## Volume Front Matter

## Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III;** a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with certain manuscript codices, corrected with the utmost diligence; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the very extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which everything that each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture and in which passages of their works.

An edition of the utmost accuracy, and easily preferable to all others if the following features are weighed: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Under the direction of J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning, Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The 1,200 volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,000 French francs; the 1,300 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 1,800 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of the Lord 662: Cyricius, Bishop of Barcelona

## Historical Notice on Cyricius

*(From Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis.)*

Cyricius, or Quiricius (Cave calls him Syricius), was bishop of Barcelona in Spain around the year of Christ 662. Lucas D’Achery published two letters of his to Hildefonsus of Toledo, together with Hildefonsus’s replies, from the Corbie Codex, in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, pages 308 and 311; they are found in a more accurate form, taken from the Hardensis Codex, in volume III of the new edition, page 314. In the first letter Cyricius thanks Hildefonsus for his work on the virginity of Saint Mary against Jovinian and Helvidius.

# In the Year of the Lord 669: Saint Hildefonsus, Bishop of Toledo

## Historical Notice on Saint Hildefonsus

*(From Antonius, Bibliotheca veterum Hispaniae.)*

### 1

Saint Hildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, flourished especially under the kings Chindaswinth and Recceswinth. Under the latter, “in the ninth year,” as Julianus says—himself also bishop of Toledo—in his brief eulogy of Hildefonsus, “he was summoned to the episcopate; he was held in honor for nine years and almost two months, on account of the merits of his life and the sustained exercise of his governance; and, when the eighteenth year of that same ruler had been completed, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, he entered upon the way of all flesh.”

He was therefore ordained in the year 659 and departed to the heavenly realm in the year 669, on January 23, the day on which his memory is recorded in the Roman Martyrology. John Mabillon reports that it is also found in the oldest surviving copy of Ado’s Martyrology.

> **Note [Col. 0009B]:** Elsewhere, “veneration”; but nothing should be changed. *Retentatio* stands for *retentio*, a frequentative for a simple form. Thus elsewhere *renotare* stands for *notare*, and in Montanus *retemperare* for *temperare*.

> **Note [Col. 0009B–C]:** In the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, second century, in the *Life of Saint Hildefonsus*, page 516, letter d, in the notes.

Clearly, everything that is said about the holy and praiseworthy deeds he performed, and that more recent books preserve, is derived from two eulogies by the most celebrated men of his age. The author of the first was Julianus, whom we mentioned above: after Quiricius, Hildefonsus’s successor as bishop of Toledo, and a contemporary of the man whom he described. The author of the second was Cixila, himself at one time—under Moorish domination—governor of that same Church, who heard the account from contemporaries.

A few poems of Saint Eugenius III also contribute something. We judge that Luitprand, Julianus, and any other pseudonymous writers whom the blind superstition of later generations venerates should be counted with these authors, since they are not even a century old and cannot themselves provide authority for ancient matters; when they remain within their proper order, they should be content to borrow from one another.

> **Note [Col. 0009C–10B]:** The learned Florez published the *Life of Hildefonsus attributed to Cixila*, collated with several codices, in volume V, beginning at page 504. In the latest Madrid collection of the Holy Fathers of Toledo, volume I, beginning at page 96, it was reprinted under Cixila’s name. Yet a Toledo codex of the twelfth or early thirteenth century bears this title: “Here begins the Life or Deeds of Saint Hildefonsus, bishop of the metropolitan see of Toledo, written by Saint Helladius, bishop of the same city, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February.” The Vatican codex formerly belonging to Christina, queen of the Swedes, no. 563, and another belonging to the King of France, volume III, page 269, no. 2359, agree with this. It is false. The Aemilianensis Codex, written in the year of Christ 994, settles the matter by its wording on folio 230: “Here begins the Life or Deeds of Saint Hildefonsus of Toledo … written by Cixila, bishop of the same city,” and so forth.

### 2

Tradition says that Hildefonsus was born at Toledo to the noble parents Stephen and Lucia, under King Witteric, in the seventh year of this century.

> **Note [Col. 0011D]:** This seemed to the Pseudo-Luitprand in the *Chronicle*, era 644.

Lucia is said to have been the full sister of Eugenius III, bishop of Toledo. While Hildefonsus was still a boy, Eugenius imbued him with the first elements of learning and with love of piety. At that time Eugenius himself was serving in an ecclesiastical office in the Church of Toledo, before he had put on the monastic habit at Zaragoza; he sent Hildefonsus to Saint Isidore at Seville to be instructed in every discipline.

> **Note [Col. 0011D]:** Morales observed this, book XII, chapter 39, and the manuscript *Acts of the Breviary of Astorga*, in Tamayo, January 23, page 247, confirm it.

Having emerged from this training, Hildefonsus soon began to display himself as a man complete in every excellence of learning and holiness. He returned to Toledo and, under Bishop Helladius, embraced the monastic discipline in the monastery of Saints Cosmas and Damian, also called Agaliense, in that city.

Near the end of his life Helladius conferred upon him the order of deacon. This occurred at the beginning of Sisenand’s reign, that is, around the year 631; Hildefonsus himself bears witness to it when speaking of Helladius in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 7.

He was then elected abbot of his own monastery, not of another, as some prefer.

> **Note [Tamaio, volume I of the *Hispanic Martyrology*, January 23, pages 255–256]:** Others think differently.

Julianus expressly says that, upon the death of his maternal uncle Eugenius, while he was still directing the monks as abbot, Hildefonsus was transferred, unwillingly and yielding to what Julianus calls “the principal violence,” to the governance of the Church of Toledo.

As abbot he was still present at the endowment of the monastery at Complutum, founded by Saint Fructuosus, in the forty-sixth year of this century.

> **Note:** Morales, book XII, chapter 26.

From there he was present at the Eighth Council of Toledo in the fifty-third year, and also at the Ninth, around the year 657, as the subscriptions show.

### 3

In the episcopal office at Toledo, to which he is believed to have been appointed two years later, he “shone like a burning torch,” as Cixila says, and “illumined all Spain” with the rays of chastity, prudence, universal Christian learning, and every heroic virtue.

He was considered worthy to transmit to posterity a memory marked and consecrated by two extraordinary benefits bestowed upon him by God.

While he was celebrating the sacred rite before Recceswinth, the virgin and martyr Leocadia appeared to him. She pointed out the place of her burial, which had until then been sought in vain, and gave thanks to the most holy man for having defended the virginity of the Mother of God in the books he had recently published. She did so in her own name.

It is a constant tradition that a fragment of the veil of this most holy martyr, his fellow citizen, cut off by Hildefonsus with a knife hastily supplied by the king, is preserved at Oviedo in the holy reliquary chest.

> **Note [Col. 0011D]:** In a certain prose text of the old office for this event, cited by Tamayo, page 260, it is said that this was done with the king’s *ganipule*. *Ganivete de mesa* is an obsolete word in our language.

> **Note [Col. 0011D]:** That knife is preserved today at Toledo in the treasury of the very eminent college of canons; it is honored and venerated with the greatest attendance of the people and neighboring inhabitants.

Not long afterward, when he came into the church on the feast of the Expectation of the Childbearing of the Blessed Virgin Mary to perform the morning office, he was granted the sight, with mortal eyes, of that same Mother of the Son of God seated in the episcopal chair. He heard her address him kindly and was permitted to adore her as she handed him a garment received from the heavenly treasury, which he alone was to wear on that solemn feast.

Cixila testifies that Hildefonsus related this together with other miracles worked through him by the Holy Spirit. One of the witnesses, Urbanus, is called by Isidore of Beja “the veteran melodist of the Church of Toledo,” that is, its cantor.

> **Note:** *Chronicle*, era 757.

The other, Evantius, was archdeacon of that same Church, distinguished “in learning, wisdom, holiness, and in every hope, faith, and charity according to the Scriptures, for the strengthening of the Church of God” in Spain, which was already groaning under captivity.

Cixila had these two as his authorities, and by their testimony established the credibility of the event, although Julianus, in the eulogy mentioned above, and Isidore of Beja, in his chronicle under era 721, where he discusses Hildefonsus, are silent about it.

### 4

The twelfth-century writer Hermannus the monk, whom the historian Vossius overlooked, strikingly confirms the report, universally current, in his *Miracles of Saint Mary of Laon*, in a letter to Bartholomew, bishop of that Church.

> **Note [Col. 0011D]:** In the brothers of Sainte-Marthe, *Gallia Christiana*, among the bishops of Laon, folio 620, part 2.

He writes:

> “When some time ago I set out for Spain to see the glorious King Hildefonsus—this was Alfonso, king of Aragon and also of Castile through his wife Urraca—the son of your maternal aunt Felicia, and we had received from him a most fortunate promise that, if you should return a second time to see him, he would give you the body of Saint Vincent the deacon and martyr, as well as the most precious chasuble which the Blessed Mother of God had given to Saint Hildefonsus, archbishop of the city of Toledo, as a reward for the three little books he had composed concerning her virginity, and so forth.”

> **Note [Col. 0011D–12D]:** Felicia, wife of King Sancho Ramírez and mother of Alfonso, was the daughter of Hildwin, count of Roucy in France, as appears from the same Hermannus, book I, chapter 2, whose words may be read in the brothers of Sainte-Marthe. Hence Surita was mistaken when he believed, in book I of the *Annals of Aragon*, chapter 19, that Felicia was the daughter of the count of Urgell. Jerome Blancas followed him in his *Commentaries on the Affairs of Aragon*, as did King Sancho IV.

But concerning this matter, reader, I ask you to consult the writings of our own scholars:

> **Note [Col. 0012D]:** A complete book on this subject exists by the Jesuit Francisco Portocarrero; and Peter Salazar de Mendoza treats it extensively in his *Life of Saint Hildefonsus*. Tamayo collected all the material under January 23 and the following January 24.

Let us not delay any longer those matters belonging to the history of Hildefonsus that are relevant to the purpose of this library.

### 5

“Julianus says that Hildefonsus wrote very many books, most distinguished for their polished style, which he judged should be divided into the following parts,” namely:

### 6

A book on the personification of his own weakness, which has been lost.

### 7

A short work *On the Virginity of Saint Mary against Three Unbelievers*.

As far as I know, this book was first published by Michael Alfonso Carranza of Valencia, a man equally pious and learned and a member of the Carmelite order. After comparing two manuscript codices, one belonging to Gregory of Miranda of Valencia, judge of matters of the faith, and the other to the Hieronymites of Gandia, he brought it out at Valencia in 1556, in octavo, under the following title:

*The short work of our most holy Father Hildefonsus, archbishop of the Church of Toledo, on the undefiled and perpetual Virginity of the holy and glorious Mother of God Mary, ἀντὶ τριῶν ἀπίστων, against three unbelievers.*

I do not believe that these Greek words came from Hildefonsus, but from some later writer who wished improperly to affect Greek learning.

> **Note [Col. 0012D]:** In the Escorial Codex, apparently from the late tenth century, shelfmark A, pluteus I, no. 9, it appears under this rubric: “Hildefonsus’s short work *On the Virginity of Saint Mary*, *Antitriapistos*”—a word written in Latin letters—“that is, against three unbelievers, composed in a sequence of synonyms,” so that it might lend antiquity to itself by means of an uncommon Greek title.

The work was composed in an arrangement of synonyms. Carranza also appended a *Life*, which Jerome Welaeus had published at Louvain in 1549 together with this same book. In 1557 I know that Basil Melanius, a monk of the Cassinese Congregation, again made this same short work public at Basel, in octavo.

### 8

Some time afterward, Franciscus Fevardentius, a Minorite, reprinted it at Paris, at Nivellius’s press, in 1577, together with other works incorrectly attributed to Hildefonsus; and Bignaeus reprinted it in the ninth volume of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers* in 1589.

The title varies in these editions. For the wording “On the undefiled and perpetual Virginity,” which appears in Carranza, the manuscripts used by Fevardentius and Constantine Cajetanus had *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary*.

In one of Cajetanus’s codices, the former copyist wrote:

> “Gomesanus, abbot of Ilde, in the region of Pamplona, gladly wrote the little work long ago most eloquently published by Saint Hildefonsus, bishop of the see of Toledo, in which there is contained a praise of the virginity of Saint Mary, the perpetual virgin.”

> **Note [Col. 0013C]:** For “Gomesanus, abbot of Ilde,” read “Gomesanus of Albailda”—not an abbot but a monk of that monastery, over which Dulquitus, or Dulcatus, presided in the region of Pamplona. This is established by the manuscript notes of the learned Andrés Marcos Burriel in the Royal Library of Madrid; he was the first to detect Constantine Cajetanus’s error, in *The Lives of the Three Benedictine Bishops*, page 141.

> **Note [Col. 0013C]:** In the *Life of the Three Benedictine Bishops* published by Constantine Cajetanus, page 141.

But we shall return to this note below.

### 9

Who the three unbelievers were is placed beyond doubt by the very form of address used in accusing them. Jovinian and Helvidius—very well-known heresiarchs of the earlier age, both refuted in particular books by the greatest doctor, Jerome—and, in third place, a certain Jew, identified only by the name of his sect, are presented here and attacked with the greatest force and vehemence of argument and doctrine.

> **Note [Col. 0013D]:** Saint Augustine attributes this heresy to Jovinian, although Saint Jerome does not mention it in the books written against him, as Erasmus notes in the argument to those books.

The first had formerly denied that Mary, the Mother of God, remained a virgin in childbirth.

> **Note [Col. 0013D]:** Helvidius maintained that, after giving birth to the Savior, the Mother of God had intercourse with Joseph, as is clear from Jerome’s book against him.

The second denied that she remained perpetually a virgin after childbirth. The third sacrilegiously rejected her bodily integrity throughout the whole time of childbearing.

Thus Hildefonsus refutes Jovinian in the first chapter—Hermannus the monk cited above calls these sections “little books”—Helvidius in the second, and the Jew in the third, together with the arguments that follow the third. This final enemy had to be overthrown with a greater force of arguments, so that Jovinian and Helvidius, who had already been attacked separately, might also be struck down anew.

### 10

The whole defense of Mary’s integrity had truly to turn on establishing by argument that the true Son of God was born from her. Once this had been granted, what sane person would afterward deny that God could enter the enclosed womb of an incorrupt mother and, having formed for himself a body there, bring it forth into the regions of daylight with the virgin’s modesty equally inviolate?

This, therefore, had to be urged at greater length against the unbelieving Jew, because it was especially opposed to his sect. Through the Jew’s body, as it were, the throats of the rest of the blind-minded Antidicomarianites had to be attacked—those whom Epiphanius calls so in the *Panarion*.

For these later opponents, although they had Christ and Christianity on their lips, are represented by almost all defenders of Mary—especially Ambrose, *Letters*, book X, letters 79 and 81, and Jerome, *Against Helvidius*—as adherents of Hebrew doctrines.

Alphonsus Vazquez of Miranda, a member of the Mercedarian order, a man of purified judgment and extensive learning, who during his lifetime was abbot of Saint Anastasia in the kingdom of Sicily, rightly understood the matter in his vernacular work on Saint Hildefonsus and his writings, book IV, chapter 4.

Gabriel Vasquez, the Jesuit, also had the same thought in his commentary on the third part of Saint Thomas, disputation 121, chapter 11, except that he asserted that Cerinthus or Carpocrates—both of whom, as is clear from Epiphanius’s first book *Against Heresies* and other sources, once taught according to Jewish belief that Jesus our Lord was born from Joseph and Mary—was being struck down in the person of the Jew whom Hildefonsus names.

But his opinion is plainly contradicted by chapters 3 and 4 of this very work. At the beginning of both chapters it is said to the Jew that the holy Virgin belongs to his own stock or nation. This cannot properly be applied to one who is not truly Jewish by origin but only by sect or heresy.

I am more inclined to think that Hildefonsus was refuting not some private individual but the entire Jewish sect, having selected one representative from among them whom he could accuse and address in so many chapters.

The following words from chapter 7 cannot have any other proper meaning:

> “For concerning the passion, insults, cross, nails, death, and burial, why should I now speak to you, when you do not doubt that you did these things?”

And shortly afterward:

> “When you are held guilty of the murder of an innocent man, and this death, cruelly inflicted by you but willingly accepted by him, and so forth.”

Gomesanus also saw this, that copyist of the book *On Virginity* used by Cajetanus, whom I have already summoned as a witness and shall often summon again.

> **Note [Col. 0013D–14D]:** The Escorial Codex mentioned above, a tenth-century manuscript, shelfmark A, pluteus I, no. 9, explains the word *Triapistos*: “The three *triapisti*,” it says, “are Jovinian, Helvidius, and the Jews.” Gomesanus’s words in the Toledo Codex are these: “Hildefonsus wounded Jovinian’s perfidy and destroyed Helvidius’s error with the dagger of the truest reason; and he also slaughtered the hardness of the Jews, not only by the testimony of angels and men—read *astipulatione* for *stipulatione*—but also by a confession uttered by demons.”

### 11

These, then, are the three unbelievers whom Hildefonsus wished to confront in this book.

Perhaps he wished, out of devotion to the most blessed Mother of God, to raise up new enemies for himself even from among enemies already defeated, so that he might exercise the style of piety, as declaimers commonly do.

His own temperament seems to have summoned him to this, as will become clear below when his letters are praised. The same appears from the testimony of Quiricius of Barcelona, which will be cited shortly, and from the words of the presbyter Gomesanus, which we shall produce below. Finally, it appears from the testimony of the fragment concerning the translation of the relics from Toledo to Asturias, which we shall also present later.

Alternatively, perhaps the shameless heresy of these enemies had acquired new adherents at this time, either in Spain or outside Spain.

> **Note [Col. 0013D–14D]:** It is scarcely credible that Hildefonsus, who was more devoted than any mortal ever was to the honor of the most blessed Virgin Mary, wished merely for the exercise of his style to raise up new enemies for himself from the tombs and to play the declaimer on a subject through which wounds once inflicted upon that most blessed Virgin by Jovinian and Helvidius would necessarily be reopened. This is appropriately noted by the editor of the latest Madrid edition of the Holy Fathers of Toledo, in the prologue to volume I of Hildefonsus’s works, page 104. Nor does this seem in any way to be inferred from Quiricius’s letter to Hildefonsus, from Gomesanus’s account, or finally from the fragment concerning the translation of the relics, which our author adduces in support of his conjecture. Indeed, since I see in Hildefonsus’s short work the line of attack directed principally, and almost exclusively, against the Jews, I believe that Hildefonsus’s controversy was with Spaniards or Hispanics who belonged to that sect, on the occasion, perhaps, of some virulent writing against the most blessed Virgin that had been published around that time. Nor should we suppose that Isidore, before Hildefonsus, in his books *Against the Jews*, or Julianus of Toledo, after him, in the *Proof of the Sixth Age*, fought with phantoms rather than with actual Jews. Do we believe that the teachers of that people were more restrained in the age of Hildefonsus than they were afterward, or even than they are now? From the twelfth century onward, down to the memory of our grandfathers and nearly to our own times, their books—*Nitzachon*, *Chizzuk Emunah*, *Tholdoth Jeshu*, and others—show that they never ceased to pour forth horrible blasphemies against the most blessed Virgin with shameless and pestilential speech. John Christopher Wagenseil collected these books and published them with refutations in *Fiery Arrows of Satan*, Altdorf, 1681. See the notice prefixed to the works of Saint Hildefonsus in the latest edition of the Holy Fathers of Toledo, volume I, page 105. Also see our discussion below, no. 346.

The latter position will certainly be held tenaciously by those who cling to figment-filled chronicles.

For Luitprand often insists in his *Chronicle*—under the years 661, no. 101, and 668—and Julianus likewise—in his *Chronicle*, nos. 337 and 338—that Hildefonsus engaged in written controversy with Theudius and Helladius, Gothic heretics who had come from Narbonne.

The foundation for this claim was provided by Roderic of Toledo, book XI *On the Affairs of Spain*, final chapter, in these words:

> “In his time, when Helvidius and Pelagius came from Gaul and infected many parts of Spain, defaming the virginity of the Blessed Virgin, Saint Hildefonsus went out against them and, by the testimonies of Sacred Scripture, by his honeyed tongue, and by the grace diffused upon his lips, refuted their doctrines and drove them, confounded, from Spain.”

The same account is followed by the *General History* commonly attributed to King Alfonso X.

I shall not vigorously oppose those who, with Roderic, maintain this position. A more suitable opportunity for resolving the matter will arise shortly afterward.

### 12

To confirm by further testimony that this work belongs to Saint Hildefonsus, Ambrosius Morales somewhere testifies that he saw a handwritten codex in which this book on the virginity of the Virgin Mother of God had been copied in the very hand of Atilanus Sentica, or Zamora, a most holy man. A note prefixed there informed him about this man.

> **Note [Col. 0015D]:** The Royal Escorial Codex mentioned above, shelfmark A, pluteus I, no. 9, is much older than Atilanus’s codex. At its end one reads: “In the name of Jesus Christ, this codex was completed by John, an unworthy notary, in era 992—that is, the year of Christ 954—on the eighth day before the Ides of March, while Ordoño was reigning in León and Fernando González was count in Castile. Thanks be to God.” Atilanus is known to have presided over the Church of Zamora from the year 990 to 1009, according to the catalogues of the bishops of that church in the learned Florez, volume XIV, page 337.

That book, which Cajetanus used, was transmitted to posterity from a very ancient manuscript written by hand and marked, not without the name of its copyist. At the end there is a note, as we have already indicated, too lengthy to reproduce here in full.

> **Note [Col. 0015D]:** It appears in the *Life of the Three Benedictine Bishops* mentioned above, page 141.

But it contains the statement that Gomesanus, abbot of Ilde—

> **Note [Col. 0015D]:** “Gomesanus, abbot of Ilde” should read “Gomesanus of Albailda,” as elsewhere.

—wrote this short work at the request of Bishop Gothiscalcus, who was passing through that place—in the region of Pamplona, as we have already said—from Aquitaine into Galicia in order to visit the body of Saint James. It further says that this same bishop transferred the work from Spain to Aquitaine in era 989, that is, in the year 951, during the winter, on the days at the beginning of January; during those very days Ranimirus, king of Galicia, died.

This is approximately what Gomesanus’s note says. The Ranimirus, or Ramirus, in question is Ramirus II, king of León, who died in January of the year 950. Accordingly, the era, or year, of the note must be corrected to this number, lest it contradict the most authoritative documents cited by Morales.

> **Note:** Morales, book XVI, chapter 20.

### 13

Jerome Higuera testifies in his notes on Luitprand that another parchment codex, written in Gothic letters 540 years earlier, was preserved at the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Toledo. It was written, as we believe, by Salomon the archpresbyter, presumably of Toledo, in era 1105, that is, in the year 1067. Higuera makes the same observation elsewhere in the same notes.

> **Note [Col. 0016C–D]:** It still exists today at Toledo in the monastery of the Holy Trinity. Its exemplar was collated with Michael Carranza’s printed edition by the learned Andrés Marcos Burriel in the Royal Library of Madrid. At its end one reads:

> “I, wretched Salomon, archpresbyter, an unworthy servant of God and sinner, wrote this book on the virginity of Saint Mary, the Virgin and Mother of the Lord, to the very end, and completed it in the city of Toledo, in the Church of Saint Mary the Virgin, under the metropolitan lord Archbishop Paschal. It is recorded on the sixth day, the third hour, on the day of Saint Cyprian the bishop, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the thousandth one-hundred-and-fifth year of the era.”

Isidore of Beja mentions the same book in his *Chronicle* in these words:

> “While the most holy Hildefonsus was then presiding, the golden mouth of honeyed eloquence in various books, and concerning the virginity of our Lady Mary, ever virgin, flourishing in bright and polished eloquence in an order of synonyms”—this is how I read it, rather than *synonyme*—“and so forth.”

> **Note [Col. 0016D]:** Sandoval published this in that form from what appears to have been a very corrupt codex. Miraeus has it differently.

The words are corrupt and have been placed in an unsuitable position, as becomes clear when the corresponding passages written by Roderic of Toledo, book II, final chapter, and book III, chapter 12, are compared with the passages that he copied from Isidore in his customary manner in both places.

### 14

The author of the *History of the Translation of the Relics from Toledo to Asturias*, which is read in Sandoval’s edition as inserted into the history of Sebastian of Salamanca—or, if it is the work of Alfonso III, surnamed the Great—mentions these relics in the account of those deposited in the holy chest at Oviedo.

Among the other relics he praises a “pallium”:

> “which the Queen of Heaven herself gave to Hildefonsus, archbishop of the see of Toledo, in return for the praises he had celebrated in honor of her own holy virginity, in which the holy and glorious bishop himself argued against the heresiarchs Helvidius and Jovinian,” and so forth.

It is perfectly clear that the reading should be “Helvidius and Jovinian,” not “Heliudius and Lovinianus.”

A manuscript existed in the library of the Church of Évora, according to Resendius.

> **Note [Col. 0016B]:** In his letter to Quevedo, *Hispania illustrata*, volume II, page 224.

It also existed in the monastery of La Mejorada, belonging to the Order of Saint Jerome, near Olmedo. Morales somewhere reports that another codex was at Saint Francis in the city of Valladolid.

> **Note:** *On the Holy Journey*, manuscript.

Constantine Cajetanus used another, very ancient codex.

> **Note [Col. 0016D]:** He reports this himself in the passage cited above, page 139.

### 15

Some may perhaps criticize the accumulation of synonyms in this book, since according to the rules of the rhetoricians it is unbecoming to express the same matter with several words that mean the same thing.

But in this Hildefonsus followed his teacher Isidore. And although at times, in great agitation of spirit, a speaker is not satisfied until he has brought forth what he has conceived within by every possible means and verbal distinction, Hildefonsus was subject to such states when he departed from ordinary usage, as though transported outside himself by the fires of love for the blessed Mother of God.

Choruses in several of Euripides’ tragedies are read as being stirred by similar emotions.

Let us proceed with Julianus to the remaining works.

### 16

A short work *On the Properties of the Persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit*.

Eisengrein calls it *On the Holy Trinity*.

> **Note [Col. 0016D]:** It is listed among the lost works of Hildefonsus by Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, volume III, page 260; William Cave, under Hildefonsus, at the year 657; and Cellier, volume XVII, chapter 37, page 713.

17. A short work of annotations on sacred matters, and a short work of annotations on the sacraments. That Julian clearly distinguished these two works is confirmed by the Casinensian manuscript, which Cajetanus saw, and by which Mabillon published them; Vincent of Beauvais likewise recognized both (*Speculum historiale*, book VII, chapter 120). But the Paris and Madrid editions of the works of Saint Isidore—which also include this work together with the catalogues of Isidore and Hildefonsus—have only one book, *Annotations on Sacred Matters*; the Frankfurt edition (*Hispania illustrata*, vol. II) has instead only *Annotations on the Sacraments*, as Henschenius also accepted.

[Note: This is likewise listed among Hildefonsus’s lost works. Whether he wrote two works, or a single work on the related subject, as seems likely, is uncertain. Julian, as in the Escorial Codex of the year 954 cited shortly above, shelfmark A, pluteus I, no. 9, entitles the work *A Short Work of Annotations on the Sacraments*; the most recent Madrid edition of the Holy Fathers of Toledo, p. 95, has *Annotations on Sacred Matters*. Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 55, lists one book of *Annotations on Sacred Matters* and one book of *Annotations on the Sacraments*.]

[Col. 0017A] 18. One book *On the Knowledge of Baptism*. Labbe reports, from Louis Jacob of Saint Charles, that this manuscript existed in the library of the Discalced Carmelites of Clermont in Auvergne, together with certain books of Ferrandus the deacon (*Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, p. 207). The Frankfurt edition has *On the Governance of Baptism*. All the others have *On the Knowledge of Baptism*.

[Note: It is found in the most recent Madrid edition of the Holy Fathers of Toledo (vol. I, p. 163), from a manuscript of the Dominican Fathers of Bayeux, from which Baluzius is said to have been the first of all to bring it to light, under this title: *Annotations on the Knowledge of Baptism*. It also appears in the 1761 Lucca edition of Baluzius’s *Miscellanea* (vol. II, p. 15).]

19. Another work *On the Progress of the Spiritual Desert*.

[Note: In the same edition of the Holy Fathers of Toledo (vol. I, beginning at p. 232), under the title *On the Journey through the Desert*.]

20. A short work of annotations on the activity of the day. Perhaps this means the spiritual exercises undertaken during the daytime. The Frankfurt edition has *on divine activity*, as Henschenius published it. Mabillon omitted this book.

[Note: Among Hildefonsus’s lost, indeed even doubtful, works. For although it occurs in Julian’s *Eulogy* in the most recent Madrid edition of the Holy Fathers of Toledo (vol. I, p. 95), and in Trithemius (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 55), Fabricius (vol. III, p. 260), Cellier (vol. XVII, chapter 37, no. 2), and the distinguished Flórez (vol. V, p. 483), it is nevertheless absent from that same work of Julian, or *Eulogy of Hildefonsus*, as it appears in the oldest of all the previously praised Escorial manuscripts of Hildefonsus’s works, from the year 954, shelfmark A, pluteus I, no. 9. I reproduce his words:

“He [Hildefonsus] certainly wrote very many books in a most polished and powerful style . . . namely, a book on the prosopopoeia of his own frailty; a book *On the Virginity of Holy Mary against Three Infidels*; a short work *On the Property of the Persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*; a short work *of Annotations on the Sacraments*; one book *On the Knowledge of Baptism*, and another *On the Spiritual Progress through the Desert*. All this he wished to have joined together in a volume of the first part, etc.”—without mentioning the short work *of Annotations on the Activity of the Day*, unless I myself happened to omit it long ago while transcribing.

“Julian says: ‘All this he wished to have joined together in a volume of the first part. Then [he said], of the second part.’”]

21. There is a book of letters in which, writing to various persons, he employed enigmatic formulas and sometimes introduced characters. In it, too, he obtained from certain people more polished replies by way of correspondence. At the end of the Pseudo-Julian system (*Adversaria*, part II, p. 143), there is indeed a collection of various poems made by him, in which he says that he collected certain letters and poems from a Gothic parchment book of Saint Justa of Toledo and sent them to Fulda—a fiction from beginning to end. These pieces are absent from this edition, and nothing further is given beyond the poems and their explanation by the same Pseudo-Julian.

I had hoped that this promiser might perhaps intend to bring forth something Hildefonsian from that richly stocked storehouse of his fictitious library of Saint Justa, especially after I had read, in his exposition of the epitaph of Saint Isidore, that the same Julian referred to certain letters from Isidore to Hildefonsus and from Hildefonsus to Isidore. But when I saw, in the edition of the works of Luitprand prepared by Don Lorenzo Ramírez (p. 515), those same letters, I believe, for which hope had been given us, under the heading “Letters of Bishops Collected by Julian,” I discovered that my curiosity had been disappointed.

22. Envy, then, of the age destroyed the most illustrious monuments of the holiest doctor that were destined for the future, monuments from which the history of his time would have been especially illuminated. Nevertheless, two letters survive among them to Cyricius, or Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona. In the first he replies to that bishop’s congratulatory letter concerning the work *On the Virginity of the Virgin Mary*, which had been sent to him; in the other he replies to Quiricus’s exhortation that similar works be published.

Lucas d’Achery, if I am not mistaken, was the first to publish these four letters of Cyriacus—or rather Quiricus—and Hildefonsus from the library of the monastery of Corbie in Gaul, in his *Spicilegium* (vol. I, p. 308). From Quiricus’s first letter, it seems clear that the book which Hildefonsus had sent him gave no occasion for a dispute with contemporaneous or coeval heretics. Are not his words perfectly clear?

“And, so to speak, he has made those things which appeared obscure, in proportion to the magnitude of their mystery, clearer than light and known to small and great alike, so that by this means Jovinianus may be blunted, Helvidius scattered, and likewise the unbelieving and treacherous-minded Jew may fall.”

[Note: None of this establishes or proves anything against what we said shortly before, namely in no. 11, note (f).]

This Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona, attended the Tenth Council of Toledo in the year 656, when Hildefonsus was still an abbot. I refer to this first letter’s opening:

“When, returning from you—that is, from this gathering at Toledo—I had returned to the places of the flock entrusted to me, exhausted by the magnitude of the labor, etc.”

Thus the title written above this letter—“Reply of Cyricius, bishop of Barcelona, to Hildefonsus, bishop of the See of Toledo, concerning the work *On the Virginity of Holy Mary*”—is plainly not the author’s own, but a copyist’s. Apart from the unusual form of designating the subject of the letter in this place, it is decisively disproved by the fact that Hildefonsus was not yet bishop of Toledo at that time.

This is confirmed for me by the titles of the second letter, in which Hildefonsus replies to Quiricus, and likewise of the fourth, a responding letter: “To the most holy and honorable lord Quiricus, bishop, Hildefonsus, your servant.” For Hildefonsus, remembering his own dignity, however humble he might be, would not have called himself the servant, but rather the brother, of another bishop.

I admit that this humble name “little servant” is found in the title of Quiricus’s third letter, and that the reciprocal address “lord” occurs in this letter and in Hildefonsus’s fourth. But it is more excusable for the bishop of Barcelona to have submitted himself to Hildefonsus, a metropolitan of superior rank, than the reverse; and in ordinary usage one person’s calling another “lord” has always been reciprocal.

23. Hildefonsus’s fourth letter has reached us truncated, breaking off sooner than it should, where he excuses himself to Quiricus for not devoting himself to writing because of the necessities of the times and fear of the evils pressing upon him.

[Note: In the most recent edition of the Holy Fathers of Toledo (vol. I, beginning at p. 256), there are two letters of Quiricus and two of Hildefonsus to Quiricus, reciprocal letters—ἀμοιβαίαι.]

So that we do not omit this point, John Mabillon also published, from the Thuan library, another letter of Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona, to Taio of Zaragoza, in the second volume of his *Analecta*. In it Quiricus replies to Taio and gives thanks for a certain *Collectaneum* sent to him from the works of Saints Gregory and Augustine; this will be mentioned again when Taio’s affairs arise.

Julian continues:

24. “He wished the third part to consist of Masses, hymns, and sermons”; therefore we place these in this catalogue of works.

25. Several Masses. At that time it was customary to compose Masses for a particular feast of Christ the Lord, Mary the Mother of God, or the saints. Cixila mentions two:

“While he was immediately shining in the office of abbot, he completed two Masses in praise of those lords—the martyrs Saints Cosmas and Damian, to whom the monastery was dedicated—for them to sing on their feast day, in a wonderful mode of melody; we have these Masses noted below.”

Shortly afterward he also mentions another Mass, for Saint Leocadia:

“He himself, immediately clasping and embracing him with his hands, is said to have uttered such vows, crying out with all the people and shouting: ‘Thanks be to God. My lady lives through the life of Hildefonsus.’ Repeating the same words, the clergy sang the ALLELUIA with great force, together with the hymn which the lord Hildefonsus himself had recently composed:

‘YOU HAVE BEEN MADE BEAUTIFUL, ALLELUIA, AND YOUR FRAGRANCE IS LIKE UNMIXED BALSAM’—

and other words which he had set down below in that very Mass and brought forth in her praise.”

Thus we see that the words commonly attributed to the martyr Leocadia—“My lady lives through the life of Hildefonsus”—are not Leocadia’s words, but those of the people acclaiming the same martyr as though she were rising again from the tomb.

[Note: By our authors Morales, book XII, chapter 39, and Mariana, book VI, chapter 10.]

26. Shortly afterward he also mentions a Mass for the Virgin Mary, or for her Annunciation. It is best to hear the words of that most serious historian, to whom we must often return as to a source:

“When the day of holy and ever-virgin Mary arrived”—this is the day instituted by the Goths at the Tenth Council of Toledo for the Blessed Virgin Mary, otherwise the Incarnation of the divine Word in her sacred womb, since, as the Fathers of the council say, “the feast of the mother is none other than the Incarnation of the Word,” on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January throughout Spain, after so many other sacred days of the Mother of God, and now also celebrated under the title of the Expectation of the Birth, or, as the common people say, *de Nuestra Señora de la O*, on account of the antiphons prescribed from this day whose opening begins with the letter O, or the interjection of invocation—“three days beforehand he performed litanies for three days and completed the aforementioned Mass”—perhaps *the Mass written below*, for he had not previously mentioned it—“to be sung in her praise; this is the seventh.”

He did not make sufficiently clear, however, whether he counted this among the Masses composed for the Blessed Virgin, or among all the Masses he composed for other solemnities.

27. We shall nevertheless add a useful notice concerning a manuscript book of the Church of Toledo, which, as appears from the catalogue we use, is the twenty-ninth of shelfmark XXX. It contains a portion of a Mozarabic Breviary and bears its title from that fact. On its ninth page, in a modern hand, the following appears, partly in Latin and partly in the vernacular language of Spain:

“This book contains the following:

[Note: The first and second Masses, which are lacking in order to complete the number seven, are those of Saints Cosmas and Damian, composed by Hildefonsus, which Cixila mentions above at no. 302. See the distinguished Flórez, vol. V, p. 511, no. 14.]

3–7. Masses of the Blessed Virgin Mary;

Office of the Annunciation, in December

[Note: That is, longer than in the Mozarabic Breviary.]

(*Más largo que en el Mozárabe*—Longer than in the Mozarabic);

Office of the Assumption of Blessed Mary;

Office of the Nativity of the Lord;

Office of Saint Stephen

[Note: It has no beginning, and two other leaves of it were bound by mistake among the Mass: *Qui non...*, of the Mother of God.]

(*No tiene principio, y otras dos hojas suyas están atrás encuadernadas entre la Misa: Qui non... de Nuestra Señora*—It has no beginning, and two other leaves of it are bound farther back among the Mass *Qui non...*, of Our Lady);

Office of Saint John the Evangelist;

Office of the Circumcision of the Lord;

Office at the Beginning of the Year;

Office of the Appearance of the Lord, or Epiphany

[Note: In the middle of it six leaves have been inserted which belong to the second or third Mass of the holy Virgin.]

(*Y en medio de él hay seis hojas, que son de arriba de la Misa 2 o 3 de Nuestra Señora*—And in the middle of it there are six leaves which belong above to the second or third Mass of Our Lady).”

The following Latin note of Juan Bautista Pérez, formerly librarian, a most learned and diligent man, follows these remarks, as is made clear by his subscription:

“This book is to be held in great esteem, for I believe that the seven Masses of Blessed Mary were composed by Doctor Hildefonsus: first, on the basis of their style; and second, because Cixila, archbishop of Toledo, says in the Life of Doctor Hildefonsus that he published seven Masses of Blessed Mary. The Mozarabs call ‘Masses’ not the entire office, but certain things like preambles, or exhortations, for the celebration of such an office.

PÉREZ.”

[Note: This sense of the word “Masses” should be added to those collected by the most learned man, John Bona, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, after others, in book I, *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 2.]

We have thought it worthwhile to draw this to the attention of those curious about antiquities, especially sacred antiquities, and of the devotees of Saint Hildefonsus.

28. They are also not unaware of what Francisco Portocarrero of the Society of Jesus left written in a vernacular book *On the Descent of Saint Mary the Virgin into the Church of Toledo* (chapter 12): namely, that Thomas de Torralba, of the same Society, saw at Worms, in a certain Gothic Missal copied by the hand of Julianus Petrus, a Mass “composed by Isidore of Seville and set to music by the lord Hildefonsus, bishop.”

Nevertheless, we wish the names of these Wormsian Fulda-forgeries, of Torralba, and of the man who conducted this German commerce with him, Hieronymus Romanus de la Higuera, to be proscribed throughout this entire work; and we insist that they be treated with equal severity whenever the occasion arises—and it arises often.

29. Hymns. As we have seen, Cixila mentions a *Canticle* which Hildefonsus composed in praise of the virgin Leocadia, perhaps the one inserted into the Gothic Breviary, commonly called the Isidorian Breviary.

[Note: It is found in Bivar, in his commentary on Dexter, p. 345.]

30. Sermons. Several bear the name of Hildefonsus although they are not his, as we shall say shortly.

[Note: The same Flórez (vol. V, beginning at p. 490) was the first to publish three sermons as though they were Hildefonsus’s. Two of them came from a thirteenth-century manuscript which happened to contain *On the Virginity of Holy Mary*, and were entitled:

I. *A Sermon for the Day of Saint Mary*. It begins: “The Lord exhorts us,” etc.

II. *Of the Same*. It begins: “Rabbi, the Son of God without beginning,” etc.

III. From a parchment Codex of Toledo (shelfmark XV, no. 13), *On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary*, under this title: “Likewise, a sermon on Saint Mary.” It begins: “Creator of all things and author of life,” etc.

There is nevertheless some difficulty. The style and phrasing of the first, especially from no. 4 onward, do not seem to me far removed from those of Hildefonsus in chapters 3, 4, and 5 of *On the Perpetual Virginity of Holy Mary*. The learned notice concerning the doubtful works of Saint Hildefonsus in the most recent edition of the Holy Fathers of Toledo should nevertheless be consulted (vol. I, beginning at p. 291).]

Julian now speaks:

“Finally, the fourth book belongs to the later part; it is composed of verse and prose, and in it epitaphs and certain epigrams are likewise recorded. He also wrote many other things, which, impeded by various occupations and troubles, he left partly begun and partly unfinished.”

On the authority of this statement we append the following writings to the catalogue we are continuing:

31. Certain epitaphs and epigrams. Some of which would have been a delight to posterity if that collection of various poems made by Julian—archpresbyter of Saint Justa and author of the *Chronicle*—and explained by scholia, which Ramírez appended to his edition of the same *Chronicle*, *Adversaria*, and the little book *On Hermitages* (Paris, 1628, at Sonnius), had transmitted the genuine offspring of a poet more pious than polished or eloquent.

That collection contains seventeen poems, or epigrams and epitaphs, twelve of which are attributed to Hildefonsus. We shall now examine them critically, using as our touchstone the material which Hieronymus Romanus de la Higuera—whom we contend to have been either the author or the peddler of this collection and of the rest of Julian’s fictions—conveniently supplied in his history of the city and kingdom of Toledo.

When Higuera wrote this history, he had already encountered these epigrams, as he himself admits in book XII, chapter 5. He says that they were shown to him by a certain Dominican friar and also sent to him from Germany.

[Note: “Thus I found it in an old book given to me by Father Fray Domingo de Medellín, a great servant of God and Master of the Order of Saint Dominic, who lives in the monastery of Saint Peter Martyr in this city. It had been taken from some verses brought to me from Germany under the title of Saint Ildefonsus, and they read as follows,” etc.]

We have attached Higuera’s vernacular words. Ambrosius Morales also copied those portions which are genuine and ancient from a certain Codex of Michael Ruiz de Azagra, which he often mentions.

[Note: Volume II, before book II, under the heading “On the aids for what follows,” folio 10, page 2; and book XII, chapter 34, folio 147, page 2, at the end.]

Yet Morales praises only those which bear Saint Eugenius as their author; none which bear Hildefonsus, so far as I have seen.

[Note: Certainly, in the Toledo Codex of Ruiz de Azagra, a copy of which is at hand, there is no poem either attributed or entitled to Hildefonsus.]

Higuera inserted certain Hildefonsian pieces, as well as other Eugeni an pieces, into his history. This will serve as our guide in reaching the point toward which the love of truth calls us.

32. The first, which begins:

“Evantius, suppliant, consecrated a temple to Luke,” etc.,

is spurious, and contains all the notions which the fabricator had formed concerning Saint Hildefonsus’s ancestry and kinship. It is unworthy of being attributed to the most holy man, from whom all the pomp of worldly pride and arrogance ought to have been absent. For it mentions his parents and grandparents, as well as his brothers and sisters. It says that his grandmother Blesilla, born of the illustrious blood of the Goths, and his father Stephen, together with Ophilo, the husband of his maternal aunt Evantia, were sons of King Athanagild.

It also calls Athanagild, as we have said, his grandfather—a man who lived as an Arian, yet was second to none in piety—and says that he built one temple for the martyrs Eulalia and another for Justa. In short, it mentions Ervig, who was inaugurated king of the Goths in the year 681, namely twelve years after Hildefonsus’s death (Morales, book XII, chapter 52, at the end, and chapter 53).

[Note: Included among the spurious works of Hildefonsus in the most recent edition of the Holy Fathers of Toledo (vol. I, p. 443).]

A scholium by the Pseudo-Julian follows, in which he attempts to confirm what was stated earlier by means of the second and third epigrams, which are genuine offspring of Saint Eugenius.

33. Hieronymus de la Higuera inserted these two pieces into his history of Toledo. Yet they speak differently in the aforementioned history and as handled by the Pseudo-Julian. To omit other matters of little importance, this half-distich:

“This temple, suppliant, Evantius consecrated in God’s honor,

Building this temple in God’s honor.”

“Here I enclosed my ancestral ashes in cut marble”—

is rendered by the *History of Toledo*, and likewise by the copy in our possession from the papers of Don Juan de Fonseca (who himself copied it from the example in which Ambrosius Morales engraved it from the Azagra Codex), after changing the first-person verbs into the third person, as follows in the Pseudo-Julian:

“This temple, suppliant, Evantius consecrated in God’s honor,

Building this temple in God’s honor.

Here he enclosed his ancestral ashes in splendid marble.”

The great difference between the two versions is that in the earlier and genuine form Eugenius makes his father Evantius speak and address Nicolaus, his parent, in this verse:

“Nicolaus, my father, for you is my highest devotion.”

But in the later and adulterated version Eugenius is made to speak and praise Evantius, perhaps as his grandfather, while Nicolaus is certainly treated as his father. The Pseudo-Julian reveals in the scholium appended below that he derived this meaning from these verses.

[Note: In the aforementioned example of the Toledo Codex of Ruiz de Azagra, most accurately collated with the autograph by the distinguished Andrés Marcos Burriel, the reading is entirely: “I consecrated,” etc., and in full:

“This hall, suppliant, Evantius, I consecrated in God’s honor,

Building this hall in God’s honor.

Here I enclosed my ancestral ashes in cut marble,” etc.,

as in Higuera’s *History of Toledo* and in the examples of Juan de Fonseca and Ambrosius Morales cited by us.

For a fuller understanding of all this, it should be known that in the Toledo Codex of Ruiz de Azagra there are three poems, namely:

I. A ten-line elegiac poem entitled *Epitaph of Nicolaus*—“To Nicolaus, the grandfather,” in the *Toledan Fathers*, p. 77—beginning: “Whoever of the sons of Romulus,” etc.;

II. An eight-line epic acrostic poem entitled “Likewise”—“To Lord Evantius,” in the *Toledan Fathers*, p. 36—beginning: “Noble and great,” etc., whose initial letters of the individual verses form the word NICOLAUS, while the final letters form EVANTIUS;

and III. finally, a ten-line elegiac poem entitled “Likewise,” as also in the *Toledan Fathers*, p. 77, beginning: “Behold, the entrance lies open,” etc.

These three poems, I say, are read continuously in the aforementioned Codex of Ruiz de Azagra, dedicated by Eugenius of Toledo to Evantius his father and Nicolaus his grandfather. In the most recent edition of the *Toledan Fathers*, however, they are separated, I do not know by what right. The acrostic—“Noble and great,” etc.—appears in the first part of Eugenius’s works, p. 36, no. 17; while the other two—“Whoever of the sons of Romulus,” etc., and “Behold, the entrance lies open,” etc.—appear in the second part of those same works, p. 77, nos. 86 and following.

This separation departs very far from the Codex of Ruiz de Azagra and considerably confuses readers. Moreover, the third verse and the two following verses of the poem “Behold, the entrance lies open,” etc., are read in the *Toledan Fathers*, p. 77, as follows:

“This hall, suppliant, Evantius consecrated in God’s honor,

Building this hall as a sacred place in God’s honor;

Here he enclosed his ancestral ashes in cut marble.”

These agree with the *Chronicle* of the Pseudo-Julian rather than with the Codex of Ruiz de Azagra, against which the works of Eugenius are said to have been collated at the beginning of the same volume. I pass over the violation of the laws of meter in the second verse, since the Codex of Ruiz de Azagra correctly reads: “I consecrated, building,” etc.]

34. Whoever corrupted the genuine work of Eugenius, or published corrupt material enlarged with commentaries, first falsely attributed this poem to Saint Hildefonsus. We are completely certain that his purpose was to trace the origins of the Barrosi, a distinguished family in that same city of Toledo, back to Evantia, Hildefonsus’s maternal aunt, Ophilo, her husband and son of King Athanagild, and Evantius, Hildefonsus’s maternal uncle.

This is clear from the following genealogical scheme of the Pseudo-Julian: under Count Ferdinand, Count of Castile, who fathered Guterius by his wife, the daughter of Roderic Armildez, the family of the Quirini of the city of Toledo was produced. Roderic himself also descended from Ophilo and Athanagild, as the same Pseudo-Julian notes elsewhere (*Chronicle*, no. 379).

This is another family of the Quirini—commonly called the Chirini—to which he wished to attach Hildefonsus, affixing to him a royal Gothic lineage.

[Col. 0023A] 35. This genealogical tree sprang from the brain of the author of this collection and luxuriated in extremely abundant branches. At the time when it was being fashioned by that same man—if God permits us to say so—within the brief and by no means ambitious display which the other genealogical scheme appended here presents, it remained contained within that narrow form; though it diverged greatly from, or rather contradicted, the original:

[Col. 0023]

[Col. 0023B] 36. Therefore, reader, regard the first description of the Hildefonsian genealogy, contained in that first poem

[Note: Namely, the poem beginning “Evantius, suppliant, consecrated a temple to Luke,” etc., discussed above at no. 32.]

and in the scholia appended to it, as spurious and mendacious. But regard the two poems attributed to Eugenius, the second and third

[Note: Namely, those beginning “Behold, the entrance lies open,” etc., and “Scatter roses, reader,” etc. They are unquestionably Eugenius’s and are found in the Codex of Ruiz de Azagra; in the most recent edition of the Holy Fathers of Toledo they are nos. 87 and 88, pp. 77 and following.]

as legitimate and genuine remains of that age.

37. The fourth poem in sequence, or the second of Hildefonsus, concerning the hospice built by his parents Stephen and Lucia, which begins:

“Lucia with Stephen as mother, but the uncle her . . .”

[Col. 0024B]

appears to be a genuine work of Hildefonsus, whom it presents. The author of the *History of Toledo* introduces it as having been sent to him from Germany with other material, not as part of Julian’s collection, whose construction had not yet occurred to him.

[Note: It seems to me equally suspect with the earlier poem, “Evantius consecrated,” etc., although it contains nothing discordant or absurd. The editor of the Holy Fathers of Toledo hesitates over it in the note, vol. I, p. 443.]

38. Passing over the fifth, for which Venantius Fortunatus supplied a suitable poem that the collector could misuse under the name of Evantia, and which we possess in this system in a strangely mutilated form—a matter for which we shall accuse the careless writer elsewhere—

[Note: Namely, Venantius Fortunatus’s *Epitaph of Hilary the Presbyter*, which appears in book IV, no. 12. Particularly amusing is the transformation of the distich of its final epigram. The Pseudo-Julian, wishing to flatter the Toledan family of the Quirini (Chirini), whom he had discussed in his *Chronicle*, no. 379, presents it in the collection of poems, p. 147, as follows:

“By the duty of burial, Evantia CHIRO

Brought these tears to her SON-IN-LAW,” etc.

as though Chirus, or Quirinus, or Chirinus, were Evantia’s son-in-law, whereas the epigram makes clear that the man was called Hilary and, after his wife had been abducted—as is stated in the same place—entered clerical service and was ordained a presbyter.

In Venantius it reads:

“By the duty of burial, lamenting for her dear one, Evantia

Brought these tears to her son-in-law,” etc.]

the sixth poem, for the tomb of Helladius, bishop of Toledo, is a genuine monument of antiquity. Yet it is evident that it has departed considerably, at the collector’s hands, from the version which was part of the history of the writing of Toledo and which we have inserted in our *History* (book XII). We shall give both versions and note the differences.

39. From the *History of Toledo*:

[Col. 0025A]

The body of Bishop Helladius rests in this tomb,

But his spirit holds the stars.

He was ruler of Toledo while he lived in the palace,

And from a monk he became abbot of Agali.

From there he was violently carried away to the city of Toledo,

Worn out by age, but vigorous in piety.

The martyr Leocadia received the remains of his body.

This house contains kings and pontiffs.

Therefore on the final day he will rise again into the air,

To receive rewards worthy of his merits.

I, Hildefonsus, whom he had made his servant,

Paid these few verses to the holy old man.

From Julian’s Collection:

[Col. 0026A]

The body of Bishop Helladius rests in this tomb,

But his spirit holds the stars.

He was a reader of Toledo while he lived in the palace,

And from a monk he became a reader of Agali.

From there he was violently carried away to the city of Toledo,

Worn out by age, but vigorous in piety.

The martyr Leocadia received the remains of his body.

This house contains kings and pontiffs.

Therefore on the final day he will rise again into the air,

To receive rewards worthy of his merits.

And already, as an old man, he had completed eighty years—

The glory of bishops, the courageous torch of God.

I, Hildefonsus, whom he had made his servant,

Paid whatever verses I could to the holy old man.

[Col. 0025B] 40. The portions set in italic type are those in which one version is observed to differ from the other. Only the collector knew the complete distich concerning Helladius’s age. But what we consider noteworthy—or rather laughable—is the substitution of the name and office *reader* for *ruler* in the fourth verse of the poem:

“And from a monk he became a reader of Agali.”

For in the third verse we have no doubt that he intended to write *ruler*, and that this is merely a typographical error. But that the collector intended Helladius to have become a reader of Agali after being a monk is made plain by the scholium appended to it, since he says that among the Benedictines the office of reader is identical with that of treasurer or steward, and that this is evident from Isidore’s book *On Offices*.

But this is an imposture committed against the true reading. For *ruler* is accustomed to signify *abbot* in Hildefonsus himself, as in *On Justus*, chapter 8. But neither Isidore in his book *On Offices*, nor anyone else, I believe, ever mentions a reader as treasurer or steward. Indeed, it would be madness to say that Helladius was placed over the treasury rather than over the entire monastery.

[Note: Our author considers this poem, as it appears in Higuera’s *History of Toledo*, “a genuine monument of antiquity”; the editor of the Holy Fathers of Toledo agrees with him (vol. I, p. 444, note). Even in its entirety, however, it does not greatly please me.]

41. The seventh poem, composed for the tomb of Eugenius, seems genuine and Hildefonsian, however much Morales disliked it; the still uncorrupted historian of Toledo also recognized it as such. We do not call the whole of it genuine, but only that portion which the same historian once recognized as genuine.

He calls it a tetrastich, whereas it appeared as an octastich in the collector; for this reason I would scarcely count the second and fourth distichs among the other two.

[Note: Namely, the poem beginning “Of Bishop Eugenius,” etc. Our editor, the editor of the Holy Fathers of Toledo, considers it interpolated, “half fabricated,” and spurious (part I, p. 444). It seems entirely suspect to me, and

“must be cut away with the sword, lest the genuine portion be dragged along with it.”]

42. I regard the eighth, composed for Saints Leander and Masson, metropolitans of Seville and Mérida; the ninth, concerning Saint Fulgentius; the tenth, concerning Saint Isidore; the eleventh, concerning Saint Florentina; and the twelfth, concerning Saint Leocadia, martyr of Toledo, as spurious.

43. Concerning the thirteenth poem, which begins:

[Col. 0025D] “This sacred cross bears the bodies of twin brothers,”

that is, of Leander, Isidore, and Florentina, buried in the same tomb, we have already said, when discussing the affairs of Fulgentius, that in the form in which it appeared in the collector it was neither Hildefonsus’s nor anyone else’s ancient work, and that it differed considerably from the form which came from the Codex of Nicolas Fabri.

44. Finally, the fourteenth poem seems to have been made in such a way that, if anything had previously been granted to others, those who use reason would henceforth withdraw all credence from it. The fabricator of the poem directed his mind toward making Saint Bonitus, bishop of Auvergne, to whom, like Hildefonsus, the Mother of God Mary is said to have appeared and given a cloak of wondrous whiteness, a descendant of the same people and family as Hildefonsus—that is, a nephew of Ophilo and Evantia, Saint Hildefonsus’s maternal aunt.

Perhaps this was so that, if the gift of the heavenly cloak once granted to Hildefonsus by the Virgin Mother of God had to be repeated in another case, it would nevertheless not leave the family, in keeping with the law of trusts.

It is established from the contemporary history of the Acts of Bonitus

[Note: In Surius and Bollandus, January 15. Also in Francisco Lanovius, *On the Holy Chancellors of France*.]

that he was born of Theodatus and Syagria “from a noble lineage belonging exclusively to the Roman senate,” to use the words of that anonymous author. How far this is from Gothic ancestry and from King Athanagild as a great-grandfather, everyone can see.

And is it not ridiculous and insane to believe that Hildefonsus, composing these verses in the name of Syagria, his maternal cousin, conceived the following thoughts because a priest had once foretold the holiness of Bonitus while he was still in his mother’s womb?

“Wonderful things they sing of the boy, destined to occur

as the ages of the world roll onward.

May God preserve these things for me.”

We could easily grant this to a frivolous woman, but we cannot grant it to the most serious and prudent Hildefonsus.

Nor did the license for fabricating matters about Bonitus stop there. The same man who, in this scholium of Julian, says that Bonitus was bishop of Auvergne when he received a garment from the Virgin Mother of God, publishes him elsewhere in the same Julian (nos. 440, 441, 442), and likewise in Luitprand’s *Pseudo-Chronicles* (under the year 859), as a bishop of Toledo—not an Auvergne bishop, but merely an Auvergnat by birth.

These matters, however, do not properly belong here, but to the place where Julian will state the grounds for their authenticity.

[Note: Namely, throughout the censure of the fictitious histories, especially book II, chapter 4, sections 6 through 9.]

45. Besides these works attributed to Hildefonsus by Julian the eulogist, there are two other short works, which he perhaps did not remember because they were not proper works but rather additions, as in fact they are, namely:

[Col. 0026D] **46.** The little book *On Illustrious Men*, also called *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, or an addition to the book of the same subject by Saint Isidore. In its preface the author himself gives himself away, describing himself as the successor of another Eugenius in the glorious see of the city of Toledo. Yet the following expansion deserves the greatest attention: “I call it glorious,” he says, “not because of the number of men, since the presence of glorious princes also makes it illustrious, but because before those who fear the Lord [Col. 0027A]—the wicked as well as the just—it is held to be a fearful place and exalted with every kind of veneration.” Without doubt he means only the presence granted him in that church, whether of Saint Leocadia the martyr or of Mary the Mother of God. From this one may conclude that he wrote this little book after the second of these two apparitions—that is, toward the end of his life. It has indeed been published, and is always published, together with the aforementioned little book of Saint Isidore.

Cardinal Caesar Baronius and Alphonsus Ciaconius possessed manuscript copies of it at Rome, and Arnold Uvion saw it in their possession [Note: [Col. 0027D] He himself reports this in *The Tree of Life*, book V, chapter 63.]. Cajetanus likewise had a copy from the library of Monte Cassino; he also reports (*Lives of Three [Saints], etc.*, p. 140) that it is found in the Vatican, though without the author’s name. Andreas Resendius likewise possessed another copy (*Letter to Quevedo*, p. 224) [Note: [Col. 0027D] It is held in the Escorial library (Digramm. et, shelf IV, no. 23), and in Flórez (vol. V, p. 473 onward).].

**47.** He also produced a supplement, or continuation, of the Chronicle of that same Saint Isidore down to his own times; it was later published together with the Chronicle of Lucas of Tuy by Franciscus Schotus, the brother of Andreas, who served as a substitute in this undertaking of publishing the authors of what is called *Illustrated Spain* (vol. IV). For Lucas of Tuy, bishop of the Church, commissioned by Queen Berengaria to write a world chronicle, laid as the foundation of this work what he knew had been written by Isidore.

This work which Tuy gives us as Isidorian is indeed somewhat different from the one commonly circulated under Isidore’s name. We said something about this when discussing Isidore. These two works also differ in their conclusion. The commonly transmitted Isidorian chronicle does not go beyond the fifth year of Heraclius and the fourth of Sisebut—that is, the year 654 of the era. Tuy, however, added the remaining years of Sisebut and the entire period of the reign and life of Suinthila, who ruled after him. I cannot easily say what judgment should be formed about this difference.

Lucas, believing that his own Chronicle of Isidore extended thus far and having divided it into two books, says that he would append a third, beginning here: “The continuation of the Chronicles of blessed Isidore, composed by blessed Hildefonsus, bishop of Toledo” [Col. 0027C]. This extends from the beginning of Sisenand to the death of Reccesvinth.

**48.** But if this work is in part genuinely Hildefonsus’s—which we can affirm only on the authority of that same Lucas of Tuy—then certainly many things stitched onto the ancient material by a new and foreign hand are present, and we know for certain that they are not Hildefonsus’s. One example is the supposed first arrival and preaching in Spain of Muhammad the false prophet, together with his expulsion through the work of Saint Isidore.

Apart from the fact that we demonstrated in its proper place that this is a tasteless fabrication, Isidore himself would certainly not have kept silent about it in either his Chronicle or his history of the Goths. The former reaches the year 616, the latter as far as 626, and both therefore extend beyond the time assigned to this childish tale of Muhammad’s expedition into Spain.

As for the statement found at the end of the first book of that same Lucas of Tuy, and within the brackets—so it is indicated—of the aforementioned Isidorian Chronicle, under the year 653, namely that in the time of Sisebut Muhammad was disgracefully driven from Spain and preached the wickedness of his impious law to foolish peoples in Africa [Col. 0027D], it is of the same character as the additions made by Hildefonsus to that work of Tuy, or by someone else: they follow popular rumors, not the true history of this depraved man.

Those who continually defend the primatial dignity of the Church of Toledo over the other churches, as though it were some Palladium of Spain, will judge this addition no differently. For here we plainly read that Saint Isidore flourished at Seville with the dignity of primate [Note: [Col. 0027D] The editor of the edition of the Fathers of Toledo expresses the same opinion about this continuation of the Chronicles in the notice prefixed to it (vol. I, p. 435). Nevertheless, in the Escorial Codex (shelf b, shelf I, no. 9) it bears this title: [Col. 0028D] *The continuation by blessed Hildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, of the History of the Goths from the time of Sisenand to Reccesvinth*.].

**49.** Similar are the inventions appended concerning the books of the holy doctor *On the Medical Art*, which are said to have been corrupted by Avicenna; concerning the transfer of the primatial see from Seville to Toledo because of Theodiscus’s apostasy; and concerning a privilege obtained by Chindaswinth from the Roman pontiff, according to which, at the pleasure of the Spanish bishops, this primatial dignity was to be either at Seville or at Toledo, and which the same king assigned to Toledo.

Yet no trace or indication whatsoever of so serious a matter—one which, as is said, depended upon the pleasure of the Spanish bishops, understood as assembled together—has been left in the Toledan councils of Chindaswinth and Reccesvinth, or in those of Wamba and his successors.

**50.** Finally, since Hildefonsus died in the eighteenth year of King Reccesvinth, as we have seen—that is, in 666—he could hardly have concluded this addition with an account of Reccesvinth’s death, unless he had employed some Pythagorean metempsychosis. Yet Lucas of Tuy believed that he did so. For the following note of this author comes after it: “Thus far blessed [Col. 0028B] Hildefonsus wrote, etc.”

Rodrigo of Toledo gives a different account; but in the printed editions his words on this matter are extremely corrupt (*Illustrated Spain*, vol. II, p. 52):

“And when blessed Isidore had written the origin of the Goths up to the fifth year of King Suinthila, Saint Hildefonsus wrote the times of the Goths, Alans, Vandals, and Sueves, from the fifth year of Suinthila up to the eighteenth of Reccesvinth, [Note: [Col. 0028D] Scotus noted in the margin of his Frankfurt edition that the words enclosed in parentheses are absent from the manuscripts. The general history likewise errs, part II, chapter 50, as does the manuscript of John Aegidius of Zamora, which used Rodrigo’s corrupt wording.] [while the younger Isidore, beginning from the creation of the world, faithfully continued the Chronicle up to the eighteenth year of Reccesvinth] and himself wrote as far as the destruction of Spain by the Arabs.”

I believe the passage should be corrected as follows:

“And when blessed Isidore had written the origin of the Goths, Alans, Vandals, and Sueves up to the fifth year of King Suinthila, Saint Hildefonsus wrote the history of the Goths from the fifth year of Suinthila up to the eighteenth year of Reccesvinth; and the younger Isidore, continuing it up to the destruction of Spain by the Arabs, himself wrote.”

Everyone can see that, read in this way, the passage proceeds on a sound footing; otherwise it is inconsistent with itself.

This is what we have considered necessary to say about this addition. Besides the aforementioned bishops of Toledo and Tuy, it is accepted by the author of the *General History*, John Aegidius of Zamora in his manuscript fragments, and John of Gerundum in the preface to his *Anacephalaeosis of Spain*. When discussing its historians, John says that Hildefonsus of Toledo and Sulpicius added to Isidore’s work something about the succession of the Goths. He should be corrected, however: instead of Sulpicius, one should believe that Julian, or the younger Isidore, was written.

Others attribute the whole work that passes itself off under Hildefonsus’s name to Lucas of Tuy. Among them is Lorenzo de Padilla, in the *Life of Saint Isidore* (*In the Work on the Saints of Spain*).

**51.** We may infer that Hildefonsus contributed something to the Office, or ecclesiastical books, of the Isidorian rite—as they call it, namely the Breviary and the Missal—from the following fact. In the synodal letter which the Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt, held under Charlemagne and attended by bishops gathered there from all sides to condemn the heresy of Felix of Urgel and Elipandus of Toledo, addressed to the bishops of Spain [Col. 0028D], they cite the testimonies of Saints Eugenius, Hildefonsus, and Julian, which Elipandus had used in his defense in the statement of faith addressed to Charlemagne. They respond as follows:

“In the same book of yours it follows: ‘Likewise, our predecessors Eugenius, Hildefonsus, and Julian, bishops of the see of Toledo, said in their teachings the following in the Mass of the Lord’s Supper:’” [Col. 0029A] “He who, through the passion of the adopted man, etc.”

One or two testimonies from this Mass and from another Mass of the Ascension of the Lord follow. To these they add:

“And the other things which you have set down from the statements of your fathers, so that it may be evident what sort of fathers you have, and so that it may be known to all from whom you have been handed over into the hands of unbelievers.”

**52.** They unjustly reproach [Note: [Col. 0029D] We formerly defended Saint Hildefonsus against the stain with which he had been branded by the Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt, who had been misled by the error of Felix and Elipandus. See volume II of the *Great Collection of the Councils of Spain*, pp. 669–670. CARDINAL DE AGUIRRE.] the calamity of captivity as though it were a punishment for false doctrine handed down by the ancient Fathers, who were truly most holy and thoroughly Catholic. Baronius expressly defends these Spanish teachers (*vol. IX*, under the year 794, no. 6 onward) against the stigma of this synodal censure, so sharply directed against them solely on account of Elipandus, who abused their teaching in support of his own faith.

The same judgment should be formed concerning what the Fathers of Frankfurt add:
