“It is better to believe the testimony of God the Father concerning his Son than that of your Hildefonsus, who composed for you such prayers in the solemn celebrations of the Mass as the universal and holy Church of God does not possess. Nor do we think that you are heard in them. And if your Hildefonsus called Christ ‘adoptive’ in his prayers, our Pope Gregory of the Roman See, the most illustrious teacher throughout the world, did not hesitate in his prayers always to call him ‘Only-Begotten.’”

Baronius and others among our own writers replied to these words as fairness required, praising other testimonies of our Saint Hildefonsus which entirely exclude from his mind and teaching the adoption of the flesh in the sense intended by Elipandus and understood by the Fathers of Frankfurt.

Since Elipandus introduced this matter into his own century—that is, the following one—it will have to be reconsidered. For the present we have cited it only to show that Hildefonsus contributed some work to the Ritual and ecclesiastical books.

**53.** To the works truly attributed to him, our own age has added certain others which either never belonged to him or to anyone else, or which cannot be shown by any adequate reasoning to be his.

Franciscus Fevardentius, a Frenchman of the Order of Friars Minor, highly skilled in the whole field of ecclesiastical history and sacred disciplines, and rightly praised by the great Baronius for his piety and learning (in the place cited above, under the year 794, no. 10), published at Paris in the previous century, in 1576, from the workshop of Nivellius, the following works attributed to Saint Hildefonsus:

1. A book *Against Those Who Dispute the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary and Her Childbearing*;
2. A homily *Against Those Who Falsely Affirm that the Virgin Mary Gave Birth to the Lord Contrary to the Law*;
3. Six sermons *On the Assumption of Blessed Mary*;
4. Two sermons *On the Nativity of Blessed Mary*;
5. A sermon *On Her Purification*.

We also have this little work published among the works of the ancient Fathers (vol. IX).

**54.** Likewise, Pedro de Alba y Astorga, a Spaniard of the same Franciscan order, published under the name of Hildefonsus a *Crown of the Blessed Virgin Mary* in the great work he himself had begun, the *Bibliotheca Virginalis*—that is, a collection of those authors who wrote particular works in praise of the Mother of God [Note: [Col. 0030D] In the explanation of Hildefonsus’s epigram on Eugenius, or in the *Collection of Various Poems*, p. 150.].

Pseudo-Julian also wished it to be believed that Hildefonsus had written the *Life of Saint Eugenius*, his predecessor—that is, the younger Eugenius [Col. 0029D] [Note: [Col. 0030D] Pseudo-Julian says that Hildefonsus wrote this Life of Eugenius for the benefit of the people of Toledo.].

More recently, the very learned Benedictine Jean Mabillon published a certain *Revelation* attributed to a certain Hildefonsus, a Spanish bishop, together with a dissertation *On Unleavened and Leavened Eucharistic Bread*, issued at Paris in 1674.

I shall now endeavor to establish that none of these works can be attributed to him, or believed to be his, with any plausibility.

**55.** To proceed in order, and first to set forth the considerations which seem to support its authenticity: Vincent of Beauvais, bishop, formerly recognized the book *Against Those Who Dispute the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary and Her Childbearing* as a work of Hildefonsus (*Historical Mirror*, book VII, chapter 120).

Michael Alphonsus Carranza, a Valencian Carmelite—the man who first published the aforementioned books *On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary*—also used in his treatise, composed to instruct a novice in this same mystery and appended to the earlier work, a testimony attributed to Hildefonsus.

There is also a historical account said to have furnished the occasion for that writing. Rodrigo of Toledo says the following in book II, at the final chapter:

“In his time, when Helvidius and Pelagius (for Jovinianus), coming from Gaul, had infected many parts of Spain, slandering the virginity of the Blessed Virgin, blessed Hildefonsus confronted them and, by testimonies from the Sacred Scriptures, by his honeyed tongue, and by grace poured upon his lips, refuted their doctrines and drove them from Spain in confusion.”

He then recounts the apparition of blessed Mary to Hildefonsus and the thanks given to him for having defended her virginity.

[Col. 0030B] **56.** But there are more numerous and weightier arguments which persuade us not to admit this book into the catalogue of Hildefonsian works.

The first, and indeed a decisive one, concerns its style, which learned judgment regards as the true and genuine mark of an author. For the language Hildefonsus uses in the work *On Virginity*, unquestionably his own, differs so greatly from that of the other little book published against the disputants that one must wonder how the most learned men have never brought the perception of this difference to the test of their own judgment.

The style of the former bears the unmistakable character of his age and of the Gothic Latin in which Hildefonsus lived and was trained: a kind of Latin expression already declining toward roughness and harshness, far removed from the purity and ease of ancient and genuine Roman diction.

This style takes particular pleasure in words either unusual or improperly employed; it recoils from a straightforward phrase and uses an unpleasant form of expression. It preserves rhythm not so much in the structure of the whole sentence, as it should, but with laborious anxiety contrives it at the end of each period [Col. 0030C]; its phraseology and diction are harsh. Unless sentences fall with corresponding words, or at least with words of the same nature and kind, and answer one another, the speech is thought to grow cold, to be without strength, and altogether ἀνάριθμος—that is, lacking rhythmic proportion.

**57.** There is also an affected piling-up of words and, so to speak, an impoverished abundance, whose entire purpose was to envelop in a heap of words, through circumlocution and anxious effort, whatever might have been expressed plainly, simply, and easily.

This was the characteristic of the eloquence of that age, and Hildefonsus, like almost all his peers in Spain, used it extensively. We criticize the age, not the men.

But the composition of the little book *Against the Disputants* displays no affectation. It has that simple and open form of expression which became common among other peoples and among writers of a later age, accompanied by only a very few harsher or more unusual words.

**58.** But lest this general indication weaken the force of the argument, let us examine these peculiarities individually in clear examples.

First, from the little book *On Virginity* we note the following words, which are insufficiently Latin or used in a Latin manner: *connectatio* for *copula*, as we believe; *fatuissimus*; *fetosa* for *feta*—a word which Saint Isidore also used in a certain hymn; *rememoratus*, as though meaning *recordatus* or *reminiscens*; *inconstabilis*; *tantumdem* for *tantum*; *ducare* for *ducere*; *vetustatus*, as though meaning *antiquatus*; *plausibilis* for *libens*; *audientia* in the sense of hearing; *monitationes* for *monitiones*; *almificus* for “sanctifying”; *impudoratus* for one who lacks modesty, whom Isidore in his glosses called *expudoratus*; *evadens* used passively for *evadibilis*; *implenitudo* and *impromptissimus*, which do not exactly deny fullness or readiness; and other such forms.

**59.** Next come affected and redundant expressions. “What [have I] brought to your hearing from an abundant harvest of infamy?”—for I prefer the uncertain reading *infamis* to *jugis*, “continual.” Of the prophetess Anna he says:

“Not long-lived in the company of a husband, remote through the lengthy duration of twelve times seven years of widowhood, and rich in supplications.”

Likewise:

“Although I have not explained all the innumerable and ineffably existing truthful witnesses of such and so great matters, etc.”

And:

“The star brought forth with a new beginning of birth and a new ceremonial display of procession.”

These are the more noteworthy examples; anyone can easily observe similar expressions scattered throughout the entire book.

I have said all this in order to assign to our holy man, the craftsman of this work, the kind of style that was the elegance of his age. Let it be said with the pardon of all pious people, and of that most holy man whose imperfect traces of speech, when I read them again, I bend down and kiss eagerly.

But in the other little work, *Against Those Who Disputed the Childbearing of Mary*, everything is different: the manner of writing is entirely different, the speech clearer and simpler, scarcely a word that offends the ear, and no affectation at all—neither in leading matters around by circumlocution nor in bringing sentences to an equal close [Col. 0031B].

**60.** Second, we are influenced by Julian’s silence concerning this work, although he described the works of others.

It is scarcely credible that so diligent and curious a cataloguer of the books which our Hildefonsus had left complete and intact could have been unaware of, or passed over, this complete and intact work, issued at a point where devotion to the Blessed Virgin was being put to the test.

For he praises only one little book, *On the Virginity of Saint Mary Against Three Unbelievers*, which is manifestly another work and different from this one.

Nor does Isidore of Paxos stray from this single work when he praises the book “which, in polished and shining eloquence and in an orderly sequence of synonyms”—you see what he means by “eloquence”—“blooms forth concerning the virginity of our Lady Mary, ever virgin.”

You would likewise say that Pelagius of Oviedo, or Sebastian of Salamanca, knew no other work—namely, the work by which the most holy doctor deserved the Marian gift of a heavenly cloak. He deserved it for the work in which “he contended,” as Pelagius says, “against the heresiarchs Helvidius and Jovinianus.” These truly are the enemies whom Hildefonsus set before himself for the exercise of combat in the one book which we maintain to be his sole work of this kind.

Quiricus also appears to have referred to this same work, and not to another written by Hildefonsus, in the same terms [Note: [Col. 0031D] In that letter preserved by d’Achery, vol. I of the *Spicilegium*, p. 308.]. Hermann the monk likewise referred to it in letters addressed to the bishop of Laon [Note: [Col. 0031D] It is found in Cajetanus at the place cited, and likewise in Mabillon, vol. II of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, p. 520.].

**61.** Third, are we to consider Hildefonsus so much of a stranger to poetry, or so inept at measuring verse—although Julian describes him to us as so devoted to that art—that he could have allowed the following to escape him?

“Thus it is, certainly, that the Church, on the authority of the holy Fathers, sings of his birth, that she has the mother’s joy together with the modesty of virginity—where men other than the eminent have emended it to ‘with the honor of virginity.’”

You recognize the verse from Sedulius’s *Paschal Work*, book II, namely from the hymn which the Church sings to the holy Mother of God: “Hail, holy parent,” etc.

The verse is, and can be, only this:

“Having the mother’s joy together with the honor of virginity.”

What, then, shall we say about that error? Did the author who uses poetry suppose that this blemish had already been contracted by Sedulius himself, or did he think otherwise? Whichever view one takes, the statement is absurd.

Hildefonsus, who was certainly not ignorant of the poetic art, could not have thought that Sedulius had stumbled so disgracefully.

**62.** Conversely, who of sound and prudent judgment could believe that the Church—that is, the whole Christian world, with so many distinguished men of letters and learning—adopted this verse for its use, whether corrupted [Col. 0032A] or already faulty, at a time when the lights of poetic art had not yet been extinguished, even in Spain itself?

Moreover, when he says that the Church sings this hymn, or this verse of the hymn, on the authority of the holy Fathers, if Hildefonsus is speaking, he must appear to be speaking of the ecclesiastical rite and the custom of chanting which, by the constitution of the Fourth and Fifth Councils of Toledo, prevailed continuously both in Spain and in the Gothic province of Narbonne—whence those whom the book is said to have accused as heretics came—not of the ordinary form of the Roman ecclesiastical office disseminated beyond those boundaries.

Yet this hymn of Sedulius was never received into the Gothic Missal.

**63.** Fourth, John Mabillon and Lucas d’Achery, Benedictines whom we have already often praised for their solid virtue, maintain—with the most certain arguments, according to the former [Note: [Col. 0031D] In his observations on certain writings of Hildefonsus, vol. II of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, p. 519, and in the preface to part II of the third century.] and with conjectures, according to the latter [Note: [Col. 0032D] In the preface to the reader of the first volume of the *Spicilegium*.]—that the book in question is not the work of Hildefonsus but of Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, who lived under Louis the Pious.

In Radbertus’s time a new opinion arose in parts of Germany concerning the manner of the birth of Christ the Savior from the womb of the Virgin Mother of God. It taught “that Christ’s infancy did not truly originate through the virginal gate of the womb in a human birth, but emerged monstrously from the hidden recess of the belly by an uncertain path of light into the air; for this is not to be born but to burst forth,” as Ratramnus says.

Ratramnus, himself a monk of Corbie and a contemporary of Radbertus, wrote this in his book *On the Fact that Christ Was Born from the Virgin, Against Those Who Think Otherwise*, published by Lucas d’Achery in the first volume of his *Spicilegium* (p. 318).

Against this book of Ratramnus—or against another author who, while asserting with the Catholics that Mary retained her virginity in childbirth, interpreted it wrongly, “denying the very thing he confessed,” when he said “that she brought forth a son in accordance with the common law of nature”—which are the words of the little work under discussion—the author took up his pen.

[Col. 0032C] **64.** Mabillon saw this work copied in manuscripts of the Corbie library with the following inscription [Note: [Col. 0032D] D’Achery published it in the preface to the reader of the first volume of the *Spicilegium* cited above.]:

“To the venerable matron of Christ, together with the sacred virgins living a monastic life at Vesona”—Mabillon believes that *Suessona* should be read—“P. R., the least of all monks. Dear women, I have decided to answer for you the question about the childbirth of the Blessed Virgin Mary recently brought to me, since I do not doubt that you love it greatly; so that from this you may know how much I love you, having long ago been your pupil from the womb and now worn out by great old age.”

Mabillon is certain that the name of Paschasius Radbertus is concealed under these larger initials, P. R. D’Achery even says that two manuscript codices of the same Corbie library have the name of Paschasius Radbertus prefixed.

He inferred, against those who maintain that Hildefonsus was the author, that the book lies outside a controversy with heretics from the fact that it attacks brothers, not enemies. Hear his words from the same preface:

“But because the shameless temerity of certain brothers is again now laboring, as it were by questioning, to investigate these matters, I have decided to write to you, women of Christ, about those things which they try to examine more curiously—note the word—against her modesty, than religiously.”

But what follows below places beyond dispute that, in this work—not Hildefonsus’s but Paschasius’s, or another’s, if for the moment we grant this to opponents of the later judgment that Paschasius was its author—Ratramnus and his work *On the Fact that Christ Was Born from the Virgin*, published by d’Achery, are attacked and refuted.

This is manifestly established by the similar features and argument of the two works.

[Col. 0033A] **65.** The following passage is from the earlier work, *On Childbearing*, or *Against Those Who Dispute*, etc.:

“For they say that the Blessed Virgin Mary could not and ought not to have given birth in any other way than according to the common law of nature and as is customary among all women, so that Christ’s birth may be called a true birth. Otherwise, they say, if he was not born as other infants are born, it is not a true birth. Therefore, lest he be thought to be a phantom, or lest he be believed to have passed through the Virgin’s womb without the process of birth, as water passes through a channel, it is pious to believe that he was born according to the law of nature in the way other infants are born, and that she gave birth in the way other women give birth. O blind piety!” he exclaims, “which thinks so impiously about the Virgin Mary, and blind presumption, which speaks so impiously about Christ!”

**66.** Now hear Ratramnus, chapter 1, after reporting the opinion of the Germans:

“Therefore,” he concludes, “Christ was not truly born, nor did Mary truly give birth.”

And shortly afterward:

“Thus neither would the mother herself be called intact, nor would the Savior’s birth from his mother be complete.”

And in chapter 2:

“But she did not give birth if the birth proceeded in any other way than through nature’s gate. Such an origin is not the Virgin’s childbirth, but properly the infant’s own emergence.”

The entire book presses the adversary with much the same argument.

The enduring disagreement among many centuries of Catholic authors concerning this question—the manner of the birth of the Lord Christ and of Mary’s childbearing—provided the occasion for this controversy, which arose in that century among those Germans, Ratramnus and Paschasius. The greater part of our theologians, with Saint Thomas as their leader, eventually settled it [Note: [Col. 0033D] See part III, question 28, article 2; compare part I, question 98, article 2 ad 4. Suárez, part III, vol. II, question 25, article 8, disputation 13, section 1. Vázquez, part III, vol. II, question 28, article 3, disputation 121, chapter 5. Durandus, *On the Four Books of Sentences*, distinction 44, question 6.].

**67.** Fifth, when Hermann the monk, writing to Bartholomew of Laon, reports that at his urging he searched for and found in the city of Châlons three little books which Hildefonsus had composed *On the Virginity of the Virgin Mary*, and for whose reward he had received from that same Mother of God a most precious chasuble, he sufficiently indicates that Hildefonsus had no other work on this subject.

The new discovery by which people are imagined to have multiplied his books—making him write separate works on virginity and childbearing—contradicts the ancient belief of his age.

**68.** Sixth, the accounts given of this book by the authors who have recently emerged are full of errors, both historical and theological. They have dared to introduce knots into the books of many ancient writers and to sell falsehoods as certainties, as though they were applauded for suddenly appearing as *deus ex machina* figures.

For they were not content merely to follow Rodrigo of Toledo’s footsteps; they themselves added new material, the restraint of which we are now undertaking.

“In his time,” says Rodrigo [Note: [Col. 0033D] Book II, chapter 22], “when Helvidius and Pelagius (Jovinianus), coming from Gaul, had infected many parts of Spain, slandering the virginity of the Blessed Virgin, blessed Hildefonsus confronted them and, by testimonies from the Sacred Scriptures, by his honeyed tongue, and by grace poured upon his lips, refuted their doctrines and drove them from Spain in confusion. Hence also, on the feast of the glorious Virgin, etc.”

He continues with the apparition of the most holy Virgin and with Hildefonsus’s being rewarded by that same Virgin Mary with a heavenly garment for having defended her virginity.

**69.** I have no doubt that this history is true, and that heretics from Gaul attempted to spread throughout Spain the poison of Helvidius, already dispelled by Jerome.

For Hildefonsus would not have revived a heresy already extinguished merely to attack it in writing—or rather, he would not rashly have presumed to raise it from the tomb and bring it back to the attention of men [Note: [Col. 0033D] Recall what was said above on this subject, no. 11 in the note.].

But we believe that Rodrigo wrote that Helvidius and Pelagius were their actual names through error. Hildefonsus set before himself for renewed refutation and condemnation the names of the ancient heretics who attacked the virginity of the Mother of God—Helvidius and Jovinianus—so that under the guise of these two anti-Marian heresiarchs he might destroy those new monsters whom he had disdained to call by their proper name.

Pelagius of Oviedo provides the clue: “He contended against the heresiarchs Helvidius and Jovinianus.” Hildefonsus added to them a third unnamed enemy, under the designation “the Jew,” joining him to the other two in the triumph, so that through all his champions he might defeat that shameless heresy.

We therefore believe that Rodrigo came to think that the other heretic from Gaul, whom our Hildefonsus confronted, had been called Helvidius.

**70.** We likewise suspect that Rodrigo’s naming Pelagius instead of Jovinianus arose from error.

John Magnus, archbishop of Uppsala, appears to have understood him in this sense in the *History of the Goths and Swedes*, published nearly a century ago by his brother and successor Olaus, book XVI, chapter 21:

“In whose time,” he says, “two heresies, Pelagian and Helvidian, bursting from Gaul into Spain, corrupted the greater part of Spain” [Note: [Col. 0033D] Thomas Tamaius improperly cites John Magnus in his notes on the Luitprandian names of these heretics, under the year 661, p. 62.].

Most of our historians [Note: [Col. 0033D] Morales, book XII, chapter 39; Padilla, century 7, chapter [Col. 0034D] 48; Vasaeus, in his Chronicle under the year 662; Mariana, book VI, chapter 10; Portocarrerus, *On the Descent of the Mother of God into the Church of Toledo*; Vázquez in his *Hildefonsus*, book IV, chapter 3, and also the theologian Vázquez, part III, disputation 121, chapter 2.] seem to have read *Helladius* in Rodrigo instead of *Helvidius*. They wrongly think these are the names of recent figures whom he used, although others retain *Helvidius* [Note: [Col. 0034D] Marieta, book V *On the Saints of Spain*, chapter 50; Higuera in his notes on Luitprand under the year 661, no. 113.].

**71.** But the man who in our own age assumed the names of Luitprand and Julian in order to cloak his fables or imaginings with the mantle of antiquity calls them not Helvidius and Pelagius, but Theudius and Helladius.

Luitprand [Note: [Col. 0034D] In the Chronicle under the year 661.] says:

“Heretics coming from Narbonne, Goths by nation, Theudius and Helladius, wandering most abominably throughout Spain and rashly holding opinions about the virginity of the Blessed Virgin Mary—that, in the manner of other women, with the virginal barriers widened, she bore Christ the Lord, true God and man, her son—Hildefonsus vigorously refuted them in speeches and fourteen books” (this is how Thomas Tamaius’s Madrid edition reads; Ramirez’s Paris edition has instead “in fourteen speeches and published books”), “beginning with the words, ‘My Lady,’ unlike that other work, *Soliloquies*. By order of King Reccesvinth, the most Catholic and serene prince, he had them corrected and compelled them to go into exile from all Spain.”

The Pseudo-Luitprand reports that they returned from exile and were expelled again from Spain after seven years, specifically driven out at Elbora—an account presumably written to please his Carpetanian countrymen and the citizens of Talavera [Note: [Col. 0034D] Under the year 668.].

Pseudo-Julian gives nearly the same account [Note: [Col. 0034D] In the *Chronicle*, no. 338]:

“He refutes the Gallic heretics Theudius and Helladius, who spoke about the manner of the childbirth of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in books which he had dedicated to the nuns of the monastery of Delivium—elsewhere called Deibium—located in the territory of Toledo [Col. 0034D]. He convenes a council of many bishops, at which Hildefonsus himself was present, together with many bishops, among whom was Saint Amandus, the first bishop [Note: [Col. 0034D] Indeed, ‘earlier’ should be read, lest we hear this calumniously.] of Traiectum and afterward of Castellon in Spain, a learned and holy man.”

And below (no. 341):

“After delivering many sermons, Saint Hildefonsus defended the miraculous manner of the childbirth of the Blessed Virgin Mary [Col. 0035A] against those heretics who said that she gave birth in the manner of other women, while nevertheless remaining a virgin—a thing that cannot happen.”

### 72

These are dreams born in the brain of the man whom we have so often condemned. He called Helladius one of the heretics because in Rodrigo of Toledo he is sometimes read as *Helladius* instead of *Helvidius*, which is the correct reading. He called Theudius the other heretic on the strength of his own single assertion—which has no foundation—as though, having partly secured for himself a good name in Rodrigo’s authority, he could safely borrow the remainder for a lie.

Moreover, these fig-tree historians act unjustly concerning their spurious Theudius and Helladius when they call them heretics because they maintained that Blessed Mary had borne Christ the Savior in the manner of other women, yet without loss of her virginity. For the author of the book himself, Hildefonsus, accused them of nothing more than shameless boldness in questioning—and this among men whom he dared to taunt as “brothers” (how far this designation is from heretics!). He most clearly distinguished this matter from the cause of the heretics and from the Helvidian heresy already defeated by Jerome.

### 73

Nor is this opinion without defenders among Catholic writers, both ancient and modern. Tertullian seems to have held it in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 4, and *Against Marcion*, book III, chapters 11 and 16; Jerome, in Letter 22 to Eustochium, *On the Preservation of Virginity*; Pope Leo, in his letter to Emperor Leo, Letter 97, chapter 3; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 51, or Letter 1 to Chelidonius; Epiphanius, in Heresy 78; [Note: Besides these, the impious Rivet praises twelve more of the holy Fathers in *Apology for the Virgin Mother of God*, book I, chapter 16.] likewise John of Damascus, in his homily *On the Dormition of Mary*; and Durandus among the Scholastics [Note: *In the Second Book of the Sentences*, distinction 44, question 6], who praises Gregory and Ambrose.

Saint Augustine accepted this manner of giving birth in the state of innocence: with the bodily members relaxed, as in conception, rather than displaced, and without injury to integrity. From him this view was adopted by Saint Thomas, part I, question 98, article 2, reply to the fourth objection; Richard, in the Second Book of the *Sentences*, distinction 20, question 4; and other more recent writers [Note: Vives, on Augustine’s *City of God*, book XIV, chapter 26; William Estius, *On the Second Book of the Sentences*, distinction 20, section 2].

Certainly Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie, whom I said held the opposite view to this opinion attributed to Hildefonsus, did not hesitate to mark as “the poison of a new perfidy” the book of Paschasius Ratbertus, since it held a different view concerning the birth of Christ the Lord from that concerning the solemn and ordinary—though intact—form of childbirth.

It has always been an uncontested Catholic article that Mary’s integrity was preserved both in conception and in childbirth. But concerning the form of the miracle by which the divine child was released from the enclosure of the virgin womb, everyone was free to speculate, although in our own day the opinion of a miracle of penetration has prevailed according to the judgment of more recent writers. On this subject, reader, I refer you to the Scholastics cited above.

### 74

How plainly do those things attributed to Luitprand reveal a recent hand and swell with foul affectation! Hildefonsus is said there—number 101—to have refuted those heretics courageously in fourteen sermons and in various books distinct from his *Soliloquies*, beginning, “My Lady.” Do you not see that one need only consult Fevardentius’s edition of the works of Saint Hildefonsus, in which thirteen sermons are assigned to him that have hitherto been unknown?

Although not all the sermons printed there concern the mystery of the undefiled and most pure birth—some concern the Assumption or the Nativity, as we shall say—the reckoning with this writer must not be conducted too strictly, since he allowed himself to be driven by no motive other than his own desire. We gladly attribute the fourteenth number to the printer instead of the thirteenth.

Likewise, Luitprand says [Note: Number 103] that Saint Hildefonsus composed, first for his private devotion, a book of *Soliloquies*, or *Synonyms*, and afterward sermons and “books in a more elegant style, so as to avert the weapon arising from diversity of style, against these heretics.”

### 75

What is added concerning a council held at Toledo on this matter is entirely false. This is so not merely because no such council is preserved in the old books alongside the other Toledan councils of earlier and later centuries, nor because its celebration at that time is confirmed by any writer of sound faith—not even by the books and sermons falsely attributed to Hildefonsus—but especially because it is perfectly clear from the Eleventh Council of Toledo, convened in the fourth year of Wamba—that is, in the year 675, six years after Hildefonsus’s death—that the Spanish bishops had not assembled for a full eighteen years beforehand.

Within that interval, besides Wamba’s four-year reign, everyone can see that the nine-year episcopate of Hildefonsus is included. And yet, failing to notice this, some among our own writers still support Julian’s council [Note: Higuera, in his notes on Luitprand, year 661, number 101], moved solely by the fact that it seems to them scarcely plausible that during the whole period of Hildefonsus, under so eminent a bishop, the light of councils should have been extinguished. Yet these men ought not to have trusted their conjectures.

### 76

When will historians of this kind cease believing, after having been taught by so many examples? This one instance alone ought to suffice: the same foolish fabulist Julian did not hesitate to say that Amandus, first bishop of Utrecht and afterward bishop of Castellón in Spain, a learned and holy man, had taken part in this Council of Toledo [Note: Number 338, in the *Chronicle*].

Saint Amandus plainly flourished in this century and is believed to have lived until his eighty-fourth year (others [Note: Mabillon, in his notes on the *Life of Saint Amandus*, p. 723] prefer his seventy-ninth year). [Note: See the Antwerp edition of the *Acts of the Saints*, 6 February, under Saint Amandus, § 2].

Yet he was bishop only of Utrecht in Belgium under Sigebert, king of Austrasia. After three years, around the year 649, with the approval, as is believed, of Pope Martin, he resigned that office [Note: Ibid., § 2] and devoted himself to a private but highly active and most holy life. He never traveled beyond Gaul and the Basques to the south, Belgium to the north, and Rome to the east—much less did he, in Spain, where the see of Castellón is placed [Note: Tamayo Salazar, *Spanish Martyrology*, vol. I, 6 February; Francisco Ruspuerta, *Ecclesiastical History of Jaén*, seventh century, chapter 2], inconsistently again place his shoulders beneath the burden from which he had once withdrawn.

### 77

Perhaps no one ever had more writers of his life and deeds than Amandus. Among them are Baudemundus, abbot of Blandinium, who wrote his testament; Alanus; Harigerus, abbot of Lobbes; and Philippus Bonaespei, who wrote in prose; while Milo, a priest of Elnone, wrote in verse. All these works still exist, and have been published either for the first time or again in the Antwerp *Acts of the Saints* and in the Parisian Benedictine editions of John Mabillon.

Since none of these writers mentions this Spanish residence or the rank he is said to have held among that people, the man must indeed be a blockhead or a tree-stump who, after so many witnesses and the very incongruity of the matter have warned him, can still be mocked by the tricks of the Toledan magician.

### 78

Perhaps the man was deluded, seizing every opportunity to adorn his native land—namely, our Spain—with stories, on the basis of the fact that the most holy bishop Amandus once undertook a sacred expedition against the Basques. More recent writers [Note: Tamayo, 6 February], following the statement of Pseudo-Julian, interpret this as referring to the office of bishop of Castellón held in Spain—Castellón de Ampurias in Catalonia—and meanwhile to a Council of Toledo convened and subscribed by that same Amandus.

But his historians narrate the matter clearly. Baudemundus writes:

> “He heard from them of a people whom antiquity called the Vaccaei [elsewhere, Vaceii], now commonly called the Vascones, deceived by excessive error, so that, devoted to auguries and every kind of superstition, they even worshiped idols as God. This people was spread out near the Pyrenean passes in rough and inaccessible places, and, relying on the agility of their warfare, frequently occupied the borders of the Franks.”

This describes the location of the people whom Amandus attacked armed with the sword of truth. When he preached the Gospel to them without success, he soon returned, he says, to the borders of the Franks. The other historians say the same.

This, then, was the journey into Spain—or so it appeared to the writer—in the brief course of which our defenders of ecclesiastical antiquity have compressed the peaceful episcopate at Castellón and the task of purifying Spain from a new error, together with a council convened so far away at Toledo.

In fact, Amandus had another concern: to turn his own Basques—for he was Aquitanian by birth—from the worship of idols and demons, not to instruct a foreign people, the Spaniards, with such exertion concerning a form of Mary’s childbirth that belongs among indifferent matters.

### 79

Do not be misled with Pseudo-Julian into believing that the event occurred within Spain and in the Pyrenean passes belonging to us, especially because Baudemundus wrote that these Basques frequently occupied the borders of the Franks and that Amandus, together with the others, returned from there to the borders of the Franks, or into Francia.

For at approximately that time *Francia* meant the territory subject to the Frankish kings. The Basques scarcely obeyed their rule; indeed, they frequently made incursions into their territory, as is clear from Arnaldo Oihenart’s *Account of Both Vasconias* [Note: Book III, chapters 1 and 2].

Concerning Rictrude, abbess of Marchiennes, born in Vasconia, the reason for her coming into Francia is promised by the author of her life; the Elnone monk Hucbaldus records this [Note: In Mabillon’s *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, vol. II, p. 941]. I have set down this one explicit testimony concerning the meaning of *Francia*, lest I weary my readers with innumerable examples.

### 80

There were, as we do not deny, two Vasconias: the Spanish one on this side of the Pyrenees, and the Gallic one beyond them [Col. 0038A]. This is well known to geographers.

But that Baudemundus is speaking of the latter and that Amandus did not extend his journey beyond it is made perfectly clear by the monk Milo. For, narrating this very expedition of Amandus, he says:

> Come, then, my Muse, unfold for me  
> The wandering Vaccaeia spread far and wide,  
> Trusting in reins and twisting weapons with its arms;  
> I beg you, mark it in common speech.  
> If you remove or alter the letters, it is called Vasconia.  
> This people, sufficiently fierce, pressing on with varied attacks,  
> Returning hostile weapons with blows and darts,  
> Had been an enemy at the outermost borders of the Franks.

This was in the time of Amandus. Later the people were subdued, for he adds:

> But now it lies peaceful beneath wound-dealing arms,  
> Its reins at last guided by wholesome counsel;  
> It does not tear with its bite, but draws all things  
> To the kisses of peace.

It is entirely certain that this refers to the Basques of the Gallic frontier, not to those of Spain, who were never subject to the Franks. Milo may perhaps be referring to the time of Dagobert, who is reported to have subdued even the fiercest Vaccaei under his authority by hostile force, in the *Acts of Saint Eligius of Noyon*, written by Saint Audoin of Rouen [Note: *Records of the Franks*, vol. I, p. 631].

Apart from Baudemundus, Fredegarius [Note: In the *Chronicle* under the year 766, in the same volume of *Records of the Franks*, p. 778] and others provide information about the Vaccaei, whose name was later replaced by that of the Vascones. Isidore records Vacca, or Vacaea, as their city [Note: *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter 2].

[Note: It is useful to set out Isidore’s passage, *Etymologies* IX.2: “Vacca,” he says, “was a town beside the Pyrenees, from which the Vaccaei were named. Concerning them the poet is believed to have said: ‘The Vaccaei wandering far and wide. These people of the Pyrenean ridges…,’” as it is read in Grialius. This is false. The word *Vaccaei* nowhere appears in the poet, nor did Isidore quote the three words “the Vaccaei wandering far and wide” from the poet, but only the first two, which occur in *Georgics* III.477:

> Of shepherds and distant pasturelands wandering far and wide.

The monk Milo seems to have had the same passage in mind in the verse:

> Come, then, Vaccaeia wandering far and wide, my Muse,

which our author cites here.

There is also in Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.42:

> …and the Barcaeans raging far and wide…

Jerome, in his letter to Marcellinus and Anapsychia, read the passage as:

> …and the Barcaeans wandering far and wide…

From this the error of Grialius may have arisen. The Barcaeans, however, were an African people and therefore do not belong here.

Grialius’s reading must therefore be restored, and Isidore’s passage punctuated as follows: “Concerning whom”—that is, the Vaccaei—“the poet is believed to have said, ‘wandering far and wide, the Vaccaei. These people of the Pyrenean ridges…’”; or, better, the word *Vaccaei* should be deleted as though it had slipped into Isidore’s text.

Isidore therefore thinks that the poet spoke of these Vaccaei, inhabitants of the Pyrenees, when he wrote “wandering far and wide,” although he did not name them—namely, the Vascones extending toward Gaul. The preceding verse, 474, had said:

> Then let him know the lofty Alps…

Servius and Philargyrius interpret the Alps in this passage as Gaul: “For in the language of the Gauls,” they say, “high mountains are called Alps.” Prudentius confirms the same interpretation in *Peristephanon*, in the hymn to Saint Lawrence.

Of these Vaccaei facing Aquitanian Gaul—who earlier had inhabited the Pyrenean ridges as wanderers and scattered peoples—after Gnaeus Pompey had subdued them and gathered them into one body, the city of Convenae in the lower mountains of Gaul, at the headwaters of the Garonne, received its name, as Isidore says a little later, and Jerome had said before him in his pamphlet *Against Vigilantius*.

Ptolemy defines the boundaries of the Spanish Vaccaei, including within them the cities of Intercatia, Porta Augusta, Viminacium, Lacobriga, Segisama Julia, Pallantia, Cauca, Pintia, Rauda, and others; so does Appian in *Iberica*, pp. 284 ff.; the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, in the route from Asturica through Cantabria to Caesaraugusta; and, among more recent writers, Arnold Oihenart, *Account of Both Vasconias*, book I, chapter 7, and Christopher Cellarius, book II, chapter 1, §65 ff.

The notes of Dominicus Vallarsius on Jerome’s letter to Riparius should be consulted: “Having first received the letters…,” which in the Verona edition of 1734 is number 109 and appears in vol. I, col. 719.]

To support this testimony, learned men bring forward further evidence [Note: Marca, *History of Béarn*, book I, chapter 12].

### 81

The brief and unsuccessful Basque expedition of Saint Amandus therefore has nothing to do with us Spaniards, however possible it may be that there were two such expeditions.

The first occurred when, having been sent into exile by Dagobert, he “attacked the homeland of Saint Rictrude”—that is, Vasconia—as Hucbaldus says in his *Life*. Henschenius assigns this event approximately to the year 634 [Note: 6 February, §10, *On the Affairs of Amandus*, p. 831].

At that time, however, Perseverantius was bishop of Castellón in Spain. He was present at the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633 and took part in the Fifth Council in 636 through a representative. Before the latter year, Amandus had been recalled from exile and summoned by Dagobert to the royal court [Note: As Henschenius observes in the same place].

Thus the Toledan impostor is not touching the date of this earlier Basque expedition with a delicate needle in order to deceive us. Nor does he touch the date of the later expedition. Although its acceptance is not precluded by the existence of another bishop of Castellón, named Marcus, who is recorded as subscribing to the Seventh Council and those following, from the year 646 through the Tenth, provided that Amandus is admitted to have returned to the Basques around the year 665 and preached the Gospel there, as Henschenius observes [Note: §14, p. 835], nevertheless the actual circumstances and success of that preaching, as we noted above, prove that this imagined episcopate of Amandus cannot belong to that period.

For this reason Henschenius rightly refutes the story of his supposed see of Castellón in Spain [Note: §22].

### 82

Nor does Pseudo-Julian, who sets no limit to his deception, stop there. He claims that in the year 650—thus we admit that his words must be read—Saint Amandus was already presiding over the Church of Castellón among us.

> “Saint Amandus,” he says [Note: *Chronicle*, number 336], “bishop of Castellón in Spain, flourished at that time; Pope Saint Martin sent him a letter.”

Certainly this pope sent a letter to Amandus, then bishop of Utrecht, who was petitioning for permission to resign that church. The letter was preserved by Philip the abbot in the *Life of Amandus* [Note: Vol. II of the *Acts of the Saints*, 6 February, p. 866], and also by Milo, his biographer [Note: In Mabillon’s *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, century or volume II, p. 719. It also appears in vol. VI of Labbe’s edition of the Councils, col. 383].

That author nevertheless continues:

> “A council against the Monothelites was convened at the urging of Amandus in the year of the Lord 650.”

This is the Lateran Synod convened immediately after the inauguration of Pope Martin I—not at the urging of Amandus, as Pseudo-Julian invents, and as the letter just mentioned itself disproves, but at the urging of the abbot Maximus, as Theophanes writes, followed by Baronius [Note: Vol. VIII, under the year 649, numbers 5 and 6].

### 83

There is still no end. We say, on the authority of Luitprand, that besides the books of *Synonyms*, Hildefonsus wrote other books and sermons in an elegant style against these heretics. Luitprand says that this is established [Note: Number 103] “by a letter of Genesius, the second of that name, abbot of Lyons—also called Abelardus—formerly abbot of Corbie and afterward bishop of Urci.”

Reader, recognize this passage of Luitprand as one of those in which his Toledan potter changes the shape of his face again and again beneath his hands. For in the Jesuit Francisco Portocarrero’s book *On the Descent of the Blessed Virgin into the Toledan Church*, chapter 14 [Note: It may be found in Thomas Tamayo’s notes on Luitprand, p. 63], the following words are transcribed from Luitprand’s *Chronicle*. They have either emerged from those we have quoted above after considerable alteration, or Luitprand now says one thing and now denies it:

> “Genesius the first, bishop of Auvergne, warns the Lord Hildefonsus by letter concerning the heresy of Jovinian, stirred up by certain people in Auvergne who said that the Blessed Virgin had remained corrupted in childbirth; and that they were making for Carpetania in order to undermine and utterly destroy the people [or rather, the nation] by their utterly false arguments against the most holy Virgin.”

Since Thomas Tamayo did not possess these words in his manuscripts of Luitprand’s *Chronicle*, he rightly says that he does not know where Portocarrero obtained them. It is well that he suspects the hand of a recent writer. The passage is indeed recent, but it belongs to the same author of the *Chronicle*, who now thinks one thing and now another, committing to the manuscript whatever came into his mind and often sending one formulation to one friend and another formulation later, differently expressed, to someone else.

### 84

You see the same monitor of Saint Hildefonsus and the same historian, Luitprand, making Genesius now Abelardus, abbot of Corbie, or the second bishop of Lyons of that name, afterward a bishop among us at Urci; and now making Genesius the first bishop of Auvergne.

Genesius, a contemporary of Hildefonsus [Note: In *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, and in the *Bishops of Clermont*, fol. 526], did indeed govern the Church of Auvergne, but he was neither first in order nor the earlier of the two men bearing that name. It is therefore not easy to determine where these insane contrivances are leading.

For Luitprand seems also to say that this same man was bishop of Lyons—unless I am mistaken. Julian may perhaps have had him in mind when he reports that there were two archbishops of Lyons named Genesius [Note: *Adversaria*, number 383], one earlier than the other.

The claim concerning a letter from Genesius to Hildefonsus plainly refers to the following passage in Laurentius Surius’s *Life of Saint Bonitus*, under 15 January:

> “This place”—he is speaking of the monastery of Magnilocum, today Manlieu in the diocese of Clermont—“the most noble bishop Genesius of the Auvergne, long ago, wished to be a monastery on his own estate, and so on. At that time the Novatian heresy, whether through the negligence or ignorance of certain people, crept into the city of Auvergne; and the impure doctrine of Jovinian also arose there. Against these heresies there exists a letter issued in the same monastery of Magnilocum, though he does not say by whom; perhaps it would at some time be worthwhile to bring it to light.”

The anonymous author preserved by Bollandus under 16 January says much the same, though Surius altered it in his customary fashion. This is the letter that Pseudo-Luitprand [Note: Number 103] intended to suggest had been sent by Genesius to Hildefonsus.

### 85

We have brought together these details about Amandus and Genesius so that it might be evident how many disturbances the fabulist stirred up on every side, and how many mutually contradictory claims he carelessly and foolishly introduced into these wretched compositions, solely in order to vindicate for Hildefonsus the book *On the Childbearing of the Virgin Mother of God*.

The first, as I believe, to observe that this book was not his was Joannes Baptista Poza, a man of exceptional talent and learning, though otherwise most unfortunate in his studies [Note: *Elucidarium of the Virgin Mary*, book IV, treatise 4, chapter 6]. He was followed by Theophilus Raynaudus [Note: *On Good and Bad Books*, part I, question 10, number 228], both Jesuits, who argued the case. Finally Lucas d’Acherius [Note: Preface to vol. I of the *Spicilegium*] and Joannes Mabillonius [Note: Preface to part II of volume III of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, p. 13], both Benedictines, argued from both reasons and written works that the book properly belongs to Paschasius Ratbertus.

[Note: The same view concerning this little work, *On the Birth or Childbearing of the Virgin Mother of God*, is held by the most recent editor of the Toledan Fathers in his notice prefixed to the doubtful works of Saint Hildefonsus, vol. I, p. 291: namely, that it belongs to Paschasius Ratbertus. The fragment attached to it from p. 318 onward is likewise his; but another fragment taken from Fevardentius and the Amelianus manuscript and appended to it from p. 328 onward is entirely anonymous (*ἀδέσποτον*). Cellier agrees, vol. XVII, p. 714, number 5; so does Cave, under Hildefonsus, vol. I, p. 590.]

Nevertheless Baronius [Note: Under the year 794, numbers 8 and 10], Bellarmine, Possevinus, and others accepted Fevardentius’s edition.

### 86

The thirteen sermons in that same edition of Fevardentius are likewise not by our Hildefonsus. They are:

1. *On the Childbearing and Purification of Saint Mary*.
2. *Against Those Who Falsely Assert That the Virgin Mary Bore the Lord Contrary to the Law*.
3, 4, 5, and 6. *On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin*.
7. *On the Same Assumption*, concerning the words of Luke, chapter 10: “Jesus entered into a certain village.”
8 and 9. *On the Same Assumption*.
10. *On the Nativity*.
11 and 12. *On the Same*.
13. *On the Purification*, concerning the words of Luke, chapter 11: “When the days of Mary’s purification had been completed.”

Hear Joannes Baptista Poza, whose words we give [Note: *Elucidarium of the Virgin*, book IV, treatise 4, chapter 6], because the *Elucidarium of the Virgin Mother*, from which these statements are taken, has come under the censure of the sacred faith of the Fathers and is not in everyone’s hands. He gives the reasons why he rejects these sermons as works of Hildefonsus:

> “In the first sermon on the Assumption,” he says, “he speaks too incautiously about the adoration of the body. In the same place there are foreign expressions and an inelegant style, alien to the genuine spirit of Hildefonsus.
>
> “In the second sermon, concerning the incorruption of the flesh, I believe I have already said enough above in the preceding volume, and so forth. Behold: this is not a sermon addressed to the people, but a fragment of some written work.
>
> “The third sermon is compiled from excerpts taken from Ambrose and Augustine.
>
> “In the fourth sermon he suggests that the Blessed Virgin had not yet obtained the resurrection of the body. And finally, in the fourth sermon he expressly professes this error.
>
> “In the fifth sermon he says: ‘Today the ministers of Tartarus do not dare to touch their captives, whom they remember to have been redeemed by the blood of him who deigned to be born of the Virgin for the salvation of the world.’
>
> “The sixth sermon contains the error mentioned above in the fourth sermon and is composed of fragments from Augustine.
>
> “The first and second sermons on the Nativity of the Virgin contain almost nothing concerning Mary’s birth. The author borrows extensively from Augustine’s second sermon on the Assumption, while concealing its title.
>
> “In the sermon on the Purification he writes certain peculiar things concerning original sin, and yet follows that erroneous teaching which denies that Christ’s body was perfect and complete in an instant. ‘We believe,’ he says, ‘that the Lord’s body was formed in the Virgin’s womb over the course of forty days,’ whereas he had written the opposite in the *Synonyms*.
>
> “All these things persuade us that these little works are not by Hildefonsus.”

We agree with him [Note: Copies of all these sermons exist in the royal library at Madrid, carefully collated with the Toledan manuscripts and with the edition of Fevardentius by the distinguished Andrés Marcos Burriel, who labored diligently on the work and collected the variant readings. Nevertheless, he persists in attributing them to Hildefonsus, as does the editor of the Toledan Fathers, vol. I, p. 329. Cellier, vol. XVII, p. 717, number 8; Cave, vol. I, p. 590; and likewise Oudinus, vol. I, col. 1683, reject them as works of Hildefonsus.]

Among the other works falsely attributed to this same Toledan pontiff is the *Life of Saint Eugenius*, his predecessor, which the spurious Julian alone attributes to him [Note: In the *Collection of Various Poems*, p. 150].

### 87

A few years ago the Franciscan Petrus Alva y Astorga published, among other Marian works drawn from a manuscript of the Church of Toledo, a *Crown of the Blessed Virgin Mary* under the name of Saint Hildefonsus. He was moved chiefly by the argument—clear from his preface—that the same manuscript contained other previously unpublished works of Hildefonsus under his explicit title and name, and that no sensible person would doubt that they were his production.

I am astonished that so many admirers and illustrators of Hildefonsus, frequently traveling to Toledo or living there, and the custodians of the Toledan library, could have allowed this to escape their notice.

In the manuscript catalogue of this library in my possession, the work is listed as follows:

> “The Crown of the Blessed Virgin with her psalter, small format.”

In the margin of the book it is noted:

> “The title is *Psalter*. It begins: ‘The psalter of Blessed Mary ever-virgin, published by Hildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, to be sung each day with devout mind.’”

The days on which it is to be recited are marked in the margin: Sunday, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday.

### 88

The same catalogue contains another manuscript entitled *The Crown of the Blessed Virgin*. Unless the numbers deceive us, both are found together in shelves I, numbers 13 and 14, among the theological manuscripts.

Nevertheless, “no one who has experience with ancient manuscripts is unaware,” Baronius says [Note: Under the year 441], “that it happens very frequently that the same volume contains not one or two, but three, four, or more treatises by different authors; and that some of them are found copied under the name of a single author. Thus, unless one has lynx-like eyes, it often happens that whatever follows in the same manuscript is attributed to the author named in its title.”

Therefore, the fact that the *Psalter* belongs to Hildefonsus does not establish that the *Crown* is his as well.

I admit that in this *Crown*, no less than in Hildefonsus’s genuine and certain works on the perpetual virginity of Blessed Mary, there are certain words of the same formation, departing from the purity of the Latin language and showing a Gothic character. One example is *nectura*, used for *nexus* or “bond,” just as the celebrated books *On Virginity* use *connectatio*. But there are many other considerations to which greater weight should be given than to this indication, since such forms occur commonly in other writers—not only of that century but of later centuries as well.

### 89

The work inserts poems, including passages belonging to others, for the most part into prose. This is not in keeping with Hildefonsus’s style, although the editor did not distinguish them.

Such are the passages concerning the name of Mary in chapter 5:

> “Concerning the name of Mary, someone says: ‘The name of Mary is gold-fragrant and aromatic, like a heavenly perfume; like the sun, radiant with light; life-giving to the dead; honey-sweet to monks; holy and leading upward; divine and ecstasy-producing.’”

And elsewhere, in chapter 6:

> “A gate closed behind and before; a road inaccessible to the true; earth drenched with heaven’s dew; Gideon’s fleece drenched; rain of divinity; calm seas, star of the sea—lest the storm overwhelm us—and the tempest everything.”

[Note: The printed text nevertheless has *via veris in via* (“a road of spring in a road”), and other passages are badly punctuated. At the end, *obruat* may perhaps have to be read instead of *omnia*.]

The entire speech of chapter 9 is likewise metrical, despite its verses being poorly constructed and mutually inconsistent. The author says:

> “These verses, which I offer to you, Lady, deign to receive, so that neither the sound may be consistent nor the judgment of the ears be able to avoid error.”

This rhythmic poetry does not belong to the age or style of Hildefonsus.

He frequently uses the testimony of others without naming them, and it would not be difficult for careful readers to discover their sources. Thus in chapter 11:

> “A certain servant and devout praiser of yours urges us in his little works to implore the protection of this star with attentive heart, saying: ‘In dangers, in doubtful circumstances, look to the star, call upon Mary; let her not depart from your heart, let her not depart from your lips.’”

[Note: The royal library also contains a little work entitled *The Crown of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, collated by the distinguished Burriel with the example published by Petrus Alva y Astorga. No sane person attributes it to Hildefonsus. The editor of the *Toledan Fathers* agrees, vol. I, p. 392.]

## Life of Saint Hildefonsus, Bishop of Toledo

[Col. 0041]

### Notice

(From Antonio Lorenza, *Library of the Toledan Fathers*)

We have thought it best to publish the deeds of Saint Hildefonsus in the very words in which they were committed to writing by Saint Julian, his disciple and successor, and by Cixila, also archbishop of Toledo, in a later age.

We did not wish, by composing a new history that would surpass them in style, to diminish the authority of the ancient records among people of our own time, who grant more than is fitting to the critical art—or rather, should we say, to their own judgment?—in matters concerning religion. These testimonies, presented in their own words, compel belief even against the will of their readers.

We also give the life written by a monk of Cerrato in the thirteenth century. It is not without authority, although in it we have corrected a few minor points from Cixila, which the monk of Cerrato seems to have drawn from a tradition that was not entirely uncorrupted by the injuries of time.

## Eulogy of Blessed Hildefonsus

From Saint Julian, in the appendix to the book *On Illustrious Men*, written by Hildefonsus himself. (C)

[Col. 0043A]

Hildefonsus, renowned in the memory of his age and adorning the centuries of our time with the richly flowing streams of his eloquence, was finally called to the chair of the Toledan see and, after Eugenius the Second, consecrated as bishop. He was a man as worthy of praise as he was abundant in the grace of virtues.

He was endowed with constant fear of God, pierced by religion and overflowing with compunction; grave in his bearing, praiseworthy in integrity, singular in patience, silent concerning secrets, supreme in wisdom, distinguished by his talent for discussion, eminent in his power of expression, and abundant in the flood of his speech. He was held in such high esteem for the grandeur of his eloquence that, while the expansive discourse of his disputations moved forward at length, it was rightly believed that not a man but God was speaking abundantly through a man.

While still living amid the beginnings of childhood, he was touched by the divine Spirit and became enamored of the life of monks. He spurned affection for his parents and for worldly possessions and sought the monastery of Agali. His father pursued his flight with furious rage, but was stopped by a single barrier in the wall. This both frustrated the furious man’s search and preserved the devotion of the fugitive.

For while his father, driven by rage, pressed toward the interior, he left behind the hiding place in which the young man was concealed. Thus he passed by what lay behind without investigating it and searched the forward places that he had already passed.

Afterward, attacking the cell at Agali with armed force and a sword, he did not find the person he sought. Returning home, he mourned him as lost.

When the man mentioned above learned that his father was absent, he immediately went to the monastery of Agali and conducted himself becomingly there as a monk for many years.

He also built a monastery of virgins in the small village of Deibium and adorned it with his own resources. Later, having been made superior, he disciplined the monks of the monastery of Agali, administered its property, and preserved its life.

After this he was forcibly brought back to Toledo and, following the death of his predecessor, installed there as bishop.

He certainly wrote very many books in a highly polished style, which the same author judged should be divided into the following sections: the book of *The Personification of One’s Own Weakness*; the booklet *On the Virginity of Saint Mary against Three Unbelievers*; the short work *On the Distinction of the Persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit*; the short work *Annotations on the Daily Office*; the short work *Annotations on Sacred Matters*; one book *On Knowledge of Baptism*; and another *On the Progress of the Spiritual Desert*. He wished all these to be joined into the volume of the first part.

The book of letters constitutes the second part. In it, writing to various persons, he employed enigmatic formulas and sometimes introduced characters. In this work he also elicited from certain people more polished responses to his writings. He wished the third part to consist of Masses, hymns, and sermons. Finally, the book of the fourth part is composed in verse and prose; in it epitaphs and certain epigrams are recorded.

He also wrote many other works, but, hindered by various occupations and troubles, he left some begun and others incomplete. Having been summoned to the episcopate in the ninth year of the glorious ruler Reccesvinth, he remained distinguished for nine years and almost two months by the merits of his life and by his continuance in office. When the eighteenth year of the aforesaid ruler had been completed, on the following day, the tenth day before the Kalends of February, he was released from the dwelling of the flesh and buried in the church of blessed Leocadia, laid at the feet of his predecessor, with whom he is believed to enjoy forever the abode of glory.

[Col. 0043]

# Here Begins the Life of Saint Hildefonsus, Metropolitan Bishop of the See of Toledo, Written by Cixila, Bishop of the Same City

[Note: [Col. 0043] We have followed the edition of Flórez, which he himself collated with numerous editions and manuscript codices, which we shall cite as follows: A. denotes the edition of Aguirre; Ae. the Aemilianus Codex, written in the middle of the eleventh century and transferred from the monastery of Saint Emilianus of La Cogolla to the Escorial; S. the Surian edition; T. the Toledo Codex; Ta. the reading of Tamayo apud the Bollandists.]

## 1

Behold the banquets of that honey-flowing lord Hildefonsus, which, snatching them from the paradise of God and scattering them throughout all Hesperia, satisfied our hunger with an immense abundance of eloquence. He was not inferior in merits to that most holy lord Isidore, from whose fountain, while still a little dependent, he drank the purest streams. For when the holy and venerable Pope Eugenius, metropolitan bishop of the See of Toledo, sent him to the aforesaid doctor, Isidore, metropolitan bishop of Seville, although he already seemed to himself somewhat learned, he was held and refined by him to such a degree—and, as they say, constrained for a time by iron—that, if anything was lacking in his knowledge, he was more fully instructed. Returning to his teacher, lord Eugenius, and still performing the office of deacon, he was appointed abbot, after not many days, in the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, situated in the suburb of Toledo.

There, immediately distinguished in his office, he composed two Masses in praise of those same lords, to be sung on their feast day, with marvelous musical modulation. You will find those Masses annotated below.

[Note: [Col. 0043C] Ae. reads “honey-flowing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0043C] The word “and” is absent in A.]

[Note: [Col. 0043C] A. reads “at some time.”]

## 2

Then, after a long time, when lord Eugenius died, he was appointed bishop in his place. His virtue immediately shone forth, fully revealed, in the Romulean see—so he calls the Toledo see because it was in the royal city of Toledo—and, like a burning torch, traversed all his Spain. His teaching still shines in the Church like the sun and the moon; his memory is held in the blessing of fragrance and in the composition of incense.

From his very cradle and from the beginning of his life he remained a eunuch, and prepared within himself a great dwelling place for the Lord. He was not cut by a material instrument, but by the divine sword; he did not cut away lust by the skill of tools, but by heavenly grace obtained holiness within himself. Suddenly inspired by a heavenly gift, shining equally with such and so great predecessors, what had been closed to them was opened to him.

[Note: [Col. 0045C] T., Ta., and Mabillon read “shining”; A. reads “burning.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045C] A. calls the Toledo see “Romulean” because it was in the royal city of Toledo. In A. the word “Church” is absent. Ta. reads “as the sun [and] moon.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045C] Ae. reads “by the handle of the hands”; Ta. “by the instrument,” or “by hand”; A. “by the material instrument of the hand.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045C] The words “within himself” are absent in A. and Ta.]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Ae. reads “breathed upon.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] A. reads “equally.”]

## 3

For the Holy Spirit, who dwelt within him, acted in such a way that what Hildefonsus concealed within, the Spirit revealed outwardly, so that the most powerful helper might appear at work in both places: to Hildefonsus the Spirit ordained what he should disclose in praise of the virgins, and revealed to him what marvelous thing he should display in the athlete, thereby declaring before human beings the merit of his faith and not leaving him who labored in the spiritual contest without the rewards of his gifts.

Thus the Spirit acted so that what had not yet been shown to the people who desired it for so many years he first revealed through Hildefonsus. When the king arrived at the royal seat, Hildefonsus, on her feast day, presented to all who were standing by the relics of his holy virgin and confessor, Leocadia, who was dedicated to God. Falling on his knees before her tomb, he saw the tomb in which her holy little body remains buried to this day leap upward. Its cover, which scarcely thirty young men could move, was raised not by human hands but by angelic ones. The veil that covered the limbs of the holy virgin appeared to come forth alive, as though she herself, while living, were sending it outward and raising it, stretched out as if by human hands. The most beautiful virgin appeared before him, obedient to his sight.

The bishops, princes, priests and deacons, clergy, and all the people cried out, with no one remaining silent: “Thanks be to God in heaven; thanks be to God on earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0045D] A. reads this way, and Cerratensis likewise writes “she herself” in the *Life of Saint Hildefonsus*. Other manuscripts have “he himself,” but the former reading must be retained by every right.]

She herself is then said immediately to have taken and clasped it in her hands and to have uttered such words as these, crying out with all the people: “Thanks be to God! My lady lives through the life of Hildefonsus.” The clergy, repeating this, sang the *Alleluia* with great force, together with the hymn that lord Hildefonsus had recently composed in her praise: “She has become beautiful, alleluia, and your fragrance is like unmixed balsam,” along with other words that he had uttered in her praise in the same Mass, which is noted below.

[Note: [Col. 0043C] A. and Ta. read “of the divine ones.”]

[Note: [Col. 0044C] The words “the Masses” are absent below in A.]

[Note: [Col. 0044C] A. reads “we have them annotated.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] A. reads “and so that he might act in both places.” This entire sentence is absent from Ta.]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] A. reads “what he should disclose in praises”; Ae. “what he should disclose in praise.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] A. and T. read “what he should reveal to them.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045B] A. reads “one.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] A. lacks the word “in.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] T. reads “he himself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] A. reads: “When the king arrived at the royal seat, the tomb,” and so forth. A. reads “the most holy.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] A. reads “so that it might leap out.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Mabillon suggests “the tomb.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] A. reads “so that her most holy little body might leap out.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Ta. reads “green”; A. reads “rose up, as though she herself, while living, were sending it outward and raising it, stretched out as if by human hands, and were being presented to the sight,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] A. reads “of the martyr.”]

[Note: [Col. 0045D] The words “so that their desires might grow” are absent from A.]

[Note: [Col. 0046C] Ae. reads “he came forward.”]

## 4

Amid the voices of the people he cried out like a bellowing ox, asking that some cutting instrument be brought, with which he might cut off what he held in his hands. No one came to him, because the people were roaring with broad blows and open mouths. For the holy virgin was also violently drawing back what she had willingly let down, so that their desires might grow.

But the former prince Reccesvinth, who was ruler at that time, laying aside his earthly glory and ferocity—for he had looked with a proud eye upon Hildefonsus when the latter reproved him for his iniquities—offered with tears a small knife that he carried in its sheath. Lowering his neck and stretching out suppliant hands from his throne, he earnestly begged that it be brought to Hildefonsus, asking that he not judge unworthy one who offered it with tears.

He took it and, with his right hand, cut off what he was already holding a little way in his left, and placed the knife itself together with the same relics in silver cases. Deeming himself unworthy, after cutting the sacred things, to touch them further with polluted hands, he ordered that a gift, so far as he was able, be bestowed upon the petitioner through a deputy in due form.

When these things had been completed, since it would be too long to explain them all in detail, everything that pertained to the use of the holy Catholic Church was accomplished everywhere in the praises of God.

[Note: [Col. 0046D] A. and Ta. read “after these things had been examined.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] T. reads “with voices.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] A. and Ta. omit the words “so that their desires might grow.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] T. reads “violently.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] Ta. and Ae. read “who, because he was rebuked by him for his iniquities”; T. “who, since he had been rebuked for his iniquities”; A. “rebuked.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] A. reads “with happiness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] Ae. reads “extending suppliant hands”; A. “extending suppliant hands.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] A. reads “more insistently.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] A. reads “in cases.” Ae. reads “he ordered the vicar to provide it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] Ae. reads “should not touch it”; A. “should touch it. The hand of the petitioner …”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] T. and Ae. read “whatever was of use.”]

## 5

After these events, the Holy Spirit performed still other miracles through him, at the very Advent of the Lord, not many days later. But since it would be lengthy to recount everything that lord Urban and lord Evantius narrated as having been done through him in the city of Toledo during his lifetime, let us proceed from many examples to a few. Those who heard these things with me will grieve, when they read this, that I have omitted so many great events, which they certainly know together with me.

[Note: [Col. 0046D] A. and Ta. read “after these digressions.”]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] Ae., A., and Ta. read “let us undertake.”]

## 6

When the day of holy Mary, ever-virgin, arrived, he performed the litanies three days beforehand and completed the above-mentioned Mass, to be sung in her praise; this was the seventh. When her holy solemnity arrived, the aforesaid king, less concerned with the fear of God and ill-conscious of his own iniquities, came prepared, according to royal custom, to hear the solemn offices.

For the servant of God Hildefonsus, relying upon an even greater gift, received with rejoicing the day of his Lady, whom he served under God as his ruler. He had composed, with the highest devotion of his heart and with musical harmony, the work we mentioned above in praise of the Mother of God, and had elegantly produced the booklet on Virginity, filled with testimonies from the Old and New Testaments in the manner of a *Synonymia*. He had adorned the magnificence of his aforesaid Lady with worthy eloquence.

When, before the hour of Matins, he rose according to his custom to perform the service of God, the deacon or subdeacon and the clergy went before him carrying torches. Suddenly, opening the doors of the atrium and entering the church, they fixed their eyes upon a heavenly radiance. Unable to endure the light, they fled trembling, leaving behind the lamps they held in their hands, and returned by the path they had come, almost dead, to their companions.

The whole congregation anxiously asked what the servant of God was doing. They saw him with angelic choirs. The guards were so suddenly terrified that, turning their backs on the church door, they returned to their own places.

[Note: [Col. 0046D] A. and T. add “on the day of the Assumption,” which Ae. lacks.]

[Note: [Col. 0046D] A. and Ta. read “three days beforehand”; another reading is “for three days.”]

[Note: [Col. 0047B] Ta. reads “while he rejoicingly undertook the celebration of his Lady … praying.” Ae. reads “Mystical”; Ta. “might seek musical [composition]”; A. “might prepare songs composed with harmonious modulation.” A. reads “God.” Ae. reads “and the vigils.”]

[Note: [Col. 0047B] A. reads “with small vessels.”]

[Note: [Col. 0047B] A. reads “fixing their gaze upon the heavenly radiance.”]

[Note: [Col. 0047B] A. and Ta. read “fleeing in terror, they left the lamps,” and so forth. Ae. reads “worthy eloquence for the magnificence and favour,” and so forth; A. “worthy eloquence and magnificence.” S. reads “had adorned the feast.”]

[Note: [Col. 0047B] A. and Ta. read “what was happening to the servant of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0047B] The words “they saw” are absent from most manuscripts, but Aguirre includes them, appropriately.]

[Note: [Col. 0047B] Ae. reads “they were terrified … they returned.”]

## 7

But he, confident in his conscience, fell before the altar of the holy Virgin and found the Lady herself seated upon an ivory chair, where the bishop was accustomed to sit and greet the people. No bishop dared approach that chair except lord Sisibertus, who afterward lost that very seat and was sent into exile.

He raised his eyes and looked around her. He saw the entire apse of the church filled with groups of virgins, singing something with melodious sweetness to the accompaniment of David’s songs. Looking at her—as he himself reported to people of good conscience and great affection—she addressed him in these words:

“Hasten to meet me, dearest servant of God. Receive from my hand this little gift, which I have brought you from the treasury of my Son. You must use the blessing of the garment brought to you only on my day. Because you have remained with the eyes of faith fixed always upon my service, because you have painted my praise so sweetly in the hearts of the faithful through the grace spread upon your lips, and because you are already adorned in this life with the garments of glory, in the future you will rejoice with the other servants of my Son in my storehouses.”

[Note: [Col. 0047B] “Ivory” is absent from A. and Ta.]

[Note: [Col. 0047B] A. and Ta. read “to sit.”]

[Note: [Col. 0047B] A. and Ta. read “to remain seated.” Ae. reads “having lost that very seat”; Ta. lacks this reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] T. and Ae. read “with songs.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] A. reads “conscious and very dear.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] Ae. reads “most upright.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] A. reads “given”; Ta. “to be given.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] A. reads “only in my service.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] A. and Ta. read “remaining with your eyes always fixed in my service.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] A. and Ta. read “and praise.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] T. has this reading; others differ.]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] A. and Ta. read “of the Church.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] A. and Ta. read “you will rejoice”; Mabillon “you will be nourished.”]

## 8

After saying these things, she departed from his sight together with the virgins and the light in which she had come. The servant of God remained as anxious to attain glory as he was certain of the victory’s palm that had been granted to him.

[Note: [Col. 0048B] Ae. and T. read “secure.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] T. reads “foreknowing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] S. reads “of the palm of victory promised to him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0048B] This is the end of the *Life* in the Aemilianus Codex. The Toledo Codex continues: “By the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and rules all things forever and ever. Amen.”]

[Col. 0047]

# Another Life of Saint Hildefonsus, Written by Rodericus Cerratensis

[Note: [Col. 0047D] This Rodericus was a Spaniard of Cerrato, of the Order of Friars Preachers. He lived in the thirteenth century and wrote a *Sanctuary*, or *Lives of the Saints*, whose deeds he collected partly from ancient breviaries of the churches and partly from historical works. The work is still unpublished, except for the Lives of certain saints that the Reverend Father Flórez made public in his *Hispania sacra*. From that work we transcribe this Life of Hildefonsus.]

## 1

Hildefonsus, a Spaniard born in the city of Toledo to noble parents, was entrusted for education to Eugenius, the noble prelate of the See of Toledo. Saint Eugenius carefully instructed him in good morals and the rudiments of letters. Observing his capacity, he sent him to blessed Isidore, archbishop of Seville, with whom the teaching of every kind of eloquence, the discipline of the arts, and the study of theology flourished so greatly that he instructed all who flocked to him according to each one’s capacity.

## 2

Hildefonsus, therefore, received kindly by blessed Isidore both because of his lineage and because of Eugenius, and subjected to his teachings, worked very hard in the study of the liberal arts and fixed his attention even more diligently upon the law of the Lord.
