Applying himself wholeheartedly, while still in tender years, to these and other honorable exercises, he offered himself as an example of human life to the young men who studied with him. He not only recalled them from unlawful things but also, by clinging to good works, trained them to do what was good.

No one applied himself to reading more diligently than he, and no one devoted himself more frequently to prayer. Yet he so distinguished the times for reading and praying from one another that neither reading hindered prayer nor prayer reading. Rather, so that he might read or pray more attentively, reading was in turn a relief from prayer, and prayer a relief from reading. Wherever he went, prayer accompanied him as he went and returned. In secular society there was nothing indecent or dishonorable in him. As a servant of Christ and an imitator of the saints, he advanced not only in wisdom but also grew marvelously in the increase of his virtues.

## 3

When his childhood had passed and he reached the age to which the delights of the flesh appeal, he wished to restrain unlawful impulses. Surrounding his body with a wall of virtues, and setting the contrary qualities of virtues against the contrary qualities of vices, he so enclosed it that not only was no entrance open to vices, but even access was barred except through the assault of temptations. For he was permitted, like the other saints, to be tempted—not for the weakening of his virtues but for the advancement of his testing.

Out of compassionate affection he stooped to the misery of the poor; through the seal of chastity he did not lose the lily of virginity. Offering to God the other adornments of virtue and pleasing God, he sacrificed himself wholly to the Lord.

## 4

Finally, abandoning secular studies, he returned to blessed Eugenius and was ordained deacon by him.

[Note: [Col. 0049C] Cerratensis is mistaken here. For it is clear from Saint Hildefonsus himself that he was ordained deacon by Saint Helladius before Saint Eugenius ascended the See of Toledo.]

To prevent his life, which he had preserved undefiled, from being stained by the enjoyment of temporal things, he vowed to serve God in the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, situated in the suburb of Toledo and anciently called the Agalian monastery, having left his parents and joined the others who lived there.

As he was going to the aforesaid place and saw his father pursuing him from a distance in furious haste, he hid himself in an old wall so that he would not be deprived of his purpose. His father, passing by the hiding place, approached the Agalian monastery with threats; failing to find him, he returned. After his father had gone back, Hildefonsus entered the monastery and received the habit.

## 5

After many years had passed, since he was considered second to no one in religious life, he became abbot. Having become abbot, he ordered the affairs of the Church and supplied everyone with what was necessary. Observing everyone’s conduct and attending to the qualities of their character, he presented himself to each according to what was necessary: gentle toward the gentle, but toward the offended he bore an offended disposition.

For:

> The Agalian abbot was a sword against offenses.

## 6

In a village then called Bisensis, he built a monastery of virgins and enriched it from his own resources. His fame spread throughout all Spain, and no one could be found holier, more worthy of approval, more eloquent, more distinguished, more upright, or more perfect in knowledge than he. After Eugenius’s death, the clergy and people brought him back to Toledo, and, with everyone praising him, he was appointed bishop.

Having become bishop, he prepared for everyone the table of preaching according to the capacity of each.

## 7

One day, as the feast of Saint Leocadia was approaching and everyone was assembling to celebrate it, while Saint Hildefonsus was praying on bended knees at her tomb, that sacred virgin presented herself to him before all who were standing there.

When the holy man approached her presence, she, as if embracing him, uttered these words:

> “My Lady lives through the life of Hildefonsus.”

I believe she uttered these words because, when faith in and the truth of the blessed Mary’s virginity had been destroyed and extinguished throughout almost all Spain by the error of unbelievers, he wrote a book on her virginity through which that faith, as though dead, revived and completely destroyed the error.

But so that he might leave the memory of the revelation to posterity, he cut off with the knife of Prince Reccesvinth, who was present at the feast, a portion of the garment that had covered her living limbs. He placed it together with the same relics in silver vessels, judging himself unworthy, after cutting the sacred things, to cut further with polluted hands.

When these things had been accomplished, everyone solemnly celebrated the Virgin’s feast.

## 8

He loved the Mother of God greatly and honored her with every reverence. In her praise he composed, in an elegant style, a distinguished volume on her most holy virginity. It pleased the Virgin herself so much that she appeared to him holding the book in her hand and gave thanks to him for such a work.

Wishing to honor her more profoundly, he decreed that her solemnity—that is, the feast of the Annunciation—should be celebrated every year on the eighth day before the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, so that, because the feast of the Annunciation often fell near the Passion or Resurrection of the Lord, it could be restored to the appointed day.

And indeed it was very fitting that the Annunciation of the Lord should be celebrated before his Nativity at the same time of year. This solemnity is celebrated throughout many churches of Spain.

## 9

As the day of the feast of the Mother of God approached, he decreed that litanies should be celebrated with fasting three days beforehand, so that the feast might be observed with greater devotion.

In the middle of the night of the feast, when he rose for Matins and the book on virginity that he had composed with marvelous eloquence was ready to be read, he prepared to complete the vigils that he had vowed to God and blessed Mary. The ministers who went before him carrying lights opened the church doors and saw inside the church a heavenly light. Unable in any way to endure it, they fled trembling like dead men, leaving behind the lights they carried.

But Hildefonsus, undaunted, entered. As he knelt before the altar according to his custom, and, confident in his conscience, looked around, he saw the Queen of Virgins seated upon the chair where he himself used to sit and preach to the people. He also saw groups of virgins praising her.

When the Virgin and the holy man looked at one another, the most holy Virgin said to him:

> “Because you have remained with a pure mind and steadfast faith in my praises, and have painted my praise in the hearts of the faithful with sweet eloquence, and have girded your loins with the belt of virginity, I have brought you from the garments of everlasting glory a garment in which you may be clothed on my day and solemnity. You shall sit in this chair. But if anyone after you should presume to put on this garment and sit in this chair, he will not escape punishment.”

Having said these things, she disappeared and left him the garment that we call the *alba*.

[Note: [Col. 0049C–D] “The *alba*,” says the most learned Mabillon, volume I of the *Benedictine Annals*, book XV, no. 10, “was sometimes absolutely what they called that chasuble, because it was made of white cloth.”]

He lived a happy life and happily departed to the Lord.

## 10

After him, when the bishop Siargius had been appointed, he said:

> “Just as I am a man, so I know that my predecessor was a man. Why should I not put on the garment in which he was clothed, since I hold the same episcopal office?”

When he had put on the garment, he was bound tightly and fell down dead. Terrified, they removed the garment and placed it in the church treasury.

[Note: [Col. 0049D–0050D] The bishop was not called Siargius but Sisibertus. He rashly decided—not to put on the sacred garment, but to sit in the chair from which the Virgin had addressed Hildefonsus, as Cixila relates. Cerratensis must therefore be corrected by Cixila. Nor did he die suddenly while sitting there; rather, somewhat later he was deposed from the episcopal see by the Fathers at the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, assembled in 693. The principal charge was that he had conspired against the king’s life; therefore he was deprived of communion and condemned to perpetual exile. It is credible that he proceeded to so great a crime from that earlier rashness, God permitting it as punishment for so great a sacrilege.]

# On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary

[Col. 0051]

# A Special Notice Concerning the Work of Saint Hildefonsus, Particularly the Book on the Perpetual Virginity of the Mother of God

In the edition of the works of Saint Hildefonsus, we have decided to preserve the order that their author, according to the testimony of Saint Julian, assigned to them while he was alive. Yet many items are missing from his catalogue, although we have collected with the utmost diligence everything we could from various places.

We have found absolutely no trace of the book *The Personification of One’s Own Weakness*, or of the two short works *Annotations on the Daily Office* and *Annotations on Sacred Matters*. We reproduce no more than two letters, taken from the more corrected edition of E. Martène. We have only a very few sermons that we can plausibly attribute to our Hildefonsus. Of the hymns, verses, epitaphs, and epigrams that composed the fourth part of his works, we have not even the slightest fragment.

In addition to the works mentioned by Saint Julian, we present as an authentic work of Hildefonsus a supplement to the book *On Illustrious Men* begun by Saint Isidore. We then give various other short works of doubtful authenticity, consigning the remaining pieces to the Appendix, since they are wrongly attributed to the holy doctor. We shall discuss some of them in their proper places.

But the chief of all Saint Hildefonsus’s works, and the one that by every right occupies the first place, is the work we now present, entitled *On the Perpetual Virginity of the Mother of God against Three Unbelievers*. It is a golden book whose excellence can never be praised according to its worth. Even if all his other monuments had perished, its praise could have transmitted Hildefonsus’s sweetest memory, together with the greatest admiration for his piety and learning, to the posterity of every future age.

It is said to have been written *ἀντὶ τριῶν ἀπίστων*—that is, “against three unbelievers”—whose names Hildefonsus disclosed: Helvidius, Jovinianus, and a Jew.

But whether by these names he intended the heresiarchs themselves who lived in the fourth century, or their disciples, who at that time were spreading their poison throughout Spain while denying the perpetual integrity of the Virgin Mother of God, is entirely unclear to us.

Some prefer the first view. They are moved both by the explicit mention of the names themselves and by the words of Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona, in his first letter to Hildefonsus. That letter contains much in praise of his doctrine and zeal, and gives him thanks for the booklet sent to him, yet says nothing indicating that Hildefonsus was dealing with heretics of his own time.

They therefore conclude that, impelled by the most ardent affection for the Mother of God and by the desire to exalt her perpetual virginity, he took up his pen while merely setting before his mind the inventions of the earlier heretics, as though he wished to contribute, together with Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and the other Fathers who had deliberately and vigorously attacked them, his own offering in the service of the Virgin Mother of God.

Others, however, think that Hildefonsus did not undertake this work without cause, nor unless he had first been provoked by the adversaries of his own time. These men, emerging in Spain as disciples of new impious teachers, had spread foul calumnies against the virginity of the Mother of God. We willingly agree with this view.

For it is not credible that Hildefonsus would have raised such horrible and unheard-of blasphemies, as though from a tomb, merely to sharpen his style against heresy—even in order to refute them forcefully—by reproducing them in a way that would offend pious ears. It would seem rash for him to have done so.

Moreover, Rodericus, archbishop of Toledo, recounts that the matter occurred as we think, in book II of *On the Affairs of Spain*, at the end of the book, in these words:

> “In his time, when Helvidius and Pelagius—he mistakenly wrote Pelagius here instead of Jovinianus, as the manuscripts of *On Virginity* commonly have—came from Gaul and infected many parts of Spain, defaming the virginity of the blessed Virgin, blessed Hildefonsus confronted them with testimonies of Sacred Scripture, honey-flowing speech, and grace spread upon his lips. He refuted their doctrines and drove them from Spain in confusion.”

This agrees with the history of the translation of the relics from Toledo to Asturias, by an unknown author. Among other things, when describing the cloak given to Hildefonsus by the blessed Virgin, he says that it was a reward “for the praises celebrated in honor of her holy virginity, where the glorious holy bishop himself contended against Heliudus and Lobinianus,” as Sandovalus incorrectly printed the names instead of Helvidius and Jovinianus.

Besides these considerations, we are moved by the words spoken by Saint Leocadia in the apparition that Cixila narrates, in praise of Hildefonsus:

> “My Lady lives through the life of Hildefonsus.”

We say that these words were spoken by Leocadia—not by the people and not by Hildefonsus himself, as some have interpreted them, deceived by the authority of a manuscript that incorrectly reads *ipse amplexans* (“he himself embracing”) instead of *ipsa* (“she herself”), contrary to the testimony of the other manuscripts, contrary to the ancient understanding of the Church of Toledo itself, contrary to the testimony of ancient writers and breviaries, and finally contrary to the genuine meaning of the words themselves.

For those words have no proper sense in the mouth of the people, and in the mouth of Hildefonsus would be improper because of the oath “by the life of Hildefonsus” and because the address “my Lady” is attributed to Leocadia. They are, however, entirely appropriate and timely in the mouth of Saint Leocadia, who spoke them before her own flock in praise of Hildefonsus. On this matter see Father Flórez, appendix 8 to volume V.

To return to our subject: those words, “My Lady lives”—that is, Mary— as Mabillon printed them from his manuscripts, sufficiently indicate that through Hildefonsus’s works the faith in perpetual virginity and pious devotion toward the Mother of God were revived in the hearts of the faithful. In those times that faith was either languishing or dead in them because of the poisonous opinions of the heretics, which he utterly overthrew in his writings.

Rodericus Cerratensis likewise gave this interpretation of those words already in the thirteenth century, in the *Life* printed above. If Hildefonsus had not been dealing with contemporary heretics, and if faith in the perpetual virginity of the Mother of God had flourished in Spain, there would certainly have been no reason to say that through him it had been brought back from death to life.

We therefore believe that at that time there were impious men who blasphemed the Mother of God, followers of ancient errors, whom Hildefonsus attacked in this booklet under the disguised names of their leaders. At the same time, under the single name “the Jew,” he undertook to destroy and overthrow the entire Jewish people, whose notorious envy of Mary’s virginity is well known.

He pierced each of them with his own weapon. In the first chapter he attacks Jovinianus, showing that Mary, who, as he admitted, had conceived as a virgin, did not lose her virginity in childbirth. In the second he overcomes Helvidius, proving that she remained a virgin throughout her entire life after giving birth. Finally, in the third chapter and those that follow, he pursues the Jew, who rejected perpetual integrity in the woman who had given birth, with innumerable testimonies of Scripture and every kind of argument. Meanwhile, he inflicts new wounds, even unto destruction and annihilation, upon the earlier enemies whom he had already defeated individually.

Some also call this book the *Book of Synonyms*, indicating by this name the style in which it was written. Certain people criticize it because they would have liked the holy doctor to have weighed every single word according to the strictest laws of rhetoric and the most minute rules of good style.

But we would wish that, when examining the writings of the holy Fathers, they would show themselves more humane and indulgent, especially since Hildefonsus did not lack an example that he could imitate without reproach: his great teacher Isidore, who used the same style in his book *On the Lamentation of the Sinful Soul* and therefore called it a *Synonymia*.

Moreover, the aforementioned manner of writing should not be judged so inappropriate to the subject. Certainly Hildefonsus, seized, as it were, by a fervor of spirit—kindled both by love for the Mother of God and by righteous anger against the blasphemers—thought it would be useful for pressing them more sharply if he burdened and almost overwhelmed them with that infinite abundance of synonyms concerning the same point, so that, crushed beneath its weight, they would not even be able to mutter against the truth.

For I do not know what power there is in words and sentences gathered into a mass: like a torrent rushing headlong with the greatest violence, they overcome every barrier, destroy everything, and carry away with them whatever they encounter.

Thus the devotion of his inflamed spirit, as well as the very nature of the subject before him, led Hildefonsus to this manner of writing, which he certainly did not use in his other short works. It is therefore rashly asserted that this style was in some sense his own and peculiar to him. In this matter, otherwise very learned men have gone astray: because of the mere difference in style, they did not hesitate immediately to deny to Hildefonsus those short works that they found did not abound in synonymous words.

We have thus far seen three editions of this work: one made by Michael Carranza, a Carmelite, at Valencia de los Edetani in 1556, and reprinted twice not long afterward outside Spain; a second prepared by Francisco Feuardent, of the Order of Friars Minor and a Parisian theologian, published at Paris in 1576, certainly fuller and more accurate than the first as a result of collation with an old manuscript; and finally a third issued by the editors of the Library of the Holy Fathers, reproduced from Feuardent’s edition itself. We confidently promise that we shall provide a fourth, more accurate edition than all of these. Three manuscript codices assisted us in this undertaking; against them we collated Feuardent’s edition. From these we introduced into the text the sounder readings, especially those confirmed by the common testimony of the codices, rejecting the printed readings; the remaining variants we recorded at the bottom of the page.

The codices we used are the following. The first [Col. 0054B], and the oldest of all, belongs to the monastery of the Shoemaker Friars of the Order of the Most Holy Trinity at Toledo, in whose archive it is preserved. It was written in the year 1067 by Salomon, archpriest of the holy Church of Toledo, under Paschal, its archbishop. When Father Flórez mentioned this prelate in volume V of *Sacred Spain*, he also, following Nicolás Antonio, supplied information about this codex. The second comes from the library of the holy Church of Toledo and was written, so far as we infer from its script, in the twelfth or thirteenth century. The third likewise comes from that library, but was brought from Gaul, where, at the command of Cardinal Amelius, it was copied in the fourteenth century from the most ancient codex of Gotescalch—and copied with the greatest accuracy. For it far surpasses the others in parchment, script, and more carefully corrected writing. Besides this book *On the Virginity of the Mother of God*, it contains the other works included in the edition of Feuardent already mentioned, namely, the little book *On the Childbearing of the Blessed Virgin* and several sermons. [Col. 0054C] But these will be treated in their proper place.

[Col. 0053]

# The One Book of Saint Hildefonsus, Bishop of Toledo, on the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary against Three Unbelievers (C)

## Here Begins the Prayer and Confession of Saint Hildefonsus

[Col. 0053D]

O God, true light, who enlighten every human being coming into this world. O God, who give wisdom [Col. 0054D] to the little ones and summon the foolish to walk along the way of prudence. O God, who make the clean from the unclean, and, taking away sins, [Note: [Col. 0053D]

“Justify the sinner without works.” This is how the Paris edition of Feuardent reads. He supplied from his own codex, as he did many other passages, the words “without works,” which were lacking in the printed edition. After more mature consideration of this passage, we too have decided to print them, not doubting that, if faith is to be placed in the manuscript codices, Saint Hildefonsus wrote in this way; for all those we have seen make this clear.

Indeed, in the codex of the convent of the Most Holy Trinity at Toledo, from the eleventh century, after this entire sentence had been erased from the middle of the parchment by some unskilled reader who seemed to think that it contained a doctrine alien to the Catholic faith, the margin of that parchment nevertheless bears the words—if not in the same hand, certainly in very similar Gothic script—written in a style characteristic of the period immediately following that century. In another, more recent codex of the holy Church of Toledo, the first parchment of this treatise has been cut away; we believe this was done deliberately and intentionally, especially since the remainder is complete and sound in every respect. Then, in the Amelian codex, which, as we noted above, was copied with the utmost care from a most ancient codex at the order of Cardinal Amelius, the words “without works” are clearly and plainly read. Finally, in the edition of this work prepared at Valencia de los Edetani in the sixteenth century by Friar Michael Carranza, the words are indeed absent, but their place is marked by an asterisk, indicating to readers—and showing that Carranza himself found the same lacuna in the manuscripts he used in preparing the work—that the gap was present there as well.

An unworthy deed! Yet no one will cease to wonder at it once he turns his mind to the earlier centuries. Perhaps it was committed by people more religious than learned, lest some ill-disposed person seize upon it as an opportunity to fabricate an error, twisting those words into a bad sense, as though Hildefonsus had said that people can be justified by faith alone, without any other disposition or good work—a proposition that later became one of the articles of Calvinist heresy. But although such concealment might be excused in Carranza’s time and in the times of others, we certainly do not now see why we should dissemble; rather, we ought openly to honor the truth, especially since no one versed in theological study can fail to see at first glance that Hildefonsus’s words can and must be understood in a Catholic and sound sense.

For the justification of the sinner—whether we consider its beginning, when God starts to soften and prepare the human heart through his actual graces, or the justification itself, as it is completed through the infusion of sanctifying grace—is always entirely gracious, and therefore does not arise from human works; otherwise, as the Apostle says (Romans 11), grace would no longer be grace. In this sense, therefore, we must interpret Hildefonsus’s statement.

Indeed, if it is understood of the beginning of justification, the phrase “without works” excludes every work of the human being, whether natural or supernatural. It would then have been spoken against Pelagius, who attributed so much to the natural powers of free will that he asserted that a person could merit the first grace by his own natural merits. If, however, it is explained of perfect justification, we shall say that he spoke in the sense in which the Apostle speaks (Romans 3): “Being justified freely by his grace.” And (Titus 3): “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us.” Do you see how, according to the Apostle, we are justified freely and not by works?

What, then? Must no work of ours, no act of faith, no act of hope, no repentance or detestation of sins precede our justification? Certainly not. What, then, does it mean when we are said to attain righteousness freely, without works? Hear the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 8: “We are said to be justified freely by God because none of those things that precede justification—whether faith or works—merits the grace of justification itself.”

Saint Thomas had earlier interpreted Paul’s words in the same sense in his exposition of that Epistle. “First,” writes the Angelic Doctor, “he shows that this kind of justification is without the law; that is, it does not arise from the works of the law. When he says ‘justified freely,’ that is, without the merit of preceding works.”

Isaiah 52: “You were sold without price, and you shall be redeemed without money.” In the same sense those words of Psalm 55 (verse 8) are to be understood: “You will save them for nothing”—that is, not through their own merit, but through God’s clemency, as Saint Jerome explains (*Dialogue 2 against the Pelagians*, toward the end).

We omit countless other testimonies of the holy Fathers supporting this view, especially those of Saint Augustine; for we are not intending to write a dissertation, but only, by the examples of others, to rescue our Hildefonsus from the suspicion that this manner of speaking may have created among the unlearned and inexperienced. From all this readers will understand that we have retained this reading for no slight reasons. We considered it wicked to reject it against the testimony of all the manuscript codices.]

You justify the sinner without works: give me light by which I may see you; give me wisdom, so that I may understand you; grant forgiveness for my iniquities, so that I may obtain your mercy. For this reason, Lord, I am conquered by love, driven by sweetness, drawn by affection, so that, as though beneath the press of sweetness, I may pour out the wine of sacred confession. And because there is no substance of good works, let there be the fruit of good confessions.

For the bonds and pressures of sins, their weight and dangers, their destruction and losses, oppress the soul devoted to iniquity; and because there is no other name given under heaven by which I can be saved except yours, Christ Jesus, Son of the living God, therefore I seek the refuge of confession, I ask for a remedy from confession, I implore assistance from the love of confession, so that I, an impious man, may love you with abundant devotion, since your mercy has washed away my abundant iniquity.

Let the heavens, then, attend, and all that is in them; let the earth attend, and all that is upon it; let the sea attend, and all that moves in it. And let them hear me, believing with devout confession that you are Christ Jesus, the Son of the living God, who came into this world not to judge me but to save me, so that, believing in your holy name, I may have eternal life.

And thus, found to be a confessor with all creatures as witnesses, may I confess you in heaven, whom I am not ashamed to confess on earth. And may you yourself rescue me from the filth of sins and from the assaults of every adversity. You whose faith my confession vindicates against the contradictions of unbelievers, stand by as my vindicator.

Hear me, then, together with the authorities of antiquity: O Moses, speaking of things more ancient; together with the prophets: Isaiah, prophesying things more powerful; together with the evangelists: Matthew, proclaiming the first things; together with the apostles: chosen Peter, preaching illustrious things; and within the whole Church of God, the throng of blessed teachers speaking what is true and expounding what brings salvation.

Hear that I certainly believe these things which you intend to preach as things to be believed; that I devoutly confess these things which you yourselves truly confess; that I myself proclaim these things which you teach must be proclaimed. Hear that I am able to give true obedience to those whom, with all my strength, you decree that the whole Church of God should obey.

Therefore, because I have believed, I shall speak; because I have heard, I shall not be silent; because I love, I shall proclaim. In everything I put forward, I suggest nothing through contention or empty glory; I establish nothing against holy truth; I seek nothing that would overthrow the truth, but only what may discover or disclose it.

[Note: [Col. 0055D] We have restored the true reading of this sentence from our manuscript codices, the Trinity codex and the Amelian codex. In Feuardent’s printed edition it read as follows: “But if … the intention of the writer, while treating the matter, should by some chance, or through the unskilled effort of the scribe, have led me, wandering and dull, there, where otherwise … the example of those who truly teach would have shone forth,” etc.]

But if—may the abundant mercy of divine compassion avert it—the intention of the writer, wandering and lacking discernment, should have led me there, through some chance occurrence or through the unskilled effort of a scribe, where the true light of sound knowledge and the true example of those who teach would have shone forth otherwise, I gratefully obey, I devoutly assent, I hasten to meet it.

Let me have nothing profane in my confession; let me hold nothing alien to devotion, which is God; let me harbor in the deepest recesses of my heart nothing that attacks the one sacred faith; absolutely nothing that conflicts with divine things, resists the holy sacraments, or opposes the sacred mysteries.

Therefore, let my superior not despise me; let my equal not disparage me; let my subordinate not insult me; let no one from the household challenge me; let no one from the marketplace slander me; let no religious person whisper against me; let no common person murmur; let no old man reject the young; let no young man scorn his contemporary; let advanced age not mock one younger in years; let the learned not reproach me; let the ignorant not cast me aside; let the more powerful not repel me; let the humbler not turn away; let the disciple not trouble me; let the servant not ridicule me; let age not accuse me; let sex not offer an excuse.

For truth remains forever. What is true lives. What proceeds from truth does not cease. Truth does not fall before falsehood. Truth is not conquered by deceptions. What is true is not changed into falsehood.

And if truth is covered by the shadows of deceit, hidden truth will reveal what is true. For what is false will not stand; what is true will not fail; what is outside the truth will be empty; what is far from the truth will fade away, because truth is God, and the things that belong to God are true, and only the things that are from God subsist through truth.

Therefore, whoever proclaims the Lord recounts the truth. Whoever speaks true things about God unfolds the knowledge of truth. Whoever asserts what is true defends the rights of truth. Whoever embraces truth loves the Lord. Whoever practices truth fulfills God’s will.

Certainly God knows hidden things; God recognizes what is concealed; God penetrates what lies hidden; God searches out secrets. Therefore he knows the one who corrupts what is true, he knows the one who changes truth, he understands the one who diminishes truth, and he plainly perceives the one who extinguishes truth.

He will come—indeed, he will come, and he is not far away. He will come from nearby; he will come from close at hand. But when he blazes forth suddenly, when he comes in majesty, when a mighty storm surrounds him, when fire goes before him, then blessed are all who truly love him; blessed are those who speak true things about him; blessed are those who do not despise the truth; blessed are those who practice justice in truth; blessed are those who preserve judgment in truth; and blessed are all who trust in him.

For the Judge will come; stern, he will confront us; feared, he will be present; terrifying, he will appear.

Let everything, therefore, look ahead, let everything attend, let everything consider that I seek nothing but the truth with my whole heart, with my whole soul, with my whole strength, with the deepest part of my heart, with all my inward being; with what I know, what I recount, and what I understand, that I seek nothing more than divine truth; that I claim nothing other than God and the things of God; that I resist only God’s adversaries; that I stand opposed only to profaners and every profanation; that, for the love of truth, I oppose only those who contradict the truth.

I do these things so that, when this life—which is a trial upon the earth—has wearied the sick person, that truth which is God may shelter the one who is to be saved and possess him, living, forever and ever. Amen.

# Chapter One

By a torrent of synonyms, he demonstrates against Jovinianus that the most blessed Mother of God remained a virgin in conception and childbirth by God’s gift and singular grace.

O my Lady, [Note: [Col. 0057D] Feuardent’s printed edition reads “and my sovereign lady.”] my sovereign lady, ruling over me, mother of my Lord, handmaid of your Son, mother of the Maker of the world: I ask you, I entreat you, I beg you, let me have the spirit of your Lord, let me have the spirit of your Son, let me have the spirit of my Redeemer, so that I may think true and worthy things about you, [Col. 0058B] speak true and worthy things about you, [Note: [Col. 0057D] Thus all our manuscript codices; Feuardent has “true and worthy” here and immediately afterward.] say about you whatever things ought to be said.

You [Note: [Col. 0057D] “For you are” is absent from the Trinity codex.] have been chosen by God, taken up by God, appointed advocate by God, near to God, clinging to God, joined to God; visited by the angel (Luke 1), greeted by the angel, blessed by the angel, called blessed by the angel; troubled in speech, astonished in thought, amazed at the greeting, marveling at the announcement of the words. [Note: [Col. 0057D] Thus all our codices; Feuardent has “at the Annunciation.”]

You hear that you have found grace with God, [Note: [Col. 0057D] “And” is absent from the Trinity and Amelian codices.] and you are commanded not to fear; you are strengthened by confidence; you are instructed by knowledge of miracles; you are raised up to the unheard-of novelty of glory.

Concerning the offspring, [Note: [Col. 0057D] Neither of these codices has “by the angel.”] you are warned by the angel about your chastity; concerning the name of the offspring, you are assured of your virginity; [Note: [Col. 0057D] The words that follow, to the end of the sentence, are likewise absent from both codices.] and after childbirth you remain whole and chaste. The angel announces to you that the holy one who will be born from you is to be called the Son of God, [Note: [Col. 0058D] Both codices read: “he is said to be called the Son of God, and what the power of the one being born is,” etc.] and wonderfully makes known what power the king who is being born possesses.

You ask how it will happen; you inquire about its origin; [Note: [Col. 0058D] The Trinity codex reads: “about the manner of the origin.”] you investigate its manner; you ask about its experience; you inquire about its order. Hear an unheard-of oracle; consider an unaccustomed work; observe an unknown mystery; attend to an unprecedented deed.

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). The whole Trinity will invisibly bring about conception in you. Only the person of the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0058D] Feuardent has “in your body,” which is absent from the Trinity and Amelian codices.] will assume flesh from you, to be born in your body. [Note: [Col. 0058D] All our codices and Feuardent read “in you”; the variant is “from you.”]

Therefore, what will be conceived in you, what will be born from you, what will come forth from you, what will be generated from you, what will be brought forth from you as a holy child will be called the Son of God. For [Note: [Col. 0058D] The Trinity and Amelian codices omit “for.”] this one will be great; this one will be the God of hosts; this one will be king of all ages; this one will be the Maker of all things.

Behold, blessed are you among women, whole among women in childbirth, mistress among handmaids, queen among sisters. Behold, from this time onward all generations will call you blessed. [Note: [Col. 0058D] The Trinity codex has “the nations.”] All the heavenly powers have known you as blessed. [Note: [Col. 0058D] Our codices do not have “you” or “all.”] All prophets proclaim you blessed; all nations celebrate you as blessed.

Blessed are you to my faith; blessed are you to my soul; blessed are you to my love; [Note: [Col. 0059C] We have restored “my” here, repeated three times, from all our codices, in place of “our,” which Feuardent printed from his own codex.] blessed are you in my praises and proclamations. I shall proclaim you for as long as you are to be proclaimed; I shall love you for as long as you are to be loved; I shall praise you for as long as you are worthy of praise; I shall serve you for as long as service is owed to your glory.

[Note: [Col. 0059D] Our manuscript codices present this passage in the following form, very different from Feuardent’s edition: “You, conceiving God alone, were finally made the bride of the Son of God. You, giving birth at once to God and human being, were made the mother of the Son of God. In receiving him, God is only your guest; in conceiving him from yourself, God was made at once an inhabitant and a human being.” Immediately afterward it continues: “Trusting the angel’s promises, you were therefore made fruitful by the gift of the Holy Spirit. You gave birth to the emperor’s Son, whom the angels adore as God in heaven. Without the partnership of a man you brought forth the Son of God, and after childbirth you remained undefiled.”

We, however, omitted all these passages, relying on the unanimous testimony of all our codices, in which they are absent. Nor do we doubt that, if they are read attentively and compared with the rest, anyone will notice that they differ from Hildefonsus’s style and are additions by another hand.]

You, receiving God alone, are the last for God the Son [the transmitted phrase *postrema Filio Deo* is elliptical and uncertain]. You, generating God and human being together, are the first for the human Son. For him, in receiving whom God is merely your guest; for him, in conceiving whom the human being is at once an inhabitant and God.

In the past, clean for God; in the present, full of human being and God; in the future, generating human being and God; [Note: [Col. 0059D] Feuardent published the following: “Remaining joyful from offspring and virginity, you rejoiced in the honor of a parent from child and modesty.” [Col. 0060C] We followed the testimony of all our codices.] joyful in childbirth and virginity, rejoicing in offspring and modesty, faithful to Son and Bridegroom.

You preserved faith with the Son so faithfully that not even he himself knew the father of his flesh. You preserved faith with the Bridegroom so faithfully that he himself knew you as mother without a man.

So much glorying in the Son as you were ignorant of the touch of every man; [Note: [Col. 0060D] Feuardent has “finally instructed.”] instructed in what you knew, taught in what you believed, assured of what you hoped for, strengthened in what you held without loss.

[Note: [Col. 0060D] This reading of our codices is better than Feuardent’s: “Hear, you; perceive, you.” We excluded “and you” on the authority of the Trinity codex.]

By hearing, understand, Jovinianus; gain wisdom in your heart, fool; recognize in your inmost being, stupid man; learn through understanding, fickle man.

I do not want you to claim that our Virgin’s modesty was corrupted by childbirth; I do not want you to tear apart her integrity by generation [Note: [Col. 0060D] Thus the Amelian and Trinity codices; Feuardent reads “take away.”]; I do not want you to split her virginity through the exit of the one being born [Note: [Col. 0060D] Feuardent reads “through the going forth.”]. I do not want you to deprive the virgin of the duty of motherhood; I do not want you to take away from the mother the fullness of virginal glory.

If you confuse one of these things, you are confused in all. If you do not understand this harmony [Note: [Col. 0060D] The Trinity codex reads “harmony” without the preposition.], you yourself have been deprived of the harmony of truth. If you argue for this discord, you will always be found discordant with justice.

If you take away from our Virgin either generation or integrity, you do God a grave injury through great disgrace. For you deny that the one whom you admit could approach a virgin without corruption was able to preserve her incorrupt. You deny that the divinity of the Almighty could do what it wished, when you insist [Note: [Col. 0060D] Thus all the codices, and the older edition; Feuardent altered it from his codex.] that he found his mother intact but left her devoted to corruption.

Thus, according to your assertion, the divinity of the Almighty did not benefit virginity but harmed it; for, by violating the glory of virginity through birth, it destroyed [Note: [Col. 0060D] All our codices read “detracted from.”] the fullness of virginity. And thereby you assert that the very one whom he had adorned by creating he disfigured by being born.

[Col. 0060A] [Note: [Col. 0060D] All our codices read this way. Feuardent differs only slightly: “Let the mouth be silenced … let the heart grow dull; let the tongue cling to the throat,” etc.]

May the heart that meditates such things grow dull—yes, grow dull; may the mouth that speaks such things be silenced; may the tongue that utters such things cling to the throat; may speech that narrates such things not arise.

For behold: a virgin from God, a virgin from a human being; a virgin with the angel bearing witness (Matthew 1); a virgin with the bridegroom as judge; a virgin before the bridegroom, a virgin with the bridegroom; an undoubted virgin, even while the bridegroom doubted.

A virgin before the Son’s coming; a virgin after the Son’s generation; a virgin with the Son’s birth; a virgin after the Son had been born. Fruitful through the Word, filled through the Word, most abundantly endowed through the Word, worthy through the Word of giving birth; human in birth, human in law, human in custom, human in condition, human in reality—but truly unharmed, incorrupt, inviolate, undefiled, wholly intact.

But by divine gift, divine favor, divine bestowal, divine contrivance, divine gift, divine concession; through a new work, a new efficacy, a new operation, a new effect, a new accomplishment; [Note: [Col. 0060D] Thus Feuardent; our codices and the ancient edition read “childbirth.”] a virgin with conception, a virgin through conception, a virgin in conception, a virgin after conception; [Note: [Col. 0060D] Our codices read this way. Feuardent has “in childbirth.”] a virgin through childbirth, a virgin with childbirth, a virgin after childbirth.

A virgin with the one who was to be born, a virgin with the one being born, a virgin after the Son had been born. Called a wife and a virgin, taken as a wife and a virgin, believed to be a wife and a virgin; together with husband [Note: [Col. 0060D] Some witnesses read “marriage.”] and offspring, an everlasting virgin.

Always unknown to marital union, unknown to embrace, unknown to touch, unknown to marital fellowship. And then certainly, then without doubt, then truly, then veritably a holy virgin, a blessed virgin, a glorious virgin, an honorable virgin.

But after the generation of the incarnate Word, after the birth of God made human, after the generation of the human being assumed into God, after the birth of the human being united to God, [Note: [Col. 0060D] The Amelian codex has “in God.”] a holier and most holy virgin, a more blessed and most blessed virgin, a more glorious and most glorious virgin, a nobler and most noble virgin, a more honorable and most honorable virgin, a more august and most august virgin.

But so that you may not remain alone entangled in the thorns of your madness, so that you may not alone be hedged in by the thorns of your folly, so that you may not alone be confined by the briars of your stupidity, so that you may not alone be pierced by the goads of your understanding, so that you may not alone be destroyed by the sharpness of your defense, [Note: [Col. 0060D] The Amelian codex has “I shall compare.”] I shall connect one equal to you, match one like you, join one similar, bind one your equal, unite one of the same kind.

# Chapter Two

He confirms the virginity of the Mother of God against Helvidius.

[Col. 0061A]

Hear, then, you too, Helvidius; attend to me, shameless man; listen to me, immodest man; look at me, indecent man; observe me, shameless man. [Note: [Col. 0061D] The Amelian codex reads “unchastity” in place of “shameless man.”]

Why are you, immodest man, agitated? Why do you, shameless man, stand before me? Why do you, indecent man, approach? Why do you come forward without reverence? Why are you troubled without shame?

Why do you confine the beginnings of our Virgin with an end in corruption? Why do you disgrace the beginnings of modesty by the outcome of enlarged procreation [Note: [Col. 0061D] Other witnesses read “of completed procreation.”]? Why do you disfigure with human union [Note: [Col. 0061D] All our codices read thus; Feuardent has “connection.”] the integrity sanctified by divinity [Note: [Col. 0061D] The Trinity codex reads “sacred.”]? [Note: [Col. 0061D] The Toledo codex reads: “I do not want you to violate the right of majesty.”]

I do not want you to violate the power of this majesty, lest with rash boldness [Note: [Col. 0061D] Thus the Amelian codex; Feuardent reads “you dare.”] you attempt to assail God’s possession; lest you harm [Note: [Col. 0061D] Thus all our codices; Feuardent reads “you dare presumptuously to despise.”] the dwelling of divinity through the presumption of contempt; lest you pierce the house of the Lord with the injuries of corruption; lest you contend that the gate of God’s house, closed at his departure [Note: [Col. 0061D] Feuardent reads “closed in his departure”; all our codices lack “in.”], could be entered by anyone at all. [Note: [Col. 0061D] The Amelian codex reads this way; Feuardent has “lest you dare to despise the dwelling of divinity through presumptuous contempt.”]

The God of hosts is lord of this possession. The King of heaven is possessor of this right. The Almighty is the builder of this structure. He alone is the one who exits and [Note: [Col. 0061D] “And” is absent in the Amelian codex.] the guardian of this gate of departure. No one entered with him; no one departed [Note: [Col. 0061D] All our codices read “returned.”]. In entering it he had no companion; in departing he had no associate.

No one knows how he entered; only his departure knows how he left. [Note: [Col. 0061D] The Amelian codex has “how he departed.”] God enters, so to speak, without clothing; yet, to speak precisely, he departs clothed in flesh. He came to the house of his own workmanship and bore only the garment of flesh. The same one who had come returned, but in a different manner from that in which he had entered; [Note: [Col. 0061D] “He himself proceeds” is found in our codices.] he himself came forth from it.

[Col. 0061C] Entering this house, he did not carry away the spoils of modesty; rather, on departing, he endowed it with integrity. [Note: [Col. 0061D] All our codices and Feuardent have “endowed”; the ancient edition has “enriched it with integrity.”]

It had indeed been cleansed by the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0061D] All our codices, together with the old edition. Feuardent has “founded.”] but it was not yet full through the Lord’s arrival. When the angel announced it, it recognized the arrival of its founder and marveled at the approach of a new encounter; it recognized that an inhabitant was within it, but did not fully penetrate how he was acting in secret.

Nevertheless, it prepared the powers of its soul for the duties of service and rendered to the Lord the rights of its condition that were owed. [Note: [Col. 0061D] Thus the Amelian codex, agreeing with the old edition. The others, with Feuardent, have “the rights owed.”]

What he, presiding in heaven, had commanded, it ministered within itself after receiving him, [Note: [Col. 0062D] All Feuardent’s codices have “it proves.”] proving that it had prepared for its Creator clean flesh together with a clean soul; these offered spiritual service to the Son in the flesh and clothed the Lord with the incorruptible [Col. 0062A] and unchangeable reality of his flesh.

When the appointed time came, it perceived that the one who had entered was departing; and, joyful in the peaceful progress of his departure, it saw him proceeding in a manner different from that in which it had known him approaching. It saw him clothed in the reality of his flesh, yet did not perceive that the integrity of its own brightness and modesty had been diminished within it; rather, it recognized that they had increased. [Note: [Col. 0062D] “It recognizes” is absent from the Amelian and Toledo codices.]

In this realm, solitude belongs only to God and the house; in this dwelling, singularity belongs only to the lodging and the guest. This place is joined to only one who approaches. This womb rejoices in the knowledge of only one, and knows the limbs of no other man than the one who alone was born.

Since, then, the Spirit of God foretold these things through the prophets, confirmed them through the teachers, defended them through the champions of truth [Note: [Col. 0062D] Toletanus reads “assertors”], and consolidated them through the eternity of the ages [Col. 0062B], what do you, deviser of a novel error [Note: [Col. 0062D] Amelianus reads “most notorious.” We, however, judge that this whole passage—on a collation of all the manuscripts (which do not sufficiently agree among themselves)—should be emended as follows: “What, most foolish slanderer of the glorious Virgin, do you defame so copiously with trifling nonsense? What mass of infamy do you dare to utter?” etc.], what do you, most foolish slanderer, what do you, lavishly, with trifling nonsense, defame her? What mass of madness [Note: [Col. 0062D] Toletanus writes “mass,” in the accusative (massam); the others, “massa.”] do you dare to utter, persist in muttering, propose in whispers, and presume to chatter, so that the habitation of God in the virginal womb, that most splendid hall of the King of virtues in the brilliance of its modesty [Note: [Col. 0062D] Trinity, Toletanus, and others read “that” (illo)], that chaste-fleshed dwelling of the Emperor of heavenly beings, that glorious place of the God whom the whole variety of places cannot contain, after God’s generation, after the incarnation of the Word, after the Lord’s birth, after the Savior’s coming forth, should produce from a fleshly man offspring of flesh destined to perish; should bring forth from a life-giving place mortal members from the seed of mortality; should bear from the enclosed garden, which produced only the flower of an extraordinary virginity, the thorns and briars of marriage [Note: [Col. 0062D] Amelianus reads “mortal,” rather than “marital”]? [Col. 0062C] From the spring marked by the virginal emergence of the one being born, should marital mire flow forth?

I wish, I wish that pain would torment the tomb of his mouth; that a bar would close his teeth [Note: [Col. 0062D] Amelianus and Toletanus have: “That pain should torment the tomb of his mouth and a bar close his teeth”]; that the immobility of his tongue would complete the pit of his mouth [Note: [Col. 0062D] Both have “thoroughly complete”]; that withdrawn air would empty the hollows of his palate; that the thickness of the air would glue together the edges of his lips—so that the stench of such words might not burst forth, so that the odor of this discourse might not waft out, so that the breath of his speech might not whisper, so that not even the faintest sound might ring, and so that struck air might not shape the most unspeakable words [Note: [Col. 0062D] All our manuscripts and Feuardent have “childish”].

For behold: in an extraordinary manner, by an extraordinary practice, in an extraordinary order, under an extraordinary law, in one person, in one body, in one condition, in one age, the honor of mother and virgin alternates; the modesty of virgin and mother alternates [Col. 0063A]; in the one giving birth, virginity alternates; in the virgin, the capacity for giving birth alternates. Neither yields to either, and each passes into the other; neither is hindered by the other, and both hasten toward one another [Note: [Col. 0063D] Amelianus reads “prosper”].

Each is preserved in its own proper state, and each passes into the other, because both are one; because the two are the same; because what is different is nevertheless identical; because what occurs is undivided; because what comes together is undiscriminated; because what supervenes is undifferentiated [Note: [Col. 0063D] We print this passage as it appears in all our manuscripts. Feuardent has a different form: “The maternal birth does not hinder the virgin, nor does the child violate the virgin; virginal modesty ennobles the mother; the child ennobles the virgin, and virginal modesty does not violate the mother.”]

The dignity of virginity does not abandon the mother; maternal birth does not hinder the virgin; the child ennobles the virgin, and virginal modesty belongs to the mother. Thus the names “mother” and “virgin” are not separated by any case, obstructed by any difficulty, harmed by any outcome, or rendered doubtful by any circumstance. Both are undivided, both inseparable; the whole is undissected, the whole indivisible. [Col. 0063B]

It happened at a certain point that she who was a virgin became a mother [Note: [Col. 0063D] All our manuscripts read “there came” (accessit)]. The time came for her to give birth, although she remained nowhere corrupted by marital intercourse [Note: [Col. 0063D] Toletanus and Amelianus read “remains”]. She was present to give birth, while the law of childbirth was unknown to her. It occurred that she should be unimpaired in her son, she who had not been diminished by a husband [Note: [Col. 0063D] Thus Amelianus and Toletanus; Feuardent and the others have the barbarous form existerat].

But this is immeasurable, incomprehensible, unspeakable, marvelous, unheard of, unseen, unknown [Note: [Col. 0063D] We have supplied “unknown” from Amelianus and Toletanus; it is absent in the others], and unprecedented: that virginity should become radiant through conception; that virginity should accompany childbirth; that birth should designate a virgin; that virginity should prove a mother; that virginity should also glorify the mother; that the gravity of motherhood should honor the virgin [Note: [Col. 0063D] Toletanus and the ancient edition read “adorn”]; that virginity should attain maternal dignity; that the dignity of virginity should be preserved by the mother’s fertility.

Thus the virgin receives the reality of motherhood. [Col. 0063C] Thus the glory of the virgin passes into the mother. Thus the name of mother comes to the virgin [Note: [Col. 0063D] All our manuscripts read “comes to the virgin.” Toletanus continues: “Thus virginal modesty remains in the mother”]; thus the virgin’s modesty remains in the mother.

So it happened, so it came to pass [Note: [Col. 0064D] Thus Trinity and Toletanus; others, with Feuardent, read “came”], so it was present, so it appeared, that if I seek a mother, she is a virgin; if I seek a virgin, she is a mother; if I seek offspring, it belongs to a virgin; if I seek modesty, it belongs altogether to a mother.

O God of all virtues! O God of all creatures! O God, maker of all things! O God, author of all wonders! You who, through all your miracles, all your signs, all your marvels, all your great deeds [Note: [Col. 0064D] All our manuscripts and Feuardent read “great works”], opening the treasures of mercy, displaying the secrets of compassion, unlocking the riches of indulgence, and pouring out streams of clemency for my salvation and the world’s, for my redemption and the world’s, for my justification and the world’s [Col. 0063D], for my liberation and the world’s [Col. 0064A], made this deed, this work, this achievement, this act marvelous without any rational account of its manner; performed it uniquely without any example of the thing itself; formed it with power without any likeness for comparison; completed it as life-giving without any comparable parallel; fashioned it immeasurably without any conceptual explanation; made it everlasting without forgetfulness, firm without defect, perpetual without interruption, and praiseworthy without end.

Through it error was removed; through it sickness was taken away; through it sin was erased; through it death was truly destroyed; through it salvation was bestowed; through it life was granted; through it heaven was opened; through it the kingdom of heaven was promised; through it we found the way to go; through it we attain the truth of arriving; through it we obtain the life of rest; through it we shall possess the everlasting vision of your sweetness [Note: [Col. 0064D] All our manuscripts, together with the old edition and Feuardent, read “we have”].

But now already, just now [Col. 0064B], here, in this place, in this condition, at this instant, and in this time, and throughout all ages of ages forever [Note: [Col. 0064D] Feuardent does not have “just now,” but it is absent from none of our manuscripts. “Forever” is found in Amelianus and Toletanus and is absent from the others].

## CHAPTER III. Saint Mary is by nation and lineage Jewish, but by faith, honor, praise, and love Christian. Finally, he proves through the oracles of several prophets that supreme virginity ought to be joined with the glory of motherhood.

What do you say, Jew [Note: [Col. 0064D] Feuardent reads “O Jew,” unlike our manuscripts]? What do you propose? What do you assert? What do you allege? What do you object [Note: [Col. 0064D] Amelianus and Toletanus read “delight in”]? Behold, our virgin is from your stock; she is from your lineage [Note: [Col. 0064D] Feuardent has “from your race,” and below “from your people,” contrary to the agreement of all our manuscripts]; she is from your root, from your nation, from your people, from your populace, from your nation, from your origin.

Yet she is from our faith, from our belief, from our assent, from our reverence, from our honoring [Col. 0064C], from our praise, from our glorification, from our affection, from our love, from our proclamation, from our acclaim, from our defense, and from our vindication.

For what the Holy Spirit said about her through the prophets [Note: [Col. 0064D] All our manuscripts and Feuardent read “foretold”], what he disclosed through oracles, made known through figures, promised through what preceded, and fulfilled through what followed—you denying, you refusing to believe, you rejecting, you repudiating, you resisting, you blaspheming—I know, I have believed, I understand, I venerate, I honor, I glorify, I embrace, I love, I cherish, I proclaim.

For grace went before me, faith filled me, mercy followed, love advanced me, and the glory of this matter exalted me.

But you, whom treachery turned aside, whom depravity seized, whom blindness visited [Col. 0064D], whom error possessed, whom obstinacy hardened [Col. 0065A], tell me: why do you not believe that a virgin gave birth among your own people? Why do you not believe that a virgin conceived without a man? Why do you not believe that a virgin carried her own son? Why do you not believe that a virgin remained a virgin after childbirth [Note: [Col. 0065D] “Without a man” is absent in Toletanus and Trinity]?

Or, smeared with that kind of falsehood, bloated with the poison of primordial treachery, relying on that argument of ancestral deceit, twisted by the craft of faithless persecution [Note: [Col. 0065D] Toletanus and Trinity read “of the prosecution”], and made exceedingly firm by that stronghold of ancient obstinacy, do you argue from the sacred Scriptures that a young woman, and not a virgin, could give birth?

You plainly lie [Note: [Col. 0065D] Thus all our manuscripts and Feuardent: “You are deceitful”]; you deceive and are deceived; you accuse falsely, attack falsely, propose falsely, contend falsely, argue falsely, and defend falsely.

For if, as you say, a young woman and not a virgin could give birth, what sign would the Lord give (Isaiah 7)? [Note: [Col. 0065D] We print this according to the unanimous testimony of our manuscripts. Feuardent has a different form: “What sign, as he promised, would the Lord give? What miracle would he perform?”] What miracle would he give? What marvelous thing would he demonstrate? What unprecedented thing would he show, if a young woman gave birth to what was customary; if a girl gave birth to what belonged to her age [Col. 0065B]; if a youthful woman gave birth to what belonged to youthful tenderness; if a woman not unequal to marriage gave birth to what belonged simultaneously to nature and time?

For whose greatest concern sometimes remains anxiously occupied with the choice of betrothed [Note: [Col. 0065D] Feuardent has “with the delay of the betrothed”; all our manuscripts read as we print]? Whose mind is extremely anxious in expectation of a future union? Whose vows, according to the experience of companions [Note: [Col. 0065D] Toletanus and Amelianus read “according to the experience of associates,” are not uncertain?

But it would truly be a sign if a virgin gave birth and remained intact. It would bring about novelty if a virgin gave birth [Note: [Col. 0065D] Feuardent inserts here: “And remained intact. It would bring about novelty if a virgin gave birth, etc.”], and shone with modesty. It would be worthy of admiration if a virgin gave birth and remained uncorrupted. A miracle would be shown if, in human conception, something occurred that human nature did not know. A sign would be given if, married to no man, a virgin became a mother [Col. 0065C] [Note: [Col. 0066D] All our manuscripts read “to no one”]. The event would become astonishing if a woman served simultaneously in both virginal and maternal offices. The wonder of the deed would be greatly increased if one woman at one time rejoiced in the rewards both of modesty and of offspring [Note: [Col. 0066D] Amelianus reads “in the deed”; Toletanus and Amelianus have a better reading than Feuardent’s “having been accomplished”].

Thus, so that you may know that this woman conceived as a sign, not in the ordinary way; that she became fruitful in wonder, not in intercourse; that she gave birth in the novelty of a miracle, not in the antiquity of marriage; that she was made fruitful in virginal incorruption, not in a marital covenant: she is the mother of God, but because of the incarnation of the Word; she is the parent of God, but because of the assumption of humanity; she is the attendant of God, but because he himself was subject to his parents [Note: [Col. 0066D] “Because of the ministry of humanity,” and so forth, Trinity]; she is the nurse of God, because kings will be his fosterers and queens his nurses (Isaiah 49) [Note: [Col. 0066D] “Because the kings who nourish him, and queens, will be nurses,” Trinity and Toletanus].

Since this son of hers is God and man, Word and flesh (John 1), divinity and humanity, he is peace for us and a stumbling-block for you; wisdom for us and foolishness for the nations (1 Corinthians 1). Therefore human things are rightly referred to God, and the things of God are referred to man. Therefore the insubstantial things of man are strengthened by participation in God [Note: [Col. 0066D] Amelianus reads “by participation”], and the substantial things of God are said to be weakened by participation in man. Therefore the highest reaches the lowest, and the lowest touches the highest; therefore the insubstantial is made solid by what is solid; therefore the extraordinary is tempered by the ordinary, and the extraordinary is exalted through the extraordinary.

So that you may not doubt that these things are true, hear the words of the Holy Spirit; hear the oracles of the prophets; hear the sayings of those who prophesied [Note: [Col. 0066D] All our manuscripts with the ancient Vulgate; Feuardent reads “the predictions”]; hear the proclamations of truth.

Isaiah says: “A child is born to us; a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9). The same Christ is a child, because he was born as man not for himself but for us; “a son is given to us,” because God the Son gave himself to be incarnate for us. And behold, he is man in that the child was born to us; but he is God, the one who was given to us as the Son of God.

Likewise David: “You made him a little lower than God” (Psalm 8). He who is said to have been made lower than God is certainly equal to God. For in that he is said to have been made lower, he is truly the humble-born man.

In the Psalms the Father speaks of him, because he is God: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109) [Note: [Col. 0066D] “Of the Son,” Trinity]. Because he is man, elsewhere it is said: “Like dew from the womb, your youth will come forth” [Note: [Col. 0066D] All our manuscripts and Feuardent read “comes forth”]. Elsewhere again: “A man was made in Zion, and he himself, the Most High, founded her” (Psalm 86). In that he was made, he was born a most humble man. In that he founded her, he is God Most High.

You will indeed be able to find many other passages—truly numerous, wholly sufficient, certainly abundant, fully overflowing—concerning the two natures joined in the union of this Christ, provided that you believe in him [Note: [Col. 0066D] Trinity reads “only if”], remain faithful to him, offer him true faith, confess him in truth, and offer him a true confession. Yet I myself, omitting nothing entirely, will weave some of these together a little later.

Since, then, the Son possesses such great glory and dignity that he is God in the assumed man, hear of what glory and nobility his mother is. In Isaiah, she is the rod that will come forth from the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11), that is, arising from his lineage [Note: [Col. 0066D] Toletanus reads “virgin”]; a rod that produced this flower, Christ, through spiritual infusion alone, without the addition of human corruption.

Again in Isaiah, she alone was the earth that, opened by faith, not by corruption, could bring forth the Savior, while the heavens dropped dew and the clouds rained down the Just One (Isaiah 45), that is, while the prophets proclaimed his coming.

In Ezekiel she is the house of God, whose utterly pure gates of modesty, standing toward the East, are always closed (Ezekiel 44) [Note: [Col. 0067D] Feuardent has “are toward the East”; “are” is absent from all our manuscripts]. She knew neither before the birth nor after the birth of this son any approach or passage of another, because the Lord alone passed through her by being born. Hence she is always closed, because she is always a virgin.

This virgin is God’s bridal chamber in the Psalm, because from her womb this incarnate God came forth like a bridegroom, leaving in her the beauty of perpetual virginity to remain [Note: [Col. 0067D] Feuardent’s edition adds “and destined to remain”; ours, as do all our manuscripts, read simply “to remain”] (Psalm 18).

Again in the Psalms she is the earth from which truth springs forth—and that same truth is Christ—and from which his righteousness looked down from heaven [Note: [Col. 0067D] Amelianus and the old edition read “God,” rather than “his”] (Psalm 84).

Again in the Psalms: “This earth has yielded its fruit” [Col. 0067B], that is, it bore our Christ, in whom our God, the same Lord God [Note: [Col. 0067D] Thus all our manuscripts and Feuardent: “that is, God, our God”], also blessed us, so that God might bless us and we might be blessed by God, the name being repeated three times. [Note: [Col. 0067D] “Which Trinity,” Trinity and Amelianus.] Let all the ends of the earth fear him as one God in the Trinity (Psalm 66).

## CHAPTER IV. He exhorts the Jew not to diminish the glory of the virgin and mother, whose disgrace redounds upon her offspring. He also shows that all the heavenly powers adore the Virgin and that all peoples flock to her, while incidentally demonstrating that the Jews’ faithlessness was divinely foretold by the ancient Fathers.

Let it now, I beg, let it now be most pleasing to you, Jew, that the glory of so great a virgin has been found in your kindred. Let it be beloved to have discovered a Virgin of such glory in your lineage. Let it be joyful that in your stock the distinction of such chastity has appeared [Col. 0067C]. Let it be delightful that in your ancestry so great a miracle has been revealed [Note: [Col. 0067D] Toletanus and Amelianus read “joyful”].

Behold, through this Virgin the whole earth has been filled with the glory of God. Through this Virgin all, from the least to the greatest, have come to know the living God. Through this Virgin all have seen the salvation of God. Through this Virgin all the ends of the earth have remembered the Lord and turned to him (Psalm 97).

All the nations adore in the presence of her Son; the kingdom belongs to her Son, and he himself will rule the nations (Psalm 21). All sing to the Lord himself, her Son, the new song of their redemption, because in being born from this Virgin he performed great deeds [Note: [Col. 0067D] Trinity and Amelianus read “in being born”].

The Lord made his salvation known through this Virgin, and before our eyes he revealed his righteousness (Psalm 97). Through this Virgin they found God [Col. 0067D] [Note: [Col. 0067D] Amelianus reads “whom”], whom they could not find through observance of the law. God came through this Virgin, and when the nations and languages had been gathered, we came and saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father (John 1).

All the nations were gathered in the name of this Lord in the midst of Jerusalem [Col. 0068A] [Note: [Col. 0068D] “In Jerusalem,” Trinity and Amelianus], which is the Vision of Peace (Jeremiah 3), that is, the universal Church, and they will no longer walk after the perversity of their heart. The Lord swore in truth and judgment. And behold, all nations bless one born of such a mother and praise him together.

Behold, this God is our strength. To him we have all come from the ends of the earth, and with Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0068D] Feuardent printed “let us come” and “let us say”; our manuscripts read “we have come” and “we say,” which agrees with what follows, “we flock together” and “we ascend”] we say: “In truth our fathers possessed a lie” (Jeremiah 16).

Behold, on the last day this mountain, the son of this virgin, has been prepared on the summit of the mountains (Isaiah 2), that is, he has been raised above our Apostles and above the majesty of all the heavenly powers. All peoples flock to him, and many nations hasten. We ascend to this Lord, the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob [Col. 0068B], which is the Church of the living God. He teaches us his ways; we walk in his paths, because the law of grace has gone forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. In it the holy apostles were commanded that we all be baptized in his name and filled with the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28).

But concerning you, because of the obstinacy of your most wicked heart, because of your impure will, because of your faithless mind, because of your evil conscience, because of your constant unbelief, because of your genuine pride, because of your deceitful obedience, because of your faithless promises, because of your unstable faith [Note: [Col. 0068D] Toletanus reads “inconstant faith”], hear the Lord proclaiming in Deuteronomy: “You will be at the head among the nations, but the unbelieving people will be at the tail” (Deuteronomy 28) [Note: [Col. 0068D] All our manuscripts and Feuardent read “they will be” (erunt). We follow all our manuscripts; Feuardent printed instead: “To whom, then, are you unbelieving, if not . . . one about to be born?”].

To whom are you unbelieving except this God, who was destined to be born in the humility of man from this Virgin? Again Jeremiah: “The house of Judah has utterly transgressed against me, says the Lord. They denied me and said: ‘He is not the one’” (Jeremiah 5) [Col. 0068C] [Note: [Col. 0068D] All our manuscripts read “me,” whereas the Vulgate at this passage in Jeremiah reads “the Lord”]. To this day, Jew, on account of this Christ, my Lord, the son of this Virgin, you say that he is not the Christ. You await another, with whom you will perish: the Antichrist.

Again Isaiah: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people that did not believe and contradicted me” (Isaiah 65). Not believing and contradicting—whom, if not this Lord? Because he was born from this Virgin [Note: [Col. 0068D] Thus all ours; Feuardent reads “deigned to be born”], they refuse to believe that he is God.

Again Jeremiah: “How can you say, ‘We are wise, and the law of God is with us’? Truly, the lying stylus of the scribes has worked deceit. The wise have been put to shame, terrified, and captured. For they have rejected the word of the Lord, and there is no wisdom in them” (Jeremiah 8) [Col. 0068D]. What word? Surely this one, made flesh from this Virgin. And what wisdom? This, namely, of God the Father, which is foolishness to the nations.

Again Isaiah: “Hear me, hard of heart, and far from righteousness: I have brought my righteousness near, and it will not be far away, and my salvation will not be delayed” (Isaiah 46). What righteousness, and what salvation, except this one [Note: [Col. 0069D] “Certainly,” absent in Feuardent but present in all ours], by whom we believers have been justified and saved?

Again Isaiah: “Bring out the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears” (Isaiah 43). Who are those who do not see and those who do not hear, except those who do not see or hear this Son of God, incarnate from a human being, and all the things that have been foretold about him in many ways [Note: [Col. 0069D] Trinity and Amelianus read “proclaimed”]?

Again in Hosea: “Woe to them, for they have departed from me; they will be devastated, because they have transgressed against me; and I redeemed them, but they spoke a lie against me” (Hosea 7) [Note: [Col. 0069D] “And” is absent from all our manuscripts]. From whom did they depart? Surely from me, whom, seeing as a humble man, they despise as God [Note: [Col. 0069D] Toletanus and the ancient edition read “despised”]. And what lie did they speak, except what we also read in Jeremiah, when he says: “He is not the one”?

And why is he not the one? Because “we saw him, and he had no appearance; and we desired one despised and last among men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity; and as one whose face was hidden and despised, so that we did not regard him” (Isaiah 53) [Col. 0069B]. By these words your unbelief is signified: Christ appeared to you to have neither appearance nor beauty, and therefore you did not regard him as God.

I have spoken swiftly; I have spoken running; I have spoken in passing [Note: [Col. 0069D] Trinity and Toletanus read “passing over”]; I have spoken rapidly, speedily, with dispatch. I have gathered what I quickly found, what I touched nearby, what I discovered close at hand, what I drew from the neighboring ground.

For if I wished—or could—be strong in expertise, watchful in prudence, lively in insight, energetic in inquiry, and not sluggish in diligence, my days would fail me, the moments would diminish, the hours would grow weary [Note: [Col. 0069D] Toletanus reads “would languish”], morning would collapse, noon would melt away [Note: [Col. 0069D] All our manuscripts read “would languish”], evening would fall; the deep night and cockcrow, twilight [Note: [Col. 0069D] Toletanus reads “twilights”], and the abundance of nights would not suffice, would not hold together [Note: [Col. 0069D] Amelianus reads “would cohere,” rather than “cohere”], for expressing or recounting matters of this kind, whether fitting to my faith or contrary to your faithlessness.

Therefore come with me now to this Virgin, lest without her you hasten to Gehenna. Come; let us hide beneath the covering of her virtue, lest you be clothed with shame as with a double cloak. Come; let us confess—I my sins of youth and ignorance, and you the sins of your sacrilege and crime—lest the heavens reveal your iniquities. Come; let us humble ourselves in the truth of confessing and praising her, lest the earth rise up against you, asserting that it has supported your faithlessness in so great a crime.

Do not be ashamed that her Son is your God, lest he himself be ashamed of you before his angels. Do not be ashamed of his words, lest he himself be ashamed of you in the register of the book of the living [Col. 0069D]. Confess him in the land of earthly beings, lest he himself fail to confess you in the land of the living. Confess that he is God and the Son of the virgin mother [Note: [Col. 0069D] “Virgin” is absent in all our manuscripts], so that he himself may confess you before the Father of his divinity [Col. 0070A]. Fear his majesty among human beings, lest his humanity cast you into Tartarus before his angels. Love him while he is patient, lest he hate you when he judges you.

I think that by the power of God I have stabbed the enemy as best I could, left him slain, cast him aside weakened, and abandoned him lifeless. Thus he is present pale, remains bloodless, suffers exhausted, stays fatigued, lies cut to pieces, falls pierced through, and perishes crushed. Nothing remains of the breath of life; nothing now remains of hope for life; he has no expectation of the return of life.
