Only one thing is lacking: that the breath of faithlessness exhales, that the faint murmur of error breathes out, that from the sepulcher of sacrilege a thin corruption should make the nostrils of the soul recoil in disgust [Note: [Col. 0070D] “Stench” is absent in Trinity and Toletanus].

But I shall return, retrace my steps, go backward, and turn back; I shall not leave until he fails; I shall not go until he perishes; I shall not proceed until, crushed beneath my feet [Note: [Col. 0070D] We have restored “crushed” from Trinity, which is certainly the true reading, although the others write “constrained”], he vanishes. Let no little worm remain from the corpse of faithlessness; let no moth of sacrilege arise from its carrion; let no kind of worm spring from the putrefaction of profanation, which, fed in the cavern of crimes by the favor of demons, even if it does not rise into a beast, may fly into a bird and applaud itself for having escaped the nets of our argument, while lamenting that it has been unable to overcome us at the root.

Let it draw its throat away from the hilt of our polished reasoning [Note: [Col. 0070D] Trinity and Amelianus add: “and, borne wandering through the airy powers by the levities of the air”], and let it hang itself by deception, to be carried wanderingly through the aerial powers; and let it, under the appearance of fear or flight, smile at the one with whom it does not agree under the hope of victory [Note: [Col. 0070D] Trinity reads “under the hope of victory”].

Therefore, lifeless enemy, listen before you speak [Col. 0070C]. Open your ear before your tongue; remove the bar from your ear before that from your mouth, so that you may know before you speak, understand before you answer, and perceive in your heart before you utter with your mouth.

And so, to know how to assert the fullness of truth concerning this truth, consider, look, see, understand, weigh, observe, attend, know, be wise, learn, and recognize that this is the very God who is from God in the truth of his own nature, the one who was made man from the Virgin in the truth of my nature [Note: [Col. 0070D] Trinity reads “who was born”]; that this is eternally everlasting, the one who, in the economy of salvation, was made temporal; that this is the one who came, though he is truly unmoved; that this is the one contained in a place, whom no place contains [Note: [Col. 0070D] Trinity and Amelianus read “held”]; that this is within a place, who is the place of all things.

For, to speak more explicitly [Note: [Col. 0070D] Feuardent reads “more exactly”; all our manuscripts read “more explicitly”], I will follow him with him as my guide; with him going before, I will run after him; with him preceding, I will go behind him; with him helping or calling me, I will enter to him. And insofar as he permits [Note: [Col. 0070D] The sounder reading, found in all our manuscripts at [Col. 0071D], in place of “you promise,” which Feuardent printed not without error], I will affirm to you, show you, explain to you, set forth, unfold, prove, and demonstrate who this very one is who came, from where he came, when he came, where he came, why he came, how he came, and what he did.

## CHAPTER V. He explains the sacred mystery of the Incarnation.

Hear now who Christ is who has come; hear now who the same one is who has come: none other than God and the almighty Lord. Malachi says:

> “The ruler will come to his holy temple, whom you seek, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Malachi 3).

[Note: Feu-ard. has *Veniet* (“will come”) instead of *Venit* (“has come”).]

Likewise, in Exodus the Father says of him to the legislators:

> “Behold, I am sending my angel, who will go before you, guard you on the way, and lead you into the place that I have prepared. Pay attention to him and listen to his voice; do not think him contemptible, because he will not forgive when you sin. And my name is in him” (Exodus 23).

[Note: Feu-ard. has *ad legislatores dicit* (“he says to the legislators”), but *dicit* is absent from all our manuscripts.]

[Note: *Te* (“you”) has been supplied from all our manuscripts.]

Because you hear “angel,” do you therefore think that he is not the creator God, but some created angel? Far from it. You are certainly driven by great madness if you believe that God bestowed upon any angel both his own power and his proper name, and that, contrary to both your voice and mine, there is not one God who made all things.

Why do you say that the angel is equal to him?

[Note: This is certainly not true; the same reading appears in the other witnesses.]

That must not be said, because it is not so; it is not true. For who among the clouds can be compared with the Lord? Or who will be like God among the sons of God (Psalm 88)—that is, among the good angels and among holy human beings, whom the mercy of divine fatherhood calls sons through the love of adoption?

Where did Christ come from?

[Note: “From where did he also come?” appears in Trinity and Amel.]

Where did he come from? Truly, he came from nowhere other than God. Hear him himself speaking through Solomon:

> “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclesiasticus 24).

Likewise, the Father says of him in the Psalms:

> “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109).

And elsewhere he himself says through Solomon:

> “Before the hills I was brought forth” (Proverbs 8).

[Note: Feu-ard. has “all the hills,” but *all* is not read in our manuscripts.]

And Zechariah says:

> “Thus says the Lord of hosts: After the glory he sent me to the nations that plundered you. For whoever touches you touches the apple of his eye. For behold, I will raise my hand against them, and they will become a spoil for those who had served them; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me” (Zechariah 2).

[Note: Trinity and Tolet. have “the Lord God.”]

Behold the almighty Lord of hosts sent by the almighty Father, the Lord God of hosts, when Christ came. He was sent to the nations after the glory of his divinity, which he possessed with the Father, when he became humble in the form of a servant, though he was equal to the Father’s divinity.

Likewise Isaiah says:

> “I am the first, and I am the last; my hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured out the heavens. I did not speak from the beginning in secret: from the time before it came to be, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48).

Behold, the one who is first and last, and the maker of all things, is sent by the Lord Father, with whom he is held to be coeternal and coequal.

When, then, did Christ come? When did he come? Let Jacob speak in the blessings of the patriarchs:

> “The ruler shall not depart from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49).

He therefore came when, through ambition, with the foreigner Herod succeeding to the kingdom, the ruler from Judah failed in Israel.

[Note: “In Jerusalem” is found in Tolet.]

At this time the one who was to be sent arrived, the one whom the nations and peoples were awaiting.

Likewise, in Daniel, when the angel spoke to him:

> “Daniel, pay attention to the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks have been shortened for your people and for your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may reach its end, iniquity may be wiped away, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, and vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Daniel 9).

The fact that this period was completed long ago is shown by the occurrence and outcome of the things foretold.

[Note: Feu-ard. writes earlier: “Where did Christ come?” None of ours has this.]

Where, then, did he come? Let Micah say:

> “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are never too little among the thousands of Judah; from you there will go forth for me the one who is to be ruler in Israel” (Micah 5).

[Note: Trinity and Amel. have “Are you perhaps?”]

This refers to his flesh; for according to his divinity, the following words are connected with it:

> “And his origin is from the days of eternity.”

David likewise says:

> “They will go from strength to strength, and the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Psalm 38).

And Jeremiah, in the book of Baruch:

> “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him: he found the whole way of knowledge and showed it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3).

[Note: Feu-ard. has: “Why did Christ come? Again, why did he come?” We print the reading found in Amel.]

Why, then, did Christ come? Through Isaiah he himself says:

> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind” (Isaiah 6).

He himself also says:

> “Behold, our God; he himself will come and save us.”

[Note: Trinity and Amel. have “He saved us.”]

Habakkuk likewise says:

> “You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your chosen ones” (Habakkuk 3).

How, then, did he come?

[Note: Amel. has “How did Christ come?”]

Certainly as one rejected and needy. Let Zechariah say:

> “Learn, daughters of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, just and saving, poor,

[Note: Trinity and Amel. have “Say.”]

and sitting upon an unbroken donkey” (Zechariah 9).

[Note: “And” is absent from Trinity and Amel.]

In the Psalm David says of him:

> “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.”

Likewise, in Isaiah, speaking in the person of God the Father:

> “Behold, my servant will understand; he will be exalted, lifted up, and very highly elevated. Just as many were astonished at you, so inglorious will his appearance be among men, and his form among the sons of men. He will sprinkle many nations. Kings will shut their mouths because of him; for those to whom nothing was announced concerning him will see, and those who have not heard will contemplate. Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And he will rise like a young shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground” (Isaiah 22);

[Note: Amel. has *Credidit* (“has believed”).]

> “There is no appearance or beauty in him; we saw him, and there was no aspect to attract us. We desired him, despised and last among men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity; his face was as though hidden and despised, so that we did not esteem him. Truly he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows; we considered him as one afflicted with leprosy, struck by God and humbled. But he was wounded because of our iniquities and crushed because of our crimes; the discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed. We all wandered like sheep; each one turned aside into his own way;

[Note: All the others, except Trinity and Amel., have “into his own way.”]

> “and the Lord laid upon him the iniquities of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth. Like a sheep he will be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he will be silent and will not open his mouth. From distress and judgment he was taken away; but who will recount his generation? For he was cut off from the land of the living; because of the crime of my people I struck him. And he will give the impious for his burial and the rich for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. And the Lord willed to crush him in weakness. If he gives his life for sin, he will see long-lived offspring

[Note: Feu-ard. adds “upon the earth,” which is lacking in both of the senior manuscripts.]

> “and the will of the Lord will prosper in his hand. Because his soul labored, he will see and be satisfied. By his knowledge the righteous one himself will justify my many servants, and he himself will bear their iniquities. Therefore I will assign him many, and he will divide the spoils of the strong, because he handed over his soul to death and was reckoned among criminals. And he himself bore the sins of many and prayed for transgressors, that they might not perish” (Isaiah 53).

Likewise, in the same prophet:

> “He will not cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets. He will not break a bruised reed, nor extinguish a smoking wick; but in truth he will teach judgment and bring forth justice, until he establishes judgment on the earth, and the nations will hope in his name” (Isaiah 42).

And in the Psalms he says of himself:

> “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 21).

## CHAPTER VI. After a prayer, he proves that the Son of holy Mary is God.

[Column 0074A]

Open, my Jesus, open my mouth, and fill it with confession of your mercy. Touch the mouth and the ear of my heart, saying:

[Note: Feu-ard.’s edition has *Effeta*, meaning “open”; we have removed the preceding words because they are absent from all our manuscripts.]

> “Be opened”;

[Note: For *ut* (“so that”), which all ours retain, Feu-ard. and have *et* (“and”).]

so that I may hear what you speak through your Holy Spirit.

[Note: Feu-ard. has “what I shall speak,” as do our manuscripts except Trinity, which reads as we have printed it. The old edition has “what may be spoken.”]

Fill my mouth with your praise, so that I may be able to recount your magnificence, confess your mercies to you, and proclaim your wonders to the sons of men, you who live and reign forever and ever. Amen.

What did you do, Lord? As far as the omnipotence of the one Trinity is concerned, all things were made through you, and without you nothing was made. But as far as it concerns the fact that you came specifically to become incarnate in your person and to appear to human beings as the Savior of all, you yourself became subject to the law, born of a woman (Galatians 4).

But let the Psalmist declare both the results of your works and the steps you took through the marvelous variety of your deeds:

> “The steps of God were seen, the steps of my God” (Psalm 67).

Those, certainly, by which you came into the world through the Virgin and by which you returned to the Father through the glory of the resurrection.

Thus the many sayings of the prophets confirm that you came, just as examples of your works demonstrate it.

Therefore, since you came into the world, let hostile Judea learn from the assertions of the law given to it what you did. First, then, Jew, when this Son of God and almighty God came invisibly to the Virgin, what did he do except—just as Isaiah says—that from the branch which had come forth, that is, from the virgin mother, from the root of Jesse’s lineage, this flower arose (Isaiah 11)?

[Note: Our manuscripts read *ascendat* (“may arise”).]

The Son was certainly born, created without any corruption, but generated solely by the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, according to the same prophet, he says (Isaiah 7) that, not in the ordinary manner of a young woman, as you falsely claim, but as I truly say, the Virgin would conceive and give birth as a sign.

Likewise, according to the same prophet, he says (Isaiah 45) that, without the approach of corruption, solely through the warmth of the Holy Spirit and the overshadowing of the power of the Most High, the earth of the body—the virginal womb—would be opened and would bring forth this Savior.

Likewise, according to Daniel, he says (Daniel 2) that this stone would be cut off—that is, drawn out—from the mountain of the Jewish people without hands that cut it, that is, without the operation of corruption; and, coming upon the earth of the whole world’s breadth, it would fill the globe with its power and establish its dominion from sea to sea.

But likewise, according to the Psalmist, he says (Psalm 18) that the bridegroom would go forth from the chamber of the virginal womb, to take that bride from all nations, the universal Church.

[Note: Feu-ard. adds “that is, the Church”; ours, as printed, omit “that is.”]

Elsewhere it is said to her:

> “Hear, daughter, the voice of God, and see the mercy of the God who goes before you. Bend the ear of your obedience, and forget the profanations of your people and the wickedness of their deeds, and do not remember the house of your father” (Psalm 44),

[Note: “House” is not read in our manuscripts.]

namely, the devil,

[Note: Amel. writes *suaves* (“pleasant things”) instead of *sive* (“or”).]

or the enticements of the world and the shameful loves of temporal things.

Likewise, according to the Psalmist, he says (Psalm 84) that from the earth of the mother’s body the truth of the flesh of the one being born would arise, and that the righteousness of divinity would look down from heaven. And thus, with God and man existing in the unity of one person, this earth of our Virgin would give the fruit of this son, while the Lord granted us the kindness of our redemption.

Likewise, according to Ezekiel, he says (Ezekiel 44) that through the gate of virginal modesty the same Lord God of Israel would go forth from this house of the mother’s womb; and since virgin integrity never knew any approach of corruption either before or after his birth, that same gate would remain closed, because it is always shut with the bolt of virginity.

The whole force of all these prophecies is directed toward this: that from the Holy Spirit and Mary, ever virgin, this Word might become flesh, God might become man, and what was divine might become human—not through any diminution of divinity, not through the destruction of eternity, not through a change in unchangeable truth, but through the assumption of flesh, through participation in humanity, through association with human nature.

[Note: Trinity has *participatio* (“participation”) rather than *participio* (“by participation”).]

And thus, in the unity of one person, the same one is the Word who is flesh, the same one is man who is God, and the same one is both divinity and humanity.

[Note: Amel. has “in unity”; the others, with Feu-ard., have “in union.”]

Accordingly, according to Jeremiah (Baruch 3), the one Christ is God, who found the whole way of wisdom and who also lived among human beings as man.

According to the Psalmist (Psalm 86), he is the man born in Zion, who founded it as the exalted God.

According to Isaiah (Isaiah 2), who says:

> “Cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is regarded as exalted,”

he is the man in whose human breath is the breath of his divinity; and he is also God, who is regarded as exalted.

According to David (Psalm 109), he is the Lord God to whom the Lord God speaks; he is the man who sits at God’s right hand.

According to Isaiah (Isaiah 9), he is the man who was born a little child for us, and he is also God, the Son of God who was given to us.

According to the Psalmist (Psalm 44), he is the God to whom it is said:

> “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever”;

he is also the man who is said to have been anointed with the oil of exultation, the Holy Spirit.

According to the word of the Lord through Jeremiah (Jeremiah 23), he is the man to whom it is said:

> “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch, and he will reign as king, and he will be wise, and he will execute judgment and righteousness upon the earth”;

[Note: Our manuscript copies read “the days will come.”]

and he is also God, when the text continues:

> “In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely; and this is the name by which they will call him: ‘The Lord our righteous God.’”

According to Micah (Micah 5), he is the man of whom it is said:

> “He will stand, see, and feed his flock”;

he is also God, when it adds:

> “They will be in the strength of the Lord and in the majesty of the name of their God; for now he will be magnified to the ends of the earth, and this man will be peace.”

Have you heard what God did when he came into the Virgin’s womb? Have you heard that, although he is God, he became man? Have you heard that, although God is one thing and man another, there is nevertheless not one God and another man, but one Lord, our Jesus Christ, the same God and man?

[Note: Trinity and Amel. have “our Lord”; Feu-ard. and another witness have “my Lord.”]

Hear now what works of miracles he performed, what deeds of wonders he accomplished, what great acts he carried out, what works of power he achieved, and what effects of his works he produced.

Certainly, recognize that the things you are about to hear were done among your nation, in your race, among your people, and among your populace.

[Column 0076B]

For the one who did these things, insofar as he is man, willed to be born from your stock, from your line, from the offspring of your race, in the reality of the flesh of my nature.

[Note: All our manuscripts and Feu-ard. read *traduce* (“stock” or “lineage”); the reading is uncertain in context.]

But I would plainly wish to set forth before the Lord and his angels, in the tribunal of the whole world, with all the nations looking on, the case of this truth to the advocates of my party against your sacrilege and unbelief, and to present the just right of my truth on the testimony of my witnesses.

[Note: We print the final member of this sentence according to all our manuscripts. Feu-ard. has: “And that I might present the truthful right … the faith of my witnesses.”]

But I see you wishing to reply through deceitful effort, perverse cunning, treacherous opposition, a faltering encounter, a depraved mind, an impure understanding, and hyperbatonic speech—that is, speech confused in every respect.

[Note: Feu-ard. printed *profanatico* (“profane”); we follow our manuscripts, which have *hyperbatonico*. This agrees remarkably with what follows, since hyperbaton makes speech disordered and obscure unless used carefully.]

You wish to refuse to accept the authors of the New Testament and to fight their assertions with the antiquity of authority.

I too shall reply: If you do not yield at all to the new advocates of truth, at least submit to truth itself, which speaks on its own behalf.

But again you object: “These things which you claim that truth has spoken were proclaimed by the heralding declarations of new preachers.”

And I shall say: Thus, as you claim, you argue on the basis of time, not authority; you dispute by choice, not by right; you narrate the case according to your will, not according to order, when you put antiquity before novelty, attack new things with old, and try to abolish new things by means of old.

Certainly this is the direct order of the dispute undertaken; this is the proper legal procedure of the case; this is the true beginning of the matter and the appropriate method of an orderly argument: that old promises should be completed by new works; that truth should exclude the shadow; that open manifestation should reveal what was uncertain and hidden; that a new faith should disclose the secrets of antiquity; that the faith arriving in the fullness of time should reveal the secrets of former ages; that the newness of religion should display hidden mysteries; and that the fullness of time should confirm the beginnings of time.

But now, why do you seek the old things that have passed away, when behold, all things have become new? Why do you remember those times on account of which these things were not done? For they were done for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

Why do you pay so much attention to the earliest prophecies, when every prophecy has already been completed by the manifestation of the accomplished event? What are you doing with the law and the prophets, when even the elements of all things testify that what they spoke up to John has been fulfilled in God, our Christ Jesus?

[Note: In place of these words all our manuscripts have: “When I see the truth, therefore, and so forth.”]

What, indeed, shall I say? That you refuse to accept the new because you despised the old; that from the point at which you appeared to have despised ancient things you attack the rights of novelty; that from the point at which you had opposed the law you reject grace; that from the point at which you had earlier contradicted the legal commandment you refuse to give faith to the Gospel; that from the point at which you had opposed the prophets you oppose the apostles; that from the point at which you did not obey your own rulers you refuse to listen to my teachers; that from the point at which you had profaned the promise of truth you now profane truth itself; that from the point at which you refused to recognize what was revealed you now refuse to know what was disclosed;

[Note: Feu-ard. has *adaperta* (“disclosed”); Trinity and Amel. have *adoperta*, which is probably the genuine reading, since the author intends to set it against the preceding *revelata* (“revealed”), which has the same meaning rather than the opposite.]

that from the point at which you were unfaithful concerning the promise of future things you are faithless in the fullness of time.

[Note: Our manuscripts have *perfidum* (“faithless,” neuter), not *perfidus* (“faithless,” masculine), as Feu-ard. prints.]

But come now: by what order can this mode of a perverse proposition be just—that, in seeking knowledge of the truth, you choose from the crowd of truthful people the individuals whom you will believe, and, while the radiant splendor of manifest truth speaks, you pay no attention?

[Note: The Tolet. manuscript has: “And while you direct yourself toward the flashing lightning of truth, you do not attend.” But if *eluxerit* (“has shone forth”) is read in place of *dixerit* (“speaks”), no reading is better than Feu-ard.’s.]

With what poisonous mouth, by what route, is this action of an agitated contest being directed, so that, while I put forward clearer judgments, you establish in your own choice what you will defend in opposition to mine?

Finally, what sort of evasion is this: that I put forward the truth, which you refuse to see, and that you attempt to argue about the investigation of that same truth?

Or what is the thrust of this heaped-up reply: that you seek advocates of truth while scorning to see the truth that has been proclaimed?

[Note: The Amel. manuscript has “so that you seek the truth through advocates,” and so forth.]

If you are permitted to choose whom you will believe, then let it also be permitted for you to choose what you will believe. If by your choice you are permitted to claim what you believe, then let it also be permitted for you to find the author of the choice in whom you will believe.

[Note: Our Tolet. manuscript has this reading. Feu-ard. and the others write: “Let it also be permitted to find by choice whom you will believe.” We are not especially satisfied with either reading; we would prefer: “Let it also be permitted to find by choice whom you will believe.” We do not sufficiently understand what it means to believe in a choice, or to find the author of the choice.]

And thus you break the rules of judgment, so that concerning choice you pronounce a judgment of whim rather than of a just dispute. For you do not say what you ought to say, but what pleases you; nor do you set forth what discovers the truth, but what conceals it, when you do not publicly believe the truth and seek it in hidden places, while truth itself loudly proclaims what is true about itself, and you inquire by debate of choice what truth possesses as truth.

Truth says of itself: “I am”; and you seek an investigator who might display the appearance of truth!

Truth says:

> “I am the way” (John 14);

and you seek the way in byways!

Truth says:

> “I am life”;

and you seek heralds of life!

Truth says:

> “Let whoever thirsts come and drink” (John 16);

and you summon one who may give drink to the thirsty!

Truth says:

> “I came forth from God and came into this world” (John 16:28);

and you choose who that person might be who can come into the world!

Truth says:

> “I and the Father are one,”

and:

> “Whoever sees me also sees the Father”;

[Note: Tolet. and Amel. have “Whoever sees me sees”; Feu-ard. and another edition have “saw, saw.”]

and you assert that he is neither from God nor able to exist as equal to him!

But because you applaud yourself among the defenders of your party, I do not want you to remain uncertain. Know for certain that those whom you summon as advocates are mine; those whom you take to yourself are close to me; and those whom you enlist are very well known to me.

For what they have placed in your ears with their own voices, they have impressed upon my heart by the power of understanding; what sounded to you adhered to me; what touched you by sound enlightened me by touch.

But now, as one who is placable, I shall yield—not defeated by the truth, but supported by it—while you, as one infamous, yield not supported by the truth, but defeated.

For your witnesses will support what I assert, strengthen what I declare, confirm what I set forth, establish what I attest, and ratify what I have introduced.

My faith is their truth; my proposition is their testimony; my knowledge is their witness; my speaking in time is their understanding in eternity; what I set forth is their confirmation;

[Note: Where Feu-ard. has *eorumdem* (“of those same people”), Amel. and Trinity write *illorum est* (“belongs to them”); conversely, below, where Feu-ard. has *dixisse illorum est*, they have another reading.]

my not being silent is their speaking.

Thus my tongue is their breath; my speech is their spirit; my word is their breathing. For the word of God that came through them has come into me; the wisdom of God that filled them has touched me; the Spirit of God who enabled them to speak has granted me to hear and announce.

Therefore their heart is my mouth; their mouth is my speech; their speech is my faith; their faith is my affirmation. Hence I say what they understand, I know what they say, I announce what they know, I do not keep silent about what they declare, and I recount what they have announced.

Because the one who lived in them lives in me; because the one who was in them is in me; because the one who spoke in them is not silent in me; because the one who remained in them until now remains in me forever.

[Note: Trinity and Amel. have “because he lives in me”; Feu-ard. printed “because he is.”]

Why, then, do you not believe the Son when he says:

> “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 17),

when it is said to the Father concerning him:

> “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Psalm 8)?

Why do you not believe the Son when he says:

> “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God,”

when the Father also says to him:

> “Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109)?

Why do you not believe the Son when he says:

> “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5),

when the Father says to him:

> “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1)?

Why do you not believe the Son when he says:

> “If you knew my Father, you would certainly know me also” (John 14),

when the Father says to him:

> “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Isaiah 2)?

## CHAPTER VII. Through the connection of the words of the Two Testaments, he teaches that Christ is both man and, certainly, the Most High God. He also depicts at length the whole life of our Savior up to the sending of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles.

[Col. 0079B] But come, let us hasten where we began; let us not cease going where we have attempted to go; let us be driven more eagerly where we have striven to advance; let us not stop walking where we began to walk. Let the soul’s steps proceed, let the foot of the mind hasten, let the knee of the heart walk. Let the knee be sound, [Note: [Col. 0079D] “With the leg,” from Am. and Trin.; the others, with Feu-ard., have “the leg.”] let the leg stand firm, let the shin support you, lest you fall upon your ankle, lest you collapse upon your sole, lest you slip with your foot; [Note: [Col. 0079D] “You slip,” all our copies and Feu-ard.; “you slide down,” which perhaps arose by combining the final syllable with the preceding verb.] strive with your whole self, equip yourself with your whole self, rise up with your whole self. Set forth what you understand; say what you know; speak what you comprehend. Bring forth what you ruminate; recount what you think; explain what you devise. Truth is present; here is truth; behold, truth is here. Those who speak what is true are ready; those who understand what is true are ready; those who set forth what is true are ready; those who defend what is true are ready. [Note: “Another ‘I’ has been added by us from all our copies.”]

I, I indeed—although you profane what is mine, I delight in your authorities. [Col. 0079C] Although you disparage what is mine, I rejoice in the eloquence of your assertions. Although you contradict what is mine, I, obedient and submissive, embrace your authorities. [Note: “The reading ‘your’ in the text we publish comes from the Amelianus Codex; in the others, as in Feu-ard., it is ‘yours.’ But the former reading seemed excellent and more correct to us.] For your things are mine in the same measure as you are alien to mine. Your things are no longer yours in the same measure as my things could in no way become yours, because your things and mine are one, in one, from one, and through one.

Tell me, then—you who neither believe the truth, nor favor the truth, nor conform to the truth, nor love the truth, nor obey the truth, nor listen to the truth—why do you despise the commands of the Most High? Why do you render void the oracles of the Maker? Why, since you cannot contemplate the secrets of Wisdom, do you attempt to attack them? Why do you foolishly disparage God’s prudence? Why, though you yourself are dust, do you add weakness to God’s power?

You who did not believe God the Father when he said to his Son, Christ my Lord, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II)—words he spoke to no other human being, because to no other human being did he grant that the nations should be his inheritance and that the ends of the earth should be his possession, which he would rule with a strong iron rod and crush like a potter’s clay vessels, not by the examples of a human decree but by the right of his own dominion—believe that same Son when he says of himself: “I and the Father are one,” and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John X), and, “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John XIV).

And through Solomon the same Wisdom, who is the Son of God, says: “When he prepared the heavens, I was there; when with a fixed law and a circle he enclosed the abysses; when he made firm the sky above and balanced the springs of the waters; when he set a boundary around the sea and appointed a law for the waters, lest they pass beyond their limits; when he suspended the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things” (Prov. VIII).

You who did not believe the Son when he spoke the truth about himself, [Col. 0080B] believe the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me, he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Luke IV). And again there: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. II).

For this is what is said through John: “And John bore witness, saying: ‘I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven,’” [Note: “Feu-ard. published ‘and remaining’; we have ‘and it remained,’ which we read in all our copies.] “and it remained upon him, and I did not know him. But the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw, and I bore witness that he is the Son of God” (John I).

You who did not believe the divine Persons speaking individually, [Note: “Individually,” from all our copies; Feu-ard. has “separately.”] believe the same undivided Trinity working and acting together. For thus it is said through Isaiah: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. XLVIII).

For behold, in the fact that the Son of God came to be incarnate through our Virgin, the whole Trinity displayed the new wonder of its operation. You, therefore, who did not believe the truth—which is supreme truth, than which nothing is truer—should not be ashamed to believe the witnesses of truth. For although these too are creatures and a created order of that truth by which they were created, and announce the full and supreme truth concerning their Creator and the truth of that Creator himself, nevertheless he is despised through them in the same way as he is believed when they are believed concerning him.

For sometimes a judge does not contend personally with the criminal, but through intermediaries compels a confession to be elicited; and it is not burdensome to him [Note: “If he should despise,” Feu-ard. published; but the very sentence itself requires a negation, which we find in all our copies.] if the judge’s messenger is not despised by one who despised the presence of the judge—provided only that he who holds the authority of judgment may obtain the fullness of the truth.

Believe, then, Peter when he says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI). For in Daniel that impious king sees this one when he says: “Behold, I see four men unbound and walking in the midst of the fire, and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of God” (Dan. III); and we truly believe that this one is the Lord and Savior.

But lest you object that in the same Daniel this Son of God is earlier called an angel, hear that same Christ, the Son of God, called an angel by Malachi: “The Ruler whom you seek shall come to his holy temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. III). [Note: “In our judgment we have restored the true reading of this passage from all our copies. Feu-ard.’s reading is: ‘Since this is nothing else, why do you doubt?’ It scarcely makes sense.”]

Since there is no reason for you to doubt this, why do you not also believe John when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John I). When through David the Father says of him: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. XLIV).

Again, why do you not believe that same John when he says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I), when the same Wisdom, who truly is the Son of God, says through Solomon: “The abysses did not yet exist, and I had already been conceived. The springs of the waters had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet stood firm with their massive weight; before the hills, I was being brought forth. He had not yet made the earth, nor the rivers, nor the hinges of the earth’s orb” (Prov. VIII). [Note: “Here Feu-ard. writes ‘before all the hills,’ as above, against the testimony of all our copies.”]

Why do you not believe Matthew when he speaks of his birth: “The generation of Christ was thus. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to have conceived in her womb from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I)? For this is what Isaiah had said: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb” [Col. 0081C] [Note: “Shall receive,” Trin. and Tolet.] “and shall bear a son; and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. VII).

Blush, impure one, and see that the same one who was born a human being is God with us.

Why do you not believe Luke when he speaks of the place of his birth: “Joseph went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David, to register with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant. And it happened that, while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her firstborn son” (Luke II)?

For this is what Micah said: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephratha, are you truly little among the thousands of Judah? From you there shall come forth for me one who is to rule in Israel, whose going forth is from the days of eternity” (Mic. V).

Why do you not believe Matthew, when he speaks of his manifestation through the star and the Magi? [Note: “And the Magi,” all our copies; “the Magi,” Feu-ard.] “When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East’” [Col. 0082A] “and we have come to worship him” (Matt. II).

And below: “When the Magi saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy; and entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they worshiped him. And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”

This too that divine Balaam brought forward in Numbers when he said: “A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” (Num. XXIV). For the Magi, coming from the regions of the East, first announced Christ’s birth by the star as its indicator, so that, when they saw a man arising at the rising of the star, they might demonstrate by the sight of the star that the man, whose coming the chief of their art had foretold beforehand, had arisen at his birth. [Note: “With its rising,” all our copies; “its rising,” Feu-ard.]

Hence Isaiah also says: “All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense, and announcing praise to the Lord” (Isa. LX).

Why do you not believe John when he says: “He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John I)? For this is also what David says: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV). And through Isaiah it is said: “Therefore my people shall know my name on that day, because I am the one who spoke; behold, I am here” (Isa. LII).

Why do you not believe that same John when he speaks of your reproach: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John I)? For this is also what was said about you through Jeremiah: [Note: “By transgressing,” Tol.] “The house of Judah has utterly transgressed against me, says the Lord. They denied me and said: ‘He is not the one’” (Jer. V).

Why do you not believe Mark when he speaks of the miracles of his works: “They brought to him all who were ill and those possessed by demons, and the whole city was gathered at the door, and he healed many who were afflicted with various diseases, and he cast out many demons” (Mark I)? For this is what Isaiah says: “Behold, our God himself will come and save us; then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear. Then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear” (Isa. XXXV). [Note: Only Feu-ard. writes “shall be opened.” The ancient edition, in agreement with all our copies, has “shall hear.”]

For what need is there now to speak to you of his passion, insults, cross, nails, death, and burial, when you do not deny that you did these things? If you did not believe that they happened, you would indeed be guilty of no slight treachery. But since you know that they happened, and do not understand that these things were done for the salvation of the world, but insist that you did such things—as it seems to you—for his disgrace, you are truly bound by the unbreakable double knot of a grave crime, when you are held guilty both of the murder of an innocent man and of refusing to believe that his death, inflicted cruelly by you but willingly accepted by him, benefited the salvation of the world.

[Col. 0083A] But since you do not deny [Note: “You do not deny” is the reading we publish from our copies, in place of “you do not reject,” which Feu-ard. has. The Trin. and Amel. Codices, however, read this entire sentence differently, and their reading is certainly not to be despised: “But why do you not deny that you acted impiously, although the whole company of the redeemed joyfully believes with me that these things were mercifully done?”] that you acted impiously, why do you not believe with me that all the deeds of the Redeemer were mercifully done for us?

Hear the power of the miracles that seem to have arisen visibly amid the very torments of punishment. [Note: In Trin. “are clearly seen” is read instead of “seem”; we do not reject that reading.]

For you wished, by sacrilegious efforts, [Note: We publish “by sacrilegious efforts” from Trin. and Amel.; the others, with Feu-ard., have “by sacrilegious ears.” We further give the variant reading of the Amelianus Codex, which reads: “For you wished, by sacrilegious efforts, to wrest from the sacred utterances the silence of miracles that were manifest, to cast darkness over his powers, and to oppose a shadow of oblivion to all his works,” etc.] to wrest from sacred utterances silence regarding things present, to consign miracles to caves and powers to hiding places, and to cast a shadow of oblivion over all his works.

But since Scripture says: “There is no wisdom, and there is no knowledge, and there is no counsel against God” (Prov. XXI), while you strive to attack him, you have been conquered; and through the wondrous exchange of the conflict, the wondrous encounter of the contest, the wondrous appearance of contradiction, and the wondrous effect of things contending with themselves, truth is drawn out of hiding, light from the cave, brilliance from darkness, a miracle from disgrace, power from weakness, victory from punishment, honor from contempt, a trophy from the cross, life from death, the living one from the tomb, a free man from the servitude of death, a victor from the underworld, and—what remains—from oblivion testimony, from silence a voice, and from what was extinguished one who can never be extinguished.

See, then, what you did not wish to see. Consider the living things you had thought extinguished. Behold throughout the whole world the glorious things that you urged should be concealed by the guards’ lies. Consider how he whom you did not wish to be remembered any longer shines in heaven and throughout the whole world, with the immensity of miracles and the universal company of the faithful.

And answer: why do you not believe Paul when he says: “For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures; and that he was buried; and that he rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures; and that he was seen by Cephas, and afterward by the eleven; then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom many remain until now; then he was seen by James; then by all the apostles” (1 Cor. XV)? [Note: “After these words, one Amelianus Codex has the following: ‘Among the seventy-two, our region likewise received into the apostolate the most noble apostle Martial, who first illuminated the western peoples sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.’ Certainly this passage seemed most suitable to an inept French copyist for celebrating the glory of his nation. From that nation, learned men contend against learned men that various disciples of the apostles were sent into Gaul in apostolic times to announce the faith; among these they number this holy Martial, allegedly the first bishop of the Lemovicians. Whatever the truth may be—and this is certainly not the place to examine it—who would not laugh at the man’s most intrusive annotation, inserted into the text of the discourse?”]

For this is also what he himself says through David: “My flesh shall rest in hope; for you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. XV). Concerning this resurrection it is also said elsewhere: “I slept, and rested, and rose again, because the Lord raised me up” (Ps. III). In these words, to sleep means nothing other than to die, and to awaken means to rise again.

Likewise in Isaiah: “Now I shall arise, says the Lord; now I shall be exalted, and now I shall be raised high” (Isa. XXXIII). Here the prophet openly declares that he would rise from the dead, be exalted in heaven, and be raised high in the kingdom.

Why do you not believe the whole Catholic Church, spread from the rising of the sun to its setting and from sea to sea, saying with one voice: “We believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who for us and for our salvation was crucified, died, and was buried, and on the third day rose alive from the dead”?

For this is what Hosea had said from the person of the saints who rose with him from the underworld on the third day: “Come, let us return to the Lord, for he has seized us and will heal us. He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight” (Hos. VI). Likewise in the same prophet: “His going forth has been prepared like the dawn.”

For this is what Luke reports: “On the first day of the week, very early,” [Note: Feu-ard. added “when the women came”; we do not read “when” in our copies.] “the women came to the tomb carrying the spices they had prepared, and they found the stone rolled away from the tomb; and entering, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus” (Luke XXIV).

Why do you not believe the same Truth when he speaks of this resurrection of his, by which, in rising again, he fulfilled what your prophet Jonah—or rather mine—had earlier prefigured in his dangers: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matt. XII), that is, in the tomb?

After those three days, just as Jonah left the beast, so he left the tomb. For he alone was free among the dead (Ps. LXXXVI), because just as he could not be held by the contagion of sin, so neither could he be held by the bond of death.

Why do you not believe Mark when he says: “The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to the disciples, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark, last chapter)? For this is what Daniel also says: “I watched in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven” (Dan. VII). He continues and says: “And he reached the Ancient of Days,” that is, the Father. After this he adds: “And they presented him before him, and he gave him power and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be corrupted.”

Why do you not believe that, by his gift, the Holy Spirit was given after his death to those who believed in him? For this is what was said through the prophet Joel: “In the last days, says the Lord, I shall pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel II).

Why do you not believe that he will come as judge, when Mark says: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory, and he will gather his elect” (Mark XIII)? For this is what David also says: “He will summon heaven above and the earth, to distinguish his people. Gather to him his saints, who establish his covenant over sacrifices. And the heavens shall proclaim his righteousness, because God is judge” (Ps. XLIX).

## CHAPTER VIII

He shows that God performed many great deeds in the glorious Virgin, from which anyone may conclude that he could easily have preserved her virginity unharmed in childbirth. Through the testimony of barren Elizabeth and others he confirms Christ’s divinity.

[Col. 0085B]

Have you heard the Father’s testimony concerning the Son? Have you heard the Son’s testimony concerning himself and the Father together? Have you heard the testimony concerning the Holy Spirit, who, in order to show that this one is the Son of God (from whom, according to his divinity, that same Spirit proceeds), descended upon him bodily according to the truth of his Incarnation, on account of whose Incarnation all these mouths of ancient and new preachers have spoken? [Note: “We would gladly delete this word, were it not supported by the testimony of all the copies and published books. For it disturbs the whole sense of the discourse; once removed, everything is clear and plain.”]

Have you heard what the Law and the Prophets, from Moses to Zechariah, have recounted? Have you heard what John his son and, thereafter, the evangelists and apostles have brought forth? Have you heard how everything that, in the earliest and latest times, through the earliest and latest prophets, with one Holy Spirit speaking all things through them, was concordantly and truthfully foretold without the slightest hesitation, has been brought together into knowledge of one reality?

Now hear the remarkable examples of diverse conditions, sexes, ages, things, and elements, so that if the marvelous words of the prophets do not move you, the contemplation of such diversity may at last move you to wonder. [Note: “At some time” appears in Amel. We place it here in place of “in some manner,” which Feu-ard. published and the others have.]

Believe first the Virgin herself, whom both the person and the nature of divinity plainly approached, and listen to what true thing she says about herself: “Behold, from this moment all generations shall call me blessed, because he who is mighty has done great things for me” (Luke I).

Those things, surely, are as worthy of wonder when they are seen as they necessarily had to be wondrously foretold so many ages beforehand and awaited even more wondrously for the redemption of the world.

For through this Virgin God was to become human, the Word was to become flesh, [Col. 0085D] and the Son of God, the Maker of all things, was to become the son of the mother whom he himself had formed. The Ruler was to become subject by being born to the handmaid whom he himself had created. Thus the handmaid would have the Lord in submission, and the Lord would have the handmaid in a position of precedence.

Thus the mother would give birth to her Maker; thus the Maker of formless matter would make the matter of his birth into a mother; and the same Maker would come forth from her whom he had made. Thus he would have as the authoress of his birth her whose making he himself had been the author.

And always different things would be harmonized: the divine would be humbled for the sake of the human, and the human raised up in the divine; what is exalted would yield to what is humble, and what is humble would be directed toward what is exalted; the strong would be weakened in humility, and the humble strengthened in the strong; God would approach a woman, and the woman bring forth a man.

In the woman’s womb the work of the Maker did not occur through the customary operation of nature, but, establishing a wonder in the greatness of the deed, just as he made everything from nothing, so he would make this one thing from what had never been heard of—a thing that would always remain wondrous.

Just as the Maker of the womb entered the Virgin’s womb and brought about a new work, doing what he had not done before, although he had foretold that it would be done, so, with the law of nature set aside in the wonder of the event, this would occur in such a way that nature itself would recognize what had been done in it, yet deny that it could be done in it, since no harmony with customary experience showed that it could happen.

Thus a human being would give birth to God; thus earth would bring forth the divine; thus virginity would give birth to offspring; thus, with the man absent, a woman would bring forth a man.

You have heard the oracle of the Virgin, who truly conceived in the womb of the flesh and truly gave birth, just as she truly received and proclaimed in the womb of the mind; for by one Spirit she was made fruitful both for faith and for offspring.

After this, hear Elizabeth, who was married, naturally barren, advanced in years, distinguished in character, full of righteousness, walking before the Lord in his commandments, remaining in the Lord’s ordinances, persevering without reproach among her neighbors, the wife of a priest, certain in prophecy, acquainted with mysteries, instructed in sacred rites, and full of the Holy Spirit.

For when this Virgin of ours greeted her—to whose glory the things we are recounting belong—the infant leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And from where is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed, because the things spoken to her by the Lord shall be fulfilled.”

Next hear the confession of the aged Simeon, who, to rebuke your unbelief, could not obtain release from the senile decay of his limbs until he saw Christ, promised beforehand by the pledge of the Holy Spirit. For this is said concerning him:

“There was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was righteous and devout, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him. And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord. And he came in the Spirit into the temple; and when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he also took him in his arms, blessed God, and said: ‘Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace; because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for revelation to the nations, and the glory of your people Israel’” (Luke II).

You have heard the aged man, worn out with years and full of the Spirit of God. Hear what is said concerning the old woman Anna, who by office was a prophetess, distinguished by lineage, [Note: “Of a very well-known tribe and family,” Tol. and Amel.] most noble by tribe and family, of David.

First a virgin in body and mind, then honorable with a husband; not long-lived in the companionship of her husband, but exceedingly long-lived through eighty-four years of widowhood; an inhabitant of the temple; austere in fasts; rich in supplications; occupied day and night in the service of God—her name was Anna. [Note: “She too,” Tol. and Amel.; where the text has “is proved to speak,” they have “speaking, she prophesies.”]

For she too is shown to speak through the Spirit of God, when it is said of her: “And coming at that very moment, she gave thanks to the Lord and spoke about Jesus to all who were awaiting the redemption of Israel” (Luke II).

After this, hear the blind man, to whom this God, speaking of himself, said: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” He answered and said: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” And Jesus said to him: “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.” And he said: “I believe, Lord.” And falling down, he worshiped him (John IX).

Believe also Martha, who, although she doubted concerning the resurrection of her brother, could not doubt concerning the Son of God. When Jesus said to her: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John XI), he immediately questioned her, adding: “Do you believe this?” She answered: “Certainly, Lord; I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into this world.”

But why am I carried on at such length and scatter myself among various things, while I strive to overcome you, convicted by the testimony of individual persons? Let me pass individually to the guarantees of the witnesses who have been pledged. For it is enough that so many people have said so much and such things about such matters, although I have not set forth all the innumerable and innumerably existing truthful witnesses of this kind and greatness, who are so much nobler and more illustrious that they are both blessed in their earthly dwelling and exalted in their heavenly habitation.

But hear the general testimony of your people; hear the universal consent of your nation [Note: “All our copies have ‘consent’; Feu-ard. published ‘concession.’] when it is said: “Therefore many of the Jews who had come to Mary and had seen what Jesus did believed in him” (John XI).

Likewise, when he was already approaching the descent from the Mount of Olives, all the crowds who were descending began joyfully to praise the Lord with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Peace in heaven and glory in the highest” (Luke XIX). [Note: Both of these same codices write here: “Who comes, the King, in the name,” etc.]

Behold, you have been convicted by the testimony of the living; I shall still convict you by the attestation of the dead. For this is said concerning the time of his death: “When he had released his spirit, behold, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose” (Matt. XXVII). [Col. 0088A] “And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many.”

Have you heard the proclamations of the living? Have you heard the attestations of the dead? It is true that you have heard; nor will you be able to deny that you heard—or rather, certainly knew—and did not wish to believe.

But if you do not believe the testimony of the living and the attestation of the dead who rose again, I ask you at least to yield, submit, and obey the one whose dominion still holds you, whose command rules you, whose prompting torments you—and believe the demon confessing the Lord. Concerning him it is said:

“A certain man who had a demon for many years met him. He wore no clothing and did not live in a house but among the tombs. When he saw Jesus, he fell down before him, cried out with a loud voice, and said: ‘What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.’ For he was commanding the unclean spirit to come out of the man. For it had seized him for many years, and he was bound with chains and fetters and kept under guard; but breaking the bonds, he was driven by the demon into the deserts. Jesus asked him, saying: ‘What is your name?’ And he said: ‘Legion,’ because many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to go into the abyss” (Luke VIII).

Believe the demon, I beg you; believe, so that, by believing what he confesses, you may escape what he deserves. And while you do not contradict his confession, contradict his work, so that, in believing what he believes, you may cease to do what he does. Thus, taking up his voice, reject his work. Thus, confessing the common Maker and Lord, cast off the yoke of his servitude. Thus, having acknowledged his confession, cease to deny what you are compelled to deny by the demon’s prompting. [Note: We rightly rejected Feu-ard.’s corrupt reading, which has “while he fills” in place of “while he drives,” retained by all our copies and the ancient edition.]

## CHAPTER IX

By the testimony of the angels and the obedience of all insensible things, he teaches that Christ is God as well as man, so that from this the Jew may plainly conclude that he was able to preserve his mother together with the beauty of her virginity.

Hitherto I have brought forward testimony from the confines of the earth, from the inhabitants of the ground, from the sharers of the field, from the earthly company: from human society, human knowledge, human report, human speech, [Note: “From the human condition.” We do not read these words in Amel. or Trin.] from the human condition. I have produced a witness, introduced testimony, offered a declaration; I have established the proposition; I have supported what I said, asserted what I intended, [Col. 0088D] strengthened what I brought forward, [Note: We could not fail to prefer the reading of one Trin. manuscript to that of the others and to admit it into the main text. Thus Feuard. reads, together with the others: “And I showed a fuller truth and confirmation, which …” The word “which” requires another antecedent to which it might refer and sufficiently indicates that the reading is corrupt.] and shown firmly, with fuller truth, what I confidently introduced in the hearing concerning this faith.

Now, much happier, much more joyful, much more exalted, much more applauding, let me adorn what has been established, beautify what is firm, embellish what is solid; and, changing the arrangement of the regions, [Note: “Region,” Amel. and Trin.] after I have been supplied with the testimony of earthly things, after I overflow with the testimony of blessed human beings, after I delight in the confession of demons, let me seek the heavens, scrutinize heavenly things, [Note: “In the heavens,” in both.] inquire among celestial beings, traverse in faith and mind the regions of heaven. There, finding defenders of my proposition, I shall bring forth from that court of the heavenly army those who by the prerogative of my faith [Note: “By the privilege”; both.] may prove it, who may join more powerfully what I have said, bind more strongly what I have proposed, fasten more firmly what I have brought forward, establish with the solidity of eternal peace what I have recounted in the exertion of my defense, and consolidate with the warmth of eternity [Note: “Strength,” Trin.] what I, made slower and sluggish by the frailty of weariness, had constructed. [Note: We have emended this passage from the single Trin. manuscript, where it reads differently in the others and in Feuard.: “And gladly I had fastened it.” What does “gladly” mean here?]

Come, holy Gabriel, [Col. 0089B] and tell us the beginning of this matter, the origin of this miracle, the commencement of this work. For in the accomplishment of this work you are the first to greet the Virgin, you are the first to announce it to the Virgin, you are the first to proclaim it to the Virgin; instructed in heaven concerning the Word of God, you reveal on earth to the Virgin the new work of his Incarnation.

“Gabriel the angel was sent,” he says [Note: “He says” is absent from all our manuscripts.] (Luke I), by the Lord to a city of Galilee whose name was Nazareth [Note: All our manuscripts have “whose”; Feuard. printed “whose name was.”], to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary. And the angel entered to her and said: “Hail, [Note: Feuard. printed “Hail Mary,” but we do not read “Mary” in any of our manuscripts.] full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women, [Note: The following words are likewise absent from our manuscripts.] and blessed is the fruit of your womb.” When she heard this, she was troubled at his saying and considered what sort of greeting this might be. And the angel said to her: “Do not be afraid, Mary; you have found favor with the Lord. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

But Mary said to the angel: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” And the angel answered and said to her: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God.”

Again: “Joseph her husband, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her secretly. But while he was considering this, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: ‘Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife; for that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit. She shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins’” (Matthew I).

Again: “The shepherds were in that same region, keeping watch and guarding the watches of the night over their flock. And behold, an angel of the Lord [Note: Feuard. printed: “stood beside them in shining clothing.” But we read these last words in none of our manuscripts.] stood beside them, and the brightness of God shone around them, and they were afraid with great fear. And the angel said to them: ‘Do not be afraid; for behold, I proclaim to you great joy, which will be for all the people. For today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David’” (Luke I).

Again, while the angel was speaking there to the shepherds: “And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger.” And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying: “Glory [Note: Trin. has “in the highest.”] to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

Why should I recount the remaining testimonies and services of the angels, when, after the testing of human endurance, angels approach him and minister to him truly as Lord and Creator (Matthew IV)? What more? Angels are the first to announce his resurrection, [Note: All our manuscripts, together with the ancient edition, have “announce.” Only Feuard. has “proclaim.”] and, having terrified the guards of the tomb, they tell the faithful that the Living One is not to be sought among the dead (Matthew XXVIII). What more? Angels accompany his ascension, and angels testify that his return will be such as was his ascent (Acts I).

Behold, the earth has been filled with witnesses on my side, because heaven and earth alike have been filled with the truth of my faith. Behold, through witnesses on your side I have affirmed what I said; behold, through witnesses on my side I have strengthened what the witnesses on your side said. And therefore, both those whom you had taken [Note: “To assist your side.” These words are absent from all our manuscripts.] to assist your side and those whom I had produced have all become mine, because I learned from their teaching what I proposed. And the testimony of those men followed my proposition precisely where their knowledge preceded my defense. [Note: All our manuscripts read “preceded” before it; Feuard. has it afterward.]

What, then, remains? That you are without anyone and have absolutely no one; that you alone are guilty before yourself, while the sincerity of my faith possesses as one body all those whom you attempted to divide from the One. After the testimony of earthly and heavenly beings had supplied defenses for my case, after living things in heaven and on earth had been found to strengthen my truth, after both earthly blessedness and angelic exaltation had unanimously affirmed what it foresaw that I had truthfully brought before your hearing, I shall now present the attentive array of insensible and unintelligent elements and things, with their most fitting instruction and very long obedience, so that in comparison they may all feel this together [Note: “Commonly,” in place of “together,” is read in Tol. and Ame. and appears in the ancient edition.] as human beings, while you either dissent like an animal or do not feel at all like a stone.

Thus let those things wrest your reason from you, so that, since you do not obtain their obedience [Note: All our manuscripts have “obtain.” The Amelian manuscript continues: “May you deservedly fall by this sensibility.”], you may deservedly bear their insensibility. For by their movements, as though by voices, they cry out that confession. But while you repel the truth with words, you now seem, as it were, not to feel even through movements.

[Note: Here we give the variant reading of the Trin. and Amel. manuscripts: “See, then, first the star of the new birth, heralding it with a new arrangement of its procession.”]

See, then, first the star, brought forth at the beginning of the new birth with a novel procession, surpassing the heavens in brightness, outshining with its radiance the neighboring choirs of stars, approaching the farthest lands with its supreme light, going before the most devoted kings as they wandered through unknown places, pointing out the lodging of the one being born, and showing with all its strength that this one alone is the God to be worshiped, to whom by its guidance it subjected the worshiping kings. [Note: All the books, both printed and manuscript, agree in the sense of this sentence, though not in the wording. The Amel. manuscript reads: “See in the first work of his work the remarkable liquid that becomes wine from water; see how it changes color …” The Tolet. manuscript reads differently: “See the signs of his first work, and the liquid of the water from which wine is made; see how it changes color …”]

See the remarkable miracle in his first works: he changes water into wine (John II). Observe how he changes its color, takes on its taste, gives it an aroma, and changes its power. And although it is not at all what it was, it nevertheless comes from nowhere other than where it came from. If you seek water, it is no longer there; if you attend to the wine, say where it came from, since the water has not flowed away. What, then? Wine neither arrived nor did water depart, except that one thing was made another, so that one thing might be another from another—not by a process of succession, but by the origin of transformation; not through an explanation of reason, but for the sake of wonder.

See the loaves and the little fish (John VI), which, though they cannot speak through themselves, speak through the mouths of those from whom they were received. [Note: “Which cannot,” all our manuscripts.] And although they cannot express the power they feel, [Note: “Nevertheless” is absent from our manuscripts.] they nevertheless express with greater power the magnitude by which they increase. [Note: Amel. and Tol. read: “They express by their increase the greatness in which they grow.” This does not please us; but if the printed text read *magnitudine* (“by greatness”) rather than *magnitudinem* (“greatness”), as the Trin. manuscript also prefers, nothing further would be desired.] For, beyond the feeding and satiety of so many thousands, broken into fours they make up a threefold number of baskets [reading uncertain], which, untouched, could not fill even one basket. [Note: Feuard. printed “divided into fours, it consumed through idleness.” We have omitted *through*, a superfluous word absent from all our manuscripts.]

See the fig tree, so swiftly stripped of what it had been that it also as quickly lost what had lived; nor could it endure to lose its greenness through age unless it also lost its green life with equal speed (Matthew XXI).

See the sea (Matthew XIV). If its wave were turned into a tongue, it would surely utter what it murmurs; but because it does not know how to speak, it proves by what it cannot say that it has done this. [Note: “Because” is absent from our manuscripts and certainly seems unnecessary.] For while it supports the footprint of the Ruler, it overwhelms that of the servant; gliding beneath the servant’s body, it becomes stone beneath the weight of the Lord. At one command it bears two acts of service: beneath the strong foot of the Creator it becomes solid, and at his nod it supports the one who obeys him, whom it had refused in fear to support. [Note: We could not decline to admit the reading of the single Amelian manuscript, passing over Feuard.’s common reading, followed by the other manuscripts: “And it supports the assisted obedient one,” etc.]

See this same sea again. When it swelled with its movements, dashed its fierce sounds against the troubles of Charybdis with foaming crash, and wearied the little boat as it rebounded upon its proud back, see how, at the command of the one ordering it, it so quickly assumed calmness [Note: We have restored “calmness” in place of “slowness” from all our manuscripts. The following words are not found in the same form in them. The Amel. manuscript reads: “So that the inhabitants, marveling at the little boat, say …”] that the sailors and the inhabitants, marveling together, said: “Who is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?” (Matthew VIII).

Again, consider the inhabitants of the sea, how they flee the disciples’ commands as though they knew them very well, and refuse to be caught for capture; yet at the will of the Maker they fill the net in such abundance that, as they are hauled out, they become a burden to those who drag the weight along (Luke V).

See the varieties of illnesses, unable to retain their critical fevers [Note: We have followed the reading of the Amel. manuscript, with which the ancient edition cited by Feuard. agrees. Although “ethical recurrences,” as Feuard. printed it and the other manuscripts have it, could be retained because of the well-known fever called “hectic” by physicians today and “ethical” by the ancients, as though habitual, the other reading seemed better to us, because it more suitably explains the holy doctor’s meaning. “Cretical” recurrences may be interpreted as the moment at which, when a fever has advanced by degrees, its crisis or judgment takes place. This is what Saint Hildefonsus says: the illnesses did not wait for that moment, but immediately left the bodies of the sick at the Savior’s presence. “Physicians call these critical days,” writes Saint Isidore, *Etymologies* IV.9, “and I believe that this name was given to them from the judgment of illness, because they, as it were, judge a person and by their sentence either punish or free him.”] (Luke IV), but leaving the great number of the sick at the Savior’s presence.

See the buried and the tombs so sever among themselves the pact of burial that they quickly drive their eternal guests back from their monuments [Note: Trin. has “the pale ones.”] for a moment: as though you saw the frightened things restore those whom they had received, as if they had held captive those whom they had violently received to keep them. See the day of darkness lay aside the garment of light at the touch of the robe, and, with an unseen effort, acquire as quickly what grew dark as it swiftly loses what shone.

See the sun lose precisely that by which it had shone in joy, so that with pale light it might bring upon itself [Note: “Indicate,” Trin.] from grief what had shone. When the clasp of its luminous bond had been loosened, it cast away the yellow garment of unbreakable brightness and gathered itself, wrapped in the double robe [Note: “A double cloak,” in Am. together with the ancient edition.] of horror, into the corner of that day. [Note: Trin. and Am. have “repelling”; Feuard. printed “refuting.”]
