See the fields rejecting the stability of their solidity, so that through trembling both their open and their unknown places fell into ruins. [Note: Amel. and Trin. have “they fell”; the latter, with Feuard., has “to fall.”] They did not, after the example of Sicilian land, collapse gradually from moment to moment, but were shaken by the trembling of a single day, because the spirit received into the earth’s bosom disturbs the former, while the glory of the Crucified disturbs the latter.

See the rocks fleeing the hardness of their weight. Through the penetration of their fissures they are dissolved, as hardness yields to dissolution and solidity [Note: All our manuscripts read “succumbs to dispersal.” Feuard. has “succumbed to dissolution.” We could not retain the past tense, since the preceding “yields” is present.] succumbs to dissolution. They testify what power belongs to the one whom they immediately receive into themselves for burial, since, trembling, they honor the one already dead with the fissures of their confession. [Note: All our manuscripts have “with their fissures.”]

## CHAPTER X. He concludes that Mary remained a virgin throughout the whole mystery of the Incarnation.

[Col. 0093B]

Now take heed, and let examples of stones split your stony breast [Note: Our manuscripts, together with the ancient edition, read “split,” in place of “cut apart,” which Feuard. printed]; and see that all these things, by their movements, their transformations, and their efforts, profess nothing other than what you alone either try to deny as uncertain or, treacherously, deny as certain. [Note: Am. and Trin. have “or uncertain.”]

There is nothing in this truth for you to doubt as certain; nothing at which you need hesitate; nothing on which you need stumble; nowhere for you to fall; nowhere for you to go astray; nowhere for you to be uncertain; nowhere for you to waver; nowhere for you to falter; nowhere for you to tremble; nowhere for you to be in doubt; nowhere for you to hesitate; nowhere for you to be uncertain; nowhere for you to limp in mind; nowhere for you to slip in faith. [Note: Feuard. has “waving,” contrary to all our manuscripts.] Everything is true, everything is just, everything is holy, everything is sacred, everything is beyond doubt, everything is faithful; everything is fixed, everything is established, everything is confirmed forever and ever. These things were done in truth and equity, which the sacred writings have sung concerning them; which the sacred page has addressed; which the sacred letters have recorded; which the most sacred law has proclaimed; which the sacred testaments command; which the most sacred books [Note: “Most sacred,” as we print from all our manuscripts, is also found in the ancient edition. Feuard. alone writes “life-giving.”] contain; which sacred decrees determine; which heavenly laws establish; which, though heaven and earth pass away, do not pass away in their eternity; which cannot pass away even when the elements pass away, until all things are fulfilled.

With the enemies conquered, adversities crushed, rivals extinguished, foes worn down, those who insulted cast prostrate, the envious thrown down, [Note: Trin. and Amel. have “destroyed.”] and all who contradicted the power of divine strength [Note: “Strength,” the same manuscripts.] subdued, I—plaintive in pious longing, eager with good desire [Note: Feuard. printed “affection”; all our manuscripts read, as we print, “desire.”], breathless with joyful hunger, most ready in grateful delight—shall direct, strive, carry out, and attempt, as I can, as I am able, as I may, and as I have strength, to fix my gaze upon this mystery, to press my dulling eyes [Note: In place of “to press,” found in our manuscripts and the ancient edition, Feuard.’s single edition has “to impose.”] into this wonder of mighty works, to plunge my eager understanding [Note: The Tol. manuscript reads “to fix,” and the ancient edition agrees.] into this secret of mystery, and to direct the dim beam of my vision toward this light of heavenly glory.

But how may I presume? How shall I begin? With what effort shall I hurry? [Note: In place of “sight,” which Feuard. corruptly printed, “effort” should be read; the manuscripts are silent, but all ours and the ancient edition have it.] With what exertion shall I attack it? With polluted lips, unclean mouth, impure tongue, foul speech, a wicked heart, an unjust mind, and ungodly deeds—so that corruption may discuss the glory of virginity, impurity may handle the praise of incorruption [Note: Amel. reads “may attempt,” but erroneously.], the shameless may speak of modesty, [Note: The Trin. manuscript reads: “that an immodest man may narrate the good of modesty.” This reading is not without merit.] and the shameless may expound the good of modesty?

Yet now, because God came to human beings so that I might be saved, cleansed, justified, and sanctified, [Note: Trin. has “to earthly things.”] heavenly things came down to the lowest things; the strong descended to the weak; eternal things were joined to temporal things; [Note: Trin. has “were joined.”] the robust were joined to the feeble [Note: We restore “to the feeble” from the Am. manuscript; the others, with Feuard., read “feeble”]; things belonging to the Lord were joined to things belonging to servants.

Full of blessed faith, to be saved by abundant mercy, to be justified by great compassion, to be made alive by divine pity, to be cleansed from every iniquity committed [Note: Except for the Trin. and Amel. manuscripts, the others have “wicked,” an unnecessary adjective, since no iniquity is not wicked], I shall speak to the angel about the festivals of joys, about the gladness of his delight, about my redemption, my salvation, and my life; I shall ask the angel, question the angel, and address the angel.

Tell me, friend of God, and nearer to all things through contemplation; speak, most eminent of creatures; recount, more powerful than creatures; [Note: Amel. and Trin. manuscripts, together with the ancient edition, have “arise.”] begin, creature who after the firmament knows no fall, magnificent in your glory, great in your creation, powerful in your order, excellent in your nature, enduring in your eternity. I do not diminish your glory, I do not lessen your greatness, I do not wear away your eternity, I do not detract from your sublimity [Note: “From the sublime,” the same manuscripts.], I do not rebel against one more powerful, because I am speaking not of your stability but of your creation.

Faith provokes me, love drives me, wonder delights me, joy makes me glad; the grace of the merciful goes before me, [Note: Tol. has “of mercy.”] and most welcome compassion follows me. [Col. 0095A]

You, holy Gabriel, angel of the Lord, who are sent to the Virgin of Israel, who come to the mother of the Lord, who hasten to the unique virginal glory in the world, tell me what is more incorrupt, more sincere, more whole, more solid: maternal virginity or the angelic condition; virginal fecundity or angelic formation [Note: Amel. has “portion”]; incorruptible virginal glory or the beginning of the angels; modesty increased by offspring or the beginning of angelic nobility.

Which is greater: virginity [Note: All our manuscripts read “virginity”; Feuard. printed “virgin.”] that bears fruit and is not corrupted, or the angelic height, part of which was cast down in ruin? Virginal beauty, which shines even after childbirth, or angelic nobility, which after the glory of its summit bears losses among its companions? Maternal integrity, which even after childbirth increases in the glory of the Virgin [Note: All our manuscripts have “after the child”;] or the angelic condition, which was injured by losses among those cast out? [Note: We print this period according to all our manuscripts, which agree in the middle of the question, except that Tolet. has: “Or your angelic multitude …” Feuard. printed: “ … from which your angelic multitude is ignorant of corruption …” But once the particle “or,” retained by all our manuscripts, is removed, this period does not agree well with the preceding ones, in which the comparison is framed through questions between the praises of the Virgin Mary and those of the angels.]

The blessedness of the mother, from which the generation of God comes forth, and which is itself ignorant of corruption—or the glory of your multitude, which suffered a diminution of part of its number before attaining stability?

It is certain that pride broke the angelic camps, presumption diminished their ranks, wickedness reduced their multitudes, and arrogance struck down their companies. But the offspring born of my Lady did not injure her virginity by entering or leaving; neither conception nor birth violated it; neither did he grieve her while dwelling within her, nor deprive her of incorruption when he departed from her.

This woman is made a virgin by conception. This woman is preserved a virgin by childbirth. This woman is kept a virgin by generation. The Son knew this woman after his departure just as he found her before conception. And certainly her virginity is always incorrupt, always whole, always uninjured, always inviolate.

For the angelic form of nature was fragile before stability, falling before firm establishment, collapsing before permanence, wavering and tottering before strength. This woman is the vessel of sanctification, the eternity of virginity, the mother of God, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, the uniquely singular temple of her Creator.

Yet the blessed condition of the angelic creature, after its establishment, is solid in goodness; after its solidity, unfailing in love of the divinity; after its firm establishment, enduring in the vision of the Lord; after its strength, inseparable from fellowship with the Godhead.

From what immense light do you come, holy Gabriel, to the Virgin [Note: Trin. and Amel. have “to the human being”]; from what blessedness do you hasten to the Virgin; from what eternity do you approach temporal things; from what glory do you hurry toward human beings? Yet everything you do—your coming from heaven, your coming to earth, your coming from God, your coming to the Virgin, your greeting of the Virgin, your announcement of a new generation—you do in obedience to the Word becoming incarnate. You prepare for God, who is about to assume a human being; you serve the one being born from a Virgin, the Son of the handmaid; you minister to the Son of the handmaid, who is about to be born in the form of a servant.

For this God who is to become incarnate is your Maker; this one, at once human and God, is your Creator; this Son of his handmaid is your Lord; this one whom you announce as about to be born in the abasement of a servant is your Ruler in the glory of the Father.

And it was fitting that an angel should announce the glory of so great a birth. It was suitable that an angel should serve the oracles of so great a dignity. It was appropriate that an angel should reveal the work of so new a generation. It was proper that an angel should disclose the secrets of so great a mystery. Thus, too, it was fitting that angelic sublimity should recount the humility of God. It was suitable that heavenly dominion, serving him, should proclaim that the Lord of all things was to be born in the form of a servant. It was worthy that angelic dignity, through a new service of majesty, should make known a new generation. It was just that angelic knowledge should demonstrate how the ineffable cause of the miracle would occur. It was most just that, at the new coming, the highest beings of heaven should precede with a new array the Ruler who was about to come forth.

Thus you were the messenger of your Lord; thus you had come, sent by your Lord; thus you fulfilled the commands of the Lord’s mission; thus, truly, you completed the decrees of the royal ordering: so that what you had learned in heaven concerning the Father’s Word you might report to the mother concerning the Word becoming incarnate; what you had brought from heavenly things you might impress upon earthly things; and how the Son of God wished to be born from a human being, you might bring into the ears of human beings [Note: Amel. has “into their ears”] and place into human hearts [Note: Amel. has “mysteries.”]

You, holy angel Gabriel, had learned from the Word what you were reporting about the Word; from the Word you had known what you were recounting about the Word that was to be known; from the Word you had drawn what you were offering to the Virgin who was to bear. [Note: From the Tol. manuscript we print “who was to bear”; the others read “which was to be drawn.”] Thus you might announce to the soul of the mother how he could become incarnate from the flesh of the mother.

The heavenly powers saw you serve the commands of the Son who was to be born. The elements saw you regard as Lord the one whom you announced as about to be born from such a lineage. The companions of your glory saw themselves bow with you before this human being. All the powers of the exalted and sublime spirits saw this human being assumed into God, and they brought forward the services of their ancient servitude with new proclamations, when the cry rang out: “Glory in the highest to this humble God, and on earth peace to people who believe in this humble God with good will” (Luke II).

He sent you, so that you might speak to the Virgin about himself, [Note: “Who had given you to know what he would be,” etc. Here we follow the Trin. and Amel. manuscripts, which offer a better reading than Feuard.: “So that you might tell the Virgin what he was and what he would be,” etc.] he who had given you knowledge of what he would be. He filled you with the knowledge of his divinity, he who made you the messenger of his humanity. He sent you to announce that he would be born in the form of a servant, he whom, in your glory, you worshiped as united with the Father’s power. He sent you openly to report him to the world, he who had instructed you in the secrets of heavenly mysteries.

Well for you, because you announce the restoration of the diminished part of your company; well for me, because through your announcement you receive me into your integrity. Well for you, because through human beings the fallen part of the angelic host is restored; well for me, because I am brought back into a share of your integrity. Well for you, because you receive human beings into your peace; well for me, because I have received your peace, which I did not deserve. Well for you, because you worship the incarnate Word; well for me, because that truth which you worship belongs to my nature. [Note: Trin. and Tol. have “that one is the truth whom you worship.”]

We are blessed, holy angel, to possess one title of the ruling God; our God has promised, through a written pledge, [Note: Feuard. printed “Holy Michael, angel,” but “Michael” is absent from all our manuscripts. Amel. and Tol. have “one” in place of “of one.”] that I should become your companion in the glory of eternity. [Note: “Glory” is absent from our manuscripts; Amel. then writes “advocacy” in the note.] He rightly promised me that I should have heaven with you, because he wished me, as he wished you, to have the one God. He marked me with the imprint of his name, because he redeemed me from the blood of that body which you worship, behold, and venerate in the Father’s seat.

It is part of your lot never to fall from the state of blessedness; it is part of mine that after my fall I may be restored through the assumption of the body of my God. It is part of your lot always to be with my God; it is part of mine that I may one day be able to be with my God. It is part of your lot never to fall away from the blessedness of your nature; it is part of mine that I may one day be restored to the dignity of my nature. It is part of your lot to worship my nature in my God; it is part of mine to be saved because my nature has been assumed in my God.

Clearly, what I recount, what I affirm, what I speak, what I declare, is true, just, and holy. And it will remain as full of heavenly understanding as it stands complete. For these things are not mine; they do not come from me; they are not from my nature; they are not from my condition; they are not from my merit.

For I am ash, earth, corruption, decay, food for worms, a companion in an unwanted yet unavoidable mortal inheritance. My dwelling is dug-out earth, my rest a mound, my house a tomb, my habitation a monument.

But these things have been revealed to me by the Father who is in heaven; I learned them from his Son, who is his wisdom; I came to know them with the Holy Spirit teaching me. These things came from heaven, because they are excellent gifts. They descended from the Father of lights, because in them there is no alteration of truth (James I).

For on earth, in your company, I have learned these things which you yourself know with me in heaven. I learned these things in the place of my pilgrimage, which you already know in the eternity of your blessedness. [Note: Our manuscripts read “of your blessedness” rather than Feuard.’s “your.”] I have received these things in the truth of my faith, which you have known in the fullness of your vision. Because you, coming from heaven, made these things known to me while performing the service of announcing the humanity that was to be assumed.

The angels testified to these things when, having attained knowledge of the birth of this human being, they proclaimed it in heavenly hymns, crying: “Glory in the highest to God, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II). The angels demonstrated these things when, after conquering the enemy’s temptation, they approached and ministered to him (Matthew IV). The angels showed these things when, marveling at the new human being ascending to the seat of the Godhead, they called to one another in alternating voices: [Note: Tolet. has: “They commanded one another with alternating voices.”]

“Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Psalm XXIII).

And when they replied, “Who is this King of glory?” the following answer confirmed it: “The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory.”

David demonstrated these things when he said: [Note: “Demonstrates,” Am. and Trin.] [Note: All our manuscripts have “Let all his angels worship him.”] “Worship him, all his angels” (Psalm XCVI). He indicates the same thing when he says: “Praise him, all his angels” (Psalm CXLVIII).

Isaiah introduces these things when he testifies that the cherubim and seraphim, moved by the exultation of this praise, continually cry out: “Holy, holy, holy” (Isaiah VI). [Note: Our manuscripts have it somewhat differently: “So that the thrice-repeated ‘Holy’ might demonstrate that, in the inseparable Trinity [Trin.: ‘the inseparable Trinity’], there is one Lord God Sabaoth.”] Thus the name “Holy,” repeated three times, demonstrates that the inseparable Trinity is one Lord God Sabaoth.

John confirms these things when he says that the living creatures of heaven have no rest, declaring the same hymn of heavenly glory (Revelation IV). He likewise indicates them when he says:

“I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne, and of the living creatures and the elders; and their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing.’ And every creature that is in heaven, and on earth, and under the earth, and those that are in the sea, and those that are in the air, I heard all saying: ‘To the one seated on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing, and honor, and glory, and power, forever and ever. Amen’” (Revelation V). [Note: We have preferred the reading of the single Amelian manuscript to the others, not without reason: where it reads “in the air,” the others, with Feuard., retain “in it,” which has no sense.]

Paul sets these matters forth fully in the Epistle to the Hebrews, takes them up, confirms them, and [Note: [Col. 0098D] “Praises,” Amelianus and the old edition.] concludes them (Colossians II). This the very Man in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily [Note: [Col. 0098D] “In whom,” Toletanus.] completes, when he says that at his coming the powers of heaven will be shaken, and that then he himself will be seen in the glory of God the Father with his angels (Mark XIII).

## CHAPTER XI. He concludes, by the testimony of the angels, that the virginity of Saint Mary, Mother of God, was preserved perpetually.

Behold, I learned from heavenly teaching not only that the angels serve my Lord, the son of his own handmaid, our Virgin, but also came to know more truly their duties through the experience of servitude. For you yourself, Gabriel, who are called “the strength of God,” came to the Virgin to announce that a man would be born who would at once destroy the aerial powers and the prince of the world [Note: [Col. 0099D] “Would conquer,” in Amelianus and Toletanus.]. Likewise, the angels announce to the shepherds the one who had been foretold by you to the Virgin as destined to be born. They too glorify as God the one of whom you had said: “He will be called the Son of God.”

Behold, the angels adore him; behold, the archangels praise him; behold, the angels sound forth a hymn to him; behold, the angels minister to him; behold, the angels proclaim that he ascends the throne of the Godhead; behold, the angels do not know how to rest in his rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0099D] We have emended “of him” from all our manuscripts, which read “of whose.”]; behold, as they hasten in his service, we recognize the angels, and we have heard that the powers of heaven are shaken. For it is certainly most fitting that the glory of the angelic dignity should serve so exalted and eternal a God, born so humbly and temporally from a Virgin.

Why? Because he was born incomprehensibly and ineffably in both births. The whole company of angels, however, was preceded by his eternity and formed by his operation. Of him it is said: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isaiah XXXV). The same thing this Virgin wonders at in your greeting: by your words she is established as a virginal mother, and when that same Virgin asks you how this would happen, you announce to her an unheard-of generation. Of you, however, it is said: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis I)—and there came to be a light of your nature, prior and superior to all creatures [Note: [Col. 0099D] The reading “superior” is supported by all manuscript copies. Feuardentius printed “posterior,” not without error.].

To him it was said: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm II; Hebrews I), something never said to any of the angels. Of the whole creation it was said: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Psalm VIII). Among all these things, the angelic substance too is found subject to him. Of him it was said: “Sit at my right hand” (Psalm CIX), something not said to the angels. Of them, because they were made, it was said: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Psalm CIII) [Note: [Col. 0099D] “Burning,” in Amelianus and Toletanus.].

Of him it was said: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Psalm XLIV). Of them it was said that the whole host of angels stands before him with trembling.

But so that I may celebrate with the heavenly powers the glory of this Lady, my Virgin, with a greater triumph, a more exalted proclamation, faithful effort, a most sincere vow [Note: [Col. 0099D] We could not retain “most sincerely,” which we read in Feuardentius: it is barbarous, and all our manuscripts write “most sincere.”], and loving desire; so that I may prefer it to enemies destined to perish, report it to brothers who love it, proclaim it to those who will learn it though they are ignorant, and commend it, once known, to those who delight in it [Note: [Col. 0099D] “To those who delight,” Amelianus and Trinitas. Toletanus has “to those who will delight in it.”]—I still desire to know, wish to understand, long to comprehend, hope to be assured, beg to be instructed, and seek to be taught what this means: “Who will recount his generation?”

If this is said of the birth of his divinity—which is certainly true, since it is said on account of these things, though not on account of these things alone [Note: [Col. 0099D] “And certainly so.” Amelianus and Trinitas have this reading and continue: “It is true, because on account of this, but not only on account of this, etc.”]—behold, this birth of the Godhead is simply this: God was born from God, God Light from God Light, God the Word from the mouth of God [Note: [Col. 0099D] “True God,” Trinitas.], God Wisdom from the heart of God, God Power from the substance of God—and all these are one God.

Again, if this was said of the birth of his humanity—which is certainly true, since it was also said on account of this—what is the generation of this Son, proclaimed so wondrously ineffable, except an incorrupt conception, a virgin giving birth, a virginal childbirth, a maternal virginity, a virginal nativity? And all these belong to a fruitful virgin, an incorrupt mother, an intact childbearing woman, an inviolate mother, an unharmed bearer of offspring. In her, diversity so harmonized, accidents so cohered, manifold things were so joined together, and converging elements so intertwined that in this one Virgin a single person came to be from two things unheard-of, though separated by an eternal law [Note: [Col. 0099D] “One person.” These words are absent from all our manuscripts.].

This, then, is truly the ineffable generation of this one and only offspring. But the Virgin says: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke I).

Let the angel answer: “The Spirit of the Lord will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0100D] We print this period according to the reading of the Amelian manuscript, which we consider preferable to all the others, although Feuardentius’s reading is not wholly to be despised: “Apart from this woman, no mother has been seen to be a virgin; but she, after being a mother, has been seen to be a virgin. After incorruption, she has been seen to become a mother; she has been seen to have genital modesty and to have offspring.” The reading of the Toletanus manuscript is certainly not so, being exceedingly corrupt. We are pleased to present it here: “Apart from this, it has not been customary for a mother to be a virgin; apart from this, however, it has been customary to be a virgin; it has been customary for a virgin to be a virgin; after being a virgin, it has been customary to be a mother; it has been customary to be an incorrupt woman; after incorruption, it has been customary to become a mother; it has been customary to have genital modesty; after genital modesty, it has been customary to have offspring.”]

Apart from this, being a virgin is customary; after being a mother, remaining a virgin is not customary. Being an incorrupt woman is customary; after incorruption, becoming a mother is not customary. Having virginal modesty is customary; after virginal modesty, having offspring is not customary. These things differ from one another by so great an eternal law of nature that a woman is never then a mother when she is a virgin, never then a virgin when she is a mother; a virgin never gives birth, nor does a mother shine with virginity; a single moment never hold her as both virgin and mother [Note: [Col. 0101D] Feuardentius printed “to be both” (“esse et matrem”). All our manuscripts lack “to be”; therefore we have excluded it.]; a single woman never rejoices in virginity together with offspring.

Hence such a generation is not uniquely a sign, not wondrously a marvel, not ineffably evident, not from something certain—for it is not a sign, not a marvel, not wondrous, not ineffable. For it is natural, customary, corruptible, and mortal. At times it is shamefully lovable; at times it is honorably hateful. At times it ought justly to be loved; at times it is justly to be hated.

But in this Virgin the ineffable generation of this Son of God joined both things together in such a way that the mother possesses herself as a virgin and the virgin possesses herself as a mother; so that the offspring has a virgin mother [Note: [Col. 0101D] Feuardentius lacks “mother,” but our manuscripts have it.], and the husband may marvel at the virgin who has given birth. Let integrity also adhere to the conception, modesty surround the conception, and virginity enclose the conceived child. Thus let birth not cleave virginity; thus let the emergence not defile modesty; thus let generation not take away integrity; thus let the reality of childbirth not extinguish the reality of virginity.

With the differences of things therefore agreeing so wondrously in one person and at one time, so that the same woman is both mother and virgin, the very virgin is also mother, never mother except when she is also virgin, and, after becoming mother, more noble as a virgin—this alone was the ineffable generation that came to pass. I consider it wondrous for this reason: I do not perceive that some explanation of how it happened lies hidden there, an explanation that cannot be revealed; rather, I perceive only that it happened—and that it is therefore a sign, a marvel, something unheard-of and unprecedented.

That it is truly ineffable is not unknown even when its own announcement is narrated. For if there were something hidden, and yet that very thing were nothing other than knowledge of its explanation, anyone capable of reasoning could to some extent grasp it by inquiry, discover it through acumen, gather it through invention, consider it through collection, meditate on it through consideration, define it through meditation, retain it through definition, express it through retention, or confirm it through expression.

But since I think that neither angels nor human beings know anything in this matter otherwise or more fully than what we learned when the angel himself announced it, I think that the angel himself was not able to recognize anything other than what he himself brought to announce to human beings. For in so great a mystery of truth, the herald could announce neither anything other than what he himself understood nor anything more than what he himself knew.

Yet what he announced he announced also to us, and made us hear it together with the Virgin, since we have learned this neither otherwise nor elsewhere than in the Virgin and with the Virgin [Note: [Col. 0101D] We read “we are convinced, and he is convinced” in our manuscript.].

If, therefore, that Virgin who was both the material of this miracle and the cause of its fulfillment learned from the angel only what could suffice for the effect of the announced event, the angel knew no more than what he said. He said only as much as made the Virgin give birth; he said only as much as fulfilled the Virgin’s conception and childbirth.

Thus the Virgin learned from the angel’s greeting only as much about her conception and childbirth as the angel’s evident announcement of this matter has taught me. But if the angel knew more than he said, how could what the Virgin heard with me suffice for the fullness of her childbirth? I say that she heard it with me because, after this announcement of her childbirth and my redemption, she heard nothing new about this matter.

If the angel knew more than he said, how did what was said fully and abundantly suffice for the completion of the event? If the angel knew more than he said, how could half-complete words more truly bring to completion a matter completed by the testimony of the heavenly powers and of all the elements [Note: [Col. 0102D] “To fulfill,” our manuscripts.]?

It therefore remains that I know only as much about this miracle as the angel said. For he said as much as he knew, and he said as much as made the Virgin give birth. But as much as he made the Virgin give birth, so much did my faith, together with the Virgin herself, come to know.

Therefore, if, according to the assumption of humanity, this ineffable generation of this offspring is the same thing as the unique incorruption of his mother alone, I rightly prefer the integrity of this mother, which could not be interrupted by the emergence of the one being born, to the angelic creation, which could fall.

I rightly prefer the virginal beauty, which could not be impaired by the birth of the one born, to the angelic condition, which could be diminished. I rightly prefer the modesty that the beginning of the one begotten could not frustrate to the angelic formation, which could be reduced. I rightly prefer the wonderfully singular virginity, which the birth of the Son of God left increased by so great a glory of incorruption, to the state of the angels, which could be shaken.

For, having assumed that flesh uniquely and uniquely glorifying it, he brought it to the Father’s throne, and subjected every blessedness of the angelic form to its dominion. In the ascent of this exalted solemnity, when God placed the assumed flesh upon the paternal throne, the nature of man found such peace with the angels, received such fellowship with the angels, and understood that it had attained such honor over the angels; it so placed above the power of angels the lowliness by which it had been despised, that this nature—in which Abraham adored an angel (Genesis XVIII), though it was not forbidden to be adored—was forbidden, in John, to adore when it wished to adore (Revelation XXII).

For in Abraham, although it was said that this nature would be assumed in Christ from his seed, it had not yet been assumed in that same Christ. Therefore the angels judged it contemptible, because the condemnation of the Creator also held it accursed, and because its assumption had not yet joined it to his union [Note: [Col. 0103D] We do not find “this” in our manuscripts.].

But in John the angels forbid this nature to adore them, because they adore this nature above themselves upon the throne of majesty. Therefore they do not despise it among those subject to it, because they behold it above themselves upon the throne of glory. They do not scorn it as contemptible among those subjected to it, because they know it united to the divine person.

And therefore they consider the incorruption of the mother’s virginity more honorable than themselves, because they behold its fruit above themselves with wonder and humility: grateful, they praise it; serving, they adore it; everlasting, they rejoice; subject, they celebrate it together [Note: [Col. 0103D] “They celebrate together,” in all our manuscripts and in Feuardentius; “they celebrate” in others.]; blessed, they see it; bowing down, they adore it [Note: [Col. 0103D] We read “bowing” in Trinitas and Toletanus.].

I think that nothing requiring reasoning remained hidden, nothing requiring examination escaped, nothing requiring further inquiry broke forth, nothing requiring investigation exceeded our grasp, and nothing unknown went away. For as much of the matter as we heard, so much do we know to have been fulfilled; as much of the matter as we heard, so much do we understand to have been accomplished; as much as we heard, so much do we know this generation to have become; as much as we heard from the angel, so much do we see completed for our redemption from the Virgin’s womb [Note: [Col. 0103D] Toletanus: “As great a matter as we heard, so great a fulfillment we know.”].

But so that the greatness of this matter may clearly raise itself above the angels; so that the incorruption of this mother alone, proclaimed as a singular sign, may transcend the exalted things of the angels; so that the ineffable generation of this incorrupt Virgin’s Son may surpass the nobility of the angels [Note: [Col. 0103D] “More noble” is lacking in Amelianus and Trinitas.]; and finally, so that, having nothing like it in all the formation of things, it may stand evident in a greatness at which angelic beauty marvels [Note: [Col. 0103D] “Nor having anything like it” is found in the same manuscripts.], consider with me the nature of things, contemplate the form of creatures, observe the diverse conditions of the whole creation, and believe John when he says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I).

See all the things he established, all the things he made, all the things that are visible and invisible [Note: [Col. 0104D] Trinitas substitutes “to be”; Amelianus, “to subsist.”], and you perceive them existing, holding the reverence of his service and maintaining the lowliness of a condition subject to him.

For if the question concerns the lands, the sea, and all that is in them, let everything hear the voice of the Lord himself, who by the force of his authority confers all things upon man: “Rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and all living creatures that move upon the earth” (Genesis I) [Note: [Col. 0104D] “Let all things hear from the Lord himself, etc.” Thus Trinitas, which lacks “his own,” found later.].

If it concerns man himself, let him too hear: “Kings of the earth, serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Psalm II).

If it concerns the heavens and the things in them, let them hear: “Your angels praised you, Lord, and sang a hymn when you completed the structure of heaven” (Psalm CXLVIII) [Note: [Col. 0104D] We have printed “when you completed,” which all manuscripts read. Feuardentius alone has “when he completes.”].

Again: “Blessed is the one whose God is his helper, whose hope is in him who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them” (Psalm CXLV) [Note: [Col. 0104D] Feuardentius printed “the God of Jacob,” but we find “Jacob” in none of our manuscripts.].

If it concerns the angels, let them hear what Paul recalls: “When he brings the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: ‘Let all his angels adore him’” (Hebrews I).

But so that I may restrain all things, as though by the fetter of their common condition, with one general statement, let everything hear under one head: “You are great, Lord, and glorious in power, unconquerable. Every creature of yours will serve you, because you spoke and they came to be; you sent your Spirit, and they were created” (Judith XVI).

If, therefore, all things that have been made serve, nothing remains equal to the Maker, because what serves the Lord belongs to the Lord. But if there is something that does not serve, it is nothing, because what does not serve has not been made. Therefore either something will exist, and it is made and serving; or it will be nothing, because what does not serve has not been made.

If, then, as is true, all things that have been made retain the debt of servitude, they do not lose the dominion of his eternal power [Note: [Col. 0104D] “They do not lose dominion,” in Trinitas and Toletanus; “they do not admit dominion,” in the old edition.]. All things yield to his majesty in proportion as they could not at all be made equal to his excellence.

And therefore, while all things serve him, the fruit of this incorruption alone is taken up into dominion over all. While all things obey, the Lord is joined to this generation alone. While all things serve, the Lord is united to this integrity alone.

For of all creatures, this alone becomes one with the Lord in person; this alone is assumed into the unity of the Creator; this alone is joined in union with the Ruler—to such an extent that God who assumes is called the Son of Man, and man who is assumed is called the Son of God.

The properties of the natures are not confused, but are joined in the unity of the person in such a way that, from the one assumed and the one assuming, neither departs from the other, nor is either separated from the other.

Since God who assumes is called the Son of Man, the evangelist expresses this by saying: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty with his angels” (Matthew XXV). This majesty, and his angels [Note: [Col. 0104D] “Could not belong to another,” Amelianus.], could not belong to any nature other than that of the Son of God, who is truly almighty God.

Again, since man who is assumed is called the Son of God, another evangelist assigns this to the Virgin, saying: “Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I).

Because of this property of the two natures joined in the unity of the person, this one Christ, God and man, has a human mother who is a virgin. Thus she generates one Son in both natures, so that the same one is the Son of God who is the Son of Man; and there is no other Son of Man than the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0105D] Feuardentius printed “than he who is the Son of God.” We retain the reading found in all our manuscripts.].

Hence this generation is more wondrous than every miracle, more powerful than every work, more august than every sign. For it so transcends all things, so surpasses all things, and so exceeds the excellence of all things that even the angels minister to this nature joined to God [Note: [Col. 0105D] We follow the reading of Amelianus and Toletanus, which we judged preferable to Feuardentius: “joined to God”; Trinitas likewise has “united to God.”], the angels serve it, the angels adore it [Note: [Col. 0105D] Amelianus and Toletanus write “him,” and shortly afterward have “and also” for “and her.”], and with infinite and tireless voices they praise it without end in the unity of the person of the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0105D] Feuardentius printed “for infinite ages,” but we find no “ages” in any of our manuscripts.].

Therefore I entreat you, holy angel, by the indivisible inheritance of our faith, by the state of your eternity, by the mystery of my redemption, and by the peace that both of us enjoy in the body of Christ Jesus [Note: [Col. 0105D] “In the body of Christ the Lord,” Amelianus.], grant me to know as much about the Virgin Mother of my Lord as you yourself know; to believe what you yourself understand; to love what you yourself love; and to enjoy the Lord in the way that you yourself enjoy him.

## CHAPTER XII. He turns his discourse to the most blessed Mother and to her glorious Son. He also concludes against the impious profaners of inviolate virginity.

But now I come to you, the one Virgin, Mother of God; I fall prostrate before you, the one work of the Incarnation of my God; I humble myself before you, the one mother found for my Lord. I beseech you, the one handmaid found for your Son, to obtain that the deeds of my sin be blotted out; to command that I be cleansed from the iniquity of my work; to make me love the glory of your virtue [Note: [Col. 0105D] Amelianus and Trinitas, as well as the old edition, read “of your virginity” instead of “of your virtue.”]; to reveal to me the abundance of your Son’s sweetness; to grant me to speak and defend the sincerity of faith in your Son [Note: [Col. 0105D] “Your sincerity and that of your Son,” Amelianus.].

Grant me also to cling to God and to you; to serve your Son and you; to minister to your Lord and to you [Note: [Col. 0105D] “To your Lord,” in all our manuscripts. Feuardentius lacks “your.”]; to him as my Maker, to you as the mother of my Maker; to him as Lord of the powers, to you as the handmaid of the Lord of all; to him as God, to you as the Mother of God; to him as my Redeemer, to you as the work of my redemption.

For what he accomplished in my redemption he formed in the reality of your person [Note: [Col. 0105D] “Established,” in Amelianus, Toletanus, and the old edition.]. In becoming my Redeemer, he was your Son. In becoming the price of my redemption, his incarnation was from your flesh.

In order to heal my wounds, he displayed from your flesh a body destined to be wounded [Note: [Col. 0106D] Feuardentius has “in which”; all our manuscripts have “in whom.”]. In order to remove my death, he drew a mortal body from the body of your mortality. In order to blot out my sins, he received without sin the body that he took from you [Note: [Col. 0106D] “Which he removed,” in all our manuscripts.]. He assumed in the reality of your body, in humility, my nature—the nature that, as my forerunner, he placed in himself above the angels in the glory of the Father’s throne.

Therefore I am your servant, because your Son is my Lord [Note: [Col. 0106D] “Because the Lord is your Son,” Amelianus.]. Therefore you are my Lady, because you are the handmaid of my Lord [Note: [Col. 0106D] “Of your Son,” likewise.]. Therefore I am the servant of the handmaid of my Lord, because you, my Lady, have become the mother of your Lord. Therefore I have become your servant, because you have become the mother of my Maker.

I beseech you, I beseech you, holy Virgin, that from that Spirit I may have Jesus from whom you gave birth to Jesus. Through that Spirit may my soul receive Jesus through whom your flesh conceived that same Jesus. From that Spirit may I know Jesus from whom you received the knowledge of having and giving birth to Jesus.

In that Spirit may I speak of Jesus in humble and exalted terms [Note: [Col. 0106D] “Humble and exalted things,” Amelianus and Toletanus, together with the old edition.], in whom you confess yourself to be the handmaid of the Lord, desiring that it be done to you according to the angel’s word. In that Spirit may I love Jesus, in whom you adore him as Lord and behold him as Son [Note: [Col. 0106D] “You may fear,” in both of the same witnesses.].

May I fear this Jesus as truly as he, being God, was truly subject to his parents (Luke II:51).

O reward of both my salvation and my life, and likewise of my glory—great in its immense abundance! O most noble title of my freedom! O splendid condition of my free birth! O my nobility’s testimony, gloriously irrevocable and perfected in the eternity of glory! Thus, though I was miserably deceived, I desire to become, for my restoration, the servant of the mother of my Lord; thus I, once separated from the fellowship of the angels in the first Adam, may deserve to be fashioned a servant of the handmaid and mother of my Maker; thus I, a fitting work in the hands of the Most High God, may obtain, in servitude to the Virgin who gives birth, to be bound in perpetual devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0106D] Am. writes “protection” in place of “life.”]

[Note: [Col. 0106D] The same witness reads “most noble title.”]

[Note: [Col. 0106D] Am. reads “from angelic fellowship”; Tol. has “led astray” for “separated.”]

[Note: [Col. 0106D] All our manuscripts read “to be cast” (*conjici*).]

[Note: [Col. 0106D] “In the devotion of servitude.” We have restored “in” from all our manuscripts.]

Grant this to me, Jesus, God and Son of man; bestow this on me, Lord of all things and son of a handmaid; lavish this upon me, humble God in man; concede this to me, gloriously human in God: that I may believe of the Virgin’s childbirth what will fulfill my faith concerning your Incarnation; that I may speak of your mother’s virginity what will fill my mouth with your praise;

[Note: [Col. 0106D] We have likewise added “of your” from our manuscripts.]

that I may love in your mother what you will perfect in me concerning love of you;

[Note: [Col. 0106D] “Of” (*de*) is absent in all our manuscripts.] that I may serve your mother in such a way that, by this, you yourself may test that I have served you; that she may so rule over me that, by this, I may know that I have pleased you; that her dominion may hold me forever, so that you may be my Lord for eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0106D] “My,” in all our manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] We print *noverim* (“may I know”) for *noverint*, following our manuscripts against Feuardentius.]

[Note: [Col. 0106D] “How eagerly I desire,” “how faithfully,” etc., are omitted in Amel.]

As eagerly as I desire to become the servant of this mistress, as faithfully as I delight in the yoke of this servitude, as completely as I long to obey her commands, as ardently as I seek no separation from her dominion, and as greedily as I desire never to be withdrawn from her service—so truly may I find the ability to serve her, so truly may I, serving her, merit her grace, so truly may I be held in her service without interruption, so truly may I nowhere be separated from the delight of her eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “To her” and “of her” are lacking in Am. and Tr.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “In servitude”; Amel. and Trin.]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “Without interruption” is supplied by Am. and Tol., which we print. Feuardentius’s “with destruction” is not satisfactory, and Cod. Trin. has “with incorruption.”]

[Note: [Col. 0107D] Before these words Feuardentius’s edition repeats the preceding sentence, “So truly may I, serving her, merit her grace”; this repetition is absent from all our manuscripts.]

And why I seek this, those who love God know; those who are faithful in God see; those who cling to the Lord behold; those who are not unknown to the Lord do not fail to understand.

But hear, you rivals; attend, you faithless; recognize this, you filled with division; understand this, you wise men of the world, who are thereby foolish in the sight of God’s wisdom, precisely insofar as you are wise in the sight of your own foolishness; who are thereby weak in the sight of God’s strength, precisely insofar as you are strong in the sight of your own sickness; who are thereby contemptible in the sight of God’s excellence, precisely insofar as you are exalted in the sight of your own misery.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] Am. and the old edition read “your foolish speech.”]

You who are thereby destroyed, as though you did not exist, by him who always is, precisely insofar as you think yourselves to exist in your own sight, although nothing is more truly existent in the sight of him for whom being is the same as always being.

You who disdain that this woman is ever-virgin; you who do not wish her son to be my Maker; you who do not wish her to be the mother of my Maker; you who scorn that she alone should have as son the one whom every creature has as its one Lord; you who do not glorify this God as her son, and do not glorify my Lord as God; you who do not call blessed the woman whom the Holy Spirit commanded all nations to call blessed (Luke I); you who corrupt the glory of incorruption by the corruption of the flesh; you who do not render honor to the Lord’s mother in order to render honor to God her son; you who do not glorify as God the one whom you see born from her as man; you who confound the distinctions of her son’s natures; you who divide the person of her son; you who infect the divinity of that son; you who disdain the true flesh and true passion of her son; you who do not believe that he fell into death through man, nor that he rose from the dead through God.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] We have restored “infect,” from Amel., instead of “corrupt,” which appears in the other witnesses.]

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “As man” is supplied by all our witnesses.]

For what fell was from man; what rose was from God. Therefore, in order that I may be the servant of her son, I earnestly desire that she should rule over me; in order that her son may rule over me, I resolve to serve her; in order that I may be proved to serve God, I seek the dominion of his mother over me as a testimony; in order that I may be a devoted servant of the begotten son, I desire to become the servant of his mother.

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “Of the one who gives birth,” Tol. and Trin.]

[Note: [Col. 0108D] “I faithfully seek servitude” is found in all witnesses, together with Feuardentius, except Amel.; we have followed Amel.]

For in this way what is done for the handmaid is referred to the Lord; what is rendered to the mother redounds to the son; what is offered to the nurse is received by the one being nourished; in this way honor passes to the king when it is offered in service to the queen.

I rejoice with the angels, I am glad with the voices of the angels, I exult with the hymns of the angels, I rejoice with the proclamations of the angels; I rejoice with my mistress, I am glad with the mother of her Lord, I exult with the handmaid of her son, I rejoice with her who was made the mother of her Maker, I delight with her from whom the Word of God was made flesh.

[Col. 0108B] Because I believed with her what she herself knows about herself together with me; because I have recognized that she is a virgin mother;

[Note: [Col. 0108D] Feuardentius has “the virgin mother who gives birth”; but since we found “who gives birth” in none of our manuscripts, we have rejected it.]

because I understand that she is a virgin who gives birth; because I know that conception did not take away her virginity; because I have learned that her unshaken virginity preceded her childbirth; because I hold that her childbirth did not abandon the glory of her virginity.

[Note: [Col. 0108D] That is, it did not forsake it, because childbirth was not separated from virginity, which it in no way harmed.]

I love all these things as truly as I know that they were truly done for me. For what was accomplished through her is with me: that from it the nature of my God might be joined to my nature, and that my nature might pass into my God; and that there might be one Christ, Word and flesh, God and man; the same Maker and made thing, the same Fashioner and fashioned thing, the same Creator and form of the created thing, the same Worker and reality of the work assumed, the same one who made and what he had made, the same one who had made and what he made.

[Col. 0108C] He himself is the one who assumes and the one assumed;

[Note: [Col. 0108D] We represent the concordant reading of our manuscripts. Feuardentius had: “And, to speak more expressly of what he himself grants me to say about himself, I shall speak,” etc.]

and, to speak more expressly of what he himself grants me to say about himself: he himself is almighty, yet for me and for my salvation he himself was emptied. He himself is strong; he himself is weak. He himself is my salvation; he himself was wounded for me. He himself is my healing; he himself was struck with a wound for me. He himself is the power of God; he himself is God humbled for me. He himself is living; he himself is dead. He himself is the life that knows no death;

[Note: [Col. 0108D] All our witnesses have “he himself is life overcoming death,” etc.]

he himself endured death and conquered it. He himself, before death, did not know how to die; he himself, after death, is without death’s dominion. He himself came from heaven; he himself entered the tomb. He himself left the tomb; he himself returned to the heavens. He himself descended into the underworld in a human soul; he himself, by divine power, freed the souls of the saints from the underworld. He himself lay in the tomb as man; he himself rose from the tomb as God. He himself frees from death; he himself is free among the dead.

And all these things are the one Christ, and all are in one and the same Christ, for the unity of the person, not for the confusion of the nature.

[Note: [Col. 0109B] Feuardentius omits both occurrences of “for”; they are found in all our witnesses.]

Therefore, trusting through the death of this Son of God, through the cross of my Redeemer; hoping through the wounds of this Maker of mine; possessing confidence and holding true hope through the blood of this Christ of mine—because my sins have been covered, because my iniquities have been forgiven, because my crimes have been taken away, because my offenses have been washed away, because my evils have been abolished,

[Note: [Col. 0110B] We print “abolished,” found in all our witnesses, instead of “forgotten,” which stood in Feuardentius’s edition.]

because my impurities have been wiped away, because the bonds of my sins have been loosed—having been cleansed by the good God, purified by the God of mercy, justified by the compassionate Judge, sanctified by the abundant Redeemer, may I be mingled with the blessed angels, associated with angelic choirs,

[Note: [Col. 0110B] Amel. has “may I be numbered among them.”]

joined to the joys of the angels, united to the angelic festivals; so that there may be glory to God in me, praise to God from me, honor to God from me; and so that there may be from God for me forgiveness, from God for me salvation, from God for me life, from God for me exultation—continually, truly, without ceasing, manifestly, from now, from this moment, from henceforth, for all time, for the whole age, and throughout all ages, world without end. Amen.

The book on the perpetual virginity of the Mother of God ends.

# [On the Knowledge of Baptism and on the Journey through the Desert]

[Col. 0109]

## A Notice to the Reader Concerning the Two Following Little Works

[Col. 0109B] In this double little work, benevolent reader, there is no need for us to delay over the question of its attribution to Saint Hildefonsus. For Saint Julianus mentions that he composed one book On the Knowledge of Baptism and another On the Progress of the Spiritual Desert; moreover, works were found under these same titles and attributed to the same holy teacher in the manuscript codex of the Dominican Fathers of Bayeux. From this manuscript Stephanus Baluzius first published them, and we have followed him in this edition.

Unless, perhaps, the difference in style should somewhat delay your judgment—a difference whose great importance for correctly judging the labors of learned men and distinguishing the genuine and authentic from the spurious we readily acknowledge. But whatever difficulty there may be will immediately disappear once you have learned from the holy teacher himself that these two little works were not so much composed and elaborated from his own material as collected from various sayings of the holy Fathers.

“Putting forward nothing unknown from our own novelties,” these are the words of Saint Hildefonsus himself at the end of the preface to the first book, “but either unlocking the admonitions of the ancients for understanding or recording them for memory. For this reason we have decided that the title of this work should be written as Annotations on the Knowledge of Baptism.”

You will therefore cease to wonder that the sayings contained in these works often bear a style other than Hildefonsus’s.

[Col. 0109D] Meanwhile, however, we wish to warn you not to think that anything should be taken away from the value of these books because they were not worked out in every respect by Hildefonsus’s own effort. For the gravity and excellence of the sayings of which they consist are such that they deserve the highest esteem both in themselves and because of the most learned and venerable Fathers of the Church from whom they were excerpted—Augustine, Gregory, and Isidore. Yet they should be valued no less because of the great authority of the compiler.

In this matter, one should consider not only the labor that Hildefonsus expended in collecting them here and there and coordinating each one toward a single goal—although this labor is neither slight nor of little usefulness to us—but above all we should admire his learning, by whose light he opened the more obscure sayings of the Fathers to our understanding.

[Col. 0110B] Besides these matters, there are two things—and they must not be passed over in silence—that we are all taught in these books by the holy teacher, and which we would wish to have fixed in the minds of all diligent readers.

First, there is the utmost diligence and unremitting labor that he devoted to examining and learning the writings of the holy Fathers, applying himself to their study day and night, so that from them, as from the purest springs, he might draw sound doctrine to offer to the faithful people, carefully avoiding, in accordance with the Apostle’s warning, profane novelties of expression.

Second, there is that profound humility of spirit by which the most holy man, though greatly endowed with intelligence and learning, accommodated ears so empty to the teaching of the ancient Fathers—as though he thought he himself knew nothing—that he preferred to transmit their sayings and opinions to us rather than his own. Nor did he conceal this fact; instead, candidly, as befitted a most holy and upright man, he professed it in the clearest words and pointed it out to us almost with his own finger, so that he would not seem to wish to deceive his readers or in some way deprive others of the praise due to them.

Therefore, we hope that we shall do something most pleasing even to Hildefonsus himself. Following the example of learned men, we did not hesitate to return to the sources indicated by the holy teacher himself and, with all the diligence we could muster and certainly no small amount of toil, to investigate and identify nearly every passage from which each saying was excerpted.

From this sufficiently arduous labor we gained the additional benefit of restoring any corrupt readings we encountered and presenting several lacunae that we found in the Baluzius edition as filled in, although they were not of great importance. We also took care that the citations from the words of Sacred Scripture should not be missing at the margins. In short, we left nothing undone that might make this edition as complete as possible, despite the extreme scarcity of all our manuscript codices.

[Col. 0111]

# One Book of Annotations on the Knowledge of Baptism by Saint Hildefonsus, Bishop of Toledo (C, G, S)*

## Preface

[Col. 0111A]

The authority of divine instruction and the antiquity of sacred fatherhood, through Scripture—which, as the Apostle says, is inspired by God and useful (II Tim. III, 16)—has both established and affirmed that the Catholic Church is born through faith, grows through instruction, endures into eternity through the glory of reward, and persists through the gift of redemption and the spirit of adoption. For the same Spirit who inspired this Scripture for the salvation of human beings also led human beings to the rewards of blessedness.

The origin of this holy Church began figuratively among human beings in time, but it will be perfected through the eternity of the gift. Among the holy angels, however, it began temporally in the appearance of truth and remains perpetually in the appearance of truth. For it was spiritually established in such a way that, after the ruin of transgression, having received solidity in the love of its Creator, it did not grow through an increase of its own nature, but remained established, restored through the bringing about of human salvation.

In the angelic condition, because part of it fell, the remainder continued in glory forever. In the human condition, because the whole nature of humanity perished through the enemy’s deception, it could not be restored in any part unless the truth of the Redeemer had wholly assumed it for its restoration.

Hence it came about that the powerful Creator repaired the angelic ruin from the very place where the merciful Redeemer, taking the nature to be restored upon himself, introduced human nature.

Therefore, while God reigns in heaven and on earth—his kingdom being the whole world, which consists of heaven and earth, and to which the entire substance of all things celestial, terrestrial, and infernal is subject—through him that blessed part of the heavenly homeland already stands without defect, toward whose advancement human nature rises daily in the elect.

For the Word of God the Father, himself God, through whom the angels and all things were made, became flesh among human beings as the head of the Church. He who was the beginning of the angelic creature was therefore also, as God and man in the unity of one person, the one Christ, head of one body composed of angels and human beings.

Hence the glorious piety and devout rejoicing of this Church gladly rejoices in the angels who stand firm and yearns for human beings who are being advanced. In the angels it celebrates the praise of the Creator; in human beings it assumes the glory of the Redeemer. In the angels it has joy without end; in human beings it desires to rejoice without end. In the angels it rejoices in their established state; in human beings, in their acquisition. There it is solid among citizens; here it is joyful among newcomers. There it rests in security; here it looks forward amid anxiety. Salvation is restoration for the former, eternity for the latter.

And just as the former will never wish to sin and will never be able to sin, so the latter are saved from the will to sin to the ability not to sin, and are brought through the effect of redemption into the fullness of their brightness.

Already, through the pledge of the Holy Spirit and the gracious mingling of the future unity, that unity has been compacted: what the angelic world endures in human beings through opposition, it firmly sustains through the aid of angelic consolation, so that angelic assistance may cherish those whom the unity of its glorious fellowship awaits during the pilgrimage of this life.

The part of this Church that is called in the present age, so that what is said may be fulfilled—“Gather us from among the nations, that we may confess your holy name and glory in your praise” (Ps. CV, 45–46)—is invited to come according to the order of the ancient tradition of the apostles and holy Fathers, and according to the instruction promulgated by divine authority. Coming, it is received in an orderly manner; received, it is advanced through the sacred orders; advanced, it is filled with the grace of sanctification.

All this remains collected, arranged, and brought together in the sequence of the present little book: we propose nothing unknown from our own novelties, but either open the admonitions of the ancients to understanding or record them for memory. For this reason we have decided that the title of this work should be written as Annotations on the Knowledge of Baptism.

## Chapter I. The Beginning of the Prayer

[Col. 0112A]

Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me, enlightening my eyes so that I may see how I may come to you; strengthening my steps in you, so that I may not transgress the way; opening my mouth, so that I may be able to speak about you—you who have given me the desire to speak about you as far as I shall be able.

And because love of neighbor adheres to your love, grant me to exercise that usefulness which may shape his salvation and reach the praise and glory of your name.

## Chapter II. That He Intends to Speak of the Mystery of the New Birth

I shall strive to pursue and explain in their proper order that generation which takes place for the generation that is to come from God: human beings are born into wrath and reborn into grace; through it, children of wrath pass into adoption as children of God; through it, those freed from the reign of sin are transferred into the kingdom of God’s glory.

Thus everyone who is to be baptized in the holy bath may see through which signs of the mysteries he is called; and everyone already baptized may remember, preserve, and venerate the rewards of the sacraments—so that, while it is recognized that the figures of so great a mystery were formerly marked out, the sacraments of those figures may afterward be understood to have been completed in eternal grace.

## Chapter III. That the Whole Trinity Is One God

There is one God: invisible, incomprehensible, immeasurable, immortal, almighty, perfect, and eternal. In him there is nothing adventitious, nothing subsequent, nothing departing. He is before all things, above all things, within all things, and outside all things.

This God is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But the Father is from no one, but from himself, and is Father alone. The Son is born from the Father and is coeternal with the Father; and he is Son alone. The Holy Spirit proceeds inseparably from the Father and the Son, and is the Holy Spirit alone.

This whole Trinity is one God, possessing nothing as one thing and subsisting as another. Rather, it is simple because what it has in itself, that it is. For no good occurs in him by participation in which he is composed; but because every good is from him, what is in him truly is in every respect.

## Chapter IV. That the Whole Trinity, One God, Made All Things

This whole Trinity, one God, made all visible and invisible things: heaven and the heavenly angelic creature with everything contained in heaven; earth and the sea with everything contained in them.

This God created all things, contains all things, governs all things, orders all things through the administration of his providence, and rules all things. All things serve him. He judges all things. Apart from him there is nothing good; from him there is nothing evil. He is powerful enough to make good even from evil. He destroys every evil. He gives every good. He preserves every good forever.

## Chapter V. That Man Was Well Created by God but Deceived for Evil by the Devil

After the creation of the other things, the human being was created by God in a good and blessed condition. Indeed, he was so blessed that, made in the image and likeness of God, he was set above all earthly things by the authority of blessedness.

The angel who, because of his pride, had been cast down from the brightness of heavenly glory, envying him this position, rebelled against the Lord his Creator and deceived the man who had been created, through the fraud of persuasion.

The deceived man was made an exile from the place of blessedness because of the transgression he had committed, and was condemned, together with all the posterity of his race, to the sentence of death.

## Chapter VI. That the Creator’s Mercy Preceded Man’s Guilt

In his eternal mercy, the Creator established that this man would be saved, and, at the very beginnings of his creation, laying down as it were the foundations of mercy, fixed the mysteries of salvation. Through the sacraments of these mysteries, the one who would someday be saved might find the remedy of the salvation that had been signified.

Thus the mercy of the Maker preceded the guilt of man. When the fullness of time had come, the antiquity of mercy would repair the fall of the human condition and, from the point at which he had marked the sacraments of his redemption at the beginning of creation, would raise it up into the eternity of future glory.

## Chapter VII. The Formation of the Church from Christ’s Side, in the Likeness of Eve’s Formation from Adam’s Side

Adam was therefore a figure of Christ, and Eve a figure of the Church. Clay was taken, and the first man, Adam, was made a living soul. Christ was incarnate, and the second man, Adam, was made a life-giving Spirit.

Adam fell asleep in sleep; Christ rested in death. Adam’s rib was removed, and a woman was fashioned. From Christ’s side blood and water flowed forth, and through these sacraments the holy Church was formed.

Flesh is not taken from the flesh of a man, as though the woman should be fashioned softer through the softness of flesh while the strength of the man’s bones remained; rather, the removal from the man of the strength of bone is the weakness of divinity, concerning which it is said: “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14). The fashioning of the woman from the strength of the man’s bone is what follows: “And he will dwell among us.”

For to take away something of strength from the man is this: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 7). To fashion the woman from the man’s strength is this: “Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor, so that by his poverty we might be enriched” (II Cor. VIII, 9).

Therefore, insofar as he was weakened in the humility of his divinity, the Church was strengthened through the assumption of humanity in him. The weak woman is rightly formed from the man’s strength, because, after the fall of guilt, the deformed human condition would not have received the image of its Maker unless the merciful Redeemer had renewed it by dying; nor would the weak and rejected condition have risen to the strength of the spirit unless humbled divinity, having been weakened, had raised it up.

## Chapter VIII. That Both Christ’s Incarnation and Death Were Prefigured at the Beginning of the First Human Beings

The woman’s form marked out this fullness of the figure of salvation through the glory of the Virgin, when it was said to the serpent: “I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed” (Gen. III, 15). This signifies that the malice of the devil’s party cannot adhere to the sacrament of redemption, which was accomplished through the man assumed from the Virgin’s womb.

Hence it is further said: “She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (ibid.). This is understood of Christ, who is the fruit of Mary’s virginal womb. That is: through the malice of his persecutors, who are your seed and whose hearts you inhabit, you will trip him so that he may die; and he, rising again, will crush your head, which is death, and you yourself, who possess the dominion of death.

The fratricide that immediately followed prefigured this humility of the Redeemer, extending even to the acceptance of death. Cain, the elder brother, devoted to earthly works, rose up and, because of the simple offering, killed his innocent companion outside the house with crude brutality, becoming a new murderer. This signified that the Jewish people, born first under the Law, would kill Christ, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, outside Jerusalem on the gibbet of the cross.

## Chapter IX. That the Whole Trinity Accomplished Christ’s Incarnation, Yet Only the Person of the Son Assumed It

[Col. 0115A]

The Son of God, coming in the fullness of time, fulfilled the rich mystery of this holy redemption, marked out in the creation of the first human beings through abundant mercy. The operation of his coming was the reality of his Incarnation.

The whole Trinity accomplished this reality of the Incarnation, because the works of the Trinity are inseparable. Yet only the person of the Son assumed it, because whatever belongs through this dispensation to the person of Christ can in no way belong to the persons of the Father or of the Holy Spirit.

For it is not permissible to say that the Father and the Spirit were born from a virgin, or hung upon the cross, or were enclosed in a tomb. All these things were fittingly and manifestly completed in the one person of Christ.

Christ, who had been appointed to complete this mystery of human redemption, arranged in the eternity of his divinity, through the presence of the humanity he assumed, completed it at the end of the ages just as he had ordained before the ages. Nothing was devised through a novelty of counsel; nothing was assumed through the addition of a new thought. It was fixed by eternal disposition and perfected through temporal dispensation.

## Chapter X. That the Law Was Given So That God Might Return to Man’s Knowledge

Since the human race had consigned its Creator to forgetfulness, the Law was given, through which the Creator of all things might be restored to the thoughts of the creature that had lost God. Through that same Law it was said: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God,” and so forth (Deut. VI, 4).

By this saying, the superstitions through which the creature was worshiped in place of the Creator were removed, and the one God who truly ought to be worshiped was openly demonstrated.

## Chapter XI. On the Periods Under Whose Distinction the World Has Stood

The world therefore stood among human beings under a threefold distinction of times. Man will stand in a fourth order in the blessedness of the ages: in the first, supremely unhappy; in the second, not fully happy; in the third, abundantly happy; in the fourth, happy with the highest and eternal happiness.

[Note: [Col. 0115D] These seem to be taken from Augustine (Book On Various Questions, question 83, 66), though not word for word.]

In the first period, man was supremely unhappy because, created in the image and likeness of God, with the devil his deceiver ruling him, he served the kingdom of sin and worshiped idols; he impiously bestowed upon creatures the honor piously owed to the Creator alone.

In the second, he was not fully happy because the Law was indeed given for the knowledge of God, but could not lead to the righteousness of God. “For if righteousness comes through the Law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. II, 21). It was given for understanding, not for the forgiveness of sin. Through it sin was recognized and punished, not healed.

It was indeed given with the enactment of sacrifices and ceremonies, so that offerings might be made to God as God had decreed, and not as the Gentiles, sacrificing to demons, offered sacrifices. Yet this observance of the Law greatly benefited human beings in its own time, because of the knowledge of God. But it did not bring full happiness because it brought nothing to perfection (Heb. VII, 19).

The succeeding period was therefore one in which the happiness begun through the letter could be perfected through the understanding of the spirit. In this time of grace, which is the third, there was abundant happiness, when Christ, prefigured in all those sacred sacrifices, was unmistakably revealed; when light succeeded shadow, truth uncertainty, manifestation figures, revelation hidden things, the Gospel the Law, the grace of sons the fear of servants, and the most welcome and open spiritual manifestation all that the letter had foreshadowed.

The fourth is the distinctive state of blessed eternity, in which, after all adversaries have been conquered, man will praise God, secure in the tranquility of incorruption.

[Col. 0116B] Therefore, in the state of the world—

[Note: [Col. 0116D] Two lines are missing here in the manuscript codex.]

…it was brought about. The third period under grace was not fully happy, in which Christ washed us from our sins in his blood; and that final period remains abundantly happy, and it is eternal, in which we shall praise God forever and ever.

## Chapter XII. On the Effort to Carry Out the Several Orders

Now, with God’s favor, whose work of mercy in human salvation we desire to know, let us suitably pursue in their proper order the effect of that salvation which is accomplished through the regeneration of grace together with the sacrament of redemption, just as divine authority and the ancient tradition of the Fathers have decreed.

## Chapter XIII. That the Restoration of the Human Race Is Recognized as Having Begun in the Very Beginnings of Causes, in Which Its Restoration Is Contained

The beginning of regeneration, whose form was completed in the fullness of time, began at the beginning of the ages. For eternal Wisdom established the figure of the sacraments in the beginnings of things in such a way that the significance ordered from ancient times might reach the end of the ages in the effectiveness of its actions.

Thus, because the sacrament of this regeneration consisted in water and the Spirit, the institution of its causes completed—or, perhaps, was completed as—the likeness of that operation, when it is said: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen.
