I, 2), so that the restoration of these things is shown to have been figured through the same elements at the beginnings of their causes.

## Chapter XIV. On John and the Baptism of Repentance, Whose Sign Is the Straw of Haircloth, by Which Little Children Are Brought for Anointing

The Lord therefore came to fulfill the fullness of our salvation—not for his own benefit but for ours. He assumed it in himself and sanctified the sacrament of baptism through himself, sending John beforehand. John’s baptism was to be a figure of the truth, not the truth itself: it summoned sinners to repentance but did not bring forgiveness of sins, as John himself said: “I baptize in water for repentance” (Matt. III, 11).

Hence little children are brought by means of the straw of haircloth to the priests for anointing, so that they may possess the sign of repentance on account of the work, since, because of their age, they cannot demonstrate the works of repentance.

Those who are older, however, when they begin to be called to the faith, themselves offer repentance for their former errors, in which they either lived generally or served idols. John commended this efficacy of repentance when it is said of him: “He came into the whole region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” (Luke III, 3).

From this it is plainly evident that John not only preached a baptism of repentance but also administered it, though he could not administer it for the forgiveness of sins. Therefore, because he could not give a baptism that would release sins, he preached it so that, just as the incarnate Word of the Father was preceded by the word of preaching, so the baptism of repentance, by which sins are released, might be preceded by his baptism, through which sins cannot be released.

## Chapter XV. That John’s Baptism Ceased When Christ’s Baptism Began; and How Christ Baptizes and Does Not Baptize

The Lord came to be baptized by a servant. Out of humility the servant objected, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matt. III, 14). Out of justice the Lord commanded, saying: “Let it be so now. For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (ibid.).

Then John’s baptism ceased, which was in repentance and in the shadow of truth, and Christ’s baptism began, which is the truth and in which the forgiveness of sins takes place. Although Christ did not baptize, but his disciples did.

[Note: [Col. 0117D] From Augustine, Tractate 15 on John, chapter 4, section 3.]

Christ baptizes and does not baptize. Both statements are true. He baptizes because he cleanses. He does not baptize because he himself does not immerse. At that time the disciples provided the service, just as ministers now provide the ministry of the body. He provided the assistance of majesty.

## Chapter XVI. That Christ Alone Baptizes, Having Reserved the Power of Baptizing for Himself Alone, Although a Good or Bad Minister May Baptize
[Note: [Col. 0117D] St. Augustine, in the same place.] Therefore he never ceases to baptize who never ceases to cleanse. Jesus baptizes until the end of the age, [Col. 0117D] because he himself cleanses. Accordingly, let a person approach the inferior minister without fear, for he has a superior teacher. Christ himself, the teacher, baptizes outwardly also, as Paul says: “As Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, cleansing her by the washing of water” (Ephesians V); and inwardly he baptizes through the infusion of the Spirit, by which the inner person is taught both to have faith and to preserve the dignity of good works.

To this certainly pertains what is said: “And John bore witness, saying: ‘For I saw the Spirit descending like a dove, and it remained upon him, and I did not know him’” (John I, 32). John knew Christ through many recognitions. For when Mary, the mother of Christ, saw Elizabeth, this John leaped in her womb (Luke I, 41). This was “the voice of one crying: Prepare the way of the Lord” (Matthew III, 3). This was the one who forbade him who had come to him to be baptized, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (ibid., 14). This was the one who pointed him out as the Lamb of God and the one who takes away the sins of the world (John I, 29).

[Note: [Col. 0117D] St. Augustine, *Tractate 5 on John*, chapter 1, section 8.] Yet this one thing he did not know about him: that he was going to retain for himself the power of baptizing, and would neither transfer nor transmit it to any servant. But whether a good servant baptized in the ministry, or an evil servant baptized in the ministry, the person being baptized would not know himself to be baptized except by him who retained the power of baptizing; and the efficacy of this sacrament would lie not in the office of the minister, but in the authority of the teacher.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the teacher ought to fortify the preaching of words with diligent prayer, so that what he is about to say may be formed more effectively by God’s power than by his own action

When someone from a pagan way of life is unwillingly urged to come to the knowledge and faith of God, the teacher should first consider the great goodness of the merciful God, of whom it is said: “Who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy II); [Note: [Col. 0117D] St. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, chapter 25] and thereafter he should act as far as he can [Note: [Col. 0117D] Acherius published from the manuscript of Bayeux *ut intelligentes ut libenter et obedienter*, etc. But in the printed books of St. Augustine, from which this passage is taken literally, we read: “So that they may listen intelligently, willingly, and obediently”; this is the reading we have followed.] so that they may listen intelligently, willingly, and obediently.

Nor should he doubt that he can accomplish this—if he can, and to the extent that he can—more through the devoutness of his prayers than through the ability of his eloquence. By praying for himself and for those whom he is about to address, he should be an orator before he is a teacher. Whether in a private conversation or in an assembly of the Church, at the very moment when he approaches to speak, before he brings forth his speaking tongue, he should lift his thirsting soul to the Lord, so that he may pour out what he has drunk, or release what has filled him. At the time of speaking itself, he should think that what the Lord says is especially appropriate to a good mind: “But when they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak; for it will be given you in that hour what you are to speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew X, 19).

If, then, the Holy Spirit speaks in those who are handed over to persecutors for Christ, [Col. 0118D] why should he not also speak in those who hand Christ over to learners? This diligence in teaching is surely appropriate for a teacher to exercise both in persuading pagans to faith and in persuading all the faithful to good works.

[Note: [Col. 0118D] We have corrected here from the printed books of St. Augustine’s *On Christian Doctrine*; therefore, in place of *quas*, which is read in Baluzius, we have similarly made the correction in many other passages, although we have not indicated it wherever the error was obvious.]

## CHAPTER XVIII. How one who is unwilling is to be approached when invited to the faith

[Note: [Col. 0118D] St. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book I, chapter 7.] When, therefore, the knowledge and faith of the one God are offered to those unwilling to believe, it should be proposed that they proceed through understanding to see what God is, and that they place him above all visible and bodily natures, and indeed above all intelligible and spiritual natures, and above all mutable things.

For all things contend eagerly for the excellence of God, and no one can be found who believes that God is something than which anything else is better. Thus everyone agrees that God is that which they place before all other things.

[Note: [Col. 0119D] St. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book I.] And since all who think anything about God think of something living, only those can form opinions about God that are neither absurd nor unworthy who think of life itself. Then they proceed to examine life itself; and if they find it without sensation, as is the life of growing things such as trees, they place above it life that possesses sensation, such as that of animals, and above this again life that possesses understanding, such as that of human beings. When they see this life still mutable, they are compelled to place above it some immutable life—namely, that life which is not at one time foolish and at another wise, but is wisdom itself.

For a wise mind has acquired wisdom; before acquiring it, it was not wise. But wisdom itself was never foolish, nor can it ever be. If they did not perceive this, they could in no way, with full confidence, place an immutably wise life above mutable life. They also see that the very rule of truth by which they proclaim that life to be better is immutable; and they see it nowhere except above their own nature, since they see themselves to be mutable.

But when, through the teacher’s persuasion, every mutable thing has truly been excluded from the honor due to the Godhead, it must be accepted that the supreme God cannot be subject to passion, that is, to mutability. And when it has been grasped that what is mutable cannot be God, it remains that one should arrive at that reality which surpasses all things and is immutable.

Once it has been inferred that the reality which is the one God, surpassing all things and remaining immutable, made all things, governs all things, judges all things, cares for all things, and that nothing among visible and invisible things exists which does not have its beginning from him and does not lie subject to his dominion, then it follows that the servitude of subject things cannot be found under any mutable creature whatsoever, but only under this one ruling God, whose substance is eternal, whose truth is immutable, and whose power remains omnipotent.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the opening of the door of faith

[Col. 0119D]

Now, when that one has unlocked the door of faith of whom it is said, “Who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens” (Revelation III, 7)—that is, the human being assumed from the seed of David, through the power of the united Godhead, opens to the hearts of believers the mysteries of his Incarnation, which the severity of unbelief cannot shut in the predestined; and he shuts the vessels of wrath by the foresight of judgment, lest the reprobate come to the blessed reward which they have rightly shut themselves out from—then what is written comes to pass: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X, 9).

For the beginnings of faith begin to be opened to the one who, regenerated through the washing, after receiving the Holy Spirit, is one to whom Christ has entrusted himself in participation in Christ’s body. And he will see that book of holy authority opened which the same victorious Lion from the tribe of Judah opened, though it had been closed in mystery by seven seals (Revelation V, 5).

That book is the whole of Holy Scripture opened, because its meaning is revealed to human beings by Christ, who alone took upon himself and wished to fulfill those things which he ordained and foreknew must be fulfilled for the salvation of the human race.

Its seven signs are these: first, incorporation; second, birth; third, passion; fourth, death; fifth, resurrection; sixth, glory; seventh, kingdom. The opening of these signs is the complete redemption of the human race; and the one who comes to it comes in this order.

## CHAPTER XX. On those who, willingly converting to the faith at first, are called catechumens, that is, hearers

[Note: [Col. 0120D] St. Isidore, book II of *On the Offices*, chapter 20.] Whoever, coming from a pagan way of life and from superstitions in which the creature is impiously worshiped instead of the Creator, wishes to believe in God at a mature age—or whether they are newly born or small children—is called a catechumen, that is, a hearer, because they first hear the command of exhortation spoken to them in the Law: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord” (Deuteronomy VI, 4); and also: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (ibid.).

They therefore hear the word of life, through which those who were children of wrath may attain the gift of grace. For since everyone who truly recognizes this says truthfully, “I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother gave birth to me in sins” (Psalm L, 7), the one who is held originally liable to the guilt of death, until through redemption he is made a child of God, will be a child of that ancient wrath which the first human being deserved by transgressing the command. The Lord says: “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. But whoever is disobedient to the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John III, 36).

He said that this wrath does not come but remains, because it does not come from the novelty of unbelief, but remains from the antiquity of transgression. No one can be saved from this wrath except through the mercy of the Savior, as the same Lord says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John VIII, 36).

These catechumens are called hearers because of the knowledge of God which God speaks to them through the priest, as through Moses, so that, abandoning the oldness of carnal life, they may come to the newness of life through the knowledge of the one God.

## CHAPTER XXI. That catechumens are to be brought to the washing through repentance; and that those whom John baptized represented catechumens

If they are adults, they come with the practice of repentance. If they are minors, they are led by ministers to the priest on coverings of haircloth as a sign of repentance, so that those who cannot perform the work of repentance themselves may have within them the sign of repentance on account of the limitation of their age; and what is marked in the sign of repentance may be regarded as present in the effect of repentance.

After the rebuke of the exorcisms, they appropriately come to the anointing with oil. Here all those baptized by John in repentance served as a figure of catechumens, so that what baptism in repentance was for them, conversion to God through repentance may be for these.

## CHAPTER XXII. Who the exorcists are, by whom catechumens and the possessed are exorcized

These persons are exorcized with exorcisms by those who are called exorcists from that name. When those assigned to such an office are ordained, as the canons command, they receive from the hand of the bishop a booklet in which the exorcisms are written, together with the authority given them to lay hands upon the possessed, whether baptized or catechumens.

## CHAPTER XXIII. What an exorcism is

[Col. 0121B]

[Note: [Col. 0121D] St. Isidore, in the place cited above.] An exorcism is a speech of rebuke directed against the unclean spirit in the possessed or in catechumens, so that through it the devil’s most wicked power, his long-standing malice, and his violent assault may be expelled and driven away.

## CHAPTER XXIV. What an exorcism will be like

The speech of an exorcism will be [Note: [Col. 0121D] Baluzius reads *nocturno*; this is our conjecture.] without bombast of words, not difficult in understanding, nor unusual in the eloquence of its construction, but simple, well composed, and ardent. It should flash with such an intensity of power that it truly demonstrates that it drives out the prince of the world by the force of its rebuke. In the spiritual contest waged against the powers of the air, it should hurl flashes of terror, so that the expulsion of the invisible enemy may be contemplated as a kind of visible conquest; thus the catechumen may be frightened by the force of what is heard, while the faithful are spurred on to undertake the struggle.

Thus, while the offices of the priests fight as the armies of God, and the faithful offer devoted attention like weapons, the one who possessed God’s creature may depart defeated, and Christ may victoriously obtain those whom he created.

## CHAPTER XXV. From where the power of exorcizing had its beginning, and in what mystery the bishop performs this through divine words

The power of exorcizing signified that event when Jesus rebuked the lunatic: “The demon went out from him” (Matthew XVII, 17). In the likeness of this dominical rebuke, the bishop also rebukes with his own voice, just as the Lord rebuked with his voice.

The bishop undertakes this very rebuke not from human conjecture, but from the authority proper to divine prophetic words, saying: “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan, and may he rebuke you who has chosen Jerusalem” (Zechariah III, 2).

Then, commanding for a second time, he says: “To you it is said, Satan: Go away.” And afterward, as with the trumpet of victory, he proclaims for the third time: “The Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (Revelation V, 5).

Then the exorcism is begun by the ministers in this way: “Your snares have been discovered.” And so the same rebuke is completed through the utterance of the exorcists, until all the catechumens have been subjected to the exorcisms.

The order has therefore been arranged in an orderly manner, so that first the speech of rebuke, arising from that cause, may begin with those words. For since an exorcism is a speech of rebuke, it properly begins by inveighing, when it starts in this way: “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan, and may he rebuke you who has chosen Jerusalem” (Zechariah III, 2).

Second, divine power is brought forward when the command of the divine words is proclaimed by saying: “Go away, Satan” (Matthew IV, 10).

Third, the power of victory is demonstrated, because Christ once conquered the devil by dying, and daily conquers him in those who believe in and follow him. Therefore the voice is raised in victory when it is said: “The Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered” (Revelation V, 5).

For this reason it is written: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John XII, 31), that is, he will be expelled from the hearts of believers. And again the Lord says: “Indeed, the captive will be taken from the strong, and what has been taken from the mighty can be rescued” (Isaiah XLIX, 25), showing that, once the devil’s dominion had been destroyed through Christ’s victory, a human being could be rescued from his captivity and saved.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That the devil’s power is taken away by exorcizing catechumens

[Note: [Col. 0121D] St. Isidore, book II of *On the Offices*, chapter 30.] The power of the devil is exorcized—that is, rebuked—and breath is blown upon those from whom the ruler of that power is expelled, so that they may renounce him under whose authority they were held liable, and, rescued from the power of darkness, may be transferred through the sacrament of baptism into the kingdom of their Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0121D] Up to this point these are the words of St. Isidore in the place cited at the margin. We do not know from where what follows was taken. From it the learned Martène concludes (*Book I of On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter I, article 6, section 14) that the Spaniards abstained for some time from this rite of putting salt into the mouths of catechumens.

If he intends this to be said of all Spain, we cannot readily grant it, since shortly before this he wrote that Isidore, the great teacher of Hildefonsus, says in the place cited above: “They [the catechumens] are first exorcized, then receive salt, and are anointed,” and proceeds there to explain the mystical meanings of salt.

Nor does it seem likely that, in so short an interval of time, this custom became so obsolete in Spain that what Hildefonsus says would have to be referred to foreign churches: “In some places, as is reported, they receive salt.” But while it is easy to deny this, it is difficult to make this statement clear.

If someone were to say that there could have been some slight difference of discipline between the Church of Seville and the Church of Toledo—although this seems to rest more on conjecture than on any positive foundation—we would not strongly object, observing that a little earlier, in chapter 21, St. Hildefonsus writes about the rite of leading younger catechumens to the priest on coverings of haircloth as a sign of repentance, a rite of which they were not yet capable; yet no mention of this rite is found in St. Isidore, as Martène himself also noted.

It is therefore credible that Hildefonsus intended not merely to indicate the custom of his own Church, in which there was no such rite of putting in salt, but also wished at the same time to defend it from all censure by the words cited above. He indicated that the matter concerned ecclesiastical discipline: since it could not be shown by any testimony of Scripture to have been commanded by the Lord, but was commended only by antiquity, it was indeed to be praised and retained wherever it flourished; but where it had not flourished, that Church was not for this reason to be condemned.]

In some places, as is reported, they receive salt, as though it signified the seasoning of wisdom. But although perhaps, as is said, this practice was commended only by antiquity, it is by no means approved everywhere. Since it is not demonstrated by any clear testimony of Holy Scripture that salt is to be given to catechumens in order that they may obtain the sacrament of faith, it therefore does no harm where it is not done.

For how can practices that are demonstrated by no continuous authority of sacred tradition—whether by figure or by direct form—to pertain properly to the matter possess the highest force?

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Gospel example according to which catechumens are anointed with oil

After the exorcisms by which the devil’s power has been rebuked and expelled, these same catechumens are anointed by them with oil that has been blessed by the priest. This anointing is commended by the great example of the Lord’s action.

For, as the evangelist Mark relates, when they had brought to Jesus a deaf and dumb man, they begged him to lay his hand upon him. And taking him aside from the crowd, he put his fingers into his ears; and spitting, he touched his tongue. Then, looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him: “Ephphetha,” which means, “Be opened.” And immediately his ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly (Mark VII, 32–33).

What does it mean that the Lord took the deaf and dumb man aside from the crowd and put his fingers into his ears so that he might hear, unless it means that the Redeemer, coming into the world, separated the human race from the crowd of demons and from the conduct of ancient works, and through the infusion of spiritual gifts gave it the hearing of faith?

For just as the Spirit is signified by the finger of God, so by the fingers the plurality of spiritual graces is signified. And what does it mean that, spitting, he touches his tongue so that he may be able to speak, unless it means that, after hearing the sacrament of faith, he causes this man both to recognize and to fulfill the mysteries of salvation?

For the Spirit of Christ is the grace of human redemption. Descending from the head of his divinity, and recognized through the mouth of his humanity, it brought its confession and praise to those who would believe.

What does it mean that, looking up to heaven, he groaned, unless it means that, possessing equality with the Father, he demonstrated the weakness of his humanity, in which he suffered for us?

And what does it mean that he said “Ephphetha,” which is explained as “Be opened,” and immediately the man’s ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke correctly? It means that, when grace and the work of redemption came upon him, he burst forth with his whole power into the praise and love of his redeemer.

Therefore he could neither remain silent nor speak crookedly, since he had received his redemption for the glory of the Redeemer, so that he might speak and speak correctly.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That readings from the prophet Isaiah, the apostle Peter, and the evangelist Mark are properly delivered in the assembly of the Church during the exorcization

For this reason, at the same time of the exorcization, the reading from the prophet Isaiah is rightly delivered in the assembly of the Church before the exorcisms are spoken. It says: “Will prey be taken from the strong, or can what has been captured from the mighty be rescued? For thus says the Lord: Indeed, the captive will be taken from the strong, and what has been taken from the mighty will be rescued” (Isaiah XLIX, 24–25).

Likewise, the reading from Peter addressed to the nations: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition, so that you may proclaim the mighty works of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter II, 9).

Likewise, the reading from the evangelist Mark, which reveals the mystery of this “Ephphetha,” which was presented and explained above: namely, that the power of God, through the victory of the cross, taking the prey of the human race from the strength of the devil, may make it a chosen race through the gift of regeneration, and also a royal priesthood through the dominion of words, the offering of innocence, and the sacrifice of a contrite spirit; infusing it with the hearing of obedience to the commandments, giving it speech of right faith, and granting it a hymn of his glory.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the mystery of salvation, which was accomplished once when Christ died, is accomplished daily in those who are known to be regenerated

What was accomplished once generally in the human race through Christ’s death is accomplished daily in particular in the washing of those who are regenerated. For when someone is converted from pagan error, after the exorcisms his ears are touched with oil so that he may receive the hearing of faith and truly become a hearer of spiritual words.

Likewise, his mouth is touched so that he may believe in his heart, for justification, the faith of the Creed handed down to him concerning the knowledge of his Redeemer, and may confess it with his mouth and proclaim it for salvation. Thus, when the bonds created by obstinacy have been released, he speaks correctly, magnifying God.

## CHAPTER XXX. What a *competens* is, and why he is so called

A catechumen becomes a *competens*. Just as he is called a hearer because he hears the knowledge of God, so, because after receiving the Creed he now asks for the grace of God, he is called a *competens*. *Competentes* means “those asking together,” just as *considentes*, *colloquentes*, and *concurrentes* mean nothing other than “those sitting together,” “speaking together,” and “running together.” Thus *competentes* are nothing other than those asking together.

But what do they ask for except the sacraments of baptism, through which they may be rescued from the power of darkness and, having received forgiveness of sins, transferred into the kingdom of almighty God?

Therefore, so that they may be worthy to receive what they ask, they must cleanse their hearts from vices and their bodies from impurities, abstaining in soul from sins and in body from feasts. Thus contrition may humble and justify the heart, while abstinence and chastity may weaken and cleanse the body, so that, once the substance of soul and body has been entirely purified, whatever contrition of heart and whatever affliction of the flesh has accomplished may wholly contribute to the dignity of the regeneration that is to be received.

Nicodemus, that ruler of the Jews, represented the significance of these things. He had come to Jesus by night and was one of those who believed in his name, seeing the signs and wonders that he performed. When the Lord Jesus was in Jerusalem at Passover, teaching on the feast day, he heard his teaching so effectively that he believed in his name; in this respect he was a catechumen, that is, a hearer.

But in that he came to him by night and said: “Rabbi, we know that you have come as a teacher from God; for no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him” (John III, 2), he showed himself to be a *competens*. For when he heard him teaching in the temple and believed after seeing the signs, he truly proved to be a hearer.

But when, although in the darkness of ignorance, he came to the light—because he came to Jesus by night—and confessed both that he was a teacher and that he had come from God, and now sought to be taught by his teaching, because he gave the teacher the honor due to him, from that point he was a *competens*. For he had believed in the teacher’s doctrine by hearing and had sought his teaching by asking for it.

He is afterward advanced to the grace of baptism when the Savior’s reply commends this to him, as follows: “Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God’” (ibid.).

What follows, then? Since it is not enough for a catechumen merely to hear the word of God, nor enough for a *competens* to ask for grace from the teaching of God, it is necessary that he be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, so that, having been reborn, he may become a participant in the body and blood of Christ. And just as he himself believed in Christ through faith, so, by participating in the body of Christ, Christ may entrust himself to him.

For this is what is said: “When he was in Jerusalem at Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name, seeing his signs which he performed. But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them” (John II, 23–24).

[Note: [Col. 0125D] St. Augustine, *Tractate 11 on John*, chapter 3, sections 3–4.] What does this mean? Behold, the Lord does not entrust himself to those who believe in him! Is he then going to entrust himself to unbelievers and to those who do not believe? Absolutely not.

But the catechumen and the *competens* already believe in Christ. Yet because they have not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, they do not participate in the body of Christ, and therefore Christ did not entrust himself to them.

If we say to catechumens, “Do you believe in Christ?” they answer, “We believe,” and they make the sign of the cross. They already bear the cross of Christ on their foreheads and are not ashamed of the cross of their Lord. Behold, they believe in his name.

Let us ask them: “Do you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink the blood of the Son of Man?” They do not know what we are saying, because Jesus has not entrusted himself to them. Yet they already have, as it were, the sign of the cross on their foreheads. They already belong to the great household.

They must be reborn; they must be made sons from servants and citizens from outsiders. For they are not nothing, since they already belong to the great household. And when they have been reborn, then Christ will entrust himself to those who participate in his body.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On handing over the Creed

Next, the Creed must be handed over, so that the one who has heard the Lord’s command and has asked for the grace of divine teaching may receive the rule of true faith, according to which he may show himself restored, both in faith and in works, through the washing of sanctification.

## CHAPTER XXXII. In what manner the Creed is constituted

[Col. 0126A]

[Note: [Col. 0125D] St. Isidore, book [II?] of *On the Offices*, chapter 24.] The Fathers said that the Creed, which the *competentes* receive, was constituted in this manner. They say that when the apostles had heard from the Lord that they should go and teach the nations, preaching the kingdom of God, and baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, they received the Holy Spirit after the Lord’s ascension, when he settled upon them in the likeness of fire and they spoke in the languages of all nations.

Thus no nation or language was unknown to them for the knowledge of the truth, but through the same Holy Spirit they spoke to everyone in every way. Since they were about to separate bodily from one another, they composed among themselves this Creed of a single preaching, so that wherever they went they would announce nothing discordant and nothing varied, but would proclaim one faith in united words. Gathering testimonies from all the sacred Scriptures, they constructed this single brief edifice of faith, concerning which it had also been said through the prophet: “For the Lord will make a brief word upon the earth” (Isaiah X, 22).

Therefore, while they were still gathered together and filled with the Holy Spirit, they set forth this brief sign of their preaching by conferring among themselves what each one thought. They established it as the rule to be given to believers, so that, since many would arise who would pretend to be apostles of Christ but would not preach Christ with sound and complete doctrine, it might be recognized by this sign that the one truly proclaimed Christ who announced him according to this apostolic rule.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the name of the Creed, and what the Creed is

[Col. 0126C]

[Note: [Col. 0126D] St. Isidore, in the place cited above.] The name *Symbolum* is translated from Greek into Latin as “collation” or “sign.” It is a covenant and a knowledge of faith, in which it is known what is believed and what is believed is in no way violated.

It is therefore a “sign” because of knowledge, and a “collation” because of the common agreement of a united definition among many. For a sign indicates something unknown, while a collation is a definition shared in common speech.

Hence, even in civil wars, because the appearance of arms, the sound of the voice, the common custom, and the method of warfare are similar, each commander assigns distinct signs to his soldiers to prevent any deception from being slipped in. These signs are called in Latin *signa* or *indicia*, so that if someone should happen to encounter a person whose allegiance was uncertain, the person could be recognized as either an enemy or one of their own when the sign was disclosed.

The holy Fathers therefore ordered that this be entrusted not to parchment but to memory, so that it would not be held by reading, which sometimes conveys the same thing even to unbelievers, but would always remain commended to the faithful through the tradition of the holy apostolic definition and the tenacity of memory.

Thus, for the firmness of the faith being initiated, the apostles, about to depart from one another, rightly established this sign of unanimity. The Creed is a sign or indication by which God is recognized. Believers receive it so that they may know how to prepare the struggle of faith against the devil. Although it contains few words, all the sacraments are contained in it.

For this reason it was gathered briefly by the apostles from all the Scriptures: because many believers either did not know letters, or, although they knew them, were prevented by worldly occupation from reading the Scriptures, they could retain this in heart and memory and possess for themselves sufficient saving knowledge.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That the Creed is to be recited on the Thursday before Easter

This Creed, which the *competentes* receive on the day of anointing—either personally, if they are adults, or through the mouths of those carrying them, if they are small children—they recite and return to the priest on the Thursday before Easter, so that, their faith having been tested, they may deservedly arrive at the nearby sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection through baptism in the sacred font.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That the Catholic faith is contained in the brevity of the Creed

[Col. 0127B]

[Note: [Col. 0127D] St. Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 1.] The Catholic faith is known to the faithful in the Creed and entrusted to memory, expressed with as much brevity of speech as the matter allowed, so that for beginners and infants—those who have been reborn in Christ but have not yet been strengthened by the most diligent and spiritual study and knowledge of the divine Scriptures—it might be established in a few words what would have to be explained in many words to those making progress and rising toward divine teaching with firm humility and charity.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The beginning of the Creed, and what belief is

The wording of the Creed is therefore this, and this is the order of the matters contained in it: “I believe in God the Father almighty.”

What is “I believe”? I make a belief; that is, I confess as true the things that I hear although they are unknown. *Credulitas*—“belief”—is so called because the mind grows strong enough to embrace things unseen and unknown.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That faith is to be placed in God alone, not in things, but concerning things

In the Creed there is firmness and a certain separation of the one faith, by which it is shown that one should believe in God alone and believe God, not believe in any other things—in other words, one should have faith in God, but not faith in things; rather, one should have faith concerning things.

One must therefore believe in God, and not in anything else, because faith in God, like the one God himself, is to be held and retained in a unique manner. Faith is to be placed in other things, but not placed above them. We therefore believe in God. We also believe that his holy Church exists. But we do not believe in the Church as we believe in God, because the Church is not God.

We believe uniquely in God. We also believe, in due sequence, that the Church belongs to him. Likewise, thereafter, we believe whatever the rule of right faith commends to us for belief: that the Father is the Father of his Son according to divine generation, in accordance with what he says to him: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm CIX, 3).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That God is omnipotent because he made all things
[Note: [Col. 0127D] St. Augustine, in the passage cited above, chapter 2.] “Almighty,” because he alone was able to do all things, who made all things; he is to be believed almighty in such a way that he made all visible and invisible things out of nothing. For nothing could exist whose creator he was not, since he was almighty. Even if he made something from something else, as man from clay, he certainly did not make it from something he himself had not made, since he had made the earth, from which clay is formed, out of nothing.

And if he had made heaven and earth themselves—that is, the world and everything in it—from some material, as it is written, “Who made the world from unseen matter” (Wis. XI, 18), or even from formless matter, it must in no way be believed that the matter from which the world was made, although formless and unseen, could in any manner have existed by itself, as though coeternal and coeval with God. Rather, whatever mode of being it possessed, so that it might exist in any fashion and be capable of receiving the forms of distinct things, it possessed only from almighty God. Through his beneficence exists not only anything that has been formed, but also anything that is capable of being formed.

The difference between the formed and the formable is that the formed has already received its form, whereas the formable can receive it. But he who gives things their form also gives them the capacity to be formed, since in and from him exists the most beautiful, unchangeable form of all things; and he alone grants each thing not merely to be beautiful, but also to be capable of being beautiful.

Therefore it is most rightly believed that God made everything out of nothing. For even if the world was made from some material, that very material was made out of nothing, so that, by God’s most orderly gift, there might first be a capacity for forms and thereafter all that has been formed might be formed.

That Father, insofar as generation in the Godhead is concerned, is equally the Father of his Son. The Son is his co-worker, since through him all things were made and without him nothing was made; he is also his Word, Truth, Power, and Wisdom.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. That the Son was made neither out of nothing nor from any material, but was ineffably begotten by the Father, being equal to him

[Note: [Col. 0128D] St. Augustine, in the cited passage, chapters 3–4.] Hence follows: We believe also in Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, our God and Lord—not separated from God the Father, but himself God and, with the Father, one God.

Thus, when God begot the Word, he begot what he himself is: neither from nothing nor from any already-made and created material, but from himself, what he himself is. Therefore the same God the Father, who both willed and was able most truly to reveal himself to minds capable of knowing, begot for the purpose of revealing himself that which is himself, namely, the Word who is God, through whom he made himself known.

This Word is also called his Power and Wisdom, because through him he worked and ordered all things. Concerning him it is therefore said: “It reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things gently” (Wis. VIII, 1).

Accordingly, the only-begotten Son of God was not made by the Father, since, as the Evangelist says, “All things were made through him” (John I, 3); nor was he begotten in time, since the eternal, wise God eternally possesses his Wisdom with him. Nor is he unequal to the Father—that is, in any respect inferior—for the Apostle also says: “Although he was established in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized” (Phil. II, 6).

But because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I), that same Wisdom which was begotten from God also deigned to be created among human beings. To this refers the statement: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways” (Prov. VIII, 22). For the beginning of his ways is the head of the Church, who is Christ clothed in humanity; through him an example of living was given to us—that is, the sure way by which we might reach God. We could not return except through humility, since we fell through pride.

Therefore, insofar as he is the only-begotten Son, he has no brothers; but insofar as he is the firstborn, he deigned to call all who are reborn into God’s grace through adoption as sons, after his primacy and through his primacy, brothers (Luke VIII, 21; Heb. II, 11).

## CHAPTER XL. That the incarnate Son was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary

[Note: [Col. 0129D] St. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 38.] “Who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.” We rightly confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God from God, was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. In both substances—namely, divine and human—he is the only Son of God the almighty Father, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds.

But how do we say that Christ was born of the Holy Spirit, if the Holy Spirit did not beget him? Or was it because he made him? Our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as he is God, made all things through himself (John I, 3); but insofar as he is human, he too was made, as the Apostle says: “Made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 3).

Yet although the whole Trinity made that creature which the Virgin conceived and bore, even though it pertains only to the person of the Son—for the works of the Trinity are not separable—why, in making it, is the Holy Spirit alone named? Or is it that whenever one of the three is named in connection with some work, the whole Trinity is understood to have acted?

Indeed it is so, and it can be demonstrated by examples. But this need not be pursued at greater length.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] In the printed editions of St. Augustine, “the Trinity is understood to have acted.”]

## CHAPTER XLI. That although the Son is said to have been born of the Holy Spirit, he is in no way the son of the Holy Spirit

[Col. 0129D]

[Note: [Col. 0129D] St. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 38.] The question arises how it can be said that he was born of the Holy Spirit, although he is in no way the son of the Holy Spirit. For although God made this world, it is not permissible to call it the Son of God, or to say that it was born of God; rather, it was made, created, founded, or established by him, or whatever similar expression we may properly use.

Here, then, when we confess that he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, it is difficult to explain how he is not the son of the Holy Spirit but is the son of the Virgin Mary, since he was born both from him and from her. Certainly, he was not born from him as from a father, but from her as from a mother.

## CHAPTER XLII. That not everything which is born from something is immediately permitted to be called a son of that same thing

[Note: [Col. 0129D] The same work, chapters 39–40.] It must not, therefore, be granted that whatever is born from something is immediately to be called the son of that same thing. To pass over the fact that a son is born from a human being in one way, but hair, a louse, or a worm in another—none of which is a son—and to pass over these examples because they are an unbecoming comparison for so great a matter, certainly no one would rightly call those who are born from water and the Holy Spirit sons of water. They are plainly called sons of God the Father and of Mother Church.

Thus the Son of God the Father was born of the Holy Spirit, but not as the son of the Holy Spirit. What we said about hair and the other examples serves only to remind us that not everything born from something can also be called its son, just as it does not follow that everyone called someone’s son was also born from the one whose son he is said to be, as is the case with those who are adopted.

They are also called sons of Gehenna, not because they were born from it, but because they were prepared for it, just as sons of the kingdom are prepared for the kingdom. Since, therefore, something may be born from something else without being a son, and conversely not everyone called a son of someone is born from the one whose son he is called, it is clear that the manner in which Christ was born of the Holy Spirit—not as a son—and of the Virgin Mary—as a son—reveals to us the grace of God.

Through this grace, without any preceding merits, from the very beginning of his nature, when he began to exist, a human being was joined to God the Word in such unity of person that the very one who was the Son of God was also the son of man, and the son of man was also the Son of God. Thus, in the assumption of human nature, that grace itself became in a certain way natural to the man, so that he could commit no sin.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] St. Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 4, § 8.] This grace was therefore signified through the Spirit, because he is properly God in such a way that he is also called the gift of God. For by the gift of God—that is, by the Holy Spirit—such great humility was granted to us by so great a God that he deigned to assume the whole human being, namely, body, soul, and spirit, in the Virgin’s womb, inhabiting the maternal body intact and leaving it intact.

## CHAPTER XLIII. That Christ, a man born of a woman, saved both sexes

[Note: [Col. 0130D] The same work, § 9.] Therefore those who deny that our same Lord Jesus Christ had Mary as his mother on earth are to be detested, since that dispensation honored both sexes, male and female, and showed that both pertain to the care of God.

[Note: [Col. 0130D] We easily corrected and restored this mutilated passage in the Baluze edition from the printed books of St. Augustine’s *On Faith and the Creed*, from which all these materials were taken. The passage was corrupt not only in the manuscript [Col. 0131D] but also in the division of the following chapter, which the scribe devised incorrectly; for the divisions of the chapters and their rough, very often half-barbarous titles did not originate with St. Hildefonsus. Accordingly, the beginning of that chapter reads: “Not only the one whom he assumed . . . but as God they worship him, through the filth of sewers, etc.” As is evident, we have assigned the preceding words to the end of this chapter, to which they certainly belong; then, warned by an asterisk of the lacuna in the manuscript, we began the following chapter with the very words with which Augustine continues. In this way the sense remains clear and correct, and the entire passage is perfectly restored.]

—not only the one whom he assumed, but also the one through whom he assumed [human nature], by bearing a man and being born of a woman.

## CHAPTER XLIV. That the Virgin’s childbirth inflicted no injury upon Christ’s divinity

[Note: [Col. 0132D] St. Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 4, § 10.] Nor should reflection upon a woman’s womb diminish this faith for us, so that such a birth of our Lord might seem to be rejected because the impure consider it impure. For the Apostle most truly says that “the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. I, 25), and that “all things are clean for the clean” (Tit. I, 15).

Those who think this should observe how the rays of the sun—which they certainly do not praise as a creature of God but worship as God—are spread through the foulness of sewers and through every horrible place, and operate there according to their nature, yet are not soiled by any contamination, even though visible light is naturally more closely associated with visible filth.

How much less, then, could the noncorporeal and invisible Word of God be polluted by a female body that was certainly chaste, most pure, and uniquely glorious, where he assumed human flesh together with soul and spirit, through whose mediation the majesty of the Word dwelt more inwardly, separated from the frailty of the human body? It is therefore evident that the Word of God could in no way be stained by the human body, by which not even the human soul itself is stained.

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning the name and judgment of Pontius Pilate

[Note: [Col. 0132D] St. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, chapter 10.] Pilate means “the mouth of a hammerer,” because when he both justifies and condemns Christ with his mouth, he strikes both ways like a hammerer. Although he avoided the counsel of the Jews, he nevertheless permitted judgment to be carried out according to the Jews’ will.

He took water and washed his hands, so that in the washing the works of the Gentiles might be cleansed, and so that he might make us strangers to the impiety of the Jews who cried, “Crucify him!” (Mark XV, 13). He was a judge compelled to pronounce sentence against God. Yet he does not condemn the one brought before him; rather, he rebukes those who brought him, in a manner bearing witness and saying: “I indeed wished to free an innocent man; but since a riot has arisen, I am a servant of the laws, and your voice pours out blood.”

## CHAPTER XLVI. Why Christ chose the death of the cross

[Col. 0131D] This Jesus, our Lord and Redeemer, although almighty, showed himself so rich in mercy that he who is life and gives life to all humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, and death on a cross (Phil. II, 8). He chose the death of the cross in order that the condemnation contracted by the transgression involving the tree in paradise might be wiped away by the gibbet of this cross.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Concerning the mystery of the cross

[Col. 0132A]

[Note: [Col. 0132D] St. Isidore, book I *On the Offices*, chapter 30.] Paul commends the mystery of the cross when he says: “So that, rooted and founded in love, you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Eph. III, 18).

That is, the cross of the Lord: its breadth is represented by the transverse beam on which the hands are extended; its length extends from the ground up to that breadth, where the entire body is affixed from the hands downward; its height extends upward from the breadth to the top, where the head is attached; its depth is what is hidden, fixed in the earth.

By this sign of the cross every Christian action is represented. In its breadth, therefore, one is to work good in Christ; in its height, to hope for heavenly mysteries and not profane them; in its depth, to remain rooted and founded in love.

The breadth of the cross is therefore the action of a good work, represented by the extension of the hands. The breadth of the cross is also perseverance in good action, which through patient endurance preserves the power of the Passion. The height of the cross is hope for future goods, through which, without profanation . . . and being rooted, they remain immovable both in perseverance amid sufferings and in reward because of true hope.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Concerning Christ’s burial

When that burial is believed, remembrance is made of the new tomb, which would provide testimony to the one who was to rise to newness of life, just as the Virgin’s womb did to the one who was to be born. For, just as no other dead person was buried in that new tomb, neither before nor afterward was anything mortal conceived there.

## CHAPTER XLIX. That Christ descended into hell neither in his divinity nor in his flesh, but in his soul

“He descended to the dead.” Since at the time of his death Christ was, according to the flesh, in the tomb, and according to his divinity was everywhere—for he himself fills heaven and earth (Jer. XXIII, 24), and is the light that shines in the darkness, although the darkness did not comprehend it (John I, 5)—it remains that he descended into hell in his soul, according to the humility of his humanity.

According to the flesh, therefore, he was in the tomb; according to the soul, in hell, at the time of his death; but according to his unchangeable divinity he was never absent from paradise. He remains and has always remained present everywhere.

There is, however, a much easier interpretation, free from various ambiguities, if Christ’s words to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43), are understood according not to what he was as man but to what he was as God.

For as man, Christ was to be in the tomb according to the flesh on that day, and in hell according to the soul. But as God, that same Christ is always everywhere. He is the Power and Wisdom of God, concerning which it is written: “It reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things gently” (Wis. VIII, 1). Wherever paradise is, therefore, whoever of the blessed is there is there with him who is everywhere.

## CHAPTER L. Concerning the sleep of death and the glory of Christ’s resurrection

“On the third day he rose alive from the dead,” according to what was said: “I slept and rested and rose, because the Lord raised me” (Ps. III, 6). That is: I slept on the cross with the sleep of death; I rested in the tomb during the three days of repose; I rose alive from the dead in the glory of the resurrection.

He rightly rose on the third day, because, taken up by the power of the whole Trinity, he both died as a man and was raised from death—the firstborn destined to have brothers whom he called into adoption as sons of God and whom he deigned to make his fellow-participants and fellow-heirs.

Thus he who alone was the only-begotten Son born from God became the firstborn from the dead among many human beings, and deigned to call servants brothers, saying: “Go, tell my brothers to go to Galilee. There they will see me” (Matt. XXVIII, 10).

## CHAPTER LI. Concerning the ascension of Christ’s body into heaven, and that one should not ask where that body itself is; what breadth of heaven has been promised to all the faithful

[Note: [Col. 0133D] St. Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 5, § 13.] “He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father.” It is excessively curious and useless to ask where and how the Lord’s body is in heaven. It must simply be believed to be in heaven.

It is not appropriate to our frailty to investigate the secrets of heaven, but rather to hold lofty and honorable thoughts, in keeping with our faith, concerning the dignity of the Lord’s body. He also promised us a place in that blessedness, saying: “They will be like the angels in heaven” (Mark XII, 25), in that city which is the mother of us all, the eternal Jerusalem in the heavenly places.

## CHAPTER LII. What “sitting” and “the right hand of God” mean

[Note: [Col. 0133D] The same work, chapter 7.] We also believe that he sits at the right hand of the Father. Yet it must not be supposed that he is circumscribed by a human form, so that when we think of him a right and left side presents itself to the mind; nor should the statement that the Father is said to sit be understood as referring to bent knees.

Otherwise we would fall into the sacrilege in which the Apostle condemns those who “exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible man” (Rom. I, 23).

To be at the right hand, therefore, is to be understood as being in the highest blessedness, where justice, peace, and joy are; just as the goats are placed at the left (Matt. XXV, 35), that is, in misery, because of the labors and torments of iniquity.

When God is said to sit, therefore, this does not signify a position of the limbs but judicial authority, which that majesty never lacks, always distributing what is appropriate to those who deserve it. At the final judgment, however, the unquestionable glory of the only Son of God, the judge of the living and the dead, will shine much more manifestly among human beings, and the truth of the man will be seen openly.

## CHAPTER LIII. What is to be understood by “the living and the dead,” whom Christ will come to judge

[Note: [Col. 0133D] The same work, chapter 8.] “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” By these names either the righteous and sinners are signified, or those whom he will find on earth alive before death at that time are called living, while the dead are those who will rise at his coming.

This temporal dispensation is not only like that generation according to God, but also was and will be. For just as our Lord was on earth, is now in heaven, and will come in glory as judge of the living and the dead, so he will come as he ascended, according to the authority contained in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts I, 11)—that is, in the same reality of flesh and the unchangeableness of the humanity he assumed.

It is in reference to this temporal dispensation that he speaks in the Apocalypse, where it is written: “Thus says the one who is, who was, and who is to come” (Rev. I, 8).

Concerning the living and the dead who are to be judged, another view held by some is not inappropriate. It says: “When it is said that he will judge the living and the dead, this does not mean that some living and others dead will come to judgment, but that he will judge soul and body together. In these terms he called souls living and bodies dead, just as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: ‘Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot do anything to the soul. Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna’” (Matt. X, 28).

## CHAPTER LIV. That the intervening dispensation of the humanity assumed made the mention of the Holy Spirit somewhat more distant from the order of the Trinity

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” What has been handed down above at somewhat greater length concerning Christ pertains to the mystery of his incarnation and Passion. Since these matters intervene as an appropriate account of his person, they have made the mention of the Holy Spirit somewhat more distant.

But if only the divine nature is considered, then, in the same way that at the beginning it is said, “I believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ his only Son, our Lord,” the Holy Spirit is joined to them. All those things mentioned concerning Christ, however, pertain, as we have said, to the dispensation of the flesh.

Thus, in the mention of the Holy Spirit, the mystery of the Trinity is completed.

## CHAPTER LV. That the Holy Spirit is God, proceeding from the Father and the Son

[Note: [Col. 0134D] This chapter, and all those that follow through chapter 71 inclusive, are taken entirely from St. Isidore (*Etymologies*, book VII, chapter 3).] The Holy Spirit is proclaimed to be God because he proceeds from the Father and the Son and possesses their substance. For he could not proceed from the Father as anything other than what the Father himself is, namely, God.

## CHAPTER LVI. Why he is called “spirit”

[Col. 0135A]

The Holy Spirit is called so according to the fact that something is described as breathing forth. And that which breathes forth certainly breathes forth by the spirit, and from this he is called spirit.

In a particular sense, however, he is called the Holy Spirit insofar as he is related to the Father and the Son, as being their Spirit. Yet the name “spirit” is not always used according to a relation to something else, but also according to what signifies a certain nature. Every incorporeal nature is called spirit in the sacred Scriptures. Hence this name applies not only to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but also to every rational creature and to the soul.

## CHAPTER LVII. Why he is called the Holy Spirit

[Col. 0135B]

He is called the Holy Spirit of God because he is the holiness of the Father and the Son. For although the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy, he alone is properly called the Holy Spirit, as the coessential and consubstantial holiness of both.

## CHAPTER LVIII. That the Holy Spirit is called neither begotten nor unbegotten, but only proceeding

The Holy Spirit is not called begotten, lest two sons be suspected in the Trinity. He is not proclaimed unbegotten, lest two fathers be believed to exist in the Trinity itself.

He is called proceeding on the testimony of the Lord, who says: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot hear them now. But the Spirit of truth will come, who will proceed from the Father, and he will receive from what is mine. He will make everything known to you” (John XVI, 12–13).

He proceeds not only by nature, however, but also proceeds continually in order to accomplish the works of the Trinity.

## CHAPTER LIX. What difference there is between the Son who is born and the Holy Spirit who proceeds

The difference between the Son who is born and the Holy Spirit who proceeds is that the Son is born from one, whereas the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Therefore the Apostle says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. VIII, 9).

## CHAPTER LX. That the Holy Spirit is called an angel in respect of his work

[Col. 0135D] The Holy Spirit is also understood as an angel in respect of his work. For it was said of him: “He will announce to you the things that are to come” (John XVI, 13). In Greek and Latin, *angelus* means “messenger.”

Hence two angels also appeared to Lot (Gen. XIX, 1), in whom the Lord is named in a singular way. We understand them to be the Son and the Holy Spirit, for the Father is never read to have been sent.

## CHAPTER LXI. Why the Holy Spirit is called the Paraclete

The Holy Spirit is called the Paraclete from consolation. For Greek *paraklēsis* is translated into Latin as “consolation.” Christ sent him to the grieving apostles after he himself had ascended into heaven from their sight.

A consoler is sent to the sorrowful, according to that saying of the same Lord: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matt. V, 4). He also said: “Then the bridegroom’s sons will mourn when the bridegroom has been taken away from them” (Matt. IX, 15).

Likewise, he is called Paraclete because he provides consolation to souls that lose temporal joy. Others translate *paracletus* into Latin as “speaker” or “advocate.” For the Holy Spirit himself speaks and teaches; through him the word of wisdom is given, and by him the sacred Scripture was inspired.

## CHAPTER LXII. Why the Holy Spirit is called sevenfold

The Holy Spirit is called sevenfold because of the gifts which, from his united fullness, each person deserves to obtain in portions according to his worthiness. For he is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of God (Isa. XI, 2).

## CHAPTER LXIII. That “an upright spirit,” “a holy spirit,” and “a princely spirit” refer to the Trinity

The princely spirit is read of in the fiftieth Psalm. Since the word “spirit” is repeated there three times, some have understood the Trinity, because it is written: “God is spirit” (John IV, 24).

What is not a body and nevertheless exists appears to remain spirit. Some therefore understand the Trinity to be signified there: the Father in the princely spirit, the Son in the upright spirit, and the Holy Spirit in the holy spirit.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Why the Holy Spirit is called a gift

[Col. 0136C]

The Holy Spirit is called a gift because he is given. The name “gift” derives from giving. It is very well known that when the Lord Jesus Christ had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, he gave the Holy Spirit, and those who believed, filled with him, spoke in the tongues of all nations.

He is the gift of God insofar as he is given to those who love God through him. In himself he is God; in relation to us he is a gift.

The Holy Spirit is eternally a gift, distributing gifts of grace to each person as he wills. He grants prophecies to whomever he wills and forgives sins to whomever he chooses. For sins are not forgiven without the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER LXV. Why the Holy Spirit is called love and grace

[Col. 0136D]

The Holy Spirit is properly called love either because he naturally joins together those from whom he proceeds and shows himself to be one with them, or because he works in us so that we may remain in God and he in us.

Therefore nothing among the gifts of God is greater than love, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit. He is also grace, which is called grace because it is given freely, not on account of our merits but by the divine will.

Just as we properly call the only-begotten Word of God by the name “Wisdom,” although the Holy Spirit and the Father are also universally wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called by the name “Love,” although the Father and the Son are also universally love.

## CHAPTER LXVI. Why the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God

[Col. 0137A]

The books of the Gospel make it perfectly clear that the Holy Spirit is the finger of God. For while one of the Evangelists says, “By the finger of God I cast out demons” (Luke XI, 20), another says the same thing in this form: “By the Spirit of God I cast out demons” (Matt. XII, 28).

The law was therefore also given as written by the finger of God on the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb (Exod. XXXI, 18). And on the fiftieth day after the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit came (Acts II, 2).

He is called the finger so that his operative power with the Father and the Son may be signified. Hence Paul also says: “All these things the one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. XII, 11).

Just as through baptism we die and are reborn in Christ, so we are marked by the Spirit, who is the finger of God and the spiritual seal.

## CHAPTER LXVII. Why the Holy Spirit is attested to have come in the form of a dove

The Holy Spirit is said to have come in the form of a dove so that his nature might be revealed through a bird characterized by simplicity and innocence. Hence the Lord says: “Be simple as doves” (Matt. X, 16). For this bird, physically speaking, lacks bile and possesses only innocence and love.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. Why the Holy Spirit is called by the name of fire

The Holy Spirit is called by the name of fire because in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts II, 3) he appeared like fire through the division of tongues and sat upon each one of them.

He gave the apostles the grace of different languages so that they might be made capable of instructing faithful peoples. The fact that he is said to have sat upon each individual means that he was not divided among many, but remained wholly in each, as is generally the nature of fire.

For kindled fire has this nature: however many people look upon it, and however many gaze upon the crest of its purple radiance, it grants as much of its light to their sight and provides as many with the service of its gift, while nevertheless remaining whole in itself.

## CHAPTER LXIX. Why the Holy Spirit is called by the name of water

[Col. 0137D] The Holy Spirit is called by the name of water in the Gospel, when the Lord cries out and says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 37).

The Evangelist explained the source of this saying: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive.”

## CHAPTER LXX. That the water of the sacrament is one thing and the water of the Holy Spirit another

But this signifies the Spirit of God. The water of the sacrament is visible; the water of the Spirit is invisible. The former washes the body and signifies what takes place in the soul. Through the Holy Spirit, however, the soul itself is cleansed and nourished.

## CHAPTER LXXI. Why the Holy Spirit is called anointing

The Holy Spirit is called anointing, as the Apostle John attests, because just as oil, by its natural weight, rises above every liquid, so at the beginning the Holy Spirit hovered over the waters.

Hence the Lord is also read to have been anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, with the Holy Spirit. The Apostle John likewise calls the Holy Spirit anointing, saying: “The anointing which you received from him remains in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you; but just as his anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John II, 27).

For he himself is the invisible anointing, the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER LXXII. That the holy Church is believed because love of neighbor is demonstrated in it

[Col. 0138B]

[Note: [Col. 0137D] St. Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 21.] “The holy catholic Church.” This faith concerns God our creator and our renewer, and up to this point it has been discussed.

But since love has been commanded to us not only toward God, when it was said, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind,” but also toward our neighbor—for he says, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII, 37, 39)—unless this faith embraces a gathering and fellowship of human beings in which brotherly love is active, it is less fruitful.

We therefore believe also in the holy Church, truly catholic.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. Concerning the name of the catholic Church

[Col. 0138C]

[Note: [Col. 0137] St. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 1, from which the following three chapters are also taken.] “Church” is Greek; in Latin it is translated as “convocation,” because it calls everyone to itself. “Catholic” means universal, καθόλου (*katholou*), that is, “according to the whole.”

For it is not confined, like the gatherings of heretics, to certain parts of the regions, but is spread and extended throughout the whole world. The Apostle also approves this when he says to the Romans: “I give thanks to my God for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Rom. I, 8).

Hence *universitas*—“universality”—is named from *una*, “one,” because it is gathered into unity. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. XII, 30); that is, whoever is not gathered by me into my unity, being separated from me, is dispersed in the destruction of dispersion.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. Why seven churches are written of, although the Church is one

Why are seven churches written of, although the Church is one, except that the one catholic Church may be signified as filled with the sevenfold Spirit? We know that Solomon likewise spoke of the Lord: “Wisdom built herself a house; she carved out seven pillars” (Prov. IX, 1).

Yet there is no doubt that these seven are one, since the Apostle says: “The Church of the living God, which is the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Tim. III, 15).

## CHAPTER LXXV. From where the Church began, and why it is called Zion or Jerusalem

[Col. 0139A]

The Church began at the place where the Holy Spirit came from heaven and filled those who were sitting together in one place.

In its present pilgrimage, the Church is called Zion because, situated in the length of this pilgrimage, it contemplates the promise of heavenly things. For this reason it received the name Zion, that is, “speculation” or “contemplation.”

Because of the peace of the future homeland, it is called Jerusalem. For Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.” There, after every adversity has been swallowed up, it will possess in present vision the peace that is Christ.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. What difference there is between the Church and the Synagogue

[Col. 0139B]

“Synagogue” is Greek for “assembly.” The Jewish people retained this as their proper name; their assembly is properly called a synagogue, although it has also been called a church.

The Apostles, however, never called ours a synagogue, but always a church, either to distinguish them or because there is some difference between an assembly, from which synagogue derives its name, and a convocation, from which church derives its name.

The distinction is that animals are accustomed to be gathered together, and we properly speak of their herds; but a convocation is something greater, appropriate to beings who use reason, such as human beings.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. That the Holy Spirit fully inspired the New and Old Testaments in the holy Church
[Col. 0139C] Into this holy Church the Holy Spirit inspired, in the Old Testament, the Law and the Prophets, and, in the New, the Gospel and the Apostles. Hence Paul also says: “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching” (II Tim. III, 16). Therefore, since it is appropriate in this place to indicate clearly and systematically, as we have learned from the records of the Fathers, which books of the New and Old Testament are believed to have been inspired by that same Holy Spirit according to the tradition of our predecessors and are known to have been handed down to the Churches of Christ:

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. Which authority of the Scriptures is to be followed first in the Churches.

[Col. 0139D] [Note: This chapter and the following two are taken from Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapters 8–9.]

Among the canonical Scriptures, therefore, that authority of the Catholic Churches is to be followed above all, among which, clearly, those Churches are to be included that have deserved to possess apostolic sees and to receive letters from them. The following rule is consequently to be observed regarding the canonical holy Scriptures: those books accepted by all the Catholic Churches are to be preferred to those which some do not accept. Among those not accepted by all, those accepted by the greater number and by the more authoritative Churches are to be preferred to those held by fewer and less authoritative Churches. But if some books are found to be accepted by the greater number and others by the more authoritative Churches—although such a situation cannot, in fact, be found—I think that they should nevertheless be regarded as possessing equal authority.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. Which books are contained in the canon of both Testaments.

[Col. 0140A]

The entire canon of Scripture, on which we now say that our consideration is to be directed, is contained in these books: the five books of Moses, namely Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy; one book of Joshua son of Nun; one of Judges; one little book called Ruth, which seems rather to belong to the beginning of the Books of Kings; then four Books of Kings, and two Books of Chronicles, not following in sequence but attached, as it were, alongside and proceeding together with them. This is the history that contains connected periods and the order of events.

There are other books, as though arranged according to a different order, which neither fit into this sequence nor follow one another: Job, Tobit, Esther, Judith, the two Books of Maccabees, and the two Books of Ezra, which seem rather to follow that ordered history, extending to the conclusion reached in the Books of Kings or Chronicles. Then come the Prophets, among whom David is represented by the one Book of Psalms; and Solomon by three books, Proverbs, the Song of Songs, and Ecclesiastes. For those two books, one entitled Wisdom and the other Ecclesiasticus, are said, because of a certain resemblance, to be Solomon’s; but it is most reliably reported that Jesus son of Sirach composed them. Nevertheless, since they have deserved to be received as possessing divine authority, they are to be counted among the prophetic books. [Note: The printed editions of *On Christian Doctrine* place this among the authoritative books.]

The remaining books are those properly called prophetic: the twelve individual books of the Twelve Prophets, which, because they have never been separated, are regarded as one. The names of these prophets are: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. Then there are four prophets of larger books: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and Ezekiel. With these forty-four books the authority of the Old Testament comes to an end.

The New Testament consists of four books of the Gospel: according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, and according to John; fourteen letters of the apostle Paul—one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, one to Philemon, and one to the Hebrews; two letters of Peter, three of John, one of Jude, and one of James; one book of the Acts of the Apostles; and one book of the Apocalypse of John.

## CHAPTER LXXX. That all the books possessing holy authority are either to be committed to memory or not to be left wholly unknown.

[Col. 0140D]

In all these books, those who fear God and are gentle through piety seek the will of God. The first observance in this work and labor is to know these books and, even if one does not yet understand them, at least to commit them to memory by reading them, or not to leave them wholly unknown.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On the remission of sins.

[Note: Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 64.]
