The remission of sins. It is rightly placed after the commemoration of our Church in the order of the confession: the remission of sins. For by this the Church that is on earth stands. By this, what had perished does not perish, but is found again. Apart from the gift of baptism, which was given against original sin, so that what was acquired through generation might be removed through regeneration, it also takes away active sins—whatever it finds to have been committed in the heart, mouth, deed, thought, or speech. Therefore, apart from this great indulgence, with which the renewal of the human being begins and in which every guilt, both innate and added, is loosed, even the rest of life, however greatly it may abound in righteousness, is not lived without the remission of sins. For the children of God, as long as they live in mortality, struggle with death.

Although it has truly been said of them, “Those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. VIII, 14), they are nevertheless stirred by the Spirit of God and, as sons of God, make progress toward God, so that even by their own spirit—especially when the corruptible body weighs them down—as sons of human beings they may, in certain human impulses, fall back upon themselves and therefore sin. There is indeed a distinction of degree; for although every crime is a sin, not every sin is therefore a crime. Accordingly, we say that the life of holy people, as long as they live in this death, can be found without crime. But if we say that we have no sin, says the holy Apostle, “we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8). Yet even concerning those crimes themselves, however serious, one must not despair of their remission in the holy Church of God for those who repent according to the measure of each person’s sin.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. That in the practice of repentance the measure of time is not to be considered, but rather that of sorrow; and that sins can be remitted only in the Church.

[Col. 0141C]

[Note: Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 65.]

In the practice of repentance, when an offense has been committed such that the offender is also separated from the body of Christ, the measure of sorrow is to be considered more than the measure of time. “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. L, 19). But because one person’s sorrow is often hidden from another and does not come to the knowledge of others through words or any other signs—although it is before him to whom it is said, “My groaning is not hidden from you” (Ps. XXXVII, 10)—the leaders of the Churches rightly establish periods of repentance, so that satisfaction may be made to the Church, in which those sins themselves are remitted; for outside it they are not remitted. It alone, properly speaking, has received the Holy Spirit as a pledge, without whom no sins are remitted, so that those whose sins are forgiven may attain eternal life.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. On the evident resurrection of the flesh.

[Note: Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 10, §23, after the middle.]

The resurrection of the flesh and eternal life. This visible substance properly called flesh must without hesitation be believed to rise again. The apostle Paul seems to point to it as with a finger when he says: “This corruptible body must put on incorruption” (I Cor. XV, 53). For in saying “this,” he directs his finger, as it were, toward it. What is visible is pointed out with a finger, since the soul too could be called corruptible, for it is corrupted by moral vices. And when we read, “this mortal body must put on immortality,” the same visible flesh is signified, because the finger is again directed toward it, as it were. The soul can likewise be called mortal as well as corruptible because of moral vices. For the soul’s death is apostasy from God (Eccli. X, 14). Sacred Scripture records this as its first sin in paradise. The body, therefore, will rise again according to the Christian faith, which cannot deceive.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. That nothing of human flesh perishes in the resurrection; but whatever has been dispersed or consumed in any kind of destruction returns wholly to the soul that animated it while it lived.

[Col. 0142B]

[Note: Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 88.]

The earthly matter from which the flesh of mortals is created does not perish for God. But whether it is dissolved into dust or ashes, scattered into whatever breath or air, changed into the substance of other bodies or into the elements themselves, or becomes the food of any animals or even human beings and is transformed into flesh, it returns in an instant to the human soul that originally animated it so that the human being might come into existence, grow, and live.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. That Almighty God wonderfully and ineffably restores, with marvelous speed at the resurrection, the whole substance of which the flesh consists. Also, on the example of a statue made of dissoluble metal, by which it is shown how the resurrection can occur.

[Col. 0142C]

[Note: The same work, chapter 89.]

The earthly matter itself, which becomes a corpse when the soul departs, will not be restored in the resurrection in such a way that, although the things that disperse and are transformed into the various kinds and forms of other things return to the body from which they dispersed, they must necessarily return to the same bodily parts in which they had been. Otherwise, if what repeated haircuts removed were returned to the hair, and what repeated trimming removed were returned to the fingernails, an excessive and indecent deformity would confront those who think about the matter and consequently do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh.

But just as, if a statue made of any dissoluble metal were melted by fire, crushed into powder, or mixed into a mass, and the craftsman wished to restore it again from the quantity of that material, it would make no difference to its completeness which particle of the material were returned to which limb of the statue, provided that the whole from which it had been formed were restored and recovered—so God, the wonderful and ineffable craftsman, will restore our flesh with marvelous and ineffable speed from the whole substance of which it had consisted. It will make no difference to its restoration whether hairs return to hairs and nails to nails, or whether what had been lost from them is changed into flesh and recalled into other parts of the body, while the craftsman’s providence ensures that nothing indecent occurs.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. On the diversity of stature and on the thinness or fatness of human bodies, in which holy bodies will possess only what is fitting.

[Col. 0143A]

[Note: Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 90.]

Nor does it follow that the stature of each person who rises again will therefore be different because the stature of each person while living was different, or that the thin will rise with the same thinness or the fat with the same fatness. But if it is the Creator’s purpose that each person’s individual character and recognizable likeness be preserved in his or her form, while all other bodily goods are restored equally, the material will be proportioned in each person so that nothing of it perishes and so that he supplies whatever anyone lacked—he who was also able to make whatever he willed from nothing.

But if there will be a rational inequality among the bodies of those who rise, just as there is among the voices that complete a song, then each person will receive from the material of his or her own body what both makes the human being suited to the angelic assemblies and introduces nothing offensive to their senses. Nothing indecorous will be there. Whatever will be, will itself teach this, because it will not be future if it is not fitting.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. That the bodies of the saints will rise spiritual, though they will not be spirits.

[Note: The same work, chapter 91.]

The bodies of the saints will therefore rise without any defect, without any deformity, just as without any corruption, burden, or difficulty; and in them there will be as much ease as there is blessedness. For this reason they are called spiritual, although they will unquestionably be bodies, not spirits. But just as what is now called an animal body is nevertheless a body and not a soul, so then there will be a spiritual body, yet it will be a body and not a spirit (I Cor. XV, 44).

Accordingly, with respect to the corruption that now weighs down the soul (Wis. IX, 15), and the vices through which the flesh lusts against the spirit (Gal. V, 17), then there will not be flesh but body, since heavenly bodies too are mentioned. Therefore it was said: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV, 50). And as though explaining what he had said, he adds: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” What he first called “flesh and blood,” he later called “corruption”; and what he first called “the kingdom of God,” he later called “incorruption.”

But with respect to substance, it will still be flesh; for this reason Christ’s body was also called flesh after the resurrection (Luke XXIV, 39). Thus the Apostle says: “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (I Cor. XV, 44), because then there will be such harmony between flesh and spirit, the spirit giving life to the flesh that is subject to it without any need of support, that nothing within us will oppose us; but just as outwardly we will suffer no enemy, so inwardly we will not suffer ourselves as enemies.

[Note: Baluzius printed: “Because of … and after the resurrection the body of Christ which was called …” We have corrected this passage in accordance with the printed editions of blessed Augustine.]

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. That the bodies of the reprobate will indeed rise, but will be eternally punished with their vices and deformities.

[Note: Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 92.]

All those who are not liberated by the one Mediator between God and human beings from that mass of perdition which came into being through the first human being will also rise, each with his or her own flesh, but so that they may be punished with the devil and his angels. Whether they rise with the vices and deformities of their bodies—whatever defective and deformed limbs they may have borne—is it necessary to labor in investigating? The uncertain condition or beauty of those whose condemnation will be certain and eternal ought not to weary us. Nor should it trouble us how their bodies will be incorruptible if they will be able to suffer. For there is no true life except where one lives happily, and no true incorruption except where health is not corrupted by any pain. But where the unhappy are not permitted to die, so to speak, death itself does not die; and where perpetual pain does not destroy but torments, corruption itself does not end. This is called the second death in the holy Scriptures (Rev. II, 11; XX, 6, 14).

[Note: The same work, chapter 93.]

Yet neither the first death, by which the soul is compelled to leave its body, nor the second, by which the soul is not permitted to leave its punitive body, would have befallen the human being if no one had sinned.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. That the punishment will be milder for original sin alone and for the least actual sin.

The punishment of those who, apart from the sin they inherited originally, added no further sin will certainly be the mildest of all; and among the other sins they added, each person will have a condemnation there that is more tolerable in proportion as his or her iniquity here was less.

## CHAPTER XC. That from death until the resurrection souls are held in hidden receptacles, either in rest or in distress.

[Col. 0144C]

[Note: The same work, chapter 109.]

During the period between a human being’s death and the final resurrection, souls are held in hidden receptacles, each according to whether it deserves rest or distress, in keeping with what it acquired in the flesh while it lived.

## CHAPTER XCI. How offerings and almsgiving by the living may benefit the souls of the departed, or may not benefit them at all.

[Note: The same work, chapter 110.]

Nor should it be denied that the souls of the departed are relieved by the piety of their living relatives when the Mediator’s sacrifice is offered for them or alms are given in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while they lived, earned the ability to be benefited by them afterward. There is a certain way of living that is not so good that it does not require these things after death, but is not so bad that these things do not benefit it after death. There is also a condition so good that it does not require them. And there is, again, a condition so bad that, when this life has passed, it cannot be helped even by these things.

## CHAPTER XCII. That eternal life is the grace of God, while the wage of sin is death.

[Note: The same work, chapter 107.]

The Apostle commends eternal life, which is the reward of good works, as the grace of God: “The wage of sin,” he says, “is death, but the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. VI, 23). A wage owed for military service is paid, not given as a gift. Therefore he said, “The wage of sin is death,” to show that death is inflicted on sin not undeservedly but as something owed. Grace, however, is not grace unless it is free. It must therefore be understood that the good merits even of the human being himself are gifts of God; and when eternal life is paid in return for them, what is paid except grace for grace?

## CHAPTER XCIII. That in this life a person acquires what may afterward bring relief or increased punishment.

[Note: Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 110.]

Accordingly, every merit is acquired here by which someone may be relieved or burdened after this life.

[Note: How corrupt the text was in this passage is evident from the reading of the Baluzius edition, which we transcribe: “But let no one hope to obtain from God after death what he neglected here. Those things which the Church regularly performs to commend the dead are contrary to the apostolic sentence, in which it is said: ‘For we shall all stand,’ and so forth.” Anyone can see how great an error was contained in these words.]

But let no one hope to obtain from God after death what he neglected here. Therefore those things which the Church regularly performs to commend the dead are not contrary to that apostolic sentence in which it is said: “For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil” (Rom. XIV, 10; II Cor. V, 10), because each person also acquired this merit for himself or herself while living in the body, so that these things might be beneficial. For they do not benefit everyone; and why do they not benefit everyone except because of the difference in the life each person led in the body?

## CHAPTER XCIV. What sacrifices and alms offered for baptized persons who have died accomplish.

When, therefore, sacrifices—whether of the altar or of any kind of alms—are offered for baptized persons who have died, for the very good they are expressions of thanksgiving; for those who are not very bad, they are acts of intercession; for the very bad, even though they provide no assistance to the dead, they are nevertheless forms of consolation for the living. For those whom they benefit, they either bring about complete remission or at least make the condemnation itself more tolerable.

## CHAPTER XCV. That after the resurrection and the completion of judgment, the individual cities will remain in angels and human beings: Christ’s in eternal glory, the devil’s in everlasting condemnation.

[Note: Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 111.]

After the resurrection, when the universal judgment has taken place and been completed, the two cities will have their respective boundaries: one belonging to Christ and the other to the devil; one to the good and the other to the evil. Each, however, will consist both of angels and of human beings. The good will have no will to sin, and the evil no ability to do so; neither will there be any condition of dying. The good will live truly and happily in eternal life, while the evil will endure unhappily in eternal death, without the power to die, since both states will be without end. Yet in blessedness one of the good will remain more excellent than another, while in misery one of the evil will remain more tolerable than another.

[Note: The same work, chapter 113.]

That perpetual death of the condemned, namely alienation from the life of God, will therefore remain without end, and it will be common to all, whatever human beings may imagine concerning the variety of punishments and the relief or interruption of pains according to their human ways of thinking. In the same way, the eternal life of the saints will remain common to all, although they will shine harmoniously with differing degrees of honor. This is the faith that is given to newly instructed Christians to be held in a few words in the Creed.

[Note: These final words are from the book *On Faith and the Creed*.]

These few words are known to the faithful, so that by believing they may be subjected to God, by being subjected may live rightly, by living rightly may cleanse the heart, and with a cleansed heart may understand what they believe.

## CHAPTER XCVI. On the remaining matters belonging to the rule of true faith.

After the Apostles’ Creed, and after those things that have been said concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit according to the ineffable nature of the Godhead, and also according to the temporal dispensation concerning the Incarnation of Christ, the following matters likewise belong to the faith and must be held with an equal strength of belief.

[Note: Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 24.]

There is one God of the New and Old Testament. These two Testaments are salutarily commended by divine authority: the former fulfilled truthfully through prophecy, the latter through history.

Nothing is to be thought concerning God or creatures together with pagans, heretics, or schismatics in those matters in which they dissent from the faith of truth; rather, only what both Testaments commend through divine utterance is to be believed.

God created heaven, earth, the sea, and all that is in them without necessity, and there is absolutely no visible or invisible substance that either is God or was not created by the good God. God is the supreme and unchangeable good, whereas the creature is inferior and mutable good.

The nature of angels and of the soul is not a part of the divine substance but a creature of God, created from nothing; and because it was created in the image of God, it is therefore incorporeal. The nature of the soul itself, however, is uncertain.

Piety in conduct must be maintained in every respect. Without it, faith in divine worship lies idle and languishes; with it, the integrity of divine worship is made complete.

God is to be loved for his own sake; one’s neighbor, in God; and one’s enemy, for God’s sake, so that love, beginning with God, may advance through one’s neighbor and, progressing, reach even one’s enemy; and thus, when it has advanced through one’s neighbor and reached one’s enemy, it may remain complete in God.

One person cannot be defiled by another’s sin where the consent of a pure will is not present.

Lawful marriages are not to be believed condemnable, although offspring born from them is believed to be subject to original sin; nevertheless, the integrity of faithful virgins or of those who practice continence is rightly taught to be preferred to marriage.

One must not think that the remedies of repentance are unnecessary for the daily transgressions of human frailty, without which we cannot exist in this life. Rather, we must confess that all sins are erased through the fruitful contrition of repentance, as the Spirit of God teaches: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin” (Ps. XXXI, 1).

No human being can be subjected to his or her head, which is Christ, by his or her own powers, but only through divine grace; nor can anyone be made firm in the unity of Christ’s Church except through perseverance in unbroken peace.

Nothing good should be thought to be credited to the free choice of the human will; rather, the entire number of the elect is acquired according to the purpose of God’s will.

Temporal goods, created by God and common to the good and the evil, are either withheld from or granted to each person by his providential ordering and administration. In the case of each believer, it is not the possession of these goods but their use that is either to be condemned or approved.

Certainly, only the good will be able to attain eternal goods in the future. We believe that the Church, formed by the pledge of these goods, is now held in expectation, possessing here the first fruits of the Spirit and in the future their perfection; here sustained in hope, there afterward satisfied in reality; here seeing through a mirror in an enigma, but in the future face to face, when faith has been brought to sight.

Until the good is perfected in us, so that we may enjoy the fullness of the supreme God, we are to know that we should enjoy God and our neighbors with delight. We must also have this hope of resurrection: we must believe that we too will rise in the same reality of the flesh in which the Lord rose from the dead, in the same body in which we exist and live—not changing our nature or sex, but merely laying aside frailty and vices.

Satan, together with his angels and worshipers, is to be condemned to everlasting fire. Nor can he ever be restored to his former, that is, angelic, dignity, from which he fell through his own impiety, as certain sacrilegious disputation maintains.

This is the true integrity of the Catholic tradition’s faith. If any one element of it is rejected, the strength of the whole faith is lost.

## CHAPTER XCVII. That after the Creed one proceeds to the font.

When all these matters have been set forth—those belonging to the rule of the one holy faith, as well as those shown to adhere to that same faith with complete firmness, by which it is fitting to instruct the candidate after the catechumenate—one proceeds to the font. The font is approached as though it were the Red Sea, so that those who served in Egypt under Pharaoh, laboring with mud and bricks made light by straw (Exod. I, 14)—that is, those who clung to the world, while the devil ruled them, hardened by the mingling of evil thoughts in earthly actions—may, with Christ as their guide, as Moses was the guide, quickly attain their liberation.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. That a human being serves the prince of this world in the world just as Israel served Pharaoh in Egypt.

Thus, under the Egyptian king, Israel is burdened with mud, straw, and bricks in the buildings of those whose liberation will perish. In the same way, before baptism, under the prince of this world, the human being is brought through the lightness of unclean thought into earthen structures, forming a wall of most wicked action. While remaining in it, the person indulges in evil pleasure according to desire and is pressed under the yoke of harmful slavery.

## CHAPTER XCIX. What the clouds and the pillar that went before the people destined for salvation signify.

Then the Lord is seen going before the people as guide on their journey: by night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud (Exod. XIII, 21–22). This same preceding cloud is Christ, who is also the pillar, because he is the uprightness, firmness, and support of our weakness. He shines not by day but by night, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind (John IX, 39)—that is, so that humble ignorance may be enlightened and swelling knowledge obscured.

Again, in another sense: the mystery of Christ is manifest as in the daytime in the flesh, as though in a cloud; but in the judgment it will be as in the terror of night, because then there will be great tribulation in the world, like fire, which will shine for the righteous and burn for the unrighteous.

Again, in another sense: in fire there is terror, but in cloud a gentle and soothing favor of vision. The day is understood as the life of the righteous, and night as the life of the sinner. Thus the pillar was shown by the cloud in the day and by fire in the night, because Almighty God will appear gentle to the righteous and terrifying to the unrighteous. When he comes in judgment, he caresses the former through the mildness of gentleness and frightens the latter through the strictness of justice.

Again, in another sense: What does it mean that the pillar of cloud went before the people by day, while the radiance of fire shone not by day but by night, except that our Redeemer, offering guidance to those who follow him by the example of his conduct, shone with no light for those who confess their righteousness, but kindled with the fire of his love those who acknowledge the darkness of their sins?

## CHAPTER C. How free will is shown, through the pillar that follows and precedes, to be governed by prevenient grace and God’s subsequent mercy.

We must certainly consider how free will, whether in us or in those who are reborn through us, can do nothing good without God’s grace. For look: the pillar that goes before the people destined for salvation leaves what is behind behind it and stands between the camps of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel, resisting the former and advancing the latter. In the fact that it first went before, it signifies that, through prevenient grace, the unwilling human being has been granted the will to desire what is good. In the fact that it protects what is behind from the rear, it signifies that what has been begun can be completed with the help of subsequent mercy, which preserves and fulfills what comes last.

There the pillar went before the people, showing the route of liberation; here grace goes before free will. There the pillar guards the rear; here mercy follows weakness. There it was sought that those who did not wish to perish might be liberated; here it is granted that those who are unwilling may will what is good. There terror is brought about when the enemies are confronted from behind; here subsequent mercy comes to meet us when weakness is assisted.

For unless help were present both in going before and in following the people being delivered, to afford the light of life when the enemy rushed upon them from behind to destroy them—as happens here—what benefit would preceding faith offer those to be baptized, unless subsequent mercy, freeing them from evil, granted that they might complete the work of faith? Therefore the light of the pillar rightly goes before the people destined for liberation, so that they cannot perish, and follows them, so that they cannot be destroyed: the grace of the Savior graciously precedes the human will so that it may will what is good, and mercifully grants it the ability to do what is good.

## CHAPTER CI. On the encounter along the journey and the entrance into the Red Sea, whose significance is represented in the waters of the font.

Moses is the leader of Israel destined for salvation. Jesus became the leader of the human being destined for redemption. Moses leaves Egypt; Jesus leaves the world. The Egyptians pursue Moses; the multitude of sins pursues Jesus.

There the sea was colored red by the redness of its shore, whence it is also called the Red Sea; here there is baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ. There the sea’s expanse is divided by the rod; here the entrance to the font is opened by the sign of the cross. There Israel enters; here the human being is immersed. There the passage through the waters is made without obstruction on dry ground; here the saving journey is accomplished through the waters.

There the pursuing Egyptians with Pharaoh are submerged; here sins with the devil are slain—not through the destruction of nature but through the loss of power. For insofar as he is the devil, he remains; insofar as he had evil power, he no longer remains. One element becomes both destruction and aid for each side: it destroys those destined to perish and advances those destined to be rescued; it slays those destined to die and helps those destined to live; it casts down those destined for ruin and sends forth those destined for deliverance.

Those who have been liberated rejoice in the glory of the Liberator and in the grace of liberation. After the sea, and after the font, it is said: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored. He cast horse and rider into the sea. The Lord is my helper and protector, and he has become my salvation” (Exod. XV, 1).

## CHAPTER CII. On the figure and type of baptism commended by the apostle Paul in the cloud and the sea.

Paul rightly commends the figure and type of this baptism when he says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud and all passed through the sea” (I Cor. X, 1). Why did they pass through the sea? As though you were asking him, he continues: “All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.” If the figure of the sea had such power, how much power will the reality of baptism have? If what was performed in figure brought the people who passed through it to the manna, what will Christ provide in the truth of his baptism for his people who have passed through him?

## CHAPTER CIII. That the passage through the sea signifies arriving at the manna, that is, coming after baptism to receive Christ’s body.

To what does Jesus lead through baptism—Jesus whom Moses then represented when he led the people through the sea—if not to the manna? What is the manna? “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (John VI, 51). The faithful, already passed through the Red Sea, receive the manna.

Therefore, since, as was said, “all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,” and the Lord says, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not see the kingdom of God” (John III, 5), the sea rightly represented water, the cloud the Holy Spirit, and the manna the bread of life. By these sacraments the human being is purified and given life, so that he may be admitted into the inheritance of the land of the living.

It has now become clear that the sea represented the font. Let the mysteries of the sacred font itself now be set forth.

## CHAPTER CIV. That the generation of created things and the regeneration of human beings take place at one time.

[Col. 0150B]

The time that coincided with the effect of this font’s new regeneration was the time when the world began to have its origin, so that the generation of created things and the regeneration of souls might coincide at one time, since both were revealed to take place in spring. For the beginning of the world arises in the first month. Likewise, in the same month Passover is commanded to take place. Thus the newness of creation begins; thus the newness of souls begins.

What was created in the world through newness reaches mortality. What, after oldness, rises again, buried in the death of Christ, reaches eternity. But how it comes about that entrance into this generation and into these purposes seems to be assigned [perhaps: “to be assigned”] at the time when there is a lawful passage from this generation into another generation is unclear. For in spring the children of Israel left Egypt and passed through the sea. At this time the Passover of our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated. This is the passage of souls from vices to virtue, from the passions of the flesh to the grace and sobriety of the mind, from the leaven of malice and wickedness to truth and sincerity.

To those who have been regenerated it is therefore said: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first for you among the months of the year” (Exod. XII, 2). For the one who is washed leaves and abandons that intelligible Pharaoh, the prince of this world, together with all his works.

## CHAPTER 105. That it is said to contain the sacrament of mysteries until the miracle of the waters is manifested on the surface

[Col. 0150D] Let us disclose, from the surface, the miracle, and from the mystery, the hidden secret of this font, into which the power of divine sanctification flows. In this font we contemplate the remarkable signs of its miracles, and an operation worthy of awe is observed, established by divine institution.

[Note: [Col. 0149D]

Many examples similar to this prodigy—whose exposition Hildefonsus pursues at greater length throughout the following chapter—occur in ecclesiastical history: waters sent down from heaven into baptismal fonts whenever the solemn time for baptism approached, in various Churches, both Eastern and Western. Sophronius is our authority for these events (whether he was the true author of the *Spiritual Meadow*, John Moschus). In chapters 214 and 215 he records two miracles of this kind customarily seen in the same province of Lycia, though in different places: one at the village of Soruba, at the foot of the mountain on which the city of the Coeanenses was situated; the other at the fortress of Cedebratis, beneath Mount Aeonander, where a baptistery stood.

It is certain, however, from the most reliable records, that such events were more frequent in the West. Hardly anyone is unaware of what Paschasius, bishop of Lilybaeum, relates in a letter addressed to Saint Leo about a small church in the Campanian town called Meltina; the letter is published among his works. The miraculous filling of this font, although it was accustomed to occur every year, became more famous and celebrated throughout almost the whole world in the year 417. At that time a dispute had arisen under Pope Innocent concerning the proper day on which Easter should be celebrated. The Westerners disagreed with the Easterners because of an error in the calculation of Easter. Thus, while the Easterners had designated 22 April, the Westerners had appointed the celebration of Easter for 25 March. It happened that in the church mentioned above, when the solemn time for baptism at Easter was approaching according to the Western calculation, the priest came to the font, as was customary, and found it dry, whereas every year they had found it filled from heaven. Accordingly, baptism was postponed until 22 April. When they approached the baptistery again on that day, they found the font filled with abundant water from heaven, exactly as before. By this event the error was detected and corrected. Paschasius relates all these things after being consulted by Saint Leo the Great about the controversy that arose in the year 444 between the Alexandrians and the Westerners concerning the proper celebration of Easter.

Cassiodorus, in *Variae* VIII, letter 33, which he wrote in the name of King Athalaric to Severus, recounts a similar miracle concerning a baptismal font in Lucania when discussing the assembly at Leucothea. Saint Gregory of Tours likewise reports such an event from Gaul in his book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, a work of the greatest authority among all people, especially in matters of local concern.

As for our Spain, Gregory of Tours himself testifies that it was not without miracles equal, indeed greater, than these. It will be worthwhile to transcribe his words from Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 24:

“There is also,” he says, “that famous miracle concerning the fonts of Spain which the province of Lusitania produces. Near Osset there is a pool, constructed long ago in a field and wonderfully fashioned from various-colored marble in the shape of a cross; above it, Christians also built a church of great splendor and height. Therefore, when the sacred day arrived after the course of the preceding year had passed—the day on which the Lord, after the traitor had been confounded, offered the mystical supper to his disciples—the citizens gathered at that place with the bishop, already anticipating the fragrance of the sacred perfume. After prayer had been offered, the priest ordered the doors of the church to be sealed with seals, awaiting the arrival of the Lord’s power. On the third day—that is, Saturday—when the people assembled for baptism, the bishop arrived with his citizens, inspected the seals, and opened the closed doors. And, wonderful to say, they found the pool that he had left empty full instead; indeed, it was so filled beyond the usual level that wheat is commonly heaped above the rims of measuring vessels. You could see the waters surging here and there, yet not flowing over to the other side. Then, after the water had been sanctified by exorcism and chrism had been sprinkled over it, the whole people drew water according to their devotion and carried home a full vessel, intending to protect their fields and vineyards by the most health-giving sprinkling. Although an uncounted number of jars were drawn from it thereafter, the level never diminished; yet, once the first infant had been immersed, the water immediately withdrew, and after all had been baptized, the waters returning into themselves—just as no one knows how they appeared at the beginning, so no one knows how they disappeared at the end.”

A little later he adds:

“Finally, when Theodegisilus, the king of that region, had seen this miracle occurring in these fonts consecrated to God, he considered the matter within himself and said: ‘It is Roman cleverness’—for the people of our religion call them Romans—‘that causes this, and it is not the power of God.’ When the following year arrived, he sealed the door with his own seals together with the bishop’s seal and stationed guards around the church, in case he might catch anyone involved in some fraud by whose ingenuity water was being introduced into the font. He did the same in another year. In the third year, having summoned a multitude of men, he ordered trenches to be dug around the basilica, lest the water might be conveyed into the font through hidden channels. The trenches were twenty-five feet deep and fifteen feet wide. Yet nothing concealed could be found. Nevertheless, as he was bringing his life to an end—and, I believe, because of the rashness of this investigation—he was not permitted to see the day of the following year on which this mystery was celebrated, because he had presumed to investigate the secret of divine power.”

Gregory relates these things about the fonts of Spain. Although historians generally accept his testimony, so that scarcely anyone now doubts the principal feature of the present miracle, they desire greater precision from Gregory of Tours in his account of the circumstances. The most eminent Baronius did not doubt the event; the distinguished Pagi was less certain, although he held it certain that similar prodigies had once been seen in Spain and Gaul. Nevertheless, when Baronius cites Gregory’s words under the year 417, he could not fail to notice that Gregory’s account was false in many of its circumstances.

“For Theodegisilus,” he says, “reigned only one year and seven months, and not in Lusitania, which obeyed Suevic kings. Moreover, Osset is a town in the territory of Hispalis, which obeyed Theodegisilus, king of the Goths. Therefore Gregory of Tours wrote rather inaccurately about events that took place outside Gaul.”

Moved perhaps by these and other considerations, we believe that the learned Juan de Mariana came to suspect that the whole story of the miraculous fonts and Theudiselo’s disbelief had been fabricated. After recounting it, he adds the following in Book V of *On the Affairs of Spain*, while discussing this same Theudiselo:

“Bishop Paschasius, as Isidore records, testified in a letter to Leo the Great that a similar prodigy occurred in Sicily; and perhaps, as the report wandered, what happened in one province was attributed to another. We are surprised that Isidore, who lived almost into his own time and reported the event from Sicily, made no mention of so remarkable an event in Spain.”

For our part, we do not depart from the common judgment of historians; and if that was once permissible, it would now be wrong for us to do so after the publication of Hildefonsus’s testimony. Although Hildefonsus does not explicitly speak of Spain, he nevertheless wonderfully confirms Gregory of Tours’s account in all the elements that constitute the core of this story. Indeed, in our judgment, both authors spoke of one and the same font, and neither of a font situated outside Spain. Their agreement in describing the font is so great, and the font they describe differs so markedly from those of the other provinces, that it is implausible—not to say impossible—that what Juan de Mariana suspected actually occurred: that, because of a wandering report, something that happened in Sicily was falsely conveyed to Gregory of Tours as having happened in our Spain.

For in the other fonts mentioned in history, almost nothing is miraculous apart from the supernatural coming and withdrawal of the waters; in ours, the heavenly arrival and departure of the water are accompanied by a thousand other wonders no less extraordinary. Gregory admits that his own fonts are surpassed by those of Spain. As for the others, it will be enough to review the testimonies cited above. In them we read nothing of the very sweet odor that appeared three days before Easter and served as a certain announcement of the coming miracle; nothing of that extraordinary abundance of water which, although rising above the lips of the font, was divinely sustained in a heap and did not flow away while surging here and there; nothing of that heavenly supply from which an almost unlimited quantity could be drawn, whether to quench the thirst of those present or to sanctify and protect their homes, without its being diminished, much less exhausted, and so forth.

All these things are recorded of our fonts by Gregory and Hildefonsus; and, what is more remarkable, they occur in precisely the same order of signs, without the slightest variation. Unless readers are reluctant to compare the two accounts with each other, they will easily discover that this is so. Let us therefore grant that the event did not occur in Lusitania but in Baetica—although, because the provinces bordered one another, the error would be easy and pardonable—and let us not deny that what Gregory relates about the unbelieving ruler could not have been done by Theudiselo or Theodegisilus. Perhaps he intended to name Theudis, who preceded him by many years in the kingdom and was no less impious. Provided we are certain of this, Spain was the theater of such great miracles.

Only one question remains: which particular church in our land witnessed such a prodigy? We have no certain knowledge of this, and in an obscure matter we do not wish rashly to advance our judgment. Gregory says that it was near Ossem, or Osset. But Saint Isidore’s silence prevents us from asserting this without qualification; his silence carries considerable weight, since he was brought up and educated near that place at Hispalis and spent his entire life there.

Without doubt, someone who has read this chapter and the next will declare that the site of the miracle can be determined with complete certainty from the many passages in which Hildefonsus seems, as though an eyewitness, to address the people present. “Whom,” such a person will say, “could he more plausibly have addressed than the people of Toledo, since the bishop of the Church of Toledo was speaking?” The learned Martène was not far from this conjecture when, relying on these same words, he supposed that Hildefonsus had witnessed such a miracle.

We, however, know—as we have often reminded our readers—that this work was assembled by the holy doctor from the opinions, homilies, sermons, and other treatises of the holy Fathers. We therefore do not rashly suspect that these two chapters contain a fragment of a speech delivered by the local bishop to a large congregation at the very place where the miracle appeared each year, in order to arouse the faithful’s wonder and move their hearts to offer the God who deserved it his due thanksgiving. Who that bishop was, however, we have sought in vain, despite applying the utmost diligence.

Another person may perhaps say: Why should Hildefonsus not plausibly be credited with it amid such darkness, since it is established that he not only recited the opinions of other Fathers but also inserted much of his own material to illustrate and confirm them? Nothing certainly prevents this, and our judgment is that there is no argument that conclusively proves the contrary. Moreover, we admit that the style, which bears the stamp of the Goths, is not foreign to Hildefonsus, nor is such a vivid description of the entire miracle beyond the powers of his exceptionally fertile mind. Therefore, by this not improbable conjecture, we willingly and gladly contribute to the glory of the Church of Toledo.

The writers of Toledo’s history are silent; but how do we know that everything was committed to writing? And even if it was, how much, and how many things, failed to reach the knowledge of later generations? In these last centuries, how many things have been drawn out of the darkness in which they lay—some brought forth by chance, others found through diligence? We need not go far. How many centuries did this very book of Hildefonsus, which we are publishing, lie hidden?

Whatever judgment should be formed on this matter, one thing certainly cannot be doubted: whoever the author of this fragment was, he deserves to be counted among the most articulate and eloquent of the Fathers of those times.]

For it possesses the likeness of prophetic power, a fixed time of certainty, a stable condition of truth, an unknown odor, moisture flowing in a dry place, an upright wave without flowing away, a supply that is not quickly emptied by drawing, a location inexhaustible in abundance, a flow that renews access to life, destruction for the removal of sins, renunciation of impiety, confession of the divine and one Trinity, an eternal remembrance in the freedom of righteousness, perpetual forgetfulness of the work of sin, and everlasting fullness in the reward of glory.

It possesses, then, the likeness of prophetic power because on the Thursday before Easter it announces the odor that it presents visibly three days later, on the Saturday of Easter. It possesses a fixed time of certainty because, as a testimony to the Lord’s resurrection, no variation of error alters its occurrence. It possesses a stable condition of truth because it preserves its event in unchanging accordance with the Easter feast. It possesses an unknown odor because it exhales a fragrance unlike the fragrance of grace. It possesses moisture flowing in a dry place because amid the dryness of rocks an abundance of waters is found without any water entering from elsewhere. It possesses an upright wave without flowing away because, although its waters move without any external motion and only through their own stillness, they do not pass beyond the boundary of the rim. It possesses a position that is quickly emptied without anyone drawing from it because, just as its abundance rushes in without anyone knowing how, so dryness comes without anyone emptying it. It possesses a flow inexhaustible in abundance because, although the water is continually taken away for drinking, the amount removed exceeds the capacity of what is retained. It possesses access to rebirth for life because those who enter it, death having been removed, are transferred into life. It possesses the destruction of sins to be put to death because the person immersed there rises purified from the old age of sin into the grace of newness. It possesses renunciation of impiety because no one approaches it except one who has renounced the devil, his angels, and all his works. It possesses confession of the divine and one Trinity because everyone who approaches it is baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. It possesses eternal remembrance in the freedom of righteousness because the one who is immersed, freed from slavery to sin, [Col. 0153C] passes into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. It possesses perpetual forgetfulness of the work of sin because, forgetting his former way of life, which lies behind him, the baptized person reaches forward through blessed hope toward the gifts of eternal rewards. It possesses perpetual fullness in the reward of glory because the person freed from the corruption of labor will praise God with the joy of exultation forever and ever.

## CHAPTER 106. On the effects of the water of the font, and on the manifest wonder of the miracle

But in order that the nature of the event may be displayed more clearly, the action must be described at greater length. Behold, we see the site of the font constructed among parched rocks and covered with dry slabs of marble. The builder’s skill joined and strengthened it with plaster, lime, wax, and marble dust so thoroughly that there is no opening through which one might enter or breathe, and no moisture from any channel is received into it.

Whence, after the completion of the entire year, does today’s glorious vision arise? Whence, after a year’s dryness, does sudden greenness appear? Whence water among the rocks? Whence water among the marble? Whence rivers in a dry place? Whence overflowing streams in parched stone? No channel of a stream is visible, no rain enters, not even the slightest dew or damp mist arrives. The roof tiles are intact, the doors are found closed, the seals are found unharmed. No unbeliever entered to mock the faith; no believer entered to provide for the faith; no one at all entered who might either counterfeit or obstruct so great a miracle.

Let that ineffable author, then, be contemplated, together with his wondrous works. From the effects of his operation the power of his work can thus be recognized.

[Col. 0155A] The day before yesterday the air was the messenger of this miracle. Since the closure of the doors denied the sight to the eyes, the power revealed the coming event to the sense of smell. The odor, I say, spread far, very far away, and gave credibility to the coming vision.

Behold, we have now arrived and see with open eyes. There we fix our gaze in amazement, and we behold the font overflowing abundantly with water, though we knew it to be dry. We see the surging depths, moved by no breeze. The waters rise into a heap, yet no overflowing beyond the boundary [F., limit] is observed. Raised without being touched by any breath, it moves; and, in the swelling of its motion, while it does not cross the rim, it contains within its elevation a storm that is boiling over. You can see the waves striking one another, the globes turning, the billows whirling; and, while the position of the place struggles with the condition of the element, neither gives way to the other.

The rocks hold an unknown liquid and rejoice that it has been born from their own barrenness, though they do not know it to have been poured in from another’s fertility. The marble compels itself to contain what it has received. But that law forbids resistance. Why does capacity not hold within measure what abundance has forced into such fullness? The waters leap beyond their proper level, yet, gathered into a mass, do not pass beyond the boundary. In their movements they now rear themselves up to a crest, now fall back into quiet, now make the surface rippled, now render the rippled variety of the surface smooth. They threaten to escape, yet do not abandon their place. They rest in every storm and move only in stillness. Free from every disturbance and agitation, they smile and applaud only through their own movements of wonder.

For the miracle to be fully enhanced, it is not enough that waters born in dust should occupy the place of parched stones, unless such abundance is present that one cannot calculate how many thousands of vessels carried away by the faith of the gathered peoples are filled. Led by the love of faith, the people press forward vigorously, crowd together competitively, and carry away water in abundance. Although the innumerable people moving to and fro obstruct one another, piety prevails and faith suffers no injury. Under the pressure, the little vessels strike against one another, and so much liquid is drawn that the floors are turned to mud.

Each person receives the remedy by which he drinks, while the abundance carried away across the breadth of the world and stored for use at home is preserved. The wonder of this abundance is immeasurable; the quantity cannot be calculated. [Note: [Col. 0155D] We have emended to *mansurae*, as it stands in Bal.] The only thing that can be understood is that more could be taken away than could be found.

The color of this water is brighter than light, its clarity purer than air. Its taste is unknown to all other tastes of water and more pleasing. Its power is gentle, its appearance beautiful, its novelty astonishing, and its age so enduring through such long duration that, although removed from the passing years, it is corrupted by no defect.

In other waters, only freshness is pleasing, and that water is more agreeable which gives off no odor. For although it may be contained in shining vessels, if it is stored overnight, it becomes thicker once its original clarity has been exhausted; having taken in a foul smell, its thickness grows heavy into sediment, and afterward the water returns to the earth. This water, however, never lacks the pleasure of clarity, odor, or taste. Thus it is new in its wonder, ancient in its creation, and constant in its uses for salvation.

Since the miracle is reported—and this too is marvelous—it cannot remain forever in the condition of a miracle; but because it comes miraculously, it departs only miraculously. For just as there is no entrance through which it flows in, so there is no passage through which it flows out. The place is found full from an unknown source and seen empty from an unknown source. Where the water escaped, just as where it entered, cannot be discovered.

What, then, can this mean except that the omnipotence of God, which miraculously poured it in, miraculously drains it away? The beginning, middle, and end are all constituted in wonder: it is born in a dry place, it lies hidden while surging and does not flow away, and it becomes dry without being emptied.

The little chamber of the font stands full. After the priest has blessed it, it sustains all the gatherings of those who come: how much is drunk bodily from it, how much is spilled onto the ground through the rush of those arriving, and how much, carried away in vessels to various lands for the sake of religion, is preserved, cannot be calculated. It certainly remains so inexhaustible for those drawing from it that it does not know how to become smaller through what has been taken away. [Note: [Col. 0155D] We print *quam* instead of *aquam*, which Bal. prints.] But when the priest has immersed the infant being baptized, immediately there is stillness; and so, visibly, that which invisibly grew from nothing returns to nothing.

These things occur in this particular font, made wondrous by the novelty of its water. But they also occur in that wondrously universal and uniquely general font, of which this font is one, signified by the prophet’s saying: “On that day there shall be a fountain opened for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing away of sin and of the menstruous woman” (Zech. XIII, 1).

It is open because it is closed to no one. Therefore we are all reborn in it; through it the sins of sinners are cleansed, and the uncleanness of the menstruous woman—that is, of unclean souls—is washed away in a saving bath. It is one for the grace of regeneration, just as there is one faith and one Church of the living God, signified by the house of David. These sacraments are fulfilled in their proper order.

## CHAPTER 107. Why and from when the font is closed during Lent and opened at Easter

Because this font is full of the mysteries of human salvation, it is rightly closed under episcopal authority after being sealed, and it is sealed so that it may be opened. It is closed during the days of Lent and opened at Easter.

The fact that it is sealed during Lent shows that, except in the event of the gravest necessity, baptism is in every way forbidden throughout the world during those days. The fact that it is opened at Easter through the bishop’s sanctification demonstrates that the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection is made accessible, in which access to life was made for humanity, so that, buried with Christ’s death through baptism, a person may rise with him in the glory of God.

Just as the universal restriction of baptism corresponds to closing the font in one place, so opening the font means granting general permission to baptize.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] This ancient custom of the Church—closing the fonts or baptisteries during Lent by sealing them with the bishop’s ring and not opening them before Easter except when serious necessity demanded it—had been neglected in some of our Churches. It was restored several years after Hildefonsus, namely in the year 694, at the seventeenth Council of Toledo, assembled from the bishops of Spain and Gaul. Its second canon decreed that all bishops were to observe it in their Churches.

It is worthy of notice that, when the Fathers of the council wished to explain first of all the mystical meaning of this rite, they used almost the very words with which Saint Hildefonsus speaks in this chapter. This shows that the Fathers had Hildefonsus’s book before their eyes when composing the canon and attributed great authority to his teaching. It is pleasing to quote the beginning of the canon:

“Although at the beginning of Lent the general administration of baptism is closed, nevertheless the order of ecclesiastical custom requires, and necessity demands, that on that same day the doors of the baptistery be closed by the bishop’s hand and sealed with his ring, and that they not be opened until the solemnity of the Lord’s Supper. This is so that, through the bishops’ seal (except in the event of the gravest necessity), it may be shown during these days that baptism and sanctification may not be administered throughout the world; and so that, when it is again opened by episcopal sanctification for the observance, it may signify that the mystery of the Lord’s Resurrection is accessible, in which access to life was made for humanity, so that, because through baptism the person has been buried in Christ’s death, he may rise with him in the glory of God.”]

The font is closed with the seal of the ring, but it is opened by the priest’s blessing and by the mysteries of the sacrament.

## CHAPTER 108. On the time and place for baptizing

[Col. 0157A]

Apostolic and paternal antiquity decreed that the celebration of baptism should take place only at two times, Easter and Pentecost, at the seats of the lawful bishops and in their presence. It also decreed that this should not be done in the neighboring churches under those bishops, lest, when gatherings of the people are divided among various places, there should be no one to receive the grace of instruction, or the venerable dignity of the bishops should be diminished.

In churches of the parishes situated at a great distance, however, it is appropriately permitted that baptism be administered, lest, when the length of the journey causes delay, the desirable grace—which ought to be conferred promptly—be postponed. Outside these two seasons, baptism is freely permitted at any time solely because of the necessity created by the danger of death.

## CHAPTER 109. On the exposition of the mysteries of the font

The priest then approaches the font; and just as Moses went in the name of the Lord, so this priest, entreating God, pours the duties of sanctification into the waters. Moses struck the waters there with his staff, and a saving path was opened (Exod. XIV, 21). Here the priest touches the waters with the sign of the wood of the cross, and the entrance to salvation is opened.

Otherwise, unless Moses had struck the waters with his staff, no passage of freedom would have opened amid the waves. Likewise now, unless the waters of the font are touched in the name and by the cross of Christ’s wood, no remedy of salvation is obtained.

He applies an exorcism, lest anything infected by the contagion of the hostile side lie hidden there. He pours in oil, so that the water may be shown to share, through the infusion of sanctification, in that sacrament over which the Spirit of God was borne in the beginning of creation. He pronounces a blessing, so that the blessing may make it powerful to abolish the curse.

## CHAPTER 110. On the steps of the font

[Note: [Col. 0158D] Taken from Saint Isidore (*On Ecclesiastical Offices*, Book II, chapter 25); the following material, through chapter 121, is drawn from there, although Hildefonsus explains it more fully.]

This font is the source of all glories. It has seven steps: three descending, because of the three things renounced—that is, the devil, his angels, his works, and his commands; and three ascending, because of the three whom we confess: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is one God in the Trinity.

The seventh is also the fourth: that is, he is “like the Son of Man,” extinguishing the furnace of fire, the support of the feet, and the foundation of the water, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

Through the three steps, therefore, the person being baptized descends when he renounces the three. In abandoning the devil’s height, he descends to the humility of Christ’s baptism. Thus, finding firm ground on the fourth step, he stands freed from the things he renounced. Then he ascends through confession of the Trinity. He himself is the seventh, the culmination of liberation, who was the fourth as the resting place of freedom.

## CHAPTER 111. On the two covenants of renunciation and belief

There are two covenants. The first is the one in which the devil is renounced, when the person says: “I renounce you, devil, and your angels, your works, and your commands,” so that he may no longer serve him either through the passions of the earthly body or through the errors of a depraved mind. Having sunk every kind of wickedness like lead, and fortified himself on the right and left by good works, he should strive to cross the seas of this world with an unhindered step.

The second is the one in which belief is placed in God in the name of the Trinity, so that, holding fast to the power of his love, the believer may remain with him in his praises throughout the everlasting ages.

## CHAPTER 112. That baptism is given in the name of the Trinity; that if any person of the Trinity is omitted in baptism, the celebration of baptism accomplishes nothing; and that Christ’s baptism was performed in the Trinity

Then, according to the Lord’s command, which says, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19), the priest adds, “that you may have eternal life,” and the person is immersed in the waters. At that moment the firm promise spoken by the Lord is shown to him: “Whoever believes in me has eternal life” (John VI, 47).

But if baptism is administered with any person of the Trinity omitted, the solemnity of baptism must be considered entirely ineffective, unless the whole Trinity is truly invoked. For the Lord’s baptism, when he was baptized by John, is likewise recognized as having been celebrated in the truth of the Trinity. When God said, “This is my Son” (Matt. III, 17), the Father was present in the voice, the Son in the reality of the body, and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove.

## CHAPTER 113. That baptism removes both original and actual sin; that no one has eternal life unless reborn; and why some profess renunciation or confession on behalf of others

For adults and those mature in age, baptism serves either for the cleansing of original guilt or for the abolition of actual sin, so that original and actual sin may be erased together by one saving benefit.

For infants it serves only this purpose: that the offense which the human race inherited through descent from Adam may be dissolved through this regeneration. If they depart from this world before being regenerated, they will not be heirs of Christ in the kingdom of God, as the Lord says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not see the kingdom of God” (John III, 3).

Finally, infants have another person profess renunciation or believe in God on their behalf because they cannot speak for themselves, just as the sick, mute, and deaf have others profess on their behalf. . . . they themselves are baptized.

## CHAPTER 114. On those who receive the baptized from the font, and what they ought to do with them

Those who receive, with devout love, people begotten for adoption as children through the Holy Spirit from the womb of Mother Church—that is, from the font of the bath—ought to admonish them thoroughly, both before they are baptized and after they have been baptized, not only by example but also by words.

Just as both sexes are reborn from the same font, so those who receive the reborn of either sex ought to possess the practice of saving instruction. They should also understand that they become sponsors. For the baptized they answer that they renounce the devil, his angels, and his works, affirming that they believe in the name of the Trinity.

Therefore both those who receive the baptized and those who are received by them must guard with complete vigilance the covenant they made with God in the sacrament of baptism, so that, while they keep what was commanded in regeneration, they may receive what was promised in recompense.

## CHAPTER 115. That regeneration is given in hope of future blessedness, not so that the penalty of temporal death may be removed

[Col. 0159C]

Although the guilt of our origin is dissolved through the benefit of regeneration, the penalty of death nevertheless remains for those whom the grace of the Savior frees from guilt. Thus a person should understand that he receives regeneration in hope of future blessedness, not so that he may escape the penalty of temporal death. For although grace has bestowed the life of eternal glory, the sentence imposed has not removed the penalty of temporal death.

## CHAPTER 116. That only priests may give baptism, except in the necessity of danger

It is certainly not permitted to deacons, clerics, or just anyone to give baptism, but only to priests, as the Lord says to the disciples alone: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John XX, 21). And again to the disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

It is therefore clear that only priests are permitted to give baptism. This ministry has not been granted even to deacons without a bishop or presbyter, unless, when those ministers are far away, the utmost necessity caused by illness or danger compels it. In such circumstances it is granted in some manner to clerics and faithful laypeople, so that no one may appear to have departed from this world without the life-giving remedy.

## CHAPTER 117. What it signifies that the infant is immersed in water in the likeness of Christ’s death; and on single and triple immersion in baptism

When the infant is immersed in the waters, he is baptized into Christ’s death, as Paul says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. We were buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. VI, 3–4).

Likewise, when the infant is brought up from the waters, it is shown that he rises with Christ, as the same Apostle continues: “Just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too should walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be united with him in his resurrection” (ibid., 4–5).

When the person is immersed once, he is baptized in the name of the one Godhead. If he is immersed three times, the number of the three days of the Lord’s burial is signified. Therefore, within the one faith, differing custom has nothing contrary to it. But because heretics commonly use the number of immersions to divide the unity of the Godhead, it is rather from God that the Church of God observes only one use of immersion.

## CHAPTER 118. On not repeating baptism
## CHAPTER 118. That Baptism Must Not Be Repeated

Once baptism has been received, it is in no way permissible to repeat it for any reason whatsoever. For just as there is one God and one faith, so there is one baptism. And as the Apostle likewise says, “Knowing that Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9), so baptism too must never be repeated in any manner.

Moreover, since there are two births—one from earth, the other from heaven; one from the flesh, the other from the Spirit; one from mortality, the other from eternity; one from male and female, the other from God and the Church—and since each of these two is single, neither can be repeated, neither the one nor [Col. 0160C] the other. Therefore, just as one who has already been born from Adam cannot be generated again from Adam, so one who has been born from Christ cannot be generated again by Christ; for just as the mother’s womb cannot be repeated, so neither can the Church’s baptism.

## CHAPTER 119. That the First Baptism Is of Water and the Second of Blood

There are three kinds of baptism. The first baptism is of water and the Spirit, concerning which we have been arguing up to this point; through it, original sins are erased by regeneration. The second is that by which each person is baptized through martyrdom in his own blood. Certainly Christ too was baptized with this same baptism, so that he might give believers in him an example in this matter as in others.

For he says to the sons of Zebedee, his disciples: “Can you drink the cup which I shall drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I shall be baptized?” (Mark 10:38)—that is: Can you drink the cup of the bitterness of suffering, and be baptized by the pouring out of your blood, just as I shall endure the disgrace of the cross and release a flowing stream of blood?

Water and blood, then, are the twofold figure of baptism. For by the one we are regenerated from the washing, and by the other we are consecrated from blood.

## CHAPTER 120. That the Third Baptism Is the Flood of Repentance in a Deluge of Tears

The third is a flood of tears, which occurs in repentance for sins. It is indeed performed laboriously, [Col. 0161A] but, through the abundant mercy of the Redeemer, it is assured of pardon.

Thus that sinful woman in the city, sitting at the Lord’s feet, washed with tears what she had defiled in herself through pleasures (Luke 7:38). O baptism full of mercy, overflowing with the Redeemer’s abundant pardon, which so swiftly washed away so long-standing a mound of crimes with a flowing flood!

Consider, whoever you are, that you are a sinner [F., you are a sinner]; or rather, consider all human beings, because every human being is a sinner, and weigh the power of this baptism. Thus a spring of tears burst forth abundantly over the sinful woman, so that it reached the feet of the Lord who remits sins. Thus a wave of lamentation rose from the depth of her heart into a heap, so that it might water the heavenly footprints of the Lord. Thus bitterness brought the force of affliction, so that she might attain the sweetness [Col. 0161B] of mercy.

For this reason that man waters his bed with tears every night (Ps. 6:7). For this reason the Ninevites, while they drenched themselves with a rain of lamentation, extinguished the fires of vengeance (Jonah 3). But he, that most gracious compassionate one, bestows an abundance of this grace upon the wretched: he who gives repentance to sinners and prepares forgiveness for sins; who punishes sin through repentance and grants the fruit of repentance; who commands the ungodly to come to him by being converted through grace, and through mercy causes the justified to depart from him in exultation.

## CHAPTER 121. That Baptism May Not Be Repeated Even in the Case of Heretics

Any heretics who, following a different schism, are shown to have received baptism with the attestation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not to be baptized again, but are to be cleansed only by chrism and the laying on of hands.

For baptism is not man’s, so that it should be repeated by man; it is Christ’s, so that it may remain through Christ. For just as there is one God and no other, and one faith in God and no other, so there is one baptism of Christ and no other.

If it were from man, it could be repeated; but because it was given immutably from Christ, it cannot be repeated. God alone is the one who baptizes, so that those who are baptized by him may become sons of God.

Therefore it makes no difference whether a believer or a heretic administers baptism. The only concern is that someone wishing to be baptized should not, through the carelessness of Christians, be led to the heretics. But even if negligence in this matter incurs blame, it can never confer permission to repeat baptism.

This sacrament is so holy and blessed that it cannot be defiled even when administered by the most wicked person. For the heretic too possesses Christ’s baptism. Yet it benefits him nothing when he carries what he received outside the unity of the faith. Once he has entered the Church, however, the baptism that he had outside, formerly leading to destruction, immediately begins to benefit him for salvation.

Hence what has been received is approved with reverence for the faith. Therefore, when he has approached, it is not fitting that it be changed, but that it be acknowledged. For since it is the sign of the King, my God, no sacrilege is committed when a deserter is corrected, and the Lord’s sign is not changed.

## CHAPTER 122. That After the Glory Is Sung in a Hymn, a Person Is to Be Advanced to Anointing

[Col. 0162A]

After a person has been immersed in water in the likeness of Christ’s death and has again been brought out of the water in hope of resurrection, a hymn of thanksgiving having been sung for his deliverance, he is advanced to the touch of the sacred chrism, so that he may be anointed with the Spirit of God and, from Christ’s anointing and name, may be and be called a Christian.

## CHAPTER 123. Concerning the Ointment of Chrism and Its Institution

The ointment of chrism was first composed and prepared by Moses in Leviticus at the Lord’s command (Lev. 8:2, 12, 13). [Note: [Col. 0161D] In the edition of Baluze, “in Exodus,” erroneously.] [Note: [Col. 0162D] St. Isidore, book II, *On Offices*, chapter 26.]

This anointing is said to have first descended upon Aaron and his sons through that same Moses as a testimony of priesthood and as a mark of holiness. [Col. 0162B] Thereafter kings were anointed with the same chrism in honor of their glory. Hence it is said concerning them: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Ps. 104:15).

Among priests and kings this mystical anointing existed only as a figure of Christ the King and Priest who was to come. For the name “Christ” is derived from chrism, because *chrisma* means anointing.

But after our Lord Jesus Christ, the true King and eternal Priest, had been anointed by God the heavenly Father with mystical ointment, according to what is said to him, “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8), not only pontiffs and kings but the whole Church is consecrated with the chrism of holy ointment, because it is the most holy member of the eternal King and Priest.

Therefore, because we are “a chosen race and a royal priesthood,” we are anointed with chrism after the washing of water, so that from the name of Christ we may be called Christians.

## CHAPTER 124. That Through Visible Anointing of the Body the Holy Spirit Invisibly Works the Anointing of the Soul

With this holy chrism a person is therefore anointed externally, and the power of the Holy Spirit enters internally, so that the whole person, cleansed by the washing, may be made wholly rich through the Spirit’s anointing.

The soul receives power from this same anointing of the Holy Spirit so that it may know God as its indwelling inhabitant, love the one whom it has received within itself, remain with him always, be ruled by him, and do his will, without grieving him; for a person has been sealed in him for the day of his redemption, so that [Col. 0162D] he may be one with Christ among Christ’s members, while he is enlivened and governed by the Spirit of Christ.

## CHAPTER 125. That the Spirit Is Given to Human Beings According to Measure, but Not to Christ

John commends this anointing when he says: “So that you may know that you have an anointing, and that the anointing which we received from him remains in us” (1 John 2). The sacrament of this anointing is the very invisible power; the invisible anointing is the Holy Spirit; the invisible anointing is that charity which, in whoever possesses it, will be like a root of life and cannot wither, even when scorched by the sun of persecution.

Everything that [Col. 0163A] is rooted in charity is nourished and never withers from the heat of adversity.

The Holy Spirit was not given to Christ according to measure, because “in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:9). In human beings, however, he is given according to the measure of discernment and grace (1 Cor. 12), so that, because the many members of Christ form one body through the gifts of their many operations, one Spirit may rule over all, and the grace of different gifts may work in each one alike.

Paul says: “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; to another faith; to another the grace of healings; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues” (1 Cor. 12).

## CHAPTER 126. Concerning the Discernment by Which the Holy Spirit Is Given to Human Beings According to Measure

[Col. 0163B]

This discernment of gifts takes place when almighty God, through the secret governance of his inward judgment, so orders all things that, while by abundant grace he raises up each person, he also places one beneath another through unequal distribution [F., even places one beneath another]; and each person recognizes that the one subject to him is better than himself in another gift, and, although he feels that he excels him in some respects, nevertheless places himself beneath the same person in others.
