Thus he orders all things: while the individual gifts belong to everyone, through a certain bond of charity all things become the possessions of each individual; and each person possesses in another what he himself has not received, so that he may humbly devote to another for possession what he himself has received.

## CHAPTER 127. Saint Pope Gregory’s Interpretation of the Sevenfold Spirit

[Col. 0163C]

This is the sevenfold Spirit, as Isaiah says: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:2).

Saint Gregory, speaking of heavenly things, reports that the prophet numbered these degrees by descending rather than ascending, namely: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear. (Book I of the *Moralia*, chapter 15.)

And since it is written, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:16), there is no doubt that one ascends from fear to wisdom, not returns from wisdom to fear; for wisdom possesses perfect charity, and it is written: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Therefore the prophet, speaking of heavenly things down toward what is below, began with wisdom and descended to fear. But we, because we are striving from earthly things toward heavenly things, should number these same degrees while ascending, so that we may be able to arrive at wisdom from fear.

In our mind, then, the first degree of ascent is the fear of the Lord; the second, piety; the third, knowledge; the fourth, fortitude; the fifth, counsel; the sixth, understanding; the seventh, wisdom.

The fear of the Lord exists in the mind. But what kind of fear is it if piety is not with it? Whoever does not know how to show mercy to his neighbor, whoever pretends not to share in his neighbor’s tribulation—such a person’s fear is nothing before the eyes of almighty God, because it has not been raised up to piety.

But piety often tends to err through disordered mercy, if it should perhaps spare what ought not to be spared. Sins that can be struck by the fires of Gehenna must be corrected by the blows of discipline. But disordered piety, when it spares temporarily, drags a person toward eternal punishment.

Therefore, so that piety may be true and ordered, it must be raised to another degree, namely knowledge, so that it may know what to punish out of mercy and what to forgive out of mercy.

But what if someone knows what ought to be done yet lacks the strength to do it? Therefore our knowledge must grow into fortitude, so that, when it sees what ought to be done, it may be able to do it through strength of mind, lest it tremble from fear and, collapsing through terror, be unable [Col. 0164B] to defend the good that it perceives.

But fortitude often, if it is imprudent and insufficiently watchful against vices, falls uselessly through its own presumption. Therefore it must ascend to counsel, so that by foresight it may fortify everything that it can courageously accomplish.

But counsel cannot exist if understanding is lacking; for someone who does not understand the evil that burdens the person acting, how can he make firm the good that helps him? Therefore let us ascend from counsel to understanding.

But what if understanding keeps watch with great acuteness and does not know how to govern itself through maturity? Therefore let one ascend from understanding to wisdom, so that wisdom may maturely arrange what understanding has discovered sharply.

Since, then, through fear we rise to piety, through piety we are led to knowledge, through knowledge we are strengthened for fortitude, through fortitude we strive toward counsel, through counsel we advance to understanding, and through understanding we arrive at the maturity of wisdom, we ascend by seven steps to the gate through which the entrance to the spiritual life is opened for us.

## CHAPTER 128. Concerning the Laying On of Hands

The Truth itself, which through itself as the way calls to itself as life, gave an example by itself of the laying on of hands. For Mark says: “When they brought little children to him so that he might touch them, he embraced them and, laying his hands upon them, blessed them” (Mark 10:13).

The meaning of this action is that, when he blesses with words, the Spirit is infused; when he touches with his hands, the operation of spiritual power is signified.

Thus the form of the laying on of hands proceeded from this divine imitation into sacred services, so that every little one—that is, every person humble in faith and spiritual obedience—might receive from God through the priest the power of sanctification.

Jesus therefore blesses by the authority of his divinity; he lays on hands so that the humanity he assumed may accomplish the effect of salvation. Jesus blesses with his mouth and touches with his hands because, in that which he is the Word, he sanctifies; in that which he became flesh, he administers the power of sanctification.

Jesus blesses and lays on hands because what the power of the Godhead signifies, the humanity of the Redeemer completes. The one Jesus calls those to be justified through his divinity and strengthens those called through his humanity.

Nothing is lacking in him for the work of salvation, when the divinity joined to humanity commands, and the humanity assumed into divinity [Col. 0165A] forms the power. One Christ, God and human, performs this act: all things render service to the invisible nature, and the visible nature carries out the authority of invisible power.

Therefore, following Christ’s example, the priest salutarily lays hands upon the faithful with a blessing, because authority has been bestowed upon him by divine authority, so that through the blessing of his mouth the infusion of the Spirit may emerge, and through the laying on of hands the touch of spiritual grace may grow strong.

## CHAPTER 129. Again Concerning the Laying On of Hands and the Holy Spirit

[Note: [Col. 0165D] St. Isidore, book II, *On Offices*, chapter 27.]

After baptism, the Holy Spirit is appropriately given with the laying on of hands. For the Acts of the Apostles shows that the Apostle did this.

It says: “It came to pass, while Apollos was at Corinth, that Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples. And he said to them: ‘Have you received the Holy Spirit after believing?’ But they said to him: ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ He said: ‘Into what, then, were you baptized?’ They said: ‘Into John’s baptism.’ Paul then said: ‘John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people that they should believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.’ When they had heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus; and when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied” (Acts 19:1–7).

Again, elsewhere: “When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had come, [Col. 0165C] they prayed for them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (Acts 8:14).

## CHAPTER 130. The Holy Spirit Is Given by God

Just as it is true that we can receive the Holy Spirit as a divine gift, so we cannot give him by our own power. Nevertheless, in order that he may be given, we invoke the Lord, the giver of that same grace, so that the grace of divine power may be conferred through the ministry of our supplication.

God cooperates in everything: he causes us to pray, the one who is blessed receives sanctification, and he infuses the fullness of sanctification.

## CHAPTER 131. Concerning the Chrism

[Col. 0165D]

[Note: [Col. 0165D] St. Isidore, cited above.] Concerning who principally performs this act, as the holy [Note: [Col. 0165D] Pope Innocent, *Letter to Decentius*. See *De Consecratione*, distinction 5, chapter “Manus.”] Pope Innocent bears witness, he says that it is not permitted to be performed by anyone other than a bishop.

For although priests are priests, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate. The right to seal or to impart the Spirit the Paraclete belongs only to bishops. This is shown not only by ecclesiastical custom, but also by the earlier passage from the Acts of the Apostles, which states that Peter and John were sent to impart the Holy Spirit to those who had already been baptized. [Col. 0166A]

Priests, whether without a bishop or in the presence of a bishop, may anoint the baptized with chrism when they baptize, but it must be chrism consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that oil; this belongs only to bishops when they impart the Spirit the Paraclete.

## CHAPTER 132. How the Baptized Person Is to Be Taught to Pray

[Note: [Col. 0166D] What he writes in the following chapters concerning the Lord’s Prayer is found in Saint Augustine’s letter to Proba, which is letter 130.]

After the washing of the font, after the newness of life, after the anointing of the Spirit, a person must be taught to pray with words of truth, so that the one who was a son of wrath in the old person may now, in heavenly regeneration, invoke the Father with devotion.

He is not to pour forth a lengthy utterance, by which he cannot escape sin (Prov. 10:19), but is to pour out prayer in the feeling of holy intention, possessing the rule of the Lord’s teaching. If he holds its power readily in prayer, he increases it more abundantly in delight, as the Psalm says: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart” (Ps. 36:4).

Accordingly, just as holy intention should not be prolonged if it cannot endure, so, if it endures, it should not be broken off too quickly. Let there be no excessive speech in prayer; but let there be abundant supplication, if fervent intention perseveres.

For to speak much is, in prayer, to conduct a necessary matter with superfluous words. But to pray much is to knock upon the one whom we entreat through a prolonged and devout stirring of the heart. Often this activity is carried on more through groans than through words, more through weeping than through expression.

He sets our tears in his sight (Ps. 55:9), and our groaning is not hidden from him (Ps. 38:10), who created all things through the Word and does not seek human words.

Words are therefore necessary for us, by which we may be reminded and may examine what we are asking—not words by which we imagine that God must either be instructed or persuaded.

## CHAPTER 133. Concerning the Lord’s Prayer

When, therefore, we say, “Our Father, who are in heaven,” we acknowledge the Creator in due order, honor the Lord with rightful reverence, and invoke the Father with devotion. We no longer waste away under fear of servitude when we trust in the Father’s love.

Nevertheless, we direct the words of this prayer to the whole Trinity, because both we and all things are from him, through him, and in him (Rom. 11:36).

[Col. 0166D] It must therefore be acknowledged that God is everywhere through the presence of his divinity, but not everywhere through the grace of his indwelling. Because of this indwelling, in which without doubt the grace of his love is recognized, we do not say, “Our Father, who are everywhere,” although that is true; rather, we say, “Our Father, who are in heaven,” so that in prayer we may commemorate his temple, which we ourselves ought also to be and, insofar as we are so, belong to his fellowship and the household of adoption.

For if the people of God, not yet made equal to his angels, [Col. 0167A] are still called his temple in this pilgrimage, how much more is his temple in heaven, where the people of angels are, to whom we shall be joined and made equal when, our pilgrimage ended, we have received what was promised?

Likewise, when we say, “Hallowed be your name,” we admonish ourselves to desire that his name, which is always holy, may also be held holy among human beings—that is, may not be despised—which benefits not God but human beings.

And in what we say, “Your kingdom come”—which will certainly come whether we wish it or not—we awaken our desire for that kingdom, so that it may come for us and we may deserve to reign in it.

When we say, “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven,” we ask him for that obedience in ourselves, so that his will may be done in us as it is done in his heavenly angels.

When we say, “Give us this day our daily bread,” by the word “today” the present time is signified. Here we either ask for that sufficiency which excels, signifying the whole by the name “bread,” or for the Sacrament of the faithful, which is necessary in this present time—not, however, for attaining the things of this present time, but that eternal happiness.

When we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” we remind ourselves both what we should ask and what we should do, so that we may deserve to receive.

When we say, “Do not bring us into temptation,” we remind ourselves to ask that, deprived of his help, we may not either consent to some temptation after being deceived or yield to it after being afflicted.

When we say, “Deliver us from evil,” we remind ourselves to consider that we are not yet in that good where we suffer no evil. This final petition, which is placed in the Lord’s Prayer, extends so broadly that a Christian placed in any tribulation gives forth groans over it, pours out tears over it, begins from it, lingers upon it, and brings his prayer to an end with it.

For these words were necessary to commend the realities themselves to our memory.

## CHAPTER 134. Concerning Prayer That Is Not Long

Whatever other words we may say—words formed beforehand by the feeling of the one praying so that it may become clear, or attended to afterward so that it may grow—we say nothing other than what is contained in this Lord’s Prayer, if we pray rightly and appropriately.

But whoever says what cannot pertain to this evangelical prayer prays carnally, even if he does not pray unlawfully. I do not know how this can be said not to be unlawful, since those who have been born again through the Spirit ought to pray only spiritually.

## CHAPTER 135. Concerning Every Petition Made by One Who Prays the Lord’s Prayer

For example, whoever says, “Glorify yourself among all the nations, as you have been glorified among us, and let your prophets be found faithful” (Ecclus. 36:18), what else does he say than, “Hallowed be your name”?

Whoever says, “God of hosts, convert us, and show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:4), what else does he say than, “Your kingdom come”?

Whoever says, “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Ps. 118:133), what else does he say than, “Your will be done in heaven and on earth”?

Whoever says, “Do not give me poverty or riches” (Prov. 30:9), what else does he say than, “Give us this day our daily bread”?

Whoever says, “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness” (Ps. 131:1), or, “Lord, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Ps. 7:4), what else does he say than, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”?

Whoever says, “Take away from me the desires of the belly and the desire for intercourse, lest it seize me” (Ecclus. 23:6), what else does he say than, “Do not bring us into temptation”?

Whoever says, “Deliver me from my enemies, and free me from those who rise up against me” (Ps. 58:2), what else does he say than, “Deliver us from evil”?

And if he should run through all the words of the holy commandments, I believe he will find nothing that this Lord’s Prayer does not contain and comprise.

Therefore it is permissible to say the same things in prayer in various words, but it is not permissible to say different things. These petitions are to be offered without wavering doubt for ourselves, for our own people, for strangers, and even for our enemies. Nevertheless, according to the closeness or distance of our relationships, the feeling of the one praying may arise or become stronger in the heart for one person or for another.

## CHAPTER 136. Concerning the Truth of Christ’s Body in the Eucharist

[Col. 0168C]

After the regeneration of spiritual birth, after the grace of heavenly anointing, after instruction in the Lord’s Prayer, and after the invocation of the divine Fatherhood, it is now fitting to proceed to participation in the heavenly nourishment.

For it belongs to those who have already been regenerated by the Father through water and the Spirit to say, “Our Father, who are in heaven,” so that they may confidently ask, saying, “Give us this day our daily bread.”

Since this bread is the living Christ, who descended from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:51), we rightly ask in this Lord’s Prayer that this same bread, Christ, be given to us daily, so that we who remain and live in Christ may not depart from his sanctification and body.

For what does God desire so much as that Christ, who is the bread of life and the bread from heaven, should dwell in us daily?

That bread was signified by the manna which those who had been delivered ate after crossing the Red Sea. For just as there, after the sea had been crossed, they ate the bread of heaven, that is, manna, so here, after the font—which bore the figure of the sea—we eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood, who said: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” [Note: [Col. 0167D] St. Augustine, *Tractate 16 on John 6.] (John 6:56).

Hence Paul says: “All were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food” [Col. 0169A] (1 Cor. 10:1). Spiritual, certainly, because that manna was a figure of the truth of Christ’s body, which we now eat.

And therefore the food is the same spiritually, but different bodily, because they ate manna, whereas we eat something else. He adds: “And all drank the same spiritual drink.” One thing for them, another for us—but in visible form, although it signified the same thing by spiritual power.

How, then, did they drink the same drink? “They drank,” he says, “from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ,” in the Word and in the flesh.

And how did they drink? The rock was struck with a rod. The twofold striking signifies the two pieces of wood of the cross. There the rock was struck with a rod, and water flowed, and they drank. Here, when Christ was suspended upon the wood of the cross, water and blood flowed; and we drink these so that we may have eternal life.

But when the same Lord says, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57), he explained what he had said. For to eat that food and drink that drink is to remain in Christ and to have him remaining in oneself.

Accordingly, whoever does not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain, unquestionably neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a reality to his own judgment.

## CHAPTER 137. What It Means to Understand Christ’s Body or Blood

What you see, then, is bread; and the cup is what your own eyes also report to you. But what your faith requires to be taught is this: the bread is Christ’s body, and the cup is Christ’s blood. This has been stated briefly, perhaps sufficiently for faith.

But faith desires instruction, for the prophet says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9).

You may therefore say to me: You have commanded us to believe; explain so that we may understand.

A thought of this kind may arise in someone’s mind: We know from where our Lord Jesus Christ received flesh—from the Virgin Mary. He was nursed as an infant, nourished, grew, reached youth, suffered persecution from the Jews, was hung upon wood, was killed upon the wood, was buried, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven on the day he willed, carried his body there, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. Now he sits there at the right hand of the Father.

How, then, is bread his body, or how is what the cup contains his blood?

Brothers, these things are called sacraments because in them one thing is seen and another understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has a spiritual fruit.

If you wish to understand Christ’s body, hear the Apostle speaking to the faithful: “You are the body of Christ and members of it” (1 Cor. 12:27).

If, then, you are Christ’s body and members, the mystery placed upon the Lord’s table is your mystery. You have received your mystery in relation to what you are; you have answered “Amen,” and by answering you have assented.

You hear “the body of Christ,” and you answer “Amen.” Be a member of Christ’s body, so that your “Amen” may be true.

Why, then, should we bring forward anything of our own here concerning the bread? Let us hear the Apostle himself again. [Col. 0170A] When he was speaking about this sacrament, he said: “One bread, one body—we who are many” (1 Cor. 10).

Understand, and rejoice: unity, piety, the truth of the flesh—one bread, one body, many.

## CHAPTER 138. As Concerning the Bread, So Also Concerning the Wine

Remember that bread is not made from one grain but from many. When bodily abstinence was imposed upon us and you began to abandon the way of life of the pagans in order to abstain from sins, cleansing yourselves through fasts, temporarily withdrawing from wives, spectacles, and more luxurious foods, and thus undergoing exorcism, the useless chaff of your former way of life having been removed—the chaff that you were then being ground down with—when you cast away the chaff of unclean conduct, you came into the brightness of a new confession. [Col. 0170B]

When you were baptized, you were, as it were, sprinkled together. When you received the fire of the Holy Spirit, you were, as it were, baked. Be what you see, and receive what you are. The Apostle said this concerning the bread.

What we should understand concerning the cup is also sufficiently shown, even without being stated. For just as, for the visible form of bread to exist, many grains are sprinkled together into one, so that what Holy Scripture says of the faithful may come about—“They had one soul and one heart in the Lord” (Acts 4:32)—so it is also with wine.

Brothers, remember from what wine is made. Many grapes hang upon a cluster, but the juice of the grapes is poured together into unity.

Thus the Lord Christ, to signify that we belong to him, willed the mystery of our peace and unity to be consecrated upon his table. Whoever receives the mystery of unity but does not hold the bond of peace does not receive the mystery for himself, but a testimony against himself.

## CHAPTER 139. Concerning the Building Up of a Person Through Repentance and Tears

After all the sacraments have been completed in full, the person newly born will for several days continually cling to the assembly and choirs of the Church, dressed in white garments. He will celebrate the sign and festivals of the holy solemnity in which, freed from the oldness of the first human being and released from the guilt of a condemned condition, he enters the presence of the Lord with rejoicing and is led among his chosen ones in gladness.

Thereafter let him remember his corrupted nature. Although he has escaped its condemnation, he has not entirely lost its frailty. Let him remain in the fear of the Lord, doing his will, loving God, and delighting in him.

And because he cannot be without sin, let him both take care to avoid sin and, persisting in the disposition of repentance with tears, continually strive to have his sins erased, until the abundant mercy of divine goodness, just as it erased original sin in the washing, also erases actual sin through lamentation.

And so, secure in the hope of future blessedness, let him complete the condition of death and rest in peace; and let him rise, reborn in every respect, destined to remain in his incorruption and in the praises of the Redeemer.

## CHAPTER 140. Prayer for the Removal of the White Garments

Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the world, whom God the Father marked out as his Son, truly human and truly born from a human being, confirm in this your household [Col. 0171A] that which, marked with your name, cleansed with sacred liquid, and filled with your Spirit, now rejoices that it has been satisfied with your body and blood and redeemed.

May they continually possess these sacraments, which they have received for the renewal of life, for the use of salvation, so that from them they may approach confidently toward the reward of blessedness.

## CHAPTER 141. Another Blessing

May the Lord Jesus Christ, who washed you with the water of his side and redeemed you by the pouring out of his blood, himself confirm in you the grace of the redemption you have received.

Through him you have been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit; may he join you to the heavenly kingdom. He who gave you the beginnings of holy faith may also grant you perfection of action and fullness [Col. 0171B] of charity.

Amen.

## CHAPTER 142. A Sermon to Be Delivered to the Infants on the Third Day after Easter for the Removal of the White Garments.

The sermon is addressed to you, infants newly born, little ones in Christ, the Church’s new offspring, the Father’s grace, the mother’s fruitfulness, a godly shoot, a new swarm, a fount of nurtured honor, and the fruit of my labor, my joy, and my crown. To all of you who stand in the Lord I speak in the words of the Apostle: “Behold, the night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Cast off the works of darkness, and put on the armor of light; let us walk honorably as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and debauchery, not in quarrelsomeness and rivalry, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII, 12–14), so that you may also put on in your life the one whom you have put on sacramentally. “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. III, 27–28).

For this is what the very substance of the sacrament contains. It is the sacrament of a new life, which begins in the present age with the forgiveness of all former sins, but will be brought to perfection in the resurrection of the dead. You have been buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, you too may walk in newness of life. You now walk by faith, as long as you are pilgrims in this mortal body. Yet Christ Jesus himself has become for you the sure way toward which you are striving, according to the human nature which he deigned to assume for our sake. For he will preserve great sweetness for those who fear him, opening and perfecting it for those who hope in him, when we receive in reality, through the light, what we have begun to possess in hope. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (I John III, 2).

He himself promised this in the Gospel: “Whoever loves me,” he says, “keeps my commandments; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and I will show myself to him” (John XIV, 21). Certainly those to whom he was speaking saw him; but they saw him in the form of a servant, in which the Father is greater than he, not in the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father. The former form he displayed to those who feared him; the latter he reserved for those who hoped in him. Therefore may he who redeemed you enlighten you, and may he who enlightened you guard you, so that he may protect you from every evil during this pilgrimage and present you glorified to himself in the future reward; through the glorious Trinity, our God, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0171]

# BOOK ON THE JOURNEY THROUGH THE DESERT, BY WHICH ONE PROCEEDS AFTER BAPTISM (C)

## CHAPTER I. On the beginning of humanity’s restoration through Christ

[Col. 0171C]

In the preceding work, through the ordered arrangement of heavenly teaching, it was shown from the beginning of humanity’s creation that the human being reached the grace of divine regeneration. In the work that follows, it is indicated how, after baptism, one hastens to reach the dwelling-place of eternal life—just as, after crossing the sea, one reaches the promised land—through observance of the divine commandments. Thus it may become clear that its outcome consists in a threefold course of events.

## CHAPTER II. On the restoration of humanity

First, when the blessed creature, having been made, fell through deception. Second, when it was restored through the Mediator’s death. Third, when it will be eternally glorified in the gift of redemption. Certainly, after the beginning of goodness, nature, corrupted through the enemy’s deception, came as far as the destruction of evil. Subsequently, restored through the Mediator’s blood, nature is led into the glory of the kingdom. Thus the devil’s kingdom was destroyed, a kingdom that endured until the Redeemer’s coming. Thus Christ’s kingdom was established in his elect and remains for ever: this will be the third and final kingdom, destined to remain in glory without end. First, therefore, humanity was created blessed; then, secondly, humanity was reborn more blessed. The intervening condition was utterly wretched, stained by every kind of misery and condemned by just retribution.

## CHAPTER III. On the Savior’s death and the regeneration of life

At the beginning, therefore, his condition was blessed; then the fall resulting from the serpent’s deception persisted for a long time in evil; thereafter, a gracious restoration came to our aid through the Savior’s death. Since the blessed beginning did not endure after deception had intervened, a life-giving regeneration came with profound mercy, so that corrupted birth might have a means by which it could be reborn from destruction to gain.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Church joined to Christ

But so that there might be a womb in which the human being, born into death, could be reborn into life, the Word of God became incarnate. Therefore, through the proclamation of the ancient Law, he formerly called from the nations the Church that had been foreknown; dying for her, he cleansed her in the bath of water and consecrated her to himself as a bride in an eternal covenant. In the manifestation of the Gospel, offering her a share in his body and blood through the sacrament of redemption, he made her his spouse and joined her to himself in the unity of communion.

## CHAPTER V. On the adoption of the children of God

From her, through the word of faith and the fruitfulness of the Holy Spirit, he creates countless people reborn each day. Embracing them as children adopted by grace, he takes them as his co-heirs in the blessedness of eternity. During the hardship of this mortality, he teaches them his law and, through his clear commandment, enlightens the eyes of the soul (Psalm XVIII, 9), so that, instructed in heart, he may lead them into the inheritance of righteousness. That this is the path of the right way, by which the liberated are led through a saving guidance to possess the kingdom, is readily known and made evident by the presentation of the passage.

## CHAPTER VI. On liberation after baptism

Therefore, after liberation from Egyptian slavery, after departure from the Egyptian dwelling-place, after the pursuit by the Egyptian army, after crossing the raging sea, after Pharaoh’s destruction, after the overthrow of the Egyptian multitude, after Israel’s rejoicing at salvation, and after the hymn of glory to God—that is, after we have left the world, after we have turned back to God, after the demons’ pursuit, after the immersion of baptism, after deprivation of the devil’s power, after the drowning of sins, after exultation over the salvation granted, and after the glory and hymn of divine praise—we must consider where we are being led and by what means we are being led, remembering that we are drawn and called by the Creator’s grace alone to the promised land, namely, the region of the land of the living, in which we shall be Christ’s co-heirs and children of the kingdom.

## CHAPTER VII. On instructing the baptized in sound doctrine

Let us now see how that wisdom of the Most High God clothes the children received from the water with paternal teachings and cherishes them with maternal compassion, instructing some who are ignorant and embracing others who are tender.

## CHAPTER VIII. On what is bitter and sweet water

[Col. 0173D]

After crossing the sea, one comes to the waters of Marah (Exod. XV, 23). That place received its name from the bitterness of its waters. Thus, after baptism, we come to knowledge of the Law. Since the mind cannot know spiritual understanding unless it first possesses knowledge of the historical account, one first comes to knowledge of the commandment. But when its surface is first tasted, because “the letter kills,” it is bitter and wearisome. Hence the course of its commandments offers no flavor of refreshment, because it brought nothing to perfection (Heb. VII, 19). We therefore learn, in due order, the killing letter. But once the faith of spiritual understanding has been received, and the wood of the Cross’s Passion has been mingled with it, it is changed into the sweetness of faith; and whatever was bitter through the letter’s influence becomes sweet through devout understanding.

## CHAPTER IX. On the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples

[Col. 0174A]

From there one comes to the twelve springs of sweet water and the seventy palm trees (ibid., 27), which show us the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples of the second order, whom the Lord is read to have sent ahead of him in pairs (Luke X, 1). From these springs and palms we drink doctrine and receive the sweet fruits of victory. Hence Elim, which is the name of that dwelling-place, is interpreted as “strong rams.” For they themselves are the sturdy leaders of the flocks and guides of the sheep, that is, teachers of the nations. It is therefore rightly that one comes to the grace of the Gospel, which through Christ’s disciples grants us both the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom and victory over spiritual wickedness.

## CHAPTER X. That one comes to the kingdom by a swift shortcut along the Gospel way

[Col. 0174B]

All the diversity of the dwellings that follows will then be set out individually through an exposition of their mysteries. But since these matters have already been arranged by the holy Fathers, we must carry forward for you the summons of evangelical grace. In it we find a more excellent way prepared through a swifter shortcut to salvation: one that does not postpone the rest of taking possession of the inheritance for forty years amid the dangers and hazards posed by enemies, but that offers the Savior’s swift and easy remedy in the one who says: “Come to me, all you who labor, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI, 28–30).

## CHAPTER XI. On attending to the work of human liberation

Let us now attend to the work of our liberation. And then let us consider the road of the journey that leads toward the dwelling-place of blessedness. Truth itself says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John VIII, 36). Behold now the true freedom: called to the Redeemer’s grace, as though we had left Egypt and Pharaoh behind, we have accepted the servitude of the devil and of sins. We passed through in the manner of baptism; in its sacrament we received all the benefits of our salvation together with the nobility of freedom. We have come to the course of the present life, and, as our age advances, we devote ourselves to acquiring knowledge. Thus, through knowledge of the Law, we approach the bitterness of the killing letter. The author of this Law is the one God who is also the author of the Gospels.

## CHAPTER XII. That one does not linger in the Law if it is understood spiritually

Yet by understanding this Law spiritually, we do not linger in its bitterness; rather, we hasten quickly to the waters of doctrine and the palms of victory, where we are satisfied with the abundance of heavenly teachings through the apostles and raised up by the triumphs of spiritual glory.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Gospel light beginning to shine

May the evangelical light shine upon us who sit in darkness and the shadow of death (Luke I, 79), the light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John I, 9). May it no longer set for us amid the assaults of temptations, but may it always shine upon us, entering us through the bestowal of mercies.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the preparation of the Incarnation, which leads us to the unchangeable truth of the Godhead

Through the assumption of flesh, the one who remains life through the power of eternity becomes our way, leading us to the sweetness of the everlasting and unchangeable truth.

## CHAPTER XV. That in the desert of holy life the pleasure of impure delight is not found

Let us now contemplate this prosperous journey undertaken by the saints in the desert, and let us be led along with them by equal imitation. It is said of those who, after crossing the Red Sea and proceeding through the deserts, confidently believed that, according to God’s true promise, they were coming to the promised land. Although the whole people, formed from a multitude of saints and a company of sinners, proceeded together under God’s protection, nevertheless Holy Scripture, presenting the better part—that of the saints, concerning whom it is said, “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Psalm XXXIII, 16)—leaves the wicked unmentioned and recounts only the action of blessedness.

Let us therefore enter with those righteous people concerning whom it is said: “They traveled through deserts that were not inhabited” (Wisdom XI, 2)—those deserts, certainly, that contain no dwellings of pleasures, no abodes of corruption, no earthly happiness that soothes only to destruction, and no delights that impede travelers hastening toward the land of the living. “They made shelters for themselves in secret places” (ibid.), because they placed the mind’s rest in the hidden recess of contemplation, not recklessly exposing themselves to enemies through stubbornness, but protecting themselves in the secrecy of readily available counsels through a saving prudence. There vain glory did not display them for their destruction, but true humility led them away from the ruin of the proud. “They stood against their enemies” (ibid., 3), because they raised the inflexible strength of the spirit against the assaults of temptations; untouched by the softness of the present life, they never bent in the ranks of spiritual warfare from the stance of holy purpose before the attack of the aerial power. “And therefore they took vengeance on their enemies” (ibid.), because, armed with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, they were not lifted up by the glory of prosperity nor crushed by the weight of adversity. They took vengeance in this way because, by conquering their enemies, they secured their own salvation; and where the adversity of vices was driven back and destroyed, there the salvation of the holy soldiers stood firm after being shaken.

“They thirsted and called upon God” (ibid., 4), because, burning with the fire of charity, they thirstingly called upon the one whom they truly loved. A great thirst of love boiled within them, and their invocation of God poured in the reward of refreshment. For the more fervent their love proved to be in the love of God, the more surely the warmth of grace came to their aid as refreshment. Hence “water was given them from the very high rock” (ibid.): because what they raised up within themselves through the ardor of love reached wholly to the streams of the highest rock—that is, of spiritual grace—and, having attained blessedness, they quenched every thirst of good desires. “They also had rest from the hard stone” (ibid.), that is, from the strong stone, because fire of charity consumes whatever was fluid; the blaze of love strengthens whatever was fragile; and blessed eternity makes firm whatever was rightly desirable to them.

## CHAPTER XVI. On entering the desert of holy life

Thus we enter the desert of holy life, where, once the moisture of all carnal pleasures has been dried up, we will find nothing that, by contrast, is beautiful to the eyes or pleasing to the sight, nothing which, when the hand of free choice is extended and the palate of thought has tasted it, can drag those already reborn back to their former destruction instead of onward to eternal purity.

There will be nothing in which the eyes’ vision may wander in lascivious sight, when we say continually: “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Psalm CXXII, 2). The ears will not be enticed by the deadly whispers of unclean birds, which either disturb the heart’s quiet by wickedly unsettling it or delight it into torpor by wickedly soothing it, when this has been meditated upon: “Therefore I shall sleep, and my heart shall keep watch” (Song V, 2). The sense of smell will not be infected by the breath of fleeting pleasure when, burning with love for the Bridegroom, we say to him: “We shall run after the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song I, 3). The taste will not be corrupted by the sourness of ancient decay when a throat seasoned by grace cries out: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Psalm CXVIII, 103).

The scurrilous tongue will not cast out falsehood and slander when, sensing the refreshment of grace, it says: “My mouth is filled with joy, and my tongue with exultation” (Psalm CXXV, 2). The heart will not grow weak through the flow of thought when it has been preserved with all vigilance. The sense of touch will not handle the uncleanness of foul activity when this has truly been brought forth: “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will surround your altar, O Lord” (Psalm XXV, 1). The steps of the spirit will not cling to a swamp of mud when firm purpose says: “He set my feet upon a rock and directed my steps” (Psalm XXXIX, 3).

The body will not lawlessly desire to be restored by the blandishments of the air when it has steadfastly affirmed: “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing” (Psalm XXII, 1). No licentious remedies for discomfort will be sought when it has been attentively said: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation” (Psalm XXVI, 1). The relief of need will not viciously seek a more luxurious appetite when true confidence cries out: “God does not kill the soul of the righteous with hunger” (Prov. X, 3). No sadness that extinguishes blessedness will cast down the soul when the joyfulness of the mind breaks forth in exultant rejoicing: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Psalm LXXXIII, 3).

The pleasure that soothes prosperity will not be attempted when the only delight, with the whole will, belongs to the one who says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm XV, 5). Finally, the one who says with Paul, “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14), will desire nothing from the world’s consolations. Every pleasurable moisture of the inner person, the fatness of corrupt activity, and the swelling of an inflated mind will be cleansed and dried up by one saving antidote, when the Lord’s command has been fulfilled: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX, 23).

## CHAPTER XVII. On the signs and leadership of the desert

O how blessed is the people who proceed through such a desert, having their Redeemer as guide and following him alone, attending to him alone, taking up either their Lord’s cross or their own! It will be their Lord’s cross when, through faith in him, they have conquered every aerial power in triumph; but it will be their own when, in imitation of their Lord’s Passion, they have fastened their flesh, with its vices, to the nails of fear. Thus, undaunted, they will cross the wasteland of the desert, because grace, the light of the merciful one, goes before them; the Redeemer himself is their guide; the glory of the Cross is the sign of victory; and the ever-present mercy of the Redeemer follows as their protection.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That the sun of righteousness, which pours in light, itself dries up the moisture of pleasure

Behold the sun of righteousness, which has shone upon us so that we may walk along the straight road in its light. By its heat it has itself dried up every fluid and flowing moisture of wounded pleasure, so that, now that we know by what straight path we should walk, we are not delayed by any touch of corruption.

Thus let those who desire the beauty of life love the austerity of the desert. Thus let those whose soul magnifies the Lord and whose spirit rejoices in God their Savior delight in the affliction of the flesh (Luke I, 47). Thus, deprived of all the consolations of the present world, the entire desert of this present life will be loved in hope of future consolation, since no better or quicker route leads to the homeland of the blessed than through the narrow passages of sufferings, as Paul says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

## CHAPTER XIX. That humanity can be saved by the grace of God alone

Now that the saving desert of righteousness has been shown to be illuminated by light and made active by heat, offering a path amid labor to travelers but amid refreshment to eternal citizens, let us see the delights that their guide administers there for their consolation through the pledge of the Holy Spirit bestowed upon them. Thus every human being, warned by consideration of his own inability and recognizing that he is bereft of merits of his own, may place his hope in God alone—God who prepares the will and grants the ability; who freely gives merits to those who do not deserve them, by which he may repay gifts; who first grants mercy and thereby gives the substance of good works, and afterward bestows the rewards; who enables his servant to do what pleases him in his service, and later rewards him by calling him to the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XX. On attending to the refreshment of eternity because of the gift of present consolation

Then, as sharply as each person can, let him gaze with wonder at what refreshment of eternity he will give there, when here he grants so great a consolation in time; what exultation there will be in the gift if so much consolation is given here in pledge; what glory will be ours upon arrival, if there is so much exultation in hope; what joy it will be to possess and behold the Redeemer in the embrace of eternal love, if there is so great a salvation in having received redemption.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the affections by which eternal blessedness is desired

O Lord, give me that fire which you sent when you came upon the earth and which you desire to burn (Luke XII, 49). Grant me to burn with the fire of charity; grant me to shine with the splendor of obedience; grant me to glow with the love of devotion; grant me not to perish amid dangers; grant me to emerge safely from dangers; grant me to hasten toward your sweetness; grant me to come peacefully to your vision; grant me to be eternally satisfied by the revelation of your vision; grant me to praise you without end throughout the eternity of the ages.

Certainly, attentive minds must consider that to await that reality is to merit this one; that to expect that is to possess this; and that to perceive that most clearly is to have truly perceived this.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the description of the pleasures whose moisture is not found in the holy desert

Now the poison of spiritual diseases is to be extinguished; in this desert it can neither arise nor flow through any moisture soaked with pleasures. The wise apostolic discourse describes it in its several forms, as though speaking to a foolish sick person whose illness is worse the less it is known: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, lust, the service of idols, sorceries, hostilities, quarrels, rivalries, anger, strife, dissensions, heresies, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. V, 19–21).

## CHAPTER XXIII. On spiritual foods prepared for the stomach of the mind

Having rejected the nausea of such fluids and freed the belly of the mind from foul decay, once the stomach has been prepared, tranquil and fit for the appetite of salvation, the same apostolic discourse next sets before it a rich feast of virtues through the fitting service of devotion and says: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, patience, gentleness, modesty, self-control, chastity. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another” (ibid., 22–26).

## CHAPTER XXIV. That Christ refreshes us on this pilgrimage with many gifts of charisms

There are also the gifts of charisms mentioned earlier, by which the Holy Spirit, together with these virtues, refreshes us on this pilgrimage. Christ gave him to us as a pledge of his goodness, so that he might not find us failing on the road, but lead us, once refreshed, into our homeland.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the sacrament of light

[Col. 0179A]

The light, namely, of the knowledge of him, concerning which we say to the Father, “In your light we shall see light” (Psalm XXXV, 10): for in the knowledge of Christ, who is light, we shall see the light, the Father, begetter of light. And this is truly so, because whoever has the Son also has the Father, and because no one knows the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him (Matt. XI, 27). Or it is also because he has given us the light of holy understanding, in which we may search out his commandments and, with his help, find the fruit of our searching.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the sacrament of oil

The oil of sanctification, by which we receive the anointing of spiritual joy, is the oil of which the prophet says: “The yoke will decay before the face of the oil” (Isa. X, 27). When we received its infusion, the yoke of sin, which had pressed upon the neck of the soul, decayed and vanished.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the sacrament of bread

The bread of heavenly manna, which he identified with the reality of his body when he said: “This is the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world” (John VI, 33).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the sacrament of water

The water of life that flowed from the rock when it was struck by the rod signifies that, in the form of the two woods of the Cross, the body of Christ, suspended upon it, would pour forth for us a life-giving drink. In the water it would display the washing of baptism, and in the blood it would effect the remission of sins. There is also there the greenness of branches, which, by their nature, provide shade for the anxious; through the leaves of doctrine they prepare knowledge; through their fruits they administer the refreshment of understanding; and through the sight of their greenness they commend eternity.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the significance of the rod

There is there the rod of Christ’s flesh, which blossomed after the dryness of death. For after it had been cut off in the Passion from the root of Jesse, it revived more vigorously after having been put to death. In the rod, that same flesh displays power to reign over all things; in the flower, the beauty of the resurrection; and in the whole company of the redeemed, glory.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the significance of the flower and the lily

[Col. 0179D]

There is there “the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II, 1), because Christ himself, arising from the shoot of virginal flesh, shone forth as the world’s beauty, and the grace of virgins’ humility gleamed forth.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the significance of the vine

There is there that evangelical vine presented by the testimony of Truth himself (John XV, 1). Open to the whole world, it offers life to those who believe in it and has those who believe in it as branches within itself for eternal life. Its grapes’ blood is the price of the world, the redemption of the faithful, the abolition of sin, and the reward of the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the significance of the pomegranate

There is there that pomegranate, symbol of the Church’s nobility, diverse in the grains of the faithful yet bound together in unity; divided according to the dwelling-place of merits yet compacted in the unity of faith; red with the title of Christ’s blood and enduring in blessed eternity.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the significance of the fig

There is also the fig tree, which, casting off the first coarse figs of the Jews’ Law, subsequently brought believers in the time of grace to the sweetness of the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That the Gentile people, or the unfruitful soul, are called a desert

[Col. 0180B]

In this desert, pools and streams of water are found commended both in prophetic words and in prophetic mysteries. Whether this refers to the Gentile people or to the unfruitful soul, it is the same reality: one that, through its uselessness, languishes without fruit and lies in the dust, and afterward pours forth the streams of holy preaching and the channels of doctrine. Even more is promised to this solitude as a great gift.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the significance of the cedar

[Note: [Col. 0179] From St. Gregory, *Book I on the Gospel*, Homily 20, § 13; from this passage the six chapters that follow are taken.]

That cedar of great fragrance, which displays virtues and signs in the activity of the saints and, with Paul, says, “We are a good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II, 15), is all the more praiseworthy in the memory of eternity insofar as it is found more pleasing and purer than the putrefaction of corruption.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the significance of the thorn

The thorn of spiritual doctrine, which, when it discusses sins and virtues, sometimes threatens eternal punishments and sometimes promises heavenly joy, pricks the hearts of its hearers so that, pierced by the pain of compunction, it compels the mind through the eyes to draw out tears as a kind of blood of the soul.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the significance of the myrtle

The myrtle possesses the virtue of self-restraint, so that it tightens loosened limbs. When, through compassionate mercy, it either brings help to afflicted neighbors or offers them words of consolation, it restores to the hope of salvation what, battered by pressures, could have been worn away through laxity.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the significance of the olive

The olive signifies mercy, because in Greek mercy is also called ἔλεος (*eleos*), and its liquid shines with the fruit of mercy, highly acceptable before the sight of God.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the significance of the fir

The fir signifies contemplation. Placed within the holy Church in earthly bodies, it already contemplates heavenly things; and although its origin is from the earth, through contemplation it now raises the summit of its crown into the ether.

## CHAPTER XL. On the significance of the elm

The elm signifies secular power. Although it serves earthly concerns and produces no fruit of spiritual virtue, it nevertheless supports holy men, filled with spiritual gifts, through its generosity; it worthily bears, as it were, a vine together with its fruits.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the significance of the box tree

The box tree signifies perpetual greenness. Although, because of the weakness of its age, it has neither height nor fruit, nevertheless, following the faith of faithful ancestors, it rejoices perpetually in the everlasting greenness of faith.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the significance of the pine

The pine is lifted high by holy purpose through the sharpness of its leaves, stirring the minds of its hearers with words of doctrine. It is stripped by no adversity of time of the greenness of eternal desire, preserving in hidden places the fruit of understanding. This fruit does not easily reveal itself to the idle unless the learner’s great attentiveness has penetrated it with something like the hammer of good study.

When it has been extracted for consumption as understanding, it both flavors the throat in speech and strengthens the stomach of the mind in understanding virtue. It brings forth resin in the sweat of endurance from the suffering of the body; when this is applied to the wounds of neighbors, it both heals the ulcer into salvation and blazes forth in good repute through its fragrance.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the significance of the cedar and cypress

The cedar and cypress together, of which it is said, “The roofs of our houses are cedar, our ceilings are cypress” (Song I, 16), signify a twofold love, namely, love of God and love of neighbor. In the saints, who are God’s dwelling-place, this love is shown to have been granted from above through the Holy Spirit, so that within the Church’s sublimity one aspect consists in love of God through the power of protection, while another aspect consists in love of neighbor through beauty.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the significance of the reed

There is there the reed of spiritual doctrine, nourished by water and receiving such grace of dignity that, progressing in the word of God, it too becomes a writer, as a teacher or preacher.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the significance of the rush

There is there the rush, raised by the same grace of doctrine. Although it cannot advance to the point of becoming a writing reed—that is, a teaching preacher—nevertheless, because it preserves the virtue of obedience, it advances in learning the law and preserves its greenness until the reward.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the significance of the lily, rose, and violet

There is also the white lily, the flower of virgins; the purple rose, the blood of martyrs; and the violet, the grace of the continent.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the significance of hyssop

[Col. 0182A]

Hyssop possesses the purifying power of the words of God. Sprinkled upon the swelling of the mind, it makes everything that puffs it up wither through the austerity of the commandment.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the significance of mustard

There is there that mustard seed likened to the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XIII, 31), exalted in seed, strength, and stalk. Its smallness in the seeds is so remarkable that, with the hope of growth, it surpasses vegetables in height and even exceeds certain shrubs. Its sowing is humble; its maturity lofty. The form of the seed cannot be cut apart. Whole, it gives off no fragrance at all; crushed, it is intolerable in smell and taste. Its stalk is so tall that it provides a secure dwelling for the birds of heaven.

It signifies faith, which is the kingdom of heaven, sown contemptibly in the humility of the teacher. When it is considered by itself, it is thought contemptible and worthless. But if it is examined attentively, first it does not admit cutting, because it has no rift of heresies. Second, it is gentle to the touch, because Christ’s yoke is easy and his burden light. Third, when rubbed through the intention and handling of the spirit, it gives off an immense fragrance and an immense flavor, so that one who thinks rightly about it says: “I sought wisdom, and it withdrew far from me” (Eccles. VII, 24), because when it is carefully examined, the strength of impenetrable mysteries is perceived. It also grows in its own strength, reaching the rewards of future things, which the souls of the faithful attain, possessing the solidity of its dwelling as the birds of heaven possess it in its branches.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the significance of the mountain, which is Christ

[Col. 0182C]

There is seen there that solitary mountain raised above the summit of all mountains (Dan. II, 35), which grew from a stone cut without hands and filled the whole globe of the earth. This means that the Word, made flesh and born from the truth of humanity without the work of marital intercourse, filled the world, because his kingdom grew above all things. It also surpassed all mountains in height, because, exalted above the excellence of angels, it took its seat in the Father’s throne.

## CHAPTER L. On the significance of Zion, which is the Church

There is there the eminent mountain of Zion, situated in the length of this desert—that is, of the pilgrimage of the present life—so that upon it we may watch for the promise of heavenly things. Hence Zion is called “watching.”

## CHAPTER LI. On the significance of Lebanon

There is there Lebanon—not that Lebanon whose forest is cut down for the destruction of the proud, but the Lebanon concerning which it is said: “The fragrance of Lebanon will come to you” (Isa. LX, 13). That is, the pleasing activity of holy souls will give off its fragrance before you.

## CHAPTER LII. On the significance of stones

There are there the living stones marked by Peter’s mouth, not subjected to being cut by any softness of vices but made solid for the service of eternity by the ardor of charity. Concerning them it is said: “Coming to the Lord, the living stone rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honored by God, you yourselves, like living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (I Peter II, 4–5).

## CHAPTER LIII. On the consolation of spiritual birds

Moreover, amid the distinct beauty of mountains and woods, which display the consolation of greenness and fruits to those who are approaching eternal rest as an exhibition of virtues, there are also clear contemplations of good birds. These either refresh God’s traveler with sweet song or delight him by the sight of grace. They remain as consolation for the traveler and, through their protective companionship, soothe the distress of the journey.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the significance of the dove

[Col. 0183B]

Columba, of course, signifies innocence flourishing in evangelical simplicity. Since it has no gall in its flesh, it is likewise free from the bitterness of anger and indignation. In the form of a dove the Father’s Spirit came upon Christ (Matt. 3:16), and the same Christ commands his disciples to be like it when he says: “Be simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16). Thus he enjoins the virtue of gentleness and simplicity, while anger, indignation, and malice alike depart.

### CHAPTER LV. On the Significance of the Pelican

The pelican signifies the Christ of unique solitude, that is, Christ brought forth from the singular womb of a virgin birth, who, uniquely generated, was kept alone in the dwelling of virginal solitude. [Col. 0183C]

### CHAPTER LVI. On the Significance of the Night-Raven

The night-raven of the ruined dwelling signifies the same Lord, who, amid the darkness of the persecutors’ treachery gathering around him in his Passion, did not choose to disregard their hearts; for he prayed to the Father for them even amid his sufferings, dwelling among them until the end of his Passion and the victory of death.

### CHAPTER LVII. On the Significance of the Sparrow

The solitary sparrow of the heavenly building signifies Christ himself. After enduring the Passion amid the dark works of the ruined people, he reclaimed the seat of heavenly glory in the freedom of the resurrection. [Col. 0183D]

### CHAPTER LVIII. On the Significance of the Eagle

The eagle signifies divine protection, of which God says: “I received you as young birds, as under the wings of an eagle, and brought you to myself” (Exod. 19:3). By spreading the wings of his hands upon the cross, Christ protected believers by receiving them; and after the setting of bodily death, he ascended to heaven on the flight of his Ascension. In John too, it flies from heavenly eminence to the Father and announces to the world what it has learned concerning the Word of God.

### CHAPTER LIX. On the Significance of the Coot

The coot, whose house is the rock, which is the guide of sparrows’ houses, signifies Christ. For Christ is the rock, the place of rest, the fixed solidity of repose, and he is the guide of all the saints to the entrance of eternal life. [Col. 0184A]

### CHAPTER LX. On the Significance of the Turtle-Dove

The ecclesial turtle-dove builds a nest for itself from the wood of the cross. In it, under the warmth of faith, it stores the little believers so that they may grow together, until, educated in the dwelling of faith, they can reach the point where they are able to take up the likeness of Christ’s Passion, bear his cross, and follow the same Lord.

### CHAPTER LXI. On the Significance of the Swallow

That keen-sighted swallow, proclaiming at the proper and improper time with a tongue of bright sound, rouses the sluggish. Flying with the freedom of living contemplation, it is known as prey to no most ravenous demonic bird. By the diligence of holy work it builds a nest of the mind, where it warms the young of its thoughts in the loving fellowship of neighbors, as in a human dwelling; then it directs them toward the work of action, for the flight of perfected virtue. [Col. 0184B]

### CHAPTER LXII. On the Significance of the Hen

The evangelical hen is brought forth in the Lord’s likeness and words: a pleasing kind, gentle, fruitful in offspring, and devoted toward its young, carefully warming its children and educating them with still greater care. It does not vary in its brood like the partridge, nor abandon what it should warm like the pheasant. Rather, when the vigorous mother has carried food to her offspring, she calls the little ones with attentive voice; drawing them inseparably along with her, she does not allow them to be frightened by the hardship either of cold or hunger. Through this image the Lord displayed his compassion and spoke to the unfaithful people, saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling. Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:37–38). Therefore, because it will not be under the wings of God’s protection . . . [lacuna]

### CHAPTER LXIII. On the Significance of the Phoenix

### CHAPTER LXIV. On the Significance of Both Serpents

. . . having stood upright, raised toward the vision of the Redeemer; for when we contemplate his exaltation upon the cross, then we understand that he walked for our defense upon the asp of sin and the basilisk of death (Ps. 90:13), and that he likewise trampled upon the lion, the devil, and the dragon, the Antichrist. Certainly all these were overcome and destroyed through the victory of his Passion for all of us who, having been conformed to his Passion, recognize ourselves crucified to the world and the world crucified to us. [Col. 0184D]

### CHAPTER LXV. Another Significance of the Serpent

There is also another serpent joined to the same head of its own. While it hides its head in the opening of a cavern for life through faith, it surrenders its body in the Passion of death, stripping off the garment of its former way of life so that it may walk in newness of life.

### CHAPTER LXVI. On the Significance of Both Lions

[Col. 0185A]

Although the lion may rage—the one who prowls about seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. 5:8)—that victorious lion from the tribe of Judah is nevertheless always with us (Rev. 5:5), defending us against him as willingly as he himself powerfully conquered him.

### CHAPTER LXVII. On the Significance of the Wolf and the Sheep

Although the wolf may attack, always panting after prey with the jaws of death, that sheep is present with us and resists him on our behalf—the one led to slaughter who did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7). It clothes and protects us against the arrows of ungodliness and against the cold with the wool of mercy, the warmth of charity, and the unconquerable strength of one who fights. [Col. 0185B]

### CHAPTER LXVIII. On the Significance of the Lamb

The immaculate Lamb himself stands there. Since he has no stain of sin, he therefore breaks the molars of this wolf and lion (Ps. 57:7), and does not allow his body to be touched by its bites. For by pouring out his own blood, he extinguished the power by which that one was accustomed to devour the life of souls, as though drinking blood. When the innocent Lamb was sacrificed and fell into death, he extinguished both its voracity and its rage: by the outpouring of his blood, he did not water the thirst for the blood of the slain but extinguished it; he did not moisten but slew; he did not temper but absorbed it. Thus, while the other greedily drained the harmful blood of souls without satisfaction, this one, pouring out his innocent blood, drained the devourer and drinker altogether. [Col. 0185C]

### CHAPTER LXIX. On the Significance of the Deer

There is also the deer running along the path of God’s commandments in the straightness of faith. It has none of the turnings of the heretical fox; hence it is said: “Straight is the deer’s course, but winding is the little fox’s.” By the harshness of its tongue it kills the serpent, because by the attack of its teaching it kills the strength of sin in the hearts of its hearers. It longs for the springs of water (Ps. 41:1), so that, reaching the living God, it may be revived by the eternal refreshment of his vision.

### CHAPTER LXX. On the Significance of the Fawns of the Doe

The fawns of the doe, representing the two peoples (Song 4:5), truly acknowledge themselves as sinners through humility; yet through charity they perceive that nothing arising from temporality obstructs those who run. Seeking the heights of contemplation, they freely climb the lofty leaps of love. When they seem to lower themselves in compassion for their neighbors, they are not injured by any precipitous fall, because they support themselves on the horns of devout virtue, lest they fall amid their neighbor’s dangers. [Col. 0185D]

### CHAPTER LXXI. On the Significance of the Horse

There is also the horse—not the one that, in confidence in itself, bears a proud rider, with whom it is hurled into the sea (Exod. 15:1), but the handsome one in battle, which carries us against the powers of the air with tireless exertion and, exalted in the name of our Lord, rescues us from dangers. [Col. 0186A]

### CHAPTER LXXII. On the Blessedness of the Holy Desert

O blessed desert, in which one travels not by the feet of the body but by the movements of the heart; in which one seeks not the ambition of possession but contemplation; where the advancing soul does not grow weary, because the journey is not completed by the bending of the knees; where one does not desire to know when refreshment will be sent, but when the perfection of refreshment will be found; where whatever else there is is nothing other than what the reward will be; where the harmony of the senses presses toward the end of labor with such a steadfastness of perseverance that no laborious action obstructs it; where there is no forgetfulness of the future, although much pressure from the present presses upon one; where something of the reward is already tasted when unwavering constancy is maintained under the weight of suffering; which is not made fruitful by the moisture of pleasures but by the warmth of charity; whose verdure is not infused by pleasurable moisture but nourished by the fervent exertions of holy watchfulness; whose durability is preserved not by interruptions of leisure but by unceasing concentration; where the fragrance of good action is scattered by no blast of worldly violence; where the pleasing sight is obstructed by no dullness; where holy labor does not grow weary of enduring its work; where every holy action is joy, and idleness is detestable and absent.

It is not so arduous that it must also be feared. Yet, being harmless in this way, it does not know the welcome of freedom mixed with defilements. It is at once pleasing and strict: pleasing in the desire for rewards, strict in the prohibition of sins. Whoever loves eternal things runs eagerly in it. Whoever clings to temporal things, bound in chains, should not fear to undertake it.

There the certainty of salvation loves adversity, while the tranquil prosperity of leisure enervates it. There love is strong as death (Song 8:6), because when the love of divinity has breathed upon a person, it holds worldly action as mortified. Every traveler runs there wounded by charity, and is ardently driven toward the reward by the goads of charity’s wound. Established in an earthly bosom, it delights in a heavenly striving. Given strength for mortal time, it possesses mortal love; and from the very source where it truly assumes the mortification of the body, it freely presses on toward the glory of immortality.

It is accessible through the footsteps of holy souls. Every future citizen of the good homeland enters it according to sex, seeks it according to age, enters it in due time, practices it through works, presses toward it through intention, and embraces it through love. The elders, with Moses and Aaron, strive through the urgency of holy service toward the brightness of inner glory. The young, through the exercise of work, subdue the battles of temptation with spiritual weapons. Women, with Miriam, resound on the tambourine with hymns to the divine glory, their flesh having been made lean; equipped with the uses of virtue, so that through the path of strong men it may be free for them to walk.

They therefore do not shrink from the attacks of hostile temptations, because by strength of soul they remain joined to the fellowship of the saints. For the same reason they are not separated by the hardship of the difficult road: they are equal in the undertaking of holy intention. They do not complain about their weakness, because through the softness of the body they bring forth the work of virtue. They regard nothing as delicate for themselves on account of bodily softness, since they also prepare their bodies to receive the swords of persecutors. They perceive nothing tender in their sex, since everything that was softly delightful has hardened toward the victory of glory.

No one, whatever his purpose or honor, sex or rank, person or lineage, will be excluded from this holy dwelling in the desert of mortal pilgrimage. It either receives and holds him for protection or sends him by the saving road to the dwelling of eternal blessedness. For there the capacity of every rank is present, rejecting no condition from itself. Whoever is rationally invigorated in it lives wisely, abides in the love of God, and presses toward the praise of divine eternity.

For in bishops there are the example of blessed living and the lofty height of heavenly glory; in priests, the honorable gravity of a blessed life; in ministers, holy life and obedient service; in the rest of the religious body, beauty of character and the observance of distinct orders; in virgins, the glory of incorruption; in the continent, the expectation of consolation; in penitents, remission granted; in the wealthy, ready generosity in the use of riches and license cut off from illicit uses; in the poor, life-giving consolation; in those possessing power and eminence of honor, true humility and restraint against excess in the exercise of authority; in married people, honorable freedom in offspring and pleasure removed from self-indulgence. This place receives all into salvation; this road sends all toward life.

Only this is required: whoever enters the territory of this religion must cling to innocence, burn with charity, and continually pant toward the manifestation of God’s glory, destined to be eternally satisfied by it. For every traveler there, the wiser and more firmly established he is in his proper order, the more certain he will be of the reward he awaits; and the more ardent he is in doing what is good, the more faithful he will be in receiving the reward. [Col. 0186D–0187C]

### CHAPTER LXXIII. Hope in God Alone

After the course of the desert has been described, spiritual refreshment attempted there, and the moisture of all vices drained away, complete tranquility will come to those who travel onward when all hope has remained firmly fixed upon God, the author of every good.

### CHAPTER LXXIV. That No One Can Be Saved without Both the Preceding and the Subsequent Mercy of God

[Col. 0187D]

Although washed in the sea of baptism, although delivered into freedom, and although we sing the song of God’s glory, we cannot be led through the stages of this present life to the possession of eternal rest unless, while we live mortally, both the light of the pillar goes before us and protection overshadows us. By these, amid the encounter with all the temptations of this world, the light of God’s prevenient grace leads the ignorant forward, while the cloud of subsequent mercy protects and strengthens the weak.

### CHAPTER LXXV. On the Following Account, Set Forth in Outline

[Col. 0188A]

Since certain good works are powerful instruments without which no human being can either be restored wholly to the Creator or be completely joined to the Redeemer, they must be briefly noted, so that the force of what has been said, held taut by its own arts, may by a diligent joining produce a solid and beautiful body of work.

### CHAPTER LXXVI. Repetition of Certain Earlier Matters

The beginnings of the restored human being, coming from the old way of life to the knowledge of God, have been set forth in the preceding work in a clear and appropriate sequence: in the exorcism of the word, the proclamation of the commandment, the anointing with oil, the reception of the Creed, the sacrament of baptism, the chrism of the Holy Spirit, and participation in the body and blood of Christ. [Col. 0188B] All these begin from hearing of faith, stand through the expectation of faith, and are completed in the love of faith.

### CHAPTER LXXVII. What Faith Is

[Note: [Col. 0187D] From Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VIII, chapter 2, no. 4.]

Faith is that by which we believe that what we are not yet able to see can come to be. For when someone sees, there is no need for him to seek faith in a matter to which he has given the testimony of vision. But if it cannot yet be seen, it is necessary that he grant faith and affirm that what he is entirely unable to see can come to be.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII. Why Faith Is So Called

[Col. 0188C]
