Faith is therefore so called because what has been agreed upon between two parties comes to be—that is, between God and the human being: so that in the present one believes in God, and in the future one believes that one will be satisfied with the sweetness of God, which he promised to those who love him.

### CHAPTER LXXIX. That Faith Concerns Both Evil and Good Things

Faith, moreover, is not only in God. For it also concerns evil things and good things, because both good and evil are believed—and this with good faith, not bad.

### CHAPTER LXXX. That Faith Concerns Past, Present, and Future Things

Faith also concerns past, present, and future things. We believe that Christ died, which is past; we believe that he sits at the right hand of the Father, which is present; we believe that he will come to judge, which is future. [Col. 0188D]

### CHAPTER LXXXI. That Faith Concerns Both One’s Own Things and Those of Others

Faith likewise concerns both one’s own things and those of others. Each person believes that he himself once began to exist and was certainly not eternal, because he began; yet he believes that he is eternal because he does not cease. We believe many things pertaining to religion not only about other human beings, but also about angels.

### CHAPTER LXXXII. That Faith and Works Joined Together Save a Person, but Separated Do Not

[Col. 0189A]

[Note: [Col. 0189D] From Isidore, *Differences*, Book II, no. 35.]

The approach of works is joined to perfect faith by a great kinship of virtue. For if neither clings to the other, both are confused by their separation, as the Apostle says: “Do you wish to know, O empty man, that faith without works is dead? Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar” (Gen. 22:9)? You see that faith cooperated with his works, and that faith was perfected by works. Scripture is fulfilled when it says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God” (Gen. 15:6; Rom. 4:3). You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (James 2:20–24). [Col. 0189B]

What, then, follows from the fact that the two are destroyed by their separation, except that they are built up by their connection? Thus, in accordance with Abraham, faith commends works, and, in accordance with the Apostle, active works give life to faith.

Moreover, as the Gospel reveals to us, faith in Christ alone commends the inheritance of eternal life, for Christ himself says: “This is eternal life, that they believe in you, the only true God, and in Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). Then the same Lord assigns to believers that the works of faith must be joined to it, and that faith alone cannot save outside the dignity of works. He himself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21). [Col. 0189C]

Faith and works, therefore, remain joined together for the state of salvation, since their wrongful mutual separation is shown to lead to the ruin of salvation.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII. On Comparisons Applied to Faith and Works

Just as the quality of some fashioned object does not consist in the beauty of the metal alone, unless the hand of the craftsman, through an orderly arrangement, impresses upon it the beauty of form, so faith without the adornment of works is found not only unbeautiful but also dead. Likewise, the lamp of faith, unless it has the nourishment of good works, is quickly seen to be extinguished.

So the bodily life of a human being, unless it is strengthened by suitable food, is brought to the decay of death. Finally, unless this living spirit gives it strength, the body will be dead. Thus the planting of a woodland, unless it grows together through streams of moisture, is immediately destroyed by the burning of drought. It follows, therefore, that works should follow preceding faith, since neither can a structure of works stand without the foundation of faith, nor can faith be without the building-up of works.

It is therefore a great happiness for a human being when that faith which works through love is fortified by the activity of love itself, so that, if the believer loves, this may be proved by the display of his works. [Col. 0189D]

### CHAPTER LXXXIV. That Hope Concerns Only Good and Future Things

Hope concerns only good things, only future things, and things belonging to the one who is said to possess hope in them. Hence the Apostle says: “Hope that is seen is not hope. For what does someone hope for when he sees it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24). [Col. 0190A]

### CHAPTER LXXXV. That Hope Is Born from Faith

From that confession of faith which is briefly contained in the Creed, and which, when considered carnally, is milk for little children but, when considered and expounded spiritually, is food for the strong, is born the good hope of the faithful, accompanied by holy charity.

### CHAPTER LXXXVI. Why Hope Is So Called

[Note: [Col. 0189D] From Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VIII, chapter 2, no. 5.]

Hope is so called because it is the foot by which one hastens. Through it we advance and patiently endure the delay of the promised good while placed amid the temptations of this age, until, possessing our souls in patience, and liberated from evil by divine assistance, we reach the blessedness that was promised, in which we will live in every good thing. [Col. 0190B]

### CHAPTER LXXXVII. That Despair Is Contrary to Hope

[Note: [Col. 0190D] From Isidore, same work.]

Despair, moreover, is contrary to hope. The foot of the soul needed for advancing and enduring is absent. For when someone, being unrighteous, loves sin, he neither endures temptation nor hopes for the crown of life.

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On Paul’s Statement, in Which He Shows Faith, Hope, and Charity Fittingly Interwoven

Paul commends the approach of this faith and the state of hope, pressing toward the reward of blessedness, in suitable words and realities, when he says:

“Having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we also have access into this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces tested character, and tested character produces hope. Hope, however, does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:1–5).

This entire passage has been compacted and joined together like a single piece of instruction, so that the three principal realities—faith, hope, and charity—are completed either by being woven through their beginning, state, and fulfillment, or are interwoven by their fulfillment. [Col. 0190D]

### CHAPTER LXXXIX. An Exposition of the Same Statement of Paul

He therefore proposed that the beginning of human salvation comes from faith, saying: “Having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God.” And, as though someone were asking through what means the effect of that peace could be brought about, he adds: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

And what does our Lord Jesus Christ himself do in this matter? It follows: “Through him we have access into this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God.”

Behold, he has foretold the beginning of faith, which, when it is in Christ, becomes justification for the believer. After justification there will be peace with God, which one reaches in due order through the grace of God. In that grace, everyone who believes now stands immovable against every adversity and glories in the hope of the children of God.

From this point the middle stages begin to become solid, whose beginnings had been faithful. First, a person is justified through faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Gal. 3:11). Then, through justification, he is reconciled to God, because “the peacemakers will be called children of God” (Matt. 5:9). These things take place through no other faith than that which is in Christ Jesus, through whom we have access to the grace of that same faith, in which we stand and glory.

This grace is prepared by God in good will for the believer. Concerning it, it has been said: “The believer stands, made firm upon the rock, which is Christ, and, hoping, glories in the inheritance of the children of God promised to him.”

This is the middle stage in which he endures the struggle of adversity and the contests of suffering. When a tormented person, whether by hidden temptations or by the open attacks of persecution, strengthened by true faith and hope, awaits invisible things, he confidently believes that what is not yet seen will come, and already embraces firmly in present expectation what future recompense will bring. He does not doubt that he will one day receive it; for in order truly to receive it, he already clearly hopes for it.

Hence Paul adds: “And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations.” What does “not only this” mean? Is there, then, another thing in which there is glorying? Indeed: the glorying in the faith received, whose reward he hopes for—the recompense of eternal life.

But he also glories in another gain, namely, in the tribulations that he is made to endure: “Knowing that tribulation produces patience.” Hence it is said: “You need patience” (Heb. 10:36). For unless patience moderates tribulation, the pressure of tribulation extinguishes the force of patience; the business of the struggle does not extend to testing but is immediately struck down into rejection.

Now the patience produced by tribulation extends to testing, so that what is endured may truly be tested if it tends toward the love of eternity. This prevents an evil murmur of the voice from hiding in the bosom of endurance, and prevents what stood solid beneath the burden of pressure from slipping into the instability of murmuring. Thus it does not lose the dignity of tested character by falling into the murmuring of rejection.

Once tested faithfulness has been found, it comes to the hope of good things. It pants for the sweetness of the Creator so greatly that it desires to depart from the body and to be with Christ (Phil. 1:23), and is so strengthened by its own solidity that it cannot be put to shame.

That salvation, therefore, which began through faith, found justification, reached the peace of God, found access to grace by being strengthened in Christ, and, standing most firmly in that grace, truly glories; which tribulation exercised and testing rendered fit—that salvation is then led by hope, without shame, toward the eternity of recompense. This happens only because “the greatest of these,” the final one, namely charity (1 Cor. 13:13), has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

During this time of hope, which is intermediate between faith and charity but never separated from either faith or charity, the exercise of good works takes place. Faith is commended by works, lest it be regarded as dead without works; hope continually practices good works, carrying its intention all the way to the salvation of perseverance and enduring whatever adversity arises from temptation or suffering. Thus it bears everything with an even temper, so that amid the narrowness of sorrows it may glory in present joy and rejoice in the expectation of future glory.

### CHAPTER XC. On Charity and Its Name

[Col. 0192B]

How much can anyone say about the good of charity, when it is enough that Paul said so much? In setting forth its virtues, he embraced them in such abundance and number as he judged its rich fruits to possess.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] From Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VIII, chapter 2, no. 5.]

The name *charity* is Greek; in Latin it is called *love* (*dilectio*). It begins from two persons: either from the human being and God, or, before God, from the human being and his neighbor. For the experience of love cannot be apparent in one person alone, because solitude has no one with whom or anything to which a person may be joined.

This love first comes from God to human beings, as John says: “Not because we loved God, but because God first loved us, giving us the pledge of the Spirit so that we might love him in works of devotion” (2 John 4:10). Then, in order that love of God may be demonstrated, love of neighbor is displayed. For the Apostle declares: “If we do not love the neighbor whom we see, how will we be able to love God whom we do not see?” (ibid., 20).

Love of neighbor is therefore evidence of love of God. And God will then be proved truly loved when the person who is a friend in God and loved for God is shown to be an enemy.

When this love truly exists, it does not know how to be cut off, because what will remain in the inheritance of eternity has no interruption. It is so adequate in the effect of its activity that, without seeking its own interests (1 Cor. 13:5), it enters into the dangers of its neighbors and, whatever gain it has undertaken, either refreshes it through sharing its own prosperity or defends it by conquering the adversity it has undertaken.

It is hostile to strong exercises of self-interest, while always eager for the salvation of its neighbor: it either does not lose what it has gained or grieves with simple compassion over what it has been unable to gain, never emptied of the reward of goodness. [Col. 0192D]

The book on the Progress of the Spiritual Desert ends here.

## [LETTERS]

[Col. 0191]

### PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING LETTERS

[Col. 0191D]

We have already stated above concerning Hildefonsus’s letters that all of them, except these two sent to Quiricus, have perished, to the great loss of his teaching. That he wrote quite a large number is indicated by the fact that they grew to the proper size of a single volume, constituting the second part of his works, as Saint Julian testifies.

As for those that we publish here, Quiricus’s letters contain the highest praise for that divine work of his on the Virginity of Saint Mary. So great a man read it not only with the greatest delight of soul and spiritual benefit, but also—something that seems miraculous—with his body broken and weakened, he was so uplifted and strengthened by the most joyful reading of the book that he immediately became fit to perform his duties. He himself, having long been absent from the choir because he was held back by illness, was thereafter able to take part in the divine praises with full strength.

In the responses of our Hildefonsus, on the other hand, profound humility of soul, joined to the highest wisdom, shines forth throughout. By this humility he turns the praises of so worthy a man entirely away from himself and demonstrates that they must be poured back upon the one God, the author of all good things.

We have followed the edition of Florez, who in volume V of *Hispania Sacra* presented Hildefonsus’s letters, and in volume XXIX presented them again, together with Quiricus’s letters, more accurately corrected for us after Acherius. [Col. 0193A]

## [LETTERS (C)]

### LETTER OF QUIRICUS, BISHOP OF BARCELONA, TO HILDEFONSUS, BISHOP OF TOLEDO

He gives thanks for the book *On the Virginity of Saint Mary* sent to him, which he praises extraordinarily, reporting the benefit he had received from reading it.

[Col. 0193B]

1. When I returned from you to the places of the fold entrusted to me, I was so weary from the magnitude of my labor and so weakened by the force of exhaustion that the state of my health allowed me neither to hurry to the sacred office nor to do anything similar. At last, while I was considering in my mind what assistance might benefit my weariness, I immediately remembered your gift.

When I read through it with strenuous attention, fixing the gaze of my mind and trying to taste everything that stood forth fragrant like spices, everything in me that was languid, worn out, or troubled by adverse health fled away. Rising into the strength of complete health, I ran vigorously to the lap of the devout and holy mother Church, and gave thanks to our only-begotten Lord and Redeemer, Jesus Christ, the Son of God. [Col. 0193C]

For it was he who, through the life-giving breath of his inspiration, had breathed into the hidden chamber of your heart and, through the anointing of the Holy Spirit, had equipped you to speak about everything concerning him. Just as the sequence of the New and Old Testaments appropriately contained the mysteries of the Lord’s Incarnation and Birth, so he made you unfold the garment of those same Scriptures with such clarity that, so to speak, you made those things which had seemed obscure according to the greatness of their mystery clearer than light and known to the small and the great alike.

Thus Jovinianus is confounded, Helvidius is scattered, and likewise the unbelieving and treacherous-minded Jew falls.

2. I rejoice in this gift of grace distributed to you by God. He who had sent Gabriel to the Virgin Mary at the fullness of time to announce that the Holy Spirit would come upon her and that the power of the Most High would overshadow her has touched the entrance of your mouth and fortified the inner chamber of your heart beforehand, making you speak about everything concerning so great a mystery as clearly as he fulfilled it truly.

For this we bless the Lord: remembering his promises, he deigns to be with us in this final age of the world. Whatever the weakness of our minds and the sluggishness of our souls, weighed down by external cares, could not sufficiently investigate in the sacred pages of Scripture, we receive from you in fullest measure, through the abundance of his grace, as instruction concerning the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation and Birth.

We give thanks to the holy Trinity, which is God, because it formed the human being in the Virgin’s womb, although, for our redemption, only the person of the Son assumed him. [Col. 0194A]

3. We also give thanks to your holiness because the one and only Son of God, who became incarnate in the Virgin’s womb, came to you and made his dwelling with you. Through you he refreshed the hunger of our famine with the abundance of his word, strengthened us with the purity of his grace, and enriched us with the gift of his truth.

May a good reward be stored up for you, my lord, before Christ our Lord and his angels. May you be joyful from the fruit of your good work, abiding amid the joys of eternal happiness, because you have made us joyful through our participation in the heavenly oracle.

4. Behold, although not as I wished, nevertheless as I was able, I have taken care to offer these words to your holiness—not with the audacity of presumption but with the affection of humility. Even if a rustic understanding was unable to shape them with sufficient polish or flavor, may charity, which invited me to offer them, inspire you to receive calmly what has been offered.

May divine grace preserve our lord in safety. Amen.

## HILDEFONSUS’S RESPONSE

He returns to God the praises he received from Quiricus.

To the most holy and venerable lord Quiricus, bishop, Hildefonsus, your servant.

1. I gave glory to my Lord Jesus when I received the letter of your blessedness, composed in the form of thanksgiving. For you yourself had also, insofar as devoted mortality could, rendered due honor to blessed immortality, preserving the balance of judgment so that you might bring praise to him alone whose work you recognize.

Since, then, the grace of God sent to you the things for which I have received from you vows of praise, let us bless him together as one—the one who, through me, supplied the material for devout expression and who, from you, received the glory of praise due to him alone. [Col. 0194C]

2. In all other respects I stand accused within myself, conscious of guilt, anxious in fear, confounded before the Judge, and shaken with terror before the Judge’s coming. Yet, because of redemption, I am faithful to redemption, destined to be saved entirely by the mercy of the Redeemer’s action.

If you ask what his work is, it is sin. If you ask what the account of my life is, it is confession of sin. If you ask what the judgment is, it is the punishment of sin.

For all these things—for my sins and for the merits of my sins—I beg you, by him whose judgment we desire to be absolved from guilt, to extend your hand of prayer on my behalf before the face of his mercy. Thus, not ensnared but assisted by your words, may I obtain pardon and be rescued from my offenses. May you earn for me that it be given or increased, so that I may speak truly about him and devoutly love what I have said about him, and so that he may be glorified in my confessions, both those of the present and those that will remain throughout the ages of eternity.

I would wish to say more if the pressure of my wretchedness allowed it. But let charity consider itself wholly satisfied that wearisome necessity permitted even this little. [Col. 0194D]

## SECOND LETTER OF QUIRICUS TO THE SAME HILDEFONSUS

He urges him to devote himself to interpreting the Scriptures.

To the most holy lord and truly specially revered by me, Hildefonsus, archbishop, Quiricus, your little servant.

### 1

Since, as you know, almighty God uses an eternal, not a new, plan for all new things, distributing among you a quantity of talents for the poverty of our age, so that we might not be weakened by extreme hunger, he has taken care to sustain us with the nourishment of your speech. And therefore, because you take care to render to the supreme Master of the household the full account of the doubling of those same talents, I beg you: if, through diligent investigation, you discover—or intend to discover—anything in the obscurities of the divine Scriptures that may benefit our dearest mother, who now groans with us on earth and to whom we sigh in heaven, do not cease suitably to bring it forth, through the utterance of your pen, for the advancement of that same holy mother. And may it be beneficial that you, my lord, who are introduced into the chamber of the eternal King, should open the garment of the sacred Scriptures and, with your accustomed labor, endeavor to make public those things that had long lain hidden beneath the covering of the elders’ garments. For, as we trust, through the distribution of heavenly grace, the door of speech has been opened to you for declaring its mystery.

The recompense of eternal reward will attend your work, when Christ, through you, has advanced the minds of the weak toward the salvation of the inner person, so that what you have initiated for the salvation of souls may grow strong in full vigor. By the scattering of spiritual seeds through the teaching of holy preaching, when you have drawn some away from error and preserved others from falling into error, you will, after the course of a long life, gather the sheaves of holy labor and obtain everlasting joys before the sight of the eternal Judge.

### 2

I therefore, whom you, my most holy lord, know to be dulled by sluggishness of mind and unskilled in the speech of preaching, suggest that you not disdain to fortify me with these gifts, so that, with the grace of the Holy Spirit supplying them, whatever you say piously, whatever you bring forth holily, and whatever you make clear rightly may be recognized by that same Holy Spirit and loved by all who are filled with him. Thus may you glorify and bear Christ in your confessions, both in the present age and throughout the ages that will endure eternally.

### 3

For the rest, when these matters have been passed over, I beg you to raise up the weak man with the hand of holy prayer and, by constant prayers before the common Lord, to obtain that, until he perfects me by the healing of his mercy, he may not withdraw his medicine from my illnesses. May the grace of Christ preserve my lord unharmed throughout the long duration of everlasting time. Amen.

## THE RESPONSE OF HILDEFONSUS

He indicates that he will gladly undertake this, but is delayed by the wickedness of the times.

To my lord Quiricus, bishop: Hildefonsus, your servant.

### 1

You command me, dearest lord, either to speak if I am silent, or, if I speak, not to remain silent; to unfold what is hidden and covered in the Lord’s garment—which has neither spot nor wrinkle—so that, by the striking of a single light, I may shine upon the desires of the faithful and extinguish the ignorance of the unbelieving. I cannot do this; but let him accomplish this glory for himself through me who raises up the oppressed, releases those bound, and gives sight to the blind.

Let him raise me to himself by the hands of the merciful cross—me who clearly fell from the hands of his divinity. Let him release me, by the commands of his mercy, from the bond of wickedness. Let him illumine me by his prevenient mercy—me whom the guilt of evil has darkened. Then, seized by Jesus, may I hear: “You are released from your infirmity”; and, immediately raised up, may I glorify him. Then also may he permit me, once released, to depart, and may I run after him in the fragrance of his ointments; and whatever I have drawn in through the breath of virtue, may I breathe out again through the breath of speech.

Let him also illumine the blind man, and when I have recognized the light of his compassion, may I and all the people likewise give praise to God.

### 2

Now certainly, because you seek not me but the glory of my Christ in me, and because I do not commend myself but ardently present my Christ as lovable to those who watch in everything I desire to say—so that, loving this beloved of mine, I may speak of him; speaking, announce him; announcing, make him known; having made him known, celebrate him; and, after celebrating him, render him praise in the hymns of angels throughout everlasting ages—I would therefore, as you command, desire to speak frequently. It is also present to me, through pious devotion, that in meditation upon the law of God neither tongue nor life should have silence. But the necessity of the times so wears down the strength of our spirits that life itself is scarcely pleasing because of the evils that threaten.

---

# THE BOOK OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS MEN OF SAINT HILDEFONSUS, BISHOP OF TOLEDO

*[Note: In the edition of Antonio Lorenza, which we follow, the work of Saint Isidore, On Illustrious Men, is printed before this book. Since it has already been reprinted among the Works of Saint Isidore (Patrologia, volume LXXXIII, column 1082), we judged it unnecessary to place it again before the eyes of readers here. EDITOR.]*

## PREFACE

### 1

The enumeration of those men by whose decrees and teachings the holy Church, spread throughout the whole world, is illuminated in what is good and defended against adversity is said to have been fully recorded, shortly after Christ’s ascension, beginning with the apostles, by the blessed and most learned presbyter Jerome. He wrote down, one by one, their names, the sequence of their times, the records of their books, and the varieties of their writings, in a laudable and necessary memorial extending to himself, with a clear style; by making them known he displayed them, and by unfolding them he entrusted them to posterity. Following him, Gennadius ran through the order of this renewed record in a similar text. Thereafter, the most prudent man, Isidore, bishop of the see of Hispalis, following the same course, added to the record whatever excellent men he found. Yet he did not depart having examined everything. After him, negligence invaded everyone in our regions, so that ancient antiquity was covered over by neglect and very many new things were hidden beneath the forgetfulness of oblivion.

### 2

But I, very far from equal to those whom the record preserves and to those whom the renewed record delighted, and sufficiently unworthy and without the resources for the whole good work, having become successor to another Eugene of holy memory in that glorious see of the city of Toledo—which I call glorious not because of the immense assembly of men, since the presence of glorious princes also makes it illustrious, but because before those who fear the Lord it is held to be a place terrible to the wicked and the just alike, and exalted in every kind of veneration—I have attempted, even without elegant learning, to mingle at least an act of good will with the glorious memory of that glorious see, lest I incur damage through silence if I were to cover with the dark cloud of silence the light of the memory of so glorious a see and of such glorious men.

### 3

For it is reported from ancient times that this could happen, as an example from a later age makes clear. Montanus, the most blessed prelate of that same see, is said to have held glowing coals taken up in his garment, for so long in order to repel from himself the disgrace of an accusation concerning married conduct, that, while consecrating the offering to the Lord, he completed the entire celebration of the Mass by himself. When this sacrifice had been completed, the fire of the coals and the beauty of the garment came into such harmony that neither did the fire extinguish the garment’s strength nor did the force of the fire damage the garment’s condition.

### 4

Again, when Justus the deacon insolently assailed Helladius, bishop of that see, with the arrogance of pride, he lived as a bishop after the death of his own pontiff, but himself wasted away. Having been turned to a reprobate mind because of his intemperance of conduct, he died in his sleep, strangled by a noose by the ministers of his altar.

### 5

Likewise, when Gerontius the presbyter, supported by the favor of the prince, brought contempt and adversity upon his successor, Bishop Justus, the power of his understanding suddenly failed so completely that, although many physicians’ treatments were applied, whatever was done as a remedy increased the disease. His disturbance of mind became so powerful that until his death it was a source of horror to the man either to share in a vision of him or to engage him in conversation.

*[Note: Thus the royal edition and the Toledo manuscript; not “by caretakers,” as in the Flórez edition.]*

### 6

Again, when Lucidius, the deacon of his successor Eugene the elder, had violently extorted the honor of the presbyterate and certain estates, being entangled in secular friendship, he reached so reprobate a mind and so excessive a condition of illness that, since he refused to live, what he lived was as much death as what he wished to die was life.

### 7

Therefore, stirred by the zeal of these good men, I have briefly recorded, with such an effort of speech as I could make, whatever ancient things I found through the accounts of the elders and whatever new things I learned from the testimony of the present age, so that I might be joined to their good memory, from whom I am separated by wicked action. Although I do not bring to them in the temple of God an abundance of teaching, I commend with faithful service the memory of those who offer it, begging everyone to commend me to the divine mercy.

For this reason I have firmly entrusted them to human memory, from which they might have slipped away. Indeed, Isidore of holy memory had recorded the most blessed Gregory; but since he said less about his works than we have learned by experience, we have set aside Isidore’s record and record in a fuller style whatever we know about him.

I. Gregory, pope of Rome.  
II. Asturius, bishop of Toledo.  
III. Montanus, bishop of Toledo.  
IV. Donatus, an African monk [Toledo manuscript: abbot of Servitanum].  
V. Aurasius, bishop of Toledo.  
VI. John, bishop of Caesaraugusta.  
VII. Helladius, bishop of Toledo.  
VIII. Justus, bishop of Toledo.  
IX. Isidore, bishop of Hispalis.  
X. Nonnitus, bishop of Gerunda.  
XI. Conantius, bishop of Palentia.  
XII. Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta.  
XIII. Eugene, bishop of Toledo.  
XIV. Eugene the second, bishop of Toledo.

## CHAPTER ONE

*[Note: The Life of Pope Gregory, which Hildefonsus says he wrote, was missing from all copies of Hildefonsus except one, that of the monastery of Font-Sanctus.]*

Gregory, pope and prelate of the Roman and apostolic see, full of compunction from the fear of God and supreme in humility, and endowed through the grace of the Holy Spirit with such a light of knowledge that not only was no one of the present age ever his equal, but no one in former times either, shone so sublimely in the perfection of all virtues that, once every comparison with illustrious men had been excluded, antiquity displays nothing similar to him. For in holiness he surpassed Antony, in eloquence Cyprian, and in wisdom Augustine.

At the beginning of his episcopate he produced the book of the Pastoral Rule, addressed to John, bishop of the see of Constantinople, in which he teaches what sort of person should come to the office of governing and how, once he has come, he should strive to live and teach those subject to him.

*[Note: Thus Isidore, although in the printed editions it reads “of Ravenna.”]*

Moreover, apart from the works of which Isidore of blessed memory makes mention, that same most excellent teacher wrote other moral books: namely, twenty-two homilies on the prophet Ezekiel, arranged in two books, in which he discussed many matters from the divine Scriptures with mystical and moral meaning, in a lucid and eloquent style.

*[Note: The Toledo manuscript and the royal edition read “lucidly.”]*

He also wrote on Solomon’s book entitled the Song of Songs, explaining the entire work in a wonderful manner by proceeding through it according to its moral meaning.

He also produced four books on the Lives of the Fathers who lived throughout Italy, joining them into a single volume, which he preferred to call the Book of Dialogues. In these books a diligent reader can easily recognize how many divine mysteries are concealed and how many marvelous lessons in the love of the heavenly homeland are contained.

Many letters of his to various persons also exist, composed in a polished and clear style. Whoever reads them through will clearly perceive that in him there was a right intention toward God and that he was diligent with every vigilance and care in his zeal for souls. Collecting these into one volume, he divided them into twelve books and decreed that it should be called the Register.

He is also said to have produced other excellent works, but they have not yet reached our hands. Yet he was most fortunate—indeed exceedingly fortunate—to whom God granted the ability to weigh all the sayings of his studies. This sublime and most blessed teacher and prelate flourished during the reign of the emperor Maurice.

## CHAPTER TWO

*[Note: Asturius, perhaps the man mentioned in the First Council of Toledo.]*

Asturius succeeded Audentius as bishop in the metropolitan city of Toledo, in the province of Carthage: an excellent man who displayed works of virtue more by the example of his life than by the pen of a writer.

*[Note: Gennadius mentions Audentius, a bishop of Spain.]*

He was blessed in his priesthood and worthy of a miracle, because he deserved to find in an earthly tomb the bodies of those with whom he was to be joined in heaven. For while he was exercising the priesthood of his see, he is said to have been warned by a divine revelation to investigate the martyrs of God buried in the municipality of Complutum, situated approximately sixty miles from his city.

*[Note: The saints Justus and Pastor, who suffered under Dacian, about whom Prudentius writes.]*

He hurried there and found those whom the earth’s mound and the oblivion of time had covered, to be brought forth into the light and glory of earthly knowledge. Once he had found them, he refused to return to his see; bound to the saints by service and constant devotion alike, he completed his final day. Nevertheless, no one occupied his see as long as he lived. Hence, according to ancient tradition, he is recognized as the ninth priest in Toledo and the first in Complutum.

## CHAPTER THREE

*[Note: We possess, still unpublished, the two letters of Montanus, archbishop of Toledo, which Hildefonsus mentions. The Turibius to whom Montanus writes was a monk of Palentia, entirely different from Saint Turibius, bishop of Asturica, whose body is venerated at Liébana among the Asturians. There is also a third Turibius, a notary of the Roman see, who is mentioned at the First Council of Braga. The aforesaid letters were later published by the eminent Cardinal Aguirre, then by P. Flórez, and finally reprinted by us in this work.]*

Montanus held the cathedral of the first see of the province of Carthage, the city of Toledo, after Celsus. A man distinguished by spiritual virtue and adorned by aptness of speech, he maintained and administered the government of his office with fitting and heavenly law and order alike.

He wrote two letters concerned with the discipline of ecclesiastical usefulness. In one of them, addressed to the inhabitants of Palentia, he is said to prohibit, with great authority, presbyters from preparing chrism and bishops from consecrating churches of another diocese and of another territory, affirming by the testimonies of the sacred writings that this is wholly impermissible.

He also rejects and reproaches the adherents of the Priscillianist sect, although they did not practice the same things, because they nevertheless retained the memory of Priscillian with affection. He recalls that, in the books sent by the most blessed Bishop Turibius to Pope Leo, the same Priscillianist heresy had been exposed, convicted, and duly rejected.

In another letter, addressed to the religious Turibius, he praises him for destroying the worship of idols and entrusts him with the authority of priestly power, by which he may restrain, with vigorous denunciation, presbyters from preparing chrism and bishops from consecrating churches belonging to another jurisdiction and another diocese.

This man is reported, according to a very ancient and trustworthy account, to have held burning coals in his garment for so long, to refute the accusation of disgrace, that he completed the entire celebration of the Mass by himself before the sacred altar of his see. When the solemn rites had been completed, neither were the coals found to have lost their fire nor the garment its beauty. Then, when thanksgiving had been rendered to God, the deceitfulness of the accuser was convicted and condemned by the simple nature of fire, and the innocence of the most blessed priest was vindicated.

*[Note: Thus Montanus subscribes at the Second Council of Toledo, in the fifth year of Amalaric.]*

He was held in glory during the reign of King Amalaric and held the dignity of the pontificate for nine years.

## CHAPTER FOUR

*[Note: John of Biclarum calls Donatus a worker of miracles, under the year 572.]*

Donatus, both by profession and by practice a monk, is said to have been a disciple of a certain hermit in Africa. Seeing the violence of barbarian peoples approaching and fearing the dispersal of the sheepfold and the dangers facing the flock of monks, he traveled to Spain by sea with nearly seventy monks and a great number of books.

With supplies and material resources provided by an illustrious and religious woman named Minicea, he appears to have built the monastery of Servitanum.

*[Note: Isidore mentions Servitanum in his work on Eutropius.]*

He is said to have been the first to bring to Spain the practice and rule of monastic observance, noble in life through examples of virtue and exalted after death through the brilliance of his memory.

*[Note: Toledo and the manuscript of Mariana in Flórez, here and in the present passage.]*

Even now, while he remains in the light of the present world and rests in the crypt of his tomb, he is reported to shine forth through certain signs of healing. Hence the inhabitants of the region are said to honor his monument.

## CHAPTER FIVE

Aurasius, bishop of the metropolitan Church of Toledo, was appointed to the priestly office after Adelphius: a good man, distinguished by the authority of his governance, well ordered in domestic affairs, and steadfastly upright amid adversities. The more temperate he was toward the gentle, the stronger he was always found against adversities.

His concern for the defense of truth was greater than his diligence in writing.

*[Note: We possess a manuscript letter of his to a certain Froganus, who favored the cause of the Jews. John Baptist Pérez himself once saw it and had it transcribed from an ancient manuscript of the library of Saint Laurence, and he annotated it. From that brief letter what Saint Hildefonsus writes here is easily confirmed: namely, that Aurasius was extremely sharp in arguing and reproving, but not very careful in writing.]*

For this reason he is regarded as equal to the most perfect men: what their preaching sowed through speech, his guardianship of the defense fortified. He lived in the priesthood during the times of the kings Witteric and Gundemar and the beginning of the reign of Sisebut, for approximately twelve years.

## CHAPTER SIX

*[Note: John, brother of Braulio, below, chapter 12.]*

John followed Maximus in the episcopate and ascended to the see of the Church of Caesaraugusta.

*[Note: Isidore writes about Maximus in On Illustrious Men, chapter 46.]*

At first he was a father of monks, and thereafter became a prelate in the governance of peoples. He was learned in the sacred writings and devoted himself more to teaching by words than by writings. He was as generous and cheerful in giving as he was cheerful in countenance.

The anointing of God’s Spirit, by which he was inwardly nourished, he displayed so clearly both in the generosity of his gifts and in the expression of his face that grace commended what was given and excused what was not given. In ecclesiastical offices he composed certain works elegantly both in sound and in speech. Among these he recorded such a subtle and useful method for determining the date of the Paschal solemnity that the reader will appreciate both the compressed brevity and the truth made manifest.

He held the dignity of the see for twelve years and attained the life for which he yearned with a desirous vow, entering into joy. He remained in the priesthood during the reigns of Kings Sisebut and Suinthila.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

Helladius obtained the place of that see after Aurasius. When he was a most illustrious official of the royal court and administrator of public affairs, he simultaneously fulfilled the vow and practice of a monk beneath secular dress.

For whenever the route of his frequent official journeys brought him to our monastery—I mean the Agalian monastery, whose reception made me a monk, and which, through God’s gift and the beauty of its enduring and manifest holiness, is known and openly renowned to all—he would put aside the pomp of his clients and secular dignity and cling so closely to the monks’ ordinary tasks that, joining their ranks, he carried bundles of straw to the oven.

Since he both loved and pursued the secrets of solitude amid the splendor and arrogance of the world, he soon abandoned everything he had known to belong to the world and came to that holy monastery, which he had often visited by vow, in order to remain there in the practice he desired.

*[Note: Thus the Toledo manuscript and Flórez; the Madrid edition reads “he approached.”]*

There he became a father to the monks and, through his merits and holy zeal, duly governed both the life of the monks and the condition of the entire monastery, enriching the common resources with abundant wealth.

From there, though his limbs were almost exhausted by old age, he was summoned to the height of the pontificate. Since he was called by force and was at once unknown there, he displayed greater examples of virtue as a bishop than he had as a monk, because he is said to have governed with great discernment the state of the world, which he had rejected through virtue.

He lavished mercies and abundant alms upon the needy, as though he believed that their limbs descended from his stomach and their entrails were warmed there.

He refused to write, because the page of his daily activity displayed what ought to have been written. When I returned to the monastery mentioned above, he made me a Levite at the end of his life. He died an old man and held the sacred government for eighteen years. He was held in glory during the reigns of Sisebut and Suinthila and at the beginning of the reign of Sisenand; thereafter, full of the good things of old age, he earned the more blessed glory of the heavenly kingdom.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

Justus, a disciple of Helladius and bound to him as his successor, was a man distinguished in bodily appearance and in the talents of his mind, subtle, and a monk from childhood. Helladius abundantly trained and instructed him in the virtue of monastic discipline, and he became the third rector of the Agalian monastery after Helladius.

Soon afterward he was installed as Helladius’s successor in the pontificate. He was sharp in intellect and adequate in eloquence, and promised to be of great benefit, had not death taken him away before a long life. He wrote a letter to Richila, father of the Agalian monastery, constructed with appropriate and sufficient argument, in which he clearly maintained that one must never abandon the flock one has received.

He was rector for three years.

*[Note: He subscribes at the Fourth Council of Toledo, in the third year of Sisenand.]*

He died during the reign of Sisenand, who, after him, departed this life on the nineteenth day.

## CHAPTER NINE

Isidore held the cathedral of the province of Baetica, the see of Hispalis, after his brother Leander: a man distinguished alike in appearance and intellect. For in speaking he attained such an abundant wealth of charm that the marvelous fullness of his discourse turned his hearers to astonishment, so that whoever had heard him once commended what he had heard only when it had been repeated many times.

*[Note: In all editions it is read twice. In the Toledo manuscript we read “these,” which does not fit unless we say that “these” was written for “he” in the nominative case. This reading would be acceptable to everyone unless one preferred to conjecture “scarcely” for “twice.”]*

He wrote works both distinguished and substantial: a book On the Origin of Offices; a book of Prefaces; a book On the Birth and Death of the Fathers; a book of Lamentation, which he himself called the Synonyms; two brief books against the wickedness of the Jews, addressed to his sister Florentina; a book On the Nature of Things, addressed to the prince Sisebut; a book of Differences; and a book of Sentences.

He also collected from various authors what he himself called Expositions of the Mysteries of the Sacraments; when these were gathered into one, the book is called Questions.

Finally, at the request of Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, he wrote the book of Etymologies. After striving to complete it for many years, he appears to have brought his final day to a close in the midst of that work.

He flourished during the reigns of Kings Reccared, Liuvanis, Witteric, Gundemar, Sisebut, Suinthila, and Sisenand, holding the honor of the pontificate for nearly forty years and displaying at once the distinguished glory and beauty of holy learning.

## CHAPTER TEN

*[Note: John of Biclarum, abbot, about whom Isidore writes in chapter 44.]*

Nonnitus succeeded John as bishop in the see of Gerunda. He was a monk by profession, transparent in simplicity, holy in his actions, and called to the pontificate not by the prolonged deliberation of men but by the swift decision of God through men. He clung earnestly to the services at the tomb of the holy martyr Felix.

*[Note: Felix, martyr of Gerunda, about whom Prudentius writes in the eighteenth poem of the Martyrs, and Eulogius.]*

He governed the Church of God more by examples of merit than by pronouncements of words. Both while dwelling in the body and while resting in the tomb, he is said to perform works of healing. He remained in office during the reigns of Kings Suinthila and Sisenand.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

*[Note: Conantius at the Council of Toledo in the year 636.]*

Conantius succeeded Maurila in the see of the Church of Palentia. He was a man grave both in the weight of his mind and in bodily appearance, eloquent in ordinary speech, and grave [Toledo manuscript: agreeable], attentive and provident in the ordering of ecclesiastical offices. For he newly produced many melodies of song. He also composed a little book of prayers concerning the propriety of all the Psalms.

*[Note: Thus he died around the year 638.]*

He lived in the pontificate for more than thirty years and was held in honor from the final period of Witteric, through the reigns of Gundemar, Sisebut, Suinthila, Sisenand, and Chintila.

## CHAPTER TWELVE

*[Note: Isidore writes to him.]*

Braulio, brother of John, succeeded to his place in Caesaraugusta after John’s death. He was joined to him by kinship, but was not at all inferior to him [another reading: exceedingly inferior] in talent.

*[Note: A manuscript copy exists.]*

He too was renowned for his songs and for certain short works. He wrote the Life of a certain monk named Aemilianus, which, in its own composition, both preserves the memory of this man and illuminates the virtue of that holy man.

He held the priesthood for approximately twenty years; when these had been completed, he ended the day of his present life.

*[Note: Thus he died around the year 646.]*

He continued in the government of the Church during the reigns of Kings Sisenand, Chintila, Tulga, and Chindaswinth.

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN

*[Note: The Goths appear to have known only two archbishops of Toledo named Eugene. Thus Hildefonsus, Julian, and Felix call the one whom we call the third “the second,” or “the other.” The antiquity of the time had buried in oblivion the first Eugene, a martyr sent to the Toledans by Dionysius the Areopagite; he is mentioned by Abbot Ilduinus and in the Life of Saint Gerard, and is finally attested by the concordant Church of Paris and Toledo. In the year of Christ 1148, Raymond, archbishop of Toledo, traveling to the Council of Rheims, came upon Eugene’s monument in Paris and was the first to report to our people the history of the event and the location of the tomb. More recently, the most religious King Philip II of Spain, after the body of this holy martyr Eugene had been brought to him from Gaul in the year 1565, received it with the most celebrated procession and presented it to the Church of Toledo.]*

Eugene, a disciple of Helladius, a companion and fellow student of Justus, succeeded Justus as bishop. A monk from childhood, he had been instructed by Helladius together with Justus in the sacred disciplines of the monastery.

Helladius brought him with him from the monastery when he was drawn into the pontificate. Eugene, in turn, was trained by him in the clerical orders and became the third rector of his see after him. What a good reward for the old man, who deserved to leave the Church of God an inheritance to be governed by two disciples and holy sons!

This Eugene was grave in conduct and bearing and skillful in intellect. For he knew the numbers, state, increase and decrease, courses and recourses of the moon with such expertise that his explanations turned the listener both to astonishment and to a desirable knowledge.

He lived in the priesthood for nearly eleven years, during the reigns of Kings Chintila, Tulga, and Chindaswinth.

## CHAPTER FOURTEEN

Eugene the second was installed as bishop after Eugene. While he was an excellent cleric of the royal Church, he took delight in the life of a monk. Making a shrewd flight, he sought the city of Caesaraugusta, where he devoted himself to the tombs of the martyrs and suitably cultivated both the studies of wisdom and the monastic purpose.

From there, forcibly brought back by royal authority and summoned to the pontificate, he lived his life more through the merits of virtues than through physical strength. For he was thin in body and small in bodily power, but his spirit burned intensely through the strength of virtue. Pursuing the force of good studies, he corrected songs corrupted by very evil uses through his knowledge of melody and restored the neglected orders and discipline of the offices.

He wrote a little book on the Holy Trinity, polished in eloquence and clear in the truth of its subject. It could have been sent at once to the regions of Libya and the East, had the seas, tossed by storms, not delayed the uncertain journey of fearful travelers.

He also wrote two short books, one composed in various meters of poetry, the other formed in prose from various works; through these he was able to commend his holy memory firmly to the industry of many.

He also revised the short books of Dracontius On the Creation of the World, which antiquity had handed down in a corrupt state. Removing or changing whatever he found unsuitable, or conjecturing better readings, he brought them into such a form of beauty that they seem to have emerged more beautifully from the craft of the corrector than from the author’s hand.

*[Note: Isidore writes about Dracontius in chapter 37. Dracontius, the poet mentioned here, is said to have long been in print, but not as Eugene corrected him. I saw this correction by Eugene in the ancient manuscript of Ruicius Azagrius mentioned above. Dracontius, as corrected by Eugene, has since been published several times: first by the learned Sirmond, then in the Library of the Fathers, and finally by us. See volume LX of this Patrologia.]*

And because that same Dracontius, by remaining entirely silent about the seventh day, appeared to have left his work incomplete, Eugene both recorded a recapitulation of the six days in individual little verses and elegantly added what seemed appropriate to him concerning the seventh day.

He was held in glory during the reigns of Kings Chindaswinth and Recceswinth. He held the dignity and glory of a priest for nearly twelve years, and after the setting of the light of this world he continues to possess a dwelling-place in the tomb in the basilica of Saint Leocadia.

Thus far Hildefonsus.

# APPENDICES

## APPENDIX ONE

### Works Doubtfully Attributed to Saint Hildefonsus

## NOTICE

When we call certain works doubtful, excellent reader, understand us to mean those works that were at some time believed, not without probable reason, to be by the holy teacher, although, as time passed and the writings were examined more carefully according to a proper standard, learned men discovered weightier reasons for judging that they should be withdrawn from the holy teacher.

Among these we give first place to the short work On the Childbearing of the Blessed Virgin Mary and Her Perpetual Virginity. We shall say a little about it beforehand, since we possess observations concerning its legitimate author by the most learned John Mabillon—*Saeculum II of the Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, in the observations on the Life of Saint Hildefonsus—which we have thought worthwhile to transcribe together with Luca D’Achery, volume I of his *Spicilegium*, folio 43 of the new edition, corrected and purged by Louis de la Barre.

“Francis Feu-Ardentius,” he says, “a Parisian theologian, published several short works of Hildefonsus in the Library of the Fathers. Among them was a book On the Virginity of Holy Mary against Three Unbelievers, whose prologue begins: ‘God, true light,’ etc., and whose opening is: ‘O my Lady! My Mistress!’ etc.

“To this book he appended another work, likewise attributed to Hildefonsus, On the Perpetual Virginity of Holy Mary and Her Childbearing, beginning as follows: ‘Although the virginity of all the Churches,’ etc.

“We have discovered by the clearest arguments that the first little book belongs to Hildefonsus, but that the later one belongs to Ratbert, abbot of Corbie. Hildefonsus published a book On Virginity full of testimonies from the Old and New Testaments, says Cixilanes; and this manner of speaking is plainly apparent in the first book, not in the later one.

“Moreover, according to Julian, Hildefonsus wrote a book On Virginity against three unbelievers—Jovinian, Helvidius, and the Jews. This is also made clear by the letter of Quiricus prefixed to Hildefonsus’s works in a manuscript. Now Hildefonsus addresses and attacks precisely these same unbelievers by name in this first book; in the later book, however, the state of the question is entirely different. Testimonies of the Fathers are repeatedly introduced in confirmation, among whom are praised and cited the *Moralia* of Gregory the Great, Augustine, Jerome, Cyril of Alexandria, Peter of Ravenna, and others whom Hildefonsus does not even greet in his own work.

“Finally, there is a great difference in style between the two works. Hildefonsus presses his opponents with clustered synonyms; Ratbert proceeds in the later book with greater gravity of sentence, a manner befitting an old man. He dedicates his work to the abbess and nuns of Saint Mary at Soissons, where he had been educated, as will become clear from the inscription of the work cited below. Hence he often calls them his dearest mothers and matrons.”

“Therefore it is not Hildefonsus but Ratbert who should be regarded as the author of this later book. In his time a certain controversy arose among Catholics concerning the manner in which blessed Mary gave birth to Christ. Some maintained that he was born by the natural and common way and law of other human beings; others, among whom was Ratbert, protested against this. This question arose in Germany, as Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie and opponent of Ratbert’s view, teaches in a short work which he composed on this subject and dedicated to someone unknown to him—not, therefore, to Ratbert, the abbot of his monastery. Ratbert appears to answer Ratramnus, addressing his opponents as ‘brothers,’ in these words: ‘But since the shameless rashness of certain brothers is again troubling itself with inquiries, as though questioning, I have decided to write to you, brides of Christ, concerning matters which they themselves are attempting to investigate more inquisitively than religiously, to the detriment of her chastity.’ And, so that you may understand the state of the controversy: ‘I do not say,’ he writes, ‘that they say she lost her virginity—she who, without knowing man, conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin—but that they deny precisely what they confess, when they say that she brought forth a son according to the common law of nature.’

“From this the great difference between the works of Hildefonsus and Ratbert is evident. Hildefonsus writes Against Three Unbelievers; Ratbert, Against the Brothers. Hildefonsus argues against Helvidius and the Jews, who deny the virginity of the Mother of God; Ratbert against Catholic theologians who admit that same virginity of the Mother of God but do not explain it correctly—men who said that Mary gave birth to Christ with the barriers of her virginity opened wide, precisely what Jovinianus, whom Hildefonsus attacks, had already wished to assert. Ratbert divided his work into two books, addressed to the nuns of Soissons, with the following inscription, as it is found in the Corbie copies: ‘To the venerable bride of Christ, together with the holy virgins living the monastic life at Vesona [read: Suessona], P. R. (that is, Paschasius Ratbert), the least of all monks.’

“If Feuardentius had seen this inscription, he would undoubtedly have assigned to Ratbert a genuine and legitimate offspring of his own. After this the book begins as follows: ‘Since all the Churches …,’ and continues as far as the middle of the short work in the Library of the Fathers. For from the place where this note occurs—‘Something is missing here’—the manuscript copies differ entirely from the printed editions. They substitute a portion of a sermon attributed to Hildefonsus, which among the printed works is entitled On the Purification of Holy Mary. The second book of Ratbert, however, is the very Homily which in the printed editions follows the aforesaid sermon, beginning with these words: ‘Among the sayings of the Holy Scriptures …’”

Up to this point the account is Acherius’ material taken from Mabillon. These considerations sufficiently and quite plainly establish that the author of this little work was someone entirely different from our Hildefonsus; and we gladly subscribe to that judgment. We have only one point on which to caution the reader here: Mabillon’s preceding arguments derive their principal force from something that can scarcely be called into doubt—namely, that Hildefonsus composed only one short work On Virginity, and that it is distinguished by so many individual characteristics, as we learned from Julianus and Cixila, that it can easily be distinguished from any other work. For if Hildefonsus had composed another work in defense of the Virgin Mother of God, directed against different opponents, we do not believe that the authors of his Life would have passed it over in silence.

Once this foundation has been laid, the entire comparison which Mabillon learnedly instituted between the two works stands on the firmest ground. It follows immediately that this other short work—which, because of its difference of style, dissimilarity of subject, and diversity of the opponents whom it attacks, cannot in any way be regarded as a portion of Hildefonsus’ work—must be assigned to another author.

As for the remaining matters, after carefully comparing Acherius’ edition with that of Feuardentius and with our manuscript Codex Amelianus, which has already been mentioned at length in the preface to the short work On Virginity, although we found that the manuscript agrees with Feuardentius, we nevertheless decided to abandon them and follow Acherius’ edition, except in one or two places. Nor was this done rashly, for this treatise is generally more correct in Acherius than in our copies, in which, as Mabillon has already indicated, the order has been disturbed and the text interpolated.

This does not mean, however, that the authority of our Codex should be undervalued. Its writing is extremely accurate, and very often agrees with Acherius’ Corbie manuscripts, confirming their reading against Feuardentius, as will appear from the variant readings. Moreover, in that very Codex we found the conclusion of the second short work in the form in which it appears in Feuardentius, but is lacking in Acherius’ edition. In our judgment, anyone who attentively reads both versions will admit that the second part of this work is mutilated in Acherius, since it ends in the middle of an exposition of a saying of Isaiah, with the discourse still hanging and incomplete. In our copies, on the other hand, it exists in complete form; there the sermon is not brought to an end until the whole sentence has been explained and appropriately applied, and the discourse concluded with the words of blessed Augustine. We therefore did not hesitate to supply from our copy what we recognized to be lacking in Acherius’ edition.

Nevertheless, it necessarily happened that two fragments, which had rightly been rejected from their proper place, remained separate. So that they might not perish altogether, we placed them before the sermons in this work: namely, the beginning of the sermon—as it appears in Feuardentius—On the Childbearing and Purification of Holy Mary, and the middle part of the treatise On Childbearing, in the same author. Having been informed of these matters, farewell.

[Col. 0207]

SHORT WORK [Note: [Col. 0207B] In Acherius this book is entitled On the Birth of the Virgin; in Feuardentius and in our Codex Amelianus its title is: Book Against Those Who Argue About the Perpetual Virginity of Holy Mary and Her Childbearing.] MORE PROBABLY TO BE ATTRIBUTED TO PASCHASIUS RATBERT, ABBOT OF OLD CORBIE, THAN TO HILDEFONSUS. (G,S)*

[VOLUME ONE.]

[Col. 0207A]

[Note: [Col. 0207B]

Thus the book begins in our copies without any preface. In the Corbie manuscripts, however, the following appears, as it was published by Acherius:

‘To the venerable bride of Christ, together with the holy virgins living the monastic life at Vesona, Paschasius Ratbert, the least of all monks.

‘I have decided to explain to you, dearest daughters, the question concerning the childbearing of blessed Mary the virgin recently brought to me, since I do not doubt that you love her exceedingly; so that from this you may know how much I love you, having long ago been your fosterling from childhood and now worn out by advanced age.’

Mabillon, together with Acherius, argues that Vesona should be read Suessona, or Suessione; Ludovicus de la Barre, however, thinks that Vesona may be retained, since in the province of Périgord in Gaul there was a city called Vesona, Vesonna, or Vesuna, as everyone knows.]

Although the virginity of blessed and glorious Mary, Mother of God, is the adornment, honor, and model of virtue of all the Churches, it is especially so for the virginal nuns, whose chastity is more particularly illumined by her virtues, shaped by her examples, and strengthened by her merits. [Note: [Col. 0208B] Thus Acherius and our manuscript Codex read, “more particularly illumined.” A little below we print “On her behalf,” as in Feuardentius and Amelianus, better than Acherius’ “Because of these things.”] Therefore, to venerate and recount with the utmost devotion of mind and heart her most sacred childbearing is a grace of divine gift. To fight and triumph on her behalf against heretical depravity, however, is the work of the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, who overshadowed her, so that without intercourse with a man and without any corruption she might give birth to God and man, and might remain ever a virgin. [Note: [Col. 0208B] Acherius has “the Lord” in place of “God.”] We read that blessed Jerome once wrote in her defense against the heretic Helvidius and his associates; and he so utterly crushed and defeated them that from then until the present no resurgence of error against her has arisen. [Note: [Col. 0208B] Feuardentius and Acherius have recidivum, ‘recurring’; Codex Amelianus differs, reading residuum, ‘remaining.’ This reading is also found in one of the other Corbie copies and is not rejected by L. de la Barre.]

But since the shameless rashness of certain brothers is again troubling itself with inquiries, as though questioning, I have decided to write to you, brides of Christ, about matters which they themselves are trying to investigate more inquisitively than religiously, to the detriment of her chastity. In investigating her childbirth and the womb of her chastity, they introduce, as though they were highly skilled physiologists, [Note: [Col. 0208B] “As though.” L. de la Barre wished these words to be enclosed in parentheses, as though added by a scribe and disruptive of the sense. We do not deny this; but no manuscript lacks them, and they are not wholly intolerable.] [Note: [Col. 0208B] Callida, ‘cleverly,’ in Amelianus.] by their own sufficiently clever argument, a filthy mixture of vices in which many dangers of error converge.

For they say that blessed Mary the virgin could not, and ought not, have given birth in any other way than according to the common law of nature and as is customary for all women, [Note: [Col. 0208B] Feuardentius lacks est, “is”; Codex Amelianus has it with Acherius.] so that Christ’s birth may truly be called a birth. [Note: [Col. 0208B] In Amelianus: alias etiam; Feuardentius alone has solus.] Otherwise, they say, if he was not born as other infants are born, it is not a true birth. And therefore, lest he be thought a phantom, or lest he be believed to have been born through the virgin’s womb without the process proper to birth, as water passes through a channel, it is pious to believe that he was born according to the law of nature in the same way as other infants are born, and that she gave birth in the same way as other women do.

O blind piety, which thinks so impiously about Mary the virgin, and blind presumption, which speaks so impiously about Christ! I do not say that they claim she lost her virginity—she who, without knowing man, conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin—but they deny precisely what they confess when they say that she brought forth a son according to the common law of nature. But if it is as they maintain and assert—which God forbid—then Mary is no longer a virgin, Christ was born under a curse, the son of wrath from sinful flesh, and she who is proclaimed blessed by the angel, still remaining under a curse, gave birth under a curse.

Otherwise, what is the reason they seek the law of nature in Mary, when everything that was in her was possessed by the Holy Spirit, whom the power of the Most High overshadowed? [Note: [Col. 0209D] Feuardentius alone reads quoniam, ‘because,’ instead of quam, ‘whom,’ as in the others.] If the power of the Most High overshadowed her from every heat of sin, then in conception and childbirth, just as she was free from every heat of lust, so also she was free from every pressure of the curse—not from herself, but by the power of the Most High, immune from it and alien to it. [Note: [Col. 0209D] Amelianus and Feuardentius read: ‘Therefore let these disputants consider the laws of nature; let them consider also the rights of divine things’—with virtutem, ‘power,’ in Feuardentius.]

Therefore let them consider the rights of divine things, since divine laws do not depend on the nature of things; rather, the laws of nature and of things are shown to flow from divine laws. [Col. 0209B] For this reason it is rash to assert of Christ that he was born according to the common law of nature, since he was begotten in the Virgin’s womb from her flesh not according to nature’s ordinary custom. Indeed, the very law of nature under which women now conceive and give birth is, so to speak, not truly the law of nature at all, but the law of curse and guilt. For unless Adam and Eve had first sinned in paradise, no one thereafter would have been born under the guilt of sin. Therefore this common law of birth belongs not to nature but to corruption and defect.

But because Mary was blessed and had no guilt of corruption, she did not give birth to Christ in pain or under corruption. If Christ was born from corruption or with pain, then he was born under a curse. Genesis bears witness concerning this curse, reporting that the Lord said to Eve: ‘Multiplying, I will multiply your pains and your conceptions’ (Gen. 3:16). Symmachus rendered this, ‘your afflictions.’ Origen and Theodotion, as well as the Septuagint, rendered it, ‘your sorrows’ and ‘groans’; and Theodotion and Symmachus used ‘hardships’ for ‘groans.’ In all these expressions the law of nature is not indicated, as these physiologists, with considerable incompetence, wish [Note: [Col. 0209D] Feuardentius: imperiose, ‘arrogantly.’], but the law of retribution is multiplied, and the cause of sin is increased: labors in childbirth, afflictions, sorrows, hardships, and groans. In Hebrew the text reads: [Hebrew text absent in the supplied source]. Therefore all women who give birth do not give birth in this way from the nature of their first origin, but from the defect of guilt and from the curse of God’s just retribution.

But blessed and most glorious Mary the virgin—not only, I say, not according to the common law of nature, but not even according to the nature of the first origin—brought forth a son, divinely begotten from her own flesh by the Holy Spirit and not from the seed of a man, God and man, without any filthy mixture of vices. Therefore her childbirth must not be treated as other births are, since, as the outstanding teacher Athanasius says, among other things, [Note: [Col. 0209D] Feuardentius writes docte, “learnedly,” in place of sicut doctor, “as a teacher.”] in the little work on his faith which he published in the form of a dialogue, ‘The Only-Begotten was incarnated through his own secret mystery, which he himself knows’ [Book IX, On His Faith, near the end]. He continues: ‘It is ours to believe, and his to know.’

Let them therefore hear that it belongs to him alone to know how he was conceived, how he dwelt in the womb, and how the Word, God and man, was born from the Virgin as one Christ. For, as he himself says, God the Word, receiving in full everything that belongs to man in order to be man, and man, having been assumed, receiving in full everything that belongs to God, could not be anything other than what God is. [Col. 0210A] Accordingly, if God the Word, by receiving in full everything that belongs to man, is man, and the assumed man, by receiving in full everything that belongs to God, is God, then assuredly he is God. [Note: [Col. 0209D] We print this passage according to Codex Amelianus and Feuardentius. In Acherius the entire following period is lacking, and the present one ends with the words, “Assuredly he is God. But if …”]

But if this is so, as he has confessed—indeed, because it is so—where, I ask, is the common law in his birth? Where is the filthy mixture of vices? For Christ, God, who never ceased to be what he was, from the time he became man and was assumed into the unity of the person, always remained and remains true God and man—not two, so that one would be God and the other man, but one and the same God and man. Although he is one thing insofar as he is God and another insofar as he is man, in both he is one God and man, because there was never a time when a mere man was conceived or born without God.

But because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit from virginal flesh and truly born as man, immediately from his conception, by an ineffable birth, true God proceeded and man was born. How, then, can that which is ineffable be called common? Or how is Christ not always wholly true God, [Note: [Col. 0209D] Amelianus and Feuardentius have qui nunquam est, ‘who never is,’ which is better than Acherius’ quicunque, ‘whoever,’ or ‘anyone whatsoever.’] who was never conceived or born without the true God? Therefore, just as he is rightly believed to have been conceived with the womb closed, so altogether he was born with the womb closed. [Note: [Col. 0210D] Feuardentius and Amelianus have a different reading: ‘For no inability belonging to man was added to him by which he might be born from the Virgin,’ and so forth.]

For no incapacity belonging to man was added to him by which he might be born from the Virgin, just as nothing was ever added to him by which he might become God and one Christ. He wished to be born in such a way, in the unity of true God and man, that everything born was truth, that the manner of his birth was ineffable, and that everything born from the Virgin was wholly credible, without the pollution of sin, just as it was without any contagion of original origin.

Therefore let the rash investigators and scrutinists of so great a mystery hear and understand that these are not the laws of humanity in birth, nor a law—not merely of condemned nature, but not even the law of the first origin before sin—according to which God and man, one Christ, should be born from the Virgin. For, as blessed Cyril says in his letter to Nestorius [middle]: ‘A common man was not born from the holy Virgin, because in the very womb of the Virgin, as he himself confesses, the Word united himself with flesh in the virginal womb and underwent a carnal generation. He made the birth of his flesh his own birth; and he who, in the form of God, made man, became man in the form of a servant.’ [Note: [Col. 0210D] Feuardentius has quia, ‘because.’] Thus, in one person, both are God by the power of the one who assumes, and both are man by the humility of the one assumed.

Accordingly, such a childbirth does not belong to the common law of nature. Just as he was wonderfully conceived, so wonderfully was God and man born. Therefore adoption did not make him a son of God like other adopted sons; rather, the nature of divinity exalted him as God’s proper Son and gave him the name that is above every name (Phil. 2:9). Thus he was wholly the Son of God, man and Word, because he was never not the Son of God, remaining eternally the Only-Begotten of the one and only Begetter.

He was therefore never conceived or born as a mere man, nor born as other infants are born, so that through the grace of adoption or through the reward of virtues the prerogative of sonship might be granted to him. [Note: [Col. 0210D] Codex Amelianus reads ex adoptionis gloria, “from the glory of adoption”; Feuardentius, aut ex molimento virtutum, “or from the achievement of virtues.”] Rather, because the Word of God became flesh, he assumed man into himself without a human person, so that Christ might be wholly God’s proper Son. [Note: [Col. 0210D] We have retained the reading of our Codex Amelianus and Feuardentius, certainly better than Acherius, who printed: ‘so that Christ might be proper, not from the gift of grace,’ and so forth.] He was not reborn through the gift of grace as others are, but with the proper identity of both natures preserved.

He did not assume the person of a man, but only man, because he himself was always the third person, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, in the Trinity of one God. [Note: [Col. 0210D] Sancto, ‘Holy,’ is lacking in Acherius but is present in Amelianus and Feuardentius.] Therefore, possessing what he had in eternity, he did not assume a person, but in time he assumed man, which he had not previously possessed. Thus the one who assumed and that which was assumed were, as blessed Augustine says in his book On Predestination, one person in the Trinity. For, as he says elsewhere, God the Word was born from the Father; the Word made flesh was born from the mother; one and the same God, the Son of God, was born before the ages and born in the age; and both births belong to one Son of God.

Accordingly, the virgin Mary is rightly called Mother of God, [Note: [Col. 0211D] Feuardentius has quae, ‘who,’ or ‘because she.’] because she gave birth to God and man: the Word made flesh—not as other infants are born, nor as men become men through the gift of grace, but, as blessed Gregory says in the Moralia, ‘with the proper identity of both natures preserved, he essentially assumed man into his own person.’ Through this wondrous mystery, the one and the same person would be both eternal from the Father and temporal from the mother, the true Son of both God and man.

For, as he says in the same Moralia, it is one thing for human beings, once born, to receive the grace of adoption through him; it is another [Col. 0211B] for one to have proceeded uniquely from the very conception as God through the power of divinity. [Note: [Col. 0211D] Feuardentius and Codex Amelianus lack unum, ‘one,’ and read: ‘it is another for one uniquely to have proceeded,’ and so forth.]

Therefore, I beg them, let them cease saying that he was born as other infants are born.
