The Virgin, Mother of God, did not give birth to him from the origin of the first transgression so that he might be reborn, but from the Holy Spirit so that he might be believed to be God: without pain or groaning, without distress or hardship, without sorrow or affliction, [Note: [Col. 0211D] Haec omnia, ‘all these things,’ is present in Acherius and Codex Amelianus but lacking in Feuardentius.] since all these things are the most just retributions and punishments of condemned flesh in its first origin.

Indeed, although blessed Mary herself was born and begotten from sinful flesh, and although she herself was sinful flesh, she was no longer such at the time when, through the prevenient grace of the Holy Spirit, she was proclaimed by the angel blessed above all women: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you’ (Luke 1:35). [Note: [Col. 0211D] In our Amelianus and Feuardentius, quando, “when,” is absent; they read: “she was no longer [such] through the prevenient …”] [Note: [Col. 0211D] Amelianus and Acherius read eodem Spiritu sancto, ‘by the same Holy Spirit’; Feuardentius lacks sancto, ‘Holy.’]

Otherwise, if she was not sanctified and cleansed by that same Holy Spirit, how was her flesh not sinful flesh? And if her flesh came from the mass of the first transgression, how was Christ the Word flesh without sin, who assumed flesh from sinful flesh, unless the Word, who became flesh, first overshadowed her, upon whom the Holy Spirit came and whom the power of the Most High wholly possessed?

Therefore her flesh was truly no longer sinful flesh, [Note: [Col. 0211D] Ejus est, ‘it is his/her,’ is present in Amelianus and Feuardentius but lacking in Acherius.] since God poured himself wholly into it, and the Word who became flesh came to us without sin. He therefore rightly not only did not observe the law of corrupted nature in his birth, [Note: [Col. 0211D] Feuardentius reads vere, ‘truly.’] but did not observe even the law of the first origin which women would have had if Eve, the mother of all, had kept the commandment in paradise.

Otherwise, since the Holy Spirit filled her, how was she not without original sin, whose birth is also proclaimed glorious, Catholic, happy, and blessed throughout the whole Church of Christ by everyone? Indeed, if she were not blessed and glorious, her feast would certainly not be celebrated everywhere by all. [Note: [Col. 0211D] Feuardentius and Amelianus read: “her feast would be celebrated everywhere by all.”] But because it is celebrated with such solemnity, the authority of the Church establishes that when she was born she was subject to no sins and, having been sanctified in the womb, did not contract original sin.

Thus, although the day of Jeremiah and that of Job are pronounced accursed (Jer. 20:14; Job 3:3)—that is, the day of their birth—the day on which Mary’s blessed birth began is pronounced blessed and is celebrated with due religious observance. If she had been in sin, it would rightly have been called accursed and mournful rather than blessed when her father was told that she had been born into the world.

But now, because blessed Mary the virgin illumines the entire Church with her blessing, she is rightly venerated as sanctified in the Holy Spirit. No one’s birth, therefore, is celebrated in the world except that of Christ, that of Mary, and that of blessed John. [Note: [Col. 0211D] The words that follow, up to ‘so also the blessed,’ are lacking in Acherius and ought not to have been omitted.] John’s is celebrated because he too is read to have been sanctified in the womb; so also the blessed virgin Mary’s would not at all be celebrated unless she had been sanctified in her mother’s womb.

But now, since she is venerated on the authority of the whole Church, it is established that she was free from all original sin. Through her not only was the curse of the mother Eve dissolved, but blessing is also granted to all. If, therefore, the illustrious and most sacred birth of the Virgin is rightly celebrated and venerated everywhere as so holy and glorious, how much more should she herself be so honored when she was most dutifully greeted by the angel as already full of grace?

For when he says to her, ‘Hail,’ he offers a heavenly service of veneration (Luke 1:28). When he says, ‘Full of grace,’ he shows that wrath has been completely expelled and declares that grace has been restored. [Note: [Col. 0212D] Where Acherius has iram expulsam, “wrath expelled,” Feuardentius has tam exclusam, “so completely excluded.”] When he says, ‘Blessed are you,’ he reveals the fruit of blessing, because when the Holy Spirit came upon her, he wholly cleansed and refined the Virgin from defilements, so that she might be holier than the stars of heaven. Moreover, when the power of the Most High wholly overshadowed her, [Note: [Col. 0212D] We judged this reading, found in Feuardentius and Amelianus, should be retained. We noticed no corruption in it, unlike the reading ‘his work in her womb,’ and so forth, which L. de la Barre attempted to emend as: ‘Immediately, the Word that was in the beginning, eternal with the Father, came into her womb so that it might become flesh,’ and so forth.] it came to pass that the Word, who in the beginning was eternal with the Father, coming into her womb, became flesh in time and dwelt among us.

Therefore let the new disputants and investigators of a new and unheard-of childbirth hear and understand, first, since they are men, how they can properly argue about the nature and sex of women; and then let them consider why they seek nature and the common law of birth where everything is divine and ineffable, and where divine power is at work. [Note: [Col. 0212D] Ut quid, ‘why,’ is retained from our copies; Acherius has ut qui.] ‘Who will recount his generation?’ says the prophet (Isa. 53:8). [Note: [Col. 0212D] Acherius lacks propheta, ‘the prophet.’] Here quis, ‘who,’ is understood in the sense of ‘no one,’ because there is no saint who can fully recount—not to mention the divine generation—even his human generation, although everyone ought to believe both.

From this, then, it follows that these men’s hesitation is superstitious and their disputation pointless, since they say that he opened the entrances of the belly and womb, and drew after him, as all others do, the pollution of blood and the filth of the afterbirth. [Note: [Col. 0212D] Feuardentius has secundas spurcitias, ‘the filth of the afterbirth’; Amelianus, immundarum spurcitias, ‘the filth of unclean things.’] In all these things groaning and pain are multiplied, and sorrow and hardships increased, so that no one gives birth to a son without them. [Note: [Col. 0212D] Acherius and Codex Amelianus have ut nemo, ‘so that no one’; Feuardentius has et nemo, ‘and no one.’]

But far be it from the hearts of the faithful to suspect anything of this kind concerning Mary the virgin, who brought blessing to the world in place of the curse of the first origin. Therefore she herself, as I have said, is proclaimed blessed among women by the angel and is most dutifully greeted as the glorious Mother of the Lord above all others (Luke 1:28). She is also pronounced blessed by Elizabeth in the spirit of prophecy, and the fruit of her womb is believed and venerated as blessed. [Note: [Col. 0213C] Feuardentius has: ‘Therefore, in and through whom.’ Shortly afterward neither Amelianus nor Feuardentius has beata Dei genitrix, ‘blessed Mother of God’; and instead of naevo, ‘blemish,’ found in Acherius, they read nodo, ‘knot.’]

Therefore, in and through whom so great a blessing blossomed and grace flowed, it must not be believed that her childbirth was subject to pains and groans in the manner of women. And because the blessed Mother of God was not subject to sorrows and hardships, she was free from every blemish of the curse. The Holy Spirit filled her, [Note: [Col. 0213D] Amelianus: ‘dedicated her wholly to the Lord.’ Feuardentius and Amelianus also have: ‘For the power …’] and dedicated her wholly to the Lord; the power of the Most High overshadowed her, [Note: [Col. 0213D] Feuardentius and Amelianus add: ‘And the Word, having taken flesh for himself from the sanctified flesh of the Virgin …’] and from the sanctified flesh of the Virgin the Word assumed flesh, [Note: [Col. 0213D] Feuardentius has: ‘and united them.’] and united them in the unity of the person.

This is what is meant by the saying, ‘The Word became flesh’ (John 1:14): not by a mingling of natures, but through the unity of the person. Therefore concerning this birth also, as I have said, we rightly believe it was said: ‘Who will recount his generation?’ (Isa. 53:8). For this birth too is ineffable: a wondrous birth of flesh—not, as these men babble, common according to the law of nature, but a sacrament of grace. [Note: [Col. 0213D] Feuardentius and Amelianus have: ‘as these men sing, common according to the law of nature,’ and so forth.]

For that God and man is born from a Virgin is not custom but mystery; not nature but power and condescension; not [Col. 0213B] the order of birth but power. Therefore human wisdom has nothing to seek in this birth except that the Word became flesh and was born as he wished, or when and how he wished. Otherwise, who could comprehend what is unheard-of and ineffable? [Note: [Col. 0213D] Feuardentius and Codex Amelianus have: ‘Or who rightly seeks an understanding of the flesh in him where everything that is narrated is divine and incomprehensible?’]

Or why should bodily understanding rightly seek anything in him when everything that is narrated is both divine and incomprehensible? For the evangelist says: ‘The generation of Christ was thus’ (Matt. 1:18). Certainly this carnal generation was thus; he did not say, ‘Thus it came to be,’ but ‘Thus it was,’ because Christ’s generation was ineffable with the Father when, through this prescribed and ineffable process, he was generated from his mother. Therefore, whatever was, always was. And whatever always existed from eternity could become in time, whatever wondrous thing was accomplished in him. [Note: [Col. 0213D] Acherius, using his own copies, printed non mirabile, ‘not wondrous.’ Whether it was rightly rejected by us, while preserving the reading of our copies, the reader may judge.]

Therefore those who say that he was born according to the common law of nature are profoundly mistaken, [Note: Amelianus’s manuscript: “Who is shown to have been conceived and born according to another law.” And shortly afterward, where Acherius has “the law of nature,” Feuardentius and Amelianus have “the law of birth.”] since he was not conceived according to that law. For this law of birth, which is now called the law of nature, derives from the fault of the first condemnation. [Col. 0213C] And therefore the Apostle says: “We were all once children of wrath, even as the others” (Ephesians 2:3).

But far be it from the hearts of the faithful to believe that Christ was born as a son of wrath, as others are born in the corruption of defilement, from which pain and groaning are multiplied. In other circumstances, according to the flesh, there is neither groaning nor pain without corruption of the womb, nor corruption without pain and groaning; groaning and corruption in the childbirth of women come only from the offense and curse of the first origin. [Note: Feuardentius and Amelianus have “pain of heart.”]

Let us therefore question those followers of the heretic Helvidius who, although they do not deny that she remained a virgin, nevertheless stain her chastity and the grace with which she is proclaimed to have been full, when they say that she gave birth according to the common law of corrupted nature. If she gave birth in this way, then she still remained, as though within the mass of the first condemnation, subject to the curse—contrary to the angel’s declaration—and the Word of the Father assumed a human being from sinful flesh (which God forbid), so that he might become flesh. [Col. 0214A]

But since it is contrary to the Catholic faith to think in this way, the blessed Virgin, full of grace, neither felt pain nor endured corruption of the womb. For to the extent that she was free from guilt, with the Holy Spirit cooperating in her, and by the power of the Most High, by which she was overshadowed, [Note: Feuardentius has “by which she was overshadowed in its entirety,” against Acherius and Amelianus.] to that same extent she was removed from the curse of the first condemnation, [Note: Amelianus’s manuscript and Feuardentius read: “And she remained entirely immune from corruption of the flesh.” We have not wished to excise these words, since the verb “remained” makes the sentence clearer.] and so completely remained immune from corruption of the flesh, as well as from the groaning and pains by which all the daughters of Eve are afflicted when they give birth.

Hence the Prophet, speaking in Christ’s person to the Father, says: “You are he who drew me from the womb; my hope from my mother’s breasts” (Psalm 21:10). Therefore, when he says, “You are he who drew me,” he declares the uniqueness of his birth: he was brought forth gently from the womb. [Note: We alter nothing in the reading of Amelianus together with Feuardentius, although Acherius reads differently: “having brought forth sweetness from the womb.”]

In every other case, anyone who comes from his mother’s womb into the light of the world comes forth only by God’s will and operation. Christ, however, was brought forth from the Virgin in a special and ineffable manner, and entered the world without distress to his mother. Therefore it is pious to believe that God and man was born into the world not like the others, but according to a new and marvelous order.

Hence Jeremiah testifies: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman will encompass a man” (Jeremiah 31:22). If it was indeed new and marvelous that the Virgin conceived without seed and without the intercourse of a man, there could have been no old or ordinary condition in the birth. Therefore it must likewise be believed that he was born into the world in a similar new and marvelous order, without pain, groaning, or any corruption of the flesh.

For this reason also, as though in thanksgiving, he says to the Father in the psalm that is wholly about him: “You are he who drew me from the womb” (Psalm 21:10). [Note: Amelianus has “openly.”] As though he were plainly saying: “You drew me forth because I did not emerge from the womb in the order in which others are born, amid the mother’s immense distress, but by a new emergence [Note: This passage is plainly mutilated in our witnesses, where it reads: “But by a new emergence, as many heretics have said,” and so on.] without violation of modesty. You indeed drew me from my mother’s womb, and I did not corrupt the organs of her integrity.”

And lest we should think that he was a phantom, as many heretics have said, he added: “My hope from my mother’s breasts.” Therefore, wherever a mother and breasts are mentioned, the reality of flesh, not a phantom, is proclaimed. Although he was born with the womb closed—having himself made it passable for himself without compromising the seal of modesty, just as he was conceived—he was nevertheless brought forth from the Virgin’s flesh, and is therefore rightly said to have been nursed at her breasts. [Note: “Because” is found in Feuardentius and Amelianus.]

Thus everything happened so that a new thing might come to be upon the earth, when the Word became flesh and was called Emmanuel, which means “God with us.” This, then, is that enclosed garden in the Song of Songs, the sealed fountain (Song of Songs 4:12): an enclosed garden, because when God entered her, he found her incorrupt; but she remained a sealed fountain when God and man was born from her, and yet he did not violate the fountain of modesty or the integrity of her blood. [Col. 0215A]

For since the blood and the fountain of modesty were not corrupted in the conception of the child through intercourse with a man, I do not believe that they ought to have been corrupted in the birth, with the mother’s torture and the defilement of honor. Hence the Church, on the authority of the holy Fathers, sings concerning his birth: “And possessing the mother’s joy,” he says, “with the modesty of virginity” (Sedulius, *Carmen*, book II). [Note: Acherius reads “with the modesty of virginity,” but shortly afterward has “they corrected it to ‘with the honor of virginity,’” which, as the following context shows, is the corrupt reading in the Corbie manuscripts.]

Here certain other distinguished men corrected the text to “with the honor of virginity.” The honor of virginity is exceedingly great if a virgin gives birth to God and man, and yet, after giving birth to a man, suffers none of the *kakiai*—κακίαι, that is, “afflictions” or “distresses”—that would compromise the seal of modesty. For *kakiai* in Greek means the afflictions by which body and soul are grievously tormented.

But blessed Mary endured none of these things. She had joy in the fruit and honor in the birth. Hence she is said to have conceived as a virgin, to have given birth, and to have remained a virgin. She is therefore said to have conceived and given birth under the same condition, and likewise to have remained a virgin under the same condition.

For women in childbirth do not ordinarily have intercourse with men [Note: “To have intercourse” is absent in Feuardentius.] so that one might claim that a virgin lost her virginity at the moment when there is neither desire nor any possibility of intercourse. Rather, the virgin’s integrity, honor, and incorruption of flesh are being commended. Otherwise, since we men do not know the nature of that sex, let us question virgins, and likewise married women joined in wedlock. Let us question virgins so that we may know what integrity of flesh and blood is; and let us question married women whether there is any corruption or pain in childbirth unless contamination of blood and reception of seed have preceded it.

We do not willingly cause you embarrassment, dearest women, since we speak of these matters only with great modesty. But it is an honor of exceptional piety for you to proclaim the chastity of the most blessed Virgin incorrupt and undefiled, and to confess that she was free from every contagion of the first origin. [Note: Feuardentius has “honor” instead of “is an honor.”]

If we question virgins about her, they know the grace of incorruption but do not know the fruitfulness of offspring. If we inquire of women dedicated to marriage, they certainly know the pressures and groanings of Eve’s curse; they know, amid hardships and sorrows, the fruitfulness of seed. But they do not know the integrity of virginity, either in conception or in childbirth.

The blessed mother of the Lord, however, remained a virgin in both respects—that is, a mother in conception and a virgin in childbirth—because in none of these matters was she defiled according to the example of other women. [Note: “Of women” is absent in Feuardentius and Amelianus.] She neither admitted Adam to herself, nor received a son from Eve’s pollution, nor gave birth to the Lord beneath the curse, amid the pains and anguish of the first condemnation.

Hence it is clear that, just as she conceived with the womb closed, so also she gave birth with the womb closed: not according to the common law of corrupted nature condemned under curses, but by the grace of the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, by which she is read to have been overshadowed.

Yet these men, with all the effort they can muster, attempt to support the claim that the Virgin gave birth in a state of corruption and to inflict insults upon her chastity. They therefore take up this passage from the Gospel: “When the days of her purification were completed, they brought Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord” (Exodus 13:2), “because every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke 2:22). [Col. 0215D]

“Behold,” they say, “when the Evangelist says that the days of her purification were completed, he shows that she was subject to the law of nature and had been defiled by impurities, and likewise that Jesus opened his mother’s womb.” [Note: Feuardentius and Amelianus have “subject to the legal law.”]

These rash advocates, who think in this way, are altogether foolish. They destroy what belongs to sound doctrine, what the rudiments of faith have entrusted to the Churches concerning Christ, and what the grace of the Holy Spirit proclaimed in the mystery. [Note: Amelianus and Feuardentius have “in the ministry” instead of “in the mystery.”]

For the completion of the days of her purification is not mentioned as though the blessed Virgin needed purification from any offense, since she gave birth to the Lord Jesus Christ, brought forth from the Holy Spirit. Rather, it is mentioned because she herself was under the law, and the Lord Jesus Christ, having been made under the law, was made of a woman (Galatians 4:5). The precepts and institutions of the ancient law [Note: Feuardentius has “of the old,” erroneously, instead of “of the ancient,” which is found in Acherius and Amelianus.] were therefore observed in him for a time, until, with the law ceasing, grace should succeed it.

This, then, is the completion of the days according to the custom of the law, not according to any need for purification, because blessed and undefiled virginity remained immaculate and incorrupt, stained by no impurities and afflicted by none of Eve’s torments.

It cannot be that, according to the angel’s declaration—the angel who brings joy to all—Christ himself brought torments upon his mother at his birth. [Col. 0216B] [Note: “Christ himself” is not found in Amelianus and is absent from Feuardentius.] Amid the watchfulness and praises of the angels, I do not believe that he brought upon his mother Eve’s groanings, pains, and sorrows.

That purification of other women was therefore one thing: in it, not only the offenses of souls but also the defects of bodies were purified. Mary’s purification was another: in it, the custom of the law was observed for no other reason than as a mystery, because she needed none of the purifications, having herself given birth to God, the purifier of all, incarnate.

Moreover, the completion of the days of her purification has no other cause than the fulfillment and custom of the law. The purification and separation of other women, however, occur for many reasons, in which both the defects of souls and the defects of bodies are cleansed. Hence seven days are designated as unclean, during which a woman is commanded to sit in the blood of her uncleanness, utterly unclean, according to the days of her separation; and thirty-three days, during which she is to sit in clean blood (Leviticus 12:2, 4). Throughout all these days the woman was nevertheless unclean and impure on account of many defects, until the condition of the whole body was restored [Note: Feuardentius has “and the beds were healed”; Amelianus, “and the bed was healed.”], the bodies were healed, and the blood, corrupted by its agitation, ceased from its fever. Then, once the impurities had been cleansed, the woman was purified by divine sacrifices and offerings.

But blessed Mary had no need of such sacrifices, since she herself gave birth to the holy Victim through whom the world was purified. For when the Evangelist says, “Because every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke 2:23), he does not say this to compel us to believe that Christ opened his mother’s womb as others do. Rather, he teaches that they presented him to the Lord in order to fulfill the custom of the law on his behalf, because every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord, in the mystery of the law and the sacrament of sacred prefiguration. [Note: “In the mystery” is better than “in the ministry,” which Feuardentius has; nevertheless, we retain the rest of his reading, which is inferior to Acherius’s: “of sacred transgression.” Amelianus’s manuscript reads “of its own prefiguration.”]

The Evangelist did not therefore introduce this testimony from the law in order to show that Christ opened the Virgin’s womb, as the other firstborn do, but to show that he was made under the law and came forth from the Virgin’s womb—not merely one who would be called holy, but one who was essentially holy, for whom every closed thing is rightly open.

[Note: What follows appears in Feuardentius’s edition and in the Amelian manuscript in the sermon on the Purification. Nevertheless, apart from the Corbie manuscripts, the context itself proves that it belongs to the present treatise, as we shall note somewhat further below. We therefore rightly follow Acherius and have excluded what appears at this point in the Amelian manuscript and Feuardentius.]

Explaining this testimony, blessed Ambrose says in the Gospel (*Book II on Luke*, chapter 2): “For it was not intercourse with a man that opened the hidden places of the virginal womb, but the Holy Spirit infused immaculate seed into the inviolate womb.” This doctor does not say that the aforementioned seed was infused in such a way that it came from elsewhere rather than from the Virgin’s flesh and blood; nor does he say that the Holy Spirit should be believed to be the source of the flesh’s seed, as Irenaeus holds. Rather, through this word the operation of the Holy Spirit is indicated. [Note: Our witnesses have “that the seed is,” instead of “seed-producing.”]

Then he added (in the same work): “For the Lord Jesus alone, among those born of woman, is holy in every respect: he did not experience the contagions of earthly corruption, because of the novelty of his immaculate birth, and by heavenly majesty he drove them away.”

And shortly afterward (in the same work): “He alone, therefore, opened the womb for himself. Nor is this surprising. For he who had said to the prophet, ‘Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you’ (Jeremiah 1:5)—he who sanctified another’s womb so that a prophet might be born—is the one who opened his mother’s womb so that he might come forth immaculate.” [Note: “Another’s” is absent in Amelianus and Feuardentius and was certainly missing.]

In these words, however, he does not seem to me to contradict himself or the other holy doctors, because he says that Christ alone opened the womb for himself. He opened it for himself, certainly, by his own power and wondrously, so that a passable path might be available to him, while the virginal womb remained closed, just as the doors remained closed when he entered through them to the disciples; and likewise just as the sealed and closed tomb remained so when, rising again, he came forth through it. [Col. 0217B]

Hence elsewhere also, in a certain hymn, he says: “The gate of Christ becomes passable, filled and overflowing with grace; the King passes through, and it remains closed.” He does not say this in such a way that you should understand him to be thinking contrary to himself, but so that you may fully recognize that Christ was born from the Virgin’s womb and through her womb, which he himself made passable.

Accordingly, he himself opened the womb for himself: for himself, indeed, because the Virgin’s womb, although closed, was open and penetrable to him. [Note: Acherius prints tamen (“nevertheless”) instead of quam (“which”), which is found in our witnesses.] When he came forth from it into the world, he left it entirely closed and sealed with the seal of modesty, since nothing is difficult for God; for, as someone has said, all nature is habitually subject to his commands.

It is therefore established beyond ambiguity that he was born in such a way that his mother’s genital passage remained hidden and closed, while by his own power he made it open for himself.

In another sense, however, he alone opened the womb of the holy Church, which he dedicated as his bride, for the generation of peoples. Concerning this womb, the prophet David sings: “The sinners are estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the womb; they have spoken falsehoods” (Psalm 57:4). Here he declares the person of the heretics, who are estranged from the womb of the Church’s integrity by mixing in falsehoods, so as to corrupt the chastity of the Church’s virginity. [Note: “By mixing in falsehoods, so as to corrupt the chastity of the Church’s integrity,” and so forth. We reproduce this passage according to our Amelian manuscript and Feuardentius’s edition, where these words—missing in Acherius—are present and sufficiently appropriate to the sense.]

The Apostle strives to preserve this chastity immaculate and to guard the Church as a virgin when he says: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). Christ opened her hidden womb when he granted the grace of rebirth through water and the Holy Spirit.

To her the prophet says: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah 54:1). Hence Anna also says in her song: “The barren woman has given birth to many, and she who had many children has grown weak” (1 Samuel 2:5).

He alone, therefore, is holy essentially—not one through whom the mother is corrupted, but one through whom the womb of the Church is opened—the firstborn among many brothers.

All the firstborn prescribed in the divine law prefigured this future mystery. [Note: Acherius read “through mouths” in his manuscripts; De la Barre had already suspected that “the former” should be read instead. We needed no conjecture, since we found “the former” in both Feuardentius and the Amelian manuscript.] They signified it in their own firstborn, not because they were truly holy, but because they were called holy according to the mystery of the law.

Otherwise, if we follow the letter of the text (Saint Ambrose, in the same work), how was every male who opened the womb holy, when it is well known that many were most wicked? Was Ahab holy, or Joram, or the others? Were the false prophets holy, whom the avenging heavenly fire consumed at Elijah’s prayer? Certainly not. But in the sacrament of the future prefiguration they were called holy, although they were not, until Christ came who was holy essentially, who would open the womb of his bride and pour into her the fruitfulness of bearing children.

For he alone was judged worthy of the Lord’s regard; no one can doubt that all the others, according to the sequence of the law, were types of what was to come. And therefore they present him to the Lord, because he is the purification of the eighth day through the resurrection in Jerusalem, so that in him every adoption of the children of God might be pardoned and offered. [Note: “Of the eighth day” is absent in our witnesses.]

For when the law says, “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exodus 13:2), it promised the truly holy birth of the Virgin—an immaculate birth that would open the womb of the Church, so that in him all other things might be sanctified and become firstborn. [Note: Acherius and the Amelian manuscript have “was promised.” Feuardentius’s “was prefigured” is not bad.]

Hence the angel expressly says to Mary: “And what will be born from you will be called holy, the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). This is not because, by being born, he corrupted his mother, whom he left an intact and inviolate virgin, but because God and man, born from her, opened the womb of the Church and made a passage for himself in his flesh. [Note: “Through the womb” is found only in Feuardentius.] In this way he preserved the Virgin’s chamber closed, so that he might show that, from a virgin mother, [Note: “Virgin” is absent in Acherius but present in Feuardentius and Amelianus; we have judged that it should be retained.] he had taken a virgin bride for himself, whom by such a great and solemn covenant of birth he showed would remain a virgin and immaculate.

Hence it is clear that he was offered according to the law, just as he was circumcised. Otherwise, he had no need of circumcision, since he drew no original sin by which Christ himself would need to be removed from his people if he were not circumcised. Yet he was circumcised because he willingly placed himself under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law; and likewise he was offered so that, for us who were guilty, he might offer in himself a sacrifice to God the Father (Galatians 4:5).

In another sense, if he were himself unclean—which God forbid—and had defiled his mother, how could he cleanse us in his offering and make us a sacrifice to God as a fragrance of sweetness? Therefore, although he himself bore our pains and carried our illnesses (Isaiah 53:4), far be it from us to suppose that he afflicted his mother’s modesty with any painful injury.

Far be it from us to suppose that the woman through whom every curse of Eve was dissolved was herself subject in childbirth to the curses of the first condemnation. [Note: Feuardentius alone has “through whom.”] Far be it from us to suppose that, where power is born, there was such a flood of defects; where the joy of all is proclaimed, that such sadness and groaning intervened; amid the movements of the angels, that she sat for seven days in uncleanness and impure blood.

If this had been the case, the shepherds could not, as I might put it, have entered to her early in the morning according to the law. But now, because the angel devotedly invites them for the purpose of proclaiming the good news, they come and see; they find and understand the word that had been proclaimed to them. [Note: Feuardentius and the Amelian manuscript have “proclaimed.”]

They must therefore in no way be believed to have found Mary alone amid such impurities, overwhelmed and wrapped in as many [Note: Feuardentius has “mysteries” instead of “miseries.”] miseries as women in childbirth ordinarily endure, while at her birth a multitude of angels sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke 2:14). Therefore, where and through whom such peace is proclaimed, I do not believe that those disgraces or pains of the flesh befell the immaculate mother. [Note: Our manuscript, together with Feuardentius, reads “through whom such great things are proclaimed”; it continues, “I do not believe that any disgrace…”]

The Magi also then reverently enter the house and find what the shepherds found: Mary, Joseph, and the child (Matthew 2:11). They find her not afflicted by pains, but attending to the child. Then they fall down and adore the one whom they find with his mother, offering gifts.

They adore, I say, her firstborn—not one who would have brothers following him, but one whom no one precedes. [Note: Feuardentius presents this passage as follows: “Although some have preferred that he be called ‘only-begotten’ rather than ‘firstborn’; and although the idiom…” The Amelian manuscript agrees with Acherius, whom we follow.]

Although some have wished him to be called “only-begotten” rather than “firstborn,” nevertheless, since it is the idiom of Scripture that whatever first opens the womb is called firstborn and is sanctified to the Lord, the Evangelist preferred to call him firstborn according to that same rite rather than only-begotten. [Col. 0219B] This does not mean that he opened the womb according to the law of nature, as is customary among other women, as these men claim, but because the one born from her was both firstborn and only-begotten, made under the divine law and under the law, so that through him the whole law might be fulfilled in spirit and in letter.

For he is also called the firstborn from the resurrection, among many brothers. Since a genus is gathered under a species, although by nature he could be called only-begotten, it was nevertheless more fitting that he be called firstborn, so that it might be an indication that already in him and through him many other brothers were being gathered as sons of the Church by grace, the womb of which he opened.

In the Old Testament also, the status of firstborn was very often given to those chosen beforehand by the grace of God. Their dignity did not come from nature, but their merit, deriving from grace, placed them first. [Note: “Merit” is absent in our witnesses.]

Therefore we too say that he is more significantly called firstborn than only-begotten, so that through him all who are gathered by grace, united with him alone, may be held among the heavenly beings.

All those firstborn consecrated to the Lord under the law bore this figure. Therefore it was right that, from among all those firstborn who opened the womb [Note: “To the Lord” is likewise absent in our witnesses.], the Lord should be offered legally among them, since all of them prefigured his form. Thus he himself would be firstborn, holding primacy in all things—not one who afflicted his mother’s womb, but one who opened the womb of the Church.

I have said these things so that the prudent reader may understand that firstborn sons are not made firstborn by the brothers who follow them. Rather, Christ is certainly called firstborn because all only-begotten sons, just as he himself was his mother’s only-begotten son, can be called firstborn; yet not every firstborn can rightly be called only-begotten. [Note: Acherius adds: “Or, from these words it is clear that all this belongs to a booklet written for readers, such as this work on the Virgin’s childbirth, and is in no way part of a sermon delivered to nuns, as it is entitled in Feuardentius’s edition.”]

From this it follows that he ought to be called firstborn, before whom no one existed and after whom no one existed, not merely one who is followed by brothers. [Note: “And after whom no one existed” is missing from our witnesses, and without it the sentence is defective.]

Christ is therefore rightly called firstborn from the Virgin—not because he afflicted the Virgin’s womb and opened the chamber of modesty, but because he who was firstborn from the beginning of all creation was born from her, both only-begotten and firstborn, in whatever manner he willed, without the groaning and pain of the woman giving birth. [Note: Acherius has “of the woman giving birth.”]

He is also rightly called firstborn from baptism, and is said to have risen as firstborn in the resurrection. [Note: Acherius adds “to be called.”] [Col. 0220A] Yet in both nature and birth, although he is called firstborn, he is rightly believed to be only-begotten, because he is the same Son of man and Son of God—not one and another, but one, and one in both.

By these rules of Catholic truth, the meaning is evident on every side: no one but a heretic says that Christ was born only according to the common law of nature, or otherwise than infants in general are born.

Although the aforementioned doctor Jerome, in the work he composed against Helvidius, may appear to have yielded to him in this matter—and in the passage where he speaks of the nine-month lodging of the womb and the lowliness of birth, which that heretic had proposed mockingly, as though it were unworthy of the divine majesty to humble itself to such great condescension as to dwell among the organs in the Virgin’s womb or to be born among female thighs, so filthy amid impurities [Note: Amelianus’s manuscript has “with impurities.”]—he in fact put forward all these arguments in reverse, as a heretic would, in order to destroy the truth of the Catholic faith.

In opposition to him, that distinguished defender of truth, not yielding as these men claim, but commending still more fully the dignity of God’s glorious humility, says (*Against Helvidius*, chapter 9): “The more lowly and dishonorable things that divine majesty accepted or endured for our sake, the more dearly it redeemed us, and the more earnestly it ought to be honored.” [Note: Feuardentius and Amelianus have “condescension.”]

With this meaning, although not, as far as I recall, in the same words, he seems to have responded to that heretic without bringing upon the blessed Virgin the disgrace of any defilement or the punishment of sin. Rather, he reverently commended the divine condescension and immense self-emptying in the form of a servant—not to show the Virgin afflicted and dishonored by the Lord, but to demonstrate even to heretics of this kind the clemency of the gracious Creator.

Therefore, he did not yield to these men who err with Helvidius, but rebuked them, so that they might learn not to defame the Virgin [Note: Acherius has “and God”; our witnesses have “the Lord.”] and not to detract from the humility of God in the form of a servant. He does not teach that her chastity was injured in any respect; rather, he triumphs in her praise. Nor did he yield even for a moment to her adversaries, since he fought for her so long and so earnestly with the sword of the word. Against her enemies God granted him such grace to resist and such power to refute that no one dares rise up against him.

I pray, most sacred virgins of Christ, through the merits you bring before God, that he who granted that man such skill in speaking and such strength to overthrow his adversaries may also grant me the grace of speech and open to me in the spirit of truth what is worthy of this mystery. Thus, through you and for your sake, O matrons of Christ, may I, who have no merits of my own to rely upon, be found worthy to defend appropriately [Note: “And indeed, to disclose the truth to believers…” is found only in Feuardentius; our Acherian manuscript agrees with it.] and the chastity of my Lord’s mother, and disclose the truth to those who do not rightly believe, so that they may come to their senses and cease any longer to speak [Note: Our witnesses have “against the truth,” where Acherius has “falsehood.”] falsehood.

They say that Christ cannot be said to have been born in any other way than according to the same condition of nature as the others, as though divine Scripture always spoke of birth under an identical condition. Yet this birth by which all are born under the lot of the curse is very different from the other birth—which would have occurred if Eve had not sinned. The former is under a curse and hardship; the latter would have borne fruit wholly in the flowering of blessing, without groaning or pain.

Therefore, I ask, let them at least grant Christ’s birth from the Virgin Mary the birth by which all would have been born according to the common law if Eve had not sinned—a birth now known to God alone and perhaps unknown to human beings—and let them not attribute to him curses, groanings, and hardships that brought sorrow to his mother instead of joy. For the more full of grace and incorrupt she was, the more free the Virgin was from the corruption of suffering, the pain of the flesh, and the impurities of disgrace; [Note: Amelianus and Acherius have “the more”; Feuardentius has “as though.”] and the more she was dedicated to the Lord by the Holy Spirit [Note: “To the Lord” is absent in Acherius.] and overshadowed by divine power.

For the Holy Spirit contains within himself his own hidden recesses, according to which birth is spoken of in different ways in the sacred Scriptures and concealed under everlasting laws. One birth is flesh from flesh, another is God from God, and others belong to innumerable kinds of things. Yet the manner of birth is not the same for all of them, nor is the order of their existence the same, although birth is equally spoken of in each case, to which it is rightly attributed that those born from another are said to have been born. [Note: Amelianus and Feuardentius have “to be born” instead of “those born.”]

Accordingly, Christ is rightly believed to have been born from the Virgin Mary in whatever manner, because he assumed flesh from her. But how that birth itself came forth to us—whether under the condition in which Eve would have given birth if she had not sinned, or in a more glorious manner, because she gave birth to God and man and remained a virgin, which Eve would not have been, nor would the other women have been while giving birth—is unnecessarily questioned.

In this work none of the saints wished to entertain doubt. Rather, all proclaim as certain by Catholic faith that she neither conceived in sin [Note: These words are absent in our Amelianus and Feuardentius.] nor gave birth in sin and pain with corruption, and that Christ drew no sin from her. If he drew no sin from her, he did not admit it either [Note: Feuardentius erroneously has “lost it”; our manuscript and Acherius agree with “admitted it.”], since in being born he did not afflict his mother’s modesty with any torments, nor in any way stain her virginity.

We do not say, then, as they claim, that he was born monstrously, but that he was born as it was long ago foreshadowed in the prophets and handed down to us by the holy Fathers: that she herself was the gate shown to Ezekiel, concerning which he says: “I saw a gate in the house of the Lord, and it was closed; and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of hosts has entered through it” (Ezekiel 44:2).

Concerning this gate, blessed Ambrose, in the same hymn of which I spoke, which he composed in honor of the most holy Virgin, says:

> “She becomes the accessible gate of Christ, filled and overflowing with grace; the King passes through, and she remains closed, as she was throughout the ages.”

Thus, when he says “she becomes accessible,” he explains himself and displays the passage of His birth; when he says “she remains closed,” he shows that what had been foretold by the prophets was fulfilled. She therefore would not be called closed if her integrity had been injured in any way; but because virginal modesty was violated in no respect, and the fountain was unsealed in no respect, the meaning is plainly evident: He came to us with the womb closed, just as He entered to the disciples through closed doors.

The disciples’ own sight then proved both facts: that the doors were closed and that the Lord, entering through those same doors, stood present before them. So also our faith holds with complete certainty both things concerning Christ: that her integrity was accessible when the Lord was born from her, and yet that the womb was not unsealed. Otherwise, how can that be said to have remained closed which was violated? Or how did the woman in childbirth bear a child without pain and without groaning, if she brought forth a son with her organs afflicted in the manner of other women? And if it opened in the way they claim, how did it remain closed, as it was before she gave birth? For those doors were not more penetrable while closed than the Virgin’s incorrupt womb.

Therefore it is rightly believed, and not without reason, that the Lord came forth to us in such a way that Christ’s birth would be proved to have been from the Virgin’s flesh, while the Virgin would be afflicted by no torments.

Some may perhaps say that a body already incorruptible and immortal would have been more able to pass through wherever it wished than it had been earlier, before it rose again. [Note: Feu-ard. has something not very different: “Therefore let no one who is of sound judgment say so.”] But no one who is of sound understanding says this, because from the moment He was conceived as man, He was the same one who had previously been God. Thus, when before His passion He walked upon the waves of the sea, He was no less man than God.

But if you consider the nature of things, either He carried a body without weight, or by His power He made the waves more solid so that they could support the body’s weight. [Note: La Barre emended this to *sustinerent* (“might support”), since in Acherius it was corruptly read as merely *sustinere*. In our Amelian and Feu-ardent manuscripts we found *sustinere possent* (“could support”), which we had no reason to emend.] And therefore, as blessed Gregory says in his homilies (Homily 26):

> “The works of our Redeemer, which cannot possibly be understood from themselves, must be weighed by reference to another of His works, so that more wondrous deeds may give faith to wondrous things.”

For, he says:

> “That body of the Lord entered to the disciples through closed doors which, plainly, came forth at His birth before human eyes from the Virgin’s closed womb.”

Then he adds:

> “What wonder, then, if after His resurrection, when He would already live forever, He entered through closed doors, since when He came to die He came forth without opening the Virgin’s womb?”

Behold what this great and eminent teacher and supreme pontiff thought about this matter—he who had read all the outstanding interpreters before him, both Latin and Greek. [Note: *Certatores* (“champions”) is the reading of Feu-ard. and Amel.] Behold how, from this one fact, which he believed no one could doubt, he confirms what might perhaps have seemed doubtful. [Note: Feu-ard. and our Amel. have it differently: “Therefore let no one who is of sound judgment greatly doubt this matter or attempt to affirm something uncertain.”]

Therefore no one who is of sound judgment, faced with a matter involving great doubt, should attempt to assert something uncertain. Since faith in that body which could be seen was wavering among those who looked on while they saw the doors closed, the Teacher of truth removed all doubt from them when He commanded them to touch and see His hands and side.

So here too this distinguished author, beginning from what he believed to be certain for everyone alike, established and confirmed a very difficult matter: that the Lord’s body entered through closed doors after the resurrection, and that it was incorruptible [Note: Feu-ard. alone reads *primo* (“first”).] and likewise tangible. Yet however He entered, the Gospel proves that He entered to the disciples through closed doors, just as He was born from the Virgin’s closed womb. [Note: Feu-ard. differs from Amel. and Acherius: “For if He was born through the vulva, as they claim, it cannot truly be said,” and so forth.]

But if it cannot rightly be said that He was born in this way through the vulva, as they wish, then neither can it be said that He entered through the doors; and yet He is demonstrably said to have entered to them, when He is reported to have stood in their midst. Likewise, He is shown to have come forth from the tomb while the monument was sealed, when the angel rolled away the stone and displayed the tomb as empty. [Note: Our Amelian and Feu-ardent manuscripts have “with the monument sealed”; Acherius printed “sealed,” which de la Barre emended.]

It is therefore plainly established that, just as that stone doorway was accessible and penetrable to Him and could not restrain the living One whom it had previously enclosed as dead beneath its seal, so also the enclosure and genital passage of the Virgin, though closed and sealed with the seal of modesty, could not, when the days of childbirth had been fulfilled, obstruct the birth because of the body’s integrity. Yet it did not need to be unsealed, because [Note: Amel. has *cogit* (“compels”).] it was not fitting that He for whom this was the mother’s honor and joy should be subjected to torment. For in her everything that was closed was accessible to God; and it was an honor because everything was divine, that which was born [lacuna].

I plainly confess that no subject for debate can be found as extensive as the question why He came forth from the sealed tomb or why He entered to the disciples through closed doors, compared with the question why He came forth from Mary the Virgin’s closed womb. In those events divine majesty is revealed; in this one divine condescension is displayed, and, according to [Note: Acherius has “humility.”] humanity, the honor due to the mother and reverence for modesty.

For this reason, too, blessed Ambrose testifies in hymnic praise (in his hymn for the Nativity of the Lord) that the enclosure of modesty remained intact and that the standards of virtue shone in her, in whom the whole majesty of the Godhead dwelt, until the fullness of time for giving birth arrived.

Therefore, in her in whom the enclosure of modesty remained whole, there was no rupture, no torment of the flesh, no foulness of that terrible condition; and in her in whom the standards of virtue flashed, no sin of original descent prevailed to afflict her. The standards of virtue shone in that sacred childbirth when the Virgin conceived without seed, the Virgin gave birth without pain and groaning, and remained a virgin with fruitful offspring. [Note: *Virgo* (“virgin”) is absent in Feu-ard. alone.]

This is indeed what it means for the enclosure of modesty to remain: that the genital secret was violated in no respect, for it was opened to Him neither in conception, nor in childbirth, nor in any confusion accompanying delivery. For the entire Church of Christ, both Roman and Greek, confidently sings this with its divine authority: that the Virgin gave birth without pain and remained inviolate, because the Holy Spirit preserved her unharmed in every respect, so that the Virgin might have a son and the honor worthy of so great a gift might be preserved for her, since her womb had been consecrated to God with such sanctification.

**The first volume on the Birth of the Virgin Mary, dedicated together with the holy virgins, ends.**

# The Second Volume on the Birth of the Virgin Begins

[Col. 0223C]

Among the sayings of the Holy Scriptures, vain and superstitious interpretation must always be avoided, because, as it is written in Proverbs, “The perverse are corrected with difficulty, and the number of fools is infinite” (Ecclesiastes 1:15). And therefore, because the rashness of certain brothers has begun to defile the mysteries of the divine gift through impudent disputation and to scrutinize the mystery of the sacred birth by needless inquiry, they prefer to err with heretics rather than correct what they think wrongly with Catholics.

Thus, because they find cracks through which their vain disputation may enter, they introduce into the churches a most foul sewer of depraved filth, bringing about the drowning of souls, when they falsely say that the Virgin Mary gave birth to the Lord according to the natural law, as other women give birth, and that she was incorrupt in childbirth for no other reason than that she did not conceive through intercourse with a man.

I believe that I have already said enough above, in the first volume, concerning her incorruption; but because these men do not accept what we have said, [Col. 0224A] they obstinately insist that virginity can be corrupted in no other way than through intercourse with a man, and that Mary ought not to be called corrupted, even though she gave birth according to the law governing all women. For, they say, even if her organs or genital secret opened in childbirth in the manner of other women so that Christ might be born, nevertheless virginity could not be corrupted; therefore the Mother of God alone remained a virgin and incorrupt after childbirth.

While they spread such and similar empty talk, [Note: Acherius has: “While they spread their own nonsense.”] they set aside the authority of the holy Fathers and defile the Catholic faith. Since they disdain to hear us, I ask them to listen to blessed Augustine, whom it is not permissible to contradict, disputing this matter, among other places, in the *Enchiridion* (chapter 34). For he says:

> “It is not lawful to say that anything belonging to human nature was lacking in that assumption. He was not born as one is born from both sexes through the concupiscence of the flesh with the burden of sin, whose guilt is washed away by regeneration; rather, He was born as it was fitting for Him to be born from a Virgin, whom the faith of His mother, not lust, had conceived. For if her integrity were corrupted even through the birth, He would no longer be born from a virgin; and the whole Church falsely—God forbid—would confess Him to have been born from the Virgin Mary, the Church which, imitating His mother, daily gives birth to His members, [Note: “And is a virgin” is found in the Amel. manuscript together with Acherius; *est* is not read in Feu-ard.] and is a virgin.”

Concerning this same work he writes quite elegantly to Volusianus, and he refers us there as well to read that book. But these men, because they are unwilling to read either that book or this passage, go astray, deceived by their own recklessness. Otherwise, as this distinguished teacher admits in the same place, if virginal integrity were corrupted even through the birth, it would not be permissible to call her a virgin, since her virginity would have been corrupted by the one born from her. And if it were corrupted even through the birth, how would the virgin be whole and unharmed?

Let these empty talkers therefore listen to so great a teacher and come to their senses, lest by their false [Note: Feu-ard. printed *affectionem* (“affection”) here.] assertion they introduce Christ as conceived in sin and born in iniquities. For [Note: The editor would gladly delete these words, which are badly inserted here, but refrained because they occur in all the manuscripts.] if He was not born from a virgin, then what the Church confesses is false, as Augustine says here; and false also is what all the Scripture of the New and Old Testaments testifies about her.

But because she remained entirely a virgin, she was pressed by no pains and was corrupted in no respect. Therefore she did not experience the impurities of childbirth, did not discharge a flow of blood, and did not endure the ruptures of her organs either within or without. [Note: *Intra extraque* (“within and without”) is the more correct reading, found only in the Amel. manuscript. Acherius and Feu-ard. printed *infra extraque* (“below and outside”). The following words we print as in our manuscripts, where the reading is better than in Acherius: “For if a woman in childbirth endured torments of this kind and such as these.”]

For if a woman in childbirth were subjected to such torments and the like, she would plainly not be a virgin, because virginal integrity would have been violated.

Here Sedulius, the rhetorician of the Roman Church, says in his *Paschal Work*:

> “For the infant, both small and great—small, that is, in bodily members [Note: Amel. and Feu-ard. have *exiguus corpore* (“small in body”); but *corpore* is plainly redundant and is absent in Acherius.] yet exalted in divinity—flowing down through the undefiled chastity of the hospitable temple, did not injure the body as He departed, which He had not injured when He came.”

If this is so—or rather, because it is so—He was not born as others are born, with the body corrupted, but God and man was born with the organs unharmed.

The same author continues:

> “Truly, this mystery of divine generation is revealed by the testimony of the Virgin’s childbirth: He who entered as the guardian of His mother’s modesty was conceived and created with her organs closed.” [Note: Acherius alone has “with her organs closed.”]

Nothing, then, could be said more plainly, nothing more clearly by these holy teachers concerning the Virgin’s childbirth, than that the whole and closed Virgin remained as she had been before she gave birth. This would certainly not be so if in childbirth she were subjected to corruption in the manner of other women.

No virgin, therefore, is subjected to sufferings of this kind; and therefore she is rightly called truly a virgin, because she is whole and incorrupt. [Note: *Esse* (“to be”) is found in Amelian and Feu-ard.] So also the blessed Mother of God, so that she may truly be called a virgin while giving birth, is rightly believed to have remained wholly closed in the manner of virgins and incorrupt. If she did not remain undefiled in this way, unlike other virgins, she would not truly be a virgin.

To demonstrate this, the prophet David, prophesying about her, says in a very fitting image:

> “He shall descend like rain upon fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth” (Psalm 71:6). [Note: Feu-ard. alone has “like falling drops upon the earth.”]

Senator Cassiodorus, explaining this verse in his exposition of the Psalms, understands the fleece as the most sacred Virgin Mary, shorn from the sheep of Israel, and compares the rain with the divinity of the Word. For just as rain comes upon fleece in complete silence, so it poured over and filled the virginal body and possessed the virginal mind.

In a wondrous manner, and by a wondrous image of comparison, he confirmed in prophecy the coming of the One descending into the Virgin’s womb: just as rain drenches fleece while leaving it whole and inviolate, so the divinity of the Word preserved the Virgin undefiled and unharmed. It found her whole and incorrupt when it descended like rain upon fleece and entered her virginal organs; and it descended also like drops falling upon the earth.

Thus the same prophet explains the perfect Incarnation of Christ in these two prophetic statements. We see the earth bring forth through falling drops, from which, when rain pours moisture upon it, every plant of the field sprouts and all the earth’s greenery arises. [Note: Feu-ard. has: “For through falling drops we say that the earth germinates.”]

So also the divinity of the Word, descending upon Mary like drops upon the earth, made her germinate the shoot of life—not from anywhere other than from herself, that is, from the Virgin’s flesh, through the infusion of divine majesty. [Note: We retain the reading of Feu-ard. and the Amelian manuscript; Acherius printed a different reading.] And therefore what was born from her was equally divine and human, so that the divinity of the Word is not believed to have been born from Mary without a human being, nor the human being without the Word; for the Word became flesh, and thus God and man are one Christ.

Moreover, by the rain that descended upon fleece he did not express the nature of germination from the fleece, but the manner of birth from the Virgin. For when rain falls upon fleece in calm weather, it preserves its integrity equally when it enters and when it flows back out; the integrity of the fleece is in no respect violated by the rain.

Thus that heavenly orator mentioned above understands and confesses the matter concerning the Virgin Mary: that she was neither corrupted at the entrance of the Son of God nor violated at His departure, but was preserved in every respect full of grace, whole, and unharmed. Neither when He entered were the womb or organs corrupted, nor when the womb was emptied were they unsealed. [Note: These words, through “nor when He enters,” are found only in Acherius.]

The genital secret remains, but closed and undefiled; the womb is emptied like fleece by the rain, but the organs are not shaken. [Note: Feu-ard. and Amel. have *cassantur* (“are shattered”); the text apparently means that they are not shaken or broken.]

By these two statements, then, as the teacher mentioned above indicates, the Holy Spirit wished to declare what Isaiah finally testifies concerning Christ, saying:

> “As rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but water the earth, soak it, and make it germinate … so shall my word be, which shall go forth from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isaiah 55:10–11). [Note: *Meum* (“my”) is absent in Acherius.]

Behold what David wished to signify by rain and what by falling drops: plainly, the infusion of the Holy Spirit and the divinity of the Word, so that it might cause germination in the Virgin’s womb and the Word might become flesh—not so that it would corrupt the virginal earth, as these men claim, but so that a shoot might burst forth from it into fruit and the earth’s integrity might remain unharmed.

If the power and nature of rain are so great that it waters and saturates the earth and makes it germinate, how much more must we believe that the Word of God, to whom belong power and might, filled the virginal organs, soaked them, and made them germinate, yet did not corrupt her by entering, just as He did not violate her by departing.

This is what David says in prayer to God the Father:

> “Let the peoples praise You,” he says; “let all the peoples praise You” (Psalm 66:4).

And lest you ask why they should praise Him, he immediately adds:

> “The earth has yielded its fruit.”

That is, the fruit of life and the fruit of incorruption; therefore the fruit from the tree of life, which is said to have been planted beside the streams of waters, and not the fruit from the tree of disobedience. For the fruit of disobedience is death, mourning, sadness, groaning, and pain. From the fruit of the tree of life, joy and life are measured rather than anxiety and grief, integrity rather than corruption and rupture of the organs.

By these examples, prophetic speech everywhere more clearly sets forth, according to the figures of allegory, the fruit of offspring and the mother’s incorruption than the punishments and retributions inflicted by the just judgment of God because of the first condemnation. Therefore the Virgin’s childbirth must be treated with greater reverence rather than scrutinizing, as one may not, the hidden places of the womb.

I recently found in a certain authoritative book, as many report, a work of blessed Augustine on the secret mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation. Among other things, it reads as though he were speaking familiarly to someone:

> “Read with fear, carefully, and come to me, and I will tell you how the Virgin conceived; for it is better that there be modesty in speech than danger in faith.”

By these words he plainly suggests how dangerous rashness is, and how cautiously and secretly such matters must be discussed with deeply religious people.

In the same work he continues, pouring out prayers to the Lord rather than words:

> “Forgive me, Christ, and spare my mouth, because in my rash narration I touch upon the mystery of Your Incarnation. Although You left the womb closed, You nevertheless allowed us to open the Gospel to unbelievers.”

Behold how, among the other mysteries, everything is attributed to God. Therefore, in the service of charity, I humbly beseech Him, because we are far too unequal to His praises.

**The treatise on the Birth of the Virgin ends.**

# Fragment of a Treatise on the Birth of the Virgin by the Same Author

[Col. 0227]

## Notice to the Reader

[Col. 0227]

Since we had decided to follow Acherius’s edition in the preceding treatise, we had resolved to append this fragment to it—both so that it might not perish altogether and because it was found in Feu-ardentius’s edition and in the Amelian manuscript, where it made up the greater part of a little book on the Birth of the Virgin, a subject certainly not unrelated to the present argument.

Now, however, after reading it more attentively, it has seemed to us not merely similar in subject but entirely identical in subject with the preceding little book. We have detected so many marks of affinity between this fragment and the other work that, if you ask us who its author is, we do not hesitate to assert that it is Paschasius Ratbertus himself, who is also the author of the preceding work. We had already suspected this from the similarity of style; now we have it fully established.

First, he addresses the nuns, just as in the preceding work, whom he frequently addresses at the end:

> “Therefore, because you have been dedicated, dearest ones, to such a great and such a spouse, etc.”

He calls the opponents whom he attacks “brothers,” just as above:

> “Therefore, so that our brothers may cease, etc.”

He pursues exactly the same argument, and concludes:

> “Therefore, let the empty talkers cease saying that He was born from the Virgin according to the common law, etc.”

Finally, what most clearly demonstrates that the author is the same, he repeatedly praises certain sentences from the preceding little book as his own. He says:

> “For if that curse still prevailed in Mary, then Christ Himself also, as has often been said, would still have been under the curse.”

Then elsewhere, near the end:

> “Let them not ascribe to the most sacred mother any insults inflicted upon her—neither groanings, nor pains, nor sorrows … because all these things, as has often been said, were punishments and retributions inflicted in the first beginning as the most just consequences of the first transgression.”

He had said almost all these things in virtually the same words in the earlier treatise.

Therefore there can no longer be any question about the author of this fragment. Indeed, we believe it to be part of the same book on the Birth of the Virgin, belonging either to the second volume or forming a third and final volume. No one will say that the address is to nuns who notices that here too the author, as in the first part, addresses the reader:

> “If you attend, reader,” he says, “to the simplicity of the statements … etc.”

For the rest, we compared Feu-ardentius with our manuscript, and from its certainly more correct reading we made many emendations.

[Col. 0227]

## Fragment

[Col. 0227]

… according to his account, which he had earlier defined clearly and briefly by saying: [Note: Feu-ardent. has *tunc* (“then”).]

> “You,” he says, “left the womb closed.”

Then he added more obscure matters concerning the mystery and said:

> “Nevertheless, I shall tell you what is accomplished in the chamber of nature.” [Note: Feu-ard. has “in the bedchamber.”]

In the Virgin’s vulva, therefore, the genital blood and her semen were the fluid. From the substance of this blood and fluid, kept hidden within, He made flesh. The Holy Spirit also came upon it and, by giving life, formed what had been joined together there by a kind of glue. Having formed it, He distinguished it into the form of a living human being, within which God was held enclosed in its bodily features. [Note: Feu-ard. has “of the Word.”]

> “Behold,” he says, “I have told you how she gave birth; she gave birth in the same way as she had previously conceived.”

In these words, if you attend, reader, to the simplicity of the statements and the familiarity of the persons involved, these are the words of blessed Augustine. But if you attend to the cunning of those who bring accusations, then neither was God the Word enclosed in any bodily features, for He is immeasurable, although He became man wholly enclosed in the womb, because the whole God assumed the whole man in the unity of His person, so that the Word might be flesh; nor did He mingle with the flesh so that the substance of the Word would be confused with it, as though two liquids had been mixed together, but He united to Himself the man whom He assumed, without division and without any commixture, into God.

And therefore, ineffably, although this author confessed as much as he was able, the Holy Spirit, by whom Christ was conceived, accomplished the work—just as there is one mother from whom He was conceived, so that two fathers might not be named.

As for the fluid of the seed and the coagulation of the moisture, which occurred through the power and might of the Word, he has spoken elegantly, in a manner appropriate to what may lawfully be said. For He Himself is that mountain of God in the Psalms, the fertile and coagulated mountain in the Virgin’s womb—not those whom some falsely supposed to be mountains made of cheese [Note: Feu-ard. has “cheese-covered.”]—but Christ alone from the Virgin is the mountain in which it pleased God the Father to dwell forever (Psalm 67:17).

And therefore He is rightly said to have been coagulated through the Holy Spirit, because just as milk is drawn out [Note: Feu-ard. has “drawn off.”] and thickened from fluid or blood, which, as physicians hold, is the woman’s semen, so He was coagulated as though from the milk of semen, so that Christ might be one, from whom God and man were conceived through the power of His divinity and by a might known to Him alone.

For, as blessed Augustine says, “conceived in the flesh, He was not made carnally; His birth from the flesh brought abundance, but did not take away the integrity of the woman giving birth.”

Therefore, dearest ones, such things and matters of this kind, as this distinguished man warned above, must be considered cautiously and understood wisely. Then, with an unambiguous heart, we must believe and confess with our mouth, as he says, that the Virgin, Mother of God, gave birth in the same way as she conceived—that is, because the undefiled Virgin conceived with her organs closed, as the holy Church confesses, so in like manner she gave birth with them closed and incorrupt, without pain, groaning, sadness, or sorrow. Thus she gave birth as she conceived.

For it could not have been otherwise, since she would not have been an incorrupt virgin, nor possessed the flower of virginity as the other virgins do, if she had been afflicted even in childbirth.

Therefore blessed Leo speaks in this way in his sermons on the Nativity of Christ:

> “He was generated by a new birth, conceived from a virgin, born from a virgin, without the concupiscence of paternal flesh and without injury to maternal integrity; for such a birth befitted the future Savior of mankind, one who would possess in Himself the nature of human substance but would know nothing of the defilements of human flesh.”

Then he says:

> “It was fitting that He who was bringing the new grace of undefiled purity to human bodies should be born according to a new order. It was fitting that, in being born, incorruption should guard the mother’s original integrity, and that the infused power of the divine Spirit should preserve the pleasing enclosure of modesty and the sanctuary of holiness; that it should raise up what had been cast down, strengthen what had been broken, and grant multiplied power of chastity for overcoming the allurements of the flesh.” [Note: The Amelian manuscript has: “which had been cast down from its state, strengthened what had been broken, etc.”]

> “Thus virginity, which in others could not remain safe while giving birth, might in others become imitable through confession and rebirth.” [Note: *Imitabilis* (“imitable”) is found in the Amel. and Feu. editions; *mutabilis* (“changeable”) is another reading.]

For, as he himself testifies, this birth, although its nature is similar in Him, has a different origin. It lacks, as we believe, human usage and custom, because it rests upon divine power: the Virgin conceived, the Virgin gave birth, and the Virgin remained a virgin.

> “Here,” he says, “the condition of the woman giving birth is not considered, but the will of the one being born, who was born man in the manner He wished and was able. If you seek the truth of nature, recognize the human material; if you examine the reason of the origin, confess the divine power.”

Again, in another sermon, concerning this same birth of Christ, he says:

> “The birth of our Lord Jesus Christ surpassed all understanding and transcended every example. It cannot be compared with any other birth, for it is singular among all births; it was announced by the archangel as being without injury to modesty.” [Note: Feu-ard. has *ulla* (“any”) here.]

> “Blessed fecundity violated sacred virginity neither in conception [Note: Feu-ard. has “which would violate.”] nor in childbirth. For when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, the unchangeable Word of God took from an undefiled body a human flesh that He made His own. That flesh, moreover, drew no contagion from concupiscence and lacked nothing belonging to the nature of soul and body.”

Therefore:

> “Let the monstrous opinions of heretics withdraw far away; let the sacrileges of their insane falsehoods withdraw into their own darkness.”

But let us, venerating the Virgin’s childbirth, adore it with the Magi, and let us see and understand that “in the beginning was the Word with the Father,” which the Lord showed us together with the shepherds, making no division in any respect between the visible and the invisible, the bodily and the incorporeal, the passible and the impassible, the form of God and the form of a servant. For although one substance remains from eternity and the other began in time, both substances nevertheless came together in one person in such a way that, unless faith believes it, speech cannot explain it.

Accordingly, the poet Prudentius, preluding to the same matter in his poem, confirms it by saying:

> The divine power weds the untouched maiden  
> With pure breath through her chaste organs.  
>   
> The birth of an unknown origin commands us to believe  
> That Christ is God: thus the unwedded Virgin,  
> Created [or: formed], is wed to the Spirit,  
> And knows nothing of the fault of love.  
>   
> Her marked maturity remains weighty, within and without  
> Unharmed, flourishing in chaste fertility.  
>   
> [Col. 0229C] Virginity and ready faith drank Christ into her womb.
of the heart, and, as she gives birth, keeps [it] in hidden places left intact. Therefore, I say, the sealed maturity remains inviolate; virginity is not violated, because the integrity of her dwelling is not corrupted.

Hence follows precisely this: that maturity, sealed, remains inwardly and outwardly unharmed, and virginity, blooming from chaste fertility, remains uninjured. If she remained blooming inwardly and outwardly, unharmed, it is clear that she was in no way contaminated—not by groaning, not by pain, nor by any corruption of flesh or blood. She was wholly radiant inwardly and outwardly, without any affliction, while she conceived, carried, and bore him; for in all these things she remained blooming, full of grace, uninjured and fruitful, giving birth while her hidden places remained intact.

For where the genital secret is corrupted, no integrity and no virginity of the mother remains—neither of nature nor of sex; where the modesty of the flesh is violated, there is no flower of integrity.

Moreover, this birth of the Mother of God was not the mother’s disgrace. At her birth, a multitude of angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14); rather, it was an honor and a joy. Therefore, as Peter of Ravenna urges in his sermon: “Let neither the conception disturb you nor the birth confuse you when you hear of them, since virginity excuses whatever belongs to human modesty. What injury to modesty is there here,” he says, “where divinity entered into communion with integrity, which had always been its companion? Where is the angel as interpreter, faith as bridesmaid, chastity as betrothal, virtue as dowry, conscience as judge, God as the cause, integrity as conception, virginity as birth, and the virgin as mother?”

And in the same passage he continues: “Fool, whence could there be defilement in the virgin mother, where there was no intercourse with a human father? Whence could there be defilement in her who neither conceived in lust nor suffered pain in giving birth?
