Whence could there be defilement in the house to which no guest came, but only the Lord, its maker, entered; he put on a garment which he did not previously possess, and left her just as he found her, closed?” [Note: “Eam quia” (“her because”), in Feuardent.] “And just as he was born alone, free among the dead, so the modesty of the mother from whom he was born alone remains entire. Therefore let none of you judge in a human manner what is accomplished through a divine sacrament. Let no one investigate a heavenly mystery by earthly reasoning. Let no one handle the mystery of novelty according to ordinary practice.” [Note: “Test” in the Amelianus Codex.] “Let no one measure what is unique by any example.” Thus far he.

We, however, say that Mary would not have been a virgin at all—at least not as other virgins are—if she had been afflicted even in childbirth. Nor do I think that any woman, if her conscience bore witness, would wish to be called undefiled, even if it were permissible for her to conceive without a man, while in childbirth she was pressed by as many and such afflictions as the other women suffer when they give birth. [Note: “Pressed,” from the Amelianus Codex; in Feuardent the reading was *perpessa* (“having suffered”), which is erroneous.]

Otherwise, what benefit would there be if she were a chaste virgin in conception but were so wretched under the curse in childbirth—afflicted by many pains and shamefully corrupted through her sufferings on account of sin? Such a virgin certainly would not have been in childbirth as she had been in conception—such and so blessed—if she had been corrupted by dreadful pains as other women are. And I do not say merely that she would not have remained a virgin in childbirth; she would not even have remained a virgin after childbirth.

Therefore, because the birth of the most holy virgin Mary was not of the sort these men assert, the most blessed Ambrose sings and prays:

> Come, Redeemer of the nations;  
> show forth the virgin’s birth;  
> let the whole world marvel:  
> such a birth befits God.

For he does not say, “Show forth the Virgin’s conception,” but “the birth,” thereby refuting these mistaken men: such and so great is that birth as befits God, and in it the whole world should marvel. For in the birth, so to speak, something more is revealed than in the conception. In the birth, the Virgin’s entire incorruption is displayed; in the conception, nothing is shown except that the Virgin became pregnant without intercourse.

For, as these men would have it, if he were born from her according to human law, she could eventually have been corrupted in childbirth, so that the human conception itself might corrupt the woman’s untouched womb. [Note: “Woman,” in Feuardent.] But because she was wholly uncorrupted in childbirth, this proves that she was also uncorrupted in conception.

Therefore blessed Ambrose, aware of so great a mystery, entreats and desires that the Virgin’s birth be shown—the birth these men do not understand—so that the Virgin may be manifested in both respects. [Note: We have emended this passage according to the Amelianus Codex. It was corrupt in Feuardent’s edition, where it reads: “For if it were as these men assert, blessed virgin Mary would not exist, so that her birth would be such as befits God,” and so forth.]

For if matters were as they assert, blessed Mary would not be a virgin, nor would her birth be such as befits God, since it would be ordinary. And if it were ordinary, according to the law of other women, it would be under the curse under which all the daughters of Eve give birth. Therefore there would be nothing in it for the whole world to marvel at, but rather something over which, God forbid, the whole world would mourn.

But now, because the enclosure of modesty remains—as this author testifies—she was not corrupted in childbirth. Therefore he is the one promised by the prophet Isaiah:

> Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son (Isaiah 7:14).

She will certainly conceive as a virgin and give birth as a virgin, because, although the entire divinity of the Word did not shrink from the Virgin’s womb, it corrupted her virginity in no respect—not in conception and not in childbirth.

Therefore, since he humbled himself so greatly as to receive the form of a servant, he did not wish to corrupt his mother—he who had come to heal what was corrupted—so that his birth might be wondrous, a birth at which the whole world would marvel. It would not be so if it were ordinary. [Note: “Would do,” in Feuardent.]

This is that notable miracle of which the aforementioned prophet sings:

> For the Lord himself will give you a sign (ibid.).

He himself, indeed, and not another. For he had given many signs through the holy Fathers and patriarchs; but this one he gave through himself, and it is exceedingly wondrous, so that the whole world might marvel at it, since it is ineffable.

Those who do not understand or believe in this twofold operation in Christ everywhere therefore go mad. In him neither divinity operated without humanity nor humanity without the divinity of the Word.

Thus, wherever divine power excels in the man Christ, it is the sacrament of the divine Word; but wherever human nature operates in him, because he assumed the form of a servant, it is the self-emptying of the divine Word. Christ is found divided in no respect, nor is the twofold operation of the two natures confused in any respect. [Note: Feuardent has *opera humana* (“human works”); and a little below, where we print *exinanitio* (“self-emptying”) from the Amelianus Codex, it has *est ex animo* (“is from the mind”).]

Therefore Christ, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, has been placed wholly as a sign for the peoples (Isaiah 11:10). And not merely as any sign, but, as Simeon says, “as a sign that will be contradicted” (Luke 2:34)—something we still see happening today. If he is contradicted everywhere even now, then he is contradicted also in the birth of his nativity.

Nor is it surprising that he has such contradictors, since all the adversaries, the companions of Antichrist, resist and contradict him. [Note: *Omnes* (“all”) is lacking in Feuardent.] Therefore we rightly execrate such men and such plagues together with Antichrist, because those whose faithlessness in slander is one will have one punishment of condemnation in their perseverance.

Accordingly, let our brothers cease from such things and sing faithfully with us, together with holy Ambrose:

> Come, Redeemer of the nations;  
> show forth the Virgin’s birth;  
> let the whole world marvel:  
> such a birth befits God.

A birth such as the Church of Christ confesses, and not such as these men falsely imagine and fabricate for themselves. [Note: Feuardent writes *ubique* (“everywhere”) instead of *utique* (“certainly”); the reading is not wrong if *post qualem* (“after what sort”) followed.]

It is not a birth in which virginal modesty is confounded, but one in which the whole world marvels and God is praised. It is not one that corrupts the mother’s womb, but one that restores what was corrupted and renews all things.

For this is that new miracle which, according to Jeremiah, the Lord promised to perform upon the earth (Jeremiah 31:22): not one in which the oldness of sin rages by corrupting virginal members, but one in which all things are renewed.

Hence Augustine, in his *Epistle to the Ephesians*:

> For what was not new in the man who was assumed by our Savior? His conception, birth, delivery, infancy, teaching, life, and virtues.

Therefore he is rightly called new in every respect, in conception as well as in birth. For if there had been any corruption in his birth, there would have been contamination by sin, on account of which the ancient curse would have raged against Mary. If that curse still prevailed in Mary, then Christ himself, as has often been said, would still have been under the curse.

But because he alone among all was free from guilt, he acted freely in being born from Mary, and freely in everything for which he came. Otherwise, if he had been defiled by his mother, or if he had corrupted his mother’s womb as though on account of sin and stained it with the filth of the first condemnation, he would not be the Son of God but an adopted son like the others—or rather, not even an adopted son, since there would be no one through whom he himself could be adopted if he were not the proper Son.

But now, as blessed Augustine testifies throughout all his writings, from the moment he began to exist, the only Son of God undoubtedly began to exist in the Virgin’s womb. He is said to have begun to exist not according to what he is as God, but according to what he graciously consented to become temporally as man. For he who had always been God began to be man: he himself, and no other, is Christ, God and man. Hence everywhere he is proclaimed by all—and by himself—as the only Son of God.

Likewise, in his epistle to Peter, Augustine says:

> In what words can the singular excellence of that flesh be explained, whose person is divine from the very moment of its assumption? For the Word became flesh in such a way that, in one person with his flesh, the Only-Begotten and eternal God was himself conceived through the conception of his flesh. While the Only-Begotten was being conceived, he began to possess the reality of flesh from the Virgin. [Note: Feuardent reads “nativity.”]

And he continues:

> This is the conclusion: God became the son of the virgin Mary, and Mary the virgin became the mother of God’s Only-Begotten Son.

Regarding this mystery, Cyril, writing to Nestorius, confesses one Christ, namely God and man—not worshiping a man together with the Word, lest thereby some division of the Spirit be introduced, but worshiping one and the same Christ in the unity of his person. His body is not alien to the Word, nor is it divided from him, because the Word became flesh, and man was so united and assumed into God that there is one God, with whom he now also sits alongside the Father, perfect in the Trinity.

Therefore he is not a recent God, nor a mere man; rather, one undivided Christ is honored and worshiped with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. [Note: “Because,” in Feuardent.]

This mystery is not the fruit of a curse, nor of the mother’s groaning in conception, nor of the laboring woman’s pain, nor of the adoption of the womb. Therefore he is not an adopted son but, so to speak, the adopter of the others. For the Virgin mother did not conceive him in iniquities, nor give birth to him in sins as the other women give birth—she who truly bore the one God in both natures, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born. She remained a virgin in childbirth just as in conception, something that could never happen to anyone else. For whatever human corruption generates in corrupted wombs cannot itself be incorrupt.

Therefore the children of corrupted nature, conceived through the intercourse of iniquity and cast forth from their mother’s womb amid pain in sins, can be nothing other than children of wrath. Hence they are regenerated through water and the Holy Spirit, so that through this regeneration they may be freed by Christ’s grace from the sins of the first condemnation and adopted as children of God.

But Christ, not an adopted son but the proper Son of God, came in the fullness of time, sent by the Father, born of a woman, made under the law (Galatians 4:4). He alone had no need of the sacrament of regeneration, nor of being reborn. [Note: Feuardent printed: “Since the true Son of God, who for us …”; the words supplied by us from the Amelianus Codex are absent there.] For in conception and birth he was nothing other than the proper Son of God, who in his goodness graciously granted us, through the washing of regeneration, the fellowship of brotherhood by the grace of adoption.

Hence John says:

> But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God (John 1:12).

The one begotten from the Father possessed this power in himself by his own nature, and not from elsewhere, so that he might be the proper Son of God and freely give the grace of adoption to whomever he wished.

And because this is so, far be it from anyone to believe that Christ was born like the others, just as he was not conceived like them, because he is the only Son of God, begotten from the Father’s nature.

Therefore let foolish disputants listen, and let them not attribute anything base, foul, or mournful to Mary, but joy; not pains, but the grace of salvation at the Savior’s birth.

Let them now hear fulfilled in the Virgin’s birth what the very clear-sighted prophet Habakkuk once saw from afar, trembling with fear and ecstasy:

> Lord, I heard your report and was afraid;  
> I considered your works and was astonished (Habakkuk 3:2, according to the Septuagint). [Note: The Amelianus Codex has “clear” (*perspicuus*); Feuardent’s edition reads “propitious” (*propitius*).]

And afterward:

> You will be known in the midst of two animals.

When he says, “You will be known,” he indicates that before he was born from Mary he was not sufficiently known. I wish these men would attend so religiously and consider the Virgin’s birth, which so great and such a prophet foresaw from afar, when he says in astonishment, fear, and trembling:

> Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid.

And so that I may speak to you, what did you hear, most holy prophet? Please tell us what you heard, which you marvel at with such astonishment, and what you saw in that report that makes you tremble so greatly.

For you do not speak of ineffable things according to ordinary usage, since you say, “I heard your report.” I do not think you are speaking conventionally. We hear someone’s voice, not someone’s hearing, because another’s hearing belongs only to the one whose hearing it is and in whom it exists.

Perhaps, therefore, your “hearing” is a reality rather than a sound—or rather, a voice which John saw when he turned around (Revelation 1:12). Perhaps, contemplating this voice, you see the consubstantial Word, on account of which you are so afraid; and thus what you hear and what you see are one and the same. Terrified by this voice and hearing, you cry out in such fear.

But lest you leave us outsiders to an understanding of this kind, you immediately add:

> You will be made known in the midst of two animals; when the years draw near, you will be known; when the time arrives, you will be revealed.

See how clearly you indicate what you heard. You heard, then, the Father’s Word, and you perceived him not through the hearing of the ear but through the hearing of the mind. This is the wondrous work that you contemplate. For you were contemplating the mystery of his incarnation and the birth of the holy Virgin.

Therefore you say: “In the midst of two animals”—recognize the manger. When the years draw near and the time arrives, understand the fullness of the time for giving birth, when God the Father, according to the Apostle (Galatians 4:4), sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law. [Note: “Born of a woman,” as in the Amelianus Codex. This is not surprising, since some are known to have read it so, although the other reading is preferable.]

Then what had been hidden for ages and generations became known to believers; what had not previously been revealed was recognized; and what had always been concealed was displayed.

Hence Isaiah says:

> You are a hidden God, and we did not know you (Isaiah 45:15). [Note: “God” is absent from Feuardent.]

He was indeed God, but hidden. Many knew that there was one God, but they did not know that he was the Son. Therefore the Father, too, was not known. But when the fullness of time came, he made himself known and revealed the Father.

Once the Son was recognized, the Father too was recognized. He was first shown in the manger by means of the star, in the midst of two animals, when it was also announced by the angel that he was the Son of the Most High.

This is that wondrous vision and that utterly ineffable hearing. This is the very same contemplation which Isaiah saw when he said:

> A child is born to us, and a son is given to us (Isaiah 9:6).

He was born for us, not for himself, and he was given to us, although he had always been born with the Father. He who was coeternal with the Father, the Only-Begotten in the nature of divinity, was the one and the same person born in time through the Virgin and given to us.

He was born for us, not for himself, because the Son was coeternal with the Father.

Therefore let empty talkers cease to say that he was born of the Virgin according to the ordinary law, he over whom all the prophets marvel. When they hear of his birth in the world, they fear and rejoice, tremble and worship, fall silent and proclaim, praising what they cannot fully express.

Therefore let us too praise and believe, dearest sisters, whatever in this birth is fully established, though we cannot penetrate it with our senses or understand it completely.

Come, brides of Christ, to the Virgin’s birth and to the manger. See, I ask you, the miracle; see the Word with the shepherds, worship him with the Magi, because the Word who was in the beginning with the Father lies in the manger, made flesh—and what then lay in the manger now reigns, seated at the Father’s right hand.

Therefore let us not regard as insignificant the bridegroom who lies so humbly in the stable. Gabriel obeys him, the angels praise him together, the star serves him, and the whole world ministers to him.

I beg you, do not investigate with these men the hidden places of the Virgin’s birth as though they had been corrupted, for they too have failed—“the investigators investigating an investigation of vanity” (Psalm 63:7)—because they think things that are unworthy of the Lord’s mother.

Rather, come with joy and see the Lord proceeding in the fullest faith, like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber—not, as these men chatter, corrupting the Virgin’s limbs with pains or violating the mother’s genital secret, but exulting divinely, as the Prophet sings, and freely proceeding from the chamber of the womb like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber, because the closed womb was made passable for him. [Note: We have emended *pervius* (“passable”) in place of *parvus* (“small”) in Feuardent; we had no hesitation, although the Amelianus Codex reads *per eum* (“through him”).]

His going forth from the highest heaven is described as strong for running his course, and his return reaches to the Father’s seat (Psalm 18:6). In all these things he proceeds as a festive bridegroom for you, virgins, and for his Church, exulting like a giant, joyful to take a wife for himself. [Note: Feuardent read “for us, virgins”; we have emended it to “for you,” although the Amelianus Codex also has “for us.” We followed its example because, at the end of this little work, where Feuardent has “our bridegroom,” the Amelianus Codex reads “your bridegroom.”]

Therefore those who say that, when he came forth from the Virgin’s womb like a joyful bridegroom, he afflicted his mother with pains, corrupted her womb, violated her chastity, multiplied sadness and hardships, and increased her groaning must not be heeded.

If this were really so, it could not very plausibly be said that the Lord proceeded like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. For when a bridegroom comes forth from his bridal chamber, he is always joyful and eager to be seen. [Note: “For the bridegroom …” These words are absent from Feuardent; only the following words appear there: “always joyful,” and so forth.]

There is no doubt that the womb of the virgin Mary is the bridal chamber in which the covenants of marriage are joined between the bridegroom and the bride when the Word becomes flesh. [Note: Feuardent reads “join.”]

For, as Cyril testifies, the flesh or body of Christ should not be understood as the bridal chamber or temple, but the Virgin’s womb, because in Christ there are not two persons, as certain heretics wished. [Note: “Because in Christ there are not two persons.” This stood in the edition and manuscript, although “there are two persons”; it was certainly corrupt, and we have therefore emended it conjecturally.]

For, as this holy man testifies, the creature was not assumed into fellowship with its Creator in such a way that the one would occupy the place of an inhabitant and the other that of a dwelling. Rather, the two natures were united to each other, and they came together in such a great unity that the distinction of both is found in one and the same Son.

Therefore, when a man is born from the virgin Mary, it is not a mere man, nor is he born according to the ordinary law of nature; it is God, the Son of God, who is born—not with him, but in him.

Likewise, when the temple of Christ’s body is dissolved according to the Gospel and raised again, God-man is dissolved into death and God-man is raised to life. For this temple is not dissolved in such a way that it is separated from the Word; rather, it is dissolved so that God may suffer and die in man.

For, as blessed Augustine says, the one who was born from the Father was born as God the Word, and from his mother the Word became flesh. Therefore one and the same God, the Son of God, was born before the ages and was born in the world, and both births belong to the one Son of God.

Indeed, he continues, the same God-man came forth from his mother’s womb; the same God-man lay made in the tomb; and the same God-man rose from the dead on the third day.

Therefore, I ask them to listen: from the moment he was conceived as God-man, Christ is in no respect dissolved. Otherwise, as the apostle John says, “Whoever dissolves Jesus Christ is not of him; this is Antichrist” (1 John 4:3).

Let them therefore cease from such ravings and confess with the holy Fathers that he was born of the virgin Mary as he graciously willed and as befitted God. Let them not attribute to the most sacred mother any insults—neither groaning, pains, hardships, bodily afflictions, nor any corruptions of dreadful sadness—for all these things, as has often been said, were imposed at the beginning as punishments and most just retributions for the first transgression.

From all these things blessed Mary was as far removed in guilt as, without doubt, she was free from pain and punishment.

For this reason, dearest sisters, rejoice in the Lord and exult together, because you have been made participants in so great a grace. Rejoice together because you have devotedly vowed to your Bridegroom, God, not only chastity but also complete and undefiled virginity.

Therefore, because you have been dedicated to such a great Bridegroom, beloved sisters, preserve your immaculate marriage and your nuptial rights, which are maintained only through complete faith and works.

Pray, I ask you, for me, because I am not worthy to join you before the throne of this Virgin in the sweet songs of the drama. May forgiveness at least be granted me through your interceding merits.

Moreover, I beg you, obtain through your prayers that this gift, although dedicated to you in rustic speech, may be graciously received by the blessed Virgin in your service. For, as you know very well, she has no need of our praises, since all that heavenly company continually celebrates her with hymn-filled melodies. [Col. 0235B; Col. 0236A]

Nor can she now be obscured by any calumnies. Exalted gloriously above the choirs of angels, she is venerated by all; and while they worship and praise the Son of God, they confess him to be her Son and recognize that the one believed and worshiped by all as coequal and consubstantial with God the Father is none other than the one born from the womb of the virgin Mary. [Note: We have emended *qui* (“who”) although both witnesses have *quam*; we have no doubt that this is the correct reading.]

Therefore, brides of Christ, look upon the cradle and the manger in such a way that you understand him always to be seated at the Father’s right hand—not now crying among the swaddling clothes or hanging on the cross, but reigning over all. As he himself testifies, all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18). Every knee bows to him—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ, your Bridegroom, is in the glory of the Father (Philippians 2:10). [Note: “Our,” in Feuardent.]

Amen.

## Another Fragment from the Little Book on the Virgin’s Birth

As it appears in Feuardent’s edition and in the Amelianus Codex, in which there is instead the opening of a certain sermon to the people.

[Col. 0235]

Whenever, beloved, something is proclaimed and exalted before you with fitting praise out of love for our Creator, in the creature he has made, it is undoubtedly referred back to the praise of him who is the author of creatures, so that the maker may be understood and praised through his creature. For, according to the Apostle, God’s invisible attributes are perceived and understood through the things that have been made (Romans 1:20).

This is just as happens, so to speak, in some admirable and wondrous work of craftsmanship: whatever in it is extolled with many and great praises is rightly regarded as wholly directed toward the glory and praise of the artisan’s hand.

But God must be praised incomparably more in his saints and proclaimed in all his works.

Hence David says:

> Praise the Lord in his saints;  
> praise him in the firmament of his power (Psalm 150:1).

For this to be done worthily, faith must first be applied, because all his works are in faith. Then understanding must be sought; otherwise, as Isaiah says, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9).

The intelligible things of God are worthily understood through those creatures which, as has been said, have been made and are being made in his saints, when they are considered in faith with the piety of devotion; and, once understood, they are truly praised in full (Romans 1:20).

This praise is pleasing in the sight of God and his angels, and is received with so much greater favor as God is more wisely believed by faith and piously seen through the same holy and true works.

Hence David, greatly rejoicing, exhorts us by repeating his appeal three times:

> Sing praises to our God;  
> sing praises;  
> sing praises to our King (Psalm 47:7);

namely, to the Father and the Son. And so that God the Trinity may be commended together with the Holy Spirit, he says:

> Sing praises wisely (ibid., verse 8).

Whoever does not rightly understand or believe these things seems to sing not wisely, I do not say, but not even profitably—he sings in vain.

Therefore, beloved, apply diligence at the festivals of all the saints, but especially at this celebration of the Mother of God, so that by understanding rightly and living correctly you may stand worthily in her praises and sing wisely to God. For whatever is most devotedly offered to his mother is undoubtedly offered to him, to whom every hidden thing rightly lies open . . . [lacuna]

# Dubious Sermons of Saint Hildefonsus

## Notice to the Reader

Do not be surprised, excellent reader, that you see the following sermons counted by us among the doubtful and uncertain works of Saint Hildefonsus, although you hear them very frequently praised as his by men who are not unlearned and although, by common opinion, they have been accepted as Hildefonsian.

We have done this neither rashly nor without the support of other men distinguished by great learning—without whose support we would never have dared to pronounce judgment on them so openly. We are not unaware how much hostility is involved in undertaking to uproot opinions in some sense consecrated by age and deeply fixed in people’s minds, nor how difficult it is for one occupied with examining and judging the works of the holy Fathers somewhat more carefully to escape the charge of excessive criticism.

Accordingly, when we say that it is very uncertain whether these sermons truly belong to Saint Hildefonsus, we do so only after serious reflection and a lengthy examination of them; after many comparisons among the sermons themselves and with the other works of the holy Doctor; with men distinguished in every branch of learning and erudition always serving as our guides; and, finally, only after being compelled by weighty arguments. It will be worthwhile to explain all this at somewhat greater length.

Nothing concerning the sermons of Saint Hildefonsus had come down to the memory of later times beyond the testimony of historians, who mention several sermons written by him and published together with his other works. Nor had later centuries seen any copy of them until the sixteenth century, when, first of all, Franciscus Feu-ardentius, a noble Parisian theologian from the family of the Friars Minor, published twelve sermons under the name of the holy Doctor from an ancient manuscript codex—which, he writes, had been brought from Spain by Gotiscalcus, bishop among the Aquitanians—together with the book *On the Perpetual Virginity of Holy Mary* and the other little book *On Childbearing*, printed above.

The otherwise exceptionally keen-sighted man was deceived, perhaps because he found sermons bearing such a title, and because the attribution did not conflict with the truth, since it was established that Saint Hildefonsus had written sermons. He was perhaps deceived because he had found the sermons inscribed with that name. Everyone received, approved, and praised the discovered and published treasure with common acclaim. Each person brought forward, embellished, and expanded Hildefonsus’s opinions. No one even slightly doubted them or applied his mind to examining them. Consequently, not long afterward the common opinion spread among all learned men that these sermons were genuine offspring of Hildefonsus.

After this, however, it happened that certain scholars, applying themselves seriously to reading them, encountered several things which at first sight seemed less acceptable in their judgment. This led them to consider bringing the sermons back for renewed examination and investigating their legitimate parentage more carefully.

The first among these to come to our attention was Father Joannes Poza. In his *Elucidarium of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, while undertaking to examine testimonies drawn from our Hildefonsus in order to illuminate the question of the undefiled conception of the Mother of God, he sought to separate uncertain and spurious passages from those that were certain and genuine.

He thought he had found many things in these sermons that were entirely alien both to Hildefonsus’s manner and style and to his doctrine and piety—things that ought not rashly, or without the most serious proofs, to be attributed to so great a Doctor. Yet no such proofs existed.

Theophilus Raynaud, having newly examined the matter, agreed with Poza’s judgment. Don Nicolaus Antonius, who followed them, likewise willingly supported the judgment of both in his *Ancient Library of Spain*, after reproducing Poza’s censure in the same words.

Afterward Father Remigius de Ceillier, in his work published in French on ecclesiastical writers, says that he cannot in any way persuade himself that the sermons in question belong to Saint Hildefonsus.

Therefore, if we follow these scholars, the aforesaid sermons must be denied to Saint Hildefonsus on two grounds: the doctrine they contain and the particular style of each one.

But, to speak frankly, we cannot approve Poza’s censure in matters concerning doctrine. For unless we are completely blind, we do not see what in them can rightly be accused of error.

The learned man considers three matters discordant with the faith and wholly intolerable to pious ears.

First, in Sermon 5, *On the Assumption*, the author is said not to affirm without hesitation that the blessed Virgin was assumed bodily into heaven—although it is pious to believe this—lest uncertain things be accepted as certain.

Second, in the preceding sermon, he dares, with a certain pious boldness, to assert that the feast of the Assumption brings some remedy and refreshment to the infernal prison, so that on that day the Tartarean ministers do not dare to reach their captives, whom they remember to have been redeemed by the blood of the Son of so great a Virgin.

Third and finally, in the homily *On the Purification*, he asserts that the body of the Lord Christ was formed in the Virgin’s womb over a period of forty days.

This is the substance of the entire censure, each point of which is easily refuted.

For the author’s doubtful statement concerning the bodily assumption of the Virgin was taken from the sermon *On the Assumption*, which he cites under the name of Saint Jerome. It certainly does not belong to Jerome, but either to Sophronius, a Greek author contemporary with Jerome, as some hold, or, as others maintain, to a much later author—though still one belonging to those earlier centuries.

That author could assert without offense that some people at that time piously believed the blessed Virgin had been assumed bodily into heaven, while it could not be affirmed without hesitation as something certain. We perceive no error in this.

Nor, if someone in Hildefonsus’s century had expressed the same judgment, would it easily have been possible to accuse him of error, since this belief was not held with certainty in all churches or by all doctors, but only in some—as is inferred from the second sermon *On the Assumption*, falsely attributed to Augustine, whose author wrote after Saint Isidore, whom he praises.

Nevertheless, once the belief was received by the universal Church and all sacred doctors agreed in that truth, anyone who dared to deny it or doubt it would not escape the charge of rashness.

The following objection is no more compelling: in second place, it was alleged that on the anniversary of her Assumption the Virgin brought refreshment and relief to those confined in the prisons of hell. For who would be surprised that a teacher of those times should have willingly indulged in such a pious boldness, as he himself calls it, in the glory of the blessed Virgin, if he knew that Saint Augustine (*Enchiridion*, chap. 112) did not dare to condemn the opinion of certain people who believed that the punishments of the damned might be mitigated to some degree at fixed intervals of time, so that God would not contain his mercies within his anger—not by bringing eternal punishment to an end, but by applying relief or interrupting the torments? Moreover, how can it be proved that the author here spoke of people eternally condemned to hell on account of grave sins, rather than of holy souls tormented in Purgatory? Indeed, the names “damned” and “captives” are applicable to these latter as well, and no one doubts that they are tormented by Tartarean ministers in the prisons of hell.

Finally, as to the last objection—that the Lord’s body was formed in the Virgin’s womb over a period of forty days—if it presents any difficulty (as certainly it does), it is no different from the difficulty found in Augustine’s words in *Book Eighty-Three Questions*, question 56. This passage appears to have been taken from there by the writer of that homily. Yet since, after the Master of the Sentences, there has been no theologian who has not interpreted Augustine’s words in a sound sense, a solution to this passage may be adapted from their commentaries. With these accusations concerning doctrine therefore dispelled, let us set forth the remaining observations by which it is demonstrated that these sermons should in no way be regarded as established works of Hildefonsus.

First, the consideration that most persuaded Feu-ardentius that these sermons were Hildefonsus’s was that he had found them in a sufficiently old manuscript together with other works of that holy doctor. But just as this circumstance magnifies the error of so great a man, so it later became clear how little weight it carried. For immediately after Hildefonsus’s little book *On the Perpetual Virginity of the Mother of God*, that manuscript also contained the other treatise *On Childbirth*, recently edited by us, which, as we have already warned, no one attributes to Hildefonsus. Although it appears under his name, long experience has shown that among the ancients, before the invention of the art of printing, it was customary to gather into the same manuscript the writings of various doctors dealing especially with the same general subject, very often without marking the difference between their authors. This practice has produced an immense number of errors concerning the genuine works of each author.

Examples abound everywhere. To mention no others, we found a similar case in our own Amelian Codex, already frequently cited in the edition of these little works. It is almost entirely copied according to the model of the codex used by Feu-ardentius: the treatises in both are the same and arranged in the same order, except that ours is more correct and contains one additional sermon, entitled *On Saint Mary*. Yet after all this we noticed that several parchment leaves had been cut away. They undoubtedly contained another treatise on the praises of the blessed Virgin, whose very full index still remains at the end of the codex, written in the same hand as the rest. Nevertheless, that little book should not on this account be considered Hildefonsus’s; it may instead be by Anselm or by someone else who wrote on the praises of blessed Mary.

Considerable weight is added to this observation by what learned men have noticed concerning the style of these works. [Col. 0239] Although they had no certain and established sermon of Hildefonsus with which to compare them, nevertheless, so far as they could infer from his other works, they saw in these writings anything but Hildefonsus. For that distinctive manner of writing and formation of the Latin language which expresses, as it were, the characteristic mark of the Gothic Fathers nowhere appears. One fact will certainly be evident to anyone who reads them with even moderate attention: they were composed in not one or two but many different styles, which reveals multiple authors. The first and the fourth, which is virtually an abridgment of the first, are said to belong to one author; the third, fifth, and sixth have the character of another; the seventh and eighth are altogether different from those preceding them; the tenth resembles none of the earlier ones. One is entirely woven from scriptural testimonies; others abound in citations from the Fathers and doctors.

The following fact is especially worthy of notice: although Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and the poet Sedulius are sometimes praised in these works, the name of Gregory the Great is nowhere heard—not, I say, of that Gregory who alone was, for our Gothic Fathers, the equal of all others; whose teaching above all delighted them; whose sayings they always had on their lips and with which they were accustomed to sprinkle every discourse. This may be seen both in Isidore’s works and in Hildefonsus’s own books *On the Annotation of Baptism* and *On the Progress of the Spiritual Desert*. Yet in his book *On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary* he made no mention of Gregory, just as he mentioned no other doctor, being wholly intent on pressing the testimonies of Scripture as circumstances required.

From all this it may reasonably be concluded that none of the first eleven sermons can be attributed to our Hildefonsus on any firm basis. Nor is the judgment concerning the last three, which we add, any more certain. The only argument for the first of these, entitled *On Saint Mary*, is that a single codex, the Amelian, presents it among the others. The two remaining sermons persuaded Father Florezius of their authenticity because, after the editors of Saint Augustine—who was believed to be their author—had rejected them as spurious, they were found in his own thirteenth-century manuscript, after the little book *On the Virginity of Saint Mary*, under the name of Saint Hildefonsus. We have seen how much weight that argument possesses in itself, unless a firmer conjecture can be drawn from style and subject matter. We leave that judgment to learned readers, who, after reading these sermons, will decide what similarity they bear both to the genuine style of the holy doctor and to the sermons preceding them. We leave the matter undecided and proceed to an accurate edition of them.

[Col. 0239]

[SERMONS (C, G, S)\*]

## SERMON ONE. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE MOST BLESSED AND GLORIOUS VIRGIN MARY

[Col. 0239A]

Today, beloved brothers, we celebrate the birthday-feast of blessed Mary; [Note: [Col. 0239C] “And now, aided by your sincere merits”—the reading of Codex Amelianus—which is more tolerable than Feu-ardentius’s: “also by your merits in heaven, etc.”] and now, aided by your sincere merits and prayers, may she deign to intervene, so that I too may be able solemnly to exhort you to advance in your salvation, and you may devoutly receive what is said, so that we may all be found worthy together in her praises. For the almighty God requires not so much the accomplishment of great things as the will. And therefore, as I believe, for your good will, beloved, he will grant the power of speaking which inexperience denies, and he has also given you the fullest grace of understanding, since we have come joyfully and devoutly to celebrate her festival, before whose bed the multitude of the heavenly host once sang:

> Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.  
> (Luke 2:14)

Therefore, let good will be ours in affection; certainly, God’s assistance will be ours in its outcome, so that we may both suitably understand the one whom we praise and religiously praise the Virgin whose solemnities we celebrate today.

Before her bed, where the child is laid in the stable, the singing angels invite us, as I have said:

> Glory to God in the highest,

to make known by their voices that the one who has been born in the flesh is both God and man. Because he is God, there is “glory in the highest,” where sin is absent and perpetual praise is proclaimed ever more fully. But because that same one is man, on earth, where sedition and wars are incessant, “peace to people of good will” is announced for the reconciliation brought by the Mediator; and thus one and the same Christ embraces both realities. Therefore, above in heaven, the glory of the citizens on high is not diminished but increased; nor below on earth, because of discord, is peace to people of good will frustrated, but it is granted.

For this reason, the choir of the holy prophets invites us to the cradle of this infant, which the angels frequent; indeed, the Wisdom of God the Father and the Holy Spirit invite us as well:

[Col. 0239C] “Before the bed of this Virgin,” they say, “frequent for us the sweet songs of drama.” For *dramaton*, dearest ones, is a kind of poem, and it is in this genre that the *Song of Songs* is understood to have been composed. Behold, we are commanded, so that charity may be commended more abundantly, to frequent in this manner of singing sweet songs in honor of this Virgin, where at times singing angels celebrate her praises, the archangel Gabriel announces the good news, the approaching star shines forth, the Magi come and adore and bring gifts, prophesying through their gifts; the shepherds hear and speak; they come, see, and understand the incarnate Word whom the Lord reveals to them.

Therefore, dearest women, where such great things are displayed, [Note: [Col. 0239C] “Strive,” Codex Amelianus.] rise, singing psalms with hymns and spiritual songs in your hearts to the Lord, and sing with the angels, [Note: [Col. 0239C] “Sing,” the same manuscript.] saying:

> Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.  
> (Luke 2:14)

For this is the mother of the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0240C] “Through whom,” Amelianus.] through whom life is restored. This is the fruitful virgin, proclaimed by many signs given by the prophets. This is she who today, when all things have been completed, is taken up into heaven: she is divested of flesh and clothed with heavenly glory.

This virgin arose from the race of Abraham, in whose seed all nations were blessed, from the tribe of Judah. Hence it was said:

> The ruler shall not fail from Judah until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.  
> (Genesis 49:10)

She is the rod from the root of Jesse, from whose root, in turn, Christ the flower ascended (Isaiah 11). She is the most illustrious Virgin, descended from the stock of David, to whom God the Father once said in the Spirit:

> I will place upon your throne the fruit of your womb.  
> (Psalm 31:11)

Behold, sons, to her all the sayings of the prophets converge; to her all the riddles of Scripture converge. From her Christ, God and man, was born formerly on earth, so that today, taken up from the body, she might be reborn in heaven. Therefore she is rightly sung as the daughter of Jerusalem, although the Most High, who once founded her, was born from her (Psalm 86).

In truth, that heavenly mother has today come to meet us, adorned with her jewels, of whom it is said:

> I saw Jerusalem descending from heaven, from God, adorned [Note: [Col. 0240C] “With pure gold,” from Codex Amelianus, in place of “by a worldly man” in Feu-ardentius.] with pure gold and inlaid with precious stones. [Note: [Col. 0240C] “With which,” Feu-ardentius.]

She has indeed descended adorned today for this reason: to carry with her the Queen of the world, namely blessed Mary, to the heights and place her upon the throne of the kingdom. Otherwise she would not have come to meet her with such official splendor, unless the festival were a great one.

Therefore, sons, or whoever you are—boys and girls, old and young alike—prepare yourselves with joyful conduct for the festival of so great a Virgin. Bring forth [Col. 0241A] choirs of spiritual joy, [Note: [Col. 0241D] “So that you may be able to recite the songs that you have heard, or that you sing,” Feu-ardentius.] so that you may teach the songs that you hear or sing. Otherwise, because praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, you are not suited to these festivals until you have stripped yourselves of vices.

Therefore she is called the star of the sea, which heaven has today received into its own dwelling, because, according to the Hebrew word, *Maria* [Note: [Col. 0241D] See Saint Bernard, homily 2, *On “Missus est.”*] is interpreted in this way. Hence act, dearest women, so that that morning star which knows no setting may arise in your hearts while you are in this world. For the sea is the present age, while the star is blessed Mary the Virgin, from whom arose the one through whom the whole world is illumined.

Approach her praise, then, with greater confidence, and be enlightened, because she is the one through whom the true light shone upon the sea of this age. She is the handmaid of the Lord, according to what she herself said after Gabriel’s ineffable promises:

> Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.  
> (Luke 1:38)

Therefore learn, dearest women, to humble yourselves; learn to be meek, because this is the one virtue in which she especially glories that the Lord looked upon her, so that you too may glory in the same humility. For she is also called the queen of our world. Act with her, so that you may be able to reign where the humble are exalted and the proud cast down; where the meek rule and those who are presently lifted up in their arrogance are reduced to servitude.

Behold, all the generations of the ages now call her blessed, for she long ago adorned herself with such great virtues that she is rightly called both bride and mother of her Creator.

Before her bed, I ask you, let there again be sung—not dirges of sorrow or laments of weeping for her funeral—but songs sweet to God, [Note: [Col. 0241D] “Set to music,” Feu-ardentius.] melodiously voiced, because today she has joyfully reached the bridal chamber of the King. The mother who gave birth has therefore arrived where the honey-sweet organs of the angels sound without ceasing, where choirs of saints, singing hymns, alternate nuptial songs from side to side, and where the epithalamia of bridegroom and bride are rendered sweet by their melodies.

To this wedding, then, the blessed Mother of God entered today with joy. She was once the temple of the Creator, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit—the sanctuary, I say, of God, because all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in her womb (Colossians 2:3), and there the Word became flesh, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells (ibid., 2:9). Yet Christ is the temple of the Word in one way, and the blessed Virgin in another, because the Virgin’s womb was like a lodging from which Christ God came forth to us, like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber, strong in power like a giant.

Moreover, Christ God and man was the one mediator between God and human beings (1 Timothy 2:5): not one being God and another man, so that the temple and the Word would be two, but one and the same Christ Jesus. When he is dissolved in death, God in his human nature, although immortal, is proclaimed dead on account of the unity [Note: [Col. 0241D] “Of substance,” Codex Amelianus, in place of “of subsistence.”] of his subsistence. Thus the one who is the temple and the one who is the Word are not different; the Word and the temple are one Christ. And because they are one and the same, he cannot be divided in his passion according to substance, nor in his majesty.

[Col. 0241D] Thus the Mother of God is also proclaimed beautiful, like a dove, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun (Song of Songs 6:9), because that dove which remained over Christ had filled her completely. Therefore, on account of this beauty of adornment, she is rightly praised as beautiful in the loveliness of her virtues.

Fair as the moon—indeed, fairer than the moon—because in her appearance the race [Note: [Col. 0241D] “Race” is found in Amelianus, in place of “nation” in Feu-ardentius.] of all the churches shines forth, illumined by the sun of justice, so that it may be able to destroy the darkness of the present life and make us all belong to that place to which the blessed Virgin has attained, where she now suffers no diminution of light, because the fruit of her labors and grace is glorious.

Therefore, beloved, imitate her while opportunity and time remain—her whom all the saints praise and love, who today has gone forth from earth to heaven, chosen as the sun. And behold, forever brighter than the sun, she triumphs crowned before the Lord. In this Virgin, as in the sun, the King once placed his tabernacle (Psalm 18:6), and the Bridegroom came forth to us from his bridal chamber, the King of virtues, the King of glory, so that all might reign through him.

O how beautiful and admirable is a chaste generation with [Note: [Col. 0241D] We have emended the reading to “brightness,” although both Codex Amelianus and Feu-ardentius’s edition plainly read “charity.” We made the emendation not so much because of the common reading, from which we often see reason to depart, but rather because of the words that follow: “And if she is renowned among virgins, and renowned with the praise of a good reputation, etc.”] brightness (Wisdom 4:1)! And if she is renowned among virgins, and renowned with the praise of a good reputation, much more so is Mary, Mother of God, who remained a virgin and yet was a fruitful mother. Her illustrious memory of virtues reigns immortally with God and human beings.

For this reason, sons, imitate her and desire her, who today, already adorned for the bridal chamber, bride and wife, mother and virgin, entered the wedding. She entered with her seal wholly intact, marked by the sign of modesty, because every virginity and chastity is honored before God, so that it may be acceptable and approved. Those who imitate her will be counted among her companions; and blessed is she who has not known a marriage-bed in sin, for she will have fruit in the visitation of holy souls (Wisdom 3:13).

Therefore, I ask you, sons, imitate the seal of your faith, blessed Mary, whom the Holy Spirit, like fire acting upon iron, wholly tempered, heated, and kindled, so that in her [Note: [Col. 0242D] “Nothing but the flame of the Holy Spirit.” Those words are absent from Feu-ardentius, but Codex Amelianus contains them.] nothing but the flame of the Holy Spirit might be seen, and nothing but the fire of the love of God might be felt.

For she is that enclosed garden of delights, the sealed fountain (Song of Songs 4:12), the well of living waters, the restoration of life, the gate of heaven, the glory of women, the summit of all virgins. Like the cedar of Lebanon, she multiplies and spreads her branches daily on earth [Note: [Col. 0242D] “Will multiply and spread,” in Feu-ardentius.] and is strengthened with roots in heaven, so that she may grow further. She is exalted like a palm tree, blooms like a beautiful olive in the fields, and [Note: [Col. 0242D] “Will bear fruit,” Amelianus; “bears fruit,” Feu-ardentius.] will bear fruit in the house of God forever (Ecclesiasticus 24:17–19).

Into that house she entered joyfully today, and the souls of all the elect who belong to her follow her. O! If we were permitted to know what joys of that life she entered today; what pleasant places of that flowering paradise; what fellowship of angels; how great the service of heaven; and what an exultant number of holy souls came to meet her! How many secrets of mysteries were shown to her today; how ineffable were the joys disclosed! I do not say that anyone could explain in words—or even worthily conceive—what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart.

Therefore, sons, contemplate the Mother of the Lord, who, like a vine, produced the sweetness of fragrance and brought forth for all nations the fruit of honor and grace (Ecclesiasticus 24:23). She blossomed as an honored mother, as the mother of beautiful love and fear, as the mother of the knowledge of God and of hope, in whom is every hope of life and virtue (ibid., 24–26). She alone shone forth as a holy virgin among women, like a lily among thorns.

A prudent virgin, a most chaste virgin, a most beautiful and fruitful virgin: beautiful and undefiled in body, radiant in spirit, clear in faith, distinguished in life, devoted to the love of virginity, [Col. 0243A] ready in every obedience to virtue, and most careful in the ministry entrusted to her. In the passion of Christ a sword pierced her soul, and the fervor of divine love refined her through every anguish.

She, then, is the one proclaimed by the prophets and also proclaimed by philosophers, greeted by the archangel, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, and overshadowed by the same Spirit. Ignorant of male seed yet made fruitful with offspring, [Note: [Col. 0243D] “Virgin” is read in Amelianus as “man”; and later, where Feu-ardentius has “who by faith,” the reading is “which by faith.”] an unmarried virgin, glorified in her son, she conceived by faith and gave birth with joy.

She was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth. The God who became man, whom the whole world cannot contain, enclosed himself within her womb. He who fills heaven and earth, for whom heaven is a throne and earth the footstool of his feet (Isaiah 66:1); he who holds the heavens in the span of his hand, weighs the mass of the earth with three fingers, and encloses it in his fist (Isaiah 40:12)—this holy Virgin wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger (Luke 2:7).

Therefore, she who feeds all things heavenly and earthly and rules them together nourished him with the milk of her flesh. At whose command all things are then governed, God as an infant lived under her discipline or authority. And, more wondrous still, the defender and creator of all fled like an exile [Note: [Col. 0243D] “Into Egypt,” Feu-ardentius.] into Egypt (Matthew 2:14).

What more is there to say? He who holds all things suspended as though on a balance was suspended upon the cross. The blessed Virgin suffered greatly over him and endured much, wounded in soul by the sword of Christ’s passion and pierced through by the weapon.

O most holy of all women, who on earth had such great and intimate companionship with God! And behold, today she is exalted beside the one whom she bore, so that she may remain glorious in heaven without end. She lived with the apostles, and as long as they were together she remained with them in unanimous prayer, conferring with them until all the mysteries of Christ’s promise were fulfilled and they themselves were scattered far and wide for the work of preaching (Acts 1:14).

Afterward, how happily she lived under the protection of the angels and the care of John! O illustrious Virgin! Behold, you remain on earth while you send your son, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, ahead to heaven; yet more blessed and fortunate, you too pass gloriously among the angels. Secure and rejoicing, you now proceed, because you know that your same son, our Lord, now sits at the right hand of the Father in the glory of his divinity [Note: [Col. 0243D] “To ascend,” according to Codex Amelianus.].

How blessed, therefore, and worthy of praise is the celebration of this day, on which the wondrous Virgin, with the praises of the heavenly host, [Note: [Col. 0244D] We have emended “below” to “within,” following Amelianus.] is received within the palace of the heavens with immense triumph! From her flesh the Lord Jesus, the Word, became flesh; he deigned to open the gates of paradise to all who believe in him. He placed his mother with him upon the throne of the kingdom, transferred her into the glory of immortality, and raised her above the choirs of angels with supreme solemnity.

Therefore, dearest women, celebrate worthily the solemnity of this day, over which the angels exult, the archangels rejoice, and that entire heavenly Jerusalem, the glorious city, celebrates. O! If we were permitted to know how great the joy and ineffable gladness there are, how great the exultation of the holy souls at the sight of such glory; how great the service of the blessed spirits and the number of angels who today came joyfully to meet the Mother of the Word of God; into what great and blessed joys she entered today—things that eye has not seen and ear has not heard!

What she received is invisible and ineffable. As has already been said, she now sees her son, our Lord Jesus Christ, whom she once grieved and suffered greatly to see hanging on the cross, exalted above all things and reigning at the right hand of the Father. Every order of heaven joyfully adores him; they cling to him in reverence, and, clinging to the immortal God, live immortally.

To him today that same blessed mother and virgin joyfully sings:

> My soul has clung to you; therefore your right hand has received me.  
> (Psalm 62:9)

For nothing is more joyful or more pleasing than what she herself sings:

> You have held my right hand; in your will you have led me, and with glory [Note: [Col. 0244D] “You have received me,” Amelianus.] received me.  
> (Psalm 72:24)

And elsewhere: [Note: [Col. 0244D] Feu-ardentius: “For what is there for me in heaven, etc.”]

> What have I in heaven, and apart from you what did I desire upon earth?  
> (ibid., 25)

As though she were saying: “I desired nothing but you, the one Lord, to see you whom I loved, whom I worshiped, whom I desired, whom I long sought with my whole heart, that you might be as you are. And behold, now I see you; now I hold you, to whom I once entrusted myself with complete devotion. I will not let go of the one whom I loved. And because my heart and my flesh have now failed through love, therefore you, God of my heart, will henceforth be my portion forever” (ibid., 26).

Then, turning to her companions—and perhaps joyfully to the other saints as well—she says today:

> As we have heard, O beloved ones, so now we see in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God, which God founded forever.

Of that glorious city things were once proclaimed to us; now we see them and enjoy them with the fullest vision of love.

Therefore, for such joys and others like them, in which the saints exult with her in glory and rejoice upon their couches (Psalm 149:5), let us also rejoice, dearest women, in the hope of the children of God, and let us implore through their intercessions that we may reach what we believe they have attained with the blessed Virgin—believing with the heart unto righteousness and confessing with the mouth unto salvation. For then are we true praisers, if we pursue what they pursued and hasten to come to that faith which works through love.

Otherwise, we are careless, vain observers and wicked praisers, if, while they are crowned and receive palms because they fought lawfully in the contest, we do not also strive, according to our measure, to reach those things worthily. For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought to walk as he walked (1 John 2:6).

Therefore, as has often been said, imitate the Mother of the Lord, who gave birth for you to an immortal bridegroom. Imitate [Col. 0244C] the saints as well, whose examples, by God’s favor, are read in great number. Follow the bridegroom, and hasten to enter where the blessed Virgin entered today, into the eternal wedding. Prepare your lamps, so that when the bridegroom comes and knocks, he may find you watchful, because blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds prepared and vigilant (Luke 12:37), just as today he found her vigilant.

Today, indeed, she deserved in great joy to hear this from the *Song of Songs*:

> Rise, come, my beloved, my bride, my dove, my undefiled one; for behold, winter has passed, the rain has gone away and departed.  
> (Song of Songs 2:10–11)

Perhaps, rejoicing at the arrival of the citizens above, she answered:

> Flowers have appeared in our land, because the time of pruning has come.  
> (ibid., 12)

And then:

> I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.  
> (Psalm 26:13)

“Those good things once promised to the saints; the good things that are in Christ Jesus, whom I bore, whom I fed and nourished, toward whom my soul long thirsted to come, to God the living fountain (Psalm 41:3). And behold, today at last, rejoicing, I come when called, and I shall appear before the face of God.”

Therefore she says:

> My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody in my glory.  
> (Psalm 107:2)

As though she were plainly saying: “I will sing and make melody in Christ, who is my glory, whom you gave me as a son, through whom not only greater glory but also adoption is granted to all. Therefore, now joyful and secure, return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you; hence I shall please him in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:9).

Blessed, then, exceedingly blessed, is the virginity that at its end is adorned with such and so many gifts, and, heaped with so many virtues, is exalted, so that today, rejoicing with jubilation, it may sing this Davidic song:

> How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord.  
> (Psalm 83:2–3)

[Note: [Col. 0245D] “As though she were plainly saying”—these words are absent from Feu-ardentius.]

As though she were plainly saying: “My heart and my flesh first rejoiced in the living God when I bore him in the flesh, when I suckled him, when I nourished him, and when I brought him to maturity. Now he himself is my king and my God, whom I bore, whom I believed in by faith, and whom I desired in my heart.”

Therefore you too, daughters, do the will of the Father, so that you may be sisters and mothers of Christ, just as he himself says:

> Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.  
> (Matthew 12:50)

Do the will of my Father. [Note: [Col. 0245D] “My” is absent from Codex Amelianus.]

Since you are now brides, love the bridegroom to whom you have vowed yourselves; and since you are daughters by adoption, [Note: [Col. 0245D] “May he recognize you as sisters,” the reading of Amelianus; “sisters” is absent from Feu-ardentius.] may the Son of the supreme King recognize you as sisters.

But lest any one of you perhaps wish to become more wanton on that account, because the name you have sought is a lofty one, it is fitting to remember that you were bought with his great blood as your dowry. Therefore, according to the Apostle:

> Glorify God and carry him in your body.  
> (1 Corinthians 6:20)

Imitate the bridegroom and love him, because you are brides. Imitate the Virgin Mother and all the saints whom you praise, because our praise does not benefit them as much as their imitation benefits us. Hence the devoted imitator pleases the bridegroom more than the idle praiser. Yet true praise is imitation in deed. For truly to praise God and the saints in him is already a work of virtue, when the mind advances, is kindled by the fire of divine love, and is strengthened upon the foundation of true humility.

With this humility, the blessed Virgin Mother, founded in Christ after all that had been divinely promised to her, said:

> Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.  
> (Luke 1:38)

Hence she also says in her song:

> Because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid, behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.  
> (ibid., 48)

Blessed and happy, therefore, is the mind which, amid outstanding virtues and an abundance of gifts, humbled itself so greatly, because [Note: [Col. 0245D] “The Lord on high,” Amelianus.] the Lord has looked upon the humble in heaven and on earth (Psalm 112:6), and knows the lofty from afar. If he seeks the humble in heaven among the angels, what do you think he seeks on earth, sons, where we are nothing but ashes and worms, except together with sin?

Therefore imitate the Mother of the Lord and obey your fathers. Humble yourselves among the virginal flowers, because the gifts of chastity and the endowments of virtue come from the grace of God. Implore him in your prayers; say with the Prophet:

> Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.  
> (Psalm 113:9)

Whoever you are, if you are what you vowed to be, it is God’s gift and the grace of the Redeemer. His, I say, are the gifts whose mother today ascended gloriously into heaven and entered the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, amid the voice of exultation and joy, where the sound of feasting is continual (Psalm 41:5–6).

Therefore, from the place where she had earlier sung:

> Taste and see that the Lord is sweet  
> (Psalm 33:9),

she now feasts and rejoices with all the saints. Concerning this enjoyment of delights the Lord says through Isaiah:

> Behold, those who serve me and who carry it together will drink in my holy courts; but you shall thirst. Behold, those who serve me shall rejoice; but you shall be put to shame. Behold, those who serve me shall exult for joy; but you shall cry out because of anguish of heart, and because of contrition of spirit you shall howl.  
> (Isaiah 65:13–14)

You have, then, daughters, the joys of eternal life, to which blessed and undefiled virginity has reached today. Strive [Col. 0246A] also to enter through the narrow gate (Luke 13:24) into the bridal chamber of your Bridegroom, whose dowry and bridal pledge you have received as a gift. Strive and take care to merit the good things promised to you, so that you may receive them [Note: [Col. 0245D] “With the remaining virgins,” Amelianus.] with the other virgins. Concerning these things each believer sings in the psalm:

> One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek.  
> (Psalm 26:4)

And:

> I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.  
> (ibid., 13)

These good things blessed Mary the Virgin received today in the greatest joy, [Note: [Col. 0246D] “She will enjoy them with the angels,” the reading of Codex Amelianus; Feu-ardentius has: “she enjoys them and with the angels, etc.”] to enjoy them forever with the angels. Today she is crowned in the kingdom prepared for her long ago together with the saints from the foundation of the world. Today she is placed upon the throne at God’s right hand, as it is sung in the Psalms:

> The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded by a variety of virtues.  
> (Psalm 44:10)

Come, I ask you, citizens of Jerusalem—whoever you are, men; whatever your state, virgins, widows, boys, or girls—and behold with complete purity of heart; look more attentively upon the Mother of the Lord, shining in the heavenly dwelling with the crown of her diadem. Come, I say, in mind, faith, and devotion, and behold her crowned on the day of her solemnity and joy with the crown of gladness and beauty with which the Lord, the Bridegroom of virgins, the King of glory and rewarder of all good things, has crowned her.

Come, I ask you, and behold, for today the ark of God’s covenant has been transferred to the heights above, gilded outwardly with virtues and fashioned inwardly with the purest gold of majesty. In it were the law of God’s covenant and the manna that had flowed down from heaven; in it also was Aaron’s rod that had blossomed. Concerning this rod David says in the Psalms: “The Lord will send forth from Zion,” he says, “the rod of your power” (Ps. 109:2). Then, addressing it directly, he says: “Rule in the midst of your enemies” (ibid.).

This rod, indeed, blossoming for us, brought forth the most peaceful fruit of salvation, which for a time germinated within the Virgin’s womb as a mystical sacrament. Hence also, concerning her, it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your navel is a turned vessel, lacking nothing of drink; and your belly is a heap of wheat, surrounded with lilies” [Col. 0246C] (Song 7:2), because Christ’s birth from the Virgin corresponds to this in every respect.

Indeed, that womb was a turned vessel.  
[Note: Amel.: “It was a turned vessel.”]

For wisdom poured itself into it; wisdom mixed its wine in the vessel, possessing an unfailing grace of knowledge and supplying the fullness of its divinity. In the Virgin’s womb, therefore, both a heap of wheat and the flowers of lilies germinated by Christ’s grace, since Christ was both a grain of wheat and a lily.  
[Note: We have corrected “grain” from our Amelian manuscript in place of “grace,” which was erroneously printed in Feu-ardent.]

He was a grain, as he says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24). But because from one and the same grain of wheat heaps of grain grew, this prophetic saying was fulfilled: “The valleys will abound in grain” (Ps. 64:14), because that dead grain produced abundant fruit.

This grain, then, was the manna; and therefore it satisfied all human beings with the perpetual harvest of heavenly gifts. Hence David says: “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” [Col. 0246D] (Ps. 80:17).

The divine utterances also testify that this grain too is a lily. “I am,” he says, “the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1).

For this reason the womb of that Virgin is represented by the ark, which contained within itself all the mysteries of the sacraments. It contained that living bread which came down from heaven (John 6:51); it also contained the law of the New Covenant, because she bore the Lawgiver, in whom are “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3).

And so, rightly, the virgin Mary was the ark of God’s sacraments. Above her, in truth, the mercy seat and the cherubim [Col. 0247A] overshadowing it on either side are represented, because no contagion of sin entered Mary from outside; rather, within her were the complete keeping of the law and the manna—which is a wondrous sacrament and the propitiation of human salvation. The propitiation was rightly placed above the ark, because he himself, the blessed God, is our propitiation above all things.

Therefore, dearest women, lift up your hearts to the heights, where today, so to speak, the ark of the covenant is carried most gloriously by the angels to the sublime realms. Fix your minds where the female sex has arrived, and where virginity consecrated to the Lord has arrived, having above it the One from whom divine responses are given to the faithful from the midst of the cherubim, and in whom reconciliation is granted to those who rightly believe.

Therefore, whatever you wish to offer to God in your minds, send it there in faith; there present your vows; from there bring back what you have obtained through your prayers, since there is no other place through which you can please God the Father except in the One in whom the Father established his entire good pleasure.

Hence, I ask you, hear him speaking to you daily from the mercy seat, because in him and from him is the sum of our redemption. And if there are any offerings that we make in faith, let us offer everything through him in whom God determined to be pleased with himself, since there is no other way by which we can please him. “This is,” he says, “my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 17:5). Therefore listen to him speaking in the Gospel; listen to him in the sacred Scriptures, in which from the beginning the Father’s will is shown through the Son.

And because today the ark of God’s covenant has been brought into that heavenly Jerusalem with joyful exultation, I ask you to celebrate the feast most devoutly with hymns and songs, with the whole assembly of the people. If David, together with all the people, judged it fitting to escort the ark of the Old Covenant with such honor, as Scripture testifies, it is much more religious that this ark should be commended with worthy praises.

For the divine word says that David and all the people went up with him to carry the ark of God, upon which the name of the God of hosts, who sits above the cherubim, had been invoked. Then, it says, David and all the people danced before the Lord with all their strength, with songs, lyres, psalteries, tambourines, sistrums, cymbals, and trumpets (2 Sam. 6:2; 1 Chron. 13:8) [Col. 0247C].

I ask you: if, in a figure, such great glory was offered with such devotion, what do you think took place today before the blessed Virgin, when she was lifted up into the heavenly Jerusalem? How great a host of saints went before her with hymns and songs?

There is no doubt that those one hundred forty-four thousand who are before the throne and the elders, holding their harps, sang with all the thunderous sound of heaven the new song which no one can sing except themselves. They themselves come festively today to meet her with their harps, and joyfully welcome the Virgin into their blessed chorus—not just any virgin, but one of the number of the wise, the first of all among the foremost, who follows the Lamb nearest of all, wherever he goes.

She too sings with them the new song of the drama, which no one can sing except one who belongs to that chorus.  
[Note: At this point Feu-ardent contains the entire sentence: “For *dramaton* is a kind of song,” etc., which appears above at the beginning of this sermon. We have omitted it because it is redundant here and is not found in the Amelian manuscript.]

The saints therefore have their instruments in heaven, with which they sing sweet songs; they have psalteries and tambourines; they also have trumpets, cymbals, and sistrums, on which each one sounds worthy praises to God in his heart. Thus, one harmony of virtues is offered daily to God with rejoicing, in a voice of exultation and gladness.

All these songs of the musical kind resounded loudly in heaven today to meet the Virgin, like the voices of harpists. Perhaps the chorus of virgins first came to meet her, among whom, as I think, were the purple flower—namely Thecla and Cecilia, Agnes also and Perpetua. Then came the praiseworthy company of widows, among whom Anna, daughter of Phanuel, goes together with all the others. Sarah also, our mother, Rebecca, and Rachel came with the holy bridesmaids.  
[Note: Amel. reads “goes”; Feu-ardent reads “saw.” This is perhaps a typographical error.]

What more need be said? Today all the flocks of every order receive her joyfully, singing “Hosanna” beforehand in a dramatic jubilation before the Mother of the supreme King, who was truly the temple of the living God and the ark of the covenant.

Before this ark, we read, King David most devoutly danced naked as a figure of Christ, and after six steps offered sacrifices. If David bore with such honor the glory of that former ark which was destined to pass away—for these events were deeds enacted in figures—how much more is the ark of the living God, from whom Christ, the power and wisdom of God, was born, brought here today with praises?

All those things were shadows of what was to come; in Mary, however, there is manifest truth. Before her, Christ the King passed by with leaps from death to life and from corruption to incorruption. Thus he led the Church, together with her Mother, back to the heights, because she is the temple of God and the ark of the New Covenant, in which the true God dwells—not in figure and riddle, but in truth. For the God-man is sacrificed for the salvation of all.

In his blood the New Covenant was confirmed, the covenant which he established with our fathers and which was stored up in the Virgin’s womb, from there being brought forth to us. That Virgin, as though she were the ark, is today brought back glorified from the captivity of this age in an angelic procession—not into the Jerusalem which the army of the Chaldeans burned or devastated, but placed in that true and heavenly Jerusalem which God, and not man, founded.

Therefore, beloved, I would have you consider more attentively with how great praises we ought to accompany the Mother of God as she proceeds to the palace of heaven, whom the heavenly host venerates today; with whom angelic legions travel; at whose arrival the order of heaven dances and the multitude of saints exults. For if there is joy in heaven over one sinner on earth who repents (Luke 15:7), much more must we believe that heaven rejoices over the arrival [Col. 0248C] and glory of so great a Virgin.

Therefore let us also, I ask you, rejoice in hymns and spiritual songs; let us jubilate to God with exultation, who loved us so greatly that he himself became man—for whose sake we exist.  
[Note: The Amelian manuscript reads: “because of whom we exist.”]

And then, although we were all children of wrath, according to the Apostle (Eph. 2:3), he made us children of God by grace, which he himself is by nature.

Therefore, I beseech you, approach such grace through faith; approach continually, and behold with Moses the great vision which he saw in the bush. Behold, I say, what has now been fulfilled, and marvel at what that great patriarch foresaw in the Spirit as destined to occur.
