Otherwise, even an event that has taken place cannot be seen except in the Spirit, because it is a great vision which no one can worthily foresee and proclaim. Hence Moses says: “I will go over and see,” he says, “this great vision” (Exod. 3:3).  
[Note: “Truly great.” We have supplied these words from our Amelian manuscript; they add considerable force to the sentence.]

Truly great. For he saw that the wild bush was burning but was not consumed, which was most wondrous. But far more wondrous was that God was wholly in the bush and was called an angel. The bodily vision was indeed very wondrous, but far more wondrous was what was understood in the Spirit: he was wholly present in the flame, and what was shown through the flame was destined to come, so that neither the flame failed nor the bush was consumed by the harmless fire.

Since the bush remained unconsumed, we believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths that the virginity of blessed Mary was preserved. For the Holy Spirit, since God is a consuming fire (Deut. 4:24), wholly inflamed and kindled her, so that she became the mother of Christ and the temple of divine majesty.

The material joined to the heat did not provide fuel for the fire [Col. 0249A], nor did the shrub feel the losses of nature, though possessed by flames. So also blessed Mary, although—as God himself testifies—no one who sees God can live (Exod. 33:20), nevertheless, receiving the whole divinity into herself through the Christ whom she bore, lived untouched; thereafter she remained more blessedly a virgin and incorrupt.

This was the great vision which Moses, passing through it in the Spirit, foresaw. Therefore, shaken with fear, he did not dare to approach, because everything he saw with his eyes was ineffable. For this reason, you also, holy women of Christ, must not undervalue the vision of understanding—the fire of divinity—which you remember shining forth in Mary. For he is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, as the voice from the bush sounded forth; he was born from her.

Therefore, the reality that we behold fulfilled and that remains for salvation is greater than the figure which passed away when the truth was manifested. Hence we also call Moses blessed, because he saw from afar such great things destined to come; but Mary is more blessed, for from her came the very vision.  
[Note: We represent the reading of our Amelian manuscript, much more correct than Feu-ardent, which printed: “He who saw such things from afar and great things”; but the very vision of Mary is more blessed.]

Concerning this vision the eminent prophet Habakkuk, trembling, sings: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I was terrified” (Hab. 3:2). He was terrified when he saw something of this kind; Moses too was terrified, because what they both saw was incomprehensible to human beings.

Let us therefore also fear, lest we perhaps drift away from so great a mystery of our redemption. And let us approach in mind with confidence, through the intercession of the most sacred Virgin, the throne of the supreme Pontiff, where he himself is sacrifice, priest, advocate, and judge for us.

And because we are less fit for this, let us ask Christ through her, whose feast we celebrate today. Let us ask with all our desires; let us implore with our prayers that she may deign to pray for us to him whom she bore. For even if we do not possess merit equal to that of Moses, the prophets, or the apostles, blessed nevertheless are those who have not seen and have believed (John 20:29).

Let us therefore also believe and praise the things that have been accomplished, seen, and believed, because they are true, so that we may attain the things promised to us.  
[Note: Feu-ardent alone reads: “And let us praise, so that we may be able to attain the things promised.” We have supplied the remainder from the Amelian manuscript.]

But since we cannot worthily praise the blessed Virgin, because our praise is inferior to her, let us venerate and love her as much as we can. Let us adore God the Father as true worshipers, in spirit and truth, as the Savior says, because God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit (John 4:23).

Otherwise, he cannot be worshiped except in spirit, nor can he rightly be served. Therefore go out from these bodily confinements; strip off the old man and put on the new, who has been created according to God (Col. 3:9–10).

Go out from this carnal love, lest the anxiety of the present life and of pleasure suffocate within you the word of life that has been sown in the heart. Rather, be strangers to the body, so that you may be present with God (2 Cor. 5:6), since those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom. 8:8).

But you, dearest women, are no longer in the flesh, for you put to death the works of the flesh within you, but live in the Spirit. Therefore, whoever is led by the Spirit of God is a child of God (ibid., 14).

And so, enlarge yourselves and raise your minds to the heights [Col. 0249D], so that you may comprehend the things in which Christ, your Bridegroom, sits and is glorified at the right hand of the Father. Thus you may worship him there on the throne where he himself is.  
[Note: The Amelian manuscript reads “who”; we have adopted that reading.]

For he is now beyond the world, where the twenty-four elders are said to sit around his throne before God, each in his seat, and to worship Christ, the King who lives forever and ever, casting their crowns before his feet—the crowns they received from him—and saying: “We give you thanks, Lord God Almighty, who are and who were, because you have taken your power and have reigned forever and ever” (Rev. 4:4).

Therefore, where they worship and in the manner in which they worship, we too ought, insofar as is permitted to mortals, to worship him even now [Col. 0250A]. For Christ is truth in the Father, and the truthful Father is wholly in Christ, his true Son, who is the one true God. He is worshiped in the Holy Spirit, because God is Trinity; and this God, the Trinity, is in his temple and not in temples made by human hands (Acts 17:24).

The temple of God is the Church, as John testifies in his Apocalypse: “And the temple of God in heaven was opened,” he says, “and the ark of his covenant was seen” (Rev. 11:19).

This ark, in truth, is not the one fashioned by Moses, but blessed Mary, who had already been transferred from here. Perhaps blessed John the Evangelist, the witness of truth, to whom she had been entrusted, recognizing her, addresses her reverently.

Because she was seen in heaven, the species is shown in the genus, just as the genus is declared through the species. Since blessed Mary was seen in the temple of God—that is, in the Church of God—and since the Church is wholly dedicated to the Lord in the fruit of her virginity, it follows that the ark of God’s covenant, namely the Mother of God herself, was rightly seen in his temple [Col. 0250B], because the Church too is a virgin.

Hence the Apostle says: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2). Therefore, most beloved women, direct your minds there, where your Bridegroom entered for us and where the blessed Virgin was seen, because her feast is rightly celebrated there, where Christ is the Bridegroom and the joys of eternal life are celebrated.

Therefore, I ask you, go out in faith, conduct, mind, and every desire for the eternal vision; and do not touch what is polluted in your actions. Ascend upward through contemplation and through a manner of life that is good, until the temple of God in heaven is opened, so that you may enter into everything where the good things promised to you are kept and where the holy Virgin is already clothed in heavenly immortality.

Let your hearts be raised in the heavenly places, where your treasure also is (Matt. 6:20). Indeed, let the treasure of the eternal inheritance itself be in your hearts, so that what is in heaven may be in you through faith.

Therefore let no one take your crown until the Bridegroom comes (Rev. 3:11); rather, may you be a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord through his grace (Isa. 62:3), he who called you to eternal joys, Jesus Christ, the Son of the Virgin, our Lord, who with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## The Second Sermon of the Same Author on the Same Assumption of Blessed Mary

Among the principal festivals of the saints, dearest women, today the distinguished and glorious solemnity of Mary, the Mother of God, has shone forth for us. On it the blessed and venerable Virgin herself was most gloriously taken up to the heavenly bridal chamber, in which, as we sing, the King of kings, the Son of the blessed Virgin Mary, sits upon a star-studded—or rather, ineffable—throne.

There thousands upon thousands of angels minister, according to Daniel’s prophecy (Dan. 7:10), and ten times a hundred thousand stand in attendance. With their praises and angelic escort, the glorious Mother of God has today been raised from the earth, lifted from the flesh, and received into heaven with triumph and exultation [Col. 0250D], and placed in paradise.

This, brothers, is the sacred and venerable solemnity prescribed and preordained before the foundation of the world; but today it has been fulfilled with exultation. For us, beloved, it is annual today; but for the angels in heaven and the citizens above it is continuous and perpetual.

But because it cannot be continuous for us in the present life, it ought to be celebrated more solemnly than all the festivals of the saints, in proportion to the ineffable privilege enjoyed by the mother of the Lord and Savior and to the gift of perpetual virginity that she possesses.

For although Christ the Lord, the just Judge, distributes rewards to each one according to his works, according to the Apostle (Rom. 2:6), nevertheless, since what this most sacred Virgin accomplished is incomparable and the gift she received ineffable, so also the reward and glory that she merited are beyond estimation and comprehension—not merely among the other sacred virgins, but even beyond all the saints.

The blessed and glorious Virgin has reached the palace of heaven, where Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, placed her within the bridal chamber at the right hand of his majesty. There he took her as the most excellent among the foremost, where, in David’s words, “the queen stands at God’s right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety” (Ps. 44:10).  
[Note: The Amelian manuscript reads: “surrounded with manifold variety.”]

This, then, is the day on which she, reborn among the daughters of Jerusalem, shone forth in beauty; on which the glorious Mother of God came forth like the dawn and follows the Lamb, more glorious than all, wherever he goes.

This, as I have said, brothers, is today’s chief and venerable festival for us; but in heaven it is more venerable to the angels and all the saints. Their joy and gladness are undoubtedly completed by the exultation of this day, when the blessed Mother of God shone brighter than the sun on the throne of glory [Col. 0251B].

For Christ, as we read, “placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18:6); from this tabernacle he himself proceeded, so to speak, like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber. Concerning this tabernacle, as though in the voice of the Mother of God, it is said: “He who created me rested in my tabernacle” (Sir. 24:13).

Therefore, without doubt, dearest brothers, the blessed Virgin, in return for so great a grace and the privilege of such great maternal honor, has today been seated in exaltation upon the throne. For although twelve thrones are mentioned, on which the company of the twelve apostles will sit when the Judge of all—the most sacred Virgin’s Son—sits upon the throne of his majesty with his senators (Matt. 19:28), there are nevertheless many others there also. Among them, twenty-four elders are said to sit in the presence of God and to worship before the throne of the living God forever and ever (Rev. 4:10).

Daniel too testifies that thrones were set in place, though he does not complete their number (Dan. 7:9).  
[Col. 0251C] Hence it is clearly established, beloved, that the throne of the most blessed Virgin, prepared before the foundation of the world, is today glorified more highly and is also venerated by the angels.  
[Note: “Is venerated” is the reading of Amel.; Feu-ardent has “is found.”]

And rightly so, because she herself became the throne of God and the bridal chamber. Coming into her womb, the Wisdom of God the Father became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). If the soul of any righteous person is the seat of wisdom, as Scripture testifies (Wis. 7), how much more was the soul of this Virgin, dearest brothers, which the Holy Spirit so filled [Note: Amel.: “filled”] even before the hour of conception that she was greeted by the angel?

For he said: “Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28). The Son of God, who is the power and [Note: “The Wisdom of God the Father”—the same wording occurs in Amel.] wisdom of the Father, immediately entered into her and so filled and possessed her that in her the Word became flesh and the whole God dwelt in man.  
[Note: Amel. reads: “the whole Christ.”]

And therefore he was wholly in us, because the whole God was in her. Thus the Virgin conceived the One whom heaven and earth cannot contain, wholly from the Holy Spirit, and bore God and man for the salvation of the world.

Therefore, beloved, consider with complete integrity of faith—consider, I say—the soul of this Virgin, for we cannot worthily know or even contemplate the commerce of so great a gift.  
[Note: We correct Feu-ardent’s “not in faith” to “not know,” from Amel.]

For this reason let us glorify the soul of this Virgin, magnifying the Lord (Luke 1:46), whom paradise received today with joy; whom the angels accompany with praises; whom the chorus of the apostles venerates; whom the white-robed martyrs bless; whom the company of the robed confessors celebrates together; whom today the host of holy virgins meets exultantly with their victorious palms.

For this is that blessed soul through whom the author of life entered the world; through whom every curse of our first parents was dissolved; and through whom heavenly blessing came into the whole world. This is the Virgin in whose womb the whole Church is betrothed (sic) and believed to be joined to God by an everlasting covenant.

For such sacraments and things of this kind, brothers, today’s festival is to be venerated—annual in such a way that it may always remain continuous and venerable in our minds. For after Christ, who is the head and God of the whole Church, this glorious Virgin shines forth, exalted even above the angelic choirs, as it is sung; most illustrious among virgins and whiter among [Col. 0252B] martyrs.

For although those crowned with martyrdom washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Rev. 7:14), this blessed and venerable Virgin is nevertheless rightly proclaimed whiter, since, although the bodies of the martyrs endured sufferings for the Lord, this wondrous Virgin is nevertheless shown, by the Lord’s testimony, to have suffered in her soul.

For Simeon—or the Lord speaking to her—says: “And a sword will pierce your own soul” (Luke 2:35). If the sword reached as far as the soul when she stood beside the cross, while the apostles fled and she saw the Lord hanging there (John 19:25), then she was more than a martyr, because inwardly she was wounded by the sword of love no less than by that of grief.

She stood ready, had the hand of the executioner not been lacking. The blessed Mother of God is rightly more than [Note: Feu-ardent printed: “She is more than a martyr-mother.” We have rejected “martyr,” since it is not found in Amel.] a mother: wounded by immeasurable love, she became a witness of the Savior [Note: Amel.: “and endured in her soul the torment of the Passion through grief”] and endured in her soul the torment of the Passion through grief.

Therefore, since this virgin and mother has now been endowed with ineffable gifts [Note: We adopt the Amelian reading “has been endowed with ineffable gifts,” because Feu-ardent’s “ineffable is” does not fit the sentence], and exalted by divine privileges, we must believe that she is today so illuminated by complete heavenly glory that no one on earth can worthily honor her with praises.

[Note: We follow Amel., from which we have supplied some words; Feu-ardent has: “Therefore, since we cannot, how much we ought.”]

Since we cannot honor her as much as we ought, the Holy Spirit must be implored—the Spirit who filled her and adorned her with the immense gifts of his generosity. The only-begotten God himself, the Son of God, must also be implored, so that according to the measure of our weakness he may deign to accept whatever praises we offer for her. For no mortal can worthily utter the praises of this most sacred Virgin, nor explain in words the mysteries accomplished in her.

Nevertheless, the archangel Gabriel, sent to her, showed how greatly she should be honored [Note: “How greatly she should be honored.” Feu-ardent lacks *sit*; Amel. supplies it] (Luke 1:26), when he first greeted her in the exercise of the veneration due to her and praised her as full of grace, proclaiming her blessed among all women. Immediately he indicated that she would become the mother of the Lord.  
[Note: Feu-ardent lacks “indicates”; it is required here.]

Otherwise, beloved, unless she were not only above women but also, in merit, above human beings, so great an archangel would not have shown her such honor in his greeting, nor brought her such great and exalted praises. And if, while she was still in mortal flesh, even before the mysteries of the sacrament had been completed, God’s archangel showed her such reverence and brought her such proclamations of praise [Col. 0253A], what do you think are the praises they offer today in heaven as they glorify the Son of God who was born from her?  
[Note: Feu-ardent reads: “Even after the mysteries of the sacrament had been completed. Thus Feu-ardent, incorrectly and contrary to the meaning of the sentence, continues: ‘God’s archangel showed reverence.’ We reproduce the reading of the Amelian manuscript, unquestionably more correct and complete.”]

For this, beloved, is Mary the Virgin, on account of whose nature Christ so often testifies in the Gospel that he himself is the Son of Man, when he says: “The Son of Man will come in the kingdom of his Father” (Matt. 16:27). And again, when he said to blessed Peter together with the others: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (ibid., 13). Finally, when he asked them: “But who do you say that I am?” (ibid., 16), Peter answered for them all: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

He did not say this to deny that he was the son of the most blessed virgin Mary, as Christ had said, but to demonstrate that the one and same person who was the Son of Man was also the Son of God. This was the faith that the Lord sought both in Peter and in the other apostles.

Therefore, beloved, let us venerate her as the mother of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; let us proclaim her as the mother of the Lord and perpetual virgin, who has today reached the bridal chamber of the eternal King, to that same wedding which was consecrated in her womb [Note: “Of her”—we have supplied this from Amel.], and for which she received, as the bride of Christ, the pledge of her dowry and the guarantee of the eternal inheritance, the Holy Spirit (Eph. 1:14).

But because we are less capable of speaking or thinking worthily about such great mysteries, let us return to the words of the blessed Virgin herself, to the beginnings of her virtues, so that from her apprenticeship in humility we may better explain how she ultimately reached such exalted splendor.  
[Note: Feu-ardent: “We may better explain it, when from the depths she reached such great magnificence of glory.” We have preferred the Amelian reading.]

For she says, among other things: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid; for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1:48).

Hence, I ask you, my brothers, listen to the mother, the prophetess of God. I call her a prophetess—indeed, to put it so, an evangelist. Listen, I ask you, virgins; let every order of women hear the humility of so great a Virgin. Do not believe that all the things she foretold through the Spirit of truth who had filled her have not already been fulfilled.

“For behold,” she says, “from now on all generations will call me blessed.” Therefore, when this holy and venerable Virgin said these words, I do not know, brothers, whether she was known to many, or whether she was known only to a few in that Jewish nation. Yet she spoke with faith and proclaimed what she knew was destined to come.

She spoke as a humble woman and handmaid, though she knew that she would be called blessed: “For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.”  
[Note: Amel.: “that all generations would call her blessed.”]

Therefore, I ask you, look upon all the lands that the sun illuminates with its light, and behold: there is now scarcely any nation, scarcely any people, that does not believe in Christ. Wherever Christ is worshiped and adored, Mary, the venerable Mother of God, blessed and happy, and also perpetual virgin, is proclaimed.

And so, brothers, it is little for one or a few to say what is proclaimed and believed by everyone everywhere. This, beloved, is what I mean: it is believed. Behold, throughout the whole world, in every people and every language, blessed Mary the Virgin is proclaimed, and as many people as there are, so many witnesses does she have.

I shall speak truly, then, when I say that she is believed because she is proclaimed. And she is proclaimed because she is truly believed to be blessed with God; now she is proclaimed everywhere with greater confidence, because she is truly and faithfully believed to be blessed.

Yet what was foretold is fulfilled in every respect: for she is called blessed and glorious on earth, while in heaven she is praised by all the saints, who behold her, and she is renowned. Hence, beloved, this glorious feast derives its glory from the fact that she is exalted and is venerated as blessed even by the angels. “For he has regarded,” she says, “the lowliness of his handmaid; for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1:48).

[Note: Feuardent: “For indeed, with wondrous devotion.”]

A wondrous utterance, full of every kind of devotion, is this: “For he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid.” She does not say, “For he has regarded my virginity,” or my innocence, or the grace of any other virtue; rather, she humbly confesses that the Lord regarded only her humility. What wondrous discipline of virtue, and what admirable wisdom! Indeed, the Virgin’s declaration is wondrous and circumspect, so that the truth might be revealed in her words without offending in any way the divine power that was magnified in her confession. Thus, when she had heard all the incomprehensible things announced to her by the angel, had believed what had never been heard before, and had also believed what Elizabeth said, she declared: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” (ibid., 46). Then she added: “For he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid; for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.”

[Col. 0254B] Yet she presumed nothing concerning herself, and in no respect thought highly of herself. Rather, she rejoiced entirely in God; her whole spirit delighted in God, and her whole soul magnified and praised the Lord. She attributed no merits to herself, and applauded herself for nothing; she sought and valued only the things that belong to God. Therefore she exults, rejoices, and is glad entirely in him. She claims for herself only the humility of a handmaid, she who is venerated by the Savior’s angel as his mother.

Yet she did not say that this same humility was anything of herself [Note: “She said that it was something,” Amel.]; but because the Most High regarded her and made her pleasing to himself, therefore, she says, “all generations will call me blessed.” O wondrous confession, and wondrous humility! She confesses the humility which, she says, was the only thing in her that he who regards all things regarded; and immediately her blessedness is proclaimed, of which the whole world is a witness today. She is believed to be blessed and to reign eternally with Christ, because what she foretold has been fulfilled. For it is written: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11; 18:14).

The holy Mother of God was exalted not only because she was found humble, but also because she was ineffably filled with grace. We venerate her while imploring her, and implore her while venerating her, that she may deign to intercede for us with our Lord, the Son of God, whom she herself bore incarnate, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III OF THE SAME AUTHOR: THE THIRD SERMON ON THE SAME ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

The glorious feast of blessed Mary the Virgin is present among us today, beloved brothers, full of joys and filled with immeasurable gifts because of her ascent. [Note: We follow the Amelian Codex; Feuardent printed: “Indeed illustrious because of her merits.”]

She is illustrious because of her merits, but far more illustrious because of the grace by which she is illumined—not only the blessed Virgin herself, but through her also the whole Church of Christ. For glorious virginity did not earn grace by merits; rather, it received the rewards of merits from grace. Therefore today’s celebration is more glorious than the birthdays of the other saints, inasmuch as the blessed Virgin and Mother of the Lord is illumined by the ineffable privileges of divine mysteries.

[Col. 0254D] For her merits increased from the very source by which she was most fully filled with grace. Thus, as to how great her merits before the Lord should be reckoned, or what rewards should be contemplated, I think no one can explain fully except one who is truly able to weigh the nature and magnitude of that grace with which she herself was filled, through whom the majesty of God came into the world.

Therefore, my brothers, this solemnity must be venerated with every service of devotion, and what is sung must be venerated as well: she has been exalted above the choirs of angels. For no human being was ever granted the privilege of such a gift—not even an angel—that a person of the Trinity, whom she had generated from her own substance, should be God.

[Note: The phrase “which he had generated” is absent from Feuardent, who shortly below has *genuit*—“he generated”—where we print the reading of Amel.]

Therefore, I ask, let the folly of the flesh be silent, and let the feast of the Mother of our Lord and Savior be celebrated worthily with praises. She is as worthy of honor as she is venerable because of grace, since her honor and glory, praise and thanksgiving, are the Redeemer’s.

Today she was summoned forth and received from the hand of the Lord an unfading crown with the palm of virginity. Today she was received upon the throne of the kingdom and took her seat. Today she entered the bridal chamber, because she was both virgin and bride. Today she heard that voice of the one who caressed her from the seat of majesty, saying: “Come, my chosen one, and I will place you upon my throne, because the king has desired your beauty.”

At that voice, we believe, the blessed soul was released with joy and exultation and proceeded to the Lord. She who had been a temple of divinity in the flesh became herself a throne. She was more beautiful and exalted than all others, to the extent that grace also shone more gloriously in her.

This, then, brothers, is the divine recompense of which it is said: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11; 18:14). [Note: “For she was established and deeply rooted in humility.” Thus the Amelian Codex, but Feuardent’s reading, which we print, is better.] For she was established in deep humility and expanded in charity; therefore today she has been exalted so sublimely.

But since we cannot investigate the height and magnificence of the throne, let us at least sometimes examine the treasures of her humility, so that thereafter, through the intervention of her merits, we may be able to reach the glory of the gifts. For humility is the guardian of the other virtues. Therefore the venerable Virgin, because she had gathered many virtues to herself, carried their guardian, humility, in her heart. After receiving grace, she increased it and confessed herself to be a handmaid, though she was the mother of the Creator.

Nothing nobler, brothers, is found than the Mother of God who professes herself a handmaid; nothing more splendid than she who chose the splendor of glory. The blessed Virgin knew that humility always pleases God. Therefore, when she was greeted by the angel’s message, she thought nothing lofty of herself and presumed nothing, but, wholly humble, directed herself toward God, to whom she attributed everything that she was and everything that she heard.

Therefore let us also learn to defer to God; let us learn always and in all things to think humbly of ourselves. Let us learn to humble ourselves, because the author of life, though he was Most High, came to us in humility in order to teach us humility, as the teacher of truth. For if someone gathers virtues without humility, he is like one carrying dust in the wind. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29).

Nor is it without reason that he especially commands mortals and fragile beings to learn humility, since even in heaven, where the Immortal reigns among the angels, he seeks what is humble. Hence the prophet David says: “Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and regards the humble in heaven and on earth?” (Psalm 112:6).

[Col. 0255D] If gentleness is required even of the angels in heaven, what do you think is required here, brothers, where pride reigns? How necessary is it for us to humble ourselves! Accordingly, we read: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Sirach 3:20), because, as Solomon says, “glory will receive the humble in spirit” (Proverbs 29:23).

The blessed Mother of God knew this, my brothers: that divine condescension looks upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at his words (Isaiah 66:2). Therefore she immediately said to the angel: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).

She does not become proud; rather, through the gift of devotion, the service of humility increases. Her privilege is enlarged in every respect, yet arrogance seizes nothing, because she does not swell with empty glory when she declares that she will soon be called blessed because of the favor granted to her humility.

Therefore she does not run about, because she is humble. For, to the degree that anyone who obeys divine commands is gentle, to that degree is one harsh who either does not believe or delays obeying what he hears. The blessed Virgin now humbles herself in everything in order to receive within herself the whole grace of the giver, because what was given to others in portions came to her all at once as the fullness of grace.

Hence the Evangelist also says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). Great indeed was the grace of the blessed Virgin Mary, and great were the rewards of eternal recompense that she earned, because she humbled herself greatly amid immense gifts and amid communion with divinity; today she is greatly exalted in glory by the Lord.

Finally, Christ came in humility to the humble Virgin whom he chose, in order to raise a triumph of salvation from such profound humility and to exalt her, as we have sung, even above the angelic choirs. This exaltation is truly a privilege of grace. Therefore these mystical mysteries of the gifts must be recalled with fear and trembling and perfect love, and by them the grace of this celebration must be measured.

Consider, therefore, brothers, with what reverence and with what service of devotion it is fitting for us to participate in such mysteries. The angel himself, not without holy fear or due honor, offered her the reverence of announcing the Gospel. For the angel perceived that the Lord was already present in a special way in the blessed Virgin, and he knew the mysteries of the divine plan that were to come.

Therefore he said so reverently: “Hail, full of grace” (Luke 1). Then observe how exalted is what he immediately adds: “The Lord is with you.” He did not say, “May the Lord be with you,” as though merely for the sake of visiting her, but “The Lord is with you,” because through you he enters into the new mystery of birth. Thus, proceeding wholly into the greeting on account of the curse of our first parents, he discloses the great oracle of blessing: “Blessed are you,” he says, “among women.”

How, then, is she now blessed, beloved? Behold: through hearing, grace is fulfilled; through hearing, faith is produced, and she believed contrary to faith. From the conception she learned to show honor to her relatives; from the birth of her son modesty grew. Chastity increased, integrity was strengthened, virginity too was made firm, and all the virtues persevered. Everything [reading uncertain: *extremuit*] trembled, and her wondrous humility had shone first.

When she had learned all these things from the angel and had been filled with heavenly gifts, she said: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” The effect immediately followed the utterance. At once the blessed Virgin became pregnant; today she has been assumed into heaven with joy. She became the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit and the council-chamber of the Word.

She is rightly called blessed among all women because all call her blessed. Grace and blessedness were bestowed upon her in a singular form so that they might be spread throughout the whole race of the Church. Therefore it is not without reason that the blessed and venerable Virgin today surpasses the whole body in her particular dignity: beyond all others she was made fruitful in the singular fruit of her offspring.

Meanwhile, she is rightly given precedence in heavenly things, since on earth she was enriched and filled above all others with divine gifts. Therefore today’s feast is most dear to all the citizens above, because it is the Assumption of the one from whose body came forth truth and righteousness, which looked down from heaven, in whom we are all justified and in whom the saints rejoice in glory (Psalm 84).

Hence, brothers, I ask that we join our vows with the citizens above and, according to the measure of our weakness, fulfill them with praises, since what was born from her is the common joy of all. They indeed come to meet her today rejoicing, and they receive her with joy, hymns, and praises. Let us accompany her with every devotion of heart and integrity of faith.

Let us accompany her in such a way that we may one day be able to reach those ineffable gifts which the blessed Mother of God received. Perhaps, therefore, some of the saints, looking from afar, asked today that question from the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a wisp of smoke from perfumes of myrrh and frankincense?”

For many ornaments of virtue were burning during her ascent, consumed in the fire of divine love. She is like a slender wisp of smoke because she is that rod from the root of Jesse which ascends today (Isaiah 11). Slender indeed and delicate, formed from the spices of every perfumer’s powder, but consumed in the fire of charity.

And she is rightly like a wisp of smoke made from spices, because she became wholly a burnt offering to God and scattered from herself the fragrances of virtue up to the heavens—not just any fragrances, but those of every perfumer’s powder.

Therefore, brothers, that angelic wonder arose not from virginity alone, which was unique in Mary, but from the immensity of grace, because all the virtues in her diffused the sweetness of fragrance from the fire of divine love, so that in her there was a model not only for virgins but also for all the churches of God.

For the virginity and life of blessed Mary were the mirror and image of all chastity, the integrity of the virtues, the adornment of modesty, and a most excellent instruction in goodness. In her, I ask, let virgins see what they ought to avoid, what they ought to correct, and what forms of honorable conduct they ought to maintain (St. Ambrose, *On Virginity*). For the first love of learning, if I may put it so, is the nobility of the teacher.

You have, therefore, virgins, the form of an excellent instruction; you have in her an exemplar of perfect virginity. Behold the way by which you must proceed; behold the blessedness and glory to which you wish to attain. You must continually pant toward it with vows and desire, so that one day you may happily reach it.

But since no one born from the propagation of the flesh shone more nobly than the Mother of God, nor did anyone more splendid than she come forth—she whom the splendor of the Father’s glory illumined ineffably and divinely; whom the power of the Most High overshadowed so that a virgin might give birth; whom divine grace filled so that a virgin might conceive; whom the wisdom of God the Father chose above all others so that she might please him; who generated the body of Christ without contamination of her own body; who, in the ardor of charity, burned all the shoots into a sweet fragrance for the Lord, so that she might become wholly a burnt offering to God—

Her flesh and blood were the origin of the most gracious Savior; her soul became the temple in which the exchange of our redemption was accomplished. Truly a good house, beloved, into which all the divinity of the Word entered at once; in which the wisdom of God the Father raised up for itself seven columns; upon which the whole house rests, and the Church is built.

What shall I say, my brothers, or what shall I speak about those mystical realities in which all human speech grows more through silence and wonder than through speaking, and for which the angels rejoice and sing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 1)?

If they sang such things then at the Virgin’s giving birth, we believe, beloved, that today they celebrate her worthy obsequies and receive with glory the mother of their Creator, rejoicing—her whom the Holy Spirit filled, whom the wisdom of the Father, namely the Son of God, possessed.

[Col. 0257D] Therefore let us also give thanks to our Creator, because the privileges of his gifts are our gifts and our dough, since the leaven that was mixed into the singular substance overflowed into the whole race, until the whole was leavened (Luke 13). Thus one body and one new dough came to be: Christ and the Church.

Therefore, beloved, it is necessary that the feast which burns in the mind through faith should also be possessed and contemplated by all in its visible reality. Let that which now shines only as believed in our hearts be glorious in our eyes. Then that feast will be continuous and eternal for us, whereas now it is present in the mind as today’s and daily feast. Thus it is rightly the feast which now burns in faith, pants in hope that we may remain, and beats in charity, so that we may enter that celebration in which the blessed and glorious Mother of God is queen, assumed today through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV OF THE SAME AUTHOR: THE FOURTH SERMON ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

[Col. 0258A]

Beloved brothers, whenever something in God’s creature is proclaimed or honored with fitting praise out of love for the Creator, it undoubtedly redounds to the praise of God, who is found to be the author of the work of creation itself. Just as, in some praiseworthy and wondrous work of craftsmanship, whatever is most highly celebrated in it is rightly understood as praise of the craftsman.

Hence it is also written in the Prophet: “Praise the Lord,” he says, “in his saints.” Therefore, beloved, I humbly implore the dignity of your grace first of all: grant pardon for my presumption or imperfection. Though I am slow in understanding and unlearned in speech, nevertheless, out of love for her, concerning whose Assumption—the Assumption of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, the Mother of the Lord—something is read, I have tried, like an infant babbling, to murmur something—like those who voluntarily thrust themselves into an undertaking they cannot worthily complete.

But the Almighty Lord requires not so much the result as the will, according to what is written: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 1).

The holy and venerable Virgin Mary, then, is the mother of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, born from the seed of Abraham and from the tribe of Judah; the rod from the root of Jesse; renowned from the stock of David; daughter of Jerusalem; star of the sea; handmaid of God; queen of the nations; lady of kings; bride of the Lord; mother of Christ; temple of the Creator; sanctuary of the Holy Spirit; like a beautiful dove; beautiful as the moon; chosen as the sun (Song 4); seal of faith; restoration of Eve; entrance of life; gate of heaven; glory of women; head of virgins; enclosed garden; sealed fountain; well of living waters.

She multiplies like the cedar of Lebanon, blossoms like the palm, and is like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God (Psalm 52). A holy virgin, a prudent virgin, and one of the number of the prudent virgins. A most beautiful virgin, a modest virgin, adorned in body, radiant in spirit, clear in faith, distinguished in mind, devoted in love of virginity, ready for obedience, careful in the ministry entrusted to her, peaceful amid persecution, and inwardly suffering with Christ in his Passion.

Foretold by the prophets of God, announced beforehand by holy philosophers, greeted by the archangel, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit and overshadowed by him; ignorant of the seed of man, fruitful in the offspring of a son: an unmarried virgin, rejoicing because of the Son, conceiving through faith, giving birth with joy; a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, a virgin after childbirth.

The whole world cannot contain him, yet this Virgin enclosed him in her sacred womb. She wrapped in swaddling clothes the one who holds the world in his handful. The one whose presence of majesty nourishes the angels in heaven, the holy Virgin nourished with the milk of a mother’s sacred breast. Moreover, the Creator of the world, at whose command the whole earth is governed, was fed as an infant at the breast of this glorious Virgin.

Under whose protection the kingdoms of the earth are guarded, with him the Virgin Mary fled into Egypt. The one who holds the whole world suspended as though on a balance, the Virgin Mary saw and gazed upon when he was fastened to the cross. The one who never lacked the presence of his majesty in heaven, the Virgin Mary is believed to have contemplated with her own eyes as he ascended into heaven.

O most blessed and holiest Mary of all women! How happily you remain on earth, you who send your son—and indeed our Lord, Redeemer, and Jesus Christ—before you into heaven! Indeed, you enter heaven much more blessedly and happily, because you know that your son sits in his glory at the right hand of the Father.

O most blessed and glorious celebration of this night, in which the venerable Virgin Mary is received with praises by the heavenly army into the palace of heaven, with ineffable triumph! From her flesh the Lord Jesus, the Word, became flesh. No believer doubts that she has been transformed for the glory of immortality and raised above the angels.

O beloved, if we were permitted to know what nevertheless neither the human mind conceives in its heart nor the mouth can express—what service of holy souls, what reverence of the rejoicing holy angelic spirits, is offered and performed in the heavenly dwelling at the arrival of the blessed soul of Mary! They joyfully behold her Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, elevated above them; beholding him, they cleave to him; cleaving to him, they live immortally in immortality.

Therefore rejoice now in what you are doing; celebrate solemnly what you are celebrating, and drive from your hearts the slothfulness of the evil body. Once it has been driven out, kindle your spirits with the flame of holy love; give understanding to the voice of the chant; sing psalms wisely.

And amid these things, I beg you to obtain pardon for me through your prayers, so that I may be included among them through the intercession of blessed Mary, whom you honor while loving her with the deepest desire of your hearts.

And because she deserved to become the mother of our Creator, may we deserve to have her interceding for us with her Son—indeed, her Lord and our Redeemer—and helping us in all things. And because she deserved to be overshadowed by the power of the Most High, may we deserve to be aided by her prayers, with the help of him who lives and reigns as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V OF THE SAME AUTHOR: THE FIFTH SERMON ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

At that time: “Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha received him into her house.” And the rest (Luke 10).

### Homily of Hildefonsus on the same reading

It seems entirely appropriate and fitting that the Fathers ordained that, in memory of the Mother of God, the Gospel reading should be recited which tells how those two sisters, sisters in mind and flesh, received the Lord Jesus as a guest.

For the one for whom Mary prepared a temple in the world, consecrated in virtue and dedicated to perpetual virginity, these women, as the Gospel relates, prepared a lodging for temporal habitation and offered the service of devout humanity and most sincere charity.

Their lives and actions were so wondrous and so celebrated in the memory of the faithful that Catholic and highly learned men rightly assert that they represent the figures of two divine ways of life. Martha, then, who cared for the household and prepared what was necessary for so great and such a guest, represented, as we have said, the figure of the active life.

Through Mary, however, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened most attentively to the conversations of his teaching, the contemplative life is clearly prefigured.

Come, beloved brothers, let us see whether our Lady—or rather, the Mother and ever-virgin Mary of our Lord and God—fully practiced both lives: the active and praiseworthy life which Martha cultivated through her work, and the excellent contemplative life which Mary obtained by listening and choosing.

We know that the beloved John, the Lord’s theologian, said little about the human and bodily actions of the Lord Jesus but said and wrote much about the nature, power, and majesty of his divinity, as the most sacred sequence of his account bears witness. [Note: Amel.: “the Evangelist.”]

So too we believe that the Mother of the Lord was not greatly occupied with active conduct, since she devoted herself wholly to divine contemplation. She did not restrict herself to the active life beyond what was fitting for the Mother of the Lord; rather, with the entire affection and desire of her mind, she raised herself toward the contemplative life.

And lest she be altogether without a share in the active life, after she had been chosen by the Lord, greeted by the angel, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, and made fruitful by the Word of God, she rose from her place and, traveling by a difficult road over the rugged mountains to undertake the laborious service of active life for her friends, entered the house of the prophet Zechariah. There, when she greeted Elizabeth, she learned in the spirit that the noble pledge had been deposited in Elizabeth’s womb (Luke 1). In these few acts, as we have said, she fulfilled Martha’s role.

If Martha was blessed because she represented the active life, how much happier were those most holy persons of whom we speak, who deserved to become possessors of such great joys and gifts?

What happiness can be greater than that, in the mother of the Lord—and, so to speak, in a royal hall, a virginal hall [Note: Amel.: “in a virginal womb”]—fruitfulness and virginity should reign? That barrenness should generate and give birth with an infertile and aged woman? That an age which had earned the name of old age and antiquity should attain the dignity of new fatherhood?

And, as blessed Jerome pursues the matter in a delightful discourse, John also leaped and rejoiced at Mary’s arrival; through the Virgin’s mouth he heard the words of the Lord [Note: Amel.: “the resounding words of the Lord”], and from his mother’s womb he eagerly desired to burst forth to meet him.

How, to what extent, and in what manner she submitted herself with the services and observances of the contemplative life together with the other Mary—let the testimony of the archangel Gabriel declare, and let the narrative of the Gospel discourse pursue it, for our smallness of speech fails when attempting to recount these things.

We know one thing with certainty: her entire life and action were always directed toward the Lord’s word. [Note: The same: “was always intent upon the Lord.”] And as it was said of the other Mary, “she chose the better part” (Luke 10), because she was the first of all women to offer her virginity to God. For this reason she deserved that the Son of God, announced by the angel, should receive from her the body of our redemption.

We have said that she was always intent upon divine contemplation; but we ought to establish this very point in Catholic terms.

To speak in ordinary human terms: where was she bodily when the angel was sent to her by God? Certainly in her parents’ house. Where was she in spirit? Indeed, as we have said, in that vision of divine contemplation. What was she doing? Living irreproachably, without prejudice to anyone, as was proper to her profession: she was praying and reading.

How was she praying? She sang the song which she uttered with the timbrel and cried aloud. What was she reading? Perhaps the testimonies of divine Scripture that related, without doubt, to that ineffable mystery which was taking place in her came before her.

Did she not believe that the Mosaic prophecy could be fulfilled in the pledge she bore? “God,” it says, “will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall hear him” (Deuteronomy 18:15).

And she saw clearly many other prophetic statements through which the truth of so great a sacrament and mystery was foreshadowed and fully declared. Did not the testimony of the patriarch Jacob seem to pertain to this, when he said: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself will be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:10)?

What is clearer than what Balaam, the diviner and false speaker [Note: Amel.: “the false-speaking man who spoke from himself”], confessed, though by God’s command he spoke truthfully? “A star,” he says, “shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” (Numbers 24:17).

The Mother of God, taken up into the citadel of divine contemplation and instructed by David’s testimonies, knew that the Lord would proceed from her like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber (Psalm 18:6), and that he would be beautiful, as the same Prophet foretold, beyond the sons of men (Psalm 44:3).

Illumined by the light of the Holy Spirit, she did not doubt that the following words, which she recalled the prophet Isaiah had spoken, pertained to her: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son. And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 7:14; 11:1).

What could be clearer? What could be more delightful? The most noble of the prophets foretells both that a virgin will give birth and that a rod will come forth from the root of Jesse.

It pleased me, therefore, to insert into this little discourse of ours the text of Psalm 86, which blessed Ambrose—a man praiseworthy in every respect and a true defender of the Catholic faith—chose to interpret so fittingly in memory of the Mother of God and the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation and birth.

Therefore, as I said, I wished to append the words of so great a bishop to my poor work, so that what the poverty of my small intellect could not worthily pursue might be ennobled and commended by the authority of so great a bishop’s words.

For the aforementioned most learned teacher says, according to the ancient interpretation (*Funeral Oration on the Death of His Brother Satyrus*): “Mother Zion will say: ‘A man, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her’” (Psalm 86:5).

He could not have a mother according to divinity, because he is the author of his mother. He became man not through divine generation but through human generation; [Note: Amel.: “Because he who.”] and he who became man was born as God-man.

Elsewhere too you have: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6). In “child” there is the name of age; in “son” there is the fullness of divinity. He was made from a mother and born from a father; nevertheless, understand him as both born and given—not divided, but one. [Note: Amel.: “For one is the Son of God, from the Father, and born from the Virgin.”]

For the one Son of God was both born from the Father and born from the Virgin, in distinct order, but converging in one name, just as the present reading teaches: “A man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her.”

Man according to the body, Most High according to power. Although God and man differ in nature, he is nevertheless the same, not another, in both. One thing, therefore, is proper to his nature, another is shared with us; yet in both there is one, and in both he is perfect.

It is therefore not surprising that God made him both Lord and Christ. He made him Jesus, that is, the one who received his name from the body; for he made the one of whom the patriarch David also writes: “Mother Zion will say: ‘A man, and a man was made in her.’”

Thus, having been made man, he is unlike us—not in divinity but in body; nor is he separated from the Father, but received in the gift.

By announcing this gift, the Virgin Mary merited conceiving the Lord; by giving birth she obtained it; and after childbirth, remaining perpetually virgin, she possessed it without corruption.

Filled, as we rightly believe, with the gifts of the same grace, she spent with him the whole period of the Lord’s infancy, boyhood, and adolescence. As the true mother of his humanity, she ministered to her son with maternal love and tenderness.

What were their conversations with one another—how sweet, how loving—when virginity shone in the mother and fruitfulness rejoiced; when humanity appeared in the son and divinity remained hidden? The extent and nature of that divine and virginal fellowship exceeds altogether the understanding not only of us but of all human beings.

Then the same one who was the Virgin Mother’s only-begotten son, when he wished to appear as the one Son of God the Father, displayed this very thing at the time of his baptism through the majesty of the Trinity: the Father was heard in a voice, the Son was seen in human form, and the Holy Spirit deigned to appear in the likeness of a dove (Matthew 3:16–17).

A great witness to the magnitude of this event, greater than the others, is a man named John, sent by God. This man, who until then had wondrously shared with the saints in knowledge of the secrets of the Lord’s Incarnation and birth, became the minister of this wondrous mystery.

Therefore, brothers, so that we may believe in our hearts and confess with our mouths that the three named, [Note: “Distinct” is absent from Feuardent.] distinct and separate persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—possess one divinity, eternity, immensity, and glory [Note: Feuardent: “universality and glory”], let the most truthful words of the prophets and the trustworthy testimonies of the apostles and evangelists admonish and teach us.

And so that the Trinity, which is supreme, simple, eternal, and incomprehensible in three persons, may be believed, confessed, and adored, let the sincerity of the Holy Scriptures invite us, and let the faithful authority of the Catholic Fathers teach us—those Fathers, namely, in whose understanding and writings the devotion and truth of faith do not waver.

After the mystery of baptism had been completed and consecrated by the presence of the entire Trinity, Jesus went into the desert by no alien spirit but by his own spirit and will. There the evil spirit found him to tempt him; but, overcome by his power, the devil withdrew from him in confusion while angels ministered to him (Matthew 4:1).

Afterward he was found by blessed John and, because of his incomparable innocence, was called by him “the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

And lest the light kindled by God be placed under a bushel, he went out into public. Because he found the whole world subject to crimes and sins, he prescribed a remedy for all and declared that the kingdom of heaven was drawing near with his coming.

And so that Isaiah’s prophecy might be fulfilled—“The people who sat in darkness have seen a great light; for those dwelling in the land and shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isaiah 9:2)—he then, with the light of his divinity going before him, called disciples from the various occupations and conditions of this life, as the Gospels relate (Luke 6:13), and chose twelve from among them, whom he called apostles. Through them he showed the human race the way of salvation.

The most holy Virgin was always present at their gatherings and always clung to their noble fellowship. She always lived with them and rejoiced to present herself frequently before the Lord’s gaze.

That truly excellent portion which Mary, the sister of Martha, represented in type and figure, the Mother of God rightly and most firmly retained; and with the apostles she discussed Christ’s human actions, which she knew more truly and particularly, so that from her they might learn how they themselves should believe the mystery of so great a matter, recount it more clearly to others, and, when the proper time came, transmit it to the world in writing without any ambiguity. She herself, as the holy evangelist John reports (John 2:1), was sometimes present at the Lord’s miracles; and in these, as well as in his other works and powers of divinity, she rejoiced beyond what can be expressed.

And if Mary (Luke 7:37), once a sinful woman toward whom he was gracious in forgiving sins, listened attentively to words from his mouth, how much more ardently did this woman, holy in mind and body, listen—she whose very Lord was also her son? Yet, in order that the prophecy of the righteous Simeon might be fulfilled, which says, “Your own soul a sword will pierce” (Luke 2:35), at the time of the Lord’s Passion she stood before the cross with the beloved disciple (John 19:25). To use the very sweet words of Ambrose (Book 10 on Luke, chapter 33), “with devout eyes she gazed, not upon the death of her pledge, but upon the salvation of the world,” where she was worthy to hear, “Behold your son”; and to the beloved disciple it was said concerning her, “Behold your mother.”

Concerning the Lord’s burial, some say that she was much more concerned than those holy women. Their opinion, unless I am mistaken, seems to be supported by that good Sedulius, an evangelical poet, eloquent speaker, and Catholic writer. For if we wish to know what the Mother of God was doing after the Lord’s resurrection, before he ascended into heaven, there can be no doubt that she frequently went around and desired to visit the places of the Lord’s birth, Passion, burial, and resurrection. In those same places she also shed tears and impressed the sweetest kisses of her most holy mouth. Then, refreshed by the sight of the Lord’s places, she returned joyfully to the refuge set before her, namely, the apostolic company.

[Note: Pasta intuitu, Amelianus; Postea intuitu, Feu-ard.: “refreshed by the sight”; “after the sight.”]

We believe that she was present at the joys of the Lord’s ascension and that, on the holy day of Pentecost, she received with the holy apostles the grace of the Holy Spirit, whom it is clear she had possessed most fully from Christ’s very conception. If anyone, moved by devotion or by devout curiosity, should still wish to investigate what she did after the Lord’s ascension, how holily and justly she lived, and with whom she dwelt, this seems to have been known only to God, to the archangel Gabriel, to whom the Lord is said to have entrusted her whole cause, and to the angels who rejoiced with her and spoke with her; and also to John, the Lord’s beloved disciple, who from the very cross received her into his charge and care (John 19:27)—namely, so that a virgin might serve a virgin and render the service of devotion and love to the Lord’s mother, who had made him worthy of this above others by her affection.

For her most pure life and conduct were not unknown to the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, or to the other apostles; nor was her holy, admirable, and praiseworthy manner of life unknown to them, since she was always with them, from the beginning of their conversion until the day on which the only-begotten Son of God, truly born as man from her in the true faith, wished to rescue her from the labors of this life and, as is believed and proclaimed, deigned to raise her above the choirs of angels to the glory prepared for her from the ages.

[Note: Ab ipso conversationis initio, Amel.: “From the very beginning of their association.”]

The whole world celebrates this day’s joy today. Today, because of the veneration of the assumption of the Mother of God, the angels rejoice, virgins give thanks, and patriarchs and prophets return praises to God, because they recognize that their foreshadowings and prophecies have been fulfilled through this same Mother of God. The apostles and evangelists exult, since in their writings they proclaim with true faith that God came in the flesh and was born of a Virgin.

Mothers also glory today, celebrating with worthy praises the solemn feast of the Mother of their God. The supreme pontiffs, confessors, and Catholic teachers rejoice, while through their teaching God’s faithful believe and worship that the Son of God assumed what he was not and did not lose what he was. They proclaim that the Mother of God gave birth as a virgin and remained a virgin after giving birth.

I shall say something more, if I dare; I shall say it with faithful boldness, with devout temerity. The whole world today rejoices and is glad with fitting jubilation; only Tartarus howls, rages, and mutters beneath its breath, because the joy and gladness of this day grants some relief and refreshment to those confined within the infernal prison.

[Note: We do not see what can rightly be censured in the meaning of this passage. If it is understood of the souls of the just who are tormented in purgatory until they have washed away the stains of lighter offenses, then in our judgment it is entirely devout and Catholic. For it is devout, and not implausible, to think that on the more solemn festivals of Mary the torments of the faithful souls mentioned above are lightened, and sometimes even brought to an end, through the prayers and merits of so great a Virgin. What, then, prevents this interpretation from being applied to this passage? Certainly not the place of purgatory, which is believed to be situated in the lower parts of the earth and therefore placed within the infernal prison. Nor the torments said to be inflicted by the Tartarean ministers; for souls undergoing purification are tormented by none other than demons. Finally, not the name “captives,” which the author of the sermon uses: souls subjected to the power of demons with respect to punishment, and detained for a time in the lower prison, may rightly be called their captives.

“Nevertheless, suppose that he is speaking of the damned, who are commonly understood by this name—those condemned to eternal punishments on account of grave crimes. What then? Is it so absurd and unheard-of that even they might receive some alleviation of their punishments, although those punishments would not for that reason ever come to an end? Yet the blessed Augustine did not regard a similar thought concerning the damned as entirely inappropriate, although he himself did not approve it. Here are his words in the Enchiridion, chapter 112, where he discusses that verse of Psalm 87: ‘God will not forget to show mercy, nor will he restrain his mercies in his anger.’

“‘This is understood without hesitation of those who are called vessels of mercy, since they too are liberated not according to their merits but by God’s mercy; or, if they think that this applies to all—including the damned—it does not therefore follow that they should suppose the damnation of those of whom it is said, “These will go into eternal punishment,” will come to an end. … Let them suppose that the punishments of the damned are mitigated to some extent at definite intervals of time, if this pleases them. For even in this way it can be understood that God’s anger remains upon them—that is, the damnation itself—yet that in his anger he does not wholly restrain his mercies: not by bringing eternal punishment to an end, but by applying or interposing some relief amid the torments. For the psalm does not say “to bring his anger to an end,” or “after his anger,” but “in his anger.” … That perpetual death of the damned, therefore—that is, alienation from the life of God—will remain without end and will be common to all, however much people may, in accordance with their human feelings, conjecture differences in punishments or relief from, or interruption of, pains.’

“Prudentius also sang things agreeing with this opinion in Hymn 5, indicating that during the Easter festival some measure of rest and relaxation is granted to the damned:

> There are also, often, for the hurtful spirits  
> Festive holidays of punishment beneath Styx.  
> On that night when the holy God returned  
> From Acherontian waters to those above,  
> Tartarus grows slack with gentler punishments;  
> And the people of the shades rejoice in the leisure  
> Of their prison, freed from the fires,  
> Nor do the rivers boil with sulfur as usual.

“Who, then, would be surprised that what Prudentius, a Christian and most devout poet, said about the Easter festival was transferred by the author of this sermon, with a certain devout ‘temerity’ (as he himself puts it), to the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary? There is therefore no appearance of error in the passage, whatever interpretation is applied to it. Nevertheless, we judge the former interpretation to be more remote from every novelty of doctrine and no less consonant with the author’s intention.”]

The Tartarean ministers, I think, do not dare today to touch their captives, whom they remember to have been redeemed by the blood of him who deigned to be born of the Virgin for the salvation of the world.

Concerning the merits of this Virgin and her most glorious assumption today, the interpreter of divine law, namely Saint Jerome, and other outstanding teachers have been able and willing to say such great and wonderful things that we neither dare nor ought to add anything to them. Whoever wishes to know fully the glory of today’s solemnity should read the sermon which the aforesaid Father Jerome delivered to the holy Paula, to her virgin daughter Eustochium, and to the other virgins—not only those present but also those who would come later.

[Note: The author of the sermon on the Assumption, addressed to Paula and Eustochium, was falsely thought to be Jerome.]

In that sermon, not only women who are virgins but also men can learn how they ought to serve the Virgin of virgins in a virginal and manly manner. Today, most reverend fathers, dearest brothers, lords and elders, mothers and sisters, let us celebrate with the utmost devotion the most celebrated feast of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, so that through her singular merit and the prayers of all the saints and holy virgins, we may deserve to have as our gracious and favorable advocate the Son of the Virgin and Bridegroom of virgins, our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## The Sixth Sermon of the Same Author on the Assumption of Blessed Mary

[Col. 0264B]

Today, dearest brothers, the glorious and perpetual virgin Mary ascended into heaven; today, rescued from the earth and from the wicked present age, secure in unfading glory, she reached the palaces of heaven. On this day, I say, she deserved to be exalted above the choirs of angels, since, as we believe, raised to the right hand of the Father, she gloriously took her seat after Christ upon the throne of the heavenly kingdom.

[Note: Feu-ard. reads: “Upon the throne of the kingdom in heaven.”]

She is rightly called and believed to be the temple of the Lord and the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit. This is that glorious virgin whose ineffable merit was foretold long beforehand both in legal figures and in the oracles of the prophets. For what else did that rod of Aaron prefigure, which, placed in the Lord’s tabernacle, was found on the third day to have blossomed, with flowers already bursting forth from its expanded leaves, and with the swelling buds formed into almonds?

This sacred rod is the virgin Mary, who, neither sown nor rooted, was made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, without any cultivator, on the third day—that is, in the third age of the world—and bore for us God and the man Christ. His twofold substance was well represented by the almond. For an almond consists of flesh, bone, and kernel; so Jesus Christ is God and man in one person. In the almond, moreover, the outer flesh is exceedingly bitter, while the inner kernel refreshes those who eat it with pleasant sweetness. So Christ, through his humanity, experienced the bitterness of suffering, while through his divinity he remained incapable of suffering.

Of this rod the prophet Isaiah had foretold: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11:1). The virgin Mary, whose ascension to heaven we celebrate today, came forth from the stock of King David, who was the son of Jesse, from a most noble lineage and royal descent. “And a flower shall rise from his root,” because that true Nazarene, Christ, the flower of purity, came into the world through her, incarnate from her.

This is that most sacred flower who speaks of himself in the nuptial song of the Church: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1). He was the flower of the field, which was neither plowed nor sown, because he appeared born of a Virgin without the agency of a man. He became the lily of the valleys because, in order to reveal an example of humility, he chose poor parents from whom he would be born, himself deigning to become poor for our sake so that by his power we might be granted a share in the riches of his divinity.

The blessed prophet Ezekiel also testifies in the prophetic spirit that he was aware of this sacred Virgin, saying: “I saw a gate in the house of the Lord closed, and the angel said to me: ‘This gate which you see shall not be opened. The Prince shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord’” (Ezekiel 44:2–3). The closed gate in the house of the Lord is the ever-untouched virgin Mary. No man shall pass through it, because Joseph did not know her. It was closed forever, because Mary is virgin before childbirth, virgin in childbirth, and virgin after childbirth.

The Prince sat in it to eat bread before the Lord, because the Son of God remained in her womb for nine months, and from there he came forth, as a bridegroom from his chamber, to eat bread before the Lord, in accordance with what he himself said: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 4:34).

Thus, foretold by so many and such great prophecies of the prophets, this holy virgin and mother of the Lord was assumed into heaven today, to receive the fruit of her merits and the rewards of her labors. For when the Son of God ascended into heaven, he left his most chaste mother on earth for a time in order to prepare for her a place of immortality in the heavenly dwellings, so that she might reign with him forever.

This is the solemnity of the present day, on which she was gloriously and happily assumed into the heavenly bridal chamber. Her feast is certainly so much more excellent than the feasts of all the saints, and so incomparably worthy of wonder, as the Mother of God herself is incomparable to the other saints and regarded as more wondrous. Hence, speaking in the person of the citizens above, the Holy Spirit, marveling at her ascension, says in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up through the desert like a little column of smoke?” (Song of Songs 3:6).

For today this virgin ascended from the desert of the present age. Therefore the souls of the elect wondered who she might be, whose dignity surpassed even the excellence of the angels by the virtues of her merits. Like a little column of smoke, she rose from spices, because delicate and refined by divine disciplines, she was filled with the many fragrances of virtues, through which every day she burned herself as a holocaust to the Lord in the fire of devout love and the desire for charity.

Nor could this holy, most sacred Virgin remain long on earth after the Lord’s ascension. The angels desired her, and heaven itself was inquiring about her ascension. Therefore the Holy Spirit invited her, saying: “Come, my dove, my immaculate one; for winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed” (Song of Songs 2:10–11). He showed how ardently he wished to assume her by repeating the invitation frequently: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come” (Song of Songs 4:8).

And beautifully she is commanded to come from Lebanon, that is, from whiteness—for Lebanon is interpreted as “whitening.” This holy virgin was whitened by virtues and made radiant by the gifts of the Holy Spirit; she preserved the simplicity of a milky dove and the immaculate brightness of virginity. Therefore she alone was worthy to be the one through whom and from whom the Son of God, coming for the reconciliation of the human race, would assume flesh.

Hence that angelic greeting was fitting for her alone: “Hail, Mary, full of grace” (Luke 1:28). For grace is given to the other elect only in part, but in this Virgin the whole fullness of grace poured itself forth. Considering this, the prophet David says: “He shall descend like rain upon a fleece” (Psalm 71:6). The fleece prefigures virginity. For just as fleece, though it comes from the body, does not submit to bodily passion, so virginity, though it exists in the flesh, knows nothing of the vices of the flesh.

He descended, therefore, like rain upon a fleece, because the heavenly rain—that is, the wave of divinity—flowed gently into the virginal fleece when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). We must not omit the point which many, out of devotion, gladly embrace: that on this day she was bodily raised by her Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, to the palaces of heaven.

[Note: We find nothing erroneous or impious to declare in this passage if we consider the period in which the author of the sermon was writing concerning the bodily assumption of the Virgin. First, the entire meaning of this passage, as also of many other parts of the sermon, is in our judgment taken from the sermon on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, which this author repeatedly cites, falsely believing it to be by Saint Jerome. Learned men, however, think it to be by some Greek author who knew Latin imperfectly—whether Sophronius, nearly contemporary with Saint Jerome, or another author, as some prefer, more than a century later.

“Further, even if this sermon had been written in the seventh century, in our judgment its author could have asserted the same thing without any qualification: namely, that the bodily assumption of the Virgin into heaven, although some may have believed it with devout faith, was at that time neither sufficiently established nor numbered among truths so evident that it would be impious in any way to doubt them. For at that time this feast was not yet celebrated by the universal Church, nor had the consensus of all teachers converged upon the truth mentioned above, as we see happening today, when the entire Catholic Church throughout the world celebrates the Virgin assumed bodily, and the suffrages of all theologians agree so completely that anyone who dared to think otherwise would rightly incur the charge of impiety and temerity.

“That it should not seem surprising that in the seventh century the author of the sermon spoke of the assumption of the Virgin’s body with such hesitation and caution, we demonstrate by the example of another sermon written for the celebration of the same feast, in that same century or perhaps later, as is gathered from the authority of Saint Isidore, whom it praises by name. This sermon had once been attributed, together with others of the same kind, to Saint Augustine, but was later rejected as spurious. Whoever its author may have been, he speaks of the Virgin’s assumption as follows, section 2:

“‘We say this, brothers, because, just as the Church of Christ has now received it as customary, the Virgin Mary is said to have been assumed into heaven on this day. But no Catholic history relates by what order she passed from here to the heavenly kingdoms. This same Church of God is said not only to reject apocryphal writings but also to be ignorant of the matter. Indeed, there are certain writings without an author’s name concerning her assumption which, as I have said, are so carefully avoided that they are not permitted to be read at all as confirmation of the truth of the matter. Hence some are troubled, because her body is not found on earth, nor is her assumption with the flesh, as it is read in the apocryphal writings, found in Catholic history. …’

“‘Nor is any Latin commentator found to have spoken openly of anything concerning her death.
