For when the blessed Ambrose was treating that verse of the Gospel which Simeon said to the Lord’s mother, “And your own soul a sword will pierce,” he said: “Neither history nor Scripture teaches that Mary ended her life by the sword.” Hence Isidore also says: “It is uncertain whether by this saying he meant the sword of the spirit or the sword of persecution.” … It remains, therefore, that a man should not deceitfully invent as an open fact what God wished to remain hidden. But the true opinion concerning her assumption is shown to be this: that, according to the Apostle, whether in the body or outside the body, since we do not know, we should believe that she was assumed above the angels.’

“These remarks have been made so that we might show, by reason and example, that the author’s statement can be defended from harsher criticism.”]

Although it is devout to believe this, we nevertheless ought not to affirm it, lest we seem to accept doubtful matters as certain.

Whether this is true or not, we ought nevertheless to believe that she reigns with her Son in the heavenly realms, and that after God she confirms us in every truth and fortifies us by her merits and prayers. If you wish to know what she did after the Lord’s ascension, this alone is certain: the holy virgin remained so in body and mind, living with the apostles until they were sent to preach in various regions.

Although all the apostles revered her and served her in the duty of love, John loved and honored her more and more particularly than the others until the end of his life. He took the Virgin entrusted to him into his care, and thus assisted and served her as a son serves his mother, remembering what he had heard from the gracious Master on the cross: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19:26).

Let us therefore celebrate with spiritual joy today’s feast of this most holy Virgin and Mother of the Lord, who, as the Gospel says, “chose the best part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). Although this is understood historically as having been said of that Mary, the sister of Lazarus, Christ’s most ardent lover, it is nevertheless believed to apply especially to the blessed Mother of God. She chose the best part because she alone was granted to be a mother without losing the seal of chastity, to receive offspring while rejoicing in incorrupt virginity.

For although there are three orders of the faithful in the Church—married people, the continent, and virgins—she alone, by an excellent and unchangeable gift, could be both mother and virgin, preserve modesty, and from her untouched womb bring forth God and man. Hence we rightly confess her to be the Mother of God.

Let us now turn our prayers and vows to the woman of whom we are speaking; let each of us ask her intercession, and let us all ask together. Let us pray that she may be our protectress in prosperity, remove harmful things, suggest what will profit us, admit the prayers of those who supplicate her into the sanctuary of divinity, and obtain for us a share in her blessedness, with the favor and help of our Lord, her Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong dominion and immortality with God the Father throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: Amelianus: “A protectress in adversity, a promoter in prosperity; may she remove …”]

## The Seventh Sermon of the Same Author on the Assumption of Blessed Mary

[Note: Amelianus has “on the Assumption,” whereas Feu-ard. has “on the Nativity,” of which there is not a word in the entire sermon.]

The celebration of this day reminds us that we ought to dwell upon the praise of the Virgin Mary, because it is truly unworthy that, on a day belonging to so great a Mother of God, the tongue of flesh should silence the praises of our Lord. On this day, indeed, blessed virgin Mary appropriately proclaims freely to that heavenly Bridegroom: “You have held my right hand, and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have taken me up” (Psalm 72:24).

Today, I say, she also appropriately hears from the Bridegroom: “Come, my beloved, my beautiful one, my dove, for behold, winter has passed, the rain has gone away” (Song of Songs 2:10–11). And the blessed woman now replies: “Flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come” (Song of Songs 2:12). “My soul shall rejoice in the Lord and delight in his salvation” (Psalm 35:9); and, “In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the meek hear and rejoice” (Psalm 33:3); and, “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13).

Let us therefore see, brothers, what kind of Virgin this is—to whom the Holy Spirit deigned to come, who was so beautiful that God chose her as his bride, and so chaste that she could be a virgin after childbirth. This is, I say, the temple of God, that sealed fountain, and the closed gate of God. Into her, therefore, the Holy Spirit descended; the power of the Most High overshadowed her; and from her Christ, powerful in works, came forth (Luke 1:35).

She is untouched by intercourse, fruitful in childbirth, a virgin in chastity. She conceived as a virgin, not from a man but from the Holy Spirit; she gave birth not in pain but in joy; she nourished the food of angels and human beings.

Certainly happy and worthy of all praise is she who, without human seed, brought forth heavenly bread for the world and gave birth to the Savior of the world! O covenant of faith! O secret of faith! The angel promises a son who will be born to the virgin; the virgin rejoices and desires to become a mother. Truly a great and saving mystery: she gave birth in such a way that she can be called both mother and virgin.

Nurse, Mary, your Creator; nurse the bread of heaven; nurse the reward of the world. Offer your breast to him who suckles, so that he may offer his cheek to the one who strikes for your sake. As a mother, provide him with temporal substance, so that he himself may grant eternal life to us and to you.

[Note: The words that follow are absent in Feu-ard., though they are necessary for the completion of the sense.]

Nurse, then, him who made you, who made you such that he himself might be made in you. Nurse him who granted you the fruit of fertility through conception and did not take away the glory of virginity through birth.

See, brothers, how worthily consecrated virginity serves the Lord, whom he deigned to love in such a way that one and the same woman could be called both virgin and mother; what grace is to be preferred and proclaimed throughout all ages—that she alone obtained the dignity of motherhood and did not lose virginal purity.

She was chosen to give birth to her Creator; finally, she was astonished that she would give birth without having known a man, since she had known no marriage chamber. O how blessed is this mother, who conceived without defilement and gave birth without pain to the remedy! Blessed, I say, is the mother through whom the life of our race was restored, who received offspring from heaven and gave birth to the Savior of the world.

For in a marvelous and ineffable manner she gave birth to the Savior of all things and to her own Savior. The intact virgin was chosen so that she might be granted the fruitfulness of a mother; and she became a fruitful mother in whom the integrity of a virgin was preserved.

For if we consider a virgin who conceived flesh without the desire of the flesh, and conceived a man without a man, and if we wish to seek the explanation, we fail in the very act of our inquiry, since it is written: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). Indeed, blessed Mary herself, whose nativity we celebrate today, conceived through believing the one whom she bore through believing.

When the angel had announced to her the Lord’s birth, she, conscious of her chastity and of the divine dispensation, is reported to have replied to the angel: “How shall this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1:34). The angel answered her with a gentle countenance: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

Do not fear childbirth, virgin, nor be afraid, nor be excessively inexperienced through fear. Only believe, and you have conceived; love, and you have given birth. For the Holy Spirit will come upon you; therefore there is no reason for you to fear. And the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore you have reason to rejoice.

[Note: Feu-ard. incorrectly reads, “nor is there reason for you to rejoice.”]

Pain would follow childbirth if lust had preceded conception. But now the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you—that is, the same Holy Spirit will refresh you beneath his shadow, so that you will not be scorched by the heat of desire.

[Note: Feu-ard.: “so that you may not be terrified in the fury of desire.” Amelianus: “so that you may not be held in the fervor …” We have not hesitated to emend the reading to “scorched” on certain conjectural grounds.]

Therefore the holy thing that will be born from you shall be called the Son of God. When Mary heard these things, already pregnant with the seed of faith and conceiving Christ in her mind before conceiving him in her womb, she answered the angel: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). Immediately, as the Virgin’s consent was revealed, the Bridegroom entered her immaculate body, and he whom the whole world cannot contain was poured into the limbs of an unmarried girl.

For hear, brothers, how the gate through which the Lord entered was always closed—the gate which the prophet Ezekiel saw in a divine vision: “I turned,” he says, “toward the way of the gate of the outer sanctuary that faced eastward; and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate which you see shall be closed and shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel shall enter and depart through it, and it shall always be closed’” (Ezekiel 44:1–2).

[Note: Feu-ard.: “Which, when it clearly showed …”]

Behold how clearly he shows us that holy Mary was always a virgin and remained a virgin: virgin before childbirth, virgin in childbirth, and virgin after childbirth. She conceived, and she is a virgin; she gives birth, and she is a virgin; she nurses, and she is a virgin.

[Note: We print the reading from Amelianus, whereas Feu-ard. printed: “For blessed Mary could be a mother; she could be a woman.”]

The virgin Mary could indeed be a mother, but she could not be a woman. A great mystery! A great gift! A great grace! A handmaid gave birth to the Lord; a creature gave birth to the Creator. With a fruitful womb and intact generative organs, the virgin mother poured forth the Lord upon the earth.

Conceiving as a virgin, giving birth as a virgin, remaining a virgin; a pregnant virgin, a fruitful virgin, an everlasting virgin.

[Note: “Remaining a virgin.” These words were absent in Feu-ard. Amelianus, moreover, writes “pregnant” in place of “fruitful.”]

Why are you amazed, O human being? God ought to be born in this way when he deigned to become man. Meanwhile, let us turn with our whole affection to the help of the blessed Virgin; with one mind and every effort let us implore her patronage. And while we attend upon her with humble service on earth, may she deign by her diligent prayer to commend us in heaven to the Lord our God, who lives and reigns as God in the Trinity throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

## The Eighth Sermon of the Same Author in Praise of the Blessed Virgin Mary

[Note: This sermon is found word for word among those once attributed to Saint Jerome and later published among the spurious works.]

Knowing, dearest brothers, that we owe much to our Creator because we were created, and more because we were redeemed, let us venerate the exchange of our redemption and that most sacred womb from which God, united to man, appeared. Even if we do not honor it for its merits, let us at least celebrate it through acts of devotion.

[Note: “Knowing” is absent in Feu-ard.]

Knowing that the darkness of our error was partly sprinkled with its radiance, because what the defiant pride and gluttony of the first mother had lost through the negligence of the first-created parents, the birth of this sacred Virgin not only restored what had been ruined but also bestowed eternal things.

[Note: Amelianus: “The first mother.”]

Therefore let us venerate with every kind of praise the mother of our Creator, who, while conceiving her Creator, displayed to us in the world the exalted Redeemer. And because she is established as a model after the likeness of her mother, our mother the Church, may she herself look upon it amid the roaring storms of the age; may she herself continually sustain it through prayer amid the world’s rushing courses.

For there is no doubt that she who deserved to give the price for the liberation of others can bestow assistance upon the liberated.

[Note: Feu-ard.: “That she who deserved to give the price for the liberated may be able to bestow assistance …”]

Meanwhile, let our prayer continually be directed to God, so that what he sanctified when he entered that womb for the honor of his name, and what we venerate with the devotion that is due, may profit us as a remedy—he who through her gave himself to us as the price of our redemption.

Blessed Mary is rightly exalted by our singular praise, for she offered the world a singular exchange.

[Note: “Singular” is absent in Feu-ard.]

She rightly rejoiced even then among women, when she carried in her chaste womb a singular remedy. She felt the weight of her womb, yet had not lost the modesty of chastity. She marveled at the signs of childbirth, though she had known no contact with a man.

O truly fruitful virginity, which, in a new and unheard-of manner, could be called both mother and virgin! She gave birth to him from whom she began; she carried him by whom she was created, since he himself is the author of Mary who was born from Mary.

Thus, in an ineffable manner, blessed Mary is both mother and virgin: she became the fruit of a foreign sojourn and suffered no loss of integrity. In her, heavenly providence so arranged the condition of the matter that she displayed obedience to the command while recognizing the honor announced by the angel.

For she does not detract from the credibility of the messenger when she understands the dignity of what was announced to her by the angel, who said: “For the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy thing that will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Having been instructed, she believed what she heard; having been sanctified, she deserved what she believed.

Finally, [Note: [Col. 0270D] The Amelian manuscript reads: “He lowered himself from such a height that the Word,” etc.] she raised herself to such a height, even to the summit of heaven, that she received the Word who was in the beginning with God—that is, the Son of God—from the highest citadel. And while he always mingled the hidden mystery of the divinity [Note: [Col. 0270D] Feu-ard reads: “and the fragility of our flesh.”] with the frailty of our flesh, divinity lay hidden in the human being, so that humanity might not perish in divinity; and, concealed beneath the veil of the assumed flesh, he redeemed the lost more preciously than if he had defended captives from the enemy threatening them.

Immense is his compassion, and his majesty is to be proclaimed above all that can be expressed! The womb of the maiden filled the palace of the Holy Spirit; the womb of the unmarried Virgin concealed the seed of the Word as it grew. The secret recesses of her body, I say, were filled, filled with the fruitfulness of the Holy Spirit; and there was hope in the birth, because there had been no pleasure in intercourse. The most beautiful mother was astonished [Note: [Col. 0270D] In Feu-ard alone one reads: “And, silently within herself, she marveled wondrously at the novelty of what had happened.”] and silently marveled within herself; she burned with the heat of uncertain reflection, and, struck by the novelty of events, was wondrously astonished. For she knew her own purity, yet marveled at the abundance of her womb.

O happy Mary! O glorious mother! O exalted mother in childbirth, in whose womb the author of heaven and earth is entrusted! O happy kisses pressed upon the lips of the nursing mother, when, amid the toys of crawling infancy, the true son from you played with you as his mother, while, as Lord from the Father, he commanded! For, conceiving your own creator, you brought him forth in time as one grown, whom before time you had possessed as the Creator. O happy childbirth—delightful to angels, awaited by the saints, necessary for the lost, fitting for the fallen! After enduring many insults in the flesh he had assumed, and at last [Note: [Col. 0270D] For “was scourged,” Feu-ard reads “burned.”] scourged with lashes, given gall to drink, and fastened to the gibbet, he showed that you were truly his mother; and by suffering torments he demonstrated that he was truly human.

But you, blessed and glorious Mary, are worthy of praise amid these things and because of these things: you merited the gift of fruitfulness in such a way that you did not lose the support of virginity. For you are blessed among women; you are preeminent among all the ranks of virgins; you follow the Lamb wherever he goes. You invite virgin choirs, estranged from the goads of the enticements of the flesh, through shining lilies and blooming roses, to drink at the fountain of eternal life. Having attained the dignity of the first rank in that most blessed region of virtues, you wander with dewy feet among the grassy choirs of paradise’s delights, advancing on tender knees, and with a happy palm you pluck unfading violets. Joined to choirs singing without end, associated with angels and archangels, you never cease to cry out “Holy” with tireless voice. But what can I say, poor in understanding, when whatever I say about you is surely less than your dignity deserves? If I call you the mother of nations, you surpass the title; if I call you the form of God, you are worthy of it; if I call you the nurse of heavenly bread, you fill us with the sweetness of milk.

Nurse, therefore, mother; nurse our food, nurse the heavenly bread, nurse the food of angels; nurse him who made you such that he himself might become in you. By his conception he brought you the gift of fruitfulness, and by his birth did not take away the honor of virginity; before he was born, he created you as the mother from whom he would be born, so that from there he might come forth like a bridegroom from his chamber and be seen by mortal eyes. How great was this condescension: that he should be created from you, whom he had created; carried in the hands that he had fashioned; suck at your breasts, which he himself had filled? What praises, then, shall we offer to God’s love? What thanks shall we give him, who loved us so greatly that for our sake he became human, [Note: [Col. 0271D] Feu-ardentius renders this poorly: “so that he might initiate the beginnings of our former condition.”] entered the womb of our condition, endured the humiliations of a newborn infant, and bore all the necessities of humanity?

Let us therefore give thanks as best we can to our Creator, and celebrate with joy the nativity [Note: [Col. 0271D] At this point the Amelian manuscript has (as it does below) *natalem*, or “conception,” namely, the active virginity of blessed Mary, which is the subject of the whole sermon.] of that most precious mother [Col. 0271C]. For it is fitting to serve her with the greatest rejoicing, through whom the insignia of virginity blossomed. Indeed, she was a virgin before marriage, a virgin in marriage; a virgin while pregnant, a virgin in childbirth, a virgin while nursing. Given to a husband, yet a mother not from a husband. For the almighty Son of the holy mother in no way took away at his birth the virginity that he chose at his own birth.

Let virgins, therefore, rejoice: a virgin bore Christ. Let them think that nothing of what they knew has been destroyed, because she remained a virgin after childbirth. Let widows rejoice as they celebrate the Virgin’s nativity: Anna, a widow, recognized the Virgin as mother. Let married women rejoice as they attend the solemnity of the blessed mother: Elizabeth, a married woman, was greeted as the Virgin Mother of the Lord. Let boys rejoice, commending continence to a boy: he himself consecrated the integrity of boyhood’s continence, who brought fruitfulness to his mother without taking away her virginity. To him be honor, glory, and power through immortal ages of ages. Amen.

## THE SAME AUTHOR’S SERMON IX: THE EIGHTH SERMON ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

[Col. 0271D]

[Note: [Col. 0272D] Almost the whole sermon is taken from the preceding sermon.]

It is therefore with good reason that holy and venerable Mary, Virgin and Mother of God, Queen of heaven and Lady of the world, is exalted by us with singular praise: she who offered the world a singular exchange. Finally, she raised herself to such a height, even to the summit of heaven, that she received the Word who was in the beginning with God from the highest citadel of heaven.

O happy Mary, worthy of every praise! O glorious mother! O exalted mother in childbirth, in whose womb the author of heaven and earth is entrusted! She is undefiled in intercourse, fruitful in childbirth, a virgin nursing the Lord of heaven, nourishing the food of angels and of human beings. O happy kisses pressed upon the lips of the nursing mother! O happy childbirth, joyful to angels, desired by saints, necessary for the lost, fitting for the fallen!

What praises, therefore, O Lady, salvation of the whole world, will the frailty of the human race render to you, which through your singular exchange found the way to restoration [Note: [Col. 0272D] Feu-ard reads: “You found it.”]? O how venerable, and more worthy of honor than all others, is this day, on which the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, departed from the world to Christ—she who knew neither sorrow after childbirth nor weariness after her passing! O wondrous bridal chamber, from which the bridegroom, beautiful in form, came forth! O light of the nations, hope of the faithful, tabernacle of glory, heavenly temple, to whom the apostles render sacred service, at whose triumph the angels sing, whom Christ embraces!

O blessed Mary, enter paradise rejoicing. You have been transferred by angels from earthly life to heavenly life, and among the choirs of virgins, like the shining sun, you have received precedence over the archangels in heaven. O most exalted one, whom paradise joyfully welcomed today; whom cherubim and seraphim accompany with praises; whom the white-robed martyrs bless; whom the robed company of the saints celebrates together; toward whom the army of all the holy virgins, exulting with their victorious palms [Note: [Col. 0272D] *Palmis*, from the Amelian manuscript; Feu-ard had *psalmis*, “with psalms,” as shortly below he had *charissima* for *clarissima*.], comes joyfully! O brightest among virgins, who today, exalted with praises and funeral rites, have been most gloriously carried into heaven with a great triumph!

Receive, therefore, most pious and most merciful Lady, whatever acts of thanksgiving, feeble and unequal to your merits, we can offer; and when you have received our vows, excuse our faults by your prayers. Admit our prayers into the sanctuary of hearing, and return to us the grace of reconciliation. Let what we have done badly be excused through you; accept what we offer; obtain what we ask. For we cannot find anyone more powerful than you to appease the Judge’s anger—you who merited becoming the mother of that same Redeemer and Judge.

Come to the aid, therefore, most pious Mother of Christ, of the wretched who flee to you; help and comfort all who trust in you. Pray for the sins of the whole world; intervene for the clergy; intercede for the company of monks; pray for the devout female sex. Let all who invoke your glorious name experience your clemency. Let compassion be yours toward the affliction of captives; let tender devotion be yours toward pilgrims to heaven.

And because you see yourself rejoicing and exulting without end in heaven, grant that you may admit to God the prayers that we pour out to you with tears, and that you may appeal to him for us as your own Son, so that, when he comes at the end of the world as Judge, we too may appear with him in glory. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## THE SAME AUTHOR’S SERMON X: ON THE PURIFICATION OF HOLY MARY

At that time, when the days of Mary’s purification according to the law of Moses had been completed, they brought the Lord Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke 2:22).

The sequence of this reading commends many things, but above all the virtue of humility, which is the mother and guardian of the other virtues, so much so that no other virtue can be possessed without it. The present reading therefore commends this virtue to us no less in the Lord and Savior than in his venerable mother. Although both of them were free from every commandment of the law, each nevertheless wished voluntarily to submit to the legal institutions in order to commend humility.

Let every pure and sinful human being therefore consider how much obedience he owes to the divine commandments, if the God-man, free from every sin, wished to humble himself so greatly for human beings. But so that we may understand how entirely God and his mother were exempt from the commandment of the law, let us examine the commandment itself more carefully.

“Any woman,” God says in the law (Leviticus 12:2–4), “who conceives and bears a male child shall be unclean for seven days. On the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised, and she herself shall remain thirty-three days in the purification of her blood.” Since, then, it declares the woman who has conceived and given birth from male seed unclean and commands her to be purified over a period of time, it certainly excludes from this requirement the woman who conceived not from male seed but through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit.

But the Lord voluntarily wished to submit himself to the law in order to free us from the curse of the law. Likewise, his undefiled mother, who knew that she owed nothing to the law, nevertheless, for the sake of humility, wished to fulfill the legal commandment, completing what the wise man said: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus 3:20).

After her days of purification had been completed—whether those of the Lord or of his mother, for mother and son were commanded to be purified in one and the same order—they brought him (there can be no doubt that this means the child Jesus), his parents bringing him to Jerusalem, to the temple of the Lord, to present him—that is, to establish and consecrate him—to the Lord.

The Hebrew boys who were brought to Jerusalem from every kingdom, if they belonged to the tribe of Levi, were detained there in the temple of the Lord to serve perpetually. If they belonged to another tribe, they were redeemed by their parents with a payment and taken back home. The purification of the boys consisted in the offering of sacrifices; that of the mothers consisted in being prohibited for forty days both from entering the temple of the Lord and from the bed of a husband—not because it is sinful to beget children from a lawful and marital union, but because even lawful and marital intercourse cannot be entirely free from the guilt of iniquity.

For we know that the goodness of marriage was divinely granted from the very beginning of the human race. Hence the Apostle undoubtedly commends honorable marriage and an undefiled marriage bed (Hebrews 13:4). Although lawful marriage is generously granted by God in faith and love, if it is not undertaken by the will of lust, it nevertheless necessarily produces offspring tainted by the sin of the first human being. Thus, although what is born from a good marriage is so good that it is not even evil if it is born without adultery or fornication, God bestowed the gift of fruitfulness upon human nature; the evil of lust, however, is not God’s creation but the punishment of sin. Therefore, a human being is not born pure from the purity of marriage, because, when sordid lust intervenes, iniquity is sown. [Note: [Col. 0273C] The Amelian manuscript reads “from impurity.”]

Hence blessed David, who knew that he had been begotten from a lawful marriage, nevertheless, conscious of this matter, lamented the stain of carnal generation with a heavy sigh, saying: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Psalm 50:7). These few remarks have been made so that we may understand that the stain of original sin consists not in lawful marriage but in the pleasure and delight of lust.

As for the fact that a woman was prohibited from entering the temple for forty days after giving birth, this appears, according to the literal sense, to have been done because the infant is formed in the womb over as many days as the mother’s purification was celebrated. For physicians—that is, those who discuss the generation of individual things—say that the seed received by the woman resembles milk during the first six days; during the following nine it is changed into blood; during the remaining twelve it becomes solid; then, during another nineteen days, it is formed through the individual outlines of the limbs; after that, until the time of birth, it increases in size.

These numbers together make forty-six. Six, nine, twelve, and nineteen likewise make forty-six, the number by which, as has been said, the infant is conceived in the mother’s womb.

Therefore even the name of the first human being, Adam, expresses the same number through the Greek letters. For according to the calculation of the Greeks, who assign a definite number to each letter, the letters make one and four, and again one and forty; these letters form the name *Adam*, while the numbers yield forty-six. [Note: [Col. 0273C] The Amelian manuscript: A is one, D four; likewise A is one, M forty.]

Hence the Jews in the Gospel (John 2:20), although ignorant of what they were saying, nevertheless spoke truthfully about the temple of the Lord’s body, which was to be destroyed by them in death and raised by him after three days: “This temple was built in forty-six years.” [Note: [Col. 0273D]

At first sight these words are admittedly rather difficult. They seem to signify that the conception of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was completed over a period of forty-six days, in the manner of other human beings. Against this, all Catholics, together with the holy Fathers, believe against the heterodox that, through the miraculous operation of the Holy Spirit, it was perfected in an instant.

Yet let us not immediately condemn the author. There is a somewhat similar passage in Saint Augustine (as we said in the note to the reader), which our author appears to have had before his eyes when composing this sermon. Augustine’s passage is in *The Eighty-Three Diverse Questions*, question 56, concerning the forty-six years in which the temple was built (John 2:20). In explaining it, after reviewing in almost the same words as our author the sequence that physicians are said to observe in the formation of the human body, and after various multiplications and combinations of the number forty-six, from which the number of days contained in nine months is finally derived, he concludes:

“Therefore it is not absurd to say that the temple was built in forty-six years, since it signified his body, so that as many days as there were years in the construction of the temple, so many days were there in the perfection of the Lord’s body.”

Since every theologian has explained this passage of Augustine with a suitable interpretation, it will not be difficult to interpret our author’s words similarly from their commentaries. Consult Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, book III, distinction 3, and the commentators on this passage of the Master. One of them now comes to mind, D. Bonaventure, who speaks as follows:

“It must be said that in Scripture a thing is frequently said to occur when it becomes known; and Augustine’s statement must be understood in this way. For although the Lord’s body was formed from the instant of conception, it did not yet appear or become perceptible because of the smallness of its bulk; but after forty-six days it was brought to such a size of perfection that it could be visible to human eyes, and so forth.”

We believe, then, that the Lord’s body was formed in the Virgin’s womb over this number of days, in accordance with the very common usage of Scripture, which takes years for days and the part for the whole. But the fact that purification is commanded to be completed not in forty-six days but in forty is a very common scriptural usage: smaller numbers are accustomed to transcend the cause and include the larger numbers within them. [Col. 0274C]

“For every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exodus 12:14). After the Lord passed through Egypt and slew the firstborn of the Egyptians and led the children of Israel out from there, he consecrated to himself all the firstborn of the children of Israel, both human and animal. The law was that animals, if they were clean, were to be offered in sacrifice; if unclean, they were either exchanged, redeemed, or killed, according to what is written in the law.

The firstborn of human beings, if he belonged to the tribe of Levi, was detained there, as has been said; if he belonged to another tribe, he was redeemed with a payment and taken back home. The payment was five shekels, according to the weight of the sanctuary, after one month.

Allegorically, all these firstborn signified that one and singular firstborn, who, although unique in the substance of God the Father, became in the substance of humanity the firstborn of every creature—that is, of all human beings—as the Apostle says of him: “He is the firstborn of the dead and the prince of the kings of the earth” (Revelation 1:5). He was truly and uniquely holy to the Lord, because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

Tropologically, we too offer all our firstborn in the Lord’s sacrifice when we attribute whatever good we conceive in our minds through his grace not to our own strength but to his grace. We redeem our unclean things with the price of five shekels when we punish with worthy satisfaction whatever wrongs we have committed through the five bodily senses.

“And to offer,” he says, “a sacrifice.” This was the sacrifice of the poor. For the law commanded (Leviticus 12:6–8) that the parents should offer for the child an unblemished lamb and a turtledove or a young pigeon. But if their means could not provide a lamb, they were to offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons.

Our Redeemer, however, mindful in every respect of our salvation, not only deigned to become human for us but also a poor human being. He wished a poor sacrifice to be offered for him and wished to be born of poor parents, so that by his poverty he might make us participants in spiritual riches and the heavenly kingdom, according to the Apostle’s words: “Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor, so that by his poverty we might be enriched” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

It is not without a mystery that these birds in particular were commanded to be offered in the Lord’s sacrifice. For by these birds, whoever was to be cleansed was commanded in the law to be purified. The dove is the simplest of animals and is free from the bitterness of gall. The turtledove, however, excels in chastity, so much so that if by chance it loses its mate, it does not thereafter seek another spouse.

The Lord’s command that these birds be offered to him in sacrifice signified that he takes delight in the most chaste simplicity of the saints as in a most pleasing sacrifice. It should also be noted that both birds habitually produce a moaning sound instead of a song, signifying the twofold lamentation of the saints in this world. They mourn both their own offenses, from which they cannot be entirely free as long as they are here, and the fact that they are delayed from the kingdom for so long.

The fact that the dove usually moves in a flock, whereas the turtledove is solitary, signifies through the dove the active life, which is shared by many, and through the turtledove the contemplative life, which can be imitated by few.

“And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon.” When the Lord came in the flesh, he received testimony not only from angels but also from every human condition, because it was fitting that the one who came for the salvation of all should receive testimony from every age, sex, and condition.

That exalted and angelic dignity had already borne witness to him when, at his birth, the angels cried out in exultation: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14). The Virgin who bore him had borne witness; the married man Zachariah, together with his wife Elizabeth, had borne witness; the child John, still in his mother’s womb, had borne witness.

It remained for some continent and elderly man to give him testimony. Such a man is introduced here, one whose assertion no one would doubt: “A man,” it says, “just and devout.” After saying “just,” it rightly added “devout,” because justice cannot in any way be preserved without the fear of God. In truth he was just, because he was awaiting not merely his own consolation but that of the whole people.

[Col. 0276A] “And he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit.” The ancient saints had a great desire to see Christ in the flesh, whom they knew through the oracles of the prophets to be destined to be born of a Virgin [Note: [Col. 0275D] The Amelian manuscript reads: “who knew him.”]—as the Lord himself made clear when he said to his disciples in the Gospel: “I tell you that many prophets and kings and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke 10:24).

This grace of merit was granted to the holy old man Simeon. He received an answer from the Holy Spirit with which he was filled: he would not see temporal death before he had first seen in the flesh Christ, who would redeem the whole human race. “And he came in the Spirit into the temple.” We must not think that he came into the temple without a body, by the spirit alone, in order to see the one whom he had long desired to see.

“And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he also took him in his arms”—that is, in his embrace.

Mystically, this holy old man represents the world, already declining as though into a long old age and burdened with advanced years. The old man therefore took the child Christ into his arms, because the world, in the final age of its existence, received the incarnate Son of God; and, stripped by him of the oldness of its sins, it was reborn into the new infancy of the Christian religion.

“And he blessed God.” This blessed old man knew that those who saw Christ in the flesh would be blessed. For this reason he desired to remain in the body for so long, until he could behold him even with bodily eyes, as though already secure concerning the redemption of the entire human race: “Now,” he said, “you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace.”

As if he were saying: “You dismiss me in peace because I see peace.” For Christ is our peace, who, according to the Apostle, was made peace and reconciliation for us by God the Father (Ephesians 2:14).

Why he wished to be dismissed in peace he makes clear: “Because,” he says, “my eyes have seen your salvation.” He calls Christ the salvation of God, through whom God the Father reconciled the world and restored the human race to eternal salvation, so that all who wished to believe in him might behold him in faith and love.

It is evident that at his first coming the Lord was by no means seen by all peoples. But when he says “before the face of all peoples,” he directs the eye of prophecy, in prophetic fashion, toward the future day of judgment [Note: [Col. 0276D] Feu-ard reads: “The prophetic eye is directed …” incorrectly.], when Christ in his humanity will be seen by all flesh, so that every eye may see him and he may repay each person according to his works.

“A light,” he says, “for revelation to the nations.” Christ became light for both peoples, the Jewish and the Gentile, because he led both from the darkness of ignorance and unbelief to the true light of divine knowledge.

More particularly, he was the glory of the people of Israel [Note: [Col. 0276D] The Amelian manuscript reads: “the glory of the people.”], because he was incarnate from that people, lived among them, and performed among them miracles previously unheard of. It should be noted that he first said that Christ came as light for the revelation of the nations, and then for the glory of the people of Israel, because, with prophetic insight, he foresaw that the nations would first be converted to the faith of Christ and that afterward the Jews would believe in him at the end of the world.

The Psalmist says something similar. After first speaking of the calling of the nations—“The Lord has made known his salvation; in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (Psalm 97:2)—he immediately added concerning the final conversion of the Jews: “He has remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel.”

The Apostle also agrees with this: “When,” he says, “the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25). The Psalmist speaks again of this conversion: “They will return in the evening and suffer hunger like dogs, and they will go around the city.” That is, the Jews, converted to the faith of Christ at the end of the world, as though at evening, will hunger for that bread which came down from heaven (John 6:59). And, in order to deserve to receive it, they will go around the city set upon Christ the mountain—that is, the holy Church—like dogs, so that the one whom they now persecute impiously like the most savage hunters they may then protect with the barking of devout commitment [Note: [Col. 0277C] Alternatively: “like a stag pursued by hunters,” according to the reading of the Amelian manuscript.].

Let these brief remarks on the text of the Gospel reading suffice. Although they reveal the reasons for this solemnity sufficiently and abundantly, it is nevertheless not inappropriate to say something more briefly about its name.

It is therefore called by the Greek name *Ypapante*, which may be rendered in Latin as “meeting.” For in Greek *ypante* means “to meet.” This festival is designated by that name because, when the Lord was brought into the temple by his parents on this day, we believe that he was met by the saints, of whom it is certain that there were very many in Jerusalem at that time.

This festival is celebrated in the month of February, which the Romans, while still pagans, named from Februus—that is, Pluto—whom they believed to be the most powerful deity of purification. [Note: [Col. 0277C]

Pliny: “In ancient times the common opinion prevailed that *februa* were all those things by which the consciences of wrongdoers were cleansed, sins erased, or the spirits of the dead made peaceful.”

Varro, *On the Life of the Roman People*: “When cakes have been made in their sacred rites, they are customarily sprinkled with a seed of spelt, and they say that by this they *februare*, that is, purify them.”

Ovid, *Fasti*, book II:

“The Roman fathers called *februa* the things of purification;

Even now many signs confirm the word’s meaning.”

And shortly afterward:

“Whatever it is by which our bodies are purified,

Among our unshorn ancestors it bore this name.”

Blessed Augustine, *The City of God*, book VII, chapter 7: “They say that the Terminalia are celebrated in the same month of February, when the purifying sacrifice called *Februum* is performed; from this the month received its name.”

The same author, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book XVIII, chapter 5: “January was named from Janus, February from the sacred *Februa* of the Luperci.”

Albinus, *On the Offices of the Church*.

Concerning this festival, the priest and distinguished teacher Bede says, *On the Times*: “Numa dedicated the second month to Februus, that is, Pluto, who was believed to have power over purifications; and it was necessary that the city be purified in that month. But Christian religion rightly changed this custom of purification, since in the same month, on the day of Saint Mary, the entire people, together with priests and ministers, proceeds devoutly through the churches and suitable places of the city while singing hymns, carrying in their hands the burning candles given by the pontiff.”

Amalarius Fortunatus, *On the Offices of the Church*, book III, chapter 43, and Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of Clergy*, book II, chapter 33, transmit the same account in the same words.

Whoever desires fuller information should consult John of Chartres, *Sermon on the Purification of Saint Mary*; Rupert, *On the Divine Offices*, book III, chapter 25; and William, bishop of Mende, *On the Reason for the Divine Offices*, book VI. FEU-ARD.]

For we say *februare*, “to purify.” In that month the city was purified. After the Romans had subjugated all nations, they imposed tribute upon them on the condition that the same tribute should be paid every fifth year. When that period had elapsed and the census had been paid, the city was purified by the whole people, as has been said, and they offered sacrifices to the spirits of the dead, by whose assistance and power they thought they had subjugated the whole world.

Christian religion suitably and devoutly changed this custom of purification, since in the same month—that is, on this day—in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, not only the clergy but also the entire people go around the places of the churches with candles and various hymns, purifying them [Note: [Col. 0278D] Feu-ard reads *lustrantibus*, “while they purify,” and shortly below, where the text has “of earthly dominion,” he printed “of eternal dominion.” Both readings have been corrected from the Amelian manuscript.]. They do this no longer in remembrance of the five-year cycle of earthly dominion, but in memory of the perpetual kingdom of heaven, when, according to the Gospel parable, all the saints, meeting Christ the Bridegroom at the end of the world with the lamps of good works, will be admitted by him into the chamber of eternal happiness.

To this chamber, may we too deserve to be admitted. Let us earnestly implore the help of the holy Mother of God, so that through her powerful intercession with the mercy of her Son she may obtain for us forgiveness of all our crimes—she who on this day underwent temporal purification without the stains of sin. Through the same Lord our Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns through ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XI: ON THE NATIVITY OF THE MOTHER OF GOD AND EVER-VIRGIN MARY

Hear, brothers, and understand. Consider how the almighty God, through his ineffable compassion, created the world, and by his supreme proprietorship fashioned the human being in his own image. He established him as a cultivator of paradise, so that he might enjoy perpetual life and rejoice daily in the companionship of the angels. But through the weakness of the flesh that he had received, he did not preserve the promise that he had received, being persuaded by the adversary, who through pride lost what he possessed and through envy harmed the human being.

For wherever he found the weaker part, there he first offered his persuasion. Through the same fall by which he himself had fallen, he struck down the human race in that man. For he said to the woman: “If you eat from this fruit, you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). This was the beginning of sin: pride, by which the human being, made from earth, conceived in his mind the desire to become equal to God. He wished to know what he could in no way possess.

Then they were cast from paradise into this world, into this valley of tears, where they ended their life in labor and sweat and left their descendants amid the same misery, because it is written: “Death ruled in Adam, and so it will rule over all his children.”

When the Creator of the world had considered all things through his wisdom [Col. 0278B] [Note: [Col. 0278D] Feu-ard reads “had created”; the Amelian manuscript’s *considerasset*, “had considered,” is better.], and saw that the world was so fragile and perishable in every respect, always inclined toward worse things, fallen from good things and rushing into evils, he grieved through his great compassion. He had created the human being in his own image out of benevolence, yet the human being had freely destroyed himself; therefore God arranged how he might restore him to the former place in which he had established him.

In his wisdom, then, he arranged from afar that he would redeem through himself what he had fashioned through himself. Through his compassion and omnipotence he wished to visit the world, so that he who had made the human being might redeem him through his visitation. He prepared a vessel for himself, so that through it he might appear to human beings. For it is written: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Proverbs 9:1)—or a temple, that is, the Virgin Mary.

Let us consider, as far as we can, for the tongue is not sufficient to express what the will desires to proclaim, how great was God’s kindness: that from so far away he should seek for himself a temple in which to dwell. For the Virgin Mary was not born in the way that boys and girls ordinarily are born, but from the barren Anna and an already elderly father, beyond the customary course of women, after the heat had grown cold and the blood in the breast had already cooled, and after every desire of lust had departed; she was born [Note: [Col. 0278D] The Amelian manuscript reads: “from a barren old woman.”].

Thus the Lord wished his mother to be born from such a vessel. We know now that, by the ordering and gracious command of the Holy Spirit, he prepared for himself a mother who surpassed all mothers. For she was such as had never before been seen and would have no successor.

An honorable day, and a sacred festival, on which the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, was born. This is our joy; this is our festival: for when he willed, he brought it about that, through his great mercy, he might visit us through the Virgin. Let us all rejoice and be glad in celebrating today’s festival of blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, because it is glorious and holy—the day on which the Redeemer of all began his wondrous visitation and deigned to recall us from captivity to our former state. May almighty God himself, we beseech you, assist us through the glorious intercession of his Mother, in whom his blessed birth was begun, so that through her intercession we may live with him who for our sake deigned to undergo death, and may thereby deserve to possess everlasting life with him; through our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ON HOLY MARY

*[From the Amelianus manuscript, from which P. Flórez first published it.]*

### [Col. 0279B]

The Creator of all and the author of life, dearly beloved brothers—as your faith knows very well—is the Lord God, for it is written: “With you, Lord, is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10). Adam, the first man, was created by God very good; but, at Eve’s urging and through the serpent’s persuasion, he was most grievously deceived. The author of death, however, is the devil, as it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world, and those who belong to his side imitate him” (Wisdom 2:24–25).

For the devil himself was rightly created by God, but he did not wish to stand in the truth; rather, as soon as he was created, through the vice of his pride and having offended the Creator, he lost his heavenly seat. Wishing to restore those seats, the Lord formed the first parents—namely Adam and his wife Eve—from earth and into earth, so that from their race he might restore the vacant ruins of heaven. But the author of death, envious of this restoration, hastened to mingle the poison of his death with the unformed source of the human race, just as one might scatter streams of birth across the fields. Thus he corrupted the human race, as though it were a single tree still tender at the root, putting forth shoots in the offspring of its propagation.

Hence the corrupted root continually and without interruption puts forth leaves, and its leaves continually wither through death. It often happens that gleaming gold is found in mud, and that from a piercing thorn a beautiful red rose emerges. Through the work of divine Providence, therefore, a shoot emerged without defect from a corrupted root; this is understood as the most blessed Virgin Mary, as the prophet Isaiah testifies when he says: “A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11:1).

The figure of this glorious Virgin, that is, holy Mary, was represented by the rod that served Aaron the priest, which the Lord commanded holy Moses to place in the tabernacle. On the following day it alone put forth leaves and produced nuts (Numbers 17:7–8), because without doubt the Virgin Mary alone was the one who bore the Lord and remained a virgin after childbirth. Through her, therefore, the author of life openly condemned the author of death, when through the Son of a woman he condemned the sin of a woman. For it is written: “Sin began with a woman, and through her we all die” (Ecclesiasticus 25:33). And again: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived” (1 Timothy 2:14). Thus, in the opposite direction, the restoration of life began with a woman, through whose Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, we all rise again, because it is written: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

Let us therefore see, dearest brothers, how these two women differ from one another. Through a crooked serpent, the author of death persuaded Eve to accept death; conversely, through the archangel Gabriel, the author of life sent the assistance of salvation to blessed Mary. The devil persuaded Eve to eat forbidden food; the angel announced to Mary that she would conceive a son through obedience to the promise.

Eve, by eating the forbidden fruit, harmed both herself and her husband; blessed Mary, by conceiving the Son given to us—as it is written, “A child is born to us, a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6)—benefited both women and men. Eve appeared to seize the essence of divinity furtively in her mind, as the utterance of the Holy Trinity testifies: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us” (Genesis 3:22). Mary, however, confesses herself to be the humble handmaid of the Lord; for she said to the angel: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).

Holy Mary, through the obedience of humility, was overshadowed by the power of the Most High’s divinity; Eve, conceiving through corruption and giving birth in sorrow, was placed under the authority of her husband. Mary, conceiving in faith through the mystery of the Holy Spirit and giving birth in joy, became one whose authority kings and princes themselves desire to accept with jubilation. Eve was sent from paradise into exile; Mary was raised from the exile of this world to heaven.

Eve, fearing after childbirth, hid herself among the trees of paradise; the rejoicing Virgin Mary, after childbirth, was surrounded by choirs of the angels of the heavenly army, who said with joy: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). Eve transmitted the human descendants born from her flesh to hell; blessed Mary directs those born from her offspring to heaven. Those born from Eve’s flesh are called children of men; those reborn from blessed Mary’s Son are not called children of men, but children of God.

Why should I linger any longer by extending this account? Eve harmed; Mary benefited. Eve mourned; Mary gave light. Let the deadly and evil-counseling hiss therefore now be silenced among women through blessed Mary, because we have all already been redeemed through the Son of the glorious Virgin Mary. Let Eve’s reproach also fall away, because through the childbirth of the holy Virgin Mary we are all joyful.

Let the assembly of Christians rejoice and be glad as it solemnly celebrates this day, because the life that Eve had destroyed is restored through blessed Mary. But rejoice even more, blessed maidens, virgins of Christ, who, following the example of the most blessed Mary, the most holy Virgin, reject carnal marriage and escape the pain of childbirth, the authority of a husband, care for the flesh, mourning for a child, and the anxieties of the world, so that you may strive to live without impediment and may prove—as the blessed Apostle exhorts us, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0279] Here the Apostle’s words needed for the continuity of the prayer are missing.]

By entreating the Lord and rejecting earthly desires, you will deserve heaven as your dowry, because, joined to blessed Mary’s bridal chamber, you will please Christ. Do not mourn funerals, since you will receive joys without end, because your beloved, Christ the Lord Jesus, lives immortally. And because Christ, your beloved, lives forever, you too will reign together with him and with all the saints.

Therefore, dearest brothers, having poured out our prayers, let us all together beseech the Lord: may he who, for our redemption and salvation, deigned to dwell with us in the holy Virgin Mary, and who makes her reign in the heavenly places above the stars of heaven and above the choirs of virgins, command that we too, aided by her merits, become participants in the assembly of the saints, so that that savage accuser may not find in our souls anything by which to destroy us; but may his boundless mercy mercifully draw us to the crown—he who lives and reigns with God the Father forever and ever. Amen.

*(Here the Amelianus manuscript ends.)*

## ALSO, SERMON XIII. FOR THE DAY OF HOLY MARY

*[Published by P. Flórez from his own thirteenth-century manuscript.]*

Our Lord God exhorts and admonishes us together, saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:5). Our God cannot be estimated, cannot be changed, cannot be numbered, as the prophet David says: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and there is no measure of his wisdom” (Psalm XIV, 6, 5). You know these things very well, dearest brothers, who firmly hold Catholic truth in your hearts; nevertheless, hear briefly what I have proposed to explain, with the Lord’s assistance.

There is one God the Father, one God the Son, and one God the Holy Spirit. Not three gods, but one God. Three in name, but one in the divinity of substance. But a heretic will say to me: “Then, if they are one, all were incarnate.” No; flesh belongs to Christ alone. For example, soul is one thing and reason another; yet reason is in the soul, and there is one soul. But the soul does one thing and reason another. The soul lives; reason understands. Life belongs to the soul, wisdom to reason. And although they are one, the soul alone receives life, while reason alone receives wisdom. So too the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, although they are one and are one God, flesh belongs to Christ alone, just as wisdom belongs to reason alone.

### [Col. 0281B]

In the sun, brightness and radiance are in a single ray; yet heat dries, while radiance illuminates. Heat receives one thing, radiance another. Although heat and radiance cannot be separated from one another, heat receives warmth, not illumination; radiance receives illumination, not warmth. They act together in one way and individually in another, yet they are not separated from one another.

So too the Son assumed flesh without abandoning the Father or being absent from the Father. The Son, I say, assumed flesh in his own particularity; nevertheless, the Father and the Holy Spirit were not absent in majesty. There is equality in divinity, and the particularity of the Son alone in the flesh; yet the divinity of the Father and the Holy Spirit never withdrew from him. Since there is one deity and one divinity, both the Father and the Holy Spirit filled Christ’s flesh—but in majesty, not by assuming it.

Do you wish to know that the Father was with him? The Lord himself says: “I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 8:16). Hear also concerning the Holy Spirit, that he was with him. The Evangelist testifies that Jesus, having come forth from the Jordan, was full of the Holy Spirit (Luke 4:1). Behold: our Lord Jesus Christ alone assumed flesh, yet the Father and the Holy Spirit were not absent in majesty. If the Father fills heaven and earth, and the Holy Spirit also fills them, they could not abandon Christ’s flesh when they remained in the unity of divinity.

Consider a lyre for this purpose, so that it may produce a musical melody in sweet sounds. Three things seem to be present together: the art, the hand, and the string. Yet one sound is heard. The art directs, the hand touches, and the string resounds. Three things indeed work together, but only the string produces the sound that is heard. Neither the art nor the hand produces the sound, yet they work together with the string. So neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumes flesh, yet they work together with the Son. Only the string strikes the sound; Christ alone received flesh. The operation consists in three, but just as the resonance of the sound belongs to the string alone, so the assumption of human flesh belongs to Christ alone.

The Jew, on the contrary, says: “Mary the Virgin could not give birth contrary to nature.” And the detestable Manichaean says: “If it was flesh, she could not have been a virgin; if a virgin gave birth, it was a phantom.” Both must be answered.

Against the Jew, an essential example may be drawn from the history of the Old Testament. The Lord commanded holy Moses that one rod be brought from each tribe (Numbers 17). Twelve rods were brought, among them the one that had belonged to Aaron the priest. Holy Moses placed them in the tabernacle of testimony. On the following day Aaron’s rod was suddenly found to have produced flowers and leaves and to have brought forth nuts.

It is pleasing to mingle this mystery, with your charity, against Jewish unbelief, where the figure of the sacrament is especially present. This rod produced what it had not previously possessed: it was neither rooted in a planting, nor dug up with a hoe, nor animated by sap, nor fertilized in a seedbed; and yet, although all the conditions required by nature were absent, the rod produced what could not have been drawn from seed or root.

Therefore, the rod could produce nuts contrary to nature, but could holy Mary the Virgin not, contrary to nature and by God’s command, give birth to the Son? Let the unbelieving Jew tell me how the dry rod flowered, put forth leaves, and produced nuts, and I will tell him how Mary conceived and bore the Son of God. Certainly, the Jew will be able to explain neither the conception of the rod nor the childbirth of the Virgin. Let him come to the Church; it will be explained to him, so that he may understand.

Nevertheless, the Virgin naturally fulfilled the course of childbirth, awaiting the time of delivery; the rod, however, had no time for budding. The Virgin gave birth after the completion of nine months; the rod put forth, on the following day, what nature had not given it. But you say that nature in no way permits the Virgin to give birth. The God who displayed a wondrous sign contrary to nature, so that a she-ass might speak (Numbers 22:28), willed to perform an even more wondrous deed: that Christ should be born from holy Mary the Virgin.

Let that cunning Manichaean hear another sacramental example. A ray of the sun penetrates glass and passes through its solidity with imperceptible subtlety; it appears the same within as without. Thus, brothers, the glass is neither violated when the ray enters nor shattered when it exits, because the glass remains intact both at its entry and at its exit. If the sun’s ray does not break glass, could the entry or departure of the Godhead have violated the Virgin’s integrity?

But why should I linger further? Let the Christian hear what the Jew or the Manichaean heretic does not wish to hear, so that the former may progress in faith as one redeemed, while the latter may fail as one hardened.

The rod of which we were speaking, Aaron’s rod, was the Virgin Mary, who conceived and bore for us the true Christ, the priest, concerning whom David sang, saying: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm CIX, 5). For in the preceding verse he had already said: “The Lord will send forth the rod of his power from Zion, and he will rule in the midst of his enemies.”

The prophet Isaiah, too, filled with the Holy Spirit, sings and says: “A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him—the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety—and he filled him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isaiah 11:1–3).

The fact, therefore, that this rod produced nuts was an image of the Lord’s body. For a nut has within its body a threefold union of substances: skin, shell, and kernel. In the skin, flesh is signified; in the shell, bones; in the kernel within, the soul. In the skin, the almond signifies the Savior’s flesh, which possessed within itself the harshness or bitterness of suffering. In the kernel, it indicates the inward sweetness of the divinity, which provides nourishment and supplies the function of light. In the shell, it signifies the intervening wood of the cross, which did not separate what was outside from what was inside, but joined earthly and heavenly things through the interposition of the wood as mediator.

But because there are some who say that it could not happen that Christ was born from the Virgin Mary, asserting in their impurity that this part of the body was shameful, we answer: if there had been any impurity there, the Lord would have purified it by his presence. Consider how the sun sends its rays everywhere—into filth, into sewers, and even into the foulest places. Impure heretic, the sun enters sewers and is not defiled; could the Godhead be defiled by the Virgin’s womb?

Where is your impious, faithless, and dark soul, which invents such things for itself while attending to spirits of error? Is it only in your head? Is it only in your eyes, and not also in your intestines, where your excrement is? Impure heretic, your soul is not defiled by your excrement, but Jesus could be defiled by his own work?

There are also those who say that holy Mary had children by Joseph after the Lord’s birth; this is forbidden to say. We answer them briefly. The genital organs from which we proceed into the world are called “gates,” and this is not merely said but also written. For holy Job says this concerning the day of his birth: “Who did not close the doors of my mother’s womb, so that she might not bear me?” (Job 3:10).

Now see, brothers, how the gate through which the Lord entered always remained closed. For the prophet Ezekiel says: “I turned toward the way of the gate of the sanctuary that faced east, and behold, it was closed. And the Lord said to me: This gate that you see shall remain closed, and it shall not be opened. No man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel shall go out through it, and it shall remain closed forever” (Ezekiel 44:1–2).

Behold, it is clearly shown to us here that holy Mary was always a virgin: a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth. Let every land therefore sing a new song to you, Lord, because you have done a new thing in heaven: that a virgin, without a man’s embrace, should conceive and give birth to a male child. She conceived, and she is a virgin; she gives birth, and she is a virgin; she nurses, and she is a virgin.

Holy Mary, heretic, could be a mother; she could not be a woman. The virgin’s breasts swell, yet the mother’s genital organs remain untouched. The one who gave birth to integrity could not be corrupted in either respect. Great merit, great gift, great grace: a handmaid bore the Lord; a creature bore the Creator; a daughter bore the Father—the daughter of divinity, the mother of humanity. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

## THE SAME AUTHOR’S SERMON XIV

*[From the same manuscript of P. Flórez.]*

Dearest brothers, the Son of God was born timelessly from the Father. What was he before he came in human form? Imagine, then, that you ask yourselves and say: “Before Christ was born from the Virgin Mary, do you suppose that he existed, or did he not exist?”

The Lord himself answers these thoughts. For when the Jews said to him, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” he answered and said: “Amen, I say to you: before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:57–58). Therefore, he existed.

But what was he? Lest someone say, “He was an angel,” hear the oracle. The holy Gospel answers you. You know that Christ existed, and you ask what he was? “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). Behold what he was. “In the beginning was the Word”; it does not say, “In the beginning the Word was made,” but, “the Word was.”

What kind of Word was it? Do you wish to hear what kind of Word? “And the Word was God.” O Word! Who can explain such a Word in words? “And the Word was God.”

But perhaps God was made by God? Far be it. How do we know that it is far from the truth? Do not say that he was made. Hear what follows in the Gospel: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). What does “all things” mean? Everything that was made by God was made through him. How, then, was he himself made? Did he make himself? Finally, if he made himself, then he existed who would make himself. If, therefore, he existed who would make himself, he was never absent.

### [Col. 0284A]

How, then, did such a Word come to be in the Virgin? How did the Word of God enter the Virgin’s womb? He did not abandon the angels; he did not abandon the Father. How, then, could he be enclosed in that womb? Far from it. He could be present there; he could not be enclosed.

“How,” he says, “could one so great be in so small a place?” Then the womb cannot contain the one whom the world cannot contain.

I am speaking with you concerning my own word. Understand this that I am saying and speaking to you. Surely we marvel at how Christ assumed flesh: he was born from the Virgin and did not depart from the Father.

Behold, before I speak the word to you, I already have the word in my heart. I could not speak to you unless I had first thought about it. When I thought about what I would say to you, the word was already in my heart. And I was seeking how what was in me might come to you. I considered what language you spoke. I found that you were Latin-speaking; therefore the word had to be presented to you in Latin. If you were Greek, I would have to speak to you in Greek, and I would present a Greek word to you.

The word that is in my heart plainly precedes these languages. I seek for it a sound, as though a vehicle by which what does not depart from me may reach you. Behold, you have heard it, and what was in my heart is now also in yours. It is in me, and it is in you. You have begun to possess it, and I have not lost it.

Just as my word assumed sound, by which it might be heard, so the Word of God assumed flesh, by which it might be seen. And just as my word, which came to you, did not depart from me, so the Word of God, when he was in his mother’s womb, did not wholly leave the Father or the heavenly things. For he who was being born in the flesh through humanity reigned and reigns everywhere with the Father through divinity.

He could thus be held in the Virgin’s womb, but he could not be enclosed. Just as human wisdom is joined to the mind without being bound by any fetter, so the great God dwelt in the Virgin’s small womb, just as he always dwells in the purest heart.

I have said what I could. And yet, what have I said? Who has said it? A human being wishes to speak about God. He is so great, so exalted, that we can neither speak about him nor ought we to remain silent about him. In our voice, let him receive devotion, not deficiency.

Thanks be to you, Lord, because I wished to speak. How far what I have said falls short of your greatness—you know. Nevertheless, with the small crumbs of your table I have fed my fellow servants. Feed inwardly those whom you have regenerated and nourished. Lord God, call us, so that we may ascend to you; strengthen us, so that we may not depart from you. So that, when you have supported us mercifully in this life and brought us to yourself without confusion, we may praise your name forever and ever. Amen.

Thanks be to God.

# SECOND APPENDIX. WORKS SPURIOUSLY ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT HILDEFONSUS

## A LITTLE BOOK ON THE CROWN OF THE VIRGIN

### PREFACE

The works which we have discovered to have been falsely attributed to Hildefonsus follow his doubtful works. Among these, the first that we encounter is a little book entitled *The Crown of the Blessed Virgin Mary*. Before all others, Peter de Alva labored to attribute it to Hildefonsus. He was a theologian of the Franciscan family, well known both for his extensive learning and, above all, for his outstanding devotion to the Mother of God, whose worship and glory he appears to have devoted himself entirely to promoting for many years.

In the second volume of his *Marian Library*, which he undertook with the greatest effort but, overtaken by death, left unfinished, he published this *Crown* under the following title: *The Crown of the Blessed Virgin Mary, by an Anonymous Author; Perhaps Hildefonsus, Archbishop of Toledo*. He admits that in an ancient manuscript of the holy Church of Toledo, from which he first published it, it was found without the author’s name. When he had searched in vain for the author and consulted catalogues of ecclesiastical writers in which authors who had composed *Crowns* for the Virgin were known to have been listed, the thought occurred to him that perhaps it ought to be attributed to no one other than Saint Hildefonsus of Toledo.

In his judgment, some considerations supported this conjecture, and he allowed himself to be moved by them all the more willingly because it seemed to him that in this way he could serve domestic honor most beautifully and honorably.

Nevertheless, although the little book was written with such piety and learning that it would have been worthy of our Hildefonsus, it contains so many distinctive features and such clear indications of another author that it cannot be attributed to Saint Hildefonsus without injustice.

For anyone who examines the matter even superficially will see that the entire style of expression is foreign to Hildefonsus and wholly conforms to the twelfth century. This is apparent from the songs or rhythms with which the discourse is everywhere sprinkled. Since these consist of Leonine verses, no one will doubt that they are later than the twelfth century. They were called Leonine either because they were invented in that century by a certain French monk named Leo, as Ducange and quite a few others maintain, or because they began to be frequently used by that same Leo in that century.

This much is certain: this kind of poetry was not in use among the Gothic Fathers, as may be established from an examination of the verses of Saint Eugenius. For the poems circulated under Hildefonsus’s name by Pseudo-Julian and others are fictitious and fabricated by their own authors’ brains.

Even if all these considerations were insufficient to establish the point, the authorities quoted in this little book, taken from Saint Bernard, seem to settle the matter and remove every doubt. See, in chapter 17, that prayer of Saint Bernard which everyone commonly recites from memory: “In dangers, in doubtful matters,” and so forth.

Accordingly, the arguments that the praised Alva gathers in favor of Saint Hildefonsus are too slight to move anyone. As for his claim that certain other works of this same holy doctor, established as genuine, are found in the same manuscript, we remember that we have often shown how little weight this carries. Nor does the antiquity of the manuscript provide any support unless it were much older than the twelfth century—which we deny.

It is indeed established that Hildefonsus, exceptionally devoted to Mary the Mother of God, wrote little works in her praise. That is true; but we know what sort of work it was and what its subject was, and we have read no work entitled *The Crown of the Virgin*. Moreover, whatever is brought forward concerning the style and the character of the entire discourse is such that it collapses entirely on its own; it has scarcely anything in common with the style of the Gothic Fathers. On this point, as we have often done elsewhere, we willingly appeal to the judgment of the discerning reader.

Whatever the case may be, the little book certainly deserves to be read by everyone; indeed, we scarcely believe that it can be read without producing some profound feeling of piety and devotion toward the Mother of God. We were necessarily obliged to publish it both because of Peter de Alva and because of the many others to whom the opinion spread from Alva that this was the offspring of our Hildefonsus.

We have proceeded as in the other cases: we have published it after collating it with and correcting it as far as we were able from the manuscript in the Library of the holy Church of Toledo, shelf V, no. 9—unquestionably different from the manuscript seen by Peter de Alva, which we ourselves were unable to find. Farewell.

## [THE LITTLE BOOK ON THE CROWN OF THE VIRGIN. (G)*]

### THE PROLOGUE TO THE CROWN OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY BEGINS

### [Col. 0285A]

“A golden crown upon her head, marked with the sign of holiness” (Ecclesiasticus 45:14).

The Scriptures teach, created things exhort, figures admonish, and nearly all the sacred pages of theological knowledge urge us to praise, bless, and proclaim the imperial majesty of the glorious Virgin, adorned with the glory of every virtue, decorated with the pearls of every spiritual gift, and illumined by the radiance of wisdom and knowledge.

We are also impelled to this by miraculous signs, by oracles fallen from heaven, by hidden mysteries, by prophetic teaching, by mystical signification, by evangelical reading, and by the apostolic trumpet.
