Prelates pant after dignities; fortresses are overthrown, cities laid waste, pestilences rage, frauds and deceptions are committed, lies are spread abroad, thefts are perpetrated, monasteries are despoiled, virgins are violated, nuns are ravished, and married women are dishonored. [Col. 0306D: Alva has “married women are violated.”]

Behold, most merciful Lady, into what misery human nature has fallen, into what sadness Mother Church has collapsed, and with what grief every creature is tormented. Therefore, tender mother, may your tender affection grieve with us; may your merciful inward parts have compassion on the human race. Stand for us before the tribunal of God; bend the sternness of God the Father; recall the sentence of the Judge; restrain the savagery of hostile piety. [F.: “impiety.”] May new peace arise from heaven; may works of piety revive in the world; may virtuous deeds flourish in the cloister. [Col. 0306D: Our manuscript reads “may they bloom again.”] May your merits be remembered in the world, and may praise and glory be given to the Lord Jesus Christ, and to the Father, and to the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## CHAPTER XVII. The placing of the most beautiful flower, namely the violet, in the sixteenth position of the Virgin’s crown

You, our Lady, are exceedingly beautiful, a most beautiful virgin unknown to man. You are beautiful among all the daughters of Jerusalem, because they are merely brides of Christ, whereas you are both mother and bride; they enjoy only the privilege of virginity, but you are made fruitful and are adorned with the privilege of virginity as with a double ornament.

You are beautiful in chaste love, more beautiful in works of devotion, and most beautiful in Christ’s virginal conception and birth. Beautiful in virginity, more beautiful in humility, most beautiful in charity. The sweetness of your character made you beautiful, the holiness of your works more beautiful, and royal majesty most beautiful. [Col. 0307A] Surrounded by the angelic powers, you remained wholly untouched, inviolate in mind and body.

You are that star of the sea, near to God at the highest pivot of heaven, toward whom worshipers of Christ sigh while sailing amid the waves of this age, that you may pour the rays of faith into our blindness—rays which unhappy humanity, stripped of righteousness, quickly cast away and rejected from itself.

Therefore, that I may deserve to be enlightened by you and saved through your merits, I offer you a most beautiful flower, namely the violet, which I now insert in the sixteenth position of your crown, so that it may be sprinkled with its gentle fragrance. For the violet is a lovely little flower of hyacinthine color, wonderfully fragrant and useful in medicine.

This flower, O Lady, greatly suits your crown, because you imitate it in the virtues. For you, holy Virgin, are the violet of purity, the violet of modesty, the violet of chastity, the violet of recovery, the violet of fragrance, the violet of sweetness, and the violet of holiness. [Col. 0307D: Our manuscript reads “the violet of recovery … the violet of fragrance.”] [Col. 0307D: The same manuscript reads “the violet of health.”]

In its hyacinthine color, resembling a serene sky, your affection is signified as lifted from earthly things to the heights. [Col. 0307D: The same source reads “your effect.”] For you, Lady, established your dwelling among the morning stars, so that with the rejoicing sons of God you might praise your Creator. You lifted your heart toward the Bridegroom seated at the right hand of Majesty.

Therefore, a certain saint says:

> You raised your holy head on high, Lady,  
> as far as he who sits upon the throne,  
> as far as the Lord of Majesty.

Moreover, the fragrance of your wondrous sweetness and the scent of your gentle and devout visitation gladden the hearts of those who love you, and by your spiritual touch you refresh and heal the sick. Another saint says the same:

> You are the patroness of the human race,  
> the singular physician of those afflicted.

### Prayer

O sweet physician, healer of souls [Col. 0307D: Alva has “healer of healed souls”], enlightener of hearts! Heal my sicknesses, illumine my blindness, enlighten my faith, strengthen my hope, and kindle my charity.

You are the shining star who gave birth to the splendor of the Father’s glory, glittering in the splendors of the saints; you announced eternal morning to us who sit in the shadow of death. Like a rising dawn, you went before the course of the eternal sun, enlightening the world with the light of grace and illuminating the holy Church with the radiance of virtues.

Your splendor enlightens heaven, illuminates the world, penetrates hell, abolishes vices, nourishes virtues, grants holiness, and obtains peace and charity for us from heaven. You also shine with innocence, radiate chastity, and are magnified with the adornment of all holiness.

You are the mother of eternal light, by whose brightness angels rejoice, human beings are glad, and spirits and souls are refreshed with special delight. You are the dawn that gives birth to the sun, whose perpetual radiance continually rejoices in the light. By his splendor you are irradiated, happily illumined, and supremely enlightened.

You are the closed gate of the temple, prepared for the Prince of kings; the consecrated house of God, sealed with the seal of the entire Trinity. You are the luminous cloud through which the darkness of sins is destroyed; the dewy cloud by which our dryness is sweetened and our barrenness made fruitful; the shining cloud by which darkness is whitened. Concerning this cloud it is said:

> O radiant cloud of light,  
> exalted in the heavens,  
> flowering branch of Jesse,  
> made fruitful by grace.  
>   
> Ark drenched with dew,  
> watered from above,  
> sprinkle our dry hearts  
> with a sweet and gracious drop.  
>   
> You are the throne of wisdom  
> and the rod of justice;  
> you, cedar of modesty,  
> vine of abundance;  
> fragrant cypress,  
> olive of gentleness.  
>   
> Lead us to the harbor of indulgence,  
> fountain of devotion.  
>   
> You, lily of chastity,  
> eastern gate,  
> dining hall of the Trinity,  
> imperial throne,  
> refuge of sinners,  
> foremost mother:  
>   
> draw us to the summit  
> of the heavens,  
> springtime flower.  
>   
> Discovery of the sacraments,  
> star of wondrous splendor,  
> preface of our law,  
> text of the supreme Teacher,  
> be our protection,  
> mother full of sweetness,  
> the work of our salvation  
> after this valley of sorrow.  
>   
> Amen.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The precious amethyst in the Virgin’s crown

Hail, holy Mother of God, golden resting place of the world’s Savior, eastern light illuminating and enlightening the breasts of the saints. Philosophy of virtue, teacher of Christians, discipline of those in the cloister, doctrine of peace, sword of the spirit, victorious helmet. Your virtue irradiates the heavens, gladdens the angels, terrifies the demons, and empties the depths of hell.

You are the imperial throne and seat of the holy Trinity, the dormitory of Jesus Christ, consecrated, sanctified, and adorned by the Holy Spirit. You are adored on earth and crowned in heaven; you bind the strong man and plunder the vessels of captivity. [Col. 0307D: Alva has “you bind the strong man.”]

You are mother of virtue, slayer of crime, key of the kingdom of heaven, mirror of chastity. Hail, beautiful virgin, joining earthly things with heavenly, uniting human beings to angels, and binding the lowest things to the highest in an everlasting covenant.

O most sincere Virgin, prefigured by the patriarchs, foretold by the prophets, preached by the apostles, and proclaimed by the teachers! Since you are illumined by so many and such great blessings and are so magnificently commended by all, it is right that I offer you something small from my poverty to glorify your venerable majesty.

Receive, therefore, graciously, Lady, the precious stone amethyst, which I place in the seventeenth position of your crown, so that it may offer you its splendor. The amethyst is partly violet and partly rose-colored, and holds the chief place among purple stones. Since you, Lady, resemble it, it ought to be placed in your diadem. [Col. 0308D: Alva has “similar.”]

For you were gracious and fragrant like the perfumed violet, and purple like the rose. In the small violet your humility is commended, and in the colored rose your charity is signified. For just as, through your conception, you made yourself the humble handmaid of God [F.: “the conception of your Son”], so, through the fiery love with which you loved him, he made you exalted in glory and honor.

Such gifts of grace and prerogatives of virtue were given to you that you surpassed not only human beings, but also angels and archangels, the principalities of heaven, the cherubim, and the ranks of seraphim.

You surpassed virgins through wondrous chastity. For your virginity was marvelous because it was joined to privileged fruitfulness. From your virginal fruitfulness you propagated for us the Redeemer of all, the Savior of those to be saved, and the Restorer of angels—something no other virgin could do.

You surpassed confessors through virtuous action. Although they performed wondrous deeds, you were superior to them in signs of virtue, labors of penance, works of mercy, fervor of spirit, and abundance of devotion.

You surpassed martyrs through triumphant victory. For no wiles of the tempter could break through the barriers of your virginity; no allurements of the seducer could soften your steadfastness; no arrows of the raging enemy could overcome your courage. [Col. 0308D: Alva printed *temptares*; he nevertheless suspected *tentaris*. The true reading is the one represented here from our manuscript.]

You surpassed the apostles through the most excellent holiness. You were superior to them in love of God, love of neighbor, knowledge of the mysteries of Jesus Christ, capacity for the mysteries of the Most High, and tasting of heavenly glory. [Col. 0309D: Alva has *compacitate*; “capacity” is conjectured.]

You surpassed patriarchs and prophets in faith, hope, and perseverance; in clearer knowledge of past and future things; and in understanding enigmas and figures.

You surpassed all choirs of heavenly spirits in purity of mind, clarity of understanding, signs, virtues, and wonders; in restraining hostile assaults; in wondrous principality; in glorious dominion; in the tranquility of peace; in the splendor of wisdom; and in the ardor of charity.

### Prayer

Since, then, sweetest Lady, all good things have been placed in your hand by God, as is clear from what precedes, I ask you to deign to receive this prayer graciously, so that you may be pleased to obtain peace and pardon for me.

> O Virgin, splendor of glory,  
> sanctified by the Spirit,  
> dove full of sighing,  
> bring us out of Egypt.  
>   
> Come to us, full of grace,  
> and defend us from the roar  
> of the evil household,  
> among the army of the righteous,  
> that we may enjoy sweet rest.  
>   
> You are adorned with necklaces  
> of gifts of grace,  
> with Christ’s grace;  
> with precious stones,  
> shining with the grace of virtues.  
>   
> You are full of wisdom  
> and every spiritual gift.  
> By your power preserve us  
> from the assaults of demons.  
>   
> Give peace to us all,  
> foremost of virgins.  
>   
> You are joined to the heavenly Bridegroom  
> by an everlasting covenant.  
> Make him shine upon us,  
> him whose mother you are believed to be.  
>   
> And since you are the ark of the covenant,  
> render him propitious to us  
> in the time of vengeance,  
> through the merits in which you rejoice.  
>   
> Help us, wretched as we are,  
> now that the star of light has risen,  
> and deign to come to us  
> on the day of our death.

## CHAPTER XIX. The clear and shining moon in the Virgin’s crown

Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, illustrious virgin, lily of paradise, because in you the angels and archangels rejoice, as do the cherubim and seraphim, the principalities and powers, and the legions of the entire heavenly army.

For you are the reconciliation of the world, the form of peace, the way of salvation, and the rule of discipline. The Savior loved you, clothed himself in your flesh, and entrusted his grace to you. Therefore, for such great benefits, the angels praise you; the dominions adore you; the principalities and powers honor and celebrate you; and the blessed seraphim, with outstretched wings, carry you before them and display you. [Col. 0309D: Our manuscript reads “and the blessed seraphim,” though perhaps “and the blessed one” was intended.]

And I, a poor and unworthy sinner, wishing to please you in some small way, place in the eighteenth position of your crown the bright and shining moon, so that it may illumine and glorify it with its splendor. For the moon receives light from the sun; it illumines the night, is friendly, spreads dew, and reveals the thief. [Col. 0309D: Alva has “and illuminating … revealing the thief”; our reading follows the manuscript, whose true wording Alva suspected.]

Since these qualities most suitably apply to you, most radiant Lady, it rightly ought to be placed in your diadem. [Col. 0310D: Alva reads “But you before it,” etc.; his conjecture, “but you in it,” is far from the true reading of our manuscript.] You, placed before that highest Majesty, fix your chaste and pure eyes upon him, eagerly thirsting and longing for almighty God seated upon the throne. He, as your friendly object of contemplation, transmits and communicates his splendor to you.

From this, Lady, you illumine the night of sinners, drive away and dispel the darkness of night, refresh and enrich the dryness of souls with grace, and expose the assemblies, illusions of the air, plots of spiritual thieves, every wickedness, and the deceits of demons.

O holy virgin of virgins, holy and blessed dining hall of the heavenly Majesty! With how many praises ought we to praise you! With how many prayers and tears ought we to incline you to defend us from these spiritual wickednesses!

For you are the glorious resting place of the Savior of the ages, who fashioned for himself from your bright and virginal flesh, in the court of your most chaste womb, a noble and honorable girdle with which to conquer the cruel prince of death.

You are also the holy, inviolate, and undefiled sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, in which that same Holy Spirit placed the treasures of his graces and gifts. For with you are hidden inexhaustible treasures of virtue and grace, peace and mercy, salvation and wisdom, honor and glory. [Col. 0310D: Our manuscript reads “of truth and grace.”]

Moreover, that same Spirit granted you that in your name every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that you, Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, are in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10). You sit at the right hand of your most loving Bridegroom and only Son, crowned conspicuously with an unfading crown shining with the radiance of seven stars, surrounded by choirs of virgins, and exalted above all the saints with wondrous glory, amid alternating angelic choirs singing hymns, among the lilies of perpetual vigor, within the court of paradise. May your Son lead us there, moved by your prayers and by this song offered to you.

### Prayer

> Hail, throne of Majesty,  
> hail, flower of humility,  
> lily of purity  
> and of the whole Divinity,  
> temple and sanctuary  
> of undefiled charity.  
>   
> Hail, virginal earth,  
> or heavenly threshing floor,  
> bearing a pleasing flower,  
> made fruitful by the Spirit.  
>   
> Divinely overshadowed,  
> you bore the incarnate Word.  
>   
> As the springtime light  
> of dawn drives away  
> the clouds of heaven  
> and gives splendor to the day,  
>   
> so the rising of your brightness,  
> bringing forth the Savior  
> in the freshness of new joy.  
> [Col. 0310D: The manuscript has *sic* instead of *ac*; somewhat below it reads *angaria* instead of *agonia*.]
>   
> In the agony of death,  
> Virgin, by your grace  
> deign to visit us,  
>   
> and after death summon us  
> to the joys above,  
> where glory is everlasting.  
>   
> Amen.

## CHAPTER XX. The placing of the precious chrysolite in the Virgin’s crown

Rejoice, Virgin daughter of Zion, and rejoice greatly, mother and bride of Christ, because the Lord is your everlasting light, and your most loving Son is your glory. May the voice of the heavenly watchmen resound in praise of you, and may the jubilation of the morning stars distill for you a song of glory and honor.

And rightly so, for heaven and earth are illumined by the light of your mercies. Who, O mother rich in compassion, can avoid the sweetness of your devotion? Through your merits the devil is confounded, hell is emptied, the world is illumined, the angel rejoices, and paradise is filled.

What thanks, venerable queen, can I, an unworthy sinner, offer you? In your holy womb lie divine mysteries; in your holy heart, the secrets of God; in your holy breast resides the wisdom of God; in your mother’s womb you were filled with grace. [Col. 0311D: The manuscript absurdly reads “in the womb of the Mother of God.”] Never polluted by any stain or defiled by any contagion, you received God chastely, clothed him in sacred flesh, and gave birth without blemish.

And because, holy Lady, you brought forth for us the sweetest child for everlasting salvation and glory, I offer you, for your praise and glory, the chrysolite, a precious stone, so that it may be nobly placed in the twentieth position of your crown. Chrysolite is adorned partly with a golden color and partly with the color of the sea. Gold expresses piety, while the color of the sea expresses bitterness. For just as gold surpasses all metals, so piety surpasses all bodily exercises, possessing the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come; and it is properly the worship of God.

You, therefore, Lady, were always devoted toward the wretched, sweet toward the afflicted, and merciful toward the poor. You were also most pure [Col. 0311D: the same source has “most pious”], wholly dedicated to divine worship: loving God with your whole heart, praising him with all your strength, tending toward him, always seeking his face, contemplating him, cleaving to him, tasting him, and drinking from the torrent of his delight.

For these reasons you carried him, made human, in your virginal womb, and gave birth without pain. [Col. 0311D: Alva has “carry him made human”; our manuscript reads “you carried his humanity.” From both readings the true text results.] You nursed him at your sacred breast, sweetly consoled him when he wept, lovingly nurtured him, and pressed sweet kisses upon him, so that you were never devoted to anything except divine things.

You were also made bitter by the persecutions and tribulations of your most loving Son, greatly distressed by his pains and sufferings, and pierced in soul by his death with a sword, as had been prophesied to you: “and a sword will pierce your own [Suppl.: ‘soul’]” (Luke 2:35).

### Prayer

Since so many distinguished things are proclaimed about you, Lady, turn your holy and devout gaze upon me, a wretched sinner deprived of every grace. Enlighten my spirit, refresh my breast, kindle my heart, vivify my soul, and renew my mind. O devout one, refresh me; prudent Virgin, instruct me; my lamp, enlighten me; my strength, strengthen me. [Col. 0311D: Alva has “recall me.”]

Through you may my action be directed; through you may my intention and affection be governed. May your light enter my heart, your love my inward parts, and your charity my inmost being, so that I may sweetly perceive, see, and understand what is pleasing and acceptable before you at all times. [Col. 0312D: Alva erroneously reads “and having received.”]

Most holy Virgin, you are the ark of the covenant, covered on every side with gold, in which are all the treasures of God’s grace and mercy. Outside you are gilded with virtues, within with innocence and devotion; within you shine with the gold of devotion, outside you glitter with works of charity and the splendor of miracles.

You are wholly pure within in mind, wholly beautiful outwardly in action, wholly without stain, wholly joined to God, shining with divine brightness and resounding with divine praises.

You are the temple of the Lord, where omnipotence is found in charity, wisdom in humility, goodness in virtue, firmness in faith, simplicity in perfection, chastity in virginity, and holiness in action and work.

You are the life of the world, medicine for languishing souls, the tree of life in the midst of paradise, whose fruit heals the contrite, restores the weak, consoles the sorrowful, and sustains the feeble.

You are also the glory of the world, the pillar of heaven, the foundation of virtue, the sword that slays the devil, and the bite of hell. You extinguish desires, cause the fruits of virtue to grow, strengthen the tempted, enlighten the blind, give drink to the thirsty, feed the hungry, fortify the dying with your sign, and lead them by saving guidance to the glory of paradise. May your blessed Son grant it to us. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXI. Here the Virgin is devoutly praised, and the *solsequium* (“sun-following flower”) is placed in her crown

As the sun rises upon the world in the highest places of God, so is your beauty, Virgin Mary, an ornament of the entire court of paradise. The King of kings, Lord and Prince of rulers, desired this beauty, effecting a wondrous exchange: giving us his divinity and taking our mortality, so that he might raise our poverty from the dung heap and wondrously adorn it with imperial scepters and an everlasting kingdom.

Therefore you are proclaimed most holy by all, because you have become the cause of all good things for us—not only of everlasting salvation but also of every virtue and holiness of life. [Col. 0312D: Alva has “everlasting.”] [Col. 0312D: Alva printed *excedas*; yet he himself recognized the true reading found in our manuscript.] From you you give us an example of good works, and you obtain from the Lord various gifts of grace. [F.: *charismata* (“gifts”) rather than *charismatum*.] Through you the sweetness of his mercy, the clemency of his devotion, and the abundance of his grace flow into us; through you divine gifts are dispensed; through you heavenly secrets are unlocked; in you heavenly mysteries lie hidden; and from you the sacraments of the Church flow forth.

You increase the joys of the angels, prepare salvation for human beings, announce peace to the earth, and incline God toward mercy. Through you light is poured into hearts, sweetness distills upon sinners, joy arises for minds, consolation for the sorrowful, a prize for those who labor, and a crown for those who contend.

You are a saving fruit, watered by a living spring and distilling the balsamic liquid of devotion. From you flow the spices of charity, the ointments of sweetness, the fragrances of virtue, and channels of tears.

You are more fragrant than cinnamon, more virtuous than cedar, more aromatic than cypress, and sweeter than spiced foods. You are the mirror of souls, angelic nectar, imperial ornament. Through you hell is broken, the captive people redeemed, and heavenly things opened.

From you proceed the flowers of roses, the lilies of the valleys, and every kind of spice. You are Indian sapphire, sparkling carbuncle; you are radiant sapphire, emerald of verdure. [Col. 0312D] In you are the treasures of precious stones, the fragrance of every ointment, the sweetness of every spice, and the brightness of all the stars.

Your virtues are more precious than gold, more fragrant than cinnamon, and more beautiful than sapphire. Your merits surpass the sweetness of ointments and the beauty of royal adornments. Your fruitfulness glows like the morning star, shines like the full moon, and gleams like the sun in heavenly power. [Col. 0312D: Our manuscript reads “in its power.”]

Therefore, for such great prerogatives of merit, I, a sinner, offer you from my poverty, in your honor and glory, the *solsequium* (“sun-following flower”), a fragrant and pleasing flower, so that it may be fastened in your crown and placed in the twentieth position. [Col. 0313A]

The *solsequium* is so called because it follows the sun. When the sun comes over it, it immediately opens itself to him as though applauding; but when he withdraws, it contracts sadly into itself, folds up, and closes. [Col. 0313D: The same source adds “as though sad, contracting itself inwardly, it folds up,” and so forth.]

You resemble it, most pure Virgin. For when the sun of justice—that is, the heavenly Word, proceeding forth but not leaving the Father’s right hand—went forth to his work, about to assume our nature, entered your womb, wishing to put on the cloak of our flesh and fashion a garment for himself from your most pure blood, how gladly and how quickly did you open your affection to him, enlarge the heights of your mind [F.: “the bosom”], extend your desire, and restrain him in the embraces of love so that he might remain with you for a long time!

But when, after his death, he withdrew himself from your sight, you remained sad and alone, grieving and lamenting, and oppressed by many calamities.

And just as the *solsequium* is pleasing to the eyes in its color, so you, through your humility and kindness, were pleasing to the eyes of the heavenly Majesty and most pleasing to the gaze of the entire holy Trinity. And just as scent refreshes the sense of smell, so the fragrance of your virginity was fragrant to the angels, offered delight to Christ’s holy maidens, provided pleasure to the Son of God, poured forth a wondrous aroma, and breathed a spirit of delight upon all the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

### Prayer

O virginal maiden, pleasing in humility, fragrant with virtues, fiery and luminous with charity! You delight and intoxicate the devout heart with wondrous sweetness; you cleanse and purify the breast; you irradiate, enlighten, and calm the soul; you illumine all the inward parts.

I ask that my affection may burn with love for you, that my soul may melt, my heart be inflamed, my inward parts be warmed by your grace, and all my interior be enriched by your sweetness. May your praise never fail from my mouth, your love from my inmost heart, or your holy name from my heart and memory.

May I always experience you as my protectress in temptation, my consoler in tribulation, my helper in dangers, my enlightener in gloom, my sweetener in bitterness, my liberator in adversity, my support in need, my consolation in the struggle of death, and my faithful guide and companion to the joys of the angels. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXII. The chrysoprase in the Virgin’s crown
A Hebrew woman caused confusion in the house of Nebuchadnezzar (Judith 14:16). The Hebrew woman is the Virgin Mary, adorned with the jewels of the virtues, called Hebrew from the patriarch Abraham; [Note: [Col. 0313D] Our manuscript reads *quae* (“who/which).] for, propagated from the root of Jesse like a tender shoot, she brought forth the most beautiful flower, our Lord Jesus Christ, by whose fragrance the dead rise again, by whose perfume [Note: [Col. 0313D] Alva reads *respergunt* (“are sprinkled”).] heaven and hell are sprinkled, and by whose sweet scent all human beings are refreshed.

But you, slender shoot of Jesse, made thin by heavenly disciplines, shoot diffusing the fragrance of charity and holiness, [Col. 0313D] shoot of dominion and power, you caused confusion in the house of Nebuchadnezzar—that is, of the devil—when you broke his tyrannical rod, extinguishing Holofernes, his prince, and taking his principality and dominion [Note: [Col. 0313D] Alva printed *a nobis* (“from us”) in place of the manuscript’s *a nobile*, evidently an error.] away from us; you made his cruel yoke rot away at the presence of the oil, and his most harsh scepter perish from oppressing us.

And therefore you are proclaimed most blessed by all: through you salvation is given to the world, joy to heaven, honor and glory to God, peace to sinners, hope to the fallen, light to the blind, grace and blessing to the Church, and everlasting blessedness to the righteous. Since, therefore, you are such and so great, and have become for us, after God, the cause of every good, I exalt you with fivefold praise, so that I may be found worthy of your grace.

Hail, queen of mercy, bride of Christ, Mother of God, daughter of the Most High Father, friend of the Holy Spirit, salvation of the world, light of the Church, sweetness of devotion.

Hail, queen of virgins, empress of angels, exultation of the good, friend of peace. Virgin mother, gracious woman, lamp of justice, teaching of holiness.

Hail, more pleasing rose, tree of life, lily of paradise, banquet-hall of the Trinity, palace of the eternal Word, blessed gate of heaven, solace in sorrow.

Hail, full of grace, mother of the poor, advocate of sinners, scepter of equity, joy of the soul, peace of the sinner, delight and gladness of the heart.

Hail, our confidence, support of the weak, splendor in darkness, foundation of faith, harbor of indulgence, way of repentance, fountain of sweetness, cause of our salvation.

But because I desire to honor you still more, I offer you the precious stone chrysoprase, which I shall arrange to fasten in the twenty-first place of your crown. [Col. 0314B] Chrysoprase gleams with a golden sheen and is adorned with a green color. [Note: [Col. 0314D] Alva adds *et quia* (“and because”).] Since you are made like it, it ought rightly to be fastened to your crown. For you shone like gold before God, and pleased him with the greenness of holy works. In gold wisdom is signified; in greenness, virginity.

You were also, Lady, a pure virgin, a holy virgin, an immaculate virgin, undefiled in mind and body. And because you dedicated yourself as a virgin to God, and were the first to vow your virginity to him, you were given exceedingly abundant knowledge and wisdom. Therefore, as a prudent virgin and wise woman, you built your house—not, I say, for yourself, but for God. For he who has his dwelling in heaven, attracted by your appearance and beauty, established his throne in your holy soul and his dwelling in your virginal womb. There he joined together the cloak of our substance, by which he conquered the enemy of the human race; from it he drew the purple blood that erased the writ of our destruction and reconciled God the almighty Father to us.

But since it is wholly unfitting that the dwelling of so great a majesty should appear unadorned [Note: [Col. 0314D] Alva reads: “it is unfitting that a dwelling not ordered for such majesty”; our manuscript reads: “not honored by such majesty.”] [Col. 0314C], he who placed his tabernacle in you adorned you with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, like the noblest ornament of seven precious stones.

First, he adorned you with the gift of wisdom, by which you were wholly raised into divine things through ecstatic love. Second, he adorned you with the gift of understanding, by which you were expanded into mysteries through hierarchical splendor. Third, with the gift of counsel, by which you became prudent, discerning, and astute through heavenly instruction. Fourth, with the gift of knowledge, by which you were educated in the Scriptures through the teaching of Christ. Fifth, with the gift of fortitude, by which you are strong, steadfast, and vigorous against every adversity. Sixth, with the gift of piety, by which you are merciful, devout, and tender-hearted because of infused charity. Seventh, with the gift of divine fear, by which you are [Note: [Col. 0314D] Our manuscript reads: “a gentle, simple mind,” etc. We believe *mente mitis* (“gentle in mind”) should be read.] simple-minded and fearful before the awesome majesty.

## PRAYER

And therefore I beg you, most merciful Lady, that your grace may fortify my forehead, enlighten my senses, make my body chaste, sanctify my senses, and inflame my heart. May power enter my soul, enlighten my conscience, and purify my flesh. May your grace and power protect me in temptation, console me in tribulation, assist me in danger, and shield me from sin.

May your grace assist me while I pray, read, meditate, speak, eat, keep vigil, and sleep. May your mercy and piety forgive my debts, increase my merits, restore what has been lost, and acquire for me blessings without measure. May your grace and power illumine my death, repel my enemy, rescue me from the [Col. 0315A] hand of hell, and lead me to the joys of paradise. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Here Orion, a brilliant star, is placed in the Virgin’s crown.

“I saw one beautiful like a dove, and roses and lilies of the valleys surrounded her.” Rightly, Lady, the Holy Spirit marvels at your ascent in this word. For you are beautiful in faith, lovely in face, graceful in mind, and fair in holiness [Note: [Col. 0315D] Alva reads *sanitate* (“in soundness/health”).]; simple as a dove and white in soul, whitened by every purity and innocence.

You are surrounded by the shining stars of angels and apostles, the fragrant roses of martyrs, the sweet-smelling violets of confessors, and the white lilies of virgins. This comparison is rational, for your innocence and purity surpass the innocence of angels, your wisdom the understanding of the apostles, your steadfastness the endurance of martyrs, your prudence the diligence of confessors, and your chastity the continence of virgins.

[Col. 0315B] For what angel is so transported in divine things? What apostle is so set aflame with love? Which of the martyrs is more steadfast in suffering? Which of the confessors is more virtuous in action? What virgin or holy woman is purer in chastity?

Therefore, since you are so wondrous in every grace, and since I wish to procure from you, Lady, that grace for myself, I present you with Orion, a bright and shining star, so that your crown may be illumined by it and it may be fastened in the twenty-second place. Orion is a brilliant star that diffuses rain.

You, Lady, were a brilliant Orion when you conceived God through faith, and you became more brilliant when you remained inviolate after childbirth; most brilliant when you were exalted in the choir of glory above the choirs of angels and archangels. And since you are a heavenly threshing-floor drenched and saturated with heavenly dew, you pour out upon us the rain of grace and devotion, the rain of repentance and contrition, the rain of sorrow and tears, and the rain of sweetness and consolation.

[Col. 0315C]

## PRAYER

O noble and generous Mother of the eternal and [Note: [Col. 0315D] Our manuscript reads “uncreated Word.”] incarnate Word of the Father, who came to the aid of the lost world through the saving fruit brought forth from your immaculate flesh by virginal purity and wondrously provided dew!

O illustrious maiden, prepared from eternity and before the ages to become the mother of the supreme King! O splendid queen, adorned by the Holy Spirit as the bride of all virtues with their jewels, desired from the first dawn, a wondrous work wonderfully fashioned and vivified by the supreme Creator in manifold beauty, most magnificently adorned with the sculpture of all holiness and perfection!

I, an unworthy and vile sinner, although polluted by vices, stained by desires, defiled by filth, disfigured by pleasures, wrapped in darkness, obscured by sins, wandering in heart, and unstable in mind, desire to exalt your majesty with praises, to proclaim your holy merits with acclamations, and to glorify the insignia of your virtues and graces with devoted titles.

But you, Lady, who have propriety in your bearing, beauty in your appearance, generosity in your hands, modesty in your eyes, eloquence on your lips, clemency in your ears, prudence in your speech, holiness in your soul, the wisdom of God in your breast, divine mysteries in your mind, the Word of the Father made human in your womb, and who are wholly surrounded by the ornaments of every grace, shining within and without with outstanding beauty: heal our sicknesses and infirmities, pour light into our senses, saturate our dry breast with wondrous unction, and fill all my innermost being with glorious illumination, so that I may offer you holy, glorious, and devout speeches, and devoutly sing to you words aflame and fragrant with your love.

For you, Lady, are she of whom it is written: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1:3).

O pure light, beautiful light, illuminating heavenly things, enlightening [Col. 0316A] earthly things, terrifying those in hell, light bringing back the erring, gladdening the sick, cheering the angels and all the saints and righteous of the court of paradise!

O light revealing mysteries, uncovering hidden things, shining upon what lies concealed! Reveal our stains, raise up our ruins, shine upon our dark and clouded places, give rest [F.: *sospitatem*, “well-being,” for *sopitatem*, “sleep/rest”] to the infirm, joy to the sorrowful, enlighten sinners toward repentance, and lead those who trust and hope in you to eternal glory. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The placing of the precious beryl stone in the Virgin’s crown.

“You shall make a lampstand of pure gold” (Exodus 25:31). You, most glorious Lady, were this lampstand, beneath which the Wisdom of God placed its lamp in order to seek the lost drachma. The daughters of Jerusalem gaze upon you most attentively, so that they may run after the fragrance of your ointments, in the light of your virtues.

You were the table through devotion to and knowledge of the divine law. In you was the setting forth of the loaves through the examples of the fathers and the practice of good works. You were the ark through the glorious treasure of fruitfulness; the golden censer of God through the devotion of prayer, which love of eternity had wholly set aglow; the urn through watchfulness; manna through the sweetness of the divine birth; the rod through royal authority; the tablets of the covenant through fullness of knowledge; the mercy-seat through the affection of piety.

In God’s tabernacle there was nothing that was not covered with gold. So you too, Lady, are like the tabernacle that the Most High sanctified [Note: [Col. 0316D] Alva reads *aedificavit* (“built”).]; you were wholly golden because you were full of charity.

You are the star of the sea, because the wretched sigh toward you and angelic spirits aspire toward you. The two cherubim overshadowing the mercy-seat are the archangel Gabriel and John the Evangelist, jubilantly singing songs of praise and glory before your throne.

From the golden censer—that is, from your virginal breast—the smoke of incense rises in the sight of the Lord, because through you, who are our chief mediatrix and advocate before God, our devotion is brought before him, and through you his mercy deigns to be reconciled to us.

Therefore, so that you may deign to pray to God for me and make him favorable to me, I offer you the precious beryl stone, so that your crown may be adorned with it and it may be placed in the twenty-third position. Beryl is a clear and green stone, possessing the power to make a person gracious and to render him unconquered against enemies.

You, Lady, represent this stone in a certain way. For through the gift of wisdom you were clear and radiant, darkened by no stain, ever polluted by no impurity, obscured by no fault. Through the grace of heavenly illumination you were like an emanation of almighty God, clear and sincere, into which nothing unclean enters.

You were clear in soul, radiant in countenance, bright in body, angelic in face; clear in discerning ambiguities, clearer in knowing mysteries, and clearest in understanding [Col. 0316D] and contemplating divine things.

And because you carried in your body the eternal wisdom of God made human, you possess illustrious veneration, perpetual brightness, and the incorruptible glory of God. The grace with which you were filled made you ever fresh and green, producing the shoot of justice, the flower of innocence, and the fruit of mercy.

For you sent forth leaves of good will, lilies of chastity, the violet of piety, roses of patience and virtue, and fruits of holy and perfect charity. From the abundance of your piety and mercy, you make your servants and those who trust in you gracious and pleasing to God and the angels through good works, and through constancy of faith you make them strong and unconquered against the assaults of demons, destined to receive heavenly glory and a crown. [Note: [Col. 0316D] The word *gloria* (“glory”) is absent from Alva’s edition.] Amen.

## CHAPTER XXV. Chamomile, the beautiful flower of the Virgin’s crown, in the final place.

[Col. 0317A]

“King Solomon made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with exceedingly pure gold; it had six steps” (1 Kings 10:18). Our Solomon, Christ the peaceful King, singular wisdom, beloved glory and power, built himself a throne—namely, your womb—in which that ineffable majesty rested.

You were an ivory throne, because there are three qualities in ivory that were fully present in you. Ivory is of wondrous whiteness, cold by nature, and born from a chaste elephant. So too you, most glorious Virgin, were white because you were separated from every pollution; very cold because you were removed from the heat of carnal desire; and born from the chaste embraces of the patriarchs.

You are therefore called great, because although many things in creation are great, nothing so magnificent has been made by the work of God’s fingers.

You are clothed in tawny gold because you are colored by the purest radiance of wisdom. [Col. 0317B] The six steps of the throne are the six works of mercy, with which you, glorious Virgin, were filled and which you expended upon your good Son. For you fed him when he was hungry, gave him to drink of virginal milk, received him in the bridal chamber of your womb, wrapped him naked in swaddling clothes, refreshed him, crying, at your sacred breast, and nourished and cherished him when he was placed in the prison of our mortality.

The two hands embracing the throne are the two lives, namely the active and the contemplative [Note: [Col. 0317C] Alva adds: “which are in you”], which in you are joined by the chain of charity.

The two lions are the archangel Gabriel and John the Evangelist, one appointed as your chaste attendant at your right and the other at your left. They are called lions because of the high-pitched roar of their lofty utterance. One of them says: “Hail, full of grace,” etc. (Luke 1:28). The other says: “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. (John 1:1).

Truly, no comparable work has been fashioned in all creation, because this surpasses the orders of angels. Therefore, most excellent Lady, exalting and surpassing all things, I promised to fashion a crown for you as for the noblest empress—not one equal to what was fitting, but one such as my smallness could discover or imagine. In its final place remains the placing of chamomile as its appropriate completion.

Chamomile is a white, spherical, round flower, pleasant in scent, adorned in the middle with a kind of golden knob. You, Lady, are appropriately compared with it. For in soul you are whitened through innocence, [Col. 0318A] in conscience clean and bright through right faith, and in body white and beautiful through virginal chastity.

Therefore, as a beautiful queen, like a dove crowded around with virginal lilies, you sing with them a new song before the Lamb standing upon Mount Zion and seated upon the throne of the Father—a song that no one can sing except those who walk in white garments and have the name of the Lamb and of his Father written on their foreheads.

For, as it is said, truth does not seek corners. Because of the truth, gentleness, and justice for which Christ’s right hand wondrously led you, you were called round, not angular.

Moreover, the fragrance of your virtues surpasses every kind of spice; the scent of your piety and mercy surpasses frankincense and balsam; the fragrance of your charity and friendship conquers the sweetness of every ointment.

In your midst you shine with a golden pallor, because the wisdom of your heart is [Note: [Col. 0317C] Alva reads *pretiosior* (“more precious”).] more beautiful than the sun, the prudence of your heart and breast is brighter than the moon, and the knowledge of your understanding [Note: [Col. 0317C] The word *scientia* (“knowledge”) was absent from Alva’s edition. Hence he suspected that *tuus intellectus* (“your understanding”) should be read.] gleams with wondrous beauty above the whole arrangement of the stars.

Nor is it surprising that you shine and gleam with wisdom, since you conceived the everlasting wisdom of God the Father in your chaste womb from the Holy Spirit and brought forth into the world, for our salvation, that same wisdom clothed in flesh.

This incarnate wisdom is [Note: [Col. 0317C] Our manuscript reads: “the true light illuminating the world,” etc.] the light illuminating the world, saving sinners, shedding radiance upon heavenly things, and joining and binding human beings and angels together in an everlasting covenant.

Therefore, concerning this crown which I promised you, Mother of God and ever-virgin, let it suffice that I have spoken thus far. If I have been able to say anything well and in a manner suited to the subject, I attribute it to divine grace and to your merits. Whatever I have uttered less correctly or less cautiously, I attribute to my foolishness and to my sins.

And because I fear [F.: *paveo*, “I fear”; the printed text has *pauco*] that I have handled so great a majesty unworthily, I ask pardon. Forgive me, most pure one, who repent and supplicate you—not offending you out of malice, but trusting, or perhaps presuming, upon your goodness.

Since you are the queen of mercies, advocate of sinners, excuser of crimes, defender of orphans [Note: [Col. 0317C] Alva reads *populorum* (“of peoples”).] [Col. 0318C], and since you dwell upon the imperial seat and reign with your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, worthy of praise and glorification, forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0317C] In our manuscript this treatise ends as follows: “Here ends. Thanks be to God.” Then the following is found:

“Take hold of her, and she will exalt you; you will be glorified by her when you have embraced her; she will give increase of graces to your head, and an illustrious crown will protect you. Glory to God in the highest, thanksgiving, and the voice of praise: he who now, through oracles fallen from heaven, now through prophetic mysteries, now through evangelical light, now through the apostolic trumpet, in many ways and by many means [perhaps: ‘summons us’], calls us to love the Virgin Mary, the most serene queen of angels.”]

Here ends the book on the praises and honor of the blessed Virgin Mary, [the remaining Latin is textually corrupt: “from twenty-four stones placed on the head in her crown; thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the whole world.”]

# CONTINUATION OF THE CHRONICLES OF BLESSED ISIDORE, ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT HILDEFONSUS

[Col. 0317]

## PREFATORY NOTE TO THE READER

[Col. 0317] Lucas of Tuy, bishop, who at the command of Queen Berengaria undertook to write the *Chronicle of the World* in the fourteenth century, was the first who, intending to lay down, as it were, the foundations of that work, thrust upon us the present continuation of the Chronicles after the chronicle written by Isidore, extending to the reign of Sisebut, as though it had been composed by Hildefonsus, bishop of Toledo—a work of which no earlier memory existed.

Where Tuy obtained it is uncertain. Some, with Lorenzo de Padilla, think that everything he sold under Hildefonsus’s name was fabricated by him. He will never persuade us to think rashly of a good man; nevertheless, we cannot sufficiently wonder at the man’s credulity, since he did not see the monstrosities of so many fables with which this whole portion of the history has been woven. Therefore there is now no historian who does not despise it as a foul fiction, wholly unworthy of having ever been attributed to Saint Hildefonsus.

Among many other things, the most mendacious compiler of trifles expressly asserts that Saint Isidore held the see of Seville as primate, introducing a certain Theodisclus as his successor, previously known to no one and recorded in no lists of bishops, deposed from his dignity because of crimes of apostasy and living in exile. On this occasion he invents the story that the primatial dignity was transferred to the Church of Toledo.

To this fable he attached another no less foolish one concerning the arrival in Spain of Mahomet, the impious prophet, and his preaching established at Córdoba. He invents the story that Mahomet, warned by the devil of the return of Master Isidore from Rome, fled, and thus escaped the bonds, prisons, and punishments that Isidore had already decreed against him.

Who could read these things, having observed the true history and chronology of the life of that infamous prophet, without laughing at such monstrosities and wondering that there were people who took pleasure in inventing or recounting so many tasteless old-womanish tales?

These points, even when merely indicated, are sufficient to persuade us of the falsity of this monument and to remove from our Hildefonsus the odium attached to it. Whoever wishes to know more should consult Don Nicolás Antonio on Saint Isidore and Hildefonsus, where he pursues these fables at length; and then Father Flórez, in volume five of *Sacred Spain* and elsewhere, where he discusses the primatial dignity of the holy Church of Toledo.

Meanwhile, we reproduce his edition according to the model of the edition made by Francisco Scotus in volume two of *Illustrated Spain*, who transcribed it from Tuy with this same title, which we place at its head.

[Col. 0319]

## HERE BEGINS THE CONTINUATION OF THE CHRONICLES OF BLESSED ISIDORE, ARCHBISHOP OF SEVILLE, COMPOSED BY BLESSED ILLEPHONSUS, ARCHBISHOP OF TOLEDO (G)

[Col. 0319A]

Since the illustrious doctor Isidore clearly and briefly revealed the ages of the world and the histories of certain emperors and kings from the beginning of the world to the time of Sisenand, king of the Goths, let us begin from the time at which he ceased, lest the memory of present heroes fade from the minds of those to come.

In the year 671 of the Era, in the eighteenth year of the reign of Heraclius, after King Suintila, Sisenand reigned for three years. He held a synod of bishops, was patient, and stood firm in the Catholic orthodox rules. He ended his life at Toledo.

In the year 674 of the Era, in the twenty-first year of the reign of Heraclius, Chintila received the kingdom. He held several synods at Toledo with the bishops and strengthened the kingdom subject to him in the Catholic faith. He reigned five years and four months.

In the sixth year of Chintila’s reign, Isidore, doctor and legislator of the Spains, standing in the church, after completing a sermon to the people and extending his hand toward heaven, blessed everyone, commended to God the flock entrusted to him until then, and fell asleep in the Lord in a most blessed sleep, adorned with a most holy old age.

For he was renowned in the spirit of prophecy, generous in almsgiving, outstanding in hospitality, serene in heart, truthful in speech, just in judgment, constant in preaching, joyful in exhortation, diligent in winning souls for God, cautious in expounding the Scriptures, prudent in counsel, humble in dress, temperate at table, devoted in prayer, distinguished in good character, always ready to die for the Church and the defense of truth, and conspicuous in every goodness.

Moreover, he was the father of clerics, teacher and sustainer of monks and nuns, consoler of the sorrowful, protection of orphans and widows, relief of the oppressed, defender of citizens, crusher of the proud, [Col. 0319C] persecutor and hammer of heretics.

He governed the archbishopric of the Church of Seville for forty years, shining with various signs of miracles, flourishing in the dignity of the primacy, and exercising in Spain the functions of the Roman pope. He taught priests, kings, and peoples the divine and human laws, and commanded them humbly to obey the Roman bishop. He brought a curse upon those unwilling to obey and separated them from the fellowship of the faithful.

He instructed the Church of Christ through many volumes of books and rested in peace in the year 680 of the Era. He summoned the bishops to a synod at Toledo and, with prophetic voice, foretold to them the day of his death and what was to come upon Spain.

“Star of righteousness, light of morals, sun of probity—

These things that holy Isidore, through whom the nourishing faith flourished,

said at the synod of Toledo:

If you preserve what is commanded to you,

Christ will preserve you in his love.

He will give grain and oil, and every best thing,

if you please him with a pure mind.

If you neglect these things, you will not escape unpunished,

since God rightly punishes evil deeds.

Then the Goths will fall in wars, and a barbarian enemy

will crush you with countless disaster, fear, and hunger.

Then turn back; then lament your crimes,

and immediately the Lord will be your helper.

Your glory will be greater, and the grace of Christ

will raise the Goths to more abundant good.”

We have recorded these things concerning his deeds among the acts of the kings because he himself was born from the illustrious stock of the Gothic kings, his father being Severianus, a Carthaginian commander.

After his death, one month later, the Catholic king Chintila died at Toledo, having met a good end. Theodisclus, a Greek by nationality, succeeded the most blessed doctor Isidore. Learned in a variety of languages and polished in outward speech, he was inwardly, as his end demonstrated, a most ravenous wolf beneath a sheep’s skin.

For he corrupted, out of hatred for the faith, certain books on the *Natures of Things*, the *Art of Medicine*, and also the *Notory Art* (*Ars notoria*), which Father Isidore had composed in eloquent style and which had not yet been made public, cutting out what was true and inserting what was false. Through a certain Arab named Avicenna, he translated them from Latin into Arabic.

When he was found to be unfaithful in these and many other matters and was proved erroneous in the articles of faith, he was degraded by a synod from the archiepiscopal dignity. For he asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ was not one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but rather an adoptive son.

As has been said, deprived of the honor of the priesthood, he went over to the Arabs, adhered to the sect of the false prophet Mahomet, and taught many detestable things under the emperor Heraclius. At that time the dignity of the primacy was transferred to the Church of Toledo.

Heraclius waged war against Chosroes, king of the Persians, in the sixth year of his reign and the sixth year of the reign of Sisebut, king of the Goths. After defeating and killing him, carrying the Lord’s cross to Jerusalem, and seeing an angel above the gates of Jerusalem, he returned from there to his own land with [Col. 0320C] great joy.

At this time, when the peoples of the East disdained to pay taxes and tribute to the Romans, they began to rebel with all their strength. Then a certain wicked preacher arose, born in Arabia, named Mahomet.

This most evil seducer, seeing that discord had arisen between the peoples of the East and the Romans, raised himself up against God and the rule of the Christians, deceitfully urging the race of the Arabs on and saying that they ought not to be subjected to the lord of another people, because the Lord would provide for them by granting them from their own race a benevolent leader whom they might have as a brother and with whom the Lord would also speak.

As he preached these and similar things in persuasive words, and seemed to perform certain feigned powers and miracles by magical arts, the Ishmaelites immediately, like brute animals without understanding, gradually changed from good to evil. Abandoning the Catholic faith, they began to believe him and to hold him in such veneration that they proclaimed him a prophet sent by God and chose him as their king, deceived by his counterfeit miracles and misled by his eloquence.

For he was handsome, eloquent, and strong, and deeply versed in magical arts. This Mahomet, prince of the Saracens and Arabs, is said to have been descended from Ishmael, the son of Abraham.

When, in his youth, he had begun to be a prudent merchant, he frequently traveled with his camels to Egypt and Palestine, and stayed with Jews and Christians, especially with a certain Antiochene monk, a friend of superstition, named John. From him he learned both the New and the Old Testament superficially and superstitiously.

As he traveled here and there with various kinds of spices and goods for the sake of profit, it happened that he entered the province of Corrozata. The mistress of this province, whose name was Cadiga, when she saw the young man, was first captivated in mind by his beauty and eloquence. She began to inspect the various wares that Mahomet had brought with him and to attach herself to him more intimately.

Mahomet artfully touched her with the phantasm of his enchantments and gradually and cunningly began to lead her into error, telling her that he was the Messiah whom the Jews were awaiting. He was aided not only by Queen Cadiga, who had been deceived by him, but also by many Jews who flocked to him from different regions.

All the Ishmaelites and Arabs also gathered around him in crowds, astonished by the novelty of the affair. He began to invent new laws for them and to hand them over to them, applying to those wicked laws corrupted testimonies from both Testaments.

He perverted the authorities of the divine writings so as to bar both Christians and Jews from disputing with the Saracens. He also issued an edict to his followers that anyone who preached anything other than what they had received from him should be punished by the sword.

The Saracens call these sacrilegious teachings the laws of God and acknowledge him as their lawgiver and messenger of God.

The aforementioned Cadiga, seeing him surrounded equally by the companionship of Jews and Saracens, supposed that divine wisdom lay hidden in him. Since she was a widow, she took him as her husband. Mahomet himself then assumed the name of king, placing upon himself the royal diadem.

Afterward he began to conduct himself vigorously in arms and to appropriate to himself the name and insignia of king and prophet.

After this he began to suffer frequent attacks of a falling disease and epileptic illness. When Queen Cadiga saw this, she was exceedingly distressed, because she had married a man whom she believed to be afflicted by the seizure of demons.

But he cleverly deceived her by soothing her fears, saying: “Because I behold the angel of the Lord Gabriel speaking with me, and because, being a carnal man, I cannot endure the splendor of his face, I fail and fall.”

While saying this, he attempted to perform certain signs and miracles by magical arts. Nevertheless, as the story goes, the devil, disguising himself as an angel of light, foretold certain future things to him.

Thus, at the beginning of his deceitful preaching, he went to Spain [Col. 0321D] and taught at Córdoba the sect of his own destruction. For he said that Jesus Christ the Lord was born of a virgin through the working of the Holy Spirit, but nevertheless was not God.

When this was reported to the most blessed Father Isidore, who was then returning from the Roman court, he immediately sent ministers to capture him. But the devil appeared to Mahomet and ordered him to flee as quickly as possible.

After his flight into Africa and Arabia, Mahomet deceived innumerable peoples. Having obtained royal power, he devastated the Roman Empire with the Ishmaelites, who believed that he received from the mouth of the archangel Gabriel the laws that he handed over to them.

In the year 656 of the Era, Mahomet invaded the regions of Arabia, Syria, and Mesopotamia hostilely with his army, and occupied both those lands and the neighboring countries through disastrous plundering.

When this was reported to Theodore, the brother of Heraclius, who then governed the regions of the East, he immediately met him near Gabatha with a large army to engage him in battle [Col. 0322A]. While they fought each other fiercely, Theodore was killed, most of the Christian army fell by the dreadful sword, and the rest were scattered in flight.

Then the Hagarenes, strengthened by the Romans’ flight, attacked Syria more boldly. They laid waste to the country and established the throne of their kingdom at Damascus, once a famous city of the Christians, and gave credence to the sayings of Mahomet, asserting that divine power lay hidden in him.

Among the other abominations that Mahomet taught, he revived the sect of Nicolas, a native of Antioch who had been one of the seven apostolic deacons and whose sect had already died out through the apostles. In the Apocalypse the Lord writes to the angel of the church at Ephesus that he hates it, saying: “You hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate” (Revelation 2:6).

In the tenth year of his reign, because he had said that he would die and rise again on the third day, one of his disciples, Albimor, wishing to discover whether he would truly rise from the dead, cunningly offered Mahomet a highly effective poison. Mahomet immediately experienced, through a sudden change, the end of his life.

Therefore he told certain people standing beside him that through water they would receive remission of sins, and he immediately died. But his disciples carefully guarded his body, expecting him to rise again.

When an excessive stench burst forth and they could no longer endure it, they departed. On the eleventh day Albimor found Mahomet’s body torn apart by dogs. He carefully gathered his bones and, with a great assembly of Saracens, buried him in Medina Ruphul, which in Latin means “City of the Messenger.”

In the year 666 of the Spanish Era, the seventeenth year of Heraclius, after Mahomet, Abubacar—chosen from among his relatives—ruled the Arabs vigorously for three years. After him Homer reigned, and triumphed in many battles; he subjected the city of Alexandria, the metropolis, to his empire. After achieving many victories by sea and land, while one day he was engaged in prayer, he was struck by an arrow shot by one of his servants and died, having completed ten years of reign. Thus the error of the Saracens had its beginning, and from the Romans they obtained many provinces and victories in various parts of the world. And, as is said, the cause of such great evils was the avarice of the Romans, who intolerably oppressed the nations subject to them under the yoke of slavery. Therefore, taking advantage of the opportunity, those nations shook Roman dominion from their necks as quickly as possible, while miserably entangling themselves in the wicked rites of Mahomet. For this was the tail of the dragon, of which it is written in the Apocalypse that it cast down from heaven a third of the stars (Apoc. 12:4). But now let the pen turn to the kings of the Goths.

In the year 680 of the Spanish Era, the twenty-sixth year of the reign of Heraclius, after King Chintila, Tulga reigned for three years. He was gentle and Catholic in every respect. He enlarged the kingdoms subject to him in peace; he was upright in judgment and distinguished for generosity and gentleness. He confirmed the synod enacted by his predecessors. He died at Toledo.

In the year 682 of the Spanish Era, the first year of the reign of the younger Heraclius, Chindaswinth reigned alone for four years and eight months; afterward he reigned together with his son Recceswinth for another six years and seven months. He obtained from the Roman pope the privilege that, according to the good pleasure of the bishops of Spain, the dignity of primacy should belong either to Seville or to Toledo; and, having instructed the Church with the bishops, he confirmed it through many synods. In his time Spain rested from every disturbance, so completely that no unbeliever was found in it, nor anyone who would take up arms in rebellion. He diligently caused the books of the holy Fathers to be sought out and firmly observed the institutions of blessed Isidore. By synodal judgment he exiled the treacherous Theodiscus, bishop of Seville, and transferred the dignity of primacy to the Church of Toledo. He died at Toledo.

In the year 686 of the Spanish Era, the first year of the reign of Constans, son of Heraclius, Recceswinth, son of Chindaswinth, reigned for six years, and afterward alone for twelve years. He loved the Catholic faith to such a degree that he was always seeking learned men who would frequently discuss the articles of faith before him. For he delighted in the divine Scriptures and adorned Christ’s altars with gold, silver, jewels, and silk with the greatest care. He held three synods with the bishops at Toledo, confirmed the laws enacted by his predecessors, and added certain others entirely fitting to upright conduct. He loved everyone wonderfully and was greatly loved by all. He was so gentle and humble that among his subjects he seemed like one of them. He ruled the kingdom subject to him in peace, and at a village called Gerticos, situated on Mount Cauriensis, he died a natural death under the emperor Constantine.

Thus far the blessed Hildefonsus, primate of Spain and archbishop of Toledo, has written; in the time of the aforesaid King Recceswinth he shone in the Church of God like the morning star among the stars, both in uprightness of character and in the brilliance of his signs. He also deserved in this present life to be honored with heavenly gifts by Mary, the perpetual Mother of God, and by Leocadia.

# EPIGRAMS ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT HILDEFONSUS BY PSEUDO-JULIAN IN A COLLECTION OF VARIOUS POEMS

## NOTICE

Even the collector’s name alone—suspected and hated by everyone—has deprived these poems of all credibility, so that there is scarcely any need now to ask why we send to the appendix, among the apocryphal works of Hildefonsus, these epigrams, almost all of which are defended by the authority and testimony of a single Pseudo-Julian, that notorious father of fables. We say “almost all,” because some of them had been produced by Jerome de la Higuera in his *History of Toledo* before Pseudo-Julian had published his dreams, and had also been cited by other earlier writers. Such are the third, for Saint Heladius, bishop of Toledo; the fourth, concerning Saint Eugenius; and the tenth, which is here entitled “On the Translation of Saint Fulgentius.” All of them, however, have been corrupted and interpolated by the collector, as we shall point out in their proper places.

Nevertheless, for that reason we do not condemn them all by one and the same judgment. We more willingly follow the judgment passed on them by the learned Nicolás Antonio, who did not dare to reject everything. He acknowledges at least three epigrams which, if cleansed of the interpolated verses—as he supposes—could be considered genuine works of Hildefonsus. They are the second, concerning the hospice built by his parents at Toledo; the third, concerning Saint Heladius; and the fourth, concerning Saint Eugenius, his uncle.

He considers the rest to be rejected as spurious, containing nothing beyond the mere inventions of an impostor. And we certainly believe that anyone who reads them a little more carefully will agree with him. We depart from him only slightly, as will appear from the observations to be appended below; and, in order to warn the reader of this varied status of the poems, we have marked them with different typefaces.

Besides these twelve epigrams drawn from the collection of Pseudo-Julian, we publish, at the end, another in honor of Saint Isidore of Seville, no less apocryphal than the others, in our judgment. It had, however, been published and attributed to Saint Hildefonsus by the author of the *Life of Saint Isidore* printed by the Bollandists, who is believed to have been Lucas of Tuy, after the other poem found in the collection as number 10, beginning, “This blessed cross bears,” and so it necessarily had to be added to the others, lest anything concerning spurious works at some time attributed to Saint Hildefonsus should be lacking in this Appendix.

## EPIGRAMS

### Note

Nicolás Antonio says that this epigram is spurious and contains all the notions that its artificer had conceived concerning Saint Hildefonsus’s lineage and kinship—unworthy of being attributed to the most holy man, from whom every trace of pride and arrogance ought to have been absent. Besides, how many false and absurd things does it contain? Let the reader note that Athanagild, king of the Goths, whom it says was second to none in piety, lived as an Arian; and then that the poet also remembers Ervig, although it is established that Ervig was inaugurated as king twelve years after Hildefonsus’s death. After this, no one will doubt that the epigram is spurious.

### FIRST EPIGRAM

The suppliant Evantius consecrated a church to Luke;

Its noble founder was Nicolaus.

Lucia was our parent; Evantia our sister,

And Eugenius, bishop of this city, our loving brother.

Lazarus, a poor man, receives from my excellent and upright mother

A house for guests and the poor.

Moreover, my grandmother Blesilla, born of the illustrious blood of the Goths,

Builds holy temples to Mark.

Moreover, her offspring, Evantia, daughter of Nicolaus,

The loving wife of Ophilo, who worshiped God,

Raises splendid temples to Peter beneath the city walls,

Also increases their revenues and fills the house with honor.

This Ophilo was a descendant of King Athanagild,

And my father was also his brother, Stephen.

King Athanagild, our grandfather, founded

The monastery and church of Eulalia;

But first he established them for Justa.

This man was pious, second to none in piety;

But secretly, because of those Goths who held power.

Sebastian has a church while Liuva reigns

Beneath the city; Ervig restores Mary’s.

Yet King Constantine also builds one for her,

And the third sacred house was at Toledo.

Live, you roofs rising to magnificent gods,

You who rule the city walls with your protection.

### II. ON THE HOSPICE BUILT BY HIS PARENTS

#### Note

Nicolás Antonio himself acknowledges this epigram as genuine. Certainly nothing decisive can be brought against it; for tradition says that Saint Hildefonsus was born of Lucia and Stephen and was the nephew of Saint Eugenius. Nicolás also says that it is cited by Jerome de la Higuera in his *History of Toledo*, as having been sent to him from Germany. Although this is not strong evidence for persuasion, we do not object to its being regarded as a work of Hildefonsus.

Lucia was his mother by Stephen, but his uncle,

Bishop Eugenius, compelled him to establish the hospice.

Lazarus the beggar possesses this place beneath the city walls,

Where the road to Complutum lies open for travelers.

### III. THE SAME AUTHOR’S SEPULCHRAL POEM FOR SAINT HELADIUS, BISHOP OF TOLEDO

#### Note

Regarding this epigram, as also the following one, we do not doubt that they are genuine monuments of antiquity. The historian de la Higuera recognized them even before the publication of the false chronicles, but without the interpolation of poems or distortion of words that the collection of Pseudo-Julian represents. For the collection mentioned above presents the second couplet of this epigram as follows:

> He was a reader at Toledo while he lived at court;  
> From a monk he became a reader of Agali.

In the first line we think “reader” is a typographical error; but the repetition of “reader” in the pentameter reveals the hand of that corruptor, Pseudo-Julian. The penultimate couplet also seems to be of the same kind; and for that reason it was omitted by the same historian in his *History of Toledo*.

In this tomb rests the body

Of Bishop Heladius, but his spirit possesses the stars.

He was ruler of Toledo while he lived at court;

From a monk he became abbot of Agali.

From there he was violently carried away to the city of Toledo,

Worn out by age, but strong in piety.

The martyr Leocadia received the remains of his body;

That house receives kings and bishops.

From there he will rise again on the final day,

To receive rewards worthy of his merits.

He had already passed eighty years as an old man,

The glory of bishops, the courageous torch of God.

I am Hildefonsus, whom he had made his minister;

I paid these whatever last honors I could to the holy old man.

### IV. FOR SAINT EUGENIUS, HIS UNCLE, BISHOP OF TOLEDO

#### Note

This epigram, which we said above was one of those that could be regarded as genuine, is fabricated in half of its text and is spurious, having been interpolated at the collector’s pleasure, according to the same Nicolás Antonio. Indeed, it gives rise to considerable suspicion that the historian de la Higuera is said to have cited it as a tetrastich, whereas here it appears as an octastich. For this reason he thinks the second and fourth couplets should be rejected; and we have therefore marked them with a different typeface. Perhaps he has discovered the truth. Yet if anyone wishes to defend the whole epigram, we shall not strongly resist.

Here lies the venerable body of Bishop Eugenius,

Whom the revered temples of Leocadia contain.

Here he became a monk, while fleeing mortal shadows,

And in old age became bishop in the land of Toledo.

His life was blessed, his character chaste and without blemish:

Such as Isidore and Leander were.

The disciple renders the last funeral services

To his beloved teacher and kinsman.

### V. ANOTHER POEM FOR SAINT LEANDER AND SAINT MASSONA, THE FORMER ARCHBISHOP OF SEVILLE, THE LATTER OF MERIDA

#### Note

Nicolás Antonio considers this fifth epigram, as well as those that follow—the sixth concerning Saint Fulgentius, the seventh concerning Saint Isidore, the eighth concerning Saint Florentina, and the ninth concerning Saint Leocadia—to be absolutely spurious. Evidently, as we think, he missed in them the Gothic antiquity which they scarcely display at all. Moreover, they rest solely on the testimony of Pseudo-Julian, and therefore each of them ought to be suspect.

Leander, outstanding father, whom Heaven receives,

Adorned with praises and distinguished by titles:

The hammer of the Arian race, and likewise its healer,

Teacher of Isidore, whom he begot for the Lord.

You also are thrice blessed, Massona, glory of the land of Merida,

Renowned for counsel, heart, and faith.

Equal in spirit, both equal in piety and praise,

And each a wall in the house of the great God.

By enduring threats you conquered the king’s rebellious spirit;

They say that he repented of his crime.

You opened the twofold heaven to the king’s offspring;

Through you one martyr flies to the stars,

While the other rises to the rosy airs of light,

And where that light is absent, there he possesses its radiance.

They say that you granted salvation to the Gothic people;

He abandoned the hated doctrine and embraced the pious one.

The victorious laurel rightly follows you,

And everlasting glory, due to such magnificent merits.

Your honor and illustrious fame will always remain,

And peoples will sing of you, but the stars sing more loudly.

For you are girded with an eternal crown of leaves

In a more splendid place among the teachers.

### VI. TO THE MOST HOLY MAN AND TEACHER FULGENTIUS

Fulgentius, whom New Carthage restored to the breezes,

And afterward, too fortunate, possessed you as a father,

Then Astigi joyfully receives you back as its father,

The stream in which the Baetis rejoices—and rejoices in you still more.

You correct the unbridled morals and educate the life of your people,

A teacher by example and by speech.

Seville itself arranges your ashes with those of your brothers;

The same urn contains three brothers together.

### VII. EPITAPH FOR SAINT ISIDORE OF SEVILLE

Your mind penetrates the heavens, while your body sleeps in this urn,

Sweet glory of your people, leader Isidore.

Receive willingly the verses consecrated to you by your disciple,

Most honored teacher, who was part and companion of your exile;

And love, after your death, in security,

The one whom you loved while alive, teacher.

Pray for us wretched ones, most illustrious teacher,

Glory of the West, honor of religion.

Grant, I beg you, a gracious hearing; cease, I pray, to be entreated,

Since peoples call upon you, and your disciple calls upon you.

Make him who is surrounded by varied cares

And beset by dense dangers enjoy the dwelling of heaven.

### VIII. TO THE HOLY VIRGIN FLORENTINA

Florentina, shining one, immortal glory of chastity,

Unstained mother and glory of the virginal choir.

You prefer poverty to riches, and Christ as husband,

Who wishes to be for you abundantly rich in possessions.

You trample beneath your feet all that the deceitful world worships;

Poor bride of God, you seek the stars of the poor man.

Rejoice in your lot, destined to enjoy it forever,

And afterward gladly follow your Lamb as his ewe.

Pour forth chaste prayers, virgin, for our guilt,

And help me yourself, whom your bridegroom has helped.

### IX. TO THE HOLY VIRGIN AND MARTYR LEOCADIA

For with what praises shall I sing of your deeds,

Leocadia, illustrious through your blood and even more illustrious through your faith,

Joined to the marriage-bed of the eternal Bridegroom,

Whom you now hold in your embrace, but without end?

You are the very glory of your Toledo, whom all Spain

Invokes and continually entreats with its prayers.

Dacian drives you on, moved by savage furies,

Thinking that he can conquer you by a cruel imprisonment.

Here, aided by the cross and by the suffering of death,

Long since worn down, you remain unconquered.

The Almighty lends a ready ear to your desires;

Struck by the lash, you fly through the stars.

And to me, thrice wretched though I resist,

You grant the grace to see you emerging from the tomb with radiant face.

In the presence of the devout people you grant that the veil be cut with iron,

And, as one who loves the Mother of God, you impart her commands.

May the heavenly ones praise you, whom the throng of the devout praises;

Remember your client, virgin, and rejoice.

Toledo calls you by the voice that you pour forth in blood;

Add your customary prayers for your fellow citizens.

### X. ON THE TRANSLATION OF THE BODY OF SAINT FULGENTIUS

#### Note

This epigram, inserted in the collection of Pseudo-Julian, is older than that collection: it is found under the name of Saint Hildefonsus in the *Life of Saint Isidore* written by the man believed to have been Lucas of Tuy. Concerning its legitimate author, we do not think a more exact judgment can be made than that pronounced by the same Nicolás Antonio, so often mentioned by us: it should be attributed neither to Hildefonsus nor to any other ancient author.
