It has nevertheless also been corrupted and most foolishly enlarged by the collector, so that he might introduce a mention of Saint Fulgentius, as appears from a comparison with the text which we transcrib[lacuna] from Lucas of Tuy:

> This blessed cross bears the bodies of twin brothers,  
> Leander and Isidore, and their father from the order of seers [reading uncertain].  
> Their third sister, Florentina, devoted forever—  
> O how well ordered a companion!—rests here worthily.  
> Isidore, placed between them, separates the limbs of the two.  
> What men they were, inquire in the books, reader.  
> You will learn that both spoke all things well,  
> Secure in hope, full of faith, and dear above all.  
> You will see that the faithful increased through their teachings,  
> And that what impious laws held was restored to the Lord.  
> And, so that you may believe that exalted men live forever,  
> Looking upward, strive to see them depicted.

This blessed cross bears the bodies of twin brothers,

Leander and Isidore, likewise from the order of seers;

Their third sister, Florentina, devoted forever—

O, how harmoniously composed, she rests here worthily!

Isidore, placed between them, separates the limbs of the earlier two.

What men they were, inquire in the books, reader.

You will learn that they spoke all things well,

Among whom Fulgentius rests here. Look upon these three,

Full of certain hope and faith, and dear above all.

You will see the faithful increased through their teachings,

And those whom impious laws held restored to the Lord.

And believe that exalted men live forever;

Looking upward, strive to see them pure.

### XI. ON SYNAGRIA, HIS MATERNAL AUNT

#### Note

It contains a thousand ridiculous inventions and a thousand fictions concerning Saint Bonitus, bishop of Clermont, in order to make him born of the same family and people as our Hildefonsus. See Nicolás Antonio.

Now I, Synagria, daughter of Ophilo, married

Theodat, equal to me in noble Auvergnian birth.

Though Ophilo was among the Goths, my husband was of Auvergnian stock,

A man of outstanding nobility and piety.

During the marriage it happened that I bore Bonitus;

He was excellent in many respects.

Wonderful things foretell what will happen to the boy

As the ages roll onward; may God preserve these things for me.

I die, while my marriage-partner and my son survive;

With my mother and my beloved father I lie.

If merciful God forgives me my many sins,

May I thereafter enjoy eternal rest.

You who read this, pour forth prayers and pray for me;

As a devout man, entreat the Godhead with constant prayer.

### XII. TO SAINT JUSTUS

#### Note

This epigram—which we find Nicolás Antonio did not annotate—contains genuine material concerning Saint Justus and seems to have been composed from the eulogy of him written by Hildefonsus, except for the explicit mention of Saint Benedict, which clearly demonstrates that the poem is later and apocryphal.

Dear father to us, Justus, in deed and name,

You yourself fulfill the number of your name.

Offspring of Heladius, a monk from childhood;

He was the splendid rule of the Benedictine choir.

You become father to many monks, and to your servant Alfonso,

Whom you nourish—Benedict, to you.

Afterward you are carried away as shepherd to the church of Toledo;

The appointed years of your episcopate were yours.

You were worthy of life, but unexpected death concealed

Many hopes for so great a bishop and father.

Swift intelligence was joined to marvelous eloquence,

And the gravity of an old man accompanied your judgment.

Your third summer had seen you as bishop;

You lie dead in the church of Leocadia.

#### Note

This epitaph exists, as we have said, in the *Life* published by the Bollandists, which is regarded as a work of Lucas of Tuy. It seems to wish to attribute it to Saint Hildefonsus; for after the poem already published above, beginning “This blessed cross bears,” which he himself says was composed by Hildefonsus, it adds, without mentioning any other author: “Another likewise,” and then describes this other epigram: “In praise of the Church,” and so forth.

Nevertheless, many things prove it to be apocryphal. For it contains almost all the fables that we refuted above in the continuation of the *Chronicle*: concerning the primacy of the Church of Seville, and concerning the refutation and expulsion of Mahomet.

Moreover, the very form of the poem reveals later centuries, in which Leonine verses began to be used long after the age of the Gothic Fathers, as we have already noted elsewhere.

## ANOTHER EPITAPH IN PRAISE OF SAINT ISIDORE, FROM HIS LIFE WRITTEN, AS IS BELIEVED, BY LUCAS OF TUY

In praise of the Church, to Christ, King of glory,

Let us sing continually;

And in a single Davidic song

Let us solemnly sing of the Virgin.

Let hymns resound with the glory of Isidore,

Remembering his merits;

Let the accumulation of praises increase, let the people rejoice,

And the angelic choirs.

Shining in our times through his character,

Faithful in the words of the Lord,

He exalted the faith and drove away the stain

Of heretical error.

Born at Carthage, knowing nothing childish

From the beginning,

He poured forth the fountain of wisdom

Throughout the regions of Spain, performing wonders.

While he presided as primate at Seville, he taught the law,

A Spaniard to Spain.

Pre-eminent in doctrine, preaching the Crucified,

He drove away idolatry.

Most noble in lineage, he stood firm

In the great works of God,

Seeking the reward of heavenly joys,

Despising temporal things.

Through the splendor of his works, a fruitful example,

He gave himself to the clergy;

Changing nothing from what was certain, wholly intent on heaven,

He overcame vices.

Here he restored the doctrines of the Romans

More widely throughout the regions of the world;

As the evening star adorns the West,

So he more brightly adorned the Church.

Orthodox, he confounded Arius,

The dreadful adversary,

With the reckoning of reason;

The bitter enemy yielded, defeated openly.

Let the devotion of the Iberian clergy

With full joy honor the Father of the fatherland;

Contemplating his doctrines, let the regions of the world praise

The teacher of the Church.

Ornament of archbishops, mirror of priests,

He wrote, composing learnedly,

Wonderful poems concerning the Catholic faith,

Piling book upon book.

The blindness of Mahomet, which was destroying ruined peoples,

Unable to refute his miracles,

Sorrowfully yielded

To the spotless man.

As he sincerely believed, so sincerely he set forth

The form of repentance.

Discerning in learning, effective in example,

Teacher of the multitude.

Who could fully bring forth or prescribe

The record of his deeds?

The tongue would not suffice, the right hand would fail

In writing each one.

Let us therefore entreat him, whose sanctity

Is firmly believed,

To defend us perpetually from the enemy’s snares

And from vices.

O suppressor of crimes, reconcile us

To the Lord by your prayer;

Comfort us in hope, remove what harms us,

And cleanse away all our defilements.

With you we honor your brother;

We ask for the intercession of Leander,

So that, hearing our prayers,

He may receive them in everlasting remembrance.

We wish to remember Fulgentius the teacher,

The companion of these brothers;

For the merit of his life, we ask

That he be concerned for our salvation.

We ask, together with the brothers,

For the outstanding virgin Florentina,

That she may come as a helper and soften the offenses

Into which we have fallen,

And that the Lord may likewise be willing to soften them.

Amen, let the clergy sing.

Through the intervention of the virgin,

Let her cleanse from the stain of sin

Those whom sin pollutes.

Let so renowned a virgin, having driven away the darkness

Of vices, plead for us,

So that he who rules all things with wondrous power

May place us in heaven.

Amen.

# In the Year of Our Lord 678. Saint Leodegarius, Bishop of Autun

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT LEODEGARIUS

### From *Gallia Christiana*, volume IV

Three ancient authors committed the life of Saint Leodegarius, or Leutgarius, to writing. The first is an anonymous author from Autun, a contemporary of the bishop, who dedicated his little work—indeed inelegantly but seriously written—to Hermenarius, bishop of Autun. The second is Ursinus, who shortly afterward, at the urging of Audulfus, abbot of Saint-Maixent, composed another work concerning the holy bishop and dedicated it to Ansoaldus, bishop of Poitiers. The third, a monk by nationality an Alamannian, dedicated his work to the abbot of the monastery of Murbach in Alsace. Finally, Audulfus, abbot of Saint-Maixent, published a little book about the miracles performed at the saint’s translation. From these sources, but especially from the first two, which deserve complete confidence, we have taken what we shall transcribe below.

Leodegarius was born of the noblest family among the Franks. His father’s name was not committed to writing. His mother was Sigrada, who, after her husband’s death, became a nun in the convent of Saint Mary at Soissons and lived so holy a life that she is mentioned in the old calendar of that nunnery—now preserved in the convent of Longpont and written five hundred years ago—on the Nones of August with an office of twelve lessons; and on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April one reads: “Commemoration of Sigrada.” She had a sister, Berswinda, wife of Athic, son of Leutharius, duke of the Alamanni, as Mabillon thought.

At the beginning of his life, his parents brought him to the palace of King Chlothar. Shortly afterward, when he was ten years old, according to Cointius, the same king entrusted him to his uncle Dido, bishop of Poitiers, to be instructed in literary studies. Under his care he made such progress in learning and piety that he became highly skilled in humane letters, most accomplished in the divine Scriptures and sacred theology, renowned for his knowledge of ecclesiastical canons and civil law, and finally adorned with every virtue, especially the beauty of chastity.

Thus, through his uncle, he was “chosen and ordained to the office of the diaconate before the age of twenty. Then, after not much time had passed, he became archdeacon and was placed over all the churches of the diocese.” Here a difficulty arises: should the “under twenty years” within which Leodegarius was raised to the diaconate refer to his age, or to the period he spent with Bishop Dido? Mabillon refers it to his age, when he says, “Within the twentieth year of his age,” and so forth. Cointius, however, refers it to the period of residence, and with very great probability: first, because the canons forbade ordaining a deacon before the age of twenty-five, and it is difficult to persuade oneself that Dido transgressed them; second, because, as the authors of the *Lives* testify, Leodegarius surpassed the others in the variety of his learning when he was ordained deacon, and an age younger than twenty does not seem capable of so many sciences; finally, because learned men understand Fortunatus’s words concerning Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, in the same sense as Mabillon, although those words are altogether similar.

Nevertheless, it is not difficult to answer these points, and the contrary opinion is not without plausibility. Whatever the case, in the office of archdeacon he gave such proofs of courage and wisdom that he far surpassed all his predecessors, brought joy to the sorrowful, recalled those burdened with crimes to the pursuit of discipline, and kept everyone to his duty.

Afterward, “when the father of the monastery founded in honor of Saint Maxentius died,” he “undertook its governance at his uncle’s command; he ruled it for nearly six years and enriched it with great resources,” according to Ursinus. Mabillon consequently infers that he changed his habit and took monastic vows, since Gregory the Great had forbidden—and the prohibition already existed before him—that clerics should be placed over monasteries.

Moved by the reputation of his wisdom and virtues, King Chlothar and his wife Bathildis asked Dido “to grant him permission to remain with them in the palace.” Dido immediately fulfilled their request and sent him “equipped with great resources and crowned with the flowers of wisdom.” He was received with the highest honor, and “within a few days,” by his virtue and integrity of character, the courtesy of his speech, and the greatest refinement and wisdom in action, he achieved such standing that the king and queen, many bishops, and the nobles held him especially dear and in the highest esteem. By common consent, and especially that of the Franks, he was judged worthy of a bishopric.

Accordingly, he was made bishop of the Church of Autun, which at that time had been vacant and afflicted for nearly two years, in the year 659, as is clear from Ursinus: “When he had energetically discharged this office for ten years,” he says, “King Chlothar, who had promoted him, departed this life.” For Chlothar died in the fourteenth year of his reign, in the year 669.

The Church of Autun, torn apart by factions, oppressed by disturbances, and stripped of its possessions, received new splendor under his governance. The anonymous author says:

> At his arrival all the adversaries of the Church and city were terrified, as were those who were constantly fighting among themselves with hatred and murder, so that they did not wish even to hear the memory of the former scandal. Those whom preaching had not led to harmony were compelled by justice and fear. How greatly his chief concern grew for the support of the poor and for the adornment of sacred things is shown by the works or register established by him, which remains at the church door; by the beauty of the vessels that gleam with golden brilliance in the service of the church; by the ornaments of the baptistery fashioned with marvelous workmanship; by the pavements and ceilings of the church; by the new construction of the atrium; by the restoration of the walls; by the repair of the houses; and so forth.

In the year 661 he held a council at Autun, at which many canons were enacted to establish and repair the discipline of the Benedictine rule in monasteries. In the tenth year of King Chlothar, in the year of Christ 666, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, Drausius, bishop of Soissons, granted a privilege to the convent of Saint Mary, which had been built in that city by Ebroin. Our Dom Michael Germain published it in the history of that monastery (p. 421). Besides the bishops of the province, the following subscribed it: Genesius of Lyons . . . Leutgarius of Autun . . . Desideratus of Chalon, Leudeboldus, and others.

While the holy bishop was thus living peacefully at Autun, and while everything was proceeding according to his wishes, certain men, driven by envy and afraid of his steadfastness, approached Ebroin, mayor of the palace of Chlothar, and accused Leodegarius before him, as though, while everyone obeyed Ebroin’s commands, Leodegarius alone despised them. Ebroin became enraged and was driven into a fury when he observed that he could not overcome the holy bishop in argument, nor obtain from him the obsequious flattery that everyone else offered; indeed, Leodegarius always remained fearless in the face of Ebroin’s attacks. These are the words of the anonymous author.

At that time, however, the tyrant could do nothing. He accomplished only this: he issued an edict “that no one from the regions of Burgundy should presume to approach the palace unless he had received his summons.” It was certainly an empty vengeance at that time; for when the childless Chlothar died in 669, Ebroin’s power and freedom fell with him.

When Ebroin determined to install Theodoric as king in place of his deceased brother, so that he himself might govern the young man’s kingdom just as he had governed Chlothar’s, the Austrasians and Burgundians decided otherwise. They summoned from Austrasia Childeric, whom fame reported to be a wise ruler, chiefly at the initiative and urging of Leodegarius. Childeric hastened there and was acclaimed king by everyone.

Abandoned by all, Ebroin took refuge in a church and escaped death only through Leodegarius’s intercession; he was then confined in the monastery of Luxeuil. Leodegarius, by contrast, obtained the highest honors, was retained at the palace, became the king’s counselor, and wielded such influence with him that he was regarded as mayor of the palace.

Ursinus speaks as follows:

> The king placed Leodegarius over his entire household and wished him to be mayor in all matters. Having received this power, he restored to their former condition whatever he discovered had been improperly introduced against the laws of the ancient kings and great nobles. He restored the entire kingdom of the Franks so completely that everyone rejoiced to have Childeric as king and Leodegarius as governor of the palace.

Nevertheless, it should not for that reason be thought that the holy bishop was actually mayor of the palace. First, that dignity was secular and therefore wholly unsuitable for a bishop; second, the anonymous author, who must unquestionably be preferred to Ursinus, says nothing of it, and indeed notes that Wulfoaldus was mayor of the entire monarchy.

Accordingly, in Ursinus I interpret “mayor of the palace,” or “governor of the palace,” in a less precise sense: namely, as referring to one whose counsels the king was accustomed to follow to the greatest extent, and on whom the whole kingdom seemed to depend. It might perhaps be said that at the beginning Leodegarius held the dignity of mayor of the palace entrusted to him for a very short time, and that, through the solicitation of the nobles, especially Wulfoaldus, it was immediately taken from him and transferred to Wulfoaldus. In this way the two authors of the *Life of Leodegarius* could be reconciled and everything made straightforward.

In the year 672, a royal diploma for the monastery of Dervensis was obtained by Bercharius, with Leodegarius, Nivardus, and Atelanus, bishops, supporting him. It was issued on the fourth day before the Nones of July, at the palace of Compiègne, in the third year of King Childeric. After the king, the bishops already named subscribed, followed by Wulfoaldus, mayor of the palace, and others.

Bercharius himself also issued a document by which he gave all his possessions, both hereditary and acquired, to the monastery called Puteolus. It was enacted in the city of Reims, on the third day before the Kalends of September, in the presence of the lord and glorious King Childeric, in the fourth year of his reign. After Nivardus, Atelanus of Laon, Leodegarius, and others subscribed.

How slippery fortune is! How uncertain the sea of the court! Leodegarius scarcely preserved Childeric’s favor and friendship for “three years.” The causes of offense and hatred were envy, slander, and admonitions that were indeed justified but troublesome. At first the prince had acted wisely in many matters, but as he grew older, yielding more than was proper to the unhealthy counsels of certain courtiers, he began to act wrongly in many ways. Since the bishop could not tolerate this, he often reproved him for violating the laws of his ancestors and for his incestuous marriage with his uncle’s daughter, threatening him with God’s vengeance unless he corrected his evil deeds.

Thus, perceiving the king’s hostility toward him, he left the court and withdrew to his own church. Shortly afterward, as the feast of Easter approached, he asked Childeric, who was then staying not far from Augustodunum, to come to his city to celebrate the mysteries of Christ’s Resurrection. The king came, but this brought about the bishop’s destruction. Hector, patrician of Marseille, had also arrived to defend his case against Praejectus, who was reclaiming certain estates from him. Leodegarius favored Hector and had received him as his guest; hence arose the courtiers’ slanders. They persuaded the king that the two men had met in order to plot criminal designs against the king and the kingdom. Inflamed almost to madness by these accusations, the king said, did, and threatened such things that Leodegarius became convinced that a plot against him had been devised unless he departed. He fled, but soldiers sent after him overtook the fugitive, reported his capture, and immediately, by the king’s command, led him away to the monastery of Luxeuil to undergo perpetual exile.

There he found Ebroinus, greeted him courteously, confessed that he had in some way sinned against him, and asked that, having mutually granted one another forgiveness, they be joined in harmony.

Shortly afterward, when Childeric had been killed, they left Luxeuil together and headed toward Augustodunum. On the way Ebroinus would have laid hands upon Leodegarius, to whom he had extended his right hand, had Genesius, bishop of Lyon, not prevented him. Leodegarius was received by his people with the greatest joy and with something like a triumph. The next day both men left the city together to go to Theodoric; but midway Ebroinus withdrew from Leodegarius’s company and hurried to his own lands.

Received by the king, Leodegarius persuaded him to appoint Leudesius, son of Erchinoald, formerly mayor of the palace under Clovis, as prefect of the palace. After returning from there, he governed his diocese peacefully. Ebroinus, wishing to cause trouble for Theodoric, put forward a false king named Clovis, whom he claimed to be the son of Clotaire. After killing Leudesius, he raised an army and conceived the plan of destroying Leodegarius, since he did not doubt that the bishop was an adversary of his tyranny. He employed the services of Waymer, duke of Champagne; Desideratus, surnamed Dido, of Chalon; and Bobo, bishop of Valence—depraved men all. Having received forces from him, they hastened to Augustodunum.

The holy bishop, moved by pity for the public devastation of his people, distributed everything he possessed—silver plates and all his household goods—to monasteries of both sexes, both in the city and in the territory of the Aedui, and to the poor. At last he voluntarily surrendered himself to his enemies. They brought him to Waymer, who, as Ebroinus had ordered, cruelly deprived him of his eyes. While this was being done, the pious and unconquerable bishop neither allowed himself to be bound nor uttered a groan; rather, he sang the praises of God and psalms.

Thus mutilated, Waymer led him away to his own house. There he was so softened by the bishop’s holy conversations that he willingly restored the church’s silver, which he had shortly before received as ransom for the Aedui. From there the holy bishop was taken to a certain monastery, where he remained hidden for almost two years and displayed outstanding examples of patience and humility.

Having gained control of affairs under Theodoric, Ebroinus ordered Leodegarius and his brother Gairinus to be brought before the king in the year 676. There the tyrant subjected both men to many insults and reproaches, to which each of them replied in these words:

> “We indeed suffer these things deservedly, because we have sinned against the Lord; but you, wretched Ebroinus, who inflict such an injury upon the Frankish people, are taking vengeance rather upon yourself while you seek to deprive others of life. You have deceived many and compelled them to be exiles from their ancestral land; but you yourself will be the greater exile, since you will soon lose both temporal and eternal glory. For while you desire to surpass all the men of Francia, you are losing the glory with which you are undeservedly endowed.”

Enraged by these words, Ebroinus ordered the two men to be separated and Gairinus to be killed at once. But Leodegarius he handed over to Waningus for harsh custody, so that by a slow punishment he might drive him to despair: his feet were slashed, his tongue cut out, and his lips mutilated. But what can savage wickedness do against God? Leodegarius, by a wondrous miracle, spoke distinctly though without a tongue; and when Winobertus and Ermenarius had treated his wounds as best they could, his lips and tongue grew back.

Moved by this, Waningus treated the martyr more gently and led him to the monastery of Fiscamnus, which he himself had founded. There he ordered that Leodegarius be kept under guard but treated more humanely. There he “remained for almost two years and displayed the great seed of his teaching among the people. Whenever he approached the company of the virgins serving God there, he spoke with such eloquence, it is said, that all who heard him marveled at how great was the clemency God had worked.” Finally, there he strove to offer the daily sacrifice.

Earlier he had written a consolatory letter to his mother, who had become a nun in the convent at Soissons—a letter worthy of a martyr and apostle in the first centuries of the Church.

At last, in the year 678, the holy bishop completed his martyrdom. The king and Ebroinus ordered him to be brought into the palace, where an assembly of nobles and bishops was then being held. To prevent him from appearing to be punished while innocent, Ebroinus persuaded Theodoric that Leodegarius had been involved in Childeric’s murder. They pressed him to acknowledge this guilt himself, but he steadfastly declared that he was innocent of so great a crime.

Nevertheless, in the synod he was treated as guilty and degraded: his priestly vestment was torn from his head, and he was then handed over to Chrodobert to be killed in a remote forest. It was ordered that his dead body be thrown into a well and that the mouth of the well be carefully sealed, so that no honor might be shown to the dead man.

Chrodobert, moved by the man’s holiness, accepted the assignment reluctantly; but fearing Ebroinus’s tyranny, he allowed four servants sent by Ebroinus to carry it out. His wife mourned that so atrocious a crime had been entrusted to her husband. Leodegarius consoled her, promising that his death would in no way be turned into a curse for her, but rather into a blessing, provided that she arranged for his body to be given burial.

Then he was led by the aforesaid attendants into the designated forest. Three of them fell at his feet and asked for pardon and forgiveness. He prayed for the welfare of all who had tormented him, gave thanks to God that he had reached this final day, and, having implored Christ’s mercy, offered his neck. The fourth of the attendants cut off his head, and thus he completed his martyrdom on 2 October, in the year 678.

[Note: The year is inferred from the anonymous author and from Ursinus. Both assert that Ebroinus was beheaded after an interval of almost three years had elapsed from the passion of Saint Leodegarius. Ebroinus, moreover, was killed in the ninth year of Theodoric’s reign, according to Sigebert—that is, in the year 681 of Christ. Therefore the holy martyr was beheaded in the year 678.]

The forest in which he ended his life lies in the territory of Arras and is still distinguished by the name of Saint Leodegarius. At the command of Chrodobert’s wife, his people secretly carried his body to Sarcinium and buried it in the oratory of the estate. There the holy martyr lay for almost three years and became famous through so many miracles that, although Ebroinus tried to conceal and suppress them in silence, they were reported throughout all Gaul. After Ebroinus had been killed, the reports reached Theodoric’s court, “who,” says the anonymous author, “believed the event with astonishment and began to venerate the martyr whom, because of the tyrant’s accusation, he had previously believed guilty.”

The translation of his sacred body was therefore considered, but a considerable dispute arose concerning the place to which it should be taken. Ansoaldus, bishop of Poitiers; Hermenarius, bishop of Augustodunum; and Vindicianus, bishop of Arras, each claimed so great a treasure for his own church. After fasting and prayers had been proclaimed, three slips of paper were placed upon the altar cloth. After the solemn celebration of Mass, a servant of Ansoaldus drew one of the slips, and by this lot the body of the blessed martyr was assigned to him. It was transferred to the monastery of Maxentius, situated in the diocese of Poitiers. So many miracles occurred along the way that anyone suffering from any illness who was able to touch with his hand either the bier or the cloth with which it was covered immediately recovered his health.

In certain Martyrologies the solemnity of this translation is recorded on 16 March, as Godefridus Henschenius reports in his dissertation on the three Dagoberts. When the Normans were ravaging the territory of Poitiers, the monks first carried his sacred remains to Armorica, then to Auvergne, and afterward to Auxerre. Finally, after a monastery had been built in his honor at Ebrolia in Auvergne, they left there the greater part of the relics of Leodegarius and his brother Guarinus, “except for the hands and the head,” which Bernard Guido, bishop of Lodève, asserts are venerated at the monastery of Maimacum.

Nevertheless, the monks of Murbach, Jumièges, and Pratelles maintain that his head is preserved in their own monasteries. The monks of Fécamp boast that they possess one arm, those of Basol another, and those of Maxentius one of the excavated eyes, as well as small portions of the body.

Perardus transmitted his testament, in which the holy martyr speaks as follows:

> “I appoint as heir the church of Saint Nazarius, the title of my episcopate, from my possessions—that is, from the estate of Mariniacum on the river Stantia, which Queen Valdechildis transferred from her own property into my own … from the estate of Tiliniacum, which by maternal right belongs to me from my grandparents and great-grandparents; likewise from the estates of Olega and Canavis, which I acquired from Bodilo and Sigrada, devoted to God, etc.”

I am not unaware that the chronological characters in the published texts are corrupt; nevertheless, I maintain that the substance of the testament itself is genuine. First, Bishop Jonas explicitly indicates this in letters for the canons of the Aedui, in which the estate is bequeathed on the condition that they pray for mercy not only for rulers, as “Saint Leodegarius instituted,” but also for the governors of the whole Church and for the entire flock of God. Second, Pope John VIII states in a diploma that the estate of Tiliniacum belonged by right of ownership to Saint Leodegarius and had been granted by him to Saint Nazarius.

Nicolaus Imblot, prefect of the Church of Augustodunum, lists the successors of Saint Leodegarius in the catalogue supplied by Demochare: Projectus or Praejectus, Herminarius, and Aubertus. Chenutius and Robertus enumerate the same men in the same order. Severtius changes the order, placing Hermenarius before Praejectus or Projectus and substituting Aubertus for the latter.

The last of these is Ansebertus, concerning whom elsewhere. As for Praejectus, it is clear from his Life that he both lived and died as bishop of Auvergne, not of Augustodunum. The error seems to have arisen from the fact that, on the vigil of Easter, this holy bishop celebrated the solemn Mass in the church of Saint Symphorianus, while the king and nobles were present. On that very sacred day, after Leodegarius and Hector had fled, he completed the remaining service at the request of the bishops—of whom there were then very many at Augustodunum.

They would have spoken somewhat more plausibly if they had asserted that Bobo had been intruded into Leodegarius’s place. Concerning him the anonymous author says, in section 10:

> “Waymerus and Dido assigned Augustodunum as a possession—or rather, for devastation—to a certain Bobo, who had recently been expelled under an anathema from the episcopate of the city of Valence. But the oppressed citizens received an adversary after they had already lost their shepherd.”

---

# The Life of Saint Leodegarius, by Ursinus, an Abbot Contemporary with Him

*[From Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict.]* (C, S)

## Author’s Prologue to Ansoaldus, Bishop

To my lord and holy pontiff, Ansoaldus, bishop of Poitiers, Ursinus, a sinner.

Obeying your command, most blessed father, I have complied with your request—pressed for the most part by Audulfus, father of the monastery of Blessed Maxentius—that I should narrate in writing a few of the many good deeds of Blessed Leodegarius’s life and passion.

I wished to publish this work in obedience to your orders, but the simplicity of my heart and my sluggish eloquence are unable to explain the praises of so great a man’s virtues. How much his patience endured in our own times he concealed from view; no one knows except him alone to whom he revealed it inwardly. Deprived of the sight of his eyes and hidden in secret retreats, who could recount what good and how much good he had accomplished, when there was no attendant present who could observe it and thus narrate what he himself could not see with his eyes?

For the outcome of his work shows outwardly how much he had accomplished while remaining hidden within. Nevertheless, insofar as his life became known to me and I learned it from the reports of many, I have not delayed, at your command, to publish it, even in rustic speech.

If I have tried to extend certain matters with somewhat lengthy wording, I have followed this course in order to set out the line of truth. If, however, I omitted anything concerning his virtues, I did not do so deliberately; rather, through ignorance, I passed it over. For this must be understood: even if someone wished to describe the deeds of this man of God in the eloquence of lofty speech, he could not speak of them more openly and without deceptive words.

Perhaps, with God’s assent, I too might have been able to narrate them in obscure and unfamiliar language. But I did not wish to do so, so that whenever rustic and uneducated people hear these things, they may understand them and, devotedly, desire to imitate the example of the man whose miracles they have understood by hearing them.

## His Passion Begins

### Chapter I. Leodegarius Is Educated First in the Palace and Then in His Uncle’s Household

Accordingly, blessed Leodegarius, born of the high and most noble lineage of the Franks, was, from the infancy of his earliest years, entrusted by his parents at the palace to Lotharius, king of the Franks. Not long afterward, the same king gave him to Dido [Al.: Duddo], bishop of the city of Poitiers and his uncle, to be instructed in literary studies.

The bishop entrusted him to a certain priest of God, a most learned man, for his education. This priest taught him diligently for many years and, once he was educated, returned him to the bishop. The bishop received him and kept him under disciplinary guardianship in his own chambers [Al.: with his chamberlains], wishing to make him like himself: just as the bishop had preserved himself chaste in body [the Carnot manuscript adds: “and in mind”], so he wished Leodegarius to become likewise.

He repeatedly admonished him with the greatest insistence to preserve his virginity [Al.: consecrate himself as a virgin] and to become a worthy vessel of election in the Church of God, because he desired [Al.: it was necessary] that Leodegarius should become bishop of this city after him.

[Note: The Carnot manuscript inserts the following passage: “Even while he was still of tender age, he possessed a mature eagerness—namely, to adhere to the sayings of his elders. If he could hear anything worthy of attention, he did not carelessly consign it to oblivion, but rather entrusted it to his tenacious memory. Even then, with a thirsty breast, he drank in the streams of teaching, which at the appropriate time he would belch forth from his honeyed throat for the instruction of others.” These words are written by Paul the Deacon about Gregory the Great, word for word. From this and other passages it is evident that the Carnot manuscript has been interpolated.]

### Chapter II. He Becomes Deacon and Then Archdeacon

When the bishop saw that Leodegarius was well suited for this work, and when he was nearly twenty years old, he was chosen for the office of deacon and consecrated by the bishop himself. Not long afterward he became archdeacon and was placed in charge, under the bishop, of all the churches of his diocese.

He was greatly devoted to the most honorable eloquence; he was tall in stature, among the handsomest of men, handsome in appearance, pleasing in speech, exceptionally sharp in intellect, provident in judgment, and fervent in zeal for God and love. As he had been admonished, he was a guardian of perpetual virginity.

He surpassed all the inhabitants of the parish [that is, the diocese] entrusted to his governance in sacred Scripture, in the teaching of the laws, and likewise in canon law. He was so suitable for all elders, equals, and subjects that his eloquence pleased everyone who spoke with him: he restored joy to the sorrowful and discipline to those committing crimes.

In a short time, under the authority of the bishop, he brought great peace to the territory of Poitiers through the prudence of his administration.

### Chapter III. He Later Becomes Abbot and Is Called to Court, Where He Is Made Bishop of the Aedui

After a certain father had died in the monastery situated in honor of Blessed Maxentius, Leodegarius assumed its governance at the bishop’s command. He ruled it vigorously for almost six years and enriched it with great resources.

But when, following the admonitions of his bishop, he was preparing himself as a suitable candidate, and when he was regarded as distinguished above all others, the fragrance of his excellence spread so far that it reached the royal palace.

At that time the younger Lotharius, together with his mother Baltechildis, was ruling the kingdom of the Franks. Having recognized Leodegarius’s prudence and wishing to have him with them at the royal court, they asked the bishop to give him permission to live with them in the palace.

The bishop immediately fulfilled their command. In obedience to their will, he appeared to send them a man enriched with great gifts and adorned with the flowers of wisdom. When the king and queen saw him, they received him honorably. Within a few days he displayed his gracious speech and goodness to such an extent that both king and queen, as well as many bishops and nobles, received him into their affection above all others.

Since they saw that he was worthy to receive the episcopal dignity, the leading Franks, by common consent, proclaimed him suitable for episcopal honor. After all had chosen him for this purpose, they made him bishop of Augustodunum, which is the city of the Aedui.

### Chapter IV. After Clotaire’s Death He Supports Childeric against Ebroinus, the Supporter of Theodoric; After Ebroinus Becomes a Monk, Leodegarius Is Placed over Childeric’s Court

[Note: Thus, in the fourth year of Clotaire’s reign, A.D. 659, Leodegarius was raised to the see of Augustodunum, since Clotaire reigned fourteen years.]

When he had governed the see vigorously for ten years, King Lotharius, who had appointed him bishop, died. When the bishop heard this, he hastened to the palace and began discussing the king with men like himself.

When they heard that Hilderic, king of the Austrasians, was governing the kingdom in his youth as well as was appropriate to his age, a faction of the Franks chose him, wishing to have him as king. Ebroinus, who had been mayor of the palace under King Lotharius, wished to substitute his brother Theodoric for him on the throne. Ebroinus himself was then hated among the Franks.

Because they feared the burden of the authority that they had endured under King Lotharius through Ebroinus, they abandoned his counsel and raised Hilderic to supreme authority over the whole Frankish kingdom.

Seeing that he had been abandoned and that his counsel counted for nothing, Ebroinus, terrified, begged the king to spare his life, provided that he abandoned everything, and to permit him to enter a monastery. The king consented to his plea, with Lord Leodegarius interceding, and immediately sent him to the monastery of Luxeuil to become a monk.

[Note: Evidently this was the abbot of the monastery of Saint Denis, as is clear from the second Life. Nevertheless, Hadrianus Valesius denies that Theodoric became a monk; he says only that Theodoric was ordered to be kept in that monastery and to wait there until his hair, having been cut, should grow back. The anonymous author supports Valesius’s opinion; here, however, Theodoric is said merely to have been given to the abbot to be preserved and nourished.]

After King Childeric had been confirmed in the kingdom, he entrusted his brother Theodoric to a certain servant of God to be kept and nourished. The king then raised the holy bishop Leodegarius over his entire household and appointed him mayor of the palace in all matters.

[Note: Hadrianus Valesius, in *The Frankish History*, book XXI, and after him Carolus le Cointe, under the year 670, interpret “mayor of the palace” here as “counselor.” They maintain that the mayoralty of the royal palace was a secular dignity, which was wholly inappropriate for a bishop.]

### Chapter V. After Three Years He Becomes Hateful to the King; He Celebrates the Easter Vigil with the King at Augustodunum

After assuming the reins of this kingdom, Leodegarius restored to their former condition whatever he found contrary to the laws of the ancient kings and the great nobles, whose lives were known to be praiseworthy. He restored all the Frankish kingdoms everywhere so thoroughly that everyone rejoiced to have Childeric as king and Leodegarius as governor of the palace.

When these affairs had been conducted with great distinction for almost three years, the Adversary—whose custom it is, through the envy of his condition, to destroy good things—began to incite the companions whom the bishop himself had chosen as partners in government. Through the evil of envy he stirred them up and sowed the tares of discord between the bishop and the king.

During those days the famous day of Easter was already approaching. The bishop then earnestly requested that the king order the most holy day to be celebrated in his city of Augustodunum. The king did not refuse and tried to fulfill the petitioner’s desire.

When the day had already approached and they were going together to celebrate the solemn Mass that is held on the Sabbath—as was the ancient custom—on the vigil of Easter,

[Note: In the second Life it is said that the king did not wish to celebrate Easter with Leodegarius, but celebrated it with Marclinus, a recluse at Saint Symphorianus.]

—and when they were both concealing within themselves the evil seed of hatred, the instigator of both evils approached the bishop and said:

“Take heed, holy bishop. Know that after the celebration of Mass you are to be killed by the king, because the wicked seed against you, which your enemies have sown—and which has long since been sown in the king’s heart as well—has been decreed to reach completion this very night.”

### Chapter VI. After the Sacred Rites He Secretly Departs; With the King’s Consent He Withdraws to Luxeuil and Is Reconciled with Ebroinus

Hearing this, the bishop concealed his reaction and delayed, showing himself cheerful. He appeared with a radiant face, considering nothing too burdensome, and completed the solemn Mass he had begun with the greatest dignity.

After he and the king had received Holy Communion, the king went to the palace to dine. The bishop, having fully completed his office and received wine with his companions—as human frailty is accustomed to do—began, fearing the king’s hostility, to discuss with them what he ought to do in this conflict.

By thinking and praying to the Lord, he found the better counsel: it was preferable for him to abandon everything and follow Christ than to give way to the king and allow the king’s hands to be stained with priestly blood on so great a feast day. Otherwise, the kingdom of the Franks might become a reproach, and through one man alone a dispute might arise among the whole people.

Then he left the king and all the exalted powers, considering as nothing whatever is valued in the world. That same night he set out with a few companions, beginning to go wherever he might become Christ’s poor man.

When the king heard this, he was greatly saddened and sent one of his faithful men with a large army after him. Pursuing him throughout that night, the man found him at dawn and brought him back in accordance with the king’s command.

The bishop then humbly begged that he be sent to the monastery of Luxeuil, where, having abandoned the world, he might devote himself to God. The king did not delay in sending him there.

When he arrived quickly at the monastery, he found Ebroinus already a cleric [that is, a monk]. Leodegarius said that he had sinned against him in some way [Al.: seriously]. They asked forgiveness of one another and stood reconciled.

At the abbot’s command, however, they were separated. For a certain period both performed penance and strove to live diligently among the monks’ quarters as though they were monks forever.

### Chapter VII. After Childeric’s Death, Leodegarius Is Recalled to His See, with Ebroinus as His Companion

At that time King Hilderic died, and his brother Theodoric was raised to the throne. When the friends of both men heard this and desired to see them, they set out with great enthusiasm to fulfill their wishes and return them to their own places.

Coming from both sides to the monastery mentioned above, they compelled the two men to leave and return to their own homes. After suffering greatly from anguish, they finally consented to the pleas of their friends, both out of love and friendship and because they had been exhausted by the long distances they had traveled.

With the blessing of the monastery’s father, bound together in the harmony of peace, Ebroinus and the bishop Leodegarius set out together and came to their city of Augustodunum. When the entire city heard this, it was stirred to joy. The citizens came out to meet them and received them with happiness and great rejoicing, because they had recovered the father and governor whose loss they had once mourned.

After welcoming him, they restored him to his former seat so that he might enjoy joy with his people. While they were celebrating together with the greatest happiness, Leodegarius wished to send Ebroinus away the next day, enriched with great gifts of honor, to his own place.

Ebroinus, however, did not allow his companions even a brief rest. He slipped away from the city by night and joined the Austrasians, who had once been his adversaries, as friends.

Not long afterward, after committing many crimes and gathering around him companions in evil, he entered the territories of the Franks by force. Acting with the utmost cruelty and tyranny, he presented himself before the glorious King Theodoric, who restored him to his former rank.

### Chapter VIII. After His Restoration, Ebroinus Plots Leodegarius’s Destruction; When the City of the Aedui Is Besieged, Leodegarius Goes Out to Meet His Enemies

Once he had become mayor of the palace, Ebroinus began to consider vengeance against the enemies who had refused to have him as their subordinate ruler. Like a roaring lion among the other beasts, his roar resounded throughout the Frankish lands. All who had once plotted evil against him were terrified, and those who remained from his slaughter fled.

During those days the man of God, Leodegarius, was residing in his city of the Aedui to restore his people. Ebroinus recalled all the evils that he believed Leodegarius had inflicted upon him with King Hilderic. He therefore began, together with the most wicked companions of his enemies, to consider how he might destroy the bishop.

Two of these advisers—namely Dido and Waymer, who had become the principal agents of the plot by name—said that they could seize the bishop from the city and take vengeance upon him, thereby satisfying Ebroinus’s malice.

[Note: Dido or Diddo “had once held command in the city of Chalon.” Waymer was duke of Champagne, as is stated in the second Life; later he became bishop of Troyes, according to the Life of Saint Praejectus, bishop. “Bercharius, abbot of Dervus, when going to Jerusalem, is said to have taken with him Waymer, guilty of Saint Leodegarius’s tortures,” says the monk of Dervus in the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Bercharius*, section 11.]

Ebroinus rejoiced at their answer and gave them a very large army. They hastened to the city of the Aedui and, surrounding it with that army, ravaged the area around the circuit of the walls.

When the man of God saw this, he was inflamed with great zeal for the people entrusted to him. Following the example of the Lord, he preferred to lay down his life for his sheep and desired to win them rather than seek his own temporal safety. He ordered all the clergy of the city to assemble and went out to meet his enemies with relics, crosses, and choirs of singers, praising God. He voluntarily offered himself for the palm of martyrdom, if only the executioner’s will should not fail.

### Chapter IX. He Is Deprived of His Eyes; He Is Detained in a Monastery for Two Years

Those who had come to punish him seized him without reverence for the relics. He is said to have cried out:

“I give thanks to almighty God the Redeemer, who has deemed me worthy to be glorified today.”

They then led him outside the city and, carrying out the orders of their prince Ebroinus, tore his eyes from his head. But when they removed human light from him outwardly, they enclosed divine light within him.

They handed him over to guards and brought him to a certain monastery, where he remained hidden for a period of two full years. There he left a great example of his humility and patience.

### Chapter X. He Is Accused before the King by Ebroinus Together with His Brother; They Reply to the Charges

At the same time, his brother Gairinus [Al.: Warinus], who, out of fear of the aforementioned Ebroinus, had wandered with other Frankish nobles whom Ebroinus had driven into exile through the regions of the Vascones [that is, the Basques], was ordered to return to the palace by command of the glorious King Theodoric and the prince Ebroinus.

At the same time it was ordered that blessed Leodegarius should leave the monastery in which he was being kept hidden and be summoned into the king’s presence.

When the two men had been brought together and presented before the rulers, they were subjected to many insults and reproaches by Ebroinus. They are said to have replied [Al.: it is conjectured]:

“We suffer these things deservedly, because we have sinned against the Lord; but greater is His clemency, since He has deemed us worthy to be called to such glory.

“But you, wretched Ebroinus, who inflict so great a punishment upon the Frankish people, are taking vengeance rather upon yourself, since you desire to deprive others of life. Indeed, you have deceived many and made them exiles from their ancestral land; but you will be the greater exile, because you are quickly losing both temporal and future glory. For while you desire to surpass all the inhabitants of the whole of Francia, you are taking away the glory that you received undeservedly.”

### Chapter XI. Guarinus, Having Received His Brother’s Admonitions, Is Buried under Stones

When Ebroinus heard this, he was filled with great fury. He ordered his servants to drag Gairinus away and separate him from his brother, so that they might be punished separately and would not enjoy uttering such words together.

As Gairinus was being led away, blessed Leodegarius addressed him:

> “Be of good courage, dearest brother, for we must suffer these things, because the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us (Romans XIII). Our sins are indeed many, but the mercy of the Almighty is greater and ever ready to wash away the offenses of those who praise Him. We suffer these things for a time because we are debtors to death; but that life awaits us, if we endure this punishment patiently, where we shall rejoice forever in heavenly glory.”

Then the servants began to bury Gairinus, who had been tied to a stake, under stones.

He prayed to the Lord, saying:

> “Good Lord Jesus, who did not come to call the righteous but sinners, receive the spirit of Your servant. You have deemed me worthy, in the likeness of the martyrs, to have this mortal life taken from me by stones; most mercifully command that forgiveness of my crimes be granted.”

As he said this, he breathed out his final spirit in prayer.

### Chapter XII. By Ebroinus’s Command, Leodegarius Is Cruelly Mutilated

Blessed Leodegarius wished to end his life together with his brother, so that they might together deserve to share in the future and blessed life.

But Ebroinus wished to delay his death, preparing eternal punishment for him through torments prolonged over a long period and preventing him from receiving the martyr’s crown—indeed, depriving him of the rewards of everlasting glory. He ordered that Leodegarius be led barefoot through a certain pool in which there were rocks sharp and cutting like nails.

Then, after he had been thrown to the ground, Ebroinus ordered that his tongue and lips be cut out. He intended that, when Leodegarius saw that his eyes had been removed, his feet pierced, and his tongue and lips cut, and when he saw that all the integrity of his limbs had been taken away and the powers of his body had everywhere been denied him—when he could not see the road with his eyes, walk the path with his feet, or praise the Creator through the use of his tongue—he would fall into blasphemy through despair and deprive himself of the salvation that he would have deserved to attain from heaven by praising God.

But God, who hears hearts without the need for words and embraces the contrite heart rather than the proud and exalted one, received the voice of the silent man more readily than that of those who speak proudly: he asked for help not through the sound of his voice but through the humility of his heart.

For when he recognized that every human defense had been lost, he begged with all his strength for divine aid to be present. As far as human impiety sought to pull him back from the heights, so far did divine piety cause him to be joined to heaven.

## Chapter XIII

### Exiled to Fiscamnus, he regains the use of his tongue

Then Ebroin summoned a certain man named Waningus and said: “Take Leodegarius, whom you once saw as such a proud man, and place him under secure custody. For the time of his calling will come, when he shall receive from his enemies what he deserves.”

Then Waningus took him and brought him to his monastery, called Fiscamnus, where there was a community of consecrated virgins presided over by Childomerga, a servant of Christ. There he remained for many days as an inhabitant under guard. His tongue, though it had been cut out, recovered its customary function, and he displayed the great seed of his teaching among the people. Whenever he entered among the company of the virgins, his words shone with such sweetness, as is reported, that all who heard them marvelled at how great a work God’s mercy had accomplished, and, turning away from evil deeds, hastened to seek the fruits of repentance. For he remained watchful day and night in the worship of God, so that he scarcely ever left the church even briefly for the necessities of the body, nor was he able to take any sleep or food.

## Chapter XIV

### His persecutors suffer punishment

At the same time the glorious king Theodoric and Ebroin summoned a synod, and, coming to a certain royal estate, caused a great multitude of bishops to be present. Among the others was Diddo, who, together with Waimer, had driven the holy man Leodegarius from the seat of his episcopate and, seduced by inducements, had delivered him over to punishment. Condemned by that same synod, Diddo received a blow upon the head and was expelled and separated from the holy congregation. Then, condemned to exile, and afterward overtaken by death, he suffered the penalty of death which corresponded to all that he had deceitfully inflicted upon the holy man.

Certain other bishops also received nearly the same punishment at the hands of the king through Ebroin at that synod and were assigned to perpetual exile. Waimer likewise received a similar sentence with the others.

Then Ebroin said to the blessed Leodegarius: “Why do you persuade so many people by your speaking? You suppose yourself to be a martyr, and for that reason you show yourself so presumptuous.”

“Much longer still,” he replied, “you will be delayed; you desire in vain to possess such a reward. For you will receive martyrdom in the manner in which you deserve it.”

Ebroin wished to extinguish him utterly, so that, since he saw that he had already been stripped of worldly glory, he might at least have prevented him from receiving the rewards of the saints. But precisely from the place where Ebroin thought he would cut him off, he caused him rather to cling to Christ, whom Ebroin wished him to abandon; for the longer his punishment was prolonged, the more his rewards increased.

## Chapter XV

### Delivered to Chrodobertus, he is illumined by heavenly light

Then he delivered him to a certain man named Chrodobertus [another reading: Ruotbertus]. “Take him,” he said, “and keep him under close guard; for the time of his death will still come.”

When Chrodobertus was leading him to his own house, he saw that Leodegarius was exhausted from the journey and from weakness, and ordered that a drink be given him for refreshment. While the cupbearer was standing before him, a great light, descending from heaven as though in the form of a circle like a wheel, shone over his head.

Then all who saw this sign trembled and said: “What is this, lord, that appears above your head—a most brilliant light sent down from heaven, as though in the form of a circle? We have never seen anything like it.”

He immediately fell to the ground and worshipped, saying: “I give thanks and praise to you, almighty God, consoler of all, who have deigned to display such a miracle over your servant.”

Then all those who saw it seemed to be in an ecstasy of mind. Yet, recovering their spirit, they glorified almighty God together and turned to one another, saying: “Truly this man is a servant of God.” And they promised that they would devote all their strength wholly to God.

From that time onward, nearly all his relatives, his wife, and the members of his household were converted to the worship of God by his preaching. Consequently, when people throughout the surrounding region heard of his reputation, they flocked to him, desiring to hear the saving word. He, for his part, did not cease instructing everyone by his preaching how they might reach the kingdom of heaven.

## Chapter XVI

### Four horsemen are sent to kill the saint

Not long afterward, when almighty God had resolved to reward his faithful servant for the gift of such great endurance, Ebroin, now hardened and wishing to complete his cruelty against him, sent after him the swiftest horsemen, men exceedingly dangerous, to kill him.

When they arrived, they took him from the house of the man to whom he had been delivered for custody and led him through unknown places until they reached a certain spot. There he stopped and said: “You need not tire yourselves by going farther, my sons. Quickly accomplish what you have come to do, and fulfil the wish of the wicked man.”

Those who had come to kill him were four in number. Three of them threw themselves at his feet, begging him to obtain forgiveness for them from God and to deign to bestow his blessing upon them. But the fourth, a proud man [Wadardus], stood there with his sword drawn, ready to kill him.

## Chapter XVII

### After prayer, he is beheaded; he is buried at Sarcingus

After he had bestowed his blessing upon them and proclaimed the word of God to his executioners, the man of God devoted himself to prayer and said:

“Lord God almighty, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have received knowledge of you; God of hosts, creator of every creature, and redeemer of the whole human race: I bless you, I glorify you, who have deigned to bring me to this day of combat. I ask and beseech you, Lord, that you yourself command the mercy of your compassion to be granted to me, and make me worthy to share in the merits of your saints and to be a companion of eternal life. Grant forgiveness to those who afflict me, because through them, most merciful Father, I believe that I shall be glorified in your sight.”

As he was saying this, the executioner stretched out his hand and, with his sword drawn, cut off his head. His body, however, is said to have remained standing upright for approximately an hour. When the swordsman saw that he did not immediately fall, he struck him with his foot so that he would fall to the ground more quickly.

Not long afterward, the executioner was seized by demons, deprived of his mind, and struck by divine vengeance. He threw himself into a fire and there ended his life.

Then, by the order of the wife of Chrodobertus, this blessed martyr was carried by servants, amid the great weeping of those who mourned, to a certain estate called Sarcingus [Sorcin]. By the command of that woman he was buried, in the little oratory, wearing the garments in which he had been slaughtered.

This is believed to have taken place on the sixth day before the Nones of October [another reading: the fifth day before the Nones]. He is said to have remained buried in that tomb for two and a half years.

# Here Begins the Translation of the Same Work

## Chapter XVIII

### Miracles performed at the tomb; sacrilegious thieves are punished after everything is restored

During these days a certain priest who served at this oratory learned that a brilliant light had shone there at night without human assistance. A great rumour therefore spread throughout the surrounding region.

When people came to the venerable oratory of this blessed martyr, he healed a great multitude afflicted with various illnesses: he gave the lame the use of their feet, granted sight to the blind, cleansed those possessed by demons, and shone forth through many miracles in the venerable dwelling-place of the martyr.

The priest of that church bears witness to this. The cleric who served that priest and was caretaker of the church was also robbed one night, so that the thieves carried away all his property. Among the stolen goods was a little shoe of the blessed martyr, which he had kept hidden out of reverence. The thief, unaware of what it was, carried it away with him.

When the cleric rose early from the oratory and went to his dwelling, he discovered that all his possessions had been stolen. He therefore hurried to the tomb of this man and begged him to restore what he had lost through theft. For that entire day and the following night he remained in prayer at the tomb, fasting and persisting in psalmody.

When he had completed his prayer and returned to his cell, he found all that he had lost, with nothing missing, together with the little shoe of the blessed martyr, preserved intact.

The thief’s master, who had sworn an oath on behalf of his servant that he had certainly not committed this crime, returned home and died. The servant, however, brought the crime he had committed to an evil conclusion.

## Chapter XIX

### Ebroin’s impious spy pays the penalty; Ebroin himself likewise

Then the fame of the blessed martyr’s holiness burst forth more and more widely. Not long afterward Ebroin learned of it through the events that took place.

When he heard this, he secretly sent a messenger who was to investigate the matter carefully and report the truth to him. The messenger obeyed his orders and approached the martyr’s tomb. After careful questioning, he learned from the custodian where the holy body rested.

But when he approached, he postponed beginning his prayer. Instead, he despised the ground, struck it with his foot, and foolishly said—for he did not know the power of God:

“A dead man certainly does not perform miracles.”

The wretched man, however, learned in his own person how powerful the holy martyr was in miracles before he could return and report to the one who had sent him. While he was setting out on his journey, he suddenly lost his life and did not report back to the one who had sent him.

When Ebroin learned these things, he kept them concealed in silence. Trembling inwardly with shame, he dared to reveal them to no one except his wife, lest perhaps, as the martyr’s glory increased, Ebroin’s own glory—since he wished to extinguish such a light—should be diminished among the people.

But during the very period in which the wretched man wished this good deed to remain hidden, the report of the blessed martyr’s aforesaid miracles spread and shone everywhere all the more.

After nearly three years had passed [Note: The anonymous author has the same wording in chapter 17: “After nearly three years had passed,” etc. From this it is possible to determine the year in which Saint Leodegarius died. Ebroin was killed in the ninth year of King Theodoric’s reign—if we believe Sigebert—in the year 681 or the following year, and indeed nearly three years after Leodegarius had suffered martyrdom. Leodegarius was therefore killed in the year of Christ 678, as Charles Le Cointe also believes.

This calculation is confirmed by the fact that Ebroin obtained the prefecture of the palace again in the first year of Theodoric’s reign. Soon afterward he began to persecute Leodegarius, who was held for two years in a certain monastery under the custody of Waimer, duke of Champagne. Later, entrusted to Waningus, he lived in exile at Fiscamnus for “many days”—that is, nearly two years. Finally, after the synod held in the sixth year of King Theodoric, as Sigebert writes, he was taken away from Chrodobertus to the district of Arras, where shortly afterward he was struck on the head on the sixth day before the Nones of October.

On that very day he is commemorated in the ancient Martyrologies, if Bede’s calendar is excepted. The reliable Usuard records it as follows: “In the territory of Arras, the passion of the blessed Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, whom Ebroin, mayor of the royal palace, afflicted with various injuries and different punishments for the sake of the truth and killed.”

Ado writes: “At Arras, in the estate of Siricynus, the passion of the blessed Leodegarius,” and so on as in Usuard, adding: “His sacred body was translated into the diocese of Poitiers and buried in the monastery of the blessed Maxentius.”

The Arratenses, or Adarctenses, were formerly called the Atrebates who lived toward the north; those toward the east were called Ostrebates, and those toward the south Austrebates, as Malbrancus rightly observed in book II, chapter 57, of *On the Morini.

Nevertheless, Sarcingus, the place of Leodegarius’s burial, and the place where he was killed—both villages being called Saint-Leodegarius—the former near the sources of the Alteia River and the latter toward the source of the Quantia, lie west of the Austrebates. The latter place, however, since it inclines somewhat toward the north, may be assigned to the Arratenses.]

In Ebroin, who had tried to extinguish this lamp, the divine saying was fulfilled: because he had killed many with swords, he himself perished by the sword.

Unhappy and wretched man! Raised to such great honours, he enjoyed among men a reputation for his ability that had spread through three parts of the world. Yet because he refused to grant forgiveness to his enemies by fulfilling God’s commandment, he caused many of them, through his vengeance, to enter the kingdom of heaven. It is therefore greatly to be feared that he who killed so many priests and nobles through the cruelty of his vengeance prepared eternal punishment for himself instead.

He lost so lofty a glory as no Frank had deserved to possess, and he lost the blessed life which he might have obtained through endurance.

## Chapter XX

After the unhappy Ebroin had ended his life, what he had concealed concerning the servant of God, driven by envy, spread far and wide with great praise. It was then reported with commendation in the palace, though it had for many days lain concealed from the enemy.

For there was a very large gathering of bishops and nobles. While they were discussing the holy martyr among themselves and marvelling at what they heard about him, the man of extraordinary holiness, Bishop Ansoaldus, introduced the following statement:

“If only I were given the choice …”

The rest is to be repeated from the Second Life, chapter 17 and following.

# The Second Life of Saint Leodegarius by an Anonymous Author

## Author’s Prologue to Bishop Ermenarius

To the truly holy lord and bishop of the city of Autun, Ermenarius, worthy of apostolic veneration:

Often ordered by you and compelled by the entreaties of spiritual brothers, I have finally undertaken to write the deeds of the blessed martyr and bishop Leodegarius.

I delayed for so long fulfilling your orders and requests because I saw a double punishment rising against me: on the one hand, I feared the darkness of ignorance and negligence; on the other, I feared that my ineptitude would be exposed to the ridicule of the prudent.

I therefore first beg your faithful devotion to pardon my rusticity, and merely to read privately, for the present, the things which I have undertaken at your command, until either you repair them with a more elevated style, or, once they have been corrected according to the judgment of other wise men, you approve a diction which, after you have read it, may please you as irreproachable.

I ask this especially: that the powers necessary to carry out this work—powers which my lack of understanding denies me—may obtain from the Lord, through the diligent effectiveness of your prayers, timely assistance.

# Here Begins the Life or Passion

## Chapter I

### Leodegarius is perfect in all things and instructed by Ado; how he conducted himself as archdeacon; he is ordained bishop of the Aeduans amid a dispute; what he accomplished in the episcopate

The glorious and distinguished Leodegarius, bishop of the city of Autun, who in Christian times became a new martyr, was nobly born according to earthly lineage. Yet, accompanied by divine grace, as he grew from earliest youth into mature strength, he proved himself distinguished above others at every rank or order to which he was advanced.

He had been carefully brought up by his maternal uncle Diddo [another reading: Ado], bishop of the city of Poitiers, a man who surpassed his relatives in an exceptional abundance of wisdom and in the wealth of his resources. He was thoroughly polished in every respect by the discipline of the various studies to which the powerful of this world customarily devote themselves. In that same city he was chosen for the archdiaconate.

The strength of his courage and wisdom suddenly shone forth in him so greatly that he appeared unequalled among his predecessors—especially since he was not ignorant of the strictness of secular law and was a formidable judge of worldly matters.

Filled with canonical doctrines, he became an outstanding teacher of the clergy. He was also vigorous in disciplining offenders, never weakened by indulgence toward the flesh; vigilant with prudent care in ecclesiastical duties; energetic in accounts; wise in counsel; and radiant in speech.

Meanwhile, the pressure of necessity arose, so that he ought to be ordained bishop in the city of Autun.

[Note: [Col. 0347D] This author omitted the abbatial charge entrusted to Leodegarius in the monastery of Saint Maxentius; this must be supplied from the First Life. After the death of Ferreolus, bishop of Autun, the dispute described here arose; [Col. 0348D] finally, after two years, Leodegarius was appointed his successor in the fourth year of King Clotarius’s reign, that is, in A.D. 658 or the following year.]

A dispute had recently arisen between two men over that same episcopate, and the conflict had continued even to the shedding of blood. When one had died there and the other had been expelled into exile for the crime he had committed, Queen Balthildis—who governed the palace of the Franks together with her son Clotarius—being, as we believe, inspired by divine counsel, sent this vigorous man to the aforesaid city to become its bishop.

Thus the Church, which had remained almost widowed for nearly two years amid worldly disorder, might be protected and strengthened by his governance, and defended against those who attacked it.

Why say more? At his arrival, all the adversaries of that Church and city were so terrified, as were those who were continually fighting among themselves with hatred and murder, that they did not wish even to hear the memory of the former scandal. What preaching had not brought to concord, justice and fear compelled.

Once he had been raised to the episcopate by the Lord’s dispensation, it would take too long to recount in detail how exceptional was his care for the nourishment of the poor. While we remain silent, his works bear witness: the register which he established and which remains at the church door; the beauty of the vessels that shine with golden splendour in the service of the church; and the ornaments of the baptistery, fashioned with wondrous workmanship.

How devoted his mind was to the love of martyrs is shown, even in our silence, by the burial of the holy martyr Symphorianus and the glorious translation of his sacred body.

His diligence is also indicated by the church’s floors and golden ceilings, the new construction of the atrium, the restoration of the city walls, and the repair of the houses. These works, raising up what had been consumed by excessive age, provide true testimony to those who see them.

Let these few things among many suffice for the present. Let us turn our discourse to the time when Christ’s athlete began the struggle against the devil.

## Chapter II

### He suffers Ebroin as an adversary

When the holy bishop Leodegarius was living happily and peacefully as bishop in the city of Autun, he renewed everything that had been ruined, instructed the clergy in the divine offices, continually admonished the people with heavenly nourishment through his preaching, supported them by the generosity of his almsgiving, and directed his whole mind toward keeping God’s commandments.

His will was so effective in everything that whatever he resolved to accomplish was granted success by the Lord without difficulty. Nor did the Almighty bestow his grace upon him without reason, since Leodegarius himself had first devoted his whole being to keeping God’s commandments.

But because malice is always opposed to good will, and the ancient serpent, in his envy, always finds people through whom to sow scandal, certain honoured men who knew nothing of spiritual matters but feared secular power saw that this man stood inflexible upon the summit of justice. They therefore began to be tormented by envious resentment and resolved to obstruct his advancement if an opportunity arose.

At that time there was, as we have said, a man named Hebroinus [another reading: Ebroinus], mayor of the palace, who governed the palace under King Clotarius. [Note: [Col. 0348D] Nothing further above concerning Ebroin.] The queen whom we mentioned above was residing in the monastery which she had previously prepared for herself.

Therefore the aforesaid envious men approached Hebroinus and stirred up his anger against the man of God. Since they found no true accusation, they fabricated a false charge, alleging that while everyone obeyed Hebroinus’s commands, Leodegarius alone, as bishop, despised them.

The aforementioned Hebroinus was so inflamed by the torch of greed and so devoted to the ambition for money that, in his presence, only those who brought more money had a just case. Some filled him with gold and silver out of fear, others to purchase justice; and the minds of certain men, grieved by the losses he had caused, had already been stirred against him.

Nor did he practise only the commerce of rapacity: for a slight offence he shed the innocent blood of many nobles.

## Chapter III

### For what reason; after Clotarius’s death, the nobles agree upon Childeric, and why; Ebroin is exiled at Luxovium, while Theodoricus, tonsured, is relegated to the monastery of Saint-Denis

Leodegarius was suspected by him because Ebroin could not overcome him in speech, because Leodegarius did not offer him the service of flattery as others did, and because Ebroin knew that he remained fearless in the face of all his threats.

At that time Ebroin had issued a tyrannical edict that no one from the regions of Burgundy should dare approach the palace unless he had received Ebroin’s command. Everyone therefore suspected, out of fear of what had happened before, that he had devised this to increase his crimes—either to condemn certain people to death or to inflict losses upon their property.

Meanwhile, while the matter remained suspended, King Lotharius was called by the Lord and departed from this life (A.D. 669). Hebroinus ought then, according to custom, to have summoned the nobles and solemnly elevated his brother Theodoricus to the kingship. Instead, swollen with the spirit of pride, he refused to summon them. [Note: [Col. 0349D] For at that time the Frankish nobles customarily assembled to establish a king, each swore allegiance to the chosen man, and, after a spear had been placed in his hand in place of a sceptre, honoured him as he sat upon a raised throne, as Hadrian Valesius observed in *Rerum Francicarum*, book XXI.]

For this reason they began to fear all the more that, while retaining the king whom he ought publicly to have raised up for the glory of the homeland, he might easily inflict harm upon him in private, since he wished him ill.

When the multitude of nobles who were hastening to meet the new king received, at Hebroinus’s command, a refusal concerning their journey, they took counsel together. Abandoning him, they all sought his younger brother Hilderic, who had received the kingdom in the south.

Those who then refused to agree with their decision either escaped by flight or submitted unwillingly, threatened with fire and at the risk of their lives.

When they had brought Hilderic into both the Neustrian and Burgundian kingdoms because of their fear of Hebroinus’s tyranny, the tyrant, recognizing that this crime of his had been carried out, fled to the altar of a church. His treasury was suddenly plundered in many places; what the wicked man had long gathered wickedly was suddenly dispersed for good.

Certain bishops then intervened, especially Bishop Leodegarius, and they did not kill him. Instead, he was sent into exile at the monastery of Luxovium, so that by repentance he might escape the crime he had committed.
