But because the dust of earthly desire had blinded the eyes of his heart, spiritual wisdom did not benefit his evil soul.

When Hilderic ordered that his own brother, for whose sake he had come, be brought before him so that he might speak with him, certain men who appeared to be among the leading figures of the kingdom and wished to please Hilderic by flattering him ordered, with reckless audacity, that their lord’s hair be cut. In this way they contrived to present him to his brother.

When the king asked him what he wished to do concerning him, Theodoricus declared only that he had been unjustly deprived of his royal position and that he awaited God in heaven as his judge.

Then he was ordered to reside at the monastery of the holy martyr Dionysius, and he remained there safely until he had grown back the hair they had cut off. The God of heaven, whom he had declared to be his judge, afterward happily permitted him to reign.

## Chapter IV

### Childeric establishes a just edict and immediately revokes it; the king is stirred against Leodegarius; corrected by him, he considers killing him

Meanwhile everyone petitioned King Hilderic to issue decrees throughout the three kingdoms he had obtained, so that each people’s law and custom might be observed, as the ancient judges had preserved them; so that governors from one province would not enter another; so that no one might assume tyranny after the manner of Hebroinus and later despise his companions as Hebroinus had done; and so that, since they recognized that they possessed the heights of power by mutual succession, no one would dare to place himself above another.

He willingly granted their requests. But, corrupted by the counsel of fools and almost pagans, and being still young in age, he suddenly opposed what he had confirmed through the counsels of wise men.

Because he knew that holy Leodegarius was conspicuous above all others for the light of wisdom, he kept him constantly with him in the palace. For this reason the envy of evil men, renewed once more, increased, and they again sought the beginnings of accusations against him. Whatever the king did, whether by a just or an unjust judgment, they said had been done through Leodegarius’s fault. Had the king obeyed his counsels, he would have walked according to the divine commandments.

But because a sentence had already come down from heaven, his heart could not grasp the discipline of justice. Thus he deserved to have the judgment which Theodoricus had declared he awaited from God brought to a swift conclusion.

When the man of God saw that the devil’s envy against him was growing hot again, he took up, according to the Apostle, the breastplate of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6:17), and entered into single combat against the ancient enemy.

Because priestly integrity does not know how to fear a king’s threats, he began to rebuke Hilderic, asking why he had so suddenly changed the ancestral customs which he had ordered to be preserved. He is also said to have told him that the queen whom he had as his wife was the daughter of his own maternal uncle, and that, unless he corrected these crimes and the other unlawful offences by amendment, he should know that divine vengeance would surely come upon him suddenly.

At first Hilderic willingly began to listen. But, anticipated by the counsels of his attendants, instead of turning Leodegarius’s words toward correction, he began to seek opportunities for his death. Those who wished to overturn justice persuaded him to do this, as did those who supported the king in his undisciplined youthful conduct, and those who had induced him to break his own decree.

All these men, and others like them who lived amid worldly pleasures, feared that the man of God would destroy their practices, since they already knew him to walk inflexibly along the path of justice. The ageing world, weighed down by vices, could not endure the manliness of this heavenly citizen.

## Chapter V

### A new charge is fabricated; the saint is sought for death on the vigil of Easter; he fearlessly approaches the king and avoids death because of the sacred day; Hector is killed

At that time there was a certain noble man named Hictor [Hector], who held the office of patrician of Marseille. As he was born from a distinguished lineage, so he surpassed others in the nobility of his family and in secular prudence.

He had come to King Hilderic on a certain matter [Note: Namely, to recover from the king the inheritance of his mother-in-law Claudia, which Claudia had left to the Church of Auvergne, having been defrauded by her daughter]. Through the intercession of the man of God he hoped to obtain what he sought, and the holy man had received him in his city as an act of hospitality, until he could commend him to the king through his intercession, as Hictor had requested.

For the aforesaid Hilderic had been asked to come to the church of Leodegarius’s city for the Easter solemnity. The envious men discovered this opportunity by which to accomplish the wickedness they had recently poured into the king’s heart.

They associated with their accusation the mayor of the palace, named Wolfaldus [another reading: Wlfoaldus], and fabricated a lying story about Leodegarius and Hictor, alleging that the two had joined together for the purpose of overthrowing royal rule and usurping the rights of power for themselves.

At that time there was also a certain man at the monastery of the holy martyr Symphorianus who wore the habit of religion but was a recluse only in body, not in mind. His name was Marcolinus [Chesnius reads: Marcolmus]. As later became publicly evident, he was instead exceedingly desirous of human praise and honours under the appearance of religion. Concerning his conduct, especially once it had become apparent to everyone, I think it better to remain silent than to speak.

The king, however, was unaware of this and regarded the aforesaid man as though he were a prophet of God in all things, because Marcolinus flattered him above all others by supporting his will in the accusations against the man of God.

On the night when the holy Easter vigil was being celebrated in the city, the king, already as though under suspicion, refused to come there [Note: Yet in the First Life it is said that he received holy communion with the king. This may perhaps be understood as having happened not in the same church but in the same city. The Acts of Saint Praejectus say that he celebrated the sacred rites before the king].

Instead, returning with a few supporters to the counsel of the aforesaid hypocrite, he now bore a hostile spirit against the servant of God and did not fear to receive the Paschal sacrifice there prematurely. Later, shamefully drunk with wine, he entered the church while the others were fasting and awaiting the sacred solemnities. Calling Leodegarius by name, he demanded him, attempting to drive him into flight and already terrifying him by threatening violence with swords among the messengers.

When repeated shouting revealed to him that Leodegarius was in the baptistery, he entered there as well. At the sight of the great radiance and the fragrance of the chrism used there for the sanctification of the baptized, he was astonished.

When Leodegarius himself answered his shout by saying, “I am here,” the king did not recognize him at all, passed by him, and sat down in the church building where the meal had been prepared.

The other bishops who had kept vigil with the man of God returned to their lodgings. But after completing the sacred office, Leodegarius fearlessly approached the king. In gentle words he asked him why he had not come before the vigil or why he persisted in anger during the solemnities of such a sacred night.

Since, in his agitation, the king could find no answer to the man’s ineffable wisdom, he said that he regarded him with suspicion for some reason.

The man of God Leodegarius therefore saw that the king’s mind was fixed upon the plan, urged by his attendants, of killing Leodegarius together with Hictor as he had decided. He also feared that Hictor, in his distress, might suffer contempt at the king’s hands.

Not fearing his own death, but considering the safety of those who had come to him for protection, he preferred for the time being to conceal himself by flight rather than provide an occasion for the solemnities of Christ’s resurrection to be stained with blood through his martyrdom, or for the church to be plundered, lest those who had gathered to him should thoughtlessly lose their lives [Note: Chesnius reads: “lest they should turn against the consul what was being done against him, and thus the same consul should lose his life”].

No one should think that he feared martyrdom to such an extent.

When, previously, a certain monk named Bercharius had announced to him during the Lord’s Supper that he would be killed, Leodegarius went to the king’s palace on the day after the Lord’s Passion and voluntarily presented himself, wishing to offer his blood to Christ on the very day on which Christ had shed his blood for the salvation of the world.

The king also wished to strike him with his own hand that day, but, out of reverence for God, was restrained by the counsel of certain wise nobles.

We must undoubtedly believe that he was then preserved by God so that, if he had perhaps incurred anything contrary through human conduct—which is not lived without fault—the furnace of prolonged persecution might burn it away, and so that afterward, as the printed text has it, “like a dry world, placed in it by the hand of his king” (*velut aridum mundum in ea de manu sui regis impositus*) [materially uncertain], he might shine through the power of his miracles like sparkling gems. [Note: [Col. 0352D] Chesnius reads: *velut arido mundo despecto in diadema sui regis impositus* (“as though, despising the dry world, placed upon the diadem of his king”). It seems that one should read: *velut aurum mundum, in ea* (that is, in the persecution) *de manu sui regis impositus* (“like pure gold, placed in it by the hand of his king”).]

When the swift persecution was stirred up against him by those who were awaiting the outcome of this opportunity, the aforementioned Hictor was killed there. Because he had attempted to defend himself manfully, he was overcome by the crowd, with the Lord permitting it, together with certain others who were accompanying him.

Nor is it believed impossible that, through the merits of the holy martyr, those souls who innocently wished to escape the storm of persecution with him were able to obtain forgiveness from God.

## Chapter VI
## Detained by Envious Men, He Is Exiled to Luxeuil

—He is rescued from impending death by Hermenarius.—

Accordingly, when Leodegarius, the servant of God, had been detained by certain men, they suddenly reported what had happened to Childeric. The man who had succeeded in apprehending Leodegarius believed that he would receive the king’s greatest favor. Then, on the advice of the nobles or bishops, it was ordered that he be taken for the time being to the monastery of Luxeuil, until they could deliberate together what they should do with so renowned a man.

Meanwhile, when those who appeared to be the chief men of the palace had been summoned by Childeric to decide what judgment they should pronounce concerning the saint of God, they answered with one accord that, if he spared his life, he should order him to remain at Luxeuil in perpetual exile. The judges’ decree was immediately confirmed, although certain bishops or priests agreed to it for the purpose of freeing him, for the present, from the king’s anger.

For the aforementioned king, misled by the counsel of wicked men, had ordered him brought from Luxeuil so that, once deposed with mockery according to the will of his accusers, he might hand him over to be killed as they wished, just as Herod had once intended to do with Peter at the Jews’ demand.

There was present, however, a venerable man, the abbot Hermenarius [another reading: Ermenarius] of the basilica of Saint Symphorianus. After the departure of the man of God, the king had entrusted the city of Augustodunum to him at the people’s request. He repeatedly threw himself at the king’s feet with immense prayers, asking that he permit Leodegarius to remain at Luxeuil and not order him brought out to satisfy the expectation of the cruel men whom the devil had inflamed against him in fury.

Thus, by such entreaties, he was then saved both from death and from the execution of the king’s order. Some people, however, falsely supposed that Hermenarius frequented the king’s residence for this reason: so that he might be the first of Leodegarius’s accusers and thus more easily be permitted to hold Leodegarius’s bishopric. But the truth was far otherwise. Since the carnal eye did not perceive his spiritual devotion, his works later bore witness on his behalf: for as long as Leodegarius remained alive in this present life, Hermenarius devotedly ministered to his needs in whatever way he could, with charity.

## CHAPTER VII

### He Is Reconciled with Ebroin

### The State of the Kingdom after Childeric’s Death

### A Comet

In those days Ebroin still remained in exile at Luxeuil, tonsured in the monastic habit and pretending to be reconciled, as though, since both had received the same sentence of exile—although the sentences were different—they were leading a life of concord.

While these things were taking place, divine vengeance did not long delay passing judgment upon Childeric. His dissolute conduct had become offensive to all the palace nobles. One of them, bearing this more impatiently than the rest, struck and killed him with a mortal wound while he was confidently hunting in the forest.

[Note: This was in the forest of Lauconia, near the royal villa of Cala. While Childeric was staying in the palace, he was cruelly killed by Bodilo, whom he had shortly before disgracefully beaten with rods, and by other attendants, together with his pregnant wife Bilichild, in the fourth year of his reign, A.D. 673. The event is described in *Gesta Francorum*, chapter 45. Their bodies, buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent, now called Saint-Germain-des-Prés, were discovered in 1656.]

Before these events had occurred, two dukes, who had been ordered to bring Saint Leodegarius from Luxeuil, had delayed there up to that time. One of their officers had conspired that, if he saw the servant of God outside Luxeuil, he would kill him by a blow of the sword. But when the moment arrived, such intolerable fear overwhelmed his heart that he publicly confessed not only that he had said this, but also that he had conceived so grave a plan against the servant of God. Trembling, he fell at his feet and begged him to forgive this wickedness.

When Childeric’s sudden death was announced, those who had been condemned to exile because of his order returned, as venomous serpents customarily emerge from their caves in spring after winter. Their fury produced great turmoil throughout the country, so that it was openly believed that the coming of Antichrist was at hand.

Those who ought to have governed the regions began to attack one another with unceasing hatred. Since no king had yet been firmly established on the throne, each person acted according to what seemed right in his own judgment, without fear of discipline. We clearly recognized that God’s anger had come upon us, for even a star appeared in the heavens, which astrologers call a comet. At its rising, they declare, famine troubles the earth, kings are changed, nations are stirred up, and the sword of destruction threatens.

All these things were then plainly shown to have occurred.

[Note: The Venerable Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 12: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 678,” he says, “a star appeared in the month of August, one called a comet, and it remained for three months,” and so forth. About that year, it is recorded in the *Acts of Saint Salaberga*, under the year 655, that Theodoric fought with Dagobert, son of Sigebert and grandson of the elder Dagobert, for the kingdom at Langres.]

But, as it is written, “fools are not corrected by words, much less by signs.” Those who had returned from exile with evil intent accused Leodegarius’s factions of having caused whatever they had endured because of their own crimes.

## CHAPTER VIII

### Leodegarius Is Protected by Religious Men

### Ebroin Leaves Luxeuil and Plans to Destroy Leodegarius; Prevented by Saint Genesius, He Is Received at Augustodunum with Leodegarius; He Approaches Theodoric, Abandoning the Monastic Habit and Returning to His Wife; He Plunders the Sacred Treasury; Again Harasses Leodegarius; He Substitutes Clovis, Son of Clotaire

During those days, the man of the Lord was being held for his protection by the dukes just mentioned, by whom he had recently been brought out of Luxeuil. For divine grace had then granted its servant this venerable dignity: in those places the aforementioned dukes, their wives, their attendants, all their households, and even the common people were so devoted to him that they did not hesitate to offer themselves on his behalf.

When those who were keeping the servant of God with them informed the other authorities who lived nearby that they had recognized divine grace resting upon God’s servant Leodegarius, those authorities were united in his aid by a religious love of Christianity. They agreed among themselves and confirmed that, while this undisciplined turmoil of domination had arisen, if anyone should perhaps wish to injure Saint Leodegarius before they had jointly raised Theodoric to the kingship, he would be protected by their assistance.

In those days Ebroin also left Luxeuil, like another Julian, having maintained a pretended monastic life. For when he was suddenly surrounded by a company of friends and servants, the exiles mentioned above, seeking his support, set him at the head of the evil which they had fabricated in their accusation, so that, using his aid or counsel, they might unanimously avenge themselves upon the man of God.

Ebroin himself lifted up his poisonous head; like a viper restoring its venom, he pretended that he was then faithful to King Theodoric and therefore hastening toward him as quickly as possible with his associates. When the man of the Lord and the companions mentioned above were traveling along the same road, they had not yet completed even a day’s journey. Before they approached the city of Augustodunum, Ebroin, pressed on by his supporters and forgetful of the friendship he had formerly promised, wished to seize him there—unless he had been prevented by the counsels of Genesius, metropolitan bishop of Lyon, or frightened by the strong force accompanying him.

Again pretending friendship, they entered the city together in a mixed company. The city and the whole Church rejoiced at the renewed presence of their shepherd. The streets were adorned; the deacons prepared candles; the clerics celebrated with antiphons; the entire city rejoiced at the arrival of its bishop after the storm of persecution.

Nor were watches of praise offered without reason, for, with the Lord present [or, according to another reading, foreknowing], he was hastening toward the crown of martyrdom. There, too, in honor of the bishop’s arrival, they prepared delights even for his adversaries.

On the following day they proceeded together, intending to reach Theodoric, king of the Franks, as a united group. Meanwhile, when they had traveled some distance toward the king, Ebroin the tyrant, nearly halfway along the route, abandoned their company and went over to his own followers. He cast off his clerical status—that is, his monastic habit—

[Note: Ebroin’s wife was Leudotrudis, who persuaded her husband to found the convent of Saint Mary at Soissons. There, without doubt, she had received the veil from the tonsured Ebroin. See the note below on Saint Leodegarius’s letter. Chesnius lacks the word *velum* (“veil”).]

—and, like a dog returning to its vomit, went back to the woman after the sacred veil. Since he could not serve in Christ’s army, he took up worldly weapons with his adversaries. Having already abandoned faith and God, he openly showed himself an enemy even of his earthly lord.

Theodoric was then residing securely at Novientum, having recovered the kingdom, when Ebroin suddenly arrived with the Austrasians. Who could fully recount the plunder then carried out from the royal treasury and from the Church’s property, which earlier Catholic princes, devoted out of love for Christianity, had bestowed upon the Lord’s sanctuary—and when even the mayor of the palace had then been killed?

[Note: This was Leudesius, son of Erchinoald, formerly mayor of the palace. Concerning his death, see *Gesta Regum Francorum*, chapter 45.]

He committed this evil because he had been armed with envious counsel by devilish men. They grieved that they had been cast down by merit, seeing the whole people faithfully turning after Theodoric, who had already been confirmed in the kingdom, and God’s servant Leodegarius residing in his own city with Theodoric’s favor. They began again to burn with envy and resentment: while the righteous stood upright, the perverse were unable to recover their position.

Since, at the devil’s urging—the devil who had stripped them of faith—they had already been blinded to the counsel of truth and found no means by which to destroy God’s holy servant, they turned to even greater ruin through a fabrication of falsehood. By this they brought great evil upon the kingdom and a devastating slaughter through the persecution of many.

Finally, they took a certain boy whom they falsely claimed to be Clotaire’s son, and, lifting him up with them in the regions of Austrasia, installed him as king.

[Note: Hadrian Valesius rightly concludes from this that, when his father died, Clotaire was scarcely four years old. Thus he reigned not merely four years, as some write, but fourteen, so that Ebroin could substitute a son for him and persuade the people of it.]

By this means they gathered a great number of people to their side, since it seemed plausible to everyone. As they subdued the country by devastating it, they issued commands to judges in the name of their false king. Whoever unwillingly refused to obey them either lost the rights of his office or, if he did not secretly escape by flight, perished by the sword.

How many people, through this cunning fabrication, believed that Theodoric was dead and that Clovis was Clotaire’s son?

The first and, as it were, the rulers of the palace in this falsehood were Desideratus, surnamed Diddo [so in most manuscripts; another reading: Dido], who had once held authority in the city of Chalon, and his colleague Abbo [another reading: Bobo], who had held the city of Valence as his domain.

Nor do such men deserve to be called bishops, since they are more vigilant in increasing their money through earthly desires or temporal profits, while they care nothing for the souls entrusted to them, for which they will have to render an account to the strict Judge.

Using the counsel of such priests and similar nobles, Ebroin the tyrant was so exalted and blinded in this world that, unrepentant, he was finally hurled into hell.

Let us return to the work we began.

## CHAPTER IX

### Ebroin Entrusts Diddo and Waimer with the Order to Destroy Leodegarius; They Besiege the City of Augustodunum

### The Saint Spends His Treasures for Pious Uses; Gives Excellent Exhortations to His People; Orders Fasts and Supplications; Asks Everyone’s Forgiveness in the Church; Forbids Battle and Inquires into the Adversaries’ Purpose

When these events had taken place and everything had unfolded in due order, after Childeric had been killed, and after the bishops and patricians, together with the nobles, had returned from Neustria or from Theodoric’s court to Burgundy and, with the kingdom secured, were residing safely in their own places, the envious men stirred up an enemy against them—namely Ebroin—and first of all against the man whom they thought had acted with King Childeric.

Then, joining themselves to the most wicked associates of his enemies in council, he began to deliberate how he might destroy that same bishop. Two of these counselors, Diddo and Waimer, who were named as the chief authors of the wickedness, said that they could seize him from the city and take vengeance upon him, thereby satisfying Ebroin’s malice.

Ebroin rejoiced at their answer and gave them a very large army. They hastened to the city of Augustodunum.

The man of the Lord, Leodegarius, was residing in his own city to restore his people. When he perceived the attack intended by the enemy, he did not allow himself to flee farther, but, fearless, awaited the Lord’s judgment concerning him.

When his relatives, clerics, and faithful people urged him to take away the treasures he himself had brought together and depart, so that, hearing of this, the enemy might desist from destroying the city or persecuting him, he refused in every way. Instead, he immediately summoned them to the treasury and assigned to them everything he had placed there, speaking as follows:

“These things that you see, brothers, I faithfully contributed here, as far as I could, for the common adornment, for as long as God wished me to enjoy the favor of earthly men. But perhaps earthly men are now angry with me because the Lord deigns to call us to the grace of heaven.

“Why should I carry away from here things which I cannot take with me into heaven? Therefore, if you approve, I choose instead to give these things for the use of the poor, rather than wander here and there through the world with this shameful burden. Let us imitate blessed Laurence, for ‘he has distributed and given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever, and his horn is exalted in glory.’”

At once he ordered the custodian to bring out the silver plates and many other vessels, and he summoned silversmiths with hammers to break into small pieces everything which he ordered to be distributed to the poor through the administration of the faithful. Whatever was suitable for ecclesiastical use he added to the service of the church.

With the same silver he relieved the poverty of many monasteries of men and women within the city and its territory. What widow, orphan, or poverty in general was then present there that did not receive consolation from his generosity?

The man of the Lord, being filled with the spirit of wisdom, spoke these words to the brothers:

“Brothers, I have now resolved to think of nothing at all belonging to this world, but rather to fear spiritual wickedness than an earthly enemy. If an earthly man has received such power from God that he can persecute, seize, destroy, burn, and kill, we cannot escape these things by evading them.

“And if we are driven from transitory possessions into discipline here, let us not despair; rather, let us rejoice in the future over forgiveness. Therefore let us fortify both our souls and the city’s defenses with virtues, lest either enemy find an entrance through which to bring danger upon us.”

Then, stirring up the entire population of that city, he went around the circuit of the walls with a three-day fast, the sign of the cross, and the relics of the saints. He touched the earth at each entrance to the gates and prayed to the Lord with tears that, if He was calling him to suffering, He would not permit the people entrusted to him to be taken captive. And so it was granted to happen.

Thus, when the people had withdrawn from every direction into the city in their fear of the enemy, had firmly closed the gateways with bolts, and had established defenses everywhere in proper order, the man of the Lord ordered everyone to enter the church. There he asked forgiveness from all together, so that, if he had rebuked any of them—as often happens—in zeal for righteousness, or had injured anyone by word, they would forgive him.

The man of God knew that, as he entered upon the path of suffering, martyrdom is of no benefit unless, after resentment has been wiped away, the heart has first been cleansed and illumined by the lamp of charity. No one there possessed a breast so hard that, even if he had been seriously injured, he would not devoutly have forgiven every evil of the heart.

After this, the city was not long surrounded by the army, and on that same day the two peoples fought fiercely until evening. But when the enemy army had encircled the city with a powerful siege and, shouting day and night like dogs, went around the walls, the man of the Lord, foreseeing the danger threatening the city, ordered all fighting upon the walls to cease and began to plead with his people in these words:

“Cease, I beg you, from fighting against these men. If they have come here solely because of me, I am ready to satisfy their will concerning myself and to appease their fury. Nevertheless, lest we seem to depart without having heard them, let one of the brothers go and ask them why they have besieged this city.”

When they had prepared a descent for Abbot Meroald through the barrier of the wall [Chesnius reads *repugnaculum*, “defensive barrier,” rather than *repagulum*], he reached Diddo and said to him:

“If we have committed these offenses against you, I ask that you meanwhile remember the Gospel saying in which the Lord said: ‘If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive your sins’ (Matthew 6:15). And this also: ‘With the judgment by which you judge, you will be judged’ (Matthew 7:2).”

At the same time he begged him to restrain the enemy and accept the ransom he desired.

But, having hardened his heart like stone, as the king of Egypt once hardened his heart, Diddo could not be softened at all by the divine words. He threatened that he would not withdraw from attacking the city until he could seize Leodegarius and satisfy the mad desire of his fury—and unless Leodegarius promised allegiance to Clovis, whom they had falsely made king.

This was merely a pretense, for they all asserted under oath that King Theodoric was dead.

## CHAPTER X

### He Refuses to Violate His Allegiance to Theodoric; While the Enemies Rage, He Offers Himself after Receiving the Eucharistic Provision; He Endures the Plucking Out of His Eyes without a Groan

### Augustodunum Is Assigned to Bobo as Plunder

When the man of the Lord had heard these words, he gave them this answer:

“Let this be known to all of you, friends and brothers as well as enemies and foes: for as long as God orders me to remain alive in this world, I will not abandon the faith which I promised before the Lord to preserve toward Theodoric. I have resolved to offer my body to death rather than shamefully strip my soul of faithfulness.”

When the enemies heard this answer, they quickly pressed in from every side with showers of weapons and fire, attempting to break into the city.

The saint then bade farewell to all the brothers, received communion of bread and wine, strengthened their uncertain hearts, and entrusted to them the memory of his passion, as Christ had entrusted it to his disciples. Fearlessly he went to the gates. When the barriers had been opened, he willingly offered himself for the citizens to their enemies.

The adversaries rejoiced and, like wolves receiving an innocent sheep as prey, seized him. He is said to have cried out:

“I give thanks to almighty God, who has deigned to glorify me today.”

They then devised an almost unspeakably wicked plan: they tore the light of his eyes from his head. In this tearing out of his eyes, he appeared to endure the cutting of the iron beyond the limits of human nature.

Many distinguished men who were present bear witness that he did not permit them to bind his hands, nor did a groan come from his mouth while his eyes were torn from his head. Instead, he continually glorified the Lord and strove to sing melodies from the Psalms.

Among the others was a certain duke of Campania named Waimer, who had come from the regions of Austrasia with Diddo to perpetrate this evil. These two assigned Augustodunum to a certain Bobo, who had recently been expelled with an anathema from the episcopate of the city of Valence, to govern—or rather to devastate—it.

The citizens, overcome and now bereft of their shepherd, received the adversary; under his administration nearly all the Church’s support was carried away. For the redemption of the city, once the opportunity arose, the church’s silver was sold for five thousand solidi, apart from the citizens’ property that was plundered.

Although the Church suffered the loss of temporal goods, the Lord permitted no one to be led away captive.

## CHAPTER XI

### The Saint Is Handed over to Waimer

### Saint Genesius Is Rescued from a Similar Fate

### Ebroin Orders Leodegarius to Be Consumed by Starvation

### Waimer Is Softened toward Him

### Leodegarius Sends the Silver Received from Waimer to the People of Augustodunum

When the enemies had joyfully divided the spoils, they handed the man of God into the custody of the aforementioned Waimer, who returned with him and the army to his own country.

Desideratus, surnamed Diddo, together with Bobo and the duke Adalric [another reading: Chaldaric], whom they wished to be patrician of the province, proceeded as far as Lyon to subdue the patriciate. They intended to remove Genesius from there, just as they had previously expelled Leodegarius from Augustodunum.

But the powerful force of the people, gathered from every side, did not permit them to break into that great city, which had God as its protector.

When those who had taken Leodegarius, the servant of God, reported to Ebroin what had happened, he ordered him to be shut away in the solitude of the forests. He also ordered a false story to be fabricated that he had died, as though he had been drowned, and commanded that a burial mound be made for him, until long starvation should consume him.

Anyone who could hear or see this believed it to be true.

[Note: Here the author appears to be referring to himself, in the same manner as Saint John in the Gospel, chapter 14: “And he who saw it has borne witness.”]

But He who fed Elijah by a raven in the wilderness did not abandon His servant there. After the martyr of God had endured a long period of hunger and starvation, Waimer remembered that human nature could not endure such treatment unless Christ’s grace sustained him. He ordered him to be brought into his own house, for his hard entrails began to be softened by compassion.

When Leodegarius had become accustomed to conversing familiarly with Waimer, he subdued and tamed Waimer’s fierceness in a short time. He converted both Waimer and his wife to the fear of God, so that Waimer devoutly offered him the church’s silver which he had recently received as the ransom of the city of Augustodunum, allowing him to do whatever he wished with it.

The man of God accepted it and sent it back to the aforementioned city through a faithful abbot named Berton. Dividing it, in accordance with the Apostle (Galatians 6:10), among “those who belong to the household of faith,” he faithfully fulfilled Waimer’s intention through an act of charity.

## CHAPTER XII

### Ebroin Rejects the Pseudo-Clovis and Becomes Theodoric’s Mayor of the Palace; He Enacts an Unjust Edict; He Rages and Runs Riot against Everyone; He Accuses Leodegarius of Childeric’s Death

### Leodegarius Encourages His Brother to Patience

Since, as was said above, the wicked Ebroin could no longer conceal his crime, he abandoned the king whom he had falsely created and returned to Theodoric’s palace. He was received through the faction of certain men and was suddenly made mayor of the palace again.

Some raised him to the summit of honor with joy, others with fear. He immediately issued an edict that, if anyone had caused loss or seized plunder from anyone during the period of turmoil, no accusation should arise from it against anyone.

This was an opportunity for him not to return the spoils which his officials had brought him from the plunder of many people.

When he began to swell with renewed pride,

[Note: Chesnius reads: “When he began to swell with renewed pride.”]

at once grieving and fearing that he might have surviving rivals whose parents he had harmed—for he had already obtained the rights of power—he doubled his malice with envy.

He began relentlessly to persecute the former nobles. Those whom he could seize he either struck down by the sword or drove into foreign lands after confiscating their property. He destroyed the monasteries of noble women and sent their leading religious women into exile.

Since he had been granted power to trample upon the adornments of jewels, he did not hesitate, like a pig, to burst into Christ’s treasures without any compassion and trample their ornaments underfoot. Because he could not look toward heaven, his heart was fixed beyond measure in the mud of earthly desires.

When the cruel Ebroin had satisfied his fury concerning the matters mentioned above, he again began to seek opportunities by which he might remove the disgrace of his cruelty from human eyes. Then he pretended that he wished to avenge Childeric’s death, although no one had wanted Childeric to die before Ebroin himself had desired it. For he did not dare publicly to persecute anyone whom he hated in any other way.

The leaders ordered Saint Leodegarius and his brother to leave the monastery in which he had been kept hidden, and commanded that he be summoned into the king’s presence.

Turning to Ebroin, Leodegarius said:

“While you desire to surpass all the inhabitants of the whole of France, you are stripping away the glory which you received unworthily.”

When the most wicked Ebroin heard this, he was filled with great fury. He ordered his attendants to drag Gairinus, Leodegarius’s brother, outside and separate him from his brother, so that they might be punished separately and not enjoy saying such things together.

As he was being led away, blessed Leodegarius addressed his brother:

“Be of good courage, dearest brother, for we must suffer these things, because ‘the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us’ (Romans 8:12). Our sins are indeed many, but the mercy of the Almighty, which is surpassingly great and always ready to wash away the offenses of those who praise Him, is greater still.

“For a time we suffer these things because we are debtors to death. But that life awaits us if we endure this punishment patiently; there we shall rejoice without end in heavenly glory.”

## CHAPTER XIII

### Gairinus Is Buried under Stones; Leodegarius Is Mutilated in His Feet, Tongue, and Lips and Handed over to Waningus for Custody; He Recovers the Use of His Voice; He Is Cared for by Hermenarius; His Tongue and Lips Grow Again

### The Author’s Age

### Leodegarius Is Brought to Fiscamnum

Then the attendants began to bury his brother, who was bound to a stake, under stones. He prayed to the Lord, saying:

“Good Lord Jesus, who did not come to call the righteous but sinners, receive the spirit of your servant. You who have deigned to take this mortal life from me by stones, in the likeness of the martyrs, mercifully command that forgiveness of my sins be granted.”

As he said this, he breathed out his final spirit in prayer.

Blessed Leodegarius desired to end his life together with his brother, so that together they might merit participation in the future blessedness. But the tyrant Ebroin wished to delay his death in order to prepare eternal punishments for him through prolonged torments and to prevent him from receiving the crown of martyrdom, so that he might instead be deprived of the rewards of everlasting glory.

He therefore ordered him to be led barefoot through a certain pool in which there were stones as sharp as cutting nails. For this reason he cruelly ordered his lips and the hollow of his face to be cut with iron. He also ordered the tip of his tongue to be cut away with iron, so that, once his eyes had been removed, his feet pierced, and his tongue and lips cut, and when he saw that every blessing had been taken from him and that the strength of his body had failed everywhere, he would be unable to see the road with his eyes, walk the path with his feet, or praise the Creator with the service of his tongue.

Thus he might fall into blasphemy in despair and deprive himself of the salvation which he would have deserved to obtain from heaven by praising God.

But God, who hears the hearts even without voices, loves a contrite heart more than one lifted up in pride and receives the voice of the silent more readily than that of the boastful. He does not demand the assistance of the voice, but humility of heart.

When Leodegarius recognized that every human defense had been taken from him, he asked with all his strength that divine assistance be present to him. As far as human impiety sought to draw him back from heaven, divine compassion made him that much more closely joined to heaven.

They therefore kept Saint Leodegarius, the Lord’s servant, alive for a longer time, intending him for punishment. Shamefully stripped, they ordered him to be dragged naked through the marshes along the streets. They handed him over, disfigured, to a man named Waringus, so that under his harsh authority he might breathe out his tortured spirit.

The wicked Ebroin said to him:

“Take Leodegarius, whom you once saw as a proud man, and place him under secure custody. The time of his calling will come, when he will receive what he has deserved from his enemies.”

Since Waringus’s residence was far away, they placed the holy martyr of God upon a wretched beast of burden. When he realized that this had been fulfilled, he took up this verse from the Psalm:

“I have become like a beast of burden, and I am always with you” (Psalm 72:23).

Although he no longer had lips or a tongue, he could not remain silent in the praises of God. His devoted mind sounded forth, with whatever voice it could, from the hidden sanctuary of his heart.

When everyone saw him severely covered in blood, they believed that he would die because of this. One of our brothers, an abbot named Winobertus, had followed the holy man of God from a distance as far as his lodging. He begged the guards to allow him secretly to approach Leodegarius and found him lying on straw, covered with an old piece of tent-cloth, breathing faintly.

Although he thought he was about to expire, he found an unexpected miracle. Amid the bloody spittle, the cut tongue, without lips, began to produce its customary speech. Because the severing of the lips had exposed the rows of teeth, they produced the sound of the words from within, by the breath that was blown through them.

Then the man who had come to keep vigil for his passing began to weep for joy and hastened to report what had happened to Bishop Hermenarius.

Hermenarius, hearing this, asked Waringus to let him enter to see the martyr of God. Permission was granted because of his own merit, for everyone feared Ebremerdus—that is, Ebroin, the son of perdition and straw of hell—the savage tyrant, as they would fear an enraged lion.

[Note: Chesnius reads: “For everyone feared the savage tyrant, Ebremerdus, as they would fear an enraged lion.”]

The same Hermenarius, of blessed memory, who was later raised to the honor of the episcopate after him, as we stated above, carefully endeavored to treat his wounds. By whatever skill he possessed, he restored him with drink and food and clothed him in the best garment he had.

They did not honor him as an ordinary earthly man, but reverently as a martyr who had been transferred from this world. For this reason they obtained from him not only forgiveness for the past, but also his favor for the future.

After Waringus had taken him to his own home, by the accompanying grace of God his lips began to grow back more quickly than nature would ordinarily allow. His tongue likewise returned, and I saw words flowing from his mouth in greater abundance than before.

When Waringus learned of this miracle, he did not harden his heart against doing him harm, as the tyrant had ordered. Instead, changing his mind and recognizing him now as God’s martyr, he took him to his own monastery, called Fiscamnum. There was a community of virgins there, presided over by Childemarca, a servant of Christ. He lived there for many days under guard.

His severed tongue recovered its customary function, and he displayed the great seed of his teaching among the people. At times he entered the company of the virgins and, as they say, shone with such sweet eloquence that all who heard him marveled at the greatness of God’s mercy and, turning away from evil works, quickly sought the fruit of repentance.

When, within a short space of time, he had recovered the function of his lips, throat, and tongue, he devoted himself to offering a daily sacrifice, since he himself had already been offered to the Lord.

As spiritual light filled him inwardly, he cared nothing for his bodily eyes. Day and night he remained constantly awake in the praises of God, scarcely ever leaving the church even briefly for the necessities of the body, in order to take a little sleep or food.

## CHAPTER XIV
The ruin of his enemies is mourned; after the bishops opposed to him have been expelled from the synod, he himself is brought before the synod; he pleads that he had no part in Childeric’s death; he foretells many things to the king; after his tunic has been torn, he is handed over to Chrodobert to be killed; he is commended by a heavenly light; he accepts the sentence of death with equanimity.

Accordingly, when, after so many scourges—as befitted a martyr—the faithful people were offering him venerable service, almighty God openly declared this to all, because a lamp cannot shine when hidden beneath a bushel. For suddenly he began to avenge his adversaries. While he remained there for nearly two years, occupied in the praises of God, they announced to him that those men had been killed or, on account of their guilt of faithlessness, driven into other regions. He grieved for them deeply, not rejoicing in their punishment, but because death had overtaken them without repentance.

At that time the glorious king Theodoric and the same Ebroin convened a synod. They assembled at a royal estate and caused a great crowd of bishops to be present. There, among the others, Dido was brought forward—the man who, together with Waim­er, had expelled the holy man Leodegarius from the seat of his episcopate and, having been enticed, had handed him over to punishment. Condemned by that very synod, he was expelled after being made bald and was separated from the holy congregation. Then, condemned to exile, he paid the penalty of death and thus discharged whatever treachery he had practiced against the holy man.

The other bishops, too, at that time received from the king, through Ebroin, an almost similar punishment in the same synod and were deported into perpetual exile. Waim­er, who had been a partner in wickedness in capturing the aforesaid servant of God in order to carry out Ebroin’s commands, had afterward been deceitfully raised to the rank of bishop by Ebroin himself because he had agreed to avenge him. After a short interval, however, he fell into Ebroin’s displeasure and, by God’s will, as we believe, was overwhelmed by many scourges. For, as the report goes, he was hanged by a noose and, condemned to a most shameful death—as befitted a betrayer of the just man—was sent to Tartarus.

The holy man of God Leodegarius was still staying in that same monastery of nuns where he had been placed under guard. Accordingly, in order to forge the martyr’s crown for him, the crafty artificer, the tyrant Ebroin, remained alive from among those men, so that he might complete whatever was still lacking for the glory of his passion.

Again the ancient serpent, envious and distressed that he had been driven from that place by the holy man’s prayers, began once more to goad Ebroin and ordered him to be brought back to the palace, so that, on the advice of the bishops, he might tear his garment and thereby forbid him to presume to offer the sacrifice any longer.

> **Note [Col. 0363D].** In this passage we observe two methods of reducing bishops to order, namely by shaving the head and by tearing the tunic. We have an example of the first method in the first rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, chapter 16, where he orders that “a monk who pursues boys or adolescents,” apart from other punishments, “shall lose the crown he wears on his head, and, disgracefully shaven, shall be exposed to reproach.” An example of the second method is found in Gregory of Tours, bishop, book V, chapter 19, where he discusses the council held at Paris in the case of Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, at the command of King Chilperic. Chilperic, pressing for Praetextatus’s deposition, demanded “either that his tunic be torn, or that the hundred and eighth psalm, which contains the Iscariot curses, be recited over his head, or at least that a judgment against him be written, so that he might never again receive communion.”

When he had been brought into the midst of them, they questioned him, seeking a statement by which he might confess himself an accomplice in Hilderic’s death. Recognizing that, through a diabolical contrivance, a conflict was again threatening him, and not wishing to excuse himself from a human offense, he nevertheless declared that he had in no way been an accomplice in this crime, but professed that God rather than men knew it.

Then they summoned him also to the same synod. Yet it is not confirmed that he was within the council itself, but rather apart from it. At that time he is said to have held a conference with the king, during which he foretold many future events that can plainly be inferred to have come to pass.

When, after long importunity, they could extract nothing else from him, they tore his tunic from the top. Then the impious tyrant ordered him to be handed over to a certain Chrodobert [variant: Ruotbert], who was at that time count of the palace, so that his present life might be taken by a stroke of the sword.

For God’s martyr rejoiced in complete endurance, since, with the Lord as his rewarder, he felt that the crown of martyrdom owed to him was drawing near. Chrodobert took him into his own house. Seeing him exhausted by the journey and by illness, he ordered that a drink be given him for refreshment.

Before the cupbearer could attend to him, a great light, as if descending from heaven in the circle of a wheel, shone upon his head. Then all who saw this sign trembled and said:

“What is this, lord, that appears above your head, shining from heaven in the form of a circle? We have never seen anything like it.”

He prostrated himself on the ground in worship and said:

“I give thanks there to you, almighty God, comforter of all, and I render praise to you, who have deigned to display such a miracle over your servant.”

Then, seeing this, all seemed to be in an ecstasy of mind. At last, having recovered their senses, they glorified almighty God together, and, turning to one another, said:

“Truly this man is a servant of God.”

They promised that they would devote themselves wholly to God to the best of their ability.

Indeed, when the aforesaid man had brought him into his house, he received such a heavenly blessing at his arrival that, when all who lived there recognized this, they confessed their own sins and hastened eagerly to the remedies of repentance. For the Lord had so illuminated his servant with this grace that wherever he had been handed over in exile so that wickedness might be inflicted upon him, all, by a reversal of fortune, offered him submissive reverence.

At last the day of his reward arrived, on which the end of his persecution was to come. Then an order was sent from the palace that Leodegarius should not live any longer. But the impious Ebroin feared that the faithful Christians might honor him with the dignity of martyrdom. Therefore he ordered that a well be sought out in the thick of the forest and that his murdered body be thrown into it, so that, with the mouth of the well blocked by earth or stones, its tomb might remain unknown to men.

Meanwhile the aforementioned Chrodobert, influenced by his preaching, had begun to be somewhat converted. Therefore, unable to bear witnessing the death of the man of God, he instructed four of his servants to carry out what had been commanded him. When this news reached his house, Chrodobert’s wife began to weep with bitter mourning, because so cruel a crime had come to her husband’s charge.

## CHAPTER XV

He consoles his host; he is led to the place of martyrdom; after commending the executioners to God, he is struck after offering his neck; the impious executioner perishes; the saint is buried.

When the man of the Lord learned that his end had now arrived, he began to console the grieving woman, saying:

“Do not, I beg you, weep because of my departure, for my death will by no means be required of you as a cause for vengeance. Rather, a blessing from heaven will be given you by God if you devoutly bury my little body in a tomb.”

After saying this, he bade farewell while the servants urged them on, and they led him into the forest to carry out the sentence that had been commanded. They had already searched for a well in which to conceal his body, as had been ordered, but could no longer find one anywhere.

They led him through unknown places until they reached a certain spot. There he stood and said:

“You need not tire yourselves by going farther, my sons. Quickly do what you have come to do, so that you may fulfill the desire of the wicked man.”

Those who were leading him to his death were four in number. Three of them fell at his feet and begged him to pardon them and to deign to bestow his blessing upon them.

> **Note [Col. 0365D].** A., “The fourth, named Wadardus”; the Chartres manuscript has *Wadhardus*.

But the fourth stood proudly, with his sword drawn and ready to kill him. After he had bestowed his blessing upon them and proclaimed the word of God to his killers, the man of God, devoting himself to prayer, said:

“Lord almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have received knowledge of you, God of hosts and creator of all creation: I bless you, I glorify you, who have deigned to bring me to this day of battle. I ask and entreat you, Lord, that you yourself command your mercy to be bestowed upon me, and make me worthy, through the merits of your saints, to share in their company and to be a companion of eternal life. Grant forgiveness to those who afflict me, because through them I believe that I shall be glorified in your sight, most merciful Father.”

Then he rose and extended his neck, reminding the swordsman to fulfill what had been commanded him. As he said these things, the executioner extended his sword and cut off his head. It is said that his upright body remained standing for about an hour. When the swordsman saw that he did not immediately fall, he struck him with his foot so that he would fall to the ground more quickly.

Not long afterward, however, his executioner was seized by demons, deprived of his senses, and struck by God’s vengeance. He threw himself into a fire and there ended his life.

Then, at the command of Chrodobert’s wife, this man’s body was secretly carried by his servants, amid the great weeping of the mourners, to a certain estate called Sarcinio.

> **Note [Col. 0365D].** Balderic, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, briefly summarizes this story in his *Chronicle of Arras*, book I, chapter 20: “In the territory of Arras Ebroin had him led away and beheaded, at the place called the Forest of Saint Leodegarius. He was buried in an estate called Sorcin, which lies on the boundary of the bishopric of Cambrai and that of Thérouanne.”

By the decision of this woman, the blessed martyr was buried in a small oratory, together with the garments in which he had been murdered.

## CHAPTER XVI

The place of burial is illumined from heaven.—Sacrilegious thieves are punished after everything is restored.—Ebroin sends an investigator to the tomb, whose impiety is punished by death.—The unrepentant Ebroin is destroyed; on what occasion.

During these days a certain priest who served in this oratory recognized that a splendid light shone there at night without human assistance. He also asserted with an oath that he had heard an angelic song there, so terrifyingly that, trembling, he withdrew lest he should be present at a spiritual vision improperly.

> **Note [Col. 0366D].** Perhaps, “alone to spiritual sight,” and so forth.

From this a great rumor spread throughout the surrounding area. The venerable martyr healed many crowds of sick people and of those afflicted by various diseases who came to his venerable prayers. He also gave the lame the power to walk, granted sight to the blind, cleansed those possessed by demons, and shone forth through many miracles in the venerable dwelling of this place. The priest of that church attests to this.

The cleric who served this priest and was guardian of the church also suffered a robbery one night. The thieves carried away all his property. Among the stolen things was a little shoe of the blessed martyr, which he had kept hidden out of reverence; the thief, unaware of what it was, carried it away with him.

When the cleric rose early from the oratory and went to his home, he found that all his possessions had been stolen. He hurried to the tomb of this man, begging him to return what he had lost by theft. For the whole of that day and the following night he remained in prayer at the tomb, fasting and persisting in psalmody.

When, after completing his prayer, he returned to his cell, he found everything that he had lost, with nothing missing, together with the blessed martyr’s little shoe, which had remained intact.

The master of the thief, who had sworn on his servant that he had certainly not committed this evil, returned home and ended his life. The servant, however, brought the crime he had committed to a wretched conclusion.

Then the fame of the holy martyr’s sanctity broke increasingly out of hiding, and soon what had happened became known to Ebroin. On hearing this, he secretly sent a messenger to investigate these matters carefully and report the truth to him.

The messenger obeyed his orders and approached the tomb. By questioning the guardian, he learned where Leodegarius lay. A blind man who had received his sight through God’s miracles told him where the saint’s body rested and served the man who had restored his sight. The messenger believed none of this. Swollen with pride, he approached but delayed applying himself to prayer; indeed, despising the ground, he struck it with his foot and foolishly said, because he did not know the power involved:

“A dead man will by no means perform miracles.”

But the wretched man, returning before he could report these things to the one who had sent him, learned in his own person how powerful the holy martyr was in miracles. While he was making the journey, he lost his life and did not report to the one who had sent him. The proud man who had not believed was dashed down and compelled to recognize the one he had despised.

When the report of so great a matter spread and brought joy to the faithful, the most wicked Ebroin, having learned these things, kept them locked within his silent heart and, trembling inwardly, dared to disclose them to no one except his wife. He feared that, as the martyr’s glory increased, his own glory among the people would be diminished, since he had desired to extinguish such a light.

For as much as that wretched man wished this good deed to remain hidden during those days, so much more widely the rumor of the aforesaid miracles of the blessed martyr spread and shone everywhere.

As soon as Ebroin learned of it fully, he did not wish to correct his evil. Rather, with his heart now blind, he was hardened together with his followers by the obstacle of unbelief. He ordered, with threats, that what Christ the Lord had deigned to display for the consolation of unbelievers, for the glory of his martyr placed upon the lampstand of the Church and for the enlightenment of the faithful, should be hidden.

For when the tyrant’s wavering and wandering mind faltered and did not turn at all toward humility or the correction of himself, the devil raised his neck against all men in the pride of arrogance beyond the usual measure.

> **Note [Col. 0367D].** Read, “had raised.”

Then Solomon’s proverb was fulfilled in him:

> “Before a man’s heart is humbled, it is exalted, and before ruin the spirit is lifted up” (Proverbs 16:18).

And so that the deed of so great a crime might not escape punishment, he himself, like a madman, sought out the moment of his death.

For, finding an opportunity, he brought such a spoliation upon a certain nobleman who at that time administered a fiscal office that he nearly took away his entire estate. Moreover, he threatened him with death.

When that man saw that, after his dispossession, the destruction of death was already threatening him, he hardened his resolve and kept watch by Ebroin’s door before dawn, waiting for him to come out.

It was Sunday, and therefore Ebroin was going out to the celebration of Matins.

> **Note [Col. 0367D].** It was therefore the custom of Christians at that time, even those who were lax or eminent, to attend the offices of Matins on Sunday.

When Ebroin had put his foot outside the threshold, the other man suddenly sprang out unexpectedly and struck him on the head with a sword. By this blow he fell into a double death.

Thus the unjust dominion was removed from his kingdom, just as once David removed the reproach from the children of Israel when the Philistine foreigner had been struck down.

## CHAPTER XVII

At what time.—A dispute arises over the body of Saint Leodegarius; Ansoald arranges for it to be taken by lot to Poitiers.—The author writes this at the request of Ermenana, abbess.—Audulf described the saint’s miracles.

After nearly three years had passed, the divine word was fulfilled concerning Ebroin, who is forever to be mourned because he had attempted to extinguish this lamp. For the man who had killed many with the sword himself perished by the sword.

Unhappy and wretched was the man who, raised to such great honors and whose reputation for ability had spread among three parts of the world, enjoyed influence among men, because he did not wish to grant forgiveness to his enemies by fulfilling God’s command. By avenging himself on them, he caused many to depart for the heavenly kingdoms.

Therefore it must be greatly feared that the man who killed so many priests and nobles by the cruelty of his vengeance had instead prepared eternal punishment for himself; that he had lost a glory so exalted that no Frank had deserved to possess its equal; and that he had lost the blessed life which he could have attained through patience.

But after the unhappy Ebroin had ended his life, what he had hidden from the servant of God, driven by envy, became widely known and was proclaimed far and wide with great praise.

After this, when the king and his palace had learned the truth about the miracles of the holy martyr—how Christ the Lord had glorified him with signs of power as a testimony to his praise—the king believed the event with admiration. He began to venerate as a martyr the man whom, previously, because of the tyrant’s accusations, he had believed guilty.

Then the matter that had been hidden for many days by his rival was reported with praise in the palace. A great multitude of the highest bishops and nobles was there. As they discussed the holy martyr among themselves and marveled at what they heard about him, the man of great sanctity, Ansoald, bishop of the city of Poitiers, introduced the following statement:

“If only I were granted the choice! For it is known that he is my kinsman, and he advanced to the grace of honor from the diocese entrusted to me. Would that I might at least deserve to have his little body with me.”

There was also present Bishop Hermenarius, who had succeeded him in the episcopate of the city of Autun. He said:

“The body of this man is rightfully given to me, since it is just that he should rest where he was a bishop.”

Then Vindicianus, bishop of Arras, in whose diocese he had been killed, is said to have replied:

“It will certainly not happen as you holy bishops have said. Let me be granted the power to possess this blessed body, since he was given to this place, where he deigns to rest.”

With the entire crowd of bishops standing by, they decided that fasts and prayers should be offered in this dispute, so that through them the Lord might deign to show in whose diocese the body ought rightfully to rest.

Those who heard this agreed to the decision. After prayer and fasting, the decision was written on three small letters and placed upon the altar, so that, when the prayer had ended, the Lord might declare into whose lot the little body of the blessed martyr would fall.

On the following day, when the prayer had been completed and the solemnities of the Mass had been concluded, one of the attendants, ordered by the bishops, put his hand beneath the cloth without knowing [variant: “unknowingly”], and the knowledge of the truth came into his hand.

When all who were present at this spectacle saw this, they recognized it and cried out that the right belonged to Bishop Ansoald, since the letter concerning this matter had appeared and showed that the matter was truly settled.

The decision having now been confirmed without ambiguity, that same bishop Ansoald ordered a certain man of God, his abbot named Audulf, to go quickly for this holy body and, with due reverence, bring it as far as the territory of Poitiers, so that its lamp might shine there forever, where it had first begun to exercise the worship of God.

Then the man of God, obeying the command of his holy bishop, went joyfully and quickly to the place where the little body had rested. When the monks and other men and women living in the surrounding area heard this, they hurried together to the place, deeply moved by great devotion.

There, when many were healed of various illnesses, they rejoiced and exulted with great praises. A crowd of many people, singing and weeping together, moved this holy body, as the glorious lord King Theodoric had ordered.

As they proceeded on the journey, the news spread throughout the places along the route. From monasteries, villages, and estates, crowds of monks and clerics began to come of their own accord from every direction, proceeding along the public road with crosses, lighted candles, and fragrant perfumes to meet them.

The multitude was so great that scarcely anyone could approach the bier or carry it upon his shoulders. For anyone who was afflicted by an illness, even if he could approach the bier and touch it with his hand, immediately returned to his former health. No one was denied healing if, with faith, he touched the fringes of the covering of this bier.

In the district of Cahors [variant: Caturvino], certain faithful brothers made requests, especially the petitions of Ermenana, the abbess—who, more insistently than the others, compelled us to write this little work about the miracles that accompanied the saint. The aforesaid Audulf sent a true account. He inserted certain details but said that, because of their multitude, they could not be written down; he would merely report how many miracles he had seen flashing forth while the body was being carried.

He asserted, he said, that if anyone wished to insert in a book all the things he had seen, the volume in writing would exceed the size of the Psalms.

We, however, briefly make known to those who desire to hear it what we have learned through that same account.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Various miracles at the saint’s bier.

In a certain estate called Gaudiacus (Jouy), there was a girl named Radinga who for seven years had lain in her parents’ house blind, mute, and paralyzed.

When her parents had brought her to the bier of the blessed martyr, she is said that same night, while overcome by sleep, to have seen two shining men on horseback standing beside her. When she awoke and wondered at the vision within herself, her eyes received sight, her feet the power to walk, and her tongue the function of speech. She herself cried out:

“I give you thanks, almighty God, who through the holy martyr Leodegarius have restored me to complete health.”

Raised up by this praise [variant: “by this calamity”], sound in all her limbs, she went with her parents to their home and afterward lived for a long time.

Next, when they had reached the territory of the city of Tours, in a nearby village called Solnacum (Sonay), a woman tormented by a demon was being dragged by her parents to the bier of the holy man. When, finally, unwilling and compelled, she arrived and touched the cloth of the bier, she was immediately cleansed of the demon. Restored to her right mind, she now wished even more to remain near the bier, because she feared that the adversary might seize her again.

After these things had occurred, the bier was brought to the city. When the bishop of that city, who at that time was the man of God Bertus [variant: Theodebertus], heard this, he came out to meet it with choirs of singers and received the bier with lamps and great honor.

As they were passing through the city, a woman accused in connection with her husband’s death was being led along with her neck and hands bound in chains. As she was dragged along, she cried:

“Help me, blessed Leodegarius, for I am dying innocent, bound by false accusers.”

When she had said this, the chain immediately broke and fell from her neck. The woman at once threw that same chain beneath the bier with her hands, and she who had been punished without cause appeared to be vindicated.

When the same bishop had carried this holy body with great praises through his diocese and had entered the territory of Poitiers, to which it had been destined, it rested for a while in a certain village called Igoranda (Ingrande).

There a certain lame man came to meet it. When he had thrown himself upon the ground in prayer before the body of the holy man, he was immediately made sound and, standing upright on his feet, returned home unharmed.

Then a woman heard of it whose hands had lost their form and whose fingers had become crooked, so that they were bent into the palms. Her nails were so hidden in the flesh that they had lost their natural function. When she approached the bier, however, she invoked the name of the Lord and the holy martyr, and her hands were straightened and restored to their former health. Giving great thanks to God, she returned home.

This miracle also must not be passed over in silence. Bishop Ansoald, the man of God, hearing that the holy body had already drawn near, sent a swift servant to his estate at Interamnis to provide an abundance of wine, so that the poor and the rest of the common people who accompanied the holy body might have refreshment.

When this had been done, not long afterward it was reported that all the vessels within the storeroom from which the wine had been taken, although they had seemed almost empty, appeared so full that the wine even overflowed onto the floor, while the vessels themselves nevertheless remained full.

Afterward, when they had reached the river Vienne at a village called Sannone, a contrary wind was rising above the swollen river, which was surging with waves. The sailors, fearing for their safety, began to forbid the travelers to enter the river.

Then the man of God, the abbot mentioned above, whose responsibility it was to carry the holy body, trusting in the merits of the holy martyr, compelled them, saying:

“Put it into the boat and cross safely, for the Lord is powerful enough, through the merit of this saint, to calm these waves.”

When it had been placed in the boat and the sailors began to navigate, the waves immediately grew calm, and they crossed the river safely.

When they had spent the night in a church, a foreign woman arrived with a blind infant. She kept vigil in prayer throughout the night, and at dawn the infant received back the sight that he had lost.

From there they proceeded directly to an estate called Gelnacum. Bishop Ansoald came out to meet them there with a multitude of clerics, common people, and the poor, with censers and the fragrance of incense, with crosses and lighted candles, and with many companies singing. Receiving this holy body, he began to proceed toward the city.

There was also a woman who had been bent over for many years, so that her head, bowed down, almost touched her knees. When she slightly raised her eyes in prayer toward the bier of the holy martyr, her body returned to its former strength.

The bishop and all who stood with him marveled at the power of God and of the most blessed martyr. Then, with songs and great praises, they reached the city.

In the suburbs there is a basilica in which the blessed Radegund rests. The bishop entered it with the holy body of the martyr. A certain paralytic was there, and at the martyr’s arrival he became well.

When the blessed body was carried to the basilica [variant: monastery] of Saint Hilary, another paralytic lying in the road touched the bier and was immediately healed.

A short time later, a blind girl invoked the holy man of God and received back the sight she had lost. She followed the bier until she reached his tomb and has continued to serve there devoutly to this day.

## CHAPTER XIX

The monks of Saint Maxentius receive the sacred body.—Other miracles.

When the holy body had been taken away from the city, and had been carried for some distance upon the shoulders of the bishop of that city together with his priests and attendants, it was brought with great rejoicing to a certain village called Zezinoialo [variant: Zizolliolo].

There a great crowd of monks from the monastery of Saint Maxentius, where he had previously been abbot, came out to meet him. They intended to receive their shepherd with great favor, and they spent the night in that church with great devotion and psalmody.

At dawn a woman approached, carrying in her arms an almost lifeless infant of nearly three years of age. The child is said to have lost his spirit before reaching the holy body. She carried him forward and placed him beneath the bier. Weeping, she invoked the holy man, saying:

“My lord, give me back my son.”

After she had cried out these prayers for nearly three hours, the child, as if awakening from a deep sleep, sought his mother with the voice he possessed and said:

“Mother, where are you?”

Rejoicing, she received back alive the son whom she had lost dead. This was a great and wondrous miracle, through which great faith in such a perfect man arose among the people, whose great glory remains in heaven.

Then the body of the most blessed martyr was lifted up and carried onward as befitted such a man. They began to go to the monastery of Saint Maxentius, where he had previously been father of the monks.

Because he had first begun there to turn the minds of perverse men toward divine worship, it is judged, by the just judgment and providence of God, that by shining forth with the highest miracles he should attach many more to the works of God through supreme examples.

As the body was being carried, two poor people—a man and his wife—met it on the road. The man had lost one eye, while his wife had lost both. When they each approached the bier, the woman received sight in her eyes, but her husband, doubting, withdrew still blind in one eye.

Before they approached, the man had been dragging his blind wife by a cord. As they departed, the wife, repaying the favor, afterward dragged her blind husband.

When the monks from that monastery had first hurried out to meet the holy man, a girl who lay paralyzed in the court of Saint Maxentius had lost the use of all her limbs, as was well known. When she heard the name of the blessed Leodegarius, one of her hands was restored to health.

When the body of the blessed martyr arrived in that court on the third day, all her disjointed limbs, with every illness removed, returned to their former functions, and she was restored completely sound.

When those who were present saw this miracle, such a multitude of people gathered from every direction that the churches and courts could scarcely contain all the crowds who arrived.

Meanwhile another woman came from far away and, when she approached the tomb of the holy martyr, received the sight of her eyes that she had lost.

A young man and a girl, both tormented by demons, arrived trembling at the place of the holy martyr. The demons were expelled through the vomiting of blood, and they returned to health.

## CHAPTER XX

The devotion of the faithful toward the sacred body; the saint is buried in a new basilica.

Many innumerable miracles were performed through the same martyr during those days. For whoever came—many sick, blind, deaf, mute, withered, lame, and tormented by demons—received the health of wholeness.

As the body was being carried along the road, the number of those bearing it was almost beyond counting. Noble matrons, wearing the adornments of their garments, offered cloaks, coverings of gold and silk, and ornaments to be placed upon the martyr’s bier. Each woman rejoiced that she was better in merit if she had first offered her vow to the Lord in honor of the martyr.

In honor of the most blessed martyr, by order of Bishop Ansoald and through the work of Abbot Audulf, father of the monastery, a building of extraordinary size was constructed. Its architecture was unlike the construction of all other basilicas.

The aforementioned bishop, wishing to fulfill his vow, came to this place with all the priests of his church, a company of nobles, and a great crowd of people. With great praises he buried there the holy body of the blessed martyr. At that place the heights of miracles are at work.

There, to the praise of Christ’s name, a joyful procession continually takes place, and it is granted that, for the healing of the people and the forgiveness of sins, all who approach in faith may obtain the fulfillment of their prayers.

Our Lord reigns, to whom belong honor and dominion, strength and power, forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER XXI

The time of the martyrdom, and so forth.

The martyrdom of Saint Leodegarius was completed on the fifth day before the Nones of October, and the dedication of his basilica on the third day before the Kalends of November; the translation of the holy body, however, took place in the middle of March.

## CONSOLATORY LETTER

Which Saint Leodegarius, bishop of the Aedui, sent to his mother, who was at Soissons in the monastery of the maidens, after the death of his brother Gairenus, after the loss of his eyes and the cutting of his lips.
