> **Note [Col. 0373C].** Ebroin founded at Soissons the monastery of Saint Mary for girls, of the order of Saint Benedict, which has flourished down to the present day, together with his wife Leutrude and his son Bovo. At first it was established in the narrow central island of the river Aisne outside the city, and afterward within the walls of the city itself. “When this monastery had thus been founded,” says the writer of the *Life of Saint Drauscio*, “Drausius gathered there a very large company of nuns and appointed over them an abbess named Aetheria (called Itheria by Leodegarius above), whom he had taken for himself from the devout monastery of Jouarre.”

> Melchior Reginald preserves, in his *Summary of the History of Soissons*, a privilege granted to this same monastery by Drausius; a fuller version is found in Bollandus, under 5 March and in the additions. It is dated “at Augusta Suessionum, in the fourteenth year of the reign of our lord King Chlothar,” and orders that the girls consecrated to God should serve “according to the rule of Saint Benedict, in the manner of the monastery of Luxeuil, which the blessed Columbanus governed.” Leodegarius above calls this same rule “the holy rule.”

> Sigrada, the mother of Leodegarius, had gone there before he began to be persecuted by Ebroin—unless, perhaps, having been exiled there by Ebroin, she willingly withdrew into the religious life.

(From Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict.) (C)

[Col. 0373B] **1.** To the lady and most holy mother Sigrada, who formerly through kinship of the flesh, but now through union of the spirit, has become a true mother; and fulfilled is that which the holy Truth says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew 12:50).

Leodegarius, servant of the servants of Jesus Christ our Savior, sends you grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. I give thanks to my God, who has not taken his mercy away from me, but has given joy and gladness to my hearing in return for our faith and patience amid all his persecutions and tribulations [Bolland.: your persecutions and tribulations], which you endured in the example of the just judgment of God, so that you might be deemed worthy of the kingdom of God. In that kingdom our Lord Jesus Christ chose you before the foundation of the world and granted you not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him.

If there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort from love, any fellowship of the spirit, any tender mercies in him, you have fulfilled the joy of the saints, and all sadness has been turned into gladness, because there was no reason for you to grieve, as the most blessed Peter says: “Though now for a little while, if necessary, you are grieved by various trials, so that the testing of your faith, much more precious than gold tested by fire, may be found” (1 Peter 1:6–7). Blessed Paul likewise bears witness, saying: “For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure,” etc. (2 Corinthians 4:17). And elsewhere: “Remember the former days, in which, after you were enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings,” etc. (Hebrews 10:32). And so that perseverance and reward might remain forever, he added, saying: “Therefore do not abandon your confidence, which has a great reward. For you need patience, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise. For yet a very little while, and the one who is to come will come; the righteous person lives by faith. But if he draws back, my soul will have no pleasure in him. We, however, are not of those who draw back to perdition, but of those who have faith for the gaining of the soul” (ibid., verses 35–39).

**2.** O lady, how great a joy you ought to have in the Lord, neither tongue can express nor page contain. You have abandoned what had to be abandoned; you have obtained what your soul desired. The Lord heard your prayer and saw your tears, which you shed before him after enduring many things; and whatever seemed for a little while to hinder you from attaining eternal blessedness, he cut away from you, so that, released from the bond of relatives and free from every fetter of this world, you might be at leisure and live for the Lord, and taste how sweet Christ is.

He is our God; he is our King; he is our Redeemer; he is the way, the truth, and the life in the knowledge of God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. He must be served forever. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Psalm 115:12). Indicating what should be rendered, he immediately adds: “I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (ibid., verse 13).

**3.** O happy death, which grants life! Happy loss of possessions, which will restore everlasting riches! Happy sorrow, which brings the joy of angels! You have now experienced how greatly the most merciful Lord Jesus Christ has taken pity on you: he has granted you spiritual devotion, observance of holy discipline, and contempt for the world; he has rescued the children of your womb from the distress of this age and from the error of the present life; and he has given the hope of eternal life to those whom you might have mourned as dead had you left them surviving in the world. For them you should not be sorrowful, but should offer manifold thanksgiving to God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Behold, the darkness that obscured the pupil of the soul has been removed; behold, the fascination and care of the present life have been cast aside. Now the naked man has no struggle to which his hand can cling, as he bears Christ’s cross after taking up the light yoke [Note: Bollandus conjectures *luctans*, “struggling.” Editorial note].

**4.** Therefore, following the Lord, with his mercy going before us, let us proceed fearlessly to the contest. He is faithful and will give us victory, because he himself will fight for us and will swiftly crush Satan beneath our feet. Behold how God calls his soldiers to battle, for whom he has prepared crowns after victory; and he clothes them with such weapons as their enemies do not possess: the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, and the helmet of salvation, with which they can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Let them pray at every moment in the Spirit with every prayer and supplication, and remain watchful in it.

**5.** Our King wishes to find in his soldiers nothing of the old weapons, nor anything of the old clothing, but wishes to test them in battle after they have been renewed. And if anything remains—God forbid—of the old custom, even if it seems small, it produces the greatest harm, especially if there is any hatred in the heart toward enemies. May God turn this away from the minds of faithful Christians.

For what virtue can be more perfect than, by loving one’s enemies, to deserve to become a child of God, and, by forgiving a debt, to deserve release from the bond of one’s sins? The Lord says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant will be also” (John 12:26). Hear him teaching what path he should be followed when he was going to the cross: “Lord Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

If the author of eternal life, who assumed flesh from the Virgin without the stain of sin, prayed for his enemies, how much more ought we, who are full of sins, to love our enemies and pray for them, so that, by imitating and following the Lord, we may deserve to have a share in his kingdom with the saints? And if there are some whom the perversity of their life has separated from our communion, nevertheless they are not to be hated for what they were created to be; rather, they are to be loved for the sake of God’s commandments.

**6.** Above all, one must beware that those whom divine mercy has freed from concern for temporal affairs do not in any way return to them, either in body or in mind. And if there are things that are lawfully owed, let them be sold, given, or even distributed to the poor with all speed [Note: Perhaps “when they have been added.” Bollandus], so that the mind may grow fervent toward the treasure of the heavenly kingdom and eternal blessedness.

In this example Mary obeyed: she sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his word, while Martha was busy with much service. She stood and said: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me.” The Lord answered her: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:39–43).

With such a blaze of love Mary longed inwardly that she even abstained from bodily service to the Lord and contemplated the power of his divinity alone, insofar as the Lord granted it to her. Therefore whoever has deserved to rise to this contemplation, and is hindered by evil obstacles, ought, while devoting himself day and night to psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs and observing obedience to the holy rule, to await the coming Lord with a burning lamp, so that when he comes and knocks, the door may immediately be opened to him. Nothing is better than the fear of God; nothing is sweeter than to breathe freely in his commandments.

**7.** O good lady, what the merciful Lord has prepared for you, eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor can it enter into the human heart. Hear and listen to how the Lord has rewarded you in the present life.

In place of the service of maidservants, he has given you all the holy brothers, who pray for you daily. In place of the service of female servants, he has given you holy sisters, whose companionship you may enjoy. In place of the labor of the present life, he has given you rest in the monastic community. In place of the loss of possessions, he has given you divine Scripture, holy meditation, and constant prayer. In place of your parents, you have the venerable and holy lady Itheria, the abbess: she is your mother, your sister, and your daughter.

You should therefore repay her in kind, because, as I am certain in Christ Jesus, you have one heart and one soul. For this reason I trust that you have accepted everything in this way, because all things have been bestowed on me by Christ through your prayer and holiness, not through my merits but solely through the mercy of Christ.

“Trustworthy is the saying and worthy of complete acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I received mercy, so that in me, the most merciful Jesus might display his patience, for the consolation of all sinners and the hope of forgiveness” (1 Timothy 1:15–16).

Because we possess little earthly substance, we have sent you something from the treasures of the sacred Scriptures. When you have read and heard it, give thanks to the Lord throughout the eternal ages. Amen.

[Note: In the Codex of Bonneval, and likewise in the Angevin, Dijon, and other manuscripts that list the bishops who were present at each synod and promulgated its canons, the following is found at the end: “The consent of Lord Leodegarius, bishop of Autun. I, Leodegarius, although an unworthy sinner and bishop, with the consent of my brothers have promised, and it has pleased us that this should be observed perpetually.” This subscription may perhaps be understood to belong to our present council. Jacob Sirmond.

To the canons edited above, Pierre de La Lande, a distinguished man, adds another from a collection of canons in the Thuana Library. Since it is there called the fourteenth, it is clear that formerly there were more than now survive, and that not all concerned monastic discipline. That they were dictated by Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, is evident from two indices of this collection. The first contains the chapters of the Greek and Latin canons, and at its end are these words: “Canons of Autun of Saint Leodegarius, bishop.” The second index reads: “The bishops who dictated these canons, whose names are missing.” At the end of this index one reads: “The consent and confirmation of Lord Leodegarius, bishop of Autun.” Labbe and Cossart.]

# SOME CANONS OF THE SYNOD CELEBRATED BY SAINT LEODEGARIUS

*(From Mansi, Expanded Collection of Councils.)*

[Col. 0377]

## NOTICE

[Col. 0377A]

In the most ancient collection of canons from the library of the church of Angers, under title XLIV, *On Monks and Monasteries*, several canons from this synod are produced. They all concern monastic discipline and are inscribed: “Canons of Autun of Saint Leodegarius, bishop.”

They are not all transcribed there, however. After omitting some, the collection gives only those that follow. Then, after repeating the inscription already given, it lists the canons in the order in which it found them. We too judge that they should be reproduced here, as a precious monument of antiquity and a clear testimony to the concern of Saint Leodegarius to restore and strengthen monastic discipline in his diocese.

[Col. 0377]

## [CANONS]

[Col. 0377]

**I.** The first title of monastic discipline is this: abbots or monks must possess nothing privately, and monks must receive their customary food and clothing from the abbot.

[lacuna]

**V.** No one among them is to dare to have godchildren.

**VI.** They are not to be found wandering about in cities. But if they are sent for the sake of the monastery’s needs, they are to be directed with letters from their abbot written to the city’s archdeacon.

[lacuna]

**VIII.** They are to be obedient to their abbot and provost.

[lacuna]

**X.** No one is to presume to maintain familiar relations with external women; and whoever is found doing so is to be corrected with greater severity. Women are under no circumstances to be permitted to enter a monastery of monks.

We establish and decree that no one is to presume to retain another man’s monk without the permission of his abbot. But when one is found wandering, he is to be recalled to his own cell and there disciplined according to the merits of his faults.

[lacuna]

**XV.** Concerning abbots and monks, it is fitting that they observe the following: whatever the canonical order or the rule [Note: “The order of the canons or the rule,” in the Einsiedeln manuscript cited by Mabillon] of Saint Benedict teaches, they must fulfill and guard in every respect. For if all these things are lawfully preserved among abbots and monasteries, then, by God’s favor, the number of monks will increase, and the whole world will be free from harmful contagions through their constant prayers.

Let all the monks be entirely obedient; let them shine with the grace of frugality; let them be fervent in the work of God, devoted to prayer, and steadfast in charity, lest through negligence or disobedience they become food for the enemy who goes about roaring and seeking whom he may devour. Let them have one heart and one soul. Let no one call anything his own, but let everything be common to them. Let them labor in common and be wholly devoted to hospitality.

Whoever attempts, by any transgression, to annul what we have dictated by God’s command for the confirmation of the monastic rule—if he is an abbot, let him be suspended from the power of communion for one year; if a provost, for two years; if a monk, let him either be beaten with rods or be suspended from communion [Note: “And from the table,” Einsiedeln manuscript], the Mass, and charity for three years.

For it is just that the seeds of vices, as they begin to steal in, should be cut away with the sickle of justice, lest, while they are nourished under the pretense of continence, they become so wild that they cannot even be cut down with axes.

[Note: The following canon also seems to belong to the synod of Autun of Saint Leodegarius. It is cited in another collection of canons from the library of Saint Benignus at Dijon and in others, and is called the first canon of Autun:]

## Canons of Autun, first series

If any priest, deacon, subdeacon, or cleric does not faithfully recite the creed which the apostles delivered under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and the faith of Saint Athanasius the bishop, let him be condemned by the bishop.

[Note: Burchard, in his *Collection of Canons*, book XIX, chapter 74, cites a canon from the Council of Autun, or, which is the same thing, the Council of Aedui, canon V. Although he took it from the council of Saint Leodegarius, it is not found there, even though it cannot conveniently be referred to any other council—for before Burchard no other Council of Autun is recorded. I therefore judged that it should rightly be referred here.

Ivo, and Labbe after him, gives a fifth canon of Autun of Saint Leodegarius that is entirely different from Burchard’s canon. But it is established that these collectors of decrees were not infrequently mistaken in assigning the numbers of canons.]

## Canon of Autun

**XIV.** Secular persons who have not received communion at Christmas, Easter, or Pentecost are not to live among Catholics. No priest who is filled with food or drunk with wine is to presume to handle the sacrifices or celebrate Mass; if anyone presumes to do so, let him lose his dignity. Women ought not to enter the altar area.

## From the Council of Aedui

**Canon V.** If any of those who serve at the Lord’s altar should suddenly fall through the lamentable weakness of the flesh, and, with the Lord looking favorably upon them, should repent worthily, so that, after mortifying the body, they offer the sacrifice of a contrite heart to the Lord, it shall remain within the bishop’s power either not to suspend those who are truly afflicted for long, or to separate the negligent from the body of the Church for an extended period.

This is to be done, however, in such a way that they may recover the places of their former offices, but may not thereafter be promoted to higher offices. If they relapse, like dogs returning to their vomit, and, like swine, emerge from their wallowing, they shall not only lose the dignity of their office, but shall receive holy communion only at the time of death.

[Col. 0379]

[Note: Published by Perardus (*Historical Monuments of Burgundy*, p. 3), whose reading we follow, and by Miraeus (*Diplomatic Works*), with the discrepancies we have placed in the margin.

Cointius and Mabillon undertook to examine it. Cointius (*Annals*, vol. III, p. 581), following Perardus, declared this to be the work of a modern author. Mabillon (*Annals*, vol. I, p. 418) acknowledged that the chronological figures were corrupt, but maintained that the substance of the testament was authentic on the basis of later instruments.

Among his posthumous works (*Annals*, vol. I, p. 530) there is also a letter in which he defends the chronological figures, though not all of them. It was not customary in this period to reckon years from the Incarnation; moreover, the year of Christ 653 does not coincide with the reign of Theuderic III, nor can the tenth indiction or the period of Leudesius, mayor of the palace, easily be reconciled with these data. He therefore thinks these marks should be deleted.

Miraeus agrees with him; in his text no chronological marks appear at all, except the seventh year of Leodegarius’s episcopate and the third year of King Theuderic. These two, however, do not agree: Leodegarius’s seventh episcopal year corresponds to A.D. 665 (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 350).

Mabillon indeed orders that the seventeenth year of his episcopate be read in place of the seventh, and conjectures that a crossed-out numeral was omitted by copyists in the apographs. He correctly connects the third year of King Theuderic with A.D. 676, in which year he believes Leodegarius’s testament should be placed. But this cannot stand, since from 674 onward Leodegarius had already been seized by Ebroin and thrown into prison, until he was killed after his eyes had been torn out. Brequigny.

Amid the doubts of such distinguished men, we have scarcely dared to attempt a new path for bringing together—and perhaps bringing back to the truth—the various opinions scattered here and there. Nevertheless, it has seemed to us at least tenable, or probable, that three chronological indications must be distinguished in this instrument.

1. Some refer to its original composition: namely, the notable confirmation by fifty-four bishops mentioned near the end, and perhaps the seventh year of Leodegarius’s episcopate, in accordance with the view of those—including Mabillon in the preface to volume II of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*—who assign the beginning of his episcopate to 659 and the council under Saint Leodegarius to 665.

2. Other indications refer to the final confirmation of this little document: namely, the third year of Theuderic’s reign and the synod of Christiac, which were inserted only at the end, as though by a second hand.

3. Finally, other indications placed at the beginning are quite certainly spurious, added by another interpolator and, unless I am mistaken, by the notary who in the tenth century recopied this instrument in the archive of the church of Aedui and produced several copies of it, when the matter, fiercely disputed on one side by the bishops and on the other by the counts of Aedui, was referred to Pope John VIII for settlement.

Given these facts, since the instrument was publicly confirmed by the aforementioned Pope John VIII, and since an enduring tradition concerning his authority remained firm in the Church of Aedui despite many attacks, indeed since the register instituted by Saint Leodegarius remained in force for many generations and continued until the fourteenth century under the name of the Denarii of Saint Leodegarius, nothing now prevents even a stricter critic from entirely adopting the opinion of the celebrated Mabillon: namely, that this instrument is defective in certain chronological indications but, in substance, should be regarded as sound and genuine.]

# THE TESTAMENT OF SAINT LEODEGARIUS

*(From D. Pitra, History of Saint Leger; Perardus, Historical Monuments of Burgundy, p. 3; Miraeus, Diplomatic Works.)*

*(Sixteenth-century old translation—from the manuscript History of the Bishops of Aedui.)*

[Note: The Latin and French versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## [TESTAMENT]

[Col. 0379B]

[In the year of the Incarnation of God and our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ 653, in the tenth indiction, with Theuderic, son of the glorious King Clothar, reigning, and Leudesius, son of Erchinoald, being mayor of the palace [Note: Miraeus entirely omitted all these words, enclosed in brackets as improperly added, and thought they should be printed in italics],] I, Leodegarius, although an unworthy bishop of Aedui, in the seventh year [Note: Mabillon adds “seventeenth”] of my episcopate, considering the various changes of earthly affairs, as well as the unavoidable end of death and the dreadful hour of judgment, terrible to all, and at the same time returning for these and similar matters to that teaching which commands: “Give, and it will be given to you,” and “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, who may receive you into heaven” (Luke 16:9); and remembering the warning of Wisdom: “A man’s riches are the ransom of his soul, and just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Proverbs 13:8);

for the love of the Divinity, for the remission of sins, and also in pious remembrance of Lord Clothar and Queen Valdechildis; for the welfare of King Theuderic, his kingdom, and all his nobles; especially for those who assisted and worked with us in the matters to be declared and acquired, I give, hand over, transfer, and establish as heir the church of blessed Nazarius, the title of my episcopate, from my possessions.

That is to say, the estate of Mariniac, which lies on the river Stantia [Miraeus: Sconem] [Note: The river Stantia, now commonly called the Canche], which the aforesaid queen transferred from her own property into my ownership and granted me by a royal charter; and likewise the estate of Tiliniac [Note: Commonly Tillenay], which comes to me by maternal right from my grandparents and great-grandparents and lies on the river Saône [Note: Commonly the Saône]; and also Olgea and the estate of Cananis [Note: Miraeus: Canapis; an estate which I acquired from Bodilo and Sigrada, devoted to God. Its land lies both below the fortress of Dijon and around it] [Note: Olgea is absent from Miraeus and has hitherto been unknown to me].

These estates, together with their livestock [Note: “And chapels with their servants,” Miraeus and the old translator. “With cattle,” in another reading. *Catallum* means the same as *capitale*, all property consisting of livestock. From *capitale* came *captale*, from *captale* *catallum*; compare French *chatel* and *catel*. Cangius. A French word of the same kind and origin, referring to the same property of an estate, is *cheptel*. It is worth noting that the old translator, like Miraeus, read “chapels with servants”], servants of both sexes, vineyards, meadows, waters, ponds, streams and backflows, woods, and pastures for larger and smaller livestock, we transfer, separate, and convey from our own property to the status of our register, which we built at the entrance of the church of Saint Nazarius, with all its appurtenances, on the following condition:

[Col. 0381D]

[Note: “By Bercarius, provost of the same church,” according to Miraeus and the old translator.

“It is certain that, besides the central charitable establishment founded at Saint-Andoche and the register of Saint-Nazarius, there were four small charitable establishments or deaconries, situated at the city’s four principal gates.

It was in the deaconry of the Saint-André gate, a little outside the city, near the field of executions, that Saint Racho was buried. In the Middle Ages this deaconry was given to La Charité-sur-Loire; it formed part of the charitable establishments of Besançon, Nevers, and even England, which constituted the endowment of La Charité-sur-Loire, as may be verified in the list of Cluniac priories (*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, pp. 1717–1719).

Near the Temple of Janus, another place of execution and justice, there was a charitable establishment still existing in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, as several documents from that period attest. When this establishment had completely disappeared, the rights and duties it represented were transferred to a house situated at the entrance to the cloister, toward the Bancs gate. The most distinctive right of the owner of the house called Genetage was to wash the bishop’s feet when that prelate took possession of his see.

Among the ancients, this act of washing the feet was the most expressive symbol of hospitality practiced, and one of the duties most strongly recommended to deacons serving in the deaconries.

The third deaconry stood where the hospital cemetery is now located, below the Rome gate. In the twelfth century the establishment was moved to the place called Mal-Dieu or Saint-Laurent.

The fourth was near Saint-Andoche, toward Fleury or Parpas.

We owe this note and several pieces of information of this kind to the gracious friendship of Abbé Devoucoux, canon of Autun, who made a special study of the antiquities of the Aedui.”]

forty brothers may receive daily rations and stipends at all times from Bercarius, provost of the same church, and from his successors, whom our successor bishops shall appoint, so that they may pray more freely for the salvation of the kingdom, its princes, and the whole world belonging to God [Miraeus: God].

But if any member of the senior hereditary families, or any person whatsoever, should presume to violate this common almsgiving of ours and the charter of this instrument, let him know that, as guilty of treason, he is to be punished before the mayor of the palace either by death or by a fine of one hundred pounds of gold.

As for our successor bishops, we wish them to observe these provisions, just as we have also bestowed many things upon them and just as they shall judge these matters worthy before God. But if thereafter anyone’s obstinacy should rise up against these provisions, let him know that he will also be condemned by the fifty-four fellow bishops who were assembled by our princes at Christiac [Note: Mabillon: Cressiac; absent from Miraeus]—in whose presence, or on whose advice, we made this donation to the church and register which we established—and by our authority, although we are at the point of death, and by the invocation of the Holy Trinity and the power of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

He shall be eternally condemned with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, who kept the money box, stole the Lord’s possessions and those of the poor, and with Dathan and Abiron, whom the earth swallowed alive in an unheard-of and desperate death, as a terror to all the living, unless he repents with worthy satisfaction. He shall be punished forever. Amen. Amen.

[Note: From these words, as from the words above—“for the salvation of the kingdom and its princes”—one may rightly conclude that great peace prevailed among the Frankish kings when this was written, and therefore that, in its substance, it was written at the beginning of Leodegarius’s episcopate, when Clothar in Neustria and Childeric in Austrasia were reigning in fraternal peace.]

Done publicly at Christiac, in the third year of the reign of King Theuderic. I, [Note: “Bishop” is absent from Miraeus] Bishop Leodegarius, subscribe to and personally confirm this donation made under anathema.

## [TESTAMENT]

[Col. 0379B]

[In the year of the Incarnation of our Savior Jesus Christ, 653, in the second indiction, with Theuderic, son of King Clothar, reigning, and Landegesus, son of Herchion, being mayor of the palace.] I, Leger, although an unworthy bishop of Autun, and in the seventh year of my episcopate, considering the changing transformations of earthly things and the unavoidable end of death, and the fearful hour of God’s judgment, likewise, for these and similar matters, returning to that teaching which says and commands: “Give, and it shall be given to you,” and “Make for yourselves friends from unrighteousness, who will receive you into heaven”; and remembering what is written: “The riches of a man are the ransom of his soul, and just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin”;

for love of divine goodness; for the remission of the sins of Lord Clothar and Queen Zelchedis; for the welfare of King Theuderic, his kingdom, and all his princes and lords, especially his lineage, who have been our coadjutors, collaborators, and donors in these goods; I give, transfer, and make heir the church of Saint Nazarius, the title of my bishopric, of all my possessions, namely:

The estate of Marignac on the river Sicanan, afterward called the Rouche, which the aforesaid queen gave me from her own property, authenticated by the royal seal; likewise the village of Telma, which comes to me through my mother and my great-grandparents, situated on the river Saône; and the village of Canabis, afterward called Chenôve, which I acquired from Baudillon and Sigrada, whose land lies both below Dijon Castle and around it.

All these villages and chapels, with their people of whatever sex, land, vineyard, countryside, two ponds, streams, woods, and pastures, great and small, we transfer from our own estate into the *matricule* which we have established at the gate of the aforesaid Saint Nazarius, with all its dependencies.

On this condition: forty brothers, each in his turn, shall receive his daily ration and stipend at all times from Bercarius, provost of the aforesaid church, and from his successors, whom our successor bishops shall appoint and establish in charge of this property, so that they may pray more solemnly to God for the welfare of the kingdom, its princes, and the whole world.

If anyone of my closest heirs or their descendants, or anyone at all, should presume to break or violate this almsgiving of ours and this testamentary codicil, let him know that he will be punished as one convicted and found guilty of treason, either by death or by a fine of one hundred pounds of gold payable to the mayor of the palace.

We also wish our successor bishops to be bound by all this, just as we have made many donations in their favor, without considering whether this was worthy before God. If any one of them should rise and rebel against this will of mine with obstinate purpose, let him know that he is excommunicated by the authority of fifty-four bishops assembled by our princes at Christiac, on whose counsel we made this donation to our aforesaid church and register.

Likewise, by our authority, although we are the last of them, we excommunicate them on behalf of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, to be eternally damned with the traitor Judas, who carried the money box and stole the goods of Our Lord, and with Dathan and Abiron, whom the earth swallowed alive in an unheard-of and desperate death, to the terror and dismay of the whole world, unless they return to repentance and complete satisfaction.

Done at the aforesaid Christiac, publicly, in the third year of King Theuderic. I, Leger, bishop, subscribe this donation with my own hand, under penalty of excommunication.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 683. POPE LEO II

[Col. 0383]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON POPE LEO II

*(From Mansi, Expanded Collection of Councils.)*
[Col. 0383C] **[Note: Leo. From the second canon of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo below it is plainly gathered that Leo was created pope in the year of our Lord 683. Since he held the papal see for only ten months and was still alive at the time the Fourteenth Council of Toledo was held—as [**Note: Binius errs here; he himself later places this Fourteenth Council of Toledo under Benedict II. Mansi.**] canon 2 of that same council plainly indicates [Col. 0383C]—it is known with the greatest certainty that he did not ascend the apostolic throne before the year of our Lord 683. Sev. Bin.]**

Leo [**Note: Codex Luc., Leo the Younger**], a Sicilian by nationality, the son of Paul, [**Note: He held the see for ten months and seventeen days. He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of July; on that day he is reckoned among the saints in the ecclesiastical calendars. He held the see for ten months and eight days. Baron. year 684, no. 1. Id.**] held the see for ten months, seventeen [eighteen] days. He was a most eloquent man, sufficiently instructed in the divine Scriptures, learned in the Greek and Latin languages, outstanding in chant and psalmody, and refined by the most subtle exercise in their meanings. He was also a scholar in language, polished by extensive reading for eloquence [**polished**], [Col. 0384C] an exhorter to every good work, imparting to many a most flourishing knowledge [**he ardently imparted their knowledge to the common people**], a lover of poverty, and a provider for the needy [**a provider for the poor**], concerned not only through the piety of his mind but also through the labor of his zeal.

[**Note: He received the holy Sixth Synod. When Leo, after the emperor had confirmed his election and had entrusted him with administering the pontificate, had received permission from that same emperor for the legates of the apostolic see to return to Rome—whom, perhaps at the persuasion of Theodore, bishop of Constantinople, he had until then detained longer at Constantinople—the emperor entrusted to them the synodal acts, written in Greek and corrupted by Theodore, as we have said, though not corrected, as he himself pretended, to be conveyed to the pope. When Saint Leo received them, he rendered them into Latin. But did he approve the same forgery corrupted by Theodore the Monothelite? Unless one declares Leo’s first letter spurious, it is necessary, according to the common judgment, to affirm that Saint Leo confirmed those acts which he had received through the legates, and which Theodore had corrupted by inserting the name of Honorius and had enlarged with numerous additions. Thus, in Leo’s defense, one must say either that the necessity of the times compelled him to undergo that most unjust condition, so that, had he not done so, the condemned heresy would have revived and the synodal acts would have had to be abolished; or that Leo, ignorant of past events, did not know the genuine acts of the synod and the defense by which Pope John and Abbot Maximus had explained and defended the letters of Honorius. But since neither alternative would leave the pope free from blame, one of the two must necessarily be maintained: either that the council’s acts had indeed remained uncorrupted before Leo’s time and were corrupted only later, when, twenty years afterward, Leo’s letter was used to begin attacking the Monothelite decrees of the synod; or that Leo’s letter itself, as Baronius asserts, is spurious. I shall discuss below in the notes to that letter the conjectures by which the author of the Annals confirms this opinion. Id.]**

He received the holy Sixth Synod, which by God’s providence had recently been celebrated in the imperial [Col. 0385A] city, written in the Greek language, under the direction and presidency of the most devout and most merciful great prince Constantine within his royal palace, called the Trullus; together with him were the legates of the apostolic see and two patriarchs, namely the patriarchs of Constantinople and Antioch, as well as one hundred and fifty bishops. At this synod Cyrus, Sergius, [**Note: Honorius. Baronius holds that in those acts which were presented to Pope Leo, the name of Honorius was deceitfully added by Theodore’s forgery. What others judge concerning this matter I have stated above. Id.**] Honorius, and Pyrrhus, Paul and Peter, as well as Macarius with his disciple Stephen, and also Polychronius, a new Simon, were condemned—those who said or preached, or were going to preach or defend anew, that there was one will and one operation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

But so that now two wills and operations of Christ, our dispenser and God our Savior, might also be proclaimed, as the same synod most carefully translated into Latin declares. Nevertheless, [**Note: Codex Luc., “which he also translated most carefully into Latin.” “Nevertheless,” etc.**] the above-mentioned defenders of the evils of heresy [**Note: Codex Luc., “of the heresy of Macarius, Stephen, Polychronius, and Anastasius, since they were unwilling,” etc.**], since they were unwilling to withdraw from their purpose, were confined in different monasteries [**in Rome by the greater number of the above-mentioned defenders, namely Macarius, Stephen, Polychronius, and Anastasius, since they were unwilling to withdraw from their purpose**].

That most holy man Leo absolved two men for receiving communion, who had been sent from the imperial city to Rome with the aforesaid Macarius and the others, because they had not yet been anathematized by the synod: namely Anastasius the presbyter and Leontius, deacon of the church of Constantinople. On the holy day of the Theophany they set forth their faith in writings of their own, in accordance with what the holy synod had decreed, anathematizing all [**the two**] heretics, as well as the aforesaid accomplices whom the holy synod or the apostolic see had anathematized.

During his pontificate, by the imperial command of the most merciful [**Note: Codex Luc., “most devout.”**] [Col. 0387A] prince, the church of Ravenna was restored under the administration of the apostolic see, after the death [**Codex Luc., “after the death.”**] of the [**Ravennate**] archbishop, who had been elected and was to come to the city of Rome for ordination according to the ancient custom [**to be ordained**]. He issued a decree, preserved in the archive of the church, that whoever was ordained archbishop should not be required, by any custom, to pay anything for the use of the pallium or for the church’s various offices. He also prohibited the anniversary or commemoration of the former bishop Maurus [**Codex Luc., “and he prohibited the celebration of the anniversary of the former bishop Maurus”]. Moreover, they restored the charter of autocephaly which they had obtained for themselves in order to remove scandals from the apostolic see.

He built a church in the city of Rome near Saint Bibiana, where he also deposited the bodies of the holy martyrs Simplicius, Faustinus, and Beatrix, together with those of other martyrs, and dedicated it in the name of the blessed apostle Paul. At the command of this gracious pontiff, a church was built near the Golden Veil in honor of the blessed Sebastian [Col. 0388A], and likewise one in honor of the martyr George.

During his pontificate, [**Note: Codex Luc., “he dedicated it on the twenty-second day of February, where he also offered gifts. During his pontificate [an intervening passage is missing].”**] on the sixteenth day [**Note: Codex Luc., “on the fifteenth day”**] of April, in the eleventh indiction, the moon suffered an eclipse. After the Lord’s Supper, for nearly the whole night it struggled with a blood-red appearance; and only after cockcrow did it gradually begin to clear and return to its proper aspect [**state**] [**Note: Codex Luc. does not contain “aspect.”**].

He held one ordination in the month of June [**May**], on the twenty-seventh day: nine presbyters, three deacons [**Note: Codex Luc., twenty-five deacons**], and twenty-three bishops in various places. He was also buried at Saint Peter the Apostle, on the fifth day before the Nones of July [**the fourth day before the Kalends of July**]. The episcopate remained vacant for two months [**Note: Codex Luc., eleven months**] and twenty-two days.

This most holy man, mentioned above, was ordained by three bishops: Andrew of Ostia, John of Porto [**who took part in the Sixth Synod**], and Placentinus of Velletri, because the Alban church had no bishop at all [**Note: Codex Luc., “because it had no Alban bishop at all.”**].

[**Note: In the entire succession of the Roman pontiffs scarcely anything appears more confused in the ancient and recent writers of history than the beginning, deeds, and death of Pope Leo II. Therefore, in order to satisfy myself and my readers, I shall touch upon and note a few matters here in advance, in outline (*ἀρκοστιγῶς*).**

**At the beginning of the year of Christ 682, on 10 January, in the tenth indiction, Pope Agatho died, or at least was buried, after occupying the see for three years, six months, and twenty-five days. By then, from 16 September, the Council of Constantinople III, or the Sixth Ecumenical Council, had been completed, while among the Latins the ninth indiction was still running. Shortly after Agatho’s death, Leo II was elected Roman pontiff.**

**When Constantine the emperor heard of Agatho’s death and Leo’s election, he wrote to Leo on 13 April—not December, as the common edition reads—a letter which survives in Greek and Latin at the end of the eighteenth session. In July of the tenth indiction, the legates sent by Pope Agatho to the general council in 680 returned, bringing its acts together with Constantine’s letter. On 15 August, in the tenth indiction, Leo II, having received confirmation, was ordained pontiff, among others by John, bishop of Porto [Col. 0386B], who had been one of the legates. It must therefore be said that he held the see for one year, ten months, and fourteen days.**

**Nevertheless, his consecration is commonly assigned to 15 August of the following year, 683, when the eleventh indiction was drawing to a close. If this is true, it must be admitted that Leo II, elected by the Romans and meanwhile performing the pontifical office with due dignity, scarcely—or hardly at all—consented to his consecration until about a year and six months later, perhaps out of the greatest humility of spirit or for other reasons.**

**In the year 683, indiction 11, on 16 April, after the Lord’s Supper, the moon struggled for nearly the whole night with a blood-red appearance, and did not begin to emerge from the darkness until cockcrow—that is, shortly after midnight, when the sixth day of the greater week had already begun—as Anastasius testifies. This eclipse therefore occurred during the pontificate of Leo, whether he was merely elected or had also been consecrated, depending on the different methods of reckoning.**

**In May of that indiction—not the tenth but the eleventh—after examining at leisure the acts of the Sixth Synod which the returning legates had brought with the emperor’s letter in July of the preceding year, Leo, whether merely elected or already solemnly ordained in the preceding year, wrote back to the emperor and approved what had been done in the Sixth Ecumenical Council. There are also those who would have Leo die in June of this year.**

**Toward the autumn of 683, with the twelfth indiction already begun, as is reasonable to believe, Leo sent the acts of the Ecumenical Council to Spain through Peter the regionary, notary of the Holy Roman Church, together with the letters which survive. But since they had been brought, on 4 November, after the Thirteenth Council of Toledo had been completed and the Fathers had been dismissed to their own cities, their reading was postponed until November of the following year, when the Fourteenth Council of Toledo was held, in the era 722.**

**Meanwhile, on 28 June 684, while the twelfth indiction was passing, Leo died. Benedict II succeeded him on 20 August; Benedict wrote to the same Peter the regionary and to King Ervig, and died on 7 May 685, in the thirteenth indiction. Those chronologists, however, who maintain that Leo died in 683 assign Benedict’s accession to 683 and assert that his pontificate, or that of his successor, lasted one year longer. But it is not necessary to overstep the limits which we and others have established.**

**For since Peter the regionary, sent by Leo to Spain in 683, remained there after the completion of the Thirteenth Council of Toledo until the Spanish bishops should subscribe to the acts of the Ecumenical Synod at the annual meeting of the next, the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, and since, upon hearing of Leo’s death, Peter perhaps pursued Leo’s instructions somewhat slowly, Benedict, his successor, shortly after his election or ordination, encouraged him by the surviving letter to carry out the ministry entrusted to him with the greatest devotion for the firmness of the apostolic faith. He did so in November of the year 684, as may be understood from canon 2 of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo.**]**

[Col. 0387]

# Letters of Pope Leo II

[**Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.**] (C, S)

## First Letter of the Emperor Constantine to Pope Leo II

[**Note: Sacred rescript. Baronius asserts, on the following conjectures, that this letter of Constantine to Leo is suspect in matters of faith. First, although Leo was created in August, the emperor did not inform him of what had been done at the synod until four months later, namely in December, whereas he ought immediately to have informed him of the state of the faith. Second, at the beginning of the letter it is stated that it was given to Leo in the tenth indiction, at which time Leo was not yet pope. For [Col. 0388D] Leo’s first year fell at the end of the eleventh indiction and the beginning of the twelfth, as is clear from what precedes. Third, the letter says that the emperor had written to Agatho concerning the convocation of the synod, whereas it is certain from what precedes that he wrote on this matter not to Agatho but to Pope Donus. See Baronius, year 683, nos. 6 and 8. Sev. Bin.]**

Copy of the divine sacred rescript of the most devout and Christ-loving emperor Constantine to Leo, the most holy and blessed pope of elder Rome, sent through those who had been dispatched from there by the surviving Agatho of holy memory. It was sent on 13 December, in the tenth indiction.

[Col. 0388C]

To Leo, the most holy and blessed archbishop of the ancient and most renowned city of Rome, and ecumenical pope.

Desiring the eternal kingdom and blessedness of heaven, and directing our pious purposes toward spiritual adoption, we meditate upon and undertake those things by which our efforts may attain a good outcome. What, then, did the Lord promise in the Gospels? “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5).

Desiring to attain this promise, by which we are raised to divine kinship and obtain the nobility of adoption, and imitating Christ himself, from whom we have received our crown and who reconciled all things to God in himself, we strive to lead our Christ-loving commonwealth toward peace and concord. Above all, however, we are concerned for the order of the holy churches of God, and we continually take care that we may establish unity of faith.

Therefore we were greatly angered, and perhaps could no longer endure, that this division, strengthened by the passage of time, should continue to such an extent that unbelievers mocked those who love Christ and took pleasure in the hatred of Christians toward one another. Abandoning their attack upon the unbelievers, the Christians armed their tongues against one another like sharpened razors, with curses and insults, and tore the faith apart through dissension. These things began before our time and advanced to such wickedness that the evil seemed incurable. To restrain it was difficult, but to neglect it was still more grievous. They provoked God, and they also provoked our gentleness.

We therefore resolved to cure the disease oppressing the churches of God by urging the priests of God, the worshipers of God, and the physicians of such evils to deliberate and confer. The Church has often been dangerously sick from the assaults of heresies; yet it received no other medicine for orthodoxy than the exhortation of devout and Christ-loving emperors and the agreement and assemblies of priests inspired by God.

For this reason we urged the blessedness of the holy Pope Agatho in our pious letters to send some who would represent his person. We also instructed the other most holy prelates that each should summon the venerable priests subject to him, so that all might assemble in our royal city preserved by God, in order to cut away the uselessness of the rotten and scandalous member, especially since it refused to accept treatment, and to strengthen the rest of Christ’s body entirely with the teaching and poultices of piety. For it is fitting to say evangelically that one member should perish so that the fullness of the whole Church may be preserved.

When, at our invitation and command, those who belonged to the party of your blessedness, together with the most holy patriarchs who occupy the sees alongside and after it, and all the other gracious bishops, had assembled and taken their seats together with our tranquil devotion to piety, a discussion of the faith was held.

When those who represented the holy Pope Agatho immediately presented his petition to our authority—namely, Abundantius, John, and John, most holy bishops; Theodore and George, most beloved presbyters; John, the most beloved archdeacon; Constantine, the venerable subdeacon; Theodore, the most beloved presbyter of the church of Ravenna; and those with them—they offered it to our serenity. When we ordered it to be read aloud before all who were present, we saw in it the mark of a sound and uncorrupted faith.

For when we weighed the evangelical and apostolic words and compared them with what had been established and defined by the holy and universal councils, and when, moreover, we compared the testimonies it presented with the writings of the Fathers, nothing discordant was found in it; rather, we perceived in it the rule of the true confession, wholly unchanged.

It was as though we beheld with the eyes of our minds Peter himself, the leader of the apostolic choir and overseer of the first chair, divinely declaring the mystery of the entire dispensation and addressing Christ through these letters: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16). For the sacred letter portrayed the whole Christ for us in its exposition. We received all of it with willing and sincere minds and embraced it, as it were, with the arms of our soul as Peter himself.

Only Macarius, together with those who had been carried away with him, abandoned us—he who, though he bore the name, was not blessed, and who had been bishop of the city of Antioch. By opposing Christ he withdrew himself from Christ’s yoke, and he leapt away from the priestly assembly. For he utterly refused to assent to the most sacred letters of Agatho, as though raging against the chief and foremost Peter himself.

There was no lack of admonition, and frequent exhortation was offered to him. We showed him every path of return. What did we not say? What did we not attempt and threaten, especially regarding those things which separate a man from the priestly college? We grieved for him—for why should we not? Out of compassion our inward parts were torn when he was separated from the Lord’s flock. But his face became like that of a harlot, and he put on the countenance of shamelessness; together with exhortation he rejected piety. He did not understand so as to understand, and he abhorred the holy word.

Why should we prolong this account, when the acts explain these matters more precisely and carefully? Since they have been sent to you, investigate through them the knowledge of all that was raised and discussed.

But because he became so hardened, stretched an iron sinew across his neck, made his face brazen, made his ears heavy so that he would not hear, and set his heart stubbornly so as not to hear the law—for the law goes forth from Zion, the doctrine from the summit of the apostolic mountain—the holy and universal council therefore stripped that same madman Macarius, together with the associates of his heresy, of the priestly habit.

All the others jointly petitioned our serenity in written prayers that we should send them to your blessedness. We therefore did so and sent them to you, entrusting their entire case to your paternal judgment.

The holy council issued a sacred and venerable definition, to which we also subscribed and which we confirmed by our pious edicts, exhorting all our Christ-loving people to obey the faith prescribed there and to invent no heretical sect whatsoever.

Glory to God, who does glorious things and has preserved the faith among us intact. For how could he not have done so upon that rock on which he founded the Church and concerning which he foretold that the gates of hell—that is, the plots of heretics—would never prevail against it? From that rock, as from the vaults of heaven, the word of the true confession shone forth, enlightened the souls of those who love Christ, and revived orthodoxy, which had grown cold.

With God’s help we have completed these things according to our desire and brought Christ’s sheep into one flock. They are no longer deceived by hireling shepherds, who are not shepherds, nor are they prey to wolves; rather, they are pastured by the one and only good shepherd, with whom you too have been commanded to feed the flock and to lay down your life for the sheep.

Therefore act manfully, take courage, and gird yourself with the sword of the word; sharpen it with divine zeal. Stand firm as a champion of piety and strive to cut away every heretical utterance and introduction. Just as Peter formerly struck and removed with the sword the organ of Jewish hearing, signifying beforehand the deafness of the legal and servile synagogue, so extend the axe of the Spirit. Every tree producing the fruit of heresy either transplant through instruction, or cut down by canonical penalties and consign to the fire of the Gehenna to come.

When all that damages the faith has been cut away on every side, may the body of the Church be strong and whole, bound and joined together by the peace of the Spirit. While that peace stands firm and unmoved, the faction and resistance of the enemies are shaken; the throne of our serenity is established upon the rock of faith; the counsels and efforts of our power are directed toward what is beneficial; and the condition of the entire Roman commonwealth is made tranquil together with the tranquility of the faith.

We further exhort your most sacred eminence to send without delay the apocrisiary appointed by you, so that he may reside in our royal city, preserved by God, and in all matters that arise—whether dogmatic, canonical, or wholly ecclesiastical—represent and exercise the person of your holiness.

Farewell in the Lord, most blessed one, and devote yourself with the greatest zeal, according to our authority, to praying for us.

**Subscription of the most devout emperor:**

May God preserve you for many years, most holy and blessed Father.

## Greek Version

**Copy of the divine sacred rescript of the most devout and Christ-loving emperor Constantine, addressed to Leo, the most holy and blessed pope of elder Rome, sent through the synodal envoys dispatched from there by Agatho, who was still alive and of holy memory. It was sent on the thirteenth day of December, in the tenth indiction.**

[Col. 0387C]

To Leo, the most holy and blessed archbishop of the ancient and most renowned city of Rome, and ecumenical pope.

Desiring the unending kingdom and blessedness of heaven, and directing our pious purpose toward spiritual adoption, we meditate upon and undertake those things which promise the attainment of what we seek. What, then, did the Lord promise in the Gospels? “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons [Col. 0387D] of God.”

Desiring to enter into this promise, which raises us to divine kinship and grants us the nobility of adoption, and imitating Christ himself, who crowned us and reconciled all things to God in himself, we strive to lead our Christ-loving commonwealth toward peace and concord. Above all, we care for the good order of God’s holy churches and continually take thought to establish the unity of the faith.

Therefore we were exceedingly and beyond measure angry, and could no longer endure that so great a division, strengthened by time, should continue to grow, so that unbelievers mocked those who love Christ and regarded the hatred of Christians toward one another as a pleasure. Abandoning their opposition to those unbelievers, they armed their tongues against one another with insults like a sharpened razor and divided the faith through dissension.

These things began before our time and advanced to such wickedness that the disease seemed incurable. To stop it was difficult, but not to stop it was more difficult still. They provoked God, and they also provoked our gentleness.

We therefore determined to heal the disease afflicting the churches of God in no other way than by urging the priests and servants of God, the physicians of such disorders, to examine the matter. The Church has often been dangerously sick from the attacks of heresies, but it received no other healing for orthodoxy than the summons of devout and Christ-loving emperors and the assent and assemblies of priests bearing God within them.

Accordingly, by our pious letters we urged the blessedness of the holy Pope Agatho to send certain men who would represent his person. We instructed the other most holy presidents that each should summon the most devout priests under his authority and gather them all together in our city, protected by God and imperial, so that they might cut out the uselessness of the rotten or scandalous member, especially when it most refused to accept treatment, and heal the rest of Christ’s body with the doctrines and poultices of piety.

For it is fitting to say in evangelical fashion, “that one member should perish and the fullness of the whole Church be preserved.” And when, according to our invitation and command, those belonging to the party of your blessedness, together with the most holy patriarchs who share your throne and sit beside you, and all the other most devout bishops, had assembled and taken their seats with our tranquil devotion, we examined the matter of the faith.

Immediately, when those representing the holy Pope Agatho brought forward his petition to our authority—namely Abundantius, John, and John, the most holy bishops; Theodore and George, the most beloved presbyters; John, the most beloved archdeacon; Constantine, the most reverent subdeacon; Theodore, the most beloved presbyter of the church of Ravenna; and those with them—they extended it before our tranquility. When we ordered it to be read aloud in the hearing of all, we discerned in it the stamp of sound and unadulterated faith.

For when we examined the evangelical and apostolic utterances, compared them with the decisions and definitions established by the holy and ecumenical councils, and compared the quotations it contained with the writings of the Fathers, finding nothing discordant, we perceived in it the statement of the true confession, unaltered.

We seemed to contemplate with the eyes of the mind Peter himself, the leader of the apostolic choir and first occupant of the chief seat, declaring the mystery of the entire dispensation as theology and addressing Christ through the writings: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

His sacred letter depicted the whole Christ for us through its word. We received it all gladly and sincerely, and embraced it with the arms of the soul as though we had received Peter himself.

Only Macarius, together with those whom he had dragged along, the man who was not blessed, deserted us. He had presided over Antioch. He withdrew himself in opposition from Christ’s yoke and leapt away from the priestly assembly, for he would not consent at all to the most holy writings of Agatho, as though raging against Peter himself, the chief apostle.

Great admonition and great entreaty were offered to him. We pointed out every path of return. What did we not say? What did we not devise concerning those things which especially [lacuna] separate a man from the priestly assembly? We grieved for him [variant: “for we grieved for him”]—for how could we not?—and our inward parts were torn by compassion when he was separated from the Lord’s flock.

But he acquired the face of a harlot and put on the countenance of shamelessness; together with entreaty he repelled piety. He did not understand so as to understand, and he despised the holy word.

Why should we lengthen our explanation of these matters, concerning which the account of what was done speaks in greater detail? Through the acts sent to you, you may trace the knowledge of everything that was raised.

But because he became so hardened, stretched an iron sinew across his neck, made his face bronze, made his ears heavy so as not to hear, and set his heart disobedient so as not to heed the law—for the law goes forth from Zion, the doctrines from the summit of the apostolic mountain—the holy and ecumenical council therefore stripped that same deranged Macarius, together with his fellow heretics, of the priestly garb.

All together they entreated our serenity in written petition that we should send these men to your blessedness. We did so and sent them to you, entrusting their entire case to your paternal judgment.

The holy synod proclaimed a divine and venerable decree, to which we also subscribed and which we confirmed through our pious edicts, urging all our Christ-loving people to follow the faith inscribed in it and to devise no heretical invention whatsoever.

Glory to God, who does glorious things, who has preserved the faith among you inviolate. For how could it not have done so, when he founded the Church upon the rock and foretold that the gates of Hades would not overcome it through heretical ambushes? From that rock, as from the arches of heaven, the word of the true confession shone forth, enlightened the souls of those who love Christ, and rekindled orthodoxy, which had grown cold.

With God inclining toward our purpose, we have completed these things and gathered Christ’s sheep into one flock. They are no longer deceived by hirelings who are not shepherds, nor are they exposed as prey to wolves; they are shepherded by the one and only good shepherd, with whom you have also been appointed to feed the flock and commanded to lay down your life for the sheep.

Therefore be courageous and strong, gird on the sword of the word, and sharpen it with divine zeal. Stand firm as a champion of piety and be eager to cut away every heretical utterance and introduction. As Peter formerly struck the organ of Jewish hearing with the sword and removed it, prefiguring the deafness of the legal and servile synagogue, so raise the axe of the Spirit.

Every tree that produces the fruit of heresy either transplant through instruction or cut down by canonical punishments and consign to the fire of the Gehenna to come. Thus, when everything that harms the faith has been cut away on every side, the body of the Church may be strong and whole, tightened and joined together by the peace of the Spirit.

While that peace remains unmoved, the stance and resistance of the enemies are shaken; the throne of our serenity is supported upon the rock of faith; the counsels and movements of our power are directed toward what is beneficial; and the condition of the entire Roman commonwealth shares in the serenity of the faith.

We urge your most holy eminence to send without delay the apocrisiary appointed by you, so that he may dwell in our royal city protected by God and, in every matter that arises—whether dogmatic, canonical, or simply ecclesiastical—represent the person of your holiness.

Be strong in the Lord, most blessed one, and rise with the utmost zeal to pray for our power.

**The signature of the most devout emperor.**

May the Divine One guard you for many years, most holy and most blessed Father.

## Letter II: Of the Same Emperor to the Roman Synod

[Col. 0393]

Copy of the divine command of the lord Constantine, addressed to the synod of the ancient apostolic see of Rome through the same men who had been sent from there to the synod.

[Col. 0393C]

To all the most holy councils everywhere belonging to the synod of the apostolic see [**In Codex Bell., “In the name of the Lord our God and Savior Jesus Christ, the most devout emperor Flavius Constantine, faithful emperor in Jesus Christ.”**]

Your sacred assembly appeared illustrious and beautiful. The Holy Spirit gathered it for the Church and armed it with the words of piety, by which the enemies lying in wait for the faith were defeated, with the teachers [**G., “the leader”**] of the priestly and pontifical order assisting the common father, indeed the universal father [**G., “assisting the universal patriarch”**], with whom you have learned to make peace and have been taught to fight together.

“For everything there is a season” (Ecclesiastes 3), as Solomon seems to say. It is good to have peace with all who are in concord concerning piety; but it is better to fight when the work of peace produces agreement in evil.

For the Lord says: “I have not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword” [Col. 0396A] (Matthew 10). The word of faith is likened to a two-edged sword, dividing and distinguishing the believer from the unbeliever; separating the kinship and agreement that incline toward impiety, but joining and attaching us to God through peace and love directed toward him.

Nothing is closer to him than the love which exists toward him through faith [**nothing is more precious than love**]. For neither father nor mother, who undergoes labor together with her children; nor brothers, bound by the necessity of nature but separated by their wills; nor the thick and not insensible bond of a legal marriage, which dissolves affection when one party is released—none of these makes men participants in the divine nature. Only faith and love toward God do so; through their embrace we have been reborn and restored, and through our devotion to the Creator we have been deemed worthy [**made worthy**].

The Savior himself said: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10).

If, then, those who have undertaken to search out the evangelical path and have obtained the pontificate of apostolic dignity despise everything and, if necessary for friendship with God, endure condemnation to the extremity of death, have they not learned to endure and undertake the hardest things when they see the faith being ravaged, through which friendship with God has been gained, and when they observe the Church attacked by the invasions of heretics?

When they perceive truth cast down by falsehood, do you suppose that, postponing offense, they will be reconciled to their enemies, forget the evangelical command, and leave the guilty unpunished? [**And how would such a thing be followed and remain unpunished?**] By no means. Taking up the armor of the Spirit, they strive to resist those who have attempted to fight against them.

Your priestly college did this also and fought for piety, assisting the common father. It bravely defeated the ranks of the heretics; but the speech is restrained by the memory of what must be said, and is prevented from going farther. For the explanation that follows is a mournful tragedy.

The bishops became inventors of heresies. Instead of peace they announced contention to the people; instead of wheat they sowed weeds in the furrows of the Church. They mixed wine with water and gave their neighbor a turbid drink of destruction. Like a wolf imitating a lamb, they feigned falsehood as truth and [**a wolf as a lamb, and a lamb as a wolf; falsehood as truth, and truth as falsehood**] rejected truth as falsehood.

All ecclesiastical affairs were thrown into confusion, since no one was present to distinguish what could cause harm. And since these things were being arranged in this way, and impiety was devouring piety, we went where it was fitting for us to direct our steps. We raised the eyes of our mind to the only wise God, who knows these things, and from him we asked in continual prayers that he grant a solution to those matters which, through interpretation, introduce doubt.

Therefore, enlightened by his sign [**spirit**], we recognize that the eyes of the Church—that is, the priests—were stirred to contemplate the truth.

We fight for the faith, attend to piety, and take care above all for the ecclesiastical condition all the more intensely because, although surrounded by civil concerns and drawn away by military deliberations, we did not fail to gather this supreme priestly assembly, so that the distance between the churches might be driven away and joined together by the bond of peace.

For we trust that our Roman commonwealth, beloved by Christ, has been joined together in the peace of the faith, and that your venerable council has now been assembled in the same way. You too were present with the universal prince of shepherds, speaking divinely with him both in spirit and in writing.

We received letters sent to us not only from his blessedness but also from your holiness. They were produced and read, and they displayed the true style of truth and portrayed the orthodox faith. They were all set forth harmoniously and without disagreement for imitation, and they agree both with synodal and with patristic teachings.

We did not neglect them but compared them [**examined them**] with the greatest care. Therefore we all agreed in mind and speech and made the same confession. We marveled exceedingly at the report of Agatho as though it were the voice of the divine Peter himself, for no one differed except one.

No one perished from among all except the son of destruction, the father of stubbornness; and he, together with his own disciples, was taken away by an angel fit for him and by his accursed company [**G., “was cut off by a destructive angel and from the most sacred company”**]. It is fitting to lament him with the prophet, since we grieved with him:

“How you have fallen from heaven, from the summit of the priesthood, O Lucifer, who rose in the morning! You were appointed to illumine the souls of the faithful with the most certain light of knowledge, yet, exalted by empty doctrines, you set the seat of arrogance among the clouds. How have you slipped into flight, avoiding the angelic ranks that imitate the multitude of such priests? Raised on the wings of pride to a lofty ruin, you have alienated yourself from the mystical table, becoming an imitator of the Jewish falling away.

“How did you not receive the exhortation of your brothers, who were celebrating the imperial and apostolic solemnity? How did you resist, though beloved by those who love you and invite you to repentance? Does one who falls not rise again, or does one who turns away not return? Why do you turn away with wicked turning, remain held in your heretical purpose, and refuse to return to piety? You are surely confounded, convicted in the matters concerning which you taught falsely.

“O madness and blindness at once! The two indeed appear to be the same. One misleads the bodily steps, the other the steps of the soul. He was not ashamed to teach badly and was ashamed to be taught well—this man who became bishop of the Antiochenes, Macarius, whom one ought not to call Macarius [**blessed**], and those who departed with him from Christ’s order. By the common judgment of the universal assembly they were rejected from priestly dignity and handed over to the examination of the most holy pope.”

The most holy council decreed an adorably sacred and venerable definition [Col. 0400A], agreeing with and following both the most holy councils and the approved Fathers. Our empire subscribed to it and confirmed it by our pious edicts, through which the whole fullness of the Church is pacified by your prayers.

Where are those who fashioned the scandal of a shattered condition [**G., heresy**]? Where are those who clothed themselves in feigned reverence [**religion**] as a pretext for false doctrine? The veils of persons have been removed; the falsehoods of the deceivers have been convicted. The wolf has cast off his skin, and the naked wolf is exposed. This remains when what had been concealed comes to light.

Pretense has been condemned; truth acts confidently. Falsehood has been exterminated, and the doctrines of the one who sowed weeds have been cut away. The wheat, which is the people beloved by Christ, is gathered into one granary, namely, the Church of Christ.

The light of orthodox faith has risen; the darkness of error is submerged. Sadness is transformed, mourning into joy, grief into gladness; everything passes over into better things.

Therefore, congratulating the churches of God which have lately received the grace of peace, we address you according to apostolic tradition: “Rejoice, rejoice, and again I say, rejoice” (Philippians 4). For the Trinity has granted us threefold joy.

Farewell, most sacred helpers of piety, praying for our empire.

**And in the emperor’s own hand:** “We have read.”

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of January at Constantinople, in the imperial palace, under the most devout and perpetual Augustus, the emperor Constantine, in the twenty-ninth year; and after his consulship, in the thirteenth year, in the tenth indiction.

## Greek Version

**Greek copy of the divine sacred rescript of the same most devout and Christ-loving emperor Constantine, addressed to the holy synod of the apostolic throne of Rome and sent through the same synodal envoys.**

[Col. 0394C]

To all the holy councils everywhere belonging to the synod of the apostolic throne.

Your radiant and universally renowned holy assembly, which the Holy Spirit gathered on behalf of the Church and armed with the words of piety, has by these means fought down those lying in ambush against the faith, with the commander, the hierarch, and the ecumenical patriarch standing beside you in battle. You have learned to make peace with him and have been taught to fight alongside him.

“For everything there is a season,” Solomon seems to say. [Col. 0394D] It was good indeed to be at peace with everyone, but only with those who agree in piety; better still is to fight when making peace produces agreement in evil. Accordingly, the Lord also said: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword.” The word of faith is compared to a two-edged sword, dividing and distinguishing the faithful from the unbelieving; cutting apart kinship and alliance with impiety, but making us familiar with and joining us to God through peace and love toward him.

For nothing is more precious than love for him through faith. Neither father nor mother, who together with their children undergo the pains of childbirth; nor brothers, bound together by the necessity of nature and dissolving their separate wills; nor the thick and scarcely unfeeling bond of legal marriage, which dissolves the relationship when one partner is separated—none of these makes us participants in the divine nature. Faith alone, directed toward God, and love do so. From their interweaving we have been reborn and refashioned, and have been deemed worthy of intimacy with the Creator.

For the Savior himself said: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me.”

If, then, those who choose to follow the evangelical path and who have received the dignity of the apostolic hierarchy despise everything, endure everything, and, if need be, gladly accept condemnation to the ultimate death because of their love for God, what will they not be willing both to suffer and to do when they see the faith—through which love for God is obtained—being attacked; when they behold the Church being ravaged by assaults of heretics; when they perceive truth being struck down by falsehood? Will they abandon the fight and the defense, reconcile themselves to the enemies, and forget the evangelical commandment? [Col. 0395C] How could this be without guilt or punishment? By no means. Therefore, having taken up the armor of the Spirit, they arm themselves against those arrayed against them.

This indeed—this very thing—your most holy assembly also demonstrated. It fought on behalf of piety by fighting alongside the common father and cutting down the heretical phalanx. But at the recollection of what is about to be said, the discourse contracts and is restrained from proceeding farther. For what follows is the description of a mournful tragedy.

The hierarchs became leaders of heresy. Instead of peace, they proclaimed strife to the people; instead of wheat, they sowed weeds in the furrows of the churches; they mixed wine with water and gave their neighbor a turbid drink of ruin.
