Likewise, in February, after the feast of Saint Valentine, a star appeared in the west at midday and declined toward the eastern regions. After this, Mount Bebius [perhaps Vesuvius], which is in Campania, erupted during the day in March, and all the surrounding places were devastated by the dust of its ash.

He bestowed honors on the clergy of the various orders on the holy day of Easter [Col. 0424A]. Immediately afterward he fell ill [Note: [Col. 0424A] Codex Luc., “being held by illness”], and died a few days later. He left thirty pounds of gold to the entire clergy, the monastery, the *diaconia* [Note: [Col. 0424A] Codex Luc., “to the deacons”], and the *mansionarii*. He made twelve bishops in various places. He was also buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the eighth day before the Ides of May, and the episcopate remained vacant for two months and fifteen days.

[Col. 0423]

## LETTERS OF BENEDICT II

*(C, S)*
[Note: [Col. 0423C] “That these two letters are not genuine but were substituted under Benedict’s name is demonstrated in broad daylight, says Baronius, by the synodal acts of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, since they profess to have received the synodal acts of the Constantinopolitan Council through Leo II’s delegate. If Leo had already done this and they had received the same documents, why was it necessary for Benedict to send them there again? It could have happened that circumstances made it necessary for them to be sent again, but this should have been expressed in the letter; nor should he have so plainly implied that he was transmitting the synodal acts of the Sixth Council to Spain for the first time. But since the latter letter is plainly identical with that written by Leo II to King Ervig, consult the censure concerning its forgery, which is set out above.”]

The following is a true and genuine letter of Pope Benedict, which he sent to the bishops of Spain, urging them to clarify what they had written somewhat obscurely concerning the will and three other chapters. It is mentioned only briefly in the acts of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo. See what I said above in the notes to the Life of Benedict II. SEV. BIN.

# FIRST LETTER. BENEDICT II TO PETER, REGIONAL NOTARY

[Col. 0423B]

He urges him to ensure that the synodal acts of the Sixth Council—on whose account he had been sent to Spain by Leo II—be authenticated by the signatures of the Spanish bishops.

Benedict the presbyter, and, in the name of God, elect of the holy apostolic see, to Peter, regional notary.

In accordance with the purpose for which the lord Pope Leo, of apostolic memory, determined that your energetic self should go to the province of Spain—to the most excellent and most Christian king, the most holy archbishops, and all the prelates of the churches established there, as well as to the glorious count—in order to make known the definition of the venerable Sixth Council, together with the acclamation, also called the *prosphoneticum*, of the most reverend bishops who assembled in that council gathered by God, addressed to the most merciful ruler and sent generally everywhere by the edict of that most devout ruler, carry out with the greatest zeal for piety the ministry entrusted to you for the firmness of our apostolic faith.

With the utmost diligence and vigilance, arrange also for the subscriptions of the most reverend bishops to be appended after the same synodal definition, so that both those most reverend bishops and the entire religious province through them may be shown to be sharers with us in the Catholic and apostolic tradition and faith; and so that, before God, to whose glory the praise and stability of the Christian faith are directed, commendation and acceptance may bring them the salvation of souls. Therefore, adorning the pious office you have undertaken with vigilance and skill, hasten to complete it; for you are storing up for yourself the fruit of a good work, and you are providing those who receive it with the means of attaining the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom through confession of the right and apostolic faith.

# SECOND LETTER. BENEDICT II TO ERVIG, THE KING

[Col. 0424C]

He indicates that he is sending Peter, the regional notary, who would bring with him the definition of the Sixth Council, together with the edict of the Emperor Constantine and the acclamatory booklet of that same council addressed to the emperor.

It appears above, col. 418, under Leo II’s own name. It begins as follows: “Since God, the one King of all, exists,” etc.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 686. POPE JOHN V

[Col. 0425]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON POPE JOHN V

*(From Mansi, Expanded Collection of the Councils)*

[Col. 0425A] [Note: [Col. 0425B] John. According to Anastasius, John V, the fifth of that name, was substituted for Benedict on 22 April in the year of the Lord 685. He was the first Roman pontiff consecrated through the unexpected authority of the Constantinopolitan emperor, and he took part in the holy Sixth Council, distinguished by the office of an apostolic legation. SEV. BIN.]

John, a Syrian by nationality, from the province of Antioch, son of Cyriacus, occupied the see for one year and nine [eleven] days. He was a very energetic man, endowed with learning, and entirely moderate. After the passing of many pontiffs—or many years—he was elected by the whole congregation in the church of the Savior called Constantiniana, according to the ancient custom, and was thereafter introduced into the episcopal residence.

While he was still a deacon, he was sent by Pope Agatho, of holy memory, to the royal city with other priests, representing the apostolic see at the holy Sixth Council, which had been assembled there through God’s providence [Cod. Luc. adds: “or celebrated”]. Afterward, when the most merciful ruler had released him, he brought great joy back with him to the Church. That is, he brought the holy Sixth Council itself, or the edict of the most merciful ruler confirming that same council.

He also brought other imperial commands relieving not a few of the grain assessments of the patrimonies of Sicily and Calabria, and likewise grain received [Cod. Luc.: “purchased”; another reading: “ordered grain”], as well as various other things that the Roman Church was annually in no way able [or “able”] to pay. He was consecrated by three bishops—the bishops of Ostia, Porto, and Velletri—just as his predecessor Pope Leo had been.

During his pontificate, the lord Justinian Augustus reigned, his father having died at the beginning of September, in the fourteenth indiction. [Col. 0426A] This most merciful ruler, with the Lord’s help, established peace with the Saracen people—who need not even be named—for ten years, by land and sea; moreover, after the province of Africa had been subdued, it was restored to the Roman Empire.

After many years had passed, he dealt with the transgression of the arrangement of the Church of Torres [in Sardinia], which Citonatus, archbishop of Cagliari, had carried out without the authority of the pontiff, since in ancient times that arrangement had belonged to the apostolic see and had been granted for a time to that Church. Later, because of the arrogance of the archbishops, they were suspended from that arrangement by papal commands, in accordance with the decision of Pope Martin, of holy memory.

After a council of priests had been held, he restored and confirmed Bishop Novellus, who had been ordained by that same archbishop, under the jurisdiction of the apostolic see. Their written declaration is preserved in the church archives [or “is kept”]. This most holy man was confined by a prolonged illness, so that he could scarcely even complete the ordination of priests.

He left to the entire clergy, monasteries, deacons, and mansionarii one thousand nine hundred solidi. He ordained thirteen bishops in various places. He was also buried at the blessed Apostle Peter on the second day of August, and the episcopate remained vacant for two months and eighteen days.

[Col. 0425]

[Note: [Col. 0425C] Exemplar. This letter appears suspect in faith, both because its chronological notice contains an obvious contradiction and because it is not credible that the emperor undertook these actions for the defense and faithful preservation of the acts of the Sixth Ecumenical Council, since Pope Nicholas I’s letter to the emperor Michael shows that he was not sound in the faith. Add that Anastasius, in the Life of Pope Conon, reports that either this letter or another of the same subject was written by the emperor to Pope Conon:

“He,” he says of Conon, “received the imperial command of the lord Justinian the ruler, in which he states that he had found the acts of the Sixth Council and had them in his possession—the acts which the lord Constantine, his father, of pious memory, had prepared—and his piety promised to guard and preserve them perpetually, undefiled and unshaken.”

On the authority of Anastasius this letter could be defended against forgery and surreptitious insertion, however defective its heading might perhaps be, if Pope Nicholas did not number its author among wicked and heretical emperors [Note: “Though he may have been bad in other matters, he was not so in matters concerning the faith sanctioned by the Sixth Council against the Monothelites.” MANSI.]. SEV. BIN.]

# EXEMPLAR OF THE DIVINE COMMAND OF JUSTINIAN AUGUSTUS

Addressed to John, Pope of the City of Rome, in confirmation of the Sixth Council of Constantinople.

[Col. 0425C] In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ: the Emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian, faithful in Jesus Christ, peaceful, pious, perpetual Augustus, [Col. 0426C] to John, the most holy and most blessed archbishop of the ancient, venerable city of Rome and universal pope.

[Col. 0427A] [Note: [Col. 0427B] The Greek text is not extant; this is an old Latin version from the earlier Royal edition. HARD.]

Since we have great zeal and great concern for the stability of the immaculate faith of Christians, we therefore trust that our most merciful God is the helper and protector of our serenity against every enemy of our commonwealth beloved by Christ. For it has become known to us that the synodal acts, and their definition—which, as is known, were established by the holy Sixth Council assembled in this God-preserved royal city during the time of our father, of holy memory—were sent back to certain judges of ours.

We certainly did not foresee that anyone else should retain them in his possession without our most pious serenity, since our God, in his abundant mercy, appointed us guardians of that same immaculate Christian faith. Accordingly, we immediately summoned our most holy and most blessed fathers and patriarchs, together with your Blessedness’s representative, the apocrisiarius; the most holy senate; the metropolitans and bishops beloved by God who reside here in the royal city; the military inhabitants of the holy palace; members of the popular associations and the excubitors; and also certain men from the armies beloved by Christ—from the imperial service preserved by God, from the Eastern [F: a conjunction is missing] and Thracian forces, likewise from the Armenian army, from the army of Italy, then from the Cabarisian and Septensian forces, as well as from Sardinia and the African army, who had come to our piety.

We ordered the aforesaid documents of the synodal acts to be brought forward and read aloud in the presence of all the persons mentioned above. After all had listened carefully, we caused them to sign the documents. The entire body of those who had heard them then handed the documents over to us, so that we might preserve them inviolate in our keeping and so that, at any time, those who do not wish to fear God might not be permitted to corrupt or alter anything contained in the aforesaid synodal acts.

These documents were fully and rightly defined in the time of our father, of holy memory, by approved holy fathers, who are known to have confirmed before our Lord Jesus Christ, the true God, the testimony of their own tongues and hands, and to have taught it in confession. We trust in our most merciful God that, for as long as our spirit, appointed by God, remains within us, we shall always preserve these documents undefiled and unaltered.

Therefore, in order to make known to your fatherly Blessedness the movements concerning this matter, we have taken care to inform your Blessedness of them.

And by the divine hand [or “divine hand”].

May the Divinity preserve you for many years, most holy and most blessed Father.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, at Constantinople, in the imperial palace, under the most pious and perpetual Augustus Justinian, in the second year of his reign and the second year after his consulship—that is, in the year of Christ 687—in the fifteenth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0427C] In the Bellovacensis manuscript the following words are appended:

“This codex was written in the time of Sergius, the most holy and most blessed pope, who died in the year 701, and is kept in the patriarchal residence of the holy Roman Church. Thanks be to God. [Col. 0428C] Amen.”]

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 690. SAINT JULIAN, BISHOP OF TOLEDO, TOGETHER WITH IDALIUS AND FELIX, BISHOPS OF BARCELONA AND TOLEDO

[Col. 0427]

# HISTORICAL NOTICES

*(From Antonio, Old Library of Spain)*

[Col. 0427C] Felix, himself once appointed to the same see, described Julian, the bishop of Toledo, in polished language, in the eulogy customarily appended to Hildefonsus’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. That this Julian was distinct from Julian Pomerius—whom Gennadius praised under the bare name of Pomerius [Note: *On Writers*, ch. 98] and whom Saint Isidore later restored to the catalogue of writers under the full name of Julian, surnamed Pomerius [Note: *On Writers*, ch. 12]—is beyond dispute. He was a writer of the fifth century, a Mauretanian who flourished in Gaul [Note: Nevertheless, Morales, *On Royal Deeds*, book XII, ch. 58; Vossius, *On Historical Literature*, book I, ch. 27; Baronius, under 8 March; Vasaeus, *Chronicle of Spain*, under the year 685; Padilla, *Ecclesiastical History of Spain*, seventh century, ch. 66.].

Nevertheless, many also maintain that the Julian of Toledo whom we are discussing was likewise surnamed Pomerius. Among them are Bellarmine [Note: *On Writers*, under the year 680], Labbe [Note: Dissertation, *On Writers*, vol. I, p. 652], and Barthius, *Adversaria*, book X, ch. 14. They rely on the testimony of Roderic of Toledo, who calls him this in book III, chapter 13, and says in book IV, chapter 3, that Urban, likewise bishop of Toledo, carried into Asturias, out of fear of the Moors, the writings of Saints Hildefonsus and Julian Pomerius. By that name, it is more likely than not that he intended no one other than our Julian.

But Roderic may plainly have been deceived by the ambiguity of the name, or some copyist may have disfigured his work by adding a spurious surname. At least, that author seems to have been responsible for others [Note: Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; and, apparently, Matamoros, *On Academies*; Roderic Sánchez of Palencia, *History of Spain*, part II, ch. 33; Alfonso de Cartagena, *Summary of the History of the Kings of Spain*, ch. 40; Lucio Marineo Siculo, *On the Affairs of Spain*, book V; Padilla, *On the Saints of Spain*, fol. 30; Eisengrein, *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*.] making one person out of two. They were further confirmed in this error by the fact that one wrote the *Prognosticum* of the future age, as appears from Felix, while the other wrote three books of *Prognostics* concerning contemplation of the future life, as appears from Honorius, following Isidore.

I have absolutely no doubt that, if this Julian, our bishop of Toledo, had borne the name Pomerius, Felix, the author of his Life, would not have concealed it. Indeed, the Pseudo-Julian in his *Chronicle*, no. 369, introduced a third Pomerius, not content with two. Yet the net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures, to use the language of Scripture.

Among later generations a report became widespread that Julian had been descended from Jews, as Roderic of Toledo himself puts it. Since the author of the Life omitted to record this, I see that some express doubt about it [Note: Vasaeus, under the year 685; Pisa, *History of Toledo*, book II, ch. 24; Tomás Tamayo, *The Truth of Dexter*, p. 125; Juan Tamayo, under 8 March.]. Nevertheless, more people believe Roderic [Note: Mariana, book VI, ch. 18; Morales, book XII, ch. 58; Diego Rodríguez de Almela, *Valerio of the Histories*, book I, ch. 5, title 1.]—and not without reason, since Isidore of Pacensis was an authority for the story in the same words [Note: Under the era 728, in the affairs of King Ervig].

Born, baptized, and educated at Toledo, he made remarkable progress in the study both of letters and of true wisdom under Eugenius II, Hildefonsus’s predecessor, together with the deacon Gudila, to whom he was bound by the closest bond of friendship. Both desired to devote themselves to the monastic life, but Felix says in the clearest terms that their devotion was frustrated. One might therefore rightly say that those who enroll Julian in the Benedictine catalogue were driven by a kind of uncontrollable impulse to favor their own cause [Note: Arnold Wion, *The Tree of Life*; Menard, book I of the *Observations on the Benedictine Martyrology*, fol. 206].

[Col. 0429C] It is therefore necessary that Julian, abbot of Saint Michael’s, was another person. He is read as having subscribed, among others, to the Eleventh Council of Toledo in that same Church of Toledo. He was a Levite, then a priest, and finally, after Quiricus—who died in 681—was elected bishop. In that priestly office he showed himself equipped with genuinely pastoral virtues, which the author of the Life enumerates individually, down to the third year of Egica, that is, the year 690 of human redemption and the final year of his episcopate.

He attended, and subscribed before the others, four councils of Toledo: the Twelfth, in 681; the Thirteenth, in 683; the Fourteenth, in 684, during the first, fourth, and fifth years of King Ervig; and the Fifteenth, in the first year of Egica, or 688 of Christian redemption.

He is listed among the saints not only in the Toletan Breviary on 8 March and in other churches of our region [Note: See Tamayo under this date, p. 125], but also in Usuard, on the sixth of the same month, as follows:

“At the city of Toledo, the death of Julian the bishop, who is held in the highest renown among the inhabitants of that place.”

Lippomano and Surius place him on 23 June, while the more recent martyrologies, together with the Roman Martyrology, place him on the eighth.

He left to posterity many monuments of his learning, though a large part of them has perished. From the list of these works, which Felix followed carefully, we know that he wrote filled with the abundance of the Holy Spirit and endowed, as Felix also says, with the overflowing fullness of a well-watered spring: in Latin, in a style elegant beyond the capacity of his age, and with an easy, copious, and pleasing intellect and expression, as Juan Mariana judged.

He has a book of *Prognostics of the Future Age*, addressed to Blessed Idalius, bishop of Barcelona, containing at its beginning a letter directed to him and a prayer. This *Prognostic of the Future Age* survives; that was the title given it by its author, as is clear from the letter of Idalius, bishop of Barcelona, at whose request Julian undertook the work. The letter was preserved for us by a codex of the monastery of Corvey, from which d’Achery inserted it into his *Spicilegium* (vol. I, p. 313). I believe this is the very letter sent to him—that is, to our Julian—by Idalius, which Felix mentions.

Felix accurately described the *Prognostic* in these words:

“The work of this codex is arranged in three books. Of these, the first has been published *On the Origin of Human Death*; the second, *On the Souls of the Dead, and Their Condition before the Resurrection of Their Bodies*; the third, *On the Final Resurrection of Bodies*.”

This division cannot have come from anyone other than the author, however much Felix may seem to imply otherwise. This is clear from the judgment of Idalius on the entire work, which we have set out below:

“In this work, although the first book may in some measure appear to inspire sinners with harshness and fear, the two books that follow raise the hearts of Christians with the greatest confidence through hope of the future resurrection and of the kingdom that Christ promised to give to the faithful.”

This *Prognostic* was published in volume nine of the *Library of the Fathers*. It had previously been published at Leipzig in Germany by Michael Blum in 1536, in quarto. Secondly, it was published at Paris in 1554, an edition mentioned by Morales (book XII, ch. 58). Andreas Resendius had this edition in view when, in his learned letter to Quevedo—worthy of such a man—he reported that, twenty years earlier, a Parisian guest had taken away his own codex of this book. He later said that he had received the book back in printed form, though it had not been cleansed of the errors with which it abounded.

Third, it was published at Douai in 1564 by Louis de Winde, though under the patronage and through the efforts of Boethius Epon, a most learned Belgian, who nevertheless seems to me to have been unaware of the earlier editions.

Manuscript codices of this work are preserved among us in the Cistercian monastery of Spina, one of which Morales saw [Note: He reports this in his unpublished account of his journey]. There, he asserts, another work entitled *On the Instruction of Novices* is placed before it. We ourselves saw one copy in quarto and another in octavo in the possession of Martín Vázquez Siruela of Seville, a prebendary and a most learned man. Another exists in the Basel library, of which Spizelius bears witness [Note: *Revealed Secrets of Libraries*, p. 40]. That is the other copy whose theft Resendius lamented.

He also wrote a book of *Responses*, addressed to the same Idalius mentioned above, in defense of the canons and laws that prohibit Christian slaves from serving unbelieving masters. This was established by the Third Council of Toledo, canon 14, and the Fourth, canon 66, and by laws 13 and 14—which are laws of Sisebut—title 2, book XII of the Visigothic Laws.

After all this, King Ervig, in the first year of his reign, renewed the same prohibition. The death penalty that Sisebut had imposed on transgressors was, however, removed and changed into a milder penalty, in laws 22, 13, and 16, title 3, of the same book XII. I hope that Julian illustrated and confirmed this law with ancient testimonies and suitable arguments in these *Responses*.

[Col. 0431A] The *Apologetic of the Faith*, which was addressed to Benedict, Pope of the City of Rome [Note: It does not survive; nevertheless, its subject and the occasion on which it was written are explained by T. II, editor of the edition of the Toletan Fathers, in the note to the Life, or Eulogy, of Saint Julian, p. 19, no. 9]. And on the occasion of this writing—

There was also another *Apologetic, On the Three Chapters*, concerning which the prelate of the City of Rome seemed, without sufficient reason, to have entertained doubts.

The matter stands as follows. Under Pope Agatho and the Emperor Constantine Pogonatus, the Sixth Ecumenical Council was held at Constantinople against the Monothelites, who denied that Christ possessed two wills corresponding to his two natures, divine and human. It was held in the year 680 and the following year.

Leo II, the pontiff who succeeded Agatho—who died in 682—after seven months in that same year, solemnly sent the principal part of its acts, namely the definition, to the Church of Spain, so that the decrees of the council might remain supported also by the authority of our own Church, as the Fathers of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo say in its second chapter.

García Loaysa published Leo’s letters to the Spanish bishops—one; another to Quiricus, then still living as bishop of Toledo; and a third to the count Simplicius—from a codex of the monastery of Saint John of the Kings at Toledo, in his notes on that council (p. 650). A fourth, addressed to King Ervig, was added by others. They all appear in the common editions of the councils [Note: Latest Paris edition, vol. VI, col. 1246]. It is not the place here to investigate whether Baronius unjustly excluded them from Leo’s monuments of established authenticity (under the year 683, no. 16, vol. VIII).

These letters of Leo were brought to Spain in the winter at the end of the year 683 or the beginning of 684, after the recently concluded Thirteenth Council of Toledo, which had been held in November 683 under King Ervig, when Julian was already bishop of Toledo, as may be gathered from canon 3 of the following Fourteenth Council.

Since it would have been inconvenient to summon once again, while the land was still gripped by the severe winter frost, as they say, the fathers who had dispersed from the city of Toledo and the national council, each to his own provincial assembly, Julian decided in the meantime to send our *Apologetic* to the same [Col. 0431C] Roman pontiff, as a confirmation of the Constantinopolitan faith, while awaiting an appropriate opportunity to convene a synod of the bishops of his diocese.

This *Apologetic* is mentioned in chapter 4 of the same Fourteenth Council of Toledo:

“Accordingly, at that time, satisfying the Roman pontiff with the responses of our apologetic reply, we decided to confirm those very acts [of Constantinople], etc.”

But to which pontiff? Not Leo, who had died shortly after sending the letter mentioned above—in the same year 683, in June—but Benedict II, his successor, who was created pontiff ten months after Leo’s death, in the year 684 [Note: Baronius, under the year 684, no. 2]. Felix expressly says this in his mention of the *Apologetic*.

A little later in the same year, a synod of the diocesan bishops of the province of Carthaginensis was convened by Julian himself—this was the Fourteenth Council of Toledo—and vicars of the metropolitans of the other provinces also attended in their name. The synod fully praised and approved the same Constantinopolitan acts (chapters 5 and following), as well as the *Apologetic* previously composed concerning them (chapter 11).

Benedict the pontiff, however, was not entirely satisfied with this writing of Julian’s *Apologetic*. Indeed, in writing back to Julian, he conveyed through one of Julian’s men certain points which seemed to him to deviate from the Church’s correct doctrine in the praised *Apologetic*: namely, that its author had said “will begot will” in divine matters, and likewise “wisdom, wisdom”; and that “there are three substances in Christ”—namely, body, soul, and divinity—along with two other points that we do not know.

After these matters had been set out more explicitly, given their correct meaning, and confirmed by testimonies of the ancient Fathers, Julian immediately prepared a response to Benedict. He mentions it himself through the voice of the Toletan Fathers who attended the Fifteenth Council. This was the other, or second, *Apologetic* mentioned by Felix, *On the Three Chapters*, concerning which the prelate of the City of Rome seemed, without sufficient reason, to have entertained doubts. The same Toletan fathers thought they would perform a worthwhile service if they inserted its wording or connected argument into the acts of that Fifteenth Council [Note: See what follows under the section “After this Symbol,” in Loaysa’s edition, p. 662].

This is correctly stated, as usual, by Ambrosius Morales, book XII, chapter 58, [Col. 0432B] and by others [Note: Baronius, under the year 685, nos. 5, 6, and 7; Loaysa, in his notes on the Fifteenth Council of Toledo; Binius, following Baronius, in his notes on the Life of Pope Benedict; Vázquez, part III, distinction 37, chapter 3, at the end; Padilla, seventh century, chapter 65].

Roderic of Toledo also relates the matter in book III, chapter 14:

“In his time”—that is, in the time of King Ervig—“the book *On the Three Substances*”—named after one of the three chapters, which perhaps had caused the greater disturbance—“which the most holy primate Julian had sent to Rome some time before, and which Benedict, the Roman pope, had ordered to be rejected because he had treated it less cautiously”—he does not imply that the matter had been carried as far as a formal condemnation—“because it said that will begot will: Saint Julian, by truthful testimonies, firmly established in this council, at the demand of the aforesaid ruler and through the statements of those whom he had sent to Rome, that it was true, through the utterances of those things [perhaps: those persons] which he had sent to Rome. He composed an *Apologetic* and sent it to Rome through his legates: a presbyter, a deacon, and a subdeacon, most learned men, servants of God in every respect, and instructed in the divine Scriptures. He sent with them also acclamatory verses, as he had formerly sent, *On the Praise of the Roman Emperor*.

“Rome received it worthily and piously and ordered it to be read by everyone. The emperor, by acclaiming, ‘Your praise, O God, is to the ends of the earth,’ caused it to be read repeatedly and made known. He also sent back a rescript to the lord Julian through the aforesaid legates, with thanks and honor, and declared that everything Julian had written was just and pious.”

[Note: [Col. 0432D] The final part reads very differently in Loaysa’s notes on the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, p. 682. In describing this passage, our author seems to have had before his eyes Roderic of Toledo’s *History*, book III, chapter 14, as it appears in volume II of *Hispania illustrata*, p. 61. The learned Flórez, vol. V, p. 298, follows Isidore of Pacensis and differs somewhat; this will be discussed more fully shortly.]

Caesar Baronius (for the year 685, nos. 5, 6, and 7) reproaches Roderic for having expressed Pope Benedict’s judgment concerning the Apologeticus too harshly, by using the term “condemnation,” and for having inserted it less cautiously than he ought, as he himself unwisely wrote. But the following words of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo concerning the same matter are plainly harsher in formulation; while omitting Benedict’s name, as was proper, they are far more pointed than Roderic’s words:

> “Now, if after these things anyone should disagree with the very doctrines of the Fathers by which these statements were set forth, we must no longer contend with such persons; rather, clinging directly to the footprints of our predecessors, our response will be exalted before the lovers of truth through divine judgment, even if by ignorant rivals it is judged obstinate.”

These words seemed to Juan de Mariana somewhat too free to befit Julian’s modesty—he was undoubtedly the author—in his conduct toward the Roman pontiff (*De rebus Hispaniae*, Book VI, chapter 18). [Note: “That discussion of Julian’s,” says Mariana (*De rebus Hispaniae* VI.18), “was celebrated with great praise by Sergius, Roman pontiff, Benedict having meanwhile died, as Roderic the bishop reports; it seemed to us somewhat too free to befit Julian’s modesty toward the Roman pontiff, supreme ruler of the Church. And indeed, few people concede to anyone else the praise of intellect; and it is difficult to maintain moderation in the heat of disputation. For Julian was at that time celebrated for the glory of his learning, etc.” Consider how much Cave builds upon this passage under the year 680, in his account of Julian of Toledo, whom he falsely calls “Pomerius,” saying in volume I, page 596:

> “In this final synod—that is, the Fifteenth Council of Toledo—Julian vigorously sought redress from Pope Benedict over his book *On Three Substances*, which Benedict had judged insufficiently orthodox after it had been brought to Italy. He served Benedict up to the Fathers of the council for ridicule as though he were some stupid doctor picked up from the crossroads, and demonstrated that the pontiff’s frivolous quibbles were to be disregarded; in them, one might say, there are almost as many blunders as words. But I pay no attention to that. I am more sharply wounded by the passage cited from Mariana. If I say that this eminent man has grievously fallen into error and has been conspicuously unjust to our Julian, I shall do so not gratuitously or of my own inclination, but compelled by love of the truth alone. The matter must be narrated in order. First of all, it must be noted from Felix that Julian wrote two Apologetic works, both of which Julian mentions in the Acts of the Fifteenth Synod, chapter 9, if we carefully weigh his somewhat obscure words.

> “The first was addressed privately to Leo II, who had sent him, for subscription by all the Fathers of Spain, the definition and acclamation, or *prosphoneticum*, of the Sixth General Council of Constantinople. Julian accepted the council’s definition, but modestly excused himself from compelling the Fathers to assemble again in synod, since they had only recently been dismissed, amid the severe heart of winter, from the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, in which they had taken part, and had scarcely yet returned to their own sees.

> “This first Apologeticus, which one might more properly call an apology—for the Greek word has both meanings—Julian more often calls the *Book of the Response of His Faith*. As the year of salvation 684 was drawing to a close, it was carried to Rome through Peter, the regional notary, who had brought the definition and *prosphoneticum* of the Constantinopolitan Council to Spain. At that time Benedict II had already succeeded Leo, who died in July of that same year, or was about to be appointed in his place.

> “In this Apologeticus, for the fuller explanation of the doctrine of Constantinople, Julian had written: ‘In divine matters, will begets will, just as wisdom begets wisdom.’

> “In the same year, 684, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, the Fourteenth Provincial Council of Carthaginensis was convened by Julian at Toledo. It consisted of seventeen bishops and was also attended by representatives of the metropolitans of the churches of Tarragona, Narbonne, Mérida, Braga, and Seville. At that council the definition and *prosphoneticum* of the Sixth Council of Constantinople were accepted by unanimous agreement of the Spanish Fathers as entirely consonant with the Nicene Council and with the general councils that had preceded it; they were subscribed and placed, after the Council of Chalcedon, in the rank, place, and order due to them.

> “At the beginning of the year of salvation 685, Julian arranged for the Acts of this Council of Toledo to be brought to Rome, sending a special messenger to Benedict, whom he himself calls ‘our man.’ The messenger presumably carried letters in which Julian declared that there were three substances in Christ, in order to refute the Apollinarians and, as he says, the hidden Manichaeans.

> “In Rome the Acts of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo were received with the greatest applause and acclamation from the Roman pontiff and all the orders. But as Julian’s messenger was preparing to return to Spain, Benedict dictated to him certain matters that he was to receive from Julian’s own mouth and report back to Julian. These concerned what Julian had written first in his letter to Leo II, transmitted through Peter the regional notary, and most recently to Benedict himself: ‘that in divine matters will is begotten by will, and that there are three substances in Christ,’ as though both statements had been expressed by Julian with insufficient caution.

> “Benedict added that he wished, and urged Julian, to fortify these statements with whatever testimonies of Sacred Scripture and the Fathers he could provide, and to make them solid. The Acts of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo show that Julian immediately and abundantly fulfilled this request.

> “This, then, is Julian’s second Apologeticus, or response, with which Benedict—and, after Benedict’s death, apparently the Roman See—seems to have been satisfied. It has perished completely, just as the earlier Apologeticus transmitted through Peter the regional notary to Leo II has perished. Cellierius teaches that nothing survives of either Apologeticus except their titles (volume XVII, page 728, no. 11).

> “From the Acts of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, chapter 9, we read:

> “‘After, therefore, the rule of this pious confession had been proclaimed with devout voices, we immediately turned our attention to those chapters for whose defense, two years earlier, Pope Benedict of blessed memory had admonished us by the indication of his letter. Yet he did not take care to record them in his own writing, but instructed that they be reported verbally to our man. To this request an adequate and appropriate response was given to him in that same year, 685. Nevertheless, now, rereading more carefully the same report of our man, we find that in that book of the Response of Our Faith which we had sent through Peter the regional notary of the Roman Church, the first chapter seemed to the aforesaid pope to have been stated by us incautiously, where, according to the divine essence, we said: “Will begot will,” etc.’

> “Meanwhile, when Julian’s messenger had returned to Spain and it became known that Benedict had admonished Julian concerning the two chapters mentioned above, not a few rumors were stirred up against him at Toledo and throughout the province by ignorant persons and by rivals, as Julian himself says. To suppress these rumors and to remove every suspicion of frivolity or error from himself, he arranged for the two disputed chapters to be examined again in the Fifteenth National Council of Toledo, consisting of sixty-one bishops, which was convened in the year 688, on the fifth day before the Ides of May.

> “They were to be refined again, as he himself says, by synodical examination, and, if they were found in every respect consonant with orthodox faith, defined and subscribed by the Fathers, and then, through salutary publication, passed into the knowledge of the people. The entire council immediately fulfilled this task.

> “From these facts we infer:

> “I. That Mariana, in the passage cited, pronounced nothing against Julian that he deserved concerning an Apologeticus he had never seen.

> “II. That he referred to Sergius, who was finally elected pontiff toward the end of the year 687, the acclamation of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo and other matters that had been accomplished by Benedict a full two years earlier.

> “III. That Roderic of Toledo was not justified in being praised as though he had attributed the encomium of the Apologeticus to Sergius, since in the commonly circulated copies of Roderic, as well as in his ancient manuscripts, Benedict is said to have been the author of that encomium.

> “There is no opportunity here to investigate where Mariana obtained his statements about Sergius and Roderic. Concerning Julian, however, I believe that this eminent man falsely persuaded himself that what is read in the Acts of the Fifteenth Council concerning the two chapters mentioned above forms part, or a fragment, of Julian’s Apologeticus addressed to Benedict, and that exactly as many severe and pointed words as are now found in the Acts of that synod formerly appeared in the Apologeticus. If this were assumed, there would be nothing surprising in his missing the honor and reverence due to the supreme pastor of the Church, or even in his missing modesty in Julian.

> “I believe that the editor of the distinguished edition of the Toledan Fathers was carried away by the same prejudice—not only in the present passage concerning our Julian, but also more generally. He treated and published the Acts of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo as almost the entire Apologeticus of Julian (volume II, page 20, in the notes), and, in order to remove from the entire council the odium arising from the harsher wording of those Acts—which odium in fact is wholly absent and never existed—he transferred it onto Julian alone, though Julian was undeserving and innocent (*Monitum* to the *Apologeticus*, page 77).

> “As for the opinions of the Fathers, the testimonies of Sacred Scripture, and the force of the arguments brought forward on Julian’s behalf in the Acts of the Fifteenth Council, I have no doubt that all of them formerly existed in his Apologeticus. But how free from venom and sharpness must they be judged to have proceeded from the mouth of a man whom Felix describes as Julian: exceedingly modest and thinking most humbly of himself! Can one who, in his letter to Idalius, calls himself unworthy of the Toledan episcopate, while calling Idalius ‘the most holy lord and brother’; who entrusts to Idalius’s prudence whatever he may find said differently from what ought to have been said in the books of the *Prognostics*, so that it may be corrected, clarified, and embellished—can such a man be believed to have been more sparing with Benedict, the prelate of the universal Church and Christ’s vicar on earth, or to have treated him less generously and courteously?

> “Nevertheless, the force and energy of his speech must have been quite different when he instructed the people entrusted to him in the doctrine of the faith before the general assembly of the Spanish Fathers over which he presided, and especially when he was cleansing himself of the suspicion and stain of frivolity or error cast upon him by rivals and detractors. For Paul, who becomes weak with the weak and scarcely endures to see his disciples saddened even for an hour, invokes an anathema not only upon himself but upon an angel from heaven if anyone should preach to them differently from himself.

> “We also know that the Fathers of the Church—Athanasius, Jerome, Augustine, and others—consistently observed this same manner of disputing in matters of faith. We have pursued these matters at somewhat greater length than our purpose required, not only because of our subject, but also in order to defend and transmit unsullied to posterity the memory of the most holy and learned prelate of the Toledan Church, in whose former offices of treasurer and canon priest we once gladly served.”

I have no doubt, however, that the common reading of Roderic is erroneous when he attributes to the emperor—namely Constantine Pogonatus, or Justinian II, his successor—who was residing at Constantinople, what took place at Rome: the reading and approval of the Apologeticus sent by Julian, which properly belonged to no one other than the supreme prelate of the Church to whom it had been addressed. [Note: The words of Roderic cited by our author are these:

> “He made an Apologeticus [Julian] and sent it to Rome … together with acclamatory verses, as he had also formerly sent them, *On the Praise of the Roman Emperor*. Rome received it worthily and piously and ordered it to be read by everyone; and the emperor, acclaiming, repeatedly made what had been read known with the words: ‘Your praise, O God, reaches the ends of the earth,’ etc.”

Loaisa has:

> “He made an Apologeticus and sent it to Rome … together with acclamatory verses, as he had also formerly sent them, *On the Praise of the Roman Emperor*. Pope Benedict received it worthily and piously and ordered it to be read by everyone; and by acclaiming, ‘Your praise, O God, reaches the ends of the earth,’ he repeatedly made the reading known.” (*Notes on the Fifteenth Council of Toledo*, page 682.)

Although these words are more tolerable than the earlier ones, they are not free from defects and therefore ought to be returned to the anvil and purified anew. As for Constantine Pogonatus, at whose urging Leo II had sent the definition and *prosphoneticum* of the Sixth General Council to the bishops of Spain for subscription, neither of Julian’s two Apologetics was brought to him, nor did either concern him. Only the Acts of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo were sent to him, at which the Spanish Fathers unanimously subscribed the definition and *prosphoneticum* of the Sixth General Council.] 

The distinguished man Ambrosius Morales, the Theseus—so to speak—of our national history, when he came to this passage, observed that many errors had entered the common books of Roderic against the testimony of the ancient manuscript codices that he states he had seen. Among them was the error we are now criticizing: the inappropriate mention of the emperor at this point. In its place, the codices clearly contain a reference to the aforementioned pontiff.

Moreover, in two Toledan codices—one belonging to the monastery of Saint John of the Kings, of the Order of Saint Francis, the other to the library of the principal church—from which I once very carefully extracted variant readings, now in my possession—the reading *atque imperatori acclamando* is consistently found in place of *atque imperator acclamando*, etc. [Note: The Escorial codices are no longer at hand; but the royal Madrid codex, apparently written around the year 1300, has: “And, acclaiming the emperor.” Its complete passage is:

> “Together with acclamatory verses, as he had also formerly sent them, concerning the praise of the Roman emperor; and Rome, receiving it worthily and piously, ordered it to be read by everyone, and, acclaiming the emperor: ‘Your praise,’ etc.”

For “concerning the praise of the Roman emperor,” I think we should restore “and in praise.” By “acclamatory verses,” as in Isidore of Beja and Roderic, I understand the subscriptions of the bishops, which were customarily written on separate lines like verses, or *stichērōs* (στιχηρῶς).]

We maintain that this reading contains nothing absurd, provided that the supreme pontiff sent to the emperor Constantine, the most religious prince who had promoted the convocation of the great Constantinopolitan Council and the condemnation of the Monothelites, a copy of the Acts of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo after they had been read and approved, accompanied by the acclamation or eulogy: “Your praise, O God, reaches the ends of the earth,” as testimony from the Spanish Church, situated at the farthest edge of the world and united in agreement with the Greek and universal Church.

Unless one prefers to correct Roderic from Isidore of Beja, whose words he often likes to borrow, so that the text should read, as it appears in Sandoval’s edition of Isidore: “and, acclaiming the supreme emperor.”

Morales and Mariana praise Pope Sergius; Mariana also praises Roderic in this matter, saying that the book had already reached the hands of Sergius, who then occupied Peter’s chair. I do not find the name of Sergius in Roderic. Moreover, since Sergius was not elevated until after the death of Benedict and of those who succeeded Benedict—John V and Conon—no earlier than the year 687, I consider it scarcely admissible that the Apologeticus mentioned by Felix was addressed to anyone other than Benedict, [Note: This matter was discussed at length above, column 432.] or received by anyone other than John, his successor, who ascended to the pontificate in November 686.

This agrees well with Julian’s own statement among the Toledan Fathers assembled for the Fifteenth Council in 688, that he had sent that writing to Rome two years earlier. He says:

> “These four specific chapters”—although I should like to know why the title of the book in Felix expresses only three—“which they urged us to make firm, after gathering together in one book of our response the Catholic doctrine of the Fathers, we had presented to that party two years earlier, so that it might be recognized what had been said, and by which teacher.”

(Loaisa’s edition, page 671.)

Before we leave this Apologeticus, one or two matters must be noted. First, Pseudo-Julian speaks falsely in the spurious chronicle (no. 361), when he says:

> “Saint Julian sends an Apologeticus with explanations to Pope Sergius, and a poem to the emperor Heraclius Justinian, in his praise. They respond to him with an elegant letter.” [Possibly: “letters.”]

Pseudo-Luitprand says similar things under the year 689. As we have already noted, Sergius was placed in Peter’s chair in 687. But Julian, in the synod held at Toledo in the following year, 688, declared that he had sent his writing to Rome two years earlier. Therefore Julian could not have sent it to Sergius, who was not yet pontiff, unless we assert that Julian wrote to Rome three times: once with the confession of the Spanish Church, or the approval of the Constantinopolitan doctrine; again, sending to Benedict privately the Apologeticus concerning the matters already mentioned; [Note: It is uncertain whether Julian sent to Benedict privately an Apologeticus concerning the three substances in Christ. The Acts of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo contain nothing except: “To this he [Benedict] was sufficiently and appropriately answered in that same year.”] and finally a third time, sending the same work under the name and authority of the council, when Sergius was already pontiff. Isidore of Beja seems to imply this.

Pseudo-Julian is plainly far from the truth, however, when he calls Justinian II, surnamed Rhinotmetus—that is, “the nose-cut,” the son of Constantine Pogonatus—“Heraclius Justinian.” All the Greeks and Latins are silent concerning this surname. Nevertheless, it may be argued on the testimony of Cardinal Baronius (*for the year 685*, no. 3) that Constantine Pogonatus, at least the father, was called by this name somewhere, namely by Luke the Sicilian, an ancient historian.

This is Peter the Sicilian, not Luke, the author of *On the Vain and Foolish Heresy of the Manichaeans*. The work was first published at Ingolstadt by Matthaeus Raderus, together with a Latin translation (1604). The aforementioned cardinal calls him sometimes Luke and sometimes Peter, as Vossius notes in his book *On Greek Historians* (Book IV, chapter 19). But the eminent man was misled by the person who supplied him with Peter the Sicilian’s Greek in Latin.

For what sounds in Baronius’s Latin as follows—

> “The bishop of Colonia in Armenia immediately reports each of these matters to the emperor Justinian Augustus, who governed the scepter of the empire after Heraclius Constantine”—

is different in Greek:

> ἀνήγαγε περὶ τούτων βασιλεῖ Ἰουστινιανῷ, τῷ μετὰ Ἠράκλειον βασιλεύσαντι.

That is: “He reported these matters to Emperor Justinian, who reigned after Heraclius.” Raderus translates this:

> “He immediately reports each of these matters to Julian Augustus, who governed the scepter of the empire after Heraclius.”

The Greek author certainly did not intend, by the name Heraclius, to signify Constantine, the father and imperial predecessor of Justinian the Younger, as Baronius thought. Rather, knowing that two Justinians had ruled the empire, one before and the other after Heraclius, he meant and indicated the latter. It is neither new nor uncommon for our pseudo-historians to fall asleep, in the company of that good Homer.

The same counterfeit Julian continues by saying that Julian of Toledo sent, along with the Apologeticus and its explanations, a poem to the emperor in his praise, and another poem to Pope Sergius. Isidore of Beja gave him the opening for this:

> “An Apologeticus was made at Rome”—he meant to say “sent to Rome”—“through his legates, etc. Again: ‘With an acclamatory verse, as he had also formerly sent, *On the Praise of the Emperor*, he sends it.” [Note: Sandoval’s edition incorrectly has “acclamatory verses.”]

Upon this foundation of Isidore—good heavens!—how lavishly the architect of Pseudo-Julian has built! We read that Hieronymus Higuera, in his notes to Luitprand (under the year 688, page 369), presented a lengthy narrative of the entire affair, with two poems: one to the emperor Justinian, the other to Pope Sergius, as though they formed part of the Chronicle.

This material was apparently once prepared for attachment to the body of the work, but was later omitted from it and left in the cabinets of the Toledan Prometheus like an inert log. From there it was finally extracted by Ramirez, [Note: He published the works of Luitprand, together with Hieronymus Higuera’s notes on the Chronicle, at Antwerp in 1611.] who impressed upon the pages a conspicuous example and trace of Toledan pottery.

For the entire passage praised by Higuera as a portion of Julian’s Chronicle is now absent from the Chronicle. Therefore we shall not credit it. It seemed unworthy of the author himself and even unfit to be mixed with the dross of Julian’s works.

In this judgment, while we lack any evidence from a Julian archbishop’s codex that would give the poems a presumption of authority, I would like those two poems—to the emperor and to Pope Sergius—to be regarded as spurious and the work of a later hand. [Note: These two epigrams appear in the latest collection of the Toledan Fathers, volume II, page 387 and following, among the works falsely attributed to Julian. Above, column 435, we explained what the acclamatory verses in the synods were.]

The well-known author Higuera intended to produce no words other than those excerpted from Pseudo-Julian’s Chronicle, although the printer, through an error, printed part of it in the round type so called and part in italic, as though the words were not by the same author. When the author says that he copied these poems from a manuscript book of Saint Justa, this must refer not to Higuera—who never used any library or codex of Saint Justa—but without doubt to the person who pretended to be Julian, archpriest of Saint Justa.

But let us proceed to other works.

### The Booklet on Remedies against Blasphemy

Together with a letter to Abbot Adrian. [Note: The curator of the latest collection of the Toledan Fathers notes that this booklet of Julian’s has certainly perished (volume II, in the note to Felix’s encomium of Julian, page XX); Cellierius likewise, volume XVII, page 738, no. 11.]

### On the Proof [or Demonstration] of the Sixth Age against the Jews

Felix says that this work has at its beginning a discourse and a letter to the lord King Ervig. He also describes the argument and division of the work:

> “The same codex is divided into three books. The first contains very many testimonies from the Old Testament, by which Christ the Son of God is clearly shown—without any calculation of years—not as one who is yet to be born, but as one already born. The sequence of the second book proceeds through the doctrine displayed by the apostles, which clearly demonstrates that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary in the fullness of time, not according to years reckoned from the beginning of the world. The course of the third book likewise shows by true testimonies that the sixth age, in which Christ was born, is undoubtedly present. In it, the five ages of the world that have passed are distinguished not by years but by a fixed boundary of generations.”

Thus far Felix.

The work exists among the works of the ancient Fathers in volume four. It had earlier, and for the first time, been brought to light at Hagenau by Johannes Secerius in 1532, in octavo, together with the *Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs*, the sons of Jacob, translated from Greek into Latin by Robert, bishop of Lincoln. Menardus Moltherus of Augsburg contributed his services to this edition, using an old exemplar belonging to Laurentius, abbot of the monastery of Eberbach in Phenigoia, and added a preface with much praise of the work.

Isidore of Beja also praised it long ago at the end of his Chronicle:

> “Thus, the most holy Julian, bishop of Toledo, wrote in the book which he composed against the Jews concerning the six ages of the world, saying,”

and Julian’s own words follow. After reproducing his complete testimony, Isidore adds:

> “Finally, the most holy and in this work exceedingly learned Julian says the following in the booklet which we have mentioned above.”

Philippus Labbeus wished to note in his *New Library of Manuscripts, or Specimen of Ancient Readings* (page 2 of the Paris edition, 1653) that he had found the calculation of years contained in the third book of this demonstration in a manuscript exemplar, arranged somewhat differently and more accurately than it appears in the Paris and Cologne editions of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*.

Consult Possevinus in the *Apparatus* (volume I, page 986), and Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book XIX, chapter 14, as well as the many other passages of his vast and learned work in which he corrects, explains, or illuminates some of Julian’s testimonies.

The author himself testifies in his preliminary letter to Ervig and at the end of the third book that he completed this work in the year of the Lord 686, under Conon, Roman pontiff, and at the command of King Ervig.

### A Book of Various Poems

This contains hymns, epitaphs, and numerous epigrams on various subjects. Thus Felix.

Our Andreas Resendius, writing to Bartholomaeus Quevedus, [Note: The learned letter appears in volume II of *Hispania Illustrata*.] says that he saw in Germany a booklet of Julian’s poems, but in the possession of a man who was unwilling to lend it even for the use of a single day.

Thomassinus [Note: *Bibliotheca Veneta*, page 9.] reports that in the library of Saint Anthony at Venice, formerly belonging to Cardinal Grimani, there is a certain little work by Julian, bishop of the Toledan Church. He says that attached to it is a little work written in poems in a very ancient script. Whether these words belong here must be left to the judgment of the reader.

For the moment we refrain from passing judgment on the poems addressed to Pope Sergius and to Justinian the Younger Caesar, until it is shown to us how they reached posterity.

### A Book of Letters

A great many, says Felix.

### A Book of Sermons

In it, Felix says, there is a short work *On the Vindication of the House of God and of Those Who Take Refuge in It*. [Note: The curator of the collection of the Toledan Fathers lists these three short works—of poems, letters, and sermons—among Julian’s lost writings (volume II, in the note to Felix’s encomium, page XX, note 13); Cellierius likewise, volume XVII, page 738, no. 11.] A book of *Responses*, discussed below, deals with the same subject.

### The Book of Ἀντικειμένων

Concerning this Felix says:

> “Likewise, a book *On Contraries*, which he wished to be designated in Greek by the title ἀντικειμένων. It is divided into two books, of which the first contains discussions of the Old Testament and the second of the New.”

Saint Isidore says in *The Etymologies*, Book II, chapter 31:

> “There are four kinds of contraries, which Aristotle calls *anticimena*, that is, opposites.”

The term τὰ κείμενα among the Greeks denotes passages—whether of Sacred Scripture or of other authors—that are proposed for explanation, and which we commonly call “texts.”

Saint John Chrysostom, in Homily 39 on Genesis, writes:

> Ἔιδετε, ἀγαπετοὶ, πῶς οὐδὲν ἀργὸν τῶν παρὰ τῇ θείᾳ γραφῇ κειμένων

that is:

> “You have seen, beloved, how nothing has been placed idly in divine Scripture.”

On the principal strength of this testimony, the most learned and diligent Petrus Lambecius, imperial historiographer and librarian of Emperor Leopold I, confirmed this use of the word in *Commentaries on the Imperial Library*, Book VI, page 71:

> “The Ἀντικείμενα, therefore, are the contrasted or opposed testimonies of both Testaments which are explained.”

This work was published long ago without the author’s name, through the efforts of Johannes Alexander Brassicanus, jurist, at Basel in 1530. It was then published from the Cologne press of Cervicornus in octavo in 1532, from a very ancient codex, if I am not mistaken, belonging to Fulda. It also appeared at Paris together with Junilius Africanus’s work on Genesis.

But Andreas Schott restored it to Julian of Toledo so that it could be inserted under his name into the great Cologne library of the ancient Fathers, where it is now read in volume XV. Following Felix’s authority, he also had another guarantor for this attribution: Samson, abbot, in a still unpublished book found by Garsia Loaisa in the library of the Toledan Church, against Hostegesis, bishop of Málaga, which was written around the year 864.

Xystus of Siena, however, [Note: Book IV of the *Bibliotheca*.] attributes this work *Ἀντικειμένων*, which begins “Why are there seven in Genesis?”, to Richard, a Cluniac monk who flourished in the twelfth century under Pope Adrian IV and Emperor Frederick I. Yet Philippus Bergomas [Note: *Supplementum*, Book XII, under the year 1149.] and Raphael Volaterranus [Note: *Anthropologia*, Book XX, under the heading “Benedict and his various order.”] attribute to Richard only one surviving historical work.

Alphonsus Castrensis [Note: Book IV of *Against Heresies*.] likewise attributes the *Ἀντικείμενα* to Salvian of Marseilles.

Leo of Ostia, Book I, chapter 33 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, and Petrus Diaconus, chapter 12 of *On Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*, testify that Bertharius, abbot of Monte Cassino, also once published a work with the same title. Leo Allatius, in *Urban Bees*, testifies that the distinguished Constantinus Cajetanus once possessed a copy attributed to this Bertharius. The most excellent and learned D. Angelus de Nuce, archbishop of Rossano and our friend, wished it to be noted that the work may still exist in the Cassinese library, in his notes on Leo’s *Chronicle* (chapter 33).

Perhaps, however, this is a different book from the preceding one, although it bears a similar title. In any event, there can be no doubt that Julian of Toledo wrote the work *Ἀντικειμένων*. [Note: In addition to the authors cited by our writer, Cellierius, volume XVII, page 738, no. 10, Du Pin, volume V, page 128 and following, and perhaps others attribute the book *Ἀντικειμένων* to Bertharius, abbot of Monte Cassino. The curator of the latest collection of the Toledan Fathers, volume II, page 141, asserts and vindicates this work as Julian’s, on the authority of Felix and Samson of Córdoba, against Cave and Fabricius.

In an Escorial codex, written in the year 1047—era 1085, as the manuscript itself states—designated Digramm. and Plut. I, no. 3, there is a letter, apparently hitherto unpublished, from a certain Tuseredus to Ascaricus, a bishop of uncertain see, which we intend to publish in its proper place. In it Tuseredus responds to Ascaricus, who had asked about certain doubts concerning Christ’s resurrection, saying:

> “But let those who contradict this”—namely, those who maintained that, when many bodies rose with Christ, they nevertheless did not ascend with him into heaven but remained on earth to die again—“and who say, ‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man,’ read the book of blessed Julian, not Pomerium but Julian of Toledo, called *Anticimena*. He composed it concerning those matters which sound contradictory in Scripture, but are not contradictory to those who seek to investigate Scripture with vigilant understanding … If the *Anticimena* is unavailable, let them turn to Augustine’s book of Homilies on John, and so forth”—namely, to chapter or question 23 of Book II, which guides the reader ascetically through the *Ἀντικειμένων* passage from the New Testament and the Gospel of Saint John, where this subject is discussed.] 

### A Book of History

Felix continues:

> “Likewise, a book of history concerning what occurred in Gaul during the time of King Wamba.”

Lucas of Tuy inserted this history into his own history. Franciscus Schott published it, with a note indicating that it was by a different author, in the fourth volume of *Hispania Illustrata*. It was also published separately, and later by Duchesne among the *Writers of Frankish History*, volume I, page 821, though with many differences.

It begins:

> “It is customary for virtue to be an incentive to courageous souls,” etc.

Traces of an author contemporary with the events and with that age survive even at the very beginning:

> “Since this account may cure the timid and the sluggish, we introduce a report of an event that occurred in our own time, so that succeeding ages may be summoned to virtue by it. Wamba was present in our days,” etc.

In my judgment, we should not believe that this history of Julian was concluded with Wamba’s triumphal entry into the city of Toledo and the words “let it acknowledge them in eternal proscriptions,” as it is in both Schott’s earlier edition and Duchesne’s later one.

For what follows the ending prescribed at this point is entirely Julian’s; it is absent from Duchesne’s edition, but appears in Schott’s as though it were already the writing of Lucas of Tuy. It begins:

> “The transgression of the faithless having been marked,” etc.

This is immediately and plainly evident to anyone who reads the passage, even inattentively.

Now that these words have for the first time been restored by us to Julian, Lucas finally attaches the continuation of his own discourse:

> “And because, through the hindrance of the author of evil,” etc.

When Vossius wrote *On Latin Historians*, he failed to notice that this history had already been made public at the time of which we are speaking. He says that he does not know whether it had seen the light, although he hoped that it would shortly do so (*On Latin Historians*, Book II, chapter 27).

Here Pseudo-Luitprand too thinks of quibbling; [Col. 0441A] but how coldly and thoughtlessly he does so [Note: [Col. 0441D] In the *Chronicle*, under the year 960, no. 361.]! “Saint Julian wrote the *Life of Saint Hildefonsus*. Felix, moreover, wrote the *Life of Saint Julian, bishop of Toledo*. He also added it to the *Chronicle*, which begins as follows: ‘In the name of the Lord begins the *Chronicle* which Saint Julian composed.’ The passage ‘Now Witiza was born…’ others attribute to Gunderic. Certainly nothing concerning the addition has hitherto been found. He is plainly false and betrays himself by his stupidity. Julian did not write a *Chronicle*, but a history of one Gallic war of King Wamba. Yet in what respect history and chronicle differ, the genuine Luitprand could not have been ignorant, since boys know it.

“Father Higuera nevertheless does not linger over the notes to this passage. For he says: ‘The *Chronicle* circulated under the name of Wulsa is also Julian’s, except that the passage concerning Witiza was added by Gunderic, although he leaves this last point as uncertain.’ If we believe him, then, our Julian wrote a *Chronicle*. This is apparently what he judged concerning Wulsa’s *Chronicle*, and, in order to advance this opinion of his, he foisted it upon this Pseudo-Luitprand of his, as well as upon his twin Julian under the year 692, no. 359, about whom we shall speak elsewhere. For those words which he notes as belonging to Felix or Gunteric are not found in Julian’s history, the one of which we are speaking. Perhaps, however, they are found in the work attributed to Wulsa, which has not yet been committed to print; but in its proper place, when we have to discuss Wulsa, we shall establish that this was genuinely the name of the author who left behind a very brief written history of the Goths down to the destruction of Spain, under which period he is believed to have lived, and that it is attributed to Julian without any reason. Indeed, this history of Julian seems to have been regarded as a continuation of Isidore’s history of the Gothic kings and of Hildefonsus’s appendix; indeed, it was even confused with Isidore’s work. For the anonymous author of the *Chronicle of Exil* attributes to Isidore, and to the history of the Goths written by him, the deeds of Wamba against the rebel Paul, as we have already said in our discussion of Isidore [Note: [Col. 0441D] The genuine history of Julian concerning Wamba, under the title *Book of the History of Gaul, which was composed during the time of Wamba, ruler of blessed memory, by Julian, bishop of the see of Toledo, from ancient codices of the church of Toledo*, together with the same work as interpolated by Lucas of Tuy, collated with it; and also *The Judgment Published against the Treachery of Tyrants*, together with the work entitled *The Insult of the Lowly Historian against the Tyranny of Gaul*, hitherto unpublished, is presented in the most recent edition of the holy Fathers of Toledo, vol. II, p. 330 onward.].”

*A Book of Sentences, collected briefly and in summary from the decade of the psalms of blessed Augustine.* Thus Felix’s statement is obscure. Unless he intended to indicate only the first decade of the psalms [Note: Saint Augustine is said to have composed a special psalter, or a very brief work stitched together from various verses of the psalms, for the use and spiritual consolation of his mother Monica. The most recent Benedictine editors, however, assign it among the spurious—or at least doubtful—writings of the holy Doctor. [Col. 0442D] Perhaps Felix had this in mind when listing Julian’s works. Cellier, vol. XVII, p. 738, no. 11, and Du Pin, vol. V, p. 124. They title the work *A Collection of Sentences from Augustine’s Commentaries on the Psalms*. Among Julian’s lost writings are also the three works that follow: I. *Extracts Collected from the Books of Saint Augustine against Julian*, etc.; II. *On Divine Judgments*, etc.; III. *Book of Responses against Those Who Persecute Those Fleeing to the Church*.].

*Extracts collected from the books of Saint Augustine against the heretic Julian.* These are those highly elaborate six books of Augustine, or at least so judged by Augustine himself (*Retractions*, book II, chapter 62), against Julian, bishop of Eclanum; concerning them, after others, our fellow Augustinian Henry of Noris treats in book I, chapter 21, of his *History of the Pelagian Controversy*.

*A little book on divine judgments, collected from the sacred books*, at the beginning of which, Felix says, there is a letter addressed to Lord Ervig during the time of his countship—that is, while he was still a count and a private citizen under Wamba, as is clear from the conclusion that we assigned to Julian’s brief history of King Wamba in the *Chronicle* of Lucas of Tuy—and sent on behalf of that little book. Ervig later conspired against the king, deposed him, and confined him in a monastery, secure in the divine judgments; but after giving Casilona, his daughter and heiress, in marriage to Egica, Wamba’s cousin, and following the proper succession to the throne, he obtained the title of a pious and moderate ruler.

*A Book of Responses against Those Who Persecute Those Fleeing to the Church.* This must have been a work different from the one Felix called *On the Vindication of the House of God and of Those Who Flee to It*, mentioned above, though concerned with the same subject. These two writings perhaps gave the Fathers of the Twelfth Council of Toledo, among whom was our Julian, the occasion to make provision concerning the immunity of sacred buildings—specifically in canon ten—since not long before, by a certain law of King Recceswinth (now the sixteenth law of title five, book six of the *Law*, as the book is called, of the Visigoths), the matter had been regulated with insufficient attention or piety toward the sanctity of churches.

*A Book of Masses divided into four parts according to the whole cycle of the year*, in which he corrected and completed some portions that had been corrupted and left incomplete through the neglect of antiquity, while he composed others entirely anew. Thus Felix. Julian, therefore, was one contributor to the complete Isidorian Missal—by which name it is commonly known—which the Mixtarabes later used, and which we discussed in the monuments of Isidore and Hildefonsus.

Felix finally says that Julian also composed *a Book of Prayers for the Feasts which the Church of Toledo customarily celebrates throughout the entire cycle of the year, partly drawn from the resources of his own talent and partly carefully corrected after having been corrupted by long antiquity, gathered together into one volume, and left to the uses of the Church of God out of love for holy religion* [Note: Of the books of Masses for the whole cycle of the year and of the other work, *Prayers for the Feasts*, etc., both of which Felix mentions, it can scarcely be determined, if passages survive in the Mixtarabic Missal or elsewhere, whether they belong to Julian, Isidore, or another author. Fragments, or a sample of them, were published by the distinguished editor of the edition of the holy Fathers of Toledo, vol. II, p. 326 onward.]. Jerome Romanus de la Higuera once informed me that this book, and indeed in a very large volume, was preserved in the library of the Church of Toledo; at the time he was reading in his papers its still unpublished history of the city and kingdom of Toledo. But in the extremely accurate copy of the catalogue of that same library which is in our possession, we encountered nothing that seemed to refer to this Book of Prayers.

To Felix’s account of Julian’s books, the following item, which is read elsewhere concerning them, should be added. For it is held with certainty to be his [Col. 0442C]:

*An Appendix to the Book, or Addition, of Saint Hildefonsus, On Illustrious Men—or rather, a single eulogy of that same holy man.* Cardinal Baronius, however, attributes it to another Julian, namely to a member of the Church of Toledo who was not a bishop but a deacon (*Annals*, vol. VIII, under the year 657, no. 43); he also says that it appears in place of a preface in a volume of Saint Hildefonsus’s works published by Franciscus Fevardentius. Manuscript books attribute it either to Julian the deacon or to Julian the bishop. Nor are these two different men. For Julian is reported still to have been a deacon when Hildefonsus went to heaven; hence he could inscribe the eulogy “Julian the deacon.” What we maintain is evident from Felix: “After the death of his predecessor, Hildefonsus of divine memory, from approximately the seventeenth year of the rule of Recceswinth, and also throughout the entire reign of Wamba, until the third year of the reign of the most glorious King Egica, he acquired a celebrated name while continuing in the honor of the diaconate, priesthood, and episcopate.” There are also codices that attribute these two eulogies, that of Hildefonsus and that of Julian, to Felix [Note: Consult the notes of Joannes Baptista Pérez on this eulogy of Hildefonsus in the Madrid edition of the works of Saint Isidore, vol. I, p. 137.]. Lipomanus and Surius published this appendix under June 23. It also appears in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, published in the Madrid edition of the works of Saint Isidore, from which Miraeus seems to have transferred it into his own work [Note: It appears in a tenth-century Escorial codex, shelfmark A, Plut. II, no. 9, and in another more recent manuscript, Digramm. and Plut. IV, no. 23.].

Henry Canisius published from a manuscript of the Bavarian library, in volume I of Bignaeus’s *Library of the Holy Fathers*, attributing to our Julian a *Commentary on the Prophet Nahum*. It is mutilated, however, or scarcely begun: the codex in question contained only an exposition of four verses of the prophet. But enough concerning Julian [Note: This commentary on the prophet Nahum was reprinted under Julian’s name in vol. II, p. 268, of the most recent collection of the holy Fathers of Toledo. The distinguished editor of that edition leaves no stone unturned in order to attribute and vindicate it as Julian’s against Natalis Alexander and others. It should be consulted. The same distinguished editor also discusses the *Chronicle of the Visigoths* circulated under the name of Wulsa, as well as the epitaphs of four Toledan bishops, Hildefonsus and Quiricus, and of King Gudila and King Wamba, which the maker of the Pseudo-Chronicles of Julian and Luitprand attributes to Julian; he rejects all of these as spurious and falsely assigned to Julian.].

Idalius appears to belong to us, if what Jerome Paulus, a very learned man, wrote about him nearly two hundred years ago, and what Franciscus Tarafa left in writing on the testimony of Hieronymus Pujades, is true: namely, that he labored over many works, of which only a few survive [Note: Book VI, *On the Crown of Catalonia*, chapter 132.].

[Col. 0443B] We certainly possess one letter and another, the first of which was addressed to Julian, whom we mentioned above in d’Achery’s *Spicilegium* (vol. I, p. 313), preserved from a manuscript of the monastery of Corbie [Note: It appears in the most recent collection of the holy Fathers of Toledo, vol. II, p. 6.]. The second follows it in the same *Spicilegium*, addressed to Sunifred, bishop of the first see of Narbonne, sending him Julian’s *Prognostic of the Future Age*, by Julian, bishop of the first see of Toledo—that is, the metropolitan bishop. [Note: This letter too was published by the distinguished Matthaeus Aymericus in the *Catalogue of the Bishops of Barcelona*, Barcelona, 1760, p. 461; he also discusses Idalius at greater length on p. 262 and following.] In this letter it should be noted that Barcelona, now so greatly expanded, was then a small city; for he says, “when I was devoted to this little city, over which I preside unworthily.”

Roderic of Toledo calls this bishop of Narbonne Sunifred in book III, chapters 42 and 13, of his *History of Spain*, and the authors of the *Gallia Christiana* follow him. He did indeed attend the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, first after the metropolitans. Since that council was celebrated in the year 688, his place there sufficiently indicates that, by the privilege of an earlier ordination, he preceded the others. Certainly, at the National Council immediately preceding this one, which is called the Thirteenth of Toledo and which was held five years earlier, the deacon Laulfus acted in the place of Idalius. Likewise, at the Twelfth Council of all Spain, held in the year 681, his name is absent; nor is any bishop of Barcelona recorded there. For this reason Pujades believes that Idalius succeeded Raymond from the year 674 (*Book VI*, chapters 123 and 127), and that he lived until 690 or thereabouts (chapter 132).

Felix praised or adorned this same Julian, bishop of Toledo, with an eulogy; Felix himself was bishop of Toledo after having been bishop of Seville, as is established by the acts of the Sixteenth Council held in that city. This eulogy is commonly appended to Hildefonsus’s little book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and to the appendix of that same Julian *On Hildefonsus* [Note: It is found in a fourteenth-century Escorial codex, Digramm. and Plut. IV, no. 23.]. He was still alive in 694, when the Seventeenth Council of Toledo was held; although the subscriptions have been lost, Roderic of Toledo shows that Julian attended it [Col. 0444B]. Pseudo-Luitprand would have us believe that this Felix had previously been bishop of Iria, that he enlarged Julian’s *Chronicle* somewhat, and that he was a great preacher, a most vigorous defender of the faith, and a devotee of the blessed Virgin Mary (*Chronicle*, under the years 693 and 700).
