There truly was a certain Felix, bishop of Iria, as we know from the subscriptions of the Twelfth Council of Toledo in 681, the Thirteenth in 683, and the Fifteenth in 688. But to establish that this Felix of Iria was subsequently raised to the episcopal dignity at Seville requires other evidence. We should also like to be informed how this same Felix continued Julian’s *Chronicle*; for we do not even trust Pseudo-Julian when he boasts that Felix was likewise the author of the little book *On the Lives of Twelve Writers* (*Chronicle*, no. 363).

# LIFE OR EULOGY OF SAINT JULIAN, BISHOP OF TOLEDO, BY FELIX, ALSO BISHOP OF TOLEDO

[Col. 0443]

## PREFATORY NOTICE

What we promised to do, and in fact did, in the *Life of Saint Hildefonsus*—namely, not to follow the deeds and life-history of the Fathers of Toledo in our own style, but occasionally to produce the more ancient testimonies of others concerning them, which would make the account more credible—we now do in the present instance as well, transcribing the *Life of Saint Julian of Toledo* from Felix, likewise archbishop of Toledo, who added his eulogy to the already frequently cited book of Saint Hildefonsus *On Illustrious Men*. There was no reason for us to prefer our own account to this narrative, which far surpasses all other testimonies both in antiquity and authority. It possesses as much antiquity as could be desired, since it was written by Felix, Julian’s contemporary and an eyewitness of almost everything he relates, who wrote these things about Julian while the memory of them was still fresh. It has no less authority, since the testimony proceeds from a man who succeeded Julian himself, after Sisbertus, in the episcopate, and governed the Church of Toledo with the highest distinction for seven years, dying in the year 700 or thereabouts. Moreover—and this is highly significant in monuments of this kind—we have brought this eulogy to light from not merely one but a great many manuscripts, which agree remarkably with one another, especially in setting out the chronology of his life, as Father Flórez rightly observed when discussing Julian in volume V of *Sacred Spain*, whose edition we reproduce. We therefore saw nothing in it that needed correction; rather, by means of its own words, we overturned several errors concerning Julian’s affairs and, as it were, dispelled them by the light supplied in the notes appended, almost all of which concern this matter. Farewell.

[Col. 0445]

## THE LIFE BEGINS (C, S)

[Col. 0445A] 1. [Note: At the very threshold one encounters the error of many who, deceived by the similarity of names, thought that our Julian was called Pomerius and was the same person as Julian Africanus. At the present time even the least learned reader scarcely needs to be warned about this, since anyone with any knowledge will not be unaware how far apart the two are. Julian Pomerius, a native of Mauritania in the province of Africa, flourished under the emperor Marcian in the middle of the fifth century, that is, two centuries before our Julian. Thus the former is praised more than once by the latter in the book *Prognostic*, and Africanus is said to have composed another similar work under the same title; hence the error of failing to distinguish the two was powerfully reinforced. A sensible reader will therefore distinguish them and reject the surname Pomerius falsely assigned to Saint Julian of Toledo, which he will search for in vain in manuscripts earlier than the twelfth century.] Julian, a disciple [Note: That Saint Eugenius, whom we number as the third, was Saint Julian’s teacher is testified by Julian himself more than once in the work *Prognostic*, pp. 58–59, in these words: “Our holy teacher Eugenius.” Why, then, Felix calls him “the second” will scarcely escape anyone. The Goths, of course, were unaware of Saint Eugenius the First, the father and founder of the Church of Toledo, whom the Gauls have venerated for nearly ten centuries and we for more than six hundred years, as we noted from Joannes Baptista Pérez in the book *On Illustrious Men*.] of the second Eugenius, metropolitan of the province of Carthage, after the blessed Quiricus, following his teacher in fourth place, attained the pontifical dignity of the royal city. He was, moreover, a native citizen of that city [Note: Apart from Julian’s birthplace, which Felix states here with complete clarity to have been Toledo, he says absolutely nothing about his lineage or parents [Col. 0446B]. Let the reader therefore beware of readily believing Isidore of Pacensis, who writes that Julian arose from the Jewish race, like a rose among thorns; for we still do not know from what sources he obtained this. Perhaps the Pacensian was mistaken here, as in many other matters that he writes about Saint Hildefonsus, although otherwise he was a historian devoted to truth. Unless we prefer to believe that there were some who, because a certain Rabbi in Spain existed named Pomerianus or Pomarius—the surname by which, as we said above, our Julian was falsely called by some—then, owing to the similarity of this surname to a Jewish name, believed our Julian also to have been a Jew, extracting, as often happens, one disgraceful error from another.], and in the principal church of that same city he was washed in the waters of holy baptism and there nourished from the very beginnings of infancy.

2. Finally, when he had reached the age of youthful maturity, he was so closely joined in a social bond to Gudila, a levite and his colleague, of holy memory, and united with him in an indivisible bond of love, that inviolable charity showed both of them to be one, while the unity established in both demonstrated that there were not two souls in them but one. Such, therefore, was the communion of the unanimity they had attained [Col. 0445B] that, according to the history of the Acts of the Apostles, they were thought to possess one heart and one soul in two bodies. For they stood prudent in counsel, united in decision, and harmonious in praiseworthy action; and, by the breathing of the divine Spirit, they delighted in enjoying the good of theoretical—that is, contemplative—rest and in being bound by the barrier of monastic discipline.

3. But because the judgment of the heavenly divine power ordained otherwise, their devotion was nevertheless frustrated. Although they did not complete the course of the journey they desired [Col. 0446A] [Note: Those who counted Saint Julian among the monks, such as Arnold Wion in *The Tree of Life* and Hugh Menard in the Benedictine *Martyrology*, perhaps never paid attention to these words of Felix, in which he most clearly testifies that they had wished to live a monastic way of life, but that, God resisting and calling them to another kind of life and conduct, Julian never attained the fulfillment of his desire.], they did not cease from the pursuit of pious devotion. And since they preferred to benefit only themselves through retreat, they later began, with ever-growing aspirations, to strive for the salvation of their neighbors. For in teaching their subjects they displayed strenuous virtue; in advancing them they were worthy of desire; in God’s service they were fervent; in their zeal for the splendor of the Lord’s house they were energetic; in obedience to their elders they were ready; and, if it were possible to obtain the benefit of all the virtues, they strove for it with ever more fervent minds. Accordingly, by the dispensation of divine judgments, Gudila, a deacon of holy memory, on the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the eighth year of the rule of Wamba, closed the final course of his life by a death marked by a worthy confession of God. His little body was honorably laid to rest and buried in the monastery of Saint Felix, which is dedicated in the village of Cabensis through the care of his most beloved companion [Col. 0446B] [Note: Eight miles—not ten, as Papebrochius says—from the city of Toledo, on the southern bank of the Tagus, there is a place called Valdecaba, which Papebrochius thinks Felix indicates here. But amid such a great distance of time, together with the confusion of places and names, just as it is not difficult to make a thousand conjectures, so it is easy to be deceived.].

4. After his departure, therefore, following a short interval of time, and after the holy Quiricus of blessed memory, that outstanding man Julian was anointed to the primacy of the aforesaid city. He deserves to be proclaimed with as great a title of praise as he was supported by the resources of diverse virtues, by which in his own time he wonderfully ordered the Church of God. Indeed, so that I may reveal the time from which he began to shine, I shall unfold it through this woven account and fabric of faithful narration. After the death of his predecessor, Hildefonsus of divine memory, from approximately the seventeenth year of the rule of Recceswinth, and throughout the entire reign of Wamba, until the third year of the reign of the most glorious King Egica, he acquired a celebrated name while continuing in the honor of the diaconate, priesthood, and episcopate [Col. 0447A] [Note: If the reader calculates, according to Felix’s testimony, the time Julian spent in the lower orders before he was raised to the episcopate [Col. 0447C], he will certainly discover that before the year 667, in which Saint Hildefonsus died, Julian had already been established in the diaconate, since Felix says that from that time he began to shine in the honor of the diaconate, priesthood, and episcopate. The reader will therefore be even more astonished at what could have been written in the breviary of the Church of Braga, most recently enlarged in 1708, under March 8, in the lessons of the second nocturn, which contain the *Life of Saint Julian of Toledo*. For it says that, before he was summoned to the Church of Toledo to succeed Quiricus, Julian had presided over Braga for thirteen full years, and that he was the same Julian who subscribed to the Third Council of Braga in these words: “I, Leodicisius, surnamed Julian.” We have not yet seen a tale more foolishly fabricated or less consistent with historical truth. If Julian was bishop of Braga for thirteen years before Quiricus’s death, this must have occurred while Hildefonsus was still alive. Yet Felix testifies that after Hildefonsus’s death Julian remained in the grades of the diaconate [Col. 0447D] and priesthood. Furthermore, in the eighth year of King Wamba, Julian was living at Toledo, where he arranged the funeral of his closest companion, the levite Gudila; but the Third Council of Braga had been celebrated three years earlier, for the eighth year of King Wamba fell in the year 679. That council, however, was celebrated in 675, as is well known. In addition, the person who subscribed to the council is called not Julian by name but Leodicisius, surnamed Julian. Nor was this Leodicisius ever numbered among the holy men. We must therefore call this an obvious and egregious error. Would that it were corrected by those whose duty it is to see that, in the histories of the saints read in the Church, one truth prevails and all fables remain as far away as possible.].

5. He was a man full of fear of the Lord, supreme in prudence, cautious in counsel, outstanding in the virtue of discernment, exceedingly devoted to almsgiving, most prompt in the relief of the wretched, devoted in supporting the oppressed, discerning in intercession, energetic in settling disputes, equitable in issuing judgments, sparing in his verdict, singular in the vindication of justice, praiseworthy in debate, unceasing in prayer, and marvelous in discharging the praises of God. If some difficulty, as commonly happens, arose in the divine offices, he was most ready to correct it; he was exceedingly attentive to the sacred lights [Col. 0447B], exceptional in the defense of all the Churches; ever watchful in governing his subjects; upright in restraining the proud; prepared to sustain the humble; generous with the authority due to him; richly endowed with the virtue of embracing humility; and, generally, conspicuous in every moral excellence. He abounded in kindness, so that there was no person in distress whom he did not wish to help; and his charity overflowed so greatly that he never ceased, out of love, to provide some good to anyone who asked him. Finally, he preferred to show himself dear to God in all things and to demonstrate himself useful to all people, so that he might please God in every respect and, for God’s sake, satisfy human beings with a devoted mind, insofar as that was possible. He equaled the worthy merits of so many noble men who had preceded him inasmuch as in no aspect of virtue did he stand beneath them [Note: What a man Julian appears in this account of Felix! No virtue whatever, whether one considers private or public life, was lacking in him. Whoever wishes to know individually the inner sentiments of devotion by which he was sometimes moved, fixed in meditation upon divine matters, should carefully read the letter of this same Julian to Idalius, bishop of Barcelona [Col. 0448B], prefixed to his work entitled *Prognostic of the Future Age* [Col. 0448C].].

6. He therefore preserved the well-ordered ecclesiastical ranks in the seat of his government with especially diligent care; he usefully restored those that had been corrupted; he instituted those that had been inadequately maintained by prudent arrangement; and he composed a great many offices with sweet-flowing melody. But now, since he shone filled with the abundance of the Holy Spirit and endowed with the overflowing fullness of a well-watered spring, learn from this point, reader, the catalogue of his books, which God brought forth through him for the benefit of His Church.

7. For he composed the book *Prognostics of the Future Age*, addressed to Idalius, bishop of blessed memory [Note: This is the very book whom we have just praised, greater than all our commendation, and the first of all that we published.], containing at its beginning a letter addressed to him and a prayer. The work of this codex is arranged in three books. The first of them concerns the origin of human death; the second, the condition of the souls of the dead before the resurrection of their bodies; the third, the final resurrection of the bodies. He also wrote a *Book of Responses*, addressed to the person mentioned above, in defense of the canons and laws by which Christian slaves are forbidden to serve unbelieving masters.

8. He also wrote [Note: This first *Apologetic* no longer exists. It will nevertheless be worthwhile to understand what it contained and on what occasion it was written. Pope Saint Leo II had sent to Spain under this title the acts of the Sixth General Council of Constantinople, together with a letter to Quiricus, bishop of Toledo, whom he believed to have been alive in 682, although he had already died two years earlier. He sent them so that the bishops of Spain might approve them, and so that the anathema pronounced by the Fathers of Constantinople against the destructive heresy of Apollinaris might be confirmed more and more by their votes. Julian, Quiricus’s successor, received Leo’s letter at the end of 683 or the beginning of 684, at which time the national Thirteenth Council of Toledo had recently been dissolved. Julian therefore considered it impossible, given the season—it was the middle of winter, and an exceptionally severe one—to summon the Fathers again, who had already been dismissed to their respective provinces. At the same time, he wished in the meantime to satisfy the holy pontiff. While a new council was being convened, he composed this first *Apologetic* and sent it to Rome. In it he testified, in his own name and that of the entire Church of Spain, that he accepted the acts of the general council and approved all the anathemas issued against the errors of Apollinaris; at the same time he indicated what the Church of Spain universally thought and firmly believed concerning Christ the Lord. This is precisely the *Apologetic* that the Fathers of the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, held in the same year, 684, praised and unanimously approved in section 4. Felix says that it was addressed to Pope Benedict because Saint Leo II had departed to heaven in that same year, 683, shortly after sending the letter; Benedict, called Benedict II, was then seated at Rome in his place.] an *Apologetic of the Faith*, addressed to Benedict, pope of the city of Rome [Col. 0449A]. He also wrote another [Note: Since we have discussed the first *Apologetic*, we should explain more fully the reason for composing this second one, which Felix indicates. After receiving Saint Julian’s first *Apologetic*, Benedict II approved the other matters contained in it, but a few points displeased him. Through a certain envoy whom he sent to Spain with his instructions, he courteously and most graciously arranged to have these points communicated to Julian. Their substance was that Julian had written that will in God generates will, just as wisdom generates wisdom; that he asserted three substances in Christ the Lord; and two other points of which we are entirely ignorant. All these statements seemed to the holy pontiff either expressed too obscurely or advanced with insufficient caution. Our Julian, informed of this, was orthodox in faith, devoted to truth, and rich in learning; he immediately prepared a response, likewise entitled an *Apologetic*. In it he explained so clearly and wisely the sense in which he had uttered the aforesaid statements, and confirmed it with so many brilliant testimonies of the holy Fathers, that he plainly demonstrated that he had spoken no differently and in no other way than Augustine, Cyril, and Isidore. Thus he showed that nothing in his confession deserved censure or reproach [Col. 0449D]. By this response he obtained from the Roman pontiff what he desired: he removed from himself every suspicion of any error and secured the pope’s approval of his teaching as orthodox and catholic. For that reason he was afterward greatly praised and commended by him, as Isidore of Pacensis asserts. No one, therefore, should be surprised that the Fathers of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, convened from all Spain in 688, after publishing their confession of faith, not only read this *Apologetic*, which Saint Julian had sent to Rome two years earlier, but also inserted almost the whole of it into the acts of the council, approved by common vote, so that its teaching might be more firmly confirmed and transmitted to posterity. We publish it among Julian’s genuine writings, transcribed from the council itself.] *Apologetic on the Three Chapters*, about which the bishop of the city of Rome seemed, apparently without reason, to have entertained doubts.

He also wrote a little book *On Remedies against Blasphemy*, with a letter to Abbot Adrian [Note: The book *On Remedies against Blasphemy* has entirely perished.]. [Note: The little work *On Demonstrating the Sixth Age against the Jews* survives; it has been reprinted more than once and finally by us.] He also wrote a book *On Demonstrating the Sixth Age*, which has at its beginning a prayer and a letter to Lord Ervig, king. This same codex, however, is divided into three books. The first contains a great many testimonies from the Old Testament, by which it is openly declared, without any calculation of years, that Christ the Son of God was not going to be born but had already been born. The sequence of the second book runs through the teaching of the apostles, which clearly shows that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary in the fullness of time, not according to years calculated from the beginning of the world [Col. 0449B]. The course of the third book likewise demonstrates by true proofs that the sixth age, in which Christ was born, had unquestionably arrived. In this work the five preceding ages of the world are distinguished not by years but by a fixed limit of generations.

9. [Note: The entire volumes of poems, letters, and sermons have perished, together with the little work *On the Vindication of the House of God*. Their loss is all the more to be lamented because many excellent documents, especially from the letters, could have been drawn from them to illuminate the ecclesiastical discipline of those times in Spain. Perhaps the following two sentences were taken from them—for no other surviving little work comes to mind to which they could belong—which Alvarus of Córdoba praises under Julian’s name in letter 10, a bishop’s letter to a bishop, among those published by Father Flórez, vol. XI of *Sacred Spain*, p. 158, in these words: “He is judged to be of unsound and empty mind who raises his feet there where the consideration of the head has not advised it”; and on p. 163, near the end: “It is no less a matter of foresight to provide for an impending necessity than to apply the rudder of complete discernment.” Likewise, the following sentence is praised by Abbot Samson in a little work published by Flórez in the same volume, where it appears on folio 386: “To refuse to assert something for the sake of the faith is the same thing as denying it.”] He also wrote a *Book of Various Poems*, containing hymns, epitaphs, and numerous epigrams on different subjects. He also wrote a *Book of Many Letters*. He also wrote a *Book of Sermons*, containing a brief work *On the Vindication of the House of God and of Those Who Flee to It* [Col. 0450A]. He also wrote a *Book of Contraries*, which he wished to designate in its title by the Greek word Ἀντικειμένων, “of Contraries” [Note: We possess this book, divided into two parts, complete, as Felix says; it was previously published and is now reprinted by us with the addition of certain questions.]. It is divided into two books: the first contains discussions of the Old Testament, and the second of the New.

10. Also a book of history concerning what happened in Gaul during the time of Prince Wamba. [Note: [Col. 0450D] This history of the deeds of King Wamba in Gaul, written by Julian and later published by others, has been more carefully edited by us. Concerning it, as also concerning the works mentioned above, our preliminary remarks should be read. But the remaining four short works, listed by Felix, have been begrudged to us and snatched away by unjust and devouring time.] Also a book of maxims, collected briefly and summarily from the ten books of the blessed Augustine on the Psalms. Also excerpts collected from the books of Saint Augustine against the heretic Julian. Also a little book on divine judgments, collected from the sacred volumes; at its beginning is a letter to Lord Ervig, sent during his tenure as count on behalf of this same little book. Also a book of replies against those who persecute persons taking refuge in the church.

11. Also a book of Masses for the entire cycle of the year, [Col. 0450B] divided into four parts; in these he corrected and completed certain items that had been corrupted and left incomplete through the negligence of antiquity, while he composed others entirely. [Note: [Col. 0450D] The Mozarabic Missal unquestionably contains Masses and prayers either composed or corrected by Julian. But, apart from those which we have published, we are completely unaware which they are; and thus we have been unable to satisfy the wishes of scholars in this matter. For we deliberately omit here the fragments praised by Elipandus in his letters, intending to republish them elsewhere. At that point we mean to investigate more at leisure whether Elipandus deceitfully corrupted the words of his predecessors or not.] Also he collected into one book a book of prayers for the festivals that the Church of Toledo was accustomed to celebrate throughout the entire cycle of the year, partly drawn from the style of his own genius and partly corrupted by ingrained antiquity, which he carefully corrected, and left it for the uses of the Church of God out of his love for holy religion.

12. [Note: [Col. 0450D] The chronology of Saint Julian’s episcopate could not have been marked by clearer indications, nor could any testimony more plainly establish the day of its beginning and end than this testimony of Felix. We therefore establish the matter as follows. Julian ended his final day of life on the day before the Nones of March—that is, on 6 March—in the era 728, which is A.D. 690, after he had spent ten years, one month, and seven days in the episcopate. It follows plainly that he was consecrated bishop in the year 680, on 29 January. For if from that day one counts ten years, one month, and seven days, one arrives again at the date of death designated by Felix. All these facts, since they are expressly derived from Felix, as you see, the most authoritative of all witnesses, agree remarkably both with one another and with the whole history of those times. For the year 680 was unquestionably the third year of Egica’s reign, which began to be reckoned from 24 November of the year 687, the day on which the king was inaugurated. Furthermore, that Julian already held the see of Toledo in the year 680 is established most clearly by the Twelfth Council of Toledo, celebrated in 681. In its first chapter the Fathers state that Wamba, after laying aside the royal diadem, announced to Julian, bishop of the see of Toledo, that he should anoint Ervig as king. But Wamba’s relinquishing of the royal scepter took place in 680; therefore Julian was then bishop of Toledo, since Wamba certainly would not have required a royal anointing except from a bishop. We assign 29 January as the date of Julian’s consecration because Felix designates 6 March as the day of his death—a date we would rashly question, since all Felix’s manuscripts agree on it, as do Loaysa, the catalogue of the Church of Toledo, and the Martyrology of Usuard; in addition, so do the corrected Roman Martyrology, edited by Pisa, and, if Tamayo is to be believed, the most ancient Breviaries of Zamora and Carthage. Ambrosius Morales therefore must not be heeded: using a corrupt manuscript, he confidently asserted that the exact date of the beginning of Julian’s episcopate could not be designated except rashly, and that no more than nine years, four months, and five or six days could be assigned to him as seated in the see of Toledo—plainly contrary to the testimony of Felix, whom he accuses of error. Nor are we troubled by the fact that our Church of Toledo now commemorates Julian on 8 March, rather than on 6 March, as it ought. The extremely ancient records cited above carry greater weight with us, both external and domestic, such as the catalogue of prelates of the very Church of Toledo, in which 6 March, not 8 March, is designated as the day of Saint Julian’s death. That date is consistently read in all the martyrologies down to that of Baronius; before it, as Papebrochius asserts, there is none that does not present Julian’s commemoration on that same sixth day. It was not Felix, then, nor his scribes, who erred in designating the sixth day, an error that supposedly passed from there into the most ancient martyrologies of foreign churches rather than into the Church of Toledo itself, “which Church, if we follow Papebrochius, adopted the celebration of Saint Julian on 8 March before Felix wrote anything about him.” How we could wish that this most learned man had produced the records of a matter so truly astonishing! We would possess an excellent basis for praising Julian: namely, that, before ten years had passed after his death—for Felix, who was still alive around the year 700, composed this eulogy before then—a day had already been solemnly appointed in the Church of Toledo for the annual liturgical commemoration of him. But Felix’s own silence overturns this conjecture, and the most ancient Breviaries of this holy Church [Col. 0452B] establish the contrary with complete clarity. In none of them, composed before the sixteenth century, is a day dedicated to Julian found. Thus the first commemoration of Saint Julian inserted into the Toledan calendar is that published in the Mozarabic Missal of the year 1500. We therefore suspect—and by no means rashly—that, because some manuscript read 8 March as the day of Julian’s death, when the composition of his ecclesiastical office was being considered, the aforesaid error entered the Toledan Breviary. Since the matter was considered unimportant and had not yet been sufficiently demonstrated and clarified, no correction was undertaken. Nevertheless, if the Lord wills, this will eventually be done, and every opportunity for others to stumble here will be removed—those who, following Papebrochius’s example, have attributed such weight to the custom of our Church that, believing it extremely ancient, they preferred to correct even the oldest manuscripts rather than correct the custom itself, which celebrates Julian on the eighth day before the Ides of March. One matter remains, which Felix did not record in his eulogy but which we have no right to omit. This is the number of the Councils of Toledo to which Julian is known to have subscribed as bishop. Four were celebrated between the year 680 and 690, when he departed to heaven: at all of them he not only took part but also presided, as far as we can infer from the position of the subscriptions. Specifically, the Twelfth Council in 681, the Thirteenth in 683, the Fourteenth in 684, and the Fifteenth in 688. Except for the Fourteenth, which was provincial, the others were national. What Julian’s role was in such assemblies, and how much authority and learning he possessed among their Fathers, can be learned nowhere better than by reading their acts. In them they repeatedly testify, in carefully chosen words, how highly they valued Julian’s judgments, words, and writings; and we think we have indicated this sufficiently in the preceding notes when speaking of his Apologetic.] He held the honor of the episcopate and the dignity of the priesthood for ten years, one month, and seven days. Overtaken by the approach of unavoidable death, in the third year of Prince Egica, on the day before the Nones of March, in the era 728, he closed the final day of his life and was thus buried by lot in the basilica of the most glorious holy virgin Leocadia.

[PROGNOSTICON.]

[Col. 0451]

NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING TREATISE.

[Col. 0451]

[Col. 0451] We give first place, excellent reader, to this little work, which its author, Saint Julian, entitled *Prognosticon of the Future Age*, because, although it was composed toward the end of his life, it far surpasses his other writings both in the dignity of its subject and in the excellence of its learning. For it treats matters extremely serious in themselves, than which scarcely anything in human life or in the whole of theology is greater. What could be more sublime, more august, and, I might almost say, more divine than the question of the state of our souls at the time of death, after death before the final judgment, and finally at the judgment itself? This is unquestionably the most agreeable and fruitful of all prognostications; everyone ought to take the greatest pleasure in knowing it, rather than in those popular divinations by which even people far from ordinary are so often captured. Nor are many other matters that he touches upon in treating this subject less worthy of knowledge: divine providence and predestination, original sin, the baptism of infants, the duties of angels toward human beings, prayers and offerings for the dead, the pious burial of corpses, infernal fire, the punishments of purgatory, and so forth. Everyone can see how important all these matters are.

[Col. 0453] The method employed in explaining them also possesses no small merit. First, the subject is distributed clearly and suitably into three books according to the threefold state of our souls: in death, after death until the final judgment, and at the judgment itself. Then each book is divided into numerous and most engaging questions—nearly all the questions that can be posed concerning the proposed subject. The author nevertheless resolves them in such a way that, using throughout the opinions of the ancient holy Fathers, he declares that he wishes to add nothing of his own beyond their statements. His manner of writing is at once extremely prudent and, in this field, entirely safe: he concludes nothing concerning religion without sacred Scripture or the tradition and authority of the Church. It also demonstrates a singular moderation of spirit, all the more worthy of praise because we understand it to have been found in a man versed in every discipline and especially learned in theological matters, one who combined constant reading of the ancients and an almost infinite power of memory with intellectual acuity and a writing ability far from ordinary. He is therefore worthy to be compared with the more learned and holier of his predecessors—not to say that he surpassed them in a certain sense.

There is no need to recall here where, on what occasion, and for whom this little work was written, since Julian himself explains everything fully in the letter that serves as a preface to the work and is addressed to Idalius, bishop of Barcelona, a sufficiently learned and exceptionally devout man who revered Julian of Toledo as a teacher of all learning and virtue.

The year, however, is not so easy to determine. If we can attain anything by conjecture, its composition seems to belong to the year 688 or 689. Julian relates that the occasion for this discussion arose from a conversation held with Idalius when the latter was staying at Toledo around Easter. It is not established that Idalius came to Toledo except for the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, which was celebrated in 688. It is also said that in that very year the king departed for war, when Julian was considering completing the work. We interpret this as referring to King Egica, since his predecessor Ervig had constantly pursued policies of peace. But Egica, who obtained the kingdom only toward the end of 687, could not have undertaken a war before 688. Be that as it may, this work must unquestionably be numbered among Julian’s final writings.

As far as we know, this treatise has now gone through the press for the fourth time. First at Leipzig in 1536, under the care of Johannes Cochlaeus; second at Paris in 1554, from the manuscript of Andrea Resendius, as is asserted; third at Douai in 1564, through the efforts of Boetius Epo, royal professor at the Academy of Douai. He acted from the same pious purpose that Johannes Cochlaeus had followed twenty-eight years earlier: namely, to defend religion, shamelessly attacked by heretics, by setting against their rashness and novelty the doctrine of all previous antiquity on the principal points at issue, as found in the testimony of a single man who had lived in the seventh century. In this connection, the preface of the aforementioned Boetius Epo to Philip II, king of Spain, prefixed to his edition, deserves to be read by everyone. Besides the profound piety and eloquence it displays, it contains great praise both of the work and of its author. All three of these editions deserve greater esteem because they were produced from different manuscript codices and therefore sometimes shed light upon one another. The other, fourth edition that we mentioned, produced by the editors of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, has no merit in itself, since it was conformed to the Douai edition.

Now receive what we have accomplished in this edition. Since we had no ancient codex at hand—for the one seen by Ambrosius de Morales in the monastery of the Cistercians at La Espina was destroyed in that lamentable fire in which the entire monastery burned down in 1731—we carefully compared the Leipzig and Douai editions with each other. We followed neither of them throughout, but corrected one from the other whenever either was plainly in error. At the same time, we recorded the variant readings of both and carefully investigated and indicated the exact passages from which the statements or words of the holy Fathers were taken, passages that the author himself had not identified; we also noted whenever the published editions differed from ours. Our work, however, was fruitless in the case of the testimonies of Saint Eugenius and Julianus Pomerius. The little works in which Julian had read the statements he cited have unquestionably perished; yet we owe these fragments to his diligence.

[Col. 0453]

THREE BOOKS OF THE *ΠΡΟΓΝΩΣΤΙΚΟΝ FUTURI SAECULI* OF SAINT JULIAN, BISHOP OF TOLEDO. (C)

[PREFACE.]

THE AUTHOR’S LETTER, WHICH SERVES AS A PREFACE IN THE OLD MANUSCRIPT CODEXES

[Col. 0453A]

To the most holy Idalius, especially dear to me in the Lord, bishop of the see of Barcelona: Julian, unworthy bishop of the see of Toledo.

Who could express with worthy feelings the remembrance of that day, made conspicuous by the clear celebration of all the redeemed, on which, while we were both staying in the royal city during the present year, we received the feast of the Lord’s Passion with the festive ardor of our hearts? [Note: [Col. 0453A] The Leipzig edition reads: “the day of the Passion of all the Redeemer . . . conspicuous, which . . .”] It happened then that, seeking the fitting silences of so great a festival, we entered a more secluded place of privacy. There, drenched by the rains of the divine Passion, we both lay upon separate beds, where, while we were commonly touched by the dart [Note: [Col. 0454A] “Mirror.” Leipzig.] of eternal light, sacred reading was taken up in our hands. In the silence of the day we read [Note: [Col. 0454A] “As we eagerly examined them, we read in prolonged silence.” The same edition.] and examined the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion, assembling the harmonies of the Gospels. But when we came to a certain desirable passage of the reading, which I cannot now recall, we were shaken, we groaned, we sighed. A certain sublime jubilation arose in our minds, and suddenly we were drawn up to a kind of citadel of contemplation. Tears that welled up interrupted the effort of reading; shared grief cast the book aside and awaited the fruitful gift of mutual conversation alone. Who could explain in writing what divine savor then touched our minds, what sweetness of heavenly love poured itself into the minds of mortals as it flowed in, or who could adequately express it in fitting words? You were then, I confess, most holy lord and brother [Note: [Col. 0455D] “Fellow bishop.” The Leipzig edition.], wasted by the twisting pains of gout, but lifted far more greatly by the hope of divine contemplation. I believe [Col. 0455B] that at that moment all the pain of bodily suffering fled from you, when that divine conversation began to take place between us. There I fully perceived how good and how delightful it is for brothers to dwell together in unity (Psalm 132:1), when that anointing of the Holy Spirit, which had descended from God our head to the hem of his garment—for perhaps we were then that garment—illuminated us with the ardor of a great and necessary inquiry. Invited, then, by these dishes of food, we began to ask one another how the souls of the dead fare before that final resurrection of their bodies, and thus, through mutual conversation, to learn what we would be after this life: so that, thinking about this matter vividly and truthfully, we might flee the present all the more certainly as we examined the future more eagerly.

From this matter, then, certain little questions arose, which, by their diversity, affected our minds not lightly [Note: [Col. 0455D] “Not slightly.” The Leipzig edition.]. But since, because of the brevity of our understanding, we were unable to gather from them an excellent solution or definition, our spirits were jointly stirred to ensure that whatever came into question for us concerning this matter should be noted down by a running pen. Thus, whatever reason required to be answered from the matter itself, and whatever had been defined according to the understanding of Catholic teachers, the memory of sacred reading would bring before us—not through the continual turning of books [Note: [Col. 0455D] “Then through turning.” The Leipzig edition.] but through the industrious exercise of living memory [Note: [Col. 0455D] “And through the industrious exercise of memory.” The Leipzig edition.]. Then I [Note: [Col. 0456D] “Therefore.” The Leipzig edition.], if I am not mistaken, urged on by you, summoned a notary and, on that same day in your presence, collected the chapters concerning the little questions mentioned above, as briefly as I could. But since your holy mind, as is its custom, is impatient in divine matters, the strength of my smallness was compelled by the most gentle authority of your intimacy and bound by the command of our inseparable fellowship, so that, as soon as I had considered the divinely granted leisure given to me, I should immediately gather together these very matters that had earlier come into question and that had already pleased us in the arrangement of headings, combine them into one short volume, and demonstrate what the authority of our predecessors had thought on the subject by adding their statements [Note: [Col. 0456D] “Also apostolic statements.” The Douai edition.]. Thus, in investigating such questions, the multitude of books would not burden the inquiring soul, but this collected brevity would satisfy the reader’s manifold thirst. Moreover, we decided, in an exchange of mutual affection, that whatever causes or little questions concerning the final resurrection of bodies might present themselves to our memory should be recorded under a similar arrangement of headings [Col. 0456B] and in the same style. In addition to these two books [Note: [Col. 0456D] “Therefore, in addition to the two books.” The Leipzig edition.], we also judged, with the sorrowful affection of a grieving heart shared between us, that a first book should be composed concerning the death of this body and should precede these two little books, formed according to the same division of headings [Note: [Col. 0456D] “Confirmed.” The Leipzig edition.]. It would raise the mind of the reader, terrified by an immoderate fear of death, through hope of heavenly joys; and thus, after the laying aside [Note: [Col. 0456D] “Disposition.” The Leipzig edition.] or reception of this body, the nature and extent of the fruit of eternal blessedness granted to holy souls would be expressed in the notation of the following books. You yourself therefore know all that was done or determined on that desirable day.

But now, because the military expedition of the glorious prince led turbulent formations of peoples away from the royal city [Col. 0456C]—which, I believe, resulted in the calm of our minds beginning to clear after the storms [Note: [Col. 0456D] “He set out with them, which, I believe, resulted in the calm of our minds after ruins, or storms, etc.” The Leipzig edition.] through gentle breezes—I happened to remember both your command and my promise. I have therefore done what I promised, though not as I ought, at least as I was able. I have formed the first book on the origin of human death; the second, on how the souls of the dead fare before the resurrection of their bodies; the third, on the resurrection itself. [Note: [Col. 0456D] “Forming the future.” The Leipzig edition.] Since I determined that the whole should exist in one volume comprising three books, I chiefly gave this book its title so that, from its better and greater part, it might be called *Προγνωστικῶν futuri saeculi*, “Prognosticon of the Future Age.” In it, however, you will find not my own examples and teaching but those of our predecessors; and yet, if my voice sounds anywhere at all, I have written in my own style nothing other than what I remember having read in their books. But if in any place I have perhaps said what ought to have been said otherwise, or rashly inserted something in a form different from that in which it ought to have been set down [Note: [Col. 0457A] “What ought to be formulated.” The Douai edition.], may the charity that bears and endures all things forgive me as I confess it. May it also obtain this from the mind [Note: [Col. 0457D] “Minds.” The Leipzig edition.] of your holiness: that what the understanding of our weakness has shaped with insufficient learning may be corrected, clarified, and adorned by your wisdom [Note: [Col. 0457D] “Your.” The Leipzig edition.]. Above all, may it obtain this through your prayers from the Lord: that whatever I, perhaps heedless, have contracted in this work by way of sins, the communion of the pious blood of Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0457D] “Our Lord Jesus Christ.” The Leipzig edition.] and our Savior may command to be erased. I was therefore pleased to form this work not merely so that I might demonstrate to readers things supposedly unknown—for I would not doubt that many had learned knowledge of these matters from the volumes of numerous books—but rather so that, collected into one place, the account of future things might touch the minds of mortals all the more forcefully because they could read what is placed here without labor, and so that the mind might be made compunct all the more at the time when this food was most readily offered to it [Note: [Col. 0457D] “Desired.” The Leipzig edition.]. Let this ordered formation of books, gathered for the sake of knowledge, suffice, so that in this mirror our mind may recognize itself. For if we carefully meditate upon what we shall be, I believe that we shall sin either rarely or never. For it is written: “Son, in all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Sirach 7:40). Having completed these matters that have been prefaced for the sake of remembrance [Note: [Col. 0458D] “For the sake of recognition, or remembrance.” The Leipzig edition.], I ask and desire this: whether this offered formation of books pleases or displeases, may it either undergo improvement under the pen of your judgment [Note: [Col. 0458D] “Its own is lacking in L.”] or be made public by the decision of your judgment [Note: [Col. 0458D] “Your is lacking in D.”].

IDALIUS’S REPLY [Note: [Col. 0458D] This letter of Idalius appears in the Leipzig edition of Johannes Cochlaeus, at the end of the *Prognosticon*; it is absent from the Douai edition.] (C)

[Col. 0457C]

To the most holy lord Julian, especially dear to me, bishop of the first see of Toledo: Idalius, bishop of the see of Barcelona.

Fearful at the remembrance of my sins and utterly terrified by the memory of my enormous crimes, I had supposed that the divine ears were completely closed to my cries, since I was not at all receiving the work you had promised. And although for this reason—now disturbed by various troubles, now deprived of the arrival of the desired opportunity, or, as often happens, held back by forgetfulness—I had brought my pleas to your holiness with alternating farewells, I nevertheless, relying on the oracle of our Savior and Redeemer, by which he consecrated his disciples when he said, “If two of you on earth agree about anything whatever they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:19), and relying also most fully on the confidence inspired by your promise, held firmly in my heart that neither truth could in any way lie nor a worshiper and disciple of truth serve falsehood. I therefore awaited the promise of your holiness, placing great hope in the Lord Jesus Christ. Yet I prayed, if not every day, at least often, that he who is present everywhere might be present as the inspirer of our hearts and at last grant fulfillment to our desires.

Now, therefore, because the Lord remembered me and made me possess the fulfillment of my prayers, he has filled my mouth with joy and my tongue with exultation: he has crowned you with the perfection of a holy work and enriched me with the fruit of your labor. I shall therefore say to him, with the exultant words of his Prophet: “Blessed is God, blessed is the Lord, day by day” (Psalm 67:20). For a certain Jew named Restitutus arrived, carrying, so to speak, like a brute animal, material appropriate for the light. He offered with both hands the book that you had undertaken to complete with studious brevity—not only from the statements of the ancient and holy Fathers but also, with Christ inspiring and teaching, through your own labor and study—and to send, through the wisdom of your holiness, to our ineptitude.

Seizing it rather than receiving it in my eagerness to know, I opened it at once and, looking up at the title, confess that I was astonished that your holiness had entrusted the transport of so valuable and splendid a merchandise to such an untrustworthy bearer, alien to the worship of the faith. But immediately, instructed by the principle according to which treasure is entrusted to earthen vessels, I gave thanks before all to the aforementioned Jew for having carried unharmed what he had received, rather than to you, considering whether perhaps you had acted through a transformation by the right hand of the Most High, so that the man accustomed to carrying perishable merchandise might be prepared for divine and eternal mysteries. Nevertheless, I understood here the humility of your holy and skillful heart. Whatever is graceful, shining, and pure in your words, by referring it with thanksgiving to God, from whose gift it comes to you, you make great and excellent; while rejecting empty glory, you strive to display that same work before the eyes of those who see it as something lowly, by appearing to have entrusted it to a bearer of inferior worth.

After examining the title written above and considering it, I could find no other name more suitable to the work than the one it seems to bear at the beginning of its volume. It is called *Prognosticon futuri saeculi*, which can appropriately be rendered in Latin as “foreknowledge of the future age.” In it, although the first book may in some measure seem to inflict harshness and fear upon sinners, the two books that follow raise the hearts of Christians with the greatest confidence through hope of the future resurrection and of the kingdom that Christ promised to give the faithful. As I read through the remaining body of the whole codex, I found what the Lord Jesus Christ says in the Gospel: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure things new and old” (Matthew 13:52). For doubts have clearly been dispelled and obscurities brought into the light, as the decrees of the ancient Fathers and the tokens of your skill’s new brevity have been brought forth through fruitful labor. Thus truth remains from their opinions, while from your labor comes a new and most truthful brevity.

Whatever, therefore, they truly, chastely, and soberly thought in matters concerning God is shared by you, since the Lord’s teaching has brought the same knowledge to you. Yet your diligence deserves equal applause because, prompted by curiosity, it has clearly opened to the sluggish and drowsy the opinions of those men collected into one place and presented in a connected account. Therefore, although they supplied the material through Christ’s gift, the full sum of the labor will nevertheless be attributed to your work. For even if gold possesses the splendor of its origin and nature, when it is skillfully shaped through forms or even varieties of figures and is elegantly polished, the craftsman’s ingenuity is rightly praised. Moved by this example, I would endeavor to exalt in praise the effectiveness of the talent that divine grace has placed in your heart and the distinguished zeal with which I know you have labored in the causes of Christ; or, since I cannot do so myself, I would ask others to praise you—were I not aware that this very thing is usually displeasing to you. I therefore have left to do what the holiness of your soul desires.

My insignificance, then—or rather the whole Church together with me, to whose knowledge our lowliness has brought the distinguished features of your work—renders to the immense and ineffable Trinity, not as many thanks as it owes, but as many as it is able to offer. For at the end of time, or, more truly, at the consummation of the world, it poured into the heart of your blessedness the gift of its grace together with the zeal for holy work, and gave to your mouth an upright and well-sounding discourse, so that it might resound by terrifying the hearts of sinners and might abundantly kindle, with heavenly fire, those devoted to good works, strengthening them in holy actions.

We then pray the most lavish mercy of the heavenly Majesty to preserve you, extending the years of your life, in the episcopate of his Church for the illumination of the faithful. May he also grant that the gift of his graces, which he has poured into your heart, may overflow so greatly that through the zealous works and teachings of your holiness he may make the Catholic people possessors of every good; and, in return for your holy diligence in labor, after the longest span of this life, may he grant you the heavenly kingdoms to possess with his saints and elect, your iniquities forgiven and your sins covered.

PRAYER OF THE SAME JULIAN TO GOD

[Col. 0460A]

Inhabiting the desert of Idumea, blind and sick, I cry out to you, Son of David: have mercy on me. For I seek my eternal homeland, Jerusalem; I long to behold its citizens, but I cannot find guides by whom I may cross over there. Therefore, you who have deigned to show yourself as the way, extend your hand to me, by which I may arrive there—not now blind, but seeing—without any obstruction from robbers. For you alone are such a way as has no robber.

Behold, my anxious heart, sighing to you for a long time over the return to that homeland, is stretched upon the rack by immeasurable concern for the things to come. I desire that, before day breaks, it may already contemplate here the joys of that future blessedness. For, seeking what benefit awaits the souls of the dead after the death of this body, and what glorification will also reach them after they receive their bodies, I have taken care, according to the measure of my strength and as far as I have been able to discern from the discussions of the elders, to collect in this work certain instruments for investigating the matter. But these things too have been stated only insofar as they can be spoken by mortals; nevertheless, not everything that must come to pass could be stated, because the paths of your judgments are inscrutable. Yet, desiring to fly into the bosom of that homeland about which such great things are told, I ask that through you, who are the way, I may walk; in you, who are the truth, may not stumble; and to you, who are the life, may arrive. Therefore, from you, who are the way to supreme happiness, may I not be separated by any misfortune or torn away by any obstacle of circumstance; but, walking in you, may I not suffer the robber when I am about to die, nor, once dead, endure an accuser. Protect me as I die with angelic watchfulness; when summoned to you, console me with the outstretched embrace of your mercy, so that, coming to you without shame, I may see the good things that are in Jerusalem.

Now, Lord, it is enough that, darkened until now by the shadows of sins, I have not perished. Therefore, so that this very thing, which I prepare for my own remedy or that of my brothers, may not become offensive in any respect, I beseech you, I implore you, by that glorious commerce of your sacred blood and by the invincible and venerable sign of your cross, that I may not be accused as reckless on account of these things, that I may not waste away as one in error, and that I may not be judged and punished with those who speak great things from their own heart, not from your Spirit. Behold, my Lord, you have before you your poor man, begging and knocking—not arrogantly defining what he does not know, but humbly desiring to recognize what ought to be known. Feed me, therefore, Lord, with all the promises of your grace. Although they cannot here be grasped, they are nevertheless believed with the firm assurance of true faith. Grant me, wretched as I am, both to await here in happiness that joy which no human pen can encompass, which no eye has seen and which has not entered into the human heart, and there to behold it with fuller evidence of its reality.

**Note:** “About which” (*de quo*). L.

# The First Book of the *Prognosticon* of Saint Julian Begins: On the Origin of Human Death

## Chapter I. How death first entered the world

The apostle Paul teaches that death entered the world through the sin of the first man: “Through one man,” he says, “sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12).

## Chapter II. That God created the angels immortal, but threatened human beings who sinned with death

Death comes to human beings from the propagation of sin. For one must not believe that God created human beings in the same way in which he had created the angels, so that, even if they sinned, they could not die at all. Rather, the human being was created in such a way that, having fulfilled the duty of obedience, angelic immortality and blessed eternity would follow without the intervention of death; but if disobedient, he would be punished by the most just death. Thus we see that those first sinful human beings were struck by death in such a way that whatever arose from their stock was likewise held subject to the same penalty. For nothing other than what they themselves had been would be born from them. Indeed, because of the magnitude of that guilt, condemnation changed nature for the worse, so that what had preceded as punishment in the first sinners would also follow by nature in the other human beings who were born.

**Note:** “In that way” (*eo modo*). L.

**Note:** “With the most just condemnation” (*damnatione justissima*). L.

**Note:** “The first sinners were thus” (*primos peccatores ita fuisse*). D.

**Note:** “What” (*quod*) is absent. D.

**Note:** “The condemnation of those natures.” D.

**Note:** “Would follow in the remaining human beings.” D.

## Chapter III. On the nature of the first human being, or on the penalty of death by which he was justly condemned after sin

**Note:** “Of the created human being.” L.

The first human being was created with such a nature that he was fully capable both of immortality and of death: he was not made immortal in such a way that, even if he sinned, he could not die; nor was he made mortal in such a way that, if he had not wished to sin, he would succumb to death. He was also endowed with freedom of choice, so that he might justly be blessed if he did not wish to sin when he could have done so, or wretched if, although he could have avoided sin, he sinned—not from any necessity, but by his own will.

And since neither a right action nor a sin can be spoken of without the keeping or abandonment of some commandment, he received a commandment after being placed in paradise: since by nature he possessed the ability both not to die and to die, either, by carrying out the life-giving commandment and being proved obedient, he would become immortal in such a way that he could no longer die; or, being detected as disobedient through its transgression, he would begin to be mortal in such a way that he could not avoid death. This seems to me to be the reason why the first human being received the commandment, and why the penalty that came upon the sinner through the merit of his transgression was just.

**Note:** “And that the penalty was just.” L.

**Note:** “And a right action—for it could not be called a sin.” D.

**Note:** D reads: “And capable of death, so that he was not immortal in such a way that, even if he sinned, etc.”

## Chapter IV. From what death received its name

Death was so called because it is bitter, or it was named from the bite of the first human being. For when the first parent of the human race touched the forbidden tree through disobedience, he incurred death through the bite.

**Note:** From this passage the reading found in certain manuscripts of Saint Isidore (*Etymologies*, Book II, chapter 2) is confirmed. In them, this other etymology of death, derived from *morsus* (“bite”), is contained in exactly these words. Since the Paris edition of Saint Isidore, older than our royal edition, had indicated this reading, we do not see why in the present edition it has not only been rejected from the text but also entirely omitted from the margin.

**Note:** The Leipzig edition continues: “And therefore death itself is certainly also called from the bite.”

## Chapter V. That there are three kinds of death

It must be understood that there are three kinds of death: bitter, premature, and natural. The death of infants is bitter; that of the young, premature; that of the old, natural.

**Note:** “And it must be understood that”: these words are absent in L.

**Note:** “Mature, that is, natural.” L.

## Chapter VI. How harsh the death of the flesh is, and that the dying often do not feel its distress

As for bodily death—that is, the separation of the soul from the body—which those who are dying undergo, it is good for no one. For it has a harsh sensation, and the force itself by which the two things that had been joined and fastened together in the living person are torn apart is contrary to nature. It continues until every sensation that arose from the very union of soul and flesh is killed and removed. Yet sometimes a single blow to the body, or a sudden snatching away of the soul, intercepts so great a distress and does not permit it to be felt because of the speed with which it comes.

**Note:** “A sensation from the spirit.” L.

**Note:** “As great as the whole distress.” L.

## Chapter VII. That the soul is often freed from sins through a harsh death

**Note:** “The death of the flesh.” L.

Whatever it is in the dying by which sensation is removed amid grievous feeling, if it is endured piously and faithfully, increases the merit of patience, but does not remove the name of punishment. Thus, although death is undoubtedly the punishment of the one who is born, perpetuated through the propagation of the first human being, nevertheless, if it is weighed according to piety and justice, it becomes the glory of the one who is reborn. And although death is the recompense of sin, it sometimes obtains that nothing be recompensed to sin.

Accordingly, blessed Gregory says:

“It is written: ‘The righteous person, whatever death may overtake him, will be in refreshment’ (Wisdom 4:7). Therefore, what does it harm the elect, who are advancing toward eternal life, if they die harshly for a short time? For perhaps there is sometimes some fault of theirs, although very small, which ought to be cut away in that same death. The man of God who was sent against Samaria, because he ate on the journey through disobedience, was killed by a lion on that same journey. But it is immediately written there that ‘the lion stood beside the donkey and did not eat from his corpse’ (1 Kings 13:28). From this it is shown that the sin of disobedience was released in the very death, because the same lion that had dared to kill him while he was alive did not dare to touch him once he had been killed. For the one who had the courage to kill him did not receive permission to eat from the corpse of the slain” (Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 24).

Therefore, one must believe that often the fear alone purifies the souls of the righteous as they depart from minor faults. For at the very departure from life the souls of the elect are terrified by immense fear, uncertain whether they are passing to reward or to punishment. Some of the elect, at their end, are purified from certain light sins; others, at the very end, become joyful through contemplation of eternal goods.

**Note:** “By enduring it.” L.

**Note:** “If they die?” L.

**Note:** “For it is written” (*item ex hoc*). D.

**Note:** “Because the same one whom he had dared to kill while alive.” L.

**Note:** “His corpse” is absent. L.

**Note:** D lacks “of goods.”

## Chapter VIII. That death is not itself any good, and yet is good for the good

Death, by which the body is separated from the soul, is often good for the good, because through it one passes to future immortality. This is not because death, which previously was evil, has itself become some good; rather, God bestowed such great grace upon faith that death—which is clearly contrary to life—became an instrument through which one might pass to life.

**Note:** “Nor is it anything good.” L.

## Chapter IX. Against those who say: If the sin of the first human being is dissolved in baptism, why does death follow baptized people?

**Note:** “May follow.” L.

Those who are troubled about why human beings suffer death, although the guilt is absolved through the grace of baptism, should pay attention.

**Note:** “Let them attend to this excellent solution of the matter.” L. For those who say these things usually put forward their objection in clever propositions:

“The death that came upon the first human being arose from the evil of disobedience, and therefore, on account of that original sin, the condition of death is imparted to each person. But we, whose original sin is dissolved in baptism, why are we held subject to the punishment of this death?”

**Note:** “Is imparted.” L.

Reason, properly brought forward, answers these objections.

**Note:** “Brought forward.” D. For the excellent teacher Augustine speaks about these matters as follows:

“For this purpose the soul is left to undergo separation from the body, even though the bond of guilt has already been removed: if the immortality of bodies immediately followed the sacrament of regeneration, faith itself would be weakened. Faith is faith precisely when what is hoped for is awaited, though it is not seen in reality” (Saint Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Book II, chapters 31–32).

**Note:** The L edition continues: “Hence Paul says in Romans: ‘We have been saved by hope. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.’”

By the strength and struggle of faith, therefore, the fear even of death had to be overcome, especially in the more advanced stages of life; this shone forth most clearly in the holy martyrs. Certainly, there would be no victory and no glory in such a struggle—for it would not even be a struggle—if, after the washing of regeneration, the saints could no longer suffer bodily death.

**Note:** “Could be a struggle.” L.

As for infants who were to be baptized, who would then hasten to baptism not for the grace of Christ but rather so that they might not be released from the body, and so that their faith would not be proved by an invisible reward but they would immediately seek and receive the payment for their work: now, through the greater and more wondrous grace of the Savior, the punishment of sin has been turned to the service of righteousness.

**Note:** The Douay edition reads differently: “But with infants to be baptized, who would not rather hasten for Christ’s grace so that he might not be released from the body? . . . but then faith itself would no longer exist, immediately seeking and receiving the reward of its work.”

**Note:** “For the uses.” L.

Julianus Pomerius also says of this:

“Therefore those who have been regenerated cannot pass from here to eternal blessedness without the death of the flesh, because all the good that the sacraments by which they are regenerated produce in them belongs not to the present life but to the future. And certainly, if all who are saved are saved by hope, and hope is not of temporal life but of eternal life, those regenerated in Christ would not be saved by hope if they appeared to wish to be reborn in Christ in order to attain the eternal blessedness that is not seen and for which hope labors, but rather to possess this visible life without end. In that case they would not be faithful, since they would have no faith in invisible things, and, made lovers of this temporal life, they would become sluggish in earning invisible goods.”

**Note:** D reads: “Lovers of this time.”

## Chapter X. That angels are present when human beings die

When, as death approaches, souls are separated from bodies, we must acknowledge that angels are present there. They receive the souls of the righteous as they depart from their bodies and introduce them into the dwellings of the pious. Thus, when the Gospel speaks of the rich man and the poor Lazarus, it is written:

“It happened that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom” (Luke 16:22).

By this statement we are most truly confirmed that, at the separation of holy souls and their departure from the body, the watchfulness of angels is always present.

**Note:** “We are confirmed.” D.

Saint Augustine also discusses this matter in the argument by which he wished to show whether the dead know what the living are doing. Introducing this into his discussion of the question mentioned above, he says:

“For if there were no angels who could be present in the places of the living and the dead, the Lord Jesus would not have said: ‘It happened that the poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom.’ Thus those who carried the one whom the Lord willed from here to there could be here now and there then” (Augustine, *On the Care to Be Shown for the Dead*, chapter 15).

The same teacher also says in his books *On the Trinity*:

“Whoever is renewed from day to day by advancing in the knowledge of God and in the righteousness and holiness of truth transfers love from temporal things to eternal things. In this progress and advance, when the final day of this life has found each person holding fast to faith in the Mediator, he will be led to the God whom he worshiped and perfected by him. He will be received by holy angels, destined at the end of the age to receive an incorruptible body, not for punishment but for glory.”

**Note:** “To the knowledge of God and the righteousness and holiness of truth, he is transferred from death to life, and from temporal things …” L.

**Note:** D lacks “the final.”

## Chapter XI. On the fear of bodily death

**Note:** “Why he.” L.

Everyone fears the death of the flesh, but few fear the death of the soul. On behalf of the death of the flesh—which will undoubtedly come someday—everyone takes care that it not come; that is why they labor. A human being who is going to die labors not to die, but does not labor not to sin, although he is going to live forever. And when he labors not to die, he labors without purpose. What he accomplishes is that death is greatly delayed, not that it is escaped. But if he does not wish to sin, he has not labored in vain, and he will live forever.

If only we could awaken human beings, and be awakened together with them, so that we might be lovers of enduring life as we are lovers of fleeting life! What does a person not do when placed in danger of death? With a sword hanging over their necks, people have betrayed whatever they had kept in reserve for their livelihood. Who did not immediately betray something to avoid being struck, and was perhaps struck after the betrayal? Who did not immediately wish to betray what he had to live on, in order to live, choosing a beggar’s life rather than a swift death?

Who, when told, “Sail, lest you die,” delayed? Who, when told, “Work, lest you die,” was lazy? God commands easy things so that we may live forever, and we neglect to obey. God does not say to you: “Lose whatever you possess, so that you may live for a short time anxiously amid labor”; rather: “Give to the poor from what you have, so that you may live forever secure and without labor.”

The lovers of temporal life accuse us—a life they possess neither whenever they wish nor for as long as they wish. Yet we do not accuse one another, though we are so lazy and lukewarm in grasping eternal life, which, if we wish it, we shall have, and which, once we have it, we shall not lose. But this death that we fear we shall have even if we do not wish it.

**Note:** “As people are lovers of fleeting life.” L.

**Note:** “What did the person do?” L.

**Note:** “That he may escape.” L.

**Note:** “He will not have labored in vain.” L.

## Chapter XII. On the difference in fear: why each person should consider whether it is more bearable to fear several kinds of death while living or to endure one of them when it occurs

The most blessed Augustine says:

“What difference does it make by what kind of death this life is ended, when the one whose life is ended is not compelled to die again? But since innumerable deaths, so to speak, threaten each mortal person amid the daily hazards of this life, as long as it remains uncertain which of them will come, I ask whether it is better to suffer one by dying, or to fear all of them while living.

**Note:** The Leipzig edition adds: “And thereafter to fear none, or always to fear all”; these words are absent from both the Maurist edition of Augustine and the Douay edition.

For I am not unaware how readily one chooses to live for a long time under fear of so many deaths rather than, by dying once, to fear none thereafter. But one thing is what the weak and fearful sense of the flesh recoils from, and another is what the carefully scrutinized reason of the mind establishes.

A death preceded by a good life must not be considered evil. For nothing makes death evil except what follows death. Therefore those who must necessarily die should not be greatly concerned with what happens to cause them to die, but with where they are compelled to go by dying. Since Christians know that the death of the devout poor man among the tongues of licking dogs was far better than that of the impious rich man in purple and fine linen, what did those dreadful kinds of death harm the dead who had lived well?” (*The City of God*, chapter 11.)

**Note:** In the Leipzig edition, from these words another chapter begins, with the title: “How those who fear bodily death may be consoled.” Thus in the Douay edition this first book consists of twenty-one chapters, and in the Leipzig edition of twenty-two.

What is this death? The abandonment of the body, the laying down of a heavy burden—but only if another burden is not carried by which the human being is hurled into Gehenna. Concerning this death the Lord says: “He who keeps my word will never see death” (John 8:51). Let us not fear this death, but fear that which is more grievous. Yet because many perversely feared this one, they fell into the other.

Some people were told: “Worship idols; if you do not, you will be killed”; or, as Nebuchadnezzar said: “If you do not do so, you will be thrown into the furnace of burning fire” (Daniel 3:15). Many were afraid and worshiped, unwilling to die—and they died. By fearing the death that cannot be escaped, they fell into the death that they could have happily escaped if they had not unhappily feared this unavoidable one.

You were born human; you are going to die. Where will you go so as not to die? What will you do so as not to die? So that your Lord might console you, since you were destined to die by necessity, he deigned to die by choice. When you see Christ dead, do you disdain to die? Therefore you are going to die; you have no way to escape this. Whether it happens today or tomorrow, it will happen; the debt must be paid.

What, then, does a person accomplish by fleeing, fearing, and hiding so as not to be found by the enemy? Is he accomplishing that he will not die? No, but only that he will die somewhat later. He does not receive security from the debt, but merely a postponement. However long it is delayed, what is delayed will nevertheless come.

Let us fear that second death, which follows this first death of the flesh. Let us therefore keep the word of God in faith, destined to arrive at the vision when we have received complete freedom. For concerning the fathers who died long ago, the Lord gave the Jews this answer, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. He is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matthew 22:32). Therefore, if they live, let us labor to live in such a way that, when we have died, we may deserve to live with them. For this is what the Lord says: “He who believes in me, even though he has died, will live” (John 11:25)—that is, he who believes in me, even though he has died for a time in the flesh, lives in the soul until the flesh also rises, never afterward to die.

**Note:** “And to fear none thereafter.” L and the edition of Saint Augustine. The Douay edition, however, reads “thereafter not to fear.”

**Note:** L omits “not.”

**Note:** L reads: “Let us fear this death,” and also lacks “which is more grievous.”

**Note:** “Without necessity, dead.” L.

**Note:** L omits the second “not.”

**Note:** “And so that, once dead, we may live together.” L.

## Chapter XIII. That Christians should not fear bodily death, because the righteous person lives by faith

As the blessed teacher and martyr Cyprian says:

“It belongs to one who does not wish to go to Christ to fear death; it belongs to one who does not believe that he is beginning to reign with Christ to be unwilling to go to Christ. For it is written: ‘The righteous person lives by faith’ (Romans 1:17). If you are righteous and live by faith, if you truly believe in God, why, since you are going to be with Christ and are secure in the Lord’s promise, do you not embrace the fact that you are being called to Christ and rejoice that you are freed from the devil?

“Finally, that righteous Simeon, who was truly righteous, had faithfully kept God’s commandments. When he had received a divine response that he would not die before he had seen the Lord’s Christ, and when the infant Christ had come into the temple with his mother, he recognized in the Spirit that Christ had been born—the one about whom he had previously been told. Having seen him, he knew that he would soon die. Therefore, joyful at his approaching death and secure in the nearness of his summons, he took the child in his arms, blessed God, and exclaimed:

‘Now, Lord, you release your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation’ (Luke 2:25–30).

Thus he proved and testified that peace for God’s servants is then free, tranquil, and at rest, when, drawn out from the storms of this world, we seek the harbor of eternal dwelling and security; when, having completed this life, we come through death to immortality. That is our peace, that faithful tranquility, that stable, firm, and everlasting security” (*On Mortality*, p. 229, Paris edition, 1726).

**Note:** The words “who was truly righteous” are absent from the Douay edition but are found in Lipsius and also in the Paris edition completed by a monk of Saint-Maur in 1726, with which we compared the other testimonies.
