We warn the reader here, however, that although the Leipzig edition of Johann Cochlaeus frequently agrees with the editions of the holy Fathers whose statements are cited in this little work, we have deliberately admitted into the text the readings of the Douay edition, although they differ somewhat from those editions, whenever they do not plainly conflict with the author’s meaning. We had two reasons for this decision. First, the agreement of the Leipzig edition with the editions of the holy Fathers seems highly suspect and appears more likely attributable to the editor’s diligence: he took care to conform the testimonies of the holy Fathers to their proper sources, noting in the margin the works from which they were taken—a diligence lacking in the Douay edition. There can therefore be no doubt that Boethius, its editor, altered nothing arbitrarily from his manuscript. Second, since Julian himself asserts that, in composing the book, he always followed the opinions and teaching of the elders, but did not always use their exact words, sometimes writing in his own style what he remembered having read in their books, no one will think that the reading of the Douay edition should be rejected merely because it does not always correspond word for word with the editions of the holy Fathers.

**Note:** “Christ already [born].” L.

**Note:** “At the divine summons.” L.

**Note:** Lipsius has *semel* (“once”) instead of *scilicet* (“namely”), which is found in the Douay edition; shortly below, the word *servis* (“servants”) is absent.

**Note:** L reads: “When this death has been extinguished in immortality,” and so forth. The Paris edition of Saint Cyprian reads: “When this death has been ended,” and below, “true peace.”

## Chapter XIV. For what reasons the fear of human death can be moderated; that we ought rather to embrace the day of death than fear it; and that a great number of loved ones awaits us there

The aforementioned teacher says:

“The kingdom of God has begun to draw near, dearest brothers; the reward of life, the joy of eternal salvation, everlasting gladness, and possession of paradise, recently lost, are now coming as the world passes away. Heavenly things are already succeeding earthly things, great things small things, and heavenly things transitory things.

**Note:** “Eternal things succeed.” L. and the edition of Saint Cyprian.

What place is there here for anxiety and concern? Who amid these things is fearful and sorrowful, except one who lacks hope and faith?” (Saint Cyprian, *On Mortality*).

The same teacher says afterward:

“What else is conducted daily in the world than a battle against the devil? What else is fought amid constant struggles than against his darts and weapons? We contend with greed, impurity, anger, and ambition; we are engaged in continual and troublesome combat with carnal vices and worldly enticements. The human mind, besieged and surrounded on every side by the devil’s assaults, scarcely meets each attack and scarcely resists. If greed has been struck down, lust rises up; if lust has been suppressed, ambition follows; if ambition has been despised, anger exasperates, pride inflates, drunkenness entices, envy breaks concord, and jealousy cuts off friendship. You are compelled to curse, which the divine law forbids; you are driven to swear oaths, which is not permitted.

“The soul suffers so many persecutions every day, the heart is pressed by so many dangers—and yet it is pleasing to remain here for a long time amid the devil’s swords, when one ought rather to desire and seek to pass more swiftly to Christ, with death coming to our aid. He himself instructs us and says: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will come into joy’ (John 16:20). Who would not wish to be free from sorrow? Who would not hasten to come to joy? And when our sorrow will come into joy, the Lord himself declares again, saying: ‘I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you’ (ibid., 22).

“Since seeing Christ is to rejoice, and our joy cannot exist unless someone has seen Christ, what blindness of mind, what madness it is to love the pressures, punishments, and tears of the world, and not rather hasten to the joy that can never be taken away! This happens because faith is lacking, because no one believes true the things that God promises—God who is truthful, whose word is eternal and firm for those who believe.

“If a serious and reputable man promised you something, you would have faith in the one making the promise and would not believe yourself deceived or misled by someone whom you knew to stand by his words and deeds. God speaks with you, and you waver faithlessly with an unbelieving mind? God promises immortality and eternity to the one departing from this world, and you doubt? This is nothing other than not knowing God; this is offending Christ, the teacher of faith, by the sin of unbelief; this is being established in the Church but not having faith in the house of faith.

“How beneficial it is to depart from this world, Christ himself, the teacher of our salvation and advantage, demonstrates. When his disciples were troubled because he said that he was now going away, he spoke to them, saying: ‘If you loved me, you would rejoice because I am going to the Father’ (John 14:28), teaching and showing that, when those we love depart from this world, we ought to rejoice rather than grieve.

“Remembering this, the blessed apostle Paul writes in his Epistle and says: ‘For me, to live is Christ and to die is gain’ (Philippians 1:21), considering it the greatest gain no longer to be held by the snares of the world, no longer to be subject to any desires and vices of the flesh, freed from pressing afflictions and released from the poisonous jaws of the devil, and to depart at Christ’s call toward the joy of eternal salvation.”

**Note:** “And is delighted.” D.

**Note:** “To hasten.” L.

**Note:** “And you will lament.” L.

**Note:** “Lovers of this time.” D.

**Note:** L reads: “Immortality and eternity.”

**Note:** “Increasing.” Douay edition.

**Note:** “In his words and promises.” L.

The same teacher also says:

“Therefore, if we believe in Christ, let us have faith in his words, and, since we will not die forever, let us come with joyful confidence to Christ, with whom we shall live and reign. In that we die for the present, we pass through death to immortality. Eternal life cannot follow unless we depart from here. This is not an exit but a passage, a crossing over to eternity after the journey through time has been completed. Who would not hasten to better things? Who would not desire more quickly to be changed and remade in the likeness of Christ and in the dignity of heavenly grace?” (Saint Cyprian, *On Mortality*).

The same:

“Coming to Christ’s seat and to the splendor of the heavenly kingdoms, one ought not to mourn and lament, but rather, according to the Lord’s promise and true faith, to rejoice in one’s departure and translation” (ibid.).

The same:

“It belongs to one who is delighted by the world, whom the age, flattering and deceiving, invites by the enticements of earthly pleasure, to wish to remain long in the world. But since the world hates the Christian, why do you love what hates you, rather than follow Christ, who redeemed and loves you?” (ibid.).

The same:

“With an undivided mind, firm faith, and the strength of a courageous spirit, let us be ready for every will of God. Once the fear of mortality has been expelled, let us think upon the immortality that follows. Let us show ourselves to be what we believe, so that we may neither mourn the departure of our loved ones nor, when the day of our own summons comes, arrive without hesitation and willingly at the Lord’s command.

“Although this has always had to be done by God’s servants, it ought now to be done much more, since the world is already collapsing and is besieged by the storms of hostile evils. Since we see that serious things have already begun and know that more serious things threaten, let us consider it the greatest gain if we depart from here more quickly.

“If, while you lived in your house, its walls were tottering with age, its roof above were trembling, and the house—already worn out and exhausted, with its buildings collapsing from old age—threatened imminent ruin, would you not move away with all speed? If, while you were sailing, a turbulent and stormy sea, with waves violently rising, announced that shipwreck was coming, would you not quickly seek the harbor?

“Behold, the world totters and collapses, and testifies to its own ruin—not through the old age of created things, but through its end. And you do not give thanks to God? Do you not rejoice that, removed by an earlier departure, you are stripped of the ruins, shipwrecks, and blows that threaten?”

**Note:** “If the walls of your dwelling.” L.

**Note:** “They would tremble.” L.

**Note:** “Not already through old age.” L.

**Note:** “For you” is absent in L.

> “Let us embrace the day that assigns each person to his own dwelling, which, having snatched us away from here and stripped us of the snares of this age, restores us to paradise and the kingdom. Who, living abroad, would not hasten [Note: “[would hasten” (*properaret*), L.] to return to his homeland? Who, hastening to sail to his own people, would not eagerly desire a favorable wind, so that he might quickly embrace those dear to him? Let us regard paradise as our homeland; we have already begun to have the patriarchs as our parents. Why do we not hasten and run, so that we may see our homeland and greet our parents? A great number of those dear to us awaits us there—a multitude of parents, brothers, and children; a frequent and abundant crowd [Col. 0471A] longs for us: already secure concerning their own safety, but still anxious about ours. How great a joy, shared by them and by us, it is to come into their sight and embrace! What delight of the heavenly kingdoms [Note: “How great the desire for the heavenly kingdoms,” Duac.] is there, without fear of dying, and what supreme and perpetual happiness in living with eternity! There is the glorious choir of the apostles; there is the number of rejoicing prophets; there is the innumerable people of martyrs. Let us hasten to these with eager desire, so that we may soon be able to be with them; let us wish that we may soon come to Christ. May God see this thought of ours; may Christ behold this purpose of our mind [Note: “of our mind” (mentis nostrae), L.], and may he grant the greater rewards of his glory to those whose longing for him has been greater.”  

## CHAPTER XV. How our will is contrary to the Lord’s Prayer, when we pray daily that God’s will be done, yet, overcome by fear of death, do not wish to pass over to him; with the example of a certain brother, to whom Christ appeared rebuking him because he feared to leave this world

The opinion of the aforementioned teacher concerning these matters is as follows. He says:

> “We must remember that we ought to do, not our own will, but God’s, according to what the Lord commanded us daily to pray. How absurd, how perverse [Note: “and how perverse,” L.], that, while we ask that God’s will be done, when God calls and summons us from this world we do not immediately obey the command of his will! We resist and struggle against it, and, like stubborn slaves, we are led into the presence of the Lord with sadness and grief, departing from here under the constraint of necessity rather than in obedience to his will; and [Note: *Et* (“and”) is absent in Lip., but present in Duac., which agrees with the edition of St. Cyprian.] we wish to be honored by him with heavenly rewards, although we come to him unwillingly. Why, then, do we pray and ask that the kingdom of heaven may come, if earthly captivity delights us? Why, in prayers frequently repeated [Note: “Reiterated,” L.], do we ask and plead that the day of the kingdom may be hastened [Note: The edition of St. Cyprian also has *acceleret* (“may hasten”); Lip. has *acceleretur* (“may be hastened”).], if our greater desires and better wishes are to serve the devil here rather than reign with Christ? Finally, so that the signs of divine providence might shine forth more clearly—namely, that the Lord, foreseeing the future, provides for the salvation of his own—when one of our colleagues and fellow priests, already exhausted by illness and anxious about approaching death, was asking that his departure be granted him, a young man appeared to him as he prayed and was almost dying. He was venerable in honor and majesty, tall in stature and radiant in appearance; while he stood beside him, human sight could scarcely discern him with bodily eyes, except that one who was about to depart from this world could already behold such a figure. The sick man, not without a certain indignation of spirit and voice, groaned at him and said: ‘You fear to suffer; you do not wish to depart. What shall I do with you?’ [Col. 0472A] This is the voice of one rebuking and admonishing him who is anxious about departure but secure concerning his summons; he does not consent to his present desire but counsels him for the future [Note: Lip. has: “and admonishing him who is anxious about persecution but secure concerning his summons, does not consent to his desire, but …”; the edition of St. Cyprian has *sollicitis … securis … desiderium*. In the remainder it agrees with the edition of Duac.].”  
> (St. Cyprian, *On Mortality*.)

## CHAPTER XVI. That we must not be broken by despair when we are troubled by approaching death

Some people are accustomed to say: “Must the Christian spirit also be troubled when death is approaching?” Those who say this should receive an answer suited to them. Christians—if there are any—who are not at all troubled when death approaches are certainly steadfast [Note: “Most steadfast,” L.]; but are they more steadfast than Christ? Who, utterly mad, would say that? What, then, is the reason that he was troubled, unless it was that he consoled the weak in his own body—that is, in his Church—through the likeness of his own weakness? Thus, if any of his own are still troubled when death approaches, they may look to him, and not on this account think themselves rejected and be swallowed up by a worse death of despair [Note: “So that, on this account, they may not think themselves rejected and be swallowed up by worse despair,” L.]. How great, therefore, is the good we ought to expect and hope for from participation in his divinity, whose troubled state calms us and whose weakness strengthens us?

For blessed Peter the apostle also, when the Lord said to him, “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” [Note: “He will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go,” L.] (John 21:18), wanted nothing other than to be released from the body and be with Christ. Yet, if it had been possible, once the distress of death had been removed, he desired eternal life; he was led unwillingly to that distress of death and left us this feeling of weakness. That no one wishes to die is so natural that even old age could not take this away from blessed Peter, to whom it was said: “When you grow old, you will be led where you do not wish to go.” Therefore, however great the distress of death may be, the power of love ought to overcome it—the love by which he is loved who, although he is our life, also chose to suffer death for us. For if death had no distress, or only a small one, the glory of the martyrs would not be so great.

## CHAPTER XVII. That at the end we must persist in prayer and commend ourselves to the prayers of the brethren

When the final hour of the due end draws near, continual prayer ought to help us [Note: “To assist us,” L.]. For if we plan to travel in this world to unknown or distant places, we sometimes commend ourselves to the prayers of the brethren, and sometimes, at the very moment of departure, we drench ourselves with a continual flood of tears [Note: “Overflowing,” L.], praying to the Lord [Note: “Praying to the Lord,” L.] that we may hasten along the paths of our journey with calm steps. And if we do these things so earnestly, while the embrace of body and soul still remains, amid the familiar things of this age [Note: Duac. has: “of flesh and soul, amid the unfamiliar things of this age.”], how much more earnestly ought we to do so at our end, when we make our passage to that region where, after the separation of body from soul has been completed, we arrive at things so unfamiliar [Note: “At such unfamiliar things,” L.] that, while we are still living here, no knowledge remains for us of whether blessed life will receive us after death, or whether, as we leave the body [Note: “From the body,” L.], we shall be snatched away to torments? Since the devil also tries to entangle the final moments of our life in his snares, if at the very departure we are fortified by the devout prayers of the brethren and by their assiduous service of psalmody, he is always driven far away and does not dare to thrust himself into the divine camp to do harm, where he hears the name of the Lord faithfully resounding from the mouths of those who sing. For we read that some people, at the hour of their departure, were freed from the devil, who stood by and lay in wait, through the prayers of the brethren and the frequent recitation of psalmody. Hence there is no doubt that when devout and truly faithful Christians depart from this world, if the diligent and frequent prayer of the brethren assists them, the bloody assault of evil spirits will not dare to touch them.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That the rites of burial and funeral care should duly be provided for the faithful

> “Although funeral care [Note: Duac. has *ratio funeris* (“the account or arrangement of the funeral”).] and the provision of burial, or the pomp of the funeral procession, are more consolations for the living than aids for the dead, nevertheless the bodies of the departed should not be despised or cast aside—especially the bodies of the righteous and the faithful, whom the Holy Spirit used as instruments and vessels for every good work [Note: “For the accomplishment of good works,” L.]. For if a father’s garment and ring, or anything of this kind, is dear to posterity in proportion to the greater affection they have for their parents, how much more must the bodies themselves in no way be disdained, bodies which we certainly wear much more closely and familiarly [Note: “Much more familiarly and closely,” L.] than any garments.”  
> (St. Augustine, *On the Care of the Dead*, chapter 3, and *City of God*, book I, chapter 13.)

Accordingly, whatever is done for the human body is not a safeguard of salvation but an act of humanity, in accordance with the affection by which no one has ever hated his own flesh. Therefore one who is able ought to care for the flesh of his neighbor when the one who cared for it has departed [Note: “As much as he can,” D.]. And if those who do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh do these things, how much more ought those who believe to do them, so that, although the body is dead, yet will one day rise and remain in eternity, such service may also in some way be a testimony to that same faith.

> “For the funerals of the righteous of ancient times were cared for with dutiful devotion, their obsequies were celebrated, and burial was provided for them (Genesis, final chapter). While still alive, they themselves also commanded their sons concerning the burial, or even the transfer, of their bodies (Genesis 47:30). Tobias, too, is commended, on the testimony of the angel, as having pleased the Lord by burying the dead (Tobit 12:12). The Lord himself, who was to rise on the third day, praises and commends for proclamation the good work of the devout woman who poured precious ointment over his limbs and did this for his burial (Matthew 26:1). Those who received his body from the cross and carefully and honorably arranged for it to be covered and buried are also commendably remembered in the Gospel (Matthew 27:59–60). Yet these authorities do not teach that any sensation exists in corpses; rather, they indicate that the bodies of the dead also belong to the providence of God, who is pleased even by such acts of devotion, for the affirmation [Note: “For the preservation,” D.] of belief in the resurrection.”  
> (St. Augustine, cited above.)

## CHAPTER XIX. Whether it benefits the dead if their bodies are buried in churches

When someone is buried near the memorials of martyrs, this benefits the deceased only in this respect: the survivor, commending him to the patronage of the martyrs, has his affection for prayer on his behalf increased. When the mind recalls where the body of one most dear has been buried, and a place bearing the name of a venerable martyr comes to mind, the affection of the person remembering and praying commends the beloved soul to that martyr. Yet it is beyond doubt that this affection, when it is shown by faithful people to their beloved dead, benefits those who, while they lived in the body, merited that such things should benefit them after this life.

(St. Augustine, *On the Care of the Dead*, chapter 4.)

## CHAPTER XX. That faith greatly benefits one buried in a church, when it is believed that he is aided by the patronage of the martyr near whom he is buried

Many of the faithful, moved by the affection of antecedent faith, order that their own bodies or those of their relatives be buried near the memorials of martyrs. I do not think that what is believed in this matter is fruitless, or that what is faithfully hoped for from divine assistance is vain—provided that those buried in churches are not bound by sins that cannot be loosed, sins preventing them from being helped after death even when sacrifices have been offered to God [Note: “Such persons,” L.].

Accordingly, if that faith is believed to possess merit by which someone praying for his deceased relative buried at a martyr’s shrine implores [Note: “Whoever, being filled with prayer for his deceased relative,” D.] God [Note: “Prays to God,” L.], how much more does that faith obtain the fruit of its hope which, while a person is still living, provides a place of remedy for his own corpse [Note: “For himself, for his own corpse,” L.]?

Indeed, Saint Augustine replied as follows to Bishop Paulinus, who had asked about this question:

> “When a faithful mother wished the body of her faithful son [Note: “Of her deceased son,” Lips. and the edition of St. Augustine.] to be placed in a martyr’s basilica, if she believed that his soul would be helped by the merits of the martyr, the very fact that she believed this was a supplication [Note: “A certain supplication,” L. and the edition of St. Augustine.], and this benefited him, if anything benefited him. And when her mind returns to that same tomb and she commends her son more and more through prayers, it is not the place of the dead body that helps the spirit of the deceased, but the living affection of the mother arising from the memory of the place. For both who he is and to whom he has been commended touch the religious mind of the one who prays—not without fruit.”  
> (St. Augustine, *On the Care of the Dead*, chapter 5.)

These, then, are the words of the most holy Augustine, by which it is believed that the faith of those who live devoutly and order the corpses of their relatives to be buried at the memorials of martyrs is not empty. Yet we have learned through many other arguments and through the examples of our ancestors that those who live wickedly to the very end of their lives are damnably buried in churches. For if they acquired no merit in this life by which such things might benefit them, it is useless to seek it after this life. Whatever is done for them can benefit them after the body only if it was acquired in the life that each person lived in the body.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning offerings made for faithful Christians who have died

In the books of the Maccabees we read that a sacrifice was offered for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:43). But even if this were nowhere read in the ancient Scriptures, the authority of the universal Church would not be of little account [Note: “The authority of the universal Church is not small,” D.], since it shines forth in this practice, in which the commemoration of the dead also has its place among the priest’s prayers poured out to the Lord God at his altar. When a sacrifice is offered to God for the spirits of the departed [Note: “Sacrifices … are offered,” L.], for those who were very good they are thanksgivings; for those who were not very good they are means of propitiation; and for those who were very evil, even if they provide no assistance to the dead, they are nevertheless consolations of whatever kind for the living. To those whom they benefit, they either bring about full remission or at least make the punishment itself more tolerable [Note: “So that the punishment itself may come to pass,” L.].

# BOOK TWO. How the souls of the dead exist before the resurrection of their bodies

## CHAPTER I. On the difference between the paradises

There is one earthly paradise, where the life of the first human beings existed bodily; but there is another, heavenly, where the souls of the blessed are transferred immediately after leaving the body and, rejoicing in worthy happiness, await the reception of their bodies.

Concerning this paradise Julianus Pomerius [Note: Julianus Pomerius, in his *Dialogue on the Nature of the Soul*, comprising eight books, book VIII—which, according to Saint Isidore, treated the resurrection, or the ends of good and evil—has entirely perished.] says:

> “Thither, too, the souls of the righteous seem to be led or to go into paradise when they depart from the body—the paradise to which the Apostle says he was caught up, surely in mind and not in body.”

Again, after a short interval, the same author says:

> “Enough has been said about the heavenly paradise [Note: “It is enough to know about the heavenly paradise,” L.], namely, that the holy souls, immediately after leaving their bodies, are sent there by God’s gift. That this ought to be believed was confirmed by our Lord Jesus Christ by his authority when he said to the thief, ‘Today you will be with me in paradise’ (Luke 23:43). Without any ambiguity he thereby proved that the heavenly paradise receives blessed souls stripped of their bodies without any interval of time.”  

## CHAPTER II. Where the paradise is in which the souls of the blessed, stripped of their bodies, rest

We read in blessed Augustine, when he was explaining in the fullest detail those words of the Apostle in which the Apostle himself recalls that he was caught up into the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2), that paradise is in the third heaven—the place into which the Apostle was caught up and where the souls of the blessed, stripped of their bodies, are placed. The same teacher defines the first heaven as corporeal, the second as spiritual, and the third as mental, into which one ascends through contemplation of the mind [Note: “Into which,” D.], asserting as follows:

> “If we rightly understand the first heaven as everything corporeal, whatever is above the waters and the earth [Note: “Whatever, in the general sense of the term,” L.], then the second is in a bodily likeness—that is, what is itself seen in bodily form, such as that disk which was lowered to Peter in ecstasy, full of animals (Acts 10:10–11) [Note: “By the spirit,” L.]. But the third is what is perceived by the mind, so hidden, remote, completely seized away from the senses of the flesh, and purified [Note: Lips. and Duac. read this way; the editions of St. Augustine have: “so hidden and remote, and completely seized away … and purified”] that it can ineffably see and hear the things that are in it, even the very substance of God and the Word, God, through whom all things were made [Note: “The Word of God, through whom all things were made,” L.], in the love of the Holy Spirit. We therefore reasonably believe that the Apostle was caught up there and that paradise may perhaps be there, better than all others; and, if one should so speak, the paradise of paradises.”  
> (St. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XII, chapter 34.)

## CHAPTER III. What is signified by Abraham’s bosom, in which the souls of the blessed are received

I do not doubt that Abraham’s bosom has been defined by the opinions of many teachers as signifying the rest of the father, or the father’s hidden place [Note: “The hidden place of eternal rest,” L.], or even paradise, since Ambrose, Augustine, and Gregory, among others, have taught with particular elegance that the bosom of so great a patriarch signified nothing other than this very thing [Note: “Than precisely that,” L.].

## CHAPTER IV. On the distinction between the infernal regions

I remember having read in the treatises of blessed Augustine about the distinction of the infernal regions. There he says more plainly that there are two infernal regions: one above the earth and the other beneath the earth, according to the voice of the Psalmist confessing to God, “You have delivered my soul from the lower hell” (Psalm 85:13). For the Son of God was sent on account of these two infernal regions, delivering us everywhere [Note: “Delivering us, of course,” in the editions of Lip. and St. Augustine]. He was sent to this hell by being born, and to that one by dying.

Speaking in this way, he says:

> “As for hell, brothers, neither have I yet experienced it, nor have you, and perhaps there will be another way, and it will not be through hell. These matters are uncertain. But because Scripture says what cannot be contradicted, ‘You have delivered my soul from the lower hell,’ we understand that there are, as it were, two hells, an upper and a lower. For where would there be a lower hell unless there were also an upper one [Note: Lips. has: “a lower hell, unless there were an upper hell”]?”  
> (St. Augustine, *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 85, verse 13, no. 17.)

The same most holy teacher also presents another opinion, saying that within hell itself there is a lower part, where that rich man was cruelly tormented, and an upper part of hell, in which Abraham rejoiced with Lazarus, where all the saints were held before Christ’s coming. Thus the aforementioned teacher says:

> “Perhaps within hell itself there is a lower part, where the impious who have committed very many sins are thrust. Indeed, concerning whether Abraham had already been in certain places within hell, we cannot determine with certainty. For Christ had not yet come to hell [Note: “The Lord had come to hell,” L. and the edition of St. Augustine] to rescue from there the souls of all the saints who had gone before, and yet Abraham was there in a place of rest. And when the rich man was being tormented in hell and saw Abraham, he lifted up his eyes. He could not see with lifted eyes unless Abraham were above and he below. And what did Abraham answer him when he said, ‘Father Abraham, send Lazarus to dip his finger in water [Note: The words “in water” are absent in L. and in the edition of St. Augustine] and let it drip upon my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame’? ‘Son,’ he said, ‘remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus bad things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tormented’ (Luke 16:24–25). And concerning this he added: ‘Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that we cannot cross from here to you [Note: “Come to you,” L.], nor can anyone cross from there to us’ (ibid., 26).”  
> (St. Augustine, cited above, no. 18.)

These, then, are perhaps the two hells: in one the souls of the saints rested, while in the other the souls of the impious are tormented.

## CHAPTER V. From what the infernal regions receive their name

*Infernus*—“hell”—is so called because it is below [Note: “The inhabitants below are called *inferi*, because they are below,” L.]. Just as, according to the body, all lower things are heavier if they maintain the proper order of their weight, so, according to the spirit, all lower things are sadder. Hence in the Greek language the origin of the name by which the infernal regions are called is said to echo the idea that they have nothing beneath them [Note: “That they have nothing pleasant beneath them,” L.; Duac. and the edition of St. Augustine omit “pleasant”].

(St. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XII, chapter 33, no. 66.)

## CHAPTER VI. What the infernal regions are like, and whether they are corporeal

> “There is, as blessed Augustine says, a certain substance of the infernal regions, but I believe it to be spiritual, not corporeal. Nor should we listen to those who assert that the infernal regions are explained as existing in this life and that they do not exist after death. Let them see how they interpret the fictions of poets; we must not depart from the authority of the divine Scriptures, which alone are to be believed concerning this matter.”  
> (St. Augustine, cited above, no. 62.)

## CHAPTER VII. Why the infernal regions are believed to be beneath the earth

“Why the infernal regions are believed to be beneath the earth, if they are not corporeal places, or why they are called the infernal regions if they are not beneath the earth, is rightly asked,” as Saint Augustine says.

The same teacher therefore says:

> “For this reason the infernal regions are said or believed to be beneath the earth: because, appropriately in the spirit, they are represented through the likeness of corporeal things. When the souls of the dead [Note: “Through those likenesses of corporeal things it is represented that the souls of the dead …,” L. and the edition of St. Augustine], deserving of the infernal regions, have sinned through love of the flesh, this is exhibited through those likenesses of corporeal things which are customarily applied to dead flesh, namely, that it be buried beneath the earth.”  
> (St. Augustine, cited above, no. 66.)

## CHAPTER VIII. That the souls of the blessed go to Christ in heaven immediately after leaving the body

Concerning these matters we read that blessed Gregory answered Peter as follows:

> “We can affirm this neither of all the righteous nor deny it of all. For there are souls of certain righteous people that are still delayed from the heavenly kingdom in certain dwellings. What else is indicated by the loss involved in this delay except that they possessed somewhat less than perfect righteousness? Yet it is clearer than daylight that the souls of the perfect righteous, as soon as they leave the prison of this flesh [Note: “Of our perfected righteous,” only the edition of D. against L. and St. Gregory.], are received into heavenly dwellings. Truth itself also testifies to this when it says: ‘Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered’ (Matthew 24:28), because where the Redeemer himself is in body, there without doubt the souls of the righteous are also gathered. Paul desires to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23). Therefore whoever does not doubt that Christ is in heaven does not deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven. He also says concerning the dissolution of his body and his dwelling in the heavenly homeland: ‘We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens’ (2 Corinthians 5:1) [Note: Lips. alone has “because we have an edifice”; farther below, the edition of St. Gregory has “but eternal”].”  
> (St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 25.)

## CHAPTER IX. That the souls of the dead are now held in certain receptacles

> “During the time that lies between a person’s death and the final resurrection, souls are held in hidden receptacles, each according to its deserts, whether of rest or of distress, in accordance with what it received while living in the flesh [Note: “While he was living,” Lip.].”  
> (St. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 109.)

## CHAPTER X. That souls which possessed something less than perfect holiness are not placed immediately in the heavenly kingdoms when they leave the body

Julianus Pomerius says:

> “Those spirits that do not depart from here with such perfect holiness that they can go into paradise immediately after laying aside their bodies, yet do not live so criminally [Note: “Not so,” L.] and damnably, or persist so in their crimes that they deserve to be condemned with the devil and his angels, will, while the Church here effectively prays for them, be purified by corrective punishments [Note: “From punishments,” L.]. They will receive their bodies together with blessed immortality, become participants in the heavenly kingdom, and remain in it without any diminution of their blessedness.”  
> (Julianus Pomerius, *Dialogue on the Nature of the Soul*, book VIII.)

## CHAPTER XI. That before the resurrection of the body God does not appear to the holy spirits of the dead as he will appear after the resurrection; and how the souls of the dead now desire to receive their bodies

On this subject blessed Augustine says:

> “If it troubles anyone [Note: “If anyone is troubled,” Lip. together with the edition of St. Augustine] why the spirits of the dead need to receive their bodies in the resurrection, if that supreme blessedness can be granted to them even without bodies, the question is indeed more difficult than can be settled perfectly in this discourse. Yet we must not doubt at all that the mind of a human being, snatched away [Note: “Caught up” (*raptam*), L.] from the senses of the flesh and, after death, having laid aside the flesh itself, having also passed beyond the likenesses of corporeal things, cannot see the unchangeable substance in the same way as the holy angels see it [Note: Duac. differs from the edition of L. and St. Augustine: “cannot live in the unchangeable substance in the same way as the angels live”], whether this is because of some more hidden cause or because there is in it a certain natural appetite to govern a body. By this appetite it is held back from proceeding with complete devotion into that highest heaven so long as the body whose governance quiets that appetite is not present.

“Moreover, if the body is such that its governance is burdensome and difficult, like this flesh which is corrupted and weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15), since it derives from the propagation of corruption, the mind is turned away all the more from the vision of the highest heaven. Therefore it had necessarily to be snatched away from the senses of that same flesh, so that it might be shown how it could grasp that vision.

“Accordingly, when in the future transformation it has received this body—not now an animal body but a spiritual one—made equal to the angels, it will possess the perfect condition of its nature, obeying and commanding, made alive and giving life, with an ineffable ease, so that what was a burden may become glory [Note: The passage is plainly corrupt in the Duac. edition, which reads: “Made equal to the angels, possessing the perfect condition of its nature, obedient, made alive and commanding, and giving life, with an inestimable happiness, so that what was …”].”  
> (St. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XII, chapter 35.)

## CHAPTER XII. That after Christ’s descent to the infernal regions, the souls of the elect are not held in those places where the souls of the patriarchs were held, but go immediately to heaven

The ancient fathers, until the Lord’s coming, were not led into the kingdom, however justly they had lived, unless he descended who by his death would open the barriers of paradise to human beings [Note: “Would open them through the intervention of his death,” L.]. For even after they had completed their righteousness, the barriers of hell held them, although in tranquility. But after the Mediator came into this world, as blessed Gregory says, we are led into the kingdom as soon as we leave the body, and without delay receive what the ancient fathers merited only after the greatest delay.

## CHAPTER XIII. That just as the souls of the saints go to heaven after their departure, so the souls of sinners are thrust into hell

If we believe, on the testimony of sacred Scripture, that the souls of the saints are in heaven, we must also believe in every respect that the souls of the wicked are in hell. For from the retribution of eternal justice by which the righteous rejoice, it necessarily follows that the unrighteous are also tormented in every respect. Just as blessedness glorifies the elect, so we must believe that from the day of their departure [Note: “That on the day,” D.] fire burns the rejected.

## CHAPTER XIV. That those who have once been cast into hell will remain there forever

It is written in the book of Solomon: “When a tree falls, whether to the south or to the north, there it will remain” (Ecclesiastes 2:3)—namely, because when, at the time of human death, either a holy or a malign spirit receives the departing soul from the prison of the flesh, it will retain it with itself forever, without any change, so that it can neither fall from an exalted state into punishment nor rise from being plunged into eternal punishments to a remedy of deliverance [Note: “Beyond, to a remedy,” L.].

## CHAPTER XV. That the soul is not deprived of its senses after the death of the body

In the writings of Cassian we read (John Cassian, *Conferences*, conference 1, chapter 14, toward the end) that after the separation from this body souls are not idle and do not feel nothing, since the rich man in hell cries out that he is being tormented in the flame and calls to the poor Lazarus (Luke 16:24). The Lord’s words from the cross to the thief likewise show this: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). The Lord would certainly not have promised this to him if he had known that after the separation of the flesh his soul would either be deprived of sensation or dissolved into nothingness. It was not his flesh, but his soul, that was to enter paradise with Christ.

By these statements, as the same teacher says, it is clearly proved that the souls of the dead are not only not deprived of their senses, but are not even without those affections—namely, hope and sadness, joy and fear—and that they already begin to have a foretaste of what is reserved for them at that universal judgment. Nor, according to the second opinion of certain unbelievers, are they dissolved into nothingness after their departure from this life [Note: “After their departure from this sojourn,” L.]; rather, they continue to exist more vividly and cling more intently to the praises of God …

Is it not beyond every absurdity—not merely foolishness but madness—to suspect even slightly that the more precious part of the human being, in which, according to the blessed Apostle, the image and likeness of God resides (1 Corinthians 11; Colossians 3:10), becomes insensible once it has laid aside this bodily burden by which it is dulled in the present, even though it contains within itself the whole power of reason and, through its participation, makes even the mute and insensible substance of the flesh perceptive [Note: “The material substance of the flesh,” L. and the edition of Cassian.]?

Since it necessarily follows, and the order of reason itself contains this conclusion, that once the mind has been stripped of this carnal grossness [Note: L. and the edition of Cassian have: “the grossness by which it is now dulled”], it restores its intellectual powers to a better state and receives them purer and more refined rather than losing them.

The blessed Apostle knows this to be so true that he even desires to depart from this flesh, so that by its separation he may be more fully joined to the Lord, saying: “I have a desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is much better” (Philippians 1:23). For while we are in the body, we are away from the Lord [Note: “Away from Christ,” L.]; and therefore we are bold and have the good will rather to be away from the body and present with the Lord. For this reason we strive, whether present or absent, to please him (2 Corinthians 5:6, 8–9). Thus he declares that the soul’s sojourn [Note: Duac. has “the soul’s communion.”] in this flesh is a pilgrimage away from the Lord and an absence from Christ, while he confesses with complete conviction [Note: “With complete confidence,” L.] that its separation from and departure out of this flesh is presence with Christ.

## CHAPTER XVI. That the soul possesses a likeness of the body and, in that same bodily likeness, experiences rest and endures torments
On the human soul, that it possesses the likeness of the body, this is the opinion of the distinguished teacher Augustine. For he says:

“I profess that the soul can possess a likeness of the body, and indeed of bodily members. Whoever denies this [Note: The Duacene edition reads: ‘Whoever denies that the soul can possess a likeness of the body and indeed of bodily members,’ etc. Here the sense is undoubtedly obscure and the text corrupt; therefore, following Lipsius, we have emended it as it is also read in Augustine. The remainder differs somewhat, but without any error or reversal of meaning; we have therefore retained the Duacene reading.] can deny that the soul is what, in dreams, sees itself walking or sitting, or moving here and there by foot or even by flight—something that does not occur without a certain bodily likeness. Therefore, if it bears this likeness even in the underworld—not a bodily likeness, but one resembling the body—then it is also rightly located in places that are not bodily but resemble bodily places, whether in rest or in sufferings” (St. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XII, chapter 33).

## CHAPTER XVII. Whether the soul, although incorporeal, is believed to be tormented by corporeal fire

If the incorporeal spirit of a living human being is held within the body, why should the spirit, although incorporeal, not also after death be held by corporeal fire [Note: “Incorporeal fire.” Lipsius.]? We say that the spirit is held by fire in the sense that it is in the torment of fire through seeing and feeling. For it suffers the fire by the very fact that it sees it, and because it sees itself being burned, it is burned [Note: “Being burned together.” Lipsius.]. Thus it comes about that a corporeal thing burns an incorporeal thing, while invisible heat and pain are drawn from visible fire, so that the incorporeal mind is also tormented by corporeal flame through corporeal fire.

Yet from the Gospel passages we can infer that the soul suffers the burning not only by seeing it but also by experiencing it. For the voice of Truth says that the rich man, after his death, was buried in hell. That his soul is held in fire is indicated by the fact that he begs Abraham, saying: “Send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24). Since, then, he declares that the sinful rich man is condemned in the flames, what wise person could deny that the souls of the reprobate are held in fires?

## CHAPTER XVIII. That there is one fire of Gehenna, but that it does not torment sinners in one manner

[Col. 0482D]

There is indeed one fire of Gehenna, but it does not torment all sinners in one manner. For each person will there feel as much punishment as his guilt demands [Note: “For each person will there feel as much punishment as his guilt demands.” Lipsius.]. Just as many people stand beneath one sun in this world, yet do not all feel the heat of that same sun equally, because one is hotter and another less so [Note: “And one more … and another less.” Lipsius.], so there, in one fire, the mode of burning is not the same for all. For what the diversity of bodies produces here [Note: “The diversity of works.” Lipsius.], the diversity of sins produces there, so that although they have a fire that is not different in kind, it nevertheless burns each of them differently.

## CHAPTER XIX. That a purgatorial fire is believed to exist after death

We have learned that a purgatorial fire exists after death, clearly defined in the opinions of many interpreters [Note: The word “clearly” is absent in Lipsius.]. Among them is the distinguished teacher Augustine. Although he testifies that it can occur for the faithful in this life, he nevertheless also declares that it will exist for certain people after death [Note: “For light sins, for certain people,” etc. Lipsius.], asserting that that purgatorial fire, which is now despised by some and considered insignificant, is much more severe than anything a person can suffer in this life (Augustine, *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 37, no. 3).

Gregory likewise says of this purgatorial fire:

“For certain light sins, a purgatorial fire is to be believed to exist before judgment, because Truth says that if anyone speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit [Note: “Against the Holy Spirit.” Lipsius.], it will not be forgiven him either in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12:32). In this statement it is understood that certain sins are forgiven in this age, but certain others in the age to come” (St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 39).

For what is denied concerning one matter plainly implies by consequence that it is granted concerning certain others. Nevertheless, as I have said, this must be understood of small and very slight sins, such as habitual idle talk, immoderate laughter, or the sin involved in managing one’s household affairs—matters that are scarcely handled without fault even by those who know how they ought to avoid fault—or an error of ignorance in matters that are not serious. All these things continue to weigh upon a person after death if they have not been forgiven while he was still living.

For when Paul says that Christ is the foundation, he adds: “If anyone builds [Note: “Builds upon it.” Lipsius.] upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood [Note: “A piece of wood.” Lipsius.], hay, straw … the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work that he built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

Although this [Note: “This” is absent in the Duacene edition.] can be understood of the fire of tribulation applied to us in this life, nevertheless, if anyone takes it to mean the fire of future purification, it must be considered with the greatest care [Note: “Carefully.” Lipsius]. For he said that a person can indeed be saved through fire—not one who builds bronze, iron, or lead upon this foundation, that is, greater and therefore more difficult sins, already insoluble—but wood, hay, and straw, that is, the smallest and lightest sins, which the fire can easily consume.

This, however, must be known: there no one will obtain purification even from the smallest sins unless, while still living in this life, he has earned that purification through good works, so that he may obtain it there.

## CHAPTER XX. That one fire is purgatorial, through which many are believed to be saved, and another is that into which the ungodly will be plunged at Christ’s judgment

From the distinction made by blessed Augustine we understand (*Second Exposition on Psalm 29*, no. 2) that one is the future fire of which it will be said to the ungodly when Christ judges: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41), and another is the fire properly called purgatorial, because of those who are saved through it.

Through that fire which is destined for the ungodly no one will be saved [Note: “For” is absent in the Duacene edition.], because, as it is written: “These will go away into eternal punishment” (ibid., 46). But through this fire, which tests and purifies, salvation is plainly promised.

For, as the aforementioned teacher says:

“But if we wish to understand that fire in this passage as the one of which the Lord says to those on the left, ‘Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire,’ so that those who build wood, hay, and straw upon this foundation may also be thought to be among them, and so that the foundation of a good work may free them from that fire after a period of punishment imposed for their evil deeds, what are we to think of those on the right, to whom it will be said, ‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you’ (ibid., 34), except that they are those who build gold, silver, and precious stones upon this foundation?

“But if, understood in this way, both groups—the right and the left—are to be sent into that fire of which it is said, ‘Yet so as through fire’ (1 Corinthians 3:15), then both are to be tested by that fire of which it is said: ‘The Day of the Lord will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is’ (1 Corinthians 3:13). If, therefore, the fire will test both—so that if someone’s work remains, that is, if what he built is not consumed by the fire, he will receive a reward, while if someone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss—then that fire is clearly not eternal.

“For only those on the left will be sent into it in the final and everlasting condemnation; but this fire tests only those on the right. It tests some of them in such a way that it neither burns nor consumes the building that it finds constructed by them upon Christ the foundation. It tests others differently: what they built is burned, and they suffer loss, but they are saved, because they held Christ firmly established as the foundation with outstanding love.

“If they are saved, they will certainly stand on the right and, together with the others, hear: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you’ (Matthew 25:34)—not on the left, where those who will not be saved will be, and therefore will hear: ‘Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire’ [Col. 0485A] (Matthew 25:41). For no one will be saved from that fire, because all who enter it will go into eternal punishment, where ‘their worm does not die and their fire is not extinguished’” (Mark 9:45).

## CHAPTER XXI. That souls endure purgatorial fire before, and not after, the last judgment

Concerning purgatorial punishments, and the fact that they occur before the last judgment, St. Augustine, setting forth a definite opinion, says:

“We indeed acknowledge that in this mortal life certain punishments are purgatorial; … but some endure temporal punishments only in this life, others after death, and others both then and now. Nevertheless, they suffer them before that most severe [Note: The Duacene edition has “last” instead of “most severe.”] and final judgment; yet not all who suffer temporal punishments after death will enter into the eternal punishments that are to follow that last judgment. For what is not forgiven to some in this age will be forgiven in the age to come, that is, so that they may not be punished with the eternal penalty of the age to come” (Augustine, *The City of God*, book XXI, chapter 13). [Note: The entire period from here through “and afterward” is absent from Lipsius.]

For how could those whose sin is forgiven in this age be punished with eternal punishment in the age to come? Accordingly, after some further discussion, the same teacher says:

“Whoever, therefore, desires to escape eternal punishments must not only be baptized but also be justified in Christ, and thus [Note: “And so.” Lipsius.] truly pass from the devil to Christ. Let no one suppose, however, that purgatorial punishments will occur except before that last and dreadful judgment” (ibid., chapter 16).

Thus, confirmed by the judgment of so great a teacher, we acknowledge that this purgatorial fire occurs before the last judgment and precedes that fire into which all the ungodly will be plunged when Christ judges.

## CHAPTER XXII. Whether those who are to be saved in purgatorial fire are believed to be tormented until the time of the resurrection, or for a shorter period

I think that, just as not all the reprobate who are to be condemned to eternal fire will burn with one and the same kind of punishment [Note: “They will be plunged into eternal fire and condemned with one and the same kind of punishment.” Lipsius.], so all those who are believed to be saved through severe purgatorial punishments will not endure the torment of spirits for one and the same span of time [Note: “They will not endure the torment of spirits over one and the same span of time.” Lipsius.]. Thus, what is brought about among the reprobate by a differentiation of punishments is brought about among those who are to be saved through fire by a measure of time.

The punishment of purgatorial fire will therefore be extended for a shorter or longer period according to the degree to which they loved temporal goods less or more [Note: “Transient goods.” Lipsius.]. In accordance with this, blessed Augustine, discussing purgatorial punishments in his works, says among other things:

“It is not incredible that something of this kind also occurs after this life; it may be asked whether it is so, and either discovered or remain hidden from some of the faithful, that through purgatorial fire they are saved more slowly or more quickly according as they loved perishing goods more or less [Note: “Their own goods.” Lipsius.]. Yet this does not apply to those of whom it has been said that they will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:10; Galatians 5:21), unless those same crimes are remitted to them through fitting repentance. I said ‘fitting,’ so that they may not be barren in almsgiving” (Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 69).

## CHAPTER XXIII. That this death of the flesh belongs to the tribulation of purgatorial fire

The distinguished teacher Augustine, discussing purgatorial punishments, says:

“Even this death of the flesh, which was conceived from the perpetration of the first sin, can belong to this tribulation, so that each person experiences the time that follows it according to the nature of his building. The persecutions also by which martyrs are crowned, and which all Christians suffer, test both buildings like fire; they consume some together with their builders, if they do not find Christ as their foundation in them, and others without their builders, if they do find him. For although with loss, they themselves will nevertheless be saved [Note: “All who belong to Christ are tested—both buildings, like fire—and some are consumed.” Lipsius.]. But they do not consume others, because they find such things in them as will remain forever.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. Whether the souls of the dead recognize one another and those whom they have never seen

That souls of the dead, stripped of their bodies [Note: “Stripped from their bodies.” Lipsius.], can recognize one another [Note: “One another” is absent in Lipsius.], the Evangelist testifies when he says:

“It happened that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom; but the rich man also died and was buried in hell. And when he lifted up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from afar [Note: “But lifting up his eyes … he saw Abraham from afar.” Lipsius; and below: “so that he may dip … in water.”] and Lazarus in his bosom. And he said: ‘Father Abraham, send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame’” (Luke 16:22–24).

Behold how the soul of the rich man recognized the spirit of the poor Lazarus. From this it must not be doubted that the spirits of the dead likewise recognize one another in that region. The good can recognize the good, and the wicked the wicked.

“For if,” says Gregory, “Abraham had not recognized Lazarus, he would certainly not have spoken to the rich man placed in torments about the rich man’s former affliction, saying that he had received evil things during his life. And if the wicked did not recognize the wicked, the rich man placed in torments would certainly not have remembered even his absent brothers. For how could he fail to recognize those who were present, when he even took care to pray on behalf of those who were absent?

“This also shows that the good recognize the wicked, and the wicked recognize the good. For the rich man is recognized by Abraham, to whom it was said: ‘You received good things during your life.’ And the chosen Lazarus is recognized by the reprobate rich man, who asks that he be sent, saying by name: ‘Send Lazarus.’ In this recognition [Note: Lipsius reads: “Send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, that he may cool my tongue. In this faithful recognition,” etc.] the abundance of recompense for both parties will increase: the good will rejoice more greatly when they see those whom they loved rejoicing with them; and the wicked will be tormented together with those whom they loved in this world [Note: Lipsius reads: “And the wicked, while they are tormented with those whom they loved in this world with contempt for God, are consumed not only by their own punishment but also …”], so that not only their own punishment but also that of the others will consume them.

“Something still more marvelous occurs among the elect: they not only recognize those whom they knew in this world, but recognize the good whom they never saw as though they had seen and known them. For when they see the ancient fathers in that eternal inheritance, those whom they have always known through their works will not be unknown to them by sight. Since there all behold God in a common brightness, what could they fail to know there, where they know the One who knows all things?” (St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 33).

## CHAPTER XXV. Whether the souls of the blessed are seen to pray for those whom they perceive to be in hell

“According to blessed Gregory, the souls of the blessed pray for their enemies at the time when they can turn their hearts toward fruitful repentance and save them through that conversion. For what else should be prayed for on behalf of enemies than what the Apostle says: that God may grant them repentance and that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will (2 Timothy 2:25–26)?

“And how will one then pray for those who can no longer be changed from iniquity to works of righteousness? The reason, therefore, why one does not then pray for people condemned to eternal fire [Note: “Eternal punishment.” Duacene edition.] is the same as the reason why one does not now pray for the devil and his angels, who have been appointed to eternal punishment.

“This same reason now prevents holy people from praying for unbelieving and ungodly men who have died: since they already know that these have been appointed to eternal punishment, they refuse to have the merit of their prayer annulled before the presence of the just Judge.

“If even now the righteous who are living do not pity the dead and unjust who are condemned, although they themselves know that they still suffer something subject to judgment in their flesh, how much more strictly will they then regard [Note: “They behold.” Duacene edition.] the torments of the wicked, when, stripped of every fault of corruption, they themselves will cling more closely and ardently to justice [Note: “More strictly.” Lipsius.]? For in this way the force of strictness absorbs their minds, because they cling to the most just Judge, so that they have no desire at all for anything that diverges from the subtlety of his inner rule” (St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 44).

## CHAPTER XXVI. Whether the souls of the dead pray for the salvation of their living loved ones

If the rich man buried in hell begs Abraham concerning his brothers, so that they may be warned lest they too come into wicked torments [Note: “Into the place of torments.” Lipsius.] (Luke 16:27–28), how can the souls of the devout, especially those established in rest, be believed to have lost their concern for their surviving loved ones?

They can therefore pray for the salvation of the living, insofar as they are permitted by the Lord. For they can certainly remember those whom they loved while they were placed in this age. The faculty by which the living were present to one another while living [Note: “Were.” Lipsius.] is to be believed not to have been lost by them, but to be freer there, where they cannot be weighed down by the burden of the body.

For according to the divine judgment, “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15). Therefore the soul, which is now weighed down by the body, becomes freer once separated from the body. After death, then, the soul possesses both an unimpaired faculty of perception and a complete memory.

Therefore the soul that uses there the sure faculty of remembrance recalls the sweetness of its loved ones. Recalling those whom it loved in this world, it can commend them in prayer to Christ, although the prayers of faithful souls may be understood as nothing other than their desire [Note: “The prayers of the souls of the faithful departed may be understood as their desires.” Lipsius.].

I also say that the Church’s custom in this matter is exceedingly widespread: when people commend themselves to those who are dying and desire that the dying remember them [Note: “The custom of the faithful, when they commend themselves … and desire ….” Lipsius.]. Thus, when martyrs were dying, the familiarity of their surviving loved ones commended itself to them. Thus every day the multitude of devout faithful entrusts itself to the elect souls being summoned from this age and asks them always to remember it.

For the faith of the living would not ask this of the dying [Note: “Of those who are departing.” Lipsius. Shortly afterward, instead of “certain,” the Duacene edition has “uncertain”; perhaps “with certainty” was intended.] if it were certain to them that the dead could help them in no way after death. But because concern of such authority does not pass away, the outcome of the matter has often proved that the things which many living people ask the dying to do for them are received without the loss caused by delay [Note: “They receive.” Lipsius.].

This, then, seems to me to be the reasoning concerning the question proposed here. Although I do not find it expressed in precisely the words in which it was elaborated by our predecessors, I nevertheless think that the authors have defined it in meaning. Yet if I should find that they have defined something on this subject, I shall follow their opinion rather than my own [Note: “If I find it, I follow their opinion rather.” Duacene edition.].

## CHAPTER XXVII. Whether the souls of the dead can grieve or rejoice over the salvation of their living loved ones, or be moved by the sorrow or any other concern of the living [Note: “Be moved” is absent in the Duacene edition.]

[Col. 0488D]

If the dead had no concern for the living, that rich man who was tormented in the underworld would certainly not have been concerned for his brothers, saying to Abraham:

“I beg you, father, to send Lazarus to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments” (Luke 16:27–28).

Thus the dead [Note: “Nevertheless, the dead.” Duacene edition.] can have concern for the living, although they do not know what is presently happening among us, just as we who are living can have concern for the dead, even though we are ignorant of what is happening among them. For if the living had no concern for the dead, we would certainly not pray for them so frequently through offerings of sacrifices [Note: “We would not so frequently offer sacrifices to the Lord,” etc. Lipsius.].

In setting forth this and similar matters in his volumes, St. Augustine gives one example that is not a little remarkable:

“We have heard,” says the same teacher, “that when a debt was demanded from a certain man, and a bond of his deceased father was produced, although the debt had already been paid by the father without the son’s knowledge, the man began to be exceedingly distressed and astonished [Note: “And astonished.” These words are absent from the Duacene edition but present in Lipsius and in the editions of St. Augustine.], because his father, when dying, had not told him what he owed, although he had also made a will.

“Then, when he was extremely anxious, the same father appeared to him in a dream and indicated where the document had been hidden [Note: “Hidden.” Thus both our editions, Lipsius and Duacene. St. Augustine’s edition reads *recautum*, and other manuscripts read *repositum*.] by which that bond had been canceled. When it was found and shown, the young man not only refuted the accusation of a false debt but also recovered his father’s acknowledgment of debt, which the father had not recovered when the money was paid.

“From this it is thought that the man’s soul had concern for his son and came to him while he slept, so that, teaching him what he did not know, it might free him from great distress [Note: “What she did not know, she freed him from great distress.” Lipsius and likewise.]” (St. Augustine, *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*, chapter 11).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and all the spirits of the blessed eagerly await rejoicing with us; and that their joy is not perfect as long as they grieve over our errors

[Col. 0490A]

Origen, the teacher, teaches the following in his doctrines:

“For the saints who depart from here do not immediately receive the complete rewards of their merits, but they also await us, even though we delay and are sluggish. Their joy is not perfect as long as they grieve over our errors and mourn our sins [Note: “Our sins.” Lipsius.].

“Perhaps you will not believe me when I say this [Note: “You believe.” Duacene edition.]. For who am I, that I should dare to affirm the judgment of so great a doctrine? But I bring forward as a witness one concerning whom there can be no doubt. For the Apostle Paul is the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.

“When writing to the Hebrews, after enumerating all the saints [Note: “The holy fathers.” Lipsius.] who were justified by faith, he adds this after everything else: ‘And all these, although commended through faith, did not yet obtain the promise from God, since God had provided something better for us, so that they might not be perfected without us’ (Hebrews 11:39–40).”

You see, then, that Abraham still awaits receiving what is perfect; Isaac also awaits, and Jacob, and all the prophets await us, so that together with us they may receive perfect blessedness.

For this reason also that mystery is preserved until the final day of the postponed judgment: there is one body that awaits justification, one body that is said to rise in judgment. Although there are many members, there is nevertheless one body” (Origen, *Homily 7 on Leviticus*).

[Note: No one should wrongly infer from this passage that Origen, and with him our Julian, held the opinion—which some of the ancients once maintained but which has now been condemned by the Church—that the souls of all the righteous, even those fully cleansed from every stain, are not granted the intuitive and beatifying vision of God before the final day of judgment.

This point is worth observing because heretics of our time who have embraced this error strongly press this passage of Origen. Although he frequently went astray in other matters, here he certainly teaches nothing alien to orthodox faith.

For he is speaking not of the essential glory of the righteous, which consists in the clear vision and enjoyment of God and which, once attained, can neither be diminished nor increased by anything, but of the joy that theologians call accidental. Since there are many things by which such joy can be increased, it will certainly not be complete before the final judgment.

Such joy is increased in the blessed, for example, by the conversion of sinners and their true repentance, as we read in the Gospel (Luke 15:7), and then by the eternal salvation of parents, friends, and loved ones; finally, it will be completed by the resurrection and glorification of each person’s own body.

The very words of the Apostle, whom Origen presented as the witness to his opinion, plainly suggest this. To pass over other entirely just interpretations, the Apostle does not say, ‘so that they might not be crowned without us,’ but ‘so that they might not attain perfection,’ or, as our Vulgate has it, ‘be made perfect’—as though he wished to signify not that the essential and chief reward of their virtues had been delayed, but a certain accidental completion of joy, which they would not receive before we departed, since it arises from our fellowship and participation in the same happiness.

Origen’s final words themselves demonstrate this. Transferring what he had stated about each of the blessed to Christ the head and exemplar of all the blessed, he concludes that even the Lord Christ, who now sits at the right hand of his Father, does not enjoy perfect joy until he is, in a certain sense, separated from his elect, of whom he is the head. Who could interpret these words as referring to anything other than an increase in accidental joy?

Moreover, what he says at the beginning—that the saints in heaven do not possess perfect joy as long as they grieve over our errors and mourn our sins—must be understood cautiously: they detest our sins and would so vehemently wish that no crime be committed by us that, if it were possible, they would grieve and shed tears out of sorrow. Scripture uses a similar manner of speaking when it says that the angels of peace weep bitterly.

Yet they already dwell and reign with Christ in the region of peace and joy, where no mourning, crying, or pain will assail them any longer, because God has wiped every tear from their eyes. Having therefore obtained a most blessed state, from which nothing whatever can cast them down, they can rejoice and be glad even more because of the things I have mentioned; but they cannot grieve at their absence or be afflicted by them.

This has perhaps gone beyond the purpose of our work. Whoever wishes to know more should consult the more distinguished theologians of the Schools on this question: Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 4, article 5; Bellarmine, *Controversies*, book I, controversy 7, chapter 2 and following chapters; and others whom there is no time to enumerate, but whose works one will not regret having read.]

“The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you.’ Even if the eye is healthy and undisturbed with respect to seeing, if the other members are lacking, what joy will it have? Or what perfection will there seem to be if it has no hands, if the feet are missing, or if the other members are absent?

“For although there is some glory belonging to the eye [Note: “There is a certain outstanding glory.” Lipsius.], it consists above all in this: either that it itself is the body’s leader, or that it is not deprived of the services of the other members.

“I think that this is also taught to us through that vision of Ezekiel, when he says that bone must be joined to bone, joint to joint, and that sinews and veins, each in its proper place, must be restored. Finally, see what the prophet says [Note: “He added.” Lipsius.]: ‘These bones.’ He did not say, ‘These are all human beings,’ but he said, ‘These bones are the house of Israel’ (Ezekiel 37:11).

“Therefore you will have joy when departing from this life, if you have been holy; but then your joy will be perfect when no member of your body is lacking [Note: “Is lacking.” Lipsius.]. For you too will await others, just as you have been awaited [Note: “Just as he himself was awaited.” Lipsius.].

“If you, who are a member, would not regard your joy as perfect if another member were lacking, how much less would our Lord and Savior, who is the head of the whole body, say that his joy is perfect while he sees something lacking from his body’s members?”

## CHAPTER XXIX. Whether the dead can know what the living are doing

“It must be admitted,” says blessed Augustine, “that the dead do not know what is being done here by the living. But while these things are being done here, they can afterward hear about them from those who depart from here and go to them by dying—not everything, certainly, but those things which are permitted to be disclosed by those who are also permitted to remember them, and which those to whom they disclose them ought to hear.

“The dead can also hear something from angels who are present at the affairs that take place here, whatever the One to whom all things are subject judges that each of them ought to hear. For if there were no angels who could be present in the places of the living and the dead, the Lord Jesus would not have said: ‘It happened that the poor man died and was carried [Note: ‘Brought.’ Lipsius.] by angels into Abraham’s bosom’ (Luke 16:22).

“The spirits of the dead can also know, through the revelation of the Spirit of God, certain things that are being done here and that it is necessary for them to know [Note: “Things that it is necessary to know.” The edition of St. Augustine continues: “or whom it is necessary should know them.”], not only present and past things but also future things, just as not all human beings knew these things while living here, but the prophets did—not even they knowing everything, but only what God’s providence judged should be revealed to them” (St. Augustine, *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*, chapter 15).

## CHAPTER XXX. Whether the dead can appear to the eyes of the living

From this the aforementioned teacher says:

“Divine Scripture testifies that some of the dead are sent to the living, just as, conversely, the Apostle was caught up from among the living into paradise. For the deceased prophet Samuel also foretold future events to the living king Saul.

“Although some think that it was not Samuel himself, and that he could not have been summoned by magical arts [Note: “Who could have been.” Lipsius.], but that some spirit corresponding to such evil practices assumed his likeness, the book of Ecclesiasticus—which is traditionally said to have been written by Jesus son of Sirach [Note: “Is read.” Lipsius.] and which, because of a certain similarity of style, is attributed to Solomon—nevertheless contains, in its praise of the fathers, the statement that Samuel prophesied even after his death [Note: “Even when dead,” in the edition of St. Augustine.] (Ecclesiasticus 46:24).

“But if this book is challenged on the basis of the Hebrew canon, since it is not found in their canon [Note: “On the basis of the Hebrews, since it is not in their canon.” Lipsius. The Duacene edition agrees with St. Augustine’s edition.], what shall we say of Moses? He certainly appears as dead in Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 34:5), and in the Gospel he is read to have appeared to the living together with Elijah, who did not die (Matthew 17:3)” (Augustine, in the work cited above).
