## CHAPTER XXXI. That it is the souls of the saints, not of the ungodly, who alone know what can be done by the living
It must be believed without qualification that, just as the living cannot take part in the deeds of the dead, so the causes and affairs of the living are unknown to the departed. Yet the souls of the saints do not suffer this ignorance [Note: [Col. 0492D] “The souls”—as we conjecture—“feel this not at all.” L.], for they know the God who sees all things and contemplate him who knows all things. For blessed Gregory too, in the *Books of Morals*, at the passage where he began to expound that testimony from the words of Job [Note: [Col. 0492D] “He appears to be expounding.” L.], where he says, “Whether his sons were noble or ignoble, he does not understand” (Job 14:21), defines the matter as follows:

> “For just as those who still live do not know in what place the souls of the dead are held, so the dead do not know how the life of those living in the flesh will afterward be ordered [Note: [Col. 0492D] “How their lives will be ordered.” L.]. For the life of the spirit is far removed from the life of the flesh; and just as bodily and incorporeal things differ in kind [Note: [Col. 0492D] “Kinds.” L.; *genere*, D. and the edition of St. Gregory by the Maurists], so also they are distinguished in knowledge. Yet this must not be understood of holy souls, because those who see within the wondrous brightness of almighty God [Note: [Col. 0492D] *Miram* is absent in L.] must in no way be believed to be ignorant of anything [Note: [Col. 0492D] L. has “that anything outside exists.”]. But because carnal people devote their love especially to their children, blessed Job asserts that after death they do not know what they loved intensely here: whether their sons are noble or ignoble, they do not know, although concern for them had always wearied them.” [Note: [Col. 0492D] “Afterward.” L.] (St. Gregory, *Morals*, Book XII, chapter 21, on Job 14:21.)

## CHAPTER XXXII. Whether, after Christ’s descent to hell, by which the way to heaven was opened to the saints, the good can see the wicked in pain, or the wicked the good established in rest

[Col. 0492D]

Behold, as the evangelist Luke testifies, we have learned that, when that rich man died and was buried in hell, while the poor man Lazarus was established in rest in Abraham’s bosom, the rich man, placed in hell, saw Abraham or Lazarus the poor man [Note: [Col. 0493D] “And Lazarus.” L.], and Abraham looked upon that rich man placed in torments [Note: [Col. 0493D] “Looked upon.” L.] (Luke 16). We understand that these things happened before Christ’s descent to hell.

But when our Lord and Savior, dying for all [Note: [Col. 0493D] “For all of us.” L.], descended to the regions below with his soul alone, he opened the gate of the heavenly paradise to the patriarchs who were being held in the places beneath the earth. Since this is so—since he both brought them out of hell and placed them in the heavenly realm—it is reasonably asked whether Abraham and the other saints can now see the souls of the wicked in hell from that place of the heavenly paradise in which they were placed when Christ rose, just as they had been able to do from the place from which they were led forth when Christ died.

As for this question, just as it now appears to be proposed by me, occupied as I am with various tumultuous affairs, I do not readily recall where I have read about it [Note: [Col. 0493D] “*Facile* is absent in L.]. I remember having read only the following on this subject in the homilies of Pope Gregory, where he says:

> “It must be believed that, before the final judgment of retribution, the unjust see certain of the just in repose, so that, when they behold and contemplate them in joy, they may be tormented not only by their own punishment but also by the blessedness of those others. But the just, established in repose, always look upon the unjust in torments [Note: [Col. 0493D] “But the just always look upon them in torments.” L.], so that their joy may increase from this: they see the evil from which they mercifully escaped, and they give greater thanks to their deliverer the more they see in others what they themselves could have suffered had they been left there. [Col. 0493C] Nor is the splendor of such great blessedness dimmed among the souls of the elect by the sight of the punishment of the condemned [Note: [Col. 0493D] “*Animas*,” both of our editions; “*animum*,” the cited edition of St. Gregory.], because, where compassion for misery no longer exists, the joy of the blessed cannot in any way be diminished. What is surprising, moreover, if, while the just behold the torments of the unjust, this serves their joys [Note: [Col. 0493D] “This increases the service of their joys.” L. alone; the cited edition of St. Gregory differs scarcely from Duac.: “may serve their joy.”], when in a painting black is laid beneath so that white or red may appear brighter? Although their own joys are fully sufficient for their enjoyment, they nevertheless undoubtedly always see the evils of the condemned, because those who see the glory of their Creator cannot fail to see anything done in creation.”  
> (St. Gregory, Book II on the Gospels, Homily 40, no. 8.)

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Against those who say that there is no life of the soul after death

[Col. 0493D]

Cassian says:

> “Those who have died in body bless and praise the Lord in spirit, according to the passage: ‘Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous’ (Daniel 3:86), and ‘Let every spirit praise the Lord’ [Col. 0494A] (Psalm 150:6). And in the Apocalypse of John the souls of those who were slain are said not only to praise God but also to intercede (Apocalypse 4). In the Gospel, too, the Lord says more explicitly to the Sadducees: ‘Have you not read what was spoken by God, who says to you: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? He is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him’ (Matthew 22:31–32; Exodus 3:6). Of these people the Apostle also says: ‘Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a holy city’” (Hebrews 11:16).  
> (John Cassian, *Conferences*, Conference 1, chapter 14.)

Although blessed Augustine and the other teachers assert this in many passages and numerous books, I shall recall one example from the aforesaid man to reinforce this assertion.

He reports that a certain Gennadius, a physician well known and highly esteemed by him, lived at Carthage. He testifies that Gennadius was extraordinarily diligent in caring for the poor and most benevolent, with the greatest readiness of spirit. Nevertheless, Gennadius doubted whether there was any life [Note: [Col. 0494D] “Any life.” L.] after death.

> “Since God therefore would in no way abandon this man’s mind and works of mercy, a conspicuous and dignified young man appeared to him in a dream and said: ‘Follow me.’ As he followed, he came to a certain city, where he began to hear, on the right-hand side [Note: [Col. 0494D] “*Parte*” is absent in L.], sounds of the sweetest singing, beyond the customary and familiar sweetness. When he was intent upon discovering what it was, he was told that they were the hymns of the blessed and the saints. What he reported seeing on the left-hand side I do not remember well. He awoke, and the dream vanished [Note: [Col. 0494D] D. has “was present.”]; he thought about it only as much as he thought about a dream.  
> 
> “On another night, behold, the same young man appeared again to the same person and asked whether he recognized him. He replied that he recognized him well and completely. Then the young man asked where he had known him. He did not fail to remember what he answered [Note: [Col. 0494D] L. has “that he answered the same thing again.”]; and he easily recounted the entire vision, and the hymns of the saints to which he had come under the young man’s guidance [Note: [Col. 0494D] L. reads: “to hear which he had come under his guidance, and, remembering the most recent event, he easily recounted it.”].  
> 
> “But the young man asked whether what he had seen, he had seen in a dream or while awake. He answered: ‘In sleep.’ Then the young man said to him: ‘You remember correctly: you saw those things in sleep; but know that even now you see me in sleep.’ When he heard this, the man believed that it was so and confirmed it by his reply.  
> 
> “Then the one who was teaching him added: ‘Where is your body now?’ He replied: ‘In my room and on my bed.’ The young man said: ‘Do you know that in that same little body your eyes are bound and closed [Note: [Col. 0494D] L. reads: “and that your eyes are not bound but closed and inactive, and that you see nothing with them”?]? He replied: ‘I know.’ Then the young man said: ‘Who, then, are these eyes with which you see me?’ Unable to find what to answer, the man fell silent.  
> 
> “When he hesitated, the young man immediately disclosed what he was trying to teach him through these questions. ‘Just as,’ he said, ‘these eyes of your flesh are now inactive while you sleep and lie on your bed, and at this moment do nothing, yet they are the eyes with which you look upon me and by which you make use of this sight, so, when you have died, although the eyes of your flesh do nothing, there will be in you a life by which you live, and a sense by which you perceive. From now on, take care not to doubt that there is life after death.’ Thus, he says, the faithful man was freed from doubt concerning this matter.”  
> (St. Augustine, Letter to Evodius 159, in the Paris edition of the Maurists.)

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Against those for whom it seems insufficient that, after the death of the flesh, the soul sees certain joyful things or feels sorrowful things in a kind of bodily likeness; and that joyful or sorrowful things there are more vivid than those that can be seen by the mind here in dreams

[Col. 0495B]

Although the visions by which souls stripped of their bodies are affected, whether for good or ill, are not bodily but resemble bodily things, and although the souls themselves appear to themselves as resembling their bodies [Note: [Col. 0495D] “*Similes*” is absent in D.], nevertheless the joy and distress are real, arising from spiritual substance [Note: [Col. 0495D] Lipsius: “But nevertheless there are true joy and true distress, made from spiritual substance.”].

For even in dreams it makes a great difference whether we are in joyful or sorrowful circumstances. Hence many people, finding themselves in situations they had desired, regretted awakening; and others, driven and tormented by terrible fears and afflictions, were afraid to sleep after they had awakened, lest they should be brought back into the same evils. Certainly there is no doubt that the things said to exist in hell are more vivid and therefore felt more intensely [Note: [Col. 0495D] Lipsius: “The things called infernal are more vivid, and for this reason are felt more intensely.”]. For those who have been deprived of their bodily senses have reported seeing things more vividly than if they had dreamed dreams [Note: [Col. 0495D] L. has “had reported.”], though less vividly than if they had died altogether.

## CHAPTER XXXV. What reward the souls of the dead are believed to possess before the final time of that resurrection

The souls of the blessed, as soon as they depart from the dwelling of this body, enjoy spiritual gladness [Note: [Col. 0495D] L. alone has “gladness.”] until the final time of that resurrection arrives, as John testifies concerning the souls of those slain for the word of God, saying: “A single white robe was given to each of them” (Apocalypse 6:11).

This, then, is the first robe: one of rest and gladness, which the soul alone enjoys after the death of the flesh. The second will be when, having received its body, it rejoices in the immortality of soul and flesh.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That immediately after laying aside this body God is seen by holy spirits

The most blessed Cyprian, a renowned teacher and marvelous master [Note: [Col. 0496D] L. has “and magnificent martyr of God.”], writing to Fortunatus on the exhortation to martyrdom, says among other things:

> “What great dignity and what great security there are in going forth joyful from here, in going forth gloriously amid pressures and anxieties; in closing for a moment the eyes by which human beings and the world were seen, and opening those same eyes immediately so that God and Christ may be seen! As great as the speed of departure is, so great is the happiness of departing [Note: [Col. 0496D] L. has “how happily one departs.”]. Suddenly you are taken away from earthly things, so that you may be placed in the heavenly kingdoms. These things must be embraced in mind and thought, and meditated upon day and night [Note: [Col. 0496D] L. has “These things by day and night.”]”  
> (Chapter 12, near the end.)

Instructed, therefore, by the exhortation of so great a teacher, we must hold faithfully that after death we shall in no way be deprived of the vision of God, but shall enjoy him with gladness, if here we have lived in deeds pleasing to him.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That even now the souls of the saints reign with Christ in heaven

[Col. 0496B]

Saint Augustine, wishing to teach with the utmost certainty that not only the souls of martyrs but also the souls of the faithful elect already reign with Christ in heaven, cites that testimony from the Apocalypse of John in which it is read that the souls of those slain for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God reign with Christ for a thousand years (Apocalypse 20:4)—that is, the souls of the martyrs, before their bodies have been restored to them.

Lest anyone suppose that only the souls of martyrs, and not those of the other faithful, reign with Christ, the same teacher adds:

> “For the souls of the pious dead are not separated from the Church, which is also now the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0496D] “The kingdom of Christ.” L.]; otherwise their memorial would not be made at the altar in the communion of Christ’s body. Nor would it be of any benefit to hasten to his baptism in times of danger, lest this life end without it [Note: [Col. 0496D] Both of our editions read “unless by it.” The better reading is undoubtedly that of the editions of St. Augustine: “lest it end without it.”]; nor would penance avail for reconciliation if someone had been separated from that same body through shamelessness or an evil conscience [Note: [Col. 0496D] Lipsius differently: “nor for reconciliation, if someone through evil penance or an evil conscience,” etc.]. Why are these things done, unless because the faithful, even when dead, are members of it? Although, therefore, they are not yet with their bodies, their souls already reign with him.”  
> (On the City of God, Book XX, chapter 9, no. 2.)

Now and daily they desire the doubling of blessedness which they will receive later, and their very desires are, in a certain sense, the words of their cry, by which they implore God to receive the resurrection of their extinguished bodies. For their great cry is their great desire. Each person cries the less, the less he desires; and he utters the greater voice into God’s ear, the more fully he pours himself into that desire. For if desire were not, in a certain sense, speech, the Prophet would not say: “The desire of their heart your ear has heard” (Psalm 9:38).

These holy souls have already been given individual white robes—that is, the very blessedness of the heavenly homeland [Note: [Col. 0497A] “Heavenly blessedness.” L.], in which they now rejoice exultantly—and they were told: “Rest for a little while longer, until the number of your fellow servants and brothers [Note: [Col. 0497A] “Your brothers.” L.] is complete” (Apocalypse 6:11).

Therefore, to say to souls that desire this, “Rest for a little while longer,” is for God, through his very presence among them, to breathe upon them the solace of consolation amid the ardor of their holy desire. Nevertheless, as we have said, their souls already reign with him, while these thousand years run their course.

Hence it is also read elsewhere in the same book: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord; from now on, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labors, for their works follow them.” The Church, therefore, now reigns with Christ, first in the living and the dead. For this reason, as the Apostle says (Romans 14:9), Christ died so that he might be Lord of both the living and the dead.

But John mentioned only the souls of the martyrs [Note: [Col. 0497A] “John” is absent in Lipsius], because it is they above all who reign after death, since they fought for the truth even unto death [Note: [Col. 0498A] “They contended.” But the reading clearly applies to the whole passage. L.]. Yet, by taking the part for the whole, we understand the other dead as well—those who belong to the Church [Note: [Col. 0498A] “Which is the kingdom of Christ.” L.], which is the kingdom of Christ.

The second book ends.

# THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS: ON THE RESURRECTION ITSELF

[Col. 0497]

## CHAPTER I. That no human being has known the time and day of the judgment

[Col. 0497B]

The Lord wished the time or day of judgment to be unknown to us. For when the disciples asked him about the final day, saying, “What will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age?” we read that the same Lord answered: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:32).

Yet, when he says that he does not know this, it must not be thought that the Son was ignorant of it; rather, he knows it in such a way that he does not wish to tell others. For when the Lord himself says through the prophet, “The day of vengeance is in my heart” (Isaiah 63:4), he indicates that he does know it, but does not wish to disclose it to others.

## CHAPTER II. Whether it is believed that there is a particular place where judgment will be carried out by the Lord

[Col. 0497C]

What I may have read on this elsewhere does not readily come to mind [Note: [Col. 0497D] “In other books.” Lipsius.]. Nevertheless, we learned from the prophecy of the prophet Joel [Note: [Col. 0497D] “We have learned.” L.] that, in the valley of Jehoshaphat, all nations are to be gathered by the Lord at the time of judgment [Note: [Col. 0497D] “Are to be judged.” L.]. For the same holy prophet says:

> “In those days and at that time, when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all nations and bring them down [Note: [Col. 0497D] L. has “into the valley.”] into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and I will enter into judgment with them there” (Joel 3:1–2).

But let us hear how blessed Jerome understands these words of the prophet, so that from his words the reader may better recognize [Note: [Col. 0497D] “May recognize.” L.] whether this place of Jehoshaphat, where judgment is said to be carried out, should be understood literally or figuratively.

Blessed Jerome says [Col. 0498B]—on this passage in Joel, though not in these exact words:

> “Jehoshaphat is interpreted as ‘the judgment of the Lord’ [Note: [Col. 0497D] “The judgment of God.” L.]. This, then, is what he says: ‘When I have had mercy on them,’ that is, on those who are reckoned by their confession of my name, ‘then I will bring all my adversaries down into the valley of Jehoshaphat,’ that is, into the valley of judgment.  
> 
> “‘All nations’ either designates all the unbelieving nations, or he means all the demons, for the same teacher continues in the same work: ‘Such persons’—that is, those whom he calls either unbelieving nations or demons—‘will not be judged on mountains, nor on plains, but in the deep and below, so that the place itself may be their punishment.’”  
> [Note: [Col. 0498D] “For them.” L.]

## CHAPTER III. That no human being knows for how many days that judgment will extend

[Col. 0498C]

> “What the whole Church of God holds in confession and profession is that Christ will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead—as the most blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0498D] L.: “We all call this the day of the final judgment, that is, the future last time.”]. We call this the day of the final judgment, that is, the last time. For how many days the future judgment will extend [Note: [Col. 0498D] “Will last.” L.] is uncertain.”  
> (Blessed Augustine, *City of God*, Book XX, chapter 1, no. 2.)

## CHAPTER IV. On the terror of Christ’s coming, and that he will come to judgment in the form in which he was judged and will carry out the judgment

[Note: [Col. 0498D] “The almighty Son of God.” L.]

Christ, the Son of God, when the world’s term has ended, will come with all the saints in the bodily form in which he ascended into heaven [Note: [Col. 0498D] “To judgment with all the saints.” L.]. When he comes from heaven to judgment, according to what he himself says in the Gospel:

> “The powers of heaven will be shaken, and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven; and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn [Note: [Col. 0499D] “They will mourn,” understood. L.], and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power. And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and they will gather his elect from the four [Note: [Col. 0499D] “Winds of heaven, from the highest parts of heaven.” L.] winds, from the highest parts of heaven to their boundaries” (Matthew 24:29–31).

The Apostle Paul also speaks in this way of the coming of the judgment [Note: [Col. 0499D] “Of his judgment.” L.]:

> “The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:15).

For, as the Psalmist proclaims, fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will surround him (Psalm 50:3), because the one who once came secretly to be judged will then come openly to judge all.

When all his saints have been gathered, he will descend from heaven [Note: [Col. 0499D] “To carry out judgment from heaven.” L.], according to what Isaiah says:

> “Behold, the Lord will come with his saints to carry out judgment” (Isaiah 3:14).

He will therefore come exceedingly fearsome and terrifying on the day of his examination [Note: [Col. 0499D] “Judgment.” L.], when he is seen in the glory of his majesty with angels and archangels, thrones and dominions, and the other powers, while heaven and earth burn and all things are shaken in terror to serve him.

## CHAPTER V. That Christ will come to judgment preceded by the cross, and that the same cross will be carried on angels’ shoulders as Christ descends from heaven

John Chrysostom, discussing this question with complete clarity and defining it, says as follows (First Homily on the Cross and the Thief):

> “Let us see how Christ will come with his cross, for it is necessary to demonstrate this very point. ‘If they say,’ he says, ‘Behold, Christ is in the storerooms; behold, he is in the wilderness, do not believe it’ (Matthew 24:26), speaking of the second coming of his glory, on account of false Christs and false prophets [Note: [Col. 0499D] “And false prophets, and the Antichrist, lest anyone.” L.], and on account of the Antichrist, lest anyone, overtaken by error, fall into a false christ.  
> 
> “Since the Antichrist will precede the coming of Christ the Savior, we must carefully beware lest, while seeking the shepherd, someone find a wolf. For this reason I tell you how you may recognize the coming of the true Shepherd. He gave this sign: it was his will that his first coming should take place secretly, and that he should seek what had been lost; but his second coming will not be like that. He simply says: ‘Just as lightning coming out [Note: [Col. 0499D] D. has “from the north.”] from the east appears in the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man’ (ibid., 27).  
> 
> “He will suddenly appear to everyone, and no one will need to ask whether Christ is here or there. For just as, when lightning flashes, we do not need to ask whether a flash has occurred, so, when the revelation of his presence shines forth, we will not need to ask whether Christ has come [Note: [Col. 0499D] “Whether he is truly Christ.” L.].  
> 
> “But what is being asked is whether he will come with the cross—for I have not forgotten the explanation already begun. Listen, then, to what follows. ‘At that time,’ he says, ‘the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light’ (ibid., 29). For such will be the eminence of Christ’s radiance that even the brightest lights of heaven will be hidden before the splendor of the divine light.  
> 
> “‘Then the stars will fall, when the sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven’ (ibid., 29–30) [Note: [Col. 0500D] “When it has appeared.” D.]. Have you considered how great is the power of the holy cross [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Of the sign, that is, of the cross.” L.]? The sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, but the cross will shine; and when the lights of heaven have been darkened and the stars have fallen, it alone will radiate, so that you may learn that the cross is brighter than the sun and the moon, whose splendor, illuminated by the divine radiance, it will surpass.  
> 
> “And just as, when a king enters a city, an army goes before him carrying royal standards and banners [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Precedes, carrying them before him.” L.], and the armed array of preparation announces the king’s entrance [Note: [Col. 0500D] “And announces it with the pomp of preparation and the clash of arms.” L.], so, when the Lord descends from heaven, an army of angels and archangels will go before him. They will carry that triumphant sign, the banner of the cross, upon their exalted shoulders, announcing to the trembling earth the divine entrance of the heavenly king.”

The same teacher repeats the following after some intervening material:

> “But why will the cross appear then, and for what reason will the Lord come with it carried before him [Note: [Col. 0500D] “The reason is clear.” L.]? It is clear: so that those who crucified the Lord of majesty may recognize the plan of their wickedness. Through this sign the shameless falsehood [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Falsehood” is absent in Lipsius.] or impiety of the Jews is exposed.  
> 
> “And because he will come bearing the cross for this very reason, hear him himself bearing witness in the Gospel: ‘Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn’ (Matthew 24:30), seeing that the cross itself is their accuser; and when it reproves them, they will recognize their sin too late and in vain confess their impious blindness.  
> 
> “Why are you surprised that he will come bearing the cross, when he will then also display the very wounds? ‘They will see,’ he says, ‘the one whom they pierced’” (John 19:37).

## CHAPTER VI. On the terror of the devil’s appearance when he is brought forth to judgment

When the devil is brought forth to be condemned, many of the elect who are to be found in the body will be shaken with fear when the Lord comes to judgment, seeing the wicked one punished by such a sentence. They will be purified by this terror, because, if any remnant of sin still remains in them from the body, they will be purified by the very fear with which they behold the devil condemned.

Hence Job says [Note: [Col. 0500D] “The Lord says this to Job.” L.]: “When he is brought forth, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified” (Job 41:16) [Note: [Col. 0500D] “Terrified.” L.], meaning by “angels” all the holy and elect.

## CHAPTER VII. That Christ, when he comes to judgment, will appear gentle to the just and terrifying to the unjust

When the Redeemer of the human race appears, he will be gentle to the just and terrifying to the unjust. The elect see as gentle the one whom the condemned behold as fearsome and terrible. But the elect will not see him as terrifying for this reason: they do not cease now to consider his terror. The condemned, on the other hand, will behold him as terrifying because now they postpone the terror of his final judgment and, what is worse, lie as though secure in their filth.

## CHAPTER VIII. That both the just and the unjust will see Christ coming in the flesh to judgment with bodily eyes

[Col. 0501B]

When Christ, the Son of God, comes to carry out judgment, all alike—the just and the unjust—will see his humanity. They will not, however, see his divinity, which is promised to be seen only by the just.

That his divinity will not be seen by the unjust is testified by Isaiah, who says: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see [Note: [Col. 0501D] “The glory of God.” L.] the majesty of God” (Isaiah 26:10).

From this it is perfectly clear that the condemned will then see his humanity, specifically that in which he was judged [Note: [Col. 0501D] “The humanity of Christ in which he was judged.” L.], so that they may grieve; but they will not see his divinity, so that they may not rejoice. For to those to whom the divinity is shown, it is certainly displayed for joy [Note: [Col. 0501D] “So that they may rejoice.” L.].

## CHAPTER IX. That not the Father but only the Son is believed to come to carry out the judgment

[Col. 0501C]

Blessed Augustine says the following concerning this (On the Gospel of John, chapter 5, Tractate 19, no. 16):

> “For the Father will not come to judge the living and the dead, yet the Father will not depart from the Son. In what sense, then, will he himself not come? Because he himself will not be seen in the judgment: ‘They will see the one whom they pierced’ [Note: [Col. 0501D] “Whom they pierced.” L.] (John 19:37). That form will be the judge which stood beneath the judge; that form will judge which was judged. For it was judged unjustly; it will judge justly.”

And when the Lord is read in the prophetic Scriptures as coming to carry out the final judgment [Note: [Col. 0501D] “To carry out the final judgment … even if no other distinction of his person is specified.” L.], even if his person is clearly presented under another distinction, Christ alone must be understood because of the judgment itself. For even if the Father will judge, he will judge through the Son [Col. 0501D] [Note: [Col. 0501D] “Through the coming of the Son of Man.” L.]. For through the manifestation of his presence he judges no one himself, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), because the man who will judge will be manifested, just as the man was judged.

## CHAPTER X. That this life is not meant when Christ descends from heaven to judge the living and the dead

We must not conclude that this pertains to the present life when Christ [Note: [Col. 0501D] “Descending from heaven, appears openly as judge to all” [Col. 0502D] L.] descends from heaven to judge the living and the dead and appears openly to human beings as judge. For, according to the statement of blessed Augustine set out above, what we profess concerning Christ as future—that he will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead—does not pertain to the life we lead here, because it is neither among the events of his life nor among those now taking place, but belongs to what will occur at the end of the age.

This is what the Apostle adds immediately afterward:

> “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:4).

When he comes, he will judge the living and the dead, because the just, who certainly live, and the unjust, who are rightly called dead, are to be judged by him. Or we may understand as “the living” those whom his coming will find here not yet dead but still living in this flesh [Col. 0502B] [Note: [Col. 0502D] “Whom it will find.” L.]; and as “the dead,” those who have departed from the body before he comes, or who will depart before his coming.

## CHAPTER XI. On the seats of those who judge

We call them *sedes*, “seats,” which the Greeks call *thronoi*, “thrones”; the Greeks call *sedes* “thrones” [Note: [Col. 0502D] “They call them chairs.” L.]. Thus, although the saints themselves are seats of God, according to what is written, “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wisdom 7), they will nevertheless have seats on which they will sit while Christ judges, according to what the Truth himself says:

> “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the seat of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning those who will sit with the Lord to judge

It is clearer than daylight that all the saints who have completely left the world will sit with the Lord and judge the others. Then what is read in the divine Scriptures will also be fulfilled:

> “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Proverbs 31:23) [Note: [Col. 0502D] “When he sits.” L.].

## CHAPTER XIII. That, in the twelve seats named by Christ, not only the twelve apostles will sit, but the whole number of the perfect, who are divided into the number twelve

Saint Augustine says the following on this subject in his treatises (On the City of God, Book XX, chapter 5, no. 3):

> “We must not think that, because the Lord said that the apostles would sit upon twelve seats [Note: [Col. 0502D] “His disciples.” L.], only twelve human beings would judge with him. For by the number twelve a certain entire multitude of preachers is signified, because of the two parts of the number seven, by which totality is often signified. These two parts—that is, three and four—multiplied one by the other make twelve. For four times three and three times four are twelve; and some other numerical principle of this kind, applicable to the matter, can perhaps be found [Note: [Col. 0503D] “Is found.” L.].  
> 
> “Otherwise, since we read that Matthias was appointed an apostle in the place of Judas the traitor, the Apostle Paul, who labored more than all of them, would have no place from which to judge. Yet he plainly shows that he belongs with the other saints to the number of judges when he says: ‘Do you not know that we shall judge angels?’ (1 Corinthians 6:3).  
> 
> “The same reasoning applies to those who are to be judged, in connection with this number twelve. For, because it was said, ‘Judging the twelve tribes of Israel,’ the tribe of Levi, which is the thirteenth, will not therefore fail to be judged by them; nor will they judge only that people and not the other nations.  
> 
> “When he says ‘in the regeneration,’ he undoubtedly wished the resurrection of the dead to be understood by the term ‘regeneration.’ For our flesh will be regenerated through incorruption just as our soul has been regenerated through faith.” [Col. 0503B]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the final resurrection of human bodies

No one who is truly a Christian ought in any way to doubt that the flesh of all human beings who have been born or will be born, and who have died or will die, will rise again. The Lord says:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when the dead who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:25).

## CHAPTER XV. That, when the seventh angel sounds the trumpet, the resurrection of the dead will occur in the twinkling of an eye

[Col. 0503C]

[Note: [Col. 0503D] We have searched for this in Jerome in vain; perhaps these are the words of another. Certainly they scarcely bear the stamp of Jerome’s style.] Blessed Jerome, in his letter to Minervius, asserting the opinions of certain people disputing about the resurrection, says: “We ask why the Apostle wrote that the dead would rise at the last trumpet (I Cor. XV, 52). For when it is called ‘the last,’ obviously others preceded it. In John’s Apocalypse (ch. XI), seven angels are described with trumpets; and as each one sounds—namely, the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth—the action accomplished by each is indicated. But when the last, that is, the seventh, resounds with the clear blast of the trumpet, [Note: [Col. 0503D] Duacensis has it somewhat differently: ‘The dead are raised in the body; receiving incorruptible bodies in place of those they previously possessed, which were corruptible.’] the dead are raised, receiving incorruptible bodies in place of the corruptible bodies they previously possessed.” Nevertheless, concerning what the Apostle says about the resurrection of the dead—that all will rise in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet—“the resurrection of the dead,” says the same teacher, “will take place with such speed that the living whom the time of consummation finds in their bodies will not be able to precede the dead rising from the underworld. For when he says that the resurrection of all will occur in a point of time, in the movement and instant of an eye, he excludes the whole fiction of a first and a second resurrection, so that some might be believed to rise first and others last.” Again, after some intervening material, he says: “We must hold this opinion: just as a light feather [Note: [Col. 0503D] Or ‘a straw,’ L.] or a thin, dry leaf is carried away by the wind and its blast and transferred from earth to a lofty place [Note: [Col. 0504D] ‘It is easily transferred.’ L.], so the bodies of all the dead will be moved at the sight and nod of God, ready for the Judge’s coming.”

## CHAPTER XVI. That resurrection pertains to all human beings, but transformation only to the saints

Behold, the Apostle says: “The trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise” [Note: [Col. 0504D] “They will rise incorruptible.” L.], “and we will be transformed” (I Cor. XV, 52). But just as the resurrection of all, both good and evil, is general, so transformation must not be believed to be common to all. For, as blessed Augustine, Jerome, Julianus Pomerius, and the others testify, resurrection will be common to all, good and evil alike, whereas transformation will be granted only to the righteous; and this plainly signifies glorification in eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XVII. That it is not an ethereal body, but the flesh we bear, which will rise without any corruption

Those who tell some fanciful story that an ethereal body will rise in place of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0504D] “Ethereal.” L.] must by no means be heeded. Rather, according to the truth of sacred history, each person will rise in the body in which he lives. For, to say nothing of the others, I will briefly repeat these words of our distinguished teacher Eugenius, bishop of the see of Toledo [Note: [Col. 0504D] L. incorrectly writes “of Toulouse.”]: “We most truly confess the resurrection of the flesh—not, as some rave, that we shall rise in an ethereal or any other flesh, but in this flesh which we possess [Note: [Col. 0504D] “And in which we live, in which also each person will deserve to receive either a crown for right deeds, or punishment for evil conduct.” L.], in this flesh in which each person will deserve to receive either a crown for right deeds or punishment for evil conduct.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. How they are to be believed to have spiritual bodies then, when the bodies that will exist are most certainly proved to be bodies, not spirits

The bodies of the saints will rise without any defect, without any deformity, [Note: [Col. 0504D] “Just as without any corruption, burden, or difficulty.” L.] without any corruption or difficulty caused by weight or burden. In them there will be as much ease as there is blessedness. For this reason they are called spiritual, although unquestionably they will be bodies [Note: [Col. 0504D] “Flesh, not spirits.”]. But just as the present body is called “animal,” although the body is not the soul, so then it will be a spiritual body, yet it will still be a body, not a spirit.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the quality of the bodies that will exist in the resurrection

“The quality of those bodies,” says Julianus Pomerius (On the Origin of the Soul), “which the wretched and the blessed will receive will indeed be equally incorruptible and immortal; but the places or merits of those who will receive them will be incomparably different and far removed from one another. Hence the Apostle says: ‘We shall all rise, but we shall not all be transformed’ (I Cor. XV, 51). By saying, ‘We shall all rise,’ he signifies one resurrection of all human beings, so that all human bodies, endowed with one incorruption and one immortality, may continue forever either in punishment or in reward. Therefore all are to be believed to rise together; but the impious to punishment, sinners to that final judgment, and all the saints to reward.

“Thus the bodies of the wretched will not be immortal and incorruptible in such a way that, because they cannot decay or die, they will admit no sensation of pain; rather, established in eternal torments, the greatest pain will neither corrupt them through torment nor destroy them. Thus immortal flesh, condemned together with its soul, lives for this purpose: that it may feel; it feels in order to suffer; it suffers in order to receive what is due to its merits.”

## CHAPTER XX. At what age or stature those who rise will exist, whether they are old, young, or infants

When most people were obstinately and variously disputing this question, blessed Augustine (The City of God, book XXII, chapters 15–16), declaring that he would provide an answer [Note: [Col. 0505D] “Offering one.” D.], says:

“If we say that the bodies of some of the larger persons are to be reduced to the measure of the Lord’s body [Note: [Col. 0505D] “The larger bodies of various people.” L.], much would perish from the bodies of many, although he promised that not even a hair would perish. It therefore remains that each person should receive his own measure, which he either possessed in youth, even if he died an old man, or would have possessed had he died earlier. And what the Apostle mentioned concerning ‘the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ’ (Eph. IV, 13), [lacuna] we understand as being said in this sense: that the bodies of the dead should rise neither below nor beyond the youthful form, but in the age and strength to which we know that Christ attained here [Note: [Col. 0505D] Lipsius: “In the strength of that age.” Saint Augustine’s edition: “In that age and strength.”]. For even the most learned men of this world have fixed youth at approximately thirty years; when its allotted span has ended, a person then begins to decline toward the deterioration of more advanced and old age. Therefore it was not said ‘according to the measure of the body’ or ‘according to the measure of stature,’ but ‘according to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.’ [Note: [Col. 0505D] Duacensis: “It will not come.”]

“Therefore all will rise as great in body as they were, or would have been, in the age of youth. Yet it will make no difference even if the form of the body is that of an infant or an old person, since no weakness of mind or of the body itself will remain” [Note: [Col. 0505D] “For merits,” in place of “of mind.” L.].

Accordingly, the aforementioned teacher adds: “If someone contends that each person will rise in the bodily condition in which he died, there is no need to fight him with laborious contradiction” [Note: [Col. 0505D] “With troublesome contradiction.” L.].

Nor will I omit what Julianus Pomerius thought about this (in his book On the Soul). “Certainly,” he says, “I consider there to be no question concerning age. For whether infants lose their life already in the womb or after birth, they are believed to rise [Note: [Col. 0505D] Duacensis: “They are believed to rise at that age.”] at the age which they surely would have reached in the following years had they lived; since, if the resurrection restores nature, nothing belonging to the fullness of nature can be lacking.”

The aforementioned teacher likewise established that the same applies to those who die at an advanced age, saying: “The person who departs from this life at an advanced or even decrepit age will rise at the age at which he was young, with the weakness of old age removed. Or, if it is more fitting for that blessed age in which all the saints will live without any diminution of their blessedness that there should be some difference of ages there, it will be such that it is no impediment or disgrace to those reigning forever” [Note: [Col. 0505D] “So that there may be nothing, I say, as an impediment.” L.]. He also adds: “What we have said concerning age may likewise be understood concerning stature.”

## CHAPTER XXI. Whether the stature or form of the bodies of those who rise will be equal or different, and whether the thin will rise with the same thinness and the fat with the same fatness

Concerning the bodily stature in which all will rise [Note: [Col. 0506D] “All generally.” L.], blessed Augustine, speaking with clear precision, says (Enchiridion, chapter 90):

“It does not follow that the stature of those who come back to life will therefore be different because the stature of the living had been different—namely, that the thin should return to life with the same thinness, or the fat with the same fatness” [Note: [Col. 0506D] “Or the thin.” L.].

“But if this is the Creator’s design: that each person’s individual character and recognizable likeness be preserved in his appearance, while all other bodily goods are made equal [Note: [Col. 0506D] Here we have preferred the reading of Lipsius and the edition of Saint Augustine to that of Duacensis, which reads: “But let this be in the Creator’s counsel, that . . . but in the other bodily goods let all things be made equal. Thus,” etc.], then the material will be so proportioned in each person that nothing of it will perish, and whatever was lacking in anyone will be supplied by the One who was able to make whatever he willed even from nothing” [Note: [Col. 0506D] The reading here in Duacensis differs also from Lipsius and Saint Augustine, which we have followed. Its wording is: “But in this way with the bodies . . . as with the voices by which a song is filled. This will happen,” etc.].

“But if there will be a rational inequality in the bodies of those who rise, as there is among the voices that fill out a song, then from each person’s bodily material this will be made to happen which restores the human being to the angelic assemblies and introduces nothing incongruous to their perceptions.”

## CHAPTER XXII. That the bodies of the saints will rise without any deformity

The bodies of all the saints will rise conspicuous with every happiness and the glory of immortality, just as without any corruption, difficulty, [Note: [Col. 0507D] “Or burden.” L.] or burden, so also without any deformity. In them, as Saint Augustine says, there will be as much ease as there is blessedness. For the same teacher also teaches that the very scars on the bodies of martyrs may indeed be seen, but that this will occur without any appearance of deformity. “For,” as the same distinguished teacher says (The City of God, book XXII, chapter 19, §3), “there will be no deformity in those bodies, but dignity; and although a certain beauty will shine in the body, it will be the beauty not of the body but of virtue.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. That it is useless to ask at what age or measure the bodies of the reprobate will rise

It is surely pointless to ask whether the reprobate will have one stature or different statures, since among those who will remain alienated from the blessed light and from the beauty of that eternal dwelling, stature—which ordinarily contributes to beauty—is not a matter for inquiry [Note: [Col. 0507D] “The word ‘not’ is absent in L.”]. For, in accordance with what a certain wise man says, where there will be the gnashing of teeth and eternal, [Note: [Col. 0507D] “Unceasing.” L.] intolerable weeping, it is futile to ask about the beauty of bodies.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That men and women will rise in their own sex

Many people, because the Apostle says, “Until we meet him as a perfect man” (Eph. IV, 13), believe that all women will rise in the male sex, on the grounds that man was made from clay, whereas woman was made from man’s side. But instructed by the opinions of Catholic teachers, we believe and hold that almighty God, who created, established, and redeemed both sexes, will restore both in the resurrection.

For when the Lord Christ was questioned about the woman who, having lost the seven husbands she had possessed, had herself also passed away, and was asked to which of them she would chiefly be restored in the resurrection, he answered: “In the resurrection women neither marry nor men take wives” (Matt. XXII, 28–30) [Note: [Col. 0507D] “They will not marry . . . they will not take wives.” L.].

From these most sacred words it is perfectly clear that there it is not sex but sexual intercourse that will be absent; nor will the nature of the flesh be changed, but its lust will be brought to an end. Blessed Augustine likewise, treating this question in his works (The City of God, book XXII, chapter 17), says:

“They seem to me to have the better understanding who do not doubt that both sexes will rise. For there will be no lust there, which is the cause of shame. Before they sinned, the man and the woman were naked and were not ashamed. Therefore bodily defects will be removed, while nature will be preserved. The female sex, however, is not a defect, but a nature which will then be free from intercourse and childbirth.”

After these matters have been set forth by the aforementioned man, there will be, as our holy teacher Eugenius [of Toledo] teaches, “such and so great a beauty of the body” [Note: [Col. 0507D] “Of the glorified body.” L.] “that it delights the sight, yet in no way bends the heart toward vice.”

## CHAPTER XXV. That no concern for food or drink will trouble those who rise

Our nature endures the necessity of food and drink so long as it remains subject to this corruptible body; these are supplied to the body, weakened by the penalty of corruption and mortality, as medicines [Note: [Col. 0507D] “The same, as it were, medicines for its weakness.” L.]. But when the resurrection of the bodies has taken place, there will be no necessity there for consuming food or drink, since this necessity belongs only to corruption in the present life, not to the incorruption or immortality that will exist after this life [Note: [Col. 0507D] “There will be no necessity there for consuming food or drink, which is attributed only to corruption in this life, not to the incorruption or immortality that will come after this life. For according to the Old [Testament], as . . .” L.].

For, as Julianus Pomerius says (Book On the Origin of the Soul): “When all corruption and mortality have been consumed, there will be no weakness of the flesh there, but nature. Here, therefore, where the flesh can die, it must be aided by food and drink, lest it succumb to death; but in that life where it cannot die, it will require no nourishment, because neither hunger nor thirst can kill what is immortal.”

If, on the other hand, someone objects that after the resurrection the Lord is said to have eaten with his disciples, and therefore those who rise are believed to eat on his example, then, “the Lord Jesus ate bread,” says the same teacher [Note: [Col. 0508D] Lipsius has simply “bread” in place of the reading here.], “not from need but from power; not to provide for the weakness of his flesh, but to show those who doubted that he had risen in true flesh. For if he had been a spirit, as they then supposed, he would not have taken any bodily food; but he did take it in order to strengthen their faith, which had begun to waver, and to show that he lacked not the ability but the necessity of eating” [Note: [Col. 0508D] “The necessity of eating.” L.].

## CHAPTER XXVI. That our nature will have no need of bodily clothing

I do not doubt that it has been established by the opinions of many teachers that in the glory of that final resurrection coverings will not be necessary for bodies. There will be no weakness by which the incorruptible and immortal flesh could be destroyed, nor [Note: [Col. 0508D] “Any sin.” D.] any sin by which the blessed soul would be forced to feel shame. So much so that our predecessors declare that those who believe such things—that is, who say that the risen will need clothing—are capable of refusing to believe all the good things said to be future.

Yet if, as some argue, there will be certain coverings or garments there, [Note: [Col. 0508D] “The incorruptible bodies will surely use incorruptible garments.” L.] they will certainly be incorruptible, as Julianus Pomerius says in the same work:

“If our flesh is changed not in kind but in quality, and is made not spirit but spiritual, it will not require material things. Either there will be no garments in the resurrection, or, if there are, [Note: [Col. 0508D] “They must be believed to be wholly incorruptible, belonging to incorruptible bodies.” L.] they must be believed incorruptible, clothing the saints in such a way that they are not distracted by any concern for themselves [Note: [Col. 0508D] Duacensis lacks ‘in.’] amid the security of that future blessedness.

“Or perhaps the garments will be of the kind in which the prophet rejoices that he is clothed under the figure of the Church, saying: ‘He clothed me with the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the garments of righteousness’ (Isa. LXI, 10). The same teacher refers the garment of salvation to the flesh and the garment of righteousness to the soul.

“The same teacher continues: If this is so, and if it is granted that those who rise will use garments, they will not be like the garments of the Israelites (Deut. VIII, 4). For although those garments were preserved for forty years by divine will, they were nevertheless worn away by ordinary age. Nor will they be like those in which Moses and Elijah appeared on the mountain with the Lord (Matt. XVII, 3), or like those in which the holy angels were seen; these too were dissolved into nothing, since they had been taken for a time from the material from which they were made [Note: [Col. 0509D] The words “from which they were made” are absent in D.]. Rather, they may be like the garments in which the risen Lord appeared clothed (Matt. XXVIII), if those garments too were not assumed temporarily for the sake of human eyes [Note: [Col. 0509D] “For human sight.” D.] but were his own.

“For if there will be garments there, whatever or of whatever kind they may be, they will be spiritual garments belonging to spiritual bodies. Thus, even if they are not naked, spiritual beings will not need material things.”

This, then, is what Julianus Pomerius says. But the clear judgment of many teachers, confirmed also by the lucid statement of our teacher Eugenius, asserts this:

“In that future glory of the resurrection, where there will be no deformity in the holy bodies and no adversity of pain or labor, the use of covering will likewise not be necessary, since Christ will be all things in all” (Col. III, 11).

## CHAPTER XXVII. On aborted fetuses, and that a human being is believed to belong to the final resurrection from the moment he begins to live in his mother’s womb

If it can be established with certainty when a human being begins to live in his mother’s womb, then from that moment it can also truly be determined that he could have died, and thus that he who had life and could die will be restored at the time of the resurrection. Blessed Augustine, not so much discussing as proposing this question, says among other things (Enchiridion, chapter 86):

“From the moment a human being begins to live, from that moment he can certainly die. Once dead, wherever death could have occurred to him, how could he not belong to the resurrection of the dead?” [Note: [Col. 0509D] Lipsius adds: “I cannot find this.”]

Julianus Pomerius likewise says: “Certainly those who are expelled from the womb will rise, if they lived; they will not rise to be judged but to be punished, because, having been condemned in Adam’s sin [Note: [Col. 0510D] “By the condemnation of Adam.” L.], they were not released from the bonds of their condemnation. Yet whether infants are deprived of life in the womb or after birth, they are believed to rise at the age which they surely would have reached in the following years had they lived; because if the resurrection restores nature, nothing belonging to the fullness of nature can be lacking.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How those who are born with a greater or smaller number of limbs, or with two heads and one body, or two bodies and one head, or in any other monstrous form, are believed to rise

On this question blessed Augustine speaks as follows (Enchiridion, chapter 87):

“Nor, he says, will the monsters who are born and live, however quickly they die, either be denied a resurrection or be believed to rise in such a way that their nature is not rather corrected and restored. Far be it from us to think that the two-membered person who was recently born in the East, about whom the most faithful brothers reported what they had seen and concerning whom the priest Jerome of blessed memory left a written account, was one double human being rather than two human beings—something that would have been the case had twins been born. [Col. 0510B]

“Thus the other cases in which individual births possess something either greater or smaller, or which are called monsters because of some excessive deformity, will in the resurrection be restored to the form of human nature, so that each soul receives its own body, and even those parts which had been born joined together remain joined to no other, but each person carries his own limbs separately, by which the integrity of the human body is completed” [Note: [Col. 0510D] “Of nature.” D.].

Julianus Pomerius, following the opinion of the aforementioned teacher, likewise says:

“This also seems to me to be understood in the following way: whether our flesh is born with fewer limbs or with more, it will rise with the customary and fitting limbs [Note: [Col. 0510D] “With its own integrity.” L.] belonging to its integrity. For both in those who have fewer and in those who have more, there is a weakness which here indeed appears contrary to nature, but in the future restoration of our body is believed to be removed, just like corruption and mortality. Thus our flesh will rise whole, with all its parts, and perfect according to the measure of its form, without diminution or addition of limbs.

“Whether two bodies are born with one head, or one body with two heads—although the manner in which these things occur is uncertain to us, and especially to me—I nevertheless declare without any ambiguity what I know with certainty: either two bodies will rise with their own heads, if two souls were born in them, since it cannot be denied that each soul will immortally receive the body it lost; or, if one soul was born, whether in one body with two heads or in two bodies with one head, it will receive one body.

“Accordingly, the nature of our flesh, whether by losing what was superfluous to it or recovering what was lacking, will be restored to its fullness. Just as it will be without any corruption, so it will be without any weakness and will remain immortally joined to its own spirit.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. That those who are now eaten by wild beasts or mutilated by various forms of tearing will possess the integrity of their bodies when they rise

“Earthly matter,” says Saint Augustine (Enchiridion, chapter 88), “from which the flesh of mortals is created, does not perish for God. However it may be dissolved into dust and ashes, dispersed into whatever breath or air, changed into the substance of whatever other bodies or into the elements themselves, or become the food and be transformed into the flesh of whatever animals or even human beings, it returns in an instant to the human soul which first animated it so that the human being might be made, grow, and live.”

Blessed Gregory, likewise raising and resolving this question in his treatises, says (On Ezekiel, book II, homily 8, §8):

“Those who say, ‘A wolf ate the flesh of a man, a lion devoured the wolf, and when the lion died it returned to dust—when that dust is raised, how is the man’s flesh separated from the flesh of the wolf and the lion?’ often make this empty little objection” [Note: [Col. 0511D] “Often those who say . . .” L.]. “To them we should give no other answer than that they should first consider how they came into this world, and then they will discover how they will rise.

“You, certainly, who are a human being and are speaking, were once in your mother’s womb a froth of blood. There you were a small, fluid lump formed from your father’s seed and your mother’s blood. Tell me, if you know, how that fluid of seed and blood hardened into bones, how it remained liquid in the marrow, how it solidified in the sinews, how it grew into flesh, how it was stretched out into the skin [Note: [Col. 0511D] D. has “in the mind” instead of “in the skin.”], how it was differentiated into hair and fingernails, so that the hair was softer than the flesh and the nails thinner than the bones but harder than the flesh.

“If, then, so many and such diverse things were distinguished from a single seed and yet remained joined in their form, why should it be surprising if almighty God can, in the resurrection of the dead, distinguish human flesh from the flesh of beasts, so that one and the same dust does not rise insofar as it is the dust of the wolf and the lion, yet does rise insofar as it is human dust?”

## CHAPTER XXX. That those who departed this life disabled will possess their limbs intact in the resurrection

If someone departs this life weak in body, mutilated, or broken, there is no doubt that he can be restored at the time of the resurrection with the integrity of his limbs [Note: [Col. 0511D] Duacensis: “If there is someone broken and mutilated who departs this life.”]. Whatever weakness or alien cruelty has made shameful or defective in him, the beauty of immortality will then restore in such a way that nothing superfluous or unbecoming, and nothing removed, will appear there to be deformed [Note: [Col. 0511D] “To them.” D.].

Thus blessed Augustine says (The City of God, book XXII, chapter 19):

“The thin and the fat need not fear that they will be there such as, if they could, they would not have wished to be even here. For all bodily beauty consists in the harmony of the parts together with a certain pleasantness of their color. Where there is no harmony of the parts, something is offensive either because it is too small or because it is too large” [Note: [Col. 0511D] Lipsius: “either because it is misshapen, or because it is too small, or because it is too large.”].

“Accordingly, there will be no deformity caused by the disproportion of the parts, since what is small will be corrected, what is less than it ought to be will be supplemented from the source known to the Creator, and what is greater than it ought to be will be removed while the integrity of the material is preserved.”

Instructed, therefore, by this teacher’s prudent definition, we should also believe that those whom we have seen with six fingers on their hands and feet will not rise with that deformity, but, with the integrity of the body preserved, they will have that number of fingers which maintains the bodily harmony of the parts. By the harmony of bodily parts I mean the arrangement established by the proper order of birth: that every human being should have two eyes, two ears, five fingers on each hand, and five fingers on each foot, with no number added or diminished that would introduce deformity into the parts. Nevertheless, nothing is to be believed to perish from the body.

For Saint Augustine says (in the same place): “Nor would I say that I think anything will perish from any body that was naturally present in it, but only what was born deformed.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. Whether whatever has been removed from our fingernails or hair by cutting or shearing is believed to be restored

Blessed Augustine says concerning this (Enchiridion, chapter 89):

“Therefore the earthly matter itself, which becomes a corpse when the soul departs, will not be restored in the resurrection in such a way that whatever is dispersed and changed into one kind of thing after another must, when it returns to the body from which it dispersed, also necessarily return to the same bodily parts where it had been [Note: [Col. 0511D] “Although.” L.]. Otherwise, if what repeated cutting removed from the hair of the head, or what repeated clipping removed from the nails, returns there, an excessive and unbecoming deformity would present itself to those who think about it and do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh.”

Therefore, as the same teacher says in another work (The City of God, book XXII, chapter 19):

“If the hair that was so often cut and the nails that were clipped will not return to their former places because of deformity [Note: [Col. 0511D] Lipsius: “If hairs so often cut, or nails clipped, return to their own places, they will not return with deformity, yet . . .” The Maurine edition comes closer to Duacensis: “If hairs . . . or nails clipped return deformed to their own places, they will not return.”], yet they will not perish for anyone who rises. For they will be changed into the same flesh and restored to other parts of the body, while the harmony of the parts is preserved” [Note: [Col. 0512D] “Of the material.” D.].

“Although what the Lord says—‘Not a hair of your head will perish’ (Luke XXI, 18)—can much more suitably be understood as referring not to the length but to the number of the hairs. Hence he also says elsewhere: ‘All the hairs of your head are numbered’ (Matt. X, 30).”

Again, the same teacher, using an illustration for this matter, says (in the same work):

“What should I now answer concerning the hair and the nails? Once it is understood that nothing will perish from the body, in such a way that there will be nothing deformed in the body, it is simultaneously understood that those things which would have made the mass excessive and deformed will themselves be added [Note: [Col. 0512D] Lipsius: “Those things that had contributed to the deformity of the form will be added to the mass.”]—not to the places where the form of the limbs would be disfigured.

“It is like a vessel made from clay: if it is reduced again to the same clay and the whole vessel is made again from the whole mass, it is not necessary that the portion of clay which had formed the handle return to the handle, or that which had formed the bottom again form the bottom, provided that the whole returns into the whole—that is, that all the clay return into the whole vessel, with no part of it lost” [Note: [Col. 0513D] “Remaining.” Lipsius: “Returning.” Maurine edition.].

Thus, as the same teacher says (Enchiridion, chapter 89), “it will not matter for the restoration of the body whether hair returns to hair and nails to nails, or whether whatever of them had perished is changed into flesh and restored to other parts of the body, with God’s providence ensuring that nothing unbecoming occurs.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. How those who have not been separated from the mass of perdition will rise

“Whoever,” says blessed Augustine (Enchiridion, chapter 92), “is not liberated from that mass of perdition which was brought about through the first human being [Note: [Col. 0513D] Lipsius: “Through the one mediator of God and human beings, they too will rise, each with his own flesh.”], will also rise with the flesh, but so as to be punished with the devil and his angels.

“Whether they rise with the defects and deformities of their bodies—those who bore defective and deformed limbs in them—why should we trouble ourselves by investigating? Their uncertain condition or beauty should not weary us, since their condemnation will be certain and everlasting. Nor should it disturb us how their body will be incorruptible if it can suffer, or how it will be corruptible if it cannot die.

“For there is no true life except where one lives happily, and no true incorruption except where health is not corrupted by any pain. But where the unhappy are not permitted to die, [Note: [Col. 0513D] Or “is absent in Lipsius.”] or, so to speak, where death itself does not die, and where everlasting pain does not destroy but afflicts, and corruption itself does not end, this is called ‘the second death’ in the Holy Scriptures” (Rev. XX, 6) [Note: [Col. 0513D] Lipsius likewise lacks “and”; consequently, it yields another sense.].

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the order of the future judgment

Just as we have said that there are some who will sit as judges with God [Note: [Col. 0514D] Lipsius: “with Christ.”], so others must be believed to exist who will be judged by the examination of those who sit in judgment. [Note: [Col. 0514D] “For there are two distinctions, as there will be orders of human beings in the judgment.” L.] There will be two distinctions or orders among the people gathered for judgment, namely the elect and the reprobate; these, however, are divided into four.

One is the order of the perfect, who judge with God, concerning whom the Lord says: “You too will sit upon twelve thrones” (Matt. XIX, 28). These are not judged, but reign. There is also another order of the elect, to whom it will be said: “I was hungry and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV, 35). These are judged and reign.

There are likewise two orders of the reprobate. One consists of those who are found outside the Church. These are not judged and perish; concerning them the Psalmist also says: “The wicked shall not rise in judgment” (Ps. I, 5). The other order of the reprobate consists of those who will be judged and perish, to whom it will be said: “I was hungry and you did not give me food; depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 41–42).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the separation of the good and the evil

Behold, the Psalmist says: “He summoned the heavens from above, and the earth, to distinguish his people” (Ps. XLIX, 4) [Note: [Col. 0514D] Lipsius: “The heaven above, and the earth, that he might distinguish.”]. What does he mean when he says, “to distinguish his people”? It means to separate the good from the evil by judgment, as sheep from goats. For then he will set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That the very separation of the good from the evil will take place through angelic ministries.

The separation, or indeed the division, of the good from the wicked is to be believed capable of being accomplished by the angels. For [Col. 0514B] when the Psalmist said: [Note: [Col. 0514D] Lipsius has the same reading that we noted above.] “He summoned the heavens above and the earth, to discern his people” (Ps. XLIX, 4), what he said—“to discern his people”—pertains to the separation of the good from the wicked. And immediately he added: “Gather his saints to him.” For to whom was it said, “Gather his saints to him,” except certainly to the angels? Thus Saint Augustine says in this passage (*Exposition on Psalm XLIX*): “The address is turned to the angels when the Prophet said: ‘Gather his saints to him.’ Certainly, so great a matter must be accomplished through angelic ministry.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That when the good have been separated to the right and the wicked to the left, the books—that is, the consciences of individuals—will be opened.

[Col. 0514C] Therefore, when the good have been separated from the wicked through angelic ministries, with the elect standing at the right and the reprobate at the left, then the books will be opened—that is, the consciences of individuals. For the apostle John says: “I saw the dead, great and small, and the books were opened; and another book was opened, which is the book of the life of each person; and the dead were judged from those books according to their deeds” (Rev. XX, 12).

By “the books” he evidently wishes all the sacred books of the New and Old Testament to be understood, in whose lives, as in books, we learn what we ought to do. But in the book of which it is said, “Another book was opened, which is the book of the life of each person,” what good each person had done or had not done is known, as it were, in the divine power.

“Which book,” as Saint Augustine says (*City of God*, book XX, chapter 14), “if understood in a bodily sense, who could estimate its magnitude or length? Or how much time could be given to reading the book in which the entire lives of all are written? Or will there be as many angels as there are human beings, so that each person will hear his life recited by the angel assigned to him? Therefore there will not be one book for all, but individual books for individuals. Yet Scripture, wishing one thing to be understood, says: ‘And another book was opened.’ A certain divine power, then, must be understood—one that will cause all a person’s deeds, whether good or evil, to be recalled to memory and perceived by the mind’s gaze with marvelous speed, so that conscience may accuse or excuse [Note: [Col. 0515D] Lipsius has “knowledge [of] conscience.”], and all together and each individually may be judged. This divine power has, appropriately, received the name ‘book.’ For in it, so to speak, whatever is recalled by its agency is read.”

Then the Lord will recall to his elect what he foretold would be mentioned in the Gospel, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: for I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; [Note: [Col. 0515D] Lipsius has, in place of this, “I was sick, and you visited me”: “I was naked, and you clothed me.”] I was sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matt. XXV, 34–36).

He will also charge those standing on the left [Col. 0515B] [Note: [Col. 0515D] “Those standing there” means the reprobate. L.] with not having done the things which he recalls those standing on the right to have done. When these two sayings of our Lord have been completed—one in which the good deeds of the elect are enumerated, the other in which the reprobate are charged with not having done them—“the wicked,” as the Truth himself says, “will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV, 46).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the evil hearing which the righteous will not fear.

After the wicked have been judged and sent into eternal fire, when the Lord says to them: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41), the righteous, who have already been placed at the right, will have no fear at all of this evil hearing. For “evil hearing” [Col. 0515C] is understood here as that with which the Lord threatens them—the everlasting fire. From this may you, O Christ, then [Note: [Col. 0515D] Lipsius has, with its customary piety: “rescue us, and enroll us among those who are to be gathered …”] rescue us by your mercy alone, and enroll us to reign together with you, our Head.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Concerning the downfall of the devil and the destruction of the wicked.

The holy apostle John, clearly indicating the devil’s descent into eternal fire, says this. After first stating: “And they were judged individually according to their deeds” (Rev. XX, 12), he briefly added how they were judged: “And death and hell,” he says, “were cast into the lake of fire” (ibid., 14). Here [Note: [Col. 0515D] Lipsius has: “under all these names.”] he signifies the devil, [Note: [Col. 0515D] Lipsius has: “because he is the author of death and of infernal punishments, together with the fellowship of all the demons.”] who is the author of death and of infernal punishments, together with the whole company of the demons. For this is what he had already said more explicitly by anticipating it above: “And the devil, who deceived them, was cast into the lake of fire and sulfur.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX. What that book is of which the apostle John says that all who are then not found written in the book of life will be cast into the lake of fire.

In his Revelation, Saint John wrote, among the other things he narrated concerning the resurrection (Rev. [Col. 0516A] XX, 15), that those who were not found written in the book of life would be cast into the lake of fire. In saying this, he certainly did not say that God suffers from forgetfulness and, as though turning through this book, comes to know what he did not know. “Rather, this book,” as Saint Augustine says (*City of God*, book XX, chapter 15), “signifies the predestination of those to whom eternal life will be given. For God does not fail to know them and read in this book in order to know them; rather, his foreknowledge of them—which cannot be deceived—is itself the book of life, in which they are written, that is, foreknown beforehand.”

## CHAPTER XL. That the bodies of the wicked will endure in the fire without being consumed.

[Col. 0516B] Saint Augustine, treating the matter through many and varied kinds of examples (*City of God*, book XXI), is clearly understood to have affirmed as certain that the bodies of the wicked will burn without being consumed, and that the fire will not destroy those very bodies; for they will burn in eternal fire and yet will not be able to die at all.

“What then?” says the same teacher (ibid., chapter 2). “I shall show from what considerations unbelievers may be convinced that living human bodies [Note: [Col. 0516D] “And living.” L.] can not only never be dissolved by death, but can also endure the torments of everlasting fire.”

Again, after some intervening discussion, he says (chapter 3): “The soul, by whose presence the body lives and is governed, can suffer pain and yet cannot die at all. Behold, a thing has been found which, while possessing the sensation of pain, is immortal. This, then, will be the condition of the bodies of the condemned which we now know to exist in the souls of all. Since this is so, what further need have we,” he says (chapter 4) [Note: [Col. 0516D] Duacensis has *aut* instead of *ait*.], “of examples of things by which we may be taught that it is not incredible for human bodies [Note: [Col. 0516D] “Destined to be punished with everlasting torment.” L.] condemned to everlasting fire not to lose their souls in the fire, to burn without injury, and to suffer without being destroyed?”

## CHAPTER XLI. How that future fire will burn the demons.

“For why,” says Saint Augustine (*City of God*, book XXI, chapter 10), “should we not say that, although in wondrous ways, nevertheless by true means even incorporeal spirits can be afflicted by the punishment of bodily fire, if the spirits of human beings, who are themselves certainly incorporeal, can now be enclosed in bodily limbs, and then can be indissolubly bound by the bonds of their bodies?” [Note: [Col. 0516D] Lipsius has *poterunt* (“will be able”), which is absent shortly thereafter.]
