Again, after some intervening discussion, the same author says: “But that Gehenna, which is also called the lake of fire and sulfur, will be a bodily fire, and it will torment the bodies of the condemned— [Note: [Col. 0516D] “Of human beings and demons.” Lipsius. “Of both human beings and demons.” The Maurist edition.] whether of human beings, or of demons; the bodies of human beings being solid, those of demons aerial; or only the bodies of human beings together with their spirits, while the demons, as spirits without bodies, remain in the bodily fires, receiving punishment but not imparting life to them. For there will be one fire, as the Truth said” (Matt. XXV, 41).

## CHAPTER XLII. Concerning the diversity of punishments according to the diversity of merits.

The mildest punishment of all will be that of those who, apart from the sin they inherited originally, added no other sin. Among the others who added sins, each will have a damnation all the more bearable there in proportion as his iniquity here was lesser. For it cannot be denied at all that even the eternal fire itself will be lighter for some and heavier for others according to the diversity of their merits, though those merits are evil—whether the force and heat of the fire itself vary according to each person’s deserved punishment, or whether the fire burns equally while being felt with unequal distress.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Against those who inquire with excessive scrupulosity what that future fire will be like or in what part of the world it may exist.

[Col. 0517B]

Compared with the knowledge of the great, the knowledge of lesser persons—if I may not rashly call it a kind of torpor in knowledge—is a kind of sluggishness in learning. Therefore, since the great and diligent have said that they did not know what they did not know, it is extremely dangerous and superfluous for us to presume to define anything about it in any way. Blessed Augustine, teaching about that very fire, appears to say this (*City of God*, book XX, chapter 16).

After introducing the future condemnation of the wicked by saying, “For when those who are not written in the book of life have been judged and sent into eternal fire,” he added: “I think that no one knows what kind of fire it will be, or in what part of the world or of creation it will exist, unless perhaps the divine Spirit has revealed it to someone.” [Note: [Col. 0517D] The text has *qui* (“which”) incorrectly in place of *quia* (“because”), according to Duacensis.]

## CHAPTER XLIV. That after the condemnation of the wicked comes the reward of the elect.

The order of the words of the Lord’s promise, by which we believe that our Lord [Note: [Col. 0517D] “The Lord Christ.” L.] will give both the kingdom to the saints and everlasting punishment to the reprobate, is such that the condemnation of the wicked comes first and the reward follows afterward, as Christ the Lord declares: “The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into life” (Matt. XXV, 46).

In the Apocalypse also we read that this order has been preserved, where it is expressly set forth. First, the punishment of the devil and all his followers is reported, and it is said: “Death and hell were cast into the lake of fire” (Rev. XX, 14). [Note: [Col. 0517D] Lipsius adds: “And everyone who was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.”] Then the future blessedness of the saints is added: “And I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. XXI, 1).

By these words it is made clear that, by the just judgment of God, punishment is first inflicted upon sinners and afterward the rewards of merit are granted to the saints. [Note: [Col. 0518D] “The gifts of rewards.” L.]

## CHAPTER XLV. That after the judgment has been completed, the form of a servant in which Christ conducts the judgment will pass away, and thus Christ will hand the kingdom over to God and the Father.

[Col. 0518A]

The form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0518D] “In which Christ is to be seen when he conducts the judgment.” L.] in which Christ will come as judge to conduct the judgment, according to what has been handed down in the writings of the elders, will pass away when the judgment has been completed—the form which he had presented for this purpose, that he might conduct the judgment.

It is said that it will “pass away,” not because it will cease to exist, but because it will pass from judgment to the kingdom. Or certainly, the Lord passes to us after the judgment, according to what blessed Gregory says (*Homilies on the Gospels*, book I, homily 13, no. 4): “Because he raises us from the form of his humanity to the contemplation of his divinity. His passing is his leading us into the vision of glory, when we shall see in divinity, after the judgment, him whom we behold in humanity at the judgment.”

Now, after the judgment, he will proceed from here and take with him the body of which he is the Head, and he will offer the kingdom to God and the Father (1 Cor. XV, 24). How, then, will he hand the kingdom over to God and the Father, except when he has shown his lovers the vision of his divinity, in which he is one with the Father? And when he has manifestly brought us, his members, to that knowledge and vision in which he is believed to be equal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, then that form will plainly be seen by the elect [Note: [Col. 0518D] “Fully.” L.], though it could not be seen by the wicked.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning the conflagration of the fire by which this world is said to perish.

It is established by the clear judgment of the elders that, when the judgment has been completed, this heaven [Col. 0518C] [Note: [Col. 0518D] “This” is absent in Duacensis.] and this earth will then cease to exist, when the new heaven and the new earth begin to exist. For this world will pass away through a transformation of things, not through complete destruction. Then the form of this world will perish in the conflagration of worldly fires, just as the Flood came about through the inundation of worldly waters.

In that conflagration of the world, as I have said, the qualities of the corruptible elements that corresponded to our corruptible bodies will utterly perish by burning. The substance itself, however, will possess those qualities which correspond to immortal bodies through a marvelous transformation, so that the world, renewed for the better, may be suitably adapted to human beings whose flesh also has been renewed for the better. [Note: [Col. 0518D] “By transformation.” L.]

## CHAPTER XLVII. That when the judgment has ended, the new heaven and the new earth will begin to exist.

[Col. 0518D]

As the most blessed Augustine says (*City of God*, book XX, chapter 16), when the judgment has been completed and ended, this heaven and this earth will then cease to exist, when the new heaven and the new earth begin to exist. For this world will pass away through a transformation of things, not through complete destruction. Hence the Apostle says: “The form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. VII, 31). Therefore it is the form that passes away [Note: [Col. 0519D] “Will pass away.” L.], not nature.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. That in the new heaven and the new earth not all who rise again, but only the saints, will exist.

According to what we read in certain manuscripts [Note: [Col. 0519D] “In some copies.” L.], sinners and the wicked, although they rise again immortal and incorruptible, will nevertheless not exist at all in the new earth, because they will be entirely excluded from that transformation of the saints.

For when the Apostle says: “We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. XV, 51), he indicates that the resurrection will generally be for everyone, but counts the transformation into glory as belonging only to the saints.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Against those who say that, if the conflagration of the world will occur after the judgment, where can the saints then be, since they will not be touched by the flame of the fire?

[Col. 0519B]

Blessed Augustine resolves this question as follows (*City of God*, book XX, chapter 18):

“Perhaps someone asks: If this world will burn after the judgment has taken place, before the new heaven and new earth are restored in its place, where will the saints be at that very time of its conflagration, since they must exist in some bodily place, possessing bodies?

“We can answer that they will be in the higher regions [Note: [Col. 0519D] “Parts.” L.], where the flame of the burning will not rise, just as the waters of the Flood did not rise. For their bodies will be of such a kind that they can be wherever they wish to be. But they will not fear the fire of that conflagration either, having been made immortal and incorruptible, just as the corruptible and mortal bodies of the three men were able to live unharmed in the blazing furnace (Dan. III, 94).”

## CHAPTER L. Concerning the reward of the saints and the kingdom, when Christ will gird himself and, passing by, minister to his own.

The reward of the saints is the vision of God, which will present us with ineffable joy. Concerning this reward, I think the prophet said: “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. LXIV, 4; 1 Cor. II, 9).

The Truth himself, also placing the manifestation of this vision as the reward and promising it to his lovers, says: “Whoever loves me will keep my commandments; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV, 21).

Indeed, according to the words of the holy Truth himself [Note: [Col. 0520D] Duacensis has: “of the Holy Trinity.”], he will then gird himself, make us recline, and, passing by, minister to us (Luke XII, 37). [Note: [Col. 0520D] Duacensis has “them” instead of “us.”]

“Therefore he girds himself,” as blessed Gregory says (*Homilies on the Gospels*, book I, homily 13, no. 4), “that is, he prepares himself for repayment. He will make us recline, that is, cause us to rest in eternal repose; for our reclining is to rest in the kingdom. But the Lord then ministers to us as he passes by, because he satisfies us with the illumination of his light. For what is said—‘He passes by’—means that he returns from judgment to the kingdom.”

## CHAPTER LI. That the wicked will then not know what is happening in the joy of the blessed, while the good will know what is happening in the punishments of the miserable.

Those who will be in punishments will not know what is happening within, in the joy of the Lord; but those who will be in that joy will know what is happening outside, in the outer darkness. Therefore the prophet said concerning the saints: “They will go out and see the limbs of human beings who transgressed against me” (Isa. final chapter, 24).

But by saying “they will go out,” he means that they will go out through knowledge, because those who are outside them will certainly not be hidden from them. For if the prophets, before these things had happened, were able to know them through whatever small measure of God was in their mortal minds, how will the immortal saints then be ignorant of things that have happened, when God will be all in all (1 Cor. XV, 28)?

## CHAPTER LII. That in this body in which we now are, we shall then be able both to be carried into the heavens and to dwell there.

Against the Platonists, who say that the human body cannot ascend into the heavens, Saint Augustine argues at length (*City of God*, book XXII, chapter 11) and establishes—also proving it through marvelous examples of reasoning—that our bodies, made immortal after the resurrection, will be held in the dwelling place of heaven.

For after the resurrection, the ascent into heaven has certainly been promised to the saints in the flesh, Christ saying to the Father: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XIX, 24). For if we are members [Note: [Col. 0520D] “Of the body.” L.] of the Head, and Christ is one in himself and in us, then wherever he ascended, we too will ascend.

## CHAPTER LIII. Whether we shall then have subtler movements of the body, or whether they will be such as they now appear to be.

Fearing to state a definitive opinion concerning the movements of the body, Saint Augustine says (*ibid.*, chapter 30):

“I do not dare to define what the movements of such bodies will be there, for I cannot even imagine it. Nevertheless, both movement and rest, as well as the very appearance of the body, will be seemly, whatever they may be, where nothing unbecoming will exist. Certainly, wherever the spirit wishes, there the body will immediately be; nor will the spirit desire anything which could not itself be seemly, nor anything which the body could not be.”

## CHAPTER LIV. Whether God will then be seen through these bodily eyes with which we now see the sun and the moon.

Saint Augustine, discussing perceptively these bodily eyes and whether we shall be able to see God through them in the future life (*ibid.*, chapter 29), says:

“When you ask me,” he says, “what these eyes will do in that spiritual body, I do not say what I already see, but I say what I believe according to what I read in the Psalm: ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’ (Ps. CXV, 1). I say, then, that they will see God in this body.

“But whether they will see him through it, just as through the body we now see the sun, the moon, the stars, the sea, and the earth and what is in it, is no small question. It is difficult to believe that the saints will then have bodies such that they will not be able to close and open their eyes whenever they wish; but it is more difficult to believe that whoever closes his eyes there will not see God.

“Therefore, far be it from us to say that the saints in that life will not see God with closed eyes, whom they will always see in spirit. But whether they will see God through these bodily eyes when they have them open—that is the question.

“For if, in the spiritual body, those very eyes will have only as much power as these eyes which we now possess, then undoubtedly God will not be able to be seen through them. Therefore, if that incorporeal nature, which is not contained in a place but is [Note: [Col. 0521D] Duacensis has “certainly.”] wholly everywhere, will be seen through them, they will have a very different power [Note: [Col. 0521D] Lipsius has *valentiae* (“capacity”) instead of *potentiae* (“power”).].” [Col. 0521B]

Therefore, according to what the same teacher affirms:

“It can happen, and it is highly credible, that we shall then see the bodily things of the new heaven and the new earth in such a way that we shall certainly see God, present and governing all bodily things, through the bodies which we shall bear and which we shall behold, wherever we direct our eyes, with the clearest vision.

“Not as now the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made (Rom. I, 20), in a mirror and in an enigma, in part (1 Cor. XIII, 12), where faith, by which we believe, has greater power in us than the appearance of the bodily things that we see with bodily eyes.

“Rather, just as now, when we see the human beings among whom we live and who exercise vital movements, we do not believe that they are alive as soon as we look at them, but see it—although we cannot see their life apart from their bodies—nevertheless perceive that life in them through their bodies, with all ambiguity removed; so, wherever we direct those spiritual lights of our bodies, we shall behold through our bodies the incorporeal God who governs all things.

“Either God will be seen through those eyes in such a way that they will possess, in such excellence of mind, something resembling that by which an incorporeal nature may be perceived—something which it is difficult or impossible to demonstrate by any examples or testimonies of the divine Scriptures—or, what is easier to understand [Note: [Col. 0521D] *Est* (“is”) is absent in Duacensis.], God will be wholly and equally visible to us: he will be seen in spirit by each of us, in each of us; he will be seen by one in another, in himself; he will be seen by one in another, in himself; he will be seen in the new heaven and in the new earth, and in every creature that will then exist; and through bodies, in every body, wherever the gaze of the spiritual eyes of the body may be directed.

“Our thoughts also will be open to one another. For then will be fulfilled what the Apostle, after saying, ‘Do not judge before the time,’ immediately added: ‘Until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and manifest the thoughts of the heart; and then each person will have praise from God’” (1 Cor. IV, 5).

## CHAPTER LV. That we shall then see God by the vision with which the angels now see him.

We read in the Gospel that Christ said: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones; for I say to you that their angels [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Their angels in heaven.” L.] in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 10). Therefore, just as they see, so shall we see, though we do not yet see.

For this reason the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. XIII, 12). This vision, then, is reserved for us as the reward of faith; concerning it the apostle John also says: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III, 2).

The face of God must be understood as his manifestation, not as some bodily member such as we possess, which we nevertheless now call by that name. We shall therefore then be like the angels, because just as they now see, so we shall see God after the resurrection.

## CHAPTER LVI. That all the saints will enjoy freedom of choice then, much firmer than in this life, although they will not be able to sin.

The whole body of teachers clearly indicates that in that life we shall possess a greater power of free choice than we possess here. For if in this life, as someone has said, most people live by free choice, where they can avoid sins but cannot be without sin, how much freer in spirit will they be there, where they will cling so closely to their God that they will be unable to be subject to any sin?

For a person becomes freer in proportion as he is more completely freed from sins. Thus, in that blessed life, they will be freer precisely because they will not be able to sin.

For, as it seems to me, if equality with the angels is promised to us, how will we then not have free choice, which they employ to praise God without ceasing? Whether this is possessed by the reprobate, however, is perhaps uncertain; for, according to the opinion of someone who hesitates concerning this question, I do not know whether those who will be alien from the life of the saints can possess any sort of free [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Either kind of free choice.” L.] choice, since, once they have been sent into punishment [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Into everlasting punishment.” L.] and the burning of flames, neither their mind nor their body will in any way be free.

## CHAPTER LVII. That there we shall possess both forgetfulness and remembrance.

[Col. 0522D]

“As far as rational knowledge is concerned [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Reasonable knowledge.” L.], each person will remember his past evils; but as far as the experience of sensation is concerned, he will be entirely forgetful of them.

“For even the most skilled physician knows almost all diseases insofar as they are known by his art, but insofar as they are felt in the body, he does not know many of them because he himself has not suffered them.

“Thus, just as there are two kinds of knowledge of evils—one by which they do not escape the mind’s capacity [Note: [Col. 0522D] Duacensis has: “one which does not escape the mind’s power”; the other, which clings to the senses of experience.”], and another by which they cling to the senses of experience—for all vices are known in one way through the teaching of wisdom and in another through the worst life of a fool—so there are also two kinds of forgetfulness.

“For the learned and educated person forgets them in one way, and the person who has experienced and suffered them in another: the former if he neglects his knowledge, the latter if he is free from misery. According to this forgetfulness, which is placed second, the saints will not remember their past evils; for they will be free from all evils, so that those evils will be entirely removed from their senses. [Note: [Col. 0523D] The word “evils” is absent in L.]

“Nevertheless, that power of knowledge which will be great in them will not fail to know not only their own past misery but also the everlasting misery of the damned. Otherwise, if they were going to be unaware that they had been miserable, how would they sing, as the Psalm says, ‘I will sing of the mercies of the Lord forever’?” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 1) [D. Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 30, no. 4]. [Note: [Col. 0523D] L. has “They will sing.”]

## CHAPTER LVIII. Concerning the diversity of merits and rewards, in which nevertheless no one will envy another.

[Col. 0523B]

“The degrees of honors and glories that will exist in that life,” as Saint Augustine says (*ibid.*, no. 2), “who is capable of imagining them, much less of expressing them? Yet there is no doubt that they will exist.

“And that great city will also possess this good: no inferior will envy any superior, just as the other angels do not now envy the archangels, as though no one wished to be what he did not receive, although he is bound to the one who received it by the most peaceful bond of concord. [Note: [Col. 0523D] We have corrected this passage according to the Maurist edition of Saint Augustine, supplying the words “what he did not receive” and leaving the rest unchanged, although that edition reads more appropriately: “and would no more wish … than the eye in the body,” and so forth. In Lipsius the passage is different and corrupt: “And in that blessed city he will see in himself this great good, that no inferior will envy any superior, just as the other angels do not envy the archangels, as though each person wished to be what he did not receive, although he is bound to the one who received it by the most peaceful bond of concord.”]

“Just as in the body the eye does not wish to be the finger, although both members are held together in the peaceful structure of the whole flesh, so one person will possess less good than another in such a way that he will also have this gift: that he will not desire more.”

## CHAPTER LIX. That the saints will praise God without weariness.

In praising God, the saints will not then encounter laborious resistance in praise itself [Note: [Col. 0524D] Lipsius lacks “laborious resistance.”], because, as the prophet says concerning them, “they will not labor or grow weary” (Isa. XL, 31). For they will enjoy the blessedness of eternity, so that their reward of blessedness will consist in their possessing an unfailing jubilation of praise.

For the Psalm says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5). The reward of virtue, therefore, will be the one who himself gave virtue.

## CHAPTER LX. That we shall see the Lord without end and that he himself is the end of our desires.

[Col. 0524A]

If, as the Apostle says, “We shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. IV, 16), it is certain that we shall see him without interruption.

“Christ, then, will be the end of our desires: he will be seen without end, loved without distaste, praised without weariness. This gift, this affection, and this activity will certainly be common to all, just as eternal life itself is common” (Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 30, no. 1).

## CHAPTER LXI. That the Lord himself will then be our reward, and that our honorable desires will then be wonderfully fulfilled.

He who created us promised that he would give us himself as our reward, and nothing is better than this.

“For what else is meant by what the Lord said through the prophet, ‘I will be their God, and they will be my people’ (Lev. XL, 31), except: ‘I will be what satisfies them; I will be whatever human beings honorably desire—life, salvation, [Note: [Col. 0524D] Lipsius adds: “virtue, abundance, glory, honor, peace, and every good.”] abundance, peace, and every good’?

“For thus also what the Apostle says is rightly understood: ‘That God may be all in all’” (1 Cor. XV, 28) [D. Augustine, *ibid*.].

## CHAPTER LXII. Concerning the endless end in which we shall praise the Lord infinitely.

Christ, our end, who perfects us, will himself be our refreshment and our praise. We shall praise him forever and ever, and, praising him without end, we shall love him.

There, as the most holy teacher Augustine says (*City of God*, book XXII, chapter 30), there will truly be the greatest Sabbath, one without evening. The Lord commended this at the beginning of the world’s works, where we read: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works [Note: [Col. 0524D] “Which he had made; and God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it,” and so forth. L.] that he had made” (Gen. II, 2), and he sanctified it because on it he rested from all his works.

For we ourselves will be the seventh day when we have been filled and perfected by his blessing. Then will be fulfilled: “Be still and know that I am God” (Ps. XLV, 11). Then truly our Sabbath will exist, whose end will not be evening, but the Lord’s Day, or the eighth day, which has been prepared by Christ’s resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0524D] “Or the eternal eighth day.” L. “As the eternal eighth day, which has been consecrated …” Maurist edition of Saint Augustine.]

There we shall be at rest and see; we shall see and love; we shall love and praise. Behold what there will be at the endless end. [Note: [Col. 0524D] Lipsius has: “For what other end is ours, except …?”] Is there any other end of ours than to arrive at the kingdom whose end is none?

[THE APOLOGETIC BOOK.]

[Col. 0525]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK.

The *Apologetic Book concerning the Three Chapters* follows the *Prognosticon*. It is unquestionably Julian’s work, sent to Benedict II, Roman pontiff, and inserted in the middle portion of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo.

We have discussed at length the date and occasion of its composition in the notes to Julian’s biography prefixed to this edition. The reader may consult them and will not doubt—and will at the same time be astonished—that otherwise highly learned and conscientious men have existed who thought that this book should be denied to Julian because some of its words seemed to them excessively harsh and alien to the modesty of so humane and holy a man.

They did not observe that, although they thought they were diverting the odium of those words from Julian, they were in fact casting it upon the entire council—a council over which Julian presided, and in which whatever he had written privately to Rome was approved and confirmed by public votes. But we deliberately pass over these matters.

The work unquestionably ought not to have been omitted from our edition, since it demonstrates Julian to be an absolutely accomplished theologian as much as—or, I do not know whether, even more than—the preceding work: a theologian who never departed by so much as a finger’s breadth from the teaching of the holy Fathers; from whose pen no word fell without deliberation, and no expression pleased him unless it had been used by the Fathers, especially in explaining the deepest mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation.

In this undertaking, no one is entirely unaware how much attention must be paid not only to the subject matter but also to the language.

Now, in order that our edition might be as thoroughly purified as possible, we kept before our eyes the two editions of the fifteenth council, produced by Garcia Loaysa and Cardinal Aguirre. We carefully collated them with two parchment manuscripts of the library of the Holy Church of Toledo. One of these began to be written in the era 986 (that is, in the year of Christ 948); the other, more recent, was completed in the era 1133, or the year of Christ 1095. From both manuscripts we corrected many things in the printed editions, as will be clear from the variant readings. We also indicated in the margin the passages of Sacred Scripture and the works of the holy Fathers cited—not without considerable care. [Note: [Col. 0525] We, however, inserted them into the text. EDIT.] Then we appended the notes of Garcia Loaysa, which shed some light upon the little work.

[Col. 0525]

THE APOLOGETIC BOOK OF SAINT JULIAN, BISHOP OF TOLEDO, ON THE THREE SUBSTANCES. FROM THE FIFTEENTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO, IN THE CONFESSION OF FAITH. (C, S)

[Col. 0525A] 1. After the rule of this pious confession had been proclaimed in devout words, we immediately turned to examining those chapters on behalf of which, two years earlier, Pope Benedict of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0525A] Pope Benedict. Benedict II succeeded Leo II. [Col. 0525B] Roderic, Archbishop of Toledo, describes this entire controversy in Book III, chapter 13, as follows: “In his time,” he says, “the book on the Three Substances, which the most holy primate Julian had previously sent to Rome, and which Pope Benedict of Rome, dealing with it insufficiently cautiously, had ordered to be rejected because ‘will generated will,’ Saint Julian, in this council, at the demand of the aforesaid ruler, confirmed by truthful testimonies, through the passages which he had sent to Rome, that it was true; and he composed an apology and sent it to Rome through his legates—a priest, a deacon, and a subdeacon, most learned men, servants of God in all things, and instructed in the divine Scriptures [Col. 0526A], together with acclamatory verses, just as he had formerly sent verses in praise of the Roman Empire. Pope Benedict, the Roman pontiff, receiving it worthily and piously, ordered it to be read by all; and by acclaiming, ‘Your praise, O God, reaches to the ends of the earth,’ he repeatedly made its reading known. He also sent his reply to Lord Julian through the aforementioned legates, with thanks and honor, and declared that everything he had written was just and pious.” Thus far Roderic. G. LOAYSA.] had warned us by the meaning of his letter. He did not, however, take care to record these matters in his own writings, but ordered them to be communicated verbally to our man; an adequate and appropriate reply was made to him in that same year. Yet now, on rereading more carefully that same communication from our man, we discovered that in that book of our Response concerning the Faith, which we had sent through Peter, regional officer of the Roman Church, the first chapter had seemed to the aforesaid pope to have been imprudently set down by us, where we said, according to the divine [Note: [Col. 0526B] Aguirre’s edition: “existence.”] essence, “Will generated will, just as wisdom generated wisdom.” Passing over these words in a careless rush of reading, that man supposed that we had used these very nouns—namely, relatively, or according to a comparison with the human mind. [Note: [Col. 0526B] Nor according to relation. The question is asked whether these names—wisdom, essence, and will—are used by the holy Fathers relatively or substantially. The Master of the Sentences resolves this question in Book I of the Sentences, distinction 27, where, following the judgment of St Augustine, he teaches that names which signify substance are said only as “that of that.” St Thomas, I, question 39, article 5, says: “Hence ‘nature from nature’ or ‘wisdom from wisdom’ is less improper than ‘essence from essence.’” Although Augustine, Book VII of On the Trinity, chapters 1 and 2, establishes this expression, “wisdom from wisdom,” and in Book XV of On the Trinity, chapter 20, this one, “will from will”: “The Son,” he says, “is called counsel from counsel and will from will, just as substance from substance and wisdom from wisdom.” Yet all holy teachers sometimes spoke more expressly than propriety of expression permits; hence forms of speech of this kind are not to be extended, but rather explained, so that abstract names are explained by concrete or personal names, as Thomas taught, I, question 39, article 1, and the Master of the Sentences, Book I, distinction 5. Therefore these propositions must be interpreted through concrete or personal names, so that when “essence from essence” or “wisdom from wisdom” is said, the sense is: the Son, who is essence and wisdom, is from the Father, who is essence and wisdom. G. LOAYSA.] And therefore [Note: [Col. 0526B] In the same work.] he was instructed to admonish us in that communication of his, saying:

“By a natural order we understand that the Word originates from the mind, as do reason and will. They cannot, however, be reversed so that one might say: just as the Word and will proceed from the mind, so also the mind proceeds from the Word or will.”

From this comparison it seemed to the Roman pontiff that “will from will” could not be said. We, however, said “will from will,” not according to this comparison with the human mind, nor according to relation, but according to essence, just as “wisdom from wisdom.” For in God, being is the same as willing, and willing the same as knowing. This, however, cannot be said of a human being. For in a human being what he is apart from willing is one thing, and willing—even apart from knowing—is another. [Note: [Col. 0528D] Loaysa: “it is for a human being.”] In God, however, it is not so, because He is a simple nature; and therefore for Him being is the same as willing and knowing. Accordingly, whoever is able to understand that we said “will from will” according to essence will not be troubled by the question that has been raised.

This is also clear to those who read and understand carefully the work already mentioned, our Response concerning the Faith, where the statement of blessed Athanasius inserted there declares that we ought to hold precisely this view, saying:

“We retain this judgment of religious belief concerning God: we must not believe that His will is one thing and His nature another.”

For if, according to what this teacher says, we ought to hold that God’s will is not one thing and His nature another, then His will is the same as His nature, and His nature the same as His substance or essence.

2. Therefore the Son of God was born from the essence of the Father: essence from essence, just as nature from nature, and substance from substance. Yet one cannot speak of two essences, two natures, or two substances, but of one essence, nature, and substance. Thus, light from light—not two lights, but one light; essence from essence—not two essences, but one essence; nature from nature—not two natures, but one nature; likewise will from will, [Col. 0527C] not two wills, but one will—for God’s will is not one thing and His nature another, as was established above through the teaching of Athanasius.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] “And therefore.” This general rule and universal axiom belongs to all theologians in the matter of the Trinity, and derives from Augustine, Book III of On the Trinity. In the preface, concerning the names of the undivided Trinity, he says: “Some things are said only of the individual persons, while others signify the unity of essence and are said both individually of each person and collectively of the common nature. There are still others that are said of God metaphorically and by way of likeness.” Ambrose says the same in the preface to Book II of On the Trinity. ID.]

And therefore whatever is said of God according to essence appears to apply commonly to each of the persons, such as wisdom and strength, and the rest. For the Father can be called wisdom, and the Son wisdom. The Father can also be called strength, and the Son can likewise be called strength. This cannot in any way be said according to that comparison with the human mind. For example, if the mind is placed in the role of the Father, the Word proceeding from the mind is understood as the Son, and the will proceeding from the mind and the Word signifies the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0528D] “As if from”: Aguirre.] Yet it does not follow that the mind, which is placed in the signification of the Father, can be said to belong to the Son or the Holy Spirit; or that the Word, understood as belonging solely to the Son, can be compared with the Father or the Holy Spirit; or that the will, understood as belonging to the person of the Holy Spirit, can be said to belong to the person of the Father or the Son. Rather, according to the comparison with the human mind, each corresponds to its own individual, so that whatever is said of one of them is not said of another at all. Likewise, when the Father is named by a relative term, He is not the same as the Son; when the Son is named, He is not the same as the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit is not the same as the Father or the Son. Thus those names that are taken by comparison from human beings are spoken according to the comparison with the human mind so that, in some manner, human weakness may be stirred toward contemplating the ineffable mystery of the divine Trinity.

3. According to this comparison, then, we were thought to have said “will from will,” although it is certainly most absurd to say or think this. Accordingly, the rule by which something is said of God according to essence is entirely different from the rule by which something is asserted of Him according to a comparison with the human mind. Therefore, agreeing with and following the judgment of the distinguished teacher Augustine, we said, according to the essence of the divine Trinity, “will from will,” just as he himself declares in the fifteenth book of On the Trinity, saying (chapter 20, no. 38):

“It is better, in my judgment, to say ‘counsel from counsel’ and ‘will from will,’ just as ‘substance from substance’ and ‘wisdom from wisdom.’”

[Col. 0528C] Here every intelligent person clearly understands that we did not err, but that they perhaps were misled by careless reading, because what we said according to essence they thought had been stated according to a comparison with the human mind. [Note: [Col. 0528D] Loaysa: “operation.”]

4. Passing also to the reconsideration of the second chapter, in which that same pope thought that we had imprudently professed three substances in Christ the Son of God: just as we will not be ashamed to defend what is true, so perhaps some will be ashamed to remain ignorant of what is true. For who does not know that every human being consists of two substances, namely, soul and body? Concerning these the Apostle speaks specifically, saying: “Although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). Likewise, the one who thirsted for God cried out in the psalm: [Note: [Col. 0529C] “My soul thirsts for You.” From Psalm 62 according to the Septuagint, which translates ἐδήψησε ἡ ψυχὴ μοῦ ποσαπλῶς ἡ σὰρξ μοῦ literally: “My soul thirsted for You; how greatly my flesh.” Saint Jerome has: “My soul thirsted for You; my flesh longed for You.” Basil (Scholia on Psalm 62), citing the words “My soul thirsted in You, how greatly,” says: “Theodotion has ‘very often’; Symmachus, ‘longs for.’ He set out all the translations in order to teach that ποσαπλῶς is not a phrase of two parts, but a single term signifying an intensification of expression. For the flesh too assents to the soul’s love and does not oppose its counsels—as though he said: ‘Both my soul and my body long for You,’ just as someone might thirst for water that is most pleasant and most clear.” The new Latin version of the Septuagint has “My soul thirsted for You,” in accordance with the sense of Hilary and Augustine. G. LOAYSA.—Cardinal Aguirre printed “My soul thirsted in You”; although that reading is indeed more common, we preferred to retain the other, which the two Toledo manuscripts exhibit. See Garcia de Loaysa’s note.] “My soul thirsts for You,” [Note: [Col. 0529D] We emend “tropically” from the two Toledo manuscripts. Loaysa and Aguirre are less correct in reading “two properly.”] he says, “how greatly, and my flesh also” (Psalm 62:2). There are also many other passages that declare that a human being consists of two substances.

5. Against this rule, however, we likewise find in Scripture that, when the flesh alone is generally named, the whole human being can be understood, or that, when the soul alone is named, the perfection of the whole human being is sometimes recognized. Therefore, when the divine nature has been joined to human nature, three substances can properly be named, and two tropically. [Note: [Col. 0529D] We emend “tropically” from the two Toledo manuscripts. Loaysa and Aguirre are less correct in reading “two properly.”] But it is one thing when the whole human being is expressed according to the proper sense, and another when the whole is understood from a part. For there is a certain mode of speech [Note: [Col. 0529D] The fifth rule of Tichonius, cited by Augustine in Book III, chapter 35, of On Christian Doctrine, and by Isidore in Book I, chapter 19, of the Sentences.—A remarkable amount of error has occurred in the editions of Loaysa and Aguirre in citing Tichonius’s rule and the places where Augustine and Isidore mention it.] frequently found in the divine Scriptures, by which the whole is signified from a part; among grammarians this trope is called synecdoche. For it is written in the book of Genesis, according to this tropical mode of expression signifying the whole from a part: “Man was made into a living soul” (Genesis 2:7), although man consists not only of soul but also of flesh. Likewise, in the same way, the whole is signified from a part when the substance of the soul is omitted and the substance of the flesh alone is named, as it is written in the psalm: “All flesh shall come to You” (Psalm 64:3), although every human being consists not only of flesh but also of soul. [Note: [Col. 0530C] The same manuscripts read “but also of soul.”] Nevertheless, when flesh alone is named, the whole human being is understood, just as, when the soul alone is named, the whole human being is understood.

For in Exodus, [Note: [Col. 0530C] The manuscripts read, “And also in Exodus.”] when Scripture likewise wished a human being [Note: [Col. 0530C] The manuscripts read “human beings.”] to be understood as the whole from a part, it says: “Seventy souls [Note: [Col. 0530C] “Seventy souls.” The passage is Exodus 1:5, where it reads: “So all the souls who came out from the thigh of Jacob were seventy”; shortly before, in the same chapter, they are said to have entered Egypt. Genesis 46 likewise says explicitly: “All the souls of the house of Jacob who entered Egypt were seventy.” The same passage occurs in Deuteronomy 10. G. LOAYSA.] entered with Jacob into Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0530D] The manuscript reads “in Egypt.”] (Exodus 1:5), although those seventy souls had not entered there without their bodies. He likewise wished the whole human being to be understood by the name of flesh when he said: “In my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19:26), although bodies will not rise without their souls.

[Col. 0530A] 6. Behold, by the usage of Sacred Scripture we have proved both that a human being is properly called by the very substances of which he consists and that, tropically, the whole human being can be understood from a part. If you ask whether there is any fault, neither should the one be said to have erred who named the whole human being from a part, nor should the one be blamed who expressed the whole human being by naming flesh and soul, because divine Scripture proves that both can be said without blame. Yet although we now hold it established that neither of these parts is to be blamed, we must ask which part may more easily serve for understanding the whole human being and, with every obscurity removed, may also be clearer: whether the one that names flesh alone while silently intending the soul to be understood there, or the one that expresses both soul and flesh and thereby says “the whole.”

[Col. 0530B] 7. To make this more clearly known, some examples must be given. Behold, according to the foregoing tropical mode of speech, called synecdoche, by which either a part is understood from the whole or the whole from a part, we find written in the psalms concerning the plague of Egypt: “He sent among them the dog-fly” (Psalm 77:45). [Note: [Col. 0530D] “The dog-fly.” Psalm 77:45 has Κυνομυία, “dog-fly,” in the Septuagint, as does Psalm 104:31; the Latin Vulgate retained the Greek word. Κυνομυία means “dog-fly,” as it is rendered here. Isidore, Etymologies, Book XII, chapter 8. G. LOAYSA.] And likewise: “He spoke, and the locust and the caterpillar came” (Psalm 104:34). Scripture wished by this form of speech that not a single fly or locust but a plurality of flies and locusts should be understood. For it was not one fly [Note: [Col. 0530D] “One fly and one locust.” A.] or one locust, but a multitude of flies and locusts, that filled Egypt. But now, if someone were to say in our manner, “God sent flies, locusts, and caterpillars into Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0530D] The manuscript reads “in Egypt.”], using the plural number—which is certainly also true—could slander arise against this part, which confesses plurality, so that it might be said not to be true, although it is indeed true concerning the multitude of locusts that filled Egypt?

The same is the case [Note: [Col. 0530D] We supplied the connective particle from the manuscripts.] where the people cried out to Moses, saying: “Pray to the Lord, that He may take away from us the serpent” (Numbers 21:7). [Note: [Col. 0530D] “That He may take away from us the serpent.” The passage is in Numbers 21, though somewhat differently; the Latin translation has not “the serpent” but “the serpents.” In the Septuagint, however, it is τὸν ὄφιν, in the singular, as here. G. LOAYSA.] Yet the people were suffering not from the affliction of one serpent [Col. 0531A] but of many serpents. [Note: [Col. 0531C] The manuscripts read “of serpents.”]

The Apostle also speaks in this manner in the passage where he says: “By the works of the law no flesh shall be justified” (Romans 3:20), as if he were saying “no human being,” wishing the whole human being to be understood from the part, namely, the flesh. Thus also concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, when it is written of Him in the Gospel, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), flesh alone is named so that the soul too might be silently understood there, according to the foregoing mode of speech by which the whole human being is understood from a part. This rule of speech was also frequently observed by the Fathers.

8. Thus blessed Cyril, in the book called the Scholia, [Note: [Col. 0531C] Cyril’s book called the Scholia. [Col. 0531D] It is sufficiently clear from our edition that this most learned man made a mistake here, since blessed Cyril wrote the words quoted by Julian in the Scholia.] perhaps commentaries on John, where in Book I, chapter 15, commenting on the words “And the Word became flesh,” says as follows (chapter 24, Paris edition of 1573):

“Having now plainly entered upon the subject of the incarnation, he most clearly relates that the only-begotten Son of God became man. For when he says, ‘And the Word became flesh,’ he says nothing other than that the Son of God, who is God by nature, became man. Nor is anything novel being stated, since divine Scripture often signifies the complete, so to speak, and whole human being by the single term ‘flesh.’ ‘I will pour out,’ Joel says, ‘from my Spirit upon all flesh’; for unless you understand the whole human being from one part, it will seem ridiculous that spirit should be given to inanimate flesh.” G. LOAYSA.]

[Col. 0531B] He says:

“It is necessary to see, then, how the Word became flesh. First, divine Scripture often names flesh and, as it were, makes it signify the whole animal from a part; and at times it likewise does the same from the soul alone. For it is written that ‘all flesh shall see the salvation of God’ (Luke 3:6). And the divine Paul himself says: ‘I did not consult flesh and blood’ (Galatians 1:16). Moses the high priest addressed those who are descended from Israel: ‘In seventy-five souls your fathers descended into Egypt’ (Exodus 1:5, according to the Septuagint). [Note: [Col. 0531D] “Seventy-five.” Thus it appears in Exodus 1 in the Septuagint edition: ἔσαν δὲ πᾶσαι ψυχαὶ ἐξ Ἰακὼβ πέντε καὶ ἑβδομηκοντα, “and all the souls from Jacob were seventy-five.” Luke has the same in Acts 7. But Genesis 46 says: “All the souls who entered with Jacob into Egypt and came out from his thigh, apart from the wives of his sons, were sixty-six; and the sons of Joseph who were born to him in the land of Egypt were two souls; all the souls of the house of Jacob who entered Egypt were seventy.” For “seventy,” the Septuagint edition has ψυχαὶ ἑβδομηκοντα πέντε, “seventy-five souls.” In Deuteronomy 10, however, the Septuagint and the Vulgate agree, and state that seventy souls descended into Egypt. Josephus also has the same in Book II, chapter 7, of his Antiquities. Jerome beautifully reconciles how there can be both seventy and seventy-five in his Questions on Genesis at this passage. ID.]

But you must not therefore say that souls descended into Egypt naked and without flesh [Note: [Col. 0532D] The manuscripts read “in Egypt.”]; nor, on the other hand, that God granted His salvation to empty bodies and mere flesh. Whenever, therefore, we hear that the Word became flesh, we understand a man formed from soul and body.” [Note: [Col. 0532D] The manuscripts read “may be understood.”]

[Col. 0531C] 9. Likewise Saint Augustine, in the book of Questions against the Apollinarians, says (Question 80):

“If whenever flesh is named and the soul is left unmentioned, it must be understood that the soul is not believed to be there [Note: [Col. 0532D] The Toledo manuscripts read “that the soul is believed to be there.”], then those about whom it is said, ‘All flesh shall see the salvation of God’ (Luke 3:6), had no souls. Nor had those to whom it is said in the psalm, ‘Hear my prayers’ [Note: [Col. 0532D] The manuscripts omit “my.”], ‘to You all flesh shall come’ (Psalm 64:3), any souls. Nor had those of whom it is said in the Gospel, ‘You have given Him authority over all flesh, so that all that You have given Him may not perish but may have eternal life’ [Note: [Col. 0532D] Aguirre: “that He may give them eternal life.”] (John 17:2), any souls. Hence it is also understood that human beings are accustomed to be signified by the naming of flesh alone, so that according to this mode of speech the statement ‘The Word became flesh’ (John 1:14) may also be understood to mean nothing other than ‘The Word became man.’ For just as, from a part, the whole is often understood when the soul alone is named—as in the statement, ‘So many souls descended into Egypt’ (Genesis 46:27; Exodus 1:5)—so again, from a part, the whole human being is understood even when flesh alone is named.” [Note: [Col. 0532D] “Flesh.” A.]

10. The same author also says in the Enchiridion (chapter 34):

“‘The Word became flesh’: the divinity assumed flesh; the divinity was not changed into flesh. Here we must understand ‘flesh’ as ‘man,’ in a mode of speech signifying the whole from a part, just as it is said: ‘By the works of the law no flesh shall be justified’ (Romans 3:20), that is, no human being.”

Therefore [Note: [Col. 0532D] Cardinal Aguirre reads: “In what manner,” which does not please us.] this is the full judgment, gathered according to the manner of the Fathers and of Scripture [Note: [Col. 0532D] Aguirre: “from the Scriptures.”]: whenever any one substance of the human being assumed by Christ is named from a part, the other is immediately understood there as well. For even if [Note: [Col. 0532D] We restore “even if” from the manuscripts in place of “if.”], according to this trope, one is left unmentioned and the other is stated, nevertheless both are understood. Let no one, then, on hearing that the whole human being can be understood from a part, say that one ought not to profess three substances in Christ, since by this mode of speech one thing is necessarily understood from another. There is therefore no difference whether one substance of the human being is named tropically or the two are named properly, since either form of speech permits us to understand and confess that the human being assumed by God exists in two substances. Accordingly, anyone who has learned this reasoning with full understanding will not hesitate to profess three substances in Christ. But where these Fathers confess, not tropically but properly, that the whole human being was assumed by Christ, they expressed it in their treatises as follows.

11. Blessed Cyril, in the book mentioned above called the Scholia (chapter 10), says [Note: [Col. 0532D] The manuscripts read, “thus he says.”], where he clearly demonstrates the truth of the three substances of Christ through a figure from the Old Testament:

“Because God the Word was truly united to humanity, while the substances nevertheless remained unconfused, the holy tabernacle was erected through the wilderness according to God’s will, and Emmanuel was represented in it in many ways. Almighty God therefore said to the divine Moses: ‘You shall make an ark [Note: [Col. 0533D] “You shall make an ark.” The passage is Exodus 25:10–11, as follows: “Make an ark of incorruptible wood, two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high, and overlay it with pure gold; inside and outside you shall overlay it.” In place of “incorruptible wood,” the Septuagint has more explicitly ἐξ ξυλὼν ἀσήπτων, “from wood that does not decay,” as Cyril reads. G. LOAYSA.] of testimony from incorruptible wood, two and a half cubits in length, a cubit and a half in width, and a cubit and a half in height, and you shall overlay it with pure gold; inside and outside you shall overlay it’ (Exodus 25:10–11).

“Let the incorruptible wood be a figure of the incorruptible body—for cedar is incorruptible—while the gold, as a material more precious than others, indicates to us the majesty of the divine substance. Observe, then: since the entire ark was overlaid with pure gold, both outside and inside, God the Word was indeed united to the holy flesh; and, as I think, this is what it means for the ark to have been overlaid with gold on the outside. But that He also made the rational soul which was in the body His own is shown by the fact that He also commanded the inside of the ark to be overlaid with gold. We know from this that the natures, or substances, remained unconfused: for the gold placed upon the wood remained what it was; the wood was indeed adorned with the beauty of the gold, yet it did not cease to be wood.”

Likewise Saint Augustine, expressing the same point in his book On the Trinity of God, says (Book XIII, chapter 17):

“Human nature could be joined to God in such a way that from two substances there would be one person, and consequently now from three—God, soul, and flesh.”

12. Since the holy Fathers teach us these things and indicate both rules of speech to us, let those who judge without partiality toward either side now at last see and decide which position can be the safer, although blame cannot fall upon either side: whether that which professes in Christ the Son of God one substance of the Word and another substance of man, understanding the whole from a part, or that which confesses that the whole human being was properly united to the Word of God in two substances. In the former position, which wishes the whole human being to be understood from a part, the deceit of heretics may lie hidden, so that, by naming either one of these substances, it suppresses the other; and thus what it does not profess with its mouth it may not confess in its heart. This is what Apollinaris did, denying that the Lord Jesus possessed human nature [Note: [Col. 0534D] Loaysa: “a soul.”], or what Manichaeus did, denying the reality of the body assumed by Christ.

In our profession, however, where, after the substance of the Word has been stated, we specifically profess the two substances of man in the one person of Christ, no fraudulent deceit can arise or even be suspected, since the whole man is plainly proclaimed to have been assumed by God. The safer position, therefore, is the one that says the whole, rather than the one that suppresses something; and what is said properly is clearer than what is established by a restricted tropical expression. [Note: [Col. 0534D] “Is formed.” A.]

But perhaps we alone say this, and do not prove it by the judgment of our predecessors?

13. Let us therefore, if it please you, summon Augustine as judge, so that we may hear which position he declares to be more secure against heretics. [Note: [Col. 0534D] The manuscripts read “and” instead of “so that.”] Thus he says in his treatise on the Creed (no. 8):

“Heretics lie in wait for the Lord’s temporal dispensation in many ways; but whoever holds the Catholic faith, believing that the whole human being was assumed by the Word of God—that is, body, soul, and spirit—is sufficiently protected against them.”

Behold, the spiritual man, considering both spiritually, [Note: [Col. 0534D] Loaysa and Aguirre read incorrectly: “Behold, we consider spiritual things . . . .” With the help of the manuscripts we have restored this passage.] has delivered his judgment and fixed his verdict, declaring that the more secure and safer position is the one that defends against heretics the whole human being, assumed by the Word of God, in two substances, flesh and soul.

14. But perhaps someone will say that here three things belonging to the human being have been named—body, soul, and spirit—and that although three are said, there are in fact two, as is demonstrated by the same Teacher in the aforementioned treatise on the Creed (no. 23):

“There are three things of which man consists: spirit, soul, and body; these are again called two, because the soul is often named together with the spirit. For a certain part of the same rational nature, which animals lack, is called spirit.”

He also explains this with clear exposition in his letter to Peter [Note: [Col. 0534D] A. reads “attains”], where he teaches that spirit and soul are one and the same and are understood to belong to one substance. For he says (Letter on the Soul and Its Origin, Book II, chapter 2):

“There are two things, soul and spirit, according to what is written: ‘You have released my soul from my spirit’ (Job 7:15, according to the Septuagint), and both belong to the nature of man, so that the whole human being is spirit, soul, and body. But sometimes these two are named together under the name ‘soul,’ as in the statement: ‘And man was made into a living soul’ [Note: [Col. 0534D] Loaysa and Aguirre read “living.” We have restored “a living soul” from the Toledo manuscripts.] (Genesis 2:7); for there the spirit too is understood. Likewise, at times both are called by the name ‘spirit,’ as in the statement: ‘And He bowed His head and gave up His spirit’ (John 19:30).”

There too the soul must necessarily be understood, and both are one and belong to one substance. Accordingly, soul and spirit, and soul and body, are the two distinct substances of the human being, which are also called different.

[Col. 0534D] 15. Therefore, in the work on our Faith already mentioned, when responding to the heresy of the Apollinarians, we said that there are three substances in Christ, [Note: [Col. 0534D] “Three substances in Christ.” Stephen, Bishop of Autun, in Book 17 of On the Sacrament of the Altar: “We believe that there were two natures in Christ, divine and human, and three substances: divine, flesh, and soul, as Athanasius attests when he says: ‘Just as a rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.’” G. LOAYSA.] as we have shown that our predecessors also taught [Note: [Col. 0535C] The manuscript reads “we show.”] [Col. 0535A]—honoring and following, namely, the judgment of the distinguished bishop of the See of Seville, which he discussed in his books On the Difference of the Nature of Christ and of Ours, where he says (Book II, no. 8, in the royal edition of 1599):

“We subsist from two substances, namely body and soul; He from three: the Word, body, and soul. Hence it is that the perfect man is proclaimed also to be perfect God.”

These, then, are a very few examples [Note: [Col. 0535C] The manuscripts read “very small.”] that we have drawn from the Fathers, so that in brief we might demonstrate what is relevant. But anyone who seeks these matters by reading them even more attentively will be able to gather many more.

16. But if anyone, with shameless face, refuses to yield even to these Fathers [Note: [Col. 0535C] “Nor,” instead of “not,” from the manuscripts] and insolently asks from where they drew these things, let him at least believe the words of the Gospels, by which Christ declares that these three substances are present in Him. For when He was asked by the Jews, “Who are You?” He answered: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25). Behold, you have one substance, that of the Godhead.

Two substances of the human being remain. To show that He had assumed true human flesh, He offered Himself to the disciples to be touched, saying: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see Me have” (Luke 24:39). [Note: [Col. 0535D] “Has” is found in the manuscripts instead of “have,” as in the text of Loaysa and Aguirre.] Behold, the substance of human flesh has been expressly stated. Likewise, to show that He had assumed the substance of a human soul, He says: “I have power to lay down My soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

17. Behold, three substances united in the one person of Christ, without confusion and inseparably: namely, divinity and humanity. Approving this by the oracles of the Gospels, we all confess with one voice and proclaim in the sentence set forth above, confessing, in accordance with the Council of Chalcedon (Act V, in the revision of the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creed), that the same Lord Jesus Christ is perfect in divinity and the same perfect in humanity; truly God and the same truly man, consisting of a rational soul and a body; according to his divinity, of one nature with the Father; according to his humanity, of one nature with us, like us in all things except sin.

Before the ages, he was born from the Father according to his divinity; but in these last days, for us and for our salvation, the same was born from Mary the virgin, God-bearer, according to his humanity: one and the same Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation. The distinctions of the natures are in no way abolished because of the union; rather, the proper character of each nature is preserved, and the two come together in one person and one state. He is not to be divided or separated into two persons, but is one and the same only-begotten Son, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ.

But if anyone thereafter, instead of being instructed by these things, should show himself opposed to this explanation that has been given, he will suffer the condemnation of the aforesaid council.

18. [Note: What these two chapters contained is still unknown. [Col. 0536C] Certainly, together with the two preceding chapters already expounded, they constitute the four special divisions of the chapters which, as is said shortly afterward, he confirmed—or made solid—by adding the testimonies of Catholic Fathers. From this we draw two conclusions: first, that the *Apologeticus* of Saint Julian ought to have been entitled not *On the Three Chapters* (as Felix writes in his eulogy), but rather *On the Four Chapters*; [Col. 0536D] second, that the Fathers of the Fifteenth Council transcribed only half of this little work, and that this alone has come down to us. G. Loaysa.]

Considering the third and fourth chapters, we have shown that not only their meaning but almost their very words were drawn from the books of the blessed Ambrose and Fulgentius, whom we know to have taught these doctrines. Since the solemn devotion of the Churches of God honors them as renowned teachers throughout the world, we must not be angry with them but rather submit to them, because whatever is thought against them is perceived to depart from the rule of right faith.

These four special divisions of the chapters, which they urged us to establish firmly, we presented for recognition, in a single book of our reply, to that party two years ago, having brought together the Catholic doctrine of the Fathers and indicating what had been said by which teacher. But if, after this, anyone should dissent in any respect even from the doctrines of the Fathers themselves, from which these statements were drawn, there is no longer any need to contend with such people. Rather, clinging directly to the footsteps of our elders, our reply will be exalted before the divine judgment among lovers of truth, even if ignorant opponents judge it to be uninstructive.

[ON THE CONFIRMATION OF THE SIXTH AGE.]

[Col. 0535]

NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK.

In the little work that follows, *On the Confirmation of the Sixth Age*, which Saint Julian composed at the request of Erwig, king of the Goths, in order to attack the Jews’ faithlessness and blindness, we ought to say a few preliminary words. Whatever needed to be said about the subject of this work, its division, and the occasion of its composition, Julian himself explains with exceptional clarity in his letter to King Erwig, which should be regarded as a fully developed prologue. We shall then briefly indicate what we have done in this new edition of his work.

Without the assistance of any manuscript codices, we consulted only the earlier editions: namely, the first, produced at Hagenau by Menrad Molther in 1532; the second, the Paris edition by the editors of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* in 1624; and the third, the Lyon edition in the same *Bibliotheca*, reprinted in 1677. We carefully corrected their errors, marking in the margin the sources from which the testimonies of Sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers were taken, and adding at the foot of the page other observations that seemed worthy of notice. Among these we included certain conjectures of the very learned Gaspar Barthius, set forth in book XIX, chapter 14, of his *Adversaria*, by which, as he thinks, some passages of this little work of Julian’s that appear corrupt could be healed and restored.

[Col. 0537]

THREE BOOKS OF SAINT JULIAN, BISHOP OF TOLEDO, ON THE CONFIRMATION OF THE SIXTH AGE. (C)

[PREFACE.]

PRAYER.

[Col. 0537A]

I shall approach you, Lord, in the humility of my spirit. I shall speak to you, because you have given me great hope and confidence. Who will rise with me against the malicious, or who will stand with me against those who speak wickedness (Psalm 93:16), unless you, Lord, help me?

You, therefore, Son of David, who came to us in the flesh when the mystery was revealed, with the nail [Note: [Col. 0537C] All those who have hitherto edited this little work of Julian prefixed to it the title *Against the Jews*, which seemed false to the learned Juan Bautista Pérez, because, as we suppose, Felix had entitled it *On the Demonstration of the Sixth Age*. We, however, [Col. 0537D] who restore this title to the little work, do not at all think that the other title, *Against the Jews*, was so wrongly employed by the rest, since Isidore of Pacensis, an author writing half a century after Felix, already entitled the book thus: “The most holy Julian, bishop of Toledo, [Col. 0538C] in the book which he wrote against the Jews on the six ages of the world,” etc. *Hispania Sacra*, vol. VIII, p. 324, 2nd ed.] of your cross, open the secrets of my heart. Send one of the seraphim, through whom that glowing coal taken from your altar (Isaiah 6:6) may cleanse my filthy [Note: [Col. 0538C] *Sordentia*: Barthius would prefer *surdentia*, as though “mute lips”; he offers many examples of this expression. His conjecture does not please us, because *sordentia labia*, “filthy lips,” agrees with the verb *depurget*, “cleanse,” whereas *surdentia* does not.] lips, clear my mind of cloud, and supply material for speech, so that my tongue, which through charity serves the usefulness of my neighbors, may not give off the stench of error [Note: [Col. 0538C] Barthius thinks that *causam*, “cause,” should be read instead of *casum*, “fall,” and that Julian wrote it that way. The conjecture is plausible.], but may resound forever with the proclamation of truth.

Meanwhile, O God, my God, illuminate with the inextinguishable flame of this coal the heart of the glorious prince, so that he may burn wholly with the fire of your charity and likewise blaze with zeal for the faith. May he strive always to preserve your bride, wandering on earth, peaceful and defended from every contagion of disease. With the hand of his power may he overthrow the poisons by which harm can be done. May he crush the authors of poison beneath the heel of faith. May he not allow a judgment of blood to come against her, so that, always rejoicing in the glory of her defense, and now reclining in her bosom, he may remain himself pure by guarding her, a virgin, clean and disciplined in faith; and afterward, reaching you, made glorious in her, may he approach ready to render you a good account of his defense of her. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0537C] *Clavo*: this is how it is read in all the printed editions. But the very learned Gaspar Barthius, in book XIX, chapter 14, of his *Adversaria*, examining at length certain passages of this little work of our Julian that seem corrupt to him—and which we have wished to indicate—thinks that *clave* should be read here instead of *clavo*, because of the following verb *adaperi*, “open.” A very prudent conjecture.]

TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS, GLORIOUS, AND REVEREND LORD ERWIG, KING, JULIAN, YOUR LITTLE SERVANT.

[Col. 0537C]

It is the custom of skilled physicians, wherever a wound spreads through the body, to forestall the substance of the wound with the knife [Note: [Col. 0538C] *Vulneris materiam*: all the editions have this reading. [Col. 0538D] Barthius corrected it to *ulceris materiam*, “the substance of the ulcer.” This is indeed more properly expressed and more consistent with the usual meaning of the words. Yet I would not dare assert that Julian, although most learned, was in his own age so concerned about the propriety of words.] and first to cut out the festering corruption at its root, before the harmful ulcer infects the healthy parts. Therefore, lest the site of the wound touch sound limbs, the skill of excision is always applied first. For contact with the wound cannot produce the cause of healing. Wherever it reaches, it makes room for the wound. Unless it is first cut away by the hand of the craftsman, it brings about the destruction of all the infected limbs.

I believe, most sacred prince, that your clemency wished to imitate the expertise of this remarkable cure. Fearing that the peoples entrusted to you by God might be touched by deadly destruction, you devise a useful kind of excision by which those who are to be saved may, through curative diligence, avoid the destructive pus of useless limbs and the incurable skin of purulent filth. For this reason you command me to apply care to the limbs that are still healthy, [Col. 0538B] lest, when diseases arise, they fall away; so that error may be cut off before an occasion for danger is generated. Thus, while their safety is prudently safeguarded, the approach of illness to be avoided may be usefully frustrated.

I would call the tongues of the Jews the corruption of these limbs that must be avoided. They think that Christ, the Son of God promised in the Law, has not yet been born, and they await another who is to come, chattering poisonous accusations: namely, that the calculation of years, counted from the beginning of the world according to the Hebrew codices, still indicates the fifth age of the world, and that Christ has not yet come—the Christ whom they believe will arrive in the sixth age of the world.

A grave evil, an intolerable and dreadful crime, is that the period of years in this error is thought to determine the date at which Christ’s birth should be recognized—as though they had read somewhere in the sacred writings that this was commanded: that, by counting the predetermined years from the beginning of the world, the time of his sacred birth could be learned.

Against this detestable error of impiety and this most manifest blindness, your august head and serene mind command me to respond in a very brief book. I, however, conscious of my weakness, would have declined the burden imposed upon me by you if I had not guarded against the ruin of souls being constructed through my silence, especially since it is one and the same thing to refuse to defend the faith and to deny it. For whenever something is done concerning God or against God, it is dangerous for a shepherd to remain silent, disgraceful to flee, and deadly to yield. The Lord recalls this with fearful force through the prophet, rebuking the sluggish negligence of shepherds: “You did not go up against the enemy, nor did you build a wall for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13:5). For this reason the same Lord, through the same prophet, declares that he will require from the watchman the blood of those souls who perish (ibid. 3:18 ff.).

Trembling at the sentence of this severity, bound both by the devout commands of your Glory and by the duties imposed by my order, I return to your Highness the honor due to obedience and to God the service owed to him. The work commanded to me I have explained obediently, as I was able, though less learnedly than I ought. I have striven to conclude this very easy little work of our reply with a threefold [Note: [Col. 0539D] *Trimodo*: Barthius conjectures *trinodo*.] division of books.

I have preserved this order of reasoning: first, in the book of this work, the Jews are to be refuted by clear and evident signs from the Old Testament, by which it is plainly declared, without any calculation of years, that Christ the Son of God was not destined to be born but was born long ago. Then, as the sequence of the second book proceeds, it is shown through the manifest teaching of the apostles that the revealed fullness of time in which Christ appeared born in the flesh was not demonstrated to the Lord’s disciples or to other believers by years collected from the beginning of the world, but was announced through the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets.

This is especially so since the Jews themselves, at that time, did not think that he was the Christ; indeed, while disputing with Christ about whether he was the Christ, they never raised against our Christ the objection that the insolent and ignorant breadth of their present argument now advances.

In the third book, the arrival of the sixth age is also demonstrated. There it is shown that the five preceding ages of the world must be distinguished not by years but by a fixed limit of generations. It is also necessarily taught there that, because of the difference in years found between the Hebrew codices and our own, the books of the translation of the Hebrews are not to be followed, but the codices of the Seventy Interpreters, to which the authority of the majority has given credence. For this third book not only discloses more clearly the distinctions of the six ages, but also shows that Christ was given in the sixth age, explains most plainly why he wished to be born in the sixth age, and dissolves every such question concerning this calculation of years.

I say, then, that we have arranged the three books composed on this question under this division because it seemed better to us that one should not first deal with such people about the question of years itself, before their falsehood has been exposed by the true divine signs and the indications of the prophets, together with the doctrines of the New Testament; only afterward should one proceed freely to confirm the sixth age.

For this reason the question of years raised by them is answered in the third book of this work, [Col. 0540B] so that the mind resisting those two preceding books may first be broken. It is fitting that the mouths of such people, soiled by carnal antiquity, should first be restrained by the sword of the Old Testament; then, struck by the powerful and new dagger of the Gospel, they should proceed to the book of the third discussion, in which they may recognize the sixth age of the world and understand that Christ was born in it.

Thus it is in no way advantageous to read one of these books and pass over another, lest the person whom the reading of all three books constrains fail to draw from them the full solidity of the teaching. Since the hostile malice of the Jews raises a question about the difference in years between our codices and theirs, we, conversely, set up a barrier based on the unfolding of the generations, which is the same in our codices and theirs. Thus, when they point to the shortness of the years for distinguishing the ages, we, by displaying the fullness of the generations, may dismiss as superfluous their question about years.

For what can years accomplish if the generations fail? The truth concerning the time of Christ’s birth must therefore be sought in the generations of the ages; it is shown through the Law and recognized through the Gospel.

Now, most gentle prince, I ask that, for the things I have said somewhat inelegantly and for having perhaps extended the subject of my speech somewhat more than was proper through the fault of loquacity, pardon be granted to me in your goodness, since your Glory imposed upon me this very necessity of responding.

Let your Highness, therefore, who has shown yourself the patron of Christ’s cause, believe that you will be saved in every way when he himself comes to judgment. Your work will then be taken into account, when the manifest day of judgment shines forth—provided, most devout prince, that you vigorously crush the necks of Christ’s enemies beneath the Lord’s service and powerfully raise the banners of the Christian faith.

BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0539]

[Col. 0539D] 1. Taking up the task of strengthening the faith of the nascent Church with suitable witnesses, I shall begin this little work with the patriarchs and prophets themselves. I shall strive, insofar as I can with God’s help, to answer the rabid barking of the Jews, who, possessed by the blind night of unbelief, not only fall into the abyss of detestable faithlessness themselves [Note: [Col. 0539] In book XVIII, chapter 1 of the *Adversaria*, at the end, Barthius conjectured that *coincidunt* should be read.] but also compel certain members of the faithful to waver. They presume, in diseased speeches, to argue by a rash calculation that Christ the Son of God has not yet come into the world for the salvation of humanity but is still to come.
