They say that the fifth age of the world is still unfolding and that the course of the sixth age, in which Christ ought to come and be born, has not yet arrived.

From this most vain opinion they dare to investigate the presence of Christ by collecting a calculation of years from the beginning of the world according to their own codices; but, once faith has been removed, all things are blind to them.

2. What, I ask, shall we answer such people, or how shall we raise weapons against the unarmed? I believe Paul declared that disputes of this kind should be avoided when he instructed his disciple Timothy. “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions,” he says; “for they contribute greatly to impiety, and their speech spreads like cancer” (2 Timothy 2:16–17, 23).

Truly foolish is the question that does not proceed from the hidden meaning of the Law. Such people must therefore be judged weak and unarmed, because they do not take up weapons from the Scriptures but bring forth unjust things [Note: [Col. 0541D] *Injusta*: Barthius read *justa* in the printed editions, which is plainly erroneous, and corrected it either to *hausta*, “things drawn out,” or, as he preferred, *scruta*, “things searched out,” so that he would have something to oppose to weapons.] from the cave of their own malice. The mouths of such people are armed not with the iron of faith but with the sword of faithlessness [Note: [Col. 0541D] *Gladio*: Barthius does not approve this reading, since he is, in our opinion, overly fastidious in judging individual words. Why does he object? Because Julian later calls them unarmed. But the learned man did not notice that Julian calls them unarmed because they raise these objections equipped with no weapons from the Scriptures.]; not with prophetic testimony but with deceitful obstinacy.

Therefore, they are in every respect rightly called unarmed, because they raise these objections equipped with no weapons from the Scriptures. Yet if they alone were perishing, perhaps we could remain unharmed through silence. But what of the fact that this kind of destruction infects the faithful as well? We must therefore strive—we who, although unworthy, are nevertheless ministers of God’s word and have received the stewardship of preaching—so that the rock of truth, cast forth through our mouth, may crush the teeth of such people. Otherwise, through our silence, those who sincerely confess Christ but are still unable to avoid Satan’s cunning may grow weak in the very truth of the faith. Thus, even if the Jew is not corrected, at least the Christian may advance.

3. Listen now, workers of impiety, wicked children—not to me, but to Christ the Lord himself, whom you strive to overcome. Listen to him answering your fathers. For in the Gospel he said to the Jews who were testing him: “You are mistaken, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God” (Matthew 22:29).

Indeed, according to Paul, Christ is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Therefore, ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. What wonder, then, if error possesses your hearts, when ignorance of the Scriptures rebukes you?

Search, therefore, the hidden fields of the Scriptures, and then you will understand the blindness of your eyes. Now, without prejudice to the Christian faith, I shall speak. Was Christ predicted anywhere in the Law or the Prophets as destined to be born specifically in the six-thousandth year? Or is it foretold anywhere, with regard to his human birth, that a calculation of years from the beginning of the world should be observed? Is it not rather the clear evidence of the testimonies that declares this very glorious birth of his?

Nevertheless, with the Lord’s help—and may he himself assist me in what follows—everything will be calculated more clearly, and it will confirm the sixth age of the world and testify that Christ was born of a virgin in the sixth age. What I say is for me to prove; it is for you to answer.

4. Where did you read the things you maliciously fabricate? Or perhaps you say this because of the opinion set forth in the Psalm, where it says: “For a thousand years in your sight are like one day” (Psalm 89:4). Do you therefore think that, just as the world is said to have been made by God in six days, so it is divided, as it were, into six ages over six thousand years? Far from it.

We do say, without error, that, in the likeness of those six days, six ages of the world are distinguished. But we do not say that those six ages are determined by six thousand years—that is, that each age is separated by a course of a thousand years.

But does that prophetic testimony mention anything here about the distinction of the ages, or does it proclaim anything about Christ’s birth? For it says, “A thousand years in your sight are like one day,” because however long a period is desired for this life, and however great the length of years in which one lives, a thousand years in the eyes of him who does not die are regarded as one passing day and therefore counted as almost nothing.

Nevertheless, some believe that, according to the number of the six days, the matter may also stand at six thousand years. But even if this were so, or even if each age had been determined by a thousand years, the disciples would not have asked the Lord about the end of the world. Knowing that the end of the world could be calculated by a definite reckoning of years, and therefore that they could know it by counting the years from the beginning of the world, they would not have attempted to learn this from the Lord. They would have been certain from the experience of past ages that each age proceeded through a thousand years.

The blessed Augustine, explaining this point, says (*Exposition on Psalm 89*, no. 5): “Men dared to presume knowledge of the times, although the Lord said to his disciples, who desired to know: ‘It is not for you to know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority’ (Acts 1:7). And they determined that this age could end after six thousand years, as though after six days. They did not consider that it was said, ‘like one day that has passed’: for when this was said, not merely one thousand years had passed.””

5. Since the objection of that foregoing opinion has thus been emptied of force, what, I ask, does the mention of the Lord’s birth in this testimony prejudice—that “a thousand years in your sight are like one day” (Psalm 89:4)? Are we to understand that a thousand years are mentioned here so that we may learn something from them concerning the time of Christ’s birth?

No one will ever find it intimated in the divine canon of books that, by applying a calculation of years from the creation of the world, one should determine the time of Christ’s birth [Note: [Col. 0543] The compilers of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* have the better reading here than the other editions, which have: “Never and nowhere, whoever he may be, in the divine books,” and so forth.].

We do indeed read in Daniel (9:24 ff.) that, after seventy weeks had elapsed, the angel foretold Christ as destined to be born and to suffer, establishing a definite calculation of years. But he who wished to calculate the future time up to Christ by a reckoning of years did not concern himself with the total of past years from the beginning of the world. He either did not foresee those years as necessary to the Lord’s incarnation, or, if he considered them necessary, he omitted them all the more deliberately and necessarily.

Thus the prophet Daniel, understanding through divine revelation the number of years, not only wrote that Christ was to come—a fact the other prophets also foretold—but also disclosed when he was to come. He arranged the kings in order, demonstrated the matter by counting the years, and foretold other clearer signs.

Since these things are so, he did not wish to collect the years from the beginning of the world to Christ’s coming—years that he had neither read were to be observed for such a question in the divine writings nor known from the examples of the preceding Fathers. He therefore taught the future courses of years concerning Christ, which he certainly understood more deeply than the others. For he himself says: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Daniel 12:4).

His knowledge was therefore manifold in this matter. Already serving, in a certain sense, the apostolic principles—“forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead”—in recognizing the birth of Christ, the Son of God, he did not attend to calculations of past years but most clearly declared the reckoning of those yet to come.

By this prophetic calculation our faith is strengthened and your faithlessness destroyed. Set out in its proper place, it will either illuminate all the darkness of your error so that you may come to life, or refute it so that you may depart into Tartarus.

6. Now, then, lest your error—God forbid—infect the Christian army in any way, everyone ought first to know this: nothing of the sort was foretold either in the Law or in the Prophets, namely, that the coming of the Lord’s incarnation should be recognized by counting the years from the beginning of the world.

Nevertheless, in many places, whether in the Law or also in the Prophets, wherever Christ is proclaimed as destined to be born, the presence of his first coming is always promised as occurring in the last days. Among us, this is understood as referring to the sixth age of the world.

These six ages are not gathered by an equal calculation of years, but are to be recognized through an arranged order of generations, just as we find three ages counted in Matthew’s Gospel. We recognize that these, too, were determined not by the passage of years but by the enumeration of generations (Matthew 1:2 ff.). The distinction of each of these ages will also be set out and displayed in the third book of this work, and its completed structure will be recognized in its proper divisions.

Therefore, the years counted from the beginning of the world do not promise through the Law or the Prophets that Christ would be born. Rather, clearer testimonies foreshadow that the event would occur which is now celebrated among us as having already passed.

Let us, then, also set aside for a little while the calculations that the patriarchs and prophets themselves did not use to determine the birth of Christ. Let us use only the testimonies by which the things that you believe are still future may be shown already to have occurred, and to have been completely fulfilled since the time of Christ’s first coming. They must no longer be awaited, because they have already passed.

Nor is it now necessary for me to gather the divine testimonies concerning Christ’s birth, death, and resurrection; many have already done this abundantly and sufficiently. I need only select and briefly present those that can show by manifest indications that Christ, the Son of God, has already come in the flesh.

7. First, therefore, I shall investigate the very signs of the times of Christ’s birth and shall proceed in orderly fashion to ask whether those times were as peaceful as the prophets foretold.

In the days of his birth, as the prophet David says, “Justice shall arise in his days, and an abundance of peace” (Psalm 71:7). Likewise, Micah, indicating both the name and the time of his birth, says:

“And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are you indeed little among the thousands of Judah? From you there shall come forth for me one who is to rule in Israel, whose coming forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity. Therefore he shall give them up until the time when she who is in labor shall give birth. The remnant of his brothers shall be converted to the children of Israel. And he shall stand and feed them in the strength of the Lord, in the majesty of the name of his God. And they shall be converted, for then he shall be magnified even to the ends of the earth, and this shall be his name’s peace” (Micah 5:2 ff.).

Let the peace of the time of his birth also be proclaimed. For how peaceful those same times were, the same prophet clearly explains shortly above, where he foretells that all wars would cease at the time when Christ ought to be born. He says:

“In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, exalted above the hills; and all peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall hasten and say: Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths. For the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many peoples and rebuke strong nations even from afar. And they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not take up sword against nation, nor shall they learn war any longer” (Micah 4:1 ff.).

Isaiah, also indicating these same signs concerning the time of Christ’s birth, says:

“In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, and let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord [Al.: “to the mountain of the Lord”] and to the house of the God of Jacob. And he shall teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths. For the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge the nations and rebuke many peoples even from afar, and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they train for battle any longer” (Isaiah 2:2 ff.).

8. Do you not now see how the oracles of these three prophets agree in every respect, as though they had been spoken by the mouth of one man? For no peace is perceived as long as wars are being waged. Once wars have been removed, what remains except an abundance of peace?

Therefore, what David says—“Justice shall arise in his days, and an abundance of peace”—Isaiah and Micah expressed concerning the wars that would cease in his days: “Nation shall not lift up sword against nation.”

When wars ceased throughout the whole world, Christ, our peace, arose. To recognize that this truly happened, if you please, examine the ancient histories of the individual nations. You will find that, up to the twenty-eighth year of Caesar Augustus—Christ was born in Judea in his forty-first year—there was discord throughout the whole world, and that individual nations burned with eagerness to wage war against neighboring peoples, so that they killed and were killed.

But when the Lord and Savior arose, when under the governor of Syria, Quirinius, the first registration was made throughout the world (Luke 2:2), and peace through the teaching of the Gospel was prepared for the Roman Empire, then all wars ceased. People were no longer trained for battle through towns and villages; rather, they were devoted to the cultivation of the fields, while only the Roman soldiers and legions were assigned the task of waging war against barbarian nations. Then that angelic chorus was fulfilled:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

In this way, justice arose in his days, and an abundance of peace. Behold the signs of the times of Christ’s birth: just as the prophets foretold that they would be peaceful, so we know that they were peaceful—but that they have already passed.

They have therefore already been fulfilled. We must not continue to believe that peaceful times are still future, since this age will close with an end characterized by wars rather than peace. The Lord said this to his disciples when they asked him for a sign of the consummation of the age:

“Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom” (Matthew 24:7), together with the other things that follow.

9. Since we have spoken first about the signs of peaceful times, let us now speak again about the last days in which the coming of the Lord and Savior was foretold as imminent.

Behold, the peaceful times of Christ’s birth were foretold by the two prophets, Micah and Isaiah; but both said that these things would occur in the last days. Why, I ask, do they indicate that these very signs of the time of Christ’s first coming would occur in the last days, yet did not attempt to disclose the mystery of so great an event through years counted from the beginning of the world? Unless, as I judge according to the weakness of my understanding, they thought it better to understand those last days as belonging to the decline of the Israelite kingdom, when the leader and prince from the tribe of Judah had failed, rather than to establish them by a calculation of years.

For if they had said, for example, “From the beginning of the world to Christ’s coming there will be so many years,” it would not sufficiently appear that anything there was to be considered “last,” since many years would still remain—namely, until the end of the world.

But because they said that the very things they had foretold concerning Christ would be fulfilled in the last days, I believe they understood those last days to be the ones that were recognized as the final days of that kingdom, when the princes from the tribe of Judah had failed. At that time, a foreigner, Herod, first succeeded to the kingship among that people, and during his reign Christ is known to have been born in Judea.

### 10

Although the “last days” may also be understood otherwise, as referring to the sixth age, which is the final age for every human being, they called these days “last,” but peaceful—days in which Christ ought to be born—which Micah foretold and Isaiah likewise announced, lest, according to your error, they should still be awaited as future. Jacob the patriarch disclosed the sign of these same days when, calling his sons to him, he likewise called those days “last” and said:

> “Gather yourselves together, that I may announce to you what will happen to you in the last days. Gather yourselves together and hear, sons of Jacob; hear Israel your father” (Gen. 49:1–2).

There also, concerning Judah, from whose seed Christ arose, he says:

> “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (ibid., 10).

Behold, it is manifest and clear that these “last days” are understood as already past, and not yet future, when the following is expressed:

> “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved.”

Behold the evident sign of the last days: when rulers or leaders from the stock of Judah ceased, the foreign king Herod succeeded to the throne, and Christ was born in Judea during his reign. These three men, filled with the divine Spirit, as though speaking with one mouth, foretold those last days in which they saw in the Spirit that this great mystery had to be fulfilled.

### 11

We have shown two signs by which we demonstrated that both the peaceful times and the last days had arrived at the time of Christ’s birth—as though we were saying that peace had arisen in the last days. Now, in the third place, it follows that we speak of the testimony of the forerunner, through which the herald’s voice disclosed the Judge’s coming.

For Malachi, almost the last prophet of the people of Israel, clearly foretold not only the sign of Christ’s birth but also that of his forerunner. He says:

> “Behold, I shall send my angel, and he will prepare the way before your face; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. 3:1).

You indeed accept this testimony as having been spoken about Elijah; we believe that it was prophesied about John, since Christ the Lord and our teacher both spoke and interpreted this very passage. Wishing it to be understood of the forerunner John, he said:

> “This is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Matt. 11:10).

Thus John came six months before Christ’s advent and pointed out with his finger the Lord himself, present in the flesh, saying:

> “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).

John bore witness to his Lord, and the voice to the Word. By bearing testimony in water, he made known that the Savior’s presence in the flesh had arrived.

The figure of this man was represented by that Iras the Adullamite whom we read about in Genesis (38:12), who came with Judah to Thamnah to shear the sheep. For Judah here signifies Christ himself, since we believe that Christ’s flesh was propagated from the stock of Judah. His shepherd, Iras the Adullamite, whose name means “testimony in water,” signifies John.

The Lord plainly came with this testimony. He possessed testimony greater than John’s, yet he used this testimony in water for the sake of the weak sheep. For Iras—the name of that shepherd—is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.” John indeed saw his brother, namely Christ, his brother according to the seed of Abraham, when he greeted him from the womb (Luke 1:41), and recognized him more perfectly from the dove. Therefore, as an Adullamite, he bore true testimony in water (John 1:32–33).

### 12

We have said that Christ was then signified through the person of Judah, and that John’s person was signified through Iras the Adullamite. The meaning of these two persons is also declared by the prophecy of the prophet Malachi, which expounds what was prophesied about Christ and John.

> “Behold,” he says, “I shall send my angel, and he will prepare the way before your face; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. 3:1, cited above).

Now consider, if you can, how he is said to be about to come suddenly to his temple, if his coming is determined by a calculation of years fixed from the beginning of the world. What occurs after a fixed number of years does not come suddenly.

But because you think that this testimony was spoken about the prophet Elijah, and because you refer the following words—“The ruler whom you seek will come to his temple”—to your Christ, whom you think will come at the end of time, I am greatly surprised that the outcome of events does not teach you the truth.

In what kind of temple of his will the ruler come, when that temple has been destroyed down to its foundations? Or, if it must be rebuilt by someone else before Christ comes, what more will your Christ have to do if everything has already been restored by another?

If, as you wish, you understand Elijah in this passage, where you hear only an angel announced, why, in the place where the same prophet foretold the time of Christ’s first coming, did he not express the name of that angel and instead conceal the name of Elijah? For the prophet who expressed Elijah’s name at the end of his prophecy because of the end of the age ought not to have been silent about Elijah’s name in the place where he merely named an angel.

For where he foretold that Elijah would come before the end of the world, he says:

> “Behold, I shall send you Elijah the prophet, the Tishbite, before the coming of the great and terrible day of the Lord, to turn the hearts of the fathers toward the sons, and the hearts of the sons toward their fathers” (Mal. 4:5–6).

Before the coming of judgment, therefore, the Lord will send Elijah to turn the hearts of the sons toward the hearts of the patriarchs and prophets, so that their descendants may believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, whom the patriarchs and prophets awaited in their prophecies.

For if the Jews still believe rightly at the present time, why does the last prophet testify that they are to be converted through Elijah? They cannot now understand the Savior whom they hear until the end of the world, when the consummation of the ages has come.

The Lord declares this through the prophet Isaiah, saying:

> “Hear, hearing, and do not understand; see the vision, and do not know. Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy and their eyes blind, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them.”

And the prophet said:

> “How long, Lord?”

And the Lord said:

> “Until the cities are made desolate, without an inhabitant, and the houses without a human being, and the land is left desolate. And the Lord will remove human beings far away. Then it will be converted, and it will be like a terebinth and like an oak that spreads its branches; the holy seed will be what remains in it” (Isa. 6:9–13).

Recognize, then, that this time of your blindness extends until the end of the world, during which you do not acknowledge the Savior. Unless you believe in Christ before Elijah comes, all of you will perish in this blindness before he arrives.

And if perhaps some from your descendants are to be saved when Elijah comes, you nevertheless, who now exist before his coming, will be confined by the grief due to death and will perish after death in everlasting punishment and torment.

### 13

There follows the fourth and most certain indication of Christ’s birth, by which the calling of the nations is commended. Through this calling Christ is proved to have been born long ago, so that he himself may be commended as the expectation of the nations.

For immediately after Christ was born, the first fruits of the nations were consecrated to the Lord, as is sufficiently and clearly shown by the mystical gifts of the Magi who came from the East (Matt. 2:1–11). Thus this too had been prophesied:

> “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents. And all the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him. And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him” (Ps. 71:10–11, 17).

Since you see that this has already been fulfilled in our Christ, it may perhaps not be necessary to set before you very many testimonies on this subject.

For once Christ had been born, he immediately received the nations as an inheritance from God the Father. David had foretold this long beforehand when he said in the person of that same Christ:

> “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:7–8).

Isaiah develops this most evident sign of the nations that would believe:

> “He will sprinkle many nations, and kings will shut their mouths because of him” (Isa. 52:15).

Again, explaining the same matter concerning Christ, he says:

> “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the nations” (Isa. 55:4).

The same prophet continues:

> “The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God” (Isa. 52:10).

If, as you say, Christ has not yet come, how do you already see him revealed in the sight of the nations? David also says:

> “The Lord has made his salvation known; he has revealed his justice in the sight of the nations” (Ps. 97:2).

Since there is one gathering of all the nations in Christ, you ought to know that what was foretold by the prophetic oracle has already been fulfilled:

> “In gathering the peoples together as one, and the kings, that they may serve the Lord” (Ps. 101:23).

How, then, do all the kings and peoples of the earth now obey him, if his birth did not precede this, and if this glorious birth of his did not provide the occasion for believing?

For it is written:

> “He who will arise to rule the nations—in him the nations will hope” (Isa. 11:10, according to the Apostle in Rom. 15:12).

Therefore, by being born or appearing, he first arose into the world, and thus the nations began to hope in him.

The same prophet further explains:

> “The root of Jesse, which stands as a sign for the peoples: the nations will entreat him, and his tomb will be glorious” (Isa. 11:10).

Behold, his glorious tomb already exists, yet his birth is not believed.

### 14

There follows thereafter the fifth manifest sign in every respect, by which his dominion is extended throughout the whole world. This too had been prophesied through David:

> “He will rule from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the world” (Ps. 71:8).

It is proved that this testimony applies to none of the kings of that people, for it is known within what boundaries that kingdom was confined.

But we see this fulfilled in Christ, whose great name is worshiped by the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting. His worship and adoration now extend not only through Judea but throughout the entire world.

The prophet Zephaniah had also foretold this when, foreseeing in the Spirit the time of the Christian religion, he said:

> “A man shall worship him from his place, all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. 2:11).

And shortly afterward:

> “I will transform the language and lineage of the peoples, so that they may all call upon the name of the Lord and serve him under one yoke” (Zeph. 3:9).

But perhaps someone may be seen shamelessly to object and say that not yet have all nations believed in Christ.

The answer is easily given: even if unbelieving peoples still exist in certain places, they do not thereby entirely escape Christ’s dominion, since they are oppressed by rulers in whose hearts Christ himself is already recognized as dwelling through faith.

Nor do I think that any nation remains that is ignorant of Christ’s name. Even if it has had no preacher, it cannot be unaware of the reputation of the faith among neighboring nations.

Having given this explanation, I ask you to answer: In what corner of the earth can the one whom you still await be born and rule, when our Christ has filled the entire world with his dominion—so completely that even the demons, which seem to lack his bodily presence, are subject to him?

But why should I delay any longer? If, I say, you do not yet believe that Christ has been born, gather the evidence from the four other signs that follow: the humiliation of your strength; the punishment that befell you after Christ’s death and resurrection; the loss of your kingdom and priesthood; and the rejection of your sacrifice.

### 15

Concerning your humiliation, by which you could be confounded after Christ’s death and resurrection, the prophet Isaiah foretold:

> “Jacob shall no longer be confounded, and his face shall no longer blush; but when he sees his children, the work of my hands, sanctifying my name in his midst” (Isa. 29:23).

Observe the time and mark the mystery: Jacob is said now to be confounded, whereas previously he was not confounded.

These days, therefore, are already passing after Christ’s coming, in which your fathers were oppressed by profound humiliation, when they saw their children—that is, the apostles and apostolic men who came from the Jewish people—performing mighty works in the midst of the nations of the Lord and preaching Christ’s name among the Gentiles.

For before Christ’s coming, Israel did not confess concerning the faith of the nations. But after Christ appeared in the flesh, and after the multitude of the nations believed in the Son of God through the preaching of the apostles, then Israel, confounded and blinded, was struck with astonishment.

Would that this humiliation were an occasion of salvation for you, rather than the grief by which you gnash your teeth within yourselves when you see Christ’s kingdom expanding in this way!

### 16

It remains now that we speak of the punishment that befell you after Christ’s death and resurrection because you fastened him to the cross.

Thus, through the prophet Hosea, the Lord himself cries out concerning this:

> “Woe to them, for they have departed from me; they shall be devastated, because they have transgressed against me. I redeemed them, and they spoke lies against me” (Hos. 7:13).

Later it is added:

> “My God has rejected them, because they did not listen to him; and they shall be wanderers among the nations” (Hos. 9:17).

Isaiah also clearly develops this. After he had said of Christ:

> “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter,”

he immediately added:

> “Because of the crime of my people I struck him, and I will give the impious for his burial, and the rich for his death” (Isa. 53:8–9).

Jeremiah likewise says:

> “Climb upon its walls and destroy them; remove its branches, for they are not the Lord’s. For it has utterly transgressed in the midst of the house of Judah, says the Lord; they denied me and said: ‘He is not the one’” (Jer. 5:10).

Behold, see how far in advance the blasphemy of your mouth was foretold.

For this is precisely the cause you now pursue when you say that Christ has not yet come, evidently awaiting another—namely, the Antichrist.

The psalmist also develops this in the person of Christ, saying:

> “But you, Lord, have mercy on me, and raise me up, that I may repay them” (Ps. 40:11).

Who could now deny this, seeing that after Christ’s death and resurrection the Jews were uprooted from their dwelling places by war and slaughter and utterly destroyed?

He was killed by them, rose to glory, and meanwhile repaid them with temporal discipline.

### 17

After this it follows that we speak of the kingdom, priesthood, and sacrifice of the Jews, which clearly ceased when Christ our Holy of Holies appeared in the world.

Although these matters are expressed with evident indications in Daniel’s prophecy and will have to be set out in their proper order, the points presently at hand must not be omitted.

We must therefore proceed to the very manifestation of the times, when the sacrifice according to Aaron had to cease and Christ’s sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek had to begin to be celebrated.

Concerning these days—namely, the loss of the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews—the prophet Hosea foretells:

> “For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without priesthood, and without manifestations” (Hos. 3:4).

Who does not see that all this has already been fulfilled in you in the very manner foretold by the prophet, as is also demonstrated by the actual consequences of events?

This too is gathered as having been clearly prophesied in the Book of Kings. For it is written:

> “A man of God came to Eli and said to him: ‘Behold, days are coming, and I will destroy your seed and the seed of your father, and there will be no elder for you in my house all your days. And I will destroy your man from my altar, so that his eyes may fail and his soul may melt away’” (1 Kings 2:27, 31 ff.).

Behold, the days that were foretold have already come, and there is no priest according to the order of Aaron.

And whoever is a man of his lineage, when he sees the sacrifice of Christians prevailing throughout the whole world while that great honor has been taken away from him, his eyes fail from the decay of grief and the pressure of bitterness (St. Augustine, *The City of God*, book 17, chapter 5).

Concerning this rejection of the former sacrifice, Malachi, showing a clear indication of the Christian faith and of your rejection, says:

> “I have no desire for you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is offered to my name; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord” (Mal. 1:10–11).

It is therefore now manifest that the rejection of the former sacrifice occurred from the time when Christ’s great name began to exist among the nations.

Even if you pass over all these things with deaf ears and minds, the events themselves stand before you. They are thrust upon your eyes, even against your will; they teach and convict you alike that what you seem to hope will be future must already be regarded as past.

### 18

There remain now the mystical signs of two patriarchs, expressed in the blessings of their sons, and that final prophecy of Daniel, concluded with the completion of the weeks. These indicate that the time of Christ’s birth has passed (Dan. 9), so clearly that no human cunning can oppose them.

If, then, we seek Christ’s flesh in the seed of Abraham, let us seek the mystical blessings in Abraham’s offspring.

Isaac, the son of Abraham, blessing his son Jacob, said:

> “May he give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth an abundance of grain and wine. And may nations serve you, and princes worship you; be lord of your brother, and may the sons of your father worship you” (Gen. 27:28–29).

This blessing of Jacob is the preaching of Christ. This is done and accomplished among all nations. The nations serve him; kings worship him. The sons of his father worship him—that is, the sons of Abraham according to faith—because Christ himself is also the son of Abraham according to the flesh (Augustine, *The City of God*, book 16, chapter 37).

Behold, Jacob, blessed with this mystical blessing of his father, also blessed Judah, the son born from him, from whose tribe Christ descended according to the flesh, from the seed of David.

> “Judah,” he says, “your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be upon the backs of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the sprout, my son, you have ascended. Reclining, you slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub; who will rouse him? A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations. Binding his colt to the vine, and the colt of his she-ass to the vine-shoot, he shall wash his robe in wine and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Gen. 49:8 ff.).

Judge and consider all these things: have they not already been completed in Christ with the clearest light?

Do not his brothers—the apostles and all his fellow heirs—praise him, seeking not their own glory but his?

Are his hands not upon the backs of his enemies? Are those who still oppose him not pressed down and bent toward the earth as the Christian peoples increase—as is still happening?

Have not the sons of Jacob worshiped him in the remnant that has come into being through the election of grace?

Is he not the lion’s cub, who became small by being born?

Did he not ascend the cross reclining, when, with his head bowed, he gave up his spirit?

Did he not sleep like a lion, because in death itself he was not conquered but conquered?

Did not the one whom no human being has seen, nor can see, raise him from the dead (John 1:18; 1 Tim. 6:16)?

For in the words “Who will rouse him?” the indication of one unknown is sufficiently expressed (from the same Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 12, chapter 42).

### 19

If you say that all these things will take place in future times and have not yet happened, see how the prophetic speech that follows dissolves this entire mistaken suspicion of yours and proves it false.

It continues:

> “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.”

The prophetic speech specifically described the time to which all these things ought to be referred. I believe that the patriarch foresaw in the Spirit these clouds of your error and foolish arguments, by which you could say—as you do say—that Christ must still be hoped for by us and that he has not yet been born, although he will be the expectation of the nations.

For this reason he foretold a specific and evident time in which Christ ought to be born: when the ruler from Judah had failed, then the glorious birth of Christ would be recognized.

For he says:

> “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.”

Christ had already come when the leader and ruler from Judah failed.

Return, therefore, to your trustworthy histories, and you will prove that this people never lacked a leader or ruler from Judah until they came to a foreign king, during whose reign Christ was born from a virgin.

### 20

But lest I appear to pursue these matters fancifully and without truth, I shall also arrange the leaders and rulers themselves in order, so that it may plainly be clear whether the succession of his lineage ever faltered from the loins of Judah, or whether there was ever a break in the series of rulers before the time of the Lord’s birth arrived.

To pass over earlier times, I shall begin counting these rulers only from the time when, after the people returned from the time of Cyrus, they began to rebuild the Temple in Judea, and continue up to Christ’s birth.

Eusebius records that they governed this people in the following order (*Demonstration of the Gospel*, book 8, demonstration 2):

> “The first to govern after Daniel’s prophecy, after the people had returned from Babylon, were Jesus son of Josedec and Zerubbabel son of Salathiel. After them, Joachin son of Jesus succeeded to the high priesthood; after him came Heli, after Heli Joaida, then John, afterward Jadus, and after him Aonias. Then Eleazar was high priest over the Jews; after him came another Aonias, then Simon, whom Aonias succeeded in the high priesthood; then Judas Maccabaeus, whom his brother Jonathan succeeded; after Jonathan, Simon, the brother of both, succeeded; then John, after whom came Aristobulus. Alexander succeeded him, and he was both king and high priest. After him, Alexandra, his wife, ruled the people with her sons Hyrcanus and Aristobulus.

> “At that time Herod, son of Antipater the Ascalonite and of his Arabian mother Cypros, killed Hyrcanus, received the kingdom of the Jews by decree of the senate, and was himself the first foreigner to rule over the Jews. During his reign Christ is recognized as having been born in Judea, when this same glorious birth of his was announced to the Hebrew shepherds by an angelic voice.”

### 21

You now know that Jacob’s prophecy has been fulfilled, and you are utterly unable to find an answer to give in the face of such a clear manifestation of events.

Or perhaps, persisting in the shameless obstinacy of your brow, you object—as your parents habitually put forward in their lies—that there is today some king of the race of Judah who appears to hold a kingdom in the remotest regions of the East?

In their blindness of mind they do not notice how greatly the falsehood of their pretense is exposed by this fact: just as no altar and no sacrifice remain, so no high priest and no priest remain among the Jews.

For the prophet Hosea cannot be a liar when he says:

> “The children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without priesthood, and without manifestations” (Hos. 3:4).

Who does not see that all these things have now been fulfilled in you?

Now, if you examine that passage in the prophet Daniel which the Lord mentioned through his angel, saying:

> “When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, let the reader understand” (Dan. 9:27),

and if, therefore, the number is also pursued by calculating the periods of the weeks, not only Christ but also the time at which he ought to come to his passion will be found—although even without a calculation of years this is declared by the manifest consequences of events.

For the moment, however, leaving aside the number of the weeks themselves, I shall first prove Christ’s coming and birth through the revelations concerning kingdoms, in accordance with Daniel’s own prophecy.

Interpreting the dream that King Nebuchadnezzar had seen concerning the statue, Daniel says:

> “You are the head of gold, O king” (Dan. 2:38–39 ff.).

By this the first kingdom, the Babylonian kingdom, is shown to have been compared with the most precious gold.

> “And after you another kingdom shall arise, inferior to you,” namely, that of the Medes and Persians, which has the likeness of silver.

> “And a third kingdom, another, of bronze,” which ruled the whole earth—signifying Alexander, the kingdom of the Macedonians, and Alexander’s successors.

The fourth kingdom, which plainly pertains to the Romans, is of iron, which crushes and subdues everything. But its feet and toes are partly iron and partly clay; this is most clearly confirmed in the present age.

For just as at the beginning nothing was stronger or harder than the Roman Empire, so at the end of events nothing is weaker, since in civil wars and against various nations it appears to need the aid of other peoples and barbarians.

Observe now what this prophet says:

> “At the end of all these kingdoms—the kingdoms of gold, silver, bronze, and iron—God of heaven will raise up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, and its kingdom shall not be handed over to another people. It shall crush and consume all these kingdoms, and it itself shall stand forever.”

This is plainly Christ’s kingdom, which was made manifest to the world during the reign of the emperor Octavian and which will certainly be eternal without end.

### 22

Yet, so that no one may regard this as doubtful, the calculation is also expressed by a number of years through the seventy weeks.

But observe now that the number of years in the weeks which Daniel understood to extend to Christ is not taken from the beginning of the world; rather, it extends from his own time to Christ’s birth.

This would have been said in vain if it had already been foretold somewhere in Scripture—namely, if an evident knowledge of Christ’s birth had been disclosed by calculating from the beginning of the world to Christ.

What need would there have been for Daniel’s prophecy to express the future times up to Christ by a calculation of years, if a clear passage of Scripture had already disclosed this by taking the calculation of years from the beginning of the world?

Tell me, then, why the preceding periods were not sought through calculations of years, when the angel foretold these future things and Daniel understood them most clearly.

Observe and understand that one and the same time concerning Christ’s birth, which the patriarch Jacob foretold through the succession of leaders and rulers from the loins of Judah, was also confirmed by the prophet Daniel through the clearest calculation of years.

To the extent that Jacob extended his prophecy concerning Christ, Daniel likewise made known both the prophecy and the number.

Jacob’s patriarchal blessing and Daniel’s calculation of years agree with such great clarity that they have no disagreement even with the histories of the nations—provided that each person carefully considers which patriarch appears to have been contemporary with which king of the world.

### 23

For it is clear that Abraham was born in the time of Ninus. When Ninus, reigning over Assyria, was in the forty-third year of his rule, Abraham is shown to have been born.

Similarly, Jacob is found to have lived in the time of Inachus, who is said to have been the first king to rule at Argos.

Moses, who is shown to be the author of this prophecy in which Jacob is reported to have said, “A ruler shall not fail from Judah” (Gen. 49:10), lived, I say, as a contemporary of Cecrops, who was the first king of the Athenians.

Thus, among the books of the translators known as the Seventy and the histories of the nations, a harmonious calculation of years will be found.

By this agreement with the histories of the nations, the Seventy Translators show one and the same end of the period. They preserve it truthfully up to Herod as the chronological limit marked by Jacob in his prophecy and expressed by Daniel when the mystery of the weeks was revealed to him.

Therefore, the years which you think must be extracted from the books of the Hebrews from the beginning of the world for the birth of Christ must be rejected; they are not necessary. Jacob was silent about them, the angel did not foretell them, Daniel himself did not choose to calculate them.

Only those years must be counted which the angel taught under the announcement of the seventy weeks.

For the angel says:

> “Attend to the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks have been shortened for your people and for your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may come to an end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Dan. 9:23–24).

### 24

Eusebius explains how the number of years in the seventy weeks of the prophecy appears to agree with the prophecy concerning Christ foretold by Jacob in the *Chronicle*. He begins calculating these same weeks from the sixty-fifth to the one hundred eighty-sixth Olympiad—that is, from the restoration of the Temple, or the time of Darius, to the death of Hyrcanus the high priest, when the priesthood from the loins of Judah ceased and the foreign king Herod succeeded, during whose reign Christ was born in Judea.

Thus the same historian, after recounting the years of Hyrcanus the high priest, continues:

> “Herod, son of Antipater the Ascalonite and of his Arabian mother Cypros, received from the Romans the chief authority over the Jews. During his reign, when Christ’s birth was near, the kingdom and priesthood of Judah, which had previously been held through the succession of the ancestors, were destroyed. The prophecy was fulfilled which speaks through Moses as follows: ‘A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations’ (Gen. 49:10).

> “At this point Christ also, whom the writing of Daniel foretells, reaches his limit. For until Herod, the *christi*—that is, the priests—were kings of the Jews. They began to rule from the sixty-fifth Olympiad, and from the restoration of the Temple under Darius until Hyrcanus and the one hundred eighty-sixth Olympiad, with 483 years having elapsed in between. Daniel also signifies these years when he says: ‘And you shall know and understand: from the beginning of the word to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until the rule of Christ, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks’ (Dan. 9:25).

> “These sixty-nine weeks make 483 years, during which the *christi*—that is, the priests, consecrated through anointing—ruled until Hyrcanus. When the last of all these had been captured by the Parthians, Herod, son of Antipater, received from Augustus and the senate Judea, which had no connection with him; and his sons ruled after him until the final captivity of Jerusalem, with high priests no longer being appointed from the succession of the priestly lineage.”

### 25

I have placed these passages here word for word in order to prove in every respect that Jacob’s prophecy and the number of the weeks in Daniel agree.

For Jacob the patriarch marked the same end of the period up to Christ which Daniel’s prophecy expressed in a calculation of years.

No one should be troubled by the fact that the seventieth week is not counted together with the sixty-nine weeks, since the truth of the matter foretold is shown to have been fulfilled within it below.

Now, in the sacred writings, one week is understood as seven years, as the Lord says to Moses:

> “You shall count seven weeks of years” (Deut. 16:9),

that is, seven times seven, which amounts to forty-nine years.

Therefore, seventy weeks make 490 years; for seventy times seven is 490 years.

Some begin calculating these seventy weeks from the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes, when it was the fourth year of the eighty-third Olympiad, and extend the number of the aforesaid weeks to the second year of the two hundred and second Olympiad, the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar.

They wish to demonstrate that within the number of those same weeks Christ was born and that he suffered at the end of the seventieth week, as the distinguished chronographer Africanus reports (Eusebius, cited above).

26. But others have taught that sixty-two and a half weeks elapsed from the first year of Darius, when Daniel also saw this vision [Col. 0556D], until the coming of Christ, because they are shown to be divided in this way in Daniel’s prophecy itself. They determine that the remaining seven and a half weeks were completed in Christ’s passion and in the overthrow of the Jews, by which they were conquered through Vespasian—following, as they do, a different order of kings and reckoning of years from that followed by those whom we mentioned earlier. As Tertullian prefaces in the book he wrote against the Jews, whose words must now be briefly set forth. For he says (Against the Jews, fol. 46, Paris edition, 1545):

“From where, then, do we show that Christ came within sixty-two and a half weeks? Let us count from the first year of Darius, since at that time the vision is shown to Daniel, which says to him: ‘Understand the prophecies of this utterance’ (Dan. IX, 25). Therefore we ought to begin counting from the first year of Darius, when Daniel saw this vision. Let us see, then, how the years are fulfilled up to the coming of Christ.

“Darius reigned nineteen years; Artaxerxes, forty. Ochus, who was also called Cyrus, twenty-four. Argus, one year. Another Darius, who was also called Melas, twenty-one years. Alexander the Macedonian, ten years. After Alexander, who had ruled in Media and Persia, which he had conquered, and had established his kingdom in Alexandria, naming that city after himself, Soter reigned there in Alexandria for thirty-five years. He was succeeded by Philadelphus, who reigned thirty-nine years. After him Esethehac reigned twenty-five years. Then Philopator, twenty-four years. Again another Esethehac, twenty-seven years. Soter, thirty-eight years. Ptolemy, thirty-seven years. Cleopatra, twenty years and five months. Again Cleopatra ruled jointly with Augustus for thirteen years. After Cleopatra, Augustus ruled for another forty-three years. For all the years of Augustus’s reign amounted to fifty-five.

“We see, then, that in the forty-first year of Augustus’s reign—that is, of the reign he held after Cleopatra’s death—Christ was born. That same Augustus survived from the time Christ was born for fifteen years. Thus, on the day of Christ’s birth, the remaining period amounts to four hundred and thirty-seven years and ten months, up to the forty-first year after Cleopatra’s death; hence sixty-two and a half weeks are completed, which amount to four hundred and thirty-seven years and six months on the day of Christ’s birth. Eternal righteousness was brought to completion, and the Holy of Holies was anointed—that is, Christ; the vision and prophecy were sealed; and sins were forgiven, sins which are remitted to all who believe in him through faith in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“But what does he mean by saying that the vision and prophecy are sealed? All the prophets announced concerning him that he would come and that he would have to suffer. Therefore, since the prophecy was fulfilled through his coming, he said that the vision and prophecy were sealed, because he himself is the seal of all the prophets, fulfilling everything that the prophets had previously announced concerning him. After his coming and passion there is no longer either vision or prophet who announces that Christ is to come.”

And a little later:

“Let us see how the other seven and a half weeks, which are divided off in the cutting away of the earlier weeks, were fulfilled in action. For after Augustus, who survived fifteen years after Christ’s birth, Tiberius Caesar succeeded him and held the empire for twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. In the fifteenth year of his reign Christ suffers. Then Gaius Caesar, also called Caligula, for three years, eight months, and thirteen days. Nero, for nine years and thirteen days. Galba, seven months and twenty-eight days. In the first year of his reign Vespasian subdued the Jews, and the total comes to fifty-two years and six months. For he reigned eleven years. And thus, on the day of their overthrow, the Jews fulfilled the seventy weeks foretold by Daniel.”

27. Attend, then, with greater diligence, and see that if you wish to count these seventy weeks according to Eusebius from the sixty-fifth to the one hundred and eighty-sixth Olympiad, you will find that after four hundred and eighty-three years the priesthood from the tribe of Judah ceased when Hyrcanus died, and that Herod, a foreign king, succeeded him; it was during Herod’s time that Christ our Lord was born.

But if you wish to reckon these same weeks according to Tertullian, you will see that in their course Christ’s birth, his passion, and the destruction of Jerusalem were completed, just as the prophet foretold. For when the angel foretold this number of weeks to Daniel, he also taught him that the Holy of Holies would be anointed, signified Christ’s very death, and did not conceal the destruction of the Jewish nation. For the angel said to Daniel:

“Daniel, I have now come forth to teach you and to make you understand. At the beginning of your prayers the word went forth; and I have come to declare to you that you are a man of desires. Therefore observe the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks are determined for your people and your holy city, so that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may come to an end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed.

“Know, therefore, and understand: from the going forth of the word to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until Christ the prince, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. And again the street shall be built, and the walls, in the distress of the times. And after the sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed; and the people with the coming prince shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end shall be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed” (Dan. IX, 22 ff.).

Behold how, after the angel foretold Christ’s killing, he announced that all these things would follow. Did all these events not happen after the Savior’s death to that city and its inhabitants? For after they cried out against the Son of God that he should be killed, vengeance from the Lord followed them after some time. A Roman army came with its commander Vespasian; the city was subdued, the Jews were conquered, and many thousands were killed. No Jew is now permitted to approach that place where they cried out for Christ to be crucified.

I say that these things happened to the Jews because of Christ, as the meaning of the Scriptures agrees with the outcome of events and the order of the times. Or, if Christ has not yet come, on whose account were they foretold as destined to suffer these things? Will they suffer them when he comes? And where now is the daughter of Zion who is to be left behind, when today she does not exist (Isa. I, 8)? Where are the cities destined to be burned, when they lie in ruins? Where is the dispersion of the nation, which is already exiled? Restore the condition of Judea as Christ would find it, and contend that another has come.

Or, if I am lying, say: Where is your kingdom? Where is your temple? Where is your priesthood? Where is your sanctuary? Where is the assembly of the prophets? Surely all these things have utterly failed, since the sacrifice has ceased, the priest has been cut off, and the former anointing has failed. If, therefore, with all these things having ceased, the anointing itself has ceased, from where will your Christ be anointed when he comes? For the Law prescribed that, in captivity, it was not permitted to prepare the royal anointing oil. From where, then, will he who is to be born in Bethlehem be anointed, or how does he proceed from Bethlehem, when absolutely no one from the offspring of Israel is in Bethlehem?

For we see that no one of Israelite descent has remained in the city of Bethlehem since it was forbidden that any Jew should remain within the borders of that region, so that what had been spoken through the prophet might also be fulfilled: “Your land is deserted, your cities are burned with fire” (which happened to them in the time of war); “foreigners shall consume your region in your presence” (Isa. I, 7).

28. What do you now answer to these things, madmen, blinded by God’s hidden justice? Where is that promised land in which you sinned while dwelling there, and from which, after it was destroyed, you departed? Do you seek the kingdom of the Jews? It does not exist. Do you seek the sacrifice of the Jews? It does not exist. Do you seek the priesthood of the Jews? It does not exist (from Augustine, Sermon 2 on Psalm 88, no. 7).

Daniel foretold that all these things would cease when he clearly prophesied that the Holy of Holies would be anointed (Dan. IX, 24). Since, therefore, you now see that all these things have been fulfilled in you, you show yourselves liars concerning Christ’s future birth by the clear evidence of your own words.

Behold, you have already been convicted by a very few testimonies that we have introduced, but they are exceedingly strong and distinguished. There are indeed many other things expressed in the divine books, but I cannot mention them all, because that would be excessive, nor many of them, because it would be lengthy. We have collected only a very small number, merely to open the way to this understanding.

And yet, among the things that have been said, whether those that can still be said from the divine books, nowhere will it be found foretold that, by calculating the years from the beginning of the world, the time of the Lord’s incarnation should be recognized. Accordingly, by this argument the shortness of the years alleged from the Hebrew codices will be disregarded as a means of determining the rule of this mystery.

Now, as we proceed to the suitable witnesses and ministers of the New Testament, let us close this book with its proper conclusion.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0559]

1. Having brought forward and set before us the patriarchs and prophets, through whose preaching we learned that Christ was born at the time when they had also declared that he would be born, and at which time we now believe that he was born, I shall now follow the times of the New Testament and inquire more carefully how they began through the announcement of an angel.

Certainly Daniel learned through an angel that mystery of the seventy weeks concerning Christ’s birth (Dan. IX, 21 ff.). Similarly, Zechariah heard from an angel who appeared to him that John, his son, was to be begotten by him (Luke I, 11 ff.). And Mary both believed and consented to the angel who announced to her that Christ was to be born from her. We see these three things, spoken and fulfilled through an angel.

It must now be carefully considered whether this angel who appeared to Zechariah and Mary also foretold those things to Daniel himself. Indeed, Daniel himself, in the book of his prophecy, when he learned through an angel that those mysteries of the weeks concerning Christ’s future birth would occur, clearly expressed the name of that angel himself. For he says:

“Behold, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen at the beginning, came swiftly flying, touched me, and said: Daniel, observe the word” (Dan., as cited above), followed by the other things mentioned there.

Likewise, in these times the remarkable name of that angel is found expressed according to the Gospel. For the same angel said to Zechariah: “I am Gabriel, who stand before God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to announce these good things to you” (Luke I, 19).

The same Gospel also says this concerning the birth of the blessed Virgin Mary: “The angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee whose name was Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph; and the virgin’s name was Mary” (ibid., 26).

2. It is now clear, therefore, that it was one and the same angel, Gabriel, who both disclosed to Daniel those predetermined times concerning Christ’s birth and showed that the Virgin’s childbirth was now present. Thus he came at the appointed time and demonstrated that what he had formerly spoken had been fulfilled through the accomplishment of the work: there faithful in the prophecy of the weeks, here faithful through the mystery revealed.

Did he foretell one thing by that reckoning of years and wish to prove something else here in Mary? He wished to leave no room for doubt or error: what he had foretold as future when those things did not yet exist, he later made manifest, so that those earlier promises would not be disbelieved.

Let us therefore follow the voice of this angel who evangelizes, and just as we proved him truthful when he spoke in prophecy, so let us recognize that he was fulfilled here when he speaks in the Gospels. For this angel said to Mary:

“Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (ibid., 31 ff.).

After some intervening material, the Gospel continues:

“When the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, she bore her only son, wrapped him in swaddling cloths, and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn. And shepherds were in that region, and behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them and said to them: ‘Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger’” (Luke II, 6 ff.).

After some further material it says:

“The shepherds came in haste and found Mary, Joseph, and the infant lying in the manger.”

When Jesus had already been born in Bethlehem of Judea, as the Gospel reports:

“Behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him.’ But when King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born. And they said to him: ‘In Bethlehem of Judea’” [Note: We believe, with blessed Jerome, Book I of his Commentary on chapter II of Matthew, that *Judaeae* in place of *Judae* is an error of the scribes. But since he himself retained that reading, and the manuscripts cited by Peter Sabbatier likewise retain it, we did not hesitate to follow the compilers of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, although other editors have restored *Judae*.]

For thus it is written through the prophet:

“And you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the princes of Judah; for from you shall go forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel” (Matt. II, 1 ff.).

3. Now I wish those who are ungrateful for the sacrament of so great a dispensation to answer me this: given the extraordinary diligence of the inquiry by which Herod questions the chief priests concerning Christ’s birth, and given the king’s great fear and the scribes’ great concern as they respond, how could this question concerning the alleged contradiction in the years not at that time have been either lightly raised from the Hebrew codices or, once raised, clearly brought forward, so that they might console themselves with their terrified king?

For it is written: “Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.” Certainly this king, although profane, had heard of the promised Christ in the books of the Hebrews; therefore he was afraid that, when Christ came, he would lose his kingdom. For if he had not heard Christ prophesied in their writings, he would certainly not have asked the chief priests and scribes where he was to be born.

But not only the king himself was troubled; all Jerusalem was troubled with him—that is, the entire assembly of teachers, all the seats of the Jews. Accordingly, when the king carefully questioned them, they brought forward the prophetic indication that Christ, the Son of God, would be born in Bethlehem of Judea.

When the king was troubled and terrified, they could have demonstrated from their books some such point concerning this reckoning of years, by which they might have clearly shown through an evident calculation of years that Christ ought not yet to be born, if they had repeatedly read this with certainty in the divine pages.

But what was not inserted in the Law and the prophets was not said by them. For those who showed from the testimony of Scripture the place where he would be born could similarly have shown when he would be born—that is, that he ought still to be awaited in the future—by a lawful reckoning of years.

Behold, the truth of their response is not believed on the basis of their persons but is confirmed on the basis of the Law. They truthfully brought forward what they knew to have been written. Nothing was introduced concerning this reckoning of years which, from their books, could be said to contradict Christ’s birth.

Moreover, at the later time, when the Jews themselves wished to know whether he was the Christ, throughout all their questions and Christ’s answers this objection concerning the years is nowhere raised by them or settled by the Lord. Finally, the Gospel reads concerning these matters:

“Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico. Therefore the Jews surrounded him and said to him: ‘How long will you keep our souls in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly’” (John X, 23–24).

Similarly, the chief priest is recorded as having said to the Lord: “I adjure you by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God” (Matt. XXVI, 63).

They also ask John whether he himself is the Christ (John I, 19 ff.), and the Gospel says that some were saying: “This is the Christ.” But others were saying: “Does the Christ come from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that the Christ comes from the offspring of David and from the village of Bethlehem, where David was?” Thus dissent arose among the crowd because of him (John VII, 41 ff.).

In such a widespread Jewish disagreement, if a reckoning of years according to their books had helped them in any way, would they not have responded more boldly on that basis and, by citing definite passages of Scripture, have proved that Christ ought not to be born at that time but should still be awaited, using the evident reckoning of years itself? Yet behold: neither the Jews’ dispute or disagreement is touched upon by any opinion concerning the years, nor is Christ’s manifestation explained by calculations of this kind.

4. Let us now see what Christ answered such people. “I speak,” he says, “and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father’s name bear witness about me” (John X, 15).

In another place he answered them as follows:

“You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth. Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life, and they are the ones that bear witness about me; yet you do not wish to come to me so that you may have life. I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive.

“Do not think that I shall accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you hope. For if you believed Moses, you would perhaps also believe me, for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John V, 33, 39 ff.).

In another place he also says concerning these matters:

“If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John XV, 22).

These are indeed the Lord’s words.

After this, let us hear how he instructed those two disciples who, after his resurrection, were going to a village called Emmaus, when he saw them doubting and conversing about his resurrection; let us hear from what source he instructed them and by what means he finally strengthened their faith. For he spoke to them as follows:

“O foolish men and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and thus enter into his glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke XXIV, 25 ff.).

Behold how Christ himself manifested himself to those who were ignorant—not through an age-old calculation of years from the beginning of the world, but through the conspicuous truth of the testimonies.

Moreover, multiple legions of demons confessed him to be truly the Son of God; the elements themselves bore witness to him; and bodies raised from the dead proclaimed him. Therefore, if you do not wish, O Jew, to believe the angels concerning Christ, believe the demons; believe the heavens announcing him, the tombs opened, and the dead rising. The angel taught that he was the Son of God; the star showed it; the worship of the Magi revealed it; the voice thundering from the cloud made it known; the dove displayed it; and John recognized it.

5. Now listen carefully to what testimony John bore to Christ, and observe it. From this point onward, let us consider whether this cloud of witnesses and such a great multitude of believers, through the coming of Christ’s past birth, proved that it had to be learned by unfolding the calculations of the whole world-age, or whether they themselves recognized it through the truth of faith and handed it on to others for discernment.

This John, therefore, the first of them, born from the womb of a barren mother, an outstanding preacher of a new life, believed that Christ was recognized through faith; he did not attempt to investigate the matter by calculating the years. For he recognized Christ both through prophetic manifestation and through the reality of his bodily presence.

Indeed, he recognized Christ by those very signs through which he had learned from Isaiah’s prophecies that Christ had been foretold. For Isaiah himself, speaking in the person of God the Father, says:

“Behold my servant; I shall receive him. My beloved, in him my soul is well pleased. I have given my Spirit upon him; he brings judgment to the nations” (Isa. XLII, 1).

In these two statements of Isaiah, in which the Father calls the Son both chosen and pleasing to him, and declares that he will give him his Spirit, this John narrates that these things had already been fulfilled at the Lord’s baptism:

“I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained upon him. And the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John I, 32 ff.).

After the Lord had been baptized, a voice also came from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17).

What Isaiah said in the Father’s voice, “I have given my Spirit upon him,” John saw fulfilled in bodily presence when he said, “I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven upon him.”

And what is written again in Isaiah, “My chosen one, in him my soul is well pleased,” is found in the Gospel to have been fulfilled when a voice came from heaven saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

The prophet Isaiah offered a special prophecy concerning the Lord, but this John, more than a prophet, pointed to the Lord with his finger and proved that these things had been specifically fulfilled in him.

6. Behold by what signs and indications John learned that Christ was the Son of God. Therefore, when the Jews asked him whether he was the Christ, he bore perfect testimony to them concerning Christ and said:

“I am not the Christ. But one stands among you whom you do not know. He is the one who was before me.”

The passage continues:

“On the following day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said: ‘This is the one about whom I said: After me comes a man who came before me, because he was before me’” (John I, 20, 26 ff.).

Indeed, when John was already held in chains, he sent two of his disciples to the Lord, saying: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Matt. XI, 3).

He greatly desired to know whether the Son of God, who already seemed to have come into the world in the flesh, would himself descend into the underworld. In this inquiry it is sufficiently apparent that, if he could have learned the coming of the world’s Redeemer by calculating the years from Adam, he would not have sought the Lord’s counsel; the calculation of the years alone would have been enough for him to know these things.

For he himself was distinguished by priestly descent and had been brought up in the Law. If, at that time, he had foreseen these objections as contrary to Christ’s birth, he could have raised them by saying: “The calculation of five thousand years has not yet been completed; Christ, who is to redeem the world, must still be awaited.” Far be it from us to think so.

That good servant of Christ raised no such objection. Instead, he trusted the answers given to him by the Lord. For he had asked the teacher through his disciples: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”

And the Lord said to them:

“Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized; and blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me” (ibid., 5–6).

Behold, John was not scandalized by Christ; rather, he bore clear testimony to Christ.

7. After him all Christ’s disciples follow, renewed by the grace of Christ’s coming. They learned that Christ the Son of God had come in the flesh, not through the laborious calculation of years but through the evident testimonies of God: believing not what is gathered according to the impious by counting on one’s fingers, but what is perceived according to the godly through the revelation of faith.

Thus Andrew makes his brother Simon Peter believe this, saying: “We have found the Messiah,” which is translated “Christ” (John I, 41).

Thus Philip, introducing Christ to Nathanael, says: “We have found Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth, whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote about” (ibid., 45).

Thus Peter himself, first of all the disciples, seeing that his preaching was not burdened by any obstacle of calculations, says:

“We make known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, having become eyewitnesses of his majesty. For he received honor and glory from God the Father, when a voice of this kind was conveyed to him: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’ And we heard this voice conveyed from heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain” (2 Peter I, 16 ff.).
