Later in the same letter he says:

“There were false prophets among this people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who, introducing destructive sects, even deny the Lord who bought them” (2 Peter II, 1).

The same Epistle continues:

“Therefore, brothers, since you know these things beforehand, beware lest, led astray by the error of the foolish, you fall from your own steadfastness” (2 Peter III, 17).

How clearly this holy apostle foretold long beforehand the wickedness of the present age, and bore witness to Christ not only by believing but also by seeing!

8. Let us continue to follow the teaching of this great apostle and see whether the many thousands of Jews converted through Peter’s preaching raised any objection concerning these years against Peter as he preached, or whether, after hearing his exhortations, they rested in faith.

For when, on the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection, the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles and they spoke of God’s mighty works in the languages of all nations, it is written:

“Peter stood up, raised his voice, and spoke, saying: ‘Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen with your ears to my words. For these men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day. But this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: “And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy”’” (Acts II, 14 ff.).

After he had convicted them concerning Christ’s passion and resurrection, he repeated:

“Therefore let the entire house of Israel know with absolute certainty that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (ibid., 36–37).

The passage immediately adds:

“When they heard this, they were pierced in their hearts. Those who received his word were baptized, and about three thousand persons were added on that day. And they persevered in the apostles’ teaching” (ibid., 41–42).

Behold, neither Peter’s preaching was subject to calculations of years, nor did that multitude of so many thousands of Jews attempt to investigate anything concerning this calculation from Peter. They believed only in the testimonies he brought forward, and, pierced in heart, they rested in faith.

9. By this same rule—and in a similar manner—James enlightens Jerusalem, Thomas India, Matthew Macedonia, and the whole remaining apostolic multitude preaches and testifies, by the same teaching, that Christ the Son of God came into the world.

For these men did not inspect from the Hebrew codices the courses of years that opposed their preaching—calculations which in any event have no bearing on the cause of Christ’s birth.

Indeed, the Jews themselves are nowhere read to have either contended with the apostles concerning this dispute about the years or resisted the apostolic statements, especially since at that time the Jews themselves still possessed their homeland and kingdom and had not yet been dispersed. They shone with such an instrument of instruction as was appropriate to the extensive honor they still enjoyed through their kingdom and dignity.

Therefore, if these men, who were neither ignorant of the Law nor less learned than the very multitude of scribes and rulers, did not at that time flatter themselves with this dispute about the years, with what face do those now raise this objection who, having been handed over to dispersion among the nations, are as far removed from knowledge of the Law as they are proved to have been expelled from their own soil?

10. Let us then pass to Paul himself, the apostle and vessel of election. He too was thoroughly trained in the Law and instructed at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts XXII, 3), and he was so well acquainted beforehand with the whole meaning of the Old Testament that it is impious to believe that anything in those writings escaped him.

For he himself says to the Galatians:

“You have heard of my former way of life in Judaism: how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and devastated it, and advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.

“But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace to reveal his Son in me, I immediately did not yield to flesh and blood” (Gal. I, 13 ff.).

Observe, I ask you, Paul’s calling: when Christ the Son of God had been revealed to him, he did not yield to flesh and blood. Therefore, once the Son of God had been revealed to him, he believed and recognized Christ who had been promised to him from the Law.

For the man who had persecuted the Church with such a furious zeal could easily have argued against it on the basis of this exceedingly vain opinion concerning the years, if he had perceived that his cause could in any way be helped by it. If he had received from the Law any information handed down concerning these numbers of years, he could certainly have used it all the more to attack the Church of God. He would have drawn from it a greater basis for resisting the Church by showing that this matter had been inserted in the Law.

For the man who said, “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Gal. IV, 3), could have said: “The fullness of time has not yet come, because the sequence of six thousand years has not been completed according to the Hebrew codices.”

Therefore he said that the fullness of time had already come because he recognized that the mystery of the times had been revealed to him. For he says to the Ephesians:

“God the Father has made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him, for the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ” (Eph. I, 9–10).

This mystery is the dispensation of the fullness of times: that all things should be completed at the appointed time. Therefore, “when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son”; he could not come earlier unless the mystery of the time had been fulfilled.

Since Christ has once been born for me, suffered, been buried, risen, and ascended victoriously to the Father, I have no need of the ancient calculation, because I now hold with certainty the revealed mystery, which is clearly recognized in the fullness of time.

In this way Paul recognized, through the mystery revealed to him, the fullness of the time in which Christ ought to be born; yet he did not learn it through those calculations of years.

Therefore, when the Galatians wished to turn to Judaism, he announced Christ to them and wrote sharply:

“I am amazed that you are so quickly transferring from him who called you into the grace of Christ to another gospel—unless there are some who trouble you and wish to overturn the Gospel of Christ. But even if we or an angel from heaven should evangelize to you contrary to what we evangelized to you, let him be accursed” (Gal. I, 6 ff.).

11. This, I say, the vessel of election and apostle of the Gentiles, in all his disputations with the Jews or Greeks, is nowhere found either to have relied upon these calculations of years while still opposing the Gospel, or to have taken pleasure in them while preaching the Gospel; [Col. 0567A] rather, by setting forth testimonies from the Law and the Prophets, he openly exposed the manifest madness of the Jews. For thus it is written of him: “But Saul grew ever stronger, affirming to the Jews who lived in Damascus [Note: [Col. 0567D] Some have published: ‘But he increased in strength and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus,’ etc. We leave untouched the reading that we found in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*], affirming that this is the Christ” (Acts 9:22). Behold: Paul affirmed that Christ had come, not by means of the completion of years derived from Hebrew manuscripts, but by the clear evidence brought forward from the divine books. For, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

“Paul and Barnabas entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day and sat down. After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying: ‘Men, brothers, if there is among you a word of exhortation for the people, speak.’ Then Paul rose, and, signaling for silence with his hand, said: ‘Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen: The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and exalted the people when they were settlers in the land of Egypt,’ etc. (Acts 13:14ff.).

From that point he continued down to the time of David, from whose offspring he showed that Christ had been born; then he explained by clear testimonies all that had been accomplished in Christ through his passion and resurrection. Yet he drew nothing from this calculation of years according to the Hebrew manuscripts. For it was not necessary for him, in proving the mystery of so great a matter, to calculate the years from the beginning of the world. Scripture continues and says: ‘According to his custom, Paul entered in to the Jews and for three Sabbaths reasoned with them from the Scriptures, explaining and demonstrating that it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and that this is Jesus Christ, whom I proclaim to you’ (Acts 17:2–3). In all these disputations, when he opened the Scriptures to the Jews every day, if he had discovered anything from this opinion about the years that contradicted his preaching, would he not immediately have made clear to them what had been concealed, or rejected what he ought to have rejected?”

12. Stephen also, the first martyr of Christ, very frequently refuted the Jews who opposed him, not by a calculation of times but by an abundance of testimonies. For thus it is written:

“Some rose from the synagogue called the Synagogue of the Libertines, and of the Cyrenians and Alexandrians, and of those who were from Cilicia and Asia, disputing with Stephen; and they were unable to resist the wisdom and the Spirit who spoke through him, because they were refuted by him with all boldness [Note: [Col. 0567D] This addition—‘because they were refuted by him with all boldness’—is absent, says Petrus Sabbatier, from the current Greek text. But Mill notes that it is read in one manuscript of Stephen, as in the Cambridge Greek manuscript: διὰ τὸ ἐλέγχεσθαι αὐτοὺς ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ μετὰ πάσης παῤῥησίας· Μὴ δυνάμενοι οὖν ἀντοφθαλμεῖν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ—‘because they were being refuted by him with all boldness. Therefore, being unable to withstand the truth.’ Bede, in his revision of his commentary on Acts, also notes that the same addition is found in the Greek; Erasmus likewise states that an old Latin manuscript has it]” (Acts 6:9–10).

Behold: we read that the Jews were refuted and convicted by Stephen, yet we find nothing in his disputations about this calculation of years. Hence he said to the Jews themselves, who were not resisting this opinion but persisting in their customary obstinacy: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did” (Acts 7:15).

[Col. 0568A] 13. What shall I now say about the apostle James, the brother of the Lord? When the Jews asked him to give testimony concerning Jesus, whom they were seeking, he taught that he was the Savior. Yet neither those who accepted his word nor those who, through the intervention of envy, separated themselves from him asked anything of him that appears to have concerned this calculation of years. Nevertheless, as a witness of the truth and as one who proclaimed this same Son of God to be Christ, he was crowned with glorious martyrdom.

James, the brother of the apostle John, likewise preached this same Son of God as Christ to the Jews. Feeling that his preaching was subject to no opinions about years, he taught at length, through divine testimonies, that all the things foretold had been fulfilled in our Lord Jesus Christ.

Finally, John, that distinguished disciple of Christ, filled with the sweetness of the Lord’s breast, commends this same truth most openly and clearly in his Epistle, saying:

“Every spirit that confesses that Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God. We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error” (1 John 4:2–3, 6).

Repeating and commending the same point, he says:

“We know that the Son of God has come, and for our sake has put on flesh, and has suffered, and has risen from the dead. He took us up and gave us understanding, so that we might know the true God and be in his true Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

He also says further:

“This is the victory that has conquered the world: your faith. And who is the one who has conquered the world, except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” (ibid., 4–5).

14. Accordingly, having accepted this definition of Christian faith, we must believe without doubt the past events narrated in the Gospels and hope without hesitation for the future. Faith is not necessary for present things that are seen and are confirmed as certain by the bodily senses; rather, firm faith must be applied to those things that are not seen as present. Thus every Christian will hold with full faith that Christ, the Son of God, was born in the past from a Virgin, and will hope without doubt that he will come to judgment. He will believe both in his past birth, by which he graciously consented to become human for our sake, and in his future promise, by which he promised that he would give the kingdom to the faithful.

Thus, by offering an unshaken faith concerning both the past and the future things said in the Gospel and apostolic writings about Christ the Son of God, each person will deserve to obtain the future kingdom with all the saints, because he has not violated the mystery of holy faith. By this faith we all live; through this faith we faithfully hope to be crowned. For “the just person lives by faith.” And how does the just person live by faith (Hab. 2:4), unless by not seeing what he believes? This, then, is the righteousness of faith by which we are justified: that we believe in him whom we do not see, and that, cleansed by faith, we may afterward see him in whom we now believe.

Certainly Christ was once born, died, and was raised from the dead; yet just as we did not see him physically being born or dying, so we have not seen him rising. Nevertheless, with undoubting faith we both truly believe and confess these things about him. This is the righteousness of faith by which we are justified and cleansed: we contemplate and believe with the eye of the heart those things that we have not seen with our eyes.

The apostles were granted the ability to see these things and to behold the Word himself incarnate in the flesh. But he commanded us to believe what he granted them to see. Faith, therefore, as has been said, concerns things that are not seen and yet are believed without doubt—that is, if you believe without hesitation what you are unable to see in the present. Christ therefore first came into the world in his own time to save the world, and he will come again in his own time to judge the world.

Accordingly, the things that are read as having been accomplished concerning him are to be believed alone; but the things promised as future are both to be believed and hoped for. Whoever therefore truly believes that he once came for the salvation of the world will not perish when he comes to judgment. If anyone doubts this faith, what does he hope for except eternal punishments?

We must therefore act so that in certain matters of faith belief may suffice even when understanding has not been attained—namely, so that, if in certain matters an explanation is not available to us, faith alone may suffice, and rational objection may not be admitted where the depth of faith is commended. For all the industry of human disputation must be set aside where faith alone is sufficient.

15. Behold, leaving the other matters unmentioned, I shall set forth two astonishing miracles concerning Christ the Son of God: his birth without a father from a virgin mother, and his entrance to the disciples through closed doors after the resurrection. If these two things could be comprehended by reason, they would not be astonishing, nor would faith possess merit when human reason supplies the proof (Gregory the Great, *Homily 26 on the Gospels*, no. 1).

For, as blessed Hilary says (*On the Trinity*, book 8, no. 10): “It brings not so much pardon as reward to be ignorant of what you believe, because the greatest recompense of faith is to hope for what you do not know.”

We must therefore rely upon faith and embrace faith, which is perfected even when understanding has been attained, through hope and charity. I ask that it suffice every Christian to believe what he cannot reach by the senses. Whoever has been granted both sublime understanding and strong faith should give thanks to God. Whoever has not been granted understanding should believe in order to understand, so that, when believing he understands what he has heard, he may, by understanding, enjoy what he has believed. Thus it will come about that belief opens understanding, and understanding, nourished by faith, reaches the crown.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0569]

## THE HEADINGS OF THE SAME AUTHOR’S THIRD BOOK BEGIN

[Note: [Col. 0569] These headings, omitted by the collectors of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, are published by us from Menrad Molther.]

So that the reader may most easily find an argument with which to respond in defense of the sixth age, let him first carefully attend to the following chapters.

[Col. 0569C]

1. That the ages of the world are recognized not by years but by generations.

2. That, whether in the Hebrew manuscripts or in those of the Septuagint translators, an equal number of years is not found for each age, so that it may be said that each age possesses such-and-such a number.

3. That, corresponding to the six days, the sixth age of humankind and the six ages of the world are likewise confirmed.

4. The distinction of the five ages arranged by generations, and the number of generations through which each age extends.

5. What is the reason that the two ages from Adam to Abraham are enclosed within ten generations, while the remaining three up to Christ are divided into fourteen generations.

6. Examples from Scripture by which we are instructed that the ages of the world ought to be reckoned not in years but in generations, because Matthew traces the royal generations of Christ, whereas Luke follows certain lines of priestly descent.

7. What is the reason that Christ was born in the sixth age of the world, since, whether the number of years appears greater or smaller, nothing impedes the fullness of the generations.

8. The calculation of the years in both sets of manuscripts, since the shorter number of years alleged from the Hebrews does not hinder the confirmation of the sixth age of the world.

9. What Epiphanius, Augustine, and Jerome thought concerning the years, and which translation each preferred.

10. A new reckoning of the years for each age according to the Septuagint translators.

[Col. 0569C]

1. Responding for the third time in this little book of the work to the slanderers of the Christian faith, who, taking the years from the beginning of the world according to the Hebrew manuscripts, recklessly maintain that the fifth age of the world is still present, I first admonish the entire Christian people of this: whenever any Christian hears a Jew calculating the ages according to the years taken from the Hebrew manuscripts, let him not bend his heart toward him so as to accept that the same ages ought to be calculated according to that number of years. Rather, let him recognize them as determined according to the established number of generations. For the ages themselves are not first known by the number of years; rather, the years themselves are gathered according to distinct ages of generations.

2. Since the individual ages do not at all end after an equal number of years—for in one place the number is greater, in another smaller, and a different number of years is found throughout the several ages—which number and how great a number of years there is is better calculated and determined within the ages themselves, according to each person’s preference. For one reaches Christ not by counting years according to the Gospel, but by reckoning generations. Therefore the ages of the world themselves must be gathered not in years but in generations.

It must by no means be done in the wrong order, so that the ages are recognized in years; rather, the years must be recognized within the ages. I shall now speak, then, and disclose the principles of the six ages.

3. In six days God made heaven and earth, and on distinct days he created every creature formed by him, beginning each day with light and bringing it to an end with evening, as Scripture says: “There was evening and morning, one day.”

[Note: [Col. 0571D] Augustine has interpretations very similar to all these concerning the six ages in book 1 of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, from no. 35 through no. 42, and in the final chapter of book 22 of *The City of God*.]

According to these numbers and principles of the six days, six ages likewise become recognizable in each human being, in which life itself is completed: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, maturity, and old age. Suppose, then, that all human beings who have existed from Adam down to the present day are like one human being; and, in the person of this one human being, place before yourself an image of the whole age of the world. You will see with the greatest ease through how many ages this world, like one human being, has passed, and in which age it now stands.

4. From Adam to the Flood extends the first age, which ends with ten generations. The second, after the Flood and up to Abraham, likewise unfolds through ten generations. The third age of the world thereafter extends to David through fourteen generations. The fourth, following this, is likewise carried through fourteen generations from David to the Babylonian captivity. Then follows the fifth age of the world, from the Babylonian captivity to Christ; it too ends with fourteen generational divisions. Finally, the sixth age of the world follows, in which Christ the Son of God is born from the Virgin Mary. No human being comprehends through how many years or generations this age extends.

5. The reason will show why those two ages before Abraham run through ten generations, while these three in the Gospel are marked by lines of fourteen generations.

From Adam to the Flood there are ten generations; this first age is assigned to infancy. And so that you may clearly know the ten names of the generations mentioned above, attend to them here in their order:

Adam begot Seth; Seth begot Enos; Enos begot Kenan; Kenan begot Mahalalel; Mahalalel begot Jared; Jared begot Enoch; Enoch begot Methuselah; Methuselah begot Lamech; Lamech [begot] Noah.

This first age, I say, is reckoned with its morning and evening. For just as each day begins with light and ends in evening, so this age began with Adam and had the Flood as its evening.

The second age, therefore, extends from the Flood to Abraham through ten corresponding lines of generations: Shem begot Arphaxad; Arphaxad begot Kenan; Kenan begot Shelah; Shelah begot Eber; Eber begot Peleg; Peleg begot Reu; Reu begot Serug; Serug begot Nahor; Nahor begot Terah; Terah begot Abraham, from whom the third age of the world begins.

This age, I say, had its morning after the passing of the Flood, while its evening was that confusion of languages. A diligent reader will find the same pattern of morning and evening renewed in the subsequent ages as well, if he seeks it.

6. Now understand the reason why these two ages end with ten generations. The first age of a human being is infancy, and the second is childhood. These two ages, apart from the five bodily senses in which natural sensation or movement exists, neither attain anything clearly through distinct understanding nor accomplish anything through active work. For action without understanding is rash, and understanding without action is sluggish.

Therefore the first period of human life, to which no proper administration is entrusted, is devoted to the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Accordingly, because of the five bodily senses alone, by which the age of such persons is shown to flourish, the same number five is doubled on account of the two sexes, since the same five bodily senses are demonstrably present in males as in females. For this reason these two ages end with the number ten in generations.

7. The three ages of the world that are reckoned in the Gospel are distinguished by twice seven generations. From Abraham to David there are fourteen generations; from David to the Babylonian captivity, fourteen generations; and from the Babylonian captivity to Christ, fourteen generations.

8. We must now see why these three ages of the world are recognized as ending with the number twice seven generations. We said above that those two ages from Adam to Abraham, like infancy and childhood, existed as devoted solely to the five bodily senses, because in these two ages nothing sublime can be grasped through understanding or formed through action. They flourish, therefore, only through the five bodily senses, as has been said.

Once infancy and childhood have been completed and adolescence follows, both distinct understanding and necessary action come to a human being. If these two are added to the five bodily senses, they make seven. If seven is again doubled on account of the two sexes, since it is understood in men just as in women, fourteen results as one number.

This, then, is the reason why those two ages run through ten generations, while these three serve through divisions of twice seven generations. We have said that there are five ages of the world, which we are to recognize not in years but in generations.

9. So that you may recognize that the ages of the world themselves ought to be learned not by calculating years but by determining generations, the holy Gospel provides sufficient proof. The three ages that it places in order from Abraham to Christ it divides by definite and determined lines of generations. For, in order to demonstrate those three divisions of the ages, it did not set forth anything concerning numbers of years, although it unfolded those three ages through fourteen generations each.

Thus it is read in Matthew’s Gospel:

“All the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David to the Babylonian captivity, fourteen generations; and from the Babylonian captivity to Christ, fourteen generations” (Matt. 1:17).

The Evangelist surely would not have observed this in distinguishing the ages—namely, that he should disclose them not by numbers of years but by generations—if he had not foreseen that this same practice had been observed in the old Law for distinguishing the ages.

According to this pattern, we find two ages—one before the Flood and the second after the Flood—brought to an end in the Book of Genesis. For, after the generations from Adam to Noah had been counted, before Noah entered the ark, and since they were certainly ten generations, Scripture says: “These are the generations of Noah” (Gen. 6:9).

Likewise, when it sets forth the sequence of the generations of the second age after the Flood, the same Scripture recalls and says: “These are the generations of Shem” (Gen. 11:10), counting the same ten generations from Shem his son to Abraham.

It deals similarly with the third age of the world. Beginning with it, the Evangelist Matthew, having arranged the divisions of the generations, explained the three ages of the world, necessarily leaving aside those two earlier ages, which, like infancy and childhood, were not suited to beget sons. For who, according to the ordinary law of nature, can beget children before the thirteenth year of his life?

Therefore, wishing to explain the generation of the Lord according to the flesh (Matt. 1:1–2), the Evangelist began to extend his account from Abraham, as from adolescence, the age at which a person can beget children, on account of the seed of Abraham in whom all the nations had been promised a blessing (Gen. 12:3).

10. Thus the explanation that has been given teaches us to seek the ages of the world not in years but in generations, because in distinguishing any age we do not find in Scripture, “These are the years of the generations,” but rather, “These are the generations.”

As was said, when the first age of the world had ended: “These are the generations of Noah.” Or, when the second age is recalled from Shem to Abraham, it is similarly written: “These are the generations of Shem.” Yet neither in the first nor in the second age of the world is it written, “These are the years of the generations,” but, “These are the generations.”

Therefore, wishing to show that the ages of the world should not be established according to an opinion about years but examined by weighing the number of generations—especially since in many passages of Scripture, where a fixed order of times is directed through generations, years are entirely omitted, yet the times of the world are not thereby frustrated in any respect—Scripture teaches that it is not enough to attend to the total number of years where the effectiveness of the ages is demonstrated through generations.

In this manner we see certain things promised by God’s law that are foretold as destined to be fulfilled not in years but in predetermined generations. It is not announced by the speech of some human prophet but marked by the very voice of God, when the Lord speaks to Abraham: “In the fourth generation the sons of Israel will return from the land of Egypt” (Gen. 15:16). This appears to have been fulfilled then not in years but in generations.

For, if you review the genealogy of Levi, you will find that the sons of Israel departed from the land of Egypt in the fourth generation. Levi begot Kohath; Kohath begot Amram; Amram begot Aaron; Aaron begot Eleazar; Eleazar begot Phinehas. Kohath, however, entered Egypt with his father Levi. Again, Eleazar left Egypt with his father Aaron. From Kohath to Eleazar four generations are counted.

11. Thus the future and complete liberation of the Israelite people from slavery was foretold by God as destined to be fulfilled not in years but in generations.

In the same way Cain’s sin is foretold as destined to be expiated by a sevenfold reckoning of generations. For Cain’s sin was dissolved in the seventh generation, since in the seventh generation Cain himself was killed by Lamech, who is the seventh from Adam.

Then the sin of Lamech himself, who is said to have killed him, is deferred for cleansing until the seventy-seventh generation, according to what is written concerning him: “Vengeance shall be taken sevenfold for Cain, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold” (Gen. 4:24).

From Adam to Christ seventy-seven generations are gathered in order, as is read in Luke’s Gospel (Luke 3:23ff.). For there the account begins with Christ himself and proceeds until it reaches Adam, or God, from whom Adam was created.

Therefore Lamech’s sin, as the sin of the whole world, was cleansed in the seventy-seventh generation, namely, at the coming of Christ. Hence the Lord himself, commending in the Gospel the mystery of this most sacred number seventy-seven, teaches that sins must be forgiven not merely seven times but also seventy-seven times (Matt. 18:22).

12. Nor do these seventy-seven lines of generations, which the historical order commends according to Luke from Adam to Christ, in any way prejudice those generations that are recalled by Matthew (Matt. 1:1ff.). Luke follows one set of generational lines, while Matthew examines another.

Luke, following the ancestry of the priestly race and beginning with Christ the Son of God, explained seventy-seven lines of generations down to Adam and to God himself, by whom Adam was formed. Matthew, however, traced the numbers of the generations of the royal line, in which he expressed the three ages of the world through divisions of fourteen generations each.

Therefore the ages of the world, which we said were five up to Christ, must be calculated not according to Luke, who traces the priestly lineage, but according to Matthew, who arranges the royal generations. For we believe that the flesh of Christ the Son of God was propagated from both lines in such a way that it flourishes through royal descent and is glorious through priestly ancestry.

According to the royal lineage that Matthew traces, with those two ages added—that is, the ages running through ten generations from Adam to Abraham—the five ages of the world must be counted. Thus the calculation of the years is to be considered, but the entire line of generations is to be examined.

13. Therefore, whenever the falsehood of the Jews, O most diligent Christian, attempts before you to define the ages of the world by the years extracted from their manuscripts, as though it could show the world’s ages determined by thousands of years, do not allow yourself to be drawn there into the spirit of error. Return instead to the spirit of truth, so that, according to the Gospel and the examples from Scripture set forth above for distinguishing these ages, you may despise that entire calculation of years according to the Hebrew manuscripts and attend only to these enumerations of generations, which you have heard were brought to an end in distinct lines from Adam to Christ.

[Col. 0575B]

14. Now, diligent reader, learn carefully the reason why he had to be born in this sixth age: namely, so that the one who had made the human being on the sixth day might also come in the sixth age of the world for the restoration of the human race.

Accordingly, now secure concerning this question of years, all the apostles and apostolic men, because the sum of these ages is established not in years but in generations, did not concern themselves with what number of years was drawn from the Hebrew manuscripts, provided that the sequence of generations was clearly complete.

For what does it matter how many years each of those men lived, provided that he knows the number of generations more fully? If something is subtracted from the number of generations, the confusion of the ages is certainly recognized. But where the full number of generations remains, what need is there to trouble over the years of the world, when the entire sum of the ages proceeds according to definite and predetermined numbers of generations?

You, Jew, learn to find the years through the generations; for you cannot know in any way how many years there have been from the beginning of the world unless you first discover this through the individual generations. If, therefore, the order of the generations is frustrated, what truth concerning the years will remain? Years cannot in any way be known through generations.

What, then? Can the matter be arranged through generations in such a way that they cannot be understood without years? A generation can be counted in either few or many years. But years cannot be found without generations.

Let me grant, then, that each generation lived for only twice ten years. Does this number of years impede me in any way, when the sequence of generations satisfies me? Therefore this must be held, and preserved with complete faith: for the recognition of the sixth age and of the Lord’s incarnation, we must observe the orders of generations distributed among the individual ages. In them not only is there no error, but a great disclosure of truth has been revealed; and we shall be secure from error to the extent that we recognize that Christ, who was born long ago, is to be reckoned by the sequence of generations.

15. Now, if you wish, apply yourselves also to the very years collected from the beginning of the world, which you collect only through the successive generations, and see whether you can still derive anything from them.

[Note: [Col. 0575D] The serious controversy, entangled in inextricable knots, concerning the number of years from the beginning of the world to the birth of Christ, which Julian begins to explain here, has been discussed by many sacred interpreters; but above all, Thomas Malvenda seems to us worthy of consultation, in his work *On Antichrist*, book 1, chapters 13 through 16.]

Although it has already been proved above that the shortness of the years extracted from the Hebrew manuscripts does not hinder or contradict the demonstration of the sixth age of the world, nevertheless, without prejudice to this question, if, for example, you wish to know only this concerning the total number of years—namely, how many years passed from the origin of the world to Christ, and which manuscripts ought therefore to be trusted, whether the Hebrew manuscripts or those according to the translators of the Septuagint—apply your living understanding here.

“For if we seek the years from the beginning of the world to the birth of Christ according to the manuscripts of the translators of the Septuagint, together also with certain subsequent histories of the nations, there are found from Adam to Christ 5,200 years. And whatever else remains according to certain historians who have written the sequence of the years of the world.”

[Note: [Col. 0576D] We note these words because Isidore of Beja cited them at the end of his *Chronicle*, vol. 8 of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 325, second edition.]

But according to your manuscripts far fewer years are found—so much so that, in the two ages alone before and after the Flood, which proceed in order up to Abraham, the difference between the two manuscripts amounts to scarcely 1,540 years and a little more.

For in that first age 1,656 years are found from Adam to the Flood, and from the Flood to Abraham 292 years are found. But according to the manuscripts of the Septuagint translators, 2,242 years are found from Adam to the Flood, and from the Flood to Abraham 1,072 years. Counted together, these two ages contain 3,314 years.

If the years from the third age up to Christ—five thousand years, together with whatever remains beyond that—are added to them, the total will be completed. Behold: a smaller number of years is found in the Hebrew manuscripts than in the manuscripts of the Septuagint translators—so much so that even up to the present day five thousand years do not yet appear to have been completed. Yet this too in no way prejudices the time of Christ’s birth, which the sequence of generations commends with such manifest evidence.

[Col. 0576D]

16. Since we have established what both manuscripts contain concerning the years themselves, it remains now to consider which manuscripts deserve greater authority. Let each person now state what he thinks.

Will this shortness of years demonstrated from the Hebrew manuscripts in any way be judged preferable to the greater number of years contained in the edition of the Septuagint translators, who translated the divine Scriptures by the gift of prophecy rather than by the task of translation, with the Lord revealing them to them, and among whom this calculation of years is also found?

[Note: [Col. 0577D] The question of which manuscripts should be followed in counting the years of the patriarchs—those of the Greek Septuagint translators or the Hebrew manuscripts—has been vigorously debated among scholars. The majority does indeed favor the Hebrew calculation. Nevertheless, there are not a few authors, and not contemptible ones, who have fought vigorously for the chronology of the Septuagint translators: Baronius in the *Apparatus to the Ecclesiastical Annals*, Joannes Morinus in *Exercitation* 7, Vossius, Paulus Pezronius in *Antiquity of Time Restored*, and others. Accordingly, it is less surprising that our Julian held the same opinion at the time when the Latin edition of the Septuagint translators was flourishing most fully in the Church. See Nat. Alexander, Dissertation 8, “On the First Age of the World,” vol. 1 of the *History of the Old Testament*.]

Therefore, for these years we must observe the authority of the Septuagint translators alone. It is rightly preferred to all editions and translations; all ecclesiastical teachers have maintained it down to the present, and in this matter especially—that is, in the calculation of years—they have followed it.

17. I shall briefly note what each of the learned men thought concerning the praise and pre-eminent authority of those venerable translators, the Seventy. Epiphanius, that distinguished bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, speaks as follows in his works concerning their praise. He says (Treatise on Measures and Weights, p. 566, Basel edition of 1560):

> “This ought to be admired, and no one should dare to consider it worthy of blame, but rather should praise the fact [Col. 0577B] that, by God’s counsel and will, seventy-two venerable men assembled on the island of Pharos, which is called Anagoge, that is, ‘upper land.’”

He continues their praise somewhat later (ibid., p. 567):

> “They were not found to be discordant,” he says, “but a wondrous work of God appeared, which must be acknowledged, because these men had received the gift of the Holy Spirit. It belonged to that Spirit alone to make those interpreters so perfectly harmonious, so that wherever a word had to be added for the sake of clarification, they all added it together, and wherever something had to be removed because of a less ornamented repetition, they all removed it together.”

There too, after other remarks, he adds:

> “Wherever something was added by those same translators, they suitably supplied expressions for the understanding and assistance of the nations [Col. 0577C] that were to be called to faith in God and were to receive the inheritance of eternal life from the divine admonitions of the Old and New Testaments.”

This, then, is what Saint Epiphanius reports.

18. But now hear also what blessed Augustine says in praise of such men. In Book XV of The City of God (chapter 23, §3), he says:

> “The Seventy interpreters are rightly believed to have received the prophetic spirit, so that, if they changed anything by its authority and said in another way what they were interpreting, no one would doubt that this too had been spoken divinely.”

The same man repeats this concerning them in Book XVIII of the same work (chapter 43, §1), saying:

> “Although there were also other interpreters who translated those sacred utterances from the Hebrew language into Greek, nevertheless this translation, which is the Septuagint, the Church has received as though it alone existed [Note: The edition reads: ‘which the Church received as though it alone existed.’], and the Greek Christian peoples use it, most of whom do not know whether any other exists. From this Septuagint translation what the Latin Church possesses was also translated into the Latin language. Hence the Church of Christ judges that no one should be preferred to the authority of so many men [Col. 0577D] chosen for this work by Eleazar, then high priest. For even if one Spirit, unquestionably divine, had not appeared in them, but these learned Seventy had compared among themselves the words of their translation in the ordinary human manner, so that whatever pleased them all might remain fixed, no interpreter ought to be placed before them.”

Let these statements concerning the praise of the Seventy interpreters suffice.

19. As for the difference in the number of years, what difference exists between the Hebrew books and our books is also discussed by the same Saint Augustine in the work mentioned above. He says (Book XV, chapter 10):

> “Between the Hebrew books and our books [Note: ‘Our books,’ say the Benedictines concerning this passage, are the Latin books then used by the Church, translated from the Greek version of the Septuagint; the Hebrew books are those translated from the Hebrew text.] there appears to be some difference in the actual number of years, though I do not know how this came about. Nevertheless, it is not so great as to deny that those men lived to such great ages. For Adam himself, the first man, is found in our books to have lived 230 years before he fathered the son who was called Seth, whereas in the Hebrew books he is said to have lived 130. But after he fathered him, he is read to have lived 700 years in our books, and 800 in theirs; and in both the total agrees. Then, through the succeeding generations, before the one whose birth is recorded was born, his father is found to have lived 100 years fewer among the Hebrews; but after he was born, the same number of years is found in our books, 100 fewer than in the Hebrew books. Thus the total of the numbers agrees on both sides. In the sixth generation the two books nowhere disagree. In the seventh, however, where Enoch, who was born, is said not to have died but, as it pleased God, to have been translated, there is the same difference as in the preceding five generations: 100 years before he fathered the son, where his age is recorded, and thus a similar agreement in the total. For, according to both books, he lived 365 years before his translation.
>
> “The eighth generation does contain some difference, but it is smaller and unlike the others. Methuselah, whom Enoch fathered, before he fathered the one who follows in that succession, according to the Hebrews lived not 100 years fewer but 20 years more. Those years are subsequently found added in our books after he fathered him, and in both the total of the whole number corresponds.
>
> “Only in the ninth generation, that is, in the years of Lamech, the son of Methuselah and the father of Noah, does the total differ, though not greatly. For he is found to have lived 24 years more in the Hebrew books than in ours. Before he fathered the son called Noah, he had six years fewer in the Hebrew books than in ours; but after he fathered him, he had 30 years more in those same books than in ours. When the former are subtracted from the latter, 24 remain, as stated.”

Thus far Saint Augustine.

20. Although the doctor above says that he does not know why it happened that in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and seventh generations 100 additional years are found according to the books of the Seventy—years which are subtracted in the Hebrew books when each man fathered his son—he nevertheless later expresses what he thinks about it. He says (same book, chapter 13):

> “In these years, in which the likeness of the same falsification is continued, so that before the son who is inserted into the succession is born, 100 years remain in one place and are lacking in another, while after his birth they remain where they had been lacking and are lacking where they had remained, so that the total agrees—and this is found in the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and seventh generations—the error itself seems to possess a certain consistency, if it may be called an error; it does not bear the appearance of chance, but of design.”

A little later he adds:

> “Clearly, the person who did this wished to persuade people that the ancients had lived for very many years, though those years were called very short, and wished to demonstrate this by the maturity of puberty, at which they would become capable of fathering children. Therefore he thought that those 100 years should be represented to unbelievers as ten of our years, lest they refuse to believe that men had lived for so long. He added 100 years wherever he did not find an age suitable for fathering children, and after the children had been born he removed those same years, so that the total might agree. In this way he wished to make credible the ages appropriate for producing offspring, while nevertheless not defrauding the total number of years lived by each person.”

21. Although this blessed doctor, extending the sharpness of his subtle intellect, debated the uncertainty of so great a matter, he explained what seemed to him to be the case not by asserting it but by conjecture. He supposed that this had been done to remedy the unbelief of those for whom it would in no way be credible that men of that age could have lived so many years unless the maturity of puberty also made their fathering of children credible—that is, so that even if they wished to reckon those very short years, they would always find an age suitable for fathering children, while they attempted to establish that ten years such as we now have represented one hundred of their years.

Yet the aforementioned doctor neither confirms nor rejects this opinion, and concludes as follows (ibid., near the end):

> “However this is understood,” he says, “whether one believes that it happened in this way or does not believe it, whether it is so or is not so, I would in no way doubt that it was rightly done.”

22. After this, directing the eye of his mind from uncertain matters to certain ones without doubt, and expressing the final judgment of his discussion concerning this very difference in years, he continues as follows (same book, chapter 14, §2):

> “It is not without significance that no one has dared to correct from the Hebrew books the many passages in which the Seventy interpreters appear to say something different. For that difference was not considered an error, nor do I in any way think it should be considered one. But where there is no scribal error, we must believe that they wished, by the divine Spirit, where the meaning was consonant with truth and proclaimed truth, to say something differently—not in the capacity of interpreters, but with the freedom of prophets. Hence the authority of the apostles is rightly found to use not only the Hebrew books but also these books themselves when it adduces testimonies from Scripture.”

In saying this, he also introduces, as a report based on conjecture, what he remembers others to have thought concerning this variation in the years. He says (same book, chapter 11):

> “They say that it is not credible that the Seventy interpreters, who translated at one and the same time and with one understanding, could have fallen into error, or that, where nothing was at stake for them, they wished to lie; but that the Jews, out of envy toward us because the Law and the Prophets passed to us through translation, changed certain things in their books so that the authority of ours might be diminished.”

23. Moreover, when this doctor mentioned the second age of the world in Book XVI of the work already mentioned (chapter 10, §2), he says:

> “In the second year after the Flood, Shem, when he was 100 years old, fathered Arphaxad. Arphaxad, when he was 135 years old, fathered Cainan. When he was 130 years old, Cainan fathered Shelah. Shelah himself was likewise 130 years old when he fathered Eber. Eber was 134 years old when he fathered Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided. Peleg himself lived 130 years and fathered Reu, who, at the age of 132, fathered Serug. The latter, at the age of 130, fathered Nahor. Nahor, at the age of 79, fathered Terah, who, at the age of 70, fathered Abraham. Thus, according to the common edition, that is, the Seventy interpreters, the years from the Flood to Abraham amount to 1,072. In the Hebrew books, however, far fewer years are said to be found, for which they offer either no explanation or one of the greatest difficulty.”

24. Blessed Augustine explained these short years of the Hebrews, for which no explanation could be given. Yet if that outstanding doctor had seen some danger to the faith—God forbid—in the shortness of the years derived from the Hebrew books, or had observed someone defending that same shortness as contrary to the time of Christ’s birth, by which the enemies of the Christian faith infer that the sixth age of the world had not yet arrived, he would have devoted himself entirely to answering it. There he would have spread the full sails of his discussion before the blowing winds, wherever the opportunity of the subject called for him to say something of that kind. He would not earlier have said, “Concerning this very difference in the years, I do not know why it happened,” when ignorance of this sort would involve the penalty of error in a matter that contradicts the mystery of the Lord’s birth.

But because in this very difference of years he saw nothing contrary to proving that the sixth age of the world had arrived, there was no reason for him to infer from this variation in the years anything that ought to be known concerning the ages, which he knew to be distinguished by predetermined generations. Whether those shorter years according to the Hebrews or these multiplied years according to our books are used, once the series of generations has been disclosed, as stated, they compel us to understand nothing other than that this is the sixth age of the world.

25. Now we must consider what Saint Jerome thought about this. In the Chronicle of Eusebius, which he translated from Greek into Latin, he wished all the years from the beginning of the world to Christ to be understood not from the Hebrew books but from the books of the Seventy interpreters, expressly stating this in his preface. He says:

> “I am not unaware that in the Hebrew books the years of the ages are found to differ, by more or less, according to what the interpreters thought should be read; and that we ought rather to follow the reading which the multitude of copies has preserved.”

These words were spoken by Jerome, a man of blessed memory, who translated the divine Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin speech. Who, I ask, does not now plainly see that we ought altogether to trust the Seventy interpreters concerning this reckoning of the years—those who, as stated, are believed to have set down that multiplied series of years not in the capacity of interpreters but with the freedom of prophets?

26. Let it suffice that it has now been proved to you that no total of years appears contrary to the time of Christ’s birth. Likewise, let it suffice that the ages of the world are distinguished not by an equal reckoning of years but by the number of generations assigned to them. Since this too has been proved to you, receive from this point onward the ages of the world themselves according to the Seventy interpreters, reckoned with their years [Note: We have no doubt that Julian had before his eyes Isidore of Seville’s Chronicle and Book V of the Etymologies when he calculated the years of the six ages. Whether he also knew what are called the Chronicles of Mellitus, published by Henry Florez in volume VI of España Sagrada, others may judge; we certainly incline too strongly toward the affirmative. In any event, Julian compiled both works and added other material lacking in them.], and finally understand in confusion what total of years each age contains within itself.

I make only this observation, lest anyone think it contradictory that in the third and fifth ages of the world the years of the generations themselves are not set down here, although those generations are listed according to the Gospel of Matthew. For in those third and fifth ages of the world the generations themselves are not set out with their years in the same manner as in the first and second ages, where both years and generations are recorded.

## FIRST AGE

[Col. 0581D] 27. After the first five days, Adam was formed on the sixth day. Adam, at the age of 230, fathered Seth. Seth, at the age of 205, fathered Enosh. Enosh, at the age of 190, fathered Cainan. Cainan, at the age of 170 [Col. 0582A], fathered Mahalalel. Mahalalel, at the age of 165, fathered Jared. Jared, at the age of 162, fathered Enoch. Enoch, at the age of 165, fathered Methuselah. Methuselah, at the age of 167, fathered Lamech. Lamech, at the age of 188, fathered Noah. Noah, at the age of 500 [Note: This is how the editors of the Library of the Fathers published the passage, undoubtedly in error. Others, in conformity with Saint Isidore, Book V of the Etymologies, chapter 39, and the Chronicle, have: ‘In Noah’s six-hundredth year the Flood occurred.’ We prefer to read: ‘Noah, at the age of 500, fathered Shem. In Noah’s six-hundredth year the Flood occurred.’ But since we lack manuscript witnesses, it is enough to draw attention to this point.], the Flood occurred.

## SECOND AGE

28. Shem [Note: This is the sole consideration that persuades us that Julian read Mellitus; for, just as here, he merely says ‘Shem fathered him in the second year after the Flood,’ and so forth, whereas Isidore writes in the Chronicle: ‘In the second year after the Flood, when Shem was 100 years old, he fathered,’ and so forth.] fathered Arphaxad in the second year after the Flood. Arphaxad, at the age of 135, fathered Cainan. Cainan, at the age of 130, fathered Shelah. Shelah, at the age of 130, fathered Eber. Eber, at the age of 134, fathered Peleg. Peleg, at the age of 130, fathered Reu. Reu, at the age of 132 [Col. 0582B], fathered Serug. Serug, at the age of 130, fathered Nahor. Nahor, at the age of 79, fathered Terah. Terah, at the age of 70, fathered Abraham.

This second age, which we said proceeds through ten generations, has one fewer according to the Hebrew books: the one named Cainan, which is included here. Nevertheless, the Seventy interpreters mention this generation, and the Gospel according to Luke confirms it.

These two ages of the world—the one before the Flood and the other after the Flood—have no difficulty in the reckoning of the years, because they proceed along direct lines of descent, one being propagated from another.

## THIRD AGE

29. The third age of the world follows. In it, years are sought after the mention of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, through the Hebrews’ servitude in Egypt and the times of the Judges, because the years themselves are not everywhere plainly revealed in the fourteen generations which Matthew records from Abraham to David.

We say this so that no one may think it contradictory that one order of generations is maintained there and another order of authorities here, where the years are being sought. There the evident sequence is solely that of the generations, which extends to Christ; here only the truth of the years is set out, placing confidence in the years as indicators of the times.

30. Abraham, at the age of 100, fathered Isaac. Isaac, at the age of 60, fathered Jacob. Jacob, at the age of 90 [Col. 0582D], fathered Joseph. Joseph lived 110 years. The Hebrews’ servitude in Egypt lasted 144 years. Moses ruled the people in the wilderness for 40 years. Joshua, 27 years. Othniel, 40 years. Ehud, 80 years. Deborah, 40 years. Gideon, 40 years. Abimelech, 3 years. Tola, 23 years. Jair, 22 years. Jephthah, 7 years. Ibzan, 7 years. Abdon, 8 years. Samson, 20 years. Eli the priest, 40 years. Samuel and Saul, 40 years.

## FOURTH AGE

31. If in this fourth age something perhaps seems contradictory to anyone because the number of fourteen generations contained in Matthew is not preserved here, let him observe that Matthew omitted three kings between King Joram and Joatham, omitting Athaliah, whereas here they are included with their years and are removed from the Gospel. This was because Joram had allied himself by marriage with the most wicked Jezebel, and for that reason his memory is removed down to the third generation, so that he might not be placed in the succession of the holy birth.

It is also especially appropriate to consider that there were more successions but fewer generations. The periods of the kings are not the same as the generations. Hence Matthew passed over those whom he did not judge to belong to the genealogy. In this way, I say, the number of fourteen generations will remain unproblematic down to Jeconiah.

32. David, 40 years. Solomon, 40 years. Rehoboam, 17 years. Abijah, 3 years. Asa, 41 years. Jehoshaphat, 25 years. Joram, 8 years. Ahaziah, 1 year. Athaliah, 7 years. Joash, 40 years. Amaziah, 29 years. Uzziah, 52 years [Col. 0583C]. Jotham, 6 years. Ahaz, 26 years. Hezekiah, 29 years. Manasseh, 55 years. Amon, 12 years. Josiah, 32 years. Jehoiakim, who is also Jeconiah, 11 years. Zedekiah, 11 years.

## FIFTH AGE

33. The fifth age extends from the Babylonian captivity to Christ. Matthew follows it through six generations, because, among the forefathers themselves, who were situated in captivity, it is not easily known how many years each one lived. Therefore the number of years in this age down to Christ is better established by learning the histories of the nations.

The captivity of the Hebrews lasted 70 years. Darius, 34 years. During his reign the captivity of the Jews ended. Xerxes, 20 years. Artaxerxes, 40 years. Darius [Note: Namely, Nothus, designated by this surname by Isidore and Mellitus in their Chronicles in order to distinguish him from the other Dariuses.], 19 years. Artaxerxes, 40 years. Artaxerxes [Note: Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, as the same Isidore and Mellitus name him in their Chronicles.], 26 years. Xerxes [Note: Xerxes is also read in Isidore, Book V of the Etymologies, but the Chronicles give the better form, as does Mellitus: Arses, son of Ochus.], 4 years. Darius [Note: Mellitus appropriately added that this Darius was the son of Arsames, to distinguish him from others of the same name.], 6 years. Alexander, 5 years. Ptolemy, 40 years. Philadelphus [Col. 0584A], 38 years. Euergetes, 26 years. Philopator, 17 years. Epiphanes, 24 years. Philometor, 35 years. Euergetes, 29 years. Soter, 17 years. Alexander, 10 years. Ptolemy, 8 years. Dionysius, 30 years. Cleopatra, 2 years. Julius Caesar, 5 years.

## SIXTH AGE

34. “Octavius [Note: This is how the editors of the Library of the Fathers published it; others have Octavianus, as do Mellitus and Saint Isidore in the Etymologies, but the Chronicle has Octavius. Isidore of Pax, who translates the words in question, has: ‘Octavianus … reigns,’ and so forth.] Caesar reigned for 56 years. In his forty-first year, according to the testimony of Tertullian and Jerome, Christ the Son of God was born of Mary ever-virgin,” and he was crucified during the reign of the emperor Tiberius, who reigned for 24 years.

From the beginning of the world, therefore, to the time of Christ’s birth, when it was the forty-first year of Octavian Caesar, there are 5,325 years. The remaining number of years from the time of Christ’s birth to the present is readily available to anyone who wishes to know and calculate it, taking the years according to the era from the Lord’s incarnation itself.

The era was established 38 years before Christ was born. It is now said that the era is 724. Therefore, subtracting the 38 years from the establishment of the era to the birth of Christ, 686 years remain. How many years the remaining period of this sixth age—that is, from the present day to the very hour of the end of the world—will extend, is known to God alone.

But now glory be to the only-begotten Christ, the Son of God, through whom that most vain opinion of yours is meanwhile plainly exposed and rejected: the opinion by which you both continue to await the sixth age of the world and pretend that this world is to last for only 6,000 years—years which you will prove already to have passed if you pay closer attention.

What you have heard must therefore be repeated.

35. We have said that from the beginning of the world to Christ there were 5,325 years. If to these are added the 686 years from the Lord’s incarnation to the present day—that is, to the time when the most serene prince Ervig is seen to be in the sixth year of his reign—the total is 6,011 years.

If you wish to calculate according to the histories of others, you may perhaps establish an even greater and more extensive number of years. Thus, I say, once 6,000 years have passed, what can you do now, false Judaism, when, having lost your kingdom and priesthood, you are dragged into error and, ignorant of the order of the generations, place your confidence regarding the future solely in the years?

Behold, you have been defeated and convicted in many ways concerning the sixth age of the world and the birth of Christ, which has already taken place. You will find nothing true to answer, because you are overcome both by the ages, once the order of the generations has been disclosed according to your own books, and by the total number of years, by which you are plainly overthrown according to the books of the common edition.

O how pitiable is your error! No prophetic history helps you; no historical sequence confirms you. You no longer see your signs; “there is no prophet any more” (Psalm LXXIII, 9). For he has commanded the clouds “not to rain rain upon you” (Isaiah V, 6). And you still say that Christ is to be born?

“I await him,” you will say, “who came into the world long ago.”

You greatly err, you are greatly foolish, you snore deeply. You have fallen grievously, O Israel; you have been struck, shattered, and crushed by your iniquities. You have lost the way. Follow the way, therefore, so that by the way you may come to salvation. Amen.

# THE TWO BOOKS OF SAINT JULIAN, BISHOP OF TOLEDO, OF ΑΝΤΙΚΕΙΜΕΝΩΝ—that is, OF CONTRADICTORY OR OPPOSING PASSAGES APPARENTLY FOUND IN BOTH TESTAMENTS

Recovered from an ancient Fulda manuscript and restored to its author.

[Col. 0585]

## PREFACE OF ANDREW SCOTUS, placed before his edition in the Cologne Great Library of the Ancient Fathers

In former times many men wrote investigations into questions concerning Sacred Scripture. Among them were Jerome and Augustine, the Church’s greatest lights. Yet the Questions on the Old and New Testaments circulated under Augustine’s name [Note: See the Benedictines’ admonition concerning this book of Questions in the Appendix to volume III of the Works of Saint Augustine, p. 34.] are not Augustine’s, but those of some heretic, as the most illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine teaches with many arguments.

Jurists strive to reconcile the Ἀντινομίαι, or “antinomies,” which they have collected from their own Digests and legal books. In sacred writings, however, as in God’s word and speech—which is itself truth—there are in reality no contradictions, but only apparent ones, which theologians of orthodox faith can easily resolve and reconcile from the holy Fathers.

An anonymous author also once appeared in this field under the title Ἀντικειμένων, that is, “Two Books of Passages of Sacred Scripture Apparently in Conflict,” one concerning the Old Testament and the other concerning the New. Some person improperly divided these into three little books by separating the apostolic letters from the Gospels, although together these constitute the New Testament.

Recently, while reading the works of the blessed Isidore and Hildefonsus on the sacred writers of the Church, we observed in the Appendix to the work of Felix that a little book by an uncertain author concerning the writings of Julian, bishop of Toledo, should be attributed to this Julian—namely, the Ἀντικειμένων—which we now at last restore to its birthplace and its proper parent, following Felix’s authority.

For he says:

> “Julian also wrote a book on Contradictions, which he wished to title Ἀντικειμένων in Greek. It is divided into two books, of which the first contains discussions concerning the Old Testament and the second concerning the New.”

Thus far Felix the Spaniard.

I remember that this little work was published by the jurist Johannes Alexander Brassicanus at Basel in 1530. Ten years later it was published at Cologne by Cervicornus from a manuscript, if I am not mistaken, of very great antiquity from Fulda. It was also printed at Paris together with Junilius on Genesis.

Seraphinus Cumiranus of Feltre, of the household of the companions of Saint Francis, later treated the same subject under the following title for a two-book work: Reconciliation of the Common Passages of Sacred Scripture That Appear to Conflict with One Another.

He wonderfully illuminated the field he had undertaken. For us, it is enough to have pointed out, as it were with a finger, the father and author. Farewell.

[Col. 0585]

## NOTICE OF THE SPANISH EDITOR

There are only a few things we need to say to the reader after Andrew Scotus, but we must by no means pass over in silence the fact that this little work had often been published before his time without the author’s name, and that he was the first to point out its true parent, as he himself says, almost with his finger.

We congratulate him on this. But what he stated somewhat cautiously, we assert as entirely established and indisputable: that no one other than our Julian was the author of this little work.

No one, indeed, has hitherto doubted that Saint Julian wrote the Ἀντικειμένων of Sacred Scripture, divided into two books, as testified by Felix, his successor. That the work we are editing is itself this treatise is shown beyond further doubt by the Apologeticus of Samson, abbot of the monastery of Pinamelaria in Baetica and parish priest of the church of Saint Zoilus, written in 864 against Hostegesis—a work published a few years ago by P. Florez in volume XI of España Sagrada.

His testimony is of such a kind that no one can resist it. For in that work the little book of Saint Julian of Toledo, the Ἀντικειμένων, is praised more than once. Not only this, but the very words themselves occur, just as they are found in the questions and answers—namely, as we also note in their places, in Questions 16, 59, 115, and 129 of the first book, and Question 48 of the second book.

By this most lucid evidence all the difficulties disappear which seemed to Guillelmus Cave and Fabricius to make the present question concerning the true author of this book exceedingly complicated.

Therefore, if there are manuscript books in Italy—such as those which Joannes Baptista Maro testifies to exist in the Anician Library, and which the archbishop of Rossano, Angelo de la Nuce, reports to exist at Monte Cassino—with the name of Saint Bertharius, who was abbot of Monte Cassino in 856 and died in 883, they should be said either to bear his name because they were copied under his care or by his work, or to contain different questions under the same title, or questions explained in different ways. Both situations are extremely common, as no one at all is unaware.

Certainly, anything else should be devised before we deprive Julian of this little work in the face of the unmistakable testimonies of Felix and Samson.

As for the present edition, since the Lyon edition of the Library of the Fathers, which alone we had at hand, was riddled with numerous errors, we took care to compare and correct the sayings of the Fathers woven throughout the entire work against better editions of their writings. We did this soberly and cautiously, keeping before our eyes the fact that Saint Julian sometimes reports not the words of the sayings so much as their meaning.

Nor did we invariably correct the words themselves whenever they differed from the printed editions, because very often Saint Julian’s reading is plausible and sometimes more probable. No one can doubt that Saint Julian had handled highly corrected manuscripts of the holy Fathers.

We then corrected the previously disordered sequence of the questions, so that henceforth the questions would follow not only the order of the books of Sacred Scripture but also the order of the chapters within each book.

In addition, from Samson’s Apologeticus we supplied Question 70 of Book I, which he cites in chapter 24 of Book II and which was missing from the other editions.

Finally, we omitted nothing that could make the edition as complete as possible.

[Col. 0587]

# [LIBRI II ANTIKEIMENON.(C)]

## ΑΝΤΙΚΕΙΜΕΝΩΝ—THAT IS, OF CONTRARIES OR OPPOSITES—BOOK ONE

Containing, in concise form, questions from the Old Testament that appear to conflict, together with clear solutions to them.

## FROM THE BOOK OF GENESIS

[Col. 0595A]

## QUESTION I (Elsewhere 3)

How is evening and morning recorded as having occurred during those first days, when the stars by which days are distinguished from nights were made on the fourth day? For on the fourth day the Lord is read as saying: “Let there be stars in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth, and divide between day and night, and let them be for signs, seasons, days, and years” (Gen. I, 14). How, then, had God already divided between day and night, if the stars accomplish this on the fourth day?

## ANSWER

We must understand that during those three days, which existed without sun or moon, the distinctions of the works themselves were named within the duration of time: “evening” [Col. 0595B] because the completed work had passed, and “morning” because the future work was beginning. This was based, of course, on the analogy of human works, since most people begin in the morning and finish toward evening. But what is said on the fourth day—“Let them divide between day and night,” and the rest—we should understand as though it said: “Let them divide day and night among themselves in such a way that day belongs to the sun, while night belongs to the moon and the other stars.” Thus, during those three days, a division had already been made between night and day, but not yet among the stars, so that it might now be certain to human beings what would appear through the stars as day and what as night.

## QUESTION II (Elsewhere 4)

Since Genesis does not say that God founded the earth on the sixth day, but only that he made the animals [Col. 0595C] and the human being (Gen. I, 24 ff.), how does the Psalmist, in the title of Psalm 92, seem to say the opposite: “A praise-song, by David, for the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded”?

## AUGUSTINE’S ANSWER (Enarration on Psalm 92, no. 1)

> [Note: [Col. 0595C] Editor: “Thus, just as God made the human being on the sixth day . . . so we find that the Lord came in the sixth age . . . so that he might be restored,” etc.] “On the sixth day God made the human being in his own image; and in the sixth age the Lord Jesus Christ came, so that the human being might be restored to the image of God. For the first period, like the first day, extended from Adam to Noah; [Col. 0596A] [Note: [Col. 0595C] Editor: “The second period, like the second day, from Noah,” etc.] the second from Noah to Abraham; the third period, like the third day, from Abraham to David; [Note: [Col. 0595C] Editor: “The fourth period, like the fourth day, from David to,” etc.] the fourth up to the Babylonian captivity; [Note: [Col. 0595C] Editor: “The fifth period, like the fifth day, from the Babylonian captivity to,” etc.] the fifth up to the preaching of John; [Note: [Col. 0596C] Editor: “The sixth day is now being lived from the preaching of John to the end.”] the sixth period, like the sixth day, from John to the end. [Note: [Col. 0596C] These words up to Paul’s statement are not found in Augustine.] On this sixth day Christ was born of the Virgin; on this day the spiritual earth was founded, that is, the Church. For no one can lay a foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus (I Cor. III, 11). Therefore, when all who believe throughout the whole earth are immovable in faith, the earth has been founded, and then the human being is made in the image of God, [Note: [Col. 0596C] You will not find there, ‘because there,’ etc.] because there he was formed.”

## QUESTION III (Elsewhere 5)

Since the angels were created on the first day and the human being on the sixth (Gen. [Col. 0596B] I, 26 ff.), how does the Lord speak to Job as though he had created the angel and the human being together? For he says: “Behold Behemoth, which I made with you” (Job XL, 10).

## GREGORY’S ANSWER (Book XXXII of the Moralia, no. 17)

> “They were created together, not by unity of time, but by the knowledge of reason. [Note: [Col. 0596C] After ‘reason,’ the edition adds: ‘together through the image of wisdom received, and not together through the joined substance of form. It is written,’ etc.] For it is written concerning the human being: ‘Let us make the human being in our image and likeness’ (Gen. I, 26). And through Ezekiel it is said to Satan: ‘You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God’ (Ezek. XXVIII, 12, 13). Therefore, in the whole creation the human being and the angel existed as created together, because the human being proceeded distinct from every irrational creature.”

## QUESTION IV (Elsewhere 14)

Since it is written in Genesis: “God made the human being in his image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26, 27), how does the prophet in Psalm 70, as though the human being had not been formed in God’s likeness, say: “God, who is like you?” (ibid., 19)?

## ANSWER

It is one thing if someone perversely wishes to become like God—that is, through pride, like the devil, who said: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14)—and another if, through obedience and fulfillment of his commandments, he bears God’s likeness [Col. 0597A] within himself. For when the human being, persuaded by the devil, perversely wished to become like God, he became captive under his deceiver. Behold, the one who had fallen from him cries out here and says: “God, who is like you?” For in that captive human being the likeness of God had perished, when through pride he desired to be like God.

But God makes us in his likeness when he urges us to cling to his commandments, when he wishes us to become such as he himself is, when through his Scripture he cries out: “Be holy, because I too am holy” (Lev. XI, 44). Likewise, when he says: “Love your enemies, pray for those who persecute you, do good to those who hate you” (Matt. V, 44), he urges us toward his likeness. Finally, what does he add? “So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” [Col. 0597B] (ibid., 45). What, then? Does he himself do this? Certainly he does, because he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust. Whoever, therefore, wishes well to his enemy is like God; and this is not pride but obedience.

Why? Because we were made in the image of God. Therefore, whoever wishes to be so like God as to stand close to him should guard his strength by him, as it is written (Ps. LVIII, 10), and not depart from him: by cleaving to him, let him be marked as though by a seal-ring upon wax. In this way he will truly guard the image to which he was made.

But if he perversely wishes to imitate God, so that, just as God has no one by whom he is ruled, he himself wishes to exercise power by his own authority, what remains except that, departing from God’s warmth, he should grow numb? Having in a certain sense become alien from the image of God, let him cry out as a captive: “Lord, who is like [Col. 0597C] you?” It is as though it were said: “Behold, I perversely wished to be like you, and I became like a beast. For under your dominion I was truly like you; but the human being, placed in honor, did not understand. He was compared with senseless animals and became like them.” [Note: [Col. 0597D] Editor: “He understood; he was compared; and he became like them.”]
