Now, therefore, no longer placed in the likeness of God but established in the likeness of beasts, he cries out when he says: “God, who is like you?” (From Augustine, Sermon 2 on Psalm 70, nos. 6–7.)

## QUESTION V (Elsewhere 12)

Since it is written: “All things were very good” (Gen. I, 31), how are certain animals called unclean in the law (Lev. XI, 4 ff.)?

## ANSWER

They were called unclean with respect to use, not creation; for it is understood that the law divinely prohibited their use as food on account of certain figures.

[Col. 0598A]

## QUESTION VI (Elsewhere 13)

Since in Genesis all things are called very good (Gen. I, 31), and many other things later are also judged under the name of goodness, and Christ likewise declares in the Gospel both a good person and a good servant (Luke VI, 45; Matt. XXV, 21, 23), why does the same Lord speak in the opposite way: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark X, 18)?

## ANSWER

There is no doubt that all the things that Scripture declares good are good in themselves. Yet if we look to the goodness of God, none of them will be pronounced good, since the Lord says: “No one is good except God alone.” In view of this, even the apostles themselves—who by the merit of their election had surpassed the goodness of the human race in many [Col. 0598B] ways—are called evil, as the Lord says to them: “If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (Matt. VII, 11).

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Samson the abbot transferred this question into Apologeticus, Book II, chapter 21, no. 7, or page 479 of volume XI of the Spanish Sacred Works.]

## QUESTION VII (Elsewhere 16)

Since God is not the author or creator of evil, as Scripture says (Gen. I, 31) that he created all things very good, how does the Lord himself speak through Isaiah as though saying the opposite: “I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evils” (Isa. XLV, 7)?

## ANSWER

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Supplied from Samson: “If all things were created good by a good creator, how does the Lord declare that he creates evils? But if these two points are considered more carefully, they will not be contrary to one another. For the Lord, creator of creatures, created all things good, and these certainly cannot be called evil by nature. Behold, therefore, the good God according to,” etc.]

The good God, as is read in Genesis, created all things good. But the evils that he said he creates, he did not likewise declare that he creates by nature. [Col. 0598C] For God does not create evils (Gregory the Great, Moralia, Book III, no. 15), which have no existence by any nature of their own. Rather, the Lord indicates that he creates evils when he forms well-created things into a scourge for us when we act badly: so that those same things are evils to sinners through the pain with which they strike, but good through the nature by which they exist. Thus poison is death to a human being, but life to a serpent.

It is rightly said: “Forming light and creating darkness,” because when the darkness of pain is created outwardly through scourges, the light of the mind is kindled inwardly through instruction. “Making peace and creating evils,” because peace with God is restored to us when those things that were well created but not rightly desired are turned into scourges that are evil for us. Through guilt we exist in discord with God. [Note: [Col. 0598D] Gregory: “we existed.”] It is therefore fitting [Col. 0598D] that through scourges we return to his peace, so that whenever something well created is turned into pain for us, the corrected mind may be humbly restored to the peace of its creator.

[Col. 0599A]

## QUESTION VIII (Elsewhere 1)

Since the first seven days are read in Genesis, during which God completed the whole creation, according to what is written: “And he rested on the seventh day from all his work” (Gen. II, 2), how does the same passage, in contrast, later mention only one day on which the entire created order of the world was made? For it says: “These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created, on the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth and every plant of the field” (ibid., 4), etc.

## ANSWER

The one who earlier related that everything was created day by day—how could he then add that everything was created together on one day, unless he wished plainly to show that the whole creation existed together in substance, but did not come forth together in form? The origin of things [Col. 0599B] was created together (Gregory the Great, Moralia, Book XXXII, no. 16), but their form was not fashioned together; and what existed together through the substance of matter did not appear together through the substance [Note: [Col. 0599D] Editor: “form.”] of form.

When it is said that heaven and earth were made together [Note: [Col. 0599D] Editor: “described”], it indicates that spiritual and bodily things were made together, together with everything that arises from heaven and everything produced from the earth. For the stars are said to have been made in heaven on the fourth day [Note: [Col. 0599D] Editor: “The sun, moon, and stars were made on the fourth day,” etc.]. But what came forth in form on the fourth day already existed in the substance of heaven through creation on the first day.

Likewise, the earth is said to have been created on the first day [Note: [Col. 0599D] Editor: “created on the first day,” etc.], while on the third day the shrubs and all the earth’s green growth are said to have been made [Note: [Col. 0599D] Editor: “described.”]. But what appeared in form on the third day had been created on the first day in the substance of the earth itself [Note: [Col. 0600D] Editor: “brought forth in form on the first day itself,” etc.] from which it arose.

[Note: [Col. 0600D] From “It is written” up to “together” is absent from the edition.] For it is written: [Col. 0599C] “He who lives forever created all things together” (Eccli. XVIII, 1).

## QUESTION IX (Elsewhere 7)

Since it is written in Genesis: “On the seventh day God rested from all his work” (ch. II, 2), how does Christ, in contrast, say in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V, 17)?

## ANSWER

He rested on the seventh day because thereafter he made no new creature. He works until now because he makes everything from those things that he made during those six mystical days: for what he then created in its beginnings, he now governs and directs through his power. Therefore, he rested from creating the kinds of creatures, but he did not cease [Col. 0599D] from the work of governing or administering everything he created.

## QUESTION X (Elsewhere 2)

Since the Genesis narrative says that the human being was created on the sixth day, how is it written there after the creation of the human being, or after the sequence of the seven days: “For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no human being to work it” (Gen. II, 5)? Why was there no human being to work the earth, when he had already been made on the sixth day?

## ANSWER

[Col. 0600A]

This is recalled by way of recapitulation: when God made the green plants of the field, it had not yet rained, and the human being had not yet been made.

## QUESTION XI (Elsewhere 15)

Since, when God made the human being, Genesis simply states: “God made the human being from the clay of the earth” (Gen. II, 7), how does the Psalmist say: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Ps. CXVIII, 73)?

## AUGUSTINE’S ANSWER (Sermon 18 on that Psalm, no. 1)

> “Why some people thought that God made the other things by his word, but made the human being, as something especially important, with his hands, I do not see—unless perhaps they think that, because the human body is read to have been formed from dust, [Col. 0600B] it could not have been made except by hands. They do not consider that what is written in the Gospel about the Word of God—‘All things were made through him’ (John I, 3)—cannot stand if the human body too was not made through the Word.
>
> “But they produce the testimony of the psalm [Note: [Col. 0600D] Editor: ‘of this psalm’] and say: ‘Behold, here the human being cries out most plainly: “Your hands made me and fashioned me”’ [Note: [Col. 0600D] Editor: “formed me”], as though it had not also been plainly said: ‘I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers’ (Ps. VIII, 4), and: ‘The heavens are the works of your hands’ (Ps. CI, 26), and, much more plainly: ‘His hands formed the dry land’ (Ps. XCIV, 5).
>
> “The hands, therefore, are the power of God. Or, if the plural number troubles them, because it does not say ‘your hand’ but ‘your hands,’ let them understand the hands of God as the power and wisdom of God (I Cor. I, 24), both of which are called one—Christ—[Col. 0600C] who is also understood as the arm of the Lord, where it is written: ‘And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’ (Isa. LIII, 1).
>
> “Or let them understand the hands of God as the Son and the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit too is a co-worker with the Father and the Son. Hence the Apostle says: ‘All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes’ (I Cor. XII, 11). For this reason he said ‘one,’ lest they think that there are as many spirits as there are works—not because the Spirit works without the Father and the Son.”

## QUESTION XII (Elsewhere 6)

Since, after the creation of Adam, Scripture specifically says: “God cast a sleep upon Adam, and took one of his ribs, and filled up flesh in its place, and God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman” [Col. 0600D] (Gen. II, 21, 22), how can the woman be said to have been created at the same time as the man, since the same Scripture says of the sixth day: “God created the human being in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he made them” (Gen. I, 27)? Behold, on the sixth day Eve is described as not yet having been made, and yet the human being is already said to be male and female.

## ANSWER

Since without doubt a female was going to proceed from Adam’s side, she was already counted in him then according to [Col. 0601A] substance, from whom she was to be produced according to form.

## QUESTION XIII (Elsewhere 10)

Since in Genesis the earlier statement concerning bodily marriage was spoken by the Lord, when he wished the woman to be subjected to the man, saying: “Your desire shall be toward him, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III, 16), how does the Lord, in contrast, speak to Abraham: “Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice” (Gen. XXI, 12)?

## ANSWER
The first statement, certainly, was uttered by the Lord concerning bodily marriage, where the wife is commanded to obey her husband. Nothing contrary to it is said here, because this does not appear to have been said about bodily marriage; rather, Sarah is here presented as a wife in the sense of the virtue of the soul, which each man is always commanded to heed—that is, whatever the virtue of our soul has suggested should be done, it should be carried out for us in every respect as though by strong men—while that statement about bodily marriage remains in force, namely, that the wife should always be subject to her husband.

## QUESTION XIV (also 8)

Since the Lord said to Noah, “The days of man shall be 120 years” (Gen. VI, 3), how is it that, contrary to this decree, men are subsequently found to have lived many more years—for example, when Jacob, questioned by Pharaoh, replied that he was 130 years old (Gen. XLVII, 9)?

### ANSWER

This should not be understood as though it had been foretold that thereafter men would not exceed 120 years of life, since we find that even after the Flood some exceeded 500 years. Rather, we must understand that God said this when Noah was approaching the end of his five hundredth year, that is, when he was completing 480 years of life—years which Scripture, according to its custom, calls “five hundred,” often signifying the largest part by naming the whole. For the Flood occurred in Noah’s six-hundredth year, in the second month (Gen. VII, 11). Thus the 120 years foretold were to be the remaining years of the lives of the people of that earlier age, after which they would be destroyed by the Flood.

## QUESTION XV (also 22)

Since clean and unclean animals were distinguished by divine law through Moses (Lev. XI, 2 ff.), how is it that, even before the Flood, the animals that were to be received into the ark are called unclean (Gen. VII, 2)?

### ANSWER

[Col. 0601D] Moses, inspired by the Holy Spirit, is the writer and author of the Pentateuch. And because a distinction between clean and unclean animals was to be set forth in Leviticus, he also called the same animals unclean in Genesis, since both books have the same author.

## QUESTION XVI (also 20)

Since in Genesis (Gen. IX, 4) and in other passages of Scripture God prohibited the Israelite people from eating blood—and especially in Leviticus, where the Lord says, “I said to the children of Israel: You shall not eat the blood of any flesh” (Lev. VII, 26)—how is it that, on the contrary, the Book of Numbers says of that same Israelite people: “He shall not lie down until he has eaten the prey and drunk the blood of the slain” (Num. XXIII, 24)?

### ANSWER

[Col. 0602A]

Let the Jews now say who this people is that makes a practice of drinking blood. For these were the things that, when they heard them in the Gospel, caused them to take offense, and they said: “Who can eat flesh and drink blood?” (John VI, 53). But the Christian people hear these words, embrace them, and follow him who says: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in yourselves; for my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (ibid., 54, 56). And certainly, because he said these things, he was wounded for our sins, as Isaiah says (Isa. LIII, 5).

We say that we drink the blood of Christ not only through the rite of the sacraments, but also when we receive his words, in which life consists, [Col. 0602B] just as he himself said: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John VI, 64). He, therefore, is the one who was wounded, whose blood we drink—that is, whose words of teaching we receive. Yet those who preached his word to us were also wounded, and when we read the words of these men also—that is, of his apostles—and obtain life from them, we drink the blood of the wounded.

## QUESTION XVII (also 9)

Since in Genesis God says to Abraham, “Know assuredly that your seed will be a sojourner in a land not its own, and they will reduce them to slavery and afflict them for 400 years” (Gen. XV, 13), how is it that, on the contrary, Exodus says: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they dwelt in Egypt, was 430 years” (Exod. XII, 40)?

### ANSWER

If these two passages are calculated more precisely, the children of Israel did not remain in Egypt under slavery for either 430 years or merely 400 years, provided the calculation is made from the very day on which Jacob or his sons entered Egypt to the final day on which they departed from there under the leadership of Moses. For it is clear that, according to the calculation of Eusebius, all the years that the Hebrews spent in Egypt amounted to 115 (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, under the year 3260 from the creation of the world).

From Abraham’s first promise, however—that is, from the seventy-fifth year of his life—until the time when Jacob entered Egypt with his sons, there were 215 years. After Jacob’s entry into Egypt, until the time when all the children of Israel went out of Egypt amid signs and wonders, another 215 years are calculated; these, added together, make 430.

Thus, so that the two passages may not disagree, if you calculate from Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, when the promise was first made to him, until the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, you will find 430 years. But if you gather the total from Isaac’s fifth year until the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, from the time when Isaac, still a little child and certainly the seed of Abraham, began to be afflicted by Ishmael, you will find 400 years, as the Lord said.

Augustine likewise writes as follows (*City of God*, book XVI, chapter 24):

> “What was said to Abraham—‘Know assuredly that he will be a sojourner,’ and the rest—was most clearly prophesied concerning the people of Israel, who were to be enslaved in Egypt. It was not that this people was to spend 400 years in that slavery under the Egyptians who afflicted them, but that within those 400 years this future event was foretold. Just as it is written concerning Terah, Abraham’s father: ‘The days of Terah in Harran were 205 years’ (Gen. XI, 32), not because all those years were spent there, but because they were completed there, so here too it is said: ‘They will reduce them to slavery and afflict them for 400 years,’ because that number was completed in the affliction, not because the whole period was spent there. Four hundred years are mentioned on account of the fullness of the number, although the actual period is somewhat longer, whether it is calculated from the time when these things were promised to Abraham or from the time when Isaac was born, on account of Abraham’s seed concerning whom these things were foretold. Thus, as we said above, from Abraham’s promise until Israel’s departure there are 430 years. The Apostle refers to these as follows: ‘Now this I say: the covenant confirmed by God was not annulled by the law, which came 430 years afterward, so as to cancel the promise’ [Note: [Col. 0603D] Editor’s text: “which was made 430 years afterward.”] (Gal. III, 17). These 430 years, therefore, could then be called 400, since they are not very much more. How much more readily could they be so called once some part of that number had already passed, since those words were shown and spoken to Abraham in a vision?”

[Note: [Col. 0603D] Editor’s text: “From Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, when the first promise was made to him, until Israel’s departure from Egypt, there were 430 years; of these, etc.”]

## QUESTION XVIII (also 17)

How was it promised to Abraham that the children of Israel would leave the land of Egypt in the fourth generation (Gen. XV, 16), when Moses says, “The children of Israel went out of Egypt in the fifth generation” (Exod. XIII, 18, according to the Septuagint)?

### ANSWER

If you count the fourth generation, you will begin counting it from the tribe of Levi; if the fifth, from Judah. Consider, therefore, the genealogy of Levi. Levi fathered Kohath; Kohath fathered Amram; Amram fathered Aaron; Aaron fathered Eleazar; and Eleazar fathered Phinehas. Kohath entered Egypt with his father Levi. Again, Eleazar departed from Egypt with his father Aaron. From Kohath to Eleazar there are four generations.

If, therefore, you wish to show how, according to Exodus, the children of Israel went out of the land of Egypt in the fifth generation, let the order of the tribe of Judah be counted for you. Judah fathered Perez; Perez, Hezron; Hezron, Aram; Aram, Amminadab; Amminadab, Nahshon; and Nahshon, Salmon. Perez entered Egypt with his father Judah. Nahshon is described as the prince of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, while his son Salmon entered the Promised Land. From Perez, therefore, to Nahshon there are five generations. Some, however, begin with Hezron and proceed to Salmon. The same calculation applies from Amram to Phinehas. Thus Jerome (*Letter 125 to Damasus*, question 2).

## QUESTION XIX (also 11)

Since, before the birth of the two brothers Esau and [Col. 0604A] Jacob, the Spirit of God says concerning them in Genesis, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. XXV, 23), how is it that, according to the history of that same book, the younger worshiped the elder—that is, when Jacob, the younger, returned from Mesopotamia, he worshiped Esau, his elder brother (Gen. XXXIII, 3)?

### ANSWER

The statement “The elder shall serve the younger” does not obstruct the truth of the historical account; rather, the Spirit of God foretold it figuratively. Accordingly, the Jewish people are signified by Esau and the Christian people by Jacob. They are therefore not contradictory: according to the historical account, the younger worshiped the elder; according to the allegorical sense, the elder served the younger.

## QUESTION XX (also 18)

Since Jacob testifies in Genesis that he saw God [Col. 0604B] (Gen. XXXII, 30), how does the Evangelist John say, “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18), while Job also agrees with him, saying, “The wisdom of God is hidden from the eyes of all the living” (Job XXVIII, 21)?

### ANSWER (from Gregory, *Moralia*, book XVIII, nos. 88–89)

Jacob saw God [Note: [Col. 0604D] Editor’s text, in both places: “the Lord”], for he said: “I have seen God face to face” (Gen., cited above). Moses saw God, concerning whom it is written: “The Lord spoke with Moses face to face” (Exod. XXXIII, 11), and so forth. Job also saw the Lord, for he said: “But now my eye sees you” (Job XLII, 5). Isaiah saw the Lord, who said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and elevated throne” (Isa. VI, 1). Micah also saw the Lord, who said: “I saw the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0604D] Editors add “sitting”] “upon his throne” (1 Kings XXII, 19).

What, then, does it mean that so many fathers of the Old Testament testified that they had seen God, while it is said of that wisdom which is God, “It is hidden from the eyes of all the living,” and John says, “No one has ever seen God,” unless it is plainly understood that, as long as one lives here in mortality, God can be seen through certain images, but cannot be seen through the very form of his nature? Thus the soul, inspired by the grace of the Spirit, sees God through certain figures, but does not reach his very essence [Note: [Col. 0604D] Editor’s text: “the very power of his essence.”]

For this reason Jacob, who testifies that he saw God, saw him only in an angel. For this reason Moses, who speaks with God face to face, says amid the very words of his conversation: “If I have found grace in your sight, show me yourself” (Exod. XXXIII, 13). Certainly, if the one with whom he was speaking was not God, he would have said, “Show me God,” and not, “Show yourself.” But if the one with whom he was speaking was God, why did he ask to see the one whom he was seeing? From this request of his it is gathered that he thirsted to behold, through the unbounded splendor of God’s nature, the one whom he had begun to see through certain images.

They therefore saw the Lord, and yet, according to John’s voice, no one has ever seen God, because those living in mortal flesh could see him through certain bounded images, but cannot see him through the unbounded light of eternity. But if, while still living in this corruptible flesh, some holy people can see him through a certain keenness of contemplation, this too does not conflict with the statement of blessed Job that we have cited, nor with that of the Evangelist John, “No one has ever seen God.” For whoever sees the wisdom that is God dies completely to this life, so that he may no longer be held by love of it.

No one who still lives according to the flesh sees him [Note: [Col. 0605D] Editor’s text: “No one who still lives according to the flesh saw her”], because no one can embrace God and the world at the same time. For the one who sees God dies precisely insofar as, either in the intention of his heart or in the accomplishment [Note: [Col. 0605D] We have substituted “accomplishment” for “affection,” following Gregory.] of his deeds, he separates himself entirely in mind from the delights of this life.

## QUESTION XXI

Since in Genesis and Exodus only seventy souls are said to have entered Egypt with Jacob (Gen. XLVI, 27; [Col. 0605B] Exod. I, 5), how is it that the Acts of the Apostles reports that seventy-five souls entered Egypt with Jacob (Acts VII, 14)?

### ANSWER

It is established that only seventy souls entered Egypt with Joseph, Ephraim, and Manasseh. Where the number seventy-five souls is reported, the writer seems, by anticipation, to have counted also the sons and grandsons of Ephraim and Manasseh, whom the account of sacred Scripture shows to have been born later in Egypt.

## QUESTION XXII (also 19)

Since, among the other patriarchs and prophets who promised Christ’s coming, Jacob specifically proclaims the incarnation of Christ and the calling of the nations, saying: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10), how does Paul say in his Letter to the Ephesians, concerning the same mystery of Christ’s incarnation: “In other generations it was not made known to the sons of men as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit, that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and fellow participants in the promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel” (Eph. III, 5–6)?

### ANSWER (from Jerome’s Commentary on this chapter of the Letter to the Ephesians)

> “Either this must be the answer: Paul carefully and expressly testified that the mystery was unknown to the sons of men, not to the sons of God, to whom it is said: ‘I said: You are gods’ (Ps. LXXXI, 6). That is, those who received the Spirit of adoption—including the patriarchs and prophets—knew the mystery of God.
>
> “Or it must be noted that Paul did not say definitively and generally that the Lord’s mystery had been entirely unknown in other generations, but that the ancient patriarchs and prophets did not know it in the manner in which it has now been revealed to his saints and apostles. For it is one thing to know future events in the Spirit, and another to see them accomplished in reality.”

Hence John is also called greater than all the prophets (Matt. XI, 9), because he saw the one whom the others foretold and pointed him out with his finger.

This must also be understood from the fact that the same apostle teaches in the same letter [Col. 0606A] (Eph. III, 10) that this mystery was manifested through the Church not only to the Gentiles but also to the principalities and powers. For this reason the same Teacher continues, saying:

> “If the manifold wisdom of God, which has now been revealed to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places through the Church, was unknown to the principalities and powers, how much more was it unknown to the patriarchs and prophets? We have shown above that they did not fail to know the mystery of Christ, but knew it in such a way that they did not know it as the apostles did. For the manifold wisdom of God has now been revealed through the Church of God both to the principalities and to the powers. God had long ago determined it in his mind as something that would come to be, and now, from what we see, we recognize that it has been accomplished. The cross of Christ, therefore, benefited not only us but also the angels and all the powers in heaven, and it opened a mystery that they had previously not known.”

Thus Jerome.

## QUESTION XXIII (also 26)

Since in Exodus the Lord commands Moses, saying, “Remove the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III, 5), how is it that in the same book those eating the Passover are commanded: “You shall eat it with your loins girded, and you shall have your sandals on your feet” (Exod. XII, 11)? Moreover, Paul commands the Ephesians to have their feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace (Eph. VI, 15).

### ANSWER

If we understand that sandals are unnecessary for the perfect but still necessary for the imperfect, there may be no contradiction: the arrangement was established according to differences of merit. Those who, like Moses and Joshua son of Nun, have already been deemed worthy to see God are more perfect than those who are advancing toward that vision and who, still placed on the way, are commanded to eat the Passover lamb with sandals on their feet.

For these people sandals are perhaps still necessary, since the examples of good fathers are judged useful to those running along the way of the Lord.

> “For what are our feet except our deeds? And what are sandals except the skins of dead animals? Sandals protect the feet. What, then, are the dead animals from whose skins our feet are protected, except the ancient fathers who went before us to our eternal homeland? When we contemplate their example [Note: [Col. 0606D] Editor’s text: “examples we behold”], we protect the feet of our deeds. To have sandals on one’s feet is to contemplate the life of the dead and to guard our footsteps from the wound of sin, so that, protected by their example, we may cross the vast wilderness of this world until we see God face to face” (Gregory the Great, *Homily 22 on the Gospels*, no. 9).

Therefore, when people come perfectly to the Lord, these sandals will perhaps no longer be necessary, since the examples of the fathers will perhaps not be necessary where God is fully known by those who see him in all things.

If, however, sandals are also understood on account of vices, this likewise creates no contradiction, since no one can see God unless he has laid aside earthly and mortal vices. Let the one who is still walking have his feet shod; but let the one who has already crossed the Jordan and entered the Promised Land bare his foot and loosen his sandal, for the place on which he stands is holy ground.

If someone is not Joshua son of Nun or an apostle, let him shoe his feet in readiness for the Gospel of peace. But if someone is an apostle and can be numbered among the Twelve, let him by no means remove his sandal on the way, nor cover his heel in order to avoid scorpions and serpents. Rather, already perfected and complete, let him live in Christ in the holy land and follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

# FROM THE BOOK OF EXODUS

## QUESTION XXIV (also 23)

Since, when the Lord had disclosed his name to Moses in Exodus, he said, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III, 14), how is it that afterward he indicates, as though in opposition, that he has another name, saying: “Go, say to the children of Israel: ‘The God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob has sent me to you’; this is my name forever” (ibid., 15)?

### AUGUSTINE’S ANSWER

Augustine, by distinguishing the two, has taught us that one pertains to the nature of divinity and the other to the assumed humanity. When God said to Moses, “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me to you,” he signified the substance of divinity. But when he says, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” he indicates the mystery of the incarnation that was assumed, because he would be recognized as having been begotten from them according to the flesh, and it is understood that he placed their names here under the veil of a mystery.

## QUESTION XXV (also 29)

Since in the Book of Exodus the Lord commands, saying, “Remember that you sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days you shall labor and do all your work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God” (Exod. XX, 8 ff.), how does he say, on the contrary, through Isaiah: “Your Sabbaths my soul has hated” (Isa. I, 13)?

### ANSWER

“Sabbath” is interpreted as “rest.” The Israelites received this spiritually as a gift, so that, under this sign, they would not be wearied in this life by any desire for earthly things. Yet the Jewish people, not understanding that the Lord had given this command spiritually, spent their Sabbaths in luxury, drunkenness, and feasting.

Therefore the Lord says that he hates such Sabbaths, because they are not those that the Lord commanded spiritually, but those that the people chose for themselves carnally. For concerning them he said: “You profaned my Sabbaths” (Ezek. XXII, 8).

Thus we recognize that the temporal Sabbath is human, while the divine Sabbath is that eternal one of which Isaiah says: “From month to month, and from Sabbath to Sabbath” (Isa. LXVI, 23). Therefore, when he says, “Your Sabbaths my soul has hated,” he does not alter the oracle of the earlier commandment; rather, he rebukes the Sabbath corrupted by the carnal people.

## QUESTION XXVI (also 24)

Since among the Ten Commandments given in Exodus the fourth commandment is found to be, “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. XX, 12), how does Christ say conversely in the Gospel, “Honor your father and your mother,” which is the first commandment in the law?

### ANSWER

There were two tablets on which Moses received the Ten Commandments in writing. Of these Ten Commandments, the three placed first pertain to love of the divine Trinity, while the remaining seven pertain to love of one’s neighbor.

The three that pertain to love of God are these: “The Lord your God is one” (Deut. VI, 4); “You shall not take the name of your God in vain”; and “Remember that the Sabbath day be sanctified” (Exod. XX, 7–8). These three were written on one tablet.

On the second tablet the remaining seven commandments were written. Therefore, “Honor your father and your mother” was written as the first commandment among the seven. If you count all ten commandments together, you will find that this is the fourth among the Ten, for a person opens his eyes through his parents, and this life takes its beginning from love of them. Hence this commandment is first among the seven.

But how is it first if it is fourth? It is first, as has been said, because it is first on the other tablet. Or, because the Ten Commandments were given first, each one of them may be called the first commandment.

## QUESTION XXVII

Since in Exodus the Lord promised longevity of life to those who honor their parents, saying, “Honor your father and your mother, so that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived upon the land” (Exod. XX, 12), how did David regard this very longevity of life as insignificant, saying, “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX, 5)? Solomon, moreover, embraces death rather than life, saying, “I praised all the dead who have already died above the living” (Eccles. IV, 2); and Jeremiah says, “Cursed be the day on which I was born” (Jer. XX, 14)—especially since we believe that many who obeyed their parents died young, while the impious toward their parents lived into extreme old age?

### ANSWER

Let the Jews and those like the Jews answer: if the length of this life is what is promised, and dwelling in the body for a long time is happiness, what does David’s lament mean, that his sojourning in life has been prolonged? If, according to Solomon, the dead are praised above the living, and according to Jeremiah the day on which we are born is cursed, how is it now promised to those who honor father and mother that they will be long-lived upon the land that the Lord their God will give them?

The land that the Lord God promises and grants to those who have left spiritual Egypt and, with all great power, have crossed the terrible wildernesses of this life must therefore be sought. They will possess the land prepared for the meek. For “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. V, 4), which is truly the land of the living, according to the words: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI, 13).

## QUESTION XXVIII (also 25)

How is it written in Exodus, “You who repay the iniquity of the fathers upon their sons and grandsons” (Exod. XXXIV, 7), when, on the contrary, Ezekiel says:

> “What is this proverb that you turn into a saying among yourselves in the land of Israel, saying: ‘The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge’? As I live, says the Lord God, this proverb shall no longer be a proverb for you in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine: as the soul of the father is mine, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins, it shall itself be punished” (Ezek. XVIII, 2 ff.)?

### ANSWER

The sins of the fathers are repaid in the sons when, on account of the parents’ guilt, the soul of their offspring is polluted by original sin. And again, the sins of the parents are not repaid in the sons, because, once we have been freed from original guilt through baptism, we no longer bear the sins of our parents, but those that we ourselves commit.

# FROM THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS

## QUESTION XXIX (also 30)

Since in the Book of Leviticus the offering of sacrifices was instituted at the Lord’s command (Lev. I, 2 ff., and often elsewhere), how does Isaiah, speaking conversely in the voice of the Lord, say: “What do I want with the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord. I am full of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fattened animals; I have not desired the blood of calves and lambs” (Isa. I, 11)?

### ANSWER

Sacrifices and the offering of victims were not principally sought by God, but were instituted so that sacrifices would not be made to idols and so that, through carnal sacrifices as through a type and image, we might pass over to spiritual sacrifices. By saying that he had not sought a sacrifice, he shows that the law is spiritual and that all the things which the Jews do carnally are to be fulfilled by us spiritually.

## QUESTION XXX (also 31)

Since in Leviticus the Lord entirely excluded leaven from sacrifices, saying, “Every offering that is offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven, and no leaven or honey shall be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord” (Lev. II, 11), how is it that later he commands a sacrifice to be placed upon leavened loaves?

### ANSWER

Observe more carefully that leavened bread is taken not for the sacrifice but for the service of the sacrifice. Let us see, then, what this means.

In the Gospels the Lord calls the human teaching of the Pharisees, who handed down human traditions and commandments, “leaven,” when he says to the disciples: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matt. XVI, 6).

Similarly, human learning includes, for example, the art of grammar, rhetoric, and even dialectic. Nothing from such learning is to be received for the sacrifice—that is, for those things that are to be believed concerning God. But lucid speech, the splendor of eloquence, and the method of argument are properly commanded to be admitted for the service of the word of God.

## QUESTION XXXI (also 33)

Since in Leviticus the Lord commanded through Moses that the high priest, when ordained, should be clothed in two tunics [Col. 0610A] (Lev. VIII, 7), how did Christ, on the contrary, prohibit his priests and apostles from having two tunics (Matt. X, 10)?

### ANSWER

The fact that Jesus commanded that two tunics should not be possessed is not contrary to the law, but goes beyond the law. Thus the law forbids murder (Exod. XX, 13), while Jesus also cuts off anger (Matt. V, 22); and when the law prohibits adultery (Exod. XX, 14), Jesus also cuts away the desire of the heart (Matt. V, 28).

In this way it might seem that the high priest there wore two tunics, while the apostles here wore one. Indeed, a plausible interpretation of this kind presents itself, but I do not confine the priestly mysteries within the narrow limits of this understanding; I think something more is indicated by this form.

[Col. 0610B] The high priest is one who possesses knowledge of the law and understands the principles of each mystery. To explain briefly, he is one who knows the law both according to the spirit and according to the letter.

That high priest whom Moses was then ordaining knew that there was a spiritual circumcision, yet he also observed circumcision of the flesh, because an uncircumcised man could not be high priest. Thus he had two tunics: one signifying the carnal mystery and the other spiritual understanding.

He knew that spiritual sacrifices ought to be offered to God, yet he also offered carnal sacrifices. For the high priest of that time could not exist unless he sacrificed victims. Thus it is appropriately said that that high priest was clothed in two tunics.

But the apostles were to say: “If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Gal. V, 2), [Col. 0610C] and: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come” (Col. II, 16). Since they completely rejected observance of the law according to the letter, did not burden the disciples with Jewish fables, and did not impose upon them a yoke that neither they nor their fathers had been able to bear (Acts XV, 10), they are rightly prohibited from having two tunics; one is sufficient for them, and it is the inner one.

For they do not want the tunic of the law that is outward and visible from above. Jesus permits them to have one tunic, and that one the inner tunic.

## QUESTION XXXII (also 28)

Since in Leviticus the Lord commands, saying, “The priest shall not be defiled among the deaths of his fellow citizens, except only for his blood relatives and close relations—that is, for his father, mother, son, daughter, brother, and virgin sister who is not married to a man; nor shall he be defiled for the prince of his people” (Lev. XXI, 1 ff.), how does he appear shortly afterward to say the opposite: “The high priest, that is, the chief priest, shall not enter at all to a dead person; he shall not be defiled even for his father or mother” (ibid., 10–11)?

### ANSWER

The first command concerns one of the lesser priests, who are not commanded to enter to any dead person except those relatives and close relations mentioned above. But the great priest, that is, the high priest, possessed something more than the other priests. For this reason, since he ought not to be moved either by pity or by affection, he was commanded not to become unclean even in the cases named above and to restrain his affection generally from every dead person.

Therefore, the first statement concerns the lesser rank of priests; the statement that follows must be understood of the high priest alone.

## QUESTION XXXIII (also 32)

How is it not contrary to the law’s command, “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy,” that Christ says, “Love your enemies” (Matt. V, 44)?

### ANSWER

Every human being, insofar as he is unjust, is to be hated; insofar as he is human, he is to be loved. This, I say, is the rule by which we hate an enemy on account of what is evil in him—that is, iniquity—and love an enemy on account of what is good in him—that is, the social and rational creature.

# FROM THE BOOK OF NUMBERS

## QUESTION XXXIV

Since the Book of Numbers says, “God is not like man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change” (Num. XXIII, 19), and Ezekiel likewise says, “The word that I have spoken shall be fulfilled, says the Lord God” (Ezek. XII, 28), how does God, on the contrary, often appear to change his decision—as happened with the Ninevites, when through Jonah he said, “Forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jon. III, 4), and immediately afterward it is said, “And shall I not spare the great city of Nineveh?” (Jon. IV, 11)—and as happened with David concerning the kingdom, when death had been promised for three days in order to devastate the people, yet within a single day it ceased by the hour of the midday meal (2 Sam. XXIV, 15)?

### ANSWER

Perhaps these statements made in the form of a question should not be taken as a fixed determination, but as a certain figure of speech that appears to indicate something intermediate, without expressing the intention of a definite and irrevocable decision. Thus the statement “When he has spoken, will he not act?” appears more restrained than if it had been written, “When he has spoken, he will act in every respect.”

But let us review the very passages of Scripture found either in Jonah or in the Books of Kings, lest there too, as is the custom of Scripture, something belonging to divine writing may be contained. Thus in Jonah:

> “And the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying: ‘Arise, go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it according to the preaching that I spoke to you’” (Jonah III, 1 ff.).

Jonah did indeed preach and said: “Three days more”—or, as the Hebrews say their text reads, “Forty days more, and Nineveh shall be destroyed.” But the men of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast, and clothed themselves in sackcloth, from the least to the greatest of them.

A little later: “And God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil ways, and he relented concerning the evil that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it” [Col. 0612A] (ibid., 10).

Observe, therefore, in the words we have taken from the prophet that the words spoken by God to the prophet do not contain the statement, “Three days more and Nineveh shall be overthrown.” Thus this utterance, which was spoken but did not come to pass, appears to have been uttered by Jonah rather than by God.

But let us also produce what is written in the Second Book of Samuel (XXIV, 11 ff.), where, after David had numbered the people:

> “The word of the Lord,” he says, “came to Gad the prophet and seer, saying: Go and speak to David: Thus says the Lord: I shall bring three things upon you; choose one of them, which I shall do to you. And Gad came to David and announced to him, saying: Either a famine will come upon your land for three years; or for three months you will flee before your enemies [Col. 0612B] who pursue you; or for three days there will be death in your land. Now therefore know and see what answer I shall give him who sent me. And David said to Gad: I am hard pressed on every side. But let me fall rather into the hands of the Lord, for his mercies are many, and let me not fall into the hands of men. And the Lord sent pestilence upon Israel from morning until the hour of the midday meal, and seventy thousand men of the people died, from Dan to Beersheba. And the angel of the Lord stretched out his hand over Jerusalem, to destroy it. And the Lord relented concerning the evil, and said to the angel who was destroying the people: It is enough; withdraw your hand.”

Observe, therefore, how even in these three threats God is not found to have spoken of three days of death. The statement is placed in Gad’s word, not in the Lord’s commands; [Col. 0612C] and not everything spoken through a prophet is always to be received as though it had been spoken by God.

Finally, through Moses God spoke many things, yet Moses also commanded certain things on his own authority—a distinction that the Lord clearly makes in the Gospels when, asked about the dismissal of a wife, he says: “Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses wrote this commandment for you, but from the beginning it was not so” (Matt. XIX, 8). You see, then, that here too God neither commanded nor wished divorce to take place, whereas Moses, because of the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, wrote that a dismissal should be granted.

Paul likewise shows this in his letters when he says concerning some matters: “The Lord commands, not I” (I Cor. VII, 10); and concerning others: “I say this, not the Lord” (ibid., 12); and again concerning others: “I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice” (ibid., 25); and again: “What I am saying, I am not saying according to the Lord” (II Cor. XI, 17). Thus, similarly, among the other prophets some things were spoken by the Lord, not by the prophet; other things by the prophets, and not by the Lord. In this way the proposed objection appears to be dissolved, since the Lord recalls and changes for the better words that are not so much his own as the prophet’s.

Yet I rather think that the earlier solution accords with the meaning of the whole of Scripture, and especially with those statements in which God is called patient, rich in mercy, and repentant concerning evils (Psal. LXXXV, 15; Joel II, 13; Jonah IV, 2); or, above all, with those general statements pronounced by Jeremiah, in which God’s mercy and incomprehensible [Col. 0613A] goodness are plainly shown: he says and does not do, speaks and does not persist.

Thus God says through Jeremiah:

> “I shall speak decisively—that is, definitively—concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to uproot and destroy them; and if that nation turns from its evils, I shall relent concerning all the evils that I had thought to do to them. And I shall speak decisively concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to rebuild and establish them; and if they do evil in my sight, so that they do not obey my voice, I shall relent concerning all the good that I had spoken of doing to them” (Jer. XVIII, 7 ff.).

How, then, can we prefer to these statements, spoken unconditionally through Jeremiah, those spoken conditionally through the prophet—unless because the former are to be confirmed for the negligent and contemptuous, while the latter are to be understood more secretly by the more perfect?

## FROM THE BOOK OF DEUTERONOMY

[Col. 0613B]

### QUESTION XXXV

How does the Lord command in Deuteronomy, “You shall swear by my name” (Deut. VI, 13), while, on the contrary, in the New Testament he appears to have commanded, “Do not swear” (Matt. V, 34)?

### GREGORY’S RESPONSE

To commit perjury is certainly a grave sin; not to swear, however, just as to swear truly, is no sin. But the person who is not accustomed to swear is farther removed from false swearing than one who is readily inclined to swear truthfully. Therefore the Lord preferred that we, by not swearing, should not depart from the truth, rather than that, while swearing truthfully, we should draw near to perjury.

The admonition not to swear is therefore a turning away from the sin of perjury. For one who swears truly does not sin at all. [Col. 0613C] Hence the Lord wished to remove every occasion of perjury when he prohibited us from swearing.

The Apostle too, in the discourses that he is reported to have delivered, neither swore nor had the habit of swearing, lest at some point, even unknowingly, he should fall into perjury. In his writings, however, where there is greater and more careful consideration, he is found to have sworn in several places—not because he thought that even swearing was sinful, but rather because he understood that the hearts of human beings, through not swearing, are more safely preserved from perjury.

### QUESTION XXXVI

Since the Lord commands in Deuteronomy, saying, “You shall worship the Lord your God” (Deut. VI, 13), how does the Psalmist, on the contrary, command us in the ninety-eighth psalm to worship the earth, saying, “Worship the footstool of his feet” (Psal. XCVIII, 5)? For this is plainly the earth, according to what another prophet says: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI, 1).

### RESPONSE  
*(From Ambrose, Book III On the Holy Spirit, chapter 11)*

The prophet says that earth is to be worshiped—the earth that the Lord Jesus assumed in taking flesh. Thus by the footstool the earth is understood, and by the earth the flesh of Christ, which even today we worship in the mystery, and which the apostles worshiped in the Lord Jesus.

For he took earth from earth, since flesh is from earth, and he received flesh from Mary’s flesh. And because in that very flesh he walked here and gave us that flesh to eat for salvation—and no one eats that flesh unless he has first worshiped it—it was discovered how the footstool of the Lord’s feet is to be worshiped, so that we not only do not sin by worshiping, but sin by failing to worship (from Augustine, *Expositions on Psalm XCVIII*, no. 9).

### QUESTION XXXVII

Since it is written in the book of Deuteronomy, “Cursed is the one who has not left offspring in Israel” (Deut. VII, 14, in the Greek codices), how, contrary to this divine sentence, did many people, both in the Old Testament and in the New, neither enter into marriage nor leave behind any offspring of their flesh, as in the Old Testament Elijah, Jeremiah, and Daniel, and in the New John the Baptist, John the Evangelist, and many others who are shown to have done likewise [Col. 0614B], leaving no offspring according to the flesh?

### RESPONSE

We find these two statements, which appear contrary to one another, explained by Origen in the following way. He says (*Homily 11 on Genesis*):

> “One who possesses consummate and perfect virtue must always be engaged in some form of instruction, and divine speech calls this instruction his spouse. In accordance with this, I think, the celibate and sterile person is subject to a curse in the Law: for if these words are thought to concern carnal offspring, all the virgins of the Church will appear to have been placed under a curse, as likewise John the Baptist and many other saints. But it is certain that they left spiritual offspring, and that each of them possessed Wisdom as a spouse, just as Paul generated children through the Gospel.”

### QUESTION XXXVIII

How can Moses say in Deuteronomy, “The Lord your God is testing you” (Deut. XIII, 3), while the Apostle James, on the contrary, proclaims, “God tests no one” (James I, 13)?

### RESPONSE

It is customarily understood that there are two kinds of testing in the sacred Scriptures: one that deceives and another that proves. In reference to the kind that proves, it is said: “The Lord your God is testing you.” In reference to the kind that deceives, the Apostle James proclaims: “God tests no one.”

## FROM THE BOOKS OF SAMUEL

### QUESTION XXXIX

When, in the First Book of Samuel, God promised the house of Eli, saying, “Thus says the Lord: Your house and the house of your father shall minister before me forever” (I Sam. II, 30), how does he, as though changing the promise, add in opposition: “Behold, the days are coming, and I shall cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there will not be an old man in your house” (ibid., 31)? And after a little he adds: “I shall raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will act according to my heart and my soul; and I shall build him a faithful house, and he shall walk before my Anointed forever” (ibid., 35).

### AUGUSTINE’S RESPONSE  
*(Book XVII of The City of God, chapter 6)*

> “Although these things were then foretold with such sublime elevation, and now shine forth with such great manifestation [Note: [Col. 0615D] The edition reads more aptly, ‘manifestation.’], nevertheless someone may not unreasonably be troubled and say: How can we be confident that everything foretold in those books as future will come to pass, if this very statement divinely spoken there—‘Your house and the house of your father shall minister before me [Note: [Col. 0615D] The edition reads, ‘shall pass before me.’] forever’—could not be fulfilled? For we see that that priesthood was changed, and that what was promised to that house cannot now be hoped for as ever to be fulfilled, since what succeeds it after its rejection and change is rather proclaimed to be eternal.

> “Whoever says this does not understand, or does not remember, that the priesthood itself according to the order of Aaron was established as a shadow of a future [Note: [Col. 0615D] The edition omits “and.”] and eternal priesthood. Consequently, when its eternity [Note: [Col. 0616D] The edition reads, “Its eternity.”] was promised, the promise was made not to the shadow and figure itself, but to that which was foreshadowed and represented through it. Yet, lest anyone think that the shadow itself would remain, its change also had to be prophesied.” [Col. 0615B]

### QUESTION XL

Since it is written in the Book of Samuel that Elijah was taken up by a whirlwind into heaven (IV Kings II, 11), how does the Lord say in the Gospel, “No one has ascended into heaven” (John III, 13)? And so forth.

### RESPONSE  
*(From Gregory the Great, Homily 29 on the Gospels, no. 5)*

One heaven is the aerial heaven, and another is the ethereal heaven. The aerial heaven is close to the earth; hence we speak of the birds of heaven, because we see them flying in the air. Elijah was therefore lifted up into the aerial heaven, so that he might suddenly be brought into a certain hidden region of the earth [Note: [Col. 0616D] The edition reads more aptly, “into a certain secret region.”], where he might already live in great repose of flesh and spirit, until he returns at the end of the world and pays the debt of death. [Col. 0615C]

## FROM ISAIAH

### QUESTION XLI *(Elsewhere 46)*

Since Isaiah says concerning the Egyptians, “They will cry out to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he will send them a savior and defender who will deliver them” (Isa. XIX, 20), how does he, seemingly in opposition, immediately add: “And the Lord will strike Egypt with a plague” (ibid., 22)?

### RESPONSE

This striking of the Lord upon the Egyptians is the act of one who spares, not of one who destroys, because through the plague of repentance he can rather lead the soul to salvation. Therefore it will not be contrary to the promise that a savior and defender will be sent to them because of the oppressor. For this blow or plague that follows is introduced not for condemnation, but for the healing of conversion.

This is the force of what is said above: “He will send them a savior and defender who will deliver them,” since it also follows: “And the Lord will strike Egypt with a plague and heal it.” To make this clearer, he added: “And they will return to the Lord, and he will be reconciled to them, and he will heal them.”

### QUESTION XLII *(Elsewhere 44)*

How can Isaiah say concerning the person of Christ the Son of God, “There is no appearance or beauty in him; and we saw him, and he had no aspect, and we desired him; despised and last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity; and as though his face were hidden and despised, so that we did not esteem him” (Isa. LIII, 2–3), while the Psalmist, on the contrary, says, “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psal. XLIV, 3)?

### RESPONSE

What Isaiah says concerning our bridegroom Christ—than whom nothing is more beautiful—that he appeared almost deformed, he says in reference to Christ’s executioners, to whom Christ himself appeared contemptible. For “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8).

What the Psalmist says, that he was more beautiful than the sons of men, is reckoned according to the faith of believers, who were worthy to see him in such a way that they confessed him, with an undivided faith, to be true God and true man. It therefore remains that he was considered deformed by his persecutors and beautiful by believers.

### QUESTION XLIII

How can Isaiah say of Christ, “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. LIII, 8), when the Evangelist, enumerating Christ’s generation, says among other things, “Now the generation of Christ was in this manner” (Matt. I, 18)?

### RESPONSE

The prophet foretold the generation of his divinity; the Evangelist, following the mystery of the Incarnation, explained Christ’s generation according to his humanity.

### QUESTION XLIV *(Elsewhere 42)*

How can Isaiah say concerning Christ, “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 9), when Paul, on the contrary, appears to have said, “He who knew no sin, for our sake he made sin” (II Cor. V, 21)?

### RESPONSE

When Isaiah says that he committed no sin, he most plainly shows that the person of the Son himself was not stained by sins. He is the lamb without stain and without sin.

When Paul says, “He who knew no sin, for our sake he made sin,” the phrase “he made” refers to the person of the Father: that is, God the Father made his Son, who committed no sin, an offering for our sins, when he permitted him to be sacrificed for the salvation of the world. [Col. 0616D]

It is said that the Father made him sin because he willed him to become an offering for sin, just as it is said, “They eat the sins of my people” (Hos. IV, 8), although it is not sins that are eaten, but offerings presented for sins.

### QUESTION XLV

Since the Lord commands the prophet Isaiah, saying, “Cry out; do not cease” (Isa. LVIII, 1), how does the Apostle, on the contrary, appear to prohibit crying out when he says, “Let all anger, indignation, and shouting be removed from you” (Eph. IV, 31)?

### RESPONSE

[Col. 0617A]

There is one kind of shouting that proceeds from preaching or petition, and another that proceeds from anger. Therefore the Apostle prohibited the shouting that proceeds from anger, not the kind by which Isaiah is commanded to preach or by which the contrite pour out groaning cries to the Lord.

### QUESTION XLVI *(Elsewhere 41)*

How can Isaiah say, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Isa. LXI, 1), and how can the other prophets, or Simeon, or Zechariah be believed to have foretold the future through the Holy Spirit, when the Gospel says, “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII, 39)?

### RESPONSE

The ancient patriarchs and prophets certainly did not foretell the future without the Holy Spirit. But when it says, “The Spirit had not yet been given,” this means that the abundance of spiritual grace had never before been given to them in the manner in which it was afterwards given, when the disciples were gathered together and spoke in the languages of all nations, and the future Church was thus proclaimed in the languages of all nations.

## FROM JEREMIAH

### QUESTION XLVII

How can Jeremiah say both things that appear contrary to one another? For he says in the voice of the Son of God:

> “The sons gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women mix fat, to make cakes for the queen of heaven, and to pour out offerings to foreign gods, and to provoke me to anger. Are they provoking me to anger? says the Lord” (Jer. VII, 18–19).

There he immediately adds, as though in opposition:

> “Behold, my fury and my indignation are kindled upon this place, upon human beings and animals” (ibid., 20), and so forth.

How can the one who had just said, “Are they provoking me to anger?” now say, “Behold, my fury and my indignation will drip upon this place”?

### RESPONSE

The meaning is this: “I do not become angry by nature; but they act in such a way that they provoke me to anger and make me appear to change my nature. Let them therefore experience me as angry, since, so far as it lies with them, they are trying to bring this about.”

### QUESTION XLVIII

Since we know that the prophet Jeremiah imposed silence upon himself with regard to preaching, in saying, “I will not remember him, nor speak any longer in his name” (Jer. XX, 9), how does he, seemingly in opposition, immediately add, “There arose in my heart something like a burning fire, shut up in my bones, and I grew faint, unable to endure it. For I heard the insults of many” (ibid., 10)?

### RESPONSE  
*(From Gregory the Great, Book XXIII of the Moralia, no. 18)*

Because he saw that he was not being heard at all, he desired silence. But when he saw the evils increasing, he did not remain in that silence. What he kept silent outwardly from weariness of speaking, he endured inwardly as a fire from the zeal of charity.

### QUESTION XLIX

Since the manifold and grievous sins of the Jews were proclaimed before Christ’s coming by the voices of the prophets, as in the statement, “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom and did not conceal it” (Isa. III, 9), and in Jeremiah, “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus on a diamond point” (Jer. XVII, 1), and so forth, how does Christ in the Gospel appear, on the contrary, to have said concerning the Jews, “If I had not come, they would not have sin” (John XV, 22)? What does this mean? Were they without any sin before Christ was born in the flesh, and did they begin to have sin only after he came?

### RESPONSE

He intended a particular sin to be understood, namely unbelief, because they did not believe in the one who justifies the ungodly.

## FROM EZEKIEL

### QUESTION L *(Elsewhere 51)*

How does the prophet Ezekiel describe the movement of the living creatures, saying, “They did not turn back as they went” (Ezek. I, 9, 14), and a little later, seemingly in opposition, add, “The living creatures went and returned”?

### RESPONSE  
*(From Gregory the Great, Book X of the Moralia, no. 31)*

The holy living creatures sometimes go and do not return at all; sometimes they go and immediately return. This means that when the minds of the elect, through the grace of the active life bestowed upon them, destroy the paths of error [Note: [Col. 0617D] The edition reads, “leave”], they do not know how to return to the evils of the world that they have abandoned.

But when, through the sharpness of contemplation, they withdraw from this same active life, they go and return. [Note: [Col. 0617D] The edition reads, “because through the fact that they remain for a long time,” etc.] Since they are not at all able to remain for long in contemplation, they pour themselves back into action, so that by exercising themselves in the things close at hand they may refresh themselves, and by contemplating they may again gain strength to rise above themselves.

### QUESTION LI *(Elsewhere 53)*

Since it is written in the Book of Ezekiel concerning the scroll that he had received, “It was in my mouth like sweet honey” (Ezek. III, 3), how does Ezekiel himself later speak of himself, saying, “I went away bitter in the indignation of my spirit” (ibid., 14)?

### RESPONSE  
*(From Gregory, Book I of the Homilies on Ezekiel, Homily 10, no. 45)*

It is indeed very strange if sweetness and bitterness can exist together. But it must be understood that when the word of God begins to grow sweet in a person’s mouth [Note: [Col. 0617D] The edition reads, “when it begins to be sweet in the mouth of the heart,” and so forth], that person’s mind undoubtedly becomes bitter against itself.

For when he learns, with no subtlety, how he ought to reproach himself, he chastises himself all the more harshly through the bitterness of repentance. This displeases him all the more in himself [Note: [Col. 0618D] The edition reads, “by which”], the more fully he sees in the sacred scroll what he ought to love concerning almighty God [Note: [Col. 0618D] The edition reads, “who”].

### QUESTION LII *(Elsewhere 50)*

If, according to Ezekiel’s words, “the righteous deeds of the righteous will be forgotten on whatever day he sins” (Ezek. XVIII, 24; XXXIII, 12–13), how is it consistent that Paul writes that “God repays each person according to his works” (Rom. II, 6), since whatever the righteous possessed from works of righteousness he lost when he sinned—especially since the Apostle Paul also writes that each person’s work, whatever it is, will be tested by fire (I Cor. III, 13), that is, that good and evil alike are to be weighed by fire?

### RESPONSE

Let us see whether perhaps the divine word finds its own resolution within itself, if we observe how it is written, for it says: “When the righteous turns away from his righteousness.” It was not enough for him to say, “When he turns away from his righteousness”; he added: “And commits every kind of ungodliness, according to all the iniquities that the wicked person has committed.”

In this he appears secretly to have inserted the following meaning: if perhaps the righteous person does not commit all the iniquities that the wicked person committed, not all his righteous deeds are removed from memory. But if he commits all the iniquities that the wicked person committed, then all his righteous deeds are finally taken from memory in his fall.

Although the Holy Spirit concealed this in the Scriptures for the sake of those who despise the riches of his goodness and patience, he did not entirely remove it. If, therefore, what Paul said is understood in this sense, it will not be wholly contrary.

The blessed Gregory also explains this testimony according to the new translation in this sense, saying:

> “When it is said, ‘The righteous dies in his sin, and the righteous deeds that he performed will not be remembered,’ we must especially consider this: when we commit evils, it is useless to recall our past good deeds, since no confidence in past good deeds ought to remain when evils are being perpetrated.”

### QUESTION LIII *(Elsewhere 52)*

Since the Lord says through Ezekiel, “I gave them statutes that were not good” (Ezek. XX, 25), how does Paul, seemingly in opposition, say, “The Law indeed is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Rom. [Col. 0619D] VII, 12)?

### RESPONSE  
*(From Gregory the Great, Book XXVIII of the Moralia, no. 41)*

Things that are evil cease to be regarded as evil in comparison with worse things, and things that are good are not regarded as good in comparison with better things. For just as, in comparison with Sodom and Samaria, it is said to the more sinful Judah, “You have justified your sisters in all your abominations that you committed” (Ezek. XVI, 51), so, in comparison with the subsequent and better commandments of the New Testament, the good commandments given to beginners are said not to be good.

### QUESTION LIV

In the vision of the spiritual building, the prophet Ezekiel first says that he saw the chambers with fronts toward the southern road. How, then, does he later add that the chamber facing the southern road belongs to the priests who keep watch in the temple guard, while the chamber facing the northern road belongs to the priests who keep watch over the service of the altar (Ezek. XL, 44–46)? If both fronts faced the southern road, how is one now said to face the southern road and the other the northern road?

### RESPONSE  
*(From Gregory the Great, Book II of the Homilies on Ezekiel, Homily 10, no. 14)*

[Col. 0620B]

From these words we recognize that the chamber of the priests who kept watch in the temple guard [Note: [Col. 0619D] The edition reads, “keep watch”] had been positioned so that it faced only the southern road. The chamber of the priests who kept watch over the service of the altar [Note: [Col. 0619D] The edition reads, “keep watch”], however, was situated in the court so that it extended toward the southern road and toward the northern side [Note: [Col. 0619D] The edition reads, “so that it extended also toward the southern road and …”]. Thus, along with the chamber of the priests who kept watch in the temple guard, it faced the southern road [Note: [Col. 0619D] The edition reads, “looked toward it”], while, apart from the chamber of those same priests, it could be seen from the northern road [Note: [Col. 0619D] The edition, after “priests,” adds “the chamber of the priests [Col. 0620D] who keep watch over the service of the altar, so that it could be seen from the northern road.”].

But what can we discern in these mystical words [Note: [Col. 0620D] The edition reads, “mystical” in the singular], except what the spiritual hearer already understands from what has been said above: that the priests of the higher order, who keep watch in the temple guard, face only the southern road, because, occupied solely with spiritual pursuits, they attend carefully to the things that belong to the love of God [Col. 0620C].

The priests of the lower order, however, who are responsible for examining the sins of transgressors, also turn their eyes toward the northern road, so that they may see what chills of torpor exist in the minds of sinners and, bringing them back through words of correction even to the groans of repentance [Note: [Col. 0620D] The edition reads, “leading them”], may, as it were, kindle them like flesh upon the Lord’s altar.

They also looked toward the southern road with the great priests [Note: [Col. 0620D] The edition reads, “may look”], because, so far as concerns themselves, they burn with the fire of charity and are kindled by the flames of the love of God. But because they frequently correct the sins of transgressors [Note: [Col. 0620D] The edition reads, “sins” in the plural], they also turn their eyes toward the northern road.

## FROM DANIEL

[Col. 0620D]

### QUESTION LV

If, after three years, as it is written at the beginning of Daniel (Dan. I, 5, 18), the young men themselves entered into the presence of Nebuchadnezzar, how is it written in the subsequent vision, “In the second year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream” (Dan. II, 1)? These statements appear to contain a major contradiction, since those very young men—who had nowhere previously been introduced and questioned in the presence of the aforesaid king except after three years—Scripture now recounts, in the second year of Nebuchadnezzar, both that Nebuchadnezzar himself saw the dream and that Daniel disclosed its interpretation.

### RESPONSE  
*(From Jerome, on Daniel, chapter II)*

The Hebrews resolve this as follows: the second year is said to refer to the second year of his reign over all the barbarian nations—not only Judea and the Chaldeans, but also the Assyrians, Egyptians, Moabites, and the other nations that, by the Lord’s grant, he had conquered.

Hence Josephus also writes in the tenth book of the *Antiquities* (chapter 12):

> “After the second year of the devastation of Egypt, King Nebuchadnezzar saw a marvelous dream.”

### QUESTION LVI *(Elsewhere 57)*

Since in the Book of Daniel, at the end of the first vision, it is written of Daniel himself, “Daniel continued until the first year of King Cyrus” (Dan. I, 21), how is it written in the same book, on the contrary, “In the third year of Cyrus king of the Persians, the word was revealed to Daniel” (Dan. X, 1)?

### RESPONSE

When it is said that Daniel continued until the first year of King Cyrus, this should not be understood as referring to the length of his life. Rather, it signifies that until the first year of Cyrus, who destroyed the empire of the Chaldeans, Daniel remained powerful in Chaldea. Afterwards he was transferred by Darius to the Medes.

Jerome likewise says in his exposition of Daniel (on chapter X, verse 1):

> “We understand that Daniel remained among the Chaldeans, clothed in his former dignity, purple and fine linen, until the first year of King Cyrus, when he overthrew the Chaldeans. Afterwards he began to be with Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of the race of the Medes, who ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldeans. Or certainly, after Darius had died—the one in whose first year he had learned the mystery of the seventy weeks—he is now reported to have seen these things in the third year of King Cyrus.”

### QUESTION LVII *(Elsewhere 56)*

Since Daniel had already foretold to King Nebuchadnezzar the fulfillment of God’s sentence, which he knew to be immutable, concerning the punishment of his kingdom, saying, “They will drive you away from human beings, and your dwelling will be with the wild beasts” (Dan. IV, 22), how does he later exhort that same Nebuchadnezzar to repentance, as though the sentence had been changed, saying, “Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you: redeem your sins by almsgiving, and your iniquities by mercies toward the poor; perhaps God will forgive your offenses” (ibid., 24)?

### RESPONSE  
*(From Jerome, on Daniel, chapter IV, verse 24; IV Kings XX, 1 ff.)*

This is easily resolved by the example of King Hezekiah, whom Isaiah had said would die, and by that of the Ninevites, to whom it had been said, “Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown” [Col. 0622A] (Jonah III, 4). Nevertheless, through Hezekiah’s prayers and the conversion of the Ninevites, God’s sentence was changed—not through any fickleness of judgment, but through the conversion of those who earned pardon.

Otherwise, in Jeremiah also God says that he threatens evils against a nation, and that if it does good he changes his threats through mercy. Again, he asserts that he promises good to one who does good, and if that person does evil, he says that he changes his sentence—not in the human being, but in the works, which have been changed. For God is angry not with human beings but with their vices; when these are no longer present in a person, he does not punish him, since the person has changed.

### QUESTION LVIII

Since in the Book of Daniel it is written that Daniel learned through the revelation interpreted by the angel, as he says, “While I, Daniel, was looking at the vision and seeking understanding, I heard the voice of a man saying: Gabriel, make this man understand the vision” (Dan. VIII, 15–16), how is it immediately added, seemingly in opposition, where Daniel himself says, “I was amazed at the vision, and there was no one to interpret it” (ibid., 27)? If there was no one to interpret it, how did the angel interpret it above?

### RESPONSE  
*(From Jerome, on this verse)*

What he means is this: he had heard about the kings, but did not know their names; he had learned the future, but wavered uncertainly about the time when the future events would occur.

## FROM THE MINOR PROPHETS

### QUESTION LIX

[Note: [Col. 0621D] Samson the abbot, Book II of the *Apology*, chapter 27, no. 6, or page 512 of volume XI of *Hispania Sacra*, translated this question as follows: “It may reasonably be asked how, in this passage (Job XXXIV, 30, which is absent from the codex or was omitted by the editor), it is said that he makes a hypocrite reign, when the prophet specifically complains about this matter, saying, ‘They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them.’ For who, thinking correctly, would say that the Lord does what he certainly does not know? But because God’s knowing means approving, and not knowing means rejecting, in a wondrous manner the Lord both makes hypocrites reign,” and so forth, as at the end here.]

Since the Lord says through the prophet Hosea concerning reprobate kings, “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. VIII, 4), how does Job, on the contrary, say, “He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” (Job XXXIV, 30)? For who, thinking correctly, would say that the Lord did what he certainly did not know?

### RESPONSE  
*(From Gregory the Great, Book XXV of the Moralia, no. 41)*

God’s knowing means approving; not knowing means rejecting. Hence he says to certain people whom he rejects, “I do not know where you come from” (Luke XIII, 25).

Sometimes it is also God’s doing to permit through anger what he forbids to be done. Hence he also asserted that he hardened the heart of the king of Egypt (Exod. IV, 21), meaning that he permitted it to be hardened.

In a wondrous manner, the Lord both makes hypocrites reign and does not know them: he makes them reign by permitting it, and does not know them by rejecting them.

### QUESTION LX

How did the prophet Amos, when questioned, answer, “I am not a prophet” (Amos VII, 14), when we know that he was a prophet and retain the words of his prophecy?

### RESPONSE  
*(From Gregory, Book II of the Moralia, no. 89)*

At the very hour when he was questioned, he perceived that the spirit of prophecy was absent from him, and truthfully gave this testimony concerning himself, saying, “I am not a prophet.” Yet he immediately continued:
