> “And now hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Your wife will fornicate in the city, and your sons and your daughters will fall by the sword, and your land will be measured with a measuring line, and you will die in a polluted land” (Amos VII, 16–17).

These words of the prophet plainly show that, while he was speaking those things concerning himself, he was filled with the prophetic spirit; and he soon deserved to possess the spirit of prophecy because he humbly acknowledged that he was not a prophet.

### QUESTION LXI

Since Zechariah says concerning those who mocked Christ, “They will look upon the one whom they pierced” (Zech. XII, 10), how does Isaiah, seemingly in opposition, appear to have said concerning them, “Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. XXVI, 10, according to the Septuagint)?

### RESPONSE

The ungodly person is blinded so that he may not see something. He will see the form of a human being, concerning which it is said, “So he will come” (Acts I, 11); but he will not see the form of God, concerning which it is said, “I will manifest myself to him” (John XIV, 21). The ungodly will not see this form; only the righteous will.

Therefore, because of the mere human form, which is to be seen by both the righteous and the unrighteous, it was said, “They will look upon the one whom they pierced.” But because of the form of God, which will be seen only by the righteous, it was said, “Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see,” and so forth.

## FROM THE BOOK OF PSALMS

### QUESTION LXII

Since David says in the fourth psalm, verse 5, “Be angry, and do not sin,” how does Paul say in his Epistles, “Put away all anger and indignation” (Col. III, 8)?

### RESPONSE

There is one kind of anger by which we are moved through zeal for justice, and another by which we are carried away through an irrational impulse. The Apostle therefore did not wish to cut away that anger which proceeds from justice, especially since he used this very testimony from the psalm in his Letter to the Ephesians, saying, “Be angry, and do not sin” (Eph. IV, 26).

It is as though he had said: “Be angry in such a way that you refrain from fault.” Rather, he wished all anger that proceeds from an irrational impulse to be removed.

### QUESTION LXIII

How can David say in the fifteenth psalm, “My flesh will rest in hope, because you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (verse 9–10), when, seemingly in opposition, he appears to say in the twenty-ninth psalm, “What benefit is there in my blood, while I descend into corruption?” (verse 10)?

### RESPONSE
What he says, “My flesh shall rest in hope, because you will not abandon my soul, etc.,” the Psalmist certainly declares affirmatively in the person of Christ, as though it were spoken from the voice of the Son of God to God the Father (excerpted from Augustine, *Expositions on the Psalms*): “My flesh will sleep in hope of the resurrection, because you will not give my soul over to the underworld to be possessed, nor will you permit my sanctified body—through which others too are to be sanctified—to decay.” But what appears to be contrary is in fact the same thing, not something different. For Christ says, in a manner, to the Father: “What benefit is there in [Col. 0624A] the shedding of my blood, if my flesh is corrupted in the same way as that of other human beings, so that I rise only at the end? Will dust—that is, the throng of the ungodly, which cannot be justified unless I rise—confess you?” Thus, understood in this way, the statements are not contradictory.

## QUESTION LXIV

Since the Psalmist says, “The pains of hell found me” (Ps. XVII, 6), and likewise, “Our God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations that found us exceedingly” (Ps. XLV, 2), how does he testify, with a change of verbal expression, not that he was found by tribulations but rather that he himself found tribulation, saying, “I found tribulation and sorrow” (Ps. CXIV, 4)?

## ANSWER

[Col. 0624B]

There are tribulations or sorrows that we find, and others that find us. For when a person, without anyone’s admonition or chastisement, considers what he has done and, entreating God, mourns and trembles, he has found tribulation and sorrow. But the person who is crushed either by another’s rebuke, by someone else’s admonition, or by punishment is found by tribulations and sorrows.

## QUESTION LXV

When the prophet David complains in the twenty-first psalm that he was not heard, saying, “My God, I will cry out by day, and you will not hear; and by night” (verse 3), etc., how does he, on the contrary, testify in the same psalm, saying, [Col. 0624C] “He did not turn his face from me; and when I cried to him, he heard me” (ibid., 25)?

## ANSWER

The Lord Christ, speaking in the person of the old human being whose mortality he bore, says that he cries day and night with words of sin and is not heard. For they are words of sin, not of righteousness, when one cries to the Lord by day—that is, in prosperity—in order that this very prosperity may not change; and when one cries by night, in order that adversity may prosper. Such a petition, therefore, is far from salvation. Hence the following words also say, “and not to my folly”—that is (from Augustine, *Expositions*, I, on this psalm), “Do not do this to my folly, but rather so that I may understand what you wish me to cry: not with words of sin and a desire for temporal [Col. 0624D] life, but with words of conversion to you for eternal life.”

Accordingly, in the words of conversion and righteousness that follow, he recalls that he was heard, saying: “He did not despise or disdain the prayer of the poor; neither did he turn his face from me; and when I cried to him, he heard me.” That is: he did not hear the one who, crying to God with words of sin, did not wish to cross this path—that is, prosperity—but he heard the prayer of the poor. Therefore, the one who earlier testifies that he cried with words of sin and was not heard himself recalls, when he entreats with words of righteousness, that he was heard. Earlier he cried with words of sin—in the person of the old human being—and was not heard. Later he cried with words of righteousness and conversion to God [Col. 0625A]—in the person of the human being belonging to the new life—and was heard.

## QUESTION LXVI

Since the Psalmist says in the twenty-fourth psalm, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (verse 10), how does he say conversely in another psalm, “All your ways are truth” (Ps. CXVIII, 151), or, as it is read in another translation, “All your commandments are truth”?

## ANSWER (From Augustine, Sermon 29 on Psalm CXVIII, no. 8)

Toward the saints, all the ways of the Lord are mercy, and all the ways of the Lord are truth: for in judging he comes to their aid, and thus mercy is not absent; and in showing mercy he presents what he promised, so that truth is not lacking. Toward all people, both those whom he liberates and those whom he condemns, all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth: for where he does not show mercy, the truth of vengeance is manifested. For he liberates many who do not deserve it, but he condemns no one who does not deserve condemnation.

## QUESTION LXVII

How does the Psalmist in the twenty-ninth psalm appear to make contradictory statements about himself? For he says, “I said in my prosperity: I shall not be moved forever” (verses 7, 8); and shortly afterward adds, “You turned your face from me, and I became troubled”?

## ANSWER

Because he became swollen with confidence in his own strength, he says, “I said in my prosperity,” etc. But shortly afterward he adds what he suffered: “You turned your face,” etc., as though he said plainly: “I thought myself strong among the virtuous, but, abandoned, I learned how great my weakness is.” Hence he says again, “I swore and determined to keep the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. CXVIII, 106). But because it was beyond his strength to remain in the observance that he had sworn to keep, he immediately, in his distress, discovered his weakness. Therefore he suddenly turned to prayer and help, saying, “I have been humbled exceedingly; give me life according to your word” (ibid., 407).

## QUESTION LXVIII

How does David say, “I said: I will confess my injustices against myself to the Lord, and you forgave” (Ps. XXXI, 5), etc., and also what is said elsewhere, “When the sinner has groaned, he will be saved” (Isa. XXX, 15, according to the Septuagint), when, on the contrary, the blind man says in the Gospel, “We know that God does not hear sinners” (John [Col. 0625D] IX, 31)?

## ANSWER

That God hears sinners is shown in many passages of Scripture, as is written concerning that publican and others in the Gospel (Luke XVIII, 14). But in saying this, the blind man speaks as one who has not yet been anointed. Therefore, it should not be understood that God does not hear sinners. If he does not hear them in miracles, he hears them concerning their sins.

## QUESTION LXIX

Since the Psalmist says in the thirty-third psalm, [Col. 0626A] “His praise shall always be in my mouth” (verse 2), how does he, conversely, use a specific number in the hundred-eighteenth psalm? For he says, “Seven times a day I have praised you” (verse 164).

## ANSWER

He assigned the number seven to praise because of the seven days in which this world is carried out, during which praise is always offered to God.

## QUESTION LXX

Since the Psalmist says, “You will save humans and beasts, Lord” (Ps. XXXV, 7), how does the apostle Paul appear to say, conversely, “Does God care about oxen?” (1 Cor. IX, 9)?

## ANSWER

Saint Augustine distinguishes these matters as follows [Col. 0626B] (*Expositions on Psalm CXLV*, nos. 13–14):

“Behold, it is said that God does not care about oxen. Again it is said, ‘You will save humans and beasts, Lord.’ Are these statements contradictory? No. With respect to the force of the commandment, God does not care about oxen. With respect to his providence over the universe, he cares for everything. What, then, does the Apostle say? Does the matter of oxen pertain to God? When he gave the commandment, ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain’ (Deut. XXV, 4), did God not think about oxen? Thus he intended to signify certain oxen. For God is not concerned to instruct us what to do with oxen. Human nature itself knows this. A human being was made so that he would know how to care for his beasts, and he did not receive commandments from God about this; rather, God implanted this understanding in his mind, so that he could do it even without a commandment. God made him such. But just as he governs the beast, though he himself must be governed by another, he received a commandment from the one who governs him. With respect to the force of the commandment, therefore, God does not care about oxen. With respect to the providence by which he created all things and governs the world, God will save humans and beasts [Note: [Col. 0625D] Here perhaps Julian resolves the question; but since Abbot Samson, whose testimony alone we rely upon, recorded nothing, we could not avoid transferring the passage through the end of the chapter.].

“Let your Charity pay attention. Perhaps someone may say to me here: ‘It belongs to the New Testament that the matter of oxen does not pertain to God. “You will save humans and beasts, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0626D] Florezius says that the words enclosed in brackets are lacking in the manuscript, but they are found in Augustine at the cited place.] belongs to the Old Testament.’ There are people who slander these things and say that the two Testaments do not agree. Perhaps, they say, one thing is stated in the Old and another in the New; and they demand from me a statement from the New Testament such [Note: [Col. 0626D] The manuscript has *denotabilem*; Augustine, however, has the word indicated by the same author.] as this: ‘You will save humans and beasts, Lord’ (Ps. XXXV, 7). What am I to do? Nothing stands so prominently at the head of the New Testament as the Gospel. In the Gospel I find that all these things pertain to God. No one can now contradict this. Surely the Apostle will not be contrary to the Gospel? Let us hear the Lord himself, the prince and teacher of the apostles. ‘Look,’ he says, ‘at the birds of the air: they do not sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them . . . . And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They do not labor or spin. But I say to you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed [Col. 0627A] like one of these. If, then, God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith?’ (Matt. VI, 26, 28 ff.). Therefore, apart from human beings, animals and plants also pertain to God’s care, so that they may be fed, not so that they may receive the law. With respect to giving the law, therefore, God does not care about oxen. But with respect to their being cared for, fed, governed, and directed, everything pertains to God.”

Hence it is also said in Matthew’s Gospel: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarius? And not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father” (Matt. X, 29). Luke says likewise: “Are not five sparrows sold for two asses, and not one of them is forgotten before God?” (Luke XII, 6). Those whom he remembers, feeds, governs, and directs, and without whom not one of them falls to the ground, are not merely with them and within them; rather, he is also in them, since he himself has powerfully ordained that they be fed, he whose equal care remains over all things.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] From this question through LXXII inclusive [Col. 0628D], our enumeration is one unit higher than that of the printed editions, because the seventieth question from Samson has been added.]

## QUESTION LXXI (Elsewhere 70)

How does the Psalmist, in the thirty-seventh psalm and in the person of Christ, say, “Those who sought my soul used force against me” (verse 13), when, conversely, in the hundred forty-first psalm, likewise in the person of Christ, rebuking them, he says, “There is no one who seeks my soul” (verse 5)? If he rebuked certain people as enemies because they did not seek his soul, were those who sought his soul therefore friends?

## ANSWER (From Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm XXXVII*, no. 18)

Christ’s soul is sought both rightly and wrongly. It is sought rightly by those who desire to be incorporated into his members; wrongly by those who use force and persecute either him or his members. Who seeks his soul rightly? The one who imitates his sufferings. Who sought his soul wrongly? Those who used force against him and crucified him.

## QUESTION LXXII

How does David say in the forty-third psalm, “Rise up; why are you sleeping, Lord?” (verse 23), while, as if in opposition, he says in the hundred twentieth psalm, “Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel” (verse 4)? If the one who guards Israel neither sleeps nor slumbers, how can the cry be addressed to him, “Rise up; why are you sleeping, Lord?”

## ANSWER

[Col. 0627D]

The Lord sleeps in the hearts of unbelievers; he does not sleep in the hearts of Christians. Therefore, when it is sung, “Rise up; why are you sleeping, Lord?” the Church cries this out on behalf of unbelievers, who believe Christ to have died but do not believe that he rose again; thus Christ is, as it were, always asleep in the hearts of such people. Because they still think Christ is dead, the request is made that he rise in them—that is, that faith be granted to them by which they may believe that he rose from the dead.

But when we sing that he “neither sleeps nor slumbers who guards Israel”—since Israel is interpreted as “seeing God”—this testimony refers only to the faithful, who confess that Christ was raised from the sleep of death, not sleeping, that is, dead, but living forever.

## QUESTION LXXIII

Since in the forty-fourth psalm, from the voice of God calling, the human soul is told, “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear” (verse 11), how does he then, mentioning another father, add conversely, “And forget your people and your father’s house”?

## ANSWER

Here God the Father calls the daughter—that is, the human soul—to leave the house of another father, namely, this world, and to strive to return to the vision of its own Creator and Father. This happens when, having died with Christ to the elements of this world (Col. II, 20), we contemplate, according to the Apostle, not the things that are seen but those that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal (2 Cor. IV, 18).

## QUESTION LXXIV

How can the same prophet David, after saying, “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High” (Ps. XLIX, 14), appear to say conversely, “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it; but you will not delight in burnt offerings” (Ps. L, 18)? How can he say that God delights and does not delight in human sacrifices?

## ANSWER

[Col. 0628C]

Visible sacrifice is the sacrament of invisible sacrifice—that is, a sacred sign. Hence the penitent man in the prophet, or the prophet himself seeking to make God propitious toward his sins, says: “If you had desired sacrifice, I would certainly have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings.” “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart.” We see how, where he says that God does not want sacrifice, he there demonstrates that God does want sacrifice. He does not want the sacrifice of slaughtered cattle, but he wants the sacrifice of a contrite heart. Therefore, by that which he said God did not want, he signifies what he then stated that God does want.

Accordingly, where it is written, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hos. VI, 6), it should be understood as nothing other than that one sacrifice is preferred to another, since what is called sacrifice by human beings is a sign of the true sacrifice. Mercy, moreover, is the true sacrifice. Hence the Apostle also says: “Do not forget to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased” (Heb. XIII, 16).

## QUESTION LXXV

Since the prophet David says, “God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteousnesses?” (Ps. XLIX, 16), how does Paul appear to command the contrary, admitting even wicked people to preaching when he says, [Col. 0629A] “Whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed” (Phil. I, 18)? And what of the Gospel saying, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII, 3)?

## ANSWER (From Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm XLIX*, no. 23)

These things were said so that those who hear need not fear, regardless of whom they hear; not so that those who say good things and do evil may be secure. But God did not wish to dismiss without reproof those who speak, lest, simply because they speak, they fall asleep secure in an evil life and say to themselves: “God will not destroy us, since through our mouths he wished such great good things to be spoken to his people.” According to this understanding, sinful preachers are admonished not to live wickedly while preaching well, not to stop their mouths from preaching righteousness.

## AUGUSTINE’S QUESTION LXXVI (From his *Exposition on this Psalm*)

Since it is written in the fifty-second psalm, “There is no one who does good, not even one” (verses 4, 5), how is the name of the good immediately added when it says, “Those who devour my people”? If there is no one who does good, not even one, who is this people called exclusively God’s people? For God’s people cannot be called such unless they do good and cling to him.

## ANSWER

Behold, in one and the same psalm both the good—that is, God’s people—are described, and the statement that there is no one who does good, not even one, is set forth in the preceding sentence. For the prophet, wishing to distinguish the sons of God from the sons of human beings, said, “There is no one who does good,” etc., referring to the sons of human beings, who are not yet sons of God. For earlier he had said of them, “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of human beings.” The same prophet said, “Those who devour my people.” Behold, here he named God’s people, which certainly refers to the sons of God. By this designation we are sons of God.

Remove, therefore, the fact that human beings are sons of God, and what remains is that they are sons of human beings—that is, reprobates and sinners—to whom the statement applies: “There is no one who does good, not even one.” But when some good people are found among the wicked, they are sons of God, who are here called God’s people. They are devoured like food, like bread, by the sons of human beings—that is, by the wicked—when they are torn apart by their persecutors. But when the wicked themselves become good, they are no longer sons of human beings but sons of God.

Therefore, if you attribute the earlier verse, “There is no one who does good,” to the sons of human beings, and assign the following verse, “Those who devour my people,” to the sons of God, there will be no contradiction in the question.

## QUESTION LXXVII

Since in the fifty-fourth psalm David invokes punishment upon certain schismatics, saying, “Let death come upon them” (verse 16), how does he appear, as if conversely, to add, “And let them descend alive into hell”?

## ANSWER

[Col. 0630A]

Recalling the event in the history of the Old Testament in which the earth swallowed Dathan and Abiron alive, while fire consumed the people who had agreed with them (Num. XVI, 31–32 ff.), the psalm says, “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell.” But if death had already come upon them, how were they descending alive to the underworld? Or how can it happen that they appear first to have entered into death and afterward are shown to descend alive into the underworld?

The statement “Let death come upon them” refers to the people who agreed with them and were consumed by fire; but what follows, “Let them descend alive into hell,” refers to the leaders of those wicked men, Dathan and Abiron, whom the earth swallowed alive. That first beginning of the schism was destroyed by a new death. Alternatively, to descend alive into hell means, while living and perceiving, to descend by an evil deed into the prison of hell.

## QUESTION LXXVIII

Since in the sixty-first psalm the prophet says, “God spoke once” (verse 12), how does he appear, as if conversely, to add, “I heard these two things,” especially since the apostle Paul also writes to the Hebrews, “In many portions and in many ways, long ago God spoke to our fathers through the prophets” (Heb. I, 1)?

## ANSWER (From Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm XVI*, no. 17 ff.)

It is extremely difficult to investigate how the words were arranged: first, “God spoke once”; then, “When he spoke once, I heard these two things.” For if he had said, “God spoke once; I heard this one thing,” he would appear to have removed part of the question, so that we would ask only what “God spoke once” means. But now we must ask both what “God spoke once” means and what “I heard these two things” means, since he spoke only once.

It must be understood, however, that among human beings, to human beings, God often spoke in many ways and in many parts, through the manifold creature. With himself, God spoke once. God begot one Word; in that Word are all things, because all things were made through the Word (John I, 3). He has one Word, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. II, 3).

The two things he says he heard are power and mercy. Precisely these: understand the power of God; understand the mercy of God. Nearly all the Scriptures are contained in these two things: for the sake of these are the prophets, the patriarchs, the law, our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the apostles, and every proclamation and celebration of the word of God in the Church.

Fear his power; love his mercy. Do not presume upon his mercy in such a way that you despise his power; and do not fear his power in such a way that you despair of his mercy. With him are power and mercy: “he humbles one and exalts another” (Ps. LXXIV, 9)—he humbles one by power and exalts another by mercy.

## QUESTION LXXIX

Since in the sixty-eighth psalm the prophet, speaking in the person of Christ, says, “I labored in crying out; my throat became hoarse” (Ps. LXVIII, 4), how does the Gospel say that during his Passion the Lord did not answer them a word? And what of Isaiah’s statement, “As a lamb before the one who shears it, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII, 7)?

## ANSWER (From Augustine, Sermon 1 on Psalm LXVIII, no. 7)

That is why he was then already silent: he was hoarse, because he had cried out so much in vain. We know that cry of his from another psalm, spoken on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?” (Ps. XXI, 2). But how great was that cry, or how prolonged, that his throat became hoarse from it?

For a long time he cried, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. XXIII, 13, 14 ff.)! For a long time he cried, “Woe to the world because of scandals” (ibid. [Col. 0631B] XVIII, 7)! And truly, how hoarsely he cried—and therefore was not understood—when the Jews said, “What does he mean? This saying is harsh. Who can hear it? We do not know what he is saying” (John VI, 61). He spoke all the words, but their throats were hoarse for them, since they did not understand his voices.

Thus, under this interpretation, the statements promised in the psalm will not be contradictory: in accordance with what he says above, the cry by which his throat is said to have become hoarse should be understood as having occurred not at the time of the Passion but before the Passion.

## QUESTION LXXX

Since the prophet, speaking in the person of Christ in the sixty-eighth psalm, first says, “I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm submerged me” (Ps. LXVIII, 3), how does he then, as if conversely, plead in what follows concerning the depth of the waters, “May the storm of the water not submerge me” (ibid., 16)? There are also other statements in the same psalm that appear contrary to one another: first he says, “In the mire of the deep” (ibid., 3); then, conversely, “Save me from the mud, so that I may not stick fast” (ibid., 15).

## ANSWER

The earlier statement, “The storm submerged me,” is understood as spoken with reference to the body, which was already being held in the Passion. But the following statement, “May the storm of the water not submerge me,” appears to be a prayer with reference to the spirit: since the body was being held for the sufferings, he at least prayed for his soul, that it not be submerged in the storm of the sufferings.

The same must be understood in the other two statements in which he says, “I am stuck in the mire of the deep,” and then repeats, “Save me from the mud, so that I may not stick fast” (from the same sermon of blessed Augustine, no. 18). According to the earlier meaning, he ought to have said, “Save me from the mud where I was,” [Note: [Col. 0631D] The edition reads, “where I had stuck.”] by rescuing me, not by preventing me from sticking fast [Note: [Col. 0631D] The edition reads, “from sticking fast.”].

Therefore, he had stuck fast in the flesh, but he had not stuck fast in the spirit. He says this from the weakness of his members. When perhaps you are seized by someone who presses you toward iniquity, your body is indeed held; bodily, you are stuck in the mire of the deep [Note: [Col. 0631D] The edition reads, “in the mire.”]. But as long as you do not consent, you have not stuck fast; if you consent, you have stuck fast. Have you stuck fast [Note: [Col. 0631D] The edition lacks: “Have you stuck fast?”]? Let your prayer be there, so that, just as your body is now held, your soul may not also be held (no. 19).

Likewise, concerning the depth of the waters: “May the storm of the water not submerge me.” But he had already been submerged. “I came into the depth of the sea, and the storm submerged me”—you said this. He was submerged according to the flesh, but not according to the spirit. To those to whom it was said, “If they persecute you in one city [Note: [Col. 0631D] The edition reads, “in one city”], flee into another” (Matt. X, 23), this was said so that they would stick fast neither in the flesh nor in the spirit.

## QUESTION LXXXI

Since we read that the fathers of the Old and New Testaments—Moses, Aaron, Elijah, Elisha, and the other saints of that time [Col. 0632B]—as well as the apostles themselves of Christ the Son of God, performed various wonders and signs, why is it written conversely in the seventy-first psalm, “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does great wonders” (Ps. LXXI, 18)?

## ANSWER

God alone performs wonders, because he himself works in all who perform them—he who alone performs wonders.

## QUESTION LXXXII

Regarding what is written in the seventy-fourth psalm, “For the cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine mixed” (Ps. LXXIV, 9): this appears contradictory, since he called the cup full of unmixed wine and then added “mixed.”

## ANSWER

[Col. 0632C]

The first question, according to what Saint Augustine says (*Exposition on this Psalm*, no. 11), arises as follows:

“‘It is full of unmixed wine mixed.’ How can it be unmixed if it is mixed? Therefore, let it not disturb you that he calls it both unmixed and mixed [Note: [Col. 0631D] The edition reads, ‘because it is both unmixed and mixed.’]: unmixed because of its purity, mixed because of its sediment” (no. 12).

“For me, the cup of unmixed wine full of mixture appears to be the law given to the Jews and all that Scripture of the Old, which is called the Testament. There are found there the weights of all the judgments, for the New Testament lies hidden there, as though in the sediment of bodily sacraments.

“Circumcision of the flesh is a matter of great sacramental significance, and from it circumcision of the heart is understood. That temple in [Note: [Col. 0632D] The edition lacks ‘in.’] Jerusalem is a matter of great sacramental significance, and from it the body of the Lord is understood. [Col. 0632D] The promised land [Note: [Col. 0632D] The edition reads, ‘land of promise.’] is understood as the kingdom of heaven. The sacrifice of victims and cattle has a great sacramental significance, but in all those kinds of sacrifices that one sacrifice and that one victim on the Lord’s cross is understood [Note: [Col. 0632D] The edition reads, ‘the Lord.’]. In place of all those sacrifices, we have one sacrifice, which they prefigured, and these things were prefigured by them [Note: [Col. 0632D] The edition reads, ‘because they prefigured these things, that is, these things were prefigured by them.’].

“That people received the law; it received righteous and good commandments. What is as righteous as: ‘You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not give false testimony; honor your father and mother; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife; you shall worship one God, and serve him alone’ (Exod. XX, 7 ff.)? All these things pertain to the wine. But those bodily things, as it were, settled to the bottom so that they might remain among them, in order that all spiritual understanding might be poured out from them [Note: [Col. 0633D] The edition reads, ‘might be poured out.’].

“The cup in the hand of the Lord—that is, in the power of the Lord—of unmixed wine—that is, of the pure law—is full of mixture—that is, with the sediment of bodily sacraments. And because he humbles this one, the proud Jew, and exalts that one, the confessing Gentile, he inclined it from one to the other—that is, from the Jewish people to the Gentile people. What did he incline? The law. It was refined; from it came spiritual understanding. Nevertheless, its sediment was not emptied, because all its bodily sacraments remained among the Jews.

“‘All the sinners of the earth shall drink.’ Who will drink? ‘All the sinners of the earth.’ The Jews were indeed sinners, but proud; and the Gentiles were sinners, but humble. All sinners will drink, but observe who drinks the sediment and who drinks the wine. For those, by drinking the sediment, vanished; these, by drinking the wine, were justified.”

## QUESTION LXXXIII

Since the Psalmist in the eighty-fourth psalm, as though recounting past events, says, “You have blessed your land, Lord; you have turned away the captivity of Jacob. You have forgiven iniquity,” etc., up to “you have turned away from the anger of your indignation” (ibid., 2 ff.), how does he immediately add, as though these things had not happened, “Convert us, O God our Savior, and turn your anger away from us. Will you be angry with us forever”? How does he narrate something as having happened and pray that it may happen?

## ANSWER (From Augustine, *Exposition on this Psalm*, no. 6)

Was it not because he wished to show that he had spoken the past-tense words prophetically? That what he said had already happened had not yet happened, he demonstrates by praying that it may happen. For the prophet would answer you in this way: “I speak of those things as having happened which I see as future. But because they have not yet happened, I pray that what I have already seen may come.”

## QUESTION LXXXIV

Since prophetic and apostolic writings proclaim concerning God that he is the same just and truthful God, especially since the Psalmist says in the eighty-fifth psalm, “And you, Lord, merciful and compassionate . . . . and . . . . truthful” [Col. 0633D] (verse 15), how does God himself appear, conversely, to have said concerning himself in the book of Job against Satan, “But you have moved me against Job, so that I might afflict him without cause” (Job II, 3)? For one who is just could not afflict without cause. And again, because he is truthful, he could not have said anything other than what he did.

## ANSWER (From Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, Book III, no. 3)

For both things to befit the just and truthful God—that he speak truth and do nothing unjust—we must recognize that blessed Job was struck both without cause in one respect and not without cause in another. Blessed Job was not struck without cause because his merit was increased; yet he was struck without cause because no offense committed by him was being punished. God therefore spoke truthfully according to the sense in which blessed Job is understood to have been struck not for punishing sins but for increasing merit.

## QUESTION LXXXV

It is asked how the two things agree with each other, namely joy and fear, according to what is written in the eighty-fifth psalm: “Let my heart rejoice, so that it may fear your name” (verse 11). How can joy be fear? Is fear not usually bitter?

## ANSWER (From Augustine, *Exposition on this Psalm*, no. 16)

One day there will be joy without fear; for now there is joy with fear. There is not [Note: [Col. 0633D] The edition reads more aptly, “There is not yet.”] complete security [Col. 0634B] or perfect joy. If there is no joy, we grow weak; if there is complete security, we rejoice wrongly. Therefore, let him sprinkle joy and inspire fear, so that through the sweetness of joy he may lead us to the seat of security. By giving fear, let him prevent us from rejoicing wrongly and departing from the way.

Therefore he says in the psalm [Note: [Col. 0633D] The edition reads, “The psalm.”]: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. II, 11). So also the Apostle says: “Work out your salvation with fear [Note: [Col. 0634D] The edition reads, “your own salvation.”] and trembling” (Phil. II, 12).

## QUESTION LXXXVI

Since in the eighty-eighth psalm it is read that God swore to David, saying, “Once I have sworn by my holiness: if I lie to David, his offspring will remain forever. And his throne like the sun before me, and like the moon it will remain forever, and the witness in heaven is faithful” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 36–37 ff.), how does he then, conversely, add, “But you have rejected and brought him to nothing; you have delayed your anointed. You have overturned the covenant of your servant,” etc., up to “you have covered him with shame”? Surely God does not promise falsely—which it would be utter madness to say—or swear falsely? Why, then, did he promise those things and do these things?

## ANSWER (From Augustine, Sermon 2 on this psalm, no. 6)

David was the one to whom all these things were promised as to be fulfilled in his offspring, who is Christ [Note: [Col. 0634D] The edition reads, “which.”]. Because of the promises, therefore, that had been made to David, people expected them to be fulfilled in David. Consequently, lest one Christian say, “He spoke about Christ,” while another said, “No, he spoke about that David,” and thus err by saying [Note: [Col. 0634D] The edition reads *videret* (“would see”) rather than *diceret* (“would say”).] that everything had been fulfilled in David, God overturned them in David. When you see that those things which necessarily must be fulfilled were not fulfilled in him, you seek another in whom they might be shown to be fulfilled. So too, in Esau and Jacob, we find the elder worshiped by the younger, since it is written, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23). When you see that this was not fulfilled in those two earlier figures, you await its fulfillment in the two peoples, because God does not deign to make a false promise.

“From your offspring,” he said to David [Note: [Col. 0634D] The edition reads, “David said.”], “I will place one upon your throne” (Ps. 131:11). He promised that something from his offspring would endure forever, and Solomon was born and became so wise that God’s promise concerning David’s offspring was thought to have been fulfilled in him. But Solomon fell (3 Kings 2:1 ff.), and gave way to hope in Christ. Since God can neither be deceived nor deceive, although he knew that Solomon would fall, he did not place his promise in him; rather, after Solomon’s fall, you were to look to God and demand your promise.

“So, Lord, have you lied, by not fulfilling what you promised and not presenting what you swore?” Perhaps at this point God would say to you: “I did indeed swear and promise, but this man did not wish to persevere.” What then? “Lord God, did you not foresee that he would not persevere?” Certainly you did. Why, then, were you promising me that this man, who would not persevere, would endure forever? Did you not say, “If they forsake my law, and do not keep my commandments, and profane my covenant” (ibid., 31 ff.), “my promise will nevertheless remain and my oath will be fulfilled”? “Once I swore by my holiness”—within, in a certain secret place, at the very fountain from which the prophets drank and then belched forth these things to us. “Once,” he says, “I swore: if I lie to David.” Present, then, what you swore; give back what you promised. It was taken away from this David so that it would not be expected in this David. Await, therefore, what I promised [Note: [Col. 0635D] The Benedictines say that this is how it reads in the manuscripts, whereas the editions have *promisit* (“he promised”). Thus our text agrees with the manuscripts.].

David himself knew this. For see what he says: “But you have rejected and reduced him to nothing.” Where, then, is what you promised? “You have delayed your anointed one.” Although he lists certain sad things, in this expression he nevertheless restores us. What you promised, O God, remains entirely; for you have not taken away your anointed one, but delayed him. In this David, therefore, in whom the ignorant expected God to fulfill his promises [Note: [Col. 0635D] The edition reads, “To this David . . .”], see what happened, so that God’s promises might be fulfilled more securely in another.

“You overturned the covenant of your servant.” For where is the old covenant of the Jews? Where is that promised land, in which they sinned while dwelling, and which, once destroyed, they abandoned? Are you looking for the kingdom of the Jews? It is no more. “You profaned his holiness upon the earth.” You showed that those holy things they possessed were earthly. “You destroyed all his walls, with which you had fortified him.” For when would he have been plundered, unless the walls had been destroyed? “You placed his fortifications in terror” [Note: [Col. 0635D] The words *in formidinem* (“in terror”) are absent from the editions.]. What does “in terror” mean? It means that this might be said to sinners: “If God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you” (Rom. 11:21).

“All who passed along the way plundered him”—that is, all the nations. By “the way,” that is, by this present life, those passing along it plundered Israel; they plundered David. First, see his fragments among all the nations. For it was said of these very people, “They will become portions for foxes” (Ps. 62:11). Scripture called wicked kings foxes: deceitful and timid men, whom another’s strength terrifies. Therefore, when the Lord himself was speaking about Herod, who threatened him, he said, “Go and tell that fox” (Luke 13:32). The king who fears no human being is himself a fox. He is not that lion from the tribe of Judah, of whom it is said, “You have gone up; lying down, you have slept like a lion” (Gen. 49:9) [Note: [Col. 0635D] The edition reads differently: “The king who fears no human being is not himself a fox: he is that lion . . . of whom it is said, ‘You have gone up; lying down, you have slept,’ etc.” Thus the king under discussion is understood as Christ; in our text, however, it is plainly Herod, who, like the unjust judge mentioned by Luke the Evangelist, did not respect any human being.].

“You went up by power; you slept by power, because you wished to sleep” [Note: [Col. 0636D] The editions add, according to the Benedictines, “because you wished to go up,” which is absent from the manuscripts. Please note again that Julian’s text agrees with the manuscripts.]. Hence also the statement, “I slept” (Ps. 3:6) [Note: [Col. 0636D] Instead of *Unde et illud*, the edition has, “Therefore in another psalm he says.”].

Those, then, of whom it had been said, “They will become portions for foxes,” are the ones of whom it is now said: “All who passed along the way plundered him; he became a reproach to his neighbors. You exalted the right hand of his enemies; you gladdened all his enemies.” Consider the Jews, and see that everything foretold has been fulfilled.

“You turned away the help of his sword”—how they once used to fight with a few men and overthrow many [Note: [Col. 0636D] The better edition lacks the particle *non* (“not”).]. “You turned away the help of his sword, and you did not assist him in battle.” Deservedly defeated, deservedly captured, deservedly alienated from his kingdom, deservedly scattered. For he lost the land on account of which he killed the Lord.

“You dissolved him from purification.” What does this mean? Among all these evils, this is a great terror. For if he has been dissolved from purification, he no longer has to be cleansed, but must be cast away. From what purification, then, is the Jew dissolved? From faith. “For we live by faith” (Hab. 2:4), and it was said concerning faith: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). Since only faith in Christ cleanses, by not believing in Christ they have been released from purification.

“You struck his throne down to the ground”; deservedly, then, you also broke it. “You shortened the days of his throne” [Note: [Col. 0636D] In the editions this was repeated here, the Benedictines say: “You shortened the days of his throne”; but it is absent from the manuscripts. Thus again Julian’s text agrees with the manuscripts.]. They thought they would reign forever. “You drenched him with shame.” All these things came upon the Jews [Note: [Col. 0636D] The edition reads *evenerunt* (“befell”) rather than *venerunt* (“came”).]. Yet Christ was not taken away, but delayed.

## QUESTION LXXXVII

Since the Psalmist says, “Who is the man who lives and will not see death?” (Ps. 88:49), how does Christ seem, by contrast, to have promised in the Gospel, saying, “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death” (John 8:51)?

## ANSWER

The Psalmist spoke of one death, while the Savior foretold another. When the Psalmist said, “Who is the man who lives and will not see death?” he was asking about bodily death and declaring with certainty that absolutely no one lives without seeing death. It was as if he said: “There is no other human being who lives and does not see death, except the one who alone rescued his soul from the hand of hell”—that is, the one who died for us and, rising again, will die no more.

But when the Lord speaks in the Gospel and promises, “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death,” he was not speaking of this bodily death, by which everyone dies, but of eternal death—that is, the death of condemnation with the devil and his angels. That is the true death; the other is a departure. In this sense, therefore, the two statements are not contradictory.

## QUESTION LXXXVIII

Since the Psalmist says, “Who will be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88:7), how does the Apostle say, “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2)?

## ANSWER  
*(From Gregory the Great, Book XVIII of the Moralia, no. 79)*

How, then, will they be like him, and how will they not be like him? They will be like this wisdom in image, but not in equality. By beholding God’s eternity, they become eternal; and while receiving the gift of his vision, they imitate, through their reception of blessedness, what they see.

Thus they are like him because they become blessed; yet they are not like the Creator, because they are creatures. They possess a certain likeness to God because they do not have an end; yet they do not possess the equality of the uncircumscribed, because they are circumscribed.

## QUESTION LXXXIX

Since David says of Christ in Psalm 109, “The Lord is at your right hand” (verse 5), as though indicating that God the Father stands at the Son’s right hand, how does Paul, apparently by contrast, declare in his Letter to the Ephesians that Christ sits at the Father’s right hand, saying, “He made him sit at his right hand in the heavenly places” (Eph. 1:20)? This is especially so since the Psalmist also testifies to the very thing Paul says at the beginning of that psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.”

## ANSWER

When it is said, “Sit at my right hand,” the Father is understood to have placed the Son at his right hand. When it is said, “The Lord is at your right hand,” the speech is directed to the Father himself, as though he were told: “O God the Father, behold, the Lord Christ, sitting at your right hand, will shatter kings on the day of his wrath.” Nevertheless, both testimonies signify that the Son sits at the Father’s right hand.

## QUESTION XC

Since the Psalmist says, “The one with haughty eyes and an insatiable heart—I did not eat with him” (Ps. 100:5), how is the Lord, by contrast, read in the Gospel to have eaten with the proud and with sinners (Matt. 10:10 ff.)?

## ANSWER  
*(From Augustine’s exposition of this psalm, nos. 8–9)*

What does “I did not eat with him” mean? It means, “I did not dine with him.” For *vesci* means “to eat.” Why, then, do we first find the Lord himself eating with the proud? For a certain proud man had invited him. He is the one who was displeased because a sinful woman, who was notorious in the city, approached the Lord’s feet (Luke 7:36 ff.). This Pharisee was proud, yet God dined with him.

How does he set this before us? When he himself did not do it, he urges us to imitate him. We see that he dined with the proud; how, then, does he forbid us to dine with them? We do dine with our brothers for the sake of some correction; we also refrain from dining with our brothers, so that they may be corrected. If we see those who are attached to us [Note: [Col. 0637D] The manuscripts have *nobis haerent* (“are attached to us”), according to the Benedictines; the Erasmian and Louvain editions instead read, “who were with us and cling to us.” Julian’s text agrees with the manuscripts, as it consistently does.] living badly, we should dine rather with strangers and pagans than with them, so that they may be ashamed and corrected, as the Apostle says: “If anyone does not obey our word by this letter, take note of him, and do not associate with him; and do not regard him as an enemy” [Note: [Col. 0637D] The editions add “with.”], “but admonish him as a brother” (2 Thess. 3:14–15).

We often do this as a remedy, and yet we frequently eat with many strangers and with impious people. What, then, does “With haughty eyes and an insatiable heart, I did not eat with him” mean? The devout heart has its feasts, and the proud heart has its feasts. He said “insatiable heart” because of the very food of proud hearts. What feeds the proud heart? If it is proud, it is envious; it cannot be otherwise. Pride is the mother of envy [Note: [Col. 0638D] The edition reads *invidiae* (“of envy”) rather than *invidentiae*.]. Every proud person, therefore, is envious. If he is envious, he feeds on the misfortunes of others. Hence the Apostle says: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5:15).

When, therefore, you see people eating in this way, do not eat with them; flee such a feast [Note: [Col. 0638D] The edition reads *videtis* (“you see”) rather than *videntes* (“seeing”).]. For they do not satisfy themselves by rejoicing in the misfortunes of others, because their hearts are insatiable. Take care that you are not caught at their feasts.

## QUESTION XCI

Since the Psalmist says in Psalm 106, “He blessed them, and they were greatly multiplied, and their livestock was not diminished” (verses 38–39), how does he seem, by contrast, to add: “They became few, and they were afflicted”?

## ANSWER  
*(From Augustine’s exposition of this psalm, nos. 13–14)*

“Livestock” and “cattle” designate those who walk simply in the Church, or calves—those who are not highly instructed, but are full of faith [Note: [Col. 0638D] The edition reads: “Livestock and cattle are called those who walk simply in the Church, but are useful; they are not highly instructed, but are full of faith.”]. He therefore blessed both the spiritual and the carnal; they were greatly multiplied, and their livestock was not diminished [Note: [Col. 0638D] The edition reads *deminuta* (“diminished”), for that is how Augustine reads it in the text of the psalm.].

This passage of the psalm refers to faithful peoples. But what follows—“They became few and were afflicted”—is said of heretics, because all who separate themselves from unity become few. They are many, but they are in unity, so long as they are not separated from unity [Note: [Col. 0638D] So the manuscripts read, according to the Benedictines; the editions instead have: “but while they are not in unity, they are separated from unity.”]. Once the multitude of unity no longer belongs to them, they are few in heresy and schism.

## QUESTION XCII

Since the Psalmist says, “The dead will not praise you, O Lord” (Ps. 113:17), how does the same Psalmist seem, by contrast, to say, “I will praise your name forever and ever” (Ps. 144:2), and also: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you forever and ever” (Ps. 83:5)?

## ANSWER  
*(From Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 144, no. 5)*

It was indeed said, “The dead will not praise you, O Lord,” but this applies to those of whom it is said, “From the dead, as though he did not exist, confession has perished” (Sir. 17:26), not to those of whom he says, “The one who believes in me, even though he dies, will live” (John 11:25). For the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is not the God [Note: [Col. 0639D] The edition lacks “God” here.] of the dead, but of the living [Note: [Col. 0639D] The edition has “God” here.].

For if you will never be anything except his, you will never cease from praising him. Hear the Apostle: “None of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord” (Matt. 22:32). For this reason, he says again, “Christ died” [Note: [Col. 0639D] The editions add “and rose again,” but elsewhere Augustine reads it as Julian does, as do the others cited by Peter Sabbatier.] “so that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living” (Rom. 14:9). Therefore, because “his greatness will have no end” (Ps. 144:3), neither will our praise—who shall please God even when we have died—have an end.

## QUESTION XCIII  
*(Elsewhere 220)*

Since the Psalmist says, “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11), one might answer him: “If everyone is a liar, then so are you; and the statement you uttered is as false as you yourself are a liar.” But if he himself is not a liar, then the statement is no longer true, because if you are truthful, not every human being is known to be a liar.

## ANSWER

We must note what precedes: “I said in the excess of my mind.” Through this excess of mind, therefore, he passed beyond himself when he made a judgment concerning the condition of humanity. It is as though he plainly said: “I uttered a true statement about the falsehood of all human beings from the place where I myself was above humanity.” He too is a liar insofar as he is human; but he is not a liar at all insofar as, through the excess of his mind, he is above humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0639D] From this question through LXXXVIII inclusive, our enumeration exceeds that found in the editions by two units, because Question LXXXIII has been inserted.]

## QUESTION XCIV

Since the Psalmist says, “For those who practice iniquity will not walk in his ways” (Ps. 118:3), how is the Apostle Paul to be believed to have walked in the ways of the Lord, when he confesses concerning himself, saying, “I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want” (Rom. 7:15)? This is especially difficult since Paul himself, by firm declarations, asserts the opposite—that he walked in the ways of the Lord—saying, “Will we not walk by the same Spirit?” (2 Cor. 12:18), and to Timothy, “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course” (2 Tim. 4:7). What does this mean? Either the saints of the Lord do not walk in the ways of the Lord, or, if they do walk in them, they do not practice iniquity. If they do not practice iniquity, they have no sin, since sin is iniquity (1 John 3:4). But how can they have no sin when it is said, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (ibid., 1:8)?

## ANSWER  
*(From Augustine’s Sermon 2 on Psalm 118, no. 2)*

If you please, let us hear the Apostle Paul himself concerning this question. Indeed, since it pleases us, let us question him. Tell us, blessed Paul: while you were still living in the flesh, did you walk in the ways of the Lord? He replies: “Did we not walk by the same Spirit? Did we not walk in the same footsteps?” (2 Cor. 12:18). And also: “For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:7); and: “I have fought the good fight” (2 Tim. 4:7), and the rest. These answers should be sufficient, by which we have learned that the Apostle Paul walked in the ways of the Lord.

But let us inquire something else of him. Tell us, I ask, Paul: when you were still living in the flesh and walking in the ways of the Lord, did you have sin, or were you without sin? Here too he replies: “Have you not read where I confess, saying, ‘I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want’?” We have heard this as well.

Now, then, let us ask the question: How did you walk in the ways of the Lord if you did the evil that you did not want, when the holy Psalmist thunders, “Those who practice iniquity will not walk in his ways,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0640D] The edition reads *psalmus* (“the psalm”) rather than *Psalmista* (“the Psalmist”).]?

Hear him immediately answering through the following statement: “If I do what I do not want,” he says, “then I myself no longer do it, but sin dwelling in me” [Note: [Col. 0640D] The edition reads: “If I do what I do not want, I myself,” he says, “do it; now,” and so forth.]. Behold how those who walk in the ways of the Lord do not practice sin and yet are not without sin: for they themselves no longer practice iniquity, but the sin that dwells in them does so [Note: [Col. 0640D] The edition reads “it” rather than “iniquity.”].

Yet this resolves the question only so that another, more difficult one arises *(from Augustine’s Sermon 3 on Psalm 118, no. 1)*. How does a person do what he himself does not do? He said both things: “I do not do what I want,” and, “It is not I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.”

We must therefore understand that when the sin dwelling in us operates in us, we ourselves do not operate it, provided that our will does not consent to it and also restrains the members of the body from obeying its desires. For what does sin accomplish against our will except unlawful desires? If the assent of the will is not given to them, some emotion is indeed stirred, but no action is released for it.

The same Apostle taught this when he said: “Therefore, let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12). There are, then, sinful desires to which he forbade us to give obedience. These desires practice sin; if we obey them, we too practice it. But if, obeying the Apostle, we do not obey them, we do not practice it; rather, the sin dwelling in us does so.

If we had no unlawful desires at all, neither we nor sin would accomplish anything evil in us. Yet the movement of unlawful desire, which we do not practice because we do not obey it, is nevertheless said to be something we do, because it is not the strength of an alien nature but our own weakness. From this weakness we shall be completely saved when we have become immortal in mind and body.

Therefore, because we walk in the ways of the Lord, we do not obey sinful desires; and because we are not without sin, we have sinful desires. Accordingly, we no longer practice them by refusing to obey them; rather, the sin dwelling in us stirs them up.

“For those who practice iniquity”—that is, those who obey sinful desires—“will not walk in the ways of the Lord.” Since “human life upon earth is a time of temptation” (Job 7:1), even if we are far from serious crimes, there is nevertheless no lack of occasions when we obey sinful desires in deed, word, or thought. While we are vigilant against greater sins, certain lesser ones creep in upon the unwary. If these are gathered together against us, then, even if they do not crush us individually by their separate movements [Note: [Col. 0641D] So the edition reads, according to the Benedictines; the manuscripts have *molibus*. Perhaps Julian followed this reading, and the typesetters or editors corrected it. In other places, as we have noted, his text consistently agrees with the manuscripts.], they nevertheless overwhelm us all together by their accumulation.

For this reason even those who walk in the ways of the Lord say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), since this prayer itself and this confession belong to the ways of the Lord, although sins themselves do not belong to them *(from the same Augustine, at the place cited above, no. 2)*.

Thus, in the ways of the Lord—which are all embraced by the one faith by which one believes in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5), and who also said, “I am the way” (John 14:6)—no one practices sins [Note: [Col. 0642D] The edition reads *peccatum* (“sin”) rather than *peccata* (“sins”).], but confesses them *(Augustine, ibid., no. 3)*. A person therefore goes astray when he sins; and for this reason the sin committed by one who strays is not attributed to the way. Those on the way of faith are regarded as not sinning, because their sins are not counted against them.

Concerning these people, the Apostle Paul, commending the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:7), showed that it is written in the Psalms [Note: [Col. 0642D] The edition more correctly reads “in the psalm”]: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 31:1–2).

Whoever walks on this way—that is, in devout faith—either does not practice sin, or, if something is committed by one who strays, it is not imputed on account of the way and is regarded as though he had not practiced it. Accordingly, the statement may also rightly be understood in this way: “Those who practice iniquity have not walked in his ways,” so that “iniquity” signifies what departs from faith or does not approach faith. Those who practice iniquity—that is, unbelief—have not walked in his ways, because they have not believed in Christ.

## QUESTION XCV

Since the Psalmist says, “In my heart I have hidden your words” (Ps. 118:11–12), and so forth, how is it consistent for him apparently to add, “Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your ordinances”?

## ANSWER  
*(From Augustine, Sermon 5 on Psalm 118, no. 4)*

How can he still seek to learn what he already keeps hidden in his heart—something he certainly would not have done unless he had learned it? The answer is that he wishes to learn them by doing them, not merely by speaking of them or retaining them in memory.

Since, as it is written in another psalm, the one who gave the law will give blessing (Ps. 83:8), he therefore says, “Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your ordinances.” Because I have hidden your words in my heart so that I may not sin against you, you gave the law; give also the blessing of grace, so that by doing I may learn what you commanded by instruction.

## QUESTION XCVI

How does David say, “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth” (Ps. 118:13), when the Apostle Paul says that God’s judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable (Rom. 11:33)? Who could proclaim all God’s judgments when he cannot search them out?

## ANSWER  
*(From Sermon 6 on the same psalm, nos. 1–2)*

Does the Church not know God’s judgments? Indeed it does. For it certainly knows to whom the Judge of the living and the dead will say, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34), and to whom he will say, “Go into eternal fire.” It knows, I say, that neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor these nor those [Note: [Col. 0642D] The edition reads, “nor those and those.”] whom the Apostle Paul lists there (1 Cor. 6:9), will possess the kingdom of God.

It knows that there will be wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, for every human soul that practices evil, for the Jew first and also for the Greek; and glory, honor, and peace for everyone who practices good, for the Jew first and also for the Greek (Rom. 2:9–10). The Church clearly knows these and similar judgments of God. Yet these are not all of them, since some are inscrutable, like a great and deep, hidden abyss.

Or are even these known to certain more excellent members of this human being who, together with his saving Head, is wholly Christ? They are perhaps called inscrutable to human beings because no one can search them out by his own powers. But why should someone be unable to do so by the gift of the Holy Spirit, if the Lord deigns to grant this to anyone?

Thus it was also said, “God dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16), and yet we hear, “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:5) [Note: [Col. 0642D] The edition reads “draw near to him,” rather than “draw near to me.”]. The question is resolved in this way: he is inaccessible by our powers, but we approach him through his gifts.

Even if no saint at all is permitted to know all God’s judgments so long as “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15)—for it is indeed a great deal for a human being, especially since, to give one example by which the vastness of God’s judgments may be inferred, no one is slow in spirit or lame in body without God’s judgment—the Church nevertheless has grounds to say, and to say truthfully, as the people of God’s possession: “With my lips I have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth.” That means: “I have kept silent about none of your judgments that you wished to make known to me through your words; I have proclaimed them all completely with my lips.”

This is what is signified: he does not say “all your judgments,” but “all the judgments of your mouth”—that is, those you have spoken to me—so that by his mouth we may understand his utterance. We know that this has been done in many revelations of the saints and in the two Testaments. The Church never ceases to proclaim all these judgments everywhere with her lips [Note: [Col. 0643D] The edition reads: “What he did for us . . . through the two Testaments, all these judgments,” and so forth.].

## QUESTION XCVII

Since the Psalmist says in Psalm 118, “I have not turned aside from your judgments” (Ps. 118:102), how does he seem, in what follows, by contrast, to ask for them, saying, “Teach me your judgments” (ibid., 108)? How, then, did he not turn aside from the judgments if he did not know them? But if he did know them, how could he ask to be taught them?

## ANSWER

Augustine explains this in the following words *(Sermon 23 on this psalm, no. 4)*: “So that we might understand that these are the words of one who is making progress and asking that what he had received be increased.”

## QUESTION XCVIII

How can statements be shown to agree when the Gospel answers, by contrast, things that appear contradictory in what the Psalmist says? Thus the Psalmist writes concerning charity: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96). And again: “You set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. 30:9). If charity, through which one reaches God, is broad, how does the Lord say in the Gospel, by contrast, “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. 7:13)?

Here are two other similar statements that seem to contradict one another. The Psalmist says: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept to difficult ways” (Ps. 16:4). And, as though by contrast, the Lord says in the Gospel: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30). How, then, is charity broad if the gate is narrow? How is the yoke easy and the burden light if, in God’s commandments, the ways that are kept are difficult?

## ANSWER  
*(From Gregory the Great, Book II of the Homilies on Ezekiel, Homily 5, no. 13)*

Charity itself quickly resolves this question for us [Note: [Col. 0643D] The Benedictines say that all their manuscripts compel them to read this way, whereas the editors thought it better to write “truth itself.” Once again Julian conforms to the manuscripts.], because the way of God is narrow for those who are beginning, but broad for those who are already living perfectly.

The things we set before the mind spiritually are difficult because they run counter to habit [Note: [Col. 0643D] The Benedictines say that all manuscripts require *usum* (“habit”); the editions read *consuetudinem* (“custom”).]; yet God’s burden is light once we have begun to bear it. Indeed, out of love for him, persecution becomes pleasing, and every affliction for him enters into the sweetness of the mind, just as the holy Apostles rejoiced when they endured scourging for the Lord (Acts 5:41).

Thus the narrow gate becomes broad for those who love; the difficult ways become smooth and level for those who run spiritually. For [Note: [Col. 0644D] The Benedictines restored *enim* (“for”) on their own authority; this is confirmed by Julian, whom they did not consult.] when the mind knows [Note: [Col. 0644D] The edition reads *scit* (“knows”) rather than *sciat* (“may know”).] that it will receive eternal joys for temporal pains, it begins to love the very thing through which [Note: [Col. 0644D] The word *per* (“through”) is absent from the editions.] it is afflicted.

## QUESTION XCIX  
*(Elsewhere 121)*

Since the Psalmist says, “Who founded the earth upon the waters?” (Ps. 135:6), how does Job say, “Who founded the earth upon nothing” (Job 26:7)?

## ANSWER

To ensure that these two statements do not seem contradictory, we have gathered the matter from the discussion of our predecessors. Ambrose also says the following, though somewhat differently (Book I of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 6):

“Let Scripture suffice concerning the nature or position of the earth. According to Job, it must be understood that he suspended the earth upon nothing.”

Philosophers likewise hold that the earth is supported by dense air and hangs motionless, like a sponge, in the midst of the air by the mass of its own substance. Thus, in an equal movement from one side to the other, as though supported by oars like wings and free on every side, it hangs suspended and cannot incline toward either side.

But concerning the Psalmist’s statement, “Who founded the earth upon the waters,” so that it may not seem contrary to the foregoing interpretation, blessed Augustine has woven the following oracle of his discussion. He says *(Exposition of Psalm 135, no. 7)*:

“What does ‘who established the earth upon the waters’ mean? This too is an obscure question, because the earth appears heavier, so that it is believed not to be carried by the waters, but rather to carry the waters. Concerning this matter, lest we appear contentiously to defend our Scriptures against those who think they have discovered these things by certain arguments, whether it is so or otherwise, we have something nearby that we may understand.

“The earth inhabited by human beings, and containing terrestrial animals, which in another passage of Scripture is called the dry land, is said to have been founded upon the waters because it rises above the waters flowing around it. For when a coastal city is said to be founded upon the sea, the sea is not beneath it in the same way that waters are beneath the vaults of caves or beneath ships floating on the surface. Rather, it is called ‘upon the sea’ because it rises above the lower sea.

“Thus Pharaoh is said to have gone out upon the water; for this is what the Greek has, whereas certain Latin manuscripts have ‘to the water’ (Exod. 14:23). So the Lord sat above the well (John 4:6), because both were higher than the river and the well—the one beside the river, the other beside the well.”

If these statements are examined according to the interpretation given above, therefore, they will in no way be contradictory to one another.

## QUESTION C  
*(Elsewhere 97)*

Since David says in Psalm 142, “No living person will be justified in your sight” (verse 2), how does Paul seem, by contrast, to say, “He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, so that we should be holy and blameless before him” (Eph. 1:4)? Either the Ephesians to whom the Apostle writes are holy and blameless before God, in which case the statement “No living person will be justified in your sight” is false; or, if no one will be justified in the sight of God, the preceding statement that they are holy and blameless in God’s sight is false.

## ANSWER

There are two ways to answer this. Paul does not say, “He chose us before the foundation of the world, when we were holy and blameless,” but, “He chose us so that we might be holy and blameless.” That is: we were not holy and blameless beforehand, so that afterward we might become so.

This can also be said of sinners who have turned to better things, and the statement remains valid: “No living person will be justified in your sight”—that is, no one will be justified throughout the whole of his life, in everything he has done during his time in this world. Paul and those like him are chosen not because they were holy and blameless; rather, they are chosen and predestined so that in the life to come they may become holy and blameless through works and virtues.

In addition, the statement should be understood in this sense: he said, “No living person will be justified in your sight”—that is, not everyone will be justified; some will be justified.

## QUESTION CI

[The supplied source ends here.]

In Psalm 144 it is written of God: “His greatness has no end” (v. 3). How, then, does Psalm 88 seem to say the contrary: “God, who is glorified in the council of the righteous, great and terrible above all who are around him” (v. 8)? If God is everywhere, who can be around him, so that he is placed, as it were, in the middle and surrounded by others? For if he has some around him, he is understood as bounded on every side, as it were. But if it is truly said of God, “His greatness has no end,” who are those who remain around him?

**RESPONSE** (From Augustine, Sermon 1 on Psalm 88, no. 8)

Unless it is because he who is everywhere chose to be born in one place according to the flesh, to live among one people, to be crucified in one place, to rise again from one place, and to ascend into heaven from one place? Where he did these things, the nations are around him. If he had remained where he did these things, he would not be great and terrible to all who are around him. But because he preached there in such a way that from there he sent preachers of his name throughout all the nations, working miracles throughout the whole world through his servants, he became great and terrible to all who are around him.

[Note: The edition reads: “throughout all the nations, throughout the whole world; working, etc.”]

### QUESTION CII (Previously 99)

When the Psalmist says, “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Psalm 144:18), how does Solomon say, “They will call upon me, and I will not answer” (Proverbs 1:28)?

**RESPONSE** (From Augustine, exposition of Psalm 144, no. 22, according to the sense, not literally)

Many call upon the Lord, but not in truth, seeking from him profits or estates of earthly things. They seek other things from him, and do not seek him himself. But those who place the Lord himself—by whom they have received the things in which they rejoice—above all the things they have received, and seek God himself not for the sake of anything else but for his own sake, and seem to love him, all these call upon the Lord in truth, and the Lord is believed to be near to them. He does not mean all indiscriminately, including those who ask evil things from him and seek transitory things, but only all those to whom he becomes near when they call upon him in truth, because they desire the things to be given them by the Lord that are pleasing to the Lord himself.

## FROM THE BOOKS OF WISDOM

### QUESTION CIII (Previously 100)

When, in the Proverbs of Solomon, Scripture speaks through the voice of God, saying, “They will call upon me, and I will not answer them” (Proverbs 1:28), how is it that Psalm 85 says, “You, Lord, are kind and gentle, and exceedingly merciful to all who call upon you” (v. 5)? If God answers all who call upon him, how does he say here, “They will call, and I will not answer them”?

**RESPONSE**

There are those who call upon God for God’s sake, and there are those who call upon him for the sake of something else that God does not wish to give. Those who ask according to the Lord’s will—things that God has certainly commanded—are found in the verse of this psalm that says, “Exceedingly merciful to all who call upon you” (from Augustine, exposition of Psalm 85, no. 8). But those who do not call upon God for God’s sake, but ask that something be given them contrary to God’s will, are rejected by the Lord’s words: “They will call, and I will not answer them.”

Some who call do not call upon the Lord; of them it is said, “They did not call upon the Lord” (Psalm 52:6). Rather, they call so that an inheritance of money and worldly rank may come to them. Whoever calls upon the Lord in this way makes him an assistant to his desires, not the fulfiller of his requests.

Consider one who calls upon God in another psalm: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek” (Psalm 26:4). What did he ask? “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” Why this? “That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord.” Therefore, if you are a lover, love him with the most sincere depths of your heart and with pure sighs; love him, cherish him, burn with desire for him, long for him, since you find nothing more delightful than he. If, then, you love and call upon God in this way, you belong to this verse: “And exceedingly merciful to all who call upon you.”

### QUESTION CIV (Previously 101)

When Solomon speaks in Proverbs about the way of iniquity, saying, “Everyone who walks in it will not return” (Proverbs 2:19), how does Paul, returning from persecution and blasphemy, say, “I was a blasphemer and a persecutor” (1 Timothy 1:13), and Peter, turning from denial to weeping, obtain Christ’s regard (Luke 22:61)?

**RESPONSE**

By himself a person can walk in that way of iniquity, but by himself he cannot return from it, except by grace.

### QUESTION CV (Previously 104)

How does Solomon command both things concerning the division of waters—that everyone should pour out his waters in the streets, and, conversely, that he should have them alone? For he says: “Let your springs flow outward, and divide your waters in the streets”; and, conversely: “Keep them for yourself alone,” and so forth (Proverbs 5:16–17).

**RESPONSE** (From Gregory the Great, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 24)

A preacher drinks water from his own cistern when, returning to his heart, he first hears himself what he says. Let him drink the streams of his own well; let him be watered by the irrigation of his own word.

[Note: The edition reads: “He drinks … if he is watered.”]

The text appropriately continues: “Let your springs flow outward, and divide your waters in the streets.”

[Note: In the edition, “your waters” is absent.]

It is right, then, that he first drink himself, and afterward flow out to others by preaching. For to make one’s springs flow outward is to pour the power of preaching into others externally. To divide one’s waters in the streets is to distribute the divine words among a great multitude of hearers according to each person’s capacity.

And because the desire for empty glory often creeps in when the word of God reaches the knowledge of many, after it has been said, “Divide your waters in the streets,” it is rightly added: “Keep them for yourself alone, and let no strangers share in them.”

[Note: Here too the edition lacks “your waters.”]

By “strangers” he means the evil spirits, of whom the voice of a tempted man says through the Prophet: “Strangers have risen against me” (Psalm 53:5). He therefore says: “Divide your waters in the streets, and keep them alone.”

[Note: The edition reads: “Divide your waters in the streets, and yet keep them alone.”]
