As if he were saying more clearly: It is necessary for you to serve preaching outwardly in such a way that you do not join yourself through pride to evil spirits, lest in the ministry of the divine word you admit your enemies as sharers with you. [Note: The edition reads “waters.”]

Thus we divide water in the streets and yet possess it alone when we spread preaching widely outwardly, yet have no desire through it to attain human praise.

### QUESTION CVI (Previously 120)

How did Solomon command, saying, “Do not fear anyone besides the Lord, my son” (Proverbs 7:2, according to the Septuagint), when the Apostle, as though preaching the contrary, says in his Letter to the Ephesians, “Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling,” and also, “Let the wife fear her husband” (Ephesians 6:5; 5:33)?

**RESPONSE**

When wives are commanded to serve their husbands, and slaves their masters, with fear, what else is meant except that this fear itself is referred to God, by whom that subjection is commanded to them, and by whom they are ordered to serve their husbands and masters?

For just as, when masters are obeyed rightly for God’s sake, those good services themselves are referred to the Lord, so, when masters are resisted, the injury itself is referred not to them but to God, as Moses says: “Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord. For what are we?” (Exodus 16:8).

### QUESTION CVII (Previously 105)

How can Solomon say, “Evil pursues sinners” (Proverbs 13:21), while Jeremiah, conversely, says, “It is well with all who transgress and act wickedly” (Jeremiah 12:1)?

**RESPONSE**

The Prophet, disputing with God about the prosperity of the ungodly, distressed on account of the affliction of the saints, seeing them subjected to various hardships and temptations, while sinners, conversely, not only passed through the course of this world without any scourge of humiliation, but even rejoiced in an abundance of riches and the highest prosperity in all things, inflamed by intolerable zeal and the fervor of his spirit, exclaims: “Why does the way of the wicked prosper? It is well with all who transgress and act wickedly.”

By saying this, the Prophet did not approve that sinners receive present goods according to their merits; rather, he anxiously complains, in a certain sense, that it is well here with those who act wickedly. Thus the two statements above are not contrary, since sinners may pursue present goods in this present age while future evil nevertheless awaits them: those who live wickedly and prosper in the present age are proclaimed suddenly to descend into hell.

### QUESTION CVIII (Previously 102)

When Solomon says, “The righteous man, eating, fills his soul, but the souls of the wicked are in want” (Proverbs 13:21), how could the Apostle Paul, who was certainly righteous, say, as though in opposition, “To this present hour we are both hungry and thirsty” (1 Corinthians 4:11), and likewise, “In hunger and thirst and in many fasts” (2 Corinthians 11:27)?

**RESPONSE**

The righteous person is nourished without interruption by the food of God’s word, in which the wicked have no share. By this heavenly bread the righteous is satisfied, while the wicked abstains from it. Therefore Paul was not saying that he was hungry for this heavenly bread, with which he was more fully satisfied, but for the bodily bread by which human life is sustained.

### QUESTION CIX (Previously 103)

When Solomon says, “The heart of the king is in the hand of God, and wherever he wishes, he will turn it” (Proverbs 21:1), how does Daniel seem, conversely, to have said about Nebuchadnezzar, “Those whom he wished he killed, and those whom he wished he struck; those whom he wished he exalted, and those whom he wished he humbled” (Daniel 5:19)? If, in such honors and punishments, exaltation and humiliation, there is neither God’s providence nor his command, but merely the will of those who strike whom they wish and exalt whom they wish, how, then, is the statement understood that the heart of the king is in God’s hand?

**RESPONSE**

Unless perhaps we should call him a holy king, one whose sin does not reign in his mortal body (Romans 6:12), and whose heart is therefore preserved because it is in God’s hand? Whatever is in the hand of God the Father, no one can snatch from it (John 10:29); and whoever has been snatched away is understood not to have been in the Lord’s hand.

### QUESTION CX (Previously 106)

When Solomon says, “Let another’s mouth praise you, and not your own, a stranger’s rather than your lips” (Proverbs 27:2), how does Job seem to have said the contrary, when he recounts his own praises in this way: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame,” and so forth (Job 29:15)?

**RESPONSE**

By saying, “Let another’s mouth praise you, and not your own,” he prohibits the desire for empty glory—that is, he teaches that when we report our good deeds to others, we should seek to increase not our own glory but God’s. For those who intend to act in a way that wins applause are rightly rejected by the Lord as unclean. It is written: “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God” (Proverbs 16:5).

But when holy men speak of good things concerning themselves, they do not act contrary to the rule of the preceding command. In the virtues they proclaim about themselves, and in the good deeds they recall having performed, they recount not their own glory but God’s glory—not so that they themselves may advance among human beings by displaying their deeds, but so that they may draw those to whom they preach toward life by their example.

Therefore, when they announce their own praises in this way, they do not praise themselves with their own mouth, because they proclaim in themselves not their own glory but the Lord’s. Hence they are not contrary to the preceding commands, because they do not speak good things about themselves with their own mouth—that is, through the vice of desiring praise—but by the Spirit of God, by whom they are inwardly moved, they certainly recount the gifts of God that they perceive in themselves. Thus they are praised, as it were, by another’s mouth, since the good qualities of such people are proclaimed by the Spirit of God, who is certainly a stranger to worldly contamination.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord. For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends” (2 Corinthians 10:17–18).

Moses too seems to have praised himself not with his own mouth but with another’s, when, compelled by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he spoke praise about himself as though about someone else, saying: “Now Moses was a very meek man, more than all the people who dwelt on the earth” (Numbers 12:3).

### QUESTION CXI (Previously 107)

When Solomon says, “One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth will stand forever” (Ecclesiastes 1:4), how does Job say that all these things are humbled and taken away (Job 24:24)?

**RESPONSE** (From Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book XVII, no. 11)

We can easily resolve this if we distinguish in what manner the earth and heaven pass away and in what manner they remain. Both pass away according to the appearance they now possess, but in their essence they subsist without end.

Hence Paul says: “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:31).

[Note: After “world,” the following words found in the edition are entirely absent here: “Hence Truth itself says: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. Hence it is said to John in an angelic voice: There will be a new heaven and a new earth. These things, indeed, …”]

These will not be newly created as something different, but these same things will be renewed. Therefore heaven and earth will pass away and will exist, because they will be cleansed by fire from the form they now possess, yet will always be preserved in their own nature.

[Note: The edition reads “passes away.”]

Hence the Psalmist also says: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Psalm 101:28). They now announce this final transformation of theirs to us through the very alternations by which they continually vary for our use. For the earth falls away from its winter appearance through dryness and becomes green through the moisture of spring; the sky is daily covered with the darkness of night and renewed by the brightness of day.

### QUESTION CXII (Previously 108)

When Solomon says, “Do not persist in an evil work” (Ecclesiastes 8:3), how does the angel speak conversely in the Apocalypse: “Let the one who does harm continue to do harm, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy” (Revelation 22:11)?

**RESPONSE**

Everyone who is truly subject to God through fear knows the will of the Lord, who commands him to turn away from evil and do good (Psalm 33:15). Therefore, when the angel says to John, “Let the one who does harm continue to do harm, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy,” he speaks not by commanding but by foretelling or prophesying.

He does not introduce a command that it is beneficial for people to do harm or make themselves filthy; rather, he foretells or prophesies what may happen to such people because of their completed iniquity.

The verse of the psalm also pertains to this, where it says, “Let the wickedness of sinners be completed” (Psalm 7:10), which Augustine explains in this way (*Exposition of this Psalm*, no. 9):

> “Let it be completed,” he says, “let it be perfected, according to what is found in the Apocalypse: ‘Let the righteous become more righteous,’ and so forth (Revelation 22:11). The wickedness of those who crucified the Son of God seems to have been completed, but greater is the wickedness of those who refuse to live rightly and hate the commands of truth, for whose sake the Son of God was crucified. “Let the wickedness of sinners therefore be completed,” he says—that is, let it reach the summit of wickedness, so that the just judgment may now come.”

### QUESTION CXIII (Previously 109)

Since there is one Church, as Solomon testifies, “My perfect one is one, my dove is one” (Song of Songs 6:8), and as the Apostle says, “The Church of the living God, which is the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15), how did John write in the Apocalypse to seven churches (Revelation 1:4)?

**RESPONSE**

Unless it is so that the one catholic Church, full of the Spirit sevenfold, may be designated, just as we know Solomon also said of the Lord: “Wisdom built herself a house; she carved out seven pillars” (Proverbs 9:1). Nevertheless, there is no doubt that these seven are one, since the Apostle says: “The Church of the living God, which is the pillar and foundation of the truth.”

### QUESTION CXIV (Previously 110)

When it is written in the book of Solomon, “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7), how is it that, conversely, in Ezekiel this same Spirit is said to move about (Ezekiel 1:13), or that in the Book of Wisdom he is called now mobile, now stable (Wisdom 7:22–23)?

**RESPONSE** (From Gregory the Great, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 5, nos. 10–11)

Why is this Spirit, who fills all things, called both mobile and stable? If we turn to the usage of ordinary human speech, we quickly discover the sense of the speaker. A person, because he moves about in the region in which he is, undoubtedly comes everywhere and is suddenly found where he is not expected. Therefore, to signify the presence of the almighty Spirit everywhere, he is called both mobile and stable.

He is stable because by nature he contains all things; but he is called mobile because he encounters everyone everywhere, even those who do not know it. Thus, as he holds all things, he is called stable; as he presents himself as present to all, he is called mobile.

It can also be understood in another way. In the hearts of the saints he always remains with respect to certain virtues; with respect to others, he comes in order to depart and departs in order to come. In faith, hope, charity, and the other good things without which one cannot reach the heavenly homeland—such as humility, charity, justice, and mercy—he does not abandon the hearts of the perfect.

But in the power of prophecy, eloquence of teaching, and performance of miracles, he is sometimes present to his chosen ones and sometimes withdraws from them. He is present so that they may be lifted up toward him; he withdraws so that they may be humbled.

[Note: The edition reads “remains.”]

[Note: The edition reads: “Why is this Spirit … called …? But if we turn to the usage …”]

[Note: The edition reads “who.”]

[Note: The edition reads “almighty.”]

[Note: The edition reads: “He is present so that they may be lifted up; and he withdraws himself so that they may be humbled,” and so forth.]

[Note: Samson presents this question in book II, chapter 27, no. 6, or page 510 of the same volume. After citing the passage from the Book of Kings, “An evil spirit from the Lord rushed upon Saul,” he says: “In discussing this in [lacuna] the *Antichimenon* [lacuna], Julian says: ‘Some ask: If it is the Lord’s, why is it evil?’ Here the one and the same spirit is called both the Lord’s and evil—the Lord’s, namely, by the permission of just authority, and so forth.”]

### QUESTION CXV (Previously 111)

Since in both Testaments the Spirit of the Lord is read to be good, as, among other passages, in Solomon: “You gave them your good Spirit, O Lord” (Nehemiah 9:20), how is it written in the Books of Kings that “an evil spirit from the Lord rushed upon Saul” (1 Kings 18:10 and 19:9), so that both descriptions are expressed—both “from the Lord” and “evil”? If it is from the Lord, why is it evil? If it is evil, how is it called the Lord’s?

**RESPONSE**

The Holy Spirit of God, who is the third person in the Trinity, is certainly good. Concerning him it is written in the Book of Wisdom that he is manifold, subtle, mobile, eloquent, undefiled, certain, sweet, loving what is good, keen, and preventing no one from doing good (Wisdom 7:22–23).

But this spirit, who is called both the Lord’s and evil, must be understood to be the devil: the Lord’s, namely, by permission of just authority, but evil through the desire of an unjust will. For everything the devil wills is unjust; yet, with God’s permission, all his power is just.

[Note: After “justa,” supply from Samson: “For of himself he unjustly desires to tempt anyone, but God justly permits those who are to be tempted to be tempted.” Thus, in these two expressions—by which the spirit is called both the Lord’s and evil—there are contained both the just power in the devil and the unjust will. “For he himself also …”]

He is called an evil spirit because of his most wicked will, and the Lord’s Spirit because of the most just power he has received (Gregory, *Moralia* II.17; XVIII.4).

### QUESTION CXVI (Previously 112)

How is it said in the Book of Wisdom to God, “Since you are just, you dispose all things justly” (Wisdom 12:15), when immediately afterward the same book says, “You condemn even one who ought not to be punished, and you regard him as a stranger to your power”? How is he just and how does he dispose all things justly, if he condemns one who ought not to be punished?

**RESPONSE** (From the same Gregory, *Moralia*, book III, no. 27)

Our Mediator certainly ought not to have been punished for himself, because he committed no contamination of guilt. But if he had not accepted what he did not owe, he would never have freed us from the death we did owe.

Therefore, since the Father is just, when he punishes the Just One he disposes all things justly, because through this he justifies all things: he condemns for sinners the one who is without sin, so that all the elect might rise to the summit of righteousness precisely because the one who is above all endured the condemnation of our injustice.

[Note: The edition reads “no guilt.”]

[Note: The edition reads “because of which.”]

### QUESTION CXVII (Previously 113)

When Solomon says, “There is a shame that brings sin,” how does he immediately add there, as though in opposition, “There is a shame that brings glory”?

[Note: The learned reader will not be surprised that our Julian attributes the Book of Ecclesiasticus to Solomon, just as it is well known that many ancient Fathers of the Church did so, including the Africans at the Third Council of Carthage, Innocent I in his letter to Exsuperius of Toulouse, Cyprian, Basil, Ambrose, and others in various places. “For this book,” says Isidore of Seville, “because of the great similarity of its meaning and equality of its eloquence, is prefaced under Solomon’s name. But it is established that it was published by Jesus son of Sirach.”]

**RESPONSE** (From the same Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 10, no. 17)

Just as modesty is praiseworthy in what is evil, so it is blameworthy in what is good. To blush at evil is wisdom; to blush at good is foolishness. Whoever is ashamed of the evils he has done, and repents of them, reaches the freedom of life; but whoever is ashamed to do good falls from the state of uprightness and moves toward condemnation.

### QUESTION CXVIII (Previously 114)

When Solomon says, “Do not repeat a word in your prayer” (Ecclesiasticus 7:15), how does Paul, as though in opposition, command, saying, “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17)?

**RESPONSE** (From the same Gregory, *Moralia*, book X, no. 28)

We must carefully remember what is said: “Do not repeat a word in your prayer.” By these words the wise man certainly does not prohibit us from frequently asking forgiveness, but from repeating our sins. As if he were saying openly: Once you have lamented the evil things you have done, do not again do what you must lament once more in your prayers. Therefore, when he forbade a word to be repeated in prayer, he did not forbid frequent prayer; he forbade the repetition of sins.

### QUESTION CXIX (Previously 115)

When Jesus son of Sirach says, “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15), how does the Apostle likewise say, “Greed is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6:10)?

[Note: Perhaps Julian had written, as above, “when Solomon says,” and someone else ineptly corrected it.]

**RESPONSE**

By saying this, the Apostle Paul, as he commonly does, explained the prophetic statement, since whether you call it “the beginning of every sin” or “the root of all evils,” you mean one and the same thing. Moreover, greed and pride are one evil to such an extent that a proud person cannot exist without greed, nor a greedy person without pride.

For the devil, in whom pride holds the chief place, was greedy for his own power and for the destruction of humanity; and humanity itself, through desire for the forbidden tree and aspiration to divine likeness, showed itself afflicted by the disease of greed.

Therefore, if we wish to complete the course of our struggle, let us first beware of greed and pride—not two evils, but one, from which all evil acts take their beginning. For without pride, what sins could even be begun, when it is said, “The beginning of every sin is pride”? Or without greed, which is the root of all evils, what evils could be done, since without the root they are either counted as nothing or are dead?

Furthermore, if I cannot commit any sin unless I consent to my own pleasure—which is the characteristic of greed—and disregard God’s commands—which is the evil of pride—how can every sin not proceed from greed, which is the root of all evils, and from pride, which is called the beginning of every sin?

Another teacher also says the following about this. He says (Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XI, nos. 18–19):

> “Since pride is love of one’s own excellence, while envy is hatred of another’s happiness, it is easy to see which gives rise to which.

[Note: The edition reads *invidia* (‘envy’).]

For by loving his own excellence, a person envies either equals, who might become equal to him; inferiors, lest they become equal to him; or superiors, because he cannot become equal to them.

[Note: The edition reads *quod* (‘because’) rather than *qui* (‘who’).] Thus, by being proud, the envious person is envious; not by being envious is each person proud. Rightly, then, the beginning of every sin is pride.
>
> “To this testimony, not inappropriately, may also be joined what the Apostle says: ‘Avarice is the root of all evils,’ if we understand avarice in a general sense, by which each person desires something more than is proper, because of his own excellence and a certain love of what is his own. Latin wisely gave this the name *privatum* (‘private’), since it is clear that the word is derived rather from loss than from increase. For every deprivation diminishes.
>
> “Thus, from the very point at which pride wishes to rise above others, it is thrust into narrowness and poverty, when it is reduced by self-love to the common detriment of the state.

[Note: The edition reads: “when, to the detriment of the common good, he is reduced from what is common to what is private through self-love.”]

> “There is also a particular kind of avarice, more commonly called love of money. By using its name to signify the species, the Apostle wished universal avarice to be understood when he said, ‘Avarice is the root of all evils.’ For by this the devil too fell, although he certainly did not love money but his own will.

[Note: The edition reads “power.”]

> “Accordingly, perverse self-love deprives the swollen spirit of holy fellowship and constricts it in misery, since through iniquity it desires to be preserved.”

[Note: The edition reads “to be satisfied.”]

### QUESTION CXX (Previously 116)

How is it written in Ecclesiasticus, “If you do good, know to whom you do good, and there will be abundant gratitude for your gifts” (Ecclesiasticus 12:1)? For this seems contrary to the command, “Do not choose whom you should benefit.”

**RESPONSE**

In the passage where it is written, “Do not choose whom you should benefit,” nothing more plausible occurs to me than what Christ says in the Gospel:

> “When you make a luncheon or a dinner, do not invite your friends, or your brothers, or your relatives, or your rich neighbors, lest perhaps they also invite you in return, and repayment be made to you. But when you make a feast, invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind; and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you” (Luke 14:12 ff.).

Therefore, this is what he means by “Do not choose whom you should benefit,” which Christ also confirms by saying, “Do not invite the rich.”

It is said, “Do not choose whom you should benefit,” as if it were said: Do not spend the use of your almsgiving on the persons of the rich, lest, by the choice of your inclination, you refresh one who is not in need while considering him, but, by choosing persons, feed a rich man. For, as a certain wise man said, “What else is it to give to one who has than to waste?”

But the statement, “If you do good, know to whom you do good,” is understood to mean that, in giving, one should consider age and weakness, and sometimes also modesty, which reveals a noble birth, so that you may give more generously to the elderly, who can no longer obtain food for themselves by their labor.

Likewise, consider bodily weakness, and then be more ready to help if someone has fallen from wealth into poverty, especially if he has lost what he possessed not through his own fault but through robbery, confiscation, or accusations.

If these things are carefully considered according to what has been said, they will in no way seem to contradict one another. In one and the same command of the Lord we find both explained. In the words, “Do not invite your friends, brothers, relatives, or the rich,” we understand the statement, “Do not choose whom you should benefit.” But what is added in the same Gospel reading—“Invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind”—pertains to what is written in Ecclesiasticus: “If you do good, know to whom you do good.”

Therefore, when it is written, “Do not choose,” it is necessary to understand implicitly: “those who have means,” as the persons whom you should benefit.

### QUESTION CXXI (Previously 117)

When it is written in the Book of Jesus son of Sirach, “Give to the good, and do not receive the sinner. Do good to the humble, and do not give to the impious; forbid giving them bread” (Ecclesiasticus 12:5–6), how does Christ seem, as though in opposition, to command in the Gospel, saying, “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6:30)?

**RESPONSE**

We find this explained by blessed Augustine in the following way. He says (*Exposition of Psalm 102*, no. 13):

> “Show mercy to the wicked, not as wicked: for the wicked person himself, insofar as he is wicked, do not receive him; that is, do not receive him with a purpose and love directed toward his wickedness.
>
> “A sinful person also comes before you. When I say, ‘A sinful person comes before you,’ I have spoken two names; these two names are not superfluous. One name refers to the fact that he is human, the other to the fact that he is a sinner. The fact that he is human is the work of God; the fact that he is a sinner is the work of the human being. Give to the work of God; do not give to the work of the human being.
>
> “What does it mean to give to the work of the human being? It is to give to hunters, actors, charioteers, and prostitutes. Why do they give? Do they perhaps give to the Lord and to those people themselves? For they do not attend there to the nature of God’s work, but to the wickedness of human work.

[Note: The passage reads somewhat differently in the edition: “He who gives to actors, who gives to charioteers (Amerbach and Erasmus conjectured, less well, ‘soothsayers’), who gives to prostitutes—why does he give? Do not they too give to human beings? Yet they do not attend there …”]

[Note: Here the hunter is, as the Benedictine editors correctly state, one who fought with wild beasts in the arena; charioteers were those who drove and managed the horses of the racing chariots in the circus.]

> “Do you wish to see what you honor in the hunter, when you dress him? If it is said to you, ‘Such are your sons,’ you say, ‘It is an insult.’

[Note: The Benedictines published this passage restored from better manuscripts, whereas in the printed editions it read quite differently: “If it is said to you concerning the prostitutes, ‘Such are your daughters,’ it is an insult,” and so forth. For this reason our Julian, as we have often noted elsewhere, consulted more accurate manuscripts of Augustine; this is also evident below in the reading ‘when you give,’ where the printed editions had ‘when you do not give.’]

> “Why is it an insult, unless because of that iniquity, unless because of that disgrace? Therefore, when you give, you do not give to strength but to disgrace. Since, then, the person who gives to the hunter does not give to the human being but to a most wicked profession—for if he were merely a human being and were not a hunter, you would not give—you honor the vice in him, not his nature.
>
> “Conversely, if you give something to a righteous person, to a prophet, or to a disciple of Christ who needs it, and do not consider that he is Christ’s disciple or God’s minister, but consider some temporal advantage—for perhaps at some time he may have been necessary to your case because you gave him something—then you have not given to a righteous person, if you have given in the same way as the other person did not give to the human being when he gave to the hunter.
>
> “If you seek such service from him, the Lord will deny you the reward of the righteous, unless you add the proper qualification. For he says: ‘Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person’ (Matthew 10:41–42)—that is, because he receives him because he is righteous—‘truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward.’
>
> “Therefore, just as you understand, ‘Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward,’ so understand: ‘Whoever receives a sinner in the name of a sinner will lose his reward.’”

[Note: The edition reads “then you have not given,” and similarly, “as the other did not give,” rather than the text above.]

[Note: The edition reads “denied you.”]

[Note: The edition reads “whoever will have received.”]

[Note: The edition reads “receiving.”]

[Note: The edition reads “whoever will have received.”]

[Note: The edition reads “receiving.”]

Therefore, with this testimony excepted from the general command that says, “Give to everyone who asks you,” the other statements will not be contrary, because in these matters the giver’s intention alone is considered. Thus it will not be contrary to the command to feed both the righteous and the sinner, provided that the service of humanity is rendered beneficially and piously: to the righteous because he is righteous, and to the sinner not because he is a sinner, but because he is a creature of God.

### QUESTION CXXII (Previously 118)

How does Solomon say, “Do not trust your enemy forever” (Ecclesiasticus 12:10), when the Lord commands in the Gospel, “Be in agreement with your adversary while you are with him on the way” (Matthew 5:25)?

**RESPONSE**

Solomon’s command not to trust an enemy is understood of the devil, so that we should never entrust ourselves to him. But when the Lord commands us to be in agreement with our adversary, this is said as a command of his law, so that, by agreeing with him, we may not be handed over to the judge and burned by him as dissenters.

### QUESTION CXXIII (Previously 119)

How does Solomon say, “Blessed is the one who has not been pierced by the sorrow of sin” (Ecclesiasticus 14:1), when James commands, “Be miserable, mourn, and weep” (James 4:9)?

**RESPONSE**

He certainly calls blessed the one who has committed no sin by which he might be pierced with sorrow. It can happen that some who live blessedly are pierced not by sorrow over crimes but by desire for eternal things. But what James commands—that one should mourn and weep—can be understood in both ways: either of those who lament their own evils, or of those who sigh solely from love of the heavenly homeland.

## FROM THE BOOK OF JOB

### QUESTION CXXIV (Previously 122)

How does Job say (Job 1:6) that Satan stood among the sons of God before the Lord, when it is written in the Gospel that they cannot see God unless they are pure in heart? For he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). How could Satan, who cannot be pure in heart, have been present before the Lord in order to see him? [Note: [Col. 0656D] The Benedictine edition reads, “how could he have been present in order to see the Lord?” But its editors note that several manuscripts read as in our text, supported by Abbot Samson in *Apology*, Book II, ch. 27, vol. II of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 512.]

**RESPONSE** *(From Gregory the Great, Moralia, Book II, §§4–5).*

We must observe that Satan is said to have been present before the Lord, but not to have seen the Lord. Satan came to be seen by the Lord, not to see the Lord. [The printed edition has more briefly: “For he came to be seen, not to see.”] He himself was in the Lord’s sight, but the Lord was not in his sight. It is like a blind man standing in the sun: he is indeed bathed in the sun’s rays, yet he does not see the light by which he is illuminated. Thus Satan was present among the angels in the Lord’s sight, because the divine power, which by its perception penetrates all things in the order of the subtler nature [the words “in the order of the subtler nature” are absent from the edition], saw the unclean spirit, although he himself did not see.

## INTERROGATION CXXV (Also numbered 123)

How can Job say: “I have sinned; what shall I do to you, O guardian of mankind?” (Job 7:20), or: “You wish to consume me for the sins of my youth” (13:26), when, on the contrary, he seems to have said: “For my heart does not reproach me throughout all my life” (27:6)? How can he deny that he is reproached by his own heart, when above he accuses himself of having sinned?

**RESPONSE** *(From the same Gregory, Moralia, Book XVIII, §§10–11).*

We must know that there are sins which the righteous cannot avoid [the edition reads: “which the righteous can avoid”; and: “there are some which even the righteous cannot avoid”]. For whose heart, while it remains in this corruptible flesh [the edition reads “while it remains,” rather than “while it subsists”], does not slip into an evil thought, even if it does not sink as far as the pit of consent? Yet merely entertaining such thoughts is itself sin [the edition reads “perverse” rather than “small”]. But when resistance is offered to the thought, the soul is freed from its shame.

The mind of the righteous, therefore, although free from perverse action, sometimes nevertheless falls into perverse thought. It slips into sin [the edition reads: “It therefore slips into sin”], because it turns aside at least in thought; yet it has no reason afterward to reproach itself with tears, because it restores itself before it falls through consent. Properly, then, the man who confessed himself a sinner [the edition reads “confessed”] does not at all confess that he is reproached by his own heart: although perhaps in thinking something unlawful he once failed to maintain uprightness, he nevertheless resisted the thought with a courageous struggle of mind.

## INTERROGATION CXXVI (Also numbered 124)

How can Job, introducing despair, say: “I despair; I shall no longer live” (Job 7:16), when he immediately adds: “Spare me, for my days are nothing”? These two expressions—“I despair” and “spare me”—do not seem to agree. For one who despairs no longer asks to be spared, while one who still desires to be spared plainly does not despair.

**RESPONSE** *(From the same Gregory, Moralia, Book VIII, §46).*

He despairs for one reason, but the holy man asks to be spared for another: namely, while through despair he abandons the good things of passing life, he rises stronger in hope to obtain the things that endure. By despairing, therefore, he is led more effectively to the hope of pardon; for he desires the things to come more certainly in proportion as he more truly abandons present things through despair.

For a righteous person to despair [the edition reads “of the righteous person”] means to abandon the goods of the present life by choosing eternity, to seek what will remain, and not to place confidence in temporal things (ibid., §45). Whoever does this [the edition reads “doing this”] asserts that he will no longer live, because each day he kills himself to the life of passion through a life-giving death. Whoever despairs in this ordered manner rightly desires to be spared.

## INTERROGATION CXXVII (Also numbered 125)

How can Job say both: “I know that you do not spare the transgressor,” and, conversely: “You have numbered my steps, and you spare my sins” (Job 9:28; 14:16)? If the transgressor is not spared, who is rescued from eternal death, since no one is found free from sin?

**RESPONSE** *(From the same Gregory, Moralia, Book IX, §54).*

The Lord does not spare the transgressor, because he does not leave sin without punishment. Either the person himself punishes it in himself through repentance, or God strikes him, taking vengeance together with the person. Sin is therefore not spared, because it is never released without retribution.

God strives to wipe away from his elect, through temporal affliction, the stains of iniquity that he does not wish to see in them forever [the Benedictines restored “that he does not wish to see” from all the manuscripts they cite; the edition had “that he does not wish to avenge.” This again shows the agreement of Julian’s text with the manuscripts]. God therefore spares, and does not spare, human sins. He does not spare them in that he does not leave sin without punishment; but he does spare when he turns the punishment inflicted toward the expiation of sins. It is rightly said that God does not spare the transgressor, because he cuts away our sins either through us or through himself, even when he releases us from them.

## INTERROGATION CXXVIII (Also numbered 126)

How can Job, who had already said above, “Nothing on earth happens without a cause,” seem afterward to add the contrary, saying: “He has multiplied my wounds even without cause” (Job 5:6; 9:17)?

**RESPONSE.**

Concerning the statement, “Nothing on earth happens without a cause,” blessed Gregory says as follows (Moralia, Book VI, §13):

> “For this reason the sluggish person often receives intelligence, so that he may be punished more justly for his negligence, because he refuses to know what he could have attained without labor. And for this reason the diligent person is sometimes burdened by slowness of understanding, so that he may find greater rewards in recompense in proportion as he labors more intensely in the pursuit of discovery [the editions add after “the diligent person”: “and the intelligent person,” words absent from all the manuscripts cited by the Benedictine editors, as they are from our text]. Nothing, therefore, is without a cause on earth, since slowness benefits the diligent person toward reward, while quickness increases the punishment of the sluggish.”

Accordingly, “nothing on earth happens without a cause” must be understood to mean: nothing happens without the cause of divine distribution or permission.

But the statement, “He has multiplied my wounds even without cause,” is understood in this way. Blessed Job, taking upon himself the voice of the human race, said this on behalf of those who, bound by the guilt of original sin [from Book IX, §32], die before they are cleansed by the grace of baptism, and who are removed from the present light before they reach the point of earning good or evil merits through active life. Since the sacraments of salvation do not free them from the guilt of their origin, and since they have done nothing of their own here, they arrive there for punishment.

For such people, being born corruptible [the Benedictine edition reads “corruptibly”; several other manuscripts read “corruptible,” as does our text] is one wound, and dying according to the flesh is another. But because eternal death also follows after death, their wounds are multiplied, by a hidden and just judgment, even without cause, insofar as human understanding can grasp it [the edition omits “insofar as human understanding can grasp it”]. Thus, whoever, without adding any personal sin, is destroyed solely because of the guilt of his origin—what is he, except one wounded without cause?

The two statements can also be understood in another way. Blessed Job was not struck so that the blow might cleanse vice in him, but so that it might increase his merit. Nothing, therefore, happens on earth without a cause, since divine punishment strikes a person either for cleansing or for testing. But here blessed Job declares that he was wounded without cause, because he was not struck so that the blow might cleanse vice in him. He speaks outwardly of himself what Truth testifies inwardly concerning him, saying: “You moved me against him, to afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3).

## INTERROGATION CXXIX (Also numbered 127)

How can Job say: “He knows both the deceiver and the one who is deceived” (ibid. 12:16), when the Lord in the Gospel seems to say to the wicked: “I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matt. 7:23)?

**RESPONSE** *(From the same Gregory, Moralia, Book II, §18).*

God’s “knowing” is sometimes said of recognizing and sometimes of approving. He knows the wicked person because he recognizes and judges him; and he does not know him because he does not approve him. He would not have judged anyone wicked if he did not recognize him. [Note: The edition reads: “And he knows the wicked person because he judges him by recognizing him (for he would not have judged anyone wicked if he did not recognize him); and yet,” etc. We leave Julian’s text untouched, since it is independently established that Abbot Samson translated it thus; see *Apology*, Book II, ch. 27, vol. II of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 513.] Yet he does not know the wicked person because he does not approve his deeds.

He therefore knows him because he detects him, and does not know him because he does not acknowledge him in the likeness of his wisdom. Thus it is said of any truthful man that he does not know falsehood—not because he does not know how to condemn it when others speak falsely, but because he both knows that very deceit in judgment and does not know it in affection: that is, he himself does not practice it, while condemning it when practiced by others [the edition reads “when it has been practiced” rather than “when practiced”].

## INTERROGATION CXXX (Also numbered 128)

When Job says, “Let not the hypocrite come into God’s sight” (Job 13:16), how does the Evangelist seem, as it were, to say the contrary: “All nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, placing the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left” (Matt. 25:32–33)?

**RESPONSE** *(From the same book, §49).*

We come into the Lord’s sight in two ways. In one way, by carefully weighing our sins here, we place ourselves in his sight and judge ourselves with tears. For whenever we bring the power of our Creator back to our awareness, we stand in his sight. Hence it is rightly said through the man of God Elijah: “The Lord, the God of Israel, lives, in whose sight I stand” (1 Kings 17:1).

In another way, we come into the Lord’s sight when, at the final judgment, we stand before his tribunal. The hypocrite, therefore, will come before the judge’s sight through the final examination. But because he now pretends not to consider and lament his faults, he refuses to come into the Lord’s sight: while he desires to please human eyes, he does not set God’s strict judgment before his own eyes.

## INTERROGATION CXXXI (Also numbered 134)

When blessed Job confesses concerning himself, “I will reproach my ways in God’s sight”; and likewise, “You wish to consume me for the sins of my youth”; and again, “You have sealed up my sins as in a purse”—how does he seem, as it were, to have said above the contrary: “If I am judged, I know that I shall be found righteous” (Job 13:15, 26; 14:17; 13:18)? For sins and righteousness cannot exist together.

**RESPONSE** *(From the same book, §51).*

By attributing iniquity to himself and his cleansing to the almighty Lord, this holy man recognizes himself as a sinner because of himself, and does not fail to recognize himself as made righteous by grace. Even while established in a righteous deed, he merited, through the abundance of grace [the edition reads “through abundant grace,” rather than “through the abundance of grace”], to endure blows; and now he rejoices to come to a just judgment [the Benedictine edition reads: “and now he rejoices to be found righteous in judgment,” etc.; earlier editions read “to find him righteous”], because he sees himself struck before the judgment.

Thus, although much later he says, “You have sealed up my sins as in a purse,” he immediately adds: “But you have healed my iniquity” [the edition reads “he adds” rather than “he added”]. Therefore, when he recalls that he will be found righteous in judgment, he does not at all deny that he was justly scourged, although through the scourging the Lord sought not to cleanse sins in him, but to increase his merits.

## INTERROGATION CXXXII (Also numbered 129)

How can Job say: “When a man has fallen asleep, he will not rise” (Job 14:12), when Paul says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51)?

**RESPONSE** *(From Moralia, Book XII, §§11–12).*

These statements are not contradictory if we attend to the sentence immediately added in Job. For after saying, “When a man has fallen asleep, he will not rise,” he immediately adds: “Until the heavens are worn away, he will not awaken, nor rise from his sleep.” It is clear that he will not rise until the heavens are worn away. For unless the end of this world has come, the human race will not awaken from the sleep of death to life.

He therefore does not indicate that humanity will not rise at all [the edition reads “absolutely not”], but that it will not rise before the destruction of the heavens [the edition reads “namely, until,” etc.].

## INTERROGATION CXXXIII (Also numbered 136)

Since Job, hoping to rise with a glorified body, says, “On the last day I shall rise from the earth, and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19:25–26), in accordance with what the Apostle also says, “This corruptible body must put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15:53), how does that same Apostle seem, on the contrary, to say: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (v. 50)?

**RESPONSE.**

Considering Adam’s sins, which arise from the corruption of flesh and blood, the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.” Yet, according to the true faith of that same Apostle, the flesh will indeed rise, in accordance with the statement: “This corruptible body must put on incorruption,” and so forth.

Since, therefore, this corruption arises from sin, sins themselves are also called by that name. If, then, by “flesh and blood” we understand corruption or sins—things which certainly arise from flesh and blood—the statements are not contradictory. Our flesh, therefore, in which we live, will possess the kingdom of God because of its good deeds; but flesh understood as corruption, because it is called by the name of flesh and blood, will not possess the divine kingdom.

## INTERROGATION CXXXIV (Also numbered 135)

Since, according to many statements of Sacred Scripture [the edition omits “according to many statements of Sacred Scripture”] (Job 34:12; Ezek. 6:10; 14:23), almighty God does nothing in vain, why does blessed Job testify that God afflicted him in vain (Job 19:6) [the edition reads “testifies”]?

**RESPONSE** *(From Moralia, Book XIV, §38).*

Our just Creator, through so many blows against blessed Job, sought not to extinguish vices but to increase merits. What he did for the increase of good merit was therefore equitable [the edition reads “through” rather than “for”]; yet what was believed to punish the cause of sin did not appear equitable [the edition reads “causes” rather than “cause”]. Hence blessed Job believed that those scourges erased his sins rather than increased his merits, and for that reason he calls the judgment inequitable, because he measures his vices [the edition reads “his life”] against the scourges.

If vices [the edition reads “life”] and scourges are weighed, therefore, what blessed Job believed was being done to him through the anger of strict judgment was not equitable. But if the judge’s mercy is considered—namely, that through the punishment of the righteous man his merits in life were increased—the judgment was equitable, or rather merciful.

## INTERROGATION CXXXV (Also numbered 131)

If perfect peace is maintained in the heights, since Job says, “Power and terror belong to him who makes peace in his heights” (Job 25:2), what does it mean that the angel says to Daniel: “I came because of your words; but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (Dan. 10:13); and shortly afterward: “Now I shall return to fight against the prince of Persia; and when I was departing, the prince of Greece appeared, coming” (v. 20)?

**RESPONSE** *(From Moralia, Book XVII, §17).*

Whom else does he call the princes of the nations, except angels who could have resisted him as he departed? How, then, can there be peace in the heights if a battle is fought among the angelic spirits themselves, who always stand before the sight of Truth?

But because particular angelic ministries have been assigned for the governance of each nation, whenever the conduct of those subject to them causes the assistance of the spirits set over them to be deserved against one another, the spirits who preside are said to come against one another.

The angel who spoke to Daniel is recognized as appointed over the captives of the Israelite people who were settled in Persia. Michael, however, is found to be set over those from the same people who had remained in the land of Judea. Hence, shortly afterward, this same angel says to Daniel: “There is no one who helps me in all these matters except Michael, your prince.” Concerning him he also says what we cited above: “And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me.” Since he is said not to be present together with him but to come to his aid, it is plainly acknowledged that he was appointed over the people who were being held captive in another region [the edition reads “captively” rather than “captive”].

What does the angel mean by saying, “I came because of your words, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me,” except that he is announcing his own works to his subjects? It is as though he openly said: “The merits of your prayers demand that the Israelite people be freed from the yoke of their captivity; but there is still something in that people which must be cleansed under Persian rule. Hence the prince of Persia rightly opposes my effort to free them [the Benedictine edition reads “so that he may oppose me concerning their liberation,” in agreement with several manuscripts; later editions read “hence he opposes their liberation,” a reading they rejected], although the tears of those who have been left in Judea also assist your prayers.”

He adds what we have mentioned: “Michael, your prince, came to help me.” And when he goes out to fight against the prince of Persia, the prince of the Greeks appears to him as he comes to battle [the edition reads: “And when he goes out in order to fight against the prince of Persia, the prince of the Greeks appears to him,” etc.]. From this it is indicated that Judea had also committed something against the Greeks, whose cause plainly resisted the liberation of that people.

The angel therefore hears the prophet’s prayers, but the prince of Persia resists, because although the life of the righteous man who prays has already demanded the liberation of the people [the edition reads “demands” rather than “has demanded”], the life of that same people still opposes it: since those who had been led into captivity have not yet been fully purified, the Persians rightly continue to rule them. Michael helps, but the prince of the Greeks comes to battle, because although the long oppression of the captives could merit pardon, the benefit of their liberation was also obstructed by what they had done against the Greeks.

It is rightly said, therefore, that the angels come against one another, because the merits of the nations entrusted to them oppose one another in turn. For the exalted spirits who preside over those nations do not contend on behalf of those acting unjustly; rather, they examine their deeds by judging them justly. When the guilt or righteousness of each nation is brought before the council of the heavenly court, its appointed guardian is said to have prevailed or not prevailed [the edition reads “either to have prevailed in the contest or not,” etc.].

Yet the one victory of them all is the supreme will of their Maker over them, whom [the edition reads “which”], while they always behold, they never will to obtain what they are unable to obtain.

## INTERROGATION CXXXVI (Also numbered 130)

Since Job says concerning the angels, “Is there any number of his armies?” (Job 25:3), how does Daniel, assigning a definite number to the angels, say: “Ten thousand times ten thousand attended him” (Dan. 7:10)?

**RESPONSE** *(From the same book of the Moralia, §18).*

Within the knowledge available to human reason, there is no number for the heavenly spirits, because no one knows how great is the multitude of the invisible army. The number of the heavenly citizens is both infinite and expressed as definite, so that it may be shown that what is countable to God is uncountable to us [the edition reads “to human beings”].

## INTERROGATION CXXXVII (Also numbered 132)

When, speaking to Job, he indicates that Behemoth is the devil’s food, saying, “He eats grass like an ox” (Job 40:10), and Isaiah says of him, “The lion shall eat straw like an ox” (Isa. 11:7), how does the prophet seem, on the contrary, to say concerning his food, “His food is choice” (Hab. 1:16)? How can this Behemoth, said to eat grass or straw, be said to consume the life of spiritual beings, if the life of carnal people is designated by the terms “grass” and “straw”? Nor will his food be choice if, while eating grass, he seizes what is carnal [the edition reads “he carries away the carnal person” rather than “he seizes what is carnal”].

**RESPONSE** *(From Book XXXII, §§18–19).*

Some people are grass before God, yet are regarded by human beings as holy, since their life displays one thing before human eyes while their conscience displays another before divine judgments. Such people are therefore choice according to human judgments, but grass before the Lord’s subtle examination [the edition reads “among” rather than “before” the Lord’s subtle examination; earlier in the sentence it reads “intends” rather than “displays”].

## INTERROGATION CXXXVIII (Also numbered 133)

When Job, reproved by the Lord, also reproves himself, saying, “Therefore I reproach myself” (Job 42:6–7), how did the Lord nevertheless prefer him to his friends, saying: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Moralia, Book XXXV, §9)? How is blessed Job reproved above, if, in comparison with his uprightness, his friends are said not to have spoken rightly before the Lord? Or is that earlier statement about him confirmed, in which the ancient enemy is told: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth” (Job 1:8)?

**RESPONSE.**

What does it mean that he is praised to the enemy, reproved in himself, and nevertheless preferred to his friends when they speak, except that the holy man surpasses all others by the virtue of his merits? Yet, precisely because he was human, he could not be without reproach before God’s eyes. In a holy person dwelling for a time in this present life, the rule of divine judgment still has something to judge, although by comparison with other human beings he already has something worthy of praise.

Blessed Job therefore believed that he was scourged because of guilt and not because of grace; he thought that vices were being cut away in him, not that merits were being increased. He is reproved insofar as he suspects that the purpose of the scourging was something else [the edition reads “because he suspects”], and yet, when his friends resisted him, he was preferred by the decree of the inner judgment. It is therefore aptly inferred [the edition reads “openly inferred”] how great his righteousness was: in opposing his friends’ words, he asserted the innocence of his conduct, and by divine judgment he was preferred even to those who defended that same divine judgment.

[Note: In this Book II, the numbering of the first edition in the Bibliotheca Patrum continues, so that this question is the one hundred thirty-seventh and the book ends with the two hundred twenty-first. We, following the better method, begin a new enumeration and henceforth do not note the old order in the margin, since this notice is sufficient. But because we have mentioned the two hundred twenty-first question, no one should wonder that we have omitted it, since it is the same as the one hundred ninety-sixth in the Bibliotheca Patrum and the sixty-first in our edition.]

# BOOK TWO: CONTAINING QUESTIONS FROM THE NEW TESTAMENT

## FROM THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

How can Christ say, “Take care not to perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6:1), and elsewhere say, “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father” (ibid. 5:16)?

**RESPONSE** *(From Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule, Part III, chapter 35).*

What does it mean that our work must be done in such a way that it is not seen, and yet we are commanded to ensure that it is seen, except that the things we do must both be hidden, so that we ourselves are not praised, and displayed, so that we may increase the praise of our heavenly Father?

For when the Lord forbade us to perform our righteousness before people, he immediately added: “In order to be seen by them.” And when he again commanded that our good works be seen by people, he immediately added: “So that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.” Thus he showed, by the conclusion of each saying, when they should be seen and when they should not be seen: the mind of the person acting should neither seek to have its work seen for its own sake nor conceal it for the sake of the glory of the heavenly Father. Hence it often happens that a good work is hidden when it is performed publicly, and public when it is carried out secretly.

## INTERROGATION II

When the Lord, teaching us to pray in the Gospel, commands us to say, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13), how does the Apostle James seem, as it were, to preach the contrary, saying, “Blessed is the man who endures temptation” (James 1:12), as well as what is written elsewhere: “Everyone who has not been tested has not been proved” (Ecclus. 34:9, 11)?

**RESPONSE.**

Who among the faithful does not know that the temptation which tests is beneficial, while that which leads into temptation is not? Cassian says the following about this:

> “The words ‘Do not lead us into temptation’ do not mean, ‘Do not permit us ever to be tempted,’ but rather, ‘Do not permit us, once placed in temptation, to be overcome.’ Job was tempted, but he was not led into temptation. Abraham and Joseph were tempted, but neither of them was led into temptation, because neither gave consent to the tempter. Finally, the prayer continues: ‘But deliver us from evil’—that is, do not permit us to be tempted by the devil beyond what we can bear (1 Cor. 10:13), but with the temptation provide an escape, so that we may be able to endure it.”

## INTERROGATION III

How can the Lord say in the Gospel, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21), while Paul says, on the contrary, “No one speaking by the Spirit of God says, ‘Jesus is accursed,’ and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3)?

**RESPONSE** *(From Augustine, Sermon on the Mount, Book II, §83).*

We cannot say that any who possess the Holy Spirit will fail to enter the kingdom of heaven if they persevere to the end; nor can we say that those who say, “Lord, Lord,” yet do not enter the kingdom of heaven possess the Holy Spirit.

How, then, does no one say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit? It is because the Apostle specifically used the verb “says,” so as to signify the will and understanding of the speaker, whereas the Lord used the verb “says” in a general sense when he said, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.” Even one who neither wills nor understands what he says may seem to say it; but a person truly says it when he expresses his will and mind through the sound of his voice.

## INTERROGATION IV

When the Lord says in the Gospel, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28), how can the Psalm say, in the person of Christ, “My soul is filled with evils” (Ps. 87:4)? Dare we say that Christ’s soul was filled with evils, when the suffering’s affliction had whatever force it had only in the flesh?

**RESPONSE** *(From Augustine, Expositions on the Psalms, on this psalm, §3).*

The soul cannot be killed by persecutors, but it can be filled with evils. We cannot say that that soul was filled with vices by which iniquity dominates a person; but perhaps it was filled with pains, through which the soul suffers together with its flesh in the Passion. Even what is called bodily pain cannot exist without the soul; for sadness, which is a pain belonging to the soul alone, inevitably precedes the bodily pain that is about to occur.

The soul, therefore, can suffer even when the body does not suffer; but the body cannot suffer without the soul. Why, then, should we not say that Christ’s soul was filled not with human sins but nevertheless with human afflictions? Another prophet says of him that he suffered for us (Isa. 53:4), and the Evangelist says: “He began to be sorrowful and deeply distressed,” while the Lord himself says: “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matt. 26:37–38).

Foreseeing these future events, the prophet who composed this psalm introduces Christ as saying: “For my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to the underworld.” He explained the same statement entirely in other words when it was said: “My soul is sorrowful even to death.” What is expressed by “My soul is sorrowful” is expressed by “My soul is filled with evils”; and what follows, “even to death,” is expressed by “my life has drawn near to the underworld.”

## INTERROGATION V

How can Christ say both in the Gospel, “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10:23), and, on the contrary, “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. But the hired man, who is not the shepherd and whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep” (John 10:11–12)?

**RESPONSE.**

We must understand these two authoritative and true statements in such a way that we do not declare them contradictory in any respect. To explain briefly: a person flees bodily without guilt when he withdraws from persecutors not out of fear but for a necessary and useful reason—that is, when he does not flee death in spirit, but preserves himself for a time for their benefit, as Paul says: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:24). This is the permitted flight, allowed to us by the Lord.

But whoever, overcome in spirit by fear of persecution or of any power, either avoids preaching the truth or chooses to change his location out of terror is condemned as a hired man, and such flight is entirely blameworthy.

We find these two statements explained by blessed Augustine in the following words (Tractate 46 on John, §§7–8):

> “We heard in the Epistle that Paul fled through a wall, being lowered in a basket (2 Cor. 11:33), so that he might escape the hands of his persecutor [the edition reads: ‘I saw Paul fleeing; he was lowered through a wall in a basket, so that he might escape the hands,’ etc.]. Was he therefore unconcerned for the sheep whom he abandoned when the wolf came? He was certainly concerned for them, but he commended them in prayer to the Shepherd sitting in heaven, while he preserved himself by fleeing for their benefit, as he says in a certain passage: ‘To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake’ (Phil. 1:24). For they had all heard from that same Shepherd: ‘If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.’
>
> “May the Lord deign to explain this question to us. Lord, you said to those whom you wished to be faithful shepherds, whom you were forming to be your members: ‘If they persecute you, flee.’ You therefore do them an injustice when you condemn hired men who flee [the edition reads: ‘hired men who see the wolf coming and flee. We ask,’ etc.]. We ask you to show us what depth this question contains. Let us knock; the one who opens will be present. But he is the doorkeeper of the door [the edition reads: ‘he will be present, the doorkeeper of the door itself, which,’ etc.], for he himself is the door.
>
> “Who is the hired man who sees the wolf and flees? He is the one who seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21; 1 Tim. 5:20), and does not dare freely rebuke the sinner. Suppose someone has sinned—he has sinned grievously, and must be rebuked and excommunicated. But once excommunicated, he will become an enemy, lie in wait, and do harm whenever he can. The person who seeks his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, so as not to lose what he pursues—the advantage of human friendship—and so as not to incur the trouble of human enmities, remains silent and does not rebuke him.
>
> “Behold, the wolf has seized the throat of the sheep [Julian’s edition read: ‘Behold, the wolf, whose throat …’ The editors perhaps erred by reading *cui* (‘whose’) instead of *ovi* (‘of the sheep’) in the manuscripts; we have corrected it from Augustine’s edition]. The devil has persuaded a believer to commit adultery; you remain silent and do not rebuke him. O hired man, you saw the wolf coming and fled.
>
> “Perhaps he replies and says: ‘Here I am; I did not flee.’ You fled because you remained silent, because you were afraid [the edition reads: ‘You fled because you remained silent; you remained silent because you were afraid’]. Fear is a flight of the spirit. You stood bodily, but fled in spirit—which was not done by the one who said: ‘Although I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit’ (Col. 2:5) [the edition omits ‘but’]. For how could he flee in spirit who, although absent in body, rebuked fornicators by letter?
>
> “Our affections are movements of the soul: joy is the soul’s expansion; sorrow, its contraction; desire, its advance; fear, its flight. You expand in soul when you take delight; you contract in soul when you are troubled; you advance in soul when you desire; you flee in soul when you are afraid.
>
> “This is why the hired man is said to flee when he sees the wolf. Why? Because he has no concern for the sheep. Why does he have no concern for the sheep? Because he is a hired man. What does it mean that he is a hired man? He seeks a temporal reward and will not dwell in the house forever [the edition reads: ‘seeking a temporal reward, and in the house,’ etc.].”

## INTERROGATION VI
How did Matthew and Luke remember the Lord’s telling his disciples not to carry even a staff (Matt. 10:10; Luke 9:3), when Mark says, “And he commanded his disciples to take nothing for the journey, except a staff only” (Mark 6:8)?

**RESPONSE** (From the same blessed Augustine, *Book II on the Agreement of the Evangelists*, nos. 73–74).

[Col. 0668A]

Both statements must be accepted as having been spoken by the Lord to the apostles. In saying this to his disciples, the Lord was doing what the Apostle Paul explains more clearly when he says: “Do you not know that [Note: [Col. 0668D] The text reads *quod* (“that”); the edition reads *quoniam* (“because”).] those who work in the temple eat what comes from the temple, and that those who serve the altar share with the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. But I have made use of none of these things” [Note: [Col. 0668D] The text reads *nullo*; the edition reads *nullius*.] (1 Cor. 9:13 ff.).

Thus, when he says that the Lord ordained this, but that he himself had not made use of it, he plainly shows that the power to use these things was granted, not that an obligation to maintain or serve them was imposed [Note: [Col. 0668D] The edition reads, “the necessity of serving,” which is less correct.]. In making this ordinance—the same ordinance that the Apostle says he made, namely, that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel—the Lord was telling the apostles not to possess or carry with them the necessities of this life, whether great or small, without anxiety. That is why he added “not even a staff,” showing that all things were to be supplied by the faithful to his ministers, who were to seek nothing superfluous.

Accordingly, by adding, “The laborer is worthy of his food” (Matt. 10:10), he made entirely clear and plain the reason and purpose of all that he was saying. The power to receive these things, therefore, he signified by the name of the staff when he said that they should take nothing for the journey except a staff only. It could also be expressed briefly in this way: “Carry no necessities with you, not even a staff—except a staff only,” so that the statement “not even a staff” may be understood to mean not even the smallest possessions; while the added phrase “except a staff only” may be understood to mean that, through the power received from the Lord and signified by the name of the staff, even those things that are not carried will not be lacking.

**QUESTION VII**

When Christ says in the Gospel, “The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart” (Matt. 12:35), how does he there seem, as it were, to say the opposite: “No one is good except God alone” (ibid. 19:17)?

**RESPONSE**

Did he not stimulate us to inquire and distinguish what it means for something to be good through another good, and what it means for something to be good through itself? How good, then, is that through which all good things exist, so that you can find absolutely nothing good that is not good from him, the one who makes good things good. For God is called good in such a way that, in comparison with him, created things are not good at all. When he is not being compared with them, however, all things may be called good that were made by a good author; but when compared with him, they should not be called good at all.

**QUESTION VIII**

Although the devil, knowing that Christ was the Son of God, plainly spoke through the multitude of demons in the Gospel, “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” (Matt. 8:29), how, by contrast, in that temptation in which Christ is said to have been taken up by the Spirit, did he test him by wondering whether he was the Christ, saying, “If you are the Christ, the Son of God, throw yourself down” (ibid. 4:6)?

**RESPONSE**

Christ became known to the demons not through that which is eternal life and unchangeable light—which illumines the godly when, by seeing through faith what is in him, their hearts are cleansed—but through certain temporal effects of his power and through the most hidden signs of his presence, which could be more perceptible to angelic senses, even those of evil spirits, than to human weakness.

Finally, when he judged that these signs should be restrained for a little while and concealed himself somewhat more deeply, the prince of the demons doubted concerning him and tested whether he was the Christ. In doing so, he examined the extent to which Christ himself allowed himself to be tested, so that he might adapt the humanity he had assumed as an example for our imitation.

After that temptation, however, when the angels, as it is written, ministered to him (Matt. 4:11)—clearly good and holy angels, and therefore beings to be feared and dreaded by unclean spirits—it became increasingly clear to the demons how great he was, so that, at his command, no one dared resist him, even though the weakness of his body appeared contemptible in him.

**QUESTION IX**

How does Christ say in the Gospel, “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father” (Matt. 18:10), when Paul, by contrast, seems to say, “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14)? If they are always in attendance, how are they said to be sent outward?

**RESPONSE** (From Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, Book II, no. 3).

If the angels were to lose sight of their Creator when they went out from him, they could neither raise up those who lie fallen nor announce the truth to those who are ignorant. Thus they are both sent and remain in attendance, because they go forth to us by spiritual presence, yet by inward contemplation they preserve themselves there from which they had departed.

**QUESTION X**

When the Lord replied to the young man who asked him and said, “Good Teacher, what must I do to have eternal life?”—“Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Matt. 19:16–17)—as though he did not wish to be understood either as good or as a teacher, how does he seem, by contrast, to say to the apostles, “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (John 13:13), and also, “Do not be called teachers, for your teacher is Christ” (Matt. 23:10)?

**RESPONSE**

The presumptuous young man, through his observance of the law and ignorance of the end of the law, which is Christ (Rom. 10:4), questioned the Lord as though he regarded him merely as a man, not as God, and as the teacher of all the commandments and of what is written in the law.

Christ, however, reproved this irreverent confession of faith concerning himself. Because he was being questioned as though he were a teacher of the law, he replied, “Why do you call me good?” And to indicate how he should be understood, he added, “No one is good except one, God.”

He therefore did not reject the name of goodness, nor refuse the name of teacher; rather, he convicted the young man’s faith, since the young man had understood nothing in him except what was bodily and carnal. For where Christ is teacher together with faith, there he praises the title so fully that he even acknowledges it; here, however, he does not recognize the title of good teacher, because the young man had understood neither that he was Lord nor that he was Christ.

**QUESTION XI**

When Christ commands his disciples, saying, “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:9), how does the Apostle Paul dare to say contrary to this, “Our fathers were all under the cloud” (1 Cor. 10:1)?

**RESPONSE**

In these two statements, unless I am mistaken, it is clear that someone is sometimes called father on account of nature. For Christ, wishing this world to be understood as the father of human beings by imitation, says, “Do not call anyone your father on earth”—that is, this world.

Paul, however, naming a father according to nature, says, “Our fathers were under the cloud.” This world is the father of human beings, since all who are carnally begotten are born from it in a carnal manner. But if this world is despised, so that one can truly say, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14), then this father—the world—is dead to such a person, and that person truly becomes an orphan whose father is the Lord.

Therefore, when Christ says, “Do not call anyone your father on earth,” he seems to be indicating this world as the father from whom he wished to turn them away, so that Christ himself might become their one Father. But when the Apostle says, “Our fathers were all under the cloud,” he was speaking of carnal generation from this world. From it they derived the origin of their flesh, and, born from human beings, they lived among human beings.

The Lord teaches that his disciples are to become orphans, to whom he says, “Do not call anyone your father on earth.” He himself provided an example of this when he said, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” (Matt. 12:48). Of these orphans it is said, “You will be the helper of the orphan” (Ps. 10:14 according to the Hebrew numbering).

Jerome says the following about this (in his commentary on Matt. 23:8):

> “It is asked why, contrary to this commandment, the Apostle said that he was a teacher of the Gentiles, or how, in ordinary speech—especially in Palestine and in the monasteries of Egypt—they call one another fathers. The solution is this: one thing is a father or teacher by nature, and another by indulgence. When we call a man father, we pay honor to his age; we do not indicate that he is the author of our life. Someone is also called teacher through association with the true teacher. And, not to repeat endlessly: just as the fact that God is the one Father by nature, and that the Son is one, does not prevent others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so likewise the one Father and Teacher does not prevent others from being called fathers and teachers in an improper sense.”

**QUESTION XII**

When the Gospel says that the disciples were sorrowful at the Lord’s passion and that the women also wept, so that it is even said of the disciples, “Their eyes were weighed down with sorrow” (Matt. 26:43), and the Lord himself said to the women, “Do not weep for me” (Luke 23:28), how does Christ himself, as it were, say the opposite in Psalm 68, speaking of the time of his passion: “I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; and for those who would comfort me, and I found none” (Ps. 68:21)?

**RESPONSE** (From Augustine, Sermon 2 on this psalm, no. 5).

The disciples and the women were sorrowful over the Lord’s bodily passion or death. The Lord, however, was pressed by another sorrow, concerning which he says, “I looked for one who would grieve with me, and I found none.” The Lord himself wished to save them, while his persecutors desired to rage. He prayed that they might be spared; they, like madmen, inflicted injury upon the good physician.

The sorrow of the disciples and women was therefore of another kind: they mourned the Lord’s flesh, which was about to die or had died. Thus he found no one who would grieve with him, because he found no companion in this sorrow. Neither the disciples nor the women were saddened by the sorrow with which the Lord suffered, but were saddened in a wholly carnal way over Christ’s mortal life, which was to be changed by death and restored by resurrection.

For he did not say, “I looked for one who would grieve, and there was none,” but “one who would grieve with me”—that is, from the very matter by which I was grieved, I found no one who would grieve. Yet in this sorrow, because Christ grieved over the blindness of those who persecuted him, he found no comforters, because he had no one who was making progress. Those who make progress are the ones who comfort us, and they are a consolation to all preachers of the truth.

**QUESTION XIII**

When, according to the Gospel, vinegar mixed with gall was offered to the Lord during his passion to drink (Matt. 27:34, 48), not as food to eat, how is it that Psalm 68, speaking in the person of Christ, recalls—and the same statement is certainly taken as a testimony concerning the Lord’s passion—“They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22)?

**RESPONSE**

If we understand the Lord’s food as the unity of his body, which he wished to signify at the time when he ate that Passover with his disciples (Luke 22:15 ff.), where he most appropriately displayed the sacrament of his body; and if we understand the gall cast into this food—that is, into the unity of Christ’s body—as representing the opponents of the Gospel, like Christ’s persecutors, then the statements read above will not be contradictory.

For the very thing they gave was not food [St. Augustine, from the same sermon, no. 6]—it was a drink—but they gave it “for food” because the Lord had already received food, and the gall was cast into it. He himself had received sweet food when he ate the Passover with his disciples, where he displayed the sacrament of his body [Note: [Col. 0671D] The edition reads, “with his disciples; there he displayed the sacrament,” etc.].
