Into this food, so sweet and pleasant—the unity of Christ that the Apostle commends when he says, “As there is one bread, we who are many are one body” [Note: [Col. 0671D] The edition reads, “Because.”] (1 Cor. 10:17)—who is it that gives gall, except the opponents of the Gospel, like those persecutors of Christ? For the Jews who crucified him walking on earth sinned less than those who despise him sitting in heaven.

What the Jews did, therefore—giving (*dantes*, “giving”; the edition reads *darent*, “they might give”) that bitter drink for the food he had already received—is done by those who, through wicked living, cause scandal in the Church. Heretics do the same by making it bitter, “but let them not exalt themselves” (Ps. 65:7). They give gall over so delightful a food. But what does the Lord do? He does not admit them to his body.

By this sacrament the Lord himself, when they offered him gall, tasted it and refused to drink it (Matt. 27:34).

**QUESTION XIV**

How does Christ say in the Gospel, “Behold, I am with you always, to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20), when elsewhere he says the same, “You always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me” (26:11)?

**RESPONSE**

When he says, “Behold, I am with you always, to the consummation of the age,” he is speaking of the presence of his majesty, by which he promised that he would in no way abandon his Church until the end. But when he says, “You will not always have me,” he is speaking of the presence of his body. It is therefore rightly understood that one statement concerns the presence of his flesh, and the other the presence of his majesty.

**QUESTION XV**

[Col. 0672C]

When Christ, forewarning and instructing his disciples in the Gospel, says, “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19), how does Peter, addressing the Jews in the Acts of the Apostles, say, “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts 2:38)? For even of those who are said to have been baptized by Philip and Paul (8:38), it is not said that they were baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, but only in the name of Jesus (19:5).

**RESPONSE** (From Vigilius of Tapsus, *Book XII on the Trinity*, in vol. VIII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon edition, 1667, p. 803).

Did the apostles become transgressors of the Savior’s command, and, in contradiction of the Savior, baptize so great a multitude? For it is not written that they baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, but only in the name of the Lord Jesus. But they are not transgressors. Far from it. For although only the name of the Son is mentioned, it nevertheless has the Father and the Holy Spirit pronounced along with it, as is sufficiently established in the holy Scriptures.

**QUESTION XVI**

When the Lord said to his disciples, “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19), why did Paul use only the name of Christ in baptism, saying, “All who have been baptized in Christ” (Rom. 6:3), when baptism is certainly not legitimate except under the name of the Trinity?

**RESPONSE**

Observe Paul’s prudence: in the present passage he wished to discuss not so much the nature of baptism as the death of Christ. In its likeness he was also urging us to die to sin and to be buried with Christ. It was plainly unsuitable that, when he was speaking about death, he should mention either the Father or the Holy Spirit.

“For the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), and rightly, where there is flesh, death is discussed. Nor would it have been suitable for him to say, “All who have been baptized in the name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit have been baptized into his death.”

## FROM THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK

[Col. 0673B]

**QUESTION XVII**

According to Matthew’s Gospel, it is said, “John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners’” (Matt. 11:18–19). How, by contrast, is it said of John, “His food was locusts and wild honey” (Mark 1:6)?

**RESPONSE**

We know John’s food and drink. It was not said that he did not drink at all, but that he did not drink wine or strong drink (Luke 1:15). He therefore drank water. His food was neither nothing at all nor everything, but locusts and wild honey.

Why, then, was it said that he came “neither eating nor drinking,” except because he did not use the kind of food by which the Jews lived? If the Lord had not used that kind of food, he would not, in comparison with John, have been called one who ate and drank.

The Lord therefore did not contradict the evangelist’s statement that John ate locusts and wild honey, since he was not speaking of those things, but reporting that John neither ate nor drank the food by which the Jews lived.

**QUESTION XVIII**

When Mark says in his Gospel of Christ, “He sat at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19), how does Stephen, by contrast, say in the Acts of the Apostles, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55)?

**RESPONSE** (From Gregory the Great, Homily 29 on the Gospels, no. 7).

[Col. 0673D]

What does it mean that Mark testifies that he saw him sitting, while Stephen testifies that he saw [Note: [Col. 0673D] The edition reads *videre* (“to see”) for *vidisse* (“saw”).] him standing? We know that sitting is the posture of one judging, while standing is the posture of one fighting or helping.

Since our Redeemer was taken up into heaven and now judges all things, and will come at the end as judge of all, Mark describes him as sitting after his ascension, because after the glory of his ascension he will be seen as judge at the end.

Stephen, however, placed in the struggle of labor [Note: [Col. 0673D] The edition reads, “in the labor of the struggle.”], saw standing the one whom he had as his helper [Col. 0674A]. For, so that Stephen might overcome the unbelief of his persecutors on earth, Christ fought for him from heaven by his grace.

## FROM THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE

**QUESTION XIX**

When the angel explains concerning Christ in the Gospel, “God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1:32), and Christ himself is called the son of David in many passages of Scripture, how does Christ himself, as it were, say the opposite to the Jews in the Gospel when he asks, “If Christ is the son of David, how does he call him Lord in the Spirit?” (Matt. 21:43)?

**RESPONSE**

This was said to the uninstructed, because although they hoped that Christ would come, they looked for him according to his humanity, not according to the fact that he is the power and wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24).

He therefore teaches there the truest and most sincere faith: Christ is both Lord of King David, insofar as he is the Word in the beginning, God with God, through whom all things were made (John 1:1 ff.), and son, insofar as he was made for David from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3).

For he does not say, “Christ is not the son of David.” Rather: if you already hold that he is his son, learn how he is also his Lord, lest you retain in Christ only what belongs to his being the son of man and abandon what belongs to his being the Son of God. In the former sense he is David’s son; in the latter, he is his Lord.

**QUESTION XX**

When the Lord says, among other things, “If anyone does not hate his wife, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26), how does Paul, by contrast, seem to say, “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church” (Eph. 5:25)? Does the judge announce one thing and the herald proclaim another? Or can we both hate and love at the same time?

**RESPONSE** (From Gregory the Great, Homily 37 on the Gospels, no. 2).

If we consider the force of the command, we can do both things with discernment [Note: [Col. 0673D] The edition reads, “we are able.”]: we can love those who are joined to us by bodily kinship and whom we recognize as our neighbors, while refusing, through hatred and avoidance, to acknowledge those whom we endure as adversaries on the way of God.

For the one who, being carnally minded, thrusts evil things upon us and is not heard is loved, as it were, through hatred. To show that this hatred toward one’s neighbors does not arise from lack of affection [Note: [Col. 0673D] This is how it is read in several manuscripts cited here by the Benedictines, although the edition previously read “affection,” as does our Julianus, who, as always, follows the better manuscripts.], but from charity, the Lord immediately added, saying, “And even his own life.”

We are therefore commanded to hate our neighbors, and to hate our own life. It is clear, then, that one ought to hate one’s neighbor while loving him—namely, to hate him in the same way as oneself. For we rightly hate our own life when we do not yield to its carnal desires, when we break its appetite and resist its pleasures. When it is despised and led toward what is better, it is loved, as it were, through hatred.

In the same way, we ought to display the discernment of hatred toward our neighbors, so that in them we love what they are and hate what obstructs us on the way of God.

## FROM THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN

**QUESTION XXI**

How did John say in the Gospel, when those questioning him asked, “I am not Elijah” (John 1:21), when the Lord says, “He is Elijah” (Matt. 11:14)?

**RESPONSE**

John answered according to the literal identity of the person; the Lord spoke according to figurative representation. John, considering the identity of his own person, answered that he was not Elijah. The Lord, however, foretold him as Elijah according to prefiguration—that is, because John had come to announce Christ’s advent in the same spirit and power of Elijah, in which Elijah will come to announce Christ’s advent.

**QUESTION XXII**

When John the Baptist pointed out the Lord who was coming to baptism, saying, “Behold, the Lamb of God,” and so forth (John 1:29), and, considering both his own humility and Christ’s divine power, said, “He who is from the earth is of the earth and speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all” (ibid. 3:31), why, when he was in prison, did he send disciples to ask, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Matt. 11:3)? It is as though he did not know the one he had pointed out, or did not know whether he was the one whom he had proclaimed by prophesying, baptizing, and pointing him out.

**RESPONSE** (From Gregory the Great, Homily 6 on the Gospels, no. 1).

This question is resolved quickly if the time and order of the events are carefully considered. When he was stationed at the waters of the Jordan, John affirmed that Christ himself was the Redeemer of the world. But when he had been sent into prison, he asked whether they should expect another [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Whether they should expect another.” Although the Benedictines did not admit these words into the text, they nevertheless note that they are found in some manuscripts.], or whether Christ himself was coming [Note: [Col. 0675D] The text reads *requirit* (“asks”); the edition reads *quaerit* (“asks/seeks”).]—not because he doubted that Christ was the Redeemer of the world, but so that he might know whether the one who had come into the world by himself would also descend by himself into the gates of the underworld [Note: [Col. 0675D] The edition reads, “of hell.”].

The one whom he had announced to the world as its forerunner by being born, he was preceding into the underworld by dying [Note: [Col. 0676D] The edition omits “by being born.”]. He therefore says, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”—as though he were saying openly: “As you have deigned to be born for human beings, indicate whether you will also deign to die for human beings, so that I, who became the forerunner of your birth, may also become the forerunner of your death and announce in the underworld that the one has come whom I already proclaimed to the world” [Note: [Col. 0676D] The edition reads, “announce to the underworld that you have come.”].

**QUESTION XXIII**

When the Truth says in the Gospel, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13), how does this same Truth seem, by contrast, to say, “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (ibid. 17:24)?

**RESPONSE** (From the same Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXVII, no. 30).

These statements do not disagree in their wording, but they kindle the zeal of our minds to investigate what appears to be discordant. For all who have been born to his faith [Note: [Col. 0676D] The edition reads, “in his faith.”] are undoubtedly his body. Since, therefore, through the wondrous dispensation of his mercy, the Lord became the head of his members, after the multitude of the reprobate had been rejected, he alone is also with us.

“No one, therefore, has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0676D] The text reads *ergo* (“therefore”); the edition reads *igitur* (“therefore”).]: because, since we have already become one with him, he who came there alone in himself returns there alone, also in us. And he who is always in heaven ascends into heaven daily, because he who remains above all things in his divinity draws the joined structure of his humanity daily into the heavens [Note: [Col. 0676D] The edition adds “himself” after “joined structure.”].

**QUESTION XXIV**

How does Christ say, “The flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64), when, by contrast, he says, “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself” (v. 54)?

**RESPONSE**

The flesh, without the life-giving Spirit, profits nothing, just as knowledge without charity puffs up rather than builds up (1 Cor. 8:1). Perhaps the Apostle is speaking of this when he says, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (15:50).

But when he says, “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself,” he wishes the sacrament of eating his flesh and drinking his blood to be understood, through which we remain in him and he in us.

**QUESTION XXV**

When Christ says in the Gospel according to John concerning the Father, “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges” (John 8:50), how does he say the opposite, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (5:22)?

**RESPONSE**

In the holy Scriptures, judgment is usually understood in two ways: once as condemnation, and once as discernment. Judgment is used in the sense of condemnation when the Gospel says, “Those who have done evil will come forth to the resurrection of judgment” (v. 29).

Judgment is also used in the sense of discernment in the Psalms, where it says, “Judge me, O God, and discern my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42:1). Thus, when the Savior says here, “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges,” he uses “judgment” in the sense of discernment, because by the discernment of judgment the Father distinguished the glory of his Son from human vanity. In this sense it is said that the Father judges.

But the statement, “All judgment has been given to the Son,” must be understood of the future judgment of examination. Accordingly, since here the Father, by judgment of discernment, separates the glory of his Son from human glory, while later the Son exercises judgment over the living and the dead with power, the statements cited do not appear contradictory in any respect.

**QUESTION XXVI**

When Christ says to the Jews in the Gospel according to John, “I know that you are Abraham’s children” (John 8:37, 44), how does he seem, as it were, immediately to say the opposite to these same Jews in the same Gospel: “You are from your father the devil”?

**RESPONSE**

When he calls the Jews children of Abraham, he testifies concerning their carnal descent, from which they certainly descended. But when he asserts that the devil is their father, he makes this known with reference to the works that they imitated.

**QUESTION XXVII**

How does Christ say on his own behalf in the Gospel, “For judgment I came into this world” (John 9:39), and, by contrast, “I did not come to judge the world” (12:47)?

**RESPONSE**

This is what he means: “I came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.” He called the discernment by which this occurs “judgment”: through it he distinguishes the cause of humble believers and confessors from that of the proud, who think that they see and are therefore blinded more severely.

Those who thought they saw, trusting in their own righteousness, were proud and blind because they did not believe in the physician. But the humble, believing because they confessed that they did not see, sought the physician so that they might deserve to see.

When he says, “I did not come to judge the world,” he is speaking of the future judgment. It is as though he said: “I came to bestow mercy, not to examine the world in judgment, as will be done in the future.”

**QUESTION XXVIII**

When the Lord, during his passion, prayed for those who were persecuting him—that is, for sinners—and, before his passion, said to the Jews themselves, “But now your sin remains” (John 9:41), how does the Apostle Paul, who came to the faith of Christ so much later, seem to say, “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Tim. 1:15)? If other sinners preceded him, how does he say that he was the first sinner? Were there no sinners before him?

**RESPONSE**

What else does “of whom I am the first” mean except that he surpassed all others—not in time, but in wickedness?

**QUESTION XXIX**

How does the Lord say, “I have other sheep that are not from this fold” (John 10:16), when he says, “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24)?

**RESPONSE**

What else does “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” mean except that he did not offer his bodily presence to any people except Israel? By saying, “I have other sheep,” however, he intended the Gentiles to be understood. He himself did not go to those Gentiles, but sent others. To the people of Israel he both sent others and came himself.

**QUESTION XXX**

How can Christ say both, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and, as it were, the opposite, “The Father is greater than I” (14:28)?

**RESPONSE**

When he said one statement according to the nature of divinity and the other according to the substance of humanity, he proclaimed nothing contradictory. When he says, “I and the Father are one,” he is speaking of the substance of divinity, by which God is from God, the Son from the Father, perfect from perfect, begotten without beginning or end.

But when he said, “The Father is greater than I,” he was speaking of the nature of humanity, according to which the Son is understood to be less than the Father.

**QUESTION XXXI**

When the Evangelist John places in the person of the Son of God the words that Isaiah wrote, “Go, say: You shall hear with your ears and shall not understand” (Isa. 6:9), namely, the words spoken by the one who was addressing Isaiah, how did Paul, by contrast, testify that it was the Holy Spirit who spoke to Isaiah (Acts 28:25–26)?

For when John wishes the Son of God to be understood as the one who said this to Isaiah—“Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them’” (John 12:39–40)—he also demonstrated the very person involved by adding, “Isaiah said this when he saw his glory and spoke of him” (v. 41).

But in the Acts of the Apostles Paul recalls that it was the Holy Spirit who spoke this testimony, saying, “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers, saying: ‘Go to this people and say: You shall hear with your ears and shall not understand,’” and so forth (Acts 28:25–26).

**RESPONSE** (From Vigilius of Tapsus, *Book XII on the Trinity*, in vol. VIII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon edition, 1677, p. 803, col. 1).

This is how Saint Augustine resolved the question [Note: [Col. 0677D] I cannot readily say why Julianus cites Augustine here, since all these words are Vigilius’s in the passage cited in the margin. Nevertheless, because among scholars it is not established—whatever Chiffletius, the editor of Vigilius’s works, may say—whether *Book XII on the Trinity* is the work of the bishop of Tapsus, we are compelled to remain in doubt and await the judgment of wiser authorities. If the Augustinian manuscripts that Julianus possessed contained this book under Augustine’s name, perhaps we are unjustly denying it to Augustine, although until now it has nowhere been published under his name.] He says against the heretics:

> “Let them declare who they wish this person to be. For perhaps they will say that he is the Son. In the Gospel *according to* [Greek: κατὰ] John [Note: *Κατά* is a Greek preposition translated into Latin as *secundum*, ‘according to’.] it is written: ‘And therefore they could not believe in Jesus, because Isaiah the prophet said: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they perhaps see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them.” Isaiah said this when he saw his glory and spoke of him’ (John 12:39–41).
>
> “And what will they make of Paul, who says that the Holy Spirit was seen in that glory by Isaiah, spoke to him, and sent him to the people to say the things mentioned above? For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘When the Jews disagreed among themselves, they departed after Paul had spoken one word: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly to our fathers through the prophet Isaiah, saying: Go to this people and say to them: You shall hear with your ears and shall not understand,”’ and so forth (Acts 28:25–26).
>
> “Behold, John says that it was the Son, while Paul says that it was the Holy Spirit who was seen by Isaiah, sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and who is worshiped, praised, and glorified by the seraphim (Isa. 6:1).
>
> “But all the Churches of Christ, from east to west, unanimously profess in the recitation of the mysteries that it is the Father who is praised by the seraphim. Let those who deny veneration to the Holy Spirit tell us which of these statements is true, or who is deceiving us: John, or Paul, or all the Churches of Christ.
>
> “For since all the Churches profess that it is the Father who is worshiped by the seraphim, while John says it is the Son and Paul says it is the Holy Spirit, if none of them is deceiving us but all speak the truth, it is plainly proved that, even when only the name of the Father is mentioned, the Son and the Holy Spirit are nevertheless pronounced along with him.
>
> “Let those who worship in this way venerate the Father and the Son, imitating the veneration of the heavenly living beings, and let them not follow their own thoughts.”

**QUESTION XXXII**
How does Christ in the Gospel say both things that appear contradictory? For he says, “I give you my peace” (John XIV, 27); and, on the contrary, “I have not come to send peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matt. X, 34).

**RESPONSE.**

The peace of Christ, which he gave to his disciples, is one thing; the peace of the world is another. Christ denies that he gives the peace which the world possesses. For he says: “My peace I give you, my peace I leave you; not as this world gives peace do I give you.” Therefore he denies that he gives his disciples the peace of the world, since elsewhere also he says: “I have not come to send peace, but a sword.”

Do you wish to see what peace God gives upon our earth? If that good earth which produces a hundredfold or sixtyfold fruit, etc. (Matt. XIII, 8), receives that peace from God of which the Apostle says: “And the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts” (Phil. IV, 7), then this is the peace which God gives upon our earth.

**QUESTION XXXIII.**

How does he say in the Gospel, “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV, 15), when shortly afterward in the same place he says: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (XVI, 12)?

**RESPONSE.**

When he says, “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you,” he did not mean that he had already made everything known, but that he had spoken of the things that he would have to make known in the future. Accordingly, there is no contradiction with the passage in which he says, “I still have many things to say to you,” since the Lord wished us, for our benefit, not to know many things at present, though he has reserved them for us to know profitably in the future.

**QUESTION XXXIV.**

When the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XV, 16), how does Paul say that he asked the Lord three times that the spirit of Satan might be taken away from him, yet was unable to obtain this (II Cor. XII, 8–9)?

**RESPONSE** *(from Gregory the Great, Homily 27 on the Gospels, no. 6).*

If the Father gives us everything that we ask in the Son’s name, what does it mean that Paul asked the Lord three times and did not deserve to be heard, but was told, “My grace is sufficient for you, for power …”? Did that outstanding teacher [Note: [Col. 0679D] Editor: “preacher.”] not ask in the Son’s name? Why, then, did he not receive what he asked? How is it true, then, that whatever we ask the Father in the Son’s name, the Father gives us, if the Apostle Paul asked in the Son’s name that the angel of Satan be taken away from him, and nevertheless did not receive what he asked?

But because the Son’s name is Jesus, and Jesus means “Savior,” or is also understood to mean “salutary,” the person who asks in the name of the Savior is the one who asks for what pertains to salvation. For if something that is not beneficial is asked, the Father is not being asked in Jesus’ name. Hence the Lord also says to those same apostles, who were still weak: “Until now you have asked nothing in my name” (John XVI, 24). It is as though he were saying plainly: “You have not asked in the name of the Savior, because you do not know how to ask for eternal salvation.” This is why Paul is not heard: if he had been freed from the temptation, it would not have benefited him for salvation.

**QUESTION XXXV.**

Since Christ is acknowledged in John’s Gospel to have said, “I have spoken openly to the world” (XVIII, 20), how does he appear, as though in opposition, to have promised his disciples in the same Gospel: “I have spoken these things to you in figures. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce the Father to you openly” (John XVI, 25)? If, then, he did not speak openly even to those disciples who were closer to him (from Augustine, *Tractate 113 on the Gospel of John*, no. 3), but promised an hour when he would speak openly, how did he speak openly to the world?

Moreover, even to those disciples themselves—as the authority of the other evangelists also testifies—he spoke much more plainly, in comparison with those who were not his disciples, when he was alone with them, removed from the crowds. For then he explained to them the parables which he presented to others in concealed form. What, then, does he mean by, “I have spoken nothing in secret” (John XVIII, 20)?

**RESPONSE.**

We must understand him to have said, “I have spoken openly to the world,” as though he had said, “Many have heard me.” The very fact of being open was, in one respect, open, and in another respect, not open. It was open because many heard him; and again it was not open because they did not understand.

When he spoke privately to his disciples, he certainly did not speak in secret. For who speaks in secret when he speaks before so many people, since it is written, “Every word shall be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XIX, 15)? This is especially true when he tells a few what he wishes to make known through them to many, as the Lord himself says to those whom he still had as a small number: “What I tell you in the darkness, say in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matt. X, 27).

Therefore, even what seemed to be spoken by him secretly was in a certain sense not spoken in secret, because it was not spoken in such a way that those to whom it had been said were to keep silent about it, but rather in such a way that it would be preached everywhere.

**FROM THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE ROMANS**

**QUESTION XXXVI.**

How does the Apostle Paul say two things about Christ that appear contradictory—namely, “Who was born from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 3), and other statements of this kind—and, on the contrary, “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer” (II Cor. V, 16)?

**RESPONSE** *(from the same Augustine, Book XI against Faustus, chapter 7).*

That the Son of God was born as a human being from the seed of David is stated by the same Apostle in one place, and is proclaimed most openly by the holy Scriptures. But what he says—“Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer”—is sufficiently explained by the context of the passage itself. In his customary manner, he contemplates our future life, which has already been completed in the man Christ Jesus, our Mediator and Head, when he rose again, with such certain hope that he considers it as though it were already present and possessed. That life, certainly, will not be according to the flesh, just as Christ’s life is no longer according to the flesh.

In this passage he calls “flesh” the carnal quality of corruption, which will no longer exist, since the changed flesh will not decay. We therefore knew Christ according to the flesh—that is, according to the mortality of the flesh—before he rose again; but now we know him no longer in that way, because, as the same Apostle says, “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more,” etc. (Rom. VI, 9). Thus the two statements do not appear to contradict one another at all: before Christ rose again, the Apostle knew that he had mortal flesh; after he rose again, he believed that he could no longer be touched by any corruption of death.

**QUESTION XXXVII.**

When Paul defines in his Letter to the Romans that Jews and Greeks are all under sin (Rom. III, 9), and on this occasion indicates that the whole human race is under sin, how does he himself seem to speak in opposition, saying, “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (IV, 15)? Or how does he say of himself, “I was once living without the law” (VII, 9), when elsewhere he says of himself that he received circumcision on the eighth day according to the law (Phil. III, 5)?

**RESPONSE** *(from Origen, on chapter III of the Epistle to the Romans).*

Among the Jews, it is clear that there is the law of Moses. Among the Gentiles, however, there is undoubtedly the law of nature, which, by the testimony of conscience, accuses the offender. Where, then, shall we find a person in whom there is no law, and who therefore does not appear to be in transgression of sin? For Paul himself also says of himself, “I was once living without the law.”

And when did Paul live without the law, when he also says of himself that he possessed circumcision on the eighth day and was a Hebrew of Hebrews (Phil. III, 5)? How, then, can it be true that he once lived without the law, when on the eighth day of his birth he received, according to the law, the sign of circumcision?

It is therefore clear that a person comes under the law when he reaches the age at which he can choose and distinguish what the law is, and that he does not previously take upon himself the external yoke of any law before he begins to possess the strength of an inner and natural law. Indeed, where he said, “I was once living without the law,” he added: “But when the commandment came, sin revived” (Rom. VII, 9). By this he shows that in childhood, before a person possesses the ability to distinguish good from evil, he is said to be without the law. Even if he sins, because the law is not yet in him, the sin is not counted against him. But when he has received the ability to distinguish good and evil, the law and its commandments are said to have come to him. Where the force of the commandment exists—that is, the conscience accusing him—the sin which had previously been dead in him is said to have revived.

**QUESTION XXXVIII.**

When the Apostle Paul writes to the Romans that Jews and Greeks are all under sin (Rom. III, 9), how does he later define that not all, but many, were constituted sinners through the disobedience of one man, saying: “Just as through the disobedience of one man the many were constituted sinners, so also through the obedience of one the many will be constituted righteous” (V, 19)?

**RESPONSE** *(from the same Origen, on chapter V, verse 19, of the Epistle to the Romans).*

We must explain how they appear to be “many sinners” and not “all,” when the same Apostle says that “all have sinned” (Rom. III, 23). To have sinned is one thing; to be a sinner is another. A sinner is one who, by committing many offenses, has already entered into the practice and, so to speak, the deliberate pursuit of sinning.

By contrast, a righteous person is not one who has done something righteous once or twice, but one who, by always acting righteously, possesses righteousness through practice and habit. For if someone is unjust in nearly everything else but once or twice performs some righteous deed, he would be said to have acted righteously in that deed in which he maintained righteousness; nevertheless, he will not for that reason be called righteous.

Likewise, a righteous person is indeed said to have sinned if at some time he commits something unlawful. Yet he will not therefore be called a sinner if he does not maintain the practice and habit of sinning. Similarly, a physician is not called a physician merely because he knows how to place a spider’s web on a lightly torn scalp, or because he knows how to foment the swelling of a wound with warm water, although even this may appear to belong to medicine. Rather, the physician is the one who possesses the practice, dedication, and discipline of healing.

From all this, I think it has been sufficiently shown that to sin is one thing, and to be a sinner is another. It is possible that all have sinned, even if they were holy, since “no one is clean from defilement, not even if his life should last a single day” (Job XIV, 4, according to the Septuagint). For who is there who has not sinned either in deed, or in word, or—even if he is extremely cautious—in thought? Therefore I said that all may rightly be said to have sinned, but that not all have become sinners; rather, many have.

**QUESTION XXXIX.**

How does Paul, writing to the Romans, testify that he does not destroy the law but confirms it, saying, “Do we destroy the law through faith? By no means; rather, we establish the law” (Rom. III, 31), when, on the contrary, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians he seems to proclaim the destruction of that same law, saying: “If the ministry of death, formed in letters and engraved on stones, came in glory—so that the children of Israel could not look intently at the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which is being destroyed—how will the ministry of the Spirit not be even more glorious?” And shortly afterward: “For if what is being destroyed came through glory, much more will what remains be in glory” (II Cor. III, 7–8, 11). How, then, does the Apostle Paul testify that he does not destroy the law but confirms it, when he proclaims that the glory of Moses’ face—which he shows to be the law—is being destroyed?

**RESPONSE** *(from the same Origen, on chapter III, verse 31, of the Epistle to the Romans).*

“What we destroy is the law” and “the law is destroyed” do not mean the same thing. Therefore, in the present passage Paul declares that he himself does not destroy the law. For even if the law is destroyed, it is destroyed by the glory that surpasses it, and not by Paul or by any other of the saints. Hence the Lord himself also said, “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17).

No saint, not even the Lord himself, will destroy the law. Rather, its temporal and passing glory is destroyed and surpassed by the eternal, abiding glory.

**QUESTION XL.**

Since the law given by God had not then been handed down to all the nations as it had been to the Jews, and since the Apostle therefore seems to say, “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. IV, 15), how can what is read in the psalm be true: “I have regarded all the sinners of the earth as transgressors” (Ps. CXVIII, 119)?

**RESPONSE.**

If there is no transgression where there is no law, why does the prophet call those who did not receive the law transgressors? But if we consider that every human race derives original sin from its first parent, that first and singular testament alone is the covenant under which all human beings—even without the law—are said to be transgressors (from Augustine, Book XVI of *The City of God*, chapter 27).

But since the law was afterward clearly given, and the Apostle says, “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression,” how can what is read in the psalm be true—“I have regarded [them] as transgressors,” etc.—unless because all who are held bound by some sin are guilty of transgressing his law?

Therefore, if even infants, as true faith maintains, are born sinners—not properly, but originally—and if we consequently confess that they need the grace of the remission of sins, then, in the same sense in which they are sinners, they are also recognized as transgressors of that law which was given in paradise. Thus both statements that are written are true: “I have regarded all the sinners of the earth as transgressors,” and “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

**QUESTION XLI.**

Is Paul believed to have lived at some time without the Mosaic law because he says, “I was once living without the law” (Rom. VII, 9), even though he expressly confesses that he was a Hebrew of Hebrews and circumcised on the eighth day according to the commandment of the law (Phil. III, 5)?

**RESPONSE.**

If the natural law is recognized as distinct from the law given to the Hebrew people, it is easier to determine of which law Paul was speaking. Origen (on chapter V, verse 13, and chapter VII, verse 9, of the Epistle to the Romans) shows that sin is dead in us without the law—that is, before the rational sense within us has become active through age. He also gives the example of a small child striking or cursing his father or mother:

“In such a case,” he maintains, “according to the law that prohibits striking or cursing one’s father or mother, sin appears to have been committed. But he says that this sin is dead, because the law is not yet present in the child to teach him that what he is doing is not permitted.”

It is certain that both Paul and all human beings once lived without this natural or rational law—that is, during childhood. For during that period all alike are not yet capable of this natural law. Otherwise, Paul’s own statement—“I was once living without the law”—would not appear to be true.

**QUESTION XLII.**

How does the Apostle say, “The law is holy, and just, and good” (Rom. VII, 12), when, on the contrary, he appears to say, “The power of sin is the law” (I Cor. XV, 56)? How does he call that law good which he declared to be the power of sin?

**RESPONSE.**

The law given by God is always good. Yet the law is called the power of sin because, through its severe enforcement, it increases the harmful pleasure of sin itself; nevertheless, even in this respect it is not evil.

**QUESTION XLIII.**

When Paul says, “Sin is not counted when there is no law” (Rom. V, 13), and also says that “through the law comes knowledge of sin” (III, 20), how did Cain, after he had sinned, say, “My sin is greater than can be forgiven” (Gen. IV, 13)? Moreover, when the patriarchs had gone down to Joseph in Egypt and were accused by him through a contrived charge, they said to one another: “We are in sin concerning our brother, because we despised the distress of his soul when he pleaded with us, and we did not listen to him; therefore this distress has come upon us” (XLII, 21). It is also clear that Job lived before the law, when he says: “Even if I have sinned unwittingly, if I concealed my sin, or was ashamed before the multitude of the people, so that I did not declare my offense” (Job XXXI, 33–34). All these men are plainly shown to have recognized their sin.

**RESPONSE.**

From these passages it is inferred that the Apostle Paul was speaking not of the law of Moses, but of the natural law written in human hearts. According to this natural law, therefore, the Apostle appears consequently to have said that every mouth must be stopped and the whole world made liable before God (Rom. III, 19). For no one is exempt from the judgment of the law that is naturally present in human beings, neither Jew nor Gentile.

**QUESTION XLIV.**

How does the Apostle Paul appear to have said two things contrary to each other? When speaking about “the body of this death,” he says, “What I do, I do not understand”; and, on the contrary, “I did not know sin except through the law,” and “through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. VII, 15, 7, and III, 20). How, then, did he not know the sin which he knew through the law?

**RESPONSE.**

When the Apostle says, “What I do, I do not know,” what else does this mean than “I do not will it, I do not approve it, I do not consent to it, I do not do it”? Otherwise this would contradict what he said above: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin,” and “I did not know sin except through the law,” etc. “In order that sin might appear to be sin, through what is good it worked death in me” (Rom. VII, 13).

How could he know through the law the sin which he does not know? How can sin appear if it is unknown? Thus “I do not know” means “I do not do”—because I commit it with no consent of my own—just as God will say to the wicked, “I do not know you” (Matt. VII, 23), although no one can be hidden from him. Similarly, it is said of Christ, “the one who did not know sin” (II Cor. V, 21), meaning “who did not commit sin.” For he did not know the thing which he condemned.

**QUESTION XLV.**

Since the Apostle Paul says that through the Holy Spirit we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII, 15), how does he again say elsewhere: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. IV, 6)? How do we cry if he himself cries within us?

**RESPONSE.**

He causes us to cry when he begins to dwell within us. What is received therefore acts so that, by asking, seeking, and knocking, it may be received more abundantly. Whether we ask for a good life or that we may live well, “all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. VIII, 14).

Thus, whether we are said to cry through the Holy Spirit or the Spirit himself is said to cry within us, there is no contradiction. When we are said to cry, we are shown to cry not from ourselves but from him; and when he is read to cry within us, what else is demonstrated but the effectiveness of his work, by which he causes us to act?

**QUESTION XLVI.**

When the Apostle, writing to the Romans, says that he awaits the adoption of the sons of God and the redemption of his body (Rom. VIII, 23), how does he say, as though he were already a son of God and had nothing further to await, “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God” (v. 16)? And again, how does he hope for the redemption of his body when he says to others, “Christ redeemed us” (Gal. III, 13)?

**RESPONSE.**

For the present, Origen resolves these matters as follows: “In my opinion,” he says, “he himself resolves this by the statement that follows.”

**QUESTION XLVII.**

When Paul, writing to the Romans, says, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom. VIII, 31), appearing to declare absolutely that no one is our adversary, how does Peter, on the contrary, seem to proclaim: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V, 8)?

**RESPONSE.**

The Apostle does say, “If God is for us, who is against us?” Not that he declares that we have absolutely no adversary, but he shows that, when God acts on our behalf, our adversary becomes contemptible and powerless.

**QUESTION XLVIII.**

When Paul says, “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII, 1), how does the Lord speak through the prophet about certain people, saying, “They have reigned, but not from me” (Hos. VIII, 4)?

**RESPONSE.**

It is as though he were saying, “Not with me favorable, but with me angry” [Note: [Col. 0685D] Samson, Book II of the *Apology*, chapter 27, no. 6, or p. 513, vol. XI of *Hispania Sacra*: “even though I am angry.”] Hence below, through the same prophet, he says: “I will give you a king,” he says, “in my wrath” (Hos. XIII, 11), by which it becomes clearer that both a good and an evil order [Note: [Col. 0686D] More suitably, Samson: “authority.”] are ordained by God—good when he is favorable, evil [Col. 0686C] when he is angry [Note: [Col. 0686D] The same: “good when he is favorable, evil when he is angry.”].

**QUESTION XLIX.**

When Paul writes to the Romans, “Let each of you please his neighbor for the good, for edification” (Rom. XV, 2), how does he say elsewhere, “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I, 10)?

**RESPONSE.**

It is one thing to make it one’s aim to please human beings in order to seek praise from them, and another to make it one’s aim to please human beings by living in a manner that is irreproachable among them, so that all who see or hear such a person may make progress through him. One must not please human beings in matters in which it is contrary to faith, uprightness, or religion to please them.

Therefore he says: “If I were pleasing human beings”—that is, unbelieving and faithless Jews—“I would not be a servant of Christ.”

**FROM THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS**

**QUESTION L.**

When the Apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, praises them at the beginning of his Epistle, saying: “I give thanks always to my God for you, for the grace of God that has been given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you, so that you lack nothing in any grace” (I Cor. I, 4 ff.), how does he then seem to follow this praise with a rebuke, saying: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you”; and again: “For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those of Chloe’s household, that there are contentions among you,” etc. (I Cor. I, 10–11)?

**RESPONSE** *(from Gregory the Great, Book I of the Homilies on Ezekiel, Homily 11, nos. 18–19).*

Behold: those whom he had praised as being rich in every word and in all knowledge, those whom he had said lacked nothing in any grace—after speaking for a little while, and gently moving toward rebuke—he reproves as divided among themselves. He first described their health and afterward exposed their wounds.

For a skilled physician, seeing that a wound had to be cut but perceiving that the patient was timid, stroked him for a long time and then suddenly struck. First he placed upon them the gentle hand of praise [Note: [Col. 0687D] The Benedictine edition has *blanda manu laudes*, “praises with a gentle hand”; but the editors themselves note that all the manuscripts have *blandam manum laudis*, “the gentle hand of praise.”] and afterward drove in the iron of rebuke.

Unless bashful minds are reproved by being first soothed, so that they hear from other matters something they can take as consolation, they immediately fall into despair under rebuke. But did Paul lie when he first said that they lacked nothing in any grace, though he was later going to say that they lacked unity? By no means. Who, even in his foolishness, would believe such things about him?

But because among the Corinthians there were some filled with every grace, while others had been shaken [Note: [Col. 0687D] Editor: “cut off.”] by favoritism toward persons, he began with praise of the perfect, so that by a restrained attack he might arrive at the correction of the weak.

**QUESTION LI.**

How can Paul say, “Do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14), and also, “Neither will cursers possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 10), when he himself pronounced a sentence of cursing, saying, “Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; God will repay him according to his works” (I Tim. IV, 14); or when he said to Ananias, “God will strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts XXIII, 3)?

**RESPONSE** *(from Gregory the Great, Book IV of the *Moralia*, no. 2).*

It must be understood that Holy Scripture mentions cursing in two ways: one which it approves and another which it condemns. A curse is pronounced in one way by a judgment of justice, and in another by the spite of vengeance.

A curse by a judgment of justice was pronounced against the first man when he sinned, when he heard: “Cursed is the earth in your labors” [Note: [Col. 0687D] Editor: “in your labor.”] (Gen. III, 1). So also the statement made to Abraham: “I will curse those who curse you” (XII, 3).

Again, because a curse is uttered through the spite of vengeance, we are warned by Paul’s proclamation: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14). God is therefore said to curse, while human beings are forbidden to curse, because what a human being does through the malice of vengeance, God does only with the scrutiny and power of justice.

When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, it bursts forth not from a desire for vengeance, but from the justice of judgment [Note: [Col. 0688D] Benedictine edition: “from the examination of justice,” as nearly all their manuscripts have it. Here Julian reads as the old editions and others do.]. For inwardly they perceive God’s subtle judgment, and they recognize which evils arising outwardly deserve to be struck by a curse. They therefore do not sin in cursing, insofar as they do not disagree with the inward judgment.

This is why Peter directed a sentence of cursing against Simon, who offered him money, saying: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts VIII, 20). By saying not “is,” but “may it be,” he showed that he had spoken these words not in the indicative but in the optative mood.

This is also why Elijah said to the two commanders of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you” (IV Kings I, 10). The outcome of the matter demonstrated how strongly the sentences of both men were confirmed by the reason of truth [Note: [Col. 0688D] This is read in all the manuscripts and in the old Paris and Basel editions, the Benedictines note, whereas in others “severity” appears instead of “truth.”]. Simon perished in eternal destruction, and a flame coming down from above consumed the two commanders of fifty [Note: [Col. 0688D] Editor: “destroyed.”].

The subsequent effect therefore testifies with what intention a sentence of cursing is pronounced. When the innocence of the one who curses remains, yet the curse absorbs the one who is cursed unto destruction, it is inferred from the outcome on both sides that the sentence against the guilty person was hurled by one inward Judge.

**QUESTION LII.**

How does the Apostle say that the divisions of grace given to us through the Spirit (I Cor. XII, 4, 11) are given according to measure (Eph. IV, 7), when the Gospel says, “God does not give the Spirit according to measure” [Col. 0688C] (John III, 34)?

**RESPONSE.**

According to the Apostle, the Spirit is given to human beings according to measure: “To one, indeed, through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit,” etc. (I Cor. XII, 8). But the Father does not give the Spirit according to measure to his only Son, because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. II, 9).

**QUESTION LIII.**

When Paul says of his fellow apostles in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, “I labored more abundantly than all of them” (I Cor. XV, 10), how does he, in the Epistle to the Ephesians, regarding himself as the least of all the elect, say: “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given, to evangelize among the Gentiles” (Eph. III, 8)?

**RESPONSE.**

I do not think that the Apostle departed from the inward conviction of his mind when he said that he was truly the least of all the saints—for example, of those who were at Ephesus, at Corinth, at Thessalonica, or who had believed throughout the whole world. Since it is a judgment of humility to call oneself the least of all the saints, it would be a charge of falsehood to conceal one thing in the heart and utter another with the tongue.

We must therefore find an explanation by which Paul was truly the least of all the saints and yet did not fall from apostolic dignity. In the Gospel the Lord says to his disciples: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be the least of all; and whoever wishes to be first, let him be the last of all” (Matt. XX, 26–27). Paul fulfilled this by his works, saying: “For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last, as men appointed to death” (I Cor. IV, 9).

Among all, therefore, who desired to be least for Christ’s sake, the Apostle Paul was even less, and for that reason greater. For he says: “I labored more than all of them”; “yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (XV, 10).

Because of this humility, although he was the least of all the saints, this grace was given to him among the Gentiles: to evangelize the unsearchable riches of Christ and to teach the dispensation of the mystery of Christ, hidden for ages in God, who created all things (Eph. III, 8–9).

**FROM THE SECOND EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS**

**QUESTION LIV.**

When Paul says of himself in the Epistle to the Corinthians, “We do not live according to the flesh, nor do we wage war according to the flesh” (II Cor. X, 3), how does he write conversely to the Romans, saying, “But I am carnal” (Rom. VII, 14)? And when elsewhere he says that Christ lives in him (Gal. II, 20), and speaks of the Holy Spirit, saying, “Because of his Spirit dwelling in us” (Rom. VIII, 11), how does he seem to speak in opposition when he says, “Good does not dwell in me,” that is, “in my flesh” (VII, 18)?

**RESPONSE.**

If these statements seem to anyone to be contrary to apostolic dignity, let him understand them as having been spoken in such a way that the Apostle did not say them of his own person, but assumed in himself the person of the weak. He will perhaps not consider them contradictory.

When he calls himself carnal and declares that good does not dwell in him, according to Origen’s account (on chapter VII, verse 14, of the Epistle to the Romans), the Apostle did not speak in his own person, but, as a teacher of the Church, assumed in himself the person of the weak, in accordance with what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “I became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak” [Col. 0689D] (I Cor. IX, 22).

Nevertheless, the blessed Augustine, writing to Pope Boniface (Book I against the Two Letters of the Pelagians, no. 17), also testifies that what he says—“But I am carnal, sold under sin”—can be understood of the Apostle’s own person, because the Apostle did not yet possess a spiritual body. In the same way he could say, “But I am mortal,” which can certainly be understood only according to the body, since he had not yet been clothed with immortality. Even if it is understood in this way, it will still not be contrary to anyone who understands it correctly.

**QUESTION LV.**

When Paul says, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19), how did Christ cry out in his Passion, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII, 46)?

**RESPONSE.**

The cry with which Christ called out, “My God, my God,” etc., must be understood not as spoken from the person of the Word, by which he remains God, one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but from the old human being—not the old human being whom he himself had assumed.

For he who, by the power of his great divinity, by which he is equal to the Father, had raised the dead, suddenly became weak in the hands of his enemies and was seized as though he were powerless [from Augustine, Sermon 1 on Psalm LXX, no. 12] [Note: [Col. 0689D] Editor: “For he, who by great divine power,” etc.]. But when would he have been seized unless they had first said in their hearts, “God has abandoned him” (Ps. LXX, 11)?

Hence came that voice on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Did God forsake Christ, when God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, and when Christ himself was God—according to the flesh, indeed, from the Jews, but “God blessed above all forever” (Rom. IX, 5)? Did God forsake him [Note: [Col. 0689D] Editor: “here, abandoned him”]? By no means.

Rather, in our old human being, it is our voice [Note: [Col. 0690D] The editor has *erat* in both places, “was.”], because our old human being was crucified together with him (VI, 6). He had received a body from that old human being, because Mary was descended from Adam. Therefore he said from the cross what they had thought: “Why have you forsaken me?”

**FROM THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE GALATIANS**

**QUESTION LVI.**

How can the Apostle Paul say, “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I, 10), when elsewhere he commanded, “Please everyone in everything, just as I also please everyone in everything” (I Cor. X, 32–33)?

**RESPONSE.**

Those who do not understand these statements consider them contradictory. But this is not so. He rightly said that he did not please human beings, because in this very matter he sought to please not human beings but God.

Likewise, he rightly commanded that human beings should be pleased—not so that this might be sought as a reward for right actions, but because no one can please God who does not make himself an example to those whom he wishes to be saved. Thus Paul both pleases and does not please (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 8), because in seeking to please, he seeks not to please himself, but to make truth itself pleasing to human beings.

**QUESTION LVII.**
How is it that the apostle Paul, when recounting in order in his Epistle to the Galatians where he first went after his conversion, says, “I went away to Arabia, and returned again to Damascus” (Gal. I, 17), whereas Luke in the Acts of the Apostles testifies that the same Paul, after receiving faith in Christ, first stayed not in Arabia but in Damascus (Acts IX, 8 ff.)?

**ANSWER.**

We find this explained as follows by blessed Jerome (*Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, Book I, chapter I, verse 17). Concerning the Apostle’s statement, “I went away to Arabia, and returned again to Damascus,” he says:

[Col. 0691A]

“It does not seem that the order of the narrative agrees, when Luke relates in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts IX, 23 ff.) that, after Paul had boldly proclaimed the Gospel in Damascus for many days following his faith in Christ, a plot was made against him; that he was let down through the wall at night in a basket; that he came to Jerusalem, attempting to join himself to the disciples; that when they avoided him and were afraid to approach him, Barnabas brought him to the apostles; and that there he related how he had seen the Lord on the road and had acted boldly in Damascus in the name of Jesus. ‘He was with them,’ he says, ‘entering and departing in Jerusalem, and acting boldly in the name of the Lord; he also spoke and disputed with the Greeks. But they sought to kill him. When the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him away to Tarsus’ (Acts IX, 28 ff.).

[Col. 0691B]

“Yet here he says that he first went to Arabia (Gal. I, 17), then returned again to Damascus, and after three years came to Jerusalem, saw Peter, and remained with him for fifteen days; and that he saw no other of the apostles except James, the Lord’s brother. So that these things might be believed as true—for to those who were absent they could appear doubtful—he confirms them under oath, saying: ‘Now, concerning the things I am writing to you, behold, before God, I do not lie’ (ibid., verse 20).

“We may suppose that, according to Luke’s account, Paul did indeed go to Jerusalem, not as though he were going to the apostles who preceded him in order to learn anything from them, but to escape the assault of persecution that had been stirred up against him in Damascus on account of the Gospel of Christ. Thus he came to Jerusalem as he might have come to any other city, and immediately departed from there because of the plot, going to Arabia or Damascus; and from there, after three years, he returned to Jerusalem to see Peter.

[Col. 0691C]

“Or certainly it may be understood in this way: immediately after he was baptized and strengthened by taking food, he was with the disciples who were in Damascus for several days; and, while everyone marveled, he immediately preached in the synagogues of the Jews that Jesus was the Son of God. Then he went to Arabia, returned from Arabia to Damascus, and remained there for three years. Scripture attests that these were many days, saying: ‘When many days had passed, the Jews took counsel to kill him. Their plot became known to Paul, and they watched the gates day and night in order to kill him. But his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket. When he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join himself to the disciples’ (Acts IX, 23 ff.).

[Col. 0691D]

“Luke passed over Arabia for this reason: perhaps Paul had accomplished nothing in Arabia that was worthy of an apostolate, and therefore Luke preferred, in his concise narrative, to mention those things that seemed worthy of the Gospel of Christ. Nor should this be attributed to the Apostle’s negligence, if he stayed in Arabia without result; rather, some divine dispensation and command may have required him to remain silent.”

### QUESTION LVIII

[Col. 0692A]

Since the apostle Paul says of himself, “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20), how does he seem, as though contradicting himself, to say: “I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh” (Rom. VII, 18)?

**ANSWER.**

These statements, which appear contradictory, are resolved in this way by blessed Augustine, who, arguing against Julian, says (*Against Julian*, Book VI, number 71):

“It is not contradictory, as you suppose, that one who says, ‘I no longer live, but Christ lives in me,’ should also say, ‘I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh.’ For to the extent that Christ lives in him, to that extent he fights against and overcomes the fact that good does not dwell in his flesh, but evil does. Indeed, no one’s spirit would rightly desire against his flesh (Gal. V, 17), unless the Holy Spirit dwelt in him.”

[Note: The Editor has *concupisceret*, “would desire.”]

[Note: The Editor has *Spiritus Christi*, “the Spirit of Christ.”]

### QUESTION LIX

[Col. 0692B]

Since Paul preaches to the Galatians, “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (ibid., 2), how does he seem, as though contradicting himself, to preach to the Romans: “Circumcision indeed profits, if you keep the law” (Rom. II, 25)? And further: “What advantage, then, has the Jew? Or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them,” and so forth (Rom. III, 1, 2).

**ANSWER.**

These two statements, which seem contradictory, are resolved as follows by blessed Jerome (*Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, Book II, chapter V, verse 2):

[Col. 0692C]

“If circumcision profits nothing for those who have been circumcised, how does circumcision profit those who keep the law? This is resolved by saying that the Epistle written to the Romans was addressed to those who had believed from both Jews and Gentiles. Paul acted in such a way that neither people would take offense, so that each community might retain its own privilege: the Gentiles were not to be circumcised, and those who had been circumcised were not to restore the foreskin.

“But when writing to the Galatians, he used a different argument. Those who had believed were not from circumcision but from the Gentiles, and circumcision could not benefit those who, after the grace of the Gospel, were returning again to the elementary practices of the law (Gal. IV, 9). The historical account in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XV, 1 ff.) relates that, when certain men arose from among the circumcised and asserted that those who had believed from the Gentiles ought to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, the elders who were in Jerusalem and the apostles, gathered together, decreed by letter that the yoke of the law should not be placed upon them and that they should observe nothing further except to keep themselves from sacrificial offerings to idols, from blood, and from fornication—or, as it is written in certain copies, also from strangled animals.

[Col. 0692D]

“And so that no doubt might remain that circumcision is of no benefit, but that Paul moderated his statement concerning circumcision in the Epistle to the Romans on account of those who had believed from the Jews, he gradually proceeds toward the later parts of that same Epistle and shows that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value, saying: ‘Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God’s commandments’ (I Cor. VII, 19).

“For circumcision is so completely nothing that it did not benefit even the Israelite people, which boasted of its circumcision, as the prophet bears witness: ‘All the nations are uncircumcised in flesh, but the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart’ (Jer. IX, 26). And the uncircumcised Melchizedek blessed the circumcised Abraham (Gen. XIV, 19).”

### QUESTION LX

Since the apostle Paul preaches in his Epistle to the Galatians, saying, “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V, 2), why does he seem in the Acts of the Apostles to have acted against his own preaching, when he himself circumcised his disciple Timothy (Acts XVI, 3)?

**ANSWER.**

[Col. 0693A]

Both actions were undertaken at the beginning of the growing Church with prudent and salutary purpose: on the one hand, carnal circumcision, which had been fulfilled in Christ, ought already to cease, as the Apostle preached; on the other hand, among those early Christians who had believed from circumcision, circumcision of the flesh was not immediately forbidden, contrary to a long-standing custom, lest this give rise to scandal in the Church. Instead, they were gradually led by persuasion toward perfect understanding.

[Col. 0693B]

Thus blessed Augustine discusses this question in his books *Against Faustus*. He says (Book XIX, chapter 17):

“The first Christians who had believed from the Jews, who had been born and instructed according to the precepts of the old law, were ordered by the apostles to preserve their ancestral rite and tradition; and those for whom this was necessary were admonished to accommodate themselves to the slowness and customs of the others.

“This is why the Apostle even circumcised Timothy, who was born of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, on account of those to whom he had come with him in such circumstances (Acts XVI, 1 ff.); and he himself observed such a custom among them, not through deceitful pretense but through prudent counsel. These practices were not harmful to those born and instructed in this way, although they were no longer necessary as signs of future things. Indeed, it was more harmful to forbid them as though they were harmful in people among whom they ought to continue.

[Col. 0693C]

“For Christ, who had come to fulfill all those prophecies, found them initiated in such a way that thereafter those who were not bound by any such necessity, but who came from the opposite wall—that is, from uncircumcision—to that cornerstone which is Christ (Eph. II, 14, 20), were not to be compelled to observe such practices.

“But if those who came from circumcision and were still devoted to such sacraments voluntarily wished to provide such accommodation, as Timothy did, they were not to be forbidden. If, however, they thought that their hope and salvation lay in such works of the law, they were to be avoided as a certain destruction.”

[Note: The Editor has *siverunt*, “allowed,” instead of *jusserunt*, “ordered.”]

[Note: The Editor has *tales*, “such,” instead of *talis*, “such a.”]

[Note: The Editor has *mortem*, “death,” instead of *morem*, “custom.”]

[Col. 0693D]

[Note: The Editor has *vetarentur*, “were to be forbidden,” instead of *vitarentur*, “were to be avoided.”]

“Thus also comes the Apostle’s statement: ‘Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.’”

### QUESTION LXI

How could Paul, who had instructed the Galatians that, if a person were overtaken in any offense, he should be restored in a spirit of gentleness (Gal. VI, 1), seem afterward to say, as though contradicting himself, to these same people: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?” (I Cor. IV, 21).

**ANSWER** *(From Jerome, Book III on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter VI, verse 1.)*

[Col. 0694A]

If he says there that he will come to sinners not in a spirit of gentleness but with a rod, how does he now, for those who have been caught in some sin, apply not a rod but a spirit of gentleness? The former statement is addressed to those who, after sinning, did not recognize their error and were unwilling to submit to their superiors and be corrected by repentance. But when a sinner, recognizing his wound, has handed himself over to a physician for treatment, a rod is not necessary there, but rather a spirit of gentleness.

### QUESTION LXII

Since Paul commands in the Epistle to the Galatians, saying, “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. VI, 2, 5), how does he seem, as though contradicting himself, to say later: “Each person will bear his own burden”? If each person will bear his own burden, one person cannot bear another’s burdens.

**ANSWER** *(From the same work, on verse 5.)*

[Col. 0694B]

We must observe that there he commanded us, while we are in this life, to support one another when we sin in this life and to help one another in the present world. Here, however, he speaks of the Lord’s judgment at the resurrection: we will be judged as sinners or as saints according to our own work, not on account of another person’s sin or by comparison with someone worse, with each person receiving according to his own work.

Although obscurely, this little statement teaches us a hidden new doctrine: while we are in the present world, we can help one another either by prayers or by counsels; but when we have come before the tribunal of Christ, neither Job, nor Daniel, nor Noah will be able to plead for anyone (Ezek. XIV, 14), but each person will bear his own burden.

[Col. 0694C]

### QUESTION LXIII

Since Paul says, “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI, 14), how is he found to have gloried in many other things, as in the passage where he says, “I will gladly glory in my weaknesses” (II Cor. XII, 9)?

**ANSWER** *(From the same work of Jerome, on verse 14.)*

[Col. 0694D]

How does he now say, “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of Christ,” when elsewhere he boasts of other things, as in the statement, “By your glory, which I have in Christ Jesus” (I Cor. XV, 31)? We must understand that all such glory, when referred to the cross, is the glory of the cross; and whatever worthy deed is accomplished in the virtues is done for the sake of the Lord’s passion.

## FROM THE EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS

### QUESTION LXIV

Since in the Epistle to the Ephesians Paul says of Christ that the Father “placed all things under his feet” (Eph. I, 22), how does he say elsewhere, “We do not yet see all things subjected to him” (Heb. II, 8)? Likewise, there is the statement, “He must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet” (I Cor. XV, 25). If all things have not yet been subjected to him, and he must reign until they are subjected to him, how has God now subjected everything beneath his feet? This is especially puzzling since Paul himself also testifies elsewhere: “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (I Cor. XV, 28).

**ANSWER** *(From the same work of Jerome, on chapter I, verse 22.)*

[Col. 0695A]

Either he mentions what is future in the present tense, as though it had already happened; or, if the statement is to be understood of the past, we must take it in this way: even those things that are not subject to him willingly serve him by the condition of their nature—for example, demons, Jews, and Gentiles.

[Col. 0695B]

They do not serve Christ, nor are they subject to his feet; yet because they were created by him for a good purpose, they are subject against their will to his power, even though they resist him by the will of free choice.

### QUESTION LXV

Since Paul urges the Ephesians to become imitators of God, saying, “Be imitators of God, as beloved children” (Eph. V, 1), how does he say to the Corinthians, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. XI, 1)?

**ANSWER** *(From the same work of Jerome, Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter V, verse 1.)*

[Col. 0695C]

The Corinthians could not immediately become imitators of Christ; it was already a great thing for them if they could become imitators of Christ’s imitator. But to the Ephesians, as to people whom he had already taught such great mysteries, he does not say, “Be my imitators,” nor “Be imitators of Christ,” but “Be imitators of God.”

This is not because being an imitator of Christ is less than being an imitator of God—for Christ is God—but because it is one thing to imitate him according to his humanity and another according to his divinity. For although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him according to the flesh (II Cor. V, 16).

Nor do I think that in all the other things God has done a human being can imitate God. Rather, for example, just as he is merciful and sends rain upon the good and the evil (Matt. V, 45), so we too should pour out our goodness upon all people. When we do this, we will be beloved children, or imitators either of Paul himself or of God.

### QUESTION LXVI

Since throughout all the divine Scriptures we acknowledge God alone as both ruler and creator of the world, how does the apostle Paul seem, in contradiction, to say:

[Col. 0695D]

“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities and the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph. VI, 12)?

**ANSWER.**

Insofar as the devil and his angels extend their kingdom through the members who belong to them, they are called by the Apostle “rulers of the world.” He called them rulers of the world because they rule the lovers of the world. They do not rule the world in the sense of being rulers of heaven and earth; rather, he calls sinners “the world.” Hence it is also written in the Gospel: “The world did not know him” (John I, 10).

## FROM THE EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 0696A]

### QUESTION LXVII

How does the apostle Paul say, “I desire to depart and be with Christ,” and also, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I, 21, 23), when he seems, in contrast, to say: “We who are in this dwelling groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (II Cor. V, 4)?

**ANSWER** *(From Gregory the Great, Book XXXI of the *Morals*, number 70.)*

[Col. 0695D]

[Note: The Editor has *videamus*, “let us see,” instead of *miremur*, “let us marvel.”]

We marvel here at Paul: how he loves what he avoids and avoids what he loves.

[Note: The Editor reads: “how he loves what he avoids, and how he avoids what he loves.”]

For behold, he both desires to die and yet fears to be stripped of the flesh. Why is this? Because, although victory brings everlasting joy, punishment nevertheless disturbs him in the present; and although love of the reward to come prevails, the assault of pain still touches the soul without sorrow.

[Col. 0696B]

For just as a brave man, when battle is already near and he is girding himself with weapons, both trembles and rages—he is seen, as it were, to be afraid through his pallor, yet is driven forward vehemently by anger—so the holy man, when he sees himself drawing near to suffering, is shaken by the weakness of his nature and strengthened by the firmness of his hope. He trembles at approaching death, yet rejoices that by dying he will live more truly.

He cannot pass to the kingdom except through the intervening passage of death. Therefore, while trusting, he seems almost to doubt; while almost doubting, he trusts; he fears while rejoicing, and rejoices while fearing, because he knows that he cannot reach the prize of rest unless he crosses with labor what lies between.

[Col. 0696C]

So, when we wish to drive illness from the body, we sorrowfully drink the bitter cup of purification; yet, certain of the health that will follow, we rejoice. Since the body cannot otherwise reach health, we willingly take in the drink what otherwise disgusts us. When the mind sees that life is contained within bitterness, it becomes cheerful even while troubled by sorrow.

[Note: The Editor has: “when battle is already near, he girds himself with weapons, trembles, and hastens,” and so forth.]

### QUESTION LXVIII

How does the apostle Paul, speaking as though in contradiction, testify at one moment that he is perfect and at another that he is imperfect? In the Epistle to the Philippians he says: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect.” Then he adds: “Therefore, as many as are perfect” (Phil. III, 12, 15).

**ANSWER.**

[Col. 0696D]

Concerning this twofold perfection, we find that blessed Ambrose understood the matter as follows. He says:
