“We have seen that it is impossible for someone living in the body to be perfectly free from blemish, since Paul himself also calls himself imperfect. For he says: ‘Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect.’ Yet shortly afterward he says: ‘Therefore, as many as are perfect.’

“Unless perhaps, because there is one perfection in this world and another after this life, we are to understand as perfect the person of whom he says to the Corinthians: ‘When that which is perfect has come’ (I Cor. XIII, 10); and elsewhere: ‘Until we all come into the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, into a perfect man, according to the measure of the fullness of the age of Christ’ (Eph. IV, 13).”

[Col. 0697A]

## FROM THE EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS

### QUESTION LXIX

When the apostle Paul, speaking of the final resurrection, says among other things, “The dead who are in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive will be caught up together with them in the air to meet Christ, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thess. IV, 15, 16), since he says, “So we shall always be,” how did John in the Apocalypse assign a fixed period to the reign of the saints, saying, “They will reign with Christ for a thousand years” (Apoc. XX, 4)?

**ANSWER.**

[Col. 0697B]

The holy Apostle would never have said of himself or of other holy people, “We will be caught up together in the clouds to meet Christ, and so we shall always be with the Lord,” if he had known that some saints, once they had received immortal bodies, would reign with Christ for a limited time.

For they will not always be with the Lord if they reign with him after the resurrection for only a thousand years. Therefore, if the “always” that is spoken of has no end, there will not be a thousand years, since when they have ended they bring an end.

But so that these statements may not be thought contradictory, the reader should understand them briefly in this way. When the Apostle says, “So we shall always be with the Lord,” he is speaking of the time of the future judgment, from which onward we will reign with Christ without end.

[Col. 0697C]

But when John says in the Apocalypse, “They will reign with Christ for a thousand years,” these thousand years are understood as the time of the present life. This is the period placed between the two advents of Christ: the first, in the incarnation, and the second, in his judgment.

He called this intervening period a thousand years, however many years its duration may encompass, either so that a part might figuratively be understood from the whole, or so that the fullness of the number called “a thousand” might include whatever time there is between Christ’s first and second advent.

The saints are said to reign with Christ for a thousand years on account of the Church of God, which, in the kingdom of faith, extends and grows in faith and works from the time of Christ’s incarnation until the time of the judgment that is to come. For to say of the saints that they will reign with Christ for a thousand years is virtually to say of the faithful elect that throughout this entire period lying between the two advents, they live faithfully with Christ in the Church.

[Col. 0697D]

## FROM THE FIRST EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO TIMOTHY

### QUESTION LXX

Since the apostle Paul says, “The law is not laid down for the righteous” (I Tim. I, 9), how does the Psalmist ask that the law be given to him, saying, “Set before me the law, O Lord, the way of your ordinances, and I will always seek it” (Ps. CXVIII, 33)?

**ANSWER** *(From Augustine, Sermon 11 on this Psalm, numbers 1 and 2.)*

[Col. 0698A]

What does it mean that he prays for the law to be set before him by the Lord, if it is not set before the righteous? Is it not set before the righteous in the same manner in which it was set before the rebellious people on tablets of stone rather than on tablets of their fleshly hearts (II Cor. III, 3), according to the Old Testament from Mount Sinai (Exod. XXXI, 18), which produces slavery, and not according to the New Testament (Gal. IV, 24)?

[Note: The Editor has “from Mount Sinai” instead of “on Mount Sinai.”]

[Note: The Editor has *servitutem*, “slavery,” instead of *servitute*, “in slavery.”]

Of the latter it was written through the prophet Jeremiah: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a New Testament with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will give my laws into their minds, and I will write them on their hearts” (Jer. XXXI, 31 ff.).

[Col. 0698B]

[Note: The Editor has *neglexi*, “I disregarded,” instead of *negligam*, “I will disregard.”]

See how this man wishes the law to be set before him by the Lord—not as it was set before the unjust and disobedient, who belonged to the Old Testament, on tablets of stone, but as it is given to the holy children of the free woman, that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem, the children of promise and the children of eternal inheritance, by the Holy Spirit as by the finger of God in the mind and written upon the heart.

[Note: The Editor has *quam* in both places, “which,” instead of *quod*, “because.”]

[Col. 0698C]

This does not mean that they retain it in memory while neglecting their life, but that they know it through understanding and practice it through love, in the breadth of love and not in the narrow confines of fear.

Why, then, does this man still ask that the law be set before him? Surely, if it had not been set before him, he would not have run along the way of God’s commandments in the breadth of his heart. But because he speaks as one who is making progress and knows that what he has advanced in is God’s gift, what else does he ask when he asks that the law be set before him except that he may progress in it more and more?

He certainly knew the law according to the letter; but because “the letter kills, while the Spirit gives life” (II Cor. III, 6), he prays that through the Spirit he may do what he knew through the letter.

[Col. 0698D]

[Note: The Editor has *proficit*, “makes progress,” instead of *profecit*, “has made progress.”]

### QUESTION LXXI

How does Paul say, “He desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II, 4), when Scripture says, in contrast, “God has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes” (Rom. IX, 18)?

**ANSWER.**

If God desires all people to be saved, how is it that all are not saved? Or if all are saved—which certainly is not the case—how is it written elsewhere, “God has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes”?

But we must understand what has been written in this way (from Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 103): when it says that he desires all people to be saved, it is as though it said that no person is saved except the one whom he himself wills to save. It does not mean that there is no human being except one whom he willed to be saved, but that no one is saved except one whom he wills to be saved.

[Col. 0699A]

Accordingly, when it says “all,” he wished a part to be understood from the whole: namely, that he desires all those to be saved whom he has chosen for salvation from every kind of human being.

Therefore this is not contrary to the statement, “God has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes.” The one on whom he has mercy is saved through mercy; the one whom he is said to have hardened is abandoned to judgment.

God is said to harden the person whom he does not wish to soften, just as he may also be said to blind the person whom he does not wish to enlighten, or to repel the person whom he has ceased to call.

### QUESTION LXXII

Since in the First Epistle to Timothy Paul commands women to remain silent in the church, saying, “I do not permit a woman to teach” (I Tim. II, 12), how does he seem, when writing to Titus, to grant women the power to teach—that is, so that they may be good teachers and teach prudence (Tit. II, 3, 4)?

**ANSWER** *(From Jerome, Commentary on the Epistles to Timothy and Titus.)*

[Col. 0699B]

These statements are resolved by the earlier teachers in such a way that they appear in no respect contradictory. The meaning is that teaching has been removed from women in relation to men, while they may teach younger women as though they were their daughters.

Therefore, when the Apostle commands women to be good teachers and to teach prudence, he permits them to teach women, not men; and this is to be done not in the church but privately, so that it does not contradict the earlier command by which he orders women to remain silent in the church.

### QUESTION LXXIII

Since the Apostle says of God, “He dwells in inaccessible light; whom no human being has seen, nor can see” (I Tim. VI, 16), how does the Psalmist say, “Come to the Lord, and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII, 6)? How, then, are we enlightened by approaching him if we do not see the very light by which we can be enlightened? But if, by approaching him, we see the very light by which we are enlightened, how is it said to be inaccessible?

**ANSWER** *(From Gregory the Great, Book VIII of the *Morals*, number 92.)*

[Col. 0699C]

In this matter we must consider that he called it “inaccessible” to a human being, that is, to one wise in human things.

[Note: The Editor has “to every human being who possesses human wisdom.” The Benedictine editors adopt this reading, although they note that some readings agree more closely with ours.]

Sacred Scripture commonly calls all followers of carnal things by the name “human beings.” Thus the Apostle says to certain people who were quarreling among themselves: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to the human being?” (I Cor. III, 3, 4). Shortly afterward he adds: “Are you not human beings?”

[Col. 0699D]

Elsewhere he gives this testimony: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9). After saying that this was hidden from human beings, he immediately adds: “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (verse 10).

[Note: The Editor adds *Deus*, “God,” after *revelavit*.]

By distinguishing himself from the designation “human,” he shows that the person who had been caught up above humanity already possessed divine understanding.

[Col. 0700A]

So also in this passage, when he declares the light of God to be inaccessible, he shows whom he means by adding: “Whom no human being has seen, nor can see.” In his customary manner, he calls all who possess human wisdom “human beings,” because those who possess divine wisdom are above human beings.

[Note: The Editor has *perhiberet*, “when he declared,” instead of *perhibet*, “when he declares.”]

## FROM THE SECOND EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO TIMOTHY

### QUESTION LXXIV

Since Paul commands Timothy, saying, “Do not contend in words” (II Tim. II, 14), how does he seem, as though contradicting himself, to have commanded Titus in the passage where he instructs him concerning what a bishop ought to be, saying, “So that he may be powerful in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it” (Tit. I, 9)?

**ANSWER.**

How these two statements, which appear contradictory, differ from one another is explained in the books of blessed Augustine *On Christian Doctrine* (Book IV, chapter 28, number 61). He says, placing Paul’s very testimony before us:

[Col. 0700B]

“Do not contend in words, for it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear.”

He immediately adds:

“This was not said so that, when adversaries attack the truth, we should say nothing in defense of the truth. Otherwise, what are we to make of the statement in which he showed what a bishop ought to be, saying among other things, ‘So that he may be powerful in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it’?

“To contend in words is not to care how error may be overcome by truth, but how one’s expression may be preferred to another’s expression. But the person who does not contend in words—whether he speaks humbly, moderately, or with grandeur—uses words so that the truth may be made evident, the truth may be pleasing, and the truth may move.”

[Col. 0700C]

Therefore, when one contends against the truth, this is the vice of vanity. But when the minister of God’s word is commanded to be powerful in sound doctrine so that those who contradict may be refuted, this is the ministry of spiritual teaching, by which one serves truth rather than vanity.

### QUESTION LXXV

How does Paul admonish Timothy, “Reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and doctrine” (II Tim. IV, 2), when, in contrast, he commands Titus, “Reprove with all authority” (Tit. II, 15)?

**ANSWER** *(From Gregory the Great, *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 16.)*

[Col. 0700D]

What does it mean that he dispenses his teaching with such skill that he places authority before one and patience before the other, except that he saw Titus to possess a spirit of gentleness and Timothy one somewhat more fervent?

[Note: The Editor reads: “so that in displaying this, he places authority before one,” and so forth.]

[Note: The Editor’s better reading is *proponat*, “places before,” instead of *praeponat*, “puts first.”]

He inflames the former through the zeal of emulation, and moderates the latter through the gentleness of patience.

## FROM THE EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO THE HEBREWS

### QUESTION LXXVI

[Col. 0700D]

Since it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews, “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. IV, 13), how does the Lord, when about to rebuke the wickedness of Sodom, seem to speak as though he were ignorant of it, saying, “I will go down and see whether they have acted according to the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. XVIII, 21)?

**ANSWER** *(From the manuscript of Gregory, Book XIX of the *Morals*, number 46.)*

[Col. 0701A]

Although all things are naked and open to his eyes, the author of our life nevertheless wished to restrain us from delivering a hasty judgment. He did not wish to judge the wickedness of the Sodomites merely on hearsay, for he says:

“The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave. I will go down and see whether they have acted according to the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

[Note: The Editor has “the wickedness of Sodom” instead of “the wickedness of the Sodomites.”]

[Col. 0701B]

Why, then, does the omnipotent Lord, who knows all things, seem to doubt before investigating, unless it is to provide us with an example of seriousness, so that we do not presume to believe people’s crimes before examining them?

Behold, he descends through angels to investigate the wickedness, and immediately strikes the guilty.

[Note: The Editor has *cognoscenda* (“to investigate,” agreeing with *mala*, “evils”) instead of *cognoscendum*.] He is patient, gentle, and the one of whom it is written, “But you, Lord, judge with tranquility” (Wis. XII, 18); he is the one of whom it is again written, “The Lord is patient, but he is a requiter” (Sir. V, 4).

When he found them involved in so great a crime, he seemed to set patience aside and did not wish to wait for the day of the final judgment to exact vengeance; instead, he forestalled the day of judgment with the fire of judgment.

Behold: when he heard of the evil, he seemed almost to believe it only with difficulty, yet, once he discovered it to be true, he struck without delay. He thereby gave us an example: greater crimes, when heard, should be believed only slowly, but once they are truly recognized, they should be punished more swiftly.

## FROM THE CATHOLIC EPISTLE OF BLESSED JAMES THE APOSTLE

### QUESTION LXXVII

How does James say, “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. II, 17, 20, 26), when Paul seems, in contrast, to say: “But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace, just as David also speaks of the blessedness of the person to whom God credits righteousness without works” (Rom. IV, 5, 6)?

**ANSWER.**
If, according to James, faith without works is dead, how does it follow, in accordance with what Paul says, that faith without works justifies the ungodly? Yet, when these statements are carefully considered, they will not be found contradictory. For, according to Paul, faith without works saves those whom faith in Christ first separates from unbelief—certainly without any preceding merits of good works. If someone believes in Christ, with all sins forgiven, he can be saved by faith alone. But then, if one who already believes and truly receives Christ’s sacraments refuses to do good, his faith, according to James, is dead. Thus, when Paul says that a believer can be saved without works, he is speaking specifically of those whom faith has first received as believers; their sin is not reckoned against them before the act, since it is wiped away by the water of baptism. But when he calls faith without works dead, he is speaking specifically of those who, after receiving faith, believe that they can be saved without works of righteousness. For the beginning of justification by God belongs to the one who believes in the Justifier. And when this faith has been justified, it clings to the soil of the soul like a root that has received rain, so that, when it begins to be cultivated by God’s law, branches may rise from it bearing the fruits of good works. The root of righteousness therefore does not come from works; rather, works come from the root of righteousness, which God brings forth in the one accepted, even without works.

In this same passage of the Apostle Paul, where he says, “But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness,” a certain teacher, explaining the passage, says:

“God justifies the ungodly who turns to him by faith alone, not by good works, which he did not possess; otherwise he would have been punished on account of his works of ungodliness. At the same time, it must be observed that he asserted that it is not a sinner but an ungodly person who is justified by faith alone—that is, one who has only recently come to believe—according to God’s purpose, by which he determined freely to forgive sins through faith alone.”

## From the First Epistle of Blessed Peter the Apostle

[Col. 0702B]

### Question 78

How can Peter say of God, “Into whom angels desire to look” (1 Peter 1:12), when Christ says in the Gospel, “Their angels always see the face of my Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10)?

### Answer

*(From Gregory the Great, Moralia, Book XVIII, no. 91)*

Does Truth proclaim one thing and the preacher of truth another? Yet, when the two statements are compared, it is recognized that they are by no means discordant. The angels both see God and desire to see him, so that they may not be deprived of the fulfillment of their desire. Desire without fulfillment produces anxiety, and anxiety produces punishment. But the blessed angels are far removed from every punishment of anxiety, because punishment and blessedness never coexist at the same time.

[Note: The edition reads more fully and somewhat differently: “God … the angels … desire to see; they thirst to behold, and they behold.” “For if they desire to see in such a way that they do not enjoy the fulfillment of their desire, desire without fulfillment,” etc. The edition reads “since” for “if.” It also reads “having been satisfied.”]

[Col. 0702C] Again, when we say that they are satisfied by the vision of God, since the Psalmist also says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm 16:15), we must consider how satiety is ordinarily followed by weariness. Therefore, so that the two statements may properly agree, let Truth say that they always see, and let the outstanding preacher say that they always desire to see. So that there may be no anxiety in desire, they are satisfied while desiring; and so that there may be no weariness in satisfaction, they desire to be satisfied.

They desire, therefore, without labor, because satisfaction accompanies their desire; and they are satisfied without weariness, because their satisfaction is always kindled by desire.

## From the First Epistle of Blessed John the Apostle

### Question 79

How can John, writing in his Epistle about love, say, “Beloved, I am not writing a new commandment to you, but an old commandment” (1 John 2:7), when the Lord himself calls love a new commandment in the Gospel, saying, “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another” (John 13:34)?

### Answer

*(From Augustine, Tractate 1 on the Epistle of John, no. 10)*

What commandment did he call old? “The one you had,” he says, “from the beginning.” It is therefore old because you have already heard it; otherwise he would contradict the Lord, who says, “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another.” But why is it an old commandment? Not because it belongs to the old person. Why, then? Because you had it from the beginning. “The old commandment” [the editions add *is* after “old”], “the word that you heard.” It is therefore old because you have already heard it.

And he shows that it is itself new when he says, “Again, I am writing a new commandment to you.” It is not another commandment, but the very same one that he called old; the same commandment is new. Why? Because “it is true in him and in us” [the editions read “in you”]. Why, then, did you hear it as old? Because you already knew it. Why is it new? Because “the darkness has passed away, and the true light is already shining” [“already” is absent from the edition]. This is why it is new: because darkness belongs to the old person, whereas light belongs to the new [the edition reads: “because darkness belongs to the old person, but light to the new person”]. The Apostle Paul says, “Put off the old person and put on the new” (Colossians 3:9–10). And again: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

### Question 80

How can John say, “Everyone who has been born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin” (1 John 3:9), when, on the contrary, he says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8)?

### Answer

*(Extracted from Augustine, Tractate 5 on the same Epistle, nos. 1–8)*

What is this sin, unless it is acting against the commandment called the love of Christ? For this was not said generally of every sin. If we understand it as referring to every sin, it will contradict the statement that says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.”

Therefore, when he says, “The one who has been born of God does not commit sin,” he means that he does not harbor hatred toward his brother and cannot sin because he does not act against love. But what he says—“If we say that we have no sin”—may be understood of sins in general.

### Question 81

How can the Apostle say, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), while the Psalmist says, on the contrary, “The pure fear of the Lord endures forever” (Psalm 18:10)?

### Answer

*(From the same Augustine, Tractates 43 on the Gospel of John, nos. 5 and 7)*

How does perfect love cast out fear, if the pure fear of the Lord endures forever and ever? There is therefore servile fear, and there is pure fear. Servile fear is fear lest you suffer punishment; pure fear is fear lest you lose righteousness. Accordingly, what the Apostle said concerns servile fear; but what the Psalmist says is to be understood of that pure fear by which we shall be joined to the Lord forever.

### Question 82

Since the Apostle John says in his Epistle, “Everyone who has been born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9), how can Isaiah, speaking in the voice of the Lord, say, “I have raised children and exalted them, but they have despised me” (Isaiah 1:2)?

### Answer

*(From Blessed Jerome on that passage of Isaiah)*

If the one who is born of God does not sin, how could they have despised him? Hence it appears that, according to the Hebrew translation, it is better to read, “I have nourished children,” rather than “I have begotten children,” lest it seem contrary to that statement found in John’s Epistle: “Everyone who has been born of God does not sin.” Therefore, if they were born of God, how could they have sinned, since everyone born of God cannot sin?

## From the Acts of the Apostles

### Question 83

Since it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that the Lord remained with his disciples for forty days after his resurrection (Acts 1:3), how can that same Lord say so contradictorily to those same disciples in the Gospel, “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you” (Luke 24:44)?

### Answer

*(From Gregory the Great, Homily 24 on the Gospels, no. 2)*

He was not absent from those to whom he was visibly present in the body; yet he now denies that he is still with them, because, in the immortality of his flesh, he differed from their mortal flesh.

The *Antikeimenon* of Saint Julian ends.

## Commentary on Nahum

### Notice concerning the following treatise

[Col. 0703D] The Commentary on the prophet Nahum which follows—an attempted work only, not a completed one—was first published by Henry Canisius, a German jurist, from a manuscript of the Bavarian Library which bore the name of St Julian, bishop of Toledo. Once made public, it was accepted by learned men and repeatedly reprinted in France by the editors of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* under Julian’s name. So far as we know, no one disputed this attribution or suspected that its author was other than our Julian, until Natalis Alexander, in Dissertation 15, century I, proposition 2, began to doubt whether it was his genuine offspring.

If we seek the true reason, it is undoubtedly no other than that the work expressly teaches St James the Apostle’s preaching in Spain, a teaching which Natalis undertakes to attack with all the force of his arguments in that dissertation. How successfully that undertaking turned out is not for us to judge here. It is enough to say and show that the evidence Natalis confidently opposed to it is, in our judgment, extremely slight—not ours alone, but also that of very weighty men, Cardinal de Aguirre (to omit others) and the most learned Bollandists, whom it will repay one to consult in their preliminary commentary, vol. VI of July, part II, §7.

The historian says that it is uncertain whether this work belongs to St Julian of Toledo, and gives three reasons. First, it was published from one manuscript, mutilated throughout and full of errors. As though many monuments of antiquity had not been published from one manuscript alone and deservedly approved by learned men—for example, to give one instance among many, the work *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, attributed to Lactantius, first published by Baluze. His second point is that it expounds only four or five verses of Nahum. If that argument had force, all published fragments and unfinished works of the holy Fathers which are universally held genuine would have to be rejected. Finally he concludes: “Those Leonine verses, read at the end of the testimony just cited concerning St James’s preaching, plainly indicate an author later than Julian.” Let the fair-minded reader see and judge. The verses are:

> Each, by his allotted portion, spread Christ without stain;  
> but through Paul he is spread throughout the whole world.

Where, pray, are the Leonine verses? As the Bollandists perceptively observed, the first has no metre at all, while the second cannot properly be called Leonine; such verses require the middle to rhyme with the end. Both may only be called similarly cadenced. But even if they were Leonine, must a work be relegated at once to a later age because of only two verses, when some such verses occur even in poets of the golden age? For example, Virgil, *Aeneid* XII:

> His right hand hurled the mouths of the swift horses;

and these two of Ovid in Ulysses’ speech:

> If you think anything remains for Troy’s fate,  
> husband, I beg you, brother, help your wife’s sister.

One or two Leonine verses, casually produced by the writer, can therefore carry no weight against the antiquity of the work.

Yet some after Natalis have embraced, as we have seen, his very slight conjectures, no better disposed than he toward Spanish matters. Among them is Fr Thomas Maria Mamachi, well known in the republic of letters both for extensive learning and singular erudition. Pursuing Natalis’s aim of attacking St James’s preaching in Spain, he answered our Flórez, writer of *Sacred Spain*, in *Christian Origins and Antiquities*, vol. II, ch. 23, and reproached him for maintaining that the book of Commentaries on Nahum, which learned men take away from Julian bishop of Toledo, ought to be ascribed to him. What does he add beyond Natalis? Only this: that Felix, when compiling a catalogue of Julian’s works in his encomium, was wholly silent about such a commentary.

But one should observe that Felix likewise did not mention the Life of St Ildefonsus, unquestionably written by Julian. Further, the Commentary in question is unfinished, as we have noted: apparently begun with great effort, but interrupted at the very outset, perhaps by death; consequently it was not published and was not sufficiently known to others. Examples of this could be supplied almost without number.

Until stronger arguments are produced, therefore, we shall never allow a book to be rashly taken from Julian when its first editor attributed it to him on the authority of a manuscript, and when Miraeus, Fabricius, Labbe, Nicolas Antonio, Aguirre, the Marquis of Mondéjar, and very many others, Spanish and foreign alike, did not take it from him.

Should anyone, with Élie Dupin and Remigius Ceillier, wish leisurely and carefully to compare this writing’s style with Julian’s other undoubted works, intending thereby to forge a stronger weapon against us, we would warn him to remember how often arguments drawn from this quarter have deceived, unless everything is considered attentively and cautiously. Such judgment requires a highly trained mind, the keenest eyesight, and the most discerning nose.

The work itself, though unfinished and mutilated, shows its author to have been deeply versed in Holy Scripture and acute in investigating its meanings. In expounding each sentence he pursues every sense: first the literal, then the allegorical, then the anagogical, and finally the moral. In this last kind he gives not one sense only, but many; one is moved to marvel both at the fertility of his mind joined to the greatest clarity, and at his learning and singular erudition joined to precision of expression. No one who has carefully read Julian’s other writings will doubt that all these literary excellences can fully belong to our Julian.

Meanwhile we have endeavoured to fulfil what was our part here. Having no copy of this Commentary except two editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, one Paris edition of 1624 and the other Lyons edition of 1677, we have done what we could: corrected typographical errors detected in them, occasionally indicated a probable means of restoring corrupt places in the text, and noted in parentheses the sources of the passages of Holy Scripture and authors cited there.

## Commentary of Saint Julian, Bishop of Toledo, on the Prophet Nahum

Published by Henry Canisius, J.C., from a manuscript codex of the Bavarian Library.

### Preface

[Col. 0705D] The prophet Nahum concerns the kingdom of the Assyrians. Historically, he speaks of the destruction of Nineveh, its capital; allegorically, of the desolation of the world; mystically, of the restoration of humankind through Christ; morally, of the restoration to former dignity, or to greater glory, of the sinner fallen into crimes.

[Col. 0706D] Nineveh was founded by Ninus, the second king of the Assyrians, and was given its name, some maintain, from his own name—or rather, according to others, from his son Ninias. Ninus, born of Belus his father and Semiramis his mother, was deceived by his mother’s fraud and, unaware of the illicit desire involved, begot Ninias by her. When he discovered this after his mother had delivered her womb of its child, abhorring his mother’s crimes, he stained its walls with blood. This city, outstanding in its time for form, situation, size, and adornment, and eminently distinguished by king, law, and people, by power, shrewdness, and constancy, sought to extend on every side the pomp of its kingdom and the pride of its luxury; it unrestrainedly loosened the reins of cruelty even against God’s people.

[Note: “Unrestrainedly” pleases us, as it is read in the manuscript and in the editors of this work in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, rather than their “before unrestrained.”]

First Sargon, then Pul, then Tiglath-pileser, and afterwards Shalmaneser carried part of that people captive; finally, under Hoshea, all Israel, conquered by Sennacherib, migrated into Assyria.

Accordingly Nahum pours forth prophecy for the consolation of the transplanted people, the strengthening of saints to be tested, the glorious expectation of those to come, the stirring of devotion in the fallen, and the thanksgiving of all. He contemplates a vision in which the overthrow of the city and destruction of the people are declared; the memory of the exiles is in some measure refreshed, the patience of the afflicted is fostered, redemption is foretold for the condemned, hope and exaltation are intimated for the fallen, and honour and incorruption are promised in common to all the faithful. The prophet prophesied in the time of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah: when the Assyrian kingdom was destroyed, Romulus was born, the first Olympiad was established by the Greeks, Rome was founded, the kingdom of the Lacedaemonians failed, that of the Macedonians began, and the poet Hesiod flourished. From the first Ninus, the second ruler of Assyria, to the thirty-sixth Sardanapalus, its last ruler, who, defeated by his standard-bearer Arsaces, burned himself in a fire, the years of the Assyrian kingdom total 1,164.

The prophet prefixes a prologue in which, according to the manner of rhetorical discourse, he makes the hearer attentive, teachable, and well-disposed. The prologue is: “The burden of Nineveh; the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.” He set down three things by which he wished to move the hearer to pardon, favour, and glory. In the burden misery is apparent; in the vision, grace; in consolation, a certain glory. To the Assyrian persecutor is assigned the weight of misery; to Israel enduring, the regard of grace; and to the same Israel returning, the likeness of some glory. Thus, upon hearing “burden,” the reader becomes attentive; by “vision,” teachable; and by Nahum—that is, “consoler”—well-disposed.

“The burden of Nineveh”: because it was overthrown by the Chaldeans. “The book of the vision”: because pardon was given to Ezra, Nehemiah, and others. “Nahum the Elkoshite”: because the liberty, grace, and glory of city, temple, and people were in some degree restored. These things we have said historically. Let us now discuss them briefly in their mystical or moral sense.

“The burden of Nineveh”: the world’s conflagration; “the book of the vision”: the resurrection of the saints; “of the consoler”: their glorification.

“The burden of Nineveh”: the damnation of the reprobate; “the book of the vision”: the choosing of the blessed; “of the consoler”: their praise for ages of ages.

“Burden,” when it is said, “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41); “vision,” when it will be said, “Come, blessed of my Father” (v. 34); “consoler,” when, being all in all, he will deliver the kingdom to God and the Father (1 Cor. 15:24, 28).

Or “burden” is the unbelief of the nations; “book of the vision,” the conversion of believers; “of the consoler,” the consummation of all things. Let the reader remember that burden among the reprobate is distress; the book of vision is grace abiding with the elect; consolation is victory over the enemy conceived by divine aid.

Burden is the weight of misery and tribulation; vision, the favour of a divine gift and an invocation of the mind; consolation, steadfastness in conflict and joy in triumph attained. In all these, the reader is made attentive, teachable, and well-disposed.

In rhetorical works, Cicero (*On Rhetorical Invention*, I.16, Geneva edition, 1743) says that goodwill is gained from four sources: the cause itself, the person of the judge, that of the opponents, and one’s own. But the saints, who die or live not for themselves but for the Lord (Rom. 14:8), and seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21), do not seek favour for themselves but refer all things to the Father of lights. Hence the Psalmist says, “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:9); and the Apostle: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). Goodwill, therefore, is gained from four things: the person of the Saviour, the form of salvation, the reason for the gift, and the fall repaired. The supreme One gave; what he bestowed was eternal; he granted it freely to the wretched. In the first is considered the immensity of power; in the second, the abundance of mercy; in the third, the liberality of grace; in the fourth, the kindness of nature: for the supreme One freely bestowed the greatest things on the wretched. Thus in the first the giver’s omnipotence is proved; in the second, his generosity; in the third, his sufficiency; in the fourth, his goodwill.

In another way, he seeks goodwill from the person of the judge, his own condition, the cause and quality of the business, and the enormity and nature of the adversary. From the judge, because he himself is mercy; from his own condition, because he is involved in misery; from the cause, on the adversary’s side because he was seduced by envy, but on his own because he is surrounded by weakness and ignorance; from the adversary’s nature, by subtlety of nature, length of life, and unremitting activity; and from its enormity, because they attack without cause, never cease even for a moment, and yield in no particular. In the first he seeks favour through the judge’s compassion; in the second through the humility of confession; in the third through life’s pilgrimage and unconquerable frailty; in the fourth through the adversary’s envy and cruelty. In the first the judge’s clemency is invoked; in the second his own need is displayed; in the third the temptation of this life is alleged; in the fourth the adversary’s envy and assault are charged. First, because the judge’s sentence is: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live” (Ezek. 33:11); second, need says: “If he shuts up, none can open” (Job 12:14); [Note: The reading *clauserit* for *incluserit*, read in the manuscript, was wrongly corrected in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, since the Vulgate reads *incluserit*; on its authority we restore this reading.] third, the misery of life: “Remember me, because my life is wind” (Job 7:7); fourth: “From the north evils are kindled over the face of the whole earth” (Jer. 1:14).

In another way, we read that the Saviour’s works were fourfold: he performed miracles, conferred benefits, suffered bitter things for us, and delivered precepts of life. In these four the hearer is made well-disposed: enlightened by his teaching, sustained by benefits, confirmed by miracles, and kindled to love by the mark of his sufferings. In the first ignorance is excluded; in the second, need; in the third, negligence; in the fourth, torpor of life and sloth of soul. In the first he receives the light of knowledge; in the second, the abundance of grace; in the third, he infers the blessedness of the kingdom; in the fourth, he longs for Christ’s love. By life-giving oracles the blind are enlightened; by miracles the fugitive is brought back; by benefits one is made devout; by the marks of the Passion one is made perfect.

He is made teachable also when, in Christ’s teaching, life, and reputation, he is taught what to hold, urged what to avoid, instructed what to fear, what to grieve for, in what to hope, and what to love: namely, to avoid vices, hold fast the counsels of life, fear the punishments of Gehenna, grieve over the misery of this exile, fix the anchor of hope in heaven, and ardently love the heavenly homeland.

He is made attentive from the greatness of punishment, when “burden” is prefixed; from the quality of joy, when “vision” follows; and from the certainty of reward, when “consoler” is added.

Since Cicero (*On Rhetorical Invention*, I.15) establishes five kinds of causes—honourable, remarkable, lowly, doubtful, and obscure—and recommends different introductions accordingly, we call this prophecy an honourable kind, not of a cause but of prophecy. In it God’s just severity toward the reprobate is shown, and his most merciful goodness toward the pious commended: in a friend, grace; in an enemy, justice; in a servant, the truth of judgment; in a hireling, the equity of reward; in a son, inheritance of the kingdom; in a bride, identity of spiritual joy.

Having thus briefly tasted the subject and intention, let us now say to what part of philosophy it belongs. Philosophy has four principal species, beneath which is contained the entire sequence of all liberal arts and of all divine discourse: theoretical, practical, physical, and logical. They often appear so interwoven and connected that they can scarcely be distinguished; at times they are so separated and alienated that they cannot be joined at all. Mathematics concerns visible figures of visible things; practice, invisible forms of visible things; physics, invisible causes; theology, invisible substances. Logic, however, provident over all, mistress of the arts and keeper of the keys of mysteries, ranges everywhere, loosening and binding forms, modes, causes, and knots with great subtlety, excellence of art, and abundance of arguments. This prophecy, because it partly concerns heavenly things and partly treats morals, belongs in part to theoretical philosophy and in part to practical.

Its method of treatment is this. First it threatens enemies, then speaks gently to the obedient. After this it introduces, as though incidentally, the coming of the Saviour. Then it presents the terrible arrival of the devastator: the Babylonians are armed and fall upon the Assyrians; Nineveh is stormed, captured, and destroyed; the temple is overthrown from its foundations; every age, sex, and condition is ruined, dashed to pieces, and consigned to slavery. Next it inveighs against her in mockery, reproaches her robberies, fornications, and sorceries, and calls her a city of blood. It also threatens destruction to Alexandria as it brings aid. Then, in mockery, it repeatedly charges the cowardice of rulers and people, calls the people effeminate, and plainly declares that their efforts are vain. Finally it rebukes the sloth of the shepherds, and so ends its prophecy.

The preface ends.

## The exposition begins

[Col. 0709D] **1. “The burden of Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.”** Some believe that the prophet placed this prologue before his prophecy; others maintain that Ezra found it. For just as, after the Law had been burned by the Chaldeans and restored by him in newly discovered letters, Ezra prefixed titles to the individual psalms, so, for instruction’s sake, he prefixed prologues to nearly every prophet. Or, if the prophet is said to have prefixed it, he speaks of himself as of another out of humility. Thus Moses, speaking of himself, said as of another: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command the children of Israel,” etc. (often in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers). So Isaiah: “The vision which Isaiah son of Amoz saw” (Isa. 1:1); Jeremiah: “The words,” he says, “of Jeremiah, who was among the priests from Anathoth” (Jer. 1:1); Micah: “The word which came to Micah of Moresheth” (Mic. 1:1). Nearly all prophets begin thus. The same is found in the New Testament: “That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter” (John 21:7). The Apostle has something similar: “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ,” etc. (Rom. 1:1). Divine writings hand down many such examples. Or, when saints begin to receive grace from God, thirsting, they entreat the Deity, thereby especially advancing and leaving posterity an example of grace.

**2. “The burden of Nineveh.”** Among the twelve prophets we read of four who used “burden” in their prophecies: Nahum, Habakkuk, Malachi, and Zechariah. The first three put it at the beginning; Zechariah in two places, in the middle and at the end. In the middle he says: “The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus its resting-place” (Zech. 9:1); at the end: “The burden of the word of the Lord upon Israel” (12:1). In Isaiah also we read eleven burdens: the burden of Babylon, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, the wilderness of the sea, Dumah, Arabia, the valley of vision, Tyre, and the beasts of the south (Isa. 13:1; 15:1; 17:1; 19:1; 21:1, 11, 13; 22:1; 23:1; 30:6). By the very character of the number these signify transgression of sin. For in ten, the number of commandments, obedience is marked; in eleven, which passes beyond it, the evil of transgression. Further, eleven curtains of goats’ hair are made in the tabernacle (Exod. 26:7), and after the traitor’s death the Saviour would not leave the apostolic choir at that number. We have said above that “burden” signifies the weight of misery. The Apostle cries: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). “If this is done in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). Thus Jeremiah, urging the faithful soul to consider this life’s misery: “If you have not been secure in a land of peace, what will you do in the pride of the Jordan?” (Jer. 12:5). And Job: “Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast, and in his angels he finds perversity; how much more those who live in houses of clay, who have an earthly foundation, will be consumed like a moth” (Job 4:18–19).

As, therefore, in divine discourse there are simply “songs” and “Song of Songs” for the immeasurable greatness of ineffable joy; “ages” and “ages of ages” for the extent of eternity; simply “sabbath” and “sabbath of sabbaths” for the blessedness of most hidden rest; simple “works” and “work of works” for venerable and mystical dignity: so individual burdens may simply mean individual crimes or kinds of tribulation, but “burdens of burdens” an excessive multitude of faults or tribulations.

**3.** There are three burdens of burdens: vanity, iniquity, and calamity—the vanity of the world, iniquity of the soul, and calamity of hell. Vanity blinds, iniquity hurls down, calamity torments. Worldly vanity removes contemplation of heavenly things; iniquity of soul removes love of God and neighbour; the calamity of Tartarus removes affection for good and devotion of soul. Vanity makes one vicious; iniquity makes one hateful; the calamity of hell makes one liable to punishment. Vanity makes one incestuous; iniquity hostile; calamity perpetually sorrowful. Vanity presses down, iniquity bends, calamity breaks.

**4.** We may say another thing about these burdens: one is carried on the head, another in the arms, another on the shoulders. Burden on the head is vanity in the mind; burden in the arms, iniquity in action; burden on the shoulders, the calamity of Gehenna. The first defiles affection, the second dishonours action, the third kills the subject. Of these three burdens Hosea says: “You ploughed impiety, reaped iniquity, and ate the fruit of falsehood” (Hos. 10:13). Impiety is ploughed when someone meditates on vanity from devotion to the world; he reaps iniquity when from unlawful thought he gathers a wicked deed; he eats the fruit of falsehood when he receives in hell according to what he did in the body. Thus unlawful things are ploughed by thought; iniquity is gathered by doing evil; its fruit is eaten by enduring punishments.

**5.** Of vanity it must be said that some are subordinate, others associated, and others set beneath. The first are carnal, the second spiritual, the third intellectual. The first give themselves to curiosity of the senses; the second to human necessity; the third strive for the truth to be contemplated. In the first order sense and thought are defiled; in the second affection is adorned and action made honourable; in the third intellect is raised and reason made vigorous. The first voluntarily subject themselves to the world; the second unwillingly serve it; the third wholly flee it. The first, therefore, are brutish, the second active, the third contemplative.

**6.** We may say similar things of iniquity. Some love iniquity but do not preach it; some both love and preach it; others preach, love, and defend it. Iniquity therefore has three principal forms: impiety, crime, and malice. Impiety is against God, crime against oneself, malice against one’s neighbour. They are impious by despising commandments, criminal by plunging themselves into vices, malicious by corrupting neighbours. The first order is those “whose god is their belly, and whose glory …” (Phil. 3:19); the second, those who “proclaimed their sins like Sodom” (Isa. 3:9); the third, those who “became like molten shields” (Job 41:6). The first are those who “cast their inmost parts upon the ground” (Ecclus. 10:10); the second, those who say, “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; for this is our portion and inheritance” (Wis. 2:8–9); the third, those who say, “The way of the Lord is not just” (Ezek. 18:25). Thus sin is committed first against the Father, second against the Son, third against the Holy Spirit: against the Father by acting against his will; against the Son against his humility; against the Holy Spirit against his love.

7. Calamity likewise has three species. The first is bitterness of conscience, the second hatred of justice, the third despair of pardon. In the first case they are wretched, because conscience gnaws at them; in the second, more wretched, because justice displeases them; in the third, because no clemency of pardon remains. Since, then, we said above that the vanity of the world, the iniquity of the soul, and the calamity of hell are burdens, it remains for us to inquire what other things are dominated by these burdens. Above, in Isaiah, we set down eleven burdens, which signify eleven kinds of vices and express eleven burdens of worldly affairs. Let us discuss first the vices, and then the affairs.

[Col. 0713A] 8. In the burden of Babylon, pride is chiefly signified. In Moab, indignation and especially arrogance; in Philistia, specifically the perverse curiosity of the senses; in Damascus, overt rapacity; in Egypt, gluttony and drunkenness altogether; in the desert of the sea, the presumption of singularity; in Dumah, superstition; in Arabia, feigned affection; in the valley of vision, the blinding of the soul; in Tyre, boasting of vices and arrogance; in the beasts of the South, the dissolution of religion is expressed. These, then, are the kinds of vices. Now let the burdens of worldly affairs follow.

9. The first of these is indeed secular power [perhaps: worldly commands]; the second, pagan learning; the third, canine eloquence; the fourth, the distinction of blood; the fifth, bodily beauty; the sixth, the honor of a spouse; the seventh, the example of offspring; the eighth, the faithfulness of friends; the ninth, the humble service of subjects; the tenth, abundance of temporal goods; the eleventh, the peaceful possession of all the foregoing. It was not my intention to discuss these more fully at present; to treat them belonged to another work. I leave it to those who are weighed down by the burden to show that they are burdens. Vanity, therefore, is assigned to worldly affairs, iniquity to vices, and calamity to the punishments of Gehenna. Since those things are called burdens and truly are burdens, these are not undeservedly called the burdens of burdens.

That vanity depresses many by its burden the Apostle testifies, saying: “The creature was subjected to vanity, unwillingly” (Rom. VIII, 20). In the Psalm we read concerning the burden of iniquity: “My iniquities have gone over my head, and like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me” (Ps. XXXVII, 5). The calamity of Gehenna also weighs down most grievously; the Savior calls it a winepress in Isaiah, saying: “I have trodden the winepress alone” (Isa. LXIII, 3). Of the first we read in Ecclesiastes: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. I, 2); of the second in Zechariah: “Iniquity sits upon the talent of lead” (Zech. V, 7–8); of the third in the Psalm: “Destruction is in their ways, and misery” (Ps. XIII, 3). A grievous yoke, therefore, lies upon the sons of Adam from the day of their departure from the womb until the day of their return to it (Ecclus. XL, 1), when they pass from vanity to iniquity, and from iniquity to calamity. There are also other burdens, very different from those mentioned above.

10. For the first belongs to administration, the second to religion, and the third to love. The first burden is borne by prelates; the second by those who have been put to death to this world; the third by those perfected in the measure [or: in the cubit]. The first strengthen the condition of the Church; the second adorn her appearance; the third commend her virtue. The first order says: “The anxiety of all the churches, my daily burden” (II Cor. XI, 28); the second: “My soul chose hanging, and my bones death” (Job VII, 15); the third: “Whether Paul, or Cephas, or Apollos, all are ours” (I Cor. III, 22). The first order consists of those who bow beneath God and bear the world (Job IX, 13); the second, of those who mortify their flesh so that they may transfer their soul to wisdom; the third, of those who wound themselves, one by one, through love of their neighbors.

11. Administration contains three burdens under itself. [Col. 0714A] The first is occupation with external affairs; the second, concern for conduct; the third, endurance of hardships. In the first, one serves the necessity of subjects; in the second, one provides for the purity of conduct; in the third, one meets adversity or pleads against it, as expediency requires. Or: the first is the business of the world; the second, vigilance over oneself; the third, concern for one’s neighbor. In the first one must be necessary; in the second honorable; in the third useful. Necessary, so that he does not desire superfluous things immoderately; honorable, so that by living effeminately he does not corrupt the conduct of others; useful, insofar as he goes before his subjects toward pardon, grace, and glory. Necessary, therefore, is life; honorable, reputation; useful, teaching. Honorable in example, useful in counsel, necessary in ministry.

12. Religion likewise consists in three things: namely, in the mortification of the flesh, devotion of the soul, and compassion for one’s neighbor. Hence the Apostle James says: “This is pure and undefiled religion: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, and to keep oneself undefiled from this world” (Jas. I, 27). He refers visitation to compassion for one’s neighbor, and undefiled preservation to the mortification of the flesh and devotion of the soul. The Savior also clearly taught this in the Gospel (Matt. VI, 2 ff.), where, speaking about religion, he instructed his disciples concerning almsgiving, prayer, and fasting: fasting he referred to mortification of the flesh; almsgiving to compassion for one’s neighbor; prayer not to the clamor of the tongue, but to devotion of the soul. Or, the first is abstinence from evil; the second, the fervor of goodness; the third, the joy of a purified soul.

[Col. 0714C] 13. Love has three burdens: for one thing is required of us by our neighbor, another by the angel, and another by God. Our neighbor demands from us the services of humanity; the angel, the desires of sincerity; God, efforts burning with every virtue and flowing with every sweetness. Our neighbor demands a devoted act, the angel seeks a sincere affection, and God requires the purest understanding. We must therefore offer our neighbor the piety of action, the angel sincerity of conduct, and God every effort of the soul and perfect charity.

14. For the Spirit praises his bride, adorned and ordered in this way, in the Song of Songs with much commendation, saying: “You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and comely, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array” (Song VI, 3). Beautiful to the world, sweet to one’s neighbor, comely to heaven. Or: beautiful in action, sweet in affection, comely in understanding. Or: beautiful in the honesty of reputation, sweet in the usefulness of teaching, comely in the necessity of an exalted life. Or: beautiful in example, sweet in speech, comely in counsel. Or: beautiful in works, sweet in conduct, comely in the mind’s ecstasies. Or: beautiful to one’s neighbor, sweet to the angel, comely to the Bridegroom.

Rightly, therefore, she is called terrible to her enemies, in whom there is found neither worldly ambition, nor injury to one’s neighbor, nor presumption concerning oneself, nor offense against the angel, nor aversion from the divine will—not even for a little while. Again, concerning the same one, through the same speaker and to the same one: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (ibid. IV, 7). Truly beautiful is she who is neither conquered by the enemy, nor corrupted by the world, nor led astray by her neighbor, nor struck down by the flesh, nor exalted by the mind. Wholly beautiful, indeed, is she whom neither action corrupts, nor affection stains, nor understanding hinders: action by iniquity, affection by vanity, understanding by the splendor of heavenly things. There is therefore no blemish in her, because in her the suggestion of the Evil One does not prevail, the threats or promise of the world are base, the flesh’s imprint lies dormant, and the mind’s arrogance is suffocated.

These, then, are the burdens of love, by which the happy soul is weighed down. May my mind be weighed down by this burden; may my soul die, crushed beneath this weight. The general burdens, therefore, are clearly fourfold. Some belong to God, some to the soul, some to the world, and some to hell. We have likewise subdivided each of these above into other categories. Now let us examine the remaining matters.

15. In the present discussion, Nineveh can be understood in four ways. Historically, it is that famous metropolis of the Assyrian kingdom; allegorically, it signifies the world; mystically, it is a type of the Church; morally, it represents the soul. Concerning the city we have already said something historically, though little. It remains, therefore, to proceed to the explanation of the other meanings. Let us first examine the interpretation of the name.

16. Nineveh is interpreted as “beautiful,” and concerning God and the world one reads in a certain philosopher:

[lacuna] You lead all things from a heavenly

Pattern: most beautiful yourself, bearing

The beautiful world in your mind and forming it in a corresponding image.

For if someone considers the craftsman, the material, the abundance of dissimilar creatures produced from it, and the divinely implanted order in things, together with their grace, then through their arrangement, order, and adornment God’s invisible things can indeed be known; his power, wisdom, and clemency can be perceived to some extent: power through arrangement, wisdom through order, and goodness through adornment. Hence, from its adornment, it also received in Greek the name κόσμος (*kosmos*). The world is the totality of all things, consisting of the four elements and rounded into the form of a complete sphere.

If you contemplate the structure of this universe, you will find that, by a marvelous design and wisdom, the composition of all things has been perfected: apt, harmonious, beautiful, and complete in all its parts. In it, not only do like things preserve harmony, but even those things which creative power brought into being come together, at wisdom’s command, into a kind of single friendship and covenant. What could be more contrary than fire and water? Yet God’s providence has so tempered them in the nature of things that they not only do not dissolve the common bond of fellowship between them, but also supply life-giving nourishment to all things that are born, so that they may endure. Every nature loves itself, and the harmony, in a marvelous way, of many dissimilar things brought together into one produces a single concord in all things.

See whether anything is lacking from the beauty of divine works; and if you perceive that nothing, not even the smallest thing, is lacking, you already have something from which to marvel at the craftsman.

17. When the Psalmist contemplated these things, he greatly admired them, saying: “How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24). Again: “I remembered the works of the Lord, for I shall remember your wonders from the beginning” (Ps. LXXVI, 12). [Col. 0716A] Again: “I will meditate on all your works, and I will exercise myself in the works of your hands” (Ps. CXLII, 5). If anyone were capable of investigating these things, he would find in them the marvelous light of God’s wisdom. Would that I could perceive these things with as much subtlety and expound them with as much appropriateness as I can love them ardently!

For I delight in speaking frequently about these matters, because it is exceedingly sweet and pleasant: the understanding is instructed by reason, the soul delights in sweetness, and the affection is stirred by wonder. Thus, astonished and admiring with the Psalmist, we cry out: “How magnificent are your works, O Lord! Your thoughts have been made exceedingly deep. The foolish man will not know, and the stupid will not understand these things” (Ps. XCI, 6–7).

Let this suffice for what has been said about the world. Now let something be brought forward concerning the beauty of the Church.

18. For the Church, the bride of Christ, the temple of the Most High, the city of the great King, flourishes with such power, beauty, and wisdom that she can neither be conquered by the enemy, nor led astray by the world or by her neighbor, nor overcome by adversity, nor bent by prosperity, nor in any way darkened by an adverse breeze. Hence the Savior says of her in the Gospel: “The rivers came, the winds blew, and they could not move her, for she was founded upon a firm rock” (Matt. VII, 25).

For this reason the Psalmist stirs us to praise, love, and enlarge her: “Set your hearts upon her strength, and distribute her houses, so that you may recount them to another generation” (Ps. XLVII, 14). For just as—so Cicero mentions at the end of the second book of the *Rhetorica* (N. 56)—certain goods of a state pertain to its preservation, while others pertain to its enlargement, so in the Church, which is the excellent city of the great King, some things pertain to beauty and others to enlargement: justice to preservation, fortitude to stability, prudence to beauty, and temperance to enlargement.

[Note: [Col. 0715] Perhaps something is missing here: “Some things pertain to health, others to stability.”]

19. There are four things that educate and adorn the soul, instruct and strengthen it: counsels, services, aids, and remedies. Counsels pertain to prudence, services to justice, aids to fortitude, and remedies to temperance. Counsels enlighten the blind; services make the devoted; aids strengthen the weak; remedies heal the sick. Counsels drive out ignorance; services, envy; aids, weakness; remedies, desire. Counsels make teachers of wisdom; services, lovers of justice; aids, defenders of truth; remedies, lovers of happiness.

Happy, therefore, is the city that neither lacks counsel, nor is without service, nor lies helpless through weakness of aid, nor is sullied by poverty of remedy. Christ bestowed these upon his Church after he had been glorified and had given the Spirit of his Father and his own; she herself first brought these forth within her for his glory. For he gave counsels of life, services of justice, aids of constancy, and remedies of repentance. Counsels, by teaching the people; services, by feeding the crowds (Matt. V, 2 ff.; XIV, 15 ff.); aids, by judging the causes of widows, orphans, and resident aliens (Deut. X, 18); remedies, by passing through the land and healing all those oppressed by the devil (Acts X, 38). He therefore gave counsels on the mountain, services beside the sea, aids in the upper room, and remedies on the cross.

20. The Church likewise received these things from her Bridegroom and used them to spread his fear, beauty, honor, and love among others. Through the counsels of divine knowledge and the light of wisdom, she joined converted philosophers to herself; through the services of mercy, she subdued the pagans; through the aids of grace, she steadfastly conquered heretics; through the remedies of repentance, she mercifully recalled schismatics.

Through counsels they come from natural ignorance, as from the eastern quarter; through services they return from the heat of desire, as from the southern region; through aids they are drawn back from the cold of wickedness, as from the northern climate; through remedies they are brought out from the setting of vices, as from the western region.

21. Her Bridegroom had promised her through the prophet Isaiah the future joy of a numerous offspring: “Behold, I will bring your seed from the East, and your children from the ends of the earth. I will say to the North: ‘Give’; and to the South: ‘Do not withhold’” (Isa. XLIII, 5–6). He had also promised her this through the mouth of the Psalmist: “Great is the Lord, and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God. Mount Zion, the sides of the North, the city of the great King, is founded in the joy of the whole earth” (Ps. XLVII, 2–3).

This is truly a city of refuge, in which pardon, freedom, and confidence are granted to those who flee for refuge through the death of the high priest (Num. XXXV, 28, 32). In it, therefore, there are commandments for preservation, counsels for stability, spiritual gifts for beauty, and remedies of repentance for enlargement. The apostles are for preservation, martyrs for stability, virgins for beauty, and confessors for the fragrance of enlargement. Charity is for preservation, humility for stability, continence for beauty, and clemency for expansion. For its preservation there are penitents; for stability, preachers; for beauty, despisers of the world; for enlargement, the married who show mercy.

22. Again, this city possesses other goods of the greatest value, which both confer health upon it, strengthen it, adorn it becomingly, and enlarge it most extensively. It is healed by evangelical grace, strengthened by apostolic teaching, adorned by the words of holy teachers, and enlarged by the decrees of orthodox fathers and by the canons.

Since, then, this city has been happily endowed by king, law, people, situation, abundance, and adornment—for its king is happiness; its law, charity; its people, the faithful, a fellowship sharing both under the king and under the law; its situation, sincerity of faith and conduct; its abundance, an overflowing wealth of doctrines and virtues; its adornment, the grace of spiritual gifts and the various kinds of processions [perhaps: professions]—since, I say, this city abounds so generously in so many and such great goods, what madness afflicts the wretched: to thirst for the wormwood of vices, to follow the shipwreck of this world, always to suffer the misfortune of life, to bear the dominion of impious tyranny, and not rather to fly to the aid of the most serene city, to the bosom of maternal charity, to the joy of angelic [Col. 0718A] happiness, and become a decurion of this king, a minister of this law, and a citizen of this city?

Of this city the Psalmist says: “Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God” (Ps. LXXXVII, 3). Again, the same writer concerning the same city: “Great is the Lord, and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God” (Ps. XLV, 2). This is that beautiful city of which the Bridegroom speaks gloriously in the Song of Songs, saying: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful. Your eyes are like those of doves” (Song IV, 1). Again, the same writer in the same book: “You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and comely, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array” (ibid. VI, 3). Again, the same writer concerning the same city in the same book: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (ibid. IV, 7). Again, the bride herself says of herself in the same book: “I am black, but beautiful, O daughter of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon” (ibid. I, 4).

23. Here a very useful division presents itself to us from the side; here an occasion for a fourfold division has been given to us. For one woman is not black but beautiful; another is black and beautiful; another is neither beautiful nor black; another is not beautiful but black. The first is the queen of heaven; the second, the bride of the Lamb on earth; the third, the wife of the world; the fourth, the consort of the devil. The first consists of those who rejoice with Christ in heaven; the second, of the faithful journeying on earth; the third, of those whom the vanity of the world has swallowed; the fourth, of those whom iniquity afflicts with punishments or calamity tortures in hell.

24. There are accordingly four kinds of betrothal by which the aforementioned classes of women are betrothed: the joy of divine contemplation, the grace of pardon, the desire of the world, and the misery of hell. To the first is betrothed the fellowship of the blessed angels; to the second, the glorious unanimity of just human beings; to the third, the pernicious vanity of the reprobate; to the fourth, the dreadful unhappiness of the worst among the dead.

The first are at rest; the second stand in battle array; the third have been shamefully cast down; the fourth have been mercifully enslaved. The first is “Jerusalem above, free, our mother” (Gal. IV, 26). The second and third are, in the Lord’s threshing floor, wheat and chaff together; the fourth is tortured among the dead with pain and misery.

In the first there is all glory and no misery; in the second, much glory but some misery; in the third, much misery but scarcely any glory; in the fourth, no glory whatsoever but every misery. The first, therefore, rejoices above with Christ; the third fornicates with the world; the fourth is tortured with the devil; the second is prepared for the Bridegroom, so that it may be black through repentance and beautiful through obedience; black through humility and beautiful through charity; black through the struggle of temptations and beautiful through constancy in virtues; black through ministry and beautiful through desire; black through the practice of religion and beautiful through the sincerity of contemplation.

The Church is black in carnal matters and beautiful in spiritual ones; black in active works and beautiful in contemplative ones. She is the queen of Ethiopia who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. You are therefore black because you are Ethiopian; beautiful because you are burning with wisdom. Black because you came from the remotest ends; beautiful because you overflow with delights.

[Col. 0719A] 25. These things are written about her in the Book of Kings:

“The queen of Sheba, having heard of Solomon’s fame and wisdom, came to Jerusalem to test him with riddles. And with her came camels bearing burdens. And she brought with her a great quantity of gold and very precious stones. She entered in to Solomon and spoke to him all that was in her heart. And Solomon explained to her all her words, and there was no word that the king omitted and did not disclose to her. And the queen of Sheba saw all Solomon’s wisdom, and the house that he had built, and his food, and the seating of his servants, and the order of his ministers, and their garments, and his cupbearers, and his holocausts which he offered in the house of the Lord; and she was astonished and said: ‘The word that I heard in my land concerning your words and your wisdom is true; and behold, I was not told even half of it.’ And she gave Solomon one hundred and twenty talents of gold, and a great quantity of spices, and very precious stones” (III Kings X, 1 ff.).

The queen of Sheba therefore came—that is, the Church from the Gentiles, long held captive under vices. For this is what Sheba means. She came to hear Solomon’s wisdom and to test him with riddles. For many uncertain matters were reported among them, concerning the creation of the world, the immortality of the soul, the future judgment, the glorification of the saints, and many other things. Coming to Christ concerning all these matters, she was fully assured.

“With her came camels bearing burdens”: that is, Gentiles bringing with them works of mercy, or various kinds of vices. “And a great quantity of gold”: namely, rational understanding. “And a precious stone”: natural intelligence. She entered through repentance to the true Solomon and spoke everything to him through confession. Solomon also explained all her words to her, because after she had been reconciled to him, she was changed into a friend and bride.

Then Jesus brought her into the wine-cellar (Song I, 4), and from there showed her the ineffable abundance of his riches. Hence he says in the Gospel: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV, 15).

She also saw his wisdom and prudence: prudence, by which he orders human affairs; wisdom, by which he governs divine things. And she saw his house (Prov. IX, 1), the mysteries of his incarnation. For she is the one whom Wisdom built for itself.

She saw also Solomon’s foods: the various kinds of piety and the diverse affections of ordered love. She saw the seating of his servants: the ecclesiastical order among bishops and priests. She saw the ranks of his ministers, namely, the differing status of the lower degrees. She saw his garments: the individual believers, or the ornaments of virtues. She saw his wine-pourers: the chosen preachers of the divine word. She saw his holocausts: undoubtedly the mysteries of prayers and supplications.

When she had seen all these things, she marveled at his answers and prudence. If anyone considers the kinds of anointings, the mystical offices of the sacraments, the devout practices of professions, the degrees of orders, the orders of dignities, the dignities of ministers, the ministers of the sacraments, and the sacraments and examples, he sees in these things the king’s marvelous power, incomprehensible wisdom, ineffable goodness, and inaccessible light.

We have said these things about the condition and beauty of the holy Church at somewhat greater length, so that it may be clear to all: if her tabernacle shines so brightly in the land of dissimulation, in the valley of weeping, how brightly must the temple above shine? For if what will be abolished shines with such glory, how much more glorious is what remains forever in glory?

26. Nineveh may also be referred to the beauty of the soul. But, so that the discourse may not run on too long, let the prophetic reading of Ezekiel suffice, where it says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, your root and your generation are from the land of Canaan,” and so forth (Ezek. XVI, 3).

Addressing the unhappy soul, the Lord convicts her, in the manner of a rhetorician, from the attributes of her person and her affair, setting before her the circumstances before, during, and after the deed. Before the deed, he declares how foul, deformed, and worthless she was; during the deed, how sincere, beautiful, and lovable; after the deed, how foul-smelling, poisonous, and utterly abhorrent she had been.

After this, having been despised, rejected, and confounded, he mercifully pursues her and kindly recalls her: by promising, he draws her back; by drawing her back, he perfects her; by perfecting her, he makes her blessed. By “the deed” I mean the grace of election.

The attributes of the person by which she is confounded and convicted are these: name, sustenance, fortune, appearance, affection, pursuits, counsels, deeds, capture, and upbringing. She is confounded from the attributes of the affair when she is convicted by its preparation, commission, outcome, time, occasion, place, means, and manner.

27. If anyone wishes to be instructed about these matters, let him discuss the sequence of the prophetic reading carefully [perhaps: explain or expound it]. I have undertaken not to teach rhetoric but to explain the prophetic reading. First, therefore, it reveals what sort of person she was through vice and what, and how great, she became through the work of grace, saying:

“Your root and your generation are from the land of Canaan. Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite. And when you were born, on the day of your birth your navel was not cut; you were not washed with water for salvation, nor rubbed with salt, nor wrapped in cloths,” and so forth.

Then, reproaching her, he adds:

“‘How long,’ he says, ‘and I passed by you, and I saw you, and behold, your time was the time of lovers. And I spread my cloak over you and covered your shame. And I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, and you became mine. And I washed you with water and cleansed your blood from you. And I anointed you with oil, and clothed you in garments of different colors, and shod you with hyacinth, and girded you with fine linen and embroidered cloth, and many colors. You ate fine flour, honey, and oil, and you became exceedingly beautiful, and you advanced to royalty. And your name went out among the nations because of your beauty, for you were perfect in my beauty which I had placed upon you,’ says the Lord” (Ezek. XVI, 3).

28. Consider the overflowing riches of divine clemency: how the most notorious of harlots, from a filthy brothel, was raised into a queen, adorned with royal attire, and sits at the summit of virtue and the pinnacle of royalty.

Truly, the riches are overflowing when he grants us not only what is necessary, but also what is useful and pleasing. If he granted only necessities, there would indeed be goodness, but not wealth. When he adds useful things to necessities, he displays the riches of his goodness. When useful things are heaped up with suitable additions, the abundance of the riches of his goodness is demonstrated.
