But when, finally, he adds to suitable things those that are also pleasing, what else does he make known except the overflowing riches of his goodness?

29. Consider each thing carefully and see how great is the clemency of our Savior and how great is his care for our salvation. First he washes her with the waters of compunction; then he clothes her with the garments of virtues; afterward he refreshes her with the delights of wisdom; finally he raises up a house for her in honor of royal happiness.

First she is washed in the waters of repentance; second, adorned with the garments of justice; third, nourished with the banquet of divine knowledge; fourth, elevated to the throne of royal dignity.

The Lord therefore says: “I spread my cloak over you.” The cloak is the protection of the angels; the covering of shame is manly repentance; the covenant is observance of the commandments; the oath is the unshakable foundation of salvation; “you became mine” means her glorification by him forever.

He washes her with the tears of repentance, cleanses her blood through works of mercy, and anoints her with the oil of joy flowing from a secure conscience. He adorns her with a variety of virtues; strengthens her affections with firm hope of heavenly things; girds her with the radiance of virginal purity; and clothes her below with spiritual manifestations of God.

He makes her mind joyful through knowledge of variety. He gives her constancy in works and perfection of obedience, the grace of teaching, and the fragrance of a good reputation. He confers upon her the beauty of wisdom, the splendor of eloquence, the brightness of innocence, and the joy of contemplative happiness.

He feeds her with knowledge of the natural law, understanding of the written law, and the grace of the Gospel. Or he refreshes her with allegorical, moral, and mystical knowledge. Or he instructs her with knowledge of worldly things, understanding of hidden causes, and wisdom concerning divine things. Or he refreshes her with purity of action, sweetness of love, and pleasantness of contemplation.

Or he teaches her knowledge of the Trinity: namely, the power of the Father, the wisdom of the Son, and the most benevolent clemency of the Holy Spirit.

Such is the beauty of the soul; such are the immortal riches conferred upon her. Thus the breast is adorned, the understanding honored, the affection purified, and the intellect glorified. Thus life is beautified, conscience cleansed, teaching commended, and reputation celebrated.

Of such a one the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song VIII, 5). Again, elsewhere, the same writer through the same speaker says: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Prov. XXXI, 29).

30. Let what has been said briefly about the beauty of the soul suffice. Now let us see which burdens belong to which things. The burden of the world is its destruction, whether through Christ into something better or at the end. The burden of the Church is the attack against heresies, schisms, and carnal conduct. The burden of the soul is the sudden assault of vices.

The first burden consists in the destruction of idolatry; the second, in the defense of justice; the third, in the restoration of innocence. Since the prophet foresaw Nineveh being overthrown, the world destroyed, the Church disturbed, and the soul attacked by vices, he says, as though giving warning beforehand: “The burden of Nineveh.” As if he were saying: “Let him be at rest; let him see that he does not fall” (I Cor. X, 12); and “let him who holds fast hold fast, until he is removed from the midst” (II Thess. II, 7).

31, 32. But he who had first set before us the anguish of the burden, lest anyone, despairing, succumb to the burden, after the sorrow of the burden supplies the joy of the vision, saying: “The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.”

The name of the book is mentioned in many places throughout the sequence of divine speech. Hence Job says: “Who will grant me a helper, that the Almighty may hear my desire? And may he himself write a book that judges, so that I may carry it on my shoulder and surround myself with it as with a crown” (Job XXXI, 35–36).

Hence Isaiah says: “The vision of all things shall be for you like the words of a sealed book, which, when they give it to one who knows letters, they will say: ‘Read this’; and he will answer: ‘I cannot, for it is sealed’” (Isa. XXIX, 11).

Hence the Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, open your mouth and eat whatever I give you. And I saw, and behold, a hand was sent to me, in which there was a rolled-up book. And he spread it out before me, and it was written within and without. And written in it were lamentations, a song, and woe. And I ate it, and it became in my mouth like sweet honey” (Ezek. II, 8–9; III, 3).

Again, Daniel speaks concerning the same book: “I watched, and behold, thrones were set up, and the Ancient of Days sat. His clothing was white like snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was a flame of fire, its wheels burning fire. A fiery and rushing stream came forth from before him. [Col. 0722C] Thousands upon thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him. Judgment sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. VIII, 9–10).

Hence Zechariah says: “I lifted up my eyes, and behold, a flying scroll. And he said to me: ‘What do you see?’ And I said: ‘Behold, I see a flying scroll. Its length is ten cubits and its breadth is ten cubits.’ And he said to me: ‘This is the curse that goes forth over the face of the whole earth’” (Zech. V, 1 ff.).

Again, in the Apocalypse concerning the same book: “And I saw in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals. And no one could open it except the lion who conquered from the tribe of Judah. For he opened it and broke its seals” (Rev. V, 1 ff.).

I have brought forward all these passages from divine speech so that it may be clear to the reader that the book has many meanings in it.

33. One book, therefore, belongs to nature; another to discipline; a third to grace. The first teaches human equity; the second, human impunity; the third, human and divine charity. The first promises serenity of conscience and conduct; the second, fertility in temporal goods; the third, the happiness of the heavenly kingdom.

The first taught the institutions of nature; the second, the decrees of bodily discipline; the third, the admonitions of grace. The first offers honorable teaching; the second, useful teaching; the third, necessary teaching. Through the first, a friend is made honorable; through the second, a servant is bound; through the third, a son is called into inheritance. The friend, so that he may return grace; the servant, so that he may not flee into idolatry; the son, so that, having spurned exile, he may hasten to his homeland.

The first teaches the honor of human society; the second tests the fear of human frailty; the third supplies the fear of divinity [perhaps: love of divinity]. The first, therefore, belongs to covenant; the second, to correction; the third, to love. The first is the reasoning of the soul; the second, the law of Moses; the third, the Gospel of Christ.

Thus the human race, first receiving the honor of the natural law, became transgressive and fell into fear; then, melting through grace into love, at last returned to its former honor.

Each of these can be called a book of vision, since through the first divine happiness can be understood, through the second the unity of the Godhead, and through the third the sameness of eternity. Through the first there is sincerity of peace; through the second, prudence; through the third, piety. Sincerity pacifies nature; prudence reads the counsel; piety, by regarding itself as existing for servants.

[Col. 0723B] ### 34.

There are also three other books through which the invisible things of God are known. The first is the structure of the world; the second, the human conscience; the third, divine predestination. For this whole world is like a book written by the finger of God—that is, created by divine power—and the individual creatures are like figures, not invented according to human preference, but established by divine will to reveal and, in a certain way, signify the invisible things of God.

Just as an illiterate person, when he sees an open book, looks at the figures but does not recognize the letters, so the foolish and merely natural person, who does not perceive the things that are God’s (I Cor. II, 14), sees outwardly the appearance of these visible creatures, but does not understand their meaning. But the spiritual person, who can discern all things (v. 15), perceives inwardly how wondrous is the Creator’s power, how worthy of reverence the Craftsman’s wisdom, and how deserving of love the goodness of the One who governs.

Therefore there is no one for whom God’s works are not wondrous, although the foolish person marvels at them only for their appearance. The wise person, however, by what he sees outwardly, searches out the profound meaning of divine wisdom—just as, in one and the same writing, one might praise its color or form in one way, but its meaning and significance in another.

It is therefore good continually to contemplate and admire God’s works, but this is proper to the person who knows how to turn the beauty of bodily things toward spiritual use. For this reason Scripture also so greatly urges us to consider God’s visible works, so that through what we behold outwardly we may come inwardly to the knowledge of truth. Hence the Psalmist recalls as though he had already done something great and declares that he will do it still, saying: “I remembered the days of old; I meditated on all your works, and I shall exercise myself in the works of your hands” (Ps. CXLII, 5).

[Col. 0723C] ### 35.

There are therefore three visible things of God: power, wisdom, and goodness. There are likewise three visible things of the world: immensity, beauty, and usefulness. Power is manifested through immensity, wisdom through beauty, and goodness through usefulness. These three things just mentioned are like exceptionally clear images of the divine thought. We must therefore ask which of them first presents itself to those who contemplate, as they come to knowledge.

Every creature, the more closely it approaches the likeness of its Creator, the more closely it declares its Creator. That visible image must first display the invisible exemplar which retains within itself the image of the divine likeness in a perfect way.

[Col. 0723D] The immensity of creatures pertains more to their essence, while their beauty pertains more to their form. But essence considered apart from form is formlessness. What is formless is like God insofar as it exists; but insofar as it lacks form, it differs from God. What therefore has form is more like God than what lacks form. Hence it is clear that the beauty of creatures, which pertains to form, is a more evident image than their immensity, which concerns essence alone.

[Col. 0724A] ### 36.

Again, the beauty of creatures, because of their natural form, pertains to their state, whereas usefulness pertains to their activity, since creatures are useful insofar as they are subjected to human beings, serve them, and render service. What pertains to state is more proper and more certain than what pertains to activity, because nature bestowed the state, whereas institutions added the activity.

The image of beauty therefore precedes immensity and usefulness together in knowledge. It does so first because it is more evident in manifestation.

The wisdom to be sought begins its inquiry from the wise image itself, because the Father is manifested through his wisdom—not only when he sent his wisdom into the flesh, but also when through his wisdom he created the world.

[Col. 0724C] ### 37.

The beauty of creatures, which we have said is the image of wisdom, embraces four things: position, motion, appearance, and quality. Among these, motion holds the more excellent place, because things closer to life are more mobile than things unable to move.

Motion, however, is fourfold: local, natural, animal, and rational. Local motion is forward and backward, to the right, to the left, upward, downward, and around; natural motion occurs in increase and decrease; animal motion in the senses and appetites; rational motion in actions and deliberations.

Rational motion is placed above all the others, because in it not only the senses are moved so as to animate, but reason also is moved so as to understand. No image among creatures can be more evident than this, because what possesses understanding displays invisible wisdom most manifestly to all.

[Col. 0724D] The first and principal image of uncreated wisdom is therefore created wisdom, that is, the rational creature. Because it is invisible in one respect and visible in another, it has become both the door and the way of contemplation. Insofar as it is invisible, it is a door; insofar as it is visible, it is a way.

It is a door because it first opens an entrance for the mind entering contemplation; it is a way because it leads the mind running toward contemplation to its goal. It is a door because in a certain manner it displays invisible things visibly; it is a way because, proceeding from visible things through invisible things, it leads us to behold the Creator of both visible and invisible things. The shrewd person can recognize this in himself.

[Col. 0725A] ### 38.

Since we have entered from visible things into invisible things through the eyes [perhaps: with the eyes] of contemplation, we have penetrated along the way of investigation far enough that we no longer doubt that the Creator of all things exists without beginning, without end, and without change.

It remains, therefore, to consider whether the invisible things of God are known from the second book, that is, from the human conscience. In the human conscience there are three things through which the invisible things of God are known in both respects—namely, the Trinity of the Persons and the unity of the Essence. These are the power of the Father, the wisdom of the Son, and the goodness of the Holy Spirit.

In the soul there are likewise three things: mind, understanding, and love. The mind indeed generates understanding from itself, one from one. When it sees that understanding to be subtle, true, fitting, and delightful, it immediately loves it and takes pleasure in it as its own. It sees and marvels at the same time; it wonders that it could have found such a thing, and rejoices.

[Col. 0725B] It desires always to look upon it, always to possess it, always to enjoy it, and always to delight in it. It is pleasing in itself, and nothing outside it is sought, because everything is loved in it. In it the contemplation of truth is delightful for seeing, pleasant for possessing, and sweet for enjoying. With it the mind rests within itself and is never wearied by the solitude of its secret place; it rejoices in this one companion, though not a solitary one.

### 39.

Consider therefore these three: mind, understanding, and love. Understanding is born from the mind; love is born from the mind and understanding together. From the mind alone comes understanding alone, because the mind alone generated it. Love, however, comes neither from the mind alone nor from understanding alone, because it proceeds from both.

First there is the mind; then the mind and understanding; afterward the mind, understanding, and love. This is indeed how it is in us, but in God reason teaches something very different. In him wisdom is always present, because he has always possessed wisdom, because he has always been wise.

[Col. 0725C] Wisdom is always from him, because, having been begotten, it is not separated from its begetter. It is always begotten, and always being begotten: neither does it begin when it is being begotten, nor cease when it has been begotten. It is always being begotten because it is eternal; it is always begotten because it is perfect.

He who begot is the Father; he who was begotten is the Son. And because he who begot has always begotten, the Father is eternal. And because he who was begotten has always been begotten, the Son is coeternal with the eternal Father.

[Col. 0725D] Likewise, he who has always possessed wisdom has always loved wisdom. He who has always loved has always possessed love. Thus love is coeternal with the eternal Father and Son, because it is the Holy Spirit.

### 40.

But since above we asserted that the Creator of all things is supremely and truly one, we must confess that these three are one in God. Since, moreover, he who was begotten cannot be the one from whom he was begotten, and likewise he who proceeds from the Begetter and the Begotten cannot be the one who is Begetter or Begotten, we are compelled by an unassailable reasoning of truth to affirm in God both a Trinity of Persons and a unity of substance.

The three are therefore one, because there is one substance in the three Persons; but the three are not one person, because just as the distinction of the Persons does not divide the unity of the Godhead, so the unity of the Godhead does not confuse the distinction of the Persons.

[Col. 0726A] Thus there is one common and equal eternity, and an eternal equality, for the three in the Godhead. What the one Godhead makes common to all cannot be unlike in each individual.

Let this already-said account of divine knowledge, which is drawn from the human conscience, suffice. But it must be understood that this knowledge is also called vision, and wisdom, and foreknowledge, and providence. It is called vision because it looks upon; wisdom because it understands; foreknowledge because it anticipates; providence because it orders.

### 41.

The first book, then, is that of the world’s creation; the second, that of human reason; the third, that of divine predestination. Through each of these the invisible things of God are known, as well as the world’s desolation, its restoration through Christ, the condition of the Church, the redemption of the soul, and the happiness of the homeland.

The individual years of the first book are like gatherings of four sheets; its leaves are the months; its pages are the days; its compositions are the totality of affairs; its color is their prosperity; its erasure or error is their adversity. When fortune smiles, the erasure shines; when it changes its expression, the sentence suffers defect.

This book is written within and without: without, in manifest affairs; within, in hidden causes. In it are also written lamentation, song, and woe. The woe of the pagans, the lamentations of heretics, and the song of Christians. For in the world there are the punishments of the wretched, the repentance of those who have fallen, and the innocence of the saints.

[Col. 0726B] ### 42.

We can say similar things about the second book. Its gatherings, as it were, are the dispositions of the soul; its leaves are its dispensations; its pages are its affections; its sentences are the intentions of the heart; the color of its letters is love of God and neighbor; its eclipse or erasure is worldly ambition and the desire of the flesh.

It too is written within and without: within, in desires; without, in actions—working outwardly, loving inwardly. In it are written lamentation, song, and woe.

[Col. 0726C] Woe is the blinding of the mind; lamentation is the confession of sins; song is the contemplation of truth. Woe is despair of salvation; lamentation is compunction for offenses; song is perfect love.

### 43.

Many subtle things could be said about the third book, but, in order to avoid length, we are compelled to hasten on to other matters.

The first book is therefore historical; the second, moral; the third, anagogical. The first is the library of affairs; the second, the canon or rule of morals; the third, the teaching and cause of all things. Each, therefore, as was stated above, is the book of Nahum’s vision.

[Col. 0726D] ### 44.

Nahum is interpreted as “consoler,” which is appropriately understood of the person of the Savior, who, according to the Apostle’s statement, “consoles us in all our tribulation” (II Cor. I, 4).

There are four principal kinds of his consolation among us. One consists in the peaceful abundance of temporal goods, another in bodily health, another in harmony of conduct, and another in the joy of contemplation. The first drives away the miseries of the world; the second, the distresses of the flesh; the third, the troubles of the mind; the fourth excludes the darkness of contemplation.

The first consolation is carnal, the second animal, the third spiritual, and the fourth intellectual. The first pacifies action, the second tranquillizes the senses, the third calms the mind, and the fourth enlightens the understanding. The first invites one to works of mercy, the second to the practices of religion, the third to the form of perfect love, and the fourth to the joy of contemplation. The first makes one a servant, the second a hired laborer, the third a son, and the fourth a spiritual spouse.

[Col. 0727A] ### 45.

Helcheseus is interpreted as “advocate.” Advocacy is needed in the prosecution of a case; advocacy is also necessary for effecting reconciliation.

There are three general kinds of prosecution, and three advocacies are necessary for us. For we bring three matters to trial.

[Note: At this point something seems to be missing. EDIT.]

Third, we examine morals and life before the judge. First we stand before a human being, second before an angel, third before God. Before a human being, by confessing sins; before an angel, by pleading for sins; before God, by awaiting judgment.

In the first case, fear of punishment brings us to trial; in the second, the condition of life; in the third, the necessity of justice. In the first case we have repentance as advocate; in the second, justice; in the third, only the mercy of the Savior.

[Col. 0727B] The first therefore concerns the confession of sins, the second the completion of this life, and the third the universal examination of all. Whoever has pleaded the first case elegantly and purely will, in the second, put on the first stole of glory, and in the third, a double one. When the first case has been rightly pleaded, he is justified; in the second, honored; in the third, glorified.

We therefore have as advocate Jesus Christ the Just (I John II, 1): in the first case, by suggesting repentance; in the second, by conferring justice; in the third, by leading us to glory. Jesus, the most merciful Savior, is therefore both advocate and consoler: consoler in misery, advocate in the case; consoler in tribulation, advocate in the pleading; consoler so that we may not succumb, advocate so that we may conquer.

[Col. 0727C] ### 46.

“The Lord is jealous and the Lord takes vengeance. The Lord takes vengeance and possesses fury; the Lord takes vengeance on his enemies and is himself angry with his adversaries” (Nahum I, 2–3).

At the beginning of the prophet’s work, we exhort the orator who swells with pride over the brilliance of his language and boasts of the flowers of ornate eloquence not to prefer the jests of Demosthenes, the flowers of Quintilian, or the colors of Cicero to the simplicity of divine speech in all its richness of color, nor to love sinful eloquence more than holy simplicity.

Although the kingdom of God is not in speech but in the power of the Spirit (I Cor. IV, 20) and in purity of soul, nevertheless divine speech contains such grace of color and such glory of power, such splendid sweetness of language and such honorable fruitfulness of works, such polish of the tongue, color of the word, fear of sin, and love of God, that by comparison Demosthenes is filthy, Quintilian lies prostrate, and Tully clings to the ground.

[Col. 0727D] But because the saints have resolved to live not for the wind but for grace, devoting themselves to virtue rather than empty glory, and not to the praise of human beings but to the Father of lights, they chose to set aside the most ornate elegance and follow what is necessary and useful instead. But enough of this. Let us continue the exposition we began.

### 47.

“The Lord is jealous,” and so forth. If you consider the whole sentence, the figure is anaphora, in which, at the end of the verse, he repeats “taking vengeance” three times through the beginnings of the clauses. But if you attend to the individual clauses, another figure, called hypozeuxis, appears, in which each sense has its own proper clause. This is also shown here, since the sense is concluded four or five times.

[Col. 0728A] A third figure, called catachresis, also intrudes: it assigns the name of one thing to another that does not possess a proper name of its own. For when fury, anger, and jealousy are attributed to God, who is impassible and unchangeable, this is said not properly but figuratively.

As to the matter itself, the rhetorical color is called frequentation. Frequentation occurs when matters scattered throughout an entire case or affair are gathered into one place, so that the speech may be weightier, sharper, or more accusatory. This is a forceful ornament, almost always necessary in conjectural argument, useful also in the other kinds of cases, and sometimes to be employed in every discourse.

[Col. 0728B] The rhetorical color apparent here is that the substance of the entire matter depends upon frequentation. These points we have distinguished [perhaps: discussed] scholastically; now let us return to the sequence of the exposition.

### 48.

The prophet therefore first sets forth the Lord’s jealousy, then vengeance in three forms, and afterward his anger and fury.

It is as though Nahum were saying to the Assyrian: “Will he abandon the bride to you, O Assyrian, whose jealous concern for her chastity rescued her from Egypt, the Red Sea, and the desert; against whose enemies multiple and most severe vengeance was inflicted; against whose foes God’s fury and indignation were kindled?”

Jealousy, according to the Apostle’s statement—“I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God, for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2)—refers to marriage. Vengeance refers to the destruction of enemies. The fury and anger of God refer to eternal punishment.

[Col. 0728C] He certainly gave this bride a betrothal-pledge in Abraham, but joined her to himself through the Law. On account of his zeal he afflicted Egypt with dreadful plagues, drowned the Egyptians, struck down countless ranks of enemies, fed her with the bread of heaven and with flesh in the desert, and then led her into the promised land.

This is the jealousy, though it appears threefold. If vengeance is referred to Israel itself, the first was for idolatry, the second for lust, and the third for gluttony. The first occurred when Israel fashioned the calf in the desert (Exod. XXXII, 4); the second when it avenged the crime committed against the Levite’s wife (Judg. XIX, 1 ff.; XX, 1 ff.); the third when Israel was struck down because of the sin of the sons of Eli (I Kings IV, 10 ff.).

Fury occurred when the ark was captured; anger, when Saul was rejected (ibid. XIII, 13 ff.; XV, 11 ff.). In the first vengeance twenty-five thousand fell; in the second, forty thousand men of Israel fell, while of Benjamin twenty-five thousand one hundred fell; in the third, four thousand men fell at first, and afterward, when the ark was captured, thirty thousand foot soldiers.

[Col. 0728D] If vengeance is understood of enemies, the first occurred in the drowning of the Egyptians (Exod. XIV, 27–28); the second in the killing of the thirty kings of the Canaanites and one additional king, and in the defeat of their peoples (Josh. XII, 1 ff.); the third in the very frequent subjugation of the Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, and others.

[Col. 0729A] The meaning is this: if the people beloved by God is handed over to you, do not boast against God. For if he has taken vengeance on it through so many and such great thousands, you will in no way escape his hands.

We have said these things historically; now let us refer them to the Church.

### 49.

The prophet, foreseeing that the Church would arise from the Gentiles and would suffer tribulations and pressures for the sake of justice, addresses her with consolation and terrifies her enemies, saying: “The Lord is jealous,” and so forth.

It is as though he were saying: “He bought you at a great price; he redeemed you with his precious blood; he called you freely from a brothel; he washed you with the water of baptism; he adorned you with the gifts of grace; and, in addition, he betrothed you as his bride and raised you to be a queen. If you [read *violaveris* (“you violate”), for the printed *violaverit*] violate his marriage, desiring a rival or the adulterer’s incestuous companionship, he, inflamed with jealousy, preserves the rights of marriage, excludes the injuries of procuring, and most severely avenges the crime of adultery.”

[Col. 0729B] ### 50.

Why, however, should vengeance be inflicted threefold? This is understood from the duties of marriage itself. There are indeed three goods of marriage: fidelity, the hope of offspring, and the unity of the sacrament. If she preserves these unviolated for her bridegroom, she hears herself commended in her bridegroom’s voice in the Song of Songs: “You are beautiful, my beloved, sweet and lovely, terrible as an army set in battle array” (Song VI, 3).

The bridegroom wishes the fidelity of the marriage bed to be firm, the offspring of the womb legitimate, and the chastity of the sacrament inviolate. Fidelity means that she must not mix Jewish faithlessness into the Gospel; legitimate offspring means that she must not follow the desire of the world; the chastity of the sacrament means that she must not slip into heresy, schisms, or idolatry.

[Col. 0729C] The Church’s fidelity is strengthened in the sacrament of baptism; offspring is produced through the preaching of truth; the sacrament consists in the spiritual union of unity. Fidelity means that she please Christ alone; offspring, that she bear children for him alone; the sacrament, that she remain one for one.

The Apostle’s statement refers to fidelity: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but her husband does” (I Cor. VII, 4). To offspring: “I want younger women to marry, bear children, and manage households” (I Tim. V, 14). To the sacrament: “I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not separate from her husband; but if she has separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband” (I Cor. VII, 10–11).

[Col. 0729D] She is therefore betrothed in water, made fruitful in blood, and joined in the Spirit. She is betrothed through the washing of baptism, made fruitful through the preaching of the Incarnation, and joined in the splendors of the saints and in blessed recompense.

By water I understand here, morally, the fullest sanctity of baptism; by blood, the newness of preaching; by Spirit, that spiritual unity by which God will be all in all (I Cor. XV, 28).

Otherwise, if the subject is faith, the Church is generated through three things, and these remain indivisible in baptism, so that none of them is separated from the connection with another. But, as blessed Ambrose tells us, they are one not by the nature of the same substance, but through the operation of the same mystery.

[Col. 0730A] For, as he says: “The Spirit recalls the mind, the water perfects it for washing, and the blood refers to the price. The Spirit makes us children of God through adoption, the water of the sacred font washes us, and the blood of the Lord redeemed us.”

[Note: Some copies read “redeems,” but Ambrose has “redeemed.”]

[Note: From here up to “blood,” this passage is absent from Ambrose.]

“These are the three that give testimony on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood” (I John V, 8). Through the sacrament of the Spirit we therefore receive one invisible testimony and another visible one.

### 51.

Through these three, then, the Church is generated and generates; she is washed and washes; she is liberated and liberates; she is renewed and renews.

In water the washing away of vices is signified; through blood redemption is made from the hand of the wicked; through the Spirit comes renewal of life. Since these three things have been bestowed upon the Church—in her birth, in her ministry, and in her power—whenever she transgresses in these matters, a threefold vengeance follows her.

[Col. 0730B] For, by the opposition of antithesis, she is stained with vices, captured by the enemy, and handed over to prison or crime for punishment in the present, and to Gehenna for punishment in the future.

Or, since there are three classes of enemies of the Church—the first without the sacrament of the Church; the second outside the Church but possessing the sacrament of the Church; the third possessing the sacrament of the Church and being within the Church—whenever the Church is oppressed by them, divine vengeance is poured out upon those same enemies. This is why the prophet places “taking vengeance” three times.

### 52.

Alternatively, the prophet addresses a faithful soul, admonishing it always to be concerned about its condition or its fall: about its condition, so that it may remain; about its fall, so that it may return. He shows how strictly the one who is ready to avenge every injury and every disobedience demands justice (II Cor. X, 6).

[Col. 0730C] He does this in five ways: either in relation to the punishment of an enemy, or the contempt of a servant, or the faithlessness of a hired laborer, or the disobedience of a son, or the irreverence of a spouse. For the Lord is served in four ways, and offended in five. One either obeys him with the disposition of a suppliant, or in hope of reward, or through the love proper to a son, or through the affection proper to a spouse. He is offended, however, in the five ways I have just set forth.

Since, therefore, the Lord is jealous for his bride and avenges irreverence toward marriage, he is “the jealous Lord.” Since he does not leave disobedience unpunished, there is added, “and taking vengeance.”

[Col. 0730D] [Note: The passage is corrupt.] The supplied text here reads: “gratiam, fraudem mercenarii, subsequitur” (“grace, the fraud of the hired laborer, follows”), but the syntax and precise sense are uncertain.

Against the contempt of the servant, there is added fourth: “the Lord takes vengeance on his enemies.”

If, according to the tradition of the teachers, we wish to distinguish between “enemy” and “adversary,” an enemy exists for a time, whereas an adversary remains perpetually in hatred; an enemy is accidental, an adversary natural. From an enemy, after victory, grace is expected; from an adversary, no trace of any pact is hoped for.

Hence a certain wise man says:

“From conquered enemies the name *hostia* (‘victim’) is derived. But for an adversary no entreaty is made under any law among the ancients.”

Hence fury is also added to enemies, while anger is assigned to adversaries. Fury is a brief agitation of the mind; anger is a grave and lasting indignation.

[Col. 0731A] Through fury, therefore, the conversion of enemies is intimated; through anger, the perpetual obstinacy of adversaries. Because the Church has enemies at one time whom at another she possesses as helpers; because she sees some now raging against her whom afterward she rejoices to see running about everywhere in her service; because she sees some now oppressing the poor whom afterward she sees devotedly distributing their resources; and because she sees some now attacking the truth whom afterward she sees as its most faithful preachers—the prophet, foreseeing this, added fury to enemies and placed anger before the obstinate.

### 53.

This distinction is clearly indicated in Isaiah, where the Lord says: “Ah! I shall be consoled over my enemies; I shall take vengeance on my adversaries” (Isa. I, 24).

You will find something similar in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “The kings of the earth and all the inhabitants of the world did not believe,” he says, “that the enemy and adversary would enter through the gates of Jerusalem” (Lam. IV, 12). The divine utterances contain many such passages.

[Col. 0731B] In Isaiah also the conversion of enemies is spoken of: “Those who slandered me will come to you and worship the traces of your feet” (Isa. LX, 14). Again, the same prophet says: “The inundation of camels will cover you; the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All those from Sheba will come, bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming praise to the Lord” (v. 6).

Again, in the same book: “Men of high rank and glory will then bow down to you; they will be yours, and peaceful kings will serve you” (Isa. XLV, 14). Again: “Every flock of Kedar will be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth will serve you” (LX, 7). Again: “In the houses where dragons and ostriches formerly lived, greenery of reed and rush will spring up” (XXXV, 7).

[Col. 0731C] In Job: “From the north smoke will proceed, and fearful praise to God” (Job XXXVII, 22). And in the Psalm: “From cursing and falsehood the end will be proclaimed.” Again, in the same Psalm: “They will return toward evening, and will suffer hunger like dogs, and will go around the city” (Ps. LVIII, 13, 15).

Again, in Job, the Lord says to him: “Will you mock him, namely Behemoth, as a bird, or bind him with your maidservants?” (Job XL, 24).

And in Obadiah, speaking of the devil under the person of Esau: “How they searched out Esau and investigated his hidden places! All the men of his covenant mocked you; they prevailed against you. All the men of your peace, who eat bread with you, will set an ambush beneath you” (Obad. I, 6–7).

And in Habakkuk, under the same figure: “Woe to him”—namely, to the devil—“who multiplies what is not his! How long does he weigh down thick mud against himself? Will not those who bite you rise up suddenly, and those who tear you apart be awakened? You will become their spoil” (Hab. II, 6–7).

[Col. 0731D] And in Zephaniah: “Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, from there my suppliants, the sons of my dispersed ones, will bring me an offering” (Zeph. III, 10).

Solomon, concerning the Church and the conversion of enemies, says: “You will be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards” (Song IV, 8).

The Savior, speaking to the Pharisees, asserts that this will happen: “Amen, I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. XXI, 31).

[Col. 0732A] The Lord is placed above each individual kind of affair because those who obey him neither through fear, nor reward, nor honor, nor affection are compelled to experience the Lord of vengeance.

The text continues.

### 54.

“The Lord is patient and great in strength, and cleansing, does not make [anyone] innocent” (Nah. I, 3).

As far as the wording is concerned, the figure is called polysyndeton. It is a statement chained together by many conjunctions, as here: “The Lord is patient, and great in strength, and cleansing,” and so forth.

As far as the meaning is concerned, because “Lord” refers to both clauses, it is shown to be hypozeuxis. The trope, that is, the mode of expression, is certainly judged by experts in the art to be catachresis: the name of one thing is assigned to another, namely patience is attributed to God, although it is properly foreign to him. For patience properly belongs to one who is accompanied by misery.

[Col. 0732B] By saying these things about the wording, we have satisfied the requirements of the art; let us also investigate the meanings hidden within it.

### 55.

First, therefore, this is said to the Assyrian, so that, because he flourishes for a time and prevails over many, he may not attribute this to his own arm but to divine judgment. By that judgment the iniquity of the Jewish people is purified and the misery of their adversaries increased, according to the saying: “Let the one who is righteous become more righteous, and let the one who is filthy become filthier still” (Rev. XXII, 11).

For the longer God’s patience is, the more severely the judge’s sentence strikes, according to the prophetic saying: “I have been silent, I have been still, I have been patient; like a woman in labor I shall cry out” (Isa. XLII, 14).

[Col. 0732C] The Lord therefore patiently permits one or the other to be afflicted and to afflict: he leads one back to innocence by cleansing him through patience, while the other, on account of the merit of his savagery, pays penalties worthy of his own injustice.

These things are said about the Assyrian. Let it now be explained how they are to be read [perhaps: understood] concerning the Church.

### 56.

“The Lord is patient,” and so forth.

[Note: Cicero, in his usual manner, expresses this more closely and elegantly: “Fortitude is the considered undertaking of dangers and endurance of labors. Its parts are magnificence, confidence, etc. Magnificence is the management and conduct of lofty matters with a certain broad and splendid conception of mind. Confidence, etc., as is nearly the case here.”]

[Col. 0732D] “Fortitude,” as Cicero says in the *Rhetorica* (Book II, no. 54), “is the pursuit of great and exalted things, contempt for lowly things, and endurance of labor with regard to usefulness.” Its parts are four: magnificence, confidence, patience, and perseverance.

Magnificence is the management of great and exalted things with a certain breadth of mind. Confidence is that by which the mind places much confidence in itself amid great and honorable matters, together with a sure hope. Patience is the voluntary and enduring bearing of difficult and arduous things for the sake of honor and usefulness. Perseverance is a stable and perpetual continuance in a course of action carefully considered.

We have prefaced all these matters because we have recognized that they will be necessary not only for the present subject but also for nearly all other tasks.

### 57.

There are therefore four things by which the Church is strengthened, tested, adorned, and preserved: commandments, scourges, spiritual gifts, and temptations. She is strengthened by commandments, tested by scourges, adorned by spiritual gifts, and preserved by temptations.

Confidence must therefore be exercised in commandments, patience displayed in scourges, magnificence possessed in spiritual gifts, and perseverance opposed to temptations.

[Col. 0733A] The prophet, foreseeing the future afflictions of the Church, the various gifts of grace, and her consolations, presents them in reverse order, whereas we shall set them forth in natural sequence.

Let the Lord be called “cleansing,” with reference first to commandments; “patient,” afterward, in scourges; then “magnificent,” in gifts; and finally “making innocent,” when one does not yield to temptations.

From the first arises confidence; from the second, patience; from the third, magnificence; from the fourth, innocence is acquired.

It must be understood that divine Scripture is accustomed to speak in such a way that the Lord is said to suffer or to do what he permits the elect to suffer or do, or what he permits to be suffered or done in them. Hence here too the Lord is called patient. The remaining description that follows is attributed to him quite properly.

### 58.

Alternatively, the passage contains four kinds of orders. The first is marital, the second virginal, the third solitary, and the fourth priestly.

[Col. 0733B] Among married people, therefore, he possesses patience; among virgins, magnificence; among solitaries, perseverance; and in the priestly order, confidence on behalf of all.

In the married state there is worldly concern; in the virginal state, angelic beauty; in the solitary state, the spiritual strength of warfare; in the priestly state, the heavenly model of innocence.

The married person thinks about the things of the world, how to please his wife (I Cor. VII, 33); the virginal person thinks about the things of God (v. 32), how to please the Creator; the solitary person considers how, by ascending from virtue to virtue, he may contemplate the Word who was in the beginning with God, with the living acuity of the mind; the priestly person considers how to present himself worthy before the eyes of the divine majesty and when it is fitting to minister the light of doctrine to the peoples.

Alternatively: “The Lord is patient” when he awaits sinners for repentance; “great in strength” when he justly punishes their impenitence; “cleansing” when he grants the grace of pardon to those who have turned back; “making innocent” when, in merciful goodness, he raises them to the heights of contemplation.

The text continues.

### 59 [Col. 0733D]

“The Lord is in the storm, and the whirlwind is his way, and the cloud is the dust of his feet” (Nahum 1:3).

Let us first attend to the letter, and afterward examine the inner meaning. First of all, it must be understood that the wording suffers an ellipsis, since the name of the third person and the nominative—which, being used intransitively, requires connection with something—are placed absolutely; and a reference is made in it when no antecedent has preceded to which the expression can refer. In saying this, I do not condemn the meaning, nor do I in any way criticize the prophetic grace, when I say that its expression is less grammatical. The prophet did not greatly concern himself with the business of grammatical form, but, thirsting for the joy of the vision, rendered obedience to the Spirit speaking inwardly.

Hence blessed Gregory says: “Far be it that the words of the heavenly oracle should be confined beneath Donatus’s rules. For the Spirit who is subject to the prophets, and who has spoken in them, demands purity of obedience, not polish of language or urbane eloquence.”

Let the construction therefore be corrected, and let it be expressed without fault in this way: “The Lord dwells in the storm, and in the whirlwind,” or “he walks in them,” or something of this sort; and then what follows is appropriate: “and in the storm and whirlwind are his ways.” The trope called *catachresis* is also employed in this passage, as above in the others.

### 60 [Cols. 0734A–B]

Once the grammatical matter has been completed, let the passage first be interpreted historically as referring to the Assyrian. Its meaning is therefore this: By his just judgment the Lord permits the raging Assyrian to commit great and countless acts of cruelty, and, as though he were a storm and whirlwind, to crush everything as he rushes about indiscriminately. But the Lord himself, who has loosened the reins of his fury, presides over him with the authority of omnipotence—an incomprehensible praise of justice—and restrains the reins of his wickedness. For in this savagery the justice of the one who presides is fulfilled: the Assyrian, although acting from an evil will, has been given official power for the purpose of judgment, so that through it he may oppress the servant, afflict the hired laborer, instruct and correct the son, overthrow the adversary, and make the just person more just and the filthy person filthier.

This also must be understood: from the beginning of the prophet up to the words, “If they are complete, and likewise numerous,” etc. (Nahum 1:12), everything is understood of the Assyrian. His wickedness is clearly indicated throughout, although the omnipotence of the one who presides mercifully moderates it.

So much concerning the Assyrian. Now let the interpretation be referred to the Church.

### 61 [Cols. 0734B–D]

There are therefore three storms of the Church and three whirlwinds belonging to her, differing according to the divisions of time. The first was that of the pagans, the second that of the heretics, and the third that of false Christians. The first tore the bodies of the apostles and martyrs; the second attempted to overthrow the bonds of the apostolic faith; the third strives daily to corrupt the forms of moral conduct.

The pagans, persecuting the faithful, believed that they were rendering service to God (John 16:2). The heretics, swollen with pride and attacking the Church, endeavored to form conventicles for themselves by preaching heretical faithlessness. False Christians, however, seeking what is their own and not what belongs to Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21), break the laws of the Church, disturb the customs of justice, and follow their own desires.

Therefore David, foreseeing these storms in the person of the Church, prays that they may arise successively, so that her members may not return to idolatry, may not be led astray into following heretical faithlessness, and may not place worldly desire before the justice of faith. He says:

“Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me up, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Psalm 68:16).

The waters are peoples, as John says in the Apocalypse (Revelation 17:15). He therefore prays that the sordid desire of a carnal people may not oppress her, that the dark subtlety of the depths of vices may not cast her down, that wickedness may not seize her into the pit and blind impiety block her return from the depth of ignorance.

The first storm consists of bodily punishments, the second of poisonous words, and the third of carnal conduct. The first labors to empty the Godhead of its omnipotence; the second strives to corrupt the integrity of faith; the third attempts to overthrow ordered charity.

### 62 [Col. 0735A]

Therefore Isaiah, foreseeing that many would depart from the path of faith and from purity of spirit, says:

“Fear, and the pit, and the snare are upon you, inhabitant of the earth” (Isaiah 24:17).

Fear, that is, of idolatry; the pit, of heretical faithlessness; the snare, of carnal desire. Fear arises from an injury done to the Godhead; the pit is dug by proud assailants of the truth; the snare holds the servants of unclean desire.

But the order of the successive wickedness is indicated by the very order of the words. For he continues:

“And it shall be that whoever flees from the sound of fear will fall into the pit, and whoever escapes from the pit will be caught in the snare” (Isaiah 24:18).

Many rejected the filth of idolatry who nevertheless suffered shipwreck in the storm of heresy. Many also escaped this, whom the flood of desire swallowed up.

The first whirlwind was before the face of the judge, the second in the conflict of battle, and the third in the assault of filthy desire. The first occurred when a Catholic was condemned by the judge; the second when a Catholic was falsely denounced by heretics; the third when carnal persons and subjects forcibly and violently wrest from saints and prelates permission to obey themselves and the flesh [read: “themselves”].

### 63 [Cols. 0735B–D]

Concerning these whirlwinds Isaiah says:

“Like whirlwinds coming from the south, it comes from the desert, from a dreadful land. A harsh vision was announced to me” (Isaiah 21:1–2).

A harsh vision, therefore, had been announced to him who foresaw storms and the aforementioned whirlwinds successively rising against the unity, purity, and charity of the Church from idolatry, heretical faithlessness, and worldly desire.

A harsh vision, I say, in which unity suffers division, the business of faith slips away, and charity endures shipwreck.

In the first whirlwind and storm are the Lord’s ways: truth in confession, steadfastness in suffering, and devotion in thanksgiving. Truth consists in confessing and boldly proclaiming the majesty of the one and supreme Godhead; steadfastness, in patiently enduring blows for the cause of truth; thanksgiving, in joyfully returning the spirit to heaven.

Three ways of departure lie before them. The first is soundness of faith, the second clarity of knowledge, and the third freedom of spirit. Through the first, grace is obtained from God; through the second, the enemy’s cunning is foreseen; through the third, the audacity of his faithlessness is overthrown. Through the first affection is stirred; through the second understanding is illuminated; through the third action is brought to completion.

The first excludes the error of faithlessness; the second, the darkness of ignorance; the third, the sluggishness of spirit and the torpor of negligence. By the first the sick person is healed; by the second the blind person is illuminated; by the third the servant is endowed with freedom.

By the first infirmity is expelled, by the second ignorance, and by the third the practice of sin. The Son heals, the Spirit illuminates, and the Father brings to completion. Doctrine heals, knowledge illuminates, and justice perfects. The Son heals through the purity of faith; the Spirit illuminates through the brightness of heavenly things; the Father brings to completion through eternal happiness.

In saying this, I do not divide the works of the Trinity, which I certainly affirm to be the same, but I speak in this way so that the distinction of the persons may be discerned in the divine gifts and operation.

In the first and second ways of the Lord there is also a threefold division. The first is voluntary mortification, the second perfect humility, and the third perfected charity. The first circumcises the action of the flesh, the second ennobles the mind, and the third orders the affections.

Through the first they return from Egypt; through the second they come from Babylon; through the third they flee the disaster of Rome. For Egypt signifies lust, drunkenness, and gluttony; Babylon, the utterly vain confusion of the senses; Rome, which is interpreted as “loftiness” or “exaltation,” signifies pride.

### 64 [Cols. 0736A–C]

Thus we are admonished by the voice of John the apostle to flee the storms and whirlwinds of this world by these ways and return to our homeland. He says:

“If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, or the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life. These are not from the Father, but from the devil” (1 John 2:15–16).

Through the first way, therefore, the sober and chaste return; through the second, the honorable and tranquil; through the third, the devout and perfect.

These things may also be referred to Christ, the head of the Church, and a storm and whirlwind may be found in his persecution and passion. Concerning this storm the Psalmist says:

“Thus you will pursue them in your storm, and in your anger you will trouble them” (Psalm 82:16).

The Lord pursued the Jews in his storm, because, while he endured from them the marks of suffering, he justly took away from them knowledge of the law and the gifts of the virtues. He pursued them in his storm because, while he endured human things from them, he not unjustly took divine things away from them.

He continues: “And in your anger you will trouble them.”

The Lord troubles some in anger and others in mercy. He troubles mercifully those whom he recalls from hell through scourges; in anger, those whom he permits to be scourged forever by a just judgment. He troubles mercifully by piercing them with compunction for their sins; in anger, by leaving them in the shipwreck of vices and in their filth.

Mercifully he sends inwardly the whirlwind of contrition and repentance; without mercy, he justly permits them to be led into the darkness of shadows and hell.

Of the first whirlwind it is said:

“The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm 33:8).

Of the second:

“Indignation and anger and tribulation through evil angels” (Psalm 77:49).

The Lord’s storm was present when he was harassed by the Jewish people; the whirlwind was present when the disciple who betrayed the pious teacher with a feigned kiss said, “Hail, Rabbi” (Matthew 26:47). The storm was present when he was scourged by the Romans (Matthew 27:26); the whirlwind, when the Jewish crowd shouted, “Crucify, crucify!” (Luke 23:21). The storm was in the garden near the estate of Gethsemane; the whirlwind, when he was led before the governor. The storm was before the cross; the whirlwind, before the judge.

### 65 [Cols. 0736D–0737C]

Yet his way through these things was threefold: truth, gentleness, and justice. The Psalmist clearly testifies to this, saying:

“Because of truth and gentleness and justice, your right hand will lead you wondrously” (Psalm 44:5).

He always maintained truth in preaching, gentleness in suffering, and justice in action. He was truthful in preaching new things; gentle in enduring human things; just in performing divine things. He taught the truth of knowledge, the gentleness of repentance, and the works of justice. Truth in confession, gentleness in interpretation, and justice in love.

First, one is to declare one’s iniquities so as to be justified; second, to receive the discipline of the Father calmly and gently when one is tested; third, to love what ought justly to be loved, according to the saying: “You shall pursue precisely what is just” (Deuteronomy 16:20).

He taught the truth of the natural law, the justice of the written law, and the gentleness of the Gospel. He taught truth, by which each person would know himself; gentleness, by which one would endure one’s neighbor; justice, by which one would worship God.

He taught the truth of his divinity, the gentleness of his humanity, and the justice of the second property of both.

Alternatively: he displayed truth in the universal examination of all; gentleness in the blessed consolation of the elect; justice in the most just condemnation of the reprobate.

Alternatively: he displayed the truth of his divinity by revealing it in judgment; the gentleness of his labor by commanding the impious; justice by rendering to each person what belonged to that person.

Because of these three things, therefore, his right hand led him wondrously, since the power of the Godhead made him free from every evil and full of every good, united him to itself in the identity of one person, made him the bridegroom of the Church and the craftsman of grace, made him judge of the whole world, and was pleased that he should become a participant in that same Godhead and glory.

Because of these three things his right hand led him wondrously: God, because he is truthful, sealed him (John 3:33); made him beautiful beyond the sons of men (Psalm 44:3, 8); and anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions. In him the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily (Colossians 2:9); to him the Father gave the Spirit without measure (John 3:34).

He wondrously created him in the Virgin’s womb; wondrously preserved him in Egypt, at sea, in the temple, on the cross, and in the tomb; wondrously glorified him in the resurrection; and, still more wondrously, exalted him to the honor and glory of that same blessedness.

The Lord’s way in storm and whirlwind was therefore threefold. Although he drank from the torrent on the way (Psalm 109:7), he became the head of the Church and immediately deserved to be exalted, because the world—or its prince—had nothing in him (John 14:30), and therefore could neither hold him nor have any claim over him.

These same matters may also be examined morally and appropriately referred to the soul that longs for heavenly things and ascends inwardly from virtue to virtue.

### 66 [Cols. 0737C–0738A]

There are therefore four storms of the soul and four whirlwinds belonging to it. The first is that of vices, the second of affairs, the third of temptations, and the fourth of useful affections. The first is of anger, the second of misery, the third of justice, and the fourth of grace.

The first hails down the flower of the virtues. The second casts down the honor of conscience. The third drives away the most sweet fragrance of contemplation. The fourth ardently carries one onward to love of heavenly things.

The first comes from the devil, the second from the world, the third from the debt of misery, and the fourth from God. The first annihilates the holiness of religion; the second disturbs the serenity of conscience; the third drives away the sweetness of the most divine fragrance; the fourth raises one to angelic purity.

The first is therefore the storm of divine indignation, the second of dispensation, the third of testing, and the fourth of love. The first brings poverty through spiritual hunger; the second lays waste spiritual vineyards and trees; the third corrupts the bridegroom’s garden and destroys the sweetness of spices; the fourth repairs every fall and transfers the soul to the brightness of heavenly things.

Thus Job, in the hope of the fallen, the consolation of the miserable, the exhortation of the tempted, and the glory of the just, says:

“You will laugh at devastation and famine, and you will not fear calamity when it comes. And you will know that your tabernacle is at peace, and, when you visit your appearance, you will not sin” (Job 5:21 ff.).

The first corrupts the action of justice; the second excludes the understanding from innocence; the third defiles the affection of wisdom; the fourth illuminates the intellect with the immortal light of wisdom.

The ways of the first are pure confession and manly repentance; of the second, contempt of the world and the solitary life; of the third, devout compunction and purity of mind; of the fourth, the silence of a purified soul and the joy of the bridegroom.

### 67 [Cols. 0738A–0739A]

But since the prophet asserts that the Lord’s ways are in the storm, not in the storms (Nahum 1:3), he speaks especially of the fourth, as may be understood.

Concerning it we read plainly in the Book of Kings. For he says:

“Elijah stood at the entrance of the cave, and behold, the spirit of the Lord passed by, overturning mountains and crushing rocks; and after the spirit, an earthquake—but the Lord was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake, a fire—but the Lord was not in the fire; and after the fire, the sound of a gentle breeze. There was the Lord” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19:11 ff.).

By the passing spirit, performing the things mentioned above, the storm of the soul is signified—that is, the bitter but useful contrition of sinners. By the earthquake, devout compunction of mind; by the fire, fervent and ordered love; by the silence, the most secret infusion of blessed contemplation.

Yet the Lord is said to be in none of the things mentioned above. He is perhaps asserted to be in the sound of the breeze, because although the mind, thoroughly pierced with compunction for its sins and devoted to the commandments, forgets what lies behind and stretches toward what lies ahead, courageously ascends from virtue to virtue, and ardently snatches itself toward sublime things, nevertheless, while caring for itself and remaining occupied with its own condition, it recognizes itself as a creature. [Note: Col. 0737D: The passage is corrupt.] Yet, because it cannot altogether transcend the condition of a creature, it falls short of the inmost clarity of contemplation, in which the presence of unbounded light is in some measure known.

For this undertaking is not accomplished by human reasoning, when the mind is inwardly flooded with divine anointing. Until the bounded mind transcends all things, it does not attain the secret joys of the One who transcends everything. Until the region of the third heaven is transcended, the pleasantness of paradise and the heavenly anointing are not experienced.

Hence Isaiah says:

“I saw the Lord seated upon a throne, lofty and raised up; and the things beneath him filled the temple” (Isaiah 6:1).

The throne is the mind withdrawn from earthly actions; lofty, when adorned with pure affections; raised up, when exalted by divine understanding and angelic perceptions.

The throne is the mind through the purpose of religion; lofty through the rigor of mortification; raised up through the virtue of love. The throne is the mind through contempt for the visible things of the world; lofty through contempt for its own visible things; raised up through transcending the invisible things of the soul.

The throne is the mind through knowledge of itself; lofty through devout and fervent love; raised up through subtle inquiry into heavenly mysteries.

Yet the Lord sits above these things; he does not dwell in them. For the mind ordered by these morals, devoted to these pursuits, and adorned with these virtues pleases him; yet through these things he in no way discloses to it the presence of his blessedness, nor unites it to himself through the grace of contemplation.

But when it has raised itself above the lofty and exalted throne, trampling underfoot the darkness of the world and surpassing the narrow limits of human knowledge, it is immediately lifted up to immortal riches.

Through the eminence of contemplation it is brought into the wine-cellar. Then it hears words that it is not permitted a human being to speak—ineffable words—and, because of the excessive sweetness of its bridegroom, it even grows weary of angelic conversations.

Hence we read in the psalm:

“Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; and Ephraim is the support of my head. Judah is my king” (Psalm 59:9).

### 68 [Cols. 0739A–B]

He named four things through which he wished to signify four spiritual degrees of advancement. Judah, who is placed last in the order of the psalm, is naturally first in the order of right living. Gilead is second, Manasseh third, and Ephraim fourth.

Judah is interpreted as “confession,” Gilead as “heap of testimony,” Manasseh as “forgetfulness,” and Ephraim as “fruitfulness.”

Confession is threefold. The first is confession of faith, the second of sin, and the third of joy. First a person believes rightly; second, lives well; third, receives the reward of faith and works.

The first hands over to the citizens of the homeland the bonds of their country; the second mercifully cares for the wounds of the fallen in the conflict of vices; the third bestows most welcome rewards upon those who struggle for their wages.

Of the first it is written in the Gospel:

“Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess before my Father” (Matthew 10:32).

Of the second Solomon says:

“Whoever conceals his crimes will not prosper, but whoever confesses them will be justified” (Proverbs 28:13).

Of the third the Psalmist says in the person of the soul exulting in hope of heavenly things:

“A sound of rejoicing and confession, the voice of one feasting” (Psalm 41:5).

The first led the martyrs to glory; the second draws sinners to pardon; the third brings combatants to the joy of the prize.

### 69 [Cols. 0739C–D]

Judah is therefore called “king of God,” because no one enters life except by the way of faith or through the truth of confession.

Judah is rightly called king, therefore, because he precedes confessors, goes before sinners, and rewards conquerors. Truly he is king, by whose aid, counsel, and strength idolatry is crushed, heretical faithlessness is defeated, the vanity and concupiscence of the world are trampled underfoot, the happiness of the kingdom is tasted in advance, and glory is possessed.

Judah therefore signifies confession; Gilead, compunction of mind; Manasseh, love strong as death (Song of Songs 8:6); Ephraim, the blessed contemplation of heavenly things.

Judah, Gilead, and Manasseh serve appropriately and please the Lord; but Ephraim’s fruit shines above all. Although he highly esteems and more closely embraces the lamentations of repentance, works of mercy, tears of piety, and vows of charity, his blessed presence is nevertheless not grasped in these things. But Ephraim, “his head,” received the presence of divinity—that is, when the mind, exalted by God, is happily united to its bridegroom and conceives from him the fruit of the Spirit.

### 70 [Cols. 0740A–B]

The first three receive great approval, but Ephraim alone becomes the support (*susceptio*) of the head, because although the signs of confession rightly please him, although the desires of compunction give off a sweet fragrance, and although the sighs of love burn with nectarous fragrance, the fruits that are especially heavenly open the joys of secret contemplation to the bride.

Mary is sought, but Martha is tolerated; Rachel is loved, but Leah gives birth. Pure Judah of the mouth, or sound confession of faith, therefore pleases; Gilead also pleases, the devotion of a cleansed mind; and the love that forgets what lies behind, strong as death, is cherished.

But above all, intellectual fruitfulness is sought and required, in which truth is contemplated, in which the bride, divinely made fruitful by the Spirit, beholds the Word with God in the beginning. This is truly the reception of the head.

Hence Solomon says in the Song of Songs:

“There are sixty queens and eighty concubines. My dove, my bride, my undefiled one, is one” (Song of Songs 6:7–8).

Hence the Savior says in the Gospel:

“Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. Mary has chosen the best part, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:41–42).

What is signified in the Book of Kings by the spirit, the earthquake, the fire, and the sound of the breeze is signified in Isaiah by the lofty and raised-up throne and the height of the Lord’s seat; and in the psalm it is signified by Judah, Gilead, Manasseh, and Ephraim, who is called the reception of the head.

We have spoken of these matters concerning the fourth storm of the soul, after the agreeable tempering of the air has been restored, after the serene face of heaven has returned, after complete happiness and perfect rest have been granted to the soul.

### 71 [Cols. 0740B–C]

We have also said that there are four whirlwinds of the soul. The first is the sudden oppression of the just; the second, the unforeseen assault of affairs; the third, the momentary invasion of temptations; the fourth, the sudden and violent disturbance of the soul arising from various preceding causes.

The storm of vices follows the first whirlwind; and the calamity of punishments follows the storm. The storm of anxieties follows the second, and the flood of crimes succeeds it. The storm of temptations precedes the third; tranquility of conscience and the grace of gifts follow it. After the fourth comes the storm of righteous affections, followed by the pleasantness of ordered love and the joyful serenity of divine contemplation.

### 72 [Cols. 0740C–D]

“And the cloud is the dust of his feet” (Nahum 1:3).

Just as the interpretation of the preceding material was fourfold, so what follows must be examined in four ways.

First, let it be read as referring to the Assyrian. It is as though he were saying: The Lord deigned to exercise his judgments over many through the Assyrian. His power was so great, the multitude of peoples so great, the rich abundance of diverse things so great, and confidence in his strong men so plentiful that, when the camps were moved for the sake of fortune or the outcome of war, the dust of his feet rose up and, like a whirlwind circling the region, turned into clouds, bringing over them darkness that shut out the light, while the sun stood in the middle of the sky.

Thus Job speaks historically of the same Assyrian:

“From the north comes smoke, and praise terrible to God” (Job 37:22).

And Isaiah says:

“Like whirlwinds coming from the south, it comes from the desert, from a dreadful land. A harsh vision was announced to me” (Isaiah 21:1–2).

But this is the historical interpretation. Allegorically, however, the prophets were the Savior’s feet, who through their utterances brought him to us incarnate at the end of the ages.

### 73

The Psalmist presented him to us, saying: “In the sun he placed his tabernacle, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. XVIII, 6). Likewise the same author: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI, 5). Hence Isaiah: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII, 14). Again, in the same book: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior” (ibid. XLV, 8). Jeremiah also says: “The Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI, 22). Again, in the same book: “This is he who devised every way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his child and to Israel his chosen one. After this he appeared upon the earth and lived among human beings” (Bar. III, 37).

Ezekiel, under the person of the Savior, sees a man clothed in linen measuring the layout of the temple (Ezek. XL, 3). [Col. 0741A] Again, under the names of the prince and the gate, he speaks of the Savior and his virgin mother, saying: “This gate shall be closed for the prince. For the Lord God himself shall enter through it, and he shall depart through it” (ibid. XLIV, 2). [Col. 0741B]

Daniel likewise, concerning his incarnation: “I was watching in the vision of the night, and behold, one like a Son of Man was coming with the clouds of heaven; he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power, honor, and a kingdom. And all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His power is an eternal power that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII, 13 ff.). Again, the same author: “Seventy weeks have been shortened for your people and your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may come to an end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (ibid. IX, 24). [Col. 0741C]

Hosea, concerning the Savior’s birth and passion, says: “Israel was a child, and I loved him; from Egypt I called my son.” Again, the same author: “I was like a nurse to Ephraim; I carried them in my arms, and they did not know that I was caring for them. In the cords of Adam I will draw them, in the bonds of love; and I shall be like one lifting a yoke from their jaws. And I bent down to him so that he might eat” (Hos. XI, 1, 3 ff.).

Joel also, concerning his birth and the sending of the Holy Spirit, says: “Now, sons of Zion, rejoice and be glad in the Lord your God, because he has given you a teacher of righteousness, and he will cause the early and the latter rain to descend upon you as at the beginning” (Joel II, 23). [Col. 0741D] Again, in the same book: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (v. 28). Again, in the same book, concerning the apostles’ preaching: “On that day the mountains shall drip sweetness, the hills shall flow with milk, and through all the channels of Judah the waters shall go; a fountain shall come forth from the house of the Lord and shall water the torrent of thorns” (Joel III, 18).

Amos, concerning the same one’s birth and passion, and the apostles’ preaching, says: “On that day I will raise up the tabernacle of David; I will rebuild the breaches of its walls, restore what has collapsed, and rebuild it as in ancient days” (Amos IX, 11). Concerning the passion: “On that day the sun shall set at midday, and I will make the earth dark in the daytime of light; I will make it like the mourning for an only-begotten son, and like a bitter day” (Amos VIII, 9–10). [Col. 0742A] Concerning the preaching: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when the plowman shall overtake the reaper and the treader of grapes the sower of seed. The mountains shall drip sweetness, and all the hills shall be cultivated” (ibid. IX, 13).

Obadiah speaks of the same one as follows: “In Mount Zion there shall be salvation, and it shall be holy” (Obad. 17).

Jonah bore the figure of the Savior both in his deeds and in his words. In his deeds, as the Savior testifies in the Gospel, saying: “Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matt. XII, 40). In another way: “Jonah rejoices while the ivy is green; Nineveh is in danger. When the gourd withers, the prophet is saddened, while the beautiful city is saved” (Jon. IV, 6 ff.).

Micah also speaks concerning the Virgin’s childbirth, the Savior’s birth, the privilege of grace, the dignity of power, the insult of the passion, and the power of preaching. Concerning the childbirth and birth: [Col. 0742B]

“And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are little among the thousands of Judah; from you there shall go forth for me one who shall be ruler in Israel. His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity. Therefore he shall give them up until the time when she who is in labor shall give birth” (Mic. V, 2–3).

Concerning the privilege of grace and the power of might:

“And this one shall be peace: when the Assyrian comes into your land and treads upon our houses, we shall raise up against him seven shepherds and eight principal men” (v. 5).

Concerning the power of preaching:

“And they shall pasture the land of Assyria with the sword and the land of Nimrod with their spears” (v. 6).

Concerning the insult of the passion:

“Now you shall be laid waste, daughter of the robber; they have laid siege against us; with a rod they have struck the cheek of the judge of Israel” (v. 1).

Nahum bears the figure of the Savior both by office and by name: by office, that of advocate; by name, that of consoler. For Nahum is said to mean “consoler,” while Helchaeseus is interpreted as “advocate.” [Col. 0742C] He says:

“Behold, upon the mountains are the feet of the one who evangelizes and announces peace. Celebrate your festivals, Judah, and fulfill your vows, because Belial shall no longer pass through you; he has been utterly destroyed” (Nah. I, 15).

“He has gone up who scatters before you, who guards the siege. Observe the road, strengthen your loins, and greatly fortify your power” (ibid. II, 1). [Col. 0742D]

Habakkuk speaks concerning the same one’s birth and passion and the apostles’ preaching. Concerning his birth:

“Write the vision; explain it upon tablets, so that the one who reads it may run, because the vision is still for a distant time, and it shall appear at the end and shall not lie. If it delays, wait for it, because when it comes, it shall come, and it shall not be late” (Hab. II, 2–3).

Again: “You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ” (ibid. III, 13).

Concerning the passion:

“His brightness shall be like light; horns are in his hands. There his strength is hidden” (ibid. IV, 5).

Again, threatening the Jewish people concerning the same matter:

“Because you have plundered many nations, those who remain of the peoples shall plunder you, because of the blood of a man and the iniquity of the land” (ibid. II, 8).

Concerning the office of preaching:

“You who ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (ibid. III, 8).

Zephaniah speaks concerning the birth:
