“Sing praise,” he says, “daughter of Zion; shout aloud, Israel; rejoice and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. The Lord, the King of Israel, is in your midst; you shall fear evil no longer. On that day it shall be said: ‘Jerusalem, do not fear; Zion, let not your hands be weakened. The Lord your God is in your midst; he himself, the Mighty One, shall save’” (Zeph. III, 14 ff.). [Col. 0743A]

The same author speaks concerning the resurrection: “Wait for me on the day of my resurrection in the future, because my judgment is to gather the nations and assemble the kingdoms” (v. 8).

Haggai speaks concerning the same one’s birth and the glorious establishment of the Church:

“Yet a little while,” says the Lord, “and I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land. I will shake all the nations, and the Desired One of all nations shall come; and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts. The glory of this last house shall be greater than that of the first, says the Lord” (Hag. II, 7 ff.).

Zechariah speaks concerning the birth:

“Rejoice greatly,” he says, “daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king is coming to you, just and saving, and he himself is poor. He shall ride upon a donkey and upon a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zech. IX, 9). [Col. 0743B]

The same author speaks concerning the passion: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (v. 11).

Again, in the person of one questioning the Savior concerning the same matter: “What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?” And he shall say to them: “With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me” (ibid. XIII, 6).

Again: “Sword, arise against my shepherd and against the man joined to me” (v. 7).

Concerning the Savior’s personal preaching and the devoted conversion of the nations to him:

“In those days ten men from every language of the nations shall seize the hem of a Jewish man’s garment, saying: ‘We shall go with you, for we have heard that God is with you’” (ibid. VIII, 23).

Again, concerning the passion: “I saw by night, and behold, a man riding upon a red horse; and he was standing among the myrtles that were in the depths” (ibid. I, 8 ff.). [Col. 0743C]

Concerning the sending of preachers:

“And after him were red, dappled, and white horses. And I said: ‘Who are these, my lord?’ And he answered: ‘These are the ones whom the Lord sent to walk throughout the earth.’ They answered: ‘We have walked throughout the earth.’ And behold, all the earth is inhabited and at rest.”

Concerning the Church’s expansion:

“My cities shall yet overflow with good things; and the Lord shall comfort Zion and shall again choose Jerusalem” (v. 17).

Again: “Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls, because of the multitude of human beings and beasts in her midst. And I shall be,” says the Lord, “a wall of fire around her, and I shall be her glory in the midst” (ibid. II, 4–5). [Col. 0743D]

These things concern the calling of the Jews. Again, concerning their rejection and the seeking of the nations:

“After the glory,” he says, “he sent me to the nations; they have plundered us” (v. 8).

Again: “Sing praise, daughter of Zion, and rejoice, because behold, I am coming and I shall dwell in your midst, says the Lord. Many nations shall join themselves to the Lord on that day, and they shall be my people” (v. 10–11).

Concerning the diversity of graces bestowed upon the Church:

“Old women and old men shall yet dwell in the streets of Jerusalem; and each man shall have his staff in his hand because of the multitude of his days. The streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing” (ibid. VIII, 4–5).

Again: “Behold, I will save my people from the land of the east and from the land of the setting sun; I will bring them here, and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem” (v. 8–9).

Again, concerning the final calling of the Jews:

“But now I shall not act toward the remnant of this people as in former days, says the Lord; rather, the seed shall be of peace. And just as you were a curse among the nations, house of Judah and house of Israel, so I shall save you, and you shall be a blessing” (Zech. VIII, 11 ff.). [Col. 0744A]

Concerning the Church’s confidence in the Lord and its supplication for the needs of the peoples:

“Virgins, ask rain from the Lord in the latter season, and the Lord will make snow and snow-rain. From him comes the corner, from him the peg, from him the battle-bow; from him every exactor goes forth together” (ibid. X, 1, 4).

Again, concerning the Savior’s birth and the fullness of graces in him:

“Behold,” he says, “I shall bring my servant, the East. For behold, the stone that I have placed before Jesus: upon one stone are seven eyes” (ibid. III, 8–9).

Concerning the example of his works and the performance of miracles:

“Behold, I shall carve its sculpture,” says the Lord, “and I shall remove the iniquity of that land on that day” (v. 9). [Col. 0744B]

Malachi speaks thus concerning the same Savior’s birth:

“For you who fear God, the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings” (Mal. IV, 2).

Concerning the glory and exultation of believers:

“You shall go forth and leap like calves from the herd, and you shall trample the wicked when they have become ashes beneath the soles of your feet, says the Lord of hosts” (v. 3).

Again: “Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face; and immediately the ruler whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (ibid. III, 1).

Again, in the same book, the Father speaking concerning the Son:

“My covenant,” he says, “was with him, a covenant of life and peace; I gave him reverence, and he revered me, and he was afraid before my name. The light of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found upon his lips. He walked with me in peace and equity, and he turned many away from iniquity” (ibid. II, 5–6). [Col. 0744C]

### 74

Thus, indeed thus, these feet brought the Savior of the world to us, bearing his figure personally through many evidences of deeds and prophesying him through mystical utterances. Hence those aforementioned feet are said to be like bronze, both because of the beauty of wisdom and because of the brilliance of the whirlwind of eloquence (Rev. I, 15; II, 18). [Col. 0744D]

For bronze is more sonorous than all other metals; it has the appearance of gold, but is far inferior to it. The saints who preceded the coming of Jesus Christ cried out longer and anxiously to those who followed them, while living in this age soberly, justly, and devoutly, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God (Tit. II, 12–13). Although they lived perfectly according to the quality of their times, they were all servants, yet none of them was Lord; one master transcendent above the heavens existed for all, and each was a disciple.

Hence Job says: “Behold, God is greater than our knowledge; none is like him among legislators” (Job XXXVI, 26). From this the Apostle says: “Moses indeed was faithful as a servant, for a testimony to the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son over his own house” (Heb. III, 5–6).

They possessed the appearance of gold, but a reality far different from it. For although they were sincere in heart, temperate in speech, free in the flesh, most holy in faith, firm in hope, rooted in charity, serving necessity, pursuing usefulness, and attending to uprightness, nevertheless none of them was entirely free from sin. None of them could become “a solitary sparrow on the housetop”; none of them could become “free among the dead” (Ps. CI, 8); no one was able to lay down his soul (Ps. LXXXVII, 6) and take it up again (John X, 18). [Col. 0745A]

Hence Job says: “Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast, and he found perversity in his angels; how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is earthly—they shall be consumed like a moth” (Job IV, 18–19). Again, in the same book: “Can a human being be compared with God, even if he possesses perfect knowledge?” (ibid. XXII, 2). Again, the same author in the same book: “Can a human being be justified when compared with God, or can one born of a woman appear clean? Behold, the moon does not shine and the stars are not clean in his sight; how much more is a human being corruption, and the son of man a worm?” (ibid. XXV, 4 ff.).

Therefore the feet of the Lord are dust because of humility of conscience, and clouds because of the obscurity of eloquence. They are dust in thinking humbly of themselves; clouds in covering heavenly mysteries with the veil of the letter: humble in life, obscure in doctrine. They are dust so that they may please; clouds lest they give pearls to swine. In another way: [Col. 0745B]

### 75

“Clouds are the dust of his feet” (Nah. I, 3). Dust is earthly understanding; cloud is passing obscurity. When the sun shines, the clouds are dispersed. Therefore the clouds are the dust of the Lord’s feet, because when the sun of righteousness shone—namely, when Christ preached and performed miracles—earthly understanding was trampled down, and spiritual and mystical knowledge was disclosed.

Hence it is written in the Psalm: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII, 12). He made darkness his hiding place because, covered beneath the veil of the prophets’ letter, he remained hidden for a long time. Hence it follows: “Dark water in the clouds of the air,” because knowledge in the prophets is obscure. It follows: “Before the brightness in his presence the clouds passed away” (v. 13). For while the Savior performed miracles, and clearly showed that the enigmas of the prophets foretold concerning him had been fulfilled in him, the dust of the historical sense immediately vanished like a cloud. [Col. 0745C] Spiritual light shone inwardly, and when the veil had been removed, the Holy of Holies was revealed.

Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “O foolish ones,” he says, “and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer, rise on the third day, and so enter into his glory?” And beginning from Moses and the prophets, he interpreted the Scriptures for them (Luke XXIV, 52 ff.).

Therefore the clouds are the dust of the Lord’s feet. The shadow flees when brightness returns; the figure passes when the truth is present. In another way: [Col. 0745D]

### 76

The apostles may be signified by the Lord’s feet, concerning whom it is written in Isaiah: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things!” (Isa. LIII, 1). Again, elsewhere concerning the same men: “Those who draw near to his feet shall receive from his teaching” (Deut. XXXIII, 3). [Col. 0746A]

These, then, were the Lord’s feet, who brought him through preaching throughout the whole world. For Peter brought him to Rome, Andrew to Achaea, John to Asia, Philip to Gaul [Note: If you prefer, understand “Gaul” not as the region of the Franks but as Galatia, which Saint Isidore of Seville writes is so called in Book XIV, chapter 3, of his *Etymologies*, after the ancient peoples of the Gauls by whom it was occupied; and from the ancient name of the Gauls . . . Galatia is now named. The Galatians, he adds in Book IX, chapter 2, are known to be Gauls. You will find this same division of the apostles among the various regions of the world in the same Isidore, chapter 81; in *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, etc.; in the Mozarabic Breviary, on the feast of Saint James son of Zebedee; and in the commentary on the Apocalypse of Saint Beatus of Liébana, edited by Henri Flórez, p. 97, Prologue to Book II. Beatus’s testimony, being at least a century later than the others, preceded by more than twenty years the discovery of Saint James’s body, since that event occurred at the beginning of the ninth century, before the year 814, as the aforementioned Flórez rightly says in vol. XIX of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 69, while Beatus wrote on the Apocalypse in the year 784, as his editor demonstrates.] [Col. 0745D] Bartholomew to Parthia, Simon to Egypt, James to Spain, Thomas to India, Matthew to Ethiopia, and Judas Thaddeus brought him to Mesopotamia. James son of Alphaeus retained him at Jerusalem. [Col. 0746D]

Each by his lot spread Christ without stain;

But through Paul he is dispersed throughout the whole world.

But since the office of preaching can scarcely be carried on for long without blemish, without the taint of a sinister disturbance—for either it is received fittingly and brings joy, or it is heard carelessly and produces torpor, or it is shamelessly despised and causes grief—therefore dust is said to be present on the feet, because a little leaven of glory clings to their conduct. [Col. 0746B]

But since it is soon driven away by the fervent light of compunction, the dust vanishes in the manner of a cloud. Hence, when the apostles returned from preaching and said, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us,” he taught them, as though rebuking them: “Do not rejoice in this, but rejoice rather because your names are written in heaven.” Again: “I was seeing Satan fall from heaven like lightning” (Luke X, 17, 20, 18).

As though he were saying to them fittingly and kindly, but secretly: If he who was made the seal of likeness, who was in the delights of God’s paradise, whose covering was every precious stone (Ezek. XXVIII, 12–13), who was created the most beautiful of all, experienced the peril of pride, suffered the misfortune of vainglory, continually grieves over his plunge into Gehenna, and laments the destruction of perpetual misery, then, following in his footsteps, you will in no way be able to escape the punishments he suffers. [Col. 0746C] For those whom the quality of their fault makes alike, the retribution of punishment necessarily makes share alike. Whoever has no middle way follows either every reward or none. For there is no fellowship between light and darkness: truth always attacks falsehood; the brightness of virtues, the shadow of vices; the vanity of the world opposes the glory of heaven; the calamity of Gehenna opposes the happiness of glory.

Hence in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters. For no one can serve God and Mammon; either he will endure one and despise the other, or he will hate one and love the other” (Matt. VI, 24). [Col. 0746D]

Therefore the dust of the Lord’s feet becomes a cloud, because although the glory of victory and gifts may lightly touch the mind, a fearful conscience, burning with excessive love, immediately washes away with tears, through affection for the divine gift, whatever earthly dust had stealthily entered. Otherwise grace would in no way persevere in them unless the creature submitted to the Creator and the human conscience humbly remained subject to God.

Hence Solomon says: “The rivers return to the place from which they flow, so that they may flow again” (Eccl. I, 7), because the mind possesses richer gifts of heavenly grace from the very place where it judges itself unworthy of such great covenants. [Col. 0747A]

Thus the dust of the feet becomes a cloud, because if anything sinister has stolen into the consciences of the saints, it immediately vanishes through the fervor of divine righteousness. The vice of vainglory must therefore be fled in every way: by it the soul’s virtue is weakened, the gift of grace diminished, the laughter of conscience darkened, and the happiness of glory lost.

### 77

For vainglory exercises in one’s character the function of a certain little serpent. There is a certain little serpent called the *hispalis*; when someone is wounded by it, he is immediately overcome by the sleep of death.

Concerning such people Hosea says: “Strangers have consumed his strength, and he did not know it; indeed, gray hairs have been scattered upon him, and he did not know it” (Hos. VII, 9). [Col. 0747B]

Strangers consume the strength of the vainglorious, but they do not know that they themselves are being devoured, because the wretched conscience, burning with love of praise, exchanges heavenly things for earthly things. While the wind of human praise pleases it instead of happy and eternal brightness, and the fading glory of the sinner is smoothed with oil, it becomes insensible to higher things, gradually becomes incapable of virtue, and, the slower and weaker it becomes with regard to divine things, the more inclined and ardent it becomes with regard to human things.

Thus external glory puts it to sleep, while inwardly the suggestion of evil spirits’ incentives kills it. And, like a madman, while dying it thinks itself alive; while insane it thinks itself playing; while it supposes that it is performing the role of glory, it vigorously conducts the business of misery. [Col. 0747C]

“Gray hairs have been scattered upon it, and it does not know it,” because while the flower of the age, the dowry of Egypt, and the dew of the world enrich, exalt, and gladden it, laying down in these things the new person, it thinks itself renewed while putting on the old.

Hence through another prophet it is said: “The Lord called you a fruitful, luxuriant, beautiful olive tree. At the sound of a great proclamation, fire has been kindled in it, and all its branches have been burned” (Jer. XI, 16).

Hence also through Jeremiah: “A swift runner, spreading out his ways. A wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of her soul she drew in the wind of her love” (ibid. II, 23–24). [Col. 0747D]

Indeed, such a soul becomes a swift runner, because, although with immense difficulty, it swiftly accomplishes whatever it sees as contributing to its temporal glory, whatever it regards as belonging to celebrated reputation and the fleeting eminence of a name, carrying it out without hesitation after setting aside the judgment of reason.

It spreads out its ways because, hastening toward glory, passing from one thing to another, it dissipates useful and honorable actions without regard for divine grace.

At times the wild ass exists in the wilderness, because the soul undertakes certain difficult things, proposes certain things difficult for many, and begins certain singular enterprises, without which the glory it desires cannot be retained.

The soul is a wild ass in the wilderness when, through love of empty glory, it is exalted by the singular height of its works. The soul is a wild ass in the desert when, anxious for the hope of glory, it persists in its arduous purpose. The soul is a wild ass in an arid land when, under the pretext of glory, it rarely bears the marks of abstinence and has been stripped of the disciplines of religion. [Col. 0748A]

But this wild ass, “in the desire of her soul, draws in the wind of her love,” because the soul anxious for praise exposes loss, profit, laughter, mourning, fame and infamy, poverty, misery, usefulness, grace, and all other such things for sale, solely so that glory may be obtained in them and through them.

Therefore, “in the desire of her soul she draws in the wind of her love,” because the mind thirsting for human favor undertakes, endures, seeks out, and embraces everything that it sees serving as evidence of its glory.

Hence Hosea says: “Ephraim feeds on wind and pursues the heat” (Hos. XII, 1), because the mind feeds on the breeze of exaltation and is lifted up by the wind of human praise while it pursues and endures the heat of an arduous religious life. [Col. 0748B]

It pursues the heat and feeds on wind because, the more outwardly it displays the appearance of abstinence and, to the eye of observance, enters more religious paths, the more quickly it gathers the flimsiest fruits of empty glory.

### 78

Again, through the same prophet concerning the same matter: “Ephraim, as he saw, Tyre vanished, which had been founded in beauty. Their glory flew away from childbirth, from the womb, from conception” (ibid. IX, 13, 11).

What sort of foundation it had, and what its beauty was, or how great, the reading of Ezekiel clearly shows, where it is said:

“Thus says the Lord: O Tyre, you have said, ‘I am perfect in beauty, and I am situated in the heart of the sea.’ Your neighbors who built you filled you with beauty. They built you with fir trees from Senir; they brought cedar from Lebanon for you. They spread out oaks from Bashan for you. They made your benches for you from Indian ivory and precious stone from the islands of Italy. Variegated linen from Egypt, violet and purple from the islands of Elishah, became your covering. The inhabitants of Sidon and Arvad were your rowers. Your wise men, O Tyre, became your pilots. Your furnishings were both useless and precious. Your warrior men hung shield and helmet upon you for your adornment. Carthaginian merchants filled your marketplaces with silver, iron, tin, and lead” (Ezek. XXVII, 3 ff.). [Col. 0748C]

This is the beauty of Tyre upon which it had been founded, as the prophetic reading records. Afterwards it follows how its glory flew away:

“Behold,” he says, “they shall take up a lamentation over you and shall mourn for you. What is like Tyre, which has become silent in the midst of the sea? By the multitude of your riches and your peoples you enriched the kings of the earth. Now you have been shattered by the sea into the depths of many waters. Your wealth and all your multitude, which were in your midst, have fallen. All the inhabitants of the islands have been astonished over you, and all the kings, struck by your tempest, have changed their faces. The merchants of the peoples have hissed over you. You have been reduced to nothing, and you shall not exist forever” (v. 32 ff.). [Col. 0748D]

Again, to the prince of the same city:

“You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God. Every precious stone was your covering. Gold was the work of your adornment, and your sockets were prepared on the day you were created. With the cherub extended and protecting, I placed you on God’s holy mountain. You walked perfect in your ways in the midst of fiery stones from the day of your creation. Your inner parts were filled with iniquity; you sinned, and I cast you out from the mind of God. Your heart was lifted up in your beauty. You destroyed your wisdom in your adornment. I cast you to the earth; I set you before the faces of kings, so that they might look upon you. In the multitude of your iniquities and in the iniquity of your fornication you polluted your sanctuary. Therefore I shall bring forth fire from your midst; it shall consume you, and I shall reduce you to ashes upon the earth in the sight of all who see you. Among the other kingdoms you shall be most humble, and you shall no longer be exalted above the nations” (ibid. XXVIII, 12 ff.). [Col. 0749A]

Behold Tyre’s exceptional foundation, its abundance of works [possibly: wealth], its friendly multitude of kings, nobles, and peoples; but afterwards it follows how its manifold glory flew away. [Col. 0749B]

### 79

It should be understood, however, that the prophetic reading, and the testimonies from which we have read the foregoing passages [possibly: “the testimonies we have read”], speaks specifically about vainglory. Therefore, since these passages are sufficiently clear in themselves and require no burdensome exposition, I shall refrain from speaking about them at greater length—especially since I see that I must hasten to investigate other matters more extensively and to make the secrets of the prophetic reading more expressly known and more clearly disclosed.

The glory of Ephraim therefore passes away from childbirth, from the womb, and from conception when the mind, previously honored by glory almost as a demigoddess, by the just judgment of God begins to suffer infamy instead of fame, misery instead of glory, hatred instead of favor, contempt instead of reverence, loss instead of profit, and hunger instead of abundance [possibly: “begins to undergo”].

Childbirth is action; the womb is intention; conception is thought. [Col. 0749C]

The glory of Ephraim therefore flies away from childbirth, from conception, and from the womb when the action of those who previously lived splendidly outwardly and gloried inwardly in the respectability of their life is disgraced, their intention corrupted, and their thought defiled.

The glory of the reprobate leads to this. But if it ever titillates the minds of the saints, it vanishes like a cloud, because as soon as they perceive outwardly the touch of this impurity, they immediately flee to the antidote of humility.

Therefore the dust of the Lord’s feet becomes clouds, because although the saints are tempted through the weakness of corruption, they nevertheless overcome through the power of reason and conquer in all things by the freely given gift of divine consolation.

Let this suffice concerning Christ’s feet. Now let what follows teach how these things are to be referred to the Church. [Col. 0749D]

### 80

Almost similar, or even identical, seem to be the things said of either of the two. For just as bridegroom and bride are two in one flesh—“this is a great sacrament,” as the Apostle says, “in Christ and in the Church” (Eph. V, 32)—so their attributes appear to be equal in unequal ways, and similarly they are dissimilar in similar ways.

Concerning the feet of the Church it is written in the *Song of Songs*: “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince!” (Song VII, 1). Sandals are made from the skins of dead animals and signify the examples of the saints’ righteousness.

### 81

Here an opportunity arose incidentally to introduce a fourfold division. For one is a daughter of the prince and his wife; another is a daughter but not a wife; another is a wife but not a daughter; another is neither wife nor daughter. [Col. 0750A]

A daughter is made by an expressed likeness to righteousness; a wife by sound preaching of the truth. She is a daughter of the Father when she retains within herself the image of the heavenly Father; she is a wife when, through the teaching of truth, she bears offspring for Christ.

The first, therefore, is the unanimous perfection of holy preachers; the second, the devoted company of simple righteous people; the third, the inquisitive multitude of carnal teachers; the fourth, the murmuring crowd of carnal or unbelieving subjects.

The first sits in the chair of righteousness; the second lies in the chamber of innocence; the third is filthy in the chair of Moses; the fourth reeks in the hovel of prostitution.

The first is crowned outwardly with glory and honor; the second is adorned inwardly with gifts of knowledge and the splendor of charisms; the third is pale within in conscience but shines outwardly in speech; the fourth is merely a snare and pit of malice. [Col. 0750B]

Of the first it is written: “She made a linen garment, sold it, and delivered a belt to the Canaanite.” Of the second: “Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she shall laugh on the last day” (Prov. XXXI, 24–25). Of the third: “A gold ring in her nostrils: a beautiful but foolish woman” (ibid. XI, 22). Of the fourth: “There is no head above the head of a serpent, and there is no wickedness above the wickedness of a woman” (Ecclus. XXV, 22–23).

### 82

The Church is therefore called the bride of the bridegroom, the prince’s daughter. She is a wife through the chastity of faith, a daughter through the sincerity of love. She is a wife according to humanity, a daughter according to divinity. She is a daughter by the dignity of creation, a wife by the kindness of redemption. She is a daughter by obeying commandments, a wife by bearing offspring through preaching.

Her steps are works of righteousness; her sandals are examples of innocence. The steps of the prince’s daughter are therefore beautiful in sandals, because the Church is expanded more and more as its preachers offer the peoples examples of innocence received from others, while they themselves display works of righteousness. [Col. 0750C]

That distinguished preacher, the vessel of election, Paul, who sowed the Gospel throughout the surrounding regions as far as Illyricum (Rom. XV, 19), demonstrated this in himself when he said:

“For me it is a very small thing to be judged by you or by a human day. For I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. IV, 3–4).

Behold innocence.

“Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burned?” (2 Cor. XI, 29).

“To the Jews I became as a Jew, to the Gentiles as a Gentile; I became all things to all, so that I might win all” (1 Cor. IX, 20 ff.). [Col. 0750D]

Behold righteousness.

### 83

The dust of the feet therefore becomes clouds, because the teachers of truth and preachers of the Church, reckoning all earthly things as dung for the love of righteousness, flee from them while despising the world’s more valued possessions; and from that very point, by conquering them more easily, they subdue the world to themselves.

And because the Church is expanded more greatly in proportion as its teachers trample more perfectly upon transitory things—for they consider that

Everything born tends toward destruction.

Again:

Everything passes away like flowing water.

Again:

Everything that has arisen perishes, and what has increased grows old; [Col. 0751A] and because here we have no abiding city, but seek the one that is to come [Hebr. XIII, 14], therefore, regarding all the glory of the world as misery, they hasten with utmost effort and anxious striving toward their homeland. And because they burn with perfect love, they earnestly strive with supreme devotion that those whom they had as companions in the misery of the world and the pilgrimage of exile, they may have as sharers in glory and blessed recompense.

The feet of the soul, however, are its affections. For just as the body is carried by the service of the feet, so the soul is moved toward various things by the impulse of its affections. The mist in the air is the power of compunction in the mind. The dust of the soul’s feet therefore becomes like mist, because if the conscience of the perfect is stained by any negligence of human life, compunction immediately arises in the devout mind from its own judgment, and through it the affection previously sullied is cleansed.

Thus I understand what is read [Note: [Col. 0751D] “In the Gospel”—unless this is an error of the copyist or printer for “in Proverbs,” I could hardly say why the author ascribes this saying to the Gospel, since it is found in Proverbs. Jerome reads the words “in the day” in Letter 46, near the end, in the edition of Marianus Victorius; Gregory the Great also reads them in Book VI of his commentary on 1 Kings, chapter 2, no. 8; and the Mozarabic Breviary, on the Saturday of the Third Sunday of Lent, at Terce. Peter Sabbatier could make good use of the testimony of all these authorities and assign this reading a place in his edition of the Sacred Bible.] in the Gospel: “The righteous man falls seven times in the day, and rises again” (Prov. XXIV, 16). Likewise, in Proverbs concerning the same subject: “The righteous man shall be confident as a lion, without fear” (ibid. XXVIII, 1). Not that a lion is never afraid, but that, overcoming fear, he immediately returns to his natural state. So too, if the righteous man should at some time fall into sin, he immediately hastens to tears and washes away his blemish in a shower of compunction.

Hence it is said to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, which are by the gate of the daughter of the multitude” (Cant. VII, 4). The dust of the soul’s feet truly becomes like mist, because if the affections of the saints are infected by any impurities, they immediately return to the heart and live in tears, saying that word of the Psalmist: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI, 3).

Hence the children of Israel are commanded to carry a peg on their belt, so that the filthy discharge of the belly may be covered with earth (Deut. XXIII, 13–14), because those who sigh for high things and love heavenly things always have genuine compunction, by which they manfully cover and wash away the excessive discharge of impure thought. What follows.

84. “Rebuking the sea and drying it up, and bringing all the rivers into the desert” (Nah. I, 4).

Let this therefore be read first concerning Assyria, then concerning the soul, next concerning Christ, and finally concerning the Church.

Concerning Assyria, it is as follows. The Lord rebukes the sea because he causes the exceedingly bitter persecution of the Assyrians to cease at the time appointed by the examination of just judgment. He dries up the sea when he utterly annihilates it. He brings all its rivers into the desert when he permits the various classes of kings, nobles, and peoples to grow weak, allows them to be conquered, endures their ruin, and permits them to be dragged down completely into nothingness.

This happened when Sennacherib’s hostile army came furiously to Jerusalem, surrounded its walls in a hostile manner, and was struck down and utterly destroyed by an angel. Thus it is read in the Book of Kings: “The angel of the Lord descended into the camp of the Assyrians in the middle of the night, and struck them, and that night eighty-four thousand men fell. And he himself fled almost alone into Nineveh, his own city” (IV Kings XIX, 35). Not long afterward, two of his sons killed him in the temple of Nesroch, his god.

Or he rebuked the sea when Sennacherib fell with his army; he dried it up when Sardanapalus, the last and lowest of the Assyrian kings, was reigning. He brought all the rivers into the desert when the Macedonian [Possibly: Median] conquered Assyria and subjected it to himself in hostile fashion.

Morally, concerning the soul: the sea is the bitterness of conscience rising from the depths of wickedness. The Lord rebukes the sea when, moved by the regard of his merciful grace, he pricks the mind disturbed by vices and embittered by sins, producing compunction. He dries it up when he completely obliterates harmful pleasures. He brings all the rivers into the desert when he utterly empties out every kind of vice, even the smallest.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash its little ones against the rock” (Ps. CXXXVI, 9). The Lord therefore rebukes the sea by leading the soul to confession; he dries it up by infusing compunction; he brings all the rivers into the desert by supplying mortification of the flesh. He rebukes the sea by exhorting to repentance; he dries it up by inspiring the grace of the virtues; he brings all the rivers into the desert by raising the soul to perfect righteousness.

85. First he infuses the bitterness of repentance; second, he supplies tranquility of conscience; third, he grants the serenity of grace. He rebukes the sea by removing crimes; he dries it up by erasing even the smallest offenses; he brings the rivers into the desert by cutting off impure desires. He rebukes the sea by erasing iniquity; he dries it up by mortifying the will; he brings the rivers into the desert by conferring purity upon the soul.

First he grants hatred of evil; second, contempt of the world; third, rejection of oneself. First the soul is given life; second, the flesh is mortified; third, the spirit is purified. It is given life through forgiveness, mortified through abstinence, and purified through perfected righteousness.

Or he brings the rivers into the desert when, after the soul has been cleansed of vices, drained of impurities, and completely stripped of heavenly disciplines, he most mercifully grants the gifts of the spirit, the rewards of grace, the light of spiritual understanding, and the sweetness of contemplative joy.

First, therefore, the soul must be cleansed through compunction; second, the wantonness of the flesh must be purified through mortification. [Col. 0752D] Third, the spirit must be adorned with gifts of grace, raised up by spiritual knowledge, and divinely enlightened through contemplation.

Hence the Psalmist says: “In a desert land, impassable and without water: so I have appeared before you in the sanctuary, that I might see your power and your glory” (Ps. LXII, 3). First, by confessing vices, the soul becomes a desert; second, by abstaining and manfully bearing the yoke of discipline, it becomes impassable to evil spirits; third, by trampling upon impure desires, it becomes without water. [Col. 0753A] Then the power of God and his glory are seen.

Power arises from the subjection of enemies; glory from the splendor of gifts. The power of God is shown in hatred of iniquity; glory in the joy of contemplating truth. The power of God is manifested when the sinner is chosen from the depths of wickedness; glory when he is raised to the state of perfect innocence. The power of God is displayed when the vanity of the world is despised; glory when heavenly happiness is felt on every side.

Let him therefore say: “Knowing that you love the purity of your creature, by purifying my mind and mortifying my flesh I immediately betook myself to holiness, so that, climbing these steps, I might at last be able to attain the blessedness of both your power and your glory.”

Hence Solomon says: “I considered,” he says, “how to withdraw my flesh, in order to transfer it to wisdom” (Eccl. II, 3).

[Col. 0753B] 86. Hence it is read in the Book of Judges that Samson replied to the solution of the question posed by his companions: “Unless you had plowed with my heifer, you would not have discovered my riddle” (Judg. XIV, 18).

The heifer is wanton flesh; the riddle is obscure speech. Concerning the heifer it is read in the Book of Jeremiah: “Egypt is a beautiful and graceful heifer; a goad will come against her from the north” (Jer. XLVI, 20). For when wanton flesh, serving pleasure and outward adornment, despises the judgment of reason and hates the workshop of seduction, incentives to lust intrude from the side of the worst adversary.

The goad of the heifer comes from the north because immediately the goad of all wickedness is present for the ostentatiously fattened and carefully prepared flesh, suggesting incentives to every impurity.

Samson, whose name is said to mean “sun,” represents the sun of righteousness; and his companions represent students of wisdom. Let it therefore be said: “Unless you had plowed with my heifer, you would not have discovered my riddle.” As if it were said: Unless the flesh is restrained and made sober, the mind can in no way raise itself freely toward heavenly things.

The heifer is plowed when the flesh is mortified. The riddle is discovered when the contemplation of heavenly mysteries is opened. Unless, therefore, the heifer is plowed, the riddle is in no way revealed, because unless the pleasurable vanity of the flesh is worn away, the sweetness of ineffable joy is not opened.

Samson’s companions therefore plow diligently with the heifer so that they may understand the proposed riddle, because the disciples of Jesus Christ, friends of truth, soberly discipline the flesh, appropriately weaken their bodies, devote themselves to hardship, and humble themselves completely; [Col. 0753D] so that they may understand obscure knowledge, penetrate the secrets of wisdom, see immortal riches, and enter the most delightful secrets of the wine cellar.

87. Abstinence is therefore of great importance: through it vices are cleansed, forgiveness obtained, grace possessed, innocence restored, and heavenly mysteries disclosed.

Abstinence, moreover, is fourfold. The first is abstinence from vices, the second from food, the third from business, and the fourth from impure desires. Concerning all these it is read in Zechariah: “The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth, shall be for you a great joy and splendid solemnities,” says the Lord of hosts (Zech. VIII, 19).

The human body is composed of the four elements. All activities are carried out through the five senses. Through observance of the Decalogue, vices are uprooted. By the number seven contemplative perfection is signified.

Therefore, through the fast of the tenth, vices are uprooted by observance of the commandments. Through abstinence associated with the number four, drunkenness and gluttony are destroyed. Through the fast of the fifth, renunciation of individual occupations is achieved. Through the moderation of the seventh, especially impure desires are driven away and the joy of contemplation is possessed. Through the fast of the tenth, all things are brought to blessedness.

Likewise, on the fourth day God created the lights of heaven (Gen. I, 14ff.). On the fifth he brought forth animals from the waters. On the seventh he rested from all his works. Through the number ten all things are blessed.

Through the fast of the fourth, therefore, the light of knowledge and the understanding of reason are supplied to us. Through abstinence of the fifth, a new and clean creature is produced from the waters of compunction. Through the fast of the seventh, we rest on the Sabbath of most secret contemplation. Through the fast of the tenth, we receive the denarius of most blessed recompense.

Through the fourth we are enlightened; through the fifth we are purified; through the seventh we are honored; through the fast of the tenth we are blessed. The first excludes iniquity and ignorance; the second, the vanity of the world and concupiscence; the third drives away weakness and sluggishness of spirit; the fourth, calamity and misery.

88. The fasts just mentioned shall therefore be for us, as Zechariah says, “a great joy and splendid solemnities” (as above), because, rightly observed by us, these fasts confer upon us the light of divine knowledge, serenity of conscience, the joy of perfect righteousness, [Col. 0754C] and, in addition, transfer us to the solemnity of heavenly joy.

The number four is a general married number; five is married but singular; seven is virgin; ten is celibate. The first both generates and is generated; the second generates but is not generated; the third is neither generated nor generates, but is subject; the fourth likewise remains the same, but is placed above.

The fast of the first therefore cuts off the foulness of illicit lust; that of the second imposes the necessity of propagating offspring; that of the third grants the honor of virginity; that of the fourth raises the celibate to the blessedness of angelic dignity.

First the married man is restrained, lest he pour himself out indiscriminately; second, he is bound more tightly, lest he offend; third, the virgin is adorned so that she may please; fourth, the celibate is raised to the heights so that he may always rejoice.

89. Abstinence was of such importance among the ancients, and was held in such reverence and observed with such care, that even among the Egyptians, in their pagan religion, no one became a chief initiate or handled sacred mysteries unless abstinence commended him as foremost above all.

Abstinence is the firm guard of Christian service, the bar of the virtues, the most savage beast against vices, the storehouse of spiritual gifts, the guesthouse of graces, and the most faithful messenger of contemplation.

We know that fasting is God’s fortress [Note: [Col. 0753D] We corrected “fortress” from the edition of Chrysologus; previously “art” had been read.] (from Sermon XII of Chrysologus), the camp of Christ, a wall against spirits [Note: [Col. 0754D] The edition of Chrysologus reads “against the spirit.”], the standard of faith, the sign of chastity, and the trophy of holiness.

Adam preserved this in paradise, but gluttony cast him out of it [Note: [Col. 0755C] The edition reads: “whom gluttony dragged away from there.”] (Gen. II, 16–17; III, 6ff.). Noah guarded this in the ark, when drunkenness submerged the world. By this Lot extinguished the fire of Sodom [Note: [Col. 0755C] The edition reads: “through this Lot extinguished the conflagration of Sodom.”], though through drunkenness he suffered the fire of incest [Note: [Col. 0755C] The edition reads: “was burned in the fire.”] (Gen. XIX, 31ff.).

By this Moses, the friend of God and sharer in the divine counsel, deserved to become what he was, when the people returned to idolatry through gluttony and drunkenness [Note: [Col. 0755D] The edition reads: “This caused Moses to be led onward by the light of divine fervor, when feasting and drunkenness darkened the Israelite people with the errors of idols.”] (Exod. XXIV, 18; XXXII, 1ff.). By this Elijah was carried up to heaven [Note: [Col. 0755D] The edition reads “brought onward.”] (III Kings XIX, 8; IV Kings II, 11). By this John was made greater than those born of women. Through this, while the Lord was fasting, the devil’s snares were exposed.

For the devil, who had despised Christ when he was eating, when he saw him not eating, suspected him to be God and confessed him to be the Son of God. “If you are the Son of God,” he says, “command that these stones be made bread. Or cast yourself down” (Matt. IV, 3, 6).

Fasting is the death of vices and the life of virtues (from Sermon 8, near the middle). Fasting is peace for the body [Note: [Col. 0755D] We corrected “peace for the body” from the edition; previously “a part of the body” had been read], the beauty of the limbs, and the adornment of life. Fasting is the strength of minds and the vigor of the soul. Fasting is the wall of chastity, the bulwark of purity, and the city of holiness. Fasting is the gymnasium of religion [Note: [Col. 0755D] The edition has, instead of “the gymnasium of religion,” “the school of merits.”], the mastery of teaching, and the discipline of disciplines. Fasting is the saving provision for the ecclesiastical way. Fasting is the unconquered leadership of Christian service.

90. (From the same author.) But in all these things fasting then flourishes and then triumphs, under the leadership of mercy, when it resists [Note: [Col. 0755D] The edition reads “fights.”]. Mercy and piety are the wings of fasting, by which it is lifted up and carried to heaven; without them it lies prostrate and rolls about on the earth.

Fasting without mercy is merely an image of hunger, but no holiness [Note: [Col. 0755D] The edition reads: “there is no image of holiness.”]. Without mercy, fasting is not a purpose of moderation but an opportunity for avarice. This is the worst kind of moderation: the more the body is dried out, the more it swells in the mind—or in the linen pouch [Note: [Col. 0755D] The edition reads: “Without piety, fasting is an opportunity for avarice, not a purpose of moderation; for this moderation, the more the body is dried out, the more the purse swells.”].

Fasting without mercy is not virtue but hypocrisy, as the Lord says: “When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites” (Matt. VI, 16). Whoever fasts but does not distribute his meal, instead storing it away, is shown to fast for greed, not for Christ.

Therefore, when fasting, let us place our meal in the hand of the poor—what the belly would have wasted. [Col. 0756A] The hand of the poor is the bosom of Abraham, where whatever the poor man receives he immediately stores away. The hand of the needy is the treasury of heaven: whatever it receives, so that it may not perish on earth, it entrusts to heaven [Note: [Col. 0755D] The edition reads: “The hand of the poor is the treasury of heaven; whatever it receives, so that it may not perish on earth, it stores in heaven.”].

“Store up for yourselves,” he says, “treasures in heaven” (v. 20). The hand of the beggar is Christ’s treasury, because whatever the poor man receives, Christ stores in the treasury of his grace [Note: [Col. 0755D] The edition reads: “Christ accepts it.”].

Give earth, therefore, to the poor, so that you may receive heaven; give a coin, so that you may receive a kingdom; give a crumb, so that you may receive everything; give to the poor, so that you may give to yourself, because whatever you give to the poor, you will possess.

The poor man seeks human mercy so that you may receive divine mercy [Note: [Col. 0756C] The edition differs: “God seeks human mercy in order to bestow divine mercy.”]. For there is mercy in heaven, and one reaches it through earthly piety [Note: [Col. 0756C] The edition reads: “through earthly acts of mercy.”]. Whoever is confident in the protection of fasting [Note: [Col. 0756C] The word “fasting” is absent from the edition] and mercy may be secure concerning forgiveness and have no doubt concerning absolution [Note: [Col. 0756D] The edition reads: “let him not doubt.”].

[Col. 0756B] 91. (From the same Sermon 8, shortly after the beginning.) Brothers, fasting hungers; fasting thirsts when it is not nourished with the food of piety or watered with the drink of mercy. Fasting grows cold, and abstinence fails, when it is not covered by the fleece [possibly: veil] of mercy [Note: [Col. 0756D] The edition reads “fasting”], when the garment of compassion has not covered it.

What spring is to the soil, mercy is to fasting. For just as the breath of spring makes the grasses of the fields flower, so the soil of fasting produces the flower of mercy [Note: [Col. 0756D] The edition reads: “so mercy brings all the seeds of fasting into flower.”].

What oil is to a lamp, piety is to fasting. For just as the richness of oil makes the lamp’s light shine through [Note: [Col. 0756D] The edition reads: “just as the richness of oil kindles the lamp’s light and, by measured nourishment, makes it shine throughout the whole night”], so piety makes fasting shine.

What the sun is to the day, almsgiving is understood [Note: [Col. 0756D] The edition reads “is known”] to be to fasting. For just as the sun’s radiance makes the day brighter and scatters all the darkness of the clouds, so almsgiving sanctifies the holiness of fasting [Col. 0756C] and, by the light of piety, excludes entirely the death of greed [Note: [Col. 0756D] In the Library of the Fathers we previously read this passage in a somewhat disordered form: “For just as the sun’s radiance makes the day brighter, so almsgiving sanctifies the holiness of fasting. And just as the same [the editors supplied ‘the same’; the manuscript read ‘all’] scatters the darkness of the clouds, so fasting entirely excludes the death of greed by the light of piety.” We have restored the text from the editions of Chrysologus.].

And, not to linger over many things [Note: [Col. 0756D] The edition more correctly reads “not to delay”], what the soul is to the body, generosity is held to be to fasting. If hypocrisy and greed are absent from fasting, generosity is brighter to the soul than the clarity of the sun is to the world.

92. (From Sermon 7.) Hypocrisy is a subtle evil, a secret poison, a hidden venom, a counterfeit of virtues, and the moth of holiness. Hypocrisy safely pretends, deceives in prosperity, lies with affected curiosity, and by a cruel art cuts down virtues with the sword of virtues: it destroys fasting through fasting, empties prayer through prayer, and overthrows mercy through compassion.

What dropsy is to bodies [Note: [Col. 0757A] We have supplied “dropsy” from Chrysologus; the editors of the Library of the Fathers substituted “hydropisis” for “hydrops,” which was read in the manuscript], hypocrisy is to souls. Dropsy thirsts while drinking; hypocrisy is intoxicated with thirst.

Hypocrite, even if your face is unkempt, your skin neglected, your countenance sad, and your appearance disfigured; even if you have found no praise among human beings, you have lost the fruit of fasting before God.

Hypocrite, you entered the waves of abstinence, climbed the billows of self-restraint, and swam across the sea of fasting; yet in the very harbor of fasting you suffered shipwreck. For you did not acquire profits but traded in vanity; because, on God’s credit, you completed a human transaction [Note: [Col. 0757B] The edition reads: “who, on God’s credit, completed a human transaction.”].

The poison of hypocrisy must therefore be fled, and its pestilence avoided: it creates diseases from remedies, produces sickness from medicine, turns holiness into a crime, makes appeasement into guilt, and generates danger from reconciliation.

A face cast down by sorrow invites [Possibly: indicates] hunger; it does not profess voluntary fasting. If he wishes to fast, why is he sad? If he does not wish to fast, why is he fasting? [Note: [Col. 0757B] We have restored this entire passage from Chrysologus himself, since it appears excessively corrupt in the *Library of the Fathers*, namely: “The poison of hypocrisy must be fled … its pestilence avoided: it produces diseases from remedies, sickness from medicine … makes appeasement into a creature, and generates danger from reconciliation. If he wishes to seek, sad; if he does not wish to fast, why deservedly such,” etc.]

Rightly is he tormented by such a transaction [Note: [Col. 0757B] The edition reads: “he lives under such punishment”], who makes vice out of virtue, falsehood out of truth, loss out of reward [Note: [Col. 0757B] The edition reads “payment”], and sin out of remission.

(Thus far the Bavarian manuscript, says Canisius: “Accordingly, either the commentary is mutilated, or certainly the holy man’s work was cut short by death; for up to this point he has explained only four verses, and not even those in their entirety.”)

[Col. 0757]

THE LIFE OF SAINT HILDEFONSUS. (C)

(You may see, most learned reader, that this Life, or Eulogy, is without doubt to be attributed to our Julian, among the prolegomena prefixed to the Works of Saint Hildefonsus, in this volume, cols. 43–44.)

[ORATIONS.]

[Col. 0757]

NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

The following Orations, although they may appear to be mere trifling fragments, are works of Saint Julian; and we were entirely unwilling either to let them perish or to leave them scattered. We were completely ignorant of the author of the first and second until we saw them quoted by Abbot Samson in Book II of his *Apologeticus*, which, as we have mentioned elsewhere, was first published by the Reverend Father Flórez in volume XI of *Hispania Sacra*.

He writes that these orations are found in the daily Mass of the Gothic rite. But, going through the Mozarabic Missal in its present form, we read the same orations in the Mass for the Sunday before the fast of the Kalends of November. The first, which is called the Illation, occupies the place of what we call the Preface; the other occurs immediately before the Lord’s Prayer.

Since, however, we found in the aforesaid Missal no name or trace of daily Mass, it is obscure to us, and not easy to determine, what Samson intended by that expression. For it does not occur to us why the Mass of the Sunday mentioned above could have been called daily, since it was read on only one day. Nor, if the aforesaid orations belonged to another Mass at that time, can we understand what sort of Mass it was that could be called daily.

To call some common Mass, as we say, a daily Mass—one that could be read on any day—seemed to us a slight conjecture. Unless someone prefers to understand “Mass” here as that particular oration which in the liturgy of the Mozarabs is called by this name: “When the catechumens are sent outside,” as Saint Isidore writes in Book IX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 19, “when the deacon cries out: ‘If any catechumen remains, let him go outside’; and hence, *missa*.” This does not satisfy us, because in this sense the *missa* always preceded the offertory, whereas each of these two orations follows the offertory, as is clear in itself and as their words sufficiently indicate.

There is almost nothing to note concerning the third oration, since it is the very one prefixed by the same holy teacher to the work *On the Proof of the Sixth Age*, and published by us above in column 537. The Mozarabs therefore recite it amid the solemnities of the Mass after the washing of the hands, in the place where we recite the oration “Receive, Holy Trinity,” and so forth.

We reprint it because of the variant readings, which we distinguish by different type. Among them one may see the not inconsiderable reading *clave*, “with a key,” rather than *clavo*, “with a nail,” which was read in the printed editions of the work *On the Proof of the Sixth Age*. This shows how correctly we said at that point that Barthius had made a very prudent conjecture: in his *Adversaria* he judged that this reading should be restored. The Toledo edition of the Mozarabic Missal of 1500 displays it, the Roman edition of 1755 retained it, and we likewise followed it in our specimen of the Mozarabic Mass, which we published at Angelópolis in 1770, when we occupied the cathedral see of Mexico.

[Col. 0757]

ORATIONS COMPOSED BY SAINT JULIAN AND FOUND IN THE MOZARABIC MISSAL

ILLATION

[Col. 0757]

It is worthy and just that we give you thanks, holy Lord, eternal Father, almighty God, through Jesus [Col. 0758] Christ your Son, our Lord. The immensity of whose divinity so ineffably surrounds all things that it remains wholly in each individual creature and dwells entire in them all. It is not diminished in the smallest things, nor increased in the greatest [Note: [Col. 0759B] Abbot Samson, Book II of the *Apologeticus*, chapter 23, no. 2, transcribes only these words: “It is worthy and just that we give you thanks, almighty God, whose divine immensity so ineffably surrounds all things that it remains wholly in each individual creature and dwells entire in them all. It is not diminished in the smallest things, nor increased in the greatest, since it is neither increased nor diminished in anything; and yet he increases gifts and diminishes them by his powerful command.” We do not know whether these final words, which we print in italics, belong to Julian.].

It is not confined by time, nor restricted by quantity. It did not begin at a beginning, nor will it be ended by a limit. By whom the whole human being was created for righteousness without sin, and after the fall was restored through the purest sacrifice of that same Christ.

Through him, whom heavenly and earthly beings alike praise in the unity of the threefold power, proclaiming a hymn in sweet harmony and saying: “Holy,” and so forth.

TO THE LORD’S PRAYER

Beloved brothers, since we are about to receive the heavenly sacrifice within mortal entrails and God as a guest within the chamber of the human breast, let us cleanse our consciences from every stain of vice [Note: [Col. 0760B] These are the words which Samson transfers in Book II of the *Apologeticus*, chapter 13, no. 2: “Beloved brothers, since we are about to receive the heavenly sacrifice within mortal members and God as a guest within the chamber of the human breast, let us cleanse our hearts from every stain of wrongdoing.”], so that there may be nothing deceitful or proud in us; but let the entire brotherhood be joined together in devotion to humility and consent in charity through the food and blood of the Lord’s body, so that with confidence we may deserve to say from the earth: “Our Father, who art,” and so forth.

ORATION TO BE RECITED IN THE MOZARABIC MASS AFTER THE WASHING OF THE HANDS

I shall approach you in the humility of my spirit; I shall speak to you, because you have given me great hope in your strength. Therefore you, Son of David, who came to us in the flesh after the mystery had been revealed, open the secrets of my heart with the key of your cross, sending one of the seraphim to cleanse my polluted lips with that glowing coal which was taken from your altar, to clear my mind of clouds, and to supply material for instruction, so that the tongue which through charity serves the benefit of its neighbors may not sound forth the fall of error, but may resound forever with the proclamation of truth.

Through you, my God, who live and reign forever and ever. [Col. 0760B] Amen.

HISTORY OF THE REBELLION OF PAUL AGAINST WAMBA, KING OF THE GOTHS, BY SAINT JULIAN, BISHOP OF TOLEDO

[Col. 0759]

PRELIMINARY NOTICE

[Col. 0759C] No one is unaware that Julian of Toledo committed to writing the history of Paul’s rebellion against Wamba, king of the Goths, and of the events carried out by Wamba on this occasion in Narbonese Gaul. For, as Felix, his encomiast, testifies, it was in all subsequent ages not only known to every historian, but also praised and commended.

Thus the author of the chronicle attributed by some to Alfonso III and by others to Sebastian, bishop of Salamanca, writes the following concerning Wamba: “If you wish to know more fully how many massacres, how many burnings of cities, how many slaughters, how many troops of Franks or Gauls were killed by Wamba, and how many famous victories he achieved as a result of the destruction of the tyrant Paul, read blessed Julian the metropolitan, who composed the history of this period with complete clarity.” We read this in Appendix 7 to volume XIII of *Hispania Sacra*.

Lucas of Tuy incorporated the same history into his own work in the thirteenth century. Andreas Schottus first published it in print in volume IV of *Hispania Illustrata*. Duchesne later reprinted it, separated from Tuy, in volume I of the *Scriptores Coaetanei* of Gallican history. Most recently of all, Father Henry Flórez published it in Spain, in volume VI of *Hispania Sacra*, collating it with a manuscript exemplar of the Royal Library of Madrid copied from a transcript by Juan Bautista Pérez. This transcript is preserved in the library of our Holy Church of Toledo among the other manuscripts donated by him. From this collation he extracted and noted variant readings and more than once corrected even Duchesne’s text.

Yet, to acknowledge the truth of the matter, none of these editions ought to be regarded as exact and perfect. Tuy, whose text Schottus published, when transcribing the history from Julian’s codex, followed his usual practice of truncating it at almost every third word or interpolating material of his own. For this reason it differs greatly from Julian’s genuine text.

Duchesne, using a single codex, frequently goes wrong through the fault of the copyist. Flórez, finally, left many passages still corrupt, which he was unable to correct even with the aid of another Madrid exemplar. We have corrected a large part of these with the help of our Toledo manuscript.

Here one cannot help wondering: since the Madrid manuscript was copied from our Perezian manuscript, how can the discrepancy between the two be as great as the variant readings will show? Is this due to the copyist’s carelessness, or to his perversity?

We, therefore, who have compared the editions mentioned above with the praised manuscript of Juan Bautista Pérez, and have also been assisted by another ancient Toledo codex containing the chronicle of Tuy, may affirm that we shall publish the author’s genuine text far more complete and corrected than the others, and shall not seem unlikely to earn our readers’ trust.

We also hope that they will not criticize our decision to publish the genuine text of the author together with Tuy’s version. We resolved to do this both so as not to burden the margins with the wearisome mass of so many variant readings, and so that anyone might easily judge at a single glance how greatly Tuy’s narrative differs from Julian’s.

When this occurred to Flórez, he deliberately refrained from doing so, lest he seem to depart from his own purpose. Since his purpose differs greatly from ours, we have no such concern.

But the Perezian copy has come down to us not only so that Julian’s writing might emerge in a more corrected form, but also in a fuller one. In it, after the historical account of the outbreak of the rebellion and the defeat of the tyrant, but before the exposition of the sentence passed against him and his associates, we find an oration inserted which the author calls an *insultatio*; we would call it a declamation.

Why the copyist of the Madrid exemplar did not wish to transcribe it, we do not sufficiently understand, unless perhaps he suspected that it had been inserted by someone else and was not composed by Julian. But we see no grounds for such a suspicion.

For this declamation, if properly considered, is exceedingly similar in character and style to the other passages before and after it: sharp, vivid, pointed, and interwoven with various tropes and figures both of words and of thought. Indeed, when I read it attentively, if one excepts that swelling of words and hardness of style—the defect of those times, almost characteristic of the Gothic race—the orator appears far from commonplace.

He attacks the province of Gaul and reproaches it not only for the corruption of its morals and faith but also for its own faithlessness, by which, like a base adulteress weary of her legitimate marriage bed, it was not ashamed to seek foreign embraces. He handles this metaphor elegantly.

Then he carefully and skillfully anticipates the empty pretexts that Gaul might wish to put forward in defense of its crime. To place the disgracefulness of its offense in the light of day, he opposes, through a most elegant antithesis, the singular clemency of the prince and his admirable moderation of spirit in the midst of victory to its shamelessness and insolence.

His sole aim in this vehement *insultatio*, as he calls it, is that Gaul, suffused with salutary shame, may thereafter refrain from such ruinous counsels and wish to safeguard its own peace and security, as well as its good name and honor.

Yet, beyond these oratorical virtues, which we have set forth and which are by no means to be despised, the author reveals a mind inflamed by pious zeal. He could not restrain himself from attacking the crime of that wicked man, who was inciting subject peoples to rebellion—if not with his hands, then at least with his pen—painting his disgrace in such dark colors that he led everyone to detest it. For it was always regarded, from ancient times, as the distinctive praise of the Spanish bishops to offer their kings loyalty and obedience everywhere and in every form of service; to regard their persons as sacred; always to defend both their rights and their authority over subject peoples, by word and in writing; and to teach, urge, and proclaim the same thing to their peoples both by their example and through unceasing exhortations, always crying out with the chief apostles: “Be subject to every creature for God’s sake, whether to the king or to governors. Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; therefore be subject by necessity, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience.”

For this reason we, the first of all, now bring this speech, hitherto unpublished, to light, and precisely in the place which it occupies in the Perez manuscript, before the account of the sentence passed against the rebels. We then recorded the variant readings, designating by D. the edition of Duchesne, by F. that of Flórez, and by Ms. the manuscript codex of the holy church of Toledo mentioned above—and these variants belong to the genuine text. In the Tudela text, however, the variants appended below are either from Schott’s edition or from the Toledo manuscript previously mentioned. We further warn the reader that Luke of Tuy, when transcribing Julian’s history, inserted some material of his own and suppressed other material that was in Julian. To make both things apparent in the present edition, we print in the Tudela text whatever has been inserted in italics, as they are called; what has been suppressed we present in the genuine Julian within asterisks.

[Col. 0761]

## LETTER OF PAUL THE PERFIDIOUS MAN WHO CAUSED THE REBELLION IN GAUL, TO WAMBA, THE GREAT TOLEDAN PRINCE

[Col. 0761C] *In the name of the Lord. Flavius Paul, anointed* [Note: F., “supreme.”] *king of the East, to Wamba* [Note: Ms., “of Wamba.”] *king of the South.*

If you have already traversed the harsh and uninhabitable crags of the mountains [Note: F., “traveled through.”], if you have already shattered with your breast, like a most powerful lion, the rugged forests dense with torrents [Note: Id., “fertile”], if you have already utterly subdued the running of the does, the leaps of the stags, and the voracity of boars and bears; if you have already vomited forth the poisons of serpents and vipers [Note: Id., singular, “the poison”], tell us, O bearer of arms; tell us, my lord, friend of forests and rocks. For all these things have also lain down, and you hasten to come to us so that you may generously unfold for us the nightingale’s song. Therefore, noble man, let your heart rise to courage, and descend as far as the Defiles [Note: F.: “he rose … to courage. Descend as far as,” etc.], for there you will find the great Opopumpeus [Note: Id., “Oppopumbeus,” adding in a note that it is a fortress in the Pyrenees], with whom you may lawfully contend.

[Col. 0763]

## [HISTORY OF PAUL’S REBELLION](C)

[Note: This and the following title are found in the manuscript; Duchesne, however, has: “History of King Wamba of Toledo, published by Julian, archbishop of the Toledan see, concerning the expedition and victory,” etc.]

## IN THE NAME OF THE LORD BEGINS THE BOOK OF THE HISTORY OF GAUL, WHICH WAS PUBLISHED IN THE TIME OF WAMBA, THE PRINCE OF DIVINE MEMORY, BY JULIAN, BISHOP OF THE TOLEDAN SEE

In the name of the holy Trinity begins the History of the most excellent King Wamba, concerning the expedition and victory [Note: Flor., “which”] by which he subdued the province of Gaul, rebelling against him, in a celebrated triumph. [Note: The “Textus Legitimus” and the “Textus Tudensis” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## AUTHENTIC TEXT

### 1

The account of triumphs, when related, usually serves as a protection for virtue and raises the minds of the young toward the standard of virtue; whatever glory has been proclaimed concerning the past does so as well. For human nature itself contains a certain sluggish inclination toward inner virtue. Hence it is found to be inclined not so much toward virtues as toward vices. Unless it is instructed and strengthened by the continual prompting of useful examples [Note: D., *quae enim* (“for indeed it”)], it remains cold and grows numb [Note: F., *praestiterit* (“has provided”)]. For this reason, so that an account of past events may be able to remedy minds grown weary, we introduce an event accomplished in our own time, by which we may summon succeeding ages to virtue. [Note: Id., “the account.”]

### 2

For in our days there appeared the illustrious prince Wamba, whom the Lord willed worthily to rule, whom priestly anointing revealed, whom the community of the whole nation and homeland elected, whom the affection of the peoples sought out, and who, before attaining the height of kingship, was very widely proclaimed by many revelations as destined to reign. While this illustrious man was performing the funeral rites and lamenting the death of the departing prince Receswinth [Note: D., “the fallen prince”; Id., “was lamenting”], suddenly everyone turned toward a single agreement. Summoned, as it were, with one mind and with a common movement of speech, they all shout with delight that they wish to have him as prince; with united voices they thunder that they want him, and no other, to rule among the Goths [Note: F., “they wished him to rule”], and in crowds they throw themselves at his feet so that he may not refuse their requests [Note: Ms., “at his own feet”].

But the man, rejecting them in every respect, choked by tearful sobs [Note: Ms., “and by tearful sobs”], is overcome by no prayers and swayed by no petition of the people. At one moment he cries out that he will not be sufficient for so many impending disasters; at another he declares himself worn out by old age. While he was resisting fiercely [Note: Ms., “while he was resisting him …”], one of the commanders, as though about to act on behalf of them all, boldly stepped into the midst and, looking at him with a threatening face, said:

“Unless you promise that you will consent to us [Note: F., “only if you promise”], know that you are to be beheaded at once by the edge of the sword. Nor shall we leave this place until either our expedition receives you as king or this bloody death, which will occur today, consumes you as one who refuses.”

### 3

Overcome not so much by their prayers as by their threats, he finally yielded and, accepting the kingship, received them into his peace [Note: Ms., “all of them.”]—yet he postponed the time of his anointing until the nineteenth day, so that he would not be consecrated as prince outside the site of the ancient royal seat. These events took place in a village which antiquity called Gerticos [Note: Ms., “a small village”], situated in the territory of Salamanca, about one hundred and twenty miles from the royal city. There, on the same day—namely, on the Kalends of September—the life of the deceased king came to an end, and the acclamation of the people which we have just described arose over the election [Note: Id., “pre-election”] of the man who was to succeed him.

*For although, from that time onward, divine providence, the panting vows of the common people, and their obedience had already surrounded the same man with the great offices of royal dignity, he nevertheless did not permit himself to be anointed by the hands of the priest until he had reached the royal city and sought the ancestral seat of antiquity [Note: Id., “the throne”], where it would be suitable for him both to receive the banners of sacred anointing [Note: Id., “of the anointing”] and patiently to endure the agreement of those who were far away in his election [Note: Ms., “on account of the pre-election of himself”]. Clearly, he did not want it to be thought that, driven by a hasty ambition for the kingship, he had usurped or stolen—rather than received from the Lord—the sign of such glory.*

Nevertheless, postponing the matter with prudent solemnity [Note: The nineteenth day of September was adopted by Juan de Mariana in his Latin history; why he inserted the twenty-ninth in the Spanish version, I do not know. We would wish this error corrected in the two latest Madrid editions], on the nineteenth day after he had received the kingship he entered the city of Toledo.

### 4

But when they had come to the place where he was to receive the sign of holy anointing, in the praetorian church, namely that of Saints Peter and Paul, he was already conspicuous in royal attire. Standing before the divine altar, he restored the faith to the people according to custom. Then, as he bent his knees, the oil of blessing was poured over his head by the hands of the holy bishop Quiricus [Note: The manuscript omits “his”], and an abundance of blessing was bestowed, so that this sign of salvation immediately shone forth.

For at once, from the very crown of his head where the oil had been poured, a vapor resembling smoke rose upward in the form of a column over his head; and from that very place on his head a bee seemed to leap forth, which clearly foretold some sign of coming prosperity [Note: F.: “which … foretold the appearance of a certain sign of prosperity.”].

*It will perhaps not be superfluous to have prefaced these matters, so that posterity may know how manfully he ruled the kingdom. He attained the height of kingship not only unwillingly, but also by proceeding in due order through such great stages and under the compelled pressure of the whole nation.*

### 5

In the glorious days of this man, the land of Gaul, the foster-mother of treachery, is branded with an infamous designation. Afflicted, as it were, by an immeasurable fever of disloyalty, it fed upon the members of the disloyal whom it had itself produced. For what cruel or slippery thing was absent there [Note: Id., “in it”], where there existed a conspirators’ gathering, the sign of treachery, obscenity of conduct, fraud in business, venal judgment, and—a brothel of Jews blaspheming against our Savior and Lord, worse than all these things?

That land thus, so to speak, prepared its own ruin through the birth of its own destruction, and from the viperous offspring of its womb nourished the snare of its own overthrow. For while it had already long been afflicted by these various fevers, suddenly, through the fall of one wicked head, a storm of disloyalty arose within it, and the ascent of treachery passed through one man to many [Note: Ms., “agreement.”]

### 6

The head of this tyranny, according to the report of his crime, was Ilderic. He was administering the affairs of the city of Nîmes under comital authority and had taken upon himself not merely the name but also the title and practice of disloyalty, joining to himself as associates in his wickedness the detestable Gumildus, bishop of the see of Maguelonne, and Ranimirus, an abbot [Note: Mariana consistently, and mistakenly, calls this abbot Remigius. The editors of the aforementioned editions would also have done well to correct this blemish].

This head of crime, while kindling the fire of his disloyalty in various places, attempted to draw the bishop of Nîmes, the blessed Aregius, into the stigma of treachery. When he saw him resisting his schemes with pure speech and steadfast heart, he deprived him of the dignity of his rank and place, loaded him with the weight of chains, and handed him over to the Franks in the regions of Gaul to be mocked. Then, in place of the removed bishop, he installed as bishop his associate in treachery, Ranimirus [Note: Ms., “Ranimirus the abbot.”]

In his election no order was observed, nor was any decision of the prince or metropolitan awaited. Instead, with a certain elevation of proud mind, against the prohibitions of the forefathers, he was ordained by only two bishops of a foreign people. After so great an act of presumption had been accomplished, the three men—those poisonous seeds of every treachery, namely Ilderic, Gumildus, and Ranimirus—established the boundaries of their conspiracy and divided the land of Gaul between themselves from the place called Camel Mountain to Nîmes, adding it to their conspiracy, so that disloyalty might thereby be separated from loyalty [Note: Id., “is separated.”]

Then, gathering their forces, they ravaged the citizens, exhausted their resources, and plundered the entire province of Gaul.

### 7

This report reached the prince, and soon, to extinguish the name of the seditious, he sent an army into Gaul under the command of Paul. Paul marched with the army at a sluggish pace [Note: F., “at a sudden pace”]; by delaying, he weakened the army. He himself also refrained from battle and did not direct the first attacks against the enemy. By such conduct he removed the minds of the young men from the fury of battle in which they were burning.

Thus Paul, transformed in mind into Saul, while unwilling to advance on behalf of the faith, attempted to act against the faith. Enticed by ambition for the kingdom, he was suddenly stripped of faith. He stained the promised loyalty of the devout prince, forgot his obligation to his homeland [Note: Ms., “obligations”], and, as someone has said, secretly seized a tyranny quickly matured and armed it publicly.
