He carried out these things by a certain secret plan, so that the royal height he desired might be seen before it could be known, after attracting to himself as associates in his treachery Ranosindus, duke of the province of Tarragona, and Hildigisus, who was still serving in the office of a *gardingus*. Intending to accomplish this wish of his perverse desire with incredible speed, as I may put it, he gathered peoples from every side and falsely announced that he was going to fight against the rebels.

*He appointed a day and designated a place to which they were to come in order to conquer Gaul [Note: Id., “to fight in Gaul.”] He learned of this through the very subtle report [Note: F., “narrative”] of certain people. Argebadus, bishop of the see of Narbonne, a man venerable in life and well suited by his concern for saving the people, tried, as was proper against a tyrant, to prevent him from entering the city.*

But this intention did not escape Paul either. Therefore, before that bishop could put what he had planned into effect, Paul suddenly entered the city of Narbonne with his army at reckless speed [Note: Ms., “with his own speed”], forestalled the bishop’s ambush by his promptness [Note: F., “by acting promptly”], and ordered the city gates to be closed under the protection of a delegated garrison of armed men [Note: Ms., “to be watched”]. When the whole army had gathered around, Paul himself, that serpentine head of treachery, stood in the midst with some of his associates and first rebuked the bishop, asking why he was trying to prevent him from entering the city.

### 8

After this, intending to reveal his plan of tyranny, changing the loyalty of the people by another argument of fraud, and inflaming each man’s spirit to inflict injuries—already decreed by fate—upon the prince Wamba, Paul himself first swore that he could no longer regard Wamba as king or remain any longer in his service [Note: Id., “I, Paul, cannot have him as king of men, and it does not have ‘him’”]. Rather, he said:

“Choose from among yourselves the head of government [Note: Id., “of the government”], to whom the whole assembly of the people may yield and whom it may appear that we should have as prince [Note: Id., “from among these.”]”

Then one of the conspirators, Ranosindus, an associate in that wicked plan, designated Paul as king for himself and wished Paul, not another, soon to become king for the peoples [Note: Id., “for other peoples.”]. But when Paul saw that the advancement of his plan was at hand, he immediately gave his consent to his own desire and even compelled them all to swear allegiance to him.

After this he seized the kingdom [Note: D., “snatched it up”] and, by wicked presumption, drew to himself through the work of treachery that troop of conspirators whom he had not captured by the advantage of arms [Note: F. has incorrectly “captured”]. For he easily made Hilderic, Gumildus, and Ranimirus associates of his treachery.

Why say more? The whole land of Gaul suddenly conspired to take up the arms of sedition, and it attempted to make not only Gaul but also part of the province of Tarragona an ally of its rebellion [Note: Ms.: “not only Gaul, but also some part of the province of Tarragona attempts the cothurnus of rebellion”]. Thus all Gaul suddenly became a gathering-place of the disloyal, a cave of treachery, an assembly of traitors [Note: Id., “of the ruined.”]

Then, wishing to increase the number of his associates in treachery, Paul brought forward and promised gifts, recruited multitudes of Franks and Vascones to fight in his support, and remained in Gaul with a multitude of enemies, awaiting the outcome of the most welcome [Note: D., “most grave”] moment at which he might advance into Spain to fight [Note: Ms., corruptly, “with intervals”] and vindicate the royal height he had obtained.

### 9

At that time, while these events were taking place in Gaul, the devout prince Wamba was advancing to conquer the fierce peoples of the Vascones and was staying in the region of Cantabria. When news of what was happening in Gaul reached the prince’s ears, the matter was immediately reported to the leading men of the palace for deliberation: whether they could proceed from there into Gaul to fight, or whether, returning to their own territory, they should gather forces from everywhere and undertake the journey of such great length with a numerous army.

When the prince himself saw many of them wavering in this twofold counsel [Note: D., “swimming”], he addressed them all with this common admonition [Note: The manuscript omits “all”; the manuscript also omits “common”]:

“Behold, young men, you have heard of the evil that has arisen, and you have learned with what defense the instigator of this sedition has armed himself. It is therefore necessary to forestall the enemy, so that he may be met in battle before he grows in his own blaze. It would be shameful for us either not to go out to meet men with whom we are about to fight or to return to our homes before they perish.

“It ought to seem disgraceful to us that a man who could not subdue our rebels with his own arms should dare to resist men of such glory, and that one who was unable to overcome the skin of a single, most contemptible man for the peace of his homeland should dare to present himself as an enemy to a nation—as though judging us everywhere to be effeminate and soft, incapable of resisting his tyranny by any arms, any strength, or any counsels.

“For what virtue does that doomed man possess if he engages in conflict with us by fighting with the strength of the Franks? We know their battle very well, and it is not uncertain. Therefore, it would be shameful for you to fear the testudo [Note: Ms., “testudine”] and battle lines of those whose courage you know to be always weaker.

*“But if he relies on the conspiracy of the Gauls, it must be considered a disgrace that the tyranny should be vindicated, so that our achievements should yield in the farthest corner of the earth [Note: The manuscript omits “our”], and that those in whom the kingdom has spread wide should be disturbed by the movements of men whom they always defend in the capacity of protectors.*

*“Whether they are Gauls or Franks, let them, if they please, consider the crime of such a great conspiracy something to be avenged [Note: Thus the manuscript; F. has: “consider the crime.” We nevertheless …]; we must vindicate the name of our glory with avenging arms [Note: D., “only.”] For we have to contend not with women but with men. Yet it remains well known that neither can the Franks ever resist the Goths, nor can the Gauls accomplish anything of great valor without our aid.*

“If you object to the lack of provisions or vehicles, it will be more glorious for us, having set everything else aside, to win triumph amid hardships than to finish carefully prepared wars amid abundance. For a more exalted virtue always ennobles strength through greater endurance than the provision of resources does [Note: The manuscript is corrupt: “For the narrower virtue always …”].

“Rise now to the standard of victory [Note: Ms., corruptly: “For the narrower … rise to victory”], destroy the name of the traitors. While the heat of passion is present, there must be no delay in hastening. While anger presses our spirits against the enemy, no hindrance should hold us back. Rather, if it can be done without interruption, we should undertake the journey we have begun; in this way the camps of our enemies can be overthrown much more easily [Note: F.: “Rather, if it could be done without interruption, we ought to undertake the journey we have begun. In this way they could much more easily,” etc.]. For, as a certain wise man says, anger is powerful when present but grows weak when delayed.

“There is therefore no need to turn back the soldier whom an eager advance has made victorious [Note: Ms., “makes victorious”]. We must not frustrate the direct route [Note: F., “There is no need for us to be frustrated by a direct journey”]. Let us therefore advance from here to inflict defeat upon the Vascones; then let us hasten at once to extinguish the name of the seditious.”

### 10

At these words everyone’s spirits grow hot, and they wish to do what is commanded. Soon he entered the regions of Vasconia with the entire army. There, for seven days, throughout the open plains in every direction [Note: F., incorrectly, “in various directions”], devastation and hostility, together with the burning of camps and houses, were carried out so forcefully that the Vascones themselves, abandoning the ferocity of their spirits, desired—not so much by prayers as by gifts—that their lives be spared and peace granted to them.

Accordingly, after receiving hostages, collecting tribute, and establishing peace, he ascended [Note: Ms., “he received”], intending to proceed by the direct route into Gaul, and passed through the cities of Calahorra and Huesca. From there he selected commanders and divided the army into three divisions: one part was to make for the Castle of Libya, which is the chief place of Cerretania; the second was to proceed through the city of Ausona toward the middle of the Pyrenees; the third was to march along the public road beside the seacoast [Note: F., “the maritime shore”]. The devout prince himself, with a numerous body of warriors, followed those who went ahead.

But because the disorderly conduct of some among our men not only thirsted for plunder but also perpetrated the crime of adultery while burning houses, the prince already mentioned avenged crimes of this and similar kinds with such force of discipline that you would have thought him imposing heavier punishments upon them than if they had acted as enemies against him. This is attested by the severed foreskins of certain adulterers, upon whom he inflicted this loss as punishment for fornication.

For he said:

“Behold, the judgment of war is already imminent, and you delight in prostituting your soul? And I believe that you are approaching the trial of battle. Take care lest you perish in your own filth. For if I do not avenge these things, I am already bound to leave this place [Note: D., “about to be bound”]. I shall go for this purpose, and I shall be seized by God’s just judgment if, seeing the wickedness of the people, I do not punish it myself [Note: F., “if I, seeing … do not punish it”]. Here the priest Eli, that man recognized in the divine Scriptures, ought to provide an example for me: when he refused to rebuke his sons for the enormity of their crimes, he heard that they had fallen in battle. He himself, following his sons, died with a broken neck.

“These things, therefore, must be feared by us; and thus, if we remain cleansed of crime, there can be no doubt that we shall win triumph over the enemy.”

Under this discipline, as has been said, the prince already mentioned led the army forward gloriously, keeping the conduct of each man under divine laws. With the passing of the days he saw both the battle arrangements and the victory of the fighting prospering for him [Note: F., “ruling”]. The first of all the rebellious cities, Barcelona, was brought under the authority of the devout prince; then Gerona was subjected.

To Amator, the venerable bishop of this city, that same pestilent Paul had sent the following letter.

### 11

[Col. 0775A] “I have heard [Note: Id., “I have heard”] that King Wamba is planning to come against us with an army, but let not your heart be troubled by this. For I do not think that this will happen [Note: D. omits “will happen”]. Nevertheless, whichever of the two of us your Holiness first sees approaching with an army [Note: F., “there your Holiness”], believe that you have him as your lord, and you ought to remain in his favor.”

The wretched man himself wrote these words, not knowing what just judgment he had pronounced against himself [Note: Id., “and not knowing”]. Accordingly, the devout prince, wisely interpreting the words of this writing, is said to have declared:

“Paul did not speak these words in his writings of his own accord [Note: Id., “Paul did not speak these words in his writings,” etc.]. But although unknowingly, I judge that here he prophesied.”

After this the prince departed from Gerona and, marching in warlike attacks [Perhaps “in wagons,” as below, section 27], reached the ridges of the Pyrenees. There, while the army rested for two days [Note: Id., “having rested”], he arranged the army across the backs of the Pyrenees in the three divisions mentioned above [Note: Id., “three troops”], and captured with a remarkable triumph of victory the Pyrenean fortresses called Collioure, Vulturaria, and the Castle of Libya [Note: Id. incorrectly, “began to capture”], subduing them completely.

A great quantity of gold and silver found in those camps fell as booty to the armies [Note: D.: “Finding much gold and silver in these camps, which … to the numerous armies”]. For an assault was made upon the fortress called the Defiles by two commanders after armies had been sent ahead. There Ranosindus and Hildigisus, together with the rest of the troop of traitors who had gathered to defend the fortress itself [Note: D., “had fought”], were also captured. Thus, with their hands bound behind their backs, they were brought before the prince.

Wittimirus, however, one of the conspirators, had been stationed at Sordonia. When he perceived that our men had broken in [Note: F., “who had shut himself in Sordonia, perceiving that our men had broken in,” etc.], he immediately fled and went to bring Paul in Narbonne news of so great a disaster. This greatly [Note: Ms., “gravely”] made the tyrant afraid.

The devout prince, after subduing the army of the aforementioned fortresses, descended to the plains beyond the crossing of the Pyrenees and waited for only two days in order to gather the army into one body [Note: Id., “to a single place”].

### 12

But when a multitude of armies gathered from different regions had increased into one body [Note: Id., incorrectly, “when an army gathered into one body”], there was no delay in taking a position. Immediately he sent the selected number of warriors, under four commanders, before him to attack Narbonne. He also dispatched another army to advance for a naval battle.

Indeed, only a very few days had passed since the rebel Paul had departed from Narbonne by a shameful flight [Note: F., “from Narbonne”], having learned that the party of the devout prince was advancing with such a fortunate outcome [Note: Id., “with a fortunate outcome”]. Paul himself, claiming that city as subject to his own authority, fortified it with a numerous garrison of traitors and entrusted the conduct of the battle to his commander Wittimirus.

When our army courteously urged him [Note: F., “exhorted him”] to surrender the city without bloodshed, he flatly refused. After the city gates had been closed [Note: Ms., “with the gates shut”], he cursed the army of the devout prince from the wall. He also heaped curses upon the prince himself and tried to drive the army away with threats [Note: F., “to throw the army into confusion”].

The multitude on our side could not tolerate this. Inflamed by a sudden kindling of their hearts [Note: D., “by a sudden accession”], they aimed a shower of weapons at the faces of the traitors. Why say more? A terrible battle was joined on both sides, and the two parties resisted each other in turn as though exchanging arrows. But when our men despaired, they not only pierced the rebels fighting on the wall with arrows, but also hurled such showers of stones into the city that the city itself seemed to be overwhelmed by the roar of voices and the clatter of stones.

Thus, from approximately the fifth hour of the day until the eighth hour of that same day, the two sides fought fiercely. But when the courage of our men grew hot [Note: F., “the spirits of our men grow hot”], they could not endure the delay of victory [The printed text has “dilationem,” “delay”; the note gives “dilectionem,” “love”], but advanced nearer to the gates to fight [Note: Id., “they advance to fight”].

Then, with a victorious hand through the Lord, they set fire to the gates, leapt upon the walls, and entered the city as victors. There they subjected the rebels to themselves. While Wittimirus, still bearing arms, was making for the church, he was thrown into confusion by the approach of our men. Behind the altar of the blessed Virgin Mary he declared that he would avenge himself—not out of reverence for the place, but with an avenging sword [Note: Id., “in reverence”]—holding a sword in his right hand and threatening each person with death.

To suppress the swelling of this madness at once [Note: Id., “the rumor”], one of our men, having cast aside his weapons along with the others, seized a board in his hand and advanced against him with a furious blow. When he tried with great force to strike him with the board, Wittimirus immediately fell trembling to the ground, was captured, and had the iron weapon removed from his hand. Then, dragged away shamefully [Note: Id., “manfully”], he was bound tightly under the weight of chains and beaten, together with his associates, with whom he had tried to defend the city.

### 13

After the city of Narbonne had been conquered and subjected, the army directed its march to pursue Paul, who had withdrawn to Nîmes in order to defend himself [Note: Id., “directs it”]. Then the cities of Béziers [Note: Ms., “Betere”] and Agde were immediately subjected.

In the city of Maguelonne, however, Gumildus, the bishop of that place, seeing the army surrounding him for a siege and observing that the city itself was being encircled not so much by those who had approached to fight by land [Note: F., “by the lands”] as by those who had traveled across the sea to wage a naval battle, was terrified by the disaster threatening him. He took the path of escape and joined himself to Paul at Nîmes [Note: D., “withdrew”].

But when the army of Spain perceived that Gumildus had escaped, it soon captured the city of Maguelonne with a victory no different from the former [Note: F. incorrectly, “began to capture”].

When our men then attempted to attack the city of Nîmes in ordered battle formation, the first phase of the fighting was assigned to four commanders with a chosen troop of warriors. Their selected young men, nearly thirty thousand in number, went ahead of the prince.

With a noble advance they hurried toward Nîmes, where Paul had gone to fight with the army of Gaul, or with the assembly of the Franks. They forestalled the ambushes of the rebels [Note: D., “the rebel, forestalling”], and after completing the course of their hurried march throughout the night, they suddenly appeared as the rising light of day began to show [Note: F., “they appeared”]. The battle lines of our men were arranged with equal preparation of arms and courage.

When the enemy saw them from the city, supposing that they would have to fight against only a few, they resolved to meet them in the open fields. But suspecting a trick and an ambush, they preferred to carry on the battle within the city from their walls [Note: The manuscript omits “their”], rather than endure outside the city the unforeseen dangers of open peril [Note: Ms., “open dangers”]. They also awaited the arrival of other peoples to assist them [Note: F., “who were attacking”].

But when the sun shone back upon the earth [Note: Id., “was poured over the earth”], our men joined battle. The first phase of the fighting was carried out amid the sounds of trumpets and a cloud of stones. As soon as the sound of the trumpets rang out, our men converged from every side with a din of voices, attacked the city walls with showers of stones [Note: Ms., “with blows”], and drove back those stationed along the wall with every kind of missile, spear, and arrow. The enemy, however, also cast weapons of many kinds at our men in resistance [Note: Id., “had weapons cast.”]

But what more can I say? The battle was fought more fiercely by both sides; each contended on an equal balance [Note: The manuscript omits “on an equal balance”]; the conflict was waged on equal terms. Neither our men nor the enemy yielded in the battle they had joined. Thus they fought throughout that entire day beneath the two-edged blade of uncertain victory [Note: F., “beneath the two-edged blade”].

14. One of the instigators of the sedition, seeing the battle being fiercely pressed and preparing to taunt our men from the wall, composed these words and shouted:

“What are you doing here,” he said, “standing fast and fighting so fiercely, you who are doomed to die? Why do you not return to your own homes? Or do you perhaps wish to meet the fate of death before the setting of your lives? Rather, why do you not seek the precipitous rocks where you may hide yourselves, when the appearance of our aid has become evident? [Note: [Col. 0779D] The manuscript has *quam*, “when”; [Col. 0780D] F. has *paruerit*, “has appeared,” instead of *apparuerit*.] Believe me, then, that I have pitied you, knowing the outcome of the affair and that [Col. 0779C] the arrival of relief is imminent. [Note: [Col. 0780D] The manuscript has *eventurum*, “about to be,” instead of *eventum*, “outcome”; F. has *superventuri*, “about to arrive,” instead of *superventurum*, “about to arrive.”] For I know very well how many kinds of auxiliary forces are coming to join us in battle. [Col. 0780A] This is now the third day since I set out from there and have been hastening here. Knowing this, therefore, I await with grief the end of your wretched display. I shall show you your prince, for whom you have come to fight, bound; I shall consign him to insults and mock him with taunts. [Note: [Col. 0780D] F. has *paruerit* rather than *apparuerit* above; the text transmitted here is punctuated and understood accordingly.] It is not expedient, then, for you to fight here so savagely on his behalf, since perhaps it is already certain that he has perished in an ambush laid by our men. And what is more serious, when our victory has become manifest, you will have no pardon thereafter.”

By saying this he not only failed to terrify our men, but kindled them more fiercely to the fury of battle. They approached the wall; they stood firm in combat more fiercely than they had begun, and vigorously renewed the battle that had been joined. [Note: [Col. 0780D] The edition has: “Approaching the wall, more fiercely than they had begun, they stood firm in combat,” and so forth.]

15. When these things had been carried on through the whole day, [Note: [Col. 0780D] The edition has *per spatia*, “through intervals,” instead of *spatio*, “through the span.”] night at last brought the battle to an end. Yet during the first heat of that day, while our men were still persisting in the fight with tireless courage, they sent word to the prince and requested that assistance be directed to them, taking no small precaution for their own safety—namely, lest they should be forestalled by the treachery of an alien people, or, with their strength exhausted, be overthrown by those against whom they were fighting and so perish.

And the matter was well handled. For when the prince learned that Paul, the leader of the tyranny, was fighting against our men, there was no further delay. With marvelous speed in arranging matters, therefore, he sent nearly ten thousand selected men from the army, under the command of the general Wandemir, to aid the combatants. [Note: [Col. 0780D] The edition has *Wandemarum*, “Wandemar,” instead of *Wandemirum*.] They were to remain awake throughout the night and complete their hastened journey, so that by their arrival they might not so much break the enemy as promptly reach our men and encourage their spirits. [Note: [Col. 0780D] The edition has *sui*, “of themselves,” instead of *suo*, “by their”; and *pervenirent*, “might reach,” instead of *praevenirent*, “might arrive before.”]

But when the exhausted guards’ watchfulness had already, in a sense, despaired of holding the enemy shut in for long, they suddenly saw the aid sent to them. At once sleep fled from their eyes, and, their spirits rejoicing and their strength restored, the battle was brought to an end by those who came to meet them. [Col. 0781A] [Note: [Col. 0781D] The manuscript has *definit occursus*, “the encounter is ended,” instead of *definitur ab occursantibus*, “is brought to an end by those coming to meet them.”]

16. Dawn had now left its saffron bed, and the hostile multitude crowded along the wall, looking out, saw through the clear line of light that the ranks of the combatants had grown more numerous than those it had seen on the previous day.

Then Paul himself, the head of the tyranny, came forward to climb a certain projecting watchtower in order to view so great a spectacle. [Note: [Col. 0781D] F. has *quodam speculo*, “a certain mirror,” instead of *quadam prominenti specula*, “a projecting watchtower.”] As soon as he saw our ranks drawn up, he immediately, so it is said, lost heart and declared in these words:

“I recognize,” he said, “that all this battle-array proceeds from my rival. This is he himself, and I think there is no other. [Note: [Col. 0781D] D. omits *hic ipse est*, “this is he himself.”] I recognize him in his arrangements.” [Note: [Col. 0781D] F. has *In suis enim eum*, “For in his own arrangements I recognize him.”]

Saying this and similar things, he recovered his courage and inflamed his men to battle.

“Do not,” he said, “be disturbed by fear. [Col. 0781B] This is that famous Gothic valor alone, which used to boast with customary recklessness that it was coming to overcome us. Believe that the prince himself is here, and his entire army. You have nothing further to fear. Their famous valor formerly served both for the defense of their own people and for the terror of other nations. But now all their strength for fighting has withered; all their knowledge of warfare has failed. They have no custom of battle, no experience of engaging in conflict. [Col. 0782A] Or, if they should join battle in a single mass, they will immediately flee to their appointed hiding places, because their degenerate spirits cannot endure the burden of combat. Indeed, when you begin to fight, you yourselves will prove the truth of what I am saying. There is therefore nothing greater for you to fear, since you see both the king and the army itself present here.”

At this, several of his men maintained that the king could not advance without standards. He replied that the king had approached with the standards of the military companies hidden, in order to make his enemies understand that another army still remained, with which he himself would later advance, as one who would come with a force more numerous than that with which he had previously arrived. [Note: [Col. 0781D] In the same manuscript, *manu* is absent.] But in saying this he was practicing deception and contriving a fraud, so that those whom he could not overcome by valor he might humble through deceitful counsel and bring to fear. [Note: [Col. 0781D] The edition corruptly reads: “But while he says all this, deception—he says—is contriving fraud.”]

17. He had not yet finished these words [Note: [Col. 0782D] F. has *expleverat*, “had completed,” instead of *compleverat*, “had finished,”] when suddenly the trumpets of war sounded among our men [Note: [Col. 0782D] The manuscript has *tubis*, “with trumpets,” instead of *tubae*, “trumpets,”] and, beginning the battle, they renewed the appearance of the previous day’s fighting. But the enemy, placing their confidence of victory more in the walls than in their own strength, remained within the city, cast javelins from the wall [Note: [Col. 0782D] F. has *spicula*, “darts,” instead of *jacula*, “javelins,”] and renewed the revived contests with our men.

Thus the impetus of battle boiled up on both sides, but the courage of our men appeared the fiercer. [Col. 0783A] For when they fought with all their strength and pierced the enemy within the city with weapons of various kinds, many men of the foreign nation, severely wounded and admiring both our courage and our steadfastness, turned upon Paul and said:

“We do not see among the Goths that sluggishness in fighting which you described. For we see in them great boldness and perseverance in winning. The wounds we have received teach us this: among other things, they hurl such powerful blows against the enemy that the crash itself terrifies one before the impact extinguishes life.”

Terrified by their words, Paul was already being shattered by blow after blow of despair.

18. But while our men, prevailing with increasing firmness, grieved that their victory was being delayed, [Note: [Col. 0783D] F. has *dimicantes*, “fighting,” instead of *dominantes*, “prevailing”; the manuscript reads *cum victoriam*, “when victory,” with the remainder differing.] they rose up with still greater determination, reckoning themselves defeated in every respect if they did not conquer quickly. Moved, therefore, by a fiercer ardor than before, they battered the city walls with continuous blows of battle almost until the fifth hour of the day, hurled showers of stones with an enormous crash, set fire to the gates by applying fire beneath them, and broke in through the small openings in the walls. [Col. 0783B]

Then, entering the city gloriously, they opened a way for themselves with the sword. But when the enemy could not withstand the fierceness of our men, they shut themselves inside the Arenas, which were enclosed by the stronger walls of an older building, seeking to fortify themselves there. [Note: [Col. 0783D] F. has *antiquioribus aedificiis*, “older buildings,” instead of *antiquioris aedificii*, “of an older building.”]

When some of our men were seen pursuing those who had rushed out for plunder, they were immediately intercepted and slaughtered before they could take refuge in that fortress of the Arenas. [Note: [Col. 0783D] The edition has *e nostris*, “from our men,” instead of *a nostris*.] Many of our common soldiers, however, who had been eager for plunder, were cut down by the sword. [Col. 0783C] [Note: [Col. 0783D] The edition has *praeventione occisi*, “killed by interception,” instead of *gladii perventione concisi*, “cut down by the sword.”]

*Not because they accomplished this openly by valor among the many, but as if in the manner of brigands: those whom they had learned had approached the enclosures [perhaps “camps”] of the Arenas for the sake of plunder, they struck down more easily, since they would not have found even two of them united together, but separated.* [Note: [Col. 0783D] The source reads *claustris*; perhaps *castris*, “camps.” The sentence is marked in the source with asterisks.]

19. A new sedition also arose among the very rebels. While the citizens or inhabitants themselves, suspecting treachery, fled to some of their own people, they killed with avenging swords those against whom suspicion had turned. Thus Paul himself, seeing one of his own household being slaughtered before him by the hands of his own men, cried out in a lamentable voice that the man was his slave, yet even then he did nothing to help the dying man. [Note: [Col. 0783D] F. omits *et*, “and”; D. has *vernulam*, “little slave,” instead of *vernulum*, “slave.”]

By now Paul himself had become bloodless and trembling, and was despised by his own men, so that one might have thought that he was entreating rather than commanding the others. [Note: [Col. 0783D] F. has *existimaretur*, “he might be thought,” instead of *extimares*, “one might have thought.”]

For he himself was now suspected by the inhabitants, together with the others who had come with him from Spain, lest he should devise their betrayal in order to secure his own release; while the Spaniards feared that, after the inhabitants had been put to death, they themselves might pass over to the prince.

Why say more? A pitiable spectacle of battle arose within the city. On both sides the more pestilential crowd fell; on both sides men were overthrown; on both sides they were slaughtered. Those who escaped our men’s swords were perishing by the swords of their own people.

The city was therefore filled with a mingled slaughter and with the corpses of the dead. [Note: [Col. 0784D] The manuscript reads: “The city was filled with mingled slaughter, with deaths and with human corpses.”]

*Wherever the sight of the eyes extended, human slaughter or herds of slaughtered animals lay exposed. [Note: [Col. 0784D] The edition reads: “Either human slaughter or animals placed beneath appeared as herds.”] The crossroads were full of corpses, and the rest of the ground was congealed with blood.* [Col. 0784A]

A pitiable funeral scene was visible in the houses, and wherever one searched the hidden parts of the dwellings, one found the dead lying there. [Note: [Col. 0784D] The edition has *patentes*, “exposed,” instead of *jacentes*, “lying.”] You could also see human corpses lying throughout the streets of the city, with a threatening expression and a certain inhuman ferocity, as though they were still stationed in the very line of battle. [Col. 0784C]

Yet their color was disfigured, their skin sallow, the horror immense, and the stench intolerable. [Note: [Col. 0784D] F. reads: “as though they had been stationed,” followed by the rest of the sentence.]

Some of the dead who had received mortal wounds even pretended to be dead in order to escape the cause of death; *yet, exhausted both by the wound in their throats and by the calamity of hunger, they themselves did not escape death—except for one, of whom it was proved that by pretending death he had purchased his life.* [Col. 0785A]

20. Paul, having now laid aside the savagery of the tyranny, lamented these and similar events with a great sigh of the heart, since he could neither resist the enemy nor in any way help his own men.

A certain man born from his own family nevertheless approached him in order to taunt him.

“Why are you standing here?” he said. “Where are your advisers, who led you to this mockery of calamity? [Note: [Col. 0785D] F. has *perduxere*, “led,” instead of *perduxerunt*.] What did it profit you to rise up against your own people, when now, amid such a great slaughter, you are able to benefit neither yourself nor your own?” [Col. 0785B]

Saying this, he taunted him, provoked less by a desire to insult than by an impulse of bitterness. But when Paul urged him with gentle words to spare his grief and not add one humiliation to another, the man at last, while still standing on the marble steps on which he had come to taunt him, made a swift descent. Thus, surrounded by his own men before Paul’s eyes, he was slaughtered and fell dead.

Paul said to them: “Why are you seeking this man?” [Note: [Col. 0785D] F. has *hinc*, “from here,” instead of *huic*, “this man.”]

“He is mine,” he replied. “Let him not perish.”

And he begged with repeated cries that the man be spared. But, already held in contempt, as though he himself too were about to die immediately, Paul could not be heard.

Then, driven by utter despair, he laid aside the royal garments which he had acquired through the ambition of tyranny rather than through lawful succession, utterly wasted away.

By a marvelous and hidden judgment of God, it happened that on the very day when the tyrant laid down the kingdom he had acquired, the religious prince received from the Lord the scepter of rule. For that day was the first of September, on which it was established that our prince had earlier assumed the royal dignity. [Note: [Col. 0785D] F. has *praedictum*, “the aforementioned,” instead of *pridem*, “earlier.”]

This, then, is the day on which, as the circle of the returning year came around, the storming of the city became manifest. On this day the royal garment assumed by the tyrant was removed; on this day bloody vengeance was inflicted upon the enemies.

21. The third day after these events had now arrived, when Paul himself, after the deep sighs of the night, awaited his final funeral. [Note: [Col. 0785D] F. has *exspectabat*, “was awaiting,” instead of *exspectat*, “awaits.”] When morning came, he began to speak with those whom he had as followers of his treason [Note: [Col. 0785D] The edition has *perditionis*, “of his destruction,” instead of *proditionis*, “of his treason,”] so that they might either bid him a final farewell or, if they could, still take some measure for their own salvation. [Col. 0786B]

Then Argebadus, bishop of the church of Narbonne, was sent by common agreement to the prince, to ask for life and to beg pardon for their offenses. For, after sacrifices had been offered to God, he was already in the very garments with which he had received the grace of communion in the holy sharing of the Lord’s body and blood—garments in which he would take care not so much to undergo the final losses of death as to be wrapped in them unburied. For burial would rightly be denied him if he should receive the death deserved for his deed.

[Note: [Col. 0785D–0786D] The manuscript is corrupt here: “For, with the offerings removed from the sacrifices, and in those very garments which some received as the grace of the Lord’s body and blood, they would take care not so much to undergo the final losses of death as to be wrapped in them unburied; for burial would be denied them if they should receive the death deserved for their deed.” The text is not clear. Lucas of Tuy offers a plainer, though shorter, version.]

Bishop Argebadus had already gone out from them to ask pardon. *And behold, seeing the prince’s swift advance with a remarkable column of warriors nearly four miles from the city,* [Col. 0787A] he leapt down from his horse to meet the prince, [Note: [Col. 0787D] F. reads *occursus*, “the encounter,” instead of *occursurus*, “about to meet”;] prostrated himself on the ground, [Note: [Col. 0787D] The edition has *desiluit*, “he leapt down,” instead of *desilivit*; it has *prostituitur*, “he is prostrated,” instead of *humo prosternitur*, “he is thrown prostrate on the ground;”] and begged pardon.

At his approach the prince held his horse for a little while and, being filled with the depths of mercy, himself also weeping, ordered that the bishop be raised from the ground.

When the man had been raised again, choked by sobs of tears, he said in a lamentable voice:

“Alas! [Note: [Col. 0787D] The edition has *En*, “Behold,” instead of *Heu*, “Alas.”] We have sinned against heaven and before you, most holy prince. We are not worthy that the outcome of your mercy should come to us, nor that the pardon granted should help us—those who have stained the faith we promised you and have fallen into so great a crime. [Note: [Col. 0787D] The edition corruptly has *summus*, “we are highest,” here and below instead of *sumus*, “we are.”]

“I beg that your mercy quickly spare us, lest the avenging sword extinguish the half-dead remnants of our people, lest the blade seek more lives than it has already claimed. Command the army now to cease from bloodshed; let citizens spare citizens. We have scarcely escaped the sword, but we beg pardon for those who are scarcely left.” [Note: [Col. 0787D] The manuscript has *venia deprecatur*, “he begs pardon,” instead of *veniam deprecamur*, “we beg pardon.”]

“Spare, then, our remnants, so that, since the slaughter of death has already spread among the rest of our people, at least some may remain for you to pity. For if you do not quickly forbid the slaughter, not even the inhabitants themselves will remain to defend the city.” [Col. 0787B]

22. Moved by these words, the religious prince was not inexorable amid his tears. *For in the deep secret place of his heart he knew that everything which was said to have perished would entirely perish for him if he did not grant pardon to the man who begged for it.* [Col. 0787D]

The prince therefore replied to the petitioner:

“Hold firmly to what I say. *Overcome by your prayers, I grant you the lives for which you have asked.* [Col. 0788A] I will not destroy them with an avenging sword. *I will shed no one’s blood today, nor will I ever extinguish a life.* Yet the offense of such men will not pass unpunished.”

The venerable man continued for a long time to press his request, asking that, since the prince had granted him their lives, he exercise no punishment against them. [Note: [Col. 0787D] F. has *diutius*, “for longer”; the manuscript has *divine*, “divinely”; we retain *diutine*, “for a long time,” from the manuscript tradition of Lucas of Tuy mentioned below.]

But the prince, suddenly made harsher by swift anger, said:

“Do not impose further conditions upon me, since it is enough that I have granted you their lives. [Note: [Col. 0787D] The edition has *imponitis*, “you impose,” instead of *imponatis*, “do not impose.”] Let it suffice for you alone that I have spared you completely; but concerning the others I promise none of these things.”

At this he grew hot with a certain burning of spirit and, advancing rapidly, hastened to take possession of the triumph of victory: *sending the embassy ahead of him so that our men would abstain from battle until the entire strength of the army, together with the prince, advanced to seize the inner parts of the city.* [Col. 0788B]

23. At last, after hastening along the route of his departure, the prince arrived at the city with an army whose terrifying display inspired amazement. *For there were there frightening standards of war. When the sun shone back from the shields, the earth itself glittered with a double light. The radiant weapons likewise increased the sun’s brilliance beyond its usual strength.*

But what can I say? Who could explain the display of the armies there, the splendor of the weapons, the appearance of the young men, and the harmony of their spirits, where divine protection was shown by an evident sign?

For, so it is reported, the army of the religious prince was seen by a man of a foreign nation to be protected by angelic sentinels, and the angels themselves, flying above the camp of that army, gave signs of their protection. [Col. 0789A]

But, leaving these and similar matters in silence for a little while, let us follow the order of the work we have undertaken.

24. When the prince perceived that the army had now been gathered into one body, stationed about one stadium from the city, he was moved by an incredible ardor of spirit. He arranged the commanders, concealed the common soldiers, divided the ranks, and instructed them in the ways by which they should complete the battle. [Note: [Col. 0789D] F. has *pugna conficeretur*, “the battle might be completed,” instead of *pugnam conficerent*, “they should complete the battle.”]

*First, however, he arranged matters as they had previously been arranged: a line of brave men along the mountain ridges and the seacoast, which are joined to the regions of Gaul, so that the free and unimpeded hand of the combatants might more quickly carry out the orders for battle, since he had perceived no hostile movement from foreign peoples.* [Note: [Col. 0789D] The edition has *ora maritima*, “the seacoast,” instead of *oram maritimam*, “the edge of the seacoast”; and *eo decertandi praelii praecepta*, “the commands for fighting that battle,” instead of *quae ... praecepta*, “the commands which...”]

Then he sent selected men from among the commanders, those superior in both strength and courage, to drag Paul and the other instigators of his sedition from the caverns of the Arenas, where they had hidden themselves to escape death.

There was no delay. When they fulfilled the commands in action, Paul himself was suddenly dragged out, together with his companions, from the hidden places of the Arenas. Thus, after being lowered over the wall, he was treated with contempt.

Then all that insolent multitude of the Gallic provinces [printed correction: “of the Gauls”] and Franks, which had gathered from various directions to fight against our men, was captured and held, together with immense treasures. [Col. 0789B]

*When that treacherous band with its king had been captured and stood together, with the army standing on the right and left,* two of our commanders, sitting on horses and extending their hands, holding Paul in their midst by his hands entangled in his hair, led him forward on foot and brought him to the prince. [Col. 0790A] [Note: [Col. 0789D] D. has *inexis ... manibus*, “with hands bound,” instead of *innexas ... capillis ejus manus*, “hands entangled in his hair”; the manuscript has *oblaturum*, “about to bring him,” instead of *oblaturi*, “about to bring him.”]

25. When the prince saw him, he stretched out his hands toward heaven with tears and said:

“I praise you, O God, King of all kings, who have humbled the proud man as one wounded, and crushed my adversaries by the strength of your arm” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 11).

The prince said this and similar things, interrupted by tears. [Note: [Col. 0789D] The manuscript has *agebat*, “was doing,” instead of *aiebat*, “was saying”; F. has *interclusis*, “with tears interrupted,” instead of *interclusus*, “interrupted by tears.”]

But as soon as the same tyrant raised his eyes and saw the prince’s face, he immediately prostrated himself on the ground and loosened his belt, already lifeless and thrown into confusion by excessive fear, without attending to what was happening to him.

It was a spectacle worthy of attention: how he had come from so lofty a height—though it was the height of a usurped rank—to this sudden humiliation and complete disgrace. [Note: [Col. 0790D] The edition corruptly reads: “It was something spectacular to the eyes, how he had found himself in sudden humiliation and public disgrace from so lofty a height, though it was the height of an acquired rank.”] It was a great thing to behold how readily the condition of affairs itself had changed: so quickly you saw cast down the man whom you had previously heard praised as glorious; and the man whom the previous day had still held as king now fall with such headlong descent into ruin. [Col. 0790B] [Note: [Col. 0790D] The edition has *facile*, “easily,” instead of *facilis*, “easy”; F. has *videre*, “to see,” instead of *videres*, “you might see.”]

The prophetic saying was fully accomplished in this man:

“I saw the wicked man exalted exceedingly, and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon. And I passed by, and behold, he was no more; I sought him, and his place was not found.” [Note: [Col. 0790D] “And I passed by...” and the remainder have been added from the manuscript.]

Why say more? When Paul himself and the other captives of this faction had already been brought before the prince’s horse and were standing there [Note: [Col. 0790D] D. has *productique*, “and brought forth,” instead of *perductique*, “and brought before,”] he said:

“Why did you break out into such madness amid so great an evil, that you repaid me evil for good? But why should I delay? Go, and remain assigned to custody until judgment is pronounced concerning you. I will grant you life, even though you do not deserve it.”

Then he divided them throughout the army and handed them over to vigilant guards. [Note: [Col. 0791D] F. omits *et*, “and”; the edition has *tradit*, “he hands over,” instead of *tradiit*, “he handed over.”] All the Franks who had been captured were nevertheless ordered to be treated honorably. Some of them were born of very noble parents and had been given as hostages. The rest were some Franks and some Saxons. [Note: [Col. 0791D] The manuscript reads *Agonibus*, an uncertain form, instead of *Saxonibus*, “Saxons.”] The king sent all of them back to their own country, honored with royal generosity, on the eighteenth day after their capture, saying that a victor ought not to be merciless toward the vanquished. [Note: [Col. 0791D] The edition has *munificenti*, “with generosity,” instead of *munificentia*, “with generosity”; and *onustos*, “laden,” instead of *honoratos*, “honored.”]

26. On the first day, the day before the Kalends of September, our men began the war against the city of Nîmes. [Note: [Col. 0791D] F. wrongly omits *pridie*, “the day before,” as the following dates show.] On the following day, the Kalends of September, the city itself was stormed. On the third day, which was the fourth day before the Nones of September, [Note: [Col. 0791D] The manuscript omits *qui fuit*, “which was,”] the tyrant Paul was captured and bound in celebrated detention.

After this, however, the spirit of the religious prince, concerned with restoring the city that had been stormed, immediately repaired the breaches in the walls, renewed the burned gates, provided burial for the unburied, restored to the inhabitants the plunder that had been taken from them, and treated whatever had been wounded with public funds. [Col. 0791B]

Nevertheless, he ordered that all the wealth of the treasure which they had captured [Note: [Col. 0791D] F. wrongly has *coeperant*, “they had begun,” instead of *ceperant*, “they had captured,”] be guarded with the greatest care—not enticed by the profit of avarice, but prompted by divine love—so that things consecrated to God could more easily be separated out [Note: [Col. 0791D] The manuscript has *secernere*, “to separate,” instead of *secerni*, “to be separated”] and restored to divine worship.

For that most wicked Paul had heaped sin upon sin by adding sacrilege to tyranny. *For, as a certain wise man says, if he had not despoiled the holy churches, there would have been nothing from which his treasury could flourish.* [Col. 0791C]

Thus it happened that very many silver vessels stolen from the Lord’s treasures, and that golden crown which the prince Reccaredus of blessed memory had offered at the body of the most blessed Felix—which Paul himself had dared to place upon his mad head—were all gathered together. He took care to separate them diligently and devotedly to restore each item, as appropriate, to the church to which it belonged. [Col. 0792A]

27. The third day after the victory had now come for the victors, and Paul himself, laden with iron, was brought with the others before the prince seated on his throne.

Then, according to the custom of the ancients, he bent the curve of his back and submitted his neck to the royal feet. Thereafter, before all the armies, he was condemned together with the others by the judgment of all to suffer death, since he had prepared death for the prince. [Note: [Col. 0791D] The manuscript has *exciperent*, “they should suffer,” instead of *exciperet*, “he should suffer”; the edition has *praeparassent*, “they had prepared,” instead of *praeparasset*, “he had prepared.”]

But no sentence of death was imposed upon them; they were merely ordered to undergo the punishment of being shaved. [Col. 0792B] [Note: [Col. 0792D] D. has “as it is ordered,” instead of *praecipitur*, “it is ordered.”]

There was nevertheless a report that some Franks were coming as quickly as possible to rescue the captive. But the prince, awaiting an opportunity to fight the Franks and desiring to avenge not only this offense but also the former injuries inflicted upon his people, endured the delay with a brave spirit and awaited their arrival each day. He was preparing in every way to fight them. [Note: [Col. 0792D] The edition reads: “But the prince endured it, awaiting their arrival, with whom he was preparing in every way to fight.”]

Yet when no Franks came forward to fight, he himself resolved to meet them first, unless the hastened counsel of his own heart and of his leading men recalled him, lest the broken promise of an agreement between the two peoples become an occasion for shedding blood.

But while, as has been said, he was preparing to wage war against them, the fourth day had already passed since he had captured Paul, *and he was nevertheless still awaiting the arrival of the opposing people.* [Col. 0793A]

But no enemy expectation, no event, no hostile gathering whatsoever appeared. For the strongly fortified cities of Gaul were already, as was reported, lamenting their final destruction, and all their citizens, lest they be forestalled by our men, had abandoned the cities and wandered far and wide in uncertain settlements, securing their lives, naturally, by hiding in concealed places.

The religious prince was also encamped with his army on the plain some distance from the city of Nîmes. [Note: [Col. 0793D] F. has *Nemauso*, “Nîmes,” instead of *Nemausensi*, “of Nîmes.”] There he established his camp and surrounded it with remarkable speed by a very strong wall. [Note: [Col. 0793D] The edition has *fortissimo*, “very strongest,” instead of *firmissimo*, “very strong.”]

While he was awaiting the arrival of the enemy there, he suddenly heard from a messenger who had hastened ahead that one of the commanders of Gaul, named Lupus, had entered the territory of Béziers in a hostile manner.

Therefore, on the fifth day after he had captured Paul, he left the city of Nîmes and, hastening rapidly with his army, attempted to forestall the enemy’s reported ambushes. [Col. 0793B] [Note: [Col. 0793D] The edition wrongly has *coeperat*, “had begun,” instead of *ceperat*, “had captured.”]

But Lupus himself, near a village called Asperianus, heard that the prince had turned back and fled in such terror that the army seemed to be missing its commander and the commander his army. For, in his flight, he neither held his own men together nor could his men in any way follow him. [Note: [Col. 0793D] The edition has *in fugiendo*, “in fleeing,” instead of *fugiendo*, “by fleeing.”]

Their hearts had been so dissolved by fear that, slipping through the mountain passes and running as they scattered along the roads, they showed that they had gained their lives by the shortcut of flight, since they already saw swords hanging over their own necks. [Col. 0794A] [Note: [Col. 0793D] The manuscript has *relucrasse*, “to have regained,” instead of *lucrasse*, “to have gained”; F. has *monstrarentur*, “they were shown,” instead of *monstrarent*, “they showed.”]

They left many spoils to our armies in this confusion, both men who could not follow them and beasts of burden or goods which they had brought with them in many wagons and which would have been sufficient for their needs. [Note: [Col. 0794D] In the same source, *et*, “and,” is absent.]

Certainly, the picked force of combatants sent by the prince could already have overtaken them in their warlike vehicles [Note: [Col. 0794D] The edition has *excursibus*, “charges,” instead of *curribus*, “vehicles”]; but their flight was so disgraceful and so swift did they reach the hiding places of their own territory that they were judged to have left no trace at all by which one might know where they had fled, hidden, or halted. [Note: [Col. 0794D] The edition has *censeretur*, singular, instead of *censerentur*, plural; D. has “with no trace,” instead of “no traces.”]

28. When the prince learned that he could not find Lupus with the others [Note: [Col. 0794D] The manuscript has *possent*, “they could,” instead of *posset*, “he could”], he proceeded peacefully toward Narbonne and entered the city as a victor. [Col. 0794B]

There he appeased by his generosity the wounds of the Narbonese province—its ravaged and devoured places, the afflictions inflicted upon that land, gasping under great fevers, by the plundering and incursions of our men. [Note: [Col. 0794D] F. has *ibi*, “there,” instead of *ubi*, “where.”] He restored the damaged order by his administration and equipped it with councils. He also established the condition of affairs in remarkable peace.

He left there a selected garrison of warriors and eradicated from it the roots of every rebellion. He drove out the Jews and appointed more merciful governors over the cities, through whom the offense of so great an evil might be appeased and the land, defiled by such foulness, might be cleansed and restored to pardon by a new baptism of judgments. [Col. 0795A]

*For inasmuch as the land of Gaul, standing upright in the pride of its customary arrogance, had raised itself on the high buskin of conceit, it was so worn down by a harsher plundering and stripped of its money and devoured of its possessions that, rightly, it may be believed through this to have lost whatever rust or wickedness it had contracted.* [Note: [Col. 0795C] F. has *fastu*, “by pride,” instead of *fastus*, “pride”; D. has *cothurnose*, “in buskin fashion,” instead of *cothurno*, “on the buskin”; the manuscript has *attulerat*, “had brought,” instead of *attollerat*, “had raised”; the edition has *deterrita*, “terrified,” instead of *detrita*, “worn down”; and *caruisse*, “to have lacked,” instead of *amisisse*, “to have lost.”]

29. After exhausting and subduing Gaul, the prince traveled safely by a direct route to Spain, fearing neither any further movement of the Gauls behind him nor any ambushes of the Franks. He knew for certain that no one remained who could either stir up battles among his own people or contrive ambushes among foreign nations. [Note: [Col. 0795C] F. has *certo*, “with certainty,” instead of *certa*, “certain”; the edition has *pugnam*, singular, “battle,” instead of *pugnas*, plural, “battles.”]

With such courage and steadfastness of spirit did he regard the barbarian peoples around him that he not only did not fear them but despised them. While he was still in Gaul, he also gave the entire army a gracious account at a place called Canaba, explaining that they had departed successfully, and immediately discharged them all from that place. [Col. 0795B] [Note: [Col. 0795C] The edition has *nuncupatur*, “is called,” instead of *nuncupabatur*, “was called.”]

He himself, reaching Elna—called Helena by one source and Herena in the manuscript—remained there for two days. [Note: [Col. 0795C] The edition and D. have *Helenam*, “Helena”; the manuscript has *Herenam*, “Herena.”]

Then he departed from there, returned to Spain with favorable successes, and reclaimed the seat of his throne six months after he had left it.

Yet it is necessary to explain with what celebrated triumph he entered the royal city, rejoicing over his enemies, so that, just as the ages to come will proclaim it a sign of his immense glory, the disgrace of the rebels may not fall from the memory of future generations. [Col. 0796A]

30. About four miles from the royal city, Paul, the prince of the tyranny, and the other instigators of his sedition were placed upon camels’ vehicles, their heads shaved, their beards removed, their feet bare, and dressed in filthy clothing or garments. [Note: [Col. 0795C] F. reads: “or in filthy garments, clothed in the garments of camels, they were placed on vehicles,” with the wording differing.]

Their king himself went ahead, deserving every disgrace of confusion, crowned with a black wreath made of leather. [Note: [Col. 0795C] The manuscript corruptly has *perdictio*, “destruction,” instead of *proditionis*, “of treason”; the edition has *coreis*, “of hides,” instead of *coriis*, “of leather.”]

After him followed his king’s ministers in a long arranged procession, all seated in the same vehicles described above, and, driven along in the same confinements or restraints, with people standing on either side, they entered the city. [Note: [Col. 0796C] The edition has *illusionibus*, “mockery,” instead of *inclusionibus*, “enclosures.”]

It must not be believed that these things happened to them without the administration of God’s just judgment. Their being seated on the vehicles, subjected before all, displayed the lofty and exalted heights of their confusion; and those who, beyond human custom, had sought lofty things through the cunning of their minds paid a still higher penalty for the wrong of their conspiracy. [Note: [Col. 0796C] F. has *doceret*, “might teach,” instead of *edoceret*, “might show”; the manuscript has *penetrant*, “they penetrate,” instead of *petierant*, “they had sought”; the edition has *conscensionis*, “of ascent,” instead of *consensionis*, “of agreement/consent.”]

Let these things, then, be preserved for succeeding ages: for the righteous, according to their desire; for the wicked, as an example; for the faithful, as a source of joy; for the faithless, as a torment. [Note: [Col. 0796C] D. has *sunt*, “they are,” instead of *sint*, “let them be.”] Thus each side, seeing itself in a certain reflection of this reading—the side that walks on straight paths may avoid the disasters of a fall, while the side that has already fallen may continually recognize itself here in the proscriptions of these men. [Col. 0797A] [Note: [Col. 0796C] The manuscript has *insecutoris posita*, “placed by the pursuer,” instead of *insecuturis reposita*, “preserved for those to come”; D. has *et quod*, “and what,” instead of *et quae*, “and which”; F. has *circuitu*, “in a circuit,” instead of *contuitu*, “in the sight/reflection.”]

[Col. 0798A] [Note: [Col. 0797A] D. and F. conclude: “Here ends the history”; the manuscript has the same wording as ours.]

Here ends the history of Paul.

THE SAME HISTORY AS IT WAS INTERPOLATED BY LUCAS OF TUY

[From the manuscripts of the library of the church of Toledo and from volume IV of *Hispania illustrata*, p. 58.]

Here begins Julian, bishop of Toledo.

TEXT OF TUY.

[Col. 0763]

[Column 0763B] **1.** A fine account of triumphs is customarily an incentive to courageous minds and raises noble spirits toward the standard of virtue, whatever glory has been proclaimed concerning past events. Human nature has, after all, a certain sluggish inclination toward inner virtue; hence it happens that people are found less eager for virtues than inclined toward vices. And unless it is equipped by the continual encouragement of useful examples and constant exhortation, it remains cold and grows numb. For this reason, so that we may be able to heal the timid and sluggish, we introduce an account of a past event carried out in our own times, by which we may urge later generations toward virtue.

[Note: [Column 0764D] In the manuscript, *incitamentum* is absent, as in the genuine Julian.]

**2.** In our days there appeared the most illustrious prince Bamba, born of royal blood, whom the Lord wished to rule worthily [Note: [Column 0764D] *Dominus* is absent from the manuscript.], whom sacred anointing adorned, [Column 0764B] whom the united people of the entire nation and homeland chose, and whom the affection of the peoples sought out. Even before he attained the heights of kingship, he was celebrated in many revelations [Note: [Column 0764D] In volume IV of *Hispania illustrata*, *relationibus* (“accounts”).] with renowned praise.

Before he became king, while he was performing the funeral rites at the death of the departing King Reccesvinth [Note: [Column 0764D] The manuscript reads *decidentis* (“falling,” or “declining”), instead of *decedentis* (“departing”).], all turned amid the very lamentations to a single accord. Moved together by one feeling, they cried out that they desired him as prince. With united voices they thundered that no one other than he could rule among the Goths. Flocking around his feet, they pressed him with tears and begged him to undertake the rule of the kingdom.

But he, whose mind courage had strengthened, yielded neither to tears, nor was he overcome by entreaties, nor was he moved by the people’s desire. Sometimes he declared that he would not be adequate to so many impending disasters; sometimes he stated that he was worn out by old age.

While he was resisting them fiercely, one of the officers of the dukes boldly stepped forward into their midst. Drawing his sword and fixing upon him a threatening look, he said:

“Unless you promise us that you will consent, know that you are about to be beheaded at once by the edge of this sword. Nor shall we leave this place until either our expedition accepts you as king, or this bloody accident of death today swallows up your refusal.”

**3.** Overcome not so much by their entreaties as by their threats, he finally yielded. Taking up the kingdom, he received everyone into his peace. Nevertheless, so that he would not receive the sacred anointing of the kingdom anywhere except at the site of the holy see of Toledo, he delayed until the nineteenth day, lest he appear to have seized or stolen the glory of kingship through ambition, and so that he might instead be seen to have received from the Lord the sign of so great a dignity.

These events took place in a village which antiquity called Gerticos. It lies in the territory of Salamanca, nearly one hundred and twenty miles from the royal city. There, on the same day—namely, on the Kalends of September—the life of the departing king ended [Note: [Column 0766D] The manuscript reads *decidentis* (“falling,” or “declining”), instead of *decedentis* (“departing”).], and the election of the aforesaid man followed.

[Column 0766C] **4.** After he entered the city of Toledo and the time came for him to receive the sign of the holy anointing, he stood conspicuous in royal dress before the divine altar. As customary, he professed the Catholic faith and, with an oath, returned his pledge of fidelity to the people; he also confirmed the good customs and laws of his royal predecessors.

Then, as he bent his knees, the oil of blessing was poured over his head by the hands of the sacred primate and bishop Quiricus [Note: [Column 0766D] The manuscript reads *Quiriaci*, instead of *Quirici*.], and an abundance of blessing was bestowed. At once a marvelous sign appeared: from the very crown of his head, where the holy oil had been poured, a kind of vapor resembling smoke rose upward in the form of a column. From that same head a bee was seen to leap forth and fly toward the heights of the air. This was certainly a sign of the happiness that would follow.

It is not within the capacity of our weakness to discuss how gloriously he ruled the kingdom thereafter [Note: [Column 0766D] *Hispania illustrata* reads *valetudinis* (“capacity,” or “strength”), instead of *valitudinis*.]

**5.** When, therefore, the kingdom was settled in peaceful quiet, the land of Gaul nourished the snare of its own overthrow. For suddenly a whirlwind of faithlessness arose there, and the agreement of treachery passed through one man to many. Rebellion against the king and the homeland was set in motion.

**6.** The report of his crime declares that Hilderic was the head of this tyranny. While governing the city of Nîmes under the authority of a count, he took upon himself not only the name but also the title and practice of faithlessness. He also joined to himself the companions of his wickedness: Gumildus [Note: [Column 0768D] The manuscript reads *Gumillum*, instead of *Gumildum*.], the detestable bishop of the see of Maguelonne, and the abbot Ramirus. With their support he summoned into the homeland, against the established laws of the Gothic kingdom, the treacherous nation of the Jews.

Thus Hilderic, the head of this crime, while kindling the fire of his faithlessness throughout various places, attempted to draw Aregius, the bishop of Nîmes, a man of blessed life, into the stigma of treachery [Note: [Column 0768D] *Hispania illustrata* reads *perfidiam notam* (“the mark of treachery”), instead of *perfidiae notam*.]. When he saw Aregius resisting his schemes with a chaste mouth and steadfast heart [Note: [Column 0768D] The manuscript has *repugnante* (“resisting”) instead of *repugnantem* (“resisting him”), as in the genuine Julian.], he deprived him of the dignity of his office, loaded him with the weight of chains, and handed him over to the Franks in the territory of Francia to be mocked. Then, in place of the removed bishop, he installed the abbot Ramirus, his companion in treachery, as bishop.

In this election no ecclesiastical order was observed, nor was any decision of the prince or metropolitan awaited. Instead, with the arrogance of pride raised up, Ramirus was ordained by only two pseudo-bishops, contrary to the prohibitions of the ancestors.

After the period of their reckless enterprise had run its course, Hilderic, Gumildus [Note: [Column 0768D] The manuscript here reads *Gunildus*.], and Ramirus established the boundaries of their conspiracy for themselves. From the place called Camel Mountain as far as Nîmes, they marked out the land of Gaul and associated it with their customary conspiracy [Note: [Column 0768D] The manuscript reads *suaeque* (“and their own”), instead of *suetae* (“customary”).]. Faithfulness was overcome by faithlessness [Note: [Column 0768D] The same source reads *superaretur* (“would be overcome”).]. Then, having gathered a force, they plundered the citizens [Note: [Column 0768D] The same source reads *depopulant* (“they plunder”), instead of *depopulantur*.], destroyed their labors, exhausted their resources, and ravaged the entire province of Gaul [Note: [Column 0768D] The same source reads *eterminant*, apparently corrupt, instead of *exterminant* (“destroy”).]

**7.** This report reached Prince Bamba, who immediately sent an army into Gaul under the command of the duke Paul, who was of the noble Greek nation, to extinguish the name of the rebels. Paul, however, advanced sluggishly with the army, abstained from battle, and used all the influence he possessed to withdraw the soldiers’ spirits from the battle-fury in which they were burning. In every respect he violated the faith he had promised to the religious prince.

He did this through a certain secret plan, intending to reach the height he desired. He drew to himself as companions in his treachery Ranosindus, duke of the province of Tarragona, and Hildigisus [Note: [Column 0768D] The same source incorrectly reads *Ildigisium*.], who was still serving in the office of gardingus.

Eager to accomplish the desire of his perverse ambition with incredible speed, he gathered people from every direction and falsely announced that he was going to fight against the rebels. When the venerable man Argebaudus [Note: [Column 0770D] The manuscript here and below reads *Argebadus*.], bishop of Narbonne, learned this through the careful report of certain people, he tried to prevent Paul from gaining access to the city.

But this opinion did not remain hidden from Paul. Therefore, before Argebaudus could put what he had planned into effect, Paul suddenly hurried with his army into the city of Narbonne and ordered the city gates to be guarded by his armed men. When the entire army had gathered around him, Paul himself, the viperous head of treachery, stood in the midst of it with certain companions. He first rebuked the bishop, asking why he was trying to bar his access to the city.

**8.** After this, the plan of his tyranny was disclosed. By various devices of fraud, estranging the peoples from their allegiance, he inflamed each person’s mind to inflict injuries upon the holy King Bamba.

Paul himself first swore that he could in no way have Bamba as king, nor remain any longer in his service. He added:

“Choose the head of the government from among yourselves, one to whom the entire multitude may yield and who may be seen to rule over you with devotion and humility.”

Ranosindus, one of the conspirators and a partner in this wicked plan, applauded him. He designated Paul as king for himself and desired Paul, and no other, to become king over the people.

At this, the other conspirators acclaimed Paul as king and inclined the minds of the entire people toward their own wishes. When Paul saw that the advancement of his plan was already assured, he immediately gave his consent to his own desire and compelled everyone to accept the matter as accomplished.

After this Paul seized the kingdom. Through the criminal audacity of treachery, he drew to himself that band of conspirators whom he had not captured by the power of arms. He easily joined to his treachery Hilderic the count and the pseudo-bishops Gumildus and Ramirus. The entire province of Gaul suddenly rushed to arms in conspiracy.

Not only Gaul but also part of the province of Tarragona attempted the high-booted stride of rebellion. All Gaul suddenly became an assembly of traitors, prepared to die in defense of treacherous wickedness.

While Paul labored to increase the number of his accomplices in iniquity, he gathered to his aid, by means of many gifts given and promised, a vast multitude of Franks and Basques. He awaited a suitable time when he could enter Spain as a combatant and reclaim the height of kingship that had been seized before his arrival.

**9.** While these things were being done in Gaul, the glorious King Bamba was engaged in subduing the rebellious Basques and was staying in the region of Cantabria.

When he received a swift message about what was happening in Gaul, the matter to be deliberated immediately became known to the leading men of the palace: whether they could proceed from there into Gaul to fight, or whether they should return to their own country, gather forces from every direction, and undertake the journey with a large army over so great a distance.

Seeing many of them wavering over this twofold plan, the prince addressed them all with this admonition:

“Look, young men: you have heard of the evil that has arisen, and you have learned what defenses the instigator of this sedition has furnished himself. It is therefore necessary to anticipate the enemy, so that he may be forestalled in war before he grows within his own conflagration.

“It would be shameful for men about to fight such enemies not to go out to meet them—or to return home before our homes perish. It ought to seem disgraceful to us that Paul, the betrayer of his homeland, who was unable to subdue our rebels by arms, should dare to resist men of such glory; and that he who could not conquer a most contemptible and unwarlike people for the sake of the homeland’s peace should dare to offer himself as an enemy to the Gothic army.

“He judges us to be wholly effeminate and weak in every respect [Note: [Column 0772D] The manuscript incorrectly reads *usquequaquam* instead of *usquequaque* (“in every respect”).], as though we were utterly unable to resist his tyranny by any strength, arms, or plans. Yet the whole world has experienced, throughout the ages, the courage and valor of the Gothic nation in the triumphs of war. What valor will that doomed man possess, even if he joins battle against us with the strength of the Franks? Their manner of fighting is well known to us and not uncertain: they have often begged the Goths, with great entreaties, for assistance in defending them against their enemies.

“It would therefore be shameful for you even for an hour to fear the battle lines of those whose courage you know always to be weaker. Whether they are Gauls or Franks, they should understand that the crime of so great a conspiracy must be punished. We must reclaim the name of our glory with avenging arms [Note: [Column 0772D] The same source reads *vindicare* (“reclaim”), instead of *vendicare*.]

“Nevertheless, you must fight not with women but with men, although it remains well known that the Franks have never been able to resist the Goths, nor the Gauls to accomplish anything of valor without them.

“If you raise the difficulty of provisions or transport, know that it is more glorious to win a triumph amid hardships than to complete carefully planned wars amid abundance. For that is always more highly esteemed which endurance ennobles more than adequate resources.

“Moreover, the scattered name of the traitors rises as a sign of victory. Let the ingratitude of the Gauls inflame your spirit, because the Franks have always oppressed them with pitiable servitude, whereas the Goths gave them the noblest freedom by the sword of war.

“Therefore, while the heat of courage remains, there must be no delay in hastening. While anger presses upon our spirits, no hesitation should impede us. Indeed, if it could be done without interruption, we should undertake the journey already begun and set out immediately; then we could much more easily overthrow the camps of our enemies [Note: [Column 0772D] The same source incorrectly reads *poterat* (“could”) instead of *poterimus* (“shall be able”).].

“For, as a certain wise man says: ‘Present anger has strength; when delayed, it grows weak.’ And also: ‘Delay harmed those who were ready.’

“There is therefore no need to turn the soldier back, since eager advance in warfare makes one victorious. Let us therefore approach and bring disaster upon the Basques [Note: [Column 0772D] The same source reads *Adhinc*, nearer *Abhinc*, as in the genuine Julian, instead of *Adhuc* (“still”).]. Then let us hasten at once to extinguish the name of the rebels.”

**10.** When the most prudent King Bamba had concluded this speech [Note: [Column 0774D] *Rex* (“king”) is absent from the manuscript.], everyone’s courage grew strong. They ardently desired to do what they were commanded, and the entire army immediately entered the region of Vasconia.

For seven days, throughout the open fields, plundering, hostility, and the burning of camps and houses were carried out with such force that the Basques, abandoning their ferocity, desired to have their lives spared and, by giving hostages, to obtain peace—not so much through entreaties as through gifts.

Accordingly, after hostages had been accepted, the customary tribute imposed, and peace arranged, they set out by a direct route toward Gaul, passing through Calahorra [Note: [Column 0774D] The manuscript reads *Galafurram*.] and Huesca.

After this, King Bamba selected commanders [Note: [Column 0774D] *Hispania illustrata* omits “selected commanders”; the genuine Julian has it, as does the manuscript.] and divided the army into three divisions. One part was to proceed toward the fortress of Libia, which is the chief city of Aquitania. The second was to make for the middle of the Pyrenees by way of the city of Ausona. The third was to advance along the public road beside the seacoast. The religious prince himself followed with a numerous force of combatants.

But because the undisciplined conduct of certain men among us not only sought plunder but also committed the crime of adultery while burning houses, the aforesaid prince punished the wickedly committed crime, along with certain other vices, with such severity of discipline that one would have thought he was imposing heavier penalties upon them than if they had acted as enemies against him.

The severed male members of those adulterers testify to this punishment: for fornication he inflicted this mutilating penalty. He said:

“Look: the judgment of war already threatens, and you wish to commit fornication so as to provoke God to anger? Since, I believe, you are approaching the test of battle, take care lest you perish in your own filth. For if I do not punish these things, I shall go from here already bound [Note: [Column 0774D] *Hispania illustrata* reads *invado* (“I invade”), instead of *vado* (“I go”).]

“Indeed, I shall go forth so that I may be seized by the just judgment of God if, seeing the people’s iniquity, I do not punish it. For he goes to war in vain to win, when iniquity accompanies him.

“You ought to take as an example that priest Eli, learned in the divine Scriptures, who neglected to rebuke his sons for their crimes and therefore learned that they had fallen in battle. He himself, following his sons, died with his neck broken.
