“These things, therefore, must be feared by us. And so, if we remain cleansed from crime, there will be no doubt that we shall gain triumph over the enemy.”

Under this discipline, as has been said, Prince Bamba gloriously led the army forward. Holding the conduct of each individual under divine rules, he saw the war arranged for him and the victory of battle advancing with the passing days.

Just as he was distinguished by his royal Gothic lineage, so he was great-hearted in mind and likewise rich in literary learning [Note: [Column 0774D] The manuscript says only: “For just as he was great-hearted in mind, so he was rich in literary learning.”]

Thus, first of all the rebellious cities, Barcelona was brought under the authority of the religious prince; then Girona was subjected. To the venerable man Amator, bishop of this city, the pestilential Paul had sent a letter written in the following sense.

[Column 0775C] **11.** “I have heard that King Bamba intends to come against us with an army. But let not your heart be troubled, for I do not think this will happen. Nevertheless, whichever of the two of us your Holiness first sees approaching with an army [Note: [Column 0776D] The manuscript reads *ibi tua* (“there your”), or perhaps *ita tua* (“thus your”), instead of *tua*.], believe that you have him as your lord and ought to remain in his affection [Note: [Column 0776D] Instead of *ipsum … dominum* (“him … as lord”), the same source has *spiritum … domini* (“the spirit … of the lord”), or perhaps *dominum* (“lord”).]”

The wretched man wrote this without knowing that he had pronounced a just judgment against himself.

When King Bamba wisely interpreted the words of this letter, he said:

“Paul did not speak from himself in this letter; but although unknowingly, I judge that he prophesied.”

After this, the prince departed from Girona and advanced with warlike incursions until he reached the ridges of the Pyrenees. There, after the army had rested for two days, he approached the spine of the Pyrenees with the three divisions of the army, as stated above [Note: [Column 0776D] The same source reads *ordivit* (“he began”), instead of *adivit* (“he approached”).] He captured and subdued, with a remarkable triumph of victory, the Pyrenean forts called Caucoliberum, Vulturaria, and Libia [Note: [Column 0776D] The same source reads *Caucoliberi, Vulturaria … Libia*.] In these camps he found a great quantity of gold and silver, which fell as booty to the abundant armies.

He had kept his hands free from every bribe, and thereby inflamed the spirits of the combatants to obtain victory.

He also captured the fortress called Clausurae. After sending the armies ahead of him, he ordered two commanders to make a breach, and through them took the fortress. There the army captured Ranosindus and Hildigisus, together with the rest of the band of traitors who had gathered to defend the fortress. With their hands bound behind their backs, they were brought before the prince.

Witimirus, one of the conspirators who had shut himself up in Sordonia, perceived that our men had broken in and immediately fled. He went to bring Paul at Narbonne the news of so great a disaster. This event shook the tyrant with great fear.

The religious prince, having subdued the army of the aforementioned forts, descended into the plains after crossing the Pyrenees and waited only two days to gather the army into one force.

**12.** When the multitude collected from different regions had grown into one body, he immediately sent a selected force of armed men under four commanders ahead of him to storm Narbonne. He dispatched another army to approach and fight by naval battle.

Indeed, only a few days had passed since the rebellious Paul had withdrawn from Narbonne in servile flight, after learning that the party of the religious prince was advancing with such favorable success.

Paul fortified the city with a large garrison of traitors and entrusted it to his commander Witimirus. When our army courteously urged him to surrender the city without bloodshed, he absolutely refused. Closing the city gates, he denounced our army with insults shouted from the walls. He heaped curses upon the religious prince and attempted to disturb the army with threats.

Unable to endure this, the courage of our side suddenly blazed up through the kindling of their hearts, and they aimed a shower of weapons at the mouths of the traitors.

A savage battle was joined on both sides, and the two parties resisted each other alternately with arrows. But when both sides fought bravely, our men hurled such heavy showers of stones into the city that, from the clamor of voices and the collision of rocks, the city seemed about to be destroyed [Note: [Column 0778D] The manuscript reads *extimaretur*, apparently incorrectly, instead of *existimaretur*.]

From approximately the fifth hour of the day until the eighth hour—*per* (“through,” or “during”) is incorrectly absent from the manuscript and is supplied here within asterisks—our men fought fiercely with the persistent use of slings.

The courage of our men then blazed up, unable to endure the delay of victory, and they approached the gates to fight at closer range. Then, by the victorious hand of God, they set fire to the gates and entered the city as victors.

While Wictimirus [Note: [Column 0778D] *Hispania illustrata* incorrectly reads *Witericus*.] was still advancing toward the church with an armed force, he was disturbed by the approach of our men. Behind the altar of the Mother of God, the wretched man declared that he would avenge himself—not out of reverence for the place, but with an avenging sword [Note: [Column 0778D] The manuscript reads *se* (“himself”), instead of *sed* (“but”).] He held a sword in his right hand and threatened each person with death.

To suppress the swelling of his madness at once, one of our men seized a board in his hand and advanced against him with a furious blow. When he attempted to strike Wictimirus with a mighty throw of the board, he immediately fell trembling to the ground. He was promptly captured, the weapon was pulled from his hand, and he was dragged away ignominiously, bound tightly under the weight of chains. He and his companions, with whom he had attempted to defend the city [Note: [Column 0778D] The same source reads *cum quibus* (“with whom”), instead of *quibus* (“with whom”).], were also subjected to beatings.

**13.** After Narbonne had been conquered and subdued, the army directed its march in pursuit of Paul, who had withdrawn to Nîmes. Then the cities of Beterris [Biterris] (Béziers) [Note: [Column 0778D] *Hispania illustrata* incorrectly reads *Beterius*.] and Agde were immediately subjected.

In the city of Maguelonne, however, Gumildus, the bishop of that place, saw the army surrounding him for the siege of his city. He saw that it was being enclosed not only by those who had come to fight by land, but also by those who had crossed by sea to engage in naval battle. Terrified by the disaster this threatened, he seized the shortest route and joined Paul at Nîmes.

When the army of Spain perceived that Gumildus had fled, it immediately captured the city of Maguelonne with a victory no less decisive. Then it advanced in a straight battle line and attempted to storm Nîmes.

The first battle force, consisting of a selected band of fighters, was sent forward under four commanders. Their vigorous young men—nearly thirty thousand—went ahead of the prince.

They reached Nîmes, where the Frankish army had gathered with Paul to seek revenge [Note: [Column 0778D] *Hispania illustrata* reads *compulerat* (“had compelled”), instead of *contulerat* (“had gathered”).] Our men had completed the whole night’s march at a hurried pace. Suddenly, as the light of day began to appear, the lines of our men became visible, arranged with equal preparation of arms and courage.

When those within the city saw them, they determined that, since they would be fighting against a few, our men should be met in the open fields. But suspecting the tricks of an ambush, they preferred to conduct the battle from within the city, stationed on the walls, rather than expose themselves outside to unforeseen accidents and dangers. They also chose to wait for the promised assistance of other peoples.

When the sun had risen, our men began the battle with the blaring of trumpets, striking the enemy with a powerful hand through arrows and stones. The traitors resisted and, like drops of rain, hurled rocks and missiles.

The battle was fought more fiercely by both sides, and they contended on equal terms. Neither our men nor the others yielded in the struggle, and the whole day was spent fighting under an uncertain fortune.

**14.** One of the instigators of the sedition, fighting fiercely and looking down from the wall, mocked our men and composed these words:

“Why do you stand here fighting so stubbornly, about to die? Why do you not return to your own homes? Or perhaps do you wish to meet the accident of death before its time? [Note: [Column 0780D] The manuscript reads *aut forte* (“or perhaps”), and so forth, rather than *an forte* (“or perhaps”).]

“Why do you not instead seek steep places among the rocks where you may hide yourselves when the appearance of our aid becomes visible? Believe that I pity you, knowing that assistance is on its way to us. I know very well that numerous forces for battle are coming to us. This is the third day since I hurried here from that place.

“Therefore, knowing this, I await with sorrow the downfall of your wretched display, and I shall show you your prince, for whom you came to fight, bound in chains. It is therefore not useful for you to struggle here so pointlessly on his behalf, since it is perhaps already established that he has perished through the ambushes of our men.

“And what is worse, once our victory has become clear, there will be no pardon for you thereafter.”

By saying this he not only failed to terrify our men, but inflamed them more fiercely to the fury of battle. They approached the wall. They held their ground in combat more fiercely than when they had begun and renewed the battle with renewed vigor.

**15.** After these events had continued throughout the whole day, night finally brought the battle to an end.

Yet during the first heat of that day, while our men still persisted in battle with tireless courage, they sent a message back to the prince and requested that assistance be sent to them. They wisely took no small care for their own safety, lest they be forestalled by the treachery of a foreign nation or, exhausted by their strength, be overthrown by the others against whom they were fighting.

The matter was well managed. When the prince learned that the tyrant Paul was fighting against our men, there was no further delay. Through the duke Wandemir he sent ten thousand selected men from the army to aid the combatants. They were to remain awake throughout the night, complete the journey at speed, and arrive quickly—not so much to break the enemy as to encourage the spirits of our men by their arrival [Note: [Column 0782D] *Tam* (“so much”) is absent from the manuscript.]

When our men saw the assistance sent to them, they were strengthened by immense joy and immediately regained their strength [Note: [Column 0782D] The manuscript reads *illico* (“immediately”), instead of *illi* (“to them”).] At once everyone resolved to join battle [Note: [Column 0782D] The same source reads *hominibus* (“men”), instead of *omnibus* (“all”).]

**16.** Dawn had already begun to appear. The multitude of the enemy, crowded along the wall and looking outward, saw through the clear ranks of light that the number of the lines of fighters had multiplied beyond what it had seen on the previous day.

At that moment Paul, the head of the treachery, went toward a certain elevated place so that he might climb up and view so great a spectacle. As soon as he saw the ordered ranks of our men, his courage fell, and he said:

“I recognize that this battle formation has been produced by my rival. This is he himself, and no other, I think; for I recognize him in his arrangements [Note: [Column 0782D] *Hoc* (“this”) is absent from the manuscript.]”

Saying this and similar things, he recovered his courage and began to encourage his men with persuasive words:

“Do not be disturbed by fear. This is merely that most famous valor of the Goths, which used to boast, with customary recklessness, that it was coming to overcome us. Believe that the prince is here, and his whole army with him.

“There is nothing more for you to fear. Formerly, indeed, the famous valor of the Goths was a defense to their own people and a terror to others; but now all their martial courage has withered, and all their knowledge of battle has failed [Note: In the manuscript, *in illis* (“in them”) is absent.] They have no custom of warfare and no experience of combat [Note: [Column 0782D] In the manuscript, *in illis* (“in them”) is absent.].

“If they join battle in a single mass [Note: [Column 0782D] *Hispania illustrata* reads *conferti* (“closely massed”) instead of *conserti*.], they will immediately fly away to their appointed hiding places, because their degenerate spirits cannot bear the weight of battle. Once you begin to fight, you will prove in action the truth of what I am saying.

“There is therefore nothing else that you need fear, especially since you see that the king and his entire army are present here.”

At this, many of his own men argued that the king could not advance without the standards bearing the signs of the army. He replied that Bamba had approached with the standards hidden for this reason: so that he might make his enemies understand that another army still remained, with which the king himself would later arrive.

“But all this,” he said, “is a deception produced by fraud, so that those whom he cannot conquer by valor he may humble into fear by cunning.”

**17.** Paul had not yet finished speaking when suddenly the trumpets of war sounded from our side. They began the battle and renewed the form of combat from the previous day.

The enemy, however, placing more confidence in the walls than in its strength to win, hurled missiles from the walls at our men and renewed the battle with them.

Thus the stimulus of battle grew hot on both sides, but the fighting courage of our men became evident with greater force. While they fought with all their strength and struck down the enemy within the city by various kinds of weapons, many of the wounded, admiring both the valor and steadfastness of the Goths, approached Paul and said:

“We do not see in the Goths the sluggishness in warfare that you described. For we see in them great daring and steadfastness in winning. These wounds that we are receiving show that they hurl such powerful blows against the enemy; indeed, the crash itself terrifies us before the blow extinguishes life.”

Terrified by their words, Paul was broken by repeated darts of despair [Note: [Column 0784D] *Hispania illustrata* reads *angebatur* (“was distressed”), instead of *frangebatur* (“was broken”).]

**18.** The Goths, fighting even more steadfastly and grieving that their victory was being delayed, rose up with fiercer courage, considering themselves defeated in every respect if they did not win quickly.

Moved, therefore, by a fiercer ardor than before, they battered the city walls with continual blows of battle until the fifth hour of the day. The men operating the slings released showers of stones with immense crashing, and, after placing fire beneath them, they burned the gates and broke through the walls [Note: [Column 0784D] “The walls” is absent at this point.]

Then, entering the city gloriously, they opened a path for themselves with the sword. When the enemy could no longer withstand the ferocity of our men, they withdrew into the Arenas, which were enclosed by the stronger walls of an ancient building, and shut themselves in there for protection.

When our men perceived this, they followed them vigorously. Before the others could take refuge in the fortress of the Arenas, our men killed many of them with the two-edged sword.

Nevertheless, many of the common soldiers among our men, who were eager for plunder, were cut down by the sword.

**19.** A new sedition also arose among the rebels. When the citizens or inhabitants themselves accused some of their own people of treason, they killed with an avenging sword those against whom suspicion had turned.

There was indeed a violent disturbance. Paul saw one of his own men being slaughtered before him by the hands of his own people [Note: [Column 0784D] The manuscript reads *a suis* (“by his own”), instead of *de suis* (“of his own”).] In a lamentable voice he cried out that the man was his servant, yet even then he could provide him no help. As a result, bloodless and trembling, Paul himself was utterly despised by his own men.

For he too was regarded as suspect by the inhabitants, together with the others who had come with him from Spain, lest he devise their betrayal in order to secure his own liberation. The Spaniards, for their part, were suspected of intending, after inflicting death on the inhabitants, to go over to the religious king.

Why say more? Within the city there arose a pitiable spectacle of battle. On both sides bands of traitors fell; on both sides they were thrown down; on both sides they were slaughtered. Those who escaped the swords of our men perished by the weapons of their own people.

The city was filled with the mingled corpses of the dead. There was also a pitiable slaughter in the houses. When one explored the hidden rooms of the buildings, one found the dead lying exposed. Through the roads [Note: [Column 0786D] The manuscript reads *duas* (“two”), instead of *vias* (“roads”).] and streets of the city one could also see human corpses lying with a threatening expression and savage ferocity, as though they were still stationed in the very battle line.

Yet their color was disfigured, their skin yellowish, their horror monstrous, and their stench unbearable. Some of those lying there, who had received mortal wounds, were still alive and pretended to be dead so that they might escape death.

**20.** Seeing these and similar events, Paul abandoned the ferocity of tyranny and was gripped by great anguish and misery of heart, since he could neither resist the enemy nor provide any help to his own men.

A certain man born from his own family nevertheless approached him to mock him.

“Why,” he said, “do you stand here? Where are your advisers, who brought you to this spectacle of calamity? What did it profit you to rise up against your own people, when now, amid so great a slaughter of death, you are entirely unable to help either yourself or your own men?”

He said this to mock Paul, provoked not so much by a desire to heap abuse upon him as by a spirit of bitterness [Note: [Column 0786D] The same source reads *tantum* (“only”), instead of *tam* (“so much”).]

Paul urged him with gentle words to spare his grief and not to add confusion to confusion. But while that man was standing on the very marble steps where he had come to mock Paul, he was surrounded by his own people before Paul’s eyes and was slaughtered.

Paul cried out trembling:

“Why are you attacking this man? He is mine. Do not let him perish!”

He begged repeatedly and lamentably that the man be spared. But Paul himself was already held in contempt, as though he too were about to die immediately, and no one could hear him.

Then, driven by complete despair, he removed, wasting away, the royal garments that he had received more through the ambition of tyranny than according to the established order.

By a wondrous and hidden judgment of God, it happened that he laid aside the tyrant’s kingdom on the very day on which the religious prince had received the scepter of rule from the Lord. For that day was the Kalends of September, on which our prince was known to have assumed the royal dignity.

On that same day, therefore, the city was breached, the tyrant Paul removed his royal garments, and bloody vengeance was inflicted upon his enemies.

## 21

The third day after these events had arrived, while Paul, after the sighs of the night, awaited his final death. Then he began to speak with those with whom he had plotted his own destruction, so that either they might bid him a final farewell or, if possible, take some measure for their own safety.

At that point Argebaudus, bishop of Narbonne, was sent by common agreement to the prince, to ask that life be granted despite their offenses and to plead for pardon. After offering sacrifices to God, he approached the prince in the very vestments in which he had performed the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. About four miles from the city he met the prince, who was surrounded by an immeasurable mass of warriors.

When the bishop saw him, he leapt down from his horse and, prostrating himself on the ground, begged for pardon. At the bishop’s approach the prince held his horse for a while; and, being filled with compassion, he too, weeping, ordered the bishop to be raised from the ground.

But the bishop, interrupted by sobs of tears, said in a mournful voice:

“Alas! We have sinned against heaven and before you, most sacred prince. We are not worthy that the outcome of your mercy should reach us. We have stained the faith we promised you and have fallen into so great a crime of apostasy.[^c0079-1] May your piety quickly spare our plea; may the avenging sword not destroy the remnants of our half-dead people, nor may the blade seek more lives than it has already begun to claim. Command your army now to cease from bloodshed, and citizen to spare citizen. We are few indeed who have escaped the sword, but on behalf of the few we implore pardon. Mercifully spare our remnants, so that, since the throat of death has already spread among the rest of our people, at least some may remain whom you can pity. For if you do not spare them quickly, not even inhabitants will remain to defend the city.”

[^c0079-1]: Note at col. 0788D: *voluti* in the *Hispania illustrata*; the reading is uncertain or corrupt.

## 22

When he heard these words, the devout prince was moved and said to the bishop with tears:

“Overcome by your prayers, I grant you the lives for which you have asked, and I shall not destroy them with an avenging sword; nor today shall I shed anyone’s blood, although an offense of this kind will not go unpunished.”

The venerable bishop continued to press him at length, asking that, since he had granted life to those men, he inflict no sentence of condemnation upon them. But the prince soon became angry and, growing harsher, said:

“From now on, do not impose other conditions upon us; it is enough that we have granted you their lives. As for you alone, let it suffice that I have spared you entirely. Regarding the others, I promise none of this.”

At this he burned with indignation and a kind of inward fury; then, advancing at a rapid pace, he hastened to the city to seize it and obtain the triumph of victory.[^c0079-2]

[^c0079-2]: Note at col. 0788D: *Et haec* (“And these things”) in the *Hispania illustrata*.

## 23

As the glorious prince approached with an incredible multitude of armies, the sun shone upon the shields, and the earth itself glittered with a double radiance.[^c0079-3] Countless terrifying standards of war were there, and the gleaming weapons themselves increased the sun’s brilliance far beyond its customary strength.

But what shall I say? Who could describe in full the army’s magnificence, the beauty of its arms, the appearance of its young men, the strength of its warriors, or the harmony of their spirits?[^c0079-^4]—especially since divine protection had plainly been present, as was clearly revealed by heavenly signs.[^c0079-5] For our army appeared to be protected by angelic sentinels, and the angels themselves seemed to extend the signs of their protection over the shining camp with flashing flight.

But let us leave such matters in silence for a little while and continue the account of the work undertaken.

[^c0079-3]: The manuscript reads *terra ipsa* (“the earth itself”); the *Hispania illustrata* reads *tamen ipse* (“yet he himself”).

[^c0079-4]: Manuscript reading: *Quid* (“what”) rather than *qui* (“who”). Another reading has *quae concordia animorum singulorum explicare* (“the harmony of each individual’s spirit”) instead of *quae concordia animorum singula explicare* (“the harmony of their spirits in detail”).

[^c0079-5]: Variant reading: *affuit* (“was present”) rather than *affuerit* (“had been present”).

## 24

When the prince perceived that the army had now been gathered into one body, positioned about a stadium’s distance from the city, he was stirred by an extraordinary surge of spirit. He appointed commanders, arranged the common soldiers, divided the battle lines, and instructed them how they should conduct the battle.

For report had brought word that the Franks were assembling to aid the traitors. Then he sent certain chosen commanders, superior in strength and courage, to drag Paul and the other instigators of the revolt from the Caves of Arenas, where they had hidden themselves while fleeing death.

There was no delay. When they had carried out the commands, Paul and his companions were suddenly dragged from their hiding places in the Arenas, lowered over the wall, and shamefully handled. Then that whole multitude of Gauls and Franks, which had gathered from every side to fight against our men, was captured and detained, together with immense treasures.

The utterly wicked Paul was carried by two of our commanders, mounted on horses, with their hands extended from either side and holding him by the hair, until they presented him to the devout prince.

## 25

When he saw him, the magnificent prince raised his hands to heaven with tears and said:

“I praise you, God, king of all kings, who have humbled the proud as one wounded, and by the strength of your arm have crushed my adversaries.”

The prince spoke these and similar words, his voice interrupted by weeping.

But as soon as that same tyrant, raising his eyes, saw the prince’s face, he immediately prostrated himself on the ground, removed his belt, and tied it around his neck. He was already as if lifeless and so confused by excessive fear that he paid no attention to what was happening to him.

It was a sight worth seeing: how Paul the reprobate had descended from so lofty a height—although he had been deprived of the rank that belonged to it—into such sudden humiliation. It was remarkable to behold how swiftly worldly circumstances had changed: to see so quickly cast down the man whom they had recently seen in glory; and the man whom the previous day had still held as king falling so precipitously into ruin.[^c0079-6]

In him the prophecy was sufficiently fulfilled which says:

“I saw the wicked man raised high and exalted like the cedars of Lebanon. I passed by, and behold, he was no more; I sought him, and his place was not found.”

What more need be said? When Paul and the other captives of this faction were already lying before the prince’s horse, the glorious prince said:

“Why did you burst forth into such madness and wickedness that you repaid me evil for good? But why should I linger here? Go, and remain under assigned guard until the severity of judgment has dealt with you. I shall grant you life, although you do not deserve it.”

Then he distributed them throughout the army and handed them over to appointed and vigilant guards.

The Franks who had been captured, however, were ordered to be treated kindly. Some of them had been born to very noble parents; they had been given as hostages to Paul the traitor so that the Franks would come to his aid. The others were Saxons. After the eighteenth day from their capture, the prince generously sent all of them back home together, laden with royal gifts, saying that a victor ought not to be harsh toward the vanquished.

[^c0079-6]: The manuscript reads *quam* (“whom”) rather than *quam … viderent* (“whom they had seen”).

## 26

On the first day of September the war against the city of Nîmes was begun by our forces; on the following day the city was breached; and on the third day, which was the fourth day before the Nones of September,[^c0079-7] the city itself was conquered in a celebrated capture.

Afterward, however, the devout prince, concerned for the restoration of the captured city, immediately repaired the hollowed-out sections of the walls, renewed the burned gates, provided burial mounds for the unburied, restored to the inhabitants the plunder that had been taken from them, and relieved every wounded condition from the public treasury.[^c0079-8]

He nevertheless ordered all the quantity of treasure that had been captured to be preserved under the most careful guard—not because he was enticed by the profit of avarice, but because he was moved by divine love: namely, so that objects consecrated to God might more easily be found and restored to divine worship.

For the utterly wicked Paul had heaped sin upon sin when he added sacrilege to tyranny. Unless he had plundered the sacred churches, he apparently did not think he had anything with which to enrich his treasury. Thus it came about that he seized very many vessels of gold and silver from the Lord’s treasuries; and that same Paul placed upon his mad head the golden crown which Reccaredus, a most Christian prince of blessed memory, had offered at the body of the most blessed Felix.

The prince ordered all these things, gathered together in one place, to be restored intact to the church to which each properly belonged.

[^c0079-7]: The first day of September was the Kalends; the fourth day before the Nones fell on 2 September.

[^c0079-8]: Manuscript variant: *quoque* (“each,” “every”) rather than *quaeque* (“everything”).

## 27

The third day after the victory had now come for the victors, and Paul, loaded with iron along with the other accomplices of his wickedness, was brought before the prince seated on his throne.

Then, according to ancient custom, bending the spine of his back, he submitted his neck to the royal feet. Thereafter, before all the armies, he was condemned, together with the others, by the judgment of everyone, to suffer death, since he had prepared death for the prince.

But the prince did not wish to destroy them by a sentence of death. Instead, he ordered that they be kept for the present, weighed down with irons, as a punishment accompanied only by the mockery of being shaved.

At that time a report was circulating that the Franks and Teutons were hastening as quickly as possible to rescue Paul. The prince, however, wished to engage the Franks more fiercely not only for this reason, but also to avenge the earlier injuries inflicted by their people, and he daily endured the waiting with still greater courage.

Since no Frank came forward to fight, he had vowed that he himself would go to meet them, unless he were restrained by the counsel of loyalty, lest the treaty of peace established between the two peoples be broken by the Goths.

As has been said, he awaited their arrival. The fourth day had already passed since he captured Paul, yet there was no expectation of an enemy, no event, no hostile assembly whatsoever. Moreover, the heavily fortified cities of Francia were already lamenting, as was reported, their final destruction; and their citizens, fearing that our forces might forestall them, had abandoned their cities and wandered far and wide through uncertain settlements, protecting their lives by hiding in concealed places.

The devout prince, for his part, was encamped in the open plain at some distance from the city of Nîmes. There he established his camp and, with remarkable speed, had the city of Nîmes restored with very strong walls and a ditch.

While he was awaiting the arrival of the enemy, a messenger suddenly arrived reporting that one of the more noble commanders of Francia, named Lupus, had entered the territory of Béziers in a hostile manner.

The prince therefore departed with swift speed and hurried forward with his army, attempting to forestall the enemy’s reported designs. But Lupus himself, hearing that the prince had turned back, was so terrified that the army seemed to lack its commander and the commander his army. In fleeing, he could neither rally his own men nor could they in any way catch up with him.

Their hearts had been so dissolved by fear that, slipping away not merely through scattered roads but over the steep slopes of the mountains—since they already saw the sword hanging over their necks—they showed that they had won their lives by the shortcut of flight. In their confusion they left much plunder to our armies, both in people who could not follow them and in pack animals and possessions that they had brought in countless wagons.

Certainly the prince could already have sent a selected force of combatants to overtake them in warlike attacks. But their flight was so swift, and they reached the hiding places of their own territory so quickly, that they were judged to have left no trace at all of where they had fled, where they were hiding, or where they had halted.

## 28

When the prince learned that Lupus and his men could not be found, he proceeded at a peaceful pace toward Narbonne and entered the city as a victor.

There the prince ordered everything that had been broken and ravaged by the enemy to be carefully restored. By royal administration he reformed the province of Narbonne, equipped it with policies, expelled the Jews, and appointed more merciful governors, through whom the offense of so great an evil might be appeased and the land, polluted by such great filth, might be admitted to pardon after being cleansed by a new baptism of heavenly institutions.

He arranged the condition of all things in remarkable peace and eradicated from the province the roots of every rebellion. He also left there a force of strong warriors.

## 29

After exhausting and subduing the Gauls, the prince safely proceeded by a direct route to Spain, fearing neither any Gallic uprising behind him nor any Frankish ambushes, since he knew for certain that none of the neighboring princes dared contend with him in strength.

He relied upon such courage and steadfastness of spirit that he not only did not fear the barbarian peoples around him but despised them. Accordingly, while he was still in Gaul, at a place called Canabat, he satisfied the entire army with a gracious address concerning what it had done bravely and successfully, and immediately released everyone from that place.

He himself also came to Elna,[^c0079-9] remained there for two days, and then departed from there and returned to Spain. In the sixth month after he had set out, he reclaimed the seat of his throne.

It is necessary to explain, at least in part, with what celebrated triumph he entered the city of Toledo, rejoicing over his enemies, so that, just as succeeding ages will praise this as a sign of his immense glory, the shame of the rebels may likewise not disappear from the memory of those to come.

[^c0079-9]: The manuscript lacks the preposition *in* (“into” or “in”), which appears in Julian’s genuine text.

## 30

For about four miles from the royal city, Paul, the prince of the tyranny, and the other instigators of his revolt were placed upon camels, their heads shaved, their beards removed, and their feet left bare, clothed in the vilest sackcloth.[^c0079-10]

At the head of the traitors rode Paul himself, the king of perdition, worthy of every disgrace of humiliation, crowned with a pitch-black crown. His long procession of followers then came after this king of theirs. All sat upon the vehicles assigned to them and, driven along amid the same mockery, entered the city while the people stood on either side, hissing at them.

Nor should it be thought that these things befell them without the ordering of God’s just judgment. They were taught, by being set upon vehicles, that the lofty and exalted heights of their pride had been cast down to the lowest place.[^c0079-11] Those who, with a pride of mind beyond human custom, had wickedly sought what was lofty were made to pay still more lofty penalties for their disgrace.[^c0079-12]

Let these things therefore be preserved for ages to come: according to their desire, for the upright; as an example, for the wicked; for joy, for the faithful; and for torment, for the unbelieving. Thus, each side beholding itself, as it were, in the mirror of this reading, the one that walks along straight paths may avoid the fall of apostasy, while the one that has already fallen may recognize itself as condemned to eternal banishment.

**Thus far Julianus.**

[^c0079-10]: The manuscript has *in capite* (“at the head”) rather than *a capite* (“from the head”). Another reading has *imponitur* (“is placed”) rather than *imponuntur* (“are placed”).

[^c0079-11]: The text has the uncertain *laesione [sessione] nimium projecta*; another reading has *in imo* (“at the bottom,” “in the lowest place”).

[^c0079-12]: The *Hispania illustrata* reads *fastu* (“with pride”) rather than *astu* (“with cunning”).

# THE BEGINNING OF THE VILE INSULT AGAINST THE TYRANNY OF GAUL

## 1

We victors take pleasure in taunting you, Gaul, for your errors—the errors through which you, wretched land, have suffered the disaster of so great a fall.

Where is that liberty of yours in which, falsely free, you applauded yourself with arrogant brow held high? Where are the raised voices with which you disparaged the strength of the Spaniards as softer than your women? Where are your movements? Where are the swelling gestures by which you rejected association with the Spaniards? (The passage concerning the neck is corrupt.) Where are the outspread heights of your mouth, with which you often swelled with pride over uncertain riches? Where are your uplifted neck and counsels, which always provided the direction of your own commanders?

What did you think would happen when, by your own deeds, you stabbed yourself, tore yourself apart with your own hands, overturned yourself by your counsels, and handed yourself over through your frauds? You hurled weapons at yourself through your own deeds when you added crime to crime: entangled in fraudulent dealings, devoted to brothels, enslaved to perjuries, and laboring over friendships with Jews rather than with the faithful of Christ.

For, holding fast to the law of adultery, you thought everything you had done honorable: to revel like cattle among herds of prostitutes, to kill friends amid banquets, to slaughter innocent souls. You pretended that you were gracious to those who arrived; yet when you had received a man with his wife and children as guests, you offered blood instead of wine, slaughtering the man, murdering his sons, and taking the surviving mother for the sport of your sexual debauchery.

## 2

Yet, even while doing these things, you do not tremble at the enormity of such a crime. Instead, beyond all this, you are emboldened by your association with the Jews, whose unbelief, if you willingly consider it, you now recognize as having passed into your own sons. Those who shone within you under the title of Christianity have been proved to have passed over to the perfidy of the Hebrews. You were always committing yourself to the judgments of those whose hearts you already knew had been rejected by God.

And how will the Jews’ accursed sanctuaries be able to be honored by you, when you had placed the care of your salvation so zealously in them?

Recognize, wretched one; recognize what you have done. Let it be enough for you that, amid your fevers, you lost your memory. Now, with the stain of fever driven away, recognize yourself as the nurse of scandal, the fuel of evil, the mother of blasphemers, the stepmother of unbelievers, the stepchild of fraudulent dealings, the material of brothels, a cavern of betrayals, a spring of perfidy, and a destroyer of souls.

## 3

For it is not enough that all this has flowed forth from your breasts. Moreover, as though something were still lacking from the crime of so great a calamity, although you had a king, you set up another king for yourself—by cunning, not by lawful order; by frauds, not by courage.

What woman has ever been found who, while having a husband, desires the company of another man without danger to herself? You alone, disregarding your own peril and not fearing to betray, set up for yourself a scepter of betrayal.

Who did these things that have been recounted? In what land did this notorious evil first appear, if not among the very breasts that nourished you?

Your mind’s womb is therefore astonishing: although pregnant with so many crimes, it did not burst; rather, it conceived pain with such astonishing capacity that in our times it gave birth to such an abundance of sorrows.

## 4

But if you claim that what you received came from elsewhere, hear whether it was done by your counsels or by those of others. Yet, by conceiving the offspring, you could not deny it.[^c0079-13]

If you received this from elsewhere, why did you nurture it instead of driving it from your borders like a rotting limb? If you yourself gave birth to it, why did you not cut off the monstrous offspring before it grew up?[^c0079-14]

Is it not rather a sign of virtue when capable women kill the monsters born from them, while it is a crime if they kill well-formed offspring, and proper order if they kill malformed ones?

But if you plead that you could not resist its strength or oppose the offspring once conceived, where are those proud heights of your mouth, where are your swelling voices, your haughty gestures, your arrogant stride, and that theatrical grandeur of speech with which you judged that not merely part of Spain, but all Spain, would in no way suffice to resist your single fist—and proclaimed this in thunderous words?

Here, then, you offered no valid excuses, although, even if you could not persist by arms, you might at least have persisted armed with faith, and might have endured the final death more faithfully amid the storms of the unbelieving.

For you had voluntarily pledged your faith to the devout prince under an invocation of the divine name, promising that you would present yourself as an enemy to his enemies and fight against the adversaries of his salvation even to the shedding of blood.

[^c0079-13]: The passage is corrupt. A conjectural reading is: “whether it was done by your counsels or by those of others; yet the conception of your offspring could not be denied.” Another possibility is: “you could not deny the conception of your offspring.”

[^c0079-14]: Conjectural reading: *necasti* (“killed”) rather than *secasti* (“cut off”).

## 5

Tell me, then: which of your people fell for the sake of the true faith? Which of your people was killed while preserving faith? Which of your people offered himself to be killed for the truth (*occisurum*; perhaps *occidendum*)? Which even desired to offer himself to be destroyed for the faith (*perempturum*; perhaps *perimendum*)?

There was no one among your people for whom the soul of his anointed king was more precious, while you, faithless in your promise and ready to perjure yourself, not only failed to extinguish the fire of unbelief that had arisen within you, but kindled it and nourished it—not merely with words, but also with deeds.

But these are the victorious signs of your customary behavior: that you do not strike the enemy but kill the citizen (*accidas*; perhaps *occidas*); perhaps defining it more advantageously for yourself to wage war against a citizen than to confront an enemy. Your strength has always been directed toward killing allies rather than adversaries.

And since you do this not with arms but rather with plots and frauds, your poisons are more to be feared than your weapons. You have destroyed more people with the antidote to your gall than with the darts of your arms.[^c0079-15]

[^c0079-15]: Conjectural reading: *confodisti* (“you pierced”) rather than *confudisti* (“you confused” or “you overthrew”).

## 6

For we have never seen your battles directed in the field against an enemy, although within the house we have felt the poisons of your heart.

We saw your battle lines prepared, but for the throats of citizens, not for the deaths of foreigners. How have you grown so dense under a cloud of cruelty that you prepared death for your liberators and punishment for your defenders?

What need had you to provoke the stronger to war and prepare destruction for the more powerful? (Perhaps read *ut validioribus*: “so as to prepare destruction for the stronger.”)

Yet you do these things not undeservedly, since, having suffered madness, you do not realize whom you dare to equal. Madmen commonly judge themselves stronger in power precisely when nature itself seems already to be standing at the point of final collapse. But they do these and other things not because they are moved by a vital sense, but because they are already wasting away in mortal dissolution.

Therefore, if after your madness you have recovered your memory, you ought to recall with what words you shouted during your fevers and whom, in your ignorance, you judged worthy of contempt.

## 7

For behold, after the most bitter fevers through which you lost your senses, the army of the Spaniards came to meet you in due time. Yet it was not the whole army, but only a certain small part gathered from it, and it completely subdued your strength, bent your necks, crushed your swelling faces, and proved what you could and could not do better by its swords than by your words.

Why, then, wretched one, do you wage war upon your victors, when you lie so miserably defeated beneath the victors’ sword?

Behold, the army of the Spaniards, with its orderly prince, bravely subdued you, stripped you of your possessions, and subjected you to servitude.

But I do not want you to complain for long that he was always harsher toward you, since you have been clothed anew by such swift benefits. Since a just servitude was owed to you according to your deserts, he acted like a truly sound head sympathizing with a sick limb: he gave you, reduced to servitude, the offering of restored liberty, and erased the old marks of your perfidy with a gentler hand.

Before you had washed away the stains you had created through repentance, he chose you as a companion of his dignity, so that, since by impious recklessness you had lost the title of liberty, you might receive a glorious testimony.

## 8

But what is surprising if he granted you these things, although you did not deserve them, when previously he had always shown himself your companion in danger and, in attacking you, had rather exposed himself to attack?

The order of these opposing roles is therefore astonishing. How great was your cruelty toward the Spaniards, and how great was the Spaniards’ compassion toward you!

They gave you peace; you devised treachery against them. They gave you defense; you devised destruction for them. They always ran to your liberation with an armed army; you stirred up foreign swords for their overthrow.

They resolved to repel the enemy from you either by force or by cunning; you, employing both shortcuts, came against the Spanish army both with your own frauds and with the strength of others.

They always sought your defense, even at their own peril; you, by contrast, prepared fortifications for their destruction, not without your own ruin.

They sought your safety and, when they could not hasten to you with arms, purchased it at a price; you determine that their death, which you could not accomplish by arms, should be bought with gifts.

When did they ever rejoice after becoming cheerful amid your wounds or delight in your deaths? Rather, whenever the report of messengers announced that you had been besieged by the enemy or battered by an enemy assault, the armed hand of the Spaniards immediately presented itself in haste for your defense; setting aside their own dangers, they fought with your enemies.

Indeed, although so many lands lay between them, they did not claim that they had endured difficult labors, provided only that you regained a condition of peace, however imperfectly.

Behold, it is now known how great an affection of compassion arose in the Spaniards and how great a storm of cruelty boiled up within you. You have experienced as both victors and merciful protectors the Spaniards whom you had assigned to contempt. But your own sons, who were brought forth from you by a viperous birth, what did they bring you except famine, pestilence, or the sword?

Let this insult, then, have been useful to you; perhaps whatever has been shouted with harsher blows may contribute to your benefit and salvation, so that the harshness of these words may be rather the cause of your correction than a performance of despair.

## 9

It remains, therefore, that you now give yourself to mournful lamentation: how worn down—or, according to the printed reading, terrified—by pallor, how discolored by wasting. Always living under this appearance of humility, blush over your former fornications, lest suppuration break out again in place of scars, lest an ulcer appear in a wound already healed, and lest a diseased lung emit anything swollen or proud.

Rather, with everything restored, let it be useful to you both to have been insulted into a condition of health and to have been taught with complete readiness. Thus, from now on, let this healthy vigor retain its memory, and let memory, made healthier, cut off from you every movement of an uplifted heart.

But if, as you are accustomed, with stubborn impulses you reject one who taunts and counsels you, I shall finally address you with these verses, by which a certain wise man is shown to have taunted death. I shall say:

> Now you yield without tears, nor do you feel the songs;  
> Let the words I speak to you serve you in place of a sword.  
> May he himself condemn your bite and conquer Tartarus,  
> He who conquered the world through the destruction of the cross.

**The insult against the province of Gaul is concluded.**

# JUDGMENT PROMULGATED AGAINST THE PERFIDY OF THE TYRANTS

*Note at col. 0801: The “Legitimate Text” and the “Tudensis Text” are printed in parallel in Migne.*

# LEGITIMATE TEXT

## 1

The marked transgression of traitors ought to be struck more severely in proportion as they appear to perpetrate certain acts through unlawful audacity.

Let those who have violated the promise of faith bear the sign of their own disgrace. Let those whom the prince’s indulgence made ungrateful carry the name of treason down to posterity.[^c0079-16] Let those who prepared the destruction of their own people be recorded among the ranks of traitors, so that those who became destroyers of their homeland may transmit the titles of their infamy through the generations of the ages.

Those to whom the prince, in his clemency, granted life shall not escape the gouging out of their eyes. They had diminished the glory of their homeland and incurred the mark of treason.[^c0079-17]

For behold, baneful perfidy came forth into the open field: joining the fellowship of the wicked to itself in bloody embraces, it stirred citizens to scandal, the populace to their own ruin, nations to the overthrow of their homeland, and the peoples not only of their own country but also of foreign lands to the death of the prince.

The earth is witness to what we say, the earth which has been worn down by their extermination. Heaven also is a witness, under which God assigned us a victorious standard.

For they broke the voluntary covenant of their promise and established a new oath of pledging, by which, having severed the voluntary promise of faith, they would reject our king chosen by God and bring upon him and his homeland destruction that had already been prepared.

By a new custom of perjury, they deceived not only their own souls but also those of many peoples, so that the prophetic oracle was fulfilled in them which says:

> “Their princes will fall into nets because of the fury of God’s anger, and there will be derision throughout the whole land.”[^c0079-18]

And likewise the passage in which Isaiah speaks of the transgressions of such men, saying:

> “They were found among my people, wicked men lying in wait like birdcatchers, setting traps and snares to capture men. As a trap full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit.”[^c0079-19]

[^c0079-16]: Variants: F has *eo* for *ideo*; D, *Habeat* for *Habeant*; F, *contingit* for *contigit*; F, *perditionis* (“of destruction”) for *proditionis* (“of treason”); F, *in* for *ad*; the manuscript, *inter cunctos perfidorum nomine* for *inter cuneos perfidorum*; and the manuscript, *paraverant* for *paravere*.

[^c0079-17]: F has *propriam* (“their own”) for *patriae* (“of the homeland”), and *incurrant* (“may incur”) for *incurrerant* (“had incurred”); it notes that Duchesne lacks the passage from *quibus ex clementia* through *incurrant*.

[^c0079-18]: The manuscript reads *subsanatio eorum* (“their derision”) for *subsannatio*.

[^c0079-19]: Variant reading: *sic* (“thus”) rather than *sicut* (“as”).

## 2

These matters, necessarily set forth beforehand, are sufficient. (F omits *et*; the manuscript has *praemissis* for *praemissa*.)

For when our most serene lord, King Wamba, sent the utterly wicked Paul to restore Gaul and to gather certain dissenters back to the faith of his majesty by a timely arrangement, Paul suddenly changed the task entrusted to him into its opposite. He not only failed to oppose the dissenters by remaining steadfast in faith, but himself made many unbelievers through his own dissent.[^c0079-20]

Turning toward tyranny against the aforesaid prince, people, and homeland, he first stripped himself of the faith he had promised and, beginning the web of his weaving, clothed himself in the stain of perjury.[^c0079-21]

Then he hurled curses against the glorious prince and publicly uttered against him every kind of insult involving detraction and injury.

After this—something impious even to say—he seized the kingdom against God’s will and compelled the peoples to swear allegiance to him in this wicked election, so that they might act against the faith they had given and bring about the death or deposition of the prince.

He observed this order above all in the succession of his perverse conditions: he dared to call our glorious lord Prince Wamba an unfortunate king. That name, according to its own interpretation, certainly signifies “unfortunate.”[^c0079-22]

Still provoked by the height of his tyrannical lot, he brought the whole province of Gaul and part of the province of Tarraconensis under the tumultuous authority of his own jurisdiction, establishing special fortifications in each and every city and appointing his own defenders in them.

[^c0079-20]: Variant reading: “he made many dissenters faithful to himself.”

[^c0079-21]: Variants: D has *sibi redditam* (“given to himself”) for *fidem redditam*; F, *gerent* for *agerent*; and F, *maculam* (“a stain”) for *macula* (“the stain”).

[^c0079-22]: Variants: D has the ungrammatical *juxta interpretatio sui* for *juxta interpretationem sui*; the manuscript omits *omnem* (“whole”); and F has *insuper* (“moreover”) for *super* (“still,” “above”).

## 3

Compelled by the wicked audacity of this affair, we were forced to take up arms and, across so many intervening lands, pursue the perfidy of the wicked.

Accordingly, to extinguish immediately the tyranny of these conspirators, we advanced fighting into the province of Tarraconensis and into Gaul. With the divine hand accompanying us, we came all the way to the cities and fortresses themselves and successfully captured these very guards and defenders of the cities and camps.[^c0079-23]

First, advancing with the army toward Barcelona, we captured Euredus, Pompedius, Guntefredus, Hunulfus the deacon, and Neufredus while reclaiming that city.

Then, reaching the Clausurae, we entered the camps themselves with the army arranged through the passes of the Pyrenees and captured the defenders of those camps, namely Ranosindus, Hildegisus, Helias, Carmennus, Maureco, Wandemirus,[^c0079-24] Dagarus, Xixan, and Luibitanus.[^c0079-25]

Proceeding in the same manner with warlike attacks, through the divisions of the armies we captured in the fortress of Caucoliber Leofredus and Gudrigildus,[^c0079-26] together with their wives.

We also hurried in the same manner into the fortress of Libya, which is the head of Cerretania.[^c0079-27] Bishop Iacinthus and Arangisclus, united in the same perfidy after the authority of the traitor Paul, were defending it.

But because Iacinthus could not defend the same fortress of Libya, he too, with God’s favor, did not escape our hands.

When the traitor Paul learned of the capture of all these men and of our entry into Gaul (*sive*; the manuscript has *suae*)—especially when he heard that the Franks whom he had sent to reclaim the Clausurae had fled—he too immediately abandoned the city of Narbonne and placed himself under the protection of flight.[^c0079-28]

There he left the city’s custodians: Ranimirus the pseudo-bishop, Wittimirus, Argemundus, and Gultricianus the chief cleric.[^c0079-29]

When Ranimirus saw the army, he too sought flight (*appetiit* in F) before the city itself was attacked. But soon captured in the territory of Béziers, he did not escape our hands.

Thus, after we had captured the aforementioned laymen Wittimirus and Argemundus, who were defending Narbonne, together with Gultricianus the chief cleric, and who were fighting fiercely against us,[^c0079-30] we subjected the city of Agde to the authority of our glorious lord. In it we captured Bishop Wilesindus*, Aragisclus, and Ranosindus*, the brother of Bishop Wilesindus.[^c0079-31]

[^c0079-23]: D has *itidem* (“likewise”) for *id est* (“namely”). The *Hispania illustrata* has *coepimus* (“we began”) instead of *cepimus* (“we captured”), evidently an error.

[^c0079-24]: Variant spelling: *Wandamirum*.

[^c0079-25]: The manuscript reads *Liuvanem* rather than *Luibitanem*.

[^c0079-26]: Variant spelling: *Guidrigildum*.

[^c0079-27]: Manuscript spelling: *aput* rather than *caput* (“head”).

[^c0079-28]: The manuscript lacks *illico* (“immediately”) in this sentence.

[^c0079-29]: The manuscript has *primiclericum* (“chief cleric”) rather than *primiclerum*.

[^c0079-30]: The *Hispania illustrata* mistakenly reads *coepissemus* (“we had begun”) rather than *cepissēmus* (“we had captured”).

[^c0079-31]: The *Hispania illustrata* has *gloriosissimi* (“most glorious”) rather than *gloriosi* (“glorious”), and *subjugavimus* (“we subjugated”) rather than *subegimus* (“we subjected”). The manuscript does not include the asterisks surrounding the names in the printed text.

### 4

And when thereafter, with divine judgments assisting us, we advanced to attack the city of Maguelone, Gumildus the bishop, having foreseen the simultaneous naval and land battle of the two armies [Note: In the manuscript, *bellum* (“battle”) is absent; in the same manuscript, *cum* (“with”) is absent], immediately abandoned that same city and, seeking flight, betook himself with the perfidious Paul to Nîmes.

When we had most gloriously captured this very city of Maguelone and its defenders, we immediately reached Nîmes, intending to fight against the perfidious Paul and his companions. There the same Paul had presented himself for battle, relying not only on the boldness of his fellow traitors but also fortified by the aid of the Franks [Note: F. reads *etiam et* (“also and”)]. Fighting most fiercely in that place and persisting in the rashness of his treachery, at last, when the same city had been breached by divine judgments and our arms, Paul was defeated, captured, and held.

It is also necessary to record his companions, whom we endured fighting fiercely against us in the same city [Note: D. reads *expugnantes*, “attacking”], and who clung most stubbornly to his treachery for as long as they were captured together with that most wicked man: namely, Gumildus the bishop, Friusclus [Note: The manuscript reads *Frugisclus*], Flodarius, Wistrimirus, Ranemundus, Andosindus, Adulfus, Maximus, *Joannes, Clerium, Anvarnus, Aquilinus, Odofredus, Iberius, Joannes, Mosamius* [Note: F. reads *Mosimus*], *Amingus, Virimar, Eumericus, Transemirus* [Note: The manuscript reads *Wazimar, Cuniericus, Trasericus*], *Bera, Ebrulfus, Recaulfus, Cottila* [Note: F. reads *et Cottila* (“and Cottila”)], *Guldramus* [Note: The manuscript reads *Guldramirus*], *Liuba, Ranila,* and *Ildericellus* [Note: F. reads *Idericellus*], except for the multitude of common people, or of Franks, which was captured in that same city.

### 5

Therefore, while this most wicked Paul, after all of us had been summoned and assembled—that is [Note: D. reads *itidem* (“likewise”)], all the elders of the palace, all the *gardingi*, the entire palatine office, and also the whole army standing in the presence of our glorious lord [Note: F. reads “most glorious”]—was standing with his aforesaid companions to be judged, the aforesaid prince addressed him under the previously mentioned charge of conspiracy, saying:

“I adjure you by the name of almighty God to contend with me in judgment at this gathering of my brothers: whether I have injured you in anything, or whether I have nourished evil in you on account of any occasion of malice, by which, being provoked, you might undertake this tyranny or dare to seize the summit of this kingdom.”

### 6

Immediately that most wicked Paul testified in a clear voice, saying:

“By God, I have neither felt that I was injured by your glory, nor have I suffered any evil from you; rather, you ordered that so much good be bestowed upon me [Note: F. reads *impertire*, “to bestow”] that I in no way deserved to receive it. Nevertheless, incited by the devil’s prompting, I did this.”

His companions mentioned above were likewise questioned, and they all answered in the same way. Thereupon the written agreements were brought forward [Note: The same edition reads *perlatae*, “brought forward”], in which, by a voluntary promise, at the election of our glorious lord King Wamba, that most wicked Paul and his companions had agreed together with us and had testified under a pledge before the divine power that they would inviolably observe faith toward him and toward the fatherland [Note: The manuscript corruptly reads *sponte*, “voluntarily”]. They had also marked these agreements with the subscriptions of their own hands.

When these agreements had been opened and read through, for the confusion of their treachery the subscription of their hands in those very agreements was displayed to them so that they might see it [Note: The same edition reads *manibus*, “hands”]. After this, other agreements were reread, to which the perfidious Paul had made the people swear. In them the following order of impiety and cruelty had been preserved: all his companions had sworn to Paul in this order, that they would be faithful to him and would fight unanimously with him against our glorious lord King Wamba [Note: The same edition omits “glorious”], and that they would fight for his overthrow or danger even to the shedding of blood, or against those who wished to defend that same lord our king [Note: The same edition adds “with him” after “king”].

In those agreements they had named the aforesaid glorious lord our king Wamba an ill-fated king, as has been stated above, together with the other detestable things found written in those agreements.

### 7

After these matters had been reviewed and read through, a sentence from the canons was brought forward from the Council of Toledo, in the seventy-fifth era [Note: D. reads “the twenty-fifth era”; but here, as in the other passages, there is an error, since it should read “the seventy-first era.” Saint Julian, writing this, refers to canon 75 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, held in A.D. 633, or era 671; the words of that canon are quoted here], where it says as follows:

“Whoever from now on among us, or among the peoples of all Spain, by any conspiracy or design, violates the oath of his faith which he has promised for the condition of the fatherland and the Gothic people, or for the preservation of the king’s safety, etc.”

Next the sentence of the law was recited, in Book II, title 1, era 6, where it says as follows [Note: This law is law 7 of Book II, title 1, of the Visigothic laws. What Julian means by “era 6” we do not clearly understand, unless he intends era 676 (A.D. 638), in which the Sixth Council of Toledo was held under King Chintila. There, in canons 12 and 18, the same sentence was imposed upon those who fled to the enemy or plotted against the safety of the prince as that imposed by the law—namely, capital punishment or the tearing out of the eyes. The author of the law appears to be Recceswinth, who held the kingdom, alone and jointly with his father, from A.D. 649 to 672]:

“Whoever, from the time of the revered-memory prince Chintila until the second year of our reign, with God’s favor, or from now and thereafter, etc.”

Instructed by the command of this sacred canon, we must no longer hesitate to punish in body and temporal goods, according to the sentence of this law, those whom those Fathers have already condemned in soul by so terrible a judgment and perpetual anathema. Therefore, in accordance with the promulgated statutes of the law [Note: The same edition reads *edicta*, “edicts”], we all determined by common agreement that the same perfidious Paul and his aforesaid companions should be condemned to the most shameful death and perish. Thus they appear to undergo the fate of everlasting destruction, since they plotted the overthrow of the fatherland and attempted to destroy the prince.

But if perhaps life should be pardoned them by the prince, let them be preserved alive only after their eyes have been torn out. We decree that all the property of Paul and his companions is to remain in the power of our glorious lord. Thus, whatever his serenity’s clemency chooses to do or judge concerning them, let unquestioned power remain with him, so that the name of the seditious may utterly perish from the earth and future ages may shrink from imitating their mournful memory, marked by these inscriptions [Note: D. reads *devotatam*, “devoted/condemned”].

*Here happily ends.*
