# TEXT OF TUY

[Col. 0801]

### 1

The marked transgression of traitors ought to be struck all the more harshly because it is seen to have been committed in illicit undertakings. Let those, therefore, to whom it happened to violate a pledged oath bear the sign of their own confusion. Let them transmit the name of perdition to posterity—those whom princely indulgence made ungrateful. Let those who prepared the destruction of their own people be marked out among the ranks of traitors, so that they may transmit through the generations of the ages the titles of their infamy—those who became destroyers of the fatherland, but whom the prince, out of clemency, allowed to live. Let those who, diminishing the glory of the fatherland, rashly incurred the mark of treason not escape the tearing out of their eyes.

Behold, ill-omened treachery has betrayed itself in the open field. By joining the fellowship of the wicked in bloody embraces, it drove citizens to scandal, the populace to the destruction of their own people, nations to the overthrow of the fatherland, and not only its own peoples but also the peoples of foreign nations to the death of the prince. The earth is a witness to what we say, the earth which has been worn away by their extermination. Heaven too is a witness, beneath which God has granted us a triumphal standard.

For when the perfidious Paul broke the voluntary covenant of his promise, he established a new oath of allegiance, by which, having severed the voluntary faith of his pledge, he would reject our divinely chosen lord King Wamba and bring upon him and the fatherland the destruction he had hastened. For, in a new form of perjury, he deceived not only his own souls but also those of many peoples, so that in them was fulfilled that prophecy of the prophet which says:

“Their princes shall fall into nets through the fury of God’s wrath [Note: The manuscript reads “the wrath of the day,” *diei*], and their mockery shall be throughout all the earth.”

And likewise what Isaiah recounts concerning the excesses of such men, saying:

“They were found among my people, the wicked who lie in wait like bird-catchers, setting snares and traps [Note: The manuscript reads *peducas*] for catching men. As a cage full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit.”

### 2

These matters, necessarily set forth beforehand, are sufficient. For when our most serene lord King Wamba sent the most wicked Paul to recover Gaul, so that he might gather certain dissenters to faith in his glory by a timely arrangement, Paul suddenly turned the task entrusted to him in the opposite direction. Not only did he fail to oppose those dissenters by remaining steadfast in the faith, but he himself made many unbelievers through his own dissent.

For, turning toward tyranny against the aforesaid prince, people, and fatherland, he first stripped himself of his pledged faith and, beginning to weave the web of his wicked design, put on the stain of treason and perjury. Then they publicly uttered curses against the glorious prince and many kinds of slanderous insults and injuries against him [Note: The manuscript reads *protestatur*, singular, “he utters”]. After this—something too wicked to mention—he seized the kingdom against God’s will and compelled the peoples to swear to him in this wicked conspiracy [Note: *Hispania illustrata* reads “of the citizens” instead of “to himself”], so that they might act against the faith pledged to the glorious prince and bring about his death or destruction.

He especially preserved this order in the sequence of the perverse agreements, daring to call our glorious lord Wamba an ill-fated king. This name, according to its meaning, signifies “unfortunate.” Moreover, impelled by the height of his tyrannical position, he subjected the whole province of Gaul and part of the province of Tarraconensis to the tumultuous rule of his own authority, establishing special garrisons in every city and appointing his own defenders in them.

### 3

Compelled by the wicked rashness of this affair, we were forced to take up arms and, across so many intervening lands, pursue the treachery of the wicked. Therefore, in order immediately to extinguish the tyranny of these conspirators, we advanced fighting into the province of Tarraconensis and into Gaul. With the divine hand accompanying us, we reached the cities and castles themselves and successfully captured these very guards and defenders of the cities and forts.

First, advancing with the army against the resisting guards at Barcelona, we captured Euredus, Pompedius, Guntifredus, the deacon Unulfus [Note: *Hispania illustrata* reads *Gutrifredum, Arnulfum*], and Neufredus, who were defending that same city [Note: The manuscript reads *vendicantes*, “claiming/defending”].

Then, coming to the Locks, we entered the forts themselves with our army deployed across the ridges of the Pyrenees and captured the defenders of those forts, namely Ranosindus, Hildegisus, Helias, Carmenus, Maureco, Vaddemirus, Diagerus, Cixanus, and Liubanes.

We also captured, as we hastened forward in warlike incursions, Leufredus and Gugidillus, together with the wives of the aforesaid men, in the fort of Caucoliberis.

We likewise entered the fort of Libia, which is the head of Ceretania, hastening there in the same manner, because Bishop Iacinthus, in agreement with Arangisclus in the same treachery, was defending it after the perfidious Paul [Note: There, *ipse* is printed instead of *episcopus*, “the bishop”]. But since Iacinthus could not defend that fort of Libia, he too, with God’s help, did not escape our hands.

When the perfidious Paul had learned of the capture of all these men, or of our entry into Gaul, through the flight of the Franks whom he had sent to defend the Locks, he too abandoned the city of Narbonne and committed himself to the protection of flight. He left there as custodians of the city itself Ramirus the pseudo-bishop, Victimirus, Argemundus, and Galtritio the chief cleric.

When Ramirus saw the army, before the city itself was attacked, he also took flight. But shortly afterward, captured in the territory of Béziers, he did not escape our hands.

When we had captured the aforesaid laymen Victimirus and Argemundus, together with Galtritio the chief cleric, who were defending Narbonne and fighting fiercely against us, we brought the city of Agde under the authority of our glorious lord and captured there Bishop Vilesmundus, Arangisclus, and Ranosindus, the brother of Bishop Vilesmundus.

### 4

After this, when with divine judgment assisting us we advanced to attack the city of Maguelone, Gumildus the bishop, when we advanced with the two armies, naval and land, immediately abandoned that city and, seeking flight, betook himself with the perfidious Paul to Nîmes.

When we had most gloriously captured this city of Maguelone and its defenders, we immediately reached Nîmes, intending to fight against the aforesaid Paul and his companions. There the same Paul had presented himself for battle, relying not only on the boldness of his fellow traitors but also fortified by the aid of the Franks.

Fighting most fiercely in that place and persisting in the rashness of his treachery, at last, when the same city had been breached by divine judgments and our arms, Paul was defeated and captured.

It is also necessary to record his companions, whom we endured fighting fiercely against us in that same city [Note: *Hispania illustrata* reads *et* (“and”) for *etiam* (“also”)], and who clung most stubbornly to his treachery for as long as they were captured together with that most wicked man: namely, Gumildus the bishop, Friuscus, Frodarius, Witimirus, Ranemundus, Adosindus, Adulfus, Maximus, and Gotila—apart from the multitude of common people, whether Franks or Saxons, which was captured in that same city.

### 5

Therefore, while this most wicked Paul, after all of us had been summoned and assembled—that is [Note: There, *nobis* (“us”) is absent, and *et* (“and”) is read in place of *id est* (“that is”)], all the elders, all the *gardingi* of the palace, the entire palatine office, and also the whole army standing in the presence of our glorious lord the king—with his aforesaid companions, was standing to be judged, the aforesaid prince addressed him concerning the conspiracy mentioned above, saying:

“I adjure you by the name of almighty God to contend with me in judgment at this assembly of our brothers: whether I have injured you in anything, or whether, on account of any kind of malice, I nourished evil in you, by which, being provoked, you might undertake this tyranny and dare to seize the summit of this kingdom.”

### 6

Immediately that most wicked Paul testified in a clear voice, saying:

“By God, I have neither felt that I was injured by your glory, nor have I suffered any evil from you; rather, your clemency ordered that so much good be bestowed upon me that I in no way deserved to receive it. Nevertheless, incited by the devil’s prompting, I did this.”

His companions mentioned above were likewise questioned, and they all answered in the same way. Thereupon the agreements were brought forward. In them, by a voluntary promise, at the election of our glorious lord King Wamba, that most wicked Paul and his companions had agreed together with us and had testified under a pledge before the divine power that they would inviolably observe faith toward him and toward the fatherland. They had also marked these pledges with the subscriptions of their own hands.

When these agreements had been read through—agreements which they themselves had maliciously abridged—for the confusion of their treachery the subscription of their hands in those same agreements was shown to them so that they might see it.

After this, other agreements were reread, to which the perfidious Paul had made the people swear. In them the following order of impiety and cruelty had been preserved: all his companions had sworn to Paul in this order, that they would be faithful to him and would fight unanimously with him against our glorious lord King Wamba, and that they would fight for his overthrow or danger even to the shedding of blood, or against those who wished to defend that same king.

The aforesaid glorious King Wamba is rashly found written in those agreements as an ill-fated king, as has been stated above.

### 7

After these matters had been reviewed and read through, a sentence from the canons was brought forward from the Council of Toledo concerning how transgressors of this kind ought to be punished.

---

# APPENDICES

## APPENDIX ONE: WORKS WRONGLY ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT JULIAN

[Col. 0809]

### Notice

We conclude in this very brief appendix all the works falsely attributed to Saint Julian—few though they are: namely, the Chronicle of the Visigothic Kings, frequently called that of Wulsa; then two poems and four epitaphs.

You ask who attributed these works to Julian. The same man who, under the fabricated names of Julian and Liutprand, composed those widely circulated chronicles distinguished by so many fables.

As for the Chronicle of the Visigoths, although it is truly a golden work—as the highly learned Joan Baptista Perez called it in the preliminary letter to volume I of Cardinal de Aguirre’s collection of councils, since by its light the sacred and secular chronology of Spain has been greatly illuminated—even so, no sufficiently solid argument proves that it should be attributed to Saint Julian.

For the whole work, as it now exists and extends down to the reign of Witiza, cannot be Julian’s. Nor, even if one says that its final chapters were written by someone continuing an earlier chronicle—which, when we consider the individual passages and observe the difference between one section and another in the designation of years and days, is almost self-evident and certain—can Julian properly be called the author of the earlier part of the chronicle.

For if we can reach anything by conjecture, the conclusion drawn from certain older manuscripts, in which the present chronicle extends only to the beginning of Ervig’s reign, as is clear from the editions of Aguirre and Vulcanius in the notes to Jordanes’ history of the Visigoths, is rather that its author was someone other than our Julian. Julian died under Egica and would scarcely have passed over in silence either the death of Ervig or Egica’s accession to the kingdom.

Moreover, if one adds that Felix makes no mention of the aforesaid chronicle in his eulogy of Julian, although he carefully recorded the history of King Wamba, one must conclude that a work of this kind was rashly attributed to Saint Julian.

Now, if you ask for its true author, we are entirely ignorant. For the fact that it is called the work of Wulsa and commonly attributed to a writer of that name—whom some have even said was a Spanish bishop—is a foul error, arising, in our judgment, from the fact that some copyist carelessly transcribed *Wulse-Gotthorum* for *Wise-Gotthorum*, which is what appears in ancient copies, and that the error then passed to others.

Certainly the name Wulsa is found nowhere among the writers of that period, still less among the bishops of Spain. On this subject one should consult Father Flórez, volume II of *España Sagrada*. We have reproduced his edition of the present Chronicle, likewise adding in the margin many variants from the manuscript of Joan Baptista Perez that we have often mentioned.

---

# CHRONICLE OF THE VISIGOTHIC KINGS

[Col. 0809]

In the four-hundredth era [407; Saint Isidore], Athanaric became the first king among the Goths. After him came Alaric. When he died in Italy, Ataulf was chosen. During his reign the Goths, abandoning Italy, occupied Gaul and afterward Spain. The years of the kings are recorded in the following summary.

1. Athanaric reigned 13 years [perhaps 12].

2. Alaric reigned 28 years in Italy.

3. Ataulf reigned 6 years [perhaps 5].

4. Sigeric [Segeric] reigned 7 years [Note: “I would prefer *days* to be read instead of *years*]; elsewhere only half a year.

5. Wallia reigned 3 years [perhaps 4].

6. Theuderic [Theudericus … 23 years] reigned 33 years [perhaps 32].

7. Thorismund [Thorismodus] reigned 3 years; elsewhere 1 [Note: This chronology should be followed, not the first].

8. Theuderic reigned 7 years; elsewhere 13 [Note: The same applies to this king].

9. Euric reigned 15 years [20], elsewhere 17 [perhaps 18] [Note: Although we believe that the computation of years which we record for Athanaric, Ataulf, Wallia, Theuderic, and Euric is more accurate than that of the other chroniclers, we nevertheless admit that in this matter he followed Saint Isidore in his History of the Goths].

10. Alaric reigned 23 years.

11. Gesaleic [Geselicus] reigned 3 years and spent 1 year in hiding; elsewhere 15 [Note: I cannot easily say why 15 is added here. As for the statement that Gesaleic reigned one year in hiding, everyone knows that this is what Saint Isidore wrote: namely, that when the king returned from Africa, out of fear of Theuderic he sought Aquitania and hid there for one year].

Theuderic ruled in Spain from Italy, acting as guardian of his grandson Amalaric, through consuls, for 41 years [Note: Not 41, but only 15 years—namely, from 511 to 526—did Theuderic act as Amalaric’s guardian. Theuderic’s reign in Italy lasted only thirty-three years according to Saint Isidore]; elsewhere 15 [“Likewise Theuderic from Italy in Spain … as guardian for 11 years”].

12. Amalaric [Amaleric] reigned 5 years.

13. Theudis reigned 16 years and 6 months; elsewhere 17 years and 5 months.

14. Theudisclus reigned 1 year, 6 months, and 13 days [5 months].

15. Agila reigned 5 years, 6 months [3 months], and 13 days.

16. Athanagild reigned 15 years and 6 months; elsewhere 14 years. The kingdom was vacant for 5 months, elsewhere 13.

17. Liuba reigned 1 year.

18. Liuvigild [Leovigild] reigned 18 years.

19. Reccared reigned 15 years, 6 months [1 month], and 10 days.

20. Again Liuba reigned 1 year; elsewhere 2 years and 6 months.

21. Witeric reigned 6 years and 10 months.

22. Gundemar reigned 1 year, 10 months, and 14 days [13].

23. Sisebut reigned 8 years, 11 months, and 16 days; elsewhere 6 months.

24. Again Reccared reigned 3 [4] years [months]; elsewhere a few days.

25. Suinthila reigned 10 years.

26. Sisenand reigned 4 years [3], 11 months, and 16 days.

27. Chintila reigned 3 years, 9 months [8], and 9 days.

28. Tulga reigned 2 years and 4 months.

29. Chindaswinth [Cindasvindus; Aguirre: Chindisvindus] reigned alone for 6 years, 8 months, and 11 days. He then reigned with his son, lord Recceswinth [Aguirre: Recesvindo], for 4 years [3], 8 months, and 11 days [Aguirre: 12]. He died on the day before the Kalends of October, in era 691.

30. Recceswinth [Reccesvindus] [Note: Henry Flórez, volume II of *España Sagrada*, part II, chapter 2, §3, proves very correctly that the word “alone” should be deleted, since Recceswinth reigned after his father’s death for only 18 years and 11 months—that is, from the first day of October 653 until 1 September 672] reigned alone for 23 years, 7 months [6], and 11 days [2].

He died on the Kalends of September, on the fourth day of the week, at the third hour, in era 710, in the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 672, in the eighth year of the nineteen-year cycle, on the third day of the lunar month. He reigned with his father for 4 years, 8 months, and 11 days.

31. The lord [glorious lord] Wamba assumed the governance of the kingdom on the same day on which Recceswinth died, on the aforesaid Kalends of September. The solemnity of his anointing was postponed until the thirteenth day [Aguirre: fourteenth] before the Kalends of October, on the twenty-first day of the moon, in the same era.

That glorious King Wamba reigned for 8 years, 1 month, and 14 days. The aforesaid prince received penance on the Sunday toward its end, at the first hour of the night, which was the day before the Ides of October, on the fifteenth day of the moon, in era 718.

32. On the following day [immediately], Monday, the glorious lord Ervig, our lord [“our lord” is absent], immediately assumed the scepter of the kingdom. This was the Ides of October, on the sixteenth day of the moon, in era 718. The solemnity of his anointing was postponed until the following Sunday, which was the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, on the twenty-second day of the moon, in the same era [Note: Aguirre edited up to this point; Maiansius, and after him the aforementioned Flórez, edited the remainder].

The glorious King Ervig reigned 7 years and 25 days. On that day, while suffering from his final illness, he chose our glorious lord Egica as his successor in the kingdom. On the following day, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, a Friday, the same lord Ervig received penance and absolved all the elders, so that together with the aforesaid prince, the glorious lord Egica, they might proceed to the seat of his kingdom at Toledo.

33. Our lord Egica was anointed king in the church of Saints Peter and Paul of Praetoria [Proetoria] on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, a Sunday, on the fifteenth day of the moon, in era 725.

34. Witiza was anointed king on the day which was the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December [Note: The same edition, and in our judgment rightly, believes that “the eighteenth” should be read], in era 738.

# APOLOGETIC POEMS BY PSEUDO-JULIAN PETER, ARCHPRIEST OF SAINT JUSTA, FALSELY ATTRIBUTED TO BLESSED JULIAN THE BISHOP

Printed by Laurentius Ramirez de Prado in the notes to Liutprand’s Chronicle, pp. 369 ff., Antwerp edition of 1640.

## Notice by the Spanish Editor

I regret, reader, having to make many observations on the two poems placed below. They were attributed to our Julian by the same Pseudo-Julian—and not merely attributed to him, but fabricated by him. The manuscript book preserved in the library of Saint Justa at Toledo, which, as he himself claims, contains these and many other poems of Saint Julian, is itself a mere invention, devised by the most mendacious of all mortals to fabricate and more easily impose his fables. The library too is fictitious.

But, to state the matter as it is, the source for fabricating the first poem, addressed to the emperor—no one having seen a copy of it before the Pseudo-Julian—was Isidore of Beja in his Chronicles, where he writes:

“Julian sent to Rome through his legates … again, with acclamatory verses, just as he had formerly sent them, concerning praise of the emperor” (*Apologeticus*), etc.

Roderic copied this passage in almost the same words in his history of Spain. From where Isidore of Beja derived it, we do not know. Certainly Felix, when speaking of the *Apologeticus* sent twice to Rome, mentions no verses.

And behold, the Pseudo-Julian immediately presents the poem itself, supposedly discovered by him alone. We reject it without hesitation because of the utterly slight authority of the man who puts it forward.

The other poem, written to Pope Sergius and extracted from the same fictitious manuscript, is even more clearly spurious. No historian even hints that such a poem was sent to the holy pontiff, much less to Sergius. When speaking of the *Apologeticus*, neither Isidore of Beja nor Roderic mentions this Sergius; and even if they did, no one could ever persuade us to accept the claim against the truth of history.

For it is established from Felix—and Julian himself also testifies in the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, held in 688—that he had sent the book *Apologeticus* to Rome two years earlier, namely in 686. At that time, after the death of Benedict II, John V was seated in Peter’s chair; he was succeeded by Conon, who died at the end of September 687.

How, then, could Julian have sent a poem with the *Apologeticus* to Sergius, the successor of Conon? It must therefore be regarded as spurious and fictitious.

## Notice of the Pseudo-Julian

Pope Benedict (II), offended … by the novelty of the expressions—namely, that will generated will, and that Christ consisted of three natures or essences—wrote courteously to him, Saint Julian, and verbally ordered the bearer to admonish him concerning these propositions.

When the holy teacher saw that some people had been scandalized by the novelty of these expressions, he sent the pope himself a responsive booklet with Peter the regional notary, and at the same time certain poems in praise of the empire. I excerpted them from the works of Saint Julian; they are as follows:

The majesty of empire extends beyond the world;

If piety is present, it flies beyond the stars.

For Caesar’s sword ought to defend the seat

Of Peter, over which God himself presides.

From him you received strength and the summit of your title;

Should you not, Caesar, be willing to offer him aid?

The glory of Roman empire brings yokes upon kings;

It moves peoples, and is present among nations.

Justiniane, by the strength of your right hand

Let every barbarian be broken, every faithless man.

With you as Caesar, let new Rome bear celebrated triumphs;

Let ancient noble Rome envy its name.

With you as Caesar, let the Church bear green laurel wreaths;

Let it carry glory away from heretical condition.

And let the impious necks of the Monothelites submit,

Holy father and shepherd, to you and to Peter the key-bearer.

May it conquer, and may the sacred see enjoy everlasting peace;

With you as Caesar, Justinian, may it hold the earth alone.

Live long, Caesar: honor willingly the commands

That Benedict gives; thus too, Caesar, you will be blessed.

He replied to Julian and still finds fault; and, after communicating his counsel with King Egica, he ordered that a national and universal council of the bishops of the Gothic people be convened at Toledo in the first year of King Egica. There, after the letters had been read, Julian explained himself and composed another *Apologeticus*, together with a poem in praise of the holy Pope Sergius, who had succeeded Benedict after others in 687; three most wise and holy men of the clergy of the holy Church of Toledo were also sent, as so great a matter required—namely Felix, archpriest; Ulisandus, archdeacon; and Musairus, chief cleric or subdeacon—with letters, the book *Apologeticus*, and the poem.

After the letters and book had been read, the holy Pope Sergius approved it and gave it to everyone to read. Having expressed thanks for their labor and piety, he sent the messengers back with relics, his blessing, and a letter of reply.

These poems are taken from the epigrams of the same Saint Julian, which are in the manuscript book of Saint Justa.

To you I gladly send this book, most holy Sergius,

You who rule and govern countless sheep.

The illustrious fame of your praises has reached us,

That you are good and merciful, a lover of piety.

In heart, voice, and manner of life you represent Christ,

Whose office you also perform on earth.

Live long for us and for the world, shining Sergius;

Julian, rejoicing, gives kisses to your feet.

Receive with a merciful countenance, most holy Sergius,

My writings; correct, O pope, my vigils.

Read through whatever our letter will teach,

And run with a gliding mind through its slight marks.

Whatever you yourself say is God’s judgment;

Whatever you say, God in heaven will deem confirmed.

The highest power has been granted by the Lord Christ;

You are able to close the heavens and to reopen them.

Therefore, Father Sergius, bless your little brother,

So that abundant grace may flow upon our head.

Remember King Egica and the faithful people;

Then bless the peoples of your bishops.

By your dew the Spanish field will bloom abundantly,

And for all time will cultivate the Catholic faith.

No savage storm, with the whirlwind of Phlegethon,

Will take it from the tongues and hearts of the faithful.

Alas for me! How I fear that evil error may entangle us,

And that we may be given as a reproach to unspeakable peoples.

Africa, full of warlike men, threatens arms,

And day by day the victorious Agarene people rage.

May this fear of mine not prove true, with Christ as avenger;

Pray for your peoples, excellent pope.

May God turn the axe away from our neck,

And, while you weep, may the merciful God grant pardon to the guilty.

---

# EPITAPHS ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT JULIAN IN THE CHRONICLE OF THE PSEUDO-LIUTPRAND

[Col. 0813]

## Notice
[Col. 0813] Of the four following epitaphs, whose omission by Nicolaus Antonius we marvel at, let the reader form the same judgment as concerning the preceding poems: that our Julian was not their author. Although it is established that he wrote many epigrams—for in that genre he yielded neither to Eugenius nor to Hildefonsus, his predecessors and teachers, and was their equal in talent and learning—we have nevertheless so far seen no genuine and unquestionable verses of Julian. For those which we now publish, after Tamaius de Vargas presented them in his *Martyrology*, rest solely upon the authority and testimony of the Pseudo-Luitprand, whom one can scarcely safely believe even when he tells the truth.

Moreover, they bear conspicuous marks of fabrication, especially the second and fourth epitaphs, so that one may easily recognize the fabricator’s ingenuity. In the epitaph of Bishop Quiricus, he confuses two well-known prelates of that name, one of Barcelona and the other of Toledo, and makes one and the same Quiricus out of the two: one who was first taken from the abbacy of Agali and appointed to the see of Barcelona, and then transferred from there to Toledo. Yet, as Father Flórez demonstrates excellently in volumes V and XXIX of the *Hispania Sacra*, the bishop of Barcelona, with whom our Hildefonsus had a close association and friendship, died at nearly the same time as Hildefonsus, around the year 667 or shortly thereafter; whereas the other, the Toledan, succeeded Saint Hildefonsus and did not die before the years 679 or 680.

Finally, in the last epitaph he invents that King Wamba, whom in his *Chronicle* he makes a native of the diocese of Segovia, had been a deacon before being raised to the kingship, ministering to the priest at the sacrifice, and had been called Peter, a name which he abandoned upon becoming king. Everyone can see how trivial, ridiculous, rashly fabricated, and fictitious all these things are.

[Col. 0813]

## [EPITAPHS]

### I. On the tomb of Saint Hildefonsus

[Col. 0813C]

The venerable body of Alfonsus lies in this stone,

[Note: [Col. 0813C] In the *Martyrology* of John Tamayo de Salazar, under 23 January, this verse and the following one are absent, so that it reads there:

[Col. 0814C] “The venerable body of Alphonsus lies in this stone,

But he shines more nobly through virtue.”

]

than whom the land of Toledo produced none better:

[the son] of Lucia and Stephen, of a noble Gothic race,

he shines yet more nobly through virtue that ennobles him.

As a young man he found the harbor and, leaving the world behind,

loved the cells of the monastery of Agali.

[Col. 0814C] From there he was carried away as bishop to the city of Toledo,

for it was his wish to dwell in his own see.

### II. On the tomb of Quiricus

[Note: [Col. 0814C] *Kiricus* is called from the Greek Κύριος (*Kyrios*), which means “Lord.”]

O Quiricus, who piously bear a name from the Lord, in word,

and who are both monk and bishop of Barcelona, hail.

Once you were the most holy abbot of Agali;

Barcelona rejoices greatly, exulting in you as its bishop.

[Col. 0815A] Piety appointed you over the Toledan fold;

yet, as a bishop who loves both sees, you behold them divided.

Nothing was ever better than one of you, nor holier than you alone;

and you die grieving over the king driven mad.

Leocadia receives you as her companion with joyful arms,

placing your body in the earth, and your rejoicing mind beneath the heights.

Rejoice in your lot, venerable Bishop Quiricus;

thus you are a lord on earth, and Lord in heaven.

### III. On the tomb of Gudila, archdeacon of Toledo

The glory of Toledo lies buried beneath this monument:

Gudila, half of my soul and half of myself.

He had possessed the character of an old man from tender youth,

and as a young man did nothing youthful here.

[Note: [Col. 0815B] In the entry for 8 March, the same source reads this pentameter as follows:

“for him, except simplicity, nothing youthful existed.”]

The Spirit of Christ dwelt in his holy breast;

he expressed Him wholly—in character, speech, and hand.

He was food for the poor, comfort for widows, and, for the sick,

welcome health: he alone was everything to the wretched.

By many merits you purchase heaven, good Gudila;

[Col. 0815B] our longing for you continues to torment us.

Mourning, we call upon him whom heaven has taken away;

and we follow the funeral with devout little tears.

We do not scatter violets, tender roses, or hoary lilies

upon the tomb, but good prayers for you.

Therefore look upon us, radiant from your heavenly citadel;

[Col. 0816A] and let love and concern for me move you, Gudila.

Drive sickness and famine away from our ancestral walls,

and hostile threats, false teachings, and deceits.

Do not disdain Toledo’s prayers and the request of your companion,

Julian, who loves you greatly and gives you this poem.

He lays your sacred bones in the holy church of Felix,

whose soul has been joined to the choirs above.

### IV. On the tomb of King Wamba

Wamba, formerly Peter, who were a minister of the Mass,

you shine as king of the Gothic people through religion.

Of your own will you did not seek the royal summit,

but, compelled, you undertook the great burden of rule.

Your hope and endeavor, relying on the power of the Mighty One,

bring you forth as one who has accomplished unprecedented deeds.

Nothing is ever more pleasing than repose of such a kind:

after the sacred scepters, you joyfully seek the monastery.

There, as a monk, you spend seven full years well;

[Col. 0816B] [Note: [Col. 0816B] The same source, in the same place.

“Then, with death offered, blessed, he goes to heaven.”]

then, with death offered, blessed, you go to heaven.

Happy Wamba, you are judged to have been in possession of a fortunate lot:

whoever treads the scepters so well will fly among the stars.

For seven years you govern the scepter of your people,

which you relinquish—not under the burden of illness, but freely yourself.

# SECOND APPENDIX

[Col. 0815]

## TWO LETTERS OF IDALIUS OF BARCELONA

*(From D’Achery,* Spicilegium*.)*

### FIRST LETTER

[Col. 0815C]

To the most holy lord Julian, especially dear to me, bishop of the first see of Toledo,

[Note: [Col. 0815D] “Bishop of the see.” Previously, “apostle” was read. This letter and the following one had already been published by Johann Cochlaeus at the end of Julian of Toledo’s books, Leipzig, 1536, as Baluzius notes; for our part, we have not had the opportunity to see that edition, nor have we made much effort to find it, since after it there was nothing in these letters that could cause us difficulty.]

Idalius, bishop of the see of Barcelona.

Terrified by the recollection of my sins and everywhere overwhelmed by the memory of my enormous crimes, I had thought that the divine ears had been completely closed to my cries, since I did not perceive the fulfillment of your promise. And although I have now been driven by various disturbances, now deprived of the outcome of the opportunity I desired, or, as usually happens, detained by forgetfulness, and have thus alternated my petitions with farewells to your holiness,

[Note: [Col. 0815D] “Alternated.” Since there were many errors in the earlier edition, which we removed with the help of a copy, we were glad to pass over the slightest matters so as not to weary the reader. But it could not be omitted that the earlier reading here was *alternam*; and shortly afterward, where you read *securavit*, we derived that reading from the copy, in which it was *sacravi*. Although the latter could not be accepted, it came closer to the true reading than the *sacre autem* printed by Acherius.]

I have nevertheless not ceased to offer prayers to your holiness. Relying upon the saying of our Savior and Redeemer, by which, speaking to the disciples, he assured them: “If two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven,” and relying most fully also upon confidence in your promise, I held firmly in my heart that neither Truth could in any way lie, nor a worshiper and disciple of Truth serve falsehood.

I therefore awaited what your holiness had promised, placing great hope in the Lord Jesus Christ. Yet I prayed—if not daily, certainly often—

[Col. 0816C] that the same one who is everywhere present

[Note: [Col. 0816D] “Is everywhere present.” The earlier edition had *ubique praesenti*. Below, in the old copy, the words *nomine Restitutus* are absent.]

and who inspires your heart might be present and at last grant fulfillment to our desires.

Now, therefore, because the Lord remembered me and made me possess what I had prayed for, he filled my mouth with joy and my tongue with exultation, since he both crowned you with the perfection of a holy work and enriched me through the accomplishment of your labor. I shall therefore say to him, in the words of his prophet and with exultation of mind: “Blessed is God, blessed is the Lord from day to day.”

For a certain Jew named Restitutus arrived, carrying, so to speak, like a brute animal, material suited to the light: a book which your holiness had taken care, with learned brevity, to complete through your own labor and study, not only from the opinions of the ancient holy Fathers but also under Christ’s inspiration and instruction, and to send to our ineptitude. With both hands he presented it. Seizing it in my eagerness to know it, rather than merely receiving it, I immediately opened it, and, looking up at the title,

[Col. 0816D] [Note: [Col. 0816D] “Looking up at the title.” Acherius printed *contra suscipiens*; I was surprised by this, but it is a minor matter, as is the reading he published in the phrase “who entrusts the treasure …”; the serious matter is that he wrote *a cultu Dei*, whereas it now reads *a cultu fidei*.]

I confess that I wondered why your holiness had entrusted the cause of so great and excellent a commodity to so untrustworthy a bearer, alien as he was from the worship of the faith. But immediately, instructed by the principle according to which a treasure is entrusted to earthen vessels, I considered why the aforesaid Jew had first delivered unharmed what he had received. Before thanking you, I reflected that perhaps you had acted through a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, so that the man who had been accustomed to transport perishable merchandise might be prepared for divine and eternal mysteries.

[Col. 0817A]

Nevertheless, in this matter I understood the humility of your holy and skillful heart. Whatever is graceful, polished, and pure in your words, you attribute with thanksgiving to God, from whose gift the great and excellent thing has come to you, and you return it to him. Yet, by rejecting empty glory, you strive to display that same thing to the eyes of those who see it as contemptible, precisely insofar as you are seen to have entrusted it to a lowly carrier.

Having therefore inspected the aforesaid book and examined its title, I could find no other name more suitable for the work than the one it itself seems to bear at the beginning of its volume. For it is called *Prognosticon of the Future Age*, which may appropriately be rendered in Latin as “Foreknowledge of the Future Age.”

In it, although the first book seems in part to instill harshness and fear in sinners, the two books that follow greatly lift the hearts of Christ’s worshipers through confidence in the future resurrection and the kingdom which Christ promised to give the faithful. As I read through the remaining body of the entire book, I found what the Lord Jesus Christ says in the Gospels: “Every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old” (Matthew 13:52).

Clearly, doubts have been dispelled and obscure matters brought into the light, since the decrees of the ancient Fathers, presented in a new brevity, have through your skill and fruitful labor been brought together and made accessible. Truth flows from their judgments, while from your labor comes a new and very brief form of truth. Whatever they truly, chastely, and soberly understood in matters concerning God is common to you with them, since the teaching of the Lord has brought you to knowledge of it.

Yet your diligence deserves equal applause because, urged on by inquiry, it has plainly opened up their collected judgments in a connected account to the lazy and sluggish. Therefore, although they supplied the material by Christ’s gift, the entire labor’s culmination will nevertheless be attributed to your work.

For gold, however much it may possess the splendor of its origin and nature, is skillfully led through forms or even varieties of figures and suitably polished; and the craftsman’s ingenuity is rightly praised.

[Note: [Col. 0817D] “Through forms or even.” To make clear what the frequently mentioned copy contributed here, the earlier edition must be reproduced. It reads: “but through forms … and, being polished by the craftsman’s skill, not imm. the preacher of this matter.”]

Moved by this example, I would endeavor to raise in praise the effectiveness of the intellect which divine grace has bestowed upon your heart, and the distinguished zeal with which I know you have labored in the causes of Christ—or, since I cannot do so myself, I would ask others to praise you—were I not aware that this very thing is usually displeasing to you.

It remains, therefore, for me to do what the soul of your holiness desires. My smallness—or rather, together with me, the whole Church, to whose knowledge our weakness has brought the distinction of your work—offers to the immense and ineffable Trinity not as many thanks as it ought, but as many as it is able, because at the end of time, or, more truly, almost at the consummation of the world, it poured into your blessed heart both the gift of its grace and the zeal for a holy work. It gave to your mouth a clear and well-sounding discourse by which it might heal the hearts of sinners through fear, and abundantly animate those devoted to good works, so that they might be strengthened in holy actions by heavenly fire.

We next pray the most lavish mercy of the heavenly Majesty to preserve you, by prolonging the years of your life, in the episcopate of his Church for the illumination of the faithful; and to permit the gift of his graces, which he has poured into your heart, to overflow, so that through your diligent works and teachings of holiness it may render the Catholic people rich in every good.

And, in return for your holy perseverance in labor, after the very long span of this life, with iniquities forgiven and sins covered, may he grant you the heavenly kingdoms to possess with his saints and elect.

### LETTER II

To the most holy and especially dear lord Zuntfredus, bishop of the first see of Narbonne, Idalius, bishop of the see of Barcelona.

The excellent work which your most blessed associate, my lord Julian, bishop of the first see of Toledo, took care to collect from the books of the ancient Catholic Fathers—not only with immense labor but also with immeasurable zeal—in remarkable and novel brevity, to gather into one volume, to call *Prognosticon of the Future Age*, and to send to our lowliness—having most earnestly charged us, at the insistent and praiseworthy urging of your blessedness, to offer it with both hands to your holiness—I, while devoted to you in this little city over which I unworthily preside, sent through this fellow-servant of mine, for presentation there at the seat of your holy sublimity.

Thus, when the bishops of your whole province have through knowledge of this work been made participants in your joy, you may command them to see by how great a light of grace the supreme Divinity has enriched your aforementioned associate for the illumination of the Church; and together they may bless the Lord God of heaven, from whose generosity this same associate of yours deserved to receive this gift.

Then may they pour out to the divine Trinity the offerings of their prayers, so that by divine grace it may protect the author of this work for so great a labor, and by divine indulgence erase the sins of our lowliness, since through him our negligence has taken care to bring them to knowledge of that by which their hearts may overflow with spiritual fruit.

I also beg you, dear lord, to command that the power of the Divinity be approached through continual prayers for the cleansing of my crimes, so that I, who am oppressed by various miseries, may deserve to be relieved by the remedies of your prayer.

Thus may you rejoice to possess the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ without end.

[Note: [Col. 0817D] “Not only with immense.” The printed editions do not yet have *ingenti*. [Col. 0818D] Below, we added *in instantia* from the cited copy, and *jubeant* as we wrote it, where it had read *jubeant cum*. From the same copy comes *libamina fundant*, where Acherius has *fundat*, and *parvitatis*, where previously there was *pravitatis*. Below, “Dear lord” is not pleasing, although it appears in our copy, and I prefer “venerable.”]

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 787. SAINT LULLUS, BISHOP OF MAINZ

[Col. 0819]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT LULLUS

*(From Fabricius,* Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.)*

[Col. 0819A]

Saint Lullus, or Lullo, also called Julius, an Englishman, after Saint Boniface his teacher, was archbishop of Mainz from the year 753 to 786 or 787. Concerning him, see Surius, 16 October; Leland, chapter 103; Bale, XIII.56; Pits, p. 156; Serarius, book IV, p. 371

[Col. 0820A] and following. “We have happened to see several of his letters,” says Flacius in the *Magdeburg Centuries*, eighth century, p. 453, “such as to Osvitha, to Leobgytha, to Gregory, to Denehard, to the Thuringians, and to Coena.” He then presents several passages from them, which may be seen there.

[Col. 0819]

## LETTERS OF SAINT LULLUS

### LETTER I. LULLUS TO DALHUNUS  
*(In the year of the Lord 752)*

[Col. 0819A]

To the most reverend brother Dalhunus, formerly my teacher, Lullus, an unworthy deacon, exercising the office of deacon without any distinction of merit: desirable salvation in the Lord.

I earnestly implore the kindness of your holiness in my deepest prayers, [Col. 0819B] asking that you deign to support the frail vessel of my mediocrity with your gracious prayers, so that, protected by the shield of your prayers’ intercession, I may deserve to reach the harbor of salvation and obtain forgiveness for my sins in this earthly prison, just as I entreated you during the past annual cycle through our brother Denewald, the bearer of my letters.

Therefore this little sheet is accompanied by the sending of humble gifts, offered with a mind not so worthy as it is devoted. Likewise, I beg you to deign to send me some little works of Bishop Aldhelm, whether in prose, meter, or rhythm, for the consolation of my pilgrimage and in memory of that blessed bishop. And indicate to me, in some words of your kindness, what your fraternity is able to accomplish regarding these requests, which I long eagerly to hear about.

I desire that you remain well and prosper through fortunate days, and that you intercede for me for many years.

It is said that King Agathocles dined from earthen vessels

and often loaded a Samian table with humble clay.

When he set golden dishes in gem-studded vessels

and mingled wealth and poverty together,

to one who asked the reason he replied: “I am a king

of Sicily, but I was born from a potter as my father.

Respect Fortune, whoever you are who suddenly

advance from a humble station into wealth.”

### LETTER II. INGALICUS TO LULLUS  
*(In the year of the Lord 752)*

To the illustrious and most beloved minister of God, Lullus: Ingalicus, your unworthy priest, yet in every respect your devoted servant, sends desirable salvation in the Lord.

The letters of your prudence and the gifts of your generosity, sent to me, have arrived. After carefully reading and considering them, and after offering the customary peaceful greeting, I understood that you had disclosed to us the various troubles and tribulations affecting you, which often beset Christ’s servants in this world, according to the Apostle’s saying: “All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution.”

Against all temptations you humbly requested the assistance of our prayers, whatever they may be. Our entire congregation has diligently endeavored to pour out prayers to the Lord for your well-being. And now, most beloved deacon, since, because of the smallness of my intellect, I have not been able to repay suitably the debt owed by writing in response to the instruction of your letters, I nevertheless know that true charity endures all things.

I have therefore taken care to send these few words of my rusticity, together with very small gifts—namely, four knives made according to our custom, a silver curling iron, and one tablecloth—through your faithful bearer, your brother, indeed ours, Aldred, solely as a remembrance of charity for your beloved presence.

I ask your fraternity to receive these things from me in the spirit in which you know they were sent. Moreover, the whole company of our brothers, together with the abbot, desires to greet in the love of God our intercessor with God, the venerable Bishop Boniface.

### LETTER III. LULLUS TO LEOBGYTHA  
*(Around the year of the Lord 752)*

To Leobgytha, my sister most beloved in Christ, Lullus, a humble servant, under the authority of the disciples of Lord Boniface: greetings in the Lord.

I do not consider your astute diligence forgetful of the evangelical saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” That poverty must be endured patiently, as the same evangelist attests when he says: “By your patience you will possess your souls.”

Keeping in my heart that saying of David, that “according to the multitude of your sorrows, the consolations of God have gladdened your soul,” I ask you not to suppose that your sincere kinship devoted to the Lord has been held in contempt or forgotten, although we are separated in bodily presence by intervals of time.

Nor should you in any way think me exhausted by your needs. Rather, know that I have been forestalled by the cunning of the devil’s deceit and wearied by the treacherous persecution of his ministers, in accordance with the prophet’s saying: “I am weary of my life because of the children of wickedness.”

Whatever your needs lack, indicate it through the returning deacon Gundwin; urge him not to grow weary in my labors, since very few are willing to share my tribulations with me.

Farewell in the Lord, interceding for me all the more earnestly the more heavily I am weighed down by distress.

### LETTER IV. LULLUS TO GREGORY  
*(In the year of the Lord 752)*

To Gregory, the shining lamp of Christ’s illustrious Church, and my most devoted helper in the teaching of divine law, adorned with the twofold honor of the priesthood and abbacy, together with the prior support of his own merits; Lullus, the least child of the orthodox mother, namely the Church, sends salutary greetings in the unfading charity of the cornerstone of both Testaments.

[Col. 0821C]

Your generous gifts reached me borne by a faithful carrier, and, as usual, they were accompanied by the sweetest greetings of your benevolent charity, which surpass every gift. When I heard and received them, I first gave abundant thanks to the most merciful God, as was fitting; then I returned due thanks to your fraternity, because I knew you to be faithful in a lesser position and quickly proved you still more faithful in a greater one.

When I learned of the successful outcome of your affairs, my sick spirit experienced both emotions: it rejoiced at the advancement of a dear companion, but grieved at the separation, because it seems intolerable to human beings when the one loved above all others is suddenly taken away. Yet I know for certain that no earthly distances can divide those whom the true love of Christ joins by an unbroken bond of kinship.

God is my witness, lest I seem to deceive you through flattery: I love you, Father, with the affection of my inner being as far as the capacity of my mind permits.

With supported and humble prayer I beg this of you: let us never allow the charity begun once in Christ to grow cold in our breast through sluggish indifference, like a small spark of a feeble fire smothered beneath the tawny ash, lest we be mocked by passersby who observe a tower whose construction has been begun.

Scripture says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.” Nor is any craftsman praised for a work begun, but for one completed. Know without any doubt that my mediocrity, however much younger in age, lower in merit and rank, and inferior in knowledge, has both kept and will keep this charity.

Concerning the seriousness of your life and the steadfastness of your mind, I have no doubt. Let us fortify ourselves with spiritual armor according to the Apostle’s command: “Praying for one another that we may be saved,” since, as James attests, the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful with God. Let us devote ourselves to this all the more diligently, the more forcefully we know ourselves to be attacked by various weapons of temptation.

The stronger right hand never ceases to assist the weaker left; and the left will not cease to serve the right, like a maidservant her mistress. That is, do not cease, by the examples of your good life, to discipline, correct, and admonish my instability, and, although absent in body, to lead me, as though present in spirit—as is your custom—toward the perfection of a better life. And I, with humble devotion and as far as my strength allows, will offer you faithful service in all things.

I beg that the exhortatory words of my mediocrity, although they may seem foolish and superfluous, not be received with displeasure by the fellowship of your charity. Charity alone demanded that I write them, without any subject matter for dictation; charity, which conquers all things, as it is written:

“Love conquers all, and let us too yield to love,” with every swelling of pride removed.

These are words of admonition which I cannot utter without risking my own condemnation: in the temporal power and earthly authority which, by God’s will, you now exercise, always remember the Lord’s saying: “My kingdom is not of this world,” and the Apostle’s: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world.”

What else is suggested by these words except that we should understand him to have said openly: “Do not fix the eye of your mind upon the one whom you see daily falling through his very ruin, but look with the whole attention of your mind upon him, and love with all your strength him who existed before all ages and remains unchanging throughout all ages, who lacks both future and past time, but possesses being eternally and essentially.”

For what is the fleeting happiness and perishable prosperity of this world except vapor and smoke? Who among the knowledgeable does not know how greatly temporal prosperity differs from eternal happiness?

Let us therefore learn to enjoy temporal power in view of eternal happiness, in comparison with which all things should become worthless to us. Let us reject costly garments, horses fed on grain, hawks and falcons with curved talons, barking dogs, the revelries of buffoons, foods and drinks of exquisite sweetness and flavor, and masses of gleaming silver and gold.

Let there not be soft repose upon a yielding mattress, nor soft pillows provided by men rather than by flaming young women. Above all, let careless intimacy with foreign women be cut off, because we are often seduced by careless security more seriously than by open temptation.

Let the secret words of divine Scripture drive out the tumultuous multitude of servants, because that is a pit to be avoided with every precaution, through which we see many fall in pitiable ruin. For often a sturdy soldier is attacked by a most violent shower of weapons all the more fiercely because he appears unconquered.

Although I clearly know that you undertook this task for the sake of winning souls and out of zeal to serve God more abundantly, nevertheless remember that a hard handle irritates a soft hand.

Therefore, dear colleague, formerly my teacher and now my pious instructor, remember your last things in all your works, and you will never sin.

My haste to come to you has been entirely denied me because of the many tribulations which, thanks be to God, we continually endure. Do not consider the greatness of this gift, but look upon the devoted mind of the sender.

Relying upon the confidence of our ancient friendship, I wish briefly to touch in this little letter upon a saying often heard among us when we commonly examined the clear words of God—not in any way referring to your pure religious character, as you well remember when it is read, but referring to a certain most wicked schismatic, who always used to swear that he would accept nothing earthly.

When suddenly, unexpectedly, like a new phantom, a bishop appeared, I feared that this would now be fulfilled to a very great extent.

May the prolixity of a longer discourse not generate weariness in the reader—for the wise use few words, while the fool is wearied by many, as I am. I beg you to wipe away the rust of this letter by correcting it, and grant indulgence for my error.

May God graciously inspire you with whatever pertains to your salvation, and may the Shepherd of shepherds preserve you unharmed with the flock entrusted to you.

I have written this with my own hand. Observe what is commanded, and you will be saved.

### LETTER V. LULLUS TO DENEHARD AND OTHERS  
*(In the year of the Lord 755)*

[Col. 0823C]

To my most beloved sons Denehard, Eanberth, Winberth, Sigeher, and Sigewald, Lullus, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

We admonish you to ask everyone serving God everywhere—the servants of God as well as the handmaids of Christ in the province of Thuringia, and the entire people—to implore the Lord’s mercy together, so that we may be freed from the impending scourge of rains.

That is: let them abstain for one week from all meat and from every drink containing honey; on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday let them fast until evening; and let each servant of God and each consecrated woman sing fifty psalms every day during that week. You priests, remember to celebrate those Masses which are customarily celebrated for storms.

We have sent you the names of Lord Romanus, the bishop, for whom each of you is to sing thirty Masses and those psalms, and to observe the fast according to our constitution. Likewise, for the two laymen named Megenfrid and Raban, let each of you sing ten Masses.

Farewell always in the Lord.

### LETTER VI. ALREDUS AND OSGIVA TO LULLUS  
*(In the year of the Lord 755)*

King Alredus and Queen Osgiva send greetings in Christ to the venerable Bishop Lullus, joined to us by perpetual friendship.

[Col. 0824A]

We received the writings of your blessedness, together with the gifts assigned in the letter, with the reverence due to our gratitude, and we gave the Almighty God the greatest thanks because, while laboring in so long a pilgrimage and contending in the struggles of Christ, he preserved you in the health for which we prayed.

Therefore, as venerable men return, we mark our joy by the testimony of sacred letters, and we ask that your episcopate deign to devote its zeal and prayer to our salvation in daily prayers.

We likewise ask that you include in the custody of your letters the names of our friends and relatives written below, and commend us to the perpetual protection of God through prayers and the celebration of Masses.

In the same way, concerning you and the names transmitted to us, we shall act according to your request, so that in all the monasteries subject to our authority they may be commended in perpetual written records and presented daily to God with the assistance of prayers.

Know also that it has greatly pleased our piety that your holiness is concerned about the disturbance of the Churches or the people; we believe that these things too have been foreseen by some providential plan of God.

We also beg you, dearest brother, to assist our embassies to your most glorious lord, King Carl—by offering counsel—so that you may cause the peace and friendship suitable to all to be firmly confirmed between us.

May the divine Majesty deign to preserve you as you labor tirelessly for the Church of Christ.

[Col. 0824C]

We have sent small gifts suited to your dignity: twelve cloaks, together with a gold ring as a larger gift toward a dowry.

### LETTER VII. PIPPIN TO LULLUS  
*(In the year of the Lord 755)*

Pippin, by the grace of God king of the Franks, an illustrious man, to the holy lord Father Lullus, bishop.

We know that your holiness is aware what mercy and compassion God has shown this land in the present year. He gave us tribulation for our sins; but after the great and astonishing tribulation, he gave us consolation, namely the abundance of the earth’s produce which we now have.

For this reason, and for our other causes, we must give him thanks, because he has deigned to console his servants through his mercy.

It seems good to us that, without imposing a fast, each bishop should hold litanies in his own parish—not with fasting, but solely in praise of God, who has given us such abundance—and that each person should give alms and feed the poor.

Arrange and order this according to our command, so that each person, whether willing or unwilling, gives his tithe.

Farewell in Christ.

### LETTER VIII. MAGINGOZ TO LULLUS  
*(In the year of the Lord 755)*

To Lullus, a magnificent priest of Christ, worthy of being embraced with reverence and love beyond measure, bishop, Magingoz, servant of the servants of God, sends everlasting greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0825A]

A clear testimony of the divine Scriptures declares that the Lord the Savior is the Truth, and that this was said of him through the prophet: “Seek his face continually.” For this reason, we greatly desire to receive from your gracious generosity a solution to a certain question which, plainly, is not easy for our feeble understanding to grasp.

Accordingly, the constitution of Christian marriage, whether in joining or separating spouses, appears to us to have been arranged by the Fathers with such diversity that scarcely one uniform judgment of theirs is apparent to our small understanding. For Isidore and Jerome seem to agree in affirming that an adulterous woman ought not to be held by the husband to whom she was joined if she joins herself to another, like a prostitute, since by impiously dividing one flesh she has rendered herself unworthy of and alien to the honor of the marriage divinely instituted; and they say that this was commanded and permitted by the Savior, when he prescribed that a wife was not to be dismissed except on account of fornication.

Augustine, however, after examining that same judgment of the Savior in a lengthy treatment, offers no clear explanation—certainly none graspable by our utter weakness—but said at the end that, as to how this command of the Savior ought to be understood, a broad and exceedingly laborious question still remained. Referring, moreover, to the woman whom the Lord freed from the accusation of the Jews, he says: “It would not be wrong for her husband to be reconciled with the woman, even though she had fallen into adultery.”

The blessed Pope Leo, however, says that when a woman’s husband has been captured by enemies, she may, compelled by her isolation, lawfully be joined to another if the captive is presumed lost; and that, should the first husband unexpectedly return, she is to be separated from the second and restored to the first. Here it seems worth noting that he immediately grants the abandoned wife permission to marry.

Among Isidore and Jerome, however, the betrayal of the marital covenant dissolves the marriage. What, then, remains for a husband or wife whom isolation presses hard, if the decree of Isidore or Jerome and that of Leo are both rightly believed to be binding, except that such a person should join himself or herself in marriage to another? I confess that I do not know.

We therefore beseech your goodness, through the charity by which Christ the Lord is always and everywhere shown to join his members to himself, that you may deign, with the Lord granting you the ability, to enlighten our ignorance and doubt, so that you may deserve to hear from the eternal Rewarder: “Well done, good servant,” and so forth.

## EPISTLE IX. MAGINGOZ TO LULLO  
*(Circa A.D. 755)*

To the most venerable lord in Christ, Lullo the bishop, Magingoz sends, humbly supplicating, the desirable greeting of everlasting blessedness in the Lord.

Your prudent eminence surely knows that, in opposition to the greatest dangers, counsel must be sought by every means, through assistance that is both sound and solidly fortified on every side. We desire, however, to make known to the graciousness of your revered charity that, oppressed on every side by griefs and fears, we await the final passing of our sister, who is breathing her last—namely, the death of her flesh—which, through the impulse of natural condition, we mourn as though it were our own. We also fear, concerning the uncertain outcome of her soul—known only to the most merciful Judge—and, in addition, concerning the very tender household of that place, that it may be dispersed, or, almost entirely lacking any firmness of counsel, that souls may perish, which is the most grievous danger.

Therefore, humbly entreating your greatness’s piety, we beseech you by Christ the Savior and by the resurrection of the dead: since we are afflicted by the troubles mentioned above, do not disdain to indicate to us by letter, through this messenger, what ought to be done after her death for the salutary stability of the little monastery, insofar as, with the Lord’s help, you are able to discern.

For, as you know, there are there the veiled daughters of our brother, toward whom perhaps the attention of the uninformed has turned. Yet none of them can as yet be judged suitable for undertaking such a burden, whether on account of age or of any firmness of understanding. We fear the ill-considered dispersal of the household unless order and stability are quickly established through an abbess.

Nor do we believe that we can find anyone either within the cell or within the community who could preserve even outwardly, in word or appearance, the necessary cohesion, apart from the little girls whom we have mentioned. We fear for them, since they would be undertaking the greatest danger, and perhaps we ourselves would be persuading them to do so.

Therefore, with repeated supplication, we beseech you through Christ the Savior not to disdain or find burdensome to reveal to us, with the speed we have requested, what you believe would be most salutary to do amid such necessities.

We desire that your blessedness may prosper, and that, by interceding for us more and more in Christ, you may advance through the whole and steadfast efforts of your heart.

Written in the service of Bishop Lullo.

## EPISTLE X. LULLUS TO THE POPE  
*(Circa A.D. 755)*

We know clearly that the holy and canonical institutions confirmed by the authority of the canons, both of our venerable bishops and also of our lord King Pippin and his counselors, must be preserved. Therefore we dare not conceal from your charity that, contrary to canon law, a certain priest has been brought into our parish by the presbyter Willefrid, having been ordained in another parish without the consent of my predecessor, Saint Boniface the archbishop, or of me, his successor. He has both despised the decrees of your institution and, having been established in our parish, spurned our authority.

Having recognized the authority of the canons, you decreed that all presbyters who are in a parish must be under the power of the bishop; that none of them should presume either to baptize or to celebrate Mass in his parish without the bishop’s command; and that all presbyters should assemble at the bishop’s council. The aforesaid presbyter, named Enred, scorned to do all these things. Therefore, according to what you established, I pronounced upon him a sentence of reprimand.

But when he still refused to repent of his past actions and did not amend, he was finally excommunicated by me according to your canonical institution. Thereafter he was received and defended by the aforesaid Willefrid.

Let your charity now judge what is right and just concerning these matters—not only concerning these, but concerning everything that he has perversely and wickedly done in his life and that has here been brought to light.

For he removed bondsmen and slaves from the churches entrusted to him. He took Faegenolph, our slave, and his two sons, Raegenolph and Amanolph, together with his wife Leobthruthe and his daughter Amalthruthe, and handed them over into Saxony in exchange for one horse, to a man named Huelp, who was to take them into Saxony.

He sent Willefrid, the son of the aforesaid Raegenolph, overseas with Enred, and Willefrid himself gave him to his own mother as a slave.

The slave and the female slave whom Aohtrich gave to our churches for the sake of his son’s soul were removed and secretly stolen by the aforesaid Willefrid. The slave’s name was Thecdo, and his wife’s name was Aotlind.

Enred the presbyter handed over Liudo, our slave, to a boy belonging to Aldbercht of Effernace, named Upbit, in exchange for one horse.

He secretly took away Erpwine, our slave, by night, while the others knew nothing of it, together with ninety-four pigs. Hredun had given him to our church.

On another occasion he took away two of our slaves, Zeitolf and Zeizhelm; and first four of our oxen, then three, and finally eight cows together with seven oxen.

The aforesaid Willefrid also took seven excellent beasts of burden, four years old, which Wenilo had given to the churches, along with many other horses bred there, and drove them to Hamulanburg.

As for the gold and silver that Regenthryth, daughter of Athuolphus, gave to our churches: two golden arm-rings and five golden sigla, worth three hundred solidi, as well as the valuables of other faithful men and women—Enred removed them from the aforesaid churches, not only gold and silver, but also clothing, weapons, and horses.

But since it would be lengthy to recount in order everything that was stolen from and stripped from the aforesaid churches, and everything done contrary to canonical institutions, we entrust these matters to your most holy judgment for correction.

## EPISTLE XI. LULLUS TO OSWITHA  
*(Circa A.D. 755)*

Lullo, the small and humble bishop, to Svithan and those subject to him.

It is an apostolic command, Oswitha, that we should diligently feed and guard the Lord’s flock, lest, found outside the sheepfold, it perish from the bites of wolves.

Trusting that you had done this and would continue to do so—for you received the discipline of regular life from the most holy man Boniface, martyr of Christ, and from his disciples—I had judged you according to the measure of your understanding. But, as I am forced to say with sadness and grief, you are proved to have acted very differently. You have neglected the souls for whom Christ died, concerning whose lives you will render an account on the day of judgment before the tribunal of Christ, when you permitted the sacredly veiled women N. and N., contrary to the statutes of the canons and the discipline of the holy rule, without my permission or counsel, and to the injury of God and of his mother, the blessed ever-virgin Mary, whose service they ought to have performed, to go freely into a distant region—into the devil’s snare, through arrogance and in order to satisfy the pleasure of lay people—to the destruction of their own souls.

You did not remember the Gospel saying: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” Nor this one: “The soul that sins shall itself die.”

But lest, perhaps, you should disregard this rebuke of mine as insignificant, I shall strike you with the apostolic word, which says: “Reprove sinners before everyone, so that the others may have fear.”

Know that you are excommunicated for such folly, together with all your people who, by consenting, have committed this offense of negligence, until you correct this fault by worthy satisfaction.

Do not receive the aforesaid wandering and disobedient women within your cell. Instead, let them remain outside the monastery, excommunicated from the Church of Christ, doing penance on bread and water until they return. You likewise must abstain from all meat and from every drink sweetened with honey.

Know that if you despise this rebuke, you despise the one who was sent by God to save sinners, namely Christ, who said in the Gospel: “Whoever despises you despises me, and whoever despises me despises the one who sent me,” namely God the almighty Father.

We desire that you turn in Christ toward better things.

## EPISTLE XII. CUTHBERT TO LULLO  
*(Circa A.D. 756)*

To the most reverend brother and, in the love of Christ, most beloved fellow bishop Lullo, and likewise to your fellow-workers, the bishops and priests of God, whose names may be held written in the book of life: Cuthbert, servant of the servants of God, together with the other fellow priests of Christ and the presbyters or abbots, sends eternal prosperity and peace in the Lord.

We therefore profess, dearest brothers, with the most sincere intention before God and his chosen angels, that whenever we hear from those who carry reports that your affection possesses a more abundant increase of peace and prosperity, an advancement of holy religion in Christ, and the fruit of sacred exhortation arising from the conduct of others, we give joyful thanks to God, the giver of all good things, rejoicing greatly and praying most earnestly for you.

Whenever, then, some injury is reported to have been done to your religion, or some harm inflicted, grief and sadness torture us. For just as we rejoice with you in Christ in your joy, so also, saddened by adversity for Christ’s sake, we suffer with you.

The various and unceasing anguishes of the tribulations that you yourselves endured, together with our beloved Father Boniface, of blessed memory, the martyr, among pagan persecutors, heretics, and schismatic deceivers, during such a dangerous and savage pilgrimage, for the love of the eternal homeland, cannot ever be erased from our memory. Since he, after the struggle of martyrdom, gloriously and happily departed with his many companions to the eternal rest of the heavenly homeland, you who survive such a man perhaps live amid various temptations with greater danger and difficulty, since it is clear that you are now deprived of so great a father and teacher.

And although the bitterness of this sorrow severely torments our hearts, a certain joy of extraordinary and novel exultation, returning frequently to our memory, often delights and softens the groaning of our pain. Recalling these things more often, we joyfully give thanks to the admirable—or rather ineffable—piety of God, because the English people, a nation from overseas, Britain, deserved to send forth from itself, far away and laudably, so distinguished a watcher over the heavenly library and so excellent a soldier of Christ, together with many well-raised and excellently instructed disciples, for spiritual combat and, by the grace of almighty God, for the salvation of many souls.

Thus, advancing as leader and standard-bearer, and by God’s assistance bravely overcoming every adversity, he brought nations wandering for a long time along byways, far and wide, from the broad and spacious chasm of eternal destruction to the radiant paths of the heavenly homeland through the encouragement of sacred exhortation and examples of piety and goodness. The actual results show more gloriously than words that this truly happened quickly, even in those places which no teacher had previously attempted to visit for the purpose of evangelizing.

Therefore, after the incomparable, world-wide mystery of apostolic election and number, and the ministry of Christ’s other disciples who were evangelizing at that time, we both love and honor him among the distinguished and excellent teachers of orthodox faith.

Accordingly, at our general synod, where we discussed more fully among ourselves both this matter and all the other matters that we now briefly set before your sanctity, we announced the day of his nativity and that of the company martyred with him, and decreed that it should be solemnly celebrated every year, since we especially seek him as our patron together with the blessed Gregory and Augustine, and unquestionably believe that we have him before Christ the Lord, whom he always loved in his life and who, by the grace he deserved from Christ, gloriously glorified him in his death.

Moreover, as we said above, we confess that we are always ready, wherever and in whatever matter we are able, to relieve and console, with paternal words and fraternal encouragement, both your vigilant care and, so to speak, the care worn down by the weariness of the absent head of the household, as well as all the servants of God subject to you.

Therefore, first, to confirm the love that the innermost chambers of our heart hold for you, let us use the language and affection of the Apostle, and say together with the Apostle: “Grace to you and peace. We give thanks to God always for all of you, making mention of you without ceasing in our prayers, remembering before our God and Father your work of faith, your labor, your charity, and your endurance in the hope of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

What was established long ago, while Boniface of venerable memory was still alive, through certain writings and faithful intermediaries, we consider it altogether necessary continually to renew among ourselves: namely, that supplications, prayers, and the remedies of Masses for us and ours—both those living here and those who have departed from here—should be offered humbly to the living God and Judge of all, in accordance with the apostolic exhortation: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved,” and so forth.

By this means we are recognized as pleasing the divine clemency, offering it the pure libations of our prayers. In this way we shall find that same clemency prospering us amid adversity. For where the Lord’s help is present, according to his promises, every adversity of the wicked is put to flight.

He himself said: “If two of you agree on earth about any matter whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.”

We judge that this must therefore be done with especially watchful diligence, because, according to the apostolic prophecies, “perilous times are now at hand,” and so forth, as he continues in that same Epistle.

There is no need to write to you about the outward attacks of calamities that, as I believe, you have frequently suffered: persecutions, plunderings, hatred, scandals, and things of this kind.

Moreover, look how greatly the condition of the Christian religion wavers in very many places, while almost everywhere, externally and internally, the order of ecclesiastical affairs is disturbed, and everywhere almost the evil sects of novel ways of life are growing up. Nor is this surprising, since, after the decrees of the ancient Fathers have been set aside and ecclesiastical laws abandoned, many people, according to their own inventions, think, affirm, and act in ways that are perverse and harmful to the salvation of many, as it is clear that a man of great authority said and did in the past year.

In response to this, what else should we, who are fearful and less inflamed by zeal for justice, do above all except continually to seek the intercession of the holy apostles, the martyrs of Christ, and the venerable bishops of the Churches of God? We should ask that, in the office to which we have been called and appointed, the grace of Christ may make us persevere through continual watchfulness; that we may not be rejected but rather accepted; not sluggish but diligent; not scattering but gathering all whom we can into unanimity of Christian religion and unity of ecclesiastical conduct.

Thus may the diligent exercise of our ministry and labor advance to the praise and glory of almighty God, so that one day, together with those who serve well and please God, we may deserve to hear: “Blessed is the servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds watching! Amen, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions.”
