For the sake of example, let us also recall more frequently to memory how the distinguished teacher and martyr, the blessed Boniface of revered memory, labored with what and how great diligence in the teaching of Christ, and how many dangers and difficulties he willingly endured for the love of Christ and the gain of souls, even unto death itself.

And since he has now become familiar to the Almighty, let your prudence carefully consider whether you ought to obey his sacred admonitions and, to the extent of your strength, follow his examples of piety. For the more he became the intimate of the one whom he loved above all, the more he will be able to obtain from him.

Therefore, if any of his subjects, to whom divine providence once advanced him in the place of a teacher, dissent from his spiritual instructions or depart through wicked conduct, he who could have been their defender at the eternal judgment will instead be their accuser, and, together with the Judge himself, will demand a strict accounting from them.

But, on the other hand, whoever properly follows the rule of his sacred instruction and teaching should know for certain that he has perpetual communion, both while living and after death, in prayer and in the celebration of Masses, as we said above, with the Roman and apostolic Church itself, from which he was sent to them as legate and teacher, and thereafter, together with it, with all of us—provided that, humbly and lovingly, for God’s sake and for eternal reward, they do not disdain to obey you, their teachers and rulers of salvation, firmly to the end.

Let them never fail as the undevoted or deceitful, but always advance as disciples of good character, faithfully adhering to their masters in Christ’s army, toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling and the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

We have written these words of greeting to your sanctity, not as though you were ignorant of or in need of the small rule of our rusticity, but for the sake of mutual charity and mutual strengthening [communion]. We testify and beseech you, by almighty God and his Son Jesus Christ, by his coming and his kingdom, that all of you, dearest brothers, together with those subject to you in Christ, may always be faithful helpers and united fellow-workers to one another in every respect, against all enemies of the orthodox faith, heretics, schismatics, and men of utterly wicked conduct.

By this you will be lovable and praiseworthy to good men, and acceptable and dear to almighty God. Thus, together with that aforesaid blessed Father and your predecessor, each of you may in the future deserve to hear from Christ, the Judge of all, the joyful voice: “Well done,” he will say, “good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord.” Amen.

May almighty God deign to preserve you all for a long time unharmed in his holy love and fear.

To the most beloved brothers and sons: Cuthbert, archbishop; to Lullo, fellow bishop.

## EPISTLE XIII. CYNEHARD TO LULLO  
*(A.D. 756)*

To the most worthy, venerable, deservedly distinguished and most excellent lord, renowned far and wide for preaching the doctrine of the Christian religion and celebrated for the most approved conduct of his life; also, not undeservedly, most dear to us because of the bond of our kinship, which must always be remembered: to Lullo the bishop, Cynehard, the unworthy, as I fear, bishop of the city of Winchester, sends from the innermost affection of his heart and vital marrow an eternal greeting in Christ.

After reading the sweetest and most gracious periods of the letter sent by your sanctity, in which we found that our smallness had been amicably greeted and admonished to preserve the same observance of unity that our predecessors faithfully maintained to the end—Lord Boniface the archbishop, the blessed confessor of Christ who is worthy of beatification; Daniel, the most learned servant of God’s people; and likewise his successor, Hunfrith, the gentlest of bishops, and so forth, matters that we believe you have remembered better—we took care to learn them through the most diligent examination of our mind as they were commended in writing, and we are making the due return of thanks insofar as we are able, since you deign to remember us across such great stretches of land and the intervening breadth of the great sea.

We also declare that we are striving, with the Lord’s favor, most diligently to fulfill everything that has been commanded at the suggestion of your sanctity—not only by providing the spiritual consolation of prayers and celebrating solemn Masses for you and for those in your regions who die in the confession of Christ, but also by making available to your participation any comforts of worldly substance that we may be able to obtain in these regions for your use.

We ask this of you in return: if you possess any comforts necessary or unknown to us, whether of spiritual knowledge, of ancient books that we do not have, or of other ecclesiastical matters, do not refuse willingly to share them with us.

Likewise, if you should acquire any books of secular learning unknown to us—for example, books on medicine, of which we have some supply, although the foreign sections that we find written in them are unknown and difficult for us to obtain—or if you can provide anything else in whatever affairs or materials that may be necessary to us, may you deign to share it, as you did when you sent the woolen garment.

We have also sent through the monasteries and churches of our diocese the names of your presbyters and deacons, monks and nuns, and others whom you sent, so that solemn Masses and the intercessions of prayers might be celebrated for them.

We humbly entreat your sanctity to do the same for those whose names we are to send to you, writing them individually together with their persons—namely, those who were especially friendly either to me or to this Church which I serve, or who were subject to or presided over it.

From our poor clothing we have also sent these small gifts for your use, though they are unworthy. Nevertheless, we ask you to accept them: one woolen tunic and another linen one, as is the custom among us; leggings and wiping-cloths; a scarf; a hood; and a short gown sewn in our manner, as a token of our fullest affection.

We earnestly ask you, in your humility, to receive these things and to keep them in remembrance of my name, at least for some period of time.

Moreover, if there is anything that ought to be communicated to your sanctity, the bearer of this little letter can explain it to you orally.

I wish you, most beloved brother, praying for me as I pray for you, to be well in the Lord, to live happily through a long age, and afterward to reach the crown of heavenly glory, distinguished lord and most excellent Father. Amen.

## EPISTLE XIV. EARDULF TO LULLO  
*(Circa A.D. 756)*

To the most reverend and, among all bishops, most beloved fellow bishop Lullo: Aeardulf, bishop of the church of Rochester, together with Aeardvulf, son of the holy Church, king of Kent, sends sincere greetings in the name of Christ.

Among other things, it is recognized as the friendly and commemorative custom of true companions that, when they cannot visit and greet one another in person because of the distances of the intervening lands or the regions of foreign provinces, they nevertheless send one another words of greeting through their faithful messengers or by letter, and discuss matters worthy and useful. This is so that the anxious mind may not be wearied for too long by uncertainty about what, through divine providence and judgment, is happening to the condition of a friend, nor groan daily in anxious uncertainty about affairs.

Therefore, first greeting you most diligently and visiting your eminence through this messenger, we desire to hear and know that you are progressing gloriously and prosperously in every respect. We earnestly desire this, and commend ourselves and our dearest ones to your blessedness with devoted prayers, so that, fortified everywhere by your sacred and God-pleasing prayers and by the support of your paternal piety, and surrounded by the wall of your protection, we may be defended against every attack of the enemy in this life, which is entirely temptation, and may deserve, through your gracious intercessions, to reach that life which is free from death and without end.

We have sent you small gifts: namely, one *reptem ruptilem* [the exact object-name is uncertain], earnestly asking you to consider the love of the sender more than the value of the gift, in hope of better things, which will come more quickly through your prayers if the Lord grants life and strength.

For we remember all the words, to be fulfilled, that came from the abundance of your heart and sounded in our ears, words that plainly showed how much you love those who love you. What else ought we to do, then, except faithfully preserve charity among ourselves for as long as, by God’s ordering and consideration of the end of all things, we shall live?

Moreover, whenever one of us, as I hope, enters first upon the happy paths of the other life, let the survivor, without delay, frequently remember and strive to support and prosper his journey from here and from there, through Masses and almsgiving, as far as he is able.

We earnestly beseech you to deign, through this most faithful brother of ours, the presbyter Laearored, to send us writings of your piety, so that through them knowledge of those matters that please you may become clear to us. For you undoubtedly possess in the aforesaid presbyter a truthful and faithful emissary between us; and therefore, through him, you will be able to disclose to us whatever you wish by the testimony of his living voice.

We have also sent you the names of our aforementioned relatives—namely, Irmigi, Noththry, and Dulicha—all virgins dedicated to God. We ask that you include them in the offerings of Masses and the intercessions of prayers, since we are likewise prepared to repay such a benefit to one another.

May God keep you unharmed and deign to preserve you, powerful in his ministry, through long stretches of time.

Aeardulf, bishop, to Lullo, fellow bishop.

## EPISTLE XV. MILRED TO LULLO  
*(Circa A.D. 756)*

To Lullo the bishop, a most loving lord and, in Christ, most dear: Milret, servant of those who serve God.

After I had unwillingly—or willingly—departed sadly from your presence and from the bodily sight of the most holy prelate and most blessed father Boniface, and after, through various events and many dangers, we reached the land of our birth by your gracious prayers, before the full circuit of a year had been completed, sad news was brought to us: the most blessed Father had departed from the prison of the flesh to the heights.

If it is permissible to call this sad, since we have deserved to send such a patron of heaven ahead to the kingdom, and since we confidently believe that, with God’s help, we are everywhere supported by his sacred intercessions. Although we mourned with many bitter tears the loss of the consolation of this present life, nevertheless he who, having shed his blood, was consecrated to Christ as a martyr—the glory and support of all whom this present homeland produced—having completed his blessed struggle, his excellent labor, and his most glorious end, greatly mitigates and soothes our deeply sorrowful hearts with a greater joy.

We mourn our own lot in this valley of tears, remaining in this life, which is wholly full of temptations. He, after completing the great labor of his pilgrimage with much sweat, has reached the most glorious martyrdom of Christ. For our transgressions, as I believe, if the Lord’s mercy permits it, he stands in the heavenly Jerusalem as a faithful intercessor, joined to the holy citizens in the most blessed lot, rejoicing upon the heavenly citadel.

I greatly desire that you bring to my knowledge everything concerning this most loving Father—his venerable life and glorious end.

Another matter concerning our fellowship comes to mind. From the depths of my heart I beseech your sweetest charity, and, as though prostrate in person at your feet, I humbly implore you to store in your heart, not as a passing memory but as a fixed remembrance, the fraternal affection that our common Father, Boniface of blessed and holy memory, joined between us through sacred words, with Christ’s charity assenting, and united by gracious utterances.

I know, without any doubt, that this will greatly benefit both you and me, if we strive to fulfill the precepts of so distinguished a teacher. Therefore, most loving prelate, do not disdain to instruct me, the least deserving in merits of all your brothers, through fraternal charity; to fortify me with sacred commands; and to support me with gracious prayers.

Accordingly, I confess and pledge by a faithful promise that, according to the measure of my strength, I shall gladly follow your sincere commands in all things. I profess before God, and desire with all the strength of my innermost being, that I preserve a faithful friendship with you in intimate charity for as long as the spirit governs these limbs and a living condition inhabits these dying members, so that, with Christ granting it, what is written may come to pass: “Everything was held in common among them.”

If almighty God grants a favorable journey, I have taken care that all these matters, which we have briefly stated, should be communicated to you more fully and orally by the bearers of this letter.

We have also sent small gifts, which we hope you will receive with the affection with which, God as witness, they were sent by us.

May Christ protect your charity as it intercedes for our transgressions.

I did not send the book of *Pyrpyri metri* [“Pyrpyri’s meter” or “the meter of Pyrpyri”], because Bishop Guthbert has still delayed returning it.

Immanuel.

Letter of Bishop Milred to be presented to Bishop Lullo.

## EPISTLE XVI. TRECEA TO LULLO  
*(Circa A.D. 756)*

To Lullo, venerably loved and delightfully honored in the Lord, bearing the episcopal insignia: Trecea, a humble native servant in Christ, sends perpetual salvation.

In the time recently past, we received with great pleasure the letter of your kindness, carried by a trustworthy messenger and brought into the presence of our mediocrity, while the inmost chambers of our hearts exulted and we gazed upon it with joyful eyes. We were especially pleased by your holy promise, which the arrangement of your written words made known: that you wished to defend our frailty by your continual and sacred prayers. Thus our imperfect mediocrity also is ready, with God assisting everywhere, to ask and implore God through inward prayers for your blessedness in almost all good things, and we show that we wish, according to our strength, to observe fraternal affection toward your clemency, with our Lord Jesus Christ teaching and saying: “This is my commandment, that you love one another.” And again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another,” and so forth. Likewise, concerning the same matter, blessed Peter, first and chief of the apostles, proclaimed this judgment, saying: “Therefore be prudent and watchful in prayers, above all having continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins,” and so forth.

Our littleness, therefore, if I am not mistaken, has been greatly strengthened by your patronage. For this reason we boldly presume to ask your blessed and truly blessed kindness to commend us, living in this valley of tears and also resting in the most glorious foreknowledge of God in Christ, to the Lord God through your continual and sacred prayers. I also, the least servant of the Church, humbly beg you before the Lord to receive me, together with my household, among your other faithful friends, with kindness, while the Lord God dispenses and rightly governs all things. I am called Aldbert by my proper name, serving in the office of the diaconate, though unworthy, so that through your most salutary intercessions I may improve the ministry of the holy order once entrusted to me and advance from day to day.

May the highest Judge of the world, from the lofty citadel of heaven, deign to watch over your kindness as you pray for us.

Farewell in the Lord.

## LETTER XVII. BOTWIN TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 756.)*

To Lullus, bishop of venerable dignity: Botwin, abbot, sends the desired salvation in Christ.

The letter of your authority, which you sent to us with devotion to divine mercy, greatly gladdened me, because you, attracted by the rain of heavenly dew, deigned to visit me, the least little servant of the servants of God, with so great a faith in divine love and with the gift of secular dignity. I give thanks to God, asking, with the desire of inward charity, that through the height of your holiness you may stand before Christ Jesus as my faithful supporter; and that in this age you may be my friend with a serene mind, if the ruler of all things judges that I must labor longer than you upon the road of this life. I weep unceasingly, praying, together with the whole company that serves Christ the Lord under my authority, that the consolations of divine mercy may be granted to your soul, so that you may likewise deign to provide me with the support of your churches.

I also send your kindness these modest gifts, namely three cloaks, hoping that they will be received.

## LETTER XVIII. WICBERT TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 756.)*

To the most holy lord Lullus, ever preserved by God, bishop: Wicbert, servant of the servants of God, abbot though unworthy, and, as God knows, wishing you well in all things and bound to you in the bond of charity.

After receiving your provision, the entire holy congregation of our monks sang individual psalters to the Lord for you, and the priests celebrated five Masses each, so that the Lord might restore your former health. I told them, in accordance with your wish, how you had instructed us to come here for a time. But they all replied with one harmonious agreement that it is our will in all things to sympathize with his illness and to show him every charity as though he were our own brother.

But now, if you wish, you may come as you would to your own house; and we, in all that we can, earnestly desire to sympathize with your illness with our former charity. We commend ourselves to your prayers, most holy Father.

To the most holy lord Lullus, bishop: Wicbert, unworthy abbot.

## LETTER XIX. DOTO TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 756.)*

To the holy lord of holy men, equal to whom in merits and loved by us with the greatest reverence, Father Lullus in Christ, fellow bishop: Doto, servant of the servants of God, and all the monks of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, living under the rule of the holy Rule, have taken care to send eternal salvation in our Lord Jesus Christ to your holiness.

For this reason we give thanks to the almighty Lord, not only because we have all things concerning you prosperous, but also because we continually and diligently implore the Lord’s mercy to grant that your life may rejoice here for many years and that there, in eternal blessedness, he may cause you to exult together with his saints in triumphs.

Moreover, although we seem to be separated by the length of the lands, distance of land does not divide in mind those whom divine charity has joined in heart. Therefore let your holiness know that, in obedience to our venerable father Dodon, abbot, and out of love and every concern for you and for your most devout holy congregation, entrusted to you by God, we shall not cease to entreat the Lord’s mercy for you in our continual prayers.

Accordingly, with the duties of greeting and humble prayer, we ask that you always keep this household of Christ and Saint Peter in your remembrance, and that you cause your intercessors, both living and dead, to be commemorated in your recompense for all your friends—both bishops and their clergy, abbots and their monks, and also abbesses and women devoted to God in this congregation of Saint Peter—so that in their sacred prayers they may continually remember it, and that through their intercessions we may at last deserve to enter the long-desired homeland of paradise.

Likewise we ask you to have the names of all your friends, living and dead, sent to us in writing by our brother Saganald, so that we may remember them in our continual prayers just as we do our other brothers.

May the grace of the heavenly King always guard you. Amen.

A brief list sent to Bishop Lullus. May Emmanuel be with us.

## LETTER XX. CYNEARD TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 756.)*

To Lord Lullus, a bishop greatly to be loved and most dear to us among all pilgrims for the love of Christ: Cineard, an unworthy bishop, as I fear, sends greetings in Christ.

We gladly receive the brother sent from you to us, together with the sweetness of your gifts, giving thanks to God and to you because you deign to remember us from such distant regions of the earth. Therefore, as we learn that you wish, we remember you insofar as, with the Lord’s help, we are permitted to do so always in our prayers, beseeching you to hold firmly to the end what you began with a faithful and most steadfast mind. Although you are beaten by many tribulations, such as almost all the saints have been accustomed to endure from the world, nevertheless, with Christ cooperating and strengthening their steadfastness, they did not fail.

We have sent a small gift, however little, solely as an expression of charity: a garment from our own clothing, just as our predecessors used to send gifts to your predecessors. We humbly beg you to deign to receive and use it in accordance with your humility and gentleness.

We always wish you to prosper in Christ and, in truth, to be happy.

## LETTER XXI. [NAME OMITTED] TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 756.)*

To the most holy and venerable bishop Lullus: a servant of the servants of God sends visceral greetings in the Lord.

I ask you, dearest brother, as I firmly believe of you, not to be forgetful, but always to recall with your most discerning mind our ancient friendship, which we had between us in the city of Maldubia, when Abbot Eaba nurtured us in loving charity. I also remember this sign: he called you Irtel by name. Therefore Abbot Hereca greets you with a holy greeting, as does the entire congregation that remains in his monastic life, because you kept us worthy of remembrance with you.

“But whoever perseveres in peace to the end will be saved.”

Farewell, beloved, happily forever; my beloved, chosen by God, because charity has no price.

Abbot Hereca made this sign.

## LETTER XXII. CUTHBERT TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 758.)*

To Lullus, the most desired and gracious friend in the love of Christ, dearest of all bishops: Cuthbert, disciple of the presbyter Bede, sends greetings.

I gratefully received the gifts of your charity, and all the more gratefully because I learned that you sent them with the deepest devotion. You sent silk, namely, for the relics of our master Bede, of blessed memory, in remembrance and veneration of him. It seems right to me that the whole English people in all the provinces, wherever they may be found, should give thanks to God, because God gave them in their nation so remarkable a man, endowed with diverse gifts, so zealous in exercising those gifts, and likewise living in good morals. I learned what I tell you through experience, having been nurtured at his feet.

You also sent me a variegated covering to cover my body against the cold. I gave it with great joy to almighty God and blessed Paul the apostle, to clothe the altar consecrated to God in his church, since I too lived under his protection in this monastery for forty-three years.

Now, because you asked for something from the little works of the blessed Father, I prepared with my boys, according to our strength, what I could for your affection. I sent you little books about the man of God Cuthbert, composed in verse and prose; and if I could have sent more, I would gladly have wished to do so. For the recent winter severely and terribly oppressed the island of our people far and wide with cold, frost, storms of wind, and rains; and therefore the scribe’s hand was delayed, lest the work should reach the number of many books.

Six years ago, moreover, through my presbyter Hunwini, who came there to your regions and desired to see Rome, I sent a few small gifts to your fraternity, namely twenty knives and a *gunna* made from otter skins. That presbyter Hunwini, however, reached the city called Beneventum and there departed from this light. Consequently, neither through him nor through any of your people have I ever received a reply as to whether these things reached you.

We have also taken care to send your fatherhood two cloaks of the finest workmanship, one white and the other dyed, together with the little books, and a cloak such as I had at hand. I ask you not to disdain my request and need. If there is someone in your diocese who can make glass vessels well, when the season is favorable, deign to send him to me. Or if perhaps such a person lies beyond your borders, under the authority of someone else, I ask your fraternity to persuade him to come to us, because we are ignorant and impoverished in this craft. If, with your diligence and God willing, one of the glassmakers is permitted to come to us, I will receive him with kindly gentleness, with life as his companion.

I would also be pleased to have a harpist who could play the harp that we call a *rotta*, because I have a harp but no craftsman. If it is not burdensome, send this man also to serve my needs. I beg you not to despise this request of mine or count it as a joke.

As for the works of blessed Bede, of venerable memory, which you do not yet possess in written form, I promise that, if we live, I will assist your wishes.

Abbot Cuthbert greets you twice and three times.

May almighty God preserve you safe forever.

## LETTER XXIII. EANVULT TO LULLUS  
*(In the year of the Lord 758.)*

To the desirable and rightly venerable lord Bishop Lullus: Eanvult, servant of Christ Jesus, together with the fellow servants who rejoice with me in these regions to draw the sweetest yoke of the Gospel for the sake of finding rest in heaven, sends perpetual salvation in the Lord.

Our heart was delighted with great joy, and our tongue sounded forth with great exultation, when so learned and holy a man sent us a letter. Therefore we earnestly beseech the paternal reverence of your charity not to refuse always to offer humble prayers to the Lord for us, remembering us.

Know that we too always remember you, if the prayer of servants so lowly has any worth before the Lord. For how greatly we rejoiced in all your progress, and how great a joy we had concerning the things that prospered for you in foreign lands . . . .

We wish you to know that, through your merits obtaining it, we shall perpetually maintain this devotion of charity, and in every way desire to merit your friendship, wishing in all things to obey the decrees of your just will. Also, when the Lord arranges it, as you enter upon the way of all the earth and are led to the rewards of eternal life, we intend then to write your venerable name together with the names of our bishops and with the names of all the former brothers of this monastery.

May heavenly grace guard the venerable crown of your fatherhood as it prays for us, dearest bishop in Christ.

. . . Written in the eleventh indiction, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June . . . . to Jul.; epistle of a bishop [the abbreviated ending is uncertain].

## LETTER XXIV. MAGINGOOZ TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 760.)*

To the venerable priest of Christ, whom we regard with particular devotion as wholly worthy of love and reverence, Bishop Lullus: Magingooz, servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual salvation in Christ.

In a recent conversation with your venerable fraternity, we learned that your prudence wished to anticipate, with a more useful counsel, the plan of one of our neighbors who, putting aside the impediment of the world, desired to enter upon the way of religion. I believe that he is designated, as though by his proper name, in these words.

Indeed, it seemed to me that the duty of due good will and charity toward him could not otherwise be fulfilled unless it were discussed with several people necessarily concerned with the same matter, lest perhaps rash presumption should overthrow this man on the very journey to which his desire leads him. But I think it necessary to provide more diligently how, or by what means, the stability of that pilgrimage—which, as you know, is most excellent . . . [lacuna] . . . may be demonstrated with every firmness of reason to those with whom the present matter must be dealt, as both possible and, if it can be done, beyond excuse.

Therefore do not disdain to inform our littleness by letter whether you think an exhortation should be sent in the common language as one letter, or whether each of us should send a letter separately. If you judge it useful that a common and single brief statement be sent by us, I ask your charitable diligence to compose it. If you think that this cannot be done successfully without some personal conference, whether with us or with other servants of God, so that the matter may be carried out with suitable counsel and complete firmness, deign to inform us of what seems to you most useful for us to do about this matter in writing, entrusting your answer to the bearer of this little letter.

We wish your goodness health and progress in Christ as it intercedes for us, with undivided desires.

For Bishop Lullus.

## LETTER XXV. CUTHBERT TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 760.)*

To Lullus, my most beloved and most faithful friend in the Lord: Abbot Cuthbert sends greetings.

I received with great gratitude the letter and gifts that your fraternity deigned to send me, namely a hairy garment and a fine linen cloth. I was all the more grateful because I have no doubt that they were sent from the depths of charity. Therefore, returning some recompense for this kindness, I too do not cease to care for you in my daily prayers.

The names of the brothers whom you sent to us are also written together with the names of the brothers of this monastery who sleep in Christ, so that I have ordered more than ninety Masses to be celebrated for them. Moreover, I took care to send, for the consolation of your pilgrimage, the book which the renowned teacher of the Church of God, Bede, composed on *The Building of the Temple*. I humbly beg your fraternity to deign to preserve firmly to the end the bonds of the friendship once agreed between us, especially in this matter: that, together with all those whom divine providence has willed to be subject to you, you may be a diligent intercessor for my infirmities before the heavenly Judge.

For Bishop Lullus.

May almighty God always preserve your fraternity in his love.

## LETTER XXVI. CENE TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 760.)*

To the most blessed lord Lullus, deserving of every honor, bishop: Coena, servant of the servants of God, sends the salvation of perpetual grace.

After receiving the letters of your blessedness, most excellent Father, I was filled with such great joy that I wept with joy from the innermost depths of my heart, considering myself blessed and certain to benefit from enjoying the friendship of so great a Father. Therefore, with every eagerness of heart, I embrace your desirable goodness and eagerly rejoice in your charity, chiefly because I remember the salutary commandments of divine love implanted in us, and because for some time I have chosen you as a supporter or counsellor in the labors of our littleness—one whom the merciful giver of all good things, through his kindly providence, has, as we believe, preordained for us in you.

Therefore, sweetest brother, to whatever regions of holy peace you call me, I come willingly, hastening and rejoicing with my whole self and with a full heart. Moreover, with many tears I earnestly beg you to deign to keep whatever small remembrance of us you can in your holy prayers, and always to preserve the promises of the goodness you have well begun, because a glorious crown of recompense is granted to perseverance, and the reward of future happiness is looked for at the end of every work.

As for what you asked about books brought to land by sea tides, it is entirely unknown to us. In addition, the books of the cosmographers have not yet come into our hands; nor do we possess any other copies except those burdensome with pictures and letters. I have often intended to write this to you, but I have not yet been able to acquire scribes. Perhaps with the help of your prayers . . . .

May the saving King preserve your holiness forever under the protection of the chosen Lady.

I know, Father, that you have not seen those things which I sent through the grace of charity.

Living happily, crowned with Christ’s triumphs,

a life for your own, a model for the age, most dear to heaven,

cultivator of justice, true lover of goodness,

defending the holy flocks with vigilant protection,

opening delightful pastures rich with flowers,

bearing a hundred sheaves when the Judge comes.

To be offered to Lullus, a most renowned bishop.

## LETTER XXVII. WIGBERT TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 760.)*

To the truly blessed lord Lullus, venerable in every duty of charity, bishop by the grace of God: Wigbert, your faithful servant and presbyter, sends the desired salvation in Christ.

With your prayers and merits assisting us, as we believe and certainly know, God’s clemency granted us prosperous journeys by land and sea after we departed from you. We found our friends and relatives safe and unharmed, and they kindly welcomed us, freely giving us everything necessary, both in fields and estates, in beasts of burden and livestock, and in other household goods.

Since we have possessed these things without any opposition until today, we ask and beseech your holy fraternity, which has always been accustomed both to help and console us, to see and consider what would be most useful for us to do. Everything is known to you—this and that—and whatever seems good to you, I confess that I have done with a glad heart and have rejected none of your salutary counsel.

If it seems good to you that we come to you, useful men, as we believe, and, as they say, good men, desire to be in our company. But if something else pleases you more, they nevertheless wish to visit you with our conversation and counsel, if this seems good to you. Make known to us what you think about this matter.

But why do I delay further, when your letter reaches us? We beg you to entrust it to this present bearer of my letter. Whatever you command or advise in it, God permitting and life accompanying us, we shall gladly do.

We have already spent much of our life, drifting and neglecting it, scattered as though outside ourselves. At last, in order that we may return to ourselves, it is necessary for us to know what is written: “The one who sows in tears will reap in joy.” Therefore we are eager to pass the remainder of our lives with your counsel.

Moreover, if any door of divine mercy has been opened in the territory of our people, namely the Saxons, take care to send us word how many, with God’s help, desire to hasten to their assistance. Consider all these matters, which we have touched on in a long letter, with your wakeful mind, deciding what is best to do, and do not let your holy kindness hesitate to inform us in writing.

Farewell.

I, Hrothuin, once something among you, now stationed here, writing, reading, and teaching what I have read, greet you warmly. I beg you to be toward me as I am toward you. Greet all who love our Lord Jesus Christ.

## LETTER XXVIII. BREGWIN TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 761.)*

To the most reverend and dearest brother in Christ, Bishop Lullus: Bregwin, servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual salvation in the name of Christ.

Many days have passed since, anxiously, I most desired that, with God favoring us, our envoy might at last find a prosperous journey to reach your blessedness. For throughout the preceding years that have recently elapsed, many and diverse disturbances were reported to exist among us in the regions of Britain and Gaul. This repeatedly hindered our desirable plan and, by causing great fear, prevented us from sending any of our people to you through such uncertain and . . . [lacuna] . . . frequently recurring attacks of wicked men in the provinces of the English or the regions of Gaul.

Now, however, since peace and protection have been undoubtedly promised us everywhere by the rulers, we have sent to your venerable fraternity this brother who bears the present letter, Hildebercht by name. I remember how we conversed with one another in the Roman city concerning the agreement of friendship, which we also confess that we shall preserve in every way.

Therefore, trusting now in the friendship of your blessedness, and wishing to do as our predecessors never ceased to do with one another, we too desire to act likewise. We send the sweetest words of greeting and peace, so that the evangelical saying may be fulfilled in us: that we may deserve to be his disciples if we have love for one another.

For this reason we have taken care to inform you that we sent your blessedness certain small gifts—not small in charity, to be sure—namely one box made from bones for priestly use, sent merely as a greeting and blessing through Ishard, a devout presbyter. We ask you to receive kindly the things that are ours, and likewise we hope to receive good things from you.

Moreover, dearest of all the brothers, I desire your loving devotion to know with certainty, God as my witness, that I willingly receive and hold more firmly your holy affection in that same place of charity and consolation of fraternal fellowship in which the love of your blessed father and predecessor Boniface has always remained unshaken and continually established. Thus between us and our people also may intimate and spiritual friendship thereafter faithfully endure, both for the remedies of our souls through prayers and the celebration of Masses, and for whatever is fitting in this life and for fraternal assistance.

I greatly desire you to fulfill, through your affection, what I have said above: greet all the priests of God and the households of blessed Boniface, Christ’s martyr, diligently and lovingly in my name, and urge them to implore the clemency of almighty God for us with earnest prayers, just as we do not cease to pray for them.

Concerning the return of the aforesaid object, whether through the words of our brother or through a letter of your fraternal piety, order us to be informed.

May the goodness of almighty God fortify us with his protection and deign continually and forever to preserve and guard the most sincere charity of your holiness for the benefit of many.

We celebrate the day of deposition of Bugga, a devout female servant of Christ, who was an honored abbess; her day of deposition was the sixth day before the Kalends of January. While she was still alive, she earnestly asked me to send this to your blessedness. As she hoped and believed, take care to do so, for her father and patron in Christ was Bishop Boniface.

## LETTER XXIX. LULLUS TO CENE  
*(Around the year of the Lord 762.)*

To Coena, brother and fellow priest, a lord most dear in merits and endowed with the insignia of the highest pontificate: Lullus, a small servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual salvation in Christ.

I humbly beg your holiness to deign to remember continually the friendship once joined between us in Christ and begun at a definite time, lest it grow old and be handed over to oblivion—the friendship we pledged before the faithful God with a solemn promise.

For the sake of Christ’s name, we ought to glory in insults and tribulations and in the exaltation of his Church, which is daily beaten, oppressed, and wearied, because the rulers of our time establish new customs and new laws according to their desires. Therefore, with a strengthened prayer, we earnestly implore your excellence to be a continual intercessor for the salvation of our soul.

For I am compelled by continual bodily illnesses and mental anxiety to depart from this sorrowful life, so full of dangers, and to render an account to the merciful and strict Judge.

I have sent your affection a small gift, namely a silk cloak, through the bearer of this letter.

I ask you to acquire and deign to send us any one of the books expounded by Bede the presbyter, of blessed memory, for the consolation of our pilgrimage: four books on the first part of Samuel, up to the death of Saul; or three books on Ezra and Nehemiah; or four books on the Gospel of Mark.

Perhaps I am asking difficult things, but I impose nothing difficult upon true charity.

## LETTER XXX. WIGBERT TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 762.)*

To the holy and most blessed lord Lullus, bishop by the grace of God, always most dear to me with every affection: Wigbert, a small servant of the household of Christ, sends unfading and everlasting health.

I have been filled with great joy, and my spirit has become very cheerful, having learned from certain people of your blessed well-being. We pray that by God’s grace you may always have it and may remember us in your holy prayers.

By God’s grace and, as we believe, with your merits assisting us, we crossed the sea safe and unharmed, reached our homeland, and, as you commanded, presented your gifts to your bishops, abbots, and friends. According to the measure of our understanding, we also took care to communicate your words and your wishes.

They did as they had been instructed, receiving everything humbly and gratefully and giving great thanks to Christ the Lord because your sublimity had deigned to visit their littleness through gifts and letters. They promised that they would always possess your communion and the continual activity of your household’s prayers. They wrote your name in their churches among those dearest to them and said that they would continually make remembrance of you, both living and dead. They also promised to send letters written as they pleased.

This bearer of the present letter can better communicate to you in words all that we have extended at length. We have taken care to send him to you as a presbyter, believing and trusting that he is a useful vessel in the house of the Lord. We earnestly ask that your holiness deign to receive and keep him kindly and honorably, if he is worthy, since he is both our friend and our relative.

We therefore cannot conceal that our friends and relatives do not wish to leave us this year. For this reason I have sent my messengers to you, humbly beseeching you through the Lord’s mercy that your clemency deign to release both the vows and the words by which I have bound myself to you, and that through your letter, returning by my messengers, you inform me what I ought to do.

For I confess to you before God that, against your will, no dignity of the world and no secular friendship can in any way retain me here, especially because I love you above all people—God is my witness. But if it seems good to you, and it is your will that I return to you more quickly, release me to the Church and to the ministry which I formerly served. I ask and beg you for one thing.

My friends and relatives promise me their land and inheritance and intend to give them to me if I decide to remain here with them; otherwise they must leave them to strangers. Therefore, my lord, consider and weigh through your prudence and understanding what seems good and right to you, and, as I have said, inform me of it by letter. For, if life accompanies me and God grants it, I intend to do what you command.

May divine mercy guard your blessedness as you pray for us forever. Amen.

I, Hrothuin, once your kinsman, greet you, earnestly asking you to forgive the ignorance of an unlearned man for whatever you find written reprehensibly. Would that, if it can be done and if it is God’s will, we might see one another face to face! Farewell, and remember us.

May Macarius, the merciful *Pantocrator* (“Ruler of All”) of the northern hall, deign to preserve you safe for a long time.

## LETTER XXXI. LULLUS TO CUTHBERT  
*(Around the year of the Lord 772.)*

To the holy and venerable brother in Christ, Cuthbert, abbot: Lullus, a small servant of the servants of God, sends perpetual salvation in Christ.

Charity, which does not know how to cease, never grows old; it can scarcely contain within itself the heat of its inward fire. Therefore our littleness was pleased to learn of your health, so that I might rejoice with you in the Lord and so that you might know what is happening to my frailty under the just judgment of God.

For continual bodily illness compels me to depart from this fleeting light and from this valley of tears, in order to render an account to the merciful and strict Judge. I therefore humbly beg you to pray earnestly to the Lord for the salvation of my soul.

We have also sent your affection a small gift, one silk cloak. We further ask you to deign to send, for the consolation not only of our pilgrimage but also of our illness, these books expounded by Bede, of blessed memory: *The Building of the Temple*, or *The Song of Songs*, or all the epigrams composed in heroic or elegiac meter. If that is not possible, send the three books on *The Building of the Temple*.

May you remain well into old age, together with all who serve the Lord God with you.

We also commend to your charity the names of our brothers and friends who have departed from this light; they are . . .

## LETTER XXXII. CYNEWULF TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 772.)*

To the most blessed lord Lullus, bishop, venerated with particular love: I, Cynewulf, king of the West Saxons, together with my bishops and also the company of my nobles, send eternal health in the Lord.

We testify to you that, according to the measure of our ability, we are ready willingly to do whatever your holiness desires or commands, just as we pledged with your predecessor, Boniface, the most reverend and holy man of God—whether in devout prayers to God or in any other matters in which human frailty, by God’s arrangement, is shown to need mutual assistance from one another.

We likewise beseech you to remember to pray to the Lord for our littleness and for the peace of our congregation, together with those who invoke the name of the Lord Jesus with you.

We entrust to your kindness this bearer of the present letter, whom we previously sent to you, because he has taken care to obey you faithfully in all things.

May almighty God, who gathers what is scattered and guards what is gathered, protect you by his grace and grant that we may see the fruit of your labor in the eternal homeland.

## LETTER XXXIII. AMALARDUS AND WIDO TO LULLUS  
*(Around the year of the Lord 774.)*
To the Lord and Father Riculfus, archbishop, whom the grace of the eternal King may deign perpetually to preserve, for the salvation of many and the defense of the Catholic Church, Amalardus and Wido, together with the entire congregation of Saint Peter from the monastery of Horbach, presume to send greetings in the Lord God our Savior.

For the rest, let it be known to Your Piety that, insofar as God deigns to hear us, we are continually your petitioners and desire to remain so with greater attentiveness. Let the greatness of Your Eminence learn that we sent our priest, named Macharius, to our churches which appear to be situated in your diocese, [Col. 0848A] so that he might perform the office there according to customary practice. But the same priest reported to us that the greatness of your authority had ordered that he should not celebrate the divine office there, because we do not know whether some report had reached the ears of Your Piety from Bishop Bernarius. For the same Lord Bishop Bernarius sent him one horse to pasture at our expense, from the resources by which we must live; we do not know whether this action was taken for that reason.

Now we beg that, once permission has been granted by you, this same priest may be allowed to render the customary service to the Lord Jesus Christ and to the relics of the saints kept in that place, lest both the house of God and the honor of those relics remain without a priest, light, and worship. Nor do we have in those regions any other priest who could perform that office there, except this one. Therefore we beseech you to grant him such an order and permission, lest, for so long as we have entreated you, the house of God and the honor of its relics remain as they now do.

May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ make you powerful in the present life and grant that you reign happily with him in eternal blessedness.

May our prayers, I beseech you, obtain access—may they obtain access—to the ears of Your Piety, chosen of God, so that a great reward for the benefit of others also may be repaid to you by the Lord Jesus Christ.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 790. ELIPANDUS, FELIX, HETERIUS, BISHOPS OF TOLEDO, URGELL, AND UXAMA, AND SAINT BEATUS THE PRIEST.

[Col. 0847]

HISTORICAL NOTICE.

(From Anton., *Bibliotheca Vetus Hispanica*)

[Col. 0847C] As the eighth century was drawing to a close, a new error, born from the ignorance of the Spanish people groaning under the yoke of the Saracens, infected the purer Christian age in which the faith of that period was alive: an error concerning the person of our Lord Christ. Yet this gave those who thought differently and correctly an opportunity to forge highly learned monuments and, through their writings, to wipe away shameful stains that would otherwise have remained had assistance not quickly been provided.

Felix, bishop of Urgell, and Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, were the foundation and occasion of the evil. Each, perhaps deceived by the contagion of those sitting upon their necks, or by that of the neighboring blaspheming Muslims, did not blush to call and teach Jesus Christ the adopted Son of God. The former Felix was condemned once at the Council of Regensburg; and again, together with Elipandus, when their heresy was condemned at Frankfurt. [Col. 0848C]

Jonas of Orléans recounts the matter more fully than others at the very beginning of his books against Claudius of Turin, in these words—not without a certain exceptional praise of our own nation:

> “It is clear that Spain produced men most eloquent and learned, and most invincible defenders of the Catholic and apostolic faith. Since their examples are worthy of imitation and their teachings worthy of being followed, since they are readily available and are embraced by the Church, the holy Church, with Christ’s favor, is rightly instructed and healthfully strengthened by them. But since she has very often produced, and to this day does not cease to produce, both heresiarchs attempting to stain the simplicity of the Catholic faith with perverse doctrines and men who oppose the authority of the holy Church of God with manifold superstitions, all the faithful have great reason to grieve. To pass over the others, there arose from that same Spain, in the time of the holy-memory, most pious and invincible Augustus Charles, a certain Felix by name, unhappy in his conduct, bishop of the city of Urgell. Joining himself to the criminal error of Elipandus, bishop of the city of Toledo, he dared to preach that, according to his humanity, Christ was not the proper Son of God but an adopted son; and by this poisonous teaching the two of them infected a large part of Spain.”

He then relates that Felix attempted to administer a draught of this poison to the Gauls and Germans; and that, by order of that same Charles the Great and with the authority of Pope Hadrian I, a synod assembled at Regensburg, or Raiginsburg—for that is how Alcuin calls it [*Against Elipandus*, book I]—condemned him, together with the author of his error, Nestorius, who was considered present.

Jacobus Sirmondus observed when this synod was held [Note: [Col. 0849C] In the notes to the *Councils of Gaul*, vol. II, p. 160], namely, in the year 792. Indeed, Felix was brought from there to Rome; in the presence of Hadrian, in the basilica of Saint Peter, he confessed his heresy and renounced it, and was freely permitted to return to his own city, as Einhard reports in his *Annals*, written under Louis the Pious [Note: [Col. 0849C] It was published among the *Writers of Germany*, anonymously, by Justus Reuber, and afterward under Einhard’s name by Duchesne, vol. II of the *Writers of France*, p. 233]. Since this author had previously been unknown [Note: [Col. 0849C] Before Duchesne’s edition of the *Contemporary Authors of Gaul*], Baronius [Note: [Col. 0849D] Vol. IX, under the year 792, no. 10; Morales, book XIII, chapter 26] and others cite him without giving his name. He also says that Felix wrote books concerning his error and sent them to Elipandus (under the year 792):

> “Urgel is a city situated on the ridge of the Pyrenees. Its bishop, Felix by name and a Spaniard by birth, having been consulted by letter by Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, etc., very rashly and thoughtlessly, and contrary to the ancient teaching of the Catholic Church, not only pronounced Christ, the Son of God, to be adopted, but also obstinately labored, in books written to the aforesaid bishop, to defend the depravity of his opinion.”

From these words the Spanish birth of Felix ought to be so indisputable that John Tamayo’s attempt to make him a Gaul is futile. For Tamayo interpolated the life of Beatus, in which we read this, published on [Col. 0849C] 19 February, although he claims to have taken it from an Asturian legendary. We shall speak of this again when treating of Beatus.

There exist, in the appendix to Alcuin’s works, letters and confessions of Felix, bishop of Urgell, and Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo—the latter confession was also published by Lalandus in the *Supplement to Sirmond’s Councils of Gaul*, p. 89. There is likewise a letter from Felix to his most beloved daughter in Christ; also a letter from Elipandus to Felix, recently converted; and finally a letter from Elipandus to Alcuin, or Albinus, containing further responses to the former letter.

Nor was this error newly born at that time. For from the year 783—if the calculation is correct and the numeral has not deceived us—in a certain manuscript codex of the Church of Toledo, in which, as in others, there is preserved a substantial work of Beatus and Heterius against this error of Elipandus, of which we shall speak shortly, there is found a letter written by Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, to a certain abbot named Fidelis, whose location we do not know, but who was living in Asturias. It appears to have been written at Toledo in October of the recently mentioned year. In that year [Note: [Col. 0849D] Morales, book XIII, chapters 25 and 26], after Silo, king of Asturias, had died, Mauregatus, the illegitimate son of Alfonso the Catholic, expelled Alfonso the Chaste and usurped the kingdom.

For the subject of this letter, see Ambrosius Morales, chapter 26. It still lies hidden in manuscript [Note: [Col. 0849D] It was partly published by the distinguished Florez, vol. V, p. 555. Only a fragment of it survives, inserted into the letter—or *Apologeticus*—of Beatus and Heterius against Elipandus, which we shall discuss in its proper place. Florez says there that Elipandus’s letter to Fidelis was written in the year of Christ 785].

This was the first writing in which Elipandus drew his pen in defense of his mad opinion. He accused Beatus, the man whom we have recently praised, and together with him Heterius, called the bishop of Oxoma, his friend and associate, because the inhabitants of Asturias, without consulting the bishop of Toledo—indeed, while he held the contrary opinion—were teaching the people what seemed right to them, something which Elipandus throws at them as though it were a reproach. He praised a certain bishop Archaricus for prudence and obedience, because Archaricus had dutifully consulted him concerning the teaching of both Beatus and Heterius.

There he also reports that, together with other Spanish bishops at Seville, he had extinguished another error concerning the celebration of Easter, that of a certain Migetius [Note: [Col. 0849D] Pope Hadrian mentions this man in his letter to all the bishops of Spain against Elipandus, which Sirmond published in vol. II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 161, and which the latest Paris edition of all the councils also contains]. He hopes similarly to extinguish the Beatian—thus he calls it after Beatus—heresy in Asturias. To this letter Beatus and Heterius, whom we shall discuss shortly, replied with an apology for the true doctrine.

Nor was Elipandus instructed or restrained by Felix’s repentance. Rather, attempting to defend once more the same cause of this error, he sent letters to Charles, king of the Franks, and also to certain bishops, “in the tenor of which,” Charles himself says [In the letter discussed below], “it was not sufficiently clear whether you intended to teach us as though by the authority of a teacher, or desired to learn from us in the humility of a disciple.”

Certainly, in those letters directed to Charles the king, Elipandus asked that the text of his treatise concerning the matter—which is the same as the letter—be read in his presence [Note: [Col. 0849D] Florez was the first to publish this letter of Elipandus to Charles the Great, from the Toledo codex mentioned above, vol. V, pp. 558 onward. In it, no. 2, we read:

> “Against the madness of this man [namely Beatus], we, unworthy and insignificant as we are, according to the limited measure of our understanding, have sent a letter to be reread and discussed by the priests subject to your rule, and to be presented to your sacred eyes [Col. 0850D], asking you by him who for your sake stretched out innocent hands upon the cross, and for your sake shed precious blood, and for your sake endured death and the tomb, and descended into hell to free the elect, and, rising for your sake, showed you the way of returning to the heavens, namely to the heavenly homeland: that you yourself may return as judge … resolve the matter with a chaste and salutary judgment, and without the oil of flattery pronounce your sentence with equal weight, etc.”

Elipandus’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, Aquitania, and Austria—or Austrasia—is found first of all in the same Toledo codex, Pluteus V, no. 16. At its end we read: “This book was written, with God’s help, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the era 1108 [A.D. 1070]. Pray for Vincent the priest, the scribe. May you have Christ the Lord as your protector. Amen.”].

Charles says that he carried this out by summoning to a council bishops from all the churches under his dominion and having the letter read before them. This was the celebrated Council of Frankfurt, or Frankford, of the year 794, though not blessed in every respect. At it the “impious and detestable heresy of Elipandus, bishop of the see of Toledo, and Felix of Urgell and their followers, who, thinking wrongly, asserted adoption in the Son of God,” was indeed solemnly anathematized, as the first canon says. [Col. 0851A] But with reckless boldness the Catholic doctrine concerning the veneration of images, the doctrine of the Second General Synod of Nicaea, was condemned in the second canon, perhaps because it had not then been adequately understood from the Greek source [Note: [Col. 0851D] Louis Maimbourg, a French Jesuit of the Society of Jesus, perhaps struck the matter sharply after proposing various conjectures concerning the difference between the two councils, in his *History of the Iconoclasts*, vol. II, book V, under the year 794. After Sirmond, John Mabillon also offered several learned observations on this Council of Frankfurt in the preface to the first part of the fourth century of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, § 3].

From this arose refutatory letters to Elipandus and, in general, to the bishops of Spain—although it is more probable that not all of them adhered to this filth. The first was attributed only to the bishops of Italy who had assembled at that council and was directed to the provinces of Galicia and Spain. The second was addressed by the bishops of Germany, Gaul, and Aquitania to the bishops of Spain. The third was Charles’s own reply to Elipandus, which he wished to be addressed to him and to the other fellow priests in the regions of Spain.

All these letters were inserted into the acts of this council [latest Paris edition, vol. VII, col. 1022], as was another letter of Pope Hadrian I [ibid., col. 1014], no longer addressed to Elipandus but against him and inscribed to the churches presided over by the Galician and Spanish bishops—for so the text reads. It had been written before the celebration of the aforesaid council, immediately after Charles had warned the pope about the letters sent to him by Elipandus [Col. 0851B]. Other letters by the same pontiff are also read in the third volume of Duchesne’s collection, the *History of the Franks*.

Alcuin also sharpened the point of his pen against Elipandus and engaged him in extensive discussion of this doctrine. I mean Alcuin, the teacher of Charles the Great, whom Charles had summoned from Britain at this very time because of his reputation for learning. In the Paris edition of Alcuin’s works of 1617, prepared by André Duchesne, one finds his exhortatory letter to Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, concerning the Catholic faith, as well as another letter from Elipandus to Alcuin containing replies to the preceding letter [Note: [Col. 0851D] Florez also incorporated this letter of Elipandus to Alcuin, or Albinus, altered from Alcuin himself, Paris edition of 1617, col. 910, into vol. V, pp. 562 onward. He also included another letter of Elipandus to Felix of Urgell, recently converted or repentant, from Ducange, in the preface to his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, nos. 29 and 31; it appears in the same volume, p. 577]. We have already mentioned this letter. There are also two treatises by Alcuin against the letter sent to him by Elipandus, in which he empties out those perverse assertions. There are likewise seven books against Felix of Urgell, published under the name of Paulinus of Aquileia in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, which the same Duchesne attributed to Alcuin [Note: [Col. 0851D] Placcius also notes this, *On Pseudonymous Writers*, p. 235].

For Paulinus, a writer of the same period and highly esteemed by Charles, wrote various works against this error. These include a treatise on the most holy Trinity against Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, and Felix, bishop of Urgell, called the *Sacrosyllabus*—this is the letter mentioned above, sent in the name of Paulinus and the other Italian bishops to the provinces of Spain—and also three books against that same Felix, bishop of Urgell, together with a letter to Charles the Great. The aforementioned André Duchesne brought these works to light from a manuscript of the Putean brothers together with the works of Alcuin. Agobard, bishop of Lyon, also issued a book directed against Felix of Urgell to Louis the emperor.

Such was the effort required to shatter with the hammer of truth the machinations of what was alleged to be a revived Nestorian error among us, and the utterly false assertions of two bishops. Yet even after the conciliar and papal anathema—the Council of Narbonne [Note: [Col. 0852D] In *Gallia Christiana*, vol. I, p. 368; Labbe’s *Synopsis*, p. 373], the Roman Council [Note: [Col. 0852D] In the same Labbe, under Leo III, in the year 799], the Council of Urgell [Note: [Col. 0852D] In Baluze’s appendix to Agobard], and the Council of Aachen [Note: [Col. 0852D] In Lalandus’s *Supplement to the Councils of Gaul*, p. 89] are praised for this by various authors—the serpent of error still raised its head in Spain among certain disciples of Elipandus. Jonas of Orléans reports that he met them in Asturias and, because after three admonitions they still persisted in the same error, avoided them as heretics.

Those who wish in some measure to excuse Elipandus’s error may consult Francisco Suárez and Gabriel Vázquez in their theological commentaries, and after them John Eusebius Nieremberg in his letter to D. Lorenzo Ramírez de Prado [Note: [Col. 0852D] In the edition of Luitprand’s works, p. 518], published by Ramírez together with the works of Luitprand.

No one among our Spanish churches had rendered greater service concerning this same matter in those very days than the Spaniard Beatus; the work of Beatus and Heterius—for Heterius was bishop of Oxoma—against Elipandus survives. Beatus of Liébana in Asturias, a learned man and, according to Alcuin’s testimony, holy both in life and in name, opposed the new doctrine of Elipandus. Since he had an intimate association with Heterius, he also inscribed Heterius’s name on the work. In a certain codex of the Church of Toledo, recently mentioned by us, it is read under this fully appropriate title:

> “To our most eminent and God-beloved Elipandus, archbishop of the see of Toledo, Heterius and Beatus send greetings in the Lord.”

It is far from the case that the proud letter of Elipandus to Abbot Fidelis, mentioned above, which criticized the work of these two men, caused lovers of the truth to abandon their purpose.

The first person, so far as I know, to bring this monument of antiquity to light was Peter Steuartius in his *Collection of Notable Authors, Both Greek and Latin, Concerning Ecclesiastical Matters* (Ingolstadt, 1616, quarto), under this title:

> “Two books of Heterius, bishop of Uxama, and Beatus the priest, against Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, concerning the adoption of Christ the Son of God.”

It was subsequently included in the fourth Paris edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. IV, and elsewhere. A manuscript survives in two codices of the Church of Toledo (Pluteus XXX, no. 13, under the name “Heterius against Elipandus”). One of these was seen by Morales, as we have already said, and by Francisco Pisa [Col. 0852C] (see *History of Toledo*, fol. 137) [Note: [Col. 0852D] We have often seen and compared these two codices with one another; from the older one, which appeared to have been written at the end of the tenth century or the beginning of the following century, we copied the exemplar now before us].

Elipandus himself mentions this work when writing to Charles, as is clear from these words of Charles’s reply (Paris edition, col. 1051):

> “You have proposed to me the example of the emperor Constantine, whose beginning you say the blessed Isidore praised, and whose end he lamented. You kindly urge that this should not happen to me through a certain Beatus, whom you have called *Antiphrasius*.”

Elipandus had used the mocking designation *Antiphrasius*—one might render it in Latin as “contradictor”—to refer to Beatus. Felix likewise agreed with him when, writing to Alcuin, he inscribed his letter:

> “To the most reverend brother Albinus the deacon, not a minister of Christ but the foulest disciple of the *Antiphrasius* Beatus” [Note: [Col. 0852D] Elipandus’s letter to Albinus or Alcuin, published by the distinguished Florez, vol. V, p. 562, bears exactly these words].

As John Mabillon most correctly emended it, this is how the letter was inscribed [preface to the first part of the fourth century of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, § 1]. Mabillon also gives two other testimonies concerning this very name *Antiphrasius*: the letter of Elipandus to Felix and the Life of Alcuin, both of which mention Beatus.

[Col. 0852D] Alvarus of Córdoba, also, an as-yet unpublished writer of the following century, praises this work of Beatus in various places in his writings, as Morales says, and there notes that Beatus had a more impeded tongue and was therefore more suited and ready for writing than for disputation.

We have not seen the passage in which he judges Beatus in this way, but only the following passage in Letter 1 to Aurelius Flavius John. Among other testimonies of the holy Fathers advanced in support of the argument of that letter, he says:

> “Also, from the book of the blessed Heterius against Helipandus”—read “of Beatus and Heterius,” for there are two men; and we do not charge Heterius and Helipandus with the aspiration-mark—

> “when he says: ‘The one who sent me is with me,’ etc.”

He confirms the correction by immediately praising the same man:

> “Likewise the aforementioned Beatus of Liébana: ‘If you wish to examine it,’ etc.”

And in another letter to the same man:

> “But as Beatus of Liébana the priest said.”

A little later in the same letter:

> “Almost of our own time, Beatus of Liébana the priest.”

In these passages he indicates either his homeland or the place where Beatus lived. In Sebastian of Salamanca, or King Alfonso, in the *Chronicle*, we read that Liébana was one of the regions into which the faithful Spanish peoples were again driven under Alfonso the Catholic, Pelagius’s son-in-law—peoples who had remained confined to certain corners of Asturias until that day because of fear of the Saracens. Sebastian names Liébana among these regions:

> “At that time,” he says, “Primorias, Liébana, Transmiera, Sopuerta, Carranza, Burgos—which is now called Castile—and part of maritime Galicia were populated.”

Today there is no certain town there, so far as I know, but a particular region of the Asturians between Oviedo and the Asturias of Saint Juliana, or Santillana as it is called: the highest and roughest part of the entire province, nine leagues long and four leagues wide. It is now called the province of Liébana and lies under the jurisdiction of the duke of Infantado.

In that region there is a town called Valle-Cavada, commonly Valcavado, near Saldaña. In its church the body of a certain holy man is reverently preserved. The people appear to prefer corruptly to call him Santo-Vieco instead of Santo Beato; and many affirm that another of his arms is openly displayed separately for veneration [Col. 0853C] [Note: [Col. 0853D] Morales, books XIII and XXVII; Lobera, *History of León*, chapter 33; Tamayo, *Spanish Martyrology*, 10 February].

The Benedictines Iepes, Wion, and Menardus say that he was their monk [Note: [Col. 0853D] Iepes, *Benedictine Chronicle*, under the year 783, vol. III, and under the year 537, chapter 3, vol. I; Wion, *Tree of Life*, book II, chapter 63; Menardus, *Appendix to the Monastic Martyrology*, letter B]; so too does the spurious Haubertus in his *Chronicle* under the year 792. Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0853D] In the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, third century, part II], however, at one time, and all the others [Note: [Col. 0853D] Morales, book XIII, chapter 26; Mariana, book VII, chapter 8; Tamayo, *Spanish Martyrology*, 19 February, p. 184; Bollandus, *Acts of the Saints*, on the same day], who did not belong to that institute, say that he was only a priest. But Mabillon withdrew his judgment when he turned to Beatus’s deeds in the first part of the fourth century, showing from Alcuin’s books and from the books of Beatus himself that Beatus had been a monk and an abbot.

From a certain legendary of an Asturian church, John Tamayo produced an account, or Life, of this Beatus under 19 February, the day on which the holy man is venerated. Those who place little or no confidence in this martyrologist do him no injustice. We shall speak of him below. Those who judge otherwise will, on the basis of this account, assign Beatus’s death to the year 798.

As for the claim recorded there and likewise by Haubertus under the year 792—that Heterius and Beatus attended the Council of Frankfurt as envoys of the Catholic Spaniards—it is refuted by the letters of the Fathers summoned to that council, praised above [Col. 0853D], and especially by the letters of King Charles directed to the bishops of Spain [Note: [Col. 0853D] Mariana agrees, in the chapter cited, as does Tamayo in the same place].

For nowhere is there any mention of Beatus as present, though the writer against Elipandus is indeed mentioned. From Charles himself we know that all the bishops under his rule, which at that time obeyed the king of the Franks, were summoned to this assembly, together with some from Britain; and finally Peter of Milan and Paulinus of Aquileia from Italy, and others from Germany, Gaul, and Aquitania—without adding any from Spain.

Paulinus of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0853D] In the *Sacrosyllabus*, or the already cited letter of the Italian bishops against Elipandus], however, says that what was added from Hesperia [Note: [Col. 0853D] Others would prefer to read Liguria, Histria, and Hesperia, or Histria, Venetia, and Emilia]—Liguria, Emilia, and Austria—belonged to Italian rather than Spanish Hesperia. For shortly before this he himself had called his own see of Aquileia, or Friuli, which is even now part of Italy, surrounded by the shores of Hesperia.

It is clear from that same letter of Paulinus, written in the synodal style, that at the time of the Council of Frankfurt Felix had not yet truly repented; or rather, that he had again fallen into error in order to defend his heresy together with Elipandus. Ado of Vienne states that he died unrepentant in exile at Lyon. People generally think differently about Elipandus [Note: [Col. 0854D] Morales, in the chapter cited; Mariana, in the chapter cited].

Indeed, if the letter of Archaricus, bishop of Braga, to Elipandus is genuine—as Tamayo says that he copied it from a manuscript [19 February, p. 187]—although in reality it had already been published among the letters of the bishops collected and annotated by Julianus, all the productions of the Higuera workshop, by D. Lorenzo Ramírez de Prado, then we certainly find there mention of a Council of Toledo summoned by Elipandus and of his recantation before the Fathers. The pseudo-Luitprand forger and the pseudo-Julian greatly embellished all this in their customary manner in several places [Note: [Col. 0854D] Luitprand under the years 795 and 810; Julianus in the *Chronicle*, nos. 402 and 411]. We shall say something about these matters shortly, after noting that, besides the aforesaid work of Beatus against Elipandus—in which, as John Mabillon observed [In the preliminary observations to the Life of Beatus], the deeds of Saint Andrew, believed to be more recent, are praised—there still exist unpublished commentaries, or a *catena*, to use the common term for a similar form of writing, on the Apocalypse, drawn from the holy Fathers, some of whom are no longer extant but are quoted there. It would therefore be exceedingly worthwhile for these works to be brought into public view after so long a silence [Note: [Col. 0854D] See Ludovicus Alcazar on the Apocalypse, p. 89]. Mabillon also desired this [Note: [Col. 0854D] We shall return below to Beatus’s genuine, hitherto unpublished commentary on the Apocalypse of John. As for the letter of Archaricus, or Arcaricus, bishop of Braga, to Elipandus, which our author mentions here while expressing doubt about its authenticity, it reveals itself as fabricated, recently or even the day before yesterday. It begins: “The letters of Your Fatherhood have wonderfully delighted me, in which you inform me that, standing before the Fathers assembled for the Council of Toledo, you adhered to the judgment of the Holy Apostolic Roman Church and willingly and readily lent your ears to the commands of the holy apostolic lord Hadrian, etc.” Can one refrain from laughter? See Tamayo, *Spanish Martyrology*, vol. I, under 19 February].

That this is the work of Beatus, however, is not doubtful among our people, although the author’s name is absent from every exemplar. There are several arguments.

First, it was dedicated to Heterius, with whom Beatus opposed Elipandus, in words that indicate their shared life and friendship:

> “I, holy Father Heterius, have dedicated these things to you at your request, for the edification of the zeal of the brothers, so that, since I enjoy you as a companion in the religious life, I may also make you a co-heir of my labor.”

Second, a parchment codex is preserved in the church of Valle-Cavada in which these commentaries were copied seven hundred years ago; and the tradition has always prevailed there that they were written by the same author whose body, buried there and reverently venerated, belongs to the holy man.

This codex was copied in the era 1008, that is, in the year of our Lord 970. Hieronymus Romanus de la Higuera left a record that he had seen it at the house of a private individual in the fourteenth book, chapter 17, of his still-manuscript *History of Toledo* [Col. 0854D] [Note: [Col. 0855D] Here our author seems to confuse the Toledo codex of Beatus and Heterius, Pluteus XIV, no. 23, which has no date attached to it, with the Elipandus codex of the same library, Pluteus V, no. 16, written by Vincent the priest in the era 1108. We said shortly before that Elipandus’s letters to the bishops of Gaul, to Charles the Great, and to Migetius are read in it].

The same author conjectures there that this is the Beatus mentioned in the Roman Martyrology and in Usuard on 9 May:

> “At the castle of Vindecinum, the deposition of Saint Beatus the confessor.”

Bede, and Galesinus following him, place him at Rome. But the castle of Vindecinum, or Vindocinum, is the city of Vendôme in Gaul. There is a parish there dedicated to Beatus, and a cave is shown in which he lived and was buried, according to Augustine Lubinus in his illustrated *Martyrology* (Table V, p. 108). The day is also different.

A similar codex was in the monastery of Saint Isidore in the city of León, likewise copied in the era 1085, or the year 1047; it is now in the possession of the most illustrious marquis of Mondéjar. Two other copies of this work also exist: the first, fairly ancient, in the library of the holy church of Oviedo; the other in the royal monastery of the Blessed Virgin of Guadalupe. Ambrosius Morales saw all of them [Note: [Col. 0855D] See him, book XIII, chapter 27].

There was another in the library of the most eminent lord D. Antonio, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church of Aragon [Col. 0855B], as our most learned friend Martín Vázquez Siruela reported to us. Yet another is in the library of the Church of Toledo, as is clear from its catalogue, which we preserve in manuscript (no. 30, 13).

We have said that there are many pseudo-historians of Toledan manufacture who excuse the Toledan bishop Elipandus, or magnify his repentance and recount his deeds: namely Julianus and Luitprandus. We shall give some examples here to demonstrate the vanity of their author.

The archdeacon Julianus says (*Chronicle*, no. 395) that there was a Toledan named Elipandus under the archbishop Cixila, at the time when Charles the Great was at Toledo, and that Charles married Galiana, daughter of Galafre, king of that city.
