According to certain authors, the emperor Louis the Pious was born from this marriage.

Such is the erudition of the great Julianus, which our countrymen marvel at, although all the ancient authorities oppose it and he wishes to be believed. Nothing is more certain [Note: [Col. 0855D] Einhard, *Life of Charles*, near the end; Paul the Deacon, *Fragment on the Ancestors and Children of Charles*, vol. II of the *History of the Franks*, p. 202; the brothers San-Marthani, *History of the House of France*, vol. I, book III, chapter 6] than that Louis was born to King Charles by his wife Hildegard of Swabia, and is said to lie near her tomb at Metz, at Saint Arnulf’s. Nothing is further from the truth than the claim that Charles was ever at Toledo or married Galiana.

For the latter story is one of those old-womanish tales that rashly burst into some of our histories [Note: [Col. 0855D] *General History of King Alfonso*, Beuter, and others, drawing from Turpin’s fabulous history, in whose chapters 1, 12, and elsewhere this stay of Charles at Toledo is recounted with other matters], and which more prudent scholars rightly reject [Note: [Col. 0856D] Morales, book XIII, chapter 20; Garibay, book XXXVII, chapter 15; Mariana, book VI, chapter 10; Pisa, *History of Toledo*, book I, chapter 17; Barreiros, *Itinerary*, fol. 98; Vasaeus, *Chronicle*, under the year 757].

He then covered the deeds of Elipandus (nos. 401 and following), saying that Elipandus was a citizen of Toledo but descended from the Goths—“Gracchi” was printed corruptly, as we believe [Note: [Col. 0856D] In the sole Paris edition of 1628]—and that, deceived by Felix and Vincent, he wrote to Charles the Great, his closest friend, concerning the adoption of Christ.

I would certainly like to find some trace of this friendship in Charles’s letter addressed to him. Under Elipandus he reports (no. 402) that the Mozarabs suffered exceedingly under the yoke of the Saracens. Yet shortly afterward (no. 411)—which would have been difficult for the Christians to achieve while enjoying the deepest peace and prosperity—Elipandus is said to have held a council of several bishops in that same city of Toledo; and this at precisely the time when, as Julianus himself says elsewhere [no. 402]:

> “The Mozarabs suffered exceedingly, provoked by the injuries of the Saracens, and for that reason many were compelled to flee to Asturias, others to Gaul.”

Thus let me attack Julianus with his own weapon; Luitprandus, whom he pretends was a man of that same age, wholly agrees with Julianus (under the year 772, no. 241, and under 786, no. 251), speaking of councils attributed to these same years.

Afterward Julianus says that Grumesindus, Elipandus’s archdeacon, and Lupus son of Andreas the Fig-tree, were sent to Charles the Great with Elipandus’s embassy and letters. The memorable deeds and family origin of that Andreas, the father of Lupus, and of the other Spanish families of the same stock—*de la Higuera*, to which the Latin surname *ficulnei* corresponds—were heaped together by Hieronymus Romanus de la Higuera, the architect, as is believed, of the pseudo-Julianus. We shall discuss these matters elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0856D] In the discussion of the spurious Julianus].

Soon afterward (no. 406) he attributes the *Apologeticus* against Elipandus solely to Bishop Heterius, without mentioning Beatus, its true author. Indeed, he later reports (nos. 409–410) that Archaricus, bishop of Braga, sent letters to Elipandus and received letters from him concerning the question of Christ’s adoption.

[Col. 0856B] But since two letters of this Arcaricus—or Archaricus—to Elipandus have been inserted into that collection of letters, which our Julian is said to have procured and left annotated in his papers, and which today has already been published together with the works of Luitprandus by Don Lorenzo Ramírez de Prado, we must pause here briefly, lest this Spanish writer, if indeed he was a writer, be dismissed by us without due acknowledgment.

Elipandus does indeed mention a certain bishop Archaricus’s having written letters to him concerning Beatus and Heterius, in the letter addressed to Abbot Fidelis that we cited above. Yet there are many features in these letters, of which we are now speaking, that strongly suggest novelty and fabrication. In the first, the title “Most Eminent” is bestowed on Elipandus by Archaricus—a form of secular ostentation more characteristic of that period than of ecclesiastical modesty—although the highly praised Ramírez has taken care to provide an extensive note here. For we possess letters of Isidore and others, indeed even of Álvarus of Córdoba, who was nearly his contemporary, that do not walk in this kind of footwear.

[Col. 0856C] There is likewise mention of the metropolitan bishops of Seville, Mérida, and Tarragona, whom Archaricus says he consulted. As for Tarragona, since the city was conquered by the Moors from the year 719 onward and utterly destroyed—as is commonly reported by the historians of Catalonia [Note: [Col. 0856D] Icart, *Grandezas de Tarragona*, chapters 9 and 21; Beuter, *Historia de España*, part I, chapter 28; Puiades, *Historia de Cataluña*, book VI, chapter 148; Zurita, book I of the *Annals of Aragon*, chapter 28]—we can scarcely believe that the Church, much less a metropolitan see, continued there. As for Mérida, there is no later mention of its bishop after Maximus, who, while the Gothic kingdom was still flourishing, took part in the fifteenth and sixteenth Councils of Toledo. The city was destroyed by the Moors, as one reads in the Arab historian Rasis (*Description of Spain*); and it suffered under their rule the things recounted in a certain letter of Louis, king of the Franks, the Pious, son of Charlemagne, which is among the letters of Einhard and was addressed to the community of Mérida [Note: [Col. 0856D] In Sirmond, after the notes on the *Capitula* of Charles the Bald; and in Tomás Tamayo, in the *Apospasmatio on the Affairs of Mérida*, published together with Paul the Deacon’s book *On the Lives of the Fathers of Mérida*, p. 151]. Concerning Seville, it is certain that John was still directing its sacred affairs shortly before this ninth century; he was held in great esteem by everyone, including the Moors. We shall speak of him at the proper place, at greater length, on account of the praise due to his learning and his monuments.

But whatever may be said about the episcopal dignity continuing in these cities, I can scarcely persuade myself that, amid the disturbances of captivity and perpetual war, that ancient organization of sacred government still survived, together with communication among metropolitan bishops separated from one another by so many parasangs; and that matters concerning religion were not instead discussed more promptly and easily among neighboring bishops.

Thirdly, it is troubling that Archaricus says he consulted Pope Adrian, and that he places this in the period when Adrian had already written to the bishops of Spain and King Charles to Elipandus letters that still exist today—for we know nothing of any others. Yet Adrian’s letter ought certainly to have mentioned that Archaricus had written to him on this matter. Adrian’s letter shows that this did not happen at all, for he addressed it as follows: “To our fellow priests presiding over the Gallic and Spanish Churches.” Among these, there can be no doubt, the bishop of Braga must also be understood. Indeed, from the very beginning he says that all of them, without exception, are “not joined to the communion of the faith with sincere minds”; and throughout the letter he calls them “deceived by the madness of their rashness, complainers, detractors, hateful to God, blind, wicked, harsh, and disorderly,” finally imposing on them, unless they repent, the ultimate anathema of all evils.

I certainly would not wish to be insulting toward so great a man and pontiff. Yet it plainly appears that he did Archaricus a grave injustice by making him primate of the bishops of Galicia: if he had consulted him, Adrian nevertheless did not mention him, but did not hesitate to stamp the same mark of error upon all the bishops of his province indiscriminately.

Fourthly, these letters are said to have been supplied by the library of Saint Justa in Toledo, as one reads in Julian’s note to the first letter. That library is nothing other than a workshop of lies, which the fig-tree Julian constructed. Therefore I still refuse to give these letters my full vote of confidence, so long as legitimate sources are lacking.

Let us now pursue the things that Julian rashly fabricated about Elipandus, by which he himself overturned his own credibility. He says (no. 411) that, in that Council of Toledo—which did not exist for us—it was decided to change the Gothic rite, because the Fathers of the Council of Italy had misunderstood, or rather had falsely attributed to the most holy Fathers Hildefonsus and Julian of Toledo, statements that they had not made concerning the adoption of Christ. In reporting this, the simpleton stumbled. For this disparagement of the learned Hildefonsus and Julian, by whose testimonies Elipandus and his followers were striving to advance their cause, is found not in the letter from the Italian bishops that he mentions, but in another letter from the bishops of Gaul and Germany to the bishops of Spain. Nor did they attribute anything falsely to Hildefonsus and Julian; they merely failed to assign to the testimonies of Hildefonsus and Julian, which Elipandus cited in his own support and which they had not seen, the place they ought properly to have occupied. Caesar Baronius did the same in our own age (*Ad ann. 794*, no. 8), as did others who have piously and prudently labored to wipe from public opinion the stains that Elipandus had cast upon those most holy pontiffs.

That Elipandus therefore repented at this council, solemnly assembled with the Moors observing and consenting, is where the matter sticks for us. I know that the records, or *Life*, of Saint Beatus—said by John Tamayo to have been drawn from the legendary of the Church of Astorga on 19 February, and from which the distinguished compilers of that great work inserted it into the *Acts of the Saints*—mention this Council of Toledo. But it was John Tamayo’s habitual practice, arising from a perverse judgment and detestable audacity, to insert into the genuine acts of the legendaries and breviaries the inventions of the pseudo-chronicles to which he adhered, as though these possessed the same texture and authority as those ecclesiastical records that preserved the ancient traditions of our nation.

Trusting in the security afforded by such rash audacity, Henschenius, in his commentary on this *Life of Beatus*, and likewise John Mabillon, the Benedictine, when discussing the acts of the saints of that order in the first part of the fourth century, accepted these acts, or this *Life*, as a genuine historical work. Led by this prejudice, Henschenius believed that John Mariana had borrowed certain words from this *Life* that he had seen, whereas it is more certain that the compiler of the *Life*, Tamayo, used Mariana’s words.

I believe, however, that all the material bearing the mark of Tamayo’s hand includes the statements about Heterius and Beatus being present at the Council of Frankfurt, as we have already said; the statements made here about a second Council of Toledo, derived, that is, from Luitprandus and Julian; and likewise the claim that Felix was a Gaul by descent, although we ought to believe the testimony of Einhard, to whom we owe greater trust than to Tamayo, and who says that Felix was a Spaniard.

Mabillon, arriving at this point with his customary acuity, saw the difficulty, setting Einhard against the alleged Gallic homeland of this Felix and observing that John Mariana did not dare to assert it—so far is Mariana from having advanced in truth by relying on this *Life*, as escaped Henschenius’s notice. Yet Mabillon unjustly attacked us as though all Spaniards adored these fables, writing: “The Spaniards are indeed amusing: if they have any rogues, they attribute them to the Franks or Gauls; but those whom they regard as more distinguished they claim for themselves, as is evident from many examples in the Spanish Martyrology.”

This writing deserves to hear these words, and sharper ones still. Yet not all Spaniards agree with him; indeed, we are ashamed whenever we take that work into our hands, and we ardently desire that a true *Martyrology of Spain* might be substituted for this work of Tamayo, defiled by countless fictions, in which truth is everywhere interpolated with falsehood, by some man who loves truth and the good name of our nation. We wished to smear these pages with this reproach directed by that most learned and modest Gallic man against us, a reproach elicited from him by our own readiness to believe anything, so that it might serve as a testimony of how necessary it is, and how much it matters to us, that we should not be so ill-spoken of: we must restore our nation to the reputation of its former sincerity and good faith, sparing neither labor nor effort, which every good and learned man ought to devote to overthrowing the monsters of our pseudo-history.

But what an elaborate invention and excavation of treasures—treasures as enviable even to Croesus as those which Hieronymus Romanus de la Higuera once boasted had been sent to him from there—is attached and, as it were, glued by that same Julian of Fulda to this Elipandian repentance and submissive attitude toward King Charles! For the whole structure rests on this foundation: namely, that Elipandus, mindful of his duty at that time, sent Charles numerous records of Spanish men of every kind, including “the Chronicles of Dexter and Maximus; fragments of Braulio, Heleca, Taio, and others,” as he says (no. 414). This is repeated offensively both by Julian himself elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0857D] In the letter to Albert of Furnes prefixed to the *Chronicle*] and by his twin, Luitprandus [Note: [Col. 0858D] In the letter to Tractemundus, to whom he dedicates the *Chronicle*] [Col. 0858D], so that the fabrication and deceit reveal themselves plainly to men who are not entirely dull-witted.

He also says that Elipandus died after having held the episcopate for nearly thirty years—that is what Julian at last taught his admirers (no. 401). In this he does not depart from Luitprandus’s reckoning (*Ad annum 782*).

[Col. 0859]

# LETTERS OF ELIPANDUS

*(From Flórez, Spain Sacred.)*

## FIRST LETTER. TO MIGETIUS THE HERETIC

[Note: [Col. 0859D] Manuscript: “Igetius.”]

[Col. 0859A]

### 1

We once received your letter, cast in the form of a little pamphlet, arising from the horrific tomb of your heart, brought forth from the ash-filled sepulcher of your breast, written not in the voice of one asking questions but with the authority of one giving instruction, so that we might read it again. We saw it, I say, we saw it, and we mocked the foolish and senseless madness of your heart. We saw it and judged the feebleness of your understanding worthy of laughter.

There we perceived that he had spoken through your mouth who said: “I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of his prophets.” There, without doubt, we saw that you are the one of whom the Psalmist says: “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit; he refused to understand, that he might do good. He devised iniquity upon his bed.” And again, concerning such men, the Prophet says elsewhere: “They have taught their tongue to speak lies; they have labored to act wickedly.”

### 2

Nevertheless, before the writings of your madness had been brought to us, before the stench of your words—most foul to us—had blown upon us, when rumor was spreading through the foolish multitude, we believed that some things about you were sound. But after we had seen the dirges of your stupidity, immediately not only we, but every rank of the Catholic faith, recoiled from you and from the whole teaching of your stench, and we shall condemn it to be struck with perpetual anathema.

For it is truly right that those whom the Son of God, by prevenient grace, does not in any way raise from the tombs of heresies should not only never dare to release them, but that his disciples should also plunge them everywhere into the deep sarcophagus of anathema, lest the stench of such words break out again. The disciples of Christ should strike such men with the sword of their mouths, so that they may not only be utterly unable to rise again, but, completely uprooted, may perish altogether—those who do not fear to tear apart the unity of the Catholic faith with poisonous assertions.

Therefore, wishing to show that you and your companions in error are fabricators of lies and adherents of perverse doctrines, and taking the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures as our support, with the Son of God going before us [Note: [Col. 0859D] Manuscript: “the Son.”] in the pillar of cloud by day and in the pillar of fire by night, armed with the zeal of faith, we advance to meet you as a true enemy of Christ, saying: “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan, and may he rebuke you who has chosen Jerusalem.” To you, Migetius, who are surnamed Satan, it is said: “Get behind me.”

It is worthy and just that one who strives to raise the heel of pride against the rule of the Catholic faith should be struck by such a goad, so that he may immediately be punished by this dagger of justice; lest we appear to have merely muttered lightly against the dog, and lest the terrified rage that barks against the holy mystery of the divine Trinity remain unchecked by the authority of the word.

Your sickness is no longer to be treated with the soothing application of wine and oil; your longstanding corruption must be cut away with a sword sharp on both sides. First we strive to batter down the tower of your pride with the battering ram of justice, lest its destructive shadow bring disease upon the faithful. First we endeavor to overthrow the structure of your madness with the stone of reason, lest it attempt to furnish the foolish with a defensive stronghold [Note: [Col. 0860D] Manuscript: “fortification.”].

This is especially because you have seized the office not of one who asks questions but of one who teaches first, although the Lord and Redeemer himself, presenting an example of humility, wished to be found not first teaching in the temple but asking questions. Hence blessed Gregory, instructing those who desire to travel the path of the right way, says:

> “Nothing is presumed to be taught without a teacher, unless it has first been learned through attentive reflection.”

And again elsewhere:

> “Silence’s discipline is, as it were, nourishment for the word; and rightly, through increasing grace, the one who has first kept silence in an orderly manner through humility receives the word of instruction. Hence Solomon says: ‘A time to keep silence, and a time to speak.’ He does not say, ‘A time to speak, and a time to keep silence’; rather, he placed keeping silence first and then added speaking.”

Blessed Ephrem, foreseeing you and those like you, spoke in this way:

> “For the one who comes to be instructed, before being instructed, already wishes to instruct others and to teach before learning. Before being educated, he wishes to promulgate a law; before he knows the order of syllables, he begins to philosophize. Before he submits for the salvation of his soul, he wishes to have subjects; before he obeys the commands of his elders, he seizes the office of one who commands; and before he is trained in the reason and virtue of discernment [Note: [Col. 0860D] Manuscript: ‘reason and the virtue of discernment.’], he usurps the right to instruct and admonish others. Therefore it is fitting that such a man should become a teacher of falsehood, refusing to be a disciple of truth, and should appear as a teacher of error, since he does not fear to assume, with brazen forehead, the authority of one who teaches [Note: [Col. 0860D] Manuscript: ‘the command of one who teaches.’].”

### 3

At the beginning of your most foul note you declare that there are three corporeal persons in the Godhead, saying that the person of the Father is specifically believed to be David, because David himself says of himself: “My heart has uttered a good word.” And again, you believe that this was said of David himself: “You will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption.”

You further assert that the person of the Son of God is the second person in the Trinity, the one assumed from the Virgin, affirming it in the apostolic words: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh.” But as the third person, the Holy Spirit, you identify with the apostle Paul, declaring that the Psalmist says of him: “The spirit of his mouth is all their power,” and that Christ the Son of God says of him: “The Spirit who proceeds from my Father—he will teach you all truth.”

All these things that spirit of error, full of falsehood, spoke falsely through your mouth. For Paul the apostle rightly spoke of you and your companions, saying: “Certain men, having gone astray, have turned to empty talk, wishing to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say nor concerning what they make assertions.”

Blessed Isidore, that outstanding teacher, also speaks of such men in his *Dogmas*:

> “Heretics do not understand the Scriptures with sound sense. Therefore they twist them toward the error of a perverse interpretation; nor do they submit themselves to the meaning of the Scriptures, but perversely drag them toward their own error.”

And again:

> “Heretics defend their lies with immense zeal and, with strenuous effort, discourage people from coming to the unity of the Church.”

Certainly, if what we have put forward is not so, how can the person of God the Father be believed to be David because he says, “My heart has uttered a good word,” when David himself expressly says of himself: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me”? And again: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.” And elsewhere: “I am the one who sinned; I acted wickedly.”

And again, when you assert that David said of himself, “You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption,” if this is so, then he spoke of himself when he said: “They pierced my hands and my feet, and they counted all my bones.” And again: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots.” And again: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

Certainly, if David himself is the person of God the Father because he said, “My heart has uttered a good word,” then he is the Father of the Son of God according to divinity, who said to the Son: “Today I have begotten you.” If David himself is the person of God the Father, then he is the one who said: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” And again: “I am God, and there is no other besides me.”

And if it is as you assert, that the words “You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption” were spoken of David, how, on the contrary, did the apostle Peter say: “David both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day, and his flesh saw corruption”?

### 4

Concerning the person of the Son, you say that it is the second person in the Trinity who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, and not the one who was begotten by the Father. If your madness raves in this way, then the Son of God arose from his mother alone [Note: [Col. 0861D] Manuscript: “origin.”]—which it is impious to say—and was not begotten without beginning by the Father.

Since in the holy Trinity nothing is believed to be corporeal, nothing greater or lesser, how can you assert that that servant-form is the second person in the Trinity, when the Son of God himself, according to the form in which he is less than the Father, testifies in his own words: “The Father is greater than I”? And concerning that form the voice of the Father speaks through the Prophet: “Behold, my servant shall understand, and he shall be exalted and lifted up,” and so forth. And shortly afterward: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before the one who shears it.”

### 5

Concerning the third person, the Holy Spirit, you say that it is Paul, claiming that Scripture speaks of him when it says: “The spirit of his mouth is all their power.” Again, because he himself speaks of himself, saying: “Not from man, nor through man, but through God the Father and through Jesus Christ,” you say that Paul, who is the Holy Spirit, proceeds from the Father and the Son.

If this is to be understood as your madness raves, then Paul himself is the Holy Spirit of whom it is said elsewhere: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.” If Paul is, as you assert, the person of the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, then he is the one who descended in the form of a dove upon the Lord being baptized in the Jordan; and again, the one who appeared in the form of fire over the heads of the disciples. Therefore Paul himself, whom we are commanded to worship and glorify together with the Father and the Son, is also the one of whom the Lord said: “When I depart, the Paraclete will come to you.”

But how can your error be accepted, when the Lord himself says of the Holy Spirit: “The spirit does not have flesh and bones”? Who has ever said that a spirit is corporeal and visible? How can your foolishness be believed, so that the things you assert are thought to have proceeded from Paul, when Scripture says of him: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils”?

How can what you assert be accepted as entirely true, when the Lord himself said to that same Paul: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? You have raged in vain against my name and stoned Stephen, my martyr; I will make you my servant”?

You say that Paul distinguishes within himself the person of the Holy Spirit, although he himself says: “I am the least of all the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.”

How can Paul himself be the person of the Holy Spirit, when, coming with Barnabas to Lycaonia [Note: [Col. 0862D] Manuscript: “Lycaonian.”], and when, out of wonder at the miracle, foolish men called one of them Jupiter and the other Mercury and wished to sacrifice to them as gods, he replied: “Men, what are you doing? We also are mortal human beings like you” [Note: [Col. 0862D] There is a short lacuna in the manuscript here; it does not, however, affect the sense.] … so that they would not sacrifice to them.

If he is the Holy Spirit, why did he endure so much suffering? Why did he finally die by the sword? Therefore—though it is also a crime to say it—the Holy Spirit endured death and the grave.

Recognize, wretched man, how many falsehoods you utter from your belly; recognize, heretic, how many evils you have brought forth from your cancerous mouth. Let that people, made into a mass of perdition and known to have been deceived by consenting to your errors, recognize this; let that people which, forestalled by the mercy of God and refusing to consent to your errors, is seen to have been snatched by the Lord’s right hand from the abyss of this heretical depravity, recognize it.

No one among the heretics is your equal; no one is your companion. The last of all in rank, you are correspondingly filled with the poison [Note: [Col. 0863D] Manuscript: “poisons.”] of all heretics; intoxicated with the deadly filth of all heretics, you are openly recognized as having been sent as Antichrist.

### 6

Tell us, glutted with the filth of all heretics, which of the holy teachers ever taught anyone to believe the Holy Trinity in the way you assert? What council instituted that the distinctions of persons should be held by the holy Catholic Church in the manner in which you distinguish them?

We, on the contrary—or rather all who think rightly and have sound understanding concerning God, according to the traditions of the Fathers, whose understanding is not carnal but spiritual, and whose word is wisdom seasoned with salt—believe that the person of God the Father almighty is the one who is like or equal to no human being [Note: [Col. 0863D] Manuscript: “like no human being”]; the one who surpasses every creature by the power of his majesty; the one who said to the Son: “Today I have begotten you.”

And again: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you”—that is, “I brought you forth from that innermost and ineffable substance of the Godhead.” And again: “My heart has uttered a good word”; concerning this the Prophet says elsewhere: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made.”

And through another prophet: “A word of righteousness shall go forth from my mouth”; concerning this the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.”

And he again says to the Son: “I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth.” Concerning him the Prophet again says: “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, my Lord, whose right hand I have grasped, so that I may subject nations before him and open doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut.”

And he again speaks to Moses, saying: “Behold, I send my angel, who will go before you and guard you on the way, and my name is in him.”

### 7

We believe that the person of the Son is not the one you assert to be equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, the one made from the seed of David according to the flesh in the last age [Note: [Col. 0863D] Here Elipandus wrongly distinguishes the person of the Son.], but the one begotten by God the Father without beginning in time.

Before the assumption of flesh, he spoke through the Prophet: “Before the hills I was in labor; when he had not yet made the earth, when he was preparing the heavens, I was present; when he enclosed the sea with its boundary and imposed a law upon the waters, I was there.”

And again: “Before every creature I proceeded from the mouth of the Most High; before he laid the mountains out upon the plain, I was with him arranging all things; I was the one in whom the Father rejoiced.”

After the assumption of flesh, we believe not in the one you assert according to the flesh, of whom he himself says, “The Father is greater than I,” but in the one of whom he himself says: “I and the Father are one.” And again: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

### 8

We likewise believe that the person of the Holy Spirit is not Paul, who was granted the ability at some point to become good from evil, but the one who, without change in himself, is naturally always good. Concerning him Scripture says: “You gave them your good Spirit, Lord, to instruct them.” And elsewhere: “You sent your Spirit, and they were created, and you will renew the face of the earth.”

And again: “Do not take your Spirit from me.” Another prophet says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me to preach peace to the peoples.”

### 9

Behold the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—spiritual, incorporeal, undivided, unconfused, coessential, consubstantial, coeternal, in one divinity, power, and majesty; without beginning, without end, always abiding.

Concerning these, the Prophet, by repeating the word three times, indicates the Trinity of persons existing in one deity [Note: [Col. 0864D] Manuscript: “existing”], saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth; the heavens and the earth are full of his glory.”

As for Paul, who at the beginning of his life was “Benjamin, a ravening wolf” and at the end became a chosen vessel, he himself testifies to this, as we have already said above, when he says: “Benjamin is a wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils.”

By these words, as blessed Gregory says, the Apostle is designated, descended from the tribe of Benjamin: in the morning he ate the prey because, at the beginning of his career, seizing as many of the faithful as he could, he satisfied his own cruelty; in the evening he divided the spoils because, later becoming faithful, he gave the faithful the sacred [Col. 0864C] Scriptures to be expounded [Note: [Col. 0864D] Manuscript: “to be explained.”].

### 10

As for your claim concerning priests—why do they declare themselves sinners if they are truly holy? Or, if they confess that they are sinners, why do they presume to approach the ministry, since the Lord himself says: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy”?

If we were to speak in such a way, each of us would be a liar like you. We too could make such claims—God forbid—if that spirit of error which is within you had instructed our inward parts. But because the one who said, “When you have done everything that has been commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants,’” is with us, we truthfully cry out with the Prophet: “We have all become unclean; all our righteousness is like a woman’s menstrual cloth.”

And again: “We have sinned and acted wickedly; departing from you, we have offended in everything.” And again with the Apostle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity.”

With what audacity do you declare yourself holy, when Scripture says: “Who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will dare to say that he is clean from sin?” And again: “No one is clean from defilement—not even one—even if his life upon the earth should last but a single day.”

For who among human beings is without complaint against him? Or who can be righteous who is born of a woman? If even the heavens are not clean in the sight of the Lord, how much more detestable and unclean is a human being?

And again the holy Fathers say in their *Dogmas*: “No holy or righteous person is without sin; yet for this reason he does not cease to be righteous or holy, since he holds fast to holiness in his intention. We acquire holiness not through the powers of nature, but through the assistance of our purpose and by grace. Therefore all the saints truthfully declare themselves sinners, because in truth they have something to lament—if not the accusation of conscience, then at least the instability and changeability of the human condition.”

Blessed Fulgentius likewise gives this instruction to Peter as he was traveling to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0865D] Manuscript: “of Jerusalem.”]:

> “Hold this most firmly, and do not doubt in any way that no one here can live without sin—not even righteous and holy persons, except for baptized infants—and that every person must continually cleanse his sins by almsgiving until the end of his present life, and humbly and sincerely ask God for forgiveness” [Note: [Col. 0865D] Something such as “it is necessary” or “it is fitting” is missing.].

Blessed John Chrysostom likewise confesses:

> “None of us is free from sin, just as no one among the dead can be free. To say something further: we too, who seem to hold the highest rank in the service of the Churches and are honored in sacred seats—we ourselves, I say, the chief priests, teachers of the peoples, and instructors, are surrounded by various troops of errors and are frequently subjected to vices. Sometimes we are even stained by the corruption of luxury. Yet we look to the mercy of the compassionate Lord, whose goodness we do not doubt in the least. For such is his generosity toward human beings that where sin abounded, there grace abounded still more.”

You too, who boast of holiness and say that you are free from sin, make it plainly understood that if you had been physically present at that time when the Lord and Redeemer, writing with his finger on the ground, said to the Jews concerning the woman caught in adultery, “If any one of you is without sin, let him cast a stone at her,” you yourself might first have incurred the crime of homicide, since you now say that you are a stranger to sin.

To whom, then, shall we say that you are like, except to the one who said: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High”? To whom are you like except that Pharisee who said to himself: “Lord, I am not like the rest of men—robbers, adulterers, and so forth”?

Why do you not remember, unhappy man, what blessed Gregory says about such people: “A man becomes like the apostate angel when he disdains to be like another human being”?

### 11

As for your attempt to argue about foods and the excrement of the belly, against the Lord’s teaching that “nothing entering the mouth defiles,” except human flesh [Note: [Col. 0865D] Manuscript: “except the flesh of a human being”], “but it is what comes out of the mouth that defiles a person”: you, on the contrary, assert from the bloody understanding of your heart that the food of unbelievers pollutes the minds of the faithful.

Yet the Apostle also says: “To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure.” And because you refuse to eat with sinners, considering yourself holier than the Lord and Redeemer and raising yourself up in the spirit of arrogance as though already without the stain of sin, although the Son of God himself—heavenly medicine and life of the dead—is often read to have eaten and drunk with tax collectors and sinners.

Nevertheless, not all were converted from the error of their way, as blessed Augustine testifies when he says:

> “Behold, everyone marveled, yet not everyone was converted. Everyone was filled with wonder at the Lord’s words, yet not everyone possessed the fullness of faith in his deeds.”

For the Lord himself also says in the Gospel concerning himself: “John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Behold, a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.’”

But to remove every remaining doubt from the faithful, the Apostle says elsewhere: “If one of the unbelievers invites you and you wish to go, eat everything that is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience.”

For among Christians it is not the kind of food that is condemned but excess; nor from all things [Note: [Col. 0866D] Something is missing between these words; the Latin is defective]—[lacuna]; but the soul ought to abstain, because, in the Apostle’s words, “the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.” For “food is for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both it and them.”

Blessed Jerome speaks in this way in his *Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*:

> “For the foods that God created, whether taken unknowingly or simply, cannot make a person common or unclean.”

Blessed Gregory likewise confirms this in his *Exposition of Ezekiel*:

> “Abstinence is indeed a great virtue; but if someone abstains from food in such a way that he judges others on account of their food, and condemns for the faithful the very foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving, what has the virtue of abstinence become for him except a snare of guilt?”

12. But when you assert that the power of God exists only in Rome, [Note: [Col. 0866D] Manuscript: “in which.”] where Christ dwells, you contradict the oracle of the Prophet, who says: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth.” You also assert that Rome alone is the catholic Church, where all the saints are, without stain or wrinkle; and that of it alone it is said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church”; and that into it “nothing defiled, nor anyone who practices abomination and falsehood, shall enter”; and that it is itself the new Jerusalem which John saw descending from heaven. That mad spirit, and the understanding produced by your folly, has taught you to understand all these things in this way. We, however, believe, on the contrary, that the Lord did not say only of Rome to Peter, “You are Peter”—that is, the firmness of faith—“and upon this rock I will build my Church,” [Note: [Col. 0867D] See no. 7.] but of the universal catholic Church spread throughout the whole world in peace. Concerning it the Lord himself bears witness, saying: “They will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”

As for your assertion that it is the Church without stain or wrinkle, and that nothing defiled or practicing abomination and falsehood will enter it: if this is so, why was Liberius, the pontiff of that same Church, condemned among the heretics? [Note: [Col. 0867D] See the same, no. 7.] Why does blessed Gregory testify that so many wicked men were in Rome? But because in every Church the wicked dwell with the good, and the reprobate with the elect, the Lord himself bears witness, saying: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals.” For no scandal can be found in that heavenly kingdom where supreme peace exists; rather, this was said of the present Church, where, as we have already said, just as in Noah’s ark, not only human beings but also beasts are known to have been present. Thus there is no doubt that within the bosom of Mother Church the wicked dwell with the good, until at the end of the age the wheat is gathered into the Lord’s barn, while the tares are burned in bundles with unquenchable fire.

13. But when you say that Rome itself is the new Jerusalem descending from heaven, whom should one believe— you or the apostle Peter? For Peter calls it Babylon, writing to certain people: “The Church which is in Babylon greets you.” Therefore, by no means should one believe that the stones of that city, or its walls, descended from heaven, as your delirious madness supposes. But if perhaps you still think that this was said of the saints, neither should that interpretation be accepted, because the saints ascend rather than descend. Rather, since Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” what else is it for the vision of peace to have newly descended, in a manner of speaking, from heaven, except the open knowledge of the faith of the Holy Trinity among all the nations predestined to life—enlightening the souls of believers by the sacrament of its holy faith and purifying them by the bath of regeneration?

## EPISTLE II. TO ABBOT FIDELIS

[Col. 0867D] (See below, the epistle of Heterius and Beatus against Elipandus, book I.)

## EPISTLE III. TO CHARLEMAGNE

To the illustrious and glorious lord, ruler of diverse nations, [the letter is addressed] in the Lord God the Father, and in the Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, and in the Holy Spirit, eternal salvation. Amen.

### 1

To glorify, with God’s help, that famous and solemn name—like an ethereal radiance before all the kings of the earth, whose reputation, like a nectarous fragrance and the precious scent of true nard, [Col. 0868A] spreads its perfume through almost the whole world—rises sweetly from our heart, from the secret place of our breast. We bow down and, prostrate upon the ground, offer prayers to the eternal King, asking that your well-being, protected by the divine right hand for the salvation of the entire catholic Church, may be preserved for a long age.

### 2

After these matters had been stated, it came to the attention of your servants that a written work of the foul-smelling Beatus of Antiphrasius had polluted with its poison the hearts of certain priests who made light of the matter. In it, the impious presbyter and false prophet asserts that the Son of God—eternally the only-begotten and without adoption—did not, at the end of time, for the salvation and redemption of the human race, assume from the Virgin’s womb a full and perfect human being, similar, kindred, and conformed to the human race in everything except the contagion of sin, [Note: [Col. 0867D] Manuscript: “contagion.”] and co-heir according to the faith of the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, evangelists, [Col. 0868B] and teachers, concerning whom the Lord said: “You are the light of the world, and you are the salt of the earth”; and, “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me.” [A lacuna in the source.] He asserts that the Son of God, in the form of a servant, with his deity emptied, in no way assumed adoption of flesh from the Virgin’s womb.

Against his madness, we, unworthy and insignificant as we are, according to the poverty of our understanding, have sent this letter to the priests subject to your authority, so that they may read it again, discuss it, and present it to your sacred eyes. We beg you by him who for you stretched innocent hands upon the cross, shed precious blood for you, endured death and the grave for you, descended into hell to liberate the elect for you, and, rising again for you, showed you the way of returning to heaven—namely, to the heavenly homeland—so that you yourself may return as arbiter and decide between Bishop Felix, whom we know to have been from his earliest years a most devoted defender of our party in the service of God, and those who defend the sacrilegious Beatus of Antiphrasius, fattened on the disgrace of the flesh. Decide with chaste and salutary judgment, and give your sentence with equal weight, without the oil of flattery. Thus may the Lord, the Son of God, subject the necks of barbarous nations and of all the proud who oppose you to the command of your power, [Note: [Col. 0868D] Manuscript: “to your authority.”] crush their teeth more severely, and reduce to dust the glory of those who contradict you.

Indeed, there were still certain necessary matters which, with God as your protector, we would have explained to your exalted rank by the running pen; but, hindered by the pressure of time, we have placed in the mouth of the bearer of this letter what we were unable to explain in words, so that he might make it known to you. Again, crushed by excessive grief, we recall to your mind a saying of the Lord that cannot be unknown to you, for he says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” And also that saying by which he freed the woman caught in adultery from the stones of the Jews and warned her not to repeat her offense. [Note: [Col. 0868D] Manuscript: “lapse.”]

### 3

Therefore, as though prostrate before your eyes, we ask with tears that you restore your servant Felix to his proper honor and restore the shepherd to the flock scattered by ravenous wolves. May Almighty God keep far from you the fate of the emperor Constantine, who, although he had been a worshiper of idolatry, was made a Christian through blessed Sylvester; afterward, through the serpent—his sister—he rejected the judgment of the three hundred and eighteen saints, was converted to the Arian doctrine, and, plunged into hell in a lamentable fall, ended his life. [Note: [Col. 0869D] See no. 4.] Concerning him blessed Isidore says: “Alas, alas! He made good use of his beginning, but had an evil end!”

Accordingly, we likewise ask that you erase from your kingdom the doctrine of the most foul Beatus of Antiphrasius, who denies that the Son of God assumed from the Virgin true flesh like ours, except for sin, [Note: [Col. 0869D] Manuscript: “sin.”] and command the people subject to you to hold the catholic faith, expressed in clear language.

[Col. 0869B] ### 4

But this too must be feared, most pious lord and our lord in Spain, [Note: [Col. 0869D] Manuscript: “little servant”; understand: the king’s rule in the regions of Spain.] lest perhaps, where—under God’s protection—no visible power of the pagans has rightly entered through your efforts, the detestable calamity of the ancient enemy should, God forbid, rule invisibly. Through the often-mentioned Beatus of Antiphrasius, devoted to the lust of the flesh, it may acquire the destruction of many souls for itself and lead them with it to be consumed in the fire of eternal burning in hell.

Let that secret chamber of your sacred breast reflect upon and ruminate what is truly pleasing to God, what makes the incense of your works fragrant in his sight, and what causes the holocaust of good odor to blaze like incense. [Note: [Col. 0869D] Manuscript: “let your charity remember.”] Let your Charity also remember that Peter, the chief of the apostles, when he ordered circumcision to be practiced among the nations, is known to have been openly, not secretly, rebuked by the younger Paul, who said: “If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” The aforementioned chief of the apostles, agreeing with reason and a friend of truth, did not disregard Paul’s sentence but immediately consented to it, remembering what is written: “If something is revealed to the younger, let the elder be silent”; and, “He is nearest to God who knows how to be silent with reason.”

For Almighty God sometimes changes his judgment, but never his counsel, as happened in the case of Hezekiah. A learned person will understand why I have said this. And this too: “Do not despise the counsel of many for the sake of one.” That is, do not alone reject the judgments of so many venerable Fathers concerning the adoption of Christ’s flesh. For it is said that you convince many by the terror of your power, not by justice. [Note: [Col. 0869D] Manuscript: “you convict by reviling.”]

May it grieve your piety that the same foul Beatus, after his conversion, boasts that he has returned again and again to the bed of a harlot, and writes throughout all regions that the glorious prince was converted from error and confirmed in the catholic faith through his horrible teaching. An unprofitable opinion has also been spread among the nations—something which is impious to believe—that you have denied Christ to be the Son of God the Father in the manner of the pagans.

Having rejected these things, we ask that your reply, secretly sent back to us, enlighten us and gladden us, and that the prayer of your servants exalt the eminence of your rule. Amen.

## EPISTLE IV. TO ALBINUS

[Col. 0870A]

### 1

To the most reverend brother Albinus, a deacon not a minister of Christ but a disciple of the most foul Antiphrasius Beatus, who arose in the time of the glorious prince in the region of Austria, [Note: [Col. 0870D] Austria was said to be the eastern part of Francia;] a new Arius, contrary to the teachings of the venerable holy Fathers Ambrose, Augustine, Isidore, and Jerome: eternal salvation from the Lord if he turns back from the way of his error, and eternal damnation if he refuses.

We received your letter, deviating from the path of right faith, horrible in its sulfurous brilliance, and written in superstitious language, at the end of July, to be read again. [Note: [Col. 0870D] Printed edition: “while rereading.”] We saw it—yes, we saw it—because that Spirit who, after the Lord’s ascension, descended upon the heads of the disciples [Note: [Col. 0870D] “descended” is missing in the source.] so that they might speak of the mighty works of God did not speak through you. Rather, it was the spirit who said: “I will be a lying spirit, like the spirit of his prophets.”

Nevertheless, may the Son of God himself, who removes the drops of rain and pours down showers like torrents—who calls the strong to their reward and strengthens the weak, in their place, for the contests; who rewards the former by receiving them and supplies the latter with strength for their labors, by which they may endure—place in my mouth a word of truth, a well-sounding word, and soothe the ear of the catholic Church, established in the name of Christ, with an answer to my hunger.

### 2

When you assert that the Son of God, according to the form of a servant, received no adoption of flesh from the glorious Virgin of God, you do not pursue the truth but show yourself full of falsehood, just as your teacher, Antiphrasius Beatus, disciple of Antichrist, foul with the uncleanness of the flesh, excluded from the altar of God, a pseudo-Christ and pseudo-prophet.

Concerning him the distinguished teacher, blessed Gregory, says: “He has lost the authority to teach whose speech is destroyed by his conduct.” But you, dearest brother, beware lest—God forbid—this be written of you: “From the root of the serpent a regulus (basilisk) has come forth, and from the hole of the asp a basilisk has come forth”—that is, Albinus, most hideous in his blackness.

Beware lest perhaps you not be a companion of the Levite Stephen, who says that he sees the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God the Father, but rather of Nicolas, whose deeds the same Son of God testifies that he hates. And again, beware lest you be unlike the Levite Vincent but like Datianus, who consecrated that same Levite to martyrdom.

### 3

And again, beware lest you be like Rufinus, who, through savage actions, became a worshiper of idolatry against blessed Felix the martyr, just as you persecute another Felix, the confessor, whom we know to have been outstanding in charity from his earliest years, chaste and adorned with good character, and whom you persecute while he lies hidden in mountains, caves, and the hollows of the earth.

Beware lest you be the one of whom the Prophet says: “The fool speaks foolishly, and his heart understands vanity.” And again: “They have taught their tongue to speak falsehood; they labored to act wickedly.” And the Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God.” The Psalmist likewise says: “Destroy the enemy and the defender.” You are recognized as both enemy and defender, because, while you appear to vindicate the deity of the Son of God, begotten from the Father before the ages, you seem to deny his humanity, assumed from the Virgin’s womb at the end of time, forgetting the judgment of the Lord, who says to his hesitating disciples: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe all that is written in the Law and the Prophets! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” And the Apostle says: “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you, so that you do not obey the truth?”

### 4

When you say in your writing that you alone, together with a few others, hold the belief retained by all Spain, remember that the Lord said: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter by it. How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it.”

Remember that the Lord said that Lazarus, a poor man covered with sores, lay at the gate of a rich man, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him anything; but dogs came and licked his sores. It happened that both died on the same day. Lazarus was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. But the rich man was buried in hell, seeking a drop from Lazarus’ finger—he who had not given him even a crumb.

### 5

Beware lest you be one of those known to possess twenty thousand servants, and therefore be puffed up by your riches and by your wisdom, which does not descend from above but is earthly, natural, and demonic.

Remember that the Lord said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them,” as is the case with Felix the confessor and his companions. [Col. 0871C] Remember what Scripture says: “Has not God chosen the poor in the world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom?” Remember what the Psalmist says: “The rich have become needy and hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.” And again: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.” And again: “He stores up treasure and does not know why he gathers it.”

I also thought this should be joined to the present matter: God the Father spoke to his servant David, saying: “When you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up from your loins one who will sit upon the throne of Israel. I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me.” And again: “The root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples, him the nations will entreat, and his tomb will be glorious.”

Behold, the Son of God, according to the form of a servant which he assumed from the Virgin, in which he is less than the Father, is God’s adoptive firstborn among many brothers according to the Apostle—not by birth (*genere*), but by adoption. Why should he not be called adoptive, since he is wholly in our condition just as he is wholly in his own, except for sin? Behold Joachim, whose daughter is recognized as the glorious Virgin Mary of God, is believed to be adoptive. Why, then, should the Lord Jesus Christ, generated from her, not be called adoptive?

### 6

Remember that the Lord said to his disciples: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me.” Concerning these holy teachers, some of whose testimonies we have cited, the Prophet says: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples.”

With these things stated, if you do not accept the testimony of so many venerable holy Fathers, give me the testimony of blessed Athanasius, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Isidore that there was no adoption of flesh and no true humanity in the Son of God, and I will agree with your errors.

For just as your foul and horrible teacher has stained Libana, so you have stained the kingdom of kingdoms, Austria. But stop uselessly stretching out lips that bark against God’s mystery. Beware lest—God forbid—you be that Behemoth whose mountains bring forth grasses for food, and with whom you sleep in the secrecy of the reed, in watery places.

Beware lest you be another Arius, who, through Arius and a woman, made the emperor Constantine—made a Christian through blessed Sylvester—a heretic. Concerning him blessed Isidore says: “Alas, alas! A good beginning, an evil end.” His depravity stained not only Gothia but also Libya, and the East and West, with its poison, down to the time of King Reccared of blessed memory.

Beware lest you be another Nebuzaradan, chief of the cooks, who destroyed the walls of Jerusalem. Beware lest you do to the glorious prince Charles what Arius did to Constantine, and let him mourn himself throughout the ages of ages.

### 7

There were many other things to be written to you, but, afflicted by the oppression of the people, we cannot write back to you about everything. Yet if you refuse to hear Moses, you will hear Pharaoh.

Moses himself said: “The Lord God will raise up a Prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as you hear me.” Behold, Moses, the adoptive son of God, says that this one is like him in flesh, not in origin, and by adoption. Yet you deny that the Son of God, of the stock of Abraham and Jesse, assumed flesh so as to be an adoptive son; and that the glorious Virgin of God, born from Joachim, was an adoptive daughter begotten from an adoptive son.

For I heard that impious presbyter, from the doctrine of the impious Beatus, saying with my own ears: “Christ Jesus, assuming flesh in his mother’s womb, did not draw it from his mother’s womb but made new flesh for himself.”

### 8

Here begin the testimonies of the venerable holy Fathers concerning adoption in the Son of God according to his humanity, and not according to his divinity.

These are the ones concerning whom the Lord Jesus Christ spoke, saying: “You are the light of the world, and you are the salt of the earth. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound, and whatever you loose will be loosed.”

Blessed Ambrose says in his *Dogmas*: “According to our usage, he is an adoptive Son and a true Son.”

Blessed Jerome likewise says: “This Son of Man is deemed worthy, through the Son of God, to be in the Son of God; adoption is not separated from nature, but nature is joined with adoption.”

Again, in his exposition of the Apocalypse: “The white gem is adoption into the Son of God.”

Blessed Augustine also says that according to his divinity the Son of God, begotten from the Father before the ages, is not a son by adoption but by origin, nor by grace but by nature; whereas according to his humanity he is called an adopted man, whose glory he sought who was born from him as his only one.

Blessed Pope Leo likewise says in his *Dogmas*: “Wholly in his own things, wholly in ours; according to his divinity he shone with miracles, and according to the humanity of the flesh he was subjected to insults.”

Behold, if he is wholly in his own things, without doubt he is also wholly in ours, except for the sin he did not commit. The Lord and Redeemer himself says according to his divinity: “I and the Father are one”; according to his humanity: “The Father is greater than I.”

### 9

Blessed Isidore, radiance of the Church, star of the West, teacher of Spain, says in the book of the *Etymologies*:

“Only-begotten” is called according to the excellence of his divinity, because he is without brothers. “Firstborn,” however, is according to his assumption of humanity, in which, through the adoption of grace, he deigned to have brothers among whom he would be firstborn.

And after some further discussion he says:

“After the fullness of time came for our salvation, he took the form of a servant and became the Son of Man. From that point, some things concerning him in Scripture follow according to the form of God, and some according to the form of a servant. For example, two statements are recalled, so that each may be referred to its proper category.

According to the form of God he said of himself, ‘I and the Father are one’; according to the form of a servant, ‘The Father is greater than I.’ But people who understand poorly what is said of what wish to transfer to the form of God those things that were said because of the form of a servant. Conversely, they wish those things that were said to distinguish the persons from one another to be names of nature and substance, and thus they create error in the faith.

Human nature was joined to the Son of God in such a way that from two substances there came to be one person. For only a human being endured the cross, but because of the unity of the person, God is also said to have endured it. Hence it is written: ‘If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.’

Therefore we confess that the Son of God was crucified, not through the power of divinity but through the weakness of humanity; not through the permanence of his own nature but through our assumption. For the Prophet also says: ‘Have mercy, Lord, on your people, over whom your name has been invoked, and on Israel, whom you have made equal to your firstborn.’

This equality is not in divinity but solely in humanity and in the adoption of flesh which he received from the Virgin. He, the one and the same God and man in two natures and one person, with his divinity preserved, endured the destruction of death.”

### 10

He himself says according to his deity: “I have the power to lay down my life, and I have the power to take it up again.” According to his humanity he says: “My Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.”

He himself, God the Son of God, says according to his humanity: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” And: “Let this cup pass from me, not as I will but as you will.”

Concerning this Son of God, the voice of the Father came down from heaven upon the disciples, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.” Again, concerning him the voice of the Father says: “Behold, my servant will understand,” and so forth. And again: “Behold my servant; I will receive him, my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased. I have given my Spirit upon him”—that Spirit, namely, full of sevenfold grace, of whom the Prophet says: “The spirit of wisdom and strength, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety.” And: “The spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him.”

Behold, God the Father is pleased with the Son, is pleased with the servant; could he be displeased with the adopted one?

Of this Son of God the Psalmist says: “He ascended on high; he led captivity captive.” Behold, he is said to be a captive; why, then, should he not be called adoptive according to the flesh?

To this Son of God the voice of the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth. You will rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you will break them.”

And concerning him the voice of the Father says: “Behold, I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth.” And again: “Behold, I will walk before you, and I will make the mountains level; I will break the iron bolts and give you hidden treasures, so that you may know that I am the Lord your God.”

Behold to whom the Father says, “I am your God”: not to him—that is, the Word—who was begotten from the Father before the ages, but to him who at the end of time became man from the Virgin Mary. Concerning him the Apostle says: “Born of a woman, born under the law, so that he might redeem those who were under the law.”

He himself, God the Son of God, says according to his divinity, in which he and the Father are one: “I will not give my glory to another.” Asking and giving are not equal: giving belongs to the master, asking to the servant.

Concerning him blessed Isidore says: “In the form of a servant, a servant; in the form of the Lord, the Lord of the servant.”

The Apostle also says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He humbled himself to death, even death on a cross.”

Concerning him the Gospel says: “Son of David, have mercy on me.” And again: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father.”

Behold, if according to his humanity he is the son of David, without doubt he is believed to be adoptive and a servant, descended from an adoptive one and a servant of God the Father, the Son himself, and the Holy Spirit, according to his humanity.

We call him adoptive only in the form of human servitude, not in the glory or substance of the divine nature.

“He is nearest to God who knows how to be silent with reason.”

But you, brother Albinus, beware lest you resemble those Levites whom the Old Testament recalls, saying: “They offered strange fire and perished, struck down by divine vengeance.”

Just so, you introduce a demonic doctrine, that of the arisen Antiphrasius Beatus—the reading *desuem* is uncertain. Your words appear outwardly honey-sweet but inwardly are more bitter than wormwood and gall. You justify works and condemn belief. May your myrrhed oil (*oleum murcatum*) not make our head fat.

### 11

Again, the testimonies of the venerable holy Fathers serving Toledo, published in the prayers of the Masses, say the following.

In the Mass of the Lord’s Supper:

“He who, through the passion of the adoptive man, while he did not spare his own body, finally—that is, again—did not spare ours.”

Likewise, in the Mass for the Tuesday of Easter:

“Look, Lord, upon the multitude of your faithful, whom through the grace of adoption you have deigned to make co-heirs with your Son.”

Likewise, in the Mass for the Thursday of Easter:

“The gift came first in adoption, but judgment still remains in conduct.”

Again, in the same Mass:

“It is worthy and just, salutary and fitting for us to give thanks, offer praises, understand your gifts, and bring vows to you, almighty Father, and to Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, who, through the passion of the adoptive man, as though he had offered certain spoils in the acquisition of the present people, presented a triumph to your piety, although he had not gone forth from heaven.”

Again, in the Mass of the Lord’s Ascension:

“Today our Savior, through the adoption of flesh, reclaimed the seat of divinity; today he brought to the Father his man, whom he offered to suffering, exalting in the heavens him whom he had humbled in hell; he who had seen burial now destined to see glory.”

Again, in the Mass of Saint Speratus:

“Only-begotten of the unbegotten Father, Son of God, coeternal and consubstantial with the Holy Spirit, who, seeking the lowest places of this world from the height of your heavenly throne, did not shrink from taking the garment of flesh of the adoptive man, and, for the liberation of the faithful, did not disdain, in the form of a servant, with your divinity preserved, to be hung upon the balance of the cross and to endure the destruction of death.”

Again, in the Mass for the dead:

“Lord Jesus Christ, who are the true life of believers, we offer this sacrifice to you for the faithful departed, beseeching you to deign to enroll among the blessed those cleansed in the fountain of regeneration and freed from the temptations of the world, and to command that those whom you made participants in adoption be made sharers in your inheritance.”

For we also sing this at the Easter vigil, as blessed Isidore says:

“He put on flesh but did not put off majesty; seeking our substance but not abandoning his own.”

### 12

Epistle of Leo to Leo Augustus: that in the one person of the Lord Jesus Christ the twofold nature of divinity and humanity must be affirmed.

Therefore, whoever is so blinded and alienated from the light of truth that they deny the truth of human flesh in the Word of God from the time of the incarnation, let them show in what respect they claim the Christian name for themselves and how they agree with the Gospel of truth—if, at the birth of the blessed Virgin, either flesh arose without divinity or divinity without flesh.

For just as it cannot be denied, as the evangelist declares, that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” so it cannot be denied, as the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims, that “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

But what reconciliation could there be by which God might again be made propitious toward the human race, unless the mediator between God and human beings, the cause of all things, assumed flesh? And by what means could he fulfill the truth of mediation unless he who in the form of God is equal to the Father also, in the form of a servant, became a participant in our condition?

This was so that the bond of death, contracted through the transgression of one, might be broken by the death of one who alone owed nothing to death. For the shedding of Christ’s blood on behalf of servants was so rich in price that, if the whole community of captives believed in its Redeemer, no bonds of the devil would remain, since, as the Apostle says, “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.” And when those born under the sentence of sin received the power to be reborn for righteousness, the gift of freedom became stronger than the corresponding debt of servitude.

What hope, then, do those retain for themselves in the protection of this sacrament who deny the reality of a human body in our Savior? Let them say by what sacrifice they were reconciled; let them say by what blood they were redeemed, since the Apostle also says: “He gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant odor.”

Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true and eternal High Priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh? Although the death of many saints was precious in the sight of the Lord, the killing of no innocent person was the redemption of the world.

The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. The courage of the faithful provides examples of patience, not gifts of righteousness. For each person’s death was singular, and no one supplied the end of another’s debt. Among all human beings, only our Lord Jesus Christ was the true spotless Lamb, in whom all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised.

Concerning them he himself said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.” For true faith, which justifies the ungodly and creates the righteous, having drawn them into participation in his humanity, obtains salvation in him. In him alone a human being finds himself innocent, possessing through God’s grace the freedom to glory in God’s power.

He who contended against the enemy of the human race in the lowliness of our flesh grants his victory to those in whose body he triumphed.

### 13.

Although, therefore, in our one Lord Jesus Christ, true God and the Son of Man, there is one person of the Word and the flesh, which possesses inseparably and indivisibly all actions, the qualities of those works must nevertheless be understood. With the contemplation of sincere faith, we must discern to what the lowliness of the flesh is raised and toward what the loftiness of the divinity inclines: what the flesh does not do without the Word, and what the Word does not accomplish without the flesh.

For without the power of the Word, the virgin would neither conceive nor give birth; and without the reality of the flesh, infancy wrapped in swaddling clothes would not lie there. Without the power of the Word, the Magi would not adore the child revealed by the star as its guide [Col. 0876C]; and without the reality of the flesh, the child would not be ordered to be taken into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution. Without the power of the Word, the voice of the Father sent from heaven would not say, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” Without the reality of the flesh, John would not proclaim, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world.” Without the power of the Word, the restoration of the weak and the giving of life to the dead would not occur; and without the reality of the flesh, food would not be necessary for the fasting person, nor sleep for the weary.

Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not declare himself equal to the Father; and without the reality of the flesh, that same one would not say that the Father is greater than he. Catholic faith accepts and defends both, believing, according to the confession of blessed Peter the apostle, that the one Christ, Son of the living God, is both human and Word [Col. 0876D].

Although, therefore, from that beginning when the Word became flesh in the Virgin’s womb, there was never any division between the two forms, and throughout all bodily growth the actions of the whole period belonged to one person, nevertheless we do not confuse those very things which were done inseparably by any commixture. Rather, from the character of these things we discern which belongs to which form.

Let those hypocrites, then, who refuse to receive the light of truth with blind minds say: in what form was Christ, the Lord of majesty, fastened to the wood of the cross? Who lay in the tomb? And when the stone of the monument had been rolled away, what flesh rose on the third day? In what form, after his resurrection, did he rebuke certain unbelieving disciples and confound the hesitation of those who doubted when he said, “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have”? And to the apostle Thomas: “Put your hand into my side, and see my hands and feet; and do not be unbelieving, but faithful.”

With how great a manifestation of his body was he already destroying the lies of the heretics, and, once the Church of Christ had seen these things and was to be instructed in doctrine, could it doubt that it ought to believe what the apostles had received for preaching?

But if heretical obstinacy does not abandon its darkness in so great a light of truth, let them show from where they promise themselves hope of eternal life, which cannot be reached except through the Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. As blessed Peter the apostle says: “There is no other name given among human beings under heaven by which we must be saved” [Col. 0877B]. Nor is there redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him who gave himself as a ransom for human beings.

And as blessed Paul the apostle proclaims: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

### 14.

Since, then, the Lord Jesus Christ is one, and in him there is wholly one and the same person of true divinity and true humanity, nevertheless the exaltation by which, as the teacher of the nations says, God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name is understood to belong to that form which was to be enriched by such an increase of glorification.

For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father, and between the Begetter and the Only-Begotten there was no distinction in essence and no difference in majesty; nor, through the ministry of the incarnation, had anything been taken away from the Word that needed to be restored by the gift of God the Father.

The form of a servant, however, through which the impassible divinity fulfilled the mystery of great piety, is human lowliness [Col. 0877D]. This was raised into the glory of divine power and, from the very conception in the Virgin, was joined to divinity and unity in such a great oneness that neither divine things were done without the human being, nor human things without God.

Therefore, just as the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, so, because he is eternally equal to God, he is said to have been exalted. For, while the unity of the person remains inseparable, one and the same person is wholly the Son of Man because of the flesh and wholly the Son of God because of the one divinity he shares with the Father.

Whatever Jesus received in the body, he received according to his humanity, which had no one to bestow it upon him. Everything the Father has, the Son also has; and what he received from the Father in the form of a servant, he himself also bestowed in the form of God. According to the form of God, he and the Father are one; but according to the form of a servant, he did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him.

According to the form of God, just as the Father has life in himself, so according to the form of a servant his soul is sorrowful unto death. The same person, as the Apostle proclaims, is both rich and poor. Rich, because, as the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Poor, however, because for our sake the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

What is his emptying, and what is his poverty, except the taking of the form of a servant, through which, by the majesty of the Word, the dispensation of human redemption was fulfilled?
