For the original bonds of our captivity could not be loosed unless there existed a human being of our race and nature who was not held by the sentence of sin and who, by his immaculate blood, would erase the deadly bond, as had been divinely ordained from the beginning.

Thus, when the fullness of the predetermined time had arrived, it came to pass that the promise, signified in many ways, reached its long-awaited fulfillment; and what had always been announced through continuous testimonies could not remain uncertain.

### 15.

The impiety of the heretics reveals that they are engaged in great sacrilege when, under the pretext of honoring divinity, they deny the reality of human flesh in Christ and suppose it pious to believe that in our Savior that which saves is not true.

Since, according to the promise extending through all ages, the world has been reconciled in Christ, if the Word had not deigned to become flesh, no flesh could have been saved. For the whole mystery of the Christian faith is disfigured by a great darkness, as the heretics wish, if the light of truth is thought to have been concealed beneath the falsehood of a phantom.

Therefore no Christian should be ashamed of the reality of our body in Christ. All the apostles, the disciples of the apostles, and all the distinguished teachers of the Churches who deserved to attain the crown of martyrdom or the glory of confession have shone in the light of this faith, proclaiming everywhere with harmonious judgments that in the Lord Jesus Christ one person of divinity and flesh must be confessed.

By what resemblance of reasoning, and by what portion of the divine books, does heretical impiety suppose itself assisted when it denies the reality of Christ’s body? The law did not cease to testify to this, the prophet did not cease to foretell it, the Gospels did not cease to teach it, nor did Christ himself cease to display it.

Let them search through the entire sequence of the Scriptures for where they may flee from their darkness, not for where they may obscure the true light. Throughout all ages they will find the truth shining so brilliantly that they will see that this great and wondrous mystery was believed from the beginning and completed at the end. Since no part of the sacred writings is silent about it, it is enough that certain harmonious signs of the truth have been made evident, by which the diligence of faith may be led into the most radiant breadth and, by the clear light of understanding, may perceive that Christians should not be ashamed but should glory with the greatest steadfastness in the Son of God, who unceasingly professes himself the Son of Man and a human being [Col. 0879A].

### 16.

So that your Piety may know that we agree with the preaching of the venerable Fathers, I thought that some statements concerning the error should be appended to this discourse. When you have reviewed them, you will find that we preach nothing other than what the holy Fathers taught us throughout the whole world and that we differ from them in no respect except from the impious heretics.

I also thought that the following should be inserted into this work, as Scripture says: “The heavens will reveal his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him.” Who are these heavens except those who will come to judgment with Christ? Among them are Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and the others whom you, Albinus, reject and judge to be heretics. Of them the Psalmist says: “The heavens declare the glory of God.”

Likewise blessed Augustine, in his letter addressed to Evodius, where he discussed the Trinity and the Dove, or the adoption of the Son of God, says after the foregoing:

“Just as the Father was in the voice that sounded, ‘You are my Son,’ and the Son in the adopted human being whom he assumed from the Virgin, and the Holy Spirit in the bodily form of a dove.”

Likewise, after some further remarks:

“And so the Son of God is said together with the human being to be adopted, and the adopted son of man is said together with the Word.”

Again, after some further remarks:

“Thus the Son of God is unchangeable and coeternal with the Father, but in the Word alone; and the Son of God suffered, but in the adopted human being alone; and the Son of God was buried, but in the adopted flesh alone [Col. 0879C]. Therefore, when words are spoken about the Son of God, one must consider in what respect they are spoken. For the number of persons was not increased by the human being who was assumed, or adopted, but the same Trinity remained. Just as in any human being, apart from that one who was singularly assumed, soul and body are one person, so in Christ the Word and the adopted human being are one person.”

Again, after some further remarks:

“Thus Christ, the Son of God and Lord of glory—and whatever of this kind is said according to the Word—is nevertheless rightly said to be the Lord of glory crucified, since he suffered this according to the adopted flesh, not according to that by which he is the Lord of glory.”

And shortly afterward:

“The Holy Spirit is said to have descended and remained upon him in bodily form as a dove. For in this way Christ is also the Rock, because it signified the adopted Christ.”

Again, after some further remarks:

“These things I have written to you concerning your two questions, namely concerning the Trinity and the Dove, in which the Holy Spirit was manifested not in his own nature but in a symbolic form. Likewise, the Son of God does not say in his own birth from the Father, ‘From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you,’ but, in the adopted human being, born from the womb of the Virgin, he was crucified by the Jews.”

### 17.

After I had read your letter again and again—sacrilegious, corrupted by deadly poison, and darkened by the gloom of ignorance—I found in it the claim that we denied that the Lord, the Son of God born from the Virgin, was not essentially God [Col. 0880A], concerning whom the Son of God himself said: “I and the Father are one.”

You ought to remember what Scripture says: “A false witness will not go unpunished”; and also: “Cursed is the person who devises evil in his heart and speaks peaceful things falsely with his lips. But God, who sees all things, will repay him according to his works.”

I certainly did not deny that the Son of God, begotten before the ages from the Father—through whom visible and invisible things, spiritual and bodily things, were made—is God not by adoption but by origin, not by grace but by nature.

### 18.

But, in accordance with the judgment of blessed Isidore, who says that there are some who think wrongly about the Son of God and transfer to his divinity what was said about him according to his humanity, and change to his humanity what was said about his divinity, our Julian nevertheless says: “The Lordly Man and the humanized God.”

### 19.

Many things still ought to have been inserted into this work, but the divine word prevents us, saying: “I will make your tongue cling to your palate, and you will be mute, so that you will not be like a man who rebukes, because it is a rebellious house.”

Therefore, woe to you, Austria; woe to you, Alexandria, which gave birth to a new Arius, namely Albinus, in the time of the glorious prince, for the overturning and obscuring of the Catholic faith.

Finally, hear blessed Cyprian speaking in this way to a certain heretic who had written to him: “You have my letters, and I have yours; both will be read in the presence of the Lord.”

Remember again that the Evangelist said: “Many of his disciples went back.” And where did they go? Let blessed Gregory answer you, saying: “After Satan.”

And again, when someone said to the Lord, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go,” he replied: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” And just as with you, if these small things are not enough for you, many will not help either.

He is nearest to God who knows how to be silent with discretion. What we have sometimes written to you in harsh language, we did at the Lord’s command through Moses, who says: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.”

### 20.

It must again be suggested to the glorious prince that he soften his anger toward his servant Felix and that the Lord not seek his blood from his hand [Col. 0880D]. For he should know with certainty that, if he despises Felix’s preaching and confirms Albinus’s position, he will share the fate of the emperor Constantine—God forbid. Blessed Isidore laments him, saying: “Alas! What grief! A good beginning, but a bad end.”

## LETTER V: TO FELIX, RECENTLY CONVERTED

### 1.

To Lord Felix:

I inform you, so that you may know, that when July was ending I received your written message, and when August was ending I wrote to you in turn. But when the opportunity arose, the letter was consumed by the present fire; and when it returned to me, I took up the labor again after nearly forty days and wrote to that pitch-black heretic Albinus as much as I could write for his confusion.

You, however, make a copy of that letter and send it onward. But now he has departed from *mele* [uncertain, as printed]; in June, at the Kalends of November, I sent you a short letter concerning our brother Militane, who thinks rightly about God. For he had also sent me four notebooks, which I forwarded against that most foul Pseudoprophet, Beatus. Inform me about the one who has been placed in Rome.

I received your letter, which had descended to me from heaven, at the end of July, and I gave immense thanks with outstretched arms to my God, who made me rejoice in your words amid the daily losses of the world in which we endure rather than live.

### 2.

But the most foul letter concerning Albinus, the son of the fire of Gehenna, a new Arius who arose in the regions of Austria in the time of the glorious prince—not a disciple of Christ but of the one who said, “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High.” Concerning him it is written: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.”

Against him I returned a reply as I wished and supported it with the judgments of the holy orthodox and Catholic writers.

But let your Holiness act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened as you remember what the Lord himself says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And again: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. Beware of people. For they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you; and you will be led before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations.”

### 3.

I sent your letter to the brothers in Córdoba who think rightly about God, and they wrote many things to me which I ought to forward for your assistance. But I sent it to be read again to the heresiarch Albinus’s teacher, Antiphrasius Beatus [Col. 0882A].

You, however, send that writing on behalf of your faithful and glorious prince before it reaches that son of death, Albinus, who does not believe in the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God. The holy Fathers and we ourselves believe this only in the form of human servitude, not in the glory or substance of the divine nature.

Concerning our brother who has died, I heard that he had instructed us to send something, and therefore I ask you to command your servant Ermedeus to inquire about the Jews who have wives and children there, to undertake the trouble, and to send us whatever God inspires. Let him do so in such a way that the other Jews who live among us do not perceive it; or, if possible, send with us one of your humble merchants who come here, and inform us what you have done concerning your intention.

In particular, send the two books of the letters of blessed Jerome and the works of blessed Isidore, which Ermedeus has and which I had sent to the brother who died. He had therefore asked me to send him any other similar works he might find.

For this reason, bring Ermedeus himself to you, instruct him with your words and in the true teaching of the faith, just as I instructed him.

### 4.

Know, however, that, already in decrepit old age, I entered my eighty-second year on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. Pray for us, as we continually do for you, so that God may join us together in the land of the living. We have also instructed all the brothers to offer sacrifice to God for you.

May I soon have the joy of receiving your reply. I commend to you this present messenger, and our priest Venerius, if it is granted that he reach you.

# CONFESSION OF FAITH OF FELIX, BISHOP OF THE SEE OF URGELL

Which he issued after rejecting his error in the presence of the council and sent to those who had formerly consented to him in that error.

*[From Mansi, enlarged Collection of Councils.]*

## NOTICE

Felix of Urgell, condemned by Leidrad and the other bishops assembled at Urgell, received from them free permission to plead his case before an assembly of bishops in the presence of the king. This was soon done at the Council of Aachen.

Alcuin relates that King Charlemagne, in order to defeat the Felician heresy, assembled a great synod of bishops in the palace at Aachen, and that, by the king’s order, he and Felix disputed there for several days. Finally Felix testified by voice and tears that he had been defeated.

Thus, after being reasonably heard and truly convicted before the priests of God and the leading men of the empire, and giving glory to God and confessing the true faith, he returned to the peace of Catholic unanimity with his disciples who were present there at that time, in the year of Christ 799.

—The Editors.

## THE CONFESSION OF FAITH OF FELIX BEGINS

In the name of God, I, Felix, formerly an unworthy bishop, to my lords and brothers in Christ, the priests Emanus and Ildesindus, and to Exsuperius, Gundefredus, Sidonius, and Ermegildus, as well as to the other priests dwelling in the parish of the Church of Urgell, and to the other faithful of the Church residing in the aforesaid charge; likewise to Vittildus the deacon and Witiricus, and to the other clergy: eternal salvation in the Lord God the Father and Jesus Christ, his true Son, our Lord and Redeemer, and in the Holy Spirit.

For the rest, we bring to your knowledge that, after I had been brought into the presence of our lord, the most pious and glorious King Charles, and presented before him, we received permission from him—just as the venerable lord Bishop Leidrad had promised us at Urgell—to present in his presence, before the bishops whom the arrangement of our glorious prince had caused to assemble before him, our opinions, which we believed we had derived from the books of the saints concerning the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God, or his naming according to his humanity.

We were to establish how our assertion might be judged valid, not by violence but by the reasoning of truth, if it were not rejected by them through the authority of the holy Fathers.

And so it happened. For, concerning the opinions we had brought forward about the aforesaid dispute—that is, concerning adoption [Col. 0883B] of the flesh and naming according to humanity—they refuted them for us on the authority of the books of the holy Fathers: namely, Bishop Cyril, blessed Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, blessed Leo, and other holy Fathers who had previously been unknown to us. They also appealed to the authority of the synod recently assembled in Rome for this purpose, at the command of our most glorious and pious lord Charles, against the letter I had formerly written to the venerable man Albinus, abbot of the Church of Tours.

At that synod, with Leo the Apostolic present, fifty-seven bishops were seated with him, together with many priests and deacons, in the house of the most blessed apostle Peter. Through the authority of all these, they excluded our aforesaid opinions—not, as has been said, by any sort of violence, but by the reasoning of truth, as was proper.

Convicted by their authority concerning the truth and by the consent of the entire universal Church, we returned, with God’s favor, wholeheartedly to the universal Church—not with any pretense or covering of falsehood, as formerly, God knows, but with true belief of heart and profession of mouth.

This we also professed in the presence of many priests and monks, expressing repentance for our former error and for the oath by which I formerly transgressed in this matter. We profess that henceforth we neither believe nor preach the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God or his naming according to humanity. Rather, as we have been instructed by the teachings of the holy Fathers, we profess that the same Lord Jesus Christ is the proper and true Son in both natures, namely divinity and humanity: the Only-Begotten of the Father, his one Son.

The properties of both natures remain intact, so that neither the divinity of the Word of God is believed to have been changed into human nature [printed readings: *natura/naturam*, *humana/humanam*], nor the humanity assumed by the Word to have been changed into divinity [printed *invidia*, corrected *in divinam*]. Rather, both—the divine and the human—have been joined and united to each other in the singularity of one person from the very conception in the Virgin’s womb, so that the one Son of the Father, true God, was brought forth from the womb of the glorious Virgin without any corruption.

The human being assumed by the Word is not thus believed to have been begotten from the substance of the Father, as the Word itself is said to be begotten “by the faithful” (*a fidelibus*; the printed text is uncertain), since he is from the substance of the mother. But because, as has been said, he was received and conceived in the very womb of the holy Virgin from the moment of conception by the one who according to his divinity exists as the true and proper Son of God, the true and proper Son of God was born from that same holy Virgin.

There is not one Son of God and another son of man, but God and man are one true and proper Son of God the Father. He is believed to be, not by adoption, appellation, or naming, but in both natures, as has been said, one true and proper Son of God the Father, according to the Apostle.

This is the confession of our faith, which, with God’s help, we learned from the holy Fathers through their writings and received and hold from the universal Church after our former error.

We exhort all of you, through the same Lord, to believe and confess this, neither diminishing nor adding anything from your own understanding, but holding without doubt, together with the universal Church, what we make known to you.

We also ask you not to disdain to implore the Lord’s mercy from the depths of your hearts for me, a wretched man, through whom the dispute in the Church has endured until now. May I, through your correction and through the prayers of Catholic priests who, unlike me, are in no way liable for a similar transgression, be able to obtain the Lord’s mercy before I depart from this mortal body.

I trust that I shall obtain this from the Lord all the more if, through me, the scandal or error in the faith that has endured until now between the two parties is corrected and settled in every respect; if all the members of the Church are joined together as one body in unity of faith and harmony of charity; and if no one among us dares thereafter to introduce scandal or any schism into the Church of God.

Rather, let all of us, thinking alike with the universal Church, which is known to be spread throughout the whole world, likewise anathematize the dispute that arose formerly—that is, the adoption of the flesh or the naming according to the humanity of the Son of God—and, as I have said, hold peace and unity of faith with all the faithful of the Church in unwavering faith and without any pretense.

Thus we may not, by agreeing with the impiety of Nestorius, who believed Christ the Lord to be a mere human being, fall somewhere in the future. He said:

“But concerning the dispensation of God, which the Lord God accomplished for our salvation in the dispensation of the Lord Christ, it is necessary to know that God the Word assumed a perfect human being from the seed of Abraham and David, according to the declaration of the divine Scriptures. He constituted according to nature what those were from whose seed he came: a perfect human being by nature, consisting of an intellectual soul and human flesh, constituted as a perfect human being according to our nature, formed by the power of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb, made from a woman and made under the law, so that he might redeem us all from the servitude of the law.

“Having previously received the predestined adoption, he came inexplicably into union with himself, making him dead according to human law, but raising him from the dead, leading him into heaven, and making him sit at the right hand of God. Therefore, having constituted him as the person over principalities, powers, dominions, virtues, and every name that is named—not only in this age but also in the age to come—he received adoration from every creature, possessing an inseparable conjunction with the divine nature, a relation to God, and an understanding that displayed adoration to every creature.

“We do not say that there are two sons or two lords, because there is one Son of the Father according to substance, God the Word, the Only-Begotten Son of the Father. Since this man has been joined and made a participant, he shares in the name and honor of the Son. The Lord according to essence is God the Word, with whom this man, joined to him, shares in honor.

“Therefore we do not say that there are two sons or two human beings, because, with the Lord and Son manifestly constituted according to substance, this man maintains an inseparable conjunction with him. Assumed for the sake of our salvation, he is granted the name and honor of the Lord and Son, not as each of us, constituted individually, is a son.

“Thus, according to blessed Paul, many are called sons, but he alone possesses this preeminence: by participating in the conjunction, adoption, and lordship of the Word of God, he removes every suspicion of duality of sons and lords.

“Having been granted to us in conjunction with the Word of the Lord, he has a good faith, understanding, and contemplation of him; and because of these he began to receive adoration from every creature through relation to God.

“Therefore we say that Christ the Son and Lord is one, through whom all things were made. Primarily, we understand God the Word substantially as the Son of God and Lord; but we also understand the assumed man from Nazareth [Possibly: Jesus of Nazareth. H.], whom God anointed with the Spirit and power, as participating in the adoption and lordship through conjunction with the Word of God. He is also the second Adam.”

This is the opinion of the heretic Nestorius, who impiously asserted that a mere human being had been conceived and born from the Virgin’s womb without God. He shamelessly preached that, after the birth of this human being, conceived and born from the same holy Virgin, the Word of God—that is, the divinity of the Son of God—descended upon him and dwelt in him above all other saints [Col. 0885D]. For this reason, just as he claimed two natures in Christ, so he also very wickedly attempted to assert two persons in him.

We, however, anathematizing his impiety, have selected certain testimonies from the books of the holy Fathers, whom the Church venerably receives, and appended them to this letter. Through them, after our former error, we returned to the way of truth, and sent them to you below. Through them you too can more fully recognize the truth of the faith concerning the stated dispute and return to the right path of faith.

Whoever dissents from these judgments of the Fathers and wishes to believe or teach otherwise than they instruct us, and presumes to believe or preach adoption and naming in the flesh of the Savior [Supply: “whoever” or “anyone.” H.], let him be anathema [Col. 0886A]. May the true and proper Son of God himself, concerning whom this is spoken, deign to free both you and us from the dart of this anathema, both here and in the future. With the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, he exists in equal and coequal glory, before all ages, now, and throughout the days of eternity.

Finally, blessed Cyril says in his treatise, among other things:

“Indeed, there is a great difference, marked by incomparable distinctions of glory and eminence, between what belongs to us and the glory and exalted prerogatives of our Savior. We are servants, but he is by nature Lord and God, although he became like us and, in a providential manner, entered into what belongs to us.

“Moreover, blessed Paul called Christ both Christ and God, saying: ‘Know and understand that every fornicator, etc., does not have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God’ (Ephesians 5). Christ alone is also truly God, who is Emmanuel. We are so by the grace of God, but the Son is not God in this way; rather, he is God by nature and in truth, although he became flesh” [Col. 0886B].

Likewise, in the same treatise, after some further remarks, he said:

“How was Christ named the proper Son of God, who was also handed over by God and the Father for the sake of the salvation and life of all? He was handed over because of our sins, and he himself bore the sins of many in his body upon the tree, according to the word of the prophet (Isaiah 53; 1 Peter 2).

“It is therefore clear that the reality assumed in the unity necessarily declared him to be the proper Son of God, who is from the holy Virgin. For the body was not, according to our condition, someone else’s, but rather was the proper body of the Word who exists from the Father and was born from her.”

Again, shortly afterward, against Nestorius:

“For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all are made alive (1 Corinthians 15). For if he did not suffer humanly for us, neither would he perform divinely the things that belong to salvation. He is said first to die as a human being, but afterward to live again because he is God by nature.

“If, therefore, according to the Scriptures, he did not suffer death in the flesh, neither is he made alive in the Spirit—that is, he did not rise again. And if this is true, our faith is vain and we are still in our sins. For we were baptized into his death, according to blessed Paul (Romans 6), and we received the forgiveness of sins through his blood.

“But if Christ is neither truly Son nor God by nature, but a mere human being according to our condition and an instrument of divinity, then we have been saved not in God, in some sense, but rather in one who, according to our condition, died for us and was raised by powers belonging to another. How, then, has death been destroyed through Christ?”

And below:

“We do not worship a mere human being—far be it from us—but rather God by nature, not failing to recognize his glory, although he became like us.”

Likewise, in the *Moralia* of blessed Gregory, pope of the city of Rome:

“And he was a great man among all the Orientals. ‘All,’ he says, ‘who stand in this East, full of faith, are rightly called Orientals.’ But because all other human beings are merely human beings, whereas he is the Orient, God and man, it is rightly said: ‘He was great among all the Orientals.’ As though it were plainly said: He surpasses all who are born to God in faith, because adoption exalts the others, but the nature of divinity exalts him.”

And again, elsewhere, the same author says:

“Because every human being is merely a human being, whereas he is God and man. There is none like him on earth, because although every adopted son makes progress toward receiving divinity, he did not receive it in such a way that he would naturally be God.”

Likewise, in the book of blessed Job:

“There is no one like our Mediator among the lawgivers, because they, called freely, return from sins to innocence. But our Redeemer is without sin, the Son without adoption, and he never committed what he rebuked” [Col. 0887B].

These judgments we previously did not understand correctly.

Likewise, blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria:

“But if anyone teaches contrary to the divine Scriptures, saying that one is the Son of God and another is the man who is from the Virgin Mary, adopted according to grace as we are—as though there were two sons, one according to nature who is from God and one according to grace who is from Mary—and if anyone says that our Lord’s flesh came from above and not from the Virgin Mary, or that the divinity was changed into flesh and confused with it, or that the Lord’s divinity was passible, or that the flesh of our Lord is unadorable like that of a human being, and is not to be adored as the flesh of the Lord and God, him the holy Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.”

Item of Saint Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, to Cledonius:

“If anyone introduces two sons, one indeed who is from God the Father, but the second who is from the mother, and not one and the same Son, and who surpasses adoption by the grace promised to those who believe, we judge him alien from our fellowship. There are two natures, God and man—for there are both soul and body—but there are not two Sons, nor two gods [Editor: ‘nor two, nor two gods’; H.].”

Item Saint Leo, pope of the city of Rome, says:

“Let the faith of right-minded people rejoice, and let them understand that there is one true Son of God, not only according to his divinity, by which he was begotten from the Father, but also according to his humanity, by which he was born from a virgin mother.”

The same author elsewhere:

“The Lord’s nature was assumed from his mother, not guilt. The form of a servant was created without servile condition, because the new was blended with the old, so that he might receive the reality of the lineage while excluding the fault of antiquity.”

# LIFE OF SAINT BEATUS, BLESSED ABBOT OF HISPANIA, BY A MORE RECENT ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

[From the Acts of the Benedictine Order, vol. V.]

[Col. 0887]

# MABILLON’S PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

1. Among the overlooked saints of the third Benedictine century, I listed this Beatus, because his commonly circulated Acts contain no mention of his monastic life. Later, however, I came upon certain arguments that prove his monastic life; indeed, I think that a man distinguished by learning and holiness may be assigned to the Benedictine family.

2. An anonymous Spanish writer, who appears to have belonged to a later age, committed the Life of Beatus to writing. John Tamayo de Salazar first published this account from the Asturician manuscript Legendary in the Spanish Martyrology, and after him John Bollandus published it in volume III of February, with a preliminary commentary by Godefridus Henschenius. The Spaniards, especially the Asturians, venerate Saint Beatus, and commonly call him Saint Bieco. John Mariana treats him at length in book VII, chapter 8, of his *History of Spain*.

3. Tamayo de Salazar wonders by what title Menardus and Yepez (Henschenius adds Wion) call Beatus a priest and monk: “since,” says Tamayo, “the unanimous opinion among writers is that he possessed only the distinction of a priest.” Tamayo’s wonder arises from ignorance of the ancient custom by which monks who had been ordained were commonly designated by the names of their orders, with the designation “monk” usually omitted and more rarely added. Thus Jerome and Bede are called priests; likewise Paschasius Radbertus is called a deacon, and others are named in the same fashion.

But lest I seem to have said this about Beatus without evidence, arguments must be brought forward, arguments with which Tamayo—and those who agree with him—will undoubtedly be satisfied. I take the first from Alcuin’s book I against Felix, where Beatus is given the title of abbot. Among the Visigoths, or Spaniards, there were no abbots other than monks and regulars. Alcuin’s words are these:

“But when you say that a certain Beatus, an abbot, and his disciple Heterius, a bishop, were the first to oppose this sect of yours, we praise them, and so forth.”

Yet lest someone perhaps reply that secular abbots also existed among the Spaniards, I offer a second argument from Beatus’s own book II against Elipandus:

“It is truly good and truly pleasant for brothers to dwell together. We left one brother in the world; behold how many we have found in the monastery. My secular brother did not love me as much as he loved my property; but the spiritual brothers, who certainly neglect what belongs to themselves, do not seek what belongs to others.”

These words can in no way suit a secular man; they necessarily apply to a monk who, after leaving one brother in the world, found far more spiritual brothers in the monastery.

These are the spiritual brothers for whose benefit Beatus composed a commentary on the Apocalypse, hitherto unpublished. In its preface Ambrosius Morales read the following words:

“I, at your request, holy Father Heterius, have dedicated this work to you for the edification and study of the brothers, so that I may make you, whose companion in the order I enjoy, also a co-heir of my labor.”

These, I say, are the words of a monk addressed to Heterius, then bishop of Osma, whom Beatus had formerly had as a disciple and fellow member of the order in the monastery. If Tamayo had read these arguments, he would doubtless have ceased to wonder that our authors called Beatus a monk; nor would he have taken it amiss that he was assigned to the Benedictine brethren.

4. Henschenius objects that, even if Beatus’s monastic status were established, he could not therefore immediately be assigned to the Benedictine order:

“since at that time there were many monasteries in Spain that had not embraced the Benedictine rule.”

He proves this from the fact that our Menardus, in his preface to the *Harmony of the Rules*, compiled by Benedict, abbot of Aniane, records one rule of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville; another of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga; and another by a second Fructuosus.

We indeed know that three rules for monks were composed among the Spaniards in the seventh century: one by Saint Isidore and two by Fructuosus, first a monk and abbot and later bishop of Braga. I do not agree with our Menardus in distinguishing two Fructuosi. I presented the arguments for this in the second century concerning the Life of Fructuosus [Note: [Col. 0889D] *Patrologia*, volume LXXXVII.]; Henschenius approved these arguments in volume II of April.

In any event, no one can rightly deny that these Rules were observed in some Spanish monasteries during the seventh century. For both Isidore and Fructuosus possessed such authority among the Spaniards that monks in that region readily accepted their Rules.

But the authority of Gregory the Great was of greater weight among them. In book II of the *Dialogues* he had praised Benedict so magnificently and commended his Rule with so distinguished an encomium. How devoted the Spaniards of that time were to Gregory is clearly shown by the fact that Chindaswinth, king of the Visigoths, sent Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, to Rome to recover the earlier part of Gregory’s *Moralia*, which was missing in that region.

Moreover, the books of the *Dialogues* were then very well known there; Isidore and Paul the deacon of Mérida praise them in the preface to the *Life of the Fathers of Mérida*. The Rule of Saint Benedict had also already been published among the Spaniards, as is clear from what I cited in the preliminary observations to the Life of Saint Fructuosus.

If, therefore, Gregory the Great already possessed such authority among the Spaniards, and if the Rule so greatly commended by him was so well known, the Spanish monks undoubtedly accepted it together with the Rules of Isidore and Fructuosus, just as is known to have happened in Gaul, where in the seventh century different Rules were received simultaneously with the Benedictine Rule in the same monasteries.

It may further be added that, as the following century was drawing to a close, Benedict, abbot of Aniane and a celebrated restorer of Benedictine discipline, was able to promote the same institution in those regions when he went to Spain to fight the Felician heresy.

Indeed, whatever primary monastic documents survive from those calamitous times—for the Moorish storm destroyed most of them—testify that the Rule of Saint Benedict was imposed upon the monks.

The first document I find is that of Fromista, an abbot who, together with his nephew Maximus the priest, founded the monastery of Saint Vincent of Oviedo in the Spanish era 819, corresponding to the year of Christ 781:

“in honor of Saint Vincent the martyr and Levite, and he received the Rule of Saint Benedict.”

(Yepez, volume III of the *Writers*, no. 18.)

The second is dated to the Spanish era 818 and concerns Adelgaster, son of King Silo, for the monastery of Obona:

“in honor of God and his blessed mother, and of Saint Michael the archangel, and of Saint John the evangelist, and of Saint Antoninus the martyr, and of Saint Benedict the abbot, whose order,” says Adelgaster, “we establish in that monastery.”

And below:

“For we give and grant by the tenor of this testament to God and blessed Mary and all the saints of God, in whose honor we found the church and monastery, and into the hand of Felix the abbot, to whom we hand over everything specified above, so that the abbot and monks may always remain in the service of God and perpetually observe the Rule of blessed Benedict.”

(The same, ibid., no. 24.)

It may further be added that all the monasteries founded in those times in Catalonia and neighboring Spain observed the same Rule, as is evident from the ancient documents reported in the Baluzian Appendix to the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, numbers 41, 62, 63, 89, 98, 132, 142, and 145.

This concludes what concerns Beatus’s monastic status.

5. Antonius Yepez conjectures which monastery’s monk he was: the monastery of Saint Thuribius of Liébana. He was led to this conclusion by the fact that a charter of that place, dated to the Spanish era 866, mentions “the religious priest lord Heterius” and the monks living there.

But if Heterius had not died by that time, he was certainly already long before bishop of Osma (Osma), and indeed bishop at the time when he wrote with Beatus against Elipandus, as is clear from his confession reported before the middle of book I:

“I, Heterius, the first, an unworthy named bishop of the see of Osma, whom the archbishop of Toledo calls a heretic, bring forth my faith before all who hear.”

He was therefore a bishop around the year 790.

I myself think that a monastery once existed at Vallis-Cava in Asturias, inhabited and governed by Beatus. For the following Life says that he withdrew there, and that place is still made illustrious by his cult and relics.

6. Beatus’s learning and doctrine were remarkable for that disastrous age of the Moors, as the two books against Elipandus demonstrate. They were published both by Beatus himself and by Heterius, his disciple, although Beatus played the principal role in that work. Elipandus attacked both men, but especially Beatus.

This is relevant to Elipandus’s letter to Fidelis:

“Let your fraternity instruct our brother Heterius, whose youth has certainly still been nourished with milk and has not yet been brought to the strength of mature understanding, because he held conference not with excellent teachers but with ignorant and schismatic men, namely Felix and Beatus Antiphrasius, equal in virtue and alike in error.”

This Felix seems to have been the abbot of Obona mentioned above, serving under the Rule of Saint Benedict. From Beatus’s association with Felix it may therefore be understood that Beatus too was attached to that Rule.

Gabriel Vasquez admits that he cannot help admiring Beatus and Heterius, because in so disastrous a time, when Spain was oppressed by the dreadful tyranny of the Moors, they illuminated so obscure a controversy through the sharpness of their intellect and their learning.

Besides these two books against Elipandus, which exist in volume VIII of the *Library of the Fathers*, Beatus also wrote a commentary on the Apocalypse, hitherto unpublished. Would that someone might finally bring it out of darkness! Morales says that he saw it in the church of Vallecava, called Valcabado by the Spaniards, not far from the town of Saldaña in the diocese of León. As I said, that place is celebrated for the memory and cult of Beatus.

Here it is worth observing that Beatus refers near the end of book I against Elipandus to the Acts of Saint Andrew the apostle, which some think to be more recent. Speaking of Christ, he says:

“This is the immaculate Lamb who, as blessed Andrew says, is sanctified daily on the altar of the cross. After all the believing people have eaten his flesh and drunk his blood, the Lamb that was sacrificed remains whole and alive.”

These very words are found in the commonly circulated Acts of Saint Andrew.

[Col. 0890]

# THE LIFE BEGINS

1. In the time of Mauregatus, king of the Asturians, there was in Toledo an archbishop named Elipandus. Amid the dreadful storms of the Agarenes, he had succeeded Cixila, his predecessor, because the fame of his learning and holiness had spread throughout all Spain.

He was descended from the Mozarabic Goths and was distinguished by the nobility of his blood. From the earliest beginnings of his literary education he had been taught by a certain Felix, a Gaul by ancestry, bishop of Urgel, later the Nestorian heretic. Against right, against the auspices, and against all human and divine writings and religious traditions, Felix taught in detail that Christ, insofar as he was man, was the adoptive son of the Father.

Elipandus had imbibed this foul doctrine from his teacher through the sacrilegious instructions of letters.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] Binius is mistaken in calling Elipandus Felix’s teacher. Certainly Dungalus calls Felix the teacher of this error.]

Following his teacher’s footsteps with rash apprehension, Elipandus first used writings and then anathema against all the bishops and priests of Spain who disregarded Felix’s opinion. Thus he stained Spain with a damnable proposition.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] John Mariana did not dare assert this, since it is clearly false from Einhard’s *Annals* under the year 792: “There is a city called Urgel situated on the ridge of the Pyrenees. Its bishop, named Felix, a Spaniard by nationality, was consulted by letter by Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, concerning what he ought to think and say about the humanity of God and our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior—whether, according to that by which he is man, he should be believed and called the proper or adoptive Son of God. Felix, very rashly and inconsiderately, and contrary to the ancient teaching of the Catholic Church, not only pronounced him adoptive, but also took care, in books written to the said bishop, to defend in writing the most perverse depravity of his opinion.”

The Spaniards are amusing in this respect: if they have any scoundrels, they attribute them to the Franks or Gauls; but the more distinguished saints they have, they claim for themselves, as is clear from many examples in the Spanish Martyrology. Claudius of Turin must be sent back to the Spaniards together with Felix. I have demonstrated in volume I of the old *Analecta* that Claudius was by origin not a Scot but a Spaniard.]

2. When he was undertaking these things, God drew sweetness from the strong one and David from the forests of the Liévana mountains, which rise between the two Asturian regions, so that he might confound all that was mighty. Like another Isaiah who did not know how to speak, God touched his lips with a burning coal and raised up in Spain a prophet who would vigorously attack the erring leaders of the Church with an iron stylus.

Nebuchadnezzar had erected a statue, exceedingly beautiful in appearance, towering in height, rich in metals, celebrated in fame, and magnificent in its adornment. Who struck down its excellence? A small stone rolling down from the mountain.

The ignorance of Belshazzar profaned the vessels of the Temple. Who exposed his arrogance and death? Two fingers and a short stylus.

Thus God, who had perceived in Elipandus a Goliath, in his error a people, in his vainglory a Nebuchadnezzar, and in his arrogance a Belshazzar, raised up from the lowliness of the people and the mountain caves a David; from an obscure populace, a stammering Isaiah; from the mountain, Beatus; and from the forests, his finger, to crush the errors of that archbishop.

3. This man, who was Beatus in both name and deed, was a Spaniard. He came from those exceedingly rugged mountains and traced his origin to the ancient Asturians. He was a priest by order [Note: [Col. 0891D] Rather, also a monk, as was proved above in Observation 3], learned in the sacred Scriptures and conspicuous for his zeal for the Catholic faith.

When he heard Elipandus’s erroneous profession, he immediately began throughout that entire region both to sow Catholic doctrine and to uproot the heretical weeds. As he resisted Elipandus’s advances, he gradually learned that his inventions were being spread abroad.

The blessed Heterius also assisted the Catholic work. He later became bishop of Osma [Note: [Col. 0891D] He too was a disciple of Beatus, as Alcuin records; his words were cited in the same Observation]. Supported by Beatus’s friendship, Heterius together with Beatus taught Catholic truth against Felix and Elipandus with manly and holy charity through writings and sermons circulating among the peoples.

Through their effectiveness, many who had drunk Elipandus’s poison and vomited forth the heretical wine returned to the bosom of Mother Church in repentant contrition.

4. Elipandus had heard of the works of the saints Heterius and Beatus. He was intensely angry with the latter [Note: [Col. 0891D] Beatus mentions his letter at the beginning of book I: “We have read the letter of your prudence, sent secretly under seal in the present year, not to us but to the abbot Fidelis, in October, in the Spanish era 823 [Col. 0892C]; we heard by report that it had arrived, but we did not see it until the sixth day before the Kalends of December.” Thus this letter was written to Fidelis in the year 785] and sent a letter to Fidelis, abbot of Asturias, complaining about the holy priests. He said that although he himself was the bishop of Toledo, they did not wish to learn from him anything concerning the doctrine of adoption, as though they despised his dignity and rank.

“Who,” he continued, “has ever heard that a man from Asturias, a mountain dweller, should presume to teach and correct the men of Toledo? Could he not have taken an example from Bishop Ascaricus [Note: [Col. 0892C] Elipandus’s published letter to Fidelis, reported in book I of Beatus the abbot, contains this example. It says: “I sent this letter of lord Bishop Ascaricus to your fraternity, dearest Fidelis, so that you may recognize how great humility reigns in the servants of Christ and how great pride reigns in the disciples of Antichrist, since lord Ascaricus wished to write these things to me not at the command of one teaching but at the request of one asking, as true humility taught him. These men, however, sometimes speaking contrary things and sometimes treating me as though I were ignorant, did not wish to ask what was right.” Ascaricus was bishop of Braga, whom Pope Adrian I censures together with Elipandus in letter 97 of the *Codex Carolinus* to the bishops of Spain], who, after hearing the antiphrasis of your Beatus, came running to our see and humbly asked what should be held?

“But just as by God’s grace victory was achieved through us and the assembly of the bishops of Spain over the Migetians of Seville, who, by deviating around the feast of Easter, spread a confused ordering of observance [Note: [Col. 0892D] Elipandus likewise boasts of this victory in the letter just mentioned to Fidelis: “What I and my other brothers had judged for so long in Seville, and with God’s help had corrected both in the Easter festivals and in their other errors—the heresy of the Migetians—they [namely Beatus and Heterius] now, on the contrary, find grounds for accusing us.” Below he says that these Migetians flourished in the borders of Baetica. Adrian censures Migetius, the founder of the sect, and his disciple Egila, in the letter cited immediately above. Thus in the text one should read “Migetians”], so in the Lord we trust that we shall uproot the Eatian heresy from the mountains of Asturias.

“I am not unaware that Heterius, being a young man, was deceived by Beatus, a wild and empty-talking man. If you approve our wishes, summon him to you immediately and point out how greatly he has erred before God, his Church, and us. If he persists in the artifices of an obstinate proposition, crush him through our correction and that of the whole Church.”

5. After some time, Beatus arrived through the favor of a visit to Adosinda [Note: [Col. 0893C] Adosinda was the daughter of King Alfonso and the wife of Silo. Mauregatus, also the son of Alfonso but by a concubine, invaded Silo’s kingdom in 783. Beatus himself says at the beginning of book I against Elipandus that he visited Adosinda with Heterius: “When we were brought to brother Fidelis—not by the compulsion of that letter, but by the recent devotion of the religious lady Adosinda—we heard that the little book of Elipandus had been publicly circulated throughout all Asturias against us and our faith. Although our faith was indivisible, the little boat began to toss among the rocks, and there were two boats. Later, when calm had returned, so that it seemed not to be divided but only one, then, speaking with one another [namely Beatus and Heterius], we said, and so forth.” From this arose the opportunity, by mutual agreement, of writing one and the same work against Elipandus. Adosinda is also mentioned below, section 8].

Fidelis the abbot showed him Elipandus’s letter. As befitted a Catholic man and defender of the faith, he summoned Heterius and wrote a complete work arranged in two books, refuting Elipandus’s errors with solid passages of sacred Scripture and powerful arguments.

When the book reached the hands of Elipandus and his other followers, they attacked it with the most vicious verbal and written wounds, among other things branding him with the name “Antiphrasius.”

But God, to whom the secrets of every heart are open, looked down from the throne of his majesty upon the spirit of Beatus’s innocence and recognized from above the priest’s pure zeal for the faith; he freed him from all the dangers posed by his enemies.

6. For Elipandus departed from Toledo and traveled through the Asturians and Galicians, infecting many in those regions with his evil opinion through the pestilential breath of his mouth.

Felix attempted to infect the Vaccaeans in Spain, the Septimani in Gaul, and others in Germany, but was driven back by the steadfast defense of all.

Thus, at Reginum, a city of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0894C] “He was led,” says Einhard, “to the king’s palace, which was then located at Reginum, a city of Bavaria [others call it Regensburg]. There, after a council of bishops had been assembled, he was heard and convicted of error; he was sent to Rome into the presence of Pope Adrian, and so forth”], he was first condemned in an assembly of bishops. Later, before Adrian, the supreme pontiff, he pretended to repent. Finally, at Frankfurt, where a council had been summoned in the presence of Charles, king of the Franks, and where the legates Theophylact and Stephen, bishops sent from Rome, and the blessed Beatus and Heterius, sent from Spain on behalf of the Catholics, were present, the error and its authors were condemned by the council’s assembly. Pope Adrian did the same.

7. When Elipandus of Toledo learned this, he decided to withdraw from his proposition. He summoned an assembly of bishops at Toledo and, in repentance, offered a written confession in which he humbly professed the Son of God to be the only-begotten and consubstantial with the Father, not adoptive but natural.

The Fathers accepted his profession with tears and granted him the benefit of reconciliation. He then received the blessed Beatus and Heterius kindly, laying aside the hostility of the former dispute. With tears and sobs he addressed them as defenders of the faith and patrons of Catholic truth.

8. Finally, when the council had been dissolved, the affairs of the faith in Spain had been well settled, and the quarrel over Felician depravity had been calmed, the holy man Beatus became the continual spiritual guide of Adosinda, the wife of King Silo, who, because of the tyranny of Mauregatus, had assumed the sacred habit.

He continued in this role until he withdrew to Vallis-Cava, devoting himself to prayers, fasts, and the study of sacred Scripture. There he composed, in marvelous order, a book on the mysteries of the Apocalypse.

At length, renowned for miracles, he commended his spirit in peaceful sleep to the Lord whom he had served, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord 798.

His body lay buried there for three years. Then it was transferred to a more honored place, while his arm was reserved for the assistance of the sick who came to his sarcophagus. Enclosed in a marble reliquary, it is preserved with the honor due to it, just as God, who lives and reigns forever and ever, promised to preserve it and the bones of his saints. Amen.

[Col. 0893]

# LETTER OF HETERIUS AND SAINT BEATUS TO ELIPANDUS

[From Galland’s *Library of the Ancient Fathers*.] (C)

# BOOK ONE

To the most eminent and beloved of God, Elipandus, archbishop of the see of Toledo: Heterius and Beatus send greetings in the Lord.

## I

We read the letter of your prudence, sent secretly under seal in the present year, not to us but to Fidelis the abbot, in October, in the Spanish era 823 [Note: [Col. 0895D] The year 785, since these authors follow the Spanish era, which differs from the Christian era by thirty-eight years]. We heard by report that it had arrived, but we did not see it until the sixth day before the Kalends of December.

When we were brought to brother Fidelis—not by the compulsion of that letter, but by the recent devotion of the religious lady Adosinda [Note: [Col. 0896D] She was the widow of King Silo]—we heard that the little book had been publicly circulated throughout all Asturias against us and our faith.

Although our faith was one and indivisible, the little boat began to toss among the rocks, and there were two boats. Later, when calm had returned, so that it seemed not divided into two but only one, then, speaking with one another, we said:

“Jesus is asleep in the boat, and we are shaken here and there by the waves and suffer the troubles of the storms, because an unbearable wind has arisen. No salvation seems possible for us unless Jesus is awakened. We must cry out with heart and voice, saying to him: ‘Lord, save us; we are perishing.’

“Then Jesus arose, who was sleeping in our boat, in which we were with Peter. Then he commanded the wind and the sea, and a great calm arose. From that time, by God’s mercy, the boat that has Peter in it is not troubled; the one that has Judas in it is troubled. For how could the boat be troubled over which he himself presided, in whom the Church’s foundation rests?”

## II

Nevertheless, many of our people, even the strongest rowers, were greatly afraid, because the little boat was tossing farther from land—that is, from the body of Christ—in the open sea. For the Lord had said to Peter:

“Put out into the deep your nets”—that is, into the depth of disputation and the sea of the Scriptures.

What is so lofty as to behold the height of riches? And what is so profound as to know the Son of God and profess the divine generation? [Note: [Col. 0896D] “To know the Son of God and to profess him, for one follows from the other.” STEVV.]

For although the human mind cannot fully comprehend this through the investigation of reason, the fullness of faith nevertheless embraces it. Although we are not permitted to know how the Son of God was born, we are nevertheless permitted to know and believe that he was truly born.

Be strong; do not be afraid. He for whom this dispute is being waged is with us.

“Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age.”

Our dispute would not be so difficult unless a virgin had given birth; and because a virgin gave birth, there is a dispute. Because the Virgin gave birth to Emmanuel—that is, “God with us”—we believe in and worship him, because there is no other God.

Finally, what is sought in persecution except that we deny Christ God? Therefore whoever does not confess Christ, true God, the son of the Virgin Mary, born from the true God, will not merit pardon.

Moreover, every spirit that does not confess that Christ has come in the flesh is not from God; that spirit is the Antichrist. For whoever denies the man has denied God, because God is man and man is God, and the only-begotten Christ, Son of God, is both God and man.

Peter, who would steer this little boat, denied the man. For he said:

“I do not know the man.”

He did not say, “I do not know God,” or “I do not know the Son of God.” But when he denied the man, he denied the Son of God as God.

And when he was questioned by the man, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” then a man answered a man and said:

“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

He denied that same Christ, the Son of the living God, when he said, “I do not know the man.”

## III

But when Peter denied him, Christ was being held bound. He stood before the governor, being struck with slaps and blows, and being spat upon. It was night; there was darkness and cold. He was in the praetorium, and the maidservant who kept the door held it closed.

The Holy Spirit had not yet been given to Peter in its fullness, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

But when Peter confessed Christ as the Son of God, Jesus was not bound, nor was he alone. A multitude followed him, and he raised their dead, illuminated their blind, cleansed their lepers, drove out demons, and healed various diseases.

He asked people who that distinguished man was considered to be among the peoples. When they offered various opinions—some saying, “You are Elijah”; others, “Jeremiah”; others, “You are John the Baptist”; and others, “You are a prophet”—then Peter, speaking among them all without any hesitation, said:

“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

The Lord proclaimed blessed the man to whom flesh and blood had not revealed this, but his Father who is in heaven.

Then Peter was also called “rock,” after he was the first to recognize Christ as the cornerstone. This is the rock of which the Father had spoken through the prophet Isaiah:

“Behold, I will place in the foundations of Zion a tested stone, chosen, a cornerstone, precious; and everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isaiah 28:16).

And surely the stone in whom he commands us to believe is God.

Of this rock the apostle Paul said:

“The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

And because [perhaps, “indeed”] all the saints who are founded upon Christ are written of as stones and rocks, whenever “rock” or “stone” is named in the sacred language in the singular, Christ alone is understood. But when “rocks” are named in the plural, they are found to be the members—namely, holy men—who are made firm by his strength [perhaps, “are expressed”].

The apostle Peter calls them stones, saying:

“You, like living stones, are being built together into a spiritual house” (2 Peter 2:5).

All these received their name not from Peter but from Christ the Rock, just as Peter did. And what he said to Peter—“Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18)—he said not to Peter alone but to all of us.

“This has not been revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., verse 17)—not to Peter alone, but also to us, who believe as Peter did and still does today.

For when today we say with our heart and mouth before the whole Church, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” he immediately responds:

“Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”

The Truth said to one person what is sufficient for all. We all believe this, but he alone confessed it.

## IV

Let the one to whom flesh and blood revealed it say:

“You are adoptive according to your humanity, and the Son of the living God according to your divinity.”

For flesh and blood had not revealed to Peter what he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Whose flesh and blood? Surely Peter’s, as though Peter’s flesh and blood had prevented Christ from being called the Son of God? Certainly not. It was the flesh and blood of the Lord himself.

In that flesh and blood, while the man was seen, what God had assumed was not believed to be what it was. For it seemed impossible to everyone that they should believe him to be God whom they saw to be a man.

And he says that such great majesty, in which the fullness of divinity dwells bodily and which the world itself cannot contain, had been enclosed in a small body of contemptible appearance:

“This flesh and blood of mine did not reveal to you that I am the Son of God, because these [perhaps, “my”]—that is, my flesh and blood—do not promise that I am to be believed to be the Son of God.””

The prophet had already said:

“He is a man, and who recognizes him?” (Isaiah 53:3).

Therefore those judging according to sight openly speak of him as Elijah, or a prophet, or one of the prophets, because they recognize him as a man in every aspect of his flesh.

“But my Father who is in heaven revealed me to you.”

## V

When did he reveal this? At what time did God speak with Peter?

“My Father who is in heaven revealed it to you.”

It is as though he had said openly:

“You believed because of the works that proclaim me to be the Son of God. You saw me raise the dead, illuminate the blind, make the deaf hear and the mute speak, walk upon the waters with dry feet, command the winds, and heal the sick by my word.

“Through these works you believed that I am the Son of God.”

For those who called him one of the prophets also saw him do these things. They all spoke falsely, because they spoke from themselves and had not received their testimony from the Father’s revelation.

Whoever speaks from himself speaks falsehood, because he thinks me to be what he sees me to be. But whoever hears from the Father speaks truth, because he draws from the truth and receives assurance from the truth.

### VI. What is the truth?

You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. For Christ himself said this: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” We were not present when the Son of God was declared by the Father. The Father alone said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him, every soul.” For when he said “every soul,” he spoke to all of us. “Every soul” means every human being, as in Genesis: “Seventy souls entered Egypt with Jacob” [Col. 0897D].

Through so many human beings, the Father cries out from heaven to us human beings on earth, so that we may hear his Son. Let us believe him and proclaim before human beings that he is the proper Son of God. Why do we doubt at the outset? If we do not believe God, whom do we believe? For everything we believe, we believe either by sight or by hearing. Sight is sometimes deceived; hearing, however, rests upon faith.

There were then those who saw Christ and believed; there were those who saw and did not believe. Now there are those who hear the Gospel and confess before human beings that Christ, the Son of God, was crucified; and there are those who insist before everyone that he is not the Son of God.

The prophets thunder, the Gospel cries out, and the same Son says through his Gospel: “Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” [Col. 0898A]. The Father says to him: “I have glorified you, and I will glorify you again.” The Father is truth, because he bears witness to the truth; he cries out to the truth, from whom he himself is truth. Truth answered Truth, who sent this truth into the world, not for himself but for us. Truth came to liars—and do we suppose that by refusing to believe it we can make it a liar?

### VII.

Truth says through the mouth of his flesh: “I am the Son of God.” And “whoever denies me denies him who sent me.” Will anyone presume to destroy this Gospel? Is it necessary to believe the Gospel in part and not believe it in part? Whoever does not believe the Gospel does not believe the Son, whose Gospel it is. And whoever does not believe the Son does not believe the Father, who sent him.

For we do not love a king if we hate his laws. Whoever does not believe the Father and the Son when they say these things is a liar, because he thinks that God has lied. If good men said such things, we would regard it as a sacrilege not to believe them. God asserts it, the Son proves it, the trembling earth bears witness: the underworld releases its captives, the seas obey, the elements serve, the rocks are split, the sun is darkened—and a heretic, though he possesses reason, argues that the son of the Virgin is not the Son of God?

### VIII.

Who is the Son of God, if not Jesus, whom the virgin Mary bore? The Father promised him to us through the Prophet, saying: “For my Son Jesus will be revealed to you” (Luke 1:31). The angel also announced this name to the Virgin: “You will call his name Jesus; he will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High.”

If what you say were true, he could then have said: “Let Jesus be called the adopted son of the Most High according to his humanity, and by no means adopted according to his divinity.” The Son himself could also have said: “God so loved the world that he gave his adopted Son into the world, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish.”

And certainly his mission is that of a human being; and the unbelievers who crucified him could see in him nothing except a human being. Yet when they crucified the human being, they crucified the Son of God; they crucified God. For me my God suffered; for me my God was crucified. And why do I say “for me”? Our God suffered for everyone.

Let us therefore say: “Rise up, O God; judge the earth.” To which God is it said, “Rise up,” if not to him who died? To which God is it said, “Judge the earth,” if not to him who was judged by the Jews? “Rise up, O God; judge the earth—you who were judged by the earth.”

Thus also Psalm 81 says: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he distinguishes among gods.” And certainly he who distinguishes among gods is God. He is not a god among gods, as the heretics assert, but the God of gods.

He who said, “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High,’” is himself the Most High God, the Son of the Virgin, concerning whom the Prophet had already said: “Behold, the exalted God will come in his strength, and no one will be like him. Who will be able to search out his ways?” (Isa. 40:10)—considering all things—and his name is above the boundaries of the earth.

He is the Lord of lords, who is the God of gods. And just as he is not one of many gods, so neither is he one of many lords, but one Lord God, as the Apostle bears witness when he says: “There is no God except one.” For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—indeed, there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we through him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him [Col. 0899A]. But not everyone possesses knowledge.

He is the Christ of christs, who is Lord of lords and God of gods.

### IX.

But he is not one of those christs of whom it was said: “Do not touch my christs” (Ps. 104:15). Nor is he one of those concerning whom the heretics say: “He is Christ, and we are christs.”

Although the saints too are christs, lords, and gods, none of them is absolutely called, in a single expression, Christ Jesus our God. None of them was called “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.” None of them died for the world. He alone did.

None of them died by his own will, or laid down his life whenever he wished, or took it up again whenever he wished; he alone did so. For he said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He did not say, “Destroy this temple, so that the Father may raise it,” but, “I will raise it.” And in the third Psalm he says: “I slept and arose.”

All this is the free power of Christ—of him who died by his own power and rose again by his own power. And whoever has power is God; not just any god, but the almighty God, because he can do all things. No one can do what the almighty God did and does.

Yet because the Father also raised him, he says in the same Psalm: “The Lord raised me.” He calls “Lord” the one whom he has as Father. For if he did not have him as Father, the apostle Peter would not have said to the Jews concerning him: “The Lord, the God of our fathers, raised his Son Jesus, whom you killed” [Col. 0899C].

He was called the Father’s servant because he emptied himself, that is, he showed himself visible to the world. “Taking the form of a servant,” the Apostle says, “he was made in the likeness of human beings and was found in appearance as a human being.”

Therefore he is the Father’s servant, although with the Father he is one Lord and one God. Yet he is neither lord nor servant to himself. He is the servant of the Father alone, because he does the Father’s will, as he himself says: “I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father.” Here he did not say “to do the will of God,” but “the will of the Father.”

Although he called God his Father, since he is also God by nature and of that same essence, nevertheless we in no way fail to understand that, remaining human, he also became human, existing under God according to the law owed to human nature [Col. 0899D].

But how could he himself be God or Lord to himself? Therefore he is the servant of the Father alone—not servant to himself, not his own servant; not lord to himself, not his own lord. Just as he is the Son of the Father alone—not his own son, not son to himself—so he is both greater and lesser than himself.

Thus, in the respect in which he is greater than himself, he is equal to the Father; in the respect in which he is lesser than himself, he is less than the Father; in the respect in which he is lesser than the Father, he is Lord of every creature; in the respect in which he is servant to the Father, he is Lord of heaven and earth, that is, of angels and human beings.

The apostle Paul bears witness to this when he says: “He humbled himself even to death, and death on a cross. Therefore God the Father also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus, the son of the Virgin Mary, every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” [Col. 0900A].

### X.

For the Father said to none of the angels: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession. You will rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you will shatter them.”

To the angels, indeed, he says: “Let all the angels of God worship him.” But to the Son he says: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”

And: “You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; all things will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail. The children of your servants will dwell securely, and their offspring will be established forever and ever.”

The Church says this about Christ. And because he came into this world humbled, made for a little while lower than the angels—and not only lower than the angels but also lower than human beings, because he was less than his parents—and [perhaps: “but”] before his passion, before his death, before his resurrection, he was thus lesser.

For after he rose from the dead, he said to his disciples: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me. As the Father sent me, so I send you.” When he had said this, he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; whose you retain, they are retained.”

And because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, he breathed that very Holy Spirit upon the apostles, so that it might be shown more clearly that the Son of God was preeminent [perhaps: that he himself was], from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds. The Holy Spirit is the third person in the Trinity; he is called the gift of the Father and the Son. Christ gave him then and afterward sent him from heaven, to show the love of God and of one’s neighbor according to those commandments on which the whole law and the prophets depend [Col. 0900C].

### XI.

He gave the Holy Spirit once on earth, on account of love of neighbor, and a second time he gave him from heaven, on account of love of God. For when he breathed upon them and they had received the Holy Spirit, he said to them: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

Where this Trinity is especially commended, we must not doubt. He is therefore the Holy Spirit who was also given from heaven on the day of Pentecost, ten days after the Lord ascended into heaven.

How is Jesus Christ not God, the Son of God, who was born of the Virgin as true God and who gives the Holy Spirit? Indeed, how great is the God who gives God! For none of his disciples gave the Holy Spirit. They prayed that he might come upon those on whom they laid hands; they themselves did not give him. The Church still preserves this practice among bishops.

### XII.

Finally, Simon Magus, when he offered money to the apostles, did not say: “Give me this power also, so that I may give the Holy Spirit,” but: “So that whoever on whom I lay hands may receive the Holy Spirit” (Acts 8:19).

For Scripture had not said earlier: “When Simon saw that the apostles gave the Holy Spirit”; rather, it said: “When Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands” [Col. 0901A].

For this reason the Lord Jesus himself not only gave the Holy Spirit as God, but also received him as a human being. Hence he is called “full of grace.” More explicitly, it is written about him in the Acts of the Apostles that “God anointed him with the Holy Spirit.”

This was not with visible oil, but with the gift of grace, which is signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized.

Nor, certainly, was Christ then anointed with the Holy Spirit when, after his baptism, the Spirit descended upon him like a dove. At that time he deigned to prefigure his body, that is, his Church, in which we who are baptized especially receive the Holy Spirit.

Rather, by that mystical and invisible anointing he is to be understood as having been anointed when the Word of God became flesh—that is, when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was joined to the Word of God in the Virgin’s womb, so that with him it became one person.

For this reason we confess him born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary. It would be utterly absurd to believe that, when he was already thirty years old and had been baptized by John, he then received the Holy Spirit. He came to John’s baptism sinless and already full of the Holy Spirit.

For if it is written even of his servant and forerunner John, “He will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb”—because, although conceived from his father, he nevertheless received the Holy Spirit while being formed in the womb—what are we to understand or believe concerning the human Christ, whose flesh was conceived not carnally but spiritually? [Col. 0901C]

### XIII.

Why have we said all this, except to establish firmly that Jesus Christ, who was born of the Virgin, is true God and the true, proper Son of God—and to deny openly that he is a god among gods, an adopted son among adopted sons, a little one among little ones, and a servant among servants, as the heretics blaspheme?

They howl; they do not expound Scripture. And because they howl, they are wolves. They walk in darkness, that is, they preach among the ignorant. They bring forward obscure and twisted arguments by which they deceive the uninformed. They try to remove the pastors of the Churches so that they may strangle the Lord’s sheep more easily.

See, brothers; do not believe them. Drive them away from you and flee from them, if you are sheep, because they do not possess the shepherd’s voice.

Our good Shepherd said to us: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.” Are they not wolves who say to you: “Believe Jesus Christ to be adopted,” and who insist that anyone who does not believe this should be exterminated?

And let the schisms of the heretics be utterly removed from your land—the metropolitan bishop and the ruler of the land punishing them in equal contest, the one with the sword of the word, the other with the rod of governance. Certainly there is already rumor, already a report, and it has been spread not only throughout Asturias but throughout all Spain and as far as Gaul, that two controversies have arisen in the Church of Asturias.

And just as there are two controversies, so there are two peoples and two Churches: one side contends with the other for the one Christ. Which side’s faith is true and which false is a major matter of inquiry; and this is not among the common people, but among bishops.

One group of bishops says that Jesus Christ is adopted according to his humanity, and by no means adopted according to his divinity. The other group says: “Unless from both natures he is the one proper Son of God the Father—not adopted, but so truly proper that he himself is the true God, the Son of God—and unless he himself who was crucified under Pontius Pilate is worshiped and honored.”

We are this latter group—that is, Heterius and Beatus, together with the others who believe likewise. Certainly we believe not only in God the almighty Father, but in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our God and Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary and suffered under Pontius Pilate [Col. 0902A].

### XIV.
