By this same means those were deceived who promised to serve God and, after professing monastic life, were enticed by the brilliance of their speech and by certain philosophical doctrines. By this means they ascended to the highest chairs, so that they might appear to ignorant people publicly as teachers, and attained the priesthood.

While at the very front of their order they pretended to humility and holiness, persuading the devout with certain arguments suited to this religious frame of mind [Note: Perhaps: “persuading with arguments suited to their exhortations”], they became like the deceptive gleam of gold. Those whom they had once enticed on the surface of their pretense, like people deceived by false and lying bronze coins, they rendered naked and wretched forever—either by recalling them to the noise of the world or by dragging them, swollen with this presumption, into heretical errors.

This is what Achan also suffered in the book of Joshua. Desiring a golden tongue from Jericho, on account of which, when the Lord became angry, many of the people perished by the hand of the enemy, he afterward deserved to be stoned by the whole people for the stolen anathema and to be condemned by the Lord to eternal death.

This signified the one who introduced into the Church the dogma of heretics or the superstitious studies of secular literature. For this is the golden tongue (Joshua VII, 21), fashioned in eloquent speech.

Arius, Sabellius, Bonosus, Marcion, Basilides, and Elipandus, archbishop of the Toletan see, were defrauded by this. For they stole golden objects from Jericho—that is, from the school of secular learning—and tried to introduce into and defile the whole Church a misguided philosophical sect, so that many would be destroyed through them.

Therefore, rejected under an anathema, as though crushed beneath a heap of stones—that is, oppressed and extinguished by a multitude of sins—they perished, just as Achan was crushed beneath a heap of stones and killed by Israel.

When his error had been destroyed, King Ai—that is, the devil, who through their impiety had cast down certain of the faithful—was again defeated and overcome, and was put to death by the people of God, suspended upon the power of the wood of the cross.

### LV

First we spoke of mixed gold—that is, the mixed doctrine of heretics—and of the pure gold stolen from Jericho, namely, heretics educated in the philosophy of the world and chosen for the priesthood.

Now, secondly, we ought carefully to investigate whether an evil intention directed toward the Scriptures, clothed in the appearance of precious metal, may deceive us.

In this matter the most cunning devil tried to impose upon the Lord Savior as though he were a pure and simple human being, supposing him to be one of the other saints. Corrupting by a malicious interpretation those things that are generally to be understood of all righteous persons, he tries to apply them particularly to the Lord Jesus Christ, who had no need of angelic protection, saying:

“For he has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may lift you up in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone.”

By cunningly appropriating the precious words of Scripture and twisting them, he considers Christ the Son of God to be one of the other human beings, because he sees him as a human being; and he turns those things that should be understood of the saints toward a contrary and harmful meaning, so that he may set before us the image of a tyrant’s face beneath the deceptive color of gold.

Therefore no one should be compared with Christ, however brilliantly he may shine in holiness, when he hears that he is called the Son of Man. Nor should anyone, by that interpretation of the devil, judge him to be one of the sons of men, concerning whom it is written: “The sons of men will hope in the protection of your wings.”

### LVI

But many heretics have arisen in the Church who said that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, was a mere human being created, but deified by grace; and they attributed to him only as much holiness as they recognized in the other saints, his servants.

Blessed Job, inspired by the spirit of prophecy, refuted this by the definition of his statement, saying: “Ethiopian topaz shall not be equaled to it” (Job XXVIII, 19).

What is Ethiopia? We should understand it as the present world, which by the blackness of its color signifies the sinful people through the ugliness of their merits. Concerning them the prophet says: “Ethiopia will first stretch out its hands to God” (Psalm LXVIII, 3). That is, before Judea believes that it will be saved, the Gentile people, blackened by sins, will offer themselves to the almighty Lord.

*Topadium*, however, is a precious stone. (And because in Greek *pan* means “all,” it is called *topadium*, as though *topazium*, because it shines in every place.)

When the Gentiles were converted to God and believed, many among them were enriched by the gift of the Spirit, so that, just as they shine with many colors, they also shine with many virtues. Yet no one should be exalted on account of the virtues he has received, as the holy man now says: “Ethiopian topaz shall not be equaled to it.”

It is as though he were saying openly: No saint, however full of virtues, yet gathered from the blackness of the world, can be equaled to him of whom this was said. For we are constrained by the very condition of corruptible nature, so that with the prophet we say: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me.”

But he alone is truly holy who, in order to overcome that very condition of corruptible nature, was not conceived through the union of carnal intercourse.

A certain heresiarch wished to make himself equal to this wisdom, as though he were a kind of Ethiopian topaz, when he said: [Note: [Col. 0927] This is the opinion of Paul of Samosata, who said: “I do not envy Christ, made God.”] “Christ was made God; if I wish, I too can become one.”

And the one who said of him in a similar sense also wished to make himself equal: “He is Christ, and we are christs. He is adoptive, and we are adoptive. He is a little one, and we are little ones. He is a servant, and we are servants.”

He thought of Jesus our Lord as God not through the mystery of his conception but through the progress of grace, perversely asserting that he was born a mere human being but advanced through merit so as to be God. From this he supposed that he and any others who become sons of God by grace could be made equal to him, not yet understanding or considering that “Ethiopian topaz shall not be equaled to it.”

For it is one thing for human beings who are born to receive adoption by grace; it is another for the one God to have proceeded uniquely from conception through the power of divinity. Nor can the glory possessed by the Only-Begotten by nature be equated with what others receive by grace.

For the mediator between God and human beings is the man Christ Jesus. He is not, as this heretic deceives us, one thing in his humanity and another in his divinity. He was not conceived and born a mere human being and then, after merit, received the status of God. Rather, when the angel announced and the Spirit came, immediately the Word was in the womb, immediately the Word became flesh within the womb.

While the unchangeable essence remained—the essence he possesses coeternally with the Father and the Holy Spirit—he assumed humanity within the Virgin’s womb. There the impassible could suffer, the immortal could die, and the eternal before the ages could be shown temporal at the end of the ages.

Thus, through the ineffable mystery of his conception and through a holy, inviolate birth, according to the truth of both natures, the same virgin was both the Lord’s servant and his mother.

Therefore Elizabeth says to her: “How is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” And the virgin herself, conceiving, says: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

And although he is one thing from the Father and another from the Virgin, he is not one person from the Father and another from the Virgin. Rather, he is the same eternal one from the Father and the same temporal one from his mother. The same one who made is the one who was made.

He is the same one who, in his divinity, is beautiful beyond the sons of men; and he is the same one of whom it was said: “We saw him, and he had no appearance; and there was in him neither form nor beauty.”

In his divinity he is the same one who existed before the ages from the Father without a mother, and the same one who, at the end of the ages, came from his mother without a father. He is the temple of the Creator and the Creator of the temple. He is the author of the work and the work of the author, remaining one from and in both natures.

He is neither confused by the union of the natures nor doubled by their distinction.

### LVII

But because we did not undertake to discuss these matters, let us return, in the order of exposition, to what we said above: no human being in whom he is human should be regarded as like him.

We must note that holy Job, in order to show that the angels are far below Christ, said: “Refined gold (*obryzum*) shall not be given for it” (Job XXVIII, 15)—that is, for the wisdom that is Christ.

And to show that even the ancient Fathers, interpreters of sacred language, are inferior to Christ, he added: “Nor shall silver be weighed in exchange for it” (ibid.). To show also that the wisdom of philosophers is far beneath Christ, he continued: “It shall not be compared with the dyed colors of India” (ibid., verse 16).

He then added: “Nor with the most precious sardonyx stone or sapphire.” And to demonstrate that no one even in that heavenly city, Jerusalem, can attain equality with the Only-Begotten, he added: “Nor shall gold or glass be equaled to it” (ibid., verse 17).

And to show that the prophets are subject to Christ, he added: “Nor shall vessels of gold, lofty and eminent, be exchanged for it; nor shall they be mentioned in comparison with it. Wisdom is drawn from hidden places” (ibid., verse 18).

### LVIII.

Finally, in order to rebuke those very heretics in the Church who, through pride, divide the faith they receive, he added: “It shall not be compared with the topaz of Ethiopia” (ibid., v. 19). As though he were plainly indicating: Those who are conceived in sins and born in sins, when they come to conversion, cannot be made equal to the God-man, even though they may appear to shine with many excellences of color. To refute their pride, he appropriately adds: “Nor shall it be matched with the purest dye” (ibid.).

Those who are truly humble and truly holy are called “the purest dyes.” They know that they do not possess the appearance of virtue from themselves, but hold it as a gift of the grace that comes upon them. They would not be dyed if they had possessed holiness by nature. They are “purest dyes” because, in humility, they preserve the grace of virtue that has come upon them and that they have received.

Hence it is said in the voice of the Bridegroom concerning the holy Church: “Who is this that ascends, made white?” (Song 4:6). Since the holy Church does not possess heavenly life by nature, but is adorned with the beauty of gifts when the Spirit comes upon her, she is remembered not as white but as made white.

It should also be noted that earlier, when he had said, “It shall not be compared with the dyed colors of India,” he did not call those same colors pure. Here, however, in order to separate the dye of the genuine virtues of God’s servants from that faction of heretical philosophers, he speaks of “purest dyes.” Those who were formerly made foul by evil works are rightly called purest dyes: when the Spirit comes upon them, they are clothed with the brightness of grace, so that they appear to be altogether different from what they were.

Thus baptism is also called a dyeing—*tinctio*—that is, our very descent into the water. We are dyed so that, having previously been unseemly through the deformity of vices, we may, once we have received faith, be made beautiful by grace and adorned with virtues.

### LIX.

Why do we say all this? Surely so that no one may presume to compare himself, among Christians, with Christ, as Elipandus does when he says: “He is Christ, and we are christs; he is a servant, and we are servants.”

When he hears the Scriptures call him “man”—the one who, for the dispensation of our redemption, was made God-man, according to the flesh from David’s utterance—he makes no distinction between the God-man, who is God by essence, God over all, and titular gods, who are not gods by essence or gods over all, but only within all.

Certainly he is said to be: “That one is man, and we are men; that one is God, and we are gods; that one is son, and we are sons; that one is Christ, and we are christs; that one is a servant, and we are servants; that one is little, and we are little ones.”

But one of us is not to be understood according to the same principle, because he is spoken of in the singular, while we are spoken of in the plural. For when he is read of in the Scriptures, we consequently understand him to be the true God, and the only one from David’s seed according to the flesh, who is “God over all, blessed forever.”

But when “God” is said in the Scriptures, it is said in the singular, not in the plural, as with “many gods” or “many lords,” because “God” is an essential name.

When, however, we read “God” in the Scriptures, we consequently understand him to be the God-man, born of the Virgin and crucified under Pontius Pilate. For God was begotten of God the unbegotten Father. Therefore we separate him from the many other men who are called gods in the plural and men in the plural. This man is God in the singular.

If you name him man, he is the true God. Just as, if you set any man before your eyes and call him flesh, he is nevertheless also soul; if you call him soul, he is nevertheless also flesh. From both—soul and flesh, of which a human being consists—there is one person, and he has one name for flesh and soul, for example, Peter.

When he speaks wisely, his flesh is seen, while his wisdom alone is heard, not seen. Yet that very wisdom is in the soul, and is heard outwardly through the flesh.

So also with Christ: his flesh was seen, while his divinity was not seen. And his wisdom, which was seen outwardly through the flesh, came from the arrangement of his divinity.

### LX.

A human being, composed of two substances, is one person, and his name is Peter. Christ, composed of three substances and two natures, is one person, and his name is Christ.

Peter died in flesh alone, not in soul. His soul ascended to heaven, while his body rests in a tomb at Rome. Yet Peter himself rests dead in the tomb, and that same Peter is alive in heaven with Christ. Peter is dead in flesh alone, and Peter is alive in soul alone. From the two there are not two Peters, but one Peter.

So also Christ has three substances: one eternal, which is equal to him with the Father—that is, immortal, as the Father is; unchangeable, as the Father is; invisible, as the Father is; without locality, as the Father is; impassible, as the Father is.

He has two temporal substances, however, which are from us: namely, a rational soul and flesh. From us the eternal one has what makes him temporal. From us God has what makes him man. From us the invisible one has what makes him visible. From us the one without locality has what makes him localized. From us the immortal one has what makes him mortal.

Thus the eternal acts temporally, the everlasting grows, the one without locality is seen, the impassible suffers, and the immortal dies—he who, wholly and without falsehood, is the one Son of God the Father.

Therefore the flesh alone that died and lay in the tomb is Christ, the Son of God. The soul alone that descended to the underworld is Christ, the Son of God. The Word of the Father, who has always remained equal to the Father, is Christ, the Son of God.

These three are not three Christs, Sons of God, but one Christ, the Son of God. Just as the two things mentioned above are not two Peters but one Peter, so these three are one Christ.

Each substance performs the whole, as one person. It is natural to him to come into this world alone, made a little lower than the angels. It is natural to him to be everywhere with the Father. It is natural to him, as the Son alone, to be localized. It is natural to him to be invisible with the Father. It is natural to him, as the Son alone, to be invisibly present. It is natural to him to be impassible with the Father. It is natural to him, as the Son alone, to be subject to suffering. It is natural to him to be immortal with the Father. It is natural to him, as the Son alone, to die.

I say that the Son alone dies, because the Son alone emptied himself. His self-emptying is his coming; his coming is his humanity. This humanity is his flesh and soul—that is, the whole and perfect man.

And that very man, the Son of God, is God. The Son alone is man, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one God. He is not one man with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but with the whole Church he is one man, because the head and the body are one person: Christ.

### LXI.

Therefore let no one say: “He is Christ, and we are christs.” From where are we called christs, if not from Christ? We are Christians from Christ, just as Hebrews are from Heber; Israelites from Jacob, who was called Israel; and Jews from Judah.

For everyone who receives a new name takes that name from one worse—or perhaps [Note: *a meliori se*: “from one better than himself”]. For example, there was a king named Vuitiza; but many today take their name from him and are called Vuitizans, even poor people, so that by the name it may be recognized that one is of royal stock and might himself have been king, if the name had made him king.

So a Christian is not therefore a christ because he gives himself the name Christian. If the name Christian made a person a christ, both good Christians and bad ones would be called christs.

He is not a Christian who does not rightly believe in Christ. He is not a christ—that is, an anointed one—who does not receive the Spirit of Christ, who teaches him that Jesus is the Son of God.

There is no Church where there is no true faith. “The righteous lives by faith.” Therefore whoever does not have true faith does not live but is dead. He cannot stand, because he lies dead. And one who is dead cannot serve the living God.

He is not one of those servants of whom the Prophet says: “Behold now, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.”

According to what the Apostle says—“until we come”—you may know how you should arrange the house of God, which is the Church.

### LXII.

The Church does not consist in walls or stones, but in the truth of its doctrines.

Yet since the visible house itself, which is called a basilica—that is, in Latin speech, a royal house—is built only with squared stones, and one stone is raised by carrying another until the building is completed, larger dressed stones are placed on the outside, while inside there are tiny stones of every sort.

What do these larger stones, each carrying another, signify except those who have followed one faith and who, by bearing one another’s burdens, grow upward in charity as the one house of the Church? Thus the law of Christ is fulfilled.

The very smallest stones are those who are nurtured by these others because they are fragile and little in understanding. All this takes place through faith and charity.

For without charity faith profits nothing. If faith alone, without charity, saved, the demons too could be saved, since, according to James, “the demons believe and tremble”; yet they do not love.

Whoever has charity and faith is a disciple of Christ. Whoever does not have charity and faith is a disciple of Antichrist and persecutes the Church, that is, the servants of Christ.

Because he does not know Christ, he does not recognize his members, and he has always been a disciple of Antichrist. Since he has not yet had an opportunity for preaching, the manner in which he would reveal himself has not been apparent.

Catholics and heretics are revealed in preaching. Catholics are always Catholics, because they are always simple and upright in heart. They always seek to conceal their good deeds and make their evil deeds public, so that people may believe them inwardly to be what they appear outwardly.

Yet they are not revealed in peace until the battle of faithlessness has arisen, as the Prophet says: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Ps. 41:9).

In the holy Scriptures, “day” sometimes signifies prosperity, while “night” signifies the tribulation of persecution. The servants of God are then revealed through faith when heretics begin to preach their heresies.

Hence the Apostle says: “There must be heresies among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest.” Catholics are then shown to be approved when the true faith is defended by them.

### LXIII.

What is a Catholic? One who has never been a heretic.

A heretic, however, from early childhood was never a Catholic, because he was never pure; under the name of holiness he was a religious hypocrite. He desired to appear holy before people, not to be holy.

At that time he was not called a heretic but a hypocrite, because inwardly he still appeared to be in the Church. But when he begins to preach to disciples and instruct them in his perverse faith, he appears as a heretic.

Then the leaf is recognized that had long lain hidden in the soil of the heart as a seed. And because, as we have said, he has always lived as a hypocrite, and human praise has nourished him, when he is reproved by Catholics he rises in pride, considers it beneath him to have asked forgiveness, and seeks his flatterers—above all, worldly ones—so that with them he may defend his perverse doctrine.

After he has deceived a very large crowd of the ignorant, he sends his letters through the various provinces, so that he may appear to have been the first to bend unsuspecting people to his faith and thus seem to agree in right belief with the whole Church.

All those who have been deceived are his children—not legitimate children, but children whom he has begotten through an adulterous word. If it had not been adulterous, the Apostle Paul would not have written to the Corinthians: “For we are not like the many, adulterating the word of God, but from sincerity; but as from God, in the sight of God, we speak in Christ.”

An adulterer in carnal intercourse does not take a wife from whom he may have children, but by committing adultery with various women seeks not children but pleasure. So too every heretic and perverse person, serving the water of the Church [Note: [Col. 0931D] Possibly, “serving vanity and empty glory.”], is rightly said to adulterate the word of God, because through sacred eloquence he desires not to beget children for God but to display his own knowledge.

When the lust for glory draws him to speak, he devotes himself more to pleasure than to generation. To adulterate the word of God is either to think about it otherwise than it is, or to seek not spiritual fruits but adulterous fruits of human praise, because he does not speak sincerely.

To speak from sincerity is to seek nothing in one’s speech beyond what is proper, but only what has been established by God. He speaks as from God when he knows that he does not possess from himself what he says, but has received it from God.

He speaks in the sight of God when, in everything he says, he does not seek human favor but directs his attention to the foreknowledge of almighty God; he seeks not his own glory but that of the Author.

### LXIV.

Whoever knows that he has received from God what he says, yet acquires personal glory by saying it, speaks as from God but not in the sight of God (2 Cor. 2:17), because, when he preaches, he regards as absent the one whom he does not set before his heart.

Holy men, however, speak both from God and in the sight of God, because they know that they have from him what they say, and they consider him present in their words as judge and author.

Therefore, when they recognize that they are despised by those near them and that their life and words do not benefit the lives of their hearers, they conceal how great their virtue is, lest, if approved speech were uselessly to reveal the secret of the heart, it should break out into empty glory.

By such people the Church is now attacked, because it does not recognize them. Concerning them the Lord said in the Gospel: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you.” And elsewhere: “If this is done in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?”

But since this is smoke, the fire itself is not yet shown. A time will come when they will persecute the Catholic Church not only with unjust words but also with cruel blows.

The Church suffers persecution from its adversaries in two ways: either by words or by swords. When it endures persecution by words, the wisdom of God’s servants is revealed. When it suffers by swords, their patience is revealed.

Even now we daily endure persecutions of words from heretics, when the heretics flatter us with deceitful and false humility. Persecutions by swords, however, will follow near the end of the world.

The grains destined to be stored in heavenly granaries are stripped from the chaff of sinners all the more truly as they are afflicted more severely. Then all the heavenly ones who have been caught up in that tribulation will remember the just time in which the Church now holds the peace of faith and tramples the proud necks of heretics—not by the power of rank, but by the yoke of reason.

### LXV.

Yet the heretic does not reason from the Scriptures, but seeks to conquer the Church with the powerful of this world. Truth can indeed be wearied, but it cannot be conquered.

At that time, in the fire of the persecution of Antichrist, God’s servants will remember those who are now planted in the faith of the Fathers amid the smoke of that fire, namely, the heretics.

Concerning this smoke and fire it is said in the Apocalypse: “And the fifth angel sounded the trumpet. And I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and the key of the pit of the abyss was given to it. And it opened the pit of the abyss. And smoke rose from the pit, like the smoke of a great furnace; and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit. And from the smoke of the pit locusts came out upon the earth, and power was given to them, as the scorpions of the earth have power” (Rev. 9:1–3).

The star that he says fell from heaven to earth signifies the heretical preachers who come out of the Church. Here “heaven” signifies the Church.

And because they will be hypocrites and pretend to holiness, they are called a star. Since they cannot possess one understanding among themselves in preaching, but all conspire against the one Church of God, they are called one star, although they are many.

Concerning these stars Job says: “Let the stars be darkened by its gloom.” That is, let the heretics—who will be hypocrites and who shine before human eyes as though by good works—be overcome by the darkness of the ancient enemy’s malice, and let them lay aside the light of praise that had shone before human judgments.

They are darkened by the gloom of night when their perverse doctrine is exposed and confounded by open error, so that without doubt they appear outwardly in their conduct to be what, inwardly within themselves, they do not fear to be before the divine judgment.

### LXVI.

“And the key of the pit of the abyss was given to it.”

We call the abyss a pit where the light of the sun does not spread. The abyss is the secret recess of their hearts, so that whatever lies hidden within may not be known unless it is revealed through the door of the tongue, and thus become known to all Catholics.

The key of the pit of the abyss is that very disclosure. “And he opened the pit of the abyss”—that is, he revealed his heart, and without any shame rises in pride against the Church, despises the Church’s preaching, and darkens it, so that it is said: “It is not as these people say, but as we say.”

“And the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit.”

The sun and the air signify the Church, of which it is said: “Beautiful as the sun, terrible as an army set in array.” The sun is darkened by the smoke of the pit when those who depart from the Church defend heretics.

“As,” he says, “the smoke of a great furnace.” For smoke precedes fire. And what is the fire except the man of sin, the son of perdition, Antichrist? And what is the smoke except his heretical ministers? Before the fire appears, the smoke of his darkness blinds the minds of weak people.

But now we already see something emerging openly from that smoke itself, when he says: “And from the smoke of the pit locusts came out upon the earth.”

What are the locusts except a multitude of people? They are called locusts, and they are also called earth. “Locusts” should be understood in reference to the mobility of their lightness, like wandering and leaping souls rushing into the pleasures of this world.

They came out upon the earth because they savor earthly things, not heavenly ones. Heretics always promise security in this world, and for that reason they savor earthly things.

The Church, however, promises security to no one, since its head showed the way of bitterness—the way he himself went before them. Therefore it is called heaven, because it savors heavenly things, not those that are earthly, according to the Apostle, who says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, not the things upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

This is not like what was said to the sinner: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.” The Church is heaven, as the Prophet bears witness when he says: “Forever, Lord, your word remains in heaven”—that is, in the Church, in which the Word of the Father remains. It does not wander about or pass away, but remains and dwells.

This Word is Jesus Christ, the only Son of God and of the virgin Mary, made flesh. Hence the present discussion is directed.

Because he is one Son of God the Father from both substances, the Law and the Gospel are his two Testaments. They are read and heard by nearly everyone; Christ is praised by everyone, yet different things are believed about Christ. They say that something belongs to Christ which is not Christ.

For he himself said to those who followed him: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.” Elsewhere he says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of it, he will not die forever but will have eternal life.”

And when he says: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth, it remains alone. But if it falls, it will save many,” all this—the flesh and blood, the bread from heaven, and the grain of wheat—is one thing, and it is one bread.

The Church eats this bread. But because different people savor different things, it has different flavors when it is eaten.

Our Lord Jesus Christ placed the grain of wheat in the earth and multiplied us. But this grain of wheat is exceedingly rich: it has marrow, it has fat, it has richness; within it is what you seek.

You seek the marrow, which is rich, and the fat of the grain satisfies you. Blessed is the one who understands the richness in this grain and looks upon its marrow.

Let us read the holy Scriptures. What else are they except the body? What is read by the tongue, grasped in syllables, and resounds in the ears and is heard by human beings—this whole thing is the body. This whole thing is the book.

But the understanding of this reading is the marrow, the richness, the fat. Unless you understand what is in the letter, you do not eat the richness of the grain.

You read the letter on the surface and do not understand the richness of the grain. You gnaw the rind and chew the leaf like a Jew.

What is this letter that you read in the Gospel or in the other holy Scriptures except the body of Christ, except the flesh of Christ, which all Christians eat? It is eaten when it is read and when it is heard.

All who receive the Gospel, praise Christ with one mouth, and bear the sign of his cross on their foreheads are called Christians by one name. Yet in food and drink, in the chair, in bed, in entering, in leaving, and in everything else, they fortify themselves with the sign of the cross, asking to be guarded and saved by Christ, and saying: “Save us, Jesus Christ, Son of God.”

And when priests and Levites in the Church give any passerby, or anyone entering the church, a prayer or blessing, when they have completed the prayer they dismiss them, saying: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us go in peace.”

If he has prayed in a house, he says it in the same way; if on the road, likewise. If at evening he has offered the lamp-lighting before the altar, it cannot be offered in any other way except by saying: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, light with peace.”

Likewise, when the service has been completed, he cannot leave without this dismissal, unless he has first said: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us go in peace.”

Thus at evening, thus in the morning, thus at all the hours in which necessary or canonical services are carried out in the church.

At Mass, not only on Sundays but also on every festival, we cry out: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men” [Note: [Col. 0935] On the use of this doxology, consult the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory.]

When the Gospel is carried by the Levite over the altar, the Levite first says: “Praise to you,” and all reply: “Praise to you, Lord Jesus Christ, King of eternal glory.”

The Gospel is preceded by the light of candles as a sign of joy and gladness, because the deacon—that is, the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ—is to proclaim such a message to the people in a clear voice.

Then he commands silence for everyone and says: “A reading from the holy Gospel according to Matthew,” or according to any one of the other three. The whole people respond: “Glory to you, Lord.”

“At that time our Lord Jesus Christ walked,” or “spoke,” or “did” the action that follows.

When this has been completed, the sacrifice is offered upon the altar—and it is wholly Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

He, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is God, the Creator of all. He alone was formed according to the form of a servant, through the operation of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Insofar as he is Creator, he possesses this naturally in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit. But insofar as he is created, he alone possesses this personally in himself: the one whose future birth according to the flesh, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven the Law and the Prophets never ceased to proclaim, just as he himself knew beforehand in words and deeds.

Indeed, in the sacrifices of fleshly victims that the holy Trinity itself—who is one God—foreknew would be offered by our fathers in the sacrifices of the New and Old Testaments, the most pleasing gift of Jesus Christ, his Son, was signified: the gift by which the Son of God alone would mercifully offer himself for us according to the flesh.

For, as the Apostle says, “he offered himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma.”

He is the true God and true high priest who, for us, entered once for all into the holy places, not in the blood of bulls and goats but in his own blood. This was signified at that time by the high priest who entered the Holy of Holies once each year.

Therefore, this is the one who, in himself alone, presented everything that he knew to be necessary for the accomplishment of our redemption: namely, he is both priest and sacrifice; he is both God and temple.

Christ himself is the priest through whom we have been reconciled. Christ himself is God, who reconciles us to himself, to the Father, and to the Holy Spirit.

He alone is priest, sacrifice, and temple—all these according to the form of a servant. He is not God alone in this respect, because in the form of God he shares this with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

### LXVII.

Therefore we have been reconciled through the one Son according to the flesh, but not to the Son alone according to divinity.

Nor can this sacrifice be offered by just any priest, but only by a holy and righteous priest. Nor can the sacrifice that is offered be eaten and drunk by just anyone, but only by those for whom it is offered—so that the priest who offers it may be without fault and so that it may be offered for the cleansing of the faulty.

Certainly all who wish to offer sacrifice to God for themselves desire and seek this.

Who, then, is as righteous and holy a priest as the only Son? [The text is uncertain: “Not because they are led to the work of life.”]

And what could be received by all with greater love and acceptance than the human flesh of Christ, which is offered for them? What is as acceptable and suitable for sacrifice as the mortal flesh of Christ? What is as pure for cleansing the faults and sins of mortals as flesh born in the womb from a virgin womb, without any contamination of carnal desire?

And what could be offered and received with greater gratitude than the flesh of our sacrifice, the perfect body of our priest, Christ?

### LXVIII.

Since four things are considered in every sacrifice—namely, to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered—this whole reality was accomplished by the one true mediator, Christ, who, through the sacrifice of peace, reconciles us to God and makes us remain one with the one to whom he offered it. He makes those for whom he offered it one in himself.

This bread that is offered upon the altar, as we have already said above, is the body of Christ, from that grain of wheat which fell into the earth and died.

From that grain many grains have arisen, which is the Church; and we too, by God’s mercy, are from it. Yet if we sow spiritually, we shall be reborn from God the Father and the Church our mother.

Of these the Evangelist said: “They were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:13).

That bread, which is the body of Christ, was baked by the wood of the cross. We shall be one bread with him. If that same cross bakes us, we shall be his body.

Whoever does not eat this bread, which is the body of Christ, cannot live. Nor can one live in the flesh who does not eat this bodily bread, as he himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of it, he will live forever” (John 6:51).

The wine that is offered upon the altar is the blood of Christ, from that true vine which said: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator.”

The Apostle said: “You, however, are branches.” Branches are watered and pruned; from them grapes are produced, that is, the saints who are born from the teaching of the apostles.

Every grape hanging from a branch is a servant of God, whether monk or layperson. The grains of the grape are its virtues: charity, chastity, humility, truth, obedience, fasting, almsgiving, prayer, vigils, a benevolent tongue, gentleness, patience, and everything else belonging to works of virtue.

A grape grows larger from many grains when it possesses many gifts of virtue within itself.

### LXIX.

The vine, as we have said, is Christ, and the Father is the cultivator. Christ alone is the vine. The Father alone is not the cultivator, because the operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is common.

Christ, insofar as he is equal to the Father, is the cultivator with the Father. Insofar as he is less than the Father, he is the true vine.

And why did he say “true vine”? Because there are wild vines and country vines, whose cultivator is not the Father; no one encloses them, no one prunes them, and no one cleanses them.

Concerning these the Lord himself says: “And my Father will cleanse him, so that he may bear more fruit.”

This is not one of those vines, but belongs to that vine which he expected to produce grapes, but which produced wild grapes. Of it the Prophet says: “Their grape is a grape of gall.”

And concerning it the Lord speaks to Jerusalem: “I planted you as a true vine; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?”

A bitter vine makes bitter wine, and it gives our Lord Jesus Christ to drink, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

When he had tasted that wine, he did not wish to drink it.

### LXX.

What is all this except that, at that time, Judea was in the Law? It did not recognize the Son of God through the Law, but denied and crucified him.

Now, in the Church, it is heretical perversity that does not recognize the Son of God through the Gospel, but says that he is a man like other men. It does not recognize his members, which is the Church, but crucifies him daily.

But since, in treating of the false vine, we have turned our discussion away from the true vine, let us return to our true vine and to our grain of wheat, without which we cannot live.

### LXXI.

Let us eat this living bread, which is broken on Christ’s table, and let us swallow it by sipping like little children, until at some point we come to solid food, so that, with the Father nourishing us—whose sons we are by grace—we may be able to know him.

This bread and wine, when eaten and drunk, becomes the body and blood of the Word. [Note: [Col. 0937D] “It becomes for us,” that is, so that he who has already become blood and body through the priest’s blessing may dwell in us, under the symbols of bread and wine. This meaning is sufficiently clear from what follows. Compare § 75 below.]

For the Lord, who in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word, because of his mercy—he who did not despise what he created—became flesh for transformation into himself and dwelt among us.

As you know, the Word himself assumed a man, that is, a rational soul and human flesh, and became man while remaining God.

Because he became man for us, he commended to us in this sacrament his body and blood, and he also made us ourselves this same thing. We have become his body through his mercy, which we have received, and we receive our body as Christ’s body.

And hear what he says: we ourselves are that body. And this is true, because there is one wheat grain, and one seed of grain, when many grains have been ground, becomes one flour. And one flour, when mixed and baked, becomes one bread.

Recall what this created thing was in the field: how the earth brought it forth, rain nourished it, and brought it to the ear; then human labor carried it to the threshing floor, threshed it, winnowed it, and stored it; it carried it, ground it, and baked it, and only with difficulty eventually brought it to bread.

This whole process is what you are.

Recall also that you did not exist, and you were created; you formed the Lord’s threshing floor through the labor of oxen—that is, through those proclaiming the Gospel. You were threshed when you were called catechumens; you were kept in the granary; you gave your names; you began to be ground by fasts and exorcisms.

Afterward you came to the water, you were mixed, and you became one bread.

### LXXII

As the favor of the Holy Spirit kindled you, you were baked together in one love of charity, in one faith and hope; you became the Lord’s bread, just as this bread, which has been consecrated upon the altar and is the body of Christ, is one bread from many grains and our one food, and is conveyed into our members. So also, when we have been united in one hope, faith, and charity, we are the Lord’s food and are transformed into his members.

Behold the Eucharist—that is, the good grace—which you have received and seen with your eyes. Just as one thing has been made from many grains, so you too must be one, loving and groaning over one faith, one hope, and undivided charity. For those who are evil seek nothing but division; the heretic seeks nothing but separation and works to tear apart rather than mend, to rupture rather than join.

He separates the Word from the flesh, preaching God separately and the man separately. He separates the head from the body, preaching the head separately and the body separately. And in his wretchedness he does not know that God and man are one Christ, and the head of his Church, in whom there are man and Christ; and that the head of Christ is God—that is, the whole divinity is the head of the man whom the Son alone assumed. And the man is the Son, the head of his Church, which is joined to that head and becomes the whole Christ—that is, head and body, one person.

Heretics are not the Lord’s food. For the Lord did not say of them: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” [Col. 0939A] “and to complete his work.” His work is one bread from many grains—that is, one soul from many souls, in one charity, one faith, and one hope [Note: [Col. 0939D] It seems that *to make* or something similar is missing.].

For if the souls whom he gathers into one faith were not God’s food, he would not say to his disciples: “I have food to eat of which you do not know.” This was fulfilled when many Samaritans believed in him and said to the woman: “We no longer believe because of your words; for we ourselves have seen and know that this man is truly the Savior of the world.”

Just as this bread, made from many grains, signifies unity, so also the wine, which has flowed from many grapes, is gathered into one whole and makes one drink. It is taken from one cup, both in its life and in its consumption, but only after the grapes have undergone pressing in the winepress. Before the winepress it cannot be called one, nor can it be drunk, because it still appears divided among the grapes—just as the grains cannot be used unless they have been threshed from the chaff.

Our persecutors themselves thresh away the chaff when we are threshed by them; they themselves [press out] the grape’s dregs when we are tormented by them. With knees bent, we ought to pray for those by whom we are made God’s food.

Just as wine after the winepress is poured into a cup, so you, after those fasts, after labor, humility, and contrition, have now come in the name of Christ as into the Lord’s cup. There you are the bread on the table, and there you are the wine in the cup. With us you are what we are; for together we are what you are. There is one cup in which we are, because there is one passion of Christ and one death by which we have all been redeemed. We drink together, although we do not live together.

### LXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0940D] Compare Saint Isidore, *Book on Ecclesiastical Offices*.]

The order of the Mass, or of the prayers by which the sacrifices offered to God are consecrated, was first established by Saint Peter; the whole world celebrates it in one and the same manner.

The first prayer of the Mass is an admonition directed to the people, so that all may be stirred up to entreat God. The second is an invocation of God, asking him mercifully to receive the prayers of the faithful and their offering. The third is poured out for those who offer, or for the faithful departed, so that through the sacrifice itself they may obtain pardon.

The fourth is introduced after these for the kiss of peace and charity, so that all, reconciled and joined together, may be united worthily through the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood; for Christ’s indivisible body does not admit dissension or the division of anyone.

The fifth is then the preface in the sanctification of the offering. In it the whole company of earthly creatures and the heavenly powers and angels is summoned to praise God, and “Hosanna in the highest” is sung: because, when the Savior, the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, was born from the line of David, the salvation of the world reached even to the heights.

The sixth then follows: the confirmation of the sacrament, so that the offering made to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit, may be confirmed as Christ’s body and blood.

The final prayer is the Lord’s Prayer, which our Lord Jesus Christ taught his disciples to pray, saying: “When you pray, say: Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew 6:9).

In this prayer, as the Fathers wrote, seven petitions are contained. In the first three, eternal things are requested; in the remaining four, temporal things, which nevertheless are requested for the sake of obtaining eternal things. For when we say, “Hallowed be your name. Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth,” these things begin here, but are hoped for in that life, where God’s sanctification, will, and kingdom will remain eternally in his saints.

Now, however, daily bread, which is given either to the soul or to the flesh, is requested in this age. Here also, after the provision of food, forgiveness is sought according to the example of brotherly forbearance. Here we ask that we may not fall into the temptation of sin. Here, finally, after everything else, we implore God’s help so that we may be freed from evils.

In that age none of these things exists. Thus the Savior taught this prayer, in which both the hope of the faithful and confession of sins are contained. Concerning it the prophet, proclaiming beforehand, says: “And everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

These, then, are the seven prayers of the sacrifice commended by evangelical teaching. Their number appears to have been established either because of the sevenfold universality of the holy Church or because of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, by whose gift the things introduced into the celebration are sanctified.

### LXXIV

The Creed, which is proclaimed by the whole people at the time of the sacrifice, was composed through the agreement of the 318 holy Fathers at the Council of Nicaea. Its rule of true faith excels through such great mysteries of the teaching of faith, and speaks concerning every part of the faith, that scarcely any heresy exists to which it does not respond through its individual words or statements.

For it tramples down all errors, impiety toward the faith, and blasphemies. Therefore it is proclaimed in all Churches with the same confession by the people.

The blessing given by priests to the people is disclosed and confirmed by the ancient blessing through Moses, because the people are commanded to be blessed under the sacrament of the threefold invocation. For the Lord says to Moses:

“Thus you shall bless my people, and I shall bless them: May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord illuminate his face upon you and have mercy on you; may the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace.”

### LXXV

The sacrifice offered to God by Christians, as we said above, was first instituted by Christ our Lord, when he commended his body and blood to the apostles before he was handed over, as it is read in the Gospel: “Jesus took bread and the cup and, blessing them, gave them to them.”

King Melchizedek of Salem first offered this sacrament figuratively as a type of Christ’s body and blood, and he was the first to express imaginatively the mystery of so great a sacrifice, presenting a likeness of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the eternal priest, to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4).

Christians were therefore commanded to celebrate this sacrifice, with the Jewish victims abandoned and brought to an end—those which they had been commanded to celebrate in the servitude of the former people.

Thus what the Lord himself did for us is enacted in us: what he offered, remaining [Forte: *more*?] from the supper until evening. For Christ had to fulfill this toward evening, so that the very hour of the sacrifice might show the evening of the world.

The apostles did not therefore partake while fasting, because it was necessary first for that figurative Passover to be fulfilled, and then for him to pass anew to the true sacrament of Passover. This was done mystically: at first the disciples did not receive the Lord’s body and blood while fasting. Now, however, they are always received fasting by the whole Church.

For it pleased the Holy Spirit, through the apostles, that in honor of so great a sacrament the Lord’s body should first enter the Christian’s mouth before any other food. Therefore this custom is observed throughout the world.

The bread that we break is Christ’s body, because he said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” The wine is his blood. And this is what is written: “I am the vine.”

But because bread strengthens the body, it is therefore called Christ’s body. Wine, because it produces blood in the flesh, is therefore referred to Christ’s blood. Although these things remain visibly present after being sanctified, through the Holy Spirit they pass into the sacrament of the divine body.

### LXXVI

Furthermore, as the most holy Cyprian says, the Lord’s cup is offered mixed with wine and water because we understand the people to be signified by the water, while the wine shows Christ’s blood.

When water is mixed into the cup, the people are united to Christ, and the congregation of believers is joined and united to him in whom it has believed. This union and conjunction of water and wine is so mingled in the Lord’s cup that the mixture cannot be separated from either, just as the Church cannot be divided from Christ.

In offering the Lord’s cup, water alone cannot be offered, any more than wine alone. For if someone offers only wine, Christ’s blood begins to exist without us; but if there is only water, the people begin to exist without Christ. When both are mixed in this way and are joined to one another in a confused union, then the spiritual and heavenly sacrament is accomplished.

Thus the cup of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be water alone or wine alone unless both are mixed together, just as neither can the Lord’s body—or [text defective] wine alone or water alone—exist unless the two have been joined to one another [Col. 0941D] and solidified in the structure of this bread. Through this sacrament also our people are shown to be united: just as many grains, gathered into one, ground together, and mixed, make one bread, so we should know that in Christ, who is the heavenly bread, we are one body, joined and united with him in our multitude.

### LXXVII

They say: A Christian ought always to receive Communion, unless some intervening sin prevents it; the Lord’s body is to be received daily. For we ask that this bread be given to us daily, at the Lord’s command, saying: “Give us this day our daily bread.”

They speak rightly, provided that they receive it with reverence, devotion, and humility, and do not do so presumptuously, trusting in their own righteousness and becoming proud. But if their sins are such that they should be removed from the altar like a dead person, they must first perform penance and then receive this saving medicine.

For whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself. To receive unworthily means to receive it at a time when one ought to be doing penance.

But if the sins are not so great that a person should be judged worthy of excommunication, he ought not to separate himself from the medicine of the Lord’s body, lest, while he is prevented from receiving by abstaining for too long, he become separated from Christ’s body.

The one who always eats the Lord’s body lives. It is also clear that those who touch the body of our Lord Jesus Christ live. Therefore one must fear that, if someone is separated from Christ’s body for too long, he may remain alienated from salvation, since the Lord himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

Whoever has now ceased to sin should not cease to receive Communion.

### LXXVIII

Married people, however, should abstain from intercourse for many days, devote themselves to prayer, and then approach Christ’s body.

Let us reread the Book of Kings, and we shall find that the priest Abimelech was unwilling to give David and his young men the bread of the Presence to eat until he had first asked whether the young men were clean from women—not from a stranger, certainly, but from a wife. And unless he had heard that they had abstained from marital relations since yesterday and the day before, he would never have granted them the bread that he had previously refused.

### LXXIX

How great is the difference between the bread of the Presence and Christ’s body; how great the difference between shadow and body, between image and truth, between representations of future things and the very things prefigured by those representations!

Therefore certain [days] should be chosen from these, during which a person may first live more continently, so that he may be able to approach so great a sacrament worthily.

### LXXX

To offer sacrifice for the repose of faithful departed persons, or to pray for them, was handed down by the apostles. The Catholic Church, established throughout the whole world, holds this everywhere.

As Saint Augustine also writes in the book of the *Enchiridion*: “There is no doubt that the souls of the dead are relieved by the piety of their living loved ones when sacrifice is offered for them or alms are given. Yet these things benefit them only if each person prepared some merit for himself while he was still living in the body. Whatever is done on their behalf does not benefit everyone, except according to the difference in the life each person led in the body.

“For the very good, they are thanksgivings; for the not very evil, they are acts of propitiation; for the very evil, even if there are no aids for the dead, they are at least consolations for the living. And those whom they benefit, they benefit either so that there may be complete remission or at least so that the damnation itself may become more bearable.”

### LXXXI

Why have we said all this, except because we are all reconciled in the one sacrifice of the Mediator? For he is the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. He is the head of the body, the Church, one person.

Therefore we eat his body and drink his blood, so that just as it is visibly incorporated into us and passes through us, so we may be transformed into him and incorporated into him—for it is a sacrament; it is a mystery.

What is a mystery except something having a secret and hidden arrangement? But what wise and prudent person can clearly grasp and retain these things without the Spirit of God, unless the Lord of all things himself, the illuminator of his mysteries, should wish to reveal everything to us when we ask and seek, as he says through the prophet Isaiah: “I shall open unseen and hidden treasures” (Isaiah 45:3)?

Again, through the Gospel’s voice he admonishes us, saying: “Ask, and you will receive; knock, and it will be opened to you; seek, and you will find.” By this saying he compels those who forget and spurs those who have grown sluggish through prolonged laziness, so that they may be neither lazy in seeking nor despairing of finding.

“For nothing,” he says, “is hidden that will not be revealed, nor concealed that will not be made known or understood. For to everyone who asks it will be given, to the one who knocks it will be opened, and the one who seeks finds.”

Christ is bread and milk, and we are children who are nourished by him. For when we say, “Our Father, who are in heaven,” we do not say it to the Father alone, nor to the Son alone, nor to the Holy Spirit alone, but to the entire Trinity, the one God.

And when we say, “Give us this day our daily bread,” we ask the one Father to give us that bread—that is, to let us know his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of it, he will live forever.”

Certainly, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he is bread for the strong, who have teeth. The Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, is bread with the Father in divinity for the strong, and he alone is milk in the flesh for the little ones. By eating this flesh and drinking this blood, the little ones come to solid food, which is the Trinity itself, one God.

Concerning this milk the apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as little ones in faith. I gave you milk to drink, not food. For you were not yet able—and indeed, even now you cannot, for you are still carnal.”

### LXXXII

First, therefore, a Christian must know that Christ himself was crucified—the one whom the Apostle says nourished the little ones like milk. His very flesh, in which his true death occurred, in which the wounds were inflicted and the blood shed, is not understood by carnal people in the same way as by spiritual people.

For carnal people, as we have said, he is milk; for spiritual people, food. Although spiritual people [Forte: *the spiritual*] do not hear more than what they hear commonly [Forte: *than those who hear commonly*] concerning Christ, they understand more about Christ. Even what both receive equally in faith is not grasped equally in the mind.

Thus Christ, preached by the apostles as crucified, was both a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, he is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

For carnal little ones, experiencing [Forte: *perishing*] this merely by believing, and for the more capable spiritual people, seeing it also by understanding: for the former he is like a drink of milk; for the latter, like solid food. To the former he is like a drink of milk; to the latter, like solid food.

This is not because those who are carnal recognized Christ differently among the crowds, while the others recognized him differently in private chambers. Rather, when Christ was publicly named, both groups heard Christ in the same way, but not all believed in the same way. Some believed; others regarded belief in such a God with contempt; others mocked the idea that such a God could exist.

### LXXXIII

The unbelieving pagans of today do the same, because God became man. It is this humility that displeases the pagans, and so they insult us, saying: “What sort of God do you worship, who was born of a woman? What sort of God do you worship, who was seized by human beings, crucified, killed, and buried?”

This is a stumbling block to the pagans; this is a stumbling block to the Jews. Since the world did not know God through wisdom, in the wisdom of God it pleased God to save believers through the foolishness of preaching.

What is wisdom except the Father’s Word? Except divinity? Except God? What is foolishness except the flesh of that Word? Except the humanity of that divinity? Except the man Christ, assumed by that very wisdom?

It was called foolishness so that through this foolishness they might come to wisdom, which is divinity, God. Yet they believed, because it pleased God to save believers through the foolishness of preaching.

Who are the believers who are saved? Those who believe that he is the true Son of God and true God, and that he alone is to be worshiped—the one whom the Jews seized, crucified, and killed, and who died.

“For we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, and now we shall be saved in his life. Therefore let us glory in God through Jesus Christ, through whom we have received reconciliation.”

Through the death of the Son we were reconciled; nevertheless, nothing in him could die except the flesh alone. This alone the Jews saw in him: what they crucified, what they killed, what died.

But when the flesh alone had died, the Son of God alone had died, because he alone came into this world, and his coming itself is the flesh. That flesh lay lifeless and dead; but the Word made flesh had not died, because the immortal and inseparable Word was with his flesh in the tomb, just as the Word made flesh was in the womb.

He remained forever equal to the Father when he lay dead in the tomb according to the flesh and descended in his soul to the underworld. He came through the flesh, and the flesh itself is his way; his coming is man, for whose sake he also labored from the journey.

But the eternal God—that is, the divinity of this man, who created the ends of the earth—will not grow faint or weary, and there is no searching out of his life.

Yet the unity of person is so great that, without hesitation, the man who died is believed to be the Son of God, true God; and the true God, the Word of the Father and Son, is believed to be true man, crucified under Pontius Pilate. The apostle Paul himself bears witness to this when he says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

And yet they crucified what they saw despised in him, not what he is as the Lord of glory.

That he is called the true Son of God and true God, the Lord himself says concerning himself: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.”

Yet the man whom God the Word alone had assumed had not at that time been placed in heaven, just as he had not brought him with himself from heaven. Thus it is also read concerning him: “The Son of Man descended from heaven,” and “the Son of God was crucified on earth.”

All this is true because from both there is one Christ, the Son of God: the one who descended from heaven is himself the Son of God who was crucified on earth under Pontius Pilate.

And when the devil tempted him, he said: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.” In another place he said: “We know that you are the Son of God, who have come to torment us before the time.”

### LXXXIV

Thus the ancient enemy recognized that the Redeemer of the human race, his divine conqueror, had come into the world. Yet before he saw him capable of suffering, when he saw that the man whom he regarded as human could suffer mortal things, whatever he had believed concerning his divinity was thrown into doubt by the arrogance of his pride.

For, understanding nothing humble except what was proud, when he saw him humble as a man, he doubted that he was God. Therefore he turned to the arguments of temptation, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread.”

Because he saw him capable of suffering, he believed that he had been born not as God but as one protected by God’s grace.

What can we say about human beings, and about how great the Son of God’s humility was, when even the devil himself—who tempted everyone to sin and recognized something of his own in them, but recognized nothing of his own in Christ—said, “For we know that you are holy,” and yet doubted that he was God?

Humility produced this doubt—that is, the humanity which he had assumed. That humanity scandalized, and still scandalizes, all the proud and arrogant.

For now, when everyone hears “Christ,” not everyone understands Christ in the same way. If you question all Christians and say, “Do you believe in Christ?” all will answer with one voice—Catholics and heretics alike, good and evil alike—and will say, “We believe.”

But heretics confess this only with their mouths; in their hearts they suppose Christ to be something that he is not. Yet throughout the whole world Christ’s good reputation resounds, because Christ’s Church is everywhere; it reads Scripture concerning Christ and praises Christ.

And although everyone thinks that he is praising Christ and speaking good things about Christ, they are nevertheless deceived, because they say something about Christ that is not Christ.

### LXXXV

No one can speak truly concerning Christ if the Holy Spirit does not speak through his mouth, as the Lord himself says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

They believe that God is God, and this is good. But when they do not believe that Christ, the crucified man, is God, this is evil. They say that they praise God and give him glory, but it is not true glory, because they are deceived. They also think good what is not good, and they think Christ to be what is not Christ.

That the only-begotten Son is not equal to the Father is not good. That the Son of the Virgin Mary is not the Son of God is not good. That the flesh of the Truth is not true flesh is not good.

For the belief that the Son is unequal to the Father is the faith of Arius. That the one whom the Virgin bore is not the Son of God is the faith of Elipandus. That the flesh of the Truth is not true flesh is the faith of the Manichaeans.

But since none of this is good, because it is not Christ, they are deceived in both respects and do not give Christ true glory, although among them a good reputation concerning Christ may appear to exist with praise.

### LXXXVI

All heretics, in fact—too many to mention—who do not think rightly concerning Christ are in error because they do not praise him with their mouths while they do not hold the truth concerning him in their hearts.

But when a Catholic rebukes them, they refuse to submit when defeated; instead, they devise a new doctrine by which they may prove their position. Arius and the others who thought Christ, the Son of God, to be something other than he was acted in this way.

Just as we are the children of those who believed in Christ in the Catholic Church as they believed, so now they are the children of the heretics who deny that Christ, a man, is God.

They bring forward new things because they want to appear wise. Concerning them the prophet says: “These are sons, like young shoots of plantings in their youth.” Their planting is not old but new. It is not from the old law, not from the prophets, not from the apostles, but from new teachers.

They are new because they are always devising something new concerning Christ. They are always young. Although there are many heresies, they change daily and discover something new each day. Even if the heresies themselves are old, they are new because they renew their teaching daily.

The errors of the old teachers are new, but the heretics themselves discover new things every day—something the Church does not do.

Heretics also disparage heretics, whose children they are through teaching and faith, and criticize their words; yet in another sense they say the very same things. With new words they are nothing other than what they themselves are, and they are always changing and numerous.

The words of the Church, however, are not numerous, nor do they change, because they are firm. They are not new, because they are all contained in the Creed. Whatever lies outside the Creed consists of the words of heretics.

### LXXXVII

Many do not understand why this statement is called the Creed. *Symbolum* is Greek; in Latin it is called “sign” and “contribution.”

It is a sign because it indicates in whom we ought to believe: in the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

We find nothing written in either the Old or the New Testament concerning what we should seek from God beyond the Creed. The Creed is also called a “contribution” because it is what many bring together into one.

For heretics come forward individually, bringing poison smeared with honey, and kill the little ones. The apostles saw this through the Holy Spirit and, having made a contribution together, composed the Creed, so that through it the Church might convict false apostles.

Our elders say that after the ascension of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they composed this Creed—briefly providing for themselves a sign of preaching—by bringing together into one what they held, so that, as they departed from one another geographically, nothing different or discordant would be preached to those who were invited to the faith of Christ.

Through this faith the Church prospers. Concerning it the prophet says: “Your children are like olive shoots around your table.”

This table is Sacred Scripture. The bread that is eaten is Christ’s body. And the body of Christ that we eat is not only the bread [Read: *bread*] and wine offered upon the altar, which are Christ’s body; the Gospel itself is also Christ’s body.

When we read and understand the Gospel, we sit as children around the table, in one contribution, and eat the heavenly bread. Those who say at every hour, “Give us this day our daily bread,” are not far from Christ’s table.

### LXXXVIII

Heretics are called “daughters,” that is, soft and wavering in faith. Of them it is said: “Their daughters are fashioned like the likeness of a temple” (Psalm 143:13).

They are called “fashioned” because the speech of heretics is contrived, while their understanding is filthy. They have ornate words drawn from secular wisdom. Hence they are called daughters arranged in order like the likeness of a temple.

A likeness of a temple is not a temple; it resembles the Church. They claim to be wise, because scarcely can a heretic be called a rustic.

“The storerooms of the heretics are full, bursting out from one thing to another” (ibid., verse 12), because they are always ready to argue. If you hold them to one testimony, they move on to another. If you hold them to the Scriptures, they bring forward their elders, who live in various provinces, and declare that they learned this from them.

When we say to them, “The Father sent the Son,” as he himself says, “The Father who sent me is greater than I,” they answer us: “God is not sent; God is not subjected; he does not serve. It is the dispensation that is sent.”

If God is everywhere, everything is in God. How can God be sent anywhere, when everything belongs to God?

It is difficult to find heretics who are uneducated. For all their teachers are equipped with knowledge of the world. They do not wish to labor in the breadth of the Scriptures; instead, they dream and snore in deep sleep, then belch forth what they have dreamed. Moreover, they insert it into books with audacity and defend it recklessly.

They do this so that they may be honored by their listeners and receive from them not only gifts of praise but also temporal support by which to live, saying to them: “If we sow spiritual things for you, it is right that we should reap your material things.”

They forget what the Apostle says: “We worked with our own hands, so as not to burden any of you.”

Many, not knowing the truth, consider such men blessed. But are those blessed who do not have, with the apostles, hands calloused through work? Who do not enter naked with a net into the sea of this age and are fishers of human beings? Who do not have muddy feet?

Certainly not, because they seek their own interests, not the things of Jesus Christ.

And where is that heretic detected in the Church who appears to display the holiness of religion, corrects vices, desires good, rejects evil, gives alms, redeems captives, receives guests, shows humanity, clothes the naked, visits the sick and imprisoned, and sometimes even chastises himself in penance, along with other similar things too numerous to list—things which he appears to do, and yet he may still be a heretic?

### LXXXIX

But you will say: “By what can it be detected who is a heretic?” There are many indications, but I shall propose three among the many by which Catholics may detect him in the Church.

First, in true faith. For through faith the abundance of life comes to human beings. God himself testified to this through the Prophet, saying: “But my righteous one lives by faith.” The Apostle Paul says to the Hebrews (10:38ff.):

> “But we, brothers, are not of withdrawal unto perdition, but of faith unto the gaining of the soul. Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen. For by faith the elders obtained testimony. By faith we understand that the ages were formed by the word of God, so that visible things might come forth from invisible things. By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was transferred so that he would not see death, and he was not found, because God transferred him. For before his transfer he had testimony that he had pleased God—but this, nevertheless, through faith. Without faith it is impossible to please God. For the one who approaches God must believe that God truly exists and that he rewards those who seek him. By faith Noah, having received an answer concerning things not yet seen, and fearing, built an ark for the salvation of his household; through it he condemned the world and was appointed heir of the righteousness that comes through faith. By faith also Abraham, when called, obeyed by departing for the place he was to receive as an inheritance. And he departed, not knowing where he was going. By faith he dwelt in the land of promise as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise. For he was awaiting the city that has foundations, whose craftsman and founder is God. By faith Sarah herself, though barren, received power for the conception of offspring, even beyond the proper time of life, because she believed that the one who had promised was faithful. Therefore from one man—and one as good as dead—there arose descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven and as countless as the sand on the seashore. All these died in faith, without receiving the promises, but seeing them and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth. For those who say such things show that they are seeking a homeland—not an earthly homeland, but a heavenly one. And indeed, if they had remembered the land from which they had departed, they would have had opportunity to return. But now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one, the Jerusalem above. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he prepared a city for them, the holy heavenly Jerusalem. By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he was offering his only-begotten son, he who had received the promises, to whom it was said: ‘In Isaac shall your offspring be called.’ He reasoned that God was able even to raise him from the dead; hence, figuratively speaking, he received him back. By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons and worshiped the top of his staff. By faith Joseph, when dying, remembered the departure of the children of Israel and gave orders concerning his bones. By faith Moses, when born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they did not fear the king’s edict.
