By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of sin for a time; he considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking toward the reward. By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger, for he endured as though seeing the invisible one. By faith he celebrated the Passover and the shedding of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them. By faith they crossed the Red Sea as though on dry land; when the Egyptians attempted this, they were swallowed up. By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelievers, because she received the spies in peace. And what more shall I say? For time would fail me if I were to speak of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, obtained promises, shut the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, recovered from weakness, became strong in war, routed foreign armies, and received back their dead by resurrection. Others were stretched out on the rack, refusing release, so that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others endured mockeries and scourging, and in addition chains and prisons. They were stoned, sawn apart, tested, and killed by the sword. They wandered about in goatskins and sheepskins, in need, oppressed, afflicted—people of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and holes in the ground. And all these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, God having provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.”

### XC

Behold these Fathers, who were still under the shadow and whom the Apostle named: they were saved through faith. For their souls he descended to the underworld and brought them with him to the heavens; yet even today those elders have not received that promise.

**[Note: That is, with respect to the body.]**

And where are those who say that those who rose with Christ ascended with Christ into heaven, with flesh and souls? They do not agree with the Apostle, who says in this passage: “They did not receive the promise, God having provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.”

How are they in heaven with their flesh, if they are still to be made perfect without us in relation to that promise?

**[Note: The passage is corrupt.]**

Or how can one part of the body of the Church—which has its head in heaven—have ascended, while another part still suffers and another lies buried? And where is what John says in the Apocalypse:

> “I saw beneath the altar the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and because of the testimony that they had” (Revelation 6:9).

They were not killed for any other reason, but because of the word of God, because of the Word made flesh, because of the testimony they had concerning Jesus Christ, whom they preached, awaited, and saw, and to whom they cried with a loud voice, saying:

> “How long, holy and true Lord, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (ibid., verse 10).

There it is also added:

> “A single white robe was given to each of them” (ibid.).

What are the single white robes except the souls alone, which still desire bodies, so that they may possess a double inheritance in their own land when the resurrection of all human beings has taken place? As it is written: not a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of sinners, as heretics falsely swear, but one resurrection of all, occurring at one time.

### XCI

To prove this more conclusively, listen to what follows:

> “A single white robe was given to each of them,”

that is, joy was given to the souls alone. And it was said to them that they should rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be completed.

But since we have not undertaken to treat these matters, let us return to the order we promised and discuss what true faith is, because without faith no one can please God.

### XCII

But since we have already spoken with the Apostle about the Old Testament, and since there is one faith and we believe in one Lord, let us come to the New Testament, with the Lord himself going before us.

By faith the Virgin herself believed the angel, saying:

> “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

By faith Elizabeth proclaimed the mother of the Lord. By faith Simeon recognized the Lord. By faith Anna praised the Lord. By faith the centurion said:

> “Lord, only say the word, and my servant will be healed.”

And the Lord, marveling, said to those who followed him:

> “I have not found such faith in Israel.”

And he said to him:

> “Go; as you have believed, so let it be done for you.”

Or what more shall I say? By faith the apostles believed. By faith the blind are enlightened. By faith various illnesses are healed. By faith the woman who touched the fringe of his garment was saved. Jesus said to her:

> “Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you.”

By faith the Canaanite woman cried out insistently, saying:

> “Lord, help me.”

Jesus answered:

> “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

And she said:

> “Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

Then Jesus answered her:

> “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you have believed.”

By faith the Gentile people believed. By faith belief still exists today.

But faith is varied in many ways, and what is not true faith is regarded as true faith. Just as the one Christ is preached in many ways, and someone is regarded as Christ who is not Christ, so a faith is considered true which is not true.

False is the faith that is without love. Accordingly, after the apostles had believed in the Lord, Jesus said:

> “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you—not as the world has peace.”

Indeed, the world’s peace is our war. “My peace I give you.” Wage war against the world, and you will have my peace.

“And by this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

Then all of them received this command from their teacher. After conferring together, they had such love that in their twelve bodies they made one soul, one heart, and one will.

And so that the Church might believe, one person did not compose the creed of faith; rather, they all supplied individual words. What they believed with their heart, they demonstrated through love.

Heretics do not do this. Each one thinks himself wise and does not consult the members of the Church or consider consultation necessary; instead, he wants everyone to bend to his new doctrine. And when a Catholic refuses to listen to him, he is stirred up into discord.

By this he is first detected: he does not have right faith.

Second, because he does not have love.

### XCIII

Third, because what the teacher is, such are his disciples. For every teacher is recognized in his disciples, just as Christ is recognized in the apostles.

Every teacher who belongs to the doctrine of Christ is first recognized by those of his household for what he is. As the Apostle taught, he must rule his own household well and have his children submissive, with complete purity. For whoever does not rule his own household well cannot show diligence in the household of God.

Everyone who nourishes disciples instructs them in true faith until Christ is formed in them, according to the Apostle Paul, who said to his disciples:

> “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.”

He also says:

> “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

Our Lord Jesus Christ could have taught his disciples in a single day, if he had wished, because he was God himself and could have inspired them in one hour with what he inspired over a long period. But this was done so that those who were to be teachers of the Churches might grow for a long time on milk and arrive with labor at solid food.

Although they labored greatly, they also erred and doubted; but their error is our correction, and their doubt is our firmness.

Peter erred because he denied the Lord. Thomas doubted the resurrection because he said:

> “Unless I see, I will not believe.”

Cleopas and the evangelist Luke doubted because they said:

> “We had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.”

And when they did not recognize Christ, he asked them why they were sad. They answered him:

> “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known the things that have happened there in these days?”

Jesus said to them:

> “What things?”

They replied:

> “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word.”

You see that they did not regard him as God, but as a prophet.

Philip doubted, saying:

> “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”

Immediately he heard:

> “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father also. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?”

Why do I say all this—that the apostles erred? Because of the heretics, who were not disciples but are teachers.

If they had labored for a long time in discipline and consultation, they would have heard there what they ought to say. There they would have been reproved so that they might amend. There they would have been corrected in the things in which they were going astray, until Christ was firmly established in them. Thus, with great labor, praying and humbling themselves, they would eventually have reached solid food.

And once they had arrived, having teeth with which to chew solid bread, they would eat it and break it for the little ones and give it to them—that is, they would answer with judgments that the little ones cannot understand by their own minds.

But because they think themselves wise and, out of contempt, refuse to do this, they become teachers of error, because they refused to be disciples of truth.

They were indeed disciples, but of secular learning. And therefore they appeared as thieves and robbers in the Church’s assembly, because they did not enter through the door, which is Christ, but came up to the first seat by another way.

From this we recognize that they are not true shepherds, because the Lord’s sheep fled from their voice—that is, from them.

### XCIV

Heretics are fully detected in the Church by these three things: faith, love, and discipline.

Whoever believes correctly but does not love is a demon. The demon believes but does not love. Such a person is not a disciple of Christ.

For everyone who loves believes. Love is understood only in good things, whereas affection may exist both in good and in evil things, because evil people have affection for one another but do not truly love one another.

Love (*dilectio*) takes its name from the binding together of two, because one loves another as oneself. The measure of love is that upon which the whole law and the prophets depend:

> “You shall love God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself.”

It remains, therefore, that whoever loves should believe correctly, because he recites the Creed. Yet he does not contend for faith alone, as the heretic does, but cries out together with the whole Church.

The heretic, wandering alone, runs through the lands seeking people who will consent to his new doctrine. The Catholic says nothing new, because he has included his entire faith in the Creed. He confirms it because he has love for his neighbor.

Then he also has hope, when he has faith and love.

Faith is so called because what has been agreed upon between two parties is brought into effect. That is, just as an agreement is made between one human being and another so that neither deceives the other. If someone lies, there is no faith.

So it is between God and humanity: if a person does not do what he promises God, there is no longer faith. Nor does God then do what he promised humanity, because the human being first violated faith.

Hope is called *spes*, as though it were a foot for advancing. Whoever promises God something but does not proceed toward him has no hope, because he does not go forward. There is no foot there, but a “footlessness,” that is, despair.

Love (*charitas*) is a Greek expression; in Latin it is called *dilectio*. These are the three things sought in the practice of religion for the worship of God in all things: faith, hope, and love.

Of these three, love is the greatest, because it begins here and has no end. Therefore God is called Love, because he has no end.

Faith and hope, however, will have an end. For when we see the God whom we believe in, we will have nothing further to believe beyond what we believe. Faith belongs to this age, because we truly believe what we are wholly unable to see. We cannot continue believing something that we see.

So also hope exists only in this age. But when we have seen the majesty of God, which he promised that we would see, we will have nothing further to hope for, because we already possess what we hoped for. And when a person has what he hoped for, he has nothing left to hope for.

### XCV

Love, however, begins here toward one’s neighbor. And when one sees God, it then becomes greater. Because here the person who loves his neighbor has lesser love; but the more he loved his neighbor, the more he will see the majesty of God there. And the less he loved his neighbor, the less he will see the majesty of God there.

Whoever has not loved—even if he fasts, prays, distributes his possessions to the poor so that he remains naked for Christ’s name, preserves his virginity, meditates day and night on the law of the Lord, knows all the Scriptures by heart, receives Communion every day, visits the sick and imprisoned, clothes the naked, washes the feet of guests, correctly believes that Christ is the Son of God, knows all his secrets, speaks in the tongues of angels, ascends the cross for Christ’s name, and sheds his blood for Christ—cannot see the majesty of God.

Without love, none of the Catholics will ever see God.

Those who do all these things but do not love will themselves say:

> “Lord, in your name we prophesied, cast out demons, and performed many mighty works.”

Then he will answer them:

> “Depart from me, workers of iniquity. I never knew you in my Father’s house.”

Ask now what is in the Father’s house. He was not in the Father’s house—that is, he did not hold to the unity of the Church.

That faith must be called true which is true and not feigned, which the holy Apostle commends, saying:

> “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.”

For since the same blessed Apostle said that we have been saved by grace through faith, and asserted that this is not from ourselves but is the gift of God, true salvation certainly will not exist where true faith does not exist.

When it is infused by God, it is undoubtedly bestowed through gratuitous generosity. And where the truth of belief exists through true faith, the truth of salvation will certainly accompany it.

Whoever deviates from true faith will not have the grace of true salvation.

### XCVI

Therefore the faithful mind must not grow sluggish in seeking an answer if something in the sacrament of faith seems ambiguous to it, especially in the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, through which righteousness was given to the ungodly, life to the dead, salvation to the weak, and the grace of true freedom to captives.

He is our bread, who came down from heaven and gives life to the world.

> “If anyone eats of it,” he says, “he will live forever.”

As the Prophet says:

> “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels.”

### XCVII

But perhaps someone will say: “Where can we find this bread that came down from heaven, and eat it? The Lord has already ascended into heaven; how shall I eat this bread and live forever? For I desire to eat this bread. And I believe that eternal life is this bread itself, that is, his body. And I say: ‘Lord, always give us this bread.’”

And in the prayer that he taught, I pray and ask:

> “Give us this day our daily bread.”

What is this bread that we ask for daily? It is our bread, and yet unless we ask for it, we do not receive it. And it truly is a body.

Listen concerning our daily bread. Ask. Receive. Eat every day.

Let us read the holy Scriptures, and we shall find this bread. I think that the Gospel is the body of Jesus; I think that the Scriptures are his teaching. And when Jesus says:

> “Whoever does not eat my flesh and drink my blood,”

although this may be understood spiritually and as a mystery, nevertheless, in bodily terms, the bread that we ask for daily—the true body of Christ and his blood—is the word of the Scriptures.

When we read it, we eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood. And we pray that we may understand these things spiritually and recognize the divinity incarnate. When we recognize that he is truly the Son of God and true God, and that there is no other God besides him who was born of the Virgin, and we worship him with the angels as the one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, we eat the bread of angels.

For the person who frequently reads Scripture, the letter itself is the body. But the spirit is in the letter. The letter itself has a spirit—that is, an understanding. Yet no one can understand that understanding without the letter, which is the body.

This understanding of the letter is not the body. But when someone begins to read the letter, which is the body, and cannot understand it, let him pray and say:

> “Our Father, who are in heaven, give us this day our daily bread,”

until he asks, until he understands.

And after he has understood, let him question the elders; let him question the Fathers, as it is written. Let them explain it to him. Then he will see whether the spirit is from God or not.

Let him not presume to preach beforehand, unless he has first tested the spirit of the letter, whether it is from God.

Consider how dangerous is the divine word that you eat. In the very Communion, recognize what you are receiving.

If a tiny crumb should fall onto the ground from the priest’s hand, everyone trembles, and one withdraws from the place where the Eucharist has fallen. It is carefully sought so that it may be placed back on the paten, because the Eucharist itself is the body of Christ. In Latin, *Eucharistia* means “good grace.” The Gospel is likewise called “good grace.”

If someone has understood the whole Gospel and has believed the miracles that he does not understand, let him seek, fear, and tremble. Let him not disdain to seek out and find the very crumb and place it on the paten—that is, in the faithful soul—for it is the body of Christ.

And if the souls of the faithful were not vessels, the Prophet would not say, speaking by the Lord’s voice:

> “Cleanse yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord.”

And the Lord himself says concerning the Apostle Paul:

> “He is a chosen vessel for me.”

Into these vessels the body of Christ is placed, which is the Eucharist, or the Word of God.

If the crumb that we have called Eucharistic should fall from the priest’s hand and he should trample it, he tramples the whole body of Christ as well.

Then he ought not to hand on the body of Christ or bear the name of “father,” but should receive it among the other children—those children who know that it is holy. But if they are questioned about the sacrament, they do not know how to give an explanation.

The same must be understood concerning the Gospel. He who is a father and announces the Gospel—the one to whom we have said that the body of Christ belongs—and who has proclaimed the whole Gospel well, if a crumb should fall from him, a crumb that he has understood, and if he does not seek out what he has misunderstood but tramples it—that is, defends it rashly—he tramples the whole body of Christ, that is, the whole Gospel.

Then he ought not, in the manner of a father, to give the body of Christ, but in the manner of a child to receive it; that is, he ought not to preach as a teacher, but receive as a disciple.

### XCVIII

Whoever believes correctly concerning the Father and the Son but does not believe correctly concerning the Holy Spirit no longer believes correctly concerning the Father.

Whoever believes correctly concerning the Son and the Father but does not believe correctly concerning the Holy Spirit no longer believes correctly concerning the Son.

Whoever believes correctly concerning the Holy Spirit but does not believe correctly concerning the Father and the Son no longer believes correctly concerning the Holy Spirit.

Whoever believes correctly concerning the whole Trinity but does not believe correctly concerning the incarnation of the Son of God no longer believes correctly concerning the whole Trinity.

So also, when someone observes the whole law of Christ but stumbles in one matter, he has violated the whole law.

If you know the law, you will also know the Gospel. For the Gospel is related to the law as a grain of wheat is to the chaff. No grain can come to maturity unless it has lain hidden within the chaff.

This is the grain of wheat that fell into the earth and did not multiply. He is Christ himself; he is the bread that we now eat.

But the grain itself also has a kernel, richness, and fatness by which we are satisfied, according to the Prophet’s saying:

> “He satisfies you with the fat of wheat.”

The richness in the grain is divinity in the flesh. The grain in the chaff is the Gospel in the law. The Gospel is hidden in the law, and Christ is hidden in the letter. Divinity is also hidden in the flesh.

Carnal Jews read the law and do not understand the Gospel. Carnal Christians read the letter and do not understand the spirit. Christians cry out “Christ” and do not understand his divinity.

Accordingly, Jews glory in the law, but they do not possess it, since they do not have the Gospel, because they do not have the bread.

Carnal readers in the Church also glory in the letter, but they do not possess it when they do not have the Spirit.

Christians glory in faith, but they do not possess Christ when they do not possess his divinity.

Therefore whoever does not possess the whole possesses nothing in part. Since the letter kills but the spirit gives life, it is necessary that the inner meanings of spiritual words penetrate us through the life-giving Spirit.

The whole of Scripture, both the Old Testament and the New, must be received according to allegorical understanding.

### XCIX

For allegory itself must be sought in the divine Scriptures in four ways.

The first is according to transference, as in:

> “The Lord was angry and came down,”

and similar expressions, in which causes and human emotions are transferred to God in order to make them known.

Another is according to representation, or *hypotyposis*, as in:

> “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho,”

and in the parable of the vineyard and the cultivators. For the order of the things done by Christ is reported as though an image of another person and affair had been fulfilled.

The third is according to comparison or likeness, as in:

> “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed,”

and similar passages. For it is not a narrative woven together as in the preceding example, but only the outcome of causes that is compared.

The fourth is according to proverbial usage, as in Solomon’s saying:

> “Drink water from your own vessels and from your own wells” (Proverbs 5:15).

Scripture wishes to admonish that carnal desire must be restrained within marital license.

The Jews do not accept these allegories of ours. Carnal Christians do not understand them, and therefore they do not confess that Christ the human being is God.

Finally, Moses veiled his face, and in this way he spoke to the people. The face of Moses’ library was veiled until Christ, and at the end of this library it was revealed.

Thus the revelation of Christ begins:

> “The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his servants what must soon take place” (Revelation 1:1).

This was revealed to John. The whole library is one book, veiled at its beginning and made manifest at its end.

This book is called the two Testaments, the Old and the New. It is one, like a single sword sharpened on both sides. It is sharpened on both sides—that is, in the law and in the Gospel—in order to arm the faithful and slay unbelievers, just as the same book testifies in the Apocalypse that a two-edged sword, that is, his word, proceeds from the Lord’s mouth.

Every library must therefore be understood in its entirety as one human being.

### C

Finally, the perfect human being consists of three things: soul, body, and spirit, as the Apostle says:

> “May the God of peace sanctify you completely, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole and blameless for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and for judgment.”

This does not mean that the soul is one substance and the spirit another, as the soul is one substance and the flesh another. Rather, the soul itself is one and the same spirit.

But while a person afflicts the outward flesh through penitence, according to the Apostle, the inward soul is renewed day by day in the knowledge of God.

And after it has come to know God, it is called spirit—that is, the contemplative servant of God—because it contemplates God.

Through the contemplative life it sees God, not in the body but in the mind. The mind is related to the activity of the soul as the head is to the body. The spirit is related to the activity of the mind as the eyes are to the head.

Just as a human being sees through the eyes and distinguishes light from darkness, and walks or works in the daytime because the light of the eyes participates in the light of the sun, and both become one light, so that spirit, which is light, participates with Christ, who is the sun, and the two become one light—that is, one spirit.

But this does not mean that the spirit we are discussing is of one nature with the Spirit of God.

### CI

When we say “light and light,” one light is illuminating and the other is illuminated. So also one thing is the sun that illuminates, and another the eyes that are illuminated.

Eyes do not see in darkness unless they participate in light, whether the light of the sun or of lamps. The sun is understood to be Christ.

The lamps are the holy Fathers—that is, the prophets, apostles, and teachers.

The darkness consists of those who do not participate in the light: the devil and his angels, evil human beings, and the sins we commit, through which we are blinded and cannot see God.

Yet he is always in the light and sees us. All the saints who are with him are in the light as well. But we think that no one sees us when we think or do evil.

Then we are not with God, but God is with us, for he is light everywhere, although we are in darkness. At that time, when we participate in their works, we are one darkness with the devil and evil people.

Thus we are not with God, while he is with us, just as a blind person does not see the light of the sun, although the sunlight illuminates his whole body. The sun has not changed; rather, the blind person has changed, having lost the light of his body.

So God never changes; it is we who change, losing the light of the soul through sin.

### CII

Why have we said all this? Because we wished to explain, by the example of the library, one human being consisting of soul, body, and spirit.

The human being consists only of two substances: body and soul. The body has a portion of the world from which it derives its origin. The soul, however, has no origin, because it is spirit and was made in the image of God.

From both together one human being is composed.

The soul itself is rational, like an angel, and understands together with the angels. And the spirit that we mentioned above is the understanding of the soul, that is, the higher understanding, which in Greek is called *anagoge*—the angelic understanding through which it sees God.

When it reaches upward, it becomes one spirit with God and the angels. When it bends toward bodily things and thinks excessively about the body, it becomes a lover of the world.

### CIII

Such a person is called “worldly” because he hates Christ.

If he had been with God, he was God—not by nature but by grace. But because he serves the world, that is, the body, he is not called the image of God but a human being.

The Prophet bears witness to this, saying:

> “And man, when he was in honor, did not understand. He was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48:13).

He is in honor when, in the higher understanding, he understands together with the angels. For this he labors, so that he may attain equality with the angels. And in the name of Jesus he asks the Father to give him daily bread, so that he may live eternally with him.

But when he labors for things that are not eternal—things earthly, bodily, and visible—he loses the image and likeness of God. He is compared with foolish beasts and becomes like them.

The one soul does all this. It is the same soul that desires heavenly and eternal things and forgets temporal things. It is also the soul that seeks earthly and temporal profits and forgets heavenly things. It cannot gain heaven and earth at the same time unless it abandons one of them.

The soul has many names according to the activities through which it moves, although it is one substance.

When it contemplates God, it is spirit. When it perceives, it is sense. When it is wise, it is *animus* (mind). When it understands, it is *mens* (understanding). When it distinguishes, it is reason. When it consents, it is will. When it remembers, it is memory. When it gives life to the limbs, it is soul.

Although these have many names, they are not divided in substance as they are in name, because all of them are one soul.

According to the part toward which it bends, it receives the name of that part, because these things I have mentioned are its parts.

We have said all this about the spirit in order to remove from heretics the basis for their slanderous argument, since we have established, according to the Apostle, that one complete and perfect human being consists of spirit, soul, and body.

### CIV

Having established this, let us return, with God illuminating us, to our library.

Just as we said that one complete human being consists of three things, so let us explain that one complete book consists of three things: the letter, tropology, and mystical understanding.

The letter is like the human body. The letter itself is history. Tropology is like the human soul. Mystical understanding is like the human spirit.

Therefore the body of sacred Scripture, as we said, is the letter. The soul is the moral sense, which is called tropological; the spirit is the higher, angelic understanding, which is called *anagoge*.

The body of the letter is present when we say:

> “The Lord was walking.”  
> “The Lord descended.”  
> “The Lord’s head, hair, eyes, ears.”  
> “The Lord swore by his soul.”

The whole history that is read and heard, contained in syllables, corrected in letters, and all similar things belonging to outward hearing, common alike to readers and hearers, is the entire body of the outward letter, just as the exterior body is the body of a human being.

If we wish to understand all that is read according to the letter—that is, according to the body of the outward letter—as it sounds to public ears, we shall be like the person who forgets heavenly things, pursues earthly profits, and loves only his body, not his soul.

Yet both of us are compared with foolish beasts. We share one comparison, though our lives are unlike: he is worldly because he loves the world, while I am religious because I love letters.

But we are both killed by one comparison—that is, by one spear—because we both love bodies and both see bodies.

There is, however, something even in the history that must be held and understood just as we hear it. We love and observe those things accordingly.

But if we reduce even those things to allegory and wish to change them, it is as though we had completely killed our own body and failed to give it what is necessary, without which the body cannot live: food, drink, sleep, and clothing.

If we do these things, there will no longer be a body that can run on behalf of the soul. Nor will the soul remain safe if it kills its own body against nature.

### CV

What are these things that we have mentioned? They are the heretics called Circumcellions, who kill themselves out of love for the martyrs. Such also are those readers who seek entirely to strip the soul of the letter from its body. For just as the body stands on its own and receives the recompense of its actions, so history sometimes stands on its own, so that nothing else is understood through meanings, comparisons, and figures, but only the body of the letter, exactly as it is heard.

History is Christ, the Son of God, born of the Virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, dead and buried. He descended into hell. On the third day he rose alive from the dead. He ascended into heaven. He sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty. This stands on its own, just as it is heard. It is not an allegory. It did not signify another Christ, as the patriarchs and prophets signified and foretold that this one would come. They foretold that he would come. They foretold not themselves, but Christ. Christ preached himself, sent by the Father, saying: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son into the world, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”

But we, together with the apostles and teachers, preach that he has already come in humility, so that he might teach us how to live; and secondly, we await him as he returns in the glory of his majesty, to demand the rule that he established and to render to each according to his works. This history, exactly as it is heard, is believed and held by the whole Church. So also the Ten Commandments of the Law, which were written on two tablets, or the Decalogue, are understood and held exactly as they are heard. All this is the body of the letter, like the body of a human being.

[Col. 0959B] ### CVI

Let us come to the moral sense of the inner letter, which we called tropological and which we also set forth in the example of the soul: how we may ascend from the body of the outer letter to the inner understanding, as to the inner rational soul. For every reader who ascends from history to moral knowledge but does not reach the spirit of the letter is like any animal, consisting only of a body.

Moral knowledge is so called from conduct—that is, according to morals. When Scripture names, for example, a human being, his conduct is understood, because he has understanding and is rational. When it names an animal, for example an ox, it is understood that the animal divides the hoof, chews the cud, and is under the yoke. When it names a donkey or any beast of burden, their conduct is understood, because they chew the cud but do not divide the hoof. When a camel is named, it is understood to chew the cud and not to divide the hoof. When a pig is named, it is understood to divide the hoof and not to chew the cud. When a lion is named, it is understood to be the strongest of all beasts. So also with a bear, wolf, or fox: according to the actions of its nature, the conduct of each is understood. The same applies to the other animals, reptiles, and birds that Holy Scripture usually mentions.

All these are to be understood as human conduct, so that through them the reader may recognize the life or conduct of human beings within the Church. But he cannot discern these kinds of conduct unless he is a complete human being—that is, spirit, soul, and body. “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one.” For just as *spiritual* derives its name from spirit, so *animal* derives from soul. “The animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God,” as the Apostle says. Likewise, *carnal* derives its name from flesh, according to the Apostle’s statement: “When I hear that there are quarrels among you, are you not carnal and walking according to the human being?”

It profits a reader nothing to recite the whole library from memory and interpret it morally if he has not reached the spirit. Why? Because he is not a complete human being—that is, spiritual—but is merely animal and carnal. No one can come to this spirit unless he has been free from external activity and has pursued the contemplative life with the whole attention of his mind.

For any carnal person can read and recite the entire library; he can also interpret it morally and say: “See what Noah signified, when he raised the ark amid the flood; what Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob signified; what Joseph, sold into Egypt, signified; what Moses, who led the people out of the land of Egypt, signified; what Joshua, who divided the promised land among them, signified; what David, king and prophet, signified. What did the prophets signify, unless all of them signified Christ?” He can also say: “See what the sun, moon, and stars signify; what the sea and fish signify; what rivers and springs signify; what mountains and hills signify; what grasses and trees signify.”

### CVII

And since most things, whether in a good or a bad sense, are to be understood in two ways, he may construct an interpretation according to the Scriptures. Nevertheless, when he comes to discuss animals and begins to ask what birds signify, what reptiles, what four-footed creatures, what clean animals, what unclean animals; what a beast signifies—that is, lions, bears, wolves, or foxes; what flocks of sheep or cattle signify, or doves or hens—then he no longer discerns what a wolf is or what a sheep is. Perhaps he himself is a wolf, walking alone in the darkness and howling, digging up and scattering the sheep that have entered under the shepherd.

For a wolf, a bear, or any beast that feeds on flesh is not under a shepherd; it is not raised in a house; it does not walk in a flock; it is not clean; and it is not suitable as human food. Clean animals, however, walk in a flock and are under a shepherd. They are enclosed and defended from beasts, and they are suitable as human food.

By this we recognize whether this interpreter is a wolf or a sheep. For if he is a sheep, he is in the flock, in the multitude, in simplicity, and under a shepherd. He is enclosed in the sheepfold; he eats the grasses of the Scriptures, not the flesh of his brother. He is the food of his master, by whom he is ruled and guarded—the one who said: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, that I may complete his work.”

But if he does not walk in a flock of sheep—that is, in the multitude of monks—even if he recites the whole library and interprets it according to moral conduct, he is not a sheep but a solitary wolf. He is a beast. He is outside the house. He finds the Lord’s sheep. He does not interpret the Scriptures—which you have heard—but howls, because he does not expound them.

What does he do? Do we not see him doing anything evil? Do not believe it. He is a hypocrite. On the surface he wears a sheep’s skin. But beneath the skin he is a wolf—that is, beneath the letter he is a heretic. He is not a complete human being. He is only soul and body; he is not spirit, but has been separated from the spirit. He wishes to separate everyone in the way that he himself has been separated. He wishes to divide them as he himself has been divided. He wishes to tear them apart as he himself has been torn apart. And therefore he comes from outside and wishes to snatch from the house, because he is not a sheep but a wolf.

For when animals, whether clean or unclean, are read of in the Scriptures, human conduct is to be understood allegorically, not according to the body of the letter as it is heard. For if there were no sheep and wolves in the Church, the Lord would not say to his disciples: “Behold, I am sending you like sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16).

The Lord commanded us to have the simplicity of the dove and to walk in one company, so that we may not plot through anyone’s deceits. Let us also have the cunning of the serpent, so that we may not be tripped up by anyone’s snares.

[Col. 0961A]

### CVIII

Why have we said all this? Because we have begun to expound one complete human being as though he were one library; and because that library is like one human being, it must be expounded according to the manner of a human being, so that it may be understood more easily. For the library is complete, and without it a human being is not complete. No one can reach Christ without it, because he himself is the perfect book.

We have spoken of the body of the letter as of the body of a human being. We have spoken of moral knowledge—that is, the understanding of conduct—and of the inner understanding of the letter, through which human conduct is recognized.

### CIX

Let us speak of the spirit of the letter, where God is found, just as we spoke of the spirit of the human being, which sees God. All these things that we have said above, and those that we still have to say, concerning both the Old and the New Testament, urge us to receive an allegorical understanding. This is indicated by what we read in the Old Testament: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak ancient riddles” (Ps. 77:2). It is also indicated by what is written in the New Testament, when it says: “Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them” (Matt. 24:34).

For in parables he both taught the believing disciples and refuted the unbelieving adversaries. The divine discourse—that is, the discourse of the prophets and apostles—has the following custom: it displays outwardly those things that are lowly and carnal, so that all who read or hear, both carnal and spiritual, may have them plainly before them. But it conceals within those things that are spiritual and beautiful, lest the dignity of the heavenly archangels should be indiscriminately exposed to everyone, and lest it should cast what is holy before dogs and pearls before swine.

And because the outer letter—that is, history, which is eloquence—is interpreted by the name of silver, while spiritual understanding is understood by the name of gold, and one Holy Spirit dictated both, Scripture truly shines according to the likeness of that silvered dove whose hindparts gleam with the radiance of shining gold: the divine Scriptures, which are plain in the letter, shine with silver, while their more hidden things glow beneath the letter with gold.

Thus, by divine providence, it was rightly arranged that the purity of those silver words, hidden from the common gaze of all as though beneath some veil of modesty, should itself be covered by Scripture, overshadowed by heavenly mysteries, just as divinity itself was concealed in its secret. For that angelic knowledge, which lay hidden beneath the letter, was manifested when Divinity itself was manifested through the flesh.

Here, in the inner letter—that is, in the spirit—are found the Lord’s inner temples; here is the Holy of Holies. Whoever enters there now speaks with the Lord, just as it is said in the Song of Songs in the voice of the bride, who is the soul: “I will rise and go around the city; through the streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him” (Song 3:2).

It is as though she openly says: “I considered all the glory of the present age; I examined the gatherings of unbelievers and the various sects of philosophers, but I did not find there the one whom my soul loves.” That is, when I had passed through such people, who are thought illustrious in the world for their varied knowledge, and when I had resisted their superstitious inventions and reproved their foolish wisdom, I found the one whom my soul loves.

For within me is that apostle who says concerning such things: “We speak wisdom among the mature—not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed; but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom that God predestined before the ages for our glory.”

And since that wisdom, which is Christ, is not found among such people, hear what follows: “None of the rulers of this age knew it; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” As it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him.”

And because, after the tablets had been dismissed and driven away, the soul finds the one whom it loves, hear what follows: “But God has revealed these things to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.”

Every discipline of religion flows from that twofold source of knowledge—that is, from what is called the active and contemplative life. The active life is the life in which one reforms one’s conduct. The contemplative life, however, is occupied with contemplation of heavenly things and with discussion of the divine Scriptures.

It cannot come to the spirit except through history, which is the body of the letter, like the body of a human being; then it must ascend to moral knowledge, which is in history as the soul of a human being is in the body; then it must ascend to the spirit, which is in moral knowledge, where God is found, just as the spirit is in the soul, where God is seen.

### CX

Behold the complete human being: body, soul, and spirit. Behold also the complete book: history, tropology, and mystical understanding. Behold also the complete Christ: Word, soul, and flesh.

If you remove one of the three from a human being—flesh, soul, or spirit—the human being is not complete. And when he is not complete, he will be an animal, because he has remained only in soul and flesh.

The same applies to this book. If you remove one of the three—history, tropology, or spiritual understanding—you have nothing by which to live, because you do not have Christ. This Scripture is the body of Christ. And this body itself is our bread.

This is the book that is sweet in the mouth and bitter in the stomach. For when it is preached, it is sweet; but when we begin to do what is written there, we cannot do so without the bitterness of repentance. And when we observe and rightly understand this Scripture, labor rightly with our whole heart, and pray for our daily bread, we ask, receive, and eat.

Then we, as complete persons, eat the complete book; and our body, which is the body of Christ, is joined to Christ the head. He is complete and perfect, and with him we are one person.

For if you remove one of Christ’s three substances—that is, if you say that one of them is not Christ—you deny the whole Christ; you deny the Father and the Holy Spirit. And when you offend against one substance of Christ, you offend against God, because Christ is God. And when you offend against God, you have nothing further against which to offend.

But you offend God when you do not eat this book. If you do not offend against the Gospel, which is the body of Christ, then you do not offend against Christ, because you eat his body.

[Col. 0963A]

### CXI

Whenever we hear the word of God, and the word of God, the flesh of Christ, and his blood are poured into our ears, what danger do we incur if we are thinking about something else? We lose that taste of sweetness that we taste, and it does not taste as it truly is.

Whatever action occupies our mind—for example, more luxurious food or drink, clothing, or any bodily matter—makes the divine word, which is our bread, have in the palate of our heart the same flavor as the action of our mind itself.

For the Jews report that when they ate manna, it tasted according to each person’s desire. For example, those who ate manna, if they desired apples, grapes, cucumbers, onions, garlic, bread, or meat, found the manna tasting according to the quality and desire of the one eating it.

So also with the flesh of Christ, which is the word of teaching—that is, the interpretation of the holy Scriptures: we receive food according to what we desire. If you are spiritual, you will find refreshment, because you eat the richest fat, which is Divinity, and you fatten yourself. If you are a sinner or proud, and so forth—things that do not belong to the spirit—you will find torments.

This book itself is Christ, written within and without. Concerning it the Apocalypse of John says: “And I saw in the right hand of the one seated on the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals. And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice: ‘Who is worthy to open the book and loose its seals?’ And no one was able, in heaven or on earth or under the earth, to open the book or look at it. And I,” he says, “wept greatly because no one was found worthy to open the book or to look at it. And one of the elders said to me: ‘Do not weep, John. Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so as to open the book and its seven seals’” (Rev. 5:2–5).

### CXII

The mighty angel who cried out was the whole of Holy Scripture. The one elder who said to John, “Do not weep,” was the whole body of the prophets, who consoled the Church, which John prefigured in his own person, because Christ alone, from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, would redeem her.

For no other was found—neither an angel in heaven, nor a living human being on earth, nor anyone buried beneath the earth—who could loose this book sealed with seven seals and open the Scriptures of the library.

Where is Elipandus, who imagines Christ to be like himself and says: “Christ is adopted, and we are adopted. He is Christ, and we are Christs. He is a little one, and we are little ones. He is a servant, and we are servants”?

Here it says: “No one was found worthy to open the book and loose its seven seals.” How, then, is he adopted along with adopted persons, when there is one book? Or perhaps you believe there are two books: one containing the letters, the other the understanding?

But here you will not be able to evade us, because there is no [read: *nullus*, “no”] book without the letter, and no letter without understanding. The letter is read in an open book, so that what is read may be understood. And when one has understood it, one already rejoices, because one finds within what one was reading outside.

If someone cuts up the book itself, he cuts up the page and the letter; he cannot cut up the understanding of the letter. And yet the outer letter and the inner understanding are one book, and it cannot exist without both. So if you prevail, separate them. But plainly you will not be able to do this.

So Christ is our book: outwardly, the page and the letter, which is the human being, body and soul; inwardly, Divinity, like understanding within the letter. The Jews were able to cut up this book, but they could neither cut up nor separate its understanding, which is his Divinity.

### CXIII

The seven seals of this book are as follows. The first is embodiment in the Virgin’s womb. The second is birth. The third is passion. The fourth is death. The fifth is resurrection. The sixth is glory. The seventh is kingdom.

Thus, while Christ completes all these things for humanity, he opened and revealed everything that had been closed and sealed in the Scriptures.

This is the one who is the book written within and without: secret and public; open and hidden; visible on its outer pages, invisible in its inner pages; comprehensible outwardly, incomprehensible inwardly.

He is written outwardly when the prophet says: “We saw him, and he had no appearance.” He is written inwardly when that same prophet says: “Who will declare his generation?”

He is written outwardly when the Father says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” He is written inwardly when the prophet says: “Beautiful beyond the sons of men.”

He is written outwardly when the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession.” He is written inwardly when the Father says: “My heart has poured forth a good word.”

He is written outwardly when the Son says: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21:2). He is written inwardly when the Son himself says: “Far from my salvation are the words of my sins”—that is, far from Divinity is the injury of humanity.

He is written outwardly when the evangelist says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” He is written inwardly when the Father says: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

He is written outwardly when the prophet says: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” He is written inwardly when the evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word.”

He is written outwardly when Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14). He is written inwardly when the Son says: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also.”

He is written outwardly when Matthew says: “Now the generation of Christ was as follows: when his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph.” He is written inwardly: “She was found to have conceived by the Holy Spirit.” What indeed did she have, except the Word, God? The Word made flesh in a woman, made under the Law.

### CXIV

He is written outwardly when the apostles, asked who the Lord was, said: “A prophet”; some said Isaiah, others Jeremiah, others John the Baptist, and others one of the prophets. He is written inwardly when Peter exclaims: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

He is written outwardly when he weeps for Lazarus and asks where they had laid him. He is written inwardly when he cries out with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out!”

He is written outwardly when Martha says: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” He is written inwardly when the Lord says: “Your brother will rise again.”

He is written outwardly when Martha hesitates to believe this, saying: “I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day.” He is written inwardly when the Lord says: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even though he has died, will live.”

Then the woman recognized the wisdom that lay hidden in the book. She exclaimed like Peter and said: “I believe, Lord, that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who has come into this world.”

He is written outwardly when the blind man cries out to the one passing by so that he may see. He is written inwardly when he stands still.

He is written outwardly when he makes mud from spittle and applies it to the man’s eyes. He is written inwardly when the man washes and sees.

He is written outwardly when the blind man himself says that he is a prophet. He is written inwardly when he believes him to be the Son of God and worships him.

He is written outwardly when John says: “Behold, the Lamb of God.” He is written inwardly: “Behold, the one who takes away the sins of the world.”

He is written outwardly: “Of whom I am not worthy to loose the strap of his sandal.” He is written inwardly: “I bear witness that this is the Son of God.”

He is written outwardly when Jeremiah says: “Like a gentle lamb carried to the sacrifice.” He is written inwardly when that same prophet says: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him.”

He is written outwardly when he himself says: “After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings.” He is written inwardly when he himself says concerning himself: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.”

He is written outwardly when that same one says: “O Lord, I am your servant and the son of your handmaid.” He is written inwardly when he himself says: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to those whom he wills.”

He is written outwardly when the Father says: “Behold my servant; I will receive him.” He is written inwardly when the Son says: “All that the Father has is mine.”

He is written outwardly when the Son says to the Father: “From my mother’s womb you are my God.” He is written inwardly when, through Zechariah, the Son himself says concerning himself: “Behold, I will stretch out my hand over you, and those who plundered you will be plundered. And you will know that I am the Lord God almighty.” [Col. 0965D] And the one who sent me is the Lord almighty.

### CXV

He is written outwardly when he himself says to the Father: “Save me from the lion’s mouth.” He is written inwardly when in the Gospel he says for the disciples: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me.” He did not say, “I ask.”

He is written outwardly when he sleeps in the boat. He is written inwardly when he commands the winds.

He is written outwardly when he fasts and hungers. He is written inwardly when he feeds many thousands of people with very few loaves.

He is written outwardly when the Jews call him a wine-drinker. He is written inwardly when he makes wine from water.

He is written outwardly when he says: “The Father is greater than I.” He is written inwardly when he says: “I and the Father are one.”

He is written outwardly when the Father says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” He is written inwardly when the Son says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.”

He is written outwardly when Isaiah says: “Say to the daughters of Zion: Behold, your king will come to you, righteous and a savior, poor, riding upon an untamed donkey.” He is written inwardly when the same prophet says: “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear. Then the lame will leap like a stag, and the tongue of the stammerers will be closed.”

He is written outwardly when through Jeremiah he himself says: “The house of Judah has transgressed with transgression against me; they denied me and said: ‘It is not he.’” He is written inwardly when he says: “If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also.”

He is written outwardly when through Isaiah he says: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger, but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood me.” He is written inwardly when through Solomon he says: “Before every creature I proceeded from the mouth of the Most High.”

He is written outwardly when Isaiah says: “And we thought him to be like a leper, struck by God and humbled.” He is written inwardly when the same prophet says: “He was offered because he himself willed it. But who will declare his generation?”

He is written outwardly when the prophet says: “The Root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples.” He is written inwardly when he says: “The nations will entreat him.”

He is written outwardly when Isaiah says: “A rod will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root.” He is written inwardly when the angel says to the Virgin: “The holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

He is written outwardly when the same angel says: “His name will be called Jesus.” He is written inwardly when he says: “He will be called the Son of the Most High.”

He is written outwardly: “And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father.” He is written inwardly: “And he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

He is written outwardly when Isaiah says: “A child is born for us.” He is written inwardly when he himself says: “A son is given to us.”

He is written outwardly when he says: “And the government was made upon his shoulder.” He is written inwardly when that same one says: “And his name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty.”

He is written outwardly when the prophet says: “And the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety. And he filled him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” He is written inwardly when the Son says of that same Holy Spirit to the apostles: “Receive the Holy Spirit.”

He is written outwardly when the Son himself says to the Jews: “If I had not come and spoken to you, you would not have sin.” He is written inwardly: “Whoever hates me hates my Father also.”

He is written outwardly when the same Son says: “It is expedient for you that I go to the Father. For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you.” He is written inwardly when he says: “I will send him to you.”

He is written outwardly: “He will glorify me.” He is written inwardly when he says: “He will take from what is mine and declare it to you.”

He is written outwardly when he says: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you, just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him.” He is written inwardly when he says: “And this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.”

He is written outwardly when he is made lower than angels and parents. He is written inwardly when he is found to be Lord of angels and human beings.

He is written outwardly when he is tempted by the devil. He is written inwardly when angels minister to him.

He is written outwardly when his mother and brothers, standing outside, seek to see him. He is written inwardly when he stretches out his hand over the apostles and says: “Behold my mother and these are my brothers, who do the will of my Father who is in heaven.”

### CXVI

He is written outwardly when he says: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone.” He is written inwardly when he says: “The day of vengeance is in my heart.”

He is written outwardly when he says to the sons of Zebedee: “To sit at my right hand is not mine to give you, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” He is written inwardly when he says: “You will sit upon thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

He is written outwardly when he says for the disciples: “Father, sanctify them in the truth.” He is written inwardly when he says: “And for them I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in the truth.”

He is written outwardly when he says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” He is written inwardly when he says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

He is written outwardly when he says: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me.” He is written inwardly when he says: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life.”

He is written outwardly when he says: “I judge no one. There is one who seeks and judges.” He is written inwardly when he says: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.”

He is written outwardly when he says: “Everyone who denies me before human beings, I will also deny before my Father who is in heaven.” He is written inwardly when he says: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I will also confess before my Father who is in heaven.”

He is written outwardly when Daniel says: “I saw, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven.” He is written inwardly when he says: “All peoples, tribes, and languages will serve him. His authority is an eternal authority that will not be taken away, and his kingdom will not be destroyed.”

He is written outwardly when Isaiah says: “Behold, my servant understands.” He is written inwardly when David says: “Who among the clouds will be equal to the Lord, or who will be like God among the sons of God?”

He is written outwardly when he himself says through Solomon: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, for his works.” He is written inwardly when he says: “Before the hills I was brought forth.”

He is written outwardly when the Apostle says: “So that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” He is written inwardly when the Son himself says concerning himself: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”

He is written outwardly when Paul says: “God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all.” He is written inwardly when the same Apostle says concerning the Son himself: “But the life I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and handed himself over for me.”

He is written outwardly when the Son says concerning himself: “God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.” He is written inwardly when Paul says: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins, to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be glory for ages of ages.”

### CXVII

And because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one will and one power, the Father sent the Son according to the Son’s being lesser; and the Son himself sent himself according to his being equal. The Father handed over and gave the Son according to the Son’s being lesser; and the Son handed over and gave himself according to his being equal to the Father.

But, as we were saying, this book is written outwardly when he is scourged and beaten. It is written inwardly when he grants healing to the sick.

It is written outwardly when he is afflicted upon the cross. It is written inwardly when he promises paradise to the thief on the cross.

It is written outwardly when, dying according to the condition of human flesh, he gives up his spirit. It is written inwardly when, during the Passion, the sun flees, the day is hidden, and the earth is shaken.

It is written outwardly when he is buried. It is written inwardly when on the third day, after the entrance of the tomb has been removed, he bursts forth into the light.

It is written outwardly when, after showing the apostles the wounds of the nails and the spear, he also asks for food. [Col. 0968C] It is written inwardly when he appears among those same apostles with the doors shut, though he had not been seen among them.

### CXVIII

But in a remarkable way, although the inner writing of the book is more obscure, the outer part troubles people’s minds all the more. And we see those things that cannot be seen through a human being; yet, for a new reason, they do not see what can be seen through a human being. For even the Manichaeans themselves believe in the Divinity: they confess that the Son is equal to God the Father, but they do not acknowledge that he possesses true flesh. With astonishing perversity, they deny what they see and confess what they do not see. They recognize the invisible in his powers; but the visible in the human being—which ought to have been more readily possible—they do not acknowledge.

So too Elipandus, together with his teaching, confesses the Son equal to God the Father in divinity, but denies him to be the Son of God in humanity. He reckons him similar to himself, and, in his madness, burst forth into such great perversity that he made no distinction of difference between himself and the Son of God, true God, when he said:

> “He is Christ, and we are christs. He is adoptive, and we are adoptive. He is a little one, and we are little ones. He is a servant, and we are servants, because visible and invisible things were not made through him.”

With the remarkable perversity of his unbelief, he confesses the inner part of the book, yet is not ashamed to deny the outer part of the book, although the book is one from both parts. And when he denies the outer part of the book, he does not possess the inner part either. For no reader can discover the meaning of the inner book without the book itself. What, then, does a man who says, “Only the inner part is the book; the outer part is not,” intend to say? Does he deny what he sees, fabricate the things he does not see, and openly mock the Church?

But he cannot mock us, because we retain the outer part of the book, while he departs empty-handed. We also possess the inner part of the book, because we hold its outer part. Blessed John signified both the invisible and the visible book—written within and without, that is, God and man—in a brief expression. For he says:

> “What was from the beginning, brothers, what we have heard.”

Behold the inner part of that book. Now open your eyes and see what follows:

> “And we have seen with our eyes, and our hands have touched concerning the Word of life.”

Behold the outer part of the book, which is subject to human eyes and hands and can both be seen and handled. Elipandus is ignorant of this outer part of the book.

That book is so open that, even if the whole world had wished to believe in it, and even if it had been ignorant of letters, no one who merely imitated him could perish. But if we speak falsely, which rustic apostles believed in him and imitated him? None of them perished except Judas, the son of perdition, who believed him to be not God but a man.

For when the Lord spoke and brought the crime into the midst, saying, “One of you will betray me,” so that the one whose conscience reproached him might repent, all, trembling, said, “Surely I am not the one, Lord?” Peter also said this: “Surely I am not the one, Lord?” James said: “Surely I am not the one, Lord?” John said: “Surely I am not the one, Lord?” And so the others also said it.

But Judas, in proportion to his pride and arrogance, held our Lord Jesus Christ in contempt. He did not wish to say, “Lord,” but said, “Surely I am not the one, Rabbi? Surely I am not the one, teacher?” It plainly appears that Christ did not dwell in him, but the one who said:

> “I will ascend into heaven; above the heights of the clouds I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High.”

Why did he disdain to say “Lord” to the Lord God, as the others did, but say, “Surely I am not the one, teacher?” The wretched man had seen with his own eyes the powers and wonders that the Lord had performed, yet denied him to his face as Lord.

### CXIX

Let the Church beware lest Elipandus perhaps belong to that same school of thought, since he disdains to call the man God. If God is a servant, then he is the servant of the entire Trinity, because the Trinity itself is God. If he is the servant of the Trinity, where does he have the Son of God who was born of the Virgin, whom the angel announced to the Virgin, saying:

> “Behold, you will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High.”

Behold Jesus, the Son of the Most High Father—not the Son of the Holy Spirit, nor the Son of the Son. How is he, then, a servant together with you? If you are a servant of God, you are the servant of the entire Trinity, that is, of the one God, because the whole Trinity is one God.

The Father is God; and Jesus, his Son, who was born of the Virgin, is God; and the Holy Spirit, the third person in the Trinity, is himself God. Behold the Trinity clearly expressed, and the three persons subsisting distinctly in themselves. Jesus Christ, who was born of the Virgin, is not the Father himself, nor the Holy Spirit.

He alone said, “Father, glorify your Son.” The Father did not say this, nor the Holy Spirit. The Father alone answered the Son: “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him.” The Son did not answer this, nor the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit alone appeared over Jesus when he was baptized; neither the Father nor the Son did so.

These three are truly three, because they are one—one in nature, that is, not one person. The one is God, the other is God, and the other is God. The one is almighty, the other is almighty, and the other is almighty. How, then, are he and you both servants of God while possessing one God? If you believe as you say, you confess Jesus not as almighty God but as your fellow servant; or else you exalt yourself so that you become a fourth almighty one; or else you abase him so that he may be like you.

### CXX

But even if he is judged humble by you, he cannot be like you, because even in his human conception he is greatly unlike you. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit, not by a man’s seed, and alone without sin. You, however, were conceived from a man’s seed, from the mass of perdition, and from the desire of both parents. Born of a woman, you were conceived in sins and born in sins.

He alone among human beings was born of a virgin; he alone was conceived without sin; he alone was born without sin. He alone was full of the Holy Spirit. You, or I, or anyone else, if we have received the Spirit, have received it from him. For he received it in such a way that we might all receive it from him: he received it in fullness, while to us he gives as much as he commands.

### CXXI

But you say, “What I say, I say only about the human being.” And what I have now said, I too have said only about the human being. Yet, even in that in which he is human, no angel is like him; nor is any human being who is born of a woman like him.

It was said of John that he would be great before the Lord. It was said of Christ, “He will be great,” but not “before the Lord,” because Jesus himself is our great Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number.

How can Jesus Christ be with the christs, the adoptive with the adoptive, the little one with the little ones, and the servant with the servants? They make so great a controversy of the inner part of the one book—which is incomprehensible and invisible—that they comprehend it, while they do not see what is visible and comprehensible, but publicly deny it.

O blindness! O ignorance of the truth! O excessive exaltation and damnable presumption concerning oneself! These are the people who, by believing in this way, place themselves above God himself.

And if, while remaining in the flesh, they still await the resurrection, and profess that they live spiritually—although they are only human beings and were made by God, and although they received from God after death the ability to possess these things—they do not believe that God could make himself a human being.

God is undoubtedly inferior to them, if he could not do what they can. For if they, while established in the flesh, can assume another nature, why could he, placed in the flesh, not preserve his own nature—that is, remain always God, without beginning to be corrupted by the corruption of human flesh?

What an extraordinary argument concerning the truth! In wishing to honor God, it judges him. For it is a greater power for an inner substance to possess divinity than for God to remain spiritually in divinity.

What, then, shall I marvel at in God, except that, although he deigned to be human, he nevertheless appeared in the human being to be God? This is marvelous; this is unique. For believing that a human being is merely human is nothing to marvel at, since all human beings are merely human. And therefore it is not marvelous that one person understands of another that he is merely human.

But this is marvelous to Christians: that Jesus, the human being, is true God, according to the prophet’s saying:

> “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone. This was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.”

It is not that he ceased to be what he had been, but that he made flesh become what God is. The true human being who was born of the Virgin is himself Jesus, the Son of God, who was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate, from both natures: not two, but the only-begotten Son of God.

And he who is the only-begotten Son of God is himself the firstborn among many brothers. Although “only-begotten” and “firstborn” refer to two natures, because of his assumed humanity he is also called the only-begotten human being, because the Only-begotten is in him.

### CXXII

Finally, the distinction between the different natures is shown by the language of the Gospels. It is therefore not fitting for our faith to believe that Jesus lies, since he is certainly the truth. He himself confesses from both natures, and from his own mouth we have learned what we say. With his own mouth he revealed both natures as belonging to himself.

He says, with respect to the divine nature, “I am.” He says, with respect to the human nature, “I am.” Sometimes he says, “I and the Father are one”; this is divine. But when he says, “I am the way,” and “I came in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me,” this is human.

He also said of himself, “The one who sent me is with me, and he has not abandoned me.” And elsewhere: “God, my God, why have you abandoned me?” In one passage he says, “The one who sent me”; in the other he says, “Why have you abandoned me?” In both passages the words “me” and “me” refer to the two natures.

When he says, “You have abandoned me,” this is human, because God had assumed a human being, and that human being was to die. But the divinity, which was life, was outside death. Therefore, through the death of the cross, he was to be abandoned until his resurrection.

This does not mean that the divinity abandoned its flesh, but that it was not to die together with its flesh. For he did not abandon his flesh by remaining with it in the tomb, just as he formed it by being born together with it in the Virgin’s womb.

> **[Note: [Col. 0971D] The negation *non* appears to be missing.]**

It is therefore fitting for our faith that the human Son should say, “Why have you abandoned me?” and that the divine Son, who is equal to the Father, should say, “The one who sent me is with me, and he has not abandoned me.”

### CXXIII

And since there is one Son from both, care must be taken lest anyone say, “The human being died, and God raised him.” Those who preach him as adoptive according to the flesh and proper according to divinity say this.

But the Lord himself rebuked them as liars when he said to the Jews:

> “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it” (John XI, 19).

He did not say, “Destroy the temple that the Father may raise,” but “I will raise it,” because it is not one who dies and another through whom the dead man rises; rather, Christ himself, one and the same, died. He himself died, and he himself is always alive, because from both there is one book, written within and without.

### CXXIV

It is written outwardly when he himself says through David:

> “I slept and rested.”
