It is written inwardly when he himself says:

> “And I arose.”

It is written outwardly when he himself says concerning the Father:

> “For the Lord raised me.”

For the Father also raised him, insofar as he is less than the Father. And the Son himself raised himself, insofar as he is equal to the Father. Likewise, he himself sent himself, insofar as he is equal to the Father. And the Father sent him into this world, insofar as he came having been made a little lower than the angels.

The interpreter of the holy Scriptures ought likewise to examine and interpret other testimonies of this kind, so that he never divides the person on account of the two substances.

In the Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, God and man, our author and redeemer, just as there is without doubt one person, so it is established that there are two substances. The divine word distinguishes this singularly in the Law, speaking to the Jews when it delivered the rite of the carnal sacrifices together with mystical and spiritual sacraments:

> “You shall eat the lamb with its head and feet, and you shall consume its entrails.”

If you inquire into or understand only the external sound of the letter, it would seem an unworthy command for such majesty that the head and feet should be joined together as food for a vile and gluttonous people, and that the entrails should be cleansed. The Holy Spirit ordained this.

Therefore let us now inquire into the entrails themselves—that is, the hidden things. Beneath the flesh of the letter lie mysteries. That lamb is undoubtedly the one of whom John the Baptist declares:

> “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sins of the world.”

In that lamb, the head is to be understood as divinity and the feet as humanity. Give the head its eminence in the creed:

> “I believe,” he says, “in his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Give the feet their earthly humility:

> “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified and buried.”

### CXXV

Concerning these feet, the Wisdom of Solomon undoubtedly gives an indication:

> “And the potter,” it says, “turning the wheel with his feet” (Wisdom XV, 7).

And what is the potter except the one who commanded us to be made from the clay of the earth, formed out of nothing? What are the feet except that, through the disciplines of the human being he assumed, he turns the whole world toward saving institutions?

Concerning this wheel we read in the Psalm:

> “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel”—

that is, through the wheel of the world the voice of the Gospel advances.

Concerning this human substance we read in Psalm LXVII:

> “That your foot may be dipped in blood; the tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.”

“Let your foot,” he says, “be dipped in blood”—that is, the assumed human being in blood. For the heavenly nature did not experience the injury of the cross; rather, through the condition of human nature he was dipped in the blood of the Passion.

On that gibbet God endured nothing by a suffering sensation, but he endured it through compassionate affection. He endured nothing on account of a difference of persons, but on account of the unity of the person. God suffered nothing through weakness, but through condescension he suffered together with humanity:

> “He who offers food to you when you are hungry cries out from heaven through the Gospel: I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink.”

For, as we have said, on account of the unity of the person, the head declares that it is fed and clothed in its members.

> “Let your foot,” he says, “be dipped in blood; the tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.”

### CXXVI

We must know when and how the tongue of Christ’s dogs was dipped in blood. The Jews, then, are dogs, barking against the truth with blasphemous speech. Their dogs’ tongue was undoubtedly dipped in the blood of the Savior when, with the devil raging within them, they cried out:

> “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

Concerning this blood of God, with the distinction between God and man clearly established, we read in the Acts of the Apostles:

> “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you as apostles to govern the Church of God.”

The following statement shows whose Church of God is meant:

> “Which he acquired with his own blood.”

Here he plainly joined heavenly and human realities under the names of divinity and blood.

Behold, the sacred Scripture figuratively proclaims Christ as a lamb. And the Holy Spirit ordained that in the head of the lamb we should understand Christ’s divinity, and in the feet of the lamb Christ’s humanity.

And this is one lamb. With what audacity do you divide him? If there is one lamb according to the head and another according to the feet, how is there one Lamb who takes away the sins of the world? For if you divide him, there are now neither two lambs nor one.

In this Lamb you will no longer be able to mock the Church of God. You have plainly appeared as a wolf, because the Lamb has overcome you. This Lamb has broken your strength. This Lamb has shaken loose the prey that you held, and has utterly destroyed the arguments of your philosophy through the innocence of his simplicity.

> “This is the spotless Lamb who, as blessed Andrew says, is sanctified daily on the altar of the cross. After the entire congregation of believers has eaten his flesh and drunk his blood, the Lamb who was sacrificed remains whole and alive.”

Although he has truly been sacrificed, although his flesh has truly been eaten by the people, and although his blood has truly been drunk, nevertheless, as I have said, he remains whole, spotless, and alive. You, however, must not divide the Lamb beyond what you have already done.

### CXXVII

But if you wish to say how he is killed daily, or how his flesh is eaten daily and his blood drunk, while he lives daily after being killed, assume the form of a disciple, so that you may be taught what you seek.

If you take this in an abusive sense, as is your custom, you do not divide the Lamb but yourself. For when the Church brings this Lamb into the midst, and you say, “He is adoptive according to the feet and not at all according to the head,” your mockery will no longer avail.

Why? Because one person and one Lamb cannot be, in part, the proper Son and, in part, adoptive—that is, in part son and in part not son, in part God and in part not God.

Do not divide him; do not tear him apart; do not split him. He abounds whole for all. He alone is sufficient for all. Yet, although you try to divide him, you will not be able to divide him. The union is inseparable.

Such was the assumption that made God man and man God, and made one Christ from both. The eminent prophet Isaiah testifies that God would come to earth in these two substances:

> “Drop down, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One.”

Concerning the human being he immediately added:

> “Let the earth open, and let it bring forth the Savior.”

For in the body of the Virgin Mary he made the purest earth fertile with a heavenly seed.

Blessed Job also, who foreshadowed not only the presence of the Redeemer but also his Passion, says:

> “Again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see the Lord” (Job XIX, 26–27).

This statement shines forth with the light of a twofold meaning. That is, Job prefigured the Church in Christ and in the Church; in his flesh he promises that he will rise again and recognize God made man in the flesh that was his own.

For just as Job’s flesh was no one other than Job, so the flesh of the Word of God was no one other than God.

> “In my flesh I shall see the Lord”—

that is, in the flesh in which I exist, in that flesh I shall rise.

The following statement confirms this, saying:

> “Whom I myself shall see, and not another, and my eyes shall behold him.”

In his own person he said this concerning the whole Church, because it will be fulfilled after the resurrection. Concerning Christ, however, the preceding interpretation contains the meaning that he would recognize his own flesh in him and acknowledge the flesh and divinity as one Christ God: in his flesh—that is, in the frailty of his human condition—he would see God as man.

### CXXVIII

It is also clear from this how we are to understand the distinction. One is that birth or nature in which, according to the Apostle, he was “made of a woman, made under the law”; another is that in which “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God”; another is that in which, created from Mary, he is humbled on earth; another is that in which, remaining without beginning, he created heaven and earth.

According to this principle Christ is to be understood as all these things in likeness, but not all these things in their proper reality. He draws the forms of names from inferior things so that he may be understood more easily. He is called at one time a lion, at another a lamb, at another bread, at another a vine. Likewise he is called a flower, a way, a door, a rock, a mountain, a cornerstone, a stone of stumbling, a foundation, a sheep, a ram, a kid, a calf, a serpent, a worm, and an eagle.

All these things are to be understood as Christ according to likeness, not according to their proper reality. If you ask me what Christ is in his proper reality, he is God and man, one person. For:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

Behold his proper reality.

### CXXIX

If you ask me about his incarnation, we state his proper reality. He is the only Son eternally begotten from the Father, begotten from eternity, equal to the one who begets him, through whom all things were made; immutable with the Father, and, having received the form of a human being, not changed.

From the incarnation he is the son of man and the Son of God. All that I have said is not likeness but reality; that is, Christ is, in his proper reality, the Son of God.

For those things that we mentioned above are likenesses of Christ; they are not Christ himself. By likeness Christ is many things that he is not in his proper reality.

But if you examine the proper realities of the things that you are accustomed to see, Christ is not a lion, because he is not a wild animal. He is not a lamb, because he is not livestock. He is not bread, because he was not produced from grass. He is not a vine, because he is not a tree. He is not a flower, because he is not the seed of a plant. He is not a way, because brute animals do not walk through him. He is not a door, because a craftsman did not make him. He is not a mountain, because he is not a forest. He is not a rock, because he is not hard and insensible. He is not a cornerstone, because he was not assembled by a builder. He is not a stone of stumbling, because he did not block the road.

He is not a sheep or a ram, because he is not horned livestock. He is not a kid, because he is not from a goat. He is not a calf, because he is not from a cow. He is not a serpent or a worm, because he is not a creeping creature. He is not an eagle, because he is not a flying creature.

He is also called a shepherd by likeness, and a book; but he is not a shepherd, because he is not the keeper of four-footed sheep. Nor is he a book, because he was not made by a writer from sheep’s skins.

The careful reader should seek to understand from these small examples, and from other similar things of this kind, what Christ is according to his proper reality and what is understood by likeness.

### CXXX

He is called a lion because of kingship and strength. A lamb because of innocence, since he came in gentleness. He is called bread because he is flesh. A vine because we have been redeemed by his blood. A flower because he is chosen. A way because through him we go to God. A door because through him we enter to God. A mountain because he is strong. A rock because he is the firmness of believers.

A cornerstone either because he *ediocise*—that is, joins—two walls, the Jewish people and the Gentiles coming to faith, into one structure, the Church; or because in himself he makes peace between angels and human beings.

> **[Note: [Col. 0975] He appears to have derived ἐδιῴκησε (*ediōikēse*) from διοικέω (*dioikeō*), meaning “administer, govern, order, arrange,” and to have rendered it in Latin characters as *ediocise*.]**

He is called a stone of stumbling because, coming in humility, the Jews or unbelieving people stumbled over him; and he became a rock of scandal, as the Apostle says:

> “To the Jews, indeed, a stumbling block.”

He is called a foundation because faith in him is most firm, or because through him the catholic Church was established.

A sheep because of patience. A ram because of sovereignty. A kid because of the likeness of sinful flesh. A calf because he was sacrificed for us. A serpent because of death and wisdom. A worm because he rose again. An eagle because after the resurrection he returned to the stars.

A shepherd because he is the guardian of human beings. A book because in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. In “wisdom” is understood the whole fullness of divinity—that is, his own, the Father’s, and the Holy Spirit’s. In “knowledge” is understood the whole fullness of our humanity, which the Son alone assumed from the Virgin, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

For when many read this book and all hear it, many suspect many things about it, and the intention is diverse. Moreover, only a few understand, and not all the wicked will understand. The learned, however, will understand, because the book is closed and sealed, yet publicly and openly revealed. Unless he himself explains himself, no unbeliever will be able to understand him. For he is opened to believers and closed to unbelievers.

Hence it is said through Daniel:

> “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied.”

And, as we said above, in the proper section of the revelation the angel says to John:

> “Seal up what the seven thunders have spoken.”

Yet at the end of that same revelation he commands:

> “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book.”

What does this mean except that, as the end of the world approaches, heavenly knowledge is opened and advances, growing more broadly together with the body?

### CXXXI

Hence it is said through Daniel:

> “Many shall pass through.”

And knowledge shall be multiplied. Already, as we said above, in the proper section of the revelation the angel says to John:

> “Seal up what the seven thunders have spoken.”

Yet at the end of the same revelation he commands:

> “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book.”

Behold the book: sealed, closed, and revealed; manifest and open, and not sealed. For the beginning of the revelation is ordered to be sealed at the head of the book, while the end of the book is forbidden to be sealed. Whatever lay hidden at the beginning in the preaching of the holy Church, the end reveals day by day.

For just as the age of each human being is described from infancy to old age, so the Church was then little, when, newly born, she could not preach the word of life. Hence it is said of her:

> “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts.”

For, before the holy Church advanced through growth in virtue, the breasts of preaching could not be offered to the weaker listeners.

The Church is called mature when, joined to the Word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit, she carries the mystery of preaching in the conception of children, because those whom she conceives by exhortation she gives birth to by conversion.

Concerning this age of hers it is said to the Lord:

> “Young women have loved you.”

All the churches that together make one catholic Church are called young women. They are no longer old through fault, but new through grace; not barren through age, but, in the age of the mind, suited to spiritual fruitfulness.

Then, when in those days the Church, weakened as though by a certain old age, does not wish to bear children through preaching, she remembers her former fruitfulness, saying that verse from Job:

> “As I was in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tabernacle.”

Although after those days in which she is brought low, she is already strengthened near the very end of time by the great power of preaching, once the Gentiles have been received in full she draws the whole Israelite people who will then be found into the bosom of faith.

For it is written:

> “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Romans XI, 25–26).

### CXXXII

But before those times there will be days in which she appears to be oppressed for a little while by adversaries, when she also remembers the days of her youth, saying:

> “As I was in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tabernacle.”

What is the tabernacle in this passage except the secrecy of the mind, the quietness of the spirit, and the contemplative life without any persecution?

Nevertheless, when at the end of the world the Church begins to be tossed by persecutions, she will not be able to possess quietness of mind. Then she recalls what the Truth itself says in the Gospel:

> “False christs and false prophets will arise, and they will give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led astray.”

At present our faithful perform wonders while suffering perversities; but then the saints will suffer perversities and perform no miracles. At that time, however, the preachers of Antichrist—that is, heretics—will perform wonders even while inflicting perversities.

Therefore he warns us, saying:

> “If they then say to you, ‘Behold, Christ is in the desert,’ do not go out. ‘Behold, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it.”

As though he were saying openly: If anyone promises you that Christ dwells in the desert of the Gentiles and in the doctrine of philosophers, or in the inner rooms of heretics who promise the secrets of God, do not go out; do not believe. This is because, in a time of persecution and distress, false prophets always find a place in which to deceive.

If anyone wishes to boast of himself under the name of Christ, do not immediately give him your faith. For just as lightning goes out from the East and appears as far as the West, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.

Do not go out; do not believe that the Son of Man is either in the desert of the nations or in the inner rooms of heretics. Rather, his faith, handed down by the apostles, shines from East to West in the catholic Churches.

### CXXXIII

Nor should this be passed over; it must be preached before the whole Church, both to the wise and to the uneducated: the Savior’s second coming is to be displayed not in humility, as before, but in glory.

It is foolish to seek him in a small place or in hiding, since he is the light of the whole world. Concerning him we read:

> “God will come openly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm will surround him.”

Understand here also the proper reality of both substances. He is believed to come in the truth of the body he assumed, and he will be called God. He was present hidden in weakness; he will be present manifest in power.

> “Fire,” he says, “will burn before him, and he will set his enemies ablaze around him.”

When the reverence surrounding his present coming will be such, consider what the form of the judgment will be. He will indeed return what he promised, but he will exact what he redeemed.

### CXXXIV

And therefore let us strive with all our strength, through his assistance, so that whatever he bestowed when he was judged, he who is to judge may find whole in us.

If, therefore, living in faith, justice, mercy, charity, and chastity, we remain in his fear, we already hold a great number of his pledges. Without doubt he will give us his kingdom. He will give us what is his to us, since he deigned to offer himself for us. Amen.

## BOOK TWO: ON CHRIST AND HIS BODY, WHICH IS THE CHURCH, AND ON THE DEVIL AND HIS BODY, WHICH IS ANTICHRIST

### I

We have written this apology [perhaps: “on account of” or “because of” your accusations], by which you never cease declaring us heretics, ignorant of the faith, and disciples of Antichrist—not in the panegyric manner of a speech of falsehood, nor with the obscurities of smoky eloquence, but in clear meaning, so that all who hear may be able to understand.

An apology is a defense in which one responds to those making accusations in defense of oneself. Therefore we have answered those who accuse us, and, with God’s illumination, have found ourselves cleansed of heresy.

A panegyric is a licentious and wanton kind of speech, used in the praises of kings, in whose composition they flatter with many falsehoods. We have not composed falsehood in our apologies in praise of any earthly king; rather, we have presented the true faith that we received from the very disciples of the Truth.

### II

But because your little books, in which you confess that we are heretics, have now been circulated publicly in various regions of the earth, so that all who read them may, according to your faith, proclaim you a Catholic teacher of the see of Toledo, a new archbishop, and us, Heterius and Beatus, ignorant and heretical men from the Lebanon and disciples of Antichrist; and because controversy has arisen on both sides and a different faith is being put forward, you inflict upon us not only ill repute but also disgrace.

“Fame” is understood both in a good and in a bad sense. “Disgrace,” however, is always turned only toward the bad. It is called *ignominia*—disgrace—because the person who is caught in some crime ceases to possess the name of honor. It is called *ignominia*, as though “without a name,” just as *ignarus* means “without knowledge,” and *ignobilis* means “without nobility.”

This is also called *infamia*, as though “without good fame.” Therefore you proclaim disgrace together with bad fame against us, so that, without distinction, you alone may appear to possess good fame in the Church.

Certainly your fame and ours are now of this kind: good fame has been added not by another but by you alone, and infamy—that is, disgrace—has also been added, so that those who had no name and cannot possess a name in comparison with me may have one.

This fame is public, and certainly no fame could exist without cause. Fame is called *fama* from *fari*, that is, “to speak,” because by speaking it spreads through the channels of tongues, resounding in the ears of those who hear.

As we have said, the word denotes both good and bad things. Since both kinds of fame exist, whether yours or ours, the matter is uncertain. Therefore the name “fame” has no secure place, because perhaps fame is false, adding much to the truth or diminishing from it.

Truth alone is sufficient for itself between the two, because nothing can be added to it or taken away from it. It is wearied until it is proved. Once it has been proved, it ceases to be called fame; from then on the matter itself is named, not fame.

A liar always fails together with his lie. He cannot be a liar without a lie for as long as he fabricates falsehood. When he abandons the lie, he ceases to be a liar.

A lie is nothing other than the absence of truth. A liar, however, is a substance; a lie is not a substance, but a quality in a substance.

Every substance created by the good God is good. But vice was not created by God; it was invented by the devil. For God the Father begot the Son, who is truth; and Truth was born from Truth, that is, substance from substance. Both together are one substance, just as both together are one truth.

The devil, however, is a good created substance, because everything that God made is very good. The devil became what he is by his own will, not by God’s creative act. He is the author of the lie, because he begot the lie. And because he begot the lie, he is the father of the lie.

For, as we said above, a lie is not a substance but only a quality. The devil alone, however, is a substance, because he is the father of a quality, not of a substance.

### III

And what is a quality? It is that which makes each thing what sort of thing it is. For in bodies there are quality and quantity. Quality is that of a body which makes it white or black; quantity, that which makes it long or short. Thus, in bodies quality refers to color, and quantity to measure.

In spiritual things, however, quality exists without quantity, as when we say, “There is an angel.” Since there is a substance of both good and evil angels, we distinguish the angel by quality when we say “a good angel” and “an evil angel.” A good angel is not good from himself, as God is, but becomes good by adhering to the good God. An evil angel, however, is evil not from the good God but from himself. Whatever is substance comes from the good God; but whatever is evil is evil from itself alone, not evil from the good God. And how did he become evil, unless he became evil by not adhering to God? Conversely, a good angel is good by adhering to God.

Why, then, did the devil not adhere to God so as to be good, except because he is a liar? For from the beginning he was a liar, according to the Lord’s saying, “and he never stood in the truth.” For truth is God, as we said above, and he scorned to stand in that truth. He devised a lie, because he wanted to seize by robbery what God possessed by nature, saying, “I shall be like the Most High.” He is therefore a liar because he spoke from his own, composed from his own, devised from his own, and learned from himself what he said. And because he learned from himself, he sought his own glory, since he spoke from himself.

Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever speaks a lie speaks from his own.” And whoever speaks from himself seeks his own glory. “I do not seek my own glory, but that of the one who sent me.”

Now the devil, who appeared as the father of lies, first deceived humanity in paradise through that very lie, saying against the Lord’s commandment: “You will be like gods if you eat from the forbidden tree.” This lie was not invented by humanity, but by the devil. Humanity did not learn what it did from itself, but, instigated by the devil, received it. Humanity became the devil’s child through the lie, because the lie itself has the devil as its father. Through this lie the human race was given to drink.

Even now, in the Church, all who are liars receive from that same spirit of error what makes them liars. Those who proclaim the truth in the Church are not truthful from themselves; rather, they receive from Truth the source from which they proclaim the truth.

### IV

We said above that Truth, the Father, begot the Son who is Truth; and that the Father, who is substance, begot the Son of his substance, through whom he established all things. Therefore the Son, God, is not from himself in the way that the Father is God from himself; rather, since he is from another—that is, from the Father—he is not from himself.

The devil, however, although he had been made good by the good God, begot a lie—not a son of his own nature, which was substance, but a quality in substance—so that this quality could exist nowhere except in substance, which is good. Thus, good can exist without evil, but evil cannot exist without good, because no evil is substance; it is only the privation of good.

Just as darkness is not any substance, but merely the absence of light; just as death is not any substance, but merely the absence of life; just as hunger is not any substance, but merely the absence of food; just as nakedness is not any substance, but merely the absence of clothing; so pride is not any substance, but the absence of humility; discord is not any substance, but the absence of charity; anger is not any substance, but the absence of patience; and likewise a lie is not any substance, but the absence of truth.

### V

You surely say that I am that lying spirit of error. When you say this, it is plainly understood that you profess yourself to be truthful when you call me a liar. For you say to your Faithful One—whom, I think, was already known to you:

> “But since I have heard that the forerunner of Antichrist has appeared in our midst, because he announces that he has already been born, I ask you to inquire from him where, or how, or when that lying spirit of the prophets who speaks in him was born, so that you may make us certain.”

Many understand this when they read the cloud of your words, which you write under allegory so that a question may arise among interpreters and so that they may explain you, as though you were a new prophet speaking enigmatically. If you should find your admirers—people able to fabricate many speculative notions as you fabricate them—and if, flattering you in the manner of a panegyric, they answer you only in order to act against us as you do, then you may regard them as most learned teachers, even though they speak a lie.

And how do you know that I am the forerunner of Antichrist, whom you specifically identify as such? You say: “He has appeared in our midst.” What does “in your midst” mean, or how many are you, in whose midst I am? You ought to name and define the character of your own party, just as you define the character of the party of Antichrist.

The name “Antichrist” sounds like one name, but there are many Antichrists. They have existed in the Church and have gone out from the Church. For the name “Antichrist” means nothing other than “one opposed to Christ.” When someone opposed to Christ is found, he appears to be a liar. When he appears to be a liar, he appears to be a son of the devil. And every liar is a son of the devil, because the devil, as we said above, is the father of lies.

### VI

Let us now inquire who the liar is. Let the apostle John speak. For he says:

> “Everyone who confesses that Jesus is not the Son of God is a liar, and he is the Antichrist.”

You say that Jesus is not the Son of God. And who is Jesus except that man who was born of the Virgin? Behold: whoever denies that this Jesus is the Son of God is the Antichrist and speaks a lie, because we all believe that Jesus is the Son of God.

Now see who the forerunner of Antichrist is who has appeared in your midst. How did he appear who was born? Before he was born, he was the forerunner of Antichrist. But after he was born, he was no longer the forerunner; he was himself the Antichrist. What is his birth except his appearance? And what is his appearance except his manifestation? And what is his manifestation except his preaching?

Before he preached, he was the forerunner of Antichrist, because he did not wish to understand Christ so as to do good; rather, he meditated iniquity on his bed and stood upon every evil way. Since he stood upon every evil way, he was without doubt the forerunner of Antichrist. And when he publicly preaches the iniquity that he meditated for so long on his bed—that is, in the secrecy of his heart—he is without doubt the Antichrist, because he denies that Jesus is the Son of God.

### VII

But perhaps you say: “How do you affirm that he is the Antichrist?” How do I affirm it? Listen: because he did not hate wickedness. The prophet said this, not I:

> “He did not wish to understand, so as to do good. He meditated iniquity on his bed; he stood upon every evil way, and he did not hate wickedness.”

These three things belong to the lie, not to the truth.

Now the Antichrist has his own antichrists. When he comes, will the Antichrist do anything other than fight against Christ, refuse his Gospel, and say, “I am Christ”? You also say: “We are christs, just as Christ is.”

And the Lord warns us, saying:

> “Pseudo-Christs and pseudo-prophets will arise; and they will give signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect.”

We have already learned this by experience, because many, even of the elect, were disturbed, although only for a short time, by this preaching of yours—contrary to truth and faith. **[Note: [Col. 0981D] “Preaching,” or something similar.]** Indeed, when we first heard it, we were all disturbed. Therefore we are not forerunners of Antichrist. Even if we erred with Peter, we now lament our errors with him, and publicly confess that Jesus is Christ, the Son of God.

And whoever does not believe as we believe, we do not doubt that he himself is the Antichrist—not that particular one who is to come in bodily form, but those whom the apostle John mentioned:

> “Now there are many Antichrists in the Church.”

They went out from us, but they were not of us; that is, they were not in our faith. For if they had been of our faith, they would certainly have remained with us. Therefore they are called antichrists after the Antichrist—that is, they are called those opposed to Christ—because they fight against Christ.

For just as Christ had David, or the others who were called christs and prefigured him, as his mediators, so that son of perdition, the Antichrist, has those who prefigure him and bear the name “Antichrist.” He is called Antichrist because he will come against Christ.

He is not called Antichrist in the way simple people understand the term—as though he were called Antichrist because he will come before Christ, that is, because Christ will come after him. It is not so. In Greek, *Antichrist* means in Latin “opposed to Christ,” for the Greek word *anti* signifies *against* in Latin.

He will falsely claim to be Christ when he comes, yet he will fight against Christ and oppose his sacraments, so as to destroy the truth of the Gospel. He will accept nothing except the Mosaic law and will urge the people toward circumcision. He will even attempt to restore the temple in Jerusalem and renew all the ceremonies of the old law.

### VIII

That man also is the Antichrist who denies that Jesus Christ is God. For, as we said, he is opposed to Christ. That man also is the Antichrist who does not believe that Jesus Christ is God but dissents from Christ in his works. He believes in Christ by faith but denies him by his actions.

Concerning such people the Apostle says:

> “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him.”

For every person departs from his Creator either in faith or in works. Just as the one who departs in faith is an Antichrist, so the one who departs from the almighty God in works is called an apostate, even if he appears to maintain the faith within the Church.

All who go out from the Church and are cut off from the unity of faith and works are believed, without doubt, to be antichrists. We, however, insofar as concerns the rule of our faith, have not gone out from the Church. We hold the faith that the universal body of believers throughout the whole world holds, the faith handed down by the apostles—whence it receives the name “catholic.”

We have nowhere else to be. When we say “catholic faith,” we mean universal faith. In Greek, universality or generality is called *catholicon*. Therefore one who is catholic cannot be a heretic. That is, one who possesses the apostolic faith held by the universal Church throughout the whole world cannot go out from the Church.

We believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our God and Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. This is the faith which, with God’s illumination, we received as handed down by his apostles, and which we hold in the catholic Church.

### IX

For the Church throughout the whole world did not learn this faith of yours. Nor has it been accustomed to believe that the visible and invisible things were made through the one who was born of the Virgin—not through the one who is Son by adoption rather than by nature, but only through the one who is not adoptive but natural.

Nor is it accustomed to say:

> “I believe in God the almighty Father, and in his Son, who emptied himself of his divinity; who appeared in the world in the form of a subordinate creature, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to Abraham in the very heat of the day; who is adoptive in his humanity, but in no way adoptive in his divinity.”

This is your faith. For it does not exist throughout the whole world. If we are not speaking the truth, let us question the entire catholic Church whether such a faith exists universally throughout the world.

Let the order of baptism be examined, and the Creed composed by the twelve apostles, which the Church has received and according to which it baptizes its children, without which baptism cannot exist. Let them also examine the Creed composed by the three hundred Fathers against your faith. If they find even one of your statements inserted there, then we have gone out from the Church.

But if, as is certainly the case, they find that this doctrine of yours is new, just as it is new to us, then you, together with your followers, have gone out from the catholic Church, which has been established universally throughout the world.

For it is clear that your faith alone has been confined within you and kept bound in the cave of your faithlessness. This heresy makes you a heretic, because you do not believe what the entire Church throughout the world believes.

Heresy is not substance, but a quality in substance. And it is not the heretic who makes the heresy; rather, heresy makes the heretic. Just as it is not the proud person who makes pride; rather, pride makes the proud person. When he abandons the pride he possesses, he ceases to be proud, because pride itself is not substance but a quality in substance.

The good God made humanity a good substance. Pride, however, is a quality in substance, born from the devil. When it enters a person, that person becomes a son of the devil, because pride was born from the devil.

Each person is then shown to be proud when he wishes to be greater than another, more than he actually is. And when he considers himself greater than another, he loses what he was; and then he loses God, from whom he is. When he has lost God, he makes himself a member of the devil, whose son he is—not by nature, but by imitation.

For his originator, the devil, was good, created by the good God. Then he became proud because he wished to be above what he was. And by wishing to be above what he was, he lost not only what he was but also merited the infernal depths of Tartarus.

Because he is the head of all the proud, he joined all proud people to himself as members in one body, as to their head, and plunged them with himself into Gehenna. Conversely, Christ, the humble one, drew the humble Church—which is his head and body—with himself to the heavenly places.

For just as pride makes the proud, so heresy makes the heretic. A person ceases to be proud when he abandons the pride he has within him. He also ceases to be a heretic when he abandons the heresy he has within him. Whoever always has heresy within him will always be a heretic, just as whoever always has pride within him will always be proud.

Heresy was invented by the devil and was born from the devil, just as pride was. Since heresy exists, is not substance, and is evil, it comes not from God but from the devil. Everything that exists and is evil, while not being substance, comes from the devil.

Every substance created by the good God is nevertheless good. It remains good so long as it has not acquired what comes from the devil.

### X

Everything that has been made by God consists of only two things: body and spirit. An angel is spirit; the world is body. Humanity alone, however, is composed of both—that is, of body and spirit.

There is a third thing, the quality of an angel and of a human being. It is neither body nor spirit, and yet it exists, because nothing that exists is nothing. This quality itself does not exist in itself but in substance, and it cannot be substance: for example, good and evil. This is a quality in substance.

We call an angel good and a human being good; we call an angel evil and a human being evil. What they are is one thing, and what they possess is another. What they are is substance; what they possess is their quality, by which it is distinguished who are good and who are evil.

An angel is called good, but goodness itself is not the angel. For an apostate angel would not have become the devil if goodness were intrinsic to him. An angel, if he is good, has goodness not from himself but from God.

One thing, therefore, is substance, and another is the goodness it possesses within itself. So also with a good human being: what is substance is one thing, and the goodness possessed within is another.

God, however, is good in himself, because goodness itself is God. His substance is not one thing and his goodness another, as with human beings and angels; rather, his very goodness is his substance.

All the works made by the good God are good. Since they remain what they were made to be, they are always good. The goodness they received from God makes them always good, provided they have not lost it.

Conversely, an evil angel and an evil human being are called evil because they have lost the good. An angel is substance, and a human being is substance. Evil, however, is not substance but the privation of good, born—or rather invented—by the devil. Through evil, those who are evil become sons of the devil.

For, as we said, it is not the evil person who makes evil; rather, evil makes the evil person. Neither an angel nor a human being is evil itself, since they are substances; rather, each possesses within itself that quality by which it appears to be evil.

Both an evil angel and an evil human being do evil to humanity. The devil is always evil because he always does evil to humanity. A human being is the devil when he does evil to another human being.

### XI

That the evil human being who does evil to another human being is called evil is shown by the Lord’s words in the Gospel to the apostles concerning Judas:

> “Did I not choose you twelve? Yet one of you is a devil.”

In sacred Scripture, a human being is called the devil, and the devil is called a human being. That the devil is called a human being is shown when the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “An enemy, a human being, did this.”

When the master of the household had fallen asleep, the enemy, the human being—the devil—sowed weeds over the good seed in the field where the Lord had sown good seed.

What, then, is the reason that makes a human being the devil and the devil a human being, except that an evil angel and an evil human being are one body? For both do evil to humanity. The human being is the devil’s body; the devil is the head of that body.

Often the words spoken by the head appear to concern the members, and from the name of the body the head is understood; likewise, from the name of the head the body is signified. Conversely, Christ and the Church are head and body, one person. When Scripture speaks of the head, it refers to the body; and when it speaks of the body, it refers to the head.

As Isaiah says:

> “He clothed me with the garment of salvation, like a bride adorned with a crown, and like a bride adorned with her jewels.”

In one person, named by two terms, he revealed both the head—that is, the bridegroom—and the Church—that is, the bride.

These, then, are the two persons read about throughout Scripture in relation to the Church: Christ and his body, and the devil and his body.

### XII

The third thing is quality: one is good and the other evil. Christ is good, and his body is good by adhering to the good. The devil is evil, although he was made good, by adhering to the lie. The human being is evil, although he was made good, by adhering to the lie.

This quality joins the two together—that is, the two substances, angel and human being—and makes the lie itself one in them. Therefore Christ, the Truth, set himself against the lie: humility against pride; charity against discord; patience against anger; goodness against wickedness; lowliness against arrogance; generosity against greed; abstinence against gluttony; sobriety against drunkenness.

**[Note: Greek Γαστριμαργία, “gluttony.”]**

Thus the good physician acted, tempering hot things with cold and cold things with hot for the sick, and promising life to those who observed the regimen. Those who drank bitter potions would return more quickly to health.

For even in the work of bodily physicians, the physicians first taste what they have prepared for the health of human beings, and then offer it to the sick to drink. So too did that merciful physician act: he first tasted the cup of bitterness, and then ordained for us to drink his body and blood, our medicine, which he prepared for us; and he left the observances of the regimen for those whom he foresaw would live with him.

### XIII

Let us now see who these people are. Not all the sick are made well through treatment, but only those who are not going to die. To those who are dying, the physician says: “Let them eat and drink whatever they wish, because they cannot live.”

These are the people who can sin but cannot repent. If they were not too delicate to repent, they would quickly return to health if they drank the cup of bitterness. Without doubt they would live and be healthy with the physician if, to the extent that the inclination of their mind had been abrupt in sinning, their devotion had been equally full in lamentation; and if they also observed the physician’s regimen that we proposed above by way of example: peace with all who are in discord, humility with all who are proud, patience with all who are angry, and the rest that we mentioned above.

These are the opposites born from the devil. Through them a person may escape the devil’s death, observe Christ’s commands, and live forever with his physician, who is life.

For just as the devil is substance and a human being is substance, so the evil that comes from the devil—heresy, pride, arrogance, and the rest—which stands between the human being and the devil, makes those who cling to it one person with the devil, head and body.

Conversely, Christ is substance and the human being is substance; and the quality with which Christ came into this world—humility, patience, obedience, and the rest derived from his example—joins those who hold to it with Christ.

This observance joins the head and the body, and the Church becomes one Christ with its head. This is the understanding intended for the reader throughout Scripture: there are only two who are opposed to one another, Christ and the devil.

There are also two cities: one of God and the other of the devil; one earthly and the other heavenly. The heavenly city belongs to Christ; the earthly belongs to Antichrist.

Christ had his prophets, who proclaimed that he would come. Antichrist also had his prophets, false priests within the law, who crucified him, saying, “He is not the one.”

Now Christ has his disciples in the Gospel, who say, “He is the one, and no other.” Antichrist also has his preachers in the Gospel, who say, “He is not the one.”

Those who say, “He is the one, and no other,” are the body of the head who knows the head; that is, they are the body of Christ because they know Christ. Whoever says, “He is not the one,” is the body of the devil, because he knows the head who separated his body from the body of Christ, just as the head itself is separated.

### XIV

The Jewish priests under the law did not recognize that Christ himself was God, the Redeemer of the world and the head of the Church; therefore they killed the head.

Now the Christian priests in the Gospel do not recognize the body as the body of the supreme head, and they kill Christ’s body. Both those priests under the law who killed the head and these priests in the Gospel who kill the body of the head are preachers of Antichrist. Both belong to one school, both to one doctrine, and both speak from one spirit.

One lying spirit is their head, whose body he too is. We said above that what the devil as head does is referred to the body of his ministers, and what the body of the devil’s ministers does is referred to the head. When the head of the Church suffers, this is referred to the body; and when the body, which is the Church, suffers, this is referred to the head.

The Church is certain concerning Christ the head, whose body it is, because Christ is the mediator. Therefore it does not doubt Christ, even if it must shed its blood for Christ.

The devil, however, is not a mediator for his own body; for he has not yet entered that condemned human being, so that the son of perdition himself may be a visible mediator between the devil and the human race. Instead, he has his false preachers, the heretics, who under the name of Christ fabricate the Christ whom the devil inspired them to fabricate, not the Christ whom Truth proclaims.

He is the devil’s body, and yet under the name of falsehood he preaches Christ and falsely claims to worship Christ. And because he boasts of wisdom, he acts against Christ, because he attacks Christ’s body. When he attacks it, he crucifies it. When he crucifies it, he does not recognize it. When he does not recognize the body, he does not recognize the head whose body it is. When he kills the body, he kills the head.

He has not yet killed the body physically, but spiritually. He kills Christ’s body when, through his philosophy, he disturbs the minds of the faithful and joins them to his own faith. He does this especially to the little ones who still live on milk—that is, who are nourished by the flesh and blood of Christ and have not yet reached the solid food of faith.

Then he takes away the milk—that is, the flesh and blood of Christ—and supplies his own milk, that is, the flesh and blood he has fabricated for himself. He takes away the breasts of the Church—that is, the two Testaments, of the Law and the Gospel—and supplies his own breasts: he interprets both the Law and the Gospel according to his perverse faith and directs those Scriptures toward that faith in the perversity he holds.

The Church is then oppressed by perversity when permission to speak is granted to wicked preachers.

### XV

Long before, Jeremiah foresaw this and said:

> “Even the lamias have uncovered the breast; they have suckled their young.”

For whom does he call lamias except heretics—those who bear a human face but, through their impiety, carry a beastlike tail? They uncover the breast when they publicly preach their error. They suckle their young when, by insinuating perversities, they nourish and strengthen the souls of their immature followers in impiety.

John agrees with this interpretation in the book of Revelation, saying:

> “And I saw another beast rising from the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and spoke like a dragon. It exercised all the authority of the first beast in its presence. It makes the earth and those who dwell in it worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed. It performs great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in the sight of human beings. And it deceives those who dwell on the earth by the signs given to it, telling them to make an image of the beast, so that they may be killed. And it causes all—the small and the great, the rich and the poor, the free and the slaves—to give them a mark upon their right hand or upon their foreheads, so that no one may buy or sell unless he has the mark, the name of the beast, or the number of its name” (Revelation 13:11–17).

### XVI

Although all this will take place physically at the time of Antichrist, it is nevertheless taking place spiritually in the Church today.

When he said, “I saw another beast rising from the earth,” he indicates that there are two beasts. The beast receives its name from *bastando*—“bearing” or “carrying.” **[Note: [Col. 0987D] Greek Βαστάζω, “I carry, bear.”]** For it feeds not on herbs but on flesh.

He called it another beast because of its function and activity. Nevertheless, it is one beast, because the entire body of the devil is one body. Every beast is an entire people: both pagans and evil Christians who oppose the Church of Christ.

Pagans openly turn away from Christ; Christians, whether good or evil, are called one Church. Yet the one Church that appears to exist is divided into three parts: one part is the Church itself, which imitates Christ. The other two parts fight against that Church: heretics and evil Christians.

The devil, who is called the dragon, is the head of these three parts: unbelievers and pagans, and evil Christians and heretics. For just as an unbeliever—a pagan or a Jew—turns away from Christ in faith, so an evil Christian turns away from Christ in works. Just as the former publicly denies that Christ is God, so the latter publicly performs evil deeds that do not please Christ.

When one part departs from Christ in faith and another in works, both are separated from the one Christ. Since they are separated from Christ, they become one body of the devil, their head. And when they become one body, they are called one beast.

### XVII

The third part belongs to the body of Antichrist—that is, the heretics—who differ greatly from that beast in their religious appearance.

Those people are adulterers; these pretend to virginity and chastity. Those are rapacious; these pretend to distribute their own possessions. Those publicly live in banquets and drunkenness; these afflict themselves with fasts and prayers. Those are wolves within and without; these are lambs outwardly but wolves within.

The devil has these as his prophets, whom he has established in the Church from his own body. He has them under the name of Christ, pretending to preach Christ while becoming the devil’s body.

Since the devil has no mediator, he has no means by which he can deceive the Church except these false prophets of his, who publicly praise and publicly preach Christ, yet under the name of Christianity deny that he is God.

The Lord calls them pseudo-Christs and pseudo-prophets in the Gospel.

**[Note: Greek Ψεῦδος, “lie,” “falsehood.”]**

They are called *pseudo-* because they arise from themselves in doctrine, assume for themselves the name of preachers, and fabricate about Christ what they have learned from themselves, not from Christ.

They place themselves above Christ’s apostles, whom the Church did not approve or choose for the apostolate; rather, they were chosen only by themselves and by temporary human favor. When they hear themselves praised by worldly people, they suppose that God regards them inwardly as such people.

Concerning them, the Lord warns his Church in Revelation, saying:

> “I know your works, your labor, and your patience, and that you cannot tolerate the wicked. You have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you have found them to be liars. You have patience and have endured for my name, and you have not grown weary.”

We have no doubt that this was spoken about those heretics called false apostles and pseudo-Christs. They claimed to be leaders of truth, but they are authors of wicked falsehood. They profess themselves good, but are shown to be worse than demons.

The catholic faith, however, exposed their lie and perversity, and through endurance suffered many things inflicted by them. “You have tested them,” he says. No one is tested except those who are within the Church. Those who are outside are plainly outside without any testing, and there is no need to test them.

The Church is tested within, because heretical perversity exists within the Church, and the Church is ravaged by it. Concerning this, the Lord says in this book:

> “I know where you dwell, where the throne of Satan is.”

The throne of Satan is those pseudo-apostles, in whom he sits within the Church of Christ. Christ is proclaimed through their mouths, and yet Christ does not speak through them. They claim to be Christ’s apostles, but they are not apostles; they are deceivers of the Church, because they do not imitate Christ’s apostles, whose name they have falsely appropriated.

### XVIII

Therefore the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

> “But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity and chastity that are in Christ Jesus. For if someone comes to you and preaches another Christ whom I did not preach to you, or if you receive another Christ whom we did not receive, or another Gospel that you did not receive, you rightly tolerate it. For I think that I have done nothing less than the great apostles among you.””

> “And if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge.”

Again, there he speaks against those false apostles:

> “But what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to cut off the opportunity of those who seek an opportunity, so that in what they boast they may be found to be like us. For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder: for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. It is therefore no great thing if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their works.”

### XIX

Thus these pseudo-Christs are rightly the third part of the body of Antichrist, the part called another beast. It would not be called another beast if it had been openly evil, if it had not been within the Church, or if it had not pretended to religious holiness.

Therefore he said:

> “And I saw another beast rising from the earth. It had two horns like a lamb and spoke like a dragon, and it exercised all the authority of the first beast.”

That is, it exercised the authority of the first people and of the devil, whom we said above is one beast in the whole body, but divided in the function of its activity.

He saw the first beast rising from the sea, but this one from the earth. The sea does one thing and the earth another. The sea is turbulent, but the earth is quiet.

The sea signifies the openly evil people of this age. The earth signifies false religion and heretical perversity, which, under the name of holiness, does not appear to fluctuate in the world but seems to maintain a kind of quiet, so that it can imitate the Church.

He saw that beast rising from the sea—that is, a people being born from a people, because there has always been an evil people. And the evil person who is always called a beast is always being born.

Likewise, he saw another beast rising from the earth, not descending from heaven. For the heavenly Jerusalem will always descend from heaven to earth, because its children are always born in humility.

The pseudo-prophet, however, will rise from the earth, because he always boasts of an earthly lineage. To rise from the earth means to be elevated by earthly glory and supported by an appearance of holiness.

Therefore it is also a beast, and it has two horns like a lamb: that is, the two Testaments, of the Law and the Gospel, through which it pretends to prophesy so that among its own it may present itself as a lamb.

### XX

And he spoke like a dragon. This is that seduction leading away from God. He presents himself as a lamb in order secretly to insert the dragon’s venom. For he would not resemble a lamb if he spoke openly like a dragon. Now he pretends to be a lamb so that he may ‘defoset’ the lamb (reading uncertain; *defoset* is transmitted as such). He speaks about God, but falsely, inventing a god for himself—not in the manner in which Scripture speaks. He speaks about God in order to turn those who seek him away from the way of truth.

He will perform signs in the sight of human beings, so that even the dead may seem to rise. That is, through his preaching many may appear to be converted and to rise from the work of death; but that resurrection is seen only in the sight of human beings. For no son of heretics who has imitated them is brought to the fruit of good works. Their wisdom is earthly, not heavenly; and it generates children of the earth, when they sprinkle the heavenly seed of the Gospel upon a carnal understanding with an earthly sense.

Therefore the Lord admonishes his Church, saying: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.” We must consider what wolves are understood to signify. They are beasts that lie in wait for the sheep who stay near the shepherds’ folds; they do not dare to enter the dwellings of houses. They watch for the sleep of the dogs, or for the shepherd’s absence or laziness. They seize the sheep’s throat in order to strangle it quickly. Wild and rapacious, and also by nature stiff in body so that they cannot easily bend themselves, they rush forward with a kind of force of their own, and therefore conceal themselves. Moreover, if they see a human being first, they are said by a certain force of nature to snatch away his voice. But if a human being sees them first, he is said to have driven them away. And therefore I must beware lest, if the grace of spiritual mysteries is unable to shine forth in today’s exposition, the wolves be thought to have seen me first and to have wrested away the customary aid of speech.

### XXI

Are these not wolves who lie in wait for Christ’s sheep? They growl around the folds more at night than during the day. At night, because they preach among the ignorant; they cannot do so by day, because they are detected by the wise. Night is ignorance, and day is wisdom. For it is always night for the faithless, who try to cover the light of Christ with their cloudy interpretations and, insofar as they can, to darken it.

Thus they linger around the folds—that is, around the seven Churches. Yet they do not dare to enter Christ’s stalls; that is, they do not presume to enter the Church, which is light. And therefore they are not healed, because Christ does not wish to bring them into his stall, in which the man who, descending from Jerusalem, fell among robbers was healed: the Samaritan bound his wounds, poured in oil and wine, placed him on his own beast, and brought him into the stall—that is, Christ brought him into his own body—and left him to the keeper of the stall, that is, to the holy bishop, to be healed. Therefore those who do not seek the physician do not receive medicine. For if they sought him, they would not openly disparage him.

They investigate the shepherd’s absence. Therefore they strive either to kill or to send into exile the shepherds of the Churches, because, while the shepherds are present, they cannot secretly devour Christ’s sheep. Thus the one who has seized the shepherd attempts to strip the Lord’s flock—those who are bodily and carnal, [Col. 0991A] [Note: Perhaps *sapiunt* (“understand”) or something similar is missing.] because they ordinarily do not turn away from their error by the intention of a spiritual mind, but are hard and rigid.

Therefore the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical person after one admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted.” The ancient interpreter of the Scriptures confines them so that they may expend their empty impulses in vain and be unable to do harm. But if they have forestalled someone by the crafty entanglement of their argument, they make him fall silent. For the one who does not confess the word of God with the same glory in which it exists is mute. Beware, therefore, lest a heretic silence you, if you do not first detect him yourself. [Note: Perhaps *serpsit* or *serpit* (“he has crept” or “he creeps”).] For he creeps while his faithlessness lies concealed. But if you recognize the fraud of his impiety, you will not be able to fear the loss of a godly voice.

Beware, therefore, the venom of crafty argument. They seek the soul, seize the throat, and inflict a wound upon the vital organs. The bites of heretics are grievous. They are even more grievous and rapacious than the beasts themselves, and know no limit either to avarice or to impiety.

### XXII

Nor should it disturb you that they seem to display human form. Although outwardly a human being is seen, inwardly a beast growls. “For by their fruits you will know them.” If someone is therefore moved by appearance, let him inquire about the fruit.

This man howls the Scriptures rather than expounding them, because he denies their author. He is the one who, when he wished to become a disciple—not simply, but deceitfully—said to the Lord: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” To him the Lord said: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests where they may rest; but the Son of Man has nowhere to recline his head.”

For he saw that the man’s mind was crooked in the manner of foxes, and that birds—that is, demons—dwelt in him. But the Lord seeks not the appearance of acts of service, but purity of mind. Accordingly, when he placed a little child in their midst, he said: “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me. And whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.” For whoever receives an imitator of Christ receives Christ; and whoever receives the image of God receives God. For the head of Christ is God—that is, his divinity—which does not dwell in a crooked mind.

Therefore, insofar as he can, let a person display sincere faith and preserve obedience to the commandments with a devout mind, lest it be said to him: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to recline his head.” For a little fox is deceitful and always intent upon ambush, so that it may practice robbery through fraud. It allows nothing to be safe, nothing undisturbed, nothing secure, seeking prey even among human dwellings and always desiring to hide in a den.

So are heretics: they do not know how to prepare a house for themselves, but try to deceive others by their entanglements. The person who possesses simplicity always dwells in a house, because he is always in charity. But a heretic is in a den, like a deceitful fox, because he is never in purity of mind; and therefore he is a deceitful fox, always plotting against that evangelical hen.

For concerning her the Lord says: “How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling? Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” The Lord wishes to gather the children of heretics, if they would come to the unity of faith; but he does not gather them, because, disagreeing among themselves and thinking different things, they do not agree.

Concerning them the Psalmist says: “Contention has been poured out upon their princes, and he led them astray in a trackless place, and not on the way.” For while they do not fear to interpret the Lord’s dispensation perversely, they lead the peoples subject to them not along the way that is Christ, but into a trackless place. Accordingly, contention is rightly said to have been poured over them, because they contradict one another with their mutual arguments.

### XXIII

Arius, accepting three persons in the Divinity, also believed in three gods. In opposition to him, Sabellius, accepting one God, believed that there was one person. Between them, holy Church, holding steadfastly to the straight path of her preaching, both proclaims one God and asserts three persons against Sabellius; and, asserting three persons, confesses one God against Arius.

### XXIV

Elipandus, bishop of the see of Toledo, through I know not what confusion arising from mixture, confuses three persons in one nature of the Godhead; and he believes that Christ, born of the Virgin, is not God but merely a human being.

### XXV

Manichaeus, however, who recognized that virginity is praised in sacred discourse, condemned marriage.

### XXVI

By contrast, Jovinianus, who discovered that marriage was permitted, despised the purity of virginity. Hence it happens that, whenever heretics are confused by perverse understanding, their wickedness agrees with itself in guilt while differing in doctrine.

### XXVII

By contrast, holy Church proceeds in ordered peace through the conflicts between both sides. Just as she knows how to accept higher things, so also she knows how to venerate lower things, so that she neither places the highest things on an equality with the lowest nor, again, despises the lowest while venerating the highest.

Heretics therefore cannot be joined into one, since, disagreeing among themselves like foxes, they dig different dens for themselves; they have lost the one house, the Church, which they once possessed. This animal is never domesticated, nor is it useful for any purpose or food. Thus heretics are never domesticated, nor are they joined to the Lord’s food. For Christ does not say of them: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven.”

In the Song of Songs the Lord commands his brothers to bind these foxes when he says: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, for our vineyard has blossomed.” In a parable in the Gospel the Lord says: “When the plants had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds appeared.” That is, as the Church progressed, numerous heresies also arose; but while the Church remained in the faith, the heresies were investigated to determine what they believed perversely.

So Samson, whose name is interpreted as “sun,” captured three hundred foxes, attached fire to their tails, and burned the fruits of the enemies. For heretics always appear at the beginning of their conversion as though distinguished by a false religion; but at the end, when they begin to preach, they drag fire behind them like a tail, being destined for the burning of Gehenna.

Therefore, when the Lord says, “Catch for us the foxes,” it is as though he says: Convict the heretics, and enclose their craftiness with testimonies from the holy Scriptures. He calls them little foxes because, in understanding nothing according to the true faith, whatever they know is insignificant. They destroy the vineyards because they overthrow the peoples, corrupting them with perverse traditions. “For our vineyard has blossomed”—that is, the Catholic Church has advanced with unceasing growth.

### XXVIII

Holy Scripture therefore rightly calls heretical people, united in one body, a beast, because what they bring forth by reading begins, as it were, under the guise of reason. But because they do not understand what they read, they nevertheless always tend toward an irrational meaning; and, like a human being ending in a beast, they become a beast when they interpret the sense of Scripture according to an understanding of evil belief.

This beast is rightly said to have two horns resembling those of a lamb, because outwardly, in the human being, it displays the lamb’s simplicity, and, through the two testaments of the Law and the Gospel, pretends with us to preach one Christ. But hear what John says about it: “And it spoke like a dragon, and it exercised all the authority of the first beast in its presence; and it makes the earth and those who dwell in it worship the first beast, whose mortal wound had been healed.”

As we have said, the dragon is called the devil. The dragon—the devil—deceived the human being in paradise by speaking and promising new falsehoods; so also the heretic, who is called a beast, speaks like a dragon, that is, like the devil in paradise. For paradise is now the Church.

Our carnal desire is seduced by the words of this serpent, and through it Adam is seduced—not Christ, but the Christian. That dragon, the devil, therefore says to the woman: “Why did the Lord command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” So the curious desire of heretics, and so perverse preachers, inflame the hearts of their hearers—represented in the figure of the woman—to love the deception of error, saying to them: “Why do you flee from possessing knowledge that is hidden and concealed? Seek out the new beyond measure, and penetrate the knowledge of good and evil.”

### XXIX

Accordingly, in Solomon, that woman representing the likeness of heretics says: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is pleasant.” Then the same dragon added: “On whatever day you eat, your eyes will immediately be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

So all heretics generally speak like a dragon when they claim the status of divinity, deceive by promising knowledge, and condemn those whom they find believing simply. And because they persuade people of wholly carnal things, they try to lead them toward the opening of carnal eyes, so that the inner eye may be blinded.

This is the speech of the heretic who speaks like a dragon and exercises all the authority of the first beast—that is, of the entire body of the devil, namely, evil people, whom he calls the first beast—as he says: “And he makes the earth and those who dwell in it worship the first beast, whose mortal wound has been healed.”

And because the beast whom he called the first is said to have seven heads and ten horns—“One of its heads he saw as though slain unto death, and its mortal wound was healed”—that head of the beast, as though slain, is the entire body of heretics. They preach Christ crucified and pretend, with their two horns, to be a lamb; nevertheless, they speak like a dragon, because they exercise all the authority of the first beast.

The ten horns of the beast, Scripture says, are to be ten kings at the end of the world. Antichrist, the eleventh, will reign over them with seven after three kings have been killed; these are the ones whom he now calls the seven heads.

The seventh head of the beast, as though slain unto death, consists of heretics who, with John, preach Christ as a lamb slain, yet deny that he is the Son of God and God, saying: “The visible and invisible things were not made through this lamb,” whom John points out with his finger: “Behold the Lamb of God! Behold the one who takes away the sins of the world!”

Whoever says these things is a beast, one of the heads of the beast—not slain as our Christ the Lamb was, but, as though slain, through a theft-like imitation of Christ. He speaks like a dragon and exercises all the authority of the first beast. For the devil devised this imitation for himself so that, under the name of religion, he might deceive not only carnal people but also the religious.

Therefore this head is said to be as though slain unto death, and its mortal wound healed—that is, as though they followed Christ crucified. It is called the devil’s imitation because, although inwardly it is a beast, outwardly it pretends to be a lamb, in the likeness of the Lamb who is Christ.

For the Church says concerning Christ: “I saw a Lamb as though slain.” And because of the sevenfold Spirit of grace, from which the seven Churches arise through the gifts of grace—the one Church that is the complete body of Christ—it says: “Having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent throughout the whole world.” For the Church, which has received the grace of the Holy Spirit, has been established throughout the entire world.

### XXX

But concerning the body of the devil, the Church speaks in a very different way. It does not call the body of the devil a lamb, nor does it attribute seven horns to it; rather, it says: “I saw a beast rising from the sea, having ten horns and seven heads; and upon its heads ten diadems, and upon its heads the name of blasphemy.” And the beast that I saw was like a leopard; its feet were like those of a bear, and its mouth like the mouth of a lion. And the dragon gave it his power and his throne. And I saw one of its heads as though slain unto death; and its mortal wound was healed. And the whole earth marveled and followed the beast; and they worshiped the dragon, because he gave authority to the beast. And they worshiped the beast, saying: ‘Who is like the beast? Or who can fight against it?’ And it was given to it to speak great blasphemy.”

All this must be understood figuratively in the Church, not as it is heard literally. For just as the lamb and the beast are opposed to one another by nature, so they must be understood allegorically through the figure. Here only two parts are to be understood: Christ and his body, and the devil and his body.

To make it easier for the Church to recognize the entire body of the devil spiritually, he has enclosed all the members of the devil in one beast. In Daniel this beast is said to be more terrifying than the other beasts—that is, it is said to be unlike the lion, the leopard, and the bear—and it is not given the name of any beast. It is merely called unlike the other beasts and terrifying.

But see how great it is outwardly, terrifying in earthly matters, when it says to the earth—that is, to earthly people: “Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?” It is said to be terrifying and unlike the other beasts. But the Lamb came and rose against it in combat, and by dying snatched away its prey.

Even today the lambs redeemed by the precious blood of the undefiled and spotless Lamb—Christ—snatch it away, through that Lamb whom God raised from the dead. This Lamb and the beast are opposed to one another in the Church. The beast that is opposed to the Lamb is not a specific but a general name, and it has many parts, represented in writing by seven distinct heads.

But in the narrative it must be understood according to the context what part of the beast is being described, since the beast consists of seven heads from one body. Sometimes he calls the devil a beast; sometimes unbelievers, that is, those without baptism; sometimes evil Christians, namely, the common people within the Church who are Christians in name only but are beasts in their works; sometimes evil rulers; sometimes heretics who think and preach wrongly about Christ; sometimes hypocrites who pretend to holiness but neither speak about Christ nor wish to know what they should say or believe.

At other times he calls them schismatics, who believe rightly and preach Christ rightly but are separated from the unity of the Church—not bodily, but in spirit. Schism takes its name from the rending of souls. A schismatic believes with the same worship and the same rite as the other religious people, but delights only in the division of the assembly, so that he is supported by no common counsel with the others; and everything he seems to do is thought holy in his own heart.

Schism arises when people say: “We are righteous; we sanctify ourselves in the world,” and other things like these. All this is described through the individual functions of the heads of one beast. They are called heads because each person follows the judgment of his own will. Only the Church acts with counsel, lest she repent after the deed.

### XXXI

To confirm this with testimonies, let us bring forth one example from the many provided by the Apostle Paul. Lest he perhaps run or have run in vain, he first sought out Peter, the chief of the apostles. Through this example the Church, which is a member of the supreme head, makes progress. All Christianity appears to be one Church.

Many people, with the whole ardor of their minds, think that they are laboring well, but it is uncertain whether they please God. There is one field, but while the master of the household slept, an enemy sowed weeds over it. When the disciples proposed to go and uproot them, our Lord forbade them, reserving for himself the separation of chaff and wheat.
