These are the vessels of wrath and the vessels of mercy that the Apostle proclaims in the house of God. The days will therefore come when, after opening the treasury of the Church, the Lord will bring forth the vessels of his wrath. When they go out, the saints will say: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us.”

No one can claim Christ’s victory for himself; no one can judge human beings before the day of judgment. If the Church has already been cleansed, what are we reserving for the Lord? There is a way that seems right to human beings, but its end leads into the depths of hell. In this error of judgment, what judgment can be certain?

Therefore, because the judgment is not certain, charity ought to be one. Yet that charity itself cannot be certain if faith is uncertain. Accordingly, the whole Church together must seek the true faith and avoid the poisons of heretics by every means.

For it is not without reason that the head of this beast is written as though slain. The beast, therefore, which he calls the person between the devil and Christ has no real personhood, because it exists only in the name by which they say that they worship Christ, who died and rose again.

This beast with two horns is the portion of the heretics together with all who agree with them, both in faith and in conduct. It is called a head as though slain—that is, deceptively Christian. Under this name they worship the devil, who devised this imitation for himself so that, under the name of Christianity, he might exclude a very large part from the Church and join it to his own head, the devil. And thus he will have a body with which he may deliver both himself and it to the depths of hell.

We worship the Lamb who was slain and rose again. They worship the beast, which bears a likeness of this kind. There are therefore three: the devil, the people, and the beast as though slain, which is the mediator among them, in whom Christ is echoed.

And because the matter falls upon the devil in part when he says that the middle beast is worshiped, the devil fills the place belonging to himself and to the heretics, through whose mouth he speaks in the Church.

### XXXII

He says that there are ten diadems upon the ten horns. This means that they praise their kings, both living and dead, and think that they have been transferred, as it were, into heaven and among the saints.

The name of blasphemy that he saw upon the seven heads means that they call themselves the Church while persecuting the Church.

The dragon is the operation of the serpent. Red is the dwelling-place of the flesh, since the dragon itself is the dwelling of the flesh. The ten horns of the dragon are the power of an alien law.

The dragon is that great ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan. He is called a dragon because he terrifies. He is great because he appears powerful and exalts himself in spirit. He is a serpent because he is not detected, but creeps and deceives without being reproved. He is called ancient because he began from the beginning and received the power of the old human being.

### XXXIII

The devil is so called because he appears to be a counselor to himself and is wise. And after he has persuaded a human being, he appears as an accuser—not of his own persuasion, but rather of the crime we have committed.

He is a leopard because he displays the variety and deceitfulness of deception. He is a bear because he represents the plundering of perceptions and evil works. He is a lion because he is the form of pride and error.

The dragon gave the beast his power and his throne because there are heretics within the Church who seem to be the Church but are not the Church. The devil speaks through their mouth, wishing to deceive those whom he seeks to mislead within the Church.

“And they worshiped the beast, saying: ‘Who is like the beast? Or who can fight against it?’” They do not say this in such words. Rather, they say: “Who is like Christ? Or who could overcome him?” They profess Christ with their tongue, but in their deeds they follow the beast.

“And he performs great signs, so that he even makes fire descend from heaven to earth in the sight of human beings.” Fire is the Holy Spirit; heaven is the Church; earth consists of those whom they baptize. He also means the other ecclesiastical orders, which are carried out through them in the Church, by which sacraments the Church is held captive by them.

The sacrament of baptism can exist not only within the Catholic Church but also among heretics who baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; yet outside the Catholic Church it cannot be beneficial. Rather, just as within the Church it brings salvation through the sacrament of baptism to those who believe rightly, so those baptized outside the Church, if they do not return to the Church, have accumulated through the same baptism destruction and confusion for themselves.

For the unity of ecclesiastical fellowship contributes so much to the salvation of baptism that the person to whom it is not given within the Church—where it ought to be given—is not saved. Nevertheless, baptism is present in a person baptized outside the Church, though especially for condemnation, since he has been separated from the Church.

But because it is clear that, wherever this baptism has been given, it is to be given only once, therefore, even if it has been given by heretics in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, it must be reverently acknowledged and must in no way be repeated.

And because all Christianity bears the name of the Church, while unbelievers who have not been baptized are said to be outside the Church, when they hear that baptized people are spoken of as outside the Church, do they suppose that this is said of unbelievers? It must not be understood in this way, as though we believed there were only two classes of human beings: one class of the baptized, which is the Church, and another class of unbelievers, which is outside the Church. Unbelievers do not possess baptism, since they do not believe Christ to be the Son of God; only Christians possess baptism.

The Christianity that has been baptized is itself divided into two parts: one that is within the Church, and that which is outside the Church. The part outside the Church is divided into two groups: heretical priests and openly evil laypeople.

The part called the Church consists of the holy and faithful, who have abandoned everything for Christ. To it he will say on the day of judgment: “You who have left everything of yours and followed me, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty in the regeneration, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

He speaks of twelve thrones because the entire Church, which has been stained by the blood of Christ’s passion, has been built upon the number twelve, the number of the apostles. For the twelve apostles are in Christ as the twelve hours of the day are in the sun.

The sun is understood as Christ, according to the saying of the Prophet: “For you who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness will rise.” And it rises only for those Christians who fear Christ—that is, who believe in Christ and imitate his footsteps—so that they are able to walk in this day.

Just as the sun makes the twelve hours of the day, while the hours do not make the sun, so Christ made and chose the twelve apostles, while the twelve apostles neither made nor chose Christ. As the Lord himself says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.”

Now they are the adopted sons who have been chosen, not the one who chose them. Yet the one who chose and those who were chosen are one day and one light: the sun is the illuminator, and the twelve hours are illuminated by the sun.

So Christ is the illuminator, and the twelve apostles are illuminated by Christ. Christ is the head, and the twelve apostles are the body of Christ; the entire Church is constituted in the number twelve, the number of the apostles. This is one day—that is, one person, Christ and the Church. Whoever walks in this day walks within the Church.

Christ sent these twelve apostles alone, like the twelve hours of the day, throughout the whole world, so that the entire multitude of believers might walk in this one day—that is, in this one Church. But none of the believers can enter there unless he has imitated Christ’s apostles. And when he has imitated them, he becomes an apostle of Christ, just as the Apostle Paul said to his disciples: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

### XXXIV

Now bishops hold the chairs of the twelve apostles if they imitate the apostles in faith, conduct, and preaching. They themselves are the Church, because they are in the apostles’ teaching. And those baptized through their hands are said to have been baptized within the Church, because they baptize no one except those who give their names.

They also instruct these people in faith and conduct—in how they should believe and how they should live—so that with their own mouths they profess the apostolic creed of faith:

“To believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, God and our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary; and in the Holy Spirit.”

In this faith they have been baptized, and they renounce the devil and his angels, his works, and his commands.

### XXXV

Some of these baptized people are handed over to the school and offered by their parents to Christ so that they may eventually become priests and serve Christ. Others are handed over only to instruction, so that they may read and know Christ, and, with blessing, take wives within the Church, so that they may serve marriage, because this too is good and is within his Church.

But the better state is the priesthood, which is within the Church and is itself the Church. Yet that other state is also good, which generates for us martyrs and priests, virgins and confessors, and in which married people live according to the Apostle Paul, who says:

“Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful. For I think this is good because of the present necessity, since it is good for a person to be so. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such people will have tribulation of the flesh, but I spare you. This, then, brothers, is the time remaining: that those who have wives should be as though they had none; and those who weep as though they were not weeping; and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away. But I want you to be without anxiety” (1 Corinthians 7:25–32).

Married people who observe this command of the Apostle are within the Church, because they are under the discipline of the apostles. If one of them commits an offense, just as he is excommunicated from the Church, so he is not received by them either.

They rightly give their tithes to God. They wash the feet of guests. They minister to the poor. They show honor to priests and share their modest means with them, because they expect to have them as future heirs. They use their wives not for lust but for the procreation of children. And they live with all people in such great charity that they are thought to be monks.

At the day of judgment these will hear from the Lord: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me. For what you did for one of these least of my brothers, you did for me.”

These are the brothers of the Lord, concerning whom he says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my mother, brother, and sister.”

### XXXVI

For if you wish to know what the will of the Father is, we can find nothing else except that we should believe in the one whom he sent—that is, believe that his Son Jesus Christ is true God. We must fear, worship, imitate, and love him, because he is the true God and eternal life, as he himself says in the Gospel:

“This is eternal life: that they know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent. This is the true God and eternal life.”

Behold the one whom the Church believes in and toward whom she strives. Whatever she does, she does through ecclesiastical teaching; whatever she asks, she asks in the name of Jesus, so that they may be eternal with Jesus and be baptized within the Church, in whose peace they persevere and through which they are also saved.

For whoever acts against this Church cannot be saved unless he returns to it, so that through it he may be saved. I believe that all who are within it are saved. Outside it, however much good a person may seem to do—even if he sheds his blood for the name of Christ—he cannot be saved unless he returns to the Catholic Church, which alone rightly believes in God, alone loves its neighbor, alone suffers for Christ, and alone dies for him.

She always wishes to rule over vices, not over brothers. Every day she fulfills the law of God, because every day she is in charity. And the more she understands, the more she labors. She suffers with all, because she grieves with all.

This is not the part that acts as we said above—the part that is outside the Church, namely, the heretics and their evil people, who receive the sacraments of the Church from them but neither possess nor proclaim to them the doctrine of salvation. They are bodies, but they do not love one another, because they are hostile to those whose members they are.

Concerning them the Apostle Paul tells the Thessalonians, when they thought that the day of judgment had arrived in Paul’s time, because he had written to them: “We who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:4).

When they were troubled by this, he later wrote to them, saying:

“But we ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, that you not be quickly shaken from your understanding or frightened, either by spirit, or by word, or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were imminent. Let no one deceive you in any way. For unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, presenting himself as though he were God.

“Do you not remember that, while I was still with you, I used to tell you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work.”

It is as though he said openly: Then Antichrist will be seen manifestly. For even now he secretly works his hidden things in the hearts of the wicked.

To say nothing of more obvious crimes, I will mention those that are committed under a pretext: behold, one person secretly envies his brother and, if he finds an opportunity, strives to overthrow him. Whose member is he, if not of the one concerning whom it is written: “Through the envy of the devil, death entered the world”?

### XXXVII

Another, thinking himself to be a man of great merit, puts himself above everyone through the swelling of his heart and believes all others inferior to him. Whose member is he, then, if not of the one of whom it is written: “He beholds every lofty thing, and he himself is king over all the sons of pride”? Another seeks honor so that he may preside over others—not because he may benefit them, but because he himself may not be subject to another. Whose member is he, then, if not of the one of whom it is written, who said: “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High”?

The devil therefore established this rule for his members, and fashioned within the Church an image under the name of Christianity; yet this party is outside the Church. The Church does not wish to dominate but to serve. For the Most High alone so rules over all that He cannot be subject to another beneath Him. The devil perversely wished to imitate Him when, seeking his own dominion, he refused to be subject to Him. He wished to acquire omnipotence by robbery, whereas the Lord possessed it by nature.

### XXXVIII

Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, although He was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. And in order to offer us an example of humility and charity, He did not humble others but Himself.

Although He was the Only-Begotten according to the excellence of divinity and had no brothers, for our sake He also became the Firstborn according to His assumption of humanity. In that humanity He graciously acquired brothers through the adoption of grace, so that He might be their Firstborn. Concerning them He Himself says through the Prophet: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one!” Here He does not mean bodily brothers but spiritual brothers—brothers concerning whom the same Lord says to the Father: “I shall declare Your name to my brothers”; brothers concerning whom He said to the women: “Go, announce to my brothers.”

Truly good and truly pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one! We left one brother in the world; behold how many we have found in the monastery! My worldly brother did not love me as much as he loved my property. But spiritual brothers neglect what belongs to themselves and do not seek what belongs to others. Thus also we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul.” And, he says, “all things were common to them,” because they possessed Christ in common.

### XXXIX

This rule, which the Church now maintains, descended from the Head Himself, whose body it also is, according to the Apostle, who says: “From whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its bonds and connections, grows for the increase of God.”

We, all His faithful, are the body of that supreme Head, Christ. The body is bound together through bonds and connections, because while the breast is joined to the head, the arms to the breast, the hands to the arms, the fingers to the hands, and the remaining limbs adhere to the limbs, the entire body is perfected.

Thus the holy apostles, because they were close to our Redeemer, were like the breast joined to the head. Because the martyrs followed them, they were like arms joined to the breast. When pastors and teachers were joined to them through good works, they became the hands of the arms.

But this entire body of our Redeemer is supplied daily in heaven through bonds and connections, because when chosen souls are led there to Him, His members are joined to Him. Concerning this it is well said: “Supplied and joined together, it grows for the increase of God.” For almighty God, our Redeemer, who has no way in which He Himself might advance, still receives increase daily through His members.

Hence it is written again: “Until we all come to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” The Church completes all this through the suffering of the flesh and the compassion of the mind. And when the body suffers here, the Head, whose body it is, suffers also, as the Apostle Paul testifies when he says: “I daily complete what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh, for His body, which is the Church.”

### XL

Our Lord and Redeemer, together with the holy Church which He redeemed according to the flesh, is one substance. The Church is the body of that Head, and Christ is the Head of this body.

The body—that is, the holy Church—rejoices in its Head when it says through the Psalmist: “But now He has exalted my head above my enemies.” Because the Church itself is also to be exalted one day, it already rejoices in heaven that its Head has been exalted above its enemies.

Therefore, when the chosen reach life, because they enter through Him as His members and come to Him, He Himself enters into Himself through Himself. For He Himself is in His members who enter; He is the Head to whom the entering members come.

Understand, then, the rule maintained by His members, the Church, which is one body in the love of the supreme Head, from whom it receives the Holy Spirit, according to the Psalmist’s words: “Like ointment upon the head, which descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. CXXXII, 2).

Consider, then, what he calls ointment. Ointment is grace; it is the blessing of divinity—just as the blessing of ointment comes from the head, that is, from divinity in Christ. God is the Head of Christ; Christ is the Head of the Church.

The ointment descended upon the man Christ. From Christ it descended to the edge of His garment, which is the Church. “Ointment from the head, which descended upon the beard.” For the beard is an indication of manhood. The head, then, is called divinity, as we have said, from which the ointment descended upon Aaron’s beard—that is, upon Christ, who is the Head of the Church.

The beard, as we have said, indicates a man, in whom we attain to a perfect man, who is Christ. And after it descended upon that beard, the same ointment descended to the edge of His garment. Thus the blessing and the dew descended upon Hermon to Mount Zion.

Hermon in our language is interpreted as *anathema*, which is the people of the Jews. The dew, therefore—that is, the Lord’s blessing—was formerly upon the Jewish people, who were afterward accursed. And that blessing, which had previously descended upon the accursed people, afterward descended upon Mount Zion, that is, the Church, which is the body of Christ.

Upon this Head of the Church the ointment descended, as the Psalmist says of Him: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, Your God, anointed You with the oil of gladness above Your companions.” The apostles are companions of Christ, but the apostles received the Holy Spirit according to a measure. In Christ, however, the whole fullness of the Holy Spirit descended, because He alone was without sin, and from His fullness the apostles received.

### XLI

You have heard what he said: “You loved righteousness.” But observe also what he says in opposition to it: “And You hated iniquity.” Hear what He received for these virtues: “Therefore,” he says, “the Lord, Your God, anointed You with the oil of gladness above Your companions.” This is said of Christ.

Jesus Christ, You were anointed so that You might anoint others with the ointment that descended upon the beard—“upon the beard,” he says, “of Aaron.” The ointment that is upon the head descended upon the beard; that is, it descended from the true God to the human being whom He graciously assumed. And from the human being whom He assumed it descended to the edge of His garment, which is what we are.

Let us see how much this holy beard and this perfect man benefit us. Who are those who advance, upon whom it descends to the edge of His garment, who can be the garment of Christ? And when they have become Christ’s garment, then Christ Himself is truly their garment, and they put on Christ.

If we are Christ’s garment, we clothe His nakedness with our faith. Behold, He hangs naked upon the cross, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles. Yet by our faith, our speech, and our confession we clothe His nakedness, and we say: “Our Lord and God is He who hangs naked upon the cross. He is truly the Son of God who suffers insults and mockery naked upon the cross, so that we might be clothed by His nakedness.”

### XLII

When the Jews hear us saying these things, they stop their ears and ridicule us because we have such a God, one who hung naked upon the cross. We withdraw from one another so completely that they do not receive us, nor do we receive them.

We flee from one enemy, the Jews, and find many enemies within the house: heretics worse than the Jews. The Jews deny Him once and say: “This one whom you say hung naked upon the cross is not God.”

When we ask them, “Who is He?” they reply: “He is a human being. For if He were God, He would not have said: ‘My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?’ Therefore you ought not so absurdly to call Him God, but only an adopted son, just as we are adopted. For neither is the one who hangs naked upon the cross the one God, nor is He the true Son of God. You do God an injury by such a belief. We honor God when we rightly say that God descended to such an indignity.”

It is a servant [or: “The Servant”] who suffers. He is the servant of God who suffers, as He Himself says of Himself: “O Lord, I am Your servant; I am Your servant and the son of Your handmaid.” And the Lord says to Him: “Behold my servant; I shall receive Him.”

Since Scripture says this truly, how can you maintain that the naked human being who hangs upon the cross, crying out that He has been forsaken by God, is God? Behold, we have also found these people to be like the Jews. The Jews stripped Christ, placed Him naked upon the cross, and He hung there dead. That nakedness, the cross, and the death cause scandal to the Jews, and they say: “He is not God.”

These heretics say the same: “He is not God.” The Jews stripped Christ of His garments; these people strip Him of faith. Christ’s nakedness caused scandal to the former; Christ’s humility causes scandal to the latter.

Therefore these are not Christ’s garment, because they do not clothe Christ with their faith but strip Him, together with the Jews, by their unbelief. The Jews praised the God of Israel, yet denied the very God of Israel whom they fastened naked to the cross. These people praise Christ, yet deny that Christ Himself, who hung naked upon the cross, is the God of Israel.

Both groups consider themselves the Lord’s people, and both profess themselves better than us in faith. Both say: “We are Israel, who rightly believe in God. You are brutish and senseless, because you regard as God a human being who died.”

Since Israel is said to mean “seeing God,” both groups profess themselves to be Israel, and both assert that they are children of God. But the Lord reproves them through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “I nourished and exalted sons, but they despised me. The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, my people has not understood me.”

He calls them His people, yet they have neither understood nor known Him. He does not understand God who does not understand Christ, because Christ is God. He does not know the God of Israel who does not know Christ, because Christ is the God of Israel.

He is not pure in heart who does not see God, the Maker of heaven and earth, who does not believe in Christ, because Christ is God, the Maker of heaven and earth. For this reason they do not see God: they do not have a pure heart. “Blessed,” He says, “are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

### XLIII

It follows, then, that those who do not understand do not see, and those who do not see walk in darkness. Hence the Psalmist also says: “They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness.”

Those who walk in darkness do not walk in the day, which is Christ and the Church. Nor can they say that verse of the psalm: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.”

And because day and night are called one day—because from the sun until the next rising of the sun it includes both day and night and is called one day—so the Church and the perversity of the heretics are light and darkness, and are called one Church.

Both read one Gospel, but both cannot be Christ’s garment. While one covers Christ’s nakedness by faith, the other proclaims Christ naked through unbelief, saying: “He is a human being; He is not God; He is not the one who made heaven and earth.”

The other proclaims Him not naked but clothed, saying: “He is God and man, and He Himself made heaven and earth—the one who hangs upon the cross between heaven and earth.”

Only the Church can say this about Christ the Head, whose body it is, because He redeemed the Church with His precious blood so that He might unite it to Himself through blood; and Christ might clothe it, and it might clothe Christ, as the Apostle Paul speaks of Him to the Ephesians: “That He might present to Himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle.”

It has neither spot nor wrinkle because it lacks both the defilement of conduct and duplicity of speech. “Not having,” he says, “spot or wrinkle”—that is, neither having a spot through sin nor a wrinkle through duplicity. For it is clean through righteousness and stretched out through single-minded intention. Therefore, having been washed so that it may have no spot, it is stretched out so that it may have no wrinkle.

It is certainly Christ’s garment. For just as the whole Church generally is called Christ’s clothing, so the souls of individuals are the clothing of the Church. Having turned from error, they surround the Church by believing in it and clinging faithfully to it. Concerning these the Lord says to that same Church through the prophet: “As I live, you shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament.”

### XLIV

Behold how the Church, through faith, conversion, and good works, is Christ’s garment. Behold how the souls of individuals, converted through the Church’s preaching and believing that forgiveness of sins exists only in it, and clinging faithfully to it, are the garment of the Church itself.

The souls gathered together as one are the garment of the Church. The whole Church is Christ’s garment, and Christ is the garment of the whole Church.

I tell you something new—or rather, not new, but something from Scripture: we are Christ’s garment. And when we clothe Him with our confession and faith, then we in turn put on Christ Himself. For the Apostle also says that Christ is our garment: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” For when we are baptized, we are clothed and covered.

### XLV

Why have I said all this? To show that believers are the garment of Christ, which descended to the edge of His garment, which descended upon the beard—“upon the beard,” he says, “of Aaron.”

Thus Aaron the priest prefigured this priest of ours, Christ, and his eight garments prefigured the whole Church. We are the figure of those garments, according to the Apostle, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, because the things that happened to them in figure have been fulfilled in us in reality.

The high priest, as we said, has eight kinds of garments. It would take too long to speak of the ephod, the tunic, the belt, the chains, the undergarments, the fringes, the footwear, and the bells, and of the virtues with which the priest must enter the temple of the Lord and the Holy of Holies.

Therefore, if we wish to belong to this priestly garment, either we are the shoulder-piece, which is interpreted as *ephod*, so that we may have good works and carry Christ’s commands upon our shoulders; or certainly we ought to be the inner tunic, a tunic that is tight and clings to the body. It is not loose or flowing, but clings entirely to the body.

You see, then, that whoever is inward, and is the inner tunic, is joined more closely to the body.

### XLVI

It would take too long to speak of the *rationale* and the manifestations. If someone is a *rationale*, which is called *logion*, it is found nowhere but on the breast. Whatever is said or done with reason is called rational; whatever is said or done without reason cannot be called rational.

You will understand the order of Scripture. Whoever is rational is the ephod, that is, the shoulder-piece; and upon the breast is prudence.

Yet it may happen that someone possesses prudence, so that he has an *augen* [perhaps Greek αὐγήν, “radiance”], that is, a *logion*, which in Latin is called rationality, and does not have an *ermonem* [perhaps *sermonem*, “discourse”], that is, a manifestation.

Whoever, therefore, is a true priest must be rational; he must have manifestations—that is, he must bring forth whatever is manifest and teach it to everyone.

### XLVII

And perhaps he does all these things, if careful and adorned chastity has not been present and he has not mortified all the impulses of the flesh, so that he may gird and mortify his loins.

Next he ought to have undergarments, so that whatever is shameful and filthy at the buttocks may, as it were, be cleansed and mortified by this belt.

Next it is said that we ought to have the *phodere* [possibly *podere*], that is, a garment of the tunic extending to the feet. The *phodere* orders, as it were, our feet. And in that *phodere* there are various flowers. There are pomegranates there, and there are also fringes.

I think that the woman suffering from an issue of blood was healed for this reason: she immediately touched the fringe. Why do I say all this? So that we may persevere in the good work that we begin all the way to the end—which reaches to the feet, if we desire to be Christ’s garment.

### XLVIII

Next consider that at the extreme feet there were pomegranates and bells, and the high priest did not enter the Holy of Holies unless those bells rang.

And what does entering the Holy of Holies mean, except that inner spiritual understanding where he speaks with the Lord?

### XLIX

Those bells and those pomegranates are diverse virtues. The priest—that is, the high priest—who carries the whole Church in himself as Christ’s garment in figure ought first to make the works of his various virtues resound through the whole Church like bells. Then all should gather for his imitation, and thus he should enter the Holy of Holies, so that whatever he has heard within concerning the Lord he may speak outwardly to the people, according to the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “So that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

When this has occurred, there will be the Church; there will be Mount Zion, because there the Lord commanded blessing. That is, the ointment that descended from the Head of divinity upon the beard—“upon the beard,” he says, “of Aaron”—which descended to the edge of His garment, which is Christ; and that blessing of dew which had descended upon Hermon reached Mount Zion—that is, it reached the Church from the Jewish people. Mount Zion is the Church, because in it the Lord commanded this blessing and life forever.

Christ is life. Whoever confesses Christ will have life forever and ever.

Yet if we belong to the Church, we defend the Church and stand in the truth of its doctrines; we are in Christ’s building. But those who are not in the Church oppose Christ’s Church.

If, then, we are in the Church, if we have the faith of the Church, the faith of the apostles, and the faith of Christ’s doctrines, we are the mountains of truth; we are Zion.

### L

Our Lord Jesus Christ is the mountain of mountains, not one of the mountains, as the heretic Elipandus asserts.

For when “mountain” is said in the singular, or “Lord” in the singular, or “Christ” in the singular, or “high priest” in the singular, or “priest” in the singular, or “offering” in the singular, or “lamb” in the singular, or “stone” in the singular, or “rock” in the singular, and other similar expressions; or certainly when “servant” is said in the singular, or “poor man” in the singular, He alone is to be understood in His own person. Thus, even in the very humility in which He is proclaimed figuratively by us, no one similar to Him is to be proclaimed.

For there are many holy human beings who become holy by believing in Him. From Him they are called gods, from Him lords, from Him christs, from Him high priests, from Him priests, from Him offerings, from Him lambs, from Him living stones, from Him strong rocks.

For this reason He became the Father’s servant, so that He might free us from many lords—that is, from many idols—and so that we might have as Lord Him alone who for our sake became a servant. We might be free through Him who alone among the dead is free and who led us to this freedom.

Without doubt, the highest freedom is believed to exist in the one in whom Christ’s service is confirmed.

For our sake He became poor, so that through His poverty we might become rich. And what is His poverty except His humanity? And what are our riches except His humanity?

“What is weak in God is stronger than human beings.” Where He descended, there we ascended. Where He humbled Himself, there He raised us up. Where He endured punishment, there He freed us from punishment. Where He died, there He gave us life. Where He rose, there He raised us up. Where He ascended, there He lifted us with Himself.

Where the Father exalted Him and gave Him a name, there He exalted us with Him and gave us all things with Him. For the Father gave Him to us, and gave us to Him; He placed Him at His right hand and caused us, His body, to sit with the Head.

### LI

Although the Head and the body are one substance, there is nevertheless a great difference between the Head and the body. They have only one sense in common, while the Head alone claims the other four.

There is therefore a great difference between Christ as man and the whole multitude of the saints, who derive their origin from Adam. With all their virtues, that entire army cannot be compared or made equal to Christ the man alone.

Christ alone could exist without them; all of them cannot live or exist without Christ.

### LII

Why have we said all this? Because we have called the Church, figuratively, Mount Zion.

We can say in the singular that Mount Zion is one Church, which is the one body of Christ. We can also call it mountains and Churches.

But we cannot call Christ alone “Christ” and “christs,” “mountain” and “mountains,” “Lord” and “lords,” “God” and “gods,” “servant” and “servants,” “poor man” and “poor men,” “little one” and “little ones,” “circumcised man” and “circumcised men,” “baptized man” and “baptized men,” “scourged man” and “scourged men,” “dead man” and “dead men.”

He alone died for all. He alone suffered these things for all. None of the saints died for another.

For when the Apostle John says: “As Christ laid down His life for us, we also ought to lay down our lives for our brothers,” anyone can indeed do this by showing compassion; but no one could do it by dying and rising again, except Christ alone, the only one without sin.

All the saints can say that saying of David: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. L, 7). Christ never said this verse.

But what did He say? “The ruler of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John XIV, 30)—that is, he found no sin in me.

Therefore, because He alone is a human being without sin, no human being is found to be like Him. He alone is the Head and is above the whole body. He is uniquely the mountain and is above all the mountains, as the prophet Micah testifies, saying:

“In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared at the summit of the mountains; it shall be exalted above the hills, and peoples shall flow to it. Many nations shall hasten and say: ‘Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and He shall teach us His ways; and we shall walk in His paths’” (Mic. IV).

The Psalmist also speaks of that mountain and of the other mountains in Psalm LXVII: “Why do you look with envy, you cheese-bearing mountains, at the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell?” (Isa. II, 2–3; Ps. LXVII, 17.) Just as He is called the mountain, so those others are called mountains. But the mountain prepared at the summit of the mountains is far higher than the mountains.

These mountains, then, are glorious because they bear that mountain, so that “whoever glories may glory in the Lord,” not in himself.

Paul the architect says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

### LIII

“Why do you look with envy at these mountains—the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell?”

Not that God does not dwell in those mountains. Indeed, He does. But through this mountain God dwells in those mountains.

For in Him alone the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily. Divinity does not dwell in Him figuratively, as in the temple built by King Solomon, but bodily. It does not dwell in Him as it does in heaven, or on earth, or in angels, or in the other saints; rather, the whole fullness of divinity—that is, of the Father and the Holy Spirit—dwells bodily in Him.

Christ Himself is also divinity by nature. Although divinity dwells in angels and in the other saints, none of them is divinity by nature as Christ is.

And because Christ, the Father, and the Holy Spirit are one divinity; because He Himself is in the Father, the Father is in Him, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both; therefore the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Him—that is, solidly and truly—according to the Apostle Paul, who says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself.”

Whether we understand this as spoken of the Father, since He Himself says, “The Father who remains in me, He Himself does the works,” and, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”; or whether it is understood in this way: “God was in Christ,” that is, the Word was in the human being, meaning that God was man.

The Word was certainly in the flesh in such a way that the Word made flesh was properly said to be one alone; that is, the human being and the Word were joined in the one person of Christ.

Why, then, do you suspect the other mountains—the mountain in which it pleased God to dwell?

He dwells in those mountains plurally in one way, and in this mountain singularly in another way. Which of those mountains, then, do you suspect to be this mountain?

For although they too are sons of God through the grace of adoption, none of them is the Only-Begotten, to whom the Father would say: “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies beneath your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1).

None of them took away the sins of the world. Of none of them was it said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Of none of them was it said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to Him.” Of none of them do we read that he is the Lord of glory.

But of Christ the Apostle said: “They crucified the Lord of glory,” because neither the Father appeared in the world, nor the Holy Spirit, but they crucified only the one Son, the Word of God the Father.

### LIV

Therefore, when you hear “Word,” beware of thinking of many words. For if you think of many words of the Father, you will understand not one Son but many sons.

Beware, then, lest the sound of the voice and the likeness of human speech deceive you. One thing is a word that has temporal duration, that is gathered into syllables, that is gathered into letters, that sounds, that is heard by the ears, that has temporal duration: one word sounds, passes away, an interval of silence occurs, another word is formed, and it follows so that it may be heard and understood. When it has been completed, a third follows; and as one word follows another, many words are produced.

The Only Son is not such a Word of the Father; the Only-Begotten God is not such a Word. God the Father is incorporeal. The incorporeal does not have a corporeal voice. If a corporeal voice is not in the Father, neither is the Son a corporeal Word.

Therefore there are not many words or many sons, but one Word, equal to the Father, which excludes both rank and number.

This is what I say because I read it; this is what I believe because I proclaim it. What the nature of this Word is, I do not know. And I know that much better than I know anything else. I know this alone clearly: that I do not know what I cannot know.

For John, whom I read, could say nothing other than what he heard: “What we have seen,” he says, “and what we have heard.” He, who reclined upon Christ’s breast, said that he knew clearly only what he had heard and seen.

Therefore it is enough for him to hear; it is not enough for me. But what he heard, he told me. And what he heard from Christ, I too cannot deny to be true concerning Christ.

Therefore what he heard, I heard. What did he hear? The Word. For he said: “What was from the beginning, what we have heard.” Then he says: “And we have seen.”

All this is true, because he heard and saw. What did he see? Certainly not divinity, which according to its nature cannot be seen. He saw Him according to my nature. For the Word is not one Son and the human being another; rather, from both there is one Only Son.

### LV

But because no one could see Him according to His own nature, He assumed my visible nature so that He might be seen according to the nature of the body.

Finally, the Holy Spirit was also seen in the form of a dove, because divinity could not be seen in the truth of its own splendor. This invisibility is one and the same for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because there is one divinity and one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But because there are three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—they do not have this in common: only the Son became man for the redemption of human beings; only the Holy Spirit descended upon the human Son in the form of a dove so that He might be seen; and only the Father cried out, “You are my beloved Son,” so that He might be heard.

### LVI

But the dove in which the Holy Spirit appeared is not called the Holy Spirit, as this human being, assumed by the Word, is called the Son. That dove is not God. This human being, however, is God.

The Father’s voice, which sounded corporeally, is not the Father. But this corporeal being who was seen is the only Son of God the Father.

The Father spoke through an assumed creature, not through His own substance, because God is invisible. The Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove through an assumed creature, not through His own nature, by which He is the invisible God.

The Son alone appeared to human beings through His own substance. He did not appear through that by which He is equal to the Father, but through that by which He came, sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit—the Son alone, who emptied Himself, that is, who alone took the form of a servant.

Therefore do not interpret according to nature what lies outside the nature of divinity. If you believe that flesh was assumed by the Word, and offer the body of Christ to be transformed upon the altars, but do not understand what is offered or to whom it is offered, and do not distinguish the nature of divinity from that of the body, the Lord immediately says to you: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.”

I do not mean that you should divide the person; rather, I mean that no one in prayers should name either the Father in place of the Son or the Son in place of the Father. And whenever one assists at the altar, prayer should always be directed to the Father.

Whoever copies prayers for himself from elsewhere should not use them unless he has first compared them with more learned brothers—that is, the prayers he proposes should first be informed by Catholics.

### LVII

Therefore the Son alone is man, and He is also equal to the Father, always in the form of God. With the Father we offer a sacrifice, and He alone, taking the form of a servant, became a priest. Through Him we can offer a living sacrifice pleasing to God.

Yet an offering could not have been offered by us if Christ had not become an offering for us. In Him the very nature of our race is a true saving offering.

For in order that the Only-Begotten, who is truly God by nature, might truly become man and priest in the person of His divinity, He did not assume the person of a human being but a nature.

For if He had assumed the nature of a human being together with a person, then in the mystery of the Incarnation there would not be one Christ, God and man, in two natures; rather, in two persons there would be one who was God and another who was man.

But Christ is one, the one Son of God and man, because the Only-Begotten Lord, who always possessed His own person, received in that same person the reality of a servant’s nature.

Therefore Christ remains inseparable. Although one nature in Him is the nature of divinity and the other is the nature of a servant, nevertheless in one and the same Christ the person of divinity was present, and that same one person is also the person of the assumed humanity.

Therefore Christ is one and the same: the one whom Scripture shows to be a little lower than the angels, having taken the form of a servant, is shown by the unity of nature to be equal to the Father.

### LVIII

In this sacrament the heretics, especially the Arians, offend most grievously. Focusing upon the priestly office in Him, they refuse to acknowledge the exaltation of His divinity.

For there are heretics who do not believe that the Son is of one divinity with the Father.

### LIX

There are also others who do not confess that the man born is the Son of God. Both groups assert that the Virgin Mother is the mother not of God but of a human being, because, they say, visible and invisible things were not made through the one who was born from the Virgin, but through the one whom God begot as equal to Himself.

### LX.

These are the heretics, such as the Manichaeans, who did not fear to deny the reality of flesh in the Son of God. The most holy Fathers appropriately and usefully placed this passage here. For when we show that, through the eternal Priest, the Lord Christ, we offer Him in our prayers, we confess that He truly possesses the flesh of our race, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.” But when it is said, “Your Son,” and we add, “who lives and reigns with You, O supreme Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” we are certainly commending that unity which the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit possess naturally.

For if we read anything of this kind in the Scriptures, as we said above, it must be referred to the unity of person. For Christ Himself alone is the priest through whom we offer the sacrifice; and we pray that through Him it may be accepted by the Father and that He may intercede with the Father for us. He Himself is God with the Father to whom we offer. He Himself is the one who intercedes with the Father for us—not by voice, but by compassion. He Himself is the one who hears with the Father; He alone intercedes with the Father for us.

Therefore our prayer should always be directed to the Father through the mediator: through the very person by whose blood we have been redeemed, whose blood we drink and whose flesh we eat, through whom we live. For just as soul and body, though of different substances, constitute one human being, so God and man, though of different substances, constitute one Christ. And thus, since He is one despite the different substances, He Himself in a certain manner intercedes for us, and He Himself in a certain manner hears us on our behalf.

### LXI.

“Then divide what is mine; divide what is his.” For I did not possess what belonged to His divinity, and He did not possess what belongs to my humanity. He took what is mine in order to impart what is His. He took it not to confuse it, but to fill it. From our condition He received something on our behalf, by which He might merit on our behalf and by which we might live in Him. He left us an example of how we should die for Him and, where He is, pass from death to the kingdom.

For no one can pass to the kingdom unless death has intervened. And therefore, while trusting, we seem almost to doubt, and while almost doubting, we trust. We rejoice while fearing, and fear while rejoicing, because we know that we cannot reach the prize of eternal rest unless we cross with labor what lies between us and it.

So, too, when we wish to drive temporary illnesses from the body, we take the bitter cup of purgation with sadness, yet rejoice in certainty about the health that will follow. For just as bodily illness is not cured without a bitter potion, so the spiritual illness of the soul is not wiped away without the lament of tears.

How, then, can He be one with us and one of our number, when He alone wiped away not His own sins but all of ours? For this reason we run through the pages of the Scriptures in their breadth, but we find no one like Him in whom He assumed the form of a servant.

### LXII.

It remains, then, that those who think Him like themselves should extort miracles from us, as unbelievers do, and say: “If what you say is true—that Jesus is the Son of God—or if you truly are His Church, perform miracles for us in His name. When you have done so, we shall believe you that the one in whom you believe is truly God.”

This is what remains for heretics as for pagans. Faith does not seek miracles. The miracle that is seen temporally does not hope for the future. To demand a present miracle is not a part of faith but a part of unbelief.

Thus the Apostle Paul, when he came to Mitylene and knew that the island was full of unbelievers, saved Publius’s father, who was afflicted with dysentery and fevers, by praying. But Timothy, his assistant in holy preaching, who was suffering from an infirmity of the stomach, he did not cure by a word; rather, he prepared to treat him by medicinal means, saying: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.”

### LXIII.

Who, then, saves the unbelieving sick man by a single prayer, but does not strengthen the sick Timothy by prayer? Clearly, the one who was dead inwardly in soul had to be healed outwardly by a miracle, so that through the power displayed externally in the body, inward power might awaken him to life.

Yet both were ill, though they were not ill in the same way. Timothy was sick in body but sound in soul; together with his teacher he preached Christ among the nations. Publius’s father, however, was sick in body but dead in soul, because he had not yet been raised through faith in Christ.

For Christ Himself said: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even though he has died, will live.” Therefore whoever does not believe that the Son of the Virgin is naturally the Son of God, true God, does not live but is dead. He is dead because he does not believe this. He would already be alive if he believed.

Therefore the one who lives inwardly no longer seeks miracles but repentance. Whoever lives inwardly in soul does not pursue the care of the body as his desire. Whoever is dead inwardly in soul does pursue the care of the body as his desire. And whoever strives to care for the body cannot know Christ.

### LXIV.

God is therefore seen more easily when, according to the Apostle, “the outward person is being corrupted.” And the more the outward person is corrupted day by day, the more the inward person is renewed day by day in the knowledge of God. The less the outward person is corrupted, the less the inward soul is renewed, and the less God is known.

It is the soul itself that must be renewed, since the Apostle calls it the temple of God. For he says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple.” The inward person was made in the image of God.

Let us therefore call forth the spirit of our mind, which is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created it, because Christ dwells in us there through faith. There there is neither Jew nor Greek; there there is neither slave nor free; there there is neither male nor female. There we cannot die when we begin to be released from the body. There we do not grow old, even if in the body we reach extreme old age.

Since this is true, and yet we seek suitable places and cannot find them, let us cleanse the inner chambers of the soul. Let us drive out every evil desire from there, prepare within our heart a secluded place of peace, and always act so that we may be the holy temple of God.

And if we wish to pray in the temple, let us pray within ourselves. For the one whom we pray to dwells there. Christ hears when He is called upon there, where He also dwells.

We believe that we shall see God—not because we see Him through the eyes of the body, as we see this sun, nor by the gaze of the mind, as each person sees himself inwardly: alive, willing, seeking, and knowing.

### LXV.

What, then, have we said? Is seeing the same as believing? Clearly, there is a great difference between the two, because present things are seen, while absent things are believed.

The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” Yet He said this to one who had seen Him and touched His scars: “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.”

If He calls blessed the one who has seen Christ and believes, how did the same Lord say elsewhere in the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God”? And the Apostle Paul says to Timothy: “No human being has seen Him, nor can see Him.”

All this was said about human beings, not about others. It was not said about those of whom we spoke above, in whose souls Christ dwells through faith—those who are the holy temple of God and in whom God dwells. The Prophet bears witness to this when he says: “The Lord is in His holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven.”

They are also called heavens, according to the testimony of Psalm 18: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” And in our daily prayer we say: “Our Father, who are in heaven,” as though we were saying openly: “You who are in the holy angels and in holy souls.”

They themselves are heaven, because they savor not earthly things but heavenly things, in accordance with the Apostle Paul’s saying: “If you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is at the right hand of God the Father.”

Whoever has risen with Christ and sets his mind on the things above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father, is now called by the sacred Scriptures not a human being but God. For he is also God, in whom God dwells, and he always sees Him because he is always in Him.

For no human being can see God. Thus the Lord Himself also questioned His disciples, saying: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” He did not say, “Who do people say that I am?” but “who the Son of Man is,” lest He appear to be asking boastfully about Himself.

Yet He asks beautifully: “Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?” For those who speak of the Son of Man are not gods but merely human beings. But those who rightly understand His divinity and say with Peter, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” are called not human beings but gods.

### LXVI.

Therefore the Apostle said: “No human being has seen Him, nor can see Him” (1 Timothy 6:16). Following ordinary human usage, he calls “human beings” those who think human things. For those who savor divine things are undoubtedly above human beings.

We shall therefore see God if we are worthy, through a heavenly manner of life, to be above human beings. Even now, according to the Apostle, “we see through a mirror, in an enigma,” through faith. But then we shall see “face to face.”

Nevertheless, we shall not see Him in the same way that He sees Himself. The Creator sees Himself in a manner vastly different from that in which the creature sees the Creator. For, in relation to God’s immensity, a certain measure of contemplation is fixed for us, because we are circumscribed by that very limitation by which we are creatures.

Thus we do not behold God in the same way that He beholds Himself. Nor do we rest in God in the same way that He rests in Himself. Our vision or rest will in some manner resemble His vision or rest, but it will not be equal to it.

So that we do not remain prostrate in ourselves, as I might put it, the wing of contemplation lifts us up. As we are raised from ourselves to behold Him, seized by the concentration of the heart and the sweetness of contemplation, we go in some manner from ourselves into Him.

Even this going of ours is less than resting. Yet to go in this way is to rest perfectly. It is therefore perfect rest, because God is seen; nevertheless, it cannot be made equal to the rest of the one who does not pass from himself into another in order to rest.

### LXVII.

There is therefore a rest that is, so to speak, both similar and dissimilar. For what His rest is, ours imitates. In order that we may be blessed and eternal forever, we imitate the Eternal; and our imitation of eternity is itself a great eternity for us.

Nor are we excluded from the one whom we can imitate. For by seeing, we share in Him, and by sharing in Him, we imitate Him.

This vision undoubtedly begins now through faith, but then it will be completed in reality, when we drink at the very fountain, Christ, the wisdom coeternal with God, which now we receive through the mouths of preachers as though through flowing streams—we who are His body.

But great will be the labor of anyone who wishes to reach those realities. For it is no small violence to the body when the flesh desires to become what God is.

God is the head of Christ’s body, as the Apostle bears witness when he says: “I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a woman is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.”

### LXVIII.

What, then, is our head except the divinity through which we receive the beginning of our existence, so that we may be creatures? For “the husband is the head of the woman; Christ is the head of the man; and God is the head of Christ.”

All this is found in Christ, who is the mediator between God and human beings. In this passage he calls the woman the people within the Church, small in understanding and carnal, who are under pastoral guidance.

The husband of this woman is their teachers. Following the apostolic example and imitating Christ’s footsteps, they govern her by educating her with such dedication that it is not enough for them to instruct her through preaching and example; following the examples of their own head, they must also lay down their lives for her.

Thus he can be her head and cling to his own head, Christ, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying.

### LXIX.

Through the man, Christ became the head of this husband. For the whole divinity is the head of the man Christ, assumed by the Word.

All this exists in the one Christ, because “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” in Him, and He Himself is the head of the whole Church.

Consider how one human being consists of soul and body, and how within the body there are these parts—flesh, bones, and head. The flesh is governed by the bones, the bones by the head, and the head by the soul.

We call the flesh the woman; we call the bones the man, the head of this woman, the flesh; we call the head the human head itself, the head of these bones; and we call the mind the head of this head. All of this exists in one human being.

So we call the head of the woman—that is, of the small people—the pastors and teachers of the Churches, as though they were the bones of the flesh. Christ is the head of the man, as though He were the head of the bones. God is the head of Christ, as though He were the mind of the head.

Although all these things exist in one human being, and the whole is itself one human being, differences are nevertheless found there, by which one part can surpass another.

Do not the bones, which are hard, surpass the flesh, which is soft? And without the bones the flesh cannot stand. So, too, the small people within the Church, who are like soft flesh, cannot stand without a teacher, who is solid like the bones.

These bones are joined to the head, through which they have life; unless they are joined to the head, through which they have life, they cannot live. So the teachers of the Churches are joined to Christ the head; unless they are joined to Christ through faith and works, they cannot live.

Now the mind surpasses the head to the degree that it is another substance, a spiritual one. So the divinity of Christ is the head both of Christ’s body—which Christ Himself contains in Himself—and of the whole fullness of His divinity and of the whole fullness of our humanity.

### LXX.

We say all this by means of a kind of comparison because of the foolishness and controversy of the heretics. They neither confess Christ the man as the Son of God, nor confess Him as one God with the Father, nor confess that there is no other God besides Him. Nor do they confess Him as one man with the whole Church.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] The passage is corrupt.]

They also deny that there is one person who is the Church and another person who is Christ the man, and another person who is the Word of the Father—so that there would be three persons: the Word, the man, and the Church, just as there are three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The Son alone became man—that is, He became a rational soul and flesh. Accordingly, the Word, soul, and flesh are indeed three substances, but there is one Christ, one only Son, one Lord of ours, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary and was crucified under Pontius Pilate.

He truly and without falsehood has the Father as God naturally, from whom He has divinity, so that He is true God and there is no other God besides Him. And truly and without falsehood He has the Virgin naturally as mother—the Virgin Mary. And He is not, together with the whole Church that He redeemed by His blood, another human being, but one person, one Christ from three substances.

This person belongs neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit but, as we have said, to the Son. The Son, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one substance and not one person; rather, there are three persons.

With the whole man Adam whom He assumed, He alone is one person and not one substance; rather, there are three substances—the Word, the soul, and the flesh—constituting the one only Son.

### LXXI.

Consider the mediator. He alone descended, because neither the Father descended nor the Holy Spirit.

And because, as we have said, He is one substance with the Father—and, as one substance, He is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and there is no other God besides Him, with whom He is one substance—there is no other God besides the Father, nor another God besides the Son, nor another God besides the Holy Spirit.

Nor is there another God besides the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Yet although together they are one God and one light, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not one person.

The Father is light because He begot light. The Son is light because He was born from light. The Holy Spirit is light because He proceeded from light unbegotten and begotten. And the three together are one light.

### LXXII.

Or perhaps you accuse me and say: “If they are one light, where is the Trinity? Perhaps the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit exist only in name, and the persons are not expressly distinguished?”

I shall answer: Far from it. The persons are expressly distinguished and subsist in their own proper identities.

For Sabellian perversity invented the idea that, since it believed in one inseparable light, it should also believe in one person, saying: “He is Himself the Father, He is Himself the Son, and He is Himself the Holy Spirit.”

### LXXIII.

Arius, on the contrary, since he believed in three persons subsisting in their own proper identities, also believed in three lights.

And because there is one light, one of them confused the persons while the other separated them. But both were blinded by the one light and confounded by the one light; that is, although they were not mingled in the one light, they were separated from the one light.

### LXXIV.

There is one light, as we have said, yet there is a Trinity in the one who begets, the one begotten, and the one proceeding. For to beget is one thing, to be begotten another, and to proceed another.

Therefore the one who begot is not the same person as the one who was begotten, because the person who begot is one person and the person who was begotten is another. One begot another, but he did not beget something different from what he is. That is, he is light, and he begot light, which is what he himself is.

Although what He begot is the very same light, He is nevertheless not Himself the one whom He begot. The light that He begot is of the same nature, but He Himself is not the person who begot the begotten light.

Nor is the one who begets and the one who is begotten the third person who proceeds from them. Rather, one person is the light who begets, another person is the light who is begotten, and another person is the light who proceeds.

Light, light, and light: one light. The one who begets, the one begotten, and the one proceeding: three persons and one light. It is as though I were to say: God, God, and God—one God.

And because God begot God, and God proceeded from God, in the one who begets, the one begotten, and the one proceeding there are three persons subsisting in their own identities, while by nature there is one God.

Therefore the Son alone became man—not in the unity of nature but in the unity of person. That is, the light eternally begotten from the Father assumed our nature. And secondly, light and body were born from the Virgin.

The light remained forever inseparable from and equal to the Father, just as the angel said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

For a shadow is represented only through light and body. The power of the Most High overshadowed her because, in her womb, incorporeal light assumed a body. From this overshadowing all believers in Christ receive refreshment of mind within themselves.

For a shadow, as we have already said, is formed from light and body. The Lord, through His divinity, is light; through the mediation of a soul, He deigned to become a body in her womb through His humanity.

Since incorporeal light was present in her womb to be conceived, and she conceived it bodily, the words “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” are spoken with reference to the body. That is: “The body of humanity receives incorporeal light of divinity within you.”

### LXXV.

Hence in the Song of Songs, in the voice of the Bridegroom, it is said: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. For your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes surpasses all spices” (Song of Songs 1:2).

You have heard, beloved brothers, the nuptial song that the Holy Spirit foretold through Solomon in the voice of the Bridegroom and the bride—that is, Christ and the Church—as an allegorical celebration of heavenly weddings.

When Christ the Bridegroom and the soul the bride pledged to one another the chaste will of marriage, they became two in one flesh—that is, God and man. These two, the Word and the soul, are one person: the Bridegroom and the bride in one flesh.

The bridal chamber of that Bridegroom was the Virgin’s womb, because in that virginal womb the two—the Bridegroom and the bride—were joined. For it is written: “And the two shall become one flesh.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh.”

For Christ and the Church are not two fleshes and two human beings but one flesh and one human being. Isaiah also very clearly remembered that the two spouses are one. For he speaks in the person of Christ and says: “As a bridegroom He placed a diadem upon me, and as a bride He adorned me with an ornament.”

One person appears to speak, and he made himself both bridegroom and bride. For they are not two but one flesh—that is, one nature of flesh and one substance of Christ and of us.

Just as Christ and the Father are one substance, so He is perfect God with the Father and perfect man with us. God and man from two natures are one person, Christ.

For “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”—that is, He dwelt in our flesh. He dwells in us when He dwells in our flesh. And the flesh of ours in which He dwells is Himself, the one who dwells there. He made Himself a house in which to dwell, and that house itself is He.

### LXXVI.

Any carpenter, for example, makes a house for himself in which to dwell, but the house itself is not the one who dwells in it. Perhaps, when that house is destroyed or burned by a persecutor, its inhabitant rises so as not to perish with it and leaves the house empty, because the house in which he lived was not himself.

It is not so that God, having become man, dwelt among us—that is, in our flesh. It is not so that the Word of the Father is one inhabitant and our flesh, which He inhabits, another, so that, when He was killed in the flesh by the Jews, the Word, the inhabitant, fled.

Far be this from Catholic faith. Rather, the Word, soul, and flesh are one person, Christ the Son of God, just as any human being is one person consisting of soul and flesh.

And when that human being is killed, it is not the soul but the flesh that is killed, and no one other than that human being dies. So Christ, the Son of God, God and man, possesses such unity of person that He who is God is Himself man.

And when the man—that is, the flesh alone—is killed, no one other than the Son of God dies—not in divinity or in soul, but in flesh alone. In that flesh the redemption of the human race was accomplished.

Therefore the whole Church confesses our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ.

### LXXVII.

Why have we said all this, except to prove that the Word made flesh is the Son of God? “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14), but He was not changed into flesh, just as a human soul is not changed into flesh.

And when the Word dwells in Christ’s flesh, He dwells in our nature, because that flesh is our flesh. The Church is joined to that flesh, and the whole Christ becomes one person, head and body.

And whenever the sacred books speak of “the man,” “the flesh,” or “the body of Christ,” not Christ alone but the whole Church is understood.

Holy Scripture has the custom of speaking about the Lord and His body—what it says about one or to one—and of displaying in one person sometimes the head and sometimes the body. Thus Isaiah, as we said above, says: “He clothed me with a garment of salvation, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride adorned with her jewels.”

Under one person and with a double designation, he revealed both the head, that is, the Bridegroom, and the Church, that is, the bride.

### LXXVIII.

Therefore the reader should carefully note in the Scriptures when the head and the body are meant, when the speech passes from either to the other, or from one to the other. In this way the discerning reader will understand what applies to the head and what applies to the body.

That Christ is the Bridegroom and the Church the bride is proved by divine Scripture, when John the Baptist speaks of Christ in the Gospel: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and listens to him, rejoices greatly at his voice.”

Another prophet also says: “I shall betroth you to myself in faith and charity.”

Finally, the heading itself makes clear that this was foretold concerning the flesh in Christ and the Church. For the Song of Songs is so called because it is above all the songs that Moses, or Miriam in Exodus, or Isaiah, or Habakkuk, or the others sang.

These songs are better, because those singers praised God with hearts and minds inflamed either by deliverance in battle, by the conduct of the people, or by wonder at divine works. But here, because the voice of God’s Church singing psalms is heard, and because divine and human things are joined to one another, it is called the Song of Songs—that is, the better of the better songs.

### LXXIX.

When it says, therefore, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. For your breasts are better than wine,” it was not speaking of a carnal kiss but of spiritual grace.

It is the voice of the venerable, immaculate virgin Church speaking to Christ, the Son of God, a thirty-year-old young man, comely and fair in form beyond the sons of men, speaking words.

For some utterances are human and others are divine oracles—“kisses.” Therefore, when the Church says, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” the Church desires to have the Bridegroom present and to hear the voice of the one who is present.

In former times the word of God customarily spoke to the Synagogue through the prophets and, as though through another’s mouth, gave the kiss of peace.

This Church, therefore, which is truly Christ’s bride, is not content merely to receive Christ’s peace through the prophets. Rather, receiving the commandments of evangelical tradition from His own mouth, she accepts from the true Bridegroom, as it were, the kiss of holiness.

Hence: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

How truly this was fulfilled can be learned from the following. Since Christ, the Son of God, deigned to come in human form and to receive flesh and soul as a bride, the Law and the Prophets came to an end, as the Evangelist says: “The Law and the Prophets lasted until John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:13). And again: “The Law was given through Moses.”

For the Church, as the Apostle defined it, is Christ’s flesh. He says: “He himself is the head of the body, the Church.”

The kiss impressed by faith and charity upon the Church occurred when the two were joined in one flesh—that is, when truth and peace embraced one another.

### LXXX.

“Truth,” he says, “sprang up from the earth”—that is, the flesh of Christ, who was born from the Virgin and whose origin is eternal.

“Peace looked down from heaven”—that is, the Word of God, who said: “I am peace.” And again: “I give you my peace.”

This is the kiss: the Word of the Father announced by the mouths of the prophets, which for many ages had hung suspended in prolonged expectation.

It was fulfilled when the day of the wedding arrived, through which the Church received the ring of faith and the wedding attendant of the heavenly marriage.

For what is dearer to Christ than the Church, for which He poured out His blood? Or what is more beloved to the Church than Christ, through whose holy and immaculate union she has brought forth a great multitude of children through the regeneration of baptism?
