We see her abundant offspring poured forth without pain. You will sense her efficacy—or, to speak more truly, her art of being born, or rather of being reborn—more than you can describe; you will understand it more than you can grasp it.

You do not see the power itself, nor recognize the art, yet you will praise with due reverence the perfect work that the teacher of wisdom and artisan Reason has brought forth in secret.

“For your breasts are good,” he says, “better than wine.”

The ancient Law indeed had two breasts, from the two tablets of stone, impressed by the finger of God, which then offered the small people the white milk of instruction. But now we recognize that the Lord’s breasts are not two but four. For the four fountains of the Gospels give believers the sweet milk of wisdom.

### LXXXI.

Finally, when the Lord promised Abraham—who is the father of both peoples, of one according to the flesh and of us according to faith—the inheritance of the future age, He required among other things this sign for the sacrifice: a three-year-old she-goat and a three-year-old heifer.

The she-goat, which has two breasts, represented the figure of the Old Testament; the heifer, which has four, represented evangelical instruction.

These are the Lord’s good breasts—that is, the fountains of the Gospels, streams of water—which are better than the wine of prophetic preaching, by which the Law is understood as old wine. The Gospel is new wine.

### LXXXII.

For in the heavenly Scriptures we read of two kinds of wine. One ran out at the wedding in Cana of Galilee; the other was made from water, and much more abundantly, through the word of God.

Hence the Savior also said: “New wine must be put into new wineskins.”

This signified the wedding of Christ and the Church: when the Word of God joined Himself to the human soul, the wine—that is, the ancient Law and prophecy—would come to an end, and another Gospel would arise from the water of baptism.

Hence believers are full of this new wine. For what is wine made from water except the soul that had previously been earthly, tasteless, and watery, but has been changed into pure wine of the spirit and made superior in flavor?

### LXXXIII.

“And the fragrance of your perfumes surpasses all spices” (Song of Songs 4:10).

The fragrance of this most holy anointing manifested the grace of the chrism, which burns and gives off a fragrance above all the perfumes of the Synagogue. For the Synagogue had an anointing made from fragrant perfumes. But Christ’s ointment descends from the sevenfold sweetness of the Holy Spirit.

Hence he adds: “Your name is an ointment poured out” (Song of Songs 1:3).

Why, then, is it called “poured out”? I shall explain briefly. The kings and priests of the ancient Law, who were anointed from the horn of chrism, were called “christs” in the Law because, by the likeness of the anointing with chrism, they received an indication of something more perfect. Accordingly, they bore the name “christs” as a shadow rather than as the reality.

But when, according to the Apostle, the fullness of divinity was completed in Christ, the name of those kings who were called christs was emptied out, so that they would no longer be regarded by this title.

The true name of Christ remains, poured out from the true ointment—that is, from the fullness of the Holy Spirit.

Elsewhere it says: “Your name is ointment poured out,” because the most sweet grace of the true name of Christ has been poured out upon all believers and has spread the fragrance of its knowledge among all the faithful; therefore it is called “poured-out ointment.”

Hence the prayers of the saints are compared in Revelation to incense.

And so it continues: “The king brought me into his chamber.” The Church speaks here, confessing Christ the Son of God as king.

What is the chamber into which Christ the king brought the Church the queen, except the hidden place of the heavenly kingdom?

For who does not know that Christ brought His Church—that is, His flesh—to the place from which He had descended without flesh, namely, from the hidden depths of heaven?

We have learned through the authority of the Apostle Paul that Christ’s flesh is the Church. He says: “The flesh of Christ, which is the Church.”

And although there are many members through the gifts of grace, the body is nevertheless one. For the Apostle says: “The body is not one member but many. If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I am not part of the body,’ is it therefore not part of the body? And if the ear should say, ‘Because I am not an eye, I am not part of the body,’ is it therefore not part of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If the whole body were hearing, where would smell be? And if all were one member, where would the body be? But as it is, there are many members, yet one body.”

What, then, is the holy Church except the body of her heavenly head?

In it one person sees lofty things as an eye; another performs what is right as a hand; another hastens to assigned duties as a foot; another understands the voice of the commandments as an ear; another distinguishes the stench of evil from the fragrance of good as a nose.

Following the pattern of bodily members, they each perform for one another the duties they have received, and from all of themselves they produce one body. While they perform different works in charity, they prevent division wherever they are held together.

If everyone did one and the same thing, the body, which consists of many members, would not exist. For it would not be joined together in many ways if the diversity of its members did not preserve this harmony.

Since the Lord therefore distributes gifts of virtue among the holy members of the Church, He sets out their measures as though they were measures of land. When one person envies another the grace given by the Lord and wishes to ascribe it to his own name, he crosses another’s boundary.

The boundary received its name from distinguishing a limit. Whoever crosses the boundary of the measure of his grace wishes to fall, because he places his foot on a precipice.

### LXXXIV.

Let each person therefore be restrained by fear of the devil’s ruin. The devil wished to be above what he was, and by losing even what he was, he was cast down from the heights and earned the depths of hell.

### LXXXV.

Therefore no one, as a member of the body, should exceed his own measure. Hence Paul says again: “To each one God has allotted a measure of faith.”

He also says: “From him the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, causes the body to grow for its building up in love.”

### LXXXVI

But since our Creator and Disposer, by a wondrous plan, bestows upon one what he denies to another, he sets limits for each in what he bestows. Whoever strives to go beyond the limits assigned to him attempts to become greater than what he has received; thus, perhaps, one who has been given only the task of disclosing the hidden meaning of the commandments may attempt also to shine through miracles. Or one whom the gift of heavenly power strengthens only for miracles may strive also to disclose the secrets of divine law.

For he stretches his foot toward a precipice who does not heed the limits of his capacities. And often he loses what he had received, because he rashly presumes and hastens to seize what he is unable to attain.

Indeed, we make proper use of the services of our bodily members when we preserve their distinct functions. We see light with our eyes, but hear a voice with our ears. If someone, reversing the order, were to apply his eyes to a voice and his ears to light, both would be exposed to ruin. If someone wished to distinguish odors with his mouth and taste flavors with his nose, he would destroy the function of both senses by perverting it. For when these members are not applied to their proper uses, they abandon their own functions and do not rise to what is foreign to them.

“To one is given the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; to another faith; to another gifts of healings; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues.”

How is it, then, that within one and the same Spirit this man excels in the word of wisdom but does not shine in the word of knowledge—that is, in teaching? Because he is capable of perceiving and discovering even what he has not grasped through diligent study. Let that other man shine in the word of knowledge, yet not grow strong in the word of wisdom, because he is capable of fulfilling as much as he says, but does not rise by his own insight to perceive anything subtle.

This man commands the elements through faith, yet does not heal bodily illnesses through the gift of healing. That man removes diseases through the power of prayer, yet does not bring back the rain by his word. This man, through the working of miracles, restores even the dead to the present life, yet, lacking the grace of prophecy, does not know what is to come. That man regards future events as though they were present, yet does not display himself in any operation of signs.

This man, through discernment of spirits, subtly perceives minds in their actions. That man examines languages of different kinds, yet does not weigh dissimilar hearts in similar matters. Another, in the one language he knows, prudently examines the force of words by interpreting them, yet patiently lacks the other good gifts that he does not possess.

### LXXXVII

Thus our Creator and Disposer orders everything so that whoever might become proud because of the gift he possesses may be humbled by the virtue he lacks. He orders everything so that, while he raises each person up through the grace bestowed upon him, he also subjects one person to another through unequal gifts; and each person may recognize that the one subject to him is better than himself in another gift.

Although he may perceive that he surpasses another in some respect [or: that another surpasses him], nevertheless he should place himself below the same person in other respects. Thus he orders everything.

And while the individual gifts which belonged to all become the property of each through a certain bond of charity, each person possesses in another what he himself has not received, while humbly offering to the other for possession what he has received.

Thus the graces are diverse, just as, as we have said, the members of the body are diverse. “Those parts of the body which we think less honorable, upon these we bestow more abundant honor; and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness. But our comely parts have no need of this.”

So it is with the wicked: when they cannot be struck by rebuke, they are covered, as it were, with a veil of honor. Here, however, we are speaking of the hidden sins of the powerful. For when they sin while others also know of it, they must be rebuked before those others, lest, if the preacher remains silent, he appear to have approved the fault; and lest this growing fault become an example which the shepherd’s tongue does not cut away.

### LXXXVIII

Therefore holy Church, through her preachers, when they rebuke evil deeds under the scrutiny of correction, moves her lips as though sparing them. Yet in sparing, she does not spare, because she does not remain silent in general about the fault of which she is silent in particular.

### LXXXIX

Therefore holy Church, which is the body of Christ, the supreme Head, insofar as it raises itself toward heavenly things, labors all the more to gather members for the Head who may become his body, according to the Apostle who says: “You are the body of Christ, and members in particular.”

One thing is a member of the body, and another is a member of a member. A member of the body is a part in relation to the whole; a member of a member is a small part in relation to a larger part. A finger is a member of a member in relation to the hand, and the hand in relation to the arm. But a member is a member of the body when that same member is considered in relation to the whole body.

For just as, in the spiritual body of the Lord, we call “members of a member” those who are governed by others in his Church, so in that rejected congregation of heretics, which is the entire body of the devil, the members are members of the flesh: those who, through wicked deeds, are joined to certain persons more wicked than themselves.

### XC

There are therefore two parts: one is the body of Christ, and the other is the body of the devil, which is called Antichrist.

For since there are two Adams, the old and the new, according to the Apostle who says, “The first Adam was made from the earth, earthly; the second Adam from heaven, heavenly,” there are now also two Adams in the Church, the earthly and the heavenly. “As is the earthly, such are those who are earthly; and as is the heavenly, such are those who are heavenly.”

The same Apostle also says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly.” These two together constitute one.

For wherever “man” is read in the sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament, the Hebrew has *Adam*. Thus, when in Latin we say what is written in the eighty-first Psalm, “But you shall die like men,” the Hebrew has, “You shall die like Adam.” And in the eighth Psalm: “What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that you visit him?”

“Man” is to be understood as Adam; “the son of man” is to be understood as our Lord Jesus Christ. He visited and remembered that old Adam, who had fallen through disobedience, when the Word became flesh within the Virgin’s womb, so that he might dwell among us.

And when the Lord said, “The Son of man will be delivered into the hands of sinners,” it was as though he said, “The Son of Adam will be delivered into the hands of sinners.”

Now, when “man” is read in the Scriptures, it has the same force as though he said “Adam”: the first man is earthly, from the earth; the second is heavenly, from heaven. Both are expressed when the Lord is called Adam and when he is called man; neither designation departs from the flesh.

### XCI

But perhaps someone asks for a more precise explanation and says: How is the second Adam called Adam, if Adam is understood as “man,” since many men existed before and after him?

### XCII

I shall answer. Many men existed before him, but all are called old; one Adam is understood as the old Adam.

Although the patriarchs and prophets, filled with the Holy Spirit, awaited Christ, and although they did not have personal guilt, nevertheless, on account of that old man they were held in the underworld. None of them could depart by his own power unless the second, new Adam descended from heaven for them.

For both those men whom he freed from the power of the devil, whom he led back with himself to heaven—whence he had descended without a man—through the new man, and those who are joined to him through faith after his ascension are, together with all these, called the new Adam and one man.

This is not to be understood carnally. When you seek the reason, the principle to be considered here is not one of flesh but of action, which the Apostle explained not according to human senses. He brings back and relates both the old Adam and our Lord Jesus Christ to the first beginnings of evil and good, establishing two vital forms in two persons: the first Adam is anyone who has walked in the footsteps of his error; the second Adam is the one who has imitated the Lord.

These are the two Adams, the new and the old, as the Apostle says: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.”

What is done outwardly in the human body is not of great significance; rather, what is done in the mind must be weighed. The new creation is made in the mind, and by this it is discerned outwardly in the body how the mind has been made new.

To the new man belongs despising the present world, not loving transient things, laying the mind profoundly low in humility before God and one’s neighbor, preserving patience under inflicted insults, and, once patience has been preserved, driving the pain of malice from the heart; giving one’s own possessions to the needy, not coveting what belongs to others; loving a friend in God and for God’s sake, and loving those who are enemies; mourning the affliction of one’s neighbor, and not rejoicing at the death of one who is an enemy.

This is the second Adam. This is the new man whom Christ led back to heaven, as he himself said to his disciples: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven.”

The Truth himself immediately agrees with this saying when he says: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me.” For the Lord does not contradict himself in his words; rather, with regard to these matters that seem discordant, he kindles the zeal of our minds to investigate them.

For all of us who have been born in his faith are undoubtedly his body. Since, therefore, through a marvelous dispensation of mercy, the Lord became the Head of his members, after the multitude of the rejected had been cast away, he alone is with us.

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven.” Since we shall already be one with him, from where he came alone in himself, there he returns alone also in us; and he who is always in heaven ascends daily to heaven.

For he who remains above all things in his divinity draws himself daily to heaven through the structure of his humanity.

Let human frailty not despair, therefore. Let it trust in the blood of the Only-Begotten. Let it behold in its own price how great is the worth of what was purchased at so great a cost. Let it carefully consider where the Head has gone before.

And let what is bound by commandments for living be strengthened by examples for hoping. Let it trust and hope for heaven, the heavenly homeland; let it know that it is a companion of the angels, and let it rejoice that, in its Head, it has been set even above the angels. Amen.

### XCIII

To the old Adam belongs seeking the present world, loving transient things out of desire, raising the mind in pride, having no patience, thinking maliciously from grief over the injury of one’s neighbor, refusing to give one’s possessions to the needy, seeking what belongs to others in order to multiply earthly profits, loving no one except oneself, returning hostility to enemies, rejoicing in the affliction of one’s neighbor, and exulting at the death of an enemy.

All these things are old, and evidently draw corruption from the root of man. This is the old Adam, who is called earthly in the sacred Scriptures. He always opposes the Church of Christ. He always gives birth to death.

This part, which gives birth to death, is called night. Baptism and all the ecclesiastical sacraments take place even among them; but since heretics, and their subjects whom they govern, separate Christ from themselves by their works, they nevertheless appear to share with us one common altar. From this they assume the name of fatherhood, by which they also presumptuously usurp the sacraments of the Church.

They do indeed beget children, but because they are the old Adam, they beget them not for life but for death. The inexperienced call them fathers; but because they do not speak what is right, the prophet calls them mute dogs, saying: “Mute dogs, unable to bark.”

### XCIV

By the fathers of heretics we mean those whom we call heresiarchs. From their perverse preaching—that is, from the seed of their speech—peoples follow, begotten in error.

Holy Church disdains to place these fathers of heretics among the dogs of the flock, because, judging them to be inventors of error, she rejects them and refuses to number them among the true Fathers. Yet because they do not hold right opinions about our Lord Jesus Christ, she will not place them with the dogs of her own flock, since she does not count them among the orthodox preachers.

It is plainly evident that Arius, Photinus, Bonosus, Macedonius, Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, Severus, and, in our own times, Elipandus, together with many like them, have attempted by teaching and persuasion to mock the Church and to appear to be fathers.

Holy universal Church, judging them by strict truth, does not number among the guardians of her flock those whom she condemns for scattering the unity of that same flock. Of them Paul says to the Ephesians: “I know that after my departure grievous wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock.”

### XCV

And because heretics sometimes imitate holiness all the more the more they flatter themselves in the error of their faithlessness, and because they appear to act greatly beyond others in outward works, holy universal Church despises all their deeds, since she knows that they do not proceed from the authority of right faith.

Through these men Antichrist begets children, whom at his most foul coming he will have as witnesses in the Church.

### XCVI

These are the testicles of Antichrist, from whose seed a perverse offspring is begotten, which is joined to the mouth of Antichrist.

Hence Job says in the voice of Antichrist: “The sinews of his testicles are intertwined” (Job 40:12). Antichrist has as many testicles as he possesses preachers of his iniquity.

Are they not his testicles who corrupt human hearts by pouring into them, through wicked persuasions, poisonous seeds of error? Aptly it is said that the sinews of his testicles are intertwined, because the arguments of his preachers are bound together by deceitful assertions, so that they may pretend to be right while persuading what is perverse; their entanglement is like a weaving of sinews, so that, once seen, it cannot be undone.

His testicles have their entangled parts from him because, beneath double arguments, they conceal the sharpness of his preachers. Often, when they infect hearts with words, they display innocence in their actions. For they would not draw good people to themselves by persuasion if they also displayed themselves as perverse in their conduct.

### XCVII

But because these testicles are bound with intertwined sinews, and present themselves as upright in order to remain hidden while they rebuke perverse things in order to corrupt others, they undoubtedly imitate their own head, who, like a lion, sits in ambush, rages through the power of an earthly summit, and flatters through the appearance of holiness.

Would that Antichrist did such things only then, in his own time, and did not even now possess these heretical testicles of lust for corrupting the faith and the innermost parts of the faithful!

### XCVIII

For evil is not infused only through the reading of the mouth; worse still, examples of evil deeds are offered by many. How many have not seen Antichrist, yet are nevertheless his testicles because they corrupt the hearts of the innocent by the example of their actions?

Whoever is lifted up in pride, whoever is tortured by the desire for avarice, whoever is loosened by the pleasures of lust, whoever relies upon the lashes of unjust and immoderate anger—what else is he but a testicle of Antichrist? By willingly entangling himself in Antichrist’s uses, he supplies others, through his example, with offspring of error.

One man acts wickedly; another is present with and adheres to those who act wickedly. He not only fails to rebuke them but even favors them. What, then, is he other than a servant of Antichrist, who has destroyed the authority of the faith promised to God by testimonies of error?

Yet when someone rebukes them, they immediately hide themselves beneath some covering of defense. Their sinews are indeed intertwined and badly entangled, so that they cannot in any way be loosened from corruption. Something in them appears that causes pain, but what wounds lies hidden.

They mix bitter things with sweet, and harmful things with flattering ones. They seek to appear admirable through power, but deceive through their art; conversations introduced beforehand are likewise laid as a foundation, and through speech they suggest about themselves what they deny by their conduct.

Hence the same holy man rightly says: “His bones are like tubes of bronze” (ibid., verse 13). His bones are compared with bronze tubes because, like bronze, they possess the sound of speaking well while lacking the sense to understand. For they assert humbly what they contemptuously reject by living proudly.

Thus Paul rightly says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.”

He speaks good things but does not follow those same good things through love. Like bronze or a cymbal, he gives back a sound, because he himself does not perceive the words he speaks.

### XCIX

Does not Elipandus send forth a cymbal-like sound from Toledo and remain senseless, because he himself does not understand the new words he speaks?

In order that a firm faith might be given to the Church, Christ chose twelve apostles. Peter, although he was first among them, did not dare to compose the Creed alone; rather, it was collected with great care by the twelve apostles and handed over to believers. Therefore whoever remains in such a confession need not fear any impending wrath.

There were twelve disciples of Christ, preachers of the faith and teachers of the nations. Since they were all one, they also commonly composed one Creed. Each individually spoke one word, mutually agreeing with the words of the one faith; there are only twelve such words.

Elipandus placed only eleven in his own confession: he exceeded the number ten by one, yet did not reach the doubled number, thirteen. These words, divided equally, make eleven and eleven, so that it might clearly be understood that he, the first of Spain, was prefiguring himself as Antichrist.

Alone he claimed to possess the whole grace of the apostles, since alone, without consultation with his brethren, he composed a document of the new faith.

### C

This man appears exceedingly proud in his arrogance, since he preached himself as a christ together with Christ. For it is said through Paul of the one whom he prefigured: “So that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God.” And again it is said through the same Apostle: “Who opposes and exalts himself and is worshiped above everything that is called God or is worshiped.”

For the holy are called pious, but they are not worshiped. Christ alone is called God and is worshiped. Antichrist has raised himself above him; his mystery we now see.

For all who are against the Church are in the body of Antichrist, concerning whom we mentioned above a single beast. When Daniel spoke of the fourth beast, supported by ten horns, he immediately added: “I considered the horns, and behold, another little horn arose from the midst of them; and three of the first horns were plucked up before it. And behold, there were eyes like the eyes of a man around it, and a mouth speaking great things” (Daniel 7:8–9).

He is described as the eleventh horn of this beast because the power of his kingdom is strengthened in iniquity; or because among the ten kings of the Romans he will be the eleventh.

Every sin is called “eleven,” because, while committing various acts, it passes beyond the ten commandments. And because sin is mourned in sackcloth, eleven curtains of sackcloth are made in the tabernacle.

Hence the eleventh Psalm says: “Save me, Lord, for the holy man has failed; for truths have been diminished among the children of men. Everyone has spoken vain things to his neighbor. They have spoken deceitful lips and a double heart. May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things.”

The tongue speaks great things when it exalts itself above all and appears great to itself.

Hence Peter, fearing that he might remain with the number eleven, sought Matthias as the twelfth by casting lots. If he had not seen that guilt was signified by the number eleven, he would not have hastened so earnestly to complete the number of the apostles as twelve.

Therefore, since transgression is expressed through the number eleven, the eleventh horn of this beast indicates the author of transgression himself.

The horn is born small because a mere human being is generated. But it grows monstrously large because it advances even to the power of angels joined to it. It uproots the three horns that are before it because it subjugates three kingdoms, all of them near to it, to its dominion.

Its eyes are like human eyes, but its mouth speaks great things, because in it a human form is seen, while by its words it raises itself above human beings.

### CI

Now I have plainly seen Elipandus as a mere human being, raising himself in such great arrogance above the whole Church that he considers everyone to be like brute animals. The words of his faith that he inserted in his letters are as contrary to the apostolic faith as they are discordant among themselves.

### CII

These words make eleven twice over, so that he might raise himself to such an extent that the Holy Spirit would appear to have descended upon him alone throughout the whole Church, just as Montanus and his two prophetesses, Prisca and Maximilla, fabricated. They believed that the coming of the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord had taken place in themselves rather than in the apostles.

Woe to that Church which is still on milk when such a person rises in preaching as Elipandus rose. Infants die who might still, in time, have reached solid food. But they die when they are deceived.

The Lord, foreknowing the future, warns his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse infants in those days. And pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath.”

It is clear from what precedes what this depends upon. When the Gospel of Christ has been preached to all nations and the consummation has come, they will see “the abomination of desolation, spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place.” Then those who are in Judea are commanded to flee to the mountains. And the one who is on the roof must not come down to take anything from his house.

Immediately it is added: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse infants in those days.” In what days? When the abomination of desolation has stood in the holy place.

And what will the abomination of desolation be except that the whole Christ—who is the Son of God and true God, the one born from the Virgin and crucified by the Jews—should be denied? The abomination of desolation will occur when Antichrist is openly received and worshiped in place of Christ, and Christ is denied to be God.

Antichrist is no longer far away, because Christ is already being denied to be God.

In the literal sense, no one doubts that this concerns the coming of Antichrist, when the magnitude of the persecution will compel flight; and it is difficult to bear little children, who, being infants at the breast, delay the flight.

Some, however, wish the siege and battle against the Jews, especially against Jerusalem, by Titus and Vespasian to be signified. They interpret winter and the Sabbath in this way also: they should not be compelled to flee at a time when the harshness of the cold does not permit fugitives to hide in fields and deserted places, and when observance of the Sabbath either makes them transgressors if they flee or subjects them to the swords of their enemies if they observe the Sabbath rest and commandments.

But this was not fulfilled in the time of Vespasian and Titus; it is fulfilled now, at the coming of Antichrist.

We, however, hearing the Lord and Savior say that those who are in Judea should flee to the mountains, understand this to mean that those who are confessors should flee to the faith and teaching of the apostles.

We also lift our eyes to the mountains, of which it is written: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come.” And elsewhere: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” And: “The mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people.” And: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

And, with the foot of the letter unshod, let us ascend Mount Sinai barefoot with Moses and say: “Passing by, I shall see this great vision,” so that we may understand pregnant souls who have conceived the beginnings of faith from the seed of doctrines and the words of God, and who say with Isaiah: “Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived and gave birth; we shall bring forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth.”

### CIII

For just as seeds are gradually formed in wombs, and it is not yet counted as homicide until the confused elements receive their own forms and limbs, so a thought conceived by reason is still held within the womb unless it breaks forth into action. It perishes as an aborted offspring when it sees the abomination of desolation standing in the Church and Satan transformed into an angel of light—that is, a heretic.

Paul speaks of such people with tears: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you. But I would like to be present with you now and change my voice, because I am perplexed about you.”

Paul wishes to change his voice in his labor, so that the speech of preaching may be turned into the roar of pain. He wishes to change his voice because those whom he had already brought forth by preaching he was again laboriously bringing to birth through reform, groaning over them.

What a roar the woman in labor uttered when, as those same people returned to their former ways, he was compelled to cry out: “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? And are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being consumed by the flesh? Or, at least, you were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?”

What a roar there was in this labor: he had brought forth, after so much time and such great effort, children conceived long before, and at some point discovered that those already born had returned to the womb of wickedness. Let us consider how much pain and labor he endured: after he had been able to bring forth from the womb what had been conceived, he was compelled once more to revive what had died.

For unless holy preachers conceived from that immense height of inward spiritual contemplation and descended to our weakness through the humblest preaching, as though through a kind of bending down, they would never beget children in the faith. They could not benefit us if they remained upright in the elevation of their own height.

Seeds perish in childbirth when they have not yet been formed in the faith, as soon as heretics begin to preach heresies. The heretics killed Paul’s disciples because they killed Christ in their hearts. Paul calls them back to one faith, saying: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.”

According to mystical interpretations, I think these souls are women. Concerning them the Apostle himself wrote: “The woman, having been deceived, was in transgression. But she will be saved through the bearing of children, if she continues in faith, charity, and holiness with modesty.”

If these souls have at some time given birth from the divine word, what has been born must necessarily grow, and first receive the milk of infancy, until it reaches solid food and the mature age of the fullness of Christ.

For everyone who is nourished with milk is inexperienced; he is a child in mind and an infant in the understanding of righteousness.

These souls, therefore, which have not yet given birth, or which have not yet been able to nourish what has been born, are quickly scandalized and perish when they hear heretical speech standing in the Church. They cannot remain steadfast in storm and persecution, especially if they have been idle in good works and have not walked in the way that is Christ.

### CIV

Concerning this abomination of heretical and perverse teaching, the Apostle said that the man of iniquity and the adversary would exalt himself against everything that is called God and religion, so that he would presume to stand in the temple of God and show that he himself is God.

According to the working of Satan, his coming makes those who have been conceived perish through abortion and prevents those who have been born from reaching childhood and full maturity.

Therefore the Lord must be entreated lest, at the beginning of faith and of growing age, the winter of cold arise—that is, the new preaching of heretics. Of this winter it is written in the voice of the bridegroom: “Already the winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed.”

*The remainder is missing from the autograph.*

## In the Year of the Lord 788

[Note: This inscription strongly betrays the ignorance and barbarism of the eighth century, as can be seen from the very solecisms with which it abounds. Consult Du Cange, in the preface to his Latin *Glossary*, concerning the causes of corrupted Latin; there one may see how far the Latin language had degenerated from its original purity under the kings of the first and second dynasties. Nor is this barbarism surprising, since corrected style did not become known until the beginning of the ninth century, as Fontanini attests in his *Vindiciae Diplomaticae*, pages 214, 215, and 238.

We extracted this from the very parchment codex of the eighth century belonging to the ancient library of the Church of Strasbourg, which Prince Louis-Constantin, Cardinal de Rohan, obtained from the Republic of Bern while he was staying in the city of Bern at the beginning of July 1774. See more concerning this codex in the first volume of our *History*, book III, pages 315 and 316.

The codex truly belongs to the eighth century and is itself an autograph. The most learned and most friendly to us, D. Sinner de Ballaigne, prefect of the Bern library, carefully examined it. From the capital or uncial letters used in the inscription, from the other characters of the codex, from the form of the letters, from the orthography according to the rules transmitted by Mabillon, and from specimens of writings of indisputable date, he judged in the preface to the catalogue of the manuscript codices of the Bern library, volume I, page 23, that no doubt remained concerning its age.

These details should be added to the praise of that outstanding man, to whom our eminent prince-bishop, greatly deserving of the literary achievements of his administration, owes in particular two ancient codices of the Church of Strasbourg.

The Codex of Rachio appears in many respects similar to the Colbertine codex of the canons, which was written at Rome at the beginning of the eighth century and now exists in Paris in the royal library, no. 3836.

P. Joseph Hartzheim published the codex of the canons that Pope Hadrian gave to King Charles in 774, from a very ancient eighth-century manuscript of the library of the metropolitan Church of Cologne, in volume I of his *Councils of Germany*, pages 131–234.]

# RACHIO, BISHOP OF STRASBOURG

[Col. 1029]

## INSCRIPTION OF THE CODEX CONTAINING THE CANONS OF THE COUNCILS AND THE DECREES OF THE PONTIFFS, WHICH CODEX BISHOP RACHIO OF STRASBOURG ORDERED TO BE WRITTEN IN THE YEAR 788

[From Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*.]

[Col. 1029D] In the name of the holy and one Trinity, in the year 788, in which our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to be born for the salvation of the world; and in the nineteenth year of the reign of our most glorious and excellent lord Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and of many peoples, and patrician of the Romans.

Therefore I, Rachio, humble servant of Christ, servant of the servants of God and of all Catholics, though a sinner, called by the grace of God bishop of the city of Strasbourg, in the fifth year of my episcopate, for the remedy of my soul’s salvation and for eternal recompense, out of love for God and for the church of Saint Mary in the city of Strasbourg, ordered this book of canons to be written, containing within itself the teaching of the holy fathers who lived rightly: the complete fullness of all the councils according to the constitution of the ancient fathers who were gathered in council at the city of Nicaea—namely, 318 bishops.

In it, for those who read, may there be present contemplation of the future and instruction for the present.

[Note: This codex, written at Rachio’s command, appears to be, as we have said, the codex of canons that Emperor Charles received from Pope Hadrian and that was subsequently received throughout Gaul and Germany. To that codex, which contained the councils of Greece and Africa, Rachio added the councils of Gaul and Spain together with the decrees of one hundred supreme pontiffs.

The decrees begin with Damasus’s letter to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, and contain none of the false decretals already circulated under the name of Isidore Mercator, or Peccator.]

*The prologue ends.*

[Note: The formula *explicit* is frequent in ancient manuscripts and derives from the Latin word *explicitus*, that is, a speech or book completed. In this sense Martial says, book XIV, epigram 1:

“Every work is completed in two verses.”

The same formula was not uncommon for marking the end of a work in the time of Saint Jerome, who writes in Letter 138 to Marcellus: “When we have completed little works, we are accustomed, to distinguish the middle from what follows, to insert *explicit*, or *feliciter*, or something of that sort.”]

# In the Year of the Lord 791  
# ANGELRAMNUS, BISHOP OF METZ

[Col. 1031]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING ANGELRAMNUS

(From *Gallia Christiana*, volume XIII.)

[Col. 1031D] Born of distinguished lineage, Angelramnus, or Ingelramnus, whom we have said was born of the brother of Chrodegang, his predecessor, was educated from childhood in the monastery of Gorze under Nargaud, master of the boys. He then moved to the monastery of Cella-Nova, now called Saint-Nabor, where for some time he professed the monastic life. After the bishopric of Metz had been vacant for two years, six months, and nineteen days, he was ordained bishop on 25 September 768, honored, as his predecessor had been, with the title of archbishop and also with the dignity of archchaplain to King Charles the Great. From that king he obtained the abbey of Senones, if he had not already possessed it before becoming bishop, and subjected it to the jurisdiction of his church. The monks were displeased that their monastery had passed from royal to episcopal authority. To reconcile the monks’ friendship to himself, he gave them the body of Saint Simeon, bishop of Metz; in their anger, they had refused to admit it into their church during the day. Because he was excessively distracted by affairs, however, he transferred the abbey to Nargaud, the Gorze monk who had instructed him.

In 770, the first year of King Carloman, he gave the monks of Gorze the village of Varenges and other gifts, on condition that they earnestly implore the Lord’s mercy for himself and his successors, the bishops of Metz, as well as for Kings Charles and Carloman and for the stability of the Frankish kingdom. Together with Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, Weomad, archbishop of Trier, and other bishops, he dedicated the church of Lorsch in 774, on the Kalends of September, in the presence of King Charles the Great, who had come there at the invitation of Gundeland, the abbot, with Queen Hildegard and his son Pepin.

We learn from the testament of Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Denis in France, drawn up in 778, that Angilramnus made certain exchanges with him concerning properties situated at a place called Salona in the diocese of Metz. These agreements, concluded at the synod of Paderborn in the ninth year of Charles’s reign with the aforesaid Bishop Angelramnus, Vilhari, archbishop of Sens, and Abbot Fulrad, were confirmed by Prince Charles himself in the following year, the tenth of his reign. By this agreement they settled that neither Angelramnus nor his successors, nor the archdeacon, should have any authority in the monastery of Salona to perform ordinations, administer chrism, or bless altar tablets, unless the abbot requested it.

Besides the abbey of Senones, he is believed to have governed the monastery of Saint-Trond. His name, inserted in the list of abbots by the author of the published chronicle of that monastery, provides some support for this. He was exceedingly devoted to the abbey of Saint-Nabor. In 787 he wrote to suppress the oppression inflicted by Count Volmar, advocate of the church of Metz, upon the monastery’s people, both through exactions and through robberies committed by his sub-advocates and officials. The monastery had consequently fallen into such poverty and misery that scarcely any brothers could be found who were willing to serve God and Saint-Nabor. To remedy this oppression, Angelramnus induced Abbot Walon and the brothers to hand over certain estates from his own prebend to the count, so that thereafter they would suffer no harassment from him.

Not content merely to secure abundance and peace for the monastery, he greatly increased its possessions and privileges and assisted in completing the buildings begun by Saint Sigibald. Indeed, when death overtook him, he was adorning the tomb of Saint Nabor, which Alcuin teaches, in epigram 64, had been completed by a deacon of the church of Metz. He granted his chapter the provostship of Milleriacum and obtained from Charles the Great a diploma issued at Quierzy in 776, by which not only the cathedral church but also the other churches and monasteries of the diocese of Metz were to be immune from secular jurisdiction; royal and imperial officials were forbidden to undertake anything against ecclesiastical persons or property.

Because of the exceptional devotion and esteem with which the king honored him, he was promoted to the dignity of archchaplain. At the same time, from Hadrian, the Roman pontiff, he received responsibility for serving the king as apocrisiarius, or apostolic envoy. Perhaps these duties, which prevented him from residing in his own diocese, gave the bishops of Gaul occasion to accuse him of violating the canons. To dispel this accusation, he composed a collection of canons, which he presented to Pope Hadrian on 19 September 785. In this work [Col. 1033C] he undertakes to prove that bishops may not be rashly accused or their reputation injured. He indicates with what caution and prudence the case of a bishop ought to be judged, and with what charity and circumspection his faults ought to be concealed. Nearly all these canons, eighty in number and for the most part extracted from the false decretals, concern the manner of proceeding in ecclesiastical cases. Some learned men consider Angelramnus their author; others judge that they were drawn from the collection of the false decretals of Isidore Mercator.

The Gregorian, or Roman, chant, which Chrodegang had attempted to introduce into the church of Metz, was far from perfect. Under Bishop Angelramnus, however, it was brought to a more regular form by Roman cantors whom King Charles the Great, having obtained them from Pope Hadrian, brought with him to France in 787. He sent one of them to Metz and another to Soissons to teach the method of singing.

At Angelramnus’s request, Paul the Deacon, surnamed Warnefrid, a Lombard by birth and later a monk of Monte Cassino, beloved by King Charles the Great for his learning, composed a history of the bishops of Metz and concluded it with this honorable apostrophe:

> Here now, most holy father Angilramnus, the course of the narrative calls for your blessedness; but I, not forgetful of my own insufficiency, do not dare unworthily to undertake matters which ought to be set forth in a grander style concerning the praiseworthy course of your life.

Another deacon of the church of Metz, named Donatus, dedicated to him a Life of Saint Trond, prefacing the work with a letter. A contemporary author who wrote an epitome in verse of the Lives of the bishops of Metz speaks of Angelramnus as follows:

> Now, the thirty-eighth shepherd,  
> Supported by his lord’s aid, Angelramnus  
> Led his sheep to the holy pastures of life,  
> At the time when the mighty King Charles,  
> Noble in arms, judgment, appearance, and spirit,  
> Received the scepter of Italy as a gift from Christ.  
> May the right hand of the Most High, at the request of blessed Stephen,  
> Protect and rule them happily forever.

Angelramnus died after twenty-three years as bishop, in 791, while accompanying King Charles on the military expedition then begun against the Huns, at a place variously named by different writers Asnaghum-Chunisberg, Asnabrug-Cumeberg, or Cummeberg. His body was brought from there to the monastery of Cella-Nova, or Saint-Nabor, and buried there. The ancient manuscripts do not agree about the day of his death; but it is preferable to follow the majority and the cathedral martyrology, which records his death on the sixth day before the Kalends of November [27 October]. His see was vacant for twenty-seven years and three months, according to the manuscript of Saint Symphorian. Madaurensis, however, who does not admit an intervening bishopric after Angelramnus’s death, extends his episcopate to fifty years and his life to the year 818. Alcuin overturns this opinion, having himself already died by 804, in epigram 164, where he testifies that Angelramnus died while adorning the tomb of Saint Nabor. He is venerated among the saints in the monastery of Saint-Nabor, where his stone tomb was discovered on 5 August 1609.

[Col. 1033]

# Collection of Canons Gathered by Angelramnus, Bishop of Metz, and Presented to Hadrian, the Supreme Pontiff

*(From Mansi, Expanded Collection of the Councils.)*

[Note: [Col. 1033] A concise transmission of the Eastern, or African, canons, which blessed Pope Hadrian gave King Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, in a single volume together with the preceding councils, for the arrangement of the Western churches, while Charles was staying at Rome. First, the canons of the apostles, numbered as chapter 1.]

Ecclesiastical regulations of the holy Fathers and apostles, issued through Clement, Roman pontiff, which are placed first, in their original order, from Greek exemplars.

[Col. 1033D]

I. A bishop shall be ordained by two or three bishops.

II. A presbyter and the other clerics shall be ordained by one bishop.

[Col. 1034D] III. Nothing else shall be offered in the sacrifice except what the Lord ordained.

IV. Fresh ears of grain, grapes, oil, and incense may be brought to the altar for blessing.

V. All other things belong in the house of the bishop and presbyter.

[Col. 1035A] VI. A presbyter shall not cast his wife away from his governance, but shall rule her chastely.

VII. Those who, after ordination, devote themselves to secular concerns shall be deposed.

VIII. Easter shall not be celebrated before the spring equinox.

IX. Let the ministers of the altar communicate after the offering has been made.

X. Let laypeople also communicate after entering the church.

XI. If anyone prays with an excommunicated person, even in a house, let him be excommunicated.

XII. If anyone prays with a condemned cleric as though with a cleric, let him be condemned.

XIII. No one shall be received without letters of commendation.

XIV. Bishops shall not invade another bishop’s parish.

[Col. 1035B] XV. Clerics shall not leave their own church without the bishop’s permission.

XVI. If a bishop retains a fugitive cleric belonging to another bishop, let him be excommunicated.

XVII. Let neither a bigamist nor a man who has a concubine be ordained.

XVIII. Husbands of corrupted women shall not be ordained.

XIX. A man who has corrupted two sisters, or his brother’s daughter . . . shall not be admitted to the clergy.

[Note: [Col. 1035] Whoever has married two sisters or a female cousin cannot be a cleric.]

XX. A cleric who becomes a surety shall be rejected.

XXI. A man made a eunuch by force may become a bishop. The one who has made him a eunuch shall not be ordained. If a cleric has made himself a eunuch, he shall be deposed.

XXII. A layman who cuts off his own member shall be excommunicated for three years.

[Col. 1035C] XXIII. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon caught in fornication, perjury, or theft shall be deposed, but not excommunicated.

XXIV. The other clerics shall likewise be judged.

XXV. Only lectors may marry. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who sins shall not beat the faithful.

XXVI. Those who have been condemned and usurp their former office shall be entirely cut off from the Church.

XXVII. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon ordained for money shall be deposed together with the one who ordained him and excommunicated like Simon Magus by Peter.

XXVIII. A bishop who obtains a church through secular powers shall be deposed.

XXIX. A presbyter who, despising his bishop, holds separate assemblies shall be deposed.

[Col. 1035D] XXX. Clerics condemned by their bishop shall not be received by others.

XXXI. Bishops, presbyters, deacons, and travelers shall be received as guests on the strength of letters of commendation, but not admitted to communion.

XXXII. Bishops shall make no arrangements without their primate, nor a primate without his suffragans, and not even in their own parishes [reading: “except in their own parishes,” Harduin].

XXXIII. A bishop who ordains clerics in another bishop’s parish without that bishop’s knowledge shall be deposed together with those whom he ordained.

XXXIV. A bishop unwilling to undertake the care of the people shall be excommunicated. Likewise clerics, if they have not instructed the people to obey their lawful bishop when the people refuse to come to them; and councils of bishops shall be held twice a year.

[Col. 1036A] XXXV. A bishop shall administer all ecclesiastical property and shall not allow any of it to be supplied to his non-poor relatives.

XXXVI. Presbyters and deacons shall do nothing without the bishop. But if ecclesiastical property and the bishop’s private property are separated from one another, and he may give the latter to whomever he wishes, then, when he dies, his relatives will not proscribe it under the pretext that it belongs to the Church.

XXXVII. All church property shall be in the bishop’s power for distribution to the poor. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who is a gambler or drunkard shall either cease or be condemned. Clerics or laypeople who commit the same offenses shall be excommunicated.

[Col. 1036B] XXXVIII. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who is a usurer shall either cease or be condemned.

XXXIX. A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who merely prays with heretics shall be excommunicated.

XL. If, however, they have urged them to clerical office, let them be condemned.

XLI. A bishop or presbyter who receives the baptism of heretics who do not baptize in the name of the Trinity shall be condemned.

XLII. A bishop or presbyter who rebaptizes someone rightly baptized, or fails to baptize someone who was not rightly baptized, shall be deposed.

XLIII. If a layman sends away his wife and marries another, or a woman dismissed by another man, let him be excommunicated.

[Col. 1036C] XLIV. If any bishop or presbyter has not baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, let him be rejected.

XLV. If any bishop or presbyter has not baptized by three immersions, let him be deposed.

The regulations of the Council of Ancyra, twenty-four in number, are earlier than those of Nicaea; nevertheless, they are placed after the Nicene regulations because of the authority of the holy and great council assembled at Nicaea.

I. Presbyters who sacrificed unwillingly but afterward resisted the pagans shall retain the honor of their own see, although deprived of office.

II. The same shall be done with deacons if they have sinned in the same way, so that mercy may be shown to those who repent worthily.

[Col. 1036D] III. Those who were forcibly dragged into sacrificing to idols shall not be separated from communion; nevertheless, they may be ordained at the discretion of the bishops.

IV. Those who unwillingly performed pagan rites shall do penance for as long as they practiced paganism.

V. Those who were not compelled to sacrifice except under extreme torture shall be received among the hearers until the great day of the Lord’s Supper; afterward they shall do penance for six years.

VI. Those who ate their own food in places of idols shall do penance for two years.

VII. Those who were frequently compelled to sacrifice shall do penance for seven years.

[Col. 1037A] VIII. Those who compelled others to sacrifice shall do penance for ten years.

IX. Incontinent deacons shall be deposed.

X. Brides shall be restored to their bridegrooms by their abductors, even if they have been violated.

XI. The fact that those to be ordained sacrificed before baptism shall not harm them.

XII. Chorepiscopi who have been corrected shall not ordain a presbyter or deacon, nor shall a presbyter do anything in a parish without the bishop’s command.

XIII. Clerics who condemn the eating of meat shall be deposed.

XIV. Whatever presbyters have sold from ecclesiastical property without the bishop shall be restored to the church.

XV. Men who have intercourse with males or animals, if not yet twenty years old, shall be admitted to communion in prayer after completing fifteen years of penance. Then, after five more years, they shall receive altar communion. If they have repeated such a crime, an even longer period of penance shall be imposed on them. Those who are already twenty years old and married and have committed such an offense shall finally communicate in prayer after completing twenty-six years of penance; then, after five years, they shall receive the sacrament of the offering. Those who are fifty years old and married and have committed such an offense shall receive communion only at the end of life.

[Col. 1037B] XVI. Men who have intercourse with males or animals shall pray only among the possessed.

XVII. If bishops who have been ordained but not received inflict the violence of sedition upon other bishops, let them be rejected.

[Col. 1037C] XVIII. Those who violate a vow of virginity shall be counted among bigamists; and virgins shall not live with anyone as though they were sisters.

XIX. If someone’s wife has committed adultery, or if a husband has committed adultery, let him or her do penance for seven years.

XX. Women who kill the children conceived through fornication shall do penance for ten years.

XXI. Voluntary homicides shall receive communion at the end of life, after continuous penance.

XXII. Involuntary homicide shall be expiated by seven or five years of penance.

XXIII. Those who seek divinations in the manner of the pagans shall do penance for five years.

XXIV. A certain man made his fiancée’s sister pregnant. Then, after the fiancée had been taken by him as his wife, her corrupted sister hanged herself. Those who were aware of this shall do penance for ten years.

And eighteen bishops subscribed: Vitalis of Antioch, Marcellus of Ancyra, Agricolaus of Caesarea, and the remaining fifteen bishops.

Regulations issued at the synod of Neocaesarea, later than the times of Ancyra and Caesarea, but earlier than those of Nicaea.

I. If a presbyter marries a wife, he shall be deposed; but if he sins through fornication or adultery, he shall be compelled to stricter penance.

II. A woman married to two brothers shall be rejected until death.

III. Nevertheless, she shall be received at the end of life if she promises that, should life be granted to her, she will not repeat such a union.

[Col. 1038A] IV. Those married many times must do penance.

V. It shall not be imputed as a fault against divine grace if the desired sexual act is not completed.

VI. A catechumen who sins and, after admonition, transgresses the commands shall be expelled.

VII. A pregnant catechumen woman shall be baptized.

VIII. Presbyters shall not attend the weddings of bigamists, because bigamy requires penance.

IX. A layman whose wife has committed adultery shall not be ordained. A cleric living with an adulterous wife shall be deposed.

X. A presbyter who confesses that he committed a crime before ordination shall not consecrate the offerings, but shall remain in his other offices. If he does not confess and cannot be convicted, he shall be left to his own judgment.

[Col. 1038B] XI. A deacon who has fallen in the same way shall be deposed.

XII. A presbyter shall not be ordained before the age of thirty.

XIII. Someone baptized during illness shall not become a presbyter except in case of necessity.

XIV. Rural presbyters shall not offer in the city before the bishop or city presbyters, unless perhaps they are summoned in the latter’s absence.

XV. There shall be seven deacons in a city, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles commands.

And the following subscribed: Vitalis of Salamis, Amphion, and the remaining bishops—nineteen in number—who assembled at Caesarea [reading: Neocaesarea].

Twenty canons of the Council of Gangra, issued after the Council of Nicaea.

[Col. 1038C]

I. If anyone detests marriage as a crime, let him be anathema.

II. If anyone condemns a person who eats meat religiously, let him be anathema.

III. If anyone teaches a slave, on religious grounds, to despise his master, let him be anathema.

IV. If anyone despises a presbyter because he is lawfully married, let him be anathema.

V. If anyone teaches that the house of God is contemptible, let him be anathema.

VI. If anyone rashly usurps ecclesiastical ministries outside the church, let him be anathema.

[Col. 1038D] VII. No one shall receive the church’s offerings outside the church without the knowledge of the bishop or his representative.

VIII. No one shall receive or distribute offerings to the poor except the bishop or his representative.

IX. No one shall condemn marriage because of virginity.

X. No one who preserves virginity shall become proud against married people.

XI. No one shall disdain agapae—that is, banquets provided for the poor.

XII. No man shall wear a cloak as a sign of continence, despising those who wear ordinary clothing.

XIII. No woman shall assume masculine dress as though for the sake of continence.

[Col. 1039A] XIV. No woman shall leave her husband out of hatred for marriage.

XV. No one shall neglect his children on the pretext of continence.

XVI. Children shall not despise their parents on the pretext of Christianity.

XVII. Women shall not have their hair cut as though for divine worship.

XVIII. No one shall fast on Sunday as though for the sake of continence.

XIX. No one shall break the church’s fasts without necessity.

XX. No one shall condemn the gatherings held in commemoration of the martyrs.

And the following subscribed: Aelianus, Eusebius, Basilius, Osius, Gregorius, and the remaining bishops, ten in number.

Twenty-five regulations issued at Antioch at the dedication ceremonies.

I. Whoever celebrates Easter with the Jews contrary to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea shall be excommunicated. A condemned cleric shall also be deprived of every external honor that the holy rule or the priesthood has bestowed.

II. Whoever withdraws from holy communion because of some intemperance, or whoever communicates with an excommunicated person, shall be excommunicated.

III. A cleric who refuses to return to his own parish shall be degraded.

IV. If a condemned bishop, presbyter, or deacon usurps his former office, he shall never be restored; and all who knowingly communicate with him after his condemnation shall be excommunicated.

V. If a cleric, despising his own bishop, gathers separately, let him be condemned irrevocably. If he does not cease disturbing the church, let him be suppressed by the other authorities.

VI. One excommunicated by his bishop shall not be received.

VII. Travelers shall not be received by another bishop without letters of commendation.

VIII. Rural presbyters cannot issue canonical letters; chorepiscopi can.

IX. Although the metropolitan is superior to the bishops of the province, he shall make no arrangements apart from them except in his own parish.

X. Chorepiscopi cannot confer the lower orders, even up to the subdiaconate. A cleric who, apart from the letters of the bishops of the province, approaches the emperor with complaints shall be deprived of honor and communion.

XI. Condemned clerics who approach the emperor shall never be restored.

XII. Whatever a bishop ordains without being requested in another’s parish shall be invalid.

XIII. If the provincial bishops disagree with the metropolitan in condemning a bishop, the case shall be settled after neighboring bishops have been summoned.

XIV. If all the provincial bishops agree in condemning one man, he need not be judged by others.

XV. [Missing.]

XVI. A bishop who invades a vacant church shall be rejected.

XVII. If anyone refuses to enter and govern the bishopric he has accepted, he shall be excommunicated.

XVIII. If anyone avoids the bishopric he has accepted through no fault of his own but because of the fault of others, he shall retain his honor.

XIX. A metropolitan shall ordain bishops only together with several other bishops.

XX. Councils of bishops shall be held twice a year in the province.

XXI. A bishop shall in no way transfer from his own parish to another.

XXII. An ordination that a bishop has usurped in another parish over another’s clerics shall be invalid.

XXIII. It shall be invalid if a bishop chooses his own successor.

XXIV. Church property shall be administered by the bishop’s judgment, but kept separate from his private property, which he may give to whomever he wishes, so that, when he dies, his private property will not be seized together with the church’s property.

XXV. A bishop may distribute ecclesiastical property to himself and others, but not to excess; rather, he shall use it for the needs of the needy.

And thirty subscribed: Eusebius of Palestine, Theodotus of Mesopotamia, Theodorus of Isauria, and the rest.

The holy synod that assembled at Laodicea in Pacatiana Phrygia issued the following fifty-nine regulations.

[Col. 1040C]

I. If some have married a second time lawfully, after a short interval of time devoted to prayer they shall be admitted to communion.

II. Communion shall be granted to those who have completed their penance.

III. Those newly baptized shall not become clerics.

IV. Ordinations shall not take place in the presence of hearers, that is, catechumens.

V. Clerics shall not be usurers in any way.

VI. Those who persist in heresy shall not be permitted to enter the house of God.

VII. Novatians, Tessarescaedecatites, and Sotiani [perhaps Photinians], when returning to the Church after renouncing heresy, shall be reconciled through anointing with chrism.

VIII. Converts from the heresy of the Cataphrygians shall be baptized.

IX. Catholics who go to the cemeteries of heretics to pray shall be excommunicated.

X. Catholics shall not enter into marriage indiscriminately with heretics.

XI. Those called presbyteresses, who preside in churches, shall not be ordained.

XII. Bishops shall be advanced with the judgment of the metropolitan and the other bishops.

XIII. Ordinations shall not be carried out by the judgment of the multitude.

[Col. 1041A] XIV. Eulogiae, that is, offerings, shall not be sent to other parishes.

XV. No one except regular cantors shall sing from the pulpit.

XVI. On Saturday the Gospels shall be read together with the other Scriptures.

XVII. Psalms shall not be continued in the church; instead, readings shall be recited after each psalm.

XVIII. The same office of prayers shall be celebrated at the ninth hour and in the evening.

XIX. After the bishops’ preaching, a prayer shall be made over the catechumens. When they have departed, a prayer shall be made over the penitents, who then approach the priest’s hand. When they have departed, the three prayers of the faithful shall be completed: the first in silence, but the second and third with the customary acclamations. After the peace has been given, the offering shall be celebrated. Only the sacred ministers shall be permitted to communicate near the altar.

[Col. 1041B] XX. Deacons shall not sit in the presence of a presbyter unless he commands it. Likewise, deacons shall be honored by those below them.

XXI. Subdeacons shall remain apart from the diaconate, that is, the secretary, and shall not touch the sacred vessels.

XXII. A subdeacon shall not wear the orarium, nor leave the doors.

XXIII. Lectors and cantors shall not read or sing with oraria.

XXIV. Clerics, continent persons, and monks shall not eat in taverns.

[Col. 1041C] XXV. Subdeacons shall not give bread or bless the chalice.

XXVI. No one may exorcize anywhere unless ordained for this by the bishop.

XXVII. Clerics invited to an agape shall not take portions belonging to the churches.

XXVIII. It is not permitted for an agape to be held or food to be eaten in churches, or couches to be spread there.

XXIX. No one shall rest on Saturday in a Judaizing manner.

XXX. Men shall not bathe with women.

XXXI. Catholics shall not give their sons or daughters in marriage to heretics, but should rather receive the heretics’ children, provided that the latter promise to become Catholics.

XXXII. No one shall receive eulogiae from heretics, for these are not blessings but curses.

[Col. 1041D] XXXIII. No one shall pray with heretics or schismatics.

XXXIV. Whoever approaches the martyrs of heretics shall be anathema.

XXXV. Whoever abandons the church and presumes to worship angels or form assemblies shall be anathema. Clerics who use incantations or amulets shall be excommunicated.

XXXVI. No one shall receive festival gifts from Jews or heretics.

XXXVII. No one shall receive unleavened bread from Jews.

XXXVIII. No one shall celebrate festivals with pagans.

[Col. 1042A] XXXIX. Bishops summoned to a synod shall not refuse to come.

XL. No cleric shall depart without canonical letters, that is, formatae.

XLI. Subdeacons shall not leave the church doors even briefly.

XLII. Clerics shall not depart without the bishop’s command.

XLIII. Women shall not enter the altar area.

XLIV. No one shall be baptized after two weeks of Lent have passed.

XLV. Those to be baptized shall learn the creed, which they shall recite to the bishop or presbyter on Thursday of Holy Week.

XLVI. Those baptized during illness shall afterward learn the faith.

[Col. 1042B] XLVII. The baptized shall be confirmed with chrism.

XLVIII. The bread of blessing shall not be offered during Lent except on Saturday or Sunday.

XLIX. No one shall break the Lenten fast on the Lord’s Supper.

L. The birthdays, or commemorations, of martyrs shall not be celebrated during Lent; their commemoration shall instead take place on Saturdays or Sundays.

LI. Weddings and the birthdays of human beings shall not be celebrated during Lent.

LII. Christians shall not applaud or dance at weddings, but shall dine reverently.

LIII. Clerics shall not attend theatrical spectacles at banquets or weddings, but shall leave before the stage performers arrive.

[Col. 1042C] LIV. No one shall hold banquets from . . . or from communal contributions [“from contributions or shared expenses,” that is, from pooled funds].

LV. Presbyters shall not enter the sacristy or sit before the bishop, but shall do so with him.

LVI. In villages or rural districts, visitors, not bishops, shall be appointed.

LVII. An offering shall not be celebrated in private houses by a bishop or presbyter.

LVIII. Popular songs shall not be sung in church; nor shall any books other than the New and Old Testaments be read in church.

And twenty-two Fathers subscribed.

Preface to the Sardican [manuscript: Serdican] or African Canons

[Col. 1042D]

There are also twenty regulations attributed to Hosius, bishop of Cordoba, which are entitled “of the forty bishops at Serdica.” [Note: [Col. 1041] Read “sixty,” as below after these Sardican canons. Harduin.] They are found not so much among the Greeks as among the Latins. It should be known that this Hosius was held in honor among the 318 Fathers of the Council of Nicaea and was sent by the Apostolic See together with the presbyters Victor and Vincentius. He is also recorded as having remained alive in Spain until the time of the emperor Constantius.

At the end of his life, however, he acted quite foolishly, as Severus Sulpicius testifies in his Chronicles, asserting that the emperor Constantius had compelled the very numerous Council of Ariminum, convened by him against the Catholic faith, to subscribe to the Arian heresy. It was therefore decided that, after an apostolic delegation had been sent, the aforesaid Hosius should be questioned as to whether the Council of Nicaea, in which he had taken part, had decreed that the Son was to be confessed as συνομούσιον, that is, “consubstantial,” with the Father, as Catholics hold, or as συνόμιον, that is, “merely similar,” as the Arians say.

But he, either becoming foolish through advanced age or concealing the truth out of deference to the emperor, is said to have replied that both sides confessed correctly, whether συνομούσιον or συνόμιον. Catholics and Arians alike mocked and rejected this answer with one voice. Finally, after this response, his name was not read among the Catholic bishops in his own city of Cordoba, where he had been bishop.

There are also ecclesiastical regulations that were very frequently written down in synodal councils in the African regions. In all these matters, however, we must follow whatever we see not to differ from the Council of Nicaea and from the holy and apostolic Roman Church.

The Ballerini present this more fully elaborated preface from Vatican manuscript no. 1337 in their preliminary dissertation to volume III of the Works of Saint Leo the Great, p. CLXXXVII [Note: [Col. 1043D] Patrologia, volume LVI, col. 11. Editor’s note], and it is given here from them. *(Mansi.)*

Moreover, there are eleven other regulations attributed to Hosius, bishop of Cordoba, entitled “of the twenty bishops at Sardica.” These too are found not so much among the Greeks as among the Latins. But since mention has been made of the aforesaid Hosius, it is necessary to make known to all Catholics that this same man was held in honor at Nicaea in Bithynia among the 318 most holy Fathers and was sent by the Apostolic See together with the presbyters Vincentius and Victor. He remained bodily in Spain until the time of the emperor Constantius.

For the aforementioned Constantius—as the very learned Sulpicius Severus reports in his Chronicles, preserving the matter with care and leaving it to our memory—assembled at Ariminum in Italy a large episcopal synod from both parts of the world. Wishing to revive the poisons of Arius against the Catholic faith and the definition of the 318 Fathers, he disturbed the Church of God by tyrannical usurpation.

[Col. 1043D] Finally, compelled either by fear of the emperor or by the presence of Taurus, to whom the execution of the matter had been entrusted in such a way that, if the greater part of the council consented to the perfidy of the Arians, he would receive the insignia of the consulship, almost all the bishops who were there subscribed. But afterward, with divine assistance inspiring them, very many repented and, having also submitted petitions to the holy Catholic Church—from which they had departed more out of necessity than by choice—returned to it.

Therefore all Catholics rightly pronounce an eternal anathema upon the Council of Ariminum. Whoever neglects to say so is not a Catholic.

As the aforementioned Sulpicius reports [Note: [Col. 1043D] But Sulpicius, *Ecclesiastical History*, does not transmit all these details], during the lengthy dispute of the synod, since, as stated above, Hosius was still alive in the time of Constantius, it was decided that an episcopal delegation should be sent to question him as to whether, in the holy and venerable gathering at Nicaea, where he had been present, the Fathers had decreed *omousion*, as we Catholics rightly confess—that is, that the Son is of one substance with the Father—or, as the Arians maintain, *omoeusion*, that is, that the Son is of similar substance with the Father.

He is said to have given this answer either because he had become foolish through advanced age or because he was currying favor with the emperor: that both positions were correct, whether *omousion* or *omoeusion*. Since his opinion had been foolishly expressed, it was mocked and rejected with one voice by all Catholics and even by the Arians. Finally, in the city of Cordoba, where he had held the bishopric, after this consultation, or response, his name was not read among the Catholic bishops who had preceded or succeeded him.

These are the regulations issued through the aforesaid Hosius and twenty bishops, with the Catholic faith preserved and unharmed, as it was expounded by the 318 Fathers at Nicaea in Bithynia. Later, in the city of Rome,

[Note: [Col. 1043D] Up to this point the Ballerini brothers followed the Vatican manuscript, indicating that what follows continues in the same manuscript; nevertheless, they omitted annotating it because part had been published by Salmon in *De l’étude des conciles*, p. 177, and another part had already been published by Dacherius in *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 507, folio edition. Accordingly, the present text is supplied from both.]

Pope Sylvester, thirty-fourth from Peter, assembled 277 Fathers in the city of Rome with the counsel of Constantine Augustus. After the Council of Nicaea he likewise condemned Arius and the other heretics and took care to establish many regulations necessary for the Church. [Col. 1044C]

Siricius, fortieth from Peter, wrote fifteen decretal chapters in response to certain necessities, after Omerius, bishop of Tarragona, had sought his advice.

Innocent, forty-second from Peter, wrote certain letters to bishops of various provinces, containing fifty-six decretal chapters.

Zosimus, forty-third from Peter, wrote a decretal letter to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, prefaced by three chapters.

Celestine, forty-fifth from Peter, wrote a letter to Venerius and the other bishops of Gaul, containing twelve chapters.

Leo, forty-seventh from Peter, wrote certain letters to bishops of various provinces, containing twenty-nine chapters. [Col. 1044D]

Hilary, forty-eighth from Peter, in the presence of bishops and forty-five presbyters, established six synodical chapters.

Felix, fiftieth from Peter, in the presence of bishops and eighty-one presbyters, established twenty-seven canonical chapters concerning bishops, presbyters, and deacons in Africa who had been rebaptized.

Gelasius, fifteenth from Peter, established twenty-seven chapters concerning ecclesiastical institutions.

Anastasius, fifty-second from Peter, established eight decretal chapters addressed to Anastasius Augustus concerning various ecclesiastical matters.
