Symmachus, fifty-third from Peter, together with bishops, presbyters, and deacons, established five synodical chapters. [Col. 1045A]

Likewise, in a second decretal of his, he established seven chapters necessary for the Church, which were confirmed with 181 bishops, presbyters, and deacons.

Gregory the teacher, sixty-sixth from Peter, wrote six synodical chapters with twenty-four bishops during the reign of Maurice Augustus.

Likewise, eleven very necessary chapters of his were written to Augustine in Britain at Augustine’s own request.

Martin, seventy-seventh from Peter, held a synod in the city of Rome with 105 Fathers against Cyrus and his associates, the heretics. He condemned those who asserted that the Son of God had one nature and one operation, and, having transcribed this decision, sent it through orthodox men to the East and West.

Gregory II, ninety-first from Peter, wrote seventeen chapters to be observed by the whole Church, together with thirty-three Fathers, and bound them under the penalty of anathema. [Col. 1045B]

## NOTE ON THE SYNODS

[Note: [Col. 1045D] What follows is supplied from the *Spicilegium*.]

A note on the little book concerning the twenty-four synods which are said to have been written before, below, or after the six synods.

The first is the Ancyran synod, said to have taken place before Nicaea but placed afterward because of its greater authority. In it eighteen Fathers established twenty-four canons, whose principal author was Vitalis, bishop of Antioch.

The second is the Neocaesarean synod, said to have taken place after the Ancyran and before Nicaea. In it thirteen Fathers established fourteen canons, whose principal author was Vitalis of Salamis.

The third is the Gangran synod, said to have taken place after Nicaea. In it sixteen Fathers established twenty canons because of certain ecclesiastical necessities, especially against Eustathius, who said that no one living in the married state, nor any believer who did not renounce everything he possessed, could have hope before God, along with many other poisonous teachings which it would take too long to enumerate. [Col. 1045C]

The fourth is the Sardican synod, in which sixty Fathers established twenty-one canons. Its principal author was Hosius, bishop of Córdoba, who also served as legate of the holy Roman Church.

The fifth is the synod of Antioch, in which thirty Fathers established twenty-five canons. Its principal author was Eusebius, bishop of Palestine.

The sixth is the Laodicean synod, in which twenty-two Fathers established fifty-eight canons. Its principal author was Bishop Theodosius.

The seventh is the Carthaginian synod, in which 217 Fathers established thirty-three [canons]. Its principal author was Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, is also said to have been present at this synod during the reign of Honorius Augustus.

The eighth is the African synod under Theodosius the Younger Augustus. In it 214 Fathers read aloud and confirmed 105 canons which are said to have been composed in various councils of the African province during the time of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. [Col. 1045D]

The ninth is the Arelate synod, in which 600 Fathers established canons. Its principal authors were Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, and Saint Marinus, bishop of Arles, during the reign of Constantine Augustus, as some assert.

The tenth is another Arelate synod, in which nineteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

The eleventh is likewise an Arelate synod, in which eighteen Fathers established canons.

The twelfth is likewise an Arelate synod, in which eleven Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

The thirteenth is likewise an Arelate synod, in which nineteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Sapapardus, bishop of Arles. [Col. 1046A]

The fourteenth is the Arausican synod, in which sixteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Bishop Hilary.

The fifteenth is the Epaunian synod, in which twenty-seven Fathers established forty canons. Its principal author was Bishop Caesarius.

The sixteenth is the Agathensian synod, in which thirty-four Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Bishop Caesarius.

The seventeenth is the Aurelian synod, in which seventy-two Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Aurelianus, bishop of Arles, during the reign of King Clovis.

The eighteenth is likewise an Aurelian synod, in which thirty-one Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Melanius, bishop of Redon.

The nineteenth is likewise an Aurelian synod, in which twenty-five Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Saint Altinus, bishop of Angers.

The twentieth is the Arvernian synod, in which fifteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Honoratus, bishop of Brevitis [reading uncertain].

The twenty-first is the Matiscan synod, in which twenty-one Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Priscus, bishop of Lyons.

The twenty-second is likewise a Matiscan synod, in which sixty-four Fathers established canons. Its principal author was again Priscus, bishop of Lyons.

The twenty-third is the Lugdunian synod, in which fourteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Philippus, bishop of Vienne.

The twenty-fourth is likewise a Lugdunian synod, in which twenty Fathers established canons. Its principal author was again Priscus, bishop of Lyons.

It is appropriate to add another very similar note, which I copied from Vatican manuscript 1342, of the ninth century, as I judged at the time. It begins as follows, without a title:

[Col. 1046C]

The Ancyran synod of eighteen Fathers, whose author was Vitalis, bishop of Antioch. The Neocaesarean synod: fourteen canons were established by seventeen Fathers. The Gangran synod against Eustathius, who said that no one could be saved unless he renounced everything. The Sardican synod, where Hosius, bishop of Córdoba, was present with sixty Fathers. The Antiochene synod, whose author was Eusebius, bishop of Palestine, with thirty Fathers. The Laodicean synod of seventeen Fathers, whose author was Bishop Theodosius. The Carthaginian synod of 218 Fathers, where Saint Augustine was present. At the African synod, 105 canons established by Aurelius the bishop were confirmed by 234 Fathers under Theodosius the Younger Augustus. The first Aurelian synod, presided over, with God’s help, by Pope Silvester during the reign of Constantine.

Another Arelate synod, whose author was Caesarius, bishop of Arles, with eighteen Fathers. Another Arelate synod with nineteen Fathers. Yet another Arelate synod with eighteen Fathers, where the aforesaid Caesarius was present. The Arausican synod of seventeen Fathers, whose author was Hilary. Another Arelate synod of seventeen Fathers, whose author was Sarpidus, bishop of Arles. The Epaunian synod of twenty-seven Fathers and sixty canons, where Caesarius was present. The Aurelian synod of seventy-two Fathers, whose author was Aurelianus, bishop of Arles. Another Aurelian synod of twenty-two Fathers, whose author was Melanius, bishop of Redon. Another Aurelian synod, whose author was Saint Altinus, bishop of Angers. The Arvernian synod of fifteen Fathers, whose author was Honoratus, bishop of Trier. The Matiscan synod of seventy-eight Fathers, whose author was Priscus, bishop of Lyons. The Lugdunian synod of twenty-eight Fathers, whose author was Philippus, bishop of Vienne. Another Lugdunian synod of twenty Fathers, whose author was the same Priscus. [Col. 1046D]

## Canons of the Sardican Council, no. 21

[Col. 1047A]

1. That a bishop be deprived of lay communion if he moves from his own city to another.

2. That a bishop not even receive lay communion at the end of his life if he has changed his see out of ambition.

3. That, in disputes between bishops, the bishops of the same province hear the case. If the condemned bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff, what he himself has decided must be observed.

4. That no one dare usurp the see of a bishop who has appealed.

5. That in a province where only one bishop remains, and he is unwilling to ordain a fellow-provincial bishop for himself, bishops of another province, summoned by the presbyters, shall ordain a bishop—even if the sole bishop who remains, after being admonished, refuses to cooperate with them. [Col. 1047B]

6. That a bishop not be ordained in villages or in small cities.

7. That a provincial synod may be reconsidered by representatives of the Roman pontiff if he himself so decrees.

8. That bishops not go to the imperial court unless summoned by the emperor or going to aid those oppressed by necessity.

9. That bishops send their deacons to the imperial court.

10. That the pope carefully examine deacons coming to Rome to the imperial court, to determine whether they have a just reason for coming. [Col. 1047C]

11. That bishops carefully examine bishops going to the imperial court, so that they do not go out of ambition.

12. That bishops be instructed by others if they do not yet know the synodical statutes.

13. That laymen not be made bishops, presbyters, or deacons, but only through the lower grades.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] The sense of the Greek canon requires the addition “unless through the grades of presbyter, etc.”]

14. That bishops not remain more than three weeks in another city, since laymen who neglect the church assembly for so long are to be excommunicated.

15. That a bishop not be absent from his own church for more than two weeks.

16. That a cleric excommunicated by his own bishop not be received by another.

17. That neighboring bishops hear a cleric excommunicated by his bishop, whether justly or unjustly; if [he was there] before the excommunication, they are in no way to excommunicate [him] for having remained so long [the wording is corrupt].

[Note: [Col. 1047D] The passage is obscure. See canon 17 of the Sardican Council itself.]

18. That no bishop ordain another bishop’s cleric in his own parish.

19. That the ordination of another bishop’s cleric without the consent of his own bishop be invalid.

20. That presbyters not remain outside their own parish for more than three weeks. [Col. 1048A]

21. That bishops expelled from their own see not be prevented from staying in another city.

The entire synod said: “Let the Catholic Church throughout the whole world observe everything that has been established.”

And sixty bishops from various provinces subscribed:

Hosius from Spain, bishop of Córdoba.

Vincentius of Capua, legate of the holy Roman Church.

Januarius of Benevento, legate of the holy Roman Church.

Calipodius of Naples, legate of the holy Roman Church.

Athanasius of Alexandria.

Marcellus from Macedonia, of Ancyra. [Col. 1048B]

Protogenes from Achaea, of Sardica.

Gaudentius from Dacia, of Naissus.

And likewise many others.

## Canons of the Carthaginian Council

After the consulship of Honorius and Theodosius Augusti, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, at Carthage, in the secretariat of the basilica of Faustus, Aurelius the pope having taken his seat together with the legates of the Roman Church—Faustinus, bishop of the church of Potentia in the Italian province of Picenum, and the presbyters Philippus and Asellus—and also Augustine, bishop of Hippo, and the remaining 217 bishops, they first read the memorandum which Pope Zosimus had sent to the aforesaid legates. Then, after also reading the twenty chapters of the Council of Nicaea, as they are found described above,

[Note: [Col. 1048D] These do not exist in this epitome; hence it appears to be mutilated.]

they established by common decree [Col. 1048C] the thirty-seven chapters that follow.

1. That the statutes of the Council of Nicaea be preserved in every respect.

2. That the holy Trinity be preached to the people of God.

3. That ministers of the altar abstain entirely, according to the teaching of the apostles.

4. That ministers of the altar abstain from their own wives.

5. That avarice be wholly avoided by clerics and that no interest be accepted on any loan.

6. That the preparation of chrism, the consecration of girls, and the public reconciliation of penitents in no way be performed by a presbyter.

7. That those placed in danger may be reconciled by a presbyter, provided that the bishop has ordered it. [Col. 1048D]

8. That criminals may not accuse bishops or persons of higher rank.

9. That a bishop or presbyter be excommunicated if he receives into communion someone excommunicated by another bishop.

10. That a presbyter be anathema if, puffed up against his bishop, he creates a schism.

11. That a bishop detained under accusation outside the time of a synod

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Add from the African ecclesiastical code: “be heard by twelve bishops.” HARD.]

12. That a bishop be ordained by no fewer than three bishops.

13. If anyone acts against his profession or subscription, let him himself be heard as a bishop in honor.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] Perhaps, “let them examine” or “let them consider.” HARD.]

14. That at Tripoli a presbyter be heard by five bishops and a deacon by three, because of the poverty of the province.

15. That clerics accused before the Church not refuse ecclesiastical judgment. And let nothing prejudice ecclesiastical judges if their sentence is overturned when an appeal has been made from them to other ecclesiastical judges of greater authority—provided that they cannot be convicted of having judged in this way after being corrupted by some desire. Likewise, let there be no appeal from judges chosen by agreement of the parties. Likewise, let the sons of priests neither exhibit nor attend secular spectacles; and let them not go where blasphemies are committed.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] The passage is corrupt.]

16. That clerics not be contractors or agents and not seek their livelihood through any dishonorable business. Likewise, let readers either be compelled to marry or profess continence. Likewise, let a cleric who lends money receive no more than he gave. Likewise, before the age of twenty-five, neither deacons are to be ordained nor virgins consecrated.

17. That each province, because of distance, have its own primate.

18. That the canons be impressed upon clerics by those who ordain them. That each province, because of distance, have its own primate (*primatum*; variant *primatem*).

[Note: [Col. 1049D] Under this number, nineteen, five titles are contained; they ought to have been distinguished so that there would be thirty-seven chapters. HARD.]

19. That neither the Eucharist nor baptism be given to the dead. That a council be held annually, to which representatives of the individual provinces shall be sent. That neither an accused bishop nor his accuser be suspended from communion unless he refuses to appear on the appointed day before the judges chosen to hear his case. That a bishop who is not in communion not celebrate communion even in his own church. That an accuser whose character appears culpable not be admitted to bring an accusation unless he wishes to assert his own causes—but not ecclesiastical causes. [Col. 1049C]

20. That an accused presbyter or deacon be examined by the bishop together with seven others in the case of a presbyter and three in the case of a deacon, whom the accused himself requested. The bishop of the place alone shall hear and conclude the cases of the remaining clerics.

[Col. 1049D]

21. That the sons of clerics not be joined in marriage to pagans, heretics, or schismatics.

22. That clerics give nothing from their possessions by way of donations to those who are not Catholics.

23. That bishops not cross the sea without consulting their primate.

24. That nothing be read in the church as attested under the name of the divine Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 1050D] The passage is corrupt.]

25. That subdeacons, deacons, presbyters, and bishops abstain from their wives; if they do not, let them be deposed. The other clerics, however, are not to be compelled to this until a more mature age. [Col. 1050A]

26. If a bishop sells the property of his church without the counsel of neighboring bishops, let him be deposed.

27. That presbyters or deacons convicted of a grave offense not receive the laying on of hands as laymen, lest rebaptized clerics be made.

28. That clerics who appeal overseas rather than to their own primates not be received into communion.

29. If an excommunicated cleric dares to communicate before his hearing, he has pronounced condemnation upon himself.

30. That an accused person or an accuser choose a place near the place from which the accused comes, if he fears some violence from the crowd. [Col. 1050B]

31. That if clerics, when their bishops wish to promote them to higher honor for the needs of the churches, do not obey, they are not to minister there in the rank from which they refused to depart.

32. That clerics leave to the Church the ecclesiastical property which they acquired from ecclesiastical resources.

33. That presbyters not sell the property of their own church, and that a bishop not usurp the property of the title of the mother church.

And they subscribed:

“I, Aurelius the bishop, have subscribed to this document reread by us.”

“I, Faustinus, bishop of the church of Potentia in the Italian province of Picenum, legate of the Roman Church, have subscribed to this document.”

“We, Philippus and Asellus, presbyters and legates of the Roman Church, have subscribed to these proceedings, reread and transmitted by us.” [Col. 1050C]

“I, Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius, legate of the council of Numidia, have subscribed to this document on behalf of myself and the same council.”

And the remaining 213 bishops subscribed, those who had assembled at the Carthaginian council.

## Canons of Various Councils of the African Province, Numbering 105

1. That nothing from the first Council of Hippo needs correction.

2. That clerics not release their sons from their authority except at the age when their own sins belong to the sons themselves. [Col. 1050D]

3. That clerics not be ordained before they have made all their own people Catholic.

4. That nothing be offered in the sacraments except bread and wine mixed with water.

5. That clerics or continent persons not visit widows or virgins except by order or permission of the bishops; and even then, not alone, but in the presence of approved persons.

6. That the bishop of the first see not be called “prince of priests” or “high priest,” but only “bishop of the first see.” [Col. 1051A]

7. That clerics not eat or drink in taverns unless travel compels it.

8. That the sacraments of the altar be celebrated only by those who are fasting.

9. That clerics not dine together in the church except out of necessity.

10. That a bishop impose penance upon penitents according to the character of their sins, and that a presbyter not reconcile penitents without consulting the bishop; that the bishop impose hands upon public penitents before the apse.

11. That a bishop or presbyter not permit consecrated virgins to wander about indiscriminately.

12. That the sick who have lost the power of speech be baptized if they have testimony of their will. Reconciliation must not be denied to actors, stage performers, or other persons of this kind. [Col. 1051B]

13. Let the passions of the martyrs be read when their anniversaries are celebrated.

14. That inquiry be made of the apostolic see whether those baptized in infancy among heretics may be ordained.

15. That rebaptisms, reordinations, and transfers of bishops not take place. That a bishop who invades another bishopric be excluded by judicial authority if he despises priestly admonitions.

16. That a bishop be ordained by no fewer than three bishops.

17. That a bishop who is to be ordained, if opposition is raised against him, be ordained only after being cleared not by three but by a greater number.

18. That the date of Easter be announced from the church of Carthage to the bishops of the African churches and be discussed. The intervention of Honoratus and Urbanus, the bishops, is [lacuna] Mauritania [lacuna].

19. That dioceses lacking their own bishops not receive bishops except with the consent of the bishop who until then has retained them without arrogance. For if he has retained them arrogantly and, desiring to lord it over the congregations, has despised his fellow bishops, he must be driven out by judicial authority not only from the dioceses he retained but also from his own church.

20. That no bishop claim another bishop’s cleric unless that cleric’s bishop grants permission. [Col. 1051D]

21. That the bishop of Carthage may ordain from any church superiors, presbyters, or bishops for other churches.

22. That no bishop claim any diocese except the one for which he was ordained.

23. That children baptized by the Donatists may be ordained to the clergy in the Catholic Church.

24. That the remains of idols or their temples be destroyed.

25. That a request be made to the emperor to establish that clerics not be compelled to give public testimony concerning the cognizance of their own case (*cognatione*; perhaps *cognitione*, “hearing” or “cognizance”). [Col. 1052A]

26. That a request be made to the emperor to abolish the assemblies of the pagans.

27. That a request be made to the emperor to prohibit theatrical spectacles on Sundays and other feast days of the saints.

28. That a request be made to the emperor to establish, under penalty of pecuniary loss, that no one defend a condemned cleric.

29. That a request be made to the emperor not to allow actors, after their conversion, to be compelled by anyone to return to their former profession.

30. That a request be made to the emperor that manumissions be celebrated in the church.

31. That the condemned Equitius be expelled by whatever means, so that he might not disturb the condition of the Church. [Col. 1052B]

32. That the Donatists be treated more mildly, so that, corrected with gentleness, they may recover from the snares of the devil.

[Note: [Col. 1051D] Read *lenius*, “more mildly.” HARD.]

33. That secular judges assist the common mother, the holy Church, in this matter, in which the authority of the bishops is despised.

34. That Donatist clerics be received into the Catholic Church with their rank, according to the circumstances of time and necessity.

35. That a delegation be sent to the Donatists to settle the matter of peace.

[Note: [Col. 1051] Read, “that a delegation be sent.” Then, in the following title, XXXVI: “against the incontinent.” HARD.]

[Lacuna] against the incontinent.

36. That bishops, presbyters, and deacons be deposed if they are found even with their wives.

37. That a bishop not be absent for a long time from his principal see.

38. That infants be baptized concerning whose baptism there is doubt. [Col. 1052C]

39. That the date of Easter and of the council be announced to everyone.

40. That a bishop serving as an interim not retain the see of a deceased bishop for long, but provide a bishop for that see within a year.

41. That defenders of the churches be requested from the emperors.

42. That bishops come to the council unless prevented by some grave necessity.

43. That an invading bishop of another bishopric be condemned if, when summoned, he refuses to come to the synod, and that another bishop be ordained.

44. That dissident peoples not prevent the bishop from [doing something] for them [lacuna]. [Col. 1052D]

45. That if a cleric, after his excommunication, refuses within a year to clear his case, he not thereafter be heard at all.

46. If a bishop ordains as the superior or cleric of his church someone received from another monastery, let him be excommunicated, and let that cleric or superior not remain in office.

47. If a bishop has preferred heretical or pagan heirs to the Church, let him be anathematized even after death, and let his name not be recited among the priests of God.

48. That altars be overturned by bishops wherever it is not established that the body or relics of any saint are buried. [Col. 1053A]

49. That whenever necessary the bishop of Carthage dictate the names of all the bishops, and that they be subscribed to the letters dictated at the council.

In the manuscript the numbers from XLIX through LX are absent.

60. That bishops who were ordained later not dare place themselves before those ordained earlier.

61. That when a bishop has been accused, his bishopric not be taken away before his case has been decided.

62. That after a bishop has been deposed, a successor be freely sought.

63. That bishops who are ordained receive from their ordainers letters bearing the date and the name of the consul, so that thereafter there may be no dispute over those ordained later or earlier. [Col. 1053B]

64. That anyone who has read even once in the church not be retained for the clergy by another church.

65. That the Donatists in each city be summoned by the bishops of both sides.

66. That the question which separated the Donatists and Catholics from one another not be treated peacefully.

[Perhaps read *ut*: “That the question … be treated peacefully.”]

67. That the Donatists who, after disregarding a peaceful warning, do not cease to harass Catholics be removed with military assistance, just as the apostle removed the conspiracy of faction-makers.

68. That bishops not easily travel overseas, if they receive [lacuna]. [Col. 1053C]

69. That a universal council not be held except because of the necessity of common cases; cases that are not common are to be judged in their own provinces.

70. If an appeal has been made, let the person against whom the appeal was made choose judges against the appellant; thereafter no appeal is permitted from them.

71. That the protection of advocates for ecclesiastical cases be requested from the emperor.

72. That congregations which have never had a bishop not receive one unless he is appointed by a plenary council of the provinces and with the consent of the primate of the bishop to whose diocese the congregation belonged.

73. That congregations converted from the Donatists may create a bishop even without consulting the council.

[Perhaps: “may appoint a bishop.”]

74. That those summoned to a synod, if they refuse to come, may be condemned as contumacious. [Col. 1053D]

75. It was resolved that the Roman and Alexandrian churches be reconciled to one another.

76. That those who desert their wives, or wives who desert their husbands, either remain in that state or be reconciled to one another according to evangelical and apostolic teaching.

77. That only those prayers, prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands be celebrated by everyone which the council has approved.

78. That anyone who requests from the emperor a hearing before the public courts be deprived of his rank. It is no impediment, however, if someone requests an episcopal judgment from the emperor.

79. If an excommunicated cleric in Africa communicates among those overseas, let him be removed from the clergy. [Col. 1054A]

80. That those going to the imperial court disclose their case either to the bishop of Carthage or to the Roman pontiff.

81. That no single bishop claim jurisdiction, against Pelagius and Caelestius, from the emperors Honorius and Theodosius.

The following eight chapters were established under anathema at the Carthaginian council.

82. That Adam died not from the necessity of nature but on account of the merit of sin.

83. That infants are baptized for the remission of sins.

84. That the grace of God not only grants the remission of sins but also provides assistance so that one may not sin. [Col. 1054B]

85. That the grace of Christ not only grants knowledge of what we should do but also inspires love in us, so that we may be able to fulfill what we know.

86. That without the grace of God we can fulfill nothing good.

87. That the saints, together with Saint John, [lacuna] not only out of humility but also on account of truth.

88. That in the Lord’s Prayer the saints say for themselves, “Forgive us our debts.”

89. That the saints truly say, “Forgive us our debts.”

90. That Catholics and Donatists living in one diocese, if, after the conversion of the Donatists, they are opposed [perhaps: “and belong to different”] sees, belong together to the see to which the Catholics had previously belonged.

91. That Catholic bishops and those converted from the Donatists divide equally those dioceses in which both Donatists and Catholics had previously lived.

92. That no bishop reclaim a diocese which another bishop, having freed it from heresy, has possessed without dispute for three years.

93. That bishops not invade congregations which they think belong to them without consulting the bishops by whom those congregations are held.

94. If a bishop, after the admonition of the bishops, has for six months neglected to make Catholic the congregations belonging to his see, whoever freed them from heresy may nevertheless hold them.

[Note: [Col. 1053D] The passage is corrupt.] [Col. 1054D]

95. That a bishop discovered to have appealed from judges jointly chosen, and who stubbornly refuses to obey them, be excommunicated by the primate until he obeys them.

96. That a bishop who is unwilling or negligent in freeing his diocese from heresy be excommunicated.

97. That bishops who falsely claim to have communicated with Donatists be deposed.

98. That clerics appealing not to African councils but to overseas councils not be received into communion by the Africans, unless necessity [perhaps “necessity for this”] has compelled them.

99. That virgins may be veiled even before the age of twenty-five, if [lacuna] they no longer admit certain things.

100. That three judges be selected from each province, so that all the bishops not be detained too long at the council.

101. That excommunicated persons not be admitted to bring accusations.

102. That no slave, freedman, person of infamous character, heretic, pagan, Jew, or person whom the public laws do not admit be admitted as an accuser. Nevertheless, none of these is denied the license to bring accusations in his own cases. [Col. 1055A]

103. That accusers who charge clerics with many crimes, if they cannot prove the first charge they bring, not be admitted to the remaining charges or as witnesses. Nor may such persons accuse, nor those whom the accuser has produced from his own household.

104. That no one be produced as a witness before the sixth year of his age.

105. That if a bishop says that someone confessed a crime to him alone, and that person denies it, the bishop not be indignant if he is not believed when he stands alone. [Col. 1055B]

For as long as a bishop avoids someone as excommunicated because that person confessed a crime to him alone, let no other bishops communicate with that same bishop for the same length of time. The bishop must take care of this, so that he does not say of anyone something which he cannot prove by other evidence.

[Col. 1055C]

And they subscribed:

[Col. 1056A]

“I, Aurelius the bishop, have subscribed to these proceedings of the statutes enacted among us.”

“I, Augustine [Faustinus], bishop of the church of Potentia in the Italian province of Picenum, legate of the Roman Church, have subscribed to these proceedings.”

“We, Philippus and Asellus, presbyters and legates of the Roman Church, have subscribed to these proceedings, which were transmitted by us to Rome.”

“I, Augustine, bishop of Hippo, legate of the province of Numidia, have subscribed to these proceedings.”

Likewise, the remaining 210 bishops subscribed.

That the aforesaid African synod of 207 bishops sent its statutes through Faustinus the bishop and Philippus and Asellus, presbyters of the same council, to Pope Boniface for confirmation; and that through the same pope it requested that copies of the Council of Nicaea be borrowed from the eastern bishops.

That Saint Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, sent authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea to the bishops of the African synod.

That Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, likewise sent authentic copies of the Council of Nicaea to the African bishops.

That copies of the Council of Nicaea reached Pope Boniface, after the consulship of Honorius and Theodosius Augusti, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, under twenty chapters, exactly as they are presented above in every respect.

That the African council, having sent a letter, asked Pope Celestine not to receive into communion in any way those excommunicated persons who fled from Africa.

## CHAPTERS OF POPE ADRIAN

Collected here and there from Greek and Latin canons, Roman synods, and the decrees of Roman bishops and rulers, and delivered at Rome by Blessed Pope Adrian to Ingilramnus, bishop of the city of Metz, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth indiction, when his case was being handled.

[Col. 1055]

## NOTICE OF J. SIRMOND CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING CHAPTERS

[Col. 1055C]

The following canons and decrees of Pope Adrian—or judgments, for they are also commonly called by these names—are so distinguished and distributed in the latest edition, which is illustrated with the notes of Antonius Augustinus, that they comprise seventy-two chapters. Nevertheless, it is certain that they originally numbered eighty. The earlier editions attest this in their titles, and Gratian and other collectors of canons acknowledge the same number when they use the testimony of these canons. Therefore, since they were confused and lacked numerical indications in our copies as well, we have restored the original number, namely eighty, by conjecture. We have also taken care to append to each canon the corresponding chapter of our kings which agrees with Adrian’s judgments. [Col. 1055D]

[Col. 1055]

## CHAPTERS

1. That whoever accuses a bishop accuses God’s ordinance.

(*Capitularia*, book VI, chapter 280; 6, question 1, “Priests.”) Whoever accuses or condemns bishops, while pursuing spiritual matters less than earthly ones, accuses God’s ordinance by which they are appointed. Hence the Prophet says: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (1 Chronicles…

XVI).

## II. Whoever has business with a bishop should first approach him privately

*(Book VI, chapter 287.)* It was decreed that any person who considers himself to have a personal case against a bishop or against the officers of a church should first approach him in a spirit of charity, so that, admonished through familiar conversation, he may remedy those matters that are being brought forward as complaints. If he wishes to postpone (differre) [or refer (deferre)] the matter, let him receive the sentence of excommunication.

## III. On the primacy of the apostolic see and on the legitimate summons of a bishop

*(Addition IV, chapter 12.)* No bishop, unless canonically summoned and heard in a legitimate synod convened at the proper time by apostolic authority—which, by the Lord’s command and through the merits of the blessed apostle Peter, has been entrusted with a unique authority for convening councils, and with a power multiply reserved to it by the decrees of the holy canons and venerable Fathers—may be heard or brought to trial concerning any crimes whatsoever. If anyone presumes otherwise, what they have done shall be brought to nothing. It shall in no way be counted among ecclesiastical acts, nor shall anything that conflicts with this have any force.

For that see, as the voice of Truth bears witness, has obtained primacy; nor would it be called first if it had another see above it. It is also the head of all the Churches, from which all have received their origin. For it did not earn its primacy through synodal institutions or any other contrivances, but through the Lord’s gift, who says: “You are Peter, and upon this Rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI), and other statements of this kind and similar ones. If anyone opposes these in a proud spirit, he shall not escape the prescriptions with impunity, but shall be subjected to the peril of his rank.

## IV. On examining the person of the accuser

*(Addition IV, chapter 11.)* It was decreed that in an accusation against clerics, the faith and life of those making the accusations should always be investigated first. For faith ought to precede all a person’s acts, because one who is doubtful in faith is an unbeliever. One must not place any trust at all in those who do not know the faith of truth or who do not lead a life of upright conduct, since such people readily and indiscriminately tear apart and accuse those who live and believe rightly and piously. Therefore their suspicion must first be examined and corrected.

## V. How a bishop is to be summoned to a synod and how the case against him is to be conducted there

*(Addition IV, chapter 11.)* The holy Roman synod said:

“These are the provisions that, henceforth, because of the plots of wicked people who indiscriminately rage against the Church and ecclesiastical men, we wish to be preserved with the greatest firmness for all ages.

“If a bishop has been accused by those accusers who are to be admitted, after he has first been approached by them charitably so that he might remedy and correct the matter itself, but has refused to correct it, then—not earlier, but only at that point—his case shall canonically be referred to the supreme primates. They shall canonically convene a council at a suitable place within the province itself, at the time prescribed by the Nicene canons, so that he may be heard therein (in eo [or ea]) by all the bishops of that province.

“He too, canonically summoned, must be present, unless illness or some other grave necessity prevents him, because no one may be accused beyond the boundaries of his province before an audience has been requested. For if he has been stripped of his possessions, or—God forbid, something that should be foreign to all the faithful—expelled from his own see, or held in some detention and separated from his sheep, then, before he has been restored to his former honor and all that the plots of his enemies had taken from him has been restored, he can neither be summoned nor judged, unless he should voluntarily choose to come on account of his necessity, though certainly not to be judged.

“He must not be compelled by anyone to answer before everything that he had lost through the insinuations of his enemies has been completely restored to his authority by an honorable council and the bishop has first been restored to his former status. Then, after he has freely and securely arranged and ordered his affairs, he shall, when canonically summoned, come at the proper time to the synod in a legitimate and canonical manner to answer the case, and, if it seems just, respond to the accusations’ propositions.

“For the greatest care must be taken that he not be compelled to answer before all these things have been done, because contention must always be avoided. No Christian can rightly regard it as permissible to deprive a bishop of his episcopate before the outcome of his case has become clear.”

*(6, question 3, “If he is ill.”)* If the bishop is ill or some grave necessity detains him, let him send a representative to the synod on his behalf. Nor should the person against whom the charge is directed be suspended from communion unless, summoned by letter on the appointed day to state his case before the chosen judges, he entirely fails to appear—that is, unless some other necessity has intervened—within the space of two or three months, or longer, as the case may require.

If both parties have come to state their cases, since one ought not to be heard without the other, the court must inquire into the conduct, faith, and reputation of the accusers, and into the intention with which they are acting. They should not be admitted for this purpose unless they are men of good conduct and upright faith, free from every suspicion and distinguished by a good life, and unless they are not infamous.

If the persons of the accusers appear culpable in the judgment of the bishops, they shall not be admitted to bring charges unless they have personal cases of their own, though not criminal or ecclesiastical ones. For an infamous person can be neither a representative nor a legal investigator.

An accuser shall not be heard in the absence of his adversary, nor shall a judgment pronounced by a judge in the absence of the other party have any validity. An absent person may neither accuse nor be accused through another. Nor shall a relative by marriage be admitted as a witness.

Therefore no one should be brought from one province to another or to the imperial court except at the report of the judge to whom an appeal has been made—that is, the plaintiff must always follow the defendant’s forum. If anyone finds that the judge is hostile to him, let him present an appeal, which must be denied to no one.

## VI. If anyone regards his metropolitan as suspect, he is to be heard before the primate

[Col. 1058D]

*(Addition IV, chapter 13.)* If anyone thinks that he is being oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him bring his case before the primate of the diocese or before the see of the city of Constantinople, and so forth.

## VII. On the order of a canonical accusation

*(Book VII, chapters 13, 338.)* We command that the order of accusation long established by canonical decrees be observed. If any cleric has been accused, the person who could be accused must not immediately be considered guilty, lest we make innocence subject to accusation. Instead, whoever brings the charge must come into court, state the accused person’s name, take up the bond of written accusation, and endure the equivalent of custody [or: guard himself]—though with due regard for rank—and must know that he has no license to lie, since the similarity of the punishment demands vengeance upon those who bring false charges.

## VIII. Accusations against clerics are to be made within the province, and those accused may appeal

*(3, question 6, “If any cleric.” — Addition IV, chapter 9.)* If any cleric has been accused of any crimes whatsoever, he shall bring forward his claims in the province in which the person accused resides, and his accuser must not suppose that he may drag him elsewhere or farther away for trial. If the accused regards the judge as suspect, he shall be permitted to appeal.

## IX. Without prejudice to the primacy of the apostolic see, each province’s synod shall administer the affairs of that province

[Col. 1059B]

*(Book VI, chapter 387.)* Without prejudice in all things to the primacy of the Roman Church, it is clear that matters belonging to each province are to be administered by the synod of that province itself, just as it is established that the Nicene Council decreed.

## X. Every accusation must be heard within the province

*(The same.)* Permission to accuse must not extend beyond the boundaries of the province. Every accusation must be heard within the province and settled by the bishops of that province.

## XI. Matters not admitted by the secular laws are to be excluded from the cases of clerics

[Col. 1059C]

*(Book VII, chapter 11.)* We decree by divine and synodal authority that accusations, accusers, and those cases which secular laws do not admit are to be completely rejected by clerics, because it is unworthy that superiors should suffer what inferiors disdain to suffer from them.

## XII. Cases are to be concluded where they arose, without prejudice to appeal

*(Book VI, chapter 287.)* The Nicene and African decrees have most prudently and justly determined that all cases are to be concluded in the places where they arose, especially since everyone is permitted, if he has been offended by the judgment of the judges, to appeal to the council of his province or even to a universal council.

## XIII. Bishops who have been expelled and stripped of their possessions are to be restored before accusation

[Col. 1059D]

*(The same.)* It was decreed that bishops who had been expelled and stripped of their possessions should first be restored to their own churches and have everything returned to them; afterward, if anyone wished to accuse them, he should do so at equal risk. We decree that the judges should be bishops who judge rightly, coming together in the church where the witnesses of each person who appeared oppressed might be present.

## XIV. A metropolitan must not hear a bishop’s case without the bishops of his province; a bishop must not hear a presbyter’s case without his own clergy

*(Addition IV, chapter 10.)* No metropolitan bishop shall hear the cases of any of his fellow bishops without the participation of all the other bishops of the province, because such proceedings will be invalid; indeed, he will have to answer for the matter in synod. Nor shall any other bishop hear the cases of his priests without the presence of his own clergy, because the bishop’s judgment will be invalid unless it is confirmed by the presence of the clergy.

## XV. The person of the accusers must be examined before everything

*(Book V, chapter 139.)* The life and character of the accusers must always first be carefully investigated, and only afterward should the charges be faithfully examined, because nothing should otherwise be done until the life of those bringing the accusation has first been examined.

## XVI. Those whose freedom is unknown must not accuse priests

*(Book VI, chapters 276–278.)* Those who are not of good conduct, or whose faith and freedom of life are unknown, cannot accuse priests, nor should persons of low status be admitted to accuse them.

## XVII. A criminal must not have the right to accuse

*(Book VII, chapter 65.)* Those who are entangled in any crimes or who are under suspicion shall not have the right to accuse their elders; only those who are free from every suspicion may do so.

## XVIII [XVI, according to Antonius Augustinus]. No bishop shall retain, ordain, or judge another bishop’s parishioner

*(Book VIII, chapter 229.)* No bishop shall presume to retain or ordain another bishop’s parishioner without that bishop’s consent, or to judge him, because just as his ordination will be invalid, so too will his judgment [or: adjudication]. For we hold that no one is bound by the sentence of another judge, but only by the sentence of his own. He who could not ordain him will in no way be able to judge him.

## XIX [XVII]. Foreign judgments are not to be accepted

*(The same, chapter 230.)* We prohibit foreign judgments by a general sanction, because it is unworthy that one should be judged by outsiders when he ought to have judges from his own province and chosen by himself.

## XX [XVIII]. A bishop must not be summoned to trial outside his province, and he may appeal if he regards the judges as suspect

*(Book VII, chapter 234.)* No bishop shall be summoned to trial outside his own province. Rather, after he has been canonically summoned, he shall be heard at a place suitable for all, at the synodal time, by all the bishops of his province, who must pronounce a concordant and canonical judgment concerning him.

If this has been granted to lesser persons, both clerics and laypeople, how much more ought it to be observed in the case of bishops? If he regards the metropolitan or the judges as suspect, or finds them hostile, he shall be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pontiff of the Roman see.

## XXI [XIX]. What persons are not to be admitted to accusation

*(3, question 1, “But all the infamous.” — Book VII, chapter 76.)* It was decreed that no slave, no freedman, and no infamous person should accuse a priest. We understand all those to be infamous whom the secular laws call infamous, as well as all those who, because of their offenses, cannot be promoted to the priesthood. For it is unworthy that those should accuse them who cannot themselves be what the others are; for just as superiors are not judged by inferiors, so neither can they be accused by them.

## XXII [XX]. Accusers must be present, and the accused must be given time to clear themselves of the charges

*(Book VII, chapter 130.)* It was decreed that no bishop should presume to judge or condemn any cleric unless the accused has legitimate accusers present and is given an opportunity to defend himself and clear himself of the charges.

## XXIII [XXI]. On bishops who appeal to the Roman pontiff

*(The same, chapter 235.)* It was decreed that, if an accused bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff, whatever he decides shall be established.

## XXIV [XXII]. Whoever accuses a cleric, if he cannot prove the charge, shall suffer the loss of his reputation

*(The same, chapter 340.)* If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or any cleric whatsoever, is accused before bishops—for it is not proper that this should occur elsewhere—by any person at all, whoever he may be, whether a man of exalted rank or of any other dignity, and if he has undertaken this kind of blameworthy accusation, he must understand that he is required to substantiate it with proofs and demonstrate it with documents.

If anyone brings charges against such persons that cannot be proved, he must understand, by the authority of this sanction, that he is to suffer the loss of his own reputation, so that, through the damage to his honor and the diminution of his standing, he may learn that he may not henceforth plot with impunity against another’s modesty; rather, let him receive upon himself the condemnation he had prepared for his brother.

## XXV [XXIII]. The distinction between primates and metropolitans

*(Book VII, chapter 341.)* No archbishop, except one who holds a primatial see, shall be called a primate, prince of priests, supreme priest, or anything of that kind. The one who sits in a metropolis shall be called simply a metropolitan or an archbishop, and, with humility, shall maintain the measure assigned to him by the canons without exceeding it.

The one who holds the first see shall be called only the bishop of the first see, while the authority of the blessed apostle Peter is always preserved in all things.

## XXVI [XXIV]. A judge must patiently hear everything that is brought forward before pronouncing judgment

*(Book V, chapter 246.)* A judge ought to investigate everything and examine the sequence of events through a complete inquiry, showing patience in questioning, proposing, and adding material, so that the action of the parties may be fully defined there. He must not wish to confront the litigants with his judgment before they have completed everything and have nothing further to propose in the case. The proceeding should be debated until the truth of the matter is reached.

He should therefore question the parties frequently, lest something be left out that ought properly to be added.

## XXVII [XXV]. On those who condemn people without examination by tyrannical power; and that bishops and presbyters must not be judged by others except by those who could ordain them

[Col. 1062A]

*(Book VII, chapter 241.)* There are some who, without examination, condemn people by tyrannical power rather than canonical authority. Just as they exalt some through the favor of partiality, so they humble others, moved by hatred and envy, and condemn them on the light breath of opinion, without proving their crimes.

Therefore, by common decree, we determine that whenever any bishop is accused, his case shall be heard after all the bishops of the same province have assembled, so that one who cannot previously be judged except by those who could have ordained him may not be judged or condemned in secret. If this is done otherwise, it shall have no force.

## XXVIII [XXVI]. Where those who have a case against a bishop or metropolitan are to be judged

[Col. 1062B]

*(The same, chapter 241.)* If a cleric or layperson has a case against his own bishop or against another bishop, or if a bishop has a case against anyone, he shall be judged before the synod of the province. If a bishop or cleric has a complaint against the metropolitan bishop of the same province, let him petition the primate of the diocese, so that he may be judged before him or before the apostolic see.

## XXIX [XXVII]. An accused bishop must be heard by all the bishops of his province

*(The same, chapter 79.)* If any bishop is accused of specific crimes, he must be heard or judged by all the bishops who are in the province.

## XXX [XXVIII]. On a bishop who ordains or judges another bishop’s parishioner

If any bishop has judged or ordained another bishop’s parishioner without the advice and consent of the parishioner’s own bishop, he must not be admitted to the common council without reprimand, so that he may no longer violate ecclesiastical canon law.

## XXXI [XXIX]. The right to accuse or testify must be closed to those who have died by divine declarations

*(2, question 7, “It was decreed concerning them.” — Book VII, chapter 242.)* It was decreed that the right to accuse priests and to testify against them be closed to those whom we know to be dead not by human but by divine declarations, because a deadly voice ought rather to be cut off (intercidi) [or forbidden (interdici)] than heard.

## XXXII [XXX]. An appeal must not be denied to the accused

*(The same, chapter 243.)* It was decreed that, if the accused regards the judge as suspect, he must be permitted to appeal, because an audience must not be denied to one who requests it.

## XXXIII [XXXI]. The confession of defendants concerning themselves must not be believed against others

*(3, question 11, “It is not to be believed.” — Book VII, chapter 244.)* The confession of those entangled in crimes must not be believed against others unless they have first proved themselves innocent, because the confession of an accused person against anyone whatsoever is dangerous and must not be admitted.

## XXXIV [XXXII]. Those who regard their judges as suspect must present an appeal

*(Book VII, chapter 170.)* If anyone finds that the judge is hostile to him, let him present an appeal, so that, when it has been granted to him, he may be heard before another judge, with the case intact and without delay.

## XXXV [XXXIII]. All who have been brought into litigation must plead nowhere except in their own forum

*(11, question 2, “A cleric or.” — Book VII, chapter 251.)* Whether cleric or layperson, if someone has been accused of a crime or summoned into litigation, he must be heard nowhere other than in his own forum, when summoned there.

## XXXVI [XXXIV]. Appellants must not be prevented by any detention

*(The same, chapter 252.)* An appellant must not be harassed by any oppressive custody, whether imprisonment or detention, if it is permitted (si liceat [or et liceat]) to remedy the appellant’s defective case through the remedy of appeal.

## XXXVII [XXXV]. Appeal is also permitted in criminal cases

Appeal is also permitted in criminal cases, and the right of appeal must not be denied to one whom the judgment has destined for punishment.

## XXXVIII. In capital cases, an absent person cannot accuse, nor can the accused be defended by another

[Col. 1063C]

*(6, question 3, “In criminal cases.” — Book VII, chapter 271.)* In criminal cases, neither may an accuser accuse someone except in person, nor may the accused be permitted to defend himself through another person.

## XXXIX [XXXVI]. On constitutions enacted against the canons and decrees or against good morals

*(Book VII, chapter 265.)* Constitutions enacted against the canons and decrees of the Roman prelates, or against good morals, have no force.

## XL [XXXVII]. A sentence not pronounced by a cleric’s own judge must not bind him

*(11, question 3, “In the case of clerics.” — Book VII, chapter 266.)* In the case of clerics, this form must be observed: no sentence pronounced by a judge who is not their own (a non suo; the printed main reading is a suo, “by their own”) shall bind any of them.

## XLI [XXXVIII]. On those who bring false charges against others

*(5, question 6, “Everyone who brings falsehoods.” — Book VI, chapter 277.)* Everyone who has brought false charges against others shall be punished and shall suffer infamy for his falsehood.

## XLII [XXXIX]. On a provincial synod being reconsidered through the vicars of the bishop of the city of Rome

*(Book VII, chapter 267.)* A provincial synod is to be reconsidered through the vicars of the Roman pontiff [or: of the city of Rome, urbis Romae], if he should decree it.

## XLIII [XL]. On those who accuse their elders

On those who come forward to accuse an elder, and that no criminal may accuse a bishop.

## XLIV [XLI]. In a capital case or a case concerning status, the parties themselves, not advocates, must conduct the case

*(2, question 6, “If at any time.” — Book VII, chapter 274.)* If a matter is brought forward in a capital case or in a case concerning status, it must be conducted by the parties themselves, not through representatives.

## XLV [XLII]. It is permitted to appeal to higher judges whenever necessity arises

*(Book V, chapter 250.)* It was decreed that whenever an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges of greater authority, a hearing must not be denied.

## XLVI [XLIII]. Metropolitans must not hear the cases of bishops unless all the bishops of the province are present

[Col. 1064B]

*(Book VII, chapter 275.)* If any metropolitan bishop attempts to act outside what belongs solely to his own parish, without the advice and consent of all the bishops of his province, he shall be subject to the peril of his rank, and what he has done shall be considered invalid and void.

But whatever it is necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of the provincial co-bishops and their Churches and clerics, and concerning the needs of secular people, must be done with the consent of all the bishops of the province—not with any arrogance of domination, but through the most humble and harmonious administration of all—just as the Lord says: “I did not come to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matthew XX); and elsewhere: “He who is greater among you shall be your minister” (Matthew XIII), and so forth.

Likewise, the provincial bishops themselves must act with his counsel, except insofar as matters concern their own parishes, in accordance with the enactments of the holy Fathers, so that the holy Trinity may be glorified harmoniously forever with one mind and one voice.

## XLVII [XLIV]. What is reproved in laypeople must be rejected even more strongly in clerics

*(Book VII, chapter 276.)* What is reproved in laypeople ought much more to be condemned beforehand in clerics.

## XLVIII. On lay and clerical despisers of the canons

Let laypeople who despise the canons be excommunicated, and let clerics be deprived of their honor.

## XLIX [XLV]. Who informers are and what penalty they incur

*(Book VII, chapter 277.)* Let the informer’s tongue be cut out, or, once convicted, let his head be cut off. Informers are those who betray others out of envy.

## L [XLVI]. On those who fabricate writings or insulting words against another’s reputation

*(The same, chapter 278.)* Whoever fabricates in public a writing or insulting words against another person’s reputation, and is found unable to prove what he wrote, shall be flogged. Whoever first finds the writing shall tear it up, if he does not wish to incur the charge of having caused the deed.

## LI [XLVII]. On one who made an accusation in anger and later withdraws it

[Col. 1065A]

*(The same, chapter 281.)* If anyone, being angry, rashly brings some charge against anyone, the insult is not to be regarded as an accusation. Rather, after being given time to consider, he must declare in writing that he will prove what he said in anger; or, if he later comes to his senses after his anger and does not wish to repeat or write what he said, he is not to be held (habeatur) [or bound, teneatur] as guilty of the crime.

## LII [XLVIII]. Whoever brings a charge must prove it, and the case must be heard where the crime was committed

*(3, question 6, “Whoever brings a charge.” — Book VII, chapter 282. — 2, question 3, “Therefore everyone who.”)* Whoever brings a charge must write that he will truly prove it, and the case must be heard where the crime was committed, so that whoever cannot prove what he charged may himself suffer the penalty he imposed.

## LIII [XLIX]. Judges must not presume to pronounce judgment in their own sentence upon an absent person’s case

*(Book VI, chapter 279.)* Let the judges of the Church beware lest they pronounce judgment while the person whose case is being debated is absent, because the judgment will be invalid; indeed, they will have to answer for the matter in synod.

## LIV [L]. On one who litigates frequently, whose accusation must not be received without examination

*(Book V, chapter 245.)* No one should receive the accusation of a person who litigates frequently and is quick to accuse without a thorough examination.

## LV [LI]. Bishops ought to correct one another if something has arisen

[Col. 1065C]

*(Book VI, chapter 301.)* Concerning accusations against bishops, the emperor Constantine said, among other things:

“Your accusations,” he said, “will have their proper time, namely, the day of the great judgment, and the judge who will then judge everyone. Therefore, as a man appointed to deal with such matters, I am not permitted to have an audience concerning priests who are simultaneously accusers and accused. It is entirely unfitting that those should be shown to be such as must be judged by others, when they themselves are rather to be judged by the Lord, concerning whom the prophet says: ‘God stood in the assembly of the gods; in the midst, God judges’ (Psalm LXXXI).

“Nor can those be condemned by human examination whom God has reserved for his own judgment.”

And other statements of this kind and similar ones.

## LVI [LII]. No one judges the supreme prelate

Nor shall the supreme prelate be judged by anyone, because the Lord says: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Luke VI).

## LVII [LIII]. A judge must not condemn the accused before he confesses or is convicted by witnesses

*(Book V, chapter 156.)* A judge examining a criminal must not pronounce a capital sentence before the accused either confesses himself guilty or is convicted by blameless witnesses.

## LVIII [LIV]. An unjust condemnation of bishops must be reconsidered by a synod

[Col. 1066A]

*(11, question 3, “That it is invalid.”)* An unjust condemnation of bishops is invalid and therefore must be reconsidered by a synod.

## LIX [LV]. No one should abandon his own Church

*(Book VII, chapter 366.)* No one should abandon his own Church for any reason so long as he is able to remain in it.

## LX [LVI]. One summoned before a judge who is not his own may remain silent if he wishes; and an appellant must be given time

*(Book VII, chapter 283.)* One who has been summoned before his own judge must state his case. One who has been summoned before a judge who is not his own may remain silent if he wishes. Whenever the accused appeals, time must be granted to him.

## LXI [LVII]. On one who acts against his own subscription

*(Book VI, chapter 232.)* If anyone acts against his own profession or written undertaking, then, if he is a cleric, let him be deposed; if he is a layperson, let him be anathematized.

## LXII [LVIII]. One who brings a false charge against a bishop, presbyter, or deacon must not receive communion even at the end

If anyone attacks a bishop, presbyter, or deacon with false charges and cannot prove them, communion must not be given to him even at the end [or: “communion is not to be given him at the end” (nisi in fine dandam ei non esse)].

## LXIII [LIX]. On notorious libels

[Col. 1066C]

*(Book VI, chapter 243.)* If anyone is found reading or singing notorious books, let him be excommunicated.

## LXIV [LX]. Bishops must not hear cases on Sundays

*(15, question 4, “No bishop.” — Book VI, chapter 245.)* No bishop or person of lower rank shall presume to judge cases on Sunday.

## LXV [LXI]. Concerning a powerful person who has stripped someone of his possessions, so that he may be excommunicated by the bishop

*(The same, chapter 246.)* If any powerful person strips anyone of his possessions and does not restore them when admonished by the bishop, let him be excommunicated.

## LXVI [LXII]. No cleric should depart from his own bishop

[Col. 1066D]

*(The same, chapter 247.)* No cleric should depart from his own bishop and transfer himself to another.

## LXVII [LXIII]. Those involved in crimes must not be admitted as accusers or witnesses

*(Book VI, chapter 298.)* Homicides, sorcerers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, ravishers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, those who have given false testimony, and those who have resorted to diviners and magicians must in no way be admitted as accusers or witnesses.

## LXVIII [LXIV]. The accusation of criminals is dangerous and must not be admitted

*(6, question 1, “Whoever brings a charge.”)* In the case of one who brings a charge, it must be ascertained whether he himself was previously a criminal, because a criminal’s declaration against anyone is dangerous and must not be admitted.

## LXIX [LXV]. Whoever helps the downfall of the wretched removes God’s vengeance from himself

*(Book VI, chapter 250.)* Every faithful person ought to come to the aid of the downfall of the wretched with whatever assistance he can, and by relieving another’s punishment remove God’s vengeance from himself [or: with whatever help he can, and by relieving another’s punishment remove God’s vengeance from himself]. For he offers the Lord prosperity who drives adversity away from the afflicted.

## LXX [LXVI]. On the danger of judges and their duty of care

*(Book VII, chapter 287.)* The danger is greater for the person who judges than for the person who is judged. Therefore everyone must take care not to judge or punish anyone unjustly.

## LXXI [LXVII]. An accusation against a teacher must be rejected

*(The same, chapter 288.)* No one should accept accusations against a teacher, because one whom God has reserved for his own judgment cannot be condemned by human examination.

## LXXII [LXVIII]. On presbyters, deacons, and the other clerics, according to the decree of Saint Sylvester and eighty-four bishops

*(Book I, chapter 139.)* A presbyter must not bring any accusation against a bishop; a deacon against a presbyter; a subdeacon against a deacon; an acolyte against a subdeacon; an exorcist against an acolyte; a lector against an exorcist; or a doorkeeper against a lector.

A prelate must not be condemned except by seventy-two witnesses. Nor shall the supreme prelate be judged by anyone, since it is written: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Luke VI).

A presbyter established in the cardinalate shall not be condemned except by sixty-four witnesses. A cardinal deacon established in the city of Rome shall not be condemned except by twenty-six witnesses. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, or lector shall not be condemned except, as it is written, by seven witnesses.

The witnesses must be free from every infamy, have wives and children, and openly preach Christ.

## LXXIII. Lay testimony against a cleric must not be accepted

[Col. 1067D]

*(6, question 1, chapter 6, “Witnesses.”)* No one shall accept the testimony of a layperson against a cleric.

## LXXIV. A cleric must not be examined in public, but in a church

No one should presume to examine any cleric in public, but only in a church, and so forth.

## LXXV [LXIX]. On bishops wishing to condemn the person by whom they were consecrated

*(Book VII, chapter 85.)* Bishops can bring no prejudice against the pontiff by whom they are proved to have been consecrated. If this is presumed, it is certainly without force and cannot in any way be considered an ecclesiastical statute.

## LXXVI [LXX]. No one must act against religion

[Col. 1068A]

*(Book V, chapter 248.)* It is not permitted for an emperor, or for anyone who safeguards piety, to presume anything against the divine commandments.

## LXXVII. The apostolic and canonical decrees must not be violated in any way

*(Book VII, chapter 90.)* Care must be taken that the apostolic or canonical decrees not be violated in any matter.

## LXXVIII. An unjust judgment of a prince, settled through fear or command, is to be annulled

*(Book V, chapter 251.)* An unjust judgment and an unjust decision arranged by judges through royal fear or command shall have no validity.

## LXXIX [LXXI]. Those who arm themselves against the Fathers are hateful to God

[Col. 1068B]

*(Book VII, chapter 287.)* God hates those who arm themselves against the Fathers so greatly that the invaders of the Fathers are marked with infamy throughout the whole world.

## LXXX [LXXII]. No king must presume to violate the judgment of this canon in any respect

*(25, question 1, “By a general decree.” — Book VI, chapter 249.)* Likewise, by a general decree we establish that an accursed anathema be imposed and that whoever henceforth believes or permits the judgment of the canons to be violated in any matter—whether king or powerful person—be regarded before God as guilty, like a betrayer of the Catholic faith.

[Col. 1068]

# NOTE OF JACQUES SIRMOND, S.J.

[Col. 1068C]

### *(The Chapters of Pope Adrian.)*

How highly these provisions were once esteemed in Gaul may be understood from the fact that they were all transferred into the books of the capitularies of the kings. It also appears that bishops sometimes proposed to observe these same provisions as law for themselves and their churches. Thus Hincmar of Laon, in the codex of Saint Mary of Verdun, has the following profession after these chapters of Adrian:

“I, Hincmar, by the mercy of God bishop of the Church of Laon, have subscribed that the decrees of these holy Fathers of the apostolic see must be obeyed. Those also who have been entrusted to me by the same authority, and who likewise agree in these matters, are concerned to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; let them share this peace with me. But if some refuse to become partners in this discipline, let them not be regarded as participants in our communion. Done at Laon, on the eighth day before the Ides of July.”

Against the authority of these provisions, however, as though they disagreed with the sacred canons, Hincmar of Reims attempts to raise objections and weaken them in his letter against his nephew, chapter 24; he also attacks this subscription of his in chapter 36.

[Col. 1068]

# NOTES OF ANTONIO AGUSTÍN, ARCHBISHOP OF TARRAGONA

Concerning the decrees of Pope Adrian, said to have been taken from Greek and Latin canons and synods, as well as from the decrees of Roman prelates and princes, and delivered to Ingelramnus, bishop of the city of Metz, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth indiction, in the year of Christ 785, as I suspect.

## Chapter I. He accuses God’s ordinance, etc.

Telesphorus uses these words in Letter 1. Hence comes chapter 8, canon 6, question 1, in Gratian, and Ivo, Part VI, chapter 314 of the *Decretum*, and Anselm, Book III, chapter 13. Pope Eusebius uses the same words in Letter 2. The words of Pope Alexander in Letters 1 and 2 are not dissimilar; from Letter 2 chapter 2, distinction 94, is taken, although Antonius Demochares [Col. 1069A] and also Antonius Contius falsely published it as Letter 10. Nor did Gratian correctly understand Alexander’s words as referring to legates of the Apostolic See, since they are spoken of all bishops.

For, writing to all the bishops, he says:

> “Whoever persecutes you persecutes the one whose legation you perform; for just as the Son of God himself was mediator between God and human beings, so you too have been appointed in the Church in his place, to perform a legation between God and human beings.”

The words reported by Gratian are appended:

> “But if anyone hinders your legation,” etc.

The Council of Tribur reports Alexander’s words in chapter 9. The capitulary uses the words of this chapter in Book VI, chapter 280, and Book VII, chapter 167; likewise Book V, chapter 170, says:

> “The disparagement of priests pertains to Christ, in whose place they perform their legation in the Church.”

You will find the same words in Book VI, chapter 98. See also Book VII, chapter 462.

## Chapter II. It was resolved that wherever…, etc.

Pope Julius testifies in chapter 7 of his letter to the Easterners that similar words belonged to the Council of Nicaea, chapter 27; Athanasius and the [Col. 1069B] other bishops assembled in the Alexandrian synod say the same in their letter to Felix II. But Anacletus says that the same rule had been handed down much earlier by the apostles, in Letter 2, from which comes chapter 15, at the end of question 3; Ivo IV, 55; Panormitanus; and V, 238 of the *Decretum*. Alexander likewise says in Letter 1 that it had been observed from the time of the apostles.

Gratian reports several of his words in question 7, chapter 16; Burchard, Book I, chapters 132 and 144, where Julius’s words are reported—not wholly incorrectly—as Alexander’s words are reported by Ivo IV, 5, 6, and by Panormitanus; Julius’s by Part V, chapter 257 of the *Decretum*; Alexander’s by Anselm, Book III, chapter 81. On the same subject there is Letter 2 of Pope Stephen, from which comes question 2, chapter 3, more fully because it is reported by Burchard, Book I, chapter 142. Likewise there are Letter 2 of Sixtus II, and, after the Council of Nicaea, the letter of Felix II, as well as those of Athanasius and the Alexandrian synod, chapter 2, and also chapter 17 of the Council of Orléans. The capitulary reports the words of this chapter in Book VI, chapter 287, etc., chapter 21, and in Book VII, chapter 135, among the additions. See also Book VII, chapter 350 of the capitulary.

## Chapter III. No bishop, unless…, etc.

These words are taken [Col. 1069C] from the Nicene synod, as Pope Julius reports in Letter 1, from which comes question 4, chapter 1, and, in different words, in Letter 2; Athanasius and the others in the Alexandrian synod likewise address them to Felix II. From this source come question 3, chapters 11 and 12, falsely inscribed to Patriarch Anastasius in a letter to Pope Felix, and likewise incorrectly reported by Ivo, Part V, chapter 15 of the *Decretum*. Felix himself says the same in his letter to the same Egyptian bishops, chapter 18.

But before the Council of Nicaea the same principle had been received from the apostles, as Pope Eleutherius testifies in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, from which comes question 6, chapter 7; Ivo IV, title 12; Panormitanus; and VI, 316 of the *Decretum*. Pope Victor says the same in Letter 1, and Sixtus II in Letter 1, from which comes III, question 6, chapter 5. Burchard reports it from Victor’s letter in Book I, chapter 176, and from Julius in chapter 144; Ivo, Book IV, title 12, chapter 2 of the *Panormia*, attributes the Victorian material to Gregory. But I write “of Julius” instead of “of Gregory,” as in Part V, chapter 257 of the *Decretum*. Victor’s successor, Zephyrinus, likewise testifies to it in Letter 1, from which comes question 4, chapter 2.

Anselm, Book III, chapter 4, reports the words of the letter incompletely. For in the books of the councils it reads:

> “Nor should it be brought to an end beforehand, as was formerly established by the apostles and their successors, by whose authority it is to be supported.”

Demochares and Contius ought not to have omitted this. The same applies to question 1, chapter 5, which is inscribed under Felix’s name. Demochares correctly notes that the same words occur in Zephyrinus’s Letter 1 and in Felix’s first letter to Paternus, although the words missing from Gratian are not noted. Contius added another error in the numbering: he calls that fifth chapter the fourth, just as he attached false numbers to other chapters.

The omitted words are: “relying on apostolic authority,” before “or let him himself confess his guilt.” Burchard, Book I, chapter 154, has, from Zephyrinus, “supported by apostolic authority”; in chapter 157, from Felix, “relying on apostolic authority.” Ivo of Chartres, IV, 12, 11, and Panormitanus have, from Zephyrinus, “by what authority the apostles were supported.” Anselm likewise has this in Book III, chapter 66, although [Col. 1070A] in chapter 65, from Felix, he reads “by apostolic authority.”

On the same matter there is Letter 1 of Pope Marcellus, from which comes chapter 15, canon 24, question 1; Anselm I, 15; and II, question 6, chapter 6, which is fuller in Anselm, Book III, chapter 7. There is also Marcellus’s Letter 2, from which comes chapter 1, distinction 17. Marcellus’s words, however, extend more broadly.

Let us add Miltiades’ letter to the bishops of Spain, part of which is reported by Burchard, Book I, chapter 2, and by Ivo, Part V, chapter 49 of the *Decretum*. These sources precede the Nicene synod. Among later sources, one should consult the letter of Stephen and the Africans to Damasus, and Damasus’s Letter 3 to the same bishops, from which comes question 6, chapter 6. Demochares and Contius printed this incorrectly. For instead of “because all may appeal,” one should write “so that all may appeal,” and the words refer to the Apostolic See. Burchard, Book I, chapter 179, has this, as does Ivo, Part V, chapter 295 of the *Decretum*. Both, however, omit the preceding words, which are very important. Ivo says that the words belong to Callistus, although they are Damasus’s.

Anselm correctly reports [Col. 1070B] the words of this chapter, with a few exceptions, at the beginning of Book II, chapter 67. The capitulary reports them in Book VI, chapter 287, and more fully in Book VII, chapter 150 among the additions.

## Chapter IV. It was resolved that always…, etc.

In the old book of Anselm of Lucca, Book III, chapter 88, everything from these words to the final chapter is said to come from the decrees of Pope Adrian. I, however, do not think that Adrian established anything here, but that he transmitted a collection to the bishop of Metz.

This chapter was formerly chapter 45 of the Council of Nicaea, as appears from Pope Julius’s letter to Eusebius, Theognius, and the other Eastern bishops, chapter 11. But before that council it belonged to many Roman pontiffs. Let us begin with Evaristus’s Letter 2, from which comes question 7, chapter 17; Ivo VII, 7; and the *Panormia*. Next comes Sixtus’s Letter 1, at the end of which, among other things, are the words reported here:

> “One who is doubtful in faith is an unbeliever,” etc.

Gregory IX has these under the title *On Heretics*, chapter 1, under the name of Stephen to all the bishops; before him, Bernard of Pavia had them in Book V, title 6, chapter 1 of the first collection of decretals. Burchard is more correct in Book [Col. 1070C] I, chapter 144, deriving them from Julius’s letter mentioned above. Ivo likewise has them in Part V, chapter 257; Antonius Contius did not alter this in the best edition of the pontifical law.

Third comes Pope Pius, Letter 1, from which comes question 4, chapter 3. Fourth is Callistus, Letter 2, from which comes question 7, chapter 18; more fully in Burchard, Book I, chapter 171, and Ivo V, 289 of the *Decretum*.
