Fifth is Fabian, Letter 1, addressed “to the sons of the apostolic and universal Church,” that is, in the Roman synod. From it comes question 4, chapter 7; more fully in Anselm, Book III, chapter 17.

Sixth is Stephen, Letter 2, containing these words:

> “The apostles, their successors, and the other holy Fathers did not wish the accusation of bishops to be made easy,” etc.

Finally comes Marcellus, Letter 2, who likewise says that the apostles and their successors established under divine adjuration that persecutions should not be carried out, etc. Gratian reports these words incorrectly in the final chapter of the distinction, and Anselm does so in VI, 187.

Let us now add a chapter of another ecumenical council, reported by Pope Nicholas in his letter to Emperor Michael. In Greek it is [Col. 1070D] chapter 6 of the Constantinopolitan synod, in Gratian IV, question 1, chapter 2; Ivo IV, 7, 10; Panormitanus; and XIV, 70 of the *Decretum*. Chapter 11 of the Council of Chalcedon is not dissimilar, from which comes chapter 46 in Gratian II, question 7; Anselm, Book XXX, chapters 114 or 115.

Add chapter 96 of the fourth Council of Carthage, and chapter 11 of the sixth Council of Toledo, from which comes Gratian’s chapter 9, question 9, falsely inscribed as coming from the seventh Council of Toledo, an attribution Demochares correctly changed. Burchard published it in Book XVI, chapter 5, from the decrees of Pope Felix, chapter 15. Indeed, Felix II’s Letter 1, chapter 11, mentions this Nicene chapter.

Finally, you will find part of the words of this chapter in the capitulary, Book V, chapters 183 and 239, and the complete chapter in Book VII, chapter 147 among the additions.

## Chapter V. The holy Roman synod said: These are…, etc.

By these words those people are deceived who think that Adrian established these canons in the Roman synod. They are, rather, the words of the synod held under Felix by seventy [Col. 1071A] bishops, as is clear from Felix’s Letter 2. That Felix lived many centuries before Adrian, under the emperors Claudius and Aurelian, is attested by Damasus. The same words occur in the capitulary, Book VII, chapter 143 among the additions.

### If any bishop is accused by those…, etc.

Gregory IX reports these words of Felix under the title *On Accusation*, chapter 2, but incorrectly says that they belong to the same Felix whose chapter this is. The former is from Felix II’s Letter 1, chapter 17; the latter from Felix I’s Letter 2. Bernard of Pavia, Book V, title 1, chapters 1 and 8, likewise reports them without observing their chronological order. Contius thinks both chapters belong to the same Felix. Burchard, Book I, chapters 169 and 174, calls both of them Felix, as does Ivo, Part V, chapters 271 and 291 of the *Decretum*.

The substance of this ruling is reported both by Athanasius and the Alexandrian synod, and by the younger Felix, in chapters 2 and 3 of Letter 1 to the same Athanasius. Athanasius testifies that this too was taken from the Nicene synod. But before that synod the same principle belonged both to Felix I and to Stephen’s Letter 2.

Next one should read [Col. 1071B] chapter 6 in Greek of the Constantinopolitan synod, and chapter 7 of the third Council of Carthage, which in Greek is chapter 19 of the Council of Carthage. From it is taken Gratian’s single chapter in IV, question 5, incorrectly inscribed as coming from the fourth Council of Carthage, as Demochares correctly notes. Burchard I, 160, gives it more uncertainly as from Carthage, chapter 19.

Ivo appears to have followed the Greek version in IV, title 2, *Panormia*, chapter 12, though corruptly; in Part V, chapter 270 of the *Decretum*, chapter 8; and more extensively from the fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 19. Both passages are corrupt. Anselm, Book III, chapter 33, follows Burchard. See the words of this subject in the additions to Book VII of the capitulary, chapter 143.

### Whoever is to be summoned at the proper place…, etc.

Besides Anselm III, 88, Burchard I, 174, and Ivo V, 292 of the *Decretum* report these words of Felix. But Felix’s letter does not read “at the time fixed by the Nicene canons,” for Felix was much earlier; it reads “at a suitable time,” that is, in autumn or summer. This is confirmed by Apostolic Canon 37 and Nicene Canon 5, from which comes chapter 1, distinction 18, although the two Antonii printed it incorrectly as:

> “so that a pure fast and a solemn offering may be presented to God.”

It should read [Col. 1071C]:

> “so that a pure and solemn offering may be presented to God.”

In Greek it is:

> τὸ δῶρον καθαρὸν προσφέρηται τῷ Θεῷ.

That is: “that a pure offering may be offered to God.”

Although we do not recognize the words “and solemn” in this passage—and although they are found in many Latin editions of these canons and in the old book of Maffei—they are not in the sixth Council of Carthage or in the translation of Dionysius Exiguus.

The rest of Felix’s wording is confirmed by the words of the Nicene council reported by Pope Julius in his letter to the Easterners, chapters 23–26, and perhaps by chapters 63, 66, or 67 of the Nicene synod. Thus Athanasius and the other Egyptians seem to testify to this in their letter to Felix II, and Felix himself to the same Egyptians in chapter 3. From this comes the final chapter of question 2, canon 5, where it is incorrectly written “Pope Felix to Anastasius,” etc. It should read “Felix II to Athanasius,” etc. The editions of the two Antonii also erred here, although Demochares could have corrected it in the additions.

Burchard, Book I, chapter 221, gives it from the decrees of Pope Felix, chapter 4; Ivo, Part V, chapter 335 of the *Decretum*. Before the Council of Nicaea there is [Col. 1071D] Pope Zephyrinus’s Letter 1, of which we spoke in chapter 3. It shares certain passages with Felix’s Letter 1 and is written in the same words; Gratian reported it badly.

There is also Pope Fabian’s Letter 3, a large part of which is found in Sixtus III’s letter to the Easterners, chapter 3. From Fabian’s letter come three chapters of Gratian, question 6, chapter 3; two chapters in Burchard I, 147–148; and two in Ivo, Part V, chapters 260–261 of the *Decretum*. Finally, Stephen’s Letter 2 establishes the same rule. Add Greek chapter 6 of the ecumenical Constantinopolitan synod. The words of this subject are found in the additions to distinction 143 of Book VII of the capitulary.

### Since anything beyond the boundaries of the province…, etc.

Pope Julius, Letter 2, chapter 32, testifies that this was established in the Nicene synod. Formerly Pope Stephen had decreed it in Letter 2, from which come question 6, chapter 4; Ivo XLV, 4; Panormitanus; Anselm III, 74; and Felix’s Letters 1 and 2, mentioned above. See below, chapter 10.

One should also consult the constitution of Valentinian and the others, Book V, title 1 of the Theodosian Code, whose words are largely repeated there. It is constitution [Col. 1072A] 10 in the complete book. Add distinction, chapter 143, in the additions to the capitulary.

### For if anyone has been stripped of his possessions…, etc.

Gratian reports these words of Felix in III, question 2, chapter 8, but incorrectly thinks that the same Felix wrote chapters 7 and 8. The former belongs to Felix II’s Letter 1, chapter 8; the latter to Felix I’s Letter 1. Burchard I, 174, reports part of these words; Ivo IV, 6, 3 and 5, Panormitanus, and V, 245 and 292 of the *Decretum* do likewise.

Many pontiffs decreed this very thing. Some assert that it was an institution of the apostles; others attribute it to the Council of Nicaea. First let us commend Zephyrinus, Letter 2, whose final chapter is question 2, chapter 2. Before the word “expelled,” the word “bishops” must be added; it is absent from Ivo IV, title 6, chapter 2 of the *Panormia*.

Second is Fabian, Letter 1, from which comes Gratian III, question 1, chapter 2. Third is Stephen, Letter 1, whose chapter is question 2, chapter 3, reported more fully by Burchard I, 142, and Ivo, Part V, chapter 255 of the *Decretum*. Fourth is Pope Caius’s letter to Bishop Felix [Col. 1072B], whose chapter appears in Gratian III, question 1, chapter 1, incorrectly printed by Demochares.

Fifth is Marcellus’s Letter 2 to the tyrant Maxentius—not to a bishop, as Gratian calls him—in distinction 96, final chapter. Anselm VI, 187, calls him simply Maxentius. Sixth is Eusebius, Marcellus’s successor, Letter 2, from which come Gratian II, question 2, chapter 4; III, question 2, chapter 6; and III, question 1, chapters 3 and 4; Ivo IV, 6, 4, 8, 7, Panormitanus; V, 249 of the *Decretum*; and Anselm III, chapters 44 and 51. Anselm reports more fully the chapter beginning “it must be restored,” namely Gratian III, question 1, chapters 3 and 4.

Seventh is Julius, Letter 2. He reports not only the words of Nicene chapter 28, which is Julius’s chapter 8, but also discusses more extensively the meaning of chapter 35 of that council. From this comes Gratian II, question 2, chapter 5.

Athanasius and the Alexandrian synod also address the same matter to Felix II, and Felix to the same people in chapters 3, 4, and 8. These come from chapters 3 and 5 of question 2, final chapter, concerning which we spoke in the second section. Stephen of the African province and the other bishops likewise wrote to Damasus, and Damasus to them in Letter 3. Isidore reports it in the prologue to the councils. There is also Leo’s letter [Col. 1072C] to the Council of Chalcedon, along with many other passages from Eusebius’s history; Nicholas cites these in Gratian XXXIII, question 2, chapter 3, as well as material from the synod of Larissa or Lampsacus and from other synods and decrees.

We shall mention Symmachus, who wrote in the Roman synod V in exactly the same words as Eusebius in Letter 2. Pope John uses the same words in Letter 2, from which comes question 1, chapter 3, reported more fully by Anselm III, 44; also question 2, chapter 7, which Ivo, Part V, chapter 249 of the *Decretum*, correctly attributes to Eusebius; and question 2, chapter 1.

Finally, Pelagius II wrote to the bishops of Italy; from this comes Gratian III, question 2, chapter 2, whose Latin text Anselm reports in Book III, chapter 59. Add chapter 143 in the additions to Book VII of the capitulary.

### For the bishop is to be deprived…, etc.

The African council uses these words of Felix in chapter 54, or, in Greek, 88 or 87. Gregory IX reports them under the title *On Judgments*, chapter 1, with some variation. Bernard of Pavia, first collection, Book II, title 1, chapter 1; Burchard, more correctly, Book I, chapter 181; Ivo, Part V, chapter 297; and the capitulary, Book [Col. 1072D] VII, chapter 143 among the additions, also report them.

### But if he is ill…, etc.

Gratian reports these words of Felix in the Roman synod in question 3, chapter 1, as though they belonged to a Roman synod in Adrian’s time. Burchard is more correct in Book I, chapter 51, giving them from the decrees of Pope Felix, chapter 11; Ivo IV, 2, 7, Panormitanus; and V, 161 of the *Decretum*. Anselm III, 88, however, gives them from Adrian’s decrees. On this matter Felix II’s Letter 1, chapter 6, should be consulted. See also the additions to chapter 143.

### Nor is he suspended from communion…, etc.

Nothing earlier exists on this matter than Apostolic Canon 74, whose form we read as preserved in the councils. These too are the words of the third Council of Carthage, chapter 7, which in Greek is chapter 19 of the Council of Carthage. From it comes the final chapter of question 3, canon 4, mentioned above. Felix II’s Letter 1, chapter 8, and the passages from Gratian and Anselm cited shortly before should be consulted, as well as the additions to chapter 143 of the capitulary.

### But if from either side…, etc.

Ivo reports these words of Felix in title 7, final chapter of the *Panormia*, and in Part V, chapter 248 of the *Decretum*. [Col. 1073A] See what we said in chapter 4 and below in chapter 15, as well as the additions to chapter 143.

### But if one of the accusers…, etc.

Gratian reports these words as Felix’s in III, question 10, final chapter, and IV, question 6, chapter 3; but in chapter 4 of the same question he attributes them to Pope Adrian. Demochares incorrectly added to Felix’s words material from chapter 13 of a decretal letter. I suspect he intended to offer Felix II’s Letter 1, chapter 13.

Ivo likewise incorrectly reports them in Part VI, chapter 418 of the *Decretum*, as words of Felix III’s second decree to the bishops of Gaul. Demochares’s words are added in the margin, “from chapter 13 of the decretal letter.” But in Part V, chapter 248, Ivo correctly has “Felix, second decree to the bishops of Gaul.”

The sixth Greek canon of the Constantinopolitan council is especially fine on this subject. A few of its words survive in Pope Nicholas’s letter to Emperor Michael, reported in Gratian III, question 4, final chapter, and IV, question 1, chapter 2; Ivo IV, 7, 20, *Panormia*, and XIV, 70 of the *Decretum*.

There is also chapter 7 of the third Council of Carthage, Greek chapter 19, a chapter of the Carthaginian synod from which Gratian’s chapter 1, question 6, is taken—not from the fourth [Col. 1073B] Council of Carthage, as the Antonian editions state. Burchard, Book I, chapter 160, gives it from the Greek version of the Council of Carthage, chapter 19. Ivo, Part V, chapter 270 of the *Decretum*, gives it from the Council of Carthage, chapter 8, incorrectly, as was said above.

At the end of Gratian IV, question 5, both Antonii printed:

> “if he proves that he did not wish to appear on the appointed day, but was unable to do so.”

Ivo’s *Panormia* has:

> “if he proves that he did not wish to appear on the appointed day, but was unable to do so.”

The *Decretum* likewise reads:

> “if he proves that he did not wish to appear on the appointed day,” etc.

Anselm has:

> “if he proves that he was unable to appear on the day.”

But the Latin councils read:

> “if he proves that he wished to appear on the appointed day, but was unable to do so.”

The Greek reads:

> ἐάν δυνηθῇ ἀποδεῖξαι, κατὰ τὴν προθεσμίαν οὐ μὴ τεθεληκέναι, ἀλλὰ μὴ δεδυνῆσθαι ἀπαντῆσθαι.

That is, literally: “if he can prove that, by the prescribed time, he had not been unwilling but had been unable to appear” (the Greek wording is itself difficult).

In the old book of Maffei it reads:

> “he proved that he did not wish to appear on the appointed day, but was unable to do so,”

which is no less corrupt.

The words of John Zonaras are:

> Ἐὰν φανῇ, μὴ ἐξ οἰκείου θελήματος καθαφρονῆσαι, ὥστε μὴ ἐκπροθέσμως ἀπαντῆσαι, ἀλλὰ μὴ δυνηθῆναι, εὔλόγου καὶ δικαίου αἰτίου.

[Col. 1073C] He says:

> “If he should show that he did not, by his own free will, disregard the matter so as not to appear on the appointed day, but was unable to do so because of a reasonable and just cause.”

The wording of the Latin councils seems clearer to me. Yet, amid such great variation, when I compare it with the Greek—which I suspect was not originally published in Greek but translated from Latin—I am more inclined to approve Burchard’s reading. Nor is it surprising if the Latin words of the African council are harsher, since scarcely any ancient writer, apart from Cyprian (whom we do not gladly find called “Coptian” in Lactantius’s account of Cyprian), can satisfy more eloquent men.

I possess an old book of Burchard, which agrees with the printed text. The words of Maffei’s book, which I know to be extremely old, do not differ greatly from Burchard’s. I add that Felix II’s Letter 1, chapter 8, contains similar words:

> “But if he has been able to prove that he did not refuse, but was unable, to come, this will harm him nothing.”

It would be stated more clearly as:

> “that he did not come, not because he was unwilling [Col. 1073D], but because he was unable.”

But enough of this.

There is also a seventh Council of Carthage, whose chapter 2 expresses a similar judgment. In Greek it is chapter 130. Gratian calls it the eighth Council of Carthage, chapter 2, cause 4, question 6; Demochares correctly observed this. Ivo likewise correctly says in Part XVI, chapter 64 of the *Decretum* that it is chapter 96 of the African council.

The capitulary reports the words of this subject with a few exceptions in Book V, chapter 241; Book VII, chapters 90 and 119; and in the additions to chapter 143.

### For an infamous person…, etc.

Gratian reports these words of Felix in the Roman synod as words of the Roman synod in III, question 7, chapter 1. Ivo, Book IV, title 7, chapter 24 of the *Panormia*, gives them as Stephen’s words to the bishops of Gaul in the second decretal, incorrectly. But in Part V, chapter 248, and Part VI, chapter 331 of the *Decretum*, he correctly gives them as Felix’s words to the bishops of Gaul and quotes many other words from the same letter.

The words reported by Gratian—“there are three, etc.”—are not from Felix’s letter, but are Gratian’s own, drawn from the *Digest*, as Contius correctly notes. Anselm [Col. 1074A] likewise correctly gives Felix’s name in Book III, chapter 7, and reports several other words. But he incorrectly inscribed it “Felix to all the bishops,” unless “of Gaul” is added. Paul should be consulted, as well as Anianus, Paul’s interpreter, Book I, title 2, *Sentences*, and Book VII, chapter 143 of the capitulary among the additions.

### But in the absence of the adversary…, etc.

Gratian correctly attributes these words to Pope Felix in III, question 9, chapters 11 and 18; Ivo IV, 7, 2, *Panormia*, V, 248, and VI, 331 of the *Decretum*; and Anselm III, 7. The same rule is found in the Nicene synod, chapters 33 and 66. Julius says that it was established in Letter 2, chapters 9 and 24.

But Telesphorus’s letter is much older, from which comes Gratian III, question 9, chapter 1, and Anselm III, 13. There is also Zephyrinus’s Letter 1, from which comes Gratian’s chapter 13; its words ought to have been distinguished from Gratian’s own words. For “unless he should have been absent,” etc., belongs to Gratian; the preceding words belong to Zephyrinus. Burchard reports them more fully in Book XVI, chapter 13:

> “This is found in the sacred books: It is not the Roman custom to condemn anyone before the accused has his accusers present and receives an opportunity to defend himself [Col. 1074B], so as to clear away the charges.”

See Acts, chapter 25. Add the additions to chapter 143.

### Nor is judgment…, etc.

Eleutherius’s letter, from which comes Gratian III, question 9, chapter 2, is also cited above. Ivo, Part VI, chapter 319 of the *Decretum*; Anselm, Book III, chapter 28; and Felix’s Letter 1 are relevant. Before Felix there was Callistus’s Letter 2, from which comes Gratian III, question 9, chapter 3; Burchard I, 171; Ivo V, 289 of the *Decretum*; and Anselm III, 34.

Add Julius’s Letter 1, chapter 3, and Damasus’s Letter 3, from which come Gratian III, question 9, chapters 5 and 6; Ivo VI, question 347 of the *Decretum*. Also add the fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 30, and what I later found: Pope Cornelius established the same rule in Letter 3, from which comes III, question 9, chapter 4; Anselm III, 37. The apostles do so in Clement, Book II, chapters 53 and 55 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*. See chapter 204 of the capitulary.

In Ivo, Part XVI, chapter 316 of the *Decretum*, see also constitution 15 of Gratian, Augustine, and the others, Book IX, title 1 of the Theodosian Code. In Anianus it is constitution 9; in the Justinian Code, constitution 14, Book IX, title 2, although it is reported too briefly. See the additions to chapter 143 of the capitulary.

### Nor may an absent person appear through another…, etc.

A similar rule is found [Col. 1074C] in chapter 58 of the Nicene council, in Julius’s Letter 2, chapter 20. Formerly Pope Hyginus used the same words at the end of Letter 1, from which comes question 7, chapter 52. Pope Lucius used different words in his letter to the bishops of Gaul and Spain. Callistus uses other words in Letter 7, from which comes question 8, chapter 1; Burchard I, 171; Ivo V, 289 of the *Decretum*; and Anselm III, 54.

Pope Stephen also has it in Letter 2, from which comes the final chapter of question 8; Burchard I, 177; Ivo IV, 7, 1, *Panormia*, and V, 293 and 328 of the *Decretum*; Anselm III, 55. Add Dionysius’s Letter 2, Marcellus’s Letter 2, from which comes chapter 5 of Gratian III, question 9; Damasus’s Letter 3, from which comes IV, question 4, chapter 2; Ivo VI, 337 of the *Decretum*; and Letter 6, from which come V, question 2, chapters 3 and 11, and XI, question 3, chapter 76.

Finally, add chapter 11 of the sixth Council of Toledo, from which comes Gratian III, question 9, chapter 9, although Gratian incorrectly attributes it to the seventh Council of Toledo, as Demochares correctly changed it. Burchard, Book XVI, chapter 5, gives it from the decrees of Pope Felix, chapter 15. I have not yet considered defending this attribution. The same wording is found in chapter 47 of the Council of Worms.

The Council of Toledo adds an exception: unless the case concerns the majesty [Col. 1074D] of the king. Burchard and Gratian omitted this. Finally, that judgment should be rendered with both parties present is also found in the apostolic constitutions under Clement’s name, Book II, chapters 53 and 55.

See below, chapter 35, and chapter 204 in the capitularies, in Ivo, Part XVI, chapter 316 of the *Decretum*. It is found in Book VII of the capitulary, chapter 354, and in the additions, chapters 103 and 143. Constitution 15 should be consulted—that is, 52. Add Paul’s *Sentences*, Book V, titles 5 and 17.

### Nor should a related person be admitted as a witness…, etc.

Gratian reports these words of Felix in III, question 9, chapter 12; Ivo, Part VI, chapter 351 of the *Decretum*; and Anselm, Book III, chapter 7. Callistus says the same concerning blood relatives in Letter 2, whose chapters are 1 and 12 of Gratian III, question 5; Burchard I, 171; Ivo IV, 8, 3, *Panormia*, and V, 289 of the *Decretum*; Anselm III, 54.

Pope Julius testifies in Letter 2, chapter 32, that this came from the Council of Nicaea. From it comes Gratian III, question 5, chapter 10; Anselm III, 21; and chapter 143 in the additions to the capitulary.

### Therefore no one is to be brought forward…, etc.

Gratian [Col. 1075A] III, question 6, chapter 16, from the Roman synod, reads *exere* instead of *exhiberi*. But in Ivo V, 248, and VI, 331 of the *Decretum*, it appears as Felix’s Letter 2. Anselm III, 88, gives it as coming from Adrian’s decrees. See the additions to chapter 143 of the capitulary.

### The plaintiff must always follow the defendant’s forum.

Alexander III and Lucius III should be consulted in Gregory IX under the title *On the Competent Forum*, chapters 5 and 8. These are taken from the first collection, Book II, title 1, chapter 7, and the second collection, Book II, title 1, chapter 2. After the Lateran Council, in Part VIII, chapter 7, you will find the matter in more words—not both chapters, but only chapter 5.

Older still is Pelagius’s rescript to Sergius the chancellor, which I have not found but which is reported by Gratian XI, question 17. Add Valentinian and Marcian’s Novel, “No one is to be brought forward,” etc., together with its interpreter Anianus, and Valentinian and Valens’s constitution 4, Book II, title 1 of the Theodosian Code, as well as Book VII, chapter 143 of the capitulary among the additions.

### But if anyone [accuses] a judge…, etc.

Ivo reports these words as Felix’s in Part V, chapter 248, and Part VI, chapter 331 [Col. 1075B] of the *Decretum*; Anselm III, 88, gives them as Adrian’s. Before Felix, Pope Fabian used the same words in Letter 3, from which comes Gratian II, question 6, chapter 22. Burchard I, chapter 148; Ivo IV, 12, 1, *Panormia*, and V, 261 of the *Decretum*, give them in different words.

Sixtus III later uses the same words in his letter to the Eastern bishops, chapter 3; Anselm III, 73. See below, chapter 32, and the additions to chapter 143 of the capitulary. Add Cornelius’s Letter 2.

## Chapter VI. But if anyone should think…, etc.

This material is no longer taken from Felix in the Roman synod, but from chapter 9 of the general Council of Chalcedon. I do not find it credible that Adrian wrote it in the form in which it was published, with headings added indicating the sources from which the material was taken. For why would Adrian say that cases of appeal were to be heard at Constantinople, and not in the Catholic Church of Rome?

I remember reading in the *Register* of blessed Gregory, Book II, chapter 54, Letter 52, from which come XI, question 1, chapter 39, and II, question 1, chapter 7, that Gregory gave a certain defensor named John, going to Spain, an index of various constitutions, whose [Col. 1075C] words are inserted so that he might use them when he arrived in the province.

Our collection is not dissimilar. I suspect that it was given in a fuller form; I know that it was also sent to the bishop of Metz, but that it reached us without the headings of the individual chapters.

This chapter appears more fully in Gratian XI, question 1, chapter 47, and Ivo, Part VI, chapter 360 of the *Decretum*; less fully in Gregory IX, under the title *On the Competent Forum*, chapter 1; in the first collection, Book II, title 2, chapter 1; Burchard II, 183; and Ivo VI, 228 of the *Decretum*.

Pope Julius testifies that chapter 21 of the Council of Nicaea was written so that judgment might be rendered in the universal Apostolic Church: Julius, Letter 2, chapter 4. Victor had previously used the same words in Letter 1, from which comes III, question 6, chapter 7. Sixtus XI did so in Letter 1, from which comes chapter 15 of the same collection; although it is inscribed to Sixtus, it belongs to Victor. Ivo IV, 12, 2, *Panormia*, and Anselm, Book II, chapter 9, report it. The same book of Sixtus has it in chapter 11; Adrian in Book III, chapter 88.

I also know that at the Council of Chalcedon, despite the opposition of Pope Leo’s legates, second place was given to the bishop of Constantinople [Col. 1075D]. Leo never approved this. Gelasius and Nicholas testify to it: they deny that he was a patriarch and say that he ought to be subject to the archbishop of Heraclea.

It is therefore preferable to believe that Adrian wrote the words of the Nicene synod rather than those of Chalcedon. Chalcedon itself has chapters 17 and 18, which confer honor on the bishop of Constantinople and assert that the honor had first been granted by the earlier Constantinopolitan ecumenical council. From chapter 17 comes question 2, chapter 1; Burchard II, 148; Anselm V, 26; Ivo II, title 1, *Panormia*. Ivo reports it more fully in Part III, chapter 106 of the *Decretum*.

Nicholas reports the words of chapter 9 of the Council of Chalcedon in his letter to Emperor Michael. His interpretation is very elaborate. In his words, as quoted in chapter 47 of Gratian’s *Decretum*, one should write “the primate,” not “the primates.” In Greek it is:

> τὸν ἔξαρχον τῆς διοικήσεως

The phrase means “the exarch of the diocese.” The interpretation is harsh if it is meant to apply only to the Roman [Col. 1076A] pontiff. This chapter is also found in the capitulary, Book VII, chapter 151 among the additions.

## Chapter VII. The order of accusation…, etc.

These words belong to Pope Eutychianus in another Roman synod, Letter 2. From it comes question 8, chapter 3. Ivo incorrectly attributes them to Sixtus in IV, 7, 22 of the *Panormia*; correctly, in Part VIII, chapter 332 of the *Decretum*, to Eutychianus. Anselm of Lucca, III, 88, as usual, attributes them to Adrian’s decrees.

I suspect that all this was taken from the final constitution of Honorius and Theodosius, Book IX, title 2 of the Justinian Code, beginning “if circumstances permit,” or that constitution was composed in Eutychianus’s words. The same constitution appears in the Theodosian Code, Book IX, title 1, final constitution. The words of this chapter occur in the capitulary, Book VII, chapter 152 among the additions, and elsewhere in Book VII, chapter 436.

### Let him take up the bond of the indictment…, etc.

These are the words of Eutychianus and the emperors. Concerning this indictment, before Eutychianus, Fabian used the same rule in Letter 3, from which comes question 3, chapter 5; more fully Ivo IV, 7, 21, *Panormia*, Part [Col. 1076B] VI, chapter 324 of the *Decretum*, and Anselm III, 79. All attribute it to Fabian’s words.

But Gratian, *On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter 22, says:

> “Hence also in the canons: If anyone, being angry,” etc.

Antonius Demochares correctly observed this. After Eutychianus, Damasus has the matter in Letter 3, from which comes question 4, chapter 2. Contius incorrectly added Gratian’s name to the words:

> “Let an indictment always be made so as to entail retaliation,”

through the word “retain.” Gratian teaches that these are Damasus’s words in I, question 3, chapter 2; Burchard XVI, 38; Ivo IV, 7, 23, *Panormia*, and VI, 348 of the *Decretum*.

Damasus treats the same matter in different words in Letter 6, from which comes III, question 9, chapter 8; Ivo VI, 348 of the *Decretum*. Sixtus III repeats Fabian’s words in his letter to the bishops of the East, chapters 3 and 4, from which comes question 8, chapter 4.

Gratian attributed this to Sixtus, but Burchard XVI, chapter 3, gives it from chapter 4 of the Council of Orange; Ivo IV, 7, 21, *Panormia*, retains Fabian’s name, as was said above.

This indictment is also mentioned in Greek chapter 6 of the Constantinopolitan council. Finally, it appears in chapter 8 of the general [Col. 1076C] Lateran Council under Innocent III, in Gregory IX, title *On Accusation*, chapter 24. See chapter 48 of this collection and the additions to capitulary chapter 151.

### Since the slanderers…, etc.

These too are the words of Fabian, Eutychianus, Damasus, and Sixtus III. Add Clement, Book II, chapter 46 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*. See below, chapter 48.

## Chapter VIII. If any cleric is accused concerning any matter…, etc.

At the beginning Pope Eleutherius used these words in his letter to the churches of Gaul; Felix soon used them in Letter 1. Pope Julius reports that they are words of the Council of Nicaea in Letter 2, chapter 22. Gratian, III, question 6, chapter 17, says that they belong to Sixtus. Ivo, Part VI, chapter 318 of the *Decretum*, attributes them to Eleutherius, and chapter 329 to Felix. Anselm, Book III, chapter 28, gives them as Eleutherius’s; chapter 88, as Adrian’s. See below, chapter 33.

Cyprian should also be consulted in his letter to Pope Cornelius, beginning:

> “I have read your letter, dearest brother,”

page 4.

These words appear to have been taken, if the chronology permits—[Note: [Col. 1075D] And indeed it does. MANSI.]—from the words of Anianus, translator [Col. 1076D] of the Novel of Valentinian and Marcian:

> “No one is to be brought forward,” etc.

They also occur in Book VII, chapter 144 of the capitulary among the additions.

### But the one who has been summoned…, etc.

Besides the authors cited above, Cornelius says in Letter 2 that this was decreed at the Council of Nicaea. In addition to Julius, Athanasius and the Alexandrian synod testify to it in their letter to Felix II; Felix himself does so to the same people in chapter 19. Gratian reports Felix’s words, with the heading omitted, even in the Antonian editions, II, question 6, chapter 16. Anselm, Book I, chapter 59, correctly attributes them to Pope Felix.

But number 2 ought to be added. See below, chapter 30.

These words too belong to Anianus—[Note: [Col. 1076D] Correct. ID.]—of whom we spoke above. See also the additions to capitulary chapter 144.

### Chapter IX

“Without prejudice to the Roman Church, etc.” These words, with a few exceptions, are cited three times by Gratian: 5, q. 6, c. 16, from the Roman synod; 5, q. 4, c. 2, theme 2, from Adrian; and 9, q. 2, c. 9, from the Council of Constantinople. They are in fact from the same Second General Council, canon 2, except for the Latin words “without prejudice to the primacy of the Roman Church in all things,” which may perhaps be Adrian’s words. Anselm, Book III, chapter 88, cites them from Adrian’s decretals. Isidore, in the preface to his Collection of Councils, cites the Constantinopolitan wording of the chapter in order to show that there were more than ten chapters of the Council of Nicaea; he does not, however, cite the words “without prejudice to the Roman Church,” etc.

I suspect that the 150 Fathers derived this from the words of chapter 5 of the Council of Nicaea. From this come Gratian 11, q. 3, c. 73, and Distinction 18, c. 3. Isidore likewise cites the words of Pope Innocent in his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, which seem to indicate that the Council of Nicaea had decreed that all cases and disputes were to be settled and conducted in the synod of the province. Besides Isidore, Gratian cites Innocent’s words at q. 1, chapter 17, assigning them only the heading “Pope Innocent”; for that reason Demochares did not add a definite location. Anselm likewise does so in Book II, chapter 53, but the passage appears in volume 1 of the councils, letter 2, chapter 3.

Contius correctly cited Isidore’s passage, but calls it chapter 25, whereas ours is chapter 27. The difference arises after chapter 9: Contius has chapter 10 beginning “Gelasian: To the Christians, etc.,” whereas mine is chapter 13. I added the numbers of the Novella and of the canon of Carthage; he omitted them.

Let us now consider whether we should defend the older decree as belonging to both the Nicene and Constantinopolitan councils, or whether these are Adrian’s words, or those additions that we suspected. Let the words of Pope Pius be read at the end of letter 2: “with the apostolic authority preserved in all respects,” etc. Before Pius, Anacletus, consecrated presbyter by blessed Peter, says the same in the final part of letter 1, from which comes 2, q. 6, c. 3. I suspect that the words “before the patrician” are corrupt and readily believe that “before the governor” should be substituted for them. For the name “patricians” was used for magistrates only many centuries after Anacletus.

Finally, the words of this chapter, except those noted at the beginning of the chapter, are cited in the Capitularies, Book VI, chapter 287.

### Chapter X

“Beyond the boundaries of the province, etc.” These words were discussed above in chapter 5, theme 2. Gratian cites them after the words of the preceding chapter, 3, q. 6, c. 16, from the Roman synod; and we do not deny that they come from the Roman synod of Felix of the seventy bishops. But the words of chapter 9, which are joined to them, were not taken from the same source, although the beginning of chapter 16 and its conclusion belong to that synod. The words of this chapter are cited in the Capitularies, Book VI, chapter 293.

“Every accusation, etc.” The Capitularies and Gratian cite these words after the preceding ones at 3, q. 6, c. 16. At the end, in place of the words “unless he is the prelate who is the accuser,” Demochares correctly substituted “unless an appeal has been made to the apostolic see.” These words occur in Pope Stephen’s letter 2 and in Gratian 3, q. 6, c. 4: “unless only,” etc.; also in Ivo IV, 5, 4, Panormia, and Anselm III, 74.

The Council of Nicaea added the same exception, omitting the words of this theme; Pope Julius attests to this in letter 2, chapter 31. After the words “beyond the boundaries of the province,” etc., the word “only” must be removed.

[Col. 1077D]

### Chapter XI

“Accusations and accusers, etc.” These words are from the Council of Nicaea, with a few exceptions, chapter 23, as Pope Julius reports in letter 2, chapter 5; Anselm III, 20. Julius repeats the same in letter 1. Earlier popes, however, had used them: Telesphorus in his letter to the bishops; Pope Stephen in letter 2, from which comes 3, q. 5, c. 8; Ivo, Part VI, chapter 315, from Telesphorus, and chapter 317 of the Decree, from Stephen.

Anselm, Book III, chapter 13, cites them from Telesphorus; chapter 18, from Stephen; chapter 88, from Adrian’s Decretals, as does Gratian 3, q. 5, c. 7, from the Roman synod held under Pope Adrian. Demochares reasonably added Damasus’s letter 3 to Stephen, but Damasus predates both Stephen and the Council of Nicaea. Pope Eusebius, letter 1, reports that this had been observed from the time of the apostles. From it comes 3, q. 5, c. 5. The fuller text is in Anselm III, 16.

The same judgment appears in the letter of Clement, Peter’s disciple and successor, letter 1, from which comes 6, q. 1, c. 5; it is given more fully in Anselm III, 1. Pope Callistus, letter 2, adds the reason, which it seemed appropriate to include:

> “For who doubts that human laws which do not conflict with reason and uprightness should be embraced, especially when they either promote the public good or defend the authority of ecclesiastical dignity and preserve it as a support?”

Let us add Eutychianus in letter 2 from the Roman synod.

After the Council of Nicaea, besides Julius and Damasus, one should consult Felix II, earlier than Damasus, in his letter to Athanasius and the Alexandrian synod, chapters 7, 9, and 14. From chapter 14 comes 3, q. 3, c. 11; Anselm III, 62. In nearly the same words, chapter 2 is found in the Seventh Council of Carthage, chapter 96 in the Latin text and chapter 130, or 129, in the Greek text. From it a portion is cited by Gratian 4, q. 1, c. 1; 4, q. 6, c. 2; Ivo IV, 7, 19, Panormia; XIV, 69; XVI, 64 of the Decree; and Anselm III, final chapter. Rabanus alone, in Book I of the *Penitential*, chapter 1, cited chapter 96 of the African Council more accurately than the others.

Finally, let us cite Pope Symmachus in the Fourth Roman Synod, and, on behalf of the same Symmachus, Ennodius’s pamphlet, which recites this chapter of the Council of Carthage. Isidore also cites these words in the preface to his Collection of Councils; but, to speak frankly, I do not recall anyone using precisely the same words as Adrian. Later I found the same material in the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 307, and only the beginning of canon 108; it also appears in the additions, chapter 148.

[Col. 1078B]

“Since it is unworthy that superiors should suffer, etc.” Gratian likewise cites these words at 3, q. 5, c. 7, attributing them to the Roman synod under Adrian. Anselm, Book III, chapter 88, cites them from Adrian’s Decretals. Their substance is said to belong to the Council of Nicaea, chapter 66, as Pope Julius reports in letter 2, chapters 28 and 36. Clement testifies that the principle came from Peter, in letter 1, from which comes 6, q. 1, c. 5, cited more fully by Anselm III, 1.

The same decree is in Zephyrinus’s letter 1, from which comes 2, q. 7, c. 11, although “of the elders in the councils” is given as “of the chief men,” as Anselm III, 58, also has it. Add Sixtus II, letter 2; Felix, letter 1; and the Julius mentioned above, letter 1. But I must admit the same thing I said shortly before: I have not found Adrian’s words previously written by others, though I have found the same judgment. See below, chapter 19, at the end. See below, distinction chapter [Col. 1078C] 307.

### Chapter XII

“Most prudently and most justly, the Nicene or African decrees, etc.” I have not read that anyone before Adrian used these words, although the judgment is expressed in many places. We have cited much from the Nicene synod confirming that cases are to be reconsidered and conducted by the synod within the province; the same is confirmed by the African decrees, chapter 5.

After writing this, I came across the letter of the African Council to Pope Celestine, in which these words occur with only slight alterations. The same appears in Greek in chapter 138 of the Council of Carthage. The same words are in the Capitularies, Book VI, chapter 287.

“To appeal to the council of his own province or even to a universal council.” These words are from the letter of the African Council to Celestine. The same judgment is found in the Council of Milevis, chapter 22; the African Council, chapter 92, Latin chapter 126 or 128 in Greek. From this come Gratian 2, q. 6, c. 33, and 11, q. 3, c. 34, where the words occur:

> “and meanwhile, whatever those appointed by them in agreement with their fellow bishops may determine.”

The council books have *finiant* (“let them finish”) instead of *definiant* (“let them determine”), and *ex consensu episcopi eos* (“with the consent of the bishop, them”) in place of the printed wording. The Greek reads:

> Καὶ τὰ μεταξὺ ποῦ τάν περατώσωσιν τῶν παρ` αὐτοῦν (sic) κατὰ συναίνεσιν τῶν ἰδίων αὐτοῦν (sic) ἐπισκόπων προσλαμβανόμενοι — “and in the meantime, let those selected from among them, with the consent of their own bishops, bring the intervening matters to a conclusion.”

A very old book has *καὶ μεταξὺ*, omitting the article *τὰ*; nevertheless I retain it, bringing the Latin into agreement with the Greek. I prefer “let them finish,” from the Greek *περατώσωσιν*. I prefer “with agreement” or “with consent.” I retain *ex* (“from”), however, and delete *episcopi eos* (“the bishops them”). The word *exhibiti* (“presented”) is not equivalent to the Greek word, which signifies those who are more readily accepted and chosen.

I understand the passage as follows: chosen from among the neighboring bishops, they are to judge; with the consent of both parties they are to be chosen—or, with the consent of the bishop from whom the appeal is made, the defendant who appealed is to choose certain persons to judge. For not all were judges; rather, a definite number of them was appointed. Thus in chapter 11 of the First Council of Carthage, from which comes 15, q. 7, c. 3, falsely attributed even in the Antonian editions to the First Council of Agde; and in chapter 10 of the Second Council of Carthage, from which comes chapter 4 of the same question in Gratian and 3, q. 8, final chapter, falsely attributed to the Third Council of Carthage. Demochares correctly published it as Burchard I, 149, from chapter 12 of the Council of Carthage; also Ivo V, 262, of the Decree; and Anselm III, 42.

Add chapter 4 of the Third Council of Carthage, from which comes 15, q. 7, c. 5, falsely attributed to the Fourth Council of Carthage; Burchard II, 205, from chapter 20 of the Council of Carthage; and Ivo VI, 280, of the Decree. Although the margin says “From Carthage 2, chapter 8,” I believe it intended to refer to chapter 10, discussed above.

The Greek texts, like Burchard, Ivo, and Anselm, have chapters 12, 14, and 20 of Carthage. The Council of Tribur, chapter 10, and Cresconius, chapter 242, likewise concern appeals overseas. Gratian moderated the provision by adding the exception at 2, q. 6, c. 34: “unless perhaps they have appealed to the Roman see.”

That exception is not found in the African councils. Chapter 61 of the African Council seems to indicate that it was rejected, but it adds *non facile*, that is, “not readily,” meaning “not frequently, but only for a serious reason.” Nevertheless, the provisions written under Aurelius of Carthage seem to have been rejected in the time of Boniface II.

His letter to Eulalius, bishop of Alexandria, should be consulted. [Note: [Col. 1079D] This is false. Mansi.] Cresconius, chapter 282, says that they are not to appeal unless the African councils are concerned, from the Council of Carthage, title 93, “On appeal to a greater council.”

Chapter 12 of the Council of Antioch exists, from which comes 22, q. 5, c. 1. Martin of Braga published it with different wording as chapter 35—not from a council of Pope Martin, as Gratian published it in chapter 5 of the same question. Gratian’s persistent error has been noted by others. One should also consult chapter 6, the Greek text of the Council of Constantinople.

### Chapter XIII

“It was resolved that expelled bishops, etc.” This matter was discussed in chapter 6, theme 3. The words themselves seem to have been taken from Zephyrinus’s letter 2, from which comes 2, q. 2, final chapter. Ivo gives a fuller version in Book IV, title 6, chapters 1 and 2 of the *Panormia*, and from Damasus’s letter 3, from which Burchard, Book I, chapter 153, and Ivo, Part V, chapter 265 of the Decree, take certain passages.

The word *placuit* (“it was resolved”) is omitted. The remainder is found in the Capitularies, Book VI, chapter 287, and Book VII, chapter 129 of the additions.

### Chapter XIV

“No metropolitan, etc.” The origin of this decree is taken from the Apostolic Canons, chapter 34 in Greek and 35 in Latin. Pope Julius testifies that the same had been established by the Council of Nicaea in chapters 51 and 61 of letter 2, chapters 14 and 23.

The same appears to be said in chapter 9 of the Council of Antioch, from which comes 9, q. 3, c. 7, and in Martin of Braga, chapter 4, from which comes chapter 1 of the same question. Earlier pontiffs are also said to have established the same rule: Hyginus, letter 1, from which comes 9, q. 3, c. 4; Burchard I, 65; and Ivo V, 174, and XIV, 72 of the Decree, the latter from Pope Callistus’s letter.

It is, however, Callistus’s letter 2 to the bishops of Gaul, from which come 9, q. 3, c. 7; Burchard I, 66; Ivo IV, 4, 2, *Panormia*; and V, 100 and 101 of the Decree. Before Callistus, Anicetus wrote to the bishops of Gaul, from whose letter come 9, q. 3, c. 5 and 6; Burchard I, 63; Ivo IV, 4, 1, *Panormia*; and V, 54 of the Decree.

After these, Pope Lucius repeats Callistus’s words in a letter to the bishops of Gaul and Spain and writes nearly the same words as this chapter. See below, chapter 43. This chapter also exists in the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 146; part of it likewise occurs in the additions, Book VII, chapter 106.

[Col. 1079D]

“Nor any other bishop, etc.” This judgment is confirmed by the words of the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 23, from which comes 15, q. 7, c. 6; Burchard I, 114; and Ivo V, 214 of the Decree.

A similar judgment is found in the Second Council of Seville, chapter 6, from which come the first and final chapters of 15, q. 7. Demochares did not publish it correctly, nor did Contius, who followed him. Add chapter 8 of Nicholas’s letter to the emperor Michael, Distinction 21, in which *praestolandum* may be changed to *postulandum*, or may be retained as a variant reading. See the Capitularies, distinction chapter 146.

### Chapter XV

“First of all, always his life, etc.” This matter was discussed in chapter 4. These words seem to be from Pope Stephen’s letter 2 and Felix II’s letter 1, chapter 13. Clement, Book II, chapter 41 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, should be consulted.

### Chapter XVI

“Those who are not of good conduct, etc.” Many pontiffs issued decrees concerning these matters. First is Anacletus, letter 1, who also uses the testimony of Clement together with his colleagues, although we do not know where Clement’s words are found. The passage occurs in Gratian 3, q. 4, c. 2, and Ivo IV, 7, 8, *Panormia*.

Second is Pius, letter 1, from which come 6, q. 1, c. 9; Ivo IV, 5, 7, *Panormia*, and V, 243 of the Decree; and 3, q. 4, c. 3.

Third is Callistus. These words seem to have been cited by Adrian in letter 2 to the bishops of Gaul, from which come 2, q. 7, c. 18; Burchard I, 171; and Ivo IV, 7, 5. This is from Felix’s letter 2, discussed above in chapter 5, theme 5; the same is in Ivo V, 289 of the Decree.

This letter of Callistus, whose words are also repeated in chapter 96 of the Fourth Council of Carthage, does not contain all the material found in Gratian. Fourth is Pontianus, letter 2, from which comes 3, q. 5, c. 4, corruptly printed; Anselm III, 16, gives it more correctly.

Fifth is Fabianus, letter 1, which he seems to have published in the Roman synod, from which comes 3, q. 4, c. 7, written much more fully by Anselm of Lucca, Book III, chapter 7. The same Fabianus also wrote letter 2 and, more fully, letter 3, whose very words Adrian cites, with a few exceptions.

The same words are repeated by Sixtus III in his letter to the Eastern bishops, chapter 2, whose wording Anselm cites in Book III, chapter 73. Before Sixtus, Stephen, letter 2, repeats much of this material. Felix II follows shortly afterward, letter 1, chapter 11, and testifies that this comes from the Council of Nicaea.

The last is Pelagius II, letter 3, from which comes 3, q. 5, c. 6; Anselm III, 59. The General Council of Constantinople also has a relevant chapter, chapter 6 in Greek. A portion is cited by Pope Nicholas III in his letter to the emperor Michael, from which come the final chapter of 4, q. 1; Ivo IV, 7, 20, *Panormia*; and XIV, 70 of the Decree. Likewise the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 21, from which comes 2, q. 7, c. 49; Anselm III, chapter 114 or 115. Finally, see Clement, Books VII, chapters 46, 47, and 53 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*.

“Nor persons of low standing, etc.” On this matter, see Anacletus, letter 2, from which come 2, q. 7, c. 15; Ivo IV, 7, 6, *Panormia*, and V, 238 of the Decree; Anselm III, 31. Deusdedit, chapter 4, reports several passages.

Evaristus also treats the subject in letter 2, from which come 2, q. 7, c. 1; Ivo IV, 5, 8, *Panormia*, and more fully Part V, chapter 240 of the Decree; and Anselm III, 12. Callistus, Fabianus, and Sixtus III are found above. Anselm III, 73.

### Chapter XVII

“Those who have been involved in certain crimes, etc.” These words are from Pope Fabianus’s letter 3 and from Sixtus III’s letter to the Eastern bishops, chapter 2; Anselm III, 73. Many others have written on the same matter.

First is Clement, letter 1, who reports the words of his teacher Peter. From it comes 6, q. 1, c. 1; Anselm III, 1. Next is Anacletus, letter 2, from which come 2, q. 7, c. 15, and 6, q. 1, c. 1. Third is Callistus, letter 1, from which comes 2, q. 7, c. 18. Fourth is Pontianus, letters 1 and 2.

Fifth is Fabianus, letter 1, from which comes 6, q. 1, c. 4, and letter 2, from which comes chapter 3 of the same question. Sixth is Eutychianus, letter 2, from the Roman synod, from which Ivo, Part VI, chapters 332 and 333 of the Decree, took more than Gratian, 2, q. 8, c. 3, and 3, q. 4, c. 11. Add Ivo IV, 8, 8, *Panormia*, and Anselm III, 25.

Seventh is Eusebius, letter 3, together with the synod, from which comes 3, q. 5, c. 9. Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 4, attributes it to the council at Theodone’s villa, chapter 3; Anselm III, 19, attributes it to Eusebius.

Eighth is Julius, letter 2, chapter 33, from which comes chapter 10 of the same question; Anselm III, 21. Julius says that this was taken from the Council of Nicaea. Ninth is Felix II, in his letter to Athanasius and the Alexandrian synod, chapter 14, from which comes 3, q. 5, c. 11; Anselm III, 62. The same Felix treats it in chapter 15 of that letter.

The last is Pelagius II, letter 3, whose words are given more fully in the council books than in Gratian 3, q. 5, c. 6, though Anselm III, 59, cites them at greater length. Chapter 6 of the Second Council of Carthage also concerns the same matter. See below, chapter 63.

### Chapter XVIII

“No bishop is to take another’s parishioner, etc.” These words are from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 26. The same words are found in chapter 14 of the Council of Mainz under Arnulf, in the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 308, and in the additions, chapter 149. Pope Julius attests to them in letter 2, chapter 6, but after the word “judge” the words “with the apostolic authority preserved in all things” are missing.

Chapter 16 of the Council of Nicaea also exists on the same subject, in both Greek and Latin, from which come Distinction 71, chapter 3; Burchard I, 109; and Ivo V, 211 of the Decree. The Apostolic Canons, chapter 35 in Greek and 36 in Latin, are similar.

Pope Callistus treats the matter more fully in letter 2, from which come three chapters of Gratian, 9, q. 2; Burchard II, 39; and Ivo VI, 140 of the Decree. Adrian’s Decretals contain chapter 15; Ivo V, 100 and 101, and XIV, 72 of the Decree, derive from Callistus’s letter.

Anselm VI, 118, cites it from Sixtus’s letter to all the bishops; chapters 119 and 120 are from Celestine. Gregory IX, under the title “Concerning Parishes,” chapter 3, attributed it to Pope Adrian, as Bernard of Pavia does in Collection 1 of the Decretals, Book III, title 25, chapter 3.

What Anselm of Lucca attributed to Sixtus we found in the second letter of Sixtus the Younger to the bishops of Spain. A large portion of it is repeated in precisely the same words under the name of Felix IV to all the bishops.

Let us add Pope Siricius, letter 4, chapter 6, and a similar passage in Innocent’s letter 2, chapter 7, where he reports that this was the judgment of the Council of Nicaea. From this chapter Gratian took chapter 2 of Distinction 71; Ivo III, 5, 73, *Panormia*. The same rule is reported by many councils: Antioch, chapters 13 and 21, from which come 9, q. 2, c. 6 and 7; Burchard I, 71 and 108; Ivo V, 176 and 210, from another version; Sardica, chapter 15 in Greek and chapters 18 and 19 in Latin, in Gratian Distinction 71, chapter 1.

This Sardican canon is mentioned in chapter 5 of the First Council of Carthage; the Council of Tribur, chapter 28; Aachen, chapter 55; and the Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, chapter 2 in Greek and chapters 2 and 3 in Latin. From these come 9, q. 2, c. 8 and 9.

The General Council of Chalcedon, chapter 20, is also relevant, from which comes Distinction 71, chapter 4, and, in another edition of Anselm, Book VII, chapter 97. In that edition, instead of Gratian’s “to be ordained in the churches of another city,” we correctly read “to be appointed in the church of another city”; the same wording occurs in the Council of Tribur, chapter 28.

> Μὴ ἐξεῖναι εἰς ἄλλης πόλεως τάττεσθαι ἐκκλησίαν

This is rendered: “It is not permitted to be assigned to the church of another city.” It is cited as 21, q. 2, c. 1. It does not come from the Seventh Council, but from the Sixth Council of Constantinople, chapter 17 in the Greek text. In the Greek manuscripts more words of the same canon are found, and instead of “appointed” they read:

> ἐν ἐτέρᾳ τάττεσθαι ἐκκλησίᾳ

“to be appointed in another church.” Thus far the Greek texts.

We also cite the Spanish synods on the same subject. Chapter 6 of the Council of Valencia not only forbids the ordination of a foreign cleric but orders that he promise to become a local cleric; it therefore calls him a resident. The First Council of Braga, chapter 26, establishes the same rule concerning orders.

From other provinces, add Eleusis, chapter 6; Auvergne, chapter 10; Chalon, chapter 13; Aachen, chapter 45, where the words of the Council of Nicaea, chapter 16, are cited; the First Council of Orange, chapters 8 and 9; Vannes, chapter 10; and the Third Council of Orléans, chapter 15. Add chapter 28 of this collection, which seems to be part of the present chapter.

After these writings, we found chapter 3 of the sixth session of the Council of Chalcedon, from which chapter 20 of the same council proceeded. It says:

> “Clerics appointed in a church may not be assigned to the church of another city, but must remain there where they were appointed to minister.”

The Greek reads:

> Κληρικοὺς εἰς ἐκκλησίας συντελοῦντας μὴ ἐξεῖναι εἰς ἄλλης πόλεως τάττεσθαι ἐκκλησίαν, ἀλλὰ στέργην ἐν ᾖ λειτουργεῖν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἠξιώθησαν.

These words are chapter 20 in Greek, where only the addition *καθὼς ἥδη ὡρίσαμεν*—“as we have already decreed”—is found, because of the third chapter mentioned above.

[Col. 1081C]

“No one is to be bound by the sentence of another judge, except his own, etc.” Besides the words of chapter 26 of the Council of Nicaea, Julius cites the same synod in chapter 34 of letter 2. Callistus does so in the letter cited above, as does Sixtus II in letter 2. Before Callistus, Zephyrinus treats the matter in letter 1.

After Callistus, Fabianus does so in letter 3, from which comes q. 6, chapter 3. Sixtus III uses precisely the same words in chapter 3 of his letter to the bishops of the East. Before Sixtus, Eusebius, letter 3, says that this was established by the apostles and their successors; Burchard I, 165, and Ivo V, 275 of the Decree, cite his words.

Somehow the words of these pontiffs appear in the constitutions of Gratian and the other emperors, Book VII, title 48, final chapter of Justinian’s Code. Zephyrinus was many centuries earlier than this, for he lived in the time of the emperor Severus. The law says that this had been established by the laws of the age. Gregory gives the same rule openly and in full in Book II, chapter 54, letter 52 of the *Register*.

Our authors seem to have delighted in Anianus’s words, or Anianus in the words of our pontiffs. The Code of Theodosius, Book IV, title 14, law 35, uses the words of this theme. The same words occur in chapter 14 of the Council of Mainz under Arnulf and in the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 308.

### Chapter XIX

“Foreign judgments, etc.” These words too are from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 53, as Pope Julius reports in the letter cited above, letter 2, chapter 16. There are also constitutions of other Roman pontiffs concerning the same matter: Hyginus, letter 1; Fabianus, letter 3; and Sixtus III, in his single letter, chapter 3, in precisely the same words, from which comes 3, q. 6, c. 12, although only the name of Pope Sixtus appears there.

Burchard I, 147, cites it from Fabianus’s letter; Ivo V, 260 of the Decree, from Felix I’s letter 2 to the bishops of Gaul. That letter was composed as the second Roman synod, discussed above in chapter 5. Anselm III, 73, cites it from Sixtus’s letter to all the Eastern bishops.

The same decree is repeated by Pope Eusebius in letter 3, as though it had been established by the apostles and their successors; Burchard I, 165, and Ivo V, 275 of the Decree, cite it. The constitution of Valentinian and the other emperors should be consulted: law 5 or 10, title 1, Book IX of the Theodosian Code.

The same words are found in the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 309, and in the additions, chapter 145.

### Chapter XX

“No bishop outside his own province, etc.” These are the words of the Council of Nicaea, chapter 54, as Pope Julius reports in letter 2, chapter 17. At the beginning, however, are the words “with the authority of the apostolic Church preserved.” Burchard, Book I, chapter 170, omits them; Ivo V, 280 of the Decree, cites the text from Julius’s letter; Anselm III, 88, from Adrian’s Decretals.

We have written much on this subject above. The words of this chapter are found in the Capitularies, chapter 314.

### Chapter XXI

“It was resolved that no slave, etc.” The beginning of this chapter is supported by decrees of many pontiffs. But it seems to have been taken from Felix the Younger’s letter to Athanasius, chapter 14, who testifies that it came from the Council of Nicaea. From Felix come Gratian 3, q. 5, c. 11, and Anselm III, 62.

The same judgment is found in chapter 2 of the Seventh Council of Carthage. A portion is cited by Gratian 4, q. 1, c. 1. In Greek it is chapter 130 or 129; in the Latin text of the African Council, chapter 96; Ivo XVI, 64, of the Decree. Rabanus gives a fuller version in chapter 1 of the *Penitential*.

The remaining material cited by Gratian comes from chapter 1 of the same Seventh, or African, Council of Carthage, chapter 95 in Latin and chapter 179 or 178 in Greek; Ivo IV, 7, 19, *Panormia*, and XIV, 69 of the Decree.

The Fourth Council of Toledo, chapters 67 and 75, decreed concerning the prohibition of freedmen alone. Concerning persons of infamous reputation, Pope Clement, letter 1, from which comes 6, q. 1, c. 5; Anselm III, 1. Likewise Pope Pontianus, letter 1, concerning slaves or those not born free.

Fabianus, letter 2, from the constitutions of the apostles or their successors, and letter 3; Sixtus III, in the second chapter of his single letter, in precisely the same words, concerning slaves, freedmen, and persons of infamous reputation.

Pope Stephen, letter 2, from which comes 3, q. 5, c. 8; Anselm III, 18. He also treats persons of infamous reputation more fully and the other matters briefly in letter 1, from which Gratian took 6, q. 1, c. 17; Burchard I, 173; Ivo IV, 7, 14, *Panormia*, and V, 291 of the Decree; Anselm III, 5.

Felix, with seventy bishops, discusses persons of infamous reputation in letter 2, as does Eutychianus in letter 2 from the synod, from which comes 3, q. 4, c. 11; Ivo IV, 88, *Panormia*; Anselm III, 25.

I add Eusebius, letter 1, and letter 3, from which comes 3, q. 5, c. 9; Anselm III, 19. Also Silvester in the Roman synod, from which comes 2, q. 4, c. 2; Ivo IV, 8, 7, *Panormia*, and VI, 334 of the Decree.

Pope Julius likewise says in letter 2, chapter 33, that the same rule concerning persons of infamous reputation and others was established at the Council of Nicaea. From this comes 3, q. 5, c. 10; Anselm III, 21.

Damasus treats the same subject in letter 3, from which Gratian took 2, q. 7, chapters 39 and 51; more fully Burchard I, 172; Ivo IV, 8, 4, *Panormia*, and V, 290 of the Decree.

Pelagius II, letter 3, from which comes 3, q. 5, c. 6; more fully Anselm III, 59. See also the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 437.

“Now all persons of infamous reputation, etc.” Pope Adrian, in Gratian 6, q. 1, c. 1; Anselm III, 88, from Adrian’s Decretals. Callistus, letter 1, and Fabianus, letters 1 and 2, also say much about this; from them come 6, q. 1, chapters 2 and 3. Eusebius, letters 1 and 2, and the other authors cited above, likewise treat the matter.

[Col. 1083A]

“And all who, because their offenses demand it, etc.” Fabianus says this in letter 2, from which Gratian took 2, q. 7, c. 38; Anselm III, 15, gives a much fuller version. Damasus, letter 3, also treats it, from which come 2, q. 7, chapters 39 and 51, discussed above.

“For just as superiors, etc.” This matter was discussed above in chapter 11.

### Chapter XXII

“It was resolved that no bishop, etc.” Much has also been written on this subject in chapter 5, theme 7. One should consult Marcellus, letter 2, from which comes 3, q. 9, c. 5, and Damasus, letter 3, from which come 3, q. 9, chapters 6 and 7. Its wording must be corrected from the councils. The text is corrupt even in the Antonian editions: “and it shall not be a province outside the homeland,” etc. It should read: “nor may it be done outside his own province.” Ivo correctly gives this in Part VI, chapter 347 of the Decree.

Damasus’s letter 6 also contains the passage, from which comes chapter 8. Gratian and Ivo VI, 348, cite it from the Decree. I have not yet found Adrian’s actual words elsewhere, except in Anselm III, 88. Pope Julius, letter 2, chapter 31, nevertheless recited the same material, perhaps from the Council of Nicaea.

### Chapter XXIII

“If an accused bishop appeals, etc.” These words are from Fabianus’s letter 3 and Sixtus III’s single letter, chapter 5. The Council of Nicaea also seems to have decreed the same, chapter 51, as Pope Julius reports in letter 2, chapter 10. It is found in the additions to the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 153, and in the earlier portion of Book VII, chapter 315.

### Chapter XXIV

“If any bishop, presbyter, etc.” These words are from Pope Caius’s letter 1, from which a portion comes in 2, q. 7, c. 75; Anselm of Lucca, Book III, chapter 45, gives it in full. Ivo of Chartres, Book IV, title 7, chapter 11, *Panormia*, gives it incompletely.

Sixtus III repeats the same words in chapter 3 of the letter cited above; Gratian attributes them to the Roman synod at 2, q. 7, c. 50. The text is corruptly printed. Demochares correctly added the reference to Sixtus III, but incorrectly omitted the word “presbyter” after “bishop.” Contius followed Demochares, as he usually does.

Later we found these words in constitution 41 of Honorius and Theodosius, Book XVI, title 2 of the Theodosian Code. How they were inserted into the papal constitutions, we do not know. The same words are also in the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 438.

“If anyone of this kind, etc.” In addition to what has been written above, add Pope Stephen’s letter 1, from which comes 6, q. 2, c. 17, discussed in chapter 19.

See chapter 75 of the Council of Elvira; the First Council of Arles, chapter 14; the Second Council of Arles, chapter 24, where the decree of the great synod—that is, the Council of Nicaea—is reported, from which comes 3, q. 10, c. 2.

See the Second Council of Braga, chapter 8, from which come 2, q. 4, c. 1; Burchard II, 202; Ivo IV, 8, 13, *Panormia*, and VI, 276 of the Decree. The penalty of retaliation was discussed above in chapter 7. See chapter 38.

### Chapter XXV

“No archbishop, except one who is a primate, etc.” This judgment is from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 47, as Pope Julius reports in letter 2, chapter 12. Athanasius and the Alexandrian synod also testify in their letter to Felix II that primates were distinguished and enumerated in that same council; Felix says the same in chapter 12 of his letter to them.

Burchard I, 163, and Ivo V, 273 of the Decree, also cite this. Chapters 6 and 7 of the Council of Nicaea are extant today, and seem to have honored the patriarchs of Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem. In Gratian, Distinction 65, chapters 6 and 7, and Anselm IV, 4, chapter 6 appears to be interpreted in the sixteenth session of the Council of Chalcedon.

An earlier mention occurs in the letters of Clement and Anacletus, which report certain remarkable things entirely unknown to me: that among the pagans there had once been chief flamens, or first flamens, and certain foremost teachers of the law.

Thus the first letter of Clement to James, brother of the Lord, says that in those same cities he had received from the apostle Peter that primates or patriarchs should be established for the bishops. Where there were other, lesser chief flamens, archbishops were to be established; in each of the other cities, one bishop.

Gratian reports this in Distinction 80, chapter 2; Burchard I, 155; and Anselm VI, 105.

No less astonishing is the wording of Anacletus’s letter 2:

> “The provinces, for the most part, were divided long before the coming of Christ,” etc.

The chapter says that in those provinces there had formerly been primates of the secular law, who could not flee to the court of the emperor or kings, etc.; they ordered that there should be patriarchs or primates.

The remaining metropolitan cities, which had lesser judges, although they were superior to counts or counties, were to have their own metropolitans, etc.; they ordered that there should be patriarchs or primates.

Gratian also reports this in Distinction 99, chapter 1; Anselm VI, 106; Ivo IV, 3, 1, *Panormia*, and V, 53 of the Decree.

The same Anacletus says in letter 3 that he had written a large volume on this subject, in which he enumerates the principal cities that had received preachers from the holy apostles and blessed Clement, or from the primates themselves. He then refers to these matters under the common designation of peoples and Christians. After that he wrote more familiarly about the three principal sees or churches: Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch.

In all these passages that are either spurious or so obscure that they offer no useful information, I am of the opinion that they should be removed from Gratian’s Decree, along with many other passages that trouble readers more than they instruct them. For by reading many chapters in that book we are not relieved but burdened with material that we could easily have done without.

But let us pursue the remaining material. From this third letter of Anacletus Gratian took, among other things, chapter 2 of Distinction 22. The subject is treated more fully in Burchard I, chapters 159 and 178, and Ivo V, 269 of the Decree.

Anicetus was the third to establish provisions on this subject, in his letter to the churches of Gaul, from which come Distinction 99, chapter 2; Ivo IV, 4, 1, *Panormia*, and V, 54 of the Decree.

Fourth is Stephen, letter 2. Gratian somehow calls him Lucinus in Distinction 80, chapter 1. Demochares correctly noted the error. Anselm VI, 109, calls him Lucius. See also the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 439.

“Either the chief of priests or the high priest, etc.” These words are from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 26; chapter 6 in the Latin text of the African Council and chapter 39 in Greek. From this comes Gratian, Distinction 99, chapter 3; Burchard I, 3; and Ivo III, 57 of the Decree. Cresconius, chapter 253, cites it from Carthage, title 6.

[Col. 1084C]

### Chapter XXVI

“A judge ought to investigate everything thoroughly, etc.” These words are Eleutherus’s, from his letter to the churches of Gaul, from which comes 30, q. 5, final chapter; Burchard XVI, 30; Ivo IV, 9, 3, and IV, 11, 12, and 13, *Panormia*. Ivo gives the same material more fully in Part VI, chapters 316 and 317 of the Decree.

Julius, letter 2, chapter 31, uses precisely the same words. See Clement’s fine admonition in Book II, chapter 41 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, and Evaristus, letter 2, from which comes 2, q. 1, c. 20; Burchard II, chapter 9; Ivo IV, *Panormia*.

Later I found that these are the words of Constantine in constitution 1, Book II, title 18 of the Theodosian Code, from which comes chapter 9, Book III, title 1 of Justinian’s Code. The same words are found in the Capitularies, Book V, chapter 246.

### Chapter XXVII

“There are some who have not been investigated, etc.” These words are found in the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 330, and in the Second Council of Seville, chapter 6, from which come 15, q. 7, chapters 1 and the final chapter.

“Whenever any of the bishops is accused, etc.” This matter has often been discussed and is still discussed, although not in the same words. See the Apostolic Canons, chapter 74; Constantinople, chapter 6; Antioch, chapter 15, from which comes 6, q. 4, c. 5; Martin of Braga, chapter 13; Eleutherus in his letter to the churches of Gaul; Fabianus, letter 3, from which come 3, q. 6, chapters 1, 2, 3, and the final chapter, in precisely the same words; Sixtus III, single letter, chapter 3, from which Anselm, Book III, chapter 83, derives his text; Stephen, letter 2; Marcellus, letter 1; Felix II, letter 1; and Innocent, letter 2, chapter 3, from which comes 11, q. 1, c. 27, discussed elsewhere in chapter 9.

These words are found in the Capitularies, distinction chapter 330.

### Chapter XXVIII

“If a cleric or layman has a case, etc.” See chapter 9 of the Council of Chalcedon, from which comes 11, q. 1, c. 47; Ivo VI, 360 of the Decree, more fully than chapter 228; Burchard II, 183; and Gregory IX, title “Concerning the Competent Forum,” chapter 1.

See Damasus, letter 3; Innocent, letter 2, chapter 3, from which come 11, q. 1, c. 27, not found by Demochares; and 3, q. 6, c. 14; Anselm II, chapter 531. Isidore, in the preface to the councils, also has the passage. [Col. 1085A] The same material is found in the Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 321.

“But if the metropolitan of the same province is opposed, etc.” This was discussed in chapter 6. Add Clement, letter 1, from which comes Distinction 80, chapter 2; Burchard I, 155; Anselm VI, 105; and Anicetus in his letter to the churches of Gaul, from which come chapter 2 of Distinction 99 and 9, q. 3, chapters 5 and 6; Burchard gives it more fully in Book I, chapter 63; Ivo IV, 4, 1, *Panormia*, and V, 54 of the Decree.

The Capitularies, Book VII, chapter 321, uses the same words.

### Chapter XXIX

If any bishop concerning specific matters, etc. This is repeated several times. See above, chapter 25. These words appear in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 104.

### Chapter XXX

If any bishop has rendered judgment, etc. I have not yet found these same words. But see chapter 16, to which this chapter ought to be joined. Later I found the same words in chapter 51 of the Second Council of Mainz, under Emperor Arnulf.

### Chapter XXXI

It was decided that they should be accused, etc. From these words onward, the decrees of Adrian are found in a certain book of Anselm and in another Veronese book of various pontiffs. But this is false. [Col. 1085B] Gratian attributes this chapter to Adrian, *Decretum* II, question 7, chapter 53; there *intercidi* should be written rather than *interdici*. Demochares notes that Pope Stephen decreed this in letter 2, but certainly the words are not the same, although part of them occurs in that letter.

By “the dead,” I understand those who are more criminal, rather than monks, as Gratian thinks. Anselm’s Veronese book also has *intercidi*, book III, chapter 88. In Eusebius’s letter 3, the ominous phrase *funestam criminosorum intercidi*—“the deadly voice of criminals must be cut off”—is written; from it come *Decretum* III, question 5, chapter 9, and Burchard III, 19. Why the criminals are called “dead” is explained by Pope Meltiades in his letter to the bishops of Spain.

Pelagius II, however, calls both groups “dead”: those guilty of crimes and the monks, in letter 3, from which come *Decretum* III, question 5, chapter 2, and II, question 7, chapter 54. Anselm gives the matter more fully in book III, chapter 59, *On Servants and Dependents*. In book VI, title 1 of Justinian’s *Code*, constitution 20 of Arcadius and Honorius has the ominous phrase *amputari potius quam audiri*—“it ought rather to be cut off than heard”—and he also reports its words. Gratian, *Decretum* III, question 11, final chapter, writes *intercidi* instead of *amputari*. [Col. 1085C] The phrase *intercidi funestam vocem*—“the deadly voice must be cut off”—is also written in letter 1 of Pope Silverius.

In Ivo, *Decree* XVI, chapter 332, from the capitularies, chapter 440, it reads: “The deadly voice ought rather to be cut off than heard.” The same words occur in book IX, title 6, constitution 3 of the *Theodosian Code*, in Anian’s book. It is constitution 2, title 3, and Anian interprets it as “to be extinguished.” Yet blessed Gregory, in book II, letter 52 of the *Register*, reports the same constitution and uses the word *interdici*—“to be prohibited.” But I judge that the books of those who write thus are corrupt. In the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 322, there is *intercidi*, as also in chapter 440.

### Chapter XXXII

It was decided that the accused, etc. This matter had been written about in chapter 8. It appears in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 313, and in the additions, chapter 317.

### Chapter XXXIII

One must not believe accusations against others, etc. Gratian reports these words from Adrian’s decree, *Decretum* III, question 11, chapter 3. The Council of Nicaea had the same ruling in chapter 55, as blessed Pope Julius reports in letter 2, chapter 18; from it comes *Decretum* XV, question 5, final chapter, where Gratian inserted the exception “except in a charge of high treason.” [Col. 1085D] Ivo does not have this exception, *Panormia* IV, 7, 17, nor in *Decree* V, chapter 288, where the words of Dionysius to Severus, his fellow bishop, are reported. That is, letter 2 should perhaps read “to the bishop of Córdoba” instead of “to his fellow bishop,” as is apparent from the letter itself.

But Pope Stephen set out the words of this chapter more fully in letter 2, from which come *Decretum* VIII, question 11, chapter 1; Burchard I, 164; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 7, 15; and *Decree* V, 274. Anselm III, 71.

These words seem to have been altered, if the times allowed it [Note: And certainly they do allow it. MANSI.], from constitution 10 of Valentinian and the other emperors, book IX, title 1 of Justinian’s *Code*, which he reports. Gratian reports the same words in the same question, chapter 2. Contius gives the emperors’ names correctly; Demochares printed them incorrectly.

Anian has the same words in book IX, title 1, constitution 7 of the *Theodosian Code* [book IV]; in the complete book it is constitution 12. Eusebius’s letter 1 also seems to have been reported corruptly by Gratian, *Decretum* V, question 5, chapter 4: instead of *rigorosus tortor*, “a harsh torturer,” it should read *religiosus*; and instead of *corpora solvuntur*, “the bodies are released,” *corpora subjiciuntur*, “the bodies are subjected.”

[Col. 1086A] Anselm III, 26, reports the letter more fully and has *religiosus terror*, “religious terror,” and *corpora solvuntur*, “the bodies are released.” Yet, since the wording of the councils is satisfactory, I do not know whether some corruption lies hidden in Eusebius’s words. See below, chapter 64. The words of this chapter appear in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 324.

### Chapter XXXIV

If anyone brings a judge against another, etc. The first part of this chapter consists of Fabian’s words in letter 3, from which come *Decretum* II, question 6, chapter 21; Burchard, 148; Anselm II, 10, with a few alterations; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 12, 1; and *Decree* IX, chapter 261, in exactly Fabian’s words. Sixtus III, as usual, has them in his single letter, chapter 3; Anselm III, 73. Felix, older than Sixtus, together with seventy bishops, has them in letter 2, as we said above, chapter 5, final topic.

### Chapter XXXV

Cleric or layman, etc. Gratian reports these as Adrian’s words, *Decretum* XI, chapter 49; likewise Anselm III, 88, and the Veronese book. They are not unlike the words of the Council of Nicaea reported by Julius in letter 2, chapter 29, and which we wrote in chapter 8.

Add Fabian’s letter 3, from which come *Decretum* III, question 6, chapter 2; [Col. 1086B] Sixtus III, in exactly the same words, chapter 3 of his single letter; and Anselm III, 73. Damasus’s letter 3 should also be consulted, from which comes *Decretum* III, question 9, chapter 7, discussed above. This is Adrian’s chapter 4 in the Populeti book. It also appears in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 332.

### Chapter XXXVI

An appellant ought not, etc. Concerning prison, see Damasus’s letter 3; Fabian’s letter 3 and Sixtus III’s single letter, chapter 3, write the remaining material. From Fabian’s letter come Gratian, *Decretum* II, question 6, chapters 1, 7, 20, and 21; but the word *carcer*—“prison”—belongs to Damasus and Adrian, not to the others.

Burchard I, 148, does not have it, nor do Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 12, 1, and *Decree* V, chapter 261, nor Anselm II, 16. All of them derive the passage from Fabian’s letter. The same material comes from Sixtus in book III, chapter 73, and from Adrian’s decrees in chapter 88, where alone prison is mentioned.

What is said at the end concerning the appeal of one being led to execution does not seem to belong to pontifical law, but to have been taken from civil law and inserted into the letters cited above. Later I came upon Anian’s interpretation of the constitutions of the *Theodosian Code*, and found nearly all these matters there in book XI, title 8, constitutions 1, [Col. 1086C] 2, and 3 of Emperor Constantine; or, in title 30, constitutions 2 and 15 of Constantine and 20 of Constantius, in the complete book. Constitution 12 under the title *On Appeals*, book VII of Justinian’s *Code*, should also be consulted.

The words of this chapter are read in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 333; the same ruling, in different words, appears in book II, chapter 251, and in the additions, chapter 106.

### Chapters XXXVII–XXXVIII
