In criminal matters, etc. Gratian attributes this to Pope Adrian, *Decretum* V, question 3, chapter 2; Ivo to Adrian, chapter 1, book IV, title 7; *Panormia* IV, 7, chapter 4; and Anselm III, 88, from Adrian’s decrees, as stated above at the end of chapter 5. This is Adrian’s chapter 1 in the Populeti book.

### Chapter XXXIX

Constitutions contrary to the canons, etc. Gratian says that these words belong to Pope Felix, *Decretum* X, chapter 4. Burchard, however, gives them from the Council of Tribur, chapter 10, and Ivo, *Decree* V, chapter 38, from a letter of Pope Adrian delivered to Ingilramnus, bishop of the city of Metz, chapter 38. In part XVI, chapter 10, Ivo follows Burchard, although the margin says that it is from the Capitularies of Pope Adrian.

Deusdedit, part I: “Adrian to Agilram.” Elsewhere: “to Bishop Gilram”; [Col. 1086D] and in part III, “Adrian to Bishop Agilram.” The wording also differs from the others. In both places it reads:

> “Constitutions contrary to the holy decrees of the Roman prelates shall have no force.”

Anselm III, 88, from Adrian’s decrees, and the Veronese book should be consulted. See also Callistus’s letter 1, from which comes *Decretum* XI, question 3, chapter 89. Gratian and Anselm III, 86, both omit these words, which we must report:

> “No emperor, nor anyone who preserves piety, is permitted to presume to do anything contrary to the divine commands.”

Marcellinus adds in letter 2:

> “nor to do anything that deviates from the evangelical, prophetic, and apostolic rules. For judgment has been entrusted,” etc.,

as in Callistus. Symmachus uses all these words in the sixth Roman synod, from which comes *Decretum* X, chapter 2.

Burchard gives them more fully in book XV, chapter 8, from the decrees of Pope Adrian, chapter 16; but I write chapter 36. Ivo, *Panormia* II, 12, 4, gives them from Symmachus’s eighth synod, and *Decree* IV, chapter 231, from Symmachus’s sixth synod; but in part XVI, chapter 9, from the Council of Pope Adrian, chapter 16, or, as I suspect, [Col. 1087A] chapter 36.

Deusdedit, in the cited part I, says that the holy martyrs of God and the Roman pontiffs Callistus and Marcellinus, as well as Symmachus and Adrian, established the same thing with one voice; this is stated in part III. The words of these pontiffs, though not all of them, are reported at the end of this collection. See chapter 70.

Add the constitution of Valentinian and Marcian, number 12, under the title *On Sacred Churches*, book I of Justinian’s *Code*, and Damasus’s letter to Aurelius of Carthage, placed at the beginning of the councils. That letter is considered suspect by many, as are several other letters attributed to the earlier Pope Damasus.

In the Populeti book, this is Adrian’s chapter 2, in these words:

> “Constitutions contrary to the most sacred decrees of the Roman prelates shall have no force.”

Elsewhere, after the words of chapter 70:

> “Anything done contrary to evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic doctrine, or to their constitutions or those of the holy Fathers, shall in every way be quashed [or: annulled].”

The words of this chapter appear in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 346, in Adrian’s letter to Bishop Angilramnus:

> “Constitutions contrary to the [Col. 1087B] holy decrees of the Roman prelates shall have no force.”

### Chapter XL

Among the clergy, etc. Gratian reports these as the words of Pope Adrian, *Decretum* XI, question 1, chapter 50; Deusdedit, part III, attributes them to Adrian in the *Register*; Anselm III, 88, gives them from Adrian’s decrees; and they occur in two places in the Veronese book.

These also seem to have been taken from the Council of Nicaea, as Julius testifies in letter 2, chapters 6 and 34, as stated in chapter 16. The words of Zephyrinus seem originally to have been in letter 1, and those of Eusebius in letter 3, followed by Julius in the chapter just mentioned. They appear in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 347.

### Chapter XLI

Everyone who makes false accusations, etc. Gratian also reports these as Adrian’s words, *Decretum* V, question 6, chapter 1. Anselm III, 88, and the Veronese book; see chapter 22, topic 1. Add Fabian’s letter 2, from which come *Decretum* III, question 1, chapter 6, and XI, question 1, chapter 32; Anselm VII, chapter 159; Deusdedit, chapter 4.

But one must consider what it means that he is handed over to the curia, which he serves all the days of his life. For how could the curia in Fabian’s time—he lived under Maximinus and Gordian—belong to the pontiffs? [Col. 1087C] The suspicion that these words belong to another author is increased by the fact that words of Augustine are quoted in them from the *Enchiridion*, chapter 79. Yet Augustine may have used Fabian’s words without naming him.

The curia is mentioned in Stephen’s letter 2, from which comes *Decretum* III, question 4, chapter 8; in Deusdedit, chapter 4—add what is written in chapter 58—and in Pope Pius’s letter 2, from which comes *Decretum* XI, question 1, chapter 19; Anselm VIII, 17.

This is Adrian’s chapter 3 in the Populeti book. The words of this chapter are found in the *Capitularies*, book VI, chapter 277, and book VII, chapters 348 and 197.

### Chapter XLII

That the provincial synod be reconsidered, etc. This chapter is said to have belonged to the Council of Nicaea, chapter 58, as Julius reports in the letter to the bishops of the East that we have often mentioned, chapter 21. Likewise, chapter 19 of that council appears in the same Julius, chapter 2. Gratian reports its words as those of Pope Sixtus, *Decretum* III, question 6, chapter 5; they are actually from Sixtus II’s letter 1.

Burchard I, 144; from Julius’s decrees, chapter 18, the same chapter 176; from the decrees of Pope Victor, chapter 1, whose letter 1 contains the same words; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 12, 11, 2, from the statements of Pope Sixtus [Col. 1087D]; the same, *Decree* V, chapter 257, as in Burchard 144. The same ruling is gathered from the words of Pope Marcellus’s letter 1, from which comes the brief chapter 6 of Gratian, *Decretum* II, question 6. Anselm of Lucca II, 7, is excellent.

There is also a similar passage in Ennodius, on behalf of Pope Symmachus, at a Roman synod, not far from the words reported by Gratian, *Decretum* XVII, chapter 6, to which he attached Symmachus’s name. The Council of Sardica is older; from it come Greek canons 3, 4, 5, and 6, from which Gratian drew *Decretum* VI, question 3, final chapter, and II, question 6, chapter 3. In the latter place Demochares falsely gives the number as chapter 7.

Pope Zosimus testifies that these canons of the Council of Sardica belonged to the Council of Nicaea, in his letter to Faustinus and the other legates at the Council of Carthage, in which blessed Aurelius and Augustine took part. Aurelius and the other Africans report the same words in their letter to Pope Boniface.

Both letters exist in Greek and Latin. The Africans denied that they found these canons to be Nicene in their books; nor did they appear in the books of Atticus of Constantinople or Cyril of Alexandria. [Col. 1088A] Although that was true, they nevertheless had existed; they could formerly have been erased by heretics, as Julius, Felix II, and Athanasius with the Alexandrians testified.

The words of this chapter also appear in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 349, and in the additions, chapter 138.

### Chapter XLIII

Concerning those who are brought to accusation, etc. We discussed this matter at the end of chapter 15. The relevant words are in the additions to the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 139.

### Chapter XLIV

If at any time, in a capital case, etc. Gratian assigns these words to Pope Adrian, *Decretum* II, question 6, chapter 39. But it should read *per procuratores*, “through procurators,” not *per exploratores*, “through informers,” as it appears in the Antonian edition. Anselm’s book III, chapter 88, from Adrian’s decrees, has *exploratores*. The words themselves do not seem to belong to pontifical law.

We have also spoken above, more than once, of accusers being present. Some material from the Council of Chalcedon, action 1, should be added. Later I found that Anian wrote these words when he added his interpretation to Paul’s *Sentences*, book V, title 37 or 39, *On Stating the Grounds of Appeals*. [Col. 1088B] The same words appear in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 357, and in the additions, chapter 140.

### Chapter XLV

It was decided that by whomsoever, etc. These are the words of the Council of Nicaea, chapter 60, as Julius testifies in chapter 22 of the cited letter to the Eastern bishops. Gratian reports them in *Decretum* II, question 6, chapter 9. Nearly the same words occur in the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 10; in Greek, chapter 15 of the Council of Carthage.

Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 12, 9; *Decree* VI, 363; Anselm, as usual, III, 88, from Adrian’s decrees. A similar ruling appears in Pope Cornelius’s letter 2, not far from the words reported by Gratian, *Decretum* III, question 9, chapter 4; Anselm III, 57. But these same words belong to Pope Lucius, in his single letter to the bishops of Gaul and Spain.

Pope Nicholas’s letter to Emperor Michael should be consulted. From it several chapters appear in Gratian, *Decretum* XXI, chapters 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9; the words relevant here are in chapter 8, although not reported in full.

The words of this chapter, with a few exceptions, are reported in the *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 250, book VII, chapter 121, and the additions, chapter 14.

### Chapter XLVI

If any metropolitan bishop, etc. [Col. 1088C] These too are from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 6, as Julius testifies above, chapter 23.

An ancient chapter on this matter is found among the Greek canons as chapter 34 and among the Latin canons of the Apostles as chapter 35. It seems to have been renewed by chapter 9 of the Council of Antioch, from which comes *Decretum* IX, question 3, chapter 2. Martin of Braga also included its words in chapter 4, and Gratian, in the same question, chapter 1, from the council of Pope Martin.

Add Pope Hyginus’s letter 1, from which comes chapter 4 of the same question; Burchard I, 65; Ivo, *Decree* V, 174, from Callistus to the bishops of Gaul. Anicetus writes more clearly to the bishops of Gaul on the same matter. Gratian reports his words in the same question, chapters 5 and 6; Burchard I, 63; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 4, 1, and *Decree* V, 54.

Callistus’s letter 2 treats the matter more fully, from which comes *Decretum* IX, question 3, chapter 7; more fully in Burchard I, 66; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 42, and *Decree* V, chapters 100 and 101.

Pope Lucius has almost the same words, addressed to the bishops of Spain and Gaul. See above, chapter 14; we say the same thing in both places, as the pontiffs themselves often do. The words of this chapter appear in book VII, chapter 358, [Col. 1088D] and in the additions, chapter 142.

### Chapter XLVII

As for laymen, etc. These words are from the First Council of Carthage, chapter 13, and from the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapters 16 and 359: Pope Adrian to Bishop Ingelramnus.

### Chapter XLVIII

That laymen who despise the canons, etc. These words are the heading of chapter 14 of the First Council of Carthage. Adrian’s chapter 5 in the Populeti book consists of these words. It may not incorrectly be Adrian’s chapter 45.

### Chapter XLIX

Let the informer’s tongue be cut out, etc. Gratian, *Decretum* V, question 6, chapter 5, from Adrian’s decree. Anselm III, chapter 88, does the same. But it was not Adrian’s role to decree this; rather, he reported what had been written in the *Theodosian Code*, or more precisely in the epitome of the constitutions of Emperor Constantine, book X, title 1, constitution 1, which in the complete book is constitution 2, title 10.

This is Adrian’s chapter 6 in the Populeti book, and it appears in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 360.

### Chapter L

Whoever attacks another’s reputation, etc. Gratian attributes this to Pope Adrian, *Decretum* V, question 1, chapter 1, and Anselm III, 88. [Col. 1089A] To me this too does not seem to derive from pontifical law. See below, chapter 59.

Later I found that Ivo, *Decree* XVI, chapter 235, mixed this ruling with others taken from the *Capitularies*—the book in which the constitutions or laws of the Frankish kings, such as Pippin, Charles, Louis, and others, were written. Later they were divided into titles and books, as in the collection of Lombard laws: in the *Capitularies* only chronological order was observed, whereas in the later collections the material was distinguished by subject.

This is Adrian’s chapter 7 in the Populeti book. But in Ivo, *Decree* IV, chapter 49, it is Adrian’s chapter 49 to Ingelram. It appears in the *Capitularies* of Benedict the Levite and in Ansegisus, book VII.

### Chapter LI

If anyone, being angry, brings a charge, etc. These are Fabian’s words in letter 3, from which come *Decretum* II, question 3, chapter 5, and *On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter 22, from the canons; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 7, 21, and *Decree* VI, 324; Anselm III, 79.

Sixtus III has the same words, as usual, in chapter 3 of his single letter. I find the same words in Anian’s edition or collection as an interpretation of constitution 3 of Emperor Constantine, book IX, title 1 of the *Theodosian Code*. These are Anian’s words. Under Alaric, king of the Goths, the constitution had previously been number 5.

Fabian lived much earlier than Constantine, since he lived under Maximinus and Gordian the African. Sixtus III lived in the time of Emperor Valentinian. These same words appear in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 364.

### Chapter LII

Let the one who brings a charge write, etc. Gratian reports these words corruptly, *Decretum* III, question 6, final chapter, from the decree of Pope Adrian. Instead of *sciat*, “let him know,” it should read *scribat*, “let him write.”

They are Fabian’s words in the cited letter 3, from which come *Decretum* II, question 9, chapter 4; III, question 6, chapter 1; and II, question 3, chapter 3. But chapter 3 is said to come from Adrian’s decree, chapter 1 from Fabian, and chapter 4 from Pope Sixtus. It is also true that the words of Sixtus III are in chapter 4 [Col. 1089B] of his single letter, under the cited distinction.

Burchard XVI, chapter 3, from the Council of Orange, chapter 4; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 7, 21, from Fabian. See chapter 7.

We should add Hincmar’s response at the synod, [Col. 1089C] written at the synod held at Saint Medard. From it come Gregory IX, chapter 1, *On the Presentation of a Written Charge*, and Gratian, *Decretum* II, question 1, chapter 9. In both places Hincmar’s name is incorrectly given, and Gratian says that it is chapter 8 of that council.

Burchard II, chapter 197, chapter 9; Ivo, *Decree* VI, chapter 269, chapter 8; Bernard of Pavia, book II, title 3, chapter 1, collection 1 of the *Decree*, does not add a number. The words of this chapter are in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 365.

### Chapter LIII

Let the judges of the Church beware, etc. Julius reports that these are the words of the Council of Nicaea, letter 2, chapter 24. Formerly they belonged to Pope Eleutherius, in a letter sent to the churches of Gaul, from which comes *Decretum* III, question 9, chapter 2.

Burchard XVI, chapter 14, gives them from Adrian’s decrees, chapter 4; Ivo, *Decree* VI, chapter 319, from Eleutherius. Likewise Anselm III, chapter 28. Although in chapter 88, from Adrian’s decrees, Pope Felix uses exactly the same words in letter 1 after the Council of Nicaea.

The same words occur in chapter 30 of the Fourth Council of Carthage, and in the *Capitularies*, book VI, chapter 279, and book VII, chapter 219.

### [Col. 1089D] Chapter LIV

Concerning one who frequently litigates, etc. Felix II has this in his letter to Athanasius and the Alexandrians, chapter 14, from which comes Gratian, *Decretum* III, question 5, chapter 11. Anselm III, chapter 62, both attribute these words to Pope Felix, but Anselm, chapter 88, attributes them to Adrian.

Add chapter 58 of the Fourth Council of Carthage; Clement, book II, from which comes *Decretum* III, question 5, chapter 4; Anselm IV, 16; and Pope Julius, letter 2, chapter 33, who testifies that this comes from the Nicene synod. From that letter come *Decretum* III, question 5, chapter 10, and Anselm III, 21.

This is Adrian’s chapter 8 in the Populeti book.

### Chapter LV

On the accusations of bishops: Constantine, etc. Some of this is from the *Tripartite History*, and some from Rufinus’s words in book X, chapter 2 of the *Ecclesiastical History*. Epiphanius Scholasticus, *Tripartite History* II, chapter 2, took it from Sozomen, book I, chapter 16.

Deusdedit, chapter 3, reports nearly the same words from the *Ecclesiastical History*. Gratian reports them briefly at the end of *Decretum* XI, question 1, chapter 5. Likewise blessed Gregory, *Register* IV, chapter 75, from which comes *Decretum* XI, question 1, chapter 42.

Add the Parisian council, book III, [Col. 1090A] chapter 8, and the *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 163, and book VII, chapter 441.

### Chapter LVI

Nor should the supreme prelate, etc. An ancient synod exists against Pope Marcellinus, later a glorious martyr. In it, three hundred bishops said:

> “No one shall ever judge the pontiff, nor shall a prelate judge his own priest, because the First See is judged by no one.”

Pope Nicholas recounts this in letter 8 to Emperor Michael, from which come *Decretum*, distinction 21, chapter 7; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 1, 6; and *Decree* V, 8.

Soon afterward there was another synod in the time of Pope Sylvester, whose final chapter reads:

> “No one shall judge—or adjudicate—the First See,” etc.

From it comes *Decretum* IX, question 3, chapter 13, under the name of Innocent; it was printed corruptly under the names of both pontiffs. Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 1, 5, attributes it to Sylvester; Anselm I, 19, more correctly IV, 39. Deusdedit, chapter 3, correctly says that these words of Adrian belong to Sylvester, at the council of 277 bishops, and from the same source reports the words of chapter 3 in a less corrupt form. They are Sylvester’s words at the Roman synod.

A third synod occurred in the time of Sixtus III. The former consul Maximus said:

> “It is not permitted [Col. 1090B] to pronounce judgment against the pontiff.”

On another day Bishop Sixtus said:

> “A servant is not above his master, nor a disciple above his teacher.”

The same Nicholas, cited above, also mentions this matter. A letter of Sixtus exists on the subject, in which he says that he had cleared himself at the synod, not because he was compelled:

> “and let no one receive accusations against a teacher.”

From this letter comes *Decretum* II, question 4, chapter 10.

The fourth synod concerned Pope Symmachus; it was the fourth Roman synod, or session. Gratian reports some material from it in *Decretum*, distinction 17, chapter 6, topic 1, including a passage of Ennodius, Symmachus’s defender, recited at the Roman synod. The same ruling also appears in Gratian, *Decretum* IX, question 3, chapter 14, under Symmachus’s name.

Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 1, 7, from Symmachus’s fifth synod; and *Decree* V, chapter 10. Gelasius was earlier than Symmachus and was a most vigorous defender of the Apostolic See, and not ineloquent, as the times permitted. In his letter to Faustus he defends the same ruling; Gratian reports his words in *Decretum* III, question 3, chapter 16.

In chapter 10, Gratian reports the words of Nicholas’s letter to Michael, in which the [Col. 1090C] same words of Gelasius are praised. In this chapter 10, “Boniface” should be written instead of “Innocent,” as is clear from the books of the councils and from Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 1, 10, and *Decree* V, 19. Anselm I, chapters 47 and 48; and, from various letters, the same author, book II, chapters 16 and 24, and more fully book XII, chapter 69.

### Chapter LVII

When a judge examines a criminal, etc. This is the ruling of the Council of Nicaea, as Julius testifies in the frequently cited letter, chapter 26.

Earlier, these were the words of Zephyrinus in letter 1 and of Pope Felix in letter 1, from which comes *Decretum* II, question 4, chapter 5. Burchard I, chapter 154, gives them from Zephyrinus; Anselm III, chapter 65, from Felix; chapter 66, from Zephyrinus; and chapter 88, from Adrian’s decrees.

The same is derived from the letter of Stephen and the African synod to Pope Damasus. Add Sixtus II’s letter, chapter 4. These are also Anian’s words in book IX, title 30, constitution 1 of the *Theodosian Code*, or title 40 in the complete book.

It is remarkable that Anian’s words and the constitution of Emperor Constantine should be used [Col. 1090D] by earlier pontiffs. It is constitution 16, book IX, title 47, also in Justinian. Gratian reports this as Constantine’s wording, *Decretum* II, question 1, chapter 2; Burchard XVI, chapter 6, from Adrian’s decrees, chapter 2—perhaps chapter 52; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 11, 4, from Constantine; Anselm III, 77, to Bishop Augustine.

This is Adrian’s chapter 9 in the Populeti book. It appears in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 170, and book V, chapter 156.

### Chapter LVIII

That an unjust judgment is invalid, etc. These words also belong to the Nicene synod, as Julius testifies, chapter 27, and to the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 28. From the latter comes *Decretum* XI, question 3, chapter 25. The same words also occur in exactly this form in Felix’s letter 1, from which comes *Decretum* III, question 6, chapter 11.

### Chapter LIX

So that no one, while in it, etc. I have not yet read these exact words. But there is a letter of Gregory to Bishop Boniface in which it is written that, if a pestilential disease or epidemic has entered a church or monastery, those whom it has not yet touched ought not to flee from the place.

A large part of this is reported in the councils as Gregory I’s letter to Augustine, and in the same councils as Gregory [Col. 1091A] III’s letter to Boniface. Evaristus’s letter 2 also exists, in which it is said that a church must not be abandoned without unavoidable necessity. From it comes *Decretum* VII, question 1, chapter 11; more fully Burchard I, 76; Ivo, *Decree* V, chapters 182 and 201; Anselm VI, 102.

Damasus’s letter 4 is an excellent one against bishops who entrust their sheep to hirelings, as prostitutes entrust their children to foreign nurses. There is also the Council of Valencia, chapter 3, against wandering clerics, and the Council of Mainz, chapter 22, taken, unless I am mistaken, from Isidore, who calls such men “hippocentaurs” in book II, chapter 3 of *The Offices*. This is written corruptly in the books of the councils. The Council of Tribur also mentions Isidore, chapter 27.

Finally, add chapter 16 of the Nicene synod, from which comes *Decretum* VII, question 1, chapter 23, which Gratian says is from the Fifth Council of Carthage. Burchard correctly gives it in book II, chapter 98; Ivo, *Decree* VI, chapter 175; and Anselm VII, 95.

The Council of Aachen, chapter 45, reports the words of the Nicene chapter. Martin of Braga published the same matter in different words, chapter 34. [Col. 1091B] Add the Council of Tarragona, chapter 11; the Second Council of Seville, chapter 3; the Council of Vernum, chapters 12 and 13; and the Second Council of Nicaea, chapter 10 (see below, chapter 66).

In Cresconius, chapter 16, we read these words: “That clerics should not abandon their own churches.” They also occur in the Apostolic Canons, titles 15 and 16; in the Council of Chalcedon, title 2; Antioch, title 3; the decrees of Pope Leo, title 38; Gelasius, title 23; and the Council of Carthage, titles 21 and 22.

Later I found the words of this chapter in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 366.

### Chapter LX

When summoned before his judge, etc. These are the words of Pope Fabian, letter 3, from which come *Decretum* III, question 6, chapter 3; Burchard XVI, chapter 10, from the decrees of Eusebius, chapter 20; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 12, 1, at the end, from Fabian; and *Decree* VI, 323.

Sixtus III has them in exactly the same words, chapter 3 of his letter to the Eastern bishops; Anselm III, 73. This matter had often been discussed. These words appear in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 367.

And when he brings an accusation, etc. Concerning adjournments, besides Fabian and Sixtus, see Eleutherius’s letter 1, from which comes *Decretum* III, question 3, chapter 3; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 9, 3; and *Decree* VI, 326.

Pope Caius, in his letter to Bishop Felix—a large part of which appears in Leo’s letter to Emperor Leo—writes close to the words reported by Gratian, *Decretum* III, question 1, chapter 1. Likewise Pope Marcellus, letter 2; Felix II, letter 1, chapters 8 and 20, from which come *Decretum* III, question 2, chapter 7, and chapters 1 and 2; Burchard I, chapter 180; Ivo IV, 8, 14, and IV, 9, 2, *Panormia*; and *Decree* V, 296.

Finally, Damasus’s letter 3 should be consulted, from which come *Decretum* III, question 1, chapter 4, and III, question 9, chapters 6 and 7; Ivo, *Panormia* IV, 1, and *Decree* V, 287, and VI, 347.

### Chapter LXI

If anyone acts against his profession, etc. These words seem to come from the Second Council of Carthage, final chapter. I find no mention of laymen there, nor in the Greek words of the Council of Carthage, chapter 13, nor in the old Latin book of Maffei, chapter 12.

Anselm IV, 88, added this ruling from the Council of Carthage, since the earlier and later material carried the heading “from the decrees of Pope Adrian.” This is Adrian’s chapter 16 in the Populeti book. See the [Col. 1091D] *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 158.

### Chapter LXII

If any of the bishops, etc. These words are from the Council of Elvira, chapter 75. See also Arles I, chapter 14, and Arles II, chapter 24, from which comes *Decretum* III, question 10, chapter 2. Gratian falsely calls it Arles III.

There it is said that this decree belongs to the Great Synod, which we understand to mean Nicaea. Add the Second Council of Braga, chapter 8, from which comes *Decretum* II, question 4, chapter 2; Burchard II, 202; and Sixtus III’s single letter, chapter 1, in which he relates that Bassus, Sixtus’s accuser, was condemned, although a viaticum was not denied to him when dying, out of mercy.

See also above, chapter 40. Clement, *Apostolic Constitutions* II, chapters 46 and 47, should be consulted. This is Adrian’s chapter 10 in the Populeti book.

### Chapter LXIII

If some are found, etc. The Council of Elvira, chapter 52, has this in different but not very dissimilar words, from which comes *Decretum* V, question 1, final chapter.

Ivo, *Decree* IV, chapter 154, from Adrian’s letter delivered to Ingilramnus, chapter 62:

> “If any are found reading notorious [Col. 1092A] books, let them be excommunicated.”

Anselm III, chapter 88, from Pope Adrian’s decrees, reports the same words that are published in the councils. The Veronese book, after some other material of Adrian’s, reads:

> “If any are found reading or singing notorious and unknown books in the church, let them be excommunicated.”

See above, chapter 48. This is Adrian’s chapter 11 in the Populeti book. The words of this chapter are reported in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 368.

### Chapter LXIV

That no bishop, or anyone below him, etc. Gratian reports these words as belonging to Pope Adrian, *Decretum* XV, question 4, final chapter. The same ruling was established by many provincial councils.

The words themselves are the title of the First Council of Tarragona, chapter 4, from which comes chapter 1 of the same question. Gratian adds another chapter, “from the council held at Ephesus in the presence of King Henry,” but *Ephesus* is corrupt. Burchard, book XIII, chapter 21, has *Esphesfurt*, the council attended by King Henry, chapter 2.

Ivo, *Decree* IV, chapter 53, has “the council held at Esphort by order of King Henry,” chapter 1. Elsewhere Burchard, book XIII, chapters 27 and 28, uses the same name, *Ersphesfurt*, and book XI, [Col. 1092B] chapter 77. Ivo likewise has *Erphot* in part XIV, chapter 125, although in part IV, chapter 59, he writes *Erphot*. The name itself is barbarous; let us write it as Burchard does. The town is mentioned in Pope Zacharias’s letter 6.

The same ruling occurs in the Second Council of Mâcon, chapter 1, at the end of which council there is an edict of King Guntram on the same matter; likewise Arles IV under Charles, chapter 16; Tours III under the same king, chapter 40; Mainz or Moguntiacum under the same king, chapter 37; and Rheims under the same king, chapter 35.

Finally, after the Sixth Ecumenical Council, in the collection of an unknown council, chapter 8, from the book of Ghent. This council seems to me to have been provincial and not much older than those mentioned above.

This is Adrian’s chapter 12 in the Populeti book, in these words:

> “No bishop, abbot, or provost below them shall presume to conduct secular cases on Sunday.”

### Chapter LXV

That if any powerful person, etc. This is taken from the heading of chapter 11 of the First Council of Toledo, from which comes *Decretum* XXIV, question 3, chapter 1. [Col. 1092C] Anselm, book VII, chapter 16, says that the *Capitularies* also report these words. The Fourteenth Council of Mâcon has a similar chapter.

This is Adrian’s chapter 13 in the Populeti book.

### Chapter LXVI

That no cleric should be removed by his bishop, etc. These words are taken from the heading of chapter 42 of the First Council of Toledo. On the same matter, see the Apostolic Canons, chapter 15. A similar provision occurs in the Council of Antioch, chapter 3, from which comes *Decretum* VII, question 1, chapter 24; Anselm VII, 195.

Clement, author of the Apostolic Canons, has it in letter 1. Burchard II, 94, and Ivo, *Decree* VI, 131, report some of his words. The same Clement, at the beginning of letter 3, gives the source of *Decretum* XI, question 3, chapter 11. The Council of Tribur reports more words, chapter 9; later *Decretum* XVI, question 1, chapter 41, is taken from the same letter; Burchard II, 93; Ivo, *Decree* II, 123; Council of Tribur, chapter 32.

Add Pope Pius’s letter 2, at the end of which comes *Decretum* XI, question 1, chapter 19; Anselm VIII, 17. Anterus should also be consulted in his letter to the bishops of Baetica and the province of Toledo, although the name “province of Toledo” is suspect, since in those times [Col. 1092D] Toledo was a less distinguished town. *Decretum* XI, question 3, chapter 14, is taken from that letter.

Finally, see the Council of Agde, chapter 2, from which comes distinction 50, chapter 21; Ivo, *Decree* VI, 366. Add chapter 5 of the English Council held at Hertford (see chapter 57).

This is Adrian’s chapter 14 in the Populeti book.

### Chapter LXVII

Murderers, sorcerers, thieves, etc. These are the words of Eusebius, letter 3, from which comes *Decretum* III, question 5, chapter 9. Burchard XVI, chapter 4, gives them from the council held at Theodonis Villa, chapter 3; Anselm III, 19, from Eusebius.

Pope Eutychianus writes the same in letter 2, from which comes *Decretum* II, question 8, chapter 3. Ivo gives it more fully in *Decree* VI, chapters 332 and 333. Felix II reports the same words in letter 1, chapter 15, and Pelagius II part of them in letter 3.

Clement’s letter 1 to James of Jerusalem is older—not “to the metropolitan,” as Gratian says, *Decretum* VI, question 1, chapter 5. Anselm III, chapter 1, should be consulted.

As for the controversy among some people concerning that letter, we leave the matter uncertain. We know that it is ancient and that much [Col. 1093A] has been reported from it by others; meanwhile, since it has not been rejected by the Roman See, we do not reject it.

There are nevertheless some passages in Clement’s letter that seem to have been added by others from Clement’s books of the *Recognitions*. We do not find these books cited or accepted by the ancient Fathers; rather, like the Apostolic Canons and Clement’s *Itinerary*, they are marked by Gelasius and the Roman synod, and by Gratian, *Decretum* XV, chapter 3.

As for this chapter, however, see what has often been said above, especially at the end of chapter 15. Later we came upon chapter 37 of part X of Ivo’s *Decree*, which says that these words come from Adrian’s letter delivered to Ingilramnus, bishop of the city of Metz—“I write *Mediomatricum*”—chapter 66.

If I had read the wording of canon 63, I would have been more pleased; but let us accept it as though it were written thus, for it is like a five-foot inscription. This is Adrian’s chapter 15 in the Populeti book. This chapter also appears in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 369.

[Col. 1093B] **CHAPTER LXVIII. “He who brings an accusation,” etc.** Gratian reports these as the words of Hadrian, VI, question 1, chapter 6, and joins to them certain words of Pope Sylvester, about which we spoke in chapter 68. Concerning this sentence, see chapter 6 of the Greek text of the Council of Constantinople, and above, chapter 31.

**CHAPTER LXIX. “Let every one of the faithful come forward,” etc.** Anselm, book III, chapter 88, took these words from the decrees of Hadrian, as he commonly does. But they are found in chapter 5 of Sixtus III’s letter to the bishops of the East; before him, in Fabian’s third letter; in chapter 2 of the fifth Council of Toledo; and in the *Capitularies*, book VI, chapter 250, and book VII, chapter 221.

“For he offers to the Lord,” etc. Gratian says, Distinction 86, chapter 3, that this, together with other statements, belongs to John VIII; and Ivo, part VI, chapter 185 of the *Decree*, attributes it to John VIII’s letter to the emperor Louis. He added certain words reported by Gratian, Distinction 10, chapter 10, from John’s seventh letter to the same Louis. But Ivo, part IV, chapter 230, has it as chapter 115.

The same Gratian and John preserve other words—“when you are able, to neglect,” etc.—which Gratian reports as belonging to Innocent, Distinction 83, chapter 3, and Deusdedit, chapter 2. Elsewhere, however, Gratian says that they belong to Anastasius and Damasus, XXIII, question 3, chapter 8. Damasus’s third letter does indeed exist, and at its conclusion are the words reported by Gratian.

Likewise, “he offers to the Lord,” etc., occurs in Anselm, book XIII, chapter 19, as in Gratian, Distinction, chapter 8. But the words “when you are able, to neglect,” etc., belong to Pope Eleutherius, at the end of his letter to the Churches of Gaul. Innocent III repeats almost the same material in the general Council of the Lateran, at the final chapter. As for the words “For he offers to the Lord,” etc., they are said to belong to chapter 2 of the eighth Council of Toledo and to the *Capitularies*, at the chapters mentioned above, 250 and 221.

**CHAPTER LXX. “There is greater danger,” etc.** We do not know where these words occur, except in Anselm III, 88, and in the books of the Councils. At last I found them in book VII, chapter 272.

**CHAPTER LXXI. “Accusations against a teacher,” etc.** Felix II, in his letter to Athanasius and the Alexandrian synod at the beginning of the Council of Nicaea, reports the words cited by Gratian, VI, question 1, chapter 12. The same Felix repeats them in chapter 20 of that letter; they are also found in Burchard, book I, chapter 180, and Ivo, part V, chapter 296 of the *Decree*.

Anacletus discusses the same matter at length in letters 1 and 2; from the second comes II, question 7, chapter 15, and the final chapter of Distinction 79. See also Ivo IV, 7, 6, *Panormia*, and part V, chapter 238 of the *Decree*; Anselm III, 32; Deusdedit, chapter 4.

The same Anacletus, in his third letter, from which come VI, question 1, chapter 15, and II, question 7, chapter 12, is cited by Anselm III, 11 and 3, and Deusdedit, chapter 3. Pius’s first letter is the source of VI, question 1, chapter 9; see also Ivo IV, 5, 7, *Panormia*, and V, 243 of the *Decree*.

Let us add these words of Sixtus III, sole letter, chapter 1: “Let no one receive accusations against a teacher” (see above, chapter 56). These words belong to Callistus, letter 1; Burchard I, 135; and Ivo V, 234 of the *Decree*. This passage also exists in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 67.

**CHAPTER LXXII. “A presbyter must not proceed against a bishop,” etc.** These are the words of Pope Sylvester at a Roman council of many bishops, chapter 3; from it come II, question 7, chapter 10; Burchard, book I, 151; Ivo, part V, chapter 264 of the *Decree*; and IV, 8, 7 of the *Panormia*. Pope Nicholas repeats the same passage in his long letter to the emperor Michael, as does chapter 12 of the second Council of Mainz under Arnulf. The *Capitularies*, book I, chapter 139, use the same words with a few additions.

“And a prelate shall not be condemned except on the testimony of witnesses,” etc. Gratian reports this in II, question 4, chapter 2; Burchard I, 151; Ivo IV, 8, 7, *Panormia*, and V, 264, and VI, 334, of the *Decree*. Deusdedit, chapter 3, does likewise.

Zephyrinus had earlier established this rule for all bishops in his first letter, from which comes chapter 154 of Burchard, book I. It was observed against Pope Marcellinus at the Council held at Sinuessa. They called that number of witnesses a *libra*, perhaps because it consisted of as many gold coins as were then marked according to the weight of a *sextula*; a *sextula* is one-sixth of an ounce. I later found the same words in chapter 12 of the Council of Mainz under Arnulf, in the *Capitularies*, chapter 139.

“Nor may the supreme prelate,” etc. We discussed these words in chapters 56 and 71. Nicholas also reports them in his letter to the emperor Michael. They are likewise found in chapter 12 of the Council of Mainz under Arnulf and in the *Capitularies*, chapter 139.

“A presbyter, or a cardinal,” etc. There is considerable variation in the number of witnesses, and also in some of the other words. What is here “established among the cardinals,” some copies read “the cardinals,” while others omit both words. Likewise, for “a cardinal deacon,” some write “the cardinals,” while others omit the expression.

The name was applied to the leading or principal men of the whole city—whether presbyters or deacons—even outside the city of Rome. See Gratian, Distinction, chapter 2; Ivo IV, 8, 7, *Panormia*, and VI, 334 of the *Decree*. Add chapter 34 of the Council of Meaux, and see Leo IX’s letter to Michael of Constantinople, 312, where the reason is given why the Romans are so called. These words are also found in the cited chapter 12 of the Council of Mainz under Arnulf and in the *Capitularies*.

“But witnesses without any,” etc. I do not see why he omitted “and accusers,” although some copies do not contain those words. Gratian reports them in the cited chapter of the Distinction as belonging to Sylvester at the synod, and in VI, question 1, chapter 6, as belonging to Pope Hadrian, after the words of chapter 64. Ivo, in the place mentioned above, attributes them to Sylvester.

Concerning the same matter, see Felix II’s letter to Athanasius and the others, chapter 5. These same words are found in chapter 12 of the Council of Mainz and, with a few alterations, in the *Capitularies*.

[Col. 1094C] **CHAPTER LXXIII. “The testimony of a layman,” etc.** The accusation could also have been joined to this, since Sylvester established in the same synod: “Let no layman dare to bring a charge against a cleric.” Gratian reports this in II, question 7, chapter 7; the emperor Louis, book II, title 51, concerning witnesses; chapter 12 of the Lombards, in different words; Burchard, book I, chapter 151; Ivo IV, 8, 7, *Panormia*, and V, 264 of the *Decree*; and Anselm III, 25.

Damasus joined accusation to testimony in his *Life of Sylvester*, as Gratian reports. The same Gratian, XI, question 1, chapter 9, reports these words in a disturbed order: “Let no one receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman.” Ivo, IV, 8, 6, *Panormia*, likewise reports Gratian’s words concerning accusation and these same words in a confused order, as does Anselm in the Roman council, chapter 14. In three editions, this variation is noted in the epilogue or epitome.

Gratian’s text seems corrupt to me. For in that synod there is no concern with laymen as defendants; the whole discussion concerns judgment in cases involving clerical defendants.

Bernard of Pavia, book II, title 13, concerning witnesses and attestations, chapter 1 of collection 1 of the decretals, gives the rule as it appears in the Councils: “Let no one accept the testimony of a layman against a cleric,” from the Council of Tribur.

On the same matter, read the sole letter of Telesphorus to all the bishops, from which comes VI, question 1, chapter 8; Ivo VI, 314 of the *Decree*; and Anselm, more fully, book III, chapter 13.

Fabian’s second letter contains both points: that laymen are customarily excluded from accusing clerics, etc. From it comes II, question 7, chapter 6; see Ivo IV, 7, 9, *Panormia*, and VI, 320 of the *Decree*.

On the same matter, Pope Stephen’s second letter is the source of Gregory IX, chapter 7, concerning accusations. The words “and all laymen,” which Bernard of Pavia had omitted in book V, title 1, chapter 7 of collection 1, are omitted there. Stephen added the reason: “Nor are those to be admitted to accuse you who do not wish to admit you in their own case.”

Add Marcellinus’s second letter, from which comes II, question 7, chapter 3. It is incorrectly inscribed “to Marcellus”; nevertheless, the second letter of Marcellus establishes the same rule in different words.

Finally, Eusebius, Marcellus’s successor, made an excellent ruling on the same matter in his first letter, at the beginning, from which comes chapter 5 of Gratian’s question, and Anselm’s fuller treatment in book III, chapter 26. I believe the words reported by Gratian in Anacletus’s chapter 14 of that question belong to Eusebius, although Demochares assigned them otherwise in the margin of that chapter.

Chapter 24 of the Council of Epaon seems contrary to all these passages, unless it is correctly understood: “We permit laymen to have the power of bringing charges against a cleric of any rank,” etc.

Although many of the passages cited above remember accusation, and only a few testimony, the rule is that one who is excluded from accusing is not to be admitted as a witness. Thus in chapter 4 of the seventh Council of Carthage—which is the African council, chapter 98 in the Latin numbering and 132 or 151 in the Greek numbering—comes chapter 1 of Gratian IV, questions 2 and 3; Burchard, book XVI, chapter 20, from the Council of Tribur, chapter 5; and Ivo IV, 8, 1, from the Council of Carthage. Pope Nicholas gives the correct version in part VI, chapter 364 of the *Decree*.

**CHAPTER LXXIV. “For no one may accuse a cleric,” etc.** This comes from the same synod of Sylvester, chapter 15; Gratian, Distinction, chapters 9 and 11, question 1; Ivo IV, 8, 6, *Panormia*; Anselm V, 23; and Damasus in his *Life of Sylvester*, as well as in his *Life of Julius*. To both men he attributes this decree, with a few alterations. But a much older version exists in the first letter of Pope Alexander, from which comes XI, question 1, chapter 15.

**CHAPTER LXXV. “The bishops to the pontiff from whom,” etc.** These words belong to Pope Marcellinus, letter 2. The synod against Polychronius of Jerusalem in the time of Pope Sylvester should be consulted; Pope Nicholas also relates it in his long letter to the emperor Michael.

**CHAPTER LXXVI. “It is not lawful for an emperor,” etc.** These words occur at the end of Pope Callistus’s first letter, at the end of Pope Marcellinus’s second letter, and in Pope Symmachus at the Roman synod, session 6, from which comes Distinction 10, chapter 2.

Burchard, book XV, chapter 8, from the decrees of Pope Hadrian, chapter 16; Ivo II, 12, 4, *Panormia*, from the eighth synod of Symmachus; and part IV, chapter 231 of the *Decree*, from the sixth synod of Symmachus, cite them. But part XVI, chapter 9, cites them from the Council of Pope Hadrian, chapter 16.

There is variation between the words of Hadrian as reported by Burchard and Ivo and those which we are discussing, as they are read in the Councils. Anselm, book III, chapter 88, from the decrees of Pope Hadrian, reports the same words as are found in the Councils. Deusdedit, chapters 1 and 3, reports the words of Callistus, Marcellinus, Symmachus, and Hadrian as do Burchard and Ivo. See chapter 37.

From the book of Populetus: Pope Hadrian—“It is not lawful,” etc.—“to presume against the commands of God, or to act by opposing them.” The words of this chapter are found in the *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 218.

**CHAPTER LXXVII. “Care must be taken lest in any respect,” etc.** These words are read only in the Councils and in Anselm, book III, chapter 88; they are not in the book of Populetus.

**CHAPTER LXXVIII. “An unjust judgment and decree,” etc.** All cite these words: Callistus, Marcellinus, Symmachus, and Burchard, as well as Ivo, part XVI, chapter 9 of the *Decree*. Gratian, XI, question 3, chapter 89, cites them from Callistus; Deusdedit, chapters 1 and 3; Anselm, book III, chapter 86, from Callistus, and chapter 88, from Hadrian. They occur in the book of Populetus as words of Pope Hadrian. They also appear in the *Capitularies*, the cited book V, chapter 251.

**CHAPTER LXXIX. “Thus God hates those who arm themselves against the Fathers,” etc.** These words belong to Pope Alexander’s first letter, to Pope Stephen’s second letter near its end, and to Eusebius’s first letter not far from its beginning. The same opinion is found in chapter 41 of the Council of Nicaea, as Pope Julius reports in his second letter, chapter 10.

Add Pope Telesphorus’s letter to all the bishops, from which comes VI, question 1, chapter 8; Ivo VI, 314 and 315 of the *Decree*; Anselm III, 13; and Fabian’s second letter on the same matter. Only Deusdedit, chapter 3, reports these as the words of Hadrian, and Anselm, III, 88, does likewise.

Stephen, mentioned above, also treats the subject in his first letter, from which comes VII, question 6, chapter 17; Burchard I, 173; Ivo IV, 7, 14, *Panormia*, and V, 291 of the *Decree*; Anselm III, 5.

Finally, Pelagius II, in his first letter, near the end, uses almost the same words in chapter 17: “He who has a judge’s herald as his accuser must not prosecute anything.” These words are found in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 374.

**CHAPTER LXXX. “Likewise, by a general decree we establish,” etc.** Gratian, LXXV, question 1, chapter 11, says that this belongs to Pope Hadrian, and adds, on his own authority, after the word “kings,” the words “and bishops.” Anselm, book III, chapter 88, does not have them, nor does book IV, chapter 40, where he says that this is chapter 48 from the decrees of Pope Hadrian.

Nevertheless, in book XVII, concerning excommunication—which for others is book XI—chapter 2, Anselm does have the words “and bishops.” Deusdedit, chapter 1, from Hadrian’s letter to Bishop Gilram, chapter 48 [perhaps 68], does not have them; neither chapters 3 and 4 from Hadrian to Bishop Agilram; nor the book of Verona, in which the letter is from Hadrian to Bishop Gelianus.

This is chapter 18 of Hadrian in the book of Populetus. With the words “By a general decree,” etc.: “Whoever henceforth, whether king, bishop, or powerful person, shall believe or permit the censure of the decrees of the Roman pontiffs to be violated in any way.” But in the *Capitularies*, book VI, chapter 249, the form of this constitution is: “Let it be observed as something accursed,” etc.

Likewise, Pope Hadrian: “By a general decree,” etc.; “of kings or bishops,” etc.

This is the end of the collection published under the name of Hadrian, in which some order and method are lacking. The matters themselves, however, are almost all excellent and were established by the ancient Fathers, so that there might be some regulation and conclusion to lawsuits and accusations.

[Col. 1096]

## OBSERVATION OF FATHER ANTONIUS PAGI

### For the year of Christ 786, §§ 3 and 4

In the Venetian edition of the Councils, eighty canons of Pope Hadrian are presented under this title:

“These chapters have been collected here and there from Greek and Latin canons and Roman synods, as well as from the decrees of Roman prelates and princes, and were delivered at Rome by the blessed Pope Hadrian to Ingilramnus, bishop of the city of Mediomatricum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the eleventh indiction, when proceedings were being conducted on account of his own case.”

The same statement appears in the later editions of the Councils, except that instead of the eleventh indiction they read the ninth, which Baronius retained. For that reason he incorrectly treated the matter as belonging to the current year, since the tenth indiction began in September.

These chapters were already attributed to Pope Hadrian in the time of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, as is clear from his work against Hincmar, bishop of Laon, chapter 24. Yet because certain ancient manuscript codices state that the chapters were collected not by Pope Hadrian but by Ingilramnus, or Angelramnus, bishop of Metz, and presented to Pope Hadrian, some today attribute them to Hadrian and others to Angelramnus.

Whatever author this collection of chapters may have had, Marca, book VII, *On the Harmony of the Canons*, chapter 20, considers it older than Isidore. He says that Isidore used these same chapters in preparing his collection of apocryphal letters.

The author reveals himself as a Spaniard in this sentence: “At the beginning of this volume we set down how a council is to be celebrated among us, so that those who wish to follow our order may know how they ought to conduct it.” For he derives the entire order of celebrating a council from the fourth Council of Toledo, as is clear from the title of that order, which appears in the first volume of the Councils as follows:

“Order for celebrating a council, written by Isidore Mercator from the fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 4, and corrected through the diligence of Garcia de Loaysa, editor of the Spanish Councils.”

Isidore Mercator’s book, brought from Spain into Gaul, was first received and published among the Gauls by Riculfus, who later succeeded Lullus as archbishop of Mainz in the following year.

Thus Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, replies to Hincmar, bishop of Laon, in work 33, chapter 24:

“Perhaps you thought that no one besides yourself possessed the same sentences—those of Hadrian or Ingilramnus—or the letters themselves collected by Isidore, and therefore you supposed that you could freely gather such materials. It is remarkable, since this land is full of those very sentences, as well as of the book of collected letters by Isidore, which Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, brought from Spain and carefully acquired, just as he did the royal chapters, and through it caused these regions to be filled with them.”

That collection was copied from the letters of Anacletus, Evaristus, and other ancient Roman pontiffs, if Antonio Augustinus is to be trusted in this matter in Dialogue XV, *On the Correction of Gratian*, where he denies that these chapters belong to Hadrian I. Or, as the aforementioned Marca believes, it was excerpted from ancient canons and genuine letters of the Roman pontiffs, and also from the laws contained in the Theodosian Code, or rather from the *Breviary* of those laws.

In these chapters, something is sometimes added to the ancient canons, while at other times certain words are removed. Such was the authority of these chapters that they were frequently copied into the capitularies of the Frankish kings, as both Antonio Augustinus and Marca state by common agreement.

Moreover, not only Marca and Antonio Augustinus but also Baronius, under the year 865, and many other learned men acknowledge that the letters of the earlier Roman pontiffs are spurious. See what we said about those letters under the year of Christ 100, § 4 and following.

[Col. 1097]

## SOME DONATIONS OF ANGELRAMNUS

### I. Angelramnus donates Faho and Gaudiacum to the monastery of Gorze (year 770)

*(From D. Calmet, History of Lorraine.)*

[Col. 1097A]

[Col. 1097B] Since Christ, the only Son of the Father, who together with the Father and the Holy Spirit created all things from nothing, did not disdain to lay down his life for his sheep and entrusted those acquired by his own blood to a servant for safekeeping, whoever receives them in trust must watch over them carefully and diligently, so that, insofar as the one who entrusted them is willing to grant him strength, he may strive not to neglect any necessities, whether spiritual or temporal, but may present to his Lord with increase the talent entrusted to him.

Therefore I, Angilramnus, in the name of God and by the grace of God bishop of the city of Metz, for the sake of divine regard, the remedy of our soul, and eternal reward, with the consent of the clergy and faithful laymen of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, our special patron, whose Church we are known to govern by the authority of Christ, donate to the monastery of Gorze, which lies under that same Church of Saint Stephen, which our predecessor, the lord Chrodegang, archbishop of blessed memory, built anew in honor of Saint Peter and the other saints, and in which he gathered a company of monks leading their lives under the holy rule, and where Saint Gorgonius, a renowned martyr, rests bodily, and where Abbot Theomarus appears to be rector under our authority, the following property belonging to the estate of Saint Stephen:

That is, in the district of Bedense, the estate called Faho, which Fredelaigus, vassal of the lord King Carloman, is now known to hold by the benefice of Saint Stephen or of us, under our lease; and likewise another estate belonging to Saint Stephen, situated in the district of Wabrince and called Gaudiacum, which Godfridus, likewise a royal dependent, appears to hold by the benefice of Saint Stephen or of us, under lease.

We wish this property to be donated to the aforesaid monastery and to the holy community living there: lands, houses, buildings, fields, meadows, pastures, vineyards, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable goods, slaves, *liti*, farm laborers, appurtenances and dependencies, with their complete customary boundaries and roads belonging or pertaining to the aforesaid estates of Faho and Gaudiacum.

Let all this serve for the increase of Saint Peter, Saint Gorgonius, or the brothers themselves, so that they may be more gladly moved to pray earnestly for us, for our illustrious king, for the stability of the Frankish kingdom, and for our successors, seeking the mercy of the Lord. And let them pay each year to the monastery and to the brothers the census which Fredelaigus and Godfridus have until now paid to Saint Stephen or to us.

When those men have departed from this light, let the brothers receive the aforesaid estates, with everything placed upon them, into their own authority, without opposition from that person, or awaiting a judge or our episcopal successors' conveyance.

I ask my successors and fellow bishops—and I presume to adjure them by the inseparable Trinity—to permit my acts to endure forever, just as they themselves desire their acts to be preserved through long ages.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 770. I, Angilramnus, sinful bishop, reread and subscribed this deed of cession made by me. Sign of Agnardus. I, Optarius, though unworthy, presbyter. Heboradus, abbot. Arthecarius, archdeacon. Andreas. Gilo, abbot. Seal of Huvinodus. Harimandus, notary. I, Ynasco, personal deacon, ordered by my lord and bishop Angilramnus, wrote and subscribed this deed of cession.

### II. Angelramnus donates the estate of Warangesi to the monastery of Gorze (year 770)

*(From D. Calmet, in the same work.)*

In the name of the Lord. Angilramnus, by the grace of God bishop of the city of Metz.

We exercise the pastoral office if, insofar as the Almighty grants us strength, we watch over the sheep entrusted to us by God in every respect, so that they do not cease to have nourishment both spiritual and bodily. And if, from the property of the Church entrusted to us for governing and administering, we grant something, as necessity requires, to churches or monasteries belonging or pertaining to that same Church, for the benefit of God’s servants or the poor, we do not consider ourselves to be acting contrary to canonical authority or the institutions of the Fathers.

Therefore, for the sake of divine regard and the remedy of our soul, with the consent of the clerics and faithful laymen of the Church of Saint Stephen, which by God’s authority we appear to govern, we donate to the monastery of Saint Peter at the place called Gorze, which our predecessor of blessed memory, the lord Chrodegang, archbishop, built anew, and to the holy community of monks dwelling there, where the illustrious and renowned martyr Saint Gorgonius rests bodily, and where Abbot Theutmarus [Theomarus] appears to preside under our authority.

We wish this donation to be perpetual and confirm it with complete devotion of mind. It consists of the estate in the district of Calvomont, called the estate of Warangesi, with its appurtenances, dependencies, and necessities: lands, fields, meadows, pastures, vineyards, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable goods, slaves, *liti* [farm laborers], tenants, money, and property of both sexes, kinds, and ages, with its complete boundaries and secure condition—in short, everything belonging or pertaining to that estate, in its entirety.

We wish it to be donated to the monastery and to the brothers.

In the same way, in that district we donate the property at Manicocurt, which Haribert donated to Saint Stephen and which his son, Chrotecarius by name, now holds under lease.

Likewise, in that district we donate the property at Rehensa-Coldocurt, which Beto assigned to Saint Stephen and which he now holds under lease, as well as the share in that estate which Vibollagus appears to hold by the benefice of Saint Stephen or of us.

Under the same condition, in that district we donate the property at the estate of Acciago, together with the church built there and everything belonging to it, which Aglebertus, son of Marcellus, is seen to possess by the benefice of Saint Stephen or of us.

We also donate the property in that district called Nodulfo, which Ilduinus appears to possess by the benefice of Saint Stephen or of us. Likewise, the property in the estate of Buxarias, which Gondolanus has until now been seen to hold by the benefice of Saint Stephen, is assigned and given to the monastery.

In the same way, we donate the properties in that district at the place called Hadulfo-curte and at Burtsolonivilla, which Maurotus donated to Saint Stephen by his will.

Under the same condition, we donate the properties in the district of Calvomont which Harbertus and Warnildis assigned to Saint Stephen by their will, and which Warnildis now appears to possess under lease, at the places called Arcas and Niguiomonte. Let them contribute to the increase of this house of God.

Likewise, we donate the properties in that district at Ilibas, above the river Cernone, which Halibert assigned to Saint Stephen and which his son Raboldus now holds under lease.

Likewise, we donate the properties above the same river Cernone which Suitbardus gave to Saint Stephen.

Under the same condition, we donate in the district of Suggentin the estate called Childufo-villa, which Count Otto now appears to possess by the benefice of Saint Stephen or of us, together with the share which Gonthadus gave to Saint Stephen and which he now holds under lease.

Let all the things included above—lands, houses, buildings, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable goods, slaves, *liti*, farm laborers, appurtenances and dependencies, with their complete boundaries and secure conditions belonging or pertaining to those properties—serve for the increase of the aforesaid monastery and the brothers, so that they may be more gladly moved to pray earnestly for us, for our illustrious kings Charles and Carloman, for the stability of the Frankish kingdom, and for our successors, seeking the mercy of the Lord.

And whoever among the men named above, or any others, appears to hold the properties mentioned above by the benefice of Saint Stephen or by leases in return for a census, let him henceforth pay to the monastery and to the brothers the census which until now he has paid as a gift for our use.

When they have departed from this light and the day of their death has arrived, after their departure let the brothers receive the properties, with everything placed upon them, into their own authority, without awaiting any contradiction from anyone, any judge, any bishop, or our successors.

I also ask my successors and lords, and presume to adjure them by the Holy Trinity, to permit my acts to endure forever, just as they themselves wish their acts to remain forever.

Done above the river Meuse, at the place called Fontanas, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 770, in the eighth indiction, with epact 19, concurrent 7, in the first year of the reign of King Carloman.

I, Angilramnus, sinful bishop, reread and subscribed this testament made by me. I, Grimaldus, abbot, subscribed. I, Helborardus, abbot, subscribed. I, Goso, abbot, subscribed. I, Sigilbertus, abbot, subscribed. Fredalius, sinful co-bishop, subscribed. Stephanus, presbyter, subscribed. Andreas subscribed. Donatus subscribed. I, Rocfridus, subscribed. Seal of Widigangus. Haymaldius subscribed. Dodonus subscribed. Hardoninus subscribed. Hildelbodus subscribed. Adulfus. I, Ynasco, ordered by my lord and bishop Angilramnus, wrote and subscribed this testament.

### III. Angelramnus donates certain estates situated in Alsace to the monastery of Saint Avold (year 787)

*(From D. Calmet, in the same work.)*

I, Engilramus, in the name of God an unworthy bishop of Metz, ought diligently to provide for all the churches entrusted to us, to establish peace for the brothers dwelling there in God, to defend them from wicked men, and to guard their property, so that they may serve God more securely.

Therefore, moved and compassionately distressed by the daily hardships and miseries of the monastery of blessed Nabor, which it suffered under the advocate and minister of Count Wolmer, our advocate, both through exactions and through the plundering which they incessantly inflicted and carried out against the men of that Church by night and by day, oppressing and afflicting them daily, so that we could no longer endure their complaints—the monastery had been reduced by all this to such poverty and misery that they could scarcely find brothers willing to serve God and Saint Nabor there, since they had no means by which to live.

At last, after taking counsel, we summoned that count and compelled him by our authority; and he ceased from this injury and rebuked his sub-advocates and ministers.

For this correction and amendment of the aforesaid monastery, Abbot Wasco and his brothers, with the counsel of us all and of the same count, so that the arrangement might be firm and valid and so that thereafter neither the count nor his successors might disturb them, permanently transferred to the count certain estates which belonged to their provision, so that from then on the count, his sub-advocates, and his ministers would inflict or impose no exaction or disturbance upon that Church or its peasants.

If, however, their peasants should rebel against them or refuse to come to justice, the aforesaid count, after being summoned by the abbot or the brothers, was to go there. The abbot, providing for him and his men for the night, was to arrange that justice be done concerning the peasants on the following day. Of the fines, the abbot was to receive two parts and the count one, and he was to be satisfied with this. The other benefits and annual services of the Church were to remain permanently in the possession of the abbot and brothers, and they were to hold them freely and peacefully, without any disturbance.

The names of the estates are these: Walo, which is near the fortress of Morspec in Alsace, near Humburo; Ropac, an estate near Jugeswile; four manses near Salrab; Cundici, with its church, an estate near Bozonisvilla. Likewise, the estate of Ostinga and nine manses at Altor, near Tanna-villa, and one mansus at Hinkinga-villa.

All these things, as they now appear to be written, we confirm and strengthen by the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and of all the saints, men and women, so that no count, advocate, or any person or man may dare to violate, break, or alter this charter, but that it may always remain firm and stable until the present day. Let all who attempt to violate or oppose it incur the wrath and curse of God and our excommunication.

Sign of Botpertus, advocate. Sign of Sigibaldus. Sign of Liepbridus, archdeacon. Sign of Mantfridus, archdeacon. Sign of Helimannus, dean. Sign of Bencenus, provost. Sign of Otto, provost.

Done in this year 29 [Note: [Col. 1101] Perhaps 19, since the twenty-ninth year of Charles the Great fell in the year of Christ 797, the year in which Angelramnus ceased to live], while the glorious King Charles was reigning, on the fifteenth day of June. Subscribed. I, Allo, notary, wrote this, and Christophorus Thilman.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 790. WICBODUS.

[Col. 1101]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON WICBODUS

*[From Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Later Latin Literature*.]*

[Col. 1101C] It is uncertain who Wicbodus was, whose *Questions on the Octateuch* were found in a codex of Saint Maximinus of Trier. Martène and Durand published only the first three chapters of Genesis in their *Amplissima Collectio*, IX, 293.

At the beginning of the codex these words appear: “Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, ordered this codex to be written for his own use.” Is he therefore that Wigbaldus who was notary and archchancellor of Charlemagne under Itherius and Rado? Or is he Widbaldus, whom, according to the Astronomer, the same prince appointed over the people of Périgueux around the year 778? This is uncertain.

[Col. 1102C] The work, however, is composed from the sayings of the holy Fathers Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, Ambrose, Hilary, Isidore, Eucherius, and Junilius, whose words it retains. And since most of Genesis almost reproduces the unaltered text of Jerome and Isidore, while the following books present only Isidore, the two scholars mentioned above did not wish to publish more. The codex itself may nevertheless be useful to those who in the future will review the works of Jerome and Isidore anew. See the *Literary History of France*, volume IV, p. 177.

## WICBODUS’S QUESTIONS ON THE OCTATEUCH

From a very ancient codex of the monastery of Saint Maximinus of Trier.

*(Martène, *Amplissima Collection of Councils*.)*

[Col. 1101]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

[Col. 1101C] I present Wigbodus’s *Questions on the Octateuch*, copied from a very ancient codex of the monastery of Saint Maximinus of Trier, at the beginning of which these words are written: “Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician [Col. 1102C] of the Romans, ordered this codex to be written for his own use.” (Such was the supreme inclination of that devout prince toward sacred matters.)

The author of the work is Wicbodus, or Wigbaldus. Whether he was that Wigbaldus who was notary of Charlemagne under the archchancellors Itherius and Rado; or Widbaldus, whom, according to the Astronomer, the same prince appointed over the people of Périgueux around the year 778; or someone else, he composed his work from the sayings of the holy Fathers, especially Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, Ambrose, Hilary, Isidore, Eucherius, and Junilius.

At times he transcribes their words pure and unadorned in a continuous sequence; sometimes he gathers passages scattered in various places into one; and at other times he expresses not their words but their meaning.

From this I conjectured—and all learned men will conjecture with me—how highly that work ought to be valued, since it had been copied at the command of so distinguished a prince for his use and represented the scriptural expositions of so many and such eminent teachers of the Church.

Yet when I examined it with some care, I noticed that most of Genesis almost merely reproduces the unaltered text of Jerome and Isidore, while the following books present only Isidore. Consequently, I did not consider the entire work worth publishing here. Learned readers, however, may perhaps find the *Questions* on the first chapters of Genesis agreeable.

[Col. 1103]

## [QUESTIONS ON THE OCTATEUCH]

## PRAISE OF THE KING. ADDRESS TO THE BOOK

[Col. 1103B]

## CHARLES, KING OF THE FRANKS AND LOMBARDS AND PATRICIAN OF THE ROMANS, ORDERED THIS CODEX TO BE WRITTEN FOR HIS OWN USE.

Who, unlearned and rustic, could ever worthily explain in metrical verses

the praises of him whom the world everywhere celebrates

under the vault of heaven,

by whose command you, O Order, have deserved to be free [Note: [Col. 1103D] Perhaps: *meruisti sorde*, “you have deserved to be free from filth”]

and to receive a shining mantle after a long time?

Begin as soon as possible to pay abundant thanks,

because you are free from the cloud of errors and are considered corrected.

Then, prostrate, ask pardon with your prayer,
And be the discerning patron of your author [*auctoris*, apparently corrupted in the source]. [Note: [Col. 1104D] Here there is a space of one verse left blank in the manuscript.]

A rough or impressed hand polished [it] by thinning [it; the wording is uncertain].

[Col. 1103C] Here, O king, you have at hand what you once ordered:

Receive it, and, fortunate one, may you use it for many years.

## EPIGRAM OF THE FOLLOWING WORK

O how greatly the proclamations of your praise shine,

King Charles, fortunate and known throughout every land.

Your command, most mighty king, prevails in the farthest regions.

Who can elegantly declare your praises

In polished speech, great one, bright beneath the vault of heaven?

Who can sing your trophies, mingled with wondrous piety,

Or unfold your riches in a lengthy poem?

Who at least could enumerate the succession of the books

Which your judgment gathers from many lands,

Renewing the writings of the holy Fathers of old?

For whatever the sacred divine volumes teach in words,

[Col. 1103D] In eloquence and meaning—whatever the ancient prophet,

Recalling the world’s beginnings, proclaims,

Whether he weaves histories or perhaps figures;

Whatever the various ages of many kings

Accomplished in ordered succession after Ruth,

Or whatever those who, after Saul had been rejected, wrote in verse

The three times fifty psalms for the Davidic kingdom;

Whatever peaceful Solomon, amid his wide dominion,

Set forth as splendid proverbs obscure in meaning;

Whatever the twice eight prophets saw after him;

Whatever gentle Job says in hidden form, though his wound is exposed.

Why should I mention Esther, or the lies of chaste Judith?

When the satrap is inflamed by the treachery of an adorned face,

While the woman remains mocking upon the obscene bed,

[Col. 1104B] And, once the head has been cut off, restrains his savage gaze?

Whatever Tobit, seeing better with his blinded body,

Whatever the author Ezra, seeing secret things, wrote down;

Whatever grace, succeeding the ancient law,

Proclaims and the miracles of the New Testament.

From one side the face of a man cries out, from another that of a lion,

And the swift eagle, and the bull strong in combat.

Whatever the four times three lambs accomplished with pure minds,

Scattering their seeds throughout the whole world;

Whatever the fourteenfold epistle of devout Paul scatters;

Whatever Peter and James, whatever Jude, and he himself

Who, having seen them, reports the secrets of heaven—John;

And whatever the truthful interpreters

Have expounded in their worthy books as many mysteries—

All these things you have held and drunk in with a thirsting mind.

[Col. 1104C] Nor, if the prophets have sung anything sacred,

Does it escape you: you recognize the laws and preserve the poetic divisions,

And commend foreign songs through your own singing.

Why should I rehearse everything? Use your learned understanding,

And whatever is known to you or understood through reading,

Turn zealously toward the work of virtue in your royal service.

But if someone from the common people, scorched by envy,

Should say, “Who is this man who alters the songs of the ancients

And inscribes empty epigrams in slight little books?”

Let him know this: fault is nowhere altered,

When he cannot refuse and a greater command compels him.

Finally, when good commands are promulgated as things to be done,

The wise person fulfills them; the madman wishes to despise them.

But if Virgil and Homer, greatest of poets,

Deserved after their deaths to undergo a new judgment—

[Col. 1104D] The judgment bestowed by your Aristarchus, Varro, and Probus—

Why should he disdain that, at a mighty prince’s command,

Little Mosaic poems should be excerpted from the Bible?

I, humble Vuigbodus, have made atonement with a heap of nuts.

Compelled by your lordly command, supreme king,

I, your little servant, have dedicated these things to you

With a devoted mind, as best I could.

## The Order of the Seven Days

The first day in the world received the beginnings of light.

The second established the heavens in their light-pouring regions.

The third gave the wave-roaming sea and the earth with its growth.

The fourth possesses Phoebus, the moon, and the stars of heaven.

The fifth, the feathered birds and swimming fish.

The sixth, the quadrupeds, creeping things, and intelligent human beings.

[Col. 1105A] The seventh is rest for the Lord, these things having been duly accomplished.

Not because the Almighty labors in human fashion,

Or, wearied by his acts, finally seeks to rest—

He who, always at rest, acts and rests in making—

But because sacred rest is covered with typical figures,

Carrying many things through signs and unfolding mysteries to us.

It is called the rest of God because, in the rightful creation of things,

It was itself the measure and the greatest end of all.

For whatever new things are made are already then shown to have been ordered.

It is called the rest of God because the Lord and Redeemer Christ,

Coming in the flesh and releasing the bonds of the flesh,

Rested on this returning day in a blessed death.

[Col. 1105B] It is called the rest of God because, after a thousand labors,

[Col. 1106A] He alone, fostering us everywhere in himself, compels us to rest in him.

No rest is granted to the wretched unless he himself receives them.

It is also called rest because, after the present activity of the world

Has run its ordered course through six ages,

It receives leisure and rests in eternal peace.

It is also called rest because this is our final lot.

For the course of life, after the pattern of the world’s mass,

Consists of six ages for human beings, and the seventh is death.

The first contains the origin of the race, simple infancy;

The second thereafter is tender childhood;

The third that follows is called maturity;

The fourth, splendid youth, bears the aid of virtue;

The fifth is burdensome old age, inclining toward the final years;

The sixth is decrepitude, which ends the span of life.

[Col. 1106B] Here ends.

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF QUESTIONS ON THE BOOK OF GENESIS, DRAWN FROM THE SAYINGS OF THE HOLY FATHERS AUGUSTINE, GREGORY, JEROME, AMBROSE, HILARY, ISIDORE, EUCHERIUS, AND JUNILIUS

[Col. 1105]

[Col. 1105B]

**Student.** First of all, my teacher, I must ask who is regarded as the author of this book which among us is called Genesis.

**Teacher.** As our elders have indicated and handed down to us, they assert that Moses was the author of this work—that is, of the five books which, according to the Greeks, are called the Pentateuch—even though the title does not say this, but the book itself reports it as though of another person: “The Lord said to Moses.” An example of this appears in the New Testament, where the apostle John, whenever he wished to report something about himself, deliberately concealed his name, saying: “Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following,” and so forth (John 21:20).

**S.** From where did Genesis receive this name?

**T.** The Seventy Interpreters, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it “In the beginning”; and in Hebrew it is written *Bresith*, which Aquila renders “at the beginning.” Therefore, according to its meaning rather than according to the translation of the word, it can be understood of Christ, who is acknowledged as the creator of heaven and earth both at the very opening of Genesis, which is the head of all the books, and at the beginning of the Gospel of John. Hence in the Psalter he says of himself: “In the head of the book it is written concerning me” (Psalm 39:8)—that is, at the beginning of Genesis. And in the Gospel: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). Therefore it should be known that among the Hebrews this book is called *Bresith*, since they have the custom of giving volumes their names from their opening words.

## In the Book of Prologues

**S.** What does Genesis describe according to the truth of its history?

**T.** It describes the structure of the world and the creation of humanity, the Flood and the division of the earth, the confusion of languages, and the deeds of all the patriarchs up to Israel’s entry into Egypt.

## JUNILIUS

**S.** I wish to know what this Scripture, speaking of the present age, signifies.

**T.** Five things: either its generation, that is, its creation; or its governance; or occurrences affecting its natures; or events arising from wills; or the subsequent results of volition.

**S.** In what ways does this Scripture signify the generation of the age?

**T.** In three ways. For something is written as having been made solely by God’s will, as in: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1); or by will together with speech, whether commanding—as in, “Let there be light,” and “Let there be a firmament”—or deliberative—as in, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.” Or by will, speech, and determination, as in: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth.” And again: “Let the earth bring forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and a fruit-bearing tree making fruit whose seed is in itself.” The other things that he works piecemeal after the seventh day until the end of the age proceed from that determination.

**S.** Is there any difference among these three?
