**T.** There is. Those things that were made solely by will or also by speech were newly made; but those made by determination are similar to the things we called newly made. Again, the former occurred during the first six days, whereas the latter continue as long as the age endures.

**S.** Give the order of the things made during the six days.

**T.** At the very beginning of creation, heaven, earth, angels, air, and water were made.

**S.** Prove that angels, waters, and air were made.

[Col. 1107A]

**T.** They are shown to have been made from other passages of Scripture, as in: “He makes his angels spirits” (Psalm 103:4); and: “Praise him, all his angels” (Psalm 148); and: “Waters that are above the heavens, praise the name of the Lord, for he spoke and they were made” (ibid., verse 5); and: “For the sea is his, and he made it” (Psalm 94:5). In the Holy Scriptures the air is usually indicated by the name “heaven,” as in “the birds of heaven,” since it is certain that birds fly through the air. We have shown that heaven was made. As for the fact that these preceded the other creatures, there is a reason concerning the angels, as Scripture demonstrates when they are placed before other creatures in praises and blessings: for it was fitting that a heavenly creature should precede earthly ones. Concerning the waters, Scripture itself says that the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.

[Col. 1107B]

**S.** Follow the order of generation.

**T.** At the beginning of the first day, light was made; on the second, the firmament was made; on the third, the sea and the things growing from the earth; on the fourth, the lights of heaven; on the fifth, the swimming and flying creatures; on the sixth, the remaining animals and humanity.

**S.** What difference is there in the making of these creatures themselves?

**T.** Some were made from nothing, such as heaven, earth, and so forth—the things we said were made up to the completion of the first day. Others, however, were made from things already made on the first day.

**S.** Give proofs of these matters.

**T.** Whenever Scripture wishes to show that things were made from something else, it either signifies this openly, as in “Let the earth bring forth,” and “Let the waters bring forth,” and similar expressions; or it indicates it through the subtle meaning of its words, as when it says, “Let there be a firmament.” This plainly signifies that something fluid and liquid had existed—that is, the waters—which, so that they might be shown as having been solidified, were called the firmament that was being made. Again, it called the lights derivative, since they were made on the fourth day, thereby showing that they were made from the light produced on the first day. In the things made on the first day, however, neither an explicit nor a subtle word declares that anything was made from something else. Nothing after the first day is shown to have been made from non-existent things, except the human soul. In this too one must observe that, while other things were made either from nothing or from things already made, humanity alone is composed from both.

**S.** What other differences do we attribute to the creatures?

**T.** The things made during the first six days did not arise naturally or through reproduction. The remaining things that are made arise naturally from the divine determination, except, of course, miracles.

**S.** Give a third difference.

**T.** Some creatures—that is, rational creatures—were made for their own sake, such as angels and human beings. The others, however, are known to have been made not for their own sake but for the sake of the angels or human beings mentioned above. Humanity, however, should be understood as having been made principally for its own sake according to the soul, and consequently according to the body.

**S.** Apart from angels and human beings, did the other creatures not need one another?

**T.** They did need one another, not for utility but for adornment. For they are useful not to themselves but to angels and human beings, for whose sake they are also known to have been made. Yet they likewise provide adornment for one another. Heaven, for example, was unadorned without the heavenly lights, and the lights themselves, lest they have been made in vain, needed the eyes of those who see. The sea was unadorned until it either received its proper place or was filled with animals. The earth was unadorned apart from the use of inhabitants or growing things, and irrational animals were unfit without human governance; grasses were superfluous in the absence of animals’ use. Thus all things needed one another, or the things that are made daily. But, as we have already said, being unadorned is one thing and being useful another: something unadorned may nevertheless be shown to be useful in itself for another.

**S.** Is there any difference in adornment itself?

**T.** There is. Some things were adorned during the six days, such as heaven with its lights, earth with its grasses, and the sea with its fish. Others are adorned as long as the world lives, such as the sea with ships, the earth with buildings and other things constructed by human skill, and humanity itself with knowledge. Others will receive their adornment in the future, such as the body receiving incorruption, mortal things receiving immortality, and the heavenly kingdom receiving the dwelling of the saints. It should also be noted concerning adornments that, in things made by human ingenuity or arts, the cause lies in human beings, whereas in the remaining things it lies in the Lord.

**S.** Give a fourth difference.

**T.** Some things emerged as though created simultaneously and suddenly, such as grasses, the lights, swimming and flying creatures, as well as terrestrial animals and quadrupeds. Others were not made simultaneously but as though with some delay, such as the sea, earth, and humanity; for humanity itself is written as having been made gradually, as were the others.

**S.** Give a fifth difference among creatures.

**T.** Some of them rule over the others by reason, namely rational creatures. Some are employed for use, such as the heavenly lights. Others obey by the necessity of nature, such as birds, quadrupeds, and things like them.

**S.** Give a sixth difference.

**T.** Those that rule over the others, namely rational creatures, are moved by will and reason. Those that are irrational either obey necessity or are moved by nature.

**S.** What materials did the things made from something else possess?

**T.** Six: earth, waters, air, fire, light, and the rib.

**S.** Give their individual origins.

**T.** From earth came green plants and animals. From the waters came the firmament, the sea, swimming creatures, and flying creatures. From earth, waters, fire, and air together came all things renewed through the succession of time. From light came the lights. From the rib came Eve.

**S.** How is it proved that fire was made, or from where, or when?

**T.** We can prove that it was made from the general statement of Scripture when it says of God: “Who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them” (Psalm 145:6), since fire is certainly also among them; and from a specific prophecy: “Praise the Lord, dragons and all abysses; fire, hail, snow, ice, and stormy wind” (Psalm 148:7). Concerning these he had said earlier: “For he spoke and they were made” (Psalm 148:5). And again: “Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord”; and he adds: “Bless the Lord, fire and heat” (Daniel 3:57, 66). Whether it was made from nothing, like the other things, or from something else, is uncertain. For many hold that it is a particle of the heavenly lights, since even now we have often seen people obtain fire in a certain way from the sun’s rays. If this is so, it was made on the first day. But Scripture more wisely called this “light” rather than “fire,” so that it might receive its name from the better use.

**S.** Give a seventh difference among creatures.

**T.** All things made from something else are bodies. Incorporeal things, however, were made neither from something else nor were other things made from them. These incorporeal things must not be understood in the same way that God is called incorporeal. In comparison with him, nothing is corporeal [read: incorporeal], just as nothing is immortal or invisible. There is one sense in which these words belong exclusively to divinity, and another in which we speak of creatures in this way, such as animals or angels.

**S.** Can we ask how God made the world?

**T.** This is asked more rashly than cautiously. For no human being is permitted to know the manner of any divine creation. If anyone knew how some things were made from nothing, he would necessarily be equal to the Creator in knowledge and power.

## AUGUSTINE

[Col. 1109C]

**S.** If God disposed all things in number, measure, and weight, where did he dispose number, measure, and weight themselves?

**T.** Number, measure, and weight are God himself. He is number without number, from whom all number comes. He is measure without measure, from whom all measure comes. He is weight without weight, from whom all weight comes. He did not see the creature outside himself or somewhere else, as human beings retain in memory what they are going to make. Every creature, therefore, is the will of the Creator. The will of the Creator is not outside the nature of the Creator; that is, where the nature is, there is the will. Yet the nature is eternal, just as the will is eternal. No new thought arises in God for forming the creature. Therefore the triune God disposed all things in himself, because in himself he possessed everything that he made. It may also be understood in another way: he disposed all things in number, measure, and weight, that is, so that everything he made would possess number, measure, and weight.

Augustine began Book I *Against the Manichaeans* in this way:

“After the manner of the Manichaeans, many unlearned and rustic people, and, so to speak, presumptuous ones, are accustomed to ask and object: ‘If at some beginning of time God made heaven and earth, what was he doing before he made heaven and earth [ [Note: [Col. 1109D] The words enclosed in brackets are not found in the printed editions.] or where was he], and what pleased him [Col. 1110A] suddenly to make what he had never before made throughout eternal ages?’ We answer them as follows.

“God created heaven and earth in the beginning—not in the beginning of time, but in Christ, when the Word was with the Father, through whom and in whom all things were made. But if we believe that God made heaven and earth at the beginning of time, we must certainly understand that before the beginning of time there was no time. For God made time as well. Therefore, before he made time, there was no time. We cannot say that there was some time when God had not yet made anything. For how could there be time that God had not made, since he himself is the maker of all times? And if time began together with heaven and earth, no time can be found in which God had not yet made heaven and earth. But when they say, ‘What suddenly pleased him?’ they speak as though some times had passed during which God did nothing. Time could not pass before God had made it, because only one who exists before times can be the maker of times.

“Certainly the Manichaeans themselves read, praise, and honor the apostle Paul, and by wrongly interpreting his letters deceive many. Let them tell us, then, what the apostle Paul said: ‘The acknowledgment of the truth that accords with the piety of God, in hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before eternal times’ (Titus 1:1). What could eternal times have had before them? Let them therefore be compelled to explain this, so that they may understand that they do not understand when they rashly wish to criticize what they ought to have investigated carefully.

“But if they do not say, ‘What suddenly pleased God to make heaven and earth?’ but remove the word ‘suddenly’ and say only, ‘What pleased God to make heaven and earth?’—we do not say that this world is coeternal with God, because this world does not possess the same eternity as God. God made the world. And if times began together with the creature that God made, for this reason they are called eternal; nevertheless, it is not eternal in the same way that God is eternal, because God exists before time and is the maker of time. Just as everything God made is very good, but is not good in the same way as God, who made it, so these things were made. He did not beget them from himself so that they would be what he is; rather, he made them from nothing, so that they would not be equal either to him by whom they were made or to his Son through whom they were made. For it is just [the printed edition has *justum*]. If they should say, ‘What pleased God to make heaven and earth?’ the answer must be given to them that they should first learn the force of the human will, since they desire to know the will of God. They desire to know the causes of God’s will, although the will of God itself is the cause of all things that exist. For if God’s will has a cause, there is something that precedes the will of God, which it is impious to believe.

“Therefore, to one who says, ‘Why did God make heaven and earth?’ the answer is: ‘Because he willed it.’ The will of God is the cause of heaven and earth, and therefore the will of God is greater than heaven and earth. But one who says, ‘Why did he will to make heaven and earth?’ [ [Note: [Col. 1111D] The words enclosed in brackets are not found in the printed editions.] or ‘Where was he before they were made?’ seeks something greater than the will of God. Nothing greater can be found. Let human rashness therefore restrain itself and not seek what does not exist, lest it fail to find what does exist. And if anyone desires to know the will of God, let him become God’s friend. Certainly, if anyone wished to know the will of a human being whose friend he was not, everyone would laugh at his foolishness or stupidity. No one becomes God’s friend except through the purest conduct and through that end of the commandment of which the Apostle says: ‘The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith’ (1 Timothy 1:5). If these people possessed this, they would not be heretics.”

But concerning what follows in the book of Genesis—“The earth, however, was invisible and unformed”—the Manichaeans criticize it by saying: “How did God make heaven and earth in the beginning, if the earth was already invisible and unformed?” Thus, because they wish to criticize the divine Scriptures before knowing them, they fail to understand even the most obvious matters. For what could have been said more clearly than this: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the earth itself, which God made, was invisible and unformed”? Before God arranged all the forms of things in their places and settings through ordered distinction, before he said, “Let there be light,” and “Let there be a firmament,” and “Let the waters be gathered,” and “Let the dry land appear,” and so forth—things which are set forth in order in that book in a manner that children can grasp—all these matters contained such great mysteries that whoever learns them will either grieve at the vanity of all heretics because they are human beings, or laugh at it because they are proud.

The book continues: “And darkness was over the abyss” (Genesis 1:2). The Manichaeans [ [Note: [Col. 1111D] The words enclosed in brackets are not found in the printed editions.] or their followers] criticize this by saying: “Was God therefore in darkness before he made the light?” They themselves are truly in the darkness of ignorance, and therefore they do not understand the light in which God was before he made this light. They know no light except what they see with bodily eyes. Therefore they worship this sun—which we see together not only with the larger beasts but also with flies and tiny worms—in such a way that they say it is a particle of that light in which God dwells.

But let us understand that there is another light in which God dwells. Of this light it is said in the Gospel: “[Note: [Col. 1111D] The printed editions read: ‘It was the true light which…’] ‘The true light was that which enlightens every human being coming into this world’” (John 1:9). The light of this sun does not enlighten the human being but the human body and mortal eyes, which are surpassed by the eyes of eagles, who are said to look upon this sun much better than we do. That other light, however, does not nourish the eyes of irrational birds but the pure hearts of those who believe in God and turn themselves from the love of visible and [Col. 1112A] temporal things toward fulfilling his commandments. All human beings can do this if they wish, because that light enlightens every human being coming into this world.

Therefore, darkness was over the abyss before this light was made. [Note: [Col. 1111D] The printed editions add here: “of which it is consequently said in this passage.”] Consequently, the passage says:

“God said, ‘Let there be light.’” For where light is not present, there is darkness—not because darkness is something, but because the absence of light is called darkness. Likewise, silence is not some thing; rather, where sound is absent, silence is spoken of. Nakedness is not some thing; rather, on a body where covering is absent, nakedness is spoken of. Emptiness is not something; rather, a place where a body is absent is called empty. Thus darkness [Note: [Col. 1112D] The printed editions lack the words “as we have already said.”], as we have already said, is not something; but where light is absent, it is called darkness.

We have said this because they are accustomed to ask: “From where did darkness itself come to be over the abyss before God made the light? Who made or begot it? Or, if no one made or begot it, was darkness eternal?”—as though darkness were something. But, as has been said, this name denotes the absence of light. Yet because these people, deceived by their fables, believed that there was a race of darkness in which bodies, forms, and souls existed in those bodies, they think that darkness is something and do not understand that darkness is perceived only when we do not see—just as we do not perceive [Note: [Col. 1112D] The printed editions read: “is not perceived.”] silence except when we do not hear.

Just as silence is nothing, so darkness is nothing. But just as they say that the race of darkness fought against God’s light, so another equally foolish person could say that a race of silent people fought against God’s voice. For the moment we do not undertake to refute and disprove those follies. Now we are setting out to defend the things they criticize in the Old Testament, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant us the ability, and to show in them that human blindness has no power against the truth of God.

The text continues.

What is written—“And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Genesis 1:2)—the Manichaeans habitually criticize in this way: “The water, then, was the dwelling place of the Spirit of God, and it contained the Spirit of God?” They try to pervert everything with a distorted mind, and they are blinded by their own wickedness. When we say, “The sun is borne over the earth,” do we mean that the sun dwells in the earth and that the earth contains the sun? Yet the Spirit of God [Note: [Col. 1112D] Read with the printed editions: “was borne over the waters.”] was not borne over the waters in the same way that the sun is borne over the earth, but in another way understood by few. That Spirit was not borne over those waters through intervals of space, as the sun is borne over the earth, but through the power of its invisible sublimity.

Let them tell us how the will of a craftsman is borne over the things that are to be fashioned. If they do not comprehend these human and everyday matters, let them fear God and seek with a simple heart what they do not understand, lest, when they wish to cut down the truth with sacrilegious words [Col. 1113A]—the truth which they cannot see—the axe return upon their own legs. For that truth cannot be cut down, since it remains unchangeable; whatever blows are launched against it rebound and return with greater force upon those who dare to strike what they ought to believe, so that they might deserve to understand.

Next they ask, and inquire mockingly, from where the water itself came over which the Spirit of God was borne. “Was it written above that God made the water?” If they asked this devoutly, they would discover how it should be understood. For the word “water” was not used in this passage so that we should understand by it the water that we can now see and touch. Nor was the earth called invisible and unformed like this earth, which can now be seen and handled.

[Col. 1113B] Rather, by the words “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1), the whole creation that God made and established is signified by the names “heaven” and “earth.” These names of visible things were used because of the weakness of children, who are less capable of comprehending invisible things. First, therefore, confused and formless matter was made, from which all the distinct and formed things were to arise. I believe that the Greeks call this *Chaos*. For elsewhere too we read in the praises of God: “You who made the world from formless matter,” and so forth; some manuscripts have “from unseen matter.”

Therefore God is rightly believed to have made everything from nothing. For even if all formed things were made from this matter, this matter itself was nevertheless made from nothing. We must not resemble those who do not believe that the omnipotent God could make anything from nothing, because they observe that craftsmen and every kind of artisan cannot construct anything unless they have material from which to construct it. Wood assists the carpenter, silver the silversmith, gold the goldsmith, and earth the potter, enabling each to complete his work. If they are not assisted by the material from which they make something, they can make nothing, since they themselves do not make that material. A carpenter does not make wood but makes something from wood; the same is true of all the other artisans.

The omnipotent God, however, needed no assistance from anything that he himself had not made in order to bring about what he willed. If some thing that he had not made assisted him in making the things he wished to make, he would not be omnipotent; and that is impious to believe.

That formless matter, therefore, which God made from nothing, was first called “heaven and earth”—not because it already was this, but because it could become this. For heaven is later written as having been made. It is as if, when considering the seed of a tree, we were to say that roots, a trunk, branches, fruit, and leaves were present—not because they already exist, but because they are going to arise from it. Thus it was said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” as though it were the seed of heaven and earth, [Note: [Col. 1113D] The printed editions read: “while the matter of heaven and earth was still in confusion.”] while the matter of heaven and earth was still confused. But because it was certain that heaven and earth would arise from it, the matter itself was already called heaven and earth.

The Lord also speaks in this manner when he says: “I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). He did not say this because it had already happened, but because it was most certainly going to happen. For a little later he says to them: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). Why, then, had he said, “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you,” unless he knew that he was going to do this? In the same way, heaven and earth could be called the matter from which heaven and earth had not yet been made, although they were not to be made from anything else. Countless such expressions are found in the divine Scriptures, just as in our ordinary speech, when we say of something we confidently hope will happen: “I consider it already done.”

He also wished this still-formless matter to be called the invisible and unformed earth [Note: [Col. 1113D] Read, with the printed editions, “to call it.”], because among all the elements of the world the earth appears less beautiful than the others. He called it invisible because of its obscurity, and unformed because of its lack of form. He also called this same matter “water,” over which the Spirit of God was borne, just as the will of an artisan is borne over the things being fashioned. Although only a few minds can grasp this, I do not know whether it can be expressed in human words even by a few people.

For this reason, too, that matter was not absurdly called “water,” because everything born on the earth—whether animals, grasses, trees, or things like them—begins to be formed and nourished from moisture. [Col. 1114C] All these names, therefore—whether heaven and earth; the invisible and unformed earth; the abyss with darkness; or the water over which the Spirit was borne—are names for formless matter, so that an unknown reality might be communicated to the inexperienced through familiar terms. It was given not one name but many, lest, if it had only one, people should suppose it to be what they were accustomed to understand by that name.

[Note: [Col. 1114D] The printed editions read: “Therefore it was called heaven.”]

It was called heaven and earth because heaven and earth were to arise from it. It was called invisible and unformed earth, and darkness over the abyss, because it was formless and could not be seen or handled in any shape, even if there had been a human being who could see and handle it. It was called water because it lay ready, pliable and yielding, for the one who worked upon it, so that all things might be formed from it. But under all these names was unseen and formless matter [Col. 1114D] from which God established the world.

[Note: [Col. 1114D] From Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book I, chapter 1.]

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” This chapter is the head of all the books, for all divine Scripture is divided into two parts: the Old Testament and the New. Some passages disclose eternal things, as in: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). Others narrate things that were made, as in: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1). Others announce future things, as in: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty” (Luke 9:26). Still others prescribe what must be done, as in: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” and so forth (Matthew 22:39).

It is divided into two parts also because some passages are expressed figuratively, as in the Song of Songs, and as in: “Adam heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the paradise” (Genesis 3:8); while others are expressed according to the truth of events, as in the account of the people leaving Egypt and walking on foot through the sea. Still others are expressed in both ways, such as the crossing of the Red Sea and those miracles which the Lord performed in the Gospel.

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

**S.** It must be investigated with the greatest care in which beginning this occurred: whether in the beginning of time, or in the beginning as the beginning of his creation, from which other things began to exist—for they were not always coeternal with God.

M. Let us say that in the beginning, which is coeternal with himself, God made heaven and earth, in the only-begotten Son, who is the wisdom of the Father; concerning him the Apostle says, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). And in the Psalm he says, “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24); and again the Apostle says, “For in him all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible” (Col. 1:16).

D. Genesis is the beginning. If “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” then the angels were made afterward. But if the angels were made beforehand, God did not create heaven and earth first of all.

M. When the stars were made together, Scripture says, “My angels praised me with a loud voice.” The stars were made on the fourth day, and the angels already existed. For they were not made on the third or the second day. In these matters the things that were made are apparent. On the third day, certainly, the earth was separated from the waters; on the second, the firmament was made, where the sun, moon, and stars move. The first day itself, however, is the angelic nature, which was first designated by the name “heaven.” Hence it is clearly shown that the first day was spiritual, that is, the angelic nature, and then this heaven which we see with our eyes. For when he says, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), he did not mean, as you say, “first of all,” but “in the beginning,” that is, in the Son—indeed, through the Son—God made every spiritual and corporeal creature, which has been called by the name of heaven and earth. For when the Jews asked him who he was, he answered that he was the Beginning: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25).

First, therefore, he wished to speak of heaven and earth as a kind of spiritual and corporeal matter, and thus to preserve the order in which they were separately made. For by “heaven” he seems to me to have meant the dark abyss of waters, Adam’s life, as it were, drifting about unless it is turned toward the Creator and becomes light, and contemplates that God is the undivided Trinity. We do not speak in such a way that this matter preceded its form as wood precedes a chest, or as the voice precedes the word; it did not precede in time, but in origin. Therefore the first creature was light—not that light which was made on the fourth day, but spiritual light, that is, the angelic nature.

Yet this must be understood: God created heaven, earth, and light together, since there is no difference except that of origin. Just as a man cannot recount two familiar parables simultaneously, so also the Lord acted: he first recounted what had origin first, and afterward what was made from it, although he had made both together. Thus what is earlier in making by origin alone is earlier in the temporal narration. Since it was necessary for Holy Scripture to recount both the events themselves and the narrated sequence of events, what was made from the former was narrated afterward for the sake of the slower understanding, so that people might be able to grasp it, since corporeal things were made from something. There is no difference between the creation of heaven and earth and that of light except the difference between a word and a voice.

D. Why did he not say, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” but “created” them?

M. Because of the formlessness of the matter.

[Col. 1116B]

D. Give the spiritual meaning.

M. Christ is the Beginning, as he himself says in the Gospel: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25). In this Beginning, therefore, God made heaven—that is, those who meditate upon and seek heavenly things. In him he also made the carnal, who have not yet put off the earthly man.

D. “But the earth was empty and void” (Gen. 1:2). Why empty and void?

M. That is, because it had not been separated from the sea; “void,” he says, because it was not enclosed by shores or adorned with its proper embellishments—that is, with trees and animals.

Likewise, spiritually understood: the earth, namely our flesh, was empty and void before it received the form of instruction.

D. Why is it said that darkness was over the face of the abyss?

[Col. 1116C]

M. Because there was no light to be poured over it; and if there had been, it would certainly have remained above it.

Also, because the air was dense and deprived of daylight.

In another sense: darkness was over the face of the abyss because the blindness of sins and the profound obscurity of ignorance covered our hearts.

D. Explain how the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.

HIERONYMUS [Note: [Col. 1115D] Hebrew Questions].

M. Where our manuscripts have *ferebatur*, “was borne,” the Hebrew has *merephet*, which we may render “was brooding” or “was warming,” in the likeness of a bird over eggs, warming them with the heat of its living body. From this we understand that the passage does not speak of the spirit of the world, as some suppose, but of the Holy Spirit, who himself is also called the vivifier of all things from the beginning. He is called the vivifier in the same way as God is called the Creator: “Send forth your Spirit,” he says, “and they will be created” (Ps. 103:30).

AUGUSTINE.

D. “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” Was he borne locally, like the sun and the stars, or in another way?

M. The Holy Spirit is God; consequently he is not contained or extended by place, nor is he subject to changes of time, but he is wholly present everywhere. In what sense, then, did he name the creature over which the Holy Spirit was said to be borne? Not locally, but in power. The Lord did not make his works out of need, but out of benevolence, and he does not need the things he made. For needy and impoverished love is subjected to the things it loves. Therefore the Holy Spirit is said to be borne over the creature because he did not operate upon that creature out of need.

AMBROSIUS [Note: [Col. 1117] Rather Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 1, chapter 7].

D. How was the Spirit of God borne over the waters?

M. As the Apostle says: “The surpassing knowledge of the love of God.” And elsewhere he says: “It surpasses every understanding.” Therefore he indicates that something had begun over which the Spirit of God was said to be borne—not locally, but by a power surpassing and excelling all things. For there are two reasons why God loves his creature: that it may exist and that it may remain. It exists by being formed, and it remains by abiding in the Creator’s command. Therefore, in order that it might exist, the Spirit of God was borne over the water; but in order that it might remain, “God saw that it was good.” For this reason he first named the things as formless and afterward named the Holy Spirit, because every weak love is placed beneath the things it loves.

FROM AUGUSTINE’S *HEXAMERON*.

D. I ask you to explain more fully and abundantly the formlessness of matter.

M. It is true and evident that everything mutable is formed from some formlessness, and the clearest reason likewise teaches that the matter of no nature could have existed except from God. Although Scripture says, “You made the world from formless matter” (Wis. 11:15), formless matter was not earlier in time than formed things, since both were created together: both what was made and that from which it was made. Just as the voice is the matter of words, while words indicate a formed voice, so God the Creator did not first make formless matter in time and afterward form it, in a second act of consideration, according to the order of the various natures. Rather, Scripture could not avoid separating in the times of its speech what God did not separate in the times of his making.

When we speak of matter and form, we understand both together, yet we cannot pronounce both together. If spiritual light was made when God said, “Let there be light,” this should not be understood as that true light coeternal with the Father through which all things were made, but as the light concerning which it could be said that wisdom was created before all things, because light was made through uncreated wisdom. How, however, both that which was illuminated and the illumination itself could have been made simultaneously, while they had to be narrated at different times, we explained shortly before when discussing matter.

AUGUSTINE.

D. “God also said, ‘Let there be light.’” Did he speak in the day, or before every day? If he spoke in the day, he spoke temporally; if he spoke temporally, he spoke through some creature. Therefore light was not the first creature.

M. He spoke neither in the day nor temporally, but before every creature he begot his Word. The speech of God, therefore, is the Word of God. But divine Scripture, accommodating itself to little ones and, in a manner, nursing them with milk so that they may advance and receive spiritual food, wished throughout the formation of creation to call this “speech.” Thus, if we ask how light was made, we hear that in the Word of God it was destined to be made, and likewise with the other things in their order. If we ask how they were made, they were in the Word of God in order to be made.

This is why it says, “God said, ‘Let there be light.’” For the divine nature does not speak in bodily ways, nor, whenever it is said that he “spoke,” did he form a word each time. He begot one Word, coeternal and consubstantial with himself, in whom he ineffably spoke all things.

ANOTHER PASSAGE.

D. “God also said, ‘Let there be light.’” Is this light visible or invisible?

M. It is called invisible because it is the angelic creation, which our eyes cannot behold. For it was reasonable that on the fourth day he should fashion in heaven the stars, which our eyes could behold.

D. Is this angelic creation temporal or eternal?

M. It was temporal in the angels, but eternal in God. It was temporal in the sense that what had been expressed by the eternal God through the coeternal Word was made in the spiritual creature that he had already made when it was said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” This speech, however, was not only without any sound but also without any bodily motion of the spiritual creature; it was, in a certain manner, impressed upon its mind and understanding by the coeternal Word of the Father.

It is exceedingly difficult to grasp how God is said to command without commanding temporally, and how the creature hears without hearing temporally—God who, by contemplation of the truth, surpasses all times—yet how this is impressed intellectually upon the creature through the coeternal Wisdom, as through an intelligible utterance transmitting itself to what lies below, so that a temporal motion might occur in temporal things, whether they were to be formed or governed.

Again: “The light was made,” he says—that is, the angelic creation—because then they began to acknowledge or understand their Creator.

D. Why does he not repeat, “And God made the light,” as he repeats this with the other creatures that he made? With the firmament, for example, he says, “Let there be a firmament,” and again, “God made the firmament.”

M. It was not necessary for him to say, “God made the light,” because it was an intellectual creature, namely, the angels. When he says, “Let there be a firmament,” or the other things among the remaining creatures, he said this in the angelic understanding. For it is not surprising if God wished first to show his holy angels, who had turned toward him in the original creation of light, what he would afterward do.

But when he says, “And God made,” that is, in the proper nature of things, it was no longer necessary to repeat this concerning the angels, because, as we have said, they had then turned toward acknowledging their Creator. For when that eternal and unchangeable Wisdom—which was not made but begotten—transfers itself into a spiritual and rational creature, as into holy souls, so that, once illuminated, they may be able to shine, a certain luminous disposition of reason is produced in them. This may be understood as “the light was made,” after God had said, “Let there be light.”

For the spiritual creation already existed, signified by the name of heaven, when it was written, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” This was not the corporeal heaven but the incorporeal heaven, in whose nature all the holy angels are understood to exist.

GREGORY.

The angels were created in such a way that, if they wished, they could remain in the light of blessedness; but if they did not wish to, they could also fall. Thus Satan fell with his legions of followers. After his fall, however, the angels who remained were so confirmed that they could not fall at all.

This is well signified at the very beginning of Genesis, in the historical account of the present book: God created heaven, which he afterward called the firmament. These, therefore, were heavens, as we have said, who were first created good, but afterward were called the firmament because they received the power of immutability, so that they might no longer fall at all.

ANOTHER PASSAGE FROM GREGORY.

“God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Gen. 1:3), and shortly afterward, “There was evening.” In this life, sin is not abandoned through the practice of righteousness in such a way that one remains unshaken in that same righteousness. For even if uprightness already expels guilt from the dwelling of the heart, the guilt that has been driven away nevertheless sits at the doors of our thoughts and knocks, asking to be admitted.

Moses indicated this spiritually when he narrated the moments of time that occurred bodily: “There was light,” and shortly afterward he added, “There was evening.” The Creator of all things, foreknowing human guilt, then expressed in time what now takes place in the mind. Light is brought toward evening because the shadow of temptation follows the brightness of uprightness.

But because the light of the elect is not extinguished by temptation, it is said that evening, not night, occurred. Temptation often conceals the light of righteousness in the hearts of the upright, but does not destroy it; it draws it, as it were, toward the pallor of trembling, but does not extinguish it completely.

AMBROSIUS.

“God also said, ‘Let there be light’”—that is, let the illumination of faith appear. On the first day he gave the light of faith, because faith is first in conversion. Hence the first commandment itself is: “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 4:6). Because of this faith, the Lord himself wished to appear visibly in the world.

Already then, according to the grace of his foreknowledge, God divided the righteous—that is, the children of God and of light—from sinners as from darkness, calling the former day and the latter night. Since the righteous are called by the name of light, hear the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

AUGUSTINE.

“And God saw that the light was good” (Gen. 1:4).

D. If God suddenly saw that the light was good, did he not know this beforehand? Did the sight give him knowledge?

M. Every work is preceded by the will. When we consider what we ought to do, we do not act in ignorance; we consider how the things that we have determined by thought should be made. If it cannot happen to a human being that he does something in ignorance, how much less can it happen to God, who made all things as he willed by his eternal and unchanging counsel?

He did not see the things made in one way and the things to be made in another. He therefore saw the things made in the same way in which he had seen them to be made.

D. “And God saw that the light was good” (Gen. 1:4). Why did he praise only the light and not the night?

M. That is because neither night nor day had yet been made, but only the angelic light. It would have been unworthy of God to praise something formless that had not yet been formed; rather, he praised that which had been formed, namely, the angelic light.

AUGUSTINE.

D. “And he divided the light from the darkness” (ibid.). Scripture says, “He divided the light from the darkness.” Everything that is divided can also exist. Therefore, just as there is an essence of light, so there is an essence of darkness. Why does Scripture not say, “God saw that the darkness was good,” as it says this of the light?

M. God created all the angels good, by a good and unchangeable will. But because he foreknew that some of them would fall through pride, by the unchangeability of his foreknowledge he divided the good from the evil.

Calling the evil “darkness” and the good “light,” he said of the latter that they were good, but in no way said this of the former, lest he seem to approve the sins that were darkness.

ANOTHER PASSAGE.

D. “He divided the light from the darkness.” What does it mean to divide the light from the darkness?

M. It means the distinction of the formed thing from the formless.

D. “And he called the light Day, and the darkness Night” (Gen. 1:5). Why did he call the light day and the darkness night, when they had not yet been formed?

M. He called the light day because “day” was named in relation to the appearance of the thing that had been made; and he called the darkness night because this night, which is well known to us, is caused by the absence of the sun over the earth. When the sun sets, we call it evening; when morning begins, we call it day.

Here “night” is the privation of work. Alternatively, night itself is called a possibility that exists in made things, from which they can come to be even if they are not changed.

[Col. 1120D]

D. “And there was evening and morning, one day” (ibid.). How is this to be understood?

M. What is evening except the completion of each individual work, and what is morning except the beginning of the works that follow?

AUGUSTINE.

D. You assert that the first day was the spiritual creature. How, then, did it have evening and morning?

M. Every creature, before it came to be in its own time, was in the Word of God, first to be known by the angels and then to be made in its own time. Therefore the creature’s knowledge of itself was evening, but in God it was morning, because the creature itself is seen more fully in the Lord than it is seen in itself. It is seen more fully in the art by which it was made than in itself, which was made.

For this reason the evangelist John says, “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3–4). All things, therefore, that were made and do not possess life are life in the Word of God, but are not life in themselves. Heaven, earth, and a stone do not possess life, yet in the Lord they are life.

Thus all the principles of creatures live in God, without beginning and unchangeably. Hence they are seen more fully by the holy angels in the Word of God, where they are life, than in themselves, because the knowledge of the angels, in comparison with God, grows dim, as it were, toward evening.

Thus there was a second day in the knowledge of the firmament; a third in the knowledge of the separation of earth and sea; a fourth in the knowledge of the sun, moon, and stars; a fifth in the knowledge of reptiles and animals; and a sixth in the knowledge of beasts of burden, wild animals, and man himself.

The knowledge was not produced six times on one day, which we understand to be the spiritual creature, that is, the angelic creature. It was made sixfold because of the perfection of the number six. But I shall gather something for you from the Holy Scriptures concerning the number and perfection of the number six. Listen willingly, and prepare yourself entirely to hear.

One cannot be divided in numbers; from it every number arises. Therefore two can be divided. If one is its part, then the division of two is into one; the division of three is also into one. What else does this number show except the Trinity who is God? For although there are three persons, they are believed to exist in the unity of one nature.

Four has two parts: its fourth is one, and its middle is two. One and two make three. Behold its parts; it neither exceeds them nor is completed by them, and therefore it is an imperfect number.

Five has only one part, which is its fifth. Six, therefore, is a perfect number because it is completed by its parts. It has one, which is its sixth; two, which is its third; and three, which is its half. One, two, and three make six.

Because of the perfection of this number, God worked on six days to make the whole creation. These three parts of the number six show us the Trinity God, who made the whole creation in number, measure, and weight.

We frequently find the perfection of the number six to be of great importance in the Holy Scriptures, especially in the Lord’s single death and his single resurrection. The death of our Lord Jesus Christ was not in the soul but only in the flesh. Our death, however, is both in the flesh and in the soul: in the soul because of sin, and in the flesh because of the punishment of sin.

Because he had no sin in his soul, he died only in the flesh, and this because of the likeness of sinful flesh that he had taken from Adam. His death, therefore, was single, while ours is twofold. His resurrection too is single, whereas our resurrection is twofold.

His death of the flesh and his resurrection; our death of the flesh and his resurrection; our death of the soul and his resurrection: our two deaths and two resurrections make four. Add our four to the Lord’s one death and one resurrection, and they make six.

Thus the Lord’s single portion and our double portion make three, and the number six has three parts, as we said above. For the thirty-six hours during which the Lord was in the underworld correspond to this single and double portion. Twelve were daylight hours, and twenty-four were nighttime hours. The twenty-four correspond to our double death, and the twelve hours to the Lord’s single death.

Indeed, his birth also has the number six. The Jews assert in the Gospel that the temple was built in forty-six years; this is understood of the Lord’s body. The forty-six years stand for days. They say that an infant is formed in the womb in forty-six days and thereafter continues to grow until the day of birth.

Forty-six times six makes 276, which makes nine months and ten days. Count, therefore, from the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when the Lord suffered—which is also believed to be when he was conceived—up to the eighth day before the Kalends of January, and you will find 276 days, a number established through the number six.

What shall we say about the woman in the Gospel whom Satan had bent double for eighteen years, and whom the Lord healed? Those years too contain the number six: three times six, ten and eight. That woman signifies the human race, which in the sixth age of the world he freed from captivity to the devil.

The first age was from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth from the Babylonian captivity to John the Baptist and the coming of the Lord the Savior; the sixth is the age now in progress, until the Most High comes for judgment.

In the sixth age, therefore, the human race is restored to the image of God. The eighteen years clearly signify not only six ages but also three periods: one before the Law, another under the Law, and a third under grace.

The year itself is also contained in the number six, for it has 365 and a quarter days. Six times sixty is 360; there remain five days and a quarter—five days of the sixth month—and yet, if you reckon that quarter as a day, the parts together make six.

Behold, insofar as God has deigned to help me, I have rendered an account of the perfection of the number six—not as much as I wished, but as much as I could.

## HERE BEGINS THE DISCUSSION OF THE SECOND DAY

“God also said, ‘Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters’” (Gen. 1:6).

AUGUSTINE [Note: [Col. 1121D] *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 2, chapters 3 and following].

[Col. 1122D]

D. The order and weight of the elements do not permit there to be a substance of water above the heavens. Water yields to earth, air yields to water, and fire yields to air. It is wholly impossible that the second element, water, should be above the fourth, fire. How, then, was it said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters”?

M. Whatever those waters may be, and of whatever kind they are, which Scripture says are above the heavens, let us have no doubt that they are there. Just as these clouds, which are certainly borne above the air, so I think it possible that thin and subtle waters are borne above the heaven.

[Col. 1123A]

For from the weight of the elements many philosophers, mocking the resurrection of the flesh, say that it cannot happen that a human being, who was certainly made from earth, should be in heaven. But Truth refutes them: it causes many earthly animals to fly in the air, and it causes fire—which is certainly the fourth element—to exist in the earth.

Therefore God’s power, which is shown capable of doing these things, can cause both man and water to exist above heaven.

But yielding to such arguments from opponents, one of our writers made a praiseworthy attempt to demonstrate the existence of waters above the heavens, so that he might establish the credibility of Scripture from visible and perceptible natures. First, he showed what was easiest: that this air is called heaven. For this reason we speak of a clear or cloudy heaven, and the flying creatures are called “the birds of heaven.”

After he had established that this air is called heaven, he wished it to be understood that it was called the firmament for no other reason than that its interval divides between the vapors of the waters and those waters which flow more thickly upon the earth. Thus he wished to show that the heaven between water and water is the air lying between the moist vapors from which the clouds above gather and the seas spread below.

Nevertheless, it may be thought that the proper weights of the elements do not prevent waters from existing even above that lofty heaven, in the minute particles by which they were also able to exist above this expanse of air. For they themselves persuade us by an extremely subtle argument that there is no body, however small, in which division comes to an end.

Therefore, if water can, as we see, be reduced to such tiny drops that they are carried vaporously above this air, why could it not also hang above that heaven, in lighter drops and lighter vapors?

Some of our people also attempt to refute them from the qualities and courses of the stars themselves. They assert that the star which they call Saturn is extremely cold and completes the zodiacal circle in thirty years.

They are therefore asked where its coldness comes from, since it ought to be hotter in proportion as it is carried through a higher heaven. For without doubt, when a rounded mass is driven by circular motion, its inner parts move more slowly and its outer parts more quickly. Whatever moves more quickly is certainly hotter.

Consequently, the star mentioned ought to have been hot rather than cold. Its coldness, therefore, is surely caused by the nearness of the waters established above the heavens.

The question is also commonly raised what form and shape the heaven should be believed to have: whether heaven, like a sphere, encloses the earth on every side, balanced at the center of the world, or whether it covers it from above on one side like a disk.

But someone says: How is it not contrary to those who attribute the figure of a sphere to heaven that our writings say, “He stretches out heaven like a skin”? One may answer that skin is stretched not only flat but also into a rounded cavity, for a wineskin and a bladder are also skin.

AMBROSIUS [Note: [Col. 1124D] Read “Augustine.”]

[Col. 1124A]

Some of the brethren also raise a question about the motion of heaven: does it stand still or does it move? For if it moves, they say, how can it be the firmament?

Let them know from this that the name “firmament” does not compel us to think that heaven stands still. It may be understood to have been called the firmament not because of standing but because of firmness, or because it is an impassable boundary between the waters above and below.

Yet this must be understood: the stars revolve, while heaven stands firm, as the poet says:

> The substance of heaven, undefiled for its own age.

We judge that the nature of the waters there is suspended not in vaporous thinness but in icy solidity, to temper the natures of the stars, lest they scorch the creatures of God placed below them by excessive heat.

We say, therefore, of those waters themselves that the smallest drops, gathered together into one, form a single collection. Because of the heaviness of their weight, the air cannot support them; rather, by spreading downward according to their weight, it gives them passage. This is rain.

They therefore wish to understand as heaven between water and water the air that lies between the moist vapors from which the clouds gather above and the seas spread below.

The second heaven is that which we see through the spirit, from which the disk filled with animals and sent to Peter descended in the ecstasy of his mind.

The third heaven is that which we know with the mind, so secret and remote—either wholly purified or snatched away from the senses of the flesh—that those things which are in that heaven are able, in the love of the Holy Spirit, ineffably to see the very substance of God, the Word through whom all things were made.

ISIDORE.

Let the heretics finally cease their madness and, confounded, acknowledge that he who could create all things from nothing could also establish that nature of waters in heaven with icy solidity.

Since they themselves say that the sphere revolves, glittering with blazing stars, did divine providence not necessarily arrange that water should overflow within and above the sphere of heaven, to temper the fires of that burning axis?

ANOTHER PASSAGE.

[Note: [Col. 1124D] Isidore on Genesis, chapter 2.]

“On the second day,” he says, “God established the firmament”—that is, the solidity of the Holy Scriptures. For in the Church the divine Scriptures are understood as the firmament, because heaven “will be folded up like a book.”

“And he separated the waters above this firmament”—that is, the heavenly peoples of the angels, who do not need to receive this firmament so that, by reading, they may hear the word of God. They always see and love him.

But he placed this firmament of his law over the weakness of the lower peoples, so that, by looking upward to it, they may learn how to distinguish between carnal and spiritual things, as between the waters above and the waters below.

“And there was evening and morning, the second day.”

## A QUESTION ARISES ABOUT THE THIRD DAY

[Col. 1125A]

D. “But God said, ‘Let the waters under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear’” (Gen. 1:9). Here too a question arises. If water covered the whole earth, there was no place for the waters to gather, since water covered the whole earth. How, then, does Scripture say, “Let the waters under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear”?

M. Water covered the whole earth like an exceedingly thin mist, which afterward was brought together and collected into one place, so that the appearance of the earth might become visible. Yet the earth, sinking down over a great extent, could also have provided hollow places to receive the waters as they flowed together, so that the dry land might appear.

AMBROSIUS.

[Col. 1125B]

We briefly remind those whom the question of when the appearance of the waters and the earth was created does not happen to move: let them understand that on this day nothing was made except the separation of these two.

When it was said, before the enumeration of the days, that “the earth was empty and void,” Scripture was indicating what kind of earth God had made. Since it had already said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” nothing else should be understood by these words except that it wished to suggest the formlessness of corporeal matter—provided that a dull understanding does not creep in and attempt to separate matter and form in time because Scripture separates them in its words.

ANOTHER PASSAGE FROM ABOVE.

[Col. 1125C]

D. “Let the waters under heaven be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.” Why, then, did he not say, “Let the dry land become visible,” or “Let the gathered water become visible”?

M. Because these are closer to the same formlessness than the heavenly bodies, or because from these, through the enumeration of the days, the weaker things are formed, he did not wish the command to be introduced in the same manner as with the things above.

FROM THE SAME SOURCE.

Spiritually. [Note: [Col. 1125D] Isidore on Genesis, chapter 2.]

“On the third day,” he says, “he gathered the lower waters, which are salty, into one place.” These are unbelieving people, shaken by the storm of desires and the waves of carnal temptations, and enclosing bitterness within themselves, as it were.

“And he separated the dry land from them”—namely, the people thirsting for the fountain of life. Thereafter he fixed the boundaries of the proud and restrained them, so that they might not disturb the dry land—that is, the soul thirsting for God—with the turbulent waves of their iniquities.

Thus it may germinate the fruits of good works according to their kind: loving its neighbor in the assistance of bodily needs, possessing within itself seed according to likeness, so that from its own weakness it may suffer with those in need and come to their aid.

It also produces a tree of strong growth and bearing fruit—that is, a benefaction by which one who suffers injury may be snatched from the hand of the powerful, while the shelter of protection is supplied through the strong support of just judgment.

The text continues:

“And God called the dry land Earth, and the gathering of the waters he called Seas” (Gen. 1:10).

Jerome, in the book of *Hebrew Questions*. It should be noted that every gathering of waters, whether salty or fresh, is called “seas” according to the idiom of the Hebrew language. Porphyry therefore falsely accuses the Evangelists of calling the Lake of Gennesaret “the sea” in order to manufacture a miracle for the ignorant, namely, that the Lord walked upon the sea, since every lake and every gathering of waters is called “seas.”

The text continues:

“And God saw that it was good, and he said, ‘Let the earth bring forth green grass,’ and so forth, up to ‘and it was so’” (Gen. 1:11).

“And the earth brought forth green grass, producing seed according to its kind.” [Note: [Col. 1126D] Gregory, *Moralia*, book 29, chapter 2.]

What is signified in this passage by grass except good action, even though we accept historically that this took place in the creation of the world? Nevertheless, we appropriately understand that the earth prefigured the Church, which germinated green grass when, made fertile by the word of God, it brought forth works of mercy.

The text continues:

And a tree producing fruit according to its kind, each having seed according to its species (Gen. I, 11). [Note: [Col. 1126D] Gregory, *Moralia*, book V, chapter 35.] A tree produces seed according to its own species when our mind gathers from itself a consideration directed toward another and brings forth the germ of a righteous work. Hence a certain wise man says: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV, 16). Hence the Gospel says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII, 12); as though it were plainly saying: Look upon your own kind in another, and from yourselves recognize what you ought to offer to others. And, as we said above, the earth signifies the Church, which both refreshes us with the nourishment of the word and guards us with the shelter of protection. By speaking it feeds, and by assisting it protects, so that it may bring forth not merely the grass of refreshment, but also, with the fruit of good works, the tree of protection.

AUGUSTINE.

D. When God said, “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation bearing seed and fruit trees,” when did he make the fruitless trees, or thorns and thistles?

[Col. 1126D] M. God made everything simultaneously, as Scripture says: “He who lives forever created all things together.” Therefore fruitless trees should in no way be called fruitless if they bring human beings assistance in some way. Indeed, if we do not find in them something to eat, we find something medicinal, and we find something useful for other purposes. Consider for yourself how many benefits they provide. Fruit-bearing trees are so called from enjoyment (*fruendo*); but if we can obtain some assistance from every tree, then rightly we call no tree fruitless. As for thistles and thorns, although they arise after human sin for the sake of toil, as Scripture says, “Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you,” it should nevertheless not be said that they first arose from the earth at that time, since they had already been made for the food of cattle and birds, not produced to increase the punishment of humanity.

“And God saw that it was good, and it was evening and morning, the third day” (Gen. I, 13).

Whenever this statement occurs to you, remember the explanation of the first day that we set out as follows: “If God suddenly saw the light in this way, that it was good,” and so forth.

BEGINNING OF THE FOURTH DAY.

“God also said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them give light upon the earth” (Gen. I, 14).

D. Did time not exist before this?

IN THE HEXAEMERON.

[Col. 1127B] M. Who does not see how obscurely it is stated that time began on the fourth day, as though the preceding three days could have passed without time, although they had the time of their own creation? Yet those three days did not have the divisions marked out by the heavenly bodies. Many inquire, with great loquacity, what kind of moon was made: whether it was a new moon or a full moon. But I shall say plainly that, whether God made a new moon or a full moon, he made it perfect. Everything that, in the course of its natural development and at the appropriate times, somehow emerges and unfolds was already contained in hidden form beforehand—not in bodily appearance or bulk, perhaps, but in the power and principle of its nature. Otherwise, perhaps, a tree that is empty of fruit and stripped of leaves during winter would have to be called imperfect at that time.

Some even dare to say that many stars are equal to the sun or larger than it, but appear small because they are farther away. And if this is so, why do they venerate these stars, which move through the constellations, even more? Why do they not declare them to be the rulers of the constellations? For although someone may insist that the retrogressions of the stars, or perhaps their slownesses, are not caused by the sun but by other, more hidden causes, it is nevertheless plainly evident from their books that they assign the sun a pre-eminent power in their delirious speculations, in which, straying from the truth, they suppose a power of the fates.

Since those heavenly bodies are not more powerful than earthly and bodily things with respect to the matters they themselves discuss, let them at least learn this at some point: when many bodies of different kinds—whether animals, grasses, or shrubs—are sown at the same moment in time, and innumerable things are born at the same moment, there are such great differences in their development, actions, and sufferings, not only in different places but even in the same places on earth, that these people truly, as the saying goes, lose sight of the stars if they consider matters in this way.

We must therefore admit that whenever they speak truly, they speak under the influence of some exceedingly hidden impulse, which human minds undergo without knowing it. When this occurs in order to deceive human beings, it is the activity of deceiving spirits. They are permitted to know certain truths about temporal matters: partly through the keenness of a subtler sense, since they possess greater vitality in more subtle bodies; partly through more cunning experience, because of the great length of their lives; and partly through the holy angels, who learn these things from almighty God, and who reveal them to the spirits at his command. He distributes human merits with the most hidden integrity of justice.

Sometimes these same wicked spirits also foretell, as though by divination, things that they themselves are going to do. It follows:

“And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars. And he placed them in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth, to rule the day and the night, and to divide the light from the darkness” (Gen. I, 16).

D. I ask you to explain how these things are to be understood according to their meaning.

ISIDORE.

M. [Note: [Col. 1127D] Isidore, *Commentary on Genesis*, chapter 2.] On the fourth day, the lights fixed in the firmament of the law shone forth: namely, the evangelists and teachers, joined to holy Scripture by their exposition and displaying the light of wisdom to all those below. At the same time there also appeared the remaining multitude of shining stars, that is, the abundance of diverse virtues in the Church. Shining in the obscurity of this life as in the night, they divide within the firmament of Scripture visible things from intelligible things, as it were between the light of the perfect and the darkness of the little ones. They are signs of virtues and miracles. They also exist for times, days, and years, because preachers live and pass away at their appointed times; but the word of the Lord will stand forever.

D. Why did the earth first bring forth vegetation, and only afterward were the lights made?

[Col. 1128C] M. Because after good works comes the illumination of light, by which to contemplate the appearance of divine power.

“And God saw that it was good, and it was evening and morning, the fourth day” (Gen. I, 18).

D. Why did he mention evening and morning, but say nothing about the night?

M. What else, then, should we call the night except the absence of light, which seemed to remain between evening and morning? Or is it because the first light signified the creation of the angels, who, contemplating their Creator with the most harmonious love and without the blindness of ignorance, never cease praising their Creator forever? Yet at the beginning and at the completion of the work they clearly understood what is called evening and morning.

BEGINNING OF THE FIFTH DAY.

[Col. 1128D]

“God also said: Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature having a living soul, and the flying creature above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven” (Gen. I, 20).

D. Why, then, did he first adorn the waters with creeping creatures, before adorning the earth with animals?

AMBROSE, IN THE HEXAEMERON.

M. There was a reason why what first appeared visibly should also first receive its adornment. Or it was because at the beginning heaven received its adornment, namely, the angels, when they were created. Likewise the earth received its adornment when he clothed it with grasses and trees. There was therefore a reason why the waters should receive their ornament from creeping creatures, and the air from flying creatures.

D. Why do we often read about the creation of heaven, earth, and sea—when they were created, or how they were created—but Scripture says nothing about the air?

M. [Note: [Col. 1129D] Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book III, chapters 1 and following.] We must not suppose that Scripture omitted any element, unless it is because it is customary for divine Scripture to call the whole world “heaven and earth.” Therefore the air must be considered to belong to heaven and earth. Whatever is humid or spread out like vapor belongs to the earth; whatever is calm and tranquil is said to belong to heaven.

That the air is like water, and is shown to be enriched by its exhalations, is evident from the fact that it produces the breath of a storm—that is, a cloud. The air is so close to heaven, in which the lights are found, that it too receives the name “heaven.” For when the psalm says, “Praise him, heavens of heavens” (Ps. CXLVIII, 4), it sufficiently appears that this air is called not only heaven but also heavens, just as lands are called “earths,” although there is one earth.

We read in one of those writings that are called canonical epistles that these aerial heavens once perished in the flood. I do not know how this can be understood except as referring to the quality of this denser air being changed into the nature of water.

Therefore, in creating the inhabitants of this lower part of the world, which is often mentioned as a whole under the name “earth,” it was appropriate that animals should first be produced from the waters, and afterward from the earth. As we have already said, the air is like water, since it is shown to be enriched by its exhalations. For this reason it is not written, “Let the waters bring forth creeping creatures possessing living souls, and let the air bring forth flying creatures that fly above the earth”; rather, both kinds of living creatures are said to have been produced from the waters.

Whatever is watery—whether it is fluid and undulating in a shifting way, or thinned and suspended like vapor, so that the former appears assigned to creeping creatures and the latter to flying creatures—is nevertheless attributed in both cases to a moist nature.

For this reason some people, with very subtle reasoning, distinguish the five bodily senses according to the four customary elements. They say that the eyes belong to fire, and the ears to pure air; smell belongs to moist air, taste to bodily humors, and touch to the earthly element. Thus all the elements are present in all things, but each receives its name from that which it possesses in greater measure.

When the body becomes excessively cold through the deprivation of heat, the sense is dulled, because the movement that comes from heat and exists in the body grows sluggish. Fire affects air, air affects moisture, and moisture affects earthly things; in other words, what is subtler penetrates what is denser. The subtler anything is in bodily nature, the nearer it is to spiritual nature.

The soul, however, in which the power of sensation resides, although it is not corporeal, exercises the power of sensation through a subtler body. It therefore possesses movement in all the senses through the subtlety of fire, but it does not reach the same thing in all of them. In sight, restrained heat reaches as far as its light. In hearing, it reaches as far as the more fluid air. In smell, it passes into pure air and reaches the moist exhalation from which this denser atmosphere subsists. In taste, it passes through this as well and reaches the denser bodily moisture. Once this has been penetrated and traversed, when it reaches earthly heaviness, it activates the final sense, that of touch.

The one who narrated the heavenly lights first, then the animals of the waters, and last the animals of the earth therefore did not fail to understand the natures of the elements. He did not omit the air; rather, he calls its purer part heaven and its denser part earth.

That we also perceive waters and winds by touch is because the solidity of earth is mixed into all the elements. Birds therefore fly in heaven—but in that heaven which the psalm also includes under the name “earth.” They do not fly in the firmament itself, but according to the firmament.

Nor am I unaware that certain philosophers assigned animals to their respective elements. They said that earthly animals included not only those that crawl and walk upon the earth, but also birds, since birds too rest upon the earth when wearied by flying. They said that aerial animals are demons, and heavenly animals are gods; the latter we call partly lights and partly angels. They assign fish and creatures of their kind to the waters, so that no element may be without its own animals.

The elements are divided into two for undergoing effects—moisture and earth—and two for producing effects—air and fire. Air extends from the boundary of luminous heaven to the fluid waters and the uncovered earth. Yet moist exhalations do not darken all of its space, but only as far as the point where earth already begins to be called by that name, as in the psalm: “Praise the Lord from the earth” (Ps. CXLVIII, 7).

The upper part of the air, because of its pure tranquility, is joined in common peace to heaven, with which it is contiguous, and is called by its name. Perhaps it was in this region that the angels who transgressed with their prince before their transgression—at that time an archangel, now the devil—were located. Some of our people think that they were heavenly or super-heavenly angels. It is not surprising that after their sin they were thrust into this darkness.

Yet in this region there is also air, and it is woven through with a thin moisture. When stirred, it produces winds; when driven with greater force, even fires; when contracted, clouds; when thickened, rain; when the clouds freeze, snow; and when denser clouds freeze more violently, hail. When stretched out, it produces clear weather. These things are administered by hidden commands and by the work of God, who governs all that he has created from the highest to the lowest.

But, as we have already said, air is produced from water. Flying creatures of heaven exist in the air, and for this reason we call birds “birds of heaven.” Demons are said to dwell in the air, and therefore the air is able to bear them, because they use an aerial form. From there they attack the human race, because as soon as they were created they were cast out of God’s sight.

Hence the Savior says in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven.” Here the question rightly arises: How is he said to have fallen, if he did not stand? But we must understand that he did not remain in the fellowship of the holy angels. As soon as he saw himself in the splendor of God, he raised himself in pride and said: “I will ascend into heaven; I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14).

Immediately he was cast down from the height of heaven into the air, together with all his followers, because they did not persevere in divine love as did those who were established in it, so that, even if they wished to sin, they could not. At the beginning, they too had free choice, just as the human race appears to have. But those who fell through their own free choice received God’s sentence: if they wished to be restored, they could not.

D. Again Scripture says: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth” (John VIII, 44). Why a murderer?
