[Col. 1131B] M. Because he first slaughtered Adam in paradise when he persuaded him to eat the fruit, and from being immortal [Perhaps: “from immortality”] he became mortal. For this reason he slaughtered the human race until the coming of the Savior.

D. How did he not stand in the truth?

M. Because he did not merit receiving what had been promised to him: that he would remain forever with his Creator together with the other angels. Instead, he was cast down to earth with his followers. There, without doubt, they suffer punishment, because sidereal fire rules over them in the air, and it has been assigned to them as a kind of prison according to their nature, until the time of the day of judgment comes, when they will be cast into everlasting fire. It follows:

“And God created the great sea creatures and every living and moving soul that the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every flying creature according to its kind” (Gen. I, 21).

D. I wish to know when the smallest fish and animals were created, including the little worms that Scripture does not mention. Since an explanation must be sought—from the largest elephant down to the smallest worm—of where they came from, Scripture has said nothing here.

M. We must understand that when God separated the waters from the waters, the smallest animals that are produced from water already existed by their nature in those waters. The worms that are found in the bodies of the dead possess in those very bodies the power by which they are born. Fish are produced from the waters, since he says, “Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature possessing a living soul.”

[Col. 1131D] D. If water covered the earth, did the earth cover the water? I ask you to explain.

M. Water covered the earth. As though some part of the earth had slipped over the water, the water was immediately forced out, and the earth returned to its place.

D. How does the psalm say that “he founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers” (Ps. XXIII, 2), if water covered the earth?

M. It speaks of the higher earth, where the mountains appear to be, or it refers to the islands, where the land is higher than the water. But this should be understood more according to its meaning: the simple in the Church are founded upon the prudent.

They are therefore called living waters, because they support those whom they see to be lower or weaker than themselves. The difference between holy rusticity and holy simplicity is as great as the distance between the moon and the stars of heaven. It follows:

“And he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea” (Gen. I, 22).

D. Why did these animals merit receiving a blessing, as did humanity?

M. That is, so that we may understand this blessing to remain in the other animals.

“And let the birds multiply upon the earth. And it was evening and morning, the fifth day.”

BEGINNING OF THE QUESTIONS ABOUT THE SIXTH DAY.

“And God said: Let the earth bring forth a living creature according to its kind: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their species. And it was so” (Gen. I, 24).

AMBROSE.

D. We must ask whether these poisonous animals possessed poison at the beginning, when they were created, as they do now.

M. We must undoubtedly understand that, just as they were then created, so they remain. Yet at the beginning they did not possess the power to cause harm, as we can demonstrate from serpents. When the viper attacked Paul’s hand, it did him no harm, because it had the power to attack but did not have the power to injure. Likewise, when Daniel was thrown into the lions’ den, the lions did him no harm.

Alternatively, these poisonous animals were created to terrify humanity, whom God knew would sin, so that humanity might understand the punishments of hell. For elsewhere he says: “Their worm does not die, and their fire is not extinguished” (Mark IX, 44). Otherwise the beasts would harm one another, although they have no basis for vengeance arising from original sin. [Note: [Col. 1131D] Saint Ambrose does not appear to say this in book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 6, where he merely says that poisonous animals were created by God to terrify human beings. [Col. 1132D]]

AMBROSE. On the creation of humanity.

“And God saw that it was good and said: Let us make humanity in our image and likeness. And God made humanity in the image of God” (Gen. I, 26).

D. First, we briefly state that it should not be understood indifferently that in the other works it says, “God said, Let there be,” whereas here God said, “Let us make.”

M. [Note: [Col. 1132D] Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book III, chapter 19.] This was to intimate, so to speak, the plurality of persons, on account of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; yet he immediately indicated that the unity of the Godhead was to be understood when he said: “And God made humanity in his image.”

Here also we must not pass over the fact that, after saying “in our image,” he immediately added, “and let humanity have dominion over the fish of the sea and the other animals devoid of reason.” Thus we understand that humanity was made in the image of God in that respect in which it surpasses irrational animals. That respect is reason itself, or the mind, or understanding.

Although it may be argued with the greatest subtlety that the human mind—in which humanity was made in the image of God—constitutes a certain rational life divided between contemplation of eternal truth and administration of temporal things, and that in this way it becomes, as it were, male and female, with one part giving counsel and the other obeying, it is nevertheless not correct to call this the image of God except insofar as it adheres to the contemplation of unchanging Truth. In symbolic reference to this, the apostle Paul calls only the man the image and glory of God.

ELSEWHERE, ISIDORE.

“And God made humanity in his image,” that is, for eternity and immortality. But “in his likeness” means that humanity would possess intellectual understanding, unlike animals, which do not know how to distinguish between good and evil.

ALSO, AUGUSTINE.

[Col. 1133B] D. What are we to understand by what is written in Genesis: “Let us make humanity in our image and likeness”?

M. In the mind, that is, in reason and understanding. When the mind thinks about eternal things, it is to be called the image of God. In thinking about eternal things, it is a man, as the apostle Paul says: “A man ought not to cover his head” (I Cor. XI, 7), since he is the image of the glory of God. That is, the more he extends himself toward what is eternal, the more he is formed according to the image of God; and therefore he should not be restrained from directing and controlling himself toward it.

But when he does or thinks about temporal things, he is called a woman. He is not then to be called the image of God, and for this reason he ought to cover his head, lest his advance toward lower things become excessive, and lest, while doing what is lawful, he desire what is unlawful.

D. “And the Lord God created humanity in his image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Gen. I, 27). Why does he say that the female was created together with the male, when she had not yet been formed?

M. Because she was going to proceed from Adam. Thus many things are hidden in the seed of a tree: first it is fixed in the root, then in the nature of the tree, afterward in the spreading of the branches, and from there in the greenness of the leaves, and so forth. In the same way, the female was hidden in Adam’s body, because she was to be fashioned from his rib. It follows.

“And he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and all living creatures that move upon the earth” (Gen. I, 28).

D. Why did humanity merit receiving this blessing?

M. So that humanity might not appear blameworthy in begetting children, and so that it might be declared that no sin would arise from it if marriage were entered lawfully.

D. If Adam was created so that he would remain immortal, why was it said to them, “Increase and multiply”?

M. This must be understood to mean that they were not to beget children according to the lust of the flesh or through any evil desire—not as people who give birth to children in pain, but as someone commands his limbs to perform some task, whether his hand in working or his foot in walking. In the same way they were to beget offspring in paradise.

D. But if they were to beget offspring in this way, why did they not come together in paradise, before they had been cast out, and beget children?

M. Because as soon as the woman was created, she transgressed, and she was cast down from lofty immortality into the depths below.

D. How, then, were their bodies to be changed if they were to remain immortal?

M. This is to be understood as follows: if they had not sinned, they could not have died at all. But after that number had been completed, their bodies were to be changed for the better, according to the number of the angels.

AUGUSTINE.

[Col. 1134B] D. Was the first human being made mortal or immortal?

M. Mortal in some respects and immortal in others. The first human being therefore had a body like ours, but without sin. He did not yet possess a law in his members resisting the law of his mind; he deserved that only after his transgression.

Adam therefore had an animal body, but, through the power of that tree which sustained him and which in paradise received the name “tree of life,” he would neither grow old nor perish. Consequently, if he had kept God’s commandment, he would afterward have been changed, by the merit of obedience, into that spiritual body which is promised to the saints in the resurrection.

Thus he could have avoided death if he had remained attached to faithful obedience toward God. He was not made unable to die, as are the other natures that cannot die at all; rather, he was made in such a way that obedience would make him immortal, while disobedience would make him mortal.

Again.

D. If Adam was immortal or mortal—and if mortal, how immortal; and if an animal, how spiritual? Or why did he share food in common with the other animals?

M. He was mortal and immortal. He was mortal because he could die; immortal because he could avoid death. If he had not sinned, he could not have died at all; but after he sinned, he became mortal.

Again.

He was mortal and immortal. He was mortal by his condition, immortal by the benefit of God, which was provided for him by the tree of life. When he sinned, he was cast out from that tree so that he could die.

D. Why, then, have we who have been reborn through Christ not received the very immortality that Adam had before his sin?

M. We did not receive what we lost in Adam, namely, an animal body; rather, we received something much better, inasmuch as the spiritual is superior to the bodily. Hence the Apostle says: “The animal body is sown; the spiritual body rises” (I Cor. XV, 44).

We did not receive the immortality of the spiritual body, but we received the righteousness from which Adam fell through sin. Concerning this the Apostle also says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. IV, 23–24).

We will therefore be renewed from the oldness of sin, not into the former animal body that Adam possessed, but into something better, namely, a spiritual body, when we become equal to the angels of God in heavenly dwelling. [Note: [Col. 1135D] Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book VI, chapter 24.]

We will also be renewed in the spirit of our mind according to the image of him who created us, which Adam lost through sin. We will also be renewed in the flesh, when this corruptible body puts on incorruption and this mortal body puts on immortality, so that it may be a spiritual body.

Adam had not yet been changed into this body, but he was going to be changed, because in the body we bear the image of the earthly human being, while in the mind we bear the image of the heavenly. Hence the Apostle says again: “If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual body, as it is written: The first human being, Adam, became a living soul; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But the spiritual was not first, rather the animal, and afterward the spiritual. The first human being was from the earth, earthly; the second human being was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly” (I Cor. XV, 44–47).

Let us also put on the image of him who is from heaven. We put on the image of the earthly human being from the beginning of the human race; but we now bear the image of the heavenly human being by faith, and we believe that we shall possess it in the resurrection.

D. Why did he not bless the trees and grasses, but humanity and the animals?

M. He blessed these latter for the propagation of offspring, or because of the distinction between male and female, or because trees do not possess the sense by which they perceive or understand. Animals perceive but do not understand; humanity both perceives and understands. Therefore he did not say to the trees, “Increase and multiply.”

“And God said: Behold, I have given you every plant bearing seed upon the earth,” and so forth, up to: “And it was so. And God saw all that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. I, 29).

D. Since God created all things good, and since nothing exists that was not made by him, where does evil come from?

AUGUSTINE.

M. Evil is not a nature; rather, it has received this name from the privation of good. Good can exist without evil, but evil cannot exist without good, nor can evil exist where good has not existed. Accordingly, we speak of a good angel and an evil angel: the good is the angel, the evil is the defect; the good is the human being, the evil is the one who is defective.

Therefore, when we say “good,” we praise nature; when we say “evil,” we identify not nature but the defect that affects a good nature.

“And it was evening and morning, the sixth day” (Gen. II, 1). It follows:

“Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment.”

BEGINNING OF THE SEVENTH DAY.

[Col. 1136A]

JEROME. [Note: [Col. 1135D] *Hebrew Questions*.]

“And God completed on the sixth day his works that he had made.”

In Hebrew it has “the seventh day” in place of “the sixth day.” We have therefore silenced the Jews who glory in the leisure of the Sabbath, since the Sabbath was already dissolved at the beginning, when God worked on the Sabbath, completing his works on it and blessing the day itself, because on it he completed everything.

D. “He blessed the seventh day,” it says, “and sanctified it” (Gen. II, 3). Why did he bless the seventh day, on which he created nothing?

M. So that he might not appear to be in need, as when a human being, tired after labor, says, “Thanks be to God, I have completed my work.” God did not act in this way. Rather, he blessed the day on which he created nothing, to show that creating all things involved no labor for him, since God merely said, “Let it be,” and they were made. For this reason he rested on the seventh day, so that he might make us rest in him.

AUGUSTINE.

D. Since rest comes only after labor, why is God said to have rested? Was he also wearied by his work, so that he was said to rest?

M. God did not rest in any creature as though he needed that creature as a good by which he might become happier, but he rested in himself. Indeed, he is not said to have rested on one of the days, but after the works of the sixth day. Hence it clearly appears that God made no creature out of need, but solely by his good will. If he rested in some creature, he would make some creature because he needed it. Therefore, since he made no creature out of need, he rested in no creature.

When Scripture says that God rested on the seventh day from all his works that he had made, I think this can be understood to mean that he did not rest because he needed that good in order to become happier. Rather, he brought the seventh day itself—that is, the angelic nature—into his rest, so that they might see in God that, just as every creature was formed, so also no creature had been made out of need, but solely from goodness. This, I think, can be understood as the rest of God.

The rest of God can also be understood in another way: namely, when he makes us rest after good works, according to the meaning of what God said to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. XXII, 12), that is, “I have made you know.” In the same way, here God is understood to rest when he grants rest to his saints.

Again, in another way.

[Note: [Col. 1136D] *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book IV, chapter 12.] God is said to rest from creating new creatures because, after the production of the works of the six days, he thereafter created no new creature. For when he says, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V, 17), this is understood not as creating a new creature, but as governing what he created.

JUNILIUS.

God is said to have rested on the seventh day, not from creating, since every creature is renewed daily by his disposition and providence, as is evident. Rather, this was signified: after those six days, he created no substantial species unknown to the world, nor any new and untried nature. For this day is the first, the second, and the last, because it is a repetition of the seventh day.

D. Why did he not bless the day on which he created the angelic light, or the day on which he completed everything?

M. He did not sanctify the day on which he began to do this, nor the day on which he completed it, lest his action appear to have been a source of joy either in the things being made or in the things already made. Rather, he sanctified the day on which he rested from them in himself, and through the seventh day he showed this rest to us.

Yet he himself was never without that rest. He signified that his rest is not attained until after the completion of the work. For this reason it is recognized that evening did not follow upon this day, since our rest, through the perfection of the work, will exist forever in joy. It follows:

“These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created, on the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth, and every plant of the field before it arose upon the earth, and every herb of the region before it sprouted” (Gen. II, 4).

D. We must inquire whether all these things were made in a single day, or over six days, as Scripture relates. And if they were made over six days, how is holy Scripture true when it says, “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclus. XVIII, 1)?

M. He created everything simultaneously according to the substance of things, but not simultaneously according to the appearance of their form. Just as a mother who nourishes an infant in her womb waits for it to grow strong, so the Lord accommodated himself to the slowness of human understanding.

In the beginning, all things were created in his presence, but they did not immediately come into visible form. When he said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” everything was then made in his presence, as we have said: whatever was going to arise from heaven and earth. Although he wished to divide these things according to their visible form over six days—for example, Scripture says that on the fourth day he placed the stars in heaven—they were nevertheless made in heaven in his presence on the first day, and on the fourth day they came into visible form.

For just as many things are hidden in a grain of seed—root, bark, leaves, fruit, and many other things that come from the tree—so all these things were first hidden with God and afterward came into visible form.

[Col. 1137D] D. If he created everything simultaneously, how is it true that we read, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V, 17)?

M. Let your learned judgment consider that, although at that time he created everything simultaneously, nevertheless he governs it daily by watering, planting, building, and other such activities. For just as a man who works a field, if he abandons it, leaves it uncultivated, so the world created by God cannot exist without God’s governance, according to the apostle Paul: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

Some wish to understand these seven days as the seven gifts of the grace of the Holy Spirit, namely: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of fear of the Lord. They say that through the spirit of wisdom God made heaven and earth; through the spirit of understanding he made the firmament and separated the waters from the waters; through the spirit of counsel he separated the waters from the dry land and caused the earth to sprout; through the spirit of fortitude he placed the luminaries in the firmament of heaven, to divide the day from the night; through the spirit of knowledge he adorned the waters with creeping creatures and the air with flying creatures; through the spirit of piety he clothed the earth with animals, created humanity, and made the other things that follow; and through the spirit of the fear of the Lord he sanctified his work on the seventh day.

So we too ought to imitate within ourselves these seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Through the spirit of wisdom we ought to make heaven and earth—that is, meditate on heavenly things and abandon earthly ones—or separate light from darkness, that is, our perfected works from the darkness of evil works.

Through the spirit of understanding we ought to make a firmament between the lower and upper waters—that is, holy discipline between vices and virtues—so that we do not incline toward vices.

Through the spirit of counsel we ought to separate the waters from the dry land—that is, rejected people from the soul that thirsts for the word of God.

Through the spirit of fortitude we ought to place luminaries in the firmament of heaven—that is, love of God and of neighbor, because Saint John said: “He who hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John 2:1).

Through the spirit of knowledge we ought to adorn the waters with creeping creatures and the other things—that is, send the voice of our hidden heart upward to heaven. Just as fish leap high with their little fins, and the birds of heaven fly through the air, so we too ought to raise our understanding toward higher things.

Through the spirit of piety we ought to make serpents and cattle and the other creatures—that is, possess simplicity and prudence, so that we may discern between good and evil; and, producing the fruit of good works, learn how we may imitate the examples of the saints, or the very truth in whose image we were made.

Through the spirit of the fear of the Lord we ought to rest in the rest of eternal life, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10).

D. “These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created, on the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 2:4). Above, seven days were counted; now one day is named, on which God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field and every plant of the region.

M. By the name of this day, according to prophecy, the whole period of this life is signified, in which heaven and earth were made—that is, in which visible creatures are ordered, governed, and exist. Hence Moses both reported distinctly that everything was created on separate days, and nevertheless added that everything was created simultaneously, saying:

“These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created, on the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it arose on the earth, and every plant of the region.”

For he who had narrated that heaven and earth, the shrub, and the plant were created on different days now declares that they were made on one day, so that he might plainly show that every creature came into existence simultaneously in substance, although it did not emerge simultaneously in form. It follows:

“For the Lord had not caused rain upon the earth, and there was no man to cultivate the earth; but a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth” (Gen. 2:5).

**AUGUSTINE.**

D. If it watered the whole earth, then it also watered the mountains, since the mountains are certainly earth. If it watered the mountains, there was a flood. And how had the earth brought forth green vegetation producing seed? Or how did man dwell on the earth if water covered the whole earth?

M. “A spring” is put in the singular for the plural. If you investigate this carefully, you will frequently find the same usage in the Holy Scriptures. Thus in the Psalm you have: “He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them, and the frog, and it destroyed them” (Ps. 77:46), although there was certainly neither one dog-fly nor one frog. Elsewhere: “The locust came” (Ps. 104:34); he does not say *locusts*, but *the locust*. Here you have the singular number for the plural, in accordance with what the noblest of poets says [Note: [Col. 1139D] *Aeneid* 2.20]:

“...and they fill the belly with armed soldiery.”

Moreover, “spring” was said on account of the unity of nature, so that in it we should understand all the springs that are on the earth, because in some manner they all flow from the nature of one abyss. When he says, “it watered the whole surface of the earth,” he does not mean that it watered the entire earth, but a part of it. A part is signified by the whole, as when we say, “Christ died; Christ rose again,” although he died and rose again only according to the flesh.

Or, as Ambrose says: “A spring was named that, having received the aid of moisture, watered the entire surface of the earth.”

Or, after paradise had been planted, that rupture of the waters was dammed back, and the spring was divided into channels to water the entire surface of the earth, just as now we see waters flow through the beds of rivers and the channels of streams, and, overflowing them, drench the neighboring places. So then, as it were from one spring, many streams proceeded.

Or one spring was named, hidden in a certain hollow of the earth, and from it all springs, small and great, proceed.

D. What, then, is the reason that this spring is plainly nowhere to be found, although it appears to have watered the whole surface of the earth?

M. Perhaps on account of the sin of our first parent, Adam, this spring was withdrawn, so that it might remove the earth’s fertility and impose greater labor upon the human race.

**ITEM ELSEWHERE: ISIDORE**

[Col. 1140A]

[Note: [Col. 1140D] Isidore, *On Genesis*, chapter 3.] “A spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.” The earth is most appropriately called the mother of the Lord, the virgin Mary, concerning whom it is written: “Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45:8). The Holy Spirit watered this earth; in the Gospels he is signified by the name of spring and water.

**ON THE INSPIRATION OF MAN**

“Then the Lord formed man from the mud of the earth” (Gen. 2:7).

D. First, the statement that God fashioned man from the mud of the earth ordinarily raises the question: what sort of mud was it, or what substance is signified by the name “mud”?, I ask you to explain this to me as well.

M. The enemies of the ancient books, who view everything carnally and therefore are always in error, sharply criticize this too: that God fashioned man from mud. They say: “Why did God make man from mud?” Was a better and heavenly material lacking, from which he could make man, so that he would form a fragile and mortal nature from the earth’s impurity?”

They do not understand, first, how many meanings “earth” and “water” have in Scripture. Mud is a mixture of water and earth. We say that the human body, after sin, began to be diseased, fragile, and destined for death. What horrifies them in our body is nothing except the mortality that we deserved by condemnation.

But what is difficult or extraordinary for God, even if he made man from the mud of this earth, in making his body such that it would not be subject to corruption, if man, keeping God’s commandment, had not wished to sin? If we say that the very form of heaven was made from nothing or from unformed matter because we believe in an almighty Craftsman, what is surprising if a body made from whatever sort of mud could be made by an almighty Craftsman such that, before sin, no distress or deprivation would torment man and no corruption would cause him to decay?

Thus it is asked to no purpose from what God made man’s body. If, however, the present passage is speaking of the formation of the body—for I have learned that some of our people understand it in this way—then, after it was said, “God formed man from the mud of the earth,” the words “according to his image and likeness” were not added because the passage is now speaking of the formation of the body. The inner man was signified when it was said, “God made man according to the image of God.”

But even if we now understand man as made from body and soul—not as the beginning of some new work, but as a careful exposition in this passage of what was briefly indicated above—then, if we understand man in this place as made from body and soul, he not implausibly received his name from that mixture of dust. For just as water gathers, glues, and holds earth together when dust is formed from their mixture, so the soul, giving life to the body’s matter, shapes it into harmonious unity and does not allow it to collapse and dissolve.

[Col. 1141A] D. [Note: [Col. 1141D] Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 14.] It may rightly be asked how those causal principles that he implanted in the world, when he first created everything simultaneously, were established. Was it that, as we have observed, all things coming into being—plants and animals—would pass through different spans of time in their formation and growth, according to the diversity of their kinds? Or was it that, as Adam is believed to have been made, they would be formed immediately, without any progression of growth, at mature human age, like water changed into wine and a rod changed into a serpent?

But why should we not believe that they possessed both possibilities, so that what was to result from them would be what the one who would bring it about had willed? For many things are future according to lower causes; but if they are so, they are truly future in God’s foreknowledge. If, however, they exist there otherwise, they are future rather as they exist there, where the one who foreknows cannot be deceived. A future old age is spoken of as present in a young man; yet it is not future if he is destined to die beforehand.

M. This will be so according to the character of the other causes, whether interwoven with the world or reserved in foreknowledge. According to certain causes of future events, Hezekiah was destined to die, but God added fifteen years to his life (Isa. 38:5), doing precisely what he had foreknown before the foundation of the world that he would do and had kept within his will.

For there it existed not only so that Adam could be made in this way, but also so that it was necessary for him to be made in this way. Nevertheless, God does not act against the cause that he unquestionably established willingly, because he does not act against his own will.

If, however, he did not initially fix all causes within the creature that was created, but reserved some in his own will, then those which he reserved in his will do not depend by necessity upon those which he created. Yet they cannot be contrary to those he reserved in his will, because God’s will cannot be contrary to itself.

Thus he established these causes in such a way that the thing whose causes they are could arise from them, but need not do so. He concealed the others in such a way that what he made possible through these causes must arise from those.

It follows:

**ITEM: AUGUSTINE**

D. “And he breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. 2:7). How do we understand this breath if God is incorporeal?

M. [Note: [Col. 1142D] Augustine, book 7 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 11 and following.] This must plainly be understood: just as he did not fashion him with bodily hands, so he did not breathe with a throat or lips. Nevertheless, we must believe and understand—and in no way doubt—that which right faith holds: the soul is from God as a thing he made, not as something of the nature of which he himself is, whether he generated it or brought it forth in some other manner.

As for the philosophers’ opinion concerning the migrations of souls, whatever its truth may be, it does not accord with the Catholic faith to believe that the souls of animals migrate into human beings or those of human beings into animals. For those accounts in which it is said that certain people seemed to remember in whose animal bodies they had been are either false stories, or this was produced in their minds through demonic deception.

If it can happen in dreams that, through a deceptive memory, a man seems to remember having been what he was not, or having done what he did not do, what is surprising if, by some just and hidden judgment of God, demons are permitted to produce something of this sort even in the hearts of those who are awake?

The Manichaeans, who either think themselves Christians or wish to be thought Christians, are worse and more detestable in this opinion concerning the transmigration or revolution of souls than those philosophers of the nations—or any other foolish men who hold this view—in that those others distinguish the nature of the soul from the nature of God. These people, however, while saying that the soul is nothing other than God’s very substance, indeed precisely what God is, do not hesitate to call it so shamefully changeable that there is no kind of grass or worm in which they do not believe it to be mixed, or into which they do not insanely suppose it can be transformed.

Accordingly, since the anterior part of the brain, from which all the senses are distributed, is situated toward the forehead, and since the organs of sensation are, as it were, in the face, I think that this is why it is written that God breathed the breath of life into man’s face.

The anterior part is appropriately placed before the posterior, because the former leads and the latter follows; from the former comes sensation, from the latter movement, just as deliberation precedes action.

And since bodily movement, which follows sensation, cannot occur without intervals of time, while we cannot act through voluntary movement across intervals of time except with the aid of memory, three chambers of the brain are identified. One is anterior, toward the face, from which all sensation comes; another is posterior, toward the crown of the head, from which all movement comes; and a third lies between the two, in which, they demonstrate, memory is active—so that, when movement follows sensation, a person may not connect what must be done with what he is doing if he has forgotten it.

When we ask from what the soul itself exists—that is, from what material, as it were, God made this breath called the soul—nothing corporeal ought to present itself. For just as God surpasses every creature, so the soul surpasses every corporeal creature in the dignity of its nature. Through light and air, which are also preeminent bodies in the world itself and possess greater efficacy for acting than material density for being acted upon, the soul administers the body, as though through things more akin to spirit than moisture and earth.

Corporeal light announces something; but to that to which it announces, it is not the same as the light. This is the soul, to which it announces, not the light that announces. And when it feels bodily affections painfully, it is distressed because its activity—by which it is present to govern the body—is hindered by the body’s disturbed condition; this distress is called pain.

The air infused into the nerves obeys the will so that it may move the limbs, but it is not itself the will. The soul is one thing, therefore, and its bodily services, vessels, or organs are other things—or whatever more suitable names may be given them.

This is made evident by the fact that a person often turns away from everything through intense concentration of thought, so that, while his eyes are open and sound, he does not notice many things placed before them. At times he even forgets where he is coming from and where he is going, and unknowingly passes by the village toward which he was heading: the nature of his body remains sound, but his attention has been summoned elsewhere.

It is believable that every body can be changed into every other body; but it is absurd to believe that any body can be changed into a soul.

Let us consider whether the following might perhaps be true—a view that seems to me more tolerable to human opinion. In those first works in which God created everything simultaneously, he may also have created the soul causally, so that the human soul would come into being when the human body was to be made. For we rightly understand neither the statement “according to his image” except of the soul, nor the statement “male and female” except of the body.

Let it therefore be believed, if no authority or truth of Scripture contradicts it, that man was made on the sixth day in such a way that the cause of his body was already in the elements of the world, while the soul itself had already been created. When the first day was established, it lay hidden in God’s works until, at its proper time, he inserted it into the body formed from mud by breathing—that is, by inspiring it.

If this is so, we shall acknowledge that the soul was not initially created among those things that would have foreknowledge of its future work, whether just or wicked. For God is not to be praised only for those to whom he gave foreknowledge, since he is rightly praised also because he created animals, to which human nature is superior, even in those who sin.

The nature of man is from God; the wickedness by which he entangles himself through misuse of free will is not. Yet if he did not possess free will, he would be less excellent within the order of created things.

We must conceive of a man living justly without foreknowledge of the future, and thus observe how the excellence of a good will is not hindered from living rightly and pleasing God by the fact that he lives in faith without knowledge of what is to come.

Whoever does not want such a creature to exist in the world contradicts God’s goodness; whoever does not want it to suffer punishment for its sins is an enemy of justice.

Through all these testimonies of divine Scripture—whose truthfulness no one doubts except an unbeliever and an impious person—we have been led to say that, from the beginning of the world, God first created everything simultaneously: some things as already-established natures, others as foreknown causes, just as the Almighty made not only present things but also future things, and then rested from the things he had made, so that thereafter, through their administration and governance, he might also create the orders of times and temporal things.

At present, however, concerning the soul that God inspired into man by breathing into his face, I affirm nothing except that it is from God in such a way that it is not God’s substance, and that it is incorporeal—that is, not a body but a spirit. It was not generated from God’s substance, nor did it proceed from God’s substance, but it was made by God. Nor was it made in such a way that the nature of a body or of an irrational soul was transformed into its nature.

**REMAINING QUESTIONS CONCERNING THE NATURE OF THE SOUL**

D. “He breathed into his face the breath of life.” What should we understand by “the breath of life”?

M. This means making the soul, as he says through Isaiah: “The spirit proceeds from me, and I have made every breath” (Isa. 56:16)—that is, every soul.

D. How is it, then, that the soul, which was created innocent, entered a body that God foreknew would sin?

M. Far be it from us to accept that the soul was created for this reason: that it should enter a body which God foreknew would sin, and that it was reserved for this purpose. If that were so, God would be the author of sin; but it is not so.

Rather, we should understand and accept that, with God inspiring it, the soul itself entered voluntarily in order to govern the body, because the body is perceived through the soul; for if the soul is absent, the body is dead.

D. What, then, is the soul? Or, if there is some thing from which souls are made, what is that thing? What is its name? What is its form? What function does it possess among created things? Does it live, or does it not? If it lives, what does it contribute to the affections of the universe? Does it lead a blessed life or a miserable one?

What, then, is the soul? It is not heaven, nor earth, nor air, nor fire, nor water, nor God, nor the stars, nor sight, nor hearing, nor taste, nor the other things—which would take too long to enumerate—that are in heaven and on earth. From where, then, is the soul?

M. The soul is given by God and made from nothing, because man, who was made from earth, returns to earth. Likewise, snow and storms, which are made from water, and air, which draws its substance from the earth, return to water, and again from the earth from which they were taken into air.

The soul, however, has no element to which it may return except its Creator, after it has departed from the body, so that, under his governance, it may receive what it deserves.

D. We must therefore inquire from where the soul comes to a man when he is born.

M. Some say that, just as flesh is born from flesh, so the soul is born from soul. But Scripture nowhere states from where the soul comes to a man when he is born, nor does it state how it was given from the woman’s own soul, as it tells how her flesh was made.

Others, however, hold the better opinion: that each person’s soul is given by God when he is born, as it is written in Isaiah: “The spirit proceeds from me, and I have made every breath” (Isa. 57:16)—that is, every soul. And as it is written in the Psalm: “He fashioned their hearts one by one” (Ps. 32:15).

Others rashly say that all souls were created when God made everything simultaneously, and are hidden in some place until a person is born, at which time his soul is given to him by God.

But in our present circumstances we must not speculate about what permits or does not permit this, or about how the soul is given to man. What Scripture nowhere relates, we cannot discern. The truth has remained silent, and Scripture says nothing else on this matter except how the soul was given by God.

D. From where, then, did our Savior receive his soul?

M. Not from Adam, but from the source from which Adam came—that is, from God. For although he descended from the propagation of sin, he was not conceived from the propagation of sin, because he himself was not sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh. He did not receive from it the guilt of dying—

D. And when the soul has departed from this body, is it corporeal or incorporeal?

M. It is indeed incorporeal.

D. How, then, is it carried if it is incorporeal?

M. It is incorporeal, but similar to bodies.

D. And where is it carried—to a corporeal place or an incorporeal one?

M. To incorporeal places similar to corporeal ones.

D. It is therefore asked: if the soul can exist without the body among the angels in perpetual blessedness without deficiency, why is it necessary for the body to rise again, so that it may clothe itself with that soul, then immortal, which it has now laid aside mortal?

[Col. 1145B] M. The administration of the body is indeed present, by which the soul is held back from proceeding to that highest state until the body rises, so that what is now a burden to it may then be its glory.

D. Why, then, is it necessary that infants whose parents—a Christian father and mother—are Christians be born again through the water of baptism?

M. Because each person is born in original sin, and unless he is reborn through the water of baptism, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.

**ON THE PLANTING OF PARADISE**

Jerome says the following in his book of *Questions*: “And the Lord God planted paradise in Eden, toward the east.” Instead of *paradise*, the Hebrew has *gan*, that is, “garden.” Moreover, *Eden* is interpreted as “delights,” for which reason Symmachus translated it “a flowering paradise.”

Likewise, what follows, “toward the east,” is written in Hebrew as *mimizra* [Note: [Col. 1145D] In the published editions of Saint Jerome, *mecedem* is read.], which Aquila rendered ἀπὸ ἀρχῆς, “from the beginning,” and which we too may translate “from the beginning.” Symmachus, however, has ἐκ πρώτης (“from the beginning”), and Theodotion ἐν πρώτοις (“at first”); both signify not “east” but “beginning.”

From this it is plainly established that, before God made heaven and earth, he had already created paradise, as it is read in Hebrew: “The Lord God had planted paradise in Eden from the beginning.”

**AUGUSTINE ON THE HEXAMERON**

“And God planted paradise in Eden, toward the east, and placed there the man whom he had formed” (Gen. 2:8). [Note: [Col. 1146D] Augustine, book 8 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 1–7.]

I am not unaware that many people have said many things about paradise. There are, however, three general opinions concerning it. One belongs to those who wish paradise to be understood only bodily; another to those who understand it only spiritually; and a third to those who understand it in both ways, bodily and spiritually.

I shall therefore say briefly that I confess the third opinion to be pleasing to me. God, then, had planted paradise in delights, that is, toward the east, and placed there the man whom he had formed. For it is written in this way because it was done in this way, as a certain wise man said: this paradise was planted in a certain place where earthly man could dwell.

Paradise is understood spiritually as the place to which the souls of the saints now go when they depart from the body; this bodily paradise was planted as its figure, in accordance with the truth of historical events.

What follows, however—“and the tree of life in the middle of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”—must be considered more carefully, lest one be compelled to interpret it allegorically and conclude that these were not trees but that something else is signified by the name “tree.”

For it is said concerning wisdom: “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her” (Prov. 3:18). Nevertheless, although the eternal Jerusalem exists in heaven, a city was also founded on earth to signify it. And although Sarah and Hagar signified the two Testaments, they were nevertheless also two actual women.

And although Christ refreshes us with spiritual water through the suffering of the cross, there was nevertheless a rock from which water flowed for the thirsty people when it was struck with a piece of wood. Concerning it Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4), not like the fatted calf that was slaughtered for the feast when the younger son returned (Luke 15:23).

In that case, the narrative itself is a figure, rather than a figurative signification of historical events. But the event concerning the rock also occurred in history, whereas the other was foretold only through figures.

So too wisdom, which is Christ himself, is the tree of life in the spiritual paradise, to which he sent the thief from the cross. Yet a tree of life was also created in the bodily paradise to signify wisdom, and God did not wish man to live bodily in paradise without the spiritual realities being presented through bodily mysteries.

The other trees therefore supplied him with food, but that tree supplied him with a sacrament. What did it signify except wisdom, concerning which it is said: “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her”? It was like the rock of which it was said: “The rock flows for those who thirst for him.”

I add this as well: although that tree provided bodily food, it was such that the body of man might be sustained in stable health—not as from ordinary food, but through some hidden inspiration of health.

Certainly, ordinary bread too possessed something more, since with one small loaf (*colliride*) God preserved a man from the need for food for forty days.

It follows:

Let us now consider why the tree of the knowledge of good and evil received this name, since God created all things very good. It must be understood as knowledge of how great the difference was between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience: if he transgressed, it would be evil for him; but if he kept the commandment of his Creator, it would be good for him, since, had he not transgressed, he would not have learned by experience the punishment.

[Col. 1146D] D. “And a spring rose from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it is divided into four heads,” or into four parts. How should this be understood?

**AUGUSTINE**

M. No one should be troubled by the fact that, among these rivers, the sources of some are said to be known, while those of others are entirely unknown. We should rather believe that, since that very place of paradise is most remote from human knowledge, four divisions of waters proceed from it, as the wholly trustworthy Scripture testifies.

But the rivers whose sources are said to be known may have flowed underground at some point and, after traversing extensive regions, emerged elsewhere, where they were reported to be known as though at their own sources. Who does not know that some waters commonly behave in this way?

**ITEM: AUGUSTINE**

The river that proceeded from Eden—that is, from delights, pleasure, and feasting—and which the prophet signifies in the Psalm when he says, “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delights” (Ps. 35:9), is divided, he says, into four parts, and signifies the four virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

Phison is said to be the Ganges, while Geon is the Nile. This may also be observed in the prophet Jeremiah. Today they are called by other names, just as the river now called the Tiber was formerly called the Albula. The Tigris and Euphrates, however, still retain the same names.

Nevertheless, these names signify spiritual virtues, as I have said; the interpretation of the names themselves also teaches this, if one considers the Hebrew or Syriac language. Thus Jerusalem, although it is a visible and earthly place, nevertheless signifies spiritually the city of peace; and Sion, although it is a mountain on earth, signifies contemplation.

This same practice is often transferred in the allegories of Scripture to the understanding of spiritual things. Thus the man who descended from Jerusalem to Jericho, as the Gospel says, was wounded on the road and left by robbers injured and half-dead (Luke 10:30). Although these places are found on earth according to the historical account, they necessarily compel spiritual interpretation.

Prudence, therefore, signifies the contemplation of truth, alien to every human mouth because it is ineffable. If you wish to express it, you give birth to it, as it were, with labor rather than bringing it forth, since the Apostle also heard there “ineffable words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak.”

This prudence circles the land that contains gold, carbuncle, and green stone—that is, the discipline of living, which, as though refined away from all earthly filth, shines like the finest gold; the truth that no falsehood overcomes, like the radiance of the carbuncle, which is not overcome by night; and eternal life, signified by the greenness of the green stone because of its vigor, which does not wither.

That river which circles the land of Ethiopia, exceedingly hot and burning, signifies fortitude, vigorous and tireless through the heat of action.

The third, the Tigris, flows toward the Assyrians and signifies temperance, which resists lust, greatly opposed to the counsels of prudence. Hence in Scripture the Assyrians are often placed in the role of adversaries.

Of the fourth river it is not said what it flows against or what land it encircles. For justice pertains to every part of the soul, since it is the soul’s order and equity, by which these three are harmoniously joined to one another: first prudence, second fortitude, third temperance; and justice is their established union and ordering.

**RECAPITULATION: ON PARADISE, THE SPRING AND RIVERS, AND THE TREE OF LIFE**

[Col. 1148A]

**ISIDORE** [Note: [Col. 1147D] *On Genesis*, chapter 3.]

“The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning.” Paradise is the Church, for this is how it is described in the Song of Songs: “My sister is a garden enclosed” (Song 4:12).

Paradise is planted from the beginning because the Catholic Church is known to have been founded by Christ, the beginning of all things.

The river flowing out from paradise bears the image of Christ flowing from the Father’s fountain. He waters his Church with the word of preaching and the gift of baptism. Of him the prophet rightly says: “The Lord our God is a glorious river leaping forth upon thirsty ground.”

The four rivers of paradise are the four Gospels, sent for preaching among all nations.

The fruit-bearing trees are all the saints; their fruits are their works.

The tree of life is the Holy of Holies, namely Christ. Whoever stretches out his hand toward him will live forever.

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the faculty of free choice, placed in the middle for discerning good and evil. Whoever, abandoning God’s grace, tastes from it will die by death.

It follows:

D. “Therefore the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it” (Gen. 2:15). What, I ask, was he to work? What was he to guard? Paradise, or something else?

M. This statement gives rise to a twofold interpretation. If man was to work paradise—that is, work at something in paradise—he worked not from the necessity of obtaining food but for enjoyment.

He had not yet sinned, nor had the earth brought forth thorns and thistles for him, so that he would eat his bread by the sweat of his face. This he deserved after sin.

Before sin, therefore, he worked paradise through cultivation not from want or necessity but, as we have said, solely by his will; and he guarded it through discipline. He did not guard paradise against beasts or any animals, but for himself—so that he would not lose through sinning what he had been able to preserve by obeying.

Or God placed the man himself in paradise to work and guard it so that he might be safe. Whichever of these interpretations is given—whether man worked paradise through cultivation and guarded it through discipline, or God worked upon the man himself so that he might be good and safe—each has a rational basis according to either interpretation.

It follows:

“And the Lord commanded him, saying: ‘From every tree of paradise you may eat, but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death’” (Gen. 2:16).

**AUGUSTINE**

D. Since God threatened man with death on the day when he touched the forbidden food, why did he not die on that same day, as Scripture says: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death”?

M. Holy Scripture very clearly [Col. 1149A] shows that there are four deaths. The first death is that of the soul, which abandons its Creator; for when it has abandoned Him, it sins. “Let the dead,” says the Lord in the Gospel, “bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22). Here you have those who, according to the soul, bury the dead, and those whom they bury, according to the flesh, are dead. This saying therefore very clearly presents two deaths: one of souls, the other of bodies. The third belongs to the soul alone, which suffers it when it has departed from the body, according to what we read in the Gospel concerning the rich man: “Father Abraham,” says the rich man, “send Lazarus to me, so that he may cool my tongue with his finger, because I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24). The fourth death occurs when the soul has received its body again, so that it may be cast into the eternal fire, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the future [Col. 1149B] judgment: “Go into the eternal fire,” and so forth. On the day, therefore, when Adam sinned, he died in his soul. For just as the body lives from the soul, so the soul, in order to live blessedly, lives from God. Thus Adam’s soul, being dead, is rightly called dead; from it three other deaths followed afterward. For in order that these might follow, the first preceded: because on the day Adam sinned, he died in his soul.

D. How could Adam fear death, when he had no knowledge of it whatsoever?

M. Just as we know the resurrection, although we have never experienced or seen it, so he also knew death. Knowing, then, that when the soul leaves the body it produces death, and that when it returns to its body it produces resurrection—behold, we know the resurrection, although we have never experienced it. So he too certainly knew death, not yet by experience but by knowledge. He knew what it was to live, and through the deprivation of life he certainly knew what death was. Thus darkness is known through the deprivation of light, and silence is known through the deprivation of sound; so Adam knew death through the deprivation of life. It follows:

AUGUSTINE.

D. The Lord also said: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (Gen. 2:18). How is this to be understood?

M. [Note: [Col. 1149D] Augustine, *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, book IX, chapter 3.] Certainly, if I am asked for what purpose this helper ought to have been made, nothing else plausibly occurs to me than that it was for the procreation of children, just as the seed has the earth as its helper, so that a shoot may arise from both. Nor do I see what could have prevented their having honorable marriage even in paradise, so that offspring might be generated from their seed without any restless ardor of lust and without any labor or pain of childbirth. This would not have been so that children might succeed their dying parents, but so that, while those who had begotten them remained in some stable condition of form and received bodily vigor from the tree of life planted there, those who were born might also be brought to the same condition. Then, when the appointed number had been completed, if all lived justly and obediently, there would be a transformation into eternal life, as may also be considered in the case of Enoch, who, after fathering children and pleasing God, was not dead but translated. Why, then, if Adam and Eve had lived justly and chastely procreated children, could they not [Col. 1150A] have yielded their place to them through translation rather than death? Since this is so, why should we not believe that before the sin they were able to command their genital members for the procreation of children in the same way as the other members, which the soul moves in any task without distress and, as it were, without the itching of pleasure? They would thus command the members by which offspring is conceived with the same act of will by which the feet are commanded when one walks, so that conception would occur without ardor and childbirth without pain.

But now, by transgressing the commandment, they deserved to experience the movement of that law which, in their members, opposes the law of the mind—the movement of conceived death. And what punishment could be more just than that the body, that is, the soul’s servant, should not obey every command, since the soul itself had refused to obey its Lord?

When therefore the Lord God had formed from the earth all the animals of the land [Col. 1150B] and all the birds of the sky, he brought them to Adam (Gen. 2:19). And so forth.

D. Did God bring all the animals and all the birds of the sky to Adam in the same way that bird-catchers or hunters bring them to their nets? Or perhaps was a voice of command produced from a cloud, which they understood as rational souls, and, hearing it, nevertheless obeyed?

M. The animals and birds did not receive this capacity so as to be capable of reason, by which they could obey their Creator. Yet within their own kind they obey God, not through a rational judgment of pleasure, but as He moves all things at fitting times, without Himself being moved temporally. He moves Himself without time and place, and He moved the created spirit without place but within time. Substance that is moved only temporally therefore precedes [Col. 1150C] substance that is moved both temporally and locally. Substance that is moved neither temporally nor locally precedes the substance that is moved temporally; the created spirit moves itself through time without place, while the body is moved through both time and place. The Creator Spirit, however, moves Himself without time and place.

Therefore the rational spirit, which is in human beings, as well as the irrational spirit, is moved even by commands. But the rational spirit has understanding, by which it can judge whether or not it should consent to commands. Animals and birds did not receive this judgment; nevertheless, according to their kind and nature, when touched by some command they are driven onward. Hence the angelic nature, carrying out God’s commands, moves every kind of animal by commands, leading them where they do not know. If human beings can tame certain kinds of animals so that they seem to fulfill certain [Col. 1150D] human wishes, how much more can angels do this?

D. What causes God, whom you assert to move, not to be moved in time, or the created spirit, which is moved in time, not to be moved also in place?

M. God, who established times and exists before times, has nothing in Him that is past or future, no new plan and no new thought, as though it were something new and newly added. For if anything were added to God, He would no longer be immutable. God is therefore immutable: nothing is added to Him, no new thought and no new plan. Hence He is not moved in time. [Col. 1151A] Bodies, however, descend from heaven and ascend into heaven in order to be moved from one place to another.

The spirit of human beings is moved in time by remembering the past, awaiting the future, and learning something new. For when I remember some reading or some city, my spirit is moved by thinking so as to remember these things; it is not thereby moved in place. But if it is moved in place, is it moved in heaven or on earth? For there is no place apart from heaven and earth. Where, then, was the spirit itself— in heaven or on earth—when it saw that reading or that city? Therefore, if it saw it in no place in order to remember it, it saw it in itself. And because it has a beginning, everything that has a beginning and time is thought. Thus, according to the reasoning given above, the created spirit can be moved through time [Col. 1151B] but not through place. The Creator Spirit is moved without time and place, whereas the body is moved through both time and place. It follows:

“Then the Lord cast a sleep upon Adam and took one of his ribs from him. ‘This one shall now be called woman, because she was taken from her man’” (Gen. 2:21).

JEROME [Note: [Col. 1151D] *Hebrew Questions*.]

“And the Lord God sent an ecstasy upon Adam.” In Hebrew, instead of *ecstasy*, that is, an excess or rapture of mind, it has *tardema*, which Aquila interpreted as καταφορὰν, “a casting down,” and Symmachus as κάρον, that is, “a heavy and profound sleep.” Finally, it follows: “and he slept.” The same word is also used for the sleep of Jonah as he snored (Jonah 1). It follows:

“This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. She shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man” [Col. 1151C] (Gen. 2:23).

It does not seem to resonate [printed editions: “sound”] in Greek and Latin why she is called “woman,” because she was taken from “man”; but the etymology is preserved in the Hebrew language: *is* means “man,” and *issa* means “woman.” She was therefore rightly called *issa* from *is*. Hence Symmachus beautifully wished to preserve the etymology even in Greek, saying: “This one shall be called ἀνδρὶς (‘man-woman’), because she was taken from ἀνδρός (‘man’).” We can render this in Latin: “This one shall be called *virago*, because she was taken from *vir*.” Theodotion, however, suspected another etymology, saying: “This one shall be called *assumption*, because she was taken from man.” For according to a variation of accent, *ishah* can also be understood to mean “assumption.”

[Note: [Col. 1151D] Augustine, *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, book IX, chapter 17.] But if the question concerns the woman who was made afterward, how that original causal condition should be understood—whether it already contained the necessity that a woman be made from the man’s side, or whether it contained only the possibility that she might be made in this way, while the necessity that she be made so was hidden in God—I shall say what seems to me to be the case.

[Note: [Col. 1151D] In the printed editions: “This entire customary course of nature has certain natural laws of its own.”]

All these customary courses of nature have certain natural laws of their own. From these, as from the beginnings of things, everything that is generated takes its origin and development at its proper time, as well as the endings and declines proper to each kind. Hence wheat does not arise from a bean, nor cattle from a human being.

Over and above this natural movement and course of things, the Creator’s power possesses within Himself the ability to make all these things other than their quasi-seminal principles would indicate. The principles governing these and similar modes exist not only in God but have also been implanted and embedded by Him in created things. Thus, for a piece of wood cut from the earth—dry, polished, and entirely without root, earth, or water—to flower suddenly and produce fruit: He did indeed give the natures He created the capacity for even this to happen through them. Yet He gave it in another manner as well: not so that they would possess this in their natural movement, but so that they might have been created in such a way that their nature would thereafter be more fully subject to His will.

God therefore has hidden within Himself the causes of certain acts, which He did not insert into created things. There also resides the grace by which sinners are saved. For as regards an unrighteous nature, corrupted by its own will, it has no means of returning to itself, but only through God’s grace. For this reason the Apostle called the mystery of His grace (Eph. 3:9) hidden—not in the world, but in God, who created all things.

Accordingly, even those things that were done miraculously, not through the natural movement of things but in order to signify this grace, had their causes hidden in God. If the making of the woman from the man’s side, and from his side while he slept, was one of these things, the original constitution of things, when it was said on the sixth day, “He made them male and female,” did not contain the determination that the female should be made in precisely this way, but only that it could happen in this way. Nor would He have acted by a changeable will against the causes He had established by His will. What would happen, so that something else entirely would not happen in the future, was hidden in God, who created all things. [Col. 1152C]

ALSO AUGUSTINE. On the Soul of the Woman.

[Note: [Col. 1152D] Book X of *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, chapters 1–15.]

Since Scripture has related how the woman was made from flesh but has been silent about the soul, it has made us all the more attentive to how those who believe that the soul is made from a man’s soul, just as flesh is made from flesh, by the seeds of both being transmitted from parents to children, can or cannot be refuted. [Note: [Col. 1152D] In Augustine: “in what way.”] For they are first moved to this position by saying that God made one soul, which He breathed into the face of the man whom He had formed from dust, and that from this one all the other human souls are subsequently created, just as all human flesh also comes from his flesh.

This suspicion is easily answered. If they think that the woman’s soul was made from the man’s soul because it is not written that God breathed into the woman’s face, why do they believe that the woman was animated from the man when even that is not written?

Let us first hold this most firmly: the nature of the soul is not transformed into the nature of the body, so that what was already a soul should become a body; nor into the nature of an irrational soul, so that what was the soul of a human being should become that of an animal; nor into the nature of God, so that what was a soul should become what God is.

[Col. 1153A] This too must be no less certain: the soul is nothing other than a creature of God.

Let us now consider whether the following statement confirms neither position but can be accommodated to both: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12).

Those who defend the propagation of souls attempt to establish their position from these words of the Apostle as follows: “If ‘sin’ or ‘sinner’ can be understood according to the flesh alone, we are not compelled by these words to believe that the soul comes from the parents. But if, although through the enticement of the flesh, it is nevertheless the soul alone that sins, how are we to understand the statement ‘in whom all sinned,’ unless the soul too was propagated from Adam, just as the flesh was?”

It is indeed most truly and most faithfully written: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). Yet I think that the flesh cannot desire without the soul, something about which every learned and unlearned person is in no doubt. Accordingly, the cause of this carnal desire is not in the soul alone, but even less is it in the flesh alone; it arises from both. It comes from the soul because without it no pleasure is perceived, and from the flesh because without it the pleasure of the flesh is not perceived.

When the Apostle speaks of the flesh desiring against the spirit, he is plainly speaking of the carnal pleasure that the spirit has from and with the flesh, opposing the pleasure that the spirit has alone. For when the spirit commands the bodily members to serve a desire by which it alone is inflamed—for example, when a book is taken up, when something is written, read, discussed, or heard, or finally when bread is broken for a hungry person—the flesh offers obedience; it does not arouse desire.

When something opposes these and similar desires, by which the soul alone desires, and that thing gives pleasure to the same soul according to the flesh, then the flesh is said to desire against the spirit. Those who are under grace contend against sin in this way: not so that this desire may not exist in their body while it remains mortal, so that it is rightly called dead, but so that it may not reign. It does not reign when one does not obey its desires.

According to this statement, we neither say anything absurd, namely, that the flesh desires without the soul, nor do we agree with the Manichaeans, who, seeing that the flesh cannot desire without the soul, supposed that the flesh possessed another soul from another nature opposed to God. [Col. 1153D]

D. Nor are we compelled to say that Christ’s grace is unnecessary for any soul when we are asked what merit the soul of an infant possesses, and why it is harmful for that soul to leave the body without having received baptism.

M. The answer given to this is that God indeed gives new souls individually to human bodies, for the purpose that, living rightly from a sinful flesh that comes from original sin and subduing carnal desires under God’s grace, they may acquire merit by which they may be transferred with the body itself to a better condition at the time of the resurrection. [Note: [Col. 1153D] The printed editions read: “so that they may be in the flesh of sin.”]

But it is necessary that they be wondrously joined to earthly and mortal members, especially members propagated from sinful flesh, so that they may first give them life and afterward, as age advances, govern them. It is as though they were weighed down by forgetfulness—if this forgetfulness may in some way be called indigestible, it is attributed to the Creator. [Note: [Col. 1153D] The printed editions read: “is attributed.”]

When the soul gradually recovers from the period of this forgetfulness, what harm is done to it if it is, as it were, briefly immersed in sleep, from which it gradually awakens and emerges into the light of understanding? But before it is able, through advancing age, to live according to the spirit, it necessarily needs the sacrament of the Mediator, so that what it cannot yet accomplish through His sacrament and faith may be accomplished through those who love it. [Note: [Col. 1154D] The printed editions read: “the sacrament,” rather than “through the sacrament.”]

“What, then,” someone says, “if its family has failed to care for this, whether through unbelief or negligence? Will that perhaps cause no harm?” [Col. 1154B] “What, then, does it profit the one who is helped?”

I confess that I have not yet heard or read anywhere what those who attempt to assert, according to the holy Scriptures—or according to what they find in them, or at least what does not conflict with them—that new souls are given to bodies not drawn from their parents, can answer on their own behalf. But even if those who affirm the transmission of souls should prevail—not by arguing but by proving their case—it would nevertheless not follow that Christ’s soul too must be believed to have come through the transmission of that transgressor.

For although Christ’s body was taken from the flesh of a woman who had been conceived from that propagation of sinful flesh, yet because He was conceived from her in the manner in which she herself had been conceived, He too was not sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh.

Finally, if I am asked from where Christ Jesus received His soul, I would prefer to hear better and more learned answers on this matter; nevertheless, according to my own capacity, I would more willingly answer that it was not from Adam, but from the source of Adam—that is, from God.

There is a passage in the Epistle written to the Hebrews that deserves very careful consideration. When, through Melchizedek, in whom a figure of this matter had preceded, Christ’s priesthood was distinguished from the priesthood of Levi, it says: “See how great this man is, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth from the firstfruits” (Heb. 7:4). Yet he himself was not tithed, whose flesh drew from that source not the heat of a wound but the material for a remedy. For since that tithing belonged to the prefiguration of the remedy, what was being tithed in Abraham’s flesh was what was being healed, not what provided the healing.

That same flesh—not Abraham’s alone, but also that of the first earthly human being—simultaneously possessed both the wound of transgression and the medicine for the wound. The latter was assumed from it, without the act of lust, from the Virgin, for the sharing of death without sin and as an example of resurrection without falsehood.

At this point they may perhaps say: “Just as He could be present there according to the flesh and yet not be tithed, why could He not also be present according to the soul without being tithed?” The answer is that in bodily seed there can be an invisible power that operates numbers incorporeally, to be distinguished by the intellect, not by the eyes, from the bodily substance perceived through sight and touch.

But why should I labor over a matter that perhaps cannot be persuaded by words to anyone unless the reader possesses such great and remarkable intelligence that it anticipates the argument before it has been completed, and yet does not wait for the whole discourse? [Note: [Col. 1155D] The printed editions read: “from the discourse.”]

I shall therefore summarize briefly. If what we said concerning the flesh could also happen concerning the soul, and if this has perhaps been understood, then the soul of Christ would be from the transmission of souls without having drawn along with it the stain of transgression. But if it could come from that source without this guilt, then it is not from that source.

As for the origin of the other souls—whether they come from parents or from above—let those prevail who can. For the time being I remain uncertain between the two positions, and at times I am moved toward one, at times toward the other. I am certain of this alone: I will never believe, with the Lord assisting my mind, that the soul is a body, or some bodily quality or conjunction—if it should be called that—which the Greeks call *harmony*, no matter who may chatter such a view. I strongly urge, as far as I am able, those whom this opinion has previously occupied, who believe that souls are propagated from parents, to consider themselves as much as possible, and meanwhile to understand that their bodies are not their souls.

For no nature is more closely related to the possibility of conceiving God incorporeally than the nature made in His image; and nothing is nearer than that one who believes the soul to be a body should also come to believe that God is a body.

D. Since Adam needed a wife to be made for him, could she not have been made in some other way than by taking a rib from him while he slept, from which the wife would be built?

M. She could have been made in another way, but He judged it more fitting that she be made in this way so that something might be signified. For just as Adam’s rib is taken while he sleeps and made into a wife, so also blood is poured from Christ’s side while He is dying, so that the Church may be built. Through participation in Christ’s body and blood, the Church becomes Christ’s wife. It follows:

D. What does Adam’s statement mean: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24)? And the blessed apostle Paul, citing this passage, explained it by saying: “This is a great mystery; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31). But how did He leave the Father, since He is of one substance with the Father?
