Or where could the Father be without the Son, when it is said of the Son Himself, who is Wisdom: “He reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)?

[Col. 1155D] M. If the Son is there wherever the Father is, the Father cannot be without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, because, just as they are inseparable in nature, so they are separable in persons. For the Son Himself says in the Gospel: “The one who sent me is with me.”

How, then, does He leave the Father and cling to His wife, that is, the Church, except in the manner described by the Apostle: “Although He was in the form of God, He did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant”?

The taking of the servant’s form is therefore itself the emptying and self-abasement. Although this emptying is not the abolition of divinity or the loss of nature, nevertheless, because of the servant’s form in which He is recognized to have appeared, He is rightly said to have left the Father. But He also left His mother, namely, the synagogue, which clung carnally to the Old Testament, and He clung to His wife, that is, the Church, so that in the peace of the New Testament the two might be one flesh. It follows:

ALSO AUGUSTINE [Note: [Col. 1156D] Book XI of *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, chapters 1–14.]

“Adam and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed” (Gen. 2:25). It is entirely true that the bodies of the two human beings living in paradise were naked, and they were not ashamed. For what could have shamed them when they had sensed no law in their members opposing the law of their mind? This was the punishment of sin that followed them after the transgression had been committed, when disobedience seized what had been forbidden and justice punished what had been done.

Before this occurred, they were naked, as it is said, [Col. 1156B] and they were not ashamed. There was no movement in the body that deserved shame; they thought nothing needed to be concealed because they had felt nothing that needed to be restrained. How they would have propagated children has already been discussed; nevertheless, it must not be believed that they would have propagated them in the manner in which they did after the crime had been committed and the foretold punishment had followed, when, before they died, death had already been conceived and was raging through the body of disobedient human beings in the most just reciprocal action of disobedient members.

“Now the serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth that the Lord God had made. He said to the woman, ‘Why has God commanded you not to eat from every tree of paradise?’” continuing to: “‘Your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil’” (Gen. 3:1).

AUGUSTINE.

D. How could the serpent speak in paradise, since to some it appears to be an irrational animal?

M. The serpent could not speak by itself, nor did it assume this ability because it had not received it from the Creator, unless indeed the devil used it, as it were, as an instrument through which to emit articulated sound. Through it he certainly spoke, and yet even the serpent did not know this. Thus a nature lacking reason is subjected to a rational nature; nevertheless, the latter does not do everything it wishes through it or in it, but only as much as it has received from God.

D. If serpents do not understand, how do they hear the words of the Marsians, so that they come out of their caves at their incantations?

[Col. 1156D] M. Although they have no understanding, they are by no means deprived of bodily sensation. They possess sight, hearing, taste, and smell. Therefore, although they hear the words of the Marsians, they do not understand them at all. They do not obey through understanding; rather, so that they may come out of their caves at the words of the Marsians, they are compelled by the devil, with God’s permission. Hence testimony is given concerning that first event, because he deceived the first human being through the serpent in paradise.

AMBROSE.

D. Why did He permit him to be tempted through this animal?

M. It is not surprising that he was tempted through the serpent, by which the devil was prefigured. The ancient enemy has a most wicked will but a most justly limited power: he always has the will to do harm, but he has no power to harm without God’s permission. [Col. 1157A]

D. Why did He permit the one whom He knew would consent to be tempted?

M. I shall say what He grants me to understand or permits me to say. It does not seem to me that a human being would have had great grounds for praise if he could live well merely because no one persuaded him to live badly, since he had both the natural capacity and the power to will not to consent to the one persuading him.

Why, then, should He not allow one whom He knew would consent to be tempted, since he would do so by his own will and through guilt, while by His justice he would be ordered through punishment? Some people are moved by this temptation of the first human being, because God permitted it to occur, as though they did not now see the entire human race being ceaselessly tempted by the devil’s snares. Why does God permit this also? Is it because virtue is tested and exercised, and because the palm of glory is greater when one does not consent after being tempted than when one could not be tempted?

Again, those mentioned above say:

“They should have made a human being who would not wish to sin at all.” [Note: [Col. 1157D] Read: “they corrupted,” as in Augustine.] We grant that the nature that would not wish to sin at all is better; let them also grant that the nature which was made so that it could refrain from sinning if it wished is not evil. The former nature exists in the holy angels, the latter in holy human beings.

Those who chose the portions of iniquity, and who corrupted an honorable nature by a blameworthy will [Note: [Col. 1157D] Read: “They corrupted by a law,” as in Augustine.], should not for that reason—because they were foreknown—have been created. For God does not need the righteousness of any upright person, much less the iniquity of the wicked.

When sound reasoning demonstrates two unequal goods, one higher and the other lower, those dull of heart do not understand when they say that both must be of the same kind. In trying to equalize kinds of goods, they reduce their number. Who would listen to them if they said: “Because the sense of sight is more excellent than the sense of hearing, there should be four eyes and no ears”? Yet if God wished it, these too would be good. How much better, then, did God will that they should be what they wished to be—good without fruitlessness, and evil without impunity.

But He foreknew that their will would be evil. Certainly He foreknew it; and because His foreknowledge cannot be deceived, the evil will is not His but theirs. [Col. 1157C]

D. Why did He create those whom He knew would become such?

M. Because just as He foresaw what evil they would do, so also He foresaw what good He Himself would bring about from their evil deeds. For He made them in such a way that they would serve others as a means of spiritual exercise and as an example provoking fear.

“So,” they say, “there is something in God’s works that needs another’s evil in order to advance toward good.” Have people become so hardened and blinded by some eagerness for contention that they neither hear nor see how, through the punishment of some, very many are corrected? What pagan, what Jew, what heretic does not prove daily in his own household what disturbance requiring discipline comes to them from the work of divine providence?

“Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all His wishes” (Ps. 110:2). He foresaw that some would be good and created them; He foresaw that some would be evil and created them. He offers Himself to the good for their enjoyment, lavishing many of His gifts even upon the evil, consulting nothing for His own advantage, and taking no advantage from the works of the good or even from the punishments of the evil.

Again:

If it is asked why the devil was permitted to tempt through the serpent, it should not seem surprising, since Christ Himself permitted demons to enter pigs (Matt. 8:31). More scrupulous inquiry is usually made concerning the very nature of the devil. Certain heretics, offended and troubled by the evil will, attempt to alienate that nature from the creation of the supreme and true God and to give it another origin opposed to God.

They cannot understand that everything which exists, insofar as it is some substance, is good, and that it cannot exist except from the living God, from whom all good comes. [Note: [Col. 1158D] Augustine has: “but that the evil will is moved disorderly.”]

Evil consists in being moved by the will in a disordered manner, preferring lower goods to higher ones. Thus it happened that the spirit of a rational creature, taking pleasure in its own power because of its excellence, swelled with pride, through which it fell from the blessedness of the spiritual paradise, and wasted away through envy.

Yet even in this spirit there is the good that it lives and gives life to a body, whether the spirit of the devil or of demons, or the soul of any human being, even a malicious and wicked one. [Col. 1158C]

Some say that the devil’s fall from the heavenly realms occurred because he envied the human being made in the image of God. But envy follows pride; it does not precede it. Envy is not the cause of becoming proud; pride is the cause of envy.

Since pride is love of one’s own excellence, while envy is hatred of another’s happiness, what arises from them is readily apparent. In loving his own excellence, a proud person envies either his equals, because they are made equal to him, or his superiors, because he is not made equal to them. In becoming proud, therefore, one becomes envious; no one becomes proud by first becoming envious.

The prophet calls him “the beginning of the Lord’s handiwork,” because He made him to be mocked by His angels. This does not mean that He created him originally for that purpose, but that, knowing he would become such by his own will as to harm the good, He created him so that He Himself might benefit the good through him. This is what it means for him to be mocked by His angels.

He is mocked in this way when the temptations by which he attempts to corrupt the saints become beneficial to them. He is therefore called the beginning of the handiwork made for mockery.

That the devil spoke through the serpent is taught by ordinary experience. For serpents, as was said above, are more strongly moved by human songs than any other kind of animal. This is no small testimony that human nature was initially seduced by the serpent’s conversation.

Demons are permitted to do this in order to preserve the memory of the first event, since they have a certain familiarity with the human race.

[Col. 1159A] D. Could this temptation have driven them from paradise, or not?

M. It should be understood that it could not have done so if they had not lifted themselves up into empty glory, when the hostile enemy promised them, saying: “If you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods.” For it is written: “Before destruction the heart is exalted.”

RECAPITULATION.

ISIDORE [Note: [Col. 1159D] *Commentary on Genesis*, chapters 4–5.]

The serpent, moreover, that was wiser than all the beasts indicates the devil, who is called a serpent because he moves about with winding cunning. But why did he deceive through the woman and not through the man? Because our reason cannot be led into sin unless pleasure first precedes it in the carnal weakness of the affections, which ought rather to obey reason as its ruling man. This is enacted in every person, in a certain hidden and secret marriage. Let us understand the suggestion as the serpent, the animal sense of the body as the woman, and reason as the man. Therefore, when an evil suggestion arises, the serpent speaks, as it were; but if thought alone takes pleasure in that suggestion, while reason restrains it so that consent to carry out the deed does not follow, the woman alone seems to have eaten what was forbidden. But if the mind itself also decides that the sin should be committed, then the man has been deceived, and the woman seems to have given food to the man. For to consent to enticement is to eat from the forbidden tree. Then, rightly, a person is expelled from blessed life as from paradise, and the sin is imputed to him, even if the deed does not follow, because although guilt is not present in the actions, the conscience nevertheless retains it in the consent. This is according to the allegorical sense.

In accordance with the metaphor, however, that cunning serpent may signify the craftiness of heretics. Some, indeed, promise more volubly and subtly the disclosure and knowledge of forbidden secrets, and display that knowledge in the human being himself, as in the tree planted in the middle of paradise. Against this serpent the Apostle cries out when he says: “I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted” (II Cor. 11:3). Our carnal desire is seduced by the words of this serpent, and through them the Christian Adam—but not Christ—is deceived.

This serpent therefore says to the woman: [Col. 1159D] “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” Thus the curious desire of heretics, thus wicked preachers, kindle the hearts of carnal hearers to love the deceit of error, saying: “Why do you flee from possessing hidden knowledge” (Prov. 9:19)? “Always seek what is new; penetrate the knowledge of good and evil.” Hence that woman in Solomon, bearing the likeness of heretics, says: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Prov. 9:17).

Then the same serpent added: “On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will immediately be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.” Thus, too, all heretics in general profess the attainment of divinity; they deceive by their promise of knowledge and criticize those whom they find believing simply. And because they persuade entirely toward carnal things, they attempt, as it were, to bring people to the opening of carnal eyes, so that the inner eye may be darkened.

The text continues:

**ISIDORE.**

“Then the woman saw that the tree was good, etc., and she took its fruit and ate” (Gen. 3:6).

The woman ate first, not the man, because carnal people are more easily persuaded to sin, and spiritual people are not so quickly deceived.

The text continues:

“And she gave it to her husband, and he ate.” This is certainly because, after the pleasure of our carnal desire, our reason too is subjected to sinning.

“And when they realized that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and covered themselves” (Gen. 3:7).

**ISIDORE.**

[Col. 1160B]

Those who embrace the harshness of the world, who burn with the itch of carnal pleasure, and who, deceived by heretical depravity, have been stripped of the grace of God, gather coverings of lies like fig leaves, making themselves girdles of depravity when they lie about the Lord or the Church. As Gregory says: “For after the sin of disobedience Adam immediately covered his shame, because he had discovered the dishonor of the flesh; and he who had refused to be subject to his Creator lost the rights over the subject flesh that he governed, so that the confusion of his disobedience might rebound upon himself, and, having been overcome, he might learn what he had lost through his pride.”

The text continues:

**AUGUSTINE.**

**D.** God brought all the animals and birds to Adam, [Col. 1160C] and, seeing them, he gave them names . . . . Shortly afterward, concerning the woman, it is said: “Then the woman saw that the tree was good for eating.” Behold, Scripture most clearly shows that the eyes of both were open. For it is not permissible to say that the first human beings were made blind. And why, shortly afterward, after the touch of the forbidden tree, does the same Scripture say: “The eyes of both were opened”?

**M.** [Note: Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XI, chapter 31.] Unless they had open eyes, he could neither have given names to the animals nor could she have seen the beauty of the tree. This is indeed true: they had open eyes. Yet unless they had been closed with respect to something, Scripture would in no way have said: “The eyes of both were opened.” They were opened, that is, to nothing other than recognizing one another, so that there might be in the members a law resisting the law of the mind, and so that there might be in those very members a movement not subject to the will—a just punishment from God, namely, that the human being who had refused to be subject to God should not have a body subject to him. Therefore the eyes of both were opened to this: that their members might be moved by desire.

The text continues:

**AUGUSTINE.**

“And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the afternoon breeze, Adam and Eve his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord among the trees of paradise” (Gen. 3:8).

**D.** I ask you, then, explain what that walking of God means.

**M.** Far be it from us to believe that God, who is Trinity, is corporeal or local merely because his walking is mentioned. Every local thing is corporeal, and every body is local. God, however, is incorporeal: he is not moved corporeally, is not contained by a place, and is not transferred from place to place. His walking must rather be understood as having taken place through some creature; and from the surrounding context of Scripture I recall from the ancients that this creature was a human being.

**GREGORY, likewise** [Note: Book XXIII of the *Morals*, chapters 3 and 10.]

When Adam heard the voice of the Lord walking in paradise at the afternoon breeze, he hid himself among the trees of paradise. Sometimes God speaks through angels by words and deeds alike, making known through certain movements what he narrates through speech. For after his sin Adam could not see God in his divinity, but he heard the words of rebuke through an angel. [Col. 1161B]

**D.** But we must ask what it means that, after the human being’s sin, the Lord no longer stands in paradise but walks.

**M.** It is plainly indicated that, when guilt entered, he showed that he had moved away from the human heart. What does “at the afternoon breeze” mean, unless that the warmer light of truth had departed and the cold of guilt was constricting the sinful soul? The first human being is found hidden at the afternoon breeze after his sin because, having lost the noonday warmth of charity, he was already sluggish beneath the shadow of sin, as though under the cold of a breeze, as it is written concerning the same sinful man: “He followed a shadow.” He had lost the warmth of charity, abandoned the true sun, and hid himself beneath the shadow of inward cold. Hence the voice of that same Truth says: “Iniquity will abound, and the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12).

Therefore, as he walked, he rebuked Adam, so that he might disclose his wickedness to blind minds not only through words but also through deeds: so that sinful man might hear through words what he had done, might see through the walking the instability of his condition after losing the state of eternity, might perceive through the breeze his torpor after the heat of charity had been expelled, and might recognize through the setting of the sun that he was drawing near to darkness.

**The foregoing author.**

**D.** “But the Lord called Adam and said: Where are you?” (Gen. 3:1). What does it mean that after the fall the Lord asks Adam, “Where are you?” Did divine power not know to what hiding places the servant had fled after his sin, when nothing is hidden from him?

**M.** Without doubt we must believe that, since all things are naked and open before his eyes. But because he saw that Adam had fallen through guilt and was, under sin, as though hidden from the eyes of Truth—for he does not approve the darkness of Adam’s error—he acts as though he does not know where the sinner is, and calls and seeks him, saying: “Adam, where are you?” By calling him, he gives a sign that he is recalling him to repentance; by seeking him, he openly indicates that he does not recognize sinners as rightly condemned. In this passage, then, let the despairing return to hope, because even the ungodly are summoned to hope for forgiveness.

He says: “I heard your voice in paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.” He said: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I had commanded you not to eat?” And Adam said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate.”

**GREGORY** [Note: Book IV of the *Morals*, chapter 27.]

It must be understood with the greatest care that sin is committed in the heart in four ways and completed in action in four ways. In the heart it is committed through suggestion, pleasure, consent, and the audacity of self-defense. Suggestion comes through the adversary, pleasure through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the audacity of self-defense through pride. The guilt that ought to terrify the mind raises it up; and while casting it down it elevates it, but by elevating it more grievously overthrows it.

Thus the ancient enemy broke the uprightness of the first human being with these four blows. As we said above, the serpent persuaded, Eve took pleasure, Adam consented, and, when questioned, he refused through audacity to confess his guilt. This same thing is enacted daily in the human race, as we know it was enacted in the first parent of our race.

The serpent persuaded because the hidden enemy secretly suggests evil to human hearts. Eve took pleasure because the carnal sense immediately submits with delight to the serpent’s words. Adam, placed above the woman, gave consent because, while the flesh is carried away into pleasure, the spirit too, weakened from its uprightness, is bent downward. And when questioned, Adam refused to confess his guilt because the spirit, having been separated from Truth through sinning, is hardened all the more wickedly by the audacity of its fall.

Adam had fled to hide himself through fear, but, when questioned, he revealed how much he still swelled with pride even while afraid. For when present punishment is feared because of sin, while the face of God that has been lost is not loved, that fear arises from pride, not from humility.

Sin is likewise completed in action in four ways. First, the hidden fault is committed; afterward the guilt is openly revealed before human eyes without shame; then it is made habitual; and finally it is nourished either by the seductions of false hope or by the miserable obstinacy of despair.

The text continues:

“And the Lord said to the woman: Why have you done this?” [Col. 1162D] She replied: “The serpent deceived me” (Gen. 3:13).

**GREGORY** [Note: Book XXII of the *Morals*, chapter 15.]

They had been questioned for this purpose: so that, by confessing, they might wipe away the sin they had committed through transgression. The serpent who had persuaded them, however, was not questioned about the guilt, since he was not to be recalled to forgiveness.

The human being was therefore asked where he was, so that after committing the guilt he might come to his senses and, by confessing, recognize how far he had withdrawn from the face of his Creator. But both chose to furnish themselves with the supports of self-defense rather than of confession. When the man tried to excuse the sin through the woman and the woman through the serpent, they increased the guilt they had attempted to defend: Adam indirectly implicating the Lord by suggesting that he himself had been the author of their sin because he had made the woman; Eve referring the guilt to the Lord because he had placed the serpent in paradise.

Having heard through the mouth of the deceiving devil, “You will be like gods,” they were unable to become like God in divinity; so, to increase their error, they tried to make God like themselves in guilt. Thus, while attempting to defend their guilt, they added to it, making it more atrocious when examined than it had been when committed.

Hence even now the branches of the human race draw bitterness from this root. When someone is reproved for his fault, he hides it beneath words of self-defense, as beneath the leaves of a tree, and, like some dark hiding place of his excuse, flees the face of his Creator by refusing to let it be known what he has done. In this concealment he hides not himself from the Lord but the Lord from himself. He acts so that he may not see the One who sees all things, not so that he himself may not be seen, because for every sinner humility of confession is the beginning of illumination.

The Lord said to the serpent: “Because you have done this, you are cursed among all living creatures and beasts of the earth. You shall walk upon your breast and eat earth all the days of your life. I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 3:14–15).

**JEROME, IN THE HEBREW QUESTIONS**

In Hebrew it reads: “You shall walk upon your breast,” that is, so that he might disclose the cunning and trickery of his thoughts [Note: The printed editions read: “the cunning and trickery”], because all his steps were wickedness [Col. 1163C] and deceit [Note: The printed editions read: “all his steps were wickedness and deceit”].

And for what follows, “You shall eat earth,” the Hebrew has *aphar*, which we can call “ash” or “dust.” “He himself shall guard your head, and you shall guard his heel”: the Hebrew has it better as, “He himself shall crush your head” [Note: The printed editions add: “and you shall crush his heel”], “and you shall lie in wait for his heel,” because the serpent hinders our steps, while the Lord will swiftly crush Satan beneath our feet.

**RECAPITULATION, likewise**

It is later said to the serpent: “You shall be cursed among all living creatures; upon your breast and belly you shall walk.” By the name “breast” the pride of the mind is signified; by the name “belly,” as the Seventy translated it, the desires of the flesh are signified. Through these two things the devil creeps toward those whom he wishes to deceive: either through earthly desire and lust or through the insane downfall of pride.

“And you shall eat earth.” That is, those whom you deceive through earthly desire will belong to you.

“All the days of your life.” That is, for the whole period during which you exercise this power, before the final punishment of judgment.

“I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed” (Gen. 3:15). [Note: Isidore, *Commentary on Genesis*, chapter 5.] The seed of the devil is perverse suggestion; the seed of the woman is the fruit of a good work, by which perverse suggestion is resisted. She will crush his head if the mind rejects him at the very beginning of an evil suggestion. He lies in wait for her heel because he strives to deceive at the end the mind that he did not deceive by his first suggestion.

Some, however, have understood the words “I will put enmity between you and the woman” as referring to the Virgin from whom the Lord was born, since at that time the Lord, who was to be born from her in order to overcome the enemy and destroy the death of which he was the author, was promised. They understand the following words, “He himself shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for his heel,” as referring to the fruit of Mary’s womb, Christ. That is: “You will cause him to stumble so that he may die, but he will rise victorious and crush your head,” which is death. As David also said, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. 99). He called the asp death, the basilisk sin, the lion the Antichrist, and the dragon the devil.

**JEROME, IN THE SAME BOOK** [Note: *Hebrew Questions*.]

“I will multiply your sorrows and your groanings” (Gen. 3:16). In Hebrew, instead of “sorrow” and “groaning,” it has “pains” and “conceptions,” and “your turning shall be toward your husband.” Aquila translated “turning” as “association”; Symmachus translated it as “desire” or “impulse.”

**ISIDORE ELSEWHERE** [Note: The same work.]

Concerning the punishment of the woman, what does it signify that she is told, “In pain you shall bear children,” unless it is this: when carnal pleasure wishes to overcome some evil habit, it suffers pains at the beginning, and thus, through a better habit, gives birth to a good work as to a child? But what he added, “And your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you,” signifies that carnal pleasure, which she had resisted with pain in order to form a good habit, now, instructed by those very pains, becomes more cautious; and, lest she fall, obeys reason and willingly serves like a woman obeying a commanding husband. Thereafter she is called the mother of the living—that is, of rightly performed deeds—to which sins are opposed and are signified by the name “the dead.”

But to Adam he said: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife rather than to me, cursed is the earth in your work; in labors you shall eat of it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth.” And the rest, up to: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:17–19).

**JEROME** [Note: *Hebrew Questions*.]

“Cursed is the earth in your works.” Here “works” signifies not the work of cultivating the soil, as many think, but sins, as it is found in Hebrew. Aquila does not differ, saying, “Cursed is the ground because of you,” and Theodotion, “Cursed is the ground (*Adama*) in your transgression.”

**GREGORY.**

**D.** “Cursed is the earth in your work.” Since the divine voice establishes the dart of the curse as something to be punished by grave vengeance, even closing the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, what does it mean that now, when the human being sins, the divine voice imposes upon the earth what the human being is forbidden to do?

**M.** [Note: Gregory, book IV of the *Morals*, chapter 3.] It must be understood that Holy Scripture speaks of a curse in two ways: one which it approves and another which it condemns. A curse is uttered in one way by the judgment of justice and in another by the spite of vengeance.

A curse by the judgment of justice was pronounced against the sinful human being when he heard: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3:17). A curse is pronounced by the judgment of justice when it is said to Abraham: “I will curse those who curse you” (Gen. 12:3).

Again, because a curse may be uttered not by the judgment of justice but by the spite of vengeance, we are warned by the voice of Paul preaching, who says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12:14). And again: “Nor will the cursers possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. 6:10).

God, therefore, is said to curse, while the human being is forbidden to curse, because what a human being does through the malice of vengeance, God does only after examination and by the power of justice. Even holy men, when they pronounce a sentence of cursing, do not burst forth into it from a desire for vengeance but from the judgment of justice. Within themselves they see the subtle judgment of God, and they recognize that the evils rising outwardly ought to be struck by a curse. They therefore do not sin in cursing, insofar as they do not disagree with the inward judgment.

Hence Peter hurled a sentence of cursing against Simon, who offered him money, saying: “May your money be with you for destruction” [Col. 1165C] (Acts 8:20). By saying not “is” but “may it be,” he showed that he had spoken these words not in the indicative but in the optative mood.

Hence Elijah said to the two captains of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you” (IV Kings 1:10). The outcome of the matter showed how strongly the sentence of both was confirmed by the reason of truth. Simon perished in eternal destruction, and fire descending from above consumed the two captains of fifty. The subsequent power testifies with what intention a sentence of cursing is pronounced. For when the innocence of the curse remains, yet the curse absorbs the one who is cursed even unto destruction, it is inferred from the outcome of both sides that the sentence against the guilty was hurled by one and the same inward Judge.

**ISIDORE** [Note: *Commentary on Genesis*, chapter 5.]

[Col. 1165D]

Now, through the sentence imposed upon the man, our reason is reproved. Having been seduced by the desire for sin and removed from the paradise of blessedness, it has the curses of earthly labor and also the pains of temporal cares, like thorns and thistles. Yet he is dismissed from the paradise of blessedness so that he may work the earth—that is, labor in this body—and acquire for himself the merit of returning to the blessed life, which is signified by the name paradise; and so that he may someday stretch out his hand toward the tree of life and live forever. The stretching out of the hand rightly signifies the cross or the torment of repentance, through which eternal life is recovered.

The text continues:

**GREGORY** [Note: Book XXV of the *Morals*, chapter 3.]

“You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). The first human being was created in such a way that, while he remained, time would pass away, but he himself would not pass away with time. He therefore stood amid the moments as they flowed by, since he was in no way tending toward the end of life through the increase of days. He stood more firmly insofar as he clung more ardently to the One who always stands.

But when he touched what was forbidden, immediately, having offended the Creator, he began to move along with time. Hence it was said to him: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” Having lost the state of immortality, the course of mortality swallowed him up; and, as he was drawn from youth to old age and from old age to death, by passing away he learned what he had been by standing still.

Because we are born from his offspring, we retain the bitterness of the root as a shoot. Since we derive our origin from him, we receive his course by being born, so that in the very daily moment in which we live we continually pass away from life. The span of life that seems to increase for us diminishes for the same reason. Infancy passes into childhood, childhood into adolescence, adolescence into youth, youth into old age, and old age into death; the course of the present life is driven toward decline by the very stages of its growth, and it always diminishes from the point at which it believes itself to be progressing within the span of life.

We cannot possess a fixed state here, where we have come only to pass away. Indeed, our very living each day is a passing away from life. The first human being could not have possessed this falling away before his sin, because while he stood, time passed by him. But after he sinned, he placed himself, as it were, upon a slippery ground of mutability; and because he ate the forbidden food, he immediately discovered the decline of his standing.

**JEROME.**

“And Adam called his wife’s name Eve, because she is the mother of all living” (Gen. 3:20). *Eve* is interpreted as “life,” or “calamity.” Concerning this the poet [Prudentius] sang:

> Eve was a dove, then white, afterward black.  
> Made through an augury by a pernicious fraud, she became poison.  
> She stained innocent Adam with filthy spots.  
> The victorious serpent soon gives the naked a covering of fig leaves.

[Col. 1166D] “And the Lord God made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife, and clothed them, and said: Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now therefore beware, lest he perhaps stretch out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever” (Gen. 3:21).

**AUGUSTINE.**

**D.** Since God is one, as Scripture says, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God,” how does he say here: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us”? For “us” suggests plurality.

[Col. 1167A] **M.** [Note: Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XI, chapter 39.] Although God is one, he is nevertheless Trinity: namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. “One of us” is said because of the plurality of persons. “Knowing good and evil” is as though he said: Just as we know the difference between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience, so Adam now understands that he was not only not made what he ought to have become, but did not even preserve what he had been made.

He also received a tunic of skin by divine providence, by which garment the mortality of the body is usually signified in the historical sense. In the allegorical sense, however, it signifies pleasures withdrawn from carnal sensations, which, as a result of the divine law, pursue and cover the person living carnally, so that he might perhaps someday turn to God and stretch out his hand toward the tree of life—that is, toward Christ—and live forever.

[Col. 1167B] “And the Lord God expelled Adam from paradise, to work the earth from which he had been taken; and he placed before the paradise of pleasure the cherubim and a flaming, turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life” (Gen. 3:24).

**JEROME** [Note: *Hebrew Questions*.]

[Col. 1168A]

Not, as some think, that God caused Adam himself, whom he had expelled, to dwell opposite the paradise of pleasure. Rather, after expelling him, he placed the cherubim and the flaming sword before the gates of paradise to guard the entrance to paradise, so that no one might be able to enter. [Note: In the printed editions these words are absent, “as others think.”]

**ISIDORE** [Note: Isidore, *Commentary on Genesis*, chapter 5.]

Through the flaming sword—that is, through temporal tribulations, by acknowledging and lamenting his sins—and through the cherubim, that is, the fullness of knowledge, which is charity, he will reach the tree of life, Christ, and live forever. For *cherubim* is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” while the turning sword placed to guard the way of the tree of life signifies, as we have said, temporal punishments. No one can reach the tree of life except through these two things: endurance of troubles and fullness of knowledge—that is, through love of God and neighbor, for the fullness of the law is charity.

**IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 797. POPE ADRIAN I**

[Col. 1167]

**THE LIFE OF POPE ADRIAN I**

[From Mansi, *Amplissima Collectio Conciliorum*.]

[Col. 1167C] **[Note: Adrianus.]** In the year 772 of our Redemption, on the ninth day of February, by the complete agreement of all, Adrian, a Roman citizen born of noble lineage—who had been accustomed to piety from childhood and had therefore been enrolled by Paul among the clergy and by Stephen among the cardinals—was unanimously elected pope. At the beginning of his pontificate he freed those who had been sent into exile from exile, and those imprisoned from their chains and prisons. Through legates he initially refused Desiderius, king of the Lombards, the friendship and alliance of peace that he requested, since Desiderius, having twice perjured himself, had broken the treaties of peace and concord that had been concluded. But when the legates also pledged their own faith under oath, he yielded to their petition, granting what they insistently demanded.

Yet scarcely had the legates been dismissed from the city when it was announced that Desiderius had invaded the duchy of Ferrara, the exarchate of Ravenna, and other cities granted to the apostolic see by the Frankish kings, and that he was preparing to besiege the city of Ravenna. Accordingly, Paul the chamberlain was sent to him to demand the return of the fortifications he had seized. He replied that this would happen only if the pope himself came to him—clearly so that, on this pretext, the sons of Carloman might be consecrated kings of Gaul; then, while rebellion was stirred up among the Franks, he himself might meanwhile subject all Italy to the Lombard kingdom.

But when Paul the chamberlain, accused of the murder of Sergius, was killed by sentence of a judge, contrary to the command and will of Pope Adrian, through the machinations of Archbishop Leo, and when nothing about his approach to the king had therefore become known to the pope, Desiderius himself sent his legates to Rome so that, with the same intention as above, they might bring the pope to him. Invited by this embassy, the pontiff replied that he would come to the king after the cities of the Roman Church, plundered and unjustly invaded, had been restored. He added that he would send an embassy in his own name and in that of the whole Church to recover the occupied cities and rights.

But when the sacrilegious king, advancing toward the destruction of himself and of his entire Lombard kingdom, not only refused to accept the condition offered but even threatened to besiege the city of Rome, the most holy pontiff, having meanwhile fortified the city, sent an embassy by sea to Charles, king of the Franks, asking him to defend the Roman Church against the Lombard invasion, following the example of his father Pippin. The most pious king would certainly have come to the aid of the endangered Church, had not Desiderius’ fraudulent account, delivered through his legates, deceived him concerning the restoration of the rights of the Roman Church.

Meanwhile Desiderius pressed for the pope’s arrival; and when the pope persisted in his earlier reply, the king approached the city with an army to besiege it. But something happened that is astonishing to hear: struck by the thunderbolt of anathema, he retreated. When Charles, king of the Franks, entered Italy to aid the Church in accordance with the pope’s repeated request, and had fruitlessly admonished the unjust king three or four times to make restitution, one night a divinely sent terror seized the enemy, so that all, struck with fear, turned their backs and fled; some, scattered, joined the forces of Charles, while others returned to their homeland.

Meanwhile the entire people voluntarily submitted to the Roman pontiff. He occupied many Lombard cities and restored them to their lawful possessor. He ordered Ticinum, to which Desiderius had fled, to be besieged. In the meantime Charles, together with his wife, whom he had ordered to come to Pavia, and with the sons of his deceased brother Carloman, set out for Rome to visit the thresholds of the holy apostles. The pontiff received him on his arrival with great joy and the acclamations of the people. After he had fulfilled the vows for which he had come to Rome and confirmed the donations that Pippin had bestowed upon the apostolic see, he returned with Adrian to the siege of Ticinum.

Soon afterward he captured the city, seized Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and all who were with him, and subjected the entire Lombard kingdom to his power. He carried the king and his wife away with him to Francia. Thus, when the Roman Church had been restored in its entirety through Charles, it triumphed over the perfidy of the Lombards.

When the most holy pontiff Adrian had himself witnessed these events, he began, in order to render due thanks to God and erect a trophy of the victory he had received, to adorn most lavishly the confession of Saint Peter, whom he had used as defender and patron; he also began to devote himself to endowing and erecting new churches, which Anastasius describes at length.

During his time King Charles repeatedly subdued the Saxons, who were constantly rebelling. Sigebert, who lived in the year 1112 of our Redemption and wrote in favor of the schismatic Emperor Henry, who unlawfully claimed for himself the investiture of all churches, says—without the authority of any earlier writer—that Charles the Great returned to Rome in the year 774 after conquering Pavia and subduing the king of the Lombards, and that a synod of fifty-three bishops was convened there:

> “At this synod,” he says, “Pope Adrian, together with the universal synod, granted him [King Charles] the right to elect the pope and to ordain the apostolic see, as well as the dignity of the principate. Moreover, he decreed that archbishops and bishops in each province should receive investiture from him, and that unless a bishop had been commended and invested by the king, he should be consecrated by no one; and he anathematized all who rebelled against this decree, ordering that, unless they repented, their goods should be confiscated.”

This is what the schismatic Sigebert wrote in favor of Emperor Henry. But who does not see that what he writes is a lie, an invention, and a fraud? Apart from the fact that he had asserted these things 342 years earlier without the authority of any other writer, he also wrote matters contrary to the best and most trustworthy authors of the life of Charles, indeed contrary to Charles’ own constitutions.

Einhard, who remained at the side of Charles the Great and wrote his life with the greatest accuracy, explicitly states that Charles himself came to Rome only four times: first, against the Lombards, in the year 773, as we have seen above; second, he came to Rome in fulfillment of a vow in the year 780; third, against the duke of Benevento, in the year 786; fourth, to restore Leo to his position in the year 800, when he was created by that same Leo emperor of the Western Empire. If what Sigebert says is true, Charles would have come to Rome not four but five times.

The constitutions of the Frankish Capitularies also contradict Sigebert. In Book I, chapter 84, they say:

> “Not ignorant of the sacred canons, we have assented to the ecclesiastical order, namely, that bishops should be chosen by the clergy and people, according to the provisions of the canons, from their own diocese, without regard to persons or gifts, for the merit of their life and the gift of their wisdom, so that by example and word they may everywhere be of benefit to those subject to them.”

Therefore he desired clergy, bishops, and pontiffs to be elected and ordained in no other way than according to the prescription of the sacred canons.

Perhaps you will say that he refused the privilege offered to him. That could be brought forward as an interpretation of this passage if it had been established by some authority; but Sigebert, having devised it from his own imagination, was the first to circulate it 342 years ago.

In the election of Adrian II, Gratian reports in Distinction 69, chapter 29, that when Adrian had been elected by the consent of the entire clergy, and the legates of Emperor Louis, then present at Rome, were displeased that they had not been invited to witness the election of the bishop, the elected pontiff replied:

> “This was omitted not because of contempt for His Augustness, but with a view to the future, lest the custom of awaiting the legates of princes in the election of Roman pontiffs should gain strength through such encouragement.”

From this it is evident that not only the laws and constitutions of the Carolingians and the very name of investiture, but also the practice of the Church and the laws of the other imperial successors, contradict the fictitious privilege.

If you say that Gratian inserted what Sigebert affirmed into his Book of Decrees, Distinction 65, canon 22, I reply that Gratian, without first conducting a more careful examination of the fraud, was, as was his custom, excessively credulous; and that Sigebert, a monk eager for honor, had written the most mendacious account in order to curry favor with the schismatic emperor, while Gratian copied almost the same words with extreme imprudence. No one, therefore, should be surprised that he inserted into his decree a history that he ought to have rejected as a little tale and an invention of a fraud.

With similar imprudence, in Distinction 63, he inserted into the canon “In the Synod” that fictitious decree which asserts that Leo VIII, at the same Roman synod, granted Otto what Pope Adrian had long ago granted to King Charles. I shall show below, in the notes to the Life of Leo VIII and to his pseudo-Roman synod held in the year 964, that all these things are fictitious and never occurred.

Paul the Deacon of Aquileia, formerly secretary to King Desiderius, was accused of the plots he had devised for Charles out of love for his lord and was sent into exile. Leo of Ostia, in *Chronicle*, Book I, chapter 17, reports the following memorable story about him: when the king, inflamed with anger, had ordered that Paul’s hands be cut off, while the nobles had said that his eyes should be torn out so that he could not write anything against the king, the king himself intervened:

> “And if we cut off his hands, where shall we be able to find so elegant a writer? And where or when shall we find such a historian?”

What histories and books he wrote in exile may be seen in the aforesaid Leo, column—.

In the fourth year of Adrian’s pontificate, Constantine Copronymus died from a divinely inflicted wound in his legs and from a very severe fever, crying out and saying:

> “While still alive, I have been handed over to unquenchable fire, and I ask that the holy Virgin and Mother of God be praised, although I was her enemy without reconciliation.”

This is what Theophanes says about Copronymus.

All the Greek writers report another memorable fact about him: when, as an infant, he was being baptized by Saint Germanus, bishop of Constantinople, he defiled and polluted the sacred font with his excrement; for this reason he received the name Copronymus. Because he delighted in magical arts, invocations and sacrifices to demons, persecutions of holy churches and of the true and immaculate faith, debauchery, horse dung, and urine, he was also surnamed Caballinus.

> “For he was so greatly delighted,” says Theosterictus, a writer of that period, in his work on Nicetas, “by filth and by the evil odor of every most impure thing, that he smeared himself with the dung of irrational animals and ordered those who were with him to do the same; he loved and received them kindly for this reason, because he was always delighted by foul-smelling things.”

Let the modern Iconoclasts see under what standard they boast and under what leader they attack the holy images. Let them recognize that the same punishment awaits them in the underworld, the foretaste of whose judgment their standard-bearer, about to die, recently experienced.

In heresy, impiety, and sacrilege, his son Leo succeeded his father, and in the fourth year of his reign he departed this life, suffering the carbuncles of hell because, through his excessive love of carbuncle stones, he had sacrilegiously placed a crown filled with precious carbuncles upon the profane head of the blessed Virgin.

> “Then,” says Theophanes, “on the sixth day before the Ides of September, in the fourth indiction, the most pious Irene, together with her son Constantine, gloriously received the empire from God.”

And so, through an empress who was a woman and a widow, and through Constantine her son, a boy and an orphan, God—wondrously—suppressed the impiety that had been aroused and the attack launched against all the churches.

During these times the Nestorian heresy revived in Spain through Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, who taught that Christ, with respect to his humanity, was the adopted Son of God, not his proper and natural Son. Since this doctrine established two persons in Christ, it introduced Nestorianism.

In the thirteenth year of Adrian’s pontificate, Paul, patriarch of Constantinople, resigned his episcopate and publicly declared, lamenting his prolonged pretense concerning the Catholic faith:

> “Unless a universal synod is held and the error that exists among you is corrected, you will have no salvation.”

Then public permission was granted to debate concerning the images. Tarasius, distinguished by his lineage, did not allow himself to be appointed in Paul’s place until he had received a promise that an ecumenical council would be celebrated concerning the case of the images.

Theophanes.

The emperors, the Augusti, announced these matters to the Roman pontiff and requested and obtained the convocation of an ecumenical synod by apostolic authority. You, reader, will learn these matters more fully from what we shall note below under the heading “Council” in the Second Council of Nicaea.

**SEV. BIN.**

Adrian, a Roman by nationality, son of Theodore, from the district of the Via Lata, sat for twenty-three years, ten months, and seventeen days. He was a very distinguished man, born of a most noble lineage and descended from very powerful Roman parents, an elegant and exceptionally handsome person, steadfast and exceedingly strong in the orthodox faith, and a defender of his fatherland and of the people entrusted to him. Manfully, with God’s aid, he resisted the enemies of the holy Church of God and the republic; he was also most merciful and a generous comforter of all the poor and needy, and an observer of ecclesiastical tradition and the teachings of the holy Fathers.

This most blessed man, after his father had died and he had been left as a small child to his most noble mother, was carefully nourished and educated, after the death of his said [holy] mother, by Father Theodatus [Theodulus], formerly consul and duke and afterward primicerius of our holy Church. From the earliest childhood of his life, while he was still a layman, he devoted himself most earnestly to spiritual pursuits and charity and modesty, persevering diligently in the church of Saint Mark, which appears to have been near his house.

There he offered frequent praises to our God day and night. Wearing sackcloth, he disciplined his body with fasts, and freely gave alms with scrupulous care to the needy and destitute, according to the strength of his means. The merits of his good actions frequently rang in the ears of all the Romans, so that the reputation of his nobility and chastity spread far and wide.

When Pope Paul of blessed memory observed the spiritual life, conduct, and outstanding character of his pious way of life, he ordered him to enter the clergy. He appointed him regional notary in the Church and afterward made him subdeacon. After the death of Pope Paul, when Lord Stephen II [Baronius: III], the younger pope, had been raised to the summit of the pontificate, he too, observing the merits of the blessed Adrian’s spiritual conduct, promoted him to the order of the diaconate.

From that time, endowed with spiritual accomplishments in many ways, he devoted the greatest care both to proclaiming the divine and evangelical words skillfully and clearly to the people and to exercising ecclesiastical tradition. Thus the grace of the Holy Spirit shone in his heart, so that he was found effective and capable in all things.

And so, when the aforementioned Pope Stephen departed this life, it came to pass that Adrian—who was loved by the Roman people with the most fervent affection—was immediately elected [raised] to the sacred height of the pontificate, as an outstanding and most holy man and worshiper of God.

On the very day of his election, at the same hour in which he was elected, he immediately caused those judges of this Roman city, both from the clergy and from the military, who had been sent into exile by Paul the chamberlain, surnamed Afiarta, and by his other impious accomplices and satellites, [to return] from exile [or: “at the departure of”] Lord Pope Stephen. He also caused the others who had been confined and shut up in strict custody to be released. Thus, with everyone rejoicing together with him, he received, under God’s auspices, his pontifical consecration.

At the very beginning of his consecration, Desiderius, king of the Lombards, sent his legates to His Blessedness: Theodocius [Theodoricus], duke of Spoleto; Tunnon [Tunnorum], duke of the royal city of Ebura; and Prandulus, his wardrobe-master. Through them he sent words of persuasion, saying that he wished to be bound together with him, as it were, in the bond of charity.

The most blessed pontiff replied to them:

> “I indeed desire to have peace with all Christians, including your king Desiderius, and I shall strive to remain in that treaty of peace which has been confirmed among the Romans, Franks, and Lombards. But how can I believe your king, in view of what my predecessor, Lord Pope Stephen of holy memory, reported to me more carefully concerning his fraudulent faith? He said that the king had lied to him about everything that he had promised him under oath upon the body of blessed Peter, for the sake of carrying out the rights of the holy Church of God; and that, merely by his own wicked device, he had caused the eyes of Christopher the primicerius and of Sergius, his son, the secundicerius, to be torn out, thereby satisfying his will against those two leading men of the Church. In this he brought us greater harm and injury.

> “For he afforded no assistance in apostolic affairs. My same predecessor also reported this to me out of the affection with which he regarded me as his little one: when he afterward sent his legates to him, namely Anastasius, the first defensor, and Gemmulus, the subdeacon, exhorting him to fulfill what he had personally promised to blessed Peter, he sent this reply through the same legates:

> “‘It is enough for the apostolic Stephen that I have removed Christopher and Sergius, who were ruling over him; he need not concern himself with seeking justice. Indeed, if I do not aid the apostolic man himself, great ruin will come upon him. For Carloman, king of the Franks, being a friend of the aforesaid Christopher and Sergius, is prepared to hasten to Rome with his armies to avenge their deaths and to seize the pontiff himself.’

> “Behold what kind of faith your King Desiderius possesses, and with what confidence we can enter into an alliance with him.”

As the most blessed Bishop Adrian continued speaking in this manner to the same legates of King Desiderius, they confirmed to him even more strongly, under oath, that their king would carry out for the distinguished pontiff and supreme shepherd all the acts of justice that he had not performed for the aforementioned Lord Pope Stephen, and that he would remain bound to him in an unbreakable bond of charity.

Trusting their oaths, His Blessedness sent his own legates to Desiderius to accomplish all these matters: Stephen, the regional notary and sacellarius, and Paul the chamberlain, together with the rest concerning this matter.

As they were departing from this Roman city and approaching Perusia [perhaps: “proceeding toward Perusia”], he joined to their commission the message [that is, “the news”] that the aforesaid Desiderius had seized the city of Faenza and the duchy of Ferrara, or Comacchio, from the exarchate of Ravenna—territories that Pippin, king of blessed memory, and his sons Charles and Carloman, the most excellent kings of the Franks and patricians of the Romans, had granted and offered to blessed Peter.

For not even two months had passed since that most holy man had attained the summit of the pontificate when the same most savage Desiderius seized those cities, constricting the city of Ravenna and its estates on every side, occupying all the Ravenna strongholds [estates], and taking away all their provisions, their households, their livestock, and everything else that seemed to be kept in those strongholds [estates].

When no hope of survival remained either for Archbishop Leo or for the aforementioned people of Ravenna, who were suffering great distress and famine, they sent their legates here to Rome—namely Julian, Peter, and Vitalian, the tribunes [or: “the tribune”]—begging with great weeping that the most holy pontiff help them as he could and fight to recover the cities. They asserted that, unless those cities were restored, they could in no way survive.

Then the beneficent pontiff, while the aforementioned legates were still in Rome, sent Stephen the sacellarius and Paul the chamberlain to the aforesaid king with letters of entreaty, asking him to restore those cities. In his letters he sternly rebuked him for having changed his mind concerning the promise he had sent through his legates, and for failing to return the rights of blessed Peter as he had promised. Moreover, he had seized those cities which his predecessors, the most blessed pontiffs Lord Stephen, Paul, and that same Stephen, had held.

When the most holy pontiff had sent such words to the insolent Desiderius, entreating, admonishing, and adjuring him, the king replied that he would not restore the cities unless the beneficent bishop first joined him so that they could speak together.

In those days it happened that the wife and sons of the former Frankish king Carloman, together with Autchar, fled to the same king of the Lombards. Desiderius strove and eagerly exerted himself to ensure that the sons of Carloman should assume the Frankish kingdom. For this reason he attempted to bring the most holy bishop to himself, so that he might anoint the aforementioned sons of Carloman as kings. He desired to introduce division into the Frankish kingdom, to separate the most blessed pontiff from the charity and affection of the most excellent Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, and to subject the whole Roman city and all Italy to the power of his Lombard kingdom.

But, with God’s favor, he could in no way accomplish this, for Adrian the pontiff proved as firm as a diamond.

The aforementioned Paul, who was still staying with Desiderius concerning this matter, firmly promised him that he would bring the most blessed pope to him, saying:

> “Even if it should be necessary for me to put a rope around his feet, I shall bring him into your presence by whatever means I can.”

And so it happened that, while Paul was on that same journey, it became publicly known that he had caused Sergius the secundicerius, who was blind and was in the storeroom, to be killed.

The most holy bishop feared that news of this might have reached Paul’s ears and that Paul might either return to the same king or turn aside from his route into Lombard territory and perpetrate further evil with Desiderius in Roman territory and in the exarchate of Ravenna—for Paul was very dear and faithful to him. Therefore the aforementioned holy pope secretly and most confidentially sent word through Julian the tribune to Leo, archbishop of the city of Ravenna, instructing him that, when Paul returned from Desiderius, he should detain him either in Ravenna or in Ariminum [detain him—variant]. This was done.

When Paul returned from that journey, he was seized in Ariminum and held in custody. Then the same blessed pontiff began carefully to investigate the death of the aforementioned Sergius the secundicerius. He summoned all the keepers of the storeroom and examined them closely as to how Sergius had been taken from that storeroom.

They replied:

> “At the first hour of the night, Calventinus the chamberlain came with Tunisson [Codex Luc. reads: Lunisson, and so everywhere], the presbyter, and Leonatius the tribune, inhabitants of the city of Anagni. He himself took away Sergius, while Lord Pope Stephen was still alive, eight days before he departed this life, and handed him over to the Campani.”

The same chamberlain was immediately brought before the court. When questioned who had ordered him to take Sergius from the aforementioned storeroom and hand him over to the Campani, he replied that he had been ordered to do so by Paul the chamberlain, surnamed Afiarta; Gregory, the regional defensor; John, the brother of Lord Pope Stephen; and Calvulus [Calventinus], the chamberlain. They had ordered him to hand Sergius over to those Campani.

The most holy bishop then sent his legates to Campania, to the city of Anagni, and had the aforementioned Tunisson [Lavisson] and Leonatius brought in. When presented before the apostolic presence and placed under severe restraint, they confessed, saying that the order to seize and kill the aforementioned Sergius had come from the aforesaid Paul the chamberlain, Gregory the regional defensor, John, the brother of the aforementioned Lord Pope Stephen, Calvulus, likewise the chamberlain, Malignus, their accomplice, and the aforementioned Paul.

Immediately the most holy pontiff sent his most faithful ministers with the aforementioned Campani, ordering them to show the place where they had killed and buried Sergius. They hurried as far as Merolana, to a painted arch beside the road [Codex Luc.: “which is beside the road”] leading to the church of the holy Mother of God at the Praesepe. There, opening a grave beside the same arch, they showed that Sergius’ body had been placed there, with his throat constricted by a rope and his entire body wounded by blows. It was therefore clearly evident that he had been suffocated and buried while still half alive.

When all the leading men of the Church and the military judges saw this, they went together with the whole people to the Lateran patriarchate. Prostrate at the apostolic feet, they earnestly begged the beneficent pontiff to order vengeance and correction for so great and unheard-of a crime: they had dared cruelly to kill a man who had repeatedly been burned by torture—something never before recorded. They declared that, unless the guilt of such a crime were expiated, this impious presumption of wicked audacity would grow excessively in the city of Rome, and evil men would thereby take courage to attempt still worse deeds.

Then the aforementioned most holy bishop, moved by the prayers of the judges and of the entire Roman people [Codex Luc.: “inclined by the prayers”], ordered that Calvulus the chamberlain and the aforementioned Campani be handed over to the prefect of the city, so that he might examine them, as murderers, before the entire people. They were led from the aforesaid patriarchate to the public prison [variant: “from the aforesaid patriarchate”], where they were examined before the entire people.

The Campani confessed in that examination just as they had before. Calvulus, however, hardened his heart and only with difficulty admitted that all these things were so; nevertheless, he lost [variant: “breathed out”] his life by a cruel death in that same prison. To cut off the guilt of so intolerable a crime, the Campani were sent into exile at Constantinople.

Afterward the aforesaid most blessed pope ordered that the bodies of Christopher and of the aforementioned Sergius, his son, be taken up, and he had them honorably buried in the church of blessed Peter.

The aforesaid beneficent pontiff sent the record of the examination—showing how Calvulus the chamberlain and the aforementioned Campani had confessed the guilt of their own crimes—to Ravenna, so that the entire matter might be read aloud to Paul.

Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, received these proceedings and immediately, without apostolic authority, handed Paul over to the consular official of the city of Ravenna. After Paul had been examined before all the people of Ravenna, the same proceedings were read to him. Thus, revealing himself guilty of so great a crime, he confessed that he had committed the offense.

Paul was examined in this way, and indeed no notice of it was given to the aforesaid most holy pontiff, either by the archbishop or by any of the people of Ravenna. His Blessedness learned of it through others.

While this was taking place, the distinguished pastor and excellent pontiff, desiring to save the soul of the aforesaid Paul so that he might not perish forever, had a petition drawn up, addressed to the Augusti Constantine and Leo, the great emperors. He informed them of the impious death of Sergius the blind man and begged their imperial clemency to receive Paul for the correction of so great a crime and order that he be kept in exile in the regions of Greece.

He also sent the same petition to the thrice-blessed Archbishop Leo, so that he might send Paul into exile at Constantinople, whether through Venice or by some other route, as he could, together with the aforesaid apostolic petition.

But the archbishop, plotting intensely against Paul, seized upon an impious pretext and sent this reply to the distinguished pontiff:

> “It is not expedient to send Paul there, since Desiderius, king of the Lombards, is holding captive with him the son of Maurice, duke of Venice. Maurice, wishing to recover his son from the king, might hand Paul over to him as a substitute.”

Behold the kind of pretext that the archbishop of the church of Ravenna craftily employed, so that he might destroy Paul. Thus he sent that petition back to the apostolic see.

Afterward, when the most holy bishop sent Gregory, his sacellarius, to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, to entreat and exhort him to restore the cities he had seized, he ordered Gregory firmly to warn Archbishop Leo to take care of Paul and, when he returned from Ticinum, to bring Paul back here to Rome with him.

When Gregory the sacellarius proceeded to the city of Ravenna, he steadfastly and firmly protested before the aforesaid archbishop and the judges of Ravenna, in accordance with the apostolic command, in the presence of Anuald the chartularius, then present there as a Roman citizen and sent there by the apostolic see, that Paul was to be kept safe and unharmed until Gregory returned from Ticinum. He stated that the apostolic authority had ordered him to bring Paul back with him to Rome and present him safe before the apostolic presence.

After making this protest to the archbishop, Gregory departed on the journey to Ticinum. Immediately the aforementioned archbishop summoned the consul of the city of Ravenna and ordered him to kill Paul.

When the aforesaid sacellarius had returned and reached Ravenna, he found that Paul had already been killed. He severely rebuked the archbishop for daring to act in this way against Paul, contrary to the apostolic command.

After several days, the same archbishop, terrified [Codex Luc.: “having become frightened”], sent his own legate, Julian the tribune, for the third time to the aforementioned most holy pope. He begged that apostolic letters and words of consolation be sent to him, as though he believed that no fault in Paul’s death would be imputed to him [Codex Luc.: “that the guilt of his death would not be imputed to him”], since the blood of an innocent man had been avenged.

But he could not in any way move the most holy pope and pontiff to yield [variant: “to incline”]. He sent him this reply:

> “Let him see for himself what he has done to Paul. Indeed, wishing to save his soul, I had resolved to subject him to penance. For this reason I sent my sacellarius here to bring him back. In fact, when the aforementioned Desiderius, king of the Lombards, carried away by the arrogance and vanity of pride, seized the cities of the exarchate of Ravenna, he immediately sent a large army and caused the territories of the cities—namely Senigallia, Montefeltro, Urbino, Gubbio, and the other Roman cities—to be occupied. They perpetrated many murders, plunderings, and burnings in those territories.

> “For when he sent a general army into the territory of Tuscia, to the city of Blera, and the people of Blera, trusting in peace, went out in a body with their wives, children, and servants to gather their own crops, the Lombards suddenly fell upon them. They killed all the leading men who were of any importance in that city, carried off much booty both in human beings and in livestock, and devastated everything around them with sword and fire.

> “The same Desiderius also ordered many evils and plunderings to be perpetrated in the territories of the Roman city and of the other cities, as has been said, and he caused the fortress of Orte to be occupied.”

For this reason the most blessed bishop repeatedly and again repeatedly sent letters of entreaty and legates to Desiderius, begging him to recover from such evils and to restore the cities he had seized.

But he was not only unwilling to restore the cities he had occupied; he also refused to withdraw from that wickedness, never ceasing, as has been said, to inflict many cruel and intolerable evils upon the territories of the Romans.

Then the aforesaid most holy pontiff summoned the aforementioned devout abbot of the monastery of the Holy Mother of God, situated in the territory of Sabina, together with twenty senior monks, servants of God, and sent them to that same Desiderius for the purpose of supplication. As they hastened to him, they reported that, falling at his feet before the judges of the Lombards, they tearfully entreated him in the name of the aforesaid vicar of blessed Peter to repent of such great evils and to restore to blessed Peter the aforementioned cities that he had taken away. But they were wholly unable to turn his heart of stone. And so those servants of God returned without result.

Desiderius himself sent his envoys—[Note: Codex Lucullanus: “more frequently, his envoys”]—to the aforementioned most blessed pontiff, namely Andrew the referendary and Stabilus the duke, so that he might join him in discussion. The gracious shepherd received them and replied as follows:

“Give this satisfaction to your king in my name: I solemnly promise you before almighty God that, if he restores to me the cities of blessed Peter which he took from me during my pontificate, whether at Pavia, Ravenna, Perugia, here in Rome, or wherever he may wish, I shall immediately hasten into his presence and join him in discussion concerning whatever concerns the salvation of the people of God on both sides. And if he perhaps doubts that I ought not to join him after he has restored those cities, let him have permission to occupy them again if I do not join him for discussion. For if he does not first restore those cities and render us justice, let him know for certain that he will never see my face.

“Therefore, behold, I shall endeavor to send my envoys as your companions to your king, so that they may receive those cities, if he is willing to restore them. From the very moment when my envoys, having received those cities, return to me and announce this, I shall immediately hasten into his presence, wherever he wishes, as I have said, in order to speak with him.”

When the Lombard envoys had hastened away and returned to their king, His Thrice-Blessedness immediately sent his own envoys to the same king Desiderius to receive those cities: Pardus, a devout hegumen—that is, a superior—of the monastery of blessed Sabas [Note: Codex Lucullanus omits “superior”], and Anastasius, the chief defender. When they were presented before him and likewise fell at his feet, entreating him with abundant tears to restore the aforesaid cities, they promised him by apostolic authority under oath that, if he restored them, the aforementioned gracious pontiff would immediately hasten to him to depart and confer with him. But they were utterly unable to soften his iron breast and hardest mind by any means, and, receiving nothing, they returned without result.

Nevertheless, the aforementioned pontiff did not cease sending envoys to him for this very purpose, both priests and men from each of the religious orders. Yet they were unable to obtain anything from him. Rather, persisting in his wickedness, he caused evils to be inflicted from every side upon many cities and territories of the Romans, and sent great threats to that eminent pontiff, declaring that he would hasten with all the armies of the Lombards to subdue the Roman city.

Because of this, the most holy pontiff, overcome with immense weeping together with his people, ordered the gates of the Roman city to be closed and had others of them blocked up with masonry [that is, closed by a wall]. While he remained in great anxiety and tribulation, compelled by necessity he sent his envoys by sea, with apostolic letters, to the most excellent Charles, king of the Franks, protected by God, and patrician of the Romans. He entreated His Excellence that, just as his father, of holy memory, Pippin, had done, he too would come to the aid of and support the holy Church of God and the afflicted Roman people and the province of the Ravenna Exarchate, and that he would exact the full rights of blessed Peter and the cities taken away by that same king Desiderius.

But although the wicked Desiderius had been unable by any deceitful stratagem to persuade the aforementioned most holy pontiff to come to him so that he might anoint the sons of the aforesaid Charles the Great as kings, and had wished to separate that gracious pontiff from the charity and affection of the often-mentioned most Christian king Charles the Great, he then, having abandoned his palace in obstinacy and audacity, set out with his own son Adalgisus and the Lombard army. He took with him the wife and sons of the aforesaid deceased Carolomannus, as well as Autcharius, who, as has been said, had fled to him. He was attempting to hasten to Rome without the knowledge of the aforementioned pontiff, sending his envoys—namely the aforementioned Andrew the referendary and two other judges from his own entourage—to announce his arrival.

When they reached Rome and were presented before the apostolic presence, the pontiff gave them this reply:

“Unless he restores to blessed Peter, as he has now promised, those cities which he took during my pontificate, and renders full justice to our side, there is no need for him to undertake the trouble of coming here, for it is utterly impossible that I should first be presented before him.”

When Desiderius received this reply, he did not turn back on that account, but continued the journey he had begun toward Rome. When the most holy chief shepherd learned that his arrival was already approaching, he gathered all the people of Tuscia, Campania, and the duchy of Perugia, together with some men from the cities of the Pentapolis, and fortified this Roman city. All were armed and ready, so that, if the king arrived, they might firmly resist him with the help of God and blessed Peter, supported by the prayers of the aforesaid most holy pontiff [perhaps: “to resist him”]. His Holiness also caused the churches of Peter and Paul to be stripped of their adornment [that is, deprived of their ornaments], and brought all their treasures and ornaments into this Roman city. He ordered all the doors of the church of blessed Peter to be closed and secured from within with earth [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “with bars”], so that, if that arrogant king should arrive without the pontiff’s permission and consent, he would have no access to enter the same church unless he broke those doors by force of arms, to the destruction of his own soul.

When he had arranged all these things, he immediately committed in writing a sentence of anathema and sent three bishops to the same king Desiderius: Eustratius of Albano, Andrew of Praeneste, and Theodosius of the city of Tivoli.
