In that same sentence of obligation and exhortation he protested against him and adjured him by all the divine mysteries that he should in no way presume to enter or trample upon the territories of the Romans without the pontiff’s absolution—neither he, nor any Lombard, nor Autcharius the Frank.

After the Lombard king had received this sentence of obligation through the aforesaid bishops, he immediately withdrew from the city of Viterbo, confounded, and returned to his own country with great reverence.

After this, envoys of the often-mentioned Charles, most excellent king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, arrived at the apostolic see: George, the most holy bishop; Gulfardus, the devout abbot and counselor; and Albinus, the king’s favorite [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “Alboinus, the favorite of the king”]. They came to determine whether he had restored the cities taken away [or: removed] and all the rights of blessed Peter, as he falsely represented when sending word to Francia and asserting that he had restored everything.

When they were satisfied that he had restored nothing, the same chief pontiff related to them everything that had occurred and dismissed them to return to Francia. He sent his own envoys with them to the aforementioned most excellent king of the Franks, bearing apostolic words of admonition, and strongly adjured him to fulfill what he had promised to blessed Peter together with his father, King Pippin of holy memory. He urged him to complete the redemption of the holy Church of God and to have everything taken away by the treacherous king of the Lombards—both the cities and the remaining rights—restored to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, without [his own] contest.

The Frankish envoys therefore proceeded with the envoys of the apostolic see and turned aside to the aforementioned Desiderius. They steadfastly entreated and exhorted him, as their king had ordered them, to restore peacefully to blessed Peter the aforesaid cities that he had taken away and to render justice to the Roman side. But they were utterly unable to obtain any of these things from him, for he declared that he would restore nothing. Having received this reply, the aforementioned Frankish envoys returned to their own land.

The envoys of the apostolic see also hastened back. Reporting everything in greater detail and announcing to the aforementioned most excellent and God-protected Charles the Great, king of the Franks, the wicked purpose of the aforesaid Desiderius, they immediately caused that most gentle and truly most Christian king Charles, king of the Franks, to send his envoys to Desiderius. They entreated him to restore peacefully the cities he had taken away and to render full justice to the Roman side. In addition, he promised to grant him fourteen thousand gold solidi, in gold and silver. But neither by entreaties nor by gifts could he turn the most savage king’s heart.

Obtaining nothing, the Frankish envoys returned to their aforementioned most Christian king. Then Charles the Great, the God-protected king, gathered the entire multitude of the armies of his Frankish kingdom. He sent part of that army to occupy the passes, while he himself, with many very brave Frankish warriors, approached those same passes by Mount Cenis [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “Sinis”], and, withdrawing to the borders of Francia, encamped there with his armies.

The aforesaid Desiderius and the entire multitude of the Lombard armies stood firmly in those passes to resist him. They attempted carefully to fortify them with structures and various stone walls. But when the aforementioned most Christian king of the Franks approached those passes, he immediately sent his envoys again to Desiderius, entreating him, as before, to accept the aforementioned amount of solidi and peacefully restore the same cities.

But he absolutely refused to yield. While that arrogant king Desiderius persisted in such hardness, and while the aforementioned most Christian king wished peacefully to receive [or: restore] the rights of blessed Peter, he sent word to the Lombard king that he should give him only three hostages, the sons of Lombard judges, in exchange for restoring those cities, and that he would immediately return home with his Frankish armies without inflicting any hostile harm [variant: “without engaging in battle”] or beginning a fight.

But even this could not bend his wicked mind. Therefore almighty God, seeing the wicked Desiderius’s treacherous iniquity and intolerable arrogance, while the Franks wished on the following day to return home, sent terror and a powerful trembling into his heart, and into that of his son Adalgisus and of all the Lombards. That same night they abandoned their own tents and all their baggage and universally took flight, with no one pursuing them.

When the Frankish armies saw this, they pursued them and killed many of them. Desiderius himself, fleeing as quickly as possible with his judges at the fastest pace, reached Pavia and endeavored to shut himself in there with those judges and with the multitude of the Lombard people. He fortified the walls of that city to resist the Frankish armies and prepared himself with his Lombards to defend his own city.

His son Adalgisus [Aldegisus], however, taking with him Autcharius the Frank, the wife, and the sons of the aforementioned Carolomannus, entered the city now called Verona, because it appeared to be the strongest of all the Lombard cities.

The remaining Lombards, scattered, returned to their own cities. Some prominent men among the Spoletans and Reatines, however, before Desiderius or his Lombard army proceeded to the passes, fled for refuge to blessed Peter and surrendered themselves to the aforementioned most holy pope Adrian. Swearing allegiance to the faith of that prince of the apostles and of the aforementioned most holy pontiff, they were tonsured according to Roman custom.

The rest also eagerly desired to surrender themselves in the service of blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “The rest also desired to surrender themselves”]. But, fearing their king, they did not dare to do so. When they had fled from the passes, and all those from the various cities of the duchy of Spoleto had returned from there, they immediately came together in a general assembly to the aforementioned gracious pontiff. Falling at his feet, they earnestly entreated His Holiness to receive them into the service of blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church and to have them tonsured according to Roman custom.

He received them and proceeded with them to the church of blessed Peter. There, all together, from the greatest to the least, under the bond of an oath, promised that they would faithfully remain in the service of that apostle of God, of his aforementioned vicar, the most holy pope Adrian, and of all his pontifical successors, together with their sons and all their descendants. After they had taken the oath, they were all tonsured according to Roman custom.

Immediately that thrice-blessed good shepherd and father, rejoicing with them all, appointed as their duke the man whom they had freely chosen for themselves: the most noble Hildeprand, who had previously fled for refuge to the apostolic see with the others.

And thus, with God’s assent, that chief pontiff brought the whole duchy of Spoleto under the law and power of blessed Peter through his own struggle [or: campaign]. Likewise, all the inhabitants of the duchies of Firmo, Auximum, and Ancona, as well as those of the Castle of Felicitas [Fulginates], returning after fleeing from the Lombard passes, came together to the aforementioned most holy pontiff and surrendered themselves to His Holiness.

After taking an oath that they would faithfully remain in the faith and service of blessed Peter, of his vicar, the aforementioned gracious pope Adrian, and of his pontifical successors, they were tonsured according to Roman custom.

Meanwhile the often-mentioned most Christian king Charles, king of the Franks, set out with his general armies and reached the city of Pavia. He surrounded it on every side and fortified it with a siege. He immediately sent to Francia and had his excellent wife, Queen Hildegard, and his noble sons brought to him at Pavia.

When he learned that the aforementioned Adalgisus had fled to Verona, he left the greater part of his armies at Pavia and himself hastened with some of the bravest Franks to that same city of Verona. When he arrived there, Autcharius, the wife, and the sons of the often-mentioned Carolomannus voluntarily surrendered themselves to that most kindly king Charles.

His Excellence received them and returned again to Pavia. Immediately sending out columns of warriors, he seized various Lombard cities situated beyond the Po and reduced them to his power.

While that Frankish king remained for six months in the siege of Pavia, greatly desiring to hasten to the threshold of the apostles, and considering that the most sacred feast of Easter was approaching, he took with him various bishops, abbots as well, judges, dukes, and counts, together with very large armies, and hastened to Rome through the regions of Tuscia. He arrived so quickly that he presented himself at the apostolic threshold on Holy Saturday itself.

When the aforementioned most blessed pope Adrian heard of his arrival—that the Frankish king had come so suddenly—he was thrown into great astonishment and ecstasy. He sent all the judges to meet him at a place called Novae, nearly thirty miles from the Roman city, where they received him with a military banner [Note: “Bandora” means a military standard].

When he had approached to within nearly one mile of the Roman city, the pope sent out all the military schools together with their patrons, and also the boys who were going to learn letters. All of them carried branches of palm and olive trees, and, singing praises with the cries of acclamation proper to those praises, they welcomed the Frankish king.

His Holiness sent venerable crosses to meet him—that is, standards, as is customary when receiving an exarch or patrician—and had him received with immense honor. When the most kindly Charles the Great, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, instituted by God, saw those most sacred crosses and standards coming to meet him, he descended from the horse on which he was seated and hastened on foot with his judges toward blessed Peter.

The aforementioned gracious pontiff, rising at dawn on that Holy Saturday, hastened with all the clergy and the Roman people to blessed Peter to receive the Frankish king. He awaited him on the steps of that apostolic hall together with his clergy.

When the same most excellent and most kindly King Charles arrived, he kissed one by one all the steps of that most sacred Church of blessed Peter. Thus he reached the aforementioned pontiff, who was standing in the atrium above the steps beside the doors of the church.

After receiving him, they embraced one another, and that most Christian king Charles took the right hand of the aforementioned pontiff. Thus they entered the same venerable hall of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. The entire clergy and all the devout servants of God sang praise to God and to His Excellence, acclaiming in a loud voice:

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” and so forth.

Then the Frankish king himself, together with that pontiff, and likewise all the bishops, abbots, judges, and all the Franks who had arrived with him, approached the confession of blessed Peter. Prostrating themselves there, they offered their own vows to our almighty God and to that same prince of the apostles, glorifying the divine power because, through the intervention and intercession of that prince of the apostles, He had granted such a victory.

When that prayer had been completed, the same Frankish king earnestly entreated the aforementioned gracious pontiff to grant him permission to enter Rome, so that he might fulfill the vows of his prayers throughout the various churches of God.

Then the most holy pope himself and the aforementioned most excellent Frankish king, together with the Roman and Frankish judges, descended together to the body of blessed Peter. After mutually strengthening one another by oath, the Frankish king immediately entered Rome on that Holy Saturday with the same pontiff, his judges, and his people.

They entered together the basilica of the Savior beside the Lateran [Lateranum]; there the aforementioned thrice-blessed pontiff celebrated the sacrament of holy baptism, the most excellent king being present with all his companions [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “until”]. Afterward the most blessed king returned to blessed Peter.

When Sunday dawned, on that most sacred feast of Easter, the most holy pontiff sent all the judges and the entire military retinue to the same king at dawn. Receiving him with great honor in the church of the Holy Mother of God at the Praesepe, he hastened there with all the Franks who had arrived with him.

After the solemn Mass had been celebrated, he proceeded with the aforementioned pontiff to the Lateran patriarchate, where they dined together at the apostolic table.

On the following day, Monday, in the same manner and according to customary practice, that distinguished father and excellent pontiff celebrated the solemn Mass in the church of blessed Peter and caused praises to be offered to almighty God and to the aforesaid most excellent king Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans.

On the third day [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “On the third day, Tuesday”], as is customary, he celebrated Mass for the same king in the church of blessed Paul the apostle.

On Wednesday, however, the aforementioned pontiff went out with his judges, both of the clergy and of the military, and joined the same king in the church of blessed Peter the apostle for a conference. He earnestly entreated him, admonished him, and strove to exhort him with paternal affection to fulfill in every respect the promise that his father, King Pippin of holy memory, and that most excellent Charles himself, together with his brother Carolomannus and all the Frankish judges, had made to blessed Peter and his vicar, the lord Stephen the Younger, pope of holy memory, when he went to Francia for the granting of various cities and territories of this province of Italy and for their being handed over to blessed Peter and all his vicars to possess forever.

He had the same promise, which had been made in Francia at a place called Quierzy, read aloud to him. That promise and all the provisions attached to it pleased him and his judges. Of his own free will, with good and willing spirit, the aforementioned most excellent and truly most Christian king Charles, king of the Franks, ordered another promise of donation to be written after the model of the earlier one by Etherius, his devout and most prudent chaplain and notary.

In it he granted those same cities and territories to blessed Peter and promised that they would be handed over to the aforesaid pontiff, with the boundaries specified as the donation itself shows: from Luni, with the island of Corsica; then to Surianus; then to Mount Bardone; then to Verceto [the text reads “in Verceto,” with the preceding place-name uncertain]; then to Parma; then to Reggio; from there to Mantua; and to the Mount [variant: bridge] of Silicis. Likewise he granted the entire Exarchate of Ravenna, as it had been in ancient times, together with the provinces of Venetia and Histria, and the whole duchies of Spoleto and Benevento.

After that donation had been made, the most Christian king of the Franks confirmed it with his own hand and caused all the bishops, abbots, dukes, and counts to be entered in it [variant: “to subscribe it”].

First they placed it upon the altar of blessed Peter, and afterward inside his holy confession. There, the Frankish king and his judges, promising under a terrible oath that they would preserve everything contained in that donation, handed it over to blessed Peter and to his vicar, the most holy pope Adrian.

The most Christian king of the Franks caused a copy of the donation to be written by that same Etherius [that is, a copy; Note: Codex Lucullanus: “on his behalf”]. For the firmest security and for the eternal remembrance of his name and of the Frankish kingdom, he placed it with his own hands inside, above the body of blessed Peter, beneath the Gospels which are kissed there.

His Excellence took other copies of the same donation with him, written by the scrivener of this holy church of ours.

After returning with his armies to Ticinum, the most excellent king of the Franks fought fiercely against and besieged the city of Pavia. While the wrath of God raged and stormed against all the Lombards who were in that city, and many had perished from illnesses or the devastation of mortality, by God’s will that same most excellent king of the Franks captured the city, together with Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and all who were with him, and subjected the entire Lombard kingdom to his power.

He took the aforementioned Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and his wife with him to Francia.

The aforementioned most blessed pontiff was indeed a lover of churches [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “of the churches of God, constantly showing great concern in caring for all those churches of God. For this co-angelic man…”].

This co-angelic man made in the church of blessed Peter the apostle a garment of marvelous beauty, made of gold and gems, bearing a representation of the story of how blessed Peter was freed from his chains by an angel.

Likewise, in the same basilica, from the entrance at the Rugas to the confession, he covered the pavement with pure silver weighing one hundred fifty pounds.

He also made in that same basilica of blessed Peter, beside the great doors, silver curtains of marvelous size, made of stauracin or quadrapola fabrics. Throughout all the arches of the basilica of that prince of the apostles he also made sixty-five curtains of Tyrian and embroidered fabrics.

Finally, His Holiness made a great lamp in the same church of blessed Peter in the form of a cross. It hangs before the presbytery and has one thousand three hundred seventy candles [Note: Codex Lucullanus: 1,365]. He established that this lamp should be lit four times a year: at the Nativity of the Lord, at Easter, on the feast of the apostles, and on the feast of the pontiff.

Likewise, the aforementioned most holy pontiff made in that basilica a silver chalice, made by casting, weighing five pounds, and placed it in the presbytery to replace one that had been lost in the time of Pope Paul.

In the church of blessed Andrew the apostle, situated beside the same church of blessed Peter the apostle, that thrice-blessed pontiff newly made a ciborium of the purest silver, weighing one hundred thirty-five pounds.

Likewise, in the church of blessed Paul the apostle, he clothed the body of that teacher of the world with silver plates weighing thirty pounds.

These were added by the same most holy pontiff because the silver that had originally been there was excessively broken.

He also made in the same basilica of blessed Paul the apostle, beside the principal doors, a large curtain of quadrapola fabrics, after the likeness of the curtain he had made in the church of blessed Peter.

He made another large curtain of quadrapola fabrics, which hangs beneath the great arch beside the altar. He also made throughout the various arches of that church seventy curtains of quadrapola fabrics.

The atrium of that church of blessed Paul, which had previously been desolate [Note: Codex Lucullanus adds: “excessively desolate”], where oxen and horses entered to graze because of the grass growing there, the same most holy pontiff, inspired by God, had paved with beautiful marble.

In the church of the Mother of God at the Praesepe, he made two garments for the principal altar: one of the purest gold and gems, bearing the Assumption of the Holy Mother of God, and another of stauracin fabric, adorned around its edges with scarlet cloth (blattin; variant: stauracio, blattis).

In that church he also made large curtains of quadrapola fabrics [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “beside the principal doors, of quadrapola fabrics”] [quadraptis, or quadruplis fabrics], after the likeness of those he had made in the church of blessed Peter.

Likewise, throughout the various arches of that basilica of the Holy Mother of God, he made, in the same manner and from quadrapola fabrics, forty-two curtains [Note: Codex Lucullanus: sixty-two].

In the basilica of the Savior of Our Lord Jesus Christ beside the Lateran, he likewise made a garment of stauracin and a large curtain of quadrapola fabrics. Throughout the various arches he also made fifty-seven silk curtains, all of quadrapola or stauracin fabrics.

In the church of blessed Lawrence the martyr outside the walls, namely where his holy body rests, he made a garment of stauracin, and in the larger church he likewise made another garment.

The roof of that basilica of blessed Lawrence the martyr, which had already been uncovered [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “of the greater basilica, which had already been uncovered, and so forth”], and its beams having been broken, he newly restored.

In the basilica of blessed Valentine he likewise made a garment of stauracin. In the basilica of blessed Pancratius he made another garment in the same manner, of stauracin.

In the church of blessed Mark, whose roof, already weakened by age, stood near collapse, he removed the extremely old beams and installed new ones. He newly made the roof and the surrounding portico, and restored the same church [Note: Codex Lucullanus reads: “and having installed other very strong ones anew,” etc.; it omits “and restored the same church”].

As for the three arches [Note: Codex Lucullanus’s first hand read: “three archways, which were also very old.” A somewhat later hand revised it to the reading found in the printed editions], which were very old, the same most blessed pontiff, adding twelve pounds of silver, newly constructed them.

He also made in the same church, over the principal altar, a garment of stauracin. Throughout the various arches of that church he made twenty-seven curtains of quadrapola fabrics, and likewise a crown of the same quadrapola fabrics, which hangs beneath a beam [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “and a curtain of the same fabrics,” and so forth].

The roof of the basilica of blessed Lawrence [lacuna] at Taurellum [Note: Codex Lucullanus: “of Lawrence, which was formerly at Taurillus,” and so forth], being extremely old, he placed new beams throughout it and restored it. He also made and offered a garment of quadrapola fabric over the altar of that church.

The basilica of blessed Felix, situated at the Principis, which was in ruins and whose roof had been uncovered, he renovated by constructing a new roof. He made a garment of quadrapola fabrics for its altar and offered it.

He also renovated the roof of the basilica of Saint Lawrence called the Damasean. There he made a garment of stauracin over its altar, and likewise another garment behind the altar, where the body of Saint Damasus rests.

He renovated the surrounding porticoes of the basilica of the apostles on the Via Lata, which his predecessor, the lord Pope Paul, had previously begun but had not completed. By God’s favor, the aforementioned most blessed pontiff repaired everything and also restored the greater roof.

When the same most blessed pontiff saw that the apse of that church was already close to collapse, he had the apse strengthened with iron grilles [perhaps: iron latticework]. Thus he restored it.

He made a garment of stauracin in the same church, over the principal altar.

The cemetery of the blessed Peter and Marcellinus on the Via Labicana, near the basilica of the blessed Helena, he likewise renovated; he also newly made its roof—that is, of Saint Tiburtius and of those same saints Peter and Marcellinus—and newly constructed its steps descending to their most sacred bodies, since there was by then no descent to those holy bodies.

In the basilica of the blessed Adrian he made silver *cerostata* weighing twelve pounds, and likewise two [silver] *laudunae* [*laudanae*], weighing eight pounds, which he placed above the *rugae* of the presbytery, where there is an arch of silver [Note: [Col. 1187D] Cod. Luc.: “He placed two *laudimae* above the *rugae* of the presbytery, where there is an arch of silver. He made, etc.”]. He also made two vestments of *stauracin*: one for the altar of the blessed Adrian and the other for the altar of Saint Martina. He further made fifteen veils of fourfold cloth (*pallia quadrapola*) in the same church.

Finally, he newly made the roof of the title-church of the blessed Prisca, which was already about to collapse and lay in ruins; there too he made a vestment of *stauracin*. In the church of the blessed Cosmas and Damian at the Three Fates he made a vestment of *stauracin*, and likewise a curtain before the apse from fourfold cloth; he also made twenty veils from the same fourfold cloth and twenty linen cloths.

For throughout the various title-churches, or other churches, and all the deaconries and monasteries [Col. 1188B] that exist within the walls of this Roman city, that most holy pontiff himself, kindled by divine inspiration, made and offered vestments from cloths—namely, *stauracin* or Tyrian cloth. And, like a good shepherd, he restored and adorned all the churches of God, both outside the walls of this Roman city and within them, for the praise of God. He also renewed the walls and towers of this Roman city, which had fallen and been destroyed down to their foundations, and usefully restored everything around them. For this he expended many stipends, both on the wages of those who constructed the wall and on their provisions, as well as on lime and various necessities, spending as much as one hundred pounds of gold.

This most blessed prelate, kindled by divine inspiration, established in the monastery of Saint Stephen at *Catabarbara*, belonging to the patrician establishment at the blessed apostles [Note: [Col. 1187D] Cod. Luc.: “to the blessed apostle Peter.”], a community of monks, appointing there an abbot and a suitable person. He decreed that they should continually offer praises in the church of the blessed Peter, as in the other monasteries, so that two monks on either side of that church might sing praises to our God, since that monastery had been plunged into great sloth, neglect, and carelessness, and no divine office was being celebrated there [Note: [Col. 1188D] Cod. Luc.: “no divine worship was being offered there.”].

This most blessed prelate newly made and established four cultivated estates (*domuscultae*) [Note: [Col. 1188D] Cod. Luc.: “He newly established a cultivated estate at the fifteenth milestone from the city of Rome at Capricorum, together with many other estates adjoining it, from his parents’ inheritance; and he founded three other cultivated estates anew. By apostolic privilege, under the obligation of great anathemas, he decreed that they should perpetually remain for the use of our brothers, Christ’s poor, and that all grain, wine, and oil should carefully be carried into the granaries and storehouses of our holy church. It is certain that he also showed great solicitude, care, and affection toward the holy and venerable patriarchal house, etc. All the intervening material is missing.”].

One of these was called Capreorum [Capracorum], situated in the territory of Vejentum, approximately fifteen miles from the city of Rome. From it he originally appeared to hold the estate itself, Capracorum, together with many other estates adjoining it, by hereditary succession from his parents [Col. 1188D]. [Col. 1189A] These had formerly been his own; he also appears to have purchased, with just compensation, many other estates, farmsteads, and properties from various persons and added them to that cultivated estate.

He decreed that this cultivated estate of Capracorum—with its properties, estates, farmsteads, vineyards, olive groves, water-mills [*aquimolae*], and everything belonging to it—should, by apostolic privilege and under the obligation of great anathemas, perpetually remain for the use of our brothers. The wheat and barley that each year was produced on the lands of that cultivated estate was to be carefully brought to the granary of our holy church and stored separately. Wine and the various legumes produced annually on the farms and lands of the aforementioned cultivated estate were likewise to be carefully transported to the storehouse of our holy church [Col. 1189B] and stored separately.

Furthermore, from the pigs that were annually fattened in the farmsteads of the often-mentioned cultivated estate, one hundred head were to be slaughtered and stored in that same storehouse.

His Beatitude decreed and promulgated, under the strongest obligations and prohibitions, that every day one hundred of our brothers, Christ’s poor—even if there should be more of them—should assemble at the Lateran patriarchate and be stationed in the portico beside the staircase ascending into the patriarchate, where those poor men are depicted. There, fifty loaves, each loaf weighing two pounds, two *decimatae* of wine, each *decimata* weighing sixty pounds, and a cauldron full of stew [Col. 1189C] were to be distributed every day by the hands of one most faithful storekeeper to those poor people. Each was to receive a portion of bread, a portion of wine—namely, a cup holding two *calices*—and also meat from the stew.

Thus his nourishing Beatitude, together with the priestly college, decreed and promulgated that none of the revenues from the crops or other resources of the aforementioned cultivated estate should be distributed or spent for any other purposes, but that everything should be devoted and perpetually distributed solely for the proper support and daily nourishment of the aforesaid brothers of ours, Christ’s poor.

The other three cultivated estates were as follows: Galeria, situated on the Via Aurelia approximately ten miles from the city of Rome, near Santa Rufina, with its estates, farmsteads, vineyards, olive groves, mills, and everything belonging to it; [Col. 1189D] and the remaining two, namely another Galeria, situated on the Via Portuensis approximately twelve miles from the city of Rome, with its estates, farmsteads, vineyards, water-mills, and the monastery of the blessed Lawrence situated on the island of the Roman port, with its associated vineyards, together with Lecticaria, which is called Asprula.

He also established another cultivated estate called Calvisianum, with its estates, farmsteads, vineyards, olive groves, water-mills, and everything belonging to it, situated on the Via Ardeatina approximately fifteen miles from the city of Rome.

These three cultivated estates—Galeria, Calvisianum, [Col. 1190A] and the other Galeria—his Beatitude decreed, by apostolic privilege and under the obligation of strong anathemas, should perpetually remain for the use and proper benefit of our holy church.

Moreover, amid all the spiritual endeavors that the same thrice-blessed and nourishing pontiff was seen to undertake both for the growth and advancement of the holy Roman Church and for the restoration of the churches of God and the improvement of divine worship, it is certain that he also showed great solicitude, care, and affection toward the holy and venerable patriarchal house.

Therefore, out of his excessive fervent love, for the honor of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and for the adornment of that holy patriarchate, he newly constructed and built there a tower [Col. 1190B] of marvelous beauty, joined to the portico that descends to the bath. There he also caused a promenade—namely, his sun-gallery—with bronze grilles to be built most beautifully. He further very usefully renovated the portico itself, which had been ruined by age. He adorned that tower and all the buildings newly constructed by him with paintings and marbles.

Thus that thrice-blessed and truly outstanding father, the good shepherd and excellent prelate, burning with such love toward his nourisher, the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, made and offered throughout that apostolic hall all its adornment: splendid objects of gold and gems, vestments, various cloths, and other ornaments of gold and silver.

He also renovated all its larger steps [Col. 1190C] ascending into the atrium, as well as the two porticoes ascending into the same church from either side. He renewed the entire pavement of the church wherever the marble had been broken, applying other, beautiful and better marble.

The porticoes on either side of the aforesaid church, in which broken beams were present and whose roof was close to collapse, he restored by installing new beams and newly constructing the roof. His Beatitude also made six images covered with silver plates. Of these, he placed three above the *rugae* at the entrance of the church [Note: [Col. 1189D] The words “of the church” are absent from Cod. Luc.], in the presbytery, where he also made a silver-covered *regulare* and placed the three aforementioned images upon it: in the middle, one bearing the painted face of the Savior; on either side, images bearing the painted likenesses of the angels, one of the blessed Michael and the other of the blessed Gabriel.

On the upper *ruga* [Note: [Col. 1190D] Cod. Luc.: “On the second *ruga*, etc.”], that is, in the middle of the presbytery, he made another silver-covered *regulare* and set upon it the remaining three images. In the middle was the prefigured face of the holy Mother of God; on the two sides was one image bearing the painted face of the holy apostle Andrew and another of Saint John the Evangelist.

All six images, as stated, were made most beautifully from silver plates and gilded. In these images he placed one hundred pounds of silver [Col. 1191A].

Now, after a period of twenty years had passed, the structure called Sabbatina had become extremely damaged. Through it water flowed by a *centenarium* into the atrium of the church of the blessed apostle Peter and likewise into the bath situated beside that church, where our brothers, Christ’s poor, who annually came to receive alms at the Easter festival, used to wash. From it, water also operated various mills at Genuculum.

But because the water from that structure flowed neither into the atrium of the blessed Peter nor within the city, since the structure, as stated, had fallen into ruin—its one hundred high arches having been built and then demolished and destroyed down to their foundations—there seemed by then to be no hope of rebuilding or restoring either those arches or the ruined structure [Note: [Col. 1191D] Cod. Luc.: “which also [concerned] the *carcorae* of that great structure, etc.”].

The most blessed and holy prelate therefore gathered a multitude of people and personally prepared them to construct and restore that structure. He devoted such care and solicitude to its construction that he renewed and restored it from its foundations.

Immediately, since the lead of that *centenarium*, through excessive neglect and carelessness, had already been secretly removed in large part, and the remaining lead had been shattered, that outstanding shepherd, adding a quantity of lead, newly made the *centenarium*. With God’s favor, he caused water to flow abundantly, as in ancient times, into the atrium of the blessed Peter, into the aforementioned bath, and also inside the city—namely, at Genuculum, where the mills operated [Col. 1191C].

The same most blessed pontiff made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul three images from silver plates, placed above the *rugae* at the entrance to the presbytery. One bore the painted face of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; on either side were images bearing painted likenesses of angels. They weighed twenty-four pounds.

He also made in the basilica of the apostles on the Via Lata twenty silk-cloth veils and twenty linen cloths. In the church of the blessed Lawrence, martyr and Levite, outside the walls of this Roman city, he made twenty veils from silk cloths and twenty linen cloths.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed Mother of God at the Martyrs [Col. 1191D], he made twenty veils from silk cloths and twenty linen cloths.

The same most holy pontiff also made in the various title-churches, for each title, twenty veils of *stauracin* or Tyrian cloth and twenty linen cloths. Altogether, this amounted to four hundred and forty silk veils.

That outstanding pontiff made gilded images from silver plates bearing the likeness of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. One was placed above the entrance of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, where the silver doors are; it weighed fifty pounds.

Likewise, in the various deaconries he made, in the same manner, six *stauracin* or Tyrian veils for each deaconry, making ninety-six veils in all.

The same most holy prelate also caused the structure called Jobia [Jovia], which had lain badly damaged for a period of twenty years, to be restored from its foundations.

Similarly, in the basilica of the blessed martyr Pancratius [Note: [Col. 1191D] Cod. Luc.: “of the martyr and Levite, which, etc.”], outside the walls of this Roman city, he made thirty-eight veils of *stauracin* or Tyrian cloth and thirty-eight linen cloths [Note: [Col. 1192D] Cod. Luc.: “forty-eight”]. In the basilica of the blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, on Mount Caelius, he made twenty veils of *stauracin* or Tyrian cloth and twenty linen cloths.

In the basilica of the blessed Apollinaris he similarly made ten veils of *octaplum* and ten linen cloths. [Col. 1192B] In the basilica of the blessed martyr Valentinus, situated outside the walls of this Roman city, he likewise made twenty-two veils of *stauracin* or *octaplum* and twenty-two linen cloths.

When the structure called Claudia appeared to have been destroyed over a period of years—it was from there that people used to bathe in the Lateran baths, and from there water used to flow into the baptistery of the church of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and into several churches on the holy day of Easter—and when only a small amount of water from the aforementioned structure was flowing inside the city, the outstanding and angelic prelate, gathering a multitude of people from the regions of Campania, personally hastened with all his strength to construct and restore that structure.

He devoted such care and solicitude to its construction that he renewed and restored it anew. Immediately, he caused water from that structure to flow abundantly, as in ancient times, into the aforesaid baths and also inside the city.

During his times, Leoninus, the deceased consul and duke, later a monk, granted three unciae of the estate of Aratiana [Aricina], which he had inherited from his parents and which lay sixteen miles from this Roman city on the Via Ardeatina, for the remission of his sins. The church of the blessed Edistus was known to stand there; that most blessed pope adorned and enlarged it with substantial construction.

To those three unciae of the aforesaid estate of Aratiana he added another six unciae purchased from Count Peter and from Agnetes, widow of Agatho the registrar [Col. 1192D], and from Theodata [Note: [Col. 1192D] Cod. Luc.: “and Theodata”], widow of the former prefecture-official Dominicus [*perfecturius* / *praefectorius*]. He also acquired the boundaries on every side. By giving worthy compensation and using force against no one, but rather—as befits a father—purchasing all the lands around that place by friendly agreement, he established that estate as a cultivated estate belonging to the blessed Peter in perpetuity. It is called the cultivated estate of Saint Edistus to this very day.

Likewise, the estate called Acatiana [Note: [Col. 1192D] Cod. Luc.: “Acutiana”], [Col. 1193A] which appears to lie beside that same cultivated estate, was granted by the same Leoninus to the blessed Peter.

The same thrice-blessed prelate also offered, in the greater basilica called “of the Holy Mother of God,” which stood beside the basilica of the blessed Lawrence, martyr and Levite, where his holy body rests outside the walls of this city of Rome, fifteen veils of *stauracin* or fourfold cloth and fifteen linen cloths.

He newly restored the roof of the title-church of the blessed Clement, which also was about to collapse and lay in ruins in the third region. He likewise renewed the church of the blessed Silvester, confessor and pontiff, situated in Orfea, which had already lain in ruins and whose roof had fallen, by making that roof anew.

Similarly, in the famous and renowned basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, celebrated throughout the entire world, that outstanding pontiff observed that the ancient beams which had stood there for ages had become extremely old. He therefore sent his treasurer Januarius [Note: [Col. 1193D] Cod. Luc.: “steward”], whom he knew to be a suitable person, and, with a multitude of people, replaced fourteen beams there. He also newly restored the entire roof and the porticoes of that basilica.

This same nourishing prelate, filled with divine inspiration and moved by mercy, saw that the structure called Virginis had been destroyed over a period of years and was full of ruins, with scarcely any water entering the city of Rome. Like the most benevolent and pious shepherd, he restored it anew and caused such an abundance of water to flow that it almost satisfied the entire city [Col. 1193C].

Finally, he newly restored the roof of the basilica of the blessed martyr Januarius, situated at the gate of the blessed Lawrence, martyr and Levite.

In the cemetery of the blessed martyrs Abdon and Sennen, outside the Porta Portuensis, he made and offered a vestment of *stauracin*.

This angelic man, kindled by divine inspiration, established three deaconries outside the gate of the blessed prince of the apostles. One was that of the holy and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, our Lady, situated in the Atrium [Note: [Col. 1193D] Cod. Luc.: “in Adrianum”]. Another was that of the aforementioned undefiled Lady, our Lady, situated outside the gate of the blessed apostle Peter, at the head of the portico. A third was the deaconry called Saint Silvester, beside the hospice of Saint Gregory.

Finding these aforementioned deaconries in obscurity and without works of mercy, this nourishing man restored them anew. There he offered many movable and immovable gifts for the remedy of his soul. He decreed that every week, on Thursday, they should proceed with psalmody [that is, the singing of psalms] from the deaconry to the bath, and that there, through orderly administration, the poor should be consoled and alms distributed.

Moreover, this often-mentioned most holy prelate, seeing in the basilica of the chosen vessel, the blessed apostle Paul, beams that had grown old through ancient age and were soon about to collapse, did as he had done above in the basilica of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. He arranged everything through his most faithful treasurer Januarius [*vestiarius*], with a multitude of people.

The thrice-blessed shepherd himself also personally and frequently visited the work and newly restored the entire basilica. He replaced thirty-five of its larger beams and newly restored it all around [Note: [Col. 1193D] Cod. Luc.: “He restored all the porticoes.”].

This thrice-blessed and apostolic man, having discovered through his most diligent investigation that the monastery of Pope Honorius was falling into extreme desolation through a certain negligence, rebuilt and endowed it anew, moved by divine inspiration. He appointed an abbot and other monks living there according to the rule, and established that they should celebrate the offices in the basilica of the Savior, also called Constantiniana, situated beside the Lateran patriarchate: namely, Matins, the First, Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours, and Vespers.

One choir consisted of the monks from the monastery of Saint Pancratius situated there, who had formerly sung alone in both places; the other choir consisted of the monks of the aforesaid monastery of Saints Andrew and Bartholomew of Pope Honorius. Thus, singing together in pious praises, they might joyfully resound with hymn-bearing choirs, offering glorious melodies to the Lord and frequently commemorating the name of the venerable pontiff, composing songs in his memory forever.

[Col. 1194C] In the cultivated estate called Capracorum, which he had offered from his own property for the nourishment of the poor to the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and his nourisher, this same most holy prelate founded and built a church from its foundations. He also adorned it magnificently and dedicated it in the name of that same God, his creator [Note: [Col. 1193D] Cod. Luc.: “He dedicated it in the name of that same apostle of God, his protector,” [Col. 1194D] etc.].

In it he deposited relics from the garments [Note: [Col. 1194D] In Cod. Luc. “from the garments” is absent] of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, of that same Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, of the twelve apostles, and of other venerable martyrs.

To this most sacred church he went with all his clergy and the Roman senate, celebrating together with great glory and rejoicing. There he made the customary great alms-distribution to Christ’s poor. He transferred and brought into it the bodies of holy martyrs and pontiffs: namely, the body of Saint Cornelius, martyr and pontiff; the body of his successor, Saint Lucius, martyr and pontiff; likewise the body of Saint Felix, martyr and pontiff; and the body of Saint Innocent, confessor and pontiff.

The nourishing holy pontiff honored them as patrons in the Lord, out of love for the holy apostolic see, in which they had presided, as was fitting [Note: [Col. 1194D] Cod. Luc.: “and, rejoicing in the Lord in their patronage, the nourishing holy pontiff honored them out of love, etc.”].

He also newly restored the roof of the title-church of the blessed martyr Susanna, situated between the two houses near Saint Quiriacus [Col. 1195A], which was already about to collapse and lay in ruins. Likewise, he newly restored the title-church of the blessed martyr Cyriacus and the church of Saint Lawrence called “at Formosa.”

He also renovated, together with its four-sided porticoes, atria, and fountains, the basilica of the Savior, also called Constantiniana, situated beside the Lateran patriarchate and lying in ruins, just as he had done with the churches of the blessed princes Peter and Paul. In it he replaced fifteen large beams.

This same nourishing prelate, finding the monastery of Saint Lawrence in the Palatine district [Note: [Col. 1195D] Cod. Luc.: “which was from the Palatine district”] abandoned, newly restored it and endowed it in every respect. He joined it to another monastery situated nearby, namely that of Saint Stephen, surnamed Baganda [Note: [Col. 1195D] Cod. Luc.: “Vaganda”], and appointed monks. He established that they should perform the office in the title-church of the blessed Mark, pontiff and confessor [Note: [Col. 1195D] Cod. Luc.: “in the territory of the blessed Mark”], namely Matins, the First, Third, and Sixth Hours, the Ninth, and Vespers, singing for the repose of his soul.

In the aforesaid basilica of Saint Mark he also made six other silver arches, weighing together fifty-five pounds. Likewise, he repaired the ministerial chalices proceeding from the Catholic [Note: [Col. 1195D] Cod. Luc.: “in the Catholic”], made of pure [Note: [Col. 1195D] Cod. Luc.: “of the purest”] gold, weighing nine and a half pounds.

This farsighted man, considering the salvation of a great multitude of people, found the portico along the bank of the river, leading to the blessed apostle Peter, narrow and confined—the route by which travelers reached that blessed prince of the apostles, Peter. Placing more than twelve thousand *tufi* in the foundations on the bank of the riverbed, he restored from its foundations to the top of the roof a portico of extraordinary size and restored it as far as the steps of the blessed Peter [Col. 1195C].

The deaconry of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary of the Greek school, called Cosmedin [Note: [Col. 1195D] In Cod. Luc. “of the Greek school” is absent], had formerly been limited in its buildings and lay in ruins. He restored it. For he demolished a huge overhanging mass of Tiburtine tuff, assembling a great multitude of people over the course of a year and burning a pile of much timber; he also cleared away the accumulation of rubble, rebuilt it from its foundations, expanded the aforesaid basilica spaciously on every side, and established three apses in it. Thus that outstanding prelate newly restored a truly magnificent Cosmedin.

Likewise, he repaired the title-church of the blessed martyr Lawrence, called that of Lucina; the church of the blessed Martin situated beside the title-church of Saint Silvester; and the basilica of the blessed martyr Agapitus situated outside the walls near Saint Lawrence [Note: [Col. 1195D] The material enclosed in brackets is absent from the Codex Lucensis. The narrative is reduced there to the following very brief notice:

“He himself, the pontiff, newly made the church of Saints Adrian and Lawrence, which had been ruined in the crypt, with secular chambers, [Col. 1196D] and offered many gifts and various veils there. This same distinguished pope magnificently adorned the altar of the blessed apostle Paul, together with the doors of his confession, with pure gold marked with sacred scenes, weighing 130 pounds. In that church he made a paten of pure gold together with a chalice, weighing together 20 pounds. He restored all the title-churches and all the cemeteries and offered gifts that cannot be counted. He also made the basilica of the monastery of the blessed Anastasius, etc.”]

These churches, which had decayed from ancient times and collapsed under the weight of ruins, the outstanding prelate, burning with love for the Holy Spirit, renewed completely and with great splendor, together with their porticoes.

He also similarly renewed from the foundations the buildings of the title-church of Saint Sixtus and the basilica of Saint Adrian. The basilica of the blessed martyr Pancratius, ruined by extreme age and overwhelmed by ruins, this same nourishing prelate restored completely and with great splendor from the foundations, together with the monastery of Saint Victor situated there.

The outstanding prelate also restored on every side the basilica of the holy Mother of God at the Manger, which had entirely decayed from ancient times, and placed twenty large beams in the roof-structure of that church.

Similarly, he renovated the basilica of Saint Eusebius on every side [Col. 1196B].

The chamber of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which had been entirely destroyed and ruined, he newly made by carving it after an ancient model and using various colors.

He newly restored the portico leading to the blessed apostle Paul, from one gate together with the church of Saint Euplus as far as the aforesaid basilica of Saint Paul. He also newly constructed the portico leading to Saint Lawrence outside the walls, from the gate as far as that same basilica.

This same nourishing father newly restored on every side the basilica of Saint Lawrence, martyr, where his holy body rests, adjoining the greater basilica that the same prelate had formerly built.

He similarly renovated on every side the church of Saint Stephen situated beside them, where the body of Saint Leo, bishop and martyr, rests [Col. 1196C], together with the cemetery of the blessed Cyriaca and its ascent.

He also completely restored the basilica of Jerusalem, situated in the Sessorian district, magnificently replacing its ancient beams, which had decayed, throughout every part.

Likewise, he entirely renewed the church of the apostles called Eudoxiana, “at the Chains.”

He also renovated with the greatest care the basilica of Saints Rufina and Secunda, situated in the episcopal estate of Silva Candida, which had decayed through ancient age, together with its baptistery.

He likewise newly restored and adorned with a structure of great size the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter situated on the Via Appia, at the place called Silice, beyond Saint Thomas the apostle, not far from the thirtieth milestone, which had been overwhelmed by desolation and ruins, together with its baptistery.

[Col. 1196D] Likewise, he entirely restored from the foundations the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian situated at the Three Fates, because its beams too had decayed and failed through extreme age.

He newly renovated in every respect the church of the blessed John the Baptist situated near the Latin Gate, which had been overwhelmed by ruins [Col. 1197A].

He also newly restored the church of the apostles outside the Appian Gate, at the third mile, in the place called the Catacombs, where the body of the blessed martyr Sebastian rests with others, since it had been overwhelmed by ruins.

He newly repaired the title-church of Pudentiana, that is, the church of Saint Potentiana, which lay in ruins. He also renewed from its foundations the basilica of Saint Theodore, situated inside the *velum* near the cultivated estate of Sulpitianus, and the basilica of Saint Peter situated in the estate of Merulana, both of which had been ruined through long ages.

During his times, Mastalus, the *primicerius*, died and left instructions that, for the sake of his soul, his own inheritance should be distributed to Christ’s poor under the authority of the aforesaid pontiff. Accordingly, the heirs of the aforesaid Mastalus, by common agreement, gave and sold to that great prelate, together with estates and farmsteads, the portion belonging to them of the church of Saint Leucius, situated on the Via Flaminia approximately five miles from the city of Rome, and two hundred gold *solidi mancusae*.

The heirs of the aforementioned Mastalus also gave their share of the estate to Christ.

The portion of Gregory, the *secundicerius*, which he was known to possess in the aforesaid farmsteads of Saint Leucius, was granted by that same Gregory to the nourishing prelate in honor of his office as *secundicerius*.

When the church of Saint Leucius had perished, surrounded by extraordinary ruins and thorn growth, the prelate newly restored it and built there, for the blessed Peter, his nourisher, a cultivated estate of marvelous size. He granted it in perpetuity and enlarged its boundaries with property both from the inheritance of Paschalis and from exchanges made with the heirs of the former Lucia, or of John the *primicerius*, or of various places [Col. 1197C].

In the basilica of the blessed Petronilla at the blessed apostle Peter he made six silver arches weighing fifty pounds.

He completely restored the title-church of Saint Praxedis, which had partly collapsed. He also newly restored the basilica of Saint Eugenia both inside and out.

Similarly, he newly restored the basilica of Saints Gordian and Epimachus; the cemetery of that church of Saints Simplicius and Aemilianus, and of the martyrs Quartus and Quintus and the blessed Sophia; together with the cemetery of Saint Tertullian outside the Latin Gate.

He also newly restored the church of the blessed Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus, and the basilica of Saint Zeno, together with the cemetery of Saints Urban, pontiff, Felicissimus and Agapitus, and the martyrs Januarius and Quirinus, all adjoining one another outside the Appian Gate in a single place. These had decayed from ancient times.

He likewise completely restored from the foundations the title-church of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary called that of Callistus, across the Tiber. Similarly, he newly restored the title-church of Saint Marcellus situated on the Via Lata.

He renovated the basilica of the cemetery of the holy martyrs Hermes, Protus, and Hyacinthus—a basilica of marvelous size.

He also magnificently restored the cemetery of Saint Felicitas on the Via Salaria, together with the churches of the martyr Saint Silvanus and of Saint Boniface, confessor and pontiff, which were all connected on the same ground.

He likewise renewed the basilica [Col. 1198A] of Saint Saturninus situated on the aforesaid Via Salaria, together with the cemetery of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria, and renovated the cemetery of Saint Hilaria.

He also newly restored the cemetery of the Jordanians—namely, of the martyrs Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis, and of the seven holy virgins.

On the same Via Salaria he renovated the cemetery of Saint Silvester, confessor and pontiff, and of many other saints, which lay in ruins. He also newly restored the church of Saint Felix situated outside the Porta Portuensis.

Likewise, he renewed the basilica of Saints Abdon and Sennen and of the blessed Candida, together with the other cemeteries of the saints, all in the same manner.

This outstanding prelate, the aforesaid [restorer] of the basilica of the blessed martyr Adrian and of Saints Cosmas and Damian, established deaconries in which he also did many good works for his perpetual memory. He granted them fields, vineyards, olive groves, male and female servants, various livestock, and movable property, so that from their revenues the poor of Christ, benefiting through the frequent distributions of the deaconry, might be nourished.

In the aforesaid diaconia of Saint Hadrian he presented twelve silver baskets, one *ama*, one bowl, one paten, one chalice, and one offertory vessel, weighing sixty-seven pounds. Likewise, through extremely diligent care and industry, he rebuilt the Sabbatine aqueduct anew from its foundations and brought flowing water to his patron, the blessed Apostle Peter—both to the fountain of the basilica [Col. 1198C], which was filled by means of vehicles, and to the atrium of that same basilica—and also provided a bath for the use of the pilgrims serving there. Moreover, he rebuilt anew the basilica of Saint Secundinus, situated in the city of Praeneste, where his body rests, since it lay in ruins.

Likewise, in the basilica of the blessed first martyr Stephen situated on Mount Caelius, which had decayed through long ages, he renewed anew the enormous beams of immense bulk, and even the portico, wonderfully, both inside and outside. Furthermore, in the basilica of blessed Eugenia, which his devotion had already restored some time before, he took diligent care there and established a monastery of girls, newly built from its foundations, [Col. 1198D] so that they might continually sing praises to God there—namely, at the first, third, and ninth hours, at evening, and at matins. In it also he presented many gifts: fields, vineyards, houses, male and female slaves, various livestock, and other movable possessions, with which he endowed it. But in the titular church of Pammachius, of Saints John and Paul, which had decayed over the passing years, he renewed all the roof and structure of that same title.

This distinguished priest, out of his great love for the confession of blessed Peter, adorned its entire interior with the purest gold, in sheets and with various scenes, elegantly, setting in place three hundred pounds by weight. Above the doorway of that same holy confession he placed thirteen pounds of the purest gold, and likewise, on the lower threshold of the confession of the apostle himself, twenty-five pounds [Col. 1199A]. He carefully renewed the appearance of the altar above that same confession and on its right and left beside the steps of the aforesaid confession, adding to it one hundred and thirty-six pounds of silver [*cariosum*]. He most brilliantly gilded its scenes with eighteen pounds of the purest gold.

At the same time, in the church of God he renewed ten *cantharae* belonging to the apostle, adding to them one hundred pounds of silver. Before the doors he made twelve silver baskets weighing thirty-six pounds. Likewise, in the tower he made twelve silver baskets weighing forty-five pounds. In the same church of blessed Peter, on various crowns, he made silver dolphins weighing one hundred pounds. In the church of the blessed Apostle Paul he placed silver dolphins, like those he had installed in the church of Saint [Col. 1199B] Peter, weighing one hundred and eighty pounds. Likewise, in the church of the Savior, called Constantinian, he made silver dolphins weighing thirty pounds.

In the church of blessed Peter he also made, for the various oratories, twelve silver baskets weighing forty pounds in all. He made silver curtains in the presbytery, on the men’s and women’s sides, weighing one hundred and thirty pounds; and also other curtains at the head of the presbytery, before the confession, weighing one hundred and four pounds in all. In the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, across the Tiber, he made five silver baskets weighing fifteen pounds in all.

Indeed, in the basilica of holy Mary, Mother of God, which is at the Praesepe, he made on her altar, at the manger itself, sheets of the purest gold painted with scenes [Col. 1199C], weighing fifteen pounds in all. He rebuilt anew the church of blessed Agnes the martyr, the basilica of blessed Emerentiana, the church of blessed Nicomedes situated outside the Nomentan Gate, and the cemetery of blessed Hippolytus the martyr beside Saint Laurence, all of which had decayed from ancient times. In the same way he restored the church of the blessed martyr of Christ, Stephen, situated beside the aforesaid cemetery of Saint Hippolytus.

In the confession of the blessed Apostle Paul he also made, of the purest gold, an image in the form of the Gospels, placed inside above his most sacred body, weighing twenty pounds. This same prelate, foremost in all good works, newly dedicated and established the monastery of Saints Hadrian and Laurence, which had been decaying in ruins from ancient times and was inhabited by laypeople like a crypt [Col. 1199D]. This distinguished bishop restored it anew in honor of the aforesaid saints, namely Hadrian and Laurence. In it he gave many gifts, in gold and silver, in fields, households, various livestock, and movable goods.

He established in the basilica of Holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, at the Praesepe, and in the other monasteries established there, that those who sang to God day and night should recite the customary praises. There, in the confession of blessed Laurence the martyr outside the wall, the aforesaid bishop made an image of the purest gold in the form of the Gospels, containing an image of blessed Laurence himself, weighing fifteen pounds [Col. 1200A].

In the church of the Savior, called Constantinian, he made three golden bowls (*gabatae*) before the entrance to the altar, weighing ten pounds. In the basilica of the blessed Mother of God at the Praesepe he made silver dolphins on various crowns, weighing twenty-four pounds.

This same outstanding and most excellent bishop made in the church of the blessed Apostle Peter, at the body, an image that had formerly been of silver, representing the Savior, the holy Mother of God, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and Andrew. Made of the purest gold and of extraordinary size, it weighed two hundred pounds.

This most elegant prelate and most steadfast preacher of the true faith sent his envoys—namely, Peter, a priest of the holy Roman Church, and Peter, a religious man and venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Sabbas [Col. 1200B], which is called New Cell—to the emperor Constantine and his mother Irene. Through his apostolic letters he exhorted them and faithfully preached in favor of the erection of the sacred images, explaining how, according to the testimony of Scripture and the tradition of approved Fathers, they had been venerated orthodoxly from ancient times until then in the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church.

The aforesaid emperors, venerating and embracing that apostolic letter, caused a council of three hundred and fifty bishops to be assembled at Nicaea. These bishops, in accordance with the teaching of the preaching of the apostolic letter, believed accordingly. In their promulgation they judged and, through the universal synod, defined with unanimous declaration that images should be erected for veneration [Col. 1200C].

The aforesaid envoys brought that synod back with them in the Greek language, together with the document signed by the sacred hands of the emperors. The distinguished bishop ordered it to be translated into Latin and likewise deposited in the sacred library, thereby creating there a worthy and perpetual memorial of the orthodox faith.

This same excellent pope adorned the altar of the blessed Apostle Paul, together with the doors of his confession, with pure gold and sacred scenes, wonderfully, weighing one hundred and thirty pounds. He also restored anew the roof and structure of the titular church of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs, which stood in ruins, placing many beams there.

Likewise, in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, he made a paten and chalice for the daily services, of the purest gold, weighing twenty-four pounds in all [Col. 1200D]. Likewise, in the church of holy Mary, Mother of God, at the Praesepe, the blessed man made a paten and a sacred chalice of refined gold, weighing twenty pounds.

In the titular church of Eudoxius—namely, that of the blessed Apostle Peter at the Chains—he made twelve baskets weighing thirty-six pounds, and thirty-five dolphins on various crowns, weighing eight pounds. He also repaired anew the church of blessed Sabina situated in the territory of Ferentinum.

This benevolent bishop made in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter a paten of refined gold together with a sacred chalice, weighing twenty pounds in all.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyr Laurence outside the wall, he made a paten of the purest gold together with a [Col. 1201A] sacred chalice, weighing fifteen pounds in all.

The administrator of the diaconia of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, because he feared the structure that seemed to stand above it, demolished the basilica over that same church, razing it from its foundations. Since he was utterly unable to restore it, this far-seeing bishop, moved by mercy and by love for those martyrs, rebuilt it from its foundations in a more spacious and splendid form.] When the most merciful bishop heard that the basilica of the monastery of the blessed Anastasius, martyr of Christ, together with its baptistery [Note: [Col. 1201D] Codex Luc., “vestiarium”], its *hegumenarchium*, and its other buildings had been burned through the negligence of the monks during the silence of night, from its foundations to the very top of the roof, he hastened there very early. He found it still burning, with only the coffin of that martyr dragged out and lying in the middle of the courtyard; all the other holy objects and sacred vessels, both in the church and in the wardrobe, had been consumed by the fire.

With his officials, he extinguished the fire in great sorrow and mutual haste. Then, with all his strength, he immediately rebuilt and restored the aforesaid church, rescued from the flaming ruins, in a better condition, together with the wardrobe, the *hegumenarchium*, and the other buildings. He also supplied it with more holy objects, sacred vessels, and ornaments than those that had been burned there.

That prelate, protected by God, as it is said, observing that the walls of this Roman city had lain in ruins for a long time, and that in many places towers had been thrown down to the ground, through his most diligent efforts gathered the entire populations both of Tuscia and Campania [Col. 1201C], together with the Roman people and their suburban communities, as well as the whole ecclesiastical patrimony. Preaching to them all and assigning the work, he restored, renewed, and adorned the entire city all around, at apostolic expense and from apostolic provisions.

In particular, on the major altar of the church of the blessed Apostle Peter he made various scenes of the purest gold, weighing five hundred and ninety-seven pounds [Note: [Col. 1201D] Codex Luc., “one hundred and ninety-two pounds”]. Inside the confession he made an image in the form of the Gospels, of refined gold, weighing twenty pounds in all, and before that same confession he made grilles of the purest gold, weighing fifty-six pounds. He also made, inside the altar, on both sides of the sacred confession, an image in the form of the Gospels; and on the lower and upper doors and grilles, as well as around the body, he used refined gold totaling one thousand three hundred and twenty-eight pounds [Note: [Col. 1201D] Codex Luc.: “in all, both on the altar and inside the sacred confession, on both sides, and in the image in the form of the Gospels, on the lower parts, and on the grille, as well as around the body, one thousand four hundred and twenty-eight pounds of refined gold,” etc.].

In the twentieth year of the aforesaid distinguished pontiff, in December, in the fifteenth indiction, the river Tiber, having left its channel and swollen, spread across the plains. Because of the excessive inundation it entered through the gate called Flaminia, tore up that gate from its foundations, and carried it as far as the arch called the Three Faccicelae [Note: [Col. 1201D] Codex Luc., “the three Catciclae”]. Meanwhile, in some places it also overtopped the walls. Beyond the basilica of Saint Mark it overturned the portico called the Palatine [Note: [Col. 1201D] Codex Luc., “regammas through the portico”]. Spreading through the streets as far as the bridge of Antoninus, it overturned that bridge’s wall, then returned and joined its own channel again, so that in the Via Lata the water rose more than two of the river’s own measures. The waters descended as far as the Gate of blessed Peter and the Milvian Bridge [Note: [Col. 1202D] Codex Luc., “the Olvian Bridge”], and, as the force of the river subsided, it receded.

It overturned houses and devastated fields, tearing up and uprooting orchards and crops. At that time most of the Romans were unable even to sow, and consequently a great tribulation threatened. When the chief bishop heard this—for the river had flowed through the city for three days as though through a channel—he gave himself over to profound lamentation. He remained prostrate on the ground in prayer, and after three days the Lord, moved by his prayers, caused the flood to cease.

The water nevertheless kept Rome inundated for many days. Then the same chief bishop, moved by divine inspiration, brought food by little boats [Note: [Col. 1202D] Codex Luc., “by sandals”] to those remaining in the Via Lata [Note: [Col. 1202D] Codex Luc., “he fed them”], so that they would not die of hunger, since they could not leave their dwellings at all [Note: [Col. 1202D] Codex Luc., “could not”] because of the excessive height of the waters. Afterwards, when the water had dried up, he consoled all those from that district of the Via Lata in their homes.

The same most sacred bishop carefully brought from the city of Perugia large bronze doors of extraordinary size and splendid workmanship and erected them in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter at the Tower [Note: [Col. 1202D] Codex Luc., “carefully erected”]. In the titular church of blessed Mark, his fosterer, he made a paten and a sacred chalice of the purest gold, weighing eleven pounds. He also made four silver chalices weighing twelve pounds.

Moreover, in the basilica of the blessed Cosmas and Damian he likewise presented a paten and chalice of refined gold, weighing eleven pounds in all. In the diaconia of Saint Hadrian he also supplied a paten and chalice [Note: [Col. 1202D] Codex Luc., “in the diaconia of Saint Hadrian, a chalice in the likeness of a paten,” etc.] of pure gold, weighing eleven pounds together. In the diaconia of the martyr Saint Hadrian he made two silver arches weighing twenty pounds.

In the basilica of Saint Martina he made three silver arches weighing thirty pounds. Moreover, in the church of ever-virgin Mary, which is called “at the Martyrs,” he renewed a silver canopy (*ciborium*) that had been worn away by age, adding sixty pounds of silver to it and newly raising it again in its former place. He also made in that venerable church a silver arch weighing twelve pounds.

This most blessed pontiff accomplished everything usefully and anew, both in almsgiving for the poor and in the adornment of the holy churches, advancing all good works. Having completed his course and most diligently preserved the orthodox faith, he ended his life at God’s summons and departed to eternal rest.

He held two ordinations in the month of March: twenty-four priests, seven deacons, and one hundred and eighty-five bishops in various places [Col. 1204A]. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter on the seventh day before the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 1203A] Codex Luc., “the sixth”], in the fourth indiction. [Note: [Col. 1204A] This Codex Luc. ends here.] He lived in the time of King Charles the Great.

[Col. 1203]

# LETTERS OF POPE HADRIAN I

## LETTER I. TO KING PIPPIN

[Col. 1203A]

Also, a copy of the letter of Pope Constantine the neophyte, addressed to Lord King Pippin. It states that he had been elected by the Roman people through violence and brought into the apostolic see, and asks that he might remain in the favor of Lord King Pippin, as his predecessors had done. It then treats of the letter of Theodore, Patriarch of Jerusalem, and of other letters of the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch. In a postscript, it concerns George, Marinus, and Peter.

“Most excellent lord,” etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, volume 98 of the *Patrologia*, column 235.

## LETTER II. TO KING PIPPIN

A copy of another letter of the same Pope Constantine the neophyte, addressed to Lord King Pippin. It contains expressions of thanks, mentions the death of Lord Pope Paul, and asks that he might remain in the favor of Lord King Pippin, as his predecessors had done.

“Most excellent lord,” etc. For the remainder, see among [Col. 1203C] the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, in the volume cited above, column 233.

## LETTER III. TO KING CHARLES

Also, a copy of a letter of the same pope, addressed to Lord King Charles. It concerns his faith and steadfastness, and Anastasius, his apostolic envoy, who had remained in Francia.

“Most excellent lord,” etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, in the volume cited above, column 311.

## LETTER IV. TO KING CHARLES

Also, a copy of a letter of the same pope, addressed to Lord King Charles. It contains thanks for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and concerns the king’s envoys, who were to come to Rome in the autumn.

[Col. 1203D] “Most excellent lord,” etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, in the volume cited above, column 291.

## LETTER V. TO KING CHARLES

Also, a copy of a letter of the same pope, addressed to Lord King Charles. It contains abundant blessings for the exaltation of the holy Church of God and concerns the letter of John, Patriarch of Grado.

“Most excellent lord,” etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, in the volume cited above, column 288.

## LETTER VI. TO KING CHARLES

Also, a copy of a letter of the same pope, addressed to Lord King Charles through Andrew and Anastasius, concerning the justice of the holy Church of God, and concerning Archbishop Leo, who had already hastened to the aforesaid lord king [Col. 1204A].

“Most excellent lord,” etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, in the volume cited above, column 286.

## LETTER VII. TO KING CHARLES

[Col. 1204B]

Also, a copy of a letter of the same pope, addressed to Lord King Charles through Abbot Gausfrid. It concerns the victory of the aforesaid king and the bishops of Pisa and Lucca, asking that, in his piety, he permit them to return to their own sees and churches.

“Most excellent lord,” etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, in the volume cited above, column 280.

## LETTER VIII. TO KING CHARLES

Also, a copy of a letter of the same pope, addressed to Lord King Charles. It concerns the faith or steadfastness of that apostolic man toward the aforesaid king.

“Most excellent lord,” etc. For the remainder, see among [Col. 1204C] the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, in the volume cited above, column 340.

## LETTER IX. TO KING CHARLES

Also, a copy of a letter of the same pope, addressed to Lord King Charles. It concerns Bishop Mauritius, whose eyes the Istrians had put out.

“Most excellent lord,” etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, in the volume cited above, column 320.

## LETTER X. TO KING CHARLES

Also, a copy of a letter of the same pope, addressed to Lord King [Lamb. adds: “Charles”]. It concerns the death of Emperor Constantine and Reginald, Duke of Chiusi. The aforesaid pope asks that the lord king not permit him to retain that [duchy], since he did not cease to commit many evils continually in the Castle of Felicitas . . . .

[Col. 1204D] “Most excellent lord,” etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, in the volume cited above, column 295.

## LETTER XI. TO KING CHARLES

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF SPAIN

Also, a copy of a letter of Pope Hadrian addressed to all the bishops residing throughout Spain, [Col. 1209A] especially Elipandus and Ascharicus with their like-minded associates, concerning their heresy and blasphemy in calling the Son of God adoptive. He reproves them on this point and on many other matters through the teachings of the holy Fathers.

He also addresses the celebration of Easter, the blood of cattle and swine, and blood from strangled animals, regarding which they preach in error that anyone who does not eat such things is ignorant and unlearned. He says that they are bound under the bond of anathema and are excluded from the Church.

Likewise, he addresses the predestination of God: if someone were predestined to good, it would not be necessary for him to resist evil; but if he were destined [Lamb., “born”] for evil, exercising good would profit him nothing. On this point he corrects them through apostolic exhortations.

He also reproves them because they say that they are not defiled by sharing a common life with Jews and unbaptized pagans, either in food or drink, or by various errors. He addresses their daughters, whom they give to pagan men; their consecrations; and women who, while their husbands are alive, take another man as husband. He also corrects them concerning free will and many other matters too lengthy to enumerate, using the traditions of the holy Fathers.

“Pope Hadrian,” etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Blessed Charles the Great, in the volume cited above, column 374.

## LETTER LIII. Granting a Privilege to the Monastery of Saint Dionysius at Paris, Permitting It to Have Its Own Bishop
