Adrian, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Maginarius, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Dionysius, the holy martyr of Christ, situated at Paris, where the venerable saint’s body rests, and through him to that same venerable monastery in perpetuity.

The summit of the supreme apostolic dignity is recognized as shining forth in the splendor of divine foresight when [Col. 1211B] it devotes itself more earnestly to the contest of labor in performing the praises of God. For this reason, the due care of the same apostolic pastoral solicitude has compelled us to publish abundantly whatever is recognized as pertaining to the stability of pious places, and to confirm for those same venerable places, by the authority of apostolic institution, the ancient custom.

Therefore, since you requested that we confirm the privilege which the apostolic authority of our predecessor, the lord Pope Stephen the Younger, of holy memory, formerly sanctioned for your aforesaid monastery, we, assenting to your wishes, entirely sanction by our apostolic insignia the decree of the institution of our aforementioned predecessor, and at the same time strengthen it by the apostolic [Col. 1211C] authority of this document forever.

Accordingly, supported by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we establish and promulgate in the aforesaid venerable monastery that it shall be entirely lawful to have a bishop there, as it was in ancient times and has continued until now. Through his preaching, the people who daily come with devout minds from various regions to the threshold of the monastery of that holy martyr of Christ may deserve to obtain a remedy for their souls.

When the bishop of the aforesaid holy place has departed from this world, and another worthy man has been elected by the abbot and monks, he shall be consecrated without any controversy, in view of the length of the journey, by the neighboring bishops, as has been customary. But if, for any reason or through envy, they delay his ordination, we grant permission for him to come to the apostolic see for the purpose of consecration, bearing with him the testimony [Col. 1211D] of the abbot and monks and the decree of election signed by their own hands, and there to receive consecration. For we do not wish the light which has until now shone there for so long through the preaching of bishops to be extinguished in our time.

No bishop shall presume to perform ordinations for the parishioners of the aforesaid monastery, in the cells, churches, titles, or oratories subject to its authority, or to undertake any other action there—whether concerning the preparation of chrism or any other matter—or to exercise coercion or summon the priests to himself. Rather, by this authority of our apostolic privilege, the bishop from that venerable monastery shall exercise the pastoral care of his ministry in the *praelatis* (“mentioned above”) [Hardouin: *praefatis* (“aforesaid”)] neighboring places, and shall carry out [Col. 1212A], with the consent of his abbot, by canonical institution and according to due order, everything that must be amended and corrected.

If, contrary to our wishes, any disagreement should arise between the neighboring bishops and the bishop of the aforesaid monastery, no one shall dare, without the abbot’s consent, to coerce the bishop of the often-mentioned monastery or to judge him in any matter. But if the abbot of that monastery should in any way wish the matter to be brought before them, let them come before our apostolic presence so that harmony may be restored.

We establish, by apostolic censure, under the solemn appeal to divine judgment and with the imposition of anathema, that none of our successors in the pontificate, nor anyone endowed with authority of any rank, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever presume to act against this command of our apostolic [Col. 1212B] privilege. Rather, we decree that it shall remain firm and stable throughout our times.

But if anyone at any time—which we in no way believe—should attempt to violate, wholly or in part, this decree of privilege confirmed by apostolic authority, and should fail to correct his presumption by suitable amendment, let him know that, by the authority of the lord blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he is bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, assigned with the devil and his most dreadful pomp to the punishment of everlasting fire, and subjected to perpetual condemnation.

But may whoever proves to be an observer and guardian of this our apostolic privilege deserve to obtain from the most merciful Lord our God the grace of blessing and eternal life.

[Col. 1212C]

Written by the hand of Christopher, notary and archivist of our see, in the month of June, in the ninth indiction. Farewell. Given on the Kalends of July, by the hand of Anastasius, first secretary, while the Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ reigns, with God the omnipotent Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. In the fifteenth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord in the apostolic and most holy see of blessed Peter, in the ninth indiction.

## LETTER LIV. TO TILPIN, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

He confirms by a new privilege the ancient rights of the church of Rheims, and orders that an investigation be made concerning Lullus, bishop of Mainz, and that a report be brought back to him.

Adrian, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy brother in Christ, Tilpin, [Col. 1212D] archbishop of the church of Rheims.

We well remember that, at the request of our spiritual son and glorious king of the Franks, Charles, and with Fulrad, the most beloved abbot and archpriest of Francia, providing you with a good testimony concerning your holiness and learning, we sent you the pallium according to custom, together with a privilege that the metropolitan church of Rheims should remain in its established condition.

Your fraternity, however, has reported to us that, when discord arose among the Franks, an archbishop of Rheims named Rigobert was removed and expelled from his see contrary to the canons, without any crime and without the consent or examination of the apostolic see, but solely because he had previously refused to join the party of the man who later took that part of the kingdom into his power—the part in which [Col. 1213A] the city of Rheims is situated. That bishopric, together with another bishopric and other churches, was given—and rather usurped—contrary to God and his authority by secular powers to a certain Milo, a cleric who possessed only the tonsure and understood nothing of ecclesiastical order. Other bishoprics belonging to the diocese of Rheims were divided in various ways; some remained for the most part without bishops; and bishops and clerics sometimes received ordination from other metropolitans and maintained improper refuges. They would not submit to judgment or coercion by their own bishops, and clerics, priests, monks, and nuns lived without ecclesiastical law, according to their own will and license.

Then Boniface, archbishop of holy memory and legate of the holy Roman Church, and the aforementioned [Col. 1213B] most beloved Fulrad, archpriest of Francia, labored greatly during the time of our predecessors Zachary and his successor Stephen so that our predecessor, the lord Zachary of good memory, might send the pallium to the archbishop of Rheims, Abel by name, at the intercession of the aforesaid Boniface. Abel was appointed by him, but he was not permitted to remain there; rather, he was expelled contrary to God’s will. The church of Rheims remained without a bishop for a long time and for many years, and the property of that bishopric was taken away and divided among laymen, as happened also with other bishoprics, but especially with the metropolitan city of Rheims.

Your fraternity has now obtained a large part of those properties from our glorious son Charles, and previously from his most glorious [Col. 1213C] brother Carloman; and in part you have restored the proper order both among the bishops and in other matters according to the canonical authority and that of the holy Roman see.

Therefore you requested that a privilege be issued for you and your church by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, of the holy Roman see, and of ourselves, so that what you already possess in a complete form may continue to remain, and so that what you do not yet possess in a complete form may, with the help of God and blessed Peter the apostle, be brought to completion through our authority.

For this reason, with ardent spirit, divine assistance, and the support of apostolic authority, we not only establish the ancient rights according to the sacred canons and the decrees of this apostolic and holy see, but also grant you new rights in recognition of your good zeal. By the authority of blessed [Col. 1213D] Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom God and our Savior Jesus Christ gave the power of binding and loosing the sins of human beings in heaven and on earth, we confirm and solidify them.

We confirm that the church of Rheims shall remain a metropolitan church, as it was in ancient times; that it shall be the principal see of its diocese; and that you, who by God’s cooperation have been ordained in that same see, shall be the primate of that diocese. We likewise confirm to you and to your successors, in perpetuity, all the cities which from ancient times have been subject to the metropolitan church of Rheims.

We further forbid anyone, in accordance with the tradition of the holy canons, to transfer or appoint there a bishop from another bishopric after your departure from this [Col. 1214A] world. Nor may anyone remove your parishes, churches, or cities, or ever divide the diocese of Rheims, but it shall remain intact as it was in ancient times, confirmed by the sacred canons, by the authority of our predecessors, and by our own authority.

No one shall ever presume or be able to remove you—or, in future times, the bishop of Rheims and primate of that diocese—from the bishopric without canonical judgment. Nor may anyone remove him by any judgment without the consent of the Roman pontiff if, during that judgment, he appeals to this holy Roman see, which is recognized as the head of the world.

Remaining subject solely to the Roman pontiff, and supported by the [Col. 1214B] authority of ourselves and of blessed Peter in this holy see, strive and labor, with the Lord’s help, to govern the diocese and parish of Rheims, subject to you, according to the holy canons and the commands of this holy see, so that with God’s help you may be able to hear, together with his elect, that desirable voice of our Lord Jesus Christ: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25).

You also brought to our attention that certain persons from that diocese of Rheims were receiving ordination from other bishops and maintaining improper refuges. We prohibit this entirely. Rather, as sacred authority teaches, both in the convocation and conduct of provincial synods and in ordinations and judgments, the church of Rheims and the archbishop [Col. 1214C] appointed over it shall possess such authority as the sacred canons and the constitutions of this holy church teach.

No one shall ever dare to inflict upon you or upon the church of Rheims any division or violence concerning matters that properly belong to it, as was done previously. For if—which we do not believe—anyone should attempt, with rash audacity, to act against this command of ours, unless he promptly corrects himself, especially after admonition, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema under God’s eternal judgment.

But whoever observes the apostolic commands and attains the standard of a right and orthodox faith shall obtain the grace of blessing.

[Col. 1214D]

We command that these matters defined by us through this document of confirmation be preserved in your church for its confirmation in perpetuity.

We also enjoin upon your fraternity that, since certain reports concerning the ordination of a bishop named Lullus of the holy church of Mainz have reached us, you should take with you Viomagus [Hardouin: or Wiomadus, bishop of Trier] and Possessor, bishops, together with the envoys of our glorious spiritual son Charles, king of the Franks, and carefully investigate everything concerning his ordination, as well as his faith and teaching, his conduct, morals, and life. If he is suitable and worthy to govern an episcopal see, let him send to us, through his envoys and with your letters and testimony—or those of the other bishops whom we have ordered to be with you—a written exposition of the catholic and orthodox faith, signed by his own hand, so that [Col. 1215A] we may send him the pallium according to custom, judge his ordination valid, and have him established as archbishop in that holy church of Mainz.

Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 1215C] The authenticity of this letter and of the matters described in it is asserted by the letters of Popes Zosimus, Boniface, Leo, Hilary, and Symmachus concerning the distinction between the metropolitans of the provinces of Vienne, Arles, Embrun, and the two Narbonnese provinces [Col. 1215D]; and also by other letters of Pope Gregory the Great to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, and Desiderius, bishop of Auxerre, concerning the granting of the pallium. Again, concerning the neglect of churches or the contempt shown toward bishops and metropolitans, one should consult the letters of Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, to which Pope Zachary replied in volume I of the Councils of Gaul.

Moreover, the date of Charlemagne’s patriciate should be noted: Pope Adrian and the Roman synod granted him that dignity, which was then useful, in the year 774, as may be read in the Decree, distinction 63, canon 22, and in the Life of that same Charles. Adrian himself shows what this dignity was by its use in the heading and subscription of his letters, as well as in their wording. Charles also indicates how highly he valued it in his congratulatory letter to Leo III, the new pope.

It should further be noted that there was some difference [Col. 1216C] between the patriciate of Charles Martel, of King Pippin, and of their sons during their father’s lifetime, and the patriciate of Charlemagne after his brother’s death as well. The Roman pontiffs granted the former merely the bare name of patrician, and only as a mark of honor, without any jurisdiction over the Senate and People of Rome; but to Charles alone, in the aforesaid year, they conferred full [Col. 1216D] jurisdiction as a reciprocal gift.

For this reason they nowhere used the title of patrician in their own letters. Charlemagne, by contrast, the great king, never omitted this title of patriciate in any of his words or deeds until he attained the dignity of emperor; indeed, he frequently joined this designation to references to the time of his reign.

Finally, Pope Adrian unequivocally preserves this honor of patriciate for Charlemagne, and honors him still more and more honorably himself—that is, above others—as the same Adrian says to that same Charlemagne.

Moreover, that bishop of Vienne to whom Pope Adrian writes is called Bertericus by Ado, also metropolitan of Vienne, in his Chronicle.

PETER DE LA LANDE]

## LETTER LV. TO BERTHERIUS, METROPOLITAN BISHOP OF VIENNE

Concerning the condition of the churches and the honor of both bishops and metropolitans, which had previously been neglected in Gaul.

Adrian, servant of the servants of God, to Bertherius, bishop of Vienne: greetings.

[Col. 1215B]

Our beloved, illustrious, and religious son Charles, king and patrician of the Romans, came to Rome and celebrated the Lord’s Pasch with us at Saint Peter’s. There, among other matters, we admonished him concerning the honor of metropolitans, concerning the cities that had been handed over to laymen, and concerning the fact that episcopal dignity had been trampled underfoot for nearly eighty years.

When the glorious king had heard these and similar matters, he promised before the body of blessed Peter the apostle that everything would be brought to us for correction. Therefore it pleased us to send to all archbishops and bishops the authority of our letters, so that, just as the individual metropolitan cities were established by ancient privileges, so they might remain; and so that each metropolis [Col. 1216A] might possess the cities subject to it, which blessed Leo and his other predecessors and successors distinguished for the individual metropolitans after the Council of Chalcedon.

Nor should any metropolis suffer prejudice on that account if we or our predecessor, at the request of pious Frankish leaders, have granted the pallium to one of its suffragan bishops. Nor should the Church suffer any damage to its order from the fact that, through the negligence of certain prelates and the ravages of barbarians, it lost and forfeited its ancient dignity, strengthened by the firmness of the Roman bishops, for sixty or eighty years or even longer, when it had enjoyed that dignity for almost countless years under the ordering of the Spirit of God.

Therefore, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we have restored to each metropolitan, according to ancient custom, his authority. We also asked our glorious and illustrious son, King [Col. 1216B] Charles, before the body of blessed Peter, to ensure that every metropolis should possess its ancient dignity.

For this reason we have sent this letter of our authority to all, and we wished you also to have it, so that you might know that the privilege which your church possessed from the time of blessed Pope Leo has been completely restored.

Given on the Kalends of January, while the most pious Augustus Constantine was reigning, with God assenting and the most pious King Charles crowned by God, in the first year of his patriciate.

## LETTER LVI. TO CONSTANTINE AND IRENE

[Note: [Col. 1215] Here it will suffice to point out in one or two words that the Greek language differs somewhat from the Latin in the following letters. EDITOR.]

[Note: [Col. 1215] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1215]

[Col. 1216C]

Adrian, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most pious and most serene lords, the emperors and triumphant victors [the Greek adds: “victors”], beloved sons in God and in our Lord Jesus Christ, Constantine and Irene, Augustuses.

God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” who rescued us from the power of darkness (2 Cor. 4) through the incarnation of his Son, the true light, in whom he was pleased that the whole fullness of the Godhead should dwell, and through whom he was pleased to renew all things, making peace in him through the blood of his cross, whether the things in heaven or those on earth (Col. 1), in the abundance of his goodness, has deigned, looking upon the face of his Church, to call your foreknown and predestined, most serene imperial clemency to the integrity of the faith, so that, with every cloud of falsehood utterly dispersed, he might through you make the truth victorious.

From the reports [Greek: “letters”] of your most pious Serenity that have reached us, we have learned this; even by hearing it, our spirit, greatly exulting, was relieved, and so great a joy of gladness arose in our heart that no human speech is sufficient to express it. Indeed, the joy now arising in us from your commands is greater than the sorrow that formerly afflicted us on account of the heresy of the schismatics.

For your very venerable commands reported what had formerly taken place in your royal city concerning the venerable images: namely, how those who reigned before you had destroyed them and treated them with dishonor and insult. Would that this not be charged against them; for it would have been better for them not to have laid their hands upon the Church. And because all the people who are in the eastern regions went astray and used them according to their own will, God has now raised you up to reign—men who seek his glory in truth and desire to hold fast what has been handed down by the teaching of the holy apostles and of all the saints together.

When we unfolded these accounts and found the venerable images commendably set forth under your most pious imperial authority, and rejected the madness of the heretics, regarding it as a dart in the judgment of divine examination against those rulers who laid their hands upon the Church, we firmly believe that your imperial power, advanced by God through triumphs, is wholly innocent of their savagery. Therefore, entreating the clemency of almighty God, we offer unending thanks; and, holding fast to what your Serenity has decreed and begun to accomplish, remain steadfast.

If you persevere and continue in the orthodox faith that you have begun, and through you the sacred and venerable images are restored in those regions to their former state, then, just as the emperor Constantine of blessed memory and blessed Helena proclaimed the orthodox faith, exalted your spiritual mother, the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church, and, together with the other orthodox emperors, venerated her as the head of all the churches, so may you be regarded as a new Constantine and a new Helena, with your most gracious name protected by God. Through them the holy catholic and apostolic Church received the strength of faith at its beginnings; and after their example your highly celebrated imperial fame, most vigorous and renowned throughout the whole world for its triumphs, is being honorably proclaimed.

But especially, if, following the traditions of the orthodox faith, you embrace the discipline of the Church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; if, as your holy imperial predecessors acted in ancient times, you honor it reverently and love its vicar from the depths of your heart; and if your empire, granted to you by God, follows their orthodox faith according to that of our holy Roman Church, then may that same prince of the apostles—he to whom the Lord God granted the power of binding and loosing sins in heaven and on earth, and who, continually acting as your protector, casts all barbarian nations beneath your feet—show you victorious everywhere.

Indeed, his sacred authority discloses the insignia of his dignity and how great a veneration must be shown by all the faithful throughout the world to his supreme see. For the Lord appointed him, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, as prince over all, and he is honored by that privilege itself through which the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to him. Thus, elevated to so eminent an honor, he merited confessing the faith upon which the Church of Christ is founded. Blessedness followed that blessed confession with its rewards: through his preaching the holy universal Church was enlightened, and from it the other churches of God received their teachings of faith.

For that same blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, who first presided over the apostolic see, left the primacy of his apostleship and the pastoral care to his successors, who would perpetually sit in his most holy see. To them he also conferred and handed down, by divine command, the authority and power that had been granted to him by our Savior, the Lord God; and they, in turn, transmitted it to their pontifical successors. Through their tradition we venerate the sacred image of Christ, of his holy Mother, of the apostles, and of all the saints.

For from the time when the doors of rest and peace were opened to the Church of Christ our God, and churches have continued to be adorned with painted images, as the blessed and most holy Pope Sylvester bears witness, this has been practiced. In the very beginnings of Christianity, when the pious emperor Constantine was being converted to the faith, the following account is read:

“When the day had passed and nocturnal silence had fallen, the time for sleep arrived. And behold, the holy apostles Peter and Paul appeared, saying: ‘Because you have put an end to your crimes and have shuddered at the shedding of innocent blood, we have been sent by Christ Jesus the Lord to give you counsel for recovering your health. Hear, therefore, our instructions and do everything that we shall indicate to you.

“‘Bishop Sylvester of the city of Rome, fleeing your persecutions, is hiding with his clergy in caves among the rocks on Mount Soracte. When you have brought him to you, he will show you a pool into which, when you have immersed yourself three times, every affliction of leprosy will leave you. When this has been done, repay your Savior in this way: let all the Roman churches throughout the world be restored at your command.

“‘For your part, purify yourself in this respect: abandoning every superstition of idols, worship and serve the one God, who is true and alone, and attain to his will.’”

Then, rising immediately from sleep, he summoned those who guarded the palace and, according to the tenor of his dream, sent them to Mount Soracte, where Saint Sylvester, received with his clergy on the estate of a certain Christian because of the persecution, was devoting himself to readings and prayers.

When he saw that he was surrounded by soldiers, he believed that he was being summoned to the crown of martyrdom. Turning to all the clergy who were with him, he said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” Setting out, therefore, as he had been instructed, he reached the king. When his arrival was announced, he entered with three presbyters and two deacons.

On entering, he said: “Peace be with you, and may victory be granted you from heaven.” When the king had received him with eager spirit and a most gracious countenance, he explained to him everything that had happened, everything that had been said, and also everything that had been revealed, according to the account given above.

At the end of his narrative, the king asked who these gods, Peter and Paul, were who had visited him for the sake of his healing and had disclosed their hiding place. Sylvester replied: “They are not gods, but worthy servants of Christ and apostles chosen by him and sent to invite the nations, so that believers might obtain salvation.”

While the pope was saying these and similar things to the Augustus, the Augustus began to ask whether he had any image depicting those apostles, so that from the painting he might learn that these were the men whom the revelation had shown him.

Then Saint Sylvester ordered a deacon to bring him an image of the apostles. When the emperor looked upon it, he began to say with a great shout that these were the very men whom he had seen, and that he ought no longer to delay the manifestation of the pool made through the Holy Spirit, which he remembered they had promised for his salvation.

Behold, as stated above, figures of the saints had existed among all Christians from the very beginnings of our faith, and sacred figures had been represented and painted in the churches of the saints. This was done so that the pagan Gentiles, seeing the depicted history of divine Scripture, might be turned from the worship of idols and the images of demons to the true light of Christianity and the worship of the love of God. Thus the outstanding father and worthy preacher, blessed Gregory, bishop of this apostolic see, says: those who do not know letters may at least read by looking at the walls what they cannot read in books.

For this reason the most approved holy Fathers decreed that the images and paintings of divine Scripture and the deeds of the saints should be painted in the churches. All orthodox and most Christian emperors, all priests and devout servants of God, and the entire assembly of Christians, having received this tradition from the holy Fathers from the beginning, reverently observed those same images and paintings as reminders of holy compunction. In those regions they continued to honor them in an orthodox manner down to the time of your great-grandfather.

But your great-grandfather, through the instigation of certain impious men, removed those sacred images; and from this a great error increased throughout the regions of Greece, and a vast scandal came upon the whole world. But woe to the one through whom scandals have come into the whole world, as the Truth itself testifies.

Therefore, bound by great sorrow, the lords Gregory and Gregory, the most blessed pontiffs who existed at that time, entreated that great-grandfather of your tranquil piety by the letters of their apostolic writings to turn back from the rashness of this new presumption and restore those images to their former state. But he was in no way moved by their most salutary entreaties.

Afterward, our holy pontifical predecessors, the lords Zacharias, Stephen, Paul, and another Stephen, repeatedly entreated the grandfather and father of your most serene Tranquility concerning the restoration of those sacred images. Likewise, our lowliness, with great humility, has earnestly endeavored to petition your most gracious imperial power with constancy.

Finally, we most insistently ask that, just as we received from the holy Fathers and our most approved pontifical predecessors the practice of depicting the history of divine Scripture in the churches as a reminder of holy action and for the instruction of the unlearned, and of setting up in the house of God the sacred image of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ according to the human form that he assumed in the incarnation, likewise depicting and venerating, out of love for them, the images of his holy Mother, the blessed apostles, prophets, martyrs, and confessors, so your most gracious imperial power may cause those regions of Greece to be brought into conformity with your orthodox faith.

Thus, as it is written, “There shall be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10). For throughout the whole world, wherever Christianity exists, these sacred images remain and are honored by all the faithful, so that through the visible face our mind may be carried, by spiritual affection, to the invisible majesty of the Godhead through contemplation of the image represented according to the flesh—the image of the flesh that the Son of God deigned to assume for our salvation.

Let us adore our same Redeemer who is in heaven, and glorify and praise him in spirit, because, as it is written, “God is spirit” (John 4); therefore we spiritually adore his divinity. Far be it from us to deify these images, as some chatterers claim. Rather, we in every way proclaim [variant: “put forward”] the affection and love that we have for God and his saints. And, according to the books of divine Scripture (Gen. 2), we possess these images as reminders for veneration, while preserving the purity of our faith.

For our Creator, the Lord God, when he had formed man from the clay of the earth according to his own image and likeness, established him, illuminating him with the ingenuity of intelligence, in the exercise of his own judgment. The first man, by his own judgment and under divine inspiration, gave proper names to all living creatures, all the birds of heaven, and all the beasts of the earth; and he permitted the living creatures to remain under those names.

Abel too, set aflame by the divine Spirit, offered the Lord gifts from the firstborn of his flock according to his own judgment and discernment. Concerning this we read: “God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts” (Gen. 4).

Noah likewise, after the flood had inundated the earth, by heavenly inspiration and according to his own judgment and personal invention, built an altar to the Lord; and from all the clean cattle and birds he offered holocausts to the Lord upon that altar.

Similarly, Abraham, as it is written, built an altar by his own judgment to the honor and glory of God who had appeared to him.

Thus Jacob, fleeing from his brother Esau, when in a dream he saw the angels of God ascending into heaven and descending by a ladder, and the Lord himself leaning upon the ladder and speaking to him, immediately arose and, according to his own judgment, took the stone that he had placed beneath his head, set it up as a pillar, poured oil over it, and called that place Bethel, saying: “There is nothing here other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28).

For this reason almighty God was by no means angered that he had set up that stone as a pillar according to his own judgment and discernment. Shortly afterward, in the history of Genesis, he is reported to have said to him: “I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the stone and vowed a vow to me.”

Behold, most serene lords, sons and great princes: everything that is prepared by human discernment for the praise of God is not to be prohibited; rather, it is entirely evident that such things are pleasing to our Creator, the Lord.

The same Jacob, finally, by his own judgment, kissed the top of the staff of his son Joseph, doing this out of the love of faith, as blessed Paul testifies in his Epistle to the Hebrews (Heb. 11). He showed honor and affection not to the staff but to the one holding it.

So too we, out of the love and affection that we have for the Lord and his saints, paint their venerable likenesses in images. We do not show honor to the boards and colors, but to those for whose honor the images exist.

Again, we read that Moses was commanded by the Lord our God: “You shall also make a mercy seat of pure gold; its length shall be two and a half cubits, and its breadth one and a half cubits. You shall also make two cherubim of gold, of beaten work, on both sides of the oracle” (Exod. 37:25). Shortly afterward, concerning the covering of the ark in which he was to place the testimony that God would give him, the text says: “From there I shall command you and speak to you” (Exod. 40), namely, from above the mercy seat and from between the cherubim that were over the ark of the testimony.

It was also commanded that cherubim be made in woven work and in various colors on the curtains and covering of the tabernacle. It must be considered, most tranquil lords, sons and great princes, that our almighty Lord deigned to speak from among those same cherubim made by human hands, for the salvation of his people.

For this reason there is no doubt that everything established in the churches of God for his praise and adornment is to be recognized as holy and venerable.

This too, most serene sons, must be added for the satisfaction of unbelievers and the guidance of those who have gone astray. God commanded his servant Moses, as the Book of Numbers records concerning the plague that had fallen upon them: “Make a serpent and set it up as a sign; whoever has been bitten and looks upon it shall live.” Moses therefore made a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign; and when those who had been bitten looked upon it, they were healed (Num. 21).

O the madness of those who rage against the Christian faith and religion, claiming that images should not be worshiped or venerated—images in which are represented the likenesses of the Savior, his Mother, and the saints, through whose virtue the world endures and the human race obtains salvation! We believe that the Israelite people were delivered from the calamity inflicted upon them by looking upon the bronze serpent, yet do we doubt that we shall be saved by looking upon and venerating the likenesses of Christ our Lord and of the saints? Far be it from us to yield assent to such wicked presumption. Let us follow the ancient traditions of the Fathers and in no way depart from their teaching.

We also read that King Solomon made cherubim in the temple that he built for the glory of God, and adorned that temple with various colors (1 Kings 6).

For this reason we and all the orthodox, in confession of our faith and for the beauty of the house of God, provide paintings with a variety of colors and ornaments, just as the prophet Isaiah foretold, saying: “On that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the Lord beside its border” [Note: [Col. 1227] In the Greek version, Isaiah 31:39, τῷ Κυρίῳ, “to the Lord.” HARD.]. “And it shall be for a sign and a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt. For they shall cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he shall send them a savior and defender who will deliver them” (Isa. 19).

As the outstanding prophet, blessed David, sang, saying: “Honor and beauty are before him” (Ps. 95). And again: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where the glory of your tabernacle dwells” (Ps. 25).

Again, announcing the coming of our Redeemer and the incarnation of the Son of God, he expressly foretold that his face should be worshiped according to the dispensation of his humanity, saying: “Your face, Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. 26). And afterward: “All the rich among the people shall entreat your face” (Ps. 44). And again: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4).

Hence blessed Augustine, that outstanding father and excellent teacher, says in his sermons of admonition: “What is the image of God other than the face of God, upon which the people of God have been marked?”

Meanwhile blessed Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, among many things in the sermon that he composed on Abraham, spoke as follows:

“I have often seen an inscription depicting the Passion, and I have not passed by the sight without tears: the work of art brings the history before the face, and so forth.”

And elsewhere, in his interpretation of the Song of Songs, as the written teaching says:

“There is a certain material, entirely composed of various dyes, which completes the imitation of a living being. For one who looks at an image completed by the same art through colors does not prefer the dyes to contemplation, but looks only upon the sight of the prototype [Greek: “original model”] represented, which the artist has displayed through the colors.”

In the epistle of blessed Basil sent to Julian the Apostate, the following is reported:

“According to what we possess by inheritance from God—our immaculate Christian faith—I confess, follow, and believe in one God the Father almighty, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit. I adore and glorify these three as one God. I also confess the incarnate dispensation of the Son and the Mother of God, holy Mary, who bore him according to the flesh.

“I also accept the holy apostles, prophets, and martyrs, who make supplication to God, because through their intercession the most merciful Lord is made favorable to me and grants me remission of my sins. For this reason I honor, adore, and specially venerate their depicted images. This has been handed down by the holy apostles and must not be prohibited; therefore in all our churches we represent their history.”

Likewise, from the same Father’s sermon on the holy Forty Martyrs:

“Writers and painters often represent the triumphs and victories of wars: some adorn them with words, others portray them upon panels, and many have been stirred to courage by both. What speech has painted in the history through hearing, silent written instruction demonstrates through imitation.”

Likewise, from blessed John, archbishop of Constantinople, also called Chrysostom, on the parable of the seed:

“If you insult the imperial garment, do you not insult the one who wears it? Do you not know that if someone inflicts an injury upon the emperor’s image, the injury is referred to the emperor himself—that is, to the ruler himself and to his dignity? Do you not know that if someone curses an image made of wood and colors, he is not judged as though he had presumptuously acted against something lifeless, but as one who has acted against the emperor? For he insults the emperor in two ways.”

And again, from a sermon of the same Father delivered on the Thursday of Easter:

“All things have been made for the glory of God and for our use: the clouds for the service of rain, the earth for the abundance of fruits, the sea, without begrudging, for those who sail. Everything serves humanity, and especially the image of God. For when imperial faces and images are brought into cities and judges and peoples come forward to meet them with praises, they do not honor the panel or the wax inscription spread over it, but the emperor’s likeness. So too creation does not honor an earthly appearance, but reverences the heavenly likeness itself.”

Similarly, we present a sermon of blessed Cyril from his interpretation of the holy Gospel according to Matthew:

“Faith depicts the Word who exists in the form of God, just as our redemption was offered to God, clothed in flesh according to us and made human.”

And shortly afterward the same author says:

“Parables fulfill for us the work of images, signifying their power, as though by the use of the eyes and the touch of the hands they also suggested those things that contemplation possesses invisibly in subtle thoughts.”

Likewise, from Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, on the Lord’s incarnation, whose beginning is: “Taking a few things sufficiently from many, we have made them known.” And afterward:

“Even the things written upon wood, when their form has been obliterated by external dirt, must necessarily be taken up again and restored in every respect, so that the image of the one whose form it is may be renewed in the same material and element. For because of that same form and material, where it is also written, it is not cast down but configured within that very material,” and so forth.

Likewise, from blessed Ambrose’s third book to the emperor Gratian, chapter nine:

“Do we divide Christ when we worship both his divinity and his flesh? Or when in him we worship both the image of God and the cross, do we divide him? Far be it from us!”

Likewise, from Saint Epiphanius of Constantia in Cyprus:

“Because the emperor possesses an image, are there therefore two emperors? Certainly not; there is one emperor even together with the image.”

Likewise, from Saint Stephen, bishop of Bostra, on the image of the saints:

“Concerning the images of the saints, we confess that every work done in the name of God is good and holy. For an image is one thing, and an idol—that is, a little statue—is another.

“When God formed Adam, that is, created him, he said: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’ (Gen. 1). And he made man in the image of God. Is man therefore an idol, that is, an idolatrous worship and impiety, because he is the image of God? By no means. For if Adam had been the image of demons, he would certainly have been rejected and unacceptable. But because he is the image of God, he is honorable and acceptable.

“Every image made in the name of the Lord, or of angels, prophets, apostles, or righteous persons is holy. It is not the wood that is worshiped, but what is seen and remembered in the wood that is honored.

“We all worship rulers and greet them, even if they are sinners. Why, then, should we not worship the holy servants of God and establish their images in their memory, so that they may not be forgotten?

“But you say that God himself forbids the worship of things made by hand. Tell me, O Jew, what is there upon the earth that has not been made by hand, since it was made by God? Was not the ark of God, fashioned and constructed from acacia wood, made by hand? And were not the altar, the mercy seat, the urn containing the manna, the table, the lampstand, and the inner and outer tabernacle works of human hands, which Solomon made? Why, then, are they called the holy of holies, although they exist as things made by hand?

“Were not the cherubim and the six-winged creatures that stood around the altar images of angels, the work of human hands? How, then, are they not rejected? Because the images of angels were made at God’s command, they are holy; and these creatures existed.

“But God cast down and condemned the idols of the nations because they were images of demons. We, however, make images in memory of the saints—of Abraham, Moses, Elijah, Isaiah, Zechariah, and the remaining prophets, apostles, and holy martyrs who were slain for the Lord—so that all who see them in an image may remember them and glorify the Lord who glorified them.

“For honor, worship, and our commendation are fitting for them according to their righteousness, so that all who see them may hasten to become imitators of their conduct.

“For what kind of honor in worship is this, except only that by which we sinners also worship and greet one another through honor and love? Thus we also worship, glorify, and stand in awe before the image of our Lord—not otherwise—for it is the image of his likeness, and he himself is depicted in it.”

[Note: [Col. 1231D] In the Greek: “But let the impious, who do not do good and do not remember the saints, not prevent those who do good, nor scandalize those who honor the saints and servants of God and remember them. For these will receive a good reward,” etc. HARD.]

Therefore, whoever is pious, does good, remembers the saints, does not prevent those who do good, and does not scandalize those who honor the saints and servants of God, but rather remembers them, will receive a good reward for good action. But the impious will have desolation and dishonor according to what they have thought, because they neglected what was just and departed from God.

For the remembrance of the saints, images are painted, worshiped, and honored, as images of the servants of God who intercede with the Godhead on our behalf. It is fitting to commemorate our leaders and to give thanks to God.

From a sermon of blessed Jerome, presbyter of Jerusalem:

“For just as God permitted every nation to worship things made by hand, but commanded the Jews [Greek adds: ‘willed them’] to honor the tablets that Moses carved, and the two golden cherubim, so he also granted us Christians the cross and the right to paint, worship, venerate, and display images of good works.”

Thus, most pious and tranquil lords and sons, we have passed briefly through these testimonies of the holy Fathers mentioned above. The history of divine Scripture in both the New and Old Testaments also bears witness to the observance of divine worship: by God’s will, things were established in the churches for the praise of God and as reminders of holy action, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers.

The history of divine Scripture has likewise sufficiently proclaimed the status of the sacred images. We have endeavored, with all humility and sincerity of heart, to make this known to your power, a Serenity strengthened by God, in the course of this apostolic petition.

We have therefore also endeavored to make known to your most gracious power what can be carefully observed in the various credible testimonies of the Fathers who established these sacred images, just as we found it in their books. With great love of heart we entreat your gentle clemency; and, as though present in person, prostrate upon the ground and fallen at your footsteps directed by God, I ask, beseech, and adjure you before God to command that these most sacred images be restored and confirmed in their former state in that royal city preserved by God and in the other regions of Greece; that you observe the tradition of this our most holy Roman Church; and that you reject and repudiate the cunning of the wicked and the heretics, so that you may be received into the arms of this holy catholic and apostolic, irreproachable Roman Church of ours.

Translation of the Roman letter of Hadrian, most holy pope of elder Rome.

[Col. 1215C]

To the most devout and most serene lords, victors, triumphant bearers of trophies, beloved children [in] God and our Lord Jesus Christ, Constantine and Irene, Augusti: Adrian, servant of the servants of God.

God, “who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ who delivered us from the power of darkness,” through the incarnation of his Son, the true light, “in whom he was pleased that all the fullness of deity should dwell, and through whom he renewed all things, making peace through the blood of his cross between the things in heaven and the things on earth,” because of the abundance of his goodness, looking upon the face of his Church, has deigned to call your piety and your foreordained serene gentleness to the perfection of the faith and to imperial dignity, so that through you he might conceal all the wickedness of falsehood and reveal the truth.

For when we learned of the letters sent to us by your serenity and piety, our heart rejoiced greatly, and we were filled with such exultation and joy as the human tongue cannot express. Such joy arose for us through your command as the blow we formerly suffered because of the schisms of heresy.

As for what is contained in your pious command concerning the former events that occurred in your imperial city on account of the venerable images—how your predecessors on the throne overturned them and brought themselves and the images into dishonor and insult—would that that sin not be reckoned against them! For it would have been better for them not to lay their hands upon the Church. For all the people who lived in the eastern regions were led astray, and each used the images according to his own will, as seemed good to him, until God raised you up to reign: you who truly seek his glory, hold fast to what was handed down by the holy apostles and all the teachers, and honor the venerable images that had been brought down through the folly of the heretics.

Now, having recently learned through your pious command your will concerning these matters, we have offered fervent prayers to almighty God on behalf of your sovereignty and have sent up glory and thanksgiving.

[Col. 1218C] Let your God-appointed empire know this with full assurance and complete certainty: if this great undertaking that you have begun is brought to completion through your mediation, if ancient orthodoxy is restored in those regions, and if the venerable images are set up again in their former restoration, you will become sharers in the divine reward of the emperor of old, Lord Constantine, and of Lady [L., blessed] Helena, who made the orthodox faith clear and firm and further exalted your holy mother, the catholic and Roman spiritual Church; and, after them, in that of your predecessors who ruled orthodoxly and prevailed [L., and who reverenced and exalted your holy catholic and apostolic spiritual mother, the Roman Church,] and, together with the other orthodox emperors, honored her as the head of all the churches.

Thus your most pious and God-given name will be proclaimed throughout the whole inhabited world as that of a new Constantine and a new Helena, through whom the holy catholic and apostolic Church is renewed.

And this will be especially so if you follow the tradition of the orthodox faith of the Church of the chief apostles, Saint Peter and Saint Paul, and embrace their vicar, just as the emperors who ruled from the beginning honored their vicar and loved him with all their heart. If your God-given sovereignty honors the most holy Roman Church of the chief apostles, to whom authority was given by God himself, the Word, to loose and bind sins in heaven and on earth, then they themselves will become protectors of your sovereignty, and every barbarian nation will be subjected beneath your feet. Wherever you go, they will make you victorious.

For those holy and chief apostles, who began the catholic and orthodox faith, established in writing that all their successors who would occupy their thrones after them should hold fast to their faith and remain in it until the consummation. Thus our Church holds fast to it and honors their holy representations.

Therefore, even to this day, our churches are adorned and beautified with their venerable images, as the most blessed and holy pope Sylvester bears witness at the beginning of our orthodox faith as Christians, when Constantine, the emperor of old, by divine dispensation, turned to the faith.

After the day had passed and night had already come, he ordered silence to be observed. While he was asleep, behold, the holy apostles Peter and Paul appeared before him and said:

“Because you permitted [printed *ἐπέτρεψας*; Ex. gives *οὐκ ἐπέστρεψας*, “you did not turn back,” or *ἔφριξας*, “you shuddered”; the transmitted alternatives are difficult] the bloodshed of infants to take place on account of the illness with which you suffer, behold, we have been sent by Christ to give you salvation. Hear, then, our admonition, and do everything that we command you. Send and summon Sylvester the bishop, who fled from you because of the persecution that you are carrying out and who is now hidden in the Soracte mountain in rocky caves with his clergy. He will prepare for you a baptismal pool of piety, in which he will baptize you; and there will be healing for you from leprosy and from every illness. When this good has come to you, immediately command that churches be renewed throughout every region of the Romans. Cleanse yourself, laying aside all worship of idols; worship God alone, the true one, and walk according to his will.”

When he awoke from sleep, he immediately gathered all the members of his palace and explained to them the meaning of his dream. At once he sent them to Mount Soracte, where Saint Sylvester was hidden with his clergy, occupied in reading books.

When Sylvester saw an army standing all around, he said to his clergy: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.”

When he came out, the soldiers told him the matter concerning which he was being sought. He then came to the emperor with three presbyters and two deacons. When he saw him, he said:

“Peace to you, O emperor, from heaven above—and victory.”

The emperor, receiving his words with a cheerful countenance and a simple heart, explained to Saint Sylvester everything that had been revealed to him. After the explanation, the emperor asked him:

“Who are the gods whom I saw, Peter and Paul?”

The most holy Sylvester answered him:

“These are not gods, but servants and disciples of our Lord Jesus Christ. He chose them to turn all the nations to faith in him.”

When he heard this, he asked him again whether there was somewhere a written account of their history. Then Saint Sylvester sent a deacon and ordered him to bring the images of the holy apostles. When the emperor saw them, he cried out loudly:

“These are the men whom I saw in the vision, and I no longer doubt. Let a baptismal pool of my salvation be prepared.”

When the pool had been prepared, he was baptized and immediately healed.

Remembering the good that had happened to him, he too began to build churches and to set up in them the same venerable images, for the worship and remembrance of our Lord Jesus Christ, who became incarnate, and of all the saints. Thus Christianity might be restored to light [L., “to the Christian faith and to light,” etc., Latin]; and to truth and desire for divine worship; and all might be freed from the idolatry of the nations and the deception of demons.

As Saint Gregory, the successor of the apostles, proclaimed, this was so that all people who were uneducated and unable to read might look upon the Gospel histories and through them be led upward to the glory and remembrance of the incarnate dispensation of our Lord and Master Jesus Christ.

All the orthodox and most Christian emperors, together with all the priests and honorable men who serve God, along with the entire most Christian people, received, maintained, and possess these same venerable images according to the ancient tradition of the holy Fathers, for remembrance and compunction of heart. To the present day they venerate them; and in those regions themselves they were venerated orthodoxly down to your great-grandfather.

But your great-grandfather, at the instigation of certain impious men, brought down the holy images in those places. From that time a great delusion increased in those regions of Greece, and a great scandal arose throughout the whole world.

But woe to those through whom scandals entered the world, as Truth itself bears witness. For this reason Gregory and Gregory, the most blessed bishops of the Roman see in our time, who lived in those days, were in great distress. They repeatedly entreated the great-grandfather of your pious serenity that the same venerable images might be restored to their proper position.

But he did not incline at all to their saving petitions [Al., requests].

Afterward our predecessors, the most holy bishops Zacharias, Stephen, Paul, and another Stephen, entreated the pope and the father of your pious sovereignty concerning the restoration of those same holy images. In the same way our unworthiness, with great humility, entreats your sovereignty: as we received from our most holy and most approved predecessors, the chief bishops, let us restore the histories in the churches for remembrance, and let us set up in the court of God the holy image of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the incarnation of his human form, together with that of his holy mother, and of the holy and blessed apostles, prophets, martyrs, and confessors; and because of our desire, let us venerate them.

Therefore let your most gentle sovereignty also command that authority be exercised in those regions of Greece and that the orthodox faith be made equal there, so that, as it is written, “There shall be one flock and one shepherd.” For throughout the whole world, wherever Christianity exists, these same venerable images are honored by all the faithful. Through the visible representation, our mind is spiritually carried toward the invisible deity of his majesty, according to the flesh that the Son of God deigned to assume for our salvation.

Let us worship our Redeemer who exists in the heavens, and, glorifying him in spirit, let us praise him; for, as it is written, “God is spirit.” In this way, while glorifying him spiritually, we worship his divinity.

God forbid that we should deify these same images, as certain people babble. Our labor and desire are directed toward the love of God and of his saints. As our divine Scripture says, we possess these same images as memorials of our worship, preserving the purity of our faith.

For the Lord our God, our maker and creator, fashioned the human being from the material of the earth according to his own image and likeness, enlightened him, and made him free in will. The first man, possessing free will, at the divine command gave individual names to all living creatures, the birds of heaven, and all the animals of the earth.

Abel, from the firstborn of his flock, freely brought gifts to the Lord God. Concerning him we read: “The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his gifts.”

Then Noah, after the flood, freely constructed and built an altar, and from all the cattle and birds he brought clean gifts together upon the altar to God.

Likewise Abraham, as it is written, freely built an altar for the honor and glory of God, as it was revealed to him.

Jacob too, having fled from the presence of his brother, saw in sleep the angels of God ascending and descending by a ladder, and the Lord speaking to him upon it. When he arose, he freely took up the stone that had been beneath his head; he set it upright and poured oil upon it, and called the place Bethel, saying:

“This is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.”

God was not at all angry with him because he had set up the stone freely. Therefore, shortly afterward in the history, he said: “I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the stone and made a vow to me.”

For, most serene children, great rulers and orthodox emperors—everything that, within human understanding, belongs to the glory of God—become pleasing to God.

Again, the same Jacob worshiped at the top of his staff, doing this in faith and love. Concerning this blessed Paul the apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews that he did not worship the staff, but the one who held it, making it an expression of love.

Thus we too, because of the desire and love that we have for the Lord and the saints, represent their likenesses in images. We do not place the honor in the wooden panel and pigments, but in those whose names the images bear.

Again, we read that a command was given by the Lord to Moses:

“You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold, two cubits [L., two and a half cubits] in length and one and a half cubits in breadth. And you shall make two golden cherubim, beaten, looking toward one another from both sides.”

And shortly afterward:

“You shall place the testimony that I shall give you upon it, to cover the ark; and I shall speak with you from above the mercy seat”—that is, from between the two cherubim standing above the ark of the testimony.

He also commanded that on the curtains and on the covering of the tabernacle there should be woven work of varied colors representing the cherubim.

It is therefore to be understood, most serene lords and children, great rulers, that our almighty Lord and God deigned to speak for the salvation of the people from between the cherubim, although they were fashioned by human hands.

It is consequently beyond doubt that everything established in the churches of God for the praise and adornment of his house must be recognized as holy and venerable.

We should add this also, most serene lords, for the instruction of unbelievers and the correction of those who have gone astray: what God commanded his servant Moses, as is read in the Book of Numbers, on account of the plague that had come upon them. He said:

“Make a serpent and set it up as a sign; and whoever is bitten and looks upon it shall live.”

So Moses made a serpent of bronze and set it up as a sign; and all those who were bitten and looked upon it were healed.

Oh, the folly of those who rage against the faith and worship of Christians! They have become accustomed not to venerate the venerable images in which are represented the histories of our Savior, of his mother, and of all the saints, whose power upholds and saves the human race.

For if we believe that the Israelite people were saved through the representation of the bronze serpent, God forbid that we should doubt, depart from the tradition of the holy Fathers, or deviate from their teaching.

King Solomon also made cherubim in the temple that he built for God, for the glory of God, and fashioned it with various colors [L., alternatively, adorned it].

Therefore we too, and all the orthodox, make the confession of our faith and the beauty of the house of God through varied colors and the adornment of paintings.

For the prophet Isaiah also said:

“On that day there shall be an altar to God in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar beside its boundary; and it shall be for a sign and for a witness to the Lord God in the land of Egypt. They shall cry out to the Lord because of those who oppress them, and he will send them a savior and champion who will deliver them.”

The psalmist David also sings, saying:

“Confession and beauty are before him.”

And again:

“Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where the dwelling of your glory resides.”

Again, announcing the coming and incarnation of the Son of God and our Savior, the same writer strongly instructed that his face, according to his incarnate dispensation, should be worshiped, saying:

“My face sought you; your face, Lord, I shall seek.”

And again:

“The rich among the people shall entreat your face.”

And again:

“The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord.”

Therefore Saint Augustine, the great teacher, said in his admonitions:

“What is the image of God except the face of God, upon which the people of God have been marked?”

Meanwhile Saint Gregory of Nyssa, bishop, composed a discourse concerning Abraham, saying:

“I have often seen the inscription of the passion, and I have not passed by without tears a work of art in which a historical subject was brought before the face;” and other passages from his interpretation of the Song of Songs, as the written teaching says:

“It is entirely a material substance, filling out through various dyes the imitation of the soul” [L., “of the living creature”].

For one who looks at the image—the panel filled out by art through colors—does not derive the likeness from the pigment, but is led upward to the contemplation of the prototype.

For in the letter of Saint Basil to Julian the Apostate it is written:

“As we have inherited from God our blameless Christian faith, I confess, follow, and believe in one almighty God: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit. These three I worship and glorify as one God. I also confess the incarnate dispensation of the Son. I further confess holy Mary, who bore him according to the flesh, to be Theotokos.

“I accept the holy apostles, prophets, and martyrs who entreat God, because through their intercession the loving God becomes gracious toward me and grants forgiveness of sins. Therefore I openly honor and worship the historical representations of their images. For this was handed down from the holy apostles and must not be prohibited; rather, in all our churches we set up their histories.”

Again, from the same saint, from his discourse on the Forty Holy Martyrs:

“Writers and painters often signify the trophies and victories of wars: the former adorn them with words, the latter engrave them on panels. Both have stirred many to heroic deeds. For what the narrative of history has written, silent painting displays through imitation.”

Again, from the discourse of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, Chrysostom, on the parable of the sower:

“If you insult a royal garment, do you not insult the one who wears it? Do you not know that whoever reviles the image made of wood and colors is not judged as having dared against something lifeless, but the insult is directed against the king?”

[“Do you not know that whoever brings insult against the image of the king directs the insult toward the king himself—that is, toward the prototype and his dignity?”]

And again, from the discourse of the same Father on the holy fifth day of Easter:

“All things were made for the glory of God, but for our use: clouds for the service of rain, earth for the production of abundant crops, sea in abundance for those who sail; all serve God [L., ‘humanity’], or rather the image of God.”

For when royal representations and images are brought into cities, and rulers and peoples meet them with praises, they do not honor the wooden panel or the wax painting, but the royal history.

So too creation does not honor the earthly appearance, but reverences the heavenly history.

Likewise, from the blessed Cyril’s interpretation of the holy Gospel according to Matthew, we quote, saying [perhaps, “he says”]:

“Faith paints the Word who exists in the form of God, just as the redemption of our life was offered to God: he assumed the likeness that belongs to us and became human.”

And again, shortly afterward, the same author says:

“Parables fulfill for us the function of images, presenting the power of the things signified as though by the placing before us of eyes and by the touch of a hand, and offering for contemplation what is invisibly contained in subtle conceptions.”

Again, from Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, whose beginning is:

“We have written sufficiently, taking a little from many sources.”

And afterward:

“Even the things painted upon wood, when the form has passed away from the external defilement, must necessarily be taken up again and united [perhaps, ‘renewed’] by the one whose form it is, so that he may be able to renew the image in the same material and element.

“For because of his form, the material also, wherever he is depicted, is not cast down, but is represented together with him in that material.”

And another passage from the blessed Ambrose, *To the Emperor Gratian*, book three, chapter nine:

“What then? When we worship both his divinity and his flesh, do we divide Christ? Or when in him we worship the divine image and the cross, do we divide him? God forbid.”

Again, from Saint Epiphanius of Constantia in Cyprus:

“If a king has an image, are there two kings? Certainly not; the king is one, together with the image.”

Again, from Saint Stephen, bishop of Bostra:

“We who confess concerning the images of the saints declare that every work done in the name of God is good and holy. For an image is one thing, and a statue [*agalma*], that is, an idol, is another.”

For when God fashioned Adam—that is, created him—he said:

“Let us make a human being according to our image and likeness.”

And he made the human being in the image of God.

What then? Because the human being is the image of God, is he a statue—that is, idolatry and impiety? By no means!

If Adam had been the image of demons, he would have been expelled and rejected. But because he is the image of God, he is honored and accepted.

For every image made in the name of the Lord, or of angels, prophets, apostles, martyrs, or righteous persons, is holy.

For it is not the wood that is worshiped, but what is contemplated and remembered in the wood that is honored.

We all worship rulers and greet them, even if they are sinners. Why then should we not worship the holy servants of God and establish and raise up their images as a memorial to them, so that they may not fall into oblivion?

But you say that God himself prohibited the worship of things made by human hands. Tell me, O Jew: what is there upon the earth that was not made by human hands after God had made it?

What then? Is the ark of God, built and fashioned from the material of setim wood, not made by human hands? And the altar, the mercy seat, the jar containing the manna, the table, the lampstand, and the inner and outer tabernacle—are these not works of human hands, which Solomon made?

And why are they called the holy of holies, although they are made by human hands?

What then? Were the cherubim and the six-winged creatures around the altar not living creatures and images of angels, works of human hands? How were they not cast out? Because by God’s command they became images of the angels, they are holy—and these were living creatures.

The idols of the nations, however, because they were images of demons, God cast down and condemned.

We make images as memorials of the saints: Abraham, Moses, Elijah, Isaiah, Zechariah, and the remaining holy prophets, apostles, and martyrs who were crushed for the Lord’s sake, so that everyone who sees them in an image may remember them and glorify the Lord who glorified them.

For honor and worship are due to them, and what we possess should be dedicated to them according to their righteousness, so that all who see them may hasten to become imitators of their conduct.

For what is the honor of worship except what we sinners also do when we worship and greet one another in honor and love?

Thus we worship our Lord—not otherwise—while glorifying and trembling before him. The image is a likeness of him, because he has been portrayed in it.

Let the impious, who do not practice what is good and do not remember the saints, not hinder those who do good, nor scandalize those who honor the saints and servants of God and remember them.

They will receive a good reward for their good deed. But the impious, according to what they have devised, will receive the ruin of dishonor, because they neglected righteousness and departed from God.

Images are painted, honored, and worshiped as memorials of the saints, who are servants of God and entreat and implore the divine majesty on our behalf.

It is also fitting to remember our leaders and to offer thanksgiving to God.

From the discourse of the blessed Jerome, presbyter of Jerusalem:

“For just as God permitted every nation to worship things made by human hands, while he approved for the Jews those tablets that Moses carved and the two golden cherubim, so also he granted to us Christians the cross and the making and worshiping of images of good works, and commanded us to display our work.”

Therefore, most devout and most serene lords and children, we have briefly reviewed these aforementioned testimonies of the holy Fathers.

The history of the divine Scripture of the Old and New Testament also bears witness concerning the preservation of divine worship: those things established in the churches for the praise of God, as memorials of pious activity and by God’s approval, accord with the tradition of the holy Fathers concerning the establishment of holy images, and with divine Scripture as it exists in painting [Θ. gives the elliptical variant *περὶ τῆς συστάσ. τ. ε. εἰ καὶ παρὰ τῆς θείας*, “concerning the establishment of the images, even if also from divine ...”; Scripture follows], as we have endeavored, with all humility and sincerity of heart, to bring before your God-authorized serenity in this apostolic statement.

Therefore, the detailed testimonies of various and highly esteemed Fathers who established these same holy images must be preserved, as we find them in their books; and we have endeavored to bring them before your most gentle empire.

I beseech your gentleness with great desire of heart, and, as though present, kneeling and crawling at your feet, I entreat you; before God I implore and adjure you: command that these same holy images be restored and firmly established in their ancient position in that very God-protected imperial city and in both regions of Greece. Preserve the tradition of this, our most sacred and holy Church, rejecting and abhorring the wickedness of impious heretics, so that you may be embraced by this holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church of ours, which is beyond comprehension [L., “inaccessible”].

# Letter 57. To Tarasius, Patriarch

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1233]

To the beloved brother Tarasius, patriarch: Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

In the pastoral cares by which it is fitting for us to feed the people of God, and while weighing with the most careful thought how the sound voice of preaching ought always to be proclaimed by the preacher, and what sort of person he ought to be in his conduct, so that through compassion he may become near to all and through his way of life distinguished among all, transferring to himself through pious mercy the infirmities of everyone, and through the highest regard for himself rising to divine things, we have considered it fitting to address your beloved holiness in sacred concord and to set forth the matter carefully.

In the synodical documents of your confession of faith, which were sent to our apostolic see through Leo, your most reverend presbyter, we found at the beginning of the first page that your reverence had been raised from the lay order and imperial administration to the summit of the sacred rank. Our soul was greatly astonished at this.

Had we not found your sincere and orthodox faith in the aforesaid synodical documents, according to the sacred creed and the practice of the six holy universal councils, and had we not found you rightly disposed concerning the venerable images, we would in no way have dared to accept such synodical documents.

But just as our heart was saddened by the inappropriate ancient separation between us, so our soul rejoiced when it found your confession and right faith.

We found in the aforesaid synodical letter of your holiness, after the fullness of faith and confession of the sacred creed and of all six holy councils, and concerning the sacred and venerable representations, a matter worthy of the highest praise and veneration. It contains the following:

“I also receive these same six holy councils, together with all the rules that were promulgated by them lawfully and divinely. Among them is contained this:

“‘In certain paintings of venerable images a lamb, traced by the finger of the Forerunner, is shown [printed *exaratus ostenditur*, “is shown, traced”; variant *demonstratus exaratur*, “is traced, pointed out”]; it has passed into a figure of grace [printed *praeteriit*, “has passed”; Greek reading *assumptus est*, “has been assumed” as a figure of grace], presenting beforehand through the Law the true Lamb, Christ our Lord. Therefore, embracing the ancient figures and shadows delivered to the Church as signs and foreshadowings of the truth, we bring forth grace and truth, receiving this as the fullness of the Law.

“‘Therefore, so that perfection may also be depicted through the work of colors in the faces of all, we decree that Christ our God, the Lamb who took away the sin of the world, be depicted from now on according to the human form, as a human character and image, in place of the former lamb. Through him we contemplate the height of the humility of God the Word (John 1), and in remembrance of his life in the flesh we are led by the hand to recall both his passion and his saving death and the redemption thereby accomplished for the world.’”

By this testimony of orthodox faith your brotherly priesthood has driven away the curiosity of the wicked and the babbling of heretics. Their evil zeal has not been received by us or by divine grace; rather, it has been judged unstable in such matters. For our own catholic and apostolic Roman Church, girded about with the belt of our mind, confesses the same thing, agreeing and harmonizing against the madness of the heretics, by whom it is shown to have been attacked and arranged in this way.

Since, therefore, your beloved holiness has promised [*pollicita*; variant *sollicita*, “has been diligent”] to honor and worship the holy images of Christ our God, who was incarnate according to the human form for us, among us, and on our behalf, and likewise those of his holy, undefiled, and truly God-bearing mother, as well as of his saints, we praise your orthodox purpose in every way, provided that you persevere as you have begun. And, as those who are concerned with pastoral care, we advise you to preserve unchangeably the orthodox faith that you have once confessed, preaching and teaching it alike.

“For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is the Lord Jesus” (I Cor. VII, as printed).

Therefore whoever holds the foundation of love for God and neighbor and of the faith that is in him has set within himself that same Jesus Christ, Son of God and man, as the foundation.

For it must be confessed that wherever Christ is the foundation, the structure of good works follows.

Truth itself says:

“He who does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but enters by another way, is a thief and a robber; but he who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10).

Again the same Savior says:

“I am the door.”

Therefore the one who enters the sheepfold through the door enters through Christ.
