He enters through Christ who, understanding and proclaiming the truth concerning the same creator and liberator of the human race, accepts the summit of governance as an office for bearing a burden, not from a desire for the glory of passing honor, and who diligently watches over the care of the flock entrusted to him, lest either perverse people speaking wickedly tear apart the sheep of God or evil spirits, persuading them to delight in vices, devastate them.

Certainly we remember that blessed Jacob, who had served for a long time for his wives, said:

[Note: From the Vulgate edition; the Greek version reads very differently. HARD.]

“For twenty years I have been with you; your sheep and goats were not barren; I did not eat the rams of your flock, nor did I show you any animal carried off by a beast. I bore every loss; whatever was lost by theft you required from me. By day and by night I was consumed by heat and frost; sleep fled from my eyes” (Gen. 31).

If, then, the one who feeds Laban’s sheep labors and keeps watch in this way, how much labor and how many vigils must the one who feeds God’s sheep undertake?

But in all these matters may he himself instruct you, who became human for our sake and deigned to become what he had made. May he pour into you the love and affection of his Holy Spirit, preserve you from every care, and open the eyes of your mind, so that through the course, struggle, and solicitude of your love, imitating our apostolic transmission of the ancient orthodox faith, the sacred and venerable icons may stand according to the ancient order in the territories of our pious emperors, so that your priesthood may thereby remain stable.

After your confession of faith, it became known to us that your venerable holiness had petitioned our orthodox defenders and champions of truth, namely our most pious emperors, who were made for the glory of God, that a universal council might be held. They promised before all their Christian people that they would piously assent to your petition and decreed that the council should be held in the imperial city.

Accordingly, just as their divine command contained, we sent beloved, approved, and prudent priests, with great desire and the greatest joy, concerning the restoration of the holy images, so that they might be reestablished in the ancient order in those regions.

But your holiness should earnestly suggest to those same most pious and triumphant emperors that, first of all, that false synod which was held irregularly and without proper deliberation [printed *insyllogistice*; variant *asyllogistice*] without the apostolic see against the tradition of the venerable Fathers and against the divine images be anathematized in the presence of our envoys; that every tares be uprooted from the Church; and that the word of our Lord Jesus Christ be fulfilled:

“The gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”

And again:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16).

The see of this apostle, holding primacy throughout the whole world, shines forth and stands as the head of all the churches of God. Therefore the blessed apostle Peter himself, feeding the Church at the Lord’s command, left nothing undone; rather, he always held and still holds the primacy.

If your holiness desires to cling to him and strives to preserve, incorrupt and undefiled, from the depth of your heart and the sincerity of your mind, the sacred and orthodox form of our apostolic see, which is the head of all the churches of God, then, truly orthodox and worshiping God, you will first offer this sacrifice to almighty God: in our name, entreat the exalted footsteps of our aforementioned most pious and God-crowned great emperors, and adjure them before God and by his fearful judgment to command that the holy images be restored and firmly established in their ancient state in that very God-preserved imperial city and everywhere, preserving the tradition of this sacred and most holy Roman Church of ours and pursuing and abhorring, through your struggle and faithful solicitude, the error of the wicked and heretics.

But if they do not restore the sacred and venerable images in those regions, we dare not receive your consecration, especially if you follow those who do not believe the truth.

Therefore, with the greatest labor, love of faith, and struggle, it is altogether fitting that your most venerable holiness should unhesitatingly restore to their ancient position in those regions the sacred images of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, of his holy mother, the ever-virgin Mary, of the holy apostles, and of all the holy prophets, martyrs, and confessors, so that with one accord we may worthily sing the prophetic song:

“Lord, save the most pious kings, and hear us on the day when we call upon you” (Ps. 19);

“For they have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the dwelling of your glory” (Ps. 25).

As for our beloved men, Peter, the archpriest of our holy Roman Church, and Peter the monk, presbyter, and abbot, who have been sent by us to the feet of the most serene and pious emperors, we ask that, for the love of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, and for our sake, you judge them worthy of every kind reception and human kindness and treat them accordingly, so that we may be able to return great thanks for this also.

May almighty God grant to preserve your love, if it remains steadfast, and cause the fruit entrusted to you to abound beyond measure, and command you to pass into everlasting joys.

May God keep you safe, most beloved brother.

# Letter of Adrian, the Most Holy Pope of Elder Rome, Translated from the Language of the Romans into the Greek Tongue

[Col. 1234]

To the beloved brother Tarasius, patriarch: Adrian, servant of the servants of God.

Considering the pastoral cares in which it is fitting to shepherd the people of God, and with the most careful reflection considering how the sound voice of preaching ought at every time to be proclaimed by the herald, and what sort of person the shepherd ought to be in compassion and conduct, so that through compassion he may become near to all and through his conduct distinguished among all; and how, through pious mercy, he may transfer to himself the illnesses of everyone, or, by the loftiest contemplation of himself, may lead all upward to divine things [L., “may himself pass over to divine things”—in the Greek, the subject is uncertain], concerning all these matters we have determined to address your beloved holiness and priestly concord and to make the word clear in detail.

In the synodical writings of your confession of faith, sent to our apostolic see through Leo, your most reverend presbyter, we found at the beginning of the first page that your reverence had been raised from the lay order and imperial service to the priestly rank. Our soul was greatly astonished at this.

Had we not found your sincere and orthodox faith in the aforesaid synodical documents of the sacred creed, according to the institution of the six holy universal councils, and had we not found you rightly disposed concerning the venerable images, we would not at all have dared to accept such synodical documents.

But as our heart was saddened by the former inappropriate separation between us [L.: “your unlawful ordination, and the inappropriate ...,” etc.; the source prints *ἀθεμίτου ὑμῶν χειρτονίας*], so our soul rejoiced when it found your confession and upright faith.

We found in the aforesaid synodical letter of your holiness, after the fullness of the faith and the confession of the sacred creed and of all six holy councils, and concerning the sacred and venerable representations, a matter worthy of praise and embrace, containing the following:

“I receive what was established by this same holy Sixth Council, together with all the canons lawfully and divinely promulgated by it” [alternative: “I receive these same six holy councils together with all the canons divinely and lawfully proclaimed by them”].

Among them it is written:

“In some paintings of venerable images a lamb is engraved, shown by the finger of the Forerunner. It was accepted as a figure of grace, presenting beforehand through the Law the true Lamb, Christ our God, to us.”

Therefore, embracing the ancient figures and shadows delivered to the Church as symbols and foreshadowings of the truth [alternative: “delivered as symbols and foreshadowings”], we prefer grace and truth, receiving this as the fulfillment of the Law.

Therefore, so that what is perfect may also be portrayed in colored representations before the faces of all, we decree that the Lamb of Christ our God, who takes away the sin of the world, be from now on set up in images according to the human form and character, in place of the former lamb. Through him we contemplate the height of the humility of God the Word, and are led by the hand toward remembrance of his life in the flesh, his passion, his saving death, and the redemption thereby accomplished for the world.

By this testimony of orthodox faith your brotherly priesthood has rejected and driven away the curiosity of the wicked and the babbling of the heretics. Their evil zeal was not accepted by us or by divine grace, but was judged unstable in such matters. For our own catholic and apostolic Roman Church, girded with the belt of the understanding, confesses the same thing, agreeing and harmonizing against the madness of the heretics, by whom it has been shown to have been attacked and opposed.

Since, then, your beloved holiness has undertaken to honor and worship the venerable images: that of Christ our God according to the human form, who became incarnate according to our condition, for us, and on our behalf; that of the holy, undefiled, and truly God-bearing mother; and those of his saints—if your orthodox intention remains as it began, we praise it altogether. As those concerned with pastoral care, we advise you to preserve unaltered the orthodox faith that you have once confessed, proclaiming and teaching it.

“For no one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.”

Who, then, holding the foundation of love for Christ and neighbor, which exists in Christ, has not set the same Jesus Christ, Son of God and man, as a foundation within himself?

For it is confessed that wherever Christ is the foundation, the building of good works follows.

Truth itself says:

“He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but enters by another way, is a thief and a robber; but he who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep.”

As the same Savior said:

“I am the door.”

Therefore that person enters the flock who enters through the door. And he who enters through the door enters through Christ: he who, understanding the truth concerning the same creator and redeemer of the human race, preserves and guards the rank of pastoral dignity and accepts the burden to be borne, not looking toward glory and passing honor, but, having taken up the flock, watches over it diligently, lest the sheep of God be corrupted either by perverse people speaking crooked things or by those persuaded by an evil spirit.

Indeed blessed Jacob, who served Laban his father-in-law for many years on account of women, is shown saying:

“For twenty years I have been with you. Your sheep and goats have not become barren [alternative: ‘have not been barren’]; I have not eaten the rams of your sheep, nor have I brought you an animal taken by a beast. I paid from myself for thefts by day and thefts by night. By day I was consumed by the heat, and by night by the frost, and sleep departed from my eyes.”

If the one who shepherds Laban’s sheep works and keeps watch in this way, how many labors and how many vigils must the one who shepherds Christ’s sheep endure?

But in all these things may he himself strengthen and teach you, who became human for our sake and deigned to become what he had made. May he pour into you the love of his Holy Spirit and desire, preserve you from every care, and open the eyes of your understanding, so that through the labor, struggle, and course of your love, imitating our apostolic transmission of the ancient orthodox faith, the sacred and venerable images may be established according to the ancient order in the territories of our pious emperors, so that through this your stable priesthood may remain.

After your confession of faith, it became known to us that your venerable holiness had asked our most pious and most orthodox emperors, zealous defenders of the truth and made faithful for the glory of God, for an ecumenical council to be held. They agreed before all their Christ-loving people, piously assenting to your petition, and decreed that the council should take place in their imperial city.

We, with great desire, as was contained in their divine command, sent genuine, approved, and prudent priests concerning the restoration of the holy images, so that they might be established in the ancient order in those regions, with the greatest joy.

But let your holiness eagerly bring before those same most pious and triumphant emperors the request that, first of all, that false synod which was held without the apostolic see, disorderly and illogically, against the tradition of the most venerable Fathers and against the divine images, be anathematized in the presence of our envoys; that every tare be uprooted from the Church; and that the word of our Lord Jesus Christ be fulfilled:

“The gates of Hades shall not prevail against it.”

And again:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”

His throne shines forth as holding primacy throughout the whole inhabited world and as the head of all the churches of God.

Therefore the same blessed Peter the apostle, shepherding the Church at the Lord’s command, left nothing undone [Al., “left nothing remaining”], but always held and still holds the primacy.

If your holiness clings to our apostolic see, which is the head of all the churches of God, and strives to preserve its sacred and orthodox form incorrupt and undefiled, from the depth of your heart and with sincere understanding, then, being truly orthodox and worshiping God, you will offer this first sacrifice to almighty God.

You will entreat, as though standing in our place, the exalted footsteps of our most pious and God-crowned great emperors; and before God [Note: Read “against” from the Latin] and his fearful judgment you will adjure them to command that the holy images be restored and proclaimed in their ancient position in that very God-protected imperial city and everywhere, preserving the tradition of this sacred and most holy Roman Church of ours. Let them drive away and abhor the error of the wicked and heretics through your struggle and most faithful labor.

But if they do not establish the sacred and venerable images in those regions, we cannot in any way dare to receive your ordination, especially if you follow those who disobey the truth.

For this reason, with the utmost labor, longing for the faith, and struggle, it is altogether fitting that your most venerable holiness should unhesitatingly raise up in the ancient order, in those regions, the sacred and venerable images of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, of his holy mother and ever-virgin Mary, of the holy apostles, and of all the holy prophets, martyrs, and confessors.

Thus, in harmony, we may worthily sing the prophetic hymn, saying:

“Lord, save our most devout kings, and hear us on whatever day we call upon you,” because they loved “the beauty of your house and the place of the dwelling of your glory.”

As for those whom we have sent—Peter, our beloved first presbyter of the holy Roman Church, and Peter the abbot, presbyter and superior—to the feet of the most serene and pious emperors, we entreat that, for love of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, and for our sake, they may be judged worthy of every assistance and human kindness and be treated accordingly, so that we may be able to offer great thanks for this also.

May almighty God approve your love, if it remains steadfast, come to your aid and preserve you, increase beyond measure the fruit entrusted to you, and command that you be transferred into everlasting joy.

May God preserve you in health, beloved brother.

# Metrical Letter of Adrian to King Charles

This letter is placed before Adrian’s book of canons in ancient manuscripts.

Divine doctrine shining forth surpasses the scepters of the kingdom.

A happy origin of kings, ever a blessed begetting.

We see the mass of the Law possessing the grace of praise.

From a righteous king is born the defender of the nourishing Church.

For heavenly discipline can never be conquered.

Already long ago, taking up the triumph of his father’s kingdom,

An example by which devoted faith rejoices in victory,

With Christ assisting, and blessed Peter the key-bearer,

He subjects all hostile nations beneath his royal feet.

Behold, a blessed root has brought forth a stock like its offspring,

Rejoicing to worship God, ever to love the divine Law,

To preserve praiseworthy faith and defend holy life,

Having the doorkeeper of heaven altogether as his helper in triumphs.

Relying upon his victorious power, he always perseveres.

Following the light of the doctrine of the apostolic see’s faith,

Great King Charles shines in this holy see.

Enriched through him with every good, it triumphs everywhere.

He has deserved always to possess a heavenly kingdom in these things.

Taking up divine weapons, he trampled proud nations.

He restored ancient gifts to his mother, the Church,

Together with great cities, boundaries, and various strongholds.

By divine strength he struck down the Lombard and Herulian peoples.

Exulting, he embraces the faith that he received from his ancestors.

This great lineage shines throughout the whole world:

Lofty, noble, resplendent, it governs diverse kingdoms.

Joyfully and swiftly, safe and sound, he comes to the thresholds of the apostles.

The whole people celebrates him with abundant praises and hymns.

He earnestly asks the highest bishop to pray for him,

That the offenses committed in his youth may be redeemed for him.

Freed through blessed intercessions, he promised in his speech to the teacher

To preserve forever the spirit of the holy Roman Church,

To protect the just decrees of his blessed protector Peter,

And, able to give more, he offered them at his confession.

To these things Bishop Adrian foretold triumphs for Christ,

That for a long time the divine right hand would protect him, with Peter and Paul accompanying him,

Granting the sword of victory and fighting on your behalf.

Unharmed, you will remain victorious with your people, for through them

You seek entrance into the city of Pavia as victor.

You will trample the necks of the wicked king Desiderius,

Overthrowing his strength and plunging him into the abyss below.

Surrounded by the kingdom of the Lombards, you will return your gift:

The sacred gifts promised to the key-bearer of Peter’s hall,

While he grants you more victory and honor as well.

May you reign through the ages here with your people, and afterward your offspring.

Never depart from the Law, observing these statutes.

[Note: Thus far Adrian’s letter, as it could be extracted from corrupt manuscripts. As for its date, since Charles came to Rome three times during Adrian’s lifetime—namely, in 774, when he was besieging Pavia; again in 781, when Adrian anointed his sons Pippin, king of Italy, and Louis, king of Aquitaine; and finally in 787, when he proceeded from there also to Capua and Benevento against Duke Grimoald—we have decided, although the matter is uncertain, to refer Adrian’s book rather to the last expedition than, as others preferred, to the first, since many things read in his letter can scarcely fit the first occasion. Sirmond.]

# A Bull of Adrian

By which he confirms the division of the diocese of Strasbourg into seven archdeaconries, the division of the bishop’s revenues from those of the chapter, and other rights of the canons of the same church; issued 4 April 784.

(From Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg.*)

[Col. 1243A] Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

[Note: The popes of the eighth century used no other title than “servant of the servants of God,” adopting it from Saint Gregory: “Gregory was the first of all,” says John the Deacon, “who rather humbly determined to be styled at the beginning of his letters ‘servant of the servants of God.’”]

It is fitting for apostolic authority to assist with kindly compassion those endowed with pious religion and to grant with eager devotion the assent sought by petitioners.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that our venerable brother and fellow bishop, Etho of Strasbourg, appeared before our apostolic authority in the presence of our most beloved son Charles, king of the Franks, and reported how, in order to lighten the work of his administration, and with the counsel and consent of the wiser men of his entire diocese, he had constituted the bishopric of Strasbourg as seven archdeaconries and had appointed over each of them, in his place, an archdeacon of good life and good conduct.

Each archdeacon, together with his archpresbyter, was to instruct his subjects usefully in God’s law by word and example, and to exercise episcopal care in every respect except the reconciliation of penitents: granting altars; closing churches in judicial order with the bishop’s seal; suspending clerics from divine office; and bringing before the presence of the aforesaid Etho or his successors for correction whatever they were unable to correct themselves.

No bishop was to have the power to remove any of the aforementioned brothers from such dignity, unless, God forbid, they became entangled in crimes for which, by canonical law, they would rightly be deposed from every episcopal vicariate.

Moreover, the same bishop informed us that he kept all episcopal property separate from the prebend of the canons, so that none of the bishops might do anything with it except by the will and election of the brothers serving God there.

They were to appoint one of their fellow canons over them, who would diligently know how to administer their property usefully day and night, and who would not disturb any brother without just cause. To such a man, with due obedience, the greatest honor and reverence after the bishop were to be shown by all.

All the benefits of the cloister, except the provostships, were to be distributed by his administration among the brothers according to each one’s need.

The bishop, however, was not to require any service from the brothers’ provost as though it were owed by obligation, except what was voluntary, apart from the canonical judgments that he was to issue in synod for individual cases.

At the request and out of affection for the aforesaid Etho, our most beloved son Charles established concerning episcopal property—namely, the mint, tolls, and other offices belonging to him—that whenever these offices changed hands, seven pounds should be contributed for the increase of his welfare: three to the provost and four to the canons collectively.

We therefore confirm this administrative arrangement, both of the king and of our brother and fellow bishop, in response to their humble petition. By the authority of God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of ourselves, we prohibit under anathema that the present bishop, any of his successors, or any person, powerful or powerless, should henceforth dare to lay hands upon it, violate any of the provisions stated above, or take anything away from the brothers.

Written by the hand of Zacharias, librarian of the holy Roman see.

Done at Rome, on the Monday of Easter, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 773, in the presence of many princes, successfully.

[Note: Pope Adrian held the pontifical see from 9 February 772 until 25 December 795, the day on which he died. Papebrock, in his *Propylaeum* to the *Acta Sanctorum* for May, p. 298, asserts that he had read no genuine bull containing years of the incarnation before Leo IX; Mabillon agrees in *De re diplomatica*, p. 185. In fact, the Dionysian era did not become consistently established in papal documents until the beginning of the eleventh century. But earlier bulls cannot therefore be called false merely because they contain that epoch, which was already well known and current at Rome in the eighth century. The Gallic authors of the *Nouvelle Diplomatique*, vol. V, p. 224, support this opinion. Moreover, the year of the incarnation found here in Adrian’s bull may have been added by Henry, bishop of Strasbourg, who copied it into his charter of the year 1205.]

# Authors of the Eighth Century, of Uncertain Date

## Isidore of Beja

### Historical Notice on Isidore of Beja

(From Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus.*)

If anything else in our affairs and among our authors is complicated and obscure, it is certainly the matter concerning Isidore, bishop of Beja. He did indeed belong to a number of other namesakes—Pellizerius has established that there were no fewer than seven writers so called (rightly, perhaps not?).

Isidore is commonly called “of Beja,” from the Lusitanian city of Pax (which they now call Beja), where he was bishop while it was still subject to the Moors [Note: Morales, book 12, chapter 40]. His name appears in the manuscripts of Complutum and Osma, attached to a certain chronicle whose title itself produces something barbarous: *Epitome of the Emperors or of the Arabs*, together with a chronicle of Spain.

This is the only edition we possess of that chronicle, prepared by Prudentius Sandoval, bishop of Pamplona, together with the other chronicles of the Spanish bishops Hydatius, Sebastian, Sampiro, and Pelagius.

This history—which is, as the most learned Peter de Marca correctly observed, a continuation of the chronicle of Isidore, bishop of Seville, *History of Béarn*, book 2, chapter 1—begins with the era 648. This must be corrected [Col. 1245C] from era 549. It is therefore the year 610, when, after Phocas was overthrown, Heraclius assumed the empire.

It extends to era 792, that is, the Christian year 754, during the reign of Constantine Copronymus—not his tenth year, as the edition prints it, but his fourteenth.

Other chronological eras, of the Arab years and of the world, given in the same edition, correspond not to this year but to the preceding one, 653 [as printed; the preceding year would be 753]: namely, Eusebian year of the world 5954, and the Arab, or Hegira, year 136. We leave this matter to the chronologists.

That this work, which the author calls an epitome, was written at this time is clear from his own words. Near the end he says:

“Thus, from the beginning of the world up to the era that has begun, seven hundred and ninety-two years have elapsed,” and so forth.

Earlier, in the same sense, though somewhat more obscurely because of the faulty reading and the tangled style, he writes:

“When era 782 had been completed and the third had already begun”—he means 783—“the sixty-eighth Roman [emperor], Constantine, son of Leo, was crowned emperor after his father, reigning for years.”

[Col. 1245D] “After so many years had been completed” should be corrected to “reigning for so many years.” For he could not otherwise have indicated how many years the prince would reign while he was still alive when the author wrote this. We therefore believe that a lacuna was left there by him, or that the adverb *so many* was inserted in its place, as though the number were to be supplied later.

“From the beginning of the world up to Constantine’s tenth year” (as we have already said, this must be corrected to the fourteenth), “the year 5954 being completed.”

He placed “the year being completed” opposite “years having been completed,” in his own barbarous fashion.

But Ambrosius Morales—whom, out of respect, we always name honorably, although in other matters he was an industrious man, perhaps more so than any other of our historians—paid too little attention to this point. When referring this Isidore to a later age, namely to the time of King García, who began to reign at León in the year 912, he makes Isidore younger than Sebastian of Salamanca, another historian of the same sort.

This is not surprising, since in truth he had nowhere seen this chronicle of Isidore, published by Sandoval and inscribed with Isidore’s name. For he attributes certain portions of this work, or epitome, to the Sebastian of Salamanca just mentioned. Anyone who observes this carefully will detect the error more than once.

Other matters that are read in Sebastian’s Chronicle he praises as Isidorian. Very often, however, he uses the testimony of Rodrigo of Toledo, Lucas of Tuy, the Arab Rhazes, and others, reporting as found in Isidore’s Chronicle or epitome what we now possess there. This would certainly have been no small fault in him if, passing over an older contemporary writer, he were to present historians nearly four centuries later as witnesses. Finally, while praising Isidore, he mentions certain matters that have disappeared from this epitome [Note: [Col. 1245D] Morales, book XII–XV, passim.]. Juan Vaseo certainly saw this Chronicle, and frequently reports from it those portions that we have in print [Note: [Col. 1245D] In the *Chronicon Hispanicum*, under the years 612–747.]; he ceases to use it when it comes to an end. Andreas Quercetanus also extracted from it certain fragments concerning [Col. 1246C] affairs in Gaul and published them in the first volume of the *Historians of Gaul*, p. 785, namely from Sandoval’s edition. Rodrigo, certainly archbishop of Toledo, made such extensive use of this history of Isidore that he often copies entire chapters from it [Note: [Col. 1245D] Book II, chapters 17, 19, 20, and 22; book III, chapters 12–15 and elsewhere, and in the *History of the Arabs*, chapter 11 and elsewhere.]. Comparing his text with Isidore’s words could be of considerable help in healing the wounds of this Chronicle. He transferred Isidore’s words not only into the history of Spain but also into the history of the Arabs, adhering to his system of reckoning, which in Isidore—apart from scribal errors—is exceedingly exact, as the already-mentioned Peter de Marca observed [Note: [Col. 1246D] Book II of the *History of Béarn*, chapter 1.]. Several manuscript copies of this history, or of the Isidorian epitome, indeed survive in Spain.

As we have said, Sandoval had two codices available [Note: [Col. 1246D] Sandoval mentions them in the heading of his edition.], one belonging to the church of Osma, without the author’s name, and the other from Alcalá. With the help of the latter, and likewise of a third copy made at the command of Cardinal Francisco Ximénez, D. Joseph Pellizerius, royal chronicler, a most diligent man, says that he corrected one of his own copies in places [Note: [Col. 1246D] In the *Annals of Spain after the Invasion of the Moors*, and in the *Pellizerian Library*, fol. 146.]. Peter de Marca saw a fourth in the library of the College of Navarre in Paris, as he himself reports in book II, chapter 1, of the *History of Béarn. Perhaps others also made their way into Portugal, since Andreas Resende, in the *Lusitanian Antiquities* (book IV), remarked, speaking of the city of Beja, that the minor works of Isidore of Beja were circulating “in a harsh and little-polished style, incomplete, and bristling with the most thorny errors.” And so it truly is, since this author has been most miserably weakened no less by his own innate and characteristic wounds than by those inflicted by copyists.

Why, then, do those among our scholars who excel in leisure and industry, and who have at hand the means to benefit the public, begrudge us a more accurate and clearer edition of this work, while neglecting other useless things, or at least things not so useful? This might indeed have been expected from the aforementioned Pellizerius, our friend, who says that he had already undertaken the more arduous labor of collation and correction—but he has now succumbed to fate as we bring these matters back to the anvil—or from D. Gaspar Ibáñez de Segovia, Marquis of Acropolis (now Marquis of Mondéjar); or from D. Juan Lucas Cortés, my fellow citizen, who, as I write, is one of the judges attending to criminal cases in the royal court at Madrid. Since he is thoroughly versed in these ancient writings and in the whole history of Spain, and has the finest manuscript codices at hand, either in his own possession or in the extensive and well-equipped library of the most excellent Count of Villa-Umbrosa, president of the High Court of Castile (now that of his most excellent widowed countess), if public affairs permit him, he ought certainly, in obedience to his inclination, to bring this and other monuments of antiquity into public view through his industry—that is, as complete and free from errors as he can make them [Col. 1247B] [Note: [Col. 1247D] Francisco Berganza, Benedictine, published at Madrid in 1729 an Isidorian Chronicle in somewhat better condition; after him the distinguished Flórez published it, collated with several ancient codices, vol. VIII, beginning at p. 274.].

Indeed, if any Chronicle of ours needs this kind of work, it is this Isidorian one, so that, disfigured only by the blows dealt by its own style, it may again appear before the eyes of men in a form consistent with itself. We said “by the blows dealt only by its own style,” since there can be no doubt that such a work came from the author’s hand: “a monstrosity rather than a Chronicle,” says Juan Vaseo [Note: [Col. 1247D] *Chronicon Hispanicum*, chapter 4, no. 11], “so prodigiously does he write, and in a Gothic rather than a Latin manner.” Resende, as we have heard, agrees with him, although he recognizes errors added to, and introduced from outside, the author’s barbarous language.

But what we have said about Isidore’s period—confirmed by the words of this same work—may perhaps be brought into dispute by the codices that attribute this epitome to Isidore the Younger. By this title another Isidore is elsewhere called, the author of a different universal Chronicle from the beginning of the world, whom we have shown in his proper place to have been bishop of Seville. Hence those who were less familiar with Isidore, bishop of Córdoba, older than the bishop of Seville and therefore called “the Elder,” persuaded themselves that not this man but the bishop of Beja [Col. 1247C]—whom, in relation to the older Isidore of Seville, they considered the Younger—was the author of both histories, the universal and the particular. It is less surprising that those who composed the General History at the command of King Alfonso X, called the Wise, fell into this error [Note: [Col. 1247D] Part II, chapter 50, p. 242.], as did Juan Gil of Zamora, the fourteenth-century Franciscan writer [Note: [Col. 1247D] *Treatise 6 of the *Adversaria*, concerning the perspicacity of philosophers and learned men of Spain.], who took that General History as his guide into error, than that Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, a twelfth-century historian, should have become stuck in the same mire. For he is the author of that work, or Chronicle, assembled from various chronicles and continued down to his own age. In its preface this author writes:

> “Dearest brothers, if you read this Chronicle, which you see before you, with a good disposition—for *bono*, not *dono*, as it was printed [Note: [Col. 1247D] By Pellizerius in his *Observations on the Chronicle of Dulcidius of Salamanca*, fol. 15. Barcelona, 1663.]—you will discover how the younger Isidore, bishop of Beja, just as he read in the Old and New Testament and understood through the Holy Spirit, so wrote fully from Adam to Noah, and to Abraham and David, and to the coming of our Redeemer; and concerning the judges and also the kings in Israel; and from there concerning the Roman kings or emperors, and the Vandals, and the Alans, and the Suevic kings of Spain, just as he diligently investigated and heard from his elders and predecessors.”

By these words, the universal Chronicle from the beginning of history, attributed to Saint Isidore of Seville, and likewise the histories of the Vandals, Alans, and Sueves, customarily attributed to that most holy bishop of Seville, are assigned to the bishop of Beja, or Isidore the Younger. Moreover, since he nowhere mentions this particular epitome of Beja, which we are now discussing, among the many chroniclers from whom Pelagius of Oviedo says he composed his historical system, it is plausible that he considered this epitome to be some portion of the aforementioned general Chronicle. In truth, they have neither eyes nor judgment who believe, whether on their own testimony or that of others, that the one universal Chronicle, as I may call it, could have flowed from the same breast and the same pen as this other work, published under the name of Isidore of Beja—one written in good Latin and free from any disgrace of language, the other barbarous and scarcely half-Latin.

Closely related to this error is the common error found in the printed history of Rodrigo of Toledo. For after it had attributed, at the end of book II, to blessed Isidore—that is, Isidore of Seville—the history of the origin of the Goths down to the fifth year of King Suinthila, and to Saint Ildefonsus the continuation of the deeds of those same Goths, Alans, Vandals, and Sueves from the fifth year of Suinthila to the eighteenth year of Recceswinth, Rodrigo is believed to have added:

> “And Isidore the Younger, who begins his Chronicle from the beginning of the world, faithfully continued it down to the eighteenth year of Recceswinth, and himself wrote as far as the destruction of Spain by the Arabs.”

Thus this second book of Rodrigo’s work concludes in the editions. But this is a gloss that should be driven out with pitchforks, and it is absent from the manuscript books. This is noted in the margin of the Frankfurt edition of this history in the *Illustrated History of Spain* [Col. 1248C]. Especially since it has already been clearly demonstrated, when we dealt with him, that Isidore of Seville wrote a Chronicle from the beginning of history, not merely from the period of the Goths; while none of the works of this Isidore of Beja, to which Rodrigo himself refers, let alone this epitome under discussion, indicates that he traced a history from that earliest beginning.

I would gladly read Rodrigo’s testimony in a slightly rearranged order, so that it is coherent and can be sustained:

> “And Isidore the Younger, because he begins his Chronicle from the beginning of the world, faithfully continued it down to the eighteenth year of Recceswinth—namely, the work begun by Ildefonsus—and he himself wrote as far as the destruction of Spain by the Arabs.”

This is true [Note: [Col. 1247D] We reproduce Rodrigo’s words with which his second book, *On the Affairs of Spain*, concludes, as they appear in a codex of the royal library at Madrid written around the year 800, namely: “And when blessed Isidore had described the origin of the Goths down to the fifth year of King Suinthila, Saint Ildefonsus described the times of the Goths, Alans, Vandals, and Sueves from the fifth year of Suinthila up to the eighteenth of Recceswinth. And Isidore the Younger, who began his Chronicle from the beginning of the world, faithfully continued it down to the eighteenth year of Recceswinth, and also wrote as far as the destruction of Spain by the Arabs.” In this passage, at least the words “down to the eighteenth year of Recceswinth” are repeated pointlessly, and they do not fit Isidore the Younger, or Isidore of Beja; nor do the preceding words, “who began his Chronicle from the beginning of the world.”].

Those seem to me to have gone astray just as much, though by another route, who multiply as many Isidores as they know works inscribed with that name. Among them I count D. Joseph Pellizerius, royal chronicler and—without prejudice to the truth—my most intimate friend [Col. 1248D] while he lived. In his observations on the Chronicle which he first published in recent years, and which he believed belonged to Dulcidius, bishop of Salamanca (fol. 16), he acknowledges no fewer than seven.

The first is Isidore of Córdoba, around the year 400, author of a commentary on the four books of Kings and of allegories of both Testaments. Pseudo-Dexter divided him into two [Note: [Col. 1249D] Under the years 384, no. 8; 423, no. 5; and 430.], both bishops of Córdoba—who perhaps never existed anywhere or at any time, as we suggested when speaking of writers of the fifth century. Pellizerius is unjust to Isidore of Seville when he denies him the book of *Allegories*.

The second of his Isidores is the recently mentioned Isidore of Seville, author of the *Etymologies*. The third is another bishop of the same see, younger than that Isidore and also bishop of Zaragoza. To this man he assigns not only the Chronicle inscribed with Isidore’s name and continued from the beginning of history down to the first year of Wamba, but also the history of the Alans, Vandals, and Sueves, which is customarily attributed equally to Isidore of Seville. In this matter we removed a second injury inflicted by Pellizerius upon the great Isidore of Seville, when we discussed the life and books of that most holy man [Col. 1249B]. All the more so because the Church of Seville records no other Isidore than this one, and the Church of Zaragoza records no Isidore at all in its catalogues of bishops. Pellizerius refers the proof of this assertion to the *Order of the Goths*—but he wrote nothing there, or elsewhere, about it. At least he says that the Chronicle of which he speaks is the one that Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, inserted in his aforementioned cento as though it belonged to Isidore of Beja, and that Lucas of Tuy continued as though it belonged to the great Isidore. This is evident from its opening: “The first among our people to compose a brief sequence of times through generations and kingdoms was Julius Africanus, etc.” That, however, is the preface to a Chronicle, not the beginning of the Chronicle itself.

Pellizerius’ fourth Isidore is the one who called himself “the Sinner” and published a collection of decretal letters and councils. But we leave it recorded, including in matters concerning Isidore, that perhaps this man was never truly the author of this work among us. His fifth Isidore is the bishop of Saetabis [Col. 1249C] [Note: [Col. 1249D] Which of the namesakes was he? For I find that two bishops named Isidore of Saetabis attended the councils of Toledo during this period. The first was the one who subscribed in fifteenth place at the twelfth council, held in the year of Christ 681; Asturius succeeded him, and his subscription appears thirty-fourth by order at the thirteenth council, held in the year of Christ 683. At the following, or fourteenth, council, the see of Saetabis is vacant. The second was the one who attended the two councils that followed, the fifteenth and sixteenth, held in the years 688 and 693; he subscribed fifty-fifth at the former and forty-second at the latter. None of these two is mentioned among writers by Julian, Felix, Honorius, or others.], to whom, he says, belongs the book *On the Signification of Names*. But is this the same as the book of *Allegories*, which Braulio calls *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels*? Or is it the glossary listed under the title of Isidore, or of Isidorian glosses? In the meantime, we await instruction from someone who may use his papers. Certainly, the author of this work, the bishop of Saetabis, is Luitprand, under the year 681, although Pellizerius attributes to him a collection of councils. I am surprised that Pellizerius, in establishing this person, has deferred to Luitprand—something he is otherwise hardly accustomed to do.

The sixth is that Isidore of Beja about whom we are now speaking, who wrote the Chronicle of the Arabs in the year 754—something that is entirely certain. Finally, the seventh is another Isidore, bishop of Beja. I do not know why he did not call this man also a bishop of Beja, since Pax, or Pax Julia, is Beja. Ambrosius Morales habitually calls him by this title of dignity when he frequently praises this history. Pellizerius says that his is the Chronicle that begins: “In six days God formed the creature of all things” [Col. 1249D]. But surely these are not the words at the beginning of that Chronicle whose preface, as we have said, is the one quoted earlier, and whose beginning differs from this Chronicle [Col. 1250A].

At least this final point—that there were two bishops of the same Pax Julia, one the author of the epitome of the emperors and Arabs that we are using, and the other, younger, who continued it, and whose continuation we lack but know only from the testimony of Morales—good faith persuades us to accept from this candid historian. It is also significant that he did not see this Isidore, the Arab chronicler, whereas he always had the later one in his hands. The former, living and writing in the year 793 under the emperor Constantine, son of Leo, of the Eastern Empire, could not, either during his life or in his writings, have reached García, king of León, and the year 940 of the era, or A.D. 902. If, therefore, we lend our ears to Pseudo-Dexter and Pellizerius, there will be two Isidores of Córdoba, two of Seville, and finally two of Beja, all writers, in addition to the one of Saetabis. But perhaps tomorrow, as the proverb has it, I shall believe nothing today.

Now that this multiplication has been brought low, and that we are content with a twofold Isidore—one of Seville and one of Beja, the latter younger in relation to the former [Note: [Col. 1249D] Elsewhere we quoted from the distinguished Flórez the testimony of Juan de Mariana concerning three Isidores: the Isidore of Córdoba, or the Elder, believed to have lived under Honorius around the year 420 and to have written certain works that do not survive; the Younger, or Isidore of Seville; and Isidore of Beja, who is likewise called “Younger” by some in relation to those earlier men, and is the author of the Chronicle under discussion. It appears in Flórez, vol. VIII, p. 267.]—let us turn to the other works of this Isidore of Beja.

He himself mentions one or two works different from this epitome, namely another *Epitome*, or a *Temporal Epitome*, as is clear from these words of his when he was discussing the battles between Belgi, commander of the eastern Arabs, and Humeia, son of Abdelmelic, commander of the western Arabs:

> “But because all Spain is by no means ignorant of it,” he says [Note: [Col. 1250D] Era 780, p. 21 of Sandoval’s edition], “this history has decided not to recount these battles, so tragic”—the printed text has *ystrayca* [Note: [Col. 1250D] *Istrayca bella*, for *tragica*. In an old Toledo manuscript of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, which we formerly collated with another recent copy and with the edition published by Grial, there appear on a blank parchment leaf the names and functions of the Muses, among which one reads:

> “Third Melpomene brings forth tragic cries with tears,”

> *traicos* being printed for *tragicos*. In Flórez’s edition, vol. VIII, p. 308, note 65, the reading is now *tam tragica bella*—“such tragic battles.”],

> “as these battles are, because in another epitome the manner in which all these things occurred remains clearly and fully written in our style.”

And later [Note: [Col. 1250D] Era 781, p. 22]:

> “Whoever, therefore, wishes to know the deeds of this matter will find everything explained point by point in the *Temporal Epitome* which we collected long ago. There he will also find written all the battles of the Moors fighting against the worship”—that is, against Christianity—“and he will read recorded the wars threatening Spain at that time.”

From this it appears that in this history he treated at length and in detail the battles of the Moors with the Goths and with one another [Col. 1250C].

Another work, called *The Words of the Days of the Age*, seems to be indicated by him in these words, while he is still dealing with the mutual slaughter of the Arabs:

> “As for the remaining deeds of these men, how they fought—is not this written in the book *The Words of the Days of the Age*, which we took care to add point by point to the preceding Chronicles?”

One might say that this book contains certain omissions, or *paraleipomena*, left out of the Chronicles of earlier periods. But whether Morales possessed either of these two works, when he so often attributes to Isidore of Beja matters not found in his published epitome; or whether Juan de Mariana possessed one, when he says that it is established from this same Isidore of Beja that our kings descended from Reccared (book VI, chapter 1), and that Roderic, the last of the Gothic kings, enlarged near the city of Córdoba a palace constructed by his father Witiza (book VI, chapter 21)—both of which you will search for in vain in the epitome—I shall answer nothing other than this: if you wish to touch the matter precisely, the examples once used by both authors should be consulted. This is what we have had to say about Isidore of Beja.

# THE CHRONICLE OF ISIDORE OF BEJA

*(From Flórez, España Sagrada.)*

## MARIANA’S TESTIMONY CONCERNING THIS CHRONICLE

### 1

It is commonly accepted, and is also received as the opinion of learned men, that there were three eminent Isidores in Spain: Isidore of Córdoba, whom Trithemius says lived under Honorius, around the year 420 of salvation; Isidore of Seville, a contemporary of Gregory the Great; and Isidore of Beja, whose period is disputed. Isidore of Córdoba is called “the Elder” by surname. The title “Younger” is commonly given to the two later men in comparison with the earlier one, and more frequently to Isidore of Seville. Isidore of Córdoba wrote nothing that survives, although Trithemius attributes certain works to him. Isidore of Seville wrote much, including, among other things, a very brief Chronicle from the beginning of the world down to the fifth year of Suinthila, king of the Goths.

### 2

Isidore of Beja composed a second Chronicle, which we present here, since it is the opinion of Vaseo that it extends to era 792—that is, that it was completed during the first years of the captivity—and is written in such a rough style that it seems to speak not in Latin but rather in some other language. This circumstance compelled us in several places to alter certain words and render them into Latin. What would you do if it were written either in Arabic or in the vernacular language of the Spaniards? It would not be any more intelligible, since so many passages are inverted and confused.

### 3

In most ancient copies it circulates without the author’s name, and Ambrosius Morales cites another Chronicle in many places under the name of Isidore of Beja, very different from this one and extending beyond the year 900 of salvation. I cannot say where he obtained it. I also saw a preface copied from a manuscript of Osma [Col. 1252A], a codex of exceptional authority, which had been prefixed to many Chronicles. It states that the Chronicle of Isidore of Beja begins from the beginning of the world and deals with the Jewish kings, Roman emperors, Vandals, Alans, and kings of Spain.

If this is true, the Chronicle of Isidore of Beja differs greatly from our present work. Nevertheless, this Chronicle must be considered to possess great authority and credibility, whoever its author may finally prove to be, especially in its treatment of the Arab kings. For this reason Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo, reproduced and translated almost the whole of it into his *History of the Arabs*. His diligence has helped us explain in Latin many passages of this Chronicle that could scarcely be understood.

### 4

The prudent reader will consider that Isidore of Beja—or whoever else was the author of this Chronicle—made a twofold error in reckoning the years of the Arabs. First, he took the beginning of his reckoning from the year of Christ 618, namely the seventh year of the reign of Heraclius [Col. 1252B]. This is a common fault shared by him with many other writers, or rather he himself may have led others into the error. Second, as a consequence of the first error, he did not compare the subsequent Arab years sufficiently accurately with our own.

Yet I do not know by what method he nevertheless followed the true reckoning from era 718 onward, bringing it into agreement with ours through the end of the book, and indeed making it entirely correct. This is the most certain indication that we have not gone astray in comparing the years of the Arabs with those of Christ.

## A SECOND TESTIMONY CONCERNING THE SAME CHRONICLE

*(D. Marca, Historia Benearnensis, Paris, 1640.)*

### 1

Among the authors of Spain there is only one, Isidore of Beja, or Isidore, bishop of Badajoz. This good man lived at the very time when the Moors entered Spain, and composed a Chronicle of the most memorable events of his age, which he added as an appendix and continuation to the Chronicle of Isidore of Seville. He brought it to an end in the year 754 of the Incarnation, which he equates with era 792 and with the year 5954 or 5950 of the world, according to the different reckonings.

Therefore one cannot obtain more reliable information about the condition of Christianity under the Saracens invading Spain than from a man who was a bishop by profession and an eyewitness of what was happening. Sandoval, bishop of Pamplona, published this author in 1615, together with Sebastian of Salamanca, Sampirus, and Pelagius. He warned his readers that very few copies of these old historians are found in Spain, and that those which remain are so damaged, defective, and corrupted that scarcely a tolerable meaning can be extracted from them without guessing.

### 2

This corruption appears greater in the printing of Isidore of Badajoz than in a manuscript copy that I collated, which is in the library of the College of Navarre in Paris, bound in the same volume with the manuscript book of Rodrigo of Toledo. Through this collation I corrected a considerable part of this little Chronicle and recovered the author’s straightforward meaning. Rodrigo followed him in his *History of the Arabs* nearly five hundred years ago, but with some errors, because he did not understand his language, which is incorrect and somewhat barbarous; moreover, he failed to render him the credit he owed, concealing his name.

### 3

The reckoning of times is very exact in this Chronicle, although certain errors, easy to correct, have slipped in through the fault of copyists. It is arranged by eras, by the years of the emperors of Constantinople, by the Arab years, and by those of the caliphs of Damascus. He places the beginning of the Arab years, or of the Hegira of Muhammad, in era 646, the seventh year of the emperor Heraclius. In that year, he writes, Muhammad, having defeated the elite of the Roman forces commanded by Theodore, brother of Heraclius, made himself master of Arabia, Syria, and Mesopotamia, and established the seat of the Arab kingdom in Damascus, the capital of Syria.

Nevertheless, on this point concerning the Hegira he does not agree with Stephen the mathematician of Alexandria. Stephen places it in the twelfth year of the emperor Heraclius, that is, in the year 622, according to the report of the emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus, which is the reckoning ordinarily followed by the ancient historians.

# [CHRONICLE]

## HERE BEGINS THE EPITOME OF THE EMPERORS, OR THE ANNALS OF THE ARABS, TOGETHER WITH THE CHRONOGRAPHY OF SPAIN, COLLECTED IN A SINGLE VOLUME

### 1

Era 649 [Note: [Col. 1253D] The Complutensian manuscript has 648.], year 57 of the Romans. Heraclius was crowned emperor and reigned for 30 years [Note: [Col. 1253D] Another reading: 29.], after 5838 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world [Note: [Col. 1253D] The Complutensian manuscript has 5838; another has 5828; but 5837 should be retained.].

Because of his love for Flavia, a most noble virgin who had been betrothed to him in Africa before he assumed power and who, by order of the ruler Phocas, had been transported from the regions of Libya to Constantinople, Heraclius plotted rebellion against Phocas together with Nicetas, master of the army. With a settled plan against the commonwealth, Heraclius, commanding the naval force, and Nicetas, the land army, agreed upon the following arrangement: whichever of them first reached Constantinople would duly be crowned on the spot and enjoy the empire.

But Heraclius, embarking from Africa with a naval force, reached the imperial city as quickly as possible by sea. Phocas offered him some resistance in battle, but the people of Byzantium captured him and struck him with a flaming sword. As soon as Heraclius saw him slaughtered, he was immediately raised to the imperial throne. Nicetas, meanwhile, penetrating the deserts, attacked Egypt, Syria, Arabia, Judaea, and Mesopotamia, vigorously pursuing the Persians and restoring the aforementioned provinces to imperial rule.

But the Persians, springing forth from their own settlements and trusting in their strength and numbers, once again stirred up and restored the neighboring provinces for themselves. The son of Chosroes, king of the Persians, fleeing his father in tumult [Note: [Col. 1253D] The manuscript of Mariana has “the opposing party.”], surrendered himself to the Roman ruler, promising to hand over the whole of Persia faithfully [Note: [Col. 1253D] The same manuscript: “truthfully”] to the aforementioned Augustus. Heraclius, however, gathering his army with all his iron-handed force, set out in pursuit of the Persians.

Then [Note: [Col. 1253D] The same manuscript: “Chosroes.”], informed of this report, Chosroes came out to resist him with the entire host of the Persians. Finally, when Heraclius and Chosroes [Col. 1253C] [Note: [Col. 1253D] The same manuscript reads “and Chosroes.”], both raging, joined battle in the same field, they agreed upon this arrangement: two warriors, chosen from the two armies, should engage in single combat, so that through them they might presage whatever they should discern concerning the outcome of the entire war from the result of that contest. Thus, under the open sky, they made this decision. They determined by their own judgment that whatever outcome Fortune should reveal through the swords of the two combatants, as we have said, would rebound upon their companions. In this way, they would be guided wholly by their auspices, so that the royal powers would immediately and without hesitation submit their necks to the victor’s yoke.

### 2

But Chosroes, proud in the manner of the Philistines [Note: [Col. 1253D] Berganza’s edition has *auctior*, “larger”; the Complutensian manuscript has *actior*, “more active.”], brought forth in battle a certain bastard as though he were another Goliath. All Heraclius’ warriors were terrified and withdrew their feet backward [Col. 1253D]. Then Heraclius, trusting in the Lord’s help, descended upon him and killed the enemy with a single spear. Breaking through the flight of the Persians, he continued striking his way as far as Susa, their chief and principal city.

At that point, with the kingdom of Chosroes destroyed and delivered into imperial rule, the people, honoring not God but Heraclius himself, and Heraclius accepting this honor with arrogance [Note: [Col. 1254D] The manuscript reads “proudly”; Sandoval’s edition reads “with the author’s approval.”], made his way back to Rome. Finally, after rewarding the army appropriately, he ascended the throne in glorious triumph.

Then, they say, many things concerning this matter came to him in a dream as a warning [Note: [Col. 1254D] The Complutensian manuscript reads: “many things happened to him.”], namely that he would be mercilessly ravaged by the mice of the desert and that he would be forewarned of this by an astrological sign through the course of the stars. This Heraclius, as we have said, subdued the rebellious Persians and restored the imperial provinces through warfare. But, deceived by the praises of the people and magnifying the honor of victory as belonging not to God but to himself, he repeatedly and gravely feared the severe warning foretold in a vision [Col. 1254B].

### 3

In his time, in era 653, the fourth year of his reign, the Slavs occupied Greece. In era 656, the seventh year of Heraclius’ reign, the Saracens claimed Syria, Arabia, and Mesopotamia—more by stealth than by courage—while Muhammad [Note: [Col. 1254D] The manuscript reads *Mahmet*; Sandoval has *Mammet*, “their leader.”], their leader, encouraged rebellion [Note: [Col. 1254D] The Complutensian manuscript reads “they took root.”]. They devastated the neighboring provinces not so much by public invasions as by secret incursions. In this way, through craft and deceit rather than courage, they stirred up all the cities adjacent to the empire; afterward, throwing off the yoke from their necks, they openly rebelled.

In era 656, the seventh year of Heraclius’ reign, they also invaded the kingdom, which they vigorously claimed through repeated battles and varying fortune [Col. 1254C]. Theodore, brother of Heraclius Augustus, fought against them in many battles. But remembering his brother’s warning about the prophesied mice, he withdrew from the battle in order to multiply and gather troops. As their slaughter increased day by day [Note: [Col. 1254D] The manuscript reads “as their fortune grew.”], fear so overwhelmed the Roman legions that, when a battle was joined near the town of Gabatha, the army was thoroughly defeated and Theodore was killed and passed from this world. Then the Saracens, firmly assured of the slaughter of so many Roman nobles, cast off their fear and mounted the throne of the kingdom at Damascus, the most splendid city of Syria.

### 4

When Muhammad’s tenth year had been completed, Abubacar, from his tribe, succeeded him on the throne, himself also undertaking considerable incursions into Roman and Persian territory [Col. 1254D]. Therefore, as we have already said, in era 653, the fourth year of Heraclius’ reign, the Arabs began to exercise tyranny. In era 656, after attacking Theodore, brother of Augustus, and wearying him in battles for nearly ten years, they finally defeated him in battle and overcame him as he resisted fiercely. Relying upon their prophet Muhammad, they openly established their kingdom at Damascus, having now thrown off their fear of the Roman name.

After Muhammad’s ten years of rule had been completed, in era 666, the seventeenth year of Heraclius’ reign, they substituted the aforementioned Abubacar, from the same tribe, in the place of his predecessor, and the Arabs struck with the sword at Persia, which had been abandoned under Roman rule [Note: [Col. 1255D] The Complutensian manuscript has 667.]. Thus, after waging war with power for nearly three years, they ruled.

### 5

In the time of this Heraclius, in era 669, the twentieth year of his reign, as the fourteenth Arab year began, Abubacar, at the end of his life, after three years had been completed, left Amer [Note: [Col. 1255D] Another manuscript: Omar.] on the throne [Col. 1255B]. Amer therefore assumed all the authority of his predecessor and remained harsh toward the people in the kingdom for ten years.

He subjected Alexandria, the most ancient and flourishing city, the metropolis of Egypt, to the yoke of tribute. When he was bringing back the triumph of victory from every region, both East and West, in land and naval warfare, he was struck with a sword by a certain slave while he was engaged in prayer. Thus, as we have said, he reached the end of his life after completing his tenth year.

### 6

In the time of this Heraclius, Sisebut, in era 650, the second year of the aforementioned emperor, while the Saracens still remained subject to Roman tribute, attempted to reconquer Iberia as a wise man and one greatly devoted to learning, for eight years. He subdued the Roman cities throughout Spain. He compelled the Jews by force to embrace the faith of Christ.

The Church proclaims the venerable Helladius, metropolitan bishop of the royal city of the see of Toledo, resplendent with the praise of holiness. Spain celebrates Isidore of Seville, metropolitan pontiff and illustrious teacher. In the seventh year of the aforementioned ruler Sisebut, Isidore held a council at Seville, in the secretary of the church of Holy Jerusalem, against the heresy of the Acephali, with great authority. Through the truthful testimony of learned men, he overcame a certain Syrian bishop of the Acephali who defended the aforementioned heresy; confirming the true decrees of the council, he condemned him by his eloquence and, by pursuing him for a long time, freed that bishop permanently from his former error.

### 7

When Reccared finally succeeded this Sisebut on the throne, he ruled for only three months. The brevity of his life records nothing worthy of note.

8. In the time of this Heraclius, Suintila, in the era 659, in the tenth year of his reign and the fourth of the Arabs, while Muhammad was ruling them, worthily assumed the reins and scepter of the kingdom of the Goths, reigning for ten years. He completed the war begun against the Romans and, by a swift victory, obtained dominion over all Hispania.

9. In the time of this Heraclius, Sisenand, in the era 669, in the twentieth year of Heraclius’s reign and the fourteenth of the Arabs, while Omar was ruling them, with the year nearly completed, invaded the Gothic kingdom through tyranny and was placed upon the royal throne for five years. In the third year of his reign, when sixty-six bishops of Toledo, Gaul, and Hispania had assembled, together with representatives of the absent bishops and the nobles of the palace, he celebrated a council in the church of Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr of Christ. This took place after Reccared, the former king of the Goths, while Isidore of Seville was still bishop and was already shining wonderfully in many books, concerning various matters.

Among the others, Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, attended this holy synod [Note: Thus M. and B.; *claruit* (“was distinguished”) in the others.], whose eloquence Rome, mother and mistress of cities, later admired greatly in the language of a letter.

10. In the time of this Heraclius, Chintila [Note: The copies have *Sinthila*.], in the era 674, in the twenty-fifth year of Heraclius’s reign and the eighteenth of the Arabs [Note: Thus B.; C. has “nineteenth.”], while Omar was ruling them, after the fifth year had been fully completed [Note: B. has “nearly completed.”] and the sixth had already begun, was placed over the Goths, reigning four years [Note: Thus the continuator of Biclar; Berg. has six.]. He held a council of twenty-four bishops at Toledo, where he illuminated ignorant minds by pouring into them much knowledge not only of worldly matters but also of divine things.

How great an assembly of holy men was gathered in the church of Saint Leocadia, virgin and martyr of Christ—composed of the representatives of the bishops sitting in council, and of the nobles of the palace who were deemed worthy to attend and who examined the council—the Book of Canons indicates. In this synod Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, excelled the other bishops and fittingly infused pious teaching into Christian minds; the Church still rereads his little works to this day.

[Col. 1256C] 11. In the time of this Heraclius, in the era 688, in the twenty-ninth year of his reign and the twenty-third of the Arabs, while Omar was ruling them in his tenth year, Tulga, of good character and Gothic stock, assumed the kingdom and ruled for two years.

12. In the era 679, in the fifty-eighth year of the Romans, Constantine, son of Heraclius, was crowned emperor. He reigned for six years, after 5,843 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world. In his time, in the era 680, in the first year of his reign and the twenty-fifth of the Arabs, Othman assumed the administration of his people and ruled for twelve years.

In the second year of his rule, extending his authority, he added Libya, Marmarica, and Pentapolis, as well as Gazania and Ethiopia, which lies above Egypt in the regions bordering the desert, to the rule and dominion of the Saracens. He made very many Persian cities tributary. Finally, he was killed in a revolt of his own people, having reigned twelve years.

13. In his time, in the era 680, in the first year of Constantine’s reign and the twenty-fifth of the Arabs, while Othman was ruling them in his second year, Chindasvinth, having invaded the Gothic kingdom through tyranny, ruled victoriously over Hispania [Note: B. has “ruled triumphally.”], and reigned for six years.

In the city of Toledo he summoned a synodal decree of thirty bishops to be celebrated in the fifth year of his reign, together with all the clergy, the representatives of those bishops whom illness or poverty prevented from being present, and the members of the palace who had earned the right to attend through their election by the body. Only the notaries required by proper procedure to read and record the proceedings were in attendance.

He sent Tajon, bishop of Zaragoza, sufficiently instructed in literary studies and a friend of the Scriptures, to Rome at his own request to obtain the remaining books of the *Moralia*. When the Roman pope kept postponing the matter from day to day, as though the book could not easily be found in the library of the Roman Church because of the multitude of books there, Tajon spent the night in prayer, imploring the Lord’s mercy at the feet of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. An angel showed him with his hand the chest in which the book was kept.

As soon as the pope realized that he had been reproved, he supplied Tajon with assistants, with the greatest reverence, for copying it, and sent it through him to the Spaniards for rereading. At that time they were attempting to recover from the books of blessed Job only the exposition that had been brought by Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, and formerly carried away with honor.

When Pope Rome questioned and adjured Bishop Tajon about how the location of those books had been shown to him so truly, after much entreaty he confessed this to him with great eagerness. One night he asked to be allowed to keep vigil among the doorkeepers of the church of blessed Peter the apostle. When permission had been obtained, at midnight, as he prostrated himself in prayer before the tomb of blessed Peter the apostle with many lamentations, a light sent from heaven shone forth. The entire church was illuminated by an indescribable radiance, so that not even the slightest gleam appeared from the church’s lamps. At the same time, together with that light, a host of saints entered, accompanied by the voices of those singing psalms and by lamps shining brightly.

Finally, when he had been terrified by overwhelming dread, and their prayer had been completed, two radiant old men from that company of saints gradually began to walk toward the place where the bishop was praying. When they found him almost dead, they greeted him gently and restored him to his senses.

They asked him why he was suffering such great exhaustion [Note: Thus B. and the Toledo manuscript; the others have *fastigium* (“summit,” “eminence”).] and why, coming from the West, he was seeking such a long sea voyage [Note: B. lacks *peteret* (“was seeking”). The others have *navigium* (“voyage”) instead of *navigerium*.]. He told them this and that, as though they were unaware of it, and they listened with interest. Then, after consoling him with many words, they showed him the place where the books lay hidden.

When he asked who that company of saints was who accompanied them with such brilliant light, they replied: “It is Peter, the apostle of Christ, and Paul with him, holding one another by the hand, together with all the successors of the Church who rest in that place.”

When he also asked who the lords were who were holding such a marvelous conversation with him, one of them replied that he was Gregory, whose book Tajon himself desired to see, and that he had therefore come to reward his immense toil and fulfill his very long desire [Note: B. has *adveneret* (“had come”); the Toledo manuscript has *advenire*, while the others use words in the singular, not the plural as in B.].

Then Tajon asked whether the learned Augustine was finally present in that holy multitude, since from his earliest infancy he had always been exceedingly eager to read Augustine’s books, just as he was those of Saint Gregory [Note: B. has *incunabilis*.]. It is reported that he answered only this: “That most illustrious man, Augustine, so welcome to the expectation of all, whom you seek, is held by a place higher than ours.”

As Tajon began to fall at their feet, that most holy man vanished from his eyes, together with the light, while the doorkeepers themselves were terrified. From that day onward, therefore, the venerable Tajon became glorious in the eyes of all at that apostolic see, whereas previously he had been despised as a weakling.

14. In the era 684, in the fifty-ninth year of the Romans, Constans, son of Constantine, was crowned emperor. He reigned for twenty-seven years, after 5,870 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world. He fought fiercely against the Arabs in a naval battle. Later, he was killed by a conspiracy at Syracuse, the renowned city of Sicily, after completing twenty-seven years of imperial rule. During his reign, when the sun was obscured at midday, the heavens revealed the stars.

15. In his time, in the era 686, in the thirtieth year of the Saracen kingdom, while Othman was ruling them in his seventh year [Note: Others have *Athuman* and *Athoman*.], Chindasvinth appointed his son Recesvinth, although disgraceful, yet well admonished [Note: B. has “moved by good advice”; M. has “yet of good character.”], to the Gothic kingdom. He reigned for twenty-four years.

He held frequent councils. While Eugenius, the pious metropolitan bishop of the royal city of Toledo, was distinguished, he splendidly gathered in one place, in the praetorian basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, forty-six bishops, an innumerable clergy, representatives of those who were absent, and the most distinguished body of palace officials. He instructed ignorant souls not only concerning worldly affairs but also concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity.

In his time an eclipse of the sun terrified Hispania, while everyone saw the stars at midday. He also witnessed an invasion of the Basques, at the cost of a considerable part of his army.

16. In his time, in the era 690, in the thirty-fifth year of the Arabs, Moabia inherited his predecessor’s seat and ruled there for twenty-five years. For five of those years he waged civil war with his own people; he spent the remaining twenty in complete prosperity, with all the people of Ishmael obedient to him.

Against him Constans Augustus assembled a thousand or more small ships and fought unsuccessfully. Fleeing with difficulty and barely escaping over the sea with a few companions, he got away. Through a commander named Abdallah, who had long held command in the conflict already described, many successful operations were also carried out in the West. He reached Tripoli, attacked Cidamus and Elemptis in battle, and, after causing many devastations, conquering various peoples, subduing extensive provinces, and receiving very many groups into the faith, he advanced into Africa with all the ranks of his warriors, still thirsting for blood.

When the battle had been prepared, the Moorish army was immediately put to flight, and all the glory of Africa, together with Count Gregory, was destroyed to the point of annihilation [Note: B. has *decoritas* (“splendor,” “glory”).]. Abdallah, laden with a rich reward, returned with all his cohorts and reached Egypt, while Moabia was completing the tenth year of his reign.

Moabia gave his son one hundred thousand men to serve him or to march against Constantinople. After they had blockaded it throughout the spring and could not endure the hardship of famine and pestilence, they abandoned the city, captured very many towns, and, laden with booty, returned safely to Damascus after two years to the king by whom they had been sent [Note: Thus the continuator of Biclar; others have “and” instead of “to.”].

Thus, after Moabia had completed twenty years of rule and the five years during which he lived through civil war, he paid the debt owed to human nature.

17. In the era 711, in the sixtieth year of the Romans, Constantine, son of Constans, was crowned emperor. He reigned fifteen years, after 5,885 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world. When he heard at Syracuse that his father had been killed in a revolt of his own people, he made for the Palace with whatever fleet he could gather and, triumphing, ascended the throne of glory.

18. In his time, in the era 716, in the fifth year of his reign and the sixty-first of the Arabs, Yzit, born to Moabia, obtained the position of ruler for three years. He was most pleasant throughout his reign and was held in the highest affection by all the nations subject to his homeland. He never sought glory for himself on account of his royal rank, as is customary among men, but lived civilly and on equal terms with everyone.

After completing three years, he left Moabia’s son as his successor, a man resembling his father in character. When he reached the height of royal power, he remitted a third of the tribute owed by everyone. After Moabia’s son had remained in the kingdom for half a year, he departed from this light.

19. In his time, in the era 716, at the beginning of the sixth year of his reign and in the sixty-second year of the Arabs, after the younger Moabia had died, the army of all the Arabs was divided between two rulers for almost four years. Such conflict remained between them that the sword devoured countless bands on both sides.

Then, for nine years, to the emperor by one of them, named Moroan [Note: Others have *Maroan*.], so that he might provide military assistance or not be hindered, there was paid for each day a sum of one thousand solidi in refined gold by weight, together with an Arabian mule and a silk-clothed saddle animal each day as a pledge of peace, so that he would not be obstructed. A beautiful cloak [Note: M. has *palla*; B. has *palla* in the margin but *polla* in the text; the continuator of Biclar has *puella*.] was also granted along with all the things mentioned above. Every captivity from former times was released, whatever had once been taken captive.

20. In his time, in the era 720, in the tenth year of his reign and the sixty-sixth of the Arabs, Abdamelic assumed the summit of royal power and reigned for twenty years.
