Pursuing his father’s rival at Mecca, he had him killed by a commander whom he had sent, at the house of Abraham, as they themselves assert, between Ur of the Chaldeans and Carrhae of Mesopotamia. In the wisest manner, he suppressed the civil wars by fighting.

24. In his time, in the era 712 [Note: Sand. has 721; B. has 712.], in the first year of his reign, the fifty-seventh of the Arabs, and the twenty-third of Moabia’s reign, Wamba was placed over the Goths and ruled for eight years.

In the third year of the era just mentioned, already contemplating the royal scepter, he renewed the city of Toledo with marvelous and elegant labor. In a sculptural work expressed in verse, he entitled it with these inscriptions, engraved in iron lettering upon polished, shining marble at the entrance of the gates:

> By God the Maker, the illustrious king Wamba  
> Raised this renowned city, extending the honor of his people.

On the memorials of the martyrs, which he inscribed above the same little towers of the gates, he likewise wrote:

> You holy servants of the Lord, whose presence shines here,  
> Guard this city and its people with your customary favor [Note: M. has “save.”].

22. In the fourth year of his reign, in the era 713, in the city of Toledo, in the atrium of the see of the blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Lord, he prepared a council of salvation in the secretarium, after eighteen years had passed amid disturbances and various disasters, like the bent woman in the Gospel. He synodically assembled all the bishops of Hispania and Gaul, with whom he also deeply lamented the times that had passed without councils [Note: B. has “without a council.”].

In this he received consolation together with such men, especially because the most holy Hildefonsus then shone forth, speaking eloquently in various books with a honey-sweet, golden mouth and treating the virginity of our Lady Mary, ever a virgin, in polished and refined language, flourishing throughout in orderly synonymy. Thus, as the anchor of faith remained fixed in his Church throughout his time, minds were truly refreshed by the little books he published and circulated through Iberia, as though by great councils of faithful readers, and the faint-hearted were greatly comforted at that time by the streams of his teaching.

23. In his time, in the era 718, in the seventh year of his reign and the sixty-second of the Arabs, when Abdallah and Moroan were beginning to fight on two sides for the kingdom, Ervigius of the Goths was consecrated to the kingdom and reigned for seven years.

During his time a severe famine devastated Hispania. In his first year, in the era 719, he splendidly convened the twelfth council of Toledo, consisting of thirty-five bishops, an immeasurable clergy, and a distinguished assembly of Christians.

During his time Julian, a bishop descended from Jewish stock, produced like a rose flower from among thorny briars, remained renowned in the teaching of Christ throughout all parts of the world. Although born of Christian parents, he was splendidly educated in every branch of wisdom at Toledo, where he was later honored with the episcopate.

[Col. 1260D] 24. In the era 726, in the sixty-first year of the Romans, Justinian was crowned emperor. Before his deposition he reigned ten years, after 5,895 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world. In his time, in the era 726, in the first year of his reign and the seventieth of the Arabs, Abdamelic had already been ruling for four years at the summit of power [Note: Thus B.; Sand. and M. have *Abdemelic*.].

25. In his time, in the era 726, in the first year of his reign and the seventieth of the Arabs, while Abdamelic was ruling in his fifth year, Egica first obtained supreme authority for the protection of the Gothic kingdom. He reigned for fifteen years.

He persecuted the Goths with a heap of deaths. Moreover, a plague of the groin fell mercilessly upon them during his time. In his first year, in the era 726, he celebrated a council at Toledo, in the praetorian church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, with all the bishops of Hispania and Gaul assembled, while Julian of blessed memory was distinguished as a teacher, together with nearly sixty bishops, a numerous body of Christians, the clergy, and all the common people fervently gathered around [Note: B. has “ordinary people.”].

In it he petitioned the synod, on various grounds and also for the absolution of the oath that he had wrongfully rendered to the aforementioned ruler Ervigius, that he might be released from it.

26. During his time, Julian, bishop of the royal city and its metropolitan, had earlier sent to Rome a book concerning the three substances. Because the Roman pope, treating it less carefully, had ordered that it be rejected—on the ground that one will had produced another will—Julian, at the demand of the aforementioned ruler, composed an apology in this council, confirming through authoritative testimonies of the elders that what he had sent to Rome was true; he had written the book two years previously.

He sent it again to Rome through his ecclesiastical legates—most learned men, a presbyter, a deacon, and a subdeacon [Note: C., M., and Sand. add: “servants of God in all things,” and so forth.]—who were instructed in the divine Scriptures in every respect and through all things. He also sent acclamatory verses, as he had previously sent them, praising the emperor.

Rome received it worthily and piously and ordered that it be read by all. With a great acclamation to the supreme emperor, it made this known:

> Your praise, O God, reaches the ends of the earth.

The Roman pope also honorably sent back a reply to Lord Julian through the aforementioned legates, with abundant thanksgiving, and declared that everything he had written was just and pious.

27. In the era 736, in the sixty-second year of the Romans, Leo was crowned emperor through tyranny. He reigned tumultuously for three years, after 5,898 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world. Having tumultuously deposed Justinian, he raised himself to the imperial power.

28. In his time, in the seven hundred thirty-sixth, thirty-seventh, and thirty-eighth eras, in the first, second, and third years of his reign, and in the seventy-ninth, eightieth, and eighty-first years of the Arabs, Abdamelic completed his thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth years of rule.

[Col. 1261D] 29. In his time, in the era 736, in the first year of Leo’s reign, the eightieth of the Arabs, and Abdamelic’s thirteenth year [Note: Others have sixteenth.], Egica, making his son Witiza his heir and partner in the kingdom, resumed rule of the Gothic kingdom.

When he succeeded his father on the throne, although he behaved recklessly, he nevertheless remained most merciful in the kingdom for fifteen years. He not only received back into favor those whom his father had condemned and held in exile, but also remained engaged in restoring their dependents [Note: M. and Sand. have the singular *clientulus*; D. Rodríguez has “as dependents.”].

For those whom his father had oppressed beneath a heavy yoke, he restored to their former joy; those whom his father had banished from their own soil, he piously [Note: B. has “with piety.”] restored through a grant. Finally, after summoning everyone, he burned in a fitting fire, before them all, the bonds that his father had deceitfully withheld [Note: Others have “under deceit.”].

He not only made the innocent free, if they wished, from an indissoluble bond, but, after restoring their possessions—already long assigned to the treasury—he also restored them to their position at court.

During the same period Felix, bishop of the royal city and see of Toledo, possessed extraordinary excellence in gravity and wisdom, and held very distinguished councils even then with both rulers.

30. In the era 838, in the sixty-third year of the Romans, Apsimarus was crowned emperor. He reigned for seven years, after 5,905 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world.

In his time, in the era 738, in the first year of his reign and the seventy-second of the Arabs, with the third year also begun, Abdamelic was ruling in his seventeenth year [Note: C. has fifteenth.]. Witiza, with his father already decrepit, ruled jointly with him.

In the era 739, unable to bear the destruction caused by the disaster just mentioned, they wandered throughout Hispania from the palace. For this reason, after his father had died a natural death, he most flourishingly resumed the kingdom for the years mentioned above, and all Hispania, relying upon great joy, rejoiced eagerly.

During the same period Gunderic, metropolitan bishop of the royal city and see of Toledo, was considered illustrious for the gift of holiness and was celebrated as the author of many miracles.

31. In the era 745, in the sixty-fourth year of the Romans, also called the sixty-first, Justinian, assisted by the wealth and strength of the Gazans, was restored to the empire. He reigned again for ten years, after 5,915 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world.

[Col. 1262C] 32. In his time, in the era stated above, in the first year of his reign and the eighty-ninth of the Arabs, Ulit resumed the kingdom among the Arabs. In Hispania, however, Witiza persevered in the kingdom in his fifteenth year.

33. In his time, in the era 748, in the third year of Justinian’s reign and the ninety-first of the Arabs, Ulit, having enlarged the kingdom, triumphed with many honors while holding the scepter of the Saracen kingdom. In accordance with what his father had set forth, he waged war against peoples for four years and reigned for nine.

He was a man of great prudence in deploying armies; although he lacked divine favor, he nevertheless broke the strength of almost all the nations nearest to him [Note: B. has “their strength.”]. He weakened Romania through constant devastation; he also brought the islands nearly to destruction; by ravaging the borders of India, he subdued them; he reduced cities to useless poverty; he afflicted castles by siege; and in the bends of Libya he subjected all Mauritania.

In the western regions also, he subdued through Muza, a commander of his army, the Gothic kingdom, which had been established with ancient solidity for nearly three hundred and fifty years from the era 400, from its own origin and beginning, and which in Hispania had been peacefully extended from Liuvigild for nearly one hundred and forty years, up to the era 750. Having taken away the kingdom, he made it tributary.

34. In his time, in the era 749, in the fourth year of his reign and the ninety-second of the Arabs, while Ulit was retaining the scepter of the kingdom for the fifth year, Ruderic, urged on by the senate, tumultuously seized the kingdom. He reigned for one year.

For when an army had been assembled against the Arabs, together with the Moors sent by Muza—namely Taric, Abuzara, and the others who had long been ravaging the province entrusted to them—and when they were simultaneously devastating many cities, he advanced to meet them in the era 750, in the fifth year of Justinian’s reign, the ninety-third of the Arabs, and the sixth of Ulit. In that battle, after the entire Gothic army had been put to flight—those who had come with him in rivalry and deceit because of their ambition for the kingdom—he fell.

Thus he lost both the kingdom and the homeland through the destruction of his rivals, while Ulit was completing his sixth year.

35. During the same period, Sinderedus, metropolitan bishop of the royal city, was distinguished for his devotion to holiness. In the Church entrusted to him, he found long-lived and deservedly honored men and goaded them with the zeal of holiness, though not according to knowledge; at the prompting of the aforementioned ruler Witiza, he did not cease to harass them during his reign.

Later, fearing the incursions of the Arabs, he approached the Roman homeland, abandoning the sheep of Christ, contrary to the decrees of the elders, not as a shepherd but as a hired man [Note: B. has “he approached the Roman homeland.”].

36. In his time, in the era 749, in the fourth year of his reign, the ninety-second of the Arabs, and the fifth of Ulit, while Hispania was being devastated by the aforementioned envoys [Note: Others have “by the aforementioned envoys,” with the words combined differently.], and while the people were engaging not only in excessive conflict with the enemy but also in internal fury, Muza himself, approaching that most wretched people, advanced through the Strait of Cádiz toward the Pillars of Hercules. As though the harbor entrances were indicated by a sign of smoke, or as though keys in his hand foretold or unlocked a passage into Hispania, he penetrated the land that had long been disastrously plundered and entirely impiously attacked.

Breaking in as far as Toledo, the royal city, he cruelly ravaged the neighboring regions under a deceitful peace. He slaughtered with the executioner’s sword certain noble elders who had somehow remained, after Oppa, son of King Egica, had fled from Toledo; and through Oppa’s agency he cut down everyone with the sword.

Thus he devastated not only Further Hispania but also Hither Hispania, as far as beyond Zaragoza, that most ancient and flourishing city, which had long since been manifestly opened to the judgment of God, with sword, famine, and captivity [*] [Note: The passages enclosed by asterisks are absent from Marca.].

He overthrew beautiful cities by burning them with fire; condemned the elders and powerful men of the age to the cross; slaughtered the young and nursing infants with daggers. While he goaded everyone with such terror, some of the remaining cities, already compelled, cried out for peace. By persuasion and mockery he deceived them through a certain stratagem, and without delay they granted what had been requested.

But when, after peace had been obtained, those terrified by fear rebelled and again fled to the mountains seeking refuge, they suffered from famine and various forms of death [*]. In that same unhappy Hispania, at Córdoba—formerly the seat of the patrician, always the wealthiest of the neighboring cities, and the source of the first delights of the kingdom of the Visigoths—they established a savage kingdom.

37. Who could tell of such dangers? Who could count such terrible shipwrecks? For even if all the limbs of the body were turned into tongues, human nature could absolutely never recount the ruins of Hispania or all its many and great evils.

But, so that I may briefly set down the scourges for the reader [Note: B. has “so that I may set down the scourges on a page”; the others have the reading given in the text.], leaving aside the countless disasters of the world from Adam until now, which the unclean enemy has cruelly inflicted upon the world through innumerable regions and cities [Note: Thus M. and B.; “which this world has inflicted” in the others], whatever captured Troy suffered according to the historical accounts, whatever the Jerusalem foretold in the prophetic utterances endured, whatever Babylon bore according to the words of Scripture, and finally whatever Rome, adorned by the renown of the apostles, accomplished through martyrdom—all of this, and so much more, Hispania, once delightful and now made wretched, experienced both in honor and in disgrace.

38. In the era 750, in the sixth year of his reign and the ninety-fourth of the Arabs, after fifteen months had elapsed, Muza, forewarned by order of the ruler, left his son Abdallaziz [Note: M. has *Abdelladiz*; C. has *Abdilazis*.] in his place. Taking selected elders of Hispania who had escaped the sword, together with gold and silver tested by the diligence of money-changers, and with a heap of distinguished ornaments, precious stones, pearls, and uniones—the things with which the ambition of matrons usually burns—and likewise with all the spoils of Hispania [Note: Thus M. and B.; the variants read *cuncta superficie*, *quod*; M. has *quae*.], too much to write down here.

Having assembled these things, he presented himself before King Ulit on his return to his homeland, in the final year of Ulit’s reign. By God’s will, he found the king angry, and on his return he was disgracefully expelled from the ruler’s presence, even to the neck, while displaying his pomp [Note: The abbot of Longuerue supplies what appears to be missing here, adding “But someone …”].

… named Theudimer, who had inflicted no small slaughter upon the Arabs in the regions of Hispania and, after being harassed for a long time, had concluded a treaty of peace with them.

Even under the Gothic kings Egica and Witiza he had triumphed in his own country in a victory over the Greeks who had come down by sea [Note: B. adds in italics, within parentheses, “in a troop”; M. and Mar. have “among the Greeks.”]. Much dignity and honor were therefore bestowed upon him. He was also sought out and praised by Eastern Christians, since such steadfastness in the true faith was found in him that all gave abundant thanks to God.

He was a lover of the Scriptures, marvelous in eloquence, and agile in battle. He was found wiser than the others even in the presence of the *Amir al-Mu’minin* [Note: Sand. and Mar. have *Amir Almuminin*.] and was honorably rewarded. The treaty that he had formerly received from Abdallaziz was firmly renewed by him.

Thus it remains established to this day, so that the Arabs’ successors may in no way dissolve so powerful a bond, and he returns joyfully to Hispania.

39. After his death, Athanaildus was held in great honor and esteem. He was in every respect a very wealthy lord and an extremely generous dispenser of money. But shortly afterward, when King Alhoozzam attacked Hispania, seized by I know not what frenzy, he inflicted no small injuries upon him and fined him twenty-seven thousand solidi.

When the army that had come with the commander Belgi heard this, within scarcely three days they prepared everything and quickly restored Alhoozzam, surnamed Abulchatar, to favor [Note: B. has “by favor of Abuliatar”;] and elevated him by rewarding him with various gifts.

40. The aforementioned Ulit, *Amir al-Mu’minin*—an expression in their language meaning “one who conducts everything prosperously”—saw the forces of all the nations, as well as the gifts of Hispania presented to him with the beauty of young women, and disregarded the great fame he saw before his eyes. He condemned Athanaildus to death, to be punished by tortures.

But when bishops and nobles, to whom he had offered many gifts from those overflowing riches, interceded for him, Ulit imposed a fine of one million one hundred thousand solidi. After reaching the end of his life, Ulit departed from this world.

Athanaildus, following the advice of the most noble man Urbanus, who had arisen in the African region under the doctrine of the Catholic faith and had come with him through all the regions of Hispania, eagerly desired to discharge it as though it were nothing and considered the burden imposed small in comparison with his great wealth.

Thus, by providing guarantors through his freedmen, he counted out the heap of coins with astonishing speed and paid the imposed sum [Note: Thus Sand. and B.; M. has “he gathers.”], and in the time of Ulit’s successor he assigned it to the treasury.

41. * [Note: The material enclosed by asterisks is absent from M. and Sand.] In his time, in the era 752, * in the eighth year of his reign and the ninety-sixth of the Arabs, after Ulit’s death, Zulema, his blood-brother, honorably succeeded him in the kingdom according to the arrangement made by his brother. He reigned for three years.

Hostile to Romania, he sent his half-brother Muzzilima, born of a different mother, with one hundred thousand armed men to destroy Romania. Muzzilima attacked Pergamum, the most ancient and flourishing city of Asia, and brought it to an end by sword and fire after it had been deceived by a stratagem [Note: B. has: “He brought Asia, attacked in war, to an end by sword and fire, after it had been deceived.” *Deceptam* is absent from C. The continuator of Biclar has the reading found in the text, which is certainly more correct; for it was not Asia but the aforementioned city of Pergamum that was destroyed.].

Then, hastening toward Constantinople, when Muzzilima saw himself endangered by various difficulties, he returned at the command of another ruler, though not very successfully.

42. During the same period, in the era 753, in the ninth year of his reign and the ninety-seventh of the Arabs, Abdallaziz pacified all Hispania under the yoke of tribute for three years. At Seville, joined in marriage to the queen of Hispania, he burned with desire for the king’s daughters and nobles’ daughters, whom he had made his concubines and imprudently distributed.

A revolt of his own people took place. While he was intent upon prayer, he was killed on the advice of Ajub. After he had held Hispania for a month, Alahor succeeded him in the kingdom of the West by the ruler’s command. The death of Abdallaziz was announced to him in such a way that it appeared as though he had attempted, on the advice of Egilo, the royal wife of the former King Ruderic whom he had taken as his consort, to turn the Arab yoke away from his neck [Note: M. and Sand. have “to overturn”;] and to resume for himself the kingdom seized in Iberia.

43. In the era 754, in the sixty-fourth year of the Romans, Philippicus was crowned emperor. He reigned civilly for a quarter of a year and one additional year, after 5,916 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world.

In his time, in the era mentioned above, in Philippicus’s first year and the ninety-eighth of the Arabs, Zulema, having resumed the Saracen kingdom, reigned for three years. The Arabs fiercely ravaged Romania. They burned Pergamum, the most ancient and flourishing city of Asia, in a retaliatory fire [Note: See section 41.].

During his time Alahor sent bands of judges throughout Hispania. By waging war and making peace, he advanced into Narbonese Gaul for nearly three years. Gradually arranging Further Hispania by assessing tribute, he raised himself toward Hither Iberia [Note: Thus Mar. and Sand.; B. has “he bent himself toward Hither Iberia.”], reigning for the years stated above.

### 44

In the era 756, the sixty-fifth year of the Romans, Anastasius was crowned emperor and reigned civilly for three-quarters of a year, the years from the beginning of the world totaling 5,918. During his time, Zulemam, holding the Arab kingdom, adopted as successors to the kingdom his paternal uncle’s son, named Omar, or his brother Izit. In Spain, however, the aforementioned Alahor, while besieging the patrician city of Córdoba, attempted anew to organize the Saracen kingdom [Note: [Col. 1266D] M. reads *patriam* (“the homeland”) instead of *patriciam*. Mar. B. lacks *regnum* (“kingdom”) and reads *obsidione* (“by siege”) in place of *obseditans* (“besieging”); M. reads *praesidio* (“by garrison”).], and restored to the Christians the property that had been taken from them [Note: [Col. 1266D] So B.; others read *resculas* (“little belongings”); M. reads *resiulas*.] for the payment of tribute into the public treasury. He imposed penalties upon the Moors who had long been traveling through Spain for the treasures they had concealed; bound in sackcloth and ashes, swarming with worms or lice [Note: [Col. 1266D] B. reads *pedunculis*.], and weighed down with imprisonment and chains, he recovered them; and by interrogation or by inflicting various punishments, he scourged them.

### 45

At the same time, in the opening of the era 757, the hundredth year of the Arabs, an eclipse of the sun occurred in Spain from the seventh hour of the day until the ninth; some people discerned that stars were visible. Most, however, maintain that this phenomenon appeared only in the time of Zama’s successor [Col. 1266D].

### 46

In the era 757, the sixty-sixth year of the Romans, Arthemius, also called Theodosius, was crowned emperor and reigned for two years, the years from the beginning of the world totaling 5,920. During his time, Omar, because of the sanctity of his law, associated his brother Izit with himself as guardian and governor of the kingdom [Col. 1267A] [Note: [Col. 1267D] M. reads: “During his time, because of the sanctity of his law, Omar associated his brother Iziz with himself in the government of the kingdom.” D. Rodriguez reads: “when he appointed him as guardian of the kingdom.”]. Omar, while every war was at rest, was of such great kindness and patience in the kingdom that even now such honor and praise are attributed to him that he is blessed above all former rulers, not only by his own people but also by outsiders. Such holiness is ascribed to him as has never been attributed to anyone from the Arab race. But his tenure of the kingdom was not prolonged for long [Note: [Col. 1267D] So M. and B.; “he fully received the government… He was exercising guardianship over his own people’s army among the Persians, and was plotting rebellion.”].

### 47

Accordingly, when Izit had fully received the government of the Saracen kingdom by succession after his brother’s death, the armies of his own people, which were exercising guardianship among the Persians, plotted rebellion and prepared civil war. Thus he sent his brother, mentioned above, named Muzilima, with an immense army. When battle had been joined in the Babylonian fields above the river Tigris, the battle line [Col. 1267B] of the tyrants immediately dissolved in an astonishing flight; and they captured Izit, the leader of the crime, but spared his life after granting him pardon.

### 48

At that time many successes came to him through fighting in the regions of the West. Through a commander named Zama, who held the command in Spain for a little less than three years, he described both farther and nearer Iberia in his own register for the payment of tribute. The estates [Note: [Col. 1268D] So B. and M.; *praedam* (“plunder”) in another reading.] and movable goods—or whatever it was that the entire Arab people in Spain had formerly recovered as undivided booty—he distributed by lot among their associates, leaving one portion to be divided among the soldiers, while he assigned a portion of every movable and immovable possession to the treasury.

Finally, he made Narbonese Gaul his own, harassed the Frankish people with repeated wars, and suitably stationed selected Saracen soldiers [Col. 1267C] in the aforementioned town of Narbonne to maintain its defenses. The aforementioned commander, advancing through the valor of his forces, reached Toulouse by fighting; he surrounded it with a siege and attempted to storm it with slings and various kinds of engines. When the Frankish peoples became certain of this news, they gathered under the commander of that people, named Eudo. There, while the battle lines of both armies clashed in a severe engagement near Toulouse, they killed Zama, commander of the Saracen army, together with part of the assembled multitude. They pursued the remaining army, which escaped by flight. Abderraman assumed their leadership for one month, until Ambiza [Note: [Col. 1268D] Another reading: Umbiza.], their governor, arrived in accordance with the supreme commands.

### 49

At the same time, Fredoarius, bishop of the see of Acci; Urbanus, a veteran and melodious teacher of the royal cathedral city of the see of Toledo; and Evantius, archdeacon of that same see, were regarded as outstanding in learning, wisdom, holiness, and in every form of hope, faith, and charity according to the Scriptures, for the strengthening of the Church of God [Col. 1267D].

### 50

In the era 758, the sixty-seventh year of the Romans, Leo was crowned emperor and reigned for twenty-four years, the years from the beginning of the world totaling 5,944 [Col. 1268A]. This Leo was experienced in military discipline. The Saracens under Omar, who had designated the kingdom for his brother, lived in quiet for a short time and achieved no success; under Izit, however, they fought many battles. When, shortly afterward, they were hastening under their king Hiscam to capture the imperial city, Leo, as we have said, received the scepter of the empire by acclamation of the entire senate.

### 51

During his time, Izit, king of the Saracens, held the original government of the kingdom in the aforementioned era. For such a rule is perpetually maintained among the Arabs: royal names are received from the ruler only through the entire succession of kings by right of precedence, so that when one ruler dies, they may approach the government without disturbance [Col. 1268B].

### 52

At the same time, in the era 759, the second year of Leo’s reign, the 103rd year of the Arabs, Ambiza recovered the government of Spain suitably for six months together with four years. He fought unsuccessfully against the Frankish people, both by planning battles himself and by pursuing them through appointed satraps [Note: [Col. 1268D] B. reads “against the peoples.”]. Through secret incursions, however, he harassed certain cities or fortresses, mutilating them by means of the wedges of his troops. Thus, by exacting doubled tribute from the Christians, he triumphed greatly in the offices of honor throughout Spain [Col. 1268B].

### 53

[The passage enclosed in brackets is absent from the printed edition. It is found in the Complutensian manuscript and, as D. Marca reports, in a Paris manuscript.]

During his time also, the Jews were tested, just as they had been in the time of Theodosius the Younger. They were seduced by a certain Jew who, receiving his name by antiphrasis, was called Serenus. He attacked them with a clouded error, proclaiming himself to be the Messiah and declaring that he would fly with them to the promised land. He ordered them to give up everything they possessed [Col. 1268C], and, having done so, they remained destitute and empty-handed. But when this reached Ambiza, he assigned to the treasury everything they had lost. He summoned Serenus to himself and asked the man, if he was the Messiah, what he intended to do concerning the things of God.]

When the aforementioned Ambiza finally renewed his expedition against the Franks, he immediately planned an incursion against them with the entire public army. But while he was rushing forward in his fury, he prepared the end of his life by his own death. He appointed Hodera, the governor of the province entrusted to him or the commander of the returning army—almost as though he were restraining it—while he lay at the point of death.

### 54

His successor immediately followed him in the era 763, almost the sixth year of the aforementioned emperor, the 107th year of the Arabs. A Saracen named Iahia, appointed at the instruction of the leaders, raged as a terrible and cruel ruler for nearly three years. With a sharp mind, he harassed the Saracens and Moors of Spain over property formerly taken in peaceful transactions and restored much to the Christians [Col. 1268D].

### 55

During his time, after completing his fourth year, Izit departed this life, leaving the kingdom to his brother Hiscam and appointing as his successor Alulit, born of his own seed after his brother. At the beginning of his authority, in the era 761, almost the fifth year of the reign of the aforementioned Leo, the 106th year of the Arabs, Hiscam, showing himself sufficiently moderate, accomplished some successes through commanders sent by him on land and sea in Roman territory [Col. 1269A]. [The words enclosed in brackets are absent from B.] In the western regions he accomplished almost nothing notable.

Then he was seized by greed, and such a collection of money was made through commanders whom he sent to the East and West [Note: [Col. 1269D] B. reads: “sent to him from the East and West.”] that no king who had preceded him had ever amassed an equal amount [Note: [Col. 1269D] So M., B., and Sand.; another reading has “collected for the kings.”]. Therefore, when considerable bands of peoples perceived that shameless greed remained in him, they divided their allegiance from his rule. After an extensive civil slaughter lasting nearly three and four years, he scarcely restored the lost provinces to his own authority [Col. 1269A].

### 56

During his time, in the era 766, the tenth year of his reign, the 111th year of the Arabs, the sixth of Hiscam, Oddifa, a man full of frivolity, received authority from the African commander, who always rejoices that the power over Spain has been assigned to him by lot at the ruler’s command. For six months he held the government without any serious burden, but, because the kingdom was so small, he initiated nothing worthy or adverse [Col. 1269B].

### 57

At the same time, in the era 767, the eleventh year of the same emperor, the 112th year of the Arabs, and the seventh of Hiscam, Antuman secretly hastened from the African regions [Note: [Col. 1269D] So M., who continues: “After him, Hiscam, as usual, while sustaining another in office for four months, invests with honors a man named Aleatan. He vigorously displays the seal, etc., for governing Spain.” After the words “secretly hastened,” B. reads: “who, while sustaining another for four months, invests Aleitan with honors, vigorously displaying the seal, etc., for governing Spain.” In place of “after him Hiscam,” D. Rodriguez, chapter 12 of *History of the Arabs*, reads “another named Alhaytam.”]. He governed Spain for five months; after that he ended his life, and another named Autuman was sent. He ruled the land for four months; after him Hiscam appointed another, named Alhaytam [Col. 1269C].

This man openly displayed the seal or principal authority sent from the aforementioned regions for governing Spain vigorously. While he ruled turbulently for ten months, by some stratagem he immediately investigated whether certain Arabs wished to deprive him of the kingdom. He therefore arrested them and for some time extorted various pretexts for rebellion from them by scourging; and, inflicting punishments as he had secretly been ordered by rivals overseas, he finally beheaded them. Among them was Zat, a Saracen by race [Note: [Col. 1269D] M. reads “of the Saracens”;], eloquent, distinguished, and an extremely wealthy lord of many things. Having tortured him under punishment, mocked him with lashes, and struck him with blows, he cut him down with a sword.

Not many days later, at the request of the people whose blood he had shed, a Saracen named Mammet was sent from the regions of Libya by command, bearing a report of concealed authority, so that Abderraman might remain in his place without delay. But when Mammet reached the seat at Córdoba, and the turbulent Abderraman had not yet been found [Note: [Col. 1270D] So M. and B.; another reading has “immediately, since he had not yet been found.”], Alhaytam was at once sternly arrested by Mammet. Since he would not leave him unpunished in prison, they flogged him severely without delay, condemned him disgracefully, shaved his head, and dragged him through the streets seated backward on a braying donkey, his face toward its rear, with his hands bound behind his back or fastened in iron chains. After not many days, they sent him under guard to be presented to the African commander [Note: [Col. 1270D] B. adds “him”], who, as they say, had secretly arranged this journey and had been warned to receive Alhaytam.

Finally, while the royal court awaited what would happen to him, the written account became entangled in many speeches and was attacked by various judgments [Note: [Col. 1270D] So B. and M.; another reading has: “The written account was entangled by many people speaking vainly and was attacked by various judgments. But since they inflicted nothing upon him…” B. has “though they inflicted nothing.”]. But since they inflicted nothing upon him, he gradually vanished from day to day and disappeared over a long period [Col. 1270B]. And because Mammet was arriving from the African regions, Alarcila had been installed in his place for one full month [Note: [Col. 1270D] M. reads: “Meanwhile, because he was from the Africans…”].

### 58

Abderraman, a warlike man, came joyfully to power in the era 769, the twelfth and a half year of the same emperor, the 113th year of the Arabs, and the ninth of Hiscam; for three years he was greatly preferred by everyone. Since he was endowed with excessive courage and glory, one of the Moorish people, named Munniz [Note: [Col. 1270D] So B.; others read Muzuu.], hearing that his own people were being oppressed with savage recklessness throughout the Libyan territories, made peace with the Franks and immediately prepared tyranny against the Saracens of Spain. Because he was highly skilled in battle, everyone who learned this divided [Note: [Col. 1270D] So M. and B.: “when everyone recognized this, the palace…” Only M. adds “they divided.”] and the condition of the palace was thrown into confusion.

But not many days later, Abderraman, disturbed while preparing a military expedition, pitilessly pursued the rebel. When he was found surrounded in the town of Cerritano, crushed by a siege and shut up within its walls for some time, he suddenly sprang into flight by God’s judgment and yielded, deprived of office. Since he had been excessively glutted with the blood of Christians, which he had innocently shed there, and since he had been greatly exhausted by burning with fire Anabadius, an illustrious bishop, and a noble youth of handsome appearance [Note: [Col. 1270D] So M. and B.; Sand. reads “he burned the beautiful and tall one.”], and had already been sufficiently condemned for this reason, he was overtaken by thirst in a city formerly abundant with flowing waters. When he could find nowhere to flee, he escaped through various winding places while the pursuing army followed him, soon to die.

And because the Frankish commander named Eudo had long before handed over his daughter to him in marriage, so that she might be joined to him as a pledge of alliance and inclined to his desires, postponing her release from the hands of her pursuers, he prepared his soul, which was destined for death [Note: [Col. 1271D] B. reads “his mind, destined for death.”]. Thus, while the public army pursued him, already wounded, he threw himself from a high pinnacle into the clefts of the rocks, mocking them; and, so that he would not be captured alive, he breathed out his life. As soon as they found him lying there, they cut off his head and presented it to the king together with the daughter of the aforementioned Eudo. The king transported her across the sea and arranged for her to be honorably sent to a mighty ruler [Col. 1271A].

### 59

Then Abderraman, seeing the land filled with his army, cut across the mountains of the Vaccaei and trampled the rough and level country alike [Note: [Col. 1271D] B. reads “and the level country.”]. He ravaged the lands of the Franks within and struck them so deeply with the sword by penetrating them that, when Eudo had prepared for battle beyond the rivers called the Garonne or Dornomia and had been scattered in flight, only God could know the number of those who died or perished [Col. 1271B].

Then the aforementioned Abderraman pursued Duke Eudo. While he desired to plunder the Church of Tours by destroying palaces and burning churches, he confronted Charles, commander of inner France, called Austrasia, a man warlike from his earliest youth and experienced in military affairs, after Eudo had warned him.

There, while both sides tormented one another for nearly seven days over the outcome of the battle, they finally prepared themselves for the line of combat. While they fought fiercely, the northern peoples remained immovable in an instant, like a wall, and, just as a belt remains bound by icy cold, they slew the Arabs with the sword. But when the Austrasian people, powerful in the mass of their bodies and striking vigorously with iron hands through the difficult ground [Col. 1271C], found the king, they killed him.

When night separated the battle, they raised their swords contemptuously. On the following day, seeing the innumerable Arab camps, they held themselves ready for battle. At dawn they looked upon the Arabs’ ordered tents and the pavilions where the standards had been set, not knowing that everything was empty and thinking that the Saracen phalanxes were prepared for battle within. They sent scouts, and found all the Ismaelite forces put to flight; all their wedges had silently withdrawn during the night and returned home [Note: [Col. 1271D] So M. and B.; another reading has “and they all withdrew in a compact wedge.”].

The Europeans, however, anxious lest the Arabs, lurking along the paths, should make some deceptive attack from concealment, were astonished on every side and searched the surrounding area in vain. Since they did not keep watch in any way against the pursuing peoples mentioned above, they divided the spoils and booty appropriately and happily returned to their own homelands.

### 60

Then, in the era 772, the fourteenth year of the same emperor, the 116th year of the Arabs, and the twelfth of Hiscam, Abdilmelic [Note: [Col. 1271D] B. reads Abdelmelic; Sand. reads Abdilmelec.] was sent from a noble family to govern Spain in accordance with the supreme commands.

When he found Spain, after so many and such great battles [Note: [Col. 1271D] B. reads “dangers.”], rich in every good thing, and filled with such flourishing prosperity after so many sufferings [Col. 1272A] that one might have said it was an imperial pomegranate, he inflicted such recklessness upon it for nearly four years that, gradually weakened by various intrigues, it remained dried up [Note: [Col. 1271D] M. and Sand. read “by various turnings … carried out.”]. His judges, seized by greed, imposed such a stain upon it through their flattery that from that time it not only appeared to decline as though dead, but also remained completely deprived of all its best things, utterly desolated and unable to recover hope [Note: [Col. 1272D] B. reads “for recovering hope.”].

For this reason, when the aforementioned Abdilmelic was warned by the supreme command that nothing prosperous was happening in the land of the Franks, he immediately leapt from Córdoba with the entire public army and attempted to overthrow the inhabitants of the Pyrenean ridges. Directing the expedition through narrow places, he accomplished nothing favorable. Convinced of the power of God, by whom the Christians—finally only a very few—held the mountain peaks and awaited mercy, he attempted the remote places on either side with a strong force, lost many of his warriors, and returned to the plains, making his way home through the wilderness [Col. 1272B].

### 61

Soon afterward, in the era 775, the seventeenth year of the Emperor Leo, the 119th year of the Arabs, and the fifteenth of Hiscam, a successor named Aucupa came to him. While all Spain trembled before his lofty power, lineage, and observance of his law, he bound his predecessor in chains and severely condemned the judges appointed by him.

Certainly, while he exaggerated the ceremonies of his law, he ordered a census of the people and energetically pursued the collection of tribute. He sent the wicked of Spain, or those entangled in various vices, across the sea on vessels. He enriched the treasury very readily from various sources; he remained abstinent from every secret gift [Note: [Col. 1272D] B. reads “concealment.”]; and he condemned no one except according to the justice of his own law.

He attempted an expedition against the Franks with a large army. Then, advancing toward the city of Zaragoza, he withdrew suitably with an immense fleet. But when he suddenly read letters sent from Africa reporting the rebellion of the Moors, he returned to Córdoba without delay with all possible speed and withdrew through the intervening promontories [Note: [Col. 1272D] Sand. reads “crossed promontories.”].

Sending Arabs without result against the Moorish fortifications, he crossed the sea in ships that had arrived in expectation. If he found among them opponents, double-dealers, or evil plotters, and heretics—whom they call augurs [Note: [Col. 1272D] So M. and Sand.; B. reads *asures*; C. reads *arueres*]—he slaughtered them with the sword [Col. 1272D].

Thus, arranging everything most carefully and keeping vigilant watch over the Tinacrian harbors [Note: [Col. 1272D] Sand. reads *trimacrios*; B. reads *Tinacrios*; M. reads *patrios*.], he mercifully restored himself to his own seat. After a short time, when the five-year period had been completed, he restored the kingdom to the aforementioned Abdilmelic; then, seized by illness, he died from the world when his disease returned to his vital organs.

### 62

At the same time, the learned men Urbanus and Evantius, sufficiently distinguished by their devotion to holiness, happily went to the Lord and rested in peace.

### 63

Abdilmelic, with everyone’s consent, was chosen as king of the Arabs in the era 780, the twenty-second year of Leo’s reign, the 124th year of the Arabs, and the twentieth of Hiscam [Col. 1273A].

[The words enclosed in brackets are found in M. and absent from the other manuscripts.] Accordingly, Hiscam, overcome by an evil deception and having loosened the reins of greed without limit, began to rage against his own people more than usual. Therefore all the peoples subject to his authority immediately rose in civil war. For the entire vast wilderness from which the Arab multitude itself arises, unable to endure the impiety of the judges, threw everything into confusion through treachery. The western region, to which the Moors are more devoted than to any other, and the region that rises toward the southern zone, all acting with one purpose, openly shook their necks free from the Arab yoke.

But when the multitude of the tyrants’ forces came to Hiscam’s hearing, he immediately supplied the African commander with a strong auxiliary force of one hundred thousand chosen soldiers. He appointed his brother Cultum commander in war over the army of the East and West [Col. 1273B; Note: B. reads: “and Zultan over the army of the East and West.”]. Once the army had been organized and counted by troops and phalanxes, they received him on African soil. Thus they decided on their own plan to proceed, ravaging the lands of the Moors and striking them with the sword, all the way to the Tangier Sea.

When the Moorish multitude recognized this, they immediately sprang from the mountainous places into battle naked, girded only with aprons before their private parts. When the brother had reached the river Maphanus, the two sides fought fiercely. The Moors displayed a dreadful color against their beautiful horses and frightened the enemy by gnashing their white teeth; consequently the Egyptian cavalry immediately recoiled in flight.

But when the Moors pressed their attack further in desperation, the Arab and Egyptian horsemen again scattered without delay because of the color of their skin, and in fear turned their backs [Col. 1273C], bringing destruction upon themselves and their mounts. While they ran across rough seas and trackless places without any restraint or restoration of their strength, that multitude perished throughout the vast desert. Thus the entire assembled force of the East and West, scattered by flight, wasted away without any remedy.

The commander of that army, named Cultum [Note: [Col. 1273D] B. reads Zultan.], was slaughtered while his companions were crushed [Note: [Col. 1273D] B. reads “terrified.”], and the whole host, against its will, was divided into three companies. One part was held by the sword or by the hands of the victors; another, wandering along the road by which it had come and attempting to return home, was slaughtered [Note: [Col. 1273D] So M.; B. reads “was prevented from returning home.”]; the third, driven into madness, hastened off somewhere unknown.

His brother Belgi, presenting himself as their commander, a man distinguished by birth and experienced in military arms [Col. 1273D], arrived—alas, how dreadful!—in Spain.

### 64

At that time, as we said above, in the era 780, the twenty-second year of the reign of Leo, and the twentieth of Hiscam, Abdilmelic ruled the Spaniards. When he learned that Belgi had arrived at the port with the aforementioned third part, he obstructed their crossing by preparing ships [Note: [Col. 1273D] B. reads “denied them the crossing.”].

But when the Moors of Spain learned that this had happened, they gathered for battle and wished, after overthrowing Abdilmelic and taking possession of his kingdom, to provide their overseas companions with a maritime crossing [Col. 1274A]. Dividing themselves into three companies, they sent one to strike the wall of the very strong city of Toledo; they directed another to Córdoba, to the seat of Abdilmelic, to slaughter him [Note: [Col. 1274D] Pellicer, *Annals*, p. 101, reads “they directed the sword toward Córdoba.”]; and they extended a third to the port of Septa [Note: [Col. 1274D] So manuscripts C. and M. and Sand.; B. reads “Septima.”] to slaughter those who had escaped from the battle mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1274D] B. reads “to keep watch over them.”].

But Abdilmelic sent the arms of both forces against them. Through his son Hemely [Note: [Col. 1274D] So B.; M. reads Humeiam; Sand. reads Humoia.], he cut down one company with the sword after it had prolonged its siege of Toledo for twenty-seven days, twelve miles from the city. Through the Arab Almuzaor, he struck back another, though at the cost of his own destruction and that of his army, and turned aside to another region. The third company, which had advanced to the city of Messula to seize those who were in charge of the transport fleet, he cut down with ships prepared, through Belgi, to whom he had earlier denied passage.

### 65

Then Abdilmelic, once the others had been terrified, withdrew to his own place. Through a letter of address he urged Belgi to return to his former island. But Belgi, anxiously and deceitfully remembering the great injuries of hunger that he had at last inflicted upon him, renewed the battles through Abderraman. He resisted the obstacles for a long time, entered Córdoba, and found Abdilmelic abandoned by his sons or by the public army, tortured with reed stakes, and grievously mangled throughout his body by the shaking of death. Finally, he killed him with the sword.

A very large army was assembled among the Easterners with the commander Belgi and among the Westerners with his son Humeya. The aforementioned era having been completed, in the stated year of the reign of Leo, the prescribed Arab year, and the already noted year of Hiscam, Amir al-Mu’minin, such battles were fought by both sides as the human tongue can scarcely narrate. But since all Spain is by no means ignorant of them, this history decided not to recount those tragic wars [Note: [Col. 1274D] So M.; B. reads “slaughtering wars.”], because in another *Epitome* it has already been plainly and fully written in our style how everything happened.

### 66

During his time, in the era 771, the twenty-third year of Leo’s reign, and the 125th year of the Arabs, the handsome Amir al-Mu’minin Alulit was elevated to the throne by everyone in the proper place. After Iziz had immediately been deprived of the kingdom, Alulit remained in power for a year and three-quarters. Then all Spain was thrown into confusion by internal fury [Col. 1274D].

### 67

In the era 782, after the completion of the twenty-fourth year of Leo’s reign, Alulit having first [reigned], Albucatur was sent in accordance with the supreme commands and quieted all the disturbances mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1274D] C. reads “by the supreme command.”].

Then Abulcatar, named Alhozan [Note: [Col. 1274D] So manuscripts C. and M. and the edition of Sand.; B. reads Alulit.], carefully took charge of the country entrusted to him. Without delay he sent an army from the overseas regions into Africa under the pretext of battle, to subdue the proud men of Spain. Because the entire East remained deceived, they rose into unheard-of battles when they heard that Alulit had been killed.

And immediately.

### 68

In the era 782, after the completion of the twenty-fourth year of Leo’s reign, the 120th year of the Arabs, at the beginning of the sixth [year], and with Iziz and Alulit having remained in the kingdom for almost a year, while Abulcatar ruled turbulently, everyone began to consider how to overthrow him from the kingdom.

Through Zumahel [Note: [Col. 1275D] So manuscript B.; M. reads Zunahel; D. Rodriguez reads Zimael.], a man girded with the authority of his people, they collectively plotted to draw him, the tyrant, into battle from the city of Córdoba, then the royal seat. Finally, when they immediately secured this through various contrivances, Zumahel, after the plan had been fixed, pretended to prepare a flight.

Then Abulcatar, with the palace army, pursued him headlong without any intervening delay. Since many of those who pursued the rebel with him were of one mind with the enemy, they hastened joyfully with the aforementioned king toward the ambush that had been arranged. Soon, when they joined battle, they fought with avenging swords. Some of the king’s companions withdrew from the battle, and immediately they overcame him when he was alone. Thus, after his own men had been killed, they pursued him as he fled together with the three who had joined him [Col. 1275B].

### 69

[The words enclosed in brackets are absent from B., M., and Sand.; they are found in C.]

During his time, the most holy man Cixila, who had persisted in God’s service from his very cradle, remained in the see of Toledo. Since the aforementioned Church had existed from the entry of the Arabs, he was ordained metropolitan. He was learned in holiness, a restorer of churches, and, in the corrupt printed reading *scptu* (sic), most steadfast in hope, faith, and charity; may his merits become known to all.

One day, a man deceived by the Sabellian heresy wished to approach before him [Col. 1275C] [Probably *coram* (“in his presence”)]. He was questioned by him as to why he was a member of such a crime, but he denied such wickedness. Immediately he was seized by a demon in such a way that the whole assembly of the church fell back in amazement. Thus, when the holy man devoted himself to prayer, he restored him to the holy Church sound and unharmed.

He also served as apostolic representative for nine years in that charity which he embraced, and he brought his life to its end.

### 70

Then they elevated Toaba, who had provided strong assistance to Zimael, to the throne of the kingdom. He concealed himself among his own people in order to restore the conflicts. Later, disastrously provoking various battles with the destruction of himself and his people, he lost himself and the multitude that agreed with him by a dreadful death.

Whoever wishes to know the events of this affair should read the individual episodes in the *Epitome of Times* that we compiled some time ago; there he will find everything explained. There too he will find written all the battles of the Moors who fought against Cultum [Note: [Col. 1275D] So M., Sand., and D. Rodriguez; B. reads Zultam. D. Nicholas Antonio, book VI, no. 66, reads “against the cult”—that is, the Christian cult—through an obvious error, for Culto is the proper name of a Muslim man.] and will find the wars threatening Spain at that time recorded.

### 71

After the completion of the era 782, and with the third [era] already beginning, the sixty-eighth year of the Romans, Constantine, the son of Leo, was crowned emperor after his father and reigned for thirty-five years [Note: [Col. 1275D] So M. The words “reigned for thirty-five years” are absent from B.; the text of that edition reads: “was crowned, with TOT years completed, etc.” It should be read: “reigning for … years,” with the number of years not expressed. By *tot*, the author indicates that it was left to others to supply the numerical notation; for when he wrote “in the tenth year of Constantine’s reign,” he entirely did not know how many years Constantine would still live.], the years from the beginning of the world up to the tenth year of Constantine totaling 5,954 [Col. 1276A].

### 72

Having been crowned with his father’s empire, the father soon closed the final day of his life. The son learned that his own empire had been seized from him by Ardabastus, who was related to him. But when Ardabastus quietly and gradually departed as a warrior to other peoples on the pretext of war, Constantine associated with himself all the palace followers and warriors. As soon as he saw Ardabastus abandoned and the entire senate empty, he hastened with the companions whom he had gathered to himself and terrified Constantine from the palace, intending to slaughter him.

When Constantine learned that Ardabastus was coming with a turbulent band of armed men, he sprang from the seat with his own supporters and sought the assistance of neighboring peoples. Finally, when he saw himself surrounded by a multitude, he hastened to seek his former seat and warned Ardabastus to leave the palace. But Ardabastus instructed the people not to open the city gates to those who were hastening.

When Constantine found the town strongly fortified, he established a very firm war, extending a siege with the forces of many surrounding peoples. After nearly three years he had worn down the city’s people with hunger. Peace was made with the citizens through intermediaries, and they presented Ardabastus to Constantine bound in chains and heavily weighed down by iron. Then, without even questioning him concerning the cause of so great a crime, he blinded him and sent him into exile, where he suffered for a long time [Col. 1276C].

### 73

During his time, Izit and all the peoples of his homeland quickly learned that Alulit had died a natural death. At the beginning of the era 783, the first year of Constantine’s reign and the 127th year of the Arabs, they substituted his brother Abrahim, whom it was known that his brother had left as deputy [Col. 1276C].

But Moroan, one of the Arabs, approached the palace [Note: [Col. 1276D] M. reads “hearing.”] and killed the man who was destined to perish. He seized the vacant empire, which had been divided among various factions, fiercely seeking war through tyranny.

### 74

In the era 784, the second year of Constantine’s reign, the 128th year of the Arabs, the aforementioned warlike Moroan, with his companions, found Abrahim with only a few men and immediately struck him with the sword as he approached the palace [Col. 1276D]. Thus, overcome by internal fury on this account, he lived turbulently for five years and carried on various wars.

He pursued from Damascus to the Babylonian fields Azali, the uncle of Abdella [Note: [Col. 1276D] Sand. reads “from Zali.”], whom a very large multitude of Ismaelites had chosen as their ruler. After crossing the Nile, Moroan was himself cast down and beheaded.

### 75

During his time, in the aforementioned era 784, the second year of Constantine’s reign, the 128th year of the Arabs, and the second of Moroan, Toaba was appointed by everyone in Spain as a warlike man of distinguished birth, after the kingdom of Abulcatar had been removed together with [Note: [Col. 1277D] *Cum* is absent from M.; Sand. does not have the words appearing between the two chronological notices in this number.] his associate Zimahel. He reigned for one year [Note: [Col. 1277D] Maz. reads “he was appointed for one year.” Pagi, year 747, no. 14.].

When he had died a natural death, Juzif was chosen by the entire senate of the palace as governor of Spain in the era 785, the third year of Constantine’s reign, the completed 129th year of the Arabs—or the beginning of the 130th—and the third of Moroan. As an elder and long-lived man, he was wonderfully acclaimed as ruler of his homeland.

Not many days later, the Arabs throughout Spain, plotting various rebellions, surrendered their souls to the underworld without achieving anything. He ordered a census to be made at the suggestion of the remaining people and commanded that the scribes remove from the public register those whom the sword had slaughtered from among the Christians paying tribute, after so many massacres of them. Although he was carefully ordering this with great recklessness, he continued to command [Col. 1277B].

76. In the sixth year of this reign, in the era 788, on the Nones of April, a Sunday, at the first hour, the second, and almost the third, as all the citizens of Córdoba looked on, three suns were seen shining in a marvelous manner and appearing pale, with a fiery or emerald-colored crescent preceding them. At their rising, by God’s command, angels—[or, according to D. Rodríguez, *Angli*, “Angles,” rather than *angeli*, “angels”]—were appointed to devastate all the inhabitants of Spain through intolerable famine.  
   
[Note: The number 77 is absent here in Sandoval and in M.; it is supplied by manuscripts C. and Maz., and by Pagi, year 746, no. 9, from which it was reprinted in edition B.]

77. At the same time, Peter, a deacon of the see of Toledo, was regarded in Spain as handsome, melodious, and exceedingly wise in all the Scriptures. For the inhabitants of Seville, on account of the erroneous Paschal observances that they had celebrated, he composed and wrote a finely arranged booklet from the Fathers and from various authorities.  
   
[Note: Maz. reads *auctoribus*, “authorities,” instead of *auctoritatibus*, “authorities.”]

78. In his time, in the era 788, in the sixth year of his reign, in the 133rd year of the Arabs, and the first of Abdella Alascemi, Moroan—as we have said, pursued by the public power—fled from the palace with an army amid the tumult of the peoples and with the public treasures. Wishing to penetrate Libya in order to renew the struggle, and now fearing nothing from Abdella, at the urging of the elders he sought the royal seat.

Abdella immediately sent after him his uncle Zali with an immense army of Arab and Persian warriors, who had hitherto honored the sun, and black-clad demons. They pursued Moroan intensely as he fled from city to city, finding no refuge because of the evils he had committed and the various deaths he had inflicted among the Saracens. They crossed the Nile, the river of Egypt, in pursuit of him.  
   
[Note: B. reads *ingesserat*, “had inflicted,” instead of *gesserat*, “had carried out.”]  
[Note: So M.; others read *insequitant*, “they pursue.”]

But when they had reached a place called in their language Azimun, they joined battle with one another and hurled weapons so violently that, after two days of merciless fighting and the slaughter of many on both sides, they cast one another down. Only on the third day, after Moroan had been overcome and killed, did they sheathe their swords and calm themselves.

[The warriors then sent the heads of the magnates to Abdella as precious spoils and rewarded the soldiers with the booty of the plunder, and they duly pacified all the former territories.  
   
Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent from B.; they are found in M. and C., though with some variation. M., except for the word *praedarum*, “of the plunder,” has the passage as printed, but then reads: “The warriors plundered them and reward them with the booty.” C. reads: “[... they] carry their own [spoils] honorably ... rewarding [them] from the booty of the plunder.” Sandoval reads: “[...] they were in their own spoils [that is, they carried their own spoils honorably],” and so forth.]

But are not the rest of their deeds—how the two sides fought one another in battle; how the wars of Spain gathered strength under the rulers Belgi, Thoaba, and Humeya or were brought to an end by Abulcatar; and under the rule of Iucif, in what order his rivals were destroyed—all these things written in the *Book of the Words of the Days of the Age*, which we have taken care to add in detail to the preceding Chronicles?

79. From the beginning of the world, therefore, up to the era that began in the year 792, in the tenth year of the reign of Constantine, the fourth of Abdella Alascemi as Commander of the Believers, the seventh of Juzif’s patriciate in Spain, and the 136th year of the Arabs, there are 5,954 years. If you wish to subtract four years from these, following certain historians who maintain by their reckoning that the age of the world amounted to precisely 5,210 years at the completion of Octavian’s fifty-sixth year of reign [Note: So M.; B. and Sandoval read: “who accurately ... in the fifty-sixth year of Octavian’s reign,” etc.], and who affirm—according to the *Ecclesiastical History* of our lord Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, book I, age VI [Note: So M.; B. and Sandoval read *aera*, “era.”]—that Christ was born in the forty-second year of the aforesaid Octavian, or now, according to the *Chronicle* of our lord Isidore, in the forty-second year, this is indeed what all the Scriptures declare.

When fourteen years are subtracted from Octavian’s fifty-six years, forty-two remain as the time of Christ’s birth. And because, at the completion of the fifth year of Julius Caesar, there are 5,154 years of the world, when Octavian’s forty-two years are added, there are 5,196 years from Adam to the birth of Christ. If the four years mentioned above—four years that some subtract from the 5,200th year of the world [Note: This is the number stated at the beginning of this paragraph; Sandoval has 798, B. 799.]—are deducted, and the 754 years of the Lord’s Incarnation, which are correctly reckoned in the era 792, are added to the previously mentioned 5,196 years, the result is 5,950 years of the world, with four years omitted and subtracted.  
   
[Note: M. reads *oblitis*, “with four years forgotten.”]  
[Note: M. gives 5950; others give 5955. The reading 5950 should be retained, since that number is composed of 754 and 5196.]

80. But since even our predecessors do not calculate the years of the world with such exact clarity that they are arranged uniformly in a single reckoning or made equal by one notation among all historians, although in this progression of years they do not differ greatly from one another, we too, following the majority who determine that Christ was born in the year 5,200, insert these four years, so that we may not wander too far from the paths of so many men—men such as these and so eminent—who have hesitated on the matter.  
   
[Note: M. adds *virorum*, “of men,” and omits the words *ubi tales tantique nutaverant viri*, “where such and so great men had hesitated,” which are found in Sandoval and B.]

For in so great a mass of time, if four years are added or subtracted, they seem in no way to prejudice the total [Note: B. reads *praedamnare*, “to prejudge/condemn beforehand”]; especially since, in the various books of the Chronicles, years advance farther and by such amounts in the total we have mentioned, and also recede, because if one counts either the beginning or the completion of a year of any reign—taking the part for the whole or the whole for the part—one cannot easily prejudice the reckoning.  
   
[Note: C. reads *et antegradentur*, “and advance beforehand.”]  
[Note: M. reads: “the total is in error, with several years added to or subtracted from the aforesaid number.”]

For, as we have said, most affirm that Christ was born in the forty-second year of Octavian; some demonstrate that he was born in the forty-first. Thus the most holy Julian, bishop of Toledo, writes in the book that he composed against the Jews concerning the six ages of the world:

> “Caesar Octavian reigned fifty-six years. In his forty-first year, according to the testimony of Tertullian and Jerome, Christ the Son of God was born of the Virgin Mary.”

Is anything here prejudiced because, according to some, the forty-second year is found, while according to others it is the forty-first? Certainly not. Rather, for this reason our predecessors counted the birth of our Savior at 5,200 years between the two editions, which it would take too long now to set down, so that the fullness of time, traced through generations and kingdoms, might be demonstrated more fully, and so that that perfect and supremely fitting number might be recalled by all. That day, together with the complete sequence of 5,200 years, might also be made more clearly known even to those who regard it lightly.

For it is fitting that his holy birth be declared more plainly, and that the number not be divided among a divergent accumulation of years, whether more or fewer. Finally, the most holy and, in this work, exceptionally learned Julian says in the little book mentioned above (*Against the Jews*, book III):

> “For if we seek the years from the beginning of the world to the birth of Christ according to the books of the Seventy Translators, together also with certain subsequent histories of the nations, there are found from Adam to Christ 5,200 years, together with whatever else remains according to certain historians who have written the sequence of the years of the world.”

# Abedoc and Ethelvulf, Abbots of Ireland

## Historical Notice on Abedoc

*(From Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Inferior Latin Literature.)*

A clerical Abedoc wrote an old Collection of Canons, under the administration of Haelhucar, an Irish abbot; the manuscript is in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, codex 572, according to Du Cange. From this old Irish Collection of Canons, which was arranged in sixty-five books in the eighth century, Lucas Dacherius published selected chapters in volume IX of the *Spicilegium Patrum*, p. 232 (new edition, volume I, p. 492). Edmund Martène supplied from the Bigot manuscript several omissions made by Dacherius, who had used two manuscripts, the Saint-Germain and Corbie copies; this material appears in volume IV of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, near the beginning.

## Historical Notice on Ethelvulf

*(From Fabricius, in the same work.)*

Ethelvulf, or Ethelvolphus, or Athulphus, or Athelulphus, son of Egbert the Great, was king of England from 836 to 857. His laws concerning payment of the denarius of Saint Peter and his hereditary letter, or Testament, are mentioned by Bale II.20 and Pits, p. 165. I judge that those laws concerning the denarius of Saint Peter are nothing other than the documents by which he donated a tenth of his father’s kingdom for the benefit of the English Church; Wilkins presents these documents, dictated and signed by Ethelvulf himself, in *Concilia Britannica*, volume I, p. 183.

# Selected Chapters

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Chapters

The Irish canons that follow were composed before the eighth century and have been selected by us from a large and ancient manuscript Collection of Canons. This Collection, consisting of sixty-five books divided into numerous chapters, teaches and establishes matters relating to sacred ordinations, the various duties of the ministers of the Church, the manner of administering the sacraments, the proper observance of ecclesiastical discipline, and the religious instruction of lay people in Christian conduct. Finally, it prescribes remedies to be applied and penances to be imposed on those who have fallen.

2. Although this Collection should by no means be despised, since it is adorned with a continuous and highly skillful sequence of passages from Holy Scripture, councils, and the holy Fathers, you may perhaps ask, reader, why we have not brought the whole of it to light. Two principal reasons especially moved us to this decision.

When we considered the many and varied collections of this kind of canons, both published and unpublished, which repeat almost the same material, we became convinced that the Collection in question would be unwelcome to learned men, for whose benefit we established the *Spicilegium* above all, if we were to offer them matters that are common and readily accessible. Then, to confess frankly, I shrank from the immense labor that would necessarily have had to be spent correcting its almost innumerable faults.

For I observed that the Collection was everywhere sprinkled with solecisms, since it had been written carelessly and incompetently by someone ignorant of the Latin language. Its words were not only inverted and barbarous, but its final syllable was repeatedly joined to the following word; a letter, and sometimes even a word, had been substituted for another; and many sentences were incomplete. Thus it was scarcely, or not even scarcely, possible to conjecture the meaning, much less to understand it.

Accordingly, we judged it worthwhile to select only the more notable passages—those that seemed to us more ancient—and especially those decreed in the Irish synods.

3. We do not deny that many obscure passages occur, either because they were copied by an ignorant man or because obscurity is, so to speak, innate among the Irish, as will be evident to anyone reading the short works and canons of Saint Patrick and certain others among the councils of Britain.

We have corrected some passages with the aid of Spelman’s *Councils of Britain*, the works of Saint Patrick edited by Ware, and a written manuscript from Saint-Germain; some we have clarified, however imperfectly, with brief notes. Among these chapters are quite a few selected canons of Saints Patrick and Gildas that have until now lain in darkness and escaped both Spelman and Ware.

We are nevertheless aware that there are canons or chapters that convey the same meaning as those found in other general and even provincial synods, sometimes in precisely the same words.

4. We have used two written manuscripts. From one, the Corbie manuscript, we extracted all these chapters of canons; the other, belonging to this library of Saint-Germain, contained another collection of various canons.

But we hesitated over whether we should add the canons placed under the vague heading “The Synod says” to the Irish material. When, however, we examined the latter manuscript more closely, we found the word *Hibernensis*, “Irish,” added in several places; and so our scruple immediately disappeared.

5. As for the author’s name, nothing certain presents itself at present, apart from the small conjecture appended by us to the Preface of the Collection. Ware seems to support this conjecture in his notes on the synod of Patrick, where, discussing a certain canon, he says:

> “Canon 25, concerning the bed of a deceased brother, is also found in manuscript excerpts from the Priestly Law of Ecgbert, archbishop of York, by the deacon Hucarius, under the heading ...”

These words indicate that Hucarius himself was engaged in the study of the Canons and, although somewhat obscurely, was their excerptor or collector.

Whether this same man was Haelucar the abbot, under whose administration Abedoc the cleric claims to have written the codex of collections, and Hucarius the deacon, we cannot readily judge—unless perhaps we say that *Hael* was added to *Hucar* or *Hucarius*. But what *Hael* denotes certainly escapes us.

# Selected Chapters from an Ancient Collection of Canons Made in Ireland around the Eighth Century

*(From Dacherius’s *Spicilegium*.) (C)*

## Collector’s Prologue

[Note: The copyist at the end of the codex seems to indicate the collector’s name quite clearly in the following manner: “I, Ardeboc the cleric, have written these Collections of fragmentary composition, under the administration of Haelhucar the abbot; here in this codex they have been gathered from the Holy Scriptures and divine sources, or from the decrees that the holy Fathers and synods established among various peoples and in various languages.”]

Seeing the immense number of synodal exemplars, and perceiving that the obscurity of many of them made them less useful to the uneducated, while also observing that the diversity of the others was discordant and more destructive than edifying, I arranged an exposition—brief, clear, and harmonious—from the vast Forest of writings into the text of a single volume. I added many things, reduced many, arranged many along the same path, and asserted many by following the meaning rather than the sequence of the words.  
   
[Note: Acherius directs that *digerens*, “arranging,” be read.]

In all this I strove for one thing alone: that, in my judgment, matters that appeared merely commendatory should not be copied. I therefore placed the names of the individual authorities before their individual testimonies, so that it might not be unclear who said what as though it were uncertain. But let this not mislead the reader: when you return to the general headings that we necessarily placed first, observe the numbers carefully. By observing them, you will find without hesitation whatever question you wish to locate.

*The Prologue ends.*

# Chapters from Book I: On the Bishop

## Chapter V — That One Man Must Not Ordain One Man

The Synod says: A bishop is to be ordained with the consent of the clergy, the laity, and all the bishops of the province, especially the metropolitan, whether by letter, authority, or personal presence.  
   
*(From canon 1 of the Council of Carthage.)*

## Chapter VII — Concerning the Man Who Is to Be Ordained

The Synod says: Before he is ordained bishop, a man must be examined to determine whether he is naturally prudent, teachable, temperate in conduct, sober, chaste, approachable toward the humble, merciful, learned, instructed in the law of the Lord, and cautious in interpreting the meanings of the Scriptures.

## Chapter VIII — On the Conduct of Bishops

The Synod says: A bishop must not invade another’s parish; he must not ordain another cleric belonging to someone else’s church; he must not presume to accept a payment for ordination; he must not presume to accept the gifts of wicked men, which the Most High rejects; he must not travel without a presbyter.

## Chapter IX — The Ages at Which a Person Is Advanced to the Episcopate

The Synod says: A boy devoted from infancy to ecclesiastical ministries shall remain a lector or exorcist until his twentieth year. He shall be an ostiarius and subdeacon for four years; a deacon for five; a presbyter at thirty; a bishop at thirty, forty, or fifty; and a priest, [Note: Something is plainly inverted here. It never happened that it was commonly believed that Christ began preaching at the age of thirty, forty, or even fifty. Therefore, it seems to me that the text originally read as follows: “He shall be made a presbyter at thirty, because Christ the preacher began at that age; a bishop at ... fifty; a priest ...”] he shall be made a priest because Christ began to preach at that age.

Second, concerning a young man who is the husband of one wife. — The same Synod says: A man who, from the beginning of adolescence until his thirtieth year, has lived honorably, content with having taken one and only one virgin wife, shall remain a subdeacon for five years and a deacon for five years; at forty he shall be a presbyter, and at fifty he shall remain a bishop.

Third, concerning an elderly layman. — The same Synod says: If a layman is of advanced age and it is necessary for him to become a bishop, he shall be a lector for two years and a subdeacon for five; after twelve years he shall be appointed presbyter or bishop.
