## Chapter XVI — That No One Ought to Judge Bishops

[Note: This refers to the book of canons that Usserius testifies he saw in the Cotton Library, *British Antiquities*, p. 557. The more learned writers commonly judge the author of this book of canons to have been Gildas, generally called “the Wise” or “the Badonic.” It appears that Gildas published these canons at the request of King Americ, so that he might restore ecclesiastical order in his kingdom, that is, in Ireland, as is related in his Life, no. 11, among the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, first century, p. 142, and elsewhere. Whether there were several Gildases, as some maintain, is not to be discussed here.]

Gildas says: Priests and bishops have a fearful judge, to whom it belongs—not to us—to judge them in both ages. Likewise, it is better not to judge fellow bishops, fellow abbots, or those subject together with us.

## Chapter XVII — That the Election of Good Men Is to Be Observed after Death, and Concerning the End of the Predecessor Bishop’s Life

[Note: Acherius says that the first part of this chapter agrees with canon 23 of the Council of Antioch. The latter part, however, is not free from corruption and can be restored from the canon itself as follows: “Let the ecclesiastical rite be observed, which provides that it must not be done otherwise than by the synod and the judgment of the bishops, who after the deceased’s falling asleep have the power to advance a worthy man.” Whether this correction will please others I do not know; to speak frankly, it does not please me. For in this chapter two canons seem to be brought together that differ from one another, although they can be reconciled in some fashion. The first, which is more general, forbids bishops to choose their own successor; the second permits them to choose one with the consent of the synod—that is, the bishops of the same province—and with the judgment of the region itself—that is, of the people. Thus the bishop does not appear to choose alone, but together with all those who possess the power of choosing.]

The Synod says: No bishop shall appoint his successor during his lifetime; after his death, good men shall choose a good man. Likewise, the Synod decreed that a bishop may appoint a successor at the end of his life with the consent of the synod and according to the judgment of the region itself, so that the appointment may not be invalid.

## Chapter XXII — On Excommunicating a Bishop Who Seizes Another’s Property

The Synod says: A bishop who seizes the parish of another bishop is to be excommunicated—unless he repents according to the lawful order—from peace, the Mass, and the table.  
   
*(From the Council of Arvernus, chapters 9 and 2; Synod of Patrick, chapter 4.)*

# From Book II: On the Presbyter or Priest

## Chapter IX — The Ways in Which the Church Now Offers Sacrifice

The Synod says: The Church now offers to the Lord in many ways: first, for herself; second, in remembrance of Jesus Christ, who said, “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians 11:24); third, for the souls of the departed.

## Chapter XIV — That a Portion of Every Dead Man’s Property Is to Be Given to Priests

The Irish Synod decreed that, for every dead person, a portion of his property should be given to the priests, because Aaron took a portion of every offering, whether from a prince or a servant; and that a common *sedatium* should be given from the property of every dead person.

## Chapter XV — On the Common *Sedatium*

The Carthaginian Synod says: Common *sedatium*, if it is small, must not be rejected; if it is large, it is to be accepted up to the value of a cow. This *sedatium* is to be avoided by a king, by a bishop who is a monk, and by brothers. The Irish Synod judged that, in this matter, the *sedatium* should be a sheep or its value, according to an established measure.

## Chapter XVI — On Communion

The same Synod says: The name “communion” signifies this: it contains viaticum, that is, protection for the journey; for it protects the soul until it stands before the tribunal, where it reports its deeds according to what it has done. Nor can the archangel lead it to life until God has judged it; nor can Satan lead it to punishment unless the Lord has condemned it.

## Chapter XX — On Giving Priests’ Surplus to the Churches

The Synod decreed that a priest should give to the church everything he has in excess, and that whatever he has left to the church, the church should deduct from his surplus.

## Chapter XXII — That Priests Must Not Accept the Gifts of the Wicked

The Synod decreed that a priest must not accept the gifts of anyone whose conscience he does not know. For to the same extent that the sacrifice does not benefit that person, the gifts of the wicked harm the priest.

## Chapter XXV — The Time During Which Priests May Be Absent from the Church, and Their Penance If They Are Absent Longer

The Irish Synod decreed that a priest may be absent from the church for one day only. If he is absent for two days, he must do penance for seven days with bread and water. If a dead person is brought to the church while he is absent, he must do penance, because he is responsible for that punishment.

Likewise, if he is absent from the church for one Sunday, he must perform penance for twenty days with bread and water; but if he is absent for two or three Sundays, he must be removed from the dignity of his rank.

## Chapter XXVI — That a Priest Must Not Regard Gifts Offered as His Own, but as the Church’s

The Synod says: Priests to whom something is donated by others, whether together with the church or separately, shall count it not as their own property but as property entrusted to the church, since the donor is understood to offer it for the redemption of his soul, not for the priest’s advantage. For it is just that, just as the priest possesses what has been entrusted to the church, so the church should possess what is left to the priest.

# From Book III: On the Deacon

## Chapter III — On the Ordination of a Deacon

The Synod says: When a deacon is ordained, only the bishop who blesses him shall place his hand on his head, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to ministry.  
   
*(From canon 4 of the fourth Council of Carthage.)*

## Chapter VII — On the Subordination of the Deacon

The Synod says: Let the deacon know himself to be the presbyter’s minister, so that the presbyters may honor the bishops.  
   
[Note: Acherius thinks this chapter should be restored from chapter 17 of the fourth Council of Carthage as follows: “Let the deacon so regard himself as the presbyter’s minister that he may know himself to be the bishop’s servant.” But this kind of correction seems to have been sought too far afield and does not sufficiently agree with what is read. Acherius also advises that the same fourth Council of Carthage should be read in the next two chapters, chapters 38 and 40.]

## Chapter VIII — On the Deacon’s Distribution of the Eucharist

The Synod says: If necessity compels, the deacon may distribute the Eucharist to the people, with the presbyter presiding.

## Chapter IX — On the Deacon’s Preaching in the Presence of Presbyters

The Synod says: When questioned in the presence of presbyters, the deacon shall speak.

## Chapter XIII — On the Ordination of a Subdeacon

The Synod says: When a subdeacon is ordained, since he does not receive the imposition of hands, he shall receive from the bishop’s hand an empty paten and an empty chalice. From the archdeacon’s hand he shall receive a pitcher with a water-cloth—that is, a vessel with water—and a hand towel.  
   
*(Book of the Sacramentary of Saint Gregory, edited by Hugh Menard, p. 234.)*

# From Book XI: On Those Who Sin While in a Rank

## Chapter III — On the Synod’s Counsel Concerning Those Who Have Fallen from Their Rank

The Irish Synod decreed: “That they should go into pilgrimage and there minister under the hand of an abbot.”  
   
[Note: Seeing that this passage was corrupt, Acherius conjectured that it might be restored as follows: “Those who have gone into pilgrimage are to be held under the authority of an abbot.” He added that the Council of Nicaea, canon 10; the fourth Council of Carthage, canon 68; the first Council of Toledo, chapters 4–13; and others oppose the other part. Perhaps that Irish synod grants this for the sake of preserving some distinction between penitents and the others who are to be advanced, establishing that after penance they are to be consecrated by the imposition of hands and minister in silence.]

The Irish interpret this more humanely, on account of the scarcity of priests: after penance, such persons are to be consecrated by the imposition of hands and minister in silence under the sign of penance until death, doing nothing according to their own will.

# From Book XII: On Fasting

## Chapter V — On Useless Fasting without Charity

Gildas says: Abstinence from bodily food without charity is useless. Better, therefore, are those who do not fast excessively and do not abstain beyond measure from God’s creation, but carefully preserve their hearts inwardly pure before the Lord, from whom they know the end of life, than those who do not eat meat, take no pleasure in worldly meals, and do not travel in vehicles or on horses, thinking themselves superior to the rest on account of these practices. Through the windows of pride, death entered into them.  
   
*(Tome I of the English Councils, p. 55.)*

## Chapter XIV — On Ending a Fast

The Synod says: For the sake of humanity, it is better, when brothers arrive, to offer the gift of love and to dissolve the strictness of abstinence and the rigor of the daily rule. For fasting is pleasing to the Lord when it has been completed by the fruits of charity.

The same Synod says: Concerning unbroken abstinence from food, the Romans establish that the coming of Christ the Bridegroom should find none of the laws of our fasts. What difference is there between a Christian and a Novatian? Is it not that the Novatian abstains continually, whereas the Christian fasts at appointed times, so that place, time, and person may be observed in every respect?

[Note: Perhaps the text should read, “that the coming of the Bridegroom may find no new laws of our fasting.” Acherius notes that *Tatianus* should be read instead of *Novatianus*, because Augustine says in *On Heresies*, chapter 25, that the Tatianists, or Encratites, asserted that it was not permitted to eat meat and that meat was in fact abominable.]

# From Book XIII: On Almsgiving

## Chapter VII — On Almsgiving Obtained through Theft or Robbery

The Synod says: Almsgiving from stolen goods or from the price of deceit is no more beneficial than if it did not exist. Yet it is better that such goods be given than that they be used among one’s own possessions, lest those possessions too be unlawful.

# From Book XV: On Care for the Dead

## Chapter II — For Whom Offerings Should Be Made

The Synod says: The Church offers for the souls of the dead in four ways. For the very good, there are thanksgivings, in which the offering has nothing to remove. For the very wicked, there are consolations for the living. For those who are not very good, the offering is made so that full remission may occur. For those who are not very wicked, it is made so that their condemnation may become more bearable.

# From Book XVI: On Testimony

## Chapter III — Those Who Must Not Be Admitted as Witnesses

The Irish Synod says: The testimony of a sinner is not accepted when he testifies against himself every day. If he has not fulfilled what he confessed at baptism, how will he be regarded as a true witness for others? How can the testimony of a worldly person, striving in this world for worldly affairs, be credible, if he has not made himself dead to the world? The testimony of a woman is not accepted, just as the apostles did not accept the testimony of the women concerning Christ’s resurrection.

## Chapter IV — That the Persons of Those Who Testify Must Be Examined

The Synod says: One must inquire into the conduct both of the accuser and of the accused; for a holy man is far more excellent than their oath.  
   
*(From the fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 96.)*

## Chapter VI — On Catholics Who Give Reckless Testimony

The Irish Synod says: If others dare to swear to what they do not know, and to what many doubt is true, following those who are worldly, they must do the penance of those who swear falsely—those who have recklessly handed their souls over to the hands of the reprobate.

## Chapter IX — On Testimony That Must Be Feared Even When Given by Many

The Synod says: The testimony even of many people must be feared if they are friends, reckless, or have been won over beforehand by payment. Hence it is said: “Gifts blind the eyes of the wise.” For this reason, too, the witnesses of the resurrection, corrupted by payment, gave false testimony.

## Chapter XIII — On Two Men Who Contradict One Another

The Synod says: Those who falsely accuse their brothers shall not communicate until the end of their lives.

# From Book XVII: On Offerings

## Chapter III — On the Three Reasons for Which Things Sanctified to God Are Withdrawn

The Synod says: Whoever withdraws consecrated Catholic offerings shall be excommunicated. Likewise: Whatever has been given in the Church of God, we do not permit to be alienated from the Church in any manner.

## Chapter V — On the Church’s More Lenient Treatment of Those Who Withdraw Offerings

The Synod says: Anyone who dares to take away offerings consecrated to God must restore to the Lord what he has withdrawn or receive satisfaction through penance.

# From Book XVIII: On the Right of Burial

## Chapter II — That One Must Be Buried in the Tomb of His Fathers

The Synod decreed: A man or woman shall be buried in the family tomb of his or her father. For it is said: “Cursed is every person who is not buried in the tomb of his fathers” (Deuteronomy 9:6).

## Chapter III — That a Person Must Be Buried in the Church to Which He Belongs as a Monk

The Synod established: If anyone has been joined to a church, he shall be buried in it.

The Irish Synod says: If a monk did not possess freedom during his life because of the abbot’s command, how much less does he possess it in death?

## Chapter VI — On the Burial of One Who Has Joined Himself to Two Abbots

The Irish Synod says: If someone has entrusted his soul and body, and everything he possesses, to God and to a superior—that is, to a holy abbot—and if afterward he has gone to another abbot and entrusted to him his soul and everything he possesses, to whom will all these things belong?

All his property will certainly belong to the first abbot, provided that he did not conceal his vow from him while he was alive. But the last abbot receives his body, clothing, horse, and cow; or, if he was of sufficiently high rank, two horses with a cart, the furnishings of his bed, and the vessel from which he drank. Nevertheless, the first abbot ought to offer prayers for the soul of the monk who has departed from him.

The same Synod says: Every buried body has, by its own right, a cow, a horse, clothing, and the furnishings of its bed. None of these is returned in satisfaction of another debt, because they are owed to the body as its customary due.

## Chapter VII — On Retaining the Dead

The same Synod says: Whoever has departed from his own church and has been buried in another church, if one of his relatives comes wishing to move the body of the dead man, he shall pay the price of the former grave—that is, a cow and his ordinary clothing—and shall ask the superior of the place to open his tomb.

But if the same household performs a work of mercy for his soul on the seventh day, the friend shall return his price and the common *sedatium*. If a priest makes the demand, it shall be so even if he is a monk; but if he is a pilgrim, he shall leave his clothing.

In the *Life of the Monks*: A certain cleric died in a church not his own and was buried there. When his relatives requested his body, it was not released but was firmly retained. When they went from there to Bishop Ovius, he said: “He must neither be retained nor released empty-handed.”

# From Book XX: On the Province

## Chapter V — On Going to Foreign Provinces for Judgment

Patrick says: If disputes arise on this island, let them be referred to the apostolic see.  
   
*(Among the short works of Patrick, canon 6.)*

# From Book XXI: On Judgment

## Chapter XII — What Judges of the Church Ought to Be Like

Patrick says:

> Judges of the Church ought not to fear human beings, but to fear God, because the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7).
>
> Judges of the Church of God ought not to possess the wisdom of the world, because the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God (1 Corinthians 3:19); rather, they ought to possess the wisdom of God.
>
> Judges of the Church ought not to accept gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the righteous (Deuteronomy 19:6).
>
> Judges of the Church ought not to show partiality in judgment, because with God there is no partiality (Ephesians 6:9).
>
> Judges of the Church ought not to possess worldly cunning, but divine examples, because a servant of God ought not to be cunning or crafty.
>
> Judges of the Church ought not to be too swift in judgment before they know what has been proved, because it is written: “Do not be a judge hastily” (Ecclesiasticus 7:6).
>
> Judges of the Church ought not to be fickle.
>
> Judges of the Church ought not to speak falsely, because falsehood is a great crime. Rather, judges of the Church ought to judge with right judgment, because in whatever judgment they have judged, they themselves will be judged.

*(From the “Proverbs of Saint Patrick,” among his short works, p. 49.)*

## Chapter XXVI — Whether Clerics’ Cases Should Be Judged before the Wicked or before the Faithful

Patrick says: Every worldly wise man, if he is wise, should not judge the judgments of the Church.  
   
*(Among the short works of Patrick, canon 1.)*

The Synod says: A cleric who brings his case, whether just or unjust, before the judgment of a judge of another faith shall be excommunicated.

## Chapter XXVII — That a Cleric May Pursue His Case without Litigation

The Synod says: No one shall presume to summon a cleric before a secular judge without the bishop’s permission. But if he has been summoned, he shall not answer; he shall neither bring nor pursue a criminal case in a secular court.

# From Book XXII: On Truth

## Chapter I — On Judging Truth, Regardless of Whose Mouth Proclaims It
Gildas: Truth shines for the wise, regardless of whose mouth it has been uttered through.

## BOOK XXIV. ON KINGSHIP

### CHAPTER III.—That the works of wicked kings destroy

[Col. 1289B]

Patrick (*On the Abuses of the Age*): The ninth degree of abuse is an unjust king. When he wishes to be ruler in himself, he does not preserve the dignity of his name; for the name “king” retains this meaning: that he should discharge the office of ruler for all his subjects. But how will he be able to correct others who does not correct his own conduct, lest it be unjust? He removes the fruits of the earth, obstructs the services of the people, prepares the deaths of dear ones, stirs up the attacks of enemies against the provinces, everywhere disturbs beasts by the tearing of quadrupeds, rouses the powers of the air, prevents the fertility of the earth and the services of the sea, kindles lightning, scorches the flowers of trees, and casts down unripe fruits. He not only darkens the face of the present kingdom, but also obscures his sons and grandsons, so that they may not obtain the inheritance of the kingdom. Because of the sins of the kings Saul and Jeroboam, Ahab and the others, God destroyed their offspring, so that they would not reign.

### CHAPTER III.—That the works of good kings build up

Patrick (same work): The justice of a just king is this: to judge no one unjustly; to be a defender of foreigners, widows, and orphans; to restrain thefts; to punish adulteries; not to support the immodest or the theatrical performers; not to exalt the wicked; to remove the ungodly from the land; not to allow parricides and perjurers to live; to defend the poor; to nourish them with alms; to appoint the just over the affairs of the kingdom; to have as counsellors elderly men who are wise and sober; not to heed the superstitions of magicians, pythonesses, and auguries; to defend his country bravely and justly against its adversaries; and to trust in God in all things.

### CHAPTER VII.—That a king should not have many wives

Synod: The greater the dignity a king has received, the greater the fear he ought to have; for many women corrupt his soul, and his mind, divided among a multitude of wives, falls especially into sin.

## BOOK XXV. ON LOTS

[Col. 1290A]

### CHAPTER V.—That a lot ought to be cast in cases of uncertainty

The Irish Synod: A lot ought to be cast either between two uncertainties, or between two equal alternatives, or between two co-Catholic parties.

## BOOK XXVII. ON CITIES OF REFUGE

### CHAPTER XI.—On the differing penance of those who voluntarily commit homicide

The Irish Synod says: All homicides, if they have been converted with their whole heart, shall undergo strict penance for seven years under the rule of a monastery.

Patrick (*Synod of Patrick*, vol. I of the *Councils of England*, p. 52): Whoever kills, commits fornication, or, in the manner of the pagans, consults a haruspex, shall perform a year of penance for each individual crime; when it has been completed, he shall afterward be released by a priest in the presence of witnesses.

## BOOK XXVIII. ON THEFT

[Note: [Col. 1289D] On this chapter you will find something in vol. I of the *Councils of England*, p. 54.]

### CHAPTER VI.—On theft committed in a church

Patrick says: [Note: [Col. 1289D] Acherius says that this twofold restitution seems foreign to the opinion of Gregory the Great in his *Responses to Augustine’s Questions*: “Far be it that the Church should receive as an increase what it seems to lose from earthly things, and seek profits from vain matters.” And in vol. I of the *Councils of England*, where this canon is reported, there is not even a word about the restitution itself.]

If anyone has stolen money either in a holy church or within a city where martyrs and the bodies of saints lie sleeping, a lot shall be cast concerning three alternatives: either his hand or foot shall be cut off, or he shall be put in prison, fasting for the period the elders determine, and he shall restore in full what he took; or he shall be sent into exile and restore double, and shall swear that he will not return until he has completed his penance. After his penance he shall be a monk.

### CHAPTER VII.—On the penance of one who steals, if the theft was not from a church

Patrick (*Synod of Patrick*, vol. I of the *Councils of England*, p. 52): Whoever commits theft shall do penance for half a year, live on bread and water for twenty days, and restore what was taken, if possible; thus he shall be received into the Church. Vinniaus says: If a cleric commits theft, he shall repay fourfold and do penance for a full year.

## BOOK XXIX. ON DEPOSITS

### CHAPTER V.—On deposits not to be returned to the Church

The Irish Synod: Every deposit shall be returned, except the deposit of the mother church of all the baptized. For just as every mother does not return to her son the deposit that has been lost, so every church ought not to return the deposits of her children, even if they have been lost.

The same synod also says: If someone guards the key of a house, and a thief digs into it and steals someone’s deposit, the person who received it shall not return it, but the entire household shall swear—how much more so if it was stolen together with his money.

## BOOK XXX. ON FATHERS AND SONS

[Col. 1291A]

### CHAPTER XV.—That parents are not to be neglected even for the sake of divine worship

Synod: Whoever leaves his parents for the sake of divine worship and does not render them their due reverence, let him be anathema (Canon 5 of the Council of Gangra).

Also: We have judged that anyone who abandons his father and mother in their need ought to be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER XIX.—On those who despise their children for the sake of religion

The holy Synod says: If anyone abandons his children, does not nourish them, and fails to do what belongs to them for the sake of divine worship, let him be anathema without dispute (Canon 6 of the same council).

[Col. 1291B] Also: Whoever begets children for the sake of posterity ought to nourish them, lest he become the murderer or destroyer of his own flesh; for Scripture says: “You shall not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58:7).

### CHAPTER XX.—That God is to be placed before children

Synod: We decree that every penitent should not leave all his possessions to his children, but should remain free and await Christ, who will provide all necessities.

## BOOK XXXI. ON PARENTS, THEIR HEIRS, AND CHILDREN

### CHAPTER X.—On preserving the inheritance for legitimate sons

The Synod says: A father ought not to defraud his son, but ought to bestow gifts and give him the inheritance.

### CHAPTER XIV.—That the Church ought to give its share to the relatives of the deceased

The Synod decreed: When someone dies, let him entrust everything he has to God, and let him give a portion to Caesar; then God will distribute it through human hands to his sons or relatives.

### CHAPTER XX.—On the provisions added by the authorities of the Church concerning female heirs

The Irish Synod: The authorities of the Church add many provisions here, so that female heirs may give fixed portions and stipulations, lest the true inheritance pass to outsiders. The Lord also says: “Their inheritance shall pass to the brothers of their father, and from them to their relatives” (Num. 27:10).

It must be determined whether they will give a portion to the Lord. If their relatives remain silent, what they give will belong to the Lord; but if they do not, it will be invalid. It must be determined what they will give by testament—that is, cows, clothing, and vessels. It must be determined what they will give to the ministers—that is, a portion of the sheep and wool. But if the ministers are relatives, they shall give them something from the inheritance; and if they have a paternal church, they shall give it something from their inheritance [Note: Acherius suggests “have a share”; but I think quite otherwise, for here I read: “and if they have a paternal church”]; and if they have begotten sons, they shall give the inheritance to the men of their choice.

### CHAPTER XXII.—On the testament of a sick person

The Irish Synod: The testament of a sick person is that he give his minister a portion of his movable substance, another portion to his heirs, and another portion to the church as the price of his burial. The inheritance, however, is divided among the kingdom, the church, and the heirs. But if he has no kingdom, a third part shall belong to the ministers; but if he does not have [an heir: the object is omitted in the printed text], the relatives and ministers shall divide it. [Note: “At this point,” Acherius observes, “there is no redundancy.” He also adds: “What is here prescribed concerning the price of burial is condemned by the Council of Enham, canon 12, and the Ecclesiastical Laws of King Cnut, chapter 20. It is likewise condemned by Gregory the Great, book VII, epistle 55, indiction 2; the Council of Meaux, canon 63; the Council of Tribur, canon 16; the Council of Clermont under Urban II, canon 8; the Council of Rome under Alexander III, canon 7; and likewise the Lateran Council under Innocent III, canon 66.”]

### CHAPTER XXIII.—On two co-heirs of two deceased fathers who disagree

Synod: Among co-heirs of two fathers who disagree, wherever age, prudence, dignity of character, and a good conscience are found, let the person who possesses them be chosen, and let what he says be believed. Or perhaps, since this resolves every uncertainty, let suitable judges interpret the matter. Also: Let the heirs of the dead be judged as follows. If one has witnesses, let him produce them. If he has none, let his age, nobility, rank, and reason be considered. But if these matters remain uncertain, let the case be determined by lot, by the truth that surpasses everything, or by true judges who do not incline to either side.

## BOOK XXXII. ON DEBTS, PLEDGES, AND INTEREST

### CHAPTER VI.—On the prompt payment of hired workers’ wages

Synod: The work of hired laborers must be considered, and then their wages are to be paid.

Also: Every hired laborer quickly consumes his work, so that he may quickly receive his payment.

Also: Every hired laborer serves for appearance’s sake; therefore an overseer must be appointed over him.

Also: “The hired man abandons the sheep insofar as he is a hired man, does not gather what is scattered, and does not tend what is broken” (John 10:12).

### CHAPTER IX.—On the amount and nature of a pledge

The Irish Synod decreed that one-fifth of the debt be given as a pledge, as it is said in the law: “He shall repay a fifth part.” If he does not redeem his pledge by the appointed time, he shall never redeem it; and he shall repay the entire debt unless you show him mercy.

## BOOK XXXIII. ON SURETIES, FIXED PORTIONS, AND STIPULATIONS

### CHAPTER II.—That a cleric ought not to be a surety

Synod: A cleric who serves as a surety shall be deposed (Apostolic Canon 20).

Patrick (*Synod of Patrick*, vol. I of the *Councils of England*, p. 52): If a cleric becomes surety for a pagan in any amount, and it happens—as is not surprising—that the pagan deceives him by some trick, he shall pay the debt from his own possessions. But if he fights with weapons, he shall be reckoned as outside the Church.

### CHAPTER III.—On persons unworthy to become sureties

The Irish Synod: Neither a foreigner, nor a strong man, nor a monk without the abbot’s command, nor a son without his father’s command, nor a woman unless she is a lady, a virgin, and holy, is worthy to become a surety.

### CHAPTER IV.—On the time when a surety ought to pay

The Irish Synod says that a surety should pay the debts for which he has pledged himself, in such a way that the debtor is given fifteen days the first time, twenty days the second time, thirty days the third time, and forty days the fourth time. Afterward he shall repay the debt without further reckoning.

Others say differently: if the pledge is made for a living person, the first time ten days should be granted and the second time five. But if it is for a dead person, thirty days.

### CHAPTER V.—How the debtor shall repay the obligation of the surety

[Note: Acherius conjectures that *solutionem* (“payment”) should be read.]

In the definition of the same synod, the debtor shall repay as much as the surety paid and as much as he has been wearied by the matter. If he is humane, the surety shall not seek interest, except to recover what he paid and the expense he incurred. But if he is inhumane, the interest shall increase for one year, and he shall repay the entire debt together with one-fifth of the debt each month.

### CHAPTER VI.—That no one ought to buy or sell without fixed portions and stipulations

[Col. 1293B]

The holy Synod decreed that every sale be confirmed in three ways: by fixed portions, by stipulations and witnesses, and by a written document in which these matters are recorded.

### CHAPTER VII.—On the nature of stipulations and witnesses

The Irish Synod: If there is one stipulation, the creditor and debtor shall cast lots [Note: A word has been added in the source text.], and one shall swear against the other. But if one of them has two or three months, or if there are several oaths, the debtor shall repay. If the stipulations disagree with one another, they shall cast lots unless there are witnesses. If one party is found to be lying, he shall either pay the debt or do penance equal in value to the debt.

### CHAPTER VIII.—On a debtor who resists

The same synod: Every debtor who resists witnesses and stipulations shall be expelled until he does penance according to the judgment of the judges.

Patrick says: For if he fights with weapons, he shall be expelled from the Church.

## BOOK XXXIV. ON OATHS

### CHAPTER V.—On fulfilling an oath

Synod: An incautious declaration is to be revoked—not as a violation of faith, but as a correction of rashness. In the Book of Kings, Saul swore to kill Jonathan, but Jonathan was not killed; nor is Saul blamed in this oath, because he swore according to his own will, not according to God’s will.

The Irish Synod: The oath of a son or daughter made without the father’s knowledge, the oath of a monk made without the abbot’s knowledge, and the oath of a child are invalid.

## BOOK XXXV. ON THE JUBILEE

### CHAPTER VII.—On the time after which neglected matters revert to the ancient right

The Irish Synod: Whatever has remained for fifty years—that is, one jubilee year—in the right of another shall pass over to the right of one person; without complaint or excommunication, it shall never return.

### CHAPTER VIII.—That the laws of the Jubilee are to be observed even in the New Testament

[Note: That is, in the Testament. Immediately after “of the seller” is read, Acherius wishes “of things sold” to be read; I think that something of another kind lies concealed here.]

[Col. 1294A]

The Synod says: As regards things sold, although they may have become customary, they never become obsolete. Nevertheless, the laws of the Jubilee—that is, of the fiftieth year—must be observed, so that uncertain matters are not confirmed by the passage of time; and therefore every transaction must be confirmed in writing.

### CHAPTER X.—Those whom the Jubilee does not affect

The Irish Synod: When others bring the Jubilee against you, you shall answer: The jubilee year applies to things sold and exchanged from the proper co-heirs to Catholic persons. It does not apply to ancient deposits; nor to things seized by force; nor to things transferred without a price; nor to things sold from the inheritances of others; nor to things transacted between the king and the Church—for just as long as the king does not withhold what belongs to the Church, so the Church shall not withhold the king’s right; nor to things transacted between brothers, because a brother defrauds his brother (*Among the Works of St. Patrick*, in the notes to the synod, p. 118).

## BOOK XXXVI. ON LEADERSHIP

### CHAPTER III.—On good leaders

The Irish Synod (in the notes on Patrick’s Canon, p. 120): [Note: If one believes Acherius, *constitui* (“to be appointed”), or something similar, must be added here; but I think quite otherwise. For the Irish Synod’s meaning is not that there must be some leader, but that, if there is one, he must be such that, etc.] Every leader ought to be like earth for support, a governor for correction, an anchor for sustaining, a hammer for striking, tongs for holding, the sun for illuminating, dew for moistening, a writing tablet for writing, a book for reading, a mirror for seeing, terror for frightening, and an image in all good things, so that he may be all things in all people (Col. 3:11).

### CHAPTER V.—That leaders are not to be blamed for a minor offense

Gildas: [Note: Who does not see that something is missing here? I read: “we who disparage our leaders.”] Miriam was condemned with leprosy when Aaron blamed Moses on account of the Ethiopian woman. We should fear this, we who disparage our leaders on account of minor faults.

### CHAPTER VII.—That leadership is not to be sought unless one has first been subject

Synod: Whoever wishes to rule ought first to be a monk; whoever wishes to inherit ought first to be devout; whoever wishes to teach ought first to be a disciple.

### CHAPTER XIV.—That a leader ought to have a minister

[Col. 1294D] Synod: A leader ought to distribute everything through the hands of ministers for the use of the parish, his subjects, and the poor.

### CHAPTER XV.—That a leader ought not to give more than small gifts without the counsel of his subjects

The Synod says: He ought to do nothing without the counsel of his subjects, except small things for the liberation of prisoners and the consolation of the poor and widows; and if the clerics are absent, then he may act (from the Council of Carthage IV, canon 32).

### CHAPTER XX.—On the consent of the people with the leader in appointing a successor

[Col. 1295A]

The Synod says: We decree that no leader is to be appointed unless the clerics and the parish have been summoned and agree together.

### CHAPTER XXIII.—On others who unworthily desire leadership, that is, beginners or those recently converted from the world

Synod: Let him learn what he is to teach; let him be reformed in what he is to hold; and, like a lamp placed upon a lampstand, let him shine, so that the opposing force of winds rushing upon it may not extinguish the flame of learning he has kindled, but increase it.

### CHAPTER XXVII.—On the penance of one who blasphemes a good leader

[Col. 1295B] Patrick says (*Among the Works of Patrick*, p. 46): Whoever, out of hatred or envy, mutters words of blasphemy against a good leader shall do penance with bread and water for seven days, following the example of Miriam, who murmured against Moses.

### CHAPTER XXIX.—That beginners ought not to preside

The Synod of the whole world and Patrick decreed (*same work*, p. 41): A beginner may in no way preside, but shall carry out his work under the authority of a Catholic abbot.

### CHAPTER XXXI.—On remaining in every calling

Gildas: Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called, so that neither a superior may be changed except by the will of his subjects, nor a subordinate occupy the place of his superior except by the counsel of an elder.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.—On expelling the worst leaders

The proud angel was cast out of heaven; Adam, after his sin, was cast from paradise onto the earth; the wicked king Jeroboam was abandoned by the ten tribes. Let all heretics, even if they are leaders of great cities, be stripped of their heresy and expelled from their seats with the consent of the synod.

### CHAPTER XXXV.—That the Church ought not to be scattered through obstinacy, but gathered like sheep into a fold

The Irish Synod: If some obstinacy has arisen between a leader and his community through disagreement, let the shepherd not reject his flock into dispersion, nor let the sheep flee from the shepherd, but let them make peace with one another, saying: “I will go in to the altar of my God” (Ps. 42:4). Gregory Nazianzen treats of this, saying: “No one has the power to drive me away from the altar.” Never defraud your fold; let the feet not rise up against the head, nor let the head regard the feet as alien to it (*In the notes to Patrick’s Canon*, p. 120).

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—That a leader ought not to regard as his own what is entrusted to him, but as belonging to the Church

Synod: Bishops to whom anything is given, either together with the Church or separately, shall count it not as their own property but among the resources of the Church.

## BOOK XXXVII. ON TEACHERS

[Col. 1296A]

### CHAPTER XVI.—On the correction of teachers, since heresy arose from them

Synod: It must be noted that heresy was spread throughout the world by the wise.

## BOOK XXXVIII. ON MONKS

### CHAPTER I.—On the name “monks”

The Irish Synod: *Monk* in Greek, *unalis* in Latin, means either one who leads a solitary life alone in the desert, or one who inhabits the world without worldly impediment, or one who, although living among many in this life, conducts himself as a solitary.

### CHAPTER IV.—That a monk ought not to be made without an abbot

[Col. 1296B] Synod: Monks ought not to exist without governance, except for a single hour, lest the wind of discord and dissension disperse the Church.

### CHAPTER V.—That a monk ought not to possess private property

Gildas says: Whatever exceeds a monk’s needs from secular possessions must be reckoned as luxury and wealth; whatever he is compelled to possess from necessity, not by choice, so that he does not fall into want, shall not be counted against him as evil.

### CHAPTER VI.—That a monk who seeks stricter discipline is not to be restrained by his abbot

Gildas says: A lenient abbot should not restrain his monk when the latter seeks stricter discipline.

### CHAPTER VII.—On receiving or not receiving monks who flee

[Col. 1296C]

Gildas says: Those who come to you from an inferior place for perfection—whose abbot has so degenerated from the work of God that he deserves not to be admitted to the table of the saints, and is burdened with the charge of fornication, not because of suspicion but because of evident misconduct—you should receive without any scruple, such monks fleeing to you from the flame of hell, and without consulting their abbot in any way.

But those whose abbot we do not exclude from the table of the saints because of infamy, we ought not to receive against his will—much less those coming from holy abbots who are suspected in no other way except that they possess flocks and vehicles, whether because of the custom of their country or because of their bodily weakness. These things harm their possessors less if they are accompanied by humility and patience than do those who draw ploughs and drive mattocks into the earth with presumption and pride. Likewise, when a ship has been wrecked, let whoever can swim swim.

### CHAPTER VIII.—That a monk ought to give his acquisitions to the abbot

The Synod says: If a monk, through obstinacy, begins to wander through deserted places and presumes to possess anything as his own, everything he acquires shall be brought to the abbot according to the monastery’s rule. He himself, like a fugitive, shall be brought back under guard.

### CHAPTER X.—That both the fugitive monk and his receiver are to be excommunicated

Patrick (*Synod of Patrick*, vol. I of the *Councils of England*, p. 52): Whoever has been excommunicated by any cleric and has been received by another shall be corrected with equal penance.

### CHAPTER XI.—That a wandering monk is to be excommunicated

[Col. 1297A]

Patrick says: A monk wandering through the parish without consulting his abbot ought to be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER XV.—That monks ought not to withdraw from the community

The Synod of Agde (canon 38): Monks are not permitted to withdraw from the community into solitary cells, unless perhaps, after approved labors, the abbots permit them to do so. Even then, however, they must remain within the same enclosure of the monastery and have separate cells.

### CHAPTER XVI.—That a monk ought not to build a cell without the abbot’s permission

The Synod of Orléans (canon 722): No monk, driven by ambition and vanity, shall presume to build a cell without the permission of his abbot.

## BOOK XXXIX. ON EXCOMMUNICATION

[Col. 1297B]

### CHAPTER I.—On the forms of excommunication

The Irish Synod names six forms: exclusion from celebration, from participation in the Mass, from cohabitation, from blessing, from peaceful conversation, and from provisions (*In the notes to Patrick’s Canon*, p. 126).

### CHAPTER IV.—That no one is to be excommunicated hastily

Gildas says (see vol. I of the *Councils of England*, p. 55): Noah did not wish to exclude his son Ham, a writer of magical arts, from the ark or from participation at the table. Abraham did not shrink from Aner and Eshcol in the defeat of the five kings. Lot did not curse the banquets of the Sodomites. Isaac did not deny Abimelech, Ochaz, and Phicol, the commander of the army, participation at his table; rather, after food and drink, they swore an oath to one another. Jacob did not fear sharing a table with his sons, whom he knew to worship idols. Joseph did not refuse to participate in Pharaoh’s table and cup. Aaron did not reject the table of the priest of the idols of Midian. Moses likewise entered into peaceful hospitality and a banquet with Jethro. Christ did not avoid the banquets of pagans, so that he might save all sinners and prostitutes.

### CHAPTER VII.—That alms from an excommunicated person are not to be accepted

Patrick (*Synod of Patrick*, vol. I of the *Councils of England*, p. 52): If any cleric has been excommunicated, neither shall his alms be received in the Church.

### CHAPTER VIII.—That an excommunicated person ought not to offer or baptize, but only to pray

[Col. 1297D] Patrick: If anyone has been excommunicated, let him pray alone from that same hour. He may neither offer nor baptize until he has corrected himself.

### CHAPTER XI.—That food and drink do not defile a person as much as evil thought and wicked action

Synod: Food and drink do not harm a person as much as evil thought and wicked action defile him. For without another you can exist, but without yourself you can never exist.

### CHAPTER XIV.—That it is better to withdraw from the wicked, lest one perish together with them

Synod: Every cleric who desires to watch a spectacle shall be degraded.

[Col. 1298A] Also: If any cleric dies in war or in a deadly quarrel, or in the games of the peoples, let no offering or prayer be requested for him; rather, let him fall into the hands of the judge. Nevertheless, he shall not be deprived of burial.

## BOOK XL. ON THE COMMENDATION OF THE DEAD

### CHAPTER II.—On a leader or bishop commending his own possessions

Synod: Every leader may commend his own possessions after death.

### CHAPTER III.—That a leader may not commend church property

Synod: Every Christian leader shall leave the Church as he found it. Unless the clerics consent, he shall commend nothing at his death, lest he be burdened with curses after death.

### CHAPTER IV.—That a leader may commend certain things from church property

The Irish Synod: At his death a leader may commend even certain things belonging to the Church—that is, the price of a female slave, or something from movable property, or from a field (*In the notes to Patrick’s Canon*, p. 120).

Also: The testament of a bishop or leader consists of ten *scriptuli* for the priest who offers sacrifice for him, a cloak for a poor person, food for a widow’s journey, and ordinary clothing for a minister; yet these provisions must be confirmed by the clerics.

### CHAPTER VIII.—On one living under a tax or census who commends nothing

The Irish Synod: Just as a monk would dare to commend nothing without the abbot’s permission, so one living under a census shall not have the power to give anything at his death unless his lord commands it.

### CHAPTER IX.—On one living under a census who commends his own possessions

The Irish Synod: If someone is under royal or abbatial rent and commends something, and his lord hears of it and remains silent for days, he cannot revoke it; otherwise it shall be invalid.

### CHAPTER X.—On the commendation of a woman living in marriage

The Irish Synod: If her husband remains silent for the prescribed days, he shall not revoke whatever she has given. But if he does not remain silent, her testament shall be invalid except with regard to her body, and to a cloak and a cow to accompany her body, if she has them. To the church in whose service she has remained, for as long as she has lived with her husband, she shall give, with her husband’s consent, one-third of her property; but her husband shall distribute it. [Note: [Col. 1297] In the manuscript of Saint-Germain there is added: “and she shall give another portion only to her father and mother.”] The rest shall belong to her husband and her children.

## BOOK XLI. ON THE CHURCH AND THE WORLD

### CHAPTER III.—That the Church is not to be stripped by the world

Synod: Thieves, robbers, and plunderers are to be expelled from the Church.

Also: If you defraud a friend, it is theft; but to defraud the Church is sacrilege.

### CHAPTER VI.—That the Church should not take everything

Synod: No one ought to defraud sons, brothers, or relatives.

[Col. 1299A] Also: Let the Church receive only God’s portion; for when the heir of the world comes, he will reclaim what belongs to the world.

### CHAPTER VII.—On two churches disputing one field

Synod: Let the field be investigated in the written documents of the two churches. If it is not found in the documents, let the elders and relatives be asked how long it was held by the other church; and if it remained there under a fixed Jubilee, let it remain there forever without reproach. But if no elders can be found, let them divide it between themselves; and let the one to whom it is closer give the other the price determined by the judges.

### CHAPTER VIII.—That the right of the Church does not perish, even if much time has passed

[Col. 1299B] Synod: If a bishop, out of humane consideration, has granted small estates to clerics or monks to cultivate or hold for a time, even if long periods of time are shown to have passed, they shall return to the Church.

### CHAPTER XV.—That the Church should not retain anyone by force

Synod: If anyone departs of his own will, let this be recorded before witnesses, and let him be left to God.

### CHAPTER XIX.—That division is better than discord

Synod: It is better to divide than always to be at odds; for division brings peace, whereas discord destroys.

### CHAPTER XXI.—How great a penalty is deserved by those who cast infants into the Church of God

[Col. 1299C] The Irish Synod: Whoever casts infants into the Church of God without the abbot’s knowledge shall do penance for three and a half years if bishops are buried there or present. But if they have committed homicide there, they shall do penance for seven years. This is taken from the fact that a bishop has seven degrees and the Church is sevenfold. But if there are no bishops and the church is small, they shall do penance for a year and a half.

### CHAPTER XXII.—On infants cast into the Church

The same synod says: A child brought in is the servant of that same church, unless he is redeemed; nor will his fault defile the church if he is unruly, provided that the church corrects the child brought in as far as it is able. If he departs from it within one hundred days, he shall have no authority, but the right shall belong to those who raised him. If the church has received money from the parents, the child shall be treated in every respect like the children of those who raised him. If the infant dies through negligence, they shall do penance for seven years, because they have killed Christ. Hence others judge that those who cast infants out should do penance for seven years, so that they may receive as much punishment as the evil they inflicted on the Church of God.

### CHAPTER XXIII.—On condemning those who seek money

Synod: If those who collect church resources for the support of life under the name of mercy are found to have redeemed no captives, let authority be taken away from them; and let what they have acquired be distributed for the redemption of captives. Let them be separated from Christians until they have performed three years of penance.

Patrick: If anyone seeks money for the redemption of a captive in the parish on his own authority, without the abbot’s permission, he deserves to be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER XXIV.—That collecting money is not blameworthy when necessity compels it

Patrick: If anyone has received the bishop’s permission and the price of a captive has been collected, demanding no more than necessity requires, let whatever remains beyond this be placed upon the altar and given to the needy and to captives.

Also: If anyone collects money under the name of mercy, let him not dare to despoil the Church of God, but let him collect from kings and peoples, for whom it is better to give than to hoard.

### CHAPTER XXV.—On the Church releasing one who is bound

The Irish Synod: If the Church releases a bound person from his bonds, let it impose upon him the bonds of the price of penance. But if he does not complete his penance and commits some evil, no curse shall come upon the Church of God. For the Church has the power of binding and loosing, is free, and everyone is indebted to it.

### CHAPTER XXVI.—That a Church living under a census does not release one who is bound

The same synod: If a Church lives under the census of a king and is bound by certain worldly cords, it is not worthy to release one who is bound; for if it releases him, it will repay the debts of his offenses.

### CHAPTER XXVII.—On the freedom of the Catholic Church, which does not repay the debts of the wicked

The same synod: The Church shall not repay the offenses of others in times of tribulation. Just as the offenses of demons do not come upon God or his angels, so the offenses of the members of the devil do not come upon the members of Christ—that is, upon the saints—nor upon monks fleeing from the Church, nor upon the worst foreigners, nor upon those who are cast upon the Church, that is, evil collectors, nor upon worldly kindreds. Rather, worldly people shall repay the Church for the offenses of other worldly people that they committed against it. Likewise, the offense of an evil brother shall not defile a religious brother, either spiritually or in worldly matters, by making him answer for that offense.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.—The order in which the offense of a sinful brother is to be charged

The same synod: First, the offense of every evil person shall come upon his property and his livestock. Second, if he has no property or livestock, it shall come upon his lands. If he has no land, it shall come upon his king. If he has no king, it shall come upon the one who supplied the weapons and clothing of the offender. If none of these is found, finally it shall come upon the one who fed him and gave him a bed. But if nothing at all is found among these, and he commits an offense in a church, the matter shall be referred to the greatest king of the province in which that church is located.

### CHAPTER XXIX.—That the guilt of sinners does not come upon the Church, even if it feeds them

The same Synod: If the Church gives food to someone who has committed an offense, the offense of the wicked person will not come upon the Church because the Church gave food to the wicked person, since it is a true dove. The dove, however, provides not only for its own chicks but for all birds that open their mouths. Thus the Church serves everyone, as the Lord says: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45).

### CHAPTER XXX.—That worldly people do not swear concerning one who has departed from the Church

The same synod: The Church defends itself even after the death of its leaders, and no oath is sworn concerning it—that is, concerning those who have departed—because their words are living. This is according to the example of Holy Scripture: “Our fathers have declared to us; they were not hidden from their children” (Ps. 77:4). And it swears concerning worldly dead people; therefore no oath is sworn concerning it, because it is free and not a prison.

## BOOK XLII. ON PLACES

### CHAPTER I.—That a church is not to be founded by unbelievers

Synod: If anyone enters a place, the church is to be founded not by unbelievers or laypeople, but by the Church.

### CHAPTER III.—On a church foundation received from unbelievers
The Synod says: Whoever builds a church, if he receives its foundation from unbelievers, shall summon the bishop and the elders; it shall be established by the bishop, and the bishop shall establish it as an offering to God and to strangers.

### CHAPTER IV.—On the conduct of a stranger who receives a place

The Synod of Patrick says (*Among the Works of Patrick*, [Col. 1301C] p. 45 and 124): If a stranger enters a parish, he shall neither baptize, offer, consecrate, nor build a church before receiving permission from the bishop of that province. This is an example of humility; for whoever seeks permission from unbelievers or laymen, and not from the bishop, is an outsider.

### CHAPTER V.—On a stranger unable to retain his place

The Irish Synod says: It has been decided that a stranger may receive a place among the monasteries; but when he has been unable to retain the place given to him, he shall return to his own monastery, from which he came. If he received it from unbelievers and was unable to retain it, he shall receive its price from the heirs; but it may not be sold to others. If he planted relics of the saints there, he may give it to other clerics, [Col. 1301D] but only to those who are perfected.

### CHAPTER VI.—On one who gives a place to someone, and how they shall separate if they part

The Irish Synod: It is proper that a prince who has not given himself or his property, but has merely preserved it for the church, if he is expelled or wishes to depart, should leave half of the seed-stock among the church’s livestock, and should leave untouched whatever was given to him, except what the necessity of that place required from him; whatever he brought with him he may take away. If he himself hired the female household servants or ministers, they shall belong to his portion; but if he hired them for the sake of the place, they shall depart with the place’s portion. All offerings of outsiders shall be divided between the prince and the church at the time of separation. But if the prince is a Catholic priest, all the labor he performed and all the furnishings of the place [Col. 1302A] shall belong to the place; and whatever he spent from the resources of the place on the workers he shall not repay, except for the major and personal objects, that is, the church’s special vessels. Others, however, have decided that what he distributed in the first year he shall not repay upon separation, because he was in need.

### CHAPTER XI.—On the boundary of a holy place, unknown and marked out by three persons

The Irish Synod: The boundary of a holy place shall have markers around it.

The Synod says: Wherever you find the sign of Christ’s cross, do not damage it.

Likewise: Three persons consecrate the boundary of a holy place: the king, the bishop, and the people.

### CHAPTER XII.—On the number of boundaries of a holy place

The same Synod established four boundaries around a holy place [Col. 1302B]: the first, into which laymen and women enter; the second, into which only clerics come. The first is called holy, the second holier, and the third holiest. Note that the name of the fourth has been lost.

### CHAPTER XV.—On the decree of the Irish concerning the violation of relics

The Irish Synod: Whoever violates the relics of bishops or martyrs by homicide shall do penance as a pilgrim for seven years; but if by theft, for three years. If, however, he kills someone within the boundary of the holy place where laymen are lodged, he shall do penance for one year. We grant pardon for the later periods for fifty days, because a place into which homicides with their spoils, thieves with their thefts, adulterers and perjurers, heralds, and magicians enter ought not to be called a holy place. [Col. 1302C] And not only must every holy place be cleansed within, but its consecrated boundaries must also be clean.

### CHAPTER XVI.—On the more serious pollution of a holy place in proportion to the number of saints in it

Patrick says: Whoever detracts from the gods, that is, from the martyrs, detracts from God; for by however many martyrs have been buried in that place, by so much does he detract from God.

### CHAPTER XXV.—On the profanation: why is holy blood more precious than a holy place?

The Synod: The blood of martyrs consecrates a place; the place does not consecrate the blood. If someone says, “The church is mine,” you shall tell him what is read in the Song: “My dove is one, and my beloved is one” (Song of Songs VI, 8). And you shall tell him: It is fitting that a son be killed in the bosom of his mother [Col. 1302D] and nurse; yet understand that only the nurse has been polluted, and that because of this pollution she is consecrated, whereas the son is dead.

Likewise Bishop Ovidius says: No one can pollute the relics whose souls, filled with the vision of God, consign worldly things to oblivion; but the souls of the martyrs beneath God’s altar cry out, saying, “Avenge our blood,” etc. (Rev. VI, 10).

### CHAPTER XXVI.—On the name of a basilica and its division

The Irish Synod: *Basilion* in Greek means “king” in Latin; hence *basilica*, “royal,” because in the earliest times only kings were buried in it, and it received its name for that reason. Other people, however, were either buried by fire or enclosed in a heap of stones.

[Col. 1303A] Likewise: [Note: [Col. 1303D] Acherius conjectured that this passage ought to be emended as follows: “No outsider shall have permission, without the prince’s permission, to divide the basilica into liberties …”] No outsider shall have the right to divide the basilica into liberties without the prince’s permission; and if anyone dares to do this, he shall repay according to the dignity of that place.

## FROM BOOK XLIII, ON WOMEN’S QUESTIONS

### CHAPTER II.—On the need to avoid pride in continence

The Synod: If anyone among those who preserve virginity for the Lord exalts himself against married people, let him be anathema (Council of Gangra, canon 9).

Likewise: Whoever preserves virginity shall do so for the Lord, not out of abhorrence of marriage; for whoever detests a faithful man and a devout woman, or considers them blameworthy, let him be anathema [Col. 1303B] (the same, canon 10).

### CHAPTER VII.—On true widows

The Synod: Widows who are supported by the church’s allowance ought to be so constantly engaged in the work of God that they assist the church by their prayers and merits (Council of Carthage IV, canon 103).

### CHAPTER VIII.—On the church’s duty to support its infirm widows

The Synod says: Young widows who are physically infirm shall be supported at the expense of the church whose widows they are.

### CHAPTER X.—On the name “veiled women”

The Irish Synod: *Pallium* is derived from *palliditas*, “paleness”; hence *palliata*, or the goddess Pallas, who is also Minerva, whose temple is pale-colored and whose priestesses were virgins called *palliatae*, that is, “veiled.” Hence [Col. 1303C] in the New Testament the term is transferred to *palliatae*, that is, “veiled women.”

### CHAPTER XI.—At what age virgins ought to be veiled

The Synod: Nuns, [Note: [Col. 1303D] Baluzius rightly observed that one should read *quamlibet vita*, “whatever their way of life.” Acherius also noted that this canon is canon 19 of the Council of Agde, in which, instead of “the twelfth,” “the fortieth” is read; reason itself indeed urges that this should be restored [Col. 1304D].] whatever their life and conduct may have been proved to be, shall not be veiled before their twelfth year of age.

## FROM BOOK XLIV, ON THE ORDER OF MARRIAGE

### CHAPTER XI.—On the times during which married people must abstain

The Irish Synod: [Note: [Col. 1304D] Acherius says that this refers to the forty days before Christ’s Nativity, likewise the forty before Easter, and the forty after Pentecost. These three Lents are mentioned in the capitulary of Charlemagne, no. 184, book VI.] During the three Lents of the year, on the Lord’s Day, on Wednesdays, and on Fridays, married couples must abstain.

Likewise: On all solemnities, and during those days when the wife is pregnant—that is, from the day on which the child begins to move in her womb until the day of her delivery [Col. 1303D].

Likewise: After childbirth, for thirty-six days if the child is male, but forty-six days if female.

Likewise: Those living in a religious habit may not be joined in marriage.

### CHAPTER XXXI.—On children born from the wives of living men who commit adultery

The Irish Synod: If anyone corrupts another man’s lawful wife [Col. 1304A] and deposits his seed so that the woman becomes pregnant, that child shall belong to the body of the man from whom he was begotten [Note: [Col. 1304D] Acherius emends this to “of the corrupter.”]. Nevertheless, he shall pay the price of the child in whatever amount the judges determine. But if the adulterer has sown seed, the corrupter shall pay nothing; nor shall one adulterer give anything to the other, unless perhaps, once the child has been acknowledged, he pays the cost of raising it.

### CHAPTER XXXII.—On excommunicating every adulterer

The Irish Synod: Every adulterer shall be excluded from concelebration, from sharing the table, from cohabitation, from blessing, from conversation, and from intercourse until he repents.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.—On receiving back an adulterous woman after penance, and on the length of the penance

[Col. 1304B] The Synod: We decree that a woman joined to another man through adultery shall be excommunicated until she performs penance; after penance she shall be reconciled to her husband.

Patrick (*Works of Saint Patrick*, p. 40): If someone’s wife has committed fornication with another man, he shall not take another wife as long as his first wife lives. If she should be converted, perform penance, and he receives her, she shall serve him as long as she lives in the capacity of a maidservant; she shall do penance for a full year on bread and water according to measure, and they shall not remain in one bed.

The Synod: He shall do penance for seven years: three strictly and four leniently. The same is to be understood of the husband if he too has committed adultery.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—On betrothed girls corrupted by others

The Synod: Betrothed girls who are afterward corrupted by others [Col. 1304C] shall, it has been decided, be taken away and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—On a woman’s inability to accuse her husband of an uncertain adultery

The Synod says: When a man’s offense remains hidden, no one should readily separate him on the basis of suspicions; he shall certainly be removed if his crime is exposed.

## FROM BOOK XLV, ON PENANCE

### CHAPTER XI.—On performing penance even in the final breath

Patrick (*Works of Saint Patrick*, p. 41): If anyone falls ill, let him perform penance, even under compulsion, because God is merciful.

### CHAPTER XIII.—On the place of penance

[Col. 1304D] The Synod says: A place for correction and penance must be considered.

## FROM BOOK XLVI, ON CENSUS REGIONS

### CHAPTER I.—On dividing a census region into three parts

The Synod: Every inheritance bound under the census of the king and the church shall be divided into three parts. The first part is given to the heirs without the casting of lots; the second to the kings. [Col. 1305A] For Christ says to Peter, “For me and for you” (Matt. XVII, 27). The third, however, is given to God, since “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness,” etc. They give a third part to God; a third part to the king who rules and supports the church with God and human beings. And three orders of columns are read of in the temple: the first, of wood without covering, that is, subjects; the second, with silver, signifying kings; the third, with gold, signifying Catholic princes.

### CHAPTER V.—On the equality of the king’s and bishop’s census

The Irish Synod says: Whoever dares to steal or seize anything belonging to the king or bishop, or to commit any offense against them, treating their displeasure lightly, shall pay the price of seven maidservants, or do penance for seven years with the bishops.

## FROM BOOK L, ON TONSURE

[Col. 1305B]

### CHAPTER VI.—On the tonsure of the Britons

Gildas says: The Britons, contrary to the whole world and hostile to Roman customs, serve the shadows of things to come with the Jews not only in the Mass but also in tonsure. [Note: [Col. 1305D] Or perhaps “rather than to the truth,” as Acherius preferred? On this chapter see the synod of Saint Patrick and Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book III, chapter 25, and book V, chapter 22.] The Romans say that the tonsure which belonged to the truth extended only from ear to ear, in contrast with the very distinctive tonsure of the magi, by which only the front of the forehead was accustomed to be covered. Patrick’s sermon testifies that the originator of this tonsure in Ireland was the swineherd of King Loigaire’s son; from him nearly all the Irish adopted this tonsure.

### CHAPTER VII.—On excommunicating clerics who are not shorn with the Roman tonsure

[Col. 1305C] Patrick: If any cleric’s hair has not been cut in the Roman manner, he ought to be excommunicated.

## FROM BOOK LI, ON TAME ANIMALS

### CHAPTER V.—On dogs

The Irish say: Whatever harm a chained dog does at night shall not be paid for by its master; but if it injures someone during the day, its master shall pay. Whatever harm a sheepdog does in a cattle-yard or in the pastures of its master’s livestock shall not be paid for by its master; but if it goes beyond the boundaries, its master shall pay for whatever harm it does.

### CHAPTER VIII.—On *pilaces*

The Irish say: [Note: [Col. 1305D] Acherius takes *pilax* to mean “cat.”] If a *pilax* does any harm at night, its master shall not pay; but during the day, if it causes injury, [Col. 1305D] he shall pay.

### CHAPTER IX.—On hens

The Irish say: If hens destroy a crop, vineyard, or small garden enclosed within a city by a fence reaching up to a man’s chin and furnished with a crown of thorns, their master shall pay; otherwise he shall not pay. But if they go outside the drying-yard, their master shall pay if they do any harm. [Note: [Col. 1305D] “Henhouse,” as Acherius conjectures? It does not seem so to me; I take *siccatorium* to mean “courtyard” [Col. 1306D].]

## FROM BOOK LII, ON MEATS

[Col. 1306A]

### CHAPTER X.—On the lawful eating of wild animals, especially deer

The Irish say: The flesh of wild animals is, as many think, unlawful to eat, because it produces more corrosion of the vital organs than nourishment. Some say that it is like other meat, because it provides nourishment to the stomach like other meat; nevertheless, the church [Note: [Col. 1306D] Acherius learned what the three kinds of flesh are from chapters 8 and 9, which for that reason he ought not to have omitted: they are those of fish, birds, and wild animals.] has consecrated these three kinds of flesh for eating.

### CHAPTER XII.—On pigs that eat human beings

Theodore says: Pigs that have tasted blood and touched it may be eaten; but if they eat while tearing apart the corpses of the dead, their flesh may not be eaten until they have grown lean.

Likewise: If a pig drinks blood, it is permitted; if it has merely tasted it, there is no consequence.

### CHAPTER XIV.—On pigs that eat carrion; on animals that consume human blood; on flesh eaten by wolves; on fish and strangled animals; on what is eaten by a hawk; and on horses

Bishop Theodore says: The Greeks do not give carrion flesh to their pigs. The hides of carrion animals may be taken for footwear, wool, and horns, but not for anything sacred. Yet if pigs happen by chance to eat carrion flesh or human blood, we do not believe that they should be cast away; nor do we believe this of hens. Animals consumed by wolves or dogs are not to be eaten, unless they are thrown to pigs and dogs; nor are deer or boars if they are found dead. Fish, however, are permitted, because they are of another nature. Birds and other animals, if they are strangled in nets, are not to be eaten. For Paul says: “Abstain from what has been strangled, from blood, and from idolatry” (Acts XXI, 25). The same applies to animals killed by a hawk. They do not prohibit horseflesh, although it is not customary to eat it.

## FROM BOOK LVI, ON HUMAN PROPERTY

### CHAPTER III.—On three beings free from another’s sin

The Irish Synod: There are three things that do not bear another’s sins: a generous man, if he keeps his house common to all; livestock, whose produce and labor are common to everyone, seeking nothing except food, and the food by which they live belongs not to human beings but to God; and a slave who faithfully serves his master. Hence Jerome says: The master’s sin does not fall upon the slave, but the slave’s sin passes to the master. Thus Balaam was ready for slaughter, unless he had been corrected through the she-ass, and the she-ass was free.

### CHAPTER IV.—On not taking livestock on account of anyone’s sin except its own

The Irish Synod says: No animal shall be condemned except for its own offense, whether by killing or injuring a human being, killing another animal, destroying hay or crops, or committing some other offense.

## FROM BOOK LVII, ON GUIDING BARBARIANS

[Col. 1307A]

### CHAPTER II.—On the penance of those who guide barbarians

The Irish Synod says: Whoever provides guidance to barbarians shall do penance for fourteen years. A barbarian means an outsider; and who is an outsider except one who, in a cruel and savage manner, lays everyone low—

### CHAPTER III.—On the law by which senators judge those who have guided barbarians to fourteen years of penance

The Irish Synod says: The senators have obtained fourteen years for this reason: if they have burned bishops’ basilicas, killed or struck down a religious man or nun, or removed innocent people from the church. The guide shall do penance for six years on his own account and seven years on account of those whom he guided.

### CHAPTER IV.—On a guide who does not accomplish the intention of his mind

The Synod: Judas incurred threefold guilt: he chose deceit, led in outsiders, and accepted the price of his deceit. The Psalm says: “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days” (Ps. LIV, 24).

## FROM BOOK LXI, ON THE CRAFT OF ARTISANS

### CHAPTER I.—The Irish say:

If an artisan makes the work of an unskilled person and supplies tools up to half the requirement, he shall receive half the price; but otherwise he shall receive a third part of his building, so that one third belongs to the workers and one third to food and tools, from which the judges shall receive their shares—that is, one judge from the artisans and another from those presiding over the church or fortress—and however much they wish, they shall assess for the work, not according to its usefulness. Afterward the artisan shall receive the price of the blessing. Other gifts shall be judged in the same way. But whoever refuses to act according to this council shall be excommunicated; no one shall receive him; and at death he shall lack communion.

## FROM BOOK LXIV, ON VARIOUS MATTERS

[Col. 1308A]

### CHAPTER V.—On Patrick’s three petitions

The Irish say: Patrick’s three petitions are these. The first is that he be given the Church’s share of a region divided into two or three parts, among its neighbours. The second is that no one should bind him by oath concerning the weak church. The third is that a cleric of like standing should be sought by a layman.

### CHAPTER VIII.—On those who think themselves just but are not

Gildas in his letters: While these people eat bread by measure, for this very reason they boast without measure; while they use water, they are simultaneously made to drink the cup of hatred; while they eat holy dishes, they practice detraction; while they spend their time in vigils, they criticize some who are weighed down by sleep. They set fasting above charity, vigils above justice, their own invention above concord, the church’s enclosure above humility, severity above humility, and, finally, a human being above God. They fast, but unless this is supported by certain virtues, it profits nothing. Those who perfect charity, however, say with the harp of the Holy Spirit: “All our righteousnesses are like a menstruous cloth” (Isa. LXIV, 6).

### CHAPTER XVII.—On the fact that admonition is better

Patrick says (*Synod of Patrick*, vol. I of the Councils of England, p. 52): It is better for us to warn the negligent beforehand, lest offenses multiply, than to condemn what has already been done, as Solomon says: “It is better to rebuke than to become angry” (Ecclus. XX, 1).

## FROM BOOK LXV, ON CONTRARIES

[Col. 1308C]

### CHAPTER II.—On the slowness of legal proceedings and their brevity

Patrick (*Works of Saint Patrick*, p. 49): Judges ought not to be so quick in judgment until they know what is right, because it is said: “Do not be a judge too quickly” (Ecclus. VII, 6). Isaiah, on the contrary: “Woe is me, because I was silent” (Isa. VI, 5).

[Col. 1307]

[Note: [Col. 1307D] Stephen Baluzius collated this little work with a manuscript codex of the church of Poitiers, now preserved in the royal library, and with another codex of the Thuane Library.]

## NOTE ON THE SYNODS

From an ancient collection written eight hundred years ago in the Remigian manuscript codex. (C)

[Col. 1307D] Note on the little book concerning the twenty-four synods which are said to have been composed before, below, or after the six synods previously mentioned.

The first is the Synod of Ancyra, which is said to have occurred before Nicaea but is placed afterward because of its greater authority. In it eighteen Fathers established twenty-four canons, whose principal author was Vitalis, bishop of Antioch. [Note: [Col. 1307D] The Thuane Codex says “Salaminus, bishop,” so that he may be the same person who formed the greater part of the immediately following Synod of Neocaesarea. In the royal codex, not twenty-four but twenty-three canons are said to have been established at Ancyra.]

The second is that of Neocaesarea, which is read as having occurred after Ancyra and before Nicaea. In it thirteen Fathers established fourteen canons, whose principal author was Vitalis Salaminus. [Note: [Col. 1308D] The Thuane Codex has sixteen Fathers.]

[Col. 1308D] The third is that of Gangra, which is read as having occurred after Nicaea. In it sixteen Fathers established twenty canons on account of certain ecclesiastical necessities, especially against Eustathius, who said that no one placed in the married state, nor any believer who did not renounce everything he possessed, had hope before God; and many other poisonous doctrines, which it would take too long to enumerate.

The fourth is that of Sardica, in which sixty Fathers established twenty-one canons. Its principal author was Hosius, bishop of Corduba and legate of the holy Roman Church.

[Col. 1309A] The fifth is the Synod of Antioch, in which thirty Fathers established twenty-five canons. Its principal author was Eusebius, bishop of Palestine.

The sixth is that of Laodicea, in which twenty-two Fathers established fifty-eight canons. Its principal author was Bishop Theodosius.

The seventh is that of Carthage, in which 217 Fathers established thirty-three canons. Its principal author was Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. It is also read that Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, was present at the same synod during the time of Emperor Honorius.

The eighth is the African synod under the younger Emperor Theodosius, in which 214 Fathers recited and confirmed 105 canons, which are said to have been written in various councils of the African province during the time of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. [Col. 1309B]
