The ninth is that of Arles, in which 600 Fathers established canons. Its principal authors were Silvester, bishop of the city of Rome, and Saint Marinus, bishop of Arles, during the time of Emperor Constantine, as some assert.

The tenth is likewise that of Arles, in which nineteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

The eleventh is likewise that of Arles, in which eighteen Fathers established canons.

The twelfth is likewise that of Arles, in which eleven Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

The thirteenth is likewise that of Arles, in which nineteen Fathers [Col. 1309C] established canons. Its principal author was Sapardus, bishop of Arles.

The fourteenth is that of Orange, in which sixteen Fathers [Col. 1310A] established canons. Its principal author was Bishop Hilary.

The fifteenth is that of Epaone, in which twenty-seven Fathers established forty canons. Its principal author was Bishop Caesarius.

The sixteenth is that of Agde, in which thirty-four Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Bishop Caesarius.

The seventeenth is that of Orléans, in which seventy-two Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Aurelianus, bishop of Arles, during the time of King Clovis. [Note: [Col. 1309C] What follows concerning the time when the Synod of Orléans was held has been added from the royal and Thuane codices.]

The eighteenth is likewise that of Orléans, in which thirty-one Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Melanius, bishop of Rennes.

[Col. 1310B] The nineteenth is likewise that of Orléans, in which twenty-five Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Saint Albinus, bishop of Angers.

The twentieth is that of Auvergne, in which fifteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Honoratus, bishop of [Note: [Col. 1309C] Acherius warns that “of Bourges” ought to be read; but in the cited codices it reads “of Brevi.”] Brevi.

The twenty-first is that of Mâcon, in which twenty-one Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Priscus, bishop of Lyon.

[Note: [Col. 1310C] It was lacking in the earlier edition and was added from the royal and Thuane codices. Baluzius notes that this Note is a fragment of a larger work, which he copied from the cited codices.] The twenty-second is likewise that of Mâcon, in which sixty-four Fathers established canons. Its principal author was likewise Priscus, bishop of Lyon.

The twenty-third is that of Lyon, in which fourteen Fathers established canons. Its principal author was Philippus, bishop of Vienne.

[Col. 1310C] The twenty-fourth is likewise that of Lyon, in which twenty Fathers established canons. Its principal author was likewise Priscus, bishop of Lyon.

# IRISH CANONS

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING CANONS (C)

[Col. 1309D] When our Acherius discovered the ancient collection of canons, composed in sixty-five books for the benefit of the Irish in the eighth century, in two very old codices—one of Corbie and the other of Paris, belonging to Saint-Germain—he selected from it only those canons that had been established especially in Ireland and had not yet seen the public light, both so as not to repeat material commonly encountered everywhere by learned men and to spare himself labor. He arranged for their publication, not without interest to students of antiquity and ecclesiastical discipline, for the benefit and use of the commonwealth of letters, in a volume of his *Spicilegium*.

But while I was staying at Rouen and examining the manuscript codices of the Bigot Library, I found among them an elegant one, written seven hundred years ago and containing the aforesaid collection; it appears once to have belonged to the monastery of Fécamp. After collating it with the published text, I noticed that it contained several important canons [Col. 1310D] that had either escaped Acherius’s eyes or, more probably, were lacking in his codices. I therefore thought it worthwhile to give them a place in this *Thesaurus of Anecdota* of ours. After the aforesaid compilation of Irish canons, the same Bigot Codex contains a Fragment of the Irish Synod, Gildas’s preface on penance, the Synod of Northern Britain, another Synod of Luci Victoria, certain excerpts from the book of David, the Synod called *Wisdom*, excerpts from books of the Romans and Franks, the canons of Adomnan, the canons of the Synod of Ireland, together with a short book on remedies for sins consisting of eight chapters, composed largely from the writings of Theodore, which have not yet been published. Although in all these works one may find something rather obscure, which seems to have been innate in the Irish, we nevertheless hope that learned men will by no means despise them.

[Col. 1311]

# IRISH CANONS TO BE ADDED TO THE PUBLISHED TEXT OF THE *SPICILEGIUM*

[From Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. IV.] (C)

## ADD TO BOOK I, AFTER CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 1311A]

A bishop shall not go out to another parish and abandon his own unless he does so by the judgment of many bishops and, above all, after a petition has been made.

## ADD TO BOOK II, AFTER CHAPTER XXII

Synod of Ferva: The gifts of the wicked, which are rejected by God, are rejected by the saints.

Likewise the Synod: The gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be refused by the priest.

## ADD AFTER THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK III, FROM BOOK IX

### On the various matters concerning clerics

A cleric shall prove his profession by his dress and bearing; he shall seek elegance neither through his heels nor through his shoes.

[Col. 1311B] A cleric shall not live with extraneous women.

A cleric shall not walk through streets and *androna* unless there is a definite and very great necessity of his office. [Note: [Col. 1311] An *andron* is a crossroads, or a place where men converse with one another. See the Glossary of Cangius.]

A cleric shall procure food and clothing for himself through craftsmanship or agriculture, provided that this does not impair his office.

A cleric who strolls through markets or the forum for any purpose other than buying something shall be degraded from his office.

A cleric who envies the progress of his brothers shall be degraded as long as he remains in this vice.

A scurrilous cleric who jokes with obscene words shall be degraded.

A cleric who perseveres in his office amid temptations shall be promoted through the ranks.

A cleric who sings during meals without edifying faith, merely tickling the ears, [Col. 1311C] shall be excluded from communion.

A cleric who breaks an imposed fast without unavoidable necessity shall be considered contemptible.

A cleric shall equally avoid the banquets and solemnities of heretics and schismatics.

A cleric, however learned in the word of God, shall seek his food through his own craft.

A cleric who considers the bishop’s severity toward him unjust shall appeal to the synod.

A cleric is not permitted to demand anyone’s death, and even after baptism we ought not to criticize the powers granted by God for the punishment of the wicked, lest we seem either to turn aside from the Lord’s discipline or to act against the Lord’s authority. All actions carried out through these powers shall be accounted for. While the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the one who pronounces their death shall be free from guilt.

Clerics who are possessed shall be degraded.

Clerics shall not have the power to associate habitually with extraneous women; they shall live only with their mother, aunt, daughter, sister, or niece, concerning all of whom it is impious to suspect anything beyond what nature establishes.

A cursing cleric, especially among priests, shall be compelled to ask pardon; if he refuses, he shall be degraded.

A cleric who turns aside from his office amid temptations or acts negligently shall be removed from his office.

A cleric who swears an oath shall be excommunicated.

A cleric shall not grow long hair or a beard, but shall shave.

A cleric shall not abandon his own church.

A cleric shall not take interest, nor pursue obscene speech. If anyone is found devising anything of this sort, he shall be expelled from the clergy.

[Col. 1312B] A cleric who has assembled for some quarrel, or who has been proved to have summoned an enemy against one of them to have him killed or injured, should more properly be called a murderer than a cleric, and should be regarded by all upright people as an outsider.

A cleric ought not to take interest, because whoever lends his money at interest shall not possess a heavenly dwelling.

## ADD TO BOOK XVI, AFTER CHAPTER XIII

### CHAPTER XIV.—On the testimony of the living concerning the dead

The holy Synod says: Whatever the living testify concerning the dead shall be given by the heirs, lest it become a sin against the dead.

### CHAPTER XIX.—On an oath taken with several persons

The Synod of Consul says: In the case of those who bring a dispute for any reason, if one party has a single witness or several witnesses and the other has no witness, the oath shall be taken with several persons.

## ADD TO BOOK XVII, AFTER CHAPTER V

### CHAPTER VI.—On those who withhold the offerings of the dead

The Synod of Valence says: Those who retain the offerings of deceased believers or return them late are to be expelled from the church as unbelievers. Such people are to be regarded as killers of the needy dead and as unbelievers in the judgment of God, in agreement with the sentence of the Fathers, which says: To take something away from a friend is theft; to defraud the church of God is sacrilege.

## ADD TO BOOK XXI

[Col. 1312D]

### CHAPTER X.—On holding to one sentence

The Synod says: If anyone dares to tear apart unity, since no human being can dissolve or censure it, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER XIII.—On the four principal ways in which judgment is perverted

[Col. 1313A]

The Synod says: Human judgment is perverted in four ways: by fear, greed, hatred, and love. By fear, when we are afraid to speak the truth because of dread of some power. By greed, when we are corrupted by the reward of some gift. A rich man often quickly corrupts a judge with gifts; but a poor man, when he has nothing to offer, is not only scorned as unworthy of a hearing but is oppressed against the truth. By hatred, when we devise hostile measures against anyone. By love, when we are content to provide a benefit to a friend or relative. By these four causes equity is often violated and innocence often harmed. Some add another way: flattery. Augustine: [Col. 1313B] It is better to suffer punishment for the truth than to receive a benefit for flattery.

### CHAPTER XX.—On not disturbing the judgment of good judges

The Synod of Laodicea: It is not permitted to challenge as invalid the judges whom common agreement has chosen; none of the bishops shall communicate with the challenger until he obeys the judges.

### CHAPTER XXXI.—On the Synod of Brenn

No cleric’s place should be taken away if he has inhabited it for the course of a year and built a church there, that is, his own house. Rather, it should without doubt be regarded as his perpetual Levitical possession, dedicated to him.

It was judged in this synod that wherever a priest has built his church, that is, his own house, within one year, his inheritance there shall be perpetual.

## BOOK XXVIII, CHAPTER VI, BEGINS AS FOLLOWS

### CHAPTER VI.—On theft committed in a church

The Irish Synod decreed: For the first theft committed in a church, the offender shall repay only the amount stolen and do penance according to the priest’s judgment. The church does this as an act of indulgence. If it is done a second time, he shall repay double or quadruple. But if the money of a worldly person has been taken from the church, and the church is Catholic and free from every census, the loss shall be restored to the owner, while the interest shall belong to the church. If, however, the church is subject to a royal census, the same loss shall be restored to the owner, while the interest shall belong to the king and the church.

## ADD TO BOOK XXXI, CHAPTER XXIII

The Synod of Ancyra decreed: If two people dispute in the absence of the dead, four shall judge; or they shall use the lot, which settles every hidden matter; or they shall divide what they dispute over; or one shall withdraw in exchange for a price; or they shall give it to the priests.

## ADD TO BOOK XXXIV, ON THE OATH

### CHAPTER XIII.—On an oath taken with several persons

The Synod of Consul: Those who dispute for any reason, if one has a single witness or several and the other has no witness, shall take the oath with several persons.

## ADD TO BOOK XXXVI, AFTER CHAPTER V

### CHAPTER VI.—On the people’s subjection to the prince

Patrick: You are ministers, and each of you shall fear his own prince, whom he attends and serves.

### CHAPTER XVIII.—On one who contradicts a prince appointing an heir
The Synod: Whoever has contradicted the decree of the prince in appointing an heir is not a Christian but a heretic.

## ADD TO BOOK XLI, AFTER CHAPTER VIII

### CHAPTER X.—On the matter that it is clear that the Church should accept everything given by enemies

The Synod: The Church should not seek things, nor reject what is given.

### CHAPTER XVI.—On the matter that one should neither eat nor sleep in a church

The Synod: One ought not to eat bodily food within the house of God, nor spread couches for sleeping. Therefore Christ drove out the sellers and buyers, [Col. 1314B] saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer.”

## ADD TO BOOK L, CHAPTER VI

### CHAPTER VI.—On clerics who do not tonsure themselves according to Roman custom

Patrick says: Any cleric, from doorkeeper to priest, who is seen without a breeches-garment that covers the shamefulness and nakedness of the belly, and who has not been tonsured according to Roman custom—and likewise any wife who does not walk with her head veiled—shall be condemned together and separated from the Church (Synod of Saint Patrick, article 6).

*(Chapter VI, however, is VII in our manuscript, and VII is VIII.)*

## IN BOOK LXIV, CHAPTER V, IT IS READ AS FOLLOWS

### CHAPTER V.—On Patrick’s four petitions

[Col. 1314C] The Irish say: “But now give thanks to your God, because the four petitions that you asked have been granted to you. The first petition is that ordination in Armagh may be performed by your favour. The second petition is that, whoever sings the hymn composed for you on the day of your departure from the body, you may judge his penance. The third petition is that the descendants of Dicuin, who kindly received you, may obtain mercy here and in the future and may not perish. The fourth petition is that all the Irish may be judged by you on the day of judgment, as it is said to the apostles, ‘And you who sit shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel’; so judge those to whom you were an apostle.”

## FRAGMENT OF THE IRISH SYNOD

The Irish Synod decreed:

[Col. 1314D] If the blood of a bishop, or of a high prince, or of a scribe, is spilled onto the ground and requires a salve, the wise judge that the one who spilled it should be crucified, or should pay seven maidservants. If it is a visible injury, he shall pay a third part in silver, and the counterpart of the crown of the head in gold, as well as the width and a comparable size of the eye in precious stone. And for the display of his bruise or wound in an assembly or in any gathering, up to the third year—or longer, if he does not grant pardon—the one who committed it shall pay the price of a maidservant.

But if the bishop’s blood does not reach the ground and does not require a salve, the hand of the striker shall be cut off, or he shall pay half the price of seven maidservants, if it was intentional; but if it was not intentional, he shall pay the price of a maidservant. [Col. 1315A] Whoever strikes or shakes a bishop without blood being spilled shall pay half the price of seven maidservants. If any of his hair has been plucked out, he shall pay twelve to twenty *sedatia* for each hair, from each of the two sides [the wording is uncertain]. Even if more has been plucked out, it is not said that it must be repaid as something belonging to him personally.

If the blood of a presbyter is spilled onto the ground so that it requires a salve, the hand of the striker shall be cut off, or he shall pay half the price of seven maidservants, if it was intentional; but if it was not intentional, the matter shall be settled by the price of a maidservant. If it does not reach the ground, the striker shall pay a maidservant; if there is a visible injury, he shall pay a third part in silver. His striking shall be compensated by the price of a maidservant; his shaking shall be settled as we stated above.

[Col. 1315B] **PATRICK SAYS.**

Everyone who dares to steal or seize anything belonging to the king, a bishop, or a scribe, or to commit anything against them, despising and treating them with contempt, shall pay the price of seven maidservants, or shall do penance for seven years with the bishop or scribe.

# THE PREFACE OF GILDAS ON PENANCE BEGINS

### I

A presbyter or deacon who commits natural fornication or sodomy, after having made the vow of a monk, shall do penance for three years, ask forgiveness at every hour, and perform an additional fast each week, except for the fifty days after the Passion: on Sunday, bread without measure and a dish somewhat enriched with butter; on the other days, a measured portion of *paximatius* bread, [Col. 1315C] and a small *misoclus* enriched with fat. He may use garden vegetables, a few eggs, and British cheese, with Roman *heminae* made according to the frailty of the body in this age. Of thin milk or *balthuta*, however, one Roman sextarius. To relieve thirst, also water in a small measure, if he is a laborer. He shall have a bed supplied with not much hay. During three Lents he shall add something according as his strength permits, always mourning his fault from the depths of his heart. Let him most willingly accept obedience in all things. After a year and a half he shall receive the Eucharist, return to peace, and sing psalms with the brothers, lest his soul perish entirely through so long a deprivation of heavenly medicine.

### II

If a monk of lower rank does penance for three years, [Col. 1315D] the measure of bread shall be increased. If he is a laborer, he shall take a Roman sextarius of milk, another of *tenucla*, and as much water as suffices for the heat of thirst.

### III

If, however, a presbyter or deacon without the vow of a monk has sinned, he shall do penance like a monk without rank. But if a monk has wished to commit the sin, he shall do penance for a year and a half. The abbot nevertheless has the power to regulate this matter, if the monk’s obedience has been pleasing to God and to his abbot.

### IV

The ancient Fathers established twelve years of penance for a presbyter and seven for a deacon.

[Col. 1316A] ### V

A monk who steals a garment or any other thing shall do penance for two years as above, if he is junior; if senior, for a full year. If he is not a monk, likewise for a year, and especially during the Lents.

### VI

If a monk vomits the sacrifice during the day because of an overflowing stomach, he must not presume to eat his supper. If it was not because of illness, he shall erase the fault through seven additional fasts; if it was because of illness and not gluttony, through four additional fasts. If it was not the sacrifice, he shall be punished with a day’s additional fast and much reprimand. If someone carelessly loses some consecrated thing by accident, he shall do penance for three Lents, leaving it to be devoured by wild animals and birds.

[Note: [Col. 1315D] The words seem to have been transposed; they should be restored as follows: “If someone carelessly loses some consecrated thing by accident, leaving it to be devoured by wild animals and birds, let him do penance for three Lents.”]

### VII

If someone, because of drunkenness, cannot sing the psalms, being stupefied and speechless, he shall be deprived of supper.

[Col. 1316B] ### VIII

One who sins with an animal shall do penance for a year; if he was alone, he shall cleanse the fault through three Lents.

### IX

Whoever has received communion from his excommunicated abbot shall do penance for forty days.

### X

One who unknowingly eats carrion shall do penance for forty days. It must nevertheless be understood that the longer someone remains in sin, the more his penance must be increased.

### XI

If some task is assigned to a person and he does not perform it out of contempt, he shall go without supper. If through forgetfulness, he shall receive half the daily ration. But if he takes another person’s task, he shall make it known to the abbot with shame, privately and with no one else listening; and he shall carry it out if ordered.

### XII

For whoever retains anger in his heart for a long time is in death.

[Col. 1316C] ### XIII

If he confesses the sin, let him fast for forty days. If he persists further in sin, let him do two periods of forty days. If he does the same thing again, let him be cut off from the body like a rotting limb, because fury nourishes homicide.

### XIV

Anyone offended by another ought to report this to the abbot—not in the spirit of an accuser, but with the disposition of one who heals—and the abbot shall decide.

### XV

Whoever has not come for the completion shall sing eight psalms in order. If, awakened, he comes after the mass,

[Note: [Col. 1316D] That is, after the prayer. In former times *missa* was called a prayer because it is sent to God; or after the mass, that is, after dismissal from the divine office.]

he shall repeat in order whatever the brothers have sung. If he comes at the second [office], he shall go without supper. If someone, through error, alters any of the sacred words where danger is noted, he shall perform a three-day fast or three additional fasts. [Col. 1316D] If he lets something sacred fall to the ground through negligence, he shall go without supper.

Whoever has been stained in sleep by a shameful fluid through his own will—if he has an abundant supply of beer and meat—shall be a *coenobium* [the wording is uncertain]. If he has sound strength, he shall keep watch standing for three hours of the night. But if he has poor food, he shall sing twenty-eight or thirty psalms while standing humbly, and compensate for it with an extraordinary task.

### XVI

For good kings we ought to offer sacred sacrifices; for wicked ones, not at all.

### XVII

Presbyters, however, are not forbidden to offer sacrifices for bishops.

[Col. 1317A] ### XVIII

Whoever is accused of some offense and, as though acting without counsel, is restrained, shall go without supper.

### XIX

Whoever breaks a hoe, and did not possess it before it was broken, shall either restore it through an extraordinary task or perform an additional fast.

### XX

Whoever sees one of the brothers transgressing the abbot’s commands ought not to conceal it from the abbot. He should first admonish the sinner, so that he may confess privately to the abbot what he is doing wrong, and the person reporting him may be found to be not so much an informer as an executor of the rule of truth.

## HERE GILDAS ENDS. THE NORTHERN SYNOD OF BRITAIN NOW BEGINS

### I

Whoever sins with a woman or with a man shall be expelled, so that he may live in a monastery in another country, and, after confessing, shall do penance for three years in confinement. Afterwards he shall be subjected to the altar as a brother. A deacon shall do penance for one year, a presbyter for three, a bishop for four, and an abbot, each deprived of his rank, according to the judgment of the teacher.

[Col. 1317B] ### II

Whoever has defiled himself shall do penance for a year in confinement. A boy of twelve years shall do forty days or three Lents; a deacon shall do one year in confinement and half a year with the brothers. A priest shall do one year in confinement and another year with the brothers.

### III

A monk who steals consecrated objects shall do penance for one year in exile and another year with the brothers. But if he has entered [Perhaps: returned], he shall suffer exile. Whoever steals food shall do one Lent; if a second time, three Lents; if a third time, a year; if a fourth time, he shall do penance in perpetual exile under another abbot.

[Col. 1317C] ### IV

The accused and the accuser shall be judged in the same manner. If the accused denies it, he shall do similar penance for a year: two days each week on bread and water, and a two-day fast at the end of every month, with all the brothers performing additional fasts and calling upon God as their judge. Those who persist in obstinacy, after the year has elapsed, shall be joined to another community under the judge’s fire and left to God’s judgment. If one of them at any time confesses, his penance shall be increased in proportion to the amount of trouble he inflicted on the other.

## THE SECOND SYNOD OF LUCI VICTORIAE BEGINS

Anyone committing theft once shall do penance for one year; if more than once, for two years. Whoever kills his brother without premeditated hatred, but in sudden anger, shall do penance for three years. [Col. 1317D] An adulterer likewise for three years.

Those who provide guides to barbarians shall do penance for fourteen years, provided that no slaughter of Christians, shedding of blood, or terrible captivity has resulted. If such things have occurred, they shall do penance for the rest of their lives, laying down their arms. If someone wishes to lead barbarians to Christians according to his intention [the wording is uncertain], he shall do penance for the rest of his life.

Whoever swears perjury shall do penance for four years. Whoever leads another who is unaware into perjury shall do penance for seven years. Whoever has been led into it unknowingly and later learns of it shall do penance for one year. But whoever suspects that he is being led into perjury and nevertheless swears shall do penance for two years, on account of his consent.

Whoever is a *moechator* (“adulterer”; the phrase *matris est* is uncertain) shall do penance for three years with perpetual pilgrimage.

[Note: [Col. 1317] That is, an adulterer; for the ancients frequently used the letter *u* for *o*.]

Whoever sins with a dog or any [Col. 1318A] animal shall do penance for two and a half years. Whoever commits a male offense, like a sodomite, shall do penance for four years. Whoever commits it upon the thighs shall do penance for three years. With the hand, whether another’s or his own, for two years.

All this that we have stated applies if a person does it after the vow of perfection. But if before the vow, one year is subtracted from each of these three penalties; from the remaining penalties, it is reduced as appropriate because he had not yet taken the vow.

# SOME EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOKS OF DAVID BEGIN

### I

Priests who are to minister in God’s temple, drinking wine and *sicera* for the sake of the appetite through negligence and not ignorance, shall do penance for four days. If through contempt of those who admonish them, forty days. Those who become drunk through ignorance shall do penance for fifteen days; through negligence, [Col. 1318B] forty; through contempt, three Lents.

Whoever, out of ordinary human kindness, compels someone to become drunk shall do penance in the same manner as the drunk person. But whoever, through hatred or lust, compels others to become drunk in order to disgrace or mock them shamefully, if he does not sufficiently repent, shall do penance as a murderer of souls.

### II

Those who fornicate with a woman betrothed to Christ or to a husband, or with a beast or a male, shall thereafter die to the world and live for God. Whoever sins with a virgin or widow not yet betrothed shall give a dowry to her parents and do penance for one year. If he has no dowry, he shall do penance for three years.

### III

A bishop who voluntarily commits homicide, or any fornication or deceit, shall do penance for thirteen years. A presbyter for seven, with bread and water, and a dish on Sunday or Saturday. A deacon for six, without rank. A monk for four, unless illness prevents them.

[Col. 1318C] ### IV

Whoever has been polluted in sleep by his own will shall rise and sing seven psalms, and live on bread and water that day. Otherwise, he shall sing thirty psalms. Whoever wished to sin in sleep but could not shall sing fifteen psalms. If he sinned but was not polluted, twenty-four; if polluted without willing it, fifteen.

### V

The ancient holy men decreed that a bishop should do penance for twenty-four years for capital sins, a presbyter for twelve, and a deacon for seven; likewise a virgin, a lector, and a religious person. An inebriated person shall do penance for four [years].

But now the penance for a fallen presbyter, and for a deacon and subdeacon, a virgin, and any person who hands another over to death, or fornicates with animals, his own sister, or another man’s [Col. 1318D] wife, or wishes to kill someone with poisons, is three years. In the first year he shall lie on the ground; in the second he shall place his head on a stone; in the third he shall lie on a board, and eat only bread, water, salt, and a small amount of vegetables. Others prefer thirty three-day fasts or additional fasts, with the food and bed stated above, from one meal at the ninth hour until the next.

There is another penance of three years, consisting of a hemina of beer or milk with bread and salt; another consists of two nights, with the allowance of a meal, during which they must beseech God for twelve hours in the order of nights and days. From this point a presbyter may not offer the sacrifice, nor may a deacon hold the chalice or ascend to a higher rank.

[Col. 1319A] ### VI

Whoever receives usury shall lose what he receives. One who lives on plunder or fraud shall do penance for half a year. Whoever secretly gives a virgin a kiss shall do a three-day penance. Whoever swears a lie in church shall repay fourfold what he swore.

## ALSO THEODORUS (Chapter 15)

Animals eaten by wolves or dogs are not to be eaten, except by pigs and dogs; nor are a stag, hind, or goats, if they are found dead.

## ALSO ADOMNAN

It is not permitted to eat the marrow of the bones of stags that wolves have eaten. Likewise, one must not eat stags whose blood we see to have flowed, however slightly.

He forbids the eating of animals whose legs have been broken in traps, affirming that their flesh is carrion because the [Col. 1319B] upper blood, which was the guardian and seat of the soul, did not flow out but coagulated within the flesh. Even if the extremity of the blood has been discharged through some outer limb, the thicker and more solid blood in which the soul had sat remains coagulated within the flesh.

Therefore, if something other than the cause of a wound has disturbed the seat of the soul, there is not a discharge of blood but an injury to an extremity. Accordingly, whoever eats that flesh should know that he has eaten flesh with blood. For when he forbade it, the issue was not the cooking of the flesh but the discharge of blood.

The foregoing must also be understood of animals that, after their ear has been cut off or torn, have died in extreme weakness. Nevertheless, we shall have their fat and hides for various uses.

## ALSO THEODORUS

[Col. 1319C] Fish, however, are permitted, because they are of another nature, even if they are found dead or strangled in nets. Birds and animals, even if they are strangled in nets, are not to be eaten. For Paul says: “Abstain from what has been strangled, from blood, and from idolatry.” Likewise, one must abstain from animals killed by a hawk.

If bees kill a person, they must be killed immediately. Their honey may nevertheless be eaten.

Animals polluted by intercourse with human beings shall be killed, and their flesh thrown to dogs. But animals that have been generated [from such intercourse] shall not be killed, where there is uncertainty.

## ALSO THE SYNOD OF WISDOM DISCUSSES TITHES AS FOLLOWS

[Note: [Col. 1319D] We gather, however uncertainly, which synod this was from a fragment of the Irish Synod, where “the wise” judge that the striker of a bishop should be crucified. Thus the Synod of Wisdom and the Irish Synod seem to constitute one and the same synod, celebrated in the time of Saint Patrick, whose ruling concerning theft committed against a bishop follows below.]

### I

The authorities say that tithes of livestock are to be offered once, and therefore shall be “holy of holies.” That is, a tenth is not owed [Col. 1319D] again from those same animals. But others affirm in good faith that every year we should give tithes to God from living and dead things, since every year we receive his gifts.

### II

Likewise, everything except the fruits of the earth is to be tithed once for the Lord, as it is said: “Whatever has once been consecrated to God shall be holy of holies for the Lord.” A tithe is not to be offered again from those things, as the teacher Columba taught. But of the fruits of the earth, a tenth part must be offered each year, because they are produced each year.

[Col. 1320A] ### III

Likewise, tithes are not only from animals; they also arise from mortal things. So too with firstfruits: that is, the first produce of every thing, and the animal that is born first in the year. Things similar to these are called firstlings; but firstborn applies only to animals—not only to human beings, but also to animals that are lawful to sacrifice.

### IV

Likewise, tithes are from livestock, and firstfruits from produce. Firstfruits are whatever is born from livestock before the others are born in that year. One should know the measure of firstfruits: this is a *gomer*, according to some, that is, nine loaves, or twelve loaves. Then the bread of the Presence consists of the material for nine or twelve loaves. Of vegetables, as much as a fist can hold.

These things should be paid at the beginning of the season, and once a year they were offered to the priests of Jerusalem. In the New [Covenant], however, each person should offer them to the monastery of which he is a monk. [Col. 1320B] Moreover, charity abounds among the same people, and firstborn offerings are made only in the case of males, never females.

### V

Likewise, according to some, if someone possesses fewer than ten [units] of property, he shall not pay tithes.

### VI

Likewise, how is it appropriate for someone to offer tithes to the Lord? If he has only one cow or ox, let him divide the price of the cow into ten parts and give a tenth to the Lord; and so with the rest.

### VII

Likewise, the Lord commands a voluntary offering. Therefore he says: “No one takes my life from me,” and so forth.

Concerning what God does not avenge, human beings also ought not to avenge themselves: and among those who quickly turn from guilt to penance, this is read in Exodus (chapter 32, verse 27 and following) concerning the worship of the calf.

[Col. 1320C] Moses stood at the gate of the camp and said: “If anyone is for God, let him join me.” And all the sons of Levi gathered to him, to whom he said: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each man put his sword upon his thigh,” and so forth, until it says: “Let each man kill his neighbor, brother, and friend.”

A little later Moses says: “You have consecrated your hands today to the Lord, each one in his son and in his brother, so that a blessing may be given to you.” It ends: “Amen.”

The people of Israel ought to have been bound by the ten commandments of the law, while God struck Egypt with ten plagues on their behalf; therefore there are ten commandments. There are also precepts in the law that God did not command, but in which he told Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, to choose seventy leaders who would judge the people with Moses. This is judgment: if we should find good judgments among the nations, [Col. 1320D] which nature teaches them and which do not displease God, we shall preserve them.

# EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOKS OF THE ROMANS AND FRANKS BEGIN

### I

If someone commits homicide in a quarrel, he shall pay three maidservants and three male slaves, and shall be secured against further claim.

### II

If someone commits homicide out of envy, he shall pay four maidservants and the same number of male slaves, and he himself shall have security.

### III

If someone is compelled in court on a charge of homicide, refuses the required dire formalities, and denies it, we order that he pay five maidservants and the same number of male slaves. Whoever causes the loss of a hand or any other limb shall receive the corresponding judgment.

[Col. 1321A] ### IV

If someone is suspected of homicide and has no means of proving—or, that is, revealing—the title of his case, he shall assemble forty-eight named men, of whom twenty-four shall swear in the church that he is telling the truth. Thus he shall depart without guilt. If he does not obtain the oath, he shall pay five maidservants and seven male slaves, and shall be secured.

### V

If a male slave kills a free man, and the free man has been killed by a blow, a staff, an axe,

[Note: [Col. 1321] It is doubtful what kind of weapon *bidubium* denotes; it is called a *falcastrum*, curved in the likeness of a sickle.]

a *bidubium*, or a knife, the homicide shall be handed over to the victim’s parents, and they shall have the freedom to do whatever they wish with him.

### VI

But if a master has entrusted weapons to a slave to carry, and he has killed a free man, he shall know that he must pay for that slave and another slave.

[Col. 1321B] ### VII

If a free man kills another person’s slave without fault, he shall restore two male slaves to the master. If he did so because of some fault of the slave, it shall be slave for slave.

### VIII

If someone in a quarrel damages a person’s hand, eye, or foot, he shall know that he must pay either a maidservant or a male slave.

### IX

If someone cuts off another’s thumb, we order that half the compensation for the damage be paid.

### X

If someone strikes a person with a spear or sword and the internal organs are exposed, he shall pay three pounds of silver.

### XI

If someone strikes another’s head as far as the scales of the brain,

[Note: That is, the membranes or scales.]

he shall pay three pounds of silver.

[Col. 1321C] ### XII

If someone slaps another and neither blood nor a bruise appears, he shall pay five silver solidi.

### XIII

If someone strikes another’s face with a slap so that blood or a bruise appears, he shall know that he must pay a maidservant.

### XIV

If someone makes a hole with a spear in another’s arm or thigh, but does not injure the limb, he shall know that he must pay two pounds of silver.

### XV

If someone commits homicide and flees, his relatives shall pay the legal compensation within a few days. Afterwards the relatives shall be restored to their homeland, or they themselves shall leave the homeland, or shall pay half the price; and thus they may sit securely in their homes.

After this, if the accused wishes to return, he shall pay what remains of the price and live in security. If meanwhile he has been killed by the relatives of the slain man, the movable property, maidservants, [Col. 1321D] or male slaves that the debtors had received shall be restored to the relatives.

### XVI

If someone throws a spear and the man is unharmed, he shall pay one pound of silver; if there is a wound, he shall know that he must pay according to the law.

### XVII

If someone fornicates with another’s wife, sister, or daughter, he shall die by death. Whoever kills him shall have no fear of liability.

### XVIII

If someone finds in a village a horse, ox, or any animal tied up for theft, or anything that has been killed, give three suitable men to swear that they have suffered no damage; if someone does not swear, let him pay.

### XIX

If someone buys a male slave, female slave, animal, or any other thing, and it has been marked with him, but he has neither an owner who vouches for it nor a guarantor, he shall know that he must pay compensation for theft.

[Col. 1322A] ### XX

If someone buys a horse from Gauls, Saxons, or any other people, in any form, he shall establish the purchase through witnesses. But if it has been marked and the witnesses on both sides have been made equal, let them divide it equally. If he has no witnesses and attempts to pursue a false claim, he shall know that he must restore threefold.

### XXI

If someone has left his neighbor’s animals unharmed in pasture and they remain there, he shall pay one scruple for two animals. If they are caught on the top of the pasture, he shall pay one scruple for four animals. If they are in a standing crop, whatever the owner swears, together with another suitable person, was the amount of damage suffered in the crop shall unquestionably be restored.

[Col. 1322B] ### XXII

If a pig remains in grain throughout the greater part of the night, four sextarii shall be paid. If through the lesser part of the night, one sextarius shall be paid.

### XXIII

If someone is convicted of fornication, he shall pay a maidservant if he does not swear an oath.

### XXIV

If someone takes a horse, cow, or any animal from a person, and the latter makes any claim for it, the debtor shall restore it together with its upkeep. Whatever has been proved, we order to be recovered.

### XXV

If pigs enter an acorn grove, the swineherd shall pay whenever they are caught. If he himself drove them in intentionally, he shall pay a larger pig.

### XXVI

A child up to twelve years of age shall receive nothing for an offense except discipline. After that age, whatever he commits or steals, he shall repay.

[Col. 1322C] ### XXVII

If a free man commits theft and is caught, he himself shall die; no one shall subject him to interrogation. This applies up to a sheep or pig; if the value is less, he shall restore threefold. A thief may be killed at night, but not by day. Whoever kills him at night has no liability.

### XXVIII

If someone has suspicion of theft and the title to the property is not deposited with him within twenty days, it shall remain so until the truth is proved.

### XXIX

If someone bound in chains refuses to come to judgment, and this is proved by witnesses, he shall be compelled to pay one pound of silver; and whatever is claimed from him, he shall restore without delay.

[Col. 1322D] ### XXX

If someone fails to pay a tribute at the proper time and is compelled by the tribute-collector to appear before the judge, then, if he has neglected it for a month after the appointed time, he shall give a pledge. If he neglects it for a second month, he shall restore double.

### XXXI

If someone has lost a maidservant or male slave and has a suspicion, twenty-four men shall be assembled by name, of whom twelve shall swear if the person who has been convicted does not restore it.

### XXXII

If someone [claims] a horse by calling men [as witnesses], nine shall swear; nothing further follows.

### XXXIII

If a male slave kills another male slave, he shall remain alive in common ownership of the masters.

[Col. 1323A] ### XXXIV

If an ox or cow kills another, the living animal and the dead one shall belong jointly to the masters.

### XXXV

If a bull kills a cow or ox, the first offense shall incur no liability; for a second offense, he shall pay compensation.

### XXXVI

If someone is brought to judgment by a judge or elders in order to swear an oath, and recognizes that it will do him no good, if he wishes to avoid it, we order that he nevertheless remain bound by this law.

### XXXVII

If someone who has committed an offense voluntarily comes to a priest for confession, we order that he be condemned by no one, provided that he restores what he took from others. If he has been convicted by someone else and is rebellious, he shall restore the price of the thing taken and shall know that he must pay threefold.

But if a layman brings a case against a cleric, [Col. 1323B] the bishops shall judge between them in court. If a cleric brings a case against a layman, they must come before the judge’s authority.

### XXXVIII

If someone leaves an inheritance at death, whatever he has entrusted in the presence of witnesses, we order all of it to remain in force, unless it is unjust.

### XXXIX

If someone gives a male slave, female slave, or native servant his freedom and liberty of his own will, no one shall be permitted to reclaim him.

### XL

If someone voluntarily gives any thing to another, we order that the recipient possess it as his private property.

### XLI

If a case has once been judged, we permit no one to judge it again.

### XLII

If a dispute arises concerning the boundary of a territory, witnesses shall be sought, and the boundary that previously existed shall remain.

[Col. 1323C] ### XLIII

If a cleric is brought into a case and has previously borne no infamy, the case shall be concluded by his oath. But if he previously bore infamy, jurors shall be appointed, and he shall weigh the case in the manner of a layman.

### XLIV

If someone summons a guarantor and then despises him, he shall be condemned according to the condition of the judgment.

### XLV

If someone buys a field or village and himself commits a capital theft, he shall die. The land he bought shall revert to the treasury. But if a son or brother, having received it as a gift, likewise commits theft and flees, he shall return a maidservant and a male slave to the treasury and possess the field in exile. If he remains innocent, let the heir be left to the inheritance.

[Col. 1323D] ### XLVI

If someone brings weapons into a church and commits a quarrel, he shall be compelled to pay one pound of silver to the church; this may be counted as alms for the needy, or he may be permitted [to do so].

### XLVII

If someone gives his daughter to a husband, he shall receive the lawful dowry. But if, by chance, death takes the husband and she wishes to marry another man, the sons shall receive the dowry. If she has no sons, it is ordered that it be given to her father.

### XLVIII

If someone buys a maidservant or male slave and a defect appears in the person before the year is complete, we order that the person be returned to his own master. But if the year has passed, whatever defect is seen in the slave shall provide no grounds for rejection.

[Col. 1324A] ### XLIX

If someone buys a horse and it has no defect up to a month later, it shall in no way be rejected.

### L

If someone strikes another and draws blood, he shall pay a cow; and if he inflicts a greater wound, we order that compensation be made according to judgment.

### LI

If someone takes another’s horse away from a robber, he shall receive an ounce if it is worth a pound of silver; but if it is worth less, he shall receive half an ounce.

### LII

If someone apprehends another’s fleeing maidservant and she is able to escape from her master, he shall properly receive a “pond of iron” [the text is uncertain].

### LIII

If someone does not report another’s horse, and he himself is able to capture it, he ought to give an ounce. No one shall consume another’s forest, *lessa*, or *alga*.

[Note: [Col. 1323] Among the English, *lessa* is land or a tenement received by lease. *Alga* is a plant growing in water.]

If he does this seriously, we order him to pay compensation for the act itself.

[Col. 1324B] ### LIV

If someone takes another’s horse and it falls into a trap, we order that he restore it to its rightful owner.

### LV

If someone wishes to sell a capital village to a threatening neighbor or voluntarily, or a house or garden, he shall have the power to do so, together with the fences that produce crops and grass.

### LVI

If a cleric strikes a layman, he shall unquestionably pay for the layman’s wound according to the layman’s order.

### LVII

If a layman strikes a cleric, let him redeem his hand according to the laws stated and do penance.

[Col. 1324C] ### LVIII

If someone is wounded while intervening in a quarrel, and a liar strikes him, he shall know that he must pay according to the wound. But if the striker is truthful, we order that the truthful and the liar each pay half in the same manner. We have likewise decreed concerning death.

### LIX

If someone, by the lawful will of the fathers, joins a wife to his son and, in addition, presumes to keep a slave-concubine for himself, he shall be excluded from the Church of God and from every Christian table, unless he is recalled to penance.

### LX

If someone wishes to keep his own maidservant in marriage, and has authority over his property, he may not later sell her if he wishes to do so. But if he wishes to sell her, we order him to be condemned, [Col. 1324D] and we place that maidservant under the authority of the priest.

### LXI

If a Catholic lets his hair grow in the barbarian manner, he shall be regarded as alienated from the Church of God and from every Christian table until he corrects the offense.

### LXII

If a dog eats anything, for the first offense nothing shall be paid on its account except the dog itself. But if it offends again, the dog’s master shall repay what it has eaten.

# THE CANONS OF ADOMNAN BEGIN

### I

Sea animals carried onto the shores, whose deaths [Col. 1325A] we do not know, may be taken in good faith, unless they are rotten.

### II

Animals falling from a cliff, if their blood has been spilled, may be taken. But if their bones are broken and blood has not flowed out, they are to be rejected.

### III

Animals that have died in the waters as carrion, whose blood remains inside, and animals caught by beasts while half-alive, may be taken by bestial men.

### IV

An animal prepared for sudden death, with its ear or another part cut off, is carrion.

### V

If pigs eat carrion, the thick or fatty flesh that is carrion and by which the pigs grow fat must be vomited up. But when they have declined and returned to their former leanness—

### VI

If they have eaten carrion once or three times, after this has passed, the contents of their bellies may be taken in [Col. 1325B] good faith.

### VII

Pigs that taste human flesh or blood are always unlawful. For in the law a horned animal, if it kills a human being, is unlawful.

### VIII

If a horse or animal strikes a person in the field belonging to its city, it shall pay half an ounce for the person whose blood has been spilled. If a person strikes an animal in his own field, nothing shall be paid on its account.

# THE CONCISE JUDGMENTS FROM BOOK III BEGIN

## On two brothers and two sisters

### I

If a man marries two sisters, or a woman two brothers, they shall be cast out from communion until death. Nevertheless, at the end of life, out of mercy, if they allow the bonds of this union to be dissolved while they are still unharmed, they shall undertake penance. But if they fail to do so, penance is difficult for those who remain in such marriages.

### II

If someone among the clergy or ministers of God starts a quarrel, he shall do penance for a week on measured bread and water, and ask forgiveness from God and his neighbor with full confession and humility, thus asking to be reconciled with God and his neighbor.

### III

If someone rises up in a scandalous spirit and resolves in his heart to strike or kill his neighbor, then, if he is a cleric, he shall do penance for half a year on measured bread and water, abstain from wine and meat for a full year, and thus be reconciled to the altar.

[Col. 1325D] ### IV

But if he is a layman, he shall do penance for a week, because he is a man of this world, and his guilt is lighter in this world and his reward smaller in the future.

### V

But if he is a cleric and strikes his brother or neighbor and spills his blood, it is one sin, as though he had killed him, but the penance is not the same. He shall do penance for a full year on bread and water and without the ministry of the clerical office. He ought to pray with weeping and tears, and shall obtain mercy from God, because Scripture says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:13); how much more one who has struck him?

[Col. 1326A]

VI. If he is a layman, let him do penance for forty days, and let him give money when the priest, or any just person, has judged it appropriate. A cleric, however, ought not to give money either to him or to that person. Therefore let him do penance with the necessary supplication.

VII. Whoever has turned back, groaned in repentance, and entered into a covenant with God: on that day his sins, which he committed in the world, will not be remembered.

VIII. If any cleric, or any sorcerous woman, deceives someone by magic, let the offender do penance for seven years, three of them with bread and water, and during the remaining years abstain from wine and meat.

IX. But if the offender has not deceived anyone, yet has given something to someone for the sake of enticing love, let the offender do penance for a full year with bread and water.

X. If any woman by her magic causes another woman to lose her child, let her do penance for half a year with bread and water, abstain from wine and meat for two years, and fast for three Lents on bread and water. But if the woman has borne a son, let her do penance for three years, as we have said concerning a cleric.

## CANONS OF THE SYNOD OF IRELAND

[In the following canons, *arreum* denotes a commutation of a period of penance.]

A year’s *arreum*: three days and nights without sitting or sleeping, except briefly; or 150 psalms with ten canticles, standing and praying at every hour; also twelve genuflections are to be made at every hour of prayer, with the palms raised above in prayer.

A year’s *arreum*: three days with a holy dead man in one tomb, without food or drink and without sleeping, girded in one’s garment, with the chanting of psalms and the observance of the hours, after confession to the priest and after the vow.

A year’s *arreum*: three days in a church without sleeping, with one’s garment around oneself, without sitting, and with the chanting of psalms and canticles without interruption; a Mass at every hour, and twelve prostrations at every hour, after confession of sins before the priest and the people and after the vow.

A year’s *arreum*: twelve three-day periods.

A year’s *arreum*: twelve days and nights on twelve measured pieces of bread made from three loaves.

A year’s *arreum*: one month in great distress, but one from which no one dies; life is thereafter resumed at the priest’s judgment.

A year’s *arreum*: forty days and nights on bread and water, with two additional observances each week, forty psalms, and forty prostrations at each hour of prayer.

A year’s *arreum*: fifty days and nights on bread and water, with sixty psalms as the measure and sixty prostrations at each hour of prayer.

A year’s *arreum*: one hundred days on bread and water, with a Mass at every hour of prayer. Their penance is to be carried out for as long as the *arreum* prescribed above lasts, without meat, wine, butter, or sweet milk.

Whoever has sinned with a dog or with any animal: two and a half years.

Whoever commits a man’s crime, as sodomites do, shall do penance for four years. But whoever [commits it] with those below shall do penance for three years, entirely on bread and water, if after the vow of perfection; but if before it, one year is to be subtracted in each of these three cases.

# ETHELVOLF THE MONK’S POEM ON THE ABBOTS AND PIOUS MEN OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT PETER ON THE ISLAND OF LINDISFARNE

*(From Mabillon, Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict.)*

[Col. 1327]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 1327A]

1. Among the ancients, I find no one who wrote about Ethelvolf the monk, author of this poem, before Harpsfeld and Pitseus. The former calls him Ethelvolf of Lindisfarne, while the latter calls him a monk of the monastery of Saint Peter among the Bernicians. Ethelvolf dedicated his poem on the abbots of his monastery to Egbert, bishop of Lindisfarne—that is, the successor of Higbald—who governed the Church of Lindisfarne for eighteen years from the year 802, as Turgot the monk testifies in Book II, chapter 5, *On the Church of Durham*. Besides this poem, the author wrote some material on the history of the English, as is clear from the following chapter, 16. He entered the monastery of Saint Peter with Wulfsige, who later became abbot, according to chapter 18; and therefore, according to chapter 22, he had first Gotfrid (whom Pitseus calls Eadfrid) and then Iglac as his teachers. Ethelvolf clearly indicates his own age not only in the dedication of his poem to Egbert, but also in chapters 17 and 18. In the final chapter he signs himself “Lupus Clarus” (“Bright Wolf”), which is the interpretation of the name Ethelvolf or Edilvolf. Pitseus divides the following book, which is a single work, into three parts, and falsely supposed that Egbert, to whom this poem was dedicated, was the archbishop of York.

[Col. 1327B]

2. I cannot easily determine whose monastery Ethelvolf was a monk of, and therefore whose abbots he commemorates here. The inscription and conclusion of the poem prove him to have been a monk of the Church of Lindisfarne; indeed, so does Ethelvolf’s own inscription, in which Edilvolf, a monk of the Church of Lindisfarne, dedicates the work to Bishop Egbert. But many considerations prevent me from believing that this Church was the one inhabited by Saint Aidan, the Irish bishop, and the other monks of that people.

First, Aidan built the monastery of Lindisfarne long before Duke Eandmund, whom Ethelvolf calls the founder of his monastery. Second, after his own monastery had already been begun, Eandmund came to Lindisfarne to Bishop Ecgfrid, according to chapter 5, in order to be instructed by him in monastic matters and to receive a teacher suitable for his own establishment. Ecgfrid agreed and granted Eandmund a priest from his monastery, who was to establish monastic rules and train the new monks in Eandmund’s cell.

[Col. 1327C]

Third, the abbots of Lindisfarne were altogether different from the abbots of Eandmund’s monastery. Eata, abbot of Melrose, presided over Lindisfarne by right in the time of Saint Cuthbert. Perhaps he was succeeded by Guthfrid, the venerable servant and priest of Christ, abbot of Lindisfarne, praised by Bede in Book V, chapter 1 of his *History*. Tilhed is also mentioned as abbot in the eighth century in the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, p. 39. But after Eandmund, the monastery was governed by Eorpuin, Aldwin, Sigbald, Sigwin, and Wulfsige, all in the eighth century.

Fourth, at the place where Eandmund’s monastery stood, there was at that time a city with clergy, according to chapter 20. I fear that this cannot be said of the monastery of Lindisfarne, which I think was then isolated. Fifth, Ethelvolf describes the location of his church in chapter 6 in a way that can scarcely be attributed to Lindisfarne. Finally, all the authors who have deliberately treated the monastery of Lindisfarne make no mention of Eandmund or of the other abbots and monks named here, as is evident from Turgot and from the *Monasticum Anglicanum*.

[Col. 1327D]

Nevertheless, both places had a church dedicated to Saint Peter. Theodore had dedicated Lindisfarne to Saint Peter, according to the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, p. 39; Eandmund’s church likewise had Saint Peter as its patron, as appears from the following chapters, 4 and 6, and an oratory of blessed Mary was attached to it, as appears from chapter 14.

Let whoever can untie these knots do so; for my part, it will be enough to have set them out. Perhaps, however, it may be said that there were two monasteries on the island of Lindisfarne, one founded by Aidan and the other by Eandmund. Yet Eandmund’s monastery seems to have been on the mainland, since Eandmund crossed from it to Lindisfarne to visit Bishop Ecgfrid, according to chapter 5. In any event, Eandmund’s monastery was situated either on the island of Lindisfarne or certainly nearby, so that Ethelvolf could call it Lindisfarne’s monastery; unless one thinks it was so called because Eandmund received the teacher of his institution from the monastery of Lindisfarne, just as New Corbie among the Saxons derived its name from Old Corbie in Gaul.

At one time it occurred to me that this might be the island of Farne, lying to the southeast of Lindisfarne; but there was no city there, only a few small huts built by Saint Cuthbert for one or two solitaries.

[Col. 1328B]

3. Whatever the solution to this difficulty may be, it is certain that many monks distinguished for piety flourished in Eandmund’s monastery, besides the six abbots mentioned above. Among them was Ultan, an excellent writer, praised in chapter 8, whose body was shortly after his death lifted from the tomb as an act of veneration. There were also the priest Fridegils, Cuicuin the smith, Merchdof, the priest and lector Iglac, and the priest Winfrid, whose deeds Ethelvolf briefly recounts here.

4. It may be regarded as certain that the writer Ultan praised in chapter 8 is different both from Ultan, the brother of Saint Fursey the abbot, and from Ultan, who wrote about the deeds of the Irish virgin Saint Brigit. The two former men lived in the seventh century, whereas the Lindisfarne Ultan flourished in the eighth.

That Ultan, the author of the *Life of Saint Brigit*, was different from the other contemporary Ultan may be inferred from the fact that Ultan, Fursey’s brother, was abbot of Peronne in Gaul and died there, while the other was bishop of Ardbraccan in the Irish region of Meath, as John Colganus relates from an ancient author.

Chilienus the monk discusses him in the metrical *Life of Saint Brigit*, published by Bollandus in the first volume for February. Its prologue is lacking; it is useful to reproduce it here from a manuscript of the Remigius monastery at Reims. This codex, identified as having been written during the pontificate of Ebbo, bishop of Reims, contains certain sermons of Saint Augustine on the Psalms, the *Enchiridion*, and the book *On the Quantity of the Soul*, together with several verses rashly attributed to him. Among these is the prologue to the aforementioned metrical *Life*, mixed in without any title with the others. It runs as follows:

## POEM

Be pleased to be present, gracious holy Virgin,

Brigit, favorable to the power of your suppliants.

If life remains my companion, you will surely know this:

that through my praises you have shone forth in heaps of glory.

[Col. 1328D]

No less than Ultan’s will our praises, O holy Virgin,

serve the devout peoples.

He was a great bishop, suited to virtues;

I shall follow and surpass him, if you grant me aid.

Thus Aileran extracted many things about your deeds

and wrote the flowers of your works in splendid volumes.

[Col. 1329A]

I shall not pass him over, if he happens to pass over it,

although he himself climbed the episcopal ranks.

For Cogitosus too, if justice prevails with you as judge,

will be utterly unequal to our undertaking.

But why should I surpass such great Fathers by my gift?

I alone shall disclose the blessed deeds of three.

And what the outstanding Fathers had published in prose,

I shall now set to music in verse.

Now accompany the path I have begun, and guard your servant;

be pleased, O maiden suited to the heavenly choirs.

And may Christ, who granted the beginning of the work,

bring it to a completed end.

[Col. 1330A]

Not because I am worthy, a sinner, to speak of such things,

but I pray, unworthy as I am, that I may become worthy.

From these verses, written in the time of Ebbo, we understand that the poet—whether he was Chilienus or someone else—lived before the ninth century, and therefore that the word *Comitissa* (“countess”), which he used, had already been accepted before that time. But these are incidental matters.

Now Ethelvolf’s poem must be presented. Thomas Gaelus, a man of singular learning and refinement, sent it to me from a manuscript in Cambridge; I confess that I already owe him much other material.

[Col. 1329]

## THE POEM BEGINS

### PREFACE OF ETHELVOLF, MONK OF THE CHURCH OF LINDISFARNE, TO EGBERT, BISHOP OF LINDISFARNE, ON THE ABBOTS OF THAT CHURCH

[Col. 1329B]

To the most excellent and beloved of friends, the great priest Egbert, presbyter [Note: [Col. 1329D] Here you see the name *presbyter* added to the title of the supreme priest—a novel usage; or should it read *episcopo*, “bishop”?], Ethelvolf, insignificant in merits, a monk of the Church of Lindisfarne, sends the greeting of deepest love.

Receive, Father, the peaceful vows of a poet in measured song,

so that with the eternal King you may obtain rest,

and seek the heavenly citadels through your shining merits.

Now, most excellent bishop, willingly remember always,

as you ascend the holy scepters of the heavenly realms,

your reward—though the transmitted reading is problematic (*calvus*, “bald,” in the phrase concerning its repayment)—

through all the seasons of your life, night and day alike.

May lofty mercy protect you and yours together.

[Col. 1329C]

Through it immense honor, shining throughout all ages,

glows with wondrous light in all the saints.

With body, mind, hand, and all the senses together,

now worshiping the lofty Lord “without faith” (*sine fide*; the reading is problematic), farewell.

### CHAPTER I. The poet’s greeting to the bishop concerning his kinsmen and the monks of his cell

When the holy hand, through your excellence, restored you to the English,

it pleased you now to accept rustic gifts.

But if rustic hearts sweat with foolish words,

rustic strings will not produce a foolish poem.

For when nobles, marked out from your own blood,

are pleasing to the Lord, you receive great joys.

Receive, learned Father, the gift of your beloved friend,

and sing thanks to Christ always and everywhere,

that shepherds pleasing to their Lord

have deserved to be born from so chosen a stock.

[Col. 1329D]

Nor should you be less willing to marvel

that monks renowned for the gift of their forebears

climb the path of light.

If among these chaste men you find anything worthy

of making you give thanks, I now especially urge you:

give thanks to the Lord.

But if otherwise, graciously deign to grant pardon

to the poet: he sang what ... [printed *notuit* is corrupt; *novit*, “he knew,” or *potuit*, “he could,” would be conjectures].

For I desire to provide this rest for your labor:

these songs, which resound as sacrifices consecrated to the Lord.

[Col. 1330A]

Whatever I advise that is burdensome, endure it modestly,

[Col. 1330B]

and let it stir no complaint in your heart.

May your mind kindly receive rest forever,

in pious prosperity in the Lord Christ.

### CHAPTER II. How, having gained the kingdom, Horret persecuted many

While Ecgfrid fell beneath the hostile sword of the Picts,

behold, Alfrid, the illegitimate brother of the English,

took possession of the kingdom

and begot a son who was renowned by name; [Note: [Col. 1329D] Bede calls this man Aldfrid, who must be distinguished from his brother Alchfrid, as I showed in the *Eulogy of Saint Cuthburga* under the year 724. Aldfrid died in 705.]

[Note: [Col. 1330D] He is called Horret in the heading; William of Malmesbury calls him Osred, in Book I, chapter 3 of *On the Kings of the English*: “Who, casting the kingdom into shadow for eleven years and leading a disgraceful life through sexual violations of nuns, was finally slain by the plots of his kinsmen.”]

and shone among the Saxon peoples, preserving the kingdom,

energetic in deeds, words, and every action.

But from his earliest years he was not restrained;

an undisciplined young man, he did not know how

to bend his wanton impulses to reason,

despising the laws of the Thunderer.

[Col. 1330C]

Excessively mighty in arms, he was bold in his own strength.

He did not honor the nobles; finally, he did not worship Christ

as was fitting. Instead, alas, he subjected his whole life

to empty actions, as long as life remained in his body.

Therefore his present age was brief,

and he could not prolong his life for long.

Thus he killed many by a pitiable death.

But he forced others to serve the supreme Father

and to remain tonsured within the enclosures of a monastery.

### CHAPTER III. How Eandmund was noble in birth and character

Among these there was a venerable shepherd named Eandmund,

that pious man joined to Christ’s companions,

who, through his deeds in the world, pressed on toward the promised rewards

which the saints receive in heaven by God’s gift.

[Col. 1330D]

Noble, and descended from a very lofty line,

he was celebrated among the peoples with the highest honor.

More noble still before the supreme Lord because of the height of his mind,

he was a venerable duke. The almighty Father,

who fashions all bodies and cleanses human minds

by removing their thorns, had made his heart pure.

Devoted with great love, he abandoned sterile military service

and served throughout his life the great Ruler

who governs all ages.

### CHAPTER IV. How, tonsured for the service of the Lord, he went to his own monastery

[Col. 1331A]

While the tyrant was slaughtering the nobles of the English excessively [Note: [Col. 1331D] This is why many lay men and women built monasteries and withdrew into them, not without the disrepute of a secular and shameful life, as Bede testifies in his letter to Egbert, bishop of York],

the aforesaid soldier entered the service of the Lord.

He rejoiced to carry upon his head the crown

which Christ once bore upon his abundant head,

when, suffering for the world, he removed the thorns of evil

and caused his blessed ones to visit life.

Nor did he alone deserve to seize the heavenly shield.

Indeed, many chosen men accompanied that same Father

and attempted to submit themselves to the Lord in the monastery.

Eandmund served Christ the gracious Lord with what he had given,

and likewise served Peter, who makes all the hosts

that render pure hearts through heavenly deeds

shine throughout all ages with flower-bearing sheaves.

[Col. 1331B]

When the Father gathered many servants into the gracious cell,

he adorned them all with sacred teachings.

The shepherd urged them to desire at least to serve their Lord,

seeking merit from the divine power,

so that the holy angel, coming from heaven with joy,

might deign to keep these servants safe;

so that the fierce wolf would not tear those subject to him,

infected by savage teeth and bites,

with sorrowful heart, but rather, strengthened by virtues

worthy of the Lord and adorned on every side,

would carry them across into the regions of light.

Instructing them in such matters, the leader taught his flock

how he might present shining sheep to Christ,

and how he might offer pious lambs to the Lamb,

who came to take away the sin of the guilty world

and made the innocent world pure by his shed blood.

[Col. 1331C]

### CHAPTER V. How, approaching the bishop, he acquired a teacher of the regular life

The pontifical summit, illustrious through the gift of merits,

was occupied by Ecgfrid [Note: [Col. 1331D] He was bishop of Lindisfarne after Eadbert, Cuthbert’s successor; he died in the year 721.], who governed the realms of the saints.

To him the shores desire to curl their pale streams,

and strive to lay bare their retreating channels,

surrounding the holy land with blue waters [Note: [Col. 1331D] That is, the holy island, or Lindisfarne, which “twice each day, when the tide of the Ocean comes in, becomes an island, and twice, when the shores are laid bare, is restored to the mainland,” as Bede says in chapter 17 of his book *On the Life of Saint Cuthbert*.],

and opening a path for the traveler when they uncover the shores.

The servant of the Lord hastened to visit him,

seeking that nourishment from the heavenly harvest

be granted to him. With ready mind the priest

opened saving words from his understanding heart

and watered the thirsty body with pious rains.

[Col. 1331D]

He drank in with attentive ears what the priest poured forth

from the depths of his heart; beneath his own breast

he received the mystical words and learned them

with keen understanding.

Moreover, gathering up what had to be transmitted by memory,

he examined everything and embraced it within the senses of his heart.

Therefore he added to his own community a suitable teacher.

[Col. 1332A]

He was a priest who established monastic laws

and instructed these new monks, reviewing the safeguards of the ancients,

whom the author of the spirit had carried to heaven.

### CHAPTER VI. How he sent a messenger to Christ’s monk

While this servant of Christ was learning that the gracious bishop

Ecgbert [Note: [Col. 1332D] It is clear from this that this Egbert, whose notice I gave under the year 729, was a bishop, although, so far as I know, he was attached to no Church; on this matter I had formerly been uncertain. At that time he was staying in the monastery called Rathmelsigi in the language of the Irish. In 723 he was transferred to Iona, where he died in 729.]

was in the lands of the Irish,

he arranged to send him a faithful servant,

asking that he properly train the monks through written rules,

consecrate an altar for him with a venerable tablet,

and, mindful of his vow, show which places were suitable

for sacred shrines to be established for the Thunderer.

The venerable bishop obeyed and complied. He strengthened the man who was going

with his words, and also enriched him with a sacred gift.

The altar-table, consecrated to the great God

under the name of Peter, came swiftly,

[Col. 1332B]

and strengthened the cell against the black enemy.

Moreover, the bishop sent the following words to the petitioner:

“Remember, brother, to keep the course of your life with blameless steps,

and to preserve your life with a chaste heart,

so that, when the struggle of the impending battle is exhausted,

you may gain the everlasting rest of heaven without end.

I confess that I have never seen with bodily sight

the lands that the Lord grants you as a great gift.

But as far as the sight of my heart was able to reach,

there is a not very high hill, bent along a sloping path,

over which the rising sun flies during the seasons of the balancing scales;

thick thorn bushes with foliage crown it.

Remember, brother, to remove these severed thorns, with all their growth,

from the level ground and ridge of the aforesaid place.

[Col. 1332C]

And in that place thus build a beautiful chapel for the Lord,

where believing hearts may pay vows

from a prayerful breast, night and day alike.”

After these words the messenger thrust his vessel through the blue waters

and hurried to carry the speech of the beloved bishop

to his Father; he reported the prophet’s words.

Then the pious man completed the roof of the beautiful temple,

covering its exterior boards with a layer of lead,

and with all his strength took care to make it ornate.

This house of the Lord—an altar beneath the central mound, as we have said—was established on earth by heavenly grace. The intervening transmitted wording, including *quae gignit odores praemites*, is corrupt or uncertain. It blazes everywhere with bright radiance, while temples to the Father of heaven and earth rise amid the ancient wild places.

While he was arranging to report these deeds to his teacher,

the messenger came to the father of the father to convey the words

and spoke thus to his pious teacher.

[Col. 1332D]

“Ecgberht, the servant of the Lord, greets you with his own voice,

and likewise your monks, whom the gentle grace of Christ,

calling them a Church, has gathered into one.

Night and day alike I do not cease to give thanks

to the supreme Ruler, who strengthens the vows of his people.

[Col. 1333A]

For I confess that I say no falsehood:

often the wicked crowd flies in and mingles with these thorns,

always trusting in weapons, streaming together from every side,

as when a crowd rushing forward hastens to plunge into these thorns.

It rejoices, always massed beneath its weapons in adversity,

and arranges many ambushes, having accomplished its deed . . . , gnashing its teeth.

It does not cease to carry the evil ones along the difficult road,

where eternal toil grants no rest to the traveler.

But thanks be to the Lord, because in our time

these places have deserved through the Lord to receive such great joys

and to exchange their former inhabitants for new settlers.

Therefore I urge all to heap magnificent praises

upon the lofty Thunderer and, with hands stretched toward the stars,

give thanks to the Lord, who sends winged birds

to answer the vows of the pious.

They hasten to the enclosure of the chapel and, borne by innumerable prayers, pass to the stars before God. The following transmitted clause—*quae fuerant pendentes, quas tamen ipse pandat* (“which had been hanging, which nevertheless he himself may reveal”)—is syntactically corrupt or uncertain.

Why should I recount everything? With the light the ministers come

from heaven above, and carry holy souls to the stars;

they praise the Lord, shining in the light,

and raise everlasting, flower-bearing crowns upon their heads.”

### CHAPTER VII. How the arrival of the messenger increased the joys of the shepherd and the brothers

While the messenger was beginning to recount these things of the poet,

Father Eandmund rejoiced with great joy in his rejoicing heart,

and gave thanks to God toward the stars.

He strove to shape his people with perfected words,

so that they might desire to hasten toward blessed life,

which in heaven can never reach an end.

Strengthened by such blessings, the monks’ hearts grow green;

the pious begin to outstrip one another in following Christ,

in gracious deeds, words, and every sense.

One, desiring to pass the night without sleep,

does not cease to stretch out holy hands in prayer.

Another, beating the marble pavement of the church with his knees,

endures the cold in icy nights; while he remains amid the fires,

he avoids the great cold.

Another, desiring to distribute his perishable riches,

wisely steals away time and hours during the dark nights

and stores up the talents entrusted to him in heaven.

Another, giving the wretched the solace of bread,

endures hunger and carries through the holy fasts.

[Col. 1333D]

Adorned with such virtues, illustrious in white garments

but interwoven with varied colors,

the Virgin and Mother appears to stand at the right hand,

she who by the power of the Ruler bears both heaven and earth.

### CHAPTER VIII. A few remarkable deeds of Father Ultan

Fame names many who lead a perfected life,

which Father Eandmund adorns with highly cultivated character.

Among them is Ultan, called by a distinguished name [Note: [Col. 1333D] This Ultan is different from Ultan, the brother of Saint Fursey, likewise an Irishman, as is clear from what has been said. He was discussed in the Second Age and is entered in the Benedictine Martyrology on 8 August. Hence, what is the date here?].

This priest was a blessed man of the Scottish race,

who could adorn books with polished letters
