and make the appearance of the characters render life itself beautiful.

[Col. 1334A]

Through this art no contemporary writer

could equal him. Nor is it surprising if such things could be done

by a worshiper of the Lord, when the Holy Spirit himself,

the author, guided his fingers and kindled his consecrated mind toward the stars.

Thus he used to visit the cell of his beloved Father,

entering and joining himself to the gracious assemblies,

and skillfully forming the monks in holy conduct:

chaste in understanding and words, in flesh and heart.

He instructed the brothers to seize the lofty lights

and strive to serve God throughout all their days,

so that in body they might enjoy the present life.

When this elect brother, filled with perfected time,

had spent many years celebrating such things for God,

at last, worn out by old age, the writer changed his earthly life

for a better one, without changing the joys of life.

[Col. 1334B]

When the earth had long gnawed at his body’s organs,

the brothers decided to raise his ashes from the tomb.

After washing the bones, they carried the remains

in clean linen into the sunlight. Suddenly two birds arrived;

they touched the linen with their feet. Their backs,

blended together in varied colors, shone with venerable beauty,

and they sang songs with their beaks.

Beautiful, they joined together in wondrous joy for all,

and moreover covered the holy skull with their wings [conjectural *alis*, “wings”; printed *aliis*, “others”].

Thus throughout the whole day they did not cease

to perform their service for the pious bones

and pour forth songs of great beauty,

until the light of the sun had wiped away all moisture

and dried the remains from the damp.

Then a certain brother, half within the shadow of death,

lay for some time; disease consumed his body,

[Col. 1334C]

and he could move no limb,

except the instrument of his tongue, which could scarcely utter words.

Lying weak, he said this to a boy:

“Run, I beg you, and bring me the arm of the Father,

with which he deserved already to paint the mystical words of the Lord.

By its sign I may be able to avoid the present danger,

or at least may Christ, through the merits of the holy man,

deign to release my sins, if I am doomed to enter

the funerals of death and deserve to ascend the path of life.”

The boy obeyed and ran to the holy linen.

He took away the pious gift and carried it back in his arms.

He brought the bone (*os*) near the dying man’s head,

and the grip of death was dissolved;

he cured the sick man by heavenly power.

Immediately the man rose, strengthened with such great force

that he could carry the healer who had healed him.

[Col. 1334D]

Then, joyful and flying from there, he carried the ruler to the linen

and gave thanks to God for so great a gift.

But a company of brothers, gathered into one number,

carried the holy bones of the pious man beneath the temple roof.

Then the melodious birds mingled with the high clouds

and avoided human sight for all time.

Meanwhile the ashes were placed with songs

within the gracious interior of the shrine;

but the rejoicing spirit now remains above the stars,

praising the Lord throughout the ages.

### CHAPTER IX. On Fridegils, the priest of Christ

There was another brother, called by the name Fridegils,

a priest and a priest of God with a pure mind.

He prepared wondrous gifts: the altars smoked with offerings,

and magnificent gifts exalted the blessed man above the stars.

In doctrine and deeds alike he was wondrous in all things,

and he shone adorned with the great grace of merits.

Strengthened by such men, the monks’ joys flourish,

and the good shepherd’s budding vows grow green.

### CHAPTER X. On the brother Cuicuin the smith

Let us be permitted to remember the brother in wondrous words,

who, mastering iron, was able to shape metals,

while the wise hammer, in various ways, subdued upon the anvil,

struck the iron amid the shrieking forge.

This Cuicuin had been called by his father’s care.

The grace of merits endows this man with life,

and crowned his own with great honor [the printed *claram*, “bright,” is left grammatically unattached in this damaged line].

[Col. 1335B]

The pious man drives away all crimes from his chaste body,

and with all his strength strives to observe Christ’s commands

in body, mind, hand, and all his senses together,

night and day alike.

He burns for true joys and, eager to acquire his own gain,

gives it generously to the needy with his hands.

Indeed, he continually carries through whole days of fasting,

as though he were celebrating the solemnities of the saints of the Lord.

While the brothers celebrate hymns in sacred harmony at night

and again begin to visit their resting places,

the brother mentioned above dwells within the enclosure of the chapel.

He does not spare his limbs from striking the marble,

and diligently entrusts himself to God and to the stars.

And again the brothers come with the light of Phoebus,

[Col. 1335C]

and desire to entrust themselves to the Lord with abundant prayers.

Joined to the holy assemblies, he delighted to recite psalms;

he commends himself to the Lord, and when the morning psalms

have been completed, how well the hammer immediately resounded

upon the struck metal, flying through the empty air as it beat.

The heat of the forge, striking the evening meal, now adorns the brothers.

While the holy man carried out such things for many years,

at last, when all labor had ceased,

the blessed brother deserved to pass into peaceful rest.

For while illnesses troubled his strong body,

a choir came from heaven with flashing light

and hastened to visit the cell of the blessed shepherd.

They took the chaste soul from its chaste body.

[Col. 1335D]

It shone exceedingly, already surpassing the sun’s lights,

and, flying with the choir, entered the heavenly citadels.

When the monk Aethuin saw this, he began to give thanks

and commended the soul to the Lord among the stars.

Therefore, when they ascend the lofty thresholds of the sun,

the angelic companies, singing their songs, close heaven

at once; from there the soul enters to receive everlasting rest,

mingled with chaste flower-bearing sheaves.

### CHAPTER XI. On the brother who, drawn from the flesh, came to life again

There was a certain brother under the holy rule of the cell,

illustrious in the world and called by the name Merchdof.

At a certain time, when illness troubled his body,

he departed from the world and, suffering, was brought

into unknown regions. The inner chambers of his heart burned,

[Col. 1336A]

and immense fear, shaking him, while threatening faces

through the darkness, terrified his soul in dense ranks;

troubled blasts assailed him in various ways.

When for a long time he was compelled, trembling,

to pass through sorrowful companies, suddenly men of shining faces

appeared to him. They had been born with tender bodies,

but illness had once driven them from the regions of life;

now blessed life had recently clothed them in white

and carried them into the heights.

When he saw them, he began to be steadier in mind,

and, rejoicing, went with them as his companions

to the judgment which the greatest judge assigns

from lofty seats to every soul departing.

With knees bent, he humbly begged him

to grant pardon to one unworthy. But he,

answering from his lofty seat, spoke thus:

[Col. 1336B]

“Since, transgressing, you placed the words of a wife first,

and did not flee while keeping faith with the marriage bed to which you had not pledged yourself,

why do you now, at the time of cold death,

ask that pardon be granted to you here,

where there is no time for pardon?”

But the children, likewise kneeling,

were preparing to call upon the nobleman for pardon for their father.

He, however, sternly ordered them to visit their lady, and according to his wife’s judgment the husband was either to receive pardon or undergo punishment.

Then, with their frightened father accompanying them,

the children hastened, exceedingly fearful, to the wife’s chambers.

They showed them from the lofty walls of the mountain’s citadel

the bright dwelling of the pious bride, shining greatly toward the stars.

The father entered, accompanied by his lofty children,

and the woman collapsed when she saw the children with her eyes.

She ordered the deceptive steps to turn away from the house.

The daughters rushed toward their mother’s holy face;

they moistened it with tears, lamenting their anger in fear,

and begged: “Mother, have mercy on us, we pray;

by the merits of your spouse, release him, joined to you,

from guilt.”

From her lofty seat, flashing radiant light,

covered over her whole body in golden garments,

rebuking her offspring (*semina*), she looked down upon her husband’s fate.

“Why, foolish man, corrupted in body and mind,

making your vows void, had you dared to contract a union,

staining your limbs in a second marriage bed [the word *natis*, “children,” in this damaged passage is syntactically unclear],

when each of you had made a covenant with the hands of the Lord

in the supreme name, before the day of death,

so that after the death of the other one might remain free from guilt?”

[Col. 1336D]

With his mouth closed, the man fell silent, his heart joyless,

and, terrified, immediately threw himself down and began

to lick the earth, covering his whole face with tears.

But she, repeating her command, ordered the fettered man

to enter the shadows of the prison,

until he had paid the full penalty for his crimes,

consumed too greatly in black flames.

The mother’s children, prostrate at her feet,

rushed about and begged in God’s name:

“Have mercy, we pray, or at least allow the husband to return to his body,

so that, living, he may deserve to expiate his crimes.”

The beloved mother consented in her troubled mind,

allowing the children to bring their father safely back to his body,

and warned him to examine his own life,

lest, coming again, he be hurled into darkness

because of his sins, where there will be perpetual shrieking and weeping.

[Col. 1337A]

Thus he was brought back again, accompanied by his white-clad children,

and reached the body, to the amazement of all,

living after death. Turned away from the regions of death,

he now learned through keen understanding how to live for Christ,

and prudently shows everyone by his life that he sees

the dreadful punishments, even should his bodily tongue fall silent.

When, as a healer, the brother applied a healing poultice

to his wounds, purified in body he left the place,

and, adorned, was believed to have deserved joyfully

to behold the inner chambers of his adorned bride.

### CHAPTER XII. On the death of Father Eandmund

After the shepherd mentioned above had long possessed the cell,

noble in eloquence and venerable in all his deeds,

when his time was full he left the company of the flesh

[Col. 1337B]

and, blessed, entered into the joys of his Christ.

Then the brotherhood placed the venerable limbs of their father

in a worthy tomb beneath the temple roof,

and, after pouring forth immense prayers with tears,

commended his soul to the Lord with sacred rites.

### CHAPTER XIII. On Eorpuin, Eandmund’s successor, and his brother Aldwin

Eorpuin succeeded him as shepherd of the entrusted flock,

an excellent priest, a devoted lover of the life.

Prudent in understanding and energetic in every action,

he gave riches to the monks with an open and generous heart,

to those whom yellow starvation oppressed,

and, in a wondrous manner, dispersed them toward certain rewards.

[The supplied source ends here, with the sentence incomplete.]

[Col. 1337C] Wealth increases; reverence for Christ is heaped up,

With gifts scattered throughout all the seasons of his life.

He was generous to the wretched, exceedingly sparing toward himself in all

Food; for he fed his body on dry provisions:

He had passed through entire days without taking any food,

Presenting his breast as a fast beneath his flying gaze.

Nor is it surprising if an outstanding prince does such things,

While greater men of goodness were present here, and these were lesser,

And while for many days they strove to render their fasts to Christ,

Lest the enemy deceive unwary minds by the sudden honor

Of virtue.

Often he himself fled through fear of the sacred people;

The faithful people were permitted to contend in accursed battles,

While Christ, granting aid from the citadel above, joined the struggle.

Thus the chosen seized from God a lofty triumph,

[Col. 1337D] And the black phalanxes judged their flight precipitous.

This pious pastor likewise completed his appointed time.

He deserved to leave his seat to a worthy kinsman.

This man had been called Alduinus by his earthly name;

In character he is true, and in all his words he stands forth,

A renowned standard-bearer, exhorting his subjects with his words,

That they might set their pious vows beyond the heavens before their prince.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Abbot Sigbald, and how he enriched the Church of Lindisfarne with many gifts and riches

The fourth pastor appears, Sigbald by his illustrious name,

A priest: he increased the monastery with many gifts,

And, zealous, founded a hall worthy of God.

This is that house which the mother of the lofty Godhead,

[Col. 1338A] Dwelling within it, preserves beneath the vault of the vast heaven.

Its joined table gleams with exceedingly beautiful panels;

In the middle stands a portico, which the saints crown with foliage,

While they close it with precious boxes containing the gifts of life.

On the western side the shining ministers gleam,

Who adorn the vault of heaven with measured harmonies.

All the saints in the middle of the chapel

Dwell there throughout all time, preserving it with handfuls

Without number; summoned to the vows of the pious,

They always defend what they receive through the merits of the saints,

If the faithful strive to hasten toward the palm of life.

Let someone count all the other lights throughout the church,

Which shine in the church and in heaven through true joys.

This priest granted God very many gifts.

This golden chalice gleams, covered with gems.

[Col. 1338B] And the gleaming silver work is fashioned in relief [on the paten].

[Note: That is, on the paten, as below, chapter 20, verse 53.]

Which that pious man gave to the hall of the great Mother.

Patched lead sheets cover the cottages with their lofty roofs.

Nor do the bronze vessels resound less joyfully for the brothers;

Bronze vessels rattle in their hollow forms, with hanging sistrums.

As the priest Sigbald entered this church with a pure mind

And prepared to visit it while celebrating Mass,

Drops of salt water began to run down from the heated springs;

The great ardor of Christ arouses them

From his pure breast, and his throat does not tremble in song.

Whenever he celebrated the holy day of the Virgin Mary—

Whether the day on which, flying, she deserved to enter the lofty heavens,

Or the day on which, born for the present world, she gave birth [to him],

Or the day on which she received the joys of exceedingly beautiful life,

Or the day on which she deserved to give birth to the Thunderer on his lofty throne,

[Col. 1338C] Or whatever day the sacred festivals of the church illumined—

On all these occasions, exceedingly joyful through holy gladness,

He restored the golden gifts of his sweet-sounding mind;

And he soothed the brothers with prayers, urging them

To celebrate the solemn festivals in honor of the pious Mother.

While this learned priest, happy through a long period,

Deserved to renew such deeds throughout the monastery,

He closed the road of this age, carried away to the halls of life.

## CHAPTER XV. On Abbot Sigwin, Sigbald’s brother and successor

After his brother had relinquished the rule of the monastery,

Sigwin, called by another name, assumed it.

He had been exceedingly generous to both the least and the greatest throughout

[Col. 1338D] His life; he bestowed riches upon the needy,

The riches which the exalted Lord had increased.

Someone had seen him, during the hours of the gloomy night,

Clothed in unusual garments, giving gifts

To wretched paupers, who, shut out at the gates, place their very cold bodies

To be warmed on the refuse heap.

And when the pious man had bestowed gleaming metal upon them,

He earnestly commanded them, entreating them by the realms of the highest Thunderer,

That they should tell no one of this throughout all the days of their lives.

But the wretched men swear that they would never tell,

For as long as they remain within the span of this present life.

When his brother saw this, while darkness thickened over the fields,

He hid himself, and, fleeing once, decided that such things

Could never be seen by anyone, since his eyes had once been able to behold them.

[Col. 1339A] And since he had always generously given to his beloved,

His riches increased in various parts of the land,

And the cultivated fields grew thick with abundant crops;

And the shepherds, having received a gift of every kind of livestock,

Did not know of any loss in the number of their flocks.

When the venerable festivals of God’s saints returned,

In two choirs beneath the vault of the church,

He mingled with the brothers and sang the psalms in song;

The sweet-sounding melodies of the antiphon poured forth.

Then the lector, resounding in articulate voice,

Well trained in the biblical books, poured forth great joys.

And when, as the day passed, they completed the chants of the Mass,

The brothers accompanied the Father to the table

With harmonious song. No one then could adequately describe

How eagerly he desired the solemn holy feasts,

[Col. 1339B] When the clergy in the city rejoiced in celebrating with their own,

And, rejoicing, filled the house with loud song.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the priest and lector Iglac

At the time when the illustrious lector, called Iglac by name,

Was accumulating worthy joys for the Father,

Of whom I spoke briefly some time ago,

While, ignorant and in every respect an unworthy writer,

I sang in verse of certain pious men of the English nation—

If anyone wishes to know these things with a learned understanding,

Let him hasten and, thirsting, plunge himself into these waters,

To the shores where the learned Father’s unlearned poems

Are celebrated; he will be able to speak of them worthily.

The present little page marks only these verses for me:

[Col. 1339C] That the Lord had surrounded the gracious table with his fingers,

And that abundant blessing descended upon the head of the saint.

Though he did not see with his eyes, he saw with a learned heart,

His spirit, deprived of the eyes of the flesh, perceiving the pious things.

He also looked out with the black eyes of his mind;

He had seen the King on high once more encircled by hands,

And, in an ecstasy of mind, a certain confessor in England

Saw a soul shining with the light of the sun.

If anyone wishes to know these things carefully throughout the world,

Let him now seek the passages mentioned above and plunge himself into their waters.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the brothers of the monastery and the death of the pastor

The priests, monks, and the rest of the brotherhood,

Whom the almighty Father granted me, unworthy though I was in my early years,

To see within the walls of the holy monastery—

Whom I myself, marveling at their wondrous deeds,

Certainly affirm to have become known in their own time—

May he not forbid his servants to imitate them in their sins;

While I still sing as a prophet, I believe that at last I shall obtain

The gifts of salvation through their prayers.

When the appointed time had been completed, the pastor had left his body

And entered the rest prepared for his merits and deeds.

The company entered in a great multitude,

And beneath the lofty cross which he himself had erected

They laid his members as a sign of sacred rest.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the priest and abbot Wulfsig

When this priest had completed his office, one called Wulfsig by name,

[Col. 1340A] He was compelled, at the pious request of the Church, to govern her camp.

At first the humble priest refused sadly,

Declaring that he was not worthy to undertake so great a burden;

But at last he rejoiced that his brother had conquered him by prayers,

And assumed the government of the rejoicing Church.

He was a humble man, strong in speech, and modest;

Very often he stretched out his pious limbs before the Lord in prayer.

To him I clung when, as a boy, I first entered

The walls of this present monastery to visit it;

Together we both sought the rest of a single house,

Until, after twice three years had passed,

The good pastor assumed the flock with modest piety.

During the dark nights, while the company of the brothers rested,

He sang hymns and psalms in frequent harmonies.

When Phoebus traverses the lowest heaven,

[Col. 1340B] He, wakeful according to his accustomed discipline,

Sang through the entire Psalter in order from his chaste breast.

And then, during the day, he completed the same psalms again,

So that in two cycles he might consume the lyrical food.

Then, rising again, while the bird proclaimed the hour,

He completed it in hymns with his accustomed red throat.

And when, in the middle of the day, the brothers began

To seek food, he, sparing of nourishment, withdrew from every meal,

And, bending his knees, beat the pavements of the chapel.

And Iris [the reading is uncertain], well adorned with divine songs,

Offers [sacrifice] to him who frees the world from evil death.

He refused to let any day pass

Without adorning himself by standing before the Lord with an abundant gift.

And when, desiring food, he instructed his body to seek it,

He embraced all that was sufficient for him in due measure,

[Col. 1340C] Despising the taking of anything beyond what was just.

By these good examples the monks’ joys increased,

And they desired to heap their prayers upon their own father.

While the pastor accomplished such things, perfected in only a few—

Alas!—years, having led his life to its blessed end,

He left his body. Accompanied by shining birds,

He entered happily the blessed camp of the saints,

Rejoicing in his heavenly lot.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the priest Winfrid

A certain brother subject to him, wondrous in body and mind,

Served him; he was called Winfrid by name.

The holy priest shone forth through illustrious deeds.

The Father embraced him with all his heart,

[Col. 1340D] Entrusted him with the faith, and placed him over the brothers’ clothing.

Devoted to God and faithful with his whole mind,

He guarded his office, supported by a firm defense.

Even when earthly care imposed its burdens,

He did not cease to offer great gifts to Christ.

But when, dying and standing before the Lord, he was compelled to leave this world,

The brother withdrew his heart from the world;

And, happily desiring to submit himself to God alone,

He humbly struck the pavement of the church among its members,

By night and by day commending to the stars in prayer

Himself and the soul of his beloved lord and father.

While the brother continued such things for a long time,

He traveled the road to heaven, not closing the joys of life,

And took the desired rest that lasts forever.

## CHAPTER XX. On the gifts of the fathers and the vows of the monks

[Col. 1341A]

The Lord adorned this monastery with the honor of the brothers.

May all now receive the greatest joys from heaven,

And strive to establish worthy praise for God.

This he granted us without our merits: he never handed us over to enemies,

Nor subjected us to the authority of the powerful men of the age.

May thanks always be given to the Lord on high without end.

Now the pious and justly benevolent nobles deserved well;

They scattered the finest seeds of a heavenly gift

Into the hearts of the brothers, and how happily the crops

Rise at the threshold of the monastery through the sweetness of heavenly dew!

By his help, because such things shine for us,

The field now smiles, blooming for the joys of Christ;

The monks rejoice throughout the monastery, the clergy in the city,

[Col. 1341B] Held together by one law: a will rejoicing in the heart.

Faith joins their numbers to the stars and gathers their numerous companies,

And at the appointed hours they commend themselves to God.

When dark night arrives, when the stars conceal their light,

They hasten from their beds at the sound of the signal,

And sing responsive songs to their own king,

Rightly praising the Thunderer with psalms and hymns.

With frequent songs they adorn the chapel with their voices,

The chapel which God and the nobles, preserving the monastery’s walls,

Had prepared to adorn with many gifts and good things.

This is that house, raised high by extended walls,

Which the bright sun, illuminating its purple hours,

Spreads with clear light throughout the shining temple.

Although there are very many ornaments of the holy sanctuary,

[Col. 1341C] Let it nevertheless be permitted to recall these few in song.

As the sky glitters with shining stars,

So, beneath the vault of the temple, all around,

Hanging lamps send trembling flames flashing in varied rows.

These things, at an earlier time, certain nobles and those of the present day

Once devoted to God with peaceful minds.

Now they took care to return them, increased by pious gifts.

For many desired to hang up cups,

[Note: That is, bowls. Thus King Egwin, as Bede reports in Book II, chapter 16 of his *History*, “in places where he saw clear springs beside public road crossings, for the refreshment of travelers, ordered bronze cups to be hung from poles that had been erected.”]

That might provide clear light to the square-shaped temple.

Others, however, fashioned standards from gleaming metal,

Which the pious bring forth as venerable miracles of Christ,

Who redeemed the world from death on the wood of the cross.

Some commanded that sacred books be written,

In which they displayed the exalted words already spoken by God the Thunderer,

Who, sounding forth, had long ago poured over the whole world;

[Col. 1341D] And a conspicuous sheet of beaten gold covers these,

Thus the saints adorn the altars of the temple.

Others covered the Lady’s table—noble by birth—

With the flames of gems and shining gold;

They properly decorated it with bright silver panels.

Anyone could see, impressed by fingers, the forms

In which the souls of the saints shine in their lofty seats.

Yet it pleased me to renew these descriptions of things,

Which a poet, learned enough to speak of them worthily,

Could adorn with wondrous modes of praise.

That golden chalice I touched earlier in verse,

And the broad paten beautifully fashioned from silver—

Its engraved surfaces aptly display figures.

While such gifts fill the inner chambers of the holy house,

Gifts that preserve the remedies of our life,

The sacred company of the brothers rightly rejoices throughout the monastery

And honors with eternal praises the giver.

[Note: See above, chapter 14.]

## CHAPTER XXI. On the spiritual songs heard in the apostles’ oratory

You too, holy house, which I once sang in verse—

[Note: See above, chapters 4 and 6.]

Which shines consecrated to God under the name of Peter—

Now let me once more recall your blessedness in a few verses.

Long ago, during the hours of black night,

[Col. 1342B] The brothers hasten, according to their accustomed discipline, to visit you after the hymns,

And complete the solemn duties of their hearts.

From there they eagerly desire to hasten to their beds.

But I, after everyone else had closed the doors, opened the hall

And entered it accompanied by another brother.

He happened at that time to be looking outside at the stars.

Suddenly, behold, an immense company came with wondrous songs,

Chanting pious hymns to the Lord and uttering them aloud;

It filled the place of ashes with exceedingly wondrous light.

Spirits entered the sanctuary shining with heavenly radiance,

And, divided into two distinct choirs, sang such hymns:

The trembling song rose to the roofs of heaven

And resounded against the lofty ceilings.

And although the building itself was not constructed, it nevertheless shines

With noble merits, which surpass the stars of heaven and the lofty mountains;

[Col. 1342C] I believe that it received help from the Lord who created it,

Who encompasses everything in heaven, on earth, and in the rivers.

When these words had sounded for a long time in two choirs of the hall,

Beneath the roof and doors of the holy place, both I

And the other brother hastened together,

To learn through our ears and eyes what we had seen.

Immediately the song, together with the light, struck the sky.

We were no longer permitted to see such things,

And, trembling, we desired to seek rest.

Nor did the companies resound only once with starry words.

Rather, the company, flashing with wondrous light

And golden voices, repeatedly strove to avoid the ashes

While the brothers remained lying on their beds during the time of the dark night.

It is established that this was accomplished for the saints by the gift of Christ,

Whose grace now always shines with a second light

[Col. 1342D] For all people on earth.

## CHAPTER XXII. The dream he saw on the Lord’s Day

It was the time of night when the bird proclaims the light,

And, after the hymns, they had relaxed their cold limbs for rest.

Stealthy sleep came upon my eyes.

Suddenly a radiant guide seemed to appear.

I, greatly frightened, followed him of my own accord,

The white man shining with bright garments,

Radiant in face and beautiful in his steps,

Walking along unknown paths.

[Col. 1343A] There was a broad field, offering the sweet fragrance

Of beautiful flowers to all who were worthy through their merits

To behold such visions.

Ruddy roses and fragrant lilies spread throughout it,

Along with many flowers of herbs whose names

My unlearned mind is certainly unable to express—

Such was the abundance of the growth.

As we both traveled along the road together,

We suddenly saw an exceedingly gleaming city;

Walls were seen to touch the dew-laden clouds.

The closed gates stood open on loosened hinges.

The radiant guide entered within, while his frightened servant followed;

The enclosures of the chapel opened,

Which had been beautifully built in the form of a cross.

But the inner house, flashing with immense brightness,

Already formed its round walls from its own stones.

[Col. 1343B] The house’s exterior, however, supported by great and small

Porticoes throughout the extent of the wall, remained standing.

From these, in the regions of the world, four pairs—eight in all—

Of elevated walls looked upward as they spread.

Between them, small cells varied in orderly arrangement,

Surrounding the temple on every side with shining fronts

And displaying a hall of marvelous marble to those who looked.

The pavements of the house beneath the middle roof of the temple

Bore golden gifts for the wondrous table.

A venerable cross, gleaming on a lofty shaft,

Rose from the top of the table, with an exceedingly gleaming emerald.

A golden sheet shone yellow with glowing gems.

While I examined such things with astonished heart,

Behold, suddenly my guide had left me,

And, descending from the temple, had hidden himself in the empty fields.

[Col. 1343C] But I, greatly trembling, bent my face toward the ground

And pleaded with Christ: “We beg for mercy;

Remember not to terrify me, frightened as I am, with hostile enemies.”

Then, turning my eyes toward the part indicated on the right,

I saw a throne properly shining with golden panels,

On which a certain venerable elder was seated.

Before his face, wreathed with golden crowns,

An altar dedicated to God sent forth its highest offering,

And from its lofty cross extended a sign.

It shone with glowing gold and splendid gems.

A garment from the east, gleaming with byssus,

Covered the summits of the crowd;

Beneath its folds it held the dedicated members

Of some saint whom I do not know.

[Col. 1343D] With such words I earnestly questioned him:

“Tell me, where does my former teacher Higlac remain?”

He immediately replied with these words:

“Remember to direct your eyes from the highest seats.”

Meanwhile, seeing the wagon by which the axle moves—when it had detained the serpent with faces turned [the wording is corrupt or uncertain]—

I was granted the opportunity to recognize a face

Known long ago from Ireland.

By his earthly name, he was called Godfridus,

My first teacher in my early years.

He had been a priest who, bent forward in prayer,

Venerated the tomb of Cuthbert with pious devotion,

Honoring it in body and mind; thus he was seen in his blessedness.

[Col. 1344A] At his back, gleaming with radiant metal,

The blessed teacher and lector Higlac sat upon a bench.

[Note: Thus they called the teachers of monasteries; so Colcu is called a lector by Alcuin in Letter 18 among the Irish letters. Pitseus praises Iglac under the year 740 and attributes to him one book on the *Life of Abbot Sigwin*. The name Iglatius appears in the Benedictine Martyrology on July 23, by mere conjecture.]

Higlac, clothed in exceedingly white garments, had shone;

He blessed me with his generous hands.

From there Godfridus, proceeding through the vast temple,

Led me through the great and small porticoes that stood open.

In all of them, surrounded everywhere by glowing capitals,

A thurible fashioned entirely from gold hung nearby.

From these, incense breathed forth to the Thunderer enthroned on high,

While wax, with flame-bearing gifts, venerated the altars.

A bright light burned throughout all the porticoes.

At last we hastened toward the western parts.

That gleaming portico shone with great honor.

Here, glowing with gold, a wondrous grace blazed forth:

An altar consecrated to God sent its gifts to the Most High.

[Col. 1344B] Here sapphire joined with beryl lay before

An outstanding throne which the Lord had made, and on which the holy Wulfsig sat,

Whom the ancient fathers desired to call by that name.

I trembled, suddenly rejoicing, as I bent forward before the holy man.

He raised his hand and blessed me with words as I departed.

From there, with my former teacher as companion, I gradually turned

Toward the summit of the monastery that faces the north,

Where many vessels gleamed with wondrous gems.

Others, made of varied gold, flashed with differing light,

And, through their adornment, could surpass all worldly metal

In the preciousness of their workmanship.

Among these, a table prepared with different foods

Offered gifts of every kind of dish.

From it he had taken a cup from a glassy vein of metal;

He had drawn with his hands the venerable gift of liquid,

[Col. 1344C] And, sacrificing with pious prayers, offered me the drink.

When I had tasted the wine of wondrous flavor,

I returned praises and thanks to the Lord in heaven.

Meanwhile the venerable priest said these things:

“This house was established by the merits of holy souls,

Whom almighty God in his mercy placed here.

No one in the Lord will feel hunger, punishments, or thirst throughout the ages;

Rather, they receive long-lasting joys,

Praising the Lord of heaven throughout all ages,

Who will grant the chosen a blessed rest without end.”

After these words, when I awoke, I began to write down the vision.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The poet’s greeting and prayer to the saints and to the Lord

[Col. 1344D] I, the wolf, renowned in my foolish heart, O exalted Father,

Composed these poems, entreating in body and mind

That the saints grant their gifts to one unworthy,

And seek pardon for him with fearful prayers.

May the Almighty always increase those who are here in merit,

So that they may receive pure faith in body and mind;

May this place always stand forth in Christ, the gracious one,

Memorable for its merits, while the monks increase them.

May almighty God be with the blessed throughout all ages,

The gentle Savior, while they desire better things.

With them, wishing to join my vows as I sing these things,

I do not cease to serve, never serving vices.

[Col. 1345A] You, Father, while reciting these things, do not despise our labors;

Rather, seeing them, hold these worthy joys dear.

Because the fathers, so illustrious through your blood,

Deserved to be what they are, I urge you to give thanks to God.

Now also deign, I beg you, to commend me to the Lord

With abundant prayers, entreating him in body and heart,

[Col. 1346A] So that here the Almighty Father may forgive the trembling poet his sins,

And not be lacking in mercy.

To him be glory, dominion, power, everlasting wisdom,

Praise and honor always remain and flourish.

May the gentle, all-sustaining Father preserve you throughout the ages,

Freeing you from the chains and scourges of hell.

[Col. 1345] Here ends the book of Ethelwolf, monk of the Church of Lindisfarne, on the abbots and miracles of that same Church.

[Col. 1345]

## Marcus, Bishop of Hydruntum

### Hymn of Marcus of Hydruntum for Great Saturday

Greek acrostic: καὶ σημερονδέ, “but today.”

*(From the Library of the Fathers.)*

[Col. 1345B] Once the wave of the sea covered the tyrant persecutor; the children of those saved buried him beneath the earth. But let us sing to the Lord like young heifers, for he has been gloriously glorified.

My Lord and my God, I shall sing to you a funeral hymn and a burial song. Your burial became for me an entrance opening the way, and your death became the slayer of death and of hell. Above, on the throne, and below, in the tomb, the supramundane and subterranean intelligences, my Savior, were shaken by your death beyond understanding; for you, the Author of life, were seen dead.

You descended to the depths of the earth in order to fill all things with your glory. For my subsistence in Adam was not hidden from you; and, when buried, you renew what was corrupt in human nature.

[Col. 1345C] You who suspended the whole earth without support upon the waters: when creation beheld you suspended on Calvary, it was held in astonishment. “There is none holy besides you, O Lord,” it cried.

You displayed the signs of your burial, multiplying the vision; and now, O Lord, you have divinely revealed your mysteries also to those who are in hell. “There is none holy besides you, O Lord,” they cry.

You stretched out your palms and united what had previously been divided. But by your arrest, Savior, in the winding-sheet and the tomb, you released those who were bound. “There is none holy besides you, O Lord,” we cry.

You, whom neither the tomb nor the seals could contain, submitted to confinement by your will. Through your deeds you made your power known, while those who sang in a divine manner proclaimed: “There is none holy besides you, O Lord,” humanly.

Foreseeing your divine self-emptying on the cross, Habakkuk cried out in astonishment: “You have cut down the power of the mighty, O good one,” having dealt with those in hell as the Almighty.

You sanctified this seventh day, which you had previously blessed by the cessation of works. For you bring forth all things and renew them, keeping Sabbath, my Savior, and restoring them.

When the strength of the stronger one conquered, your soul was separated from your flesh for a time. For your Word, by its strength, tears apart both the bonds of death and of hell.

When hell encountered the Word, it became bitter, seeing a mortal made divine, marked with the bruises of scourges and made all-powerful; yet it recoiled from the terrible form.

Your *deiparentia* (“God-bearing” dispensation), O Christ, having become compassionate toward us, caused Isaiah, seeing the light that knows no evening and keeping vigil through the night, to cry out: “The dead shall rise, and those who are in the tombs shall be raised, and all who are on earth shall rejoice.”

You renew earthly beings, though you are the Creator who came from dust; and the winding-sheet and the tomb, showing that you coexisted with them, reveal the mystery of the Word. The beautiful Counselor foretells in you the counsel of the one who gives birth to you, O magnificent one, who renews me.

Through death you transform what is mortal; through the tomb you make what is corruptible incorruptible, most fittingly. You immortalize what you have assumed, for your flesh did not know corruption, O Lord, nor was your soul wondrously abandoned in hell.

Coming forth from the incorrupt one and piercing the rib, my Creator, you effected from it the restoration of Eve. Having become Adam, you were wondrously lulled by life-giving sleep, and, as the Almighty, you raised life from sleep and corruption.

## PETER THE ARCHDEACON

### QUESTIONS ON THE PROPHET DANIEL EXPLAINED BY PETER THE ARCHDEACON

*(From Martène, enlarged Collection.)*

[Col. 1347A]

### PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

Among the various concerns of Charlemagne, his exceptional diligence in restoring the study of sacred letters deserves foremost attention. Believing that empires flourished especially when men distinguished by virtue and learning shone within them, he entirely neglected nothing that might enable him to summon learned men from every direction, with whose assistance he could revive the liberal arts, disciplines, and every science in his realms. He strained every effort to rekindle among his people the study of sacred Scripture, which had almost died out. He himself testifies to this in the preface to the Homiliary of Paul, a monk of the monastery of Casino, which was prepared at his command:

“Because,” he says, “we are concerned that the condition of our churches may always advance toward better things, we strive with vigilant zeal in letters to restore the workshop of our ancestors, which had almost been obliterated through their negligence; and, for learning the books of the sacred writings thoroughly, we also invite others by our example, insofar as we are able. Among these works, long ago, with God assisting us in all things, we corrected exactly all the books of the Old and New Testament, which had been corrupted through the carelessness of scribes.”

Therefore it ought by no means to seem surprising if the most devout prince ordered the following Questions on Daniel, which we here publish from a very ancient codex of the monastery of Stavelot, to be transcribed from the authentic work of Peter the archdeacon. We have not yet been able to determine who that Peter the archdeacon was, unless perhaps he was the Peter the deacon through whom Saint Gregory composed his books of the *Dialogues*. We await the judgment of scholars on this matter.

[Col. 1347]

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF VARIOUS LITTLE QUESTIONS WITH THEIR ANSWERS, WHICH LORD KING CHARLES ORDERED TO BE TRANSCRIBED FROM THE AUTHENTIC WORK OF PETER THE ARCHDEACON

[Col. 1347C]

### 1. What are those kingdoms that King Nebuchadnezzar saw in his vision (Dan. II, 31)?

In the head of the statue the Babylonian kingdom is indicated; after it comes that of the Medes and Persians, which has the likeness of silver; and the third kingdom signifies Alexander, the kingdom of the Macedonians and Alexander’s successors, which has the likeness of bronze. The fourth kingdom clearly belongs to the Romans; it is iron, which crushes and subdues everything. But its feet and toes are partly iron and partly clay, as is most clearly confirmed in the present age. For just as nothing was stronger or harder than the Roman empire at its beginning, so at the end of things nothing is weaker.

### 2. It is asked whether Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah were eunuchs or not

They appear to have been eunuchs, according to what we read: “The king said to Ashpenaz, chief of his eunuchs, that he should bring in some of the sons of Israel and of royal and tyrannical lineage, boys in whom there was no blemish” (Dan. I, 3); and according to what Isaiah had said to Hezekiah: “They shall take some of your offspring and make them eunuchs in the house of the king” (Isa. XXXIX, 7). But when we consider the phrase “in whom there was no blemish,” we find that they were not eunuchs.

### 3. If it is a sin to learn the wisdom and teaching of the Babylonians, why did Daniel learn what was not permitted?

If Daniel had known that the wisdom of the Chaldeans was sinful, he would never have consented to learn what was forbidden, just as he did not want to eat from the king’s table or drink his wine, lest he be defiled (Dan. I, 8). Moses, too, had learned all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

### 4. It is asked whether Daniel and the three boys learned the wisdom promised by Greek education

No, but the teaching of a barbarian people, by which the Chaldeans philosophize even to this day.

### 5. What does it mean when we read: “In the second year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream” (Dan. II, 1)? If the boys entered his presence after three years, as he himself had ordered, how is it said that he saw the dream in the second year of his reign?

Here he calls it the second year of his reign over all the barbarian nations—not only the Jews and Chaldeans, but also the Assyrians, Egyptians, Moabites, and the remaining peoples whom, with the Lord’s permission, he had conquered. Hence Josephus also says: “After the second year of the devastation of Egypt, King Nebuchadnezzar saw a marvelous dream.”

### 6. What does it mean that Nebuchadnezzar deserved to see a dream containing so great a mystery? Can we believe that such merit was obtained by a very wicked man?

He did not see it because of merit, but so that God might be glorified when the holy man interpreted what he had seen. Pharaoh likewise did not deserve to see his dream, but it was given so that Joseph might be placed over them all.

[Col. 1349A]

### 7. [Note: One question is missing here, perhaps: “What is the difference between diviners, magicians, and sorcerers?”]

Diviners—that is, enchanters—are those who accomplish a matter by words; magicians are those who philosophize about individual things; sorcerers are those who use blood.

### 8. What does it mean that Nebuchadnezzar said, “I saw a dream, and my mind was confused; I do not know what I saw” (Dan. II, 3), when afterward, when Daniel reported it, he testified that he had seen what Daniel said?

A certain shadow, and, so to speak, a breath and trace of the dream, remained in the king’s heart, so that when others reported it he could remember what he had seen and would not be deceived by liars. Up to this point the passages that have been read are related in the Hebrew language. From here to the vision of the third year of King Belshazzar, which Daniel saw at Susa, they are indeed written in Hebrew letters, but in the Chaldean language, which he here calls Syriac.

### 9. What does it mean when we read: “And the herald cried out loudly: To you it is said, peoples, tribes, and languages: at the hour when you hear the sound of the trumpet, pipe, lyre, sambuca, psaltery, symphony, and every kind of music, fall down and worship the golden statue which King Nebuchadnezzar has erected. But whoever does not fall down and worship it will at that same hour be cast into a burning furnace of fire” (Dan. III, 4)? Could all the peoples of every nation have gathered in the field of Dura, in a small place? Theodotion translated this place as Deira instead of Dura, Symmachus as Dora, and the Septuagint as *Periboaon*; it is interpreted as “enclosure” or “confined place.”

It is not that all the peoples could have gathered in the field of Dura and worshiped the golden statue, but that, in the persons of the rulers of all the nations, all the nations and peoples are believed to have worshiped.

### 10. What is to be understood by the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar made (Dan. III, 1)?

By that king and by the statue we understand all heretics, who compose a false doctrine with the brilliance of secular eloquence.

### 11. What is naphtha (Dan. III, 46)?

Olive stones that are thrown away, dried olive lees; and naphtha is called in Greek *pyrni*, from the fact that it feeds fire.

### 12. What provinces did King Nebuchadnezzar hold?

The East, Asia, Europe, and Libya.

[Col. 1349D]

### 13. How was rule preserved for seven years for a man without a mind, and how was so powerful a kingdom without a king for so long (Dan. IV, 30)? Or, if another succeeded him in the kingdom, how great must we judge that man’s madness to have been, if he surrendered the power which he had possessed for so long—especially since the histories of the Chaldeans contain nothing of this kind, nor could it have happened that those who wrote about lesser matters would have omitted greater ones?

Some, because they do not find this in the histories, want to understand the devil by Nebuchadnezzar; this must not be accepted. For who does not know that deranged men live like brute animals in the fields and wooded places? What is surprising if, to display God’s power and humble the pride of kings, this judgment of God was imposed? Greek and Roman histories, too, have reported that much more incredible things happened to human beings. The fables even tell that Scylla, the Chimera, the Hydra, and centaurs were birds and wild beasts fashioned from human beings.

### 14. Why is Daniel, whom we read to have been a worshiper of God, called chief of all the diviners, as it is written: “Belshazzar, he said, is chief of the diviners, whom I know to have the spirit of the holy gods in you” (Dan. IV, 6)?

It is not surprising that he was appointed chief of all the diviners, since, at the king’s command, he had learned the wisdom of the Chaldeans and had been found ten times wiser than them all.

### 15. If Daniel foretold the sentence of God, which cannot be changed (Dan. IV, 24), how does he urge almsgiving and mercy toward the poor, so that the sentence of God might be changed?

The matter is easily resolved by the example of King Hezekiah, whom Isaiah had said was going to die (Isa. XXXVIII, 1), and by that of the Ninevites: “Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown” (Jon. III, 4). Nevertheless, in response to the prayers of Hezekiah and the Ninevites, God’s sentence was changed—not through any fickleness in his judgment, but through their conversion.

[The supplied source ends here.]

## 16. Who was that Belshazzar of whom it is written: “Belshazzar the king made a great banquet for a thousand of his nobles” (Dan. 5:1)?

[Col. 1350C] It should be understood that he was not the son of Nebuchadnezzar, as many readers suppose, but, according to Abherosus [Note: [Col. 1349D] Orosius above in the manuscript, in an ancient hand, perhaps the same one.], who wrote a history of Chaldaea, and Josephus, who follows Berossus: after Nebuchadnezzar, who reigned for forty-three years, Evil-merodach succeeded to his kingdom. In the first year of his reign he raised Jehoiachin, king of Judah, from prison. After the death of Evil-merodach, his son Neriglissar succeeded to his father’s kingdom; after him, in turn, his son Labashi-Marduk; when Labashi-Marduk died, his son Belshazzar held the kingdom. He was killed by Darius, king of the Medes, who was the maternal uncle of Cyrus, king of the Persians.

## 17. Why, then, does he call Nebuchadnezzar the father of Belshazzar (Dan. 5:2)?

This should cause no error for those familiar with the practice of Holy Scripture, by which all great-grandfathers and ancestors are called fathers.

## 18. Why is it read, “He shall be clothed in purple and shall have a golden chain around his neck”? Why did the translator render *chain* in the feminine gender?

He did so instructed by an example. Cicero, in his *Marius*, used *chain* in the feminine gender, whereas Titus Livius used it in the masculine.

## 19. Who was that queen who entered to Belshazzar when she heard what had happened (Dan. 5:10)?

Josephus writes that she was Belshazzar’s grandmother [Note: [Col. 1350D] Josephus does indeed write that she was Belshazzar’s grandmother, *Jewish Antiquities*, Book X, chapter 10. But we possess no work of Origen on Daniel.], while Origen says that she was his mother.

[Col. 1351A] ## 20. Why are the joints of the writing hand said to have appeared opposite the lampstand (Dan. 5:5)?

So that they might not appear too far away.

## 21. After Belshazzar had been killed and Babylon had been besieged by the Medes and Persians—namely, Darius and Cyrus—why did Darius alone succeed to the kingdom, and not Cyrus with him, since Cyrus likewise began to rule the Babylonian kingdom with him (Dan. 5:30)?

The order is determined by age, kinship, and the kingdom. Darius was sixty-two years old; and we read that the kingdom of the Medes was greater than that of the Persians. As the maternal uncle, who was senior according to natural right, he ought to be regarded as the successor to the kingdom.

It should be understood what the writing was that the joints wrote: “Mane, Thecel, Phares.” [Col. 1351B] “Mane: God has numbered your kingdom and brought it to an end. Thecel: You have been weighed in the balance and found wanting. Phares: Your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians” (Dan. 5:25).

## 22. What does it mean when we read: “Moreover, the king was planning to set Daniel over the entire kingdom; therefore the officials and satraps sought an occasion so that they might find something against Daniel on the king’s side” (Dan. 9:5)? What does “that they might find something against Daniel on the king’s side” mean?

The king’s side means the queen, or his concubines and other wives who sleep beside him. They therefore sought an opportunity in matters of this kind: whether in speech, touch, or gesture they might accuse Daniel. But they could find no cause or suspicion, because he was a eunuch. [Col. 1351C]

## 23. What does it mean when we read that Daniel bent his knees three times a day (Dan. 6:10)? What times does this indicate?

The three times at which, according to ecclesiastical tradition, the knees should be bent before God are understood as the third, sixth, and ninth hours. Thus, at the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles; at the sixth hour Peter went up to the upper room, wishing to eat; and at the ninth hour Peter and John were going to the temple.

## 24. What does it mean when we read: “Daniel continued until the first year of King Cyrus” (Dan. 1:21), since elsewhere it is written: “In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia the word was revealed to Daniel, whose name was Belshazzar” (Dan. [Col. 1351D] 10:1)?

This signifies that until the first year of Cyrus, the king who destroyed the Chaldaean empire, Daniel was powerful in Chaldaea; afterward, he was transferred by Darius to the Medes.

## 25. What does Daniel mean when he says: “I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were fighting upon the great sea, and four great beasts were coming up from the sea, different from one another” (Dan. 7:2)?

The four winds of heaven are four angelic powers, to whom the principal kingdoms have been entrusted. The sea signifies this world and this age, overflowing with false and bitter waves. The four great beasts, the angel says, are four kingdoms that will arise from the earth. [Col. 1352A]

## 26. What does it mean when we read: “The first was like a lioness and had the wings of an eagle. I watched until its wings were plucked off; it was lifted up from the earth, stood on its feet like a man, and a man’s heart was given to it” (Dan. 7:4)?

The Babylonian kingdom is called not a lion but a lioness because of its savagery and cruelty, or because of its luxury and its life devoted to lust.

## 27. Why was the most powerful kingdom seen in the form not of a lion but of a lioness?

Because those who have written about the nature of animals say that lionesses are more ferocious, especially when they are raising cubs, and that they are always eager for mating.

[Col. 1352B] ## 28. What does it mean when it is written that it had the wings of an eagle?

It signifies the pride of the most powerful kingdom, whose prince speaks through Isaiah: “I will set my throne above the stars of heaven; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13).

## 29. Why is it said to have the wings of an eagle and not of another bird?

Because the eagle lives for a very long time, and the Assyrian kingdom dominated for many generations.

## 30. What should be understood by the statement: “Its wings were plucked off”?

It signifies the other kingdoms over which it had previously ruled and with which it had flown throughout the world.

## 31. What does it mean when it is said: “It stood on its feet like a man, and a man’s heart was given to it” (Dan. 7:4)?

[Col. 1352C] Nebuchadnezzar may be understood: after he lost the kingdom and his glory was taken away, he was restored again to his former rank, learned that he was not a lioness but a human being, and received back the heart that he had lost.

It may also be understood differently of the Chaldaean kingdom: after Belshazzar had been killed and the Medes and Persians had succeeded to the empire, the Babylonians understood that they were human beings of humble and fragile nature (Dan. 4:31).

## 32. What does it mean when we read: “And behold, another beast, like a bear, stood on one side; three rows were in its mouth and in its teeth, and thus they said to it: ‘Arise, eat much flesh’” (Dan. 7:5)?

The second beast, like a bear, is the one of which we read in the vision of the statue: “Its breast and arms were of silver.” Because of its harshness and ferocity it is compared with a bear. [Col. 1352D] It stood on one side because, as the Hebrews say, the Medes and Persians did nothing cruel against Israel; hence in Zechariah they are also called white horses (Zech. 6:3).

## 33–34. What is meant by the three rows that were in its mouth and in its teeth?

One interpreter explained this by saying that the Persian kingdom was divided among three rulers, as we read of the three officials who presided over 120 satraps. But by the three rows in the mouth of the Persian king and in his teeth we should understand three kingdoms—the Babylonian, Median, and Persian kingdoms—which were brought together into one.

## 35. Why was it said to it: “Arise, eat much flesh”?

[Col. 1353A] It signifies the time when, under Ahasuerus, whom the Septuagint call Artaxerxes, at Haman’s suggestion all the Jews were ordered to be slaughtered on a single day.

## 36. What does it mean when we read: “After this I looked, and behold, another, like a leopard, and it had four wings upon it, and the beast had four heads; and authority was given to it” (Dan. 7:6)?

The third kingdom, that of the Macedonians, of which we also read in the statue, “Its belly and thighs were of bronze” (Dan. 2:32), is compared with a leopard, the swiftest of beasts, which rushes headlong toward blood and leaps to its death.

By the four wings Alexander’s victory is signified, for nothing was swifter than it. From Illyria and the Adriatic Sea to the Indian Ocean and the River Ganges, he advanced not so much through battles as through victories, and in six years subjected to himself part of Europe [Col. 1353B] and all Asia.

## 37. What is meant by the four heads?

He means the same commanders who afterward became successors to the kingdom: Ptolemy, Seleucus, Philip, and Antigonus.

## 38. What is meant by “authority was given to it”?

It is shown that this was not the work of Alexander’s strength but of the Lord’s will.

## 39. What does he mean when he says: “After this I looked in the night vision, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and wondrous and exceedingly strong; it had great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the remainder with its feet” (Dan. 7:7)?

The fourth is the Roman empire, of which it is said in the statue: “Its legs were of iron” (Dan. 2:33).

## 40. Why did he previously compare the three kingdoms with beasts—the lioness, the bear, and the leopard—but compare the Roman kingdom with no beast?

Because, in order to make the beast terrifying, he kept its name silent, so that we might understand the Romans as whatever among the beasts we had imagined to be most terrifying. But the Hebrews think that what is left unsaid here is expressed in the Psalm: “The boar from the forest ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast devoured it” (Ps. 79:41).

## 41. What does it mean that it was “devouring and crushing, and trampling the remainder with its feet”?

It signifies all the nations, whether killed by them or subjected to them through tribute and slavery.

## 42. What does it mean when he says: “And it had ten horns” (Dan. 7:7)?

[Col. 1353D] Some identify the four successors of Alexander and then enumerate ten kings, down to Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, who were exceedingly savage. But it is better to believe what all the ecclesiastical teachers have handed down: at the consummation of the world, when the Roman kingdom is to be destroyed, there will be ten kings who will divide the Roman world among themselves, and an eleventh, a little king, will arise. He will overcome three of the ten kings—the king of the Egyptians, the king of Africa, and the king of Ethiopia. After these have been killed, seven other kings will also submit their necks to the victor.

He says of this horn: “There were eyes like human eyes in this horn” (Dan. 7:8), lest we should think, according to the opinion of some, that he is either the devil or a demon, but rather one of human beings, in whom Satan in his entirety will dwell. He will have a mouth speaking great things, so that he will dare to sit in the temple of God, making himself like God.

## 43. What does it mean when he says: “I watched until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat down” (Dan. 7:9)?

The thrones that Daniel saw seem to me to be those whom John calls twenty-four thrones. The Ancient of Days is the one who, in John, sits alone upon the throne. The Son of Man, who came to the Ancient of Days, is the one whom John calls “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David” (Rev. 5:5).

## 44. What does it mean that “the judgment sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. 7:10)?

The consciences and works of each person, whether good or bad, are all revealed on both sides. The good book is the one we often read of, the book of the living. The evil book is like the one held in the hand of the accuser, who is the enemy and avenger, of whom we also read in the Apocalypse: “the accuser of our brothers” (Rev. 12:10). This book is earthly.

## 45. What does it mean: “I saw that the beast was killed, and its body perished and was given to be burned with fire; the authority of the other beasts was also taken away, and periods of life were appointed for them until a time and times” (Dan. 7:11)?

In the one Roman empire, because of the blaspheming Antichrist, all the kingdoms were destroyed together. There will no longer be an earthly empire, but the fellowship of the saints and the coming of the triumphant Son of God.

## 46. What does it mean when he says: “They shall be delivered into his hand for a time and times and half a time” (Dan. 7:25)?

During those times the saints will be handed over to the power of the Antichrist, so that the Jews may be condemned, since they did not believe the truth but accepted a lie. Concerning those times the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matt. 24:22).

“I, Daniel, was greatly troubled by my thoughts, and my appearance was changed within me; but I kept the word in my heart” (Dan. 7:28).

Up to this point Daniel’s book was written in the Chaldaean language; the rest, which follows to the end of the volume, we read in Hebrew.

## 47. Susa is the capital of the region of the Elamites. [Col. 1354D] If it is a fortress, how can it be a capital (Dan. 8:2)?

Not because the capital city is a fortress, but because it was built with such strength that it appeared to be a fortress.

## 48. What does it mean when we read: “I saw in the vision that I was above the gate of Ulai”? What is Ulai (ibid.)?

It should be understood that Ulai is the name of a place or gate, just as at Troy there is the Scaean Gate, and among the Romans the Carmental Gate; each has the origin of its name from its own particular circumstances.

## 49. What does it mean when he says: “And behold, one ram stood before the marsh, or before the gate, having high horns, one higher than the other and growing” (ibid. 3)?

He calls Darius the ram—the maternal uncle of Cyrus—who, after Astyages, his maternal grandfather, ruled over the Medes and Persians together with his uncle Darius, whom the Greeks call Cyaxares. [Col. 1355A]

## 50. What does it mean when he says: “Afterward I saw the ram pushing with its horns toward the east, the north, and the south” (Dan. 8:4)?

It does not refer to that ram himself, namely Cyrus or Darius, but to the ram of the same kingdom—that is, the other Darius, who was the last king of Persian power and whom Alexander, son of Philip and king of the Macedonians, defeated.

Both Greek and Latin histories relate that this Darius was a most powerful and wealthy king.

## 51. “Behold, a he-goat was coming from the west over the face of the whole earth, and it did not touch the ground. The he-goat had a conspicuous horn between its eyes, and it came up to the horned ram that I had seen standing before the gate; and it ran toward it in the force of its strength. When it came near the ram, it shattered its two horns, and the ram could not resist it. When it had thrown it to the ground, it trampled it, and no one could deliver it from its hand. The he-goat became exceedingly great; and when it had grown, the great horn was broken, and four horns arose beneath it, toward the four winds of heaven. From one of them another little horn arose and became great” (ibid. 5).

The he-goat that came from the west and, because of its extreme speed, seemed not to touch the ground is Alexander, king of the Greeks. After overthrowing Thebes, he took up arms against the Persians, defeated the commanders of Darius, and finally struck down the ram himself. He broke its two horns—the Medes and the Persians—threw it beneath his feet, and subjected both horns to his rule.

The great horn is Alexander himself, the first king. When he died in Babylon in the thirty-second year of his age, four of his commanders arose in his place and divided the empire among themselves. Ptolemy, son of Lagus, held Egypt; Philip, also called Arrhidaeus, the brother of Alexander, held Macedonia; Seleucus Nicator held Syria, Babylon, and all the kingdoms of the East; Antigonus ruled Asia.

## 52. What does it mean when he says: “He was magnified even against the Prince of the host” (ibid. 11)?

This was said of Epiphanes, the son of Seleucus, who was also called Philopator, because he rose up against God, persecuted his saints, removed the regular sacrifice, and brought about the sin of desolation. The sanctuary and the host were trampled underfoot.

One angel asks another angel how long, by God’s judgment, the temple would remain desolate under Antiochus, king of Syria, and how long the image of Jupiter would stand in the temple of God. Antiochus had indeed placed a statue of Jupiter in the temple of God.

## 53. “And he said: ‘Until evening and morning, two thousand three hundred days; then the sanctuary shall be cleansed’” (ibid. 14).

In the 143rd year from Seleucus, who was the first to reign in Syria after Alexander, we read that Antiochus entered Jerusalem and devastated everything. In the third year he returned and placed a statue of Jupiter in the temple. From that time until Judas Maccabaeus, six years, 2,300 days, and three months of Jerusalem’s devastation and the temple’s pollution were completed, after which the temple was purified.

## 54. What does it mean when he says: “And behold, there stood before me one having the appearance of a man” (ibid. 15)?

Angels are not men, but they appear in the form of men. Thus, at the oak of Mamre, three men appeared to Abraham; they were certainly not men, and one of them was worshiped as the Lord. Hence the Savior also says in the Gospel: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

## 55. What does it mean when he says: “And I heard the voice of a man between [Col. 1356B] Ulai; he called and said: ‘Gabriel, make him understand this vision’” (Dan. 8:16)? Who was the one who commanded Gabriel to make Daniel understand the vision?

The Jews believe that it was Michael.

## 56. Why is Gabriel called to make him understand, and why is no other angel called?

Because the vision concerned battles and the conflicts of kings, or rather the succession of kingdoms. It was fitting that Gabriel, who has charge over battles, should be assigned to this task.

## 57. Why, at the time when the Lord was to be born, was Gabriel sent to Zechariah and Mary, and not another angel?

Because, as has been said, Gabriel has charge over battles: he came to declare war against demons and to triumph over the world. [Col. 1356C]

## 58. Concerning what Daniel says: “And I, Daniel, languished and was sick for days” (Dan. 8:27).

This is like what we read in Genesis about Abraham: after he had heard God speaking to him, he said that he was earth and ashes (Gen. 18:27).

## 59. What does it mean when he says: “I was astonished at the vision, and there was no one to interpret it” (Dan. 8:27)? If there was no one to interpret it, how did the angel interpret it above?

What he means is that he had heard of the kings but did not know their names; he had learned what was to come, but he wavered uncertainly about the time at which it would come.

## 60. “In the first year of Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of Median descent, who ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldaeans” [Col. 1356D] (Dan. 9:1).

This is the Darius who, together with Cyrus, defeated the Chaldaeans and Babylonians. We should not think that he was the Darius in whose second year the temple was built—the Darius whom Porphyry conjectured in order to extend Daniel’s chronology—or the Darius who was defeated by Alexander, king of the Macedonians.

He therefore adds the father’s name and the victory by which the first ruler of Median descent overthrew the Chaldaean kingdom, in order to remove, on account of the similarity of names, an error in reading.

## 61. What does it mean that the Lord assigned human beings 120 years in Genesis?

It means that those who are unwilling to repent during so long a time—that is, for one hundred years—will certainly not be granted the completion of the remaining twenty. He brings upon them earlier what he had afterward threatened.

## 62. What does Daniel mean when he says: “The curse and the detestation have come upon us, which are written in the book of Moses, the servant of God” (Dan. 9:11)? In which book of Moses?

In Deuteronomy we read the curses and blessings of God, which he afterward pronounced on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal over the righteous and sinners (Deut. 27:14).

## 63. What does it mean when we read in the Psalm: “The Lord awoke like one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome by wine” (Ps. 77:65)?

Our wickedness intoxicates God. When it is rebuked in us, he is said to awaken and to rise from his drunkenness, so that he may make us, who are drunk with sin, awaken to righteousness. When we are rebuked on account of our sins, God watches over us and visits us. But when we are abandoned by God and not judged, we are unworthy of the Lord’s correction; then he is said to sleep. [Col. 1357B]

## 64. What does the angel say to Daniel: “Therefore take heed of the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks have been shortened for your people and for your holy city; you shall know and understand from the going forth of the word that the answer be given and Jerusalem be built, until Christ the prince: seven weeks and sixty-two weeks” (Dan. 9:23 ff.)?

It is clear that the angel answered these things neither without purpose nor without the inspiration of God. This interpretation seems to require careful and attentive reasoning, [Col. 1357C] so that the reader may pay close attention and investigate the reasons for the division in the angel’s statement: “From the going forth of the word that the answer be given and Jerusalem be built, until Christ the prince” (ibid. 25).

We think that the rulers meant here are none other than those who governed the Jewish people after this prophecy and the return from Babylon. These were the high priests, whom Scripture calls *christs*—that is, anointed ones. Their chief was Jesus, son of Jehozadak, the high priest; they continued until the coming of the Lord and Savior.

The prophet’s oracle signifies these men when it says: “From the going forth of the word that the answer be given and Jerusalem be built, until Christ the prince, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks”—that is, seven weeks and afterward sixty-two, making 483 years, counted from Cyrus.

Lest we seem merely to assert an audacious opinion without proving what we say, let us enumerate those who governed the people as christs—that is, as anointed high priests—from Jesus, son of Jehozadak, until the Savior’s coming.

First, as we have already said, after Daniel’s prophecy, which was given under King Cyrus, and after the people returned from Babylon, Jesus, son of Jehozadak, was high priest, together with Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel. They laid the foundations of the temple. When the work was hindered by the Samaritans and the other surrounding nations, seven weeks of years were completed—that is, forty-nine years during which the temple remained unfinished. The prophecy separates these from the remaining sixty-two weeks. Thus the Jews also speak to the Lord in the Gospel from this understanding: “The temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” (John 2:20).

There are indeed that many years from the first year of King Cyrus, who granted liberty to those Jews who wished to return to their homeland, until the sixth year of King Darius, under whom the entire work of the temple was completed. Josephus adds another three years, during which the temple colonnades and certain other remaining works were completed. These, added to the forty-six years, make forty-nine years, that is, seven weeks of years.

They count the remaining sixty-two weeks from the seventh year of that same Darius. At that time Jesus, son of Jehozadak, and Zerubbabel, now older, governed the people; under them Haggai [Col. 1358B] and Zechariah prophesied.

After them, Ezra and Nehemiah came from Babylon and built the city walls, while Joiakim, son of Jesus surnamed Jehozadak, held the high priesthood. After him Eliashib succeeded to the priesthood, then Joiada, afterward Johanan, and after Johanan Jaddua. During Jaddua’s lifetime Alexander, king of the Macedonians, founded Alexandria, as Josephus relates, and came to Jerusalem, where he sacrificed victims in the temple.

After Alexander’s death, in the 113th Olympiad, in the 236th year of the Persian kingdom—which had begun in the first year of the Olympiad—and after the death of Jaddua the priest, who had presided over the temple under Alexander, Onias assumed the high priesthood. At that time Seleucus, having conquered Babylon, placed the diadem of all Asia upon his head. [Col. 1358C]

In the twelfth year after Alexander’s death, to which time all the years from Cyrus’s reign are reckoned as 248, the book of Maccabees counts the beginning of the Greek kingdom.

After Onias, Eleazar was high priest over the Jews. During his tenure the seventy translators are said to have translated the holy Scriptures into the Greek language at Alexandria.

After him came another Onias, who was succeeded by Simon. While Simon ruled the people, Jesus, son of Sirach, wrote the book called in Greek *Panareth*. Another Onias succeeded him in the high priesthood. During his time Antiochus compelled the Jews to sacrifice to the gods of the nations.

After Onias’s death, Judas Maccabaeus purified the temple and shattered the idols. His brother Jonathan succeeded him, and after Jonathan, Simon, the brother of both, ruled the people.

At Simon’s death, the 277th year of the Syrian kingdom was completed, and the first book of Maccabees contains the history down to that time. From the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, to the end of the first volume of Maccabees and the death of Simon the high priest, 425 years are reckoned. [Col. 1358D]

After Simon, John held the high priesthood for twenty-nine years. When he died, Aristobulus governed the people for one year. He was the first of those who, having returned from Babylon, assumed the diadem, the mark of royal power, together with the honor of the high priesthood.

His successor was Alexander, at once king and high priest, who ruled the people for twenty-seven years. From the first year of King Cyrus and the return of the captives who wished to come to Judaea, 483 years are reckoned. These comprise seven and sixty-two weeks, that is, sixty-nine weeks altogether. Throughout this entire period high priests governed the Jewish people; I now believe that these are the ones called “anointed princes.”

After the death of the last of them, Alexander, the Jewish people were harassed by rebellions, scattered here and there into various factions, and without any leader. Alexandra, also called Salina, the wife of Alexander, eventually held the power. She reserved the high priesthood for her son Hyrcanus but gave the kingdom to her other son Aristobulus, who held it for ten years.

While the brothers were fighting one another in civil rebellion and drawing the Jewish people into their competing factions, Gnaeus Pompey, commander of the Roman army, arrived. He captured Jerusalem and entered as far as the inner sanctuaries of the temple, which were called the Holy of Holies. He bound Aristobulus and sent him to Rome, reserving him for his triumph, and handed the high priesthood to his brother Hyrcanus.

Then, for the first time, the Jewish people became tributary to the Romans.

After Hyrcanus, Herod, son of Antipater, had Hyrcanus killed, received the kingdom of the Jews by decree of the senate, and became the first foreigner to rule the Jews.

We have explained these matters as best we could. Eusebius also offers another explanation; if we wished to translate it into Latin, we would enlarge the length of the book. This, then, is the sense of his interpretation.

From the sixth year of Darius, who reigned over Persia after Cyrus and his son Cambyses, when the work on the temple was completed, until Herod and Caesar Augustus, he counts seven weeks and sixty-two weeks, making 483 years. At that time Christ—that is, Hyrcanus, the last high priest of the Maccabaean line—was slaughtered by Herod, and, in accordance with the law, the succession of God’s priests came to an end.

Africanus spoke as follows about the seventy weeks in the fifth volume of his *Chronology*:

> “The passage that we read in Daniel concerning the seventy weeks contains many remarkable and extraordinary matters, which it would now take too long to discuss. Therefore, insofar as the present work is concerned, we must discuss the chronology. There can be no doubt that the prophecy concerns the coming of Christ, who appeared to the world after the seventy weeks.
