After him, transgressions were completed, sin reached its end, iniquity was erased, and everlasting righteousness was proclaimed, surpassing the righteousness of the law. The vision and the prophecy were fulfilled, because the law and the prophets continued [Col. 1359D] until John the Baptist.

> “The angel himself speaks of seventy weeks of years—that is, 490 years—from the going forth of the word that the answer be given and Jerusalem be built, beginning in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians.

> “Nehemiah, the king’s cupbearer, as we read in the book of Ezra, asked the king and received a reply that Jerusalem should be rebuilt. This was the word that granted permission for the city to be built and enclosed with walls, since until that time it had been exposed to the incursions of neighboring nations.

> “For when King Cyrus had granted permission to those who wished to return to Jerusalem, Jesus the high priest and Zerubbabel, and afterward Ezra the priest and the others who wished to travel with them, attempted to build the temple, the city, and its walls. The surrounding nations prevented the work from being completed, as though the king had not ordered it. The work therefore remained unfinished until Nehemiah and the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes.

> “At that time 115 years of the Persian kingdom had passed, while it was the 185th year of Jerusalem’s captivity. Then, for the first time, Artaxerxes ordered the walls of Jerusalem to be built. Nehemiah supervised the work; the public square was built and the walls were enclosed. From that time, if you wish to count seventy weeks of years up to Christ, you will be able to find them.

> “But if we wish to take the beginning of these weeks from that earlier time, the periods will not coincide and we will find many contradictions. For if seventy weeks are counted from Cyrus and his first act of clemency, by which the captivity of the Jews was relaxed, we will find more than one hundred years, exceeding the established number of weeks—and even more if we add the day on which the angel spoke to Daniel, or if you wish to take the beginning of the weeks from the beginning of the captivity.

> “The Persian kingdom continued for 230 years until the beginning of the Macedonians, and the Macedonians themselves reigned for 300 years. From then until the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Christ suffered, sixty years are reckoned. These figures together make 590 years, leaving one hundred years over.

> “But from the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes until Christ, seventy weeks are completed according to the lunar reckoning of the Hebrews, who count their months not according to the course of the sun but according to that of the moon.

> “For from the 115th year of the Persian kingdom, when Artaxerxes was in the twentieth year of his reign, and it was the fourth year of the 83rd Olympiad, until the 202nd Olympiad and its second year, the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, 475 years are collected. These make 490 Hebrew years according to the lunar months, as we have said. According to their reckoning, the months can consist of twenty-nine and a half days each, so that over 490 years the solar cycle has 365 days and a quarter of a day more, and over twelve months of each year eleven days and a quarter of a day more are found. This is why the Greeks and Jews make three intercalary months over eight years.

> “For if you reckon eight times eleven and a quarter, you will make ninety days—that is, three months. In 475 years there will be fifty-nine such periods of eight years and three months. Together these amount, more or less, to fifteen years. If you add these to the 475 years, you will make seventy weeks of years—that is, 490 years altogether.”

This is what Africanus said in the same words that we have reproduced.

## 65. What does it mean when he says: “He confirmed a covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall cease” (Dan. 9:27)?

Eusebius interprets it as follows: while Herod ruled among the Jews and Augustus among the Romans, Christ was born. According to the evangelist John, he preached the Gospel for three years and six months and confirmed the worship of God among many, unquestionably among the apostles and believers.

After the Lord’s passion, in the middle of the week, sacrifice and offering again ceased.

Most people extend one week of years to seventy years, as Eusebius says. Counting a decade for each year of the week, they want the period from Christ’s passion until Nero’s reign to be thirty-five years, when Roman arms were first moved against the Jews; this is said to be half of the seventy-year week.

Afterward, from Vespasian and Titus onward, when Jerusalem and the temple were burned, until Trajan, there were another thirty-five years. This, they say, completes the week about which the angel speaks to Daniel.

## 66. What does it mean when he says: “Understand and calculate from the issuing of the word to answer me” [Col. 1361B]?

We should also calculate from the first year of Darius, when Daniel saw this vision. Let us see how the years are fulfilled up to Christ’s coming.

Darius reigned for nineteen years; Artaxerxes for forty; Ochus, also called Cyrus, for fourteen; Argus for one year; another Darius, also called Melas, for twenty years; Alexander of Macedon for ten years.

After him, Soter reigned in Alexandria for thirty-five years; he was succeeded by Philadelphus, who reigned for thirty-eight years. After him came Euergetes, for twenty-five years; then Philopator, for seventeen years; after him Epiphanes, for twenty-four years; then another Euergetes, for twenty-seven years; Soter, for thirty-eight years; Ptolemy, for thirty-seven years.

Cleopatra reigned for twenty years and five months. Afterward Cleopatra reigned together with Augustus for thirteen years. After Cleopatra, Augustus ruled for another forty-three years, since all the years of Augustus’s reign numbered fifty-six.

In the forty-first year of Augustus’s reign—the reign that began after Cleopatra’s death—Christ was born. Augustus himself survived from the time of Christ’s birth for fifteen years.

The remaining period up to the day of Christ’s birth, in the forty-first year of Augustus, amounts to 437 years and five months. Thus sixty-two and a half weeks are completed, making 437 years and six months; everlasting righteousness was manifested, and the Holy of Holies was anointed, that is, Christ.

Some, however, say that “the vision” [perhaps “Jesus”] and “the prophecy” are sealed, because all the prophets announced concerning him that he would come and would suffer. Since prophecy was fulfilled through his coming, they say that the vision and prophecy are sealed, because he is the seal of all the prophets, fulfilling everything that the prophets had previously announced about him.

[Col. 1362A] **67. What does he mean by saying: “In the third year of Cyrus king of the Persians, a word was revealed to Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar” (Dan. 10:1), when at the end of the first vision we read: “Daniel continued until the first year of Cyrus the king” (Dan. 1:21)—did he continue until his first year?**

We understand, therefore, that he remained among the Chaldeans in his former rank, clothed in purple and fine linen, until the first year of Cyrus the king, when he overthrew the Chaldeans; afterward he came to be with Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of Median descent, who ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldeans. Or, alternatively, Darius had already died—during whose first year he had learned the mystery of the seventy weeks—and now he is said to have seen these things in the third year of King Cyrus.

[Col. 1362B] **68. What does he mean when he says: “And I, from the first year of Darius the Mede, stood to strengthen and fortify him” (Dan. 11:1)?**

“I stood,” he says, “in the sight of God, and I asked for his mercy on behalf of the one who loved me, that either he himself or his kingdom might be strengthened and fortified”—the one who, for my protection, also sealed the lions’ den with his ring, so that my adversaries might not kill me. Alexander, however, after founding Alexandria, died by poison when he was thirty-two years old and was in the twelfth year of his reign in Babylon.

**69. What do they mean by saying, “And after some years they shall form an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the South shall come to the king of the North to make friendship; but she shall not retain the strength of her arm, nor shall her offspring stand; and she herself shall be handed over, together with those who brought her, her young men, and those who supported her in those times” (ibid. 6)?**

This is what is now meant: for many years Ptolemy Philadelphus and Antiochus, who was called Theos, that is, “God,” would make alliances. The daughter of the king of the South—that is, of Ptolemy—would come to the king of the North, that is, to Antiochus, so that she might join her father and her husband in alliance. “But she shall not be able,” he says, “to prevail, nor shall her offspring stand in the kingdom of Syria”; rather, Berenice herself and those who had brought her would be killed. King Antiochus also, who strengthened him—that is, through whom he was able to prevail—was killed by his wife’s poison. For his former wife Laodice killed him by means of her agents, because the king called Berenice his consort [Col. 1362D] in the kingdom and this woman his concubine.

**Here ends the work.**

[Col. 1363]

# CATULFUS

## CATULFUS’S EPISTOLARY INSTRUCTION TO THE BLESSED KING CHARLES

*(From Duchesne, Historical Writers of France.)*

[Col. 1363A] To the most pious lord king, exalted by the grace of God, to the truly most dear Charles, most upright in the kingdom of Christ: the least Catulfus, yet your little servant, with a pure heart, sends greetings in the Holy Spirit.

My lord king, I therefore beg you always to remember him who, as I believe, created you from nothing and made you great from the least beginnings. For an earthly parent contributes nothing except that he emits or receives bodily fluid, the material from which conception occurs, with the accompanying sensation of pleasure; and then, insofar as it is not sin, the matter is from God. Everything else, however, is from God: conception itself, the formation of the body, the breathing-in of the soul, safe birth, and everything thereafter by which a human being is preserved according to the will of God. It is his gift that we live, [Col. 1363B] and breathe, according to the saying: “The breath of man is in the hand of God.” Likewise: “Your hands made me,” and so forth.

These things are common to all human beings. But with particular and special blessings, O my king, your King honored you above your contemporaries and blessed you with a crown of glory above your predecessors. First, through the dignity of the king and queen, and indeed beyond that: through their prayers, especially those of your mother, who specially prayed to God, as it pleased him; hence you were conceived and born—indeed, from God, my king, and consider this statement carefully.

Second, you are the firstborn and shall receive his blessing, as it is written, according to the saying: “Every firstborn that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.”

Third, God protected you in every way from the plots of your brother, as we read of Jacob [Col. 1363C] and Esau.

Fourth, you received the kingdom together with your brother of the Franks.

Fifth, and no small sign of blessedness, God transferred him from the earthly kingdom and exalted you over this entire kingdom without bloodshed. . . . . . Wonderful piety and great mercy of God on that day with the Frankish army. A fool. . . . . . a wise man in need of grace, or—

Sixth, the army of the Lombards was put to flight before your face without open battle.

Seventh, you entered the Alps while your enemies were fleeing; you also captured the exceedingly wealthy city, Pavia, together with its king, without bloodshed and with all its treasures.

Eighth, you entered golden and imperial Rome and gently received from the King of kings the kingdoms of Italy with all their riches.

In how many ways, moreover, have your enemies been put to flight before your face and have you emerged victorious! [Col. 1363D] [Col. 1364A] And this was fulfilled in you which is read in the Psalms, although it is understood especially of Christ and David: “I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them,” and so forth. Likewise, in the person of God the Father: “And I shall put his enemies to flight.” And again: “I shall make him firstborn,” and so forth. Likewise in Moses: “God fights for us.” Likewise Saint Paul: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” So also concerning Joshua, David, Hezekiah, Judas Maccabee, and others.

Now therefore, my lord king, for these many blessings, give glory night and day, together with all your armies, to God the King of kings, and offer thanksgiving with your whole kingdom, because he himself has exalted you to the honor and glory of the kingdom of Europe—and he will still grant you greater things than those mentioned above, if you exalt him together with his own in this way.

Always remember, therefore, my king, [Col. 1364B] God your King, with fear and love: you are in his place over all his members, to guard and govern them and to render an account on the day of judgment, even through yourself. The bishop is in second place; he stands in the place of Christ alone.

Therefore, consider carefully among yourselves how to establish God’s law over God’s people, as your God, whose place you occupy, said in the Psalm: “And now, O kings, understand,” and so forth. Likewise: “Serve the Lord in fear,” and so forth. Likewise: “Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry,” and so forth. There are very many examples, so that you may exalt the law.

First, I write a few things to you, as the canons set forth and as the law of all Christianity contains by God’s command. After faith in God, love, and fear, see that you frequently have the *Enchiridion*, that is, the “Manual,” the law of your God written in your hands, so that you may read it all the days of your life, and so that you may be instructed in divine wisdom and secular letters, as David, Solomon, and the other kings were.

God also said to Moses concerning kings: “When he has sat upon the throne of his kingdom, the Book of the Law shall never depart from his hands”; let him not have many wives, nor be proud over his contemporaries, nor exalted, nor envious, and so forth (Deut. 17).

But . . . . . judge between the poor and the powerful, and rescue the poor from the hand of the powerful; never sell a Christian or hand him over to a pagan people—woe, woe!—joining a member of Christ to a member of the devil, losing a soul, with its price demanded before the throne of Christ.

Clothe Christ’s bride with ornaments above all else, that is, establish the greatest privileges for the churches; govern the life of monks and canons together with your bishops, and likewise the monasteries of virgins—not through laymen, which is a crime . . . . . but correct them through spiritual shepherds.

Above all: God-fearing [men], as it is written in the law—bishops, priests, deacons, and the others, counts, centenaries, commanders of fifties, decans, and the rest—not accepting gifts, so that the law of God may be destroyed [lacuna] of money, but arranging all things with you in the fear of God, according to the law. For not all who are called bishops are bishops. So with the counts, and so also with the others.

O, o, woe, woe! You must support with yourself the few firm pillars—as I fear, the camps of God. There are eight particular pillars of a just king. Pay close attention to them.

The first is truth in royal affairs.

The second is patience in every matter.

The third is generosity in gifts.

The fourth is persuasiveness in speech.

The fifth is the correction and restraint of evil people.

The sixth is the raising and exaltation of good people.

The seventh is the lightness of taxation among the people.

The eighth is equity of judgment between rich and poor.

If you earnestly preserve these eight pillars, then you will be a king—for “king” is derived from governing, just as “kingdom” is derived from kings—and your kingdom will be blessed together with your days, your wife, and your sons. Then there will be tranquility of air and weather, fertility of land and sea and of everything born in them; you will also rule happily over many peoples, and your enemies will fall before your face, and so forth.

By contrast, as Saint Patrick said, because of an unjust king there will be misfortune for the king himself, discord among his wife and children, [Col. 1365C] dissension among the peoples, famine, pestilence, infertility of the land and sea, and crops of the earth struck by various storms; he will be defeated by his enemies and driven from his kingdom. You have sufficient examples in these days and among your fathers, such as Waepero, Desiderius and his son, and their kingdoms, and so forth; likewise Rehoboam, Ahaz, Ahab, and the other kings of the Jews who did evil in the sight of the Lord and did not walk in God’s commandments.

Therefore, my king, read all these things and consider them carefully, lest you lose your honor here and in the future. Rather, take good counsel with your wise men; take counsel especially with those who fear God. From among them, choose men throughout the cities, monasteries, and your entire kingdom to renew the laws and destroy injustices. And choose those who know the law and do not accept gifts but arrange what is right—that is, approved bishops and counts, and so forth—so that you may be able to uproot thorns, thistles, and the scandals of vices from your kingdom, and piously govern the army of Christians, the members of Christ.

In the first place, concerning the shepherds mentioned above: the canons command, and the first law of the whole world, the Roman law—indeed, God himself—commands [Col. 1366A] that the graves of Christians should have peace. If not, let them be punished according to the law.

Sorcerers, poisoners, storm-makers, witches, pythonesses, thieves, murderers—especially in the churches of God—[lacuna; uncertain reading: *trias*], adulterers, plunderers, false witnesses in public, or those who seize Christians and hand them over to paganism; perjurers, especially in the Church of God; counterfeiters of money . . . . . not returning it; despoilers of churches; abductors or robbers of widows, orphans, and the fatherless; . . . . . those who inflict injury; abductors of widows, virgins, or consecrated women; . . . . . . . . . and all incestuous acts.

Correct or condemn these and similar offenses according to the punishment of the law. . . . . . . . . . . You are God’s minister in all these matters and his avenger, and so forth. . . . . . . . And exalt him in all the matters mentioned above in praise, because he has honorably exalted you above all the predecessors [Col. 1366B] of your people, according to the saying: “Exalt the Lord our God,” and so forth. Likewise: “Sing joyfully to God, all the earth.” Likewise: “Let all the earth adore you.” Likewise: “Let all the kings of the earth give thanks to you, Lord, and let them sing to the Lord in hymns,” and so forth.

Therefore, my king, if this counsel pleases you, establish, for all these matters, for yourself and for the army of Christians, one day each year after a fast, in honor of the Holy Trinity and its unity, of the angels, and of all the saints, to be celebrated throughout your kingdom. With the counsel of the Frankish synod, establish that the Mass of Saint Michael and the Passion of Saint Peter be celebrated publicly throughout your kingdom.

When you do these and similar things, then surely, with great happiness and blessedness, you and the members of Christ with you will reign here and in the future [Col. 1366C] with the angels and archangels without end, and with all the saints you will remain in joy forever and ever. Amen.

These few things, my lord king, I have selected from many, as they came to mind. Although I am rustic and ignorant, I nevertheless thought it pleasing to write to you for the sake of your piety, trusting that pardon will be granted for my foolishness and that your reward with God will become greater.

Fare well in God. Live happily forever.

Let us always sing honor well to the King of kings.

For Christ and holy Peter, without end,

with triple harmony, my King Charles of the peoples,

let us praise the Holy Trinity, yet the one God.

Why, then, does he strongly enlarge your kingdom without war?

[Col. 1366D] Here God, your helper, always stands powerfully beside you,

he who has always taken away impious wars from you throughout the world,

who at once overwhelmed the weak and honored the humble.

For you are also worthy of the name by which the gracious God is called.

May glory always belong to the Trinity, yet to the One together.

O, o, the days are near. Let whoever now holds continue to hold until the half is completed. Read and understand carefully.

[Col. 1367]

# CONSTANS THE PRIEST

## THE TREATISE OF CONSTANS THE PRIEST ON THE PASSION OF THE BLESSED MARTYR EMMERAMMUS

*(From Pez, Library of Anecdotes.)*

[Col. 1367A] Since the power of holy religion, operating through love from its very origin, has always caused the most peaceful fruits of justice to spread through senses trained by it in holy men pleasing to God, it has nevertheless been especially celebrated through the struggles of the blessed martyrs of Christ and magnified by their glorious triumphs.

But when the fervor of both kinds of love shone more brightly through the hearts of all the faithful, and when, through the soundness of its strength, it irresistibly expanded by means of a twofold and manifold propagation, then the ardor of divine charity kindled far beyond comparison the minds of those who served as recruits of the heavenly King and gloried in contempt of the world; and it inflamed them uniquely above all others with desire for him.

For those have clung more closely to the Lord through the affection of love who have become most like him [Col. 1367B] through the bitterness of suffering. They must have bound themselves to him more firmly by the bond of charity, for whose sake they did not spare themselves even unto the shedding of blood.

In view of this, earthly things are contemptible and heavenly things are desired; everything that passes away is worthless, while what remains is precious. For the sake of attaining this, at the end the executioner is asked to tear, the torturer not to spare, and the swordsman to strike. Content with this alone, they are ready to expend body and soul.

The Apostle, burning with this fire of charity, entered the field of combat and exulted triumphantly, saying: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. Nor do I regard my life as more precious to myself.” For him also, “to live was Christ and to die was gain.”

These, then, the most eager followers of Christ’s sufferings [Col. 1367C] and lovers of him even unto death—these, I say, most valiant athletes, commanders of heavenly wars, instructed by the judgment of the holy apostle Peter, who says: “Beloved, Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps”—fortified with spiritual weapons, freed from every worldly desire, skilled in military discipline, experienced in all things before and during battle, taking possession of the stadium of the raging world, attentive to the trumpet of evangelical command, challenged the enemy and stirred up the boldness of rebels. They terrified those who had been roused and crushed those whom they had struck.

At last [Col. 1367D], led by the glory of their victories, they met the mass of what had to be conquered; and, endowed with everlasting glory, they reached their King, under whose gaze and with whose help they had fought. [Col. 1368A] Once considered wretched by human judgment, and condemned as impious, they are now joined to eternal joys and have become like the angels of God.

Among this most excellent class of conquerors, blessed martyr Emmerammus—whose day of passion, or birthday, has today dawned with joyful solemnity—possesses a dignity of such glory that, if it is insufficient to believe in earthly achievements, it may be confirmed by the proofs of heavenly virtues. These shine all the more abundantly for each believer insofar as he has conceived in his heart and demonstrated by his works the faith that burned in Emmerammus’s breast.

He, promoted through every degree of merit to the honor of the episcopate, and an investigator of the laws of the Lord by day and by night, kindled with that same most fervent fire of divinity of which we have spoken, sighed with the whole desire of his mind for the palm of martyrdom [Col. 1368B]. Following Solomon’s exhortation, he was moved to emulate the spending of his flesh for the love of Christ, so that, having sat at the great table, he too might remember to prepare such things.

He was also admonished by the evangelical saying: “No one has greater love than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends.” Wishing, insofar as he could, to repay this benefit to the Redeemer, he was driven toward it by anxious turmoil of spirit and not without the undertaking of great deeds.

Finally, since his native land denied him the opportunity for suffering, he gathered his strength and went out seeking an idolatrous enemy through the worship of truth (*cultu veritatis*, read from the fused OCR *cultoveritatis*). In this he imitated the example of the ancient patriarch, to whom it was divinely commanded by an oracle: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, [Col. 1368C] and come into the land that I shall show you.”

Intent upon this course of divine warfare as a mighty warrior, he was nevertheless restrained by heavenly governance and, of necessity, settled where he least intended. Thus he did not advance where his desire for the crown was striving to take him. For a different reason, he nevertheless obtained the same honor of martyrdom that he thirsted for.

When an opportunity arose to fulfill Solomon’s saying, “Rescue those who are being led to death,” whether he was carrying out that command or a guilty person might die in sins, he poured himself out entirely in compassion and truly became an imitator of his Lord, who bore the sins of others in his body upon the cross. He himself endured the punishments of the wretched, which they feared, and the venerable priest did not refuse to bear the Lord’s cross through the reproach of the shameful crime they had committed when they fell into sexual violation.

What, my brothers? Have you ever seen anything like this deed? What glory do you think can be compared with that of this martyr and priest?

Elijah and John, rebuking the adulteries of royal spouses, were both taken up into heaven: the one by a chariot, the other through martyrdom. But surely their circumstances were easier and their necessity less pressing. For even among fools there are those who consider the cause of one rebuked for incest far more honorable than that of incest committed. Both of them were pursued for the truth only by lustful men.

But this man, allowing the violators to transfer their crime onto himself, with only one priest left among mortals as witness to his innocence, chose rather to let his own life be stained for a time by profane suspicion—so that it might be cleansed by God, who knows secrets, in whatever manner he wished—than to allow the lives of the guilty to be ended through various kinds of torture.

For remembering the Lord’s saying, “I do not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should be converted and live,” he preserved those who confessed their sins to him for correction; and he permitted himself to be sacrificed as a most pleasing offering to God for their deaths.

A deadly executioner, driven by Satan’s savage rage, rushed upon him; and he dragged away the holy bishop of God, abandoned by his innocent companions in flight, according to what is written: “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.”

At the will of the cruel beast, this ram, a most sacred victim chosen for God, is torn apart throughout his body.

[Col. 1369C]

His mouth, both hands, and ravaged temples; his ears torn away, and his nose cut off in a pitiable wound:

his brain, too, always illumined by the light of wisdom, was deprived of the light of his eyes; although the inward vision of his spirit, brighter even than the worldly sun, shone with the unfailing clarity of its steadfastness.

His tongue also, the minister of the heavenly oracle, bringing forth new and old things from the hidden secret of the fountain, according to what reason had determined, the pestilential surgeon tore out by the roots from the chamber of his holy mouth.

Insane fury did not consider that “the lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” Even in the very sex, that is, in those limbs that should not be mentioned in him, reckless and perverse savagery, alas, exercised its judgment.

Thus, O Christ, the strength of those who serve you—the priest and victim of your flock—fortified by the shield of endurance, with you standing beside him and numbering all the wounds inflicted upon him for the sake of love for you, was carried by an angelic procession and the glory of triumphs, crowned with a hundredfold martyr’s crown, and ascended to the heavenly court. In him was fulfilled what Solomon admonishes: “Do not fear to be justified even unto death, because God’s reward remains forever.” And the Psalmist: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; they shall not be shaken forever.” Likewise the apostle James: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life.”

[Col. 1370B] Let Rome, therefore, be renowned for Laurence; Jerusalem illustrious for Stephen; Carthage noble for Cyprian; Smyrna for Polycarp; Spain distinguished for the great Cucuphas. But let our Regensburg rejoice wonderfully in its priest and martyr Emmerammus, hoping for no less a benefit of grace from this patron than any of those cities receives from its most indulgent father.

We therefore offer you thanks in honor of the Divinity, O thrice and four times happy and most blessed bishop, honored by heaven and earth. Your cause among all the martyrs was singular, more grievous than every punishment and more cruel than every torture devised.

For it is not punishment that makes a martyr, but the cause. This cause set you above the blood of Stephen, the flames of Laurence, the pyre of Polycarp, the triumph of the Theban Legion, and finally [Col. 1370C] the struggles of all Christ’s athletes. For you were crowned in heaven by your King as many times as you were mutilated by the severing of limbs in your most holy body.

In humiliation your judgment was taken away; you endured the raging tyrant like a peaceful sheep and bore the anger of the executioners with the quietest patience.

Therefore, most holy bishop, as we stand before you and on this most sacred day of your passion offer, however humbly, the vows of our praise in service, deign to visit us with the gift of heavenly blessing; excuse the sins of your people and, through continual intercession, arrange the guidance of our life before him who is the very fountain of mercy.

[Col. 1369]

# GARNERIUS, ABBOT

[Note: [Col. 1369D] Morinus preserved for us only the Gallican version of the address of Garnier the abbot to King Aistulf, and did not mention the source from which he had taken this address [Col. 1370D]. We therefore thought it best to reprint it in the same language as Morinus.]

## EMBASSY TO KING AISTULF

*(Morin, History of the Origin and Progress of the Temporal Sovereignty of the Popes.)*

[Col. 1369D] Pope Stephen III, pressed more severely than ever by the king of the Lombards, had no hope left except in the valor and piety of the Franks. At the beginning of these new disturbances, therefore, he wrote to King Pepin and his sons, warning them of Aistulf’s treachery, explaining to them the outrages he committed daily against the Romans, and chiefly begging them to compel him by their authority to carry out the donation they had made to the Holy See, of which he had fulfilled no provision.

In response to these complaints, Pepin sent an abbot of great authority named Garnier, to investigate the truth and urge the Lombards to keep their promise. Garnier went to Aistulf to try to dissuade him from attacking Rome and to advise him to give the pope some satisfaction. Having obtained an audience, he spoke to him in this manner:

“Sire, the king of France, my master, has sent me to Your Majesty to beg you to cease molesting the pope and the Romans and to fulfill your promise by placing the exarchate of Ravenna in the hands of His Holiness, under the conditions agreed upon with him and Your Majesty.

“My master the king greatly desires the honor of your friendship and to live in good understanding with you and with all Christian princes. He believes that a good peace is preferable to the hope of victory, and that it is a Christian and more glorious act to settle all his disputes by reason rather than by the outcome of a battle.

“Nevertheless, Sire, I am commanded by him, if his prayers are not powerful enough to persuade you to return the exarchate to the pope, to declare to you that he will once again cross the mountains to compel you by force; and that there is neither difficulty, danger, nor power capable of preventing him from risking his life and his state in order to restore the honor and liberty of the Holy See.

“All Europe knows that you are full of courage and valor; but you have also experienced God’s blessing upon the arms of my master. You know the great victories he has won over the rebels of his kingdom, over the Saracens, the Bavarians, the Germans, and the Saxons; how his whole life has been spent amid arms and battles, without tasting the delights of cities; how from his birth he was raised beneath his father’s laurels, and how, since his father’s death, he has never ceased to conquer.

“For this reason, my profession, which cannot be reconciled with the shedding of blood and which obliges me personally to seek peace among Christians, gives me the boldness to beg Your Majesty to consider religiously within yourself how rarely events correspond to our hopes; that nothing is more faithless than prosperity, nor anything more hazardous than placing present possessions at risk for the appearance of a future advantage.

“The hearts of the wisest grieve and wither at the thought of the future, and after a thousand painful anxieties the mind foresees everything except what is actually destined to happen to it. Let Your Majesty, Sire, consider not only what you may gain by war [Col. 1372A] but also what you may lose.

“Stability accompanies only the happiness that comes from God; as for human beings, he gives them no other portion of it in this life than thought and desire. But, Sire, there are no undertakings or actions over which uncertainty rules more than over those of war.

“War is like dice: once they have been cast, the outcome is no longer in our power; we must submit to the lot fortune assigns. One lost battle is enough to destroy the conquests of many centuries. Histories and human memory are full of such examples.

“Your Majesty need not go far to learn this. I shall take the liberty of begging you most humbly to look at what has happened to you. How quickly and against all appearances did my master the king cross the Alps, compel your captains to abandon the countryside, and go to lay siege before the capital city of your kingdom!

“It is this victory, joined to so many others, that makes him slow to undertake a new war and that advised him to send me to Your Majesty, to beg and demand that you fulfill the conditions of the treaty made with the Holy See. For the continuation of his good fortune restrains the passionate desires of his courage and makes him consider all the more the instability of human affairs, precisely because he seems farther removed from it.

“Let Your Majesty, Sire, therefore not entrust so much glory and power as you possess to the faithlessness of a single day [Col. 1372C]; and let the fulfillment of your promise be more highly commended to you than the hope of retaining a small province.

“Justice, not the extent of provinces, is the true greatness of kings, and returning to each person what belongs to him is the unshakable foundation of their states. Whatever they unite to their empires by another means resembles the feet of Nebuchadnezzar’s statue, which were made of iron and clay: *Non adhaerebunt sibi*, says the Spirit of God, *sicuti ferrum misceri non potest testae*—‘They shall not cleave to one another, just as iron cannot be mixed with clay.’

“This union brings the curse of heaven upon the whole body of the statue, which is a holy hieroglyph of the empires of the world; for a stone descending from the mountain reduced to dust the iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold of which it was composed.

“Therefore, Sire, give satisfaction to the pope. The submission that princes render to the Church is always glorious for them. Otherwise, this stone will once again descend like a torrent from the mountains and burst like a thunderbolt upon the gates of Pavia.”

# ANONYMOUS, EIGHTH CENTURY

[Col. 1373]

## I. LETTER OF AN UNKNOWN WRITER TO KING PEPIN

*(From Duchesne, Historical Writers of France.)*

[Col. 1373A] To the most merciful lord, chosen and exalted by God, to the most magnificent King Pepin: his humble servant and little client, your diligent ambassador in all things, through this letter wishes and sends your greatness everlasting salvation in the Lord of lords.

I therefore give thanks to almighty God that, with the greatest prosperity, I arrived in the service of my lord; received by him with his customary kindness, I stand graciously in his presence.

I was questioned by that most pious king about many matters concerning your regions, and in all the inquiries I deserved to be heard willingly. The Almighty furnished me with such answers that they refreshed his mind like the sweetest melody and with the joy of sacred delight.

[Col. 1373B] For this reason, his ineffable clemency has, as is fitting, the best disposition toward Your Excellency.

Since, however, your servant can recount all that was said to you in person, there were certain unequal or hostile men (*expares*), whom I thought to be friends, running with poisoned hearts, who, before I arrived, attempted to accuse my wretchedness. But he who knows the hidden things of all took pity on his servant, and their machinations began to help rather than inflict any deception.

All the things which they attempted secretly, by lying, to accuse before illustrious ears [uncertain: *nisi sunt accusare*], that same most merciful king deigned kindly to recount to me, his servant, before all the princes [Col. 1374A]; the aforesaid man can relate all these things more wisely in your hearing. Do not doubt that you have him as one of your true friends and a faithful little servant, for, to the extent that his mind was able, he strove manfully before our lord for your advancement in glory.

Our man, whom I loved in your affection as my own soul, was not ashamed to test his arrows against my death, nor at least to utter untrue words against me in the king’s presence. But he who reduced the counsel of the wicked Ahithophel to nothing wished suddenly to crush his evil as well; and by the grace of the Lord he kindly granted that I should be found worthy.

For I, your little servant, have arranged [Col. 1374B] to send my messenger to you in your service as soon as I am able. But now, on the occasion of the present, I send you through him, as a token of blessing, a small gift—not, however, with a small affection of goodwill: eleven cushions . . . . . . . May you deign to regard them with your most serene countenance.

I commend myself and all [uncertain: *rex sancti il. ac nostras*]; and for all our relatives, your little servants, I ask God [to grant] many happy years under the protection of your wings (*alarum*, read for *aliarum*) [lacuna] to Your Serenity.

As soon as you have received this little written notice, you will be handed over to be devoured by fire.*

[Col. 1373]

## II. LETTER OF A MONK TO AN ABBOT

[Col. 1373C] Dear to the dear, beloved to the most beloved, a son in Christ to his father: the humble N. to N., abbot, eternal salvation in the Lord.

Two things are simultaneously present in our mind—namely, wonder and sadness. Why? Because, after we were separated from your affection in body, though not in mind, we have not been able to become certain of your desirable prosperity—which, God is our witness, we always desire to hear and see—either through a messenger or through your honey-sweet letters. [Col. 1373D] Let your wisdom therefore know that we have decided to send our pack animals to the palace on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, and afterward to remain there for three days on account of the work of the Church; then, with the Lord’s help, we wish to follow them promptly, with the intention that we may be at Mainz on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September. For if it should please you, as you have arranged, to come through us, then we shall have to arrange our journey according to your wishes.

For there is no reason—apart from those matters which we cannot change by any human ingenuity—that could cause us to abandon your wishes, insofar as we are able with Christ’s help. [Col. 1374D] We went, moreover, to your little estate at the place called [illegible]; we inspected the estate itself, ordered our meal to be brought there from our own supplies, and, together with our own and your faithful dependents, rejoiced there in your love. From there, catching fish by boat, we reached the estate [lacuna]. Tassilo, however, as we hope, your faithful servant, prudently gave us an answer in every respect concerning the matters we had asked of him. And we think that, if you approve him and entrust him with some service according to your knowledge or instruction, he will take care thereafter to please you.

Finally, we ask that you instruct that provost of yours to strive to make a good agreement, according to your promise, concerning that estate which your charity bestowed upon us, so that from this there may accrue a reward for both us and you. [Col. 1376A] Concerning the lead and the timber likewise give orders, so that, according to your wishes, we may transport them by boat from that holy place to the place where the Signa flows into the sea, in such a way that you may thereby have as intercessors my holy lord, that lover of yours, together with all the saints whose relics we possess in the monastery.

May almighty God preserve you healthy and unharmed in the present age during his times, and in the future make you joyful with the holy angels. Amen.

[Col. 1375]

## III. A Bishop’s Admonition to the Priests Subject to Him and to the Other Ministers of Every Ecclesiastical Order

*(From Martène, Amplissima Collectio.)*

[Col. 1375B] Brother priests, you are fellow workers with us in the Lord’s order, and we, although unworthy, occupy the place of Aaron, while you occupy the place of Eleazar and Ithamar. We act in the place of the twelve apostles; you, in the place of the seventy-two disciples. We are your shepherds; you are shepherds of the people entrusted to you. We shall render an account concerning you to the supreme Shepherd, our Lord Jesus Christ; you, concerning the people entrusted to you. Therefore, dearest brothers, consider your danger. We admonish and entreat your brotherhood, therefore, to commit to memory what we suggest to you and to strive to carry it out in practice.

**I.** First of all, we admonish you that your life and conduct be irreproachable: specifically, that your dwelling be near the church and that you have no women in your house. [Col. 1375C]

**II.** Rise every night for the vigils; chant your offices at the appointed hours.

**III.** Perform the solemn celebrations of the Mass reverently; receive the body and blood of the Lord with fear and reverence; wash and wipe the sacred vessels with your own hands.

**IV.** Let no one sing unless he is fasting; let no one sing who does not receive Communion.

**V.** Let no one sing without an amice, alb, stole, fanon, and chasuble. Let these vestments be clean, and let them be used for no other purposes.

**VI.** Let no one presume to celebrate Mass in the alb that he uses for his ordinary purposes [Alt.: “to sing,” here and below]. [Col. 1376B] Let no one dare to celebrate Mass in a wooden or glass chalice.

**VII.** Let no woman approach the altar or touch the Lord’s chalice.

**VIII.** Let the corporal be perfectly clean. Let the altar be covered with clean cloths. Let nothing be placed on the altar except reliquaries and relics, [Alt., or perhaps] the four Gospels, and a pyx containing the Lord’s body for Communion to the sick; let everything else be stored in a clean place.

**IX.** Let each person have a Missal, [Note: [Col. 1375D] Some confuse the Plenary with the Missal; some distinguish them in this way: the Missal is an ecclesiastical book containing the office of the Masses, while the Plenary is a book containing the Epistles and Gospels. Nevertheless, I would judge that the Missal is plenary—that is, a book in which are contained not only the canon, prayers, and prefaces, but also the Epistles and Gospels, in short everything that is sung in the choir.] a Plenary, a Lectionary, an Antiphonary, and both books of the Forty Homilies. [Note: [Col. 1376D] In the Victorinus manuscript both books of the Forty Homilies are missing.]

**X.** A place in the sacristy or beside the altar must be prepared where water may be poured out when the sacred vessels are washed; and there let a clean vessel filled with water hang, in which the priest may wash his hands after Communion. [Col. 1376C]

**XI.** Let the churches be well roofed and vaulted, and let the church courtyard be enclosed by walls on every side. [Note: [Col. 1376D] Victorinus: “fortified by an enclosure.”]

**XII.** Let no one sing Mass outside the church, in private houses or in unconsecrated places; nor let him sing alone. [Note: [Col. 1376D] In Victorinus, “nor let him sing alone” is absent.]

**XIII.** Let every priest have a cleric who can read the Epistle or the lesson, answer him at Mass, and sing psalms with him.

**XIV.** Visit the sick, reconcile them to God, anoint them with holy oil, and give them Communion with your own hand. Let no one presume to entrust Communion to a layman or a woman to carry to the sick.

**XV.** [Note: [Col. 1376D] In the Victorinus manuscript this article reads: “Let none of you demand a reward or gift for baptizing infants, reconciling the sick, or burying the dead.” The rest is omitted.] Let no one sell the sacred chrism; let no one demand a price for baptisms, for the Lord’s body, for reconciliation, for burial, or for the consecration of churches; nor let anyone seize another’s churches by means of money. [Col. 1377A]

**XVI.** Take care that through your negligence no infant dies without baptism.

**XVII.** Let none of you be a drunkard or quarrelsome. [Note: [Col. 1377D] The Victorinus manuscript adds: “because it is not fitting for a servant of the Lord to quarrel.”] Let no one carry weapons during a riot. [Note: [Col. 1377D] Victorinus adds: “because our weapons ought to be spiritual.”] Let no one devote himself to the amusements of dogs or birds; let no one drink in taverns.

**XVIII.** Let each of you, according to his understanding, proclaim to his people on Sunday or on feast days something from the Gospel, the Epistle, or some other divine Scripture. [Note: [Col. 1377D] The Victorinus manuscript reads: “Announce the Gospel or the Apostle on Sundays or feast days. You ought to preach the word of God.”]

**XIX.** Let him care for the poor, strangers, and orphans, and invite them to dinner, so that in these and similar matters others may take an example from you. [Note: [Col. 1377D] The Victorinus manuscript states the entire article in the second person and then adds: “Be hospitable, so that others may take a good example from you.”]

**XX.** Every Sunday before Mass, prepare holy water with which the people and the places belonging to the faithful may be sprinkled. [Col. 1377B] [Note: [Col. 1377D] Victorinus: “Let the people be sprinkled,” omitting “and the places belonging to the faithful,” and adding: “And have a vessel for this alone.”]

**XXI.** Let sacred vessels or priestly vestments not be given as pledges to a merchant or to any secular person. [Note: [Col. 1377D] Victorinus: “Do not give them as security to a merchant or tavern keeper.”]

**XXII.** Let none of you bring an unworthy penitent to reconciliation for any reason whatsoever, or give him a certificate of reconciliation.

**XXIII.** Let none of you exact interest, and let him be a tenant of his senior. [Note: [Col. 1377D] Victorinus: “of new interest.”] Know that the property and resources acquired after the day of your ordination belong to the church which you serve.

**XXIV.** Let no one acquire a church without our knowledge and consent. [Note: [Col. 1377D] The Victorinus manuscript adds: “Let no one supplant another’s church by means of money.”] Let no one obtain a church through the power of secular persons; let no one abandon the church to which he has been appointed and migrate to another for the sake of profit. [Col. 1377C]

**XXV.** Let no one hold several churches without the assistance of other priests; under no circumstances is one church to be divided among several persons.

**XXVI.** Let no one receive another’s parishioner for Mass, except while traveling or if it should be agreeable to him. Let no one sing in another’s parish without that priest’s permission. [Note: [Col. 1378D] Victorinus: “without the will or request of his own priest.”]

**XXVII.** Let no one receive a tithe belonging to another.

**XXVIII.** Let no one invite a penitent to eat meat or drink wine unless he has first given alms for him on that occasion.

**XXIX.** [Note: [Col. 1378D] This article is missing from the Victorinus manuscript.] Let no one presume to baptize except on the vigils of Easter and Pentecost, unless there is danger of death. [Col. 1377D]

[Col. 1378A] **XXX.** Let each person have a baptismal font; if he cannot have one of stone, let him have another vessel prepared solely for this purpose. [Note: [Col. 1378D] Victorinus adds: “in which nothing else is done.”]

**XXXI.** Instruct all your parishioners in the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.

**XXXII.** Enjoin upon them the fast of the Ember Days, the Rogations, and the Greater Litany. [Note: [Col. 1378D] Victorinus: “Instruct your peoples to observe these in every way.”]

**XXXIII.** On the Wednesday before Lent, invite them to confession and impose penance upon them according to the nature of their offense—not according to your own judgment, but as it is written in the penitential book.

**XXXIV.** Three times a year—namely, at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost—let all the faithful receive Communion. [Note: [Col. 1378D] Victorinus: “Admonish all the faithful to approach for Communion of the body and blood.”]

**XXXV.** At appointed times, let married persons abstain from their wives. [Col. 1378B] [Note: [Col. 1378D] Victorinus: “Exhort them to abstain.”]

**XXXVI.** On feast days, let them receive eulogies after Mass.

**XXXVII.** [Note: [Col. 1378D] In the Victorinus manuscript, “let no priest travel without a stole” is absent.] Let no priest travel without a stole; let no one wear lay clothing; let no one sell, exchange, or alienate by any means any property, possession, or serf belonging to the church.

**XXXVIII.** Let each person celebrate the Lord’s Day and the other feasts from evening to evening. [Note: [Col. 1378D] Victorinus: “Teach them to celebrate without servile work.”]

**XXXIX.** Completely prohibit women’s songs and dances in the church courtyard.

**XL.** Prohibit, under solemn adjuration of almighty God, the devilish songs that the common people customarily sing over the dead at night, and the laughter that they practice. [Col. 1378C]

**XLI.** [Note: [Col. 1378D] Victorinus: “Do not communicate with the excommunicated; let no one presume to sing Mass for them, and announce this also to the peoples entrusted to you.”] Do not sing Mass for the excommunicated, and absolutely forbid the people entrusted to you to do so.

**XLII.** Let no priest attend weddings.

**XLIII.** [Note: [Col. 1378D] The Victorinus manuscript reads: “Announce to everyone that no one …”] Let no one take a wife unless the marriage has been publicly celebrated. Let no one commit abduction. Let no one take his near kinswoman. Let no one marry another man’s betrothed.

**XLIV.** Let each person make his swineherds and other servants come to Mass on Sundays and feast days.

**XLV.** Let godparents either teach, or have taught, their spiritual children the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.

[Col. 1379A] **XLVI.** Let the chrism always be kept under lock and key. [Note: [Col. 1379A] Victorinus adds: “or under seal,”] on account of certain unbelievers.

**XLVII.** [Note: [Col. 1379A] The following material is absent from the Victorinus manuscript; in its place the following is read: “But we wish, dearest brothers, that you strive, insofar as human weakness permits, to fulfill by good works what you have received through our tradition, with the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, through all ages of ages. Amen.”] Let every priest have a written exposition of the Creed or of the Lord’s Prayer, according to the tradition of the orthodox Fathers, and let him understand it fully; from it, by preaching, let him continually instruct the people entrusted to him. Let him fully understand the prayers of the Mass, the preface of the canon, and the canon itself, so that he can recite them from memory and distinctly. Let him know at least the literal sense of the Epistles and Gospel. Let him retain the words and divisions of the Psalms by heart. Let him know how to recite distinctly, in the singular and plural, the exorcisms and prayers for making a catechumen, for consecrating baptism, and the prayers over a male and a female. Let him also have the order of baptism, the order for assisting the sick, the order of reconciliation according to the authority of the canons, the order for anointing the sick, and the order for the funerals of the dead; likewise the exorcisms and prayers over salt and water, the nocturnal and diurnal chant, the computus—if not the greater, at least the lesser, that is, the epacts, concurrents, and regular terms—the Martyrology, and the Penitential.

[Col. 1379]

## IV. A Treatise: Whether Souls Departing from Human Bodies Are Immediately Led to Glory or Punishment, or Whether They Await the Day of Judgment without Glory or Punishment

[Note: [Col. 1379D] Laurentius Zacagnius noted that he had taken this treatise from the very ancient Roman Casanatense manuscript, written in the year 812. He intended to commit it to the press, but death prevented him.] *(From Mai, Script. vett. Nova Collectio.)* (C,G)*

[Col. 1379B] That ancient serpent, which long ago sharpened the tongues of heretics against the Catholic faith, now also strives, after their perpetual silence, to open the lips of a certain Arseniot, infected with the poison of his error, for renewed blasphemies. [Note: [Col. 1380D] A certain Arsenius, whom Paschasius Ratbertus calls a second Jeremiah, is mentioned in the prologue of *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. ZACAGNIUS.] For, hissing through this same man, it mutters—if the matter is indeed as report has spread about him—that before the final day of judgment no elect person enters the kingdom of heaven and no reprobate penetrates the places of hell.

If this dogma of a wicked heresy is admitted even for a moment, it is plainly shown to inflict great harm upon the faithful: it makes them both sluggish in seeking the joys of life and excessively careless in avoiding the punishments of Gehenna. Against him, however, I have an easy contest, because all defenders of the true faith destroy his effort along with me. No patriarch agrees with him, no prophet, no apostle: [Col. 1379D] not Moses, not David, not Solomon, not the prophet Isaiah, nor any other prophet after Isaiah; not the apostle Peter, not Paul, not John, not Matthew, not Judas, not James, not Luke, not Mark. Nor has any interpreter of the Catholic faith after these ever been found to have attempted to teach this error. And, to mention outstanding men among the many: Gregory of Nazianzus did not teach it; nor John of Constantinople, Hilary of Poitiers, Ambrose of Milan, Augustine of Hippo, Jerome of Bethlehem, Cyril of Alexandria, nor did Pope Gregory of Rome teach this.

I have certainly read much of these men in their holy treatises, but nowhere have I found anything like this view. Who does not see how great is the rashness, how great the folly, of a single lying little man wishing to engage, without a witness, against so many truthful witnesses of distinguished virtue? Yet what we assert in bare words in defense of the truth must be investigated more fully in clothed and developed statements.

Following, therefore, the Scripture of truth, let us show first, if you please, that before the Mediator’s coming in the flesh all the reprobate and all the elect descended to hell, although different merits established a great gulf between the former and the latter; and then that after his most sacred death both the elect reached the heavenly kingdoms and the reprobate reached places of punishment.

That sinners descended to the lower regions before the Wisdom of God was incarnate is attested by Mosaic authority, which says that Dathan and Abiron and their companions, when the earth swallowed them, “went down alive into hell.” This statement concerns certain individuals in particular; in general, however, the same conclusion is equally declared by David’s sentence: “Like sheep they are placed in hell, and death shall feed upon them” (Psalm 48:15). In the book entitled the Wisdom of Solomon, after recounting many of the miseries of the reprobate, Wisdom concludes by saying: “Such things the sinners said in hell” (Wisdom 5:14). [Col. 1381A]

That the elect also entered certain places of the lower regions, although perhaps not all of them, is likewise attested by their own statements. For the blessed patriarch Jacob, overcome by grief at the loss of one son and soothed by no consolation from the others, said: “I shall go down to my son mourning into hell” (Genesis 37:35). Job too, praised by the Lord above all the righteous of his time, speaks of himself, saying: “All that I have shall descend into the deepest hell” (Job 17:16). And again: “If I endure,” he says, “hell is my house” (ibid., verse 13). Once more, pleading with God, he says: “Who will grant me that you protect me in hell and hide me until your fury passes?” (Job 14:13.) David also, chosen as Christ’s father according to the flesh, asks knowingly concerning himself and all the living: “Who is the person who lives and shall not see death? Or who shall rescue his soul from the hand of hell?” (Psalm 88:49.) As though he were plainly saying: as far as the present time is concerned, no one at all.

Christ, therefore, had to be awaited in order to free the souls of the elect from hell. John the Baptist, while imprisoned, sent his disciples to him and asked: “Are you he who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Luke 7:19.) In these words it must plainly be observed that the spirit of prophetic vision, which had already taught the same John about the past, had not yet made him certain about the future. Thus, although he knew for certain that the one who had already come had arrived, he was still uncertain whether he was the one who was to come.

Because the Redeemer of the world had come into the world by being born, the blessed Baptist already knew this clearly, according to what he had cried out beforehand concerning him: “I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1:34). And to his disciples: “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God” (ibid., verse 36). But whether, by dying, he himself would come to the lower regions, he had not yet recognized at all. Hence the preceding question: “Are you he who is to come, or should we expect another?” As though he were saying to him: “You who are soon to descend openly to the prisons of your own people, make clear whether I should announce that you are the liberator who will come to them—the one whom I have already proclaimed to the world as having come—or another, whom until now I have not known to be sent in your place. Will you draw us out from there through the blood of your most sacred Passion, or another of an unknown mission?”

Because he did this not through someone else but through himself, he conveyed the answer obliquely to the aforesaid John. Zachariah, however, made it more explicit: he narrated as already accomplished what he foresaw would most certainly happen. Thus he says directly to the one who took the captives of the lower regions: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zechariah 9:11).

And who are these prisoners except, as Jerome teaches, the righteous of ancient times? And why were they prisoners except because of the guilt of the first transgression? And what is this pit in which they were held captive except the places of the lower regions, where, as it is said, there is no water—that is, no rest whatsoever? Hence also the passage in which the rich man, burning there, asks for a drop of water to cool his tongue and does not find one.

But if this is so, how is Abraham separated from him and at rest with Lazarus, while a great gulf has been fixed between the elect and the reprobate so that they cannot cross to one another? [Col. 1382A]

Or perhaps the gulf placed between the good and the wicked divides not distances between places but the merits of their deeds? It would be astonishing—indeed, very astonishing—if you hold this view. For Job, who had no equal on earth, declared that he would go to places of punishment when he said: “Let me mourn my sorrow before I go and do not return, to a land that is dark and covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness” (Job 10:20–22).

Far be it from us to suppose that Abraham and Job were separated there in their places, since here faith and works had joined them inseparably, and that one of them was assigned there to rest, the other to misery; that one of them was in light while the other sat there in the gloom of death. Let us therefore see whether Job, after being brought to the dark land covered with the gloom of death and to the land of misery and darkness, was nevertheless placed in Abraham’s rest.

Finally, when he uttered with greater sorrow the words quoted above—“All that I have shall descend to the deepest hell”—he immediately added, with presumptive doubt: “Do you suppose that at least there I shall have rest?” (Job 27:16.)

In saying these things, we do not rashly assert that places were not divided among the elect and the reprobate in the lower regions, since it could have been that merit alone separated the two groups, just as justice alone distinguished the ministers of the king of Babylon from Daniel’s companions: the same flame of the furnace consumed the former and preserved the latter. Similarly, the water of the Red Sea provided the Israelites a path for obtaining manna, while it supplied the Egyptians with a pitfall for the punishment of death.

We therefore say, with great authority, that these were places of punishment, which Christ judged must be traversed by himself for the deliverance of his own. Peter bears witness to this when he says of him: “Whom God raised from the dead, having loosed the pains of hell, because it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24).

In these words we must carefully observe that no one in the lower regions was free from the bonds of pain except the one who alone truly said: “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 87:5). Therefore he alone could not be held bound by the infernal hand, because he alone had no sin by which he could be confined in the bonds of its pains. And for that reason he alone was able to free others from the pains of hell: he himself had not experienced those same pains.

I know that one among the great interpreters understood these words in such a way that Christ loosed the aforesaid pains not among the patriarchs and prophets but among others situated far from their dwelling places; nevertheless, he did not dare to say that those whom he freed from the same bonds of pain were not elect. If he did say this, he would plainly appear to be a liar.

Let us concede, then, that they were not patriarchs and prophets but other elect persons who, possessing less than perfect righteousness, had been bound by the pains of hell. But if there was complete rest and complete consolation there for the patriarchs and prophets, what need did they have of awaiting Christ? Was John not a prophet and more than a prophet, who, as we recalled above, in the person of himself and the other prophets, sought the Redeemer of the world, saying: “Are you he who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Luke 7:19.)

Certainly these prisoners were awaiting him in the pit where there is no water; and it is strange if they were bound by other chains than those which Peter narrates were loosed through Christ. This question constrains us once more to explain how Lazarus was being comforted in Abraham’s bosom if he was held bound by the bonds of pain.

Let us distinguish between one pain and another, and, as I think, we shall resolve the question more easily. The wicked and the righteous were therefore tormented together in the lower regions, but the two groups were not tormented in the same way. The wicked suffered the whole torment of the fire of Gehenna; the righteous, only the sadness of the mind. The former suffered because they burned outwardly; the latter because they mourned inwardly. The former could not be comforted, because in their torments they had no refreshment; the latter, although they were saddened because they were exiled for a long time from their heavenly homeland, were nevertheless comforted because the external burning of the reprobate did not afflict them.

Thus, when it is said of the pit that there is no water in it, this refers not to the inward pain of the elect but to the outward burning fire of the reprobate. Since this fire is avenging, not even a single drop of water is available for refreshment. If the rich man had not known that it could be drawn from the streams of the elect, he would not have said to Abraham: “Send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24).

We therefore say plainly that it is not contradictory for the righteous of ancient times to have been bound in the lower regions by the bonds of pain. But what follows? Whether the judgment we have expressed concerning hell in this matter is certain or doubtful— [Note: [Col. 1383D] Namely, whether the issue concerns the manner of suffering or the infernal dwelling shared by the righteous and the unrighteous.]—this at least we affirm with complete truth: the Son of God, paying the death he did not owe on our behalf, brought only his own out from there, after the pains of hell had been loosed, however this may have occurred and whoever may have been involved.

As he himself had long before foretold through Hosea: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hosea 13:14). In these words we must carefully consider that our Redeemer utterly destroyed death, but only in the part that he swallowed; in the part that remained, death continued to exist. Let it therefore be said, “I shall be your death, O death,” as though it meant: “In the prey that I seize, I utterly destroy you.” “I shall be your bite, O hell”—that is, “I do not swallow you whole, but by biting a part of you, I consume it.” For, as the Catholic faith has established, he brought no others from there to the realms above through his most blessed Passion except his own.

But now the order of our discussion demands that, after the deliverance of the ancient righteous from the lower regions, we show where the souls of the perfected are now received. The Teacher of heaven, who never deceived anyone, established the following judgment concerning this matter, saying: “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12).

O teacher of a new error, do the violent seize the kingdom of heaven only on the day of judgment, as the devil has constructed through your mouth, and not rather from the days of John? [lacuna]

[One folio is missing here.]

[lacuna] If you approve, let these passages from among the many suffice. But if, because of my insignificant person, even these are called into doubt, I consider it necessary, by the general judgment of Catholics, to establish myself as a truthful witness in what I have said.

For in the work On Ecclesiastical Dogma, [Note: [Col. 1383D] This is Gennadius’s On Ecclesiastical Dogma, published among the works of Saint Augustine, to whom it is wrongly attributed. There still exists in the Vatican Library, manuscript 5845, a collection of canons by Dionysius Exiguus, with an ancient appendix extending to the time of Charlemagne; that manuscript too was written in his age. In this appendix Gennadius’s On Ecclesiastical Dogma is found under the name of Saint Augustine. From this it can be inferred why this anonymous author, contemporary with Charlemagne, asserts that Gennadius’s book was accepted throughout the whole world by everyone: it had evidently been inserted into the collections of canons that were then especially influential. Zacagnius.] a work comprising distinct statements in a single volume, accepted by everyone throughout the world, defended by all, and celebrated with the highest praise, the forty-fifth chapter states:

> “Before the Lord’s Passion, all the souls of the saints were held in hell under the debt of Adam’s transgression, until by the Lord’s authority they were freed from servile condition through his death, which he did not owe.”

In the following chapter, the forty-sixth, there is likewise an authoritative statement:

> “After the Lord’s ascension into heaven, all the souls of the saints are with Christ, and, departing from the body, they go to Christ, awaiting the resurrection of their bodies, so that together with him they may likewise be changed into complete and perfect blessedness. In the same way, the souls of sinners, placed in hell under fear, await the resurrection of their bodies, so that together with them they may be turned toward eternal punishment.”

This is the single, unique, and general judgment of all the Fathers who preceded and followed. Rightly agreeing with it, blessed Gregory, Pope of Rome and bishop of the apostolic see—the last of the interpreters, but outstanding among nearly all of them—answered the inquiry of his interlocutor in the fourth book of the *Dialogues*, saying:

> “It is certain that the souls of the perfect righteous, as soon as they leave the prison of this flesh, are received into heavenly dwellings. Truth itself also bears witness to this, saying: ‘Wherever the body shall be, there the eagles will be gathered’ (Luke 17:37), because where our Redeemer is in body, there the souls of the righteous are gathered. Paul also desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ. Therefore, whoever does not doubt that Christ is in heaven will not deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven. He also says concerning the dissolution of his body and his dwelling in the heavenly homeland: ‘We know that if our earthly house, which has no inhabitant, is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made by hand, eternal in the heavens’” (2 Corinthians 5:1). [Col. 1384D]

This is what he says about the righteous and the perfect. But what about the wicked? He says to the same interlocutor:

> “Because you have believed, in accordance with the testimony of sacred Scripture, that the souls of the saints are in heaven, you must believe in every respect that the souls of the wicked are in hell. For by the retribution of the inner justice through which the righteous rejoice, it is necessary in every respect that the unrighteous also be tormented. For just as blessedness gladdens the elect, so we must believe that, from the day of their departure, fire burns the reprobate.”

That most truthful teacher demonstrated all these points not only through verbal statements but also through examples of actual events. In the book mentioned above he related that the soul of Germanus the bishop was carried into heaven by angels in a sphere of fire; that the soul of Saint Benedict was led to the heavenly region along a road spread with cloths; that the soul of a paralytic servant of a hospice was received amid the inner praises of heaven and lifted above its highest vaults; that the soul of the holy virgin Scholastica was led in the form of a dove to the ethereal bridal chamber; and that the soul of the venerable Romula was taken up to eternal life with heavenly rites.

He also said that the spirit of his aunt Gordiana was consigned to the fires of Gehenna, and that the monk Hilliricianus, led to the regions below, saw the powerful and rich of this age hanging amid the flames.

Enough; it is more than enough. Who among the faithful can doubt this matter any longer? This witness too is entirely adequate, and it is impious to oppose his judgments.

Therefore I want you to know that you have been admonished: all of you whom that most ignorant man has attempted, through the winding paths of lies, to turn aside from heavenly wisdom. As you press forward in the ranks of faith, do not let the cracked croaking of a little frog divert you from the journey you have begun; follow instead the clearly resounding blast of the trumpet of the heavenly city. [Col. 1386B]

This is my prayer to God on your behalf; this is also my greeting to you. Amen.

[Col. 1385]

## V. A Letter of a Certain Person: What Is *Ceroma*?

*(From Book IV of Baluze’s Miscellanies.)*

[Col. 1385B] Our friend Fredilo recently brought me the little question submitted by your reverence, in which you asked what distinguished men properly understood *ceroma* to be. The word is found in authors who were highly accomplished in the disciplines of the liberal arts, and also among our own writers who in their age earned the palm of Roman eloquence.

Although those who draw the sinews, marrow, and, as the saying goes, the very blood from the books of the ancients judge us to be children and weaklings, pursuing rather the profundity of meanings than the lowliness of words, it nevertheless seems more appropriate for us to climb from the primary matters to the secondary than, neglecting the primary, to rush rashly toward the secondary. For since the power of eloquence is formed by the splendor of words and the weight of meanings, the beauty of words must first be sought, and only then the strength and inner light of meanings.

For this reason, students must always preserve the illumination and meaning of the selection of words, lest, once the rule of the teachers has been violated, confused and disorderly inventions which it hands down burst forth. These general observations refute rash and extraordinary presumption. Let us now consider this particular word.

And so that a clearer path may open for establishing the matter, I think we must go back somewhat further.

The games that young men staged on feast days for religious purposes, to entertain the people, and on whose account spectacles of various kinds were permitted to the public, were called gymnastic, gladiatorial, circus, or theatrical games. Yet the devil, under the invocation of gods—or rather demons—wished these games to be exhibited by mortals, so that, under the pretext of piety and religion, he might transfer the souls of the wretched into his own jurisdiction [Col. 1386B–C].

The principal game, which we have said was gymnastic, consisted in the glory of speed and strength. The place where the athletes trained was called a gymnasium, and those who trained there were called athletes. The types of gymnastic games are said to have been running, jumping, throwing, strength, and wrestling. But because in earlier times athletes exercised while girded and were not naked, until one of them, with his belt loosened, fell prostrate and died during a contest, the custom is said to have arisen that thereafter young men should exercise naked, wearing only loincloths around the part of the body requiring concealment.

The athletes, however, are called by a Greek designation derived from the embracing and joining of the sides: they contend at close quarters and remain pressed together, so that neither might deceive or hinder the other by any chance or trick [Col. 1386D], their bodies rubbed with an oily liquid. The exercise itself was properly called *ceroma*. The place assigned to wrestling was called the *palaestra*. This name derives its etymology either from wrestling or from the movement of an urn—that is, of a lot—because the participants were assigned by lot to the *palaestra*.

The meaning of the proverb is therefore this: “He loses both the oil and the expense who sends oxen to the *ceroma*.” Just as a stupid and brutish animal, although strong and vigorous, is useless for an accomplished art, which is practiced not only through strength but also through subtlety and intelligence because of the manifold interweaving of the limbs, so those are judged inert who, having been assigned from the earliest periods of childhood to school exercises, do not admit into themselves the study of the various disciplines. Untrained and feeble, like stupid and senseless animals, they are rejected from the profound and multifaceted investigation of things. The proverb mentioned above is rightly sung about them.

And because the athletes themselves were nourished with foods proper to this art, such as *coliphia*, by which their strength was increased and the fitness and efficiency of their bodies were not endangered, the proverb accordingly adds that the expense is also lost when things are improperly forced upon the negligent and those least suited to receive them.

Some have understood *ceroma* to mean a certain technique of painting according to ancient practice. To prevent the face and beauty of a painting from being obliterated by the passage of time, wax was mixed into it, a modest fire being applied to this compound, so that, with the colors and wax harmonizing in due proportion, neither beauty and grace would be lacking from the colors nor transparency from the wax.
