There is no doubt that this kind of painting was also mentioned by Boethius, a most learned man, and continued to flourish in his own time [Col. 1388A].

Those who held this opinion were led to it by a certain bending of the name, so that, for example, just as *homo* is thought to derive from *humus*, so *ceroma* was thought to originate from *cera*. But even the meaning itself shows that this was not understood with sufficient judgment. Therefore, I believe that the preceding explanation—which is judged safer, more esoteric, and more ancient—will satisfy you and, in your prudence, extinguish the nonsense of those who devise various explanations.

I have set this out before your prudent judgment, dearest of men, concerning a small matter and without deceit. I ask your cultivated prudence, while avoiding the disdainful brows of the fastidious, to keep among yourselves what a faithful spirit and the not-frivolous affection of a friend have sent. For the rest, may it please you, while preserving the stability of our friendship, to inform me in your writings, as I request, which interpretation you have chosen. I do not wish either to incur the impropriety of excessive talkativeness or, conversely, to be rightly condemned in matters that ought to be expressed on the charge of silence [Col. 1388B].

## VI. The Apparition of Saint Michael the Archangel in the Western Regions, That Is, on Mount Tumba in Gaul

Written by an anonymous author before the tenth century.

*(From Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict.)*

[Col. 1387]

### Preliminary Observations

[Col. 1387C] It will not be out of place to digress slightly beyond our boundaries, in order to make room for the celebrated apparition of Saint Michael, which brought no small splendor to the affairs of our order. For it provided the occasion for constructing the highly distinguished monastery of Saint Michael on Mount Tumba, also called the Peril of the Sea. Richard I, duke of the Normans, granted it to Benedictine monks, excluding the clerics who had previously occupied the mountain, because of their looser way of life.

The fame and popularity of the place were increased by the religious devotion of the monks, who built a magnificent basilica on the narrow edge of the steep mountain. It was two hundred and thirty-eight feet long and one hundred and thirty-five feet high. The regular monastic buildings stood somewhat lower around the basilica. At the same time, on the northern slope of the mountain there arose a town which, both through the protection of its patron and through its situation, was a very strong fortress against the enemies of Gaul.

For the sake of fulfilling vows, pilgrims frequently converged there from almost all of Europe. Among them, many kings of Gaul—namely Louis VII and Saint Louis, [Col. 1387D] Philip III, Charles VI, Louis XI, and even Henry II, king of England—deigned to honor the place with their presence. There Louis XI, already mentioned, established the equestrian order of Saint Michael, whose general chapter it long remained customary to convene there each year.

William Major, elected bishop of Angers in 1291, removed a certain Colin from an incestuous relationship, imposing this penalty: “that on Pentecost Day he should publicly receive in his church from a priest the bag and staff, as is customary, and then proceed barefoot to the Mount of Blessed Michael on Mount Tumba; and that the priest should there explain to the people the reason why the said Colin was going to the Mount of Blessed Michael, and what had been imposed upon him on our behalf as punishment for the said public incest.” So William himself says in the nineteenth chapter of his book *On His Deeds*, in volume ten of Acher’s *Spicilegium* [Col. 1388C].

2. The old charters of the place assign the time of the apparition to the year 708; they assign the dedication of the church constructed by Saint Autbert to the following year, when Childebert III ruled the Franks. Rodulfus Glaber, in the *Life of King Robert*, praises the church of Saint Michael, “which,” he says, “established on a certain promontory of the shore of the Ocean Sea, is still held venerable throughout the whole world.”

Indeed, according to William of Jumièges, a monk, in book V, chapter 4, “Ethelred, king of England, ordered his nobles in royal fashion to go through all Normandy and destroy it with plunder and fire, sparing only the Mount of the Archangel Michael” [Col. 1388D]. Moreover, in the Council of Oxford in 1222, the bishops of England decreed “that the dedication of Saint Michael on Mount Tumba should be celebrated with the utmost devotion by the rectors of churches”—a practice once observed throughout the entire province of Second Lyonnaise and in many other churches of the kingdom of Gaul.

3. The anonymous author who wrote the following history of the apparition and dedication lived shortly after the time when these events occurred, certainly before monks were introduced there [Col. 1389A], that is, before the year 960. Our Saint-Germain manuscript, which we used, was written at the command of Adrald, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in the year 1060, as the following verses, written by Ingelard, the monk and copyist, testify:

> At the behest of Lord Abbot Adrald, adorned with excellence,  
> Sigwinus, a certain monk and prior, modest in skill,  
> Devoted to books, their gracious restorer,  
> Ordered this book to be written.  
> Whoever takes it away shall perish accursed in the end.  
> Ingelard, an honorable scribe, adorned this work.

Besides this anonymous work, there is another composition on the same subject in the library of the monastery of Saint Michael, interpolated in some places.

[Col. 1389]

## Here Begins the Account of the Apparition of Saint Michael

### Chapter I. In the Reign of King Childebert, Saint Michael Appears in Gaul, Once the Patron of the Synagogue, Now of the Church

[Col. 1389B]

After the Frankish people, marked by the grace of Christ, had everywhere subdued far and wide the proud necks of the provinces, while King Childebert vigorously governed the monarchy of the whole western and northern regions, as well as the southern part—for almighty God rules not only over all peoples but also over all the regions of the subject spirits of the world that he himself created—the blessed archangel, one of the seven who always stand in the presence of the Lord, and who is also read to be the governor of paradise, destined to place the souls of the saved in the region of peace, after that manifestation [Col. 1389C] in which he showed himself on Mount Garganus for adoration and glorification, in whatever manner and way he willed, as is recorded in writing [Note: [Col. 1389D] Mount Garganus, six miles from the new Sipontum, or Manfredonia, a maritime city of Apulia, was consecrated by the apparition and cult of Saint Michael the archangel under Pope Gelasius I.], after these things had been accomplished through the blessed archangel and all nations had been illumined by Christ’s grace, learn in the eastern regions of Romania by what signs that same most blessed prince of the heavenly citizens chose to reveal himself as leader of the western peoples.

For just as he once granted the Israelite people, blessed among the patriarchs, the aid of protection, so he himself might become the guardian and guide of those sons called through adoption. For we read in the vision of the prophet Daniel that the angel said to him: “There is no one who helps me in all these things except Michael, your prince” (Dan. 10:21). “Your prince,” he says—that is, the prince of the Jewish people.

But when Christ the Lord came in his own person and was not received by his own, but rather betrayed, and when he returned to the Father, the observance of the ancient law was abolished and the wondrous mystery of evangelical proclamation was established. As the apostles’ sound went out through the whole earth, the ceremonies of sacred worship were transferred through the ministries of angels.

For ecclesiastical history relates that after the Lord’s passion and ascension into heaven, after the long-awaited fulfillment of the Israelites [Col. 1390A], when the time of the destruction of the city and temple approached—which the Savior had foretold in sacred speech with human tears—the Church at Jerusalem, instructed by the Godhead, spread throughout the whole world to preach the Gospel to the nations.

When people gathered from every place and awaited the day of the Paschal festival, while the priests observed the customary vigils, the watchmen suddenly heard voices saying: “Let us depart from these dwellings.” These voices, suddenly uttered by angels and announcing the departure of the blessed spirits, signified that the angelic ministry was being transferred to the Church of the nations. From this it is plainly indicated that blessed Michael the archangel received among the election of the nations the same ministry that he had once exercised among God’s people [Col. 1390B].

The devotion of the faithful believes that these things are so because of the display of signs. He wished to make himself known to mortals in the times of our age, so that the human race might recognize that it had been summoned into the fellowship of the elect spirits. Finally, we must consider with what mystery he foresaw a place for mortals in the western regions, where from the whole world a devout multitude of the faithful flows together, reverently imploring angelic assistance.

### Chapter II. The Situation of the Place

This place [Note: [Col. 1389D] Odo, abbot of Glanfeuil, in a letter to Adelmodus, and certain others call the mountain “the Two Tumbas,” evidently because of the mountain’s two ridges, which will be mentioned below. Here one cannot help marveling at the audacity of the pseudo-chronologist who wrote under the name and mask of Lucius Dexter, who twists all these matters toward Spain, assigning them to the year 526 of Christ.] is called Tumba by the inhabitants because, rising high as though emerging from the sands in the manner of a tomb, it extends for a distance of two hundred cubits. Surrounded on every side by the Ocean Sea, it provides the narrow expanse of a remarkable island between the mouths where the rivers Sée [Al., Sei; commonly Sée] and Sélune flow into the sea, while also providing the inhabitants with a considerable area on either side.

In length and breadth, from the base where it rises, it does not differ greatly, as is conjectured, from the structure by which the increase of the human race was saved—or rather preserved [that is, Noah’s ark]. Situated about six miles from the city of Avranches and looking toward the west, it separates the district of Avranches from Brittany.

No worldly activity can be carried on there. It is a place suited only to those who intend to venerate Christ diligently, and it receives those whom the ardent love of virtue lifts toward the heavens. An abundance of fish is found there, gathered for the most part by the inflow of rivers and sea. To those viewing it from afar, it seems to be nothing other than a spacious—or rather beautiful—tower [Col. 1390D].

But the sea, in its retreat, twice provides devout peoples with the desired path to those seeking the threshold of the blessed archangel Michael. In the beginning, as we were able to learn from truthful narrators, the place was enclosed by a very dense forest, lying, as is estimated, six miles from the waters of the Ocean [Note: [Col. 1390D] The Chesne manuscript reads: “eight miles distant from the Ocean, as is estimated,” and so forth.], and offering the wild beasts very deep hiding places.

And because remote places of the desert are usually most pleasing to those who wish, through the subtlety of contemplation, to investigate the more secret things of heaven [Col. 1391A], we learn that monks once inhabited the place. Even now there remain there two churches [Note: [Col. 1391D] Namely, one in honor of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, and another in honor of Saint Symphorian; neither now survives.] constructed by the hands of the ancients.

Those monks, serving the Lord there, were sustained by the providence of the God who governs all things. A certain priest from a village called Asteriacus (Beauvoir) supplied them with assistance in the following manner. Since they lacked food, without which human life cannot be sustained, he would load an ass with provisions stuffed into it with genuine affection; the smoke carrying the signal would rise and seek the heights of heaven. Thus, under the guidance of an invisible leader, he went through trackless places and returned, bearing the Lord’s commands and what was necessary for them.

But because this place was being prepared by God’s will for a future miracle and for the veneration of his holy archangel, the sea, which had been far away, gradually rose and by its power leveled the entire forest and reduced everything to the form of sand, providing a path for the people of the earth so that God’s wonders might be proclaimed [Col. 1391B].

Now we must come to the manner in which that same prince of the blessed spirits, through an angelic revelation, dedicated the aforesaid place.

### Chapter III. The Construction of the Place Through Angelic Revelation

At a certain time, when Autbert, the most religious and God-beloved bishop of the aforementioned city [Note: [Col. 1391D] Not Camaracum, as Baronius thought, deceived by the name of Autbert, who was a bishop of Cambrai long before him.], had given himself over to sleep, he was warned by an angelic revelation to build a church in honor of the archangel on the summit of the place already mentioned, so that the venerable commemoration celebrated on Mount Garganus might be celebrated in the sea with no lesser rejoicing.

But while the priest reflected upon the apostle’s words, “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1), he was warned in a repeated vision to carry out what he had been commanded. And because the spirit of the prophets is not always subject to the prophets, the bishop still delayed construction, but sought intercession so that he might be able to learn the will of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the most blessed archangel concerning this undertaking.

At that same time it happened that someone secretly stole another man’s bull, through the prompting of wickedness, and placed it on the summit of the same rock, so that, when the owner of the young bull lost hope of finding it, the wicked thief might make a shameful profit from it.

Meanwhile, in a third admonition, the venerable bishop was more sternly pressed [Note: [Col. 1392D] This was certainly the place to discuss that impression by which Michael is said to have struck Autbert’s hesitant head all the way through.], so that he who had not obeyed after being warned twice would go more quickly to the place, while knowing that he could not leave it until he had completed what he had been ordered to do [Col. 1391D].

As confirmation of his faith, a rock is still shown there, apparently inscribed by a human finger, on which the aforementioned bishop sat until he brought the work to completion. When the bishop asked what place might be suitable for the construction, an angelic response instructed him that the church should be built where the hidden and tethered bull was located [Col. 1392A]. When he inquired about the size and extent of the place, he learned from the same response that he should establish the dimensions of the building according to the circuit that he saw the young bull had worn down.

After this, the bull was ordered to be returned to its rightful owner. The venerable bishop, therefore, certain of the vision, entered the aforesaid place with hymns and praises and began to carry out the commanded work. Having gathered a very large crowd of peasants, he cleared the place and leveled it into an open area. In its middle stood two rocks, which the hands of many workers could neither move nor detach from their position.

When they had remained stuck there for a long time and could find no way forward, a vision appeared during the following night to a man named Bainus in a village called Icius (Huynes). He had twelve sons and held great honor among his people [Col. 1392B]. In the vision he was instructed to join the laborers and apply himself to the work. He hastened to the place with his sons to fulfill what he had been ordered to do.

When he arrived, relying on the aid of Saint Michael the archangel, he moved the immense mass, which human strength could not move, with such astonishing ease that it seemed to have no weight at all [Note: [Col. 1392D] Namely, Bainus with his twelve sons. Yet popular tradition says that a single child accomplished this by pushing it with his foot.]. Everyone together praised God and Saint Michael the archangel and devoted themselves more earnestly to the work they had begun.

When the aforementioned bishop was still uncertain as he considered the size of the structure to be built, at midnight, just as once happened to Gideon as a sign of victory, dew lay upon the summit of the mountain; but where the foundations were to be laid [Col. 1392C], there was dryness. The bishop was told: “Go, and lay the foundations as you see marked.” He immediately gave thanks to almighty God, invoked the help of Saint Michael the archangel, rose up joyful and glad, and undertook that work.

He therefore constructed a building not high in the loftiness of its roof, but round like a crypt, with a capacity, as is estimated, of one hundred men. He wished to make it equal in form to the one on Mount Garganus. It was made in the manner of a steep crag, through angelic arrangement, as a dwelling for earthborn human beings to the praise and glory of God. It clearly taught that the aid of the divine gift must always be sought in the heavens, and that the stars of heaven must be penetrated by the lofty gaze of contemplation, rather than that human hearts should be fixed upon earthly and muddy swamps.

When this had been built after not much time, with God’s aid, while Autbert, the man of God and bishop, remained anxious because he saw that he lacked tokens from the holy archangel, blessed Michael warned the priest to send brothers as quickly as possible to Garganus, to the place where the memory of the most holy archangel was reverently honored, and to receive with the greatest gratitude the blessing—or gift [that is, a present]—which they would bring back with the angel’s patronage.

### Chapter IV. How the Sacred Token Was Brought from Garganus

[Col. 1393A]

Meanwhile, the messengers reached the place. They were received most kindly by the abbot of that place, given fresh clothing, and relieved from the fatigue of so long a journey. They disclosed everything that had occurred in their region, as well as the purpose for which they had come.

When the abbot had reported these words to the bishop of the place [Note: [Col. 1393D] Sixteen secular canons now occupy the place; they are called Garganics.], both men offered abundant praise to almighty God, who deigns to provide assistance through his ministers to earthborn creatures weakened by the frailty of nature.

Then, with the reverence that was fitting, they took from the place the tokens by which the blessed archangel had commended his memory to the faithful: namely, part of the red little cloak that the archangel himself had placed on Mount Garganus above the altar that he had built with his own hand, and part of the marble upon which he had stood, where his footprints still remain visible. He handed these over to the aforementioned brothers to be brought back to the sacred place, adding the condition that those whom one cause—angelic revelation—had joined together should also be bound together eternally by a single bond of charity.

### Chapter V. The Arrival of the Relics  
*Alternative: On the Reception of the Angelic Protection*

Meanwhile, the exalted messengers returned. After covering many stretches of the journey, they reached the place from which they had departed on the very day when the building was completed on the mountain already mentioned in the western regions. They seemed to be entering a new world, which they had first left filled with dense thickets.

As they approached, Autbert, the priest of the Lord, came to meet them with great praises, spiritual songs, and indescribable joy. He brought to all on the sacred mountain the angelic protection destined to benefit mortals.

It cannot be said how much joy and gladness the surrounding province experienced at the arrival—as I may put it—of the angel. For the people saw that, by divine provision, an immeasurable heavenly gift was being granted to them: they were worthy to possess the blessed archangel Michael, prince of the heavenly army, as their standard-bearer. They also came to know the signs and wonders that the Lord works for mortals through his minister. During the stages of this journey, twelve blind people were given sight, and many afflicted by various illnesses were restored to their former health.

Moreover, a certain woman deprived of sight, from a village called Asteriacus, while following the precious gifts of the exalted archangel Michael, received her sight by divine action as soon as she reached the plain of the sea’s sands [Note: [Col. 1393D] The place is now called Beauvoir because the woman recovered her sight there; formerly it was called Asteriacus.]. She marveled that she had suddenly been changed from darkness into light [Col. 1394A]. Even to this day the Lord does not cease to work these same things in that place through his exalted minister, to the praise and glory of his name.

Therefore, on that day, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, when the venerable dedication of the church had been completed [Note: [Col. 1393D] Nothing is said here about the rite of dedication allegedly celebrated by Christ the Savior; indeed, below, in chapter 7, Autbert himself is said to have dedicated the place.], the man of God Autbert, after arranging everything carefully and in due order, also established the offices of the clerics serving there [Note: [Col. 1394D] Odo, abbot of Glanfeuil, in a letter to Agelmodus, bishop of Le Mans, concerning the discovery of the life of Saint Maurus, mentions “a certain cleric named Peter, who had traveled to Rome from the district of Avranches, from the place of Saint Michael called the Two Tumbas.”]. He assigned twelve of them to remain there and perpetually persist in the service of the most blessed archangel Michael according to the proper observances, although later successors of the blessed man appointed clerics of a different number in the same place.

He also transferred to that place, from his episcopal estate and through those serving him, the villages of Icius (Huyne), already mentioned, and Genitius (Genet).

### Chapter VI. The Acquisition of Water Through Angelic Revelation

[Col. 1394B]

Meanwhile, when the same bishop had surveyed everything and seen that it had been carried out in suitable order, he judged that one thing, which appeared very difficult, should be requested from the holy archangel: namely, the element of water, without which the life of mortals cannot exist.

Concerning this, he sought the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the holy archangel together with the flock entrusted to him, asking that he who once brought drink from a rock for a thirsty people might deign to remove the scarcity of water from his servants. At last, through an angelic manifestation, he learned the place where, when a hollow opening was cut into the steep rock, an abundant supply of water was immediately found in a wondrous manner, sufficient to provide the inhabitants with a suitable supply.

That the water flowing forth was healthful to drink was demonstrated in many ways. For it quickly brings relief to those suffering from fever whenever the desire to drink it arises [Note: [Col. 1394D] Up to this point, our manuscript extends.].

### Chapter VII. Miracles Performed in the Same Place

At the basilica of the blessed archangel, with his assistance, innumerable miracles are performed. The blind are given sight there, the lame recover their ability to walk, the deaf receive hearing, and unclean spirits are driven from possessed bodies, our Lord God providing aid through the ministry of angels.

The venerable bishop Autbert had dedicated the aforesaid place in honor of the most holy archangel Michael. The other churches that are now seen to have increased to the number eleven were built by the hands of the faithful as devotion and love grew; in them divine benefits are bestowed, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 1395]

## VII. Deeds of Lord Dagobert, King of the Franks, Son of Clotaire II

Written by an anonymous monk of the monastery of Saint-Denis, a contemporary author.

*(From Duchesne, Hist. Franc. Script.)*

### Chapter I. Concerning Clotaire, Dagobert’s Father

[Col. 1395]

Clotaire, the son of Chilperic, was the fourth king after Clovis, who was the first of the Frankish kings to be converted to the worship of God through the teaching of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims [Col. 1395B]. Clotaire inherited the kingdom. Having attained the dignity elaborated by his ancestors, he accomplished many things with vigor; above all, he left posterity this memorable indication of his power: when the Saxons rebelled against him, he subdued them by force of arms so completely that he killed all the male inhabitants of that land who exceeded in height the length of the sword that he happened at that time to carry. He did this so that remembrance of that sword, whether life-giving or deadly, might cut off from the younger men the audacity of arrogance.

Such then was the power of the Franks, such the boldness of kings. How and in what manner he accomplished this will be explained more fully and in its proper order below.

That same King Clotaire was devoted to patience, educated in letters, fearful of God, a great benefactor of churches and priests [Col. 1395C], giving alms to the poor and showing himself kind and full of piety. He was an outstanding warrior and made excessive and very frequent use of hunting wild beasts.

### Chapter II. Concerning Dagobert’s Childhood

He had a son named Dagobert, whom he had fathered by Queen Bertedrude, destined to succeed his father and worthy both in ability and strength. While still in his childhood, he was entrusted by his venerable and most holy father to Arnulf, bishop of the city of Metz, so that Arnulf might bring him up according to his wisdom, show him the path of the Christian religion, and be his guardian and attendant.

When, as is customary among the Frankish people, he exercised himself in hunting during adolescence, he set out one day to pursue a stag. The animal was easily found. With packs of dogs barking and pursuing it competitively, it ran through forests and mountains with the speed attributed to that creature, crossing whatever rivers it encountered, and tried to escape the skill of the dogs.

At last, overcome, it made its way to a village called Catulliacus. This lies about five miles from the city called Lutetia or Paris. For in that city the kings of the Franks were accustomed especially to exercise their sovereignty.

### Chapter III. Concerning the Blessed Martyr Dionysius and His Companions, and the Church That Blessed Geneviève Built over Them

In that village, during the time of Domitian, who was the second after Nero to take up arms against Christians, the most blessed Dionysius, the first bishop of the aforementioned city, was killed in sight of the city itself for the name of Christ, together with Rusticus and Eleutherius, one of whom was a priest and the other a deacon [Col. 1396A–B].

A certain married woman named Catulla, from whom they say the village took its name, secretly committed them to burial, since she did not dare to do so openly. Nevertheless, she marked the tomb so that knowledge of what had happened might remain for later generations.

Thus an incomparable treasure lay hidden for a long time, and apart from its reputation the place had nothing conspicuous. Although certain gifts had been bestowed there by earlier kings because of the frequent miracles that took place there, the site itself was at that time under the authority of the bishop of Paris, who assigned it by right of benefice to whichever cleric he wished.

The cleric to whom it was granted appeared to accumulate the proceeds for his own use—not the honor of the place but earthly profit—in the way that can still be seen in certain places today. For this reason, as we have said, the site was greatly neglected [Col. 1396C].

Only a worthless little chapel, which, as was reported, blessed Geneviève had devoutly built over the holy martyrs, did not adequately enclose the bodies of such great martyrs. This continued until, as I shall explain in due course, their name began to benefit the world. Through God’s providence, the place, which was illuminated, though secretly, by patrons so great, so certain, and so ancient, was advanced to exceptional distinction.

### Chapter IV. Concerning the Stag That Took Refuge in the Martyrs’ Church While Dagobert Pursued It

But to return to my subject: after wandering for a long time here and there through the village, the stag entered the church of the blessed martyrs [Col. 1396D] and settled there.

The dogs pressed after it. Although the same entrance stood open to them as to the stag, and although no visible guard was present to drive them away, the holy martyrs would not allow their dwelling to be violated by the entrance of unclean creatures. You would have seen the stag find a secure refuge on one side, while on the other the dogs announced its presence by barking and were kept from entering the church by divine power.

Dagobert arrived at a rapid run and marveled at the spectacle worthy of wonder; he was astonished and embraced the place. The report then stirred the neighboring people generally, encouraging both Dagobert above all and the others to love and venerate the saints. And, to speak truthfully—as later events made clear—Dagobert had no place that was either sweeter or more pleasing.

### Chapter V. Concerning the Death of Dagobert’s Mother

[Col. 1397A]

In the thirty-sixth year of Clotaire’s reign, Queen Bertedrude, Dagobert’s mother, died. Clotaire had loved her with unique affection, and all the nobles, recognizing her goodness, had loved her greatly.

After her death, King Clotaire took another wife named Sichilde, by whom he had a son named Hairbert.

### Chapter VI. Concerning Duke Sadregiselus and How Dagobert Dishonored Him

Dagobert therefore grew daily in virtue as well as in age, and continually gave signs that inspired the greatest hope for the future king. His father Clotaire had placed a certain Sadregiselus, whom he considered a man of proven loyalty, in charge of affairs under him, entrusting him especially with the dukedom of Aquitaine.

Raised up by such an excessive pride of rank [Col. 1397B], Sadregiselus could not tolerate the more prosperous conduct of Dagobert, the king’s son, partly because of the arrogance arising from the power conferred upon him and partly because he was troubled by the hope of the kingdom. Nor could he long conceal what he was plotting, even under a pretended show of affection.

Since fear of the father prevented him from being openly hostile, he repeatedly revealed himself as Dagobert’s hidden enemy through contemptuous behavior. There was, to be sure, a youthful excuse based on age: lest an inexperienced mind acquire arrogance from subjection to princes, or lest prematurely attained dominion withdraw the unformed youth from the discipline of training.

A report so damaging to Sadregiselus therefore reached Dagobert. Although Dagobert had already discovered the matter through his own ability, the judgment of others was brought forward to establish it more fully. Since he was not strong enough to bring Sadregiselus back into order immediately, Dagobert decided to await a broader opportunity, one in which he could investigate the matter more effectively and attempt against his rival whatever he deserved [Col. 1397C].

Clotaire went hunting one day and happened to withdraw some distance away. It also happened that Dagobert and the aforementioned duke remained at home. Dagobert, finding the desired opportunity presented to him, summoned the duke to him and ordered him to dine with him.

Sadregiselus, thinking of nothing less than what was about to happen, behaved casually and failed to offer the honor owed to the future—or rather already reigning—lord. Three times Dagobert extended cups to him, and, worthy to suffer the vengeance due for his earlier insolence, Sadregiselus accepted them as though they had been offered not by his lord but by an unfortunate companion.

Dagobert then began to set forth how Sadregiselus had been disloyal to his father, a rival to himself, and hated by his associates. He said that the annoyances of a servant ought not to be delayed for long, and that his own injuries should not remain unavenged lest such great arrogance grow to immeasurable proportions [Col. 1397D].

He therefore ordered Sadregiselus to be beaten with whips. Then, after shaving off his beard—for at that time this was considered the principal form of humiliation—he disfigured him. Thus, unexpectedly, the man who, through the success of his affairs, had been anticipating himself as the future king learned, by this warning, how far he was from that dignity.

### Chapter VII. How Sadregiselus, Having Been Dishonored, Presented Himself to Clotaire, and How Dagobert Took Refuge in the Aforesaid Church of the Martyrs
On Clotarius’s return, Sadregiselus, dishonored by these insults, presented himself to him and, weeping, reported what else he had suffered publicly and from whom. The king, deeply angered by the injuries inflicted on his duke, and furiously threatening his son with many punishments, ordered Dagobert to be summoned before him. When Dagobert learned of this, since neither resistance was right nor escape possible, he rightly believed that he could submit himself to him if, by taking refuge in the aforesaid church, he might incline his father’s anger through the intercession of the blessed martyrs. He therefore undertook a very secure flight and, just as he had seen a stag take refuge there while pursued, so he too went there while pursued by his father. By this action he showed that he trusted that those who had driven dogs away from the entrance of their church could also protect him from the king’s pursuit. Nor did the outcome disappoint his hope.

### CHAPTER VIII—How Clotarius sent men to drag him away from there

When Clotarius heard that he had sought the protection of the saints, he was inflamed with still greater anger and sent attendants to bring him away from there and present him to the king with the utmost speed. They hastened to carry out what had been commanded. But when they were on their way to the holy place and were no more than one mile distant, they were prevented by divine will from proceeding farther along the road. They returned to their lord and disclosed what had happened to them. Distrusting their good faith—since they had preferred their love for his son to obedience to his command—he chose others to carry out cleverly what the first men had neglected. These too suffered the same experience, and, on their return, repeated the same report. Yet even this did not cool the king’s fury, and he attempted to accomplish himself what he had been unable to accomplish through his servants.

### CHAPTER IX—How the martyrs appeared to Dagobert in a dream

Meanwhile, while these things were taking place, sleep suddenly seized Dagobert as he lay prostrate before the martyrs with a humble heart. As he lay there face downward, three men stood before him, distinguished both by the features of their bodies and by the radiance of their clothing. While he gazed at them in astonishment, one of them, who appeared to surpass his companions in venerable whiteness of hair and authority, addressed him thus:

“Know, young man, that we are those whom, as you have heard from the report of fame, suffered for Christ: Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius; and that our bodies are buried here. But because the poverty of the burial you see and the lowliness of this house have obscured our fame, if you promise to depart adorned with the remembrance of us, we can free you from the distress you are suffering and, with God’s assistance, provide you help in all things. And so that you may not think that the phantasm of a dream has deceived you, receive a sign supported by truth. Once the earth covering our monuments has been removed, the inscriptions on each one will reveal which tomb it contains.”

Immediately he awoke, wrote down the names he had heard, and, rejoicing greatly in the martyrs’ address, bound himself by a vow that he afterwards fulfilled with the greatest devotion.

### CHAPTER X—How Clotarius himself wished to drag him away from there but was entirely unable to do so

After this Clotarius, wishing—as I have said—to tear his son away from the memorial of the saints, approached accompanied by a large number of men. But because divine power exercises its will upon kings no less than upon other human beings, he who had accused others of weakness became weak himself, so that he might plainly understand that, though he was powerful, he had to yield to those more powerful than he. The martyrs were protecting the fugitive, and, conversely, were keeping his enemies far from their inner sanctuary.

### CHAPTER XI—How Clotarius forgave his son’s fault and reverently honored the same place

[Col. 1399A]

Thus defeated, and astonished at the magnitude of what had occurred, Clotarius laid aside his fury and again became a father to his son: he forgave his fault and promised him safety. At last, permission having been granted to depart, he approached the church of the blessed martyrs and humbly invoked them as his patrons, having experienced the manifest evidence of their power. When he recognized how greatly their merits had commended themselves to him, he offered very large quantities of gold and silver to adorn their memorials and donated numerous and excellent estates to enhance the magnificence of the place.

### CHAPTER XII—How Clotarius made Dagobert his associate in the kingdom

In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Clotarius made his son Dagobert his associate in the kingdom and established him as king over the Austrasians, retaining for himself the territories bounded on the side of Neustria and Burgundy by the Ardennes and the Vosges.

### CHAPTER XIII—How Dagobert took Gomatrude in marriage and how contention arose between him and his father

In the forty-second year of Clotarius’s reign, Dagobert, in royal dress and at his father’s command, came honorably with the dukes to Clippiacum, near Paris. There he took Gomatrude, the sister of Queen Sichildis, in marriage. After the wedding, on the third day a serious dispute arose between Clotarius and his son Dagobert. Dagobert demanded that everything belonging to the kingdom of the Austrasians be placed under his authority. But Clotarius vehemently refused, wishing to concede nothing of this to him.

The two kings therefore selected twelve Franks so that the dispute might be settled through their deliberation. Among them Lord Arnulf, bishop of Metz, was chosen with the other bishops, so that, with the utmost kindness, as befitted his holiness, he might speak between father and son in the cause of peace. At last the father was reconciled with his son by the bishops and the wisest nobles. He restored to him the settled territory belonging to the kingdom of the Austrasians, retaining for himself only the lands situated this side of the Loire and in the region of Provence.

### CHAPTER XIV—How Dagobert, sent by his father into Austrasia, fought against Bertoaldus, and how Clotarius, coming to his aid, killed Bertoaldus

[Col. 1399D]

Dagobert, then, a very handsome young man, capable and energetic, and highly esteemed for his intelligence and resourcefulness in every respect, was sent by his father to rule in Hoste [perhaps *Austria*] with Duke Pippin. The superior Austrasian Franks, gathered together, established Dagobert as their king. In those days the excessively rebellious Saxons, under Duke Bertoaldus, stirred up an army of many peoples against Dagobert, king of the Austrasians.

Dagobert also gathered a very large army, crossed the Rhine, and did not hesitate to go out to battle against the Saxons. While they were fighting fiercely, Dagobert was struck on the helmet of his head, and a piece of his head, together with his hair, was cut off and fell to the ground. His shield-bearer Adtira, who was standing behind him, picked it up. Seeing that his army had been wounded, Dagobert said to the young man:

“Go quickly and hasten, carrying the hair from my head. Tell my father to come and help us before the entire army falls.”

He immediately set out, crossed the Rhine, and, since King Clotarius was staying there at that time, reached Longolarium in the Ardennes forest. When he had reported what had happened and presented the king with the severed piece of his son’s head, the king, overcome with intense grief, rose at once during the night amid the blaring of trumpets and the army of the Franks. He quickly crossed the Rhine and arrived with the utmost speed to aid his son.

When they had joined together and, in cheerful spirits, clapped hands joyfully, they pitched their tents as they advanced above the River Weser. Duke Bertoaldus of the Saxons, standing on the opposite bank of the river and prepared to proceed to battle, heard the uproar of the Franks and asked what it was. They answered:

“Lord King Clotarius has arrived, and for that reason the Franks are rejoicing.”

He replied with a burst of laughter:

“You are lying in your madness because you fear us so greatly. We have heard that Clotarius, whom you claim to have with you, is dead.”

The king, standing on the riverbank with his helmet on his head and his hair wrapped in a mixture of gray, heard this and immediately removed the helmet from his head. When Bertoaldus saw the king’s head uncovered, he recognized him and mocked him, saying:

“So you were here, you beast of burden?”

When the king heard this, he was greatly angered and took the insult very hard. Impatiently entering the River Weser, he swam across it on his swift horse and, fierce at heart as he was, pursued Bertoaldus. The army of the Franks followed the king and, swimming, barely crossed the river with Dagobert through its enormous whirlpools.

King Clotarius pursued Bertoaldus and fought fiercely with him. Bertoaldus said to him:

“O king, withdraw from me, lest I perhaps kill you. If you prevail against me, everyone will say that you killed your servant Bertoaldus, a pagan. But if I kill you, then a great report will be heard among all nations: that the strongest king of the Franks was killed by his servant.”

But the king did not yield at all to his words. Roaring with anger, he rose against him more and more fiercely. The horsemen following the king from a distance shouted:

“Take courage against your adversary, lord king!”

The king’s hands were very heavy. He was wearing a coat of mail, and the water that filled his bosom as he swam across the river had made all his clothing extremely heavy. After they had fought for a long time and with great effort, the king at last rose against Bertoaldus and killed him. Taking his head upon a spear, he returned to the Franks. They had been mourning, for they did not know what had happened to the king, but when they saw him they rejoiced with great joy.

The king then devastated the entire land of the Saxons and killed the whole population, leaving no larger living man there than the length of his sword, which they call a *spatha*, seemed to measure. He established this sign in that region, so that later generations might learn how great had been the treachery of the Saxons, how powerful the might of the Franks, and how greatly the anger of kings, once provoked, prevailed.

### CHAPTER XV—On the death of King Clotarius and how Dagobert succeeded him in the kingdom

In the forty-fifth year of his reign, the great King Clotarius died and was buried in the suburb of Paris, in the church of Saint Vincent. When Dagobert heard that his father had died, he ordered all the leading men over whom he ruled in Austrasia to advance the army. He sent envoys to Burgundy and Neustria, so that they might undoubtedly establish him as ruler of the kingdom.

When he had reached Rheims, it is known that, following an urgent appeal, all the bishops and dukes of the kingdom of Burgundy surrendered themselves there. The bishops and nobles of Neustria, too, and a very large part of the kingdom, strove to seek Dagobert.

### CHAPTER XVI—On Dagobert’s brother Hairbert and how Dagobert granted him a portion of the kingdom

His brother Hairbert, however, was trying to take possession of the kingdom if he could. But his intention achieved little because of his simplicity. Brunulfus, who had been the brother of Queen Sichildis, wishing to establish his nephew Hairbert in the kingdom, had begun plotting against Dagobert. But the outcome later revealed the reversal of this undertaking.

After Dagobert had occupied Clotarius’s kingdom, both Neustria and Burgundy, and had seized the treasures and reduced them under his authority, he was at last moved by mercy and piety and, following wise counsel, decided to grant his brother Hairbert the counties and cities this side of the Loire and the frontier extending toward the region of Gascony and the Pyrenees—enough for his brother to conduct his affairs and live in private clothing, as a private person.

Specifically, he granted Hairbert to govern the county of Toulouse, Cahors, Agen, Périgueux, and Saintes, together with whatever territory was bounded by these places toward the Pyrenees. He also confirmed this by a pact, so that Hairbert would never again presume to demand from Dagobert any part of their father’s kingdom.

Hairbert, choosing Toulouse as his seat, ruled in the region of Aquitaine. Three years after he had begun to reign, he defeated all Gascony with an army, brought it back under his authority, and made the extent of his kingdom somewhat larger.

### CHAPTER XVII—How King Dagobert sought the bodies of the holy martyrs Dionysius and his companions, adorned the church, and covered with silver the apse beneath which they rest

Dagobert, therefore, retaining his father’s kingdom with God’s favor, came to the place mentioned above, mindful of the vow already described, among the other praiseworthy things he accomplished. Seeking the bodies of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, he found their names arranged on the sarcophagi. On the tenth day before the Kalends of May, he transferred them with the utmost reverence to another place in the same village and adorned their memorials with pure gold and the purest gems.

Although he had constructed the church himself from its foundations and had furnished its interior with wondrous beauty, he also covered the outside, above, with the purest silver—the apse beneath which he had buried the venerable bodies of the martyrs—so that he might more fully satisfy the desire of his devout heart.

### CHAPTER XVIII—How he annually granted one hundred solidi from the tolls of Marseille for the lights of that church

From the toll revenue that was paid to him each year from Marseille, he also granted one hundred solidi for the lights of the same church, on the condition that the royal agents would diligently purchase oil with it, according to the arrangement of the *catabolus*, as though for the king’s use, and finally deliver it annually to the envoys of that place.

He also took care to confirm the matter by an order providing that, both at Marseille and at Valencia, Fosses, and Lyon, or wherever the route passed through the remaining places, all tolls on the six wagons by which this was apparently transported would be entirely remitted until they reached the basilica itself.

### CHAPTER XIX—On the treasury that he ordered to be made before the horn of the altar of that church, and ordered one hundred solidi to be paid there annually

He also ordered a treasury to be made of silver before the horn of the altar of the same church, so that the food brought by donors might, through the hand of the priest, be distributed as substance to the poor, in order that almsgiving of this kind might be performed in secret, according to the Gospel, and that the almighty Lord, who sees all hidden things, might restore it to each person a hundredfold in eternal recompense.

Into this treasury the same king also arranged for one hundred solidi to be brought each year, from the Kalends of one September to the Kalends of the next, as an eternal recompense. He issued an order that thereafter he himself, his sons, and those who later succeeded as kings of the Franks should not fail, at the appointed time and without interruption, to deposit there the prescribed number of solidi from the public treasury as the year’s cycle returned.

No one was to remove these one hundred solidi for any other purpose: they were to be distributed entirely among the poor. So long as the kingdom endured, they were to be brought at the proper time by the succeeding kings into the aforesaid treasury, so that through this contribution, together with whatever the Lord might will to be added there by other people, the poor and pilgrims might be refreshed throughout unshaken ages.

### CHAPTER XX—On the golden cross that the same king ordered to be made there

He also ordered a great cross to be made of pure gold and the most precious gems, to be placed behind the golden altar, with distinguished workmanship and the most secure subtlety of art. Blessed Eligius, who at that time was regarded as the supreme goldsmith in the kingdom, while energetically preparing other objects belonging to the adornment of the basilica, magnificently ornamented it with elegant and refined ingenuity, aided by holiness.

Indeed, more recent goldsmiths are accustomed to assert that at the present time scarcely anyone remains who, however skilled he may be in other works, could, over the course of many years, achieve a complete understanding of this kind of gem-setting and inlay work, since the practice has fallen out of use.

He also devoutly ordered that throughout the church garments woven with gold and richly adorned with various kinds of pearls be hung on the walls, columns, and arches, so that it might appear to surpass the adornments of other churches and, blooming everywhere with incomparable brilliance, might shine adorned with every earthly beauty and illumined with inestimable splendor. And so that divine praise might continually be offered there by the worshipers of God, he added numerous and very extensive estates.

### CHAPTER XXI—On his entry into Burgundy, the fear of the nobles, the joy of the poor, and the death of Brunulfus

[Col. 1403B]

When he had already been reigning for seven years over most of his father’s kingdom, as I mentioned above, he entered Burgundy surrounded by a large company. His arrival inspired such fear in the bishops, nobles, and other dukes residing in the kingdom of Burgundy that all were filled with amazement. To the poor seeking justice, however, it brought immense joy.

When he came to the city of Langres, he administered such justice to all his subjects, both the exalted and the poor, that he was believed to have been wholly pleasing to God. No reward intervened with him, nor was there any acceptance of persons; only the justice that the Most High loved held sway.

Then, residing at Dijon, or rather at Latona, for several days, he devoted himself with the entire population of his kingdom to the administration of justice with such intensity that, filled with desire for this benevolence, he neither slept nor satisfied himself with food. He thought most earnestly about ensuring that everyone would depart from his presence having received justice.

On the same day on which he hastened to leave Latona and proceed to Chalon, before daylight he entered a bath and there ordered Brunulfus, the uncle of his brother Hairbert, to be killed because of his infidelity. He was killed by the dukes Amalgarius and Arnebertus and by Willibadus the patrician.

### CHAPTER XXII—How he left Gomatrude and married Nanthildis

When he proceeded to Chalon, intent on completing the administration of justice that he had begun out of love for justice, he then went through Autun to Auxerre, and from there through the city of Sens came to Paris. There, with the advice of the Franks, he left Queen Gomatrude at the estate of Romiliacum because she was barren. He took as his wife a certain girl named Nanthildis, of exceedingly beautiful appearance, and elevated her as queen.

Until that time, from the beginning of his reign, he had governed the royal position in Austrasia with such prosperity—at first following the counsel of blessed Arnulf, bishop of the city of Metz, and of Pippin, mayor of the palace—that he enjoyed from all peoples the praise of immense honor.

His judicial power had shaken such a strong fear in everyone that they even hastened, out of devotion, to place themselves under his authority. Thus even the peoples living around the frontier of the Avars and Slavs eagerly sought him, so that he might go happily behind them; indeed, the Avars, the Slavs, and the nations of the other peoples confidently promised, by public act, that they would submit themselves to his authority.

After the departure of blessed Arnulf, he continued to use the counsel of Pippin, mayor of the palace, and of Chunibert, bishop of the city of Cologne. Strongly advised by them, he embraced the love of prosperity and justice. Until he reached the city of Paris, as I mentioned above, he was so raised up by the favor of all the peoples subject to him that none of the preceding kings of the Franks had surpassed him in praise.

When he came to the venerable tombs of the blessed martyrs Dionysius and his companions, he prayed to the Lord that, through the intercession of those martyrs, he might complete the vows he had undertaken. In order to reconcile those same martyrs more fully to himself, he immediately transferred Stirpiniacum, an estate in the county of Vexin, to their basilica by a charter of his authority.

### CHAPTER XXIII—What kind of king Dagobert was

King Dagobert himself was a most eminent ruler and king, very cautious and shrewd in intelligence. Toward the well-disposed and faithful to him he was gentle; toward rebels and traitors, however, he appeared exceedingly terrifying in his kingdom.

Governing the royal scepters excellently and showing himself exceptionally kind to the devout, he nevertheless, like a fiery lion crushing the necks of rebels, very often triumphed over the ferocity of foreign peoples through the surrounding strength of his courage.

Toward churches, priests, the poor, and pilgrims he had been an extraordinarily generous benefactor. Constantly engaging in athletic exercises and hunts, he was energetic and incomparable in every form of bodily agility.

Although, in human fashion, burdened by the weight of the kingdom and led astray by the volatility of youth, he handled certain reprehensible matters concerning religion less carefully or otherwise than he ought—for no one can be perfect in all things—it must nevertheless be believed that the distribution of such abundant alms and the prayers of the saints—whose memorials he tirelessly endeavored to adorn and whose basilicas he enriched for the redemption of his soul, above all earlier kings—could very easily obtain from the most merciful Lord a gracious pardon for him.

### CHAPTER XXIV—How he took Ragnetrude to his bed and fathered a son by her, and how he sent an embassy to the Emperor Heraclius

[Col. 1404D]

In the eighth year of his reign, while he was traveling through Austrasia in royal state and was exceedingly sad because he had been unable to have a son who would reign after him, he took a certain girl named Ragnetrude to his bed. By her, in that year, through the Lord’s bounty, he had a son, obtained through many prayers and generous almsgiving.

His brother, King Hairbert, came from Orléans and received the child from the holy font. When the venerable man Amandus, bishop of the city of Tongeren, was blessing the child and making him a catechumen, and, after the prayer had ended, no one in the army of so great a multitude had answered “Amen,” the Lord opened the mouth of the child, who was no more than forty days old, and, with everyone listening, he answered, “Amen.”

The holy bishop immediately regenerated him through sacred baptism, and, giving him the name Sigebert, the Lord filled the kings and both armies with great joy and amazement through this sign.

Now a certain Ega, one of the leading men, was constantly present in Dagobert’s council together with the other Neustrian nobles. In that year the envoys of King Dagobert whom he had sent to the Emperor Heraclius—Servatus and Paternus by name—returned to him, reporting that they had established peace with Heraclius.

### CHAPTER XXV—On the death of Haribert and how Dagobert reduced his kingdom and treasures under his authority

[Col. 1405B]

Although the Emperor Heraclius was highly educated in letters, he eventually became an exceptionally skilled astrologer. When he perceived from the signs of the stars that, by divine will, his empire was to be devastated by circumcised peoples, he sent to Dagobert, king of the Franks, asking him to order all the Jews in his kingdom to be baptized according to the Catholic faith.

King Dagobert, seizing this opportunity and moved by zeal for God, took counsel with the bishops and wise men and immediately ordered all the Jews who refused to receive the renewal of sacred baptism to be expelled from the borders of his kingdom.

The king carried this out with the greatest zeal. But the warning given to Heraclius had concerned not the Jews but the Agarenes—that is, the Saracens—a circumcised people. For it is known that his empire was later seized and violently ravaged by them.

In the ninth year of Dagobert’s reign, his brother Hairbert died, leaving a young son named Childeric, who also died shortly afterward. King Dagobert immediately reduced all Hairbert’s kingdom, together with Gascony, under his own authority.

He also sent a certain duke named Barontus to bring Hairbert’s treasures and present them to him. Barontus is known to have caused serious loss: acting faithlessly, he stole from the treasures and fraudulently made off with a very great amount.

### CHAPTER XXVI—On the death of Landegiselus, who was the brother of Queen Nanthildis

At the same time, Landegiselus, the brother of Queen Nanthildis, died and, at the king’s command, was honorably buried in the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius and his companions.

The queen entreated him, for the burial of her brother, to assign to the basilica of the aforesaid martyrs the estate of Alateum, situated in the county of Paris, since the aforesaid Landegiselus, while alive, had obtained that little estate through a royal charter.

The king gladly agreed and immediately ordered a charter concerning the aforesaid estate of Alateum to be drawn up. He subscribed it with the authority of his own confirmation and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of his ring.

### CHAPTER XXVII—On the beginning of the conflict between Dagobert, king of the Franks, and Samo, king of the Slavs

In that year the Slavs, called Wends, whose kingdom Samo held, killed Frankish merchants in great numbers and stripped them of their possessions. This was the beginning of the conflict between Dagobert, king of the Franks, and Samo, king of the Slavs.

Dagobert therefore sent Sicharius [another reading: Suharius] as envoy to Samo and asked him to make just reparation for the merchants whom his people had killed and whose possessions they had unlawfully seized.

Samo, unwilling to see Sicharius, was nevertheless approached by him when Sicharius, dressed in Slavic fashion, came with his companions into Samo’s presence. Sicharius reported everything that had been entrusted to him, and, concerning these and the other disputes that had arisen between the parties, asked that justice be rendered mutually, since Samo and the people of his kingdom owed service to King Dagobert.

Samo, already wounded by this reply, said:

“The land we possess belongs to Dagobert, and we are his, provided that he intends to preserve friendship with us.”

Sicharius said:

“It is impossible for Christians and servants of God to join friendship with dogs.”

Samo, in turn, said:

“If you are servants of God and we are God’s dogs, since you continually act against him, we are permitted to tear you apart with our bites.”

Sicharius was immediately expelled from Samo’s presence.

When this had been reported to King Dagobert, he immediately ordered an army to be mobilized from the entire kingdom of Austrasia against Samo and the Wends. The army entered the land of the Wends in three divisions. The Lombards also went hostilely against the Slavs to aid Dagobert.

The Slavs, however, restoring their forces in these and other places, were defeated by the army of the Alamanni under Duke Rodobertus in the region where it had entered. The Lombards likewise won a victory together with Dagobert, and the Alamanni and Lombards carried away with them a very large number of captives from the Slavs.

The king, after devastating that land, returned to his own kingdom.

### CHAPTER XXVIII—On the conflict between the Avars and Bulgars, and how Dagobert ordered the Bulgars who had come to him to be killed

In that same year a violent conflict arose between the Avars, also called Huns, and the kingdom of Spain, because they were disputing among themselves which party should inherit the kingdom: one side consisting of Avars and the other of Bulgars.

After gathering a multitude and fighting one another, the Bulgars were at last defeated by the Avars. The defeated Bulgars, nine thousand in number with their wives and children, were expelled from Pannonia and sought King Dagobert, asking him to receive them for settlement in the land of the Franks.

The king ordered them to be received in Bavaria for the winter, provided that he might discuss with the Franks what should be done with them. When they had been dispersed among the houses of the Bavarians to spend the winter, the king, following the wise counsel of the Franks, ordered the Bavarians to kill those Bulgars, with their wives and children, during a single night, each host killing the people lodged in his house.

The Bavarians immediately carried this out, and not one of them survived.

### CHAPTER XXIX—On the death of Sisebodus, king of Spain, and the golden dish that Sisenandus had promised King Dagobert

[Col. 1407A]

I shall not omit what happened at that time in the region of Spain and to its kings.

After the death of Sisebodus, a most merciful king, whose successor Sentila had become king about a year earlier, Sentila was exceedingly unjust toward his own people and incurred the hatred of all the leading men of his kingdom. With the counsel of the others, a certain Sisenandus, one of the nobles, sought King Dagobert, asking him to provide military assistance so that he might drive Sentila from the kingdom.

In return for this favor, he promised to give the king a most noble golden dish from the treasures of the Goths, which King Thuresmodus had received from the patrician Aetius, weighing five hundred measures of gold.

King Dagobert, being energetic in battle, ordered the whole kingdom of Burgundy to be summoned by right of war to assist Sisenandus. He appointed the dukes Abundantius and Venerandus over it.

When it became known in Spain that the army of the Franks was being assembled to assist Sisenandus, the entire Gothic army submitted itself to Sisenandus’s authority. The dukes Abundantius and Venerandus of King Dagobert, together with the army from Toulouse, advanced with Sisenandus only as far as the city of Zaragoza. There all the Goths gathered from the kingdom of Spain elevated Sisenandus to the kingship.

Abundantius and Venerandus, honored with gifts, returned with the army from Toulouse to their own seats.

Finally, King Dagobert sent an embassy to King Sisenandus through Duke Amalgarius and Venerandus, asking him to send the dish he had promised. When that dish had been handed over by Sisenandus to the envoys, the Goths seized it on the way and would not allow them to take it away.

Later, after the envoys had traveled about, the king received from Sisenandus two hundred thousand solidi as the price of the dish itself. It is said that King Dagobert devoutly offered that silver for the construction of the church of Saint Dionysius the martyr, together with many other ornaments.

At that time miracles occurred there through the intercession of the martyrs with such great frequency that people afflicted by every kind of illness came from all directions and sought that place with devout hearts; restored to health, they returned joyfully to their homes.

When the king saw this, he unhesitatingly offered whatever precious objects could be found in his treasures to adorn that place. He also established there a *matricula*, a hospice, and various other institutions, so that the poor of both sexes, as well as those who had been deemed worthy to receive health through the help of the saints, might thereafter be supported by his alms, and those who wished might remain in the service of the Church as an act of thanksgiving.

### CHAPTER XXX—How Dagobert marched against the Wends with an army and how he remitted the tribute of the Saxons

In the tenth year of his reign, when he had been informed that the army of the Wends had entered Thuringia, he lost no time. Advancing from the kingdom of Austrasia from the city of Metz, he crossed the Ardennes and attacked Mainz. Preparing to cross the Rhine, he had with him a picked force of brave men from Neustria and Burgundy, together with dukes and counts.

The Saxons sent envoys to him, asking that he remit the tribute they paid to the fiscal authorities. They promised that, by their own efforts and for their own advantage, they would resist the Wends and guard the frontier of the Franks in those regions.

King Dagobert, having received the counsel of the Neustrians, granted them what they requested. The Saxons who had come to present this petition confirmed the agreement by oaths made over weapons, according to their custom, on behalf of all the Saxons.

But this promise achieved little in practice. Nevertheless, by Dagobert’s order, the Saxons have continued to be exempt from the tribute they had been accustomed to pay. Each year they had been assessed by the elder Clotarius at five hundred tribute-cows, but King Dagobert then annulled this obligation.

### CHAPTER XXXI—How Dagobert elevated his son to the kingdom of Austrasia

In the eleventh year of his reign, when the Wends, at Samo’s command, were again raging fiercely and, frequently crossing their own frontier, were entering Thuringia and the other counties to ravage the kingdom of the Franks, King Dagobert came to the city of Metz.

With the counsel of the bishops and nobles, and with the consent of all the leading men of the kingdom, he elevated his son Sigebert to the kingdom of Austrasia and permitted him to have the city of Metz as his seat. He appointed Chunibert, bishop of Cologne, and Adalgisus, duke of the palace, to govern the kingdom, and handed over to his son a treasure sufficient for his needs.

He elevated him worthily, as was fitting, with the honor of this dignity and determined that everything he had granted him should be strengthened by royal orders. Thereafter Sigebert, through the efforts of the Austrasians, is known to have usefully defended the frontier and the kingdom of the Franks against the Wends.

### CHAPTER XXXII—How Hludowicus was born to him from Nanthildis, and how he divided his kingdom between him and Sigebert
When, in the twelfth year of King Dagobert’s reign, a son named Hludowius [in some copies, Clodoveus] had been born to him by Queen Nanthildis [Col. 1408D], he is known to have confirmed, at the counsel and urging of the Neustrians, by a bond of agreement with his son Sigebert, the following arrangement: all the leading men and bishops of Austrasia, together with the other dukes, placing their hands in Sigebert’s hands, further confirmed by oath that Neptricum and Burgundy, their order having been secured, should belong to the kingdom of Hludowius after the departure of King Dagobert.

Austrasia, likewise secured by the same arrangement—for it was equal both in population and in extent—was to belong to the kingdom of Sigebert and to remain wholly subject to him; and whatever had formerly belonged to the kingdom of the Austrasians, King Sigebert was to receive under his authority to govern and possess perpetually. The sole exception was the duchy of Dentilon, which had been wickedly taken away from the Austrasians: it was to be restored to the Neustrians [Col. 1409A] and placed under the rule of Hludowius.

Yet the Austrasians appear to have confirmed these agreements under compulsion, driven by fear of King Dagobert, whether willingly or unwillingly; and it is established that they were preserved thereafter under Kings Sigebert and Hludowius.

### CHAPTER XXXIII  
### How he granted to the Church of Christ’s martyrs Dionysius and his companions certain plots of land within and outside Paris, together with the gate of that city and all its tolls

About this time King Dagobert returned to Paris. His love for the aforementioned martyr Dionysius and his companions grew ever stronger because of the splendid miracles that the Lord daily performed at their venerable tombs. He therefore granted to their basilica certain plots of land within and outside the city of Paris, together with the gate of that city [Col. 1409B] situated beside the Prison of Glaucinus, which at that time was supervised by his merchant Solomon, along with all the tolls that appeared to serve his treasury. By the authority of his charter he confirmed that this grant should remain perpetual, affirming it by his own signature and the impression of his ring.

### CHAPTER XXXIV  
### How he granted the annual market held after the martyrs’ feast to the brothers residing there

At the same time he granted to that holy place and to the brothers serving God and the holy martyrs there the annual market held near the same monastery after the feast of those most illustrious martyrs. He then took care to confirm the following provision [Col. 1409C]: whatever tolls, or whatever the treasury might have been entitled to expect from them, and whatever could lawfully have been exacted by any judicial authority in that city or in all the other places designated within the district of Paris—from the feast itself until that market ended—should, as an eternal recompense and so that those servants of God might at all future times be moved to pray more devotedly to God’s mercy on his behalf, be permanently assigned in full, without any exception or diminution, for their use.

### CHAPTER XXXV  
### On the death of Sadregiselus, and how the king granted to the aforesaid church all his possessions that had been received into the treasury

In the thirteenth year of his reign, when Sadregiselus, duke of the Aquitanians [Col. 1409D], had been killed by certain men—he of whom we spoke above, whom Dagobert, because he had shown contempt for him, ordered in his childhood to be beaten with rods and disfigured by the shaving of his beard, and who, fearing his father on that account, had sought the protection of the holy martyrs—Sadregiselus had sons being educated in the palace. Although they could very easily have avenged their father’s death, they were unwilling to do so; consequently, they were later rebuked by the nobles of the kingdom according to Roman law and lost all their paternal possessions.

When everything had been received into the royal treasury, the most excellent King Dagobert most devoutly granted to the Church of Christ’s martyrs Dionysius and his companions the villas of the aforementioned Sadregiselus: Novientum in the district of Angers [Col. 1410A], Barciacum, Nuiliacum, Podentiniacum, Pascellarias, and Anglarias in the district of Poitiers, as well as many others with saltworks beside the sea, whose names we have thought it too lengthy to list here. He assigned half of them for the support of the brothers serving God there, and instituted them to sing psalms in ordered groups after the manner of the monasteries of Agaunum and Saint Martin at Tours. He granted the other half to the matricularii and servants of that church, wishing to retain nothing from them for his own use.

He inserted the names of these same villas individually within the conclusion of a single charter and confirmed it by his own signature and the impression of his ring. If anyone wishes to investigate their names more carefully, let him seek the charter itself in the archive of that church [Col. 1410B]; there, I believe, he will find the names of twenty-seven villas inserted.

### CHAPTER XXXVI  
### On the army that he sent into Wasconia

Finally, in the fourteenth year of his reign, when the Wascones were violently rebelling and carrying out many raids in the Frankish kingdom formerly held by Haribertus, King Dagobert ordered an army to advance from the whole kingdom of Burgundy. He appointed at its head Adoindus the referendary, who had proved himself brave in many battles during the time of the former King Theoderic.

Ten dukes were sent with him, together with their armies: Harimbertus, Amalgarius, Leudobertus, Wandalmarus, Waldericus, Ermenricus, Barontus, and Hairhardus, of Frankish origin; Ramelenus, of Roman origin; Willebadus the patrician, of Burgundian origin; and Agino, of Saxon origin [Col. 1410C]—besides very many counts who had no duke over them. All these proceeded into Wasconia with the army.

When the entire land of Wasconia had been filled with the Burgundian army, the Wascones came out from the crags between the mountains and hastened to battle. When they had begun to fight, they turned their backs, as was their custom, as soon as they perceived that they were going to be overcome. Giving themselves concealment in the jaws of the valleys and on the peaks of the mountains, they hid themselves among the rocks of that mountain, placing themselves in the safest locations.

The army, pursuing them from behind with its dukes, put a very great number of captives in chains, defeated the Wascones, killed a multitude of them, and burned all their houses [Col. 1410D], stripping them of their livestock and possessions. At last, overcome and subdued, the Wascones asked the aforesaid dukes for pardon and peace. They promised that, once presented before the glory and presence of King Dagobert, they would surrender themselves to his authority and fulfill everything imposed upon them by him.

The king’s army would have returned safely to its homeland without any injury if the duke Harimbertus, together with the older and nobler men of his army, had not through negligence been killed by the Wascones in the valley of Robola. The army of the Franks, which had entered Wasconia from Burgundy, returned to its own homes after achieving victory.

### CHAPTER XXXVII  
### How he made the church of the aforesaid martyrs heir to certain villas, and how he granted the brothers residing there one hundred cows each year from the duchy of Le Mans

[Col. 1411A]

At the same time, the most devout King Dagobert made the Church of Christ’s martyrs Dionysius and his companions heir, by the subscriptions to his own charters, to Campania, a villa situated in the district of Camliacum, which a certain matron named Theodila had given to the king; to Tibernione [Tivernione], situated in the district of Orléans, which the same king had exchanged with Saint Ferreolus, bishop of Autun; and also to Upper Clippiacum, Idcina, Salice, and Aquaputta, all situated in the district of Paris.

He likewise made it heir to Latiniacum, situated in the territory of Meaux, which the king himself had exchanged from his own treasury with Duke Bobo and Tacilo, count of the palace [Col. 1411B]. Ever seeking the aid of the saints against visible and invisible adversaries, he acted so that, just as the aforementioned martyrs had promised him in a dream during his youth that they would rescue him from impending troubles, they might bring him the assistance they had promised both in life and after death.

Moreover, he appears to have granted for all future time, by the subscription of his own charter, one hundred cows from the duchy of Le Mans, which were paid to him each year, to the brothers serving God there, so that they might be moved to pray more devotedly to the Lord and the holy martyrs on his behalf.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### How he sent his messengers to Judicail in Britain

[Col. 1411C]

After this, King Dagobert, residing in the palace at Clippiacum, sent messengers to Britain, demanding that the Britons make amends for what they had committed against his men and surrender themselves to his authority. Otherwise, the aforesaid Burgundian army, which had been in Wasconia, would immediately invade Britain.

When King Judicail of the Britons heard this, he came swiftly to Clippiacum to Lord King Dagobert with many gifts. There he asked pardon and promised to make amends for everything that the Britons of his kingdom had unlawfully perpetrated there against the dukes of the Franks. He further swore that he and the kingdom of Britain, which he ruled, would henceforth and forever remain subject to the authority of King Dagobert and to all future kings of the Franks [Col. 1411D].

Nevertheless, Judicail refused to recline at table for a meal with King Dagobert, because Judicail was religious and greatly feared God. When the king had taken his seat at table, Judicail left the palace and went to the residence of Dado the referendary, who was called Audoenus and later became bishop of Rouen. Since Judicail knew that Dado followed a holy religious life, he went to dinner with him.

The next day Judicail took leave of King Dagobert and returned to Britain. The king nevertheless honored him appropriately with gifts.

### CHAPTER XXXIX  
### How he enriched nearly all the monasteries of his kingdom by his testament, through which he also granted the villa of Brunadum to Saint Dionysius

In that same year, after King Dagobert had subjugated all the peoples surrounding his kingdom, and peace had already been firmly established with the Lord’s help, and after he had designated his sons Sigebert and Hludowius as kings, as we have said above, he acted on counsel inspired by God. Having summoned his sons and all the leading men of the entire kingdom, he established a general assembly in the palace of Bigargium on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.
