When, according to the custom of the Frankish kings, he was seated crowned upon a golden throne, with everyone standing before him, he began as follows:

“Listen to me, O you kings and dearest sons, and all you nobles and most valiant dukes of our kingdom. Before the sudden transition of death occurs, we must keep watch for the salvation of the soul, lest it find someone unprepared, take away the present light without any reprieve, and hand him over to perpetual darkness and eternal [Col. 1412B] torments.

“Rather, while he still possesses the right of freedom, let him seek to purchase everlasting life from perishable possessions for the sake of eternal dwelling places, so that he may obtain a desirable place among the company of the just, prepare the Lord as his recompense, and take care to distribute transitory goods to the venerable places of the saints in the support of the poor, so that from the Lord himself he may deserve to be refreshed among the morning stars by the fruit of the unfailing Paraclete.

“From that living fountain, no cup is withheld from one who asks in perfect faith, nor is its channel diminished; rather, whoever draws from it is watered with heavenly sweetness, and the fragrance of the pleasant balm of paradise breathes upon him.

“Therefore, examining my conscience and the excesses of my heart, considering the judgment of the heavenly King and fearing his tribunal, also fearing the punishments of wretched men, but above all desiring the infinite glory of the just, and taking care lest the final day, according to the Lord’s dispensation, find us sluggish regarding the memory of the saints or the consolation of the needy, it has seemed good to us, with sound mind and sound counsel—and, as we have already said, the devotion of the soul has urged us—to draw up a testament for eternal recompense.

“In it we order that almost all the basilicas of the saints named in our kingdom in our time be made heirs through our own donations. For an unalterable benefaction, we have decided to confirm four copies in one wording and at one moment, with all of you as witnesses; and whatever we have now given everywhere to the places of the saints, we have set down in a similar notation below.

“Of these copies, we send one to Lyon in Gaul; another we entrust to the archive of the church at Paris; a third we give to Lord Abbo to keep at Metz; and the fourth, which we also hold in our hands, we order to be placed in our treasury.

“This, then, is our own devotion, and this is the consolation of our Lord, who graciously receives perfected vows: namely, that whoever here gives sustenance to holy places, priests, and the needy will have firm confidence on the day of necessity, for, as Scripture bears witness, ‘He who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord,’ and the Ruler of Olympus will repay him in turn.

“Therefore, as we have said, concern for the remedy of our soul has instructed us that after our departure, whenever God shall command it, the priests who at that time hold responsibility for the offices in the places written below should, exactly as this present document states, receive without awaiting anyone’s transfer and immediately, with complete integrity, the property belonging to us. Thereafter they shall regard all of it as belonging to the aforesaid holy places, and under full immunity it shall perpetually profit them there for our reward.

“When each of them has received what was assigned to him at that time, let him enter our name in the book of life without fail and commemorate it on every Sunday and on all principal feasts of the saints.

“But what we confidently believe pertains more fully to the healing of our soul: by this document we adjure you priests who at that time reside in those holy places and perform their offices without negligence, by the heavenly King, that after each of you has received what was assigned to him, you celebrate Masses for us for three successive years and offer sacrifices without fail to the most merciful King for the burden of our committed sins to be forgiven.

“This testament, with the Lord as judge and witness, we entrust especially through this document, with the consent of all who are present, to our dearest sons, Kings Sigebert and Hludowius, whom Christ’s bounty has granted us as offspring, and to whatever sons the Lord may yet give us who are to succeed us. We charge you to preserve this common decree of ours in every respect and not presume to tear apart these grants of ours.

“Rather, by the Trinity of the almighty Name, by the powers of the archangels, patriarchs [Col. 1413C] and prophets, apostles and martyrs, and all the saints, by the fearful day of judgment, and by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, before whose presence we seem destined to rise again, we adjure you to guard perpetually, with stable firmness, our enactments that the present document declares.

“We shall now strive to confirm these testamentary charters for our perpetual reward by our own ratification; and we order all of you bishops, abbots, nobles, and distinguished men who are present to affirm them by your subscriptions or marks.

“Again and again, as we have said above, we admonish you kings and dearest sons, and those who shall later succeed us, that you presume in no way to tear apart what we have done, if you wish what you establish after our departure to remain unshaken. For do not doubt this: you too will have successors, and if you do not preserve our enactments, you should not believe that your own enactments will remain secure.”

When the king had most prudently concluded this speech, with everyone listening attentively, all gladly wished him a long life and peace for the kingdom; then the aforesaid testament was eagerly confirmed both by the king himself and by all the leading men of the kingdom.

In it, mindful also of his particular patron, Lord Dionysius, although he had already granted him very many estates, he took care to insert a villa called Braunadum. After duly arranging everything that pertained to the honor of the kingdom, he allowed everyone to return joyfully to his own home.

The testament that he had ordered to be placed in his treasury is still reverently preserved today in the archive of the Church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius and his companions.

### CHAPTER XL  
### He gives the monks of Saint Dionysius eight thousand pounds of lead to cover the basilica

Finally, at the same time, he granted eight thousand pounds of lead—which was paid to him from the taxed metalworks every second year—for roofing the same church of the aforesaid blessed martyrs. He arranged that in alternate years it should be brought from the royal estates and from the same villas that he had previously granted to that holy place, and that it should be delivered by the people or treasurers of that venerable monastery, so that, just as he had most devoutly caused the basilica of those martyrs to be roofed, so the almighty God, through their intercession, might protect him beneath the shadow of his wings [Col. 1414B].

He also took care to confirm the matter by a charter, so that in all future time the same grant might be preserved inviolate by the succeeding kings.

### CHAPTER XLI  
### How the Wascones, with their duke, submitted themselves to his authority

In the fifteenth year of Dagobert’s reign, all the senior men of that land, together with Duke Hamandus, came to the king at Clippiacum. There, terrified by royal authority, they took refuge in the church of Saint Dionysius the martyr.

By the clemency of King Dagobert, out of reverence for Saint Dionysius, their lives were spared. There they confirmed their oaths and promised that at all times they would be faithful to the king, his sons, and the kingdom of the Franks [Col. 1414C]. But what they proved afterward by the outcome was that, as usual, they had always deceived him. With the king’s permission, they returned to the land of Wasconia.

### CHAPTER XLII  
### On the death of King Dagobert, and what he did while lying in that illness

It would be a lengthy task to demonstrate in the present work how prudent that same King Dagobert was in counsel, how cautious in judgment, how vigorous in military discipline, how generous in almsgiving, how zealous in establishing the peace of the churches, and above all how devoted he was to enriching the monasteries of the saints. It is also less necessary and, especially for avoiding the weariness of readers who grow impatient, undesirable, since clear evidence of these matters, impossible to erase with time, is everywhere present.

Therefore, turning now to describe his death, I shall briefly relate what he did while in that illness and also one miracle that I found in a very ancient document which, as was reported, the blessed Bishop Audoenus had written, and which occurred to that renowned king after his death.

After his glorious administration of the kingdom, in the sixteenth year after he had acquired the kingdom, he began to fall ill with dysentery at the villa of Spinogilum on the River Seine, not far from Paris. From there his men carried him to the basilica of Saint Dionysius the martyr.

After a few days, when he felt the danger to his life approaching, he ordered his counsellor Ega to come to him as quickly as possible. Entrusting Queen Nanthildis and his son Hludowius to him, and knowing that he himself was about to depart, he nevertheless regarded Ega’s counsel as extremely valuable, since with his assistance his son could govern the kingdom vigorously.

Then, having summoned the leading men of the palace and commended his son and wife to them, and them likewise to his son with the oath of fidelity, as was customary, he ordered a charter to be made for the matricularii of the aforesaid basilica of the blessed martyrs from the villas of Acuciacum, Cusdunum, and even Magno-villare, Mediano-villare, and Gellis. In it he also inserted Sarclidas, which he had previously granted to them.

While all the nobles were overwhelmed with grief, he consoled them most graciously with what strength he possessed. Among other things, whose recollection would take too long, he said:

“Although every wretched human being, as long as he is safe and well, ought always to keep before his eyes the future examination of the almighty God’s judgment, nevertheless, when placed in illness he must in no way despair of his most merciful compassion. Rather, he ought to watch over the salvation of his soul more attentively and, as far as possible, redeem himself from his own possessions through the support of the poor, so that after death he may obtain an eternal recompense from the most merciful Judge.

“Therefore, for the remedy of my soul, to the matricularii of the basilica of Lord Dionysius, our particular patron, in which that precious martyr rests bodily with his companions, and in which we desire to be buried, we now grant in full the villas contained in this present charter. Just as they have until now been possessed by our treasury, so, by our indulgence, for the salvation of our soul and for the stability of our sons, they shall, both now and in the future, perpetually benefit the aforementioned matricularii who serve in the aforesaid basilica or its atrium.

“No one among our sons or among any future kings who succeed us, neither bishop nor abbot of that monastery, shall ever presume to take these villas, or Sarclidas, which we previously granted to those same brothers, away from them, if he does not wish to incur the anger of God and the offense of Lord Dionysius. If anyone presumes to do so, let him render an account of the matter before the tribunal of our Lord Jesus Christ, together with the holy martyr and those matricularii.

“For, by God’s gift, as we believe, the annual sustenance derived from these possessions will be sufficient for the aforementioned poor, so that, nourished by our alms, they and their successors may always be more fully and devoutly pleased to pray for our soul.

“We ourselves are now no longer able to subscribe this present charter, because, as the illness grows stronger, the pen trembles in our hand. Therefore we ask our dearest son, King Hludowius, to affirm this charter with the mark of his name, to offer it to Dado, and for our nobles to subscribe it.”

When the king had finished speaking, his son, King Hludowius, subscribed the charter according to his father’s command, with the referendary Dado presenting it. All the nobles who were present confirmed it with their own subscriptions.

When these matters had thus been completed, a few days later, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, the most Christian King Dagobert was taken from human affairs [Col. 1416A]. An intolerable mourning suddenly filled the palace, and the whole kingdom was seized by the bitterest lamentation over his death.

### CHAPTER XLIII  
### On his burial in the church of Saint Dionysius, and how, while still alive, he established there the order of psalm-singing

Embalmed with spices and carried amid immense grief and a great multitude of people, he was transferred to the basilica of the most blessed martyrs. As we said above, he himself had fittingly adorned it with gold, gems, and many precious materials, and had ordered it to be magnificently constructed all around. He was honorably buried beside their tomb on the right side.

Such great riches, villas, and possessions in many places had been bestowed there by him that, even here—so as to avoid the weariness of certain readers, as I have already said—they are scarcely listed, although many people still marvel at his devotion of spirit.

He had established there an order of psalm-singers after the manner of the monasteries of Agaunum and Saint Martin at Tours; but the laxity of Abbot Agiulfus [Haigulfus] is known to have opposed that institution.

### CHAPTER XLIV  
### On the embassy of Ansoaldus and the revelation of a servant of God, by which they liberated the soul of King Dagobert

At that time, as it happened, the illustrious defender of the Church of Poitiers, Ansoaldus, was conducting an embassy in the region of Sicily. After completing it, while returning with naval assistance, he landed at a small island on which a very venerable old man named John led a solitary life [Col. 1416C]. Many people who traveled by sea frequently came to him so that they might be strengthened by the consolation of his prayer.

By divine will Ansoaldus landed on this island, redeemed by the merits of so great a man. While conversing with him about the joys of heaven, the old man asked him whence and why he had come. When the old man had learned that he was from Gaul and the reason for which Ansoaldus had been sent, he asked him to explain the character and devotion of Dagobert, king of the Franks.

When Ansoaldus had done so carefully, the old man added that one day, when he had yielded briefly to sleep—for he was already weakened by age and exhausted by vigils—a man venerable with gray hair had approached him, awakened him, and urged him to rise quickly and pray to divine mercy for the soul of Dagobert, king of the Franks, because he had breathed out his spirit that very day.

When he hastened to do this, he saw, not far away on the open sea, terrifying spirits dragging the bound King Dagobert about in a small boat across the waters and hauling him toward the regions of Vulcan, while also inflicting blows upon him. Dagobert himself was calling continually upon the blessed martyrs Dionysius and Mauritius and the most holy confessor Martin for his liberation.

Immediately the heavens thundered, and lightning was scattered through the storm. Suddenly, amid these events, most excellent men appeared, clothed in garments white as snow. Trembling, he asked them who they were. They replied that they were those whom Dagobert had called to his aid—namely, Dionysius, Mauritius, and Martin—and that they had come to place him, once rescued, in Abraham’s bosom.

Thus, swiftly pursuing the enemies of the human race [Col. 1417A], they lifted with them into the heavens the soul that those enemies had tormented with blows and threats, singing:

“Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken, O Lord; he shall dwell in your courts. We shall be filled with the good things of your house. Holy is your temple, marvelous in righteousness.”

These things, among others, were reported in the aforementioned document. They may appear, in my judgment, not merely plausible but entirely true. For although that same king had enriched churches far and wide, he had especially endowed these with abundant wealth. Thus, after his death, he called upon the aid of those whom he remembered having loved above all others.

### CHAPTER XLV  
### On his son Hludowius, and how he succeeded him in the kingdom

After the departure of King Dagobert, his son Hludowius, still of tender age, assumed his father’s kingdom. All the dukes of Neustria and Burgundy raised him to the kingship at the villa of Massollacum [Col. 1417B].

Ega, who had been King Dagobert’s counsellor, governed the palace and the kingdom fittingly during the first year of Hludowius’s reign and into the approaching second year, together with Queen Nanthildis, whom that king had left behind. Among all the leading men of Neptricum, he acted most prudently and was endowed with great patience; he was superior to all the others.

He was noble by birth, rich in possessions, devoted to justice, learned in speech, and ready with answers. He was, however, slandered by many because he was devoted to avarice.

### CHAPTER XLVI  
### On his treasures, how they were divided among his sons, and on the deaths of Pippinus and Ega, who had been counsellors of King Dagobert

After the death of King Dagobert, I shall not omit the manner in which his treasures were divided among his sons; rather, I shall set it down in the sequence of this little book in clear order.

When Pippinus, the mayor of the palace, and the other dukes of Austrasia, who until Dagobert’s death had been held under his authority, unanimously sought Sigebert, Pippinus and Chunibertus—who had previously been joined to one another by the bonds of friendship—recently bound themselves together with a strong and firm promise to preserve their friendship between them perpetually, as before.

Drawing all the Austrasian dukes prudently and graciously to themselves, and governing them kindly, they secured their friendship for perpetual observance.

Messengers were therefore dispatched to demand from Queen Nanthildis and Hludowius the portion of their father Dagobert’s treasures due to Sigebert, which Sigebert was to have. A formal assembly was convened for its delivery.

Accordingly, Chunibertus, bishop of the city of Cologne, and Pippinus, mayor of the palace, accompanied by certain leading men of Austrasia, were sent by Sigebert and arrived at the villa of Compendium. There, at the command of Nanthildis and King Hludowius, the treasures of the blessed-memory King Dagobert were presented through the insistence of Ega, mayor of the palace, and were divided on an equal scale [Col. 1417D].

They nevertheless reserved a third part of everything that King Dagobert had acquired after Queen Nanthildis had begun to reign.

Chunibertus and Pippinus, mayor of the palace, had Sigebert’s portion brought to Metz. There it was presented and recorded before King Sigebert.

After nearly a full year had passed, Pippinus died. His death caused no small grief to everyone in Austrasia, because they had loved him exceedingly for his devotion to justice and his goodness [Col. 1418A]. Ega too, in the third year of King Hludowius, was afflicted by fever at the villa of Clippiacum and died.

### CHAPTER XLVII  
### On Herchinoaldus and Flaucatus, who were mayors of the palace after Ega

After his departure, Herchinoaldus, who on his mother’s side had been related by blood to King Dagobert, became mayor of the palace of Hludowius.

He was a patient man, full of goodness, cautious in judgment, humbly revering all servants of God and all priests, endowed with possessions in measured abundance, and held in extraordinary esteem by all the leading men of the kingdom.

In the fourth year of King Hludowius’s reign, when Queen Nanthildis, after Ega’s departure, had come with her son to Orléans in the kingdom of Burgundy [Col. 1418B], she ordered all the senior bishops, together with the dukes and leading men of that kingdom, to come to her. Drawing each of them to herself with the greatest kindness, she appointed Flaucatus, a Frank by birth, mayor of the palace in the kingdom of Burgundy. With the election of the bishops and dukes, she confirmed him in this rank of honor and betrothed to him her niece, named Ragneberta.

### CHAPTER XLVIII  
### On the testament of Queen Nanthildis and her death

At that time she ordered a testament to be drawn up concerning the villas with which King Dagobert and his son Hludowius had enriched her, assigning them to suitable holy places. In it she also ordered the villa of Latiniacum, situated in Brie [Col. 1418C], to be inserted as a grant to the basilica of Lord Dionysius.

She ordered three copies of it to be written in identical wording, one of which is preserved to this day in the archives of the aforesaid church.

When these matters had been arranged, her affairs had prospered, and her son was already ruling usefully in Neptricum and Burgundy, Queen Nanthildis died. She was buried in the church of the blessed martyrs Dionysius and his companions beside King Dagobert, in the same tomb.

### CHAPTER XLIX  
### On Hludowius, how he renewed the charters that his father had granted to Saint Dionysius, and how he ordered the silver from the aforesaid apse to be distributed to the poor

Then their son Hludowius, after his parents had departed from this world, as we have said above, succeeded to the kingdom. He too took care, in his own time, to renew the charters that his glorious father, confirming them by his own authority, had granted to the church of the aforesaid holy martyrs, and to confirm them by his own signature and likewise by the impression of his ring [Col. 1418D].

In the fourteenth year of his reign, the apse beneath which the bodies of the aforementioned martyrs of Christ, Dionysius and his companions, rest had been covered on the outside above with a silver covering by his illustrious father, the king, with the greatest devotion, as I have related.

At the urging and counsel of certain people, he ordered that the silver from above that apse be distributed to Christ’s poor, the needy, and pilgrims, since, as is reported, a severe famine prevailed at that time. He also gave a charter of this kind to Abbot Aigulfus, who then had charge of that monastery, ordering him [Col. 1419A] to undertake faithfully, with fear of God, the fulfillment of this command and not to fear any demand either from his bishop—for at that time the monastery still appeared to be subject to the authority of the bishop of the Church of Paris—or from any other person.

### CHAPTER L  
### How the same King Hludowius freed the aforesaid place from the domination of the bishop of Paris through a privilege and the confirmation of the holy bishops
In the course of time, in the sixteenth year of his reign, King Hludowius, residing at Clichy, summoned the bishops and also the leading men of the kingdom. Adorned, as was customary, with the royal insignia, and among the other principal matters for which, as we have said, he had assembled the nobles to deliberate for the welfare of the kingdom, he began, impelled by divine providence, as follows:

“We ought diligently, in accordance with our father’s instruction, to show reverence to the holy places of the saints, so that on the day of necessity we may have them as patrons and defenders against invisible enemies. Therefore, lords and most holy priests, and also princes of our kingdom and palace, listen attentively to the counsel which, as I believe, almighty God has deigned to implant in our heart; and, if you judge it useful, deliberate upon it beneficially with me, under Christ’s protection.

“Indeed, almighty God the Father, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has illumined the hearts of holy Christians through the mystery of the incarnation of his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and through the enlightening of the Holy Spirit. For love and desire of him, amid the glorious triumphs of the martyrs, the most blessed Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius deserved to receive the palm of victory and the glorious crown. In their basilica, where they appear to rest, Christ has deigned for a long time to perform no small number of miracles, to the praise of his name. In that place also our parents, lord Dagobert and lady Nanthild, appear to rest, so that through the intercession of those saints they may deserve to share in the heavenly kingdom and possess eternal life.

“And since that holy place is seen to have been enriched with possessions by those same princes, by other ancient kings, and by Christians who feared God, out of love for God and to attain eternal life, it is our sincere devotion and petition that the apostolic man Landeric, bishop of the Church of Paris, ought—if it seems right to you—to make and confirm a privilege for that holy place, for the abbot and the brothers residing there, for their future tranquility. Thus the congregation may more easily pray continually at the thresholds of those martyrs for divine mercy on behalf of the stability of our kingdom. The bishop himself, in accordance with our devout petition, is also recognized as ready and willing to grant and confirm this.

“We, for the reverence of those martyrs and for the confirmation of our own reward, wish at this present time to confirm, together with you, a decree of the following kind: if anything has been assigned to that holy place in villages, slaves, or any other possessions by ancient kings, by our parents, or by people fearing God, out of love for God, or if anything should subsequently be added there—since, as we have said, that holy place appears to have been enriched by the munificence of our parents—let no bishop, whether one now present or any future successor, nor their agents, nor any other person, be able in any manner to remove anything from that place, to usurp any authority for himself in that monastery, to diminish anything under the pretext of an exchange without the will of that congregation or our permission, or to remove cups, crosses, altar vestments, sacred books, silver, gold, or anything whatever that has been or shall be presented there; nor let anyone presume to carry such things away to the city.

“But let that holy congregation be permitted to possess perpetually whatever has been assigned there by a rightful grant, so that it may be the more attentive and constant in praying to the Lord for the souls of our parents and for the stability of our kingdom.

“For the love of God, the reverence of those holy martyrs, and the attainment of eternal life, we wish, with your most welcome counsel and with complete willingness, to grant this benefaction to that holy place. It shall be arranged in this manner: just as in the time of our lord and father the order of psalmody was established there in groups, or just as it is maintained day and night in the monastery of Saint Maurice at Agaune and of Saint Martin at Tours, so it shall be celebrated in that place throughout all future time.”

Thus, while all the princes of the kingdom listened carefully with astonished ears to the king addressing them, the bishops who were present, approving the king’s excellent devotion, confirmed the decree made by the king in the manner written above; and the king, the bishops, and the princes who were present all affixed their confirmation.

Among them were several bishops whom the holy Church today does not hesitate to regard as most holy, since the Lord continues to perform no small miracles at their venerable tombs: namely, blessed Audoenus and Saint Rado, his brother; blessed Palladius; Saint Clarus; lord Eligius; Saint Sulpicius; blessed Aubertus; lord Castadius; Saint Etherius; and many others, including the venerable Landeric, bishop of Paris, who willingly consented to and confirmed the aforesaid privilege.

### CHAPTER LI.—How he broke the bone of Saint Dionysius’s arm and, as a result, first lost his senses and afterward his life together with his kingdom

[Col. 1420D]

Thus King Hludowius, throughout all his days, possessed the kingship in his realm without wars. But once, driven by fortune, in the final years of his life he came to the bodies of the aforementioned martyrs, ostensibly for the sake of prayer. Wishing to have their relics with him, he ordered the tomb to be uncovered. When he saw the body of the blessed and most distinguished martyr and bishop Dionysius, he irreverently, though eagerly, broke and seized a bone of his arm. Immediately he was struck with terror and fell into madness.

Such terror, fear, and darkness filled the place that all who were present, overwhelmed by the greatest dread, sought safety in flight. Afterward, in order to recover his senses, he gave certain estates to that place. The bone that he had taken from the holy body he also adorned with gold and gems in wondrous workmanship and placed back there. [Col. 1422A] But although he recovered his senses to some small degree, he did not regain them completely; and after two years he ended his life together with his kingdom.

The Deeds of lord King Dagobert end happily.

[Col. 1421]

## VIII. DEEDS OF THE FRANKISH KINGS

Partly from the *History* of Gregory of Tours, whose name the most ancient manuscripts also bear, and partly taken from elsewhere, carried down as far as King Theodoric II; by an unknown author who lived in the time of that same Theodoric. (From Duchesne, *Writers of the Histories of the Franks*.)

[Note: [Col. 1421] The “Editio Freheri” and the “Codex Cameracensis” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

The edition of Marquard Freher, palatine councillor, collated with various manuscript codices belonging to the library of the most distinguished Alexander Petavius, senator of Paris, and also enlarged for the first time by an appendix extending as far as King Pippin. There is also added a comparison of these Deeds with another history by a writer who appears to be older, since he ends with Chramn, son of Chlothar I. From a very ancient manuscript exemplar of the church of Cambrai.

## DEEDS OF THE FRANKISH KINGS

From the edition of Marquard Freher.

### CHAPTER I.—On the origin and deeds of the Franks, and their successive struggles

[Col. 1421B]

Let us set forth the beginning and origin of the Frankish people, and the deeds of their kings. There is, then, in Asia a town of the Trojans, where there is a city called Ilium, in which King Aeneas reigned. That people was strong and powerful, its men warriors and exceedingly rebellious, provoking restless conflicts and waging war against the neighboring peoples all around.

The kings of the Greeks rose up against Aeneas, king of the Trojans, with a great army. They fought against him with great slaughter, and there the very large army of the Trojans was overthrown. King Aeneas fled and shut himself up in the city of Ilium. They fought against that city for ten years. Then, when the city itself had been conquered, King Aeneas fled with the rest of his men to Italy, in order to establish those peoples there so that they might bring him assistance.

But two of his leading men, Priam and Antenor, fled with twelve thousand other men from the Trojan army in ships. Entering the banks of the river Tanais, they sailed through the Maeotian marshes and reached the neighboring borders of Pannonia, occupying the territories beside the Maeotian marshes. They began to build a city as a memorial [Alternative: “in memory”] of themselves, and called it Sicambria. There they lived for many years and grew into a great people.

### CHAPTER II.—How the people of the Alans rebelled against the emperor Valentinian, how the Franks defeated them, and tribute was granted to the Franks

At that time the emperor Valentinian governed the Roman Empire. At that time the extremely savage people of the Alans rebelled against the aforesaid emperor. He therefore stirred up a great Roman army, drew up his battle line against them, overcame them, crushed them, and defeated them.

The Alans, struck down near the river Danube, fled and entered the Maeotian marshes. Then the emperor said: “If anyone can enter these marshes and drive out from them this rebellious people of the Alans, I will grant him tribute for ten years.”

Then the Franks, who had been expelled from Troy, gathered and set an ambush on the opposite side, as they had been instructed, through unknown hiding places. Entering the Maeotian marshes with the rest of the Roman army, they drove the Alans out and struck them down with the sword.

Then the emperor Valentinian called them “FRANKS” in the Attic language, which is translated into Latin as *feri*, that is, “fierce,” from the hardness or ferocity of their hearts.

### CHAPTER III.—How the emperor sent tax collectors so that the Franks might pay tribute

After ten years had passed, the emperor sent tax collectors, together with a chief commander from the Roman senate, to recover the tribute that had been omitted from the Frankish people.

But they, being exceedingly barbarous, adopted a treacherous and foolish plan and said among themselves: “The emperor, with the Roman army, was unable to drive the rebellious people of the Alans from their hiding place in the marshes. But we, who defeated them, why should we pay tribute? Let us rise up against this chief commander and these tax collectors, attack them, and refuse to pay tribute to the Romans, lest, if they subjugate us, we should never be free.”

Then they lay in ambush and killed them.

### CHAPTER IV.—How the same emperor stirred up an army against the Franks; their arrival in the regions of the Rhine; and their first king

When the emperor heard this, he was moved to great anger and ordered an army to be assembled against the Roman enemy. Adding the auxiliaries of many other peoples, together with Aristarсus, commander of the army, they drew up their battle line against the Franks.

There was a great slaughter on both sides. When the Franks saw that they could not withstand such a large army, they were heavily defeated and fled. Their leader Priam also fell there.

Having departed from Sicambria, they came to the farthest regions of the Rhine, in the towns of Germany, and settled there with their princes, Marchomir, son of Priam, and Sunno, son of Antenor. They lived there for many years.

When Sunno died, they took counsel and decided that, under one authority, they should have one leader. They asked Marchomir for advice, so that they might have a single king like the other peoples. He gave them his advice, and they chose Faramund, the son of Marchomir himself, and lifted him up as their long-haired king.

Then they also began to have a law, which their earlier pagan counselors, named Wisovast, Wisogast, Arogast, and Salegast, discussed in the villages of Germany, namely Bodecheim, Salecheim, and Widecheim [Alternative: “that is, Salegagme in Bothagam and Wisogagme in Wilegam”].

### CHAPTER V.—On the death of King Pharamund, his son Chlodio, and the invasion of Gaul by the Huns

When Faramund had died, they raised his long-haired son Chlodio to his father’s kingship. At that time they first elevated long-haired kings.

Proceeding cautiously to the borders of the Thuringians, they settled there. King Chlodio lived in the fortress of Dispargum, in the territory of the Thuringians, in the region of Germany.

For this reason all the regions of the peoples beyond the river Rhine are called by the name “Germany,” because in Germany there are extremely savage bodies, a most ferocious, harsh, and violent race, and peoples always untamed and exceedingly fierce. Scripture reports that they consisted of one hundred districts.

At that time, in these regions on this side of the Rhine as far as the river Loire, Romans lived; beyond the Loire, the Goths ruled. The Burgundians, who were Arians, also lived beside the river Rhône, which flows past the city of Lyon.

King Chlodio sent scouts from the fortress of Dispargum among the Thuringians as far as the city of Cambrai. He later crossed the Rhine with a large army and, after overthrowing a large number of the Roman people, put the enemy to flight. Entering the Carbonaria Forest, he took the city of Tournai. From there he hastened to the city of Cambrai. After remaining there for a short time, he killed the Romans whom he found there. From there he occupied everything as far as the river Somme.

When King Chlodio died, Meroveus was raised to the kingship. Chlodio had reigned for twenty years. From Meroveus, that worthy king who was elevated to the kingship of the Franks, the Frankish kings were famously called Merovingians. Meroveus himself fathered a son named Childeric, the father of the most exalted King Chlodoveus.

At that time the Franks were still fanatical, worshiping idols and images rather than the Lord of heaven and earth, who had created them.

At that time in this part of Gaul there was Egidius, a Roman commander, sent by the emperor (Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapter 10).

### CHAPTER VI.—How King Childeric was expelled from the kingdom

King Childeric, son of Meroveus, as we have said, was exceedingly lustful. While he ruled over the Franks, he began to debauch their daughters and violate them by force. The Franks, greatly angered by this, wanted to kill him and expel him from the kingdom.

When he heard of this, he went to Thuringia and summoned his friend and counselor, named Wiomad. He sought his advice concerning how he might calm the rage of the furious Franks. They agreed upon a sign by which he could know with certainty whether they might at some time return to peace, and by which they could recognize one another.

They then divided one gold coin between them as a sign. King Childeric carried one half with him, while Wiomad kept the other half, saying: “When I send this other half to you, know that I have reconciled the Franks to you; then return safely in peace.”

Childeric therefore went to Thuringia, to King Bisinus and his wife Basina, and hid there.

### CHAPTER VII.—How the Franks set up the Roman Egidius over themselves, then deposed him and received Childeric

The Franks, having abandoned Childeric, raised Egidius, a Roman leader, over themselves as king—a bad, extremely foolish, and absurd decision.

After he had ruled over them for eight years, Wiomad, his counselor, pretended to enter into a close bond of friendship with him and urged Egidius deceitfully to oppress certain Franks. Egidius listened to his advice and tried craftily to oppress them.

Fearing this, the Franks, overcome by great fury, sought advice from Wiomad about what they should do. He said to them:

“Do you not remember how the Romans, by oppressing your people, drove them from their own land? You also expelled your useful and vigorous king and set over yourselves this soldier of the Roman emperor, cruel, arrogant, and proud. You did this without counsel; you acted badly, not well.”

They replied: “Because he abused our daughters without restraint. We regret having acted against our king. If only we might deserve to find him and have him reign over us in peace!”

Then that friend of the king sent the half of the solidus which they had previously divided between them, saying: “Return to the Frankish kingdom, because everything has been pacified.”

Recognizing this sign, the golden half, Childeric understood with certainty that he was desired by the Franks. At their request, he returned to his kingdom. While he had been in Thuringia, King Childeric had slept with Basina, the queen and wife of King Bisinus. Returning to the Franks, he was restored to his kingdom.

They expelled Egidius, the Roman leader, from their kingdom. Basina, that queen, the wife of Bisinus, king of the Thuringians, abandoned her husband and came to Childeric.

When he asked her what she wanted, or for what reason she had come to him from such a distant region, she is said to have replied:

“I know your worth and your beauty, and that you are capable and vigorous; therefore I have come to live with you. Indeed, if I had known of someone more worthy than you at the farthest ends of the sea, I would have sought him out and lived with him.”

He rejoiced and took her as his wife. Afterward she conceived by him and gave birth to a son, whom she named Chlodoveus. He became a great king above all the kings of the Franks, an exceptionally warlike and outstanding fighter.

### CHAPTER VIII.—How the city of Agrippina was captured, concerning the death of Egidius, and concerning Adouagrius, leader of the Saxons

In those days the Franks captured the city of Agrippina on the Rhine and called it Cologne. There they killed a great many Romans who belonged to the faction of Egidius.

Egidius then escaped by flight. They came to the city of Trier on the river Moselle, ravaging those lands and burning and capturing the city itself. For it had previously been shattered and afflicted by the Huns.

At that time Egidius, the Roman leader and tyrant, died. His son Syagrius succeeded to his rule and lived in the city of Soissons, where he also maintained the seat of his kingdom.

Then King Childeric, having raised a large army, marched against the enemy as far as the city of Orléans and also ravaged those lands.

Adouagrius [Odouacrius], leader of the Saxons, came with a naval force to the city of Angers and at that time devastated the people with great slaughter. Adouagrius therefore took hostages from Angers and from other cities.

When Adouagrius was returning from Angers, King Childeric arrived there with the Frankish army. After killing Count Paul, who was in command of that city, he captured the city itself and burned with fire the house [church] that was in it.

### CHAPTER IX.—On the death of Childeric and Chlodoveus’s war against Syagrius

(Gregory, Book II, chapter 27.)

At that time King Childeric of the Franks died; he had reigned for twenty-four years. His son Chlodoveus then astutely assumed the Frankish kingdom.

In the fifth year of Chlodoveus’s reign, Syagrius, son of Egidius and king of the Romans, was residing in the city of Soissons, which his father had held. Chlodoveus came against him with his kinsman Ranacarius [Alternative: Ragneharius] and an army.

They met in battle and fought one another fiercely. When Syagrius saw that his army had been defeated, he fled and sought refuge with Alaric, king of the Goths, at Toulouse.

Chlodoveus sent messengers to Alaric, ordering him to hand over Syagrius; if he did not wish to hand him over, he was to prepare for battle. Fearing the anger of the Franks, he handed Syagrius over to Chlodoveus’s messengers.

When Syagrius had been presented to Chlodoveus, Chlodoveus ordered him to be killed. He took his entire kingdom and treasures under his own authority.

### CHAPTER X.—The bishop’s petition to King Chlodoveus that he return a vessel, and how the conquered Thuringians served under tribute

[Col. 1429A]

At that time many churches were plundered by Chlodoveus’s army, for he was then a fanatic and a pagan.

From one church his army had taken a beautifully made vessel of remarkable size [Alternative: “a small vessel”], together with the church’s furnishings and many ornaments. The bishop of that church sent messengers to the king, begging that, if he did not deserve to receive anything else from the church’s sacred vessels, he should at least order that vessel to be returned.

When the king heard this, he said to the ecclesiastical messengers: “Follow us to the city of Soissons, because there all the things that have been acquired will be divided. If that vessel falls to me as my share, we shall fulfill what the bishop requests.”

When the king came to the city of Soissons, he requested that all the captured booty be brought into the midst, saying: “I ask you, bravest warriors, not to refuse to give me this vessel.”

When the king had said this, those Franks who were well disposed said to him: “Glorious king, everything you see is yours, and we are subject to your authority. Do whatever seems good to you. No one dares resist your power.”

After they had said this kindly, one light-minded Frank, with a loud shout, raised his battle-axe, which is called a *francisca*, and struck the vessel, saying: “You shall receive nothing from here, king, except what true lot has given you.”

When everyone was struck with astonishment, the king patiently endured the insult. He took the vessel and returned it to the ecclesiastical messenger, while concealing his anger in his heart.

A year later, King Chlodoveus ordered his entire army to come equipped with arms, intending to display in the Field of Mars the brilliance of all their weapons and to inspect them. When the king had gone around the entire army, he came to the man who had previously struck the vessel and said to him:

“No one has a weapon as neglected and filthy as yours, for neither your shield, spear, nor battle-axe is serviceable.”

The king took his battle-axe, that is, his double-bladed axe, and threw it to the ground. When the man bent down to pick it up, the king immediately raised his own battle-axe with both hands and buried it in the man’s head, saying: “That is what you did to the vessel in the city of Soissons the previous year.”

After the man had died, the king ordered the rest of the army to withdraw peacefully from that field to their homes. From then on, great panic and fear arose among the Frankish people because of this incident.

In the tenth year of his reign, Chlodoveus then marched into Thuringia with a very large army and struck down the Thuringians with a great blow. After defeating that people and ravaging their entire land, he made the Thuringians tributaries of the Franks.

### CHAPTER XI.—How Aurelianus, Chlodoveus’s envoy, dressed in foreign garb, arranged Chrodchilde for his lord

(Gregory, Book II, chapter 28.)

At that time Gundeveus, king of the Burgundians, who is said to have been descended from King Athanaric, reigned. He had four sons: Gundobad, Godegisel, Chilperic, and Godomar.

Gundobad therefore killed his brother Chilperic with the sword and ordered his wife to be drowned after a stone had been tied around her neck. Of her two daughters, one was called Chrona; he condemned her to exile after changing her clothing, while he kept the younger, named Chrothilde [Alternatives: Chrodilde and Chrochilde], in the house.

Since Chlodoveus frequently sent embassies to Burgundy, the envoys found the girl Chrothildis there. When they saw that she was beautiful, elegant, and wise, they reported this to Chlodoveus.

On hearing it, he again sent an embassy to Gundobad, his own envoy Aurelianus, asking him to give him his niece Chrothilde. Chrothildis was a Christian.

One Sunday, when Chrothildis had come to the solemn celebration of Mass, Aurelianus, Chlodoveus’s envoy, took poor clothing. He left the fine garments that he had brought with him [Alternative: “in which he had been dressed”] with his companions in the woods, and sat among the poor in front of the church’s alms-house.

When the celebration of Mass had ended, Chrothildis, according to her usual custom, began distributing alms to the poor. When she came to Aurelianus, who was pretending to be poor, she placed a gold coin in his hand. He kissed the girl’s hand and carefully drew back her cloak.

Afterward she entered her chamber and sent her maidservant to summon that stranger. He held in his hand a ring from King Chlodoveus and also kept the other hidden betrothal ornaments in his bag. When he departed, he secretly left the bag in a place behind the door of the chamber.

Chrothildis said to him: “Tell me, young man, why are you pretending to be poor, and for what reason did you draw back my cloak?”

He replied: “I beg you, let your servant speak with you in private.”

She said: “Speak.”

He began: “My lord, Chlodoveus, king of the Franks, sent me to you. He wishes to take you as his queen. Here is his ring and the other betrothal ornaments.”

He looked back behind the door of the chamber, but did not find his bag. Terrified by this, he began to fear.

She, for her part, anxiously searched everywhere, saying: “Who has taken this poor man’s bag?” Immediately it was produced. When it was opened, she took out the hidden betrothal ornaments.

She accepted the ring that King Chlodoveus had sent through Aurelianus and placed it in the treasury of her uncle. She asked Chlodoveus’s health to be conveyed to him and ordered the following message to be delivered:

“A Christian woman may not marry a pagan. See to it that no one learns of this matter. But let it happen as the Lord my God, whom I confess before everyone, wills. Go now in peace.”

He returned and reported these things to his lord.

### CHAPTER XII.—How King Chlodoveus sent to Gundobad for his bride Chrodchilde

In the following year Chlodoveus sent his envoy Aurelianus to Gundobad for his bride Chrothilde.

When Gundobad heard this, he was terrified in his heart and said: “Let all my most valiant Burgundian counselors and friends know what opportunity King Chlodoveus is seeking against us, since he has never known my niece.”

He said to Aurelianus: “You have come to spy out our houses under the pretext of seeking [or asking for] her. Report to your lord that he has spoken falsely in vain by claiming to have my niece as his bride.”

Aurelianus, however, spoke firmly to him, saying: “My lord, King Chlodoveus, sends you this message: If you wish to give him his bride, prepare for him a designated place wherever you wish, so that he may receive his bride Chrothilde. But if you do not wish to do so, he intends to come against you with the Frankish army.”

Gundobad replied: “Let him come wherever he wishes; I too intend to go against him with a great Burgundian army, so that he may depart in ruin toward destruction for what he has perpetrated before many peoples, and so that the blood of many who have been shed by your hands may be avenged.”

When the Burgundians who were his counselors heard this, they greatly feared the anger of the Franks and of Chlodoveus. They gave Gundobad this advice:

“Let the king inquire of his public servants and chamberlains whether gifts were ever conveyed by the stratagem of King Chlodoveus’s envoys [Alternative: ‘carried away and brought’]. Thus no pretext may be found against your people and your kingdom, and you may be able to defeat him in victory, since Chlodoveus’s wickedness is exceedingly furious.”

As was customary, the Burgundians gave this advice to their king. When they searched, they found in the king’s treasury a ring bearing the inscription or image of Chlodoveus [Alternatives: “marked” and “engraved”].

Then King Gundobad, greatly grieved, ordered the girl to be questioned about the matter.

She said: “I know, my lord king, that some years ago small golden gifts were brought to you as presents by Chlodoveus’s messengers, and that a small ring was placed in the hand of me, your maidservant. I myself put it away in your treasury.”

He said: “This was done simply and without counsel.”

In anger, he took her and handed her over to Aurelianus, Chlodoveus’s envoy.

Aurelianus and his companions received Chrothilde with great joy and gladness and brought her to Chlodoveus in the city of Soissons in Francia. King Chlodoveus rejoiced and took her as his wife.

When evening came, the time when they were to recline together according to the marriage custom, she, following the practice of her wisdom and trusting in the Lord, said:

“From now on, my lord king, listen to your maidservant speaking, and deign to grant what I ask before your servant joins your lordship.”

The king said: “Ask whatever you wish, and I will grant it to you.”

She asked:

“First, I ask that you believe in God the Father almighty of heaven, who created you.

“Second, confess the Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, who redeemed you, the King of all kings, sent by the Father from heaven.

“Third, confess the Holy Spirit, confirmer and enlightener of all the righteous.

“Recognize the entire ineffable majesty and coeternal omnipotence, believe what you have recognized, and abandon the empty idols, which are not gods but vain carved images; burn them, and restore the holy churches that you have burned.

“Moreover, remember, I beg you, that you must seek the portion belonging to my father and mother, whom my uncle Gundobad unjustly killed. Thus may the Lord avenge their blood.”

Chlodoveus said: “One difficult thing remains in what you ask: that I abandon my gods and worship your God. As for the other thing you request, I shall do it as I am able.”

But she pressed her request again and, supplicating him once more, said:

“This above all I beg: worship the Lord God almighty, who is in heaven.”

### CHAPTER XIII.—How Chlodoveus again sent to Gundobad for Chrodchilde’s treasure

Chlodoveus again sent Aurelianus to Gundobad in Burgundy for the treasure of his queen Chrothilde.

Gundobad, moved to anger, said: “Shall my kingdom or my treasures be handed over to Chlodoveus? Did I not warn you, Aurelianus, not to come again to my kingdom to spy out my property? By the safety of the princes I warn you, and I promise under oath: return quickly and leave me. Otherwise I shall kill you.”

Aurelianus replied:

“My lord King Chlodoveus lives, as do the leading men of the courageous Franks in his kingdom [and the Franks who are with him], and I do not fear your threats so long as my lord is alive. Thus your own son [Alternative: ‘kinsman’], my lord King Chlodoveus, commands you: he will meet you with his army for the treasure of his wife, my lady.”

The Burgundians, as was customary, gave counsel to their king Gundobad and said:

“Give your niece something from the portion of her treasure that falls to her, because this is judged to be just. Have a treaty and peace with Chlodoveus and the Frankish people, lest they fall upon our land, for that people is extremely fierce [Alternative: ‘strong and fierce’], existing without God.”

Gundobad heard their advice and, through the hands of Aurelianus, gave to Chlodoveus’s side the greatest part of his treasure. He sent his niece Queen Chrothilde the most precious furnishings.

He also handed over much gold and silver and the most beautiful works to the envoy, saying: “What remains except that I divide my whole kingdom with Chlodoveus?”

He said to Aurelianus: “Return to your lord, because you have what you can bring him—many gifts for which you have not labored.”

Aurelianus replied: “Your son, King Chlodoveus, is my lord; everything that is yours will be held in common.”

The wise men of the Burgundians said: “Long live the king who has such *leudes* [Alternative: *leodi*—retainers or dependents].”

Aurelianus returned with many treasures to his lord in Francia.

At that time King Chlodoveus had a son by a concubine named Theuderic.

### CHAPTER XIV.—Chrodchildis’s preaching to Chlodoveus, urging him to believe in the King of kings

In those days Chlodoveus extended and enlarged his kingdom as far as the Seine. Later he occupied territory as far as the river Loire.

Aurelianus took the fortress of the people of Melun and received it as a duchy.

Chrothildis conceived and gave birth to a son whom she wished to consecrate in baptism. At that time Chlodoveus did not believe in the Lord God of heaven. The queen preached to him every day, but he did not wish to listen to her.

Meanwhile the queen prepared her son for baptism and adorned the church with veils and curtains, in case she might somehow pierce the king’s heart and move him to believe [Alternative version: “The queen, attempting the same thing, prepared everything that seemed necessary for baptism and secretly presented her veiled and swaddled son to be baptized, so that the king’s mind might be more effectively pierced and moved to believe.”]

The boy was baptized, and she named him Ingomir while he was clothed in the white baptismal garment; he died in that same garment.

The king was deeply saddened by his death and, rebuking her, said: “If the boy had been dedicated in the name of my gods, he would certainly have lived. Because he was baptized in the name of your God, he could not live.”

The queen replied: “I give thanks to God because he did not deem me unworthy, but deigned to receive my firstborn from my womb into his kingdom. I retain no grief in my heart on this account.”

Afterward she gave birth to another son, whom she named Chlodomir after he was baptized. When he began to fall ill, the king said:

“It can only be that the same thing will happen to this boy as happened to his brother, so that, baptized in the name of your God, he will soon die.”

But when the queen prayed, and the Lord’s mercy went before him, he recovered his health.

The queen also did not cease preaching to the king that he should worship the true God and abandon the empty idols that he worshiped. Yet she could in no way move his mind to belief, until at last he undertook war against the Alamans and the Suebi, in which he was compelled to confess the one whom he had previously denied.

## CHAPTER XV — The War against the Alamanni, in which Chlodoveus, compelled by necessity, invokes the true God for aid and is baptized by Saint Remedius

When the armies of the Franks and the Alamanni were fighting one another, Chlodoveus’s army began to suffer very heavily. Aurilianus, looking at the king, said: “My lord king, believe only in the Lord of heaven, whom my lady Queen Chrothildis proclaims.”

Then, raising his eyes to heaven and moved to tears, he said: “Jesus Christ, whom my queen Chrothildis proclaims to be the Son of the living God, who comes to the aid of those in tribulation and gives help to those who hope in you, I devoutly ask for your assistance: if you grant me victory over these enemies, and I experience that power which the peoples proclaim concerning you, I will believe in you and be baptized in your name. For I have invoked my gods, and, as I now discover, they have withdrawn from my aid. Therefore I believe that they possess no power, since when invoked by those who believe in them they do not come to their assistance. I invoke you as the true God and Lord, and I desire to believe in you—only deliver me from my adversaries.”

While he was crying out these prayers, the Alamanni fled and turned their backs. When they saw that their king had been killed, they submitted themselves to Chlodoveus’s power, saying: “Spare us, we beg you, lord king, lest more of the people perish, [Col. 1435B] for we are now yours.”

Then the king ordered the impending slaughter to cease. He captured the Alamanni and made them and their land tributary under his yoke. After winning the victory, he returned to Francia to his queen and told her how, through invoking the name of Jesus Christ, he had been deemed worthy to obtain victory.

These things took place in the fifteenth year of Chlodoveus’s reign. Then the queen secretly summoned Saint Remedius [Remigius], bishop of the city of Rheims, asking him to show the king the way of salvation by preaching to him.

The blessed bishop summoned the king to baptism and asked his permission to speak with him. The king said to him: “I will gladly listen to you, most blessed Father. But one matter remains: the people who follow me do not wish to abandon their gods. I will go and exhort them according to your word.”

Accordingly, the king went to the people and began to exhort them. But, with the mercy of God going before them and by his power, all the Frankish people acclaimed him, saying resolutely: “[Col. 1436A] We now abandon mortal gods, glorious king, and are ready to worship and believe in the true and immortal God whom Remedius proclaims.”

They reported this to Saint Remedius. He, filled with great joy, ordered the baptismal font to be prepared. The streets were shaded by curtains painted with divine histories; churches were being constructed; the baptistery was being arranged; balsam and other fragrances filled the air. For the Lord supplied such grace among the people that they thought themselves filled with the perfumes of paradise.

The king therefore first asked Saint Remedius to baptize him. The new Constantine came to baptism, having renounced the devil and his pomp (Gregory, Book II, chapter 31). When he entered for baptism, the holy man of God addressed the king in eloquent speech:

“Bend your neck humbly, Sicamber; adore what you have burned, and burn what you have adored.” [Col. 1436B]

Saint Remedius was a wise and exceedingly holy man, an outstanding rhetorician, distinguished in virtues: he restored sight to the blind, restored life to the dead, and expelled demons.

Accordingly, the king confessed almighty God in the Trinity and was baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He was then anointed with sacred chrism, with the sign of the holy cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

More than three thousand men from his army were baptized. His sisters, Alboflidis and Landehildis, were baptized on the same day. Afterwards the entire Frankish people were baptized with glory.

## CHAPTER XVI — How the Burgundians, defeated by Chlodoveus, submitted themselves to his dominion; and concerning the devouring of human beings by wild beasts

[Col. 1436C]

(Gregory, Book II, chapter 32.) After this, Chlodoveus marched against Gundobad [Gundebaud] and his brother Godeghisel, having raised a large Frankish army. When they heard this, they assembled a very large Burgundian army. They came to the fortress of Dijon on the river Ouche [variant: Oscara], and there Chlodoveus, Gundobad, and Godeghisel fought one another with great ferocity. The Burgundians turned their backs. Chlodoveus, as usual, proved victorious.

When the Burgundian army had been shattered, Gundobad and Godeghisel fled and barely escaped. Gundobad entered the city of Avignon on the Rhône and shut himself inside it. King Chlodoveus pursued him there and laid siege to the city. Since the Franks could not break into the city itself, they devastated the region severely.

Gundobad therefore sent his wise counsellor, named Aredius, to calm the anger of the furious King Chlodoveus by his excellent counsel. They gave him countless gifts, great quantities of gold and silver, and subjected themselves to Chlodoveus’s tribute. King Chlodoveus, having taken the treasures and a very great amount of booty, returned victorious with the Frankish army.

At this time there was a very great earthquake in the city of Vienne, where many churches and the houses of many people were shaken and overturned. Many wild beasts—wolves, bears, and deer—wandered there. Entering through the city gate, they devoured very many people. They did this throughout the entire year. (Gregory, Book II, chapter 34.)

When the solemn day of the holy feast of Easter arrived, Saint Mamertus, who was bishop in that city, was celebrating the solemn Mass [variant: sacrifices] during the vigil. The royal palace in the city was also set on fire by divine flame. As these things were taking place and the Ascension of the Lord was approaching, the holy man of God proclaimed a three-day fast among the people, with groaning and contrition of spirit. He established an order of prayer, a schedule of eating, and a cheerful distribution of alms.

Then [variant: “and with contrition of spirit these things were always celebrated in those times. Then”] that tribulation and destruction ceased. From then onward, all the churches of God and priests, imitating this example, have been known to celebrate these three-day litanies everywhere down to the present.

## CHAPTER XVII — Concerning the miracles of God shown to Chlodoveus, and how, after defeating the Goths, he killed Alaric

(Gregory, Book II, chapter 37.) In those days, when King Chlodoveus had come to the city of Paris, he said to the queen and to his people: “It greatly troubles me [variant: ‘it seems harsh’] that the Arian Goths hold the best part of Gaul. Let us go with God’s help and drive them from that land, subjecting it to our rule, because it is exceedingly good.”

This plan pleased the Frankish nobles. Then Queen Chrothildis gave the king this counsel: “By his deeds, the Lord God,” she said, “will grant victory into the hands of my lord the king. But listen to your servant, and let us build a church in honor of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that he may be your helper in war.”

The king replied: “I approve what you advise; let us do so.”

Then the king threw his battle-axe, called a francisca, straight before him and said: “Let the church of the blessed apostles be built when we return with God’s help.”

The king then mobilized his entire army, the Frankish people, and directed them toward Poitiers. At that time King Alaric of the Goths was staying there.

When a large part of the enemy army was passing through the territory of Tours [variant: Torinicum], the king ordered, out of reverence for Saint Martin, that they take nothing except grass to sustain their horses. The king therefore sent messengers to the basilica of blessed Martin with many gifts and his swiftest horse, which he loved greatly, and said: “Go, and perhaps you will receive something from the holy discourse of the sacred Scriptures as an indication of victory.”

After the gifts had been presented, the messenger said: “If you are my helper, O God, and if you will deliver this unbelieving people into my hands, deign, Saint Martin, at the entrance to your basilica, to reveal to me whether you are favorable to me, your servant, so that I may know.”

When the servants arrived at the church of blessed Martin and had entered [variant: reached] the threshold, the church’s first cantor began this antiphon:

“You have girded me, Lord, for battle, and have placed those rising against me beneath my feet; you have given me the backs of my enemies, and you have destroyed those who hate me.”

When they heard this psalmody, they gave thanks to the Lord, left the king’s horse there along with many other gifts, and joyfully and exultantly reported the matter to the king.

When the king came with his army to the river Vienne, he could not find the place where he ought to ford it, for it had overflowed because of the abundance of rain. He begged the Lord to show him a ford and remained there that night.

At dawn, by God’s will [variant: nod], a hind of marvelous size went before them and showed them the ford. When it had crossed, the people also followed and crossed.

When the king came to the city of Poitiers, he pitched his tents at some distance from the church of Saint Hilary. That night a fiery beacon [variant: fiery object] was seen to come forth from the church. It appeared above the tents to aid King Chlodoveus, through the power of blessed Hilary.

The king therefore ordered his army not to take from that district either food or any supplies, nor even booty.

King Chlodoveus met Alaric, king of the Goths, on the plain of Vogladis [variant: Vocladinense], on the river Clain, ten miles from the city of Poitiers. When they fought one another, the Goths, suffering a severe defeat with their king, turned their backs, and King Chlodoveus, as usual, proved victorious.

As he was killing Alaric, two Goths struck him from the front in the side with spears. But because of the coat of mail he was wearing, they did not bruise him [variant: did him no harm]. The Lord was helping him in everything he undertook.

At that time a very large number of Arverni, who had come with their leader Apollinaris, fell beneath the Frankish sword, together with many senators.

Amalric, Alaric’s son, escaped from this battle by flight and skillfully recovered his father’s kingdom in Spain. Chlodoveus sent his son Theuderic through the cities of Albia and Rodez toward the Arverni. Advancing, he subjected all those cities, from the borders of the Goths to Burgundy, and restored them to his father’s power.

Alaric reigned for twelve years. Chlodoveus also remained for the entire winter at the city of Bordeaux [variant: Burdalense]. He took very many treasures belonging to King Alaric from Toulouse. After taking all those cities, he came to the city of Ecolosina, and God granted it such favor at his arrival that its walls collapsed completely.

After killing the Goths who were there, he seized the city itself. Having thus subjected all their land, he ordered Franks to remain in Saintonge [variant: Santoneum] and Bordeaux, to defend the Gothic people (Gregory, Book II, chapter 38).

Then he returned to the city of Tours and gave many gifts to the basilica of blessed Martin. The horse that he had previously sent to that church was given to its sacristans. He sent one hundred solidi for the horse, so that he might receive it back. When the money had been given, the horse would not move at all.

Then he said: “Give them another hundred solidi.” When the additional solidi had been given, the horse immediately moved freely away.

The king then said joyfully: “Truly blessed Martin is good in assistance, but expensive in business.”

At that time King Chlodoveus received from the Emperor Anastasius letters appointing him consul. Dressed in a purple tunic, with a golden crown on his head, the king mounted his horse in the basilica of blessed Martin. In the courtyard between the city and the church of blessed Martin, in the presence of the people, he scattered [variant: distributed] gold and silver with his own hand and dispensed it with the greatest generosity.

From that day he was called both consul and Augustus. Leaving Tours, he came to the city of Paris and established there the seat of his kingdom.

## CHAPTER XVIII — The war of Chlodoveus against his kinsman Ragnacharius

[Col. 1440B]

(Gregory, Book II, chapter 42.) After this he took up arms against his kinsman Ragnacharius [variants: Ragneharius and Regnaharius]. Ragnacharius was at the city of Cambrai, unrestrained in luxury. He also had a counsellor named Faro, equally sullied and mired in filth.

Whenever a gift or some food was brought to him, he would say: “Let these be for me and for my counsellor Faro.”

For this reason the Franks who were with him became indignant and consented to Chlodoveus, urging him against Ragnacharius. Chlodoveus gave them payment for this purpose: golden belts and armlets, but inside they were made of bronze and copper [variant: brass] covered with gold. They had been deceitfully made as a gift for Ragnacharius’s retainers, so that they might induce him to attack Chlodoveus.

When Chlodoveus had mobilized his army against his kinsman Ragnacharius, Ragnacharius sent scouts to find out whose army was stronger. When questioned, they answered falsely: “Your army and that of your counsellor Faro are stronger.”

Chlodoveus and Ragnacharius then came to battle and fought one another fiercely. When Ragnacharius saw that his army had been defeated, he tried to flee. But the very traitors seized him, bound his hands behind his back, and presented him, together with his brother Richarius, to Chlodoveus.

Chlodoveus said to him: “Why have you humiliated our people by allowing yourself to be bound? Would it not have been better for you to die?”

He raised his battle-axe, drove it into Ragnacharius’s head, and he died.

Turning to Ragnacharius’s brother, he said: “If you had given your brother assistance, he would not have been bound.” He likewise struck him in the head and killed him, and he died.

After their deaths, the traitors discovered that the gold they had received from Chlodoveus was debased, and they reported this to the king. The king replied: “Such gold is deserved by one who betrays his lord to death. Let it be enough for you merely to be granted your lives, lest you perish amid torments.”

When they heard this, they desired only to retain grace and life, saying that this would be sufficient for them.

Ragnacharius had the following relatives: his brother Regnemirus [variant: Rignemiris], who was killed at the city of Le Mans by order of King Chlodoveus.

When these men had died or been killed, Chlodoveus took possession of their entire kingdom and treasures. After killing many great kings and his own relatives, King Chlodoveus subsequently died in peace and was buried in the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter, which he and his queen had built (Gregory, Book II, chapter 43).

He died in the fifth year after he fought Alaric, king of the Goths. He reigned for thirty years in all. From the death of Saint Martin to the death of King Chlodoveus there were 112 years.

Queen Chrothildis, after her husband’s death, frequently went to the city of Tours, remained for a very long time at the basilica of blessed Martin, and served the Lord; she seldom visited Paris.

## CHAPTER XIX — The death of Chlodoveus, the succession of his four sons to the kingdom, and the invasion of Gaul by the Danes

[Col. 1441B]

(Gregory, Book III, chapters 1–3.) After the death of her husband, King Chlodoveus, his four sons—Theuderic, Chlodomir, Childebert, and Chlotarius—divided his kingdom equally.

At that time Theuderic also had a son named Theudobert, vigorous and capable. They rose to great power.

Amalric, son of Alaric, king of the Goths, asked for their sister in marriage. They did not refuse him; they sent her with excellent ornaments, and he took her as his wife.

At that time the Danes, with their king named Chochilago [variants: Chohilaicus and Cochilag], attacked Gaul with a naval army across the open sea. They devastated the pagus of the Attoarii and other districts belonging to Theuderic, took captives, and filled their ships with prisoners. Entering the open sea, their king remained on the seashore [variant: “They filled their ships with booty and a multitude of captives; cutting across the open sea, they drove their ships forward, while their king with his army sat on the seashore”].

When this was reported to Theuderic, he sent his son Theudobert with a large army to those regions. Overtaking the Danes, Theudobert fought them with great slaughter, killed their king after defeating them, took the booty, and restored it to his own land.

## CHAPTER XX — How Chlodomir, Childebert, and Chlodarius began war against the Burgundians

(Gregory, Book III, chapters 6 and 3.) In those days, when Queen Chrothildis had come to Paris, she said to her sons: “I do not regret, my sons, that I raised you tenderly. Therefore, I beg you, be angered by my injury and avenge the death of my father and mother.”

When they heard this, they were stirred to great anger. With a very large army they marched into Burgundy against the kings Sismund and Godomar [variants: Sigismund and Gotmar], the sons of Gundobad.

At that time King Sismund was building in Burgundy the monastery of the holy martyrs of Agaunum—namely, of Saint Maurice and his companions, numbering 6,600.

The Burgundians, however, raised an army against King Chlodomir and his brothers Childebert and Chlotarius, the sons of Chlodoveus. When they fought one another, the Burgundians were defeated and fled with Godomar.

Sismund, while fleeing toward the saints of Agaunum, was overtaken by Chlodomir. Chlodomir seized him with his wife and children, brought them as captives to the district of Orléans, and ordered them to be thrown into prison.

The blessed Avitus, then a holy man and abbot in the city of Orléans, pleaded with Chlodomir [Chlodomer] not to kill them. But Chlodomir would not listen to him.

Then he killed Sismund, his wife, and his children, and threw them into a well at a place called Columna in the village.

## CHAPTER XXI — How Chlodomir again defeated the Burgundians and was killed

After this Chlodomir once more mobilized his army and marched into Burgundy against Godomar [variant: Gaismar]. When he had come with a large army to the district of Vienne, at a place called Visoroncia [Visroncia], Godomar deployed his people and fought Chlodomir.

The Burgundians, suffering a severe defeat with Godomar, fled. When Chlodomir pursued them, he rushed too far ahead. Overtaking them on an exceptionally swift horse, he entered into their midst.

But he was struck from the opposite side, fell, and died.

When the Franks saw this, they were moved by immense grief and anger. They pursued Godomar and destroyed him, killed the Burgundians, devastated all the regions, and slaughtered everyone from child to old man. Then they returned.

When Chlotarius heard this, he took his brother’s wife, named Gundeuca, in marriage.

Queen Chrothildis was raising Chlodomir’s orphaned sons—Theudoaldus, Guntharius, and Chlodoaldus—keeping them with her.

## CHAPTER XXII — The great slaughter in which the Franks defeated the Thuringians, and concerning their king Ermenfred

(Gregory, Book III, chapter 7.) At that time Theuderic, his son Theudobert [variant: Theutbert], and King Chlotarius crossed the Rhine with the Frankish army and marched into Thuringia against Ermenfred, king of the Thuringians.

When the Thuringians heard this, they dug ditches by deceit and covered them above with sods. When the armies came together there for battle, the Franks realized that their horses had fallen into the ditches and became very angry.

Ermenfred fled with the Thuringians as far as the river Unstrut, and the Franks pursued him there. But after recovering their strength, the Thuringians resisted the Franks.

There was such slaughter of the Thuringians there [Col. 1442D] that the river itself was filled with their corpses. The Franks crossed over them and trampled them as though over a bridge. They devastated that entire region, carried away captives, and plundered everything.

Ermenfred barely escaped by flight. The Franks returned with much booty and plunder.

Ermenfred had two brothers, Balderic and Bertecharius [variants: Berecarius and Bertarius].

(Gregory, Book III, chapter 8.) After this, Theuderic, having given his word to King Ermenfred, had him come to him at the city of Tolbiac. While they were conversing on the city wall, Ermenfred was pushed from the wall, fell to the ground, and died. Theuderic asked [variant: ordered] that his children be killed.

## CHAPTER XXIII — The war waged by Childebert against the Goths, and the killing of Amalric

[Col. 1443A]

(Gregory, Book III, chapter 10.) Childebert was staying in the city of Clermont. His sister, the wife of Amalric, king of the Goths—the girl’s name was Queen Clothildis [variant: Chlodchildis]—sent messengers to him from Spain, saying how many evils Amalric had inflicted upon her and how he plotted against her on account of the Catholic faith.

For when she went to the church of Christ to pray, he would throw dung and many foul substances upon her, and he beat her so severely that she vomited blood. She collected the blood in her handkerchief and sent it to her brother, saying: “Avenge [variant: Vindicate], dearest brother, my suffering and injury, my most beloved lord.”

When King Childebert heard this, he was moved to great anger, gathered a very large army, marched into Spain, and entered battle with Amalric.

The Goths were severely defeated [variant: struck down], and Amalric turned to flight and prepared ships for escape. As he tried to reach the ships, Childebert’s army pursued him.
