Seeing that he was defeated, Amalric tried to flee to a Christian church. But before he reached the entrance to the church, a certain Frank struck him with a lance, and he died there.

Childebert then ravaged Spain and entered the city of Toledo, from which he took great treasures. He returned together with his sister. But, from some danger threatening her, she died of illness during the journey. She was carried to Paris and buried in the basilica of Saint Peter beside her father.

Among the remaining treasures, Childebert brought ecclesiastical vessels: from the vessels of Solomon, sixty most precious chalices, fifteen dishes, and twenty Gospel chests of purest gold, embossed and decorated with jeweled work.

He did not wish to break them up, but distributed and dispensed everything among the churches.

## CHAPTER XXIV — Childebert and Chlodtharius, after devising an impious plan, kill their nephews and seize their father’s kingdom

(Gregory, Book III, chapter 18.) In those days Queen Chrothildis was residing in Paris. King Childebert saw that the aforesaid queen, their mother, was raising the sons of her elder son Chlodomir and loved them very much. Thinking that she wished to make them kings, he said to his brother Chlotarius:

“Our mother is keeping the sons of our brother with her and delights in keeping them; she wishes to raise them to their father’s kingdom. Therefore, after taking counsel, we must decide what to do with them. Either we shall shear them, or we shall kill them, and divide their father’s kingdom between ourselves.”

They sent Arcadius, a noble and capable man, to the queen in Paris, deceitfully saying: “Tell our mother to send us the sons of our brother, our nephews, so that we may make them kings.”

Believing that this was true, she joyfully sent them to the brothers.

But they immediately sent Arcadius back to the queen, saying: “Here are scissors, and here is a sword. Thus your sons command: if you wish to shear them or to kill them with the sword.”

Overcome by excessive grief and bitterness of heart, she said with tears: “Distress presses upon me from every side. If they are not to reign, what benefit was it for me to raise them? It is better for them to die than to be shorn.”

But Arcadius deceitfully reported to them the opposite, saying: “The queen says: ‘I prefer that they be killed rather than shorn.’”

Without delay, Chlotarius seized the elder boy, threw him to the ground, and drove a knife into his armpit. Pierced through, he died immediately.

When the younger brother saw this, he threw himself at Childebert’s feet, saying with tears: “Help me, most merciful father, lest I too perish like my brother.”

Then Childebert, moved to tears, said: “I beg you, dearest brother, deign to grant this boy his life; I will give you as much as you wish for it.”

But Chlotarius, inflamed with anger, said to him: “Cast him away from you, or you will certainly die for him. You are the one who devised this evil plan, and now you wish to free him.”

When Childebert heard this, he threw the boy away from him. Chlotarius dashed him to the ground, drove a knife into his armpit, and killed him like his brother. He likewise slaughtered their attendants and, having mounted horses, departed.

When the queen heard this, she was crushed by overwhelming grief. She prepared their little bodies and, with great psalmody and immeasurable mourning, carried them to Paris and buried them in the basilica of Saint Peter.

One of them was ten years old and the other seven.

The third, named Chlodoaldus, escaped and was freed through the assistance of courageous boys. Afterwards, abandoning his earthly kingdom, he cut his own hair with his own hand, became a cleric, and was ordained a presbyter distinguished by good works. Later, full of virtues, he departed to the Lord.

He lies buried at Nogent, in the suburb of Paris.

Queen Chrothildis, overflowing in almsgiving, lived continually with the greatest abstinence and sobriety of life.

## CHAPTER XXV — The death of Theuderic, the reign of Theudobert, and the war against Chlodtharius

(Gregory, Book III, chapter 28.) In those days King Theuderic died. He had reigned for twenty-three years.

His son Theudobert [variant: Theutbert] received his kingdom.

After this, Childebert and Theudobert mobilized an army and prepared to march against Chlotarius.

When Chlotarius heard this and saw that he could not resist their army, he fled into a forest at Aurilianum [variant: Arelaunum]. He made barricades and placed all his hope in God’s mercy.

When Queen Chrothildis heard this, she went to the tomb of blessed Martin. Prostrate there in prayer, she kept vigil throughout the night, begging the Lord that civil war should not arise among her sons.

When the enemies had assembled with large armies against Chlotarius, intending to kill him the following day, a tremendous storm arose at dawn in the place where they had gathered. It tore apart the tents with flashes of lightning and overturned everything, while rains accompanied by powerful thunder poured down.

They fell prostrate upon the ground, struck by heavy hail and severely battered [variant: thrown into confusion]. No shelter remained for them except their shields, since they were especially afraid of being consumed by heavenly fire.

Their horses were scattered so widely that they could scarcely be found within twenty stadia. Many of the men were not found at all.

Then, whether struck by stones or thrown to the ground, they repented and begged God’s forgiveness because they had wished to act so against their own blood.

But not a single drop of rain fell upon Chlotarius, nor was the sound of thunder heard there; they did not even feel a breath [variant: a stirring] of wind in that place.

They sent messengers asking for peace and concord. When these were granted, they returned to their own lands.

## CHAPTER XXVI — How Childebert and Chlodtharius marched into Spain, besieged Zaragoza, and how the Lombards lived under tribute

[Col. 1445B]

(Gregory, Book III, chapter 28.) After this, Childebert and Chlotarius again mobilized a large army and marched into Spain. Entering it, they ravaged and burned the land and killed its people. They surrounded and besieged the city of Zaragoza.

The people held under siege there turned to God in such humility that they clothed themselves in haircloth, sprinkled their heads with ashes, and went around the city walls singing psalms with the tunic of the martyr Vincent.

The women likewise followed, dressed in black cloaks, with their hair unbound and weeping, so that the fast of the Ninevites might be celebrated there.

When the kings saw this, they thought the people were practicing some kind of sorcery. They seized a peasant from the city and questioned him about what they were doing.

He replied: “My lord, they are carrying the tunic of the martyr Vincent, and with it they pray that the Lord may have mercy on them.”

The king said: “Go, tell the bishop of the city to come to us confidently, without any hesitation.”

When the man had reported this to the bishop, the bishop immediately came to them with gifts.

Childebert asked him to give him relics of blessed Vincent. The bishop gave him Vincent’s stole.

Then the kings mentioned above, having acquired the greater part of Spain, returned with many treasures and spoils.

When Childebert came to Paris, he built a church in honor of the martyr Saint Vincent.

Then King Theudobert, son of Theuderic, went into Italy with a very large army. After defeating and overthrowing the Lombards, he devastated the greater part of that land, subjected the Lombards to tribute [variant: made them tributary to himself], and returned with much booty.

[Note: [Col. 1445D] The following material has been added from the codex of the illustrious man François de Thou.]

But because that land and its regions are said to be unhealthy, his army was afflicted by various fevers.

It is also said that at that time he advanced as far as the city of Pavia, to which he sent Buccelenus. After capturing lesser Italy and reducing it to the authority of the aforementioned king, Buccelenus sought greater Italy.

There he fought Belisarius [variant: Belsuarius] many times and won the victory. When the emperor saw that Belisarius was repeatedly defeated, he removed him and appointed Narses in his place. He appointed Belisarius count of the stable [master of the horse].

Buccelenus then waged great battles against Narses. After capturing all Italy, he extended his territory as far as the sea.

He sent great treasures from Italy to Theudobert.

When this became known to Narses and the emperor, the emperor hired foreign peoples with money and sent them to support Narses. Buccelenus later engaged them in battle, was defeated, and withdrew.

Afterwards Buccelenus occupied Sicily, exacted tribute from it as well, and sent it to the king.

## CHAPTER XXVII — The death of Theudobert, Chrodchilde, and Theudoaldus; how Chlodcharius received the kingdom; and the war against the Saxons

(Gregory, Book III, chapter 36; Book IV, chapters 1–2.) After this, King Theudobert fell ill, was seized by a severe fever, and died. He had reigned for fourteen years.

His kingdom in the upper Frankish regions, in Austrasia, was received by his son Theudoaldus.

Then the most glorious Queen Chrothildis, of blessed memory and distinguished by good works, departed to the Lord at the city of Tours, full of days.

She was carried to Paris with great psalmody and buried in the sanctuary of the basilica of Saint Peter beside her husband, King Chlodoveus. Her sons, Kings Childebert and Chlotarius, buried her there. The most blessed Genovefa was also buried there.

King Chlotarius had seven sons by different women. By Ingundis he had Guntharius, Childeric, Haribertus [Charibertus], Guntram, Sigibert, and a daughter, Chlodsinda.

By Heregund [variants: Charegund], Ingundis’s sister, he had Chilperic.

By Gunsina [variants: Gunsinde and Gunsinane] he had Chramnus.

Because of his love for Ingundis, since she was beautiful and attractive, and because he himself was exceedingly lustful, he took her sister Heregund in marriage.

King Theudoaldus, son of King Theudobert, died in Austrasia after falling ill with a severe fever. He had reigned for seven years, and King Chlotarius took possession of his kingdom together with many treasures.

In that year, when the Saxons rebelled, King Chlotarius mobilized the Frankish army and fought them on the river Weser. He killed their very large army and devastated their land, traversing all Thuringia and laying it waste because they had given assistance to the Saxons.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — How Chramnus conspired against his father with Childebert, and concerning the death of Childebert
(Greg. book IV, ch. 10.) Chramnus, then, the son of Chlothar, was exceedingly handsome and well formed, as well as bold and clever. When his father had sent him beyond the Loire to act in his place, he began to oppress the region very unjustly. When this had been reported to his father, he ordered him to come to him [Note: [Col. 1446D] Up to this point, the Cambrai manuscript.]. But Chramnus refused to carry out his father’s command, acting still more harshly. He took as his wife Chalda, the daughter of Willehari [Al., Wilicharius]. After seizing many treasures and coming to Paris, he was bound by an oath to his cousin King Childebert, swearing that he was his father’s most determined enemy.

When King Childebert began to fall ill, lying in Paris for a very long time with fevers, he died [Col. 1447A] and was buried in the basilica of the blessed martyr Vincent, which he himself had built. King Chlothar took possession of his kingdom and treasures. Since Chramnus could not escape from his father, he went to Brittany. There he and his wife and children [Al., daughters] hid with Cunobert, king of the Britons. His father-in-law Willehari, however, fled to Tours, to the basilica of Saint Martin.

Then that very basilica was set on fire because of the sins of Willehari and his wife. Later King Chlothar ordered it to be covered with tin and restored it with the same elegance it had previously possessed. After this, King Chlothar, gathering a large army, advanced angrily against Chramnus in Brittany. Chramnus too, fearing nothing, went out to battle against his father with Cunibert [Al., Conobert and Conobrus], king of the Britons.

When they were fighting one another fiercely, King Chlothar, moved to tears, said: “Look down from heaven, O Lord, and judge justly; impose the judgment which you once imposed between Absalom and his father David.” As they engaged one another, the king of the Britons was put to flight and fell there. While Chramnus was attempting to escape by flight, and had ships prepared at sea, he was overcome, captured, and bound by his father’s army while trying to rescue his wife and daughters.

When this was reported to King Chlothar, he ordered him to be consumed by fire together with his wife and daughters. They were shut inside the hut of a poor woman; Chramnus was stretched out upon a bench and strangled with a scarf [that is, strangled]. Then the little house itself was set on fire over them, and he was burned together with his wife and daughters.

## CHAPTER XXIX — The time when Saint Medard passed away; the death of Chlodchar, and how his sons succeeded to the kingdom

[Col. 1447C]

(Greg., book IV, ch. 19.) At that time also, in those days, the most blessed Bishop Medard, full of illustrious virtues and glory, departed to the Lord. King Chlothar buried him gloriously in the city of Soissons with great psalmody, granting many estates there. King Chlothar then went to the tomb of Saint Martin; there he prayed for a very long time, bestowed many gifts, and offered numerous donations throughout the basilicas of the saints.

After this, while he was hunting in the Cottian Forest, he was seized by a severe fever. From there he returned to Compendium, a royal palace. When he was suffering grievously there, he said: “Woe, woe! What do you suppose that heavenly King is like, who kills such great kings in this way?” In this distress he gave up his spirit. He had reigned for fifty-one years [Al., but he died in the fifty-first year of his reign]. His four sons carried him with great honor to the city of Soissons and buried him in the basilica of the blessed Medard.

After their father’s death, Chilperic took the treasures that had been gathered at the estate of Brinnacum [Al., Brinago and Brinnacum], went to the more powerful Franks, gave them many gifts, and brought them under his authority. Soon he entered Paris and occupied King Childebert’s seat. But he was not permitted to possess it for long. For his brothers joined together, expelled him from there, and the four of them—namely Charibert [Cherebert], Guntramnus, [Col. 1448A] Chilperic, and Sigibert—made a lawful division among themselves.

Charibert received Childebert’s kingdom and established his seat at Paris. Guntramnus received Chlodomer’s kingdom and established his seat at Orléans. Chilperic received the kingdom of his father Chlothar and established his seat in the city of Soissons. Sigibert received Theuderic’s kingdom and established his seat in the city of Reims.

## CHAPTER XXX — How the Huns, attacking Gaul, were overthrown; the war between Sigibert and Chilperic; and Charibert’s wives

(Greg. book IV, chs. 23 and 26.) After the death of King Chlothar, the Huns, stirred up under their king Caganus, planned to come into Gaul. Sigibert marched an army against them and, fighting them bravely, overthrew and defeated them, putting them to flight at the sword’s edge. But afterward their king sought friendship with Sigibert and requested peace with him through envoys [Al., made peace with him], and returned to his own land.

While Sigibert was staying there, his brother Chilperic gathered an army, invaded Reims, and devastated Champagne, setting it on fire and plundering it. Sigibert, returning victorious from the Huns, gathered an army against Chilperic and occupied the city of Soissons. There he found Theudebert, Chilperic’s son, seized him, and sent him into exile [relegated him]. He also advanced against Chilperic and began a war. After Chilperic was defeated and put to flight, Sigibert restored his cities to his own dominion [recalled them under his rule].

He ordered Chilperic’s son Theudobert to be kept for a full year at the estate of Ponticon [Col. 1448C]. Later, being merciful by nature, he returned him safely to his father, enriched with gifts, after requiring him to swear that he would never act against him. This oath, however, was later broken when sins multiplied.

King Charibert took Ingoberga [Al., Ingodoterga] as his wife. That queen had two girls, daughters of a certain poor man, exceedingly beautiful and attractive. The elder was named Marcouefa [Marcoueva], while the younger was called Merofledis. King Charibert had fallen deeply in love with them. Ingoberga also harassed them with intense hatred on that account. Indeed, she ordered their father to become a wool worker. For this reason the king became extremely angry with Ingoberga, left her, and took Merofledis as his wife.

Afterward he also joined her sister Marcouefa to himself in marriage [Col. 1448D]. For this reason both of them were excommunicated by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris. But when the king refused to leave her, she was struck down by God’s judgment and died.

## CHAPTER XXXI — The death of Charibert; how Sigibert took Brunchild as his wife, Chilperic took Galsuint, and concerning Fredegund

(Greg. book IV, chs. 27 and 28.) Not long afterward King Charibert also died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Romanus at the fortress of Blavia.

King Sigibert, seeing that his brothers were taking wives unworthy of themselves and joining servant women to themselves in marriage, sent an embassy to Spain and sought Brunchild, the daughter of King Athanagild, with many gifts. She was an elegant, beautiful, [Col. 1449A] and intelligent girl. Her father did not refuse, but sent her to the aforesaid king with great treasures. He received her as his wife with great display and immense joy.

Since she was subject to the Arian law, King Sigibert ordered her to be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity. Having professed the Catholic faith, she was thoroughly instructed in it. When King Chilperic saw this, since he already had several wives, he sought Brunchild’s sister, named Galsuinda [Gailsuinda], promising through envoys that he would dismiss his other wives. When her father heard these promises, he sent his daughter to him with many treasures. Galsuinda was older than Brunchild.

Chilperic received her in marriage with great joy. She was anointed in the name of the Holy Trinity and became a great Christian woman [a woman of great holiness]. But through the hatred of Fredegund, his exceedingly wicked concubine, a great scandal arose between them. Galsuinda said that she could no longer endure such injuries from the king because of Fredegund’s hostility. She therefore asked him, leaving behind the treasures she had brought with her from Spain, to let her return freely to her father in her homeland.

He, however, flattered her with gentle words. Then, on the advice of the most wicked Fredegund, he strangled her at night in her bed. After her death, God displayed miracles on her behalf. When this had happened, Chilperic’s brothers, indignant, wanted to expel him from the kingdom.

At that time King Chilperic had three sons by his queen Audovera: Theudobert [Theutbert], Meroveus, and [Col. 1449C] Chlodoveus. Now let us return to what we began, namely, how Fredegund deceived her mistress, Queen Audovera.

Fredegund herself had come from the lowest household. When King Chilperic had gone out on campaign with his brother Sigibert against the Saxons, Queen Audovera remained pregnant and gave birth to a daughter. Fredegund craftily gave her this advice, saying: “My lady, behold, our lord the king is returning victorious. How can he joyfully receive his daughter if she has not been baptized?”

When the queen heard this, she ordered a baptistery to be prepared and summoned the bishop who was to baptize the child. When the bishop arrived, there was no married woman present to receive the girl. Fredegund said: “Shall we be able to find someone like you to receive her? You yourself receive her now.”

Hearing this, Audovera received her from the sacred font. When the king returned victorious, Fredegund went out to meet him, saying: “Thanks be to God, because our lord the king has received victory over his adversaries; and a daughter has been born to you. With whom will my lord the king sleep tonight? For my lady the queen is your daughter’s godmother, through your daughter Childesinde [Al., Chelsindane].”

He replied: “If I cannot sleep with her, I shall sleep with you.”

When the king had entered his hall, Queen Audovera came toward him with the girl herself. The king said to her: “You have done an unspeakable thing through your simplicity. You can no longer be my wife.” He ordered her to put on the sacred veil [Col. 1450A], together with her daughter; and he gave her many estates and villas. He condemned the bishop who had baptized her to exile. Fredegund, however, he joined to himself as queen.

## CHAPTER XXXII — The war between Sigibert and Chilperic, and the death of Sigibert

(Greg. book IV, chs. 37, 43, 49, 50, and 51.) At that time the Emperor Justinian died in the city of Constantinople, and Justin took up [Al., received] the empire. Chlodoveus, Chilperic’s younger son, also went as far as the city of Bordeaux [Al., Burdigala and Burgundigala]. While he was residing there without anyone troubling him, a certain Sigulf, sent by King Sigibert’s party, confronted him with an army. As Chlodoveus fled, Sigulf pursued him with trumpets and horns as though he were pursuing a fleeing stag. Chlodoveus barely reached his father in Paris, exhausted by the journey.

Chilperic also sent his elder son Theudobert, who had previously sworn allegiance to Sigibert, beyond the Loire with an army [Al., with a hostile force]. He went forth and invaded the cities of his uncle Sigibert, namely Tours, Poitiers, and the others. At Poitiers he fought against the duke Gundoald; Gundoald’s army was beaten and fled. Theudobert inflicted a great slaughter there upon Gundoald’s army.

From there he gathered his army and went to Limoges and Cahors. He devastated them, burned many churches, removed [abolished] their sacred furnishings, killed clerics, threw down men’s monasteries, violated girls’ monasteries, and laid everything waste. At that time there was a worse groaning in the churches than during the persecution of the emperors Maximian and Diocletian [Col. 1450C].

When Chilperic saw these quarrels being spread between the brothers, he again gathered an army and advanced as far as Reims, burning and fighting everywhere. When Sigibert heard this, he summoned the peoples who live beyond the Rhine, came to Paris, and prepared to march against his brother. He sent messengers to the people of Dunois and Touraine, ordering them to march against Theudobert.

They disregarded this and the king sent the dukes Godegisil and Guntramnus at their head. Gathering an army, they marched against Theudobert. He remained with only a few after abandoning his own men, but nevertheless did not hesitate to go out to battle. When they came to blows, Theudobert [Theutbert] was defeated and struck down; he died there. The duke Aunulf gathered him up and carried him to the city of Ecolosina [Col. 1450D], where he was buried.

Chilperic, fleeing through Rouen with his wife and sons, entered the city of Tournai, where he shut himself in and fortified himself. Sigibert took possession of the cities located beyond Paris, as far as Rouen. Returning from there and entering Paris, he was met there by Brunchild with her sons.

Then the Franks who had formerly looked to the elder Childebert sent an embassy to Sigibert, asking him to come to them. There, after abandoning Chilperic, they established Sigibert as their king. When he heard this, he sent orders that they besiege his brother in the aforesaid city of Tournai, saying that he would follow them with an army.

The blessed Bishop Germanus said to him: “If you go and do not wish to kill your brother, you will return alive and victorious. But if you contemplate anything else, you will die. For the Lord says through Solomon: ‘The pit that you prepare for your brother, you will fall into it.’”

He neglected to heed this. When he came to an estate called Victoriacum, his entire army gathered around him. They placed him upon a shield and raised him up as their king.

Then Fredegund, remembering her arts, intoxicated two boys from Tournai and said to them: “Go to Sigibert’s war band and pretend that you are going to raise him above you as king; then kill him. If you escape alive, I shall honor you and your descendants magnificently. But if you fall, I shall distribute many alms on your behalf among the holy places.”

They came to him without hesitation and, while pretending to present another matter, drew their knives—what the common people call scramsaxes [Al., scramxaxes—longer Saxon knives and swords]—and struck him on both sides. Crying out and collapsing, he gave up his spirit shortly afterward. The murderers also fell there.

Chilperic, unaware of his brother’s death and of what Fredegund had done, hesitated uncertainly, wondering whether or not he could escape the distress inflicted on him by his brother’s army. At last Fredegund told him everything about his brother’s death.

King Chilperic then left Tournai with his attendants, his wife, and his sons. He buried Sigibert, dressed in splendid garments, at the village of Lambres. Later they buried him at Soissons, in the basilica of Saint Medard, beside his father Chlothar. He died in the fourteenth year of his reign [Col. 1451C], at the age of forty.

After King Sigibert had been killed at the estate of Victoriacum, Queen Brunhild remained in Paris with her sons, full of grief and not knowing what she should do. Duke Gundoald secretly seized her little son Childebert during the night, carried him away, and fled with him to Austrasia. After gathering the peoples over whom his father had ruled, he established him as king.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — How Brunchild was confined in exile, how Meroveus took her as his wife, and the war of the Champenois

(Greg. book V, chs. 2, 3, 8, and 22.) King Chilperic came to Paris, seized Brunhild, and confined her in exile at the city of Rouen. He took away her treasures, which she had brought to Paris, and ordered her daughters to be kept in the city of Meaux [Col. 1451D].

After this Chilperic sent his son Meroveus with an army beyond the Loire. But Meroveus abandoned his father’s orders, returned through the territory of Le Mans, and came to Rouen, pretending that he wished to visit his mother Audovera. There he joined himself to Queen Brunhild and took her as his wife.

When Chilperic heard that he had taken his uncle’s wife contrary to divine law and canon law, he became extremely bitter and hastened to that city. When Meroveus and Brunhild learned that he had decided to separate them, they fled to the basilica of Saint Martin, which was built of wooden boards above the wall.

Since the king could not drive them out by stratagem, he deceitfully swore to them: “If it is God’s will, I myself shall not try to separate them.” Trusting this oath, they left the basilica. After deceitfully kissing them and receiving them graciously, the king feasted with them.

A few days later he returned to Soissons with Meroveus. While he was staying there, an army from Champagne gathered against Chilperic. Chilperic likewise drew up his army against them. But the Champenois were heavily beaten and fled; he killed many very noble men there.

After these events, King Chilperic suspected Meroveus in this battle because of his marriage to Brunhild and her sorcery, with Fredegund plotting against him. He stripped Meroveus of his weapons and entrusted him to guards, considering [Al., consulting] what he ought to do with him.

After this, by Chilperic’s order, Meroveus was tonsured, ordained a priest, clothed in priestly garments, and sent to the monastery of Aninsula in the territory of Le Mans, so that he might live there according to the rule.

At that time also the blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, full of days and great virtues, departed to the Lord and was buried with glory and the greatest psalmody in the basilica of the blessed martyr Vincent.

After this Childebert the younger sent an embassy to Chilperic concerning his mother Brunhild. She was returned peacefully. At that time Samson, Chilperic’s son, died.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — Concerning the exceedingly wicked assessments that Chilperic ordered to be made

(Greg. book V, ch. 28.) King Chilperic ordered new and severe assessments [Col. 1452C] to be made throughout his entire kingdom on the advice of Fredegund. For this reason many people abandoned those cities and their own possessions and sought other kingdoms, saying that it was better for them to live abroad than to be subjected to such danger.

The assessment had been established as follows: the owner of land was to pay one amphora of wine for each arepennis. They did the same with the remaining lands and with every form of property. The same was done with regard to slaves. The people, greatly oppressed, cried out to the Lord.

At that time King Chilperic fell seriously ill. When he recovered [Al., grew better], his younger son, who had not yet been baptized, began to fall ill. After being baptized, he barely recovered. His elder brother, named Chlodobertus, was also struck by this illness and became extremely sick [Al., with a severe wasting disease].

Fredegund, overwhelmed by grief and lamentation for her sons, said to the king, repenting too late [Al., already repenting]: “For a long time divine mercy has tolerated us while we acted wickedly. For he has often struck us with fevers and other evils, and we have neglected to reform. Behold, we are now losing our sons; behold, the tears of the poor, the lamentations of widows, and the sighs of orphans are killing them. Behold, immeasurable weights of gold and silver, storerooms and granaries overflowing with fullness—and we do not know for whom we are gathering these things. Behold, we are losing what we possessed most beautiful. Of what use will all these things be to us? Now, let my counsel please you: order us to return what we have wrongfully seized, and order the new assessments that we unjustly and wickedly established to be burned [Al., consumed by fire], so that, if we lose our children, we may at least escape eternal punishment.”

Then the king, touched in heart, handed over all the unjust assessments to be burned in the fire. After this his little son died. They carried him with great mourning to Paris and buried him in the basilica of the blessed martyr Dionysius.

Thereafter, when their other son Chlodobertus [Al., Robertus] was extremely ill, they placed him on a litter and carried him to Soissons [Al., Sexons], to the basilica of Saint Medard. Throwing themselves before the holy tomb, they made vows on his behalf. But at midnight he weakened and died. They buried him in the basilica of the holy martyrs Crispinus and Crispinianus.

There was great mourning among all the people. Women, taking up mourning garments with the men, wept, clothed in black, and beating their breasts accompanied the funeral [Col. 1453B]. King Chilperic also bestowed many gifts and donations upon churches and the poor, as well as many estates.

## CHAPTER XXXV — Concerning the emperors Justin and Tiberius, the subjugation of Italy, the death of King Guntramnus, and how Chilperic was killed through Fredegund’s contrivance

(Gregor. book V, ch. 30.) At that time also the Emperor Justin, having become insane, died in the thirteenth year of his reign in the city of Constantinople. Tiberius assumed the empire. After this Theuderic, Chilperic’s young son, died.

In those days Fredegund gave birth to a boy whom they named Chlothar. He later became a great king and fathered Dagobert.

In those same days King Childebert went to Italy, once again acquired it for the part of Austrasia that he ruled, and subjected it to tribute [Col. 1453C]. At that time also the greatest discord arose between Chilperic and his nephew Childebert. Fredegund and Brunhild continually provoked them against one another on both sides.

At that time also the illustrious King Guntramnus, of blessed memory, Chilperic’s brother, died. He was buried in the city of Chalon in Burgundy, in the basilica of the blessed martyr Marcellus. He had reigned for thirty-one years.

Fredegund then sent her daughter, named Rihgund [Al., Riccund and Ricohund], with great wealth and countless treasures, to Leovigild, king of Spain, to be the wife of his son, accompanied by a great embassy of Goths. Fredegund was a beautiful and exceedingly clever queen, as well as an adulteress.

At that time Landericus was in King Chilperic’s court, an able and vigorous man. The queen mentioned above loved him greatly, because he engaged in lust with her.

One day, early in the morning, when the king was leaving the estate of Calinsa [Callense] in the territory of Paris to go hunting, and when he loved Fredegund exceedingly, he returned from the horse stable to a chamber of the palace. She was washing her head with water in that chamber. Coming up behind her, the king struck her on the buttocks with a stick.

Thinking it was Landericus, she said: “Why are you doing this, Landericus?” Looking up [Al., looking back], she saw that it was the king and was terribly frightened. The king, becoming very sad, went on to the hunt.

Fredegund then summoned Landericus and told him everything the king had done, saying: “Consider what you must do, because tomorrow we shall go out to terrible tortures.”

Landericus, saddened in spirit and moved to tears, said: “My eyes saw you at such an evil hour. Where can I flee from my lord the king? I do not know what I should do, for distress presses upon me from every side.”

She said to him: “Do not be afraid. Listen to my counsel, and let us do this thing, so that we do not die. When the king returns from the hunt late at night, as twilight darkens, let us send someone to kill him; and let heralds proclaim that it was an ambush laid by Childebert. When he is dead, let us reign with my son Chlothar.”

It happened that, at the beginning of the night, when King Chilperic was returning from the hunt [Col. 1454B], certain flattering young men, intoxicated with wine and sent by Fredegund, struck the king in the belly with scramsaxes as he dismounted from his horse, while the other people were proceeding to their lodgings [Al., accommodations]. Crying out, he expired and died.

The flatterers whom the queen had deceitfully sent also shouted: “An ambush! An ambush was laid by King Childebert of Austrasia against our lord the king!” The army then ran about in every direction, but, finding nothing, returned to its own quarters.

Bishop Mallulf [Al., Mathulf] of Senlis, who was then present in the palace, had him dressed in royal garments and, placing him in a boat, carried him with hymns and great psalmody, together with Queen Fredegund and the rest of the army, to the city of Paris [Col. 1454C]. There they buried him in the basilica of the blessed martyr Vincent. He had reigned for twenty-three years.

## CHAPTER XXXVI — How Fredegund waged war against the Austrasians, defeated them, and burned Champagne

Fredegund remained in the kingdom with her young son King Chlothar and with Landericus, whom she had appointed [Al., they chose] mayor of the palace. The Franks also established the aforesaid little King Chlothar over them as king.

When King Childebert of Austrasia, Sigibert’s son and Chilperic’s nephew, heard of the evil deeds of his aunt Queen Fredegund, he gathered an army. After his cousin Guntramnus died, he had taken possession of the kingdom of Burgundy.

The Burgundians, Austrasians, and the senior Franks then gathered a great army and, advancing through Champagne, entered the district of Soissons [Al., the Soissons district] with their patricians Gundoald and Wintrio, devastating it [Col. 1454D].

When Fredegund heard this, she gathered an army with Landericus and the other Frankish leaders. Coming to the estate of Brinnacum, she gave the Franks many gifts and presents and encouraged them to fight against their enemies.

When she saw that the Austrasian army, united and gathered together, was exceedingly large, she gave this counsel to the Franks who were with her: “Let us rise against them at night with lamps. Let our companions who go before us carry branches of trees in their hands, and let bells be tied above the horses, so that their sentries and guards may not be able to recognize us. At daybreak let us rush upon them [Col. 1455A], and perhaps we shall defeat them.”

This counsel pleased them. When the assembly had been announced, they were to gather for battle on the appointed day at a place called Truccia in the district of Soissons [Truncia, in the Saxon district].

As she had advised, she rose at night with weapons and branches in her hands, along with the other things mentioned above. Mounting their horses and carrying the little King Chlothar in her arms, they reached Trucciacum [Al., Trunciacum].

When the Austrasian enemy guards saw branches of trees, as though on mountains, among the Frankish line, and heard the ringing of bells, one guard said to his companion: “Were there not open fields in that place and that place yesterday? How is it that we now see forests?”

The other, mocking him, said: “Surely you were drunk; now you are delirious. Do you not hear the bells of our horses grazing beside that very forest?”

While this was happening and dawn was beginning, the Franks with Fredegund and the little Chlothar rushed upon the sleeping Austrasians and Burgundians with the blaring of trumpets. They killed most of that army, and an innumerable multitude of that very great host, from the greatest to the least, fell there.

Gundoald and Witrio [Al., Wintrio] escaped only with difficulty by flight. Landericus pursued Witrio, but Witrio escaped with the help of an exceptionally swift horse. Fredegund, with the remainder of the army, advanced as far as Reims, burned and devastated Champagne, and returned to the city of Soissons with much booty and spoils [Col. 1455C] with her army.

## CHAPTER XXXVII — The death of Fredegund and Theudobert’s war against Chlothar

At that time King Childebert of Austrasia had two sons: the elder, Theudobert, by a concubine, and the younger, Theuderic, by the queen. He sent the latter with his grandmother Brunichild to Burgundy, into the kingdom of King Guntramnus.

At that time the younger King Childebert died, having reigned for twenty years. His son Theudobert was established in his father’s kingdom in Austria [Al., Austrasia], while Theuderic was established in Burgundy.

At that time also Queen Fredegund, old and full of days, died and was buried in Paris in the basilica of the blessed martyr Vincent.

King Theuderic of Burgundy was exceedingly handsome, vigorous, and clever. On the advice of his grandmother Brunhild, he gathered a very large army from Burgundy and sent it against his cousin Chlothar. When Chlothar heard this, he quickly advanced against him with a Frankish army.

They met with their armies in the district of Sens, on the river Aroanna. When they joined battle, such a slaughter of both peoples took place there that the riverbed itself was filled with human corpses, and the water could no longer flow at all [Al., changed the water’s usual course], so much blood had been poured out.

During that very struggle an angel of the Lord was seen with a drawn sword over that people. When King Chlothar saw that his army had been wounded, he fled [Col. 1456A], entered the fortress of Miclitanum [Al., Militonum and Miclitonum] beside the Seine, and from there made his way into the city of Paris.

Theuderic, devastating and burning that region, returned as far as the village of Sciona [Isquina] with much spoil. Chlothar, returning from Paris, hastened as far as the forest of Arelaunum [Al., Erelaunum and Aurellanum].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — Brunchild’s wicked counsel and how Theuderic killed his brother

Brunchild repeatedly supplied her grandson King Theuderic with worse counsels out of envy, saying: “Why do you neglect and fail to seek your father’s treasure and kingdom from the hands of Theudobert, when you know with absolute certainty that he is not your brother, because he is the son of your father’s harlot, born in adultery?”

When Theuderic heard this, being harsh by nature, he gathered a very large army and sent it against his brother Theudobert. They met for battle at the fortress of Tolbiacum.

When they were fighting one another fiercely, Theudobert, seeing that his army had been wounded, fled and entered the city of Cologne. Theuderic burned and devastated the land of the Ripuarian people [Al., Ribarien people].

The people of that region then submitted themselves to his power, saying: “Spare us, most merciful king. We are already subject to you; do not oppress us further.”

He replied: “Either bring Theudobert to me alive, or cut off his head and bring it to me, if you wish me to spare you.”

When they heard this, they entered the city and, lying to him about one thing instead of another, said: “This is what your brother commands: ‘Return my father’s treasure, which you are keeping with you; afterward he will return with his army.’”

While they were telling Theudobert these lies, he entered the palace of his treasure with them. As he was searching through the chest for his treasures’ ornaments, one of them drew his sword and struck him from behind in the neck, cutting off his head.

They lifted him over the wall of the city of Cologne. When Theuderic saw this, he seized the city itself and took great treasures.

After he had received oaths from the Frankish nobles in the basilica of the blessed martyr Gereon, it seemed to him that he had been deceitfully struck in the side. He said: “Guard the doors. I do not know which of these perjured Ripuarians struck me” [Col. 1456D].

When they had turned back his garments, they found nothing except a small purple mark. From there King Theuderic returned with much spoil, together with the daughter of his brother King Theudobert and his two little sons, and went back to the city of Metz, where Queen Brunhild had arrived. He seized Theudobert’s sons, the boys, and killed them.

## CHAPTER XXXIX — How Theuderic wished to take his niece as his wife, and how Brunchild killed Theuderic

King Theuderic, seeing that Theudobert’s daughter, his niece, was beautiful, wished to join her to himself in marriage. Brunhild said to him: “How can you take the daughter of your brother?”

He replied: “Did you not tell me that he was not my brother? Why have you brought this sin upon me, enemy, wicked woman, and guilty cause of death, so that I might kill my brother and my kinsmen?”

He drew his sword [Al., knife] and wished to run her through. But she was rescued by those standing nearby and escaped by slipping into a bedroom of the house.

After this, consumed by intense hatred [Al., terrified], she sent him a poisoned drink through the hands of cruel servants. He drank the poison at once, unaware of the deceit; then, weakening, he gave up [Al., breathed out] his wicked spirit.

After he had died, Brunnild herself wickedly slaughtered his little sons. She killed the younger boy in white clothing by smashing his brains against a stone.

## CHAPTER XL — How the Austrasians and the other Franks raised Chlodchar to sole kingship and condemned Brunchild to death
[Col. 1457B] After these kings had died, the Burgundians and Austrasians, having made peace with the Franks, established King Chlothar as their sole monarch over all three kingdoms. King Chlothar, having assembled an army, then went to Burgundy. By a deceitful promise, pretending that he wished to take Brunhilda as his wife, he had caused her to come to him. Believing him, she came to him dressed in royal attire. When he saw her, he said:

“Enemy of the Lord, why did you persist in committing so many evils, so that you did not fear to kill such a noble royal offspring through your wicked deeds, and did not hesitate to perpetrate so great a crime?”

Then, when the assembled army of Franks and Burgundians was shouting that Brunhilda was deserving of the most shameful death, King Chlothar ordered her [Col. 1457C] to be lifted onto a camel and led around the entire army; afterward she was bound by the feet to untamed horses, and she died with her limbs torn apart. Finally, her tomb was consumed by fire, and her bones were burned. The king, having established peace throughout the surrounding region, returned.

## CHAPTER XLI — How the Saxons entered battle against Dagobert, and Chlothar killed their commander, leaving no man among them taller than his sword

At that time, after Landeric, there was a nobleman named Gundoald [Al.: Godolandus and Gundobaldus], chief officer of the household at the royal court, an outstanding and industrious man. At that time King Chlothar had a son named Dagobert, an able and vigorous boy, clever and resourceful in everything. When he had grown up, the king sent him, together with Duke Pippin, to reign in Austrasia. The leading Austrasian Franks [Col. 1457D], assembled together, made Dagobert their king.

In those days the rebellious Saxons stirred up a very large army of many peoples against King Dagobert and Chlothar. Dagobert, having gathered a very large force, crossed the Rhine and did not hesitate to go out to battle against the Saxons. While they were fighting fiercely, Dagobert was struck on the helmet of his head, and a portion of his hair was cut off and fell to the ground. His shield-bearer, standing behind him, picked it up. But when he saw his people harmed, he said to his servant:

“Go quickly and hasten with the lock of my hair to my father, so that he may [Col. 1458A] come to our aid before the entire army falls.”

The boy ran swiftly, crossed the Rhine River, and entered the Ardennes Forest. King Chlothar had arrived there with a very large army. When the hurried messenger appeared, bringing the king the lock cut from his son’s hair, the king, overcome by immense grief, rose during the night amid the tumult of the troops, crossed the Rhine with his army, and hastened to his son’s aid.

When they had joined together and clapped their hands with joyful hearts, they pitched their tents facing the River Weser. Berthoald, the duke of the Saxons, stood on the opposite bank of this river, prepared either to come to an agreement or to fight. Hearing the tumult of the people, he asked what it was. They replied:

“Lord King Chlothar [Col. 1458B] has come, and for that reason the Franks are rejoicing.”

He answered with a mocking laugh [Al.: a loud laugh]:

“You are lying; you are afraid to rave, when you say that you have Chlothar with you, since we have learned by report [Al.: have learned by hearsay] that Chlothar is dead.”

The king, standing there, was clothed in a coat of mail and had a helmet on his head; he wrapped his hair, streaked with gray, around himself. When the king’s head appeared uncovered beneath the helmet, Berthoald recognized that it was the king and said:

“So you are here, [uncertain corrupt reading], you beast?” [Al.: “You braying and neighing beast!”]

When the king heard this, he was greatly angered by the insult. Entering the River Weser with his swiftest horse, he swam across it and, savage in spirit, pursued Berthoald. The Frankish army followed the king, and, swimming with Dagobert, they scarcely crossed the river through its immense depths.

King Chlothar [Col. 1458C], pursuing Berthoald, struggled fiercely with him. Berthoald said:

“Withdraw from me, I beg you [Al.: O king], lest I perhaps kill you. For if you prevail against me, everyone will say that you killed your servant Berthoald, a pagan. But if I kill you, a great report will be heard among all peoples: that the strongest king of the Franks was killed by a servant.”

The king did not at all yield to his words; rather, his courage rose still more against and over him. One of the king’s horsemen, who had followed him from a distance, shouted:

“Take courage, take courage against your adversary, my lord king!”

The king’s hands had already become very heavy, for he was wearing armor. Rising over him, the king killed Berthoald and lifted his head upon a spear.

Returning [Col. 1458D] to the Franks, he found them mourning, for they did not know what had happened to the king. When they saw him, however, they rejoiced with great joy.

The king then laid waste the entire land of the Saxons and killed that people. He left no taller man alive there than his own sword—which they call a *spatha*—was long [Al.: except one who could equal the height of his sword]. He established this as a sign in that region. The victorious king returned to his own land.

## CHAPTER XLII — On the death of Chlodcharius and the reign of Dagobert

In the course of time, King Chlothar died, an old man and full of days; he had reigned forty-four years. His son King Dagobert wisely assumed his kingdom as sole monarch over all three realms. He was [Col. 1459A] a very powerful king in war, a nourisher of the Franks, most severe in judgments, and generous toward churches. He was the first to order that abundant funds from the royal treasury be distributed as alms through the churches of the saints. He established peace throughout his entire kingdom. His fame resounded among many peoples, and he inspired fear and dread in all the surrounding kingdoms. Peaceful like Solomon, he held the kingdom of the Franks in tranquility.

At that time the blessed Bishop Audoenus also arose and shone forth. When the distinguished chief officer Gundoald died, King Dagobert appointed Erconald [Al.: Archenald]—an illustrious man—as chief officer of the household. The aforementioned king had two sons by his queen Nanthilde [Al.: Lanthilde], who was of Saxon descent: Sigibert and Chlodoveus. He sent his elder son Sigibert [Col. 1459B], together with Duke Pippin, to be established in Austrasia for the kingdom [Al.: to reign]. But he kept the younger Chlodoveus with him.

## CHAPTER XLIII — On the death of Dagobert and Sigibert, and the reign of Chlodoveus

After this, King Dagobert was seized by a severe fever and died while ill at the estate of Spinogil in the district of Paris [Al.: in the Parisian district], and was buried in the basilica of the blessed martyr Dionysius. The Franks mourned him for many days; he had reigned thirty-four years.

The Franks made his son Chlodoveus their king. He took as his wife Bathild, of Saxon descent, a very beautiful and highly capable woman.

After this, when Pippin died, King Sigibert of the Austrasians appointed his son Grimoald chief officer of the household [Col. 1459C]. In the course of time, when King Sigibert died, Grimoald, the chief officer, cut the hair of his little son Dagobert, and sent him through Dido, bishop of the city of Poitiers, to Scotland to live as a pilgrim; he established his own son in the kingdom.

Therefore the Franks, stirred up and exceedingly indignant, prepared an ambush for Grimoald. Seizing him, they brought him before King Chlodoveus for condemnation [Al.: They seized him and sent him to King Chlodoveus for condemnation, since he was deserving of death. Another version has: They removed him from power and handed the kingdom over to Chlodoveus]. He was imprisoned in the city of Paris, confined in the torment of fetters, and, as he was deserving of death, ended his life by death because of the crime he had committed against his lord.

## CHAPTER XLIV — At what time the kingdom of the Franks collapsed, and on the death of Chlodoveus and the reign of Chlodcharius

[Col. 1459D]

At that time Chlodoveus, instigated by the devil, cut off the arm of the blessed martyr Dionysius. During the same period the kingdom of the Franks collapsed through disastrous calamities. Chlodoveus himself was devoted to every kind of filth: he was a fornicator and mocker of women, satisfied with gluttony and drunkenness. History recalls nothing worthy concerning his death and end. Many writers condemn his end; because they do not know the end of his wickedness, they report and relate different accounts about him, one thing in place of another.

For by Queen Bathild he had three sons: Chlothar, Childeric, and Theuderic. When the aforesaid King Chlodoveus was approaching death—he had reigned [Col. 1460A] sixteen years—the Franks made Chlothar, the eldest of the three boys, their king, to reign together with his mother the queen.

## CHAPTER XLV — How Ebroin was chosen chief officer, and King Chlodcharius died, and Theuderic and Childeric assumed the kingdom

At that time, when Erchonaldo [Al.: Erchenold] the chief officer died, the Franks, wavering in uncertainty, made a predetermined decision and appointed Ebroin chief officer of the household at the royal court, elevating him to this dignity.

In those days the boy King Chlothar died; he had reigned four years. His brother Theuderic was raised as king of the Franks. His other brother Childeric went to assume the kingdom in Austrasia together with Duke Vulfald.

At that time the Franks prepared an ambush against Ebroin [Col. 1460B], rose up against Theuderic, and drove him from the kingdom. They forcibly cut off the hair of both men and burned it; they shaved Ebroin and sent him to the monastery of Luxovium in Burgundy. They also sent an embassy to Austrasia on Childeric’s behalf and secured his return. He came together with Duke Vulfoald and was raised to the kingdom of the Franks.

Childeric himself, however, was extremely frivolous and conducted everything recklessly, until the greatest hatred and scandal grew up among them, oppressing the Franks severely. Among them was a certain Frank named Bodolenus [Al.: Bodilenus and Bodilo], whom he ordered to be stretched out on a stake and beaten severely, without regard to law.

When the Franks saw this, Ingobert and Amalbert in particular, together with the other leading men of the Franks, were stirred to great anger. Raising a revolt against Childeric [Col. 1460C], Bodolenus rose against him with the other conspirators and killed the king, together with his pregnant queen—a deed painful to relate. Vulfoald barely escaped by flight and returned to Austrasia.

The Franks then chose Leudesius, the noble son of Erchinald [Al.: Archenold], as chief officer of the palace. The blessed Leudegarius, bishop of Autun, and his brother Gerinus were also involved in this counsel from Burgundy and gave their consent.

Ebroin, having received this counsel, allowed his hair to grow, gathered allies to help him, and came out of the monastery of Luxovium in a hostile manner, returning to Francia with an armed force. He sent to the blessed Audoenus to ask what counsel he should give him. But Audoenus sent him only this written message through intermediaries:

“Let Fredegund come to your mind.” [Col. 1460D]

Being as clever as he was, Ebroin understood. Rising during the night, he mobilized an army and came as far as the River Yser [Al.: to the Yser]. After killing the guards, he crossed the Yser at Saint-Maxentius. There he killed those of his conspirators whom he found.

Leudesius, together with King Theuderic and a great many companions, escaped by flight. Ebroin pursued them as far as the estate of Bacio [Al.: Stoacio], where he seized the royal treasures. Afterward he came to Crisciago [Al.: Crisiacum] and recovered the king. He deceitfully sent word to Leudesius, having given his pledge, to come to him. When this had been done, he killed Leudesius and shrewdly recovered the chief command.

He ordered the holy Bishop Leudegarius to be beaten with various punishments and struck with the sword. He condemned his brother Gairoenus [Al.: [Col. 1461A] Cerinus and Garinus] to harsh punishment. The other Franks, their companions, barely escaped by flight. Some, driven into exile, wandered about and were deprived of their possessions.

## CHAPTER XLVI — How Martin and Pippin, dukes of the Austrasians, waged war against Ebroin and Theuderic

At that time, when Vulfoald departed from Austrasia, Martin and Pippin, the younger son of Ansigisel, ruled in Austrasia after the deaths of the kings. At last these dukes, having turned against Ebroin in hatred, mobilized a very large army of Austrasians and directed their battle line against King Theuderic and Ebroin.

King Theuderic and Ebroin came against them with an army at a place called [Col. 1461B] Lucofao [Al.: Lucofao and Lucofago]. Joining battle, they struck one another down in a great slaughter, and an immeasurable multitude of people fell there. The Austrasians were defeated, fled, and turned their backs. Ebroin pursued them with a most cruel slaughter and devastated a large part of that region.

Martin escaped by flight, entered Laon Clavatus, and shut himself up there. Pippin escaped in another direction. Ebroin, having achieved victory, returned and came with a large army to the estate of Ercherego [Al.: Ercheco and Ercariaco]. He sent messengers to Martin, so that, after giving an oath, he might come confidently to King Theuderic. They swore this deceitfully and falsely over empty chests. Martin, believing them, came to Ercherego and was killed there together with his companions.

## CHAPTER XLVII — How Ebroin was killed, Waratto was appointed chief officer, and Saint Audoenus departed to the Lord

[Col. 1461C]

Ebroin was oppressing the Franks ever more cruelly. But while he was preparing an ambush for a Frank named Ermenfrid, Ermenfrid learned of it, attacked him during the night, and killed him brutally; then he fled and escaped to Pippin in Austrasia.

The Franks, after taking counsel, appointed Waratto, an illustrious man, in his place as chief officer of the palace by order of the king. Waratto then received hostages from the aforementioned Pippin and made peace with him.

At that time Waratto had a capable and industrious son, fierce in spirit and harsh in character, a plotter against his father and one who was trying to displace him from his honorable position. His name was Gislemar [Col. 1461D]. The blessed Bishop Audoenus warned him not to commit this wickedness against his father. Gislemar scorned listening to him, and wars among themselves and many disputes arose between Gislemar and Pippin.

Struck by God because of the injuries he had inflicted on his father and his other cruel sins, Gislemar breathed out his wicked spirit, just as Saint Audoenus had foretold to him. When he had died, Waratto again held his former office.

In those days Audoenus, bishop of Rouen, full of days and illustrious for his virtues, departed to the Lord at the royal estate of Clippiago in the suburb of the city of Paris. He was buried with great glory in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter in the city of Rouen.

## CHAPTER XLVIII — How Waratto died and Bertharius was appointed in his place, and Pippin, after defeating them, brought the chief office under his own power

[Col. 1462A]

In the course of time, the aforementioned Waratto died. He had a noble and clever wife named Ansefledis [Al.: Ansfledis and Ansafilidis].

The Franks, inclining in different directions and wavering, appointed a certain Bertharius [Al.: Bertharius] as chief officer of the household. He was short in stature, undistinguished in wisdom, and useless in counsel; they appointed him while wandering uncertainly.

The Franks were divided among themselves. Pippin rose up in Austrasia, mobilized a very large army, and directed his battle line against King Theuderic and Bertharius. When they met for battle at a place called Textricius, and fought one another there, King Theuderic and Bertharius [Col. 1462B], the chief officer, turned their backs. Pippin emerged victorious.

As time passed, Bertharius himself was killed by his flatterers, at the instigation [Al.: through the plotting] of Ansfled. After this Pippin became chief ruler and chief officer together with King Theuderic. Having taken the treasures, he left a certain Nortbert [Al.: Nordebert] of his own people with the king and returned to Austrasia.

Pippin had a most noble and wise wife named Plectrudis. By her he had two sons. The elder was named Drocus [Al.: Drogo], and the younger Grimoald. Drocus received the duchy of Champagne.

## CHAPTER XLIX — On the death of Theuderic, and the reigns of Chlodoveus and Childebert, and Grimoald as chief officer

King Theuderic died; he had reigned nineteen years [Col. 1462C] [Al.: eighteen]. His son Chlodoveus, a boy born of Queen Chlothild [Al.: Rotild], assumed the royal seat. Not long afterward the boy King Chlodoveus himself died; he had reigned two years.

His brother Childebert, an illustrious man, was established in the kingdom. At that time Nortbert also died. Grimoald, the younger son of Prince Pippin, became chief officer at the court of King Childebert.

Pippin himself waged many wars against the pagan Ratbod and other rulers, against the Suebi and very many peoples. Grimoald had a son by a concubine, named Theudoald. At about the same time Pippin’s son Drocus died. The aforementioned Prince Pippin had a son by another wife, named Charles, an elegant, outstanding, [Col. 1462D] and useful man.

## CHAPTER L — On the passing of Childebert and the reign of Dagobert; how Grimoald was killed, and how Theudoald sought his father’s office

Then King Childebert, just and of blessed memory, departed to the Lord. He had reigned eighteen years [Al.: nineteen] and was buried at the monastery of Cauciago [Al.: Causiaco], in the basilica of the holy martyr Stephen.

His son Dagobert reigned in his place. Grimoald at that time had a wife in marriage named Teutsinda [Al.: Theodesinda], daughter of the pagan Duke Ratbod. Grimoald himself was a pious, modest, and just chief officer.

At that same time, when his father Duke Pippin was ill, Grimoald went to visit him. Without delay, in the basilica of the holy martyr Landebert at Liège [Al.: Leodicum], he was killed by Rangarius, a pagan, the son of Belial [Al.: Beluabi].

His son Theudoald, at the command of his grandfather Pippin, was established at the royal court in the exalted office of his father.

## CHAPTER LI — On the death of Pippin, the wars among the Franks themselves, and how, after Theudoald fled, Ragenfred was raised to the chief command

At that time Pippin, seized by a severe fever, died. He had held the chief command under the kings mentioned above for twenty-seven years. Plectrudis, together with her grandsons and the king, governed everything under a prudent administration.

In those days, at the devil’s instigation, the Franks again attacked one another in the Forest of Cuise and struck each other down in an exceedingly harsh slaughter. Theudoald escaped by flight and was rescued.

At that time there was a violent persecution. After Theudoald had fled, they chose Ragenfred as chief officer [Al.: as chief of the palace]. Having mobilized an army with the king, Ragenfred crossed the Forest of Carbonaria, reached the River Meuse, and devastated and burned those lands. He made an alliance with the pagan Duke Radbod.

During these events Charles was being held under guard, having been captured by the woman Plectrudis; with the Lord’s help, he barely escaped.

## CHAPTER LII — On the death of Dagobert and the reign of Chilperic, and how Charles waged war against Ratbod

In the following period King Dagobert died while ill; he had reigned five years. After this the Franks established in the kingdom a former cleric named Daniel, allowing his hair to grow [Col. 1463C], and gave him the name Chilperic.

At that same time, having again mobilized an army, they came as far as the River Meuse itself, directing their battle line against Charles. On the other side the Frisians [Al.: Fresians] also rose up with Duke Ratbod.

Charles attacked the Frisians, but there suffered a very great loss among his companions and withdrew by flight.

## CHAPTER LIII — How Charles fought against Chilperic and Ragenfred at a place called Vinciacus, and, after defeating and routing them, brought the whole kingdom of the Franks under his power

As time passed, Chilperic himself again entered the Forest of Ardennes with Ragenfred [Al.: Raganfred], having mobilized an army; they reached the River Rhine and the city of Cologne [Col. 1463D], devastating the land. After receiving a great treasure from the noblewoman Plectrudis, they returned joyfully.

But at a place called Amblava they suffered a great loss when Charles attacked them. At that time the aforementioned Charles again rose up for battle against Chilperic and Ragenfred, having mobilized an army. They too gathered their forces in opposition and hastened to prepare for battle.

Charles asked that peace be made. When they refused, they went out to battle at a place called Vinciacus [Al.: Viciccus], as Sunday was dawning, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, during Lent. While they fought fiercely, Chilperic and Ragenfred turned their backs. Charles emerged victorious.

After devastating and capturing those regions, Charles returned to Austrasia with much booty and came to the city of Cologne, where he caused a revolt. He disputed with the noblewoman Plectrudis, shrewdly recovered his father’s treasures, and established for himself a king named Chlotar.

Chilperic and Ragenfred then sought Duke Eudo’s help. Eudo mobilized an army and marched against Charles, but Charles steadfastly and fearlessly met him. Eudo fled and returned to the city of Paris.

Chilperic withdrew beyond the Loire with the royal treasures he had taken. Charles pursued him but did not find him. The aforementioned King Chlotar died that year.

In the following year Charles sent an embassy to Eudo and made an alliance with him. Eudo returned King Chilperic together with many gifts, but Chilperic did not remain long in the kingdom. Afterward he died and was buried in the city of Noyon; he had reigned five and a half years.

The Franks then established Theuderic II, the son of the younger Dagobert, who had been raised at the monastery of Cala, as their king. He remains in the kingdom to this day.

# HISTORY OF THE FRANKS

From a manuscript codex of the church of Cambrai.

[Col. 1421]

[Col. 1421D] I. Let us set forth the beginnings of the kingdoms of the Franks, their origin and that of those peoples, and their deeds.

There is in Asia a Trojan town where there is a city called Ilium, in which Aeneas reigned. That people was strong and powerful, composed of warrior men, exceedingly rebellious, provoking restless conflicts and subduing the neighboring peoples all around.

The kings of the Greeks rose up against Aeneas with a large army, fought against him in a great slaughter, and there a great number of the Trojan people were overwhelmed. Aeneas fled and shut himself up in the city of Ilium. They fought against that city for ten years.

When the city had been conquered, the tyrant Aeneas fled to Italy to settle peoples there for battle. Others among the leaders, namely Priam and Antenor, with the rest of the Trojan army—twelve thousand entering ships—departed and came as far as the banks of the River Tanais [Col. 1422D].

Entering the Maeotian marshes, they sailed until they reached the territory of Pannonia near the Maeotian marshes. They began to build a city as a memorial to themselves and called it Sicambria. They lived there for many years and grew into a great people.

## II.

At that same time the wicked and most evil people of the Alamanni [Al.: Alans] rebelled against Valentinian, emperor of the Romans and of the peoples. He then mobilized a great Roman army, marched against them, engaged them in battle, overcame them, and defeated them.

They, beaten beside the River Danube, fled and entered the Maeotian marshes. The emperor said:

“Whoever can enter these marshes and drive out this wicked people, I will grant them tribute payments and gifts for ten years.”

Then the Trojans assembled and set an ambush, as they had been instructed and as they knew how. They entered the Maeotian marshes with another Roman force, drove the Alamanni out, and struck them down with the edge of the sword [Col. 1423C].

Then the emperor Valentinian called them “FRANKS” in the Attic language—that is, “savage”—because of the hardness or boldness of their hearts.

## III.

After ten years had passed, the aforementioned emperor sent tax collectors, together with a senior commander from the Roman senate, so that they might exact the customary tribute from the Frankish people.

But they, being cruel and most savage, after adopting a foolish plan, said to one another [Col. 1423D]:

“The emperor, with the Roman army, could not drive the Alamanni from the hiding places of the marshes, a strong and rebellious people. We, who defeated them, why should we pay tribute? Let us rise against this senior commander and these tax collectors, strike them, take away everything they have with them, and pay no tribute to the Romans. Then we shall remain free forever.”

Having prepared an ambush, they killed them.

## IV.

When the emperor heard this, he was inflamed with immense fury and anger. He ordered the Roman army and the forces of other peoples to be mobilized, together with Arestarchus, the commander of the army, and they directed their battle line against the Franks.

There was a great slaughter of both peoples. When the Franks saw that they could not withstand so great an army, they were killed and beaten and fled. Their strongest man, Priam, fell there.

Leaving Sicambria, they came to the farthest regions of the River Rhine, in the towns of Germany. There they settled with their leaders Marchomir, son of Priam, and Sunno, son of Antenor. They lived there for many years.

When Sunno died, they decided to establish one king over themselves, like the other peoples. Marchomir also gave them this advice. They chose his son Faramund and raised him as their long-haired king.

Then they began to have laws, which their earlier pagan leaders had drawn up, bearing these names: Vuisowastus, Vuisogastus, Arogastus, and Salegastus. Beyond the Rhine are villages named Vibothagin, Salechagin, and Vuidechagin.

[Col. 1424D] V. When King Faramund died, they raised his long-haired son Chlodio to his father’s kingdom. From that time they began to have long-haired kings.

Coming shrewdly into the territory of the Thuringians, they settled there. King Chlodio lived at the fortress of Dispargum, in the territory of the Thuringians, in the region of Germany.

At that time Romans lived in these regions on this side of the Rhine as far as the River Loire; beyond the Loire the Goths ruled. The Burgundians, then, were held in paganism and the wicked Arian doctrine, dwelling beside the River Rhône, which lies adjacent [sic] to the city of Lyon.

King Chlodio sent scouts from the fortress of Dispargum in Thuringia as far as the city of Cambrai. He later crossed the Rhine with a large army and killed and drove away many Romans. Entering the Forest of Carbonaria, he took the city of Tournai. From there he came as far as the city of Cambrai and settled there. In a short time he killed the Romans whom he found there. From there he occupied territory as far as the River Somme.

When King Chlodio died, Merovech, a member of his family, received his kingdom. Chlodio had reigned twenty years. From King Merovech the Franks were called Merovingians.

At the same time the Huns crossed the Rhine, burned Metz, destroyed Trier, overran Tongeren, and reached as far as Orléans. At that time the holy Bishop Anianus, illustrious for his virtues, was there. When Aetius, the Roman patrician, and Tursomodus, king of the Goths, came to him, and with the Lord’s help, the Huns, together with their king Attila, were defeated and overthrown at that very city through the prayers of Saint Anianus.

## VI.

Merovech himself fathered a son named Childeric, who was the father of the famous and most powerful King Chlodoveus.

At that time the Franks were pagans and fanatics, worshiping idols and images rather than the God of heaven and earth who had created them.

At that time there was in this part of Gaul, from among the Romans, a king named Aegidius, sent by the emperor.

Childeric, the son of King Merovech, was exceedingly licentious. While reigning over the Franks, he began to seduce and violate their daughters. They, greatly enraged and indignant at this, wanted to kill him and drive him from the kingdom.

When he heard this, he called his friend, a prudent counselor named Viomadus. He sought counsel with him about how the anger of the furious Franks might be appeased.

Then they established a sign between themselves, so that he would know by a definite indication whether he might at some time return to peace; they would recognize one another by that sign. They divided one gold coin between them as a token. King Childeric carried one half with him, while Viomadus kept the other part, saying:

“When I send this other half to you, know that I have the Franks reconciled with you, and return safely in peace.”

King Childeric therefore went to Thuringia and hid with a king named Bisinus and his wife.

## VII.

The Franks, having abandoned Childeric, established the Roman leader Aegidius [Col. 1426D] as their king, adopting an evil plan.

When he had reigned over them for eight years, Viomadus pretended to form a friendship with him, so that he might learn what he was thinking. He urged Aegidius deceitfully to oppress certain Franks.

When Aegidius heard his counsel, he began to oppress them more harshly. They, turned toward fear and revolt, again sought advice from Viomadus about what they should do. He said to them:

“Why do you not remember how the Romans, oppressing your people, drove them out? They expelled them from their land. But you have expelled your own king, a useful and wise man, and raised over yourselves this proud and arrogant soldier of the emperor. You did not make a good decision, but a very bad one.”

They replied:

“He was indeed harsh to us; we regret having done this against our king. If only we might find him and have him reign over us in peace!”

Then that friend of the king sent the half of the solidus which they had previously divided between them, saying [Col. 1427C]:

“Return to the kingdom of the Franks, for everything has been pacified.”

When Childeric recognized this sign, the half of the gold coin, he understood with certainty that the Franks desired him. At their request he returned to his kingdom. While he had been in Thuringia, King Childeric had committed adultery with Basina, queen and wife of King Bisinus.

When he was received back into the kingdom of the Franks, they drove the Roman leader Aegidius from power. Basina, the queen of Bisinus, king of the Thuringians, abandoned her husband and came to Childeric.

When he asked her what she sought and for what reason she had come to him from so distant a region, she is said to have replied:

“I know your worth and beauty, and that you are capable and wise; therefore I have come to live with you. For if I had known someone more worthy than you at the farthest ends of the sea, I would have sought him and joined myself to him.”

Rejoicing, he took her as his wife. She conceived by him and bore a son, whom she named Chlodoveus. He became a great king above all the kings of the Franks and a most powerful warrior.

## VIII.

In those days the Franks captured the city of Agrippina on the Rhine and called it Cologne, as though colonists had settled in it. They killed many Romans there who belonged to Aegidius’s party. Aegidius himself fled and escaped.

They then came to the city of Trier on the River Moselle, devastated those lands, and captured the city after setting it on fire.

After this Aegidius, the Roman king, died. His son Syagrius [Col. 1428C] succeeded to his kingdom and established the seat of his rule in the city of Soissons.

King Childeric then mobilized a very large army of Frankish troops and reached the city of Orléans, also devastating those lands. Adovacrius, duke of the Saxons, came by sea with a naval force as far as the city of Angers and burned that land, causing a great slaughter there.

As Adovacrius was returning from Angers, King Childeric of the Franks arrived there with a mobilized army. He killed Count Paulus, who was then there, and captured the city itself. He burned the house that was in that city and then returned.

## IX.

After this King Childeric died; he had reigned twenty-four years. His son Chlodoveus vigorously assumed the kingdom of the Franks.

In the fifth year of Chlodoveus’s reign, Syagrius, son of Aegidius, was residing in the city of Soissons, which his father had held. Chlodoveus came against him with his kinsman Ragnacharius and an army.

When they met for battle and fought one another fiercely, Syagrius, seeing that his army had been wounded, fled and escaped to Alaric, king of the Goths, at the city of Toulouse.

Chlodoveus sent messengers to Alaric, ordering him to hand over Syagrius; if he would not hand him over, he should prepare for battle. Fearing the anger of the Franks, Alaric handed Syagrius over to Chlodoveus’s messengers. When Syagrius had been brought before him, Chlodoveus ordered him killed, and Chlodoveus took possession of his entire kingdom and treasures.

[Col. 1429C] **X.** At that time many churches were plundered by Chlodovechus’s army. He himself was then a fanatic and a pagan. From a certain church his enemies carried off a pitcher of remarkable size and beauty, together with other ecclesiastical vessels and many ornaments. The bishop of that church sent his representatives to the king, begging that, if he did not deserve to recover the other vessels of the church, at least he might order that pitcher to be returned. Hearing this, the king said to the ecclesiastical envoys:

“Follow us as far as the city of Soissons, because there all the things that have been acquired will be divided. If that pitcher comes to me in my share, I shall fulfill what the bishop requests.”

When the king arrived at Soissons, he ordered all the captured booty to be brought into the midst, saying:

“I ask you, bravest and noblest warriors, not to refuse to give me this pitcher.”

When the king had said this, those Franks who were well disposed replied:

“Everything that you see, glorious king, is yours, and we are subjected to your authority. Do what seems good to you. No one has dared resist your power.”

After they had spoken kindly to him, one frivolous Frank, with a loud shout, raised his battle-axe—which is called a *francisca*—and struck that pitcher, saying:

“You shall receive nothing from here, O king, except what the true lot shall have given you.”

When everyone was astonished, the king, consigning his injury to patience, returned the pitcher he had received to the ecclesiastical messenger, while concealing his anger in his heart.
