When a year had passed, King Chlodovechus ordered his entire army to come to the military inspection, intending to inspect the gleam of their weapons on the Field of March. When the king had gone around the whole army, he came to that man who had previously struck the pitcher and said to him:

“No one has weapons as neglected and filthy as yours, for neither shield, nor spear, nor battle-axe is serviceable to you.”

The king took his *francisca*, that is, his battle-axe, and threw it onto the ground. When the man bent down to pick it up, the king immediately raised his own hands and drove his battle-axe into his head, saying:

“This is how you acted toward that pitcher at Soissons the previous year.”

After the man had died, the king ordered the army to withdraw peacefully from that field to their homes. From that time a great fear and trembling arose among the Frankish people on account of this event.

In the tenth year of his reign, Chlodovechus set out for Thuringia with a great Frankish army, and struck down the Thuringians with a great slaughter. After conquering their people and laying waste the whole land, he compelled them to serve under tribute.

*(Chapters 11, 12, and 13 do not differ from the commonly circulated Deeds.)*

[Col. 1433D] **XIV.** At that time Chlodovechus extended and enlarged his kingdom as far as the Seine. Later he occupied as far as the Loire River. Aurelianus also took the castle of Melun and the whole duchy of that region.

Then Chrodchildis conceived by Chlodovechus and gave birth to a son, whom she wished to consecrate in baptism. For the king did not believe in the Lord God. The queen preached to him every day, but he refused to listen to her.

Meanwhile the queen prepared her son for baptism and adorned the church with hangings and curtains, so that the king’s heart might be pierced toward belief. The boy was baptized, and she named him Ingomer while he was still in the white baptismal garments; but while wearing those very white garments he fell ill and died.

The king was exceedingly grieved on his account and reproached her, saying:

“If the boy had been dedicated in the name of my gods, he would certainly have lived. Because he was baptized in the name of your God, he could not live.”

But the queen said:

“I give thanks to God, because he has not judged me unworthy, but has deigned to receive my firstborn from my womb into his kingdom. I retain no grief in my heart on this account.”

After this she bore another son, whom, after he had been baptized, she named Chlodomir. When he too began to fall ill, the king said:

“It cannot be otherwise than that the same thing should happen to this child as happened to his brother, so that, baptized in the name of your Christ, he may quickly die.”

But while the queen prayed, and the Lord’s mercy went before him, the child recovered his health.

The queen did not cease preaching to the king that he should worship the true God and abandon the empty idols he worshiped. But she could in no way move his mind toward belief, until at last war arose against the Alamanni and the Suebi; in that war he was compelled to confess the one whom he had previously denied.

**XV.** It happened, while the armies of the Franks and Alamanni were fighting one another, that Chlodovechus’s people were falling in very great numbers. Aurelianus, seeing this, said to the king:

“My lord king, believe only in the God of heaven whom your queen proclaims.”

Then, raising his eyes to heaven and moved to tears, he said:

“Jesus Christ, whom my wife Chrodchildis proclaims to be the Son of the living God, who gives aid in tribulation and gives help to those who hope in you, I devoutly ask for your assistance. If you grant me victory over these enemies, and I experience that power which the peoples proclaim to be yours, I shall believe in you and be baptized in your name.

“For I have called upon my gods, and I see that they have withdrawn far from my aid. Therefore I believe that they have no power, since they do not assist those who believe in them. I call upon you, the true God and Lord, and desire to believe in you—only deliver me from my adversaries.”

When he cried out these words in prayer, the Alamanni fled and turned their backs. When they saw that their king was dead, they submitted themselves to Chlodovechus, saying:

“Spare us, we beg you, lord king, lest more of the people perish. We are now yours.”

Then the king ordered the slaughter, which was already imminent, to cease, and took the Alamanni themselves captive, or placed their land under the yoke of tribute.

After achieving victory, he returned to Francia to his queen and told her how, through calling upon the name of Jesus Christ, he had deserved to obtain victory. This occurred in the fifteenth year of Chlodovechus’s reign.

Then the queen secretly summoned Saint Remigius, bishop of the city of Rheims, begging him to show the king the way of salvation. The priest urged him to come to baptism. He replied:

“I shall gladly listen to you, most blessed Father. But one thing remains: the people who follow me do not wish to abandon their gods. Nevertheless, I shall go and exhort them according to your word.”

The king assembled with the people and began to exhort them. But, by the prevenient mercy and power of God, all the Frankish people cried out with one voice:

“We abandon mortal gods, glorious king, and are ready to believe in the true and immortal God whom Remigius proclaims.”

This was announced to Saint Remigius. He, filled with great joy, ordered the baptismal font to be prepared. The streets were shaded with hangings painted by divine art; churches were constructed; the baptistery was arranged; waxen candles gave off the scent of balsam. The Lord supplied such grace among the people that they thought themselves placed amid the fragrances of paradise.

Therefore the king first asked to be baptized by Saint Remigius. The new Constantine came to baptism, having renounced the pomp of the devil. When he entered for baptism, the saint said with eloquent speech:

“Gently lower your neck, Sicamber. Adore what you have burned, and burn what you have adored.”

Saint Remigius was a most learned man, an excellent rhetorician, and great in virtues. Then the king confessed almighty God in the Trinity, was baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and was anointed with sacred chrism with the sign of the holy cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.

More than three thousand men from his army were baptized. His sisters were baptized that same day, bearing the names Albofledis and Landechildis. Later the entire Frankish people were baptized.

**XVI.** After this Chlodovechus marched against Gundobad and his brother Godeghisel with a large Frankish army. Hearing this, they summoned a great multitude of Burgundians and prepared for battle.

They came to the castle of Dijon on the Ouche River, and there fought one another fiercely. Gundobad and Godeghisel’s Burgundians were thoroughly beaten and turned their backs in flight before Chlodovechus. As usual, Chlodovechus emerged victorious.

After the Burgundian army had been defeated, Gundobad and Godeghisel fled and barely escaped. Gundobad entered the city of Avignon on the Rhône and shut himself in there. Chlodovechus pursued him, besieging him so that he might draw him out of the city and kill him.

When Gundobad heard this, he was terrified with fear, dreading that sudden death might overtake him. He nevertheless had with him a distinguished man named Aridius, energetic and wise. He summoned him and said:

“Distress surrounds me on every side, and I do not know what to do, because these barbarians have come upon us to destroy the whole region after killing us.”

Aridius replied:

“You must soften the ferocity of this man, lest you perish. Therefore, if it pleases you, I shall pretend to flee from you and pass over to him. When I have approached him, I shall arrange that he harm neither you nor this region. Only endeavor to fulfill whatever counsel he entrusts to you through me, until the Lord in his mercy deigns to make your cause prosper.”

He replied:

“I shall do whatever you command.”

When he had said this, Aridius took his leave and departed. Going to King Chlodovechus, he said:

“Behold, most merciful king, I, your humble servant, come to your power, abandoning that most wretched Gundobad. If your mercy deigns to receive me, you and your descendants shall possess me as an upright and faithful servant.”

Chlodovechus received him most readily and kept him with him. For he was agreeable in conversation, energetic in counsel, just in judgment, and faithful in matters entrusted to him.

Finally, while Chlodovechus and his entire army were encamped around the city walls, Aridius said:

“If your majesty’s glory would graciously hear a few words from my humility, O king, I would offer counsel with complete fidelity, although you have no need of it. It will be suitable both for you and for the cities through which you intend to pass.”

“Why,” he said, “do you retain the army when your enemy is shut up in a very strongly fortified place? You lay waste the fields, consume the estates, cut down the vines, fell the olive trees, and destroy all the produce of the region. Meanwhile you achieve nothing against him either. Send an embassy instead and impose a tribute for him to pay you every year. Thus the region will remain safe, and you will rule forever over one who pays tribute. If he refuses, then you may do whatever you please.”

The king accepted this counsel and ordered the enemy of the homeland to return to his own country. Then he sent an embassy to Gundobad, ordering him to pay the tribute imposed upon him each year. Gundobad paid what was due immediately and promised that he would continue to pay thereafter.

Chlodovechus, however, took away the treasures and returned victorious with very great booty.

In these times there was an earthquake in the city of Vienne, and so forth, as in the commonly circulated Deeds, up to these words of chapter 28: “But Chramnus did not wish to carry out his father’s command.”

# APPENDIX A: FROM THEODORIC II TO KING PIPPIN, NOW ADDED FOR THE FIRST TIME

From the manuscript codex of Alexander Petavius, royal senator.

At that time Pope Gregory sent from the city of Rome to the aforementioned prince Charles an embassy bearing the keys of the venerable tomb, together with the chains of Saint Peter and great and countless gifts—something that had never happened before and had never been heard of—on the agreed terms that he should withdraw from the emperor’s party and that the Roman consulship should be conferred upon the aforesaid prince Charles.

The prince therefore received the embassy with magnificent honor, bestowed precious gifts, and sent it back to Rome with its envoys.

Likewise, after seeking the advice of his nobles, the aforementioned prince divided the kingdoms among his sons. For this reason he gave Austrasia, Swabia—that is, Alemannia—and Touraine [perhaps Thuringia] to his firstborn, named Carloman. To his other and younger son, named Pippin, he entrusted Burgundy, Austria, and the province.

That year Pippin, having gathered an army with his uncle Duke Hildebrand, a multitude of nobles, and a host of very many retainers, set out for Burgundy and occupied the boundaries of the regions in advance.

Meanwhile new signs appeared in the sun, moon, and stars, and the most sacred order of Easter was also disturbed.

Prince Charles enriched the basilica of the holy martyr Dionysius at Paris with many gifts. He came to the palace estate of Carriacum [another reading: Carisiacum] on the Isère River, was seized by a severe fever, and died. He held the principate for twenty-seven years. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November and was buried in the basilica of the holy martyr Dionysius.

His daughter Hiltrudis, acting on the counsel of her stepmother, fraudulently crossed the Rhine with the help of her companions and reached Duke Ottilo of Bavaria. He joined her to himself in marriage against the will and counsel of her brothers.

[Col. 1465A] Meanwhile, when the Basques were rebelling in the region of Aquitaine under Duke Hunuald, formerly the son of Eudo, the princes and brothers Carloman and Pippin assembled an army. They crossed the Loire at the city of Orléans, crushed the Romans, and advanced as far as the city of Bourges, burning its suburbs with fire.

Pursuing Duke Hunuald, they put him to flight. After capturing much booty, … they returned victorious around the time of autumn.

In the same year they again moved their army against the Alamanni and pitched camp above the Danube River. Remaining there until the Alamanni saw that they had been defeated, they gave hostages, promised obedience, offered gifts, and, asking for peace, submitted themselves to their authority.

Returning from there, in the second year they moved an army into Bavaria against their kinsman Ottilo, who was in rebellion. They came and pitched camp on the river called the Lech. The Bavarian army was on the opposite side.

Seeing one another from either side, the Franks, provoked by the taunts of that people, exposed themselves to danger until the eleventh day, passing through deserted and impassable places where no path had ever been open to mortal man. At night they burst in upon the enemy, and, when the armies had been divided, battle was joined.

The aforesaid Duke Ottilo, seeing his army defeated, barely escaped disgracefully by fleeing beyond the river Inn with a few men. After these triumphs had been accomplished, the aforesaid princes returned victorious to their own lands.

After three years had passed, Carloman again invaded the borders of the Saxons with an army, since they were in rebellion. Having captured the inhabitants who appeared to border on his kingdom, he successfully brought them under his control without the danger of battle. Very many of them became Christians and were baptized.

At the same time, when Theodobald, son of Duke Godfrey, was in rebellion, Pippin expelled him from his homeland by the strength of his army. After putting him to flight, Pippin renewed for himself the duchy of that place and returned victorious.

In the following year the illustrious brothers, provoked by the insolence of the Basques, again came together as far as the Loire River. Seeing this, the Basques hastened to seek peace, promising that they would carry out Pippin’s will in everything. They obtained by entreaties that he return from their borders after receiving gifts.

After these events, in the following year, when the Alamanni had broken faith with Carloman, he entered their homeland with great fury and a large army, and slaughtered with the sword very many of those who had proved rebellious.

After these events, in the following year Carloman, inflamed by religious devotion, entrusted his kingdom, together with his son Drogo, to the hands of his brother Pippin. He came to Rome to the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, intending to persevere in the monastic order. By this succession Pippin was strengthened in the kingdom.

In the same year the Saxons attempted to rebel. For this reason Pippin was compelled to forestall them with an army. The kings of the Wends and of the Frisians also came with one accord to assist him. Seeing this, the Saxons were overcome by fear. Many of them were slaughtered, more were led into captivity, and their regions were burned with fire.

They sought peace, submitted themselves to Frankish law, as was customary, and promised that from that time forward they would pay in full the tributes that they had formerly paid to Chlothar.

Among them also, a very great multitude, seeing that they could not rebel against the Frankish assault, deprived of their own strength, asked that the sacraments of Christianity be conferred upon them.

After this had occurred, the Bavarians broke the faith which they had previously promised. For this reason Prince Pippin moved an army and entered their homeland. They fled beyond the river Inn with their wives and children.

The aforesaid prince pitched camp on the bank of the Inn and prepared a naval battle in order to pursue them to destruction. Seeing that they could not escape, the Bavarians sent envoys with many gifts, submitted themselves to his authority, and gave oaths or hostages, promising that they would never again prove rebellious.

The prince returned to Francia, and the land rested from wars for two years. During that time, after a report had been sent with the counsel of the Franks and authority had been received from the apostolic see, Pippin himself, with the consent of the Franks and the consecration of the bishops, was elevated to the kingdom.

[Thus far the manuscript codex.]

[Col. 1465]

# IX. CHRONICLE OF THE BISHOPS OF METZ BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

*(From Dom Calmet, History of Lorraine.)*

[Col. 1465]

[Col. 1465D] [Note: This illustrious man is Chrodegang, bishop, of whom Paul the Deacon writes in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz* (volume 95 of this *Patrologia*, col. 699). [Col. 1466D] This chronicle, which we reprint from Dom Calmet, begins with Bishop Angerannus, in whom Paul the Deacon concluded his *Deeds*.]

The illustrious man was succeeded by Lord Angerannus [another reading: Angilramnus], thirty-eighth in order. He was archchaplain of the palace of Charlemagne.

In his time the transfer of imperial power from the Greeks to the kings of the Franks took place, as it is said, in the following manner. The Romans, filled with furious zeal, seized Pope Leo III and wished to deprive him of his eyes, but they could not extinguish his sight completely. He fled to Charles, by whom he was honorably received; and, having been brought back to Rome with the support of an army, he was restored to his see.

For this reason, by that same pope, Charlemagne was anointed emperor in the church of Saint Peter on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, in the year 801 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

The aforesaid Angerannus, among his other good works, built the monastery of Nova Cella, in which he also rests. He governed the bishopric for thirty-three years under the popes Hadrian, the aforementioned Leo, and Stephen III. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

[Note: Elsewhere, the seventh day before the Kalends of November; elsewhere, the fourth; and in some copies, the fifth.]

After him Gundulfus, thirty-ninth bishop of Metz, was elevated; he was venerable in conduct and faith. He sat for six years during the time of Louis the Pious, under the popes Paschal and Eugenius. He died on the seventh day before the Ides of September.

After him the fortieth to ascend to the summit of the priesthood of the Church of Metz was Drogo, son of the emperor Charlemagne. He sat for thirty-two years under the popes Valentine, Gregory IV, and Sergius.

He was elevated to the honor of archbishop and served as administrator of the sacred palace.

[Note: That is, archchaplain.]

He raised from the ground the body of Saint Glodesindis, a virgin. He accomplished very many magnificent deeds, as one who exercised apostolic authority beyond the Alps throughout all Gaul.

He died in Burgundy on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

[Note: Another reading: December.]

His body was brought back from there and buried in the church of Saint John the Evangelist at Metz, where the emperor Louis the Pious, his brother, also rests in peace, together with their mother, Queen Hildegard.

[Col. 1467C] Adventius succeeded him in the bishopric, forty-first among the bishops of Metz, born of a comparatively noble family. He enlarged the church of Saint Stephen in its ornaments and treasures.

In his time Hincmar was archbishop of Rheims. Together with Adventius, at Metz, he crowned Charles after Lothair, his nephew, had been slain by divine judgment.

[Note: I read *fratruele*, that is, “his brother’s son.”]

Adventius sat for seventeen years under the popes Leo VI, Benedict, and Nicholas. Nicholas condemned Thiegaud, archbishop of Trier, and Gunther, archbishop of Cologne, supporters of King Lothair’s adultery, and annulled the council which they had held at Metz.

The aforesaid Adventius was buried at Metz in the chapel of Saint Gall. He died on the second day before the Kalends of October.

[Note: Another reading: the day before the Kalends of September.]

After him Walo was elected forty-second bishop.

He sat for six years and fifteen days.

[Note: Elsewhere: five years.]

He served under Pope John VII.

[Note: Elsewhere: John VIII.]

From him he also received the pallium. While Walo was fighting with his men against the Normans, who were then raiding Gaul, he was cut down on the third day before the Nones of April.

[Note: The fourth day before the Ides of April, in the year 883.]

His body was brought back to Metz and buried in the Church of the Savior, which he himself had built.

[Col. 1468A] Lord Robert, reformer of monasteries and of the city walls, forty-third, succeeded him. He sat for thirty-four years.

[Note: Elsewhere: thirty-three.]

He served under the popes John XI and Leo V, during the reigns of the younger kings Carloman, Louis, and Charles.

This Robert was of distinguished Alamannian lineage. He earned the pallium from the Roman pope. He either changed or renewed many of the ornaments of the monasteries, together with walls that had collapsed from age.

He died on the fourth day before the Nones of January and was buried in the church of Saint Gall.

Wigericus, forty-fourth, succeeded Robert. He sat for ten years and thirty days. He died at Metz on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March.

In his time the Hungarians, ravaging Gaul for a second time, reduced many cities and churches to ashes, and the relics of many saints were transferred from place to place. Arnulf was then reigning.

[Col. 1468B] The forty-fifth, Lord Adelbero, worthy of remembrance, succeeded Wigericus. Among his many works, he rebuilt almost completely the monastery of Gorze, which had nearly collapsed, supplying it with lands and buildings and surrounding it with a wall. In a similar manner he provided many benefits for the church of Saint Arnulf at Metz.

He sat for thirty years.

[Note: Another reading: thirty-five years.]

He also sat for nine months and twenty-five days. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of May. He awaits the day of resurrection at Gorze.

Theodoric, forty-sixth, succeeded to his episcopal mitre. He honorably built the monastery of the holy martyr Vincent in the suburb of Metz.

[Note: On the Island of the city.]

He adorned it with many relics of the saints, which he had brought with him from Italy.

[Note: Concerning that translation, see the booklet published in volume 5 of the *Spicilegium*, and the words of Sigebert under the year 970.]

His deeds are recorded. He flourished under the first emperor Otto, son of King Henry of Lorraine.

While the aforesaid Otto was reigning—

[Note: Under Otto II; Sigebert says that he died in the year 984.]

—a famous battle took place in Calabria between him and the Saracens, in which an innumerable multitude of Christians died victorious on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August.

A divine vision of the following kind was revealed to the blessed Bishop Odelric of Bavaria.

[Note: Udalric, bishop of Augsburg. Concerning the disaster inflicted upon Emperor Otto I in the year 469, see Sigebert at the relevant place in his *Chronicle*.]

He seemed to see the just Lord and Judge, in the likeness of Jesus Christ, seated upon a lofty throne, with the whole order of heaven standing around him. The examination of the balance was prepared, and the question was debated: to whom would victory belong, to the pagans or to those who profess Christ?

The iniquity and sin of the Christians had increased to such an extent that they were judged destined to be subjected to the sword of the Saracens.

The holy priest awoke and disclosed the vision to the army. They therefore applied themselves together to prayers and fasts, placing their hope of salvation in a pure confession.

Meanwhile a multitude of common people, weakened by hunger and want, withdrew from the army and arranged to fight the Saracens, preferring to perish by the sword rather than by hunger.

Thus divine mercy, which always provides for the salvation of souls, permitted them to be slain in the present life, while providing that the glory of eternal rest should be given to them.

After this tearful slaughter had taken place, while the common soldiery acted without the king’s knowledge, blessed Bishop Odelric was again carried away in a vision and, once more, as at first, saw our Redeemer and Judge upon his throne. His glorious mother Mary, together with the whole order of heaven, was pleading with him not to allow the offenses of those who confessed him to be punished by a victory of the heathen.

The balance was set up a second time, and the equality of the faithful and the unfaithful on both sides was considered. The repentance of the faithful, proceeding from the groaning of the heart, outweighed the natural justice of the law.

Behold, the martyr Lawrence was also present, whose feast day was approaching. Representing the cruelty of the torments completed in himself and his compassion for the faithful people, he obtained victory, together with the heavenly host, for the faithful people.

The priest therefore hastened to send a messenger to the emperor and ordered him to engage the enemy. Battle was joined under invocation of Christ and his martyr Lawrence. The enemy turned their backs; faith was strengthened; impiety was weakened. From that time the feast of Saint Lawrence was celebrated with greater solemnity.

His kinsman Adelbero succeeded him, the forty-seventh bishop of Metz, concerning whom many things are read that have been honorably written.

He renewed the monastery of the holy martyr Symphorian. Above all, however, he brought to completion other monasteries which his predecessors had merely begun.

Whoever wishes to know his deeds should deign to read what has been written about him. He sat for twenty-eight years. He died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January.

He was buried in the church of Saint Symphorian, where the bishops Saint Aepletius, Pappolus, Goericus, Godo, Aptatus, and Felix, distinguished by their merits, also rest.

The forty-eighth, Theodoric II, ascended to the bishopric after him. He built the principal monastery of the city for Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, having obtained the saint’s arm from the city of Besançon.

[Note: Or Byzantium. See Sigebert under the years 1004 and 1009. Sigebert under the year 1047.]

A considerable disagreement arose between him and the emperor Henry. For the sake of assistance, he distributed many ecclesiastical estates over a period of ten years, as the succession of modern accounts relates.

He ruled the see with authority for thirty years. He died on the second day before the Kalends of May and was buried in the church of Saint Stephen.

In his time Abbot Guarinus built a basilica for Saint Arnulf, which Saint Leo IX dedicated and exalted with his privilege.

[Col. 1469D] Adelbero, venerable for holiness and religious devotion, forty-ninth, succeeded him. He was a lover of peace and a restorer of monasteries.

During his time the following presided over the Roman Church: Saint Leo IX, formerly bishop of Toul; Stephen, also called Frederick, son of Duke Gothelon; and Alexander, whom Hildebrand succeeded, the one called Gregory VII.

Adelbero enlarged with his own estates the church of Saint Savior within the city, in which he rests. He died on the Ides of November, while Henry II was reigning after Conrad.

[Note: Henry III, son of Henry II and grandson of Conrad.]

From the Church of Liège, Lord Herimannus was summoned and ordained fiftieth bishop of Metz.

[Col. 1470A] At that time a great schism arose between the kingdom and the priesthood. Thus king was set over king and pope over pope; and this continued for a long time, from which point discipline declined from its former vigor.

This Bishop Herimannus, admonished by a vision, raised from the ground Saint Clement, the first teacher of the people of Metz, and died on the third day.

The blessed Clement, when carried to the mother church, gladdened the people with the greatest miracles for three days.

After the bishop’s death, he showed no signs for two days. The citizens therefore, astonished, became sad; but soon joy returned, and the cause was disclosed.

For it was revealed to a certain religious man named Lubricus, founder of the church of Saint Peter of Mount Briance, that during that delay in the signs, blessed Clement had fought most fiercely before Christ’s tribunal for the soul of the aforesaid bishop against the devil.

The enemy accused him of having acted fickly through fear of death during the dissension between kingdom and priesthood, preferring by flight to forestall the persecutions and seizures of his church, after violating the oath that is required according to imperial custom.

But blessed Clement, the shepherd, undertaking the cause of his vicar, poured out prayers on bended knee for each matter before the most merciful Judge.

What more is there to say? The divine judgment, bent by the priest’s supplication, granted pardon and ordered the accuser to keep silence under a curse.

Although there is no delay in the efficacy of divine power, nevertheless, because the essence of the Trinity judges all things in the person of Christ’s humanity, delays are said to occur according to the order of providence.

This Bishop Herimannus, taken from the Church of Liège, was buried in the church of Saint Peter at Metz, while Gregory VII presided over the universal Church and the empire was wavering. He died on the fourth day before the Nones of May, and the bishopric remained vacant for many years.

When the sea of the world was therefore tossing as if under the southwest and north winds, the Catholic people of Metz, setting aside imperial fear, elected as bishop Lord Poppo, a noble person from the Church of Trier who agreed with the Catholics. His consecration was celebrated by a legate of the apostolic see.

Imperial power, striving to impose another—namely, Adalbero—the people of Metz, firm in faith, resisted. Just as earlier they had expelled the intruders Bruno and Walo, so they also deposed this third Adalbero, excommunicated, not without great labor and danger to their possessions.

As an undaunted standard-bearer in this struggle and fearless in every conflict, Lord Adelbero, later glorious archbishop of Trier, advanced from rank to rank. From his very childhood, so to speak, he had fought in the camps of the Church for the Catholic faith, until from the schism he brought the trophy of peace to the Church.

After the death of Lord Poppo, who had proved a kindly provider for the clergy in his time, they received as bishop for the course of his life the magnificent and noble Lord Stephen, taken from the archbishopric of Vienne, consecrated by apostolic blessing in the city of Rome, and honored with the dignity of the pallium, while preserving the privilege of the Church of Trier.

Since he still flourishes in life and remains vigorous in age, let the temptation of pride arising from the plague of flattery be silent, and let prayers be offered to God for his continual zeal.

# FIRST APPENDIX: FROM ABOUT THE YEAR 1120 TO 1200

Lord Stephen, illustrious by the excellence of his lineage among both Burgundians and Lorrainers, but more illustrious in virtue and nobility of spirit, succeeded Lord Poppo in the year of the Lord 1120, namely in the second year of Pope Calixtus.

Being Calixtus’s nephew through his sister, and not yet having received the regalia from Henry V, who at that time held the stronghold of the empire, he was consecrated in the city of Rome by that supreme pontiff while the schism between kingdom and priesthood was still continuing, and was honored both with the dignity of the pallium and with the title of cardinal.

Excluded from the city of Metz for two years and more—because he did not yet possess the favor of the aforesaid prince—he celebrated his first ordinations in the place called Mount Saint-Quentin. Relying on the assistance of his brother, the count of Bar, and of his other kinsmen and friends, he recovered with astonishing speed all the estates of the bishopric that had been occupied by tyrants, except Rumilly.

[Col. 1471C] Immediately after his recent elevation, he destroyed and leveled with a strong hand the castle of Terli, which was extremely dangerous to travelers passing through those regions; the castle of the Duke at Vic; the fortification situated in a marshy place between Vic and Marsal; and likewise the castle of the count of Hombourg, which, adjoining Marsal, had long been burdensome and harmful to the entire town.

As time passed, having won imperial favor, he ascended without interruption from strength to strength. He fortified the castle called Rambervillers. He granted the noble castle of Lucelbourg, which had descended to him by hereditary right, to blessed Stephen.

The castle of Hombourg, which had descended to him by feudal right and had later been occupied by the duke of Lorraine after the death of Count Hugh, he acquired for himself and his descendants, with the assistance of Lord Frederick his father, to be held freely forever.

He also acquired for himself and for his church in perpetuity the castle of Viviers, and Duke of Luxembourg’s portion in the castle of Rucey, with all its appurtenances.

He also vigorously subdued the castle of Mirabel and Falcon’s Mount, as well as the rebellions of Danubri and Aspermont, after fortifications had been established before those castles.

At Spinal he powerfully recovered the tower called Moron, which had been occupied by the duke. Much later, because of the insolence and excessive abuses of the advocate, he besieged and captured the upper castle with the help of Duke Matthew.

Then, in recompense for this service, the duke received from him by feudal right the advocacy of Spinal.

The duke, in turn, freely and peacefully granted to blessed Stephen of Metz the allod that he possessed at Vic, to be held for all time.

The same venerable bishop, after he had blockaded for a full year and more the fortress called Petra pertusata [Note: [Col. 1471] Also Petra pertusa, Pierre-Percée, east of Badonviller], having strengthened three fortifications around it—whose traces are visible to this day—finally compelled it to surrender. Since grievous injuries had often been inflicted upon him through the fortress of Deulewart, he at last stormed it and reduced it to ashes and dust. Nevertheless, he also demolished and overturned the fortified tower at Thiecurt [Thiecourt or Thiaucourt], and the fortress situated at a place called Walteri mons [Vatimont], which were grievously harassing the bishopric. [Col. 1472B]

Nor should it be omitted among his outstanding deeds that, when a certain duke was waging war against him [La guerre; *verra* or *Werra*], he magnanimously besieged his fortress of Prigney and would unquestionably have captured it, its walls already breached, had his brother, the count of Bar, not prevented a victory already prepared and imminent. If I wished to enumerate his renowned deeds, worthy of the annals, and to set them forth in writing, the parchment would fail before the subject did.

Having sat for fourteen years under the apostolic pontiffs Callistus, Honorius, Innocent, Celestine, Lucius, Eugene, Anastasius, and Hadrian, and under the Roman princes Henry V, Lothair, Conrad, and Frederick, he migrated as a Catholic to the Lord on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, full of years and merits, while the schism of Alexander [Col. 1472C] and Victor, which had already begun, was in progress; and he deserved to be buried beside the entrance to the choir of Saint Stephen, on its right-hand side.

In the year of the Lord 1164, the lord Theoderic succeeded him, son of his brother, the count of Bar [Reginald], truly related to him both in character and in blood. His greatest concern and special care was that, under the fear of justice, the boldness both of brigands and of robbers should be restrained, and that innocence should be safe among the wicked; and wherever malice had been accustomed to rule, that the power to act maliciously should be curbed. He provided for the peace and tranquillity of the churches and for the interests of all those subject to him with such diligence that knight, clergy, and people feared him as a lord and loved him as a father. [Col. 1472D]

When he prudently and diligently confronted the evils and injuries that could daily be inflicted upon the bishopric through the fortress of Habundanges, if any other powerful man had acquired it, he acquired it for himself and his successors and built there an excellent residence.

He likewise acquired for himself and his successors Wersmnesperc and Radonis-villa [Perhaps Raville]. He made the fortress of Conflans [Conflans-en-Jarnisy] stronger than it had been and adorned it with a noble palace. When the cardinals of the heresiarch Octavian entered the city of Metz with the emperor’s very splendid envoy and attempted to compel the entire clergy to swear obedience to their idol, he bravely resisted them face to face and made them withdraw in complete shame and confusion, their business entirely unfinished, for the sake of which they had come. As a result of this deed, many cities of the Empire took from it both an example and the courage to emulate his virtue and likewise despise them. [Col. 1473A]

He sat for nine years and seven months under the supreme pontiff Alexander III, while Frederick was emperor. Because of the dangers that threatened from the schism, which was still continuing, he feared to ascend to the priestly rank and episcopal consecration; and, having remained only an elected bishop and deacon, he died as a Catholic on the third day before the Ides of August, armed with the shield of faith amid all the storms and tempests of that great schism. His sarcophagus is separated from the tomb of his predecessor and uncle, the lord Stephen, only by the entrance to the choir, so that those whom love and blood had united in life are separated in death by only a small distance between their resting places. [Col. 1473B]

By the common election of the clergy and the applause of both the knights and the citizens, he had as his successor a noble man worthy of perpetual remembrance, the lord Frederick of Plujosa. He acquired Anerey [Note: Also Ennery] for Saint Stephen. Although this man was afflicted both by extreme old age and by an incurable illness, he never laid aside his manly spirit, his generosity, or his courtliness, to which he had been devoted from the cradle. Divine mercy provided most excellently in this respect: he preserved his own powers and those of the churches entrusted to him so intact that, under his rule, they suffered no diminution and absolutely no loss. [Col. 1473D]

After he had sat for two years and as many months under the aforesaid supreme pontiff Alexander, while Frederick was emperor, remaining only an elected bishop and deacon because of the aforementioned dangers of the schism, he migrated as a Catholic to the Lord on the fifth day before the Kalends of October. He was buried in the oratory called that of Saint Gall, before the altar of blessed John the Evangelist, as he himself had requested when at the point of death. [Col. 1473C]

The fifty-fifth bishop succeeding him was Theoderic, son of the duke of Lorraine. His father, Duke Matthew, immediately after his son’s enthronement, solemnly made a donation upon the altar and bestowed upon Saint Stephen of Metz his fortress of Surkes [Note: Also Sierck], which he held as allodial property; he also placed in the hands of the same son the advocacy of Spinal, which the lord Stephen had conferred upon him, and completely renounced it [Note: *Werpire*: to abandon, relinquish, or cede; French *déguerpir*].

This bishop recovered for himself and his successors the tower situated in the middle of the fortress of Luzemburc [Luxembourg, between Phalsbourg and Saverne], which the count of Salverna [Sarverden] then held, after capturing the count himself. He sat for six years and a little more under Pope Alexander and his uncle Frederick, the emperor. He would also have accomplished other deeds worthy of arms had he not felt the strong hand of Alexander III, who annulled his election because it had been conducted while he was below the canonical orders. [Col. 1473D]

After the bishopric had remained vacant for nearly a year, in the year of the Lord 1180 it received as successor the lord Bertrannus, born in the regions of Saxony, distinguished indeed by birth, wholly commendable for the honesty of his life and character, and exceptionally learned in both divine and human law. When he had been elected at Bremen, he too had experienced the severity of Alexander III, who likewise annulled his election on this pretext, because it had been conducted while he was below the canonical orders. Public report declared that this had been done more out of hatred for the emperor Frederick, to whom he was exceedingly dear and close, than from love of justice. But blessed is the fall that is repaired for the better: he fell there so that he might rise stronger. Divine providence plainly wished him to be transferred here, so that he might prosper more greatly here and bear richer fruit. [Col. 1474A]

His beginnings and first deeds among us were these. He quickly and more easily than could be believed or hoped recalled to his own hand and table nearly all his vineyards, which his predecessor had exposed to creditors; and by imperial justice and the judgment of the princes he prudently and courageously recovered the estate of Archansiacum [Argansy or Algancy], which his same predecessor had pledged to the count of Dasburc for seven hundred pounds. [Col. 1474B]

Thereafter he built a noble residence at Vicus [the town of Vic], and acquired the fortress of Bascurt [Bassecourt] for himself and his successors. Nor should it be passed over in silence that, in the course of time, he destroyed with a strong and powerful hand a certain fortress built by Waltran, a man of the count of Bascurt, not far from Saleburc [Sarbourg], and highly harmful to the bishopric in those regions.

While matters stood thus, and he was diligently attending to the affairs of peace, religion, and justice, behold: as though the Lord wished to test him in a furnace and make his virtue shine amid the storms and tempests of this world, he permitted him to be scourged for a time by an unexpected persecution. For when he had received the lord Folmar, elect of Trier and consecrated by the supreme pontiff Urban III against the will of the emperor Frederick, in accordance with the command of that supreme prelate—which he neither ought nor dared to oppose—and, wishing to render to Caesar the things that were Caesar’s and to God the things that were God’s, had shown the respect that was due, the prince was stirred to anger and indignation. He ordered all his property to be confiscated and caused the entire bishopric of Metz to be seized [Note: Also *saisiri*, that is, to be seized and confiscated; in French, *saisir*] by his ministeriales in vengeance for this deed, as though it were some monstrous and detestable sacrilege to obey the supreme pontiff and to fear God more than man. [Col. 1474C–D]

When he heard this, he provided for the safety of his person by the protection of flight, like another Athanasius, and went to Cologne. There, in the church of Saint Gereon, where he had formerly been a canon, he cast the anchor of his hope and found there both asylum and a homeland in exile. There he received from his brothers and fellow canons, as well as from the entire clergy of Cologne and especially from the illustrious metropolitan Philip, such great respect for his person and merits, such compassion for his humiliation, and such assistance from their generosity for all his needs, that their hospitality and his exile almost made him forget his homeland. [Col. 1475A]

After two full years, when the serenity of imperial favor had been restored to him by divine assistance and by the many supplications of both princes and others, he at last returned to his church—our long-desired Job, but one restored by no means to twice his former possessions. For although, when he departed, he had left wine in the cellars, grain in the granaries, and other goods in abundance, on his return he found everything so emptied and utterly exhausted that he had to devote himself once more to renewed cares and labors and gird himself, as though from the beginning, to acquire all that is necessary for human use. May divine mercy deign to grant increase to his years and merits, and may there not be lacking someone who, in the proper place and time, will hand down his subsequent deeds to the annals and bring them to the knowledge of posterity.

## SECOND APPENDIX

Brought down to the year 1260.

[Col. 1475B]

After the lord Bertrannus, of blessed memory, the lord Conrad was elevated to the bishopric of Metz. He was a vigorous man, descended from the Teutonic race, distinguished by blood but nobler in character and virtue, and adorned among the princes of the Empire by personal beauty and bodily elegance. He had also been bishop of Speyer and chancellor of the imperial court. As a prudent and faithful steward, with discretion of mind accompanying his fidelity, he managed the affairs of the Empire so well that, not sleeping lazily over the talent entrusted to him but keeping vigilant watch, he was able to render his lord a full account of it and enter joyfully into the rest of his lord. [Col. 1475C]

Loving the beauty of the house of the Lord and the place of his dwelling, he adorned the church of Metz with exquisite ornaments. In the town of Vic, which at that time was not enclosed by any fortified defense, he established a noble fortress with high walls and towers. Although he was drawn away for most of his time to the imperial business entrusted to him and could scarcely show his presence in the diocese of Metz except rarely and briefly, nevertheless, in his absence, the reputation of his probity, prudence, and virtue acted in his place. He protected and defended the territory of the bishopric of Metz courageously against strong, noble, and powerful men as though he were present, and wisely restrained the violence of rebels both by arms and by sagacity. In the thirteenth year of his episcopate, therefore, he happily ended his life and was buried in the choir of the church of Speyer. [Col. 1475D]

The lord John, brother of the lord of Asperimont, succeeded him. The nobility of illustrious blood adorned him outwardly, while the gravity of his character illumined him inwardly. Although he was still in the flower of youth and had not reached the years required in episcopal elections, his blameless life more than made up for his lack of age. With the agreement of the clergy and the accompanying joy of the people, he was appointed bishop of Verdun. There, progressing from day to day and from good to better, he continued and increased the reputation of his goodness so greatly that, on account of the merit of his goodness and actions, he was unanimously transferred to the bishopric of Metz. [Col. 1476A]

O ineffable man! Clothed in the breastplate of justice, armed with the shield of continence, protected by the helmet of patience, and surrounded by the weapons of the virtues, he nourished those who saw him by the grace of his countenance and refreshed those who heard him by the honeyed modesty of his words. He attended the humble with dove-like simplicity, assisted his superiors with serpentine cunning, and resisted tyrants with leonine fierceness.

While he was constantly vigilant over the affairs of the church of Metz, the illustrious count of Dauborc [Dagsbourg] entered the way of all flesh. His daughter, who had succeeded to her father’s inheritance as his sole heir, earnestly asked the bishop to return to her the fief that her father had held from the bishop of Metz. The bishop returned it to her, not without the supplication and request of many nobles, [Col. 1476B] but with this condition added: if she should die without an heir of her own body, the fief itself would return in full right to the church of Metz. The condition was secured by authentic seals and likewise strengthened by the testimony of witnesses.

But when the same countess died without an heir of her own body, by a hidden judgment of God, the lord Walter, duke of Limburg and count of Luxembourg, and many other noble and powerful men of the Empire, her kinsmen and supporters, wickedly seized the fortresses belonging to the aforesaid fief, together with their dependencies, attempting to usurp and retain them under their authority forever, contrary to the obligation of the aforementioned condition. The bishop, however, who possessed a manly and courageous spirit, who was neither elated in prosperity nor cast down in adversity, resisted them powerfully and openly, with prudence accompanying his strength. Through the long danger of wars, amid the clash of arms and a labyrinth of expenses, he labored tirelessly for so long that divine providence, which does not err in its ordering of things, brought the matter to a favorable conclusion. [Col. 1476C]

For that same bishop acquired the county of Metz and four noble fortresses—namely Saraborc, Alba [Sar-albe], Turquestein, and Arestein—which belonged to the aforesaid fief, together with their dependencies, and bestowed them upon the church of Metz to possess forever. In acquiring them—not to mention the strength of the fortresses and the beauty of the sites—he doubled the revenues of his bishopric. Moreover, he exchanged the advocacy of Marsal, in which the advocate possessed much more than the lord, for certain vineyards that were of little value by comparison; and by this exchange he greatly improved the condition of his church.

When these matters had prospered for him and there was now a place for tranquillity and peace, the enemy sowed weeds and stirred up the plague of discord between him and his citizens of Metz. The aforesaid citizens, from whose fat iniquity had proceeded, lifted up in pride, burned the bishop’s town called Chates [Châtel-devant-Metz, to the west, near Saint-Germain], before Metz, blinded one cleric, and inflicted many other injuries that it would be lengthy to commit to the memory of writing. [Col. 1477A]

Since the bishop could not overlook this, after giving suitable warning, he excommunicated the citizens; and, aggravating his hand against them, he placed the city under ecclesiastical interdict. Finally, leaving the city, he withdrew to the mountain of the fortress called Saint-Germain, which he had fortified before Metz. After him, the honorable and vigorous lineage of Porta-Salis [the quarter or lineage of Porte-Seille] was also driven from the city because of the civil hatred that lay concealed among the citizens, and especially because that lineage faithfully supported the bishop in his right and adhered commendably to him. Thus not even one member of that lineage or of those attached to it remained in the city. They all departed from it and withdrew to the said fortress, their houses being utterly destroyed and all their possessions left in the city confiscated.

When the same bishop could not restrain the malice of the aforesaid citizens [Col. 1477B] by the spiritual sword, he invoked the aid of the secular arm—namely, the duke of Lorraine and the count of Bar, his faithful allies. By the bond of confederation and the intervention of an oath, a cord difficult to break, he bound them to his aid against the citizens of Metz by the right of the fidelity they owed him. But since faith is nowhere secure and brotherly favor is rare, those nobles, corrupted also by money, which often blinds even those who see it, not only abandoned the bishop whom they ought to have supported, not without the mark of treachery, but even dared to oppose him. While the danger of war continued between them for three years, those nobles and the commune of Metz, together with them, unexpectedly besieged the aforesaid lineage in the aforementioned fortress. [Col. 1477C]

When the bishop heard this—steadfast beyond steadfastness, firm in faith like Abraham, not lacking the wisdom of Solomon, not without Job’s patience, and supported by the hope of Simeon—some of his faithful clerics and laymen had abandoned him. His brother was not with him, having gone to France so that he might return with an armed force and assist him; nor could the bishop of Verdun, his kinsman, who would gladly have stood by him with a powerful hand, reach him. With fortune so greatly hostile to him, another man might have fallen into the eclipse of despair, so that no hope at all would remain for his recovery. But this man, gathering again the strength of his spirit, turned to Germany, among foreign peoples, where he sought the aid of illustrious men, the counts of Eurestein and Daborc, and many other nobles who were powerful in the possession of military forces. [Col. 1477D]

They unanimously supported him, both by entreaty and by payment; having gathered a great army, they followed him and advanced so far that they reached the river Moselle.

When some of his men advised that they should not cross the river that night, and that the bishop should not permit men exhausted by the long journey to undergo further labor by crossing that night but should postpone the crossing and give rest to the men and animals, he—who was guided more by his own judgment and ingenuity than by that of others, trusting himself more than them—forded the river Moselle with a large army, to the astonishment of many, although his adversaries firmly believed that he would not cross the Moselle thereafter. Thus not one person remained who did not cross the river. [Col. 1478A]

A marvelous thing! For if they had not crossed that night, the river rose so greatly during that very night that by morning they could not possibly have crossed it. And so those who were besieged in the fortress—whose blood their fellow citizens thirsted for savagely, and who, unable to expect relief for more than eight days, were being exposed to the danger of death—were aided by the Savior, who wills all people to be saved and no one to perish. He gave the bishop the will to cross, and the bishop crossed. Entering the lands of the aforesaid nobles, and placing the anchor of his hope in the Lord, he chose rather to entrust himself and his men to the hazard of Mars than to leave the right of his church undefended and expose his friends to the danger of death. [Col. 1478B]

When he was ready to fight them in the midst of the lands of the duke and the count, where the commune of the citizens of Metz was also present, and when the battle lines had already been drawn up in terrible array on either side, the venerable bishop of Toul came forward into the midst, kneeling, beseeching, praying, and urging the bishop of Metz to receive words of peace.

The same bishop, moved by compassion for that lineage, neither forgetful nor ungrateful for the fidelity they had long practiced toward their lords with devoted zeal, was led by pity [Note: That is, compassion; French *pitié*] to free them without danger to their persons or property, since no means of redemption or liberation was open to them except through his mediation. And because the outcomes of wars are uncertain, he chose, for their liberation, the certainty of settlement and peace. [Col. 1478C]

Thus he, moved by compassion for his people, and his adversaries, upon whom fear and trembling had suddenly fallen, brought the plague of a most grievous war to an end through a joyful peace and praiseworthy concord, with the mediation of the bishop of Toul, amid the abundant tears of many and to the confusion of the enemy of the human race. The same bishop and the faithful, strong, and steadfast lineage of Porta-Salis returned joyfully to their own homes.

In the fifteenth year of his episcopate, while the lord Pope Innocent IV presided and the lord Frederick, son of the lord Emperor Henry, reigned, he happily completed his life and was buried in the choir of the major church of Metz. (Year 1238.) [Col. 1478D]

For this man possessed what is rarely found in this age:

> A gentle life, clean hands, chaste flesh.

After him, in the vineyard of the Lord, a fruitful planting flourished harmoniously in the church of Metz: the native-born and reverend father James, bishop of Metz, descended from royal stock, brother of the noble man Matthew [Note: That is, Matthew], duke of Lorraine, and born of his father Frederick [Note: That is, Frederick], formerly duke of Lorraine, and of the sister of the count of Bar.

This bishop, born of a noble lineage, shone more brilliantly through his virtues and character. In him everything that virtues desire came together: the friendship of peace, the desire for chastity, vigor in power, distinction in vigor, kindness, wisdom tempered by prudence; and in him justice joined these elements, beauty without the envy of goodness, while implanted virtue shone forth. By the strength of peace he stifled discord; he remained unshaken amid prosperity and adversity and was surrounded on every side by the adornments of character. [Col. 1479A]

The sun and moon marveled at the beauty of his virtues. While he reigned, the concord of the whole homeland applauded him; but after his removal [Note: That is, his death], a plague did not leave it, since there is no one to heal the wounds of the troubled homeland or to extend a compassionate hand to one lying prostrate and shaken.

The diocese of Metz, which under his shadow had been the homeland’s strength and fortress of power, became weak in its resources through his eclipse and was grievously shaken by swelling storms. The Lord’s flock now almost appeared deprived of pastoral governance. In his time he bent the reins over the surrounding affairs and confined everything within the rule of law; breaking the efforts of greed, he restrained its unlawful bites. He seemed everywhere to repair, at marvelous expense, all the buildings of his diocese that had been ruined by age, strengthening weak villages, fortresses, and castles and constructing new ones; and he adorned the same diocese with very many possessions newly acquired.

At the town of Saleborc [Sarbourg], whose construction had been begun with ardent desire in the time of his predecessor, he completed the work with notable fortifications, towers and ditches, and the strongest defenses of walls. He repaired for the better the towers and walls of Alba [Sar-albe], Herrestein, and Druchetin [Turkestein], digging new cisterns. He also fortified the towns of Vic and Marsal so thoroughly that they could not be conquered by hostile attacks. Around the town of Rambervilleir, which had been surrounded by hedges, he built an enclosure of very strong walls and encircled it with the splendor of twenty-four tall towers [Note: That is, he fortified it, from *fulcio*, “to support”]. He repaired the fortress of Spinal and the town with great fortifications, and adorned the fortress of Conflans, which had nearly collapsed from the wasting of age, with towers and walls, protecting it with deep ditches. [Col. 1479B–D]

Moreover, beside the old Homborc, the watchtower of the whole world, he built a new fortress on the summit of a certain deserted mountain, still called Homborc, at enormous labor and immeasurable expense, for the defense of the entire bishopric. There the castles of the knights, citizens, inhabitants, and bishop stand out splendidly, separated from one another and distinguished by the height of their walls, the strength of their towers, and the beauty of their buildings. From the revenues of the episcopal table he established secular canons there, with sufficient revenues, appointed for the worship of the divine majesty; and he further adorned the place by constructing ponds and mills. [Col. 1479D–Col. 1480A]

Likewise, in the abbeys of Belli-Prati [Beaupré, Cistercian Order] and Salli-Vallis [Salival, Premonstratensian Order], and in other places, he erected innumerable buildings at great expense. Moreover, he acquired the fief of Albo-Monte, yielding revenues with all its dependencies, to be possessed perpetually by the bishop of Metz.

Furthermore, when the Church had drawn up its battle line against Conrad, son of the emperor Frederick, after a sentence of deposition had been pronounced against him, the same lord James came with a powerful force and an uplifted arm to the aid of the Church. Through the strength and skill of his virtue and military forces, he wonderfully put the aforesaid Conrad to flight and defeated him, sparing no immeasurable expense. [Col. 1480B]

Likewise, he acquired forever for the bishopric the fief of Maurimont, yielding revenues with its dependencies; the fief of Ruckesvignes, yielding revenues with its dependencies; and the fief of Gabondanges [Note: Habundanges is mentioned above], with its dependencies, from the illustrious man T., count called Soibert.

From the illustrious lord Henry of Salmis he acquired the fief of Pierrepersie [Note: From *petra pertusa*, “pierced stone,” mentioned above], with its dependencies and revenues, together with the homages attached to it. From the lord T. of Creincort he acquired houses with their dependencies. From the lord Wericus, called Le Vogien, he acquired a portion of his advocacy of the Valley of Faus. From the lord Peter, son of the lord Peter, formerly a knight of the New Castle, he acquired the advocacy of Castris before Metz [Châtel-devant-Metz]. He also acquired the advocacy of Metz from the advocate. [Col. 1480C]

When discord [Note: the words “there arose” are missing] existed between him and F. [Note: Frederick], duke of Lorraine, his nephew, because he was demanding from him the portion of his inheritance that came to him through his father and mother, he eventually obtained, retained, and held by peaceful agreement whatever the same duke possessed at Marsal, Vic, Remereville, Corbesal [Courbesaul], Sellacort, Rembervilleir, Sorneville, Villeines, and Bissoncourt, as is more fully contained in the documents drawn up concerning this matter. All these things, acquired through the aforesaid peace, the same bishop bestowed upon the bishopric of Metz, as is more fully contained in his documents.

After prudently governing the diocese for twenty-two years in both temporal and spiritual matters, he thereafter triumphantly fell asleep with the fathers in the Lord.

Done in the year 1260, in the month of September, while Pope Alexander IV presided in the supreme pontificate.

# ECCLESIASTICAL MONUMENTS OF THE EIGHTH CENTURY

[Col. 1481]

## NOTICE OF THE EDITOR OF THE *PATROLOGIA*

[Col. 1481]

This would be the place to reprint the many penitential books of the eighth century by authors of uncertain name, especially the *Penitential Books* edited by Marino in the appendix to his treatise on the sacrament of penance and by Martène in volume VII of the *Amplissima Collectio of Ancient Writers*. After more mature consideration, however, we judged it preferable to extend these monuments of ecclesiastical discipline to the tenth or perhaps the eleventh century, so that, after many works had been collected into one, the reader would not be burdened by the tedium of repeated investigations. We yielded our hands all the more willingly in this matter by departing from our order because, as we have heard, special studies by learned men are being prepared in Germany that will shed great light upon these ancient Penitentials.

# EXPOSITION OF THE ROMAN MASS BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR WHO SEEMS TO HAVE WRITTEN NINE HUNDRED YEARS AGO

(From Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church.*)

[Col. 1481]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 1481B]

Here we present an ancient exposition of the Roman Mass from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Alban at Angers, written seven hundred years ago. We may hope that, at least on account of its antiquity, it will not be unwelcome to devout readers. We believe that it is more than nine hundred years old, and three considerations seem to persuade us that it was written before the rites of the Roman liturgy were introduced into Gaul.

First, there is the title itself. For it appears to have been entitled *Exposition of the Roman Mass* in order to distinguish it from the other liturgies then in use, especially the Gallican liturgy.

Next is the word *contestatio*, which the author uses to designate the Preface, since that is the name by which it is customarily called in the Gallican liturgy.

Finally, toward the end the author speaks of the dismissal of the catechumens as a rite still customary in his own time, in these words:

> “The Mass, properly speaking, is at the time of the sacrifice, when the catechumens are sent outside, the deacon crying out: ‘If anyone remains, let him go outside.’ If this rite had already become obsolete when that author was writing, he would have said, not ‘they are sent outside,’ but ‘they were sent outside.’”

[Col. 1481]

# HERE BEGINS THE EXPOSITION OF THE ROMAN MASS

[Col. 1481D]

Whenever the battle lines and camps of different and opposing parties are drawn up against one another, the commanders of the troops customarily encourage each their own subordinates with exhortatory speeches, recalling the ancient victories and brave deeds of their ancestors, and declaring that God always becomes their helper in times of tribulation, and that with him it makes no difference whether he saves through many or through few. Thus, while the soldiers about to fight listen to the words of their exhorting commander, they recover some strength from the examples of their ancestors, place their highest hopes in God, and humbly advance to destroy the enemy camps, committing themselves wholly to God’s judgment; and, with him fighting on every side, they obtain victory. A trumpet is also sounded amid the very conflicts of the combatants, so that the spirit may continually be roused to hope of victory; and the more powerful the blast, the stronger the spirit becomes for battle.

Accordingly, following this military custom, the leaders of the churches have also established that, in celebrating the solemnities of the Masses, first the antiphons at the entrance should be sung, filled with praises of God and victories, through the glory of the holy and undivided Trinity. Then should be said:

> Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.

After this, a prophetic or apostolic reading, full of holy and salutary admonition, should be recited; and the Lord’s evangelical teaching, sounding forth more fully and more loftily like a trumpet, should follow the teaching of all the prophets and apostles, with the sweetnesses of wholesome song interposed and the praises of God sung in more exalted melody.

But why should we pursue each detail, when it is clear that we ought always to pray and never grow weary? What we ought to pray for, our Lord and Savior himself declares:

> Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation.

The chief of the apostles, Peter, also admonishes us, saying:

> Be sober and watchful in your prayers.

Why? Because, he says,

> your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.

If, therefore, we must watch and pray so that we may not enter into temptation, and if temptation is directed against us by the devil, our adversary, it is evident against what enemy battle line we must fight, and which enemies blessed Paul the Apostle sets, so to speak, before our eyes when he says:

> Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

These are those most powerful and most experienced enemies who cannot be defeated except by constant prayer. The same Apostle warns us, saying:

> Pray without ceasing.

For this battle, therefore, people assemble in the house of the Lord at the sacred solemnities, while the Lord himself says:

> My house shall be called a house of prayer.

But since the mind, divided among many things and disturbed by the commotion of worldly cares, cannot immediately upon entering the church forget all the anxieties of this world, so that we may be able to pour forth a purer and more attentive prayer to the Lord, the antiphon at the entrance is sung; and, with sweet melody interposed, the following are also proclaimed with mournful and extended voices:

> Kyrie eleison—that is, Lord, have mercy on us;  
> Christe eleison—that is, Christ, have mercy on us.

A prophetic, apostolic, and evangelical reading is recited. This is a preparation and an awakening of minds, so that the mind of the people, gradually drawn away from all these worldly thoughts, may be led to think about and desire heavenly things. Thus, at the time when the priest greets them and admonishes them to have their hearts on high, they may be able to answer with complete truth:

> We have them with the Lord.

For if, at the time of this very demanding response, anyone’s mind is weighed down and oppressed by worldly cares, and, while falsely claiming, protests that he has his heart on high with the Lord, he incurs punishment precisely where he could have earned forgiveness; he is struck down by the enemy precisely where he could have overcome the enemy. For it is written:

> The mouth that lies kills the soul;

and:

> He will destroy all who speak lies.

The mind of those who pray must therefore be purified and, with God’s help, lifted toward thinking about and desiring heavenly things, so that it may escape the punishment of lying and, the more vigorously it defeats its enemies by prayer, either overthrow or put them to flight.

For we must understand that, just as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul; and just as the body dies when the soul departs, so the soul dies when God departs. But if the mouth that lies kills the soul, then the mouth that speaks truth also gives life to the soul. When the mouth lies and God departs, the soul dies; but when the mouth speaks the truth and God draws near, the soul is given life—at least in those words that are good, that are spoken for the edification required by the occasion, and that give grace to those who hear them. Finally, each person’s soul among those standing there will then merit being given life by God’s mercy to the extent that he answers the priest’s admonition—“Have your heart on high”—more truthfully with his mouth; and he will be mortified by God’s displeasure all the more severely the more falsely he presumes to answer this in God’s sight.

This too must be considered with the utmost attention: although the human body has eyes, ears, nostrils, a mouth, hands, and feet, yet, when abandoned by the soul, it cannot see with its eyes, hear with its ears, smell anything with its nostrils, taste anything with its mouth, perform any work with its hands, or walk in any way with its feet. When the soul remains in the body, however, it sees through the eye, hears through the ear, smells through the nostrils, speaks through the mouth, touches something with the hands, and supplies the feet with the power to walk.

Since, therefore, the eye of the soul is that faculty by which God is either understood or seen; the ear, that by which one humbly obeys his voice; the nostrils, those by which the good fragrance of Christ is perceived; the mouth, that by which his sweetness is tasted; the hand, that by which one performs God’s work; and the foot, that by which one does not cease to advance in that same work—when God, who gives life to the soul, departs from the soul, the soul can do none of these things without him. It can neither understand nor see the Lord with a pure heart, nor incline its ear to the words of his mouth, nor receive the fragrance of his knowledge unto life, nor taste and see how sweet the Lord is, nor even conceive or perform any good work, nor run with a heart expanded by love along the way of the divine commandments.

For just as the human body receives from the soul the power to do anything, so the soul also always receives from God the power for every good thing, which it then supplies to the body. Therefore, after all that we have mentioned above, once the priest has received the people’s offering and commended it to God meanwhile in a brief prayer, he immediately breaks forth into these words:

> The Lord be with you.

Nor will we be able to raise our hearts on high, offer worthy thanks to God, or obtain that our voices may be joined to the praises of the heavenly powers, unless God is the life of our souls—namely, by his own life. The Lord Jesus, who said of himself, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life,” was also about to ascend into heaven when he promised his disciples, saying:

> Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.

And elsewhere in the Gospel he says:

> Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.

The priest therefore greets the people when he says, “The Lord be with you,” and prays that, just as the Lord has deigned to promise, he may be with his Church, in which not only two or three are gathered in his name, but also an innumerable multitude of people who believe in him.

This word of greeting—“The Lord be with you”—was not invented and composed by human ingenuity, but was adopted on heavenly and divine authority. For in the Old Testament we read that Gideon, one of the judges of the people of Israel, heard himself greeted by an angel with the words:

> The Lord is with you, most valiant of men.

And in the New Testament the angel is recorded as having greeted Mary, the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mother of God, with these words:

> Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with you.

Again, through the prophet Malachi, he says:

> The priest’s lips shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.

If, therefore, the priest who guards knowledge and announces the precepts of God’s law to the people is the angel of the Lord of hosts, then it is entirely fitting and appropriate that he should greet the people with the words by which those spirits of the heavenly homeland, endowed with the name and dignity of angels, are recorded as having greeted human beings to whom they were sent to announce something.

Nor should every priest be puffed up by this title. For it was not said that every priest is the angel of the Lord of hosts, but only that priest whose lips guard knowledge and from whose mouth the law of God, when sought, is taught. Therefore, let the one who delights in this title strive above all to possess knowledge of the divine law through understanding and to guard it through practice. Let him strive to announce to the people that same law of God, which he both understands and practices. Only then may someone confidently consider himself worthy of so great a title, namely, to be called—and to be—the angel of the Lord of hosts.

I also think that this must in no way be omitted: when bishops greet the people, they customarily proclaim not only “The Lord be with you,” but also “Peace be with you,” or “Peace to you.” Indeed, this too is not without a great mystery. For the Lord says of himself in the Gospel:

> I am the good shepherd,

and shortly afterward:

> As the Father knows me and I know the Father, so I lay down my life for my sheep.

After his resurrection, when commending these same sheep to the apostles, he also said to the most blessed Peter:

> Feed my sheep.

And, in assigning him this charge, he added that he should imitate him by dying for them:

> When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.

The evangelist says that he spoke this, signifying by what death he would glorify God.

It is therefore clear that the Lord Jesus Christ, the good shepherd, when leaving the world and returning to the Father, left Peter to feed his sheep, and in Peter the other fellow apostles of Peter, as well as all the successors of the apostles—that is, the bishops—in their proper place. These are the men who, in love and in age, assume Peter’s care: that is, they not only love the Lord Jesus, the chief of shepherds, more than others do, but are also prepared to undergo death for the sheep entrusted to them.

Acting, therefore, in the place and stead of the supreme Shepherd, they appropriately greet the sheep entrusted to them with the voice of that same supreme Shepherd. It is written in the Gospel that, when the Lord entered to his disciples through closed doors and stood among them, he greeted them with these words:

> Peace be with you.

We know that he did the same in other places also.

The bishops therefore greet the people with the voice of the supreme Shepherd, to show that, acting in the place of the supreme Shepherd, they must not only feed his sheep but also willingly embrace death for them.

Having gladly received this holy and salutary prayer and greeting of the priest, the people, lest they appear ungrateful for his greeting, greet the priest in return, saying:

> And with your spirit.

They pray that the Lord may also deign to be with the priest’s spirit. The priest therefore receives no small grace of greeting in return from the people. For just as he alone, in greeting them, prayed that the Lord might deign to be with everyone, so he himself is also greeted in return by everyone, who pray that the Lord may be with his spirit—namely, that just as the Lord is wholly with the entire people, so he may also be wholly with the priest’s spirit. For God is spirit, and therefore the people implore that he may be with the priest’s spirit.

> Lift up your hearts.

The priest, having been greeted so benevolently and reverently by the people, admonishes them to have their hearts on high, so that they may deserve to receive what they ask from the Lord.

Nor can we receive anything from above if we have hearts directed downward. What does it mean to have one’s heart on high except to seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God? What does it mean to have one’s heart on high except to set one’s mind on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth?

> For you have died, says the Apostle, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.

We ought, therefore, with all earthly desires put to death, to sigh for our life, which is hidden with Christ in God, and continually raise our hearts toward it. Those who love the world and the things that are in the world do not do this. For, as the Apostle John says:

> Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world.
