Whoever, therefore, does not mortify within himself the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes through self-restraint, but rather gives them life through lack of restraint, loves the world and the things that are in the world. But whoever loves the world, as the same Apostle says,

> does not have the love of the Father in him.

Therefore we ought to love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our mind, and with all our strength, and our neighbors—all human beings, that is—as ourselves. For if, with the inspiration of God’s grace, we are able to fulfill this, the love of the world will be able to find no place in our heart or mind. Rather, with all worldly desires trampled down and put to death, we shall be able to answer the priest who admonishes us with complete truth:

> We have them with the Lord.

If we take care to have our hearts on high, a reward of no small magnitude is promised to us. For the Apostle mentioned above says concerning those who love the world and the things that are in the world:

> The world passes away, and its desire.

But concerning those who strive to love God with their whole heart:

> Whoever does the will of the Lord remains forever, just as he himself remains forever.

Those, therefore, who incline their hearts downward and pursue the world and its desires like brute animals will themselves also pass away when the world and its desires pass away—not to a place where they may remain happily, but where they may perish eternally in misery and wretchedness.

But those who raise their hearts to God through love and continually desire their life, hidden with Christ in God, can say with the Apostle Paul:

> Yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me;

and:

> The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world;

and:

> Our way of life is in heaven.

These unquestionably do the will of the Lord. They will not pass away and perish along with the world and its desires as they pass away; rather, since the Lord remains forever, because they have done his will, they too will remain forever.

> Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.

Blessed John the Baptist says in the Gospel:

> A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.

And lest you think that you can possess something you have not received, Paul completes this very statement:

> What do you have that you did not receive?

Again, the Savior says to his disciples:

> Without me you can do nothing.

As he speaks within him, the blessed Apostle James says:

> Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration.

If, therefore, no one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven, and no one has anything that he has not received, from where could anyone receive or possess so great a love that he might always have his heart with God, unless it had been given to him from heaven? And if we can do nothing without him, through whom could we despise the world and the things that are in the world, and breathe out our whole mind and bodily strength for God alone, unless through him without whom we can do nothing?

Or how can we raise our hearts on high, when every good gift and every perfect gift descends from the Father of lights, unless the Father of lights himself confers upon us so great a gift of his grace?

The priest therefore urges us who have received such great benefits from God not to be ungrateful to the giver of benefits for the benefits received. Instead, while offering him worthy thanks for such great benefits, we should not attribute to ourselves what we do, but to him who works all things in all people, and who works in us both the willing and the doing according to his good will. Thus, while we recognize that we have nothing from ourselves and refer entirely to God everything that we have received through his gift, and while mindful of our humility we are not lifted into pride, through which we might fall into the condemnation of the devil, God may be honored in all things, through whom we possess this very humility as well.

The people, having gladly received this holy and salutary admonition, respond to the priest with great devotion:

> It is worthy and just.

Nothing is more unworthy than for anyone to be ungrateful to God, the giver of all benefits, for his benefits. Nothing is more worthy, certainly, than always to give thanks to him with all humility, even for the gifts of his grace. Through this we not only become mindful of our humility and he is praised in all things, but we also merit and obtain from him greater and more abundant benefits.

What is more unjust than to rebel against God for his benefits and swell with a proud mind? Finally, by God’s law we are commanded not to return evil for evil to our neighbors. If, therefore, it is unjust to return evil for evil to one’s neighbor, how much more unjust should we consider it to return the evils of pride to our Maker and Redeemer, the God of our neighbors, in exchange for the good things of his grace?

After this, the priest, now confident in the people’s devotion and confirming their response with a most truthful attestation—whence, unless I am mistaken, the following prayer is commonly called the “Attestation”—also raises his whole mind on high and beseeches God in exalted words:

> It is truly worthy, etc., through “to give thanks.”

> For all have sinned, says the Apostle, and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

It is therefore unquestionably worthy that the one who freely justified all sinners by his grace should receive thanks offered to him by all. It is entirely just that, because all have sinned, all lack the glory of God, and all have been justified freely by his grace when they were unable to possess merit, they should at least not cease to give thanks.

Indeed, thanksgiving is so just an offering before God that he requires it from us not only while we are established in the corruptibility of the present life, but also in the future, when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption and this mortal shall have put on immortality, and the God of gods shall be seen without interruption as he is. The Prophet bears witness to this when he says:

> Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they shall praise you.

But since the praises and thanks rendered by us to God benefit not God but us, “It is fitting and salutary” is added in this great supplication. For he is “fitting” according to nature, being called just from the equality of nature.

God created the human being not twisted by any perversity, but upright and just in every goodness, in his own image and likeness, so that he might live soberly, justly, and piously not only in that earthly happiness of paradise, but also, at some point established in a greater and spiritual happiness, might praise his Creator without end.

It is fitting, therefore, that if we wish to be just according to our nature, we should always strive to do that for which we were created: namely, while living in the present life according to the equality of our nature, to return unceasing thanks to our Creator for his benefits, and continually to desire that we may do the same in the future with our whole heart. For this is so salutary for us that we cannot possibly be saved in any other way.

Because it is fitting, we owe this to our Creator by the duty proper to our nature; because it is salutary, it is also unquestionably necessary for our eternal salvation. Whenever, therefore, as was said above, we offer praises and thanks to God, we discharge this obligation to him both because of the duty of our nature and because of the necessity of our salvation. Yet we profit him, who lacks nothing, in no way.

But anyone who wishes may carefully consider how greatly we fail if we neglect this, in the fall of our first parent. He was created in the image and likeness of God, destined eventually to be brought to equality and fellowship with the angels, and to be raised to the vision and praise of his own Creator. He was the cultivator of paradise and ruler over everything—the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts, and the whole earth. Yet, while avoiding sins and abounding in justice, he was first corrupted through pride. He not only proved ungrateful to his Creator, but desired to be like God, indeed to become God. He not only failed to attain that future happiness of his, but also lost the happiness he possessed, and encountered—or fell into—such great miseries of mortality, frailty, and calamity that everyone recognizes them by experiencing and seeing them rather than by reading about them, both in himself and in others.

Therefore, in order that we may attain from this most wretched unhappiness to that most blessed happiness, it is worthy and just before God, and fitting and salutary for us, always and everywhere to give thanks to God our Father:

Always, so that we may neither murmur over adversities nor be lifted into pride by prosperity, but may recognize that adversities come to us as the due consequence of our sins, while prosperity comes from divine condescension and mercy; and, regarding our Father’s chastisements, may beseech God that they may benefit us for salvation.

[Note: Something is missing here in the manuscript, such as “that he may be entreated” or “that he may be asked,” or something similar; or, better, *Dei* should be written in the genitive case.]

And, concerning his free goodness, let us ask that these things may not benefit us toward ruin. Let us always, gentle and humble, offer unceasing thanks, so that what the Prophet says may be fulfilled in us:

> I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth.

Then, finally, it will come to pass that we do the same everywhere—that is, in every place. For we cannot remain in any place in this world where we are not either refreshed by prosperity or afflicted by adversity.

What follows is:

> Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God.

Although “holy Lord,” “almighty Father,” and “eternal God” refer to one and the same being, these words are not repeated through needless verbosity but are proclaimed so many times because of his great veneration. For, as the Apostle says, there are many gods and many lords. Anyone who has a slave is also rightly called a lord; but a human lord who has a human being as a slave always needs service from his slave. He alone, however, is the holy Lord to whom the Prophet humbly sings and says:

> I said to the Lord, “You are my God, for you have no need of my goods.”

A human being, then, as a lord who needs the service of a slave, can be a lord because he has a slave; but he cannot be God because he needs a slave. God, however, is Lord because he needs no one’s service and, as the Psalmist says, all things serve him; he is God because he needs no one’s service. Hence he is also called the holy Lord.

For just as in the Old Testament the vessels consecrated to the Lord, the bread of the Presence, the priestly garments, and the flesh of the sacrifices are called holy because no one may touch, eat, or wear them except those to whom this has been permitted by God’s law, while they are wholly set apart from everyone else, so God the Lord is called holy because his dominion is entirely separated, without comparison, from human dominion.

He is also called God the almighty Father, so that no other may be understood to be the almighty Father besides him. For human beings, in order to be fathers of their children, must first be sons of their own fathers. God, however, is called the almighty Father because he was able not only, through the Son, to create all things from nothing and, with him, to govern all things without any labor, but also, as Father alone, not as Son, was able to beget from his own substance a Son coeternal with him, without any diminution or change. For he is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who begot a Son coeternal with himself, and from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.

He is also called the eternal God because, as the Apostle says, there are many gods, concerning whom it is written in the psalm:

> The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken;

and:

> I said, “You are gods”;

and:

> For the Lord is a great God, and a great king above all gods.

There are therefore holy angels of the Lord, and holy human beings are also gods; but they are called gods by name not by eternity, but by grace. For what has been made changeable cannot be eternal.

If the holy angels had not been created by God, we would in no way say:

> Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord,

and immediately add:

> Bless the Lord, angels of the Lord.

For whatever has not been created by God is consequently not God’s work. Likewise, when the Prophet invites not only the powers, the sun and moon, all the stars, the light, the heavens of heavens, and the waters above the heavens to praise the name of the Lord, but also all the angels, he adds:

> For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.

He plainly shows that, just like the other things he mentioned, the angels too are God’s creation and work. And if they had not been created changeable, no small part of them would ever have fallen through pride, incurring the diabolical misery while possessed of angelic dignity.

Now whoever does not know that all things are both created and changeable is not a human being but a beast. God, therefore, who had no beginning and will have no end, receiving nothing changeable and possessing nothing perishable, the Creator of all and created by no one, is alone and uniquely eternal.

To this holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, we who, through the fault of our first parent, have also become needy, weak, and temporal are unable by ourselves to offer either praises or thanks. But because the only-begotten Son of God, equally holy, equally almighty, and equally eternal with God the Father, has become mediator between us and him, through him we receive whatever heavenly grace we possess, and through him we ought to give thanks to God the Father for the benefits that he has conferred upon us through the Son.

For just as we possess nothing from ourselves, so we can offer thanks through ourselves for nothing. Since God is just in himself and immortal, while we are unjust and mortal in ourselves, God could neither spare the unjust through his justice nor in any way assist mortals through his immortality.

Therefore, the Son of God, so that he might mercifully redeem those whom he could justly punish if he wished, accepted our mortality while remaining immortal. Thus there might be one in whom the just one could unjustly taste the death that we unjust people had justly incurred; and the devil, through whose envy death entered the world, might unjustly kill the one just man and destroy all the unjust whom he appeared, as it were, to kill unjustly.

For he did not compel our first parents in paradise through threats to eat from the forbidden tree, but persuaded them through fraudulent promises. He did not use force, but gave advice; and for this reason he possessed the human being as though justly, since the human being had voluntarily subjected himself to him.

Therefore, when the Son of God was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.

For this reason God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father [lacuna].

For he is the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus. If he were pure God, there would be no other before whom he could intercede; if pure human being, there would be no one able to reconcile. Moreover, join this: God is in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. The very one with whom business must be transacted, the very one who acts, is both the one sent and the one returned, just as he himself was judged and will himself judge.

He therefore sits at the right hand of the Father, as the Apostle says, and intercedes for us as our priest, to whom it is said:

> You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

While placed on earth, he offered himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma, so that we too might present our bodies as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God, our rational service—not calves, nor the blood of bulls or goats. For it is written:

> I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks;

and:

> Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?

Rather, let us offer what follows:

> Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God, and pay your vows to the Most High.

These are the spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God which the chief of the apostles, Peter, says we ought to offer to God through Jesus Christ. Since the offering of thanks also belongs to these spiritual sacrifices, it is truly worthy and just, fitting and salutary, that we always and everywhere give thanks to the holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God.

> Through Christ our Lord.

For he truly is our Lord, who redeemed us from the slavery of the devil and from our vain way of life, not with corruptible gold and silver but with his precious blood. The blessed Apostle Paul also speaks of this price:

> You are not your own, for you were bought at a great price.

We therefore do not belong to ourselves, but are his servants, since he bought us at the great price of his blood.

It follows:

> Through whom the majesty, etc., up to “they celebrate with exultation.”

Angels are called *angeloi* in Greek, but in Latin they are interpreted as “messengers,” because they announce the Lord’s will to human beings [Col. 1491D]. The designation “angels” is the name of an office, not of a nature: they are always spirits, but they are called angels only when they are sent. The Dominions are so called because they are certain spirits of the heavenly homeland who exercise dominion over the lower ranks of angels. The Powers are those to whom hostile forces are subject; they are therefore called “Powers,” because evil spirits are restrained by their authority, so that they cannot harm as much as they desire. The Virtues are those angels through whom signs and miracles are performed in the world, and for this reason they are called Virtues. The Seraphim likewise are a multitude of angels; their name is interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as “burning” or “kindling.” They are called “burning” because no angel stands between them and God, and therefore, the nearer they stand before him, the more they are inflamed by the brilliance of the divine light.

The holy angels, then, who after the fall of the devil and his angels were established in the perseverance of eternal blessedness, and who attained such strength of steadfastness that they can no longer be turned aside by any fall or brought down by any pride, but remain firmly in the love and contemplation of God, find nothing sweet except him by whom they were created. They are also placed over places and over individual human beings. These, I say, such praiseworthy ministers of the divine majesty—of whom our Lord and Savior also says in the Gospel that they always see the face of the Father—despite such great dignity do not praise themselves or seek their own glory, but honor the majesty of the Father, whose grace has bestowed all these things upon them [Col. 1492B].

Let us therefore, human beings, imitate them as far as we can. Let us not exalt ourselves because of God’s gifts of grace, but rather let us continually return praise to him for his gifts. If those who have already been endowed with such steadfastness that they fear no fall at all continually submit themselves with complete reverence to the divine majesty, how much more ought a human being—dust, and a son of man, a worm—who, as blessed Job says, “comes forth like a flower, and is crushed, and flees like a shadow,” and never remains in the same condition, always to subject himself to his Creator with all humility, continually praising and justifying him, while always reproaching and accusing himself?

And if those spirits of the heavenly homeland who are given the name “Dominions,” because they rule over the other ranks of angels, do not exalt themselves over their dominion but reverently adore the majesty of their own Creator, how much more must a human being who is placed over other human beings in no way become inflated, but always think with a humble heart that the Lord of both himself and his subjects is in heaven!

For if, as the Psalmist says, “every living man is altogether vanity,” why does earth and ashes grow proud? And if the Powers, whom the holy Job calls “terrible,” are feared by the devil and his angels, and those beings, restrained by the authority of the Powers, cannot harm as much as they wish—if, I say, these Powers, so strong, so powerful, and so fearsome, submit themselves with complete trembling to the divine majesty and attribute such dignity as they possess to the grace of their Creator, how much more ought a human being, who fears not only that evil spirits may overcome him but even fears the worms themselves, always to keep the fear of God before his eyes, and always to tremble and be deeply afraid of him, even if he is feared by someone else!

That the heavens, together with the heavenly Virtues, celebrate the majesty of God the Father with shared exultation and praise is to be understood in this way: every creature praises God not with its voice but by its work, because the Creator is consequently understood from his creatures, and the magnificence of God is displayed in each of his works and effects.

Likewise, when the angels are said to praise, the Dominions to adore, and the Powers to tremble, this should not be understood as though the angels who praise the majesty of God neither adore nor tremble, as the Dominions and Powers do; or as though the Dominions who adore neither praise nor tremble, as the angels and Powers do; or again as though the Powers who tremble neither praise nor adore, as the angels and Dominions do [Col. 1493A]. Rather, whatever is said of each should be understood equally of all. For since it is written, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; for ever and ever they shall praise you,” anyone who believes that the Dominions and Powers dwell in the house of the Lord should not doubt that they praise the Lord for ever and ever.

For Virtues are also mentioned in the same way as angels: “Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his virtues.” Again, since it is written that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth,” if we believe that every knee of the heavenly beings bows at the name of Jesus, we shall not doubt that not only the Dominions but all the orders of angels adore both the Son and the Father [Col. 1493B].

As for the statement that the Powers tremble before the majesty of God the Father, this is not because of fear of punishment, which they do not deserve, nor because of fear of offending the Creator, which they can no longer incur, but because of reverence and honor for the divine majesty.

There are, in fact, three kinds of fear. The first is fear of punishment, of which it is said in the Psalm, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Those who have this fear begin to fear lest they be punished by the Lord for their sins. There is also fear of offending, by which God is feared by those who love him, lest he be offended even in some small matter. Of this it is said to Abraham, “Now I know that you fear God, and you have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake.” Elsewhere this same fear is called perfect love, as it is written: “Perfect love casts out fear”—namely, the fear that we placed first. The same apostle says of it: “Whoever fears is not perfected in love, because fear has punishment.”

The third kind of fear proceeds from reverence and honor. It is this by which the Powers are now said to tremble before the majesty of God. Of it, too, it is written: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever.” In the life to come there will be neither the first nor the second kind of fear; only this third kind will remain for ever and ever [Col. 1493C].

It is not only the Powers, of course, who tremble, but all the spirits of the heavenly homeland. For since the Lord says, “Whoever honors me, I will glorify; but those who despise me shall be held of no account,” it is clear that all the heavenly orders of ministers are glorified by the Creator to such an extent because he himself is honored by them all with the greatest trembling and reverence [Col. 1493D]. Finally, if they did not honor him, it is certain that they would despise him; and if they despised him, they would undoubtedly not be glorified by him but would be held of no account—like the devil and his angels, who despised him by failing to honor him, and who, by honoring themselves, fell into the disgrace and dishonor of perpetual condemnation.

In what follows also, when it is said, “The heavens, the powers of the heavens, and the blessed Seraphim celebrate with shared exultation,” it is plainly shown that the trembling of the Powers proceeds not from fear of punishment but from the honor of reverence. If the divine majesty is trembled at by all, then the blessed Seraphim, who are said to exult, must also be understood to tremble. And if the exultation of the blessed Seraphim is shared with the exultation of the other spirits [Col. 1494A], it is evident that all the orders of the good heavenly spirits both tremble before the divine majesty with exultation and exult with trembling.

I mean that trembling of which the Prophet, addressing those who tremble, gives this admonition: “Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word.” The spirit of the speaker so precisely distinguished the merits of his hearers that, although all heard him crying out, he understood the words to be addressed to the one who trembled at God’s word not through the guilt of conscience but through the effect of reverence.

Hear, then, David trembling with joy and desire: “Serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling.” And since that heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, and we believe that as many human beings ascend there as elect angels remained there, according to what is written, “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God,” it remains that those human beings who return to the heavenly homeland should also imitate there something of those ranks, revering them. Hence it immediately follows:

“With whom also our voices, etc.”

In these words the priest prays on behalf of everyone, asking that the voices of human beings, who praise the Lord with the angels’ words in humble confession, may be graciously admitted—or, that is, received and accepted—together with the blessed Seraphim.

The prophet Isaiah testifies that he saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and the Seraphim, each of whom had six wings: with two they covered his face, with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew, crying out to one another and saying:

“Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of your glory.”

The holy Church, placed on earth, therefore imitates that part of itself which has been established in heaven—not only because it praises God with humble confession, but also because it celebrates the same praises with the same words and meanings. For it follows that there should be one praise among those whose future dwelling in the house of the Lord will be one and the same.

When we say “Holy” three times in praise of God, we venerate the Trinity of persons in the ineffable mystery of the unity of the Godhead. When, however, we confess the Lord God of Sabaoth only once, we proclaim in heavenly words one God in the Trinity. For *Sabaoth* is translated from Hebrew into Latin as “of armies” or “of virtues.” This is also very frequently read in the Prophets, who say, “Thus says the Lord God of armies,” and in the Psalm it is openly said in the voice of the angels, “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of virtues” [Col. 1494D].

What follows—“The heavens and the earth are full of your glory”—shows the immensity of the divine majesty. It cannot be measured by any method or estimation. The world cannot contain it; rather, it fills the world in such a way that it itself contains the world and is not contained by the world. It is above, below, outside, and within the world: above by governing, below by sustaining, outside by directing, and within by filling. It is diffused through all things in such a way that it is not a quality of the world but the substance that creates the world, governing it without labor and containing it without burden.

Yet it is not diffused through intervals of space like a mass; it is not half in one half and half in another, and thus wholly throughout. It is not so. It is wholly in the whole heaven, wholly in the whole earth, wholly in each part, and wholly throughout all things. It is contained by no place but is wholly everywhere in itself: thus the Father, thus the Son, and thus also the Holy Spirit—one God, an undivided Trinity [Col. 1495A].

Then follows:

“Hosanna in the highest.”

“Hosanna” is interpreted as “save,” with either “your people” or “the whole world” understood. The words “in the highest” are added because Christ’s coming is not only the salvation of human beings but of the whole world, joining earthly things with heavenly things, so that every knee—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—may bow before him [Col. 1495B].

It follows:

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

This is said only of the Son of God, as the Savior himself confirms in the Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and you will receive him.”

When all that we have mentioned above has been completed, and a great silence has been made all around, the priest, with his mind fixed upon God, begins to consecrate the saving sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood. He offers it generally for the holy Catholic Church of God, for his male and female servants, and for all who stand around, whose faith is known to him and whose devotion is recognized, and who offer that same sacrifice for themselves and all that belongs to them, for the redemption of their souls, and for the hope of their salvation and safety [Col. 1495C].

He also calls upon the glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, together with the blessed apostles and martyrs of God and all the saints, for aid in his supplication, so that through their merits and prayers we may in all things be fortified by his protection.

Moreover, he prays that the Lord, being appeased, may accept the offering of his entire household, command it to be carried by the hands of his holy angel to his sublime altar, order our days in his peace, rescue us from eternal damnation, and number us among his elect flock.

All this is done in commemoration of the Lord’s death, which he tasted for a time, and by which the only-begotten Son of God mercifully freed us from condemnation to eternal death [Col. 1495D]. For he himself took bread and the cup into his holy and venerable hands, raised his eyes to heaven, gave thanks and blessed them, and gave them to his disciples to eat and drink, affirming that they were his body and blood. He said: “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me.”

This singular victim saves the soul from eternal destruction. Through its mystery it renews for us the death of the only-begotten Son, who, although he has risen from the dead and now dies no more, and although death no longer rules over him, is nevertheless, living immortal and incorruptible in himself, sacrificed again for us in this mystery of the sacred offering. His flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people; his blood is poured out no longer into the hands of unbelievers [Col. 1496A] but into the mouths of the faithful.

Let us therefore consider what kind of sacrifice this is for us, since it continually imitates the passion of the only-begotten Son for our absolution. For what believer could doubt that, at the very hour of the offering, the heavens are opened at the priest’s voice, that in the mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present, that the highest and lowest are joined, that earthly things are united with heavenly things, and that one reality is made from visible and invisible things?

For this reason these sacraments are called by secret powers—or sacred things are called *sacramenta*—because divine power works the salvation of these sacraments more secretly beneath the covering of bodily things. Therefore, whether they are administered within the Church of God by good or by wicked ministers, the gifts are nevertheless mystically enlivened by the Holy Spirit, who once appeared in apostolic times through visible works. These gifts are neither increased by the merits of good ministers nor diminished by those of wicked ones, because “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.”

I therefore think that this consecration of the Lord’s body and blood is always celebrated in silence because the Holy Spirit, remaining in them, secretly brings about the same effect of the sacraments. Hence it is called *mysterium* in Greek, because it has a hidden and concealed arrangement.

Yet when the priest performs these things, he must sacrifice himself to God in contrition of heart, because whoever celebrates the mysteries of the Lord’s passion must imitate what he performs. Thus he will truly be a sacrifice for us when he has made us ourselves a sacrifice.

“Instructed by saving precepts and formed by divine teaching” [Col. 1496C] “we dare to say”:

“Our Father, who are in heaven.”

Everything that is reported as spoken and done by divine power is a wonder even to the heavenly beings and is terrifying in its awe to mortals. But nothing so astonishes heaven, frightens earth, and causes the whole creation to tremble as the fact that a servant hears the Lord called “Father,” that the guilty person names his judge “Father,” and that an earthly creature, by its own voice, adopts itself as a son of God.

Yet we dare, because the presumption belongs not to the speaker where there is the authority of the one who commands. He himself wished us to say this, he who taught us to pray in this way: “Our Father, who are in heaven.” This does not mean that he is not on earth, but so that by this offspring you may know yourself to be heavenly. And if you confess yourself to be a son of God, live as a son of God, so that in conduct, life, and virtues you may be able to respond to such a Father [Col. 1497A].

“Hallowed be your name.”

Because you have been called a Christian by Christ, you ask that the privilege of so great a name be hallowed in you. For the name of God, which is holy in itself and for itself, is either sanctified in us by our growth [possibly: “by our conduct”], or blasphemed among the nations by our growth [or conduct].

“Your kingdom come.”

He himself says: “The kingdom of God is within you.” If it is within us, why do we pray that it may come? It exists in faith, in hope, and in expectation, but we pray that it may now come. It comes to us—not to him who reigns with the Father and always remains in his bosom—but it comes to us [Note: [Col. 1497D] Something is missing here in the manuscript]: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world” [Col. 1497B].

We say, “Your kingdom come,” so that God may reign in us in such a way that death ceases to reign in us and sin ceases to reign. “Death reigned,” he says, “from Adam until Moses.” And elsewhere: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body.”

“Your will be done, on earth as in heaven.”

Many things are now done on earth according to the will of the devil, according to the wickedness of the world, and according to the desire of the flesh. In heaven, however, nothing is done except the will of the Lord. We therefore ask that, once the devil has been destroyed, the world renewed, the body changed, the dominion of death abolished, and the rule of sin removed, there may be one and the same will of God in heaven and on earth, in God and in human beings.

“Give us this day our daily bread.”

After the heavenly kingdom we are not commanded to ask for earthly bread [Col. 1497C], since he himself forbids this when he says: “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat or what you shall drink.” But because he himself is the bread that came down from heaven, we ask and pray that we may receive from the banquet of the holy altar, for the strength of body and mind, that very bread by which we shall live eternally each day—that is, continually—today, that is, in the present life.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

By saying this, human being, you have given yourself the measure of indulgence and the limit of forgiveness: you ask the Lord to forgive you only as much as you yourself forgive your fellow servant. Therefore forgive completely the one who has offended you, if you wish to owe the Lord nothing for your own offenses. Forgive another for your own sake, if you wish to avoid the sentence of the Judge.

“And do not lead us into temptation.”

God, as it is written, tempts no one. But he is said to tempt when he abandons those who stubbornly proceed to the snares of temptation. Thus Adam fell into the ambushes of the tempter when he despised the commands of his Creator. The human being revealed by whom and through what he would be tempted when he said:

“But deliver us from evil” [Col. 1497D];

that is, from the devil, who is both the author and the origin of every evil. The devil was heavenly by nature; now he is spiritual wickedness. Older than the world in age, he is worn smooth by his practice of harming and exceedingly skilled in the art of inflicting injury. Hence he is now called not merely “evil” but “evil itself,” since everything that is evil comes from him [Col. 1498A].

This is why the human being cannot be freed by his own strength, bound as he is by carnal chains. We must therefore ask that God deliver us from the devil, who provided Christ to the earth so that Christ might conquer the devil. Let the human being cry out—let him cry out to God: “Deliver us from evil,” so that, with Christ alone conquering, he may be freed from so great an evil.

We have received the hearing of faith; we have heard the form of the Lord’s prayer. Christ teaches us to pray briefly because he wishes to grant our petitions quickly. Or what will he not give to those who ask, who gave himself to those who did not ask? Or what delay will he make in answering, who anticipated the vows of suppliants in dictating their prayers?

Nor should we be troubled by what certain people are accustomed to assert: “If God knows what we pray for, and knows before we ask what we need, we speak uselessly to one who already knows.” We are not narrators but petitioners. It is one thing to narrate to someone who does not know, another to ask someone who does know. In the former case there is information; here there is obedience. There we faithfully make something known; here we humbly beseech [Col. 1498B].

“Amen.” They placed this as the seal of the Lord’s Prayer, where we can faithfully say it. It follows:

“Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord, from all evils, past, present, and future.”

All the evils from which we ask the Lord to deliver us are either past, present, or future sins. For, above all other evils, we pray that they may not come in what follows, when it is said: “Graciously grant peace in our days.”

As the Savior says in the Gospel, “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin,” the priest therefore prays that, by releasing us from past sins and granting continual protection against present and future sins, the Lord may deign to free us from every evil [Col. 1498C]. For by committing sin we are all slaves of sin. Nor can we be freed from this kind of servitude in any other way except through the Lord’s mercy. No one can forgive sins or preserve anyone from temptation except God alone. He forgives sins not only directly but also through servants subject to him, to whom he wishes to entrust this power. To them it is said in the Gospel: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven.”

It should certainly be noted that the God whom we call “Father” in the Lord’s Prayer we call “Lord” in this prayer. We presume the former on the authority of God; the latter we offer as the duty of our devotion. In the former, grace makes us confess that we are God’s children; in the latter, nature makes us confess that we are his servants. Yet we cannot serve him worthily unless we first cease to serve sins. For the Savior says in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters.”

We therefore ask, to express it in the words of the Apostle, that, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, we may have our fruit in sanctification and our end in eternal life.

It follows:

“And with the intercession of the blessed Virgin, etc.”

When the holy Church is battered by the storm of persecution, it is accustomed to triumph most gloriously in its stronger members, but to suffer a very grave collapse in the weaker. It must be admitted that it experiences great losses in both groups, that is, among the weaker and the stronger. For when the fire of persecution consumes everything, some of the weak, tested, withdraw from the faith and perish; by their own destruction they also cause the hearts of their brothers to fear. Likewise, although the very strongest offer spectacles of their martyrdom that are wondrous to God, the angels, and human beings, they can nevertheless benefit others by example alone, not also by the word of preaching [Col. 1499A].

The priest therefore prays in these words that, just as God protects us from the stain of sins in times of prosperity, so also he may turn away the adversities of persecution from us, so that neither the weak, overcome by terror or punishment, may withdraw from the faith, nor the strong and steadfast be hindered from the duty of preaching and fraternal exhortation.

Since it is certain that the saints, after departing this life and remaining with Christ, continually pray for their brothers who remain in this world, he asks that he may obtain this through the intercessions of the blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of the greatest apostles, Peter and Paul, before God [Col. 1499B].

It follows:

“That, aided by the help of mercy, etc.”

Here is why we pray to be freed by the Lord from all evils and to be granted peace in our times: namely, so that, freed from sin and secure from every disturbance, we may be able to serve the Lord our God without fear, in holiness and righteousness, before him all our days.

Since we can neither receive nor accomplish this except through the help of the Savior, it rightly follows:

“Through the Lord, etc.” [Col. 1499C]

For our Lord and Savior himself, who with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit is one Godhead, one equality of life, and one power of giving life, says to the disciples in the Gospel: “I am the vine, and you are the branches. Whoever remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing.”

A little earlier he had said: “As a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can one who does not remain in me.”

If anyone wishes to know what it means to remain in him, let him hear him say: “As the Father loved me, so I have loved you; remain in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.”

If anyone also wishes to know what kind and how great a punishment threatens those who do not remain in him, let him hear the same voice announce: “But if anyone does not remain in me, he is cut off like a branch and is cast out, and he withers; and they gather them and throw them into the fire, and they burn.”

I think it more pleasing to hear what he himself adds concerning those who remain in him: “If you remain in me and my words remain in you, ask whatever you wish and it will be done for you” [Col. 1499D].

*Christus* is Greek; in Latin it means “anointed.” Of him the Prophet sings in the Psalm: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.”

Of him also Peter, the chief of the apostles, says in the Acts of the Apostles to Cornelius and those who were present with him: “You know what word came to all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John preached: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power” [Col. 1500A]. What the Prophet calls “the oil of gladness,” the Apostle calls “the Holy Spirit and the power of God.”

*Jehesus* [Jesus] is interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as “Savior.” The angel plainly testifies to this when he speaks to Joseph in a dream about Mary, saying: “She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jehesus; for he will save his people from their sins.”

Then, before communion, the priest cries out and says:

“May the peace of the Lord be always with you.”

Nothing without peace is pleasing to God. Nor can the one who said, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me and I in him,” remain in a heart stained by hatred and dissension. For God is not a God of dissension but of peace [Col. 1500B].

The priest therefore prays and warns that the Lord’s peace may be with us, so that the reception of the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jehesus Christ may benefit us not for guilt but for the remission of all sins. For whoever eats the Lord’s body, as the Apostle says, and drinks his cup unworthily, eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

Again, the Savior says in the Gospel: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” Therefore, if we do not eat and drink, we shall not have life in ourselves; but if we eat and drink unworthily, we shall eat and drink judgment upon ourselves.

The soul must therefore be purified, and, as far as lies within us, peace must be maintained with everyone, so that by worthily receiving the Lord’s body and blood we may escape both death and judgment and may deserve to receive life and healing through their reception [Col. 1500C].

When the following is cried out by the singers during communion:

“Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us,”

this is done so that what the blessed apostle John says may be fulfilled in us: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all injustice.”

How this happens, the same apostle shows a little earlier: “If we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jehesus his Son cleanses us from every sin” [Col. 1500D].

Again, he says later: “My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jehesus Christ the righteous; and he is the expiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world.”

These words make sufficiently clear how consistently the blessed John the Baptist testifies in the Gospel concerning our Lord and Savior when he says: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.” Of him also the prophet Isaiah says: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth; in his humiliation judgment was taken away from him.”

After the clergy or people have received communion, the prayer is customarily collected, and the deacon immediately cries out [Col. 1501A]:

“Go, the dismissal is made.”

The term *missa* properly refers to the time of the sacrifice when the catechumens are sent outside, while the Levite cries out: “If any catechumen remains, let him go outside.” It is called *missa* for this reason: those who are known not yet to have been reborn cannot be present at the sacraments of the altar [Col. 1502A].

May he himself, who commanded these heavenly and supremely saving sacraments to be celebrated in his memory, grant that we who have now been reborn by the grace of God from water and the Holy Spirit may worthily participate in them. To him, with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, belong glory and honor, might and power, for ever and ever. Amen.

# Diplomas of Pepin and Carloman, Kings of the Franks

And selected monuments of certain more distinguished Franks and Germans of the eighth century.

## I. The Capitulary of Carloman, the Prince, A.D. 742

*(Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae, etc.)*

[Col. 1501A]

The manuscripts by whose aid we have revised this constitution are the following:

1. Manuscript C of the Vatican Library, Palatine no. 577, from the end of the eighth century or the beginning of the ninth; from it Holstenius had formerly published an edition [Col. 1501C].

2. Manuscript C of the Royal Bavarian Library at Munich, formerly from Mainz, used by the distinguished Würdtwein in editing the letters of Saint Boniface, from the ninth century; several passages of it were collated again by the highly distinguished Pföringer.

3. Manuscript C of the Imperial Library at Vienna, numbered among the Theological manuscripts as no. 259, from the ninth century, which Serrarius also used in his edition.

4. Manuscript C of the Court Library at Karlsruhe, in parchment, from the tenth century, collated by the highly distinguished F. Molter, prefect of that library.

5. Manuscript C of the Royal Bavarian Library at Munich, formerly from Freising, marked C. F. 25, from the tenth century, collated by our Boehmer with the printed editions.

6. Manuscript C of Saint Mark’s Library at Venice, on paper, from the fifteenth century, which I myself collated with the printed editions, as I did manuscripts 1 and 3.

Since these very ancient manuscripts disagree unanimously with the printed editions, I am inclined to think that the latter were corrupted by the use of Benedict’s text. I have judged that the division into chapters, unknown to the manuscripts and received by Baluzius from Sirmondus, should be retained [Col. 1501D].

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, Carloman, duke and prince of the Franks, in the year 742 from the incarnation of Christ, on the second day before the Kalends of May, with the counsel of the servants of God and of my nobles, assembled the bishops who are in my kingdom, together with the presbyters, for a council and synod out of fear of Christ. These were Boniface the archbishop, Burghard, Wirtziburgensis [Note: [Col. 1501D] of Würzburg], Regenfrid, Coloniensis [Note: [Col. 1501D] of Cologne], Hwitanus, Buraburgensis [Note: [Col. 1501D] of Büraburg], Vuillabaldus, Eichstetensis [Note: [Col. 1502D] of Eichstätt], Dodanus, and Eddanus, Argentoratensis [Note: [Col. 1502D] of Strasbourg], together with their presbyters, so that they might give me counsel concerning how the law of God and ecclesiastical religion—which had been scattered and had collapsed in the days of former princes—might be restored, and how the Christian people might attain the salvation of their souls and not perish after being deceived by false priests.

By the counsel of my priests and nobles we appointed bishops throughout the cities and established over them Archbishop Boniface, who was sent by Saint Peter. We decreed that a synod should be assembled every year, so that, in our presence, the decrees of the canons and the rights of the Church might be restored and Christian religion corrected. We restored and returned to the churches the money that had been defrauded from them. We removed from the churches’ funds and degraded false presbyters, as well as adulterous or fornicator deacons and clerics, and compelled them to do penance [Col. 1502A].

### 2.

We altogether prohibited the servants of God from carrying weapons, fighting, or going on campaign or to war, except only those who have been chosen for the sake of the divine mystery—namely, to complete the solemn rites of the Mass and to carry the relics or patronage of the saints.

That is, the prince shall have with him one or two bishops together with chaplain-presbyters, and each prefect shall have one presbyter who can judge and prescribe penance to people confessing their sins [Col. 1502D].

We likewise prohibited all servants of God from hunting and wandering through the forests with dogs. Similarly, they are not to keep hawks or falcons.

3. We decreed likewise, in accordance with the holy canons, that every presbyter living in a parish be subject to the bishop in whose parish he resides; and that every Lent he render and present to the bishop an account of and the order of his ministry, whether concerning baptism, the Catholic faith, prayers, or the order of the Masses [Col. 1503A]. And whenever, according to canon law, the bishop travels through the parish among the people to confirm them, the presbyter must always be ready to receive the bishop, with the gathering and assistance of the people who are to be confirmed there. And on Maundy Thursday he must always request new chrism from the bishop, so that the bishop may stand as a witness to his chastity, life, faith, and teaching.

4. We decree that, in accordance with canonical precaution, no unknown bishops or presbyters arriving from anywhere be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry before synodal examination.

5. We decreed that, according to the canons, every bishop exercise vigilance in his parish, with the assistance of the *gravio*, who is the defender of the Church, so that the people of God do not practice pagan rites [Col. 1503B], but reject and cast away every impurity of heathenism: sacrifices for the dead; sorcerers or diviners; amulets and auguries; incantations; and sacrificial offerings which foolish people make beside churches according to pagan custom, under the names of holy martyrs or confessors, provoking God and his saints to anger; likewise those sacrilegious fires which they call *nied fyr* [“need-fire”]; and every pagan observance, whatever it may be, they must diligently prohibit.

6. We likewise decree that, after this synod, which was held on the second day before the Kalends of May, whoever among the servants of God or handmaids of Christ falls into the crime of fornication shall perform penance in prison on bread and water. If he was an ordained presbyter, he shall remain in prison for two years, and before that he shall be seen to have been scourged and flayed, after which the bishop may increase the punishment [Col. 1503C]. If a cleric or monk falls into this sin, after the third scourging he shall be sent to prison and perform penance there for a full year. Likewise, veiled nuns shall be held to the same penance, and all the hair of her head shall be shaved.

7. We decreed likewise that presbyters and deacons use not cloaks, as laymen do, but chasubles, according to the custom of the servants of God. No one shall permit a woman to live in his house. Monks and handmaids of God in monasteries shall strive to be organized and live according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, governing their own way of life [Note: [Col. 1503] Cf. Benedict, 1, 2.—Goldastus joins the two conclusions.].

## II. CAPITULARY OF THE PRINCE CARLOMANN, AT LIFTINAS, A.D. 743

[Col. 1503D]

This capitulary follows immediately after the capitulary of the year 742 in the following manuscripts: 1. the Palatine manuscript, no. 577; 2. the Mainz manuscript, now Munich; 3. the Vienna manuscript; 4. the Karlsruhe manuscript; and 6. the Venetian manuscript of Saint Mark. In manuscripts 1, 3, and 4 it is entitled: “Concerning another synodal assembly.” Goldastus gave a text emended with the aid of the Mainz manuscript. I have retained the division into chapters made by Baluze.

1. Now, in this synodal assembly, which was gathered on the Kalends of March at the place called Liftinas, all the venerable priests of God, together with the counts and prefects, agreeing with the decrees of the preceding synod, confirmed them [Col. 1504A] and promised that they wished to fulfill and observe them. And all the clergy of the ecclesiastical order—bishops, presbyters, and deacons together with the clerics—accepting the canons of the ancient fathers, promised that they wished to restore ecclesiastical laws in conduct, teaching, and ministry. The abbots and monks received the Rule of the holy Father Benedict, in order to restore the standard of regular life. We command that clerics who are fornicators and adulterers, and who have defiled holy places or monasteries while previously holding them, be removed from them and brought to penance. If, after this decree, they fall into the crime of fornication or adultery, they shall undergo the judgment of the preceding synod. The same applies to monks and nuns.

2. We decree likewise, with the counsel of the servants of God [Col. 1504B] and the Christian people, that, because of the imminent wars and persecutions of the other peoples who surround us, we may, with God’s indulgence, retain for some time a portion of the Church’s property under a precarious tenure and census, in aid of our army, on the condition that each year a solidus—that is, twelve denarii—be paid to the church or monastery from each household. The arrangement shall be such that, if the person to whom the property was lent dies, the Church shall be restored to possession of its own property. Again, if necessity requires the prince to order it, the precarious grant shall be renewed and a new document written. It must be strictly observed that the church or monasteries whose property has been granted on this precarious basis do not suffer want or poverty. But if poverty compels it, the full possession shall be restored to the church and the house of God [Col. 1504C].

3. We likewise command that, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, adulteries and incestuous marriages that are not lawful be prohibited and corrected by the judgment of the bishops; and that Christian slaves not be handed over to pagans.

4. We decreed likewise, as my father had previously commanded, that anyone who practices pagan observances in any matter be fined and condemned to fifteen solidi.

## III. CAPITULARY OF THE PRINCE PIPPIN, AT SOISSONS, A.D. 744

We have revised this constitution, formerly published by Sirmond with the aid of the Beauvais, Flemish, and Metz manuscripts and corrected by Baluze on the authority of the Metz manuscript, with the assistance of the following manuscripts: 1. Vatican manuscript no. 3827, formerly belonging to Saint Peter of Beauvais, eleventh century; 2. the Royal Paris manuscript among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75, tenth century, which plainly agrees with the Metz manuscript.

In the name of God the Trinity. In the seven hundred and forty-fourth year from the incarnation of Christ, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, under the fourteenth lunar day, in the second year of Childeric, king of the Franks, I, Pippin, duke and prince of the Franks—since it is not unknown to many how, in the name of God, with the agreement of the bishops, priests, or servants of God assembled in council, and of the counts and nobles of the Franks, we resolved to hold a synod or council at the city of Soissons [Col. 1505A]—did so in the name of God.

First, we established the Catholic faith which the 318 bishops established at the Council of Nicaea, so that it might be proclaimed throughout all our region, together with the canonical judgments of the other holy fathers, which they established in their synods; and so that the law of God and the ecclesiastical rule might be restored, since they had collapsed in ruins during the days of earlier princes.

2. Therefore, with the agreement of the bishops, priests, and servants of God, and by the counsel of my nobles, we decreed that each year we ought to renew the synod, so that the Christian people might attain the salvation of souls and heresy might not rise again among the people, as we found in Adalbert a heresy which twenty-three bishops publicly condemned with one voice. Many other priests likewise, with the consent of the prince and the people, condemned that same Adalbert, so that the people might not perish any longer, deceived by false priests [Col. 1505B].

3. Therefore, by the counsel of the priests and my nobles, we established legitimate bishops in the cities. For this reason we appointed over them the archbishops Abel [Note: [Col. 1505D] Of Rheims.] and Ardobert [Note: [Col. 1506D] Of Sens.], so that both bishops and the rest of the people might have recourse to them or to their judgments in every ecclesiastical necessity. The order of monks and handmaids of God shall remain stable according to the holy Rule. From the ecclesiastical goods that have been handed over, the monks and handmaids of God shall be supported until their needs have been satisfied; and whatever remains shall be assessed as a census. They shall not perform military service for the abbot, but shall send only as many men of their own as required. All clerics shall abstain from fornication, shall not wear lay clothing, shall not hunt with dogs, and shall not carry hawks.

4. Likewise we decreed that laymen live lawfully, abstain from various forms of fornication, consent to no perjury in the church, give no false testimony, and preserve the Church of God in every necessity. Every presbyter who is in a parish shall obey and be subject to the bishop, and shall always render to the bishop, on Maundy Thursday, an account of and the order of his ministry, and request chrism and oil. When, according to canon law, the bishop travels through the parish to confirm the people, bishops, abbots, or presbyters shall be ready to receive the bishop with the assistance required in the circumstances [Col. 1505D].

5. We decree that bishops or presbyters arriving from other regions not be received into the ministry of the Church unless they have first been examined by the bishop whose parish it is.

6. We decree absolutely that every bishop exercise vigilance in his parish so that the Christian people do not become pagan. In every city he shall establish lawful markets and measures, according to the abundance of the season.

7. Likewise we decree that all the little crosses which Adalbert had planted throughout the parishes [Col. 1506A] be consumed by fire.

8. Likewise we decree that no cleric have a woman living with him in his house, except his mother, sister, or niece.

9. Likewise we decree that no layman have a woman consecrated to God as his wife, nor his own kinswoman; that no man take another man’s wife while her husband lives, nor a woman take another man while her husband lives; for a husband ought not to dismiss his wife except when fornication has been discovered.

10. If anyone wishes to transgress this decree, which twenty-three bishops, together with other priests and servants of God, established with the consent of Prince Pippin and by the counsel of the nobles of the Franks, or wishes to violate or disregard the law [Col. 1506B], let him be judged by the prince himself, or by the bishops or counts, and let each pay the composition prescribed in the law, each according to his order. And if we observe all these things that are written above, may we find the mercy of Christ throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

+ Sign of the illustrious man Pippin, mayor of the palace.

+ Sign of Radobodo.

+ Sign of Aribert.

+ Sign of Helmigaud.

## IV. CAPITULARY OF KING PIPPIN, AT VERBERIE, A.D. 753

[Col. 1506C] We have revised the text of this constitution, published by Sirmond and Baluze from the manuscript of Saint Vincent of Metz and attributed by Sirmond, on the basis of Regino, to the assembly at Verberie, with the aid of the distinguished tenth-century Royal Paris manuscript I among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75. It also survives, as the distinguished Pforinger indicates, in manuscript 2, the Royal Munich manuscript of Ansegisus, formerly Augsburg. The evidence of Pippin’s charters dated at Verberie in March 753 seems to prove that the assembly at Verberie was held in 753, and not earlier, as Sirmond and Baluze wrote, when it is established that Pippin was made king at Soissons.

1. In the third degree they shall be separated, and, after having performed penance, if they so wish, they have permission to join themselves to others. But if they are found in the fourth degree of relationship, we do not separate them, but prescribe penance for them. Nevertheless, if the act has not yet occurred, we grant no permission to enter into a union in the fourth generation [Col. 1506D].

2. If anyone lives with his stepdaughter, he may have neither her mother nor her daughter, and neither he nor she may ever join themselves to others at any time. Nevertheless, his wife, if she so wishes and cannot remain continent, may marry another, provided that, after learning that her husband had committed adultery with his daughter, she has no carnal relations with him except by voluntarily abstaining.

3. If a presbyter has his niece as his wife, he shall dismiss her and lose his clerical rank. If another man has taken her, he shall reject her from himself. If he cannot remain continent, he may take another, since it is reprehensible for another man to have a priest’s abandoned wife.

4. However a woman may have received the veil, let her remain in it, unless someone veiled her against her will while she protested. Nevertheless, she should be admonished to remain with her veil if she wishes. If a presbyter has veiled her against her will and while she protested, he shall lose his clerical rank for this reason. If it happens that a woman presumes to veil herself without the agreement of her husband, it shall be in her husband’s power either that she remain in it or that she not.

5. If a woman has conspired with other men to kill her husband, and the husband has killed one of them in defending himself, and can prove this, the man may dismiss that wife and, if he wishes, take another [Col. 1507B]. [The woman who plotted the ambush, after being subjected to penance, shall remain without hope of marriage.]

6. If a freeborn man has taken a female slave as his wife, believing her to be freeborn, and the woman is later enslaved, [if he can redeem her from slavery, let him do so]; if she cannot be redeemed, he may, if he wishes, take another. Likewise, if a freeborn woman takes a male slave believing him freeborn, and he is later enslaved for whatever reason—unless he sold himself because poverty and hunger compelled him to do so, with her consent, and was freed from hunger by the price of her husband—she may, if she wishes, dismiss him; and if she cannot remain continent, she may marry another. Likewise, in the case of a woman who has sold herself with her husband’s consent, the same rule may apply if they separate [Col. 1507C]. Nevertheless, both must perform penance. For those who have been freed from such necessity by the price of their spouse ought to remain in such a marriage and not separate.

7. If a male slave has a female slave as his concubine, he may, if he wishes, dismiss her and take a mate of his own status, a female slave of his master; but it is better for him to retain his own female slave.

8. If a slave who has received his freedom from his master later commits adultery with the master’s female slave, then, if the master wishes it, whether he wishes it or not, he shall have her as his wife. If he dismisses her and marries another, he must absolutely dismiss the later wife and receive the woman with whom he previously committed adultery; or, while she lives, he may have no other woman.

9. If, compelled by unavoidable necessity, someone has fled to another duchy or province, or has followed his lord, to whom he could not deny his allegiance, and his wife, although she is able and can do so, refuses to follow him out of love of her relatives or her property, she shall remain unmarried for all time, as long as the husband whom she did not follow lives. But that husband, who fled to another place because necessity compelled him [if he never hopes to return to his homeland], may, if he cannot remain continent, take another wife with penance [Col. 1508A].

10. If a son sleeps with his stepmother, his father’s wife, neither he nor she may enter into marriage. But the man, if he wishes, may have another wife; nevertheless, it is better to abstain.

11. If anyone sleeps with his stepdaughter, the same judgment shall apply; and the same applies if he sleeps with his wife’s sister.

12. Whoever sleeps with two sisters, one of whom had previously been his wife, shall have neither of them; nor shall that adulterous sister, nor the man who committed adultery with her, ever take another spouse.

13. Whoever knows that his wife is a female slave and has voluntarily taken her shall remain with her thereafter always [Col. 1508B].

14. Presbyters are not to be ordained by bishops traveling through the provinces. If those presbyters are good, let them be consecrated again.

15. A degraded presbyter may, when certain necessity compels it and there is danger of death, baptize a sick person if no one else is present.

16. Clerics are not to carry weapons.

17. If a woman protests that her husband has never lived with her, let them go to the cross; and if it proves true, let them separate, and let her do what she wishes.

18. Whoever lives with his wife’s cousin shall lose his own wife and have no other. Let the woman whom he had do what she wishes. The Church does not accept this.

19. If a male or female slave has been separated from another because of a sale, they are to be admonished to remain so if we cannot reunite them [Col. 1508C].

20. A *cartellarius* who has lived with a female slave and, after dismissing her when she has received freedom from her master according to the law, has taken another, must dismiss the later woman.

21. Whoever has dismissed his wife in order that she receive the veil shall not take another [Note: [Col. 1507D] Baluze observed that Regino also cites several other chapters of the synod of Verberie; they are found in the capitulary of Compiègne (below, col. 1513), chapters 11, 13, 15, 17, 18, 21, and 22, apart from this passage in Regino, book II, chapter 223: “If a free man kills his father or mother, brother or maternal uncle, let him lose his own inheritance” [Col. 1508D]. Likewise concerning incest: “Let the bishops strive to investigate incestuous persons. If they are unwilling to repent, let them be expelled from the Church until they return to penance. If they are unwilling to obey the priests, they must be restrained by secular discipline.”]

## V. THE DOUBLE CAPITULARY OF KING PIPPIN, AT VERNEUIL, A.D. 755

We have revised the constitutions of the assembly at Verneuil with the aid of the following manuscripts: 1. the Palatine Vatican manuscript no. 577, from the end of the eighth or beginning of the ninth century, folios 71 and following; 2. Vatican manuscript no. 3827, eleventh century, formerly belonging to Saint Peter of Beauvais, folios 1–2; 3. the Royal Paris manuscript among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75, tenth century. Sirmond had published them with the aid of the same Beauvais manuscript and the manuscript of Saint Vincent of Metz. Although the edition rightly relies chiefly on the Palatine manuscript, it differs especially from earlier editions in presenting a restored text and in completing the earlier capitulary in twelve chapters; the later one is preserved in chapters 13–25 of the Beauvais manuscript and in the Paris manuscript, with which the Metz manuscript agrees.

### HERE BEGINS THE SYNOD HELD AT THE PALACE OF VERNEUIL

The sacred rules of the ancient fathers, issued as the most upright standards of the Catholic Church for the correction of mortals, would indeed have sufficed if their most holy laws had remained unharmed [Col. 1509A]. But because, as certain unsuitable circumstances arose and troubled times followed, some matters were neglected through the negligence resulting from this situation, the most glorious and religious illustrious man, Pippin, king of the Franks, therefore caused nearly all the bishops of Gaul to assemble in council at the public palace of Verneuil, wishing to restore the canonical institutions at least in part. Since the means are not now available to restore everything, he nevertheless wishes some correction to be made in what he knows to be greatly contrary to the Church of God. And if God grants him peaceful times and tranquil circumstances, he desires, according to the holy canons [Col. 1509B], with fuller assistance from divine grace, to preserve thereafter everything more fully, better, more perfectly, and in its entirety. When this has been done, let those provisions cease which, because necessity compelled it, have been excerpted more leniently from the sacred canons; and let the aforesaid canonical laws remain most firm, whole, and inviolate. Meanwhile, however, we wish these matters, as far as we can do so better, to remain unshaken and inviolable. The provisions promulgated for our common correction are set out below in distinct chapters. Issued on the second day before the Ides of July, in the fourth year of the reign of our lord Pippin, most glorious king.

1. Chapter one: That there ought to be bishops in each individual city.

2. The bishops whom we have appointed in place of metropolitans [Col. 1509C] shall be obeyed in all things by the other bishops, according to canonical institution, until we amend this more fully in accordance with canonical constitution.

3. Every bishop shall have authority in his parish over the clergy, regulars, and secular persons, for correction and amendment according to the spiritual canonical order, so that they may live in a manner pleasing to God.

4. A synod shall be held twice a year. The first synod shall be held in the first month, that is, at the Kalends of March, wherever the lord king orders, in his presence. The second synod shall be held at the Kalends of October, either at Soissons or elsewhere, wherever the bishops themselves agree at the Kalends of March. The bishops whom we have now appointed in place of metropolitans shall assemble there. The other bishops, abbots, or presbyters whom these metropolitans order to come to them shall also be brought together there at this second synod [Col. 1509D].

5. Monasteries, both of men and of women, shall live regularly according to the Rule. If they refuse to do this, the bishop in whose parish they are found must correct the matter. If he cannot, he shall report it to the man whom we have appointed metropolitan, and he shall arrange for its correction. If he too cannot correct it, they shall come before the public synod and receive a canonical sentence there. If anyone disregards the public synod, he shall either lose his rank or be excommunicated by all the bishops [Col. 1510A], and a person shall be appointed in his place at that synod, according to the word and will of the lord king or with the consent of the servants of God, to govern that flock according to the holy Rule.

6. We decree that no abbess presume to have two monasteries, nor to leave the monastery, except when compelled by hostile attack. But the lord king says that he wishes, whenever he orders any of those abbesses to come to him—once a year and with the consent of the bishop in whose parish she is—that some of them then come to him; and, by his order, if necessity arises, she may go elsewhere, but she must not stay anywhere, whether in villages [or other] places, except only as quickly as possible for going and returning. She must not leave her monastery [Col. 1510B] before sending her messenger to the lord king. If the king orders her to come, she shall come; otherwise, she shall remain in the monastery until we amend this more fully according to the canons. Likewise, the nuns must not leave the monastery. If any one of them falls into some lapse, she shall perform penance within the monastery by the counsel of the bishop. If it is necessary to bring some matter concerning their needs before the lord king or the synod, their superior or messenger must do so. Whatever gifts they wish to send to the palace, they shall send through their messengers. If there are monasteries whose poverty prevents them from fulfilling their Rule, that bishop shall ascertain the truth of the matter and report it to the lord king, so that he may arrange its correction from his alms [Col. 1510C]. If veiled women are presently found gathered there who do not wish to live regularly and are not worthy to live together with the others, the bishop or abbess shall provide a suitable place where they are to live separately under guard in a place of punishment, or work with their hands at whatever the abbess orders, until, once they have been tested, they are received into the community if they are worthy.

7. There shall be no public baptistery in any parish except where the bishop whose parish it is has established one. Only if necessity arises because of illness or some other necessity shall those presbyters whom the bishop has appointed in that parish have permission to baptize wherever the occasion occurs, so that no one dies entirely without baptism.

8. Concerning presbyters: all presbyters who are in a parish must be under the authority of the bishop in matters concerning their order. No presbyter shall presume, in that parish, either to baptize or to celebrate Mass without the permission of the bishop whose parish it is. All presbyters shall assemble at the bishop’s council. If they refuse to do what is set out above, both they and their protectors shall be judged according to canonical institution [Col. 1510D].

9. Concerning the forms of excommunication, both for clerics and for laypeople. If a presbyter has been degraded by his bishop and afterward, in contempt, presumes to perform anything belonging to his office without authorization, and is then corrected and excommunicated by the bishop [Col. 1511A], anyone who knowingly communicates with him shall know that he is excommunicated. Likewise, whatever cleric, layman, or woman commits incest, refuses to amend after being corrected by the bishop, and is excommunicated by him, anyone who communicates with that person shall likewise be excommunicated. So that you may know the nature of this excommunication: the person must not enter a church, take food or drink with any Christian, accept anyone’s gifts, offer a kiss, join in prayer, or give a greeting before being reconciled by the bishop.
