If anyone protests that he has been unjustly excommunicated, he shall have permission to come to the metropolitan bishop and be judged there according to canonical institution; meanwhile, he must observe his excommunication [Col. 1511B]. If anyone disregards all these provisions and the bishop is entirely unable to correct the matter, he shall be condemned to exile by the king’s judgment.

10. Monks who truly live according to the Rule are not to be permitted to wander to Rome or elsewhere, unless they are carrying out the obedience of their abbot. If such a situation should occur—which God forbid—and the abbot is found to be lax or negligent, or the monastery falls into the hands of laypeople, and the bishop cannot correct the matter, and there are monks there who, for the sake of God and the salvation of their souls, wish to migrate from that monastery to another, they shall have permission to do so with the consent of their bishop, so that they may save their souls.

11. Concerning those men who say that they have tonsured themselves for God [Col. 1511C], but now possess property or money and are neither under the authority of a bishop nor living according to a monastic rule: it has been decided that they shall be in a monastery under regular discipline, or under the authority of a bishop according to canonical order. If they act otherwise and, after being corrected by their bishop, refuse to amend, let them be excommunicated. The same arrangement shall be observed for veiled handmaids of God.

12. From canon 20 of Chalcedon: concerning the non-reception of clerics from another church and those who receive them without letters of commendation. Clerics serving in a church, as has already been established, may not serve in the church of another city or in the power of laypeople, but must remain where they first deserved to minister, except those who, having lost their homeland, have come to another church out of necessity. If, after this, any bishop or layman receives a cleric belonging to another church, except for a reasonable defense, it has been decided that both the one who receives him and the one who is received shall be suspended from communion until the transferred cleric has been made to return to his own church [Col. 1511D].

Manuscripts 2 and 3 continue as follows:

13. Concerning bishops without a fixed see, who have no parishes and whose ordination we do not know how it occurred: it has been decided, in accordance with the institutions of the holy fathers, that they may neither minister in another’s parish nor perform any ordination without the permission of the bishop whose parish it is. If anyone presumes to do this, he shall be suspended from office [Col. 1512A] until he comes to the synod concerning the matter and receives a sentence there according to canonical institution, except when traveling. If any cleric or layman defends such a bishop, or a presbyter, without the permission of the bishop whose parish it is, he shall be excommunicated until correction.

14. Concerning Sunday: because it has been taught to the people that on Sunday they ought not to travel with horses as with oxen and wagons, nor prepare anything for food, nor perform any work pertaining to the cleaning of the house or of a person—practices which are shown to belong more to Jewish superstition than to Christian observance—we decree that on Sunday whatever was previously permitted shall be permitted. As for agricultural work [Col. 1512B]—plowing, cutting in the vineyard, threshing, clearing land, or repairing hedges—we have judged that people should abstain from these, so that they may more easily come to church and devote themselves to prayer. If anyone is found engaged in the prohibited works listed above, the manner in which he must amend shall not be determined by lay enforcement but by the correction of priests.

15. All laymen, noble and ignoble alike, shall celebrate public weddings.

16. From canon 3 of Chalcedon: clerics are not to be agents in secular affairs; that is, they are not to undertake secular business, except in cases concerning the churches, orphans, or widows, when their bishop [or abbot] directs them to do so.

17. From canon 25 of Chalcedon: after the death of a bishop, the bishopric may not remain without a pastor for more than three months [Col. 1512C], unless such a great necessity arises that this cannot in any way be done. A bishop is to be ordained especially at the next synod when the opportunity arises.

18. No cleric shall appear before public lay courts without the permission of his bishop or abbot, according to canon 8 of the Council of Carthage. As it is written there: “Whoever, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, wishes to clear himself in public courts, even if a judgment is issued in his favor, shall lose his position. This applies in a criminal judgment. In a civil case, however, let him lose what he has won if he wishes to retain his position. For since the authority of the Church is open to him everywhere for choosing judges, he judges himself unworthy of fellowship with his brothers if, thinking ill of the whole Church, he seeks assistance from a secular court, when the Apostle commands that the cases of private Christians be brought before the Church and settled there” [Col. 1512D]. And above all, he must not cause trouble for the lord king in such cases.

19. Concerning immunities: all immunities throughout all the churches are to be preserved.

20. At another synod you granted us that, in those monasteries where monks or nuns had lived according to the Rule, the abbots or abbesses should render an account to the lord king if the monastery was royal, or to that bishop if it was episcopal, concerning what you had allotted to them from those properties so that they might live. The same applies to those villages.

21. The presbyteries which by law belong to a certain bishopric are to be held by those bishops, as you previously stated at another synod [Col. 1513A].

22. Concerning pilgrims who travel for God: no tolls are to be collected from them. As for the other tolls, let it be done as you granted: they may pass wherever legitimate exemptions have not been granted.

23. At their courts, counts or judges shall first hear and decide the cases of widows, orphans, and churches, as an act of almsgiving for the lord king; afterward, let the other cases be judged reasonably according to justice.

24. No one shall obtain an ecclesiastical rank or honor through money, because this appears to be the Simoniac heresy.

25. No bishop, abbot, or layman shall, in order to administer justice, accept a *sportula* contrary to the prohibition; for wherever such gifts intervene, justice is nullified [Col. 1513B].

## VI. CAPITULARY OF KING PIPPIN, AT COMPIÈGNE, A.D. 757

These chapters are found in the following manuscript: 1. the Royal Paris manuscript marked among the *Supplementa Latina* as no. 75, immediately after the chapters of Verberie, from which Regino also lists several of its chapters among those of Verberie. They also exist in 2. the Royal Munich manuscript, formerly Augsburg. Sirmond, the first editor from the Metz manuscript, assigned the year on the basis of the Annals of Einhard.

### HERE BEGINS THE DECREE MADE AT THE PUBLIC PALACE OF COMPIÈGNE

[Note: [Col. 1513D] The first three chapters are joined together in the printed editions.]

1. If persons are found joined in the fourth degree [of relationship], we do not separate them [Col. 1513C].

2. But if they are found in the third degree, they shall be separated.

3. And those in whom one belongs to the fourth degree and the other to the third, and who are found joined together, we separate.

4. If two people are related in the third degree, whether a man or a woman, or one in the third and the other in the fourth, and one dies, the survivor may not take the deceased person’s spouse. If they are found to have done so, they shall be separated. The same law applies to men and women.

5. If a woman puts a veil on her head without her husband’s permission, and this pleases the husband, he shall receive her again into marriage.

6. If anyone gives his Frankish stepdaughter, against her will and against the will of her mother and relatives, to a freeborn man, a slave, or a cleric [Col. 1513D], and she refuses to have him and leaves him, her relatives have the power to give her another husband. If she has another whom she later marries, they shall not be separated.

7. If a Frankish man takes a woman believing that she is freeborn, and later discovers that she is not freeborn, he may dismiss her if he wishes and take another. The same applies to a freeborn woman.

8. If a freeborn woman takes a slave, knowing at the time that he is a slave, she shall have him as long as she lives. The same law applies to men and women.

9. A Frankish man received a benefice from his lord, and took his vassal with him. The lord later died and left that vassal there. Afterward another man received the benefice, and, so that he might have the vassal more securely, gave him a woman from that benefice. He had her for some time; then, after dismissing her, he returned to the relatives of his deceased lord and took a wife there, whom he now has. It has been decided that he shall keep the woman whom he took afterward [Col. 1514A].

10. If a man, having taken a wife, discovers that she has been violated by his brother, and, after dismissing her, takes another and discovers that she too has been violated, the second wife is his lawful wife, because the man himself was not a virgin at that time. If afterward he takes a third, he shall return to the middle one; and the later woman shall have the power to join herself to another man [Col. 1514B].

11. If any man has a legitimate wife, and his brother commits adultery with her, that brother and that woman who committed the adultery shall never have a marriage together while they live. The man whose wife she was may, if he wishes, take another.

12. If someone has been baptized by a priest who was himself unbaptized, and the Holy Trinity was invoked in that baptism, he has been baptized, as Pope Sergius said. Nevertheless, he requires the laying on of the bishop’s hands. [Bishop Georgius of Rome and John the sacellarius held this opinion.]

13. If a father has violated his son’s betrothed, and afterward the son takes her, his father shall not thereafter have a wife, nor shall that woman have a husband, because it was not said that her father had remained with her. But his son, who acted in ignorance, shall take a legitimate wife.

14. In whatever manner a woman has voluntarily received the holy veil, let her remain in it and not abandon it. Georgius, bishop of Rome, and John the sacellarius agreed.

15. If anyone has held his stepson or stepdaughter before a bishop for confirmation, he shall be separated from his wife and shall not take another. Likewise, the woman shall not take another. [Georgius agreed.]

16. If a man dismisses his wife and grants her permission, for the sake of religion, to serve God within a monastery, or grants her permission outside a monastery to take the veil—as we have said, for God’s sake—the man shall take a legitimate wife. The woman shall do likewise. Georgius agreed.

17. If a man has remained in adultery with a mother and daughter, while the mother did not know that he had been with her daughter and the daughter likewise did not know that he had been with her mother, then, if that man afterward takes a wife, he shall dismiss her and shall have no wife until the day of his death. The woman whom he dismisses shall take a husband. The mother and daughter with whom he remained in adultery, both being unaware that he had been with mother and daughter, may have husbands. But if this crime comes to their knowledge, they shall dismiss their husbands and perform penance, and their husbands shall afterward take wives.

18. The same applies to two sisters: if a man has remained in adultery with one and publicly taken the other, he shall have no wife until the day of his death. If the two sisters were unaware, they may have husbands. But if it comes to their knowledge, they shall observe the rule stated above.

19. If a leprous man has a healthy wife, and he wishes to grant her permission to take a husband, the woman may take one if she wishes. The same applies to the man.

20. If a man has taken a woman and lived with her for some time, and the woman says that he did not remain with her, while the man says that he did, the truth shall be established according to the man’s testimony, because he is the head of the woman. Concerning a woman who says that her husband did not render marital intercourse to her, Georgius agreed.

21. If people flee into another country because of a feud and leave their wives, neither those men nor those women shall enter into marriage. [Georgius agreed.]

22. Concerning incest. If a man has committed incest with his mother, or with his godmother at the font and at his confirmation, or with a mother and daughter, or with two sisters, or with his brother’s or sister’s daughter, or with a niece, or with a female cousin or a more distant female cousin, or with his paternal or maternal aunt, he shall lose his property for these crimes, if he has any. And if he refuses to correct himself, no one shall receive him or give him food. If anyone does so, he shall pay 60 solidi to the lord king until that man has corrected himself. If he has no money and is free, he shall be put in prison until satisfaction has been made. If he is a slave or freedman, he shall be beaten with many blows. And if his master permits him to fall again into such a crime, that master shall pay 60 solidi to the king.

23. As for ecclesiastics, if the offender is a person of rank, he shall lose his office. Lesser clerics shall be beaten and sent to prison.

24. Concerning priests and clerics, we order that the bishop’s archdeacon, together with the count, summon them to the synod. If anyone refuses, the count shall have him compelled, and that priest or his advocate shall pay 40 solidi and come to the synod. The bishop shall have that priest or cleric judged according to canonical authority; he shall nevertheless pay 40 solidi. If anyone forcibly obstructs a priest, cleric, or incestuous person, then the count shall cause that person, placed under sureties, to come before the king together with the bishop’s envoy; and the lord king shall compel him, so that the others may amend their conduct.

## VII. Council of Attigny, A.D. 765

In the Vatican Library manuscript Palatinus 577, from the end of the eighth century, folio 6, only the names of the bishops and abbots who attended the great council held by Pippin at Attigny are preserved. Labbe published them from Holstenius’s papers in *Councils*, volume VI, page 1702; we present them again, transcribed from the unique manuscript.

The names of the bishops and abbots who gathered at the royal estate of Attigny for the sake of religion and the salvation of souls, and who, at the synodal council, wisely and beneficially defined various matters, established this also by the common decree of all: whenever any one of those whose names [Note: The manuscript reads “at daybreak.”] are written below in this list departs from this world, one hundred psalters shall be sung, and his own priests shall celebrate one hundred special Masses. The bishop himself shall complete thirty Masses personally, unless prevented by illness or some other impediment. Then he shall ask another bishop to celebrate them on his behalf. The abbots who are not bishops shall ask bishops to complete those thirty Masses in their place; their priests shall celebrate one hundred Masses, and the monks shall remember to sing one hundred psalters.

## VIII. The Capitular of King Pippin, of Uncertain Date

These chapters, first published by Pierre Pithou from what appears to have been a manuscript of Saint Vincent of Metz, and afterward reproduced by Goldast, Lindenbrog, Sirmond, and Baluze, we have revised with the aid of the royal manuscript Paris, *Supplementa Latina* no. 75, from the tenth century. At chapters 4–7 we have appended the readings of that same manuscript, which were incorrectly added to the chapters of the Synod of Ver.

Since the date and place of promulgation of the constitution are unknown, Goldast and Baluze, guided by the place where Pithou’s manuscript was found and by a statement in the *Annals of Metz* under the year 756, assigned it to the city of Metz, dating it respectively to 755 and 756; Sirmond assigned it to the year 753. But since there is no evidence even of a council held at Metz, the matter remains entirely uncertain. Perhaps the chapters were issued at the Council of Attigny.

### The Chapters of Another Synod Held under the Same Lord King Pippin Begin

**Chapter 1. Concerning incest.** If a man has committed incest in any of these cases—with a woman consecrated to God, or with his co-godmother (*commater*), or with his spiritual godmother at the font and at episcopal confirmation, or with a mother and daughter, or with two sisters, or with his brother’s daughter, or his sister’s daughter, or a niece, or with a female cousin or more distant female cousin, or with a paternal or maternal aunt—he shall lose his property for these crimes, if he has any. If he refuses to correct himself, no one shall receive him or give him food. If anyone does so, he shall pay 60 solidi to the lord king until that man has corrected himself. If he has no money and is free, he shall be put in prison until satisfaction has been made. If he is a slave or freedman, he shall be beaten with many blows. And if his master permits him to fall again into such a crime, that master shall pay those 60 solidi to the lord king.

2. As for ecclesiastics who have committed the crimes mentioned above, if the offender is a person of rank, he shall lose his office; lesser clerics shall be beaten or confined in prison.

3. Concerning priests and clerics, we order that the bishop’s archdeacon, together with the count, summon them to the synod. If anyone refuses, the count shall have him compelled, so that the priest or his advocate shall pay 60 solidi and go to the synod. The bishop shall have that priest or cleric judged according to canonical authority. The 60 solidi from that case shall be paid into the royal chapel. If anyone forcibly obstructs a priest, cleric, or incestuous person, then the count shall cause that person, placed under sureties, to come before the king together with the bishop’s envoy; and the lord king shall compel him, so that the others may amend their conduct.

[Note: Here Sirmond, and Baluze following him, inserted chapters 13 and 14 of Benedict’s Book I. Since these are absent both from the Paris manuscript and from Pithou’s edition, they should not have been admitted into the text. The matters there attributed to the constitution at Ver cannot be found in the capitular of the year 755. They are as follows:

“IV. Concerning those men who hold ecclesiastical properties by the word of the lord king: it has been ordered that they must make good, according to what they hold from those properties, the churches from which they come, and the houses of the bishopric or monastery to which they are known to belong; and they must pay there in full those rents, and those tithes and ninths, just as we ordered them at Ver. Whoever does not do this shall lose those properties.

“V. Concerning those who hold those villages or those churches: the rents and the wax which for a long time they have rendered to that bishopric, we have now ordered them to render in the same way. Whoever does not do this shall pay sixty solidi.”]

4. Concerning tolls, we order that no one collect a toll from provisions or carts, since these are not merchandise. The same applies to pack animals wherever they go. We likewise establish this concerning pilgrims who, for God’s sake, travel to Rome or elsewhere: you shall not detain them for any reason at bridges, sluices, or crossings, nor shall you bring any charge against a pilgrim on account of his bag [Note: That is, a traveling bag], nor collect any toll from them. If anyone does so, whoever proves the matter shall receive thirty of the sixty solidi, and the other thirty shall be paid into the royal chapel.

5. Concerning coinage, we establish that a pound by weight shall contain no more than 22 solidi; from those 22 solidi the moneyer shall receive 1 solidus and return the remaining coins to their owner.

6. Let immunities be preserved.

7. Concerning the administration of justice: let all administer justice, both public officials and ecclesiastics. If anyone comes to the palace on account of his case, although he has not previously brought it before that count in the assembly before the *rachimburgi*, or if his case has previously been heard before the count in the assembly before the *rachimburgi* and he has refused to accept what they lawfully judged for him, then, if he comes to the palace on account of those cases, let him be beaten. If he is a person of higher rank, the matter shall be at the king’s discretion.

If he complains that the law was not judged for him, then he shall have permission to come to the palace concerning that case. If he can prove that the law was not judged for him, the king shall have him make compensation according to the law against the person concerned. If the count or the *rachimburgi* can prove that they judged the law for him and he refused to accept it, the king shall have him make compensation to them.

The same applies to ecclesiastics: if they come to the palace to complain about their case against their superior, they shall be beaten, unless their superior has sent them concerning his own case.

## Encyclical Concerning the Performance of Litanies

Goldast assigned this letter, published from a manuscript in the Vienna Library, catalogued as Theologia 259, a ninth-century parchment manuscript among the letters of Saint Boniface, to the year 764; Baluze preserved it. Although no evident indication of that year appears in it, it is easy to believe that it was promulgated around that time, since the extremely severe winter of 764 and the incursions of Waifar into the Frankish kingdom, especially those of 761, could rightly have been called tribulations. From the annals of Moissac, which assign the famine that followed the winter to the year 762, we learn that famine followed after the winter had ended. It may therefore perhaps be conjectured that the constitution should be assigned to the following year. We have restored the text according to the Vienna manuscript.

Pippin, by the grace of God illustrious king of the Franks, to the holy lord Father Lullo, bishop. [Note: The manuscript reads “Lul., bishop.”]

We know, Your Holiness, what piety and mercy God has shown this year in this land. He sent tribulation on account of our sins; but after the great and astonishing tribulation, he gave consolation and an abundance of the fruits of the earth, which we now possess. For this and for our other reasons, we must give him thanks, because he has deigned, through his mercy, to console his servants.

It seems good to us that, without imposing a fast, each bishop should hold litanies in his diocese—not with fasting, but solely in praise of God, who has given us such abundance. Let every person give alms of his own and feed the poor. And take care to foresee and order, by our command, that every person, whether willing or unwilling, give his tithe.

Farewell in Christ.

## IX. The Aquitanian Capitular of King Pippin, A.D. 768

This appears here for the first time from the Vossian manuscript of the ninth century, folio 128. I have assigned it to Pippin’s final year. Considering chapters 1, 3, 9, 10, and 12, which seem especially to concern Aquitaine, and the capitulary of Charlemagne, from which it is clear that Pippin’s chapters 1–7, 9, and 12 had the force of law among the Aquitanians, I am convinced that this constitution was promulgated only after Waifar had been killed, when Aquitaine appeared to have been completely subdued.

### The Chapters Begin Which Our Father Pippin, of Blessed Memory, Established Synodally, and Which We Wish the People to Observe

1. Let those churches of God that have been deserted be restored, both by bishops and abbots and by laymen who hold benefices from them.

2. Let those bishops, abbots, and abbesses live according to the holy order.

3. Let whatever bishops, abbots, abbesses, or other priests require from the property of the churches for their own needs be possessed peacefully and in due order, as was already established at our synod [Note: At Bourges, A.D. 767]. If anyone has afterward taken anything from it, let him return it in full.

4. Let them take no more from the poor than they are lawfully bound to render.

5. Whoever among us holds a benefice shall work diligently there and maintain it well. Whoever does not wish to do this shall relinquish the benefice and retain his own property.

6. Whoever travels on the road, whether for military purposes or to a court, shall take nothing from his equal, except what he can buy or obtain by agreement, apart from grass, water, and wood. If the circumstances require it, let no one forbid him lodging.

7. Whoever, when he has come before us, takes anything from his equal or forcibly deprives him of it shall make triple compensation according to his law.

8. If anyone brings a complaint before us, he shall have permission to come to us, and no one shall detain him by force.

9. Concerning those benefices over which there is a dispute, we wish the persons to whom we previously gave them to retain them.

10. Let all people have their own law, both Romans and Salian Franks; and if someone has come from another province, let him live according to the law of his own homeland.

11. Let all lay and secular persons who hold church property receive grants of precarious tenure for it.

12. Whatever our envoys, together with the leading men of the country, agree upon for our benefit or for the benefit of the holy Church, let no one presume to contest.

The chapters of the late Pippin end.

## X. The Judgment of King Pippin by Which the Estate of Abaciacum in the County of Le Mans and a Portion of Sibriacum in the County of Matriacum Were Vindicated for the Dionysian Monks (A.D. 752)

(From Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, page 491.)

Pippin, illustrious king of the Franks. When, in God’s name, we were seated at Vermeria in our palace, together with our nobles and faithful men, to hear everyone’s cases and settle them by just judgment [Note: Vermeria, commonly Verberie, near the River Oise, where it receives the small river Ottenette, on the road from Senlis to Compiègne], there came the venerable Fulradus, abbot of the basilica of our special patron, the lord Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily. He brought a claim against a certain man named Gislemarus, demanding from him a certain estate of Saint Dionysius called Abaciacum, in the county of Le Mans and also of Oximense, as well as the portion at Sibriacum in the county of Matriacum which a woman named Joba, the mother of Gislemarus, had transferred by her testament to the aforesaid house of Saint Dionysius, having acted as its donor before King Chilperic. Gislemarus was wrongfully and unjustly retaining these properties.

Gislemarus himself was present, and therefore could in no way deny the matter. Instead, he acknowledged on the spot that his mother Joba had donated the above-mentioned estate of Abaciacum, in its entirety, in the county of Matriacum, to the house of Saint Dionysius by her own authority. Accordingly, in the present proceeding he appeared to have revested Fulradus, on behalf of Saint Dionysius, by his pledge, with the estates named above, Abaciacum and Sibriacum—that is, with everything that the aforesaid Joba, his mother, had donated to the house of Saint Dionysius or had held in those estates. He then declared by his staff that, in every respect, he had withdrawn from the matter against Fulradus, abbot, on behalf of Saint Dionysius.

Therefore, together with our nobles and faithful men—namely Milo, Rotgarius, Helmengandus, Chrothardus, Charichardus, Autgarius, and Wicbertus, our count of the palace, along with many others—we appeared to have judged as follows: since Gislemarus was present and could offer no explanation, we order that, because this matter was conducted and carried out in this way, Fulradus, the abbot, and his successors shall have the estates named above—Abaciacum in its entirety, with all its adjacent lands and appurtenances, wholly and completely, as an uncontested property—and also Sibriacum in the county of Matriacum, namely together with lands, buildings erected upon them, resident tenants, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, vine-plots and under-vineyards, mills, flocks with shepherds of both sexes, and everything that Joba donated by her testament to the house of Saint Dionysius, or in which she had previously acted as donor, before Chilperic, our predecessor in kingship, and Hugh, the predecessor of Fulradus the abbot. Having examined those testaments, let Fulradus hold these properties vindicated and cleared against Gislemarus. Henceforth, let all litigation between them concerning this matter be settled and at rest forever.

Issued [Note: If Pippin was crowned after the Kalends of March in the year 752, this judgment must be moved to the year 753] on the Kalends of March, in the first year of our reign, at Vermeria, successfully.

## XI. Royal Writ of King Pippin Obtained by Sigobaldus, Abbot of the Monastery of Anisola (A.D. 752)

(From Martène, volume I of the *Amplissima Collectio*.)

To all holy, apostolic, and venerable Fathers in Christ, all bishops and abbots, counts, officers of the royal household, vicars, centenarii, and all our agents, both present and future: Pippin, illustrious king of the Franks, wishing you well.

Let your charity and diligence know that Sigobaldus, abbot of the monastery of Anisola, which was built in honor of Saint Carilefus the confessor in the county of Le Mans, in the district of Labrocinus, came to us and fully commended to our hand, by his own authority, himself, the holy congregation over which he presides, and all their property. We have received and retain him and his congregation with willing spirit under our protection.

He asked—as is human—that, whenever he, the abbot, departs from this life, or whenever his successors who receive the burden of the abbacy after him succeed, no other abbot should enter that house of Saint Carilefus except one whom that holy congregation chooses from among itself and has as its abbot.

Therefore we have given him this document, confirmed by our own hand, through which we wholly ask and command you neither to presume to disturb or condemn the abbots of that place, their subordinate authorities, or the men who appear to depend upon them legally, nor to take away or diminish their possessions—unless, as we have said, they may live and remain in peace and full security under our protection and defense, and continually pray more earnestly to the Lord’s mercy on our behalf.

If cases of this kind arise against the abbots of that monastery from an adversary, or if they arise from their own men, and cannot be rightly and reasonably settled in the county without expense to them, let such cases in every respect remain suspended or reserved until they come before us. Then let them receive judgment before us according to law and justice. And so that you may believe this more certainly, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and sealed it with our ring.

Sign of Pippin, king of the Franks.

Chrodingus, ordered to review it, has reviewed it.

Given in the month of April, on the 25th day, in the first year of King Pippin’s reign. Done at the public palace of Arestal.

## XII. Royal Writ of Pippin under Boniface Concerning the Property of the Church of Saint Martin (A.D. 753)

(From D. Bouquet, from Haeda.)

[Col. 1522A]

Pippin, king of the Franks. Let it be known to all our agents, both present and future: it is fitting for everyone to lend a kindly ear to princely clemency, especially when we recognize that, for the benefit of souls, something has been granted by preceding kings and princes, our parents, to the churches. We ought to consider such grants with devoted mind and not refuse appropriate benefits, so that we may deserve to share in the reward, but rather confirm them by the strongest legal authority in our decrees.

Therefore the apostolic man and Father in Christ, Boniface, bishop of the city of Utrecht, brought before our royal clemency the fact that our predecessors and relatives, the late King Chlothar and the late Theudebert, by their authorities subscribed with their own hands, had granted in full and without diminution, from the estates of the church of Saint Martin which it presently possessed, and from whatever would thereafter be assigned to it by God-fearing people, that no public judge should enter those estates to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings or requisitions, take sureties, compel the men of that church in any matter, or demand any payment.

The aforesaid bishop Boniface showed us for rereading the orders of those princes and the confirmations of those kings, strengthened by their hands, and asserted that the benefit granted to that same church of Saint Martin by the aforesaid princes had been preserved to the present day. But, for the sake of security, he asked our Highness that our authority should once again generally confirm this concerning the same church of Saint Martin.

Out of reverence for that holy place, so that we may deserve to share in the reward, we have appeared to grant his petition with complete willingness and to confirm it in every respect. Therefore, commanding, we order that, just as it is established that the aforesaid princes granted complete immunity to the estates of the said church of Saint Martin, without the entry of judges, so henceforth, with the Lord’s help, the authorities of the earlier princes shall be preserved in every respect.

Neither you, nor your juniors or successors, nor anyone whatsoever possessing judicial power, shall presume to enter the estates of the aforesaid church which it is known to possess anywhere in our kingdom at the present time, or which will thereafter be granted or assigned to it by God-fearing people—whether free persons, dependents, or persons of any nation reside in the aforesaid estates of that church, or whether anything reverts by lawful title to that bishopric or to the church of Saint Martin—for the purpose of hearing cases, exacting fines, taking sureties, making lodgings or requisitions, compelling the men of that church for any reason, or demanding any payment.

Rather, just as these benefits were granted by the aforesaid princes to the above-named church and preserved until now, so let them be preserved thereafter; and whatever additional provisions fall under this our authority shall remain unshaken forever, by this general confirmation in God’s name. Whatever our treasury could hope to receive from them shall forever contribute to the increase of the church’s lights. And so that this authority may remain valid both in the present and in future times, with God’s help, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by our own hand.

[Col. 1523B]

Sign of the glorious Pippin, king of the Franks.

Wineramus has reviewed it.

## XIII. Royal Writ of King Pippin for the Monastery of Murbach (A.D. 753)

(From D. Bouquet, *Collection of the Histories of France*.)

Pippin, illustrious king of the Franks. It is fitting for everyone to lend a kindly ear to princely clemency, especially when we recognize that, for the benefit of souls, something has been granted by preceding kings, our predecessors, to the churches. We ought to consider this with devoted mind and not refuse any benefits, so that we may deserve to share in the reward, but rather confirm them by the strongest legal authority in our decrees.

Therefore Baldebertus, venerable man and, by God’s gift, abbot of the monastery of Vivarius of the Pilgrims, which is situated in the Alsatian county on the River Murbach and was built in honor of Saint Leodegarius, Saint Peter the Apostle, Saint Mary, and the other saints, where he is known to serve with a very large company of monks, brought before our royal clemency the fact that our predecessors had once, by their authorities subscribed with their own hands, granted complete immunity for the estates of that holy church which it presently possessed—both from the gifts of princes, including Eberhard, who founded that monastery from his alms, and from the generosity of the people of the county, as well as from whatever would thereafter be assigned there by God-fearing people.

They granted that no public judge should dare enter the estates or property of that church, either to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings or requisitions, take sureties, compel the men of that church in any case, or demand any payment there.

The aforesaid abbot Baldebertus, rector of that monastery, showed us for rereading the writ of the aforesaid predecessors [the text reads: *antecessorum* [lacuna] *dictorum*] and their confirmation, and asserted that the benefit granted to that same church had been preserved until now. But, for the sake of security, he asked our Highness that our authority should once again generally confirm this concerning that monastery and those monks.

Out of reverence for that place, so that we may deserve to share in the reward, we have appeared to grant his petition with complete willingness and to confirm it in every respect. Therefore, commanding, we order that no public judge enter the property or resources of that church to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings or requisitions, take sureties, compel the men of that church—both free and enslaved—who appear to dwell upon their lands or otherwise belong there, or demand any payments.

Rather, just as this benefit was granted by our aforesaid predecessors and, by the authority of the earlier princes, has until now been preserved for that church, so let it remain henceforth, by our authority, generally undisturbed. Whatever our treasury could hope to receive from it shall contribute to the increase of the lights of that lord Leodegarius, Saint Peter, and Saint Mary, for the stability of our kingdom. And so that this authority may remain valid in present and future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

## XIV. Diploma of King Pippin for the Fair of Saint Denis (A.D. 753)

(From Felibien, in the *Probative Documents of the History of the Abbey of Saint Denis*, page 24, from D. Bouquet.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man. To all dukes, [Col. 1524C] counts, *grafiones*, household officials, vicars, centenaries, and all officials, both present and future, as well as all our envoys traveling everywhere from the palace.

Let your prudence or dignity know that the venerable man Folrad, abbot of the basilica of our special patron Saint Denis, where that precious lord is seen to rest bodily with his companions, and the abbot himself with a very large company of monks are seen to dwell in that monastery and to serve the Lord, sent a petition to us and reported that for a long time the earlier kings—lord Dagobert and Chlodovius, and afterward Childeric and Theuderic, and the former kings Chlothar and Hilbert—as well as our maternal uncle Grimoald, mayor of the palace, and those earlier rulers themselves, had granted or confirmed to the house of Saint Denis in full all the tolls within the county of Paris from all merchants—Saxons, Frisians, and other peoples indiscriminately—from whatever counties or provinces they came for the feast of Saint Denis the martyr, both in the market itself and in the city of Paris, on that occasion, and through the villages and fields, both there and elsewhere, to trade, carry on various commerce, and purchase wine in the ports and along the various rivers on which they arrived for that feast. Accordingly, they had granted or confirmed that the toll from that occasion should belong in its entirety to the house of Saint Denis. For this reason they presented to us the commands and confirmations of the earlier kings [Col. 1524D] to be reread.

After those commands and confirmations had been reread and examined, together with the judgment established against King Hilbert and our maternal uncle Grimoald, mayor of the palace—a judgment which the agents of Saint Denis had established against the illustrious man Grimoald, mayor of the palace—they presented the document to us for rereading. Afterward Abbot Folrad and the monks of Saint Denis reported, and said this: that the toll from that market, throughout their villages and fields, ought to come wholly to the house of Saint Denis without the entry of a judge. They also said that, in the years before us, when Charles had been expelled [Note: [Col. 1525D] Mabillon, in Book VI of *De re diplomatica*, conjectures that those disturbances of Soanachildis and Gairefred occurred after the death of Theuderic of Châlons, when the leading men were disputing over supreme authority, during the five-year interregnum that intervened before the beginning of Childeric’s reign. Mabillon’s conjecture is strengthened, as he himself observes, by the authority of the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*, from chapter 10 in Acherius, *Spicilegium*, volume 3, where Abbot Wido is said to have been accused before Prince Charles of having plotted a conspiracy against him with others, and therefore to have been condemned to decapitation after the year 738, when the aforesaid Wido assumed authority over the monastery of Fontenelle. From this it is therefore clear that the conspiracy against Charles took place at that time, and from this diploma we understand that Soanachildis and Gairefred were among its participants.] through the ambition of Soanachildis, while Gairefred, count of Paris, lay in wait, they had caused four denarii to be exacted by way of a levy from each free man among the merchants and market-goers [Col. 1525B], and had taken this from them unjustly. Later Count Gairehard of Paris and his officials, having found that levy there as an established custom, exacted it from those same men: from every free man of whatever nation who came to that market, they exacted four denarii from his person, if he was free; but if he was a slave, he had to swear that he was a slave, and when those men had sworn that oath, they gave five denarii for it.

The agents of Saint Denis, Abbot Folrad, and the monks said that through this custom the market had been diminished or stripped of its resources, and that the merchants and all the peoples who were accustomed to come to that market avoided it for this reason; thus the toll belonging to the house of God had been reduced or taken away. Gairehard himself said that he had introduced no other custom into that market except what had previously been introduced by permission of Soanachildis and the aforesaid Gairefred, and what he had found there; nor did he wish to conduct matters otherwise than as the lord king desired, or as had long been the custom there in the time of the kings, or otherwise than that the toll had been granted or confirmed in its entirety to that house of God.

When we found that this matter had been handled and carried out in this way, they presented to us for rereading, together with many of our faithful men, the commands and confirmations of the earlier kings. These were Milon, Helmegand, Hildegarius, Chrothard, Drogo, Baugulf, Gislehard, Leuthfred, Raulco, Theuderic, Maganarius, Nithad, Waltharius, Vulfarius, and Wicbert, our count of the palace. In their presence we were seen to have judged, decreed, confirmed, and once again newly granted the following: from this day forward, no one exercising judicial authority, whether in the market itself, through their fields, at their ports, or from their men or merchants, nor from any peoples whatsoever who come to the aforesaid market, nor through their villages, nor from ships, ports, carts, or pack animals, shall presume to exact any toll, market fee, wheel fee, bridge fee, port fee, passage fee, *cispitaticum*, change fee, or any other exaction or customary payment, nor those four denarii from all the peoples who come there to that market—the payment which, as we have mentioned above, Soanachildis and Gairefred imposed as a custom upon those merchants—whether within the county of Paris, or in the city itself on that occasion, or anywhere else where they come for that holy feast. You, your subordinates, or your successors shall presume to exact or demand no exaction or obstruction [Col. 1526A] from them. Instead, as we have said, whatever our treasury or any of our officials might perhaps have hoped to receive from it on our behalf, all of that toll, in its entirety, shall be granted, assigned, and established as belonging to the house of God, so that in future times it may remain confirmed and established by our authority and that of the earlier kings.

For the sake of God and out of reverence for the aforesaid Saint Denis the martyr, for the remedy of our soul, for the stability of the Frankish kingdom, and for our sons and their descendants, we have granted and confirmed all this for the lights of the house of Saint Denis, and for the monks, the poor, and the pilgrims, as part of our almsgiving, so that they may be more eager to pray earnestly to the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom and for all our people, and so that it may contribute to the increase of that house of God for all ages, eternal and everlasting. And so that this confirmation of ours, having examined the judgment of King Hilbert and of the other kings, as well as that of our maternal uncle Grimoald, mayor of the palace, may be held more firmly and preserved perpetually for that holy house of God, we have decreed that it be subscribed below by our hand and sealed below with our ring.

Sign of our lord Pippin, most glorious king.

At his command, I have reviewed and subscribed it.

Given on the eighteenth day of the month of July, in the second year of our reign, happily, in the name of God.

### XV. Command of King Pippin confirming the villa of Taberniacus in the county of Paris (754).

(From Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 493.)

[Col. 1526D]

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man. We believe that we shall be joined to the eternal Judge in reward if we recognize what has been assigned to the places of the saints and, through the commands of the earlier kings subscribed by their hands and confirmed there, affirm it by our own proclamation for the love of God and in return for the saints’ merits.

Therefore let your prudence know that, at the petition of the venerable man Fulrad, abbot of the basilica of our special patron Saint Denis, where that precious martyr is seen to rest bodily with his companions, and where the abbot himself is seen to dwell with a very large company of monks and is known to serve the Lord, they reported to us that, some years ago, the illustrious man Guntald had assigned and confirmed to that basilica of lord Denis, for the remedy of his soul and with all its appurtenances, a certain villa called Taberniacus, situated in the county of Paris. Later John held that estate by a precarious grant at the petition of the illustrious man Ebroin, mayor of the palace. Likewise Frodoïn and Geruntus held it by precarious grants from Saint Denis. They presented to us for rereading the aforesaid grant or confirmation, as well as those precarious grants of the earlier king, lord Childebert, and the precarious grant of our maternal uncle Grimoald, mayor of the palace.

Since, through the unjust greed of evil men, that villa of Taberniacus had been taken away from or diminished for the house of Saint Denis, the abbot and the congregation asked our royal highness that we should secure it by our confirmation and decision. Whatever our *casindus* Teudbert held by our benefice in the above-named villa of Taberniacus—that is, together with its lands, houses, buildings, defenses, male and female slaves, tenants, inquilines, resident dependents, freedmen, and slaves, both those born there and those transferred from elsewhere, rural and urban people, [Col. 1527C] wooded lands and vineyards beneath the vines, cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards, forests, meadows, pastures, and courses of waters, livestock, possessions, movable and immovable property, every kind of cattle, and the whole revenue with its appurtenances and dependencies, both within and outside the boundaries; all acquired properties; whatever can be said or named; also those tenant holdings at Acebrelidus and Walion; and that fiscal *Warinna* through which my customary due is drawn, which Teudbert held with respect to that villa; and whatever had long before been regarded as belonging to or possessed by that villa—in the name of God, by our authority and confirmation, and for the stability of our kingdom, we grant and confirm to the aforementioned house of Saint Denis the said villa of Taberniacus, with all its integrity and security.

Whatever the rector or the congregation of Saint Denis may wish to do with it, let them have completely free and firm authority in every respect to do so. By the force of this authority of ours, let the aforesaid Abbot Fulrad hold it confirmed in his right and dominion, with the grace of God and of us, for the benefit of Saint Denis. And so that it may remain undisturbed for all ages and future times, we have decreed that it be affirmed below by our hand and sealed with our ring.

Sign of the illustrious and most glorious lord Pippin, king.

Widmar, at his command, reviewed it.

Given in the third year of our reign, at Vermeria in the palace.

### XVI. Command of King Pippin granting the monastery of Saint Denis a fortress at Mount Saint Michael in the county of Verdun (755).

(From Felibianus, *Probationes Historiae sancti Dionysii*, p. 25; from D. Bouquet.)

[Col. 1528A]

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man. It ought to be the supreme care and greatest concern of princes to examine diligently whatever is requested by the priests of Christ for the needs of the churches of God, not to deny them appropriate and suitable benefits, but to put into effect, in God’s name, whatever is undertaken for God’s sake.

Therefore let the prudence of all the faithful of God and of us, present and future, know that, for the love of God and of Saint Denis, our special patron, under whose authority Abbot Folrad is recognized as presiding and serving as custodian, we have granted to the place called Mount Saint Michael the Archangel, situated in the county of Verdun on the river Marsupia (the Marsoupe), the site and fortress which Fulfoald once gave to us for his life, because he wished to build that fortress there to receive our enemies, as was proved; and for this reason he was sent to prison. But Abbot Folrad and the congregation of Saint Denis entreated us on his behalf, and we forgave him his life, for the love of God and of lord Denis.

Therefore, for our reward and for the remedy of the soul of our lord father Charles, we give that site and fortress to the monastery of blessed lord Denis, where we were brought up, together with all the things belonging or pertaining to it: male and female slaves, lands, houses, buildings, vineyards, forests, meadows, pastures, waters and courses of waters, movable and immovable property, and whatever can be said or named, together with the clerics who are seen to serve there.

Accordingly, by this present command of ours we order and establish that, just as it is established that we acquired that site and fortress by right and the law of the Franks in our palace, so in our time and in future times Abbot Folrad and his successors, and the congregation of that holy place, shall have, hold, and possess the aforesaid place perpetually for that holy basilica. May this make them more eager always to pray without ceasing, day and night, for us and our sons, for the stability of our kingdom and of the Franks, and to implore the mercy of the Lord. As they have promised us, each day they shall recite our name both in the Masses and in their private prayers at the tomb of Saint Denis. If hereafter we are able to find an opportunity to do something for them in any place, we willingly intend to grant it to them.

And so that this authority or command of ours, which they requested of us concerning that holy house of God, may be beneficial and remain undisturbed and firm for all ages and future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 1529A] Sign of the most glorious lord Pippin, king. At his command, he reviewed and subscribed it.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth year of our reign, at Compiègne, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### XVII. Diploma of King Pippin for the monastery of Nantua (757).

(From Guichenon, in *Probationes Historiae Sebusianae*, p. 213; from D. Bouquet.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, to all bishops, counts, dukes, abbots, household officials, centenaries, vicars, and our judges, and to all our envoys traveling about.

Know that we believe the protection of our kingdom to be greatly increased if, through benevolent deliberation, we grant benefits [lacuna] suitable to the churches or places of the saints [Col. 1529B] and, with the Lord’s protection, contribute to their lasting endurance.

Therefore let your prudence know that, at the petition of the venerable man Siagrius, abbot of the monastery of Nantua, which was built in honor of blessed Mary, Mother of God, and of the apostle Saint Peter and the other saints, we have judged it appropriate to grant the following benefit for eternal recompense: no public judge shall presume to enter the villas of that monastery, which it appears to possess at the present time, whether through our gift or anyone else’s, or which divine piety may hereafter wish to enlarge in the right of that holy monastery, in order to hear cases or exact fines from any direction. Rather, the abbot himself, or his monks and their successors, shall carry out these matters under our dominion for the name of the Lord.

Therefore, being concerned that neither you, nor your subordinates or successors, nor any public judicial authority, under any pretext, should presume to enter the villas located anywhere in our kingdom, by God’s favor, belonging to that monastery [lacuna]—whether granted by royal generosity, by private persons, or by good men, or to be granted in the future—to hear disputes, exact fines for any cause, take lodging or sureties, disturb or condemn them on this account; for those persons serve there by lawful summons. Nor shall the treasury exact fines from the other servants who are seen to serve that monastery according to lawful order, within its fields, boundaries, or limits, or upon the lands of the aforesaid monastery; rather, whatever the treasury might have hoped to receive from them, through our indulgence, for future salvation, shall forever be applied by our authority to the lights of those holy places [Col. 1529D]. We have granted and bestowed all this by full donation for the name of the Lord, for the salvation of our soul, and for our succeeding descendants. Neither royal majesty nor the savage greed of judges shall attempt to oppose it.

And so that this present authority may remain inviolate, by God’s favor, for present and future times, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Sign of Pippin, most glorious king.

In the name of God, Badillo wrote this on the tenth day of August, in the sixth year of the reign. Enacted publicly at the palace of Attigny.

### XVIII. [Note: [Col. 1529D] This judgment is noteworthy both because of the judicial procedure of that time and because of the “nights” of legal delay, for which the parties were ordered to assemble at the palace so that the case might be decided before the king. For when the envoys themselves were unable to settle the dispute, the parties were summoned to the king’s hearing so that the matter might be decided in his presence. Among the ancient Franks, such days of postponement were commonly called “nights.” Charlemagne’s judgment for the year 812 likewise discusses these nights. An earlier example is found in the judgment of King Theuderic, son of the younger Chlodoveus, concerning the villa of Hildulf, where a postponement of forty nights is similarly mentioned. This manner of speaking continued into the twelfth century, as we learn from Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, in Book II, Letter 17, to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres: “In this matter,” he says, “we do not request nights according to the customs of laymen, but postponements according to the ordinances of the canons.” See the learned annotation of Sirmond on this passage, where he brings together various passages from the Capitularies.] Judgment concerning all the tolls of the market of Saint Denis, adjudicated to that monastery against Gerard, count of Paris (758).

(From Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man. The agents of Saint Denis and Abbot Folrad—Aderulf and Rodegarius—came to the palace at Compiègne on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eighth year of our reign, when we were seated to hear everyone’s cases and determine just judgments. They were seen to have brought an action against Gerard, count of Paris, because he was unjustly claiming and retaining the toll within Paris from ships, as well as the rolling and wheel tolls of the bridges, which the agents of the holy lord Denis had always received from ancient times, from the day when it had been assigned to Saint Denis.

The aforesaid Count Gerard replied that he was claiming that toll in no other way than his predecessors, who had been counts before him, had retained it for their own benefit. The aforesaid agents of Saint Denis, however, argued against him and produced the command of King Dagobert, showing how he had established that market in the county and afterward assigned and confirmed it, together with all the tolls, for the benefit of Saint Denis.

Lord King Pippin himself affirmed that, from his childhood onward, he had always seen those tolls held and collected for the benefit of Saint Denis. But Count Gerard in no way consented to this. They then established such a judgment that they should come together again at the same palace for the legally appointed nights and, before the aforementioned lord Pippin, should settle the dispute, as the law prescribed.

Finally, when the aforesaid envoys and advocates of Saint Denis, Aderulf and Rotgarius, came to the agreed hearing on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, they presented witnesses who had received those tolls in Paris, with all their integrity, for the benefit of Saint Denis. Then Widon, Raulco, Milo, Helmengand, Rothard, Gislehard, and many others, together with Wicbert, our count of the palace, adjudged that the party of Saint Denis, or its aforesaid advocates, ought to prove this. They were seen to have done so in the present matter.

The aforesaid Count Gerard then replied that he did not wish to do otherwise than as the law required and as the lord king and his faithful men who were seated there desired. Accordingly, Gerard himself declared before them that he withdrew from the aforesaid tolls. Therefore, it was then appropriate and necessary for them to receive such a record of this act that, from this day forward, the party of Saint Denis and its agents might remain secure and undisturbed with respect to those tolls, so that thereafter the dispute between them might at all times be quiet and settled.

Sign + of the most glorious lord Pippin, king.

At his command, I have reviewed and subscribed it.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of November, in the year stated above, happily, in the name of God.

### XIX. Diploma of Pippin, king of the Franks, by which he confirms the possessions of the monastery of Honau. Given on 15 December 759.

(From Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man. To all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, household officials, vicars, centenaries, and all our envoys traveling about, present and future.

Know that we believe the protection of our kingdom to be greatly increased if, through benevolent deliberation, we grant suitable benefits to the churches and, with the Lord’s protection, trust that they will endure securely.

Therefore let your prudence know that, at the petition of the venerable man Dubanus, bishop, we are seen to have granted the following benefit for eternal recompense: no public judge shall at any time presume to enter the villas or property of the church of Saint Michael the Archangel, belonging to the monastery built on the island of the Rhine called Honau, which it appears to possess at the present time through our gift, or anyone else’s, or which divine piety may hereafter wish to enlarge in the right of that holy place, in order to hear cases or exact fines from any direction. Rather, the aforesaid Dubanus and his successors shall be able to rule those possessions under the full protection of immunity, for the name of the Lord and of Saint Michael.

Therefore we order that neither you, nor your subordinates or successors, nor any public judicial authority, at any time presume to enter the villas located anywhere in our kingdom and granted to that church, whether by royal generosity, private generosity, or the generosity of good men, or which in the future may be granted by those who fear God, in order to hear disputes, exact fines for any cause, or take lodging, provisions, or sureties. Rather, whatever the treasury might hope to receive from the servants who reside within the fields or vineyards, or upon the lands of the aforesaid church of Saint Michael [Col. 1532A], or who reside elsewhere and are seen to belong there according to lawful order, whether in fines or from any other source, shall, through our indulgence and for future salvation, be applied forever to the lights of that church by the hand of its agents. We have granted this with complete devotion for the name of the Lord, for the remedy of our soul, and for our succeeding descendants. Neither royal majesty nor the harsh greed of any judges shall attempt to oppose it.

And so that this present authority may remain, with God’s help, for present and future times, we have decreed that it be affirmed below by our hand and sealed with our ring.

Sign + of Pippin, most glorious king.

[Col. 1532B] In the name of God, Baddilo [Note: [Col. 1531D] Baddilo, the chancellor, wrote many charters of Pippin from the years 757, 762, and 766; see Bouquet, vol. V, pp. 702, 705, and 706.] reviewed and wrote it.

Given on the fifteenth day of September, in the seventh year of the reign of King Pippin. Enacted at Düren [Note: [Col. 1531D] Düren, or Dura, in German *Düren*, which the ancients called *Marcodurum*, a settlement of the Ubii, was formerly a notable royal palace; it is now a city of the duchy of Jülich in the Westphalian circle, approximately halfway between Aachen and Cologne, ten leagues distant from the latter. Many synods were held there under King Pippin and his son Charlemagne. Consult Michael Germanus, “On the Palaces of the Frankish Kings,” in Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, Book IV, p. 281.], happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### XX. Diploma of King Pippin by which he confirms the property and rights of the abbey of Murbach (760).

(From Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*.)

Pippin, illustrious king of the Franks. It is proper for the chief clemency of all to lend a kindly ear, and especially, when we approve that benefits granted by earlier kings, our predecessors, to the churches have contributed to the salvation of souls, we ought to weigh them with devout mind and not deny suitable benefits, so that we may deserve to share in the reward, but rather confirm them with the strongest legal force through our proclamation.

Therefore the venerable man Baldobert, by the grace of God abbot of the monastery of the Pilgrims’ Dwelling, which is situated in the county of Alsace on the river Murbach and was built in honor of Saint Leodegarius, the apostle Peter, Saint Mary, and the other saints, and who is known to serve there with a very large company of monks, reported to our royal clemency that our predecessors had once granted, through their authorities subscribed by their hands, complete immunity for the villas of that church which it possessed at that time—both from the gifts of princes and of Eberhard, who founded that monastery through his almsgiving, and from the generosity of the inhabitants of the county, and from whatever had thereafter been assigned there by men who feared God—so that no public judge should enter the villas or property of that church, whether to hear cases, exact fines, provide lodging or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of that church for any causes, or demand any payment.

For this reason the aforesaid Abbot Baldobert, rector of that monastery, showed us the command and confirmation of the aforementioned predecessors of ours for rereading, and asserted that this benefit had until now been preserved with respect to him and the aforesaid church. But, for the sake of securing the confirmation, he asked our highness that our authority should once again confirm this generally with respect to that monastery and those monks. Know that, out of reverence for that place and so that we may deserve to be joined to the reward, we are seen to have granted his petition with fullest willingness and to have confirmed it in every respect.

Therefore we order that no public judge enter the property or possessions of that church to hear cases, exact fines, provide lodging or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of that church, free or slaves, who are seen to dwell upon their lands or *micio* [reading uncertain] and are regarded as belonging there, for any causes, or demand any payment. Rather, just as the beneficial grant of our aforementioned predecessors, examined and supported by the authority of the earlier princes, has until now remained established for that church, so henceforth by our authority it shall remain generally undisturbed. Whatever our treasury might have been able to claim from it shall forever contribute to the lights of that lord Leodegarius, Saint Peter, and Saint Mary, for the stability of our kingdom.

And so that this authority may be evident to present and future times, we have strengthened it below with our hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

### XXI. [Note: [Col. 1533D] This charter exists in Mabillon, *Annales ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. II, p. 697; Eckhard, *Origines Habsburgicae*, p. 102; Bouquet, vol. V, p. 705; and in Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*, vol. I, p. 35, but all of them are corrupt.] Diploma of Pippin, king of the Franks, for the monastery of Honau, given around 760.

(From Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*.)

[Col. 1533C]

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to the holy and apostolic lords, venerable Fathers in Christ, all bishops, abbots, and illustrious and magnificent men—dukes, counts, household officials, vicars, centenaries, and all officials [Note: [Col. 1533D] That is, generally all the king’s officials, from which arose the French expression *Les gens de nos cours*, “the people of our courts.”].

We consider it right that we bring to fulfillment, with Christ as guide, the petitions of priests that concern the advancement of holy places. Therefore the Father in Christ, Dubanus, bishop and abbot of the monastery of Honau in the county of Alsace on the river Rhine, built in honor of Saint Michael [Col. 1533D], Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and the other saints, petitioned the majesty of our glorious kingdom that, since that monastery appears to have been built through the donations of our predecessors and the assistance of men who fear God, we should generally confirm by our command the whole body of its possessions—both what earlier abbots had cultivated there, and what Dubanus himself is seen to have increased or acquired from the property of the monastery known to have been there, and what is presently possessed by that holy place. Let your greatness have no doubt that we have granted this out of divine regard and for the increase of our reward.

We have also decreed to strengthen, for perpetual stability, the privilege of that monastery, which it is seen to have merited according to the institution of the ancient Fathers and the other bishops, and which is known to have been sheltered by our authority, or by that of the other successors according to the laws of our predecessors, according to which it had been protected by our earlier command against prohibition [Note: [Col. 1533D] He clearly means the diploma of the year 759, no. 21.].

Therefore we order that all the possessions of that monastery—whatever has been lawfully acquired or obtained there by royal grant, by the gift of private persons, by earlier abbots, or by Bishop or Abbot Dubanus, indeed whatever has been properly acquired from any sources, and whatever the dominion of that holy monastery of Honau is seen presently to possess with due equity, from villas, houses, slaves, vineyards, forests, meadows, pastures, or any benefits whatsoever—supported by this authority, may, with Christ as guide, contribute to its increase there, both in the present and in future times, without anyone’s unlawful disputes.

Whatever that monastery has been granted until now and preserved up to this point, or confirmed for it by our predecessors, the kings, let it likewise hereafter, with all superfluous disturbances removed, remain in its proper order through time, with the Lord’s help, under our protection. And whenever necessity arises, may you and your successors furnish just assistance in the affairs of that monastery, so that its congregation may be more eager continually to implore the mercy of the Lord for our salvation and for the stability of our kingdom.

And so that this command may endure with firm stability, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by our own hand and sealed with our ring.

Sign + of the most glorious lord Pippin, king.

Wulmar [Note: [Col. 1533D] The same as Widmar, who wrote Pippin’s charters of the years 753 and 760, above.] reviewed and wrote it at his command.

### XXII. Pippin, king of the Franks, confirms to Archbishop Wiomad and the Church of Trier the churches of Saints Maximinus, Paulinus, Eucharius, and Oreu, Saint Martin, and whatever the Church of Trier has and shall have on this side of the Rhine and the Loire, and confirms that it is free from tallages and tolls [Note: [Col. 1534D] Mabillon mentions this diploma in *De re diplomatica*, Book II, chapter 3, no. 6, and in *Annales Benedictini*, vol. II, Book XXIII, no. 50; he judges that it is not free from interpolations, including the indiction, which is unusual for that age. The form of the invocation and address also seems corrupt to him, although he finds nothing in the text that invalidates it. The substance of the diploma should seem all the less false because the author of the *Deeds of Trier*, chapter 39, in Leibniz’s edition, writes of the matter itself as follows: “Nevertheless, Wiomad obtained from that same Pippin a command of royal authority concerning the cell of Saint Maximinus and other property of the Church of Trier, and from Charlemagne, son of Pippin; whoever wishes to know about this will be able to find it.” This Pippinian document is subsequently mentioned in a command of King Louis from the year 902.] (761).

(From Hontheim, *History of Trier*.)

[Col. 1534D]

In the name of the eternal Lord God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior. Pippin, by divinely ordained providence [Col. 1535A] king of the Franks.

If, through the gift of our generosity, we confer some benefit upon places dedicated to God, relieve ecclesiastical needs at the petitions of our priests, and protect them with royal defense, we firmly believe that this will benefit us both in passing through this mortal, temporal life and in attaining eternal blessedness. Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Wiomadus [Note: [Col. 1535D] Wiomadus … archbishop. The title “archbishop” before the ninth century is exceedingly rare in the West and is not free from suspicion. See Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book II, chapter 2, no. 3. Nevertheless, there is no reason to doubt that Wiomadus was already at that time presiding over the church of Trier. His immediate predecessor Milo had ceased to live by about the year 753. See Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. II, book XXII, no. 74; Eckhart, *Frankish Affairs*, book XXIII, no. 126. Add the Testament of the Holy Savior, year 762, note f. Wiomadus had previously been abbot of Saint Maximinus.] archbishop of the holy church of Trier presented to our presence a charter of the earlier Frankish kings, in which it was inserted that our predecessors, namely all the Frankish kings, had confirmed by their authority all the property that good and holy men, out of regard for divine contemplation, had transferred to the church of Saint Peter of Trier, so that their kingdom might be protected by heavenly aid and that afterward they might reign in heaven with Christ, King of kings.

For the security of the matter, the aforesaid prelate Wiomadus asked our highness that, following the custom of our father and of the preceding kings, we should order such a charter of our authority to be made concerning these same possessions, for the love of God and in reverence for Saint Peter. We willingly granted his petition and decreed that this charter of our authority be made for that church, out of love for divine worship and for the remedy of our soul. By it we prescribe and order that all estates or possessions belonging to the church of Saint Peter in the city of Trier—namely, the cell of Saint Maximinus [Col. 1535C], which was built in the territory of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles; the churches of Saint Paulinus and Saint Eucharius; and the monastery of Saint Mary, which the lord bishop Modoaldus built from the foundations for that church in the territory of Saint Peter, and which is called Orca; and the church of Saint Martin built in the district of Ambitivo [Note: [Col. 1536D] In the district of Ambitivo. Browerus, in the *Annals of Trier*, book VII, no. 197, reads *Ambitarino*, but even so this would not provide the designation of a proper district. More correctly, therefore, in the Carolingian charter of the year 773 the church of Saint Martin is called “in the district of Megin,” namely the present collegiate church of Saints Martin and Severus of the monastery of Meinfeld.]—as well as the other basilicas, castles, villages, estates, vineyards, woods, dependents, and everything that, by God’s gift, may henceforth be added to that church, situated in our kingdom this side of the Rhine and Loire rivers, shall remain perpetually subject to the right and power of Saint Peter’s church of Trier and of its bishop.

Moreover, in the same way we decree that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority [Col. 1536A], shall dare in our time or in that of our successors to enter the monasteries, churches, castles, villages, fields, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid church—whether beyond or beside the Rhine or Loire, in the districts or territories within the power of our kingdom where the said church possesses them, or where divine piety may henceforth increase them in the right of that holy place—for the purpose of hearing cases, exacting fines, taxes, or any assessments, requisitioning lodgings or transport services, taking sureties, distraining the men of that church, demanding unjust exactions, or collecting tolls; nor shall they presume in any way to exact the things mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid prelate and his successors be permitted to possess forever, in peace and in full, all the aforementioned monasteries, estates [Col. 1536B], villages, and castles with their appurtenances, for the remedy of our soul and of the souls of our parents; to obey our command faithfully; and, together with the clergy and people subject to them, continually to implore God’s boundless mercy for our safety, that of our wife and offspring, and of the whole kingdom granted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his most compassionate mercy.

Whatever the treasury had the right to demand from the aforesaid church’s possessions, we have granted in full to that church, so that forever it may serve as an increase and supplement for the performance of God’s service.

Therefore, so that this authority of our charter may possess fuller force in God’s name, be more truly believed by the faithful of God’s holy church and by our own faithful, present and future [Col. 1536C], and be more carefully preserved by our successors, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Pippin, most excellent king.

I, Joseph, subdeacon, acting in the place of Wulfard, have authenticated it.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the thirteenth indiction, in the ninth year of the reign of the illustrious king.

Done at Tulpiac, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

## XXIII. Charter of King Pippin by which he grants the estate of Tinningen [Note: [Col. 1536D] The seal has been torn away from the original. From an ancient parchment we learn how extensive this possession was; it reads: “In the estate of Tinninga, which lies in Swabia, when Pippin handed it over to Saint Boniface, there were found twenty-three households and fifty royal hides; 300 rights; meadowland for 400 wagonloads; 52 horses; 54 foals; 80 unbroken horses; 58 cows with 55 calves; 200 sheep; 90 pigs; 27 hides of *lidi* with their holdings; 9 mills; and 3 churches with their holdings.”] to the church of Fulda (year 762).

(From D. Bouquet, vol. V, after Schannat.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

As the Apostle says, “We brought nothing into this world,” and there is no doubt that we shall be able to take nothing from it away with us, except what, with devout mind and by God’s inspiration, we seem to grant to holy places for the salvation of our souls.
