Therefore let your greatness and prudence know that, for the name of the Lord and for eternal reward, from this present day we give to the monastery called Fulda, which has been built in honor of the holy Savior by Saint Boniface with a new work, where that precious martyr rests in body—indeed, with the greatest devotion we hand over—the estate called Thininga, situated in the district of Rezi beside the river called the Agira, in its entirety, with everything that appears to belong or pertain to that estate: lands, homesteads with the people dwelling in them, slaves, woods, boundaries or marches, fields, meadows [Col. 1537B], pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, and every kind of appurtenance, all wholly and completely, as we have said.

From this present day we give it perpetually for possession to the monastery of Saint Salvator, where the precious martyr Saint Boniface rests in body, beside the river Fulda, through this deed of transfer, for the increase of our reward. Thus, from this day forward, the administrators of that monastery shall hold and possess the estate called Tininga, with all its appurtenances and dependencies, for the benefit of that church, and it shall forever serve them as an increase. So that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved better for many ages, we have confirmed it below and sealed it with our ring.

[Col. 1537C] Sign of Pippin, most glorious king.

Hitherius, in the place of Baddilo. Given in the month of June, in the ninth year of our reign. Done at the public palace of Attigny.

## XXIV. Testament of the Holy Savior, which King Pippin ordered to be made for the abbey [Note: [Col. 1537D] Prüm, from the stream Pronaeus on the border of the Ardennes, a seat beloved by the Carolingian family, was once sought out and frequented by people of every rank, not so much because of the site’s convenience as because of the exceptional renown of its monastic discipline. It far surpassed other places, whether one considers the dignity of its religion, the fame of the most learned and otherwise distinguished men who professed there, or finally the extent of its ancient power and the splendor of its continuing princely dignity. Compare Bertrada’s charter for the year 721, where the monastery’s first celebrated foundations are recorded (*Patrologia Latina*, vol. LXXXVIII, col. 1274).] of Prüm (year 762).

(From Hontheim, *History of Trier*.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

Since it is clear that divine providence has brought us to the throne of the kingdom, we ought to undertake in God’s name those things by which we may rather obtain the grace and will of the Most High. For we remember the Gospel itself, in which he says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

And since kings reign from God, and he has entrusted peoples and kingdoms to us to govern according to his mercy, we must see to it that we are exalted rulers for the needy and that we do not neglect to govern and care for the poor for the love of Christ. For God commanded Moses the lawgiver to arrange the tabernacle of the propitiatory [Col. 1538A]; and we know that King Solomon adorned with gold and stones the temple built in his name.

Although we cannot equal those works in greatness, we nevertheless desire, with the Lord’s cooperation, to offer him what we can more easily from the possessions we have. For, as the Apostle says, we brought nothing into this world, nor can we carry anything out of it; but we believe that whatever we seem, with devout mind, to distribute to the Lord from transitory possessions contributes to the salvation of the soul.

Therefore, since it is known to all, both to neighboring and to foreign peoples, that we and our wife Bertrada, out of love for the holy Savior, the holy mother of God Mary, the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 1538B], Saint John the Baptist, the martyrs Saints Stephen, Dionysius, and Maurice, and the confessors Martin, Vedast, and Germanus, have built a monastery on property belonging to us, situated within the boundaries of Bidgau and the Ardennes [Note: [Col. 1538D] Where the stream called Berdenbach enters the Prüm. The Pronnaea and Nims—rivers celebrated by Ausonius in *Mosella*, verse 354—rise in the mountains of the Eifel and flow from there like paired streams, separated by a short interval, until, joined to the Sûre, they carry their waters with it into the Moselle.], where the stream called Berdenbach enters the Prüm; and since in the church of that monastery we have seemed to deposit relics of the sandals of our Lord Jesus Christ, of his mother Mary, and of the other saints whom we have mentioned above; and since we have established monks there, who are to be wholly trained under the rule of holy conduct and according to the example of the preceding Fathers [lacuna], so that those called solitary monks may, under the Lord’s guidance, rejoice through the ages in perfect quiet [Col. 1538C], living under the holy rule and following the life of the blessed Fathers, and may more fully implore the Lord’s mercy, under Christ’s governance, for the condition of the Church, the longevity of our kingdom, our wife and children, and the Catholic people—

it must nevertheless be provided that, since this monastery has been founded by us as a new work for the love of Christ, we should determine how the priests and monks who will be there are henceforth to live and enjoy consolation and tranquility; and that the shepherd to whom he has entrusted the care of his flock should not find the sheep scattered, but that they may be joined together and offer praises to almighty God day and night.

Therefore, with heavenly grace inspiring us, both I and my wife Bertrada give to that most sacred place, which we built in honor of the holy Savior and Saint Mary, our property [Note: [Col. 1538D] In the district of Charos. Papebrochius describes this district from an unpublished manuscript of Alexander Wiltheim, in appendix 3 to Henschenius’s *Exegesis on the Bishops of Tongeren and Maastricht.] in the district of Charos, the estate called Rumeresheim: both the portion that came to me from my father Charles and the portion of Bertrada herself that her father Herebert left her as dowry, with their appurtenances and in their entirety, except for certain slaves named Wucdramno, Arnulph, Crodoald, Wanulf, Ghiorin, Chrodramno, Wulfrid, Tancrad, Adalbert, Beringhis, Offred, Matalfred, Walafred, Madalfred, Airoin, Arefred, Adaliv, Umnelin of Bertelinde, Gunbert, Harelinde, Wnild or Charde, Sigfrid, Ratleo, Dulodulf and Lufus, Mulfus, Ratgar of Gerolinde, Hildoarance, Winead, Aznarane, Alpelinde, Magnelinde, and Zebelinde.

We have retained these slaves for our own service. As for the rest, we transfer and convey the estate itself, in its entirety, to that holy place, within whose boundary the monastery of the holy Savior has been founded, together with the dwelling above the Prüm where the stream called Escutmisbach flows into the Prüm, which is built upon the boundary of the aforesaid estate.

Likewise, we give to the aforesaid monastery, in the district of Moselgau beside the river Moselle, our estates called Meringum (Mering) and Scoacum (Schweich), together with their revenue [Note: [Col. 1559D] *Meritum*, that is, income or yield. Du Cange, *Glossary*, under this word], boundaries, and appurtenances.

We also give our estate in the district of Bidgau called Marciacum (Mertich), together with its revenues and appurtenances.

Likewise, we give to that monastery our estate in the district of Eifelgau, the estate of Sarabodis (Sarensdorf), together with its full property, boundaries, and appurtenances, as it was possessed by Garabert.

We transfer two other places in Carasco to the same monastery, Wathit-Lendorp and Birgisburias, with all their adjacent lands and appurtenances.

Likewise, in the district of the Ribuarian Franks, we give that portion in Reginbach (Reinbach) which our vassal Aglibert held as a benefice and which my father Charles left to me as allodial property, as well as the other portion in that estate which Heribert left to my wife Bertrada as allodial property.

We also confirm there those possessions that had previously been assigned to that church by written charters, in their entirety.

We therefore transfer to the most sacred place described above a cell belonging to us by proprietary right in the district of Speyer, built in honor of Saint Medardus, with its estates and appurtenances, which Herliband, Weolentio, and Bagulf handed over to me, wholly and completely, including both the church’s services and the other possessions belonging there.

We also give to that monastery another cell called Casleoca, situated within the boundaries of Senciacum and built in honor of Saint Peter, with all its adjacent lands and appurtenances.

We further confirm to that holy place a third cell called Ruivinium [Col. 1540A], in the district of Lomme beside the river Meuse, built in honor of Saint Mary, with all its revenues and appurtenances.

Under the following condition, therefore, we confirm the aforesaid possessions—both estates and cells—to that monastery in their entirety: together with lands, houses, buildings, resident inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, money, livestock of both sexes, and herds with their shepherds—in short, everything and in every respect. From the present day and henceforth, without any impediment, let the aforesaid possessions forever contribute to the increase of the already-mentioned monastery of the holy Savior.

Nevertheless, we wish that the monastery of the holy Savior, and the possessions belonging to it—both those confirmed by our authority and those that God-fearing people may henceforth contribute—remain under our power or protection, or that of our heirs; and that the community which we have introduced into that monastery, together with the abbot named Assuerus [Note: [Col. 1559D] The abbot named Assuerus. Wandelbert, a writer of Prüm living at approximately this time, stated in the *Acts of Saint Goar* that Assuerus and the first inhabitants of the monastery of Prüm were of Roman language and stock—that is, what all learned men understand and what the acts of Saint Goar clearly demonstrate: Gauls.], or his successors, so long as they wish, with God’s help, to serve there under the holy rule, shall remain there.

We shall not introduce an abbot or monk from another community contrary to our order, nor shall our heirs do so.

And because we wish that the monastery be secure from all secular administration, our clemency must provide by a salutary ordinance for the future peace of the brothers dwelling there, so that, with God’s grace assisting them, they may persevere in God’s service.

We also grant you by our authority that, from the community of the lords, bishops Romanus and Wolfrannus [Note: [Col. 1559D] From the community of the bishops Romanus and Wolfrannus [Col. 1540D]. Romanus and Wolfrannus were successive bishops of Meaux, and introduced regular discipline into the monastery of the Holy Cross, or Saint Faron, within the city of Meaux beside the river Marne. Hence that community took its name from these reformers, and the first monks of Prüm were summoned from this monastery of Meaux.], whom we have gathered in this monastery of the holy Savior, whenever the abbot departs this life, you shall, with our consent and yours, regularly elect an abbot for yourselves from that same community.

And so that you may delight perpetually to implore the mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ for the remedy of our soul, of our wife and offspring, and of our successors, and for the stability of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his gracious mercy; to persevere day and night in his praises; and, putting aside thoughts of temporal things, to devote yourselves with free minds to contemplating heavenly joys, we prescribe that no bishop or secular person inflict any prejudice or burden upon you.

If the monks are seen to conduct themselves there regularly and faithfully on behalf of us or our heirs, our heirs shall protect them in our monastery, “by no contrivances” (*per nullas artes*; syntactically defective in the transmitted text), as they have appeared. With God as author, we have established that place; thus let it remain unshaken forever, for the increase of our soul and of the souls of our heirs.

And so that this authority of ours may be held more firmly and preserved better forever, we have decreed that it be strengthened by our own hand.

I, Pippin, and my wife Bertrada.

Sign of Charles, my son, consenting.

Sign of Carloman, his son, consenting.

Sign of Genebaud, bishop.

Sign of Gaurlen, bishop.

Sign of Fulcar, bishop.

Sign of Adalfred, bishop.

Sign of Wulfrannus, bishop.

Sign of Megingaud, bishop.

Sign of Bertelinus, bishop.

Sign of Basinus, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 1541C] Sign of Wiomadus, bishop. I have no doubt that this is our Wiomadus, archbishop of Trier. For in the following year, 763, he was already seated in the see of Trier. When Cancor, count of the Rhine, and his mother Willisvinda, under the auspices of their kinsman Ruotgang, or Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, were laying the foundations of the monastery of Lorsch not far from Worms, Wiomadus, together with Bishops Alberic and John, confirmed the charters drawn up in that same year, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, preserved in Tolner’s *Palatine Diplomatic Code*, p. 2, as follows: “I, Wiomadus [corruptly printed as Automadus], bishop of Trier, have subscribed.” Browerus therefore appears to date Wiomadus’s accession too late when he places its beginning only in the year 767. The other bishops who affixed their signs were Genebaud of Laon; Gaulonus of Le Mans, also called Gauzlenus; Fulcar of Tongeren; Adalfred of Noyon; Wulfrannus of Meaux; Megingaud of Würzburg; Berthelinus of Cologne; and Basinus of Speyer. From the notable presence of so many bishops and counts it may be inferred that Pippin summoned them to obtain their counsel in matters of great importance; they were not required merely to confirm the endowment.] Sign of Wiomadus, bishop.

Sign of Droco, count [Note: [Col. 1541D] Droco, count, etc. Droco seems to have been count of the district of Maingau, whom Emperor Louis mentions as already dead in a charter issued in the first year of his empire, recorded by the *Lorsch Chronicle*. Warinus was count of the district of Lobdengau, and is mentioned in the twenty-first Fulda tradition, given in the twelfth year of Pippin’s reign. The other Warinus was colleague of Count Ruthard and royal chamberlain in Alemannia. Gumbert may perhaps be Count Cunibert of the district of Worms, mentioned in the Fulda tradition of the year 779. Waltarius may be the man whom Wandelbert, in book 1 of *The Miracles of Saint Goar*, chapter 9, calls noble according to the world and testifies was still alive in his own time. More detailed investigations of these counts are owed to the industry of the illustrious Eckhart, *Frankish Affairs*, book XXIV, no. 65.].

Sign of Theodard, count.

Sign of Warinus, count.

Sign of Welant, count.

Sign of Bangulf, count.

Sign of Gerhard, count.

Sign of Troania, count.

Sign of Waltarius, count.

Sign of Herloin, count.

Sign of Warinus, count.

Sign [Col. 1541B] of Gumbert, count.

In God’s name, Bradilo [Baddilo] reviewed and subscribed.

Done in the month of August, on the thirteenth day, in the eleventh year of the reign of Pippin, glorious king.

Done at the public estate of Trisgodros, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## XXV. Charter of King Pippin concerning the construction and endowment of the monastery of Prüm (year 762)

(From Mabillon, cited above.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

Since it is clear that divine providence has anointed us to the throne of the kingdom, we ought to undertake in God’s name those things by which we may rather obtain the grace and will of the Most High. For we remember the Gospel itself, in which he says: “Whoever does the will of my Father, who is in heaven, will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

And since kings reign from God, and he has entrusted peoples and kingdoms to us to govern according to his mercy, we must see to it that we are exalted rulers amid wealth and do not neglect to govern and care for the poor for the love of Christ. For God commanded Moses the lawgiver to adorn the tabernacle of the propitiatory; and we know that King Solomon adorned with gold and stones the temple built in his name.

Although we cannot equal those works in greatness, we nevertheless desire, with the Lord’s cooperation, to offer him what we can more easily from the possessions we have. For, as the Apostle says, we brought nothing into this world, and there is no doubt that we cannot carry anything out of it; but we believe that only whatever we seem, with devout mind, to distribute to the Lord from transitory possessions contributes to the salvation of the soul.

Therefore, since it is known to all, both to neighboring and foreign peoples, that we and our wife Bertrada, out of love for the holy Savior, the holy mother of God Mary, the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, Saint John the Baptist, the holy martyrs Stephen, Dionysius, and Maurice, and the confessors Martin, Vedast, and Germanus, have built a monastery on property belonging to us, situated within the boundaries of Bidgau (Bidburg) and the Ardennes, where the stream called Berdenbach enters the Prüm; and since in the church of that monastery we have seemed to deposit relics of the sandals of our Lord Jesus Christ, of his mother Mary, and of the other saints whom we mentioned above; and since we have established monks there, who are to be wholly trained under the rule of holy conduct and according to the example of the preceding Fathers, so that those called solitary monks may, under the Lord’s guidance, rejoice through the ages in perfect quiet, living under the holy rule and following the life of the blessed Fathers, and may more fully implore the Lord’s mercy, under Christ’s governance, for the condition of the Church and the longevity of our kingdom, as well as for our wife and children and the Catholic people—

it must nevertheless be provided that, since this monastery has been founded by us as a new work for the love of Christ, we should determine how the priests and monks who will be there are henceforth to live and enjoy consolation and tranquility; and that the shepherd to whom he has entrusted the care of his flock should not find the sheep scattered, but that they may be joined together and offer praises to almighty God day and night.

Therefore, with heavenly grace inspiring us, I and my wife Bertrada together give to that most sacred place, which we built in honor of the holy Savior and Saint Mary, our property in the district of Chorosvilla, the estate called Rumeresheim: both the portion that came to me from my father Charles and the portion of Bertrada herself that her father Heribert left her as dowry, with its appurtenances and in its entirety, except for certain slaves.

We have retained these slaves for our own service. As for the rest, we transfer and convey the estate itself, in its entirety, to that holy place, within whose boundary the monastery of the holy Savior has been founded; and also the dwelling above the Prüm where the stream called Escutmisbach flows into the Prüm, which is built upon the boundary of the aforesaid estate.

Likewise, we give to the aforesaid monastery, in the district of Moselgau beside the river Moselle, our estates called Meringum (Mering) and Sacocum (Schweich), together with their revenues, boundaries, and appurtenances.

We also give our estate in Bidgau, called Marciacum (Mertich), together with its revenues and appurtenances.

Likewise, we give to that monastery our estate in the district of Eifelgau, the estate of Sarabodis (Sarensdorf), together with its full property, boundaries, and appurtenances, as it was possessed by Garabert.

We transfer two other places in Carasio to the same monastery, Wathitlindorff and Birgisburias, with all their adjacent lands and appurtenances.

Likewise, in the district of the Ribuarian Franks, we give that portion in Reginbach (Rheimbach) which our vassal Aglibert held as a benefice and which my father Charles left to me as allodial property, as well as the other portion in that estate which Heribert left to my wife Bertrada as allodial property.

We also confirm there those possessions that had previously been assigned to that church by written charters, in their entirety.

We therefore transfer to the most sacred place described above a cell belonging to us by proprietary right in the place called Altrepio, beside the river Rhine, in the district of Speyer, built in honor of Saint Medardus, with its estates and appurtenances, which Herliband, Wiolentio, and Bagulf handed over to me, wholly and completely, including both the church’s services and the other possessions belonging there.

We also give to that monastery another cell called Gasteacum, situated within the boundaries of Senciacum and built in honor of Saint Peter, with all its adjacent lands and appurtenances.

We further confirm to that holy place a third cell called Ruivinium, in the district of Lomme beside the river Meuse, built in honor of Saint Mary, with all its revenues and appurtenances.

Under the following condition, therefore, we confirm the aforesaid possessions—both estates and cells—to that monastery in their entirety: together with lands, houses, buildings, resident inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields [Col. 1544A], meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, money, livestock of both sexes, and herds with their shepherds—in short, everything and in every respect. From the present day and henceforth, without any impediment, let the aforesaid possessions forever contribute to the increase of the already-mentioned monastery of the holy Savior.

Nevertheless, we wish that the monastery of the holy Savior, and the possessions belonging to it—both those confirmed by our authority and those that God-fearing people may henceforth contribute—remain under our power or protection, or that of our heirs; and that the community which we have introduced into that monastery, together with the abbot named Assuerus and his successors, so long as they wish, with God’s help, to serve there under the holy rule [Col. 1544B], remain there.

We shall not introduce an abbot or monk from another community there contrary to our order, nor shall our heirs do so.

And because we wish that the monastery be secure from all secular administration, our clemency must provide by a salutary ordinance for the future peace of the brothers dwelling there, so that, with God’s grace assisting them, they may persevere in God’s service.

We also grant you by our authority that, from the community of the lords, bishops Romanus and Wolfrannus, whom we have gathered in this monastery of the holy Savior, whenever the abbot departs this life, you shall, with our consent and yours, regularly elect an abbot for yourselves from that same community.

And so that you may delight perpetually to implore the mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ for the remedy of our soul, of our wife and offspring, and of our successors, and for the stability of the whole empire granted to us by God and to be preserved forever by his gracious mercy; to persevere day and night in his praises; and, putting aside thoughts of temporal things, to devote yourselves with free minds to contemplating heavenly joys, we prescribe that no bishop or secular person inflict any prejudice or burden upon you.

If the monks are seen to conduct themselves there regularly and faithfully on behalf of us or our heirs, our heirs shall protect them in this monastery, “by no contrivances” (*per nullas artes*; syntactically defective in the transmitted text), as they have appeared. With God as author, we have established that place; thus let it remain unshaken forever, for the increase of our soul and of the souls of our heirs.

And so that this authority of ours may be held firmly and preserved better forever, we have decreed that it be strengthened by our own hand.

I, Pippin, and my wife Bertrada.

Sign of Charles, my son, consenting.

Sign of Carloman, his son, consenting.

Sign of Genebaud, bishop.

Sign of Gaulonus, bishop.

Sign of Fulcaric, bishop.

Sign of Adalfred, bishop.

Sign of Wulfrannus, bishop.

Sign of Megingaud, bishop.

Sign of Berthelinus, bishop.

Sign of Basinus, bishop.

Sign of Wiomadus, bishop.

Sign of Droco, count.

Sign of Theodard, count.

Sign of Warinus, count.

Sign of Welant, count.

Sign of Gangulf, count.

Sign of Gerhard, count.

Sign of Froamed, count.

Sign of Waltharius, count.

Sign of Horloin, count.

Sign of Gumbert, count.

Sign of Raculf, count.

Sign of Warinus, count.

In God’s name, Bradilo reviewed and subscribed.

Done in the month of August, on the thirteenth day, in the eleventh year of the reign of Pippin, glorious king.

Done at the public estate of Trisgodios, happily in God’s name. Amen.

## XXVI. Charter by which King Pippin confirms all his possessions to the monastery of Honau (undated)

(From Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to the holy and apostolic lords and venerable Fathers in Christ, to all bishops, abbots, and illustrious and magnificent men—dukes, counts, household officers, vicars, centenarii, and all administrators [Col. 1545B].

We deem it right that we bring to completion, with Christ as our guide, the petitions of priests that concern the advancement of holy places. Therefore, in Christ the Father Dubanus, bishop or abbot of the monastery of Hohenaugia in the Alsatian district, upon the Rhine River, which was built in honor of Saint Michael, Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and the other saints, petitioned the majesty of our glorious kingdom that, since the monastery itself appears to have been built from the gifts of our predecessors or of God-fearing men, we should generally confirm by our command the whole body of its possessions: both what the abbots who preceded him had acquired there, and what Dubanus himself appears to have increased or acquired from the property of the monastery known to have been there, and what that holy place presently possesses. Your Greatness does not doubt that you have granted this to us out of regard for God and for the increase of our reward.

He also asked that we confirm the privilege of that monastery, which, in accordance with the institution of the ancient Fathers and of the other bishops, they appear to have merited, and which is known to have been established by our authority or by that of the other kings who succeeded our predecessors; according to which, before it had been fortified by our earlier command against those seeking to harm it, we decreed that it should be strengthened for perpetual stability.

Therefore we decree and command that all the possessions of that monastery—whatever has been lawfully acquired or obtained by royal grant, by the gifts of private persons, by the abbots who preceded him, or by Dubanus, bishop or abbot there; indeed, whatever has been rightly acquired from any property whatsoever; whatever the lordship of that holy monastery of Hohenaug, throughout the present time, is seen to possess in villages, houses, dependents, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, or any other benefits in accordance with equity—supported by this authority, may advance and increase there, with Christ as its guide, without unlawful disputes by anyone, both now and in the future.

Whatever that monastery has hitherto been granted and preserved, or whatever has been confirmed around it by our predecessors, may likewise continue thereafter in its proper order, with every superfluous disturbance removed, through the ages, with the Lord’s help. You and your successors, whenever necessity arises in the affairs of that monastery, shall provide it with just assistance, so that the congregation of that monastery may be more gladly moved continually to implore the mercy of God for our salvation and for the stability of our kingdom.

And so that this command may endure with firm stability, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by our own hand and sealed with our ring.

**Sign of the most glorious lord Pippin, king.**

Wulmar, commanded to do so, examined and wrote this.

## XXVII. Immunity granted to the abbey of Prüm by King Pippin (763)

*(In Hontheim, History of Trier.)*

**[Column 1546B]**

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, household officers, deputies, centenarii, and all our traveling envoys.

We believe that the protection of our kingdom is greatly increased if, by benevolent deliberation, we grant suitable benefits to holy places or churches; and, with the Lord’s protection, we trust that these will endure securely.

Therefore let your prudence know how we appear to have granted the following benefit to the monastery called Prüm, which we newly built in honor of the holy Savior, where the venerable man Assuerus appears to preside as abbot, for eternal recompense: in the villages of that holy place which it appears presently to possess, whether by our gift or by anyone else’s, and in those which divine piety may thereafter wish to enlarge in the right of that monastery and its rectors, no public judge shall at any time presume to enter without our command or that of our heirs, either to hear cases or to exact fines from anywhere. We have granted this instead to that monastery and its rectors. Under the name of immunity, they shall remain at peace in the Lord under our protection and defense, and that of our heirs.

Therefore, establishing this, we command that neither you, nor your juniors or successors, nor any public judicial authority, at any time presume to enter the villages of that monastery of Prüm, wherever in our kingdoms they may be, whether granted by royal generosity or by that of private persons, or which by Christ’s favor may be granted in the future, in order to hear disputes; nor may you exact fines for any causes, nor take lodgings, provisions, or sureties.

Rather, whatever the fisc might have hoped to receive from the servants or ecclesiastical persons living within the fields, boundaries, or lands of the aforesaid monastery—whether in fines or from any other source—shall, by our indulgence, permanently contribute to the lamps of that same monastery, through the hands of its agents. What we have granted to that monastery in honor of the Lord’s name and for the remedy of our soul, or what our succeeding offspring may grant with full devotion, let neither royal majesty nor the savage greed of any judge attempt to oppose.

And so that this authority may remain inviolate, with God’s help, both in the present and in future times, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand, and we have ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of the glorious lord Pippin, king.** In the name of God, Bernericus, acting in place of Baddilo, examined and subscribed.

Given on the third day before the Nones of August, in the twelfth year of the reign of our lord Pippin.

Executed at the public palace of Massario.

[Note: Massario was a public palace—namely Marsana, Marsna, or Marna—near Maastricht, not far from the River Meuse, in the district and county of Moselani or Lower Masau, one league from Maastricht toward the Meuse, today Meerssen. Mabillon discusses it more fully in *De Re Diplomatica*, book IV, p. 299; *Chronicon Gottwicense*, preliminary volume, book III, p. 491.]

In the name of God. Successfully. Amen.

[Note: Compare the similar privilege of Charlemagne for the year 775, *Patrologia*, vol. 98.]

## XXVIII. Testament of Heddo, bishop of Strasbourg, or charter of the foundation and donation of the monastery of Ettenheim, 13 March 763

[Note: The original of this testament perished, although it still existed at the beginning of the twelfth century. “In the year 1121 of the Lord’s incarnation, this charter was renewed and written by the younger Chunrad, abbot of the monastery of Ettenheim, in the fourteenth indiction.” Arbogastus Elnhart, canon of the collegiate church of Saint Thomas and judge and official of the court of Strasbourg, had this charter, thus renewed and transcribed on parchment at the request of Heinrich Reiff, abbot, copied by a public imperial and episcopal-court notary on 7 October 1457; he acknowledged it before summoned witnesses and had it sealed with the court’s seal. Hence this authenticated copy deserves complete credence.

“Muratóri writes in *Antiquities of Medieval Italy*, vol. III, dissertation 34, p. 34: ‘There are copies which were once approved by expert judges, or which have reached us transcribed by trustworthy notaries, and which show no defect in the originals themselves. For copies of such weight and authority are available to us that they take the place of the archetypes.’

This testament is found, though less accurately, in Guillimann, *On the Bishops of Strasbourg*, p. 106; Lunig, *Ecclesiastical Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 866; Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, vol. V, p. 643; Eccard, *Origins of the Habsburgs and Austria*, p. 143; La Guille, *History of Alsace*, proofs, p. 16; and Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*, vol. I, p. 37. In addition to Heddo’s testament, Schoepflin reproduced the entire charter of Arbogastus Elnhart in which it is inserted. It is enough to note it here in order to establish the testament’s authenticity.]

*(In Grandidier, History of the Church of Strasbourg.)*

**[Column 1547B]**

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. I, Heddo, a sinner in God’s name, called bishop of the city of Strasbourg, since it was known to me that our predecessor, the lord Wicgerinus, bishop, had built anew a little monastery in the Black Forest,

[Note: [Column 1547D] At the foot of the Black Forest, where one enters the valley called Munsterthal, on the borders of Breisgau and Ortenau.]

in the Ettenheim March,

[Note: [Columns 1547D–1548B] This march lies eastward at the extremity of, and within the territorial lordship of, the bishopric of Strasbourg. The boundaries of this march at that time cannot be determined from Heddo’s testament. Today it includes the following places: the town of Ettenheim in the middle; to the east, Dorlebach, Schweighausen, Mittelbach, the abbey of Ettenheim, the church of Saint Landelin, and Munchweyer; to the west, Grafenhausen, Cappel, and Rust; to the north, Orswihr, Altorf, and Wahlburg; and to the south, Ettenheimweiler and Ringsheim.]

at a place called

[Note: [Columns 1548B–1548D] This cell was formerly situated where the village of Munchweyer now stands; deriving its German name from the monks’ cell, it is still watered by the little stream Undussa, or Undis. From the place where Wicgerinus had founded the first cell, Heddo transferred it to another place, where the abbey now stands. From that time—whether from the name of the march or from the name of its renewer Etto—the monastery was called Ettenheim. Its abbey church is still dedicated to the Blessed Virgin assumed into heaven. The Annals of Blessed Frowin, abbot of Engelberg, written in 1175, whose autograph survives in Muri Abbey, describe the foundation of Ettenheim Abbey as follows: “831. Etho, first abbot of Augia, afterwards also promoted by Charles to the episcopal church of Strasbourg, before long renewed the monastery of Ettenheim bearing his own name, built long before his time and called by another name, but then almost fallen into ruin.” The distinguished patron of this work, the most illustrious Beatus Fidelis von Zurlauben, Baron of Thurn and Gestelenburg, marshal of the royal fortresses in France, sent us this transcription from the autograph itself. We also owe to him the geographical notes inserted throughout our charters, namely those concerning Switzerland. Here we render to that most illustrious man and friend a public memorial of gratitude and friendship.]

the Monks’ Cell beside the little river Undussa, in honor of holy Mary ever-virgin, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Peter the apostle, and the other saints, and had gathered monks there and given something from the property of Saint Mary to that place;

[Note: That is, from the goods or revenues of his cathedral church of Strasbourg.]

and since we afterward found that little monastery deserted through the negligence of our predecessors,

[Note: Between Wicgerinus and Heddo, bishops of Strasbourg, were Wandelfridus and Avlidulphus, who expelled the monks and restored the goods of the little monastery founded by Wicgerinus to the cathedral church.]

it pleased us, by the permission of our lord Pippin, the glorious king, that we should gather monks there who ought to live according to the rule of Saint Benedict. This I did, and I appointed there as abbot a most reverend man named Hildolfus.

[Note: Hildolphus was therefore the monastery’s first abbot, not Heddo himself. Following Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. VI, p. 187, the editors of *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 865, call Heddo abbot for eight years, confusing him with a certain Utho, bishop and abbot of the monastery of Ettenheim, who lived around 830.]

I also gave to that monastery, with the agreement of the glorious king Pippin and of our brothers—that is, our fellow citizens living in the bishopric—for the support of those monks, whatever we acquired from Duke Ernnust, namely the properties specified in the district of Breisgau:

[Note: Besselius, *Gottwicense Chronicle*, book IV, vol. II, p. 564, describes the district of Breisgau, modern Breisgau, as separated from Ortenau by the River Bleichen.]

the estate which Ernnust himself held in the village called Forcheim,

[Note: A village still existing near Endingen in Breisgau.]

or in Baldingen,

[Note: Also a village in Breisgau, at the same distance from Endingen.]

and in Roswilare,

[Note: Today Rothweil, a league from Breisach.]

and in Wellengen,

[Note: Today Wellingen, a village in Breisgau.]

and in Riegola,

[Note: Today Riegel, a large village in Breisgau, watered by the River Elz.]

or whatever Ernnust himself appeared to possess in Alamannia or in Mordunouwa.

Moreover, with the permission of the aforesaid king Pippin and the consent of everyone living in the bishopric, we granted to those same brothers serving God there, from the property of Saint Mary, the town of Endingen,

[Note: Today the town of Endingen in Breisgau, the ancient patrimony of the Usenberg dynasty.]

with everything that appears to belong to our fisc; and in Burcheim,

[Note: Burckheim, a small town in Breisgau with a castle on the Rhine, one and a half leagues below Old Breisach.]

and in Gruningen,

[Note: Today Groningen, a village one league from Breisach.]

or in Mordunowa,

[Note: For the district of Mordunowa, in the duchy of Alamannia near the Rhine between Alsace and Breisgau, see Besselius, cited work, vol. II, p. 690.]

in the village called Chipinheim,

[Note: Today Kippenheim, a large village in the margraviate of Baden, in the lordship of Mahlberg. The right of patronage there is exercised alternately by the abbot of Ettenheim and the margrave of Baden, with whom he also divides the tithes.]

and in Schopfheim, or in Mutherisheim,

[Note: Either the village of Oberschoffen in the margraviate of Baden and lordship of Mahlberg, or the neighboring village of Niderschopffen, a fief of the bishopric of Strasbourg granted to the lords of Franckenstein.]

whatever we acquired there.

[Note: Mutherisheim is today the village of Mittersen, situated in the territory of the prince of Nassau-Usingen and in the lordship of Lahr.]

We also granted to those same monks, in the village called Rustum,

[Note: Today Ruest, a fief of the bishopric of Strasbourg held by the lords Boeckel von Böcklinsau. The abbey of Ettenheim possesses the right of patronage there and also shares the tithes with the parish priest.]

situated on the bank of the Rhine, the right, between the Rhine and the River Helzaha,

[Note: Today the river in Breisgau called the Elz, rising toward the town of Elzach in the Black Forest.]

to make meadows, fishponds, and mills; to fish with our fishermen; and also to catch fish with a seine, with half of everything in each case.

We also gave in that same village our servant named Thuhari, with his wife named Eberhilde, his children, and all his possessions, to the aforesaid cell for perpetual service.

In our city of Strasbourg we gave one curia,

[Note: This curia in Strasbourg was a house with a garden at the edge of the city, not far from the Butchers’ Gate, near the church of Saint Nicholas.]

with the dependents whom Thengarius acquired there and held from our benefice; and outside the city, one garden which Magilindis held with her daughter Ercalinde; and in the village of Hugesperga,

[Note: Hausbergen near Strasbourg.]

one mansus belonging to the hospital.

We also granted the basilicas which appeared to belong to our right: one in Ethenheim,

[Note: The town of Ettenheim belongs to the bishop of Strasbourg. Yet the abbey enjoys there the right of patronage and all the tithes. A house near the town gate also belongs to the Ettenheim monastery; it is called Freyhoff, that is, a free and immune court.]

in honor of holy Mary; another in Rustum,

[Note: Today Ruest. The church of this village is still dedicated to Saint Peter in Chains.]

the aforesaid village, in honor of Saint Peter the apostle; and on the other side of the Rhine, in the village called Hepheka,

[Note: Today Epfich, a large village of Alsace belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg.]

in honor of blessed Mary; and in Beneveldim,

[Note: Today the small town of Benfelden, belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg. Its parish church still exists, dedicated to Saint Lawrence.]

the basilica of Saints Sixtus and Lawrence, with two hides and all their tithes, which appear to be subject to them. We granted these for the support of the monks, so that they might have free authority over them in every respect for their benefit.

We also gave in the town of Rubiacum,

[Note: Ruffach, a town of the bishopric of Strasbourg in Alsace, the chief place of the Upper Mundat.]

two hides with their houses, vineyards, and the dependents listed below: Wolfger, Gantzfrid, Udalharius with his wife and children, Landulfus, Fanagulfus, and Blidulfus with his children; and in the village of Marsalla,

[Note: Marsal, a town of Lorraine, seven leagues from Nancy, where saltworks already existed in those times. Heddo granted the Ettenheim abbey half a salt pan (*une demi-poêle*). On the ancient saltworks of Marsal, see Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, vol. III, dissertation on the saltworks, and *Description of Lorraine*, vol. I, p. 744.]

half a salt pan to the aforesaid cell for the support of the monks.

In the region of Argovia,

[Note: Here Argovia is understood more broadly than in our times. The name denotes the entire tract along the Aare as far as Lake Thun, beyond the limits of modern Aargau. See Besselius, *Gottwicense Chronicle*, vol. II, book IV, p. 547.]

we also gave all the basilicas and all the tithes, namely in Spietz,

[Note: Today Spiez, a small town with an excellent castle, which, together with the town’s territory, belongs under the title of barony to Lord Albert of Erlach, formerly commander of the Swiss royal guard under the Most Christian King, and later prefect at Gottstatt and Frutigen in the name of the Bernese. Spiez lies on the southern side of Lake Thun, in the territory of the Bernese Republic. Formerly it belonged to the diocese of Constance, in the tract of Upper Aargau. This barony initially belonged to the neighboring barons of Strättligen, who were also lords of Scherzligen; afterward it passed to the nobles of Bubenberg, then of Diesbach, and finally, in 1516, to the nobles of Erlach, one branch of whom still holds it. See Leu, *Historical Lexicon of Switzerland*, vol. XVII, p. 400.]

and in Scartilinga,

[Note: Today Scherzligen, also called Scherlingen, a village on the River Aare in the upper tract of ancient Aargau, where Lake Thun flows into the Aare, one quarter of a league from the town of Thun, in the prefecture of Thun and the territory of the Bernese Republic. Jurisdiction over Scherzligen was formerly held by the baron of Strättligen, whose seat appeared to be in the castle of that name, now partly ruined, above Thun. Consult Leu, *Swiss Lexicon*, vol. XVI, p. 301.]

or in Biberussa,

[Note: Today the village of Biberisch or Bibersch, in the old Aargau tract along the Aare, now situated in the territory of Solothurn and the prefecture called Kriegstetten. Consult the same work by Leu, vol. IV, pp. 9 and 11.]

and in the other places subject to our authority. We gave and transferred to the same monastery and to the monks all the revenues which until now we have held in our power from that land, for the honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his most merciful mother, holy Mary ever-virgin, and of Saint John the Baptist, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and all the saints whose memory is celebrated there daily, for the increase of the reward of eternal life and for the peace of the entire province.

They shall have completely free and most secure authority over all of it, to possess, hold, give, or do whatever they wish for the benefit of the monastery or of the monks.

These aforesaid goods and places, which we have transferred to the aforementioned cell, and which, with God’s help, we may still acquire for that cell, we have established, with the counsel of the aforesaid glorious king Pippin and the consent of all his friends and princes, and have judged by perpetual law to be fully sufficient for the daily support of thirty brothers and those who serve them daily, so that, leading a cenobitic life and obeying the rule of Saint Benedict in all things, their prayer may never cease to petition in God’s sight for the salvation and prosperity of kings, as well as for the stability of all Christendom and religion.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—I myself, or any of my successors, or anyone at all, should come against this testament, which I asked to have made and written out in good faith,

[Note: At that time *testamentum* meant any donation, or any charter written as evidence of a donation or gift. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. VI, p. 1100; Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, book I, p. 5; and *The New Treatise on Diplomatics*, vol. I, p. 395. Maffei proves that the name *testamentum* was applied to various types of charters, *History of Diplomatics*, p. 48. The royal testaments mentioned in the Ripuarian Law, in Bouquet, vol. IV, p. 247, are nothing other than diplomas of donation. This meaning of *testamentum* remained common for many centuries, and examples survive even from the end of the eleventh century.]

or should attempt to violate it, or should become its claimant, let him fear that he will incur the anger of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and the offense of holy Mary, Saint Peter the apostle, and all the saints, and that he will suffer the punishments of hell; moreover, compelled by the fisc, let him pay to the parties of that monastery ten pounds of gold and thirty pounds by weight of silver, and let him have no power to reclaim whatever he claims. Thus may this donation, made by my will, remain firm and inviolate forever, supported by formal stipulation.

And so that this letter, or this testament, may remain firm and valid at all times, I ask and humbly beseech my successors to preserve uncorrupted our acts, which have been confirmed by royal authority, for the increase of eternal recompense, if they themselves also wish their acts to remain preserved, supported by stipulation.

This testament was executed in the city of Strasbourg on the third day before the Ides of March, in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord Pippin, the glorious king, and of the venerable bishop Heddo.

[Note: Conrad, the abbot who first renewed this charter in 1121, added a false era of the Incarnation: “Executed in the year 709 from the Incarnation of the Lord.” But the original charter certainly did not contain it, since this era was not then in use. These later additions detract nothing from the truth of the original. Mabillon proves that the document rests on established facts, *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 242. Strict critics accepted this rule, among them Lenglet, *Method for Studying History*, vol. II, p. 390, Paris edition of 1729, and *Encyclopedic Dictionary*, vol. IV, p. 1019—although he was otherwise extremely hostile to ancient diplomas.]

I, Heddo, a sinner in God’s name, called bishop by God’s mercy, have reread and subscribed this testament made by me.

**Sign of Count Chrodardus.**

[Note: Chrodardus was a count of the fisc and a powerful lord in Alsace, Ortenau, and Breisgau. Chrodhardus is listed among the nobles of France in charters of King Pippin for the abbey of Saint-Denis from the years 752, 753, and 759, in Felibien, *Proofs*, pp. XXIV and XXVIII, and in Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, pp. 491 and 493. We strongly suspect, with Schoepflin, *Illustrated Alsace*, vol. I, pp. 668 and 787, that this Chrodardus was the same as Count Ruthard or Rodard, founder of the abbeys of Schwarzach and Gengenbach. For pronunciation with *Ch* was very common in ancient times in proper names.]

In the name of Christ, I, Remedius, a sinner and bishop, reread the acts of my predecessor, Bishop Heddo, and consented and subscribed.

[Note: Remedius was Heddo’s successor in the church of Strasbourg, and subscribed his predecessor’s privilege. At that time, as Mabillon notes, it was customary for episcopal privileges to be confirmed by their successors not through the granting of a new privilege but solely by adding a subscription to the original. Heddo’s own charter proves this practice, since he asks his successors to confirm his testament. Numerous examples from the fifth through the thirteenth century, cited by the authors of *The New Treatise on Diplomatics*, vol. V, pp. 2–15, prove it as well. Cointius therefore wrongly concludes from this testament that Remigius had already been ordained bishop at that time; yet on p. 669 of the same volume and p. 157 of volume VI he asserts that Heddo had already resigned his bishopric.]

I, Einhardus, having been expressly requested, wrote and subscribed.

## XXIX. Egidius, an illustrious man who became a monk, makes a notable donation to the monastery of Prüm (764)

*(In Hontheim, History of Trier.)*

**[Column 1552B]**

Since human frailty or the vicissitudes of the human race fear the final term of life through sudden transition, it is necessary that this should not find anyone unprepared. Whoever wishes to receive the salvation of his soul ought and fittingly should strive to redeem it from his own possessions.

Therefore I, Egidius, in God’s name, reflecting upon the fallibility of human life, have determined that, for eternal recompense and the remission of my sins, I may deserve to obtain pardon from the most merciful Lord in eternal blessedness. I give, and wish it to remain perpetually given, to the monastery of the holy Savior, built in the territory of Ardennes beside the River Prüm, where the venerable man Assuerus the abbot and a very large company of monks appear to be gathered, and where I laid down the hair of my head for the Lord’s name.

These are my villages called Caveniacum and Novavilla in the district of Celmanicum, with all their appurtenances,

[Note: In the district of Celmanicum, that is, Cenomannicum. From this Martène and Durand conclude that Egidius was a Gaul, and perhaps a relative of Assuerus, whom the people of Prüm make a count of Anjou, since he possessed so many extensive lands in Gaul, especially in the district of Anjou and neighboring regions.]

and whatever there appeared to serve me.

Likewise I give my villages called Nuilliacum, Duciacum, Flaviacum, Calviniacum, Juliacum, Caniacum, and Cubicium, situated in the district of Rodonicum, with all their appurtenances and whatever belongs to those villages and appeared there to serve me. From this present day I give them in their entirety to the house of the holy Savior.

Likewise, the other property which I have transferred to the holy Savior I give to that holy place, so that my children—Aginaldus, Bertricus, Botlenus, and Paulus—may cultivate it under your *precaria*,

[Note: “Under your *precaria,” that is, under the title of a *precaria*, by which someone held an estate only for life and in usufruct, while full ownership thereafter passed to another.]

and so that you may impose upon them whatever rent seems proper to you, which they shall pay you each year. After his death, each of them shall cause whatever he held under the *precaria*, together with all improved property, to return in its entirety to the aforesaid house of God and into its ownership, without any *marritione* (obstruction; the term is uncertain) or contention.

These are Comnis, Viva-aqua, Caihaco, Fol, Patriniacum, and Altiacum, situated in the district of Celmanicum, with all their appurtenances and in their entirety.

Likewise I give the other villages called Calvono, Laviniacum, Averiacum, Aurudum, Serant, Colridum, Bron, one quarter of Serant, and Duniacum, situated in the district of Anjou, with their appurtenances and in their entirety.

Likewise I give the other villages called Druvium, Palriciacum, Quevum, Bursinas, Piriallum, Dimisiniacum, Cuptiagum, and Balatiagum, situated in the district of Rodonicum, with their appurtenances and in their entirety.

And the other property not mentioned above in this document, whether I acquired it, whether my predecessors left it to me, or whether it is to be sought and has been found, I give to the house of the holy Savior. From this present day I give in its entirety whatever came to me from the share of my father Beririgus, from the share of my mother Viventiana, through purchase, or through any acquisition known to have come to me: lands, houses, buildings, resident dependents, servants, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills,

[Note: Mills.]

together with shepherds and flocks of livestock of both sexes, movable and immovable property—whatever can be said or named, and whatever appears presently to belong or pertain to the places named above, with every appurtenance—so that the whole and entire property may from this day be given and confirmed to that holy place.

Thus, from this day you shall have completely free and most secure authority in all respects to possess, hold, or do with it whatever you choose.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—if I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs, or any opposing person or anyone at all, should decide to come against this letter of my donation, which I have decreed should be made for the Lord’s name and in reverence for that holy place, or should attempt to violate it, or should become its claimant, let him receive upon himself the anger of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; let him appear excluded from the thresholds of the churches and from the fellowship of the saints; and, moreover, compelled by the fisc, let him pay to the parties of that monastery five pounds of gold and twenty pounds by weight of silver. Let no claimant have power to recover what he claims. Rather, let this present donation of my will remain firm and inviolate forever, supported by formal stipulation.

Executed at the public monastery of Prüm, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fourteenth year of the reign of our lord Pippin, the most glorious king.

## XXX. Privilege of King Pippin for the monastery of Saint Maximin (765)

*(In Hontheim, same work.)*

**[Column 1554B]**
With our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ promising eternal life in the Gospel, we believe without doubt and with full and complete faith, that it will be repaid to us in the age to come if we confirm the stability and tranquility of monasteries and, with God’s gift, increase ecclesiastical possessions under protection.

Therefore I, Pippin, by the grace of God king of the Franks, declare in this testament to all future kings forever that I hold under royal authority a certain monastery where Saint Maximinus, God’s bishop, lies buried in body—namely, one constructed in the suburb of Trier and dedicated [Col. 1554C] in honor of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist. I decree that this monastery, together with its treasury and the entire abbacy, shall always remain under the abbot of that place, since I understand that it was established in this way by kings in earlier times.

For this reason I decree that the present abbot, Utilradus, and all future abbots of that place, together with the monks and the abbacy, shall remain forever under the protection of the kings, so that, freed from every disturbance, they may serve God with spiritual joy. I also grant the aforesaid monks, by royal authority, the election of their abbot, so that they may have the power to choose whomever or whatever number they wish, on the condition that he observe the Rule with those subject to him.

But if anyone—which may it not happen—should wish to violate this charter, or inflict any harm upon the household of that place [Col. 1554D] in any matter against the abbot’s will, let him incur the anger of God and forever be held guilty of an offense against royal majesty. And so that this document may be firm, we ordered it to be authenticated with our seal.

Adalolfus countersigned.

Given in the month of January. In the public palace—that is, Ingelheim, not Mainz—in the [uncertain: “ñ m”] fourteenth year of our reign, prosperously.

[Note: [Col. 1553D] Zyllesius appended a seal engraved in bronze from the original document. [Col. 1554D] It represents this Pippin beardless, with the inscription: “+ PIPPINUS IMPERATOR,” a suspicious feature not unnoticed by others. Heineccius, On Seals, book 1, chapter 10, no. 8, especially deserves to be read here: “It is certainly strange that Pippin calls himself emperor, since he never aspired to this dignity; strange, too, that he omitted the title ‘king of the Franks,’ which even Charlemagne himself, although already raised to imperial dignity, did not abandon; and strange likewise that in the diploma he uses one title, [Col. 1555D] and in the seal another. … I know, of course, that kings have sometimes claimed the title of emperor, as is known and attested of the Bulgarians, Anglo-Saxons, and others. I also know that Frankish kings occasionally found this pleasing. Thus Baltherus calls Clovis emperor in the Life of Saint Fridolin, abbot, no. 30. Finally, I am not unaware that this same Pippin is also hailed as emperor by Suger, book 2 of On His Administration. But these rare examples do not yet establish that Pippin himself appended that title to his name.” I pass over the other suspicious features in this charter, among which the very opening of the diploma is particularly significant, since it is unusual for the Carolingians.]

## XXXI. Testament of Tello, bishop of Chur (766)

(From Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*)

[Col. 1555A]

In the name of the Holy Trinity.

When we desire to recall the mystery, and to remember continually the benefits of the Most High bestowed upon the human race; when the Lord our God Jesus Christ deigned to descend from the bosom of the Father to redeem us, and deigned, not for my merits but by his clemency, to place me also, unworthy and least of all God’s servants, among the bishops of his Church; and when I consider my misery, as well as the misfortune of my frailty, which I desire to remember not on account of any merits of mine but because of his immense mercy—still, as I am wrapped in my own sins and those of my neighbors, inherited through our first parent, and as I contemplate the uncertain end of this life and regain hope, since the Lord himself mercifully promises sinners that those who wish may redeem their sins through almsgiving:

For I, the unworthy Tello, called bishop, do not attribute what is mine to him, but return what is his, since he himself grants it. For he says through the prophet: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.” And, so that I may say it, as the same prophet says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.”

And since we know that three churches of this holy Mary, ever-virgin mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Saint Martin, and of Saint Peter have been built in this place, as well as churches of the other saints whose names have been established here; and since we know that the dwelling of many servants of God, a monastery of those living under the Rule, has been built in the place called Desertina, which I, the unworthy and sinful bishop Tello, appear to possess and use at my own expense beyond what I ought:

For the washing away of my many sins and those of my parents, I give and transfer to that church of Saint Mary, Saint Martin, and Saint Peter the property of my grandfather Jactatus and my grandmother Salvia, of my father Victor, the illustrious governor, and my mother Teusinda, of my maternal uncle Vigilius the bishop, of my brothers Zaccon, Jactatus, and Vigilius, of my nephew Victor and my sister Salvia, and of my nieces Teusinda and Odda.

And since Scripture further says that whoever possesses church property or holds any property of his own, the canons testify, must be joined to the church’s possessions, therefore I, Tello, sinful and ordained bishop, in accordance with the testimonies confirmed above, after my death or departure, cede to the aforesaid holy church of Saint Mary, Saint Martin, and Saint Peter the revenue which I establish and determine shall exist forever. I transfer it from my right into its right and dominion, and convey it forever.

This consists of the land or inheritance of my father Victor, the illustrious governor, whatever he acquired through individual instruments, obtained by whatever means, and which the Lord has deigned to give me through his generosity:

My estate at Secanium: first, the hall with an upper room, beneath it the heated rooms, above it other heated rooms, beneath it the cellar, kitchen, and room; around the estate, the stable, storehouses, presses, and other guest quarters or cellars; and everything belonging to that estate, all in its entirety.

Likewise, the small estate with its fruit trees; likewise, the gardens and vineyards beneath the estate, entirely.

Likewise, in the fortress of Sala, the masonry structure beneath the cellars, the presses in that fortress, and whatever lawfully belongs to me there, all in its entirety.

Likewise, at Vicus, my estate with its storehouses and barn, with everything belonging to that estate, together with its entrance, entirely.

Likewise, in the territories, a field at Buliu, sixty-five modia, bordering on that estate, and on the other side on Saint Columbanus; a field across from Vicus, ten modia, bordering on Gallonicus, and on the other side on Amantius; a field at Stava, eighteen modia, bordering on Victor’s property, and on the other side on the road; a field at Sarrs, eighty modia, bordering on Saint Columbanus, and on the other side on the road; a field at Astireda, fifty modia, bordering on Calausion’s property, and on the other side on Vigilius’s; a field at Renium, thirty modia, bordering on Lobecenus’s, and on the other side on Viventius’s; a field at Renium, forty modia, bordering on Jactatus’s, and on the other side on Ursecenus’s; a field in that same place, bordering on Paulus’s, twelve modia; a field before Sala, two modia; a field beneath Sala, six modia, bordering on the road; a field at Alevenoce, thirty modia, bordering on Saint Columbanus, with a house, two storehouses, an estate and its entrance, and its kennels, the field itself bordering on the road; another field, ten modia, bordering on Solemnus’s property and on Saint Martin’s.

At the summit of Levenoce, Roncale with its building, entirely.

Likewise, the meadow-estate beneath Secanium, sixty loads, with its building, bordering on Saint Columbanus, and on the other side on the road; another meadow-estate beneath Vicus, ten loads, bordering on Saint Columbanus on both sides; another meadow-estate, eight loads, bordering on the estate.

A meadow at Heretes, sixty loads, bordering on Saint Mary’s, and on the other side on the road.

A meadow at Levenoce, fifteen loads, bordering on Saint Columbanus, and on the other side on Vedalio; whatever I appear to possess in that Levenoce, entirely.

Likewise, in the alpine pasture of Agise, one hundred loads.

A meadow at Castrices in Roncale, twenty loads, bordering on Augustus’s property, and on the other side on the road.

A meadow above the rocks of Roncale, thirty loads, bordering on Saint Martin’s, and on the other side on Vederanion’s property.

And above the steps of Falaria, six loads, bordering on Saint Stephen’s, and on the other side on Lobo’s.

Likewise, in Flemme, Roncale, entirely.

Likewise, of the tenants of that estate at Secanium: Ariscius, Gaudentius, Exoberius, Calanho, Valerius, Anulfus, Crespio, and Jactatus. All these, with their wives and sons, their fields, meadows, and everything belonging to those tenant holdings, together with all their property, entirely.

Likewise, of the Spehatici: Froncio, Projectus, Evalus, Flechosvus, Lobecinus, Aurelius, Victor, Saturninus, Masso, Rusticus, Desiderius, and Lobucio. All these, with their wives and sons, their fields, meadows, and everything belonging to those holdings, together with all their property, entirely.

Amantius, the person, except for the land alone belonging to Saint Mary; Auster with his brother; Aurelianus, Praestantius, Valerius, Viventius, and Columba. Let all these, with their wives and sons and everything they appear to cultivate, return in the same manner as the preceding ones.

Likewise, my estate called Iliande: the hall with its cellar, and everything that appears to be held around that hall, entirely; presses, storehouses, barns, estates, gardens, all with their entrance; whatever appears to be held around that estate and lawfully belongs to me, entirely.

A field beneath Lobene, sixty modia, bordering on Saint Martin’s; a field at the estate, fifteen modia, bordering on Saint Mary’s; a field at Aflupius, six modia, bordering on Quartinus’s; a field at Roncale, six modia; a field before Vicus, six modia, bordering on the road.

Likewise, a meadow at Campaniola, ten loads, bordering on Saint Mary’s.

A meadow at Logorion, ten loads, bordering on Saint Mary’s.

Likewise, above the rocks, my estate with its house, storehouses, presses, garden, and everything belonging to that estate, entirely; a field, sixty modia; a meadow, one hundred loads.

Another place, Maniniocum: a field, twenty modia; another meadow at Naulo, forty loads. Let all these be given to the aforesaid church.

Likewise, the tenants of that estate at Iliande: Sporcius and Vidalinus. Let these two, with their wives and sons, their fields and meadows, and all their property, be given in full.

Likewise, Despicus, Vidalianus, Maurentius, Martinus, Calvolus, and Lidorius. All these, with their wives and sons and all their property, entirely.

Lopus and Ursocius, who are without land: let they too be given to the holy church.

Likewise, my estate at Bregelo, which I add to that monastery of Saint Mary, Saint Martin, and Saint Peter.

Likewise, at Muricia, the hall with cellar, heated rooms, upper room, presses, stable, barns, storehouses, garden, estate, and everything belonging to that estate, together with its entrance, all in its entirety.

Likewise, a field at Ruane, thirty-five modia, bordering on the river, and on the other side on Saint Mary’s; a field at Ruane itself, four modia, bordering on Julianus’s, and on the other side on Canis’s; a field across the river, eleven modia, bordering on Projectus’s, and on the other side on the river; a field above the Castle, eight modia, bordering on Silvio’s, and on the other side on Evalus’s; a field at that estate, eight modia, bordering on Julianus’s; a field at Vorce, sixty modia, bordering on Vicaon’s, and on the other side on the road, with its building, estate, and entrance, all in its entirety.

Likewise, at Selaunus, my estate with its storehouses, barns, presses, all its appurtenances, and everything belonging to that estate, entirely.

Likewise, a field at Feniles, eighty modia, bordering on that estate; a field at Arduna, sixteen modia, bordering on Evalus’s, and on the other side on Juventius’s; a field at Vicinaves, seventeen modia, bordering on Lomelengus’s, and on the other side on Saint Martin’s.

Likewise, a meadow at Sorella, eight loads, bordering on Lidorius’s; the meadow of Anives at Curtinum, twelve loads, bordering on the abbess’s property; a meadow at Esce, twenty loads, bordering on Beravius’s; a meadow at Colimne, five loads; a meadow at the Rhine, twenty loads, bordering on Victuruccio’s, and on the other side on Julianus’s; a meadow at Ruane, ten loads, bordering on Saint Martin’s; a meadow at Vallecava, four loads, bordering on the road; a meadow at Macene, twenty-five loads, bordering on the road, and on the other side on Crespio’s.

Likewise, the tenants of that estate at Taurentum: Laurentius and Lopus. Let these two, with all their property, be given in full.

From Selaune: Lidorius, Maurus, Befanius, and Sicharius. Let all these, with their wives and sons and all their property, be given in full.

Likewise, Specius of Andeste, Amantius, Montanarius, Exoberius, Frictellinus, and Johannes. Let all these, with their wives and sons and all their property, be given in full.

Likewise, from that estate, Maurelius, Dominicus, and Donadus. Let all these, with their wives and sons, their fields, meadows, and whatever belongs around those houses, be given in full.

Leo alone.

Fescianus, with his wife and sons, his fields and meadows and all his property, entirely. Let all these return after our death to that monastery of Saint Mary, Saint Martin, and Saint Peter.

Likewise, at Maile, fields, meadows, building-plots, gardens with fruit trees, whatever lawfully belongs to me—apart from the land belonging to churches—my share in full; and apart from the tenant holding which I granted to my young man Senator for his service at Maile.

Likewise, at Canpellos, fields, meadows, building-plots, gardens with their fruit trees, and everything lawfully belonging to me, all in its entirety.

Likewise, let the Plain Forest above Maile, as much as lawfully belongs to me, be given and granted to that monastery of Saint Mary, Saint Martin, and Saint Peter.

Likewise, the woodlands and fruit-bearing terraces (*scalae*) which we give to the monastery named above, above Iliande, as much as belongs to me, entirely.

Likewise, at Rucene, my estate with its hall, cellar, heated room, upper room, presses, stable, barn, storehouse, garden, and everything belonging around that estate, with its entrance and exit, with waters and pastures in the forests; likewise, Roboredum beneath Rucene, entirely.

Likewise, the Alps which we give to the monastery named above: Naulo, half; Mendane with its Secivus, entirely.

At Fadohine, my share in full.

At Ceipene, my share in full.

Likewise, we make provision concerning our dependents, to whom we have granted [property] during our lifetime and to whom we grant [it] after our death.

First, Lidorius holds the holding cultivated by Vidales. Let it return after our death to that monastery with all its appurtenances; likewise the land which Lidorius himself possesses. We give him fields and meadows, seventy modia. Whatever he appears to have beyond this number shall return to the monastery named above.

Likewise, Alecus holds at Iliande a field of forty modia; let it return after our death to that monastery.

Likewise, Gaudentius holds a field of fifteen modia; let it return to that monastery after our death.

Likewise, Crescentianus holds a holding at Rucene and four modia at Renium; let it return in the manner stated above.

Likewise, Leontius the chamberlain holds five modia at Helanengum.

Likewise, the priest Vigilius holds three modia at Helarinengum; let it return after our death to that monastery.

Likewise, Goncio holds at Vorce a field of eighty modia; let it return after our death to that monastery.

Likewise, Vadardus holds a field of fifty modia; let it return after our death to that monastery.

Likewise, Januarius holds at Taurentum two tenant holdings, apart from the people; let they return to that monastery after our death.

Likewise, the holding held by the priest Silvanus, with fields, meadows, halls, gardens, buildings, all its appurtenances, and our servant named Viventius, who lives in that house: let all these return after our death to that monastery.

Likewise, the tenant holdings held by the priest Lopus at Falaria—one with a person, the other without a person—together with a meadow of fifteen loads and a field at Roncalina of twenty modia: let all these, both the servants and the land, return after our death to that monastery.

Likewise, the holding at Falaria cultivated by Jactatus: we give it to our young man Senator, both while we are alive and after our death, for him to possess.

Likewise, the holding held by Amichus: let it return after our death to that church.

Likewise, the holding held by Laveso at Flemme and cultivated by Orsianus: let it return after our death to that monastery.

Likewise, at Valendanus, Majorinus holds a field of twenty-five modia; let it return after our death to that monastery.

Likewise, at Amede, let Majorinus retain under protection the holding which he possesses, and let Majorinus himself, together with that holding, be given to that monastery as sustenance, with his wife and sons. But if he withdraws himself from that place, let that possession remain permanently in the monastery, and let no one be permitted to remove it from there.

Likewise, the land held by Drucio at Castrice: let it return after our death to the monastery named above, and we shall establish that Drucio himself has been entrusted to that holy place.

We establish this settlement, and whatever we have forgotten or have not written in this donation to the saints—apart from the fourth part which we left to our estate at Fluminus—let the release from all our property remain as it has been written.

And while Almighty God grants me life in this world, let everything remain under my authority. After my death, let this donation remain firm, concerning fields, meadows, halls, gardens, buildings, mills, Alps, forests, waters, pastures, appurtenances, vineyards, fruit trees, livestock, large and small, bronze objects, iron fittings, harnesses, vessels, utensils, every movable and immovable thing, and whatever belongs to human life. Let it be given and granted to that monastery of Saint Mary, Saint Martin, or Saint Peter, which is called Desertina.

If anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether I myself, which may it not be, or any of my heirs or heirs presumptive, whether born of the male or female sex, whether descended from known or unknown, pretended kinships, whether near to me by my family or distantly related, or any outsider, great or small, acting in court, exercising care or royal power, or acting through some power granted by royalty, or through an agitated ducal presence, or through gifts of money, or, absurdly and arrogantly, relying upon his own power, should believe or dare to remove any of these things from these churches, and act against this deed of ours or against the command of my father, who ordered that it be done—that this written statement of our property and resources should be made, whether concerning property acquired by agreement, property owned, or anything acquired by whatever transaction or acquisition and known to have come to us—

We decree that this settlement for the redemption of our sins shall stand and be confirmed in the fellowship of the saints. I, unworthy, of sound mind and healthy heart, while alive, have taken care to fulfill my father’s commands and my own wishes, so that, for myself and for all my parents whose names have been written above, we may deserve to obtain forgiveness for our sins from the Most High Judge.

For this reason I have appointed the Creator of the world as judge and intermediary, so that he may become hostile to anyone who dares to violate or attempt to attack this deed, or by any means presumes to raise a complaint against these churches.

First, let him incur the anger of our Lord Jesus Christ, and let him be anathematized by the Holy Trinity—that is, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Likewise, on the day of judgment let him descend on the left hand with the impious into the depths of hell, as did Dathan, Abiron, and Korah, who stood rebellious against Moses. Let him, like them, sink himself into the earth’s chasm. And, like Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, let him hang himself in a noose; let him possess body and soul in a punishment of Gehenna without end.

And whatever the divine mercy shall mercifully decree to pardon of the sins of ourselves, our parents, and our dependents on account of these things, let all those sins come upon him, and let him receive condemnation with the devil and his ministers, and appear excluded from the fellowship of all catholic believers.

Moreover, at the resurrection of the human race, let seven condemnations of death fall upon him in the lake of fire.

The first condemnation: separation from the saints.

The second: rejection from the face of the Lord.

The third: descent into hell.

The fourth: repayment for his deed.

The fifth: without repentance, because there will be no forgiveness.

The sixth: torment without end.

The seventh: the end of all punishments shall never come, and he shall be excluded from the fellowship of those who serve there day and night.

In addition to all this, let him be liable to pay to the agents of the churches mentioned above twenty pounds of gold and forty pounds of silver. Let his claim obtain no effect whatsoever, but let him become, as is fitting, confounded in all things.

And let my cession, which I requested to be made with willing purpose and devoted mind, possess unshaken validity at all times and forever, with a stipulation appended.

In the fifteenth year under the reign of our lord King Pippin, that is, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, this charter of donation to the saints was made. It was enacted at Chur, in the public city, in the presence of many good men as witnesses.

+ The mark of the hand of Lord Tello, bishop and donor, who ordered this to be done and confirmed it with my own hand.

+ The mark of the priest Silvanus, witness.

+ The mark of the hand of Justinianus, judge, witness.

+ The mark of Praesens, court witness.

+ The mark of Lobucio of Amede, court witness.

+ The mark of Constantius of Senegaune, court witness.

+ The mark of Lobucio of Maile, military witness.

+ The mark of Paulus of Tremine, military witness.

+ The mark of Claudius of Chur, court witness.

+ The mark of Ursecenus of Scanavicus, court witness.
