+ The mark of Victor, son of Praestantius, military witness.

+ The mark of Justinianus of Vicus Meldone, military witness.

+ The mark of Foscio of Pogium, military witness.

And I, Foscio the priest, ordered by my lord Tello, bishop, wrote this donation and subscribed it with my own hand.

## XXXII. Pippin’s royal decree by which he restores the estate of Exona to the monastery of Saint Denis (766)

(From D. Bouquet, volume V)

[Col. 1561C]

Pippin, illustrious man, king of the Franks.

We believe that we shall be joined to a reward before the eternal Judge if we acknowledge that what was assigned to holy places and confirmed there by the signed hand of earlier kings has been affirmed by our own royal declarations, for the love of God and the recompense of the saints.

Therefore the venerable man Folradus, abbot of the basilica of our particular patron, Saint Denis, where that precious martyr appears to rest bodily with his companions, together with the abbot and a very large company of monks who dwell there and are known to serve the Lord, sent us a petition. They reported that Chlothar, king of the Franks, had assigned by his decree to that house of the lord Denis an estate called Exona, situated on the river Exona in the Parisian district; and that afterward Clovis, king of the Franks, had again confirmed it to that basilica by his decree.

The abbot therefore showed us those decrees to read again. In them we found that, through the wicked greed of evil men, the estate of Exona had later been removed from or diminished in relation to that house of Saint Denis.

The abbot and that congregation asked our royal highness that, by our confirmation and decision, we should issue such a decree that, just as the estate has until now been possessed by Count Remehone through our beneficence, with all its boundaries and appurtenances, so it should benefit that monastery and the monks serving there in its entirety, for the provision of the church’s lights and the support of the poor, and that the monks might be more pleased to pray more attentively day and night for us, for our brother of good memory, the late Kallomagnus (Charlemagne), and for our succeeding descendants, entreating the Lord’s mercy.

Therefore, let the aforesaid estate, together with all public tolls, lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, servants, vineyards, forests, fields, meadows, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, and mills, as we have said above, be held, possessed, and owned in its entirety by the aforesaid monastery and its rectors. Let it be confirmed to that house of God, as our alms and as an offering for our brother, in full legal right forever, without anyone’s claim of restitution.

And so that this cession may be held more firmly, we have confirmed it below and have taken care to authenticate it with our ring.

The mark + of Pippin, most glorious king.

In the name of God, Baddilo recognized it.

Given in the month of July, in the fifteenth year of our reign, publicly in the city of Orléans. Itherius wrote it successfully. Amen.

## XXXIII. Pippin’s donation to the monastery of Saint Antoninus (767)

(*History of Languedoc*, volume I, documents, p. 23)

A record of the transfer and confirmation carried out by Lord Pippin, most serene king of the Franks and Aquitanians, in the presence and by the hand of Fedancius, abbot of the church of Saint Antoninus the martyr, which is situated in the valley called Nobilis, where it is known that the boundary lies in the district of Rodez.

Religious men were present as witnesses to this transfer: namely, in the presence of Abbot Fedancius, Hildebold, archbishop of the see of Reims, and also Aimarus, archbishop of the see of Bourges, together with a company of twelve other bishops. Among them was Justinus, a bishop afflicted by jaundice, who, prostrated before the altar where the head of Saint Antoninus, the most glorious martyr, was kept, was suddenly protected by divine assistance and freed through the martyr’s intercession.

While this company was assembled, a crowd of soldiers and counts was also present, among them Count Bertalargus, Vulfrandus, Botelinus, and the Palatine counts, together with sixteen others.

All these men, with one voice, judged and proclaimed, along with the great crowd of people who were there, that the house of God ought to be increased for the love and reverence of blessed Antoninus the martyr, who had always been a defender and protector of the king and his entire army.

In response to their acclamation, Pippin, the most serene king, agreed that the house of God should be increased by royal donations. Therefore, after consulting his magnates, he transferred as property to the head and altar of the blessed martyr Antoninus the monastery of the apostle Saint Peter called Mormacus, situated in the district of Catucirno on the river Avarion, where it rests in God’s honor and blessing. He transferred it also to the venerable man Abbot Fedancius and to the monks and clerics dwelling there, present and future.

The whole monastery aforesaid, in its entirety, together with its dependencies—namely, two other churches, one called Mornagallus and the other the chapel of Saint Felix the martyr—together with the monks, servants, and all possessions that belonged to it and that, with the Lord’s assent, would be granted in the future; with vineyards, gardens, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters and watercourses, fishing-weirs, and mills—everything beyond the river, [by] nine cubits—he gave from the boundary of Mount Cussonus to the middle of the ear and as far as the mouth of the ancient vessel.

Everything enclosed within those boundaries, in its entirety, he gave as an allodial possession to the aforesaid house of God.

But if any emperor, king, duke, count, viscount, abbot, or any person, great or small, should wish to remove the aforesaid things from the house of God, let him be struck by the sword of anathema of all the bishops mentioned above and buried in hell with Dathan and Abiron.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of April, in the sixteenth year of the reign of Pippin, most serene emperor. Sigiltredus wrote it.

The mark of Pippin the king. +

## XXXIV. Pippin’s royal decree by which he grants the estate of Autmundistat to the church of Fulda (768)

(From D. Bouquet, volume V, based on Schannat)

Pippin, illustrious man, king of the Franks.

Since Scripture admonishes us that each person ought steadfastly to prepare himself so that, when he comes into the presence of the heavenly Judge, he may deserve to hear that gracious word of the Lord in which all the righteous will rejoice because of their good deeds, therefore, considering—as we believe, for our salvation—how, from the earthly possessions which divine mercy has deigned abundantly to grant us in this world, we ought at least to distribute something among the poor, so that we may be able to obtain his mercy, we therefore give, for the remedy of our soul and for our brother of good memory, the late Carloman, to the monastery of Fulda, where the lord Boniface rests bodily, an estate called Autmundistast, situated in the district of Maingau on the river Riechina, with all its boundaries and appurtenances.

Let the aforesaid estate, in its entirety, benefit that monastery and the monks serving there, for the provision of the lights of that church and the support of the poor, and let it be an increase there, so that the monks may be more pleased to pray more attentively day and night for us, for our brother, and for our succeeding offspring, entreating the Lord’s mercy.

Therefore, let the aforesaid estate, together with lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, servants, forests, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, as we have said above, and everything that at the present time appears to be our possession there, be held, possessed, and owned in its entirety by the aforesaid monastery and its rectors. Let it be confirmed to that house of God, as our alms and as an offering for our brother, in full legal right forever, without anyone’s claim of restitution.

And so that this cession may be held more firmly, we have confirmed it below and have taken care to authenticate it with our ring.

The mark + of Pippin, most glorious king.

In the name of God, Baddilo recognized and subscribed.

Given in the month of July, in the fifteenth year of our reign, publicly at the city of Orléans. In the name of God, Itherius wrote it successfully.

[Note: [Col. 1563D] In this original document, the chancellor’s subscription is placed opposite the king’s subscription, with a seal between them, displaying an image resembling a shaggy head impressed in a hollow of wax. Badillo, the chancellor, unusually uses an invocation when subscribing; likewise Itherius, who under Pippin performed no office other than that of notary, whatever Mabillon may allege to the contrary in *On Diplomatics*, book II, chapter 12.]

## XXXV. Letter of Sighifridus, nobleman in Alsace, to his son Altmannus, assigning extensive property to the Gregorian monastery (768)

(From Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Records*)

[Col. 1564B]

To my dearest and most beloved son, Altmannus.

I, Sighifridus, in the name of God, considering, for the love of God, that I should transfer to you my possessions in the district of Alsace, declare that these possessions are in estates called, at the boundary of Sigolt [Note: [Col. 1563D] Sigoltzheim near Kaysersberg.], the estate of Altheim [Note: [Col. 1563D] Rappoltsweiler, Ribanviler.], and two other estates called Saxones [Note: [Col. 1563D] A village between Kellenberg and Ostheim, now vanished.]; and in the estate or boundary of Heiderheim [Note: [Col. 1563D] Sassenheim.]; and in the estate or boundary of Tessinheim [Note: [Col. 1564D] Heitern, somewhat above Neuf-Brisach; *Alsatia illustrata*, volume I, p. 723.]; and in the estate of Tuginisheim [Note: [Col. 1564D] Fessenheim.], which lies in the boundary of Heruncheim [Note: [Col. 1564D] Ensisheim, a town of Upper Alsace; same work, volume I, p. 721.]; and in that boundary of Heruncheim [Note: [Col. 1564D] Dessenheim, an hour’s distance above Neuf-Brisach; *Alsatia illustrata*, volume I, p. 733.], woodland from which fifty pigs can be fattened, and in that boundary of Heruncheim [Note: [Col. 1564D] The chapel commonly called Dinsen remains there; same work, volume I, p. 733.], meadows from which one hundred and thirty cartloads of hay can be cut, except for those portions which we have donated to the houses of God.

Again, I give and transfer the possessions named above, which we mentioned earlier, both houses and estates, with buildings, servants, vineyards, lands, fields, meadows, forests, waters and watercourses.

If I myself, or any of my heirs or heirs presumptive, or any opposing person, should attempt to act against this transfer or wish to violate it, let him first incur the anger of God in punishment, appear excommunicated from every threshold of the saints, and, together with the treasury, be compelled to pay three ounces of gold and five pounds of silver.

Acted in the village of Heruncheim [Note: [Col. 1564D] Herckheim, a village two hours above Colmar; ibid., vol. I, p. 724], publicly. Sign of Sighifridus, who requested that this conveyance be made: + sign of Luitgher + sign of Sighimundus + sign of Marcoldu + sign of Siwalfuinus + sign of Horsenenus + sign of Eborninus + sign of Raffaldus + sign of Bero. Given on the Lord’s day, the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the eighteenth year of the reign of the most glorious lord King Pippin.

I, Hurulfus, an unworthy sinner and priest, wrote and subscribed this conveyance at the request of the parties.

### XXXVI. Pippin’s royal charter by which the Aequalina forest is granted to the monastery of Saint-Denis (year 768)

(From D. Bouquet.)

Pippin, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all officials, both present and future. It is desirable to earn eternal things from what is transitory, and to gain everlasting joys by distributing perishable substance. Therefore, considering this very matter, we donate to the basilica of Saint Dionysius, where that precious saint rests bodily with his holy companions, and where Abbot Fulradus appears to preside as rector, and we wish the gift to belong perpetually to that holy place, for the remedy of our soul and also because it is to be the place of burial for my body. This is our forest called Aequalina (the forest of Iveline), with all its rights and substance, whatever appears to pertain or belong to that forest, just as it has until now been possessed by us.

Therefore, by this charter, we order more particularly and wish it to be established perpetually that the aforesaid Aequalina forest, with all its entirety and whatever within or outside it pertains to it, namely: manses, lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, dependants, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable goods, money, livestock of both sexes, herds with their shepherds, as well as various kinds of wild animals, and also the forest-wardens with their dwellings, living in different places within the forest: namely, Cotonariae (Couvières), with all their entirety; at Ulfrasiaga, two manses; Humlonariae, in its entirety; likewise Visiniolum and Ursionavillare; at Putiolae (Puisieux), two manses; and Adsummumbragium [Note: [Col. 1565D] Felibianus reads Assummunbragium; he published the same charter from the original in the *Probationes Historiae Abbatiae* [Col. 1566D] *Sancti Dionysii*.], in its entirety except for half a mansus; at Villarcellum (Villarceau), one mansus; at Brogaria, one mansus; Actricomons, in its entirety; likewise Asbertovicinium; at Villare (Villiers), two manses; at Popiniaga, one mansus; and likewise at Vallis: everything and in every respect, as we have said, whole and entire, except only what is known to have previously been granted from it to holy places by written charters [Col. 1565D], namely, to Saint Germanus of Paris, to the cell called Fossatis, situated in the Parisian territory, to Saint Benedict of the monastery of Floriacum, to the Church of Saint Mary in the city of Chartres, to Saint Mary of the monastery of Argentogilum, and to Saint Peter of the Church of Poitiers. The remainder, however, shall from this day forward belong perpetually to the aforesaid monastery for possession.

The boundaries of this forest are as follows: on one side, the aforesaid Cotonariae, Watreiae, Sarnetum (Sernay), and the old monastery; on the other side [Col. 1566A], Epanevilla, the aforesaid Putiolae, and Rumbelitto (Rambouillet); on the third side, Hermolitum (Hermeray); on the fourth side, Adtanevilla (Attainville), Burdoniacum (Bourdonné), Condatum (Condé), and Vitriacum; on the fifth side, Pincionmons (Montfort) and Villare.

From this day forward, let the rectors of that holy place have, hold, possess, and enjoy all the things specified above, under the title of immunity, for the use of the said monastery. Nevertheless, we wish and command that no presumption of judicial authority, on any pretext or for the purpose of exercising hunting rights, should ever dare to enter within those boundaries without the permission of the rector of that monastery; but, just as we have granted it as our alms, so let it be preserved in every respect forever.

To make this charter more firmly established, we have decreed that it be confirmed below.

Sign + of Pippin, glorious king.

[Note: [Col. 1566D] Felibianus adds the following from the original.] Hitherius examined and subscribed.

Given in the month of September, in the seventeenth year of our reign. Acted successfully in the monastery of Saint-Denis.

### XXXVII. Pippin’s royal charter concerning the immunity of the monastery of Saint-Denis (year 768)

(From D. Bouquet, vol. V.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man. From the beginning of our reign I have watched over its establishment and complete support, with the help of the Lord, and for that good work, with the counsel of the bishops and the elder nobles, we ought to renew immunity for the confirmation of our kingdom and reward, and for attaining eternal life; and so we have done. Therefore it is fitting for the chief clemency, among other petitions, to receive favorably and bring to effect what is proposed for salvation and requested for the divine name, so that eternal things may be acquired from the perishable things of the present age, according to the Lord’s command: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9). Therefore, from the mammon of iniquity, according to his saying, we ought to purchase eternal heavenly things; and when we bestow suitable benefits upon priests, may we thereby deserve to have the Lord as our retributor [Col. 1566D] [“the Lord as retributor”] in the eternal dwelling places.

Therefore the venerable man Fulradus, abbot of the basilica of our special patron, the lord martyr Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily, petitioned the clemency of our kingdom. He stated that, from the kings who preceded us, complete immunity had long ago been granted to the estates of the aforesaid holy basilica, and he affirms that he has those charters in his possession and that this immunity has until now been preserved inviolate. He therefore requested that, for the security of the matter, we should once again confirm by our authority, concerning that holy place and the people who, with their property, give or donate themselves to that basilica, what earlier kings had granted and confirmed to the basilica by their authorities; and that we should grant and confirm this anew to the said abbot.

Therefore let your greatness and prudence know that, out of reverence for that holy place and for the peace of those who serve God there, we have again granted and confirmed our most willing favor in every respect. Accordingly, by this charter, which we specifically decree and wish to remain in force forever, we command that neither you, nor your juniors or successors, nor anyone invested with judicial authority, should at any time presume to enter the estates of the aforesaid holy basilica of the lord Dionysius, wherever they may be, in whatever counties within our kingdom, by God’s favor, they may be situated, which the monastery appears to possess or control at present, or which has been granted there by God-fearing people through lawful instruments, or may hereafter be added and assigned; nor should anyone enter to hear lawsuits, take sureties, demand fines, provide lodgings, require provisions, or exact any other payments.

Whatever our fiscus might otherwise have hoped to receive from them is entirely and in every respect granted and assigned for the benefit of our reward, together with all fines, as has been said, upon examination of the charters of earlier kings and according to what our present authority appears to contain. Whatever that holy place appears to possess at present, as we have said, and whatever may later be added or bestowed there by God-fearing people or by us, or whatever persons may lawfully and reasonably give themselves with all their property to that monastery and assign or confirm their possessions there by lawful instruments, shall from this day forward remain under complete immunity, quiet and secure.

And, as has been said, whatever our fiscus might perhaps have hoped to receive from them shall be granted and assigned in its entirety and in every respect, perpetually, for the lamps, stipends, and support of the poor of that monastery, in response to our petitions, so that they may be more inclined to pray earnestly for the stability of our kingdom and for all our peoples to the mercy of the Lord.

To ensure that this authority remains perpetually firm and inviolate for our times and those to come, and that it may be preserved and maintained unharmed through the ages, and that it may be more readily believed by all judges, we have taken care to mark it with our own hand.

Sign + of Pippin, most glorious king.

Hitherius examined and subscribed.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, in the seventeenth year of our reign. Acted in the monastery of Saint-Denis itself.

### XXXVIII. Pippin’s charter confirming the privileges of the monastery of Saint-Denis (year 768)

(From D. Bouquet, vol. V.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man. From the beginning of our reign I have watched over its establishment and complete support, with the help of the Lord, and for that good work, undertaken with the counsel of the bishops and elder nobles for the confirmation of our kingdom, for reward, for attaining eternal life, and out of reverence for Saint Dionysius the martyr, Saint Rusticus, and Saint Eleutherius—who, in glorious and triumphant devotion, obtained the crown of martyrdom for the love of Christ—we ought to renew by our gift a privilege for their basilica, where they appear to rest and shine forth in miracles, and for the monks who appear to serve there, living according to the evangelical freedom and the rule, just as the ancient fathers and earlier kings confirmed. And so we have done.

Therefore it is fitting for the chief clemency, among other petitions, to receive favorably and bring to effect what is proposed for salvation or requested for the divine name, so that it may become a conjunction of reward, when a petition is granted for the peace of God’s servants or the suitability of venerable places.

The almighty Father, who said that light should shine forth from darkness, illumined the hearts of holy Christians through the mystery of the Incarnation of his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and through the illumination of the Holy Spirit. For his love and desire, among the other glorious triumphs of the martyrs, the blessed Dionysius and the often-mentioned Rusticus and Eleutherius—the first to come after the apostles into this province of Gaul under the commissioning of blessed Clement, successor of the apostle Peter—while preaching there the baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins and striving in this way, deserved to receive the palm of martyrdom and glorious crowns.

In their basilica, where their bodies appear to rest, Christ has deigned to perform through them, for many years and up to the present, no small number of miracles and mighty works. The lord Dagobert, formerly king, also appears to rest there. May we, through the intercession of those saints, deserve to share in the heavenly kingdom with all the saints and receive eternal life.

Therefore the venerable man Folradus, abbot of that basilica of our special patron, the lord Dionysius, judged it necessary to petition the clemency of our kingdom. He stated that, for a long time, a complete privilege had been granted to that basilica of the lord Dionysius by the bishops of the city of Paris, and had been confirmed from that time until now by the earlier kings, our ancestors. He affirms that he has that privilege, as well as the charters and confirmations, in his possession. But for complete security, the abbot Folradus himself asked our highness that we should confirm this anew by our charter. Let your greatness know that we have willingly received this most religious petition and confirmed it in every respect.

Since the aforesaid princes, other ancient kings, and Christian people who feared God appear to have enriched that temple and holy place with possessions out of love for God and for eternal life, it is our complete devotion, as we have stated above, that we should make or confirm a privilege for that holy place, for the abbot and the brothers residing there, for their future peace, so that the congregation may more easily pray continually at the thresholds and tombs of those martyrs for the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore, by this text of our authority, according to what was established by the aforesaid privilege of the bishops and confirmed by earlier kings, and out of reverence for those martyrs, we confirm that whatever has been assigned to that holy place—whether villages, dependants, or any other goods or persons—by ancient princes or by God-fearing people out of love for God, or whatever may hereafter be added, since that holy place appears to have been enriched and endowed by the munificence of kings, no bishop, whether present or future, nor their successors or administrators, nor any other person, may in any manner remove anything from that place, usurp any authority over that monastery, or make anything under the title of an exchange without the will of the abbot, the congregation, or our permission.

Nor may they remove or diminish chalices, crosses, altar vestments, sacred books, gold, silver, or any object whatsoever that has been given there or may hereafter be given, nor may they take such things to the city; they are entirely forbidden and must not presume to do so. Rather, let the holy congregation and that holy place possess perpetually whatever has been granted to them by lawful assignment.

We have also been pleased to insert the following into this privilege of our serenity: when the abbot of that house of God has been summoned from this world by divine will, let the holy congregation itself choose from among its members someone whom they find good and suitable, capable of governing and directing the burden of the abbacy according to the holy rule. When they have agreed unanimously, he shall, by authority granted by us or by our successors, be installed as abbot in that house of God, so that they may continually implore the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom, for all our peoples, and for the salvation of the country.

Because, out of love for God, reverence for those holy martyrs, and the attainment of eternal life, we appear to have granted this benefit to that holy place and monastery with the agreement of the bishops, nobles, illustrious men, and our leading men, with most grateful spirit and complete devotion, we stipulate that, just as in the time of earlier kings a psalmody was established there in the holy basilica by companies [Col. 1570A], so it shall be celebrated perpetually in that holy place, day and night, as the holy order teaches.

We are confident that this authority, with Christ assisting us in all things, helps those who consent to it and despises those who wish to destroy it. To give it firmer force, and so that, with God’s help, it may be preserved unharmed and maintained through the ages for our times and those to come, we have taken care to mark it with our own hand.

Sign + of Pippin, most glorious king.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, in the seventeenth year of our reign. Acted in the monastery of Saint-Denis itself.

### XXXIX. [Note: [Col. 1569D] Felibien published it in *Histoire de Saint-Denys*, *Preuves*, p. XXX; Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book VI, p. 495; and Bouquet, in *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. V, p. 708. But not with sufficient accuracy. We give it corrected, as the aforementioned D. La Forcade transmitted it to us from the original.] Diploma of Pippin, king of the Franks, by which he confirms to Fulradus, abbot of Saint-Denis and his chaplain, the conveyance made to him by Wido, lord of Alsace, of Gemar, Saint-Hippolyte, Ensheim, Schaeffersheim, Grusenheim, and Rappolsweiler. Given 23 September 768

(From Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*.)

Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all bishops, abbots, counts, nobles, and our envoys traveling everywhere from our palace.

Since, by the mercy of God, we appear to govern the kingdoms of the earth, we ought continually to consider them in God’s name, so that our favor may protect those whose care appears to have been entrusted to us, and so that we may defend and support by the right path those who need protection. For above all, our honor must continually shine in the case of those who not only appear to have preserved their faith toward us inviolate in every respect, but also do not cease to offer the constant service of all their united strength.

Therefore we rightly judge that those who are known to perform such services, and who enable their lives to be lived peacefully in our times, should by the firmest right be able in future, under Christ’s protection, to rule without disturbance the things granted by us with free authority.

Accordingly, since it is known to many that our faithful and God-favored venerable man Fulradus, our chaplain and archpresbyter [Note: [Col. 1569D] Fulradus is called “the most beloved abbot and archpresbyter of Gaul” in Pope Adrian’s letter to Tilpinus, archbishop of Reims, written around the year [Col. 1570D] 775, in Flodoardus, *History of the Church of Reims*, book II, chapter 17. Charlemagne calls him his palace chaplain in a diploma for the monastery of Salon, dated 777, in Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 499], recently came to us and was almost exposed to mortal danger through the hardship of the journey, he therefore handed over to us property belonging to him which a certain man named Wido [Note: [Col. 1570D] Schoepflinus proves that Wido was a powerful lord of many places in Alsace, *Alsatia illustrata*, vol. I, p. 667] had assigned to him, so that we might confirm that property for the salvation of Wido’s soul to holy places.

But since, through the assistance of divine mercy, he was restored again to his former health, we appear to have returned the aforesaid property to Fulradus himself. Yet, fearing that after some period of time certain people, out of greed, might seek the aforesaid property or bring a legal claim against him on that account, he therefore asked our highness that we should generally confirm that conveyance by a charter of our own. Know that we have granted this with grateful spirit and confirmed it in every respect.

We therefore command that the aforesaid venerable man Fulradus, our chaplain, may have, hold, give, sell, and exchange the property that the aforesaid Wido gave him, namely Ghosmari [Note: [Col. 1571C] Ghosmari, called Guirmari in Fulradus’s testament, is today the small town of Gemar, situated on the royal road leading from Sélestat to Colmar], Audaldovilare [Note: [Col. 1571C] Today a small town in Lorraine, named Saint-Hippolyte after the relics of Saint Hippolytus, commonly Sant-Bilt; concerning it, see Calmet, *Notice de la Lorraine*, vol. I, p. 572], Ansulfishaim [Note: [Col. 1571D] Ansulfisheim, which Fulradus’s testament calls Ansulsesheim, is not Ansolsheim near Colmar, as Schoepflinus thinks, *Alsatia illustrata*, vol. I, p. 715. Rather, it is the village of Aneschaim or Ensheim, two hours from Strasbourg, belonging to the lords Zorn of Plobsheim, formerly an ancient fief of the dukes of Lorraine together with the town of Saint-Hippolyte. At Ensheim there is a court belonging to the Strasbourg hospital, still called the court of Saint-Dionysius], Suntor [Note: [Col. 1571D] Suntor, which Fulradus calls Scaserisheim in his testament, is the village of Schaeffersheim near Erstein, belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg. Schoepflinus, *Alsatia illustrata*, vol. I, p. 733, interprets Suntor as Sundhofen, a village one league from Colmar. But, besides the fact that he himself cites evidence that at that time neither Sundhofen nor its tithes belonged to Fulradus, the interpreter of this name is Fulradus’s testament of the year 777 itself: when listing the places assigned to him by Wido, it says not Suntor but Scaserishaim], Grucinhaim [Note: [Col. 1572C] Grusenheim, a village between the Rhine and the Ill, belonging to the Rathsamhausen family], Ratberto Villare [Note: [Col. 1572D] Today Rappolsweiler, in French Ribeauvillé, a small town of Upper Alsace], and whatever the aforesaid Wido appears to possess through the precarial grant of Fulradus [Note: [Col. 1572D] We shall explain the precarial charter below, no. 49, in the notes to the testament of Remigius, bishop of Strasbourg].

Fulradus handed this property over to us, in its entirety: lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, dependants, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable goods, money, livestock of both sexes, herds with their shepherds, and every kind of household equipment, whatever is known to have come lawfully to Wido from his father, his mother, or anywhere else; everything that he appears to have possessed in Alsace and in the Mortenau. All of it, entire and complete, was his possession in those counties, and he gave it to Fulradus; and Fulradus, as we have said, gave it to us during his illness; and we have now again given it to Fulradus.

From this day forward, by our munificence, he shall have permission to possess, hold, give, sell, and exchange that property. If, for the love of Christ and as a remedy for his soul, he wishes to assign it to holy places, wherever he pleases, he shall, with our permission and without disturbance from any judge or from the fiscus, and without opposition from Wido’s heirs, have completely free and firm authority in every respect to do with that property whatever he wishes.

To make this authority more firmly established and better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it below and sealed it with our ring.

Sign + of Pippin, most glorious king. Hitherius examined and subscribed [Note: [Col. 1572D] Hitherius, Pippin’s archchancellor, continued to hold the same office from the beginning of Charlemagne’s reign, according to Bouquet, vol. V, p. 695].

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, in the seventeenth year of our reign [Note: [Col. 1572D] Mabillon assigns this diploma to the year 767, but incorrectly. For it is clear from the *Annals of Einhard*, in Bouquet, vol. V, p. 200, and from other sources, that in September 767 Pippin was waging war on the banks of the Garonne, in the farthest regions of Aquitaine. Therefore, with Bouquet, we assign this diploma to the year 768. At that time Pippin was ill in the monastery of Saint-Denis itself, according to the anonymous continuator of the Fredegarian Chronicle, in the same Bouquet, p. 9; he died there on 24 September, the day after this diploma was granted]. Acted in the monastery of Saint-Denis itself.

### XL. Charter of King Carloman, brother of Charlemagne, by which he confirms the immunities of the monastery of Saint-Denis and exemption from tolls for all who come to the festival or market of Saint-Denis (year 769)

(From Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*.)

Carloman, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, household officers, vicars, centenarii, and all officials, both present and future, as well as all our envoys traveling everywhere.

Therefore let your prudence and greatness know that the venerable man Fulradus, abbot of the basilica of our special patron Saint Dionysius, where that precious lord appears to rest bodily, and the abbot himself together with a very large company [Col. 1572B] of monks, who appear to dwell in that monastery and are known to serve the Lord, sent a petition and informed us that the lord Pippin, of good memory, formerly king and our father, and the other predecessors who held the governance of the kingdom of the Franks before him and before us, had granted by their charters and confirmed by their sealed authority the following benefit to the house of Saint Dionysius in the county of Paris: concerning the festival of Saint Dionysius, our patron, and concerning the villages and fields, both there and elsewhere, for those who come to conduct various kinds of business, carry on extensive trade, or purchase wine in the ports and on the various rivers leading to that festival, they had granted or confirmed the tolls in their entirety to the house of Saint Dionysius in the county of Paris.

They therefore presented to us the charters of the aforesaid men, as well as the judicial decisions and confirmations of earlier kings, for reading, just as has been inserted above. After those charters, decisions, and confirmations had been reread and examined, they also presented for our reading the judgment by which the agents of Saint Dionysius had prevailed over the agents of earlier judges, issued by the lord Pippin, of good memory, our father and formerly king, by Childebert, and also by Grimoald, mayor of the palace.

Afterward Fulradus himself and the monks of Saint Dionysius stated and reported that the tolls from the villages and fields belonging to them, entirely without the intervention of a judge, ought to belong to the house of the lord Dionysius; and Fulradus, our abbot and chaplain, affirmed that he had brought back in his possession the judicial decision and confirmation of our lord and father Pippin, most glorious king, and that this had been the custom of kings there for a long time, and that the tolls had been granted and preserved in their entirety for that house of God.

When we found that this matter had been conducted and carried out in this way by the earlier kings, they presented such charters and confirmations to us for rereading. We therefore granted anew that from this day no one exercising judicial authority, whether in that market, through their fields, at the ports, from their people, their merchants, or people of any nation who come to the aforesaid market, nor through their villages, ships, ports, carts, or pack animals, should presume to demand or exact any toll, road tax, wheel tax, bridge tax, port tax, salt tax, cispitaticum, market tax, or any other customary exaction.

Nor may anyone demand the four-denarius payment from people of all nations who come there to that market, which Count Sonachildis and Count Guaireridus, as we mentioned above, imposed as a customary payment on the merchants; nor may anyone demand any exaction or impose any opposition within the county of Paris, in that city, or anywhere else from those who come to that festival. Neither you, nor your juniors or successors, may presume to demand or exact anything.

Except, as we have said, whatever our fiscus might perhaps have hoped to receive for our share and for all our officials: the whole toll, in every respect, shall be granted, assigned, and adjudicated in its entirety to that house of God, so that in future it may be confirmed and adjudicated by our authority and that of earlier kings.

Since we have granted and confirmed this for God, out of reverence for the aforesaid martyr Saint Dionysius, for the remedy of our soul, for the stability of the kingdom of the Franks, and for our nobles and their posterity, let it be used for lamps in the house of Saint Dionysius, and for the monks, the poor, and pilgrims. We grant and confirm this entirely as our alms, so that they may be more inclined to pray earnestly for the stability of our kingdom and for all our peoples to the mercy of the Lord, and so that it may contribute to the increase of that house of God for all ages, present and future.

To make this confirmation of ours firmer, after examination of the charters and judicial decisions adjudicated by King Pippin and the other kings, and so that it may be preserved perpetually concerning that house of God, we have decreed that it be signed below by our hand and sealed below with our ring.

Sign + of Carloman, most glorious king.

Maginarius examined and subscribed.

Given in the month of January, in the first year of our reign. Acted successfully in the public palace at Salmunciacum, in the name of God.

### XLI. Charter of King Carloman for the monastery of Saint Gregory (year 769)

[Note: [Col. 1573D] It appears in a defective form in Lunig, *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, continuation 1, p. 1097, and in Bouquet, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. V, p. 715.]

(From Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*.)

Carloman, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. Garinus, count, we believe that this unquestionably pertains to the stability of our kingdom in God’s name: when the petitions of priests or churches are brought before our ears, we bring them to effect. Therefore let your greatness and prudence know that, for the sake of our reward, we have granted and bestowed from our fiscus, near Aufoldus [Note: [Col. 1573D] Aufoldus, Aufholz, commonly Ufholz, a village near the town of Sennheim], by our munificence, full and complete grace and such a benefit upon the venerable man Restoinus, abbot of the little monastery between the two Fachinae [Note: [Col. 1573D] Also Fachina, German Fecht], that whatever he might be able to purchase from our fiscal people, or add or acquire from any transaction, our serenity should generally confirm for that monastery, for Abbot Restoinus and his successors.

For we command that neither you, nor your juniors or successors, should in any way act contrary to this. Whatever, as we have said, the aforesaid Abbot Restuinus may acquire by our munificence, whether by purchase or by any acquisition, and add or acquire for that little monastery [lacuna] no fiscal official on our behalf shall demand anything from him on that account. Rather, under the title of immunity, let him be permitted to live and reside peacefully with the abbot himself and C[lacuna]onaculis [uncertain], who appear to serve that little monastery, or with their successors, so that they may be more inclined to pray for the stability of our kingdom [lacuna] and for ours [uncertain].

And so that this charter may possess fuller force, we have decreed that it be strengthened by the marks of our hand above.

Maginarius examined and subscribed.

[Col. 1574D] Sign + of Carloman, most glorious king. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the first year of the reign of our lord Carloman, most glorious king. Acted successfully at the palace of Attiniacum [Note: [Col. 1573D] Attiniacum, an ancient palace of the kings of France, was situated on the Aisne in Charlemagne’s portion of the kingdom. From this diploma we infer that Carloman was then staying there with his brother. Something similar is indicated by the Annals of Tilianus of the Franks under the year 769, where Charles is said to have joined his brother Carloman at a place called Duas Dives while traveling from Aachen, where he had celebrated Christmas, into Aquitaine. By Duas Dives perhaps Dusiacum is meant, which, like Attiniacum and not far from it, lay on Charles’s route to Aquitaine. In this way Carloman appears to have accompanied his brother from Dusiacum to the palace at Attiniacum and to have remained there for some time], in the name of God.

### XLII. [Note: [Col. 1575D] This diploma was discovered in the corner of the tower of the priory house of the monastery of Argentogilum by the most distinguished and learned abbot, Lord Claude Fleury, prior of that place.] Charter of King Carloman concerning the immunity of the church of Argentogilum (year 769)

(From D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*, from the original.)

[Col. 1575A]

Carolomannus, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. For it is fitting that royal clemency willingly bestow suitable benefits upon its faithful, and that it carry into effect and confirm what justice has demanded. We wish to confirm by our own decrees the benefits known to have been granted by our predecessors, so that they may be more pleased faithfully to serve under our rule.

Therefore Sagrata, abbess of the monastery of Argentolaium in Christ the Lord, addressed the clemency of our kingdom, representing [Col. 1575B] that our predecessor, the late king, through his authority and with the confirmation of his own hand, had granted or confirmed complete immunity for all the estates of her church, without the entry of judges, so that neither a public judge might enter those estates to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings, or demand any other public payment, nor might he interfere with anything that our treasury could have received from the estates of the aforesaid monastery.

She therefore affirmed that she possessed the precepts of our predecessors through their own hands, and she produced them at the present time to be read; she also asserted that the benefit had been granted to her by those kings and that, at the present time, she was to maintain or preserve it from those same authorities. But for complete security she requested that our highness confirm this more fully by our authority. Let your prudence and greatness therefore know that, for the love of God, we have anew confirmed and granted this benefit with the fullest willingness.

Accordingly, we order that, just as the aforesaid monastery, or the aforementioned abbess Ailina, has obtained from those kings, our predecessors, through their precepts confirmed by their hands, complete immunity for all its estates without the entry of judges, so now and in future this benefit shall be preserved by the same monastery. Neither you, nor your juniors or successors, nor any judicial authority, shall presume to enter the courts of that monastery or of the aforementioned abbess Ailina to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings, or demand any other public payment—whatever our treasury could hope to receive from them—unless this remains perpetually undisturbed by our indulgence. And so that this authority may remain firm, we have decreed that it be confirmed below with the mark of our hand.

**Sign (+) of the lord Carolomannus, the most glorious king.**

Maginarius: I have examined and subscribed.

Given in the month of November, in the second year of our reign. Enacted at the public palace of Pontio, happily, in the name of God.

### XLIII. Carolomannus renders justice to the monastery of Prüm concerning the place called Benutfeld (770)

*(From Hontheim, History of Trier.)*

Carolomannus, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. We ask royal clemency and exhort the minds of our faithful that, toward those who have maintained unblemished faith and true loyalty both toward our father and toward us up to the present, they may show favor to their petition in whatever they have disclosed to our ears. We know that their minds, which we now hold under our dominion, are becoming increasingly cheerful and ready each day for our service. [Col. 1576B]

Therefore our faithful, God willing, the illustrious man Dirodoinus, count of our palace, made known to the clemency of our kingdom, with God’s help, that our predecessors, formerly kings established by God, through written instruments and a series of charters, had granted and confirmed by their authorities and the confirmation of their hands, both to their family and to the descendants who followed from it, a certain forest in the place called Benutfeld, within the centena of Belslango [Note: [Col. 1575D] Just as districts (*pagi*) were divided into counties, so these were divided into hundreds (*centenae*); the hundred of Belslango was therefore a part of the larger district of Ardenne.], within the vast Ardenne. He brought before us for rereading the royal grants concerning that forest and informed us that royal agents (*peractores*) had unjustly invaded part of it, and that my father, Pippinus, the most glorious king, had transferred possession of that forest to the aforesaid Dirodoinus and his legitimate children.

He had transferred possession to them, since the matter had been fully argued before us; and since we have learned, both through truthful men [Note: [Col. 1576D] *Per veragos homines*: that is, truthful persons, or trustworthy witnesses. Du Fresne, *Glossary*, under this word, new edition.] and through royal confirmations, that justice belonged to him and his legitimate children [Note: [Col. 1576D] *Gamaladiones* are what legitimate children, born from lawful marriages, are called, in distinction from natural children. See Du Fresne, *Glossary*, under “Gamales.”], we render him justice concerning the place called Benezvelt, from the spring that is in that estate. Within each portion they are to have whatever pertains to us. Formerly our officials unjustly denied this to him and his legitimate children; and within the boundary there was a vein or channel of that spring extending around various places, which our judges, on our behalf, unjustly denied to them.

[Note: [Col. 1576D] *Manu vestita fecisset* means that he had transferred possession to him.]

We order that from this day forward the aforesaid forest, with the portions belonging to our said men, and in future times as well, shall not be taken away, diminished, or denied by any public judge from those portions. Within the boundary of the spring, they shall have each portion, both in forests and in lands, fields, meadows, cultivated ground, open country, pastures, waters and watercourses, appurtenances and dependencies—in short, everything in its entirety, as we have said. The said Dirodoinus, his legitimate children, and their descendants shall possess it as vindicated and adjudicated; and whatever they wish to do with that forest, they shall have by our authority. They shall hold and possess it and leave it to their descendants to possess. Whatever they may wish to do with it, they shall have, by our authority, free and most secure power in every respect.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved better through the ages, we have decreed that it be confirmed below with our own hand and ordered that it be sealed with our ring.

**Sign (+) of Carolomannus, the glorious king.**

Mainarius: I have examined.

Given in the month of May, in the second year of our reign.

Enacted at the public palace of Brocmagad, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### XLIV. Charter of Carolomannus, king of Austrasia, by which he confirms the possessions of the monastery of Honau, issued in March 770

[Note: [Col. 1577C] This charter exists in a corrupt form in Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 698; Eccard, *Origins of the Austrian Habsburgs*, p. 103; and Bouquet, vol. V, p. 720. It is more correctly printed in Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*, vol. I, p. 43.]

*(From Grandidier, History of the Church of Strasbourg.)*

[Col. 1577B]

Carolomannus, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. To all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, household officers, vicars, centenarii, and all our traveling envoys, both present and future.

Know that we believe the greatest increase of strength for our kingdom lies in granting suitable benefits to the estates of churches through benevolent deliberation, and, with the Lord’s protection, we trust that they will endure securely. Therefore let your prudence know that, at the petition of the venerable man Stephen, abbot, we appear to have granted the following benefit for eternal reward, namely, etc. (What follows here agrees entirely with the words of the charter of Pippinus, king of the Franks, from the year 759, printed in column 1531, except that “Stephen” is read here in place of “Dubanus.”)

And so that this present authority may remain inviolate, with God’s help, both now and in future times, we have decreed that it be confirmed below by our hand and ordered that it be sealed with our ring.

**Sign (+) of Carolomannus, the most glorious king.**

Maginarius: I have examined and subscribed.

Given in the month of March, in the second year of our reign.

[Note: [Col. 1577D] Father Germon rejects and condemns charters of kings in which the day of the month is not assigned, *Disputations* I, p. 257, and *Disputations* II, pp. 101 and 105. Fontanini, *Vindication of Diplomas*, p. 339, and the French authors of the *New Diplomatics*, vol. IV, p. 659, learnedly refute Germon; even today, royal edicts of France often give the month and year without the day.]

Enacted at the public palace of Theudonevilla, happily, in the name of God.

[Note: [Col. 1577D] Today Thionville, a strongly fortified town in the duchy of Luxembourg, concerning which see Germanus in Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Practice*, book IV, p. 329.]

### XLV. Charter of Carolomannus, king of Austrasia, by which he confirms to the monastery of Novientum, or Ebersheim, the possessions that Adalricus, duke of Alsace, had granted to the same monastery. Given 6 May 770

[Note: [Col. 1577D] This charter was never published. However, a spurious diploma of the same year, attributed to Charlemagne and presented in authentic form, exists in the Ebersheim cartulary; see *Patrologia*, vol. XCVII, col. 1080.]

*(From Grandidier, ibid.)*

[Col. 1578A]

Carolomannus, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man.

[Note: [Col. 1577D] Carolomannus, the younger son of King Pippinus and brother of Charlemagne, was already crowned king by Pope Stephen in 754. After his father’s death in 768 he obtained the government of Austrasia, over which he ruled for only three years and approximately three months. He died at Salmuntiacum on 4 December 771.]

Since we have learned from Scripture that “the king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters every evil with his gaze,” [Note: [Col. 1578D] Proverbs, chapter XX, verse 8.] we therefore believe that this is fulfilled through us, who administer the responsibility of so great a name, if we strive to enrich and exalt the venerable places of God’s churches through the advantage of some gift; and we have no doubt that this will greatly benefit us and the stability of our kingdom.

[Col. 1578B] Therefore let the sagacity of all God’s faithful and ours, both present and future, know how [Note: [Col. 1578D] Isenhardus is called the successor of Abbot Benedict in the chronicle of Novientum. In a certain manuscript we read that this Isenhardus is mentioned in an instrument of exchange, when, in Charlemagne’s time, certain estates were exchanged between Novientum and a certain nobleman named Riehbold in the ban of Uttenheim. This instrument is unknown to us.] Isenhardus, abbot of the monastery called Novientum, situated in the Alsatian district on the river Ill, approached the clemency of our kingdom. The illustrious man Adalricus, also called Athicus, duke, and his wife Bersvinda, in the name of Christ and in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Saint Maurice the Martyr, and his companions, had newly built it on their own property. Isenhardus petitioned us to renew the privileges that our father, Pippinus, of pious memory, [Note: [Col. 1578D] The chronicle of Novientum records that, in the time of Abbot Benedict, who succeeded Columbanus, King Pippinus granted the monastery of Novientum immunity together with all its appurtenances. The present charter of privilege, now lost, is evidently remembered here by his son Carolomannus.] and his predecessors, namely, the kings of the Franks, had conferred upon that monastery and upon the places belonging to the support of the brothers serving God there.

Therefore, by the authority of royal majesty, confirming the enactments of our predecessors, we decree that, in the estates which the aforementioned duke assigned as a dowry to the church of the aforesaid monastery, together with all their appurtenances—namely, churches, fields, plots, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, resident dependents, slaves, meadows, pastures, forests, hunting rights, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, roads and trackless ways, exits and entrances, things sought and to be sought, and all utilities whatever belonging to the said properties—that is:

At Wishuvilare, situated in the district of Brisigau on the bank of the Rhine, with all its appurtenances [Col. 1579A].

[Note: [Col. 1578D] Today Weisweiler in Breisgau, a village on the Rhine where the abbey has lost its revenues.]

At Sulza, with everything belonging to it;

[Note: [Col. 1579C] Today the small town of Sulz, or Ober-Sulz, situated in the upper Mundat, only half a league from Gebweiler.]

At Burchheim;

[Note: [Col. 1579C] The village of Burgheim near Oberenheim, subject to the jurisdiction of the city of Strasbourg.]

At Lagelenheim;

[Note: [Col. 1579C] Today Lagelnheim, a league and a half from Colmar, situated on the river Ill.]

At Gruzenheim;

[Note: [Col. 1579C–D] Today Grusenheim, between Sélestat and Colmar, belonging to the lords of Rathsamhausen. The Ebersheim abbey possesses a manorial court there and shares the tithes of the Grusenheim district with the parish priest. It also formerly enjoyed the right of patronage there, down to the year 1749.]

At Sigoltesheim;

[Note: [Col. 1579D] Today Sigolsheim, or Savamont, a village of Upper Alsace near Kientzheim, where the abbey still has a manorial court.]

At Racenhusen;

[Note: [Col. 1579D] Today Rathsamhausen near Sélestat, belonging to the lords of that name. The Ebersheim abbey enjoys the tithes there.]

At Oleswilern;

[Note: [Col. 1579D] Today Orschweiler, a village two leagues above Rouffach, where the abbey possesses certain revenues.]

At Scerenwilere;

[Note: [Col. 1579D] Today Scherweiler, situated opposite Sélestat at the foot of the Vosges, at the entrance to the Villé valley, belonging to the lord of Choiseul. The aforesaid abbey has some possessions there.]

At Sarmeresheim;

[Note: [Col. 1579D; 1580C] Today Sermersheim, above Benfeld, situated on the river Ill and belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg. The Ebersheim abbey shares the tithes there with the parish priest and also enjoys a manorial court and the right of patronage.]

At Hudenheim;

[Note: [Col. 1580C] Today Huttenheim, two leagues below Ebersheim, belonging to the same bishop of Strasbourg.]

At Northus;

[Note: [Col. 1580C–D] Today Northausen, commonly called Nartz, near Erstein, also belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg. The abbey exchanged its possessions at Northausen with the major chapter of Strasbourg for properties at Kogenheim.]

—with the entire tithe of those properties.

Let no public judge or judicial authority presume to enter there, constrain any person, hear cases, take fines, make lodgings or provisions there, or make any claim for our treasury. Instead, the aforesaid abbot Isenhardus and his successors shall possess those things with full authority, increasing and improving them.

And so that this authority of ours may remain firm and inviolate, we have signed it below with the subscriptions of our hands and sealed it below with our ring.

[Col. 1579B] **Sign of the lord Carolomannus, the most glorious king, in the name of Christ.**

[Note: [Col. 1580D] Maginarius was Carolomannus’s chancellor and examined all the charters of that king.]

Maginarius: I have examined and subscribed.

Given on the day before the Nones of May, in the second year of our reign.

Enacted at Bruocmagad [Note: [Col. 1580D] An ancient place of the Triboci, called Brocomagus, described by Schoepflin, *Illustrated Alsace*, vol. I, pp. 57 and 231. It was destroyed under the Alemanni and later became a royal palace. Today it is the village of Brumat, or Brumpt, in Alsace, belonging to the house of Hesse-Darmstadt. Martène, *Ancient Monuments*, vol. I, p. 32, contains another precept of Carolomannus for the monastery of Prüm, also issued at Brocmagad in May of the second year of his reign.] at the public palace, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### XLVII. Privilege of King Carolomannus for the monastery of Grandval (770)

[Note: [Col. 1580D] This charter is presented in interpolated form by Labbe, *Miscellanies*, chapters 6 and 7, section 1; Cointius, *Annals of the Franks*, vol. V, year 769, p. 745; and Bouquet, *Scriptores of Frankish Affairs*, vol. V, p. 716.]

*(From Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*.)*

Carolomannus, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards. Let it be known to all bishops, dukes, abbots, counts, household officers, vicars, centenarii, and all our traveling envoys.

Whenever the rightful petition of priests, which will benefit the needs and places of the saints, reaches the ears of our clemency, it ought also to be such that, once heard and effectively committed in the name of the Lord, we may deserve to obtain forgiveness from the eternal recompensor; and it should please them continually to pray for the stability of our kingdom and faithfully to assist our kingdom in every respect.

Therefore let your greatness or prudence know that, concerning the monastery of Grandval, built in honor of the holy virgin Mary, and the cell of Verteme in honor of Saint Paul [Note: [Col. 1580D] The cell of Saint Paul at Werd. See Urstis, *Chronicle of Basel*, p. 7.], and the cell of Saint Ursicinus the Confessor subject to it, where the venerable abbot Gundoaldus appears to preside, a petition was sent and it was made known that our father, King Pippinus, of good memory, and the other kings who before him and before us held the governance of the Frankish kingdom, had granted to the said house, through the confirmation of their hands, the following benefit: the estates of those kings were to enjoy complete immunity, according to their precepts, in accordance with what our predecessors had granted from their authority to the said house, and they had received it fully and completely [lacuna] or, for the peace of that house and its aforesaid successors, we have appeared to have granted it [lacuna].

Therefore, by this special precept of ours, we have decreed and ordained that it shall be perpetual [lacuna]. We shall grant that neither you [lacuna], nor your successors, nor anyone invested with judicial authority, in the courts or estates of that monastery or in the buildings belonging to them, in any districts or territories, whether in what it appears to possess or govern at the present time, or in what it may yet acquire, increase, improve, or obtain through the gift of kings or queens, through a contribution of the people, by purchase, or by any other means, shall presume to hear cases, exact fines, take sureties, make lodgings or provisions, constrain persons, constrain the officers, servants, or resident dependents of the monastery, or demand or exact any public payments.

Whatever would otherwise be rendered from these things to our treasury or to counts shall be entirely excluded. No judicial authority nor our traveling envoys shall presume [the construction is corrupt]; all their estates are to stand under the name of immunity, together with all granted fines and public payments and everything stated above. Thus the abbot Gundoaldus and his successors may possess and govern all this in the name of the Lord at all times.

We have granted this to those monasteries and to the monks who are or have been there, for the increase of our reward, in such a way that nothing contained above, which was granted to them by our clemency, may be challenged, whether in our times or in times to come, or at any time whatsoever. It shall remain perpetually unimpaired and undisturbed, except insofar as what was granted through this our precept is concerned.

And so that this authority of ours may be held more firmly and preserved better through the ages, we have signed it below with the subscriptions of our hands and sealed it below with our ring.

[Note: [Col. 1581C–D] Carolomannus had already been crowned by Pope Stephen in 754. After the death of his father Pippinus in 768, he ruled part of Austrasia and Burgundy together with half of Aquitaine. The duchy of Alemannia belonged to Austrasia, under which were Alsace and the territory of the monastery of Grandval. He died in 771.]

### XLVII. Charter of King Carolomannus by which he grants the estates of Faberola and Norontum to the monastery of Saint-Denis (771)

*(From D. Bouquet, *Collection of the Histories of France*.)*

[Col. 1581B]

Carolomannus, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. Since Scripture admonishes us that each person ought to prepare himself steadfastly so that, when he comes into the presence of the heavenly Judge, he may deserve to hear that gracious word of the Lord, at which all the righteous will rejoice because of their good works, we therefore, as we believe wisely, consider how from the earthly goods that heavenly grace has graciously bestowed upon us in abundance in this age, we ought at least to distribute something among the poor, so that we may be able to obtain the mercy of the Most High.

For this reason we cede and donate, as a remedy for our soul and for the soul of our late father Pippinus, to the monastery of Saint Dionysius the Martyr, where the precious lord rests bodily with his companions, and we wish the donation to belong to the aforesaid holy place. These are the estates that our father had formerly assigned through our hands to that house of God, namely Faberola, situated in the district of Madrie, and Norontum in the district of Chartres, with all their entirety and appurtenances, to the same monastery and to the monks dwelling there, for the provision of the church’s lamps and the support of the poor. The aforesaid estates are to benefit the monastery’s increase, just as they were possessed by our vassal Audegarius, and so that the monks may be more pleased to implore the Lord’s mercy more attentively, day and night, for us and for our father.

Therefore we cede and donate the aforesaid estates of Faberola and Norontum to the holy place, together with lands, houses, buildings, resident dependents, slaves, vineyards, forests, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, mills, flocks with their shepherds—in short, everything in its entirety, as we have said. Whatever possession now appears to belong to us there, the aforesaid monastery and its administrators shall have, hold, and possess perpetually, in our times and in times to come. It shall remain assigned to that house of God as our alms, with full legal confirmation, forever, without anyone’s claim or recovery.

And so that this authority may remain firm and undisturbed, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign (+) of Charles the Great, the most glorious king.**

Maginarius: I have examined and subscribed.

Given in the month of December, in the fourth year of our reign.

Enacted at the public palace of Salmunciacum [Note: [Col. 1581D] Salmonciacum, commonly Samoney, below Laon toward the east, on the road leading toward Notre-Dame de Liesse.], happily, in the name of God.

### XLVIII. Testament of Remigius, bishop of Strasbourg, or charter of donation of the monasteries of Aschovia and Werd to the church of Strasbourg. 15 March 778

[Note: [Col. 1581D] This distinguished testament has nowhere been published. Nevertheless, Koenigshovius and Wimphelingius had seen it; see *On the Bishops of Strasbourg*, p. 21, where they make some mention of it.]

*(From Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*.)*
[Col. 1582C] + In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, on the Ides of March, in the tenth year of the reign of our lord, the most glorious King Charles. I, therefore, Remigius, although the most worthless sinner, servant of the servants of God [Note: [Col. 1581D] Augustine was the first to use this formula in a letter that he wrote around the year 412 to the widow Proba: “Augustine, bishop, servant of Christ and of Christ’s servants, etc.,” among Augustine’s works, vol. II, Letter 130.], by the grace of God bishop of the city of Strasbourg, of sound mind and sound judgment [Note: [Col. 1581D] According to Labeo, this condition was required for making a testament under Roman law. Digest, book XXVIII, title 1, law 2.], have made this testament [Note: [Col. 1581D] This testament is an outstanding monument of Roman jurisprudence as it existed at that time in Alsace [Col. 1582C] in the eighth century. Remigius’s testament conforms in every respect to the Roman laws and to the formulas prescribed by Marculf, book II, chapter 17, in Bouquet, vol. IV, p. 493; by the Lindenbrogian formula 72, in the same work, p. 554; and by the Baluzian formula 28, ibid., p. 586. Nor should the critic be surprised that this form was prescribed by Roman laws. We have examined authentic testaments written in almost the same formulas: those of Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, from the year 475; Remigius of Reims, from 535; Caesarius of Arles, from 542; Aredius, abbot of Attanum, from 572; Bertramnus, bishop of Le Mans, from 610; Abbo the patrician, from 739; and others. It should be noted that the scribe of the Remigian testament drew straight lines on the parchment in order to preserve the regularity of the letters or characters; this had already been prescribed long ago by Basil, Letter 178: “Draw the outlines of the letters perfectly, and arrange their forms in proper order.”] which I established with complete devotion and a single purpose, which I myself dictated and wrote and subscribed with my own hands, with the legally required number of witnesses present, who, having been requested by us, subscribed below or strengthened it with their own handwritten seals [Note: [Col. 1582D] It is appropriate to record each witness employed in a testament, identifying who he was and whose testament he signed. This is prescribed by the Roman laws, Digest, book XXVIII, title 1, law 30. Saint Aredius, abbot of Attanum, observed the same condition when he wrote in his testament of the year 572 [Col. 1583C]: “Which I myself, Aredius, wrote with my own hand and delivered to a sufficient number of witnesses for subscription, etc.”; in Ruinart, among the works of Gregory of Tours, p. 1308.], and which testament I wish to possess the fullest validity in place of every codicil; and if anyone should wish to invalidate it under civil or praetorian law, as though I had died intestate, and so that this may not happen, let witnesses be provided for this heir of mine, the holy church, and for my lady Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, of Strasbourg, where the mercy of God and the compassion of holy Mary commanded me, a sinner, to hold the honor of the episcopate. Therefore, my sweetest lady, holy Mary, I appoint you my heir and choose and decree you in all things, and I commend under your protection everything decreed by me; and with respect to what is contained below, written in this testament, you, most pious and sweetest lady, shall possess full power before the God of heaven and earth to have my will fulfilled and completed in every respect [Col. 1583B] [Note: [Col. 1583C] The testament of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, reported by Terrasson among the Monuments of Ancient Roman Jurisprudence, p. 90, and more briefly by Marlotus, History of Reims, book II, chapter 12, contains almost the same language: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; glory to God, amen. I, Remigius, bishop of the city of Reims, being in possession of the priesthood, have established my testament under praetorian law, and have ordered it to be valid in place of codicils [Col. 1583D] should anything required by law appear to be lacking. Whenever I, Remigius, bishop, have departed from this light, you shall be my heir, holy and venerable church of the city of Reims, etc.” Likewise, in the testament of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, in Baronius, Annals, under the year 508, no. 23, these words are read: “I have established this testament of mine, or subscribed it with my own hand, and have strengthened it under praetorian or civil law and in place of those codicils,” etc. See also the testament of Saint Bertramnus, bishop of Le Mans, from the year 610, in Mabillon, Old Analecta, vol. III, p. 112 of the first edition, and the testament of Abbo the patrician, from the year 739, in the same author, On Diplomatics, p. 507.]. Therefore, my sweetest lady, holy Mary, when God commands me by his summons to depart from this light and this frail body, you, my lady and heir, shall stand as my heir. Therefore, to you, my sweetest lady, my heir, holy Mary, I give, and wish to be given in perpetuity, on the condition that, as long as God grants me time to live, and to my niece Scholastica and my grandnephew Raderamnus [Note: [Col. 1583D] It is probable that Remigius, bishop of Strasbourg, had Hugh the count as his father and Adalric, duke of Alsace, as his grandfather. Hence Remigius had the brothers Bodolus and Bleonus. Codex Diplomaticus, vol. I, no. 45, p. 79. Thus Scholastica, Remigius’s niece, was the daughter either of Bodolus [Col. 1584C] or of Bleonus—more probably of Bodolus, since the record states that Bleonus fathered only one son, named Hugh.], whatever I appear to possess in the Alsatian district, on the island called Hascgaugia [Note: [Col. 1584C] Hascgaugia, or Eschau, is an island between the Rhine and the Ill, above Strasbourg. Formerly it was a Benedictine nunnery, whose property passed to the bishop of Strasbourg and thence to the major chapter of that church, which to this day enjoys the right of patronage at Eschau and shares the tithes with the parish priest. The village of Eschau itself, near the nunnery, is a fief of Lichtenberg granted to the Rathsamhausens.], upon the river Ill, and that island is in the district of Blabodsaime [Note: [Col. 1584C] The village of Blobsheim near Eschau, belonging to the lords of Kempffer and Güntzer.], and in the district of Quibilisheime [Note: [Col. 1584D] Wibolsheim, a village a quarter of a league from Eschau, with which it forms one parish and one district], together with the basilica built upon it, which I constructed anew and consecrated, where I buried my lady, holy Sophia [Note: [Col. 1584D] Behind the altar at Aschoviae a stone tomb can still be seen which, they say, contains the relics of Saint Sophia and her daughters Faith, Hope, and Charity.], and gave a place of burial to her most precious body, which the lord Pope Adrian, supreme pontiff, gave me to serve, and which I myself transported from the city of Rome to this region upon my shoulders, with my ministers, with great ceremony. Therefore, my sweetest lady and heir, holy Mary, to you I give the body of Saint Sophia; and I also commend to you the church itself, which we dedicated in honor of Saint Trophimus [Note: [Col. 1584D] The parish church at Eschau; it is still dedicated to Saint Trophimus the martyr.], where Saint Sophia, having been appointed there, rests bodily, together with the island of Ascgaugia, portions of which the religious women Roduna and Adala, abbess [Note: [Col. 1584D] Roduna, or Ruchuina, and Adala, who successively presided as abbesses over the monastery of Aschau, are said in the record no. 45 of the Codex Diplomaticus, vol. I, p. 79, to have been daughters of Bodolus, whom we stated above to have been the brother of Bishop Remigius. In Schoepflin, Alsatian Diplomatic Documents, vol. I, p. 33, there is a charter of Adala from the year 754 in which she says: “I, therefore, Adala, daughter of Bodolus, consecrated to God.”], transferred and donated to us and to Saint Sophia, or confirmed the charters before witnesses. Therefore, to you, my sweetest lady and heir, holy Mary, I give and hand over the island itself for the remedy of my soul and for eternal recompense, so that I may deserve to obtain everlasting forgiveness from the merciful Lord. And you, my most pious lady, deign to pray for me to the Lord Jesus Christ, whom you were worthy to bear in your womb, so that he may grant eternal forgiveness to me, a sinner. Therefore, my sweetest lady and heir, I hand over to you the aforementioned island of Aschaugia [Col. 1584B] in its entirety and in full possession, with its basilicas, houses, buildings, courtyards, orchards, slaves, vineyards, woods, meadows, fields, ploughlands, grain mills, pastures, livestock of both sexes, greater and lesser, slaves, and livestock, waters and flowing streams, and whatever can be said or named; whatever lawful possession of mine now appears to be there; whatever appears to pertain to that holy place and was donated there by good men through written charters; and whatever I acquired there, or was handed over to me, or acquired by a title of purchase. And I again, by title of donation, have assigned to that holy place and to you, my sweetest lady, holy Mary, in the manner written above, handed over and transferred it, so that you may deign to pray for my sins, that I may deserve to receive forgiveness and lessen the burden of my sins. Likewise, to you, my sweetest lady and heir, I give, in another small district [Note: [Col. 1584D] Smaller districts, or subdistricts, were called pagelli. Thus the district of Uri in Switzerland is called the pagellus of Uri in the charters that Louis the German granted to the abbey of Zurich in the years 853 and 854.], Aragougense [Col. 1585A] [Note: [Col. 1585B] That is, Aargau or Ergau. Taking its name from the river Aare, it lay between the Reuss and the Aare and was formerly a smaller part of Burgundy. Hergott’s etymology of Aargau, which he cites after Zeiler and Besold in Genealogy of the Habsburgs, vol. I, book I, chapter 4, p. 28, is ridiculous: he derives the name from a German word said to mean the same as *geehrtes Land*, that is, “honored region.”], a small monastery called Werith [Note: [Col. 1585B] That is, Werd or Schoenenwerd, a monastery now made a collegiate church. The place of Schoenenwerd lies in the territory of the republic of Solothurn, on the public road running from Aargau to Olten, opposite the Solothurn castle of Gösgen. Formerly it belonged to the prefecture of Olten; now it is incorporated into the prefecture of Gösgen.], on the river Aare [Note: [Col. 1585C] The Aare, or Arola, in French *l’Aar*. That the Aare was often called by the name *Araris* is proved by Walafrid Strabo, Ekkehard, Hepidannus, and Notker, whose testimonies are cited by Schoepflin, Illustrated Alsace, vol. I, p. 629. Glareanus uses the word *Araris* in the same sense in his panegyric of this river.], and that island is Grechchinbach [Note: [Col. 1585C] Grechchinbach, today Gretzenbach, a village in whose parish the district of Schoenenwerd is situated. Its original name was Grenzenbach, because at its boundary (*Grenzen*) it contained the island of Werith or Werd, as the testament itself suggests. Gretzenbach is situated in the territory of the republic of Solothurn and in the prefecture of Gösgen. The right of presentation to the parish now belongs to the collegiate church of Schoenenwerd. It is a member of the rural chapter called Willisau in the diocese of Constance. See Leu, *Helvetisches Lexicon*, vol. IX, p. 219.], which Bishop Rapert built anew, and he himself handed it over to me by means of his knife [Note: [Col. 1585C] Investiture or transfer formerly took place either by a charter or by certain symbols that actually signified the transfer of the thing into another’s ownership. On investitures by means of a knife, see Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. III, p. 1527. A singular example of this is provided by the Exchange of Sisenandus, in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, book VI, p. 542: “And according to my law, by knife and knotted staff, or *guaso* of the land, I make bodily investiture for you on your behalf, for you to hold as your property,” etc. The authors of the Gallic *New Diplomatic Treatise*, vol. IV, p. 648, describe investiture by a knife as follows: “The knife was one of the most ordinary signs of investiture.
