Often it was folded before being presented to the head or to some member of the chapter or community in whose favor the donation was made, or before being offered upon the altar of the church where the donor wished to consecrate to God the goods he had received.” See also the dissertation on the symbolic transfer of rights, published at Altdorf in 1748.”] before witnesses, and afterward his brothers, Rapert’s brothers, Ertulfus and Cundbertus, demanded the small monastery, and I reinvested them in it [Note: [Col. 1585D] To reinvest is to clothe again, or to restore to possession one who had been stripped of it. Du Cange, vol. V, p. 1421.]. But afterward, thanks be to God and to good men who intervened, and because of the gift [*xenium*] [Note: [Col. 1586B] *Xenium*, that is, a payment made in place of a gift. Du Cange, vol. VI, p. 1784.] that I gave, or because of my benefice, which I granted to them by a *precaria* [Note: [Col. 1586B] A *precaria* is a document or charter by which someone receives an allodial estate or landed property from a church, subject to an annual rent, to use during his lifetime, holding it precariously. Du Cange, vol. V, p. 794. This testament itself indicates the meaning of *precaria*. The ancient jurists Ulpian and Paulus say that a *precarium* in the praetor’s edict is what is granted for use, at the request of the petitioner, for as long as the grantor permits. See the discussion of *precariae* in the *New Diplomatic Treatise*, vol. I, p. 265, and vol. V, p. 694.], while they lived, and they paid us rent from it, and after their death we were to recall to our lordship both the benefice and what had been Rapert’s property by allodial right, then Rapert’s brothers again handed the small monastery over to us [Col. 1585B] before witnesses, or made a charter of transfer to us, and reinvested us in the small monastery, and by means of a staff [Note: [Col. 1586C] A *festuca* was a small fragment, twig, or reed that was cast into someone’s lap or handed into his hands as a sign of transfer, so that the recipient might remember that the transaction had been firmly established, and that it had the same measure of stability as the staff he held firmly in his hands. Concerning the *festuca*, the Gallic authors of the *New Diplomatic Treatise*, vol. IV, p. 644, state: “Among the Germans, Franks, and others, stipulation was made by the seller or donor by throwing straw into the lap of the purchaser or recipient. Stipulation was also made either by breaking the straw or by inserting it into a charter as a form of investiture. The practice of breaking the straw was common among contracting parties. When necessary, they verified their agreements by bringing from both sides the pieces of the broken stick or broken straw.” And vol. V, p. 637, note: “The ancient Germans, and especially the Franks, used straw as a symbol of the act by which they delivered something. This straw was placed in the hand of the person receiving the promised thing, and he attached this symbol to the charter of transfer, that is, to the act by which the thing itself was given.” The method of handing over and transferring ownership and dominion of things by means of a *festuca* remained in use in Germany from the twelfth through the sixteenth century, as examples show, in Haltaus, *German Glossary of the Middle Ages*, pp. 782 and 1284, under the words *Halm* and *Verschiessen*. In the German charter of John of Werde, landgrave of Alsace, from the year 1296, for the monastery of Saint Mark at Strasbourg, in Schilter, *Glossary*, p. 543, mention is made of a staff-investiture: “He has handed over these same goods into our hands and surrendered to us the right of ownership of these same goods with a stalk, as is customary.”] they made an exit from the small monastery for themselves before witnesses, just as the law of the Alamanni required [Col. 1586A] [Note: [Col. 1586D] See the pact of the Salic Law, title 49, in Eccard, p. 92, and Bouquet, vol. IV, p. 150.]. Therefore, to you, my sweetest lady and heir, holy Mary, I give the small monastery called Werith, which is dedicated to the honor of Saint Leodegarius the martyr, at the boundary of Grechchinbach, on the island upon the river Aare, both for the salvation of my soul and for the remedy of the soul of Bishop Rapert, so that you may intercede for us, that we may deserve to be aided by God, that our offenses may be erased, and that we may deserve to receive everlasting forgiveness from the merciful Lord. Therefore, to you, my sweetest lady and heir, holy Mary, I give the aforementioned small monastery in its entirety and in full possession, with its basilicas, houses, buildings, all adjoining properties and appurtenances, villages, courtyards, farmsteads, homesteads, lands, ploughlands, slaves, fields, meadows, woods, vineyards, mills, pastures, waters and flowing streams, livestock of both sexes, greater and lesser, movable and immovable property, whatever can be said or named, whatever I appear to possess today, and whatever belongs to the monastery and was assigned to the holy place of Saint Leodegarius by good men through charters of transfer, grant, and sale. To you, my sweetest lady and heir, holy Mary, I hand over and transfer all these things named above, in the manner stated above. I myself, my niece Scholastica, and my grandnephew Raderamnus, for as long as we live, are to hold them through your benefice, my lady, and through that of my successors who then appear to be in office, under usufruct; and each year, on the feast of Saint Mary at the dedication of the altar itself, which we have now dedicated, we are to give twenty silver solidi as rent. We wish our clerical canons to receive those solidi there as our alms, so that they may be more gladly inclined to serve God and Saint Mary day and night, to pray to God for us, and so that our names may be written in the book of life, and so that my little body may rest in that crypt which I built anew. I wish, beseech and implore, and charge my successors, that under no pretext may you have permission to drive my niece Scholastica or my grandnephew Raderamnus out of this benefice that I have given—namely, from that cell of Saint Sophia on the island of Aschaugia and from that small monastery in Aargau called Werida. And if you disregard these provisions or wish to do anything other than what I have written above, may you be required to give an account of it before the tribunal of Christ, and may you have no power to do so. [Col. 1587C] And when I, Remigius, and Scholastica and Raderamnus have completed the course of our lives, you, holy Church, holy Mary, and your agents, shall recall all of it, complete and entire, into your power and lordship, just as it was possessed by us; and, holy Mary, our heir, may it perpetually benefit you as an increase. We also wish and beseech that after our departure no person at any time should hold those little cells, Aschaugia and Werida, which I gave to Saint Mary, as a benefice. But if any man or any other person at any time, by any device whatsoever, should attempt to act against this testament, which I made of my own free will under divine inspiration and which I myself wrote, or should wish to oppose it, diminish it, or violate it, may he first incur the wrath of God, and may he stand excommunicated before God and holy Mary by the bishop who is then in office; and on that dreadful day, when the strict examiner arrives, may he depart guilty and condemned; and furthermore, may he be compelled to pay to the holy agents of the holy church of Saint Mary, my heir, together with the most sacred treasury, five pounds of gold and twenty-five weights of silver; and may he not be able to recover what he claims; and nevertheless may this present testamentary document remain firm and stable, with stipulation appended. Done in the city of Strasbourg. I have recorded the day [Note: [Col. 1587C] The formula “I have recorded the day” was frequently used, especially in the eighth century, as the authors of the Gallic *New Diplomatic Treatise*, vol. IV, p. 655, testify.] and the year stated above.

I, Remigius, a sinner, bishop by the grace of God, reread this testament made by me in honor of holy Mary, which I myself wrote with my hands and which I requested to be written above. And I, Gislebertus, as if a sinful bishop [Note: [Col. 1587C] Gislebertus was bishop of Tournai and Noyon. He is mentioned by Sirmond, vol. II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 66, among the twelve bishops sent from France who attended the Roman council in April 769 [Col. 1587D]. The author of the brief chronicle of Saint-Denis, reported by Bouquet, vol. V of the *Writers of Frankish Affairs*, p. 29, states that Bishop Gislebertus died in the year 782. Alcuin, abbot, composed his epitaph.]. I, Willibaldus, bishop, subscribed [Note: [Col. 1587D] Saint Willibaldus was the first bishop of the church of Eichstätt, or Aureatensis; he was consecrated in the year 741 by Saint Boniface and held the episcopate until the year 786 or 787, as Cointius proves, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. VI, p. 353. Among the fathers of the council of Attigny in 765, Willibaldus subscribed as bishop of the monastery of Eichstätt. Falckenstein discusses Saint Willibaldus more fully in *Antiquities of the Nordgau Church of Eichstätt*, pp. 1–19, and in the *Diplomatic Register of the Antiquities of the Nordgau*, pp. 445–468.]. Sign of Garibaldi. I, Weomadus, bishop [Note: [Col. 1587D] Weomadus was then bishop of Trier; he died in the year 781, as may be seen in Brower and Hontheim, the historians of the church of Trier.]. I, in the name of God, Waldericus, called bishop [Note: [Col. 1588C] Waldericus was bishop of Lorsch and Passau; in 774 he succeeded Wisericus and died in 804. See Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. VI, pp. 87 and 651; Hundius, *Metropolis of Salzburg*, vol. I, p. 195, edition of 1719; and Hanzisius, *Sacred Germany*, vol. I, pp. 138–145.]. I, Walabertus, called bishop [Note: [Col. 1588C] Three bishops named Walabertus were prominent in the eighth century [Col. 1588D]. The first was Baldebertus, or Adalbertus, who became bishop of Chur after being abbot of Pfäfers and is said to have died in 754 with a reputation for holiness; he therefore does not belong to our charter of 778. The second was Baldebertus, or Baldobertus, who succeeded Romani in the abbacy of Murbach in 755 and was designated with the title of bishop in the charters of that abbey in 760 and 761, according to the custom of the time. Baldebertus died in 762, as the Nazarene Annals testify, whose author was an anonymous monk of the abbey of Murbach, in Freher, *Corpus of the Ancient History of the Franks*, p. 886. The third was Walabertus, or Baldobertus, who succeeded Wallo or Wallanus in the bishopric of Basel and is wrongly confused with Baldobertus of Murbach. Walabertus of Basel, who subscribed our charter, had already subscribed the charter of Heddo in 748 and had attended the council of Attigny in 765.]. Sign of Hullind. Sign of Lantfridi. Sign of Balldne. Sign of Harbaldi. Sign of Friderichd. Sign of Ralhinfridi, who likewise consented for the share of his wife Harilandae [Col. 1588C].

In the name of God, I, Remigius, a sinner and bishop, made this testament in honor of the Lord and of holy Mary of Strasbourg, concerning Aschagia, which is in the district of Wibilesheim and also in the district of Bladbotesheim, for the remedy of my soul together with the holy body of Saint Sophia; likewise, in another place called Werida, the small monastery situated in the district of Grechchinbach [Col. 1589A], for the remedy of my soul and for the soul of Bishop Ratberti [Note: [Col. 1589A] The law of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian prescribes the signs of the witnesses, book XXI, title “On Testaments”: “We decree that the conclusion of a testament shall consist of the subscriptions and seals of the witnesses” [Col. 1590A].]. Sign of Anteneri. Sign of Licenzid. Sign of Erineneberti. Sign of Raderamind. Sign of Waidegirst. Sign of Venantie. Sign of Scholastice. Sign of Erinenegunde. Sign of Maurind. Sign of Ugindne. Sign of Audeberti. Sign of Widerici. Sign of Udone. Sign of Uribid. Sign of Anausoni. Sign of Berngrid. Sign of Alione. Sign of Hardrind. Sign of Rotmundi. Sign of Apponi. Sign of Ulaholfe. Sign of Scaione. Sign of Haimone. Sign of Wanbaldi. Sign of Hildibrandi. Sign of Wolfgrinid. Sign of Leoloind. Sign of Audrild. Sign of Erhusto, cleric. Sign of Hilderici, cleric. Sign of Gerwigo, cleric. Sign of Udalmannid. Sign of Nandwigo, cleric. Sign of Hildimund. Sign of Hildiberti.

## The Single Book *On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary against Three Unbelievers*

53. Prayer and confession of Saint Hildefonsus. 53.

**Chapter I.** By a torrent of synonyms he demonstrates against Jovinian that the most blessed Mother of God remained a virgin in conception and childbirth by God’s gift and through singular grace. 58.

**Chapter II.** He confirms the virginity of the Mother of God against Helvidius. 61.

**Chapter III.** That Saint Mary is Jewish by nation and lineage, but Christian by faith, honor, praise, and love. Finally, by the oracles of several prophets he proves that supreme virginity ought to be joined with the glory of motherhood. 64.

**Chapter IV.** He urges the Jew not to diminish the glory of the virgin and mother, whose disgrace rebounds upon her offspring. He also shows that all heavenly powers adore the Virgin and that all peoples flock to her; incidentally, he demonstrates that the perfidy of the Jews was divinely foretold by the ancient fathers. 67.

**Chapter V.** He explains the sacred mystery of the Incarnation. 71.

**Chapter VI.** After a prayer, he proves that the son of Saint Mary is God. 74.

**Chapter VII.** By connecting the words of both Testaments, he teaches that Christ is man and likewise truly the most high God. He also gives a full portrayal of the whole life of our Savior, up to the sending of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles. 79.

**Chapter VIII.** He shows that God performed many great wonders in the glorious Virgin, from which anyone may infer that he could easily have preserved her virginity unharmed in childbirth. By the testimony of barren Elizabeth and of others he confirms Christ’s divinity. 85.

**Chapter IX.** By the testimony of the angels and by the obedience of all insensible things, he teaches that Christ is God just as he is man, so that the Jew may plainly infer that he was able to preserve his mother together with the beauty of her virginity. 88.

**Chapter X.** He concludes that Mary remained a virgin throughout the entire mystery of the Incarnation. 93.

**Chapter XI.** By angelic testimony he concludes that the virginity of Saint Mary, the Mother of God, was preserved forever. 99.

**Chapter XII.** He turns his discourse to the most blessed mother and to her glorious Son. He also concludes against the impious profaners of her inviolate virginity. 105.

Notice. 109.

## One Book of Annotations on Knowledge of Baptism

**Chapter IV.** That the whole Trinity, one God, made all things. 113.

# Saint Leodegarius, Bishop of Autun

329. Historical Notice.

**Life of Saint Leodegarius**, by Ursinus, his contemporary and abbot. 335.

Author’s prologue. 335.

**Chapter I.** Leodegarius is educated both at the palace and in his uncle’s household. 336.

**Chapter II.** He is made deacon, then archdeacon. 336.

**Chapter III.** Then abbot. Summoned to court, he is made bishop of the Aedui. 337.

**Chapter IV.** After Chlothar’s death, he supports Childeric against Ebroin, the supporter of Theuderic. After Ebroin becomes a monk, he is placed in charge of Childeric’s court. 337.

**Chapter V.** After three years he becomes hateful to the king. He celebrates the vigil of Easter with the king at Autun. 338.

**Chapter VI.** After the sacred rites are completed, he secretly departs. With the king’s consent he withdraws to Luxeuil and is reconciled with Ebroin. 338.

**Chapter VII.** After Childeric’s death he is recalled to his see, with Ebroin as his companion. 339.

**Chapter VIII.** Restored to power, Ebroin considers destroying Leodegarius. When the city of Autun is besieged, Leodegarius goes out to meet the enemies. 340.

**Chapter IX.** He is deprived of his eyes. He is held in a monastery for two years. 340.

**Chapter X.** He is accused before the king by Ebroin together with his brother. They answer the charges brought against them. 341.

**Chapter XI.** Guarinus, after accepting his brother’s admonitions, is buried beneath stones. 341.

**Chapter XII.** By Ebroin’s order, Leodegarius is cruelly mutilated. 341.

**Chapter XIII.** Exiled to Fiscamnum, he regains the use of his tongue. 342.

**Chapter XIV.** His persecutors pay the penalty. 342.

**Chapter XV.** Handed over to Chrodobertus, he is illumined by heavenly light. 343.

**Chapter XVI.** Four horsemen are sent to kill the Saint. 343.

**Chapter XVII.** After making a prayer, he is struck in the head. He is buried at Sarcing. 343.

**Chapter XVIII.** Miracles occur at his tomb. Sacrilegious thieves are punished after everything is restored. 344.

**Chapter XIX.** Ebroin’s impious spy suffers punishment, and Ebroin himself likewise. 345.

**Chapter XX.** 346.

## Another Life of Saint Leodegarius, by an Anonymous Author

345. Author’s prologue. 345.

**Chapter I.** Leodegarius is perfect in all things and is instructed by Ado. His conduct as archdeacon. He is ordained bishop of the Aedui after a dispute has arisen. What he did as bishop. 347.

**Chapter II.** He suffers Ebroin as his adversary. 348.

**Chapter III.** For what reason. After Chlothar’s death, the nobles agree upon Childeric. Why. Ebroin, opposed to them, is exiled at Luxeuil. The tonsured Theuderic is relegated to the monastery of Saint Denis. 349.

**Chapter IV.** Childeric issues a just edict and soon revokes it. The king is stirred against Leodegarius. Rebuked by him, he considers killing him. 350.

**Chapter V.** A new pretext is offered. During the vigil of Easter the Saint is sought for execution. He fearlessly approaches the king. He avoids death because of the sacred day. Hector is killed. 350.

**Chapter VI.** Detained by jealous men, he is exiled to Luxeuil. He is freed from imminent death through Hermenarius. 352.

**Chapter VII.** He is reconciled with Ebroin. The state of the kingdom after Childeric’s death. A comet. 353.

**Chapter VIII.** Leodegarius is protected by religious men. Ebroin leaves Luxeuil and considers destroying Leodegarius; hindered by Saint Genesius, he is received at Autun together with Leodegarius. He approaches Theuderic, casts off his monastic garment, and resumes his wife. He plunders the sacred treasury, persecutes Leodegarius again, and substitutes Clodoveus, the son of Chlothar. 354.

**Chapter IX.** Ebroin entrusts Dido and Waimero with the order to destroy Leodegarius. They besiege the city of Autun. The Saint spends his treasures for pious uses; gives excellent admonitions to his people; orders fasts and supplications; asks everyone’s forgiveness in the church; and, forbidding battle, investigates the counsel of his adversaries. 356.

**Chapter X.** He refuses to violate his loyalty to Theuderic; while the enemies rage, he offers himself after receiving the viaticum; he endures the removal of his eyes without a groan. Autun is assigned to Bobo as plunder. 358.

**Chapter XI.** The Saint is entrusted to Waimero. Saint Genesius is rescued from a similar fate. Ebroin orders Leodegarius to be consumed by starvation. Waimero becomes gentler toward him, and Leodegarius sends the silver received from Waimero to the people of Autun. 359.

**Chapter XII.** After rejecting Pseudo-Clodoveus, Ebroin becomes mayor of the palace of Theuderic. He issues an unjust edict; rages and ravages against everyone; and accuses Leodegarius of Childeric’s murder. Leodegarius urges Germanus to patience. 360.

**Chapter XIII.** Gairinus is buried beneath stones. Leodegarius is mutilated in his feet, tongue, and lips and handed over to Waningo for custody. He recovers the use of his voice; Hermanarius treats him; his tongue and lips grow back. The author’s age. Leodegarius is taken to Fiscamnum. 361.

**Chapter XIV.** He mourns the downfall of his enemies. After bishops opposed to him have been expelled from the synod, he himself is brought before the synod. He denies responsibility for Childeric’s murder; foretells many things to the king; after his tunic has been torn, he is handed over to Chrodobertus to be killed; he is commended by heavenly light; and he receives the sentence of death with equanimity. 363.

**Chapter XV.** He consoles his hostess. Led to the place of martyrdom, he commends the executioners to God and, presenting his neck, remains standing after being struck. The impious executioner perishes. The Saint is buried. 365.

**Chapter XVI.** The place of burial is illumined from heaven. Sacrilegious thieves are punished after everything is restored. Ebroin sends a spy to the tomb, whose impiety is punished by death. Ebroin dies unrepentant; on what occasion. 366.

**Chapter XVII.** At what time. A dispute arises over Saint Leodegarius’s body. Ansoaldus arranges by lot for it to be carried to Poitiers. At the request of Abbess Ermenana, the author writes this. Audulfus wrote the Saint’s miracles. 368.

**Chapter XVIII.** Various miracles at the Saint’s bier. 370.

**Chapter XIX.** The monks of Saint Maxentius receive the sacred body. Other miracles. 371.

**Chapter XX.** The devotion of the faithful toward the sacred body. The Saint is buried in a new basilica. 372.

**Chapter XXI.** The time of the martyrdom, and related matters. 374.

**CHAPTER XXVI.—**Whether the souls of the dead pray for the salvation of their living loved ones. 487  
**CHAPTER XXVII.—**Whether the souls of the dead can be saddened or gladdened on account of the salvation of their living loved ones, or be moved by sadness or any concern for human beings. 488  
**CHAPTER XXVIII.—**That the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and all the spirits of the blessed eagerly await rejoicing with us; and that they do not possess perfect joy so long as they grieve over our errors. 489  
**CHAPTER XXIX.—**Whether the dead can know what the living are doing. 491  
**CHAPTER XXX.—**Whether the dead can appear to the eyes of the living. 491  
**CHAPTER XXXI.—**That it is only the souls of the saints, not of the impious, that know what can be done by the living. 492  
**CHAPTER XXXII.—**Whether, after Christ’s coming to the regions below, when the way to heaven was opened for the saints, the good can see the wicked established in suffering, or the wicked see the good established in rest. 492  
[Col. 1600] **CHAPTER XXXIII.—**Against those who say that the soul has no life after death. 493  
**CHAPTER XXXIV.—**Against those for whom it seems insufficient that after the death of the flesh the soul sees certain joys or feels sorrows in a bodily likeness; and that the joys and sorrows there are more vivid than those the mind can see here in a dream. 495  
**CHAPTER XXXV.—**What reward the souls of the dead are believed to possess before the final time of that resurrection. 495  
**CHAPTER XXXVI.—**That immediately after laying aside this body God is seen by the holy spirits. 495  
**CHAPTER XXXVII.—**That even now the souls of the saints reign with Christ in heaven. 496  

**BOOK THREE.—ON THE RESURRECTION ITSELF.** 497  
**CHAPTER ONE.—**That no human being knows the time and day of judgment. 497  
**CHAPTER II.—**Whether a particular place is believed to exist where judgment will be conducted by the Lord. 497  
**CHAPTER III.—**That no human being knows over how many days that future judgment will extend. 498  
**CHAPTER IV.—**On the terror of Christ’s coming, and that he will come to judgment in the form in which he was judged, and will conduct the judgment in that form. 498  
**CHAPTER V.—**That Christ will come to judgment preceded by the cross, and that the same cross will be carried on the shoulders of angels as Christ descends from heaven. 499  
**CHAPTER VI.—**On the terror of the devil’s appearance, when he has been raised up so that he may be brought to judgment. 500  
**CHAPTER VII.—**That Christ, coming to judgment, will appear gentle to the righteous and terrifying to the unrighteous. 501  
**CHAPTER VIII.—**That the righteous and the unrighteous will see Christ coming in the flesh to judgment with their fleshly eyes. 501  
**CHAPTER IX.—**That it is believed that not the Father but only the Son will come to conduct judgment. 501  
**CHAPTER X.—**That this does not belong to the present life, when Christ will descend from heaven to judge the living and the dead. 501  
**CHAPTER XI.—**On the seats of those who judge. 502  
**CHAPTER XII.—**On those who will sit with the Lord to judge. 502  
**CHAPTER XIII.—**That in the twelve seats named by Christ not only the twelve apostles will sit, but the entire number of the perfect, who are divided into the number twelve. 502  
**CHAPTER XIV.—**On the final resurrection of human bodies. 503  
**CHAPTER XV.—**That when the seventh angel sounds the trumpet, the dead will be resurrected in the twinkling of an eye. 503  
**CHAPTER XVI.—**That resurrection pertains to all human beings, but transformation only to the saints. 504  
**CHAPTER XVII.—**That it is not an airy body but the flesh we bear that will rise without any corruption. 504  
**CHAPTER XVIII.—**How they are believed then to have spiritual bodies, when the bodies that will exist are most truly shown to be bodies, not spirits. 504  
**CHAPTER XIX.—**On the quality of the bodies that will exist in the resurrection. 504  
**CHAPTER XX.—**At what age or stature those who rise will exist, whether they are old, young, or infants. 505  
**CHAPTER XXI.—**Whether the stature or form of the bodies that rise will be equal or diverse, and whether the thin will rise with the same thinness and the fat with the same fatness. 506  
**CHAPTER XXII.—**That the bodies of the saints will rise without any deformity. 506  
**CHAPTER XXIII.—**That it is superfluous to ask at what age or in what measure the bodies of the reprobate will rise. 507  
**CHAPTER XXIV.—**That men and women will rise in their own sex. 507  
**CHAPTER XXV.—**That no concern for food or drink will trouble those who rise. 508  
**CHAPTER XXVI.—**That our nature will not need bodily clothing. 508  
**CHAPTER XXVII.—**On aborted fetuses; and that from the moment a human being begins to live in the mother’s womb, he is then believed to belong to the final resurrection. 509  
**CHAPTER XXVIII.—**How those who are born with a greater or lesser number of limbs, or with two heads and one body, or two bodies and one head, or with any other monstrous form, are believed to rise. 510  
**CHAPTER XXIX.—**That those who are now eaten by beasts or torn apart by various forms of mutilation will, when they rise, possess the integrity of their bodies. 510  
**CHAPTER XXX.—**That those who left this life disabled will possess all their limbs intact in the resurrection. 511  
[Col. 1601] **CHAPTER XXXI.—**Whether in the resurrection whatever has been removed from our nails or hair by clipping or cutting is believed to be restored. 512  
**CHAPTER XXXII.—**How those who have not been separated from the mass of perdition will rise. 513  
**CHAPTER XXXIII.—**On the order of the future judgment. 513  
**CHAPTER XXXIV.—**On the separation of the good and the wicked. 514  
**CHAPTER XXXV.—**That this separation of the good from the wicked will be carried out through angelic ministries. 514  
**CHAPTER XXXVI.—**That once the good have been separated to the right and the wicked to the left, books will be opened—that is, the consciences of each individual. 514  
**CHAPTER XXXVII.—**On the evil hearing that the righteous will not fear. 515  
**CHAPTER XXXVIII.—**On the devil’s downfall and the destruction of the impious. 515  
**CHAPTER XXXIX.—**What that book is of which the apostle John says that all who are then not found written in the book of life will be cast into the lake of fire. 515  
**CHAPTER XL.—**That in the fire of the impious their bodies will endure without being consumed. 516  
**CHAPTER XLI.—**How that future fire will burn the demons. 516  
**CHAPTER XLII.—**On the diversity of punishments according to the diversity of merits. 517  
**CHAPTER XLIII.—**Against those who inquire with excessive precision what that future fire will be like or in what part of the world it can exist. 517  
**CHAPTER XLIV.—**That after the condemnation of the impious comes the reward of the elect. 517  
**CHAPTER XLV.—**That once judgment has been completed, the form of the servant in which Christ will conduct judgment will pass away, and thus Christ will hand over the kingdom to God the Father. 518  
**CHAPTER XLVI.—**On the conflagration by which this world is said to perish. 518  
**CHAPTER XLVII.—**That when judgment is finished, a new heaven and a new earth will begin to exist. 518  
**CHAPTER XLVIII.—**That in the new heaven and the new earth not all who rise will exist, but only the saints. 519  
**CHAPTER XLIX.—**Against those who say: “If the world will be consumed by fire after judgment has taken place, where then can the saints be, who are not touched by the flame of the conflagration?” 519  
**CHAPTER L.—**On the reward and kingdom of the saints, when Christ will gird himself and, passing among them, serve them. 519  
**CHAPTER LI.—**That the wicked will then not know what is taking place in the joy of the blessed, but the good will know what is taking place in the punishments of the wretched. 520  
**CHAPTER LII.—**That in this body in which we now are we will then be able both to be carried and to dwell in heaven. 520  
**CHAPTER LIII.—**Whether we will then have subtler bodily movements, or whether they will be such as they now appear to be. 520  
**CHAPTER LIV.—**Whether God will then be seen through these bodily eyes with which we now see the sun and moon. 520  
**CHAPTER LV.—**That we will then see God by the vision with which the angels now see him. 522  
**CHAPTER LVI.—**That all the saints will use freedom of choice much more firmly established than in this life, although they will not be able to sin. 522  
**CHAPTER LVII.—**That there we will possess both forgetfulness and memory. 522  
**CHAPTER LVIII.—**On the diversity of merits and rewards, in which nevertheless no one will envy another. 523  
**CHAPTER LIX.—**That the saints will praise God without weariness. 523  
**CHAPTER LX.—**That we will see the Lord without end, and that he himself is the end of our desires. 524  
**CHAPTER LXI.—**That the Lord himself will then be our reward, and that our honorable desires will then be wondrously fulfilled. 524  
**CHAPTER LXII.—**On the endless end, in which we will praise the Lord infinitely. 524

**POPE ADRIAN I.**
## Life of Pope Adrian I. 1167

## Letters of Pope Adrian I. 1203

### First Letter, to King Pippin

Also, a copy of the letter of Pope Constantine, a neophyte, addressed to the lord King Pippin, in which it is stated that he was elected by the Roman people through violence and installed in the apostolic see, asking that he might remain in the favor of the lord King Pippin, as his predecessors had done. And likewise from the letter of Theodore, patriarch of Jerusalem, and from other letters of the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch. And in the insertion, concerning George, Marinus, and Peter. 1203

### Letter II, to King Pippin

A copy of the same Pope Constantine’s letter, addressed to the lord King Pippin, containing expressions of thanks and an account of the death of the lord Pope Paul; he asks that he may remain in the favor of the lord King Pippin, as his predecessors had done. 1203

### Letter III, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, in which it speaks of his faith and steadfastness, and of Anastasius, his apostolic envoy, who had stayed in Francia. 1203

### Letter IV, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, containing expressions of thanks for the exaltation of God’s holy Church, and concerning the king’s envoys, who were to come to Rome in the autumn season. 1203

### Letter V, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, containing abundant blessings for the exaltation of God’s holy Church, and concerning the letter of John, patriarch of Grado. 1203

### Letter VI, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles through Andrew and Anastasius, concerning the rights of God’s holy Church, and concerning Leo the archbishop, who had already set out for the aforementioned lord king. 1203

### Letter VII, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles through Abbot Gausfridus, concerning the victory of the aforementioned king and concerning the bishops of Pisa and Lucca, asking that, in his piety, he permit them to return to their own sees and churches. 1203

[Col. 1604] **Letter VIII, to King Charles**

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the faith or steadfastness of the apostolic bishop toward the aforementioned king. 1204

### Letter IX, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning Bishop Mauritius, whose eyes the Histrians had torn out. 1204

### Letter X, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord [Lamb. adds: Charles] King, concerning the death of the Emperor Constantine and Reginald, duke of Chiusi. The aforementioned pope asks that the lord king not permit him to retain the aforesaid [duchy], because he did not cease continually perpetrating many evils in the Castellum Felicitatis. [lacuna] 1204

### Letter XI, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the framework, or beams, or timber that was needed for constructing that church of Saint Peter, and concerning the holy body requested by Fulgatus (Fulradus). 1204

### Letter XII, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the exaltation of the holy Church and concerning the apostolic bishop’s prayers. 1204

### Letter XIII, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, in which it is stated that the Neapolitans, together with the Greeks, had invaded the city of Terracina. 1205

### Letter XIV, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the sale of slaves to the pagan people of the Saracens. The aforementioned pope excuses the Romans, saying that they had never committed such a crime, but that they had been handed over by the Lombards and the Greeks. 1205

### Letter XV, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the large beams for restoring churches, which the lord king had ordered him to be given. He says that the officials, through negligence, had done nothing about it, as they had been instructed by the said king; and concerning tin for reroofing that church of Saint Peter. 1205

### Letter XVI, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the mosaic work (*mosivum*, *musivum*) and marble of the palace of the city of Ravenna (*Ravennatae*, *Ravennatis*). The aforementioned pope says that he willingly surrenders them to the lord king’s authority, or for whatever he might wish to do with them. 1205

### Letter XVII, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the territory of Sabina: how Itherius and Maginarius, the lord king’s envoys, wished to restore that territory in its entirety to the domain of Saint Peter, but were wholly unable to do so because of wicked men. 1205

### Letter XVIII, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, containing expressions of thanks for the exaltation of God’s holy Church, and concerning the territory of Sabina, namely, how the aforesaid king had promised Saint Peter that he would order it to be restored in its entirety. 1205

### Letter XIX, to King Charles

Also, the letter of the same pope addressed to the lord King Charles, containing expressions of thanks for the labors undertaken on behalf of blessed Peter, and commending Bishop George to him. 1205

### Letter XX, to King Charles

He explains how he settled the dispute of the monks who had been sent to him. He also states that Abbot Potho wished to travel to King Charles with ten monks, so that there too he might clear himself of the charges brought against him. 1206

### Letter XXI, to King Charles

Paul the presbyter, Venerandus the presbyter, Foroaldus, Adalbertus, Gaudiosus, Benedictus the deacon, Josue the deacon, Hermenfridus, Raginbertus, Autscarius (Lamb., Autcarius), Gregorius, Agemodus, David, Gaidualdus, Ariolfus, Stephanus, Garibaldus, Gregorius, Savinus, Aldosinto, Rothbertus, Rathis, Haribertus, Leo, Martinianus, Allo, Majo, Beaptulfus (Lamb., Scaptulfus), Cunualdus, Leminosus, Magnus, Ursus, Authaldus, Aldefusus, Petrus Ansualdus, Allo, Petrus, Gratiosus Faroaldus, Ursus, Adualdus. 1206

### Letter XXII, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the monastery of Saint Hilary the Confessor at Calligata. He asks that neither it nor the hospices situated among the Alpine passes, which receive pilgrims, be allowed to be attacked by any person, great or small; and that he order Gundibrand, duke of Florence, to restore what he had taken from the same monastery. 1206

### Letter XXIII, to King Charles

[Col. 1605] Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the faith or love which he had promised to hold toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, asking that it remain firm and indissoluble, and that no crafty deception be able to separate his spirit from love for the apostolic bishop. 1206

### Letter XXIV, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the consecration of Bishop Peter and concerning the territory of Sabina. 1206

### Letter XXV, to King Charles

Concerning bishops and presbyters, that they should not put on military armor but spiritual armor—that is, devote themselves to fasts and prayers—and concerning the sale or capture of people, or other unlawful causes perpetrated by wicked men; also concerning the vision of the monk John, which appeared false or empty. 1206

### Letter XXVI, to King Charles

Also, a letter addressed to the lord King Charles, containing expressions of thanks for the exaltation of God’s holy Church, and concerning the territory of Sabina: how Maginarius (*Machinarius*), the most faithful servant of that exalted king, wished to restore that territory in its entirety to the domain of Saint Peter, but was wholly unable to do so because of wicked and perverse men. 1207

### Letter XXVII, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Vincent, who had been accused before the lord king although innocent and taken away from there. He asks that the king receive him most mercifully, with gracious favor and the greatest goodwill, because false crimes had been charged against him. 1207

### Letter XXVIII, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, containing expressions of thanks and blessings for the cross that he had sent him, and concerning the territories of Populonia and Roselle, asking that the lord king send suitable envoys who should restore those cities, together with their suburbs (*suburbana*, *suburbanis*), to him in their entirety. 1207

### Letter XXIX, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, containing expressions of thanks and blessings for the exaltation of God’s holy Church, and concerning the sacramentary attributed to Saint Gregory, which the lord king had requested and had sent through John, monk and abbot of the city of Ravenna. 1207

### Letter XXX, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning Constantine and Paul, the apostolic bishop’s dukes, who had been falsely accused before the aforementioned king by wicked men. He asks that the king kindly receive one of them—namely Paul, whom he had sent to be presented before him. 1207

### Letter XXXI, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the Venetians (*Veneciis*; Lamb., *Veneticis*), asking that they be expelled from Ravenna and the Pentapolis; and concerning Duke Garamannus, who had violently invaded or stripped the possessions of the church of Ravenna. 1207

### Letter XXXII, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, containing expressions of thanks, and concerning Roselle, Populonia, and the cities of Benevento, as well as the plots of the Greeks. 1207

### Letter XXXIII, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the envoys of King Offa of the English, who were to travel to Rome together with the envoys of the aforementioned King Charles; and concerning how the aforesaid pope had received the English envoys honorably, as the aforementioned King Charles had instructed him through his legates; and also concerning other matters. 1208

### Letter XXXIV, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the Persian booty taken in Greek territory and concerning the discord that existed among them. 1208

### Letter XXXV, to King Charles

Also, a copy of the same pope’s letter addressed to the lord King Charles, concerning the dioceses or parishes of bishops in the regions of Italy and Tuscany, which they were invading against one another; and concerning monastic clothing, which they abandoned contrary to the holy canons, putting on secular clothing again and joining themselves in unlawful marriage. 1208

### Letter XXXVI, to Bishop Egila

Also, a copy of Pope Adrian’s letter sent to Bishop Egila in the regions of Spain, concerning the preservation of orthodox faith, and concerning the observance of fasting on Friday and Saturday. 1208

### Letter XXXVII, to Bishop Egila

Also, a copy [Col. 1606] of Pope Adrian’s letter to Bishop Egila and to the presbyter John, concerning their ordination or steadfastness, to be preached in the regions of Spain; concerning the Easter festival; concerning the predestination of human beings, whether to good or to evil; concerning their pollution in food as well as drink; concerning various errors; and concerning their false priests, who take wives whose husbands are still alive; also concerning free will and many other matters that had arisen in those regions against the Catholic faith. 1208

### Letter XXXVIII, to the Bishops of Spain

Also, a copy of Pope Adrian’s letter addressed to all the bishops residing throughout Spain, especially Elipandus and Ascaricus together with their associates, concerning their heresy or blasphemy in calling the Son of God adoptive. He rebukes them on many points by the authority of the holy Fathers. He also addresses the Easter festival, the blood of cattle and swine, and blood from strangled animals, which they preach as an error, saying that anyone who does not eat such things is ignorant and uneducated; he declares that they are bound under the sentence of anathema and excluded from the Church.

Likewise, concerning the predestination of God: if someone had been predestined to good, it was not necessary for him to resist evil; but if he were known (*notus*; Lamb., *natus*, “born”) to evil, exercising good would profit him nothing. On this point he corrects them through apostolic exhortations.

He also rebukes them because they say that, by sharing a common life with Jews and unbaptized pagans, in food as well as drink, they are polluted in nothing; and concerning their daughters, whom they give to gentile people; concerning their ordinations; concerning women who take another husband while their first husband is alive; and likewise concerning free will and many other matters, which it would be tedious to enumerate, correcting them in accordance with the traditions of the holy Fathers. 1208

### Letter XXXIX, to King Charles

He asks the king, first, to receive his son, then newly born, at the baptismal font; next, to continue exalting the Church in imitation of Constantine, both by granting promised gifts and by restoring in various places the estates taken from the Lombards. 1208

### Letter XL, to King Charles

He asks that the king restrain Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, who was arrogating to himself the rights of the Roman Church in the Exarchate and the Pentapolis. 1209

### Letter XLI, to King Charles

He complains that he has been despised by Bishop Possessor and Abbot Rabigaudus, Charles’s envoys. He asks that the king console his grief and promptly order the duchy of Spoleto, which he had offered to Saint Peter, actually to be handed over. 1209

### Letter XLII, to King Charles

He asks for assistance against four dukes of Italy, who were conspiring among themselves and with the Greeks against the Roman Church and Charles. 1209

### Letter XLIII, to King Charles

He expresses his joy that he had learned from Charles’s envoys that Charles himself would shortly be coming to Rome. 1209

### Letter XLIV, to King Charles

Concerning the Saxons who had returned to paganism, he explains what penance should be imposed on them if they wished to return again to the Church. 1209

### Letter XLV, to King Charles

After presenting arguments of mutual goodwill, he replies that he is striving to prevent the bishops of the Lombards from invading one another’s dioceses; and concerning the consecrations of bishops throughout Italy and Tuscany, he urges that careful precautions be taken so that they may be carried out according to the canons. Finally, he advises that those who travel back and forth to the king or to the pontiff should not go without letters from the king and the pontiff. 1209

### Letter XLVI, to King Charles

He congratulates Charles on the subjugation of the Saxons and their conversion to the worship of Christ and baptism; at Charles’s request, he orders three days of litanies on this account. 1210

### Letter XLVII, to King Charles

He grants the use of the pallium to Ermembert, archbishop of Bourges. 1210

### Letter XLVIII, to King Charles

He replies concerning the elections of the bishops of Ravenna: that they have customarily been carried out by the clergy and people, without the intervention of royal envoys, after receiving the admonition of the Roman pontiff and in accordance with the canons. 1210

### Letter XLIX, to King Charles

He reports that Charles’s envoys had been forced to flee from Benevento because the widow of Duke Arichis and the Beneventans had conspired with the Greeks against Charles and the Roman Church. 1210

### Letter L, to King Charles

He traces the Beneventan conspiracy back to its beginning under Duke Arichis and explains it more fully, as he had learned it from Gregory, presbyter of Capua. 1210

### Letter LI, to King Charles

He confirms that Adalgis had come into Calabria. He asks that troops be sent against him and that the cities in the duchy of Benevento promised to the Church be ordered to be handed over through the king’s envoys. 1210

### Letter LII, to King Charles

The objections against the Seventh Synod are refuted. 1210

### Letter LIII

By this letter, the monastery of Saint Dionysius at Paris is granted the privilege of being permitted to have its own bishop. 1211

### Letter LIV, to Tilpin, Archbishop of Reims

He confirms, by a new privilege, the ancient rights of the church of Reims, and orders that an investigation be made concerning Lullus, bishop of Mainz, and that the results be reported to him. 1211

### Letter LV, to Bertherius, Metropolitan Bishop of Vienne

Concerning the condition of the churches and the honor of both bishops and metropolitans, formerly neglected in Gaul. 1212
